# Binding and Decorative Endpaper

->**Decorative Pattern**<-

This page displays a repeating ornamental design characteristic of historical bookbinding. The pattern features alternating floral and geometric motifs printed in a warm orange-brown pigment on a tan surface. On the left edge, the dark leather of the spine is visible where it meets the decorative board.

<note>Decorative endpapers like this were common in high-quality bindings from the 17th through the 19th centuries. They served both to beautify the volume and to hide the structural "turn-ins" of the leather or cloth covering the heavy boards of the book.</note>

The motif consists of stylized blossoms enclosed within diamond-shaped frames, a style often achieved through block-printing or stamping. This visual element provides a transition between the protective exterior of the manuscript and the written contents within.

# Blank Opening Leaf

This page of the manuscript is **blank** and contains no written text. In historical bookbinding, it was common to include one or more empty leaves at the start of a volume to protect the primary text from wear and environmental damage.

The surface of the <term>parchment</term> <note>A writing surface made from specially prepared animal skins, typically from sheep, calves, or goats.</note> exhibits several characteristics of its great age:

*   **Foxing**: There are numerous small, reddish-brown spots visible across the page. 
<note>This is known as <term>foxing</term>, a type of age-related browning caused by fungal growth or the oxidation of iron minerals within the material.</note>
*   **Staining**: Notable marks are present, particularly in the top right corner.
<note>These stains are likely the result of historic moisture exposure or oils from the hands of readers over several centuries.</note>
*   **Creasing**: The page shows signs of physical stress and folding.

At the bottom right, there is a modern watermark from the digitization process.

<note>While this page lacks writing, its physical condition provides scholars with information about how the book was stored and handled throughout its history. The heavy wear on these initial pages suggests the volume was frequently consulted.</note>

The text establishes the value of preserving knowledge through books as a form of "monument" more lasting than stone.</meta>

# TO THE MOST NOBLE
# as well as Most Magnificent Father in Christ
# and Most Reverend Lord, Lord Guillaume de Poupet, <term>Hæteriarch</term><note>A title for a high-ranking official or leader of a group; here it likely refers to his status within his ecclesiastical order.</note> and Abbot in Upper Burgundy of the Monasteries of Baume, Gigny, and Balerne, and most worthy lord of other places, and his most learned patron, to be honored above all.

->ADAM HENRI PETRI<-
->SENDS HIS GREATEST GREETINGS.<-

<image-desc>Large historiated woodcut initial 'N' depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or saint) seated at a desk with books, within a decorative architectural frame.</image-desc>**By nature**, all men are so constituted that they wish for their memory never to be abolished. Hence monarchs, kings, and princes have been accustomed to adorn their palaces and houses with every sumptuous and most precious thing, and likewise to build magnificent temples and tombs. An example of this is the one which Queen Artemisia is said to have built so magnificently in the town of **HALICARNASSUS** for her husband **MAUSOLUS**, which was considered one of the seven wonders of the world due to the admiration for such an immense work. Truly, she attempted this for no other reason than to preserve the memory of her husband, whom she pursued with incomparable love. We read that the **EGYPTIAN** kings did the same thing, who, to leave their memory forever to posterity, constructed and cultivated Pyramids, Labyrinths, and most beautiful gardens. Nor did those ancients build their temples, cities, and citadels, or theaters and amphitheaters, for any other cause than to prepare for themselves an everlasting memory among posterity.

However, the efforts of all these are far exceeded by the monuments of Philosophers and learned men. By these works, they have not only secured for themselves a name and fame that will never be abolished, but at the same time have greatly helped posterity. There were not a few such even among the <term>pagans</term><note>original: "Ethnics", referring to the non-Christian classical world.</note>, among whom we rightly attribute the first place to that Prince of Philosophers, **ARISTOTLE**. Besides his other labors <note>original: "lucubrationes", referring to works produced by lamplight or late-night study.</note> which can never be praised enough, he was also the first to teach the kings of Egypt to arrange books in order, and stood as the founder of the **LIBRARY OF ALEXANDRIA**, in which some thousands of books were collected. This was truly a treasure most worthy of royal wealth as a monument. To which pursuit, even in the age of our ancestors, princes—especially ecclesiastical ones—

<meta>This page continues the dedication by Adam Henri Petri to Guillaume de Poupet. Following the previous page’s discussion on monuments and pyramids, Petri transitions to the importance of libraries and manuscript preservation as the ultimate "monuments" of the mind, specifically introducing the works of Marsilio Ficino.</meta>

# Preface.

...they applied themselves, and even now today they apply themselves most greatly, as some of their most well-equipped libraries testify. Among these, especially in Germany, that library of **FULDA** <note>The Abbey of Fulda was one of the most important centers of learning in the Middle Ages, famous for its massive collection of manuscripts.</note> must certainly be numbered in no last place; you could hardly find any other older or richer, especially in parchment and manuscript books. I hear they were organized into forty-eight categories, containing authors of every kind. We read that the monks spent more or less seven hundred years writing and transcribing them. 

Not only does this library provide a supply of various copies to any most diligent printers, but the riches of **ITALIAN** libraries are also by far the greatest. This is shown by so many distinguished authors published for the first time in our era, whom **ITALY** alone has shared with us. Among these is also our **MARSILIO FICINO**, an **ITALIAN** by nation, a **FLORENTINE** by homeland, son of the most famous physician Ficino, a Platonic Philosopher, Physician, and Theologian, rescued from the bowels of moths and beetles <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for recovering neglected or decaying manuscripts from archives where they were being eaten by insects.</note>. 

I now offer to your excellence, with all readiness, his various labors (some of which now come into public view for the first time), most happily divided into two volumes and printed at my father’s expense. 

The **FIRST** volume contains all those things which that man wrote—not by explaining the writings of others, but separately by his own **THALIA** <note>original: "Thalia"; the Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, here used to mean Ficino's own original creative inspiration or unique voice.</note>—various short works of different arguments. We have arranged these in this order, not without a certain plan: namely, that the noble volume titled **ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION** should claim the first place for itself, than which hardly anything more beautiful, useful, or more worthy of a Christian man can be found. 

In the second place, we have put the *Platonic Theology* **ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS**. In this work, whatever was previously treated and disputed by the ancient philosophers is more fully embraced, such as: the divine essence, ideas, divine providence, the soul of the world, intelligences, celestial spheres, paradise, the four elements, purgatory, limbo, hell, matter, form, kinds of causes, chance and fortune, fate, motion, the infinite, place, vacuum, time, the eternity of the world, the intellectual soul, the souls of brutes and vegetables, nations, demons, resurrection, miracles, in dreams, prophets, religion, and other things of this kind. He concluded the treatment of these matters in eighteen books with summary and succinct brevity. Here, besides Platonic matters, the greatest mysteries and most hidden things are explained; many secrets also from the sacred scriptures and from the writings of Christians, both ancient and modern, are unearthed and elucidated, and all things are made familiar to the learned. 

Indeed, that commentary **ON THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE ROMANS** earned the third place, never seen until now, in which the chief heads of the whole Christian religion are most learnedly treated; specifically, for instance, on the ascent into the third heaven, on the eternal and temporal birth of **CHRIST**, the reasons for the Trinity, how the divine Word assumed human nature; furthermore, on the world, on adoration, the spiritual worship of God, on various rites of sacrifices, the power of the Gospel, double faith, charity, the difference between opinion, science, and faith. Likewise, on the worship of the Gentiles,

# Preface.

Of the Gentiles, under the Mosaic law, the impiety of the Gentiles, and how they recognized God having been taught by divine instruction; how the invisible things of God are known through visible things. Furthermore, concerning the triple cause within God, and the triple divine cognition as if in a triple heaven; how the impious fall from guilt into punishment, and from punishment back into guilt; concerning the persistence of unbelievers, the divine judgment, the retribution for works, eternal punishment, the steps to the Father, the proud struggle against God and divine vengeance, and innumerable other matters which are noted in the individual chapters. 

**Fourth** follows a most elegant and at once most Christian book of **SERMONS**, in which, besides pious dogmas, various passages of the Evangelists are explained. In these, he wishes nothing to be promulgated by himself (which is also to be understood of all his other books) except as much as the Christian religion and the Catholic Church can endure and agree upon. 

**Fifth** are contained in this first Volume, the three books **ON THE TRIPLE LIFE**. Of these, the first treats the health of scholars, from which one may recognize how much he loved students of literature and sought their advantage; for which benefit, indeed, all students, both young and old alike, rightly owe him great thanks, for from this they emerge instructed in how they might rightly order their lives while engaged in letters. The second book concerns the prolongation of life—that is, by what remedy we ought to extend our life so that we might enjoy a long-lasting and prosperous health. The third concerns obtaining life from the heavens: and this book is clearly to be sought after and read by everyone, so that, being instructed, we may eventually acquire that celestial life in the heavenly fatherland with the Sacrosanct and individual Trinity—**FATHER, SON, and HOLY SPIRIT**—and there, having laid down this mass of the body, enjoy true joy. 

**Sixth**, the **APOLOGY** <note>A "defense" or formal justification of his views.</note> follows these in place, in which he deals with medical matters, Astrology, the life of the world, magic, and the **MAGI** <note>The "Wise Men" from the East who visited the infant Jesus; Ficino argues their "magic" was a legitimate study of nature.</note> who immediately greeted **CHRIST THE BEST AND GREATEST**. At the end of this, a most beautiful **LETTER** is also placed, concerning how security and tranquility of mind are necessary for life. 

Then is added to this the **Antidote against Epidemics**, which that most serious author had written in his own vernacular tongue—that is, **Tuscan** <note>Ficino originally wrote this plague manual in Italian (Tuscan) to ensure it was accessible to the general public during outbreaks.</note>—at the urging of the prayers and requests of certain friends; it was finally gifted with Latinity <note>Translated into Latin.</note> by **GIROLAMO RICCI OF PAVIA**. If your Excellency should deign to read this when your mind is quiet from greater business, there will be, joined with the fruitfulness, elegance, and ornament of the language, a certain pleasure and no common utility. For it teaches not only the cure of an evil <term>spreading as an epidemic <note>original: "ἐπιδημίως"</note></term> and currently present, but also with what healings or medicines this pestilence can be kept away from bodies. 

In the **seventh** place, we have set that work of **LETTERS** divided into twelve books, into which other small books and dialogues discussing various matters are inserted (as can always be seen in their proper place). 

The **eighth** place, however, is occupied by those two books, the first **ON THE SUN**, the other **ON LIGHT**. In the former, **ON THE SUN**, many things indeed most worthy of knowledge and pleasant are shown: such as what its nature, force, and power are; how it stands in relation to all other stars and planets; also its likeness to **GOD** the creator of all things, and many other things of this kind. Concerning **LIGHT**, almost no fewer things are shown, as one may read in the inscriptions of the individual chapters.

<meta>This page concludes the introductory overview of the first volume of Marsilio Ficino’s collected works. Having previously listed his theological and medical treatises, the text now focuses on his philosophical roots, specifically his early work on pleasure and the perceived harmony between the philosophy of Plato and the laws of Moses.</meta>

# Preface.

Finally, that first Volume is most happily concluded with the book on **pleasure**, which however (as the story goes) he wrote first of all in his youth, when he was twenty-four years old. This was certainly no ordinary demonstration of a most talented and learned young man’s work, from which we can clearly understand that he was already deeply engaged in philosophy and had studied and read many books by many philosophers from every school of thought. For in this work, the thoughts and opinions of the **Platonists, Pythagoreans, Peripatetics, Stoics, Sceptics, Epicureans**, and almost all other sects—which had long since been debated by those very groups—are recounted.

However, in this our age, you will find very few young men who devote themselves to **Platonic** philosophy or turn their minds toward it. This is a cause for regret, since there is almost no philosophy that approaches more closely to the divine books of Moses than this; indeed, it is said that **Plato** himself was not ignorant of them, having traveled to **Egypt** where it is reported he studied them. For **Numenius** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Eastern wisdom</note> the Pythagorean, whom **Origen** <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian</note> ranks above not only the Pythagoreans but almost all philosophers, having read both the books of Moses and of Plato, used to say that he recognized Moses within **Plato**, and that **Plato** was nothing else than **Moses** speaking in the Attic <note>The dialect of Athens; the quote "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?" was famous in the Renaissance</note> tongue.

In his books, the subject matter is nearly the same as that of **Moses**: such as the idea that there is one principle of all things, **God**; that the world was brought forth by **God** for the sake of His goodness; and that in the beginning **God** created heaven and earth with all their adornment, and all these things would remain according to the purpose of His will. He wrote that **God** made man in His own likeness, as master of earthly things but a worshiper of God Himself; that men were created from the earth and placed under the guard of divine spirits; that they received the law from a messenger of **God** alone; and finally, that after the course of the world (at **God's** command) they would rise again. 

He placed our happiness in the enjoyment of **God** alone, stated that the world was arranged by the Word <note>original: "Verbo", referring to the Logos or divine reason</note> of **God**, and that **God** is the measure of all things. Finally, he preached to all that whether they descend into hell or ascend into heaven, the divine judge is found everywhere. He taught that **God** is the leader and cause of all things, Father and Son, and that the highest good is established in His love; that all things exist by His grace and He is the cause of all good things. Furthermore, he distinguished the blessed spirits in this order: some reflect the power of **God** as the efficient cause, others His wisdom as the pattern, and others His goodness as the end of all things—and other matters of this kind, which are certainly entirely in harmony with the Mosaic doctrine.

These, therefore, **Reverend Father**, are the highlights of this first Volume, in which (as far as I can tell) there is absolutely nothing that could displease readers, for all things agree with Holy Scripture and contain nothing discordant with it. We dedicate these books of such a great philosopher to **your Dignity**, **Most Reverend Prelate**, both on account of those many and distinguished virtues of yours, and also because of your excellent learning, your singular knowledge of the sacred languages and scriptures (which is greatly to be praised in you), and also for your supreme humanity and benevolence toward all—especially toward those who surpass others in learning, doctrine, and integrity of character, whom you invite to you of your own accord and receive kindly when they come,

<meta>catchword: receive,</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces Marsilio Ficino’s early work on pleasure and argues for the profound compatibility between Platonic philosophy and the Judeo-Christian tradition, famously labeling Plato as a "Greek-speaking Moses." The text concludes with a formal dedication to a high-ranking church official, praising his support for scholars.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the preface, transitioning from a discussion of Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical influences to a personal dedication. # Preface.

...you welcome them, treat them generously, and dismiss them with honor, desiring them to return to you more frequently. If you notice any who are striving toward virtue and proper studies, you always keep them in your sight, and you foster, adorn, and protect their pursuits to the best of your ability. 

Furthermore, the greatest thing that moved me—and what I consider to be your highest quality—is that through right judgment and careful consideration, you have recognized the true purpose for which **Monasteries** and **Colleges** were built and instituted. Namely, that they should be schools for the sacred scriptures and for the other arts and disciplines useful to the **Church of Christ**, in which adolescents and youth, free from other cares and distractions, may be instructed in both the best morals and the finest disciplines. 

I have perceived these praiseworthy qualities in you not only from the reports of my teacher and your most noble nephews, the **Perrons**, <note>original: "Peranorum"</note> but also from the most distinguished **Gilbert Cousin of Nozeroy**, <note>Gilbert Cousin (1506–1572), also known as Gilbertus Cognatus, was a prominent French humanist and secretary to Erasmus</note> a man of universal learning and most devoted to you. Moreover, I have seen and known these things for myself while present at **Baume**, **Salins**, and **Lons-le-Saunier**, <note>Towns in the Franche-Comté region where the patron held influence or residences</note> within your various residences at different times.

But truly, lest I dull your ears with a longer speech, it remains for me to earnestly ask of **Your Excellency** <note>original: "T. E." for "Tua Excellentia"</note> that you receive this gift kindly and humanely. Do not value the gift itself as much as the spirit of the one presenting it; I ask that you deign to receive it now with the same countenance with which you would welcome a friend. May you enjoy it in such a way that you possess **a sound mind in a sound body**; <note>original: "mens sana, in corpore sano," a famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal</note> for you are worthy to live among the learned for as long as possible. 

Farewell, foremost of Abbots. 

**Basel**, on the **Ides of March**, <note>March 15th</note> in the Year from the Virgin’s birth, **1561**.

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine on the Christian Religion, to
### Lorenzo de' Medici, Savior of the Fatherland, Preface.

->*That there is a very great kinship between wisdom and religion.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a classical or mythological scene with figures in a landscape, possibly representing a pastoral or scholarly setting.</image-desc> THE ETERNAL wisdom of God decreed that divine mysteries, at least in the very beginnings of religion, should be handled only by those who were true lovers of true wisdom <note>original: "veræ sapientiæ amatores", a literal translation of the word 'philosophers'</note>. Thus it happened that among the ancients, the same individuals who investigated the causes of things also diligently administered the sacrifices to the supreme Cause of all things; among all nations, the same men existed as both philosophers and priests. Nor was this done without justice. For since the soul (as our Plato <note>Ficino refers to Plato as "ours" because he dedicated his life to translating and reviving Platonic thought in the Renaissance</note> prefers) can fly back to the heavenly father and homeland by only two wings—that is, by the intellect and the will—and since the philosopher relies chiefly on the intellect and the priest on the will, and the intellect illuminates the will, while the will sets the intellect on fire, it is fitting that those who first discovered divine things through intelligence (either by their own effort or by divine touch) should be the first to have most rightly worshipped divine things through the will, and to have propagated their right worship and method of devotion to others.

Therefore, the Prophets of the Hebrews and the Essenes <note>A Jewish sect known for communal living and asceticism</note> applied themselves to both wisdom and the priesthood simultaneously. The philosophers among the Persians were called Magi <note>original: "magi", meaning wise men or priests</note> because they presided over sacred rites. The Indians consulted the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanas"</note> regarding the nature of things and the purification of souls at the same time. Among the Egyptians, the mathematicians and metaphysicians performed the duties of both the priesthood and the kingship. Among the Ethiopians, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," ancient ascetic sages</note> were simultaneously teachers of philosophy and leaders of religion. The same custom existed in Greece under Linus, Orpheus, Musaeus, Eumolpus, Melampus, Trophimus, Aglaophemus, and Pythagoras. The same was true in Gaul under the governance of the Druids. Who could be ignorant of how much the study of wisdom and sacred rites was combined among the Romans in Numa Pompilius, Valerius Soranus, Marcus Varro, and many others? Finally, who does not know how great and how true the learning was in the ancient bishops and priests of the Christians?

O happy ages, which preserved this divine bond of wisdom and religion intact, especially among the Hebrews and Christians! O ages at last too unhappy, when the separation of Pallas and Themis <note>original: "Palladis, Themidisque"; Pallas Athena represents wisdom/science, while Themis represents divine law and justice</note>—that is, of wisdom and honesty—resulted in a miserable divorce. Oh, the wickedness! Thus "that which is holy is given to the dogs." <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6</note> For learning has been largely transferred to the profane, where for the most part it has turned into an instrument of iniquity and lust, and should be called malice rather than science. Moreover, the most precious pearls of religion are often handled by the ignorant, and are trampled by them as if by swine. For often the sluggish care of the ignorant and the idle seems better called superstition than religion. Thus, neither do the former sincerely understand the truth (which, as a divine thing, shines only in the eyes of the pious), nor do the latter, as far as is in them, rightly worship God or govern sacred matters, being utterly ignorant of divine and human affairs.

How long shall we endure this hard and miserable lot of an iron age? O men, citizens of the heavenly fatherland and inhabitants of the earth, let us at last free philosophy—that sacred gift of God—from impiety if we can; and we can if we will. Let us redeem holy religion, according to our strength, from execrable ignorance. I therefore exhort and pray all philosophers to either fully embrace religion or at least touch upon it; and I pray priests to diligently apply themselves to the study of legitimate wisdom. How much I have progressed or will progress in this matter, I do not know; yet I have tried and shall not cease to try, not relying on my own meager talent, but trusting in the mercy and strength of God. Your grandfather, the great-hearted Lorenzo, the great Cosimo, and then your pious father Piero, nourished me from my tender years with their resources so that I might be able to philosophize. You, recently wishing to join the study of philosophy in me (as you have been accustomed to do in several others) with the duty of piety, have [honored] your Marsilio Ficino with the priesthood, and

<summary>This preface introduces Marsilio Ficino’s argument that philosophy and religion were historically united and must be reunited to prevent science from becoming "malice" and religion from becoming "superstition." He appeals to Lorenzo de' Medici to support this reconciliation, citing his family's long-standing patronage of Ficino's work.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Christian religion, philosophy and religion, Plato, priesthood, Cosimo de' Medici, Piero de' Medici, Renaissance Neoplatonism</keywords>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: light</meta>

...indeed honorably, you have decorated me. Would that I myself had never failed nor fail myself, since indeed the favor and help of God Himself, and of the Physicians <note>original: "Medicumq;" – a clever pun on the Medici family name, suggesting they are the 'doctors' or healers of the state</note> has never been lacking. However, so that I might further win divine grace for myself, and show my gratitude to you, and not fail my own potential, as soon as I was initiated into the sacred rites of the priesthood, I composed a work concerning the Christian religion. This work I decided must be dedicated to you, both as the author <note>original: "authori" – here meaning the patron or instigator of his career</note> of this my profession, and as an outstanding foster-son of wisdom and a cultivator of piety.

<margin>Religion is most unique to man and is truthful. Chapter I.</margin>

We see individual talents of the human race appearing in certain beasts, at least according to a certain likeness—except for religion. Brute animals show no sign of religion; thus, the lifting up of the mind to God, the king of heaven, is as unique to us as the upright posture of the body is unique to us. Divine worship is almost as natural to men as neighing is to horses or barking to dogs. But if someone more curious should assert that some beasts also occasionally venerate the celestial bodies—which I do not believe at all—the Platonists <note>The followers of Plato, whom Ficino spent his life translating and interpreting</note> will answer: beasts of this kind are doing something else when they seem to honor the heavens; or if by chance they do honor them, they nevertheless do not know what they are doing; or if they do know, then they also must be participants in intelligence and immortality. 

But in truth, to return to the point, man—the most perfect animal—is most powerful in that specific quality and most distinguished from the lower animals by that which joins him to the most perfect, that is, to divine things. Again, if man is the most perfect of mortal animals, it is precisely because of that gift which he alone possesses among them, and which is not shared with other animals; that gift is religion. Therefore, through religion, he is most perfect. If religion were empty, man would conversely be the most imperfect of all, because through it he would be the most insane and the most miserable. For indeed, many men cast aside all the comforts of temporal life—and certainly all men cast aside many—and undergo hardships, either out of love or fear of God. Truly, no other animal abstains from present goods for the sake of the worship of God and the expectation of the future. Add to this that the sting of conscience continually pricks us alone; the fear of divine vengeance and of the underworld most sharply torments us. If therefore religion (as we have said) is vain, no animal is more foolish or unhappy than man; man would thus be the most imperfect of all because of religion, yet a little while ago he appeared more perfect than all because of it. 

Now, he cannot suffer such contrary things through the same part of himself, being both supremely perfect and extremely imperfect because of it. Therefore, religion is true—especially because just as nothing can become freezing cold by proximity to fire, so man cannot become most foolish and most miserable from the fact that he alone clings to God, who is most wise and most blessed. Nor can God, who is supreme truth and goodness, deceive the human race, His own offspring. A natural and common opinion about God has been inserted into us by God, the common origin and prince of natures. 

Furthermore, we ought to remember that a prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium" – used here to mean a natural instinctual foresight</note> which comes from an entire species of animal turns out to be true, because it occurs by the instinct of universal and particular nature. Many reptiles crawl out from the depths of the earth when the sun rises; the gloom of the air portends certain things; a great crowd of crows flies in the evening from a certain quarter of the sky; winds are foretold, and innumerable other things of this same kind. By the common prophecy of men, religion is also true; for all men, always and everywhere, worship God for the sake of a future life. It is true, therefore, that God provides for us and that there will be another life, provided that the most perfect species of animals possesses that most true judgment which is the most natural of all to it. Moreover, it appears that the assertion of religion is such, not only because it belongs to every man alone, but also because all human opinions, affections, customs, and laws are changed—except for a certain common religion. If someone is found entirely devoid of all religion, it is because he is outside the nature of the human species, being either a certain monster from the beginning or defiled by the contagion of another monster.

<margin>On the divinity of the soul derived from religion, Chapter II.</margin>

Our Plato, in the *Protagoras*, wishes it to be the greatest sign of our divinity that we alone on earth, as participants in a divine lot on account of a certain kinship, recognize God and desire Him; we invoke Him as our author, love Him as a father, venerate Him as a king, and fear Him as Lord. For just as the Sun is not perceived without the Sun, and just as the air is not heard without air, and the eye full of light sees...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that religion is the defining, natural characteristic of humanity, distinguishing humans from animals. He posits that if religion were false, humans would be the most miserable of creatures, which contradicts the logic of nature and God's goodness.</summary>
<keywords>humanity vs. animals, natural law, Platonism, divine providence, immortality of the soul, conscience, instinct, Lorenzo de' Medici</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on why religion is unique to humanity. The text begins mid-sentence, completing a comparison between physical senses and the spiritual recognition of God, likely following a thought about how the eye requires light to see.</meta>

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION
<meta>catchword: Every</meta>

light, and the ear filled with air hears the resonating air, so also God is not known without God. But a mind full of God is raised up toward God only in so much as it, being illustrated by divine light, recognizes God, and being kindled by divine heat, thirsts for Him. For no one is raised to that which is above and infinite, except by the power of something superior and infinite. Hence the mind is made into a temple of God, as Sextus the Pythagorean <note>original: "Xistus Pythagoricus" – Ficino refers to the *Sentences of Sextus*, a collection of moral maxims which he believed were written by a follower of Pythagoras, though they are now considered early Christian wisdom literature</note> believes; he thinks the temple of the true and eternal God will never fall into ruin. The human mind dwells upon God daily, the heart burns for God, the breast sighs for God, the tongue sings of Him, and the head, hands, and knees adore Him; even the crafts of men reflect Him. If God does not hear these things, He is ignorant; if He does not listen, He is ungrateful and entirely cruel, if He compels us to cry out daily to One who does not listen. But God, who is infinite wisdom, goodness, and clarity, cannot be ignorant, ungrateful, or cruel. Furthermore, since a superior mind comprehends an inferior one rather than the other way around, if the human mind reaches toward the divine mind, it is necessary that the human be comprehended and governed by the divine.

->*Let adolescents beware, lest they easily pass judgment on religion.*<-
->Chapter III.<-

Although man by nature is religious at any age—excepting a very few, and those indeed corrupted—two ages, as Plato writes, are more religious: namely childhood and old age. For children are born and raised religious, and they remain very firm in religion until reason is awakened in adolescence. Reason, by its nature, seeks out the causes and explanations of individual things. If, in this age, young people either take up those studies or fall into those conversations in which the causes of things are diligently scrutinized, they begin to want to assert almost nothing unless they have perceived the reason for it themselves. Then, for the first time, they cast religion largely behind their backs, unless perhaps they commit themselves to the laws and the counsel of their elders. This is because the most hidden reasons for divine things are perceived only after a long time and with the most exquisite diligence by a purified mind.

Those adolescents do not yet reach reasons of this kind, and because they assert almost nothing for which they do not see a reason, if they trust in their own judgment, they neglect religion in a way. Some, established in this opinion because of pride and a lack of self-control, give themselves over to Aristippean pleasures <note>original: "Aristippicis uoluptatibus" – referring to Aristippus, a Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure is the highest good</note>, thinking at last of nothing more regarding religion than if it were old wives' tales. Others, however, because of their gentleness and modesty, purify the mind from the senses in the Pythagorean rite through moral, physical, mathematical, and metaphysical disciplines. They do this so that they—unlike those "superior" ones mentioned before—are not forced to be blinded by suddenly directing eyes that are still bleary toward the divine Sun, but rather they progress step by step. 

First, let them look upon the divine light in moral matters, just as one sees the light of the sun upon the earth. Second, in physics, as if in water. Third, in mathematics, as if in the Moon. Fourth, in metaphysics, let them clearly and healthfully perceive the light in the Sun itself, both the super-celestial and the celestial. Orpheus calls these people the legitimate priests of the Muses; in their more mature age, they finally feel much better about religion, just as we read in Plato's *Letter to King Dionysius*, in the *Phaedrus*, in the first book of the *Republic*, and the tenth book of the *Laws*. 

Plato warns young men not to rashly pass judgment on divine matters, but to believe the laws until age itself teaches them—either through those levels of discipline we have described, or through experience, or through a certain separation of the soul from the body which a moderate old age brings. In that age, the soul, seeing things separated from bodies as if from nearby, discerns them more clearly than it was accustomed to do. One must always remember that wisdom cannot exist in youths according to nature, and nothing in judging or acting is more dangerous than an audacity born of ignorance, and an ignorant audacity. Wisdom without audacity is indeed beneficial, though perhaps not magnificent enough, but it never hinders; however, audacity without wisdom is like a certain untamed and utterly unbridled wild beast. Since we have disputed very extensively concerning the common truth of religion, the providence of God, and the divinity of souls in our *Theology* <note>original: "theologia nostra" – Ficino refers to his major work, the *Platonic Theology*, where he argues for the immortality of the soul</note>, let these brief sayings suffice for the present, for we are hastening toward the mystery of the Christian religion.

<meta>This page continues from the end of Chapter III, where Ficino warned young people against judging religion too hastily. It moves into a broader philosophical defense of the variety of religions and the specific authenticity of the Christian faith.</meta>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>Every religion has something of good in it, provided it is directed toward God himself, the creator of all; the Christian religion is pure. Chapter IV.</margin>

Nothing displeases God more than being despised, and nothing pleases Him more than being adored. He punishes men who are to some extent transgressors of divine laws more lightly, but those rebelling through ingratitude, malice, and pride, He strikes down from His empire with lightning. For this reason, divine providence does not permit any region of the world at any time to be entirely devoid of all religion, although He allows various rites of worship to be observed in different places and times. Perhaps indeed such variety, by God's ordering, produces a certain wonderful beauty in the universe. To the greatest King, it is truly more a matter of concern that He be honored than whether He is honored by these or those specific gestures. King Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> was honored in as many different ways as the nations he ruled, whether he traveled to them himself or sent his ambassadors. He approved of everything done for his glory in some measure, yet he held one way more acceptable than another. 

One must judge the King of the world in the same way. He prefers to be worshipped in any way, even clumsily—provided it is done in a human spirit—rather than to be worshipped in no way at all through pride. He either corrects immoderate men (who are nonetheless His subjects) like a father, or at least afflicts them less harshly. But the impious and entirely ungrateful, who are willfully rebellious, He exterminates and torments like an enemy. While God does not utterly reject any human worship undertaken for His sake—just as He utterly rejects voluntary impiety—there is one which He approves most of all, and indeed, alone. God in Himself is the highest good, the truth of things, and the light and favor of minds. Therefore, those worship God purely above all others—indeed, they alone do so—who diligently venerate Him with action, goodness, truth of speech, clarity of mind (as much as they are able), and with the charity they owe Him. Such people are, as we shall show, whoever adores God in the way that Christ, the master of life, and his disciples commanded.

<margin>The disciples of Christ deceived no one. Chapter V.</margin>

If the disciples of Christ had intended to introduce a fiction for the sake of deceiving the human race, they certainly would have sought some method of easier persuasion. On the contrary, they did the opposite: they undertook a task that was the most difficult of all things, both to believe and to observe. Consider also how many difficult circumstances they faced, if you consider the times, places, and persons: namely, in learned times, in the greatest cities full of every kind of doctrine, against the powerful, the princes, and the learned and numerous, when they themselves were most weak, destitute of all things, unrefined from the start, and very few. For Christ left eleven Apostles, and those seventy-two disciples of Christ were governed by the Apostles. One may hear Paul saying to the Corinthians: *See your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and God chose the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, and those things which are not, to destroy those things which are.* <note>original: "Videte uocationem uestram..." – 1 Corinthians 1:26-28</note>

Therefore, they are not to be believed to have fabricated this, especially because, with the highest harmony of good morals and opinions among themselves, they persevered bravely until the end in a matter that was the most arduous of all. Otherwise, they would have obtained nothing, nor did they themselves receive or expect any reward for such great labor in this life, nor did they promise it to the people. And this is what Paul says: *If in this life only we hope in Christ, we are more miserable than all men.* <note>original: "Si in hac uita tantum speramus..." – 1 Corinthians 15:19</note> They often foretold they would die for the faith, and afterward that all who followed their discipline would suffer bitter and unspeakable things. To say nothing of the fact that they cast aside whatever goods are held by mortals and commanded them to be cast aside; nor did they whisper in corners, but boldly spread their doctrine openly to the common people. Indeed, Paul, even with a chain bound around his neck, preached publicly, whence he writes to the Philippians: *The things concerning me have turned out more for the progress of the Gospel, so that my chains became manifest in Christ Jesus in the whole palace and in all other places.* <note>original: "Quæ circa me sunt..." – Philippians 1:12-13</note> And elsewhere he says: *The Gospel has now been preached to every creature under heaven.* <note>Colossians 1:23</note> Again, in the Acts of the Apostles: *None of these things were done in corners.* <note>Acts 26:26</note> For so Christ commanded his disciples in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke: *What I tell you in the dark,* etc. <note>Matthew 10:27</note> They believed, therefore, that they were preaching the truth to men; indeed, they certainly understood what they were preaching. Hence that saying of Peter: *Always be ready to give satisfaction to everyone asking you for a reason for the hope and faith that is in you.* <note>1 Peter 3:15</note> Hence that saying of Paul to the Corinthians: *I run thus, not as if toward uncertainty; I fight thus, not as if beating the air, but I punish my body*

<meta>catchword: body</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that God prefers any form of sincere religious worship over prideful atheism, though Christianity is the only "pure" faith. He then defends the historical credibility of the Apostles, noting they had no worldly incentive to lie and faced extreme hardship to spread their message.</summary>

[I punish] my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps after I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. <note>original: "corpus meum, & in ſeruitutem redigo, ne forte cum alijs prædicauerim, ipſe reprobus efficiar." A quote from 1 Corinthians 9:27.</note> For this reason, Paul and Apollos <note>A contemporary of Paul mentioned in the New Testament as an eloquent speaker and leader in the early Church.</note> everywhere discussed the mysteries of Christ with learned men, bringing forward the volumes of the Prophets. Paul often commands his disciples, especially the priests, to diligently apply themselves to the deep understanding of the prophets. Therefore, they believed and understood—as I have said—what they were preaching. Otherwise, they would never have submitted themselves so fearlessly and so willingly to continuous labors, dangers, beatings, and certain death for the sake of asserting that discipline. For the glory of Christ, Paul labored continuously through every kind of affliction for thirty-seven years, beyond what can be believed, even until his final breath. Peter labored for the same amount of time; John the Evangelist labored for sixty-eight years, and the others similarly throughout their entire lives.

->*In what spirit the disciples of Christ labored. Chapter VI.*<-

In what spirit the disciples of Christ labored, Paul declares in the Epistle to the Romans. "Who," he says, "shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: 'For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.'" <note>original: "Quia propter te mortificamur tota die, æſtimati ſumus ſicut oues occiſionis."</note> "For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor virtues, nor things present, nor things to come, nor fortitude, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." After he had enumerated to the Corinthians many kinds of labors and torments which he had both endured and was still enduring, he added that he rejoiced, gloried, and was strengthened in these things. The same man writes to the Philippians while he was a prisoner at Rome: "I shall not be put to shame in anything, but with all confidence, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death; for to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain." <note>original: "mihi enim uiuere Chriſto eſt, & mori lucrum."</note> "But if living in the flesh is the fruit of my labor, I do not know what I should choose; I am constrained by two choices. For I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and this indeed is much better for me; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake." He adds divine thoughts in this manner: "And confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with all of you for your progress and joy of faith, so that your rejoicing may abound in Christ Jesus in me, through my coming to you again." And a little later: "Unto you it is given for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him, having the same struggle which you both saw in me and now hear of me." He was indeed freed from chains, as he predicted, and returned to them.

The same to the Colossians: "Remain grounded in faith, stable and immovable from the hope of the Gospel which you have heard, which has been preached to every creature under heaven, of which I, Paul, have been made a minister; I who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fulfill those things that are lacking of the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for his body’s sake, which is the Church." <note>original: "adimpleo ea, quæ deſunt paſſionum Chriſti in carne mea, pro corpore eius, quod eſt Eccleſia." This is a famous and difficult theological passage suggesting the Church continues the redemptive work of Christ.</note> The same to the Thessalonians: "Let no one be moved by these tribulations; for you yourselves know that we are appointed to this. For when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we would suffer tribulations, just as it has happened, and you know." The same to Timothy: "God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of sobriety. Therefore, do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but labor together in the Gospel according to the power of God." And a little later: "For the Gospel I suffer these things, but I am not put to shame. For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep that which I have committed to him until that day." 

Again, after a few words: "In the preaching of the Gospel I labor even unto chains, as if I were an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound. Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus, with heavenly glory. It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us. But if we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself." <note>original: "Si uerò non credimus, ille fidelis permanet, negare ſeipſum non poteſt."</note> Likewise: "You know what persecutions and sufferings I endured at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and from them all the Lord delivered me. And all who want to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution." Similarly to the Corinthians: "We always carry around in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh." Whence he says to the Galatians: "I [bear] the marks of the Lord Je-" <note>The text cuts off here at the "marks" (stigmata) of Jesus mentioned in Galatians 6:17.</note>

[...the marks of the Lord Je]sus I bear in my body. <note>original: "su in corpore meo porto," completing Galatians 6:17: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body."</note> Again to the Corinthians: *I think God has displayed us Apostles last, as those destined for death, because we have been made a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:9. And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him. For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory which shall be revealed in us. For the expectation of the creature waits for the revelation of the sons of God.* <note>Romans 8:15-19. "Abba" is an Aramaic term for "Father," used here to show a familiar intimacy with God.</note>

For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation which happened to us in Asia, because we were burdened beyond measure.* Likewise: *I abound with joy in all our tribulation. Wherefore he says to the Ephesians: *I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles, beseech you not to faint in my tribulations for you, which is your glory.* Finally, he says that he performs his embassy for Christ in chains. To the Philippians he says that he counts all things, even the greatest, as nothing, and considers them as dung, so that he may gain Christ and be a partner in his suffering, conformed to his death, to merit his resurrection. <note>Philippians 3:8-11.</note> Likewise: *Our conversation is in heaven.* <note>term: "conversation" (conversatio). In this context, it refers to "citizenship" or "way of life."</note> *From whence also we look for our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, conformed to the body of his clarity, according to his operation, by which he is also able to subject all things to himself. Therefore, my most beloved and most longed-for brothers, my joy and my crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my beloved.*

To the Thessalonians: *You also became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit. You know, brothers, that our entrance to you was not in vain, but having suffered before and being treated with insults—as you know happened in Philippi—we preached the Gospel to you in the Lord with great confidence and solicitude. You became imitators of the churches of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus; for you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen, just as they did from the Jews. We were comforted in you, brothers, in all our tribulation and necessity through your faith, because now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.*

Furthermore, he exhorts the Hebrews thus: *Recall the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you sustained a great conflict of sufferings; on the one hand, being made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations, and on the other, becoming companions of those living in such a way. Therefore, do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward.* <note>Hebrews 10:32-35.</note> Likewise: *Having therefore a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to the confession of our hope.* Likewise: *And we, having so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience the race set before us, looking to the author and finisher of faith, Jesus,*

[...not I, but Christ lives in me. I live by faith in the Son of God,] Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and sits at the right hand of the throne of God. <note>original: "Iesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, confusione cōtempta, atq; in dextra sedis Dei sedet." Hebrews 12:2.</note> But I know not by what spirit I am compelled to return to those things he wrote to the Corinthians: *I have been in many more labors, in prisons more frequently, in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty stripes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I was in the depth of the sea. I have been in journeys often, in perils of rivers, in perils of robbers, in perils from my own nation, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brothers; in labor and in hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness. Besides those things that are without, there is my daily pressure: the care for all the Churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn? If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things which concern my weakness. The God and Father of our Lord knows—He who is blessed forever—that I do not lie.* <note>2 Corinthians 11:23-31. Ficino uses this "litany of hardships" to prove Paul had no worldly motive for his preaching.</note> *At Damascus, the Governor of the nation under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes to seize me, and through a window in a basket I was let down by the wall, and so I escaped his hands.* He even praises the Corinthians for what they endure: *if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face.* <note>2 Corinthians 11:20.</note> However, he reveals that he himself did not contend for his own glory, but for the glory of Christ alone, saying: *Among you one says, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos"; are you not mere men? For what is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of Him in whom you believed, and to each as the Lord has given. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. He who plants and he who waters are one.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:4-8.</note> *Therefore, let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.* But hear this also: *Charity does not seek its own, it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails.* <note>1 Corinthians 13:5-8.</note> Similar to this is that word from the Epistle of John: *Fear is not in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear.* <note>1 John 4:18.</note> Let us now conclude the words of Paul with his Epistle to Timothy: *For this we labor and are cursed, because we hope in the living God. This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.* <note>1 Timothy 4:10 and 1:15. Where the standard Bible says "chief of sinners," Ficino's Latin uses "primus" (first).</note> *But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Christ Jesus might show all patience, for an instruction to those who are to believe in Him for eternal life. To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever.*

These are the words of Paul the Apostle. John the Apostle also, in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, calls himself a witness and a partner in the sufferings of Christ, and exhorts certain peoples to patience. He highly commends many for their patience in his Epistles, as do the other Apostles and Evangelists. Finally, Luke the Evangelist writes that the Apostles, having been beaten by the Jews, went out rejoicing because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the name of Christ. <note>Acts 5:41.</note> Furthermore, they established that nothing should be possessed as their own among themselves and their followers, and they wished for the administration of goods to be separate from the Apostles. <note>Acts 4:32 and 6:2-4.</note> He adds that when a certain Cornelius wished to worship Peter, he was rebuked and forbidden by Peter. <note>Acts 10:25-26.</note> Moreover, when the Lycaonians <note>The people of Lystra in Lycaonia (modern Turkey).</note> wished to offer sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas as if they were gods because of their miracles, they were not permitted by them. John also, in the Apocalypse, forbade himself to be worshipped. From this it is clear that the Apostles sought not their own advantage or honor, but the glory of Christ alone. If anyone, therefore, suspects that the Apostles were faking, he either has never read these and similar things, or he is out of his mind.

-> The Disciples of Christ were deceived by no one. Chapter VII. <-

The disciples of Christ and their followers saw far more manifest and greater miracles than we did. For although we were born and educated in this religion, we would not labor so much for a familiar thing as they labored for a new and, so to speak, monstrous <note>original: "monstruosa." In Ficino's time, this meant something "unheard of" or "supernatural," appearing to defy the natural order of the world.</note> thing—for the more "monstrous" it appeared, the more it required clear signs and portents from the beginning to be believed. For who would easily believe that a certain young man, illiterate, the son of a carpenter (as was thought), a beggar, infamous, and publicly put to death by execution, was the very Divine Mind itself—which is always in God, through which all things are always made and governed? For this has never been believed of anyone else, that...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S BOOK</header>

...as Luke the Evangelist writes, when Paul the Apostle was disputing this matter before King Agrippa and Porcius Festus, the governor of Judea, Festus cried out: *“You are mad, Paul; your great learning is driving you mad.”* <note>original: "insanis ô Paule, multæ literæ te insanire compellunt." Acts 26:24.</note> To this also pertains that saying of Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> to the Roman judges: *“We too once laughed at these things; we are of your kind. Christians are made, not born.”* <note>original: "Hæc & nos risimus aliquando, de uestris sumus, fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani."</note> It must be thought, therefore, that those who asserted these things, and those who gave faith to the ones asserting them, had seen miracles openly worthy of God. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: *“The Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified—a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.”* <note>1 Corinthians 1:22–25.</note> Paul—a noble man, powerful, most wise, and most brave—could have been led by miracles alone, and those indeed most manifest, to suddenly turn from the most bitter enemy of Christians into their most bitter defender, and to voluntarily subject himself to so many hardships for the sake of Christ’s love alone, such as no one could number. For truly, as recorded by Luke, God predicted: *“This man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name's sake.”* <note>Acts 9:15–16.</note> Therefore, it is in no way to be believed that the heralds of Christ were deceived by anyone’s tricks. For the writings and deeds both of Christ’s disciples and of those who in that time suddenly, and with the greatest danger, received this sort of teaching, testify to men of holy mind that the first-fruits of the Christians were such that they neither wished to deceive, nor could they have been deceived in any way. What was the cause that so many—Jews as well as Gentiles, most learned in every discipline, and many wealthy men—leaving behind their possessions and pleasures, preferred to die cruelly with those rustic and beggarly disciples of Christ rather than to live with the delights of the world? Let us hear that divine man, Tertullian of Carthage, crying out in his *Apology* to the Roman judges: *“But go on, good governors, crucify, torture, condemn, and grind us down; for your injustice is the proof of our innocence. Therefore God allows us to suffer these things. For recently, by condemning a Christian woman to a pander rather than a lion, you confessed that a stain upon our chastity is considered by us more atrocious than any punishment or any death. Yet your exquisite cruelty profits you nothing; it is rather a lure to our sect. We become more numerous every time we are harvested by you; the blood of Christians is seed. We have filled all your places. If it were not permitted in this teaching to be killed rather than to kill, we could have fought against you—unarmed and not as rebels, but merely as dissenters—by the envy of a simple divorce. For if such a vast force of men had broken away from you to some remote place in the world, the loss of so many citizens would surely have undermined your rule; indeed, it would have punished you by desertion alone. Without a doubt, you would have been terrified at your own solitude, at the silence of affairs, and in the stupor of a city that was as if dead, you would have searched for someone to rule; for you have Christians as nearly all your citizens.”* <note>A famous passage from Tertullian’s "Apologia," emphasizing that persecution only made the Church grow—often summarized as "the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church."</note> Origen also, in the fourth book of *Peri Archon* <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a Greek scholar and early Christian theologian. "Peri Archon" is his "On First Principles."</note>, says that innumerable men in every region of the world, having abandoned their ancestral laws, suddenly accepted the Christian law, and most willingly and daily endure every kind of torture and death for his glory. Now indeed, if I wished to count the thousands of men excellent in every doctrine, and especially in Philosophy, who were the disciples and successors of Christ's disciples, and who in a long line up to the times of the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan emperor who attempted to reverse the Christianization of the Roman Empire.</note> defended Christ among swords and fire by their holiness, voice, writings, long labor, danger, and death, I would be forced to compose a work of no small length—to say nothing of the thousands upon thousands of Orators and Philosophers among the Greeks, Barbarians, and Latins who, after Julian, spent their whole lives most holily in Christian work.

-> The Christian religion is founded on the power of God alone. Chapter VIII. <-

If the Christian religion was by no means founded on human power, or wisdom, or pleasure, but indeed arose so suddenly and was spread so quickly through the whole world against the will and resistance of many powerful and learned men and human delights—as Paul writes to the Romans, that their faith is proclaimed in the whole world, and to the Colossians, that the Gospel is in the whole world; and John also says: *“Whatever is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith”*—then it is necessary that this very religion was founded on divine power, wisdom, and hope. What of the fact that many centuries before, in a long sequence by many Prophets and Sibyls... <note>Ficino often cites the Sibyls (ancient pagan prophetesses) alongside Biblical prophets to show that even the pagan world anticipated Christ.</note>

### A 5
<note>Signature mark A 5 indicates this is the fifth leaf of the first gathering of the book.</note>

By the Sibyls <note>The Sibyls were ancient pagan prophetesses whom early Christian theologians, including Ficino, believed had foretold the coming of Christ to the Gentiles.</note>, each of these things was predicted, as we shall show in what follows. What of the fact that Christ, the master of life, predicted by his own death that persecution would be everywhere against his disciples? He foretold the propagation and immutability of his religion, the miserable ruin of the Jews soon to come, the conversion of the Gentiles, and the persistence of certain Jews in their stubbornness until the end of the world. He both predicted this himself and inspired his disciples to say it. And what is marvelous is that Christ prescribed the siege that would occur on the Sabbath, the destruction by famine and the sword to be brought by the Gentiles, the unheard-of slaughter, and furthermore the captivity of the Jews among all nations, no differently before it happened than Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Jewish historian who recorded the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD in his work *The Jewish War*.</note> wrote it after the ruin. 

Furthermore, it is worth hearing what sort of sermon Jesus used, and each of his disciples used, to persuade their listeners: "Give all things to the poor, reject your dearest ones, offer your cheeks to the one who strikes you, do good to your enemies, hold this life and all its delights as nothing, deny yourselves, sustain this cross of ours—this terrible cross—and follow us as we first pray." For if you follow us, without a doubt you will undergo throughout your whole life whatever mortals consider to be evils. These were their words. O persuasion, full of every kind of dissuasion! Do we think that Demosthenes or Cicero <note>The most famous orators of Ancient Greece and Rome, respectively.</note> could have persuaded anyone of anything by this reasoning? 

Yet that sermon—or rather, the preacher—suddenly persuaded many great men. But from where? It was done by God, a thing more wonderful than any miracle; for indeed, as those who heard him testify, Jesus spoke "not as the Scribes and Pharisees, but as one having power." <note>original: "loquebať Ieſus nõ ſicut Scribæ & Phariſæi, ſed tanquam poteſtatem habens." Matthew 7:29.</note> They were persuaded to such an extent that Christ’s followers always loved him more than is possible for human nature according to its own strength, which no one will deny who has considered their works and writings with an open mind; for all of that is divine. 

If there is anyone who doubts, let him read and re-read diligently the books of the Prophets, the Evangelists, and the Apostles; let him also read the commentaries of those who were as they were at that time. The truth of this matter will immediately shine forth, for in those books there is a new force, a singular simplicity, sobriety, ardor, gravity, depth, and majesty. This indicates that neither divine power nor flame is absent from them, and that truth itself needs no deceit of words, nor does divine power require human machines. 

Add to this that in so many volumes of the Old and New Testaments, nothing is found that is not in harmony—a thing not granted to others, and the greatest sign of divine truth. Those writers have a certain pious and august quality, and what is marvelous is that it is common among them all but entirely foreign to all others, which signifies that God inspired all of them above all others. What shall we say to the fact that while all other writers hesitate and waver, they nevertheless doubt nothing, but—O almighty God—speak with such certainty, just as they performed the hardest tasks with such fortitude. 

Listen to that fisherman, John the Evangelist: *“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life; and the life itself was made known, and we have seen, and testify, and announce to you eternal life, which was with the Father and appeared to us. That which we have seen and heard we announce to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. And these things we write to you, that you may rejoice, and your joy may be full; and this is the announcement which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him there is no darkness.”* <note>original: "Quod fuit ab initio, quod audiui mus..." 1 John 1:1–5.</note> 

Again, consider in these words with what affirmation he speaks: *“God has testified concerning his Son, and this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has life; he who has not the Son of God does not have life. These things I write to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence we have toward God, that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us; and we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we ask of him. We know that whoever is born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world is placed in the power of the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life.”* <note>1 John 5:9–20.</note> 

Likewise: *“There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one; and there are three who give testimony on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater.”* <note>1 John 5:7–9. This passage is known as the "Johannine Comma," a famous Trinitarian verse.</note> Do not wonder, brothers,

Item elsewhere: he who saw has borne witness, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he tells the truth. Again elsewhere: *Now the son of man is glorified, and God is glorified in him; if God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him immediately.* I do not know if anyone could pronounce anything more simply and affirm it more effectively at the same time. Let us conclude the words of John with this undoubted sentiment of his: *I love you in the truth, and not I alone, but all who have known the truth for the sake of the truth which remains in us, and will be with us forever.*

James speaks thus to the twelve tribes scattered abroad: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience; but let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach, and it will be given to him; but let him ask in faith, hesitating in nothing. 

And a little later: Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning. For by his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of beginning <note>original: "initium". In this context, it refers to "firstfruits," the first and best of a harvest dedicated to God.</note> of his creatures. 

Let us also hear the confidence of Peter: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his possession, that you may proclaim the virtues <note>original: "uirtutis". Here meaning the powers or miraculous excellencies of God.</note> of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Do not tremble, but rejoice in sharing the sufferings of Christ, so that you may rejoice exultantly in the revelation of his glory. If you are reproached in the name of Jesus Christ, you are blessed, because that which is of honor, glory, and the power of God, and which is his spirit, rests upon you. Therefore, the elders <note>original: "seniores". The Greek term is 'presbyteroi', referring to community leaders.</note> who are among you, I, a fellow-elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, who am also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed in the future, beseech you: feed the flock of God that is among you, providing for it not by constraint but spontaneously, according to God. And the God of all grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, and consolidate you; to him be glory and dominion forever and ever, amen. The same elsewhere: For we have not followed unlearned fables in making known to you the power and foreknowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were made eyewitnesses <note>original: "speculatores". Literally 'watchers' or 'observers'.</note> of his majesty.

The Lord is indeed the spirit; and where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. We truly all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from clarity to clarity <note>original: "a claritate in claritatem". For we have not preached ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves your servants through Jesus. Because God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to the illumination of the knowledge of the clarity of God in the face of Christ Jesus. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the loftiness of the power may be from God and not from us. In all things we suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed; we are diminished, but not destitute; we suffer persecution, but we are not forsaken; we are cast down, but we do not perish.
