day by day. For that which is momentary and light in our present tribulation works in us an eternal weight of glory beyond measure in the highest. While we look not at things which are seen, but at things which are not seen; for things which are seen are temporal, but things which are not seen are eternal. For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens. These things were written to the **Corinthians**. To **Timothy** he admonished thus: "Be watchful in all things, and labor, do the work of an Evangelist, fulfill your ministry, be sober; for I am now being sacrificed, and the time of my dissolution is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the future there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day, and not only to me, but to all who love his coming." In these words, he prophesied that his own martyrdom <note>Ficino highlights Paul’s personal conviction as evidence of the faith's truth.</note> was imminent, which followed shortly thereafter. I cannot restrain myself from adding to these how surely he asserted, and with what majesty he sang of the eternal generation and power of the Son of God in the **Epistle to the Hebrews**: "God, who in manifold ways and in many modes spoke of old to the fathers in the Prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages. Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, making purification for sins, sits at the right hand of the majesty on high, being made so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they," and so following. Regarding the same Son of God, he says in the following: "For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. There is no creature invisible in his sight; all things are naked and open to his eyes, of whom we speak." To the **Colossians**: "The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were founded, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all, and all things consist in him, and he is the head of the body of the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might hold the primacy; because in him it pleased all the fullness of the divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth." 

But lest I be compelled to proceed further through those things to be wondered at regarding the Son of God in the **Epistle to the Ephesians**, the **Colossians**, the **Philippians**, and regarding the Holy Spirit to the **Corinthians**, and regarding the other <term>mysteries of Theology</term> <note>original: "Theologiæ myſterijs" — refers to the deep, hidden truths of divine revelation.</note> which he pours forth elsewhere like the firmest oracles, I shall encompass it in one word. If anyone reads the sacred writings diligently, they will be forced to confess that the Christian law consists of divine power. Indeed, our heroes <note>Ficino often refers to the Apostles and Martyrs as "heroes" in the classical sense of semi-divine or extraordinary figures.</note> cling steadfastly to an immovable foundation, clear in mind, fervent in will, simple and certain in words, tireless in action, invincible in purpose. Others, too anxiously, hunt for little reasons through roundabout ways, and (as David says) like the impious, they wander about in a certain circuit, being sufficient leaders for neither themselves nor others. Finally, if purity is the most proper quality of religion, this is certainly the most divine, which admits neither the base superstitions of the later Jews and the most filthy delusions of the **Talmud** <note>original: "Talmut"</note>, nor the obscene and wicked fables of the Gentiles, nor the abominable license of the **Muhammadans** <note>original: "Mahumethenſium"</note> and the absurdities of the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>. It promises not earthly rewards, like other laws, but celestial ones; nor does it command the killing of adversaries of its faith and law, as the Talmud and the Quran command, but rather that they be taught by reason, or converted by prayer, or tolerated with patience. As appeared most clearly in the reality of the first Christians, it not only cuts away vices but uproots them, and persuades to virtues by doing before persuading. For such was their condition perhaps, that they could not persuade otherwise than by practicing both virtues and miracles. Moreover, it fervently practices virtues not for the sake of ambition, or pleasure, or human tranquility, but for the grace of God alone, and it tramples this whole world underfoot and holds it for nothing, so that it may attain the other world.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the Christian religion. On the previous page, he cited the Apostle Paul’s conviction and the Epistle to the Hebrews to prove the divine nature of Christ. Here, he begins Chapter 9, shifting focus to refute the idea that Christianity's rise was governed by astrology or "fate," arguing instead for its purely divine origin.</meta>

-># THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

<margin>The authority of Christ is not from the stars, but from God. Chapter 9.</margin>

In our Theology <note>Ficino refers here to his major work, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>, we have proven that common religion originates neither from the stars, nor from certain men, nor from a disease, but from God, and from human form within our common nature. At present, however, we shall briefly demonstrate that the Christian law does not exist, nor is it preserved, by some fate of the stars. The coming of Christ, as something divine, was predicted from the beginning of the world by the Prophets and the Sibyls <note>The Sibyls were legendary ancient prophetesses whom Renaissance thinkers believed had predicted Christ to the pagan world.</note>, who were not skilled in astrology, but were divinely inspired. Add to this that the celestial spheres, acting as universal and remote causes, usually bring particular effects on earth to completion only through certain convenient means. Yet, all human affairs not only failed to supply such means to the Christians, but are recorded to have been utterly opposed to them for three hundred years. Hence, when Paul, disputing with the Jews at Rome according to Luke <note>Original: "apud Lucam," referring to the Acts of the Apostles written by Luke.</note>, said, "For the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain," the Jews replied, "We have found that this sect is everywhere spoken against." Because of this very thing, **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note> exclaimed: "When truth began by being hated, as soon as it appeared it was an enemy; it has as many foes as there are strangers—specifically the Jews out of rivalry, the soldiers out of extortion, and by nature even our own domestics. We are besieged daily, we are betrayed daily, we are crushed in our very meetings and congregations." Likewise: "Truth asks for nothing on behalf of its cause, because it does not wonder at its condition; it knows it acts as a pilgrim on earth, and thus easily finds enemies among strangers. Furthermore, it has its genus, home, hope, grace, and dignity in the heavens; it only desires one thing meanwhile: that it not be condemned while unknown. For what is more unjust than for men to hate what they are ignorant of, even if the thing deserves hatred?" Likewise: "We prove both points from one another: that they are ignorant while they hate, and that they hate unjustly while they are ignorant." Thus far Tertullian.

Furthermore, bodily causes induce laws that are either for pleasure, or ambition, or certainly nothing more than civil; the Christian law damns or overcomes all these things. Likewise, the celestial spheres cannot instill a desire higher than the heavens themselves; Christian piety despises the celestial spheres and transcends them, worshipping only the God above the heaven, inasmuch as it is born not from the heaven or celestial spirits, but from the only super-celestial God. Innumerable people among all nations have willingly offered themselves to wounds and certain death for the sake of Christ’s name, for the sake of divine blessedness alone. When else has celestial motion produced such struggles? What wise man was ever able to spread his doctrine to the whole world through piety alone? Yet God, on account of virtue alone, is believed everywhere, even in the face of ancient custom and power. If these things proceeded from the stars, surely someone else would have had the same or a similar birth by the necessity of the stars. For what fate confirmed that the Creator of the universe himself taught, and continues to teach, that there is no power in the fates? How, then, does fate contradict itself and proclaim that it does not exist?

**Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop.</note> confirmed these things thus: "Those who, for the sake of the Gospel preaching, either struggled for many years or are struggling even now—how have so many in our memory been compelled toward one will, one faith, the same virtue of soul, and the same way of living at different times? Who of sound mind could ever believe that young and old alike, men and women, slaves and free, learned and unlearned—not born in one climate of the world, nor in the same hour, but everywhere on earth and at different times—were forced by the stars to prefer one and the same new and unheard-of doctrine (and indeed with the danger of death) over the rites of their fathers, preferring the dogmas of true philosophy and a hard life over luxuries?" Thus far Eusebius. 

Therefore, one should not listen to certain impious men and foolish followers of fate, who at the very beginning of the Christian religion pronounced that it would fall as soon as it had completed three hundred and sixty-five years, and they confirmed this by a certain oracle. Nor let any astrologer ever dare to pronounce that it will fail, for it depends not on the temporal motion of the heavens, but on the eternal stability of God; it has stood from the beginning of the world until the time of the **Emperor Octavian** <note>Augustus Caesar.</note> in the proclamations of the Prophets and the expectation of the people. Since then, it has endured until our time—for one thousand, four hundred, and seventy-four years—despite the heavens and the earth being unwilling. God exterminated its first persecutors, namely the Jews, for this very reason (as we shall show elsewhere), and defended it from the long-lasting and cruel persecution of the Pagans and heretics. Therefore, this religion can never be abolished, for it has God as its avenger and guardian; even if it is poorly administered by its own people and cruelly attacked by enemies, it stands by God’s governance, being treated no less poorly by its own than by strangers. Finally, if things go prosperously for Christians...

### ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...human affairs follow, ceremonies will not cease; if many adversities happen, this religion will grow at last and be perfected. For since it arose from a certain extreme and long-lasting adversity, and grew to adulthood, it must necessarily be nourished and fully completed by the same.

<margin>The authority of Christ was by no means without miracles. Chapter 10.</margin>

But those seem to me to deserve sharp rebuke, magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Ficino is addressing his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici ("the Magnificent"), the de facto ruler of Florence.</note>, who every day so stubbornly and imprudently demand new miracles to confirm the faith of Christ. For if they are rare, they are wonders; if they happened very frequently, they would seem either artificial or natural. Let it suffice for us to know that the world once began and endured—not without manifest miracles—such miraculously established institutions and works. Furthermore, even the Pagans, Jews, and Muslims have conceded to us that Christ performed miracles.

The miracles concerning the star from the East, the eclipse of the Sun, the earthquake, the rending of the temple, and many other things manifest to many thousands of men, were daily preached and written about openly by the disciples of Christ, both in Judea and elsewhere. This was done at a time when innumerable people were still alive who had been adults when Christ died; they could have very easily refuted those disciples—who were destitute of all worldly power—if they had not spoken the truth. By what means would Herod have perpetrated such an abominable and dangerous crime, when he killed so many infants and even his own son, unless he had been terrified by some new and stupendous wonder? Indeed, when he first committed this act, it was reported to Augustus. 

Listen to **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Latin writer. The anecdote he relates is a famous pun on the fact that Herod, as a Jew, would not eat pork: in Greek, the words for "pig" (*hys*) and "son" (*hyios*) sound similar.</note>: "When Augustus had heard that among the boys under two years old whom Herod, King of the Jews, ordered to be killed in Syria, his own son was also slain, he said: 'It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son.'" <note>original: "præstat Herodis porcum esse quàm filium"</note>

It is worth the effort to hear first about the earthquake, for he says: "The greatest earthquake in the memory of mortals occurred during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, with twelve cities of Asia being prostrated." Perhaps that was the earthquake that happened during the passion of Jesus Christ, both because he says it was such that its like had never been seen, and because it was in Asia and under the rule of Tiberius, which is precisely where and when Christ suffered. 

**Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> writes that he read in the commentaries of the Pagans that in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, a failure of the Sun occurred, Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake, and many houses collapsed in the city of Nicaea; all of which agree with the events of the Savior’s passion. **Phlegon** <note>Phlegon of Tralles, a 2nd-century Greek secular historian whose lost works are often cited by early Christians as external proof of the Gospel narrative.</note>, who is an excellent counter of the Olympiads, also writes about these things in his thirteenth book, saying: "In the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad, a failure of the Sun occurred, great and excelling all that had happened before it; day was turned into dark night at the sixth hour, so that the stars were seen in the sky, and an earthquake in Bithynia overturned many houses of the city of Nicaea." Thus says Phlegon. 

The Gospel of John provides an argument for this matter—that the Savior suffered in this year—in which it is written: that after the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the Lord preached for three years. **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the famous Jewish historian.</note>, a native Jewish writer, also testifies that around these times, on the day of Pentecost, the priests first felt certain sounds in the holy places, and then a sudden voice erupted from the inner sanctuary of the temple saying: "Let us depart from these seats." Thus far Eusebius. 

That Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius is also declared by **Luke the Evangelist**, who says Christ was baptized in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as he was approaching his thirtieth year. Eusebius calculates that Christ was born in the forty-second year of the Empire of Augustus, and began to preach the Gospel in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. 

**Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>Dionysius was a member of the Athenian judicial council (the Areopagus) converted by St. Paul. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, he was believed to be the author of highly influential mystical texts.</note>, the most excellent of the Athenian philosophers, and **Apollophanes**, a distinguished sophist powerful in the knowledge of natural things, were together at Heliopolis <note>A major city in ancient Egypt, known as a center of learning.</note> on the day Jesus was being killed. They then saw the globe of the Moon—outside the time of its normal conjunction—miraculously falling upon the Sun from the East, and they observed it miraculously blocking the Sun's diameter from the ninth hour until evening; and that such an occurrence reached even to the edge of the solar body, and only then sprang back from the opposite side of the diameter. When they clearly recognized that these things had happened contrary to the entire order of nature, Dionysius was utterly stunned, and Apollophanes, turning to Dionysius, exclaimed: "O noble Dionysius, these are surely changes in divine affairs!" Dionysius the Areopagite writes these things to the wise Polycarp, and asks him to go to Apollophanes himself (who was still living and not yet a Christian), who would neither deny that those things happened contrary to the order of nature, nor further despise the Christian truth, but would instead humbly [accept it].

<summary>Ficino cites various historical and pagan authorities, such as Macrobius, Phlegon, and Josephus, to prove that the miracles surrounding Christ's life and death were objective historical facts witnessed by non-Christians. He highlights the earthquake and the miraculous eclipse during the crucifixion as celestial evidence of Christ's divinity.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...undertaking to record these monuments, Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> affirms that Christ was fixed to the cross on the 20th day of March. However, a certain astrologer named Esculus <note>Likely Cecco d'Ascoli (1257–1327), an Italian encyclopedist and astrologer.</note>, although he was not very religious, nevertheless asserts through astrological calculation that it is certain that on the day Christ was crucified, the Sun was in the first degree of <term>Aries</term><note>The first sign of the zodiac; its first degree marks the vernal equinox.</note> and the Moon was at the beginning of <term>Libra</term>. He concludes that an eclipse could not have happened according to the laws of nature, both because it was a <term>full moon</term><note>Solar eclipses naturally only occur during a New Moon, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun. At Passover, the moon is full.</note> (whereas a solar eclipse must happen at the new moon), and because that eclipse began from the East, while a natural eclipse usually begins from the West. Others claim the Sun was in Pisces and the Moon in Virgo, yet they reach the same conclusion regarding the eclipse as Esculus. The Jews show the same thing; following the command of their law, they always celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the lunar cycle, and it was during Passover that they sacrificed Jesus. Moreover, there truly was an eclipse, for it was not possible to lie about such a manifest event at that time; for these things were preached and written in the same century and among the same people where such miracles were said to have occurred.

That miracle in the heavens was performed solely for the sake of Christ. For what has ever happened, either then or at any other time, more miraculous than Christ, whether beneath the heavens or above them? Regarding him, his herald Paul says: *God exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.* <note>original: "Deus exaltavit illum, & donavit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen..." — Philippians 2:9-11.</note> And what increases our wonder is that the tongues of men confessed this after he had emptied himself into the form of a servant, having been made humble and obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. If the world confessed that a man in such a lowly state and condition was the Supreme God without miracles, this alone would surpass the wonder of all other miracles.

I cannot be persuaded that John the Evangelist—a writer most simple and sober of all—would have dared to cry out with such a miraculous voice unless he had seen many miracles: *There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I do not think the world itself could contain the books that should be written.* <note>original: "Sunt & alia multa, quæ fecit Iesus..." — John 21:25.</note> I pass over the fact that the Evangelists often say Jesus miraculously cured thousands of the sick at once. The great Paul teaches us what kind of preaching the Apostles used, by which so many people were converted; for he says to the Corinthians: *I, brothers, when I came to you, came not in loftiness of speech or wisdom, declaring to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged myself not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified; and I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling; and my speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of power, so that your faith should not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. However, we speak wisdom among the perfect.* <note>original: "Ego fratres cum venissem ad vos..." — 1 Corinthians 2:1-6.</note> In another Letter to the same people, he says: *The signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds.* <note>original: "Signa Apostolatus mei facta sunt..." — 2 Corinthians 12:12.</note>

But let us hear what he writes to the Thessalonians: *You know that our Gospel was not unto you in word only, but in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much fullness.* <note>original: "Scis quod Evangelium nostrum non fuit..." — 1 Thessalonians 1:5.</note> Was the most prudent Paul so forgetful of himself, or did he think the people to whom he wrote were so forgetful, that he would mention he had performed wonders among them if he had not? Refutation and infamy would have been close at hand if he had happened to lie. He also writes to the Romans about the wonders performed by him; from these and similar accounts, we conclude that miracles were not lacking in those times. By their virtue, the house of God was then built as a model and light—indeed, as our dwelling place—which, as Paul says, *is the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of truth; and manifestly great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed in the world, and taken up in glory.* <note>original: "magnum est pietatis sacramentum..." — 1 Timothy 3:16.</note> These things he wrote to Timothy.

Why then do we unbelievers chatter? Why do we further demand such bold proofs? Is there a lawsuit every day (with the Great God among us) before a judge? Is God compelled at every moment of time—both for each of us and for posterity who will ask the same—to redeem His authority with miracles? Is He compelled to step out into the theater at anyone’s whim like some mercenary magician? <note>original: "tanquam præstigiator aliquis mercenarius"</note> Yet it is not natural or fitting to compel even man—an animal free by nature—with violent signs, but rather to entice him with inspirations and teachings; for virtue and happiness are promised to the willing, not the coerced. The authority of the teacher is confirmed by believing, not by endless questioning. Moreover, there are few who are worthy to see miracles, and very few worthy to receive them. Miracles among men are fittingly performed by God for the most part through the souls of men who are greatly separated from their bodies and joined to God, acting as His instruments.

<summary>Ficino argues for the historical truth of Christ's miracles, citing astronomical anomalies during the crucifixion and the bold testimonies of St. Paul. He concludes that demanding constant new miracles is irrational, as faith should be led by divine inspiration and the established authority of the Church.</summary>

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

monuments. Immerse yourselves, therefore, in the mud of the body, O wretched souls, so that you may see celestial wonders: O how foolishly you desire to see sublime things with your head bowed toward the earth; you wish to be carried to the heights by portents, rather than climbing by the steps of virtue. What is more miraculous, what is more divine on earth, than a mind that is entirely master of its own body? Let us experience this command if we can—and we can, if we wish—then we will not only see miracles, but we ourselves will perform them.

I certainly believe that even for us who are undeserving, certain wonderful signs are often performed by divine power in various places, but not all things are open to everyone. Many things are also not written down, or if written, are not believed; some quite detestable men seem to give occasion for this doubt, who introduce false prodigies in imitation of true ones. Imitation and resemblance necessarily follow the true thing that is being imitated; a counterfeit coin would not be introduced unless a legitimate coin had once existed, and false miracles would not be fabricated unless men had been invited to faith or imitation by true miracles. 

The miracles that Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> says he saw, and those that Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> relates, are such that they should not lack faith. I have indeed heard that in our own times, and even in our city of Florence, wonderful and yet believable things have happened, though some are more hidden. But one thing is most manifest to many thousands of people who saw it and are still alive, which we have received from many trustworthy sources as having happened in Ancona in the year of our Lord 1470. A certain girl, because of a terrible contraction of the nerves from her earliest infancy, used her buttocks for walking instead of her legs. Furthermore, Bindellus, a Florentine, could say nothing for many years because of a bruising of the throat and chest; both of them, when they had humbly commended themselves to the Divine Mary in that same place, immediately became healthy. They had been known as infirm to the whole people for many years, and afterwards, for four years continuously, they have been healthy before all the people. 

Do not wonder, Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent," Ficino's patron and the ruler of Florence.</note>, that Marsilio Ficino, a student of philosophy, should introduce miracles: for the things we write are true, and it is the duty of a philosopher to confirm individual points with their own reasons. Natural things have their own reasons, which are according to nature; divine things, however, have reasons of this kind which are above nature—both metaphysical proofs and, most especially, miracles. For God proves His mysteries and confirms His precepts not so much by words as by miraculous works; whence that saying: *If you do not wish to believe words, believe works.* <note>John 10:38</note>

->Authority among the Gentiles. Chapter XI.<-

No one has ever denied Christian miracles, although some have attributed them to the power of demons, not knowing that demons are accustomed to spread either their own worship or vices and eventually pestilential dissensions; however, these things are entirely foreign to those Christian heroes. But how can that religion have its origin from demons which condemned and overthrew the worship of demons, and put the demons themselves to flight, and continues to do so? Almost the entire world suddenly worshipped Christ and still does, except for a few wandering moneylenders <note>A common medieval and Renaissance rhetorical trope referring to Jewish communities.</note> who, being entirely enslaved to greed, cannot think rightly about divine things. 

Truly, all the Gentiles <note>The "pagan" nations, specifically the Greeks and Romans.</note> agreed that Jesus was either God Himself or certainly divine. The Milesian Apollo <note>The oracle of Apollo at Didyma near Miletus.</note>, when consulted, thus commended Christ: "He was mortal in body, a wise worker of portents, but under Chaldean leaders, he was seized by arms and suffered a bitter death by nails and clubs." Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher who was often critical of Christianity but is quoted here for his "admissions."</note> in his book *On Oracles* says that the gods pronounced Christ to be most pious and asserted that he had escaped as an immortal, testifying most kindly about him. He adds that the goddess Hecate replied to those questioning her about the soul of Christ: "That soul is of a man most excellent in piety; they worship this soul as one free from harshness." And after many things Hecate added: "Christ himself, being pious, ascended into heaven as the pious do." 

Do not, therefore, detract from him; Porphyry himself concedes that Christ was both wise and pious, although he calls Christians partly unlearned and partly magicians, clearly contradicting both the truth and himself. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> writes in his *Apology* that when Pilate reported to the Emperor Tiberius about the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred it to the Senate so that the Christian rites might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by a decree of the Fathers <note>The Roman Senators.</note>, it was decided to eliminate the Christians from the city, it was because the judgment of this matter had not been brought to the Senate first. For there was an ancient decree that no God should be consecrated without the authority of the Senate. Tiberius, by an edict, threatened the accusers of the Christians with death; many senators and Roman knights were killed. Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the historian of the early Church.</note> confirms the same. Vespasian...

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: & and that</meta>

Vespasian and Titus, having heard of the works of Christ, feared his power. Hadrian, as Julius Capitolinus <note>One of the authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note> relates, determined to build temples to Christ and to receive him among the gods. For this reason, he ordered temples without idols to be built in all cities. Today, because they have no statues of deities, these are still called "Hadrian’s temples." It was said he prepared them for this purpose, but he was prevented by those who, consulting the sacred rites, found that everyone would become Christian if that wish were fulfilled, and the remaining temples would be deserted. Alexander Severus also intended to build temples to Christ, but he did not succeed; he used to pray in the mornings in his private chapel before a statue of Christ. So says Capitolinus. 

But hear what Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), known as the "Father of Church History."</note> reports concerning Hadrian: Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, and Aristides the Athenian philosopher, gave books they had composed in defense of the Christian religion to Hadrian. And Serenus Granius, a most noble legate, sent letters to the Emperor, saying it was unjust for the blood of innocent men to be condemned by the shouts of the mob, and for them to be made guilty of no crime other than their name and sect. Moved by these things, Hadrian wrote to the proconsul Minucius Fundanus that Christians should not be condemned without an objective charge of crime—a copy of which letter survives to our own age. So says Eusebius.

Antoninus Pius, when he heard that Christians frequently used this proverb: *What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another*, <note>original: "Quod tibi fieri non uis, alteri ne feceris"</note> examined the life of Christ and consecrated a statue to him as to a God. I truly believe he was greatly led to this by Justin the Philosopher, <note>Saint Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist.</note> who dedicated a book written in defense of our religion to him. 

Philip is recorded by Eusebius as the first of the emperors to become a Christian; for the earlier ones worshipped Jesus not alone, but along with the other gods—though they all seem to have feared their own people more than God. Finally, Constantine, when he had more clearly experienced the miracles of Christ in his own affairs, feared God more than the people; he worshipped Christ alone and openly, overturned the temples of idols, and built precious temples to Christ everywhere. Eusebius, who flourished in Constantine's time, writes these things about him. 

It is well established that those princes who raged most cruelly against the Christians were led by a certain cruel nature and reckless agitation rather than by any reason of justice—as anyone would see who considers those insane men like Nero and Domitian, who abounded in Rome in those times. Regarding such judges, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note> says our sect ought to glory, because nothing but some great good could be condemned by them. Such persecutors of ours were always unjust, impious, shameful, and condemned by all the people. The more moderate princes, however, conducted themselves more honorably toward Christians. 

Furthermore, whichever princes raged most monstrously above the rest, such as Nero and Domitian, paid miserable penalties. I shall omit how the betrayer of Christ, Judas, suddenly hanged himself with a noose, which Christ’s disciples spoke and wrote of publicly in those times. Moreover, Pontius Pilate, the condemner of Christ, eventually falling into many calamities, killed himself with his own hand—which Eusebius asserts he read in the historians of the Greeks and Romans. Similar was the end of the first Herod, <note>Herod the Great.</note> who killed himself; and similar was the end of the second, <note>Herod Agrippa I.</note> who, immediately after the killing of James and the imprisonment of Peter, perished when struck by an angel, as Luke <note>Referring to the author of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 12:23).</note> testifies. And as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> says: he saw an angel standing over his head, the minister of his destruction, and then, after being gravely tortured, he violently cut short his life. 

Add to this that the Emperor Aurelian, when he first moved a persecution against the Christians, was first terrified by a lightning bolt and soon afterward killed. Julian the Apostate <note>Roman Emperor (r. 361–363 AD) who rejected Christianity in favor of Neoplatonic paganism.</note> also, setting out against the Persians, had vowed Christian blood to the gods after his victory; but on the journey itself, he lost his army to hunger and thirst, and he himself was ignominiously killed. Diocletian killed himself. Maximian was shamefully slain. 

Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that Celsus the Epicurean, and also Porphyry, Julian, and Proclus the Platonists—and several others distinguished in learning—impiously armed their tongues and pens against Christian piety. They did this partly out of an insane arrogance and partly to please their own people and the powerful. While the weapons of the powerful and of the world raged against piety, these men undoubtedly declared by their very opposition that the fathers of our religion were by no means to be despised. Illustrious philosophers deigned to engage in contest with them and were convinced by them; thus, the religion itself did not arise by human force, as it so wonderfully overcame human wisdom and power. This is what God foretold through Isaiah: *I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject.* <note>Isaiah 29:14</note> And the Apostle Paul confirmed this, saying: *The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God,* <note>1 Corinthians 3:19</note> and, *The foolishness of God is wiser than men.* <note>1 Corinthians 1:25</note>

<summary>Ficino catalogs the reactions of Roman Emperors and pagan philosophers to Christianity, arguing that "good" rulers respected Christ while "bad" persecutors met violent ends, proving the faith's divine protection.</summary>

### ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...and the weakness of God is stronger than men. <note>original: "quod infirmum est Dei, fortius est hominibus"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:25.</note> And elsewhere, this vigorous soldier of Christ <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> cries out in this manner: "The weapons of our warfare are not worldly, but are powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds and arguments, and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God; and furthermore, for bringing every intellect into captivity in obedience to Christ, and for being ready to punish all disobedience." <note>A translation of 2 Corinthians 10:4-6.</note> Rightly, therefore, did Gamaliel, the great teacher of the Hebrews, fear these weapons when he advised that they should not persecute the teaching of Jesus. For if it were of God, it could not be hindered; but if it were not of God, it would—like other fabrications that occurred in those times—last only a short time. <note>Gamaliel was a leading authority in the Sanhedrin; this refers to his speech in Acts 5:38-39.</note> That divine Plotinus, the prince of Platonic interpreters, as well as Numenius, Iamblichus, and Amelius, also feared those weapons; they strove not to reject Christian Theology, but rather to emulate it. <note>These were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who lived in the 3rd and 4th centuries AD.</note> At nearly the same time, and much more so, did Arnobius the African, a most famous rhetorician, fear them. While he was still an idolater, he was driven toward Christian belief by dreams, yet he could not obtain formal acceptance into the faith from the bishop because he had always attacked it. Therefore, as Jerome says, he stayed up at night to compose most brilliant books against his former religion, and finally obtained his request, offering these books as if they were hostages of his piety. <note>Arnobius of Sicca (c. 255–330 AD) wrote *Adversus Nationes* ("Against the Pagans") to prove the sincerity of his conversion.</note>

<margin>The authority of Christ among the followers of Muhammad. Chapter 12.</margin>

The followers of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahumethenses"; used here to refer to Muslims.</note> seem to be Christians in a certain way, although they are followers of the Arian and Manichaean sects. <note>Ficino categorized Islam as a Christian heresy, specifically linking it to Arianism (which denied Christ's full divinity) and Manichaeism (a dualistic faith).</note> Certainly, their leader Muhammad confesses that Jesus Christ is the power, wisdom, soul, breath, spirit, and word of God, born of the Virgin Mary—a perpetual virgin—by a certain divine inspiration. He confesses that Jesus raised the dead and performed many other miracles by divine power beyond all others; that he was more sublime than all the prophets of the Hebrews, and that the Hebrews would have no prophet after Jesus. Indeed, he places him before all men, and Mary before all women. He adds that the body of Jesus ascended incorrupt into heaven. He places Christians far ahead of the Jews and utterly detests the Jews. All these things are in his book, the Quran. <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> Hence, his followers do not initiate Jews into their sacred rites until they confess that the ancient sacraments of the Christians are true and good. And those who visit the tomb of Muhammad are not considered sufficiently purified unless they also visit the tomb of Christ. Anyone who mentions the name of Christ or Mary insultingly is severely punished by them. They have one type of religious order dedicated to Elijah, another to John the Baptist, and another—indeed the most principal one—dedicated to Jesus Christ. They celebrate the Prophets and the Gospels, for they learned from Muhammad in the Quran that the Quran is an affirmation and declaration of the Hebrew Prophets and the Gospel. It is read in the same place that no one will be perfect unless he obeys the Old and New Testaments, and the Quran besides, because it is the assembly and declaration of both. Whenever he names the Gospel, which he does often, he calls the book by its own title, "the Luminous," and sometimes even adds that the Gospel is the light of the testament, a correct discipline and path for those who fear God. Furthermore, he introduces God speaking in the Quran in this way: "While we have preferred some Prophets over others and have spoken to them, we have specifically conferred our soul upon Christ the son of Mary, providing him with strength and power beyond the rest." 

However, there appear to be two principal errors of Muhammad. The first is that although he places a certain divinity in Christ—far greater than in all men, whether present, past, or future—he nevertheless seems in some places to want that divinity to be distinct from and lesser than the substance of the Supreme God. He certainly received this from the Arians, but in this he fights against himself, for the titles he attributes to Christ signify that his divinity is the same as that of the Supreme God. The other error of Muhammad—and indeed a more manifest one—is that when those henchmen of the priests who were trying to lay hands on Jesus fell down, God (as Muhammad thinks) suddenly and secretly snatched Jesus away to heaven. When they had risen, they seized another person who looked like Jesus, beat him, and fixed him to a cross. He seems to have received this from the Manichaeans. <note>This refers to the Docetic view of the crucifixion found in the Quran (Surah 4:157), suggesting someone else was substituted for Jesus.</note> There is no need for me to refute errors of this kind; for whoever has refuted the Arian and Manichaean heresies is seen to have also refuted Muhammad. We can conclude that the Christian law is admitted by all sects—Gentiles, Jews, and followers of Muhammad—to be truly the most excellent of all. For each of these, although they may prefer their own heresy to others due to a certain natural affection, custom, or fabrication, they [regard] the Christian...

<summary>Ficino argues for the universal excellence of Christianity by citing the respect shown to it by Neo-Platonic philosophers and the Quran. He characterizes Islam as a Christian heresy that acknowledges Jesus's miracles and Mary's virtues while erring on Christ's nature and the reality of the crucifixion.</summary>

### On the generation of the Son of God in eternity. Chapter XIII.

Every life generates its offspring within itself before it does so externally, and the more excellent the life is, the more internal is the offspring it generates for itself. Thus, the vegetative life, both in trees and in animals, first generates a seed—a sort of "internal tree" or "internal animal"—within its own body before it either casts it out or produces an external tree or animal from it. Likewise, the sensitive life, which is more excellent than the vegetative, produces within itself through the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia," referring to the faculty that forms mental images.</note> an image and intention of things before it moves the limbs and crafts anything in external matter. But that first offspring of the imagination, because it is in the soul itself, is therefore closer to the soul than the offspring of the vegetative life, which is not in the soul but in the body.

Likewise, the rational life, which is more excellent than the sensitive, gives birth within itself to the <term>reason</term> <note>original: "rationem," meaning both a logical principle and a thought.</note> of both things and of itself, as a kind of offspring, before it brings it into the light either by speaking or by acting. That first offspring of reason is closer to the soul than the offspring of the imagination. For the rational power is reflected upon its own offspring, and through that offspring upon itself, by seeking, knowing, and loving its own act and its very self—something the imagination does not do. Likewise, the angelic life, more excellent than the rational, produces notions of itself and of things within itself by a certain divine instinct, before it brings them forth into the matter of the world. This offspring is more internal to the angel than reason is to the soul, because it is neither stirred up by external objects one by one, nor is it subject to change.

For this reason, the divine life—because it is the most eminent and the most fruitful of all—generates an offspring most similar to itself far more than any other life does. It generates this offspring within itself before it gives birth; I say it generates "inside" by the act of understanding. Insofar as God perfectly understands himself, and in himself understands all things, he conceives within himself a perfect notion of his whole self and of all things. This notion is indeed an equal and full image of God, and a more-than-full model of the world. <note>Ficino is describing the "Logos" or the "Word" as the internal thought of God.</note>

Orpheus called this "Pallas," born from the head of Jove alone. <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom, famously sprang fully formed from the head of Zeus (Jupiter/Jove).</note> Plato, in his *Letter to Hermias*, named this the "Son of the Father God," and in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato in the Renaissance.</note> he called it the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "logon," from the Greek "Logos."</note>—that is, reason and speech—saying: "The Word, most divine of all, adorned this visible world." Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Egyptian figure thought to be a contemporary of Moses, whose writings Ficino translated.</note> often makes mention of the Word and the Son of God, and even of the Spirit. Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, highly respected by Renaissance Platonists.</note> also attributed an intellectual offspring to God. These men said what they could, and they did so with God's help. But God alone understands this, as does anyone to whom God has wished to reveal it.

The fruitfulness of God—which is a "good" that is infinite in act—propagates itself infinitely from eternity through the nature of the immense, eternal Good. However, whatever is outside of God is finite; therefore, God propagates himself within himself, where surely the Son of an infinite Father is himself infinite. It is necessary that an offspring of this kind be much more "intimate" (if I may put it that way) to God than that angelic notion is to the angelic mind. In an angel, since "being" is one thing and "understanding" is another, the notion that is generated by understanding is different from the essence of the angel itself. In God, however, because "being" and "understanding" are the same, the notion that God always produces by understanding himself—always as the most exact image of himself—is identical in essence to the one who generates it, although by a certain wondrous "relation" it is distinguished as the "begotten" from the "begetter."

Finally, God—knowing his own infinite goodness from eternity through this eternal notion—breathes out <note>original: "spirat," the root of "Spirit."</note> an infinite love within himself toward himself through that same notion from eternity. Therefore, the Father, the Son, and the Loving Spirit are called "three persons" by theologians; they agree entirely with one another in divine nature, so that there is one single and simple God, yet they differ by a certain inconceivable relation. Thus, in the order of things, we have two extremes and two means: in any angel, as some wish it, there is one angelic person in one species of its nature. Conversely, in a pregnant woman, there are several persons in several natures. On the other hand, in any animal nature, there are many individuals in one person <note>Ficino likely refers to the "animal soul" as a single faculty governing many parts.</note>; but in God, there are several persons in one nature.

But enough of these things for the present—or rather, never enough; for the sufficiency of this contemplation is to be sought not from philosophers, but from those heroic leaders of the Christians, and from God himself. For rightly did Isaiah say: "What eye has not seen, what ear has not heard, what has not entered into the heart of man, God has revealed to those who love him." <note>Ficino attributes this to Isaiah, though it is famously quoted by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:9 (based on Isaiah 64:4).</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that just as all life generates offspring internally before externally, God eternally generates a perfect internal image of Himself (the Son/Word). He links this Christian doctrine of the Trinity to ancient "pagan" wisdom from Orpheus, Plato, and Hermes Trismegistus.</summary>

<keywords>Trinity, Logos, Divine Generation, Platonism, Marsilio Ficino, Orpheus, Hermes Trismegistus, Zoroaster, Intelligence, Holy Spirit</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Marsilio Ficino, transitioning from the internal "generation" of the Divine Word discussed in Chapter 13 to a cosmic map of the universe in Chapter 14. Here, he describes how the physical heavens, the angelic hierarchies, and human souls are arranged in concentric circles around the Holy Trinity.</meta>

ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.

B 2

->The order of the heavens, angels, and souls around the Trinity like spheres<-
->around a center. Chapter 14.<-

Above the four elements <note>The traditional physical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, which are changeable in both substance and quality, there are the seven heavens of the Planets; these do not change in substance, but are changed in a certain way by their quality or disposition. Because their motion is, as it were, wandering <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note>, the eighth heaven is placed above them, whose motion is more ordered. However, that heaven has two motions: namely, from the East to the West, and vice versa. It also possesses at least two qualities, namely brightness and splendor. Therefore, one ascends from it to the crystalline heaven, whose motion is simple from the East, and whose quality is also simple—that is, brightness. But because it is superior in its state of motion, and its light is superior in brightness, one ascends from this to the **Empyrean** <term>Empyrean</term> <note>From the Greek *empyros*, meaning "in fire"; in medieval cosmology, this was the highest heaven, composed of pure light and fire, and the dwelling place of God.</note>, which is entirely stable and completely radiant. The Empyrean is rightly matched to the stability and light of the Trinity, while the remaining nine heavens are matched to the nine orders of angels.

For, as it pleases **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century theologian whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" became the standard for Christian angelology.</note>, there are three hierarchies of divine spirits, each of which contains three orders. Each order, as certain theologians calculate, contains many legions. They think a legion consists of 6,666 units, and that there are as many legions in each order as there are units in a single legion. But I agree more with Dionysius, who says that the multitude of those spirits is so great that it exceeds the capacity of human calculation. 

The one essence of God is drawn into a threefold number of Persons; this threefold number is encircled by the threefold number of hierarchies and the ninefold number of angelic orders, acting as spiritual spheres. The first hierarchy is attributed to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Spirit. 
In the first hierarchy:
*   The **Seraphim** contemplate the Father in himself. 
*   The **Cherubim** contemplate the Father insofar as he generates the Son. 
*   The **Thrones** contemplate the Father as he, with the Son, produces the Spirit. 

In the second: 
*   The **Dominations** contemplate the Son in himself. 
*   The **Virtues** contemplate the Son flowing from the Father. 
*   The **Powers** contemplate the Son as he, with the Father, produces the Spirit. 

In the third: 
*   The **Principalities** contemplate the Spirit in himself. 
*   The **Archangels** contemplate the Spirit coming from the Father and the Son. 
*   The **Angels** contemplate the Spirit proceeding from the Son and the Father. 

Although each order (as we have said) looks upon God primarily for different reasons, every one of them nevertheless sees the entire Trinity and everything within it. 

They have, moreover (as Dionysius wishes), another difference: the first hierarchy draws its "liquid" <note>original: "liquorem," here referring to the flow of divine grace or wisdom.</note> from the Trinity alone; the second through the first; and the third through the second and first. Likewise, the Seraphim observe the order of divine providence in the goodness of God as the *end* <note>The final goal or purpose.</note>; the Cherubim observe it in the essence of God as the *form*. The Thrones, finally, observe it in itself; the rest then descend to active works. 

The **Dominations**, like architects, give the commands that the others execute. The **Virtues** then carry them out; they move the heavens and join together as instruments of God to perform miracles. The **Powers** ward off those things that seem able to disturb the order of divine government. The others then descend more toward human affairs. The **Principalities** take care of public matters: Nations, Princes, and Magistrates. The **Archangels** direct divine worship for individuals and are present at sacred rites. The **Angels** arrange smaller matters and stand by as guardians for each individual. 

Just as there are nine orders of angels, so the souls of the blessed are distributed into nine orders. For every soul ascends to that order and that spirit as if to its own **star** (as **Plato** says in the *Timaeus*), to which it made itself similar during life. For although our souls, while they are in the body, constitute a fourth hierarchy below the Moon, they are able—because of the free movement of their rational nature—to ascend through all the kind spirits and descend through the malignant ones. This is especially true since they hold the middle position of all things, and therefore contain certain qualities of all things within themselves, which allows for the widest possible progression of souls. The end of the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the dwelling place of the blessed; Ficino identifies it here with the sphere of the Moon.</note> is the Moon, the boundary of life and death (as the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed in the transmigration of souls.</note> maintain). Whatever is below it is assigned to death and the underworld, where there are as many degrees of punishment, according to the crowds of malignant spirits, as there are rewards in the heavens according to the orders of the kind ones. For nine times the winding **Styx** <note>The river of the underworld.</note> 

->confines the wretched, just as the Elysian fields nine times<-
->embrace the blessed.<-

<summary>Ficino maps the structure of the universe, aligning the ten heavens with the Holy Trinity and the nine angelic orders. He explains how human souls, occupying a middle ground, can ascend to these celestial ranks based on their conduct in life.</summary>

THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

### The generation of the Son in eternity, and his manifestation in time.
->Chapter XV.<-

Before the beginning of the temporal world, there is an eternal world, which is indeed the model <note>original: *exemplar*; in Platonic thought, this is the perfect "blueprint" or ideal form of the universe.</note> for this world. This is the logic and the intelligible Word <note>original: *Verbum*; the divine Reason or Logos.</note> of the world’s architect, the splendor of his glory, and the very image of his substance. A Word of this kind is always with God, and is God Himself; through this, the divine power from eternity spoke within itself, both of itself and of all other things, and by speaking, impressed them inwardly. Through this same Word, at a certain time, both the ages and all things that exist within the ages were expressed outwardly. These divine oracles, following the mysteries of the Prophets, were poured down from heaven to men by those celestial spirits, John the Evangelist and Paul the Apostle. 

However, the human race eventually fell away from God, and since it had fallen to the lowest depths, it could never rise back toward God without God’s help. Yet, human minds had to rise back at some point, lest they should have been created by God in vain—for they were created by Him for the sake of attaining Him. Humans had once been formed through the Word of God; therefore, they had to be reformed through that same Word. And rightly so: for the darkness of the human intellect had to be driven away by the light of the intellectual Word, and the rational creature <note>original: *rationale animal*.</note> had to be corrected by the Reason of God. 

Therefore, at the times appointed by the divine will, God created through the Word a certain rational human soul, which at that same moment He joined—through the divine spirit—to the tender offspring of the virginal womb at the moment of conception. At that same moment, the Word itself assumed human nature; and just as one man is made from an immortal soul and a mortal body, so from that man and the Word of God, Christ was made—both God and man. Thus, infinite goodness, which wishes to communicate itself to all, then communicated itself to all in the most fitting way possible: when it joined to itself man, in whom, as if in a middle species of things, all things are contained. <note>Ficino views humanity as the "center" or "bond" of the universe, containing elements of both the divine/intellectual and the physical/material.</note> Nor did the divine majesty change its "seat" at that time, since it is always everywhere; nor did the divine sublimity cast itself down into human things as if by a defect, but rather it elevated human things to itself. Nor could the infinite light of the divine Sun ever be stained in any way by its joining with man; rather, man was super-illuminated and perfected by it. Just as increases or decreases in a man pertain only to the body and never penetrate the soul, so in Christ, human suffering pertained specifically to the man and did not penetrate the divinity. Therefore, as a man, Christ suffered human things; as God, He performed divine works.

->It was fitting for God to join Himself to man.<-
->Chapter XVI.<-

Why was God once made man? So that man might one day, in a certain way, be made God. For a person can, in a certain way, become divine if they desire and strive to be divine by a natural instinct. However, one cannot rise up into God unless God at some point draws them upward, just as He previously drew them to desire it. 

But let us return to this matter from another principle. The supreme craftsman <term>Opifex</term> <note>Ficino uses the term *Opifex* to describe God as the Divine Architect or Artisan of the universe, a concept heavily influenced by Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> ought to produce a supreme and manifest work—one so great that no greater work can be made. Clearly, the supreme God must make such a work; it is either purely uncreated, purely created, or composed of both. The first is not a "manifest work," but the craftsman himself, for only God is He who does not depend on another. The second, being entirely finite, is separated from the infinite God by an immense and infinite distance. In this gap, by reason of the interval itself and the infinity of God, another work and yet another more excellent one can always be made. 

Therefore, no simple creature <note>A "simple" creature refers to something that is only one kind of thing, like a purely physical stone or a purely spiritual angel.</note> can be that supreme work which we seek; rather, we trust that such a work is finally found in the highest degree if something unique is discovered that is composed of both the highest Creator and a creature at once. By reason of the creature, it is called a "work"; but by reason of the Creator, God is able to make such an immense work, and He knows how, and He wills it, for God is immense power, wisdom, and goodness. Therefore, the creature had to be joined to the Creator at some point. 

Those things that are above the rational soul are only eternal; those below it are only temporal; but the soul itself is partly eternal and partly temporal. It imitates God by its unity, the angels by its intellect, its own species by its reason, the beasts by its senses, plants by its nutrition, and things lacking essence by its life. Thus, the human creature is in a certain way "all things"—a point we have discussed more broadly in our *Theology* <note>Ficino is likely referring to his major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note>—especially since he is made of a body composed of the powers of all things, and is most balanced, like the heavens. It is fitting, moreover, for the entire creation to be joined in some way to God, the common leader of all—not indeed in a scattered way, because

<meta>catchword: sim, (beginning of 'simul' - 'together' or 'at once')</meta>
<vocab>Marsilio Ficino, Word (Verbum), Incarnation, Creature, Craftsman (Opifex), Rational Soul, Theology, Microcosm</vocab>

<summary>Ficino explains the Incarnation of Christ as the necessary "re-forming" of humanity by the same divine Word that first created it. He argues that man is the "middle" of the universe, and therefore the most fitting point for God to join with His creation to produce His most perfect work.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of why God chose to become human. On the previous page, he discussed how humanity, having fallen, required the Word (the Logos) to be reformed. Here, he explains that because humanity occupies the "middle" of creation, it is the perfect bridge for God to unite with all of existence.</meta>

ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.
B 3
<meta>catchword: as if</meta>

...since God is the highest unity—or rather, the ultimate oneness—it is necessary for God to be united to human nature, in which all things are contained. For if He were joined only to those things that are above human nature, as if to the furthest extremes of created things, such a union would reach neither the middle of things nor the other extremes. Similarly, if He joined Himself to those things which are below us, He would have skipped the middle. Truly, the infinite Unity has united His works in the highest degree, both to one another and to Himself, since from the beginning He enclosed all things within man, and thereafter bound man to Himself. Perhaps because of what we said above, the Prophet Habakkuk <note>original: "Abacuc"; Ficino is quoting Habakkuk 3:2.</note> says: *O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years you will make it known; when you are angry, you will remember mercy.* This is because that work is fulfilled in the "middle" species of things, which is composed of both worlds—namely, of eternity and of time. Some add that this also refers to the middle of the world’s course; for they wish for the course of the world—though not the world itself—to be completed in ten thousand years <note>Ficino refers to a medieval and Renaissance chronological theory that the "age of the world" would last a specific cycle, with Christ appearing at the midpoint.</note>, since motion was established for the sake of rest. They argue that in this middle of the world’s course, God showed Himself to men so that His coming would be equally distant from both extremes of the ages, lest either the expectation of His future coming be drawn out too long, or the memory of His past coming be entirely erased. But God, the regulator of times, will have seen to the timing Himself.

If it is characteristic of goodness to pour out and communicate itself, and since God is the infinite good, He must fulfill all modes of communication. These, indeed, appear to be four: by presence, by power, by unity of essence, and by unity of person. The first is fulfilled in all things, for God is present everywhere. The second is propagated through all forms, even the smallest, for every form has some effective power from God, though matter itself does not. The third occurs only within God, for the essence of God cannot become the essence of another; otherwise, either that which is infinite would become finite, or that which is finite would become infinite. The fourth mode of communication [unity of person] cannot occur in things lacking reason; for to those who entirely lack nature, knowledge, and the love of God, a divine union according to person is not fitting. 

Nor was it necessary for one person to be made from an angel and God; for no remedy remains for the wretched [fallen] angels since they lack repentance, and for the rest of the angels, that ancient possession of divine light is sufficient for their beatitude. Indeed, that light in the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, characterized by fiery love.</note> becomes, in a certain way, a "Seraphic" light; in the Cherubim <note>The second order of angels, characterized by fullness of knowledge.</note>, it becomes "Cherubic," and similarly in the others—just as the light of the Sun, while passing through glass of various colors, transforms itself into various colors. However, God in man rightly renders the man divine. For just as in natural things the most excellent natural composite, such as a rational animal, is made from the lowest matter and the highest form, so almost in divine things, from the highest spirit—namely God—and the lowest, the human soul, there is produced a "divine assumption" <note>term: *assumptum*; the theological concept that the Divine Word "assumed" or took on a human nature.</note> more excellent than all others. It was not enough for man that a ray infused by God should be stirred up in his mind, for because of the senses, man wanders away from the mind. It was necessary, therefore, in a certain man—namely Jesus—for the soul to be joined to the divine Sun in such a way that a bounty of rays might overflow into his body and to the senses of men.

->*What sort of union exists between God and man.*<-
->Chapter XVII.<-

**S**ince the union of God to man was made according to the divine person rather than according to the divine nature, it follows that when the Word is united to man, it is not necessary for the Father and the Spirit to be united in the same way; for although they agree in nature, they differ among themselves by the property of their person. Therefore, just as in the Trinity three persons exist in the same nature, so in Christ one person exists in three natures: God, the soul, and the body. In this state, the man is compared to God just as the hand is to the soul, or rather, the tongue to the intellect. For God does not properly become the "natural form" of the man, but the man becomes the proper and conjoined instrument of God, for the most excellent performance of God’s own works. 

However, there are not two persons in Christ, but one: namely, the person of the Word conjoined, not to a human person, but to a human nature. For just as the rational soul exists in its own being, through which its body also exists, so the Son of God—and much more so—exists in the being of His own person, and raises human nature up to that being. Furthermore, just as a word conceived in our mind is imperceptible, but when brought forth by the voice it becomes perceptible, so the Word of the divine mind remains invisible from eternity in God, but through the assumption of man, He was made visible. Christ is therefore the Word, which the divine mind speaks within itself from eternity by understanding itself and all things with itself, now brought forth by the divine spirit, and [clothed in] a human body...

<summary>Ficino argues that God’s incarnation as a human was necessary because humanity sits at the center of creation. He defines the Incarnation as a "union of person" where the eternal Word (the Son) uses human nature as an instrument, similar to how a thought becomes audible when spoken.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s theological argument for the necessity of the Incarnation. On the previous page, he established that humanity occupies a central "middle" position in the universe, making it the ideal bridge for God to unite with all of creation. Here, he explores the logical "fittingness" of God becoming man to repair the damage of the Fall.</meta>

BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
B 3

...as if taking up a voice, and making the divine will known to those who hear. Indeed, He made the divine will known to each person only as much as they were able to grasp. To all, however, He grants eternal happiness if they practice this in this brief life. He handed down many excellent precepts, but encompassed everything in a few words when He commanded: Love God with your whole heart, love men as yourself, and do not do to others what you do not wish done to you.

->*How fitting the union of God and man is.* Chapter XVIII.<-

It is no less a task to reform what is deformed than it is to form it simply from the beginning; indeed, "well-being" is no less a thing than "simply being." It was fitting, therefore, for God, the maker of all things, to perfect those things which had failed, just as He had created all things through the inaudible word <note>original: "insensibile uerbum"; referring to the Logos as the internal thought or "unheard" Word of God before creation.</note>. For what else are creatures but certain voices of God's thoughts brought forth? So, through the Word made somehow perceptible to the senses <note>original: "sensibile," meaning able to be experienced through sight, touch, or sound.</note>, He reforms the things of the sensory world. Since God does all things powerfully, wisely, and benevolently, it was fitting to restore them in such a way that He showed His power, wisdom, and benevolence. What is more powerful than to bring together extremes into one person and to bring the infinite back to the highest? What is wiser than for the beauty of the universe to become a wondrous bond of the first and last reason? What is more benevolent than for God, the Lord of the universe, to take the form of a servant for the sake of the salvation of a delinquent servant? Thus He both declared and acted so that nothing in the world would be deformed, and nothing at all should be despised, when He joined earthly things to the King of Heavens and, in a way, made them equal to celestial things. Furthermore, since man had fallen away from the most powerful, wise, and kind God, he had consequently collapsed into weakness, ignorance, and malice. Because of this, turning from pious to profane, he was now entirely unfit to imitate divine virtue, to know the light, or finally to love goodness. Therefore, so that man might rise again from this ruin to the heights, it was most fitting for the sublime God to stretch out His hand from on high to this man, specifically by this means: that He might make Himself visible, lovable, and imitable to him. There was no more suitable way for this than for God to become man, so that man—who had now become physical and gasped for physical things—might now more clearly know and more ardently love God as both physical and human, and might more easily and diligently imitate Him and become blessed. Finally, man could not be perfectly healed unless he recovered the innocence of his mind, the friendship of God, and his own excellence, which was subject to God alone from the beginning according to nature. He could not obtain excellence unless the healer was God, to whom alone man is subject by nature; nor could he obtain God’s friendship unless there were a suitable mediator <note>original: "conciliatorem," a reconciler or go-between.</note> who could stretch his hand to both parties, and who was in some way related and a friend to the extremes of both. There is no such person at all unless he is simultaneously God and man. Nor could he recover innocence unless the fault was dismissed, which justice does not allow to be dismissed without satisfaction <note>The legal and theological concept of "satisfaction" (satisfactio) implies paying a debt or making amends for an offense.</note>. Only God could make satisfaction for the whole human race; yet it was not fitting for anyone to suffer except the man who had sinned, nor could God Himself suffer <note>The divine nature is considered "impassible" or unable to suffer; therefore, a human nature was needed to experience pain and death.</note>. Thus it was appropriate that the human race, created through God, should now be mended by God having become man. Therefore, excellence could not be gained except through the most excellent healer, nor friendship reconciled except through the most friendly mediator, nor innocence recovered except through the most sufficient provider of satisfaction. Now, the most excellent healer is God alone; the most friendly mediator is man; and He properly appears to be the most sufficient provider of satisfaction because He is equally God and man. Therefore, it was very fitting for human healing, as John says: "The divine Word put on human flesh," so that just as the human race had been created through the eternal Word but had fallen into sin by abandoning the inspired Word, so it might be redeemed from sin through the visible Word.

->*The coming of Christ gives happiness through faith, hope, and charity.*<-
->Chapter XIX.<-

No one can attain the happiness that consists in divine contemplation unless they love God ardently. We cannot love God ardently unless we hope to be able to reach Him eventually. We cannot hope unless we first believe both that God exists and that we can one day enjoy God. Therefore, God, the father and healer of men, having sometimes clothed Himself in humanity in wondrous ways, offered Himself to our senses, so that through those very senses—which we use and trust the most—we might see His body and miracles and [know] that He is God...

<vocab>Marsilio Ficino, Incarnation, Happiness, Redemption, Satisfaction, The Word, Wisdom, Benevolence</vocab>

<summary>Ficino argues that the Incarnation was the most logical and fitting way to restore humanity, as it required a mediator who was both divine (to provide satisfaction for sin) and human (to represent the offending party). He concludes that this union allows humans to know and love God through their senses, leading to faith, hope, and eventual happiness.</summary>
