<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the Incarnation. Having established that the "Word made visible" (Christ) is the bridge between the divine and the physical, he now argues that this union provides humanity with the certainty and hope necessary for salvation, while also addressing the logical necessity of the God-man to repair the "infinite" damage caused by original sin.</meta>

ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION
B 4

...we might be more certain of God. From this, faith arose as the foundation of knowledge. Indeed, whoever believes that He descended into the heavy mass of the body for the sake of healing the human race will now hope to obtain even the greatest things from God. Whoever sees these great benefits in part, and in part hopes for them, cannot help but love Him, unless they are utterly senseless and ungrateful. Again, when you understand that God has been joined to the soul by a certain union of person, you ought to hope that the soul can eventually be joined to God by a certain union of operation—in which the highest happiness consists. You ought also to desire to cling to God above all others, for He alone has poured Himself entirely into the soul and body of man. Furthermore, because God joined Himself to man without a medium <note>original: "absque medio"; meaning there is no intermediary layer between the divine and human in the person of Christ.</note>, we must remember that our happiness consists in this: that we cling to God without a medium. And because friendship exists between equals, while you consider that God has in some way made Himself equal to man, you must neither deny God’s friendship toward you, nor abandon your own toward God. Let men therefore cease—let them now cease—to distrust their own divinity; it is because of this distrust that they plunge themselves into mortal things. Let them revere themselves as divine beings, and let them hope they can ascend to God, since the divine majesty has deigned, in a certain way, to descend to them. Let them love God with their whole heart, so that they may be transformed into Him, who out of His immense love wonderfully transformed Himself into man.

->*The coming of Christ was useful for lightening the weight of sin.*<-
->Chapter XX.<-

The soul is the life of the body; God is the life of the soul. The order of nature requires that the body obey the soul, and the soul obey God. The order of justice requires that if the soul disagrees with God, the body—by the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis pœna"; the law of an eye for an eye, where the punishment fits the crime.</note>—should disagree with the soul, and the senses should disagree with reason. The soul of our first parent rebelled against God, and the body rebelled against the soul. The first rebellion was a sin; the second was a certain punishment for that sin, and a sin itself, because it detracted from reason and from God. From that first rebel, a certain "flavor" of this rebellious disposition flowed into everyone, spreading like streams from a fountain. This, then, is original sin <note>original: "originale uitium," or original fault.</note>, the source of all other evils of the soul and body. The volumes of the Hebrews testify to this; their divinity is proven by their supreme antiquity above all others, the consensus of nearly everyone, their spread through the whole world, their unwearied duration, their harmony, majesty, sobriety, and miracles. From this comes that opinion of the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and philosophers.</note> descending from Zoroaster: namely, that all evils of the body proceed from the evils of the soul, and if the soul is cured, other evils are avoided. Plato hints at this in the *Timaeus*, but declares it clearly in the *Charmides*. 

But to return to the point: a rebellion of this kind, because it detracted from the majesty of the infinite God, rendered mortals utterly unfit for infinite happiness; nor could they be set right except by the infinite God. Yet they had to be set right eventually, lest they should have been ordained by God for happiness from the beginning in vain. Sin was committed through pleasure; it had to be purged through the opposite of pleasure: pain. In a way, all human nature sinned once in that man who acted on behalf of all; similarly, in a way, everyone must suffer once in someone who also acts on behalf of all—someone who agrees with God far more than the first man disagreed. After Adam, however, only He who was inwardly joined to God, the creator of all, could act on behalf of all. Therefore, He was both God and man at once: God, so that He might embrace all and be able to wash away an infinite fault; man, so that He might be able to suffer for the fault, and so that a man might suffer just as a man had sinned. Thus, the punishment and merit of that man had an infinite power, insofar as He was truly joined to the infinite God. For a certain infinite punishment and merit were needed to utterly wash away an infinite fault.

->*Christ fulfilled the perfect kind of instruction.*<-
->Chapter XXI.<-

Divine providence wished to omit no kind of training for its children. Instruction, however, is twofold: namely, through doctrine and through example. Perfect doctrine is that which cannot rightly be doubted, the kind which is granted to be in God alone. Therefore, God the Father sent a certain teacher to men who was God, so that it would not be fitting to doubt His doctrine; and also one who was man, so that He Himself could truly perform all human duties and endure all labors for the sake of what is honorable and for God. By this example, He might perfectly instruct men in virtue. For deeds move us much more than words, especially in moral discipline, whose proper end is found in action. That He was...

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
B 4

...miracles declared him to be God, so that his doctrine might find faith among those who are teachable; but his sufferings declared him to be truly human. Therefore, no room for excuse seems left to us—unless we wish to be excessively stubborn—if we arrogantly strive to reject his doctrine as if it were less than true. His divinity and miracles cry out against such a rejection. If we find his teaching too hard for us, the humanity and the labors of that teacher and leader show humans that the things a man endured are indeed possible. Finally, because the greatest of sins consists in this: that we cling too much to bodily things or depart from spiritual ones, Christ, the master of life, through his doctrine and his life, sent as it were a sword and a fire into the world. This is a **cleansing power** <note>original: "virtutem purgatoriam"</note>, so that once souls are purified, he might cut to the quick and consume all the **kindling-wood of bodily vices** <note>original: "corporalium vitiorum fomites"; a common theological term for the leftover inclinations toward sin.</note>. He himself also voluntarily and gladly endured everything that others flee from as if they were evils: wandering, hunger, thirst, nakedness, infamy, insults, beatings, a short life, and a shameful and most bitter death. On the other hand, he fled from those things that others pursue as if they were good, so that by this reasoning he might show us that the things we call "evils" are not true evils, nor are the things we call "goods" true goods. He showed that there is nothing in bodily things that should be valued at any price, but that whatever exists besides God should be considered a dream of a thin shadow. Since he lacked all the things desired by mortals as "goods," he certainly earned the right—solely through miracles, and he earned it suddenly—to be regarded throughout the entire world as the Supreme God, a status he holds to this very day. The Hebrews call the Prophets holy men; the Gentiles call them "excellent men," and when they name them "gods," they understand them to be men who have already been made divine and are ministers of God. The followers of Muhammad believe their king Muhammad—son of Abdallah, son of Abdul-Muttalib <note>original: "Abdal mutabilis"; likely a transcription error for Abdul-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad.</note>, the King of Arabia—was a pure man but a messenger of God; he calls himself such in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>. He adds that he himself was sent by God with the force of arms, while Christ was sent with the power of miracles, and that God made Jesus a miracle for men and Mary a miracle. Rightly, Christ alone deserved this status through stupendous works, which neither many Princes—striving for it with threats and favors—nor Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher often compared to Jesus in antiquity because of his reported miracles.</note>, and many other philosophers could achieve through their wonderful wisdom and long lives. This is true even though Iamblichus of Chalcis celebrated Pythagoras with long disputation, Philostratus celebrated Apollonius with eloquence, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of early Christianity.</note> with sharp arguments, and many Princes celebrated them with all their might.

->*Christ expelled errors and revealed the truth.* Chapter XXII.<-

Before the coming of Christ, many gods—or rather, demons—were worshipped throughout almost the entire world, and their priests were indeed evil, as the philosopher Oenomaus confesses. Who would not see that they were evil, those who cared nothing for the purification of souls, gave counsel only concerning earthly matters, and always demanded earthly things from their worshippers? They commanded the most obscene and cruel sacrifices to be made, and by their oracles, they sowed a great many discords. Everywhere, living tyrants were worshipped in place of demons (that is, in place of the blessed), and the souls of men who were partly unrestrained and partly wicked were worshipped. The human race was once oppressed by these most savage monsters. It was not an armed Hercules, but the unarmed Christ who then extinguished them when he blunted the power of the malignant demons. Plutarch writes that it is the opinion of the Barbarians <note>In this context, non-Greeks.</note> that demons of the air can suffer disturbances and even death. He also brings forward the testimony of many that it was discovered by certain signs, during the reign of the Emperor Tiberius, that the great demon **Pan** and many other demons had clearly wailed and then died. Proclus the Platonist also proves that this is possible. We, however, know that Christ at that very time entered **Limbo** <note>original: "limbum"; the place where the souls of the righteous were said to wait before the Resurrection.</note> and rose again. Furthermore, Plutarch writes that the oracles in his time, with one or two exceptions, were already extinguished throughout the whole world. Hear with what a voice Porphyry complains about this: "Afterwards," he says, "since Jesus is worshipped, we can obtain no benefit from the gods." If they are gods, O Porphyry, why do they not suppress the power of Jesus with their own strength? But let us hear that great man Tertullian <note>An early Christian author and apologist from North Africa.</note> pleading before the Roman judges: "Let someone be brought here before your tribunals who is known to be driven by a demon. If that spirit is commanded to speak by any Christian, he will as truly confess himself to be a demon as he elsewhere falsely claimed to be a God. Likewise, let someone be produced of those who are thought to be possessed by a god; unless all such spirits confess themselves to be demons—not daring to lie to a Christian—then shed the blood of that most persistent Christian on the spot." What work is more manifest than this? What...

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

What proof could be more reliable than this? The simplicity of truth stands in the open, supported by its own power; there is no reason to suspect that these things are done by magic or some similar deception. Just as our entire mastery and power over those spirits <note>Ficino refers to demons or "fallen" spirits common in late antique thought.</note> is effective through the name of Christ, so too by our touch and our breath, they depart against their will from the bodies they inhabit—grieving and blushing in our presence. Believe them when they tell the truth about themselves, for you usually believe them when they lie. No one lies to their own disgrace, but rather to their honor; yet when Christians compel them to prove the truth, they openly deny that they are Gods, and they answer that there is no other God besides the one to whom we are devoted. Thus far, **Tertullian** <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was an early Christian author from Carthage who wrote extensively against paganism.</note> has spoken. **Lactantius** writes that in his own time, this was publicly proven every day: when the Gentiles were sacrificing to their demons, if anyone was present wearing the **sign of the cross** on their forehead, the consulted prophet could not give responses, nor could the demons depict future events in the entrails of the beasts. He says this was the primary reason why wicked kings persecuted Christians: they did not realize that by the sign of the cross, as if by something more powerful, the demons were put to flight as the weaker party. For good reason did **Socrates, Plato, and Varro**—though secretly because of the crowds—deride the superstitions of the Gentiles. Finally, Jesus destroyed those superstitions so that humanity would not be destroyed. Shortly before the light of Christ, the Greeks and Romans had begun to be corrupted more and more every day by the contagious impiety of **Aristippus and Epicurus** <note>Ficino views Epicureanism and the Cyrenaic school of Aristippus as "contagious" because they prioritized physical pleasure and denied divine providence.</note>. Innumerable martyrs, following the example of Christ, appeared everywhere among the nations—some unlettered, some highly learned. Because they utterly despised this present life for the sake of the one God and the life to come, they offered to humanity a most healthy medicine against that Aristippian and Epicurean poison. Furthermore, most unjust laws existed among many nations. The Persians knew their own mothers in unspeakable marriages. The Scythians sacrificed humans to demons. The Massagetae and Derbices sacrificed their neighbors and kin when they had grown old, and feasted on their flesh. The Bactrians threw the elderly to dogs bred specifically for this purpose. The Scythians buried alive those who had been loved by the deceased. The Tybareni used to cast their elders off cliffs. The Hyrcanians and Caspians were accustomed to throw people to predatory birds and dogs—the former while they were alive, the latter when dead. These and many other acts of the same kind were performed most religiously by the ancients. Then, by the preaching of Christ and his disciples alone, this most savage plague was driven out from everywhere; it even happened that fewer people are now seized by demons or kill themselves. Before the coming of Christ, the Jews for the most part only touched the surface of the **Mosaic Law** and their Prophets; Christ and his disciples, however, taught most perfectly how to penetrate the deep meanings of the divine mind with **lynx-like eyes** <note>original: "linceis... oculis"; a common Renaissance metaphor for exceptionally sharp or penetrating vision.</note>—indeed, with divine eyes. Even the Jew **Philo** testifies to this where, in his discussion on contemplation, he commends the sharpness and holiness of the Christians. The **Ancient Theology** <term>Prisca Theologia: the concept that a single, true theology exists which flows through all religions and was anciently given by God to prophets and philosophers.</term> of the Gentiles—in which **Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Aglaophemus, and Pythagoras** agreed—is entirely contained in the volumes of our **Plato**. Plato prophesied in his *Letters* that mysteries of this kind could finally be made manifest to humans after many centuries. This indeed happened, for in the times of Philo and Numenius, the mind of the ancient theologians first began to be understood in the Platonic writings—namely, immediately after the sermons and writings of the Apostles and their disciples. For the **Platonists** used the divine light of the Christians to interpret the divine Plato. This is why the great **Basil and Augustine** prove that the Platonists usurped the mysteries of **John the Evangelist** for themselves. I have certainly found that the principal mysteries of Numenius, Philo, Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus were received from John, Paul, Hierotheus, and Dionysius the Areopagite. For whatever magnificent things they said about the divine mind, the angels, and other things pertaining to Theology, they clearly usurped from them.

To this place, then—to him, I say—let us turn our eyes and our mind; he will teach us true wisdom, he who suddenly made unlearned little men wise. He will teach us upright justice, he who possessed nothing as his own, and gave what was his to God and m—

### THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...and he bestowed these virtues upon men. To God, he gave a fatherly and more than fatherly veneration; to men, a brotherly benevolence and care. In him was found the highest magnanimity and fortitude, for he desired nothing on earth as being "great," and feared nothing as being "harsh." He displayed a singular temperance, in whom the first impulses of the soul—which were themselves gentle and proper—scarcely appeared. He showed an incredible gentleness, through which we might utterly expel pride, that plague of human society. For who was gentler than he, who, while being the highest of all, made himself equal to the lowest? He showed a most ardent charity toward all people, for he lived not for himself alone, but for the entire human race; he even died willingly to redeem others from death. He is the most perfect rule for both contemplation and action, for he frequently devoted himself to the contemplation of divine matters and even more often to curing the errors and diseases of men.

We have many writers from the beginning who are witnesses to this life, all of whom are of the highest gravity. There are also countless followers, and finally, the entire world itself. Christ showed himself publicly to men for a short time. He did not remain longer than was proper for him, yet that time was sufficient for us; indeed, he performed so many miracles that John says if they were written down one by one, the world itself could not contain the books. <note>Ficino is paraphrasing the conclusion of the Gospel of John (21:25).</note> It is said that more than fourteen people wrote about his life, as it was so famous and miraculous to all. However, only those who wrote not with a human hand, but a divine one, are in use—or ever were. These are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

Matthew wrote in Hebrew; Jerome states that in his own time, this Hebrew text still existed in the **Library of Pamphilus**, <note>A famous library in Caesarea established by the martyr Pamphilus.</note> and that the opportunity to transcribe it was provided by the Nazarenes, who used this volume in Bersabe and throughout Syria. **Pantaenus** <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and missionary.</note> the Stoic, a martyr for Christ, when he had penetrated as far as inner India preaching the words of Christ, found there the seeds of the Apostle Bartholomew and the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, which he brought back with him. This is recorded by **Eusebius**. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> The other three, who are called the Evangelists, wrote in Greek. Among the ancient Christians, a "Fifth Gospel" was also read, which was called the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*; it was sufficiently approved by **Ignatius** and **Origen**, and was translated from the Hebrew language into Greek and Latin by **Jerome**.

This is according to Jerome. In this, the Christian truth shines most brightly: the assembly of Christians from the very beginning did not rashly admit just any writers, but only those who were holy, simple, sober, and most select. Those among the first who are held in high esteem either heard Christ himself or heard his disciples; although they wrote in different languages, times, and places, and did not see one another's writings (except perhaps John), they nevertheless confirmed the same truths everywhere, guided by that same truth. Occasionally, a certain dissonance or dissimilarity appears in very minor matters, but never a true contradiction. From this, it appears that each wrote the history separately from the others, yet none of them wrote separately from the truth.

Indeed, they preached miracles so numerous, so great, and so public—performed over so many years in Judea and Jerusalem where they were said to have occurred—that it is certain they preached the absolute truth. How could they have succeeded in establishing such a difficult matter among highly learned men by asserting falsehoods? Why would they be admired if they had said things that fought against each other? Unless those leaders had truly agreed with one another, the Christian kingdom would have been immediately scattered. The Evangelists and Apostles spoke much in common regarding the life and teaching of Christ, yet each brought something unique to the fore. For if everyone had said everything, the number of writers would seem superfluous; if each had said only unique and new things, the continuity and authority of the history would be destroyed. Certainly—and this is the marvel—the writings of Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Peter, Paul, James, and Jude are such that multiple witnesses are present for the principal matters. And if we listen to all the witnesses, we see that nothing has been repeated superfluously or improperly.

<margin>The Authority of the Sibyls. Chapter 24.</margin>

He affirms, moreover, that the Sibylline books were kept in a shrine among the Romans, where they were guarded by the "Fifteen Men" <note>The *Quindecimviri sacris faciundis*, a Roman priestly college.</note> and certain priests destined for this task. **Livy** adds that the Romans restored those six books of the Cumaean Sibyl (which had been burned by a certain old woman during the reign of Tarquin) using verses from other Sibyls, whom they sent for

### ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...they collected them very diligently through legates across the world. Thus, they held three books of the **Cumaean Sibyl**, and the rest belonged to others. These books were not distinguished by any title or name of which Sibyl they belonged to, except for the **Erythraean Sibyl**, who inserted her own name into her poem. The Romans consulted these poems regarding matters of the greatest importance, and no one was permitted to look upon them at will. However, I believe that **Maro** <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> was permitted to read them due to his friendship with **Augustus**, and **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who served as an advisor to Emperor Constantine; he often cited pagan sources to prove Christian truths.</note> due to his intimacy with **Constantine**, along with several other great and learned men, with the occasional permission of the emperor and the guardians. Therefore, Lactantius, as a familiar of Constantine, was able to take the testimonies of the Sibyls which he brings forward concerning Christ from their books, which were still extant at that time, as Rome had not yet been plundered by anyone. He wrote these things to Constantine, and thus he could not lie to either the learned emperor or the other scholars, of whom there was then an abundance in both Italy and Greece—some of whom were still severely slandering Christian writers over even the smallest details.

Did not **Virgil** read in those same Sibylline books what the Prophets and Evangelists say about Christ? And what is most significant, he recognized that the promises of the **Cumaean Sibyl** from the text—as I believe—matched those times in which Jesus was born. Although he twisted the Sibyl’s oracles to flatter **Pollio** <note>Gaius Asinius Pollio, a Roman consul and patron of Virgil.</note> by applying them to his recently born son named **Saloninus**, nothing in those prophecies could fit Saloninus (who died as a boy and accomplished nothing); however, everything he read there fits **Jesus**, who arose during those times.

But what did Virgil find there (evidently at such a time)? He found that in the final age of expectation, a great order would be born anew, descending from the eternal age—that is, the eternal Son depending on the eternal Father would eventually be born in time. Specifically, it would be a time when the **Virgin** would bloom and the **Golden Age** <note>original: "aurea aetas," a mythical period of primordial peace and prosperity.</note> would return—that is, the Son would sprout from the virgin, and an age of true and blessed doctrine would flourish, and a **"new progeny"** would be sent down from high heaven. These words explain the preceding ones, for we know the Sibyl predicted that a boy would be born of a Virgin, since she added that he is a "new progeny"—that is, born in a new way, not from the earth but from heaven, proceeding from God, in whom he had existed from eternity. Virgil’s own verses are as follows:

->*The final age of the Cumaean song has now arrived.*<-
->*A great order of ages is born anew.*<-
->*Now the Virgin also returns, and the reign of Saturn returns.*<-
->*Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.*<-
<note>original: "Ultima Cumæi uenit iam carminis ætas. / Magnus ab integro ſeclorum naſcitur ordo. / Iam redit & uirgo, redeunt Saturnia regna. / Iam noua progenies cœlo demittitur alto." These are the famous opening lines of Virgil's Fourth Eclogue.</note>

I truly believe that Virgil wove these poems together from such words of the Sibyl as I described just above. Virgil adds what I believe he read in the Sibyl: namely, that at his birth, the **iron age** would return to **golden**, and at that time, there would be the "glory of the age." All this seems to pertain to the cleansing of souls and the doctrine of Christ, and that the "traces of ancient fraud" would be rendered void. I think he had read in the Sibyl that **original sin** <term>originalis culpa: the Christian doctrine that humanity inherited a state of sin from the first humans</term>—which we conceived from the beginning through diabolical fraud—ought to be wiped away. However, since he by no means understood such mysteries, he composed the Sibyl’s words into a poem so that they would seem to present another meaning. Maro adds:

->*That this progeny will receive the life of a God, and see*<-
->*heroes mixed with gods, and he himself will be seen by them.*<-
->*And he will rule a pacified world with his father's virtues.*<-
<note>original: "Quod huiusmodi progenies Deum uitam accipiet, diuisq; uidebit / permixtos heroas, & ipſe uidebitur illis. / Pacatumq; reget patrijis uirtutibus orbem."</note>

It seems he read there that this offspring would be God born of God, governing and judging the entire world by the power of God the Father, and that nothing divine would be a secret to him, and that he would have all the angels as his ministers. The poet adds that at the same time the **serpent** would fall, along with the deceptive poisonous herb, and after many things he adds:

->*Yet a few traces of the ancient fraud will remain.*<-

In what sense Virgil wrote these things, I do not know; it is enough for us that he had from the Sibyl (whom he did not understand) the deeds of that offspring. The "serpent"—that is, the evil demon—would fall, and the poisonous and deceptive herb—that is, the power of demons which, before Christ, deceived men with false religion as if it were true, and had deceived them from the beginning in the guise of a serpent and by the occasion of a certain plant <note>A reference to the Tree of Knowledge in the Garden of Eden.</note>—would be tamed. The demon still tries souls after Christ, though he does not succeed as before; for this reason, it was said that "a few traces of fraud will remain." **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was generally an opponent of Christianity, making his "confession" here particularly valuable to Ficino’s argument.</note> also confesses that mortals were accustomed to being led into crimes and false religions by malignant demons, and he discusses this diligently in his book *On Abstinence*. Furthermore, Virgil addresses that progeny thus:

->*Enter upon your great honors, the time will soon be here,*<-
->*dear offspring of the gods, great increase of Jove!*<-
<note>original: "Aggredere ô magnos, aderit iam tempus honores. / Chara Deum Soboles, magnum Iouis incrementum." Note that "Jove" or Jupiter was the supreme Roman god, whom Ficino interprets here as a pagan name for the true God.</note>

I believe the poet learned from the Cumaean Sibyl that this most expected man would be the offspring of God, not of a man, and (than which nothing greater can be expressed) that he would be the **"great increase of God"**—that is, the eternal branch of God and his propagation into temporal and sensory things, through which the kingdom of God—that is, the number of the blessed—would grow. I know that such prudence was in...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the Roman poet Virgil was not merely writing poetry for his patron, but was actually recording genuine ancient prophecies about the coming of Christ found in the Sibylline books. # THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...piety, and modesty, such that I cannot imagine he would have used such a vast hyperbole <note>An intentional exaggeration for rhetorical effect.</note> toward the infant son of a private citizen, Pollio <note>Gaius Asinius Pollio was a Roman consul and friend of Virgil; Virgil’s famous Fourth Eclogue was dedicated to him.</note>, unless he had drawn such exceedingly great things from the Sibylline poems. Even a Sibyl would never have pronounced such wondrous things about a simple man who was not God. But hear what a proud hyperbole Virgil adds: *Look upon the world nodding with its interconnected weight, the lands and the expanses of the sea, and the deep heaven. Look how all things rejoice in the coming age.* <note>original: "Aspice connexo nutantem pondere mundum. Terrasque tractusque maris, cœlumque profundum. Aspice uenturo lętentur ut omnia seclo." These lines are from Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, which many Renaissance thinkers viewed as a pagan prophecy of the Nativity.</note> Perhaps the Sibyl had written: *That offspring of God is to be honored by the elements and the heavens.* Heaven honored Jesus with an eclipse; the air and fire with a long-haired radiance <note>Referring to the Star of Bethlehem, often interpreted as a comet.</note>; the water when it obeyed his words and supported his feet; the earth with an earthquake when he was fixed to the cross during the reign of Tiberius. Finally, the Poet exclaims, although he is ignorant of what he seeks: *O, may the final part of my life remain so long!* Perhaps the Sibyl—just as the Prophets also desired—hoped to see the day of Christ and only then depart from life. When Simeon had long desired this and achieved it in his old age, he exclaimed: *Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace, according to your word. For my eyes have seen your salvation* <note>The "Nunc Dimittis," a traditional Christian prayer found in the Gospel of Luke 2:29–30.</note> and what follows.

->*Testimonies of the Sibyls concerning Christ. Chapter XXV.*<-

As we said previously, the Roman Senate held the Sibylline books. In them, Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who acted as an advisor to Emperor Constantine.</note>, a familiar of the Emperor Constantine, read certain things clearly pertaining to Christ, the Son of God. First indeed is that of the **Erythraean Sibyl**, where she proclaims God as the nourisher and creator of all, who granted the sweet spirit to everyone and made him the prince of all gods. And again she says: *God gave him to be honored by faithful men.* And another Sibyl commanded that he must be recognized, saying: *Recognize him as your God, who is the Son of God.* This is what is read in David: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* <note>Psalm 110:1.</note> Also: *From the womb before the morning star I begot you.* <note>Psalm 110:3.</note> Also: *The Lord said to me, you are my son, today I have begotten you.* <note>Psalm 2:7.</note> And in Solomon: *God created me in the beginning of his ways, for his works before the ages; he established me in the beginning before he made the earth.* And a little later: *When he prepared the heavens, I was present with him,* and the rest. <note>Proverbs 8:22–27.</note> Furthermore, Lactantius collected from the Sibylline books such things concerning the works and death of Christ: *There will be a resurrection of the dead, the running of the lame will be swift, the deaf shall hear, the blind shall see, and the speechless shall speak.* Thus Isaiah also sang: *Be strengthened, you relaxed hands; be comforted, you weak knees; you who are of a fearful heart, do not fear, do not be afraid; our Lord will repay judgment, he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame man shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be plain; for water has broken out in the desert, and a stream in the thirsty land,* which signifies the time of Baptism.

But let us follow what Lactantius collected from the Sibyls: *With five loaves and two fish at the same time, he will satisfy five thousand men in the wilderness, and taking up the remains, he will fill twelve baskets for the hope of many. He will restrain the winds with a word; he will smooth the raging sea with feet of peace, and treading upon the waves with faith, he will walk across. He will dissolve the diseases of men, bring the dead to life, and drive away pains from many, doing all things by a word and curing every infirmity. Wretched, ignominious, and without form—so that he may offer hope to the wretched—he will come into the unjust hands of the unfaithful, and they will give God blows with incestuous hands, and spit poisonous spit in his pure mouth. He will truly give his holy back simply to the scourges, and receiving blows he will be silent, lest anyone recognize what the word is or where it comes from, so that he may speak to the dead; and he will be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar; they will show this table of hospitality. For you yourself, foolish nation, did not understand your God, playing with the minds of mortals, but you crowned him with thorns and mixed the horrid gall. Truly, the veil of the temple shall be torn, and at midday there shall be a night exceedingly dark for three hours, and he will end the fate of death. After taking up sleep for three days, he will then emerge from the dead and come to the light, shown as the first to the called ones by the principle of resurrection. When these things I have spoken are perfected, every law shall be dissolved in him.*

Also, it is said elsewhere by the Sibyl that the race of the Jews will be blessed and heavenly, clearly because of the excellence of Christ, by whose grace many Jews adhering to him turned out divine before others. The Erythraean Sibyl added: *They will call the Sibyl insane and a liar; but when all things have been done, then they will remember me, and no longer will anyone call me a liar, but a Prophet of the great God.* Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who also cited the Sibylline oracles in his work 'The City of God'.</note> brings forward many things of the Erythraean Sibyl...

ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.
<meta>Catchword: Of Apollo [original: Apollinis]</meta>

The Sibylline poems, translated into the Latin language, which the Greek saw in the presence of Flaccianus <note>A Roman official mentioned by St. Augustine; Flaccianus was a proconsul of Africa known for his learning.</note>, a man most famous for his learning, contained an acrostic—the first letters of each line formed a sequence—so that these words could be read in them: **Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.** <note>original: "Iesus Christus Dei filius Saluator." This refers to a famous acrostic mentioned by St. Augustine in *The City of God*, which allegedly appeared in the Erythraean Sibyl’s verses.</note> In those poems, the resurrection of bodies is described, the changing of the ages, the coming of God to judge, and the eternal rewards and punishments of men. Certain things of this kind are also read in the works of **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as a contemporary of Moses and a source of "Ancient Theology" (*Prisca Theologia*).</note>. **Plato**, too, when asked how long one should rest in his teachings, is recorded to have replied: until some more sacred person appears on earth who will open the fountain of all truth, whom everyone should then follow.

### On the Authority of the Prophets, the Nobility of the Old Testament, and the Excellence of the New. Chapter XXVI.

**Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 1st-century convert of St. Paul, though the writings attributed to him (the Pseudo-Dionysian Corpus) are now dated to the 5th century.</note> writes to the wise Polycarp that the Persians, Babylonians, and Egyptians noted in their Annals certain miracles as if they were divine, and that they worshiped and still worship those wonders which the Hebrews narrate were performed by God through his own people regarding the stopping and reversing of the celestial bodies. **Plato** did not remain silent about the regression of the Sun and the flood of water or the destruction by fire. Many witnesses from among the Gentiles are cited for these things by **Josephus**, **Aristobulus**, **Tertullian**, and **Eusebius**—namely, **Berosus the Chaldean**, **Manetho the Egyptian**, **Hiram** <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> **of Tyre**, King of the Phoenicians, **Mendesius**, **Ptolemy**, **Menander**, **Ephesius**, **Demetrius Phalereus**, **King Juba**, **Thallus**, **Apion**, **Nicolaus**, **Molon of Damascus**, **Hesiod**, **Hecataeus**, **Hellanicus**, **Acusilaus**, **Ephorus**, **Theophilus**, **Manasses**, **Aristophanes**, **Hermogenes**, **Euhemerus**, **Conon**, **Zophyrus**, **Abydenus**, **Hestiaeus**, the **Sibyl**, **Eupolemus**, **Alexander**, **Artapanus**, **Melo**, **Theodorus**, **Philo the Gentile**, **Aristeas**, **Ezekiel**, **Timochares**, **Polyhistor**, **Numenius**, **Choerilus**, **Sanchuniathon the African**, **Alpheus**, and **Megasthenes**.

These individuals confirmed almost every single point—and certainly all of them together confirmed everything—pertaining to the antiquity that precedes all others, the wondrous deeds, the supreme doctrine of the Hebrews, and the miracles of the Bible. From these it appears, as **Clement of Alexandria**, **Atticus the Platonist**, **Eusebius**, and **Aristobulus** prove, that the Gentiles clearly usurped whatever excellent dogmas and mysteries they possessed from the Jews. However, those things which are contained as simple history among the Jews were translated by the Gentiles into poetic fables, as the fall of **Phaethon** and the story of **Deucalion** <note>Phaethon's scorched earth and Deucalion's flood were seen by Renaissance thinkers as pagan memories of the biblical stories of Joshua's sun standing still and Noah's Ark.</note> declare, as well as many other such tales. Plato imitated the Jews to such an extent that **Numenius the Pythagorean** said: "What is Plato but Moses speaking in the <term>Attic language</term> <note>The dialect of ancient Athens; the phrase implies Plato is a Greek-speaking version of the Jewish lawgiver.</note>?" He adds in his book *On the Good* that **Pythagoras** also followed Jewish dogmas.

Plato says in the *Epinomis* that the cause of the sciences was a certain "barbarian" <note>In Greek context, "barbarian" meant anyone non-Greek; here, Ficino interprets it as referring to the Hebrews.</note> who first discovered these things, and he later adds that everything flowed from the Egyptians and Syrians. Indeed, a certain part of Judea, which **Pliny** calls Galilee, was always held by writers to be in Syria, and among the ancients it was also called part of Phoenicia, as **Eusebius** proves. **Proclus the Platonist** also venerates Syrian and Phoenician Theology before all others. **Pliny** says that the Phoenicians were the inventors of letters and of <term>Astrology</term> <note>In this period, astrology and astronomy were often used interchangeably as the study of the stars.</note>; those who praise the Chaldeans seem to extol the Jews, who were also named Chaldeans (as **Lactantius** proves). For this reason, I believe, **Orpheus** said that God was known only to a certain "Chaldean," meaning either **Enoch**, **Abraham**, or **Moses**.

The Platonists wish for **Zoroaster** to be meant by Orpheus; but Zoroaster, as **Didymus** claims in his commentaries on Genesis, was the son of **Ham**, the son of **Noah**, and was called **Canaan** by the Hebrews, who (as Eusebius proves) was still alive in the time of Abraham. We must remember that the gifts and praises of the Jews could easily pass to the Egyptians, for they were always neighbors and intermingled. **Alexander** and **Eupolemus** write that **Abraham** was the most outstanding of all in holiness and wisdom; they say he taught astrology first to the Chaldeans, then to the Phoenicians, and finally to the Egyptian priests, and that he used to say he received it from the successors of **Enoch**, who was its discoverer and was named **Atlas**. **Julius Firmicus** the astronomer calls Abraham "divine" on account of his wonderful wisdom. **Artapanus** shows that whatever things are said of **Mercury Trismegistus** were present in and performed by **Moses**, and that he was called Mercury himself, and moreover, was **Musaeus** <note>A legendary polymath and poet of ancient Greece.</note>. No one will doubt that the doctrine of the Gentiles grew from Moses if they hear **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who was actually a critic of Christianity, but here cited as a historical witness.</note> saying, by the testimony of the ancient **Sanchuniathon**, that Moses lived fifteen hundred years before the first of the Greek philosophers. The same Porphyry, in his book *On Oracles*, brings forward...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the superiority and antiquity of Jewish and Christian wisdom over pagan philosophy. Ficino moves from discussing the Sibyls and Hermes Trismegistus to the historical authority of the Hebrew tradition and the relationship between the Old and New Testaments.</meta>

THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

The oracle of Apollo <note>original: "Apollinis oraculum"</note>, which contains the statement that the illustrious and very holy Hebrew nation knew before others, received, and handed down true wisdom, the best worship of God, and the blessed life. Furthermore, in the book *On Abstinence*, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher; though often a critic of Christianity, Ficino cites him here to validate the holiness of the Jewish Essenes.</note> honors certain religious men and philosophers of the Jews whom they call Essenes <note>An ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period.</note> with such great praise that he shows them to be before all others—even Prophets, holy men, and divine beings. For the same point, he also uses the testimony of the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> Theophrastus, who says that they assiduously devote themselves to fasting and prayer, and that the ancient Jews were philosophers by nature. 

Not without reason. For the Sibylline books called the race of Jews "heavenly and blessed." Clearchus the Peripatetic writes that Aristotle was a Jew. He also writes that the philosophers among the Indians, known as the Calani, were Jews. Moreover, Megasthenes <note>A Greek ethnographer and explorer of the 4th century BCE.</note> asserts that the Brahmans, the philosophers of India, descended from the Jews. Ambrose, if I remember correctly, shows that Pythagoras was born of a Jewish father. I pass over the fact that Strabo, Justin, Pliny, and Cornelius Tacitus could not remain silent about the antiquity and wisdom of the Jews. 

Therefore, the antiquity of the Jews is not to be undervalued. We may infer that their writings were not despised by the Gentiles—indeed, they were even adopted—from the fact that Aristobulus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who argued that Greek philosophers borrowed from Moses.</note> proves the volumes of Moses were translated into the Greek language before Alexander and before the Persian Empire, and the entire Bible during the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus. Demetrius of Phalerum, the Peripatetic, led the King [Ptolemy] to this translation (as Aristeas, who was present, testifies); in a letter to the King himself, he says he had read certain volumes of the Jews translated long ago, which were of such great wonder that the Jewish legal sanction alone seems entirely whole and divine. Hecataeus of Abdera confirms the same regarding that law. 

Why did Ptolemy purchase that translation with almost innumerable gifts? Why did he treat the translators and the High Priest with such great honor after they had translated it? Whoever doubts this should read Aristeas and Josephus. Nothing more need be said. Tell me, please, what kind of place do you think Jerusalem was, where the High Priest chose seventy-two men from among the rest—the most outstanding, and highly skilled in both the Hebrew and Greek languages. <note>This refers to the legendary origin of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> Pliny rightly calls Jerusalem the most famous city of all the cities of the East; Aristeas and the philosopher Hecataeus have narrated most copiously that it was also the most vast and best fortified. Josephus and Eusebius show that it was so spacious that, during the siege by the Romans, over eleven hundred thousand <note>1.1 million.</note> Jews perished in that city; furthermore, more than ninety thousand were sold into slavery. 

But it was not our purpose to argue about the earthly qualities of that city, but about its heavenly gifts. If anyone wishes to know these, let them not only consider what we have narrated above, but even more, let them read and reread their writings. They will finally discover how weighty is the authority of the Prophets, whose laws and oracles the Jews, Christians, and Muslims—and to put it briefly, all nations sustained by the earth—have believed and obeyed for so many centuries. 

Indeed, Christian doctrine surpasses the Mosaic just as the "purgatorial virtue" surpasses "civil virtue." <note>term: Purgatorial vs. Civil Virtue. In Neoplatonism, civil virtues govern social conduct, while purgatorial virtues (purgatoriae virtutes) purify the soul for divine contemplation.</note> In the Gospels, Christ runs through all the thorns of vices; those which Moses had lopped off in that more uncultivated age (for he taught to keep such an order), Christ himself utterly roots out. Where Moses condemned the act, Christ denounces even the one who thinks of adultery or murder as already an adulterer and murderer. Nor does he further permit one tooth to be extracted for one tooth for the sake of revenge, but he commands that the other cheek be meekly offered to the one who strikes, and that good be repaid for evil. "If your eye or your right hand troubles you," he says, "pluck it out and cut it off"; that is, utterly extinguish the very first incitement to lust or revenge. There are many other things of this same kind, from which it appears that the New Testament is the absolute end <note>The "end" here means the "fulfillment" or "goal."</note> of the Old Testament, and is as much more excellent than the Old as the goal exceeds those things which lead to the goal.

-> Testimonies of the Prophets concerning Christ. Chapter XXVI. <-

"Search the scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; those are the ones which bear witness of me." <note>John 5:39</note> With this voice in the Gospel of John, our Jesus cries out against the Jews with the greatest confidence, as one who knows that the testimonies of his divinity will not be lacking to those who seek them in abundance. But he warns that they should not so much touch the rinds <note>original: "cortices" (the outer bark or skin).</note> of the divine oracles as they should strive to search the marrow <note>original: "medullas" (the core or essence).</note>. For God had foretold through the Prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world." <note>Psalm 78:2</note> The Jews have a twofold volume of sacred writings from the ancients: one in Hebrew...

[Written] in Hebrew letters and the Hebrew language; the other in the Chaldean language <note>Referring to the Targums, ancient Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible used in Jewish liturgy.</note> but written in Hebrew letters. As Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible.</note> and Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and author of the *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note> testify, no one has ever dared to contradict the Chaldean text. Therefore, both have equal authority among them, and the meaning is the same; but what is briefer or more obscure in one is often more extensive and clearer in the other. The same logic applies to the sacred scriptures among us, which we have translated into the Greek language by the seventy-two Jews <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, and again from Hebrew and Greek into Latin by Jerome. But let us now hear the testimonies of the Prophets.

Jeremiah. "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth," and a little further: "And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our Righteous One" <note>original: "Dominus iustus noster"</note>. Where the Hebrew says "David," the Chaldean has "Messiah." When he says "behold, the days are coming," he shows that the Messiah would come without long delay after Jeremiah; this would indeed be false if he were still yet to come. Furthermore, he reveals that the Messiah would be God; for where the translation says "Lord" <note>original: "Dominus"</note>, the Hebrews have that <term>Tetragrammaton (YHWH): The four-letter, unpronounceable name of God, considered the most sacred in the Hebrew tradition.</term> name, that is, of four letters, which is so to be venerated before other divine names that it applies to no creature. Moses the Egyptian discusses this extensively in his book *On Direction* <note>Referring to Maimonides’ *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>. Hence Abba the Jew in the book of Lamentations, where the question is asked what the name of the Messiah is, answers: "Adonai is his name," placing there that Tetragrammaton name and citing that passage of Jeremiah: "This is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our Righteous One." Moreover, one should not say "he shall call," but "they shall call"; for so the Chaldean translation and the seventy translators taught.

Isaiah. "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government is placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the world to come, Prince of Peace." This is the Hebrew. Their Chaldean text has: "An infant is given to us, and he shall receive the law upon himself to keep it, and his name shall be called from of old: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, remaining into the ages of ages, the Messiah, in whose days peace shall be multiplied." It shows that the Messiah would be God, and his kingdom spiritual and of another world. He was to come while Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar, under whose reign Christ was born.</note> was ruling, under whom there was universal and long-lasting peace, the widest and most fortunate monarchy of the world, and a census <note>original: "descriptio"</note> of the whole globe. That these things cannot be adapted to King Hezekiah is obvious, because it adds: "his empire shall be multiplied and of his peace there shall be no end." Also: "he shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to confirm it and strengthen it forever." These things can only pertain to the divine peace of souls and a spiritual empire. Hence, Moses the Egyptian, in his *Letter to the Africans*, explains those six names—namely, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the world to come, Prince of Peace—as referring to the child born as the Messiah. But why does the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint.</note> put only "Angel of Great Counsel" in place of those six words? Because when they were interpreting the divine utterances for Ptolemy the Gentile, they often either omitted or changed things pertaining to the divinity of Christ, lest he perhaps think that the Jews considered the Messiah to be God insofar as he was a man, and a God different from the High God, making two Gods. But the Hebrew text, the Chaldean, and the translation from the Hebrew declare the divinity of Christ. Indeed, certain Jews are to be laughed at who want to say "he shall call" <note>original: "uocabit"</note> rather than "he shall be called" <note>original: "uocabitur"</note> in the words of Isaiah above. For the Seventy translators rendered it "he shall be called," and the Chaldean translation shows it must be said as "he shall be called."

Micah. "And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are by no means the least among the thousands of Judah; for from you shall go forth he who is to be the ruler of Israel, and his going forth is as from the beginning, from the days of eternity." After "shall go forth," the Chaldean text adds "the Messiah," showing that the Messiah existed from eternity as God, and was to go forth from Bethlehem as a man. Therefore, whoever explains this as referring to King Hezekiah—a mere man and temporal—is clearly raving. Moreover, Rabbi Solomon applies it to the King Messiah.

Zechariah. "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your king comes to you, holy (otherwise: righteous) and a savior, himself poor, riding upon a donkey and its foal. And I will destroy the chariot and Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem; the bow of war shall be dissipated, and he shall speak peace to the nations, and his powers shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth." Rabbi Solomon the Jew, explaining this passage, says these words can only be understood concerning the King Messiah, with whom the other Jews agree. From this, it is clear that the Messiah was to come to Jerusalem as a poor man and upon a donkey, and that his kingdom would not be earthly, and [that] salvation...

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
## ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

He speaks of him saving souls rather than bodies, and through holiness alone—indeed, even through death. For Zechariah adds: "As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, you have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit," <note>Zechariah 9:11</note> that is, the ancients from Limbo <note>In medieval theology, the "Limbo of the Fathers" was the place where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ were held until his resurrection.</note>. Such things are read concerning the throne of Jesus, whom Zechariah hints will be both man and God when he said that he would be poor, riding upon a peaceful donkey, using no weapons but only the doctrine of peace; and yet he calls him "Savior" and "King," reigning everywhere. This, however, is the office of God.

Jacob says in Genesis: "The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations." <note>Genesis 49:10</note> Where the Hebrew text has "leader" <note>original: "dux"</note>, the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary used in synagogues.</note> has "scribe" from the children of his children. Where the Hebrew says "he who," the Chaldean has "Messiah." Where it says "and he shall be," etc., the Hebrew truth has: "To him the nations shall be gathered." It is certain that Jacob speaks of the Messiah's coming, for the Chaldean volume declares it so; following this, Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270), a prominent medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note>, and Chalchadias, and Chanihis the Jews confess that the words there concern the Messiah. That Jesus was the Messiah is certain, because he called the Gentiles and saved them just as he did the Jews, and by them he is more greatly worshipped; and also because around his time the scepter was taken away from the Jews. And since one thousand four hundred and seventy-four years <note>This identifies the date of Ficino's writing as approximately 1474 AD.</note> have already passed from then until us, the Jewish power has not yet been restored. Nor is it permitted to imagine, as the Jewish old wives do, that a kingdom still remains for them in Babylonia or beyond the Caspian Mountains. For all history cries out against this; indeed, even Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), the most famous Jewish philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> and other Hebrew doctors affirm that it was never permitted, nor could it ever be permitted, for any Jew outside the land of promise to judge in criminal cases. He, therefore, who attributes a kingdom to the Jews exiled outside of Judea, is clearly raving. Let us listen.

The prophecy of Hosea: "For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an altar." <note>Hosea 3:4</note> We see that such is the present condition of the Jews, and all interpreters of the Prophets, both Jews and Christians, confirm that the Prophet spoke of these times. That the Jews today lack a legitimate sacrifice is evident, because their law approves only those Jewish sacrifices which are performed in the land of promise. Some Jews object that the scepter was taken from Judah a hundred years before Jesus—specifically when the power over affairs was transferred to the Maccabean priests, who were not from the tribe of Judah but of Levi, as Josephus <note>The Romano-Jewish historian Titus Flavius Josephus.</note> relates; Jesus, however, was born in the time of Herod, who is said to have succeeded the Maccabees. To this there is a triple response. First, since the Maccabees were of the tribe of Judah at least according to the maternal line, during their reign the power of Judah was not entirely removed. Second, the Prophet Jacob did not mean this or that tribe, but the entire Jewish people. Third, as all the Hebrew doctors agree, there was always among them a certain council of seventy wise men, to whose judgment the sentences of more serious matters belonged. They called this council the *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Camedrim"</note>; it was like a senate, adhering to a living prince, and in the case of a deceased prince, acting in the prince's stead. This had been established by Moses himself, and in the Babylonian captivity it sat with the Jewish leaders in Babylon, and after the return it sat with those leaders in the fatherland. The authority of this council lasted until King Herod, who was born of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother (as Josephus says) and received the kingdom of the Jews from the Romans, under whom Jesus was born. For Herod killed all the men of that college and abolished that council, which the Jews also confirm in the Jerusalem book *Sanhedrin* <note>The Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin.</note> and in the book *Avodah Zarah* <note>original: "Abodazara"; a Talmudic tractate regarding "Foreign Worship" or idolatry.</note>. Then, therefore, not only was the scepter taken from Judah, but also the scribe from his sons, which the Chaldean text had predicted. Therefore, when Herod, who was a foreigner, assumed the kingdom and moreover killed as many as he could find of the royal line of David, then properly the Kingdom of the Jews was utterly removed; finally, when he destroyed the council, then the scribe is considered to have been taken from the sons of Judah. Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the 4th-century church historian.</note> writes that the Emperors Vespasian and Domitian ordered everyone of the lineage of David to be killed, so that no remnant of the Jewish kingdom would remain. For they too feared the coming of Christ, just as Herod did from the beginning. Eusebius took this from Hegesippus <note>An early Christian chronicler whose works are mostly lost except for fragments in Eusebius.</note>.

Haggai: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet one little while, and I will move the heaven, and the earth, the sea, and the dry land, and the desired of all nations shall come. The glory of this last house shall be greater than that of the first." <note>Haggai 2:6-9</note> "Yet one little while" signifies to us today

He uses historical sources like Josephus and Jewish commentaries to show that the "scepter of Judah" was only truly removed with Herod's foreign usurpation.</summary>

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION
C
<meta>catchword: ptem;</meta>

That the Messiah came long ago, I shall prove by "the shaking of the heavens"—namely, through the eclipse during the Passion <note>The darkness reported during the crucifixion of Jesus</note>, and also through that star seen by the Magi—and "the shaking of the earth," specifically through the earthquake at the Passion. Furthermore, there was that earthquake which Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian</note> writes occurred in Judea during the reign of Herod, which was so terrible that neighboring nations believed all the towns of Judea had collapsed. Were not movements made throughout the whole world then, when at the birth of Jesus, the entire globe was registered by the edict of Caesar Augustus? For everyone from all sides was compelled to return to their own country so that each might be properly enrolled. At that time, Josephus asserts that Judea was troubled by many slaughters because of the faction of Judas the Galilean <note>A Jewish leader who led a resistance against the Roman census in 6 AD</note> against the Romans. He "shook the sea," as it were, when Christ commanded the sea and the winds. When the prophet adds that the second temple would be more blessed than the first <note>Haggai 2:9</note>, he means this because it would receive the Messiah; for in all other respects, it was more lowly and wretched. Every one of these details fits Jesus the Nazarene alone, especially since he came as the "desired of the nations" <note>original: "desideratus Gentibus"</note>; for he saved the Gentiles more than the Jews, since he was more honored by them. Let the Jews not wait for the construction of a third temple under a new Messiah, for Haggai called the second temple the "last."

Malachi says: "Behold, I send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before my face, and suddenly the Lord whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, even the messenger of the covenant whom you desire; behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts, and who shall endure the day of his coming?" <note>Malachi 3:1–2</note> "Behold I send," and again, "Behold he comes." This declares not so great a delay as the Jews imagine, but a swift arrival of the Messiah; therefore, he is not yet to come in the future. The "messenger" who prepared the way signifies John the Baptist, the herald of Christ. "Before my face" shows that John the Baptist would preach before Christ, and that Christ himself is God. For God himself, who is speaking, calls the face of Christ his own face. The "messenger of the covenant" <note>term: "Angelus testamenti"</note> points to the Messiah as the bringer of the New Testament. "And who shall endure" designates the difficulty in recognizing the Messiah and the stubbornness of many. Add to this the ruin of the Jews and the fall of idolatry.

Isaiah says: "The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways plain, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God." <note>Isaiah 40:3–5</note> These things are nearly identical to the previous points and are manifest.

Daniel says: "Seventy weeks are shortened" (otherwise translated as "decreed") "upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be finished, and sin may come to an end, and iniquity be blotted out, and everlasting righteousness be brought in, and vision and prophecy be fulfilled, and the Saint of Saints be anointed." <note>Daniel 9:24</note> Moses of Tyre, Hyoces, David, Chalchadias, and Abraham—all Jewish scholars—have explained Daniel in such a way that four hundred and ninety years <note>term: "hebdomadæ" (weeks). In biblical prophecy, a "week" often represents seven years; 70 weeks equals 490 years.</note> passed from the destruction of the first temple to the destruction of the second temple, and that the Messiah would be born around the end of this time. Nicholas of Lyra <note>c. 1270–1349, a highly influential Franciscan Bible commentator</note> also computes the weeks in such a way that Christ suffered within them. He proves that such was Daniel's intention. Barachias the Jew, in his book *On the Order of the World* <note>original: "de ordine mundi," referring to the *Seder Olam*</note>, explains that passage of Isaiah: "My salvation is near to come and my righteousness to be revealed." There, he says that the phrase "my righteousness" signifies that Messiah of whom Daniel spoke, that "everlasting righteousness might be brought in." Similarly, Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides (1194–1270)</note>, explaining the words spoken to Daniel by the angel, says: "Everlasting righteousness and the sanctuary of sanctuaries" (or "the Saint of Saints") "is none other than the Messiah himself, the sanctified one from the sons of David"—this is his view, and rightly so. For David sang: "In his days shall righteousness spring up." And Jeremiah: "This is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our Just One." <note>Jeremiah 23:6</note> Truly, Jesus blotted out the ruin of original transgression and granted the grace and righteousness of the Gospel. But lest anyone be allowed to imagine that Daniel’s weeks are cycles of months, or hundreds, or thousands, or ages, it must be remembered that in a certain book of the Jews regarding the order of the world, all their writers clearly agree on this: that these are weeks of years only. Solomon and Moses of Gerona testify to the same in their commentaries on Daniel, confessing that the Jewish sacrifice was taken away in the last of those weeks, during the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans; and Solomon himself asserts that Daniel’s weeks end at the destruction of the second temple. It is certainly predicted by Daniel that this would occur either at the end of those weeks, or at least after sixty-two weeks. For so it is foretold by Daniel: "And after seven weeks..."

<summary>Ficino uses prophecies from Haggai, Malachi, Isaiah, and Daniel to argue that the Messiah’s arrival was tied to the era of the Second Temple and the Roman census. He cites both Christian and Jewish scholars to confirm that Daniel's "seventy weeks" refer to a specific 490-year period ending with Christ and the Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s chronological and prophetic proof for the arrival of Christ. ### THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...[seven,] and sixty-two <note>Ficino is continuing the quotation of Daniel 9:25–26, referring to "weeks" of years</note> weeks, Christ <note>original: "Christus"</note> shall be slain (another word for "chrism," that is, the anointing <note>original: "unctio"</note> of priests) and the judgment <note>Often translated in Bibles as "he shall have nothing"</note> shall not be in him; the people, with a leader who is to come, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be devastation. Certainly, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> testifies, after Herod, the priests were by no means appointed by succession from the priestly lineage or for a lifelong term according to the Law of Moses. Instead, any common persons, even the most ignoble, would buy the priesthood every year from the prince or the Romans. Some people, because they cannot otherwise avoid the true arguments of the Christians regarding this passage, say that Daniel erred here, though he spoke well everywhere else. But such little men should be left to themselves, as they contradict themselves and err both here and elsewhere. For there are those among them who dare to change the dates of Jesus, which are well known to all; these are refuted by Josephus where he writes of the times of Jesus, and where he says: In the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate undertook the governorship of Judea, and remained there for ten continuous years. Indeed, Cornelius Tacitus, a Gentile <note>original: "Gentilis," meaning a non-Christian/pagan Roman</note>, says that Christ was killed by Pontius Pilate, the procurator of Judea, during the reign of Tiberius.

However, to put the whole matter in order, there have been many opinions among the Talmudists <note>original: "Talmuticos," meaning the authoritative Jewish commentators on the law</note> regarding the coming of the Messiah. **The first** is that of Hyocis <note>Likely Rabbi Jose ben Halafta</note>, who in the book *Cederlophan* <note>original: "Cederlophan," a corruption of *Seder Olam*, or "Order of the World"</note>, explained the limit of the seventy weeks just as we said above. **The second** is that of Habaquibe <note>Rabbi Akiva</note>, who, following the computation of Daniel, thought the Messiah would come at the destruction of the Second Temple; he therefore followed a certain foolish and warlike man named Ventozaram <note>Simon bar Kokhba, or Bar Koziba</note>, who then claimed to be the Messiah. A massive crowd of Jews followed him forty-eight years after the destruction of Jerusalem, as they themselves say. Thus, almost all gathered in the town of Bitera <note>Bethar</note> and rebelled against the Romans, since they trusted greatly in the fortune and arms of that leader. But the Emperor Hadrian, having besieged the city, killed Ventozaram along with all his followers. The Jews have all this recorded in the book *Demay* <note>The Talmudic tractate *Demai*</note>.

**The third opinion** the Jews take from the book of ordinary judges <note>Likely referring to the *Avodah Zarah* or the *Tanna Devei Eliyahu*</note>, which carries no small authority among them; there it is treated that the age of the world is six thousand years: two thousand are attributed to vanity or emptiness, two thousand to the Law, and two thousand to the Messiah. They say these things were spoken by a certain disciple of Elijah, the son of the widow of Sarepta, whom Elijah had raised from the dead. But according to the Hebrew computation, two thousand years flowed from Adam to Abraham, which were the years of "vanity." From him to Jesus the Nazarene were also two thousand years, which were the years of the "Law." Therefore, the years that follow Jesus seem to have begun from the Messiah according to the Jewish computation, especially since it is asserted in that book that four thousand years intervene from the beginning of the world to the Messiah. According to the computation of all the Hebrews, the world today is in its five thousandth, two hundredth, thirty-fourth year <note>AM 5234, which corresponds to the late 15th century</note>; therefore, the Messiah came long ago.

**The fourth opinion** was that of a certain great man whom they called "The Rabbi" <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, who says in the book *Camedrim* <note>The Talmudic tractate *Sanhedrin*</note>: All the deadlines assigned for the coming of the Messiah have already passed, and redemption consists in repentance alone. Although he perhaps was not speaking of Christian repentance, he could not entirely suppress the truth. At the same time, someone else, relying on this man's authority because he believed all the deadlines had passed, cried out: "Woe to the souls of those who calculate the dates of the Messiah!"

**The fifth** was that of Chahadia <note>Saadia Gaon</note>, who in the book *On Beliefs* <note>original: "de credendis," likely *Emunot ve-Deot*</note>, concluded by diligent numbering a certain deadline for the Messiah, which passed more than three hundred and forty years ago.

**The sixth** was that of Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note>, a man of the highest authority among the Jews; although in his commentary on Deuteronomy he forbids inquiring into the times of the Messiah, he nevertheless writes in a certain *Letter to the African Jews* that he holds from the most certain tradition of the ancients that the Messiah would be born in the four thousandth, four hundredth, and seventy-fourth year from the beginning of the world. By their own computation, this time preceded us by seven hundred and sixty years.

**The seventh** was that of Moses of Gerona <note>Nachmanides</note>, who in his *Commentaries on the Pentateuch* affirms the Messiah would arise in the year five thousand, one hundred and eighteen from the creation of the world. Levi ben Gerson <note>original: "Leui Benguerfon," also known as Gersonides</note> agreed with him in his *Commentaries on Daniel*, but this deadline preceded us by more than a hundred years.

In vain, therefore, do the Jews look further for a Messiah; indeed, whoever has expected one after Jesus has been deceived. For they did not consider what Daniel said elsewhere: In the days of those kings, the God of heaven shall raise up a kingdom <note>Daniel 2:44</note> that shall never be destroyed—namely, the heavenly kingdom of Christ. Tell me, I ask you, O Jews, why did those divine Magi, intending to see the Messiah, set out for Jerusalem immediately upon the birth of Jesus...

<summary>Ficino argues that the 70-weeks prophecy of Daniel and various Jewish chronological traditions (including the Talmud, Maimonides, and Nachmanides) all prove that the Messiah's time has already passed, concluding that Jesus is the only possible fulfillment.</summary>
