C 2
<meta>catchword: Not</meta>

...were convicted <note>This is the ending of a word from the previous page, likely "convicti sunt," referring to the persecution of early Christians mentioned by Tacitus</note>, and Herod, having inquired of the legal experts about the time and homeland of the Messiah <note>original: "Messiae"</note>, killed those infants and even his own son. This is testified by Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman philosopher and grammarian</note>, both a philosopher and a pagan <note>original: "Gentilis"</note>, for no other reason than that it seemed to the wise that those places and times belonged to the Messiah. From this, many skilled men venerated Jesus while he lived as if he were a divinity: Nathanael and Nicodemus, and others whom John the Evangelist calls "princes," who secretly worshipped him for fear of the Jews. It is also for this reason that many people around the time of Jesus boasted that they themselves were the Messiah, even though, as Gamaliel says, they vanished suddenly as frauds. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian</note> relates that under Felix, the procurator of Judea, many arose who deceived the people with their persuasions. Among others was a certain Egyptian false prophet <note>original: "Pseudoprophetam"</note>, who, having joined many to himself in a great endeavor, was crushed by the army of Felix. These accounts are consistent with the Acts of the Apostles, in which it is said to Paul by the Tribune: "Are you not that Egyptian who in these days stirred up a revolt and led four thousand men out into the desert?" Because the Tribune did not recognize Paul, he suspected he might be that Egyptian. There also arose, as Luke the Evangelist says and Josephus confirms, under Quirinius <note>original: "Cyrino"</note>, the governor of Syria, a certain Judas of Galilee at the time of the census enrollment; he deceived the people, but he himself perished shortly after, and all who followed him were dispersed. There was also a certain Theudas, about whom Luke and Josephus write very similar things, and likewise Simon Magus. Furthermore, there was Barchosibas <note>Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 CE)</note>, of whom Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous Jewish scholar Maimonides</note>, the most learned of the Jews, says in his book on Judges: "Achilayl <note>Ficino's transcription of Rabbi Akiva</note>, wise above the rest of the Jews, and all the legal experts of his time, asserted that Barchosibas, a most warlike leader, was the Messiah, until he was killed by Hadrian because of his crimes." Thus says Moses <note>Maimonides</note>. Eusebius also mentions this, following the history of Aristo of Pella, who says: from that time on, the entire Jewish nation was completely barred by the decrees of Hadrian even from the sight of Judea, and the region of Jerusalem was renamed Aelia, after Aelius Hadrian. It is also read in the Talmud <note>original: "Talmut"</note>—that is, the specific doctrine of the Jews—in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Camedrin"</note>, that Barchosibas himself reigned for thirty-five years and was accustomed to say he was the Messiah, and that the wise Achilayl <note>Rabbi Akiva</note> agreed with him. It is necessary, then, that Barchosibas existed very close to the times of Jesus.

Why, therefore, do you most stubborn men wait any longer, when long ago all the wise men of your race judged that the age of Jesus belonged to the Christ? Why did you rebel so many times against the Romans shortly after Jesus, to your own misery, unless because it then seemed to all of you that the promises of the Prophets were about to reach their fulfillment? Suetonius, a pagan <note>original: "Gentilis"</note>, testifies to this. He says: "An ancient and constant opinion had spread throughout the whole East, that it was in the fates that at that time, those coming out of Judea would master the highest power of things." He says the Jews rebelled and perished because of this: for truly, you were then suddenly expecting a certain armed Christ who would establish a perpetual world monarchy in Judea. How much wiser than you was Virgil, who thought the prophecies of the Sibyl <note>Ancient prophetesses of the Greco-Roman world</note> about the King of the world could agree with and be fulfilled in the times of Jesus—but we have discussed this elsewhere. Josephus writes that before the siege of Jerusalem, a certain oracle was found in the sacred scriptures which designated that at the same time, a man would come forth from their region who would possess the empire of the whole world. Some suspect this omen declared Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor, 69–79 CE</note>. But Vespasian did not rule over any others than those nations which seemed subject to the Roman Empire; hence these oracles should be referred to Christ, to whom the Father had said: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession" <note>Psalm 2:8</note>. And it was his voice that went out into all the earth through his Apostles at that same time.

**Isaiah:** "The Lord of hosts is he, sanctify him; he is your fear, he is your terror, and he shall be to you for a sanctification, and for a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel, and for a snare and a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and many among them shall stumble" <note>Isaiah 8:13–15</note>. Also: "I will place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and everyone who believes in him shall not be confounded" <note>A combination of Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16</note>. From these passages, it is clear that the expected Christ is God, and he himself made the souls of believers holy; and for his sake the two houses of Israel were destined to fall—namely, the royal house and the priestly house—and that not all, but many were going to be stubborn, while those who were going to believe could not be confounded. Nor is it permitted to interpret the "two houses" as "two kings," as some pervert the text. For it is the custom of Hebrew writers to name the entire series of priests as one "priestly house," and the entire series of kings as one "royal house," that is, the House of David.

**Jeremiah:** "And when you have multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, says the Lord..."

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s theological argument, moving from historical Roman witnesses to the testimony of Hebrew prophets and even Islamic texts to prove that the era of the Old Testament has ended and the Messiah has arrived. He focuses on the transition from "images" (rituals) to "substance" (Christ).</meta>

### THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO ###
<meta>catchword: -ries</meta>

"They shall say no more, 'The Ark of the Covenant of the Lord,' nor shall it enter into their hearts, nor shall they remember it, nor shall it be visited, nor shall it be made anymore" <note>Ficino is quoting Jeremiah 3:16</note>; this is because after the Messiah (which even Muhammad <note>original: "Mahumetes"</note> considers right), both the ranks and the ceremonies of the Old Testament ceased—and not without reason. For those were images of future sacraments; but when the substance is present, what need is there for an image?

Isaiah says: "Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a male child" <note>Isaiah 66:7</note>. The most ancient Hebrew commentaries explain this as meaning that before he was born who reduced the Jews to their final servitude—that is, Titus <note>The Roman Emperor who destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem in 70 AD</note>—their redeemer had already been born. Hence the Chaldean text <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> has: "Distress shall not yet come to him, and trembling with the pains of labor shall not yet come to him; the Messiah shall be revealed." In this same Chaldean text, the Hebrew Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Targum on the Prophets</note> says: "Before distress came to her, she was saved; and before the pains of labor came to her, the Messiah was revealed." Similarly, the wise Samuel affirms the same in that place. From all these things, it appears that the Messiah was born before the destruction of Jerusalem. Indeed, many of the Hebrews concede that he was born on the very day the city was destroyed. Then, according to their custom, they flee to absurdities, saying that he is hidden until God commands that he show himself openly to everyone. Others place him on Mount Sinai with the angels; others sequester him beyond the Caspian Mountains; others depict him wandering here and there as a beggar, confounding one another in their own madness and discord.

Isaiah says: "The Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a Virgin <note>original: "Virgo"</note> shall conceive in her womb, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel" <note>Isaiah 7:14</note>. In Hebrew it is *Hahalma* <note>original: "Hahalma," referring to the Hebrew 'Almah' (הָעַלְמָה)</note>, which signifies a "hidden and preserved girl." *Emmanuel* <note>original: "Emanuel"</note> truly signifies "God with us," because he who was to be born of that girl was going to be not only man, but also God. From a girl, I say, who was always a Virgin; for a birth of this kind is promised as a certain miraculous sign, about which David says: "Truth has sprung out of the earth" <note>Psalm 85:11</note>. And Isaiah says elsewhere: "Let the heavens drop down from above, and let the clouds put on justice; let the earth be opened, and let a savior bud forth. For I, the Lord God, have created him" <note>Isaiah 45:8</note>. We see in the human species two extremes and two means: each of us is born from a man and a woman; Adam from neither; Eve from a man alone by divine power; Jesus from a woman alone by the divine spirit. The King of the Arabs, Muhammad, also greatly admires and venerates this mystery in his Dialogue; also in the Qur'an <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>, compelled by the truth, he says: "Jesus son of Mary, messenger of God, and his spirit, and the word of Mary was sent from heaven."

Daniel says: "I saw in a night vision, and behold, in the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man coming, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and those who assisted brought him forward, and there was given to him a kingdom, and honor, and empire, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him; and his power is an eternal power, which shall never pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be corrupted" <note>Daniel 7:13-14</note>. For all Jewish interpreters explain this parable as being about the King Messiah, although here the final coming of Christ is treated. And by these words Daniel signifies that God would come under the habit of a man, and that the kingdom of Christ would be not temporal, but eternal and spiritual. In this, Isaiah agrees, to whom God speaks thus regarding Christ: "I will give you hidden and invisible treasures."

Hosea says: "I will call those who were not my people, 'my people,' and her who was not beloved, 'beloved,' and her who had not obtained mercy, 'one who has obtained mercy,' and it shall be in the place where it was said, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called the children of the living God" <note>Hosea 2:23 and 1:10</note>. In these words the conversion of the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish nations</note> and the stubbornness of the Jews is predicted, such as it was regarding Jesus.

Isaiah says: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me. But all day long I have stretched out my hands to a people that does not believe, but speaks against me" <note>Isaiah 65:1-2</note>. In these is the same prophecy as a little above.

David says: "The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner; this is the Lord’s doing, that is, it is wonderful in our eyes; this is the day which the Lord has made, let us exult and be glad in it. O Lord, save me; o Lord, grant good prosperity; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" <note>Psalm 118:22-26</note>. Jesus, rejected as useless by the wicked, was made by divine power into the head of the corner, to which two walls are joined—that is, the Gentiles, and those who were converted from the Jews.

Malachi says: "I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I have no accepted sacrifice from your hands, for from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name shall be glorified among the Gentiles" <note>Malachi 1:10-11</note>. He highlights the "cornerstone" metaphor to explain how Christ unites both Gentiles and converted Jews into a new spiritual kingdom.</summary>

...of various ceremonies, and the approval of the faithful Gentiles at the coming of Christ.

Isaiah: "I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, so that you may be salvation even to the ends of the earth." <note>Isaiah 49:6</note>

Isaiah: "I come to gather all nations and tongues, and they shall come and see my glory; and I will set a sign among them, and I will send those who are saved from among them to the nations far off, who have not heard of my glory, and they shall declare my glory among the nations; and I will take from them Priests and Levites, says the Lord." <note>Isaiah 66:18-21</note> And elsewhere in the same prophet, God addresses the Messiah in this way: "It is too small a thing that you should be my servant to support the tribes of Jacob and to convert the dregs of Israel; I have given you as a light to the nations." <note>Isaiah 49:6; Ficino uses "feces" (dregs/remnant) for the Hebrew "netsire" (preserved ones)</note> Likewise: "The first shall say to Zion: Behold, here I am; and I will give a Gospel-bearer to Jerusalem. I looked, and there was no man, nor anyone among them who could take counsel, and when questioned, could see the word; behold, they are all unjust, and their works are vain." <note>Isaiah 41:27-29. Ficino translates "Euangelistam" for the "bringer of good tidings"</note> And in the following chapter he adds: "Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I have put my spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not cry out, nor show favoritism to any person; he shall not break the bruised reed, until he establishes judgment on the earth, and the islands shall look for his law." <note>Isaiah 42:1-4</note> Again elsewhere: "I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah one to possess my mountains; and my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall be hungry; my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be ashamed; and you shall leave your name as an oath to my chosen ones, and the Lord shall slay you, and call his servants by another name." <note>Isaiah 65:9-15</note> The same prophet in another place has God speaking thus: "Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me." <note>Isaiah 1:3</note> Again: "By hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and their ears are heavy of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them." <note>Isaiah 6:9-10</note> "I will send those who are saved from among them to the nations"—that is, the disciples of the Messiah, who escaped the hands of the Jews, to convert the Gentiles. "I will send and I will take"—that is, from the number of the Gentiles who will be converted, I will establish legitimate Priests. From this it is clear that even the Gentiles could be raised to the dignity of the Israelites. Whence **Rabbi Auanis** <note>Original: "Rauanais Iudæus," referring to the medieval commentator Abraham ibn Ezra</note> says in his commentaries on Exodus: "In the time of the Messiah, the converted Gentiles will be priests, ministering to the Lord." "It is too small a thing that you should be": through these words it is clear that the Messiah was to be sent for the salvation not only of the Hebrews, but also of the Gentiles, just as he says "the first to Zion." **Solomon the Jew** <note>Original: "Salomon Iudæus," referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki)</note>, the interpreter, in explaining this passage, says all these things are to be understood concerning the King Messiah and the final redemption. The **Chaldean translation of Jonathan** <note>The Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic paraphrase of the prophets</note> reveals the same. In these words of Isaiah, it appears that Christ was to preach first and properly among the Jews, and there establish the Gospels and Evangelists; but because they were to be wicked and persistent in their ways, he adds: "There was no man," and therefore "he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles"—that is, among the Gentiles, through his disciples, he will spread the Gospel doctrine. And to show that the Gospel judgments were to be promulgated in the highest humility, not in magnificence, nor in the tumult and sound of trumpets like the Law of Moses, he added: "He shall not cry out." In the remaining words, Isaiah reveals that the Messiah would descend from Jacob, and that his followers would for the most part be foreigners, who would be the "chosen ones" before God; and these would no longer be called Israelites, but by another name, namely, "Christians." He also reveals that the Jews would oppose the Messiah and pay the penalty, just as happened formerly in the time of Jesus; even the eternal stubbornness of the Jews, such as we experience today.

**Jeremiah**: "The turtledove and the swallow and the sparrow have known their time and observed the times of their coming; but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us'? In vain has the false pen [of the scribes] worked. The wise scribes are confounded, they are terrified and caught, because they have rejected the word of the Lord." <note>Jeremiah 8:7-9</note> Why do the Prophets often narrate things that are to come as if they were past? Because in the Divine Mind, to which all things are present, they see those things as present; and after they have seen them, they speak of them as past—that is, as things manifest and so fully completed. But let us return to Jeremiah. Here, in the words above, he declares that the Scribes would not perfectly know the time of Christ's coming, nor the time of the harvest; nor is that surprising, for the interpretation of the divine sense is most difficult for the unjust. To this agrees what is read in Deuteronomy: "May the Lord strike you with madness <note>Original: "amantia," likely a typo for "amentia"</note> and blindness and astonishment of mind, and may you grope at midday as the blind man is wont to grope." <note>Deuteronomy 28:28-29</note> Midday is the light of the works of Christ, in which very many Jews were blinded. Also Jeremiah elsewhere: "O Lord my God, to you the Gentiles shall come from the ends of the earth, and shall say, <unclear>that</unclear> our [ancestors have inherited] lies..." <note>Jeremiah 16:19</note>

<summary>Ficino uses various Old Testament prophecies, primarily from Isaiah and Jeremiah, to argue that the Messiah's mission was always intended to extend to the Gentiles and that the Jews' rejection of him was divinely foretold. He cites Jewish commentators like Rashi and Ibn Ezra to support his claim that the Messiah would bring a new law and a new name (Christian) to his followers.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO #
38
<meta>catchword: Christ</meta>

...for our fathers possessed idols, and there was no utility in them; if a man makes gods for himself, they will not be gods. <note>Jeremiah 16:19-20</note> In these words, it is predicted that idols would fall because of the Messiah, which was accomplished through Jesus. To this corresponds that passage of Isaiah where, speaking of Christ, he says: "He will teach us his ways," and after many words: "In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his images of gold, which he had made for himself to worship." <note>Isaiah 2:3, 2:20</note> Daniel signifies the same thing when, speaking of Christ, he says that a stone cut without hands shall crush the statue woven of iron and composed of gold and silver. <note>Daniel 2:34-35</note> The "stone cut without hands" is Jesus, afflicted by the power of the Priests; he, without hands—that is, without human violence—crushed the "statue," which represents idolatry, for it worshipped statues. This statue, I say, was fourfold, for it was scattered throughout the four principal kingdoms of the world: namely, the Chaldeans, Medes, Greeks, and Romans. Jeremiah says the same elsewhere: "The Lord shall be terrible over them, and shall consume all the gods of the earth; and every man from his own place shall adore him, even all the islands of the Gentiles." <note>Zephaniah 2:11; Ficino attributes this to Jeremiah, likely from memory or a shared manuscript tradition</note>

Isaiah says: "For the Lord has mingled for you a spirit of deep sleep, and will close your eyes; he will cover your prophets and your princes who see visions. And the vision of all will be to you like the words of a sealed book. When they deliver it to one who is learned, saying, 'Read this,' he will answer, 'I cannot, for it is sealed.' And the book shall be given to one who is unlearned, and it shall be said to him, 'Read,' and he will answer, 'I do not know letters.' And the Lord said: 'Because this people draws near with their mouth and glorifies me with their lips, but their heart is far from me, and they have feared me by the commandment and doctrines of men, therefore, behold, I will proceed to cause admiration in this people by a great and wonderful miracle: for wisdom shall perish from their wise men, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hidden.'" <note>Isaiah 29:10-14</note> Again elsewhere: "God has given them a spirit of compunction: eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, even until this day." <note>Romans 11:8, quoting Isaiah 29:10 and Deuteronomy 29:4</note> All these things predict that many Jews, both the learned and the unlearned, because of their crimes and impiety, would not recognize the prophecies of the expected Christ, nor Christ himself when present. Because of this error, they remain in misery today until the end of the age, which, as we said elsewhere, Hosea sang: "The children of Israel shall sit for many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an <term>Ephod</term> <note>A ceremonial vestment worn by the High Priest</note>, and without <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Small household idols or cult objects sometimes used for divination</note>." <note>Hosea 3:4</note> But because they are believed to eventually trust in our Christ near the end of the age, he adds: "And afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek the Lord their God, and David their king." <note>Hosea 3:5</note> The <note>original: "Translatio Chaldæa"</note> Chaldean translation <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> contains: "And they shall obey the Messiah the son of David their king, and they shall fear the Lord." In the Hebrew it is held: "And they shall flow to the Lord and to his goodness in the last days." No one should understand this as referring to the Babylonian captivity, during which they had honored kings and leaders for a time, as the fourth book of Kings <note>Known today as 2 Kings</note> teaches us; there it is recorded that the King of Babylon placed Jehoiachin, the king of Judah, on a royal throne along with other kings, and the rest of his kin were similarly honored—honors of which they are deprived today. They also lack sacrifice and an altar, since they lack the Temple arranged by the Mosaic law. They lack the Ephod, that is, the priestly garment, and the Teraphim, which is a certain instrument constructed according to the rite of idolatry for foretelling the future. By these words, it is signified that the Jews today worship neither the true God legitimately nor idols; whereas in other times, they either worshipped God rightly or worshipped idols. But "after many days" and "in the last days"—that is, after many centuries, such as these since Jesus, and near the end of the world—they shall return and seek their God, namely the God of their fathers, and David their king, which means the Messiah born of the lineage of David, as the Chaldean translation teaches. Truly, the liberation from Babylon was not after many centuries or in the last times. Let no one understand that the Messiah is only then to come for the first time; for to remove this error, the Prophet did not say "Their king shall come," but "they shall return and seek him," as if he had already come long ago but they had departed and neglected him, and were now about to seek him. The Chaldean words declare this when they say: "They shall obey the Messiah," as people who had previously been stubborn. Of these, Isaiah says: "Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall his countenance now be ashamed; for when he shall see his children sanctifying my name, they shall also sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall preach the God of Israel; and those who erred in spirit shall know understanding, and the murmurers shall learn the law." <note>Isaiah 29:22-24</note> In these words, the confusion of Jacob is removed because from his lineage, and as if his children, were the Apostles who exalted Jesus, through whose doctrine all the Jews shall finally believe in Christ. Paul proves this most sharply in the Epistle to the Romans. <note>Romans 11:25-26</note> Therefore, speaking of the first coming of Christ, Isaiah says: "In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence, and everyone who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy in that day"—that is, in the time of light—the "bud of the Lord" being Christ. <note>Isaiah 4:2-3</note>

<summary>Ficino interprets various Old Testament prophecies (Isaiah, Daniel, Hosea) to explain the Jewish rejection of Jesus and their current diaspora, arguing that they will eventually convert to Christianity at the end of time. He specifically identifies the "stone cut without hands" from Daniel's vision as Jesus destroying the pagan idolatry of the Roman, Greek, Median, and Chaldean empires.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the Christian religion, moving from general prophecies about the fall of idols to specific evidence for Christ’s divinity found in the Hebrew scriptures and the historical witness of Jewish converts. # ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION #

39
<sig>C 4</sig>

Christ, the Son of God, is revealed through the magnificence of his works and wonders. The phrase "Everyone who is left" <note>original: "Omnis qui relictus"; a reference to Isaiah 4:3</note> signifies the disciples of Christ, who were few in number and abandoned by almost everyone—the holy remnant of Christ. These remnants will be exalted with Christ at his second coming. Meanwhile, what should be said of the Jews? Only a few, rarely chosen, will be among the elect; for of them, that saying of Isaiah is understood: "And there shall be left in it as a gleaning of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives in the top of a branch." <note>Isaiah 17:6</note> For after they were shaken off from the natural tree because of their faithlessness (as the Apostle Paul says) and separated from the root of the olive, some were still left there, or rather, were seen to be grafted in again from time to time. 

Such a man was Euaristus the Hebrew, an illustrious man who was the seventh <term>Pontiff</term> <note>The early title for the Bishop of Rome or Pope</note> of the Christians after the blessed Peter; he lived most worthily in that high dignity for more than ten years and died a martyr. Furthermore, in the time of Julian, a Jewish man most holily ruled the first <term>Episcopate</term> <note>The office or district of a bishop</note> of Spain. Petrus Alfonsus, of that same race, also wrote a *Dialogue* against the faithlessness of the Jews. Alfonso of Burgos, a supreme scholar of metaphysics, embraced the faith of Christ in the sixtieth year of his age and wrote many outstanding works against the Jewish position. What shall I say of Nicholas of Lyra, a man of great learning and most holy? What of Jerome the Physician, who disputed subtly against the Jews in the time of Pope Benedict? There were many others in number, though few produced in each century, of whom I believe the saying of Jeremiah was spoken: "I will take you, one from a city and two from a family (otherwise, a congregation), and I will bring you into Zion," <note>Jeremiah 3:14</note> meaning the heavenly Zion. Paul of Burgos, a distinguished theologian and Bishop, treated these matters diligently.

**David:** "He shall descend like rain upon the fleece," <note>Psalm 72:6; in the Latin Vulgate, "vellus" (fleece) is used where modern English Bibles usually say "mown grass."</note> that is, unknown to many; and he adds, "in his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace."

**Isaiah:** "In his days justice shall arise, and a multitude of peace." <note>Ficino attributes this to Isaiah, though it mirrors Psalm 72:7</note> Jesus was born while Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note> was Emperor; against the original justice lost through the root of Adam, he introduced Evangelical grace and justice. Octavian’s empire was also most just. There was such great peace throughout the entire world at that time as had never been greater or more lasting. Hence Virgil says: "The gates of war shall be closed," etc. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.294</note> This peace persevered after Jesus for thirty-seven years.

**Isaiah:** "Egypt has laboured, and the merchandise of Ethiopia and of Saba; men of stature shall pass over to you, and shall be your servants; they shall walk after you bound in irons, and they shall adore you, and shall make supplication to you: only in you is God, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we knew it not, the God of Israel the Savior; all that resist you shall be confounded and ashamed, and they shall fall into confusion." <note>Isaiah 45:14-16</note> These things show how the empires of the Gentiles were at some point to be subjected to Christ. Likewise, they show that Christ was to be God the Savior, unknown for a time but afterward adored, and that his adversaries—namely, the obstinate and idolatrous Jerusalem—must likewise fall, just as it happened. That Christ was also to be a man, Isaiah reveals thus: "God shall send them a man, and he shall save them, and judging he shall heal them." <note>Isaiah 19:20</note> He rightly names him the Messiah Savior and one who will save, for he was called Jesus—that is, "Savior." He shows, however, that he will heal minds by judgment, not bodies by violence and arms. Again, that Christ is God, David speaking of God reveals: "He sent his word, and healed them from their destructions" <note>Psalm 107:20</note>; therefore Abraham recognized God in the form of a man and adored him as the King of all. Similarly, God appeared to Joshua <note>original: "Iesu"; the Latin name for Jesus and Joshua is the same</note>, the successor of Moses, and likewise to Jacob.

**Jeremiah:** "This is our God, and no other shall be accounted of in comparison to him, who found out all the way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men." <note>Baruch 3:36-38; in the Renaissance, the Book of Baruch was often cited as Jeremiah</note> Through these words, the Messiah is shown to be both God and man. The same is said elsewhere: "And he is a man, and who has known him?" as if to say, because of his humility and the pride of men, many were ignorant of him. It is no wonder that many Jews, being little pious, did not recognize the profound mystery of the Messiah and the divinity of Jesus. Yet many Jews, partly pious and partly learned, knew him from the beginning; for Christ converted many thousands of Jews to his law, and his disciples converted many more. Even Muhammad affirms in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> that those Jews who believed in Jesus were preferred by God far above the other Jews. These, together with the Gentiles, called the Messiah (as Jeremiah prophesied elsewhere) "The Lord our Just One," <note>Jeremiah 23:6</note> and they called him truly, for he would not have permitted himself to be falsely called God.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the Hebrew prophets and ancient Jewish commentators (rabbis) anticipated the arrival of Jesus Christ as both God and man. It follows the previous page's discussion of how even after the Jewish rejection of Christ, some Jewish scholars and leaders converted and recognized him.</meta>

-># THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO #<-

40

**Moses:** In the Book of Numbers, it is written: "A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall spring forth from Israel." <note>Numbers 24:17; original: "In numeris orietur ſtella ex Iacob, & exurget homo ex Iſraël"</note> Through these words and those mentioned above, the Messiah is shown to be both God and man. The prophet Ezekiel, when depicting God, places Him in human form upon a sapphire throne, precisely because God was destined to become man. For this reason, Rabbi Joanna <note>Likely Rabbi Johanan bar Nappaha, a major 3rd-century scholar</note> says in his commentaries on the Psalter that while the Jews were liberated from other captivities by various leaders, the final redemption was to be fulfilled by God in His own person. Through this, he concedes that the Messiah is God, and explains that verse: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God and has shone light upon us." <note>Psalm 118:26-27</note>

**David:** Speaking of Christ—who is more excellent than all other "anointed ones" <term>Christos</term> <note>In Greek, *Christos* means "anointed," just as *Messiah* does in Hebrew. Ficino is noting that while many kings were anointed, Jesus is the "most" anointed.</note> of God—he says: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." <note>Psalm 45:7</note> Here he declares him to be a man, though just shortly before he had shown him to be God, saying: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of righteousness." <note>Psalm 45:6</note> That David is speaking of the Messiah is proven by the fact that where the Hebrew text says "beautiful in form above the sons of men," the Chaldean translation <term>Targum</term> <note>The Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues</note> by Jonathan—which among the Jews is equal in authority to the Hebrew text—has: "Your beauty, O King Messiah, is greater than that of the sons of men." Everyone rightly yields to the authority of this translation, for it was arranged by Jonathan, a great man, by the consensus and from the mouths of Eleazar and Joshua, most excellent men, long before the destruction of the Temple. And all the ancient Talmudic Hebrews affirm that it descended from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. Moved by these words of David and similar ones, Rabbi Abba <note>A 3rd-century Babylonian rabbi often cited in the Zohar</note> asks in his commentaries on Genesis what Daniel means when he says of God: "He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with him." <note>Daniel 2:22</note> He answers: "This light is surely the light of the King Messiah," of whom it is said in the Psalm, "In your light we shall see light." <note>Psalm 36:9</note> Thus says the Rabbi. Here he confesses that the divine light which is always with God, and is God Himself, is the light of the Messiah—and is the Messiah himself. Furthermore, that ancient and illustrious theologian Rabbi Neuma <note>Likely Nehuniah ben Ha-Kana, to whom many mystical works were attributed</note> in the book titled *The Luminous*, explaining the saying of Solomon in Proverbs, "The righteous is an everlasting foundation," <note>Proverbs 10:25</note> asks what this means and answers concerning the Messiah in this way: "Whom else does God have, or will He have, as a 'righteous one' in His world, who is beloved to Him because he sustains the whole universe? He is its foundation, he governs the world, and he brings it about that the world is governed; he is the foundation of all souls." This is why it is said, "The righteous is an everlasting foundation." Thus says the Rabbi. From these words, it is clear that the Messiah is not only man, but also God. David himself reveals the same elsewhere: "A man shall say 'Mother Zion,' and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her." <note>Psalm 87:5</note> This means that God, who founded Zion, was born in that very place as a man, and he calls Zion "mother."

**Isaiah:** "In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall rise up to rule the nations, in him shall the nations hope, and his rest shall be glorious." <note>Isaiah 11:10</note> And elsewhere: "A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the spirit of God shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him." <note>Isaiah 11:1-3</note> Jesse was the father of David. By these words, therefore, the prophet predicted that the Messiah would spring from David's lineage, that he would benefit the Gentiles more than the Jews, and that he would rule with spiritual rather than physical weapons—just as Jesus did. The same Isaiah, speaking as the person of Christ, says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind." <note>Isaiah 61:1</note> Here it is declared that the Messiah would be born of the Holy Spirit, and that Christ would be named so only by divine anointing. Likewise, he would preach the Gospel to the poor, remit sins, and drive out ignorance.

**David:** "The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba shall bring presents." <note>Psalm 72:10</note>

**Isaiah:** "All those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and incense, and announcing praise to the Lord." <note>Isaiah 60:6</note> These things happened partly immediately after Jesus was born, and partly after his ascension, especially from the reign of Constantine down to these present times. And elsewhere: "Out of Egypt I called my son." <note>Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15</note> Again elsewhere: "He shall be called a Nazarene." <note>Matthew 2:23</note> Our Jesus, having returned from Egypt, lived in Nazareth and was surnamed the Nazarene.

<summary>Ficino uses quotes from Moses, David, and Isaiah, alongside interpretations from Jewish rabbis and the Targum, to argue that the Messiah was always intended to be a divine-human figure who would rule spiritually rather than politically.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s presentation of Old Testament prophecies that he believes point directly to Jesus Christ. Having previously cited Moses, Ezekiel, and David, he now turns to Zechariah, the Book of Wisdom (attributed here to Solomon), and the "Suffering Servant" prophecies of Isaiah to demonstrate that the Messiah was destined to suffer before being glorified.</meta>

-># ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION #<-

41

**Zechariah:** The Lord God showed me Jesus <note>original: "Iefum"; in the Old Testament context of Zechariah 3, this refers to Joshua the High Priest, but Ficino uses the Latin name *Iesus* to emphasize the prophetic link to Jesus of Nazareth.</note> the high priest, standing before the face of the angel of the Lord, and the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: "May the Lord command you, He who has chosen Jerusalem; is this not a brand plucked from the fire?" And Jesus was dressed in filthy garments, and stood before the face of the angel. And [the angel] responded and said to those standing before his face: "Take the filthy garments off him, and clothe him with a robe reaching to the ankles, and place a clean turban upon his head." And they covered him with a garment and placed a clean turban upon his head. The angel of the Lord stood by and testified to him, saying: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and keep my precepts, you shall judge my house, and I will give you some of those who are standing here to walk among them." <note>Zechariah 3:1–7</note> Listen then, O Jesus the high priest. The words of the Prophet, because they portend the future, designate a man who is like an extinguished brand—contemptible and filthy at first, but afterwards adorned by God and made Judge of the divine house. These things fit God-Jesus the Nazarene, not Joshua son of Nun or Joshua son of Jozadak, who lived before Zechariah and neither suffered nor performed such things.

**Solomon** in the Book of Wisdom: "Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is useless to us, and he reproaches us for our sins against the law; he promises that he has the knowledge of God and calls himself the son of God. He has become a grievance to us even in our thoughts; he is heavy for us even to look upon, because his life is unlike others, and his ways are changed. We are esteemed by him as triflers, and he abstains from our ways as from filth; he prefers the latter end of the just, and boasts that he has God for his father. Let us see then if his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him; let us examine him with outrages and tortures, that we may know his reverence and prove his patience. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death." <note>Wisdom 2:12–20; although now considered Deuterocanonical, in Ficino's time this was widely attributed to Solomon.</note> They thought these things and were led astray, for their own malice blinded them, and they did not know the sacraments <note>original: "sacramenta"; here meaning "mysteries" or "hidden plans"</note> of God. Thus says Solomon, and nothing could be clearer. God rightly permits those who were blind and cruel toward the Prophets—the heralds of the Messiah—to be likewise toward the Messiah himself.

**Isaiah:** Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and glorified, and shall be exceeding high. Just as many were astonished at you, so shall his glory be stripped away from men—your appearance and your glory from men. So shall many nations marvel at him, and kings shall shut their mouths; for they to whom it was not told of him shall see, and they who heard not shall understand. Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? We have announced before him as a weakling, and as a root in parched ground. He has no beauty nor glory, and we saw him, and he had no appearance nor comeliness; but his appearance was lacking in honor before all men, a man placed in affliction, and knowing how to bear infirmity. Because his face was turned away, he was despised and not esteemed. He carries our sins and grieves for us, and we thought him to be as if a leper, struck by God and humbled <note>original margin: "otherwise: in sorrow, in a stroke, and in affliction"</note>; but he was wounded for our iniquities and weakened for our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, every man has wandered from his own way, and the Lord delivered him for our sins. And because he was afflicted, he opened not his mouth; he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opened not his mouth. In his humility his judgment was taken away; who shall declare his generation? For his life shall be taken from the earth. For the iniquities of my people he was led to death. And I will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he did no iniquity, nor was guile found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to cleanse him of his stroke. If you lay down your soul for sin, you shall see a long-lived seed, and the Lord willed to take away his soul from sorrow, to show him light, and to form his understanding, to justify the just one who serves many well, and he himself carried their sins. Therefore he shall inherit many, and shall divide the spoils of the strong. Because his soul was delivered unto death, and he was esteemed among the wicked; and he carried the sins of many, and for their sins he was delivered. <note>Isaiah 52:13–53:12; the famous "Suffering Servant" passage.</note> Now, that Isaiah spoke in the words above concerning the final redemption which was to be received through the Messiah is clear through a certain prologue set forth by him in these words: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and preaches peace, who announces..." <note>Isaiah 52:7; the text cuts off here to match the catchword "annunciantis" for the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino uses Zechariah’s vision of the High Priest and Isaiah’s "Suffering Servant" to argue that the Messiah was prophetically destined to appear in a humble, suffering form before his eventual glorification. He emphasizes that these descriptions uniquely fit Jesus of Nazareth rather than historical Jewish figures.</summary>

proclaiming good, preaching salvation, saying: Your God shall reign, O Zion. And below: The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. And below: For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you. <note>These citations are from Isaiah 52:7, 10, and 12.</note> All agree, both Jews and Christians, that these and many similar things there pertain to the Messiah. Then he adds: "Behold, my servant <note>original: "puer" (boy or servant). The Latin "puer" mirrors the Greek "pais," which can mean both son/child and servant/attendant.</note> shall understand" (otherwise "my servant" <note>original: "servus meus"</note>), meaning that this servant is the Messiah. The Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary used in Jewish liturgy.</note> also declares it in this manner: "Behold, my servant the Messiah shall understand." Furthermore, that this Messiah is God, the Jewish Talmudic interpreters expounding Isaiah here show it thus: "He shall be exalted more than Abraham, raised higher than Moses, and shall be exceedingly sublime, more so than the angels." How truly precious such a redemption through the Messiah is, is evident from that passage of Isaiah: "Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation; you shall not be confounded, and you shall not be ashamed forever and ever." <note>Isaiah 45:17</note> Therefore, the salvation to come through the Messiah was not to be physical or temporal, like the deliverances from Egypt or Babylon and similar events, but spiritual and everlasting.

Although that prophecy of Isaiah, "Behold, [my servant] shall understand," clearly pertains to our Jesus, nevertheless Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105). He was a seminal medieval commentator who often argued that the "Servant" in Isaiah 53 referred to the collective nation of Israel suffering in exile.</note>—a man of perverse will—dared to pervert those words, twisting them to refer to the Jewish people living in their current misery. The Chaldean translation contradicts him, as we have said. All the ancient Jewish interpreters of the Prophets also speak against him, for they maintain that this servant is the Messiah, much more sublime than the angels—an excellence that cannot apply to this lowly and sinful Jewish populace. Hence, Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>Moses ben Nahman, or Nachmanides (1194–1270). Ficino notes that Nachmanides preserved older Messianic interpretations even while remaining within the Jewish tradition.</note>, despising this Solomon [Rashi], followed the ancients. Thus, in his commentaries, he says that the King Messiah will give his heart to pray for Israel; he will even undergo fasts for them and suffer the lowest things, citing that passage of Isaiah: "But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes." <note>Isaiah 53:5</note>

And although the Jewish "dregs" <note>original: "fex" (literally 'dregs' or 'sediment'). Ficino employs the harsh, disparaging polemical language common in 15th-century theological debates.</note> are today much afflicted, and as if wounded and bruised in almost the same way that Isaiah depicts the servant of God as afflicted, nevertheless the words of Isaiah can in no way fit this people; indeed, six principal signs show this to us.

**First**, although this people is heavily oppressed, they do not suffer this because of the iniquities and crimes of the Gentiles, such that through the sufferings and merits of the Jews, the Gentiles who afflict them might obtain pardon and salvation from God; on the contrary, all Jews expect vengeance from God against the Gentiles. Therefore, when Isaiah asserts of the servant of God that by his bruises others are healed, and that God placed the iniquity of all others upon him, he certainly is not speaking of the Jewish people, for whose punishments others are not saved, but as they themselves assert, are punished.

The **second** sign: Isaiah says that this servant of God committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. But the Jews are enslaved to greed, usury, lying, and crimes. And even they themselves admit they live in this misery because of their crimes, and compelled by the authority of Deuteronomy, they confess that if they were to set aside their depravity and turn back to God, they would be immediately liberated. Hence their teachers, confessing that this misery arises from their sins, inquire what those sins might be. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] blames the worship of the calf made in the desert—a crime God had long ago punished and forgiven before Jesus. Others blame various individual sins; others want it to be a hidden sin for whose guilt they pay the penalties.

The **third** sign: Isaiah says at the end of the chapter that this servant of God prayed for transgressors. The Jews, on the other hand, at least three times every day in their execrable rites, call down the most terrible curses upon the Roman Empire, the Church of Christ, and all nations except for the Jews; and in their Talmudic constitutions, they are commanded to harm Christians however they can, whether by force, fraud, or deceit.

**Fourth**: in what way can the instruction and discipline of peace, which Isaiah says is in the servant of God, be placed in this unlearned and perverse Jewish populace?

**Fifth**: in what way is this people more sublime than the angels of God, as all the ancient Jews undoubtedly agreed that servant of God to be?

**Sixth**: since Isaiah says, "Led to death for the iniquities of my people," who does not see that the servant of God who is led to death is one person, and the people of God for whose iniquities he is killed is another? Unless perhaps someone wants Isaiah—the most elegant of all writers—to have spoken so absurdly as to mean: "My people were led to death for the iniquities of my people." Therefore, if the Jewish people have no sin, Isaiah speaks falsely here of the Jewish people; if they do have sin, he speaks falsely immediately after when he adds, "he committed no iniquity"—if indeed he is speaking of the people then. Therefore, that servant of God can in no way be the people. But

It is worthwhile to arrange the very words of Isaiah into twelve Conclusions, just as Paul, the Bishop of Burgos and an eminent theologian, has done. <note>Paulus Burgensis (c. 1350–1435) was a Jewish convert to Christianity and a highly influential biblical scholar whose "Additiones" to Nicholas of Lyra's commentary were standard in Ficino's time.</note> **First**, the Servant of God described by Isaiah is more excellent than all creatures, for he says: *he shall be exalted and lifted up, etc.* **Second**, he was a small child from the beginning and had a humble origin, for he says: *he grew up like a tender plant, and like a root out of thirsty ground.* **Third**, in his progress he was despised and held as nothing, for he says: *we saw him despised and the last of men, and we did not esteem him.* **Fourth**, he was wounded on account of our iniquities, specifically to purge them. Whence it is said: *and by his bruises we are healed*; and below: *my righteous servant shall himself justify many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities.* **Fifth**, all the righteous except him, by common law, have wandered from the way of salvation, but he himself bore the iniquity of all—that is, he paid the penalty for all. Hence that saying: *all we like sheep have gone astray, and God laid on him the iniquity of us all.* **Sixth**, he willingly endured these punishments, and even death after them, of which it is said: *he was offered because he himself willed it, and shall be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the shearer.* <note>original: "oblatus est, quia ipse uoluit" — a traditional Latin phrasing of Isaiah 53:7 emphasizing the voluntary nature of Christ's sacrifice.</note> The Jews, however, endure their sufferings not willingly, but with a reluctant and sick soul. **Seventh**, this happened because of the crime and iniquities of the people, though he was innocent. Regarding this he says: *for the crime of my people I struck him,* and of the same we read below: *who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.* **Eighth**, because that servant of God, having gained the victory, was to divide the spoils of the strong because he delivered his life to death. To this pertains: *Therefore I will allot many to him, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he surrendered his soul to death.* **Ninth**, he was to be thought of as a wicked man, on account of which he says: *And he was counted among the criminals.* **Tenth**, although such a servant could sufficiently sustain and delete the sins of everyone through what he endured, he did not, in effect, wash away the evils of all, but of many; wherefore he added: *and he himself bore the sins of many.* **Eleventh**, such was the charity in him that he even prayed to God for his enemies and his murderers; to this he adds: *he prayed for the transgressors.* **Twelfth**, the things handed down in this prophecy exceed the powers of natural talent, wherefore he exclaimed: *who has believed our report?* All these things fit only Jesus the Nazarene.

**Jeremiah**: *The breath of our mouth, the Lord Christ, was captured in our sins, to whom we said: in his shadow we shall live among the Nations.* <note>original: "Spiritus oris nostri Dominus Christus..." quoting Lamentations 4:20. In the Latin Vulgate, "Christus" is the translation for "Anointed."</note> Likewise: *On that day you shall not be confounded for all your inventions which you have done against me, for then I will take away from you the depravities of your injury, and you shall no longer add to your pride over my holy mountain, and I will leave in you a people mild and humble, and those who remain in Israel shall fear in the name of the Lord.* Likewise: *Lord, show me that I may know, then I saw their meditations; I was led like an innocent lamb to the victim; they devised schemes against me, saying: "Come, let us put wood into his bread, and let us erase his life from the earth, and his memory shall be no more."* <note>original: "mittamus lignum in panem eius" (let us put wood in his bread) from Jeremiah 11:19. Early Christian writers interpreted "wood" as the Cross and "bread" as the body of Christ.</note> Likewise: *She who gives birth is terrified, and her soul is weary, and the Sun went down for her while it was still midday; she is confounded and cursed; the rest of them I will give to the sword in the sight of their enemies.* Likewise: *I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance into the hands of its enemies; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it has raised its voice against me, therefore I have hated it.* In these passages, Jeremiah teaches that the Messiah was to be captured to purge our sins and to be afflicted, and that God would eventually leave that people for the first humble <term>Christians</term> <note>followers of Christ</note> who were subject to persecutions. For he intends the "remnant of Israel" to be the Apostles and Martyrs. After this, he also makes mention of the wood of the cross, and the eclipse at noon while Christ was suffering. He also adds the martyrdoms of the Christians, and the vengeance against the stubborn people of the Jews; finally, he adds that the people of God rose up like a lion against Christ, who was like a lamb, and therefore God will exterminate that people.

**Solomon**: *If you turn away from me, says the Lord, and do not keep my truth, I will reject Israel from the land which I gave them, and this house shall be a desert, and everyone who passes by it shall be amazed and say: "For what reason has the Lord done these evils to this land and to this house?" and they shall say: "Because they left the Lord their God and persecuted their most beloved king and God, and crucified him in great humility; because of this, God brought these evils upon them."* <note>This is a Christianized paraphrase of 1 Kings 9:6-9 or 2 Chronicles 7:19-22, common in medieval polemics to link the Temple's destruction directly to the Crucifixion.</note> Thus he spoke. Who then will deny that Jesus the Nazarene was the Messiah, and was man as well as God?

**Ezra**: *This Passover is our Savior and our refuge; consider that we have*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the Christian religion by citing Old Testament prophecies and historical testimonies. Having previously discussed the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah, he now moves into specific chronological and celestial arguments regarding the Passion, drawing on Ezra and the timing of the Passover, followed by a series of shorter prophetic proofs from the Minor Prophets.</meta>

<meta>catchword: born</meta>

...let us humble him upon the wood <note>original: "humiliare eum in ligno." This refers to the Cross.</note>, and after these things we shall hope in him, lest this place be deserted for all time, says the Lord God of power. If you do not believe in him, nor listen to his annunciation, you shall be a derision among the Nations. These are his words, and nothing is clearer than them. No less does that saying of Moses agree: *I am God, I will move you to jealousy; not with a nation against a nation, but I will send a foolish nation to provoke you to anger.* <note>Ficino is paraphrasing Deuteronomy 32:21 to show the transition of God's favor from the Jews to the Gentiles.</note> Above all other words of Ezra, those must be especially considered: that the Jews were going to humble the Savior—that is, Jesus, whose name signifies "Savior"—upon the wood at the time of the Passover. It is necessary to remember again that the law commanded the Jews to celebrate the Passover and sacrifice the lamb on the fourteenth day of the Moon. 

From this, Anatolius the Alexandrian philosopher <note>Anatolius (c. 230–283 AD) was a scientist and Bishop of Laodicea who wrote on the calculation of Easter.</note> subtly proves—first by reasons, then by law, and also by the authority of Philo, Josephus, Agathobulus, and Aristobulus—that the Mosaic ritual for celebrating the Passover was correct and customary in the month of March, after both the Sun and the Moon have passed the vernal equinox, and when the Moon is opposite the Sun. Hence Polycrates, a disciple of the disciples of the Apostles, asserts that the Apostles and their successors were also accustomed to celebrate the Passover according to the Jewish custom on the fourteenth day of the Moon, when the Jewish people made the Unleavened Bread <note>original: "Azyma."</note>. Why mention these things? So that we may confirm what we have said elsewhere: namely, that the eclipse of the Sun which occurred during Christ's suffering was not natural. <note>A solar eclipse is physically impossible during a full moon (Passover); Ficino uses this to argue the darkness at the Crucifixion was a miracle.</note> That it did occur, Lucian of Antioch testified thus before the tribunal of his judge: "Search your own Annals, and you will find that in the times of Pilate, while Christ was suffering, the Sun fled and the day was interrupted by darkness." Tertullian also cried out to the judges: "You have this event of the world recorded in your Annals."

**Isaiah:** *I the Lord God have called thee in justice, and will take thee by the hand, and preserve thee, and I have given thee for a covenant of my people, for a light of the Gentiles: That thou mightest open the eyes of the blind, and bring forth the prisoner out of liberty, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.* These are his words, in which God addresses Christ. He sends him to introduce the New Testament, to convert the Gentiles no less than the Jews, to release those bound in Limbo, and to purge sins. Elsewhere in Isaiah, Christ speaks thus: *I am not rebellious, neither do I go back: I have given my body to the strikers, and my cheeks to them that plucked them: I have not turned away my face from the foulness of spitting.* Likewise: *In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for a sign of the people, him the Gentiles shall beseech, and his sepulcher shall be glorious.* All these things happened to Jesus of Nazareth.

**Amos:** *And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord, the Sun shall go down at midday, and I will make the earth dark in the day of light: And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation.* In the day, namely, in which the Messiah suffers, the Sun shall go down; this signifies the eclipse of the Sun at noon while Jesus was suffering—Jesus, who is the "day of light," the light of light. After these things, God established as a perpetual vengeance that the Jews should be harassed daily, repeating the Lamentations of Jeremiah and similar complaints.

**Ezekiel:** *I have exalted the humble tree.* <note>Ezekiel 17:24, interpreted here as the Cross.</note>

**Job:** *Who would give us of his flesh, that we might be filled?*

**Zechariah:** *With these I was wounded.* <note>Zechariah 13:6.</note> Also elsewhere, concerning God saving Jerusalem, he says: *I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of power: and they shall look upon me, whom they have pierced: and they shall mourn for him as one mourneth for an only son.* These are his words. He who as God pours out the spirit of grace and power is pierced as a man; and therefore, we should understand that Christ was composed of different natures, working miracles by one nature and suffering terrible things by the other. Zechariah spoke in the first person, namely *I will pour out*, and in the second, *they shall pour out upon him*—that is: I, as God, (they shall look upon me whom they pierced), namely as a man; and they shall mourn over him, namely the man assumed by me, God. It is not permitted for anyone to forge the text to say "they shall look upon *him*," for every Bible, both Hebrew and Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean (Aramaic/Targum versions of the Bible)</note>, says "they shall look upon *me*." *They shall mourn*, that is, they shall pay the penalty in this world and the next. But in what way does he pour out the spirit of grace if they are to mourn over him? Certainly, he pours out the grace of the Holy Spirit and the liberation from ancient sins (for he freed those willing from the underworld); he also pours out the spirit of power to punish the unbelievers, for it is they who mourn.

**Habakkuk:** *In the midst of two animals you shall be known; you went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones; you sent death upon the heads of the enemies.* By "two animals" is meant the two Testaments; again, the two Prophets on Mount Tabor, Moses and Elijah; again, the two thieves on the cross. Perhaps even the two brute animals, when...

<summary>Ficino synthesizes prophetic texts from Ezra, Isaiah, Amos, and Zechariah to argue for the divinity of Christ and the miraculous nature of the solar eclipse during the Crucifixion. He emphasizes that the specific timing of the Passover makes a natural eclipse impossible, thus proving a divine sign.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that Old Testament prophecies accurately predicted the life of Jesus. Having established the timing of the Passion in the previous section, he now compiles a "florilegium" (a collection of excerpts) from the Psalms and the Prophets to demonstrate that every detail of Christ’s suffering, rejection by the Jews, and eventual victory was foretold centuries in advance.</meta>

-># ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION<-
<meta>catchword: Joel:</meta>

He was born in stables for the salvation of your people, so that you might make the souls of believers safe from the underworld. He calls the stubborn Hebrews "enemies."

David often speaks under his own name concerning the Messiah, whom he knew would sprout from his own lineage; thus he says: *Scourges were gathered over me, and I did not know it; they were separated, yet not struck with remorse; they tempted me, they mocked me with scorn, and they gnashed their teeth over me.* <note>Psalm 35:15–16. Ficino interprets David’s personal laments as "typological" prophecies—events in David’s life that prefigure Christ.</note> *They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink; many dogs have surrounded me, a council of the wicked has besieged me. They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones. But they themselves contemplated and watched me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.* <note>These verses from Psalms 69 and 22 are central to Christian Passion narratives.</note> *They will hunt for the soul of the just man, and will condemn innocent blood, and the Lord has become a refuge for me. You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you will establish me as the head of the Nations; a people I have not known has served me; at the hearing of the ear, they obeyed me.* <note>Psalm 18:43–44. This refers to the "Gentiles" (Nations) accepting Christ while his own people rejected him.</note> *Let these things be written for another generation, and the people who shall be created will praise the Lord. The Lord has made known his salvation; he has revealed his justice before the sight of the Nations. I will give you the Nations as your inheritance; the kings of the earth stood by, and the princes came together as one against the Lord, and against his Christ.* <note>Psalm 2. The word "Christ" here translates the Hebrew "Messiah," meaning the Anointed One.</note> *Let their table become a snare before them, a retribution, and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so they may not see, and keep their backs always bent. Pour out your wrath upon them; let the fury of your anger seize them. Let their habitation become a desert, and let there be no one to dwell in their tents. Because they persecuted the one whom you sent, and they added to the pain of my wounds. Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your justice. Let them be blotted out from the book of the living, and not be written among the just.* <note>Psalm 69:22–28. Ficino uses these "imprecatory psalms" to explain the historical dispersion and suffering of the Jewish people as a divine consequence for the Crucifixion.</note> *I am poor and suffering; your salvation, O God, has taken me up.* King David was not poor, but the Messiah, born from him, was to be born poor. Concerning Judas the betrayer, David predicted this: *He who eats bread with me shall lift up his heel against me.* <note>Psalm 41:9.</note> Regarding the Jews again: *Thus they hated me without cause,* concerning whom the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> prophesied: *They will always fill up the measure of their sins, for the wrath of God has come upon them to the very end.* Thus he foretold the eternal stubbornness and misery of the Jews. But why should I pass over what Jeremiah openly foretold regarding the sale of Christ by Judas, and the price, and the purchase of the field, just as it is handed down in the Gospel? For he says: *And they took thirty silver pieces, the price of the one who was appraised, whom they appraised from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, just as the Lord appointed for me.* <note>This prophecy is found in Zechariah 11:12–13, though the Gospel of Matthew (27:9) and Ficino attribute it to Jeremiah. This was a common attribution in early modern theology.</note> Matthew adds that even in his own time, that field bought with the price of Christ was called the "Field of Blood." Regarding the resurrection of Christ, David says: *My flesh shall rest in hope, because you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption,* <note>Psalm 16:10.</note> because, clearly, Christ did not decay. Again: *Lord, you have led my soul out of hell; I slept and took my rest, and I rose up, because the Lord took me up. I have risen and am still with you.* David agrees.

Hosea says: *He will heal us after two days; on the third day we shall rise again,* or thus: *Come, let us return to God, for he himself has seized us and he will save us; he will strike and he will cure us; he will visit us after two days. On the third day he will raise us up, and we shall come into his sight.* <note>Hosea 6:1–2.</note> Again: *Death is swallowed up in victory; where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?* <note>Hosea 13:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:55.</note> which clearly signifies, through the resurrection of Christ, the resurrection of our own bodies as well. For just as in one Adam we all fell and died, so in one Christ we are all cleansed and rise again; the Apostle Paul speaks on this with subtlety and divinity.

And why was the Prophet Jonah taken up by the belly of the vast fish and returned living to the light on the third day, if not to signify the resurrection of Christ? Indeed, the deeds of the Old Testament are no less figurative of the New than are the words. For the New is the end of the Old in no other way than as the absolute coloring and perfected painting of a certain sketch <note>original: "adumbrationis," referring to a shadow-outline or preliminary drawing.</note>; therefore, the New Testament is much more excellent than the Old.

David sang of the Lord's ascension in this way: *God ascends with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet. Sing to the Lord, who ascends above the heaven of heavens to the East. You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have given gifts to men.* <note>Psalms 47 and 68.</note> He also sings of the sending of the Holy Spirit: *You shall send forth your spirit and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.* <note>Psalm 104:30.</note>

### MARSILIO FICINO’S BOOK

**Joel:** *And it shall come to pass after this, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions; and even upon my servants and my handmaids, in those days, will I pour out my spirit.* <note>original: "Effundam de spiritu meo..." Joel 2:28–29. This is the text famously quoted by Saint Peter on the day of Pentecost.</note> After the arrival of Christ, not only the Apostles, but very many others—women as well as men, Gentiles as well as Jews, the learned and the unlearned, the old and the young—received the gifts and the marvelous grace of the Holy Spirit.

**Isaiah:** *In other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, but not even so will they hear me, says the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 28:11–12. Ficino uses this to explain the "Gift of Tongues" and the subsequent Jewish rejection of the Gospel.</note> And so it was that although the Apostles were previously unrefined, once they had received the gift of the Holy Spirit, they suddenly poured forth divine mysteries in various languages; nevertheless, not all the Jews believed.

**Ezekiel:** *I will put my spirit within your hearts.* And elsewhere concerning <term>Baptism</term> <note>The Christian rite of initiation using water for the forgiveness of sins.</note> he says: *I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your filthiness, and from all your idols I will cleanse you.* The doctors of the Jews, where they interpret their book on Jonah, and where they explain the <term>Talmud</term> <note>original: "Talmut." The central text of Rabbinic Judaism. Ficino refers to Jewish interpretations that he claims support Christian views of the Messiah.</note>—namely their new ordinances made after the time of Jesus—bring forward a prophecy of this kind to prove that in the time of the Messiah, not only the Jews but also any of the Gentiles will wash away the filth of their sins by a certain sprinkling of water.

**Isaiah, in his song, says:** *You shall draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior, and you shall say in that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name (the Savior’s)*—that is, the name of Jesus the Messiah, for "Jesus" means "Savior." *Confess to the Lord*, because the worship of the one God is introduced through Christ, as idols cease to be. A little later, he adds the preaching of the Apostles among the Gentiles in this way: *Sing to the Lord, for he has done magnificently; announce this in all the earth.* But because Christ was born in Judea, he added: *Exult and praise, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.*

**The Prophet David** treats many clear things concerning Christ in the second, third, fifteenth, twenty-first, and many other Psalms. But the mission of the Apostles to far-off nations is shown through this: *Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.*

**Isaiah, concerning the Messiah and the mission of the Apostles, says:** *How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, of those who preach good things.* He also foresaw and had a foretaste of the afflictions of the Apostles: *For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.* <note>Ficino blends Isaiah 52:7 and Psalm 44:22 to show that the Apostles' success was joined with suffering.</note> **Origen**, in the third book of his commentaries on Genesis, speaks thus: "Thomas, as has been handed down to us, was allotted the Parthians; Matthew, Ethiopia; Bartholomew, Inner India; Andrew, Scythia; John, Asia; Peter is found to have traveled through Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, and Cappadocia, and the other neighboring provinces, preaching only to the Jews, and at last stayed in Rome, where he was crucified with his head downward, which he himself prayed to be done so, lest he should seem to be made equal to the Lord." <note>Origen was a 3rd-century Christian scholar. The story of Peter’s upside-down crucifixion is a traditional mark of his humility.</note> What shall I say of Paul, who filled the land with the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, and underwent martyrdom under Nero at the end? Thus says Origen. Also **Thaddeus**, one of the seventy disciples of Christ, having set out beyond the Euphrates and preaching the Gospel in the city of **Edessa**, converted the whole kingdom of King **Abgar** to Christ, and miraculously freed Abgar himself from a certain incurable disease. For Christ had previously promised Abgar by letter that this would happen, when he had been asked by him through a letter to set out to cure him. **Eusebius** <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> read these things written in the Syrian language in the public histories of the city of Edessa, where Abgar had reigned, and translated them into Greek.

-> Solutions to doubts concerning the Prophets. Chapter XXVIII. <-

We must now explain certain words of the Prophets which, when not sufficiently understood, provide an occasion for the stubborn and dull-witted Jews to refuse to confess that Jesus was the Messiah—that is, the true Christ.

**Isaiah:** *It shall be in the last days*—that is, in the final times of the Prophets, and at the end of the Jewish kingdom and priesthood. For it is not in the "last days" of the physical world, as some dream, that he wants Christ to come for the first time; otherwise, he would be almost useless, or at least useful only for a short time.
