...his instruction would be, but in the final days of the Prophets, the priesthood, and the Jewish kingdom. These three things ceased under Jesus of Nazareth, and it follows: *The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains.* <note>original: "Mons domus Domini..." Isaiah 2:2.</note> Because of this, certain Jews rave, saying that at the coming of the Messiah, God will transport Mount Tabor, Mount Sinai, and Mount Carmel all the way to Jerusalem, and place Mount Zion upon their peaks. These dull-witted little men always drag the incorporeal works of an incorporeal God down to physical bodies.

But in truth, <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> the Jew explains Isaiah much more correctly here, saying that Mount Zion would surpass the other mountains not by the height of the place, but by the magnitude of its miracles. Now, our Jesus enlightened the man born blind on that mountain, cured the paralytic, and performed many other miracles there; finally, he poured the Holy Spirit from heaven into his disciples there. After this follows: *And all nations shall flow to him,* <note>Isaiah 2:2.</note> that is, many from among all nations. Similarly, they say that "every animal" was in Noah's ark, meaning some from every kind of animal.

*Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be trained for battle anymore.* <note>Isaiah 2:4.</note> This word "anymore" <note>original: "ultra."</note> does not signify an eternal peace for the world, but a universal and long-lasting one. Indeed, there was such great peace in the time of Jesus, as we have said elsewhere, that <term>Virgil</term> <note>Ficino uses the name "Maro." Virgil was the Roman poet who famously wrote of a coming "Golden Age."</note> sang that the gates of war were then closed. The Hebrews have it in the fourth book of Kings: *The raiding bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel.* <note>2 Kings 6:23. In the Vulgate, 1 and 2 Kings are called 3 and 4 Kings.</note> Nevertheless, after that time, it is recorded that the Syrians frequently invaded the land of Israel. Therefore, "no more" or "anymore" signifies "until a certain time." <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), a Christian historian who argued that the Pax Romana was divinely ordained to facilitate the spread of the Gospel.</note> records that after Jesus until his own time—that is, the time of Constantine—there did not occur so many overthrows of kingdoms and slaughters of peoples as had occurred before.

Likewise, the same Isaiah says elsewhere concerning the time of the Messiah: *The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat.* <note>Isaiah 11:6.</note> Although the High Priest Eleazar and Aristobulus before Christ, and <term>Philo</term> <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who used allegory to harmonize the Hebrew Bible with Greek philosophy.</note> after Christ—the wisest of the Jewish interpreters—judged that the sacred scriptures ought to be explained through <term>allegory</term> <note>A method of interpretation that looks for a hidden spiritual or symbolic meaning behind the literal words.</note> on account of their mystical sense, and they even attempted this themselves, nevertheless the childish minds of many Jews expect an entirely <term>Golden Age</term> <note>A mythical era of peace and prosperity often described by ancient poets.</note> during the Messiah’s reign, such as the words and colors of the poets depict.

However, while Jesus lived, the golden truth, tranquility of mind, and eternal fruit shone sufficiently in the souls of those who were not stubborn. After him, because of his works and teaching, whoever wishes can take possession of that Golden Age; eternal peace with God has been reconciled for men through Jesus. Furthermore, for many years, the "wolf"—that is, a more powerful prince or people—did not devour the "lamb"—that is, a weaker prince or people. Before Jesus, the Gentiles and Jews were in total discord among themselves in all things; after him, many from the Jews and a great many from the Gentiles lived and continue to live in harmony of customs and opinions under his teaching. Daily, in many places, the bites of venomous animals were rendered harmless by the miracles of the Apostles; each of these things seems to belong to the Golden Age. But the Golden Age must be placed in the fruits of the soul rather than the body. Truly, the trifles of the poets should be left to children.

<term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Referring to Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential Jewish philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> also judged this, for he says here in the *Book of Judges*: "Beware lest you think that in the time of the Messiah the order of the world and the progression of natural things will be different than it usually is." As for what Isaiah says—*The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,* and so forth—it is enigmatic; for it signifies that Israel will live in peace with the wicked men of this world, who are symbolized by wolves and leopards. These are his words.

Moses says in <term>Deuteronomy</term>: *If you have been scattered to the ends of heaven, from there the Lord your God will draw you back, and will take you, and bring you into the land which your fathers possessed.* <note>Deuteronomy 30:4–5.</note> Because of this, the Jews, expecting to be gathered by the help of Christ, do not confess that Jesus was the true Christ since they were scattered because of him. To them it must be answered: this oracle was fulfilled at the time when they were liberated from the Babylonian servitude. For then, as <term>Ezra</term> <note>Referring to the Book of Ezra in the Bible.</note> testifies, King Cyrus not only permitted all the Jews to return to their fatherland, but even offered gifts to those returning.

But if anyone should argue that a gathering of this kind belongs to the Messiah, I will say that through Jesus, souls scattered because of sin have been sufficiently gathered into the heavenly fatherland—whoever so willed—for that is called by David the "land of the living." *I believe,* he said, *to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.* <note>original: "terra uiuentium." Psalm 27:13.</note> Hence Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Another name for Maimonides.</note> says in his commentary on Deuteronomy that this divine good, which is intelligible, is called by many names in the sacred scriptures: it is called the mountain of God, and the holy place...

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...His holy place, the place of the sanctuary, the holy way, the courts of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the house of the Lord, the gate of the Lord. <note>original: "locus sanctuarij, uia sancta, atria Domini..."</note> These are his words. <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famed medieval commentator whose works Ficino studied to find common ground or points of refutation.</note> also, and <term>Rabbi Abba</term> <note>A prominent scholar mentioned in the Talmud.</note> consider the building of the temple described by <term>Ezekiel</term> to belong to the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore, those who hope for a visible temple to be built by the Messiah are foolish; foolish again are those who expect the people of Israel to be gathered by him in a specific physical place; and thirdly, those who think all Jews will be saved in the time of the Messiah are foolish. 

Let us hear <term>Jeremiah</term> speaking thus: *Return, O backsliding children, says the Lord, for I am your Husband, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion, and I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine.* <note>Jeremiah 3:14–15.</note> Indeed, these words are to be understood regarding the final redemption, which was to be fulfilled through the Messiah, and not concerning the redemption from Babylonian slavery, as some believe. For in the same context, it is read: *At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all nations shall be gathered to it in the name of the Lord.* <note>Jeremiah 3:17.</note> Because of this, Rabbi Solomon, in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>original: "Camedrin." A major tractate of the Talmud that discusses legal matters and the coming of the Messiah.</note> explains the aforementioned words of Jeremiah—namely, *I will take you one from a city and two from a family*—as referring to that final redemption which they expect. For he says there: *I will choose the righteous and bring them into Zion.* 

From this, it is clear that in the final redemption through the Messiah, not all Israelites are saved, but only the righteous. These, however, are far fewer than the unrighteous, who are not saved; therefore the Prophet said: *one from a city and two from a family* (or otherwise, *from a congregation*), as if to say, very few will be chosen out of many. Again, in the same place, one of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> says: Just as out of the six hundred thousand men who went out of Egypt, only two—namely <term>Caleb and Joshua</term>—are recorded to have entered the promised land, so it shall be in the time of the Messiah. For it is written thus in <term>Hosea</term>: *And she shall sing there as in the days of her youth, and as in the days of her coming up out of the land of Egypt.* <note>Hosea 2:15. Ficino uses this to show that the "new" exodus under the Messiah will mirror the old one, where only a faithful few succeeded.</note>

<term>Zechariah</term>, speaking of Christ, says: *He built a temple to the Lord.* <note>Zechariah 6:12.</note> The Jews expect Christ to construct a most vast structure on earth out of dead stones. Jesus, however, built a sublime and heavenly temple out of living stones of souls, surely by divine art. But these people are also refuted by the preceding arguments.

Jeremiah says: *In his days*—namely, the Messiah's—*Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely.* <note>Jeremiah 23:6.</note> They want those days which he names to belong to Christ, by whose hands they hope to be led back into that ancient and earthly kingdom, and to be enriched with earthly wealth according to their desire. But we say that through the grace and teaching of Christ, the souls of those who are willing—both of the remaining Gentiles and of the Jews—are cleansed from that ancient fault <note>The "ancient fault" refers to Original Sin inherited from Adam.</note>. Through this cleansing, the body may inhabit this world with such confidence that after the dissolution of the body, they may fly back to the heavenly realms. 

*Judah*, that is, the human race—which has its whole origin from Judah, that is, from Judea—will be saved, namely if it so chooses. But from what will it be saved? Namely, from the guilt conceived through <term>Adam</term>, and it will inhabit heaven. We ought to remember that in the Sacred Scriptures, *Israel* sometimes signifies men of whatever race, provided they follow the true worship of the God of Israel, even if they are not descended from Israel (or Jacob) according to blood. 

Therefore, <term>Isaiah</term>, where he treats the propagation of the people of Israel through the calling of the Gentiles under the teaching of the Messiah, says: *I will pour my spirit upon your seed*, and so forth, *and they shall spring up among the grass like willows by the flowing waters.* <note>Isaiah 44:3–4.</note> And in the same context, he declares that this propagation of the seed of Israel or Jacob is not to be understood only according to physical lineage. For this reason, he adds: *This one says, "I am the Lord's," and that one shall be called by the name of Jacob, and another shall write on his hand "To the Lord," and shall be likened to the name of Israel.* <note>Isaiah 44:5.</note> He who says, "I am the Lord's Israel," is so according to the flesh, of whom it is also added, "and he shall be called by the name of Jacob." That which follows in the text after these things belongs to those who are similar to Israel in belief and character; hence Rabbi Solomon, where he interprets these words—*and shall be likened to the name of Israel*—says: *These are they who are converted from the worship of the Gentiles to the true worship of God; for they are worthy to be called by the name of Israel.* Thus says Solomon. 

Therefore, when the Prophets say that Israel shall be saved under the Messiah, they do not mean this specific race of men, but all who make themselves similar to Israel and Jacob in worship and life. But if you wish for these names, "Judah" and "Israel," in that text of Jeremiah to signify only the specific people of God, so be it. But those who denied the Son of God have degenerated and were punished by the Romans; whereas those among the Jews who followed him—and they were indeed many and great men—were truly to be called by the name of Israel, and the foremost among them, with the sign

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...the believers, by a certain sign given from God, fled before the siege of the city of Jerusalem into the kingdom of King <term>Agrippa</term> <note>Herod Agrippa II, who ruled parts of Judea and was an ally to Rome during the Jewish-Roman War.</note>, who was a friend to the Romans, and they were saved. Wherefore David says: *You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow.* <note>original Latin: "Dedisti metuentibus te significationem, ut fugiant à facie arcus." From Psalm 60:4.</note> It is worthy of no small consideration that the Apostle Paul truly prophesied: namely, that some Jews would be obstinate until all the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish peoples.</note> everywhere are converted to Christ, and finally that they too will be completely converted at the end of the ages. He also brought forward that prophecy: *There shall come out of Zion He who shall deliver, and shall turn away captivity from Jacob, and this is my Covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins.* <note>Quoting Romans 11:26–27, which references Isaiah 59:20.</note> Thus, at last, in the appointed times, Judah shall be saved, and there shall be then, as was divinely predicted, one shepherd and one sheepfold; then shall be fulfilled that word of Zechariah: *In that day the Lord shall be one, and His name one.* Also that of Zephaniah: *Then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve Him with one shoulder.* <note>Zephaniah 3:9. "One shoulder" implies serving with a single, united effort.</note> Add again that of Ezekiel: *Then I will turn the captivity of Jacob and have mercy on the house of Israel.* To which this is similar: *I will bring back your captivity from all places.* 

But when shall these things be? Every day, those Jews who so desire are liberated from the captivity of both sin and men through the Messiah. However, this will appear most especially when they desire it most—that is, at the second coming of Christ, near the end of the world’s course. Then the Messiah will wage those battles with certain weapons against the impious, which Zechariah predicts regarding the future war of Jerusalem, and later adds: *In that day the Lord shall be one.* Then the Messiah will powerfully pour out His wrath upon the nations and kingdoms, just as the prophet Zephaniah threatens, where he adds: *Then I will restore to the peoples...* At that time, the battle of <term>Gog and Magog</term> <note>Symbolic enemies of God’s people described in Ezekiel 38–39.</note> described by Ezekiel will be fulfilled; when it is finished, Ezekiel predicts the redemption of Israel will occur: *Then I will turn the captivity.* Christ, therefore, in His first coming, gently remitted the sins of those who were willing through His doctrine, example, and works. In His second coming, He will undertake the matter more forcefully; He will purge more sharply, and by force He will cleanse the obstinate along with their leader, the <term>Antichrist</term>, for the order of divine discipline requires such a nature.

Daniel says: *I beheld in a vision of the night, and behold, one like the Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven.* Because of these and similar passages, the Jews expect a Christ who is not humble in appearance and fortune—as we have received Jesus—but magnificent and powerful, not knowing that His advent is twofold. He came once in humility to be judged; He will come at the last in magnificence to judge. That Daniel is speaking there about the final judgment of the world is apparent when he adds: *The thrones were set, and the books were opened.* Indeed, we have demonstrated in previous sections through many oracles of the Prophets that the first advent was to be humble, concerning which David says: *But I am a worm and no man, a reproach of men and the outcast of the people; all who see me have derided me; they have spoken with their lips and wagged their head. He hoped in the Lord, let Him deliver him, let Him save him because He desires him; for You are He who drew me from the belly. My hope from my mother’s breasts, upon You I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly, You are my God, do not depart from me.* <note>Psalm 22:6–11.</note> He adds many more things there that most clearly pertain to the same subject. 

Some of the Jews, when they read different oracles regarding different arrivals, introduced <term>two Messiahs</term>: one the "Son of Joseph"—that is, descending from the father Ephraim through a long line—who would be subject to suffering and slaughter; the other descending from David, whom they are accustomed to call the "Son of David," who would raise the other slain Messiah and powerfully restore the kingdom of Israel. But these people are clearly raving. For the Sacred Scriptures intend the salvation of the human race to depend on one, through one, and toward one; and when they speak of the Messiah, they almost always call him the offspring of David, or from there, but never the offspring of the father Ephraim. Hence, <term>Rabbi Moses</term> <note>Maimonides (1138–1204). Ficino refers to his "Book of Judges" (Sefer Shoftim) within the Mishneh Torah.</note> in the *Book of Judges*, bringing forward all the principal opinions concerning the Messiah, concludes that the Messiah will be of the lineage of David and makes no mention of another Messiah. They are insane, therefore, who fruitlessly introduce twins when one is sufficient. How much more rightly do we, through the one Jesus, fulfill all the prophecies, however diverse they may be. For He was judged by worldly men as humble once—the son of a certain Joseph by a kind of adoption, or by reputation and guardianship, and also the son of King David through His mother, who descended from David—and He shall also judge the world once with greatest power.

Isaiah says: *The light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun.* He is not speaking here of the time of the first advent, in which the accustomed order of the world was not to be changed (as we have said elsewhere), but of the age after the second coming of Christ. For the celestial bodies or elements will not cease after the final judgment, but rather their motion, which was instituted for the sake of rest, will cease; and then, with light overflowing in beau—

...the whole universe, he adds: *Then the wound of the people shall be healed, and the pressure of its blow,* <note>original: "Tūc ſanabiť uulnus populi & preſſura plagę eius." That many Prophets of the Hebrews foretold this is a matter of doubt to no one.

**Isaiah:** *He shall see a long-lived seed.*

**David:** *I will establish his seed for ever and ever.* In these two prophecies, Christ is promised as a spiritual seed, not a physical one; likewise a spiritual priesthood and kingdom, when it is said in David: *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,* and *I will establish his throne as the days of heaven.* Again: *Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of direction is the rod of your kingdom.* And shortly after he adds what pertains to the name of the Messiah <note>The word "Messiah" comes from the Hebrew *Mashiach*, meaning "The Anointed One."</note>, saying: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.* For he was anointed and consecrated more excellently than all kings—namely, because it was by God, and for eternity. Rightly had he said above that he was a priest according to the order of <term>Melchizedek</term>. For this Melchizedek is recorded in the sacred volumes to have been a priest of the Most High God, but one who was not anointed with common oil, nor one who received the priesthood through hereditary succession, as was the custom among the Hebrews. Therefore, Christ is predicted to be a priest according to his order, because he is consecrated not by the liquid of oil, but by the power of the heavenly Spirit.

Nathan also was commanded by God to prophesy to King David concerning the Messiah himself who was to be born from his lineage, in these words: *When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come from your womb.* This person, therefore, who is born after David's death, cannot be Solomon; rather, he is the Messiah, the eternal King, not a temporal one like Solomon, and one who builds not a temporal temple like Solomon, but an eternal temple for God. For God speaks thus to Nathan: *And I will restore his kingdom; he shall build a house for my name, and I will direct his throne even unto eternity. I will be to him as a father, and he shall be to me as a son.* This is because the Messiah is more the Son of God than the son of David. Shortly after he adds: *And his kingdom shall be forever before me,* namely, because it is in spiritual goods, not physical ones. Therefore he adds: *And his throne shall be raised up even unto eternity.*

Muhammad, understanding this kingdom better than the stubborn Jews, says in the <term>Alcoran</term> <note>The Quran. Renaissance scholars often cited it to find common ground or to use it as an "external witness" against Jewish or pagan arguments.</note>: *The Word of God, Jesus Christ, son of Mary, was sent by the Creator of the world to be the face of all nations in this age and the future one.* Such was the kingdom of Jesus of Nazareth, as is promised to Christ by the Prophets; therefore he himself said: *My kingdom is not of this world.* And to his successors, the Popes, he properly left authority in spiritual matters; nor does the substantial and chief jurisdiction of the Popes, insofar as they are Popes and vicars of Christ, extend further than the end of the world. Indeed, the lordship and administration of earthly things is accessory to the Popes, as if an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that isn't essential to the nature of a thing. Ficino argues that ruling land is not essential to being a Pope.</note>; not insofar as they are vicars of God, but insofar as they are the heirs of <term>Constantine Caesar</term> <note>A reference to the "Donation of Constantine," a document then believed to have granted the Popes temporal power over the Western Roman Empire.</note>. These things were said, however, not to take away the authority of temporal things from the Pope—for he truly possesses it, though as a certain "accident" without which a true Pope once existed for three hundred years, and can exist—but so that we may more easily avoid the arrows of the Jews with this truth.

For where Daniel signifies four kingdoms under the figures of four beasts, all the Jews wish the fourth beast to be understood as the Roman Empire. Since Daniel says the fourth beast must be destroyed by a kingdom raised up by the God of heaven, the Jews explain that the Roman Empire must be destroyed at the arrival of the Messiah. They add that the kingdom of the Church is entirely the same as that ancient Roman one, though narrower. From this they conclude that the Empire is a kingdom that must be dissolved after the Messiah they expect. They confirm this from the fact that Daniel says: *A little horn grew out of the fourth beast, which spoke words against the Most High,* such as they want Jesus and his vicar to have been. But this kind of scheme is false, both because the nature of the Roman kingdom consists in physical things, while the nature of the Christian kingdom consists in entirely incorporeal things. Therefore they are different kingdoms. From this we see even today that our Emperor is distinct from the Pope. Furthermore, Daniel says that the horn made war against the Saints and prevailed over them. This can in no way be said of Jesus or his vicar who is like him.

Add that in the same place Daniel predicts the fourth beast will perish when he comes *as a Son of Man in the clouds of heaven.* All this is to be fulfilled in the second coming of Christ, when he shall come with majesty and supreme power to judge. But in no way in the first coming, in which he is foretold by Daniel as coming not as a powerful and magnificent one, but like a *stone cut out and rejected.* <note>Referencing Daniel 2 and Psalm 118, symbolizing Christ’s humble first coming.</note> That "horn," however, will be the Antichrist—"little" indeed, because the Antichrist draws his origin from the lowliest dregs of the Jews. It is attached to the fourth beast, that is, of tyrannical power...

He also distinguishes between the essential spiritual power of the Papacy and its "accidental" temporal power derived from the Roman Empire.</summary>

Here, he focuses on the "fourth beast" (Rome) and how its eventual fall coincides with the arrival of the Antichrist and the second coming of Christ. He then shifts to Chapter 29, an polemical argument regarding the historical suffering of the Jewish people as a consequence of rejecting Jesus.</meta>

...power. For this beast signifies the universal tyranny of the world, from the beginning of Rome until the end of the world, which is destined to fall along with the supreme tyrant Antichrist during the second coming of Christ for judgment, near the end of the world. For Daniel says: *The judgment sat*, <note>original: "Iudicium ſedit" — Daniel 7:10.</note> and he says again, *immediately the end*. There are those who wish that by that "horn" <note>Referring to the "Little Horn" of Daniel 7:8.</note> is signified not only the Antichrist, but also the tyrannical heresy and the heretical tyranny of Muhammad, the king of the Arabs; for they say he is an image of the Antichrist, just as John the Baptist was an image of Christ. Moreover, that the fourth beast signifies a universal tyranny in every part of the world, arising from the first Romans down to the Antichrist and the end of the world, is clear from this: that even all the Jews agree that by the first beast is signified the universal tyranny of the world from the beginning of the world until Nebuchadnezzar. For the outcomes of things ought to correspond to their beginnings by a certain proportion.

<margin>Against the Jews, because they are wretched as a vengeance for Christ. Chapter XXIX.</margin>

If anyone considers the histories of the Hebrews, he will find that they were never oppressed by a heavy calamity except when they perpetrated some most shameful crime. Before the Babylonian servitude, they fell into idolatry and filled the streets of the city of Jerusalem with the blood of the Prophets (as is read in the Book of Kings) and committed other similar crimes; for that reason, they suffered a servitude of seventy years in the Babylonian region. Then, up until the times of our Jesus Christ, they lived justly enough; but they treated him no differently than the Prophets sent before him for his sake. Since, however, after they killed Jesus, they are punished longer and more bitterly than ever before, it is necessary that they then perpetrated a crime more monstrous than idolatry and the slaughter of the Prophets. Whence Jeremiah says: *They did not hear me, nor did they incline their ear, but they stiffened their neck and acted worse than their fathers.* <note>Jeremiah 7:26</note> This indeed shows that Jesus was the true Messiah, and more than a Prophet, and more than a divine man—indeed, that he was truly God. 

Tell me, I pray, you Jews, why in that volume of yours of new laws, the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism. Ficino views it here with the typical hostility of 15th-century Christian polemics.</note>, which you composed nearly four hundred years after Jesus, did you establish laws against Christians more cruel than Nero and Domitian <note>Two Roman Emperors famous for their persecution of early Christians.</note> could devise? Yet you were dispersed not by Christians, but by idolatrous Romans. Why with such poisonous curses do you especially imprecate the gravest evils upon us at least three times every day in your sacred rites, when we pray to God for you and are even milder toward you than the Muhammadans? Do you think the Christian law is more ignoble than the Muhammadan law? No, it is far more excellent. 

But nature herself, as I believe, secretly goads your minds to hatred of Christians, because clearly, on account of Jesus Christ, divine justice has scattered you. One can see in what way you opened the door for Christian vengeance, albeit unknowingly. Truly, because many among you, on account of impious negligence and ignorance of the Scriptures, did not believe that the unarmed Jesus was the true Messiah. Therefore, soon either expecting (as <term>Suetonius</term> <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian who noted a prophecy that "men coming from Judea would rule the world."</note> says) or already having (as many among you thought) another who was powerful in arms, you boldly rebelled against the Romans; because of which rebellion the city was utterly overturned, and men were killed and dispersed. We have these things from Suetonius. 

You are lost, therefore, because you did not believe in Jesus Christ, which we can indeed confirm by the words of your own <term>Josephus</term> <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian whose works are a primary source for the destruction of Jerusalem.</note>, who brings forward many signs of Divine indignation against the Jews, and most evident and horrific miracles. He affirms that in the height of the celebration, your city of Jerusalem—into which then nearly all of Judea had flocked for the sake of the <gloss>unleavened bread</gloss> <note>The feast of Passover.</note>—was besieged by the Romans. It is certain that either in those same days or in those years you killed Jesus. Josephus adds that Titus, who had besieged the city, was accustomed to say that because of many portents God was so angry with the Jews that he feared he too might be angered if he forgave them. And so, although it were not Titus, and likewise Vespasian, yet by the impulse of God, it was acted more cruelly—indeed more justly—than the Romans were ever elsewhere accustomed. Indeed, in that city more than eleven hundred thousand <note>1,100,000</note> Jews perished by hunger and the sword, while more than ninety thousand captives were sold. Thus says Josephus, who was also present. And <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian.</note> repeats this. 

Josephus adds these things: when Titus, going around, had thoroughly seen the trenches filled with the corpses of the dead, and the native earth soaked with the gore of human bodies, he, raised to heaven with a great groan and hands held up, called God as a witness that this was not his work. Then he adds this: "I think indeed that even if the arms of the Romans had ceased for a little while against the impious, the city would have paid the penalty of death either by a gaping of the earth, or by floods of water, or by Sodom-like fires and lightning sent from heaven, which city had brought forth a present generation of men much more ill-fated than those, because they had endured such things, and more wicked..."

<meta>This page continues Chapter XXIX of Marsilio Ficino’s *On the Christian Religion*. On the previous page, Ficino argued that the Jewish people suffered historical calamities only after committing great sins. Here, he provides historical accounts—citing Philostratus, Suetonius, and Josephus—to argue that the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD was divine punishment for the death of Christ and James the Just, preceded by supernatural omens.</meta>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...had attacked the Divinity, for which the entire nation equally deserved to be destroyed. Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–247 AD), a Greek sophist.</note> confirms the same in his *Life of Apollonius of Tyana* with these words: "Titus, having captured Jerusalem, had filled all the surrounding places with corpses. The neighboring nations wished to crown him for the victory, but he responded that he was unworthy of such an honor. For he himself had not been the author of such deeds, but had merely lent his hands to God, who was demonstrating His wrath against the Jews." Thus says Philostratus. Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor and father of Titus.</note> was present at that siege; when the city was destroyed and he had triumphed over the Jews—just as Suetonius <note>Roman historian, author of *The Twelve Caesars*.</note> narrates—he immediately performed two miracles in the presence of the people. For he cured a blind man and a lame man by touch alone. Yet it is recorded that he never did anything of the kind before or after, as if he had performed those miracles by divine help, immediately after he had avenged **Christian blood** by divine impulse. Although he was a reasonably just man, he did not possess such holiness, learning, or skill that he would seem able to perform miracles on his own. 

Clement and Hegesippus, disciples of the Apostles, write: James, the brother of the Lord, was so outstanding in justice in the opinion of everyone that even the most prudent of the Jews believed this was the cause of the siege of Jerusalem under Vespasian—which followed immediately after the death of James—because they had laid wicked hands upon him. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian.</note> clearly indicates that it seemed so to him through these words: "All these things," he says, "had happened to the Jews as vengeance for James the Just, who was the brother of Jesus, who is called the Christ." The Jews killed this man, whom everyone confessed to be the most just and pious of men; so says Josephus. 

Moreover, that God destroyed them for the sake of avenging **Christian blood** is evident from the fact that they committed no other crime in those times for which God should seem to be so sharply indignant; yet He was entirely indignant, as Josephus himself, who was present, reveals in the seventh book of *The Jewish War*. He says: "Certain most wicked men and deceivers, prophesying lies, persuaded the unhappy common people not to believe the evident signs and indications of divine wrath, by which the future slaughter of both the city and the nation was openly portended. But like madmen who had neither eyes nor soul, they scorned everything that was announced from heaven. For a star shining brightly, exactly like a sword, appeared to hang over the city, and a comet furthermore was seen to burn with deadly flames for an entire year. 

But even before the time of the slaughter and the war, when the people gathered for the feast day of the Unleavened Bread <note>original: "Azymorum" — referring to Passover.</note>, on the eighth day of the month of Xanthicus (which is April), at the ninth hour of the night, such a great flash of light surrounded the altar and the temple that everyone thought it had become bright daylight; it remained for half an hour. To the unskilled and ignorant it seemed a prosperous sign. But the omen of destruction was not hidden from the legal experts, the learned, and the upright teachers. 

In that same festival, a heifer brought for sacrifice and standing by the altars gave birth to a lamb right in the hands of the ministers. Furthermore, the gate of the inner shrine which faced the East—which was made of solid bronze and was of such immense weight that it required twenty men pushing with their greatest effort to close it, and was secured with iron bars and bolts and held fast by pins sunk deep into the floor—suddenly appeared to have opened of its own accord at the sixth hour of the night. 

But even after the festival day had passed, a few days later, on the twenty-first day of the month of Artemisios (that is, May), a prodigious sight appeared, almost exceeding belief; it would certainly be thought false had not the following ruin of evils confirmed the testimony of the eyes. For near sunset, chariots and four-horse teams were seen being carried through the air throughout the whole region, and cohorts of armed men were seen mixing among the clouds and surrounding the cities with unexpected battle-lines. 

On another feast day, which is called Pentecost, the priests entered the temple at night to complete the mysteries according to custom. First they felt certain movements and noises, then they suddenly heard voices saying: 'Let us migrate from here.' 

To these things another more terrible thing is added: a certain Jesus, the son of Ananias, a common and rustic man, four years before the war—when the city remained in peace and abundance—began to cry out suddenly on the feast day of Tabernacles: 'A voice from the East, a voice from the West, a voice from the four winds, woe upon Jerusalem and upon the temple, woe upon the bridegrooms and the brides, woe upon the whole people!' He went around all the streets day and night without ceasing, shouting this, until certain leaders among the people, moved by indignation at the ill-omened prophecy, seized the man and afflicted him with many lashes. But he said nothing in his own defense, nor did he plead with those standing around, but repeated the same cries with equal persistence and shouting. Then the leaders, understanding (as was the case) that the man was moved by a divine power, led him to the Roman Judge, before whom...

### ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

D 3

...he was mangled by whips even to the bones, yet he shed neither prayers nor tears; instead, emitting the same voice miserably and with a certain wailing, he uttered it at almost every lash. You might also add this: "Woe, woe to Jerusalem!" <note>Ficino is quoting Flavius Josephus, *The Jewish War* 6.5.3, regarding a man named Jesus, son of Ananias, who prophesied the city's destruction for years before the Roman siege.</note> So far, Josephus. But before him, Jesus had sadly foretold these things thus: **Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in those days. Pray, however, that your flight may not be in winter, nor on the Sabbath. For there will then be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall ever be.** Therefore, seeing the city, Jesus wept over it, saying: **If you also had known on this day what leads to your peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes, because days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and they will encircle you and press upon you from every side, and they will bring you and your children to the ground, and there will be great distress upon the land for this people, and they will fall by the edge of the sword, and be led captive into all nations. And Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near.** <note>These are composite quotations from the Gospels of Matthew (24) and Luke (19 and 21).</note> He also predicted other similar things; if anyone compares these with the history written by Josephus, he will not be able to doubt the divinity of Christ.

What else will you say to this, O miserable ones? For you were not afflicted only once, or for a short time—as usually happens to those who pay penalties for human offenses—but you wander everywhere and always in misery, as if paying penalties to the eternal God for the crime of treason against His majesty. Nor is this indeed an injustice. For you always sin, both because you are obstinate and because you disparage the mystery of Christ. Although many nations have resisted the Christians, you have been punished more rigidly by law than others, and you will be punished, because you—who were once honored by God above all others—were excessively ungrateful, and you killed the Prophets and Christ. You were the first of all to oppose the Christians, both in Judea by robbery and murder, and everywhere among the nations by treachery. You stirred up the powers of the Gentiles everywhere against them, which is why, by the example and instigation of many Jews, Christians were torn apart in every direction. But the heavenly Leader restored His army, though it was slaughtered on all sides, in wondrous ways, and increased it miraculously.

Even Muhammad confesses that you were scattered as a vengeance for Christ; he says in the Quran: **God snatched the soul of Jesus from the hands of the Jews, brought Him back to Himself and exalted Him, and placed the followers of Christ above his persecutors even until the judgment and end of the world. He decreed, moreover, that the unbelieving Jews, deprived of every avenger and protector, would be afflicted with the greatest torments in this life and the next.** <note>Ficino refers to the medieval Latin understanding of Quranic verses such as 3:54-55 and 4:157-158.</note> But listen to your "Moses the Egyptian" <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> in the *Book of Ordinary Judges* <note>Referring to the *Mishneh Torah*, specifically the "Laws of Kings and Their Wars" (Hilkhot Melakhim) 11:4, which discusses Jesus as a failed Messiah whose actions led to Israel's ruin.</note> saying: **Jesus of Nazareth appeared to be the Messiah, and was killed by the sentence of the judges; he was the cause for Israel being destroyed by the sword.**

Indeed, divine justice—although it oppressed you with various and heavy calamities and slaughters almost every year immediately after Jesus until the time of Titus (as Florus, Josephus, Philo, and Eusebius show)—nevertheless delayed that ultimate destruction of your city until the fortieth year after Jesus. This was done so that you might have time for repentance, and so that the beginning of the Christian law might become more clearly known to all ages from such a great city of yours, removed from the confusion of things and times. It also happened so that, while the city still stood, the Christians could be more violently tortured by you, and thus more accurately tested. 

However, Christ punished you by the hands of idolaters, not Christians, to show that His Christians ought to live and be able to reign without any violence. And He punished so miraculously that Christ predicted nothing more miserable had ever been or would be, just as Josephus confirmed. Read the fifth book of Josephus regarding these matters; <note>The account of the famine is actually found in Book 6 of *The Jewish War*.</note> you will see that even mothers devoured their own sons because of hunger. But to comprehend everything in brief: no tragedy more mournful can be imagined. Your own people once predicted that this misery would be the vengeance for Christ. For when Pilate said, **I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you see to it,** they responded: **His blood be upon us and upon our children.**

<meta>This page continues Chapter XXIX of Marsilio Ficino’s *On the Christian Religion*. The previous page analyzed the destruction of Jerusalem through the lens of Roman historians and Gospel prophecies. This page organizes the arguments into three specific points (chapters) to prove that the Jewish Diaspora is a divine punishment for the death of Jesus.</meta>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

->A resumption of the proof concerning the Christian retribution, divided into three points.<-

But since you diligently devise various causes every day for this calamity of yours, in order to escape the blame for the Christian slaughter, let us repeat the whole matter from the beginning and collect it into three points. We consider it necessary that three things especially concur in that crime, by the fault of which you are scattered. The first indeed is that which we touched upon from the beginning: namely, that it is much more grievous than that fault for which you were once dispersed into Babylon, and at least as much more grievous as your condition after Jesus is worse than it was in that dispersion. This calamity is said to have begun from the unspeakable slaughter of your people and a most base sale <note>Ficino refers to the historical accounts of Jewish captives being sold into slavery by the Romans after the fall of Jerusalem.</note>—frequently indeed at other times, and severely before Titus, and after Jesus, but especially at Jerusalem under Titus, and in Mesopotamia under Trajan, and at Betar under Hadrian, and everywhere under Gallus—which certainly did not happen in that dispersion which was before Christ. Add to this that under Claudius, beyond all other calamities, God also oppressed you with extreme famine, as Luke says, which Josephus also asserts was great in Judea during the time of Claudius. <note>Ficino cites Acts 11:28 (attributed to Luke) and Flavius Josephus (*Antiquities* 20.2.5) regarding a famine in the mid-1st century AD.</note> Again, in other dispersions, you had honored leaders of your own race everywhere, and you preserved the legitimate and intact worship of your sacred rites; but in this one, by no means. Furthermore, God then consoled you by the mission of Prophets, who either promised a swift liberation, such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel, or showed it to be already imminent, such as Daniel, Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah. From this it appears that God then held you as sons, not as enemies as He does today. For you have had no Prophet after Jesus, which the Psalm threatened you with: **"Now there is no Prophet, and he shall know you no more."** <note>original: "Iam non est Propheta, & uos non cognoscet amplius." A reference to Psalm 74:9.</note> Why has God for so long now entirely deprived you of life—for the most part—and of the Priesthood, the kingdom, and the Prophets? To show that you are devoid of all divine hope and inheritance, as rebels long ago rejected. How then can you expect the Messiah from Him? From whom you do not even obtain the heralds and likenesses of the Messiah. Lastly, at other times you were exiled for a certain brief time and to certain regions; after Jesus, you have been exterminated for a very long time, indeed universally and through the whole world, as those who properly offended against God Himself—who is always and everywhere—when you destroyed Jesus. When you killed the Prophets, you sinned against God’s messengers; when you worshipped idols, you took away the kingdom from God as much as was in your power; what remained for you, except to vent your rage against the very person of God? If, therefore, by killing Jesus you committed a crime greater than the slaughter of the Prophets and idolatry, then you certainly vented your rage against God; and conversely, if you ever laid impious hands upon God, it could only have been done then, when you laid them upon Jesus, who alone in the whole world, by his virtues and wonders alone, showed himself to be the true Son of the most high God, and God. Let this much be said concerning the first point.

In the second place, it pertains to this guilt of yours, because of which you wander as miserable exiles, that it is common to all of you, everywhere and always; for you individually and continually lead a miserable life among all nations. No other crime can be imagined with which you are individually and constantly infected, except that you disapprove of the life of Jesus and his disciples, but approve of the slaughter, for which reason you are participants in the Christian slaughter; which Jeremiah touched upon thus: **"Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? For you have all transgressed against me."** <note>original: "Quid uultis mecum iudicio contendere? omnes enim uos deliquistis in me." Reference to Jeremiah 2:29.</note> Since you indeed find fault with the calf fashioned in the world, or the slaughter of the Prophets, or any other of the monstrous crimes of your ancestors, and you lack any inclination toward either killing Prophets or fashioning idols, it follows that you are in no way properly participants in those crimes. Therefore, those who think you are weighed down by this calamity because of the idols worshipped or the Prophets killed are raving.

The third thing which pertains to the cause of such great misery seems to be that the guilt is hidden and unknown to you; for in that Talmudic book which is titled *Megillah*, <note>original: "Magnila." Ficino refers to the Talmudic tractate Megillah 3a or 6a, discussing the causes of the exile.</note> it is asked why the end of the affliction was foretold for those wandering in Babylonia, which Jeremiah thus testifies: **"After seventy years have been completed in Babylon, I will visit you."** <note>original: "Postquam completi fuerint in Babylone septuaginta anni, uisitabo uos." Reference to Jeremiah 29:10.</note> But for those wandering after Titus, no end of miseries was ever foretold. To this, it is answered there briefly: "Then the end of evils was shown to them, just as the fault for which they suffered the evils was open; but for these, to whom the fault is unknown, the end is also unknown." So it says there. Indeed, no other common crime of yours is entirely unknown to all of you, except that which your ancestors committed against Jesus, and which you approve.

**ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION**

**For not only do you not know it to be an evil, but since it is the very worst thing, you think it to be the best.**

->Confirmation of our arguments from Jewish sources against the Jews concerning the sacred books. Chapter XXX.<-

You Jews carry around everywhere, and always—by God's will <note>original: *Deo uolente*</note>—the Hebrew books of the Prophets. From these, anyone can understand that Christians did not invent the prophecies of the Prophets, as David touched upon: "My God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not slay them, lest they should ever forget your law; scatter them in your power." <note>original: *Deus meus demonstrauit mihi de inimicis meis, ne occideris eos, ne quando obliuiscantur legem tuam, dispergere eos in uirtute tua* (Psalm 59:11-12).</note> Thus, you are unwilling witnesses to our truth everywhere. We also possess the sacred writings of the Prophets, translated by many into the Greek and Latin tongues after the time of Christ. Furthermore, we have that translation made under King Ptolemy, more than three hundred years before Christ, by seventy-two Jews <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. While "Septuagint" means 70, tradition often cites 72 translators—six from each of the twelve tribes.</note> chosen from all the people by Eleazar the High Priest as the most excellent of all. Aristeas the Greek, a member of that king’s household who was present, writes of this, as does Josephus. They add that for the sake of this translation, the king redeemed one hundred thousand Jews who were serving in Egypt from slavery with his own money, gave incredible gifts to the Temple and the High Priest, and honored the translators in a marvelous manner. I use this translation more willingly so that I may convict this faithless Jewish commonry with the distinguished weapons of those illustrious Jews. Nor should it be thought that those volumes, which had already been spread throughout the world long ago, were corrupted by Christians—especially by the first Christians, who, venerating them as a thing sent from heaven, defended their mysteries with their own blood.

->Concerning miracles.<-

I come now to the miracles, which you do not indeed deny; rather, in many of your histories, you confirm that both the Apostles and Jesus performed miracles. But some among you say that Jesus, as a healer among the Egyptians during a few years of his childhood, learned magic at most—a matter exceedingly difficult, which so many and such great philosophers, flocking there from all sides even in their mature age, could not learn even in the smallest part after many years. For what magician, when he had been publicly seized and killed with the greatest ignominy, could immediately achieve being regarded everywhere as the Supreme God? What magic did those unrefined fishermen use after Jesus was dead? It is necessary that they performed miracles; otherwise, the slain Jesus would have completely lost all authority in a short time. If they were magicians, why did they not, as ambitious men usually do, preach themselves rather than Jesus—a beggar publicly put to death by an infamous end? Indeed, by what art did those rustic fishermen ensnare Paul and Apollos—Jews who were the most learned of all men—and many other highly educated and famous individuals to endure death? Or how did Paul similarly entrap Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite, the most excellent of all Platonic philosophers, and others like them? What pleasure, what utility was offered to them by magic, when they were daily in peril, not for their own sake, but for the love of Christ?

Hence Justin, an excellent Philosopher, in the book he wrote to the Emperor Antoninus on behalf of our religion, says: "I myself, having been instructed in the Platonic sects, when hearing the Christians being reviled and seeing them fearless in facing death and enduring every punishment, considered that it was impossible for them to live in wickedness and lust." <note>A reference to Justin Martyr's *Second Apology*.</note> These are his words. But hear freely Tertullian, who lived near the time of Justin, crying out thus to the Roman judges: "Nature has drenched every evil thing in either fear or shame. Finally, evildoers long to hide; they avoid appearing; they tremble when caught; they deny when accused; even when tortured, they do not easily or always confess; certainly, when condemned, they grieve, they rave against themselves, and they attribute the impulses of an evil mind to fate or the stars. For they do not want it to be their own, because they recognize it as evil. But what is there like this among Christians? No one is ashamed, no one repents, except clearly for not having been a Christian sooner. If he is marked, he glories; if he is accused, he does not defend himself; when questioned, he confesses even of his own accord; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of evil is this, which lacks the fear, shame, evasion, repentance, and lamentation of a martyr’s <note>Tertullian uses "martyrialis" to contrast the "evil" of the Christian with the "evil" of a common criminal.</note> suffering? What kind of evil is this,"

He further defends the legitimacy of Christ's miracles by citing the transformation of the Apostles and the testimonies of early Church Fathers like Justin Martyr and Tertullian.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

<meta>catchword: whose</meta>

...whose defendant rejoices, whose accusation is a prayer, and whose punishment is happiness. <note>Ficino is continuing a thought from the previous page about the unique nature of Christian martyrdom, where the accused finds joy in their faith.</note> He moreover refutes the rashness of the Gentile judges, because they cruelly condemned Christians for the mere name of their sect without ever discovering any actual crime. They neither inquired what such a sect believed, nor did they wish to hear it from the Christians themselves. Finally, as I have said elsewhere, the most holy purpose of this discipline clearly declares that Christ and his disciples performed miracles not by magic, but by divinity. There exists among you a book on the life of Jesus of Nazareth <note>Likely referring to the *Toledot Yeshu*, a medieval Jewish polemic that Ficino repurposes here.</note>, in which it is read that Jesus, among other miracles—many of which are narrated there—even raised the dead. This was because, clearly, he alone knew how to correctly pronounce that proper name of God, which is to be venerated by you above all others. Because it consists of only four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note>, and is indeed the most difficult of all names to pronounce, it sounds roughly in this manner: *Hiehouahi* <note>original: *Hiehouahi*. An early attempt to transliterate the Hebrew name of God, often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh.</note>, which is to say: He was, He is, He shall be; and the greater part of the Hebrews hold this opinion. If this is so, since nothing is held more holy among you than this name, and therefore it cannot be used to confirm anything profane, then without doubt the doctrine of our Christ is divine. For as you say, it was established by the power of that most divine name, and as we assert, it was established by the power of God.

->*Testimony of John the Baptist and Josephus.*<-

Cease now to rave, O Jews, as insane as you are wretched. Do you not believe that divine man whom the whole world honors without controversy, John the Baptist? He was, as Josephus says, in truth and in public estimation the very pattern of all virtues. To him, as if to an oracle, a vast multitude of Jews and others flowed together from everywhere. These are the words of your own Josephus. Now, that same John undoubtedly affirmed openly that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah, and commanded all to follow him. Otherwise, not everyone who spoke of Jesus at that time would have begun their accounts with John’s testimony and confirmation, celebrating him with such wonderful praises. It is evident to everyone that the lives of Jesus and John are narrated together by the Evangelists. Since Muhammad <note>original: *Mahumethes*</note> was not ignorant of their friendship, he sang the birth, life, and praises of both John the Baptist and Jesus in the same chapter of the Quran <note>original: *Alcorani*. Referring to Surah Maryam or Surah Al-Imran.</note>. There he called Jesus the Spirit and the Word of God, and in the same place he said that John was a great Prophet and a confirmer of the divine word. Certainly, John confirmed it in such a way that Jesus received his first disciples from him.

Finally, hear what your Josephus says of Christ in the books *On the Antiquity of the Jews* <note>The *Antiquities of the Jews* by Flavius Josephus.</note>, which he wrote in Greek. This was read in ancient copies, both Greek and Latin, even before the time of Constantine, and it is still read today, as Jerome and Eusebius testify. Nor could books that were so widely dispersed and held in the highest authority by everyone be so corrupted, especially at a time when Christians were most subject to slanderers everywhere. I do not find that any of those enemies noted that the books of Josephus or the Prophets had been corrupted.

But let us come to Josephus. "At that same time," he says, "there was Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man, for he was a doer of wonderful works and a teacher of those people who gladly hear what is true, and he joined to himself many of the Jews and many also from the Gentiles. This was Christ (as he was believed). When Pilate, upon the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had decreed that he should be led to the cross, those who had loved him from the beginning did not desert him. For he appeared to them again alive on the third day, just as the divinely inspired Prophets had predicted these and countless other future miracles concerning him. But to this very day, both the name and the race of the Christians, who are named after him, persevere." <note>This famous passage is known as the *Testimonium Flavianum*. While its total authenticity is debated by modern scholars, Ficino uses it as a core historical proof.</note> In another place he also says: "Ananias the younger, a bold and insolent man in his character, accusing the brother of Jesus, who is called Christ, James by name, and many others as though they were acting against the law, delivered them to be stoned. Those who seemed to be the most moderate of the city, and to have a concern for the integrity of the law, took this heavily, and sent secretly to the king, asking him to write to Ananias not to perpetrate such things, since he had not acted rightly before." These are the words of Josephus in the twentieth book of the *Antiquities*.

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION
## On the resurrection of Christ.

D 5
<meta>catchword: baptized</meta>

As for the other miracles of Jesus—since they were many, performed often and in the presence of the people, and are celebrated by many—you do not dare to deny them. However, concerning the Resurrection, although many have written about it, you deny it entirely because it was not known to everyone. Yet you see this confirmed by Josephus <note>Ficino refers to the *Testimonium Flavianum*, a passage in Flavius Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews* (18.3.3) that mentions Jesus’s resurrection. While debated by modern scholars, Renaissance thinkers viewed it as definitive proof.</note>. Or do you not know that the body of Jesus, which after the resurrection had been made entirely immortal and divine, was not fitting to be seen by the eyes of just any mortals, but only by those who had been appointed by God as witnesses for others? Moreover, they saw Jesus raised from the dead over forty days, frequently and many times; not only the Apostles or disciples, but even more than five hundred brothers gathered together at once, as the Apostle Paul testifies, saying that many of them were still living when he wrote those things <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:6.</note>. Not only do those men testify that Jesus truly rose; so too do thousands upon thousands of men, both Jews and Gentiles, who—just as those others did—most willingly underwent certain and most bitter deaths for the glory of being killed publicly and ignominiously for Jesus. Therefore, that story invented by you is to be mocked: that the disciples snatched his body from the tomb and hid it among the plants in the gardens, but shortly after it was found by spies sent for this very purpose by the High Priest <note>Ficino is refuting the "theft hypothesis" found in Jewish polemics like the *Toledot Yeshu*, which claimed the body was hidden in a garden.</note>. O how excessively reckless and foolish you are! Why did you not hang that corpse in the forum? If you were striving to utterly destroy the glory of Jesus, in that way everyone would have immediately abandoned the Nazarene sect.

->Confirmation of the Trinity of God and the divinity of Christ from Jewish sources:<-
->Chapter XXXI.<-

Why do you revile the divine Trinity, being entirely ignorant of your own mysteries? Read the commentaries of your own interpreters on the Psalm: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken, and called the earth" <note>original: *Deus Deus Dominus locutus est* (Psalm 50:1). Ficino highlights the repetition of divine names as a hint of the Trinity.</note>. For in those it is asked why the Psalm calls upon God three times, and they answered: clearly to show that God created the world by these three names, according to the three properties by which the world was created. These are indeed: wisdom, knowledge, and understanding, just as it is read in the Proverbs of Solomon: "The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, he established the heavens by understanding, and by his knowledge the depths break forth." God is also named three times in Exodus: "I am the Lord your God, a jealous God." Behold, three divine names according to the three properties of God by which all things were established. It is read similarly in the Book of Joshua: "The God of gods, the Lord himself knows" <note>original: *Deus Deus Dominus ipse scit* (Joshua 22:22).</note>. You will find a similar exposition in your commentaries on Genesis, especially in that part: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth," where Rabbi Eleazar says: "The world was not created except through the Word, or with the Word of God, just as it is held in the Psalm: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made." And it follows in the same place: Rabbi Simeon says, "God breathed or blew the Holy Spirit, and the world was created, just as it is read in the Psalm: By the breath of his mouth is all their power (otherwise, their host)." <note>Rabbi Eleazar and Rabbi Simeon (Shimon bar Yochai) were figures frequently cited by Christian Kabbalists to show that Jewish tradition supported the concepts of the "Word" (Logos) and the "Spirit" as creative forces.</note> You deny that God has a natural son—that is, one of the same nature—yet God says in the Psalms: "You are my son, today I have begotten you." Nor can this be said of angels or souls, which were not begotten, but created. For they did not proceed from the substance of God, but from nothing; therefore, even if they are sometimes called "sons of God" in the sacred scriptures, they are never said by God to be "begotten." But he said "today," that is, in eternity—"today" meaning in that present state of eternity which has neither beginning nor end. For whatever is of the substance of God and within God is eternal. Therefore, in the Psalm: "Give the king your judgment, O God," where it is clearly treated as being about the Son of God, it is said of that very Son: "His name shall endure for ages, and his name remains before the sun." That this refers to the eternal Son of God is declared by the fact that where our translation says "remains," the Hebrew text has *ynnon* <note>original: *ynnon* (Yinnon). In Jewish tradition (Psalm 72:17), Yinnon is considered one of the names of the Messiah.</note>, which indeed is a word derived from *nyn* <note>original: *nyn* (nin), meaning progeny or son.</note>; *nyn* is "son." What else, therefore, does *ynnon* signify than the son, the begotten, the born, and the perfect? Solomon in Proverbs is a witness that God has a son: "Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters as in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name? And what is his son's name, if you know?" Hear moreover Isaiah crying out to God: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth." The "thrice Holy" signifies the Trinity of divine persons; "Lord," in the singular, signifies the unique substance of God. "All the earth is full of his glory" signifies the assumption of humanity made by the Word of God, for in the same place Isaiah placed God on a throne in the figure of a man.

...spoke. Moreover, so that he might show that you would not sufficiently understand mysteries of this kind, he adds much concerning your blindness, deafness, and stubbornness, which we have recounted elsewhere. He also introduces God speaking in another place: *Come near to me, hear these things; from the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time that they were done, I was there; and now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit.* <note>original: "Accedite ad me, audite hæc à principio, nō in abscondito locutus sum..." — A quote from Isaiah 48:16. Ficino interprets the "me" being sent as the pre-existent Christ.</note> Therefore, he who from the beginning—namely, of the Law—did not speak in secret—specifically because he spoke openly on Mount Sinai in the hearing of everyone, and who was also there at that time, being himself God the author of the Law—is now sent by God; that is, the Son, God begotten of God the Father, has assumed human nature. The Spirit of God also sends him, since the union of God and man was brought about through the Holy Spirit. Each of these who sends is necessarily God, since he who is sent is God; and although God is one, there is nevertheless a certain, though unthinkable, distinction between those who send and the one who is sent. Moreover, that the one who is introduced here as speaking is God himself is clear from what precedes it, for he says: *I am the first, and I am the last; my hand founded the earth.* <note>Isaiah 48:12-13.</note> It is also clear from what follows, for after all the things we have cited, it is added: *Thus says the Lord your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.* 

But one may also hear David crying out: *Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there.* <note>Psalm 139:7-8.</note> In these words, he intends the Spirit of God to be everywhere, yet Jews and Christians alike hold that only God is everywhere. It is established, therefore, that this Spirit is not some "breathing" external to God, but is the Holy Spirit and exists as God, of whom Job says: *The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.* <note>Job 33:4.</note> To make a human being—that is, the soul—and to give life is the duty of God alone. 

Furthermore, in those commentaries of yours on Genesis <note>referring to Midrashic or Rabbinic traditions</note>, it is asked what that "spirit of God" is which was "hovering over the waters," and the answer is given there: "This is the spirit of the Messiah," of whom we read in Isaiah, *and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding.* <note>Isaiah 11:2.</note> From this it is clear both that the Spirit is God and that the Messiah is God. Likewise, in the same commentaries, Rabbi Simeon <note>Likely Simeon bar Yochai, to whom the Zohar is traditionally attributed.</note> says: "What is that which we read in the Psalm, *by the spirit of his mouth is all their power?*" <note>Psalm 33:6.</note> and he answers: "This means God breathed the spirit of his mouth, and the world was created." 

To this is added what Rabbi Moses Gerundensis <note><term>Rabbi Moses Gerundensis</term> is the Latin name for Nahmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note> says in explaining *In the beginning God created heaven and earth*: "In the beginning," he says, "that is, in Wisdom, which is the principle of principles." And therefore, in the Jerusalem translation <note>The <term>Jerusalem Targum</term>, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, in place of "In the beginning," it says "In wisdom." Moreover, that there is in God a certain Wisdom conceived by God from eternity like an offspring, the Prophet Solomon reveals, introducing Wisdom speaking thus: *Listen, for I am about to speak of great things... The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he did anything from the beginning; I was ordained from eternity, and of old, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the springs of water had not yet broken forth, nor had the mountains settled with their heavy mass; before all the hills I was being birthed. He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the hinges of the world. When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when with a fixed law and circle he enclosed the depths... I was with him, composing all things. I rejoiced before him at all times.* <note>Proverbs 8:22-30. This passage was central to early Christian arguments for the divinity of Christ as the "Logos" or Wisdom of God.</note> In these words it is clear that Wisdom of this kind was not only conceived from eternity but was also "being birthed"—nay, was already present as a completed being, and rejoiced, and as if distinct from the generator by its own nature, was with him, composing all things as if it were God itself. And although it is begotten of the father, it nevertheless always existed simultaneously with the father; for things which happen without motion are performed in an instant; such things, while they are being made, already are. Just as air, while it is being illuminated, is already illuminated, and the truth and reason of things, while being understood, is already understood. Therefore, the Word and Reason of God itself, because it is begotten without motion and in an intelligible manner, is already born while it is being conceived; while it is being born, it is simultaneously present, and simultaneously composes all things.

This was a most ancient opinion among your fathers, for Moses says: *In the beginning Heloym created...* and so forth. *Heloym* is plural, for its singular is *Heluel*. <note>Ficino is discussing the Hebrew name for God, <term>Elohim</term> (plural), and its singular form <term>Eloah</term>. He argues the plural name used with a singular verb (*creavit*) points to the Trinity.</note> Yet "created" is singular. Surely because in the one and simple essence of God there is a certain number of persons, Moses and many other Hebrews used this manner of speaking regarding God alone, using a plural name with a singular verb, and vice versa. A similar number in God is signified even in the last book of Joshua: *You will not be able to serve the Lord, because he is the holy God*; the Hebrew truth holds: *because the Heloym are holy.* Again, Jeremiah: *You have perverted the words of the living God, the Lord...*

<summary>Ficino argues for the divinity of Christ and the Trinity by citing Hebrew scripture and Rabbinic authorities, specifically interpreting "Wisdom" and the plural name "Elohim" as evidence of multiple persons within the one God.</summary>
