<meta>This page continues from page 52. Ficino is in the middle of a complex theological argument, using Hebrew grammar and biblical phrasing to prove that the "oneness" of God in the Old Testament actually implies a Trinity of persons. He specifically focuses on the plural noun 'Elohim' used with singular verbs.</meta>

...of the armies of our God, the Hebrew truth <note>original: "Hebraica ueritas" — a term often used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> has *Elohim chayim*, <note>original: "Heloym haym"</note> that is, "of the living Gods." However, what follows is singular, just as we have it. The plural name of God is joined to a plural verb in the second book of Kings: *What nation is like the people of Israel? For whose sake God went to redeem them for himself as a people.* The Hebrew truth says *iv'ru Elohim*, <note>original: "iuerunt Heloym"</note> that is, "Gods went." <note>Ficino is pointing out that the Latin verb "iuerunt" is plural, which he argues reflects a plural nature in the divine.</note> Likewise, in Ecclesiastes, one reads: *Who is the man who can follow the King, his Maker?* The Hebrew text says: *Who is the man who may enter after the King, they who have already made him?* 

When David speaks to God himself, he says: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.* Does he not place a certain difference in God between the one who is anointed and the one who anoints—or rather, those who anoint? For he touched upon the Son, who is anointed, and the Father and the Spirit, when he said of those who anoint: "God, God." That he speaks to God himself is clear from the preceding words, for he foretold: *Your throne, O God.* But also when he says of the Lord his God: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand,* does he not signify a personal difference between him who sits at the right hand and him near whom he sits? That these two agree in nature, the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> demonstrates, for it says: *The Lord said to his Word.* It appears also through those things which follow in the same Psalm: *From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you,* that is, before anything was created, from my innermost substance and within, which is appropriate only to God the Son of God. Yet two persons are shown even when it is said, "I have begotten you," for the begetter and the begotten differ in person. 

Why do we wander further? Moses declares the matter itself, for he says: *God said, let us make man in our image and likeness,* and adds, *God made man.* In this speech, he attributes a singular property to God twice, and a plural one twice, so that he might more effectively declare that within the unity of essence there is a number of persons. Hence God, speaking to Moses, says: *I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.* The first part designates that there is one substance of God; then, by the threefold repetition, he reveals the number of the three persons. 

But one must remember that although in a human craftsman, power, wisdom, and will (or goodness) differ in a certain way, nevertheless no one says because of this kind of difference, "that craftsman they made" or "those craftsmen he made," because those three do not constitute different persons. Only in God, and as if always, the sacred scriptures join the plural with the singular, because clearly in him alone there is a unique nature and three persons; and in him there are not only three powers, as in a craftsman, but also three persons distinguished from one another and united in a certain miraculous way.

->*Confirmation of the Messiah's passion against the Jews, from Jewish sources.*<-
### Chapter XXXII.

You mock us, you ridiculous people, because we believe the Messiah was to suffer for original sin; however, that he was to suffer many and grave things, we have already shown often in the preceding pages, first by reasoning and then from the mind of both your Prophets and your interpreters. But I know what you wanted: namely, that God by his own liberality or clemency would forgive the sins of men without the passion of the Messiah. Have you forgotten that ancient maxim which has always held great weight among your teachers: that God governs all things, especially human things, by a double measure—namely, mercy and justice? *All the ways of the Lord,* says David, *are mercy and truth,* that is, justice. Again: *Holy and terrible is his name.* 

Your interpreters want the measure of mercy to be signified in sacred scripture where it says *Adonai* [Lord], but the measure of justice where it says *Elohim*, <note>original: "Eloyn"</note> that is, "God." Therefore, Rabbi Joshua, <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Joshua ben Levi, a famous 3rd-century scholar.</note> considering the power of both names joined together in Moses' words: *The Lord God sent Adam out from the garden of pleasure to cultivate the earth,* says: "With a certain measure of justice and mercy God created Adam; with the same he gave him the commandment; with the same he cast him out." This is from Joshua. Because, clearly, not only in the expulsion, but also in the creation and the commandment of Moses, "the Lord God" similarly brings forth fruit. For God used justice in creating Adam, because he formed him in no other way than that he should correspond both to his "Idea" (which is always in God, through which he forms) and to the divine goodness for whose sake he forms. He used mercy again because, with no preceding merits of Adam, he bestowed life and other goods upon him. He was merciful in commanding, he who abundantly granted the use of almost innumerable fruits. He was, moreover, just, he who prohibited the eating of the tree of knowledge of good and evil with certain threats.

### Page 60

For it was fitting that man, by some law, should acknowledge and declare himself to be subject to God. Ultimately, God was just when He punished man with expulsion after his transgression <note>original: "praeuaricationem" — referring to the Fall of Adam and Eve</note>; yet He was also profoundly merciful, since He afflicted him with a finite punishment even though man, by offending an infinite God, had in a sense sinned infinitely. Do you then wish for Adam and the human race—his offspring—to be reconciled to God the Creator under the Messiah without that bond of mercy and justice, that is, through mercy alone? Far be it from us. Remember that which you repeat daily from Deuteronomy: *The works of God are perfect, and all His ways are judgments. A faithful God without any iniquity, He is righteous and just.* <note>original: "Dei perfecta sunt opera, & omnes uiæ eius iudicia. Deus fidelis absque ulla iniquitate, rectus & iustus est." - Deuteronomy 32:4</note> Therefore, it was consistent with God's mercy that He should eventually reconcile the human race to Himself, but consistent with His justice that some <term>satisfaction</term> <note>In theology, "satisfaction" is the idea of making amends or paying a debt to restore justice after a sin has been committed.</note> should intervene, or at least that the Messiah should satisfy for the rest. Of Him, Isaiah says: *All we like sheep have gone astray, and man has wandered from his path,* <note>original: "Omnes nos sicut oues errauimus, & homo a uia sua errauit." - Isaiah 53:6</note> that is, all men have erred because Adam, the father of all, wandered from his path. He then adds concerning the Messiah: *and God placed upon him the iniquity of us all.* 

I know, however, that you are accustomed to object here as follows: It is absurd to believe that the greatest of crimes—which many committed in killing the Messiah—could wash away the crimes of men; nor does the passion of one man satisfy for the sins of all; nor is it just for the innocent Messiah to satisfy for other guilty parties. We, however, respond briefly in this way: It was not by the crime of the murderers, but by the virtue of the Messiah in enduring evils, that evils were deleted. Therefore, in the suffering Christ, there was a greater charity and virtue than there was hatred and vice in all the transgressors, and the life of Christ alone was more worthy than the lives of all others together. Therefore, when He gave His life for all, He satisfied far more than was sufficient. Furthermore, one person can satisfy for another, as we see happening every day in civil matters; for satisfaction consists in outward acts, and for these, both instruments and friends can be accepted. But because <term>penitence</term> involves the internal act of the mind and will, that penitence belongs to the one who sinned; therefore, any sinners must be affected by penitence for their own faults. Thus, God the Messiah is seen to have satisfied for everyone. Then that saying of Isaiah is fulfilled: *Truly he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows; he was bruised for our crimes, and by his bruises we are healed.* <note>original: "Vere languores nostros ipse tulit... liuore eius sanati sumus." - Isaiah 53:4-5</note> Nevertheless, we do not escape here without punishment, for from the beginning of the world to the end, we undergo many hardships because of that <term>original sin</term>. In Christ, however, the passion was brief, the virtue and perfection were wondrous, and the happiness is everlasting. 

God had decreed from eternity that the Messiah would be the redeemer of the human race—a "redeemer," I say, who would redeem us from the slavery of deadly guilt. Of this, Isaiah says: *A redeemer shall come from Zion.* And this is the excellent dignity in the Messiah, which He would have lacked unless He had deleted the stains of the people through the sacrifice of His own flesh. We have found in sacred histories that holy men always accustomed themselves to appease God by the offering of sacrifices—especially by the sprinkling of blood—to obtain gifts from Him, to deliver the people from imminent dangers, to ratify divine laws, and once a year to purge the sins of the people. Even the Gentiles imitated this, though not lawfully. 

But let us come for now to the Hebrews. First, we read in Genesis where Noah, after that common flood, built an altar to the Lord on which he offered burnt offerings; for this reason, God was appeased and decreed that no further flood of this kind should happen to the world. For it follows in the same place: *The Lord smelled a sweet odor, and the Lord said to him: I will never again curse the earth because of man.* <note>original: "odoratus est Dominus odorem suauitatis... nequaquam ultra maledicam terræ propter hominem." - Genesis 8:21</note> Second, also in Genesis, where Abraham was first ready to sacrifice his son by God's command, and then, prohibited by God through an angel, he finally offered a ram and slaughtered it to God. Because of this will and victim, God promised Abraham a singular gift with a sworn oath: that all Nations (whosoever wish) would be saved in his seed. Third, it is found in Exodus, for there the people are delivered from the Egyptian calamity by the sprinkling of the blood of the Paschal lamb on the doorposts and thresholds of their houses. *I will see the blood,* He says, *and I will pass over, and there shall be no destroying plague among you.* <note>Exodus 12:13</note> Fourth, also in Exodus, where Moses, wishing to ratify the law received from God, sprinkles the blood of victims over the people so that the covenant between God and men might be confirmed by this method. For so it is read there: *Moses, taking the blood, sprinkled it on the people and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.* <note>Exodus 24:8</note> Fifth, in Leviticus, the Day of Atonement is treated, concerning which it is read: *On this day the atonement*

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

### Page 41

On that day there shall be expiation, and a cleansing from all your sins; before the Lord you shall be cleansed. For indeed, the High Priest, entering the Holy of Holies once every year, would pour out the blood of the sacrifices before the Mercy Seat <note>original: "Propitiatorio" — the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant, where God's presence was said to dwell</note> and upon the Mercy Seat. And by this blood, according to divine institution, the filth of the people was wiped away. The reason for this ordinance is assigned there in this manner: "for the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given that blood to you so that you may make expiation upon my altar for your souls, because blood is made for the atonement of the soul." <note>original: "anima carnis in sanguine est... quia sanguis pro animæ piaculo fit" — citing Leviticus 17:11</note> These five things we have recounted—and even greater things than these—were required to be included in the cleansing and liberation of the people under the Messiah. Rightly, therefore, he offered himself to God for all as a sacrifice of his own blood; the sprinkling of this blood, as the most perfect sacrifice, was foreshadowed in all the earlier sacrifices as if by signs. This was seen especially in the offering of Isaac by his father, and in the Passover <note>original: "Pascha"</note>. Add also to this the circumcision of all male children. Moreover, divine mercy did not wish for all men to pour out their lives with their blood for their sins, but that one should shed his blood for everyone, and for this reason, He exalted him above the rest. Although this sprinkling of blood was an impious slaughter from the perspective of the murderers, yet from the perspective of the ready will of Christ, who most willingly offered himself, it is judged to have been a divine sacrifice. Indeed, you used to signify this every year through the slaughter of the Passover lamb as a sign of your expiation and salvation; and finally, in the slaughter of the Passover lamb—namely, the gentle Jesus our Savior—it was fulfilled, which is also repeated in a certain way daily in the Eucharist <note>The Christian sacrament of the Lord's Supper, which Ficino views as the ongoing memorial of this one sacrifice.</note>. Thus, therefore, Christ Jesus is a Priest forever, sacrificing himself once to God the Father; he alone was able to cleanse others perfectly, since he was neither impure himself, nor did he need burnt offerings for the sake of his own cleansing, as did the other priests before him. He perfectly cleansed human filth and his own family <note>Meaning the human race or the Church</note> not with the blood of beasts, nor with anything impure or belonging to another, but with human blood—pure and his own. The divine Apostle Paul speaks of these things in the Epistle to the Hebrews. For this reason, the release from sins through the passion of Christ was more fitting than if God had forgiven them by absolute power; for besides the fact that it was done this way for the sake of God’s justice and mercy, and again to show the most excellent virtue of Christ, this mystery also contributed more than anything else to human instruction—namely, by the example of obedience, gentleness, charity, greatness of soul, strength, contempt for mortal things, and desire for eternal things. Thus, that saying of Isaiah is fulfilled: *the chastisement of our peace was upon him* <note>original: "disciplina pacis nostræ super eum" — Isaiah 53:5</note>; for he indeed brought it about that we have peace with God, and he taught us to have it with one another. *By his bruises we are healed* <note>original: "Liuore eius sanati sumus"</note>, not only because he made satisfaction for us, but also because he instructed us with teachings and examples.

->*Confirmation of original sin, and because of this, the passion of the Messiah, from Jewish sources against the Jews. Chapter XXXIIII.*<-

You often find fault with our doctrine of original guilt, as those who do not know how to interpret your own Prophets; for we learned these things from them. Isaiah cries out to the people thus: *Your first father sinned, and your interpreters have transgressed against me, and I have contaminated* (otherwise: *Profaned*) *the holy princes, and I have given Jacob to destruction, and Israel to reproach.* <note>original: "Pater tuus primus peccauit... Israel in blasphemiam" — Isaiah 43:27-28</note> The "first father" is clearly Adam, who sinned when he neglected the divine command. Therefore the "holy princes"—that is, the Patriarchs and the rest of the righteous descending from him—were "contaminated," which is to say, they were separated from the divine vision as if they were profane, just as those who are contaminated were separated from the Temple. Moreover, the punishment for that first sin passed into all those descending from Adam, since after the transgression God threatened Adam thus: *Cursed is the ground in your work; in labor you shall eat from it,* etc. And also to the woman: *In pain you shall bring forth children,* etc. Since, therefore, that punishment passed into all, the guilt also passed into all. For it is not likely that in all men there would be such long-lasting punishment so far removed from guilt. Hear again what God says to the people in Isaiah: *You have made me serve in your sins,* because the Lord God, for the sake of expiating the crimes of the servant-people, took on the form of a servant. God could not serve insofar as He was God; therefore He served insofar as He was man. The Messiah was, therefore, God and man, which is also clear through what follows: *You have provided me labor in your iniquities,* that is, punishments because of your iniquity. *Fear not, my servant Jacob, I* <meta>catchword: I (ego)</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S BOOK

### Page 62

"I am he, who will blot out your sins" <note>original: "ego sum, qui delebo peccata tua" — citing Isaiah 43:25</note>; that is to say, although your transgression is so heavy that it cannot be expiated by human means alone, I, as both God and man, will expiate it thoroughly. Regarding Baptism and the Holy Spirit, he adds the following: "I will pour out water upon the thirsty; I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your stock." Perhaps in these words is also signified the water which the pierced side of Christ poured forth, and the spirit of life which he gave up on the cross for our sake. Read the commentaries of your ancient elders on Genesis, especially in that part where Moses says: "These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created." You will find there that all things were created by God as entirely perfect from the beginning, but immediately after the sin of the first parent <note>Adam</note>, all things—and human things especially—degenerated from their perfection. They shall not return to their pristine state until the "Son of Pharez" comes—that is, the Messiah, who descended from Pharez <note>Phares or Perez, an ancestor of King David; in Jewish tradition, the "Son of Pharez" is a title for the Messiah</note>. From these things you can infer that the vices of the first parents were transferred to their descendants, and were to be healed through the Messiah. But he healed them in one way at his first coming, and shall heal them in another at his second.

Many of your own doctors also believe that the Prophets and the holy Fathers of the Old Testament descended to the underworld <note>original: "inferos" — often translated as Hell, but here referring to Sheol or Limbo</note> before the arrival of the Messiah. They prove this from what is said by God to Abraham in Genesis: "You shall go to your fathers." From this, Rabbi Rhahamon <note>Likely a reference to a Midrashic or medieval Jewish commentator</note> argues that because the fathers of Abraham worshipped idols (as is read in the Book of Joshua), Abraham must have descended to the underworld when he went to them. The same is handed down regarding Isaac in Genesis: "Isaac passed away and died, and was added to his people." The same is said there of Jacob, and the same of David in the third book of Kings <note>modern 1 Kings 2:10</note>: "David slept with his fathers." Regarding all of these, Rabbi Rhahamon similarly argues that they were sent to the places of those who were unjust and worshipped idols; but Christ, by his death, liberated the holy Fathers from death—that is, from the darkness of their souls.

Zechariah touched upon this thus: "As for you also, by the blood of your Covenant, you have sent forth your prisoners out of the lake in which there is no water" <note>Zechariah 9:11</note>; that is, he led the saints out of <term>Limbo</term> <note>the "edge" of hell where the righteous of the Old Testament awaited the Messiah</note>, a dry place devoid of light and joy. Therefore, it is not a Christian invention that the great Messiah, through his labors and passions, was meant to redeem the souls of the Fathers and their descendants from the underworld. Rather, many of the ancient Jews also held this view, especially the aforementioned Rhahamon, and furthermore Osuas Hanna, Habba Juda, who in the Talmudic <note>original: "Talmuticis"</note> disputes—after many points pertaining to this—also bring forward that passage of Hosea for this purpose: "I will deliver them from the hand of death, I will return them from death." Likewise that passage of Isaiah: "The redeemed of the Lord shall return, and come into Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads." They interpret "Zion" as the heavenly fatherland, and rightly so, for there is no everlasting praise and joy on earth.

Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>The famous scholar Nachmanides</note> agrees with these points; indeed, all Jews confess that the Patriarchs and Saints do not enter Paradise before the arrival of the Messiah, but remain in its outskirts until the "Son of Pharez" comes—that is, Christ the son of David—and this is because of the sin of Adam. And since these things are so, some among you, not sufficiently learned, nevertheless deny that <term>original sin</term> <note>the Christian doctrine that humanity inherits a state of sin from Adam</note> was transferred to descendants and had to be expiated through Christ, as if it were not fitting for there to be such a long-lasting punishment for everyone without personal fault. Why then did Moses write in Genesis that after the transgression of Adam, God placed the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to block the way to the Tree of Life, unless it was to signify that, because of a certain likeness and a fault contracted from the first parents, the entrance to Paradise is blocked to all? 

We ought to remember that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is so difficult, so precious, that it can and should be hindered not only by the individual, daily sins of each person, but also by the common vice of the whole of human nature, contracted from the origin of the first parents at birth. And although the Saints before Christ might have freed and cleansed themselves from their own personal sins by the strength of human virtue—wherefore they did not deserve to be tortured in the underworld—nevertheless, no one's virtue was sufficient to remove that obstacle which consisted of the common guilt of all human nature and to lay open the entrance to Paradise. But the guilt and obligation of this kind was dissolved by the passion of Christ for all in common. For God, as Isaiah says, placed upon him the sin of us all; through him, therefore, he opened the gates of the heavenly fatherland. Jeremiah signified this mystery thus: "We have sinned against you, O expectation of Israel, Savior in time of tribulation. Why will you be as a stranger in the land, and as a traveler turning aside to stay? Why will you be like a wandering man, and like one who cannot save? But you are in us, O Lord, and your holy name..."

Here, he addresses the specific mechanics of Original Sin: why physical suffering remains after Christ’s redemption, how sin is transmitted biologically, and how it can be considered "voluntary" even in an infant.</meta>

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

### Page 63

...[Your name] is called upon us, do not forsake us, O Lord our God <note>original: "invocatum est super nos, ne derelinquas nos Domine Deus noster" — quoting Jeremiah 14:9</note>. Some among you ask why Christ, by deleting our guilt, did not also delete that punishment: *In the sweat of your face* <note>Genesis 3:19</note> and *in pain you shall bring forth children* <note>Genesis 3:16</note>, and the like. It is so that by these daily stings we may recognize how terrible it was, and is, to despise God’s commands, and so that through the exercise of moral virtues we may make more progress toward achieving eternal happiness. To this is added the fact that the redemption, victory, freedom, abundance, and peace which were promised to us in the time of the Messiah perhaps pertained to spiritual things, which contribute to happiness, rather than to bodily things, which either do not contribute or even hinder it. Thus, by the passion and a true faith in Christ, that original sin was taken away, at least regarding the guilt which blocks ultimate happiness; however, those laborious things were left behind, which not only do not hinder us, but actually lead us forward. 

But you object with that passage from Ezekiel: *The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father* <note>Ezekiel 18:20</note>. We, however, explain it thus: namely, that the son is not punished for the sin of the father if he is entirely free of the guilt; but all were born as participants in that first fault. For just as daily vices pass from father to son through imitation, so the first vice passes through origin <term>original sin: the theological concept that the first sin of Adam is inherited by all humans as a corrupted nature</term>. Nor is it a wonder that the vice of the first parent passed to his descendants, for we recognize daily in children the gestures, affections, and habits of both grandfathers and fathers. For nature is so arranged that the body and soul agree in a certain harmonious proportion and come together as one; the movements of the body easily and most vehemently penetrate into the soul, and those of the soul into the body. The soul of the son is not drawn out from either the body or the soul of the father, but the body is generated as such, and with a certain propensity, from the body of the parent. Thus *the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the sons are set on edge* <note>Ezekiel 18:2</note>; the soul, because of its kinship and affection for its own body, is made a participant in that propensity in some way—especially according to its lower power, which is close to the body and agrees with it greatly. Then the higher power of the soul often obeys a certain natural interior love, almost as the lower power obeys the body—it obeys, I say, in a similar way, but not equally. Now, a movement which is an action in the soul becomes a passion in the body; what is a passion in the body becomes a sensation and compassion in the soul. An affection which is a punishment for guilt in the body is guilt in the soul.

Furthermore, you object in this manner: "Sin is so voluntary that if it were not voluntary, it would not be sin" <note>This is a famous definition of sin by St. Augustine</note>. But original sin is called a stain contracted by origin from a parent. Since it is not voluntary in the offspring, it is not sin. On the contrary, it is sin, since it is a certain crookedness declining from the right path and unfit for achieving the goal, just like a defect in a person who is lame. It is sin, I say, not so much of the individual nature as of the common nature. Moreover, it becomes voluntary in some way in the offspring insofar as the child willingly follows this sort of propensity; it is voluntary, furthermore, not so much by the offspring's own will as by the will of Adam himself. He, by the motion of generation, moves everyone who sprouts from his lineage in some way, not otherwise than the will of a single soul moves many members of the body to an act. Therefore, just as the movement of the foot is called voluntary not by the foot's own will, but by the common will of the soul which first moves the limbs—and similarly the movement of the head, the hand, and the rest—so that crookedness natural to man is judged voluntary because of the will of Adam moving everyone, rather than because of one's own will. 

There are some among you who argue against us with this reasoning: if sin was poured into us from our first parents because we were in them and received human nature from them, by that same logic, every single sin of every ancestor from the beginning of the world until now would necessarily be inflicted upon us at our birth. Our theologians respond to this that no vice of either the first parent or the others is necessarily passed down to those being born, except for the first one. For a human generates a human like himself not in individual number, but in species <term>species vs. individual: in Aristotelian logic, you inherit traits that make you "human" (species), but not necessarily the specific skills or habits of your father (individual)</term>. And for that reason, things that belong specifically to each person's individual personality are not passed to children from their origin, but things that pertain to the species are. For a musician or a philosopher does not generate a musician or a philosopher. Yet a human who sees, hears, and has two feet—unless something hinders it—generates a two-footed human capable of seeing and hearing. The first vice, however, escaped the natural grasp of the human species <note>meaning it corrupted the "blueprint" of humanity itself</note>; the rest are additional and become the specific property of individuals. I know you usually object here that Adam's sin, because it proceeded from the specific act of his own free will, belonged to his individual person rather than to the species. To this, following the mind of our theologians, I respond thus: To the person...

<meta>catchword: person [sonam]</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that Original Sin is a defect of the human species inherited from Adam, comparing it to physical traits. He argues that while individual sins are not inherited, Adam's first sin corrupted the "common nature" of humanity, making it a shared spiritual "crookedness."</summary>

--- Page 100 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s theological explanation of how original sin is transmitted and how Christ’s sacrifice rectifies it. It transitions from the mechanics of Baptism to a new chapter (34) defending the replacement of Old Testament laws with the New Covenant.</meta>

...to the **person** of each individual, something pertains in two ways: either according to the person themselves, or by some gift of grace. Similarly, something can belong to nature in two ways: either according to nature itself—namely, that which flows from the principles and elements of nature—or by a gift of supernatural grace. **Original justice** <note>original: "Originalem iustitiam" — the state of perfect moral and physical harmony humans enjoyed before the Fall</note> was not something human nature possessed from its own internal principles from the beginning; rather, it was a gift of divine grace which is understood to have been granted to all of human nature at its origin in our first parent <note>Adam</note>. He lost this gift because of the fault of the first sin. Therefore, just as that original justice would have been preserved in his descendants along with the propagation of nature had he not sinned, so too a certain opposing perversity and crookedness is passed down in succession with that nature. For this reason, a vice of this sort became a matter of nature rather than of the person. Other vices—whether of Adam or of others—do indeed deprave individuals, not in terms of what belongs to nature, but in terms of what belongs to the person; therefore, they are not necessarily spread to sons and grandsons.

What then did the **passion of Christ** bestow upon us? By removing the obstacle of original guilt, he threw open **Paradise**, which holy men were unable to enter before him. If Adam had not sinned, would he and the other righteous people have been blessed? They certainly would have possessed Paradise, but an earthly one. However, the coming of God in the person of Christ made us sharers in a **heavenly Paradise**; thus there was more gain in the power of Christ than there was loss in the vice of Adam. Adam's vice, in itself, did not bring the torment of the underworld upon us, but merely took away the earthly Paradise; Christ’s power protects us from the underworld and grants the heavenly Paradise. Hence the Apostle Paul says: *Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more* <note>original: "Ubi abundauit peccatum, superabundauit & gratia" — Romans 5:20</note>. 

I omit those lesser points: that through Christ, the devil—once the prince of this world (that is, of worldly men)—was cast out; he no longer deludes us through idolatry, nor does he afflict the souls and bodies of so many nations as sharply as he used to, unless it is occasionally permitted by God for a certain purpose. Through faith in the **Messiah** who has already come, we resist the devil; through faith in the Messiah who was to come, the saints before Christ resisted the devil. Yet no one then could so escape the devil's hand as to avoid entering a certain lower region, that is, **Limbo** <note>original: "lymbi" — the "Limbo of the Fathers" where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ’s redemption</note>. As David sang: *Who is the man who lives and shall not see death, and shall deliver his soul from the hand of the underworld?* <note>original: "Quis est homo qui uiuet, & non uidebit mortem, & liberabit animam suam de manu inferni" — Psalm 89:48</note> Against that poison and its like, the power, passion, mysteries, teaching, example, and faith of Christ provide us with abundant remedies. 

Above all, **Baptism**, in the power of the Holy Spirit and the faith of Christ, dissolves that guilt and obligation in the soul of the one washed by Baptism, though it does not root out the inclination toward sin implanted in the nature of the body. For the Spirit and the spiritual mystery properly regard the spirit and the will, not the body. Thus it happens that those generated from the body of a baptized person, because they are born "unclean" <note>carrying original sin</note>, are themselves also in need of Baptism. Each individual must daily acknowledge the gift of purification from the mystery of Christ, just like a grain of wheat: even if it has been cleaned by skill, it still produces unclean grains, such that they need that skill again. For the skill had cleaned the property of the individual grain, rather than the nature of the species or its power of generation.

-> Proof that the ceremonies of the Old Testament were deservedly consumed and completed <-
-> by the arrival of the New, based on Jewish writings against the Jews. <-
-> **Chapter XXXIIII.** <-

If the kingdom of the **Old Testament**, the Prophecy, the priesthood, and the sacrifice were meant to be taken away by divine institution upon the introduction of a certain **New Testament**—at the time of the Messiah, the eternal king and priest and the end of the Prophets, as we have shown elsewhere—how much more did those minor ceremonies, which were of little importance, vanish? I have declared this elsewhere from several predictions of the Prophets. Indeed, those ceremonies foretold Christian things and ceremonies no differently than the prophecies did. Once the oracles of the Prophets were finally fulfilled, the ceremonies were deservedly consumed. Yet you Jews still hold onto them stubbornly <note>original: "mordicus" — literally "with your teeth"</note>, being more persistent than others, bringing up that passage of **Moses** in **Deuteronomy** against us: *And now, Israel, hear the precepts and judgments which I teach you, so that by doing them you may live, and entering in, you may possess the land which the Lord God of our fathers is going to give us; you shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor shall you take away from it.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:1-2</note> These words must be considered diligently. Moses is speaking to the flock subject to him; for he says, *Hear, O Israel*. He did not say, "Nothing shall be added or diminished by anyone," but rather, *You* <note>the people</note> shall not add...

He begins a new chapter arguing that Old Testament ceremonies were always intended to be temporary precursors to the New Covenant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the transition from the Old Mosaic Law to the New Christian Law. He moves from discussing the nature of Christ’s sacrifice to scriptural proofs that the Old Law was always intended to be surpassed by a "New Covenant" brought by the Messiah.</meta>

-> ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION <-

...neither shall you add to it, nor shall you take away from it. <note>Referring to the prohibition in Deuteronomy 12:32</note> Therefore, he [Moses] took away the power of changing the law from the subject flock. But from God, who is above Moses, or from the extraordinary messenger <note>the Messiah</note> who would have the power of changing it from God, he did not take it away.

Jeremiah cries out thus: "Behold, the days are coming," says the Lord, "and I will complete (others say: *I will finish*) for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a new covenant (others say: *Testament*); not according to the Testament (others say: *pact*) which I arranged (others say: *I made*) with their fathers on the day that I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—the pact which they made void (others say: *since they did not remain in my Testament*) and I neglected them (others say: *I grew weary of them*)," says the Lord. "But this will be the Testament (others say: *pact*) which I shall establish with the house of Israel. After those days," says the Lord, "I will give my law into their mind (others say: *into their bowels*) and I will write it upon their heart; and I will see them, and I will be to them as God, and they shall be to me as a people. And each one shall teach his neighbor and each one his brother, saying: 'Know the Lord,' for everyone shall know me—namely, that I alone am God." And it follows: "from the greatest even to the least, for I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will no longer remember their sins." <note>original: Jeremiah 31:31-34</note> In these words, God promises that at some point He would arrange a new pact and Testament, and hand down a new law differing from that which He had given to Moses after He had liberated the Jews from the Egyptians. He would write it no longer on stone tablets and scrolls, but in the minds of men—as if that first law could be erased, but the second could not. And once the New Testament was introduced, the ancient ceremonies, according to a spiritual understanding, ought to have been preserved. <note>Ficino suggests that the rituals of the Old Law were meant to be understood symbolically once the New Law arrived.</note> Certainly, as the Apostle Paul says, when the Prophet mentions a "new pact and Testament," it signifies that the other is growing old and is able to fail. <note>Hebrews 8:13</note>

But when did these things happen? When was that fulfilled: "I will see them, and I will be to them as God"? God always sees men through His intellect, but He saw them moreover with His physical eyes when He assumed the form of a man—a man, I say, who truly was considered God by men. Of whom David said: "The God of gods shall be seen in Zion," <note>Psalm 84:7</note> and Zechariah: "You are God, and God is in you, nor is there God without you." <note>Zechariah 8:23, often interpreted by Ficino as a prophecy of the Incarnation.</note> From these things, the divinity of the Messiah, the founder of the new Testament and pact, is shown; the distinction of the divine persons <note>the Trinity</note> is also signified.

But lest anyone be troubled that there are different words in various translations—here "pact," there "Testament"—it should be known that this word was introduced by Jeremiah as *Berith* <note>Hebrew: בְּרִית</note>, which signifies law, pact, covenant, and Testament alike. Your own interpreters confess that this "new law" is understood to be the law of the Messiah; hence the Talmudic doctors <note>the Jewish rabbis of the Talmud</note> say the law of the Messiah will be more excellent than the Mosaic law. Read their short commentaries on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes. There you will find these words: "Every law of the present age is a kind of vanity compared to the law of the future age—that is, to the law of the Messiah." For in what follows, the matter is declared thus: "Every law which anyone learns in this age is a vain thing if compared to the law of the Messiah." These are their words.

You see, therefore, that the law of the Messiah is different from the law of Moses, and that the Mosaic ceremonies completely vanish in the sight of the Messiah. The law of Moses is called "vain," not in an absolute sense, but in relation to the law of Christ; for it is more outstanding than all others. But why vain? Because through "civil" virtues <note>virtues concerning social conduct and politics</note> it can only direct the human race toward its use in this world, not toward the goal of heavenly blessedness. The Christian law, through the "purgatory" virtues <note>virtues that cleanse the soul of earthly attachments</note> of a soul being purified, leads perfectly to the "exemplary" virtues <note>the perfect forms of virtue existing in the mind of God</note> and to heavenly happiness. For perfect happiness is not given except to souls perfectly purged; the Mosaic law does not effect this, but the Christian law does. The Mosaic law is therefore a kind of preparation for the law of Christ—much like a preliminary exercise is a preparation for a perfect habit or skill. When someone possesses the skill itself, they no longer need the preparation.

Moreover, you yourselves confess, as we said above, that under the law of Moses the Saints did not enter Paradise but awaited the law and grace of the Messiah. For this reason, I believe, Moses promises only temporal rewards to those who keep his law; for that doctrine cannot aspire to anything greater. Moses opens the whole matter thus in Deuteronomy: "I will raise up for them a Prophet from the midst of their brothers like unto you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all the things that I command him. If anyone will not hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I will stand as an avenger." <note>Deuteronomy 18:18-19</note> Do you not see that God was going to create a certain Prophet among your people besides Moses? One who would have the authority to establish laws from the beginning. To him, it is permitted to change all things as he judges best—to change, I say, the "image" into the "substance," so that he may perfect what was imperfect. By divine command, you ought to believe everything from him no less than from Moses; and because you did not believe everyone or everything, as God threatened, you were exterminated...

<summary>Ficino argues that the Hebrew Bible and Talmudic tradition both point toward a New Law (the Christian Law) that would eventually supersede the Mosaic Law. He explains that while Moses provided a preparation through civil virtue, only the Messiah provides the "purgatory" virtues necessary to enter Paradise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of Christianity against alternative religious frameworks, specifically addressing Islamic and Jewish perspectives on the nature of prophecy and the duration of the Mosaic Law. He focuses on the linguistic distinctions in the Hebrew Bible to argue that the Old Law was intended to be temporary.</meta>

### MARSILIO FICINO’S BOOK

...you were born. Let the Arabs not imagine that Muhammad was such a king, or rather a tyrant, whose law did not merely constrain the Mosaic law (which was already quite free in itself), but relaxed it far too much; Muhammad is one to whom neither the timing, nor the location, nor any words of the Prophets are suited. But how could Muhammad be that supreme Prophet who was to be raised up from the people of the Jews, when he himself confesses in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> that Jesus of Nazareth was the last of the Hebrews and the highest Prophet? 

The Jews of the past, especially those in Africa, were warned by these words of Moses and were expecting the Messiah to be the founder of a new law. But Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher known as Rambam</note> wrote to them that God did not promise a law-giving Prophet, but only a foreteller of future events. He claimed that God wanted to drive away from the Jews the practice of omens used by the Canaanites, and thus said to them: "These nations, whose land you shall possess, listen to soothsayers and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 18:14</note>—meaning that you should foreknow the future not through omens, but through Prophets sent by God. Therefore, he adds: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your own nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him." <note>Deuteronomy 18:15</note> This was the message of Rabbi Moses to the Africans. We also affirm that these words of Moses should be explained exactly as the African Rabbi Moses explained them. 

But let us consider the great Moses speaking later in that same chapter of Deuteronomy: "According to all that you asked of the Lord your God in Horeb <note>Mount Sinai</note>, when the assembly was gathered, and you said: 'Let me not hear the voice of the Lord my God any longer, and let me not see this great fire anymore, lest I die.'" And the Lord said: "They have spoken well in everything they said; I will raise up for them a Prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And if anyone will not listen to the words he speaks, I will be the avenger." <note>Deuteronomy 18:16-19</note> 

You see that the people, when the law was delivered on Mount Horeb, were terrified by the fire and other horrifying signs, and then asked God not to speak to the people in that manner anymore. Therefore, God promised that at another time, He would deliver the law to the people without any terror through a certain Prophet who would be a true man, just like Moses. In the earlier words of the chapter, then, Moses speaks of a Prophet who announces the future (of which there were many). In the following words, however, he speaks of a law-giving Prophet (such as we maintain Jesus of Nazareth was). 

But I know it troubles you greatly that Moses commanded his mandates to be observed always. Remember what your own grammarians discuss: that the terms pertaining to "forever" are twofold. Some refer to eternity absolutely, while others refer to eternity only under a certain condition. 

In the first category is *Selah* <note>original: "Cela"</note>; where the Psalm says in our version, "they shall praise you forever and ever," the Hebrew uses *Selah*. Also in that category is *Netzach* <note>original: "Necali"</note>; where the Psalm in Greek and Latin says, "He shall live forever," the Hebrew sounds like *Netzach*. 

In the second category, the Hebrew word is *olam* <term>olam: a Hebrew word often translated as "forever" but which can also mean a specific "age" or "world-era"</term>, and the Latin is *saeculum* (an age). In this way, it says in Deuteronomy regarding a purchased servant: "He shall be your servant *olam*," <note>Deuteronomy 15:17</note> that is, "for an age"—meaning for the "age" of your life or the servant's life and no longer. Thus, "age" there does not signify the total duration of all things, but the duration of this or that man. 

When Moses commands ceremonies to be observed regarding the Sabbath, Passover, Pentecost, the Feast of Tabernacles, the Day of Atonement, and similar things, he never uses those words that signify absolute eternity. He uses only *olam*, which signifies a specific "age"—that is, the entire age of the Old Testament, until the New Testament is established through the Messiah. Then the old ceremonies, just as they seem to wither, shall bloom again, and they are fulfilled in the new ones rather than being destroyed. Thus our Jesus fulfilled the Law when he perfected what had been imperfect. 

And this very perfection of the Christian law declares it to be the end and the final limit of the duration of the Mosaic constitutions. This is what God had predicted through Jeremiah, as we said, promising a New Law different from the Mosaic one. If anyone asks in what way the New Law is more perfect than the Old, let him consider five principal excellences of the New (that is, the Christian) Law, as far as this topic is concerned:

**First**, the Mosaic Law was delivered on tablets of stone, which are perishable; the New Law was, as Jeremiah says, to be branded upon hearts and minds. This signifies that this new discipline is more spiritual—and indeed eternal—since like the natural law, it is imprinted upon eternal minds forever. The Old Law, however, being subject to time, was given only for a time. 

**Second**, that Old constitution, besides...

<summary>Ficino argues that the "eternal" nature of Mosaic law was linguistically intended to be temporary (an "age") and that Deuteronomy prophesied a new law-giving Prophet (Jesus) to replace the terrifying delivery of the Law at Sinai with a spiritual one written on the heart.</summary>

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION
E 3

...those things which pertain to the natural law, bound only the Israelite nation (to whom it was given). Hence the Psalmist says of God: "He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel; he has not dealt so with any other nation, and his judgments he has not made manifest to them." <note>Psalm 147:19–20</note> The New Law, however, binds everyone no differently than the natural law does. For this reason, Isaiah says of the Messiah and his doctrine: "Until he sets judgment on the earth, and the islands shall wait for his law." <note>Isaiah 42:4</note> Third, the ancient decrees (excepting those which belong to natural right) are said to have bound the subject people not everywhere, but only in the region of the promised land. The words of Deuteronomy declare this: "You know that I have taught you precepts and justices, just as the Lord my God commanded me, so that you should do them in the land which you are to possess." <note>Deuteronomy 4:5</note> Again: "And he commanded me at that same time to teach you the ceremonies and judgments which you ought to do in the land which you are to possess." <note>Deuteronomy 4:14</note> And again: "But you, stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments, and ceremonies, and judgments, which you shall teach them, so that they may do them in the land which I will give them for a possession." <note>Deuteronomy 5:31</note> But the laws of the Messiah are to be observed everywhere, no less than natural laws; therefore, in Malachi, God at one point rejects the old sacrifices: "I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive an offering from your hand." <note>Malachi 1:10</note> Then he adds: "For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place sacrifice is made, and a pure offering is offered to my name." <note>Malachi 1:11</note> Therefore, the sacred rites which under the Old Law were permitted to be celebrated only in the temples and tabernacles of the promised land, were at some point—namely, under the Messiah—to be pleasing to God everywhere. Fourth, the Old Law promises only physical and temporal goods and threatens physical evils, as is clear in Leviticus and often elsewhere. The New Law promises spiritual and eternal things. Fifth, the Old Law introduces only civil virtues and common morals, by which it cuts away outward disturbances. The New Law introduces "purgative" virtues <note>A Neoplatonic term for virtues that purify the soul from earthly attachments</note> and the virtues of the purified mind, by which it uproots the passions and commits the fuel of vices to oblivion as if to a fire. But why is this? Because God had decided to educate a people who were still unrefined <note>original: "rudem"</note> with lighter disciplines, as was appropriate, and to move them by more manifest goods and evils; this even Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher Maimonides</note> confesses in his commentaries on the book *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Camedrim," referring to the Talmudic tractate on the high court</note>. But truly, by the time of Christ, the people had already emerged more learned. Then (as Isaiah says) "the earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea." <note>Isaiah 11:9</note> Then, therefore, God provoked and formed the human race with truer rewards and more exacting institutions. Justly, then, as the New Law arrives like a "form" <note>An Aristotelian term meaning the defining principle that gives shape to matter</note>, the old law, acting as a preparation, either departs or passes into the new, and is fulfilled in the new. Rabbi Moses could by no means remain silent on this in Deuteronomy, where he divides the age of the world into two eras: namely, the present era and the era of the Messiah. And the Talmudic interpreters, as we have said elsewhere, maintain that the "present world" and the "future world" are the eras of the Law and of the Messiah, and they admit that the "vain" law of this era belongs to the law of the Messiah—as if the old era and the old law are finished and fulfilled in the law of Christ.

->*The Distinction of the Precepts of Moses.*<-

The principal precepts of Moses are those contained in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>; for these were given by God directly on stone tablets to the entire people, and then enclosed as perpetual things in the Ark of the Covenant within the Holy of Holies. The others, however, are more minor, given through Moses and inscribed by him on parchment, and placed outside the Holy of Holies. Among these, some are simply moral; because they imitate the law of nature, they are nearly eternal, just like the principal ones. Others pertain to judgments, which are not fixed in the judgment of equity but vary as the practical use of things requires. Others, again, pertain to ceremonies, which are indeed of small importance; for like certain "Pythagorean symbols" <note>Ficino compares Jewish rituals to the symbolic, cryptic maxims of Pythagoras, which he believed held hidden spiritual truths</note>, they are referred to the portending or signifying of something else. For he who is commanded to abstain from pork is commanded to avoid the life of a pig; and he who is commanded to rest his body on the Sabbath is commanded to rest his mind in contemplation. These and similar things were brought back to their intended meaning and effect through Christ. Therefore, to sacrifice to God, and that a thief should restore what was taken, and similar things, belong to natural and moral law, and are therefore commanded to be kept always. But to sacrifice...

He uses scriptural citations and the authority of Jewish scholars like Maimonides to claim that the Old Law's ceremonies were symbolic precursors to Christian truths.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO
# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...by this agreement, and on this or that day, such or such things; again, to restore fourfold, or double, and similar matters, are either ceremonial or judicial. They were able to be changed and indeed ought to have been changed, according as it is appropriate for places, times, and persons. In matters of this kind, a change occurred not only under Christ—and occurred by right—but even among the ancients. For in the first age, by divine institution, humans were not permitted to eat anything except plants, just as <term>Genesis</term><note>The first book of the Bible, meaning "origin."</note> teaches us. Yet in the second age, after that flood of the world, God granting it, it was permitted to eat animals, which is also declared in Genesis. 

Hence, among your own people in the book <term>Bereshit Rabbah</term><note>original: "Berefith Rabba." A famous collection of ancient Jewish explanations and stories (Midrash) regarding the Book of Genesis.</note>, specifically in the commentaries on Genesis, while that verse of the Psalm is being explained—*The Lord sets the prisoners free*—it is said: "Every beast which in this age (namely the age of the Law) is considered unclean, shall be made clean by God in the future age (namely the age of the Messiah), just as the beasts were clean for the sons of Noah, though they had not been clean for those who came before." And just as God granted only plants as clean to the older generations, and then granted every animal as clean to the sons of Noah, so in the future age God will grant whatever he previously prohibited. These things are stated there. From these points, it is clear that in the age of the Messiah, those minute institutions of the old age were to be dissolved as if they were now empty and superfluous. O Jews, do you still demand more witnesses? Although they are not necessary, I will nevertheless bring forward some from the many who remain.

**Malachi:** *My covenant shall be with him of life and of peace, and I gave it to him that he might fear me with awe, and stand in reverence before the face of my name. The law of truth shall be in his mouth; walking with me in peace, he shall direct others and turn many from iniquity, for the lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.* <note>Malachi 2:5–7</note> In these words, God promises His covenant anew through the Messiah—a covenant, I say, of peace to be reconciled between God and men, from which the life of men proceeds. Again, He promises him a mild and, as it were, humble life. He also promises a priesthood, and that he will convert men not by force and arms, but by peace and knowledge—not all men, but many. Again, he says that men will receive a new law from him. For whom do all these things fit, if not Jesus the Nazarene?

**Nahum:** *I will destroy the graven and molten images; I will prepare your burial, for behold upon the mountains the swift feet of him who brings good tidings and announces peace. Celebrate your feast days, O Judah, fulfill your vows, for they shall no longer continue to pass into old age; it is finished, it is consumed, it is taken away. He has ascended who breathes into your face, rescuing you from tribulation.* <note>Nahum 1:14–2:1. Ficino's Latin text blends these prophetic verses to emphasize the end of the old order.</note> Here, he clearly portends the fall of idols at the coming of the Messiah, the fulfillment of the prophecies and the Old Testament, the consumption of the ancient ceremonies, the removal of the Jewish kingdom, the preaching of Gospel peace, the ascension of Christ, the breathing of the Holy Spirit, and finally the liberation from tribulation (namely, that of the underworld).

**Micah:** *The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he shall judge among many peoples, and shall rebuke and direct strong nations even far away.* <note>Micah 4:2–3</note> By these words, it was signified that the Messiah would bring a new doctrine and a law beyond that of Moses, which would proceed not from Sinai, like that old law, but from Zion; nor would it instruct only the Jews, as that one did, but it would be propagated everywhere by the speech of the preaching Apostles, and it would abolish the customs of the strong nations.

**Isaiah:** *Thus says the Lord to the men of Judah who dwell in Jerusalem: Renew novelty among yourselves, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the Lord your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and there be no one to extinguish it.* <note>Though attributed here to Isaiah, this quote is found in Jeremiah 4:3–4. Ficino likely quotes from a collection of "testimonies" where attributions were sometimes mixed.</note>

**Moses:** *In the final days, the Lord will circumcise your heart to love the Lord your God.* <note>Deuteronomy 30:6</note>

**Joshua son of Nun**<note>original: "Iesus Naue." In Latin, the name Joshua is the same as Jesus. Ficino views the Old Testament Joshua as a "type" or symbolic precursor to Jesus Christ.</note>, who bore the figure of Jesus Christ, said: *The Lord said to Joshua, make for yourself stone knives, very sharp, and sit, and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time*—namely, by the circumcision of the heart. By these three oracles, it was shown that physical circumcision was to be changed into spiritual circumcision under Christ; the former merely cut the outer skin, but the latter purges and washes the whole person. Therefore, why must boys pour out blood on the eighth day after Jesus has come? Spare your little children, O Jews—you who are as cruel as you are superstitious—spare your little children as soon as they are born.

# ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

Jesus, having once been circumcised in full, shed his blood once for all people. For if circumcision, the first of the ceremonies, was not intended to be permanent—seeing as it was not established from the beginning, but only under Abraham, and since any person could be righteous without it before then—how much less permanent are the remaining ceremonies? Why then do you continue to observe the **Sabbaths**? Truly, the **Lord’s Day** <note>Sunday</note> was once foreshadowed for you by the Sabbath. Why do you still sacrifice temporal victims? All of those seem to have reached their end in the eternal victim, Jesus. Why do you daily restore the ancient priests in vain? They, as the least of men, represented Jesus the eternal priest; he is the true priest forever according to the order of **Melchizedek** <note>A mysterious priest-king mentioned in Genesis who is seen as a forerunner of Christ because he offered bread and wine rather than animal sacrifices</note>. Finally, why do you look for a king any longer? That temporal kingdom of yours was transferred long ago to Christ, the eternal king. And when you said, or read, O wretched ones, "**Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews**" <note>original: "Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudæorum"</note>, you then received a dying man, a living God, the unique, final, and perpetual king. Indeed, your own Moses signified this to us when he handed down the rite for appointing a High Priest; through the sacrament of a certain mystic oil, he named him **Christ** <note>Meaning "Anointed One." In Hebrew, "Messiah."</note>. Again, when he appointed a king as his successor, he gave the name **Jesus** <note>original: "Iesum." Specifically referring to Joshua, whose name in Greek and Latin is identical to Jesus.</note> to him who had previously been called **Hoshea** <note>original: "Auses." Moses changed the name of his successor from Hoshea to Joshua (Numbers 13:16).</note>. Thus, through these twin signs of naming—the one expressing the insignia of the Priesthood, the other of the Kingdom—Jesus was named as one who was equally King and High Priest.

->*On the authority of Christian doctrine.* Chapter XXXV.<-

Many things confirm the doctrine of Christ. First, the predictions of the **Sibyls** <note>Pagan prophetesses from antiquity who were believed by Renaissance scholars to have predicted the coming of Christ</note> and the Prophets. Then, the holiness and miracles of Christ and the Christians. To this is added that incredibly wondrous depth and majesty perceived in their sober style. Though they were previously unrefined men and fishermen—especially **Peter**, **James**, and **John**—and not to mention **Paul**, who, although a most learned man before his conversion, nevertheless rises in his Epistles far above human capacity. What is more august than the letters of Peter? What is more venerable than the Epistle of James or Jude? What shall we say of John’s **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note>? That book displays a heavenly countenance and contains as many mysteries as it does words. What of his Epistles? In them, without the deceptive paint of fancy words, there is a nectar-like sweetness and a divine sense. His Gospel seems to have been written by the hands of God, not man. When **Amelius the Platonist** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> read it, he swore by Jove that this "Barbarian" (meaning the Jew, John) had briefly summarized the very things concerning divine reason, the beginning, and the arrangement of things that **Plato** and **Heraclitus** <note>original: "Heraclius"</note> had disputed. **Simplicianus** <note>A mentor to St. Augustine</note> says he heard a certain Platonist say that the prologue of this Gospel should be written in golden letters everywhere on the highest peaks of the temples. Finally, all these men were the same in their speech as they were in their lives. For just as they were most gentle in their social interaction, yet most brave and constant in dangers and labors, so in speaking they were equally humble and exalted. Philosophers consider such combinations to be above nature. Thus their master, Christ, made those unlettered men and fishermen into "fishers of men," as he had promised. And what is wonderful is that after his ascension into heaven, he suddenly and miraculously taught them—while they were still unrefined—by a certain breath from heaven, to such an extent that they immediately excelled in all languages and doctrines before all the people. A sign of this is that they themselves taught very many learned men, and many who excelled in wisdom most willingly submitted their necks to the yoke of these men. **Hierotheus**, **Dionysius the Areopagite**, and **Justin**—all Platonists whose writings are full of all wisdom—took up the cross of Christ along with the Apostle. Furthermore, **Pantaenus** the Stoic, **Quadratus**, **Agrippa**, **Aristides**, **Luke**, and **Mark** the philosophers, **Tenas**, and **Apollos**, who was most skilled in Jewish law. What shall I say of the wise **Ignatius**, a disciple of Christ and Bishop of Antioch? While he was being led to Rome in chains to be devoured by beasts, he wrote many letters during that very journey concerning martyrdom and Christian doctrine—to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians <note>original: "Thraces"</note>, Smyrnaeans, Philadelphians, to Polycarp, and to the Romans. In his Letter to the Romans, he says: "From Syria all the way to Rome, I fight with beasts; meanwhile, bound night and day, I fight with ten leopards—that is, the soldiers who guard me—who become worse even when I treat them well. Their iniquity is my instruction, but I am not justified because of it. May I enjoy the beasts that are prepared for me, which I even pray will be ready for me..."

<summary>This page argues that the Jewish law's rituals were temporary figures fulfilled by Jesus as the eternal King and Priest, while defending the divine authority of the New Testament through the miraculous wisdom of the Apostles and the conversion of great philosophers.</summary>

# THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...to be delivered to destruction, and to be enticed to be eaten, lest, as happened with other martyrs, the beasts do not dare to touch my body. But if they are unwilling to come, I will use force so that I may be devoured. Forgive me, my little children, for I know what is profitable for me. Now I begin to be a disciple; shall I not fail in those things which are seen, so that I may find Jesus Christ? Let fire, the cross, wild beasts, the breaking of bones, the severing of limbs, the crushing of the whole body, and all the torments sought by the devil's art come upon me, provided that I, as a brother, reach Jesus Christ. <note>These are the words of Ignatius of Antioch, an early Christian bishop and martyr, writing to the Romans as he was being transported to his execution.</note> These were his words. And when he had already been condemned to the beasts and heard the lions roaring, in his passion for suffering he said: "I am ground by the teeth of lions, so that I may emerge as pure bread." <note>original: "dentibus leonum molar, ut panis mundus euadam"</note>

**Polycarp** also, the Bishop of the Smyrneans and companion of **John the Evangelist**, a great teacher of Asia, was often asked by the Judge to deny Jesus; he replied that he could not deny the one whom he had served happily for eighty-six years. Thus, since he burned entirely with the love of Christ, he endured the flames of fire and death most easily. The people of Smyrna wrote these things about him to the Churches of Pontus.

**Justin**, that **Platonist** <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), who retained his philosopher’s cloak after converting to Christianity</note>, having heard the book of the Apostles which he offered to the judges in defense of our religion, and having numbered many illustrious martyrs, prophesied that he too would be consumed by martyrdom through the snares of a certain **Cynic** (or rather, a marauder). He said: "And I indeed hope that I shall suffer snares from one of these, against whom I stand for the truth; I hope to be struck by a staff or a club." Certainly, this was to be expected from **Crescens**—not a **Philosopher**, but a **Philopompos** <note>A pun in Greek: "philosopher" means lover of wisdom; Ficino calls him a "philopompos," meaning a lover of vanity or worldly display.</note>. And so it happened, and Justin bore it as bravely as he had clearly foreseen.

**John the Evangelist** had also foreseen this, and at the end of his Gospel he predicted that although he might suffer extremes, he could not be killed. And in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, among other calamities of the Christians, he most clearly predicted that which occurred under the Prince **Valerian**. Regarding this, **Dionysius**, the Bishop of Alexandria and a martyr of that time, said: "It was revealed to John that he should speak, and there was given to him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies, and power was given to him for forty-two months." Both of these were fulfilled in Valerian. These are the words of Dionysius.

But it was fitting that before other martyrs, that cousin of Christ, **Simeon**, should stand; after long-lasting torments, he also willingly endured the cross when he was one hundred and twenty years old. But behold, a vast multitude of men excellent in every doctrine now offers itself to me: **Timothy**, **Titus**, **Clement of Rome**, **Barnabas**, **John the Elder**, **Aristion**, **Sophistenes**, **Silvanus**, **Sosipater**, **Demophilus**, **Dorotheus**, **Philemon**, **Andronicus**, **Urban**, **Lucius**, **Jason**, **Tertius**, **Crescens**, **Linus**, **Cletus**, **Paul**, **Sergius** the proconsul of Cyprus, **Silas**, **Hegesippus** the Jew, **Crispus**, **Epaphras**, **Demas**, **Mark**, **Aristarchus**, **Epaphroditus**, **Tychicus**, **Onesimus**, **Euodus**, **Papias**, **Hermas**, **Justus**, **Gaius**, and **Melito**, the Asian philosopher, who composed a book for Christ addressed to **Marcus Antoninus Verus** <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note>. And many other very wise men, disciples of the Apostles, of whom one looked upon the other’s cross without fear, soon expected his own with an untamed spirit, and bore it unconquered.

Other wise men imitated these: **Theophilus**, **Dionysius**, **Pinytus** of Crete, **Tatian**, **Philip**, **Musanus**, **Modestus** the philosopher, **Bardaisan** the Syrian (a dialectician and mathematician), and **Apollinaris** the philosopher. These two gave books for our religion to Marcus Antoninus Verus. Also **Victor**, **Irenaeus**, **Rhodon**, **Clement of Alexandria**, and the most learned **Miltiades**, who also delivered a book for the Christian religion to Marcus Antoninus. **Apollonius** the philosopher, a senator of the city of Rome and a martyr for Christ, who, under **Commodus** and **Severus**, composed a distinguished volume to give an account of his faith. Also **Apollonius**, **Abel**, **Serapion**, **Bacchylus**, **Polycrates**, **Heraclitus**, **Maximus**, **Candidus**, **Apion**, **Sextus**, **Arabianus**, **Narcissus**, **Judas**, and **Tertullian**, a fountain of learning, who flourished under the Emperor Severus and cried out thus against the judges:

"We speak, and we speak openly; and while you torture us, torn and bloody we shout: We worship God through Christ! Consider him a man; through him and in him, God wishes himself to be known and worshipped. We give thanks for your sentences; when we are condemned by you, we are acquitted by God."

**Ammonius of Alexandria**, a noble Platonist; **Leonides** the wise, father of **Origen**; and Origen himself, a man of learning and a life remarkably admirable, whom **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and famous critic of Christianity</note> placed above all those of his century in learning. Origen refuted the disputations of **Celsus** the Epicurean against the Christians in eight volumes, and wrote as much concerning Christian doctrine as one could scarcely read in a very long lifetime. He, as **Eusebius** says, endured frequent torments unheard of in all centuries for the glory of Christ. His illustrious disciples **Plutarch**, **Heraclides**, **Hero**, and the two **Serenuses** were crowned with martyrdom for Christ. **Tryphon** follows...
