Next follow Trypho and Ambrose, disciples of Origen; Minutius, Gaius, Beryllus, Hippolytus, Alexander, Julius Africanus, Geminus, Theodorus, Cornelius, and Cyprian—the African martyr, most outstanding in wisdom and eloquence. Then Pontius, the disciple of Cyprian; Dionysius, Novatian, Marcion, Archelaus, and Anatolius, the famous Alexandrian philosopher. Then Victorinus, the most wealthy martyr Pamphilus and his disciple Eusebius of Caesarea (who was much like his master), Pierius, Lucian, Phileas, Arnobius, and Lactantius the rhetorician. Also Methodius, the distinguished philosopher who refuted the disputations of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher and a prominent intellectual opponent of Christianity.</note> against us in an extraordinary volume. Then Juvencus, Eustathius, Marcellus, Athanasius the Great, Anthony, Basil, Theodore, Eusebius of Emesa, Triphyllus, Lucifer, Eusebius of Vercelli, Acacius, Serapion, and Hilary the Great. Then Victorinus, Titus, Damasus, Apollinaris, Gregory of Elvira <note>original: "Gregorius Bedicus," likely referring to Gregory Baeticus of Elvira.</note>, Pacian, Phoebadius, and Didymus of Alexandria, a divine man, along with his pupil Ambrose of Alexandria. Then Optatus the African, Achillius, Cyril, Cuzonis, Epiphanius, and Ephrem the Syrian. Then Basil the Great and his brother Gregory <note>Gregory of Nyssa</note>, and Gregory Nazianzen, surnamed "The Theologian." This Gregory responded subtly and copiously to the invectives launched by the Emperor Julian against the Christians. <note>Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), known as "the Apostate," attempted to revive traditional Roman polytheism and authored "Against the Galilaeans."</note> Then Diodorus, Ambrose, Evagrius, Maximus the Philosopher, John Chrysostom, Gelasius, Theotimus the Just, Amphilochius, Sophronius, and others almost innumerable—men outstanding in learning. Some of these defended the glory of Christ before the Emperor Julian, and some during his reign, doing so amidst swords and fire, with pen, tongue, life, and death. For this reason, they are called martyrs, as they are witnesses <note>The Greek word "martys" (μάρτυς) literally means "witness."</note> to Christian glory.

Jerome numbers among those first Christians Josephus, Seneca, and Philo. <note>Jerome included these non-Christian writers (the Jewish historians Josephus and Philo, and the Roman Stoic Seneca) in his "On Illustrious Men" because of their positive mentions of Christians or supposed correspondence with Apostles.</note> He also notes seventy-two heresies of sharp-witted men that gushed forth immediately after the beginning of this religion—partly from human pride and partly from the cunning of demons—who honored Christ himself, though not correctly as others did. Now truly, if I wished to count the Jeromes, Ambroses, Augustines, Gregories, and other innumerable men most excellent in knowledge—Greeks, Barbarians, and Latins—who labored for the glory of Christ for a very long time after Julian the Apostate by writing sharply and elegantly and by living holily, arithmetic calculation itself would fail me. The Christian law is at least as much more excellent than the others as there were more learned men, and men always more learned, more eloquent, and holier than those who followed other paths.

If logicians, orators, or poets had laid the first foundation of this religion, we might suspect that the common people had been deceived by human cunning; or if all the learned had always rejected it, we might judge it perhaps worthy of contempt. If princes, either from the beginning or shortly thereafter, had entirely favored this law, we might think—as we think of certain other religions—that the weaker were coerced by the more powerful, and that their successors then, as often happens, "drank in that law with their mother's milk." 

Therefore, Divine Providence willed that the simple truth of its religion should take its first origin from men who were initially unrefined and simple, and that the clever and learned should be happily ensnared by the simple and unrefined. Moreover, Providence permitted its religion to be cruelly attacked everywhere by the powerful of the nations for more than three hundred years, so that the number of learned witnesses and the faithful might be greater, and the authority of the matter itself might be truer, more certain, and more firm; for it is easy to maintain faith in prosperity, but difficult in adversity.

That the Christians were tortured with the most exquisite torments is testified to by Cornelius Tacitus (even setting aside our own histories). However, he disparaged the Christians, I believe, to flatter the sensibilities of his own age. Tertullian showed that Tacitus even lied in his history when he said that the Jews worship the head of a donkey. <note>Tacitus, in his "Histories," repeated a common ancient slur that the Jews worshipped an ass in the Temple.</note> Yet in that same history, he wrote that when Pompey peered into the secrets of the Jews, he found no image among them. Therefore, from this one lie, learn to recognize the rest. To this is added what Irenaeus testifies: that suspicion arose against our people at that time as if we were impious and impure for no other reason than the completely incestuous and cursed lives of certain Gnostic heretics. But this infamy did not last long once the truth began to reveal itself.

Lucian the Gentile <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian satirist who wrote in Greek.</note>, mocking a certain sophist named Peregrinus—and as he describes him, a "not quite legitimate" Christian—as a show-off and a braggart, says: "This man, moreover, learned the wonderful wisdom of the Christians from their priests and teachers, who, worshiping that great man crucified in Palestine, despise all other religions. By the law of their master, they are bound to one another in brotherly charity; they hope to be eternal, led by which hope these wretched little people <note>original: "miselli"</note> despise this life and its goods, and daily offer themselves up voluntarily to slaughter." Thus says Lucian. That he lied about Peregrinus out of hatred is testified to by Aulus Gellius...

# MARSILIUS FICINO'S BOOK
->Page 74<-

...of Peregrinus, his close associate, for he shows that this Peregrinus was a grave and steadfast man and a true philosopher. <note>original: "Peregrini". This refers to Peregrinus Proteus (c. 100–165 AD), a Cynic philosopher who was once a Christian leader before returning to paganism and eventually self-immolating.</note> Pliny the Younger complained in a letter to Trajan that the cities of the Christians were being slaughtered, even though they do nothing against Roman law, except that they sing hymns before dawn to a certain "Christ as God." <note>original: "Plinius secundus in Epistola ad Traianum". This refers to the famous correspondence (Epistulae 10.96) between Pliny, governor of Bithynia, and Emperor Trajan around 112 AD.</note> To maintain their discipline, they forbid homicide, theft, adultery, robbery, and similar crimes. Trajan, however, wrote back that while Christians should not be sought out, if they were reported, they must be punished. Tertullian refutes this sentence with the following logic: "O judgment confused by necessity! He denies they should be sought out as if they were innocent, yet commands they be punished as if they were guilty. He spares and rages; he ignores and punishes. Why do you entrap yourself with such a judgment? If you condemn them, why not search for them? If you do not search for them, why not also acquit them?" <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage. This quote is from his *Apology*.</note> He also subtly refutes the vain rumors that had arisen against Christian customs, showing that action was taken against Christians not for any crime, but for the mere name of their sect.

And, as we have said elsewhere, Serenus Granius made a similar complaint in a letter to Hadrian. <note>Serenus Granius was a Proconsul of Asia.</note> Whereupon Hadrian wrote to Minutius Fundanus, the proconsul of Asia, that he should not allow harmless Christians to be disturbed, nor should the opportunity for robbery be granted to their accusers. Our Eusebius provides the full letter of Hadrian. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History," preserved these documents in his *Ecclesiastical History*.</note> Melito, Bishop of Sardis, also wrote a book to the Emperor Antoninus in defense of our religion, in which he recounts an edict of Antoninus to the people of Asia. <note>Antoninus Pius (reigned 138–161 AD).</note> In it, the Emperor rebukes them for disturbing the worship of the immortal God whom the Christians revere, and for pursuing Christians even unto death. He adds in the same edict that many judges from the provinces had written to his father about these matters in the past, and many had recently written to him; finally, he decreed what his father had also decreed: that no one should pursue Christians solely for the fact that they are Christians, unless they are perhaps proven to be plotting something against the state of the Roman Empire.

I believe Antoninus also feared Christ for this reason: his brother Marcus Aurelius wrote that when his army was in danger from thirst among the Germans, he obtained very heavy rains from God through the prayers of certain Christian soldiers, contrary to everyone's hopes. <note>original: "frater eius M. Aurelius". Marcus Aurelius was actually the adopted son and successor of Antoninus Pius. The event described is the famous "Miracle of the Thundering Legion" (c. 174 AD).</note> By this rain, the thirst of his own men was quenched and the enemy was put to flight by the force of lightning; because of the miracle of this remarkable deed, he renamed that legion the "Thundering Legion." Apollinaris and Tertullian write of these things. Tertullian adds that letters from the Emperor Marcus still exist in which these matters are more clearly indicated. Eusebius adds that this miracle was also recorded by pagan historians, although they omitted the fact that it was accomplished through the prayers of Christians.

The calamity of the Christians, therefore, happened mostly either because of the ignorant common people or because of impious rulers, the chief of whom was Nero. Suetonius relates that Christians were afflicted by Nero solely because they were introducing a new religion, which he called "maleficent"—that is, magical. <note>original: "maleficam, id est magicam". Suetonius, in *Life of Nero* 16.2, uses the word "maleficae" to describe Christianity; Ficino interprets this as "magic" because the Romans often attributed Christian miracles to the dark arts.</note> For many, seeing miracles, attributed to demons what was actually of God. But infinite truth and goodness declared its truth through the lies of its enemies, and converted the evils of men into good. God also allows the assembly of his saints to be agitated either by heretics or by enemies until the end of the world. God does not force men toward salvation, whom He created free from the beginning, but He draws individuals by constant inspirations. If any come to Him, He toughens them with labors and exercises them with adversities; just as fire tests gold, so He proves the soul with difficulty. Those who persevere to the end shall finally shine happily with divine light, like gold purified by fire.

Muhammad highly approves of those first Christians and confesses that Christian doctrine—that is, the books of the Evangelists and Apostles—received marvelous authority from God Himself, and he places them above the Old Testament. <note>original: "Mahumethes". Ficino is referring to the Quranic recognition of Jesus (*Isa*) and the Gospel (*Injil*).</note> But he says these books were corrupted by Christians after the time of the Apostles. A man as cunning as he was warlike devised this entire scheme because he asserts that he was promised by Christ in the clearest words, who said in the Gospel: "I predict to you that after me a certain messenger of God named Muhammad shall come; he is clearly the spirit of truth, who will teach you all things." <note>Muhammad (c. 570–632 AD). Ficino is addressing the Islamic claim that Jesus predicted Muhammad (referencing the *Paraclete* in John 14:16-26, which Islamic tradition often identifies with Muhammad).</note> In the first place, a scheme of this kind, though it found a place among brutish and cowardly men (for such are the followers of Muhammad) through both force and deceit, is nevertheless utterly ridiculous to great and wise men. # ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION

...it would have been the case that they should have removed the name of Muhammad from the Gospel rather than the names of Pilate, or Judas, or the Antichrist, or even the Devil. Moreover, after the coming of Muhammad, Muhammad himself would have been more likely to be honored by those who cherished the Gospel than to have his name removed. But he himself falsely wished to attach his name to the place where, in the Gospel of John, Christ promises the Holy Spirit. <note>original: "Spiritum sanctum". Muhammad is often identified in Islamic tradition with the "Paraclete" or Comforter promised by Jesus in John 14:16.</note> The pouring out of this Spirit was promised to his Apostles not long after Jesus's resurrection, not six hundred years later to the Arabs. Furthermore, a man was not promised, but an incorporeal spirit and truth. And with all the leaders of the Christians in agreement—especially those who were witnesses to the promise through both words and letters—this Spirit breathed fortunately and shone forth on the fiftieth day after the resurrection. <note>This refers to Pentecost, the "fiftieth day" (quinquagesimo die), when Christians believe the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples.</note>

Next, in what way is it likely that all Christians would have dared to change those volumes which, at that time, they venerated most highly as having been given from heaven? If any impious people had dared to do so, they, being few and reckless, would have been immediately convicted by the many who were prudent, and they would not have prevailed. Again, if the sacred volumes had been corrupted everywhere among all nations, many would have noticed it suddenly if the rest of the copies elsewhere had cried out against it. But it is entirely impossible to utterly adulterate books published in different languages, places, and times, which were so widely and suddenly scattered and so frequently used. Why did the sects of the heretics bring forward different interpretations rather than different texts?

We have heard from many Ethiopians, and indeed learned ones, that their sacred volumes in "Barbaric" letters <note>original: "Barbaris literis". Ficino likely refers to the Ge'ez script used in Ethiopia.</note> are entirely similar to those existing among the Greeks and Latins. Riccoldo of Monte Croce, the theologian, writes that in Asia he read entirely the same texts among the Jacobite and Nestorian Christian heretics as exist among us. <note>original: "Richoldus Ebron". This refers to Riccoldo da Monte di Croce (c. 1243–1320), a Dominican missionary famous for his travels in the East and his polemical works on Islam.</note>

Hence, it is clear that the Old Testament itself is preserved correctly by the Christians. For although we have many translations published both before and after Christ—some more free, such as those made by the Jews themselves, others observed word-for-word, especially by Jerome—nevertheless, the principal mysteries of Jesus Christ, indeed nearly all of them, are found similarly everywhere. <note>original: "Hieronymo". St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> And the word-for-word translation of Jerome was admitted by all Jews as true, and it is indeed most sufficient for confirming Jesus. Also most true is that translation which was published by the seventy-two Jews before Christ; it exists similarly among the Greek, Latin, and "Barbaric" Christians. <note>term: <term>Septuagint</term>—The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to seventy-two Jewish scholars in the 3rd century BC.</note> Tertullian even asserts that in his own time, the first copies of this, both Hebrew and Greek, existed at the Serapeum in the libraries of Ptolemy. <note>original: "Serapium in Ptolemæi bibliothecis". The Serapeum was a temple in Alexandria that housed part of the famous Great Library.</note>

Nor was such a translation corrupted long ago by the Apostles or their successors, both because it was difficult to corrupt codices that were widely circulated and so preserved, and because it is entirely foolish to believe that so many and such great men would have adulterated the testimonies of the Jews to bring to life the slain Jesus, only to lose themselves. Finally, the frequent objections, slanders, and traps laid for Christians from every side, and the often-repeated disputes, warned Christians to keep the correct course of the scriptures. If anyone ever hears from the followers of Muhammad that something pertaining to Muhammad was subtracted from the Old Testament, let him respond that in no way could the Jews have ever agreed with the Christians to do this. For the Old Testament, neither among the Jews nor among the Christians, favors the followers of Muhammad in any way.

But to return to the New Testament: that this itself is sincere is established from the disciples of the Apostles and the successors of those disciples, who provide testimony to the sincerity of the text in both works and writings. It is also established from the very ancient councils frequently held, where codices carried about by ten thousand of the most learned men were examined with the utmost precision; hence nothing was ever admitted by the Church without the strictest examination.

Furthermore, Muhammad prattles that the successors of the Apostles added that part to the Gospels—for instance, that the man Jesus was the supreme God and truly died. <note>original: "Garrit præterea Mahumethes". Ficino uses the dismissive verb *garrit* (chatters/prattles) to describe Muhammad's claims.</note> First of all, this is connected so often in the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists, and in such an order and with such consistency, that it could in no way be an addition. Secondly, nothing is more difficult to persuade someone of than that a man is the supreme God, nor does anything seem more discordant to proclaim than that the true God truly died. Did they then add this so that they might more easily persuade people of what was being preached? Almost nothing was said by them, except this very thing, that would either disturb the faithless Jews—who did not grasp that union of God and man—or offend the Romans, the masters of the world...

### THE BOOK OF MARSILIO FICINO

...lords, who had forbidden anyone from being called "God" without the authority of the Senate. They desired many gods—and not even supreme ones—whereas the Christians called Jesus both supreme and the only God without the Senate's approval. The Christians knew that, for this reason alone, they had entered upon an altogether arduous task and were in great danger among both Jews and Gentiles. 

Regarding what Muhammad <note>original: "Mahumethes"</note> says was added [to the scriptures], it does not seem to be an addition at all, but rather something placed there with great courage and simplicity from the beginning. Yet he himself seems to have not understood the profound mysteries of the Christians at all, even though he read them. For where he reads that Jesus is the Son of God and is God, he thinks that the Christians are introducing two gods there: namely, a Father and a Son. In the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> he detests this binary number of gods, which is actually foreign to Christians, who believe in one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 

Although he may not know how, Muhammad is nevertheless moved by the miracles of Christ and confesses him to be the Son of God and God when he names him the "breath of God," the "spirit," "God’s own soul," the "power of God," and the "Word of God," born of a perpetual virgin by the breathing of God. Furthermore, whenever he happens upon the name of the Trinity—being a man entirely ignorant of such a great matter—he falsely and foolishly slanders Christians by claiming they worship three gods. He was unable to distinguish the properties of the divine Persons while simultaneously preserving the unity of the divine substance. Yet, compelled by the truth, he himself depicts God speaking of Himself in the plural number everywhere [in the Quran]. This was also observed by Moses, who in Genesis sometimes attributed a singular name and verb to God, and sometimes a plural one, certainly preserving the unity of substance in God while simultaneously acknowledging the number of Persons. God said: *Let us make man in our image and likeness*, <note>Genesis 1:26</note> along with many other even clearer examples. 

But hear how Muhammad makes God speak to Mary, the best of all women, who was never touched by any man: *We breathed our soul into her, and we set her and her son as a manifest miracle.* Likewise: *Though we sent many messengers, we finally sent Christ, the son of Mary, whose followers were faithful, with gentle and constant hearts. We gave the Gospel to him, so that through it men might attain the love and grace of God.* Again: *We bestowed much goodness upon Christ, and we placed him over the children of Israel as a teacher.* Likewise: *We sent Christ for the fulfillment of the divine law; we made Christ and Mary a miracle, and we gave them the best place in Paradise to inhabit*, and he says similar things often. 

Therefore, even if it cannot be denied that he was arrogant, he seems to be blamed for ignorance no less than for arrogance. For he tempered his arrogance significantly when he said in the Quran that he neither performed miracles nor would perform them; that he was ignorant of many things; and that he was a mere man (though a messenger inspired by God) and could not grant the forgiveness of sins. He forbade himself to be invoked or worshipped, and he further confessed that there were some things in his books whose truth might be doubted. From this, it appears he was not the Spirit of Truth himself. He also detracted much from the authority of the Quran when he said: *Whoever worships one God and lives honestly—whether he be Jew, Christian, or Saracen <note>A common medieval term for Muslims</note>—will follow after the mercy and salvation of God.* 

Indeed, he most clearly confesses the authority of the Gospel when he calls it "light," "direction," and "perfection." Hence, the followers of Muhammad, with his permission, confess that with the arrival of the New Testament, the rites of the Old Testament rightly ceased for the most part. They understand the Old and New Testaments in the way that Muhammad explained and commanded, who asserted that he was the truest interpreter of both. They approve of the creation of the world, the progeny of Adam, the entire Hebrew history, and the teaching of Christ. They expect the Antichrist to be an utterly evil man, whom they believe will be killed by Christ. Likewise, they accept the resurrection of bodies, the final judgment, and eternal punishments and rewards; they place Christ sitting nearest to God. The Muhammadans even use the daily prayer to God that we use—the *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note> and the rest—but where we say *and lead us not into temptation*, they say,

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s treatise. # ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION:

->*The cause of the error of the Jews, the Muslims, and the Pagans.*<-
->Chapter XXXVII.<-

One may ask, therefore: what is the cause that still holds many Jews in their unbelief <note>original: "perfidia." In a 15th-century context, this term referred to a refusal to accept the Christian faith rather than "treachery" in the modern sense.</note>? It is the divine depth of the Prophetic and Christian mysteries; because they are divine, they cannot be penetrated by human intelligence, and vice versa. Furthermore, it is the character of the wretched and mercenary Jews, which is utterly unrefined and stubborn. There is an insatiable greed, both for preserving what is theirs and for the practice of usury <term>usury: the lending of money at interest, which was a common stereotype and point of theological contention</term>, as well as a natural love for their own kind and an innate hatred of Christians. 

What, however, after the time of the blessed Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), often credited with the conversion of various "barbarian" tribes to orthodox Christianity</note>, drew so many Barbarians into heresy? It was the great difficulty of interpreting the divine scriptures, the excessively ignorant nature of the Barbarian peoples, the violent hand of Muhammad, the king of the Arabs, and the laws of the seven kings of his family who succeeded him in order. Added to this was a wider license for worldly behavior. 

But what once turned the Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> away from the true religion of the Hebrews? The commands of ambitious princes, an unlearned age, widespread license, and the deception of malignant demons. Subsequently, the charms and flatteries of the Poets increased the error. Indeed, ancestral custom and long-standing habit easily hold everyone in any kind of error. However, custom cannot hold legitimate Christians in error, for they have, from the beginning, embraced a religion that is removed from error.

There is no need for me to confirm with a long dispute those things which Christ and his disciples proposed as matters to be believed, hoped for, and acted upon. For they possess enough truth and authority since we have already proved that they proceed from divine truth. Therefore, we shall assign the greatest reason for Christian institutions and promises by saying, in the manner of the Pythagoreans <note>The followers of Pythagoras were famous for accepting the word of their master without further question, a practice known as "Ipse dixit" or "He himself said it."</note>: "He said so." 

We must remember, however, that we ought not to be troubled if we are less capable of grasping these things; for I judge this to be the greatest sign of their divinity. Indeed, if our mind could thoroughly comprehend them, they would be smaller than our mind; if they are such [that we can understand them], they cannot be divine. For if they are divine, they exceed every capacity of the human mind. Faith, as Aristotle maintains, is the foundation of knowledge; and by faith alone, as the Platonists prove, do we approach God. David says: "I believed, and therefore I have spoken" <note>A reference to Psalm 116:10</note>. Therefore, by believing and approaching the fountain of truth and goodness, we shall drink deeply of a wise and blessed life.

->**MARSILIO**<-

# MARSILIO FICINO
## the Florentine’s Preface to the Platonic Theo-
### logy on the immortality of souls, to Lauren-
### tium de' Medici. <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and Ficino’s primary patron.</note>

Plato, the father of philosophers, great-hearted Lorenzo, understood that just as the sense of sight relates to the light of the Sun, so all minds relate to God; therefore, he understood that minds can never know anything without the light of God. Rightly, then, he judged it just and pious that since the human mind receives everything from God, it should refer everything back to God. Thus, whether we philosophize about morals, we must recognize that the soul is to be purified so that, having finally become more serene, it may perceive the divine light and worship God. Or, if we investigate the causes of things, the causes must be sought so that we may finally find the Cause of causes itself, and having found it, venerate it. Nor does our Plato only exhort others to this duty of piety; he himself excels at it most of all. Thus it happened that he himself is called "divine" without controversy, and his doctrine is called "Theology" among all nations, since he never treats anything—whether moral, logical, mathematical, or physical—without soon leading it back, with the highest piety, to the contemplation and worship of God.

Because, indeed, he considers the soul to be like a mirror in which the image of the divine face easily reflects, he therefore diligently tracks God Himself through every individual footprint, and turns everywhere toward the appearance of the soul. He understands that the famous oracle, "Know thyself," <note>original: "nosce te ipsum." This was the famous inscription at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note> warns us above all that whoever desires to recognize God must first know himself. For this reason, whoever reads most diligently the Platonic works (all of which I have long since translated into Latin) will certainly achieve many things, but these two above all: the pious worship of God through knowledge, and the divinity of souls. In these two things consist the universal perception of reality, the entire institution of life, and all happiness. This is especially true since Plato feels so strongly about these matters that Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity who, like Ficino, saw Platonism as a precursor to Christian truth.</note> chose him from the entire number of philosophers to be imitated as the one closest of all to Christian truth, asserting that the Platonists would be Christians if only a few things were changed.

I, truly, having long relied on the authority of Aurelius Augustine and led by the greatest charity toward the human race, decided to express a certain "likeness" of Plato himself that is very similar to Christian truth. I have applied myself diligently to those two points I mentioned above all others, and therefore I judged that this entire work should be titled *The Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*. In composing this, my chief plan was that in the divinity of the created mind itself—as if in a mirror positioned in the middle of all things—we might both behold the works of the Creator and contemplate and worship the Creator’s mind.

I believe (and not with a vain faith) that this was decreed by divine providence: that the perverse minds of many, which do not easily yield to the authority of divine law alone, might find rest at last in Platonic reasons which greatly support religion. Furthermore, those who impiously separate the study of philosophy too much from holy religion may eventually recognize that they wander no differently than someone who, out of love for wisdom, separates it from the honor of Wisdom itself, or separates true intelligence from a righteous will. Finally, those who think only of things perceived through the body, and who unhappily prefer the shadows of things to the real things themselves, may at last be reminded by Platonic reason to contemplate sublime things beyond the senses and happily prefer the things themselves to their shadows. 

Almighty God commands this first of all. Human affairs absolutely demand this. The celestial Plato once accomplished this easily among his own people, with God’s breathing upon him. At last, we ourselves have labored in this demanding work to imitate Plato for our own people, though relying solely on divine aid. But I wish that we have completed it with as much truth as we have treated it with veneration for divine truth, so much so that we wish nothing of ours to be approved except that which the divine law confirms. 

I have judged that this work itself should be dedicated to you, Great-hearted Lorenzo, above all others. This is not to reveal philosophical matters to you, which you have long since debated, so that I might seem to be publishing the secrets of the ancients to you (who have already attained these things with a certain wonderful genius) as much as to others. Rather, it is because we have obtained, through your benefit, that leisure in which we could more easily philosophize. Our Plato seems to congratulate us greatly on this duty toward you, since you have joined philosophy together with the highest authority in public affairs—something he once most greatly desired in great men.

# PLATONIC THEO-
## logy, on the immortality of souls,
### authored by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine,
-> BOOK ONE. <-

-> *If the soul were not immortal, no animal would be more unhappy than man.* Chapter 1. <-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a classical figure (possibly a deity or personification) seated amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

Since the human race, on account of the restlessness of the soul, the weakness of the body, and the lack of all things, leads a harder life on earth than the beasts, if nature had assigned to it exactly the same limit of living as it did to other animals, no animal would be more unhappy than man. But since it is impossible that man—who through the worship of God comes closer than all other mortals to God, the author of happiness—should be the most unhappy of all. And since it is only after the death of the body <note>original: *post mortem*. The OCR "p̄dst" is a common abbreviation for "post".</note> that he can be made more blessed, it seems necessary that some light remains for our souls as they depart from this prison. But if human minds never look back at their own light, enclosed in darkness and a blind prison, we are often forced to doubt our own divinity. Let us break, I pray, heavenly souls longing for a heavenly fatherland, let us break as soon as possible the chains of earthly shackles, so that, lifted on Platonic wings and with God as our guide, we may fly more freely to the ethereal seat, where we will immediately and happily contemplate the excellence of our race.

Furthermore, so that it may clearly appear by what means human minds are best able to loosen their mortal enclosures, see their own immortality, and attain happiness, we will attempt in the following discussion to demonstrate to the best of our ability that beyond this sluggish mass of bodies, where the inquiry of the followers of Democritus, the Cyrenaics, and the Epicureans <note>Three schools of ancient Greek philosophy that were materialistic, believing that only physical matter exists.</note> ended, there is some active quality and power, toward which the investigation of the Stoics and Cynics directed itself.

Above quality, however—which is divided and entirely changed along with the dimensions of matter—there exists a certain more excellent form which, although it is changed in a certain way, nonetheless does not admit division in the body. In this form, the ancient theologians placed the seat of the rational soul. Heraclitus, Marcus Varro, and Marcus Manilius <note>Classical thinkers who, according to Ficino, recognized the soul as something higher than mere physical matter but still tied to the celestial bodies or a world-spirit.</note> ascended this far.

Above the rational soul, there exists an angelic mind, which is not only undivided but also immutable; in this, Anaxagoras and Hermotimus seem to have rested. Finally, over the eye of this mind, which desires and receives the light of truth, presides the divine Sun itself, toward which our Plato ordered, taught, and strove for us to direct the purified gaze of the mind. Accordingly, when we have ascended to this point, we will compare these <term>five degrees</term> <note>Ficino’s "Great Chain of Being": Body, Quality, Soul, Angel, and God. The Soul is the middle point, connecting the physical and spiritual worlds.</note> of all things in turn: namely, the mass of the body, quality, soul, angel, and God. Since, however, the class of the rational soul itself, holding the middle position among these degrees, appears as the bond of all nature—it rules qualities and bodies, and joins itself to the angel and to God—we will show it to be utterly indissoluble while it connects the degrees of nature, most excellent while it presides over the machinery of the world, and most blessed while it winds its way into divine things. That our soul indeed behaves in this way and is such, we will assert first by general reasons, second by specific arguments, third by signs, and fourth by the resolution of questions.

-> *The body does nothing by its own nature.* Chapter 2. <-

Since, according to Plato, the body consists of a certain matter and quantity, and it belongs to matter only to be extended and to be acted upon, and extension and being acted upon are themselves certain <term>passions</term> <note>original: *passiones*. In Renaissance philosophy, a "passion" is something a thing *undergoes* or *suffers*, rather than an action it performs.</note>. Quantity, moreover, is either nothing other than the extension of matter itself, or if it is something else, it is still such a thing that it is always subject to division and [inseparable from] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note> matter—

<meta>This page continues the argument for the immortality of the soul by distinguishing between physical "quantity" (size and mass) and "quality" (the essential powers of a thing). Ficino is moving up the "Great Chain of Being" from the purely material body to the soul.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL <note>original: DE IMMORTALI AMOR, likely an abbreviated form of *De Immortalitate Animorum*</note> BOOK I
<meta>catchword: where itself</meta>

they have the same nature, they act in the same way. Moreover, things exist not through their mass in this or that species, but through this or that form; therefore, they operate through form. This is especially true since the agent approaches the patient <note>The "patient" is the thing being acted upon.</note> through the qualities of its form first, rather than through the boundaries of its quantity. The power of a form passes into foreign matter more effectively than the dimension of its quantity, and it reaches individual points of matter not by measurement, but by quality. Thus, water makes things cold through its coldness. Fire heats through its heat rather than through its bulk. For fire does not burn because it is very large, but because it is very hot. And if all its heat were reduced, as if to a single point, it would be most powerful for burning because of that maximum union. Thus, action arises by the benefit of quality, especially when it is compressed into a narrow space. 

From this, it follows that natural causes produce effects similar to the qualities of the causes, rather than equal to their quantity. And if it happens that equal effects occasionally arise, they must first have appeared through similar qualities, as if the action is carried out through qualities; afterwards, by necessity, the effects reflect their causes in and through those qualities. For this reason, almost all newborn children are similar to their parents in their complexion <note>original: *complexione*, referring to the balance of bodily humors</note> and shape, but they are more rarely and only later equal to them in size. 

But who has not seen this? For if you approach a large body, you do not become large yourself; but if you approach a hot one, you certainly become hot. Nor do you perceive quantity with any sense unless quality has first moved that sense. For who can judge how large a wall is unless color and light have brought that very magnitude to the eye? Furthermore, the judgment of quantity is lost sooner and more easily due to distance than the judgment of light and color, as if the efficacy of movement lies in the quality. This is clearly confirmed by the fact that any object always moves our desire by reason of its "goodness" (which is a quality), not by reason of its "greatness" or "multitude." Otherwise, we would always choose things that are larger or more numerous. But in fact, in those things we consider evil, we choose the smaller or fewer. 

Moreover, quality cannot be a body <note>Ficino uses "body" to mean a physical, three-dimensional object.</note> because two bodies cannot be entirely fused in the same place without mutual obstruction, yet many qualities are blended together in the same place. Indeed, in the substance of honey, the yellow color, the sweetness, and the scent—three qualities—are found everywhere together. For every little drop of honey is yellow, sweet, and pleasant to the nose. Added to this is the fact that every body, by its nature, is extended in length, breadth, and depth. Quality, however, does not seem to be extended by its own nature. For if it were, there would be no quality that was not extended. Yet certain unextended qualities exist in a point, in unity, in number, in harmony, and in virtues. 

Quality, therefore, is not a body, especially because if extension were natural to it, the wider it became, the stronger it would become. However, it becomes weaker by dispersion. Therefore, quality, which is in a certain way indivisible in itself, is divided within the dimension of a body. Indeed, division happens only by reason of quantity, since division is always led from one thing into many. Yet quality preserves even in a body a certain property of its indivisible nature. For as the followers of Plato <note>original: *Platonici*</note> believe, the whiteness that is in any part of a white body should not properly be called a "part" of that whiteness which is in the whole body; rather, it should be called the "whiteness of the part" rather than a "part of the whiteness." Certainly, if you divide a white body into several parts, the same essential nature <note>original: *ratio*</note> of whiteness will remain in each individual part. The power and action remain similar, even if the amplitude is not the same or equal. Therefore, division does not properly belong to quality, but to the body by reason of its quantity. Action belongs chiefly to quality when it is reduced to a small space. This quality is certainly not a body, and it becomes most incorporeal when it is gathered into a point. From this, it follows that operation arises not from the matter of bodies, but by the power of an incorporeal nature.

---

-> Above the form divided in the body stands the indivisible form, that is, the soul. Chapter III. <-

**W**e have thus ascended from the body to quality. Following the Platonic custom, we call every "divided form in a body" a quality. But should we stop at this step, after the manner of the Stoics and the Cyrenaics? <note>Two ancient schools of philosophy that Ficino argues were too focused on the material world.</note> Not at all. Quality is a certain kind of form. The nature of a form is simple, effective, and agile in action. For this reason, form is often called "act" <note>original: *actus*, meaning the realization of a potential</note> by physicists. A nature of this kind is stained in the lap of matter; from being simple it becomes divisible and impure; from being active it becomes subject to passion; from being agile it becomes sluggish. Therefore, this is neither a pure form, nor a true one, nor a perfect one. This cannot be the "first form" if it is not pure. For every thing must exist in its pure state, at least according to its genus, before it is defiled. Likewise, it cannot be the first form if it is not true. From where does the mind conclude that this form is not entirely true? Unless from...

This serves as a stepping stone to prove the existence of the soul as an indivisible, higher form of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s exploration of the hierarchy of being. Having discussed physical mass and the properties of bodies, he now argues that "quality"—the physical characteristics of things—cannot be the ultimate source or "first form" of reality because it is dependent, imperfect, and often deceptive compared to the higher truths found in the mind.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
<meta>catchword: efficiency</meta>

where the mind itself discerns something truer, compared to which this [sensible world] falls short and is somehow proven to be false. Where exactly does the mind see this true form? Surely it perceives it either outside of itself or within. If it looks outside itself: then certainly somewhere in nature there exists a true form superior to physical quality. If the mind gazes upon it within itself, then the true form is not lacking to the mind; therefore, it is not lacking to the world. Furthermore, truth is certainly more powerful than falsehood, since truth can exist without falsehood, while falsehood cannot stand without truth. For nothing is called "false" unless it is at least true that it is false. Nor does falsehood have any power unless it is true that it has power, nor is it truly understood to be false except through the truth. Nor is something called "false" unless it deceives, and it does not deceive except through an image of the truth. If, therefore, truth is more powerful than falsehood, and if the "less-than-true" form—namely, physical quality—exists in the order of things, then much more so is a "true form" to be found in the order of things. This is especially true since the intelligible form <note>The "intelligible form" refers to a concept or essence understood by the mind, rather than seen by the eyes.</note> ought to be as much more excellent and true than the sensible form as the intellect is more excellent and true than the senses. 

Through these points, it has become clear that quality cannot be the "first form," both because it is not pure and because it is not true. It is also evident because it is not perfect. For the first thing in any genus <note>term: *genus*—a category or class of things.</note> is the principle of the entire genus. That which is the principle of others contains the things that follow it. Therefore, nothing of its own kind is lacking to that which is first in its kind. Just as the Sun, if it is the first among shining things, lacks no degree of light. Other shining things below it, such as the stars and the elements, do not grasp the total fullness of light. Since, therefore, the "first form" embraces all the perfections of forms and thus cannot be imperfect, it is rightly concluded that the form which is called "imperfect" [quality] cannot be the first. 

Add to this that because quality is so inherent in matter that it is extended and divided along with it, it becomes (so to speak) entirely material. And if it were separated from matter, it would be destroyed. For this reason, it does not sustain itself, but is sustained by matter as its subject. But that which cannot sustain itself can much less exist through itself. Thus, since it lies within another, it certainly depends on another. For quality arises at a certain time, as it changes and perishes. Nothing, however, ever arises from itself. For that which provides a beginning to a thing generated must precede that which is generated. But nothing precedes itself. Therefore, since quality arises from another, and nothing can arise except from something superior, quality cannot be the principle of nature. 

But from where does it draw its origin? Surely not from matter? Not at all: Since matter is a common and formless subject, and for that reason—insofar as it is in itself—it relates equally to all forms always and everywhere. Whence does it happen, then, that it is adorned by different forms at different times and places, unless it is from something superior that affects it differently here and there, now and then? Furthermore, if matter were to give form to itself, we ask whether it possesses that form by its own power *before* it is about to provide it to itself, or whether it does not. If it does not have it, it cannot even conceive it; if it does have it, it is certainly not "prime matter" <note>term: *materia prima*—pure matter without any shape or quality, the lowest level of existence.</note> but rather something composed of matter and the power of form. And regarding this very power, we shall inquire similarly: does it have it from itself, or from another? If it has it from another, it also has its form from another. If from itself, does it possess this similarly through another power likewise its own (and thus we shall proceed into infinity), or rather does it possess that power not through another power, but through its essence? If this is so, the essence of matter will be the same as the power or the substance that produces forms, and it will be the source of forms rather than their subject—indeed, it would be form rather than matter, and the most excellent form of all, a form intolerant of all division. It would not fluctuate (as it does now) with the variety of gliding forms, but through an everlasting essence it would be endowed with everlasting forms. 

From these things, it is gathered that matter does not have by its own nature any power to procreate forms, because a formless subject cannot form itself, since it can do nothing at all; for action proceeds from form, from which "being" also proceeds. And just as the matter that is subject to art, even though it is not lacking form, is nevertheless led to the form of the craft not by itself, but by the form of the art, certainly the matter that is subject to nature, since it is formless, is led to a natural form not by itself, but by the nature of form.

From where, then, will quality come? Perhaps from another quality, as for example one fire generates another? Not even that. For because quality cannot exist without the fuel of matter, it does not dominate its own matter, and much less will it dominate the matter of another. Therefore, the quality of some body cannot form another body by its own power alone. A natural body, indeed, does nothing through its mass—which is subject only to being acted upon—and it does not act sufficiently through quality. For since quality does not have the sufficiency of existing, it does not provide to the body the suffi—

He concludes that matter is passive and formless, requiring a superior, non-material power to give it shape and identity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s argument that physical qualities are insufficient to be primary causes. On the previous page, he established that the human mind perceives "true forms" that are superior to the physical world; here, he applies this logic to the chain of causality, arguing that physical elements like fire must be instruments of a higher, non-physical substance.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 1.
<meta>catchword: for</meta>
<sig>F</sig>

sufficiency of existence does not grant the body sufficiency of action. Indeed, because a specific fire was first generated by something else before it could generate another thing itself, it is more appropriate for it to be viewed as an effect rather than an agent. It is an innate condition of an "effect" that it depends on something else. Therefore, whenever fire performs an action, it acts as the <term>instrument</term><note>Ficino uses "instrument" in the Aristotelian sense: a tool used by a higher cause (like a hammer used by a carpenter) that has no power of its own to create the finished design.</note> of a superior cause. For if this or that specific fire were the "first" or "highest" cause of generating fire, then—since an entire category of things flows from the first cause of that category—it would produce the entirety of fire everywhere and always. Thus, it would create both itself and every fire that existed before it and will exist after it. 

Since, therefore, this or that fire is not the primary cause of such generation, we must ask: of what cause is it an instrument? Is it the instrument of another fire? Certainly not. First, because that cause is equal, not superior. Second, because that fire from which this one previously flowed is either already extinguished or very far away. Or is it perhaps an instrument of the other elements? Not that either. For the principle of generating fire is not found in the dissimilar and contrary elements <note>The four elements (earth, water, air, fire) were thought to be opposites; therefore, water cannot be the underlying cause that tells fire how to be fire.</note> such that this fire would be subjected to them as an instrument to generate another. 

Is it then an instrument of the heavens? Not at all. For this fire cannot become an instrument of that most distant celestial body except through a medium. Yet these intermediate bodies are unsuitable. Rather, between the heavens (or the sphere of fire) and the dissimilar elements, one would sooner have to place a specific fire to generate this fire on earth than the other way around. We shall argue similarly regarding every specific species of natural things. 

For this reason, beyond all such physical forms, there must exist and preside over all things a certain **incorporeal substance** <note>A non-physical reality, such as the soul or a divine intellect.</note> penetrating through bodies, whose instruments are the physical qualities. For in what way could individual qualities, which are by their nature unstable and disordered, maintain a stable order in the succession of generation, unless they were governed by the stable order of a higher cause? Or how could they always return to the same effects through the fixed cycles of time, unless there were one and the same cause which, leading them at any time, led them similarly at these appointed times? 

The human mind daily raises itself from particular forms to universal and absolute ones. Likewise, it is accustomed to ascend from supernatural forms bound to specific matter, through mathematics (which suffices for specific matter), to metaphysics (which requires neither specific nor uncertain matter). Furthermore, it raises itself from dimensions, which lack both position and parts, to the **point** without parts (but which relates to position); then from points to **numbers**, which require parts but not position; and finally from numbers to **Unity**, which needs neither position nor any parts. 

And beyond an individual but accidental unity, the mind transfers itself to **substantial unity**—that is, to Form—and to an individual essence, which is the foundation and origin of all accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties like color or size, whereas "substance" is what a thing truly is.</note> at once, serving as a fixed axis, remaining in itself, while the accidents are inherently changeable and always clinging to something else. If the human mind has such great power for rational ascent—even though it is a part of the universe and hindered by bodily chains—the universe surely possesses a much greater power within itself for the same purpose, especially since the order of the lowest mind takes its origin from the order of the universe. 

Where the power to act flourishes more strongly, there it is naturally brought into action more fully and more quickly. To this we add that if every kind of thing is reduced to something unique in its own kind that is in some way indivisible (upon whose simplicity they depend)—for instance, motion and time reduce to the **moment**, natural form to the **minimum natural degree**, geometric dimensions to the **sign** (or point), and numbers to **Unity**—why should the category of substance not also be reduced to an **indivisible substance**? 

Just as all shapes that share in inequality are referred back to the circle (the most equal of all), and the circle is referred to the indivisible center (the beginning of all equality), so too should accidental and divisible forms be reduced to a substantial and divisible form, and such a form reduced to a **substantial and indivisible** one. And just as there is a substantial and bodily form above "quality" (which is free from weakening even though it may decrease), so above this there must be a substantial form that neither weakens nor decreases, so that the ascent toward what is better may be perfected in what is best. Such will be the **incorporeal substance**, which primarily possesses this: that by its nature it cannot be diminished; it must subsist somewhere in nature according to its own form. For indivisible and simple things are necessarily prior to divisible and composite ones. For each thing must exist before it is extended and swollen. These latter things need the former, not the other way around. From those...

<summary>Ficino argues that physical elements and qualities are merely "instruments" of a higher power. He uses a mathematical hierarchy—moving from dimensions to points to Unity—to demonstrate that all physical reality must eventually be grounded in an indivisible, incorporeal substance.</summary>

On the previous page, he argued that specific instances of fire are merely "instruments" of a higher power. Here, he explores how "Life" and "Form" act upon "Matter," drawing on ancient authorities to show that physical matter is too passive to act on its own.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

For these things <note>referring to the physical forms we see</note> take their beginning from those <note>higher, spiritual forms</note> and find their completion in them. Therefore, if these physical things exist in the nature of things according to their own specific form, it is much more necessary that their source-category be found somewhere else according to its own true form. Truly, because nature moves its own matter more effectively and better than human art moves its own material, we conclude that the primary form in nature dominates its matter more than the primary form in art dominates its material. If it dominates more, two things are concluded: first, that it is closer to the matter in terms of position than art is; and second, that it excels its matter in substance more than art does, and can exist more easily through itself without that matter. This same reasoning moves me greatly: all qualities that exist from a form in something else, whenever they generate, they generate forms in something else. For they cannot produce an offspring more free than they themselves are. Therefore, it <note>the physical quality</note> generates forms in the womb of matter; but matter itself, which does not lie within another thing, is made and preserved only by that form which does not lie in another. For matter arises neither from itself—since it is imperfect and does not act of itself—nor from qualities—which it precedes—but from a certain form that precedes matter. Such a form is entirely incorporeal. Upon the power and operation of such a form are founded the powers and operations of qualities, just as their works are poured over the work of that higher form. But more on this elsewhere.

Now, however, we must remember that matter itself (as <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure viewed by Ficino as a source of ancient, divine wisdom</note> and the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> believe) is formless—not quite "nothing," but "next to nothing"—because it is primarily and infinitely passive. From this, <term>Plotinus</term><note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note> thinks it follows that the immediate disposition of matter itself—that is, dimension and quality—is something most empty; and however small it is, the whole thing is a certain "passion" <note>original: "passio," meaning a state of being acted upon rather than acting</note>. For dimensions are nothing other than the extensions of matter itself, and qualities are nothing other than its affections—fleeting shadows, so to speak, like the shadows of tall trees in a rushing stream. Finally, he concludes that neither matter (since it is the primary passive thing) nor dimensions or qualities (since they are the primary "passions" of the primary passive thing) can be the primary principles of actions. 

So says Plotinus. But certain others distinguish it differently, though toward the same end. They say that matter itself can certainly do nothing; and quantity—if it is the passive extension of matter proceeding from some cause that extends matter—likewise does nothing, since it is the perpetual "passion" of the primary passive thing. But if quantity is like a form through which the cause that moves matter extends that matter, then perhaps it acts somewhat upon its own matter (because it is the medium by which that cause seems to extend the matter), but it performs absolutely nothing upon outside matter, because it always forces the agent to remain distant from the patient, which hinders action. Quality, however, according to the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught</note>, does perform something on both its own and outside matter. 

But if our reasoning leads us from matter (which acts on no matter) to quality (which in some way moves both) by way of the middle ground of quantity (which only works in some way on its own matter), shall we jump from quantity (which in no way moves outside matter) without any middle step to that thing which moves outside matter entirely? Not at all. Quality is very close to quantity. Therefore, quality is not entirely sufficient for external action. If, therefore, it "limps" in its ability to act, it must be directed by a superior substance that is entirely powerful. Quality rightly "limps" because at the very moment it is born, it is spread out through the width and depth of matter and is submerged, as if in the <term>River Lethe</term><note>The mythological river of forgetfulness; here Ficino means that the quality loses its divine power as it is drowned in physical matter</note>. Thus it happens that before it can act at all, it is in a sense overcome by the matter that infects it. Its power, therefore, never conquers matter through itself. For that reason, it will never move anything through itself unless it is strengthened by a superior cause. 

It is indeed strengthened and led by a certain **Life**, which generates life and sense even from non-living mud (as when frogs and flies are born), and from one shapeless matter procreates various and most beautiful flowers through various and most beautiful seeds—which, since they are often not found in the dung itself, must necessarily be in Life itself. It also forces scattered materials into an order. Order proceeds from reason. Reason consists in life; Life consists in a certain indivisible power. For death occurs through division and falling apart. Again, from the collision of cold bodies, Life generates fire. And when the reflection of rays in a mirror, or hot iron through the accidental quality of fire, heats wool, that Life—through the vital seeds of fire—produces the substantial species of fire in the wool. Finally, because we believe there is something in us that does not consume nourishment violently, but cooks and digests it sweetly and in an orderly way: something that so wonderfully brings non-living food back to a living form; something that moves heavy things upward and light things downward without manifest violence, beyond or rather above their nature, according to the use <meta>catchword: of life</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that physical matter and qualities are too passive and "weakened" by their material state to be primary causes. He concludes that "Life," a superior and indivisible power, must be the force that organizes matter, creates life from decay, and directs physical processes.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK I.

F 2

...[incorporeal] <note>completing the word "incorporea" from the previous page</note> as the requirements of life demand, and it transfers this power continually. It is this which reconciles conflicting things among themselves and overcomes them to form a unity. Certainly, it is not a simple fiery heat, nor any other quality of conflicting elements, nor a divisible nature, nor a bare property of nature, but rather a certain superior, indivisible, and life-giving power. 

Consider this just as it is within us, so it is in the universe. And from these points, conclude that bodily forms do not possess a sufficient power of generation from one another, but instead demand some higher cause above them. If this superior cause were itself a form similarly joined to matter, it would descend in turn from another higher substance. Finally, so that the progression does not go on to infinity, we must arrive at some form that is mixed with no bodies. 

Indeed, such is the power in the category of forms for this purpose—that they can exist separate from matter—that even if someone were to say that they are joined to it by their own nature, but are separated only by the contemplation of minds, they would at least be forced to admit that the minds themselves are separate, since they are the ones separating the other things. 

This appears again from the fact that substance is prior to quantity <note>the mathematical property of being measurable or divisible</note> and other accidents <note>non-essential qualities</note> by its very nature and dignity. And because what is prior can exist apart from what is posterior, there can be a certain substance without the division of quantity; and if it can be, it certainly is so at some point, lest this perfection be lacking in nature, and lest this potential be in vain. For in those things pertaining to the primary order of the universe, the situation is such that whatever *can* be either already *is*—as the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physici"</note> believe, so that no change happens in eternal things—or at least it will be at some point, so that nothing remains forever empty. 

And if life, which by natural origin alone precedes sensation, already exists somewhere by itself without sensation, much more so does substance—which excels quantity in both dignity and origin—now exist in the order of things apart from quantity. This is especially true since the universe is more perfect if certain substances are freed from the chains of quantity than if there were certain lives devoid of sensation. 

Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd</note>, following the opinion of Aristotle, proves that the bodily and substantial form of the heavens lacks matter, because there is no potential there for different forms, which is the specific nature of matter. Yet dimension exists there, and he judges such a form to be a "middle" between natural forms and divine forms. Natural forms exist together with matter and quantity, while divine forms are entirely absolute from both; the form of the heavens is the middle between them, so that one does not pass from one extreme to the other without a middle ground. Therefore, he deems it consistent that it exists with quantity, but without matter. 

From this, we argue in this manner: since substantial form usually lies in matter rather than in quantity, and has a greater proportion with matter than with quantity according to the order of its type and nature, if it can exist anywhere without matter, it can much more easily exist somewhere apart from quantity. 

Furthermore, as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> holds, there are three types of bodies. For some are (to use his words) both material and composite, such as those composed of the four elements. Furthermore, there are the spheres of the elements, which are material but in some way simple. Finally, there are the celestial bodies, which are both simple and immaterial at the same time. He also posits three types of forms, not unlike Averroes. For he wants the general definition of forms to be this: "Form is that by which something distinctly exists and acts in reality <note>original: "actu"</note>." In this definition, no dimensions are included at all, though a subject is perhaps signified in some way when it is said, "that by which something," and the rest that follows. From this, he concludes: if some forms exist without a subject matter, like the celestial ones, many more forms can and should exist without dimension. 

Likewise, Proclus and Syrianus <note>Proclus's teacher</note> argue toward the same point. That which is always extended by another is necessarily bound by dimensions. But that which extends [others] is not. Therefore, since matter is always extended by another, it is necessarily subject to dimensions. However, because each thing is in itself in some way before it is extended, matter can be thought of as indivisible. Therefore, that principle by which it is extended can not only be thought of, but can even exist, without dimensions. 

Furthermore, every divisible thing is a certain "one whole" constituted from many parts. Unless these parts had something one and the same in themselves common to all, they would never complete that whole. For "one" is only made by "one." Again, unless they were participants in unity, none of the parts would be one, but would be infinitely many, and any part would be innumerably infinite. But that "one" implanted in those parts is not divided individually among them, for it too would then need something else to bind it. Therefore, it is the same and whole in each part. Such a thing must be incorporeal. Likewise, since every corporeal thing is a certain "one whole" made of parts,

He cites Averroes and Proclus to show that just as celestial bodies exist without ordinary matter, higher souls and minds exist without physical extension.</summary>

### MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...[among the par]ties <note>completing the word "partibus" from the previous page</note>, there is a certain cause of that union. Does the whole itself unite the parts, or do the parts unite the whole? Or does something higher—which is neither a part of that thing nor the whole made of parts—unite the parts to each other and to the whole? The "whole" follows from the parts rather than uniting them. And if we admit there is something that unites the parts, it must be incorporeal <note>non-physical</note>. For if it were also divisible, it would similarly require something else to unite it. If the parts unite the whole, that is absurd, for then unity would be created by a multitude (which is the opposite of unity), whereas union ought to be created by unity itself. It remains, then, that besides the individual parts and the whole, there must be something "one" present as the cause of that harmony. This cause must be incorporeal, so that it is not forced to require a link for itself, which would lead us into an infinite chain of causes.

For this reason, we should not believe that any form divided within a body is the pinnacle of nature or the principle <note>the fundamental source or origin</note> of things—especially since the principle of things must have been, and will be, eternal by its own power. It must have always been; for it could not have come from itself at some point (as it would have existed before itself), nor from another (as nothing exists before the first). Other things, truly, would never exist unless the first had existed beforehand. It must also always remain; for if the principle is extinguished, the universe collapses, and neither the principle itself nor anything else can be reborn. It is necessary, therefore, that it possesses an infinite power through which it lives infinitely from itself. It cannot have this if it is corporeal <note>made of physical matter</note>. For if it had infinite dimensions, nothing else would exist in the world besides itself. If its dimensions were finite, its power would also be finite. 

I pass over for now (what we shall show elsewhere) that neither a body nor a corporeal form—being both needy and changeable—can be a sufficient principle of motion. Instead, every corporeal thing is moved by another. An <term>Architect</term> <note>original: "architectum," referring to God as the master builder of the universe</note> who is mixed with and stained by his handiwork cannot master that work; the Architect—the first builder of the world's work—must be perfect. 

Therefore, let us transcend corporeal form and consider now the first thing that we encounter next. Just as we ascended from the body as the lowest level to corporeal form as a sort of middle ground (because it has something of the body as it spreads through the body, yet lacks something of it since it is not itself composed of matter and form), let us now move from this middle ground to a more sublime, incorporeal form. This form has nothing of the body, but distributes qualities to bodies. Because it subsists through itself, it is called "true form and essence"—the <term>Third Essence</term>, I say, which in its proper place we shall also call the **rational soul**. This is accompanied by the irrational soul, just as a shadow follows a body. That essence is judged by the Platonists to be both true and immortal because it does not require parts into which it might one day be dissolved (and through which its power, once dispersed, would be weakened), nor is it bound to a subject from which it might vanish if abandoned, nor is it mixed with a contrary form by which it might be corrupted. It is not confined by place, nor subject to time or motion, because of the indivisible and self-abiding simplicity of its substance.

->*The rational soul is immobile through its substance, mobile through its operation, and partly immobile and partly mobile through its power. Chapter 4.*<-

What shall we say is the nature of this third essence? Is it entirely immobile <note>unchanging/unmoving</note>, or rather mobile? Certainly, it is not entirely immobile, because it is the source of the flowing qualities in matter, which lack all rest. Every cause acts according to its own nature, and therefore it is necessary that some power and image of the cause be preserved in the work. If that essence which is the cause of qualities were entirely immobile, then because it would act through its immobile nature, the quality descending from it would retain some immobile nature within itself. But the opposite occurs. For there are three things in a quality: essence, power, and action; all of these are involved in motion. Its essence is generated and corrupted, and generation and corruption are achieved through motion. Its power, too, is intensified or diminished by its nature—for example, heat may burn more or less intensely. That which is more or less hot at different times is undoubtedly changing. Its action suffers the same. Since the action of fire is heating, it does not heat water in an instant, but over time. Action over time is called "motion" by everyone; therefore, quality is subject to motion in every respect. This appears clearly from the fact that the affection of the body, which is produced through qualities, cannot remain exactly the same and similar through any delay of time, but is always changing, now into one proportion of degrees and now another, for better or for worse. Indeed, if anyone...
