### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK I.
<sig>F 3</sig>

If anyone should say that a bodily affection <note>a state or condition of the body</note> remained for an hour, the Platonists will ask him this: when the hour is finished, is the power within that affection equal to what it was at the beginning of the hour? If the power is not equal, then certainly it did not "stand still" for an hour, since during that hour it was changed according to its potential. If it is said that an equal power remains, then that affection will endure for yet another hour. For equal powers produce equal results. Therefore, if it remained for an hour through such a force, it will remain for another hour through an equal force. When the second hour is finished, they will similarly ask about that power, whether it be equal or unequal. If unequal, it did not stand still. If equal, it will stand for just as long again. They will proceed similarly afterward into infinity, and they will show that the nature of the body—if it stood still for even half an hour—would remain forever. 

In truth, the complexion <note>term: <term>complexio</term> refers to the specific balance of the four humors or elements in a physical body</note> of any body never thrives forever according to itself, since all are quickly extinguished and perish; thus, they persevere as the same for scarcely a moment of time. And because they begin and end in the same moment—and in beginning and ending, the most complete state of being is least possessed, whereas a complete act of being is necessary for acting—it seems to confirm what we proved in the previous discussion: that there is no sufficient principle of action within physical qualities. 

But to return to the question proposed here: if there is in these qualities (as far as they are concerned) a motion entirely devoid of stability, in what way can they be produced by a cause that is at such a distance from them that it possesses a stability devoid of all motion? If all things pass from one extreme to the other through a middle point—as from winter through spring into summer, or from summer into winter through autumn—certainly between a quality that is entirely mobile and an essence that is entirely immobile, something must necessarily be placed which is partly immobile and partly mobile. 

Therefore, that substance which is the immediate parent of qualities cannot be entirely immobile. What then shall we say? Shall we assert that this substance is also entirely mobile? Not at all. For it would either be in the category of bodily qualities (a category in which we cannot stop our search), or the cause—which is located in a higher category—would not exceed its effect with sufficient perfection if the substance which is the cause of quality wavered no less than the quality itself. For this reason, that substance partly stands still and is partly moved. It has three things within itself: essence, power, and operation. Which of these will stand? Which will be moved? Certainly, the operation <note>the external activity or function</note> cannot stand still if the two preceding things are changed. Nor can the essence be moved without the following things being moved. Therefore, the first will stand still—namely, the essence itself—and the last will be changed—namely, the operation. But what of the power, the middle between both? It too will partly stand and partly be changed.

-> *Above the mobile soul is the immobile angel.* Chapter V. <-

Thus far we have found a certain form above the complexion of the body, which we shall call the rational soul; its essence always remains the same, which is signified by the stability of the will and the memory. Its operation, however, is changed by the fact that it does not think all things at once, but step-by-step; nor does it nourish, increase, and generate the body in a single moment, but over time. Its natural power remains, because its natural vigor thrives perennially and is not weakened. Its acquired power <note>skills or knowledge gained through practice</note> changes, because it passes from potential into act, and from act into habit, and vice versa. Heraclitus, Varro, and Manilius <note>Heraclitus (philosopher of flux), Varro (Roman scholar), and Manilius (astronomical poet) were seen by Ficino as thinkers who reached the level of the soul but went no higher</note> ascended this far. 

But we must ascend higher, since this form cannot be the principle of all nature. For a stable operation, which completes its work most perfectly in a single moment, is more perfect than one which requires time. A life that is united with itself all at once, not distant from itself, is more complete than one which is stretched out through different moments of time and is somehow distracted from itself according to internal acts and feelings. Therefore, above this form—whose external operation wanders through time and whose life (that is, internal operation) is dispersed in a kind of flux—there must be placed another, higher form, whose operation is stable and whose life is entirely unified at once. For perfect things must always be placed before imperfect ones, because just as perfect things in any category are those which are such by their own nature, so imperfect things are those which are not such by themselves—otherwise they would be most perfectly so. If, then, imperfect things are not such by themselves, they are compelled to be so by higher things. Likewise, that which is moved breaks out from potential and rest into act, and seeks some limit and end to its motion, as if it were insufficient for itself and lacked that toward which it moves...

He defines the soul as having a stable essence but changing operations, necessitating a higher, completely stable reality above it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the soul, because it moves and changes its state of understanding, must be preceded by a higher, stable principle called "Mind" or "Intellect." This follows the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being: Body, Quality, Soul, Mind, and God.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

...it turns itself. <note>original: "se confert"</note> But truly, above that which moves from leisure into act, there exists something always that is full and perennial act. Above that which is changed because of deficiency, there necessarily exists something that is not moved, either because it is never in need of anything or is already most full. This is especially true since that which is moved is moved by a desire for improvement; it could not improve except by attaining a better and more excellent nature. It would not possess the thing it seeks through the motion itself, but would acquire it after the motion—not indeed from itself (for why then would it have needed to change?), but from some other "richer" source. For that which by its own nature lacks a boundary <note>original: "termino"; here meaning a limit or a state of completion</note> must be bounded by another more perfect thing. A mobile thing by its own nature lacks a boundary because it does not rest within itself. And if such a thing were the principle <note>the fundamental source or starting point</note> of all things—making all things changeable through its own changeable operation—there would be no stability in the world. 

But now, a certain stability in things is so necessary that even motion itself is not without stability. For unless a thing which is said to be affected in various ways through motion remains the same in its substance for some time, it would neither change its conditions nor vary little by little, but would cease to exist entirely in an instant. Even the most orderly revolution of the heavens around the same center and the same poles—the equality of their motions and the return of the stars to their places—shares in some form of stability. 

And just as that which stands still does so because of unity, and is united in its stability (which we shall explain elsewhere), so too that which moves does so because of stability, and "stands" even within its motion. It moves, I say, because of stability—that is, because of a certain stability of the moving power; for if that power did not remain in its own vigor, no order would be preserved in the motion, nor would the motion continue for even a moment. Furthermore, it "stands" in motion—that is, it perseveres in the same, or equal, or similar pattern of movement. There are also many things that, even if they are moved according to one kind of motion, are nevertheless not moved according to other kinds; therefore, they are partly moved and partly at rest. 

Add to this that since the primary matter <note>term: <term>materia prima</term>; the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe</note> of things is everlasting, that which is changed through a shift in its physical form is nonetheless compelled to remain the same in the meantime through its matter. Therefore, much more can and should a thing remain the same in its substance while it is being changed according to its quantity, quality, or location. Why say more? That which in no way remains stable while it admits change is forced to lose both its existence and its motion at the same time. If, therefore, there is any stability in things, the principle of things cannot be mobile. 

Therefore, that which is mobile is not the principle of nature. Thus, there is something above the soul. For the soul, which by its nature is indifferent to understanding or not understanding, is moved back and forth from one state to the other. It must be determined toward understanding by an influx from something else that is always "in act" <note>term: <term>actus</term>; a state of being fully realized or active rather than just having the potential to be</note> in that category. Such a thing is that which is always understanding, or always "intelligible in act," which is the same thing. 

Furthermore, whatever is "such" only in part is made so only by that which exists as "such" according to its whole self. For example, wood that is hot in one part is made hot by fire, which is hot in its entirety. Because a thing that is "such" by its own nature—like heat—is encompassed by its own nature as a whole, it is therefore entirely characterized by that quality. Conversely, that which is "such" only in part is not so by its own self. 

But this third essence—namely, the soul—is not understanding <note>original: "intelligentia"</note> according to its whole self. For it has certain other natures besides intelligence that are devoid of intelligence <note>such as the functions of growth or movement</note>. Therefore, the "mind" within the soul is indeed a part of the soul. It is also, in a way, a part of a "Mind"—I mean a higher Mind—which is entirely and solely Mind. Indeed, if the soul possessed mind from itself, the reason for producing mind would reside in the very substance of the soul. Then the whole soul would be mind—and a whole and perfect mind at that—and every soul would have a mind, because the "definition" of a soul is found in every soul. And just as moving the body belongs to every individual soul because it suits the soul by its nature, so the faculty of understanding would belong to all souls, even those of beasts, if it belonged to the soul by its own nature. 

And if it is necessary that there be a more effective nature above one that is less effective—and the mind which is in the soul neither produces any work outside itself by its own act alone, nor commands the effective power of its soul—there must be a Mind above it that is the producer of some work by its own act and the master of effective power. 

Rightly, therefore, just as this mind is the "head" of the soul (its most excellent part), so the head of *this* mind—which does not belong to itself but to the soul, and is not absolute but drawn down to the capacity of this soul, not clear but obscure and in a way doubtful—the head of *this* mind, I say, is a certain Mind that exists within itself, free and lucid. 

In this, certainly, the "Riddle of the Magi" <note>A reference to the *Prisca Theologia* (Ancient Theology), where Ficino links Plato to ancient Egyptian or Persian wisdom</note> is unraveled: There is a thing that is lucid on all sides; there is a thing that is obscure on all sides; and there is a middle thing, partly lucid and partly obscure. In the order of bodies, the thing that is lucid on all sides is any star...

He uses the "Riddle of the Magi" to illustrate the hierarchy of light/intelligence between stars, souls, and the divine Mind.</summary>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK I ###

->F 4<-

...above the moon, the air is dark on all sides; the Moon is in the middle. In the order of spirits, however, the **mind** is full of light, the **irrational soul** is empty, and the **rational soul** holds the middle ground; in one part it possesses intellectual light, while in another part it lacks it. And that part which it receives from God—just as the Moon receives light from the Sun—it receives differently at different times, and thus changes its "shape." <note>Ficino is comparing the changing phases of the moon to the way the human soul fluctuates in its understanding and virtue.</note> Therefore, an angel is rightly placed above the soul, who, like any star above the moon, always shines totally and in the same manner by the light of its own "Sun" <note>Original: "sui Solis"; referring to God as the source of light for the angels.</note>. Indeed, where a superior nature touches an inferior one, it reaches the highest level of the inferior from its own lowest grade. For instance, the lowest part of fire touches the highest part of air. 

Since the intellectual nature is superior to the bodily nature, it touches the body in such a way that whatever is most excellent among bodies participates in the intellectual soul, while the inferior bodies, which are many, do not. According to the **Platonists**, the most excellent bodies belong to the heavenly inhabitants, the <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings.</note>, and men. But are the minds assigned to such bodies the highest of all minds? Not at all; otherwise, an inferior nature would attain the peak of a superior nature without a middle step. Therefore, just as there are many bodies without minds below the bodies endowed with mind, so too above the minds implanted in bodies, there are many minds assigned to no bodies at all. Indeed, these are far more numerous than the species of bodies, since (as we shall show elsewhere) rational souls are positioned between eternity and time. The excellence of eternity seems to require that there be more species and perfections within it, in a sense, than there are in time. 

I set aside for now (though we will demonstrate it elsewhere) that the interval between souls and the **First Principle** <note>God</note> is infinite, while the space between souls and matter is finite. Thus, it should seem a surprise to no one that there can be many more grades of angels above souls than there are grades of forms below souls. Furthermore, when one thing is made out of two, and that which is less perfect is found to exist somewhere by itself apart from the other, much more can that other part—which is more perfect and less needy—exist somewhere without the lesser part. Now, a "living being" <note>Original: "animal"</note> is made from an intellectual substance (that is, the rational soul) and a body. We see many bodies exist and live without this kind of intellect. What then prevents there being many minds not united to bodies? Such minds would indeed be above the souls that are united to bodies. 

Accordingly, minds joined to bodies, insofar as they are such, do not fulfill the species of "living being" on their own, but are parts of a composite species. For the most part, in order to understand, they look toward those things which are perceived by the senses; for this reason, they are in a way imperfect and act imperfectly. If, therefore, one must ascend from the imperfect in any genus to the perfect things which are prior by nature, it follows that reason leads us from joined minds to **separated minds**, which both sufficiently fulfill their own species and, by understanding, look toward those things which are in themselves intelligible. 

The mind itself, because it does not necessarily depend on the body through its intelligence and will, naturally separates forms and occupies itself with separated things; and because it makes progress through rest rather than through motion, it is by nature free from the body and from motion. Therefore, it is more suited to its nature to live apart from the body and motion than to live within the body and motion. Nevertheless, many minds lead a mobile life in bodies; therefore, much more so, and in much greater numbers, do minds lead an immobile life without bodies. Who would deny that it is more fitting for an incorporeal substance, according to the nature of its genus, to be outside a body than in a body? Consequently, there ought to be more species of that substance separated from the body than joined to it. For that which is natural to any genus exists within it for the most part. 

Such indeed are the **angels**, who, if they move the bodies of the world, are themselves in no way moved when those bodies are moved. Yet souls, while they move bodies, are also moved themselves. A mover that travels along with the moved body does not maintain a perpetual and stable tenor and order of moving unless an **immovable mover** <note>The "unmoved mover" is a concept from Aristotle and Plato: a primary cause of all motion that does not itself move.</note> presides over it. Therefore, the perpetual order of the world's revolution testifies that there are some immobile movers above the souls. Because the elements consist of the fluidity of matter and are always infecting one another, they would observe no order of themselves unless they were ruled by the highly ordered law of celestial motion. But since even the heaven is of itself perpetually immobile <note>Ficino likely means the *essence* or *driving force* of the heaven, or its lack of change in substance despite its rotation.</note>, and therefore in need, the stable order in its motion does not come from itself, but from a supreme mover that is altogether immobile and indivisible. For a stable union does not persist in things so diverse and mobile unless it comes from a most stable and most unified axis, which is ultimately traced back to unity itself and to a state of rest. Truly, just as a mobile thing relates to a mobile thing, so too does a mover relate to a mover. Therefore, just as an element which is moved in a mobile way...

# MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

...just as the heaven which is moved is reduced to that which is moved stably, so the varied and changing motor of the mobile heaven is reduced to a stable and united motor; finally, the stable and united is reduced to state and unity itself. Truly, that action which is called "to move" follows the mover, and that passion which is "to be moved" follows this action, and it is never the other way around. For prior things are not led by posterior things, but the reverse. Therefore, it is much more possible for that action called "to move" to exist somewhere without the passion of "being moved," than for such passion to exist apart from action. Nevertheless, such passion exists in bodies apart from action <note>That is, a physical object can be moved without it being the primary cause of motion in something else.</note>: therefore, somewhere there will be action far removed from passion, so that just as bodies are moved but do not move, so the angels may move things without being moved themselves. Concerning these, **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino often cites the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to the ancient sage Zoroaster to harmonize Platonic thought with ancient mystery traditions.</note> says:

> O all you intellectual sustainers of the world, inflexible. 
> <note>Original Greek: ὦ πᾶς κόσμου ἐχένοφες ἀνοχέα: ἀκαμπᾶ.</note>

This means that the world has intellectual rulers who are immobile. Therefore, just as qualities that are entirely mobile precede the soul (which is partly mobile and partly immobile), so the souls are preceded by the entirely immobile angels. **Aristotle**, in the eleventh book of *Divine Matters* <note>Referring to Book XII (Lambda) of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, which was often called "Theology" or "Divine Matters" in the Renaissance.</note>, proves that angels exist and that they are many in this way: It is necessary that the continuous, ordered, and—as far as it is in itself—unfailing motion of the heaven be produced by a motor that is moved neither in itself nor by accident. Since, however, there are many such motions in the heaven, distinct from one another and different in kind and power, it is necessary that they be produced by many such motors. These motors must not be bodies, lest they be forced to be moved by something else while they move, which would lead necessarily to an infinite regress. Nor, again, can they be forms within a body, lest they happen to be moved along with the body they move. For one must arrive at a most perfect motor—that is, an immobile one—lest any transgression ever occur in the movements. Such motors are "Minds" <note>Original: "Mentes"; in this context, purely intellectual beings without physical bodies.</note>, since in forms entirely released from matter, the thing understood and the understanding spirit are the same. Thus says Aristotle. 

The **Hebrews** and later philosophers call those minds "Angels" and "Messengers." **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath whose works on Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism were foundational for Medieval and Renaissance thinkers.</note> argues in one place that the chief among these are no fewer than ten, but elsewhere he seems to indicate many more. Aristotle, however, says they are no fewer than the celestial motions, and confesses that he calculated that number by probable reason, or that it must be left to those wiser than himself. It is as if he suspected that those minds ought to be numbered according to their own proper and chief action—that is, intelligence—rather than according to a common and secondary action—that is, motion. Furthermore, since they are the *ends* (goals) of the motions, he perhaps prophesied that they were not to be numbered according to the number of motions. Indeed, there may be as many minds as possible which are not distributed for the purpose of moving bodies. 

For this reason, we have not only indicated previously that angels are almost innumerable, but we show it now in this way: If the species of natural things in matter—whichever are in a subject—are narrow, yet are distinguished among themselves not by the subject but by their own nature and are expanded into a great number, how much more are those distances which live in themselves above matter distinct through themselves? They are amplified into almost innumerable species by a certain wonderful fertility of their absolute kind. Furthermore, the <term>intelligible genus</term> <note>The realm of things that can be understood by the mind alone, as opposed to the "sensible genus" perceived by the senses.</note> seems by its very nature more capable of being multiplied than the corporeal. For numbers, dimensions, figures, proportions, the rarity of bodies, and the speed of motions are always limited within bodies themselves, but in the mind they are extended at will without limit. Again, those things which are particular in matter become universal in the mind. Finally, the intellect thinks at its own will of countless other things beyond all bodies, both incorporeal and corporeal. 

Since, therefore, the intelligible genus can be amplified much more than the sensible, and such a good power in the universe ought not to be forever empty, there are undoubtedly now in act many more species of <term>separated substances</term> <note>Substances that exist "separately" from physical matter; i.e., angels or pure intellects.</note> than there are species of corporeal things. This is especially true since a more excellent power adopts its own act for itself in the universe both more fully and earlier than a weaker power. Finally, since the order of the universe is disposed as well as possible under an infinite Good, it seems entirely to require that the things which are better within it should be multiplied, as far as possible, beyond the quantity of the inferior things—especially since the lower things were established for the sake of the higher. We see this clearly in the spheres of the world themselves. For the more mobile a sphere is, the larger it is, so much so that earth and water, if compared to the higher spheres, are thought of as a point compared to a circumference. What dimension is in bodies, number seems to be in incorporeal things. Therefore, it is fitting that intellectual substances, seeing as they are the best...

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK I #

F 5

...these minds are the best, and exist through themselves; they are the ends of all corporeal things, which were created for their sake. They are far more numerous than the movements of the celestial spheres or all physical bodies, as **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and Neoplatonist, whom Ficino believed was the direct disciple of the Apostle Paul. His *Celestial Hierarchy* is the source for the nine orders of angels.</note> testifies, saying that the separate species of intellectual beings are more numerous than those of physical things. Justly, the most powerful creator of the universe was able, knew how, and willed to make his work as similar to himself as possible. He created this most similar likeness specifically within this domain of power: he extended the absolute minds (which are most like Him) beyond the forms joined to matter by an immense space (if I may put it that way). Hence the saying of the **Prophet Daniel**: *Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.* <note>Daniel 7:10. Ficino uses this biblical passage to support the idea of an almost infinite number of angelic beings.</note> In distinguishing the orders of angels, Dionysius primarily uses the numbers three and nine, and sometimes seven. Furthermore, we find the number twelve used in the Christian mysteries. **Iamblichus** and **Proclus**, the Platonists who came after Dionysius, observed the same. For they divide the supreme and middle angels by the numbers three and nine; those following by seven; and the last orders on all sides by the number twelve. Because, among the Platonists, the levels of physical bodies are shadows of rational souls, and the levels of souls are images of angels, some distinguish the orders of angels according to the orders of both bodies and souls. But more on these matters elsewhere.

->*Above the angel is God, because the soul is a mobile multitude, the angel an immobile multitude, and God an immobile unity.* Chapter VI.<-

<margin>God is</margin>
The Platonists judge the Angel to be entirely immobile in essence, power, and action, because it is always the same, possesses equal power, always understands all things simultaneously, wills the same things, and, as far as it is within itself, acts instantly in whatever it does. These are the views of the Platonists. What others might say, I shall say elsewhere. However, reason does not yet permit us to rest here with **Anaxagoras** and **Hermotimus** <note>Pre-Socratic philosophers who proposed that "Mind" (Nous) was the primary cause of the world, though Ficino finds their definitions incomplete.</note>, but commands us to ascend higher. Furthermore, because the soul is "mobile" <note>In this context, "mobile" means changing or transitioning from one thought to another, rather than physical movement.</note>, it passes from one thing to another. Therefore, it possesses one thing and then another. That which possesses "this and that" also possesses "multitude" <note>A technical term meaning "plurality" or "complexity."</note>. For this reason, the soul is a certain multitude within itself—a *mobile multitude*, I say. The Angel, which immediately precedes the soul, cannot be an *immobile unity*, because two such things—one being a mobile multitude and the other an immobile unity—seem to be too far apart. For "unity" is the opposite of "multitude," and "immobile" is the opposite of "mobile." Since these things are opposed in every part, they cannot follow each other directly, but require a middle link to join them. Yet the Angel precedes the soul (the mobile multitude) without any middle link. Therefore, the Angel cannot be an immobile unity, lest two extremes be joined without a middle. It is certainly immobile, as we proved above; therefore, it is not a unity. It remains that the Angel is an *immobile multitude*, where it agrees with the soul in being a "multitude," but differs because the soul is mobile and the Angel is immobile. We are certainly forced to place some kind of multitude in the Angel. But of what kind? The kind that befits the intellect: that is, they possess essence and being, the power of understanding, the act of intellection, and many "species" <note>The intellectual "forms" or "blueprints" of things.</note> of the things understood. But since the Angel is not entirely simple but possesses number—and above number there must be Unity, because unity is the origin of every number and needs no union, whereas a multitude by its nature requires a union—it is necessary that above the Angel there be something else, which is not only immobile but entirely One and Simple. That indeed is **God**, who is as much the most powerful of all things as He is the simplest of all. Indeed, union consists in simplicity, and power in unity. Let no one dare to say that God is composed of many parts, because if He were properly "composed," He would consist of something that acts as a subject and something that acts as a form. Thus, God would not be most perfect in every way, since one part in Him would be less perfect than the whole. He would not be the highest agent, because He would not act through His whole self in whatever He does, but through one part—that is, the form. He would not be the most blessed, because He would not enjoy Himself everywhere. For He would not embrace His whole self in any given member. He would see something in Himself other than God, since the part and the whole are not the same. He will certainly be more blessed if whatever He sees in Himself *is* Himself, if He is nowhere lacking to Himself, but meets His whole self everywhere. Finally, that part which was positioned in God as a "subject," because it is conceived of in terms of forms, cannot form itself. The other part...

### MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY ###

...which performed the role of form, because it does not consist in itself, much less can it exist by itself; therefore, this composite "god" <note>Ficino refers here to the "Mind" or "Angel," which some ancient philosophers mistakenly identified as the supreme deity.</note> will be formed by some superior form, and that higher form will rather be God. This is the first discourse through which we prove that God is above the angel. Furthermore, as your eye is to your body, so your mind is to your soul. For your mind is the eye of your soul. Again, just as the light of the Sun relates to the physical eye, so the light of truth relates to the eye of the soul. Therefore, just as the physical eye is not the light, but a power capable of receiving light, so the mind, which is the eye of the soul, is not truth itself, even though it grasps truth. For your mind seeks the truth. Truth, however, does not seek itself, nor does truth admit anything false, through which your soul is often deceived. Imagine in your mind that your eye grows so large that it occupies your entire body, and the various species of limbs having been removed, the entire body is one single eye. If this eye sees anything further, it will certainly see nothing other than that same light of the Sun which it looked upon while it was narrow. Indeed, it will receive that same light more abundantly, and it will behold the colors of bodies within that light from every side, all at once in a single gaze; it will not turn here or there to see, but while remaining at rest, it will contemplate all things equally.

Yet even then, the light will be one thing, and the eye another. For if sight is established for the purpose of comprehending light, sight is one thing and light is another. And the light has no need for sight, since the light itself has no need to receive light. Imagine again that your mind grows so strong over the soul that, after the remaining parts of the soul pertaining to imagination, sensation, and generation are deleted, the entire soul is one single and solitary mind; this mind, left alone and pure, will be an angel. This vast mind, I say, will behold the same truth that the narrow mind had seen, but it will receive it more abundantly, and in it, it will behold all true things with a single intuition—to speak in a **Platonic** manner—and it will not hunt now for one thing and then for another. Yet even then, the mind will be one thing, and truth another. This is what **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino often cites Zoroaster as an ancient authority (the "Chaldaean Oracles") who pre-dated and influenced Plato.</note> reveals:
<margin>Learn the intelligible, since it exists outside the mind. <note>original: "Μάθε τὸ νοητὸν, ἐπεὶ νόου ἔξω ὑπάρχει."</note></margin>
That is, "Know that the intelligible itself is outside the mind." Truly, if the mind is established to perceive truth, then the mind that lacks truth is one thing, and the truth is another. Nor does truth itself have need of a mind through which it might grasp truth. Furthermore, if the mind itself were the same as truth itself, every mind would be truthful, and every true thing would share in mind. But as it is, human minds are deceived, and many things are true in some way which lack a mind. Truth is not only something other than mind, but also something superior. For the mind needs truth, whereas truth does not require the mind. And the empire of truth spreads more widely than that of the mind. For intellectual art is found in individual forms, but by no means in unformed matter. Yet matter is "truly" called matter, and is in truth the subject of all natural things. But if truth is above the mind, and that which is superior does not lack the goods of the inferior, the clarity of the mind is not absent from the truth. Yet these are not two distinct things—namely clarity and truth—but a most simple truth that is in no way hidden from itself; just as if light, although it does not have an eye distinct from itself, were nevertheless not hidden from itself. For God is the most clear truth and the most true clarity or "seeing," a light seeing itself, a sight shining by itself, the source of intellectual clarity and light, by whose light (and only by whose light) the clarity of the mind perceives. And just as wood is called hot through a certain participation, while fire is hot according to its form, and finally the Sun is hot in a more excellent way according to its eminent power and the cause of heat; so the soul has a part of the mind, the angel has the form of the mind, and God is the most effective origin of the mind. And, to speak in the manner of **Plotinus**, God is intellection <note>The act of understanding or the pure activity of thought.</note> itself, not existing in some intellect as a potentiality, nor of truth as if of an object, but existing in itself and of itself. It is as if vision were neither in some eye, nor the vision of an external light, but remained in itself and were a vision of itself. For wherever the intellect is placed as a power of understanding, even if it understands itself, nevertheless, by the reasoning that it is "intelligible" [the object of thought], it is said to be in some way prior to itself by the reasoning that it is considered "intellectual" [the subject of thought]. For the intelligible, as something prior and more excellent, moves, forms, and perfects the intellectual power as something subsequent and inferior. Therefore, some call God by the name of the "intelligible" or of "intellection" rather than of the "intellect," although even these names do not fit God in an entirely proper sense. But more on these things elsewhere. Added to this is that the soul's work is to provide vital movement (since it is life...

<meta>In the previous page, Ficino argued that the Mind (the angelic level of reality) acts as the eye of the soul, receiving the light of truth from a higher source. Here, he moves to the highest level of his hierarchy: the Good (God), explaining why the Good must be superior to the Mind.</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK I. ###

(Life itself is a certain [quality]) <note>This opening phrase completes a sentence from the previous page, establishing that while the soul provides life, the mind provides something more universal.</note> but the work of the **Mind** is to order things through forms. For the Mind is itself a certain species <note>original: *species*; here meaning a formal, intelligible structure or "look"</note> and it operates according to species, which we observe within our own minds. That vital motion is poured through all living things, but it does not apply to things lacking life. However, the ordering through forms belongs even to things that are not living. For indeed, these things do not lack order and species. Therefore, the Mind surpasses the Soul by as great an interval as the order of form is more widely spread than life. 

Yet, because that first formless matter of things lies beyond the order of forms—and within it lie hidden certain "seeds" (if I may call them that) of sprouting forms—the duty of the Mind, which is limited by forms, does not encompass these formless things. Nevertheless, this matter is in some way good, because it is desirous of the Good (that is, of form), because it is exposed to receiving the Good, and because it is necessary for a good world. These seeds are also good, because they are the beginnings of good forms. At the very least, then, **Goodness** surpasses the Mind by as great an interval as the bounty of the Good extends further than the bounty of species. For the more powerful a thing is, the further it extends its operation. 

To these points, we may add arguments of the following kind. All things desire the Good, but not all things desire the Mind; for not all things are capable of attaining mind and wisdom, and therefore there are many things that do not desire them, lest they desire in vain. If all things that can desire turn toward the Good, but not all turn toward the Mind, and if the source of a thing’s origin is the same place toward which it returns, then all things proceed from the Good, not from the Mind. Therefore, the **Good**, rather than the Mind, is the first cause of things. 

Furthermore, those things that possess Mind do not yet stop there, but still seek the Good. For the property of the Mind is a certain striving <note>original: *nixus*; a concentrated effort or internal pressure toward a goal</note> toward understanding. After this striving, the Mind is either in a worse state, a better state, or the same state. It is not in a worse state, because the operation itself is a certain perfection, and nothing falls into a worse state except by force or ignorance, neither of which applies to a pure and free Mind. It is not in the same state, for it would strive in vain if it made no progress, and nothing strives toward what it already possesses. Therefore, it endeavors so that it may be in a better state; thus, the Mind is not the Good itself, for nothing is better than the Good. So the Mind, by the act of understanding, drinks in goodness, but it drinks it from elsewhere. For if it held goodness within itself, there would be no need for striving to progress by its operation. That source from which it drinks goodness is the Good itself, which exists above the Mind, since it pours the fluid of its own advancement into the Mind. 

Furthermore, we seek wisdom and mind only by the impulse of reason, but we seek the Good even before every incitement of reason; every appetite of ours is always toward the Good, but not all are always toward the Mind. We desire intelligence for the sake of the Good, not the other way around. Therefore, nature values the Good more than the Mind, since it draws us toward the Good earlier, more often, and more powerfully. Hence, some people think they have enough in Philosophy if they merely *seem* to have wisdom, even if they do not; yet they do not think they have enough in life unless they truly possess that which they judge to be especially good for themselves.

If the Good is judged more precious than the Mind by natural instinct, it is also judged more eminent. From this it follows that the act of understanding is not enough for us, unless we understand both well and for a good purpose. For we often reject knowledge for a time if we suspect it will be bad or troublesome for us. But we can never reject the Good itself. We also often prefer pleasure to the speculation of things; but to the Good itself—insofar as it is the Good—we can never prefer anything. Nothing is more necessary than the incitement of the Good, since no one can "not want" the Good itself. Yet nothing is more voluntary than the incitement of the Good. For we want all things for the sake of the Good—indeed, we want the Good everywhere in all things—so willingly and so pleasantly that we wish, moreover, to be unable to "not want" it. Since, therefore, in the Good the highest necessity concurs with the highest liberty, and since the empire of the Good is both supremely necessary for its subjects and supremely voluntary, it is clear from this that all things lead their origin from here as from their source, and all things aspire toward this place as 
-> toward their homeland. <-

THEOLO-

## ology, on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
-> BOOK II. <-

-> Unity, truth, and goodness are the same thing, and there is nothing above them. Chapter I. <-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a classical or mythological scene with figures in a landscape.</image-desc> We have already shown by three arguments that there is something above the angel <note>In Ficino's system, the "angelic" level refers to pure Intellect or Mind—the realm of perfect ideas that exists above the human soul but below God.</note>. First, we showed that above the angel is the most simple Unity; second, Truth; and third, Goodness. These three are one and the same. For the highest unity is nothing other than the highest simplicity. Because of this simplicity of unity, any thing is pure and true. For wine is indeed "true" when it is pure wine <note>Ficino uses the analogy of "pure wine" to explain that something is most truly itself when it is not mixed with anything else; likewise, the ultimate Truth must be perfectly simple and unmixed.</note>. Thus, the truth of things consists in that simple unity. Furthermore, because of that same simple and pure unity, all things are good. For anything is in a good state when it is united to itself and to its own principle, and remains pure, not mixing with lower things. And if the unity, truth, and goodness of things consist in the same point, then that which is the first "One," "True," and "Good" above all things must rightly be the same thing. 

That the principle of all things lies in these is evidenced by the fact that traces of them are found in all things, as if all things flowed from them; moreover, all things desire these, as they seek to return to their own principle. For every individual thing is both a participant in and hungry for unity, truth, and goodness. Above Unity there is nothing else, because nothing is more powerful than unity, since union provides perfection and power to all. However, if you wish for there to be something above it, two absurdities immediately follow. For if Unity is under some higher principle, it is surely a participant of that higher thing. Lower things always receive something from higher causes. Thus, this would not be Unity itself, but something composed of a certain unity and a power received from above; it would therefore be a kind of "many," not unity. Furthermore, that which is placed above unity would participate in no unity at all. For a higher principle receives nothing from a lower one regarding its own nature. Therefore, it would be either nothing, or a "many" utterly deprived of union, of which no part would be a single "one." Neither would the whole "many" be one, nor would there be any communion among the parts, either with each other or with the whole. 

Again, there is nothing above Truth. For by similar reasoning, Truth itself would not be Truth, but some "true thing" composed of a certain truth and a portion of that higher thing. And that which is located above it, since it is neither truth nor a participant in truth, would be utterly false—and thus nothing. Nor can anything be more excellent than truth, unless by the power of truth it is undoubtedly true that such a thing is more excellent. Likewise, there is nothing above Goodness. For this would not be pure goodness, but some "good thing," a goodness defiled by the mixing of something else. And that which is placed before Goodness would be utterly evil. For it would not be good, since it would be beyond the boundaries of goodness. Nor would it be better than goodness, since nothing is "better" except by having a greater portion of goodness. 

How evil could exceed goodness, I do not see, since "excess" and "dominion" belong to goodness, for they are desirable things, just as good things are. Therefore, evil would overcome goodness by the very nature of goodness, and goodness would provide the power of dominion to evil <note>Ficino is using logic to show that the concept of "better" or "higher" inherently requires "goodness." If you try to put something "above" Goodness, you are trapped in a logical contradiction.</note>. Furthermore, if there is another principle of things above Goodness itself, it would surely bestow some gift from itself upon things, as every superior cause is accustomed to do. Furthermore, Goodness itself bestows its gift on all—that is, a certain goodness to each. We must ask, then, regarding that gift which descends from the higher principle: is it better than the gift of goodness, or not? It cannot be better. For whatever is called "better" is called so because of a greater portion of goodness. Yet it is absurd for the gift of a higher principle not to be better than the gift of a lower cause. Added to this is the fact that since all things desire the Good, if there is another principle above the Good itself, we ask whether they desire it or not. If they are said to desire it, it follows that they seek something...

<summary>Ficino begins Book II by arguing that the ultimate principle of reality (God) consists of Unity, Truth, and Goodness as a single, simple identity. He uses logical proofs to show that nothing can exist "above" these qualities, as the very concepts of existence and excellence depend upon them.</summary>
<keywords>Unity, Truth, Goodness, Neo-Platonism, Divine Simplicity, Hierarchy of Being, Marsilio Ficino, First Principle</keywords>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK III

...beyond and more than the good. If they <note>Referring to the "effects" or created things mentioned in the preceding argument.</note> were denied the desire for that, it would indeed be a foolish thing to say, for it would mean that effects do not seek the first cause by which they are preserved. Furthermore, goodness itself would be compelled to desire a higher principle, which is absurd. For every reason for desiring is enclosed within goodness itself. Therefore, nothing exists above goodness that can be loved. Thus, there is no principle above it. Wherefore, that unity, truth, and goodness which we find above the angel <note>In Ficino's hierarchy, the "angel" represents pure Intellect. He argues that even Intellect is a "multitude" of ideas, so there must be a "One" above it.</note>, according to the mind of Plato, is the principle of all things: God, the one, the true, and the good.

-> *There are not several gods equal to each other.* Chapter II. <-

Truly, there are not several gods, because there cannot be several first principles. But let us suppose (if it pleases) that there are "twin" gods—namely, two principles of the whole world, this one and that one. We must ask: is this one under that one, or that one under this one, or are both equal? If one is under the other, the one that is superior will clearly be the principle, and the other not at all. If they are equal, we ask whether they differ from each other entirely, or agree entirely, or partly differ and partly agree. 

The first option <note>That they differ entirely.</note> will not be granted. For they agree at least in this: that they both exist, they both act, and they are both equally called the principles of things. And if they did not harmonize in any way, there would be no concord in the machine of the world <note>original: "machina mundi." A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a finely-tuned, integrated system.</note>. If we admit the second option—that they agree entirely—then they are no longer two, but (as we desire) one. 

But if the third option is given—that they partly agree in nature and partly disagree—then certainly, because they cannot both agree and disagree through the very same trait, there must be one common nature in both through which they agree, and additionally, two specific natures in those two through which they disagree. And so, neither of them will be simple, but each will be a composite of a common nature and a specific property. Neither will be the "first" thing, because each depends on whatever reconciled those different parts into one. Neither would be self-sufficient, since the whole needs its parts, and one part needs the other. Neither would be all-powerful, since it is not entirely unified. 

Moreover, that common nature through which both are equal would be the "principle" rather than those two individual beings. Indeed, the true principle would be whatever gave that common nature to those two diverse beings. For this one nature which lies within others, and is restricted by the limitations of others, must have flowed from that absolute Unity which, consisting in itself, is narrowed by no limit. Thus, that common nature, as it comes to both from elsewhere, must come from a higher principle. 

Furthermore, those two specific natures through which they differ must come to them from the outside. For besides those, nothing remains in either of them except the one common nature; if those two additional specific natures were born absolutely from that common nature, they would no longer be diverse (as the Metaphysicians argue), but there would be one and the same property for both, flowing from the same source. It would flow out by the absolute mode of mere nature and flow back in. If, therefore, two absolute properties exist in them, they necessarily arrive from the outside. Therefore, each receives the property of its essence from elsewhere. And because each obtains its own specific nature from elsewhere, neither exists through itself, but is made by a higher principle. 

In any category of things, however, that which is the highest of that category is only one. For if there were two "highest lights," both would agree in the fact that they are the highest light, and in that, they are one. But if they are two distinct things, they must differ by some other nature rather than by the light itself. Therefore, another nature besides light would be present, and by its "contagion," the light would become dim and would no longer be the highest. So it is also with the highest heat: it is not mixed with cold or other things; for if it is mixed, it is certainly hindered, and it could be made more intense if it were purified. 

Therefore, the highest in any category is only one, and consists of only that one nature. For instance, the highest light is one—not two lights—and it is only light, not light and something else at the same time. God is the highest of all things. Therefore, God is one and simple: namely, one supreme unity, one supreme truth, and one supreme goodness. One God. One, I say, according to the Platonists <note>original: "Platonicos." Ficino refers here to the tradition of Neoplatonism (Plotinus, Proclus, etc.) which he synthesized with Christian theology.</note>, for a threefold reason. First, because he is the highest unity. For any "highest" thing is unique; and what is more unique than the highest unity? Every multitude of innumerable things is reduced to its own specific unity: the multitude of innumerable men to one human species <note>original: "species." In the Aristotelian and Platonic sense, a 'species' is the universal form or blueprint that makes a thing what it is.</note>. Of horses to one equine species, and similarly for others. Then take all these specific unities, which are limited in number—that is, the species of things—and gather them into one common unity, namely...

<summary>Ficino argues for the absolute oneness of God, the first principle, by demonstrating that multiple "equal" gods would lead to logical contradictions and would require a higher power to unify them. He uses the analogy of light and heat to show that the "highest" form of any quality must be singular and unmixed.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK III

...indeed of evils. For just as God, who is the author of all good things, is his own good and is devoid of all evil, so the opposite principle—the supreme evil—would be deprived of every good. This principle, therefore, would neither act, nor know, nor live, nor even exist at all. For to exist, to live, and to know are themselves goods and things to be desired.

---

->*There are not several gods, one above another without end. Chapter III.*<-

<margin>There are not several gods, one above another without end.</margin>
Moreover, someone might perhaps grant us that there is indeed a God above the angel <note>In Ficino’s system, the "Angel" is the rank of pure Intellect, which sits below God but above the Soul.</note>, and that there is one God in the sense that there are not many gods equal to one another, yet they might still suggest that there is one God above another in an endless chain. Although we believe this was refuted by our previous arguments, we shall disprove it more clearly with further reasons. If the gods were innumerable in this way, the causes of things would be infinite, surpassing each other in countless steps; for if these gods are the causes of things, and countless gods are ranked one above the other, then there would also be innumerable effects in the world. Every cause produces its own specific effect within the order of things, and just as the causes surpass each other, so too would the effects. Therefore, there would be infinite effects descending downward, failing one after another in countless steps, if the causes were an infinite series surpassing each other. And since a higher cause always casts its power further in producing effects than a lower one, the reach of these effects would be infinite if the ascent of causes were infinite. Who cannot see how absurd this is? First, if there is no "first" among things, there can be no "subsequent" things at all. For all things are pulled along by the first; if that first point exists nowhere, there will be no source from which the outflow of things—which must flow from somewhere else—could ever begin. 

Next, we see that in the natural world some things possess more perfection than others. This power of perfection increases as we ascend and decreases as we descend. It follows that the natural force of things is gradually weakened as it moves downward. Thus, it is forced to fail entirely at some point, having been diminished bit by bit. Therefore, it is impossible for one thing to exist beneath another without end. If there are not innumerable effects, there cannot be innumerable causes. Indeed, by the very fact that perfection grows as one ascends, it is perfectly clear that it must eventually reach a "highest" point. Why do we judge the soul to be better than the body, unless it is because the soul is closer to the highest goodness? If there were no such thing as a "highest" goodness, but one simply ascended from good to better into infinity, the body would be distant from that highest goodness by an infinite interval—and the soul would be distant by a similar infinite interval. One infinity is not "larger" or "smaller" than another infinity. There would be no rational measure or ideal standard by which one thing could be preferred over another. 

Consequently, the soul would be no closer or more suited to goodness itself than the body; therefore the soul would not be "better," nor would an angel be better than a soul. Furthermore, whatever flows from another is unstable by its very nature, because on its own it is nothing, and it only comes into being through a kind of "flow" from its source. If there is no "first" thing in reality, every thing would simply emanate from another; thus all things would be unstable. Nowhere would there be unity, equality, likeness, stability, order, or restoration. But since we clearly see these qualities in the world, the flow of things trickling from another must be guided and contained by the stability of some "hinge" <term>cardinis</term> <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a door hinge or a celestial axis to describe a fixed point that allows motion but does not move itself.</note> that does not trickle from anything else. Just as the endless flow of liquid must be stopped by something solid rather than another liquid, so must the chain of causes end in a solid foundation. 

Finally, every higher grade acts upon the one below it and receives something from the one above it. If there is no first grade and no last grade, every "middle" grade would depend on an infinite number of higher grades, and in turn produce an infinite number of lower grades. Therefore, it would receive innumerable perfections from above (since it receives some good from every cause), and it would bestow infinite gifts on those below. It would thus possess immense power and be full of infinite perfections. In such a case, all things would be equally infinite; one thing would not be more excellent than another, and a cause would not be better than its own work. Or perhaps every thing would be "infinitely finite," because it would be surpassed in countless ways by its predecessors. Conversely, it would be "infinite" because it would surpass an infinite number of followers. Nor could there ever be true knowledge, since an infinite series of causes cannot be grasped by the mind. Nor would there be anything in the universe to move or satisfy our desire <note>In Platonic philosophy, all movement is driven by "appetite" or desire for the Good.</note> if there were no first principle and ultimate end. It is by the power of this end that all desire is moved and finds its rest. Therefore, let there be one single principle of all things. Let it be called **Unity**, which towers above all things through its most excellent simplicity; **Truth**, because by producing things it gives being to all; and **Goodness**, because by calling things back to itself, it provides and...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino refutes the idea of an infinite regress of gods or causes, arguing that without a single, fixed "First Principle" (God), there could be no order, no varying degrees of perfection, and no ultimate purpose in the universe.</summary>

### MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
<meta>Catchword: God is</meta>

...persists and flourishes. And as the theology of John the Apostle—the most divine of all theologians, whom the Platonist Amelius <note>Amelius (3rd century AD) was a prominent Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus; Ficino highlights him here to show that even "pagan" Platonists respected the Gospel of John.</note> gladly embraces—teaches: he calls Unity the Principle; Truth the "reason" or logic of that Principle; and Goodness the love of that rational Principle. And let this very substance—namely Unity, true Good, or the one good Truth, or the one true Goodness—be the one, good, and true God. But because he is Unity, he is therefore Truth; because he is true Unity, he is therefore Goodness. In Unity, he enfolds all things; in Truth, he unfolds them; through Goodness, he pours them forth. Indeed, after all things have flowed out from there, they flow back through Goodness, are reshaped through Truth, and are restored into one through Unity.

-> God's power is infinite. Chapter IV. <-

Just as infinite weakness is found in the greatest dispersion, so infinite power resides in the highest unity. By its very nature, "Act" <note>In this context, "Act" or "Activity" refers to the state of being fully realized and operational, the opposite of "Potential," which is just the possibility of being.</note> does not include a limit. For to be subjected to a limit is a form of "passion" <note>original: "passio" – in medieval philosophy, this means the state of being acted upon by something else.</note>, which is the opposite of Act. Therefore, Act does not suffer a limit except insofar as it rests upon some subject where there is a degree of passive potential. But the Divine Act subsists in itself. 

Effective power itself, insofar as it is power, does not contain a fixed number of degrees. For what prevents this power, as power, from being thought of or existing in one number just as in another? For this reason, it does not receive a limit of its degrees from anywhere else, except either from the passive potential with which it is mixed, or from a limiting cause. But the divine power is pure and supreme. "Being" itself, when considered absolutely, is immense, because it can be communicated to and thought of in infinite things and in innumerable ways. Therefore, if the being of anything is finite, that being must be limited either by its cause or by its subject. Neither of these applies to God. In that infinite Being itself, there is infinite power, just as in a finite being, there is finite power. 

In pure nothingness, there is no state of being, whether real or imaginary. For who could define "nothing" according to a logic of being? Therefore, in pure Being itself, there is nothing—whether by real or imaginary logic—of a lack of being or a potential toward non-being. Therefore, that which pertains to his eternity can neither be forced nor even thought "not to be," nor can any degree of power that can be imagined by the mind be lacking in him. Otherwise the mind, which is an effect of God, could extend itself beyond God, since the mind is always able to imagine a greater degree than any finite number of degrees. Indeed, the mind would have been oriented toward an infinite progression in vain unless some infinite end was to be found. 

And because nothing of the true and the good is lacking to Truth and Goodness themselves, all degrees are present in them—whatever can be understood as true, and whatever can be desired as good. Such degrees are innumerable. Furthermore, every agent is more powerful the further it brings a potential for "suffering" <note>Meaning the potential to be changed or acted upon.</note> into a state of "act." Indeed, greater power is needed to heat water than to heat air. But that which does not exist at all is infinitely distant from being an "act," nor does it have any potential to receive an act; we shall discuss this more clearly in what follows. Therefore, whether God creates something anew from nothing, or continually brings forth and preserves the primary matter of bodies and the essence of minds and souls from no prior subject, he undoubtedly possesses an immense power of acting, since they always depend on the first act—that is, the divine act. 

What more? The movement and order of this vast and complex machine [the universe], so steady through so many centuries, teaches us that the power in the Governor is tireless and therefore infinite. For a finite power, in an infinite time—or even in a long but finite time—becomes exhausted and falters. From the infinite power of God, therefore, all intellects receive the ability to understand always and firmly; souls receive the ability to reason without end; and matter receives an unending potential for receiving forms. From this power, movement and time are able to flow without limit, and the generation of things also (as the natural philosophers say) is able to continue in an alternating and innumerable succession. For they think that infinite action and motion take their origin from infinite power, and that whatever things are said to be infinite—whether in potential or in some other way—are such and are judged to be such through the supreme, existing infinite Act. Hence the divine nature is named by Orpheus <term>the infinite end</term> <note>original Greek: ἀτελής τε τελευτή (ateles te teleute). Ficino interprets this Orphic fragment as meaning a "limitless limit" or a goal that can never be exhausted.</note>, that is, the limitless limit.

<summary>This page concludes Ficino's synthesis of the Platonic "One" with the Christian Trinity and begins an argument for God's infinite power. He posits that because God is "Pure Act" without any passive matter to limit him, his power must be limitless, as evidenced by the eternal order of the cosmos and the human mind's ability to conceive of infinity.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.
G
<meta>Catchword: tant, infi</meta>

-> *God is always.* Chapter V. <-

If any thing is more lasting to the degree that the power <note>original: "uirtus" — in this context, it refers to an inherent capacity or strength of being, not just moral virtue.</note> through which it remains and is preserved is more potent, then God, through His infinite power, remains in the infinite Himself and preserves all other things. Likewise, divine truth precedes the beginning of all things and follows the end of all things. For even before the beginning of anything, it was true that that beginning would come to be; and after every end of anything, it will be true that that end has occurred. Whatever is true at any time is true because of Truth itself. If, however, Truth itself were said to have begun at some point, then long before that, through that very same Truth, it would have been true that Truth was going to begin. And if it were imagined to come to an end, even afterwards, through that same Truth, it would be true that Truth had ceased. Therefore, Truth can be thought of as neither ever beginning nor ever ending.

Furthermore, if God exists entirely above motion and time, He does not undergo temporal change from a "before" to an "after" according to being and non-being. It follows that if God is the highest necessity of being—which we shall show in the following sections—He never could have, nor will He ever be able to, not exist. Finally, if whatever is born at some time is made from something prior, and whatever is dissolved is resolved into something older, then that which is first cannot have begun or ceased. 

We frequently contemplate in our minds a certain simple duration without beginning or end, and we call it (so to speak) sempiternity <note>original: "sempiternitas" — a term used to describe everlastingness or duration without end, often distinguished from "eternity" (aeturnitas), which exists entirely outside of time.</note>, which is indeed God Himself, even if we barely discern it. For every simple infinity is God Himself. However, our phantasy <note>original: "phantasia" — the faculty of the mind that creates and stores mental images of physical things.</note> prevents us from discerning this, for it immediately clothes and confuses that simple and consistent sempiternity with a certain manifold flow; thus it deceives us, drawing us toward the accidental flow of time, which is actually the substantial state of eternity. And so it drives us to think that what is God is actually time. God, being eternal, then offers Himself to us, but wrapped in time. No one, however, ought to doubt that God is "always," since God is the very "always" itself; indeed, sempiternity itself is God. And those things which are called sempiternal are properly those things which God propagates through Himself and into Himself.

---

-> *God is everywhere.* Chapter VI. <-

From the points above, we can prove that God is everywhere. Just as a body touches that in which it exists through the dimensions of quantity, so an incorporeal substance touches through power. For this reason, just as if there were an infinite dimension of body in nature, it would be everywhere, so because there is an immense power of an incorporeal substance, this substance is necessarily everywhere. 

And just as a particular cause is present to a particular effect—as fire is present to the wood it ignites—so a universal cause is present to a universal effect. Wherever, therefore, that which is a universal effect is found or thought to be, there also is God, who is the universal cause. Wherever there is any work that must be done through a certain cause alone and without a medium <note>i.e., without an intermediary or middle-man.</note>, there its cause must be. But everywhere there is something that can subsist through God alone by way of creation. That thing is "prime matter" <note>original: "materia prima" — the most basic, formless stuff from which all physical things are made.</note> in bodies, and "essence" in spirits.

It is desirable, as a good, to be present everywhere at once, almost no less than to "be always"; and in the First Good, nothing of the good is lacking. God is not prohibited by anything from penetrating through all things, for nothing resists infinite purity and power. The nature of God does not suffer a limit of place around itself, just as it does not suffer a limit of dignity within itself; for if the highest infinity itself suffers nothing finite, it follows that God does not have a finite presence of space, just as He does not have finite power, action, or duration. 

Nor should it be thought that the Good itself is less present to the whole world than the soul is to the whole body. For the world is less in relation to God than the body is to the soul, and the world needs God more than the body needs the soul. The "Good" is broader than "Life," because it applies to more things; it is also more necessary to the world than life. For if life were removed, the world would indeed cease to move, but if the Good were removed, it would cease to be. If, therefore, in the one living body of the world, a certain single life is everywhere—which we will show elsewhere—much more is the one Good itself everywhere, even outside the world. If the first "patient" <note>original: "patiens" — the passive recipient of action, referring here to matter and essence.</note>, which is matter and essence, is propagated through all things, much more does the first "agent" <note>the active force or creator.</note>, which is God, propagate Himself through all things and beyond all things. It is not fitting for the mind's machinery to progress further than the presence of the Good. But the mind indeed progresses through the immense. And the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, whom Ficino sought to reconcile with Christian doctrine.</note> think it fitting... <note>original: "infi..." — likely "infinitum," indicating the sentence continues regarding the infinite.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues for God's eternity and omnipresence, stating that God exists as "Truth" and "Goodness" beyond the limits of time and space, acting as the universal cause that sustains all existence.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...exist, the infinite good, by overflowing through the immeasurable, pours itself out so completely that it leaves no part of the universe—whether real or imagined beyond the world—destitute of its presence. Indeed, if the nature of the Good is to amplify itself, the infinite Good amplifies itself infinitely. It is difficult to find where God is, because He is "nowhere," in the sense that He is not confined by the limits of any subject or place. It is even more difficult to find where He is *not*, because He is within all things: He is that in which they exist, through which they are made, and through which they are preserved everywhere. God is in all things for this reason: because all things are in Him. If they were not in Him, they would be nowhere, and they would not exist at all. It is through God that this very concept of "where" exists and is called "everywhere." Through God—acting as both a guide and a light—whatever anyone does or seeks, they do and seek it somewhere. Nothing is desired anywhere except the Good; nothing is found anywhere except the True. God is all Good; God is all Truth. 

Add to this that God is amplitude and fullness itself. I do not see, therefore, why He should not amplify Himself through all things and fill every single part. If visible light (which belongs to something and exists in something, and is finite) can spread itself through the whole world, surely the invisible Light (which belongs to itself and is infinite within itself) amplifies itself through the world and beyond the world. For just as finite light receives from the infinite Light the power to shine and to shine brightly, it also receives the power to shine as widely as possible. If things fare so poorly when the sun’s light is absent for even a short time—whether through an eclipse or through the night—how much worse do we think they would fare if God were always absent from them? Rather, why should we not believe that if He were absent for even a moment, that which is Being itself would suddenly collapse into nothingness? Orpheus wisely said in his *Hymn to Saturn*:

> <note>original Greek: "ὃς ναίεις ϰατὰ πάντα μέρη ϰόσμοιο γιμάρχα"</note>
> Who dwells in all parts of the world, prince of generation. <note>Orpheus was a legendary poet-prophet; Ficino viewed him as one of the "ancient theologians" whose hymns contained hidden Platonic truths.</note>

We often imagine a certain purest capacity, which no limits anywhere can contain, but which contains everything that can exist or be imagined. Since that pure infinity itself is nothing other than God, when we imagine that capacity, we are thinking of God Himself, even if we do not fully realize it.

For <term>Phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of "Imagination" or "Fancy," which Ficino distinguishes from higher Reason because it deals only with physical images and dimensions.</note> soon deceives us with its tricks, suddenly substituting for the divine rays some stretch of lines in length, breadth, and depth; it thus compels us to see the divine light as a mere dimension or a void. It deceives us again when we consider that God fills all things completely, for then it persuades us that He is somehow "placed" within things.

But in truth, He is "everywhere" in such a way that the very thing called "everywhere" exists in Him. Indeed, He is Himself "everywhere," containing Himself and all other things. Those things which are said to be "everywhere" besides Him are properly those things which He amplifies through Himself within Himself. <term>Ratio</term> <note>Reason or the higher intellect.</note> dictates that what we call "everywhere" is nothing other than the universal nature of things, and that this nature is God. Therefore, when we say God is everywhere, it should be understood that He is in Himself, and vice versa. Furthermore, God is absent from nowhere, if that which is called "everywhere" is absent from nowhere. Phantasia, however, thinks the nature of things is only this bodily machine; it cries out that "everywhere" is nothing but the total extension of physical things, and since it thinks this extension is the largest thing possible, it doubts that God can fill it all. Reason, on the contrary, cries out that the bodily machine is a thin and meager shadow, divided into countless small parts and particles of parts; it has an endless smallness and a limited greatness. Reason asserts that what is truly "Great" is that in which nothing is small, in which whatever exists is the whole, and is equally great. And just as the whole is folded within everything that is inside, so the whole is unfolded through everything that is outside. 

Thus God, standing firm in Himself, exists everywhere. The world is not extended through God, but the world is extended through God as far as it is able. And just as the world attains the divine power (which is infinite) only in a finite way, so it follows His presence (which shines immeasurably in all directions) only within a certain finite location. The world does not move forward in a straight line to reach God, who is never absent, but it revolves as best it can around Him; rather, it revolves *within* Him, only where the location and motion are prescribed by divine law. Anebo and Abamon <note>Priests mentioned in Iamblichus’s *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, a text Ficino translated.</note> the Egyptian priests, as well as the Platonists Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Julian, wished to argue that not only God, but every Mind—whether angelic or animal—pours itself out as a whole through the immeasurable. They held that spirits of this kind exist everywhere within one another without mutual confusion, just as different habits...

He distinguishes between the deceptive faculty of Imagination, which sees space as physical dimensions, and Reason, which understands God as the "invisible light" sustaining all existence.</summary>
