<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book II, Chapter VI of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. While the previous page focused on God’s omnipresence, this page shifts to the omnipresence of the "rational spirit" or human mind, arguing that because the mind is an image of God and is not bound by matter, it shares in God's ability to be "everywhere" and "always."</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II

<note>original: "bitus" – the full word is "habitus"</note> ...habits of virtues in the soul, and the various images of colors in the air; their opinion rests on these foundations. Forms lower than the rational spirit <note>referring to physical or animal souls</note> are restricted by the specific and limited matter from which they arise. However, because rational spirits do not spring from matter in any way, they possess no fixed dimension within themselves, nor are they bound to any physical size. Therefore, since they regard every part of any space equally, they are either nowhere or they are in the entire universe. It cannot be said that things which truly exist are entirely nowhere; therefore, they are never absent. 

Every mind is, in a way, eternal. What is eternal, although it is indivisible in terms of time, nevertheless extends itself through the entire course of time. In the same way, although it is indivisible in terms of space, it is dilated through all space. And just as time relates to eternity, so does the temporal relate to the eternal. The moments of time always find the moment of eternity; likewise, the points of a physical body always find the point of the eternal spirit everywhere. Just as an eternal thing is always outside of time, so it seems to be everywhere outside of place. Whatever moments of time flow by, they run into the point of eternity. Whatever line is drawn, it touches that point. Whatever space is stretched out, it finds the eternal thing. 

What is the most important thing that can be everywhere? Certainly, it is that which physical dimension does not oppose. Again, what can exist always? That which the action of quality does not conquer. Since quality is much more effective than quantity, whatever can exist always (because quality does not prevent it) can even more easily exist everywhere (because dimension does not prevent it). Local motion—which is external motion—appears more perfect in any thing the more the internal nature of that thing is effective. Therefore, for a thing to propagate itself through all things (imitating local motion), there must first be within the thing itself a perpetual preserving power, which is called "intrinsic perfection." To whatever thing this intrinsic perfection belongs, there follows an "extrinsic dilation" through universal space. It is more excellent to *be always* (which is internal) than to *be everywhere* (which is external). Therefore, what can exist always can much more easily exist everywhere. For it is easier to exceed sluggish dimensions <note>the heavy, unmoving nature of physical matter</note> than the powerful movement of quality and time.

The mind, both to itself and to others, signifies the nature, counsel, and affection of God more than anything else; it proceeds from God like a word—or rather, like the meaning of a word from the one speaking God. Since the one who speaks is wherever the word is, it follows that the mind is everywhere, just as God is everywhere. The mind is immeasurable in its thought and affection, just as it perceives and desires the immeasurable machine <note>the universe</note>, and runs through it with its own operation. An operation cannot shine where it is not, nor can such an operation be wider than its essence. Therefore, the mind exists in the infinite. 

The goal of fire is the hollow of the highest heaven. Therefore, any small flame, if nothing prevented it, would fly up to that point; and when it reached that hollow, if it had sufficient size, it would amplify itself through the whole space so that it might enjoy all that is natural to it. If it were indivisible, it would strive to be whole in every point of that space, so that it might enjoy the whole everywhere. The aim and goal of the mind is Truth and Goodness itself—that is, God. Toward this, the mind runs by a certain essential instinct <term>instinctus</term> (a natural, divinely-planted drive), first like fire, then with life, and then with intellect. There is nothing to stop the essence of the mind from penetrating all the way to God; for the body does not resist the spirit, and the spirit resists it even less. And God penetrates all things. 

Therefore, the mind always reaches God through this essential instinct—and everywhere too. For it strives for this very thing, and it has no assigned dimension or natural need for a specific location that would prevent it from being everywhere. And because it acts wherever it is, it follows that it lives and understands everywhere, always in God. Although all minds exist through the infinite, some seem to direct certain actions more clearly toward one region of the infinite than another: angelic minds by governing, and animal minds by giving life. It is just as if many candles were lit in the same hall: their individual lights fill the entire hall, joined together but not mixed, for one light can be separated from another. Even if these lights are spread through the whole hall, each is still directed back to its individual candle. It can happen, however, that a mind thinks it is only in the body it rules, even though it is everywhere beyond the body—just as our mind, although it is in this whole body, is thought by many Philosophers to be only in the heart. These are their views on the mind. Let us now return to God.

<meta>This page continues the argument for God’s nature following Chapter VI. While the previous page discussed how the human mind, as an image of God, participates in a kind of omnipresence, Chapter VII turns to God as the ultimate source of action, preservation, and existence for all things.</meta>

MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

->*God acts upon and preserves everything, and works all things in all.*<-

### Chapter VII.

Through the preceding arguments, we have shown that God exists, and that He is one, the first, and infinite in power, duration, and space. From these points, that which Parmenides the Pythagorean said of God in his book on truth and opinion is confirmed: "one, immobile, infinite being" <note>original: "ὁν ἓν ἀκίνητον ἄπειρον"</note>. Next, we shall prove that God acts upon and preserves all things, and works all things in all, in the following way. 

If God is the most <term>simple</term> <note>In this context, "simple" means having no parts or components; pure and undivided.</note> unity, and this unity alone exists in nature because it is the highest, then whatever exists besides God is multiple and composite. For all multiplicity descends from unity, and every composition comes from the purity of the simple. If God is the highest truth, and nothing can exist without truth—for how can anything be, unless it truly is what it is said to be, and its very existence is true?—then all things proceed from God. 

If God is the highest goodness, and goodness by its very nature communicates itself most greatly, then God imparts Himself to all things. Therefore, all things seek the good; because they were born from the good, they seek their origin, so that they may be perfected by the same source from which they were created. 

Every individual thing is always doing something, and it acts more effectively the better it is within its own <term>species</term> <note>A "species" refers to the specific kind or category of being a thing belongs to.</note>. Those things that belong to a better species act the most, and everything works to produce things like itself according to its strength—even things similar in species, if possible. Furthermore, every action is done for the sake of the good. Therefore, every action in all things happens from the good, through the good, and toward the good. Thus, the highest goodness acts because it is goodness; it acts always because it is the highest; and because it is not limited to any one species but is equally common to all species, it acts upon all. 

Moreover, since God is not mixed with any one thing, He exists not as a leader of one specific thing, but as the common leader of all. If He is common, a common duty belongs to Him. Existence itself is common to all things. Therefore, existence, wherever it may be, depends upon God. This is what Zoroaster touched upon mystically: 
"All things are born from one fire," <note>original: "ἐστὶ πάντα πυρὸς ἑνὸς ἐκγεγαῶτα"</note>
that is, all things are generated from a single fire. 

Furthermore, the lower bodies of the world move from non-being into being, and pass from being into non-being. The higher bodies change from one way of being to another, or from one mode of existence to another. Therefore, all these things are, by their own nature, equally inclined toward being or non-being. If there were nothing else above such bodies, they either would never have received existence at all, or if they had, they would have all flowed away long ago. They would not have received it because, if they are equally inclined by nature toward being and non-being, they do not determine themselves toward being. They would have flowed away long ago because they are fluid by nature; if they were not held together by something more stable, they would have long since dissolved into nothingness. 

Therefore, an incorporeal and stable substance presides over the moving bodies of the world. If this substance were equally inclined toward being and non-being, like the bodies, it would again require something else to define it. Finally, then, there must be one substance that exists <term>necessarily</term> <note>A "necessary" being is one that cannot fail to exist and does not depend on anything else for its existence.</note> through itself, and this will be entirely simple. Indeed, if it were composed of parts, it would not exist through itself, but through the coming together of its parts and through the one who reconciled those diverse parts to each other. Indeed, it would be just as subject to the dissolution of its parts as it was to their connection; therefore, it would not exist by necessity, since through dissolution it could at some point cease to be. Such a substance is God: a simple substance, subsisting necessarily through itself. For this reason, Orpheus called God "Necessity":
"For strong necessity rules over all," <note>original: "δεινὴ γὰρ ἀνάγκη πάντα κρατεῖ"</note>
that is, powerful necessity dominates all things. 

If God is the highest necessity of being, and that which is highest in any category is unique, then no thing besides God will be such a necessity of being. For if you wish an angel also to be such a thing, so that there are two "highest necessities," God and the angel, you would be forced to explain in what way the angel differs from God. It cannot be in the necessity of being itself, for in that, you have posited them to be one. Therefore, there must be something else in the angel besides that necessity by which it can differ from God. Consequently, the angel will not be the "highest necessity," since it is not pure and solitary necessity, but a mixture. Whatever is highest in any category must have the pure nature of that category, unmixed with other things, so that it is not diminished by the mixture. You would also be forced to answer: from where does the angel have 그 property added to its necessity? Is it from its own necessity, or from elsewhere? If the first is granted, God will have that same property proceeding from a similar necessity of His own. Therefore, through that...

<summary>Ficino argues that God is the unique, simple, and necessary source of all existence and action. Drawing on "Ancient Theology" sources like Parmenides, Zoroaster, and Orpheus, he explains that all things depend on God for their stability and being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from Chapter VII. Ficino is transitioning from the definition of God as the "Highest Good" to a discussion of God as the "Universal Cause" who not only creates but actively sustains the existence of all things, including angels, the world, and human minds.</meta>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK II.</header>
<sig>G 3</sig>

->**God acts upon and preserves everything, and works all things in all.**<-

An angel is not distinguished from God [by its own essence]. If the alternative is granted—that it is distinguished—it follows that the angel's own nature is born from something other than the angel itself, because it acquires the property by which it is distinguished from the outside. Whatever depends on another is not necessarily through itself. Therefore, neither an angel, nor any other thing, is the necessity of being, but God alone. 

If nothing besides God exists necessarily through itself, then all things receive their being from God. From this, the profane opinion of certain Physicists <note>Ficino refers here to "Physicists" in the ancient sense: natural philosophers, likely targeting those who followed a strictly Aristotelian or materialistic view of an eternal, independent universe.</note> is condemned, who believe that matter, the world, and mind <note>original: "mentem"</note> have not only always existed, but also in no way depend on God in their essence—even if they admit they depend on Him in action, for they confess that all things are moved and work toward the good as their end. 

They ought to consider that whatever cannot suffice for itself in operating, but requires sufficiency from an external end, is much less able to suffice for itself in its essence, since it has its essence from an external principle. For if it belongs to the same one to perfect as to effect <note>original: "perficere cuius efficere" — meaning the one who finishes a thing is the same one who brings it into being</note>, just as all things are perfected by the Good as their end, so they are effected by the same Good as their principle. And since essence is most perfect in its source, if any of those three [matter, world, mind] were the source of its own essence, the substance of each would be equally perfect both in relation to one another and to God. Nor would they turn toward God, but toward themselves as their own end and perfection.

As art is related to nature, so is nature related to God. Works of art remain uncorrupted only as long as they are preserved by the power of nature. Just as a statue stands for a long time through the natural solidity of stone or bronze, so all natural things remain only as long as they are preserved by the influx of God. And just as nature brings motion to its works, so God grants being to nature. Works of nature are moved only as long as nature moves them. Therefore, nature exists only as long as God preserves it in existence. 

Furthermore, this entire work of God either was always or began to be at some point. If it always was, a first moment cannot be assigned in which it received being from God before all others. Therefore, either it received it at no moment—which is false—or it receives it at every moment, which is nothing other than being continually preserved by Him. But if it began to be at some point, it needs God much more as a preserver, whom it would need even if it were eternal. 

Generally, what belongs to a thing according to its nature belongs to it before what comes from outside. But for a work, it is natural not to be, since it would not have existed if a cause had not approached; it is through a cause that it exists. Therefore, not being belongs to it before being does. Thus, it belongs to it to be preserved by a cause before it belongs to it to be by itself. And because what is natural is never lost, it is always such that if the power of the cause were removed, it would not persist in being, since it was such from the beginning naturally that it could not come into being apart from the action of the cause.

We properly call God the **Cause**, who alone effects any thing in its entirety, and is not thought to need the help of another or to borrow matter from elsewhere. Rather, every thing is compelled to depend entirely on Him always, as a shadow <note>original: "umbra"</note> depends on a body. Indeed, when a cause effects the whole of its effect, and the effect—if compared to the substance of the cause—is something imaginary and vain rather than substantial, then surely the effect, being vain in itself, needs the continuous support of the cause, and the cause that made the whole preserves the whole. 

If the world is compared to God—the finite to the infinite—it is more vain and shadow-like than if the finite shadow of a finite body were compared to the body. Finally, the supreme cause of things rules them inwardly, if things do not merely flow from it once, but also depend on it assiduously, just as images are produced by bodies and preserved in mirrors <note>original: "specula"</note>. 

Therefore, since God acts upon and preserves all things, He works in all things; that is, the subsequent causes of things do nothing without divine power and action. If God grants being and act <note>original: "actu"</note> to an angel and preserves them, He also grants the power of acting and the action itself, and preserves them. Thus, whatever an angel operates naturally, it operates by the power of God, just as an instrument acts by the power of the craftsman. 

Therefore, God acts not only upon the angel, but even upon the work of the angel itself; and God effects the angel’s work much more than the angel does, since He Himself is the first origin of the action. If this work done by the angel moves something else, it moves it through that same power of God through which it was made by the angel. Wherefore, by the power of God, whatever happens anywhere happens, by whomever it is done—especially since all things that act in some way provide being to their work. I say **being** in this way or that, such or such. Thus all things acting under God concur toward one common effect, which is **being**. Many and diverse agents do not conspire into one work, which is being, except because they themselves are one; and they are not one, except because they are under the One, and toward...

He asserts that all secondary causes, such as angels or nature, only operate through God's continuous preservation and power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that God is the primary cause of all things. In the previous page, Ficino argued against the "Physicists" who claimed the world exists independently. Here, he explains how God's power flows through all secondary causes and why God acts by his very nature rather than through labor or complex deliberation.</meta>

### PLATONIC THEOLOGY BY MARSILIO FICINO

one. Therefore, the other agents operate by the power of the one first agent, God. Do we not arrange the order of causes according to the order of their effects? The first effect of all is <term>being</term> <note>original: "esse" — the pure state of existing before any specific qualities are added.</note>; indeed, the remaining effects are nothing other than certain determinations and properties of being itself. For each thing is first according to its nature, and then it is "this" or "that," of such a kind or another. Add to this that the very last thing to be lost is "being," for a thing stops being "of such a kind" before it simply stops "being" at all. Therefore, being itself is the proper effect of that agent which is the beginning and the end of all things. 

And if other agents contribute anything to this, they do so by the power of the first agent. They themselves, as inferiors of a narrower command, do nothing else except distinguish that universal power and action of God—which tends toward universal being everywhere—here and there with God's help; they introduce certain qualities of being rather than the nature of existing itself. 

Indeed, the divine power distinguishes itself into various effects through various means, just as the light of the Sun, which in itself is equally disposed toward any color, will produce two splendors on the floor—one red and one green—if it penetrates through two glass windows, one of which is red and the other green. That both are "splendor" comes simply from the light. But that one is red and the other green also comes from the light, yet only insofar as it penetrates through this or that glass, shaping itself in different ways. 

Let us conclude first: the first cause acts more vehemently in any effect than the remaining causes do, because the "footprint" impressed by it—namely, <term>being</term>—is both impressed first and deleted last, compared to the footprints of the other causes, as if it were impressed more strongly. Secondly, the other causes fix their own footprints upon the footprint of the first cause; just as they necessarily ground all their works in the work of the first cause, so they stabilize their powers and actions in His power and action.

->*God acts through his very being in whatever he does.* Chapter VIII.<-

But lest any <term>Epicurean</term> <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Epicurus, who Ficino often critiques for suggesting that gods are indifferent to the world or that the universe is purely material.</note> say that if God does many things, he must be bothered by deliberation and burdened by work, one must remember that because God can produce his work through his being alone, he does not need deliberation or choice. For if the divine being itself were not so great that it was able to operate through itself, but needed some "counsel" <note>original: "consilio" — intentional deliberation or planning.</note> that was different from being itself, then certainly nothing's "being" would operate anything through itself. 

Yet we see that the qualities of bodies act upon each other without deliberation. Does not the Sun illuminate the world, and fire heat, and the soul nourish the body through its <term>being</term> rather than through choice? Furthermore, even those things that act through choice also do something through their natural being—that is, through a power naturally implanted in being itself. Truly, although the human soul does many things by choice, it nonetheless gives life to the body without choice, simply by being. Is not choice itself, in a way, a work of the soul? And is not this kind of work produced from the soul's being without a preceding choice? Otherwise, that preceding choice would need another preceding choice, and that one another, and so on. Thus, any work of the soul would require innumerable choices before it began to happen, and it would never begin to happen, since one cannot cross the infinite. 

Let us gather the argument thus: if action performed through natural being is present in all things, but action performed by choosing is not (since bodies choose nothing), and if the action of choice and deliberation is always preceded by the action performed through being and nature, it is plainly clear that this action which happens by being itself belongs to the universal and first cause, which is God. Thus, the first and common action belongs to the first and common agent. 

Action that happens through being happens without care or labor. Thus the Sun, in one act, most easily illuminates nearly infinite things, and generates life by illuminating. Fire most easily heats many things; the soul nourishes the body and digests many things in it simultaneously without anxiety or labor. Thus God, through his being—which is a kind of most simple center of things from which the rest are drawn like lines—vibrates whatever depends on it with the easiest nod. 

However, there is this difference between the first agent and the other agents: the first agent is said to operate through being in such a way that he acts through *pure* being, while the others act through being—that is, through some natural or, so to speak, essential power. Therefore, the operation that proceeds from deliberation is preceded by the operation performed by essential power, and this in turn is preceded by that which happens from pure being. And just as that which happens by power is easier than that which happens by deliberation, so much easier is that which is fulfilled by pure being than that which is done by power.

<summary>Ficino explains that God, as the First Cause, provides the fundamental gift of "being" to all things, while secondary causes merely shape that being. He argues that God acts effortlessly through his pure essence, rather than through the labor of deliberation, using the Sun's light as a primary metaphor.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the discussion of God as the primary cause of all being. Having established that God is the source of existence, Ficino now moves to explain how God possesses an intellect and how He understands both Himself and the specific, individual things in the universe.</meta>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.</header>
<sig>G 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: circo (likely "circum" or "circiter" in the original Latin)</meta>

->**God understands himself first, and also individual things.**<-

->Chapter IX.<-

The intellect would never become capable of understanding an object unless there were some kinship between itself and that object. Therefore, since there is a kinship between the intellect and the thing understood, the same path that allows something to become "intelligible" <note>original: "intelligibile" — capable of being understood by a mind.</note> also allows it to become an intellect. However, the only way for any thing to reach that point where it is both understood and capable of being understood—that is, in such a way that it can be properly grasped—is by its departure from **matter**. This is because things are properly understood only when they are thought of separately from matter and the conditions of matter. Therefore, by that same departure from the physical, one can reach the state of being an intellect. Indeed, if being separated from matter is the reason why any "form" <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "form" is the essential nature or blueprint of a thing, distinct from its physical material.</note> becomes one with the intellect, then being even more removed from matter is the reason why a thing is a perfect, understanding intellect. Because no one is more remote from matter than God, no one understands more precisely than He.

Furthermore, intelligence is desirable as a "good," for through it every thing is able to enjoy itself and all other things. But to the **First Good**—which is God—nothing of the "good" is lacking. Add to this that every cause acts through its form, and the greater a cause is, the greater the form through which it acts. God is the greatest cause; therefore, the greatest form is in God. But nowhere is form greater than in the mind. God, therefore, possesses a mind. This is also proven by the fact that it is not fitting for minds to be the instruments of a "mover" <note>The "prime mover" is a philosophical term for the ultimate cause of motion and change in the universe.</note> who lacks a mind Himself. Yet all minds are the instruments of God.

To this same point, it is also true that since in God essence and operation <note>original: "essentia & operatio" — what God *is* and what God *does*.</note> are the same thing, it follows that His operation must be of the kind that does not pass into external matter, but remains within the agent as its own perfection rather than the perfection of the matter. Such is the nature of knowledge and desire. In God, therefore, there is at least knowledge—specifically, intelligence—or something even more eminent than intelligence itself. And because the intelligence of God is the "first intelligence," and whatever is first in any category is pure, solitary, and exists in itself, therefore in God *being* and *understanding* are entirely the same. If "being" were one thing and "understanding" another, we would be forced to place that intelligence within something else—namely, within an essence. 

Likewise, if the first intelligence is there, it is surely most perfect. Such perfection is found when the intellect is as close as possible to the object it must comprehend. In this way, knowledge is entirely certain, lacking nothing, and most full. But the intelligence is closest to the object being known when the understanding thing understands **itself**. Therefore, the proper intelligence of God is that He understands Himself—especially since, if God's intelligence were perfected by some external object, God's essence would be perfected by that same object (since they are the same), and God would then be "made" by something else. Who would say the divine mind follows external things in order to understand, when external things are forced to follow the divine mind in order to exist? Who would place the proper object of the divine mind outside of God, when no power can exceed its own object, yet God exceeds all things immeasurably? 

When we attribute the names "intellect" and "intelligence" to God, it must be understood that these titles are applied according to Him being the **cause** of such things, rather than by Him sharing their limited structure. For we properly consider an **angel** to be a "mind," but God is above the whole category of minds, so that He is the "Mind of minds" and the "Light of lights." 

God understands whatever He understands in a way that is "above" intelligence; and to come to our main point, He understands individual things. For whatever an intellect does, it does by its own nature, and thus it acts by understanding. Therefore, whatever He makes, He understands, as is evident in the arts and in planning. Since God acts through His very being, and that being does not lack intellect—indeed, His being and His understanding are the same due to God's supreme simplicity—it must be that He operates by understanding. His knowledge extends as far as His operation does, since in the most simple God, voluntary knowledge and operation are the same. His operation extends through all things down to the very smallest. Therefore, God understands all the smallest things. This is especially true because whoever knows all the causes of the smallest things understands the smallest things themselves. God is ignorant of no cause, for He knows Himself. He is the cause of all things; therefore, knowing the first and highest of causes, and the cause of all things, He knows them all. 

He knows them, I say, distinctly and most clearly. For while He sees Himself, who is the cause of the angel, He sees the angel most clearly. While He gazes upon the angel, He gazes through it (if necessary) at its works as if through their own cause; and through those works, He sees their own effects most plainly. Thus, He clearly discerns the highest cause of the lowest things, the intermediate causes, and the immediate ones. However, there is no need for God to look outside of Himself at subsequent causes to see the ultimate effects, since He Himself is the first origin of their very being and the cause of existence for all that follows. This—

<summary>Ficino argues that God possesses a perfect intellect that is identical to His very being, primarily understanding Himself as the source of all existence. Because He is the cause of everything, His internal self-knowledge naturally encompasses every individual thing in the universe, down to the smallest detail.</summary>

<keywords>Divine Intellect, Platonic Theology, First Cause, Divine Simplicity, Knowledge of Individuals, Essence and Operation, Mind of minds</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 103 regarding God’s intellect. The catchword "circo" from the previous page completes the word "idcirco" (therefore) at the start of this page. Ficino is transitioning from the fact that God understands Himself to the fact that He understands every individual thing in creation.</meta>

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

Therefore <note>original: "idcirco"</note>, while He looks into Himself, He looks into the total being of any and all things. I say the "total being" plainly and distinctly. For if He knows Himself perfectly, He comprehends His entire power. His power, however, is spread through every single thing. Thus, He knows individual things. Likewise, while He sees His own essence and the goodness that is to be communicated to things, He sees in how many ways that goodness of His can be shared. Furthermore, things are made as varied in nature as there are various ways the divine essence and goodness are communicated. Therefore, through the distinct knowledge of His own goodness, He sees the distinct properties of individual things. For no kind of understanding should be missing from the Supreme Intelligence. For this reason, God possesses an understanding not only of general categories <term>genera</term> and species, as some have wished to believe, but also of individual, singular things. Indeed, the knowledge of any thing is desirable as a kind of "good," and no good is lacking in God. 

Add to this that a higher power ought to know whatever a lower power knows, and something more besides, which is apparent in our own souls. For what the five individual senses receive separately, the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or imagination was considered a "lower" mental power that combined sensory data into images.</note> discerns collectively. What the phantasy sees in many images, the intellect sees in one, and it sees individual things more clearly than the phantasy does; moreover, the intellect sees the universal reasons of things which the phantasy does not know. In this way, God, by a single power, knows whatever we know through our three powers—that is, through the senses, the phantasy, and the intellect. Therefore, He perceives both universals and individuals. He perceives, I say, all modes of being, because He sees the origin of being and comprehends the entire nature of "being" itself. If this is so, He certainly inspects individual things, which are distinguished from one another by their various modes of being. Hence Orpheus says:
<note>original Greek: "καὶ διὸ: ὄμμα τέλειον..."</note>
"The perfect eye of Jove <note>Ficino uses the Greek 'Zeus/Jupiter' to represent the supreme Divine Mind.</note>, since whatever happens among us, both fate and the mind of Jove see all things throughout the universe." 

Therefore, let no one put faith in Epicurus or Averroes <note>Averroes was a 12th-century philosopher who famously argued that God only knows universal truths, not lowly individual details, to protect God's dignity.</note>, who say that the knowledge of the lowliest things is unworthy of the divine majesty. For God does not perceive things in themselves, but in Himself; not through their images, but through His own essence. He is not distracted by many things, but beholds all things as one. He never labors, because He does not "seek" knowledge, but possesses it. He is not diverted from weightier matters to consider lighter ones, because He sees both these and those with the same glance—just like the eye, which beholds many stars in the sky with a single gaze. Are you ignorant, O impious Averroes, that the good of the universal order itself is more excellent than the quality of any individual part? Certainly, since even your Aristotle, in the eleventh book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "diuinor. 11" refers to the 'Divine Books', a common title for the Metaphysics.</note>, affirms that individual parts are referred to the good of the order which is in the whole, as if to their final end. If, therefore, God knows any other changeable thing (which you do not deny), He will especially know the order of the universe. An order of this kind cannot be understood unless the more precious and the more lowly things are distinguished between themselves, for the whole order consists in the intervals and proportions between them. Remember, moreover, that these very things which are commonly called "vile" <note>meaning cheap, common, or lowly</note> were each constructed with a certain most exact skill, just like those things which are considered most precious. Furthermore, certain things, when considered alone, usually seem less beautiful, yet in this whole order, and in the Ordainer of the whole Himself, they harmonize most aptly both with themselves and with all others. Orpheus sang of this whole concept in his hymn to Apollo:
<note>original Greek: "ἔχας δε τε πείρατα κόσμου..."</note>
"You hold the boundaries of the whole world. The beginning and the end are your care; through you all things flourish. You tune the whole sphere with a resonant lyre."

-> **God understands infinite things. Chapter X.** <-

True reason teaches us that God knows not only individual and lowliest things, but even infinite things. If God knows His power perfectly, He knows distinctly all that His power contains. For the quantity of a power is considered according to the quantity of the things it can do. But since the power of God is infinite, it extends itself to things that are innumerable. Therefore, God knows the innumerable. God's knowledge reaches deeply through all those things which are said "to be," in whatever way they exist or are said to exist. Thus it is necessary that He plainly understands not only those things which exist in act, but also whatever things are said to be "in potential" <note>things that could exist but currently do not.</note>. Among things...

He concludes by asserting that God’s infinite power allows Him to know even infinite and potential things.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s exploration of the Divine Intellect from page 104. Having established that God knows individual things, he now addresses the concept of infinity: how a single, simple God can comprehend the infinite variety and number of things in the universe without becoming "divided" or "limited" Himself.</meta>

<page-num>105</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.</header>

In natural things, however, there are some that are infinite, if not in act <term>actually existing</term>, then at least in potential <term>the capacity to become</term>. Namely: the capacity of matter, the progression of motion and time, the succession of generation, the division of the continuous, and the multiplication of number. God, therefore, clearly understands infinite things, just as "unity" <note>In Platonic thought, the number One (Unity) is the source of all numbers.</note>—which is the principle of numbers—would see infinite numbers in act, if it saw those numbers which are within it according to potential. For unity is, according to potential, every number. God gazes upon all things through His own essence as if through a certain model <term>exemplar</term>. Since, however, there is infinite perfection in this essence, innumerable things can be expressed according to its likeness, so that they might gradually advance for the better through innumerable degrees of perfection. This is because neither a single thing formed from it, nor any finite multitude of such things, can ever exhaust the entire perfection of an infinite model. And so, always and without any end, there remains a new way in which something else is able to imitate that very model further. God, therefore, through the innumerable degrees of the infinite model, gazes upon innumerable images. In God, "to be" and "to understand" are entirely the same thing; and therefore, just as His being is infinite, so His understanding is infinite. Since the human intellect has the power to recognize those things which are infinite in potential, it can multiply the types of numbers unto infinity, and proceed at will in many other things without end. But if the divine intellect does not understand things that are infinite in act, but only gazes upon a certain fixed number, I ask: can He understand further, or can He not? If He can, then God does not actually understand all those things which He has the power to understand. If He cannot, then the human intellect is able to know more things than the divine. Both conclusions are absurd. He therefore understands things that are infinite in act. For this reason, since the divine mind is infinite, it is deservedly named by the Orphics <note>Followers of the legendary poet Orpheus, whom Ficino considered a "theologian" precursor to Plato.</note> the **infinite eye** <note>original Greek: ἄπειρον ὄμμα</note>. From this, the impious error of those philosophers is refuted who thought that God sees only finite things, because they believed that whatever is seen by Him is "comprehended," and whatever is comprehended is necessarily "finished" or "finite." To these people we respond for the present that God, and the things seen within God by Himself, are the same. Therefore, whoever says these things are comprehended by God says nothing other than that they are comprehended by themselves. It would indeed be absurd for an infinite thing to be comprehended <note>In Latin, *comprehendere* means both to understand and to physically grasp/limit.</note> by another. However, to be comprehended by oneself is not absurd. This is actually nothing other than the thing extending through itself and being fully equal to itself. Therefore, the infinite God does not limit Himself when He inspects His infinity in an infinite way; rather, He confirms His own infinity. Nor is it absurd for God to discern innumerable things. For He does not discern them by counting them out step-by-step, but by gazing upon them all at once. And just as He sees many things as one, while He observes them through a single form in a single act, so He sees an infinite multitude as if it were finite—that is, as a certain thing entirely simple in essence, but in a certain way multiple in its logic. This is because He considers His own form (which is truly one) as "all-formed" in its power and respect; it is just as if the light of the Sun, the source of all colors—which is (so to speak) "one-colored"—were to perceive itself as "all-colored."

---

->*God possesses a will, and through it He effects all things outside Himself.*<-
->Chapter XI.<-

Every cause acts through some form, and produces its effect in a form somewhat similar to itself; therefore, it is necessary that the form of the effect be understood by the cause. Since God is the cause of all things, it is necessary that the forms of all things be in Him. God is, therefore, an "all-formed" essence. Hence that Orphic saying: **Jupiter is the form of all** <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς εἰδὼς πάντων</note>. Just as in pure potential (that is, matter) all natural forms exist according to a certain confused potentiality, so it is necessary that in "pure act" <note>A philosophical term for a being that is fully realized and has no unrealized potential; i.e., God.</note> (that is, God), all forms exist according to a distinct act. But are these forms in God distinct according to a certain natural mode—the way light, heat, dryness, and lightness are in fire—and does He act through them led by a certain necessity of His nature? Not at all.

The first reason: Since God made all things, if He works through forms of this kind, He would be much more multiple and composite than any other cause, whether those forms in Him were essential or accidental. However, He must be the simplest of all things, and therefore they cannot be essential. For no essence would be less "one" within itself than the divine essence. Nor, again, can they be accidental. For in what way can God receive qualities? Not from elsewhere, since He cannot be acted upon by anything. Not from Himself, for if He receives them from Himself, to the extent that He gives them, He acts as...

He begins a new chapter explaining that God acts through His will and contains the "forms" of all created things within His simple essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from page 105 regarding God’s infinite understanding. Having argued that God understands infinite things through His own essence, Ficino now transitions into explaining why God’s creative power and knowledge operate through intellect and will rather than through "blind" natural necessity.</meta>

<page-num>106</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

it performs the role of the efficient cause <term>the active force that brings something about</term>; in so far as it receives, it performs the role of the subject <term>the thing acted upon</term>. However, the First Agent and "Pure Act" <note>original: "purus actus" — a philosophical term for a being that is fully realized and has no unrealized potential</note>, to whom all things are subject, cannot undergo the condition of being a subject. Likewise, substance does not depend on an accident, even though an accident depends on a substance. That which does not depend on another is able to exist at some point apart from that other. Therefore, a certain substance can exist apart from the conditions and limits of accidents. Whatever freedom and good can possibly exist anywhere, all of that can exist through the power of the highest principle and good. For this reason, God is already in act that very substance which is able to be—indeed, which is—free from all accidents.

It leads to the same conclusion that effects are found in a more excellent way within their higher causes than they are in themselves; and for that reason, they are in the Highest Cause in some most excellent way. Since, however, the effects of God are substances in themselves, they should by no means exist in God as if they were accidents <term>secondary properties like color or size</term>. Yet, there are not many substances in Him; rather, there is one certain substance there—that is, the very substance of God. For it is necessary that all things be found in God in the most perfect way, and be united to Him, and to each other, most perfectly. They cannot exist in a more sublime way in God, nor be more sublimely united to God and to themselves, than if they are God Himself within God. Therefore, the forms of things are not in God as distinct according to the mode of nature <note>i.e., they are not separate physical entities inside Him</note>, by which He would be led to act by a certain natural necessity—no differently than fire is led to burn.

### Second Reason
The nature of each thing is a single form and a power determined toward one specific work in a certain way, doing whatever it does with its whole impetus and doing so by necessity. Indeed, the warm nature of fire performs one specific work—namely, heating—and it always heats with the same intensity; as far as it is able, it exerts every degree of heat everywhere. Therefore, the fact that this matter is heated by one degree and that matter by two degrees does not proceed from the arrangement of the agent <note>the fire</note>, but from the order of degrees found in the preparation of the materials. Thus, fire does not "master" its total work, for it is not the author of the order of degrees within that work. And if it were to generate two heats outside of subjects, because it would act with its whole self on both, they would both be equal; indeed, even now, it generates entirely similar and equal heats in subjects that are entirely similar. Nature is certainly able to produce different results either through different media or from different materials; but if the diversity of media and materials is removed, it produces either a single thing or something very similar, nor can it fail to act when matter is present. 

God alone, however, procreates the primary matter of bodies and the many essences of minds and souls without any intermediate subject. These are indeed vastly different from one another and distinguished among themselves by many degrees of perfection. Rightly so, because God is the First Agent, He masters His entire work to such an extent that He Himself is able to bring about both the forms, the order of those forms, and the distinction of their degrees. Yet no agent would produce fewer or less varied effects than God—indeed, God would act entirely as one—if He operated solely through the mode of "mere nature," since the divine nature is the simplest of all. Therefore, He is not driven to act by natural instinct.

### Third Reason
If intelligence is effective in us, and more effective in the angels, it must be most effective in God. In God, His nature and His intelligence are the same. Likewise, the mode of natural operation and the mode of intellectual operation are usually the same everywhere. For both nature and intelligence act through form and produce something similar in form. Therefore, God should not be said to act either through "bare nature" or through an "added intelligence," but rather through an intellectual nature and a natural intelligence. Because God is the first, common, and most blessed cause, a natural operation suits Him, which is prior to others, more universal, and easier. Again, because He is the most precious cause, an intellectual operation suits Him, which is prior in dignity in us (though not in time), and is therefore first in the order of things; as something precious, it befits only the most excellent species. Therefore, the proper operation of God is both of these. Among the Platonists, however, there is only one property of the divine essence insofar as He is God. Therefore, both are the same operation in God.

### Fourth Reason
Bare nature regards this or that specific good; intellectual nature regards the universal good. Therefore, a cause which acts through bare nature is compared to a cause which acts through intellectual nature in the same way a specific cause is compared to a universal cause, or a laborer to an architect. Thus, the Architect of the world operates through intellectual nature, in so far as it is intellectual.

### Fifth Reason
That operation above all others suits God by which He neither falls from His state nor from His simplicity. Such, primarily, is the operation of the mind. For a natural operation begins from the agent but ends in the object sought, just as heating moves from the fire into the wood. Intellectual [operation]...

<summary>Ficino argues that God creates and governs the universe through an "intellectual nature" rather than blind necessity. He posits that since God is the First Cause, all effects (substances) exist within Him in a more perfect, unified way as His own essence, allowing Him to master the variety and degrees of creation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the Divine Mind. Having established that God knows all things through His own essence, Ficino now explains how God can contain the "Blueprints" (Ideas) of all diverse things without losing His perfect simplicity. He then transitions to arguing that God creates not by a blind necessity of nature, but through a combination of Intellect and Will.</meta>

<page-num>107</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK II.</header>

...lectual nature <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the nature of an intellectual agent.</note> or it retains both boundaries within the agent. Through this intellectual nature, God—while He is occupied with Himself in contemplating His own being—turns all external things in every direction. As Parmenides the Pythagorean says: "He rotates the moving orb of the world while He Himself remains motionless." Furthermore, it is necessary for God to be utterly uniform <term>meaning "of one form" or simple</term>, because He exists above the forms of all things. Indeed, He is also all-formed <note>The original Latin "uniformem" here is likely a scribal or printer error for "omniformem" (all-formed), as the next sentence confirms.</note>, because He is the shaper of all things. Only an intellectual nature allows Him to be uniform and all-formed at the same time; for through this, the Form of God, by gazing upon itself, conceives of itself as the proper "blueprint" or reason for all forms.

For He sees within Himself whatever is proper to each thing, while He discerns to what degree any given thing is able to imitate the Divine Form, or in what way it falls short. For instance, while He understands His own form as a mode of life, but not of cognition, He conceives—so to speak—the form and "Idea" of plants. But when He understands it as a mode of cognition, yet not as the specific intelligence belonging to a rational being, He conceives the "Idea" of an animal, and others in the same manner. Indeed, in all things that happen not by chance, but by nature or by purpose, it is necessary that the end-goal of the impulse be the form of the finished work. The acting cause, however, does not direct its action toward a form through anything else other than a form remaining within itself. Nor does it direct itself toward specific forms in any other way than through either specific forms or specific reasons <term>ratios or blueprints</term> of forms conceived within itself. 

Since, therefore, the wonderful order of the world cannot consist of a chance devoid of order, it is necessary that in the intelligence of the Creator Himself there be a form, according to whose likeness the effect is produced. And since, in God’s purpose, the order of the universe is the most powerful thing, the primary "Idea" in His mind is the Idea of the universal order. However, the reason for the order and the whole cannot be possessed unless the specific reasons for all the parts from which the whole is constructed are also possessed. Just as an architect cannot conceive the appearance of a building unless he has conceived the specific reasons for its parts. Properly, therefore, the reasons for all things exist in God; nor do the species of things have their distinctness from any other source than from that which gives them their very existence. 

Nor is the Divine simplicity any less simple because of the multitude of Ideas, since through one form and one single gaze He contains them all. Nor is the Divine essence called an "Idea" insofar as it is simply essence, but insofar as it is the exemplar <term>the original model or pattern</term> of this or that species. Therefore, to the extent that many "reasons" are understood to come from one essence, to that extent they are called "many Ideas." These sorts of relations, by which the Ideas are multiplied, are not produced by the things themselves, but rather by the Divine intellect comparing its own essence to the things. Nor are these relations "real" (so to speak) in the same way as those by which the Persons of the Trinity are said to be distinguished, but rather they are "intellectual" relations. 

Under one Idea, many things are both known and made. Some things are even perceived through the Idea of others: for example, evil and privation are known through the Idea of the good and of "habit" <term>the presence of a quality</term>; and, as some think, matter is known through the Idea of form. The properties of a substance are also known through the Idea of the substance, while common qualities are designated by their own proper Ideas. In the same way, an Architect, through the form of the house itself, effects all the "accidents" <term>secondary features like size or shadows</term> which accompany the house from the beginning; but those things which happen to the house after it is already made—such as paintings and similar things—are arranged through other Ideas. But we have now discussed Ideas here at greater length than we intended, having seized the opportunity as if by chance. This, however—even if certain dogs bark otherwise—is the most certain opinion of our Plato and the Platonists. We have touched upon this above, and we shall declare it more extensively elsewhere.

***

Hitherto we have proved that the First Cause works His various effects through a manifold order of wisdom, rather than through the necessity of a naked and simple nature. We shall prove next, God willing, that He does not work His external effects through mere intelligence unless the assent of the **Will** is added; which was indeed the purpose of this discussion.

**The First Reason.** The First Cause directs all things through itself (as we shall show in what follows) toward the best end, through the straightest ways, in the most fitting manner. It cannot do this unless, through the intellect, it anticipates the end, discerns the paths, and measures the proportion that exists between the paths and the end; and again, through the **will**, approves the end and chooses such a path over others. Hence Plato, in the *Timaeus*, *Phaedo*, *Philebus*, and *Statesman*, detests those philosophers who refer the causes of natural things either to fortune or to the necessity of matter or nature. He himself considers natural things to be certain instruments of intelligence rather than the primary agents, and he everywhere reduces individual effects chiefly to the final, efficient, and formal causes. For this reason, if someone asks why the earth is round, he answers: because it participates in the Idea of roundness, according to whose likeness the Wisdom that is the "Artisan of the World" <note>original: "mundi artifex"</note> disposed the earth, because He judged and **willed** that it would be better for it to be so for the sake of the Good itself.

**The Second Reason.** What accompanies whatever exists, belongs to being insofar as it is being. What...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that God does not create out of a blind, mechanical necessity, but through an act of Intellect and Will. He transitions from discussing how God "sees" or "knows" the blueprints of creation to explaining why the "Will" is the specific faculty that brings things into existence.</meta>

<page-num>105</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...such a quality must be found in that which is the first being. For whatever exists has this nature: it seeks a good that is absent, and it rests most willingly in a good that is present. To be sure, nature without senses acts through a certain "inclination"; nature with senses acts through "appetite"; and an intellect acts through "will." Therefore, since God is (to speak in the Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripatetico more"; refers to the followers of Aristotle</note> manner) the first being, who could deny that the Divine Intellect—through the will—gladly embraces its own present good, which is the sum of all good? For just as He sees all true things within His own truth (which become true because He illuminates them), so too He wills all good things within His own goodness (which are born from His own expansion and become good as He perfects them). Any mind, however, produces works more through *willing* than through *seeing*. For by seeing, the mind folds forms inward; by willing, it unfolds them outward. By seeing, it looks toward the truth, which possesses its own purity; by willing, it reaches toward the good, which possesses its own "diffusion" <note>Ficino means that goodness naturally spreads itself and creates others</note>.

**The third reason.** The knowledge of the senses and the intellect, because it is something like an "imaginary" thing within creatures, produces no substantial effect except through "affection" (the stirrings of the heart or will), which seems to be something essential. Thus, the more intensely one’s being is moved by affection, the more powerfully one acts. This is shown in a certain way by the eye of the ostrich, which gazes most greedily and intently upon its egg <note>There was a common medieval belief that ostriches hatched their eggs simply by staring at them with intense heat and focus</note>. If God’s intelligence is more effective in creating than the ostrich’s gaze is in brooding—indeed, if it is of infinite efficacy (which is clear from the fact that He requires neither a subject, nor an instrument, nor time in creating)—we can conclude that the affection of the will is most powerful within the divine intelligence. Add to this that it must be most joyful, provided that the intelligence, which is most perfect and always focused upon an untainted and most perfect object, must be most sweet in every way.

**The fourth reason.** Where there is no will (which is the mind’s inclination toward the good), there is no pleasure of the mind (which is the expansion of the will into the good and the resting of the will in the good). If there is no pleasure there where the Good itself resides, then pleasure—which exists everywhere only by reason of the good—will exist nowhere. Therefore, in the Good itself, there is pleasure and will. If an affection of this kind is the beginning of generation in creatures, it is certainly the origin of creation in the Creator Himself.

**The fifth reason.** If all agents, whether acting according to nature or according to art, always order their works toward an "end" (that is, toward a good), and they achieve this by their own goodness, they receive this order of "hoping" from the first agent. Since that first agent is the Good itself, it is clear that He orders His works toward the best end. For if particular goods order individual things toward some good because they are good and because they are ordered by the Supreme Good, how much more will the Universal Good order all things toward the good—namely, toward the Universal Good? God, therefore, leads all things toward Himself as their end. For no end of divine action exists outside of God, since the end is located in the same order as that which acts toward the end; it is a certain good, and it moves the agent to act. But nothing is located in the same order as God, except God Himself. God does not serve a good that is foreign to Him. For the sum of all good never serves a particular good; moreover, God is not moved by anyone else. If God’s end is His very own goodness, then God, in His own way, desires and loves His goodness. But since God is intellectual and His goodness is intelligible, He loves it with an intellectual love. Love of this kind resides in the will. Therefore, God wills Himself. I say He wills Himself as the end of Himself and of all things. Furthermore, from the willing of the "end" comes the operation regarding those things that are directed toward that end. For this reason, the Divine Will (as Plato says in the *Timaeus*) is the beginning of all creatures. The same is read very frequently in the works of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurium Trismegistum"; the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note>. For they think that the principle of the universe ought to have the most perfect mode of action; that is, that He should be the absolute Lord of the act of making through His will, just as He is the absolute Lord of the things made—a Lord, I say, disposing things by free will. For if He acted by the necessity of either nature or intelligence, He would act upon all things at once and upon infinite things at once; He would also coerce each thing and snatch them away in an instant.

-> *The will of God is at once necessary and free, and He acts freely.* <-
-> Chapter XII. <-

I believe it has been sufficiently proven that God procreates individual things not by a necessity of nature or intelligence, but by the command of His will. However, I believe it must now be demonstrated how His will is simultaneously necessary and free.

**The first reason.** Let everyone beware most diligently, lest by chance they fall into such rash impiety...

# DE IMMORTAL. ANIMOR. LIB. II.
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.

...falls into the error of suspecting that God exists or operates by chance. If nothing in the natural world ever happens by chance—for instance, it does not happen by chance that fire is hot and provides heat, but rather it *must* be so—and if it is natural for the highest being to exist and the highest activity to act, it follows that God, who is the highest being (and even more than being) and the highest activity, in no way exists or acts according to chance. Where there is more reason, there is less chance; in God, who is supreme reason or the very fountain of reason, nothing fortuitous can be imagined. If chance does not produce reason—since it is the opposite of reason, or rather the lack or defect of reason—how could it produce either God or any divine action that is superior to all reason? If God is that very rule which orders all things so perfectly that He removes all chance from the things that follow closely after Him, how could it be that He Himself exists or operates by chance? Therefore, God does not exist and act by mere chance—otherwise no order would ever be found anywhere—but as was fitting, or rather, as is fitting. It is fitting because it is beautiful. Indeed, Beauty <note>original: "decor"; refers to the aesthetic and moral fitness of the divine order</note> itself is God, from whom and through whom all fitting things are made. Rather, He acts as is necessary. I say "necessary" by way of Necessity itself. For God is Necessity itself, through whom all other things that are necessary possess their necessity. Therefore, God is as He is. He acts as He acts. And since no necessity stands above His necessity, there resides the highest liberty. Liberty is desirable as a good. In the highest goodness, however, is found whatever can ever be desired as a good. He is free who lives as he wills. Above all others, Goodness itself lives as it wills; every will desires the life of Goodness, and no will desires anything except through it. God is what He is in such a way that He could not have been anything else (because He is, so to speak, all being and all power); indeed, He would not even have *willed* to be otherwise, because He is all good. To be able or to will to be otherwise would be a sign of weakness and foolishness, falling toward the worse, or rather, into nothingness.

**The second reason.** If the impulse toward the good in individuals is the most necessary and the most voluntary and spontaneous thing of all, then certainly in the Good itself the highest necessity of nature concurs with the highest freedom of will, as we have proved elsewhere. There, the necessity of nature confirms the freedom of the will, and freedom agrees with necessity, to the point that God is necessarily free and voluntary, and voluntarily necessary.

**The third reason.** As long as a thing lacks the good itself, it is dissatisfied with itself and seeks something else beyond itself. But when it becomes a participant in the good, it is pleased with itself and wills itself; it is now as it wants to be. The more it attains this, the more it pleases itself, and the more it is as it perhaps wills itself to be. Therefore, the Good itself has this primary characteristic: it wills itself most intensely, is pleased with itself, and is exactly as it wills itself to be.

**The fourth reason.** If things are less "slavish" and more "their own masters" <term>sui iuris; a legal term meaning independent or having full legal capacity</term> the closer they approach God, then God is the ultimate master of Himself. Not only does He will to be as He is by His own nature, but He is entirely as He wills to be. Furthermore, He does whatever He wills, and for the sake of whatever He wills. No agent anywhere would be the free principle of its own action or set the end for its action unless the Principle and End of the universe were the Master of His own action and had established the end for His own activity. But let us return to the point.

**The fifth reason.** In those things where these three—namely, *being*, *understanding*, and *willing*—actually differ from one another, there is no absolute freedom. In such things, the manner of willing follows the rule of understanding, understanding follows the condition of being, and finally, being follows the one who gave it being. But in God, being, understanding, and willing are one and the same thing. Therefore, through His will, He is so much the master of His own intelligence and essence that He not only wills to be as He is and as He is understood by His own nature, but He also understands and exists exactly as He wills. For this reason, perhaps, the followers of Zoroaster <note>Ficino often cites "Zoroaster" as a source of ancient wisdom, or "Prisca Theologia," often conflating him with Neoplatonic ideas</note> claim that God, in a certain sense, "acts" Himself. Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who was Ficino’s primary philosophical inspiration</note> explained this in roughly the following way: God is an act, not of another, nor concerning another, but of Himself and concerning Himself. For He is an act remaining within Himself. Since this act is infinitely fertile because of the nature of infinite good, He does not lack an "acted" thing—that is, something generated—specifically an infinite "acted" thing. But since God alone is infinite, both through His inward act and by Himself, that which is "acted" (generated) there within God is God Himself. God is a watchful and perpetual act, from Himself, in Himself, and entirely concerning Himself. Therefore, just as He acts and is watchful, so exactly does He exist. The entire thrust of the divine act turns around itself. While He rests upon Himself, He "acts" Himself in a certain way—that is, He begets Himself—because if He looked elsewhere, He would lose Himself. Therefore, the divine being

He concludes by citing Plotinus to explain that God is a perpetual activity that "begets" Himself through His own infinite goodness.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.

...divine, it is an act toward Himself, whereas not to be divine would be an act toward another. God wills Himself. For Him, to will, to act, and even to be are entirely the same. Therefore, by willing Himself, He acts upon Himself—that is, He produces Himself, or rather, He establishes or marks Himself in being. From this, **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired</note> wants it concluded that God does not exist by some chance occurrence, or because necessity forced Him, but exists as He Himself is vigilant, active, and willing. But let God Himself see to these matters; for our part, we wish only to affirm everywhere what is worthy of God—such as what we proposed before: namely, that in God, the highest necessity meets the highest freedom.

**The Sixth Reason.** Divine goodness alone is the absolute object of the divine mind. For any power can be equal to its object, but it can never exceed it. There is nothing outside of God that God cannot exceed. However, God wills Himself by a certain absolute necessity of the will. For all things necessarily will their own ultimate end. Divine goodness is the ultimate end of God, for the sake of which He wills whatever He wills. Either we must admit that God wills nothing and is devoid of all "taste" <note>original: "gustus"; here meaning the experiential "savor" or appreciation of goodness</note>—which is absurd—or we must affirm that if He wills anything, He necessarily wills Himself, especially since in God, being and willing are the same. By willing Himself, He wills all other things; as they exist in God, they are God Himself; as they flow from God, they are images of the divine countenance, and are directed toward the divine goodness to reflect and confirm it as if toward their chief end. Yet, that act of divine will, which is absolutely necessary regarding divine goodness, is called by some "not absolutely necessary" regarding creatures. For although the will necessarily wills the end itself, it wills the things directed toward that end by a conditional necessity—or even sometimes by no necessity at all, if the end can be possessed without those specific things. And divine goodness does not need creatures.

**The Seventh Reason.** This is supported by the fact that God, in willing His own goodness, wills other goods only as images of it. Since divine goodness is immeasurable, countless images can be shaped according to its model—countless, I say, beyond those that are formed in these current ages. Therefore, if He necessarily willed every individual thing that could imitate His goodness simply because He wills His own goodness, He would certainly have to will the existence of infinite creatures representing divine goodness in infinite ways. If He willed it, they would certainly exist. But in this matter, one should remember the view of our **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, the "splendor of Theology." Although an act of the divine will can be said to be necessary based on a condition or a position—for instance, after He has once willed a thing, since the divine will is as immutable as His essence—nevertheless, by its own nature, that act does not have the same relationship of absolute necessity toward its effects as it has toward Himself.

**The Eighth Reason.** If God is the perfect cause of **being** <term>ens: a technical term for existence in its most general sense</term>, and being is the proper effect of God, then God's act can extend at least as far as the potential of being can extend—especially since passive potential must be led by a higher act. Within this potential of being is contained everything that does not contradict the logic of being, just as within the potential of bodily nature lies everything that does not take away that bodily nature. Nothing can be imagined that is repugnant to the logic of being, except its opposite—that is, what is called "non-being." Contradiction <note>original: "contractio"; likely a typo in the original Latin for "contradictio" given the context</note> alone includes the logic of non-being. Therefore, whatever includes no contradiction—as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about while debating</note> believe—is included within the potential of being, and God can bring all those things to pass. This is confirmed by the fact that the mind, excluding contradiction, can stretch itself through the entire, even immense, breadth of being. The creative power of God should not be less wide than the mind's ability to conceive. Furthermore, if the divine intellect perceives countless goods, and His will can turn toward everything the intellect offers as good, it follows that God's will is not bound to finite objects; thus His power extends to the infinite. Why mention this? So that you may understand that whatever does not include a contradiction is subject to divine power. And since there are many things not found in the nature of things which, if they existed, would introduce no contradiction (as is especially clear regarding the number, size, and distances of the stars), you should know that many things are contained under divine power which are never found in the order of things. Since God does some of the things He is able to do and does not do others, He works such things not by any necessity of nature, intellect, or will, but by the free choice of the will.

**The Ninth Reason.** Not without justice should God be said to operate by a certain choice (so to speak).

<summary>Ficino argues that while God necessarily wills His own goodness, His creation of the world is a free act rather than a forced necessity. He integrates the views of Plotinus and Thomas Aquinas to show that God's power extends to everything logically possible, though He chooses which possibilities to realize.</summary>
