# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.

Since indeed all agents, whatever they may be, that act through something else and are led to perform their work, must be traced back to a **first agent** <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, the "First Agent" or "First Mover" is God, the ultimate source of all movement and action in the universe</note>, which acts through itself in such a way that it leads itself to act—that is, so that it turns itself entirely toward its own action. It follows, then, that this agent understands and wills to work, or not to work, and again to work in this way or in another. No one is ignorant of the fact that those things which proceed from God in this manner proceed by free choice. Yet no wise person is unaware that in God, this choice does not differ from His very essence. 

But lest anyone should perhaps think that the divine will, if it looks toward created things, inflicts violence upon individuals, one must remember that the will of God <note>original: "male," likely a transcription error for "malle" or "magis"</note> prefers the good of the whole universe more than the apparent convenience of any small part. For in that universal good, the image of divine goodness shines more clearly, and that good seems to consist in a certain order. An exact order, however, requires that all levels of things be contained within the universe, so that some causes are stable and others are mobile; and those that are mobile produce effects that are, in addition, more wandering and occur in a certain variable way. For the effect of proximate causes <note>The immediate or "nearby" causes in a chain of events</note> seems to imitate the manner of those causes rather than the remote ones. 

God, however, wills not only that things themselves exist, but also the modes of being which are required for them as a consequence. Since it is appropriate for certain things, according to the mode of their nature, to be in some way **contingent** <term>Contingency: The quality of being able to happen or not happen, or to be different than it is; the opposite of necessity</term>, God chooses for something (as certain theologians say) to happen in a way according to contingency. Yet nothing deviates so much that it disturbs the order of the universe or escapes the providence of the One who ordered it.

<margin>God loves and provides. Chapter 13.</margin>

IF God is pleased with Himself, and if He loves Himself, He surely loves His own images and His works. A craftsman loves the works he has made from external material. A parent loves a son much more, whom he has generated from his own internal matter—even though he first received that matter from elsewhere (while eating). God loves any of His works more ardently, since He did not receive His matter from elsewhere; rather, He who formed the work also created the matter itself. Thus, He alone is the cause of the entire work. 

If God loves His works to such a degree, He wills good for them, and what He wills, He achieves. Therefore, He disposes them well, and by His supreme goodness, He disposes them in the best possible way. For just as the fertility and the inclination to act in all agents is born from the fertility of the First Agent, so the diligence in guarding one's works is inserted into each thing by the "first diligence" of the First Agent, who is the manager of all things as if they were His children. The greater the fertility in Him compared to others, the more diligent is His providence. 

Again, God does all things for His own sake. If He acted for any end other than Himself, God's action would depend on that end; therefore, the will to act would depend on it, and consequently God Himself would depend on it, since God and God's will are the same. If He makes all things for His own end, and He Himself is the highest good, He disposes all things toward the good (as **Plato** wishes in the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue where Plato describes the creation of the world by a benevolent Craftsman or "Demiurge"</note>), so that each individual thing, according to its nature, may receive divine goodness. 

Furthermore, since all things desire the "good," and the desire for the good is itself good—and therefore comes from the First Good itself, from which all good things come—it follows that, enticed by divine goodness, all things desire that same divine goodness. Who, then, would deny that God governs things, when they are directed toward a good end? How would the elements and members of the world—which by their nature are contraries, fighting amongst themselves in form and power—come together into one? How could they remain joined to each other for so long and exchange their natures and motions with each other, unless they were connected by some more excellent power? 

Moreover, if the government of the world were left to these members that are contrary to one another, they would remain balanced by their own weights and separated in their places; they would not mix. And even if they were mixed, they would do nothing other than be hot, cold, dry, moist, arid, or dense, and other things of that kind. They would establish no order of forms, figures, or revolutions. For indeed, even in the arts, the material does not create this kind of order, nor do the tools; only the thought of the craftsman does. And if the heavens in some way rule the elements, they do not rule so much that they themselves are not ruled from elsewhere. For such a great diversity of forms, powers, and motions in the heavens is directed into a single stable order, not by the celestial bodies themselves (which are diverse and mobile by nature), but by a superior power that is entirely self-sufficient and stable. 

Finally, a natural agent—whether it be elemental or celestial—is always dependent on something else, both because it is mobile (and therefore needy and imperfect) and because it acts by the necessity of its nature, acting with its whole self in whatever it does. Therefore, it receives from a certain celestial ruler a measure and a mode of acting through certain degrees suitable to a certain end. For heat, whether according to form or according to power, simply everywhere and altogether...

<summary>Ficino argues that God, as the First Agent, governs the universe through a combination of absolute necessity and free choice, ensuring that even contingent events serve the universal good. He emphasizes that God's providence is an act of love for His creation, analogous to a craftsman's love for his work or a parent's love for a child.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.

...and completely dissolves it, while the cold, in truth, condenses it. Therefore, that it should dissolve the one so usefully and suitably, just as it condenses the other by a similar logic, and that they do this continuously and in the most orderly fashion, they receive not from simple nature, nor from chance, but from a supernal cause. And because the spheres, by their continuous motion, are constantly departing from their present state and do not rest in themselves, they both exist and are moved by another, in whom the end resides, for whose sake they are moved and act; for indeed, the end necessarily precedes the motions toward that end by a certain intention. Hence Aristotle says in his books on divine matters <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, specifically Book XII, where he discusses the "Unmoved Mover"</note>: "Just as the order of the parts of an army toward each other and toward the whole proceeds from the order of the whole toward one leader, so the order of the parts of the world toward each other and toward the whole depends on the order of the whole toward God." From this he concludes that just as the order of the army is in its leader, so the order of the whole world is in God, the one and only prince of the world. 

Furthermore, the parts of the world and any small bodies proceed toward a certain end through a most orderly path and in the most suitable ways—or for the most part so proceed—that they very often carry out their works as well as they possibly can, just as if they possessed an art within them, and indeed a most perfect art. In fact, they advance by such a marvelous logic that they would surpass human art and reason. And since these bodies are themselves ignorant of their own motion, and therefore do not know how to prescribe for themselves the end toward which they tend—not by chance, but by necessity—yet nevertheless have that end prescribed (otherwise they would not act toward this end more than any other), it is certain that the end is prescribed for them by another, an end which they seek, and by whose wisdom they are led to that end, just as arrows are directed to a target by the skill of an archer. 

Where is this wisdom? If it is in the highest God, then God provides for things, since He reconciles conflicting things with each other so that they do not destroy one another in turn, and leads all things toward the best ends. But if it is in any other angelic mind or soul below God, know that God moves all things that are below Him. Therefore, if an angelic mind or a certain soul rules the world and leads it toward the good, it certainly does so both led by God and by the power of God. For this reason, God is the first and highest ruler, who can provide for all things, if He can make all things through intellect; since it is more excellent to make through intelligence than to consider and preserve things already made. He also knows how to rule all things, if He was not ignorant of how to make them. Finally, He wishes to govern and guard what is His own—those things He Himself made—to which He does not begrudge the gifts of well-being, after He did not begrudge them the gift of being. 

Moreover, He governs each thing with a marvelous ease. For He does not handle foreign materials which He received from elsewhere, but His own, which He makes Himself. Nor does He touch them from the outside, but stirs them from within. For He is present in the innermost parts of all things. Nor does He labor over many things, but through His very being, which is the universal hinge <note>original: "cardo," meaning a pivot or essential point upon which everything turns</note> of all things, He turns the hinges that follow: that is, essence, life, mind, soul, nature, and matter. And (as a Platonist would say) through the hinge proper to each order, He turns that order itself; that is, through one essence, all essences; through one life, all lives; through one mind, all minds; through one soul likewise, individual souls; through nature, natures; and through matter, materials. Nothing resists His decree, because He surpasses all things by an immense interval. Concerning the divine nature, Orpheus sang: 
"turning a swift current on a perpetual hinge" <note>original Greek: ἀγνάῳ στροφάλιγγι θοὸν ῥῦμα δινεύεσκ</note>. 

It has been discovered that in an animal there is a certain nerve near the nape of the neck <term>nucha: a medieval anatomical term for the back of the neck or the spinal marrow</term>; those who pull it move all the limbs of the animal together in such a way that each part is moved by its own proper motions. Aristotle writes in his book *On the World* that the members of the world are moved by God by a similar kind of touch. There he asserts providence most clearly. He also signifies this in the tenth book of his *Ethics* and in his *Physics*, where he proves that nature everywhere looks toward a certain and optimal end, and that its works are the works of an intelligence that does not err.

In Florence, we saw a mechanical shrine <note>original: "tabernaculum," here referring to a complex mechanical display or clockwork cabinet</note> made by a German craftsman, in which the statues of various animals, connected and balanced by a single ball, were moved simultaneously by different motions through the movement of that ball itself. Some ran to the right, others to the left, up and down; some rose from a sitting position, others leaned down from a standing one; some were crowning others, while some were wounding others. The sounds of trumpets and horns, as well as the songs of birds, were heard, and many other things happened there at once, and many similar things followed in just one moment from a single ball. Thus God, through His very being (which in reality is the same as His understanding and willing, and which is a certain most simple center of all things, from which, as we have said elsewhere, all other things are drawn out like lines), vibrates whatever depends on Him with the easiest nod of His will. Let Lucretius the Epicurean <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, a Roman poet who argued the world was formed by the random collision of atoms</note> be silent, then, who wants the world to be made and moved by chance, and who [deprives it] of the constant state of a most beautiful order...

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK II.
H
<meta>catchword: for such</meta>

...[Lucretius] thinks that a stable state proceeds from an unstable and shapeless lack of order, as if one were to believe that wisdom is born from foolishness, and light from darkness. Or you, Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), the Roman poet whose work *On the Nature of Things* argued that the world was formed by the random collision of atoms without divine intervention.</note>, every time you are moved by chance without a plan, a purpose, or a mind, do you always proceed by a single straight path to one and the same certain destination? Not at all; rather, you wander here and there. Or when you handle stones without any technical skill <term>ars: here meaning "craftsmanship" or "applied knowledge"</term> or a prescribed goal, do you then construct a building with perfectly ordered walls woven together, beautiful to look at and most convenient to use? Not at all; instead, you create a shapeless and useless heap. 

Consider plants and animals, whose individual members are so arranged that one is placed for the sake of another, and one serves the other. Certainly, if even one part is removed, the entire structure is almost dissolved. Finally, all the limbs are arranged for the sake of the whole composite being, and the composite itself—that is, the plant and the animal—is equipped with suitable instruments for the necessary works of its own nature. Food, habitats, and seasons are provided for all; the earth and water prepare elements for these, and the heavens temper the water and the earth. 

At last, all parts of the world converge toward a single beauty of the whole world in such a way that nothing can be taken away and nothing added. If you were to provide for trees and animals with all your planning, would you have provided differently? Not differently, and yet not as well. Therefore, a Plan better than your plan arranges these things. Otherwise, you would see every day that many of their members as well as their instruments were missing everywhere; likewise, dogs would be born from the seed of a horse, figs from apples, and human limbs would be joined to lions or the limbs of donkeys to humans; stars would fall, and stones would rise. 

But now, because the individual parts of the world, born from certain seeds, endowed with distinct shapes, seek and return to certain goals by a straight path, at fitting times and in the most beautiful and convenient orders, it follows that they are moved in the same way as those things which are moved by human skill and planning. If they are moved in the same way, then it is by almost the same skill and the same plan—and by one so much more excellent as they are more beautifully and stably ordered. By a plan, I say, that is not hesitant or shifting, but completely certain and immediate, acting by intuition <term>intuitus: a direct, instant "seeing" of the truth or the goal, as opposed to "discursive" reasoning step-by-step</term> rather than by a long chain of reasoning. For if there is no delay in the work, nor any transgression or retraction anywhere, there is no ambiguity in the maker. 

We call an intuition of this kind a "plan" by a certain metaphor—not because some things are investigated from others in that Mind, but because some things are made for the sake of others. Idle men are accustomed to debate about their crafts; but he who perfectly masters a skill no longer debates anything, but acts by habit, just as nature acts by forms. If most perfect skill exists anywhere, it is certainly there from which this wonderful work of the world is arranged. 

Perhaps you will place skill of this kind in a "nature" that is devoid of all feeling. But I will say that you yourself lack feeling if you are so alienated from sense that you do not perceive this: if even the smallest earthly beasts have feeling, it is much more necessary for the whole world and the Nature that is the maker of all things to have feeling—a rational feeling, I say, if she orders her works more rationally than human reason does. 

Daily habit, however, diminishes our wonder. But if your parents had raised you from infancy in a house closed on all sides, so that you had not seen this wonderful beauty of the world before your thirtieth year, and then the house were suddenly opened and it was shown to you, you would undoubtedly have wondered at the new spectacle of these things to such an extent that, although you were previously doubtful, you could never doubt afterward that all things are made and governed by the providence of a single most wise craftsman. 

Therefore, we must admit, Lucretius, that since the parts and effects of the world proceed in a constant order, the whole world itself cannot proceed now, or have come forth from the beginning, without constancy and order. Let us admit, finally, that the world is neither moved by its own accord without life, nor has it turned so equally for so long without a most powerful life, nor with such order without a most wise mind, nor so excellently and conveniently without the highest good. Rather, a certain single life, the queen of the single mundane body, excelling in power, wisdom, and goodness, leads the world most providently from the beginning and continually toward the best. This is either the highest God, or the handmaiden of the highest God <note>This likely refers to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, which Ficino describes as the intermediary through which God governs the physical realm.</note>. If it is the highest God, God certainly provides. If it is God’s handmaiden, God still provides, since the first principle acts and moves all things for His own sake. Orpheus spoke divinely concerning Jove:

> God is the beginning of all, and the end of all. <note>original Greek: "πάντων μὲν θεὸς ἀρχὴ πάντων, πάντων τε τελευτή"</note>

That is, he is the parent, beginning, and end of all things. Therefore, if the life of the world provides, having surely been led by God, it provides toward the end intended by God; thus, finally, all things are directed toward the goodness of God. And since this goodness has care for its whole work, it certainly neglects no parts. For from the individual parts...

<summary>Ficino argues that the intricate, functional order of plants, animals, and the cosmos proves they were designed by a divine Mind. He uses a thought experiment about a man seeing the world for the first time to illustrate that only habit prevents us from seeing nature as a product of supreme providence.</summary>
<keywords>divine providence, Lucretius, argument from design, teleology, World Soul, Orpheus, craftsmanship, cosmic order</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s argument for divine design over random chance. Having used the analogy of a building to mock Lucretius's materialism on the previous page, Ficino now transitions to explaining how the "Providence" (divine foresight and care) of God maintains the order of the entire universe while simultaneously preserving the free will of the human soul.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
### BOOK II.

For from these things consists the best state and condition of the whole composite. Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek figure viewed by Renaissance thinkers as a primary theologian who anticipated Christian truths.</note> expressed this whole idea thus:

-> You see all things, you hear all things, and you govern all things. <- 
<note>Original Greek: "πάντ’ ἐσορᾶς, καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούεις πάντα βραβεύεις"</note>

That is, you look into all things within, you hear all things within, and you distribute all things. Since indeed the whole structure of the world was established for the sake of reflecting the grace of divine goodness, and the parts of the world were joined together for the sake of that very structure, one should not demand absolute perfection in every single part of this work, but rather as much as suffices to indicate the higher perfection of its author according to its capacities. Nor should one demand every possible perfection in any given part of the world, but only that which harmonizes with the other parts and benefits the whole. Thus, although at times some condition of a particular small part of the world might seem blameworthy in itself, yet if it is compared to the state of the whole, we will find that the world could not be well-arranged in any other way than this. Truly, the founder of the universe refers the whole not to any individual parts, but rather the parts to the whole. Deservedly, therefore, things which in some places regarding the parts seem either evil or deformed, ultimately turn out for the ornament and good of the whole. For this reason, in the works of Orpheus, God is called:

-> Eternal life and immortal providence. <- 
<note>Original Greek: "ἀίδιος ζωὴ, καὶ ἀθανάτη πρόνοια"</note>

Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian sage whom Ficino believed was a contemporary of Moses.</note> says that this providence is the guardian of the human race; and Plato, in the fourth book of *The Laws*, says that God contains the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of all things, surrounding all and rightly arranging each one. He is favorable to gentle and religious men, but punishes the proud and the impious. Nor does Plato think that the freedom of our choice <term>arbitrij libertatem: also known as "free will"</term> is removed by divine providence; rather, he thinks it is preserved. He reveals this in the tenth book of the *Republic*, also in the book *On Kingship*, and in the *Critias*, because God does not act so much by knowing as by willing. Otherwise, He would have made and would be making all things at once, and He would also be the maker of evils. 

Likewise, just as the future outcomes of things are written in the foreknowledge of God, so also are the causes of those outcomes and their modes of acting. And just as our works are known to God, so too is our will, which is the cause of our works and our free mode of acting. For just as He foresees that you will do a certain thing, so He foresees that you will do it in such a way—that is, voluntarily and freely. Therefore, if divine foresight makes our works necessary by establishing a certain condition, it likewise makes necessary—that is, confirms—our mode of acting, which is the freedom of our judgment. Since God, the regulator of all natures, preserves for each thing the nature He had given it and does not take it away. Thus, while He rules all things, He rules each thing according to its own nature: as elements rise, He leads them to their ascent; as they fall, He leads them to their descent. If He rules the motion of animals, because that motion is destined to proceed by its own nature, He contributes to their walking. If He leads the heavens, because they are naturally rotatable due to their roundness, He contributes to the path of their circuit. If He strikes <note>Ficino uses "pulsat" (strikes/beats) to describe how God influences the soul, like a musician striking a string.</note> the souls—because they are freely rotatable upward and downward—He strikes them freely as well, so that He allures them, rather than dragging or forcing them, but instead persuades them. Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet; like Orpheus, Ficino viewed him as part of the "Ancient Theology" (*prisca theologia*) leading toward Plato.</note> testifies to this thus:

-> The Father does not instill fear, but pours forth persuasion. <- 
<note>Original Greek: "πατὴρ οὐ φόβον ἐμβράσκει, πειθὼ δ’ ἐπιχέει."</note>

But because the first mover must prevail and dominate, He therefore so constrains souls toward the good (as Plato wishes) that they cannot *not* want the good itself. For all things necessarily want the good; it is for the sake of the good that they want whatever they want, just as they necessarily do not want evil itself, for which reason they reject whatever they reject. For if the proper object of appetite is the good itself, certainly goodness is the very reason for the appetite to desire whatever it desires; just as in every color, the sight sees nothing but the light. And if it should desire to desire nothing further, it chooses this very vacation from desiring as something good. The soul, therefore, is necessarily carried toward the good. But because God must reserve for the soul its own proper nature, He therefore leaves to it a free judgment through which it may deliberate on what is to be done in its own way, and from many things proposed to it, judge one better than another, and choose what it has deemed more fit for attaining the good.

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe’s perfection lies in the harmony of its parts rather than in any single part, and that God’s providence governs the world through persuasion and the preservation of natural laws, specifically upholding human free will by directing the soul toward the "Good" without using force.</summary>

<keywords>Providence, Divine Goodness, Free Will, Orpheus, Plato, Zoroaster, The Good, Universal Harmony, Human Agency</keywords>

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY
## regarding the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
#### BOOK III.

->*The descent occurs through five levels, the same levels through which the ascent was made; these levels are appropriately compared to one another. Chapter I.*<-

We have ascended so far from the body into quality, from quality into the soul, from the soul into the angel, and from the angel into God—the one, the true, and the good, the author and ruler of all things. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, the ancient Greek philosopher who believed numbers were the essence of reality; Ficino often blends their math-based mysticism with Plato’s philosophy.</note> call the Body "the many"; Quality they call "many and one"; the Soul "one and many"; the Angel "one-many"; and finally God "one." They say this because the body is undetermined to any specific form and is by its very nature endlessly divisible; they say its matter would flow into infinity unless a form stopped it and unified it. Quality contributes to bounding matter within a specific form; it is, in a way, indivisible in its own nature, but becomes divisible through its mixture with the body. The Soul bounds matter with form, and is divisible neither in itself nor through the contamination of the body, but is a "moving multiplicity." The Angel <note>In Ficino's system, the "Angel" refers to the Angelic Mind or Pure Intellect, the level of reality just below God that contains the "Ideas" of all things.</note> is a vessel for all forms and is an "immobile multiplicity." God is an immobile unity above all forms. They say that God is entirely indissoluble in Himself, because He is unity and stability itself. Bodies, however, composed of elements, are entirely dissoluble because in them multiplicity exceeds unity, and motion exceeds stability. But angels, souls, the celestial spheres, and the stars appear to be dissoluble in a way, insofar as they have parts, yet they are nonetheless indissoluble because within them unity and stability outweigh multiplicity and motion. Here, then, is that divine knot <note>A concept from Plato’s dialogue "Timaeus," where the Creator binds the world together with a "knot" of mathematical and spiritual proportions that only He can untie.</note> by which God (as Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato’s "Timaeus."</note> believes) preserves these things—which are naturally dissoluble—as forever indissoluble.

The gift of unity and stability is so powerful that it only seems to be overcome by its opposites at the very lowest level of the universe. Yet even there it still conquers in a way, since it always guards matter itself—though subject to infinite multiplicity and change—keeping it permanent in its unity of substance and order. God is certainly unity, as we have proved. He is also immobile, because He is not moved by another (since nothing is more powerful than Him), nor by Himself, because He cannot move toward something better (since He is goodness itself). No one moves themselves toward something worse of their own accord. And if God were said to "flow" from one thing into another, we would ask whether He acquires anything new or nothing at all. If He acquires nothing new, He has not changed. If He acquires something new, He did not possess everything before. He who does not possess everything is not God. Because He is everywhere, He does not change place; because He is the end <note>The final goal or purpose.</note> of all things, He does not move toward anything else; because He is most simple, He is immobile even within Himself. For if He were moved within Himself, He would either move one part of Himself toward another, or at least gather some new things into Himself along with the old. He would be in substance what He was before, and would additionally put on a new form, and thus could not be "most simple." Finally, God is unity itself. Unity is the foundation of stability itself, because just as motion proceeds in multiplicity, so stability rests upon unity. For in any nature, that is said to "stand" which possesses one continuous state within itself so that it does not depart from the unity of its nature. Who would say that the foundation of all stability is changeable? We can confirm these reasons through that argument of Pythagorean number. Whatever, it says, changes according to past and future has a certain "privation" <note>In philosophy, a "privation" is the lack or absence of something that should be present. Change implies you "lack" what you are about to become.</note> mixed in; for the future is not yet, and the past is no longer. In God, however, since He is the first being and the highest act <term>Act (actus): In the philosophy of the time, "act" or "actuality" means something is fully realized and complete, having no "potential" left to fulfill; God is "pure act."</term>, there is no privation; He is therefore immutable. The Angel is also immobile, because he draws good through himself from God, the fountain of all goodness, without any intermediary; he is filled from there in a single point of eternity and always remains most full of goodness. Since every effect produced outside its cause preserves something of the cause and yet ends up lower than its cause, the angel—created closest to God—preserves something of God, but also loses something.

<summary>Ficino defines the five levels of existence (Body, Quality, Soul, Angel, God) and argues that God is absolute Unity and Stability. He explains that while the physical world is subject to change and decay, higher beings like souls and angels are preserved from dissolution by their proximity to God's unchanging nature.</summary>
<keywords>Great Chain of Being, five levels of reality, divine knot, stability, immutability, pure act, Timaeus, Pythagoras, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Book III, Chapter I, which defines the hierarchy of the universe. The previous page ended while describing the Angel as "immobi..."—completing here as "immobile multitude." The catchword for the next page is "corpus" (body).</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY
<meta>catchword: body.</meta>

God indeed possesses unity and stability; an angel cannot retain both. For if he did, he would be God himself, and not an angel. Nor does he lose both, lest the first and nearest work of God should turn out to be most unlike its maker. What then? Shall he retain unity alone, or stability? He cannot retain unity alone without stability, for unity itself is utterly immobile. Therefore, he will retain stability, but will fall away from simple unity, so that the angel is an **immobile multitude**. Nor do we assign multitude to the angel unjustly; for if he were a perfect and most absolute unity, he would be the highest and infinite power, since power consists in unity. Infinite power is God himself alone. Furthermore, if it is characteristic of a body to receive and to suffer <note>In this philosophical context, "to suffer" (passio) means to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note>, and characteristic of an incorporeal nature to give and to act, then in a corporeal nature there is said to be "power"—specifically, a power that is (as the theologians say) receptive and passive—while in an incorporeal nature there is **act**, that is, the efficacy for acting. For this reason, because **quality** is in a certain way incorporeal in itself, it sometimes possesses a force for acting, whence it is also named an "act." But because it is received and divided within matter, and thereby becomes in some sense corporeal, it is not "pure act," but is defiled by the "passion" (the being-acted-upon) of the body. It is established, therefore, that quality consists of both act and potentiality. <term>Act and Potentiality</term> <note>Scholastic terms: 'Act' (actus) refers to the full realization or presence of a thing's nature, while 'potentiality' (potentia) refers to its capacity to become something else or to be acted upon.</note> Now, although the **soul** is separable from matter, and is for that reason called an act and is foreign to the suffering of the body, it is nevertheless not yet "pure act," for it is mobile. If something is moved, it acquires through that motion what it previously lacked; insofar as it lacked it, it possesses that power which we call a receptive and, in a sense, passive potentiality. Insofar as it performs some action by moving, it is an act; and while it is acquiring something, it is also being made into an act.

The soul is therefore composed of potentiality and act. But is an angel "pure act"? Not at all. Clearly God is, because He is entirely distant from matter (in which there is passive potentiality without any power of acting); therefore He is understood to be pure vigor of acting, set apart from the nature of receiving and suffering. If God is pure act, an angel cannot be such, because that which is one in itself never becomes many except by the addition of a foreign nature. The nature and definition of pure act itself is unique, which is certainly in God, as is evident. But if it were also said to be in an angel, we would ask whether there is anything else in the angel besides "act," or not. If nothing, then only one "pure act" remains. Indeed, the act attributed to the angel would not differ from the act of God, since nothing would be in either except act, and act by its very definition is one. But if something is added to the angel besides act, the angel is no longer pure act, but is stained by a mixture; he is not "absolute act," but rather "this or that kind of act." Just as light which is green or red is not pure light, but is simultaneously light and some quality of the elements through which it becomes red or green. For this reason, the angel is also composed of act and potentiality. And this is what Plato means in the *Philebus*, where he says that God is the "limit" of all things, devoid of the infinite, but that all other things besides Him are composed of "limit" and "infinite." <note>Plato’s Philebus 23c-26d discusses the four kinds of being: Limit, the Unlimited, the Mixture, and the Cause.</note> He calls "act" the limit, and "potentiality" the infinite—which, being indeterminate in itself, is limited and formed by the act. But to come to the point: the potentiality of the angel is in his essence, which is in a certain sense made by God before it is formed by Him. For in the first moment of his creation, the angel simply *is*; in the next, he is illuminated by his author so that he may be intelligent and formed. Therefore, that essence is in the beginning in some way formless, and is set forth like a certain passive subject for the act of understanding and for receiving the adornment of forms and ideas. Concerning this, Zoroaster says:

> For the Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the second mind. <note>original Greek: "πάντα γὰρ ἐξετέλεσε πατὴρ, καὶ νῷ παρέδωκε δευτέρῳ." Ficino quotes the Chaldean Oracles, which he attributed to Zoroaster. The "second mind" refers to the Angelic Intellect.</note>

The angel is therefore a multitude, since he consists of many things. An **immobile multitude**, I say. In this he is certainly lower than God, because he is not true unity like God. In this he approaches God, because he is almost (if I may say so) immobile like God. Correcty, then, after God (immobile unity) is placed the angel (immobile multitude). After the angel is the soul, which is even further distant from God because it is a **mobile multitude**. It is indeed a multitude, since nothing after God can be the simplest unity. It is in a certain way mobile because, receding further from God, it becomes close to the qualities of bodies, which are entirely agitated. If it were entirely immobile, it would certainly be an angel; if it were entirely mobile, it would be a quality. However, there must be some middle ground between the angel and the qualities of bodies, lest it be entirely mobile. Its substance will stand firm, and will not change into more or less, or into this or that. However, its operation will flow, now this way, now that, acting in various and different ways. But quality is lower than the soul, since it is changed through both essence and operation. Lower than quality is the body.

<summary>Ficino defines the hierarchy of being by comparing God (pure act and immobile unity), Angels (immobile multitude), and Souls (mobile multitude). He argues that only God is "pure act," while all other beings, including angels and souls, are a mixture of act and potentiality.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV

H 3

<meta>catchword: who pro-</meta>

and is changed. **Body** is lower than **quality**. For quality both moves and is moved—since it moves bodies. The body is indeed moved, yet it moves nothing. <note>original: "Corpus mouet quidem, mouet nihil." In this context, Ficino likely means the body is the subject of motion but lacks the internal power to initiate motion in others.</note> An angel, for its part, does not possess its status as a single entity or as a pure **act** from itself, but from God, who is truly One and the most pure Act. However, the fact that an angel is a "multitude" (through its potential for receiving and undergoing change) comes from itself; for in being produced outside of God, it falls away from the perfection of its creator. Therefore, multitude is natural to the angel. 

Similarly, the **soul**, though it is a single substance and a stable act by its essence, does not obtain this from itself, but shares in it from God through a single and most stable act. Yet, that it is multiple and passive, it possesses from itself, because it is ranked below God. Finally, that it is mobile, it possesses from itself because it is ranked below the angel. Therefore, just as unity is natural to God and multitude to the angel, so **motion** is natural to the soul. 

The light of God produces the angel—specifically, under the shadow of God; the light of God produces the soul under the shadow of the angel. From the single act of God, the angel acquires stable unity, but under the shadow of God, it falls into multitude. Through the light of God, the soul attains its state; under the shadow of God, it attains multitude; and under the shadow of the angel, it attains change. God is the fountain of unity; the angel is the fountain of multitude; the soul is the fountain of motion. God is unity through Himself; the angel is one through God, but multiple through himself. The soul is one through God; through the shadow of God (that is, because it exists beneath God along with the angel), it is multiple; and through itself, it is mobile. 

**Quality**, through the higher levels, has the power to move something; through itself, it has the property of being mixed with matter. The **body**, through quality, has the power to act; through itself alone, it has only the capacity to suffer <note>To "suffer" (pati) here means to be the passive recipient of an action or change.</note>. Quality exceeds the body by one degree, because it moves the body; it yields to the soul by at least one degree, because it is moved by the soul. The soul exceeds quality by at least one degree, because it is moved from within itself; it yields to the angel by one degree, because it is subject to change. The angel exceeds the soul by one degree, because it remains stable; it yields to God by one degree, because it is multiple. Yet God, through this "One," surpasses all things into infinity. As Zoroaster sang:

-> The Father snatched himself away, <-
-> nor did he shut up his own fire even in the intellect that follows him. <-
<note>original Greek: "ἑαυτὸν ὁ πατὴρ ἥρπασεν / οὐδ’ ἐν δυνάμει μὲν νοερᾷ κλείσας ἴδιον πῦρ" — These are lines from the Chaldean Oracles, which Ficino attributed to the ancient sage Zoroaster.</note>

That is to say, the Father withdrew by His own power, and did not include His own fire (His essence) even within the Mind <note>The "Mind" or "Intellect" (mens) here refers to the Angelic tier of being.</note> that follows Him. It is as if he were to say: God has no comparison with the rest. 

The body is moved only by another, for it does nothing by its own nature. Quality moves another and is moved by another. The soul indeed moves another, but it is moved by itself. The angel moves other things (that is, it acts upon them) and is itself stable, but it is not stable through itself; for it stands by means of divine unity. For what else is "to stand" (as we have said) than to persevere in the unity of one’s own nature? It also moves through God. For by the power of the **First Act**, all agents do whatever they do. God moves and acts upon all things through Himself, being himself stable through Himself. 

Certainly, because all things that are "such-and-such" through another must be traced back to a "first something" that is "such-and-such" through itself, we have therefore referred all things that are stable and moving through another to God (who is stable through Himself and moving through Himself). And whatever things are mobile by another—namely, bodies and qualities—we have referred to the soul, which is mobile through itself. I say "mobile through itself" because if you descend from God through the angel, both God and the angel will appear stable to you, and the first thing you encounter that is mobile is the soul. 

Moreover, whatever is the "first" of its kind in any category is "such-and-such" through itself; for example, that which is first luminous or hot is bright or hot through its own nature. Thus, since the soul is the **first mobile** thing among all things that are mobile, it is certainly mobile through itself. A sign of this is that bodies lacking a soul are only moved by external impulse, while those that have a soul move of their own accord and in any direction. And since the soul grants to bodies the ability to be moved, in a certain way, toward any direction by themselves, it follows that the soul itself is truly and primarily mobile through itself. It is the **first mobile**, since through its presence there appears in the body a certain image of a self-moving faculty, and there is motion in every direction; this signifies that the soul is the fountain of motion, from which free and universal agitation flows forth. 

By these arguments, I believe that Pythagorean riddle used by Xenocrates is solved: namely, that "the soul is a self-moving number." <term>Self-moving number</term> <note>Xenocrates, a student of Plato, defined the soul this way. Ficino interprets "number" not as a literal digit, but as a "multiple nature."</note> "Number" means a multiple nature; "self-moving" means changeable by its own inherent property. Many things (as we have already indicated) declare to us that such a nature must exist somewhere. First, because everything that is "such" through another is reduced to something that is "such" through itself. Second, because since there are many things moved by another, if *all* things were such, we would either wander into infinity or revolve in the same circle (so that the first motor and the last would be the same, and cause and effect would be the same), and there would be no order in things. Therefore, we are compelled to arrive at some motor that is no longer moved by another. But that motor...

<summary>Ficino defines the soul as the "fountain of motion" and the "first mobile," situated between the stable Angel and the passive Body. He uses this hierarchy to explain Xenocrates' famous definition of the soul as a "self-moving number."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book IV concerning the soul as the "mean" or middle link in the hierarchy of existence. Having established that the soul possesses motion naturally (unlike the stable Angel or the inert Body), Ficino now provides four specific reasons why a self-moving soul is necessary to the structure of the universe and resolves a potential contradiction regarding whether the soul is moved by God or by itself.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

<page-num>118</page-num>

<meta>catchword: Souls</meta>

...[the soul], which most closely precedes bodies that are moved by another, is not altogether immobile. For since these two are far apart—that which is moved by another and that which is entirely stable—their middle point is that which is changeable by itself. Third, because if any thing is moved better the closer it is to the mover, and if the most perfect motion is to be reached, it is necessary that somewhere there exists something in which the essence of the moved and the mover is the same <note>Ficino is arguing that for motion to exist in the physical world, there must be a "Self-Mover" where the power to move and the capacity to be moved reside in one substance—the soul.</note>. Fourth, because if something is to be moved, it is necessary either for the mover to turn toward the thing being moved, or vice versa, or both in turn. 

Let us suppose, then, that only God, angels, and bodies exist in nature. The former [God and angels] do not approach the latter [bodies] because they are immutable; nor do the latter approach the former, because they are by their own nature inert. Therefore, there would be no motion at all in the world. Thus, there must be a certain nature that is spontaneously changeable, which by its own power approaches bodies to wake them from their lethargy; and being ever-wakeful itself, it experiences its own powers within itself before it exerts them upon the body. In this way, just as a bodily substance is produced by a spiritual substance, a bodily motion may be produced by a spiritual motion.

I believe <term>Plato</term><note>The 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher whose works Ficino translated and sought to reconcile with Christian theology.</note> understood this in the *Laws*, where he says: "If all things now stood still, and a little later something had to be moved, what would be moved first?" Clearly, that very thing which is agile toward motion by its own power, being closer to the virtue of moving, and whose motion the other things subject to motion would then follow. This he calls in the *Phaedrus* the "fountain and principle of motion." <note>original: "fontem & principium motionis"</note> It is the "fountain" because it has motion from within itself; it is the "principle" because it pours it out into others.

But here a doubt arises. If God and the angel move something, and the soul is in turn stirred by them, how then is it moved by itself? Let us respond in this manner: When <term>Apelles</term><note>A famous painter of ancient Greece, often used in Renaissance texts as the archetype of the artist-soul.</note> looked upon a meadow, he attempted to paint it with colors on a panel. The meadow, indeed, showed itself all at once, and suddenly ignited Apelles's desire. This kind of showing and igniting can be called an "act," since it does something, but it is by no means "motion," because it is not carried out step-by-step. For **motion** is an act running through moments of time. However, the acts of considering and painting that take place in Apelles are called "motion" because they are carried out little by little; for now he looks at one flower, now another, and he paints them in the same way. 

Certainly, the meadow causes Apelles's soul to see it and desire to paint it, but it does so all at once. But the fact that now one blade of grass is seen and now another, through different moments of time, and is expressed in the same way—this is not caused by the meadow itself, but by Apelles's soul. Its nature is such that it does not look upon or represent various things simultaneously, but gradually. Therefore, the beginning and the end of this motion (which is in the seeing and painting) is the meadow. For from there the painter’s consideration began, and toward the same point his desire tends. But the **fountain** through which such an act is done gradually and in time—and is called "motion"—is the soul of the painter himself. 

Similarly, among the Platonists, the rational soul contemplates or divines God and the angel in a kind of perpetual light, and it desires to paint itself in their likeness. Then, by forming itself little by little through speculation, morals, and action, it moves itself. This motion flows properly from the nature of the soul itself, as if from its own fountain of motion—that is, of temporal operation—yet it is incited by higher beings as if by an external beginning and end. The infusion that flows from higher beings into the soul is single, stable, sudden, and eternal; and as far as it is in itself, it also works similar things in the soul: namely, things that are sudden, stable, and eternal. 

However, the fact that the operations and works of the soul happen and change gradually through time proceeds from the soul's own nature, which is weaker than the higher beings. But take this whole matter by way of an example: The Sun has light from itself; it pours it in a single moment into **Mercury**. Mercury also receives all its light in a moment and remains thereafter completely full. The Sun pours the same light in a moment into the **Moon**. The Moon does not receive it in a moment, but over time. For as it turns toward the Sun in different ways at different times, so it receives light in different ways, and by its own nature it is varied by the succession of light. The Sun signifies God, Mercury signifies the angel, and the Moon signifies the soul. What I say about Mercury, understand to be said similarly of all the stars above the Moon. For just as those stars are related to the Sun, so are the angels related to God. But the soul alone stands in relation to God as the Moon does to the Sun. Therefore, nothing prevents the soul from descending from divine things and receiving divine things, and yet being moved by its own nature, so that it can always be moved and live.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is the necessary "Self-Mover" that bridges the gap between the eternal, unmoving divine and the inert physical body. He uses the analogy of a painter and the phases of the moon to explain how the soul receives eternal truths but processes them through time and gradual motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s hierarchy within the universe. In the previous section, Ficino argued that the soul must be a "self-mover" to bridge the gap between the unmoving divine and the inert physical world. Here, he formalizes the "five levels of nature" and defines the soul as the "third essence"—the indispensable bond that holds the cosmos together.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK III.

->*The soul is the middle level of things, and it connects all levels, both the higher and the lower, into one, while it both ascends to the heavens and descends to the depths.* Chapter 11.<-

But so that we may finally reach that which we desire, let us once again collect all things into five levels. We place God and the angel at the summit of nature, and body and quality <note>In this context, "quality" refers to the accidental properties of matter, like heat or color, which are less stable than the objects themselves.</note> at the bottom; but the soul we place in the middle between those highest and these lowest things. We rightly call this the "third and middle essence" in the Platonic manner, since it is the middle point for all things and the third from every direction. If you descend from God, you find the soul at the third level of descent. If you ascend from the body, you find it at the third level of ascent. We consider an essence of this kind to be absolutely necessary in nature. For the angel indeed, as the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Ficino refers to the tradition of Plato and his later followers like Plotinus, who viewed the universe as a series of descending levels of reality.</note> say, truly *is*—that is, it stands forever. Quality "becomes"—that is, it is moved at some time. Therefore, quality differs entirely from the angel, both because quality moves while the angel remains still, and because quality exists only at certain times while the angel is forever. Consequently, there is a need for a middle ground that agrees partly with the angel and partly with quality. What might that be? Is it something that *is* (meaning it remains stable within) only sometimes? No. For such a thing is not found; that which remains internal for any length of time—whether by itself or by its immediate state—remains so forever. Therefore, the middle will be that which *is* forever, but is also "becoming"—that is, it moves. Because it exists forever, it agrees with the angel; because it moves, it agrees with quality. From this it follows that there must be a third essence in the middle of these, which is always moving and living, and by its own motion diffuses life into bodies. 

It is rightly said by the Platonists that above that which exists in a part of time, there is that which exists through all time; above that, in turn, is that which exists through eternity; and finally, above that eternity stands the One. But between those things that are eternal alone, and those that are temporal alone, the soul exists as a kind of bond between both. Indeed, in this regard, the principal parts of the world-body are in some way similar. There are those who place the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the universe, believed by medieval thinkers to be the dwelling place of God and the angels.</note> as entirely immobile in eternity, while the other spheres are in eternity and time simultaneously, and finally composite things are in time alone. Similarly, they place pure intellects in the first level, but "animal" intellects <note>Intellects associated with living souls that animate bodies.</note> in the second, and finally bodily souls in the third.

But to return to our proposal: every work consisting of many parts is most perfect when it is so joined from its members that it becomes one thing throughout, consistent and harmonious with itself, and not easily scattered. Nature clearly demonstrates this in the temperament of the four elements, where earth and fire—which are far apart—are joined through air and water. Much more so must we find a connection of parts in the universal work of God, so that the work of the one God may also be one. God and body are the extremes in nature, and they do not bind to one another. Indeed, God is entirely uplifted; he neglects bodies. Rightly, the most perfect creature closest to God would be entirely divine and pass into God. Quality also does not connect the extremes, for it sinks toward the body and leaves the higher things behind; having left behind the incorporeal, it becomes corporeal. Up to this point, all things are extremes, and the higher and lower things flee from each other, lacking a fitting bond. 

But that third essence, placed between them, is of such a nature that it holds the higher things and does not desert the lower; and thus, in the soul, the highest things are linked with the lowest. For it is immobile, yet it is also mobile. On one side it agrees with the higher, on the other with the lower. If it agrees with both, it desires both. Therefore, by a certain natural instinct, it ascends to the heights and descends to the depths. And while it ascends, it does not desert the lower things; and while it descends, it does not leave the sublime. For if it were to desert either one, it would sink toward the other extreme, and it would no longer be a true bond for the world. Indeed, it does the same as the air between fire and water; air agrees with fire in heat, and with water in moisture. In the one direction, it is always hot with fire; in the other, it is moist with water. There it is thinned and becomes bright like fire; here, in turn, it grows dull like water. 

Nay, it does the same as the light of the Sun. For light descends from the Sun into fire and fills the fire, yet it does not desert the Sun. It always clings to the Sun, and always fills the fire. It perfects the air, and even though the air is tainted, the light is not tainted. Similarly, it is necessary for the third essence to cling to divine things and fill mortal things at the same time. While it clings to the divine, it is spiritually united to them, and because spiritual union produces knowledge, the soul "knows." While it fills bodies, moving them from within, it gives them life. It is therefore the mirror of divine things, the life of mortals, and the connection of both. But how is it joined to bodies? Does it perhaps touch one single point of a body when it enters it, and is thus said to be united to bodies? Not at all. For then it would be united to a point, not a body, and neither would the whole body—

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the soul must be both unified and present throughout the entire body to act as the "bond of the world." On the previous page, he established the soul as the middle level of existence.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...then it would vivify that body, but only a single point would live, with the rest of the body lacking life. Indeed, if it always remained gathered into one point, thus united to itself, it would be the same as an angel, which is far removed from the body. Or at the very least, it would cling to divine things in that way, while abandoning bodies altogether. Therefore, it is not joined to merely one point of the body, but to many, and thus it fills the parts of the body. 

But does it fill them in the same way that whiteness fills white flesh? Or in the way any quality fills its own matter? Not at all. For if it did, it would be the same as a quality, and having abandoned divine things, it would sink entirely into the body. Whiteness is in the whole of the flesh in such a way that it is extended and divided equally into many parts with the flesh; a part of the whiteness (according to the <term>Physicians</term> <note>original: "Physicos"; here meaning natural philosophers or scientists who study the physical world.</note>) is in a part of the flesh, and a larger part of the whiteness is in a larger part of the flesh, while a smaller part is in a smaller part. Thus, whiteness is made corporeal. That essence which we consider the "third" <note>The soul is the "third essence" because it sits in the middle of Ficino's five levels: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Body.</note> would suffer the same fate if it were spread into the body no differently than that quality; having been dragged to the other extreme of nature, it would cease to be the **bond of the world** <note>original: "copula mundi"; the soul’s role as the connective tissue of the universe.</note>. 

For this reason, when it enters the body, it is present as a whole in every individual particle of the body; it is neither divided nor pulled apart into any parts in order to stand by the parts of the body that are distant from one another. For it touches the body through an **indivisible power**, not through the breadth of physical size. Therefore, remaining whole and simple, it is present as a whole and indivisible to every individual part. Just as a voice and its meaning are, in a way, simultaneously in every part of a house, since the whole is heard and understood almost simultaneously in every single corner. 

Nor is it impossible for this essence—since it is an indivisible thing existing in itself—to be present as a whole to the vast mass of the body. Indeed, because it is both indivisible and not enclosed by a location, it can penetrate and encompass the whole of whatever is in that location. For the extension of physical size, wherever it is found, prevents such power and presence; thus, a thing extended by size cannot be as a whole in many places at once. Furthermore, even a thing that is indivisible but fixed to a physical size (like a point marked on a line as its boundary) cannot be as a whole throughout all parts of the body. Thus, a point designated somewhere on a line of a circle is neither in all the other lines, nor is it spread through the whole line or circle. 

However, the point that is the **center of the circle**, which belongs to no specific line, is found in a certain way in all the lines that are drawn from there to the circumference. And while no point marked on the circumference looks upon the whole circle equally, the center—which is not properly fixed to any part of the circumference—looks around at the entire circle equally. Therefore, a thing that is divisible cannot be as a whole in many places at once, nor can a thing that, though indivisible, has a fixed position in another divisible thing. 

But that "third essence" is neither extended (for then it would be a quality) nor is it located anywhere within extension (for it would not move freely by itself if it did not exist by itself). Therefore, it is like a point living within itself, and is entirely free from all size and location. Thus, it encompasses every location of the body equally, and when it enters the body—because it is not a point belonging to any specific size—it is not restricted to any one point of physical size. Indeed, since it is outside the category of size, it is not determined to touch any specific point of size, but is like the **center in all lines** and in the whole circle. 

From this it follows that this essence is both **divisible and indivisible** at the same time. 
*   **Divisible**, because through the division of the body it spreads its vital shadow, communicating itself to different parts of the body. 
*   **Indivisible**, because it stands present as a whole and simple. 
*   **Divisible**, I say, because its shadow is in the whole divisible body. 
*   **Indivisible**, because it is present as a whole in every part of the body in an indivisible manner. 
*   **Indivisible** again, because it has a stable and united substance. 
*   **Divisible**, because it is divided into many through its operation, as it works through motion and time. 
*   **Indivisible** thirdly, because it receives higher things, which are perfectly united. 
*   **Divisible**, because it declines toward lower things, which are greatly divided. 

Such a nature seems most necessary in the order of the world so that—after God and the angel, who are indivisible according to both time and dimension, and above the body and qualities, which are scattered by time and dimension—there may be a suitable middle ground. This middle is divided in a certain way by the passage of time, yet is not divided by physical dimension. Nor does it always remain gathered within its own nature like the higher things, nor is it torn into parts like the lower, but it is equally indivisible and divisible. This is that very essence which **Timaeus the Locrian** and **Plato** <note>Ficino refers to the *Timaeus*, a dialogue where Plato discusses the creation of the soul from "Same" (indivisible) and "Different" (divisible) components.</note> in their book on the world said consists of an indivisible and divisible nature. This is that which inserts itself into mortal things, and neither...

<summary>Ficino defines the soul as an "indivisible-divisible" essence that acts as the center of the body's circle, present everywhere at once without being physically spread out. This unique "middle" nature allows the soul to bridge the gap between eternal unity and material fragmentation.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK III.

->H 5<-

the soul itself would become mortal. For just as it inserts itself into the body as a whole, without being torn apart, so it also withdraws as a whole, not scattered. And because it governs bodies while also clinging to divine things, it is the mistress of bodies, not their mere companion. This is the greatest of miracles in nature. For other things under God are single individuals in themselves; this essence is all things at once. It possesses within itself the images of divine things upon which it depends, as well as the <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the formal blueprints or rational principles of physical things.</note> and models of lower things, which it also, in a certain way, produces. And since it is the middle point of all things, it possesses the powers of all. If this is so, it passes into all things. And because it is the true connection of all that exists, while it migrates into one thing, it does not desert another; rather, it migrates into each individual thing and always preserves them all together, so that it may rightly be called the center of nature, the middle of the universe, the chain of the world, the face of all things, and the **knot and bond of the world** <note>original: "nodusq; & copula mundi"; one of Ficino's most famous descriptions of the soul's role in the Great Chain of Being.</note>.

What the nature of this third essence is, we have (as I judge) said enough. However, that this is the proper seat of the rational soul is most easily seen from this: the definition of the rational soul is "life that understands through <term>discourse</term> <note>original: "discurrendo"; the process of reasoning step-by-step from one premise to another, distinguished from the instant intuition of angels.</note> and gives life to a body in time." This is the very same condition as that of the third essence. For it lives, it understands, and it provides life to the body. That it lives is apparent, since we say those things on earth are "alive" which are moved by their own internal power through every part—up, down, forward, backward, to the right, and to the left. Thus plants and animals are moved. Therefore, where there is an internal and shared movement, there is life. Life, I say, is the internal power of moving itself. A power of this kind is found especially where the fountain and origin of all agitation is, and the first movement. For internal and shared movement is greatest where it is the "first." Now, the first movement is placed in that third essence. Therefore, life is there—a life of such a kind that bodies live and move by participating in it. For by its nature, it is the closest life to bodies. Therefore, that third essence is the life that gives life to bodies.

It is also an understanding essence. Indeed, if movement is perfect anywhere, it is certainly most perfect where it is first. For no perfection descends into later movements unless it comes from the first. Therefore, the movement in the third essence is the most perfect of all motions. This is the motion which departs as little as possible from its source, which is joined most closely to its foundation, which is uniquely and supremely constant, and which is sufficient unto itself, imitating the most perfect shape. Such a motion is a **circuit** <note>original: "circuitus"; circular motion was considered the most perfect and eternal form of movement in Platonic and Aristotelian thought.</note>, as is clear to everyone, which alone among all motions is everlasting. Other motions reach some limit beyond which they cannot proceed, since there is no infinite space anywhere. But a circuit, as it repeats the same path once, so it seeks it a second, third, and fourth time by a similar logic; its end and its beginning are the same, and therefore when it seems to finish, it is then that it begins. 

Thus, an everlasting circuit is proper to the third essence, so that through movement it is reflected back into itself in a circle. It is fitting that if it moves from itself, it also moves into itself, so that some end of the motion is created where there was a beginning. Indeed, the cause of the motion itself produces the movement for its own sake. Therefore, that essence, beginning from itself, is perpetually revolved back into itself, unfolding its powers from the highest things through the middle to the lowest, and likewise folding the lowest things back through the middle to the highest. If this is so, it notices itself and what it possesses within. If it notices, it certainly knows. And it knows by understanding, as it recognizes its own spiritual essence, which is absolute and free from the limits of matter. For the knowledge of such things is called **intellection** <note>original: "intellectio"; the act of the intellect grasping a truth.</note>. 

In ourselves, we clearly see that knowledge is nothing other than a spiritual union with some spiritual form. Sight sees by being joined to the spiritual image of colors through its own spirit. But when joined to matter, it perceives nothing—which is obvious if someone places a solid body directly over the sharp point of the eye. Our mind also understands things by being united through spiritual power to the forms and reasons of physical things. Similarly, when the third essence (which is indeed spiritual) is joined to itself, it notices and understands itself in a spiritual way. It also understands divine things, to which it clings as closely as possible in a spiritual manner. It understands corporeal things as well, toward which it declines by its very nature. It knows, I say, by moving through time in discourse, since it is mobile through its operation. 

From all this, a certain definition of the third essence is gathered: namely, a life that gives life to bodies by its nature. It also knows itself, divine things, and natural things through discourse. Whoever cannot see that this is also the definition of the rational soul is himself lacking a rational soul. Therefore, the rational soul has its seat in the third essence, occupies the middle region of nature, and connects all things into one.

<summary>Ficino defines the rational soul as the "Third Essence," a metaphysical bridge that links the eternal divine realm with the physical world. He argues that the soul is the "bond of the world" (copula mundi) because it possesses the ability to move in an eternal cognitive circle, understanding both the highest spiritual truths and the lowest material forms.</summary>

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY
## on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
-> BOOK IV. <-

*There are three levels of rational souls: in the first is the Soul of the World; in the second are the souls of the spheres; in the third are the souls of the living beings which are contained within each individual sphere. Chapter I.*

In the beginning, we accepted five levels [of reality] by ascending; then we compared them to one another by descending; third, we placed the rational soul in their middle. Next, we shall examine the levels of this soul just as the <term>Mercurial theologians</term> <note>original: "Mercuriales Theologi"; Ficino refers to the followers of the legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, whom he believed anticipated Christian and Platonic truths.</note> are accustomed to do. Generation is the principle of nutrition and growth. For nowhere can anything be nourished or increased without the generation of certain parts. Now, we have established that where nutrition and growth follow generation, life and soul are present. We see the Earth, indeed, generate innumerable trees and living things from its own seeds, and like a nurse, cause them to grow. It even grows stones like its own teeth, and grasses like hair, as long as they cling to the roots; if these are plucked or torn out from the earth, they do not grow. Who would say the womb of this woman <note>Ficino frequently personifies the Earth as a maternal, living organism.</note> lacks life, she who brings forth and feeds so many offspring of her own accord—who sustains herself, and whose back produces teeth and hair? The same logic applies to the body of water. Therefore, water and earth possess a soul. This is true unless, perhaps, someone were to say that those living things which seem to lack their own seeds—and which we say are made by the soul of the earth or water—are not born from such a soul, but from the <term>influxes</term> <note>original: "influxibus"; the spiritual or astrological "outflow" of power from the heavens into the material world.</note> of celestial minds.

But the Platonists will deny that those influxes—since they are merely <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like color) that cannot exist without a "substantia" (substance) to hold it.</note> far removed from their own vital substances—could generate a vital substance here. This is because an accident cannot generate a substance unless it is subjected as an instrument of a substance—and a "proximate" (nearby) substance at that. For an instrument is not moved toward the form of an art if it is separated from the craftsman. Thus, that influx of celestial life, if it is removed from life itself, will not generate a vital form. Rightly, the celestial impulse is determined toward generating a specific life within any given element by the common life of that entire element (since the impulse is common to every element), and it is submitted to that element as an instrument. But the impulse itself will not generate life in any way by itself. For since nothing acts beyond its own degree, an accident can in no way generate a substance; it can only prepare matter through a certain "accidental preparation." It is necessary, therefore, for this life to be within the elements as an internal builder. Reason persuades us of this: both that an active substance is needed to generate a substance, and that for a perfect action, the perfect presence of the agent itself is required. When a physical substance is applied to another physical substance for some action, that which is substantial in the agent remains outside, while that which penetrates inside is entirely accidental. But there is a need for a *penetrating* substance so that a substance may result from it, and result perfectly. Such a substance is incorporeal and living. Furthermore, because natural causes act through their own nature, they are directed toward a certain effect by the fixed principle of their nature. Otherwise, they would not incline toward this effect any more than toward that one. Thus, to the extent that they fit the work to be done, they operate, and vice versa. For this reason, the herbs and living things that seem to be born in the earth through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactione"; the historical (and now scientificially debunked) theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter.</note> alone must arise from their own specific causes no less than those born through propagation. But where are these specific causes? Without a doubt, the specific causes of earthly lives are in the Earthly Life [the Soul of the Earth]. For even if you attribute them to celestial souls, those celestial and common impulses must still be contracted into earthly and particular souls through the universal Soul of the Earth. In this way, you may proceed from the celestial and common to its opposite—the earthly and particular—through a corresponding middle, which is the earthly and common. Again, if you place those causes which are called "specific" in the gathering of many agents, you will finally be forced to assign one certain determined cause of a proper order, which [unites] the various causes;

<summary>Ficino argues that the elements of Earth and Water are not dead matter but living beings with their own souls. He uses the analogy of the Earth as a mother and the concept of "spontaneous generation" to prove that an internal, vital substance—rather than just distant celestial influence—is necessary to create life.</summary>
