In the preceding section, Ficino began arguing that the elements of Earth and Water possess their own souls, which act as intermediaries between the divine mind and physical matter. He is now explaining how these souls use "seminal reasons" (formative blueprints) to generate life.</meta>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV.</header>

...and flowing together from here and there, may order and determine them toward their own proper effect. Therefore, those causes will exist in the soul of the earth, which through the natural idea and <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: "rationem"; in Platonic thought, this refers to a 'Logos' or formative blueprint that exists within the soul to guide the development of physical forms.</note> of the vine, and through the principle of many lives, will produce flies. It will, I say, produce such things in matter, having been previously disposed in this or that way by the soul itself, while the soul contracts the instincts of the world in this or that way to dispose the matter. 

Furthermore, if human art is nothing other than a certain imitation of nature, and if this art builds its works through certain principles of operation, nature itself acts in a similar way—and with an art that is all the more vivid and wise, the more effectively it works and the more beautiful the things it produces. And if human art possesses living principles—even though it creates works that are not alive, nor does it introduce primary or complete forms—how much more must we believe that the living principles of nature are present, which generate living things and produce primary and complete forms? 

**What is human art?** A certain nature treating matter from the outside. **What is nature?** Art tempering matter from within, as if a woodworker were inside the wood. <note>This is one of Ficino's most famous analogies: while a human carpenter must hack at a piece of timber from the outside, Nature is like a craftsman who lives inside the tree, pushing it into its shape from the center.</note> 

But if human art, although it remains outside the matter, nevertheless agrees with and approaches the work to be made so closely that it completes certain works according to certain ideas, how much more will "natural art" fulfill this? For natural art does not merely touch the surface of matter with hands or other external instruments—as the soul of a **Geometer** touches the dust when he draws figures on the ground—but rather it acts just as the Geometric mind builds an internal "imaginary matter" <note>original: "materiam phantasticam"; the mental space where we visualize shapes.</note>. For just as the mind of the Geometer, while it revolves the principles of figures within itself, forms the <term>imagination</term> from within with the images of those figures, and through this also forms the <term>spirit</term> <note>In Ficino's medical-philosophy, the 'spirit' is a subtle vapor that connects the soul to the body.</note> without any labor or deliberation; so in the natural art, a certain divine wisdom, through intellectual principles, imbues the life-giving and motive power joined to it with natural seeds, and through this, it most easily forms matter from within. 

**What is a craft?** The mind of the craftsman in separate matter. **What is a work of nature?** The mind of nature in joined matter. Therefore, the order of this work is as much more similar to the order found in natural art than the order of human craft is to human art, as matter is closer to nature than to man, and nature rules over matter more than man does. 

Therefore, will you doubt to place certain principles for certain works within nature? Indeed, just as human art, because it touches only the surface of matter and builds through external principles, similarly produces only external forms, so it is clear that natural art—because it begets or draws out substantial forms from the very depth of matter—works through essential and perpetual principles. 

Many living creatures, both on land and in the water, are born from <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactione"; the pre-modern belief in 'spontaneous generation,' where life was thought to emerge from decaying organic matter without parents.</note> alone without any physical seed. Many others sprout from seeds cast far off by an animal, long afterward, partly with some external warmth assisting them, and partly without any visible warmth. All herbs and trees, although they are mostly propagated by sowing or planting, nevertheless grow spontaneously every day in many places without seed or physical germ—not to mention that many Philosophers believe that after the miraculous floods of the world, even the more "perfect" animals were procreated from the earth. 

Nevertheless, it is necessary that certain things arise from certain specific seeds, and that those things which pass from potentiality into actual existence are led into that existence by some cause which already possesses such a state within itself, either as an equal or as something superior. Nor should it be thought sufficient if the "universal and remote cause" <note>likely referring to the Sun or the Heavens</note> is merely superior; otherwise, any of the most imperfect causes among us could produce the most perfect things simply by the power of the heavens. 

All these things signify that everywhere throughout the earth and water, there exist spiritual and life-giving seeds of all things within a certain artistic and vital nature. This nature begets things by itself wherever physical seeds are missing; it fosters seeds left behind by animals; and from a rotten grape-seed (which is of a single and lowly nature) it generates a varied, ordered, and precious vine, evidently by its own various and precious principles. 

This same vital nature draws out the substantial forms of the elements from the very depth of matter itself, where physical bodies cannot penetrate. Furthermore, it leads the elemental qualities—which by themselves would only burn or freeze and the like—to the most beautiful variety of colors and shapes, and to the vigor of life. Besides, when fire is created from the collision of cold bodies—where fire did not previously exist except in a certain potentiality, and even then, one remote from actual existence—nature itself generates fire through a most effective "principle of fire." And wherever accidental qualities alone appear to contribute something to generation—which nevertheless are by no means sufficient by themselves without some substance suitable for the effect—nature itself takes the place of the generative substance. Moreover, mixed bodies, which because of their earthly or watery...

He argues that the Soul of the Earth functions like a Geometer’s mind, shaping physical reality from the inside out.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument from Book IV regarding the hierarchy of existence. He is moving from the "seminal reasons" found in the elements of Earth and Water to the specific powers of minerals and plants, eventually arguing for the necessity of a World Soul as an intermediary between the Divine Mind and physical matter.</meta>

-> **MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGIAN** <-

The thickness of water and the density of earth are, in themselves, sluggish and base. Yet, nature raises up within them certain wonderful actions, even to the point of fascinating and strengthening the souls of men—effects that could not be achieved without the power of a soul, and indeed a most potent one. For by the power of a living and wise nature, which is infused into these very bodies, the herb <term>vervain</term> <note>original: "hierobotanum"; literally "holy herb," often associated with medicinal and ritual use in antiquity.</note> contributes to divinations, as the Magi say. According to the physicians, **Agate** aids the sight, blunts the effects of poison, and provides strength and eloquence; the presence of a **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"; can refer to diamond or any extremely hard stone like adamant.</note> takes away from a Magnet what it has snatched. **Carnelian** stops the flow of blood and mitigates anger; **Onyx** kindles anger and causes terror in dreams. Finally, **Coral** (as Metrodorus and Zoroaster testify) removes insane terrors and repels lightning and hail. Certainly, that nature which performs such things is superior to our own minds and to the weather; thus, it must be infused into these lowest little bodies so that it may elevate these base things, beyond their own natures, to the actions of the higher realms. 

Strato and Chrysippus <note>Strato of Lampsacus was a Peripatetic philosopher; Chrysippus was a leader of the Stoic school. Both held varying views on the vitality of the cosmos.</note> would admit that a life of this kind is infused into the world, but they would assert that this life is itself the **Supreme God**. The Platonists, however, will deny this. They argue that above that life which belongs to something else and exists *in* something, there must be a life that belongs to itself and consists *in* itself. Indeed, the life of a worldly sphere is no less familiar to its own sphere than the human soul is to the human body. Therefore, the life of a sphere—whether of a part or the whole—is neither the "First Life" nor God. 

For the **Supreme God** is the **Supreme Unity**. According to the Platonists, a certain multitude might perhaps proceed immediately from the Supreme Unity, but not such a great diversity and discord of qualities that corrupt one another. Furthermore, nothing evil or deformed is close to the Supreme Goodness and Beauty; yet many evil and deformed things occur in the realm of matter. Moreover, if God is **Being Itself**, He cannot be the "form" of matter; for such a form would not be *Being* itself, but merely a *principle of being*. And because God is "Being"—so to speak—so absolute that He does not exist within any specific essence, He is much less present within matter. 

Likewise, since God is the first efficient cause, He performs all His works primarily; however, the "form of matter" does not perform all things primarily. For the composite whole acts primarily, rather than a mere part of the composite. Again, the parts of a composite exist in a state of potentiality relative to the actualization of the whole. In God, however, there is no potentiality for any further action. Therefore, a single living animal is not made from God and matter, as the **Almarians** <note>original: "Almariani"; followers of Amalric of Bena, a 12th-century theologian accused of pantheism for claiming God was the formal principle of all things.</note> foolishly believe. 

A rational animal moves of its own accord, which is why it can be moved or not moved, and moved now faster, now slower. That which is of such a nature does not persist in perpetual and equal motion except by the law of something higher that is in no way changed. Therefore, **God is not the soul of any globe**, lest a single animal be fashioned from Him and that globe, and He be forced to have a leader above Himself. 

But shall we then concede that the life of a sphere is an **Angel**, and that natural forms proceed from the "Ideas" of the angelic mind? Not at all. For just as a body is necessarily prepared by a certain essence for a certain life, so it is prepared by a certain life for a certain mind. This is why Plato says in the *Timaeus* that God joined **mind to soul**, and **soul to body**. It is as if a bright mind cannot be coupled to an opaque body except through a transparent soul. Just as a shining body is joined to a dense one through a "diaphanous" (that is, transparent) medium—so that what possesses light in itself and offers it to others may be joined to that which lacks light and blocks light—they are joined by a middle nature which, though it lacks light of its own, does not block the entry of light. 

And if the operation of our mind is perfected through a certain separation from matter, the operation of the angelic mind (which is perfect within the intellectual genus) is far removed from matter. Since an angel is nothing other than Mind, and by the very nature of how it operates as a Mind it flees matter, in what way could the substance of an angel be directly attached to matter? 

It is fitting that, just as the particular minds of men reach and move their particular bodies through their own souls (that is, through vital powers), so the universal minds of the spheres embrace and lead their universal bodies through souls. In this way, those spheres will possess an innate life, and the divine minds will by no means be cast down from their sublime state. Above the lives of the spheres—which are simultaneously intellectual and vital—there will be **Angelic lives**, which exist as purely intellectual. Above these, however, will be **God**, the **Life of lives**. 

Furthermore, if the angelic mind is indivisible and immutable, and entirely above place and time, it will in no way fit a body that is divisible, mutable, and subject to place and time. Nor could it produce such forms within that body unless a **Soul** intervened. Because the soul is indivisible and above place, it can be formed or led by the angel; but because the soul is mutable and has some relationship to time, it accords with matter. Thus, the soul leads the forms it has received from above down into itself, toward a mutable and temporal nature, through which they pass most easily into the body.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the "World Soul" in Book IV of his Platonic Theology. Having established that even minerals and plants possess a form of vitality, he now explains the hierarchical descent of power from God through the celestial spheres down to the elemental world, arguing that every part of the universe—including the Earth itself—is animated by a rational soul.</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV

...is also mutable, and within it, things become divisible. It is therefore the view of the **Platonists** <note>Ficino refers to the tradition of Plato and his later followers, like Plotinus and Proclus, who saw the world as a living organism.</note> that God forms angels through Himself, souls through the angels, and finally matter through these souls. They believe that forms gradually degenerate from the highest life and act to such a degree that, by the time they reach matter, they no longer truly live, nor do they appear effective. Indeed, passing from God into an angel, they transition from a single essence into multiple qualities; from the angel into the soul, they pass from a state of rest into a certain effective motion; and from the soul into the body, they pass from a vital and active motion into the passive change of a mortal nature. 

For this reason, if life is implanted in water and earth, and yet this life is not God (lest the infinite Act be bound to the lowest potential), nor is it an angel (lest the brightest mind be placed too close to the darkest nature), it follows then that water and earth must possess souls. By the craftsmanship of these souls, these spheres are adorned with most precious things, just as the individual little souls of aquatic and terrestrial animals—guided by the soul of their own sphere—paint and shape their little bodies through implanted seeds in a most pleasing way. A single soul suffices for the terrestrial globe, since it is entirely one, with its parts joined into a single mass. A single soul also suffices for the orb of water. It is necessary, however, that the souls of these two be distinct pairs, differing from one another in species, as is shown by the natures of their bodies, which differ in species, qualities, and dispositions. 

If such globes, which are removed from the purity of spirit due to their thickness and narrowness, live by their own souls, then all the higher globes live much more so, for they are both purer and much more vast, and by their nourishment the earth and water bring forth life. Let air have its own soul, and fire its own, by the same reasoning that earth and water have theirs. Similarly, let the eight globes of the heavens have eight souls, for there were eight heavens according to the ancients. 

On the earth, there are many animals that have their own souls distinct from the common soul of the earth, because they move from place to place (which the earth does not do) and because they live even when separated from the earth (which stones and plants do not do, for they live through the soul of the earth, not their own). These animals raise themselves high above the earth either by flight or by buildings and machines. In the water, likewise, there are many animals living by their own souls. If, therefore, water and earth were made fertile and adorned by God, why should air and fire not also contain many of their own souls and their own animals, in addition to their common souls? 

Argue the same for the spheres of the heavens: since the stars differ among themselves in size, light, power, and motion, and each performs its own circuits, they also possess souls that differ in species. These stars adorn the heavens just as aquatic animals adorn the water and terrestrial animals adorn the earth. We shall clearly perceive those celestial animals on account of their great abundance of light, and also the terrestrial and aquatic ones, because they are both near to us and show themselves to our eyes by their thickness. But we do not see the aerial and fiery ones, because we do not even perceive the elements of fire and air themselves; they appear to the eyes of earth-dwellers neither by the benefit of vast light nor by the thickness of their mass. 

It is necessary that the soul of the earth itself be **rational**, since certain animals of the earth are not lacking in reason—especially since the works of the earth are more beautiful than the works of men. If the soul of this lowest globe is not devoid of reason, then neither are the souls of the higher globes lacking in reason. In earth and water, there is such a distinction of parts that some terrestrial bodies are less pure, while others are most pure. The former have irrational souls, the latter rational ones. The same is true in water, where there are irrational fish in the muddy parts of the water. There are also water-demons <note>original: "dæmones"; in this context, intermediary spirits or nature-spirits rather than evil beings.</note> whom Orpheus calls **Nereids** <note>In Greek mythology, these are sea nymphs; Ficino treats them here as actual biological/spiritual entities inhabiting the higher vapors of water.</note>, dwelling in certain higher exhalations of water, such as those in this cloudy air. Their bodies are sometimes seen by those with sharper eyes, especially in Persia and Africa, as Zoroaster believes. 

**Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> adds that only those daemons are seen in whose bodies fire abounds alongside the exhalation of water, and that this happens in the East and the South. Furthermore, those can be touched in whom there is much earth in addition; he says such beings existed in his own time among the **Tuscans** <note>The people of Etruria/Tuscany, famous in antiquity for their divination and contact with the spirit world.</note>. But in all the globes above the water, there are no living beings unless they are composed of reason, since those globes are not divided into thick and thin parts, and whatever is there is far purer than aquatic exhalations. 

But let us be permitted here to converse for a moment with the **Pythagoreans**. Since every multitude must be gathered into a small number, and a small number into a few units, and a few units into a single unity, therefore the innumerable crowd of souls living in any sphere of the world must be reduced to a few more excellent souls in that same sphere—say, **twelve princes**. But why specifically to twelve princes? Because just as the single body of the world contains twelve limbs according to the ancients (and these contain many joints), so the one **World Soul** <term>anima mundi</term> <note>The vital principle that Platonists believed gave life and order to the entire universe.</note> contains twelve souls, and these contain many more, but it contains them in such a way...

<summary>Ficino argues for a hierarchy of souls, asserting that every element and celestial sphere is governed by a rational soul and populated by beings (from animals to daemons) appropriate to their purity. He concludes by using Pythagorean numerology to suggest that the vast number of souls is organized under twelve principal governing souls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book IV of the Platonic Theology. In the preceding text, Ficino argued that the Earth and other elemental spheres possess souls. Here, he explores the mathematical and harmonic order of these souls, specifically why the number twelve is central to the structure of the cosmos and the various types of human life.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...contain very many souls, so that they first contain twelve principal ones. Why? Because since the soul of each sphere was selected from the first group of twelve souls and adapted to its sphere, it rightly returns again to the number twelve. We see the sign of this number in the first sphere and the last. In the first sphere, indeed, we discern twelve celestial animals through the **Zodiac**. In each of these, there is a certain principal star, acting as the heart of that animal depicted in the heavens. In that heart, the soul of the entire principal constellation lives its life. Therefore, twelve divine souls are placed there by the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized the mathematical harmony of the universe.</note>. In the heart of **Aries** is Pallas. In the heart of **Taurus**, Venus. In **Gemini**, a particular Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo, the sun god.</note>. In **Cancer**, Mercury. In **Leo**, a particular Jupiter. In **Virgo**, Ceres. In **Libra**, Vulcan. In **Scorpio**, Mars. In **Sagittarius**, Diana. In **Capricorn**, Vesta. In **Aquarius**, Juno. In **Pisces**, Neptune.

In the last sphere as well—namely the Earth—there are twelve types of human life. For humans live their lives through **reason** (assigned to the brain), through **anger** <note>original: "ira" - in this context, it refers to the "spirited" part of the soul (thymos), responsible for courage and social standing.</note> (assigned to the heart), and through **desire** (attributed to the liver). If anyone were to use none of these powers, they would not even breathe. If someone lived by reason alone, they would no longer be human—indeed, it is impossible for a soul joined to a body to proceed by reason alone. Likewise, one cannot use the power of anger alone, because this always serves either reason or desire. Nor can one live by desire alone, for this is always strengthened either by depraved reason or by spirited anger. Therefore, it is necessary to proceed either through all those powers or through two of them. 

The **first** human life, then, will be that which uses reason the most, anger less, and desire the least. 
The **second**, which uses reason more, desire less, and anger the least. 
The **third**, which uses anger more, reason less, and lust the least. 
The **fourth**, which uses anger more, desire less, and reason the least. 
The **fifth**, which uses lust a lot, reason a little, and anger very little. 
The **sixth**, which uses lust a lot, anger a little, and reason very little. 

Thus, six types of life are fashioned from the shared use of three powers. Six others are born from the use of two powers. In the first, reason overcomes anger; in the second, the opposite; in the third, reason overcomes desire; in the fourth, the opposite; in the fifth, anger dominates desire; in the sixth, the opposite. 

If the number twelve is observed in the two extreme spheres of the world <note>The highest heaven and the Earth.</note>, it is also observed in the middle ones. For this reason, as we began a little while ago, let us reduce the many souls living in any sphere back to the twelve principal souls living in that same sphere in an orderly way. Let us again take the twelve princes in any one of the twelve spheres—for there are that many spheres in the ancient world. Let us refer those to the twelve common souls of those spheres. Then, refer the twelve souls of the spheres back to the one soul of matter itself. 

But since the soul participates in the **Mind**, and above a participating nature there must be a nature that is full in itself, the genus of souls is therefore raised up to free Minds <note>Intellects or angelic beings.</note>, and the Minds are finally raised to a single **Mind**. And since the single Mind is both "mind" and "one," it must be raised simply to **The One**, which is not "this one" or "that one"—such as one mind or one soul—but the One itself. This is what Pythagoras calls the **Universal Apollo**. For he wishes for <term>Apollo</term> <note>original: "Ἀπόλλωνα"</note> to be so named as if it were <term>The Simple One</term> <note>original: "ἀπλῶν" (haplon)</note>, which means "simple," and as if it were <term>Away from the Many</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν πολλῶν" (apo ton pollon)</note>, which means "removed from multitude." He calls the same thing <term>The Good</term> <note>original: "τ’ ἀγαθὸν"</note>, that is, goodness itself, since the goodness and perfection of anything consists in its unity; thus, if goodness and union are the same thing within objects, then above objects the first "One" and the first "Good" must also be the same. 

Wherefore, the first One and Good presides most closely over the single Mind; the single Mind presides over many Minds—perhaps first over twelve leading Minds—and over the twelve groups of twelve under them, and many more thereafter; and finally over the one Soul of the World. The one Soul of the World presides over the twelve souls of the twelve spheres. These twelve souls preside over twelve groups of twelve souls. That is to say, the soul of each sphere presides over the twelve most excellent souls in its own sphere. Finally, the twelve groups of twelve preside over innumerable souls. For in any sphere, those twelve principal souls lead the other souls of that sphere. Moreover, this choir of **Muses** sings and dances perpetually (as **Orpheus** says) in musical measures at the command of Apollo himself:
> <term>You weave all things together, tuning your many-voiced lyre.</term> <note>original: "σὺ δὲ πάντα πλέκεις κιθάρην πολυκρέκτο ἁρμόζας"</note>
That is: *You temper the whole of heaven with your tuneful lyre.* 

But we have conversed enough with the Pythagoreans for now. Let us return to the established Platonic order. We have proved by one reason that the spheres of the world are alive; let us proceed to another. Since we see the spheres of the world moving, and we devise certain movers for them—and since we know, furthermore, that there cannot be one sphere above another or one mover above another without end—we are forced to admit...

He outlines a hierarchy where all souls and minds eventually trace back to a single "One," identified as Apollo or the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument for the soul's immortality by examining the nature of celestial motion. Ficino moves from discussing the number of souls in the spheres to the specific internal principles (souls) that drive their motion, arguing that physical qualities alone cannot explain the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>117</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV</header>

...some sphere which is moved first. If it is moved first, it is certainly moved by an **internal principle**. For (as we touched upon above) that which is primarily hot or cold is heated or cooled by an internal heat or cold. For we have said that whatever is such-and-such through another must always be reduced to something that is such-and-such through itself. And if even the smallest particles of the world possess, in a certain way, the powers of their own motions and works within themselves—as is apparent in the parts of the elements, in herbs, and in living creatures—how much more do the vast spheres of the world possess within themselves the principles of their own rotations? These are, I say, the most **intimate principles** <note>original: "familiarissima"; meaning principles that are perfectly adapted and closely joined to the substance of the spheres.</note>, to which the spheres are more closely joined than our bodies are to our souls. Indeed, a motion is more natural and effective the more closely the thing being moved is joined to its mover. Now, the motion of the heavens is more removed from violence, and is more natural and effective, than all others. 

But what are those principles? Are they some kind of qualities? For example, the parts of the elements seem to be moved by **gravity** and **levity** <note>In Aristotelian physics, "gravity" is the natural tendency to move downward, and "levity" is the tendency to move upward.</note>, and to operate through heat and cold; are the spheres of the world thus revolved through qualities of this kind? By no means. For a quality, because it is limited by position and parts and is bound to one specific piece of matter, also acts in a limited way and becomes exhausted, so that it cannot move either forever or always in the same manner. Furthermore, any quality performs a single work and is moved toward a single destination. What does heat do but produce heat, or cold produce coldness? Levity draws only upward, while gravity draws only downward. Therefore, a quality by its own nature will never produce an effect contrary to its principal work; it will never return spontaneously to the place from which it departed, nor will it spontaneously depart from the place to which it naturally brought itself. 

The heavens, however, move always uniformly, yet produce various and mutually contrary effects, and they dispose the lower matter toward this diversity in contrary ways. The heavens induce various configurations and have no fixed end-point in their circuit; rather, whatever point you mark upon the back of the heavens, any part of the heaven approaches it and recedes from it again most easily and an infinite number of times, and not through any violence. For that which is violent is neither long-lasting, nor does it persist over the same and orderly course. Add to this that since the heaven is revolved by contrary motions at the same time, if it were led by a quality, it would certainly be moved by contrary qualities. Yet contrary qualities and natures cannot exist there, where there is no strife and no destruction. 

Likewise, since nature is determined, and therefore cannot seek an indeterminate and diverse end (such as motion is), it moves only for the sake of **rest**. But circular motion, by its very nature, is not directed toward rest; therefore, it is neither driven by nature, nor, if it were ever to rest, would it be stopped by nature. Furthermore, a quality extended in a body is unable to reflect back upon itself since it is bound to the body. In what way, then, will a quality give the heaven a revolution into itself, when the quality does not have the power of reflecting upon itself? 

Likewise, since a body acts in no way through its own nature, but through a quality, and a quality provides force to a body not by its own leadership but only insofar as it is itself moved from elsewhere, if some quality moves the heaven, that quality is meanwhile being moved from elsewhere. What is it that moves the quality? Is it God? Not at all; God, the **Prime Cause**, since He infinitely exceeds all things, is not "intimate" to any specific body, but is equally common to all and independent from all. For if God were the specific mover of any one body, He would no longer be the God of all. Therefore, in order to be the God of all, He is not the specific governor of any one thing. 

The spheres, nevertheless, require (as we have said) the most intimate movers. And because they are distinct from one another and are driven by different motions, they require different and specific movers, since there must be a proportion between the mover and the whole thing moved. Nor should we approve the opinion of those who distribute movers to the spheres in such a way that God is assigned to the first sphere, and the remaining **intellects** <note>Ficino refers to the "Intelligences" or angelic beings that traditional medieval and Renaissance cosmology believed moved the celestial orbs.</note> to the others. For since the distribution is made according to proportion, just as the spheres agree with one another in nature and order, so God and the intellects would correspond to one another; thus God would not surpass the remaining intellects except by as much as the first sphere surpasses the rest, and He would not be infinite. He would also be composed of a common nature (by which He would agree with the others) and a specific nature (by which He would be distinguished). 

Furthermore, if God is **Goodness** itself, and Goodness moves any thing as the "desirable" moves the "desire," then God moves the heaven as an **end** <note>The "final cause" or goal toward which something strives.</note>. But a body is not moved toward an external end except through some internal form that is desirous of that end and is the producer of the motion. Therefore, there is within the heaven a **form** <note>In this context, "form" refers to the rational soul of the sphere.</note> that is desirous of the Prime Goodness and is the producer of motion. This eagerness is neither blind, like that of stones, nor irrational, like that of beasts. For how could an eagerness that is so close to the Prime Truth and Wisdom be blind and irrational? Especially since it moves with a greater

...moves its body in an orderly fashion, more so than our own reason moves ours. Therefore, God does not move the heavens <term>proximè</term> <note>meaning "immediately" or "directly," without an intermediary</note>, but rather through a certain form proper to the heaven itself, which possesses life and reason and is desirous of divine goodness. And if anyone should say that the heavens are moved by some "tempering" <note>original: "temperatione"; referring to a mechanical balance or physical arrangement</note>, just as the spheres of Archimedes <note>A reference to a famous mechanical planetarium or "orrery" attributed to the ancient mathematician Archimedes</note> once revolved, he will be compelled to confess that this very tempering is no less substantial, vital, and rational than the tempering by which the limbs of terrestrial animals are moved; for the former is closer to the first substance, to life, and to reason, and it appears more uniform both in its nature and in its motions. 

But is that mover perhaps an **angel**? Not at all; for celestial life itself is most intimately familiar with the heaven, and in a certain way, it runs around together with its own body. An angel, however, is neither a "familiar" mover, nor is it moved. Indeed, above a mobile mover, it is fitting that there be another mover who is immobile. Furthermore, an angel is entirely stable. From that which is altogether stable, such a sudden and varied motion does not proceed. If, therefore, the angel is entirely stable, and the heaven is moved by another, they certainly require some "middle" which is **self-moving**. For a thing that is self-moving follows directly after a thing that is entirely stable, and a thing moved by another follows after that. 

Indeed, a thing that is self-moving, in that it changes, agrees with the thing that is changed by another. Yet, in that it rules itself—because it thus maintains itself in its own nature and does not fall from its seat—it agrees with that thing which remains entirely permanent. What, then, is this self-moving thing that revolves the heaven directly? It is nothing other than the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note>. For it is the soul which is both self-moving and provides the trace of such motion to bodies. For even if a remote mover is said to move the heaven, it will not grant the act of motion to the heaven until it has infused a motive power joined to the heaven. 

A power of this kind ought not to be extended along with the heaven, for otherwise it would depart from itself, and therefore could not perpetually grant the heaven the faculty of returning to itself. It will, therefore, be **indivisible**, yet not restricted by dimensions like a point, because it could not then freely revolve itself and the dimensions from the same point back to the same point. It is, however, present as a whole everywhere in the whole heaven, so that it may move the whole most effectively. Thus, that joined power—indivisible, free everywhere, and equal—is the **rational soul**. By its presence, the heaven lives; its motion is life-giving, since it gives life to all things. 

Finally, since those instruments in animals live through which souls generate living things, who can doubt that the heaven lives? For it is the instrument of some life for the generation of living beings. Is not spontaneous motion (so to speak), wherever it exists, a sign of internal life? And such motion is greatest where there is a natural circuit. For what is moved more spontaneously than that which naturally recurs into itself, rolls around a natural axis, and stays within its own natural surface? Therefore, life is intrinsic to no body more than to the spheres of the world. 

Nor should we doubt that a single "animal" is formed from the spheres and the divine souls. For it is the property of matter to receive form, and of form to embrace and lead matter; and this "whole" is more perfectly realized where both the matter and the form are more excellent. Who, then, would deny that from those souls (which are more excellent than ours) and from those spheres (which are simpler and more enduring than our bodies, and which contain, draw, and generate our own) a single, **indissoluble animal** is produced? Are those celestial bodies not almost spiritual on account of their wonderful simplicity and thinness? Therefore, they are more easily animated by the presence of spirits than sulfur is ignited by the presence of fire. For in this way, the body is joined to the most excellent thing—that is, the intellectual soul—to such a degree that they are never dissolved. 

If, therefore, mixed bodies become more capable of life and knowledge the more they depart from the "intemperance" of elemental qualities and approach the "tempering" of celestial bodies, then without a doubt, the celestial bodies themselves are most capable of life and knowledge. Furthermore, the genus of minds is more sublime than the heaven, and is more akin to the heaven than to the earth. Therefore, since there are many minds joined to earthly bodies as forms, it is necessary that minds—more numerous, more primary, and more great—are joined as forms to celestial bodies rather than to earthly ones.

The Platonists judge that not only the heavens, but also the **elements** live, as we have said. For when they see all the spheres of the world, and many composite things besides that are attached to them, moved by an intrinsic motion without an external pusher, they judge that souls are within them. And if anyone asks about the ascent and descent of the elements and composite things, the Platonists will answer that this too occurs through the soul of its own sphere, which—just like a magnet draws iron—recalls the particles of its own sphere back to itself. Whence it also happens that the motion...

<summary>Ficino argues that the heavens are moved by rational, self-moving souls rather than directly by God or immobile angels, characterizing the universe as a single, indissoluble living animal. He asserts that celestial bodies, due to their purity and "tempering," are the most perfect recipients of life and intelligence.</summary>

Having argued that an angel—being perfectly stable—cannot be the immediate cause of the varied and sudden movements of the celestial bodies, he now moves to demonstrate that these bodies must be moved by a "World Soul" and individual souls within the spheres themselves, using analogies from physics and biology.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV</header>
<sig>I</sig>

...of a stone descending from on high, which becomes faster the closer it approaches the earth; and similarly, the motion of a rising flame, which becomes swifter the closer it gets to the heavens. Indeed, since the soul of the sphere <note>the celestial shells that carry the planets and stars</note> pulls more vehemently from close by, the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi"; the vital principle that animates the entire universe like a single organism</note> also draws it toward that same place. And just as if people saw the movement of iron itself but did not see the magnet, they would think the iron moved by its own power while it was being drawn by the magnet—so now, those who do not understand the souls of the spheres believe that any little bodies <note>original: "corpuscula"</note> move by themselves. Yet, since no mind of any craftsman moves limbs or instruments as correctly as those little bodies are moved in the world, it is necessary that those bodies are moved and guided not by a lifeless quality alone, but by an artistic nature. 

Furthermore, the <term>natural motion</term> <note>the inherent movement of an object toward its proper place in the universe</note> of the elements is that which does not cross the boundaries of nature and of its natural place—that is, a perpetual circuit within its own place and natural sphere, most similar to its own shape. Fire and air circle around, as does the Moon, which the revolution of the "long-haired stars" <note>original: "crinitarum"; referring to comets</note> indicates. Water circles in a constant ebbing and flowing. If the Earth moved (as Aegetias <note>likely Hegesias of Cyrene, though the attribution is rare in this context</note> wished), it would move in a circle; though as most people believe, it remains still throughout its surface. Its parts circle the center of the world in a certain way, insofar as they press against one another from all sides around it with an everlasting effort. 

However, ascending or descending is not properly a "natural motion," but rather a sudden <term>restoration</term> <note>original: "restitutio"; the process of a displaced object returning to its proper natural level</note> through a straight line toward its natural place and motion. Because this motion is terminated by another and is always directed through a single path, it clearly shows us that the parts of the elements are not at all stirred by themselves. For otherwise, they would also rest of their own accord, nor would they always take the same path; and water might occasionally not cool the nearby air, or might not flow down into a precipice. For even if the souls of the spheres always maintain the same steady course, we must not think that the "little souls"—that is, the specific powers of the elemental parts—would maintain such an order if they were present in them as movers, since our own souls do not maintain it. 

The growth of plants and stones is truly from the soul of the earth; therefore, they grow only as long as they are attached to the earth. The bodies of beasts and humans live separately from the spheres because they have their own souls, which is indicated by their shape, equipped with various instruments <note>the organs of the body</note> entirely unlike the shapes of the spheres; it is also indicated by their <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of physical humors</note>, which is most foreign to the complexion of the spheres. 

As a movable object relates to another movable object, so does a mover relate to a mover. Therefore, as body relates to body, so soul relates to soul. Thus, bodies that are separated from one another by position, nature, shape, and quantity also have a separate motion and species and soul; but those that are joined have a joined soul. Yet, there is one Soul of the World over every individual thing. For there must be one living work of one living Creator. It is not one living thing unless it is through one life. It does not have one life unless it has one soul. Rightly, since there lies hidden (as most people argue) in all the spheres one first and formless matter in itself, there is one soul for it. 

What else is the cause—even though the members of the world are contrary to each other—that they still harmonize into one and communicate their powers to one another, unless it is because one soul tempers the humors of this huge animal, however diverse they may be? It continues the members, though separated by position and quality, in a harmony of life and motion. From where else does it happen that lower things follow the nods of higher things, and all members of the world (so to speak) suffer together in turn, unless from one common nature, and one nature from one soul? This divine animal <note>the Universe</note> ought to be no less united than any other animal, seeing as it is the most powerful of all. Therefore, if among other animals any body is governed through its own single soul, much more are the members of this worldly animal bound together through one soul. 

If this soul relates to its body as ours does to ours, it is no differently whole in every part of the world than our soul is whole in every part of our body; otherwise, it could not perfectly connect, enliven, and move the universe. As nature relates to the body, so the soul relates to nature. Therefore, just as in the universal body the "universal nature" is everywhere, so in universal nature, the universal soul is everywhere. Moreover, the disposition of worldly movements shows that the souls of the spheres are rational, always proceeding toward that which is better and more beautiful. For just as a motion so swift, free, and long-lasting comes from an innermost life, so such a wonderful order of moving, and such an artistic progression, proceeds from a most wise art of that very life. For that which directs the spheres always toward the same thing through the same means is not some necessity lacking life, as is commonly thought, but a complete art and a happy wisdom, which, because it does not err in its deliberation as mortals are accustomed to do, does not wander in its motion and work. Of—

He distinguishes between the universal soul of the earth and the individual souls of humans and animals, using the analogy of a magnet to describe the invisible influence of souls on matter.</summary>

Having established the necessity of motion in the previous page, he now aligns this Platonic view with the teachings of the "Magi," Aristotle, and Christian theologians like Augustine and Aquinas.</meta>

<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

Finally, that the heavens are moved by a certain intelligence is also proven to us by this argument: the body of the heavens, through its movements, so organizes the elements and disposes composite things that intellectual souls may be infused into those composite bodies—souls which are, in truth, far more excellent than the celestial body itself. Therefore, since the corporeal nature of the heavens does not act or dispose anything above its own species by itself, it is certainly guided in this very action and disposition—where it leads to the form of a perfect mind—by the **Divine Mind** as an instrument is guided by an artisan. This mind, indeed, dwells within its own soul, since the soul of the most excellent body must be the most excellent of souls.

There are three principal rulers over the world (as the Magi <note>Ficino refers to the "Zoroastrian" or Persian sages, whom he believed possessed ancient wisdom compatible with Christianity.</note> believe): **Oromasis, Mitris, and Arimanis**—that is, God, Mind, and Soul. Unity is the property of God, order the property of mind, and motion the property of the soul. From God alone comes that first unity of parts and of the whole within the world. From the Mind, by the power of God, comes the order of those united parts. From the Soul, by the power of the higher principles, comes the motion of the ordered work. The soul moves the world changeably through itself; it moves it orderly through the mind; and it perseveres always in this one duty through the eternal unity of God Himself. Thus, these three traces of those three principles (as I have said) are seen in the world, which Plato seems to have touched upon in his *Letter to King Dionysius* <note>Referring to the pseudo-Platonic Second Letter, which mentions "three kings" or principles.</note>, a passage we have explained more extensively in our book *On Love*. I pass over the fact that any natural species has from God that it exists and is one; it has its order from God through the Mind; and it has its perpetuity from both; but from the Soul and the heavens, it has the property of being manifold in its particulars and changeable. For since Mind and Soul are procreated directly from an entirely immovable cause through its very substance, they emerge as altogether immutable substances. However, because natural species emanate from stable causes (that is, God and Mind) through causes that are mobile in their action (that is, souls and the heavens), they are also changeable in their substance in a certain way, although by the gift of the stable causes they seem perpetual through the continuous succession of individuals. For from whatever source the mobile causes possess the perpetuity of their motion, from that same source their effects possess the continuous succession of their generation. That the celestial spheres have souls is confessed not only by the Platonists, but also by all the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note>, as Aristotle teaches in the second book of *On the Heavens*, again in the 7th and 8th books of *Physics*, the 2nd book of *On the Soul*, and the 11th book of *Metaphysics*. Theophrastus, the disciple of Aristotle, also says this in his book *On the Heavens*. Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>Influential Islamic philosophers whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance scholasticism.</note> confirmed this most strongly. Augustine Aurelius in his *Enchiridion*, and Thomas Aquinas in the second book of *Against the Gentiles*, teach that, as far as Christian doctrine is concerned, it makes no difference whether the celestial bodies have souls or not.

But as to whether the spheres of the elements <note>The regions of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire that were thought to sit beneath the Moon.</note> live: although this is clearly established among the Platonists, the ancient Peripatetics said nothing about them; however, some more recent ones are in doubt, because the elements seem to have been instituted for the sake of composite things, and are as much "viler" than composites as they are closer to matter. But to this, the Platonists will respond that the whole spheres of the elements were indeed instituted for the sake of the whole world, not for the sake of this or that composite thing; but the particles of the elements—which are both separated from the integrity of the whole element and mixed into this or that composite body—are mixed for the sake of such a small body. And although the qualities of these particles are closest to <term>prime matter</term> <note>Pure potentiality without form; the lowest rung of existence.</note>, the whole elements, because they are numbered in the order of the principal members of the world, are very close both to the form of the entire world and to the universal pattern and purpose of the Supreme Architect, as well as to the divine influences of the celestial minds and spheres, which flow down into particles and mixed small bodies only through the whole elements. And in this way, the globes of the elements become worthy receptacles for rational souls. There are, furthermore, in fire and air—on account of their position and transparency corresponding to the heavens—certain parts that correspond, as it were, to the stars of that region. These parts, through certain noble and direct influences, are sufficiently prepared to receive minds. However, the thicker parts of either water or earth, or of fire and air diffused within the lands, do not deserve to receive souls from their own globes, because they both lose the dignity of the globes and do not preserve their own simplicity and purity on account of the force of external bodies. But if they are mixed together more diligently until, through a long-lasting tempering of qualities, they recover a certain equality similar to the equality of the spheres, they first achieve certain wonderful operations in the mixtures, then life in plants, then sensation, and finally reason. If anyone desires to know the names of the divine spirits, let him know that the Theology of Orpheus <note>The mystical tradition attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus.</note> divides the souls of the spheres in such a way that each...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from the previous page regarding the "double power" of the celestial soul: one power directed toward divine contemplation and the other toward the animation and governance of the physical spheres.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV.</header>

...has a twofold power: one situated in the act of knowing, the other in the act of giving life to and ruling the body of the sphere. Therefore, in the element of Earth, Orpheus <note>Ficino frequently cites the legendary poet Orpheus, believing him to be a primary source of the "Ancient Theology" that leads to Plato.</note> names that [contemplative] power **Pluto**, and this [life-giving] one **Proserpina**. In Water, he calls that one **Oceanus**, and this one **Thetis**. In Air, he calls them the thunderer **Jupiter** and **Juno**. In Fire, **Phanes** and **Aurora**. 

In the soul of the lunar sphere, he calls that first power **Bacchus Licnitus** <note>original: "Bacchum Licnitum," referring to Dionysus as the infant in the winnowing-fan, a symbol of purification.</note>, and this second one a **Muse**. Again, in the soul of the sphere of Mercury, he calls that power **Bacchus Silenus**, and this one **Euterpe**. In the sphere of Venus, **Lysius** and **Erato**. In the sphere of the Sun, **Trietericus** and **Melpomene**. In the sphere of Mars, **Bassareus** and **Clio**. In the sphere of Jupiter, **Sabasius** and **Terpsichore**. In the sphere of Saturn, **Amphietus** and **Polyhymnia**. In the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, located beyond the seven planetary spheres.</note>, **Pericionius** and **Urania**. Finally, in the Soul of the World itself, he calls the primary power **Bacchus Eribromus**, and the second power the Muse **Calliope**. 

For this reason, according to Orpheus, a specific **Bacchus** presides over each individual Muse; by this, he signifies that the powers of the Muses are "intoxicated" by the nectar of divine knowledge. Thus, the nine Muses, together with the nine Bacchuses, revel in a divine frenzy <note>The term "debacchantur" suggests the wild, ecstatic worship associated with Bacchus/Dionysus, here used as a metaphor for intellectual ecstasy.</note> around the one **Apollo**—that is, around the splendor of the **Invisible Sun**. 

But let these remarks concerning the names of the divine souls suffice. Let us briefly conclude this entire discussion with this reasoning: we should say, in the manner of the ancients, that those people are to be utterly laughed at who admit that the impure parts of the elements (from which living animals are made) possess life and reason, yet deny life and reason to the whole and pure elements. It is as if they believe the part to be better than the whole, or wish for the world to lack life and sense—the very world which nevertheless gives life to plants (which do not grow from seed) and gives sense to animals (which are not produced through sexual union).

Therefore, we gather three grades of rational souls:
1. In the first grade is the one **Soul of the World**.
2. In the second are the **twelve souls** of the twelve spheres.
3. In the third are the **many souls** contained within each of the spheres.

All these things pertaining to the souls of the spheres are narrated from the opinion of the Platonists; they should only be finally affirmed when they have been approved by the careful examination of a Christian council. For even Plato himself, in the *Epinomis*, where he speaks in his own person, says this regarding these divisions: "It is impossible that the earth, the heaven, and all the stars, and the great masses composed of them—unless a soul were present in each, or within them—could be revolved with such exquisite reason through years, months, and days, and provide all good things to us all."

->The souls of the spheres move the spheres through the law of fate, and they move<-
->in a circle because they themselves are circles.<-

## Chapter II.

**I**n what way do celestial souls move their spheres? Certainly (as pleases the Platonists) just as your soul moves your body: through **appetite** <note>Here, "appetite" means a directed desire or inclination.</note>. That appetite is also excited there by thought, and thought in that place is excited by the **fatal law** <note>The "law of fate" or "providential order" inherent in the soul's nature.</note> of that soul. Therefore, Plato says in his book *The Statesman*: "Fate and innate desire move the heaven." This is a concept he seems to have received from **Zoroaster**, from whom all the wisdom of the ancient theologians flowed. For Zoroaster, when speaking of the heaven, says:

> It is carried along by a celestial impulse, and runs on a wheel near to necessity. <note>Original Greek: "αἰθίῳ βολῇ φέρεται, καὶ τροχῷ ἐγγὺς ἀνάγκης"</note>

That is to say, it is carried by an eternal will, and always runs by the works of necessity. We shall understand this clearly if we consider the order of things in this way. There is something called "**above all**," and there is something "**below all**." 

That which is said to be "above all" is **God**, who cannot properly be called "the all," since He is the simplest Unity above all number. "Below all" are these individual bodies. It is necessary, therefore, that between that which is above all and that which is below all, there be a medium. That medium is the "All" itself, the whole, the accumulation of all things. 

However, this "All" or "Whole" will be threefold. The first "All" depends directly upon the Unity of God itself. Therefore, it must be as united as possible, since it is made most similar to Unity itself. Now, a thing can be united in three ways: in **Essence**, in **Point**, and in **Moment**. 
1. In **Essence**: so that it is one substance, not composed of many substances. 
2. In **Point**: so that it is not dispersed into many parts, through which it would be forced to be distracted into many points of space. 
3. In **Moment**: so that whatever it can possess, it attains in the blink of an eye, and does not become different through various moments of time. 

Therefore, that "All" which comes immediately from God is united in all these ways, making it most similar to Him. This is the **Angel** <note>Ficino uses "Angel" to describe the Neo-Platonic "Mind" (Nous) or "Intellect," the first creation after God.</note>. Although it might be called changeable in a certain way because it depends on another, nevertheless, because it is procreated closest to the infinite state of God and is turned toward Him without a mediator, it emerges as entirely stable.

<summary>Ficino maps the Orphic names of deities and Muses to the celestial spheres, arguing that the universe's order requires it to be animated by rational souls. He then begins a hierarchy of being, placing the "Angel" as the first and most unified creation between God and the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s exploration of the ontological hierarchy—the levels of reality—moving from the absolute Unity of God down through the angelic Mind, the Soul, and finally to Matter. He focuses here on how Time and Place emerge as the soul descends into the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>132</page-num>
# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

Next follows the second totality <note>This "second totality" refers to the Soul, following the first totality which is the Angelic Mind.</note>, which, because it hangs from the One by a kind of secondary intention, already loses one mode of unity while retaining two: it remains one indeed in its essence and as a single point, but it becomes various through its moments. Such is the soul. The third totality is the matter of the world, which is a substance further removed; it is not only varied in its moments like the soul, but is also spread out through the points of space. But why, in this descent, is **time** found before **place**? Firstly, because time is the companion of some spiritual action, whereas place is the companion of the body; therefore, time stays closer to the spirit and its efficacy than place does. Secondly, because one must descend step-by-step from unity into multiplicity. Whenever the essence of a thing undergoes the multiplicity of place, its operation also suffers the numbering of time, but the reverse is not true. For the essence can surpass the operation in its union and perfection, but never the other way around. 

Finally, any individual members of the world are said to be not "the all," but "under the all." For this reason, an **angel** contains within itself all the <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes." These are the divine blueprints or formative patterns of all created things.</note> of all things—all of them, I say, in stable possession and in active expression simultaneously. The **soul**, in turn, contains them all, but in stable possession and not in active expression. **Matter** contains them all indeed in potentiality, but not in possession or expression; rather, it receives them all through succession. It is truly necessary that the soul itself be, in a certain way, all things, of which Zoroaster <note>The legendary Persian sage whom the Renaissance Platonists believed was a predecessor to Plato.</note> says: 

*And the world contains many fullnesses of its depths.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἴσχ’ ἡ κόσμῳ πολλὰ πληρώματα κόλπων." Ficino interprets these "depths" as the various levels of reality the soul fills.</note>

For if the soul is the middle between the highest and lowest things, it necessarily contains within itself the gifts and images of those highest things, and the powers and models of the lowest. But in that part where it communicates with the angelic mind, it becomes like an angel; in the other part, it is dissimilar. Therefore, the souls of the celestial spheres possess all Ideas simultaneously in their minds, both in possession and in active expression. In their powers that move the bodies [of the planets], they again possess all the seeds of things to be generated, in possession and habit together, but not in expression. Their middle part, namely **reason**, follows the mind; because their bodies are most perfect and lack almost nothing, they are governed by the lowest part of the soul only by the laws of fate. Thus, the middle part of the celestial souls, which is mobile by its nature, becomes stable and absorbed by the mind because it is at leisure from any bodily labor.

In us, however, because of the poverty and needs of our bodies, our middle part [reason] is also moved just like the lowest part, because the difficult and laborious administration of the body forces it to be so. Yet, a certain motion also appears (as **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> wishes) in the rational part of the celestial souls themselves. Since it flows from God (the Unity of all things), first through its own unity (which is the head of its mind) and then through its mind (which is the head of its reason), it also flows back through its mind and its unity into God, the Unity of all. Indeed, the soul first naturally desires God himself, secondly understands Him, thirdly loves Him intellectually, and fourthly attains Him through a kind of loving union. 

The Platonists call an action that passes through middle steps to a certain end "motion." If it passes through time, they call it **temporal motion**; but if it passes in a single moment, they call it **eternal motion**, such as exists in the reason of the celestial souls. Although this middle part of theirs, being turned toward the mind, sees all rational principles simultaneously, its lowest part—being most closely related to changeable bodies—is not of such great power that it can be carried toward all the seeds of things in a single act. Yet it desires to be carried toward all things in act, so that all things in its power are not there in vain. 

It is therefore carried toward them with a manifold striving; now it attains this thing in act, now that thing, but it loses the former in act when it runs into the next. It does not, therefore, embrace all things at once, but is always striving toward all. Thus it is always running, and a "course" of this kind is the **first motion**. The interval of this course is the **first time**. The world runs according to that course. The times of the world flow according to that time. I think this is the very thing that (as it is found in **Orpheus**) "changes the forms of **Proteus**." <note>Proteus was the shapeshifting sea god of Greek myth. Ficino uses him as a metaphor for the Soul's constant movement and change as it interacts with the physical world.</note> 

Since those seeds are limited to a certain number, and the soul runs forever, it passes through all of them in a certain span of time. Once these are completed, it is either forced to rest (as it seems to us) or to run back gradually through all of them again, and to re-weave the same web of generation in the world, as it pleased **Zoroaster**, who thinks that when the same causes eventually return in their entirety, the same effects likewise return. By this reasoning, both he and many other of his successors confirmed the **resurrection of human bodies**. The Platonists wanted the interval of the universal circuit to be completed in thirty-six thousand solar years, which they call the **Great World Year**. **Mercury** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom.</note> calls the end of this year the "old age of the world"; Plato, in his book on the kingship of the world <note>Likely referring to the "Statesman" (Politicus), where Plato discusses the cosmic cycles of the world.</note>, calls it "restitution." But so that the manner of moving the heavens may be [explained] more clearly...

He introduces the concept of the "Great Year," a 36,000-year cycle after which the universe and human history supposedly repeat themselves, a concept he links to the idea of resurrection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s discussion of how the Soul acts as a bridge between the eternal Mind and the moving physical world. Having established that the Soul contains the principles of all things in a state of "multiplicity in time," he now explains the mechanism by which the Soul translates these internal ideas into the actual physical rotation of the heavens.</meta>

<page-num>133</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IV.</header>

To understand this, consider an example. Euclid <note>Euclid of Megara (c. 435–365 BCE), a devoted student of Socrates who reportedly risked his life to travel from Megara to Athens to hear Socrates speak.</note> thinks at night about traveling from Megara to Athens to hear Socrates, and he takes up a lantern. First, through a general thought, he maps out the entire journey in his mind. From this universal intention, however, no specific step is actually taken unless a particular thought intervenes to designate the very first step. Therefore, the lantern first illuminates the first step; the imagination immediately thinks of this step, the appetite chooses it, and the feet perform it. Once this is done, the lantern reveals the second step; Euclid immediately thinks of it, desires it, and performs it. He does the same for the third step and all others. 

In the same way, they believe this happens in the soul of the sphere <note>The "soul of the sphere" is the intelligence that governs a specific celestial body, like the Sun or a planet.</note>. There, the mind and its reason generally establish as many figures in the heavens and forms in matter as it perceives in the <term>ideas</term> <note>original: "ideas." In Platonic thought, these are the eternal, perfect blueprints of things existing in the Divine Mind.</note> and concepts within an angel—concepts formed by the power of God Himself. The soul does this so that it may, according to its own strength, produce a worldly work of the same kind that God produces as an angelic work, thus imitating the **First Craftsman**. 

However, the soul does not begin to move the heavens or perform any work unless its **motive power** (which is its lowest part) brings forth one specific kind of its <term>seeds</term> <note>original: "seminum." Ficino uses "seeds" or "seminal reasons" to describe the formative powers latent in the soul that generate physical forms.</note> before the others, offering it, as it were, to the "eyes." As soon as the force of one specific kind of seed prevails over the other seeds, the imagination itself (which is linked to this lowest power) thinks of it, desires it, and unfolds that same thing in the heavens, forming it in the elements; it creates a sequence in the heavens and brings it to birth in the elements. This happens in the same way through a sequence of succession in other seeds. 

In this series of fatal succession consists the **Law**; in that thought consists **Desire**. Thus, the heaven is moved by **Fate** and an **innate desire**, in much the same way that the spirits and humors <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were thin vapors that carried the soul's commands to the body, and "humors" were the primary bodily fluids.</note> within us are vibrated and formed by intense thought and emotion. Nor should you think that such new effects in the world, or such varied figures in the heavens, are unfolded by the mover except through new and varied "affections" (dispositions) of those souls. For from a cause that is entirely stable, only a stable work is produced. 

Nor should we think that the Soul of the Heaven grows weary by moving, even if our own soul does. For motors that are not stretched out alongside the thing they move do not usually tire—especially if they are very close to that infinite state which is the goal of all motions. Furthermore, just as the lowest and most earthly body is clumsy and unfit for motion, so is the sublime body [of the heavens] agile. If even a light breeze stirs up dust, and the wind trapped in the bowels of the earth shakes mountains, will you wonder that sublime souls can rotate the thinnest bodies with the slightest nod? This is especially true since they move them around a natural axis and within their own boundary, and these bodies are more led to this kind of motion by natural instinct than a heavy body is led to descend when our soul leads our body down a slope. Indeed, the body of the heaven is just as balanced and easily moved to any position around its center as elemental matter is to any form—indeed, much more so. 

Therefore, just as efficacy in moving belongs to the soul, so a readiness to be moved belongs to the [celestial] body. For since the body is made from "act" (form), it exists in act and is directed toward act; for this reason, its nature is to always be exercised through its forms. But because it has both a substance and a quality that are divisible, whatever it does or suffers is forced into a divisible mode—that is, to act and suffer according to **motion**. 

The motion of the celestial bodies and its variety contributes to the generation and diversity of things to be born. For the soul adorns the heaven with various figures and transmits celestial powers more intensely into the elements. It moves the elements and forces them to be mixed together in many ways; it illuminates and nourishes their sphere from all sides through a kind of rhythmic change. Furthermore, the matter of the world itself cannot hold all heavenly figures at once, nor all forms under heaven at once (since many are contrary to each other). Yet it desires all of them everywhere, as if they were the perfections of its own nature. Hence, it is made prone to **eternal motion**, so that what it cannot achieve all at once in a single state, it may at least achieve in some way through succession. 

But why do the spheres rotate specifically in a **circle**? Although I have just suggested the reason, let us begin from a deeper point. 

**God** is a single circle, because He is from Himself (like a circle) and directed toward Himself; He has no beginning or end outside Himself, but beginning in Himself, He finds His limit in Himself. 

An **Angel** is a double circle: first because it returns to the place from which it flowed while it understands and loves its Author [God], and second because it considers itself. 

the **Soul** is a triple circuit: because it looks back to God, because it considers itself, and because it descends from the causes of things to their effects, and then ascends again from effects to causes. 

If these three motors of the heavens move in a circuit, what prevents the heaven itself from being swept into a circuit? And since the heaven imitates these higher causes in its figure and its substance, why should it not also imitate them in its motion and operation? The heaven is subject to the moving soul, and that is where its motion begins. Once one part of the heaven begins to move, because of its continuity...

<summary>Ficino explains that the Soul moves the heavens by manifesting internal "seeds" or ideas one by one, much like a traveler uses a lantern to see a path step-by-step. He argues that celestial motion is circular because it imitates the recursive, self-reflective nature of God, Angels, and the Soul.</summary>
