<meta>This page continues Ficino’s explanation of celestial mechanics. He moves from the psychological impulse of the Soul to the physical manifestation of that impulse as circular motion. He argues that the heavens move because they are attempting to imitate the omnipresence of the Soul within the constraints of a physical body.</meta>

<page-num>134</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

[One part] draws another with it, and pushes another, and they necessarily turn back upon themselves in a circle. The heaven cannot stand still, since its soul does not know how to rest, yet the heaven does not wish to abandon its natural place. Thus it happens that it revolves around the same point, and the heaven is always mobile in the same place; likewise the earth (which is most distant from it) is always immobile. That which is always moved necessarily returns to the same point, for no space of physical things is infinite. Furthermore, Plato says in the book *The Statesman* <note>original: "in libro de regno." Ficino refers to Plato's *Politicus*, often titled *De Regno* (On Kingship) in Latin translations.</note>: "A state entirely devoid of change belongs only to the most divine of all things. But the world, because it is a body, already degenerates from the dignity of divine things; therefore, it cannot be altogether immutable. Yet, because it is very close to divine things, it was fitting for it to be moved with a circular motion." This motion, because it revolves in the same place, around the same center, and according to the same principles in a similar and perpetual continuation, departs as little as possible from local stability. These are his words.

Add to this that among all types of motion, only local motion <note>The movement of an object from one place to another.</note>—because it is, as it were, external—is not forced to change the substance or natural quality of its subject. In the same way, among local motions, the circuit or revolution seems able to be called "non-motion," because it alone does not change its place. If someone wished for the heaven to stand still, let him fix the heaven of Saturn <note>In the Ptolemaic system, Saturn was the highest of the seven planetary spheres.</note> upon its axis whenever he pleases. Then one semicircle of that sphere would be over us, and the other over the head of the <term>Antipodes</term> <note>Those living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. However, since all parts of this sphere are most similar to one another without any natural difference, there is no reason why one part should be here rather than another. Therefore, the lower semicircle—because it fits our location just as well as it fits the region of the Antipodes—will strive to be here just as it is there; and the upper semicircle, because of that same fitness, will strive to be there just as it was here. From this struggle, one part will push the other, while every part, because of this equal fitness, will wish to be everywhere equally.

Indeed, the concave surface of the eighth sphere <note>The "Firmament" or the sphere of the fixed stars, which sits just outside the planetary spheres.</note> is the natural place for the sphere of Saturn. There, the outer curve of Saturn's sphere touches the inner curve of the eighth. Because every particle of this [Saturn's] sphere fits equally with every particle of the eighth, it yearns to touch all of its particles. If it were at rest, individual parts would touch individual parts, but no single part could touch them all. By running, however, it nearly achieves what it could not achieve while resting; such is the "greed" of this sphere for that one.

Furthermore, the whole soul of the sphere of Saturn is present at once in every point of the sphere. This sphere, eager to enjoy its soul, therefore "runs" so that it may enjoy the whole soul through all of its own parts everywhere. It flies most rapidly so that, as far as is possible, it may be everywhere at once, just as the soul is everywhere at once. And because it never finds the soul standing still, the sphere itself never rests.

And just as the soul is constantly revolved around God as if around a center, so the body, drawn by the soul, is always revolved around the soul as if around a center. Yet the heaven stands on the same axis because the soul, through its participation in the <term>Mind</term> <note>The "Divine Mind" or *Mens*, which is the level of reality above the Soul in Neoplatonism.</note>, participates in a certain rest. All rational souls do this in their bodies. All bodies do this in relation to their souls, whether we speak of the souls of the spheres and stars, or of <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or guardians, not necessarily evil "demons."</note> and men. And if this is less apparent in our own thick, physical bodies, it nevertheless happens in the <term>ethereal garment</term> <note>original: "aetherio animæ indumento." Often called the "astral body" or "spiritus," a subtle vehicle that connects the soul to the physical body.</note> of the soul, which Zoroaster <note>The legendary Persian sage, whom Ficino believed was a source of ancient "Platonic" wisdom.</note> willed to revolve constantly within us.

Finally, let us conclude this discussion of the motion of the heaven with this thought: Neither the body of the heaven which is moved, nor the "mover" which is moved toward the motion of the heaven, is the primary ruler and end of this motion, lest labor or weariness should occur in such motion.

->For motion is always produced and governed<-
->toward the stable and around the stable.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of celestial motion to the specific arguments for the immortality of the human soul. Ficino begins Book V of his treatise by defining the Soul as the "Third Essence"—the crucial middle link in the universe that connects the eternal, unchanging divine realm with the temporary, moving physical world. He argues that because the soul moves itself in a circular, spiritual pattern, it can never "run out" of life.</meta>

# PLATONIC THEO-
## logy, on the immortality of souls,

->by the same author, Ficino,<-

### BOOK V.

->*Every rational soul is immortal. The first reason: because it is moved by itself, and in a circle. Chapter I.*<-

<note>Decorative woodcut initial: A man in a landscape with trees and a building</note>
As we place all souls in the rank of the <term>third essence</term> <note>Ficino’s "Third Essence" refers to the Soul's position in the hierarchy of the universe: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Matter. Being in the middle, the Soul acts as the "bond of the world."</note>, and for this common reason we maintain they are immortal: because they are moved primarily, and because they are moved primarily, they are moved in a circle. Therefore, because they are moved primarily, they are moved always. For where the first motion is, there is perpetual motion. For if the fountain of motion should dry up, nothing further in nature will be moved. Likewise, that which moves primarily provides both internal and external motion to itself. Internal motion is life; therefore, it supplies life to itself. And because it never deserts itself—since a perpetual love of self exists in every nature—it never ceases to live. For if that which is moved by another remains in motion only as long as it adheres to its mover, how much more so that which is moved by itself? Because it is one and the same as its own mover, it is never deserted by that mover and never ceases to be moved. Furthermore, if it were imagined to perish at some point, it would either cease to exist before it ceased to move, or the reverse, or both simultaneously. The first is impossible, because motion cannot remain separate from the essence. The second is impossible because the motion is spontaneous; for motion is the constant companion of that which originates its own movement. The third is impossible because a destructive change can never erupt from within that source from which the vital and life-giving motion arises. But such a change will not happen from the outside either, for the fountain of motion is not moved from any other source. This is surely the property of the third essence; and since all rational souls fall under this common definition, the same property applies to them all. They are also immortal because, by the nature of the third essence and the primary motion, they are driven in a circle. For if they are moved in a circle, they never stop. A circuit does not exhaust its strength but gathers its own forces back into itself, and when it is thought to fail, it renews itself. I shall pass over for now that reasoning of <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>Ancient Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) who taught that the soul is immortal and undergoes reincarnation.</note> which shows that in a sphere there is no beginning or end; therefore, that which is moved in a sphere has neither ever begun to move nor will it ever cease. Moreover, rational souls are certain spiritual spheres that perform a spiritual circuit within themselves, since the very bodies which are their shadows possess such a shape and motion. Thus, just as visible spheres and circuits are the shadows of invisible spheres and circuits, if the shadows are perpetual, how much more will those substances be perpetual? These substances perform the act of motion through a power that lacks a limit, without an end. Nor is there anything contrary to them by which they might be destroyed, just as there is no motion contrary to their own motion, which is a circuit.

->*Second reason: because it stands through its substance. Chapter II.*<-

**A**nd so, the previous reasoning has demonstrated that the soul is immortal through its motion. The same thing is also demonstrated through the stability of the soul. When we name the "soul," we wish the genus of rational souls to be understood. For we do not properly call irrational lives "souls," but rather idols and images of souls. If that third essence (about which we have said so much), although it is moved through its operation, nevertheless remains stable through its substance, it follows that the soul—which is the same as that essence—is not changed in its substance. Moreover, what is of such a kind never ceases to exist.

<page-num>436</page-num>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

### The third reason: because it clings to divine things. Chapter III.

**I**f two certain things placed at the lowest level of nature—namely, matter and quantity—are <term>passive</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "passive" things are those that are acted upon, rather than causing action themselves.</note>, and two others at the highest level are <term>active</term>—God and the angel—how shall the soul and quality, which occupy the middle region between the passive and the active, behave? In this way, surely: both turn out to be partakers of passion (being acted upon). But because quality is inherent in things that suffer (physical bodies), it receives passion entirely through its operation and its very essence. The soul, however, which stands further away, even if it perceives some bodily passion in its faculty of operating, is nevertheless free from passion in its essence. And just as the body, made of matter and quantity, renders the quality inherent in it subject to corruption, so God and the angel, being active, make the soul—which is closest to them and set apart from the body—immortal by their own divinity.

### The fourth reason: because it rules over matter. Chapter IV.

**B**ut its immortality appears most clearly in this: that the very primary matter of things, which is moved and formed by the soul, must be perpetual. Art imitates nature. Art performs its works in this order: namely, it imprints various forms upon a certain underlying matter, none of which the matter possesses as its own. For clay has no specific form of any particular vessel as its own, but instead takes on various forms in turn from the potter; and when the vessels are broken, the clay remains, from which others may be remade. Therefore, nature itself, the artisan of things, has a certain underlying matter for itself that is devoid of all forms, prepared equally to receive them all. For just as at the highest level of things there is <term>pure act</term> <note>original: "actus purus." This refers to God, who is fully realized and unchanging, with no unfulfilled potential.</note>, needing nothing and the producer of all forms, so at the lowest level there must be something that is <term>pure potentiality</term> <note>original: "pure potentia." This is Prime Matter, which has no form of its own but can become anything.</note>, lacking all things, and itself formless though capable of receiving all forms.

Thus, a universal matter—an indifferent recipient for any forms whatsoever—stands beneath the universal artisan. This is called **prime matter**, which is equally subject to the forms of the elements and other bodies. At one moment it receives this form from a natural force, at another moment that form, and it has none as its own by its nature. For these would not be the lowest things if they possessed any perfection or natural power of acting from their own form, nor would they be fit for another form that was contrary to their own. For if coldness were the natural property of matter, how could it ever receive heat? And if it were naturally moist, how could it receive dryness?

Observe the mutual changing of the elements if you wish to find this hidden matter. For when we see where the appearance of earth was before, and later the appearance of water appears there, we cannot say that the form of water which recently arrived is received into the form of earth; for these are in a way opposite to each other, since earth contains dryness and water contains moisture. Therefore, the form of earth does not receive the form of water, but as the watery appearance approaches, the earth-form departs into <term>chaos</term> <note>Here, "chaos" refers to the unformed state of matter between the loss of one form and the gain of another.</note>. But the form of water cannot exist without a subject, nor does a new subject arrive in the generation of water. Therefore, the same matter that had been subject to the earthly form now undergoes the form of water. 

And this is the argument used by <term>Timaeus the Pythagorean</term> <note>A character in Plato's dialogues (and a historical figure) to whom the creation story of the universe was attributed.</note>. Likewise, when the Sun, by striking the sea with its rays, thins the water into vapors and generates air from the water, it certainly has drawn some small portion of the watery body out of the element of water. We ask, then, whether it first reduced that small portion of water into nothing and afterwards generated air, or whether it preserved something of the water? If it reduced the water entirely to nothing, the intention of nature would be toward evil (which is impossible, since nature is always directed toward the good, as it is governed by the supreme goodness of God). Furthermore, "being" itself—which is the special gift of the eternal God—would sometimes be withdrawn from things by causes following after God. This cannot happen, since God always preserves by His own influence what He has once given, and no violence from any agent can oppose Him. 

For things lower than God do not have absolute "being" in its entirety, but rather a specific "being"—this kind of being or that; therefore, they do not have the power to take away "being" entirely, but only to change it from this mode to that. It would also follow that the Sun would be generating that new air out of nothing if it had consumed the whole prior portion of water into nothing. But natural agents are unable to make anything out of nothing. For it is easier to make something out of any existing thing than out of nothing. Yet they cannot generate just any thing from any seed: never pears from wheat, figs from millet, or an eagle from the seed of a man. Much less could they [create] from nothing any—

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because it occupies a middle ground near the divine and because it governs "prime matter," the indestructible substrate of the physical world that changes form but is never reduced to nothing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous chapter regarding the soul's relationship with matter. Ficino is in the middle of explaining that matter itself is indestructible, which serves as a foundation for his larger argument that the soul, being superior to matter, must also be immortal.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>BOOK V ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL</header>

...generate anything out of nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo aliquid generare." A fundamental principle of ancient philosophy was that nothing comes from nothing and nothing returns to absolute non-existence.</note>. By this reasoning, it is shown that the Sun could not turn that portion of water drawn from the sea into nothing. Therefore, something of its prior nature remains within it. What is that thing? To be sure, that water was cold and humid. The coldness departs, but the humidity remains—as the **Platonists** believe—which is common to both air and water. If humidity remains, there also remains some <term>matter</term> <note>In this context, "matter" refers to "Prime Matter," the underlying "stuff" of the universe that has no shape or quality of its own until a "form" is impressed upon it.</note> subjected to that humidity. For humidity is not a <term>form</term> <note>A "form" is the essence or definition of a thing; for example, "water-ness" is the form that makes matter behave like water.</note> separated from bodies. Thus, the matter which previously lay hidden under the coldness of water now lurks under the heat of the air.

Indeed, when fire is made from air, it also loses its humidity and receives dryness. Matter of this kind, which is so thinned out through <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The process of becoming less dense, like water turning into steam.</note> that it ascends into the form of fire, in turn descends through density: it swells into air, is later condensed into water, and finally grows heavy into earth. You see how one single matter is clothed in all forms in turn, while it both ascends through rarefaction and descends through density. This matter is one, both because one is sufficient for one world, and because—since it is formless—it has nothing by which it can be distinguished into many parts within itself.

But if the whole universe ends in a single "formable" thing, it is agreeable that it must begin from a single **Formatter**, and that the whole is subject to Him. But of this we have spoken elsewhere and shall speak again. Indeed, this matter is never destroyed, because it is the foundation of the whole of physical nature; were it destroyed, the entire **machine of the world** would collapse. Nor is it ever dissolved into parts, because it is not constituted of parts by its own nature. For parts are created through <term>quantity</term>, but matter precedes quantity. It is, in fact, the <term>substrate</term> <note>The underlying layer that supports qualities like color, weight, or size.</note> of both quantity and quality. It is necessary that the substrate always precedes that thing which lies within it. 

Nor will it be destroyed by the arrival of any contrary quality. Indeed, no quality is contrary to matter itself, because by its nature it receives all qualities equally, and no form that needs the support of matter is repugnant to it. For it would be repugnant to itself if it destroyed its own foundation. Nor does matter need some other seat or location, lest by the removal of that seat it might fall into the abyss. For matter itself is the primary support of all things; and if some violence were to destroy it, it would either lead it into nothingness or transform it into something else. 

The first cannot happen. For whatever acts, does so out of a natural appetite to propagate its own perfection, so that it may generate something else as similar to itself as possible. This is clear in the elements, plants, and animals, where it appears that the natural appetite is directed toward the **Good**—namely toward life, toward being, and the like—and not toward their contraries. This is because this appetite was inserted into all subsequent things by the **Supreme Good** (as we have said). For from whence things are, from there they are moved, and toward that place all things are carried. Therefore, every appetite and operation of all things, arising from the Good, tends toward and is reflected back into the Good.

Furthermore, one who wishes to remove matter entirely from the midst of things cannot establish his own new work anywhere once the foundation of all generable forms has ceased to exist. Thus, matter would be lost, and nothing new would be produced. For that which is to be made anew, if it requires matter, can no longer be made if matter is removed; if it does not require matter, it is free from it. That which is free from matter towers above it and is procreated by its Author separately from matter. Therefore, while its Author acts upon it, because He fashions it far removed from matter, He brings no violence upon matter, nor does He move matter in any way during that thing's generation, for the work to be finished does not require it. Therefore, that which begets a new thing—whatever kind it may be, whether needing matter or foreign to it—does not lead matter into nothingness.

Or perhaps He will change it into something else, so that one part of matter remains while another part perishes? Not at all. For matter is simple; it is not composed of "matter and form," since it is the **first and formless power**, nor does it require a certain collection of parts for its existence, since by its natural origin it precedes the dimensions of quantity. Moreover, if it were so changed that something remained after the change was complete, what would that thing be? Would it be matter? If it is matter, it does not yet seem to have been changed into something else, since it remains. If it is quantity or quality, that is indeed absurd, because these cannot remain without matter. If some form remains that towers above matter, what was the need to lose the matter? This form would become a total stranger, which is in no way made from matter and is produced far away from it. Rather, because matter is one thing and a form removed from it is entirely another, nothing of the matter is left behind by that changed, distant form.

Let us therefore conclude thus: Matter cannot be changed from what it is in any other way than if it were turned into nothing. Nature does not allow anything to be turned into nothing. Therefore, matter does not perish. Much less will that natural power perish which is the **mistress of matter**. The mistress of matter is that efficient power which forms it. That power which first moves it, forms it. The **source of motion is the rational soul**, to which qualities serve as instruments for moving matter. And...

<meta>This page continues Ficino's argument from Chapter IV. Having established that matter is indestructible, he now moves to the "Fifth Reason" for the soul's immortality: its independence from matter. He uses the Aristotelian framework of the four causes to show that the soul (the "third essence") is higher in the hierarchy of being than physical bodies or qualities.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<meta>catchword: Par- (Partially)</meta>

<margin>☛</margin> Every rational soul, by the nature of its <term>third essence</term> <note>Ficino organizes the universe into five levels: God, Angel, Soul (the Third Essence), Quality, and Body. The soul is the "middle" or "third" rank.</note>, presides over the whole of matter. But more on this elsewhere. Indeed, God as Unity produces matter; the Angel (as the Platonists believe) strengthens and orders it; and the immortal soul moves and forms it. God is Unity, who gives units of being to immortal matter. The Angel is the immortal order, who provides order to immortal matter. The Soul is immortal life, which, by moving, provides life to immortal matter.

### Fifth reason: because it is free from matter. Chapter V.

**P**hysicists <note>In the 15th century, "Physicists" referred to natural philosophers who studied the "physics" or nature of the world.</note> count four causes of natural things: the <term>efficient</term> <note>The agent that brings a thing into being.</note>, the <term>final</term> <note>The purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note>, the <term>material</term>, and the <term>formal</term>. The efficient cause of man is universal nature and man himself; the final cause is human happiness; the material cause is the body; and the formal cause is the soul. Whenever something is said to exist "through itself," it is understood to exist without a cause. Whenever it exists "through another," it exists through a cause. God alone exists "through Himself" in such a way that He exists through no cause; for this reason, He is entirely through Himself, because He excludes all four types of causes from Himself. A natural body exists entirely "through another," for it includes all four causes at once. Below God, nothing can exist that lacks an efficient cause and a goal. Since God is the one maker of all things and their end, nothing besides God will be found that should be called existing "through itself" in a way that lacks an efficient cause and a goal. 

However, it is not fitting that everything beneath God should exist "through another" in a way that they are *entirely* through another. Surely these two states—"entirely through oneself" and "entirely through another"—are separated from each other by a very long interval; therefore, between these two, there is a need for a middle point that is somewhat similar to both. Since every agent acts according to its own nature, it is necessary that the work made most closely by it—because it is drawn immediately from the agent’s nature—appears as similar to it as possible. Therefore, that which is made most closely and with a primary purpose (so to speak) by God, must not turn out to be utterly dissimilar to God. 

Thus, between God and the body there are some things which are not said to exist "entirely through another." Such a thing appears to be <term>quality</term> <note>Such as heat, color, or sweetness, which are not physical objects themselves but "qualities" of objects.</note>, which is not produced through four causes like a body, but depends only on three causes. A body has matter and form as its causes, as well as an efficient and a final cause; but quality does not have "form" as its formal cause. For quality is itself a certain kind of form. No form, insofar as it is a form, is itself "formed" by another; however, a quality is still produced by something and is directed toward a certain end by the agent, and it also depends on matter. For, as if from a cause, such an offspring is led out into the light from the "pregnant womb of matter," and it is extended and divided along with that matter. Therefore, quality surpasses the body by one degree, because it is in some way said to exist "through itself," since it is not formed by another. 

But why should the <term>third essence</term> <note>The Soul.</note>, which is more sublime than quality, not also surpass quality by at least one degree, just as quality certainly surpasses the body by one? But how? Not by the fact that the essence lacks an efficient or final cause, since this belongs to God alone. Nor by this, that this essence does not have a form as its cause, for quality possesses that same trait. It remains that it surpasses quality only in this: that it does not depend on matter, which is not at all true of quality. Thus, it is necessary to proceed step by step from four opposites into four opposites through three and two, so that just as we ascended above the four causes of the body into the three causes of quality, so we may ascend above the three causes of quality into the two causes of the third essence. 

Therefore, this essence will have only an efficient and a final cause, but it will not have a formal or material cause. Finally, the Angel surpasses this essence by one degree, because the Angel neither depends on matter nor is inclined toward matter, since it is occupied most closely by God. Although the third essence does not depend on matter, nevertheless, being made further from God and near to matter, it is in a certain way inclined toward it; because of this inclination, it is called "soul." And although it is inclined, it does not depend on it, which we have demonstrated by many reasons. 

The first is what we have already assigned. The second is that if this essence were submerged in matter, it would never emerge into divine things, which are most remote from matter; and thus it would not be a fitting "knot of the world," because it would not connect the lowest things with the highest. The third is that since it is moved primarily, it is necessarily moved through itself freely in a circle. If it is moved through itself, it certainly operates through itself. If this is so, it also exists through itself, enslaved to no bodies. If it is moved freely, it is not bound to matter. If it revolves in a circle, it recovers itself into itself, leaving matter behind. The fourth is that if it dominates matter by moving and forming it first, it is not mixed with matter. Through these points, it appears that the essence which is the seat of the soul—which Plato also calls the "mixing bowl" <note>original: "pateram." Referring to the *Crater* in Plato's *Timaeus*, where the Creator mixed the elements of the World Soul.</note> of souls in the *Timaeus*—has no origin from bodies, and also is not composed of quantitative parts.

He explains that while the soul "inclines" toward the body to give it life, its ability to contemplate divine things and its self-governed movement prove it is an independent, immortal substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Fifth Reason for the immortality of the soul, focusing on why the soul cannot be broken apart or corrupted by physical forces. It then transitions into the Sixth Reason, which uses geometric and logical arguments to show that the soul, being indivisible, cannot be "touched" or harmed by divisible, material qualities.</meta>

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V.</header>
<meta>catchword: Seventh</meta>

its parts; for such parts exist only in bodies and qualities, and not in forms separated from the body. Therefore, the soul will not be dissipated by being dissolved into any parts. Indeed, it has no distance between parts, since it is not divided within the body; nor will it ever fail because it is withdrawn from some support. For that essence, which is by its nature the mistress of bodies, requires no bodily foundation. Nor will it perish because the contrary and clashing forces of the elements <note>In ancient and Renaissance science, the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) were thought to be in constant conflict; the soul, being spiritual, is above this struggle.</note> might sometimes disturb it; for these clash only within matter. But the soul is placed by God above matter, so that the storm of the elements and the inequality of competing qualities cannot reach it. Furthermore, it will never be stained by sometimes receiving a quality that is foreign or hostile to its nature, which might bring a harmful <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passionem." In this context, "passion" means a state of being acted upon or undergoing a change, often a destructive one, rather than just an emotion.</note> upon it. For the first subject exposed to passion is matter; it is through matter that both the quantity embedded in it and the quality adhering to that quantity are exposed to passion. Therefore, that essence which is separated from matter—that is, a power that is separable—has no power within itself by which it might receive anything foreign or hostile, and thus be subjected to passion.

## Sixth reason: because it is indivisible. Chapter VI.

**P**re-eminently, since the soul is indivisible, it does not receive divisible and corporeal qualities. For that which is divisible cannot touch what is indivisible. For if an indivisible thing is said to be touched by something divisible, we must ask whether this divisible thing touches that indivisible thing with a certain point of itself, or with some divisible part of itself. If you admit the first, then it is only a point that touches the thing; and so it is not a divisible thing, but something indivisible that touches that indivisible thing. But if you say that it touches it with some divisible part of itself, then we reason as follows: If this divisible thing touches what you call indivisible through some divisible part of itself, it is necessary that the other thing is also touched through a similarly divisible part of its own. For how can this touch that, unless that is also touched? And how can this touch that through several of its parts, unless that is also touched through parts of itself? Indeed, to the extent that this touches, to that extent that is touched. Therefore, the thing you claimed was indivisible is forced to be divisible the moment it is granted that it is touched by a divisible thing.

Therefore, that indivisible essence of the soul is never touched by any divisible quality. I say it is not touched by a "straight line," nor even by a "reflected" one. Not by a straight line, because the soul itself does not receive a quality running directly against it. Not by a reflected one, because since it is exempt from the body, it is not snatched away by the force and fury of the qualities boiling in the body, and therefore it is not corrupted by any of them. Or perhaps it will be corrupted by some indivisible quality that it might easily receive? Not at all. For the reception of indivisible qualities perfects the thing that receives them; it does not corrupt it. This is evident from those indivisible images of things <note>Ficino refers to "species" or mental images that enter the mind or are reflected in a mirror—they convey information without physically changing the object.</note> which are received by water, mirrors, and the soul, both through sense and through reason. 

In truth, one thing does not act upon another for any other reason than to show its own form to the other. Indeed, all things are led to act for the sake of propagating their own nature. But no corporeal thing can, or even strives to, generate its own bodily form within the essence of the soul, which is so segregated from matter that bodily forms have no entry into it. But could God or an Angel introduce a new form into the soul through which the soul might be disturbed? Not at all; because if they create any form subsisting through itself, they create it apart from the soul; therefore the soul is not disturbed by its creation. If, however, they infuse some power into the soul, such a power is beneficial, since it comes from the highest causes which are the preservers of the soul itself. Therefore, the soul does not perish through such a power, but is preserved.

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

## Seventh Reason: Because the soul has its own being within its own essence.
### Chapter VII.

**W**e call one thing "essence" and another thing "being." By **essence**, we mean the rationale of a thing which is understood through its definition. By **being**, however, we mean the act of that essence and its presence in the nature of things. Take for example a *Crinita* <note>original: "Crinita," literally a "hairy star," the Latin term for a comet.</note>; the essence of a comet is this rationale and definition: "a dry vapor ignited by fire in the upper air, moving in an orderly circle through the air." This definition remains true today even if no comet happens to be shining anywhere at this moment. But the **being** of such a comet is said to occur when that specific nature of the comet (which is described by the definition every day) actually shines somewhere right now. This "being" does not occur without a specific place and time. For that essence only becomes present here or there, at this hour or that. Therefore, the **being** of natural things requires a specific place and time, but their **essence** does not. For that rationale of the comet is true even if no comet is currently burning anywhere. Indeed, if that definition included a specific time and place—such as "today here" or "tomorrow there," at the same hour and in the same region of the air where one comet exists—then all comets would have to exist at once. For the common essence and rationale of the comet is the same in every individual comet. But if this rationale were bound to a specific place and time, all comets would be restricted to those same limits of space and time—just as the power of reason, because it is included in the definition of "man," belongs to every individual human being.

Thus, the essence and the being of natural things differ in this way: "being" is bound to a specific place and time, but "essence," as far as its own nature is concerned, relates equally to almost all time and every place. For humanity itself can exist no less in other ages than in our own, and no less in the East than in the West. Yet Plato and Socrates, in order to exist and live, require this or that specific place and time. In "humanity," the essence is described; in these specific men, "being" is observed. Therefore, essence is excluded from the limits of specific time and place. Because of this, it requires no place for its own preservation by its nature, nor does it have boundaries of time by which it might eventually be surpassed, since it is exempt from such boundaries. Therefore, it flourishes everywhere and always. Thus, every essence, according to itself, is said to be immortal.

The essence of every form is such by its nature. However, when the Author of forms <note>Ficino refers here to God as the Creator.</note> gives birth to essences and brings them into being, He determines some to such a "being" that they exist only within a body; hence the "being" of such an essence or form is constricted by the agent to physical conditions. When "being" is constricted to a body, it also limits the essence to those same boundaries. The conditions of natural bodies are that they fill a place and are moved by time. Therefore, that form—which by itself would have existed beyond a specific time and place—now undergoes its own time and place. Because it undergoes time, it begins gradually, changes, and ceases. Because it undergoes place, while the body in which it lies receives contrary qualities every day, that form is also disturbed by the "storm" of such qualities and becomes mortal. Such are the forms and qualities of bodies.

However, the Author brings other essences of forms into being in such a way that they do not obtain their "being" in some other thing or matter, but contain it within themselves. Such are all forms that are foreign to any dealings with matter. For they have their being in themselves, not in matter. Now, whatever is received from another is usually received according to the capacity of the thing that receives it, and is drawn to its properties. But every essence is immortal by itself. Therefore, the "being" which is received by that essence—since it is received by an immortal thing in an immortal way—is made immortal. Therefore, a form that is separated from the company of matter is immortal on all sides; that is, as much according to its "being" as according to its "essence." Such is the <term>third essence</term> <note>In Ficino’s hierarchy of reality, the soul is the "third essence," the middle link that connects the eternal divine world with the temporal material world.</note>, the fountain of rational souls.

***

## Eighth Reason: Because the soul has its own proper being and never departs from its own form.
### Chapter VIII.

**G**eneration and corruption are opposed to each other in such a way that they tend toward contradictions; generation is a path toward **being**, while corruption is a path toward **non-being**. Each thing tends toward being because it receives a certain form. It tends toward non-being because it is forced to lose its form. In the arts, no work is "such a thing" because of its matter, but because of its form. A bronze horse or man is not called such because of the matter of the bronze...

<summary>Ficino argues that while individual physical things exist in specific times and places (and thus die), the "essence" or definition of a thing is timeless and immortal. Because the rational soul is a form that exists independently of matter, it possesses its "being" within its own immortal essence, making it inherently undying.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical exploration of "being" and "essence" in Book V. The previous page established that while a definition (essence) is eternal, the actual existence (being) of a physical object depends on specific conditions. Here, Ficino transitions from physical objects to the metaphysical nature of the soul.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V.
<meta>catchword: ...tence [essentia]</meta>

is said to be so, because although bronze is equally prepared to take on the figures of all animals, it is called a horse or a man only because of a certain form and likeness provided by the craftsman. This part of the bronze is called a horse, that part a man. Similarly in nature, matter is not the reason why Plato is a man, or why a fig is a tree. For the same primary matter of the world is common to humans, beasts, and trees; and that same matter existed many centuries before Plato, and will exist many after Plato, yet Plato himself does not. Therefore, Plato does not possess a human appearance because of matter, but because of a specific <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of humors and physical qualities in a body.</note> of the body and a soul, which are called **forms**. We must judge other things similarly and conclude summarizedly: anything whatsoever has its own proper "being," nature, and species—distinct from others—because of its **form**.

For this reason, whatever ceases to exist loses its "being" precisely because it is separated from its own proper form, just as its "being" had previously begun when it obtained that form. Therefore, a thing composed of matter and form—for example, fire, which is composed of its mass and its natural heat—perishes when it is separated from its form. The coldness of water or earth can work its way into the matter of the fire and thereby expel the heat, which is the natural form of the fire; once expelled, it ceases to be fire. Thus, that fire composed of matter and a certain heat loses its "being" when it loses its heat—its substantial form, I mean, along with its properties, which for the sake of argument we now call "heat" (since it lacks a more obvious name). But what about the heat itself? It loses its "being" because it is a form, and "being" comes from form; it ceases when it is driven out of that matter. 

For in naturally composite things, "being" is granted to the whole, not to the individual parts. Indeed, the "being" of the fire itself belongs properly to the composite, not to the matter alone, nor to the heat alone. For when heat was drawn out from the "seed" of the matter by a natural agent during the generation of the fire, it was extended through all the matter of the fire under the condition that it depended entirely upon it. The heat did not have a "being" proper to itself; rather, through the common "being" of the whole fire, the heat was also said to "be." However, that common "being" ceases when those two parts are separated from one another. When the common "being" ceases, the form—which flourished through that common "being"—also perishes. Matter, however, does not perish, because it immediately takes on another form through which it may exist; thus, while it loses a specific heat, it loses its "fiery being." When it receives a certain coldness or moisture, it may take on an "earthy" or "horsey" being. 

Conclude, then, that a composite thing, such as fire or water, perishes when it is separated from its form; but that form is lost when it departs from the "law of the former." The Sun, which generated the fire, acted as the "former" of the fire. It drew out the heat from the fuel into that matter under the law that it should be contained within the "being" of the whole composite. This law is transgressed when it departs from that matter. It departs when it is put to flight by the cold. If, therefore, something departs neither from its own form nor from the law of its "former," in what way can it perish? For the "being" of everything proceeds from its form and is preserved by the law of its "former."

*The soul, however, because of the property of that third essence, is a certain "mere form"; it is not composed of matter and form, nor is it "lying" within matter. Therefore, remaining within itself, whatever is within it is nothing other than form. Its own essence, therefore, is not formed by anything else, but it is the form of itself—that is, it is form itself. Now, there is nothing that can be separated from its own essence by itself, because nothing departs from itself. Indeed, all things, by natural instinct and perpetual effort, preserve themselves as much as they can and cling to themselves. Therefore, if the soul is never separated from itself and is its own form, it is never separated from its form. Thus, it never ceases to exist, since "being" is always drawn from form. It is not separated from itself by its own will, as we have said. But neither is it forced by external violence to withdraw from itself, because whatever it receives from the outside, it receives in its own specific way. The soul is clearly spiritual and absolute from place and time; therefore, it receives all things in a spiritual and absolute manner. Now, when spiritual and absolute things are taken up by something, they by no means destroy it. For spiritual reception, even when it occurs in bodies, does not corrupt those bodies (though they are unlike itself), as seen in the reception of images in water or a mirror. Much less, then, will it corrupt a spiritual thing that is similar to itself. Furthermore, since that absolute thing which was imagined to be received by the essence of the soul is eternal, why should it destroy its own vessel? Is it to feed itself from that vessel's matter? No, since that which is eternal does not need food. Is it to propagate itself and generate something like itself from that matter? Not at all. For that which remains always the same does not need propagation, nor can it generate something perpetual out of a corruptible thing. Therefore, it does not corrupt anything to generate a perpetual likeness of itself. In no way, therefore, can anything take hold of the essence of the soul* <note>original: "capere," translated here as "take hold of" or "seize," continuing the thought that the soul cannot be overtaken or destroyed by external forces.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that unlike physical objects (composites of matter and form), the soul is a "pure form" and its own essence. Because nothing can be separated from itself, the soul cannot be separated from the form that gives it life, making it naturally immortal.</summary>

[...capac]ity to take from which it might be destroyed. Justly, it cannot receive anything harmful at all, since it lacks matter, which is called the first and proper receptacle of such <term>passions</term> <note>In this context, "passions" refers to "undergoing" or being affected by external change or decay, rather than emotions.</note>. Nay, indeed, if this essence is its own form, nothing will ever fall between it and its form. For if any middle thing were to fall between it and its form, that thing would surely become closer to the form than its own essence. But the essence itself is its very form. Thus something would become closer to it than it is to itself, which is the most absurd of all things. Therefore, nothing inserts itself as a middle between it and its form. If this is so, it is not separated from its form by any intervening thing. But neither is it separated by its own will, wherefore in no way does it depart from itself and its form. Nor does it depart by the law of things formed: since indeed it was created by that law, that it might consist in itself. And it always remains so. For from that state it is cast down by no one. Not by itself, for any thing whatever preserves its own species and dignity for itself according to its power. Not by higher causes, because those causes, by the same law they produced it, also maintain it in the same state. Not by lower things. For the higher is not conquered by the lower. Therefore the soul, because it is pure form, and thus departs neither from its own form nor from the law of the Former <note>original: "formantis"; referring to God as the shaper or creator of forms.</note>, remains without a doubt immortal.

->*Ninth reason, because "to be" belongs to it through itself. Chapter IX.*<-

That which belongs to something <term>through itself</term> <note>original: "per se"; a philosophical term meaning a quality is essential to the thing's nature, not accidental.</note> is never separated from it. Roundness is in a circle by its very nature, and therefore there is never a circle without roundness. But roundness is sometimes in wood, not because it is wood (for otherwise all wood would be round), but because it receives a circular figure from a craftsman, which roundness accompanies, and so it is then forced to take on roundness. Wood sometimes ceases to be round as soon as it first ceases to be circular, and then it remains wood, but not round. But a circular figure is so necessarily round that if it ceased to be round, it would also cease to be circular. Similarly, heat belongs to fire through itself, moisture to water, and light to the Sun. In no other way does "to be" <note>original: "esse"; here meaning the act of existing.</note> belong to form through itself. For whatever a thing is in any species, that which it is it certainly obtains from a certain proper form leading to such a species. Since therefore a proper "being" belongs to each thing through its proper form, it follows that "to be" generally and simply belongs to it through the very genus of form. Whence it is necessary that the form itself be called the source of being, and exist through itself. 

But if it were said to exist through something else, we would ask whether that through which the form is said to exist has the nature of form or of matter. Not matter, because we see in individual composite things that the "being" of each is its own property, and does not follow matter. Therefore, even in this very form through which composite things exist, that through which the form itself exists does not have the power of matter, but of form. Thus the question returns to the same point: whether that other form through which the form exists, is through itself, or through something else? If through itself, then it is established that form must be called the source of being. But if through another, then we shall ask as before, and there will be a progression into infinity. 

Wherefore, "to be" belongs to form through itself. But indeed the Founder of forms, for a certain end and the integrity of the worldly work, produces forms in existence with such a distinction that He determines each naturally to a certain way of being: some to exist in a body, and others to exist in themselves without matter. A form impressed upon matter does not properly "exist," nor does it have its own proper "being," but it is called that by which the composite itself is, and it exists through the common "being" of the whole. If "to be" belongs to form through itself, this form which is in the body [the soul], because it is itself also a form, certainly has this property: that "to be" belongs to it through itself. 

But how, since it depends on matter and is contained under the "being" of the whole composite? Pay attention: "to be" belongs to it through itself—that is, it follows it through itself; it follows, I say, through itself, that is, according to its nature. For what else does "through itself" mean than "through its nature"? Its nature is such as its maker assigned to it. The Maker, however, decreed that it should inhere in matter. This, therefore, is its nature: to inhere in matter. Existence follows it through this nature. Therefore, existence follows it through itself—that is, as it inheres in matter. Thus, in a certain way, it belongs to it to be fixed in matter before it belongs to it to exist. Wherefore it exists as long as it clings to matter. However, it does not always cling, because matter, being ready for all forms, often gives place to contrary forms that drive out the previous forms. Therefore it does not exist always. But that form which is so determined toward being by the Founder that it consists in itself apart from the body, also because it is a form, has this property: that "to be" [belongs to it]

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a "pure form" and since the very nature of form is to be the source of existence, the soul cannot be separated from life. He distinguishes between material forms that perish when matter changes and the soul, which exists independently of physical corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration that the soul, as a "pure form" or "separate form," possesses existence by its very nature. Ficino is refuting potential objections that would compare the soul's existence to temporary physical properties like the heat of fire.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V.

...it belongs to itself through itself—through its own nature, I say. The nature assigned to it is to cling to itself. Therefore, its being follows it insofar as it clings to itself; that is, its existence follows it, not springing at all from a subject <note>In medieval philosophy, a "subject" usually refers to physical matter that "underlies" properties. Ficino is saying the soul's existence doesn't depend on being attached to matter.</note>. And as often as you say "being follows it through itself," you say just as often "being follows it as it clings to itself." Nothing, however, departs from itself. For what falls between "self" and "itself" that could separate it from itself? If it exists as long as it clings to itself, and because it clings always, it exists always. Such a form indeed is the soul. Therefore, it is immortal. 

But someone might object to this reasoning thus: *just as fire is hot through itself, it is hot always while it exists, yet it is not always [existing], from which it follows that it is not absolutely hot always; so also the soul's essence, because it is properly and truly a form subsisting in itself, is therefore through itself, and because it is through itself, it exists always—namely, while it exists. It does not, however, exist forever. Therefore, it is not always.* 

This objection is judged ridiculous for two reasons. First, it is self-contradictory in its construction. *That form exists through itself, therefore it always exists—namely, while it exists—but it does not exist always.* For here there are four statements, of which the second, which says *Therefore it always exists*, contradicts this later one which infers *But it does not exist always.* Next, an objection of this kind abounds in superfluities when it adds: *namely, while it exists*. For this phrase *while it exists* cannot be said to be anything other than that first phrase where it is said *it always exists*. Otherwise, there would be a double "is" and a double "being" in the same thing, and the thing would not exist as one, but as two. Hence it follows that the "is" which is placed when *namely, while it exists* is added, is that same "is" which had already been placed when it was said earlier, *it exists always*. Things that are the same must be treated by the same logic. Therefore, if the first "is" is uttered absolutely, so the second "is" ought to be uttered absolutely without that phrase *namely, while it exists*. Therefore one ought to say: *It is, it always is, it is*, but not add *namely, while it exists.* Or if you add that later part to the first "is," then add it to the second, and third, into infinity, and you will never find the first root of being by which it belongs to that thing to exist and exist always. But what has no root of being is nothing at all. 

Come now, stay your step. *That separated form, such as the soul is, exists through itself; therefore, it exists always.* Nay, even if being and being hot were exactly the same, when you composed it thus: *Because fire is hot through itself, it is hot always*, you would immediately add: *Being hot and being are the same; therefore it is, and always.* But now you cannot conclude in that way, because being and being hot are not the same; otherwise, whatever things *are* would be hot, and whatever stops being hot would stop being, which does not happen. Therefore fire, always while it exists, is hot, because in a certain way it "is" first and is "hot" afterwards. And because being comes before being hot, and is something other than being hot, heat seems to be in the essence of fire through some medium, so that first the essence of fire is placed, second its being, and in the third place, its being hot. Nay indeed, the essence of fire obtains being through the fact that it clings to matter. For in a certain way it lies hidden in the womb of matter before it is brought into the light. And just as it lay hidden before it existed, so also it clings afterwards, so that it does not cease to exist. It also obtains heat through the fact that it possesses being. Therefore it stops being hot when it stops being; it stops being when it stops clinging <note>That is, when the fire's form is separated from the fuel/matter.</note>. But the soul's essence, since it is an unattached form, obtains being through itself, and in it, being itself is the first and proper <term>act</term> <note>In this context, "act" (actus) refers to the state of being real or "in act," rather than just a potentiality.</note> of the essence; nor is there any bond through which being is connected with essence, which, upon being loosened, would cause dissolution. And although both being hot and being belong to the essence of fire through some condition, being belongs to the essence of the soul not through any condition, but absolutely. Therefore, although fire exists and is hot always with a certain condition, the soul nonetheless always exists absolutely.

### *The tenth reason: because "through itself" refers to God.* Cap. X.

**I**f, however, there should seem to be any condition by virtue of which the soul exists always, it is not through any relation to bodies, whose help it does not need, but in relation to the First Cause <note>A standard philosophical term for God as the origin of all things.</note>, from which it descends. But since a relation of this kind is completed through the very nature of the soul itself, nothing prevents the soul from existing through itself and absolutely, and always without condition. This we shall investigate by this reasoning: since all things depend on the first cause of things, individual things remain in their own being to the extent that they are related to the first cause. Moreover, they look back to it as they carry some likeness of it. That cause is <gloss>pure</gloss> act...

<summary>Ficino refutes the argument that the soul's existence is temporary by distinguishing between accidental properties (like the heat of fire) and essential existence. He concludes that the soul's "being" is an absolute act derived directly from its likeness to the First Cause (God).</summary>

...that [First Cause] is the purest act <note>original: "actus purissimus." In Aristotelian and Platonic thought, "act" or "actuality" refers to the fulfillment of a thing's potential. God is "pure act" because He is fully realized with no potential to be anything other than what He is.</note>, most foreign to every property of matter. To this act, lower things are judged similar not by their matter, but rather by their form (which exists as a certain act). Thus it happens that all things look back to the first cause through their form. Therefore, whatever things are composed of matter and form—such as the elements and mixed bodies—look back to the first cause not through themselves, nor through their whole nature, but only through that part of themselves which is called form.

Argue in this way: As they are referred to the first principle, so they exist; but they are referred through something else, therefore they exist through something else. Things that exist through something else are not stable; for if left to themselves, they vanish into nothing. In themselves, therefore, they are nothing, whatever they may be that exists through something else. Such indeed are natural bodies. But what of corporal forms? Certainly they are similar. For the form implanted in bodies has indeed lost its excellence and turned out entirely corporal, since it has now undergone all the conditions of the body. There are two conditions of the body: extension according to place, and change according to time. But the form immersed in bodies is stretched out with the width of the body, and is changed as the body is altered. Since, therefore, it has been made entirely corporal and stripped of its former excellence, it by no means exists through itself (as we have said elsewhere), nor does it have any being of its own, but is so joined with matter that the being of the whole is one. If therefore it is not through itself, it certainly does not act through itself. Therefore, if it is referred to the first cause, it will be referred through something else, namely through that by which it exists. 

But it exists through another more sublime form, free from matter, on which it also continually hangs into matter—just as an image in a mirror hangs from a man’s face—through which it is also constantly referred to the first cause. If therefore the corporal form exists entirely through something else, since it is also referred to the first principle through something else, what then is that through which both the natural body and its form are referred to the first? Surely it is that **third essence**, <note>In Ficino's cosmic hierarchy, the "Third Essence" is the Soul, which sits between the eternal (God/Angel) and the temporal (Quality/Matter).</note> which we have long since placed above the qualities of bodies. An essence of this kind refers the qualities of bodies to God in the same way in which it brings them about in matter. But it brings them about by its operation, and its operation is mobile. Therefore, through agitation it generates, and through agitation it also refers. Thus it refers wonderfully. 

From this it follows that natural bodies and their forms—because they are referred to God through something else and through motion—neither exist through themselves nor are stable, but they waver entirely and perish. But the third essence, because it is its own form—indeed, it is that very form, and a form free from matter—is therefore referred to God through itself. As it is referred, so it exists. Therefore, it also exists through itself. But it is referred through its essence, and that is stable. For this reason, being referred to the stable God through its own stable essence, it remains stable. Truly, this essence is the cause of its own relation, the principle of perfection. It never deserts itself; therefore it never ceases to refer itself, never ceases to perfect itself by referring. God indeed always overflows; she <note>Ficino uses the feminine "illa" to refer to the Soul (Anima).</note> always drinks. Therefore, both on the part of what is drunk and the one drinking, she always drinks Being itself and remains immortal.

---

### Eleventh reason: Because the soul is not composed of any potentiality into which it can be resolved. Chapter XI.

**J**ust as generation occurs through the joining of form with matter, so decay <term>corruption|the philosophical term for the breakdown or destruction of a composite thing</term> occurs through the separation of form from matter. Where there is no joining of these things, no separation happens. Such a composition does not exist in the soul. But let us pursue this reason more broadly. In the decay of any thing, the act of the thing itself is lost, but after it, there remains something that was underlying that act—like some receptive potentiality <term>potentia|the capacity to be something else or to receive a form</term>—so that the decay does not end in nothingness, just as generation does not happen out of nothing. 

A thing composed of form and matter is resolved back into matter. Also, that form which had been drawn out from the "kindling" <note>original: "fomite." Ficino uses this term to describe the latent potentiality in matter to produce physical forms.</note> of matter is led back into the kindling of matter. But in the soul, its act is its very being. Its essence and substance is that very potentiality which underlies the act of being. For in absolute forms <note>Forms that exist independently of matter, such as the soul or angels.</note> there is almost no other composition than that of essence and being, or something similar. Essence takes the place of matter and potentiality; being takes the place of form and act. If the soul is destroyed, its being is entirely lost. But is the essence also lost? Not at all. For no thing is resolved into nothing, because a thing that is so simple that it cannot be resolved otherwise than into nothing is also such that it was made by God through creation out of nothing. But that which is such is subject to its author, God, alone. But the vital and beneficial influence of God destroys nothing. Therefore, if the soul is destroyed...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul (the "Third Essence") is immortal because it exists through its own stable nature rather than through a physical subject, and lacks the matter-form composition that allows physical things to decay.</summary>

is constructed, for although it might lose its "being," <note>original: "esse." In this context, "being" refers to the specific act of existing in time and space.</note> nevertheless its essence remains. This is also evident from the fact that the more noble a thing is, the nobler is its matter and the nobler its form. Souls are significantly more excellent than bodies. Therefore, beneath their "being"—as if beneath a form and an "act" <note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian philosophy, an "act" or "actuality" is the realization of a possibility. The soul is the "act" of the body.</note>—there lies a certain matter and "potential," <note>original: "potentia." Potentiality is the capacity to become something or receive a form.</note> if any lies there at all, which is more excellent than that found under the form and "being" of any body whatsoever. That which holds the place of prime matter and potential in souls is their very essence. Thus, their essence is more eminent than the matter of bodies. The matter of bodies is incorruptible; therefore, is it any wonder if that [spiritual] essence can be incorruptible? From this it follows that if the soul were ever imagined to lose its "being," the essence and substance would necessarily still remain. If this remains, it certainly exists. If it still exists, "being" has not yet been lost. Thus, if the soul were said to be corrupted, it necessarily remains even after corruption; indeed, it even lives. For the "being" of the soul is nothing other than living.

But lest anyone say that the soul's "being" itself is dissolved into essence, and that essence no longer exists because it is without "act" (even if the "potential" perhaps remains somewhere), one must remember that this essence cannot be reduced to physical matter or the potential of matter. This is because it neither consists of matter as a part of itself, nor does it sprout from the potential of matter. Furthermore, it cannot be dissolved into the potential of any acting cause, except perhaps into the power of God, who alone created the soul. Yet the soul does not die for the reason that it is resolved back into the "First Life." <note>Ficino refers to God as the source of all life.</note> It would die only if, having been brought back into God, it ceased to be a soul. 

But just as the shape of wax impressed by a seal is not destroyed when it is perfectly matched to the seal, but is instead restored to its own likeness, so too the essence of the soul—if it is ever moved toward the "Idea" <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal patterns in the divine mind according to which all things are made.</note> through which God had arranged it in a certain species of being—is confirmed in its original "being." For a subsequent "act" is greatly strengthened by the "First Act." Indeed, how can God be the "limit" toward which corruption tends, since He is the "efficient limit" from whom and by whom all creation and generation is derived? Or in what way does God, who is "pure act," concur in the composition of the soul as it is born? It is so that, just as a bodily form is made from the potential of matter and an added "act" of potential—and finally the "act" of that form is resolved back into that potential—likewise from a certain power of God and a certain added "act," a soul is made, which might finally be resolved into the power of God as if into matter. For He who is the "First Act" never plays the part of matter.

Someone might assert that the essence of the soul is resolved neither into matter nor into God, but that it immediately withdraws into itself once its prior "being" is removed. Truly, just as bodily matter cannot exist without a bodily "act," neither can spiritual matter exist apart from a spiritual one. For this reason, the essence which belongs to the matter of spiritual things, and is compared to spiritual "being" as if to a certain "act," is never separated from "being"—from spiritual "being," I say. 

Unless perhaps someone should say that the essence of the soul, while it puts off one "being," puts on another, and that this essence varies such turns in spiritual "being" just as matter varies in its forms. That would be absurd to say: first, because the essence of spiritual things is more stable than the matter of physical things; and second, because since the essence of the soul is the soul's own proper "reason," <note>original: "ratio." Here meaning its defining principle or formula.</note> it does not look toward "one being and then another" equally, but only toward "soul-like being," specifically according to the soul's certain species. Common matter can indeed exist without this "act" or that one, but "proper matter" <note>A technical term for matter already prepared for a specific form.</note> cannot exist without its "proper act." Therefore, the essence of the soul, which exists in such a species of souls, will never receive the "act" of another species of souls, nor will that essence migrate again within the same species from this soul into that one, lest it be as changeable as the matter of bodies. Indeed, if the matter of the heavens is always content with the same form (as most people believe), is it any wonder that the spiritual matter of the soul is always content with the same "act of being"? That essence is life; this "being" is living. Therefore, it always lives.

## Twelfth reason: because it does not have within itself the potential for non-being. Chapter XII.

**N**o thing is ever corrupted unless it has within itself the potential for non-being. For if it were unable "not to be," it would never cease to exist. The soul has no such potential, because among the Platonists the soul is nothing other than a "simple form" subsisting through itself, perfect and complete in its essence, and leading to the production of the species of a living thing. The "act of existing" is there—namely, in that complete and perfect form itself. For each thing exists through the integrity of its form. Therefore, the proper subject of "being" itself in that case is its own form and essence. Where, then, will there be the potential for non-being? Which is...

opposite. Is it in "being" <note>original: "esse." In Scholastic philosophy, "being" is the act of existing.</note> itself? But how can one thing have the repugnant force to seize its own opposite? Or is it in the essence itself? Not here either. For if the essence, by the fact that it is a simple and integral form, is the proper subject of its own being, how can it have the potential for non-being, which is said to be its opposite? For in what way does the proper substance of fire, which is the proper subject for heat, have any potential to receive cold? By what means could it both receive cold and remain fire? Even in those very corporal and mortal substances, there is no potential for non-being insofar as they are complete substances in their own species and endowed with form (for it is according to this that they exist). Rather, they have this potential only insofar as they are underlain by prime matter <note>original: "materia prima." The most basic, formless "stuff" of the physical world which has the capacity to take on any shape but possesses none of its own.</note>, which never rests under any one such form. But this matter is absent from the soul. Therefore, the potential for non-being is nowhere found in the soul. It is, therefore, immortal. 

But let us explain this reasoning more clearly. In those things composed of form and matter, it happens that the matter in some way precedes the work itself. For who would doubt that matter exists in some way before it is formed? I take this matter that precedes the making of the work, and I ask: is it necessary, impossible, or perhaps possible that the work should come from the nature of this matter? It is not necessary, because if it were, the power of the matter would immediately through itself give necessity to the work, and it would not require any more excellent thing to form it; but as it is, it does require it, because that which is unformed cannot form itself. Therefore, as far as the matter is concerned, the future work is not necessary. Is it then impossible? Not this either. For if it were, the matter would be so unsuited to that work that it could never be led toward its form and effect. If, regarding the matter, the work to be done is neither necessary nor impossible, it remains that it is "possible." For this "possible" is the middle ground between those two—I mean, the possibility to be and not to be. For if by the nature of the matter it were possible only "to be," it would undoubtedly be "necessary." If by its nature it were only possible "not to be," it would be "impossible." 

Wherefore, since by the nature of the matter the work itself is equally possible "to be" and "not to be," it is established that in the matter itself, as far as the making of the work is concerned, there is a potential <term>potential (potentia) <gloss>the capacity or "power" for something to happen or exist, which has not yet been realized.</gloss></term> for both being and non-being. Since matter is simple and not composed of multiple natures, this same nature of matter is the potential for both being and non-being, because it is indifferent to both and is not determined to one or the other by itself. It therefore requires a higher agent to determine it toward "being" by forming it. It receives from that agent the form of a lion, from which a lion is made; and this matter of the lion, which previously held in itself the potential to be a lion and not to be a lion, is now determined toward being a lion. 

But does that same indifferent potential for both still remain in the prime matter? If it did not remain, the nature of matter would immediately cease, and nothing would be made or consist of matter if, as soon as something is made, prime matter were deprived of its nature and perished. Therefore, since it remains even after the lion has been generated, that same potential remains—not in the matter specifically close to the lion, but in the prime matter—a potential, I say, for being and non-being alike. It follows that just as the lion began to be at some point through that potential (when previously it was not), so through that same potential it ceases to be at some point after it has existed. Because a potential indifferent to either extreme is either turned toward neither, or it is turned toward both equally and in turn; and just as it was turned toward "being" from "not being," so in turn it is turned from "being" into "not being." And from this follows the corruption of corporal things.

But the rational soul, since it is a simple form from which motion arises in composite things, could not have been made from any preceding matter and subsequent form; and since it is a form subsisting in itself, not leaning on matter (because it proceeds by judging both above and below matter), it is not composed of some potential of matter—as if by a beginning of the soul—with an act of potential added—as if by the soul's perfection. Therefore, it neither consists of matter nor exists from it. If it is such, it proceeded from nothing into the light. Therefore, God alone is its author, as we shall show elsewhere. Yet this soul would never have been made unless it were possible for it to be made. Therefore, a "potential for being born" preceded our soul. Where was that potential? Not in the soul, which did not yet exist. Not in a part of the soul, which is simple and is created as a whole, not in parts. Not in any matter, since the soul does not depend on matter. Not in nothingness, for the potential for being is not grounded in nothingness. For how could one opposite be the foundation for its opposite and contradictory? "Being" and "not-being" are contradictories. It remains that this potential is grounded in the soul's only author, God. Therefore, the "potential for being" through which the soul is produced is God himself, who alone is immortal and stable. As for the potentials according to the harmony...
