The act corresponds [to the power]. Therefore, that act corresponding to the divine power is stable through its essence. Such an act is the soul. And just as there is the same power in God through which God is able to make the soul and the soul is able to be made, so in the soul there is the same act—that is, the same striving—through which both the soul subsists in its own nature and God establishes it within itself. Thus it happens that God has no less a desire to establish the soul in its nature than the soul has to subsist in the same. Since the soul is subject to God alone, if it were to be destroyed by anyone, it must be destroyed by Him. Yet it cannot be destroyed by Him. For how can a cause that produces and preserves something also be its corrupter? Or in what way is the Good itself harmful to anything? Or how can the first and infinite life be the origin of death for anyone? 

Someone might say: God does not destroy the soul by inserting some new force, but by taking away the force previously granted to it—that is, by withdrawing His influence, through which the soul had lived; just as one who creates their image in a mirror by looking into it stops producing the image by withdrawing their face. But we showed a little earlier that this cannot happen there <note>Ficino argues that the soul is a "substantial form"—a permanent thing—unlike a mirror reflection, which is merely an "accidental" appearance that vanishes when the source moves.</note>. Again, if God now pours life into the soul and later does not, a change occurs there from "pouring in" to "not pouring in." I ask: does the soul stop drinking in life, or does God stop pouring it? The soul does not stop drinking it in, since the infusion of life happens within the essence of the soul, because life is the first act of the essence as soon as it receives being <note>original: "esse." In this context, "being" is the basic act of existing.</note>. The soul’s essence is immobile, because it depends without any medium <note>original: "sine medio." Without an intermediary, such as an angel or a physical process.</note> upon the stable God, because it is perfected by standing still and resting: it is disturbed by motion, it reaches for stable things, it rules over falling things, it halts moving things, it collects scattered things, it reconciles opposing things. 

Nor is there in it that potential to "be" and "not to be" equally, such as exists in bodies, which is the beginning of all change. Therefore, the essence of the soul never ceases to receive the act of life, and God never ceases to pour it in. For God has indicated that He will only cease pouring His power into those things in which He inserted from their origin that inclination toward non-existence. Furthermore, God, the institutor of nature, never withdraws anything from a thing that is proper to that thing. Life is proper to the soul—perpetual life, I say—because insofar as it is rational, even without instruction or practice, it generates within itself every day through the power of its nature alone absolute species <note>original: "species absolutas." These are pure mental concepts or forms of things, independent of physical matter.</note>, through which it moves closest to the eternal Ideas <note>original: "ideas." In Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all reality existing in the Divine Mind.</note>. If it is natural for the rational soul to ascend to the Ideas, it is natural for it to rest in the Ideas, so that just as it lived by them naturally, it may live in them naturally; and that which was working according to its nature constantly toward perpetual things, may one day work according to its nature perpetually among perpetual things. And because every Idea is eternal life, whoever can attain an Idea according to their own nature through the mode of the Idea, can also through an eternal mode attain everlasting life.

***

### Thirteenth reason: Because it receives "being" from God without a medium. Chapter XIII.

**A**lthough Plotinus and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who lived in the 3rd and 5th centuries AD.</note> and several other Platonists think the soul is made by an angel, I more willingly follow Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian of the late 5th century, then believed to be the disciple of St. Paul.</note>, Origen, and Aurelius Augustine, the most excellent Platonists, who think the soul is procreated by the one God. Indeed, I am confident this can be demonstrated by this reasoning. The soul is a form so simple and so free that it is neither composed of many parts nor torn out from the bowels of matter. Therefore, when it is made, it cannot be generated from any pre-existing things. For it is not fashioned from diverse things placed far apart and then forced into one, since it lacks parts. Nor is it made from the "fuel" of matter, first unformed and then formed, since it is above matter. Therefore, it is made from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo." A core Christian doctrine meaning creation did not use pre-existing material.</note>. 

But to make something from nothing is proper to God alone. For from the order of works, the order of causes is investigated, because the effect is suited to the causes. Wherefore we must trace back proper effects to their proper causes, and that which is found in common among all proper effects, we must refer back to a cause common to all. Thus, since among all things, besides the proper conditions of each individual thing, "being" itself is found common to all, we ought to assign individual causes for individual conditions and qualities, but for "being" itself, which is the one thing common to all, we must assign one cause common to all. The one cause common to all is God Himself. Therefore, God is truly the cause of *being*; but for being *this or that*, or *in this way or that*, there are certain other causes besides God. Thus, that you *are*, you have from God alone; that you are *a man*, you also have from a human being; and that you are *hot*, you have from fire. God will give being to works; other diverse causes [give] di...

<meta>catchword: quia</meta>

...diverse modes of being, and these indeed by the power of God. That Being which follows nothingness is called "absolute being," for immediately after "nothing" follows "to be" in its simplest sense. After simple Being follows "to be this or that," or "to be such and such"—for instance, to be a man or a horse, to be white or black. For nothing can become "this" or "that" or "such" unless it first *is*, so that it may become this or that. Therefore, being "such" or "this" or "that" does not follow immediately after nothingness, but rather after simple and absolute Being itself. Since it is God's unique property to grant this common and absolute Being to all things, and since that Being follows nothingness before all other modes of being, it is the office of God alone to produce something into Being out of nothing. Thus, the first thing given to all—namely, Being itself—comes from the First Cause; secondary or tertiary gifts <note>Ficino refers to specific qualities or forms (like being a specific person or being a certain color) as "secondary" gifts compared to the primary gift of existence.</note> come from subsequent causes.

Certainly, whatever participates in a certain nature cannot produce that nature in its absolute form. This is because whatever is "such-and-such" through <term>participation</term> <note>In Platonic thought, individual things (like a single human) "participate" in a universal Form (like Humanity). No individual *is* the Form itself.</note> necessarily follows that which is "absolutely such," and indeed exists through it. Whatever it is, if it were to beget something, then surely that which is later would be begetting the thing that is prior to it—and even begetting its own cause—at which point it would also be begetting itself. Therefore, Ariston <note>original: "Aristo"; the father of the philosopher Plato.</note>, because he was not "Man" in an absolute sense, but this specific man constituted in specific matter, did not beget "Humanity" itself in its absolute form, but rather *this* man—namely, Plato—and in such matter.

But since, regarding the nature of being, everything beneath God <term>participates</term> in Being itself and does not possess "to be" simply, but rather "to be such" or "to be that," determined within a certain essence and species, it follows that no thing subject to God produces Being itself. Instead, it grants a certain mode of being to a certain matter. Consequently, such a thing always requires a prior foundation for its work. Furthermore, both art and nature, in whatever they do, produce an "act" <note>The "act" (actus) is the realized or finished state of something that was previously just a possibility.</note> out of a certain potential. A sculptor makes a statue in *act* out of stone that has been prepared so that it already possesses the statue in potential. A man begets a man from seed, in whose power the man resides. That matter from which art and nature make something is sometimes very obedient and fit for the work, and sometimes less fit, so that the potential of the matter is sometimes further from and sometimes closer to the act of the work being fashioned. The potential of air is a short distance from the effect of fire, but the potential of water is far from it. Thus, it is easy to kindle fire from air, but difficult from water. From this, it appears that the agent must be all the more powerful as the interval between the potential and the act is wider. But the distance between *nothing* and *being* is infinite—both because in nothingness there is no proportion to being, and because no distance can be greater than this, nor even imagined.

Only that power which has no proportion to other powers and has no limit can transcend a distance lacking proportion and limit. God alone is a power of this kind, for all other things are exceeded by the power of God. Therefore, God alone produces something into Being out of nothing. Furthermore, every thing besides God himself is called a "creature" by theologians, and is necessarily composed of four things.

For this reason, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Pythagoras, whom Ficino believed held views compatible with Christianity and Plato.</note> place "four elements" not only in bodies, but in spirits as well, because both consist of **essence**, **being**, **power**, and **action**. Truly, in them, essence is one thing and Being is another. For *Being* is the act of *Essence*. If there were no essence there for such an act to adhere to, it would be a "pure and infinite act," because it would be circumscribed by nothing. But this belongs to God alone. Again, Being itself would be absolute, free from any participation in another.

Every such thing is unique in its nature. It belongs, therefore, to God alone. Rightly, then, a creature is not its own Being, because it cannot be its own act of being since it has some mixture of "passive potential" within itself (because it is subject to God), and potential is the opposite of act. Because operation <note>Here, "operation" (operatio) refers to the activity or functioning of a thing, such as thinking or moving.</note> differs from essence even more than Being itself does—for an essence exists before it operates—therefore, where there is a distinction between essence and Being, there is a much greater distinction between operation and essence. Operation is the act of essential power, just as Being is the act of essence. Because a created essence is not its own act, it is also not its own operation; otherwise, such an operation would be self-subsisting and entirely free from the limits of a participant. We have said that such a thing is unique and infinite. But does operation differ from Being in the same way it is shown to differ from essence? Without a doubt. For operation is twofold: one flows outside the operator, like heating; the other remains inside, like knowledge and will. That which flows out undoubtedly differs from Being (which does not flow out from the thing itself); that which remains also differs for the same reason...

<summary>Ficino argues that only God can create out of nothing because the distance between nothingness and existence is infinite, requiring an infinite power. He also defines the four metaphysical components of all created things—essence, being, power, and action—distinguishing them from God, who is "pure act."</summary>
<keywords>Creation ex nihilo, absolute being, Ariston, Plato, potential and act, Pythagorean four elements, metaphysics, essence vs existence</keywords>

Here, he explains why no creature—not even an angel—can act as an intermediary in the creation of the soul, and why the soul is naturally immortal due to its direct link to God.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V. #

<sig>K 3</sig>

->anima<-

...because the being of a creature is enclosed within a certain specific kind of thing. Such activity wanders through many categories; indeed, the intellect and will themselves range through infinite ones. For the object of the former is truth itself, and of the latter is goodness itself. Now, truth and goodness are at least as wide-reaching as that which is called "being" itself. Activity derives its specific nature from its object; therefore, such an activity takes on the forms of all things. 

But does activity differ from power <note>original: *virtute*</note>, and power from essence and being? Certainly. First, because an act is always distinct from potential <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "potential" is the capacity to be something, while "act" is the fulfillment or reality of that thing.</note>. Reason, which is an act, differs from power and essence (which are forms of potential), just as power differs from "being" (which is an act) and from essence. This is because powers are distinguished by their acts, since a specific power corresponds to its own specific act. The act of an essence is *to be*; the act of a power is *activity*. Therefore, essence and power are as distant from one another as being is from activity. 

Why all these many details? So that you may understand that the activity of any creature is bound to its power, and its power and being are bound to its essence. No creature acts directly through its own substance, but through an "acting power," which is a quality or an <term>accidental property</term> <note>An "accident" is a characteristic that can change without destroying the thing itself—like the color of a person’s hair—as opposed to the "essence," which is what the thing is at its core.</note>, since it is distinct from the substance in every way. Thus, whenever something acts, it directly produces certain qualities, and it gives the kind of "being" that it has itself—that is, a being that always relies on something else. Such things, however, require a pre-existing foundation. Things that require a foundation cannot be created out of nothing. Therefore, no creature creates anything—and rightly so. Because its activity and power are attached to something else, and whatever is attached is not free or complete but is limited by the capacity of what receives it, they are bounded by the limits of their own subject. 

Creation, however, requires an infinite power. Thus, the soul is created by God alone. But perhaps someone will think the soul is made by God in such a way that it is brought about through an angel as a medium <note>an intermediary</note>, with God as the craftsman and the angel as the instrument. This opinion seems absurd because an instrument’s nature is such that it is moved by another to move something else, affecting a certain subject and transferring the form of the primary agent over an interval of time. Creation, however, neither requires a subject [matter] nor occurs through movement or time. Furthermore, if the work of creation requires immense power, what could be more absurd than to suggest that the infinite power in God must first be limited in an angel (whose nature is finite) before performing a work that belongs to infinite power? From the above, we conclude that the soul is produced by the highest God without any intermediary.

Why are the angel and the soul not equal in perfection, since both depend directly on God? Because God produces the angel according to one <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonism, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints in the mind of God.</note> and the soul according to another. He makes the former according to a higher Idea and the latter according to a lower one, just as a man and a horse painted by the same artist are not equally beautiful. The figure of the man is more beautiful than the horse because the painter expressed the man’s image according to a more beautiful model <note>original: *exemplar*</note> in his mind than that of the horse. 

But let us now conclude this reasoning: If the essence of the soul is made directly by God, nothing stands between it and God (its preserver) to separate it from Him. And if it needs God alone to be made, it needs God alone to remain. Because God preserves created things through the same power by which He created them, just as the soul proceeded from nothing into being by God’s infinite goodness, so it remains in being far from nothingness by that same power, as a life very close to God and most similar to the divine life. This will be true if the soul either lacks a beginning and an end, like God, or if it had a beginning, it shall at least have no end. 

It is the opinion of <term>Timaeus</term> and Plato <note>A reference to the *Timaeus*, Plato's dialogue on the creation of the physical world.</note> that God, the craftsman of the world, creates His works through Ideas—that is, exemplary and absolute blueprints. Therefore, whatever is created directly through such an Idea always remains as it is; however, what is created subsequently <note>through a secondary cause</note> does not necessarily remain so forever. For the effect closest to the cause must emerge most similar to it, while the more remote effect is less similar and becomes increasingly dissimilar. Thus, an Idea is a power both within itself and eternal. The power that comes directly from it is not within itself—rather, it is in something else—but it exists forever. But that which follows afterward can neither remain the same nor endure forever by its own nature. Since the rational soul is made directly through the Idea of Life, it is a form that is always living by the power of its direct origin. The irrational soul <note>The "animal soul" associated with basic life functions and instincts, but not reason.</note>, however, since it proceeds from there through the rational soul, lives only for a time. That which is created by the Idea alone through direct action is made entirely stable and possesses a stable essence. But that which is born from an Idea through the soul as a medium is born through a mutable action and is forced to derive a nature that is changeable in itself. I say "in itself," because life from...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul must be created directly by God because creation requires infinite power, which no creature (even an angel) possesses. He concludes that because the soul is a direct "effect" of God's eternal Idea of Life, it is inherently immortal and stable.</summary>

...they believe that the life impressed upon the ethereal vehicle <note>The "ethereal vehicle" or *pneuma* was a subtle, star-like body that Neoplatonists believed served as an intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>—as if on an eternal mirror—always accompanies the soul that impresses it. However, the life impressed upon the composite and perishable body does not accompany it forever. Indeed, they think that because the soul's substance lives forever, the ethereal body nearest to it is perpetually animated, while the elemental body <note>The physical body made of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> receives life from the soul through that vehicle only for a time. But more on these matters elsewhere.

<margin>H</margin>
### Fourteenth argument: because it is life by itself. Chapter 14.

**T**he soul is essence, and it is also life. In the previous arguments, we showed it to be immortal because it is an essence existing by itself; but for now, we demonstrate its immortality because it is a life living by itself. Furthermore, the soul is life by its very essence, because everything that is within it is life. For if there were anything in it that was not life, that part would certainly not be "soul," and the whole entity would be called "something animated" <note>original: *animatum quiddam*</note> rather than "the soul" itself. Let us therefore admit that the entire essence of the soul is life. If it is entirely life, it must certainly be called "life by itself" according to the form of life. For that which lives through another—not being alive by its own nature—is composed of two parts: namely, its own nature (which is not alive in itself) and that life received from elsewhere. Thus, conclude: if a thing that lives through another is not entirely life, it follows that a thing which is entirely life must live by itself. Therefore, the soul, which is entirely life, lives by itself—especially since it is moved by itself. If this is so, it is life by its very nature.

The essence of the soul is therefore life. A sign of this is that whatever the soul joins, it provides with life, as if it were by its own nature the very thing it grants to another. Hence, when the soul departs, the body ceases to live; yet while it is present in the body, it never for a moment ceases to perform the works of life by vivifying <note>term: <term>Vivifying</term> (Latin: *vivificatio*), the act of giving life or making something alive.</note> the body. Therefore, the perennial act of the soul is vivification. A perennial action is the proper action of a thing. Thus, to vivify is the soul's proper action. To vivify, moreover, is proper to life itself, just as to heat is proper to heat. Therefore, the essence of the soul is life.

Consider another proof: once a body is prepared, the soul immediately vivifies it. It gives life either by its being, or by desire, or by knowledge and deliberation. If the soul vivified the body by knowledge and deliberation, everyone would know what the soul creates and nourishes in the internal organs at every moment, and what the arrangement of that internal work is; and unless they knew it, these things would not happen. But could it be by desire? Not even that; otherwise, as long as the mind wished to be in the body, it would remain there, and he who hates the company of the body would depart from it instantly. It remains, then, that the soul vivifies the body by its very being—that is, by a natural power. If it vivifies by its very being, it is life (or a living thing) through its own essence, just as a thing that heats by its very being is heat (or a hot thing) through its essence or power.

Conclude, then, that the essence of the soul is a certain kind of life. If you do not wish to call it "life living by itself" (in the same way you usually call heat "something heating by itself"), you are at least forced by the previous points to admit that the soul is a substance made vital by its own life, just as you say fire is a substance made hot by its own heat. I care very little which of these you choose, for what we seek follows from both. But I am led by the previous arguments to call the soul "life by itself"—a natural life, I say, and a vital form.

Now, death is in some way called the opposite of life and the vital form, or it is some death-bearing quality of form, just as coldness is the opposite of heat, and dryness the opposite of moisture. But such is the nature of opposite forms that none of them admits its opposite; just as heat does not admit cold, nor does a substance to which one of those forms is proper admit the opposite form of its own nature. For example, fire (to which heat is proper) does not admit cold so as to be both fire and cold at the same time; rather, both the heat and the fire depart or are destroyed when the cold arrives, rather than the heat or the fire becoming cold. Therefore, each of them is (so to speak) "un-chillable," since it cannot become a participant in cold.

Similarly, because the soul is either natural life itself or possesses life as its natural attendant, it does not admit death (as I have said), which is its opposite. If it does not admit death, it is essentially immortal, just as fire is "un-chillable" because it does not admit cold. If being "un-chillable" were the same as being "indestructible," fire would not only not grow cold, it would also never be destroyed. As it stands, however, fire is destroyed rather than becoming cold. But since "immortal" is the same as "indestructible," the soul—which is called immortal because it does not admit death—is also indestructible. Therefore, when death arrives, the soul is not destroyed by its departure. This entire preceding discussion is encompassed in these words of Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster was the legendary ancient Persian prophet; Ficino and his contemporaries believed the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to him were a source of ancient, divine wisdom that agreed with Plato.</note>:

Immortal <note>original Greek: ἀθάνατος</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because its very essence is "life." Just as fire cannot become cold without ceasing to be fire, the soul cannot admit death; however, unlike fire, the soul is an indestructible substance that continues to exist after departing from the body.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V.

<term>It remains immortal and is the mistress of life.</term> <note>original Greek: ἀθάνατός τε μένει, καὶ ζωῆς δέσποτίς ἐστι.</note>

That is to say, it remains immortal and is the mistress of life. It is as if he were to say that it remains immortal because it has life as its constant attendant, just as the Sun has light or a comet has its "hair" <note>Referring to the tail of a comet, often called "hair" (comam) in Latin and Greek.</note>. Here, a follower of Strato <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a philosopher who focused on natural science and often leaned toward materialistic explanations.</note> or some Epicurean might argue thus: "Certainly the soul does not receive death, because when the death-bearing quality arrives, the soul departs and ceases to exist. If it ceases to exist, it certainly receives nothing." But we, O Epicurus, are not so foolish as to be unaware that death cannot be "received" by anyone—partly because death is nothingness (and what is nothing cannot be possessed), and partly because neither the living nor the dead can grasp it. The living cannot, because while they live, they are away from death; the dead cannot because, if they no longer exist (as you believe), they receive nothing, and if they survive (as our people hold), they are still away from death. 

Let us stop playing with words. Listen to what we mean when we say the soul does not receive death: we mean that it does not admit into itself any death-bearing quality through which it would cease to live. Truly, contrary qualities do not receive one another; instead, they alternately put each other to flight and flee. Therefore, heat by its very nature not only does not receive cold, but does not even allow cold to come near its location. For those things which differ by the widest interval in their nature put each other to flight and flee as far as possible. Since these forms are such by their own nature, if they existed in their pure and solitary state, and were contraries just as they are now, they would never approach one another. Nature would keep them dissociated, and there would be no intermediate reconciler present for them. 

They would certainly be like this if heat existed by itself, separated from matter, so that it had nothing mixed in it except heat; and likewise for cold. As it stands, heat lies in matter, which by its own nature is no less ready for cold than for heat. Matter opens its bosom to the arriving cold; once the cold has entered, it thrusts the heat out. The heat, thus driven out, is extinguished, since it was brought into being by its Author under the condition that it would remain only as long as it was cherished in that bosom of matter. For this reason, forms that are supported by matter—though they do not "receive" their contrary forms—are nevertheless destroyed by their onset and proximity. 

But those things which remain in themselves, even if they sometimes seem to cling to matter, actually sustain the matter rather than being sustained by it. They cannot admit a force contrary to themselves. Rather, if any force comes to the lap of matter, it stains the qualities and forms bound to the matter, but it does not touch that form which stands above matter. Such is the soul—the rational soul, I say—which, since it is the source of motion and the mover of bodies, cannot be changed from its state by bodies. And since it has life innate to its own species as its own property, it always lives without the "labor" of living, especially as long as it lives within itself. 

However, when it approaches a body, it pours out from itself an irrational life (to speak in the Platonic manner) like a shadow. The soul itself is the true soul and the source of animal life; it supplies such life to the body for a time, but much more does it supply life to itself forever, since it never deserts itself, nor is it compelled to desert itself by the body, whose quality does not pass into an incorporeal form. Again, it is not forced to do this by other souls, whose duty is to give life, not to destroy it. 

Without doubt, the rational soul is judged to be such a thing. But the irrational soul <note>Usually referring to the "sensitive" or "vegetative" soul found in animals and plants.</note> is not a true soul, because it is neither a true essence nor a true life. It is not a true essence because it does not exist through itself; indeed, it does not operate through itself, since it does nothing without the instruments of the body. It is not a true life because it is deprived of the freedom of motion. For it is not led by itself, but is dragged by force by those things which are presented to the senses. 

Therefore, many Platonists say that the rational soul is both soul and self-subsisting life, vivifying the body from itself. But they think the irrational form is an "animation" or "vivification" of the body rather than a soul. Xenocrates, Speusippus, Numenius, and Plotinus <note>Key figures in the lineage of Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> think even this irrational form is immortal, but Porphyry, Proclus, and many others deny it. Nor should we wonder if many Platonists think some souls are true and others are false. For the variety of things is woven together by appropriate intervals. God is true Goodness. An angel is an image of goodness, but is true Intellect. The rational soul is an image of intellect, but is the true Soul. The irrational soul is an image of the soul, but is true Nature. The quality divided within matter is an image of nature, and the true instrument of natural agents. 

But we must remember that those who think our lower souls are eternal—and even the souls of plants—followed the Egyptians and the Pythagoreans. They believed that human souls are minds that have fallen into reason and sense, while the souls of brutes are our souls fallen entirely into sense and generation; and finally, the souls of plants are those same souls fallen entirely into the power of reproduction, and that all are able to return to the su... <note>Ficino is describing the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the migration of souls between different levels of life.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the rational soul is immortal because it is the source of life and motion, distinguishing it from "irrational" life which is merely a shadow or animation dependent on the body. He maps out a hierarchy of existence from God down to material qualities, referencing various Greek and Egyptian philosophical traditions regarding the soul's nature and descent.</summary>

->## The fifteenth reason. Because life is more excellent than the body.<-
->### Chapter XV.<-

The **rational soul** is true, natural life. True life is, of itself, the shaper and ruler of the body, and therefore it is far more excellent than the body. Although a body may be turned into various qualities, or even divided into parts a thousand times, it never ceases to be a body; for the nature of a divisible body always remains, since parts can be divided into smaller particles without end. Therefore, how much more should the rational soul (which is the true life of the body), no matter how much it might be changed, never cease to be life? <margin>*</margin> We judge the force of this argument to consist primarily in the fact that the **third essence** <term>third essence: In Ficino’s hierarchy of being, the Soul sits in the middle—the "third" rank—connecting the higher realms of God and Intellect with the lower realms of Quality and Matter.</term>, which is the seat of rational souls, possesses three gifts because it occupies the middle point of all things. 

The first gift is that the true images of divine things shine within it. The second is that it forms and contains the entire physical machine of the world. The third is that it reconciles divine and physical things with one another. All these gifts show that the soul is eternal. 

Regarding the first: if in the category of bodies there are some eternal things <note>Ficino refers to the "celestial bodies" (planets and stars), which ancient and medieval science considered incorruptible and eternal.</note> in which there are mere shadows of divine things, then how much more eternal are rational souls, the most excellent of all souls, in which the eternal images of divine things reside? For in divine matters, life exists prior to splendor, since their splendor is both a reflection and an outpouring of life. Therefore, the abundance of immortal life flows into the soul from that source before the splendor of divine images does. 

Regarding the second: if the rational soul is the principle of forming and containing, it can lose neither its own form nor its natural stability. Indeed, since the entire category of "living things" is more excellent than the entire category of "bodies," and since in all the members of the world there are some physical things that are eternal, it is probable that in all these there are eternal souls. For who would deny that the category of souls has a perpetual "head"—in which the rational souls are—when the physical world has perpetual members everywhere? 

Regarding the third: if the soul is the source of universal reconciliation and the bond of the world, it cannot be pulled apart or dissolved. For if the bond of the universe were loosened, what else could ever be bound together? 

We shall further confirm these Platonic mysteries with the opinion of Saint Augustine. If the rational soul perished when the body died, it would necessarily change as the body changed. But it is not changed by the body. For the soul itself is the **principle of motion** <note>The starting point or cause of movement.</note>. Thus, when it seems to be changed by the body, it is actually the soul changing both itself and the body, leading them as it commands. If the soul very often moves the body while remaining itself unmoved, it is far more likely that, because it halts and contains the body, it halts and contains itself. For that which stands firm while moving another can certainly stand firm forever in sustaining and containing itself. 

Who does not know that when a body—either one's own or another's—is moved by the mind, both the motion itself and the thing moved do not possess all their parts at once, but rather slip away from the future into the present and the past? Yet in the mind at that very time, there exists simultaneously the unchanging plan of the entire work: the intention for the present task, the memory of the past, and the expectation of the future. In that place, the intention of the mind regarding things that do not exist is the mind itself, while it connects into one both those things that do not yet exist and those that exist no longer. Regarding temporal things, the soul is above time; regarding moving things, it is unmoving. Why then should its substance not become immortal when dealing with mortal things? Indeed, why should it not become perpetual itself when attaining perpetual things, seeing as it remains unmoving while handling moving things? 

Furthermore, if it is not so much the bulk of the body as its **form** <term>form: or "species"; the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</term> that makes it a body (for a body is more of a "body" the more beautiful and shapely it is, and less so the more foul and deformed it is—a defect occurring not by a cutting away of bulk, but by a loss of form), then we must believe that the mind—from which, as from a principle, the body is given the form through which it exists and the connection of parts through which it holds together—is never deprived of its own form or the union through which it is and remains a mind. After all, the body is never entirely deprived of all form and the union through which it remains a body; yet the soul does not pass from form to form <note>The soul does not shift between different "types" of existence the way matter changes its shape or appearance.</note> as the body does. For change descends from the soul into the body, and the soul is more stable than the body. Therefore, if the body always remains in the physical category, the soul remains always in its living form; nor will it be changed from one soul to another within that living form, for there is no underlying **matter** <note>In Aristotelian terms, matter is the "stuff" that allows one thing to change into another; Ficino argues the soul lacks this kind of material instability.</note> through which such a change could occur. If such a change does not happen, and the mind cannot exist unless it lives, then it can never...

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by defining it as the "third essence" that bonds the divine and physical worlds, acting as the stable principle of motion and form for the body. Drawing on Augustine, he asserts that because the soul remains stable while managing time and movement, it must be inherently eternal.</summary>

<sig>K 5</sig>

...indeed the soul dies. But if anyone should say that we ought not to fear that kind of death for the soul by which it is reduced to nothing, but rather the kind by which we say things are "dead" simply because they lack life, let him consider that no thing can ever lack its own self. The soul, however, is a form of life itself. From this, we understand that whatever is "animated" is alive, while everything "inanimate" that is capable of being animated is understood as dead—that is, deprived of life. Therefore, the soul cannot die. For if it could ever be deprived of life, it would not be a true soul, but merely something "animated," or some shadow of a soul. If such a thought is absurd, then this kind of death is even less to be feared by the soul, since it certainly cannot be feared by life itself. For truly, if the soul dies when life deserts it, then that very life which deserts it is much better understood to be the true soul; thus, whatever is deserted by life would no longer be the soul, but rather the soul would be that very life which does the deserting. Whatever is said to be dead because it is deserted by life is understood to have been deserted by the soul. However, since this life which deserts dying things is the soul itself, and the soul does not desert itself, then the soul does not die—unless, perhaps, we are forced to believe that "true life" is merely a certain "temperament" <note>In ancient medicine and philosophy, a "temperament" was the specific balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note> of the body, or something that follows from it, as **Aristoxenus** and **Dicaearchus** <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek music theorist who argued the soul was a "tuning" or harmony of the body; Dicaearchus was a student of Aristotle who similarly argued the soul was not a separate substance.</note> once believed.

Surely these men would never have held such a view if they had been able to see those things which truly exist and remain unchangeable, using a mind that had been alienated and purged from the habits of the body. For who, looking closely at themselves, has not experienced that they understand something more purely the further they are able to remove and withdraw the mind's attention from the senses of the body? If the soul belonged to the physical temperament of the body, this could certainly not happen. For a thing that had no nature of its own and did not subsist by itself—but was instead an inseparable bodily form within a physical subject—could in no way attempt to turn itself away from that same body to perceive intelligible things. Nor could it, in so far as it succeeded, gaze upon them and become better and more excellent through that vision. Indeed, such a form (or even the bodily temperament itself, which is created by a specific mixing of those four natures of which the body consists) can in no way turn itself away from the subject in which it exists inseparably.

Furthermore, since a harmony of humors is merely a composite accident <note>An "accident" is a philosophical term for a property that can change without destroying the thing itself (like hair color), as opposed to an "essence."</note>, if the soul were either that harmony or dependent upon it, it would in no way be able to know, desire, or grasp the principles of simple substances and things. To this we add that the things the soul understands when it turns away from the body are certainly not physical, and yet they are the most real of all things. For they always remain the same; and nothing could be said more absurdly than that the things we see with our eyes exist, but the things we discern with our intelligence do not—especially since it would be madness to doubt that intelligence is incomparably superior to the eyes. 

Now, since the soul gazes upon these intelligible things (which always remain the same) without any physical instrument, it shows clearly enough that it is joined to them in a wondrous and incomparable way—specifically, not according to physical location. For either they are in the soul, or the soul is in them, or both exist by themselves. If the first is true, the soul is not a <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "harmonia" — here referring to the soul as a musical-style tuning of the body's elements.</note> of the body, nor is it enslaved to such a harmony. For anything of that sort cannot be separated from the body as its subject; therefore, whatever is in it would be just as bound to the body as the harmony itself is. But the human body is changeable; therefore, those principles of things which are in the contemplating mind would also be changeable if the mind were tied to a changeable body. But those principles cannot be changeable. For it is always true in the same way that two and four make six, and that the ratio of two to four is the same as four to eight, and many other things of this kind. Principles of this sort exist inseparably in the mind, which always and suddenly uses them at will. 

In these principles consists the art of reasoning, which is not at all separated from the rational soul. For if that "artful reason"—or the rational art which is a collection of principles—were separated from the soul, it would either exist nowhere, or in something non-living, or in a living thing. One cannot say that eternal and unchangeable principles exist nowhere. It is also impossible for true principles to exist in a non-living thing, since life is the foundation of reason. If, however, artful reason passes from one life to another, does it not do so more conveniently than when one person teaches others? Yet since that does not happen (for no one forgets by teaching others), no such "passage" occurs. Therefore, Art exists inseparably in the soul. It would also exist in the body if the soul were a harmony of the body; for that reason, both reason itself and the soul would be as changeable as the body. But since such reason is unchangeable—and therefore the essence of the soul in which it exists as a subject is also unchangeable—the soul is not a temperament of the body. And...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a mere byproduct or "harmony" of the body because it is capable of grasping eternal, unchanging truths (like mathematics) that the physical body cannot contain. Since the objects of reason are immortal and immutable, the soul that holds them must also be immortal.</summary>

Let it suffice to have argued in this way from that first part of the previous division, in which it was granted that <term>reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationes*. In the Platonic tradition, these are the eternal, unchanging blueprints or mathematical principles of things.</note> exist within the soul. Furthermore, if anyone admits the second part—namely, that the soul exists within those reasons—the same conclusion follows. For in what way can the soul be a "temperament" of the body if it is located within the "reason of things" as its subject, a reason which is separated from the body? After all, a temperament of the body cannot be anywhere except in the body. If you grant the third part of that division—namely, that both the soul and the reason of things are self-subsisting substances—then the soul will subsist by itself and will not be bound to the temperament of the body. Finally, whichever part of the division you take, this one reason above all persuades us that the soul does not lie within the <term>complexion</term><note>Latin: *complexio*. This refers to the physical "weaving together" or combination of the four elements and humors that make up the body.</note> of the body as if that were its origin. If it were, it would not mingle itself so greedily, so easily, and so diligently with immutable reasons while we are philosophizing (setting aside the changeable body), nor would it be better off when it is within those reasons than when it is in the body. However, it is as much better off in those reasons than in the body as it lives more excellently in them than in itself. And it lives more excellently in them to the degree that it acts more perfectly. Indeed, it acts more perfectly within them because it understands more truly, desires more peacefully, and enjoys them more sweetly, fully, and securely. And since the soul itself is often out of harmony with itself—both in its speculation and in its morals—even while the body is in harmony with itself, and conversely, the soul may be in harmony while the body is out of harmony, anyone who does not see that the soul does not consist in the harmony of the body is himself out of harmony with the truth.

But to return to **Aurelius** <note>Aurelius Augustine (St. Augustine). Ficino is paraphrasing Augustine's *Soliloquies*, Book II.</note>, a certain question perhaps arises here: whether the soul, just as it does not perish, might also not be changed into a "worse essence." For it might seem to someone—and not without reason—that while this logic proves the soul cannot come to nothing, it might perhaps be turned into a body. If that which was previously a soul were made into a body, it would certainly not "not exist" entirely. 

But this cannot happen unless either the soul itself wills it, or it is forced by another. Yet the soul could not immediately become a body even if it desired it or were forced to. For while it follows that it *must* become a body if it necessarily wills it or is forced, it does not follow that it *can* become a body simply because it wills it or is forced. However, it will never will it. For every appetite the soul has toward the body is either to possess it, to give it life, to "fabricate" it in some way, or to provide for it in whatever manner. None of these things can happen unless the soul itself is better than the body. But if it were to *become* a body, it would certainly not be better than a body. Therefore, it will not will to be a body; nor is there any surer argument for this than when the soul asks this of itself. For it easily finds that it has no appetite except for acting, knowing, feeling, or at the very least, living, insofar as its power allows. 

If, however, it is forced to be a body, by whom is it forced? By just anyone? Surely by one more powerful. Therefore, it cannot be forced by a body, for in no way is any body more powerful than any soul. A more powerful soul, moreover, does not force anything except what is subject to its power. Nor is a soul subject to the power of another soul in any way, except through its own desires. Therefore, that other soul forces it no more than its own desires allow. But it has been said that the soul cannot have a desire to be a body. It is also manifest that the soul reaches the fulfillment of none of its desires while it is losing all desire—and it loses all desire when it becomes a body. Therefore, it cannot be forced to become a body by one who has no power to force it except through subjected desires. 

Furthermore, whichever soul has another soul in its power, it must necessarily want to have it in its power as a soul rather than as a body, whether to provide for it out of goodness or to rule over it out of malice. Therefore, it will not want the other to become a body. Finally, that forcing soul is either a living being (an animal) or it lacks a body. But if it lacks a body, it is not in this world; and if that is so, it is supremely good and cannot wish so foul a change upon another. If, however, it is a living being, either the one it forces is also a living being, or it is not. If it is not, nothing can be forced by another. For one who is "at the peak"—that is, one who is unattached—has no superior and thus is not forced. If, however, it is in a body, it is in turn forced toward whatever it is forced to by the one who is at the peak, through the body. But who would doubt that such a great change could in no way happen to the soul through a body? It would only happen if the body were more powerful than the soul. However, whatever it is that the soul is forced to do through the body, it is forced not through the body itself, but through its own desires, about which enough has been said. Moreover, that which is "better" than the rational soul is, by everyone's agreement, the Divine; the Divine certainly looks out for the soul, and therefore the soul cannot be forced by Him to be converted into a body. 

If, therefore, the soul suffers this neither by its own will nor by the force of another, from where could it suffer it? Or because sleep often overcomes us against our will, must we fear that by some such defect the soul might be turned into a body? As if, truly, because our limbs...

He further demonstrates that the soul can never "degrade" into becoming a body, as neither its own will, nor a higher power, nor the physical body itself could or would cause such a transformation.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK V

...they wither, it does not mean that the soul becomes weaker in any part. However, it does not perceive sensible things <note>Things that can be detected by the five senses.</note> because whatever it is that causes sleep originates from the body and operates within the body. For sleep lulls and somehow closes the bodily senses, yet in such a way that the soul yields to such a communion with the body willingly; for such a change—which restores the body from its labors—is according to nature. This, however, does not take away from the soul the power of either perceiving or understanding. For the soul has the images of sensible things ready at hand with such an expressive likeness that, at that very time, they cannot be distinguished from those things of which they are images. And if the soul understands anything, it is equally true for the one sleeping as for the one awake. 

For example, if during sleep it seems to you that you were debating, and following true <term>reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationes*. These are the logical or mathematical principles that the soul uses to reach truth.</note> in the debate you learned something, these same things remain unchangeable even when you wake up, even though the rest are found to be false—such as the place where the debate occurred, the person with whom the debate seemed to be held, the words themselves used during the dream-debate, and other things of this sort which are perceived by the senses and performed by those who are awake. These things pass away, yet they do not in any part overtake the eternal presence of true reasons. From this it is gathered that by such a change of the body, which is sleep, not the power of the soul itself but the life of the body can be diminished. 

Finally, although they occupy a place in the body, the soul is not locally joined to those highest and eternal reasons, which remain unchangeably and are not contained in a place. The soul is affected by these before the body is—and not only before, but also more. For it is as much "prior" as it is closer to them; and by that same cause it is as much "more" affected as it is better than the body. Let this "closeness" be understood not by physical location, but by the order of nature. By this order, it is understood that <term>form</term><note>Latin: *species*. This refers to the defining structure, beauty, or "look" that gives a physical object its specific identity.</note> is granted to the body by the highest Essence through the soul, by which the body is whatever it is. Therefore, the body subsists through the soul, and it exists by the very fact that it is animated, whether universally like the world, or particularly like each individual animal within the world. 

Wherefore, it would follow that the soul would have to become a body through a soul, which is not possible. Because that does not happen (for while the soul remains in that which is soul, the body subsists through it—the soul giving form, not taking it away), the soul cannot be changed into a body. For if it does not hand over the form which it receives from the Highest Good, the body does not exist through it; and if it does not exist through the soul, it either does not exist at all, or it receives form as closely as the soul does. But it does not become a body [in that way], because if it received form as closely, it would be the same thing as the soul. Is the soul not better by the very fact that it receives form more closely? The body would receive it just as closely if it did not receive it through the soul; for with nothing placed in between, it would certainly receive it just as closely. 

Nor can any suitable medium be found between the highest life—which is unchangeable wisdom and truth—and that which is the last thing to be given life, which is the body, except the life-giving soul. If the soul hands over form to the body so that it may be a body as far as it is, it certainly does not lose its form by handing it over. If it were to transmute itself into a body, it would be losing its form. Therefore, the soul does not become a body, whether through itself (because the body only exists through the soul while the soul remains a soul) or through another. This can also be said of the irrational soul or "life-force," in that the rational soul is not converted into it either. For unless it were subjected to the rational soul in a lower order, it would receive form equally and be the same. Therefore, more powerful things hand over the form received from the Highest Beauty to weaker things by a natural order. And certainly, when they hand it over, they do not lose it. Those things which are weaker exist only to the extent that the form by which they exist is handed to them by more powerful things, which are indeed both more powerful and better. This is granted to those natures which are not more powerful than smaller masses because of a larger physical bulk, but are more powerful because they are better by that same form, without any swelling of local magnitude—the soul is of this kind, better and more powerful than the body. Wherefore, since the body subsists through the soul (as has been said), the soul can in no way be converted into a body. For no body exists except by receiving form through the soul. But

->for the soul to become a body, it would happen not by receiving form, but by<-
->losing it. And for that reason, it can in no<-
->way happen.<-

# THE PLATONIC THE-
## ology, on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
#### BOOK VI.

->*Reduction of the opinions concerning the soul into five categories.*<-
->Chapter I.<-

H<note>The letter 'H' begins with a large decorative woodcut initial depicting human figures and scrolling foliage.</note>ad I once discussed these matters in the Regnano countryside at the house of Giovanni Cavalcanti, our unique friend, on the Calends of March <note>March 1st.</note> under a Laurel tree. Three of our principal close associates were present at these discussions: Cristoforo Landino, Bernardo Nuthius, and Giorgio Antonio Vespucci—men most illustrious in their integrity and learning. After these things had been heard with the greatest attention, Giovanni said, "Marsilio Ficino, it cannot be said how much I have been delighted by the preceding discussion. But I desire this in addition: that since you have discussed the common immortality of rational souls, you might next, if it pleases you, discuss more diligently the immortality of our own soul with its specific <term>reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationibus*. In this context, it refers to logical arguments or governing principles.</note>. I agree indeed that there are five levels of things, just as you arranged them in the previous discussion, and that that <term>third essence</term><note>In Ficino’s system, the "Third Essence" is the Soul, which sits exactly in the middle of the five levels of reality: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Matter.</note> holds the middle rank among them, which is released from matter and is perpetual. Furthermore, I do not doubt that celestial souls are placed in the rank of that essence. I also think it probable that our own mind is placed there. However, I judge that this cannot be fully affirmed until all the opinions of the Philosophers concerning the human soul are reduced to five categories, and after four have been refuted, the last one is held.

For either the soul is some very thin little body spread throughout this thicker body—whether it be fiery, as Democritus, Leucippus, and Hipparchus think; or airy, as Anaximenes, Diogenes Apolloniates, and Critias; or watery, as Hippias; or earthy, as Hesiod and Pronopides; or consisting of fire and air, as Boethus and Epicurus; or of water and earth, as Xenophantes. Or the soul is something better—that is, not the mass of a little body itself properly speaking, but some quality of it spread through the parts of the little body, such as heat, or a warm <term>complexion</term><note>Latin: *complexio*. The physical temperament or combination of qualities in a living body.</note>, which Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Antipater, and Posidonius seem to have intended. Or it is something purer, like some lucid point of that quality assigned to a certain more powerful part of the quality and the body itself—say, the heart or the brain—residing there and governing the remaining members from there, as is found in Chrysippus, Archelaus, and Heraclides Ponticus. Or it is something still more free, like a point affixed to no part, but secluded from every determined location, and present as a whole to every part of the body, but of such a kind that it is dependent on the nature of the body itself. Dependent, I say, in two ways: either because the complexion of the body generated it, or because, although the complexion did not generate it, nevertheless its progenitor, whoever he may be, led it out from the power of matter and its vitals—that is, he brought it into the light from some seed or beginning, or proportion of matter itself, and utterly devoted it to matter as if to a natural womb.

This is the opinion which Xenophanes of Colophon, Asclepiades, Aristoxenus, and Critolaus follow, among whom the soul is either a certain power of the body agile for movement, or a <term>harmony</term><note>Latin: *harmonia*. A famous ancient theory that the soul is not a thing, but the "tuning" or balance of the body's physical parts.</note> of the bodily parts.

Or finally, the human soul is something divine—that is, something indivisible, standing as a whole in every part of the body, and so produced by an incorporeal author that it depends only on the power of the agent, not on the beginning, capacity, or nourishment of matter, just as the ancient Theologians teach us: Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus <note>Latin: *Mercurius*.</note>, Orpheus, Aglaophemus, Pythagoras, and Plato, whose footsteps Aristotle the physicist follows for the most part. Aside from these five opinions, no others are found. You, however, will have shown at last that immortality belongs to us when, having rejected the four superior opinions, you shall have proved...

## Common Philosophers, not persuaded by any reason but deceived by a corrupt habit, posited that the soul is corporeal.
### Chapter II.

**I** consider, in the first place, that those common philosophers who thought the soul was corporeal—following one of those four opinions <note>Referring to various ancient materialist theories of the soul (e.g., as breath, fire, or blood).</note>—were not persuaded by any reason, but were driven into this opinion by a certain long and most unfortunate habit. There appear to be three principal duties of our soul: for it acts **in** the body, it acts **through** the body, and it also operates **by itself**. It acts **in** the body through that power which the Peripatetics call "vegetative," but which our Platonists call "nature," when it generates, nourishes, and increases the body. It acts **through** the body according to the senses, both the external—when it sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches—and the internal, when it revolves within itself the images (the remnants, as it were, of the senses) of those bodies which it perceived from without. It acts **by itself** when it neither touches bodies through the external senses nor recollects images of bodies through the internal sense, but the true and incorporeal power of the soul itself investigates and discovers something incorporeal, which is neither a body nor the image of any body. This action, indeed, we call "intelligence." You have, therefore, natural action, sensation, and intelligence. 

The soul uses natural action immediately upon entering the body in the womb; it uses sensation a little later, specifically once the human is born; it uses pure intelligence only with difficulty and at last when the body is fully grown. Indeed, a great many people almost never use it, especially those who are still children even at thirty years of age. If you were to ask that "natural" power what the soul is, it would undoubtedly answer that it is a body. For that power touches nothing else but the body. If you ask the external sense, it will likewise answer "body." The eyes will ascribe a certain shape and color to the soul; the ears, a voice; smell, an odor; taste, a flavor; and touch will ascribe weight, solidity, heat, and the like. And if you were to inquire about the soul from the "internal sense" <note>Latin: *sensum interiorem*, often called the *phantasia* or imagination, which processes sensory data.</note>, which feeds on the remnants of the external senses, it too will paint the soul with the likenesses of bodies, for it has nothing else it can apply. 

Our unhappy youth, nourished by these unlearned teachers, forces us through all our life to think foolishly about the soul while we imagine it to be corporeal, guided by these "learned" masters who perceive only bodily things. But this error seems to have arisen most especially—or rather, been confirmed—because if ever we flee from these three teachers (treating them as mere <term>Sophists</term><note>Rhetoricians who use clever but fallacious arguments.</note>) and take refuge in the Mind, that mistress of wisdom, and ask her what the soul is, she answers that it is such as she herself sees. But alas, in what state does she see it? How foul! How miserable! Certainly not such as it once descended from heaven. Instead, she sees that natural power of the soul, the builder of the body, polluted by the decay of the four humors (in which it is submerged) and suffocated by the fatness of the limbs. She looks upon the external senses, which incline everywhere toward bodies, acting through the body and being acted upon by bodies. She sees also the internal sense, which they call the <term>phantasia</term><note>The faculty of imagination that stores sensory images.</note>, covered by various shapes and qualities of diverse bodies, as if swallowed through the senses. 

Therefore, while the Mind looks upon the soul wrapped in a corporeal garment and notices its inclination and appetite toward bodies, she certainly answers that it is corporeal. It is no different than if some child, immediately upon being born, had been so smeared with mud that throughout his whole childhood he was covered in a clay shell; if he were later asked, "What is your little body like, O boy?", would he not answer that it is made of mud? Wash the body, boy...

Ficino is now moving from a historical overview of materialist philosophers to a direct, poetic exhortation to the reader to recognize the soul's non-physical nature.</meta>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...body, wipe the flesh from the clods of earth, and you will see yourself as a creature of flesh, not of clay <note>Ficino uses "clay" to represent the lowest material element and "flesh" to represent a slightly higher, more animated state, urging the reader to peel back layers of materiality to find the soul.</note>. Dismiss the senses, O wretched ones—those far too impious teachers. Interrogate only the pious mind, but on this condition: that you show it a soul that is pure, just as you received it, not enslaved to the body nor filthy with the stains of vice. The mind will immediately respond that the soul is not only incorporeal <note>non-physical</note>, but divine. You are something great, O soul, if small things do not satisfy you. You are the best, if evils displease you. You are the most beautiful, if you shudder at the base. You are eternal, if you hold temporal things in low esteem. Since you are such, if you desire to find yourself, I beseech you: seek yourself there where such things exist. 

Truly, great things exist only where no place imposes a limit or end. The best things are where nothing adverse happens. The most beautiful are where nothing is out of harmony. The eternal are where there is no failure. Seek yourself, therefore, outside the world. But so that you may seek and find yourself, fly outside—or rather, look outside. For you are already "outside" while you yourself embrace the world. But you think you are in the lowest part of the world because you do not perceive yourself flying above the heavens; instead, you see your shadow—the body—in the lowest place. It is just as if a boy standing over a well should think he is at the bottom of the well because he does not turn his gaze toward himself, but only looks at his shadow at the bottom. Or as if a bird flying in the air believes it is flying on the ground because it sees its shadow on the earth. 

Therefore, leaving behind the narrowness of this shadow, return to yourself; thus you will return to what is vast. Know that there is an immense spaciousness in the spirit, but in the body, so to speak, an infinite narrowness. This can be seen from the fact that numbers—which are close to spiritual nature—lack physical position and measure things according to their "form," whether those things are non-physical or physical. Numbers are nothing other than repetitions of "Unity" itself, and Unity is non-physical, because everything physical is multiple <note>In Platonic thought, a physical object can always be divided into parts, but the concept of "One" is indivisible and therefore spiritual.</note>. Numbers, I say, which are spiritual, can increase without end, yet they do not decrease without end <note>Ficino observes that you can always add 1 to a number (infinite growth), but in the physical world, things have a limit to how much they can grow, while they can be divided infinitely (infinite shrinkage).</note>. Magnitude, by contrast, has a limit to its growth, though it has no limit to its decrease. 

Why do you value the judgment of the senses so highly, unhappy ones? They are so deceived by false images that sight judges the Sun—which is much larger than the Earth—to be barely three feet wide <note>original: "bicubitum"</note>. It judges the sky, which moves most rapidly, to be standing still. It sees a straight oar in the water as broken and bent. It sees the shore running while the ship itself is moving. Often, hearing indicates that a voice is coming from somewhere other than its source. How often does taste judge sweet things to be bitter, and infinite other errors of this kind? 

Who corrects the errors of the senses? Reason. That which corrects and perfects is more noble than that which is corrected. Therefore, Reason is more diligent and truthful than sense. Reason judges that something non-physical can be found, and Reason itself is always occupied with such things. It is therefore true, by the judgment of Reason, that something non-physical exists somewhere, just as it is true, by the judgment of the senses, that many physical things exist in the world. However, the judgment of the senses is mistaken in this: that it affirms nothing exists *except* the body. In the same way, the judgment of Reason would be mistaken if it perchance asserted that nothing physical exists in the world. As it stands, Reason is so far from falsehood that it even corrects the fallacies of the senses. 

Indeed, the powers of sensing are so deceptive that they are not only corrected by Reason, but even condemned by one another. If you committed yourself to sight alone, you would say nothing else exists in the world except what is seen in the light; you would say voices, smells, and other things that are not seen do not exist at all. If you trusted only your ears, you would deny that colors exist. If you trusted only smell, you would think there are only odors in the world. And so it must be thought of the others. Just as each sense denies that anything exists beyond its own domain—and yet we condemn one sense by means of another and find that something else exists beyond what is proper to a single sense—so too all the senses conspiring together deny that anything can exist in nature that is not a body. 

Nonetheless, Reason, refuting them all, proclaims that something non-physical also exists; and it proclaims this truly, and much more truly than the senses, which are both condemned by one another and refuted by Reason. For what is more foolish than to grant that we surpass the beasts in Reason, and to confess that those things we perceive by sense (which some beasts perceive even more sharply) truly exist, but then to contend that what we behold with the eye of Reason is nothing? For no animal would be more foolish than man if that power of the soul which is unique to man—more so than the senses, which he shares with the beasts—were deceptive. It is a crime to say the king of animals is the most senseless of all. Only he will be most senseless who does not admit that the object of the mind is as much more excellent than the object of the senses as the mind is more excellent than the sense. Therefore, non-physical natures are truly found in a more excellent kind of substance than physical ones, especially because if the ob-

## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VI

...pertain <note>The Latin catchword "nere" on the previous page completes the word "pertinere" (to pertain/belong) here.</note>. If the objects of the mind move it, just as the objects of sense move the senses, then those very objects of the mind must possess some substance in themselves so that they are able to move the mind. But if it is said that the intellect is not moved at all by its objects, then it will already be sufficiently proven that the intellect itself is an incorporeal nature, since while it fashions its own thoughts, it is not moved by anything else and builds incorporeal structures. 

One must remember, however, that just as a child born blind finds it difficult to believe in the variety of colors and the existence of light—even though nothing is clearer than light to other people—so the soul, recently enveloped in the darkness of the body, can hardly be brought to believe that any incorporeal light exists, even though nothing in the order of things is more manifest to the angels than that light. Plato laments this at length in the seventh book of the *Republic* <note>original: "septimo de republica"; this refers to the famous Allegory of the Cave, where prisoners mistake shadows for reality</note>, and Aristotle confirms this in the second book of his divine matters <note>original: "secundo diuinorum"; referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, Book II (alpha elatton)</note>, saying that the human intellect is related to those things which are by nature most manifest in the order of things just as the eye of an owl is related to the light of the Sun.

Therefore, let those paltry philosophers <note>term: "minuti Philosophi" — a dismissive term for materialists who believe only what they can touch</note> eventually come to their senses, for they rely only on the evidence of the senses and cannot conceive of the soul being incorporeal and divine. Let them notice at last that through long habituation with the body, they have become so "corporealized" that they deservedly know nothing except the body or things born from the body. Let them become pure, and they will perceive pure things. Let them eventually experience within themselves—for they can if they only wish—what they have long searched for in the universe: they certainly perceive composite things <note>physical objects made of both matter and form</note>, and they perceive many forms within those composites. Furthermore, they desire some forms that are set apart outside of these composites. They themselves are composed of soul and body. They have a life handed over from the soul to the body, and they also have the life of the soul itself flourishing within itself. Let them, therefore, look down upon the former and look up to the latter. 

Let the soul lead an intellectual life separate from the body; once separated, they will immediately reach the "separated forms" <note>Platonic Ideas or Essences that exist independently of physical matter</note>, and they will soon prove by the fact itself the Socratic opinion: that above the forms which lie within shaped subjects <note>which are imperfect</note>, there are forms in themselves that are perfect, from which the formless subjects are shaped. There is only one way not only to reach but even to possess these incorporeal things: namely, to make oneself incorporeal. This means to recall the mind, as much as one is able, from motion, sense, emotion, and bodily imagination. 

For in this way, experience itself will reveal, first, what the pure soul is—that is, reason living with itself and greedily occupying itself around the light of truth. Second, it reveals what an angel is—that is, a pure intellect already rejoicing in the infused light of truth. Third, when the soul itself, like an angel, rejoices in the full light of truth, it will perceive that God is Truth itself, shining and rejoicing in itself; it will see the Light itself rejoicing in its own truth, and Joy itself shining with its own truth. 

We shall begin to understand somewhat that the error of the common people is born from bodily habit if we consider an alternative form of upbringing, such as the one Avicenna devised in the sixth book of his *Natural Philosophy* <note>Ficino refers to the "Floating Man" thought experiment by the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina (Avicenna) found in his *De Anima* (On the Soul)</note>. 

"Let some man be created by God suddenly," says Avicenna, "established in a perfect age, but so disposed that he perceives nothing through any of the five senses." A man's mind affected in this way will still think of something, since he is in an adult age where the structure of the body does not disturb the intelligence, nor is he occupied by the works of the senses which hinder the operation of the mind. And there is indeed something present that can be understood: for the very substance of the soul is present to the mind. Therefore, the mind, disturbed by nothing, will think of the substance of the soul present to itself. 

But what kind of thing will it think it is? Will it think it is colored, long, or wide? Not at all; for a blind man does not perceive such things. Will it think it is sounding, or sweet-smelling, and such? Not these either. For it has not yet received such things through the senses so that it could assign such a nature to the soul. Therefore, that soul will be able to attribute nothing corporeal to itself. What then will it assert about itself? Certainly, at least that which is offered to its first intuition. This is its own essence; wherefore it will affirm that it exists, yet it will perceive nothing corporeal in itself. Thus, it will affirm that it is entirely incorporeal. Nor could it even imagine itself to be a body, just as the souls of the common people—now created and educated differently—cannot consider themselves incorporeal. 

But if someone should say that the soul affirms nothing of itself regarding these bodies which we receive through the five senses, but rather some other body of a different nature, this is quite vain. For if even now, when we have perceived so many various bodies, we cannot devise anything new that is not either in these things or at least composed or elicited from them, how could the mind, ignorant of these bodies in that state, fashion the nature of a new body? Furthermore, even if it were possible for it to think up some member of its own body, it would in no way think that it belonged to its own substance.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind must be incorporeal because it can contemplate perfect, non-physical forms, and utilizes Avicenna's "Floating Man" thought experiment to prove that the soul's self-awareness is independent of sensory input.</summary>
