...pertain <note>The Latin text begins with "nere," completing the word "pertinere" (to pertain/belong) from the previous page.</note>. Therefore, that soul will affirm that it exists, yet it will not affirm anything corporeal. Indeed, these two things are different from one another: that which is affirmed, and that which is not affirmed at all. Therefore, in that consideration, the essence of the soul will be something beyond the body. Moreover, we believe the judgment of that consideration to be true because it would follow the absolutely pure nature of the soul, not images received from the outside. Such a judgment would therefore be entirely natural, and for that reason, most true. Thus, if the soul should later "wake up"—as we are now—and begin to perceive through the senses, it will not be (as we often are) completely unfit for the investigation of spiritual things. Instead, it will possess a more convenient path through which it may eventually prepare itself for the consideration of its own self, so that it may declare itself to be something beyond the body. Miserable souls now lack this path, for through nature and the senses, they have touched upon bodies—both their own and those of others—before they ever touched upon or considered themselves. From this arises that wretched and pervasive error: that they are unable to see themselves clearly, apart from the stain of the body.

Thus far, let it suffice to have recounted the hypothetical upbringing <note>original: "educationem fictam"; Ficino refers to Avicenna’s thought experiment as a "fictional education" or "upbringing" because it imagines a soul created in a vacuum.</note> devised by Avicenna. Next, let us briefly touch upon the sort of upbringing our Plato describes in the seventh book of the *Republic*.

*Imagine, he says, a certain cave underground, and in it men who have been nourished from childhood, their necks and hands tied behind their backs, and their feet bound to certain columns, so that they can neither move anywhere nor look at anything except what appears in the part of the cave placed within their sight. But behind their backs, let a lamp be lit on high, and between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk about, talking to one another, carrying in their hands various likenesses of trees and animals. Those who are thus bound will never truly see either themselves or any of the other things we have mentioned, but only the shadows of themselves or of others which, because of the fire lit behind them, are cast upon the opposite side of the cave before their eyes. For this reason, they will think that they are nothing other than their own shadows, and that other things are nothing but those shadows, or they will suppose that light itself is nothing other than that meager reflection which appears there. If, however, one of those who are bound should by chance be released, and suddenly be forced to look back toward the lamp and the other things behind him, he will immediately grow dizzy and suffer pain; because of the brightness, he will be unable to look upon the things whose shadows he saw just a moment before. Much more would this misfortune befall him if he were suddenly dragged up from the cave toward the celestial light of day. Therefore, he must be led forth not suddenly, but gradually, by suitable steps, from the shadows of things to the things themselves, and likewise from the image of light to the light itself. This must be done so that he sees those things that are in the cave first in the water, before he looks upon the things themselves. Again, for those things which are outside the cave among us, he should first look at them here by night by the light of the Moon—and similarly at terrestrial things—and likewise at the celestial things in heaven only by night. Afterward, by day, he may look at the Sun itself and the things seen under the Sun: first in the water, then in the things themselves, and finally he may look up at the Sun in the heavens. By this method especially, he will easily and purely discern each thing, and he will realize that he had been blind, deceived, and miserable when he was occupied with the meager shadows of things while bound in the cave. Furthermore, just as that cave relates to this world which we call the "visible" world, so this world relates to that which we call the "invisible" and "divine." Indeed, here miserable souls, enclosed in the darkness of a dying body and in a blind prison, never see themselves or anything else truly, nor the true Sun, but rather the shadows of themselves and others, and a certain faint image of the true Sun. For true minds, the true essence of each thing, and the true Sun exist only in the invisible world; if we attempt to look upon these suddenly, without the proper steps of upbringing and discipline, we immediately grow dizzy and suffer pain. But when we are led through suitable steps of character, doctrine, and time, we purely discern and judge those people to be blind and miserable who are deceived, occupied, and oppressed by the false shadows and images of this world. Nevertheless, when the soul descends from the immense light of the invisible world into the dark body to rule and move it, overwhelmed by new darknesses contrary to its nature, it is compelled to be blind and stumble for a long time. Add to this that, because of the sudden and massive change for the worse, it is forced to be "sick" for a long time, and is affected almost like those who are mocked and distressed by false images due to frenzy, sleep, or drunkenness. Or certainly, its condition is no different than if someone were suddenly plunged from the light of the Sun into that cavern which we described.*

He argues that the material world is merely a shadow of the true, invisible reality, and the transition between these realms requires a gradual "education" or purification.</summary>

Therefore, the mind, disturbed by nothing, will think upon the substance of the soul present to itself.

<margin>7th [Book] of the Republic</margin>
Let it suffice to have related thus far the thought experiment <note>original: "educationem fictam," literally a "fictional upbringing" or "imaginary education"</note> described by Avicenna <note>Avicenna (980–1037) was a Persian philosopher. His "Floating Man" argument suggests that if a person were created in a void with no sensory input, they would still know they exist, proving the soul is distinct from the body.</note>. <margin>The Cave</margin>
Imagine, he says, a certain cave underground, and in it men raised from childhood with their necks and hands bound behind them, and their feet tied to certain columns, so that they can neither move at all, nor see anything except what appears in the part of the cave placed within their view. Behind their backs, however, let a lamp be lit high up; and between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk about and speak to one another, carrying in their hands various statues of trees and animals. Those who are so bound will never truly see either themselves or any of the other things we have described; they will see only the shadows of themselves or of the others, which—because of the fire lit behind them—are cast upon the opposite wall of the cave before their eyes. For this reason, they will believe that they themselves are nothing other than their shadows, and that other things are nothing but those shadows; or they will think that light itself is nothing other than that meager reflection which appears there. 

But if one of these bound men were by chance released, and suddenly compelled to look back toward the lamp and the other things that follow beneath it, he will immediately grow dizzy and feel pain; because of the brightness, he will be unable to look upon those things whose shadows he was seeing just a moment before. Much more would this misfortune happen to him if he were suddenly dragged up from the cave toward the celestial light of day. Therefore, he must be led forth not suddenly, but gradually by appropriate steps, from the shadows of things to the things themselves, and likewise from the image of light to the light itself. Thus, he should first see the things that are within the cave in the water, before he inspects them in themselves. Again, for those things that are outside the cave among us, he should first look at them by night by the light of the Moon, and then look at these earthly things in themselves; likewise, let him look upon the heavenly things in the sky only at night. Afterward, however, by day, let him look upon both the Sun itself and the things seen under the Sun—first in the water, then in themselves—and finally let him gaze upon the Sun in the heaven. 

By this method especially, he will discern each thing clearly and easily, and he will realize that he had been blind, deceived, and miserable when he was occupied with the meager shadows of things while bound in the cavern. Therefore, the same comparison that exists between that cave and this realm which we call "visible," exists also between this world and that which we call "invisible and divine." For here, wretched souls, enclosed in the darkness of a dying body and a blind prison, never see themselves or anything else truly, nor do they see the true Sun; rather, they behold only shadows of themselves and others, and a certain faint image of the true Sun. For true minds, true things, and the true Sun exist only in the invisible world; if we attempt to behold these suddenly, without the appropriate steps of education and discipline, we immediately grow dizzy and suffer. But when we are led through the appropriate stages of character, learning, and time, we clearly discern and judge that those who are deceived, occupied, and weighed down by the false shadows and images of this world are blind and miserable. **Nevertheless**, when the soul descends from the immense light of the invisible world into the dark body to rule and move it, it is overwhelmed by a new darkness contrary to its nature, and is compelled to be blind and to stumble for a long time. Add to this that, because of the sudden and massive change for the worse, it is forced to be "sick" for a long time, and is affected almost like those who are mocked and troubled by false images due to frenzy <note>original: "phrenesim," a state of delirium or mental agitation</note>, sleep, or drunkenness. Or certainly, it is no different than if someone were suddenly <margin>just as</margin> [cast down] from the light of the Sun into that cavern which we have described.

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK VI.

...be cast down. For he will be so overwhelmed by new darkness that either in no way, or only with great difficulty at last under that meager light of the cavern, can he discern only those shadows which we have described. Furthermore, on account of that sudden change for the worse, he will fall into various diseases of both the senses and the body.

->These things are from Plato in the seventh book of the Republic.<-

But let us return at last to those things which we had established from the beginning. Rise up, I beseech you, souls of mortals now immersed in bodies; you will immediately find your nature beyond the limits of the body. Since indeed the body is long, wide, and deep. But because no body is infinite, it therefore has a limit of depth; it ends in a surface that lacks depth. You have already a surface, long and wide indeed like a body, but lacking depth, and rising from this one part toward the incorporeal. By the surface also, width is limited; it is terminated at a long line, having neither depth nor width. You have a line approaching the spirit in two parts <note>i.e., it has shed two of the three dimensions of matter</note>. But because this very length of the line is limited, it is led to a point, deprived not only of depth and width, but also of length. You have a point verging on incorporeal nature in three parts. But because this is the limit of a line, it therefore has a certain position in the body; it neither fills the whole nor gives life. 

Separate it, if you please, from the line. It can, however, be separated from the line at least by thought, because it is the limit of the line and exists in some way in itself before it terminates the line. Because that which is prior <note>original: "prius," a logical priority</note> may be separated from that which is posterior. You have the point, in a certain way (that is, in thought), released from the line, now departing from the body by a fourth degree. In this very release, it attains the ability to look upon all parts of the body equally. It is founded through them all and moves them; here the irrational soul <term>irrational soul (anima irrationalis) — the part of the soul shared with animals, responsible for basic life, growth, and sensory perception</term> has its seat. 

And because rational thought is not deceived in ascending, just as it found the point free from the body in thought, so in truth it will find a point—that is, an indivisible something <note>original: "indiuiduum aliquid"</note>—actually released from the body, which not only fills the body and moves it, but is itself freely moved and raised to the things above, which is now called by the name of **Unity**. Here the rational soul flourishes, in the fifth degree, foreign to the mass of the body. If something is as much more impure as it lacks more and suffers more, then the body is more impure than the surface. For it requires more dimensions in order to be, and is divided into more parts. The surface, by a similar reasoning, yields to the line, the line to the point, and the point finally to Unity, which requires neither dimensions nor position. If the most perfect of these is substantial Unity—and because it is the most perfect, it is therefore the most powerful and most true—and these things are something and exist, who would deny that Unity truly exists? 

Therefore, what prevents the soul from being something, and indeed great in power, even if it is not something great in quantity? Come now, gather the fiery form <note>Ficino often uses the "fiery form" as a metaphor for the soul or the "spiritus" that mediates between soul and body</note> which in your three-cubit-tall body is three cubits long, and collect it entirely into the center of the heart. From this it will grow as much in power as it has grown in union—no differently than the rays of the Sun collected in the center of a concave bronze mirror, which are strengthened to such an extent that, leaping back from there, they suddenly attack and consume even the hardest things. Subtract that little portion of the heart by which that form of fire is held down; let there remain the indivisible form—agile, hot, and shining, both differently than before and more wonderfully. Because it is indivisible and agile according to its whole self, it may illuminate the whole body equally. Because it glows incredibly, let it be vital and life-giving. Because it shines miraculously, let it perceive. Let it understand moreover, if it is reflected back into itself and raised upward. 

Hitherto, proceeding step by step through those things which are touched, you have found the soul when you proceeded from the solid body to something like a point that is entirely free. Again, through those things which are seen with the eyes, examine the soul. Why, I ask, do you doubt that there is something spiritual in nature, when you see spirit in a certain way with your very eyes? You know that the light of the Sun is manifest to the eye and is not a body for this reason: because in a moment it pours itself into all things, and once infused, it does not break bodies, nor is it stained. Behold, you see spirit. Why do you deny it? Or perhaps you will deny that which you do not see exists? If that is the case, you will say that the spheres of air, fire, and heaven—which are more excellent than water and earth—are nothing because they are not seen. Thus the greatest and most excellent part of the world, because it is not visible, will be nothing. 

But let us return to light. In this way you will deny that light is in the sphere of fire, because it is not perceived by the eyes. But the brightness of the Sun itself would exist even if it were not seen, since it exists now and is not seen by owls; and some of its splendor, mixed with vapors, is seen by us rather than the light itself, but we conjecture that it exists somewhere from this splendor of its. So too, we conjecture from the stars themselves that a spiritual light exists in celestial souls...

<summary>Ficino uses a geometric ladder—from 3D bodies to dimensionless "Unity"—to argue that the soul is an indivisible, non-material power. He further uses the analogy of light and sunbeams to explain how the soul can be invisible yet more real and powerful than the visible body.</summary>

<page-num>362</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...we conjecture by the light of that <note>i.e., the divine or celestial light</note>, which is its image. Do you not know that the act of light is nothing other than to shine, and to glow all the more brightly the further it is separated from gross bodies <note>original: "crassis corporibus," referring to dense, physical matter</note>? Separate light itself from all matter and it will glow more marvelously; indeed, it lives most fully when it is about to live <note>Ficino implies that light's "life" is its activity and radiance</note>. For where its "act" <term>actus: the expression of a thing's true nature or power</term> increases, life also increases, especially since all these things live through its heat. It will also feel, so to speak, since all things feel through its rays; yet it will not be sensed at all, for by its thinness it will escape the sharp gaze of the eyes, and by the abundance of its intelligible brilliance, it will surpass the capacity of earthly sight. 

You know that in the sphere of the elements, the lowest fire declines so far toward the nature of the highest air, while conversely the highest air is raised so far toward that fire, that the fire almost seems to be nothing but thin air, and that air a thicker fire; so much so that whoever sees that air can affirm without lying that he has seen fire. The same comparison applies to the lowest mind—which is the rational soul—in relation to that sublime body which is the heavens. Therefore, the soul is in a sense a thin heaven, and the heaven is a thicker soul. And he who looks up at the heaven beholds the soul. 

Think of a geometric point: because it looks equally toward every part of the space surrounding it, if it ever moves, it moves in a circle. Thus, what was a point appears to emerge as a circumference, where the circumference is truly the point running around and unfolded outward. The point, however, is the circumference rolled up around a stable center <note>literally "hinge" or "axis"</note>. Think again of a spark of invisible light: because it exists above every place, it pours itself equally into every part of space, and while it moves in a circuit, a flaming orb is produced. I say an orb manifest to the eyes, where the spark is compressed flame, and the flame is the spark poured forth. 

The soul is a spark of this kind; the ethereal body is the flame. And as great as the variety of spiritual light is in rational souls, so great is the variety of visible light in their own celestial bodies. And that light follows the spiritual light just as the pale orb in the clouds <note>a halo or reflection</note> follows the light of the Moon. There is, however, this difference among rational souls: the souls of the fixed stars and planets are surrounded only by a lucid body; all other souls are surrounded by twin bodies—one lucid and one opaque—or certainly one very bright and the other less so. It seems to be the same light which, while it remains a spark, truly feels but is not felt; but when it is unfolded into a flame, it is indeed felt but itself feels no more. And just as anyone would lack sense who, seeing the flame, denied he saw the spark, so too will he lack a soul <note>i.e., lose his spiritual nature</note> who, while looking up at the ethereal globes as the circuits of souls, does not perceive that souls are within them as centers, nor grants that souls are globes of light folded up, and globes are souls unfolded. This is what Heraclitus meant:
->**A dry light is the wisest soul**<- 
<note>original Greek: "αὐη ξηρη ψυχη σοφωτατη". Ficino uses the "dryness" of light to represent purity from the "moisture" of material corruption.</note>
That is, a dry light is the most wise soul. From this it follows that nothing is more pleasing or more marvelous to the mind than light, nor can the soul dwell anywhere else than in the light of spirits while it inhabits the earth. 

Now, therefore, you have found even here that the soul is like an invisible light—life-giving, sensing, intelligible, and intelligent. And a little before, you found it to be like a point free from the body, agile of itself, warming, life-giving, sensing, and capable of higher things, which is called a certain substantial unity. And let this be a first excursion and a sort of prelude, by which that unhappy lack of confidence may be removed—a doubt which leads the minds of common people very far away from the confession of spiritual things.

### The soul is not a body, or a form divided in the body, as is shown through the natural power of the soul. Chapter IV.

**T**he order of the proposed question requires that in the first part of the following disputation we show, through the natural power of the soul, that the human soul is primarily not a body, and partly also that it is not a form divided in the body. In the second part, through the power of sensing, we shall demonstrate the same: namely, that the soul is an indivisible form; and we shall further add that it is not attached to any one member of the body, but is poured as a whole through every single part. In the third part, through the power of understanding, we shall confirm the same: namely, that it is an impartible <note>indivisible</note> form, everywhere whole; and we shall add that it draws no origin from matter. For thus the human soul reaches that third essence, which is...

will pertain to the eternal, and will be deservedly judged immortal. Now indeed, having invoked the divine power, let us approach the first part of the discussion in this manner.

### *First reason: Because the soul is the principle of nourishment, and of acting in any other way. Chapter IV.*

**L**iving beings and green plants are bodies; logs and rocks torn from the earth are also bodies. Those former bodies grow together <note>original: "coalescunt," referring to the biological process of cells or parts integrating during growth</note>, while these latter do not at all. What then is the principle of nourishment in the former? It is not bodily matter, for otherwise other bodies would also be nourished, since such matter is common to all of them. Since, therefore, that power through which they grow is something other than bodily matter, and that power is nothing other than the <term>nutritive soul: the basic level of the soul responsible for growth and sustenance</term>, it follows that such a soul is not a body. 

But if someone should object in this way: "On the contrary, it is indeed a body, not just any body, but a specific kind, affected in such a way as is proper to the nature of plants and living beings, and not shared with dry rocks and fire," we will ask him about this specific and certain body which he calls the soul. Does it contain two things within itself—namely, a bodily mass and, in addition, a certain "affection" <note>here meaning a specific state or quality</note> through which it is called such and is a certain and proper body—or does it have nothing beyond the matter common to all bodies everywhere? If he answers that it has nothing besides this common mass, that objection was entirely vain, by which it was said that not just any body is a soul, but a specific body disposed in a certain way. 

For it does not become such a body, disposed in a certain way, except through that very quality and a certain proper "affection" added to the body itself; through this, it is not only a body, but a specific *kind* of body, by which it also differs from any other body. Therefore, if there is nothing there besides the common mass of the body alone, and since that mass is also in dry logs and rocks, these too would have a soul through which they would be nourished. Because this is clearly false, it is necessary that this specific body which the adversary called a soul contains not only the matter of the body, but also some quality or <term>form: the essential identity or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is</term>. And it is not named "soul" because of the matter of the body itself, since matter belongs to all bodies, even those lacking life. It remains that it is named so because of the form—the <term>vivifying form: the life-giving essence</term>, I say. For that is proper to the soul. 

Therefore, we shall call that vivifying form the "soul," but that matter to which it is joined, we shall say is neither the soul nor a part of the soul, but something "of the souls," because it is a participant in life from that source. The present reasoning is greatly confirmed by the opinion we introduced at the beginning, when we argued that a body can do nothing of itself; for we see that when the soul enters bodies, many operations proceed from them, which both arrive with the soul and cease to occur after its departure. Therefore, we conclude that the soul, which is the principle of such operations, is not a body.

### *Second reason: Neither is an animated body the soul, nor an inanimate one. Chapter V.*

**W**hat kind of body do you want the soul to be: an animated one or an inanimate one? You will not say "inanimate," for how can the soul give life to another if it is itself an inanimate body? Nor can you say it is an animated body, because if the soul is called an "animated body," then certainly that body, after it is called "animated," is called so because of some soul. Concerning that soul, I ask again: is it a body or not? If it is a body, is it animated or inanimate? 

If the answer is "inanimate," it is indeed absurd. If "animated," you will be forced to ask again about that soul by which it is said to be animated. And so you will be forced to proceed into infinity <note>a logical fallacy where an explanation requires a previous explanation forever, never reaching a first cause</note> as long as you assert that the soul is a body, and you will always be compelled to answer absurdly. For both responses seem delirious: that the soul is either animated or inanimate. It is like saying of "Wisdom" that it is either wise or foolish, or of "Light" that it is either illuminated or dark. 

For just as light is not dark (which would be the opposite of its nature) nor is it "illuminated" by something else (since it is itself the primary light), so the soul is neither "inanimate" (since it gives life) nor "animated" through something else, since the soul is itself properly that through which anything is actually animated. And if you refer the soul to something else by which it might be animated, I will similarly refer that "something else" to another, and that again to another, and never stop...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because life (nourishment and growth) requires a "vivifying form" that matter alone lacks. He also demonstrates through logic that the soul cannot be an "animated body," as this leads to an infinite regress, proving the soul is the primary source of life itself.</summary>

<keywords>nutritive soul, vivifying form, incorporeality, infinite regress, biological principle, animated vs inanimate, logic of life</keywords>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...I will never stop <note>The Latin text begins mid-word, "bo," completing "dubitabo" (I will doubt) or a similar verb from the previous page</note>, or if I do stop, I will certainly rest in this: that I say either that very thing which was first proposed, or something following it, is neither animated nor vivified by another, but is itself properly through itself that which animates and vivifies another. I shall call such a thing "soul" and "life" properly, and not anything else. Perhaps, in order to avoid that infinite regress and those delirious responses, you might assert that the soul is a body, yet you will claim it is not an animated body, but an **animal body**; not a vivified body, but a **living body**. 

If this is so, you are turned back to the same point. Indeed, I will ask whether it is a soul by that reason <note>original: "ratio," here meaning the underlying nature or logic of its being</note> by which it is a body, or by some other reason—namely, by some new addition through which it is called "animal" and "living"? Certainly, it is not by the reason of being a body. For if that were so, all bodies would be souls and would display the operations of life. It follows that some other nature must be present there besides the nature of the body, through which that body is called "living" and "animal." That nature I shall call **life** properly, and **soul**.

### Third reason: It is neither a dense body, nor a subtle one. Chapter VI.

**I**s the soul a dense body, such as water or earth and the like? Or is it rather a subtle and rare one, like fire and air? The first cannot be said, since the office of the soul is to penetrate bodies most easily, to fill them, and to move them. For such an operation, dense bodies are most unsuitable. The second option might perhaps seem more probable: that the soul is a rare body, like fire or air. 

But if it is said to be fire, is it a soul by the reason that it is fire, or by some other reason? If it were said to be a soul by the reason that it is fire, then surely any fire would be a soul, and all ignited things would be living. Therefore, it is by another reason. The same must be asked of air, and the conclusion must be drawn: the soul must always be sought beyond the nature of the body. 

Nor should anyone bring forward some <term>fifth body: the "quintessence" or aether, a theoretical fifth element believed to be more refined than the four earthly elements</term>, most thin and refined, which, when infused into denser bodies, becomes their soul. For the same question will return: whether that little body is a soul through its matter, or through some way added onto the matter. If the first is said, all bodies will be souls, because matter underlies them all. If the second, we will have achieved what we desire: that the soul must be referred to some power that is, in a way, **incorporeal**.

Certain brief arguments of this kind are offered by some: If the soul is said to be divisible, one asks whether its parts live as the whole does, or not? If they live, the soul is in each of its individual particles as a whole; thus, it does not require quantity, since it is not diminished by division. If they do not live, then life would consist of non-living things, which is impossible. 

Again, every body can be known by one of the five senses, but the soul by none. Every body is circumscribed by some shape or boundary, but the soul not at all. Every body necessarily performs its operation through an interval of time (for since it is divisible in its essence, it is much more so in its action), but the soul often operates in a **moment of time** <note>Ficino argues that mental acts, unlike physical ones, can be instantaneous</note>. A body is in a place through quantity rather than through essence, because it fills a place on account of its quantity; the soul is present to the body through essence, for as it is present to it, it gives it **being**. Being is given through essence, just as being wise is given through wisdom; therefore, the soul is present through essence. A body is in another thing in such a way that it is contained by that in which it is placed, and is exceeded by it; the soul is not contained in the body, but is **containing** it. For she herself perfects, contains, and leads the body. Finally, the soul is more excellent than any body and the whole body; therefore, it is more excellent than the lines and points which are in bodies as if in a subject. The indivisible is more excellent than the divisible. The soul, therefore, is more indivisible than either a line or a point.

### Fourth reason. The body is composed of matter and form. Chapter VII.

**A** natural body is composed of **matter and form**. An animal is a natural body. Therefore, matter is in it, and form. It consists, moreover, of soul and body. The body indeed is not the natural form, because a natural form is the form *of something*, and is in something as if in a certain subject that is formed. But the body is the form of nothing, nor is it in any subject, but in a place. It remains that the soul is the form, most especially because it is the proper and internal principle of operations and motions; indeed, it is even the principle of **being** for the animal. All of this pertains to the form. It is...

<meta>catchword: therefore (igitur)</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body (neither dense nor subtle) because life is an essential quality rather than a material one. He defines the soul as the "form" of the body—the internal principle that gives a living being its existence and motion.</summary>

<meta>catchword: into one</meta>

Therefore, the soul is **form**. <note>In this philosophical context, "form" (forma) refers to the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is, rather than just its outward shape.</note> But if the soul itself were also a body, there would still be a need for some other form for both the soul and the body, through which both together could be called a single living being. We would then more properly call that other form the "soul." For it is through the soul, as if through a form, that the body—which previously has only the potential for life—becomes actually living and a living being in reality.

The soul, therefore, is solely form, especially because if you were to claim it has two parts—namely, matter and form—three absurdities would follow. **First**, the soul would not form the body according to its whole self, because it would not form the body through its matter-part; yet it is necessary for a proper form to perfect its proper matter according to its entire essence. **Second**, that part of the soul called "form" would be the perfection of two different matters of the same kind, which nature does not allow; just as nature does not allow two forms of the same kind to inform the same matter. **Third**, because the soul would be transmuted into these lower bodies, and vice versa, if it possessed matter in common with them. This is considered <term>unspeakable</term> <note>original: "nefas," a term suggesting something that is not only logically impossible but almost a violation of divine or natural law</note>, because if a mutual exchange of bodies and souls were to occur, there would much more easily occur a transmutation of any soul into any other soul, and again of any body into any other body.

Let the soul, therefore, be form alone. A form, I say, that is not **accidental**, but **substantial**. <note>A "substantial form" gives a thing its primary existence (like being a human), whereas an "accidental form" is a non-essential quality (like being tan or sitting down).</note> For since the soul itself is the ruler and mover of the body—holding it together, making it stand, and turning it—it is more excellent than the body. The body is a substance. Truly, no <term>accident</term> <note>A property that cannot exist on its own, like "redness"</note> is nobler than a substance. Furthermore, a mover, insofar as it is the principle of motion, does not depend for its existence upon that which is moved. Therefore, the soul, which is truly the mover of the body, does not depend on the body like a servant; thus, it is not an accident of the body.

Moreover, whatever receives opposite qualities in turn while remaining the same thing itself is a substance. The soul, remaining the same, receives now this opinion and now that (which are contrary to each other), as well as knowledge and ignorance, and conflicting emotions; therefore, the soul is a substance. A substance, I say, acting as a kind of substantial form. But a form is not a body, because every body is defined by some form. A form, by the very reason that it is a form, cannot itself be formed <note>meaning it cannot be the passive material that receives a shape</note>. From this, it follows that the soul is not a body. 

I set aside for now the reasons showing that our soul cannot be an accident; for if it were attached to a subject by some necessity, it could not resist that subject, nor could it ever reflect upon itself, nor could it rise above the category of accidents to the category of substance, nor could it properly define substance, or distinguish it from accidents, or rightly measure by how great a distance it surpasses accidents.

---

->*Fifth reason. The body is by its nature dispersed. Chapter VIII.*<-

# C
ORPUS <note>The woodcut initial 'C' begins "Corpus" (The body)</note> by its nature is entirely dispersed. **First**, because it undergoes the distance of parts, so that one part is always in a different place from another. **Second**, because it is continually changing. For if it is subject to time, then just as different moments succeed one another in time, so the conditions of the body vary at every single moment. This variation, which occurs even in the heavens, happens much more so in the elements <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, fire</note> due to the rotation of the heavens. **Third**, because it is subject to contrary qualities, such as heat and cold and the like.

From this it follows that it is against the nature of the body to come together into one, to remain similar, and to be consistent with itself. For the very extension of quantity compels the parts of the body to remain disjoined. Constant motion forces its nature to change, so that it does not possess its attributes all at once, but loses one while seeking another. The contrariety of qualities drives one to flee the other, and through this flight, the composite body itself is dissipated.

Although it appears through these points that a body, by its nature, can in no way stand firmly in unity, nevertheless any body is in some way bound together in its parts, with all parts conspiring into a single joining of the whole body. There is, therefore, something in the body beyond the nature of the body itself which unites it, stays it, and contains it. It unites, I say, the distance of the parts; it stays the perpetual flux; it contains within itself, through its own simple harmony, the discordant qualities of the body. What is this? Is it a body? If it is a body, it likewise needs another thing to connect it. What else is that? Is it a body? If it is a body, it needs yet another. Therefore, one must confess that there can be no unity in bodies, no constancy, and no concord, unless there is within them some **incorporeal power**. 

Therefore, if the soul is also said to be a body, it would itself also need some bond. We shall call this kind of bonding power the "soul"—or rather the "virtue of the soul"—rather than the thing which is bound, since we see that it is the property of the soul to [unite] contrary humors and diverse members...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul must be a "substantial form" rather than a physical body or a mere accidental quality, because it provides unity and stability to the otherwise dispersed and ever-changing material body.</summary>

to bind into one single living composite, which, when the soul departs, everything dissolves. Therefore, the soul is not a body, but the innermost bond of the body, or a binding substance. Nor is it a form divided through the body. For such a form (as the Platonists think) would lose its nature of simplicity and constancy in the body, whereby it would, like the body itself, need another container that stands one in itself, not at all dissipated by the division of the body. If anyone asks from where stones and wood obtain the union of their parts, the Platonists will respond that as long as they are attached to the earth, they obtain both union and growth from the soul of the earth; but after they are torn away, they no longer obtain growth, but only union. <note>Ficino refers here to the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, a Platonic concept suggesting the Earth itself is a living organism that provides life and structure to things attached to it.</note>

### Sixth argument. Two bodies are not in the same place. Chapter IX.

**T**wo bodies cannot be completely equalized within the same place. For if they must be entirely in the same place, they must first be divided into parts, and then those parts must be joined to each other. If these parts are indivisible, then those bodies have already been resolved into <term>indivisibles</term> <note>original: "individua," referring to atoms or the smallest possible units of matter that cannot be split further.</note>. And since they were composed of these same units and are not dissolved, it follows that the magnitude of the body has grown out of certain indivisible points. But this could not happen, because indivisible points gathered together never create a magnitude. However, if those parts were divisible, each would be a body by itself and would have its own specific location separate from the other; thus, there would not be two bodies in one place, but rather many small bodies in many small compartments. 

If, therefore, two bodies cannot be equalized in the same place, the soul—which pours itself everywhere into the living body and extends itself through every point of the body—is not a body. Furthermore, that it is everywhere in the body is evident from the fact that nothing is more intrinsic to an essence than "being." Therefore, the form through which substantial being is granted both to the whole body and to its parts is innermost to the whole and the parts. And because as a thing stands in relation to being, so it also stands in relation to "one," the soul—which gives being through itself—is also united through itself without any intermediary to the whole body. 

That it grants substantial being is evident from the fact that once the soul is removed, all the limbs change their <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem," meaning their essential nature or form. A dead eye is an "eye" in name only, as it no longer performs the function of seeing.</note>. Because being flows from essence, and operation from power, the soul—which grants being and operation to each individual limb—also communicates its essence and power to each one. For it provides being and operation in the same way that it is united. Therefore, if it provides these to each part, it is united to each part. Is it not true that if any natural body lacking a soul is a single thing through a single form existing in the whole and the parts, how much more will an animated body be one through a soul present to the whole and the parts? 

But if the soul were in only one limb, it would be the form of that limb alone, and there would be other forms for the rest; hence, a truly single natural body would not be fashioned from all the limbs, but rather an aggregate thing, like a house made of walls. Nor would there be in any part of the animal a consensus and harmony toward every other part, as there is now, unless the various limbs were glued together by one soul—just as all joints are not contracted by the pull of a nerve unless it is the same nerve in all of them. Add to this that in any portion of the body, however tiny, there is life, and in most parts, motion and sense. These powers and operations of the soul are innermost. A power and action that is innermost to some agent does not exist without the substance of that agent. The soul is therefore in those parts, if it flourishes and acts in them; and when it moves in its own way, it does not dissipate the body, because no pain is produced from the motion of the soul through the body. 

Yet perpetual pain would occur in the body if its parts were dissipated and disturbed by the motion of the soul. They would undoubtedly be dissipated if the soul were a body, since the soul moves through the body in its own perpetual motion. By what logic, then, shall the soul be a body, when it is everywhere through the body and fills and penetrates the whole from every side without any injury to the body? Furthermore, if it were a solid body, it would either not fill the whole body (and thus the whole would not live), or if it did fill it, it would break and be broken by the penetration, and perpetual pain would arise within us. But if the soul were a fluid and unstable body, it would neither bind nor firmly solidify the body of the living being, but it would itself (as we said above) need some other bond by whose stability it might be strengthened, ruled, and moved. We shall more willingly call that bond the "soul," or rather the **virtue** <note>original: "uirtutem," meaning power or effective force.</note> of the soul. Indeed, the virtue of the soul in the body is almost the same as the power of rennet in milk, by which it is curdled; or the force of a magnet in iron, by which it is drawn and suspended; or the tempering of art in a **clock**, by which it is ruled, moved, and sounds in a wonderful order. The soul itself is not...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a body because two physical bodies cannot occupy the same space. He describes the soul as an indivisible "bond" that provides existence and unity to every part of the living body simultaneously.</summary>

[the soul's] power is not from the tempering of humors, but is a certain substantial form, simple and indivisible, which by natural power and art tempers the spirits, the humors, and the limbs.

### *Seventh argument. A body is not all in many places at once. Chapter X.*

**N**either bodies nor forms divided through bodies can be simultaneously in several parts or places. The seminary power <term>seminary power</term> <note>original: "vis seminaria," the latent creative force within a seed or "semen" that directs the growth and biological blueprint of a living thing.</note> is whole in any particle of the seed. In as many particles as the seed is divided, just as many animals arise, which appears most clearly in the eggs of fish. If a whole animal sprouts from any little drop of seed, the whole seminary power is hidden there. But this power is the soul's instrument, serving the process of generation. Therefore, much more so is the whole soul present in any particle of the seed and the body. Since, therefore, the whole power of the soul is in individual parts, is not the vegetative power <note>The "vegetative soul" was the lowest level of soul in Aristotelian/Platonic thought, responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> whole in any seed of a plant, since it certainly produces a complete plant from any part? The vegetative soul is first captured in a tiny root or germ, then as the tree grows, it pours itself through all the branches. Finally, when the branches are dried or cut off, it contracts itself back into the root. Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) and Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) were the founding philosophers of Neoplatonism, a school of thought that deeply influenced Ficino.</note> believe that this soul lacks physical quantity, for it equally encloses the smallest things and fills the largest.

### *Eighth argument. The soul is life, or the fountain of life. Chapter XI.*

**W**e think the soul is a certain nature which is either life itself, or has life as its companion and handmaid, since bodies obtain life through the soul. A body is necessarily divided into several parts. For one type of body is composed of several elements, while another is an element—not at all gathered from other elements, but constituted of form and matter. If you say the soul is a body constructed from several elements, we will ask whether those elements, each by itself apart from the others, have life, or whether none do, but when gathered together they give birth to life, or whether one certain thing among them possesses life. 

If each of them has life by itself, there are as many souls there as there are elements. Nor is there one soul fused from many parts, but many souls inhabiting the same seat. If none of them has life, they will never create life by mutual meeting. And if life is born in their meeting, it is certainly not by their own power, since they themselves lack life, but rather that life will be born by the power of something ordering that meeting—especially since it must be admitted that even if life is fused by the meeting of many, they do not meet in just any way, but only if they meet by a certain reason and path is life produced in them. Thus the innermost arranger of that certain meeting will be the soul itself, providing life in its own way to the gathering elements. 

If, however, you say that one certain element out of many has life, that alone will be the soul itself, nor will it need those other elements in order for the soul to generate. For which reason the soul must in no way be thought to be a body constituted of several elements. But it is not even a single element, because any element is composed of matter and form. If it lived, it would not live through matter, since formless matter cannot provide life either to something else or to itself. Therefore, such a thing would live through form. Form, therefore, would be the soul. 

Furthermore, if the soul is a body—whether it be an element or something similar, and whether simple or composite—it will certainly be, so to speak, affected in a similar way: namely, hot or cold, dry or moist, light or heavy, rare or dense, fluid, solid, white, black, and such things. Thus a hot thing will only heat. If it is light, it will seek the heights; and whatever kind of body it is, it will operate according to its own nature, and will never perform an action opposite to the state of its own nature. For a cold thing does not heat. Moreover, every body has a certain and determined nature and form, just as its place is limited, its time is fixed, and its power is finite. Therefore, the operation of each body is determined and does not extend to contrary effects. 

But the soul is seen to have power over any contraries. For both in the diverse bodies of animals and in the same body, it effects many things that are repugnant to one another. It stops, moves, contracts, extends, thins, thickens, sharpens, blunts, opens, closes, pours, and solidifies. It hands over contrary smells, tastes, and colors, and opposite powers and shapes to the humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were believed to control health and temperament in pre-modern medicine.</note> and limbs; it moves light spirits downward to the feet and leads heavy humors upward to the head,

which is against the nature of bodies. It drives the body in every direction: upward against the weight of heavy elements, downward against the rising nature of light ones, sideways and in a circle against every physical tendency. Since it produces almost all contrary effects and is capable of such opposing movements that it moves beyond the natural order of bodies, who would be so mad as to admit that the soul is either a body, or its quality, or something belonging to a quality?

## Ninth Argument. A body does not move itself. Chapter XII.

**T**hat which is truly and primarily mobile of itself <note>original: "per seipsum mobile"</note>—in such a way that it is entirely the same thing as both the source and the recipient of motion—ought to be mobile of itself according to its whole self. This appears in all other things that are called such "of themselves" or "primarily." For example, what is clear in this way is clear throughout its whole self. What is good in this way is entirely good. What is understood in this way is entirely intellectual. For an essence that primarily pours out some quality and primarily embraces and receives it, because it performs both perfectly, it effects both through the whole. 

However, it is necessary that somewhere in nature an essence be found that is mobile in that way "through itself" or "from itself," and that the soul is such a thing, as we demonstrated in the preceding books. Even if a body were imagined to be mobile of itself and primarily, it could not yet be such according to its whole self, because every part of it would have to be moved by itself, as would the parts of those parts and the tiny particles. For if there were even one particle in the body that did not move itself, that body would not be mobile from itself according to its whole self; thus, it would not truly and primarily be such, but would be such only through the participation and presence of something else that is primarily so. 

Therefore, for it to be perfectly mobile of itself, one would have to grant that any of its particles are moved by themselves. These are divided infinitely; hence there will be innumerable particles moving themselves. What moves, acts; what acts, exists in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" refers to the fulfillment of a possibility, as opposed to "potentiality." Ficino argues that if parts moved themselves, they would have independent actual existence, leading to an infinite number of independent beings within a single body.</note>. Therefore, there will be infinite parts in actuality driving themselves, and infinite movers in any body of the world. Indeed, those parts would not even be parts of another body by the very fact that they exist by their own action, but each would stand as a whole by itself, and there would be an infinite multitude of little bodies existing in actuality. 

However, it is impossible for such a multitude to exist in nature. Since, therefore, the parts of a body cannot be infinite in actuality—indeed, they cannot even truly exist in actuality at all, since they have no being of their own but are contained under the being of the whole composite—it follows that the parts of a body do not move themselves, lest they be forced to exist in actuality because of this, and be utterly infinite in actuality. Let us conclude, therefore, that a body cannot be truly and primarily mobile of itself, since this cannot belong to it according to its whole self, given that its parts are not able to achieve moving themselves. 

Let us proceed toward the same point by another way. When someone asserts that a body moves itself, he is forced to admit one of these four things: either one part of the body is moved by another, or the whole is moved by a part, or a part is moved by the whole, or the whole is moved by the whole—that is, all parts are moved by all parts. 

If the first is affirmed, since one part is one thing and another part is something else, it is not the *same* thing moving itself, but rather one thing moving another. Nor will that composite body truly move itself from this, since it is constituted of parts that do not move themselves, but it will have two distinct things within it, one of which moves the other. If you take the second branch of that division—namely, that a part moves the whole—or the third—namely, that the whole moves a part—that composite is still not truly driving itself. For we mean the part to be one thing and the whole another. And that part which moves the whole certainly moves all the parts, and therefore it even changes itself among the number of other parts. 

Similarly, if the whole is said to move a part, it moves that one part through all the other parts; therefore, it drives only one certain thing, in a sense, through itself. You see that in these two branches of division it cannot be said that the whole moves itself except through that part of itself which drives itself, and not at all through the others. And so, that whole will not really be mobile of itself, but perhaps only that part of the whole will be; and yet it will not even be a "part" of it, since it performs an action by itself. But if you grant the fourth, namely that the whole is moved by the whole, since the whole is perhaps nothing other than all the parts together, you will admit that all parts are changed by all parts, where that composite ought to be affirmed to move itself for no other reason than because every part of it drives itself. On which account, [it leads] always back to the part <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "retreat" or "take refuge."</note>

you are forced to retreat, intending to claim that a body is mobile of itself <note>original: "per se mobile"</note>. We reject this first because a composite body will not be properly mobile of itself, since it borrows that property from its parts. For it is said to be self-moving only by reason of its parts. Even if it is established that such a body is, in a way, all its parts at once, the motion of this kind seems to be received from the individual parts, just as it receives its substance from the individuals. 

Tell me, I ask, about that part or those parts by reason of which the whole is asserted to move itself (because they move themselves): are they indivisible? If they are, then surely that which moves itself is not a body, but something indivisible within the body, by whose impulse the body also seems to be carried along of its own accord. But if they are divisible, we shall divide that part just as we have already split the whole, and by the same reasoning we will find that it can in no way be claimed of those parts that they move of themselves, except by reason of even smaller particles that move themselves. We shall investigate those particles similarly, and since they can be distributed into infinity, we will always find new and more numerous movers, and we will never arrive at a single one, since by dividing we always have many. Nor will we ever reach the first movers or the first one, since we likewise divide infinitely. 

Therefore, nowhere in the substance of a body is there a single and first mover of itself; for this reason, it has no origin of its own motion within itself through which it could truly move another by its own power. Instead, we are compelled to arrive at something indivisible <note>original: "impartibile," meaning having no physical parts</note> from which the origin of all bodily agitation is born. Now, the internal driver of the body is the soul. While the soul is present, bodies are carried along in every direction and in a certain way of their own accord; but when the soul is absent, they require an external mover. If the soul were also a body, it too would require a mover—an external mover, I say—if indeed all living things move without an external push. That most internal mover will indeed be the soul itself, which must move of itself, since bodies seem to have the power of moving themselves through the soul.

Every such thing must be traced back to some nature that is truly the driver of itself. Thus the soul properly moves of itself, if other things obtain the faculty of moving themselves through participation in it. Therefore, the soul is not a body, nor is it a form scattered through a body. For such a form is also unable to move itself according to the reasons given above, being subject to the same conditions as the body, as has been shown. 

This excludes that quibble by which some strive to show that a certain body moves of itself. They say it is composed of matter and form, or of the four elements, in such a way that a certain nature results—beyond the matter, the form, and the four elements—which is the "integrity of the whole." They claim this integrity moves itself because it has the power to move through its form, and the capacity to be moved through its matter. Such an objection carries no weight against the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, like Ficino himself.</note>, both because the root of the power to move will be in one essence, and the root of being moved will be in another. However, one must arrive at a single essence which is both the fountain and the receptacle of motion and life, just as one arrives at an essence which is the root and foundation of both light and heat. Furthermore, if that nature which is the "integrity of the whole" is extended in quantity <note>i.e., takes up physical space</note>, it could no more move itself than the physical mass itself, as we showed above. 

But if it is indivisible, then (as we desired) we have already arrived at an incorporeal nature in which the power of driving itself resides. This does not mean it acts upon itself and suffers <note>meaning to be acted upon or to receive an impression</note> itself. For motion in the soul does not signify a transition from an agent to a patient <note>The "agent" is the doer; the "patient" is the one receiving the action.</note>, but a natural change of that essence by which it varies the turns of its own affections. Thus it runs through itself without another driving it—just as fire is hot of itself without another heating it, and without one part of it pouring heat into another part. 

Therefore, since animal motion is not from the body (which is sluggish by nature), nor from the composite alone (in which there is no power of moving if it is joined from parts that have no power for motion), it is necessarily from the soul. If the soul grants the animal the power to move from rest into action, it grants this to itself much more and much earlier. For whatever good or vital act is transferred from a cause into an effect is first unfolded in the cause. For in this way heat is hot and boils within itself before it heats other matter; and living bodies swell with seeds and conceive offspring within themselves before they give birth. Therefore, while the soul unfolds the vital progression from potentiality into act within itself, it is said to move itself. The Platonists properly call "motion" in the soul **action**, because it exists in its own fountain and forms and drives the body. But they call "motion" in the body **passion**. And since the corporeal mass of the universe must also be moved by another, they conclude that the motion of the universal body is a "passion" resulting from the motion of the universal soul, just as...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 149 (numbered 169 in some sequences), where Ficino asserts that a body cannot be the primary source of its own motion. He now transitions into defining the specific "vital motion" of the soul as the true source of activity.</meta>

rather than from some action of those parts. And just as in every category, the imperfect things are always reduced to the perfect, so they refer the imperfect motion of the body back to the motion of the soul as the perfect form in that very category of motion. Furthermore, when it is asked what kind of motion primarily moves the soul, they <note>Ficino refers here to the Platonists, likely Plotinus or Proclus.</note> respond: not a physical motion, for the soul is incorporeal; not an imaginable motion, for it lacks a shape; and not a non-cognitive motion, for it is not ignorant of itself; but rather a motion according to its **vital essence**. For just as the act of essence is "to be," and the act of the intellect itself is "to understand," so the act of life is "to live." For the soul does not possess a life that comes from the outside, but one from itself; and to use their words, the soul is **life generating and producing itself.** <note>original: "anima est uita se generans & producens"</note>

Indeed, all life is motion. Therefore, if every living thing is moved, then that which lives through itself <note>original: "per se," meaning by its own nature</note> is also moved through itself. And that which always lives is also always moved—not, of course, with an intellectual motion, but with a **vital** one. For this reason, it is always moved, and yet not always. For the mind exists according to its potential, but life exists according to its act. Finally, the essence always lives and exercises a perpetual internal motion, because essential life is always mobile. However, the powers and acts that occur regarding both life and the intellect can sometimes be interrupted or go astray. 

But let us now return to where we digressed. This third following reason persuades us of the same thing. All motions are these: **alteration, generation, corruption, increase, decrease, condensation, rarefaction, and progression.** <note>These are the eight types of change or motion defined in Aristotelian and Platonic physics.</note> Can a body move itself according to *alteration*? Not at all. For if it must heat itself, it must already possess the heat which it would give to itself. Yet it must also *not* have it, if it is to be the receiver of it. For no one receives what they already possess. Therefore, to perform the heating, it is already hot; to be heated, it is not yet hot. It is ridiculous to say that something both has and does not have something at the same time—unless, perhaps, someone says that water has a certain "potential coldness" which it retains even after being heated by fire, through which it returns to "actual coldness" once removed from the fire. To this the Platonists will respond: either that water is cooled by external elements, or, if its actual quality (which leans somewhat toward an incorporeal nature) sprouts from that internal power of productive quality (a power which is much closer to an incorporeal nature), it follows that a power of this kind flows from a certain substance that exists as entirely incorporeal. Such a substance will be the principle of motion in the body.

Therefore, no body moves itself by alteration. But neither does it **generate** itself, because that which generates something else gives "being" to the thing generated. Thus the parent has the "being" which it grants to the offspring. That which is generated receives its "being" from elsewhere, as it does not possess it itself. Therefore, nothing can grant "being" to itself. For it would both have it and not have it at the same time. And since the generator precedes the generated, one who is the generator and the generated of himself (according to a finite nature) would be both prior to and posterior to himself at the same time—which no one would imagine in a finite nature. Furthermore, a body cannot **corrupt** <note>In this context, "corrupt" means to decay or cease to exist.</note> itself. Since every thing generates its offspring from its own nature, and therefore brings forth something compatible with itself and not contrary, it follows that the natural instinct of every thing—which is a kind of "offspring" of its essence and its very being—does not rise up against its own essence and being.

Therefore, no thing is led by its own instinct toward non-being—not only its own, but not even that of anything else. Rather, since the effort of every thing proceeds toward preserving itself, it will not turn toward the opposite. Moreover, a body does not **increase** or **decrease** itself. For that cannot happen without alteration, and even a certain generation and corruption. For we grow and shrink through the alteration of qualities. While we grow, new parts of the body are generated in us; while we shrink, old parts are corrupted. Therefore, if increase and decrease require alteration, generation, and corruption, a body—which does not move itself through alteration, generation, or corruption—certainly does not move itself by increasing or decreasing. Nor does it **condense** or **rarefy** itself, since these also do not happen without alteration. Perhaps someone might say: a body is at least changed in its place through **progression** <note>local motion or traveling</note> or rotation. This is also impossible to say. For if it is powerless regarding those internal motions already mentioned, it will be much more powerless regarding external ones. I call "external motions" rotation and progression, which tend toward boundaries more remote than internal motions. Thus, if a body is not able to be moved through itself toward its own internal boundaries, how can it be moved toward foreign boundaries? Wherefore, let us now conclude thus: no other motions appear in bodies...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Ficino established that bodies do not move themselves but are moved by an internal nature. Here, he identifies this nature as the soul and describes how the soul contains the patterns for all types of physical motion.</meta>

<page-num>171</page-num>

-># ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS: BOOK VI<-

...besides those eight <note>Likely referring to the eight types of motion or categories of change discussed in preceding chapters.</note> already numbered. They are not driven by any of those through themselves. Therefore, in no way are bodies moved by themselves. However, they are moved (as is evident to anyone) by a certain nature acting from within, even without external impulses. No Platonist would deny that this is the soul, because it is possible for the soul to be moved through itself, since in it are found other motions of a different nature besides those eight. As far as the part that rules the body is concerned, there is found in the soul a temporal alternation of seeds <note>original: "seminum." In Platonic thought, these "seminal reasons" are the formative principles that govern the growth and development of physical things.</note> emerging in it at different times to generate bodily things. But as far as the part of the soul engaged in cognition is concerned, there is within it a temporal discourse <term>discursio: the process of moving from one thought to another or from premises to a conclusion</term> from one thought or affection to another; a temporal ascent from the final effects of nature to the highest principles through middle causes, and conversely, a descent from the highest principles through middle causes to the final effects. These discourses are certain motions and are proper to the nature of the mind, as we have declared elsewhere. For they do not suit God or the angels, who possess and see all things simultaneously. They do not belong to bodies, which do nothing through themselves. Nor do they belong to bodily forms, which are not moved toward incorporeal things. Indeed, discourses of this kind, leading us to divine things, elevate us above the nature of the body. But neither a body nor anything else is able to be raised above its own nature through itself. Therefore, such revolutions, which are foreign to bodies yet reside in the mind, testify that the soul cannot be a body or a form divided within a body—especially since the soul is driven through these by its own nature and power (that is, it is moved through itself), which a body cannot do.

Furthermore, there appear in the soul the exemplars <note>The "blueprints" or archetypal patterns.</note> of bodily motions: of **generation**, when it clings to divine things; of **corruption**, when it clings to mortal things; of **increase**, when it remembers; of **decrease**, when it forgets; of **alteration**, when it varies its succession of affections; of **condensation**, as when it suddenly contemplates something or collects itself; of **rarefaction**, as when it discourses or is distracted by many things; and of **progression** in a straight line, when it first touches upon external things. There is **circular** motion, however, when it either resolves an effect into its cause within things themselves and deduces an effect from its cause, or when it reflects back upon itself to be considered. Again, it seems to be moved in a **straight line** when it declines toward the body and the senses; in an **oblique line**, when it reflects upon itself or an angel; in a **circle**, when it turns toward God, its beginning and end; **upward** toward universals; **downward** toward particulars; and also to the **right** and **left**, namely into opposite differences of a genus. Finally, **forward** and **backward**, when it turns itself toward natural causes or effects. Who, therefore, would deny that the soul is the source of motions, since within it are its own motions and the exemplars of bodily motions? In these, contrary to the nature of the body, the soul in a certain way generates itself, or (as I might say) as it were corrupts, increases, diminishes, and transfers itself, and the rest. Rightly, therefore, through its presence, living bodies acquire this faculty so that they may alter, nourish, and increase themselves while they generate something from themselves within themselves; and again, so that they may walk from themselves to wherever they judge they must go. None of these things are performed by those which do not live, as if spontaneous motion were proper to life.

***

### Tenth reason. The soul does not grow according to the growth of this body. Chapter XIII.

**S**ince the soul is a body <note>Ficino is using a "reduction to absurdity" argument here: "If the soul were a body..."</note>, it certainly fills this solid body that you see, so that the whole may live; and it is itself a thin and agile body, as the speed of the mind indicates. Therefore, if you divide the body of a living creature into limbs—just as all parts of a body are themselves bodies—so those little bodies that remain in the severed limbs are parts of the soul, especially since the soul of a single thing is of one whole nature so that it may join diverse parts. Therefore, arms and legs separated from the body will live, move, and feel for a time; and the soul which remains in the rest of the body (which often lives for ten years after arms and legs have been amputated) will be much smaller than before; therefore it will be faint-hearted, dull, and forgetful. Indeed, let us also argue thus: If the soul is a body, completely equaling the magnitude and quantity of this visible body, it will grow as the body grows and decrease as it decreases. In a vast body, the mind will be more magnificent and divine. And in the same man, when the soul grows as the body reaches adolescence, it will be necessary that it grows through the addition of a body similar to itself. Does food of this kind live in itself before it is taken up by the soul, or not? If it does not live, in what way does it provide and increase the life of the soul—that which lacks life itself—and before it borrows life from the soul, it must itself borrow life from the soul. If it does live, then it already has a soul. Thus, new souls would be swallowed by us daily for the sake of our own...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is the primary source of motion, containing mental archetypes for all physical changes, and refutes the idea of a physical soul by showing the logical absurdities of growth and amputation.</summary>
<keywords>self-motion, seminal reasons, discursive thought, circular motion, refutation of materialism, growth, soul-body relationship, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

Having argued that the soul is the internal source of motion, he now addresses the soul's substance, arguing that it cannot be a physical body or a mere mixture of elements (humors) because it maintains a stable identity, memory, and knowledge over time, despite the physical body's constant state of change.</meta>
