# MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...this soul's nourishment. Moreover, nourishment always passes into the nature of that which is nourished. Thus, many souls would be lost daily by nature so that one soul might be preserved—a thing which the goodness of nature does not allow. Indeed, our prior soul would not even be saved if its substance were continually slipping away, forcing it to constantly adopt new souls to perpetually renew itself.

But in what way does a fresh soul agree with the one that came before? How is it that if something is continually flowing out from our soul, and nourishment flows into the soul—just as we see happening in the flesh—the will remains the same in most matters always? How do the same character, the same opinion, the same knowledge, and the perpetual memory of the same thing remain? How is it that after a decade, we immediately recognize those things we had seen ten years before, unless the images of those same things, once received, are still preserved unharmed within us? Who preserves them except the same mind that had received and judged them? In what way does it preserve them if the mind itself is not preserved? By what logic will images and knowledge stand still if the mind does not?

Nor should anyone say that the soul stands still for a long time provided the body remains. For what body under the heavens can remain in the same state for long, when the heavens themselves run their course so swiftly? Furthermore, if there were some body of such a kind that it remained for a while, subtle and agile bodies would nonetheless be the least likely of all to persist. Yet if the soul were a body, it would have to be of the thinnest sort so that, infused through the organs, it might most easily give life to all things. Therefore, even bones and nerves would last longer than the soul; indeed, even flesh, which nevertheless falls away in a short time and is renewed daily. The soul would be like a certain breath <note>original: "flatus"</note>, utterly unstable and vanishing at every single moment; for which reason it would not preserve the knowledge of things and images for even a single day.

The same would also happen if the soul were a "quality" or a certain <term>complexion</term> <note>complexio: in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance or mixture of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental temperament.</note> of the humors and members. For quality and humor flow in the same way, and during the very process of nutrition, the soul would flow out and flow back just like the body; the animal would not consist of its form any more than its own matter. Neither the numerical unity of the animal would be preserved, nor the continuation of the motion of nourishment or growth. Nor would there be in the living thing any power to order these motions, which would be so consistent within itself that it could impose both the order of their progression and a limit to that progression—determining how far one ought to be nourished or grown. For it is necessary that the ruler who orders and halts moving things must be stable within itself.

Someone might perhaps object in this way: We see that in our body, the same shape <note>original: "figura"</note> remains for a very long time, even though the flesh falls away and flows back. In a similar way, therefore, what prevents the same images of known things from remaining in the soul, even if the substance of the soul is changed from the old into a new one?

We respond that neither does the same shape remain entirely, nor is it completely similar; rather, as the flesh departs, the prior shape frequently departs as well. In the recent flesh, a new shape, somewhat similar to the prior one, is rebuilt. This is done by a certain most stable "artificer" <note>original: "artifice." Ficino views the soul as an internal craftsman or architect of the body.</note> who wards off destruction; who, since he remains always the same and possesses within himself the <term>reasons and seeds</term> <note>original: "rationes et semina." These are the formative principles or "blueprints" in the soul that govern physical development.</note> for disposing the members of the familiar body, can hand over a complexion similar to the previous ones to the new humors flowing in daily. He can provide a shape to the recent flesh similar to the old, not unlike a face which, looking down upon a river from above, paints the flowing waves and new waters at every moment with new images of itself, so that the same face seems to persist in different waves.

However, that innermost and stable builder of the body is the soul. If the soul itself were to flow, certainly the body would not carry similar likenesses and shapes for long, nor would the soul retain similar knowledge. For then, neither would the soul itself hold those things it had seen, nor would there be anyone present to either stabilize them in the mind or generate others similar to the previous ones. For it must not be said that when the soul possessing the image of a thing flows away, it "insinuates" that same image into the soul flowing in; for no quality can pass from an old subject into a new subject. Nor does that prior, vanishing soul fashion another or similar image in the incoming soul. For to fashion <note>original: "figurare"</note>, since it is an action, requires a perfect agent. That soul, while it perishes, is itself failing, and cannot then bring a new soul to perfection. Moreover, a new soul cannot form itself, especially at that very moment in which it is born, because even then it is imperfect.

# PLATONIC THE-
## ology, on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
### BOOK VII.

> *The soul is not a body or a form divided within the body, nor is it some point of such a form; rather, it is a form that is whole in any part of the body, as is shown through the power of sensation. The first reason: The body does not contain images suitable for sense. Chapter I.*

I know not how in the previous argument we stumbled into the second part of this discussion, in which we are to prove our proposition through the power of sensation. Let us therefore follow this part further. If a body ever receives anything, it receives it in a bodily manner—that is, the parts of the thing are received into its own parts. Nor can it receive a thing larger than itself, just as wax receiving a shape from a seal never accepts a shape larger than the wax itself. If the wax had sensation by which it could judge the magnitude of the shape, it would clearly judge it to be only as large as itself. Nor can it receive another shape in turn unless it either loses the first one, or both become so confused within it that they can hardly be distinguished from one another. 

Thus, if the soul were a body, it would receive the images of bodies through the eye in a bodily manner, so that the image of <note>Ficino uses these famous figures to illustrate his logical points about perception.</note> Plato in the eye of Socrates would be no larger than Socrates’ eye. In this way, Socrates’ soul would not think Plato to be any larger than his own eye, or certainly no larger than the brain into which the image is transferred from the eye. Finally, it would think him no larger than the size of the Socratic body itself. For if the soul of Socrates is large, it is not larger than his own body. Therefore, if it receives the image of Plato within its whole self, it receives it no larger than itself; for which reason it would never judge anything to be larger than the Socratic body. 

Furthermore, when it receives the images of <note>Xenophon, Alcibiades, and Phaedrus were students or associates of Socrates, often appearing in Plato's dialogues.</note> Xenophon, Alcibiades, and Phaedrus, it would then either lose the image of Plato, or hold them all so confused together that it could not distinguish one from the other. Conclude also in this way: The soul is either a solid body or a fluid one. If it is solid, it is hardly shaped by bodies, and teachability and sharpness of mind perish; and once one shape of one thing is received, it either does not receive others, or if it receives one after another, they are all obscured by each other. If it is a shifting <note>original: "labile," meaning unstable or flowing.</note> body, it holds no shapes and has no memory at all. 

Moreover, is it not clear that the same thing seen in a tiny mirror appears small, but in a larger one appears larger? For instance, if you look at your face in my pupil, and then in a mirror, you will pronounce it small in the former and large in the latter. For bodies are judged larger or smaller according to the size or smallness of the mirrors themselves. But in the soul of a human, the images of almost all bodies shine, through which the soul judges bodies to be as great as they actually are. There is no body so vast, so immense, that the soul cannot either behold or think of it, and it can always conceive of another body larger than the one already thought of. 

From this it appears that there is no prescribed limit of magnitude for the soul, both regarding those things which it is to comprehend and regarding the soul's own proper substance. For if it had any proper magnitude in itself, it would be especially as great as the size of its own body. Consequently, in such a tiny animal mirror, things so various, so clear, and so immense could not shine, since they usually appear larger or smaller according to the different size of mirrors. 

Yet we should not think that the spiritual images of colors are either made by bodies or received in mirrors and the brain. For these are nothing other than the splendors of light striking bodies. Although that visible light flashes in bodies, it is nevertheless made and preserved by the invisible light of celestial <note>original: "animorum," here referring to the higher intellectual beings or "minds" in the cosmic hierarchy.</note> souls, which overflows from a vast abundance and becomes clear. It is not attached to any bodies, yet it can be joined to the light of our <term>spirit<note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "spirit" (spiritus) is a subtle, airy substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the incorporeal soul.</note></term>, which depends on our soul, and can offer its splendors to it. Furthermore, the meanings of words reaching the hearing, which are themselves also spiritual, are neither made by the body nor fixed in the body, but are transmitted from the soul

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because it can perceive and conceive of things far larger than the human body, such as the vastness of the universe. He uses analogies of mirrors and wax seals to demonstrate that if the soul were material, our perception would be limited by our physical size.</summary>

...great size does not help, but rather hinders; if, I say, the outer sight <note>original: "exterior acies"</note> has no need of physical magnitude to perceive even the smallest things, what shall we say of that inner vision and the **common sense**? <term>common sense</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the 'common sense' (sensus communis) was the internal faculty that gathered and unified data from the five external senses.</note> The more this inner faculty is superior and sharper than the individual senses, the more self-sufficient it must be; and it will be more self-sufficient if it requires no bodily quantity at all. Finally, the very substance of the soul, which is the foundation of the senses, will be more sufficient than any sense if it does not lack quantity. Who could say that the soul requires the dimensions of physical size, since the magnitude of the body neither contributes to nor harms the soul's gifts? If size were necessarily helpful, a **bee** would not be more skillful than a **sheep**, nor a **fox** more cunning than a **pig**, nor a **monkey** more ingenious than a **donkey**, nor a **lion** bolder than an **ox**. If size were necessarily harmful, an **elephant** would not be wiser than a **horse**, nor a **dog** keener than a **lamb**. But if the body's quantity has no power over those faculties of the soul that deal with the quantity of bodies, we must believe it has much less power over that faculty of the soul which transcends bodily quantity—namely, **reason**, which we shall discuss in its proper place.

### Fourth reason. If the sense is divisible, the sensible image within it will be divided. Chapter IIII.

**S**uppose, if you wish, that this internal sight is stretched out through a bodily mass; attend to what follows. When it captures or conceives the image of an external color, it receives it in its own way—that is, a bodily way. An image of this kind is divided among the parts of this sight, and one part of the sight looks at one part of the color, and another part looks at another; thus, there will be nothing in us that grasps the visible color as a whole. Yet, it is necessary that a single comprehension of a single thing be made by a single perceiver. And if you say that the perceiver is a certain form of the whole composite, common to all its parts, we must ask: is this form divisible? From this, the same question will return: if it is indivisible, then we must place the power of comprehension in an indivisible force.

It is necessary, therefore, for the sense to be free of bodily magnitude. This is especially true because if the sense were large, it would not fit small things, nor would it perceive them as a whole, but only that part of itself which is equal to the small thing would feel them. If the sense were small, it would not contain large things; if it were medium-sized, it would not match the extremes. But if you wish to divide the sensible color along with the sense, in what way will you distribute it? Will you fit an equal part to an equal part? You cannot. For the sense is not equal in size to every object that must be sensed. Into how many parts will you distribute both? Into parts limited in number and naturally smallest in order? If you do this, you will not find a single comprehension of a single thing. 

Rather, following the manner of the **Mathematicians**, I think you would divide them into all the parts they possess. Thus, you would cut both the sight and the color into infinite particles, and individual parts of the sight would sense individual portions of the color. In this way, there would be innumerable "sights" there, innumerable colors seen, and innumerable acts of seeing. Thus, a single color could never strike the sight without an infinite number of sights seeing infinite colors infinitely at that same moment. Such a thing cannot even be imagined. Perhaps, to avoid these monstrosities, we might suggest that the *whole* sight feels, while its *parts* do not. But this is also rash. For how can things that lack sensation generate a sensing substance? They cannot. Therefore, those parts that are devoid of feeling will not constitute the sense itself. 

Or shall we say that each individual part of the sight feels, but does so through the same complete vision of the whole sight, sensing the whole form and the parts together with the whole? No. First, because it is not the "form" <note>original: "species"</note> that is seen, but the color itself through the form. Second, because an operation that arises from a gathering of distinct parts also arises through a gathering of moments and is completed bit by bit; yet sensation happens suddenly, which signifies that the power of sensing is **indivisible**. Finally, if each part of the sight is sufficient by itself for seeing, why are more parts needed? If it is not sufficient, then a sensing thing is being made out of a non-sensing thing. This is impossible unless those parts are gathered into one by some higher sensing power. But that higher power would be the soul itself rather than the sense. Therefore, we shall never escape these mad responses as long as we 

-> affirm that the sense is divisible. Let the sense therefore be indivisible, and let the soul <-
-> be such, which is the source of indivisible power <-
-> and its subject. <-

## MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

### Fifth reason. The soul feels everywhere as a whole. Chapter V.

**A**re you unaware that a part of any body cannot be equal to its whole? Consequently, a quality <note>original: "fortunam," here referring to an accidental property or state</note> which is of such a nature that it is stretched through different parts of a body cannot exist as a whole in any single part of that body; otherwise, the part would be equal to the whole. I admit these points. What follows? Surely the soul is present as a whole in any part of the body, because it feels the suffering <term>suffering</term> <note>original: "passionem," meaning a physical sensation or something the body undergoes, often painful.</note> of any bodily particle as a whole. For if, by some unfortunate accident, the foot feels pain, the eye is immediately turned there, the hand is moved at once, the mouth cries out, and the other members react almost similarly. This certainly would never happen unless that which belongs to the soul within all parts of the body also felt the sensation in the foot. And it could not feel what happened there if it were absent. Nor should one believe that this happens by some "messenger," for a messenger does not feel what he reports—if he does not feel it, he does not truly report it. Nor can a suffering that occurs through the continuity of physical mass always happen in such a way that it cannot remain hidden from the other parts of the soul located elsewhere, because pain is not always present everywhere. 

But the soul feels as a whole that which happens in a tiny part of the foot, and it feels it only there, where it happens. Therefore, the soul is present as a whole to each individual part at once, since as a whole it feels in each part at once. However, in the case of physical forms spread through a body—for example, whiteness—the same thing happens to them as to the body: namely, the suffering of one part does not necessarily change all the other parts. For what prevents one part of a body and its whiteness from being stained and defiled while the rest remains unpolluted? But nothing happens in any single particle of a living creature that does not immediately concern the soul as a whole. 

Our Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whom Ficino treats as a bridge between Platonic philosophy and Christian theology.</note> confirms this Platonic mystery as follows: "The soul is extended through the whole body which it animates, not by local diffusion, but by a certain **vital intention**. <term>vital intention</term> <note>A philosophical concept where the soul is present throughout the body not by filling space like a liquid, but through its active, life-giving power.</note> For through all particles it is present as a whole at once; it is not smaller in smaller parts, nor larger in larger parts; but in some places it is more intense, in others more relaxed, and yet it is whole in all and whole in each individual part. For otherwise, it would not feel as a whole whatever it feels in the body, even if it is not felt in the whole body. For when something is touched in a tiny point of the flesh, although that place is not only not the whole body but barely seems to be in the body at all, it does not escape the soul as a whole. Nor does that which is felt run through all the parts of the body, but it is felt only where it happens. From where, then, does it reach the whole soul immediately, if it does not happen in the whole body? Nor does the soul desert the other parts to be there as a whole. For those other parts continue to live by its presence even where no such thing happened. But if both were to happen at once, neither would escape the whole soul." Thus says Aurelius <note>Aurelius Augustine.</note>. 

But perhaps you will say that the soul is indeed stretched through the entire body in such a way that part of it is in the foot, part in the leg, another in the thigh, the chest, the neck, and the highest part in the brain, where the **principal judgment** <term>principal judgment</term> <note>The "hegemonikon" or ruling faculty of the soul, often localized in the brain by Renaissance thinkers.</note> occurs. You might argue that the pain of the foot is not judged by the power of the soul sitting in the brain because that power is also present in the foot, but because, by a certain succession, one part of the soul announces the suffering of the foot to another, all the way to the brain. Surely you will not deny that these lower parts of the soul feel, since it clearly appears that suffering is perceived in those limbs. If the suffering of the foot is to be announced to the brain, it is announced either because the intermediate members suffer step-by-step, or because, although they do not suffer themselves, they nonetheless feel the pain of the foot and report it to the brain. Certainly, the whole body does not always suffer equally, nor is the torment in the middle limbs the same as that in the foot, but rather a certain distressing perception of that torment. 

Therefore, in all parts, there is a certain distress and sense. Note what follows from this: the part of the soul in the foot will feel the torment of the foot; the part in the leg will feel not the foot's torment, but the leg's distress (for it feels only where it is, and feels only the suffering that runs into it). The part in the knee will similarly perceive only the suffering present there, and the others likewise. Finally, that judicial power of the brain will notice only the distress present to itself. If the soul were physical, the parts of the soul from the foot to the brain would be almost innumerable, just like the parts of the body. Therefore, once the foot is struck against a stone, there would not be one single and sudden act of feeling, but many step-by-step and almost innumerable pains would occur, just like innumerable perceptions; and after all these, that part of the soul in which the principal sense resides would feel (which is a wicked thing to suggest). It would feel not the suffering of the foot, but only its own; nor would it ever judge where the injury is or where help is needed, nor would the members of the body turn toward the foot by its command. 

To avoid these absurdities, it must be admitted that the soul's entire judicial power, together with the entire substance of the soul itself, is present to each individual limb, so that whatever happens anywhere, the whole soul immediately senses it beforehand without a messenger; the whole soul suffers with itself and harmonizes with itself, and suddenly applies all the powers of the soul and all parts of the body by its command to the healing of the injured part. And thus, whatever and however much there is of the soul...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is an indivisible whole present in every part of the body simultaneously. He uses the immediate, coordinated bodily response to a foot injury to prove that the soul does not rely on "messengers" or step-by-step transmission but perceives sensations as a unified whole.</summary>

of the soul is in any of the limbs, it is not absent from any other limb, because in any part it moves whatever it wishes toward whatever it chooses. The body and the form spread through it, or a point of that form, are not of such a kind that they can be whole in many places at once, and entirely suffer and act together with themselves in their parts without any delay. The soul, therefore, is far different from them. Nor should those many animals disturb us whose bodies, when they are cut, move and feel in both parts uselessly, as if the soul were as long as the body, since when the body is cut into separate bodies, the soul also seems to be cut into souls. For the soul is not divided first; rather, it perishes as soon as that specific structure of the body to which it was assigned is dissolved. However, new souls are suddenly produced from the **life of the world** <note>original: *vita mundi*, referring to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, which Ficino believes provides life to lower organisms</note> in those fragments that are suitable for receiving a soul. For the nature of those parts is the same as the nature of the whole was. And because such souls are so lowly that they have very few powers and operations, and therefore need very few instruments, it happens that the body suffices for them even if it is not equipped with various specialized organs—which does not suffice for more perfect souls, which live through this in individual limbs.

If a piece of wood is cut at a point, although this point is indivisible, it nevertheless perishes, and in the two fragments, two new extreme points seem to be reborn. If you break a mirror in which the image of your face was appearing, the image is not first cut, but it departs, and two images are recreated by you in the two mirrors instead of one. If you divide this name **Lucifer** <note>The "Morning Star" or Venus. Ficino uses this as a linguistic analogy: the word's meaning is its "soul," its sounds are its "body."</note>—in which the voice holds the place of the body and the meaning holds the place of the soul—into two parts, such as "luci" and "fer," that original meaning by which the planet Venus was designated first ceases to be; it is not, however, divided (for the meaning of a name is indivisible, as we shall show elsewhere). Yet there are still two specific meanings in the two parts, through which these kinds of words survive as if they had souls: "luci" through the meaning of "light," and "fer" through some meaning of "bringing" <note>original: *lationis*. *Luci-fer* literally means "light-bringer" in Latin.</note>. What, therefore, prevents reptiles from having an indivisible soul according to the Platonists, even though their divided limbs continue to live?

## Sixth ratio. The soul does not necessarily suffer by sensing.
### Cap. VI.

**T**he soul itself (as true philosophy teaches), since it is most pure, is coupled to this thick and earthy body far distant from it only through a certain very thin and very bright little body which we call the **spirit** <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus*. In Renaissance medicine/philosophy, this was a subtle vapor that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the material flesh.</note>, generated from the heat of the heart from the thinnest part of the blood, and spread from there through the entire body. Easily insinuating itself into this spirit, which is most akin to it, the soul first pours itself through this whole spirit, and then, by this medium, through the entire body. It first provides life and motion to the body and makes it a living thing; through this spirit, it rules and moves the body, and whatever flows from the body into this spirit, the soul perceives immediately as being present to itself. We call this perception **sensation**. Then it notices and judges this perception, which notice we wish to call **imagination** <term>imagination</term> <note>original: *phantasia*. Not just "make-believe," but the faculty that processes and judges sensory data.</note>.

What is the point of this? When a doctor cuts the outermost skin of the body, the flesh is broken, and the spirit is dissolved and contracted. **Touch**, which is the universal sense of the soul through all the limbs, feels all these things; the imagination judges them and suffers with them. How can the flesh be cut without the spirit spread through it being partly dissolved with the loosened flesh, and partly fleeing into itself and being contracted? How could the dissolution and contraction of the spirit be hidden from its own soul? And if it is not hidden, why should the soul not be distressed by the destruction of its own work? For the spirit and the body are the work of the soul, and all things love their own proper work. 

In the flesh there is indeed suffering; in the spirit, torment; in touch, sensation; and in the imagination, compassion and "suffering-with" (if I may speak so). To summarize: in both the flesh and the spirit, let there be a certain destructive dissolution or contraction that corrupts the substance; let us call this a harmful injury. Does such an injury also pass into the soul? Not at all. For such an injury destroys substance; it therefore destroys the power of the substance itself, and consequently destroys the operation of that power. Therefore, in any injury of the flesh and spirit, even the lightest, the substance of the soul present in them would be similarly injured, its power would be injured much more, and its operation would be injured too. Sensation and imagination are powers of the soul; sensing and judging through the senses are the actions of these powers. Therefore, if that division were to pass into the substance of the soul, we would neither feel it, nor judge what kind of injury it is, where it comes from, or how it should be helped; instead, it would either be hidden from the soul entirely, or something very small would be perceived and falsely judged by the soul. And since the soul is whole everywhere, if it were in a part of the body—

He introduces the "spirit" as the luminous medium through which the immaterial soul governs the body and experiences sensation without itself being physically damaged.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from page 177, concluding a discussion on how the soul's presence throughout the body allows it to perceive sensations without being physically divided. It transitions into Chapter VII and VIII of Book VII, focusing on why the soul cannot be a mere "quality" or "complexion" (a mixture of physical elements) of the body.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGIAN<-

[of the bo]dy is cut <note>original: *corporis*. The first syllable is on the previous page.</note> it suffers, it suffers as a whole. Indeed, the same whole soul which is there is also throughout the whole body; therefore, it suffers through the entire body. If it suffers everywhere, it cannot perceive and announce that this passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to a passive experience or something being acted upon, rather than an emotion.</note> is more in one part of the living being than in another. Furthermore, since the passion is one thing and the judgment of the passion is another, and passion is always judged by something else, if passion were present in the judgment itself, there would be a further need for some other judgment by which the passive judgment might be judged. If that too were passive, there would again be a need for another. For this reason, one must finally arrive at a judge that is free from passion. While this judge judges the passions of the body, if it receives any bodily quality from them, it undoubtedly suffers. If it does not receive one, it is not formed by the body. Therefore, such a judge must be of a kind that receives neither passions nor forms from bodies. However, the soul could not be such a thing if it were either a very thin body submerged in this body, or some affection of this body, or a certain point of affection. 

**Augustine** and **Plotinus** prove these Platonic views thus: It seems to me that when the soul feels in the body, it does not suffer anything from it, but acts more attentively in response to the body's passions. And these actions—whether easy because of harmony or difficult because of discord—do not escape its notice. And this is the whole of what is called "to sense." But this sense, which is present even when nothing is being sensed, exists as if through a bodily instrument; this instrument is moved by the soul with such a temperament that it becomes more ready to perform actions with attention toward the passions of the body, so that it may join like to like and repel what is harmful. 

Furthermore, the soul acts (as I believe) through something luminous in the eyes, through something airy, most clear and mobile in the ears, through something misty in the nostrils, something humid in the mouth, and something earthy and, as it were, muddy in the touch <note>Ficino is aligning the five senses with the four elements plus a "misty" or "luminous" spirit, a common Neoplatonic theory of perception.</note>. Moreover, it performs all these things in stillness if those things which are in the living being cling together in a unity of health by a certain familiar consensus. However, when those things are applied which affect the body with some "otherness" (so to speak), the soul performs more attentive actions, adapted to its specific places or instruments, and then it is said to "sense." To these actions it freely associates agreeable things and troublesomely resists disagreeable ones. I think the soul exhibits these operations toward the passions of the body when it senses, rather than receiving those same passions. When the airy spirit of the ear is struck by a sound, the soul—which before such a percussion was nourishing the body of the ears in silence—nourishes it then more attentively; and to do this is "to act," not "to suffer." An attentive operation does not escape the notice of the soul that is performing it. To not escape notice is to sense. In short, sense is either the more attentive noticing of that operation, or a judgment of a bodily passion and quality, excited by that attentive action of the soul.

---

### *Seventh reason. Specific reasons through the natural and sensitive soul, that the soul is not a divisible form, because the work of a quality is one. Chapter VII.*

**A**lthough by the previous reasons we have proved not only that the soul is not a body, but also that it is not a form spread through bodies, nevertheless we think this second part should be shown through its own specific arguments. And so that we may speak more conveniently about this matter, we shall (as we have said elsewhere) call such a form both a **quality** and an **affection** of the body, after the manner of the Platonists. If the soul were a bodily quality, it would either be a simple quality, or a complexion, or a form bound to these. It cannot be simple. For any simple quality, or a form following it (as we have declared elsewhere), performs only one thing and does not extend to opposites; yet the soul performs very many things, and even contrary things. Nor will it be a **complexion** <note>original: *complexio*, meaning the specific mixture of the four humors or elements that determines a body's temperament.</note>, or a form following a complexion, because in such a thing one specific quality always dominates over the others, and its operation flourishes in the body before all others. The soul is bound to no single quality, nor to any single movement.

---

### *Eighth reason. Complexion acts through the force of qualities. Chapter VIII.*

**T**he action of a complexion and its form is always carried out through the qualities from which it is composed; and therefore a complexion never performs anything so sublime that the forces of the qualities do not extend to it. The work of heat is to penetrate and dissolve; but the nutritive power of the soul, using heat as an instrument, does not only dissolve food (which is the proper function of heat), but also cooks and digests it, and leads it to the form of living flesh and the human figure, which

<meta>This page continues the seventh book of Ficino's "Platonic Theology," where he is systematically refuting various materialist definitions of the soul. Having previously argued that the soul is not a body, he now argues it is not a mere physical property (an accident) such as heat, a "complexion" (the balance of elements), or "harmony."</meta>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VII<-

the action of heat exceeds in power. The growth of a living being also cannot arise from heat as the primary cause, for growth does not happen except through nourishment, and it is led to a certain limit of size and a certain shape. Heat, however, if given matter, spreads itself without a fixed limit or shape. Since it is necessary for the limit and shape to be prescribed for the work by the primary agent, it is clear that heat cannot be the primary craftsman <note>original: *fabrum*</note> of growth; indeed, no other accidental form can do this if heat, which is the most excellent of them all, cannot. Yet growth is achieved by the soul. From this, it is concluded that the soul is not an accidental form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accidental form" is a quality like color or heat that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, whereas a "substantial form" defines what the thing is.</note>, which we must prove very frequently. It is also concluded that the soul is not composed of accidental forms, because such a composition could not rationally order qualities that wander without fixed limits, degrees, proportions, or shapes into these very things. Finally, it is concluded that the soul is not some substantial form of an element or a mixture. For the movement of such a form is directed toward a single limit, as we have said, but growth extends equally into every part.

### Ninth argument. Complexion is an accidental form. Chapter IX.

**C**omplexion <note>original: *complexio*. In medieval medicine and philosophy, this refers to the specific "mixture" or temperament of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</note> is a certain nature constituted, in a way, by contrary qualities, which holds a sort of middle ground between them. From this, it follows that it cannot be a substantial form, because it does not subsist in itself, but in that body which is the subject of those contrary qualities. Because these qualities fight against each other, they do not naturally support one another; however, when they are received by matter and mixed together, they generate a "complexion." Therefore, this complexion is not a substance, both for the reason I have stated and because it has something contrary to itself—namely, the excess of some external quality that pulls its combination apart. Furthermore, it admits of "more" and "less." For the nature, power, and operation of a complexion can be intensified or relaxed. 

Substance, however, has no contrary proper to itself, since the very contrariety of things exists in a different category than substance—that is, in the category of quality. Nor is substance in its own nature either intensified into "more" or relaxed into "less," such that this or that substance might be more or less what it is once it is a substance; for example, this stone is not more or less a stone than that one. Since, therefore, complexion is not a substance, if the soul is a substance, it is not a complexion. That the soul is indeed a substance is clear from this: through the soul, the living being receives a certain and substantial nature and name of its species and genus. Through this soul, this thing is a dog; through that one, that thing is a horse; through another, that thing is a man. 

That quality which is an accident comes to its subject after that subject is already perfected in its species. The soul, however, builds its own body for itself, preserves it once made, and while it fails, repairs it, binding the fighting elements into one. When the soul departs, the body falls away, and neither the former complexion nor the species is retained. Such a thing is necessarily the nutritive soul <note>The "nutritive soul" is the most basic level of life, responsible for growth and reproduction, shared by plants and animals.</note>. Nor should it be said that the soul which is only nutritive constructs the body in such a way that the sensitive soul <note>The "sensitive soul" allows for movement and perception in animals.</note> later arrives as a kind of accident to a body already perfected. For the body suitable for a nutritive soul must have instruments for sensing and moving forward. The nutritive soul, insofar as it is such, will only make instruments for nourishing; but the soul will make other instruments for the sake of those powers whose use the instruments are to serve. Nor are there two different souls in the same body, one of which builds instruments for the other. Indeed, that which nourishes is the same as that which senses. Certainly, disturbances of the senses hinder or increase the work of nourishing. For sorrow of the imagination <note>original: *phantasiae*. This refers to the internal sense that processes images.</note> weakens it, while joy strengthens it, as if there were one soul in man to which both duties belong. Therefore, it is a substance, because it is the artisan of the body, not its servant. Thus, it is not a complexion.

### Tenth argument. The harmony of the complexion does nothing to the body. Chapter X.

**N**or should it be allowed for Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who famously argued the soul was a "harmony" of the body’s physical parts.</note> or other musicians to dream that the soul is a certain harmony produced from the complexion itself. For in that case, the soul would likewise not be a substance, but an accident. Does not harmony draw its entire power from the strings? It does not exist as anything through itself, nor is it able to effect anything at all in the strings. Indeed, harmony itself does not move the strings, but harmony is born when they are moved from elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues Book VII of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." Ficino is currently presenting a series of arguments to prove that the soul is an independent substance and not merely a byproduct of the body's physical state. Specifically, he is refuting the "harmony theory"—the idea that the soul is just the "tuning" or "balance" of the body's parts.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

Therefore, if the soul were a harmony of <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) thought to determine health and temperament.</note> composed in a certain way, it would depend entirely on them. It would not move them itself; rather, the soul would arise only when those humors were stirred by something else. It would not rule them; instead, they would rule and support the soul. Consequently, there would be no movements in the body other than those dictated by the condition of the humors, and no works beyond their command—even though such things clearly exist, as we described above. There would be no artistic shape, no deliberate arrangement. The mind would never resist bodily impulses, nor would it reflect upon itself, nor would it connect things separated from the body to things within it. It would perform no action by itself if it did not exist through itself in any way. But we have spoken of this elsewhere and shall speak of it again.

---

### Eleventh argument. Harmony exists in every composite body. Chapter XI.

**I**n every body composed of many things, there is some harmony of its parts through which they sound together in mutual agreement. Therefore, if harmony itself were the soul, any composite bodies whatsoever would be alive and grow together. Perhaps you will say that the soul is indeed a harmony—that is, a fitting together and a consonance—but not just *any* harmony; rather, it is one blended in a 
<margin>cer-</margin>tain and specific way. You see then that the definition of "soul" and "consonance" is not the same, since a thing is not a soul simply because it is a consonance, but because it is arranged in a specific way. This specific manner of arrangement does not derive its nature from the "fitting together" itself, otherwise it would be present in every instance of fitting together. Does it then come from some other external principle? Indeed, it does. However, that external factor is not enough. For that which is outside the harmony does not constantly and naturally move and temper it. There lies hidden, therefore, in the consonance of the humors a certain power more excellent than bodily consonance that acts as a regulator. By tempering the humors in its own way within living bodies, it makes their "fitting together" specific and different from other bodies. This specific vital harmony is produced by the life-giving spirit lurking within.

---

### Twelfth argument. Harmony is understood either as the composition of the limbs itself, or as some ratio of that composition. Chapter XII.

**W**hen someone asserts that the soul is a harmony <note>original: *consonantiam*</note>, I believe they can mean two things: either the actual composition of the humors and limbs, or some <term>ratio</term> <note>original: *rationem*. Here meaning a mathematical proportion or governing principle.</note> of that composition. Surely the soul is not the composition itself, because then every part of the soul would have to be a composition of some parts of the body. We clearly cannot assign how this would happen. The composition of the body is manifest to natural philosophers, but the soul is unknown to them. It is difficult to know how the soul is composed of its powers—namely, intellect, sense, appetite, and the rest. It is even more difficult to know how the individual powers themselves are composed. Furthermore, composition is nothing other than the union of many things, and many things are not united except by "the one." By "the one," I mean something that exists within the many, so that they are glued together by an internal bond. Therefore, that one power implanted in the limbs, from which the union of the limbs arises, is the soul itself rather than the union resulting from it. Nor is the soul the ratio of the composition itself. For since different ratios and proportions of composition exist in different limbs of the body, each limb would possess its own individual soul—the bone one soul, the nerve another, the flesh another, and so on for the rest, since these limbs are composed of different proportions. We would never be able to assign a single life to one living creature unless we granted it a single form, one mover, and one ruler: that is, one soul. We also see that the principle of harmony applies more to the qualities of the body than to the soul. Health is a harmony of humors; strength is a harmony of bones and nerves. Beauty is, in a way, a harmony of limbs and colors. But as for sense and intellect—which are simple acts of a nature I cannot fully describe—I do not know what kind of "harmonies" they could be. When we know the substance of a thing, we can easily judge its accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like height or color, as opposed to the "substance" or essence of a thing.</note> from that. Therefore, because we easily judge things pertaining to health, strength, and beauty once the proportion of the humors or limbs is known, it is clear that these three consist in that proportion. But because, even when such a proportion is discovered, we still do not clearly discern the powers, affections, acts, or habits of the soul, it is certain that the substance of the soul does not consist in that proportion at all.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a mere "harmony" or mathematical ratio of bodily parts, because the soul rules the body rather than being dependent on it, and the soul's unity cannot be explained by the body's diverse physical proportions.</summary>

Having previously argued that the soul cannot be a mere byproduct of the body's physical components, Ficino now uses specific philosophical arguments (Ratios 13 through 15) to demonstrate that the soul’s ability to process non-material information and maintain its identity despite internal conflict proves it is not a "harmony" of the body’s fluids.</meta>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VII<-

For who, once those things <note>The physical mechanisms of the body</note> are discovered, would immediately boast that he has discovered the very nature of sensing and understanding? Aristotle considers the nature of things known better than Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) was a Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine," while Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was the philosopher who defined the soul's functions.</note> does, but Hippocrates considers their proportion more diligently.

### Thirteenth argument. The harmony of humors perceives nothing without matter. Chapter XIII.

**W**hatever produces an effect must be more excellent than the effect it produces. The more a thing is free from matter, the more sublime it is. Therefore, a cause must always be more free from matter than its effect. Consequently, no effect can be more free from matter than its own cause. The power of nutrition is somewhat free from matter, as it has been demonstrated elsewhere to perform many tasks above and beyond the ordinary behavior of the elements. The power of sensation is even more free from matter, because in the very act of sensing, it receives the <term>forms</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "form" is the essential nature or design of a thing, separate from its physical substance.</note> of things without the matter of the things themselves. For the sense of sight does not receive the color of a wall along with the wall itself; rather, it reaches a spiritual image of the color. Intelligence does this to a much greater degree, as will appear in what follows. Since, therefore, these powers of the soul are largely free from matter, they cannot proceed from a cause that is material or merely a measurement of matter. 

<term>Humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed by ancient doctors to control health and personality.</note> are entirely corporeal; for this reason, humors can in no way produce powers of this kind through some mixture or "consonance" of their own—much less can they produce the soul itself, which is the fountain of such powers. Indeed, if the soul had its substance in the qualities of the humors, whatever it perceived, it would receive through the affections of those humors. But through those humors, only physical forms are received. For through heat and dryness, the soul would not receive a spiritual image of fire, but the physical substance of fire itself. Likewise, through cold and moisture, it would receive the earth itself. Then the earth itself, because it would receive things in the same way as the soul, would also feel in the same way. A stone would do the same, and so would everything else.

### Fourteenth argument. That which is more in tune is more of a harmony. Chapter XIV.

**H**armony consists in the sounding together of many things, such that when strings are more in tune, there is more harmony, and when they are less in tune, there is less. The soul of a wicked man is least "in tune" with itself, for his senses disagree with his reason, and his appetites also fight amongst themselves. The soul of a virtuous man, however, is in tune in every respect. Now, if the soul were a harmony, the soul of the virtuous man—which is more in tune—would be "more" of a harmony, and therefore "more" of a soul. Since the soul is a kind of life, he would also be "more" alive. Thus, the soul of a virtuous man would be more vigorous, bolder, and more robust than that of a thief. Yet the soul of a thief digests food just as well as the soul of a just man, nor is the thief less able to produce offspring, or support and move his limbs, or discover things sharply, remember firmly, speak elegantly, or live for a long time.

### Fifteenth argument. Harmony admits nothing dissonant. Chapter XV.

**T**rue harmony, to proceed more correctly, admits nothing dissonant so long as it remains a harmony. If it is a harmony, it is in consonance; if it is out of tune, it is not a harmony. But do we not see our own soul continually distracted by "dissonant" opinions and passions, and yet it remains a true soul and equally full of life? Do not object that while discord of the passions does not destroy the soul, discord of the elements and humors does. Furthermore, if the soul cannot perish from its own internal dissonance, it cannot perish from any other. The internal dissonance proper to the human soul is that which belongs to every soul: namely, the disagreement of opinions and passions. This discord does not affect bodies that lack life, yet it strikes the souls of all mortals. If such disagreement does not cast those vital senses from their station, then the discord of humors—which is further removed from the nature of the soul—is even less likely to dissipate the soul's natural state. Certainly, if the soul's existence depended on the "tuning" of the humors, it would be dissipated if those humors became even slightly out of tune. Therefore, nothing prevents the parts of the soul and body from being far out of tune while the soul remains a true and vital soul; but harmony does not allow for this. Therefore, anyone who calls the soul a "harmony" is in error.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a "harmony" of the body because the soul perceives non-material forms and maintains its existence even when its internal thoughts and desires are in conflict.</summary>

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY,
## on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author Ficino,
### BOOK VIII.

> *The soul is an indivisible form, whole everywhere, and draws no origin from matter; therefore, it is immortal, as is shown through the power of understanding. The soul ascends through four stages to the spirit. The first argument.*

### Chapter I.

We shall now approach that part of the discussion which demonstrates our proposition through the power of understanding, after first explaining how our soul, according to the opinion of the Platonists, ascends from the body to the spirit through four stages of knowing, the last of which is intelligence. For it ascends through sense, imagination, phantasy, and intelligence. 

Through sense, Socrates sees Plato, where he reaches an incorporeal likeness of Plato without Plato’s matter through his eyes; yet he does so on the condition that the eye does not see Plato unless the physical body of Plato is actually present. 

Next, even when Plato is absent, Socrates thinks of the color and shape he had seen through internal imagination, as well as that sweet voice he had heard and the other things he had received through the five senses. This kind of imagination rises above matter more than sense does, both because it does not require the presence of those bodies to think of them, and because it alone performs whatever all five senses together achieve. Yet it is not entirely pure, because it tastes of nothing other than what the sense has received or conceived. Sense revolves around bodies; imagination revolves around the images of bodies received or conceived through the senses. 

A little later, through phantasy <note>In Ficino’s psychology, *phantasia* is a higher "judgmental" faculty than simple imagination; it interprets and evaluates the images stored in the mind.</note>, Socrates begins to judge this universal likeness of Plato which imagination itself had collected through the five senses. He thinks: "Who is this with such a tall body, broad forehead, wide shoulders, white complexion, grey eyes, raised eyebrows, aquiline nose, small mouth, and sweet voice? This is Plato—a beautiful man, a good man, and a most beloved disciple." 

You see how much the phantasy of Socrates excels his imagination. Imagination itself collected such an image of Plato, but it did not know whom that image designated or what kind of person it represented; phantasy now discerns that it is the image of *this* man who is called Plato, a beautiful image of a man who is both good and a friend. Therefore, in these things, phantasy already possesses some sense of substance (as some believe) and of beauty, goodness, and friendship. 

The Platonists, however, deny that substance is truly known by phantasy, since it does not recognize the *reason* <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning the underlying logical definition or essence.</note> of substance. Imagination does not even suspect the substance of a thing, but only its surface and exterior "painting." Phantasy at least guesses at the substance when it pronounces, "That man approaching is someone, and he is Plato."

And it even seems to "dream" of incorporeal things in a way, while it judges Plato to be beautiful, good, a friend, or a disciple. For beauty, goodness, friendship, and learning are incorporeal things, open neither to the senses nor to imagination. These sorts of conceptions of the phantasy are called the <term>incorporeal intentions</term> <note>Technical term: "intentio" refers to the mental representation or the "aiming" of the mind at an object’s non-physical qualities.</note> of bodies.

But the soul does not yet fly entirely above matter, both because phantasy does not recognize that these intentions are incorporeal, and because this phantasy of Socrates inspects specifically *this* man—namely Plato—in this place and position, at this time and hour of the day, this specific beauty, this specific goodness, and so on. In this way, it depicts Plato within itself under the same conditions in which he exists in matter. 

But while phantasy wanders around the individual conditions of this man, the intellect conceives universal reasons, and both carry out their work at the same time. For intelligence reasons thus: "Whatever kind of man Plato is, Antisthenes <note>A follower of Socrates and founder of Cynic philosophy.</note> is almost the same, and so is Xenophon <note>A student of Socrates, famous as a historian and soldier.</note>; they are similar in appearance, equally beautiful, and good friends and disciples in the same way." Therefore, in these three, there is one...

<summary>Ficino describes the four-stage ascent of the soul's cognition from physical sensation to intellectual abstraction, using Socrates's perception of Plato as a primary example. This process demonstrates how the soul moves from material particulars to immaterial, universal truths.</summary>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII.</header>

...common humanity, through which they are equally humans, a single nature of beauty, and also one of goodness, through which they are equally beautiful and equally good. Humanity itself, which is common to these individuals, also exists as common to countless others who are, were, or will be, at whatever time and in whatever place they may be born; similarly with beauty and the rest. But what I say regarding humanity, consider it said regarding the others as well. If, therefore, humanity communicates itself equally to individual persons, places, and times, it is bound to no single person, no place, and no time. A nature of this kind seems to transcend the individual conditions of bodies. It is, therefore, in its own way, incorporeal according to itself; and because it pours itself into individual bodies—whereby it is both in another and in many—there must exist, above that which is in another, that which remains in itself. And above that "one" which is in many, there must be the "One Itself" which subsists in itself. Therefore, above all bodies there stands a certain concept <term>ratio (reason/concept): the underlying logic or formal definition of a thing</term> and an Idea of humanity itself. By a certain participation <note>In Platonic thought, "participation" describes how physical things share in the qualities of a higher, perfect "Idea."</note> in this, or a likeness to it, all humans—whoever they are—become humans. Indeed, that nature which is common to individual persons does not happen by chance, because it is always ordered in a similar way; nor does it subsist through itself, since it cannot stand on its own, for it requires the foundation of matter. It is produced, therefore, by a certain cause, yet it is not produced by matter (which does not shape itself), nor by a single person (who cannot work upon everyone, and who, whatever he does, acts for himself and not for what is common to the rest). It is not produced by all persons together, who, insofar as they differ from one another, do not create something common but rather diverse things; insofar as they agree, they agree through this very nature—indeed, they exist through it—which is as much prior to them as it is simpler than they are. For various properties come upon this nature, as if upon a prior thing, to constitute individual persons. Nevertheless, this nature is formed by a single form, since it is one; this form must exist above the multitude of persons, so that it too is not made by another, and that one again by another without end. Thus we ascend to the Divine Idea, which is necessarily above all things, so that it may act equally upon all and reconcile them in a common nature. If we must rise from the part which is under the whole to the whole, and from this to that which is above the whole, then we rightly rise from individual persons—who exist in parts of space and time—to the nature common to them in itself, which exists as if through all space and all time; and from this to the concept which exists above all space and time, which Plato calls an Idea.

The intellect next receives the Divine Idea itself, whether within itself or existing in the divine light. For reason dictates that natural species <note>original: "species naturales." In this context, these are the essential forms of natural kinds (like "horse" or "man") that do not change even as individuals die.</note>, which are eternal, cannot come from a shifting cause; otherwise, having been made through motion, they would eventually fail. Yet they were made, because they are parts of the universe, which is composed from elsewhere; and they are all from a single cause. Indeed, they are so ordered among themselves that in one nature they lead to one work and end. From this, the human intellect concludes that above the shifting world, in the immobile mind that moves the world, there are concepts of the natural species—the "blueprints" <note>original: "exemplaria"</note>—not in a physical or animal nature (for they would be shifting), but in an intellectual, or rather, an intelligible nature; for intelligible things must be placed within the highest Intelligible. 

However, such a complex argument is not strictly necessary for the intellect to reach the common concepts of things. On the contrary, just as the phantasy <note>Ficino uses "phantasy" as a higher faculty than "imagination," capable of forming judgments about sensory images.</note> by its own nature judges things individually, so the intellect, by a natural power, acts immediately without any long discourse. As soon as that individual image of Plato is depicted in the phantasy, the intellect suddenly—having dismissed this "certain man"—thinks of that human nature common to all, as well as the Idea. Once that beauty and goodness are painted there, it immediately thinks of the universal nature of beauty and goodness, and a concept positioned in no certain matter, no specific place or time, but either in all matter or as something absolute from matter, simply subsisting in itself. 

Wherefore the sense is occupied with bodies, the imagination with the images of bodies, the phantasy with the individual intentions <note>In medieval philosophy, an "intention" is the mental representation of a thing's qualities.</note> of those images, and the intellect with the common natures and entirely incorporeal concepts of those individual intentions. But one must remember that the intellect knows not only the universal nature, but also the particular; otherwise, it could not compare the two with each other. Moreover, it knows all the powers below itself and their acts, since it compares them all to itself. Yet almost everyone agrees that the universal nature is known by it before the particular. Indeed, you act primarily according to the nature of the intelligible form. Since that form is conceived through a certain abstraction, it is absolute; hence it primarily reflects a universal nature. The intellect acquires this power from its own virtue, in which and from which it exists, as if the intellect itself were absolute. But from the image which is in the phantasy, only the particular is represented, which indeed par—

He describes a hierarchy of cognition moving from the physical body to the Divine Idea, asserting that the intellect naturally recognizes eternal, universal truths that exist beyond time and space.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the immortality of the soul from Book VIII. Having previously discussed how the mind abstracts universal Ideas from individual physical things, he now turns to the soul's growth and nourishment, distinguishing its "spiritual food" (Truth) from the "physical food" of the body.</meta>

<page-num>185</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII.</header>
<sig>M 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: materia (matter)</meta>

...we grow. The soul very often acquires knowledge and <term>magnanimity (greatness of soul): the virtue of being high-minded and courageous</term> suddenly; the body, however, can neither give nor receive anything except over time. Finally, the virtue of the soul is a certain "equality" or harmony, as the <term>Magi (the wise men of the East): Ficino often references ancient Persian or "Zoroastrian" wisdom as a precursor to Plato</term> hand down, through which the soul is in harmony both with itself and with the Good itself. 

If by some means a square-shaped line were made circular, it would come out more perfect—not because it became longer, but because it became more "equal" <note>By "equal," Ficino means symmetrical and uniform, qualities Platonists associated with divine perfection.</note>. Again, if a lyre is tuned, it will be more perfect—not because it becomes larger, but more harmonious. In this way, when a youth grows in virtue, the soul does not grow in quantity, but advances in a certain spiritual equality and harmony. 

Nor should anyone object that when the body is neither weighed down by too much food nor weakened by hunger, but is moderately nourished, the soul is similarly nurtured and becomes stronger in that state, and the opposite happens otherwise. For while it is true that the soul is at its strongest in that state of the human person, this does not happen because it is nourished in the same way as the body, but because the soul by its nature governs the body. When the body itself is sick or burdened, the soul is so occupied in caring for and ruling it that it is not intent on seeking the truth. But when the body is quiet, the mind contemplates freely, and then it most especially feeds on its own nourishment. 

And what other food shall we say the soul has, except that for which it always hungers and thirsts, in which part it rejoices most of all, and which, once taken, causes it to grow and be filled? Every soul, at every age and continuously, desires **Truth** above all else. This is what craftsmen seek in every art, and in any matter, children even ask curiously what the reality of the thing is. They do not do this once or twice or three times a day, like physical eating, but they investigate the truth in all affairs at every moment. 

Furthermore, out of zeal for acquiring truth, we frequently skip the nourishment of the body; we spare neither time nor money, nor do we fear weakening the body through labors—for when the body is weakened, the soul becomes more "sinewy" <note>original: "neruosior" – meaning more vigorous or spiritually strong</note>. The soul itself desires this truth, not the body. Indeed, truth does not increase the body; rather, the study of it often hinders the body. Moreover, the soul seeks it for its own sake, not for the body's. For what could it contribute to the body? If truth ever seems to benefit the body, it does not happen because of the truth itself, but because of some physical advantage that follows from the truth having been known. 

In fact, even if no utility follows from it, the soul searches for truth studiously. Even when the body is full of its own foods, the soul still hungers and thirsts for truth. When truth is found, the soul exults—not just for a time, as with physical needs, but it rejoices perpetually. It is illuminated, it grows, and it becomes so magnificent that, because of its own greatness, those things which usually seem greatest to a "starving little soul" <note>original: "animulæ"</note> seem tiny to it. By this nourishment, the soul becomes invincible, temperate, just, a governor and master of men, higher than the heavens, equal to the angels, and similar to God. 

Who, then, would doubt further that **Truth** is the natural food of the human mind? All minds desire this same food, and every mind desires it always. This stable consensus of desire signifies that minds agree with one another wonderfully, and that any mind remains stable in its own nature—since their appetite does not vary or change like the appetite of the senses. Sensory appetite differs according to the diversity of bodies and changes with the body's transformation; the senses follow the changeability of bodies, but the mind follows the stability of divine things. For the mind hates the body's nourishment and feeds on the same food as the celestial and eternal minds. 

This food is Truth. Truth, however, is not corporeal; otherwise, it would not be present in incorporeal things. But as it is, truth exists in God, in angels, and in numbers, which are both incorporeal and true. And since incorporeal things are truer than bodies to the extent that they are purer and firmer, it follows that truth exists in them rather than in bodies. 

Indeed—what is more—truth is not properly in bodies at all. In these, there are two things: <term>matter (materia)</term> and <term>form (forma)</term>. Truth is not in the matter. For through matter, nothing is truly in any "species" of things; a human is not truly anything through matter, nor a horse, and so on. Nor does truth lie in the physical form of the body, since it is not a "true form" whose power is stained by matter. 

Mathematicians testify to this, for they do not find true figures in bodies. For a "true circle" placed on a "true plane" would roll continuously; reason compels this to happen, since that circle would touch the plane at a single point, and a body cannot remain at rest on a single point. No one has ever seen these things in physical bodies. Therefore, true figures are not in bodies, because perhaps even the true principles of figures are not there (at least as far as the senses are concerned), such as points, lines, and surfaces. Reason shows that a true point must lack length, a true line must lack width, and a true surface must lack depth. Such things in...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's true nourishment is incorporeal Truth, which allows it to grow in virtue and harmony independently of the body's physical needs. He concludes that "true" forms and mathematical principles do not exist in the physical world of matter, but only in the mind and divine realm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the soul is incorporeal because its primary characteristics—virtues and knowledge—do not have physical dimensions. Following the previous page's discussion on the soul's growth, Ficino now proves that virtue is an indivisible "quality," which implies the soul itself must be indivisible and non-physical.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII.</header>
<meta>catchword: distinctas (distinct)</meta>

The indivisible virtue of the human soul is a <term>quality: a property or characteristic of a thing that is not a physical part of its substance</term>. Therefore, the soul is not a body. This demonstration will be considered sufficient if we can show two things clearly: namely, that virtue is a quality of the soul, and that this very virtue is indivisible. First, it is most evident to everyone that a soul becomes—and is called—this or that because of the presence of virtue; it is called wise, prudent, just, brave, and temperate. Furthermore, virtue can be absent from the soul while the soul remains <note>original: "abesse uirtus ab anima potest anima remanente." Ficino is using a classic Aristotelian definition: a quality is something that can come or go without the thing itself being destroyed.</note>. This is precisely the nature of qualities.

Secondly, we show that virtue is indivisible in the following way: there are two kinds of virtues—those in the intellect, and those in the <term>appetite: the soul's faculty of desiring or willing</term>, whether it be the rational or irrational appetite. The former are called <term>speculative: relating to deep contemplation or theoretical knowledge</term>, while the latter are called moral. The speculative ones are so named because they are acquired by contemplating, and once acquired, they are exercised in contemplating. The moral ones are so named because they are acquired through <term>character and habit: "mores" in Latin</term>, and once acquired, they consist in character and the practice of works. In the first category belong the wisdom of divine things, the science of natural things, the prudence of civil affairs, and the art of human works. In the second category are justice, which gives to each person their own; fortitude, which, being ready for honorable works, casts off the obstacle of fear; and temperance, which repels the softness of lust (which is the other obstacle to honorable deeds). These indeed are the descriptions of the virtues according to Plato.

If there were any corporeal size in these virtues, then the larger a person was, the wiser and more just they could become; nor could small men surpass or equal large men in virtue. Again, knowledge which is the understanding of the largest bodies would be more extensive and clearer than knowledge of smaller ones. But we know many things whose physical size we cannot match, and the entire soul perceives a large thing just as well as a small one. In summary, what else is speculative virtue but a clarity of the intellect? What else is moral virtue but a steady heat of the appetite, ignited by the clarity of the intellect? 

That clarity does not happen bit by bit, even though we approach it step by step. Just as a hare is suddenly seen after a long search following many tracks, so everyone notices in themselves, after a lengthy investigation, that in a single moment they behold what is true regarding the matter they sought. Suddenly the light of truth (as Plato says) shines out in the soul; it is not suddenly forced out of things, but rather out of a long discussion, like a spark from a stone struck repeatedly. Similarly, through long habit, youth is disposed toward character, until just a tiny bit is missing to ignite that steady and rational heat of the appetite; it is not yet sufficiently ignited, and moral virtue is not yet held; but by repeated inspiration, the heat of the appetite finally blazes up, sufficient for virtue. What more? When a mirror is turned toward the Sun, light reflects in the mirror in a moment; when wool is placed under that mirror, as soon as it is ready, fire is ignited within it. Therefore, both the sudden splendor occurs in the mirror and the sudden fire in the wool. No differently does the sudden clarity of truth occur in the intellect, and from there, a sudden blazing in the appetite.

Consider it again in this way: Speculative virtue is a certain knowledge of truth. If it were put together gradually, one part would be held now, while another part would be missing and sought after. Insofar as a part of the truth was held, we would indeed know; but insofar as a part was missing, we would also not know. Thus, we would both know and not know the same thing at the same time. Not even a drunkard would dream of such a thing. For this reason, speculative virtue does not progress gradually from one part of itself to another, but shines out as a whole and all at once. Moral virtue, too, is a certain constant will choosing whatever reason has dictated. If it had many parts and occurred gradually, a part of this will would be present while a part would still be absent. Insofar as a part is present, we will it; insofar as a part is absent, we also do not will it. Thus, we would both will and not will the same thing at the same time through the same power of the soul. This is like a monster. 

Therefore, since virtue comes into being in an indivisible moment, it is itself also indivisible—provided that the nature of each thing follows its own origin, especially since it has an indivisible end. Why should that whose birth and end are indivisible not itself also be indivisible? What is the end of virtue? The end of moral virtue is to purify and separate the soul from the divisible body; the end of speculative virtue is to comprehend the incorporeal and universal reasons of things, placed far away from divisible bodies. You see that the end of both virtues, like their origin, is something indivisible. Thus, both virtues show that they must be judged as indivisible. Both virtues show this kind of nature in themselves most especially in this: that many sciences exist in the intellect at the same time, and many moral virtues exist in the appetite at the same time, and they do not confuse each other by their number, but rather increase and illuminate one another. And we perceive the conception of one science in us separately from another, so that we can think of one without considering the other. Consequently, we have such ideas of crafts in the mind—unified, I say, yet equally distinct...

<summary>Ficino argues that virtue is an indivisible quality of the soul, proving this through the suddenness of intellectual "enlightenment" and the consistency of moral will. He concludes that since virtue is non-physical and indivisible, the soul that contains it must also be incorporeal.</summary>
