The previous page established that the soul is not a body because it possesses virtues, which are non-physical qualities. Here, Ficino expands on how these intellectual concepts and moral virtues are interconnected and indivisible, further proving the soul’s incorporeal and immortal nature.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...so distinct that we are able to speak according to the pattern of a single idea and create something specific to it, even if we do nothing toward a further pattern of conception. Bodies cannot be such <term>intellectual insights: the specific acts or objects of pure understanding</term>, which remain in the same bosom of the <term>soul</term> in such a way that they neither thrust themselves out and push each other away, nor confuse themselves through mutual mixing. The same reasoning applies to the moral virtues. Furthermore, since there are many intellectual insights in the soul of a wise person, each of them is found whole within every other. Surely, one who is skilled in <term>geometry</term> or <term>theology</term> possesses a first proposition of that faculty, a second, a third, and so on, and progresses from the knowledge of one into the knowledge of another. If the first teaches the second, and the second the third—and whoever teaches something possesses within himself that which is taught—it follows that in any preceding proposition, all subsequent ones are contained. Indeed, the preceding ones are likewise present in every subsequent one. For we often tend to investigate preceding things by the evidence of those that follow. And this is not without reason. Indeed, the images of causes shine forth in their effects. By this series of things, it happens that a wise person, having thought out any single proposition, very swiftly runs through many, and thus perceives many—indeed, all—in one. Therefore, every intellectual insight is in every other, and each one is contained whole in every single one.

The same occurs in the moral virtues; for once one of them is acquired, all are immediately held. For who will distribute justly if he either fears threats or serves lust? Who will bravely overcome fear if he is softened by lust? Who will tame desires if he succumbs to dread? Finally, who will lead an honest life unless, through prudence, he has established the best end of life and chosen the more righteous ways to that end? Or who will look prudently if the edge of the mind is clouded by the fog of vices? Therefore, these virtues are so connected to one another that all are in one, and every virtue is understood whole in every single one, just as the entire faculty of geometry lies hidden in its chief proposition—indeed, in any of them—since through the sagacity of a skillful mind, all are drawn out from any single proposition. 

However, a divisible quality cannot be present as a whole in many things at once. Surely it is in only one thing—that is, in one body—and it extends its other parts through the other parts of the body; its entire quantity is not present in every single part of the body. Therefore, those intellectual insights and character traits are entirely indivisible. For this reason, the soul can be neither a body nor a form divided through a body, since the soul itself is the subject of these indivisible qualities. Therefore, just as he is delirious who either asks how large knowledge or justice is, or thinks that Geometry is smaller than the body of the geometer, so too does he show contempt who either asks how large the soul is or believes it to be smaller than the body, since it is in no way corporeal. For not only does it receive incorporeal things, but it also creates many incorporeal things within itself while it conceives the <term>species: the mental forms or "blueprints" of things</term>, reasons, and habits of things—especially when it fashions the definitions of incorporeal things. Who, then, would say that she <note>Ficino uses "she" because the Latin word for soul, "anima," is feminine.</note> who is the cause of incorporeal things is herself corporeal? Or that she is mortal, who is the subject of the virtues? For it is the duty of the virtues to resist mortal things; indeed, the speculative virtue flees them, and the moral virtue puts them to flight. A quality cannot resist its own subject; rather, that which is the natural receptacle of those qualities—whose specific nature is to oppose and command mortal things—is necessarily immortal. The force of this reason consists mostly in this: the soul is not only the subject of such qualities, but also the principle <note>Here, "principle" means the starting point or source.</note> of them; therefore, they obtain that nature which resists mortal things from the soul.

### Fourth argument. Universal species and intelligible concepts cannot be received by a body. Chapter IV.

**A**ll the Greek Platonists hold this view. We can likewise confirm it by the opinion of the Arabic Platonists. The <term>intellect</term> does not understand a thing—for instance, "man"—unless it acquires a certain universal form representing "men," which they call the intelligible form and species. Having acquired this, it judges what the nature of man is: "man is a rational animal." This judgment is called both a concept and a <term>conception</term> of the mind, as well as the reason and definition of the thing to be known, which we are also accustomed to call science. If the intellect were stretched out by the width of a body, both the intelligible form and the conception would adhere to the width of the body. In this very width, two things are considered: namely, the point and the extension of width. Therefore, the seat of that form and conception will be either the point alone...

<meta>catchword: point</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is indivisible and immortal because it contains interconnected virtues and intellectual concepts that do not occupy physical space. He also begins a new argument stating that the intellect's ability to grasp "universal" concepts (like the definition of a human) proves it cannot be a physical, extended body.</summary>
<keywords>indivisibility, virtues, geometry, intellect, universal forms, species, immortality, incorporeality, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

--- Page 222 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book VIII of the Platonic Theology. In the preceding text, Ficino argued that the soul cannot be a body because it possesses intellectual and moral virtues that do not behave like physical matter. Here, he employs geometric and logical proofs to show that the intellect cannot be located in a single physical point nor spread across a physical extension.</meta>

<page-num>189</page-num>
-> ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII <-

...some point of the body, or an extension. But if neither ought to be granted, as we shall demonstrate, it follows that the intellect is in no way extended in the body. Let us first show that a point cannot be such a seat. First, indeed, it must be observed that a point does not exist by itself, but is so attached to the measurement of a body that it is always its boundary. If, by its nature, it receives something, it certainly never receives anything except some boundary of some magnitude which is contained in that measurement of the body of which the point is the boundary; thus, just as a bodily measurement receives the magnitude of an incoming thing, so the boundary of such a measurement receives the boundary of that magnitude. Therefore, whatever is said to be received by a point of a body is not free from magnitude. Consequently, if a point were the receptacle of an <term>intellectual form: the pure concept or "idea" of a thing held in the mind</term>, it would be impossible for that <note>original: "species"</note> <term>species: the mental representation or "look" of an object</term> not to be divisible, having its boundary in the point of the body while its remaining parts reside in the width of the body. However, we shall prove in what follows that such a form is indivisible.

Furthermore, if it is said that a point receives that form in such a way that the point alone is its seat and foundation, and that through this the form remains separated from the width of the body, then it would be necessary for the point also to be disconnected from that width—especially since nothing is a proper subject of any <term>accident: a quality that exists in something else, like "redness" in an apple</term> unless it properly exists in <term>actuality: "actu," meaning something that is fully real and present, rather than just possible</term>. A point of this kind would be separated from the line; it would neither be a part of the line nor the boundary of the width, and the line would be terminated by some other point closest to this one. Again, that other point would likewise exist in its own actuality, by which it too could become the seat of an accidental form, and it would also be separated from the line, especially since the logic of all points is the same. The result of this is either that there is no point in a line—which is the height of folly to say (for it would lack boundaries)—or that the length of a line is composed of points, which is also ridiculous to say, because a point added to a point does not increase length. 

This is perceived by the following reasoning: if three points are imagined succeeding one another in turn, we shall ask whether the middle point among them forces the two outer points to be so distant from each other that they do not touch, or whether it does not hinder the meeting of the outer points. If it forces them to be distant, it certainly does not touch one of them with the same part of itself as it touches the other; otherwise, it would not keep them apart. But if it faces one of the outer points with one part of itself and the other with another part, then it is constituted of two parts, and is not a point, since it is divisible. Therefore, we are forced to admit that a middle point does not prevent the meeting of others. Thus, all things would be in all things, nor would any length be created by their meeting, since no interval is born between other points through a middle point. 

If some length of a body does not consist of points, no point is found in it which could at any time become so actual by itself that it could become the subject of an intellectual form. Perhaps someone might say that a point is in the body not in actuality, but in <term>potentiality: "potentia," the capacity to be something that is not yet realized</term>, and through that very potentiality, it becomes the subject of an intellectual form. Although this has already been refuted, it is refuted again as follows: points of this kind, both because they are potential rather than actual, and because they are infinite, are in no way distinguished from one another such that one of them should receive that form rather than another. Therefore, all of them receive it. Because of this, the intellect will either receive in actuality infinite forms of every single thing to be understood at the same time, or it will understand the same thing infinitely and simultaneously through infinite points. Both are impossible: that there should be infinite forms in actuality, and that there should be infinite acts of understanding at the same time. Through these arguments, it is manifest that a point of the body cannot be the seat of an intellectual species. 

But could the very continuation of points or the extension of the body be the seat? By no means. For every form that is received in a divisible subject becomes divisible, just as the whiteness of snow is divided by the division of the snow. Thus, if that species is received by the width of the body, let it be wide and divisible. Yet it is impossible for it to become such a thing, which I shall show as follows. If a species is cut into parts, those parts are said to be either entirely similar or dissimilar. But neither of these is to be admitted. It must not be admitted that they are entirely similar because, if they are so similar that the complete definition <note>original: "ratio"</note> of the whole species is in any part—just as the complete definition of the whole water is preserved in individual drops of water—then certainly the intellect would behold the whole in any part, and one part of the species would suffice for the understanding of the whole thing; the others would be superfluous. Furthermore, through such a species, which is everywhere entirely similar to itself and by such similarity deceives the intellect led from there to cognition, the judgment of the intellect would be utterly confused in discerning parts from the whole—both in any of the constituent parts and especially in that thing which is composed of various natures; nor could it discern parts from parts, or from the whole. Yet, in truth, the nature of a part as a part is one thing, and the nature of the whole as a whole is another...

<summary>Ficino uses geometric proofs to argue that the human intellect cannot be located in a physical point or bodily extension, as points are indivisible boundaries and cannot host the complex, indivisible nature of thought without leading to logical absurdities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VIII of the Platonic Theology. Having previously argued that the intellect cannot be localized in a physical point, he now addresses the impossibility of the intellectual "species" (the mental concept) being divided across a physical extension like a body. He focuses on why a mental concept cannot be made of parts in the same way matter is.</meta>

<page-num>196</page-num>

### MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY ###

And this is always affirmed through the judgment of the mind, since neither can the whole itself be a part, nor can a part be the whole. Therefore, we think it must be denied that the parts of a <term>species: the mental form or "look" of an object held in the mind</term> are entirely similar to one another. This is primarily because when the mind understands the parts of a thing as parts, and understands the whole as it is a whole, it truly distinguishes the whole from the parts. It could not truly make this distinction unless there were some natural distinction within them. It follows that the parts of an <term>intelligible species: a concept understood by the intellect rather than the senses</term>—if indeed it has parts—must differ from the whole by some natural variety. 

Another reason is added: namely, that parts which are entirely similar to each other and to the whole, when they compose a whole by joining together, do not complete that whole except by an increase in number or magnitude. We see this in grains of wheat or drops of water. For where the form does not vary, yet some internal change occurs, there is in some way an increase or a decrease. Therefore, if that mental species grows together from such parts, it would be a mere number, or something numerical, or a heap, or a continuous physical thing. Consequently, through such a species we would understand only numbers and numerical magnitudes or figures; the species would then belong to the <term>imagination and phantasy: the faculties that deal with sensory images</term> rather than to the mind. From this, it is concluded that an intelligible form is by no means divided into parts that are similar to each other. 

Is it perhaps cut into dissimilar parts, just as an animal’s body is divided into bones, flesh, and nerves? Not at all. For through this form, the mind knows what the <term>substance: the essential nature or "whatness"</term> of a thing is, as we have said. The substance of a thing is most fully grasped by a <term>definition</term>. A definition consists of a <term>genus: a general category (e.g., "animal")</term> and a <term>difference: the specific trait that distinguishes a species within a genus (e.g., "rational")</term>. For example, the definition of a "man" consists of "animal" and "rational." "Animal" is the genus, through which man agrees in common with other animals. "Rational" is the difference, through which he differs from animals lacking reason. Therefore, if there were any diversity of parts in that mental form, it would most likely be through the genus and the difference. Let these two be, if you wish, the parts of the intelligible form, and let them be extended across a physical width.

Listen to what follows from this. Because the parts of a body can be divided infinitely, both the genus and the difference would be sliced without end along with them. There would be innumerable genera and innumerable differences in a single definition. In truth, it would not be a definition at all, because it could not be grasped by the intellect if it were infinite, nor would it be enclosed by its own boundaries. And (what is more absurd) we would either infinitely replicate the same genera and differences, or we would ascend from a genus into another genus infinitely by resolving it, or descend from a difference into another difference by dividing it. Such an ascent and descent is impossible, because true reason finally reaches the primary genera of things and the ultimate differences, beyond which it is not permitted to go. For "substance" is the supreme genus in man, which cannot be resolved into another genus. Likewise, the "certain power of discourse" <note>original: "Certa uerò discurrendi potentia", referring to the human ability to reason step-by-step</note> is the ultimate difference, which cannot be narrowed into another difference. 

This error is increased above all by the fact that if genus and difference exist in a thing, they will be infinite in actuality. For those things which grant essence to a thing and belong to the natural order exist in nature in actuality and truth; they are not merely imagined by human thought. But nature does not allow any such multitude to be actually innumerable, especially in a body—in which there would nevertheless be an innumerable multitude if innumerable genera and differences were divided equally through the parts of the body, for there would be just as many portions of the body itself. 

Furthermore, we question the <term>Epicureans: followers of Epicurus, here used to describe those who believe the soul is material</term>, who divide the species in the intellect just like a form in a body, and place one part of it in one part of the mind. For example: placing the Genus in the right part of the mind and the Difference in the left. Why should the right part suit the genus more, or the left the difference? Is not any part of the mind equally "mind"? Otherwise, a mind would be made of mindless parts. Therefore, any small particle of the mind regards both the genus and the difference equally; thus, any part receives both. But if any part receives both, and both are in each part, it follows that they are not separated from each other. 

Yet, as the Epicureans would have it, chance causes one of those two to fall to the right and the other to the left. But let them answer us: do they then remain distinct in this way, or do they mix together? If they grant the first, it follows that knowledge is not born from it. For no definition is made from a genus and difference that are separated from each other. In neither of them, when placed apart, is there perfect knowledge of the thing itself. They must be mixed into one, so that one knowledge of one thing can be held by one mind, through one definition, at one time. It is necessary for both to be in the whole mind so that it may truly be understood. For what is in only a part of the mind is not yet fully understood. Indeed, action belongs to the whole thing, not to a part. Therefore, one must confess that those parts are unified.

<summary>Ficino argues that intellectual concepts (species) cannot be physically extended or divided like matter; if they were, definitions like "rational animal" would be split apart and become nonsensical or infinitely divisible.</summary>
<keywords>intellect, species, genus, difference, definition, Epicureans, indivisibility of the soul, substance, rational animal, mental forms</keywords>

Here, Ficino examines whether these concepts are mixed by chance or by a mind, and why they cannot be physically divisible.</meta>

<meta>catchword: nullo</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII.

But from where are they mixed? Is it by chance or by a mind? By chance, they <note>original: "inquiunt" — referring to the Epicureans</note> say. To say this is a great wickedness. For such a mixture would happen only very rarely, and when it did happen, they would finally have to concede that those things thus united are incorporeal—which is exactly what we maintain. They will eventually concede, then, that they are mixed by a mind. From this concession, we will immediately infer two points. First, that the mind is incorporeal, if it brings the forms it receives into an incorporeal state; this opinion opposes the <term>Epicureans: followers of Epicurus who believed the soul was made of physical atoms</term>. Second, that the mixture made by the mind would not be true unless there were some such union in the things themselves. For whatever is fashioned by the mind contrary to the nature of things is a figment rather than <term>knowledge: original "scientia," meaning certain or systematic understanding</term>. It is entirely necessary that <term>genera: the general categories (like "animal")</term> and <term>differences: the specific traits that distinguish species (like "rational")</term> be joined or separated by nature, not by a figment or physical placement of the mind. For if it were done by a figment of the mind, we would be erring, not learning. But if it were by placement—such that the genus is in the right part of the mind and the difference is in the left—then, because the mind is allowed to resolve these common concepts, the mind would divide them. Through this very division, they would be cut in a bodily manner; one half of the genus would be left in one half of the right side, and the other half would be left in the other. The same would happen to the difference. It would be possible to divide them again. From this, a mangling would follow, not a resolution; and while we were tearing apart these common concepts, we would destroy knowledge. But if those common concepts are not mangled by division, but the genus remains whole in any part of itself (and similarly the difference), then they will no longer be corporeal, because they do not require a fixed quantity. Furthermore, anyone who cuts in this way will find innumerable genera and just as many differences. And the multitude of these would not consist of nature, but would be born from the mind's machination.

Perhaps the Epicureans, to avoid these objections, will no longer grant that the <term>intelligible species: the mental form or concept of an object</term> is composed of genus and difference, but of other parts. We, however, will ask whether a part of the species (whatever it may be) differs from the whole species or not. If it does not differ, then surely that which does not differ from the whole will not be a part, but will be the whole; nor will that species be a composite if it differs in nothing from its parts, because it thus lacks a diversity of parts. Therefore, they will admit that a part of the species differs from the species itself. We will then ask them how it differs. If not as a genus or difference differs from a species (as we have shown), then perhaps at least as one species differs from another, such as a figure differs from a color? But this cannot be admitted. For such a species is not "within" another species. A figure is not contained under color. Yet a part is within the whole and is contained by it. Perhaps, to prove that this species and mental conception has parts contained under it, they will flee to numbers; they might infer that a species differs from its parts just as four differs from two, or two from one. Although we have refuted this above, we shall strike it down again thus: Do they want those parts of the species and conception—which they call "knowledge"—to be themselves acts of knowledge? If they do not, they would be creating knowledge out of ignorance, as if they were constructing "whiteness" out of shapes. If they do want them to be knowledge, we argue against them thus: It is established among philosophers that any knowledge has its own object in which it is occupied, which they call the "thing known." Let them declare to us whether those instances of knowledge, which are parts of a single science, ought to have an object: is the specific "thing known" of each part the same as that of the whole, or is it different? If they answer it is the same, then none of them will be a part, but each will be the whole, since it is equal to the whole. For where objects are equal, the knowledges are also equal. But if they admit it is different, that absurdity follows again: that the knowledge of the whole "thing known" will exist apart from the knowledge of the parts, and the whole will not be known from the cognition of the parts where individual knowledges do not concur into a universal knowledge. 

But let us proceed again. The mind, for the most part, understands the very <term>reason: original "ratio," here meaning the underlying principle or logic</term> of things as both one and universal—as, for example, "goodness" itself, which is equally common to many good things.

<margin>About</margin> A reason of this kind, insofar as it is one and universal, is also simple. The "reason" of God or an angel, whenever it is truly known, is judged as indivisible. These reasons are called <term>intelligible essences: the core realities of things that can be grasped by the intellect</term>; our mind would never know them unless it had their forms within itself as images. For if in the act of knowing the mind does something, and it does not act unless it exists, and it does not act except insofar as it is "in act" <note>meaning: actively functioning</note>, and it becomes "in act" through a form, then it never contemplates essences unless it is adorned by their forms. Such forms, though they are sometimes called "intelligible," should more properly be called "intellectual," while the essences are "intelligible." This is the custom of the ancient <term>Platonists: followers of Plato's philosophy</term>. If such a form (the image of such an essence) in our mind were scattered into parts, then those parts would either be such that none of them regards the essence itself, or one regards it but another does not, or all of them do. If the first is granted, then that whole form will in no way regard the essence, since there is no regard in the parts. For as the whole form consists of parts, the regard of the whole is gathered from the regards of the parts. But if...

<summary>Ficino argues that mental concepts cannot be physical or divisible because knowledge requires a unified understanding of universal "reasons" or essences. If the mind were physical, concepts like "goodness" would be mangled by division rather than understood as whole, simple truths.</summary>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY.<-

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...in no way regards the essence, it will not be its image, nor will it contribute to the understanding of it. If the second point is granted—that a part does not regard the essence—then it has nothing to do with the <term>intellectual form: the mental concept or "idea" of a thing</term>, since it does not look toward the <term>intelligible essence: the true nature of a thing that can only be understood by the mind</term>. But if the third point is granted, we will immediately ask: does each part have the same outlook, or do some have one and others another? If the answer is that they have the same outlook, then they cannot have the same outlook unless each reflects the whole essence; in that case, none of those parts would be a "part" of the intellectual form, but each would be the whole. One would suffice for knowing, and the others would be superfluous—and there would be an infinite number of them in reality if they were cut by the division of a body and yet contributed to the action of knowing.

However, if they have different outlooks, this can only happen if individual parts of the form look at as many parts of the essence, since the "intellectual" (the mind's grasp) must be equal to the "intelligible" (the thing being grasped). It would follow that the essence itself is divisible, even though true reason concludes that it is <term>simple: in philosophy, "simple" means "not made of parts," as opposed to "composite"</term>. Nor could reason judge it to be simple unless it gazed upon it with a single, simple outlook. With a multiple outlook of diverse parts, it would judge it to be multiple. We believe, however, that they <note>original: "eos" — likely referring to materialist philosophers like the Epicureans</note> fell into this error because they observed that some sciences deal with composite things. Such is the science of "man," who is composed of "animal" and "rational," as if from his genus and his difference. Such is the science of the <term>septenary: the number seven</term> and the <term>denary: the number ten</term>, and other numbers which are gathered from numbers or units.

But we think that man, insofar as he is man, is something one and simple, because his <term>form: the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing</term> is one. The proof of this is that "man" is not divided into several "men." For whether you divide him according to <term>species: the specific category or type</term> into genus and difference, neither of those is "man." Or if you divide him according to individual parts into head, chest, and thigh, none of those is "man." You indeed cut the body because you tear it into members, which are bodies, but you do not cut the "man," because you do not cut him into "men." Whatever is such a thing in itself, and is not divided into more such things, is certainly—insofar as it is such—individual and simple.

The number ten also, insofar as it is "ten-ness," is not divided; for it is only one species and one form, which we cannot partition into several "tens." If we partition it, we partition the number into other numbers, but we do not partition the "ten-ness," because we do not distribute it into "tens." Nor is it an obstacle that the genus and difference seem to be included in the species; for there are not two forms in it, but one. For although it is one thing in the order of reality to be an "animal" and another to be "rational," in a human being they are the same, and (to speak in the Platonic way) the very nature of man is a certain "rationality." Rationality in man is nothing other than "animality" itself led into the act of reason. Such a simple form is the foundation of a simple species, which does not distribute itself into individual men but communicates itself as a whole to each individual, and through this, each individual is one.

However, they differ through other things that are adjacent from the outside, which belong not at all to the species. This signifies the simplicity of the species, which is also significantly shown by the fact that a species does not admit "more" or "less," but stands in a certain fixed degree of nature, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away without the species itself being changed. The species of numbers testify to this: the number seven is a certain species of number; add one to it, and you will create a new species, namely the number eight. Subtract one, and you have the number six, again a new species of number. Since, in truth, knowledge is not properly held regarding individuals or genera, but regarding species—for individuals, because they are innumerable and change, are neither grasped nor held firmly, and genera, because of their confusion, are not perfectly discerned in themselves—since, I say, knowledge is of species, and species are simple, knowledge of them is also simple, provided that knowledge is the attainment of truth.

Truth is the alignment <note>original: "adaequatio" — the classical definition of truth as "adaequatio rei et intellectus" (the correspondence of the thing and the mind)</note> of things with minds. Let neither the multitude of words nor the variety of multiple thoughts disturb us, from which knowledge perhaps seems to be forged. These are indeed preparations for knowledge or its attendants. Knowledge is a unique act, or a habit, a "touch," I say—a simple intuition of a simple form, of an individual truth. A sudden light of intelligence. But from this, their error is more evidently refuted: that there are many sciences regarding things that are undoubtedly indivisible. For who could divide <term>unity</term>? Who likewise could divide simplicity and purity? Who could divide "being itself" simply? Furthermore, whatever we divide, we divide into parts that exist "before" the whole. But these things are composed of no preceding parts. Indeed, we resolve "man" into "animal" and "rational," and "animal" into "body" and "the nature of sensing," and "body" into...

<summary>Ficino argues that the "species" or essential forms of things (like "humanity" or the number ten) are simple and indivisible, even if the physical objects they inhabit are not. He defines knowledge as a single, simple mental "touch" or intuition of these indivisible truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book VIII of the *Platonic Theology*, where he argues for the immortality of the soul by examining the nature of the mind. substance and quantity—substance in its being and its self-sufficiency of subsisting. Into what parts we might resolve "being" itself, I do not know, unless perhaps Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino’s work is largely a commentary and expansion on his ideas.</note> and Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a late antique philosopher who systematized Neoplatonic thought.</note> resolve it into unity and multitude; yet they do not resolve unity itself any further. No one resolves unity into numbers, no one a point into magnitudes, no one the ultimate form of a thing into another form, or prime matter into [some other] matter. Finally, no one will refer those simple concepts of our mind—which always shine within us regarding the principles of the sciences—to "un-conceived" things, or to things more known or prior. Where <term>resolution: the process of breaking a complex idea down into its simplest components</term> stops, division stops; where division ends, perfect simplicity possesses the field. 

Therefore, it must be concluded that the first concepts of the mind are <term>simple: in this philosophical context, "simple" means "not made of parts" and therefore indestructible</term>, and those things which are known from them are partly such that, although they seem to be divided, they are nevertheless known by that ratio which is least divided, and therefore the notion of them is indivisible. Partly they are such that they are entirely simple, and for that reason their perception is simple, provided that the intelligence is equal to the things understood. Thus the concept, the notion, and the perception are simple; the <term>intelligible forms: the abstract "blueprints" or ideas of things</term> from which these are born are also simple. 

If this is so, the mind too is simple, which is the subject of simple things. And since the simpler a thing is, the more indissoluble it is, and the mind reaches the highest degree of simplicity (as we have said), it also attains the highest degree of an indissoluble nature in its living. For intelligence is the reflection of life upon itself <note>original: "Intelligentia enim est vitae reflexio in seipsam." This is a key Neoplatonic definition: consciousness is life turning back to look at itself.</note>. Therefore, if through the intelligence which follows life, it reaches the highest simplicity (which precedes an indissoluble nature), how much more does it attain an indissoluble degree through that life which is prior to intelligence—a degree that is [only] posterior to simplicity itself.

***

## Fifth argument. If the mind is a body, it understands by touching and by running through. Chapter V.

**S**hould the mind be a body, or a form spread out through the magnitude of a body, it possesses two things within itself, as we have indicated elsewhere: namely, a point and <term>latitude: here meaning spatial extension or breadth</term>. It is then enslaved to the same conditions as a body. Therefore, it would not comprehend things to be understood in any other way than by touching them, enlarging itself through them, and running across them like a body. 

Either, then, it will be said to touch by a point alone so that it may understand, or by latitude alone, or by both. If it uses a point alone, and requires touch for the sake of knowing, it will not know the magnitudes of things; for through a point it reaches points, not magnitudes. And even if it did reach them, it would never recognize them as a whole or in their entirety. For the points in the mind would be infinite, as are the points in a magnitude. The "heap" of the former is the intellect, and the "heap" of the latter is, in a way, magnitude. It is not possible to travel through the infinite. Therefore, the mind as a whole will never understand, nor will it understand a magnitude as a whole. 

Therefore, it does not use a point alone. Does it then use latitude alone for touching? By no means. For it would only know those things which are touched by that latitude. These, however, are only the things that are themselves extended in latitude. But as it is, we know many other things besides these. 

Some will flee to this: they will confess that the mind uses both for knowing—a point for simple things, and latitude for others. This appears plausible, yet it is not true. First, through a point it will only reach those simple things which are applied to a body as a point, but it will not reach <term>abstract forms: ideas separated from physical matter</term> or numbers. Next, through its latitude it will run through the entire magnitude of the body to be known, so that it may understand the whole. However, no latitude can run through any space of magnitude unless, by any part of itself, it runs through any part of that space lengthwise. Therefore, the mind, by running through them in order, will apply its individual parts to each part of the body to be known, and by applying them, it will know them. But it will apply parts that are, in a sense, infinite. For the mind will have just as many parts if it exists as a bodily latitude. Thus, in a brief time, it would understand any portion of that body almost innumerably, and it would apprehend the body itself according to its almost infinite particles known innumerably, and in infinite (so to speak) turns. 

But let us briefly conclude this argument with a certain noble sentiment of our Plotinus: Whatever things are understood are either simple by their own nature, or at least they become understood when they become simple through resolution. Because indivisible things are captured by indivisible things, that power in us which captures such things is indivisible. If, therefore, the mind is said to be bodily, it nevertheless does not capture [things] by its latitude.

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind must be a "simple" (non-composite) substance because it perceives indivisible truths, and concludes that if the mind were a physical body, it would be mathematically impossible for it to process information through "touch" or "extension."</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

...it [the mind] receives those things, but rather by something indivisible. If it receives through this [indivisible part] alone, it understands through this alone. Therefore, this indivisible part of it alone will truly be the mind. What need is there for the remaining parts for it to be an intellect, since other parts are not needed for understanding once that one indivisible thing suffices? This one thing, therefore, is the mind; hold onto this, set aside the rest, and you have grasped the <term>simple mind</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "simple" means "not made of parts." Because it has no parts, it cannot be broken down or destroyed, which is central to Ficino's argument for immortality.</note>. Its simplicity is also apparent from the fact that it perceives a point without length, a line without width, a surface without depth, numbers without position, and beauty without any mixture of ugliness. For it discerns these things separately by contemplating them, and it does not contemplate them differently than how it receives them. A bodily form, however, cannot receive these things separately in such a way. 

If the fact that the soul grasps simple and indivisible things clearly shows it to be simple and indivisible, it declares this much more clearly by the fact that whatever things would be simple or indivisible in themselves—and yet because they are joined with other things, they turn out to be composite and divisible—the soul separates from their opposites and renders them entirely simple and indivisible. It could not, however, restore to them a simple and indivisible nature unless it were itself simple and indivisible. Finally, if it restores purity to things that are stained, it is itself outside of and above that stain.

->1.<-

->*Sixth argument. The intellect receives whatever it grasps according to its whole self, which it would not do if it were corporeal. Chapter VI.*<-

<margin>d</margin>
**N**o body contains anything within itself except through that <term>proportionality of quantity</term> <note>Ficino is arguing that physical objects occupy space based on their size—a big box holds a big object. He argues the mind doesn't work this way.</note> by which it grasps the whole thing with its whole self, but a part with a part, and a larger part of the contained thing with a larger part of itself, and a smaller part with a smaller part. The intellect does not grasp things in this way, for it grasps whatever it receives with its whole self. Indeed, it receives in the same way that it understands, and it understands whatever it understands with its whole self. 

For if anyone were to say that the intellect has two bodily parts, one of which grasps and understands a thing while the other does not, we would refute him by asserting that the intellect is truly that part which grasps and understands the thing—since "intellect" is named from the act of understanding—while that part which does not understand is not the intellect. Therefore, that nature which is truly the intellect grasps and knows any thing to be understood with its whole self. Consequently, when it understands a human body, it understands the members of that body as well; it knows the whole human body with its whole self, and it knows any of its members with its whole self. For he who compares any member to another, and relates any members to the whole, must necessarily know the individual members as well as the whole body with the same [faculty]. 

You must not suppose two parts in the intellect, one of which knows one member and the other knows another. For that comparison could be made through neither of those parts. If it receives as it knows, it certainly receives both the whole body and the individual members of the body with its whole self. Yet no body, and no bodily form, can grasp anything in this way, nor can one body be made equal to all bodies alike. For how could the body of a dog be made equal to the body of an ant, a horse, an elephant, or the sun? But the mind is made equal to all bodies, both the greatest and the smallest alike, since by understanding it encompasses all things in a similar way. Nor is it equal to these only, but in a certain way it equals itself to the <term>highest equality</term> <note>Ficino refers to the mathematical and metaphysical concept of "Equality" itself (the Form of Equality), which the mind uses as a cosmic yardstick to judge how similar or different objects are.</note>, while it correctly measures all things—whether more or less equal—by approaching that highest equality. Here, the mind places itself in the middle between any given things as a participant in equality and as equality itself. But if it is made equal most closely to the highest equality, it is not struck by the injustice of unequal qualities.

->*Seventh argument. The intellect, by receiving the forms of things, does not lose its own form, whereas bodies do. Chapter VII.*<-

**B**odies are accustomed to lose their own forms when they receive the forms of other bodies. For how will water take on the heat of fire unless it sheds its own coldness? But if, when an outside form is received, the original one remains, it becomes more imperfect; as when sweetness remains in wine, but water is poured into it, the sweetness becomes a weaker flavor. The mind, however, receives the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas" - here meaning the essential definitions or "blueprints" of things.</note> of all things while it recognizes them all and revolves those known things within itself; yet by receiving them, it does not lose or weaken its own form. Indeed, since the character of any form is always designated by its operation, and the operation of the intellect is intelligence, it follows... <note>original: "sequitur" - the text cuts off here at the catchword for the next page.</note>

He also notes that unlike physical matter, the mind is not changed or weakened when it "takes in" new information or forms.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII. #

...so that the form of the intellect is—if I may put it this way—<term>natural intellectuality</term> <note>original: "intellectualitas naturalis". This refers to the mind's inherent power to think, which exists even before it begins to process specific information.</note> itself, which is judged to be most perfect when its operation is the most perfect intelligence. This intelligence is more perfect the more forms of things it reaches, for it becomes loftier, faster, and clearer. Therefore, the intellect, by receiving the forms of all bodies, not only does not lose or diminish its own form, but—contrary to the nature of a physical body—perfects it to the highest degree. It penetrates the substances of these things and sees all things within each individual; while in simple things it sees mixtures through composition, in mixed things it gazes upon simple elements through <term>resolution</term> <note>The process of breaking a complex object down into its basic parts to understand its essence.</note>. Therefore, the mind seems to be present in all things in such a way that it is itself all things within each individual. Furthermore, it exists outside and above all corporeal things. Otherwise, it would be unable to separate these from incorporeal things or distinguish one from the other. If it exists in all corporeal things, is all things, and is even outside all things, it rules over all by its very nature. For this reason, it cannot be cast down from its state by the violence of any physical body.

### *Eighth reason. The form in the mind is universal: Such a thing cannot exist in the body. Chapter VIII.* ###

**T**he body, and form extended through a body, are so material (so to speak) and so bound to a particular place and time that they possess no universal power. For the more something approaches corporeal matter, the narrower it becomes; the further it recedes, the wider it grows. Therefore, if the intellect were a body, or a form spread through a body, then all the forms it received—even if they were universal in themselves—would at least become entirely particular and material within it. This is because forms in a subject restricted by the <term>passions</term> <note>original: "passionibus". In Renaissance philosophy, "passions" refer to the physical limitations or external influences that affect matter, such as being stuck in one place or time.</note> of matter retain no power to represent anything universal. 

Thus, whatever the intellect thought, it would think through a material form bound by singular conditions. Since the true operation of any thing follows the form of the thing doing the work, an intellect operating through such a material form—that is, thinking—would operate only in a singular way. And as the operation is, so the work always is. Therefore, an intellect thinking only of singulars would only ever know singular things, and would never recognize anything common or universal. It would revolve around one man in its thoughts—say, Socrates or Plato—but would not recognize the human nature that is equally common to both. It would never establish a universal rule in morality or the arts, nor would it ever create a law that applies to many human actions. 

If the mind, even without choosing to or through daily habit, produces universal forms within itself, it follows that the mind is itself their natural source and natural receptacle. Forms of this kind are not at all bound to specific matter; therefore, the mind is neither tied to matter nor will it ever be destroyed. For destruction arises from the traps and instabilities of matter.

### *Ninth reason. Minds embrace one another; bodies not at all. Chapter IX.* ###

**T**wo physical bodies cannot contain each other in mutual embraces. For that which contains another by its physical size is larger than the thing it contains. One body cannot be both larger and narrower than another single body at the same time. For example, the sphere of Saturn surrounds and contains the sphere of Jupiter, but the reverse is not true. However, one mind contains another, and is equally contained by that same mind. My mind considers yours, and yours considers mine. Thus, our minds, by considering each other, take hold of each other in turn; by taking hold, they understand; by understanding, they embrace. 

And—what is even greater—one mind embraces all minds when it considers the nature of all minds together. Therefore, if any mind gazes upon any other mind—which it can certainly do if it pays attention—then every mind is enclosed within every other mind. This is impossible for bodies. 

If every species of thing is immortal, it follows that a singular substance that equals itself to its own species is immortal. Moreover, any mind looks into any other (if the opportunity arises) and sees in individuals the species of all things, where it equals itself to its species through the <term>reflected act</term> <note>original: "actum reflexum". This is the mind’s ability to turn its attention back upon its own thinking process.</note>, which is knowledge. Therefore, also through the direct act, which is life, it previously equaled itself to that same species. If this is so, it follows that either every mind has always existed or will exist, just like the species of minds itself, or at least it will exist forever in the same way.

->N 2<-
->Decima<-

### Tenth Argument: The Mind Operates Through All Bodies, and Above Bodies. Chapter X. ###

Since the form <note>In Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy, "form" refers to the essential nature or blueprint of a thing that determines its characteristics and actions.</note> of a thing is the principle of its operation, every thing acts according to its <term>genus</term> <note>original: "genus". A broad category or class, such as "animal" or "body."</note>. From this, all things generate offspring similar to themselves in <term>species</term> <note>original: "species". A specific type within a genus, such as "dog" or "human."</note>, as far as they are able, but nothing acts beyond its own genus. Indeed, even these lower things do not operate beyond their species (for a dog never generates a sheep), and much less do they operate at a level above their own species. For how could a dog procreate a human? Thus it happens that a body cannot extend its power of acting beyond its own genus, and much less above its own nature. Therefore, it will never reach, attain, or produce either any other body or incorporeal things.

If the intellect were a body, it would be some certain body of a specific species. From this, two absurdities would follow. First, it would neither receive nor conceive the forms of many other bodies. It would not receive the forms of bodies similar to itself, since it would already possess them. For how could fire receive the form of another fire? <note>Ficino uses the logic that if the mind were made of fire, it couldn't "perceive" fire because it wouldn't have the necessary distinction between the perceiver and the perceived.</note> Furthermore, it would by no means conceive or give birth to the forms of dissimilar bodies, for every nature gives birth to something like itself. However, in order to understand, it must first receive the form of the thing to be understood, then from that form conceive the definition or the rational principle of the thing; only then is the act of <term>intellection</term> <note>The process of the mind grasping a truth or essence.</note> perfected. Therefore, the intellect would know very few bodies if it were a body itself, since it could not receive the form of a similar body, nor conceive the form of a dissimilar body—and it cannot understand unless it both receives and conceives. 

Even if it were somehow possible for it to receive or conceive some corporeal form, it would surely do so only according to its own nature. If it received a form from elsewhere, it would drag it into its own nature. If it conceived from itself, it would give birth according to its own nature. Therefore, through any form received or even conceived by it, it would always grasp only a certain specific species of body fitting and suitable to itself, and it would not consider the vast diversity of corporeal categories. Yet, we see now that the mind not only notices whatever bodies exist, but also fashions infinitely more and varied ones as it pleases.

The second absurdity that would follow if the intellect were a body is that it would not transcend the order of bodies, since bodies almost never operate beyond their species, and certainly never above their genus. Therefore, the mind would never know incorporeal things. Which of these do you think is more excellent: substance or action? Substance, certainly, which is the cause of the action itself. We must therefore be careful not to admit that an operation is at any time loftier than its substance. But the mind’s operation would be loftier than its substance if its substance were merely a certain body, yet its intelligence encompassed both all bodies and incorporeal things. For this reason, it is not a body, since it apprehends even incorporeal things beyond any bodies. 

Furthermore, it is not even a form "mixed" with a body <note>A "mixed form" refers to a soul or life-force that is so tied to matter that it cannot exist or function without it, like the "soul" of a plant.</note>. For just as a mixed form becomes divisible through the division of the body, so it becomes whatever it is through the quality of the body. Therefore, the mind would contract a certain quality for itself from the body; through this quality, the mind would be limited to a certain species of corporeal things and would know only that certain species, just as sight is limited to colors through the eye. And it would not receive forms most similar to itself, as we have said, nor those most dissimilar. 

This is the opinion of Aristotle, approved by the Platonists. But the Platonists add that if the mind were mixed, it would not grasp incorporeal things, because that which is mixed does not comprehend pure things; nor would it strive to reach anything separated from the body, for otherwise it would strive to be separated and dissolved from the body. Nor would it know in any way other than how it is moved, as is the habit of material power. But now, it does not act as it is moved, but as it creates species for itself; thus it abstracts, reasons, and reflects upon itself as if without end. 

Let no <term>Epicurean</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus, who argued that the soul was material and died with the body.</note> noise this in our ears, denying that the intellect grasps incorporeal things. Truly, it both always desires them and grasps them alone with the greatest pleasure, as things most like itself. Not only does it desire and grasp them, but it even procreates them. For what else are we striving for now in these disputes, if not to fashion something with the "hands of our mind" (so to speak) that is most foreign to the body? We have already fashioned it and are fashioning it, and we touch it with the very hands of the mind; and before we fashioned it, we looked forward to its fashioning. Indeed, as soon as we resolved to show that the soul is incorporeal, we already saw some level of incorporeal nature, to which we might lead...

<meta>catchword: ...the soul</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind cannot be physical because physical things are limited to their own kind, whereas the mind can conceive of all types of bodies and even non-physical (incorporeal) realities. He refutes the Epicurean view by pointing out that the very act of philosophizing about the soul proves the mind's ability to create and "touch" non-material ideas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Tenth Argument" from Book VIII, Chapter 10 of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology. The previous page established that the mind must be incorporeal because it can conceive of all types of bodies without being restricted to the nature of any single one.</meta>

...we were seeking the soul. What do we do daily in disputing? Whenever we assert that a thing exists which indeed exists, but has no length, width, depth, or any quality or figure, we certainly create in the mind a certain spirit above the body and the passions of the body. There indeed our mind is, where it gives birth; it gives birth, I say, to an offspring like itself, in no way more sublime than its own substance. Therefore, our mind towers above bodies and the conditions of bodies. For which reason it is neither closed in by place, nor circumscribed by the limits of time. It can therefore be everywhere and always. For that reason, nothing prevents it from being eternal.

### Eleventh ratio: The mind profits by rest, the body by motion. Chapter XI. ###

**N**ever does a body receive a new form except through motion. For through "alteration" (as the natural philosophers <note>original: "physici". In the Renaissance, this referred to those who studied "physics" or the natural world.</note> say) form is induced into matter. The mind, however, neither receives forms through motion, nor is it moved in the act of receiving. The more it achieves rest from all the motion of disturbances and affairs, the more it profits in contemplation <note>original: "speculando". This refers to the intellectual act of looking at or reflecting on truths.</note>. In this also its eternity appears, because by its own nature it desires only the contemplation of truth, and therefore rest, without which contemplation is not perfected. But the body profits by motion, because it was born through motion. That which therefore profits by standing still <note>original: "stando". Used here to mean stability or lack of physical change.</note> depends on a state of rest; therefore it has a stable and perpetual substance.

### Twelfth ratio: Things that are contrary in matter are not contrary in the mind. Chapter XII. ###

**T**he forms of contrary elements, while they are in matter, are contrary among themselves, because they repel and destroy each other. In the mind they are not contrary, because there they not only do not repel each other, but they even help one another. Indeed, our mind holds the forms of contrary elements at the same time when it considers the elements together. It also simultaneously grasps good and evil, useful and useless, beautiful and deformed, light and darkness, voice and silence, sweet and bitter, and the rest; and from the knowledge of one contrary, it judges the other more purely. Therefore it is not corporeal, nor even properly corruptible. For that which is corrupted is most often corrupted by its contrary. What, however, can be contrary to the mind, which has such power over contraries that it takes away contrariety from them and reconciles enemies with its own peace? Nor again is it corruptible because it might be separated from its preservers. For if it reconciles foreign and contrary things to foreign and contrary things, much more does it move itself toward both its causes and its preservers.

### Thirteenth ratio: The mind is not changed by receiving forms. Chapter XIII. ###

**W**hen the form of any body is truly received by another body, it renders that which receives it entirely like the body by which the form is granted; just as when the flame of fire is received by wood, it makes the wood hot and fiery. But that flame shining in a far-distant mirror does not make the mirror hot or fiery, because it is not truly received by it, since because of the distance it is not prepared for the true flame of fire. Indeed, in no way is that little flame—that is, that image of the flame—fixed in the body of the mirror, since it is spiritual; rather, it is in the spiritual light of the Sun, which surrounds the surface of the mirror. Images of things of this kind are produced not by these bodies whose images they are (for a body does not procreate something incorporeal), but by the spiritual light poured around the bodies. The light itself is also not born from the mass <note>original: "glebo". Literally a clod of earth, here referring to the physical bulk of the sun.</note> of the Sun, but from the soul of the Sun, whose light, while it is invisible within itself, becomes visible when poured out further, in which light the soul itself also becomes conspicuous. For as it pleases the Orphics <note>Followers of the mystical teachings attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus.</note> and Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who emphasized the role of fire and change.</note>, light is nothing other than the visible soul—whence all things come back to life through this—while the soul is invisible light. But let us not wander further; the forms or images of bodies are not in mirrors. The mind, however, receives the forms of all bodies when it judges concerning bodies. Does it receive them truly? Truly indeed. For as it receives, so it judges; it judges truly, therefore it receives truly; it receives from itself.

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by showing that the mind operates through rest rather than physical motion and can harmonize opposing concepts that would normally destroy each other in the physical world. He further explores the nature of light as a "visible soul," illustrating how the mind receives spiritual forms without undergoing physical change.</summary>

(as the Platonists believe) when the mind is stirred by the images <note>original: "simulachris." These are the sensory reflections or "shadows" of higher realities that prompt the mind to remember its innate knowledge.</note> of bodies, it brings into the light the forms which lie hidden in the depths of the mind. It follows that where a form is more perfect, it is also truer; and we have declared elsewhere—and will declare again—how much more perfect the form of bodies is in the mind than it is in the bodies themselves. From this it is clear that the "human nature" in Plato or Socrates belongs to Plato alone or Socrates alone. However, that human nature which is conceived by the mind—when it considers the conditions of humanity under a single definition of "man"—has power over every individual man, since it indeed embraces them all. Furthermore, if the truth of any thing consists in its pure integrity (or integral purity), and yet a form does not retain its full power in matter because of the mixing of passion <note>original: "passionis." In this context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or "suffering" the limitations of physical matter.</note> and is surrounded by external accidents, then every thing is found more truly in the mind. There, the Idea of the thing (a naturally implanted concept) gives birth to a notion of the thing, necessarily including everything essential and utterly excluding everything superfluous. The mind, therefore, captures the forms of bodies so truly that it possesses them even more truly than the matter of the bodies does. 

Therefore, if the mind were something corporeal, it would be rendered exactly like the bodies it perceives. It would become water when it understood water, and fire when it understood fire. And because it understands heat and cold at the same time, it would become contrary things simultaneously. In reality, however, it receives the forms of all things without being cast down from its own state; rather, it is perfected by receiving them. From this it appears that the intellect is not corporeal. It also appears not to be mortal. For the intellect receives whatever it receives in accordance with its own manner of being. Its being is purely intellectual. Therefore, it does not receive anything except by understanding. Through this kind of reception, it does not fail, but rather profits. Thus, it receives nothing from elsewhere that might change or destroy it; and what is more, it gains so much in receiving all forms that it even seems to gain from "evils." If the mind becomes more perfect the more things it knows, it is certainly more perfect if it discerns the privations, defects, and evils of things than if it were ignorant of them. Therefore, things which are in themselves evil and harmful become good and healthy in the mind. That nature is far from being destroyed by evil and harmful things when it converts those very evils into goods, such that all things are "good" for it.

### Fourteenth reason. The operation of the body tends toward composite things, that of the mind toward simple things. Chapter XIV. ###

**T**he operation of every thing always follows the being of that thing, so that the operation belongs to the same thing as the being. The mode of operating is the same as the mode of being, and the work produced by the operation is similar to the operator. In things composed of matter and corporeal form, "being" does not belong specifically to the matter or to the form, but to the whole "composite" <note>term: "composite" <gloss>A philosophical term for any physical object made of two parts: matter (stuff) and form (the blueprint or essence).</gloss></note> created from the joining of both. Therefore, the operation belongs properly to the composite itself; for this reason, it operates in a composite way and produces a composite work. We observe this in elements, plants, and animals, which generate composite works just as they themselves are composite. If the intellect were some body composed of matter and form, since its operation is "intelligence," this intelligence would always be limited to something composite; thus, it would never understand anything except composite things. 

But in fact, our mind so far excels natural composition that it resolves composite bodies into matter and form, and contemplates each one separately. Yet each of these, in itself, is "simple" <note>term: "simple" <gloss>In Platonic thought, "simple" means something that is not made of parts and therefore cannot be broken down or destroyed.</gloss></note>. In this especially its excellence is seen: that it comprehends as "true" those things which are in a certain way "false" in matter—such as geometric figures and the principles of those figures. Those things which are impure in matter, the mind discerns as pure. For the mind judges according to their own proper ratios those qualities which, in matter, are mixed together and overlapping with their opposites. Things which are many in themselves, the mind views as one—as when it sees infinite individual men under the single "species" of Man. Things which are moving in themselves, it contemplates as stable—as when it gathers together the parts of time (which flow away in themselves) and connects the past and future to the present. Things which are distant in themselves, it very often gazes upon as united—as when it sees the whole world in a single point. Neither the intervals of time nor the spaces of place restrain the mind's intuition. It treats things which are (so to speak) dead as if they were living. For stones, which lack life, the mind possesses as "living" within itself when it compares them to the "First Life" from which they were made. It treats corruptible things as if they were perpetual—as when the mind, by its own intuition, exempts from time and place those individual bodies which are normally subject to them. From all these things, it is gathered that the intellect is not something corporeal, since it operates in a far different way than bodies do, nor...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind's ability to understand universal concepts and "simple" essences proves it is not a physical body. Because the mind can unite distant objects, bridge past and future, and see the eternal within the corruptible, it must possess a non-material and immortal nature.</summary>

He concludes that the mind's purity allows it to free itself from the "passions" or limitations that affect physical bodies.</meta>

...to be impure, infected, dispersed, changeable, and corruptible, since the mind, by its own power, frees even those things which are like that from such suffering <note>original: "passionibus." In this philosophical context, "passions" refer to the state of being acted upon or modified by external physical forces.</note>.

### The Fifteenth Reason. The action of the mind ends in the action itself; the action of the body ends in a body. Chapter 15.

**N**o action of a body properly ends in the action itself, but instead passes into some external matter. For if it ended in the action, that action would remain within the thing doing the work, where it would work upon itself—for example, fire would heat itself. But this cannot be done by a body; because if a body does not act of its own accord <term>ex se: by its own power or from within itself</term>, it likewise does not act upon itself. Furthermore, if whatever a body does, it does by moving, then certainly since bodies cannot move themselves, they cannot act upon themselves. 

However, we see that the operation of the mind—namely, the understanding itself—ends in itself. It does not do anything externally through itself, unless perhaps it occasionally moves the will, which, having moved the arms, produces some work outside that had been thought out. We say, however, that sense <note>sensory perception</note> flows out of itself in a way. Because it is moved from elsewhere, it looks toward things that are foreign to it, and operates for the sake of an external goal; nor is it conscious of itself. The mind, on the contrary, moves freely; it inspects itself and its own contents, and operates for its own sake. 

Therefore, according to Plato, "essence" is called a "standing" <note>original: "status." A state of stability or being.</note>, because if it were without life, it would be sluggish. "Life" is called "motion" because it now goes out into action. "Mind" is called "reflection" <term>reflexio: a bending back or self-consciousness</term>, because without this, life would flow out into some external work. But the mind stops the vital motion of essence within itself and reflects it back into the essence through a certain self-awareness. It also draws all other things toward itself, considering things more as they exist as ideas within the mind than as they exist as things outside. 

It is also called "infinite reflection" because the human mind is not only limited to its operation once, but countless times, as when it notices that it understands something, and recognizes that it notices it; and when it wants to want something, and wants that it should want to want it, and so on in the same way, where either one operation is limited by another into infinity, or the same operation is folded back upon itself countless times. From this it is clear that the intellect is not only incorporeal <note>not made of physical matter</note>, but also immortal. For if it always forms and perfects itself through its own operation—by always understanding and willing—this is nothing other than to continually make, or preserve, or renew itself. This is what the Apostle Paul called by the name of "daily renewal" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:16: "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day."</note>. 

From this it follows that the mind never falls away or is absent from its own perfecter or preserver, since it can never be absent from itself; and therefore it is always being formed and perfected. Furthermore, if the goal of natural reproduction is a kind of immortality <note>The survival of the species through children.</note>, then much more so is immortality the goal of intellectual "birth." But because nature produces offspring outside of itself, immortality is fulfilled in the succession of those being born. Since the mind, however, generates within itself both itself and other things—insofar as it conceives the reasons <note>original: "rationes." In Platonic thought, these are the rational principles or "Logoi" of things.</note> of both itself and all others, whether it understands itself or other things—it follows that the power of this immortality is preserved within the mind, which is the mother. 

Here also lies an argument of this sort: it is more excellent "to be well" <note>to live a good, virtuous, or perfected life</note> than "to be" simply. Therefore, whoever provides "being well" for themselves is much more able to provide "being" for themselves. The intellect seems to give "being well" to itself when it forms and perfects itself both through contemplation and through morals. For this reason, it can also provide "being" for itself according to its form in such a way that it never ceases to be. 

I will set aside what Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a prominent Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino.</note> says: that the soul, since it is the principle of generation <note>the starting point of life and creation</note>, generates and brings itself to life in such a way that it has its essence from itself. In short, concerning every indivisible substance existing in its own essence, he affirms that it both produces and contains itself. However, concerning every divisible substance—even the heavens themselves—he says it must necessarily be produced and contained from elsewhere. But he may see to that himself. 

There also lies another argument of this kind: when the intellect first grasps and loves its own operation, and then its own power and substance, then it undoubtedly acts upon itself. Therefore, it also acts by itself <term>per se: through itself</term>. For nothing is placed as a medium between the intellect and itself. Add to this that just as a body does not work on itself because it does not act from itself, so the intellect is judged to work from itself because it works in itself. If it acts from itself into itself, then it also acts through itself. For if both ends of the action are within it, then the middle is too. What, therefore, prevents the intellect, when separated from the body, from working and living—especially since its operation, which is completed from itself into itself through itself, necessarily happens and resides within itself? But this will be explained more clearly thus: if the operation of the mind properly ends in the mind itself, the mind itself is in a way the end of its own operation...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind is immortal because its actions are self-contained and self-reflective, unlike physical bodies which only act on external things. By constantly thinking and willing, the mind essentially preserves and "renews" its own existence, making it independent of the body.</summary>
