<meta>This page continues the "Fifteenth Reason" from the previous page, where Ficino argues that the mind's operations end within itself, unlike physical actions. He is establishing that the mind is a self-sustaining, "self-moving" entity, which is a core Platonic argument for the immortality of the soul.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...is the end. Indeed, the end and the beginning of any thing are the same, since all things seek their own origin and set it before themselves as the goal <note>original: "finem"</note> of their motion. Therefore, the substance of the mind is the principle <term>principium: the starting point or source</term> of its own operation; thus it operates through itself, which our Plato calls "being moved by oneself" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where he defines the soul as that which moves itself.</note>. As it operates, so it lives—for life is an internal operation—and thus it lives through itself. As it lives, so it also exists, for life is the first act of existence. It exists, therefore, similarly through itself. What prevents it from existing forever, seeing as it is the cause of itself? I say cause not in the "efficient" sense <note>the external force that makes something happen</note>, but in the "formal" sense, by whose power existence is granted and preserved. 

Quality and life, whose entire operation flows out into other things, necessarily fail according to their nature in four ways. **First**, because by flowing out, it wavers and requires external support. **Second**, by spreading thin, it is weakened. **Third**, while it flows into other things, it is defiled by foreign elements. **Fourth**, because of this need, weakness, and defilement, it is eventually forced to fall away from its own nature. 

If this is so, it follows that the rational life which flows back into itself sustains itself, is not weakened, is not defiled, and does not fall away. Justly, as the life which is forced to flow entirely outside of itself—when it departs from life—tends toward and is consumed in death; so the life which overflows back into itself grows and is perfected into life. Finally, if a more abundant motion is the sign of a more abundant life, the rational life—which exercises, fills, and defines every kind of motion—also fills every kind of living. Therefore, neither the deprivation of life nor any condition subject to death is mixed into it. We have declared elsewhere that the mind itself exercises all species of motion in the body, fulfills the patterns of all motions within itself, and terminates all motion in itself and its own beginning through its own reflections.

---

### Sixteenth Reason. The corporal form does not have infinite power;
->the mind does. Chapter XVI.<-

**I**t is established among Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicos," referring to those who study the physical world</note> that corporal form, especially that of the elements, is so limited that it can in no way possess any infinite or untiring power. The mind, however, wanders without limit and is never fatigued. First, it is as if it were without limit within itself, for it understands itself. Therefore, its perfect act of understanding is revolved from the very substance of the mind back into the same. This revolution is an infinite motion. For it does not set out toward any external limit to be acquired, which once obtained would bring it to rest, but rather it circles its own substance, greedy for itself. Indeed, this greed for itself is never extinguished. Therefore, the substance which, through desire for itself, has once begun to meet itself from all sides and to behold itself from every angle by circling itself, will—with that same desire perpetually urging it—perpetually embrace itself in the same way by its own will. 

Therefore, the motion of the intellect, because it is circular and wound around itself, is surely everlasting insofar as it is intellectual. It also lacks an end, as we have said, for the reason that understanding is folded back upon itself infinitely. For someone who understands either themselves or anything else can understand their own understanding, just as they understand the thing itself; and likewise another understanding, and another, without end, as long as they know the thing and notice that they know it. Again, the fact that they notice this is not hidden from them, and so on without limit. 

Such a course of understanding is accompanied by that rational appetite which they call the **will**. This will certainly wills itself, or anything else, and wills that it wills, and again wills that it should will, and so on thereafter. Furthermore, the mind divides bodies into many parts, and the parts into particles; it increases numbers above numbers without end. It discovers the modes of shapes and their mutual proportions, and even the innumerable comparisons of numbers; it extends a line above the heavens beyond every limit. It produces time into the past without a beginning and into the future without an end. Nor does it only think of another time more ancient and more extensive than all time, but it also always thinks of another place larger than all space. It also fashions innumerable degrees in individual qualities. 

Added to this is the fact that the mind is not content with one specific kind of thing, as the senses are. It is not content with colors alone, like sight, nor sounds alone, like hearing, but it runs through all things—through all things, I say, not only those which are, but those which have been or will be. Nor that alone, but also through those things which neither are, nor have been, nor ever will be. For it devises many things that could perhaps exist but will never happen, and it fashions many things that perhaps can never exist. Yet these things which the mind paints by itself within itself seem to exist no less in the nature of things than what it paints through the tongue in the air, or through the hand upon a wall. Also new...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind is immortal because it is self-moved and self-sustaining, unlike physical bodies which decay when they act upon external matter. He highlights the mind's infinite capacity to reflect upon itself, its ability to conceive of infinite time and space, and its power to imagine things that do not exist.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK VIII.

...and always constructs the appearances of things by its own power and a certain order, and again renews others. Does the mind not also, after it has ascended step by step through the spheres of the world <note>The "spheres of the world" refers to the traditional Ptolemaic model of nested celestial orbits (Moon, Sun, planets) through which the soul was thought to travel.</note>, consider the angels in such a way that it always sees one higher than another? Nor does it ever find one so sublime that it cannot find another at least one degree greater, and again another at yet another degree. 

And it does this for as long as it declares each angel to be finite; for from any finite spirit, it finds another that is higher. And thus it would progress without end, unless it imposed a limit upon itself and concluded that there is some infinite spirit which surpasses every angel that exists—or can even be thought of—by innumerable degrees.

Who is it that progresses infinitely? Who, in a sense, terminates this infinite progress? Who attains that infinite limit of progression? Surely the mind does these things. Therefore, the power of the mind is in a sense infinite. This is evident in the fact that it finds not only the infinite <term>act: the state of being fully realized or active (God)</term>, which is God, but also infinite <term>potentiality: the capacity to become or receive forms (prime matter)</term>, which is the matter subject to God, suited to receive innumerable forms from Him. Hence also we find an infinite cycle of generation, which can be poured from the infinite act into infinite potentiality through infinite time.

This appears again from the fact that the mind grasps the universal reasons <note>original: "rationes," referring to the underlying logical structures or "blueprints" of things.</note> of things. Under any universal—whether a species or a genus—innumerable things are contained. It gathers innumerable men under the human species in perpetual succession; likewise, it gathers infinite individuals under other species into a single species, many species into one genus, many genera into one essence, and one essence into the divine unity, truth, and goodness. 

Conversely, from this unity, it descends step by step into an infinite multitude. Truly a wondrous power, which makes infinite things one, and makes one thing infinite! To this power, there is almost no specific degree in nature, insofar as it penetrates all things upward and downward. It has no specific location, insofar as it is stopped nowhere. It has no fixed and limited power, insofar as it works equally toward all things. 

It also seems to me to demonstrate the indeterminate <note>original: "interminatam," meaning "unbounded" or "without end."</note> force of the mind above all others, that it finds infinity itself to exist, and defines what and of what sort it is. Since knowledge is perfected through a certain equating of the mind with the things known, the mind is in a way made equal to the known infinity. But that which is equal to infinity must itself be infinite. 

Just as time, which measures motion by a certain succession, must be infinite if motion is infinite, how much more must the mind be infinite, which measures not only motion and time with a stable notion, but infinity itself? Since it is necessary for a measure to have a proportion to what it measures, and there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite.

The same is clearly shown by the fact that the mind passes from considering non-being into being, and vice versa. Now, being and non-being are separated by an immense interval. There must be an immense power to traverse an immense space. And who denies that the mind runs there? For we comprehend by the most certain reasons the creation that happens from non-being to being, and the destruction <note>original: "interitum," referring to the corruption or passing away of physical things.</note> that happens the opposite way. We describe the nature of both extremes, and we grasp with the intellect the force of common being itself, which communicates itself through innumerable modes of existing to the things born from its progression.

Finally, to sum up: the fact that the hunger of the body, thirst, and sleep are quickly satisfied with a little, while the fire of the mind is never extinguished—whether it looks toward human or divine things—serves as testimony that there is an infinite power in the mind. If it craves human things, what pile of riches, what greatness of empire can limit it? If it craves divine things, it is filled by no knowledge of created and finite things. It deservedly never rests unless it grasps the infinite God, who fills its infinite capacity flowing from Himself. 

If the mind were finite, it would either be filled by some finite thing, or at least its thirst would be eased by one. In reality, however, by the attainment of any finite things, its thirst is not only not extinguished, but burns more fiercely. This is because the more it grasps, the closer it approaches the infinite God through a kind of preparation; it burns more as it is made closer to its own fire, and runs more greedily as it nears the infinite end of its motion. The element of fire does the same when it withdraws into its own sphere. 

A stone does the same thing even more clearly when it descends from on high; the closer it gets to the earth, the more violently it is carried toward the earth. Who would say the mind is an elemental body, or anything corporeal, if it possesses infinite power? A power, I say, of persevering and grasping, as well as surrounding and traversing—whether it has this power of itself, or (to speak more truly)...

He concludes that the mind's restless search for the infinite proves its non-material nature and its orientation toward God.</summary>

...by a certain divine amplification. That is to say, insofar as the absolute infinity of God implants an intellectual and vital infinity into the minds and souls that hang most closely from Him, He preserves it continually and, in an infinite principle, recalls that infinity back to its end. For if a similar communicated quality is everywhere accustomed to flow from an absolute quality, what wonder is it that such an infinite quality—or rather, such an infinite thing—should flow from absolute infinity? This occurs foremost in minds and souls, through which the Platonists believe that an infinite succession of time and generation also proceeds in the world. Who, therefore, will be so mad as to wish that the mind should have some limit in its duration, when it has no limit in its power—at least when so amplified—nor in its operation? It is as if it could have a limit outside itself which it does not have within itself. If life precedes intelligence in its origin, and intelligence exceeds life in value, and the human soul is endowed with such dignity that an in some sense infinite power of understanding and willing has been granted to it, then an infinite power of living ought to have been granted to the same soul much earlier and much more significantly.

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY, on the immortality of souls,
->by the same author, Ficino,<-
## BOOK IX.

->*It is proven through the rational power that the soul is not only an indivisible form, but also does not depend on the body, so that immortality may be more clearly demonstrated.*<-
->*The first reason: because the mind reflects upon itself.*<-
### Chapter I.

Hitherto we have proven through the rational power that the soul is an indivisible and immortal form. Next, it must be proven that it does not depend on the body, from which its immortality is properly concluded. Divisible things <note>Ficino is referring to material objects, which take up space and can be cut into parts.</note> do not reflect into themselves at all. But if someone should say that a certain divisible thing is revolved into itself, we shall immediately ask him: Does one part of this thing turn into another part, or a part into the whole, or the whole into a part, or rather the whole into the whole itself? If the first is given, it is not the same thing turning into itself, since the parts are diverse from one another. If the second or third is granted, the same follows: for the part is one thing, and the whole is another. Only the fourth mode seems to remain: that the whole is turned into the whole. This happens in no other way than if all the parts are turned into all the parts. Let it be so. Finally, after a conversion of this kind has been made, we shall ask whether any part remains in the thing outside of another, or differing from another, or none. If one remains, then one part will be in this position or mode, and another in that, and thus they will not yet have been converted into one another. But if none remains, certainly no part in that thing will be distant or clearly different. That which is such is entirely <term>indivisible: something that cannot be split into parts (Latin: "individuum")</term>, so that it is constituted neither from parts of quantity, nor from matter and form. Therefore, either a thing does not reflect into itself, or if it does reflect, it is indivisible. 

We have said elsewhere that the soul revolves into itself in four ways: namely, through the intellect into its own nature, when it seeks, finds, and considers itself; through the will into that same nature, when it affects and loves itself; through the intellect into the act of understanding itself, when it both understands a thing and understands that it understands; and through the will into the act of the will, when it both wills something and wills that it wills. And Plato attributes these four "wheels" to the <term>chariot of the soul: a famous metaphor from Plato's "Phaedrus" describing the soul's journey and nature</term>, and I believe this to be that fourfold fountain of perpetual nature which Pythagoras said was granted to the souls of men by Jove <note>Jove is another name for Jupiter/Zeus, often representing the supreme Divine Intellect in Ficino's philosophy.</note>. If no divisible thing returns into itself, surely this rational chariot of ours, which recurs into itself through four wheels, and that innermost fountain itself, which flows back into itself through four surges, is simple and altogether indivisible. Truly, a conversion of this kind is not from body to body, but from soul to soul, which [is clear] from many other things above, and here from...

<summary>Ficino argues that because the human mind can grasp infinity and reflect upon itself (knowing that it knows), it must be an indivisible, non-material substance. He transitions into Book IX by using the geometric logic of "reflection" to prove the soul is independent of the body.</summary>

<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.</header>

...it has been proven to be indivisible because it returns into itself. Therefore, such a return <note>original: *conuersio*, a technical Neoplatonic term for the soul's ability to turn its attention inward to its own essence</note> is free from the body, since it neither begins from the body nor returns back into it. Much more is the substance of the soul free from the body, if the "return" which is its motion is free from the body. Thus, the rational soul in no way depends on the body for its existence, just as it does not depend on it for its movement or operation. Likewise, if it reflects upon itself through its operation, it also reflects upon itself through its essence. Thus, the essence of the soul turns back into itself. From wherever the return of a thing happens, from that same place is its departure, and vice versa. Therefore, the soul, which turns into itself, comes from itself. I say "from itself" in three primary ways: First, according to its **form**, because it is not shaped by any other form; otherwise it would not return to itself, but to that other form. Secondly, according to its **foundation**, because it is not supported by another. For this form—which leans upon itself when it reaches toward itself—does not rest upon another. Thirdly, according to **simplicity**, because it does not consist of parts. For in what way can that form, which is folded entirely into its own center, be spread out across a surface of parts? That which exists from itself in this way exists always; for that which ceases to be does so either because it is abandoned by its forming cause, or because it is deserted by its foundation, or because it is dissolved into parts. But that which returns to itself is not dissolved, because it is an individual <note>Meaning "undivided" or "indivisible" here</note>; it is not abandoned by its forming cause, because it is its own form; and because it remains within itself, it is never deserted by its foundation.

---

### Second reason. The more the mind is separated from the body, the better it fares. Chapter 11. <note>Likely intended as Chapter 2 (II) in the original manuscript sequence, despite the "11" in the text.</note>

**I**f the soul drew any origin from the body, the more closely it clung to the body, the better it would fare. For any thing is preserved and perfected by its own origin. But now the opposite happens. The most excellent parts of the soul are the intellect and the will; yet when we are occupied with bodily things, the intellect either perceives nothing at all or perceives unclearly, being deceived by the senses and imagination; and the will is afflicted while it is vexed by many cares from that source. On the contrary, when the soul despises bodily things, and—with the senses lulled to sleep and the clouds of phantasms expelled—the mind contemplates something by itself, then the intellect perceives clearly and shines most brightly. This is also apparent in those who, through the quiet of sleep or any other alienation from the body, deliver prophecies. Therefore some (as <term>Plato</term> says in the <term>Crito</term> and the <term>Apology</term>) <note>Plato’s accounts of the trial and death of Socrates</note> predict future events when they are near death, as if they then see those things ordained among the higher powers, to which the mind is joined by its <term>very own</term> <note>original: *suapte*</note> nature, provided it is not hindered by the body. 

Hence <term>Socrates</term>, when dragged into court by false accusers, first predicted to the judges their future repentance, to the accusers their ruin, and to the city sedition; then, in prison, he pre-marked the day of his death, which had been shown to him by a divine power through rest. Likewise <term>Theramenes</term> <note>An Athenian statesman executed by the "Thirty Tyrants"</note>, when he had been cast into prison and was drinking the poison, prophesied the approaching death of his adversary <term>Critias</term>, which followed shortly after. A certain man of Rhodes while dying (as <term>Posidonius the Stoic</term> writes) named six of his peers and said who would die first, who second, and who thereafter. <term>Aristotle</term> also writes that his friend <term>Eudemus of Cyprus</term>, when he had come to the town of <term>Pherae in Thessaly</term>, fell gravely ill; and there appeared to him in his rest a young man of remarkable face, who said that he would soon recover, and within a few days <term>Alexander</term>, the tyrant of that town, would perish, and Eudemus himself would return home five years later. Shortly after, Eudemus recovered, the tyrant was slain, and after five years had passed, Eudemus died—and thus his soul "returned home" to its fatherland. Did not <term>Calanus the Indian</term> <note>A gymnosophist or "naked philosopher" who accompanied Alexander the Great</note>, when about to die, also announce his death to <term>King Alexander</term>? And <term>Pherecydes of Syros</term> <note>A 6th-century BCE thinker and teacher of Pythagoras</note>, while dying, prophesied to the Ephesians victory against the Magnesians. Many other things of this same kind are read.

Not only does the intellect see many things clearly while we live apart from the contagion of the body, but the will is also filled; it is not afflicted by any disturbances, but rejoices exceedingly in divine things as if they were most similar to itself. From this it follows that the body is not the origin of the mind, if the further the mind departs from it, the more perfectly it fares. It also follows that if the more the mind is immersed in this body, the more it fails, and the further it departs, the more it profits, then the mind will be most perfect when it has flown away entirely from this body. But destruction does not come from that which brings the highest perfection; rather, it is the beginning of a complete life.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is independent of the body because it can reflect upon itself and because its highest powers, intellect and will, perform best when the body is dormant or dying, as seen in historical instances of prophecy.</summary>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...to such an extent that it is perpetual. For by what change will the soul ever fail, since it does not perish by departing from the body—a change than which no greater can happen to it?

->The Third Argument: The Mind Opposes the Body.<-
->Chapter III.<-

**N**o thing can, by its own nature, oppose its own origin; otherwise, it would be driven by its own accord toward its own destruction, which necessarily follows when the origin is lost. Furthermore, whatever an effect performs, it does so by the power and help of its origin. Therefore, if it fought against its cause, in that struggle the cause would be opposing itself. The soul opposes and is adverse to our body, and indeed to all bodies. Therefore, it does not take its origin from any body. Its two principal duties are **contemplation** <term>speculari: the act of observing higher truths</term> and **deliberation** <term>consultare: the process of reasoning about actions</term>. In both, it opposes bodies. First, let us see how it opposes the body in contemplation. Daily, in many ways, external bodies—variously disposed—move the sensory instruments of our body in such a way that they deceive us for a time. <note>Ficino refers to optical illusions or sensory errors caused by physical conditions.</note> Reason <term>ratio</term> amends and corrects this deception, as we have described more fully elsewhere, where reason judges differently than either an external body suggests or our own body reports; it often judges in the opposite way. In this matter, the soul condemns the condition <term>affectionem: the impression or state</term> of both its own body and that of others.

Let us set aside for now the contemplation of other things and take up the highest contemplation of the Highest [God], so that we may know how much the mind in that act refutes the nature of the body. The imagination <term>phantasia</term> follows the external senses, and the senses follow the disposition of one’s own body and other bodies. Therefore, we attribute the judgment of the senses and the imagination to the disposition of bodies, and we say that this judgment is made according to a bodily condition. When our soul, desiring to find what God is, asks such teachers, the imagination—a teacher and craftsman far too rash—constructs a kind of statue from five materials, the most beautiful of all that the external senses have offered to it from the world. However, it does this in such a way as to make those materials even more excellent than how it received them from the world through the senses. 

The imagination, therefore, offers to us a light so bright that no other could seem more radiant. It is so vast that none could be larger, spread almost through an immense void, adorned with innumerable colors, and revolving in a circle; because of this revolution, it resounds with the sweetest melodies, which both fill and soothe the ears. It smells of the most pleasant odors. It also abounds in every flavor that can be fashioned as the sweetest of all. To the touch, it is wonderfully soft, delicate, smooth, and tempered. The imagination proclaims that *this* is God. The bodily world gives us nothing more beautiful. The bodily sense neither reaches anything better nor reports anything more excellent. The imagination—the friend of the senses—fashions nothing more sublime. 

But meanwhile reason <term>ratio</term>, looking down from the highest watchtower of the mind at the games of the imagination, proclaims: "Beware, little soul, beware the tricks of that empty sophist! You seek God? Receive a light as much brighter than the light of the Sun as the Sun's light is brighter than darkness—a light to which the Sun's light, even if it were a million times clearer, would seem like a shadow.

And also receive it as something so subtle that it escapes the edge of sight. Do not spread it through empty space, lest it consist of parts and thus require the support of parts and location. Gather the whole (if you can) into a point <note>original: *punctum* — here used as a metaphysical term for an indivisible center of unity</note> so that it may be infinitely powerful from this infinite union. Then, let it be (if you please) present everywhere, not scattered in space, but whole in every place, standing by any thing you like. Let it not be stained by the multiple variety of colors. For pure light is more splendid than colored light. Let it not revolve or sound, for I do not want that light to be moved or struck or broken. And I judge stillness <note>original: *statum*, referring to a state of permanent stability</note> to be more perfect than motion. Remove also smells, tastes, and tangible softness; let it not be composed of a coarser nature. Here shines what space does not hold. Here sounds what time does not seize. Here smells what the wind does not scatter. Here is tasted what greed does not diminish. Here stays what satiety <note>The original text reads *facietas*, likely a misspelling of *satietas* (fullness/satiety)</note> does not tear away." 

Do you desire to look upon the face of God again? Look at the whole world full of the Sun's light. Look at the light in the matter of the world, full of all the forms of all things, and moving. Subtract, I pray, the matter from the light; leave the rest, and suddenly you have the **soul**—that is, an incorporeal light, containing all forms, but changeable. Take away change from this soulful light, and you have now attained the **angelic intellect**—that is, an incorporeal light, containing all forms, and unchangeable.

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.

Remove from this that diversity through which any form is different from light, and is infused into light from elsewhere, so that the essence of light and of any form is the same, and light itself forms itself, and through its own forms, it forms all things. This light shines infinitely, because it shines by its own nature; it is neither tainted nor contracted by the mixture of anything else. It is through all things because it is in nothing; it is in nothing so that it may shine abundantly through all things. It lives of itself and provides life to all, since its shadow—such as the light of the Sun—is the only thing that gives life in bodies. It perceives all things and grants perception, if indeed its shadow awakens all senses in everyone. Finally, it loves each thing, if indeed all things are most truly its own. Therefore, what is the light of the Sun? The shadow of God. Therefore, what is God? God is the Sun of the Sun. The light of the Sun is God in the body of the world. God is the Sun above the angelic intellects. This is yours, O soul; this is your God. Your <term>phantasia: the power of the soul that produces internal images based on sensory data</term> had shown you his shadow; such is the shadow of God, that it is the most beautiful of sensible things. How great do you think the light of God is? If the shadow of God shines so much, how much does the light of God blaze? You love the light of the Sun everywhere above all others—indeed, you love it alone. Love God alone, O soul, the only light. Love the infinite light of the benevolent God infinitely. You will shine now, and you will be delighted infinitely. Why then do you turn away? Face his countenance, and you shall rejoice forever. But do not be moved, I pray, to touch it, for it is stability itself; do not be distracted through various things to grasp it, for it is unity itself. Stop your motion, gather your multiplicity, and you will immediately reach God, who has already reached deep within you for a long time. 

In this investigation—O immortal God!—how much the mind opposes all bodies, how much it destroys their images and deceptions! How much it condemns the <term>phantasia</term> and the senses, the companions of bodies! Surely, just as the mind is a substance through itself, drawing no origin from any body, so it sometimes performs its own work through itself without any bodily support—indeed (what is more marvelous) even against any machinations of the body. Certainly, in its operation, it would never sever itself from every bodily stain unless, much more so in its essence, it were most alien to every bodily root. And because it cannot oppose the universal nature of bodies through any power of the body (for a part does not rise above the whole), it follows that it acts through its own power in the present without the aid of physical things; therefore, it can do so much more in the future. 

We have already said enough about how the mind opposes the body in <term>speculando: contemplation or the observation of higher truths</term>. Let us speak next of how much it opposes in <term>consultando: deliberation or the process of reasoning about actions</term>. Often, when the stomach is hungry, or the lungs are thirsty, or the brain is heavy with sleep, or the reproductive organs are swelling with seed, the sense—the companion of the body—invites one to food, drink, sleep, and intercourse. It incites, I say, or rather it reports the body's incitements to the soul. But Reason, for the sake of contemplation or virtue, judges that one must abstain from these; and as it pleases, we frequently abstain. When an insult or injury is inflicted, the blood around the heart is inflamed for vengeance. Then the motive power of the soul—the companion and guest of the body—moves the feet and hands to take revenge; yet Reason sometimes, for the sake of peace and quiet, orders one to stop and restrains them. When dangers are presented, the heart often trembles, but Reason commands one to run into battle for the sake of protecting the fatherland; hence, even with an unwilling heart, one goes against the enemy. 

Now, the ends toward which Reason deliberates in this way are incorporeal—namely, truth and virtue. When our Plato <note>original: "Plato noster"</note>, that celestial man, chose the unhealthy site of the Academy <note>The Academy was located in a marshy area of Athens; Plato reportedly chose it so that the struggle against poor health would help discipline the mind.</note> in Attica to dwell in for the sake of taming the body, was his soul not opposing the nature of the body? When Xenocrates, the beloved disciple of Plato, and Origen, their follower, cut off their own genitals so that they might utterly extinguish the fires of lust, was the unconquered soul not declaring war on the members of the body? Before these, the Persian Magi, the Egyptian priests, and the Pythagorean philosophers abstained from wine and meat to weaken Lust <note>original: "Venerem," referring to the goddess Venus or sexual desire</note>. I pass over those ancient priests consecrated to the Great Mother <note>Cybele</note> or to Saturn. The former castrated themselves; the latter tortured themselves. I pass over the first-fruits of the Christians, than whom the world has never seen anything stronger or more marvelous. 

Therefore, let no one object to us that there were once only a few, or that there are very few today, who resist the passions of the body. On the contrary, we all resist daily: some for the sake of health, others for honor, others for peace, others for justice, for the contemplation of God, or for blessedness. And even if we never broke the impulses of the body, the struggle itself, which is continuous within us, would be enough to show that the soul opposes the body. If there were no other nature in us but the bodily one, as soon as a bodily affection drew us toward something, we would rush headlong like brute animals; we would have no hesitation or deliberation as to whether that thing toward which the body entices us ought to be done. For nothing fights against itself. Yet there is almost always a struggle within us brought against us by the body as a whole. There is therefore in

<meta>This page continues Ficino's argument regarding the soul's independence from the physical body. Having previously discussed the soul as a form of divine light, he now explains how the soul transcends the "humors" of the body and even celestial influences, using the metaphor of a mother and child to describe the relationship between the soul and the physical form.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...something in us beyond the body itself, removed from its stock. Removed, I say, both from the nature of all <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed in pre-modern medicine to determine health and temperament</term> and elements, so that it can resist all their inclinations and transcend them through thought and affection, and also from all celestial nature infused into these humors by the heavens and brought to their specific property. Thus, it can sometimes oppose celestial inclinations—which the <term>Astrologers: in Ficino's time, astrology was a serious science studying how stars influenced the physical body and "lower" soul</term> themselves concede to us—and always conceive of and cultivate a certain substance far superior to the heavens. I set aside the fact that whatever is produced by the corporeal and mobile power of the heavens is itself both corporeal and entirely mobile, and cannot exceed a corporeal and mobile nature. Therefore, the soul can live separately from both elemental nature and from the celestial nature infused into the elements. But if any of the Platonists should say that the soul is always in a "celestial vehicle" <note>original: *vehiculo caelesti*; the "astral body" or etheric shell that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul between the stars and the earth</note>, we shall respond that the soul does not depend on the vehicle, but the vehicle on the soul; and among the Platonists, the eternal soul always gives life to the eternal vehicle. But let us return to the established order.

And let us not be disturbed by the fact that the soul often obeys the body, because it does not obey by force, but by the love with which it is affected toward the body—which lives through the soul—as toward a son and its own work. A mother loves her son as her own work; a small son desires food beyond measure; the mother commands him to abstain; the boy then falls silent and rests if he has been well-bred, but if poorly, he cries out and disturbs the house. The mother takes pity on her weeping son, whom she loves too much, yet she does not agree to let him take food unless she first judges by consulting herself that he can taste something without harm to his body, or if some damage is caused, that it can be easily cured by medicine. Only then does the son receive food. The mother is not forced by the small son, but the love for her own work allures the mother to obey her son. She complies at last as she deems compliance necessary. She often judges truly, but sometimes she is deceived, because being too eager to comply, she does not examine the outcomes diligently enough. The same is the similarity of the soul to the body. 

Furthermore, if it were natural for the soul to succumb to the body, every soul would always yield to the senses. However, since it resists quite often by deliberating, if it ever consents, it does not obey by nature or violence, but by love, by which the highest power of the soul affects the middle, the middle the lowest, and the lowest affects the <term>vital complexion: the unique balance of qualities and humors that sustains life in a specific body</term>, and the vital complexion affects the body. Indeed, the Platonists think that from the substance of the rational soul, like from the Sun, an irrational life for the body is poured out like light, and that the former is affected toward the latter as toward an offspring. To receive this offspring, the body (as the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world</note> teaches) is prepared by celestial souls. But what shall we say to this: when some soul destroys its own body, whether it does so by deliberation, or indignation, or fear, or grief? How would it ever attempt this if the body were the origin of the soul, since no appetite in nature can rise up against itself? No brute animal kills itself by choice, because no stimulus can arise in their soul, which sprouts from the body, that is against the body. But man, although he is a more prudent animal, nevertheless does this often, prophesying (as I believe) that he will survive after the body, and that he is unburdening himself of the body’s heavy load rather than losing himself.

### *Fourth Reason: The soul operates freely.*
->Chapter IV.<-

**W**e shall recognize most especially that the human soul does not arise in any way from the body if we comprehend by proper reason how free the <term>choice: *arbitrium*, or free will</term> in it is. For that which is bound to a body, whose nature is determined, cannot have a free and unrestrained operation. Certainly, no action proceeds from some general consideration unless some particular estimation intervenes, because movements and actions take place concerning particulars. For example, when someone considers in general that physical exercise is useful; although he considers it so, he is not yet exercising until he first deliberates how many modes of exercise there are and which are most beneficial. But when he has chosen one particular exercise above the many, then he begins the work. If it is walking, he walks; if riding, he rides. The intellect, by its nature, is occupied with the conception of universal reasons. Therefore, so that some action may proceed from its apprehension, it is necessary for its universal conception to be led down to certain particulars. A universal notion, by its power, contains many—indeed, infinite—singular things...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul’s ability to resist physical urges and even commit suicide proves it is superior to and independent of the body. He further introduces the concept of free will, noting that the soul's ability to choose between particular actions based on universal concepts distinguishes it from physical matter.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, celestial vehicle, free will, Timaeus, humors, rational soul, suicide, universal vs. particular</keywords>

Having previously argued that the soul is independent of the body's physical "humors," he now focuses on the faculty of free will, contrasting human deliberation with the fixed instincts of animals and the mechanical nature of plants.</meta>

<page-num>207</page-num>
# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.
<meta>catchword: if any</meta>

...contains [specifics], just as the general category of exercise contains countless modes of training. Therefore, that universal notion can be derived equally toward different individual cases. Such a derivation is followed by a judgment concerning things to be done. Consequently, a different judgment can follow. Thus, the judgment of the **intellect** regarding actions to be performed is not, by its own nature, determined to one single thing. It is, therefore, **free**.

Indeed, some things lack freedom of judgment because they have no judgment at all, such as **plants**. Others, although they have judgment, have it determined by nature toward one specific thing, such as **beasts**. For a sheep, by <term>natural estimation: an innate ability in animals to perceive utility or danger without reasoning</term>, judges a wolf to be harmful to itself and flees; nor can it *not* flee, as nature impels it. By natural instinct, swallows are driven to build nests, bees to hives, and spiders to webs. For this reason, all animals of the same species always build their works in the same way; they never learn, nor do they ever vary, because the natural blueprint by which they are led is present from the beginning and remains the same. 

**Humans**, however, both learn and constantly vary their works, yet they possess one single nature from the beginning. They are not, therefore, drawn to act by nature, but they direct themselves at different times in different ways by their own **deliberation**. For why do we think it happens that trees and beasts never err in certain movements, arts, and choices, while man errs very often? Certainly not because a more perfect intellect exists in them—for they possess no intellect at all—but because they are led by the **Divine Intellect**, which never errs. Man, however, is led by his own intellect, which is said to be capable of error. Yet, if ever the human intellect rests from its own actions for a time, it too is then led by God and does not err, which is made clear by prophecies and miracles. And if man were always led by God, just as other creatures are, he would err as much less than they do as his "instrument" is more perfect. Conversely, if other creatures led themselves as man does, they would err more, insofar as they have been allotted a less perfect species. 

Since, therefore, man does not have a judgment regarding actions that is determined by nature to one thing, he is necessarily **free**. Moreover, we gather that he judges freely from the fact that he leads himself to the act of judging. That he leads himself is clear from the fact that he <term>reflects: the soul's ability to "turn back" and examine its own thoughts</term> upon his own judgment. That he reflects is clear from the fact that he knows he is judging and defines the judgment itself. 

The intellect attains this freedom by its own power. For the intellect apprehends not only "this" or "that" good thing, but the <term>common good: the universal concept of Goodness itself, rather than a specific physical pleasure</term>. Since the intellect moves the **will** through a "form" <note>original: *formam*; here meaning a mental concept or idea</note> it has grasped, and since in all things the mover and the moved must match in proportion, the **rational will** is not determined by nature except toward that common good itself. Under that common good, all individual goods are contained. Therefore, whatever is offered to the will as "good," the will can be inclined toward it, with no natural inclination toward the opposite preventing it. 

This is indeed signified by what we said above: that man chooses many things against the utility and pleasure of his physical nature. He very often prescribes for himself an order of life that is harmful to the body; he hates the body, weakens it, and kills it—something beasts never do, whose every impulse and action serves the body's utility. 

It is worthwhile to consider that certain things are called "necessary" by the **Philosophers**, some "impossible," and some "middle" or "possible." Among possible things, some happen for the most part, some more rarely, and some occur almost equally. They believe this order is most fitting for the universe. Again, they affirm that some things are "natural" and others "voluntary." They add, furthermore, that there would never be a power capable of choosing between two equal outcomes unless it resided in **voluntary agents**. For natural agents are determined rather than voluntary. Finally, they prove that the natural duties of any species cannot be in vain; and the duty of man is **deliberation**. Yet it would be in vain to deliberate between opposites if one could not choose and act upon either one as the deliberation suggests.

But the freedom of our soul will be found especially if we see more clearly how the souls of **beasts** are moved. When a brute animal is hungry, if its food is placed before its eyes, its soul judges such fodder to be suitable for itself; its appetite desires it and moves its limbs toward it. We ask: where does that movement of the limbs come from? Without doubt, it is from the appetite. Where does the movement of appetite come from? From the judgment. For from the fact that it judged the food to match its needs, it immediately desired it. Where does the judgment come from? From the "form" of the food appearing to its eyes, and from the internal need of such a body. For as often as such a body is hungry and such an apple is shown to its sight, so often does that soul judge that the apple suits it, and desires it. It is certain that the principle of that movement is not in the soul, but in the body—in the body, I say, [seeking] its fodder...

<summary>Ficino argues that humans possess free will because the intellect can contemplate the "universal good" rather than being driven by specific physical instincts. Unlike animals, who are moved automatically by bodily needs and guided by a perfect Divine Intellect, humans deliberate, learn, and can even choose actions that harm their own physical bodies.</summary>

<keywords>free will, intellect, natural instinct, deliberation, animal vs human, universal good, rational will, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

->**THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY OF MARSILIO FICINO**<-
<meta>image quality: excellent; catchword: rum (likely for "moribus" or "continuorum")</meta>

# THE PLATONIC THEOLOGY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...similarly disposed, and the body of the brute animal <note>Latin: *bruti*</note> is so affected. Therefore, that soul does not properly lead the body, nor is it properly moved by itself; rather, the nature of the food as much as the nature of its own body draws it, and by this pull, the limbs are also snatched along. We shall bring forward four signs of this matter.

First, when such food is shown and the body is so affected, the soul immediately judges and desires it; nor, after it has perceived the appearance <note>Latin: *figuram*</note> of the fodder, does it defer its judgment and desire for any time, even the shortest. It is as if that soul brings almost nothing of its own power into the process, but once the cause of judgment is presented, the effect of judging follows immediately. And not without reason: for form is the principle of acting, just as the heat of fire is the principle of heating. Now, some forms are impressed by nature, such as heat and lightness in fire; others are apprehended, such as the <term>species: a mental representation or "image" of an object used in sensory perception</term> of food through sight. The appetite and movement of fire follow its impressed form. The judgment and appetite of a beast so affected follow that apprehended form of the food. Therefore, the principle of this movement is the food and its form. And just as fire is not moved by itself—because it cannot fail to ascend when nothing stands in its way, nor can it fail to burn when something is present to be burnt—so a beast is not moved by itself, because it cannot help but be carried toward those things which are offered in this or that way.

The **second sign** is that the irrational soul never judges, desires, or pursues anything except what pertains to the use of the body. For in every one of its actions, the end is the comfort of the body. Now, the ultimate end in things is nearly the same as the principle. The principle of fire is the <term>concave of the Moon: in ancient cosmology, the sphere just below the moon where the element of fire naturally rises</term>; the concave of the Moon is the end of fiery movement, because every cause acts and moves toward its own end. Therefore, in a brute animal, the principle of actions is the nature of the body or the bodily soul. It is not a pure soul, but a corporeal one, serving the whole of nature and the <term>natural craftsman: a reference to the "anima mundi" or the biological forces of nature</term> of life, since the preservation of corporeal nature and life is the end of its acting.

The **third sign** is that a beast never **regrets** <note>Latin: *pœnitet*</note> having acted in this or that way, nor does it retract anything or amend it. This signifies that there is only one principle of acting there, since there is no conflict. Certainly, corporeal life moves it as its own proper end. Therefore, nothing else is present there besides corporeal life to move it.

The **fourth sign** is that (as we said above) there is no diversity in the works of brute animals of the same species. One spider does not weave its web differently than another. All swallows likewise make their nests in the same way, and each one every year in the same manner; just as all fire heats similarly, every stone descends similarly, and every plant sprouts similarly according to its species. For the nature of each thing is a certain single form attached to itself, and a certain power implanted from the beginning, through which—being always one and the same—one and the same work is always produced. Therefore, the souls of beasts, following natural instinct, preserve the tenor familiar to their species.

The same thing happens to us whenever reason is sluggish and we live according to the whim of the senses and the <term>phantasy: the faculty of the soul that processes sensory images</term>. But when reason is awakened and intent, we deliberate for a long time on things to be done; we condemn the whim of the phantasy, and we act differently than the nature of external bodies or our own limbs might demand. And if ever we indulge them, we regret it and try to amend it; we often tame the nature of the body and subject it. For we act not only through those images received or conceived by the encounter with bodies, but also through **universal species and reasons** of things. These are partly inherent in the soul and partly produced by its own peculiar power, where the principle of acting is our own form rather than the body's—produced by us, not received from the body—created according to the mode of the soul rather than the mode of bodies, and common to infinite modes of acting.

Therefore, we are not bound to one single way of acting, but we range freely through them all. For we have in the mind a certain **common exemplar of goods**, comparing individual things to it; we either reject them or approve them more or less. We are not ourselves drawn by the things themselves or the body, but rather we draw the things themselves to the exemplar, and the body to the mind. Therefore, even while the state of things and the body remains the same, we often choose differently—at one time one way, at another time another. And while the state becomes different, we often choose similarly; indeed, almost in the same moment, because of various conjectures proposed by reason, even while bodily things remain the same, our choices are in a way various and contrary. For by **deliberation**, it happens that we do not subject the soul to things, but things to our soul. Truly, as **Plotinus** often says and **Proclus** confirms, we have proof of this in the sciences and in morals. In the sciences, it is in this way: when we are content with the contemplation <note>Latin: *speculatione*</note> of truth alone, communicating nothing at all with the body, nor desiring to do anything outside ourselves, who does not see that our contemplation is in no way dependent on the body? Likewise in morals...

<summary>Ficino contrasts animal instinct with human reason, arguing that while animals are mechanically driven by bodily needs and external stimuli, humans possess free will through universal rational concepts and deliberation. He cites the lack of variety in animal behavior and the human capacity for regret as evidence of the soul's independence from the body.</summary>

<page-num>209</page-num>
# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.
<sig>O</sig>

...in this way: When we direct all of life’s pursuits toward our soul to adorn it with morals, who would not understand that the soul is the goal <note>Latin: *finem*</note> of our duties, and therefore the soul is the very origin of those same duties? The <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in ancient medicine to determine temperament and health</term> are not the origins of these actions, because the humors do not invite one to do anything against or above their own body. Nor are the heavens <note>Ficino refers here to the celestial bodies and astrological influence</note> the origin, which move through the humors—for the body of the heavens is far remote, and it does not move our four humors before it moves the four elements, nor will it move the soul unless the humors are agitated first. Yet the soul opposes the agitation of the humors; it despises their impulses through the focus of contemplation, restrains them through the pursuit of morals, and breaks them through the industry of the arts. 

No one was more naturally inclined toward love than **Socrates**, or toward lust and drunkenness than **Alciphron of Megara**, yet no one emerged more continent than them through study. Did not **Xenocrates**, **Demosthenes**, and **Cleanthes** <note>Famous Greek philosophers and orators known for their self-discipline</note> repel the impediments of nature through their diligence? If we resist the humors, we also resist the elements and the heavens; indeed, if we are not subject to the heavens, we are much less subject to other physical bodies. 

That the human soul is not subject to the heavens is apparent from this: first, it foresees future events through knowledge, then it either avoids them through prudence or considers them of no account through magnanimity—as if nothing pertains to the man himself (who is the soul) but rather to the **soul's prison** <note>Latin: *animi carcerem*; a classic Platonic metaphor for the physical body</note>. Furthermore, the soul uses prosperous fortune happily because of temperance, and adverse fortune excellently because of endurance, so that both contribute equally to its virtue and well-being. By what logic does one follow a fate that they precede, or necessarily undergo what they avoid through diligence? Or how could nature be a source of dread to one who often despises it? Or how could he be conquered by "good" things who directs them toward his own happiness? Or how would he be overcome by "evils" who turns evils into goods? Or is he compelled by any necessity who, while he willingly agrees with the divine will for the sake of piety, makes even those things which are necessary and seem terrifying to be voluntary and light?

We demonstrate the same point again through the **intellect** and the **will**. First, through the intellect: A celestial body has a form that is corporeal, singular, local, and temporal. The form through which every mind understands is incorporeal, universal, and absolute. Therefore, this does not take its origin from the heavens. For a form that is enclosed in a specific place <note>Latin: *alicubi clauditur*</note> does not generate an absolute form. Therefore, the heavens do not generate any form in the intellect. 

Could it be that the heavens produce "intelligence" within the soul? By no means. For intelligence follows the form of the intellect. Therefore, that which cannot provide the form will not provide the intelligence. In general, no body understands anything through its own form, for such a form is entirely singular. Much less will it generate intelligence in another. Since, therefore, the intellect has neither its own action nor the principle of its action from the heavens, it is not subject to a celestial body—especially because our soul, according to that power by which it is joined to those things said to be above the heavens, is not only not subject to the heavens but even rules over them. For insofar as the soul understands the truth, it is joined to the **angels** who rule the heavens. It understands only to the extent that it receives **intellectual light** from that source. Thus it is established that the intellect is not subject to the heavens.

In the same way, it will be established that the **will** is not subject to them. Surely those things which happen by nature are led to their end by determined means, which is why they almost always proceed in the same way. Nature is determined toward one specific thing; however, the choices <note>Latin: *electiones*</note> of a human tend toward their end by various paths, both in morals and in crafts. Furthermore, things of the same species do not differ among themselves in their natural actions. Just as every swallow (as we have said) builds its nest in the same way, so every intellect similarly understands those first principles of arts and morals which are known to everyone by nature. And every will similarly desires "the good" itself, because the will desires the good according to nature. Indeed, such is the nature of man that just as the intellect relates to the principle of contemplation (which is that which is everywhere manifestly true), so the will relates to the principle of action (which is the good itself), and we all necessarily assent to both. 

But **choice** <note>Latin: *electio*</note> is a certain action following the human species, just like the discourse of reason. These two are unique to man. Thus, if men reasoned by natural instinct, there would be one and the same opinion for all men in every single thing; likewise, if they chose by the guidance of nature, there would be one choice for all. But as it is, different people choose different things in different ways, just as they judge variously by reasoning. For this reason, the heavens do not move our will by natural instinct, though they do move the body. From the motion of the body, the sense follows or announces a feeling. From this, the will is often enticed. However, this enticement is not a necessary cause of choice, because the will sometimes assents to it and sometimes not at all. Nor does the human body perceive only from celestial bodies...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that the human soul is independent of astrological influence and bodily humors because it can consciously oppose physical impulses and perceive universal, incorporeal truths. He distinguishes between natural instinct, which is uniform, and human choice, which is varied and governed by reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the human soul is not bound by the stars. He transitions from discussing the physical humors to the logic of astrological influence, citing Ptolemy to show that celestial causes are universal and remote, whereas earthly effects depend on local, contingent conditions and the soul's own nature.</meta>

<page-num>210</page-num>

-># MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...body or the senses are moved. For even **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> himself concedes that particular effects concerning matter by no means follow the celestial bodies in an absolute way. This is because the heavens are universal and remote causes, and they only act insofar as intermediate causes allow; furthermore, the changeable disposition of matter—which is subject to contrary causes—receives that influence differently at different times and places. Indeed, we prove this daily by experience itself, especially in those who, though born at the same time, follow the nature of their species and individuality, as well as their location, nourishment, and habit. Consequently, they behave in a different manner, even though the same moment of birth should have made them behave entirely alike. 

Rightly, therefore, **Ptolemy** instructs <term>Astrologers</term> to offer a general and possible opinion rather than a distinct and necessary judgment. He adds that wisdom can either resist the stars when they threaten or favor them when they promise well. Therefore, we should not believe those who assert a "fate" by saying that every single thing proceeds from determined causes, and that once a cause is set, the effect necessarily follows. 

First of all, an effect does not necessarily come from a remote cause, even if that cause is necessary, unless the intermediate cause is also necessary. This is just like in logical arguments: from a necessary major premise and a contingent minor premise, a necessary conclusion does not usually follow. <note>Ficino uses a rule of Aristotelian logic: a conclusion follows the "weaker" part of the premises. If the circumstances on Earth are changeable (contingent), the result cannot be "necessary" or "fated," even if the stars themselves move by necessity.</note> Between celestial causes and earthly effects, the intermediate causes are the <term>elemental virtues: the inherent powers of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire)</term>, whether simple, mixed, active, or passive; these are certainly contingent and changeable, and they can very often be hindered by one another. Furthermore, even when this or that determined and sufficient cause for an effect is present, it is not necessary for the effect to follow immediately, since it can be hindered by the clash of another cause. For often there is a sufficient cause for <term>bile</term> from one side, but a sufficient cause for <term>phlegm</term> from the other, and they can hinder each other in turn.

Lastly, we cannot designate determined causes for everything. For the fact that you are white, you have a specific cause; likewise, you have another specific cause for being a <term>grammarian: in the Renaissance, this referred to a scholar of classical literature and language</term>. However, for the fact that whiteness and scholarship happen to meet in the same person, you have no specific cause. For if the meeting of these two things I mentioned proceeded from some common and determined cause, they would certainly have some fixed order between them. Regarding any effect, therefore, we shall say that it does not proceed from its cause among us by necessity, because it could be hindered by some other cause meeting it by accident.

And although someone might trace a concurrent cause back to a higher cause, no one can trace the *occurrence of the meeting itself*—which causes the hindrance—to a single cause, so as to prove that a hindrance of this kind proceeds from some celestial principle. For this reason, those things which pertain to the body do not necessarily follow the stars; much less are the actions of the soul subject to the stars. 

Nor should anyone dare to say that the minds of men are moved by celestial minds through the heavens as if through some instrument or medium. For minds are more in harmony with other minds than they are with bodies; therefore, the heaven is not placed between those [divine] minds and ours. Rather, our minds hold the middle ground between those minds and the heavens. Because of this, the heavens ought to be moved by the divine spirits through the minds of men, rather than our minds being moved by the divine through the heavens. 

Perhaps someone might say that our minds are stirred by those higher minds without any medium. Let them stir us then, if they please—or rather, let them lead us. For in this way, the minds of men will be divine if they are moved directly by the divine. For they will be close to them by nature. Otherwise, they would be moved through some other nature closer to them, as if through a medium. They will certainly be closer to the divine than the globe of heaven is, since they are moved from there without the heaven's help. 

Now, if they think the heaven will be perpetual, why should the soul of man not also be eternal, since it is closer to the divine? Furthermore, the infusion that passes into lower minds from the superior and angelic ones should be called <term>illumination</term> rather than motion. For those higher minds give in their own way, and our minds receive in their own way, and both are intellects. Therefore, that which is given and that which is received is intellectual light. This does not prevent our soul from turning toward that light in its own way, using it according to its nature, and freely reasoning and choosing through it—especially because our soul sometimes turns itself toward the worse side in its deliberations, whereas the instinct of divine minds would always pull toward the best. 

Wherefore, the human soul draws the inspiration of the gods into its own nature. In that higher realm, the inspiration descends as something stable; the soul itself makes it "mobile" (active and changeable), since the soul itself is mobile, and thereafter acts in a mobile way. Thus, nothing stands in the way of the soul’s action being free, since it is subject to no moving power strictly its own. **Plotinus**, **Proclus**, and **Avicenna** <note>Neoplatonic and Islamic philosophers who argued for the soul's agency and the role of the stars as signs rather than absolute causes</note> argue that celestial motions are not the causes of lower things, but rather instruments for the divine movers, just like...

<summary>Ficino argues against astrological determinism, asserting that while stars provide universal causes, earthly effects are contingent and human minds are free. He positions the human soul as closer to the divine than the physical heavens, receiving divine influence as "illumination" which the soul then uses freely.</summary>

<sig>O 2</sig>

...obedient to the craftsmen <note>The "craftsmen" here refers to the celestial or divine movers who direct the universe</note>, whose various thoughts are indicated to us through celestial bodies, shapes, and motions—as if by their own eyes and nods—and portend future things. They add that the conceptions of the divine are unfolded through celestial arrangements as if through letters; and just as birds are believed to show through their flight and cries to the <term>auspices and augurs</term> <note>Ancient Roman priests who interpreted the will of the gods from the behavior of birds</note> not what the birds themselves are doing, but what they signify, so the heavens signify to us daily through shapes and motions those things that happen from elsewhere. 

Indeed, **Astrologers** show this when, in judging someone’s <term>genesis</term> <note>original: "genesi"; refers to a birth chart or horoscope</note>, they bring forth many things pertaining to parents, ancestors, brothers, wives, friends, and enemies, whose fortune does not depend on the birth of another, but is merely signified by it. If, therefore, corporeal things (as we have also proved above) are subjected to the celestial instruments of the higher movers neither properly nor entirely, much less is the Mind itself subjected. If its character and skills are ever predicted by **Astrologers**, they produce them through signs rather than through causes. 

For the higher movers not only think out for themselves those things of which they are the causes, but also those things of which our minds will be the causes, and they often demonstrate these through celestial nods. Our mind and will declare most clearly that they are not subjected when the mind is carried away to such an extent that it almost wishes for itself alone. For then it frees itself in a certain way from other creatures and is almost entirely content with itself. Again, this is seen when it reflects upon itself in its own act in a circle. For a spiritual circuit does not serve an external boundary. 

Furthermore, the mind is not subjected when it wills one thing because of one conjecture and does not will another because of another, but even wills that it be able to will and not will equally. In this matter, it seems indifferent to willing and not willing alike, and bound to absolutely nothing. Likewise, it is free when it chooses the highest rest from any desire; for then it dissolves the pull of every specific object. This power, which meanwhile governs every act, serves no specific object of its own. 

But let us explain all this more clearly. As often as some good is proposed to us, the soul can reason in this way: "Because the greatest good is liberty, I wish to experience it within myself at some point. Therefore, I prefer to be my own master now by retaining the act of choosing, rather than to serve by willing this or that." Yet it chooses liberty as a good, which it often postpones at other times for the sake of other goods. We choose none of the goods necessarily, therefore, although we necessarily will "the Good" itself. 

Finally, either motion is nowhere free, or it is free where it is first. It is first in the soul. It is necessary, however, for the first thing to be free, if indeed whatever is such in the first degree is such through itself. For who would doubt that the motion of action begins by descending from that point where the motion of inquiry ends by ascending? It ends, truly, in the command of the soul itself, as when I say that I do this for the sake of that, and that for the sake of the other, and that because I want to, and I want to because it pleases me. And it pleases me, moreover, to want that which pleases. I add even further that if by chance I did not want to, I would want not to want. **Plato** often calls this <note>original: "per se moueri"</note> "to be moved by oneself," which is to say, to act through oneself and freely. From this, he wishes it to be established that he who acts freely lives free, so that he is subjected to the impulse of no particular thing, whether good or evil; and he who lives free is never destroyed, for he is not struck by violence.

->### Fifth argument. The mind operates without the body. Chapter V.<-

**T**he mode of operating follows the mode of existing. Therefore, if the soul exists in some way through the body, it never acts without the body or the help of the body. Now, however, the opposite occurs; therefore, it does not exist through the body. Let us first hear **Plato's** mind concerning the mode of knowing by which the human soul operates. Since the soul is much more excellent than the body, and that which constantly forms a thing is more excellent than the thing formed, therefore no bodies—whether they be outside of us or within—paint their forms or images in the soul. Instead, by their certain qualities, powers, or images, they strike that warm and vital vapor <note>Ficino refers to the "spiritus," a subtle substance that bridges the gap between the material body and the immaterial soul</note> which is in a certain way the knot of the body and the soul, and is called "spirit" by the **Physicians**. 

For if those bodies agree with this spirit in matter, but do not agree with the soul, it is more reasonable that the spirit be formed by them rather than the soul—which is so far from being formed by the body that it is itself, in truth, both the form of the body and its <term>formatrix</term> <note>The "formative power" or the active principle that gives shape and life to the body</note>. It is the formatrix of its own body through nature, and of other things in part. The rational soul, therefore, which is the source of corporeal motions, moves the bodies themselves, but is not moved by the bodies. It would be moved by them if it were formed by them. But the spirit, which is the chariot of the soul, is struck by various bodies. This kind of striking is not hidden...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul possesses free will and is not strictly caused by the stars, which act only as signs. He begins a new argument stating that because the soul can act independently of the body, its existence must also be independent of it.</summary>
