<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the independence of the soul from the body. Having previously argued that the mind is not subject to the stars, he now explores how the soul's higher functions—specifically the intellect—differ from sensory perception and imagination by operating without physical instruments.</meta>

<page-num>212</page-num>

-># MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...the soul. Since such an affection or agitation of the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; in Ficino's medical-philosophy, "spirit" is a subtle, vaporous substance that mediates between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note> does not escape the soul, we are said to perceive. Immediately, from this sudden act of sensing, the soul's inner power is stirred to another work very similar to it. For when it has reached colors through the spirit of the eye, sounds through the spirit of the ears, and other things through the others, by its own power—through which it presides over bodies and possesses their "seeds" <note>Ficino refers to "semina rationes," the formative principles or blueprints of physical things held within the soul</note>—it does so no less in the act of knowing than in its power of nourishing. It soon either conceives within itself entirely spiritual images [simulacra] anew, or gives birth to those previously conceived, and gathers them into one. We have called this **imagination** in the preceding sections.

We later placed **phantasy** <note>Ficino distinguishes between "imagination" (storing sensory data) and "phantasy" (processing and judging those images)</note> slightly above this, ranging through the images of bodies in a nearly similar way. Finally, we declared the **intellect** to be more eminent by a long interval. When the soul senses something, it is said among the <term>Platonists</term> to operate through the body, not because the soul and the body sense together simultaneously. For just as the soul is the source of living (as Plato says), so it is the source of sensing. Furthermore, objects are often present to the eyes or ears, yet if the mind is more intently agitating something within itself, they are not sensed until the mind returns to such things—as if these limbs do not have the power of sensing, but rather the inner nature of our mind itself possesses it. 

Yet this power of sensing does not sense unless the **corporeal spirit** is agitated by bodies. Therefore, when the soul is said to act through imagination or phantasy with the help of the body, it is because it revolves through individual images that represent individual bodies, which were conceived through the impulse made upon the corporeal spirit by those bodies. And also because there is such a great kinship between these internal images and the spirit, that a vibration of the spirit always follows an internal revolution of images; and conversely, a revolution of images for the most part accompanies the vibration of this spirit. 

When the soul contemplates and chooses something through the **intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentiam"; the highest intuitive function of the intellect</note>, it is said to operate both without the body and without the help of the body. This is because it sees and chooses something entirely foreign to them, even without that impulse of the spirit and without the images collected from it. I will pass over for now the fact that the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who generally argued that all knowledge begins with sensory experience</note> place all powers of sensing in the soul according to their origin, but in the "composite" <note>The unified being of body and soul together</note> according to their form, while they locate the power of understanding in the soul alone. In this way, they believe the former act through the body, but the latter even without the body. Nevertheless, the soul naturally turns itself toward the images of corporeal sense as long as it naturally inhabits the body.

The following signs will show us that this last operation [the intellect] sometimes occurs without corporeal aid, while those former operations [sensation and imagination] always occur through the help of the body. 

**First**, the very power of the soul that uses the body, whatever it may be, does not perceive its own instrument. For who tastes their own tongue with the sense of taste? Who has known the nature of spirits and images through imagination or phantasy? Such a nature is scarcely recognized even after long discussions of the mind; yet it would be open to everyone, and most easily, if it were known through imagination and phantasy. 

**Second sign**. Such a power using the body, as we have said, knows neither itself nor its own action. If vision properly perceived that it was seeing by the very fact that it sees, then whenever we saw something, we would notice that we were seeing—which does not happen at all. For often we see a person present with our eyes open, but because the inner power of the soul is then intent on something else, we do not notice that we see at all; it is as if an act of this kind is perceived not by vision, but by a certain interior power when it is unhindered. Furthermore, the acts of seeing and similar acts are in a certain way incorporeal, but those senses only know corporeal things. If these powers are ignorant of their own actions, they are also ignorant of themselves. For what else is a certain power but a principle of operating in a certain and proper way? Therefore, he who does not know the operation does not know the mode of operating, and does not know the proper principle of operating in such a way. Thus, the five senses are ignorant of themselves. But neither do imagination and phantasy know themselves. For since all people always use these two powers of the soul, everyone would most easily know what nature these powers have. Yet in truth, those who have sought it through a long examination of the mind have scarcely understood it.

**Third sign**, when something intense is presented to these powers that agitates them violently, it occupies them so completely that weaker things are not well perceived, neither at that same time nor for a while afterward. Our eye, sometimes overwhelmed by the opposing rays of the Sun, cannot discern other colors then, nor for some space of time afterward. The same happens to the ears from a great crash and thunder. The same also to the other senses. The same to imagination and phantasy whenever they are occupied by certain horrendous images.

He provides "signs" or proofs of this independence, such as the fact that senses cannot perceive their own physical organs or their own internal operations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s systematic proof for the immortality of the soul. Having established that the soul operates through a subtle "spirit," he now distinguishes the lower sensory powers from the higher intellect by demonstrating that the senses are dependent on physical conditions and instruments, whereas the intellect is not.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>

->## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.<-

This shows that the activity of such powers concurs with the vibration of the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the soul</note>, and vice versa. Just as the senses and movement of a spider—who remains in the middle of her web with the threads stretched out on all sides—follows the trembling of the web whenever flies fly into it, so conversely the trembling of the web follows the movement of the spider. Indeed, this demonstrates that those powers are close to matter, since they are often overcome by an object, and the remains of bodily passions remaining in the spirit for a time may throw them into confusion.

**The fourth sign** is that by a more powerful object, not only is the act of discerning confused, but injury and distress occur within us, as if the bodily spirit were wounded; thus some offense happens to these powers as well, from a certain mutual use.

**The fifth sign** is that they do not apprehend a quality or image that is familiar to themselves. The eye does not see its own whiteness or the image through which it gazes. Touch does not judge its own heat. Furthermore, if some foreign heat becomes familiar to the sense of touch itself, it does not feel it, as usually happens in those who suffer from a **hectic fever** <note>a persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</note>, whose sense of touch does not perceive the fever at all. The imagination and **phantasy** <note>the faculty that processes and judges mental images</note> are also entirely ignorant of their own power, habit, and the images they have conceived. For reason only discovers such things with difficulty.

**The sixth sign**: after the seventh or eighth **seven-year period** <note>original: "septenarium"; Ficino refers to the "climacteric" years of life, roughly ages 49 to 56</note> of age, when the **complexion** <note>the balance of humors/qualities in the body</note> of the body begins to decline gradually toward an earthy quality, and the spirits are either dissolved or overly thickened and cooled, the sight grows dim, hearing is dulled, smell is obstructed, taste becomes stiff, touch withers, and the usual speed of imagination and phantasy is slowed down.

**The seventh sign**: the longer the senses work, the more they feel weakened, and they perceive worse and more confusedly. For if you stare fixedly at something for an hour, your vision will grow misty, because since the spirits are dissolved or obscured, the qualities and images of sensible things that you perceive do not shine clearly within them.

**The eighth sign**: they reach a certain fixed class of things, not all classes; each of the five senses has its own class of qualities (as is evident), while imagination and phantasy have the specific conditions of these qualities. These and other similar things usually happen to the powers of the soul when using the body; but the opposite happens to the **intellect**. Therefore, the intellect does not use the body. Now observe how these opposites apply to the mind. Those lower powers are ignorant of themselves, but the mind knows itself. For it discovers that it exists, what species of things it belongs to, and what power it possesses. Those powers have certain instruments, yet they are ignorant of them. The intellect has no instrument; and if it had one, it would know it, since it knows both itself and other things. And that instrument would be placed between itself and other things.

But if someone should say that the mind has an instrument, we shall ask whether it is bodily or of some other nature. If he answers that it is bodily, he will be refuted by the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>refers to the followers of Aristotle, who argued that the mind must be "unmixed" with matter to know all things</note> argument. Every bodily instrument is contained within some species of bodies by some form proper to itself. If the intellect were to use such an instrument, it would not judge truly regarding bodily things. For whatever might be perceived through such an instrument, being infected by its quality, would not appear exactly as it truly was, but rather as the instrument was—just as through red eyes the air appears red, and through yellow eyes it appears yellow. For this reason, the pupil of the eye lacks all color, so that it can receive all colors in their pure state. Thus it would be necessary for the mind's instrument to lack every bodily quality, so that the mind might discern all things purely through it. Yet it would not lack every quality if it were a body, for it would then possess some quality. And the quality it possessed, it would not receive from outside. Thus the mind would not know qualities similar to that one through the instrument, just as the sense of touch—whose instrument has a certain heat—does not feel a heat exactly like its own.

But it would not even discern qualities dissimilar to its own in a pure state, because those qualities would be infected by the instrument's quality before the mind could notice them. Finally, through an instrument that was a body—which would be in some certain class of bodies, and which would be something singular, circumscribed by place and time—the mind would not know anything more excellent than bodies, nor even all of those, but only a certain class of bodily things, just as each of the five senses perceives classes of bodily things through individual instruments. Lastly, it would not comprehend anything **universal** through a particular instrument. Yet we experience that we know universals through the mind: when we find that things which seem different agree together in some nature; when we reduce individual things into one species; and when, comparing a singular and proper thing with what is common, we judge that the universal differs from the particular.

...us. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the comparison of objects.</note> However, we cannot compare these two things with each other except through a single power that encompasses both. Whenever by right reason we distinguish a certain genus of most true things from every genus of bodies—in such a way that we see nothing corporeal in that genus—we reject everything that can be called corporeal. Yet we cannot reject all corporeal things through a corporeal **instrument** <term>instrumentum: a physical organ or tool, like the eye for seeing</term>, because at the very least that instrument itself cannot be cast aside by that very same instrument. Furthermore, when we behold an abstract **species** <note>original: "specie"; here meaning an intellectual form or idea</note>, and through it we unite ourselves to abstract forms and reasons, and unite them to ourselves, then a corporeal instrument placed between them would be a hindrance rather than a help. For it is utterly different from them, and far inferior, and brings about distance much more than union. Since these things are so, the mind cannot use any corporeal instrument. But could it use some other kind? Absolutely none. For if anyone joins any other instrument to it, we will ask whether the mind can understand anything without it, or nothing? If it can, it does not need the instrument. But someone might say it cannot. We, on the contrary, assert that it can. For by now everyone will admit that the intellect knows itself, and in this cognition it uses no instrument. For if it used something to grasp itself, that thing would certainly fall as a medium between the mind and the mind's own essence; the essence would be grasped by the mind through that medium, so that something external would be closer to the mind than the mind's own essence. And when the power of the mind is reflected back upon its own power, or act upon act, no instrument is placed in between. For a medium is usually employed for the sake of suitability with the extremes. Yet no instrument is more suitable with power and act than the power and act themselves. Everyone will also confess that if the intellect has an instrument, it is not ignorant of it. For we seem to not be ignorant of it primarily because we assert that it exists, and we hear that it is of such a nature as to serve the intellect. Moreover, if the intellect knows itself, and also external objects, it is necessary that it also sometimes knows the instrument through which it passes from itself into the objects of understanding. Furthermore, when it turns itself toward its own act through objects already known, and through that act toward its power and substance, is it not forced in this very regression to also run into its own instrument, if it has one, since that would be the medium between the act of the mind and its power? In that case, it is forced to recognize its own instrument. But does the mind recognize its instrument through some other instrument, or not? If through another, I ask about yet another and another, back to infinity. If through none, then it does not need an instrument for knowing, since it knows the instrument itself without one. In that case, what is called an "instrument" is really an object rather than a medium. And if it passes from this to something else by knowing, it does not run from a medium to an object, but from a prior object to a subsequent object. But perhaps someone will say that the instrument is known by the mind not through some other instrument, but through the instrument itself. I, however, would ask whether this is through the essence of the instrument or through its image? Not the first, because the mind would then always know it, since it is always related to it in the same way. But if it happens through an image, then that which was called an instrument is instead an object that is known, rather than an instrument through which something is known. And the image itself can be known with no intervening instrument, since it necessarily precedes the instrument, insofar as it is the medium between the instrument and the soul. By now, therefore, the intellect knows both itself and what is outside itself without any instrument. Consequently, by the very fact that we think of truly **simple** <note>meaning "uncomposed" or "not made of parts"</note> things and true **simplicity**, the Platonists conclude that what thinks in us in this way is neither composed of intellect and instrument, nor made of soul and body, but that the mind exists as something simple and alone. Therefore, the mind operates **by itself** <note>original: "per se"</note>, and in this way Plato also says it is **moved by itself** <note>original: "per se moueri"</note>. Therefore it lives by itself, and lives forever.

Let us proceed to the third sign. Those lower powers are confused by a violent object, such that they do not discern weaker things. The mind, on the contrary, when it sees magnificent and arduous things, then both within them and after them it discerns smaller and lighter things more clearly and easily, inasmuch as the mind is great and is nourished and grows by great things. Let us proceed to the fourth sign, and the rest. Other powers are offended by a powerful object; the mind is offended by the consideration of nothing, no matter how immense, as if it were not subject to any certain proportion of **humors** <note>the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, etc.) believed to control health and temperament</note>. To be sure, it finds the greatest things more slowly, because it does not seek things that are explained by foreign [physical] matters. Once unencumbered, it finds them more quickly, and then shines forth wonderfully through its discoveries, as if it were entirely prepared for them; then it is filled with incomparable pleasure, as if it were as close to them as possible. Who does not see here that the power of the mind is in a certain way infinite, since no...

He concludes that because the mind operates independently of the body, it possesses a self-sustaining life and is therefore immortal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument from Book IX of the Platonic Theology, where he asserts that the mind is distinct from the body and its sensory organs. Having previously discussed how the mind lacks a physical medium, he now moves to show how the mind's self-contained nature and its survival during physical decline prove its immortality.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX.</header>

...is it overcome by no finite object? Furthermore, other powers, qualities, and images are ignorant of the things familiar to them, but what of its own familiar things does the mind not know? For it defines familiarity itself, beholds itself, and understands its own act, the **species** <term>species: the mental form or "image" through which the mind recognizes a concept</term> through which it understands, and its own **habits** <term>habitus: a stable disposition or acquired skill, like knowing a language even when not speaking it</term> and virtues. The mind, therefore, dwells with itself; it is its own home. Since any thing is preserved in its natural place, the mind is preserved by itself and remains forever unharmed. 

Added to this is the fact that those who are stronger, as far as natural and sensory operations are concerned, are often better off than others, yet this is not always or even often the case regarding intelligence—as if intelligence were not a companion of the body. Furthermore, the nature of the senses fails in its operation during old age, but the eye of the mind then discerns more clearly once the clouds of youthful vices have been chased away. For as Plato divinely said: "the virtue of the soul does not flourish unless the virtue of the body fades." The edge of the mind is not sharpened unless the edge of the body is blunted. At that time, wisdom regarding divine things flourishes, while human prudence is consumed, and equity and constancy prevail.

And what is more—lest anyone think otherwise—the very power of sensing, which resides in the soul, is not lost to old age or disease, even though its action may be interrupted by a damaged eye because objects are not represented clearly enough. For even if a pen is broken, the act of writing stops, but the art of writing remains whole in the soul. That the art suffered no loss thereby is evident from the fact that, in the meantime, the person "writes" within himself, and once the pen is restored, he writes at his own will. The same would happen if a tongue-tied person’s tongue were cured, or a lame man’s foot. The same if the eye of a blind or bleary-eyed person were cured, as if the damage were in the body, not in the soul. For often, once the eye is cleansed, we see immediately. This either would not happen, or would happen only much later after the body was healed, if the power of seeing itself had failed, for it would require a certain time for its own restoration after the body required time for its own.

Aristotle wisely said: "If you were to provide an old man with the eye of a youth, he would see exactly like a youth." If the senses, which are assigned to specific parts of the body, lose no power even when those parts are damaged or aged, then the mind, which is assigned to no part, will never fail, even if the whole body is damaged. 

Here, that reasoning occurs to you which Socrates brings forward in the tenth book of Plato's *Republic*: "That thing," he says, "will not perish by a disease of the body which does not fail by its own disease." <note>This refers to the argument in Republic 608d-611a that the soul's "disease" is injustice/vice, which makes it bad but does not dissolve its existence.</note> Our body does not perish by another's disease, but by its own. Even if it perishes by faulty food or rotten air, it does not perish until these cause it to fall into its own disease, by which it is properly dissolved. And if it does not perish by its own disease, it will never perish by another’s. For if it is not harmed by a fever, it will not be harmed by unhealthy food or air. 

The soul, however, does not perish by its own flaw—that is, by iniquity. For an unjust soul is no less a soul and no less vital than if it were just. Therefore, it does not perish by a disease of the body. Furthermore, a disease of the body does not bring upon the soul the soul's own specific vice, since the soul does not become more unjust because the body is sick; rather, it is often corrected and makes progress in the pursuit of character. Therefore, bodily disease not only fails to destroy the soul, it does not even corrupt it. 

And if the mind seems at times to be harmed when the body is sick, it is not actually so. The mind is perhaps idle there, or acting within itself, or occupied with human business; it is not harmed. When Socrates was either playing with his children or caring for them while they were ill, he did not lose his habit of higher philosophy, even if he was not philosophizing at all at that moment, or at least not excellently, while he distracted the act of his knowledge toward the consideration of baser things. Our soul often plays with the body in its pleasures. In the body's illnesses, the soul rules and cares for it. In both states, that sublime consideration of reason is interrupted or relaxed, because it is either idle for a time or too anxiously occupied with baser business; but once matters are settled, it rises again. 

Nature is arranged so that we are not sufficient for different works at the same time, so far as human strength is concerned. Guests intent on a banquet do not hear the melodies of the lyre well. While the soul is busy digesting food in the stomach, it relaxes the duty of human contemplation; therefore we seem dull at that time. When it speculates more attentively, food is digested with difficulty. Hence, those who practice philosophy are often weak in body but not in soul; rather, they excel in intelligence as much as they fail in body. 

Therefore, what wonder is it if, while the body is feverish, the soul—being most intent on sustaining and caring for the sick—ceases from contemplation? Or if it uses its intellect less when it is very busy building a child's body or sustaining a decrepit one? And when black vapors occupy the spirit of the brain, and having vibrated it, stir up horrible images in the **phantasy** <term>phantasy: the imagination or the faculty that processes sensory images</term>, whereby almost the entire power of the soul is directed toward the phantasy by the novelty of the foul spectacle, would you wonder if in the meantime it intermits its work...

<note>original: "contemplandi, quod tandem uaporibus resolutis instaurat"</note> ...of contemplating, which it restores at length once the vapors have dissipated. Often, even when the vapors are boiling, reason itself remains ever-vigilant and refutes the illusions of images. This happens in those who suffer from vertigo <term>vertigo: a sensation of spinning or dizziness</term>; their reason denies that the sky or earth is falling, even though their senses suggest it. Likewise, those who are driven to madness by a dog’s bite <note>rabies</note>, or are goaded by a demonic fury, sometimes realize the onset of their insanity even in the very rush of that madness. And those who are terrified by horrific nightmares protest against their **imagination**, often saying to themselves that they are dreaming. Therefore, the mind does not always need the lower powers; it often remains idle while they are active, and is active when they are idle, condemning their chatter and commanding them to be silent.

If anyone should say that the mind requires those lower powers to be "awakened," and therefore cannot operate at all without them, I respond as follows: as long as the soul inhabits the body, it is always occupied with the body's upkeep. Because it is distracted by many things far removed from the divine, it does not turn toward the intuition of divine things unless it is awakened by grasping certain clearer likenesses of them through its "attendant" powers <note>original: "pedissequas," referring to the lower sensory and imaginative faculties that serve the intellect</term>—powers which the soul uses most frequently. However, after the soul has sufficiently turned itself toward the divine, and through frequent turning has become ready for the infusion of divine truths, it no longer needs the service of those lower powers for its contemplation. Indeed, it puts them to sleep as much as it can so as not to be hindered by them. It would always gladly persist in that state, were it not for the urgent necessity of caring for the body. This signifies that the mind can continue its speculation by itself; and when it is no longer pulled back from this by the care of the body, it will speculate freely through itself without the ministry of other powers—provided it was at least not hindered by them before. 

But as long as it is enclosed in the body, because it relies on the ministry of the senses to prepare its "turning," it happens that when the body is injured and the **spirit** <term>spiritus: in Renaissance medicine, a subtle vapor that connects the soul to the body</term> is clouded over, the mind is not easily awakened to true speculation. This is because objects are not clearly represented, nor is there a clear perception in the senses and the imagination. It also happens that some people appear more gifted than others due to the diversity of these spirits. However, I believe the difference between men in learning the arts should be attributed not so much to talent as to a difference in **will**. For anyone can achieve even the greatest things if they strive with zeal. 

Furthermore, it happens that some people are called "mindless" because they either do not use their mind or they abuse it; indeed, all the soul’s attention in these people is overly occupied with the more violent illusions of the imagination. But once the bile—whether black or yellow <note>the humors associated with melancholy and anger</note>—which causes the illusion is cleared away, they suddenly return to their senses, proving they never actually lost their mind. I will pass over the arguments of **Origen** and **Plotinus**, who claim that human souls are, in a way, minds fallen from their original purity. They fell into bodies when their focus shifted from the "Ideas" in the mind to the life-giving power of bodies. The more intensely and deeply some souls turned toward matter than others, the less intellectual light (as they say) do they retain. From this comes the great diversity of talent and character among souls. The ethereal bodies of souls also contribute to this, being adapted to the various figures and stars of the heavens. Finally, the variety of human lineages brings about a variety of talents. 

Even if one does not grant that souls existed in time before the body, but wishes to imitate the Platonists in part, one might say that souls—at the very moment they are created and begin to function in the body—are affected and disposed much as Origen and Plotinus argue. Certainly, some angelic minds fell toward lower things while others did not; and of those that fell, some fell more and others less. But human minds, being the lowest of all, all tend by natural instinct toward the natural realm and bodies from the moment they are created; some merge themselves more deeply than others into the **river Lethe** <note>In mythology, the river of forgetfulness; Ficino uses it here as a metaphor for material existence</note>—that is, into matter. In this way, Pamphilus seems to have amended Origen as far as he could. But more on these things elsewhere. 

Now, let us return to our purpose. If someone seems to lose their memory because of a head injury, the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</term> will answer that the images of things held in the spirit of the brain are confused, but the **species** <term>species: the mental forms or concepts</term> in the mind are not properly harmed; rather (if I may put it this way), they are merely idle. For as long as the mind inhabits the body, it must gaze upon the "species" of physical things not without the physical images of those things. The **Platonists** would add that to the extent the soul's attention is intensely occupied with healing the injured limb, its cognition or memory is diminished or interrupted. **Avicenna** and **Alganteles** <note>Al-Ghazali</note> would say the mind, having turned toward lower things, is diverted from a certain "Divine Mind," upon which they believe every act of understanding continuously depends. Truly, because **Lucretius** <note>A Roman poet and Epicurean who argued for the mortality of the soul</note> distrusts immortality primarily for this reason—that the powers of the soul seem to fail when death is imminent—it must be noted that...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind's essential faculties remain intact even during madness, illness, or sleep, suggesting the soul's independence from the body. He cites various philosophical traditions to explain why physical injury or focus on matter can temporarily obscure the mind's operation without destroying it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Ninth Book of the "Platonic Theology," where he presents specific "signs" or proofs that the human soul is immortal. Having previously discussed how the mind remains active even when the body is compromised, he now moves through the sixth, seventh, and eighth arguments, focusing on the mind's independence from physical exhaustion and its ability to grasp universal concepts beyond the material realm.</meta>

<page-num>217</page-num>

-> # ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK IX. <-

...that the life of the body consists in the balance of moisture and heat; therefore, the body dies when either heat dissolves the moisture, or moisture extinguishes the heat.

Since moisture is the fuel of heat, and heat is the vehicle of the **spirit** <term>spirit: in Renaissance medicine, a subtle substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the incorporeal soul</term>, and the spirit is the reconciler of the soul to the body, it happens that when moisture is gradually dissolved in the limbs of the body, the soul also gradually leaves the limbs. And because it is then less occupied with ruling the body than usual, it gathers itself into its own mind, perceives secrets, and foretells the future. Let us reject the Lucretian suspicion <note>original: "Lucretiana suspicio"; referring to the Roman poet Lucretius, who argued in *De Rerum Natura* that the soul is made of atoms and dies with the body</note>—namely, that the soul will die with the body—since the soul is actually strengthened when the body is weakened. And since union is the opposite of dissolution, the mind must be thought to be furthest from dissolution at the very time when it most collects itself into itself and, laying aside its "animal nature" <note>the biological functions of life</note>, rises into the intellect. This clearly happens in a death that occurs due to "dissolution" <note>a gradual natural decline</note>. 

But in a death that occurs due to the "extinction of the vital soul," the soul's power is focused on curing the fluids and swellings, the senses are focused on judging pains, and the **imagination** is focused on viewing the images stirred up by the vapors of the humors. Because of this, reason temporarily lets go of its duty—just as it often does in sleep—only to resume it after the "clatter of death," just as it is accustomed to waking after dreams. That it does not lose its powers and gifts at that very time is proven by this: many who are called back to life from the brink of death by the diligence of doctors do not recover their bodily strength for a long time, or ever; yet, once the excess moisture is purged, their mental clarity returns immediately. It is as if the body's strength had been extinguished, but the light of the mind had merely been hidden, like fire under ashes, rather than vanishing. Who would say that the exit from life is the same for the body and the soul, when their return is not the same? For the body returns with difficulty and late, but the mind returns easily and suddenly. Nor has it lost anything of itself at that time, since it suddenly brings back into the light both its natural and acquired gifts, no less than it was accustomed to before. It is like one who had collected his belongings rather than scattering them, prepared like a snake to shed its old skin <note>original: "exuuias exuendas"</note>, about to emerge from those enclosures into the light, living and whole, just as it was once sent forth into the light from the mother’s womb. Thus, the wise man thinks that when he leaves the body, he is not being deprived of a part of himself, but is being freed from a most troublesome burden.

And that is enough concerning the **sixth sign**. Now receive the **seventh sign**: The senses are fatigued by daily work, but the mind never is. The longer you look at something, the more blurred your vision becomes. But the longer you investigate something with the intellect, the more clearly you understand it. Every work of the body and the senses is worn out by use, but the work of the mind is strengthened. Nevertheless, the head is often weighed down by long thinking and the eye grows dim, because the exercise of the mind is frequently accompanied by the movements of the **imagination**, these by the vibration of the **spirit**, and this by injury to the brain or eye. But the "edge" of the mind itself becomes lighter and sharper. Certainly, it would remain directed upward without any intermission, were it not that, out of pity for this body entrusted to it, it interrupted its own proper work for the sake of refreshing the body. This is clearly seen in those who, while contemplating something intently, grow weary and find the body hard to bear; in them, the mind ceases its work somewhat unwillingly, while the body and senses cease most willingly, as if it were not the mind that is fatigued by working, but the body. That which is untiring is also immortal.

The **eighth sign** is that other powers are restricted to a specific category of things, but the mind is restricted to none. For what is there in the number of things that are said "to be," toward which the edge of the mind cannot be directed? It grasps the nature and power of "Being" <term>Being (ens): the most universal concept in philosophy, encompassing everything that exists</term> itself, its essence and its definition; and under these, all things that exist are contained. It also finds the difference between "being" and "non-being," and thus knows both; it divides "being" into its parts and particles when it arranges various genera and species of things under the concept of existence. And, what is greater, it ascends *above* "Being" itself and descends *below* "Being," when it places the "One" itself and the "Good" itself above existence, and places "Matter" or the "privations of things" below existence. The mind is bound to no single category of things if it encompasses all things. It has nothing outside itself by which it could be destroyed, because in a certain way it closes all things within itself.

Let us conclude the dispute in this way: if the human soul existed in some way *through* the body, it would never act without the body's instrument or help. But it does act without the use of the body through understanding and willing, as we have shown through these eight signs. Therefore, it does not exist *through* the body. Therefore, it exists either through itself or through divine things. If it exists through itself, it never deserts itself; if it exists through divine things, then it is eternal because of those eternal causes.

He concludes that since the mind can grasp universal concepts like "Being" and the "Good" without physical tools, it must be an eternal entity.</summary>

# Sixth Reason. The soul agrees partly with divine things, partly indeed with animals. Chapter VI.

**I**f the human soul sprang from matter (which they call the **Lethean river** <note>original: "fluuium Lethæum"; in Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness. Ficino uses it here as a metaphor for the material world, which causes the soul to forget its divine origin</note>), it would never join in activity with divine things, which do not spring from that river. Indeed, we shall demonstrate that the soul corresponds with those divine things in activity, and even in essence and life, in this way. Since we see that all things act most effectively when they are mature and perfect in their own species, we are compelled to assert that God—because He is the most perfect of all—is not idle, but is active, since activity is a sign of perfection. Indeed, we ourselves would not act at all unless He acted, by whose movement we are moved, just as by His making we exist, and by His breathing we live and draw breath. But what is this activity of God? It is not one that begins from elsewhere or tends toward some other place, lest God be forced to depend on something external. Therefore, the activity of God is a certain perpetual **turning back into Himself** <term>turning back: "conversio in seipsum," a Neoplatonic concept where a perfect being finds its fulfillment by looking inward at its own nature</term>, through which He may enjoy and rejoice in Himself. Thus, He contemplates Himself; by contemplating Himself, He sees His own power; and by beholding this, He discerns whatever He is able to do. Therefore, He perceives both Himself and His entire work at once in a single act; by perceiving, He conceives all things within Himself; and by conceiving, He brings forth outside Himself whatever He wills. The activity in His holy ministers and celestial spirits is almost similar; for they too behold themselves and their own works, as well as God and divine works. Certainly, contemplation alone is suited to them, because it is the most perfect of all activities.

This is also apparent in us. This activity does not require external matter, as craftsmanship does; nor does it require bodily instruments, as the senses do; nor is it moved from elsewhere or tend toward another place, like other activities; nor does it shape foreign matter, but rather cultivates and adorns the mind. Since it is not terminated by anything else, but defines itself within itself, it does not tire quickly like other actions, but remains tireless. It is neither troublesome nor lacking, as those others are, but is easy, full, and bathed in incomparable joy. If, therefore, any of the activities within us is to be attributed to the higher divinities, it is certainly **contemplation** <note>Ficino views the intellectual life of study and meditation as the highest human calling because it mimics the life of God</note>, the happiest of all activities. From these points, it is clear that the human soul corresponds with divine things in contemplation. We do not doubt that the human also corresponds with **beasts** <note>original: "bestijs"; referring to non-rational animals</note> in nutrition, sensation, and the affections of the body. Furthermore, certain activities directed toward objects appropriate to them require certain corresponding powers and substances; and the proportion of one object to another is the same as the proportion of one activity to another. The comparison of power and essence to another power and essence is also the same. Thus, just as within us that which pertains to the use of the body is an activity shared with the animals toward an object common to them, so a nature common to them appears. This is the activity of nourishing and sensing, and the power and temperament of the body, which in us are fleeting, just as they are in the beasts.

It is also necessary that there be found in us a power and substance common to those celestial beings, from which may spring that activity which we have in common with them toward an object common to us and to them. For this reason, just as the nature of nourishing and sensing and the bodily temperament in us are in a way fleeting—since they are occupied with fleeting things and are shared with fleeting animals—so the power of contemplating will be immortal, since it is occupied with immortal things and is shared with the immortals. For the same activity cannot proceed except from the same nature and power.

But who would doubt that our contemplation is very similar to that of the higher beings? For through it, the mind—like those celestial beings—considers itself and its own works, and investigates the higher causes and their effects. Likewise, it ascends from lower effects through intermediate causes up to the Supreme Cause, and in turn returns in a circle from the Supreme Cause down to the lowest outcomes. There, the mind is seen to embrace the entire series of the divine work by no other power than the divine, and to look around like some sort of God. Not only, indeed, does the soul have intelligence in common with the divinities, but also **will**, since it desires their happiness. It possesses, moreover, a similar action, insofar as it acts freely and commands its own body much as they do. From all these things, it is concluded that our soul agrees in essence with the celestial beings. If it has an essence common to and close to them, and they have no origin from matter, it follows that our soul also has no such origin. Furthermore, if those divinities are everlasting because they always move the spheres of the world in the same order and are never tired, it follows that the essence of the mind...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul occupies a middle ground between animals and God. Because humans can perform "contemplation"—a tireless, joyful, and self-reflective activity shared with divine beings—the soul must possess an immortal essence similar to those heavenly powers.</summary>

...its essence is eternal, since a limited and mobile life is in no way the closest thing to an unlimited and immobile life. Indeed, the soul corresponds even more with those divine things in the immortality of its life than it does in its understanding of truth and its desire for happiness, just as life itself is prior to understanding or will. And if the will is the striving of the intellect, and the intellect is the highest peak of a maturing life, the mind is directed toward a right will only through true understanding, and toward this understanding only through a true and mature life. It possesses a right will because it carries itself toward the first and total Good. It possesses true understanding, both because it is not deceived insofar as it is intellect, and because it possesses within itself the true **rational principles** <term>rational principles: "rationes," referring to the Platonic Ideas or blueprints of all things contained within the mind</term> of all things, as we shall show elsewhere. Therefore, it must necessarily possess a true and mature life. Such a life is one that is not subject to death. 

That famous argument of **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian theologian who blended Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine</note> favors our reasoning greatly, where he says: All natures that participate in the same principle are similar to each other, just as eyes are similar because they all participate in light; since by their nature they are all similarly turned toward the light, they are all similar, yet one is sharper than another according to their different participation in the light. All **rational substances** participate in God, since they are all turned toward God; therefore they are similar both among themselves and to Him. Thus, just as the higher ones are immortal, such as the angels, so too are the lower ones, such as souls. Indeed, all are immortal because they are similar to the immortal God. That very **turning back toward God** <term>turning back: "conversio," the Neoplatonic process where a created being returns its focus to its divine source</term> demonstrates this similarity; for the higher angels turn toward Him as if toward the Sun, like stars, while the soul turns toward the same as if it were the Moon. Although the soul is changed by a certain cycle of divine light—and therefore receives it in a mutable way—it nevertheless perceives it by an **unquenchable reason** <note>original: "inextinguibili... ratione"</note>. For it comprehends by certain reasons both that this light is unquenchable and the reason why it is so.

## *Objection of the Epicureans and the response regarding the tempering of things.*
### *Chapter VII.*

->**D**icaearchus<- <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who argued that the soul is mortal and merely a "tempering" of the body's elements</note>, or some **Epicurean** <note>Followers of Epicurus, who held that the soul is composed of atoms and dissolves at death</note>, will fight back against these points, claiming it is like a monster to suggest that a thing could be partly incorruptible and partly subject to corruption. But we shall assert that the order of nature cannot be preserved without this. There are some bodies entirely removed from all corruption, such as the heavens, of which neither the sphere itself nor any particle is corrupted. There are also bodies completely opposite to these, namely those that are entirely perishable, such as wood, stones, metals, and other things composed of the four elements. Indeed, some particles of wood eventually rot, and then the whole piece of wood itself ceases to be wood—although whatever is so composed consists of both the incorruptible and the corruptible at least in this: that it has within itself **prime matter** <term>prime matter: "materia prima," the underlying, eternal substrate of all physical things that remains even when a specific form is destroyed</term> which is perpetual, but a form that is mortal. 

Therefore, the union of mortals with immortals is neither impossible nor rare. But let us return to the established order. There are also middle bodies, namely the spheres of the four elements, which are partly incorruptible and partly corruptible. The entire sphere of an element preserves its own appearance, its own position, and its own continuity, yet some of its particles are sometimes destroyed here and restored there. Since bodies have been established either by spirits or for the sake of spirits, the order of bodies must proceed from the order of spirits, or at least imitate the order of spirits. There are, therefore, some spirits that are entirely immortal, such as angels, whose entire substance is never changed, nor is any power or activity. There are others that are entirely mortal, as the common opinion holds—namely the souls of **brutes** <note>animals</note>, whose power and activity are changed, and whose entire substance is changed as well. 

Furthermore, there must be spirits that are a "mean" between both, so that there may be a single, uninterrupted weaving together of all nature. These will remain throughout their entire substance, but will change through certain parts. Such are our souls especially; their shared contemplation, will, and action with the celestial beings forces their substances to be perpetual. However, that shared activity with mortal brutes—entirely enslaved to the care of the mortal body—indicates to us that some powers or activities will eventually cease. Since natural affections are founded in their own proper natures, and different affections exist in different natures, and yet we see that our souls have an affection for eternal things as well as an affection for temporal things, we rightly say that they are composed of two natures: the eternal and the temporal, just-as <note>This "just-as" (quemadmo-) is a catchword, leading into the first word of the next page</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul occupies a middle ground in the universe, sharing immortality with angels and God while maintaining a temporary connection to the physical world of animals and elements. He refutes the Epicurean claim that a single entity cannot have both corruptible and incorruptible parts by pointing to the hierarchy of nature.</summary>

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY
## On the immortality of souls,
->by the same author, Ficino,<-
->BOOK X.<-

->*The first reason. Just as the last thing in the order of bodies is incorruptible, so too is the last thing in the order of minds. Chapter I.*<-

**S**ince the order of bodies is situated beneath the order of intellects and depends upon it, the order of bodies follows the order of intellects in the same way that a footprint follows the foot itself, or a shadow follows the body. Therefore, the kind of order we see in bodies is nearly the same as the one we should imagine exists in minds. In the order of bodies, we see a "sublime body"—namely, the highest heaven—which contains in its nature all the powers for producing all **forms** <term>forms: "formæ," the essential blueprints or natures of things in Platonic philosophy</term>. Through these powers, which are active and effective, it disposes the lower bodies to receive various shapes. Thus, by the various powers of its nature and the various configurations of its motion, it moves and forms the lower bodies in different ways, so that it may rightly be said that the highest heaven encompasses the forms of the remaining bodies either in act or through active power. 

We can assert that the bodies following it are so subject to it that they possess those same forms in a certain **passive potentiality** <term>passive potentiality: "potentia passiva," the capacity to receive an influence or be shaped by another</term> and receive them in actuality from that heaven. However, such an order is maintained that the higher a body is beneath that heaven, the more **active power** <term>active power: "potentia activa," the ability to exert influence or create change</term> it has, and the less passive it is. For that which is closest to the "First" receives and is acted upon by that single First thing, yet it acts upon many others. That which is placed in the next grade is acted upon even more and acts less, since it is now influenced by two things—the first and the second—and it pours out what it has received into the things that follow, until one arrives at a certain "lowest matter." This matter, since it receives from all things above it, bestows nothing on anything else. Thus, in its passive potentiality, it indeed possesses all forms, which it receives through a sequence by being acted upon by higher things; but in its effective power, it possesses none.

Imagine the same thing in the case of minds, whose principle is God. He possesses all **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental concepts or "Ideas" that allow for the understanding of reality</term> in a single act of His own; He distributes them to all and receives from none. The minds following Him receive everything from there, and they relate to one another in such a way that the higher mind distributes those ideas and light, as it were, to the lower. Therefore, the higher a mind is, the fewer things it is subject to, and the more things it presides over. It is acted upon by fewer things in its receiving, and it acts upon more things in its distributing.

Finally, the lowest mind must be such that it is the opposite of the First Principle: it should receive from all and bestow upon none. According to its nature, it should possess those ideas in passive potentiality, but possess no active ones, since it does not pass ideas along to any intellect placed beneath it. Indeed, in the First, there is only the active power of ideas; in the following ones, there is active and passive power in sequence; and in the lowest mind, there is only passive power. 

Thus, God occupies the rank of the "highest heaven," the middle minds take the place of the middle bodies, and the lowest intellect occupies the place of "lowest matter." This lowest intellect, by its nature, receives all intelligible concepts in actuality through a certain succession—or rather, it "sees" them—but it does not contemplate them all at once, just as matter receives the forms of bodies by succeeding from one to another. Because this matter is not made from any preceding matter (and thus requires an infinite Creator), it is created by—or flows from—God alone. For it is fitting that a simple potentiality be made by a simple Act. Since God extends His action beyond the actions of all other agents, He alone makes matter, which holds the lowest grade in nature. If God alone creates matter, which is the lowest of corporeal things, then He alone creates that mind which is the lowest of intellects. If matter is the work of all divine works most remote from God, while the intellectual race is the closest, and if matter can exist apart from the mind, then the mind can much more easily exist apart from matter. If the lowest intellect in the genus of intellectual things holds a rank similar to that of matter in the genus of natural things, and matter cannot be made by any natural power, it follows that the lowest intellect cannot be made by any kind of intellect that exists within that genus. But if an intellect of this kind is from no intellect of the same genus...

<meta>catchword: read (lectu)</meta>

<summary>Ficino establishes a parallel between the physical hierarchy (heaven to matter) and the intellectual hierarchy (God to the human mind), arguing that the human mind is a "simple potentiality" created directly by God. He suggests that if the lowest form of matter can exist, then the human mind, which is higher in the chain of being, must certainly be able to exist independently of the body.</summary>

Following the introduction of the hierarchy of being on the previous page, Ficino here details the "Great Chain of Being," showing how every level of creation—from minerals to the highest intellects—overlaps and connects to the next.</meta>

...are closer to plants, since their brilliance and splendor reflect white and purple flowers. Among plants, the truffle <note>original: "tuber"</note> surpasses metals because it is more clearly nourished and grows, yet only slightly, because it does not have a varied order of parts. The most noble trees are close to beasts; they have roots in place of a mouth, and branches like legs, arms, and the like. Some trees even have both sexes, male and female, which is why when planted near each other they sprout more abundantly. Among the beasts, oysters surpass plants in only one respect: they have the sense of touch; yet being fixed to the earth, they are nourished almost like trees. Many small beasts are also born spontaneously without mating, just like herbs. There are also monkeys, dogs, horses, and elephants, and other beasts very similar to humans in certain shapes, gestures, and skills. There are dull and lazy men who (as it appears) are also very close to these; and there are heroic men, leaders of others, who are most closely related to the higher divinities. 

Furthermore, there must be spirits <term>spirits: "daemones," which in the Platonic tradition refers to intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil "demons"</term> joined to men by familiarity. Plato maintains that the miracles of the magic art were discovered through their instruction, just as through the instruction of men, some beasts closer to us often perform wonders beyond their own species. And these spirits or heroes are so close to us in affection, just as they are in nature and position, that they are affected by certain human disturbances; some favor certain persons and places, while others oppose them. Indeed, the Egyptians—whom *Origen*, *Numenius*, and *Porphyry* follow <note>These are influential ancient theologians and philosophers: Origen was a Christian, while Numenius and Porphyry were Platonists</note>—claim there are many spirits who raise souls to higher things, and many who twist them toward lower things. They say the worst spirits are in the west, and evil ones also in the northern region, while good ones are in the south, and the best dwell in the eastern region. 

Among them, higher spirits rule over the lower ones, and above these are others whom they call **angels**. Likewise, the Platonists place **archangels** above angels, and **principalities** <term>principalities: "principatus," a high-ranking order in the traditional celestial hierarchy</term> above archangels. Above the principalities, they place certain **intellects** who are already designated "lords" by a certain participation, always full of the most high God and drunk on divine nectar <note>A metaphor for being filled with divine wisdom and joy</note>. 

If in all kinds of things we admit that the lowest parts of a preceding order are joined with the highest of the succeeding order, and are in some way blended together, why should we not admit that the lowest intellect is so joined with the highest of the sensitive souls? Thus, while the sensitive soul is mortal, it may have some image of intellect (as is manifest in the most sagacious beasts), and the lowest intellect, although it is divine, may nonetheless have a certain sensitive and brute nature through which it properly inclines toward earthly bodies. This is especially fitting since not only the human mind, but all others that are in some way "impure," should harmonize with purer bodies. Indeed, all rational souls are "impure" minds; though they are pure as souls, they are "impure" minds because they are **animal minds** <term>animal minds: "mentes animales," meaning minds that act as the animating principle (anima) for a physical body</term>. I say these minds are so dedicated to moving bodies that they imprint their vital and animal footprints upon them. 

**Pure minds**, however, are those that are minds alone; they do not pour out from themselves "animal shadows" immersed in ruling bodies. According to Plato, the **pure bodies** are the twelve spheres of the world: the eight heavens and the four elements beneath the heavens. Furthermore, there are certain most precious parts within each of these spheres. Therefore, rational souls are present in all spheres, arranged step by step according to their dignity. But Plato calls the single soul of the entire cosmic machine **Jupiter** <note>In this context, Jupiter represents the "World Soul" that animates the entire universe</note>, and he calls the twelve souls of the spheres the "twelve gods who follow in Jupiter's train." To the purer parts of the spheres, he similarly attributes souls that participate in mind—namely, to the stars and planets, which he also calls gods. To the regions of fire, he assigns spirits and fiery heroes. To the clear air, aerial ones. To the misty air, aquatic spirits and heroes. Finally, he couples minds with the purer parts of the earth, which are called **humans** dwelling on the ground. Sometimes spirits and heroes are also placed on the earth. And he locates a great many crowds of spirits and heroes not only beneath the Moon, but even in the heavens beyond the stars. 

But in all spheres, beyond the leading spirits and heroes, he places **particular souls**—whether spirit-like, heroic, or human—which do not always follow eternal things like those leaders do, but follow eternal and temporal things by turns. These souls change their bodies and their lives, sometimes ascending toward the better, sometimes descending toward the worse. Accordingly, for as many stars as there are, just as many crowds of spirits, heroes, and souls are subject to them: Saturnian ones under Saturn, Jovian ones under Jupiter, Martian ones under Mars, and so on in order. I pass over the fact that he thinks "all things are in all things," but in the earth they are in an earthly way, in the water in an aquatic way, and similarly in the air and fire. In the heaven, they are according to the celestial nature. All things in the Moon are according to the lunar nature, and in the other spheres in the same manner, so that any sphere in its own way and with its own quality...

<summary>Ficino explains the continuity of the universe through a hierarchy where every level of being overlaps with the next, connecting minerals, plants, animals, humans, spirits, and the celestial spheres. He argues that human souls are "animal minds" that bridge the gap between pure divine intellect and the physical world.</summary>

...so that the whole world may be a single totality. But let us now conclude what we have proposed. There will be some spirits existing outside the body and perpetual, and likewise some opposite to them existing in the body and mortal. Therefore, there must be middle spirits, who either exist outside the body and are mortal—which is impossible—or who exist within a body but are immortal. The first group consists of the heavenly minds, which they call the most pure **angels**, who are distinguished among themselves by many degrees. Opposite to them are the souls of **beasts**. The **rational souls** will hold the middle position, being as it were certain "lower angels." Nor is it absurd for an immortal spirit to exist in some body, since one can even find an immortal body, such as the heavens and any entire sphere of the universe. Indeed, it is fitting for perpetual spirits to be present as forms for all the principal bodies of the world. Since (as most people think) matter is perpetual in all things, it is necessary that matter be overcome everywhere by certain forms. 

The opinion of the Egyptians leads to the same point, confirmed by all the Platonists and especially by Proclus: namely, that for the harmony of the world to be perfect, there must be not only certain rational and immortal animals, and conversely animals that are both irrational and mortal, but also many middle beings between these which are indeed rational but mortal—not only on earth, but also in the other elements. Thus, not only do men have eternal souls in a mortal body, but there are also many **daemons** <term>daemons: in the Platonic tradition, "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediary beings or "guardian spirits" that bridge the gap between gods and humans</term>, some close to us and some far more sublime, whose bodies are born and perish, although they live longer than ours, degree by degree. For they do not think it fitting to descend suddenly from the celestial animals—who are rational, eternal, and most happy—to the earthly animals who are rational but most unhappy and very short-lived. Instead, there should be degrees of rational animals who are happier and longer-lived than humans, though not eternal, nor perfectly blessed in body or soul. 

Plutarch and his associates, the philosopher Demetrius and the rhetorician Aemilianus, affirm the same. They testify from many wonders that happened in their times that the **Great Pan** <note>Ficino refers to a famous story from Plutarch’s "The Obsolescence of Oracles" where a voice announces "Great Pan is dead," signaling a shift in the spiritual order</note>, a great daemon, and many other daemons first wailed and then even died. Therefore, the fellowship of the eternal mind with the human body, however fleeting it may be, is not as absurd as Epicurus and Lucretius <note>Epicurus and Lucretius were famous ancient materialists who argued the soul dies with the body</note> believe, especially since our mind is the "last" or lowest of the minds, just as the Moon is the last of the stars; and as the Moon is related to the Sun, so our mind is related to God. 

The Moon revolves around the Sun in such a way that it shines at different times and takes on various shapes, yet it is never deprived of its total capacity for receiving light. Furthermore, it has something bright in itself, and something dark. Finally, it has an opaque quality that prevents it from shining entirely. Similarly, the human mind always shines with the ray of the **Divine Sun**, but in different ways at different times; and though its "shape" changes, it never shines in its entirety. Nor does that which shines within it shine equally. Besides its divine and rational power, there lies beneath it an opaque part, void of reason, which—just as that lunar opacity turns toward the elements—inclines toward matter and the body, and is left devoid of light.

Therefore, it seems consistent with the natural order of things that the lowest mind, although it is eternal, can be joined with a body, even a perishing one. I pass over the fact that Xenocrates and Speusippus, Iamblichus and Plutarch, think that an eternal power proceeds from eternity itself, reaching not only to the lowest minds which reflect back upon it, but even to the souls of beasts. Numenius, moreover, extends this even to plants. Finally, Plotinus extends it even to nature itself. We, however, follow Porphyry and Proclus, believing that eternal life and knowledge proceed only so far as a "turning back" <note>original: "conversio," the Platonic idea that a being must consciously "turn back" toward its creator to share in its eternity</note> is required. For those things retain a certain share in eternity which are reflected back into it, both by their own reason and by grace, and not only by a movement that is external and common, but by their own proper movement. 

But has the human body really been granted such dignity that it deserves to host an eternal mind? Without a doubt. We should not be troubled by the fact that nature equipped the bodies of beasts with various defenses and provided aids for their food, while giving us no such thing. For she did not wish to deform the delicate balance of our body, nor could she provide innumerable defenses or tools for the infinite actions of man, which follow from his **infinite thought**. Instead, as Aristotle says, when she gave him a mind and a **hand**, she granted him all arts and all instruments. She easily equipped the beasts with limited protections, because...

...equipped them, so that the specific actions of the imagination might be executed by a nature directed toward a certain end. But we consider our bodies to be suitable guest-houses for the mind, partly because of our upright figure—looking not at the ground, but gazing upward, and recognizing heaven as its own proper homeland—and partly because of the truly wonderful beauty of our various limbs. It is also because the purest elements, fire and air, are very powerful within us, which is indicated by the agility of the body, its tall stature, and its upright gaze. But it is most of all because of our very temperate **complexion** <term>complexion: In medieval and Renaissance medicine, the "complexion" (Latin: *complexio*) refers to the specific balance or "tempering" of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) and the four humors within an individual.</term>, which is signified by the delicate, smooth, firm, and bright softness of the flesh, which occurs only through the most exact balancing of the elements. 

The eagle surpasses man in sight, many birds in hearing, the dog in smell; but no animal surpasses him in taste or touch. This is clearly seen from the fact that men indulge more immoderately in feasts, drinking, and sexual matters than beasts, even if they are sometimes restrained by reason. For it is natural for them to pursue those pleasures more greedily than beasts, as they feel them more acutely. Those three higher senses <note>Sight, hearing, and smell.</note> are most desired when the brain is dry. God did not grant this dryness to man, whose brain never rests, lest perhaps if it were naturally dry, it might be parched more quickly than is proper by its continuous activity. 

Taste is nothing other than a kind of touch of the tongue. Since touch is a universal sense—belonging to every animal and to the whole body—wherever it is most acute, it declares that the body possesses the best complexion. This is primarily because touch occurs in the nerves; when nerves are drier, they feel poorly, but where touch is sharp, it signifies a presence of softness that tempers the dryness of the nerves. Furthermore, the instruments of the senses should never actually possess those qualities which the sense is about to perceive. The pupil lacks colors, hearing lacks sounds, smell lacks odors, and the tongue lacks flavors. Since touch deals with the four qualities of the elements <note>Hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, it must either lack them entirely—which is impossible in a composite body—or be far removed from their excess, so that no single quality seems to dominate its instrument, but rather a kind of harmony exists, as if the qualities had been expelled. 

Nevertheless, there was a need for a great deal of earth and water to be within us according to their mass, so that the abundance of the mass of water and earth might temper the much more powerful force of fire and air. We were also given a larger brain and a warmer heart than other living creatures: the former to provide for **contemplation** <note>original: "speculationi"</note> through various instruments, the latter to ensure that many bright **spirits** <term>spirits: In Ficinian physiology, "spirits" (spiritus) are subtle, airy vapors generated by the heart that act as the primary vehicle for the soul to move the body and process sensory data.</term> are present for the brain. The head is also suspended high, so that the filth of heavy humors does not descend to the brain and stain the purity of the spirits. The intense coldness and moisture of the brain, as well as the heat and dryness of the heart, temper each other as well as all the limbs. 

Therefore, man seems to have the most temperate complexion of all. If it were earthy, like that of almost all beasts, we would be covered in horns, teeth, claws, harder beaks, and rough, hairy skin or scales. But now, on the contrary, the human body is so fashioned that it is neither parched by an excess of heat and dryness, nor stiff or sluggish from too much cold, nor fluid and slippery from superfluous moisture, but is equally delicate and solid. This is also understood from the foods we constantly eat—airy, sweet, ground, refined, liquified, cooked, and very temperate—whereas beasts eat the opposite. As one's complexion is, so are the foods one desires; and whatever foods one uses, such a complexion one becomes. 

Let us conclude, then, that man was born for contemplation, as **Anaxagoras** <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE): A Pre-Socratic philosopher who, when asked why it is better to be born than not, replied: "To behold the heavens and the whole order of the universe."</note> said, since both his brain and the rest of his body are so constituted as to serve the continuous duty of contemplation. This requires both a softness of the brain and a temperate complexion of the body—the former so it is not dried out too much by speculating, the latter so it is not turned away from contemplation by a tumult of humors. 

Since there is such a great and sublime moderation in our body that it imitates the temperance of heaven, it is no wonder if a heavenly soul inhabits this temple, so similar to heaven, for a time. Yet it is not infused into the flesh first, but is led through suitable intermediaries, as the **Persian Magi** <note>Magi: Ancient Persian priests associated with Zoroaster. Ficino viewed them as part of a lineage of "ancient theologians" who possessed divine wisdom before the time of Plato.</note> teach. First, in its descent from heaven, it is wrapped in an aerial body, then in a spirit generated from the heart, which in us is most temperate and luminous, like heaven. Through these intermediaries, it is enclosed in the thicker body. It becomes equally close to all of these, even though it pours itself from one into another, just as the heat of fire clings most closely to air and water, although it is drawn toward the water through the air. And rightly is the immortal soul joined to mortal bodies through that **immortal, ethereal body** <note>The "astral body" or "chariot of the soul" (ochema), a staple of Neoplatonic thought.</note>. Indeed, it always inhabits that perpetual body...

He explains how the soul descends from heaven through a series of subtle, intermediary bodies—aerial and spiritual—before joining with the physical flesh.</summary>
