# MARSILII FICINI’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

These things are mortal only for a brief time, so that the soul should deservedly be called a certain God, or a star surrounded by a cloud, or a demon <note>original: "dæmon"; in the Platonic sense, this refers to a guardian spirit or a being intermediate between gods and mortals, not an evil spirit.</note>, not an inhabitant of the earth, but a guest. Guest, know yourself; know that you are a citizen of a heavenly fatherland, a citizen born to contemplate heavenly things. Remember that if your end is contemplation, your life is increased and perfected by contemplating. Since, indeed, the life of the body is somewhat slackened by this very pursuit, it follows that in the very loss and destruction of the bodily life, your own life does not decrease, but grows.

->*Second reason. Just as in natural things there is a resolution toward first matter,*<-
->*which is immortal, so too there is one toward the ultimate form, which is immortal.*<-
->Chapter III.<-

**T**he order of natural bodies is so established that it descends into first matter and ascends into the ultimate form. And the more any matter approaches first matter, the more powerful a matter it is—that is, a truer and purer matter. The more any form approaches the ultimate form, the more perfect a form it is. For first matter is the matter of matters; the ultimate form is the form of forms. Take this example of what we mean: We divide the body of an animal into limbs as if into its own matter; any limb into four humors, which are a kind of matter for the limb. Similarly, any humor into the four elements. But an element we divide into simple matter, at which it is finally necessary to arrive, lest we descend into infinity, or be compelled conversely to ascend without end. For nowhere will there be a mixed act if nowhere there were mixed potential; and nowhere again will pure act be found if nowhere pure potential could be discovered. And since action has its beginning from pure act, and passion <note>In this philosophical context, "passion" (passio) refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an impression, the opposite of "action."</note> from pure potential, actions and passions would exist nowhere. Therefore, there must be a simple matter. This simple matter, which is subject to the form of an element, is called <term>first matter: In Platonic and Aristotelian thought, the most basic, formless stuff out of which all physical things are made.</term>. Since the Architect of nature himself, in fabricating bodies, takes this naked matter in the beginning, he soon clothes it with the qualities and forms of the elements, then leads the elements into the appearance of humors, thereafter arranges the humors into the forms of limbs, adds to the limbs the appearance of nourishing, to this the form of sensing, and finally to this the form of understanding. 

But the intellectual nature is twofold. One is so foreign to bodies that it provides no life to them; this, therefore, is not called a form of matter or of a body, and that order of bodies does not terminate in this nature of the mind as its own form. According to Plato, the sublime angels hold this rank. But there is another nature of the mind which, joined to the body, conspires with it as if by a certain covenant; the progression of bodies ascends into this as the ultimate form of matter. There are two boundaries of this progression: matter is the lowest, and this mind is the highest. Since they are most distantly separated from each other, they have opposite conditions. Therefore, just as first matter is mere matter, by its nature entirely devoid of form and subject to all forms and matters, so that ultimate form—namely, the mind—is mere form, that is, entirely devoid of matter, presiding over all forms and their matters. 

Likewise, just as first matter is most distantly separated from "first being" and is closest to nothingness—wherefore it is placed by Plato between being and nothingness—so the ultimate form is most distantly separated from nothingness, and is as close as possible to "first being." From this, three things follow. First, that the ultimate form does not spring from matter in any part; second, that it is made by God alone; and third, that it can remain immortal. The first of these is concluded from the first comparison we introduced; the second from the second; and the third follows from both the first and the second. From the first thus: if it is entirely devoid of corporeal matter, which is the beginning of destructive change, it is far from destruction. And if it is the wonderful head of things, it neither succumbs to wonderful things, nor does it undergo any change except a vital one. From the second thus: if the boundary closest to nothingness does not tend toward nothingness, what wonder if the boundary furthest removed from nothingness, and closest to "first being," is neither ever cast out from being, nor pushed into nothingness? Again, the nature of form is more perfect than that of matter, since matter is perfected and adorned by form. Therefore, just as by descending step by step from matter to matter, we arrive at the <unclear>f</unclear>irst matter of bodies which is eternal, so also by ascending from form to form, we are gradually carried forward into the eternal ultimate form of bodies, lest the ascent be more imperfect than the descent, and the highest boundary be more imperfect than the lowest. It is fitting that...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind is the "ultimate form" of the physical world, serving as the immortal peak of a hierarchy that mirrors the immortality of "first matter" at the bottom. He concludes that because the mind is closest to "first being" (God) and furthest from nothingness, it must be immortal.</summary>

Ficino argues that while nature creates intermediate forms as steps toward a goal, the human soul is the final destination and thus shares in divine eternity.</meta>

<page-num>227</page-num>
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK X.

The intellectual form, toward which the effort of all universal nature tends as if to its goal, is so absolute and consummate that it is far removed from death. However, it is not necessary for middle forms to be immortal, for nature seems to value them little, choosing them not for their own sake, but rather for the sake of the ultimate form. In this respect, they clearly appear to be certain preparations of matter to receive the ultimate form, rather than principal forms existing in their own right. Through them, as if by paths, the very motion and impulse of nature pass; in the final form, nature halts its motion. Deservedly, therefore, those middle forms shall pass from being into non-being, while that final form shall rest in being, so that nature's end may remain without end <note>The Latin "sine fine" is a wordplay: nature's "end" (goal) remains "without end" (eternal).</note>. We say, however, that the entire effort of universal nature is directed toward this above all: that an intellectual animal exists because the intellect is present in a body. But for the intellect to exist in itself, only a divine action can grant that. And since it depends only upon eternity itself, it shall be eternal. 

Regarding the intellectual animal, what shall we say? The Magi <note>Wise men or followers of Zoroaster often cited by Ficino as part of a lineage of "ancient theology" that prefigured Christianity.</note> do not doubt that it too would have remained in its own temperance, 
<margin>Plato in Charmides</margin>
as Plato writes in the *Charmides*, provided that the soul had remained in its own—that is, divine—temperance. For from the soul proceeds all the harmony and discord of the body. The Mosaic and Christian law teach precisely the same thing. Truly, that which the universal order once lost due to the disordered movement of the soul must eventually be brought back into order as order itself prevails; on this not only Moses, but Zoroaster, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, and Plato agree. But more on these things elsewhere. Now let us conclude what was proposed. 

Let both limits of the bodily order be perpetual: the lowest <note>Referring to "first matter" discussed on the previous page.</note> and the highest. Indeed, the ancient theologians thought the highest limit and the ultimate form to be the rational soul, with whom 
<margin>Aristotle, Book 12 of the Metaphysics</margin>
Aristotle agrees in his twelfth book on divine things, where, disputing about efficient and formal causes, he says: the causes that move matter precede it, but forms do not. However, it must be investigated whether any form remains after matter. For in some cases nothing prevents this, as if the soul were such a thing—not the whole soul, but the intellect. 
<margin>The same, Book 2 of the Physics</margin>
He says the same in his second book on natural things: the investigation of the natural philosopher extends as far as that form which is both separate and yet in matter—which he indicates to you is the human soul, and so all the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" (covered walkway) where they studied in Athens.</note> explain it. 

We, however, think that both the ancient theologians and Aristotle arrived at this opinion through a certain reasoning. That just as a <term>temperate complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio temperata"; in medieval medicine and philosophy, this refers to a perfect, balanced mixture of the four humors or elements.</note> is the goal toward which all natural motions and complexions are directed, so the rational soul, which a temperate complexion serves, is the goal of all natural forms. Again, the condition of the ultimate form is that it be neither entirely absolute nor entirely immersed in bodies. If it were entirely free and performed nothing through the body, it would not be the form of the body. If it were entirely overwhelmed and did nothing without the body, it would not be the ultimate form. For there would be a form beyond this one—whichever was found to be such that it was partly joined to the body and partly not joined. 

Certainly, there must be some such form, so that between that angelic substance (which is entirely separate from the body and performs nothing through it) and the other form (entirely joined to the body and performing everything through the body, such as the soul of beasts), there is a certain middle form, partly joined to the body and partly separate, so that it performs some things through the body and some through itself. Such is every rational soul, because it both rules the body and contemplates. The human soul is also such beyond doubt, for it carries out the works of nourishing and sensing through bodily instruments, but perfects the act of understanding and choosing through itself. 

Thus the angel, both in substance and in operation, is separate from matter and is wholly in eternity because he is wholly in a stable state. The souls of brutes are joined through both substance and operation and are wholly in time, because they are changed through both. Rational souls, because they must be partly joined and partly separate, and could not be separate in any respect if they were joined in substance, are necessarily separate (or separable) in substance; this is because they have no origin from matter or from bodily agents and instruments. They are, however, joined through operations—not all operations, but the lowest ones—and this is not by violence, but by love. Whence, according to the Chaldeans <note>Referring to the "Chaldean Oracles," a collection of mystical texts highly valued by Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note>, they are on the boundary of eternity and time. In substance, they are in eternity; in operations, they are in time. For the former remains, while the latter are changed. For it is fitting that between that which is entirely eternal and that which is thoroughly temporal, there should be something partly eternal and partly temporal. And between that which always is and that which comes into being at a specific time, there should be something that is always coming into being. Such a thing is the heaven: its substance is always permanent, and yet it is mobile.

<meta>catchword: These</meta>

Again, the very matter of the world and its very—if I may put it this way—corporeity <note>original: "corporeitas"; the state of having a physical body</note> are of such a nature. Furthermore, the soul is almost like this: it is always flowing in its effects and actions, even though its substance remains stable. For this reason, it inclines toward bodies, which are additionally in a state of flow through their very substance. Such a soul is truly the **ultimate form** of the body, because it gives shape to and rules the body. Yet it so nearly exceeds the nature of the body that it exists within the light of the intellect; and having progressed only a little further, it would leave the limits of the body entirely behind. Indeed, it is far more separated from the body than joined to it. For it communicates only a part of itself to the body—namely, a lower power which it holds in common with "brute" animals and plants.

But its principal part, which is very similar to divine things and in which the whole essence of the rational soul consists, it keeps set apart from the body in its essence, as it also does in its actions. Whenever it operates through the intellect, it betakes itself by a primary and natural instinct to "separated reasons" <note>The Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms" which exist independently of the physical world.</note>, a point which all the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> concede. However, the soul turns itself toward individual and joined physical forms not by a primary or direct act, but by a second and "oblique" one, insofar as it reflects back upon the images from which it first produced its mental concepts. Who then does not see that the rational power is more separated than joined? Since it turns toward separated things directly and primarily, but turns toward joined physical things only obliquely and through a subsequent act. It attains what it desires most when it departs furthest from the body. On the contrary, when it descends through the senses to bodies, it is deceived and disturbed by countless passions. Now, it cannot be similar to mortal things if it is deceived and troubled by their very presence. Rather, it is similar to divine things, as **Plato** teaches in the *Phaedo*, because the more closely it adheres to them, the more it becomes clear and rejoices. Anything rests peacefully in its natural place but is distressed in an alien one. Hence, among the **Platonists**, it is clear that the natural seat of intelligence is not in mortal bodies, insofar as they are mortal. Therefore, there is very little distance remaining before the rational soul is entirely separated from the body. It is therefore the **ultimate form**, since above it there is no other form of the body, while below it there are many forms arranged so that, approaching this soul step by step, they are raised up as if above matter.

->The Epicurean’s objection and the response, concerning forms most like God.<-
### Chapter IV.

"Are we dreaming?" says **Epicurus**, when we assert that forms can in any way exceed the matter by which they are sustained. He thinks they are so entirely swallowed up by matter that it is impossible for even the most excellent form to perform any action beyond the material realm. 

We, however, believe that all the works of nature (as **Plato** writes in the *Philebus* and **Aristotle** confirms) are perfected by a certain divine intelligence. This intelligence revolves the heavens like its instruments and, as Plato says, drives the "celestial chariot," and from there it shapes this lower matter of the elements. Just as in the arts the form of a work has a triple grade—first in the mind of the craftsman, second in the instruments he moves, and third in the matter shaped by them—so too the forms of things which God generates or creates here through the motions of the heavens are first in God Himself, then in the heavens as if in streams or seats, and finally in this lower matter. 

It is necessary for this matter, since it is so moved by divine intelligence, to receive and display some most exact reflection of that divine intelligence. We see this even in nature and the arts. For the vital nature of the soul moves the matter of the food we consume through natural heat (acting as an instrument) and makes that food "vital" or living. This life granted to the food does not imitate the form of the *heat*, but the form of the *soul*. For heat does not generate life on its own. Similarly, a painter, using his instrument—the brush—marks a form onto a wall; that form is not similar to the brush, but rather to his mind, which first conceived it and later gave it birth. Therefore, both according to nature and according to art, the form of the work reflects the form of the agent who made it. 

Yet in this, we find a triple grade. We see one form closer to matter than to the agent, another closer to the agent than to matter, and some middle form. Take a natural example: the soul, through its instrument of natural heat, bestows a triple form on digested food. To the thicker parts of the food, it bestows the form of bones. To the thinnest parts, it mostly applies the form of its own **spirit** <note><term>Spirit</term>: In Ficino's philosophy, "spiritus" is a subtle, airy vapor that serves as the physical link between the immaterial soul and the heavy body.</note>, because it creates spirit from them. Finally, to the middle parts, it provides the form of flesh and nerves.

<summary>Ficino defines the rational soul as the "ultimate form" that naturally seeks divine truths over material sensations. He refutes Epicurean materialism by arguing that nature acts like a divine artist, imprinting higher spiritual forms onto lower matter through a hierarchical process.</summary>

<keywords>ultimate form, rational soul, Epicureanism, materialism, Platonic Ideas, divine intelligence, spiritus, hierarchy of nature, Phaedo, Philebus</keywords>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 10.

That natural heat <note>original: "naturalis ille calor"; in Renaissance medicine, this was the internal heat that maintained life and digestion</note> performs all these functions, not by its own power, but by the power of the soul. By its own nature, heat only burns and dissolves, but for works of this kind, it is tempered by the soul’s virtue. The form of **bones** is the most remote from the soul and closest to matter. Indeed, there is no sensation in the bones. The form of **flesh** and **nerves** is closer to the soul than that of the bones, for sensation occurs through these. I mean these five senses, which nonetheless do not depart very far from the body, since they never act except when external bodies are present. Finally, the form of the **spirits** <term>spirits: "spiritus," thin, vaporous substances believed to carry the soul's commands to the limbs and bring sensory data back to the brain</term> is closest to the soul, seeing as these serve the imagination and phantasy—the more excellent powers of the soul—in a certain way.

You have an example of this in nature; take an additional example from the arts. Surely the instruments used by craftsmen have only their own specific nature and shape; they do not possess the beauty of the craftsman's own intelligence. Yet through these tools, the craftsman’s mind carries out three kinds of things: some very close to himself, others very remote, and others in the middle. Truly, all the works of a craftsman that pertain to sight or hearing declare almost the entire genius of the craftsman. Those pertaining to the three remaining senses do so very little. For in the preparation of odors and flavors, or the tempering of bedding and baths, the intention of the craftsman hardly appears, if at all. But in **paintings** and **buildings**, the counsel and wisdom of the craftsman shine forth. Furthermore, the arrangement and, as it were, a certain "figure" of the mind itself can be seen there. For the mind expresses and shapes itself in those works just as the face of a man looking into a mirror shapes itself in the mirror.

But the artistic mind brings itself into the light most of all in **speech**, **song**, and **sounds**. In these, the entire disposition and will of the mind are most clearly designated; and whatever the emotion of the artist may be, his works are accustomed to excite that same emotion in us: a mournful voice often compels us to weep, a furious one to rage, and a playful one to be wanton. Therefore, these works—belonging to both sight and hearing—are closest to the artist's mind, while those belonging to the three remaining senses are, as we said, the most remote. Those operations pertaining to bodily exercises, whether for games or war, are in the middle.

From where else are art and nature so tempered for the arrangement of their works, if not from God, the institutor of nature and the arts? God, therefore, tempers His works in bodies in a similar way, so that He Himself generates a triple grade of forms in the matter subject to Him: namely, forms close to Himself, those most remote, and those in the middle. And since whatever moves matter moves it for no other reason than to raise it up into the **image of His own face**, and because God's judgment cannot be deceived, it is necessary that in matter which has been agitated for a long time, the face of God the Craftsman should shine back more expressively. Indeed, it must shine as much more expressively than the faces of other movers <note>Ficino compares God's creative power to other "movers" like the planets or nature itself</note> in other materials as God is more powerful than others in moving and drawing matter. Therefore, the face of God must eventually shine forth so similarly in matter that nothing more similar could possibly break through. As long as it results in something mortal, it does not perfectly fulfill the image. Surely it would be more similar if it were always similar—that is, if it rose up **immortal**. Therefore, some immortal form is made in matter. If any such form exists, it will be that which is the ultimate, which, just as it is most remote from matter by being the last, so it is closest to God, and therefore most like Him. There is no doubt that the **rational soul** is such a form. But let us open this matter more plainly.

## A clearer response regarding the levels of forms. Chapter V.

In the beginning, God affects and disposes **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality</term> in a certain way to produce the species of natural things through "primary qualities": through rarity, density, lightness, heaviness, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. These are certainly called qualities and preparations of matter rather than principal forms and species, because any of these applies to many species and they are often increased or diminished. However, the species of things (as the physicists agree) do not change in this way. Qualities often come and go while the species remains. Who would deny that heat and cold are common to many species of trees and animals, and that these qualities in living beings vary according to "more or less" while the species of the living being remains the same? They are, therefore, very similar to matter, since like matter they are subject to many species, and they do not by their presence alone distinguish the species of things from one another. Let them be called, therefore, "affections" and "preparations" of matter for receiving species. Therefore, through the extension of quantity which is familiar to it and common to many, matter is spread out <note>original: "pandis"; this is the catchword for the next page</note> by qualities of this kind...

He begins a technical explanation of how God prepares "prime matter" through physical qualities like heat and density to eventually receive the soul.</summary>

[which] opens its bosom. Indeed, once prepared through these qualities to receive species, matter immediately receives the forms and species of the elements from the Divine Mind, the architect of the whole world. It receives the species of **fire** when it has been prepared through heat, dryness, thinness, and lightness. It receives the species of **earth** when prepared through coldness, dryness, thickness, gravity, and the rest, each according to its own rationale. These forms of the elements surpass those initial preparations because they are the goals toward which the preparations were aimed, because they distinguish the specific types of matter, and they remain, in a sense, more stable. For we see the coldness of water change more quickly than the species of "water" itself, and similarly in other things. 

Nevertheless, these forms are entirely immersed in matter, because they are not resolved into other species or principal forms; rather, as soon as matter is affected by qualities, they are led into the lap of shapeless matter nearby. Because of the passive nature of matter, they are scarcely capable of a single action. What else does fire do except burn? Nor do they perform any work except insofar as those preparations of matter assist them, because they act no further than heat, cold, the dry, and the rest are able. Furthermore, they have only a single motion and a single place. 

Yet, there is a certain order among the forms of the elements. For the form of fire—because it is freer from matter than the others due to its wonderful thinness—is more effective in acting and further removed from the infection of passivity. Next, the Mind gathers these four elements into one, and through their various blendings, it creates various species of **stones** and **metals**, and similar things which are called "mixtures." The forms of these things excel the forms of the elements in this: they are resolved, in a sense, into other primary forms, and they are not created except in more carefully crafted matter. They also perform some work for which the forms of the elements and those dispositions of matter are not sufficient. 

For it is not through elemental qualities <note>i.e., simply being hot or cold</note> that <term>Jasper</term> <note>original: "Iaspis"; believed in the Renaissance to have protective and medicinal properties</note> induces labor, or that <term>Sapphire</term> <note>original: "Zaphirus"</note> drives away harmful visions, checks sweat, and confers grace, or that <term>Emerald</term> <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note> extinguishes lust, or that <term>Amethyst</term> <note>original: "Amethystus"</note> soothes drunkenness. For many other things that have similar qualities would produce the same effects. Rather, they do these things from a certain virtue <note>power or essence</note> granted to such species by the souls of the spheres <note>the celestial bodies/planets, which Ficino believed influenced earthly matter</note>. But they are not far removed from matter, since a virtue of this kind is physical and is transmitted through the bodies of the spheres. And although they perform some operation such as we have described, no work remains completed by them through such virtue. Moreover, these have one motion and one place, according to whichever element prevails in their mixture. Generally, among these forms, those are more effective in whose mixture the purer elements dominate the thicker ones.

The forms of **plants** follow, which are superior to the former because they perform a work of utility using the qualities of the elements as instruments, which the previous forms cannot do. They propagate plants similar to themselves in species, which is not granted to the forms of those mixtures <note>minerals</note>. By nourishing themselves, they carry out motions toward all parts of their location, contrary to the nature of the heavy elements that prevail in their mixture. They have obtained a body distinguished by different members—branches, shoots, a trunk, and roots—as if there were many virtues in these forms, requiring many and various instruments to fulfill their duties. 

They also manifest a likeness to certain celestial virtues and motions. To virtues, insofar as they perform some actions for which elemental qualities are not sufficient. To motions, because they produce movement in every direction, almost in a circle; and from an internal principle, like the heavens, they move their own bodies. Furthermore, they arrange all their members toward some principal part of themselves, just as the Mover of the World <note>God or the World Soul</note> acts upon all the spheres as one. But they still incline too much toward the matter of the elements, because they perform no work unless they use the forms of the elements by heating, cooling, and so on in the same manner.

The **souls of brutes** <note>animals</note> follow, which are superior to the souls of plants because they are similar to the celestial nature not only in moving, but also in a sense in knowing. Those celestial virtues know all things; the souls of beasts also know something, and they have a spiritual operation. For the act of sense and imagination is "spiritual" <note>incorporeal or involving "spiritus"</note> through the spiritual images of the objects themselves. Nor do they perform the act of sensing through any quality of the elements; for when they sense something, they do not sense by cooling it. Yet these forms are still involved with matter, because they exercise the acts of the senses through physical instruments, nor do they perceive anything except what is physical and particular, and they always obey the utility of the body.

Finally, the **soul of man** towers over all of these; it becomes similar to the celestial minds not only in cognition, but even in the *kind* of cognition it possesses. For it understands, just as they do. For which operation neither the qualities of the elements nor any instrument...

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 10

...something corporeal composed of them converges. This signifies above all else that the nature of this mind is excluded from the shackles of matter, since it has been granted an operation that is free from any commerce with matter. For matter indeed hinders the power of knowing; this is clear because the forms of the elements, of mixtures, and of plants—which are close to matter—know nothing. Even in animals, those parts serve more senses where thicker matter is less prevalent, such as the head; there, the sense becomes sharper where the instrument is purer and the **spirits** <note>original: "spiritus" — in Renaissance medicine, these were subtle, vapor-like substances that carried sensory information through the nerves</note> are most abundant. For this reason, sight—being purer than the rest—perceives more quickly and sharply, and imprints the marks of things more deeply within us. Therefore, we recognize things more clearly after a long time through those things which pertain to sight than through the evidence of the other senses. Even in our dreams, things seen offer themselves to us more often than things heard. 

Matter does not only hinder the power of knowing, but also the object to be known. For this reason, when the very mass of things weighs upon a sense, we perceive it either not at all or only with difficulty. Furthermore, the forms of things offer themselves to us first, and through them we understand matter, as it were, by implication. Moreover, we necessarily infer privations through habits, and matter through a certain relation to form. However, we do not think of all forms through a relation to matter, which signifies that matter depends on the genus of forms, and that there are some forms free from matter. Again, we know things most clearly and firmly when we contemplate the very **rational principles** <note>original: "rationes" — the underlying logical or divine blueprints of things</note> of things without the conditions of matter. 

If matter is an obstacle both to the power of knowing and to the object of knowledge, it follows that the soul which perceives and imagines anything is not composed of matter; indeed, it is not even a form divided by quantity, provided that in the act of knowing itself a miraculous and mutual union and penetration occurs between the apprehended form and the apprehending power. Surely, the dimension of quantity would prohibit all of this. And if we conclude through the lower forms of knowledge that the soul is not made of matter, we can conclude through the supreme knowledge—namely, through **intelligence**—that the soul is not "of" matter. Just as that which knows without matter exists without it, so that which understands without the conditions of matter must stand far apart from the "passions" <note>the passive or reactive states</note> of matter itself. 

For if the human soul were such a form that it was referred back to matter as its origin, it would not know any forms except through some relation to matter. But as it is, as if the mistress of matter, the soul subjects matter to forms when it relates matter to those forms; and like God, it relates subsequent forms to the **First Form**, and to God Himself. Indeed, the soul rises above matter most of all in this: that it also raises itself above itself, and is closest to God because it leads all forms back into God. 

From these things it is clearly established—the very thing we have been seeking for a long time—namely, that the **rational soul** emerges as the most similar to God among all the forms of the body. It reaches such a point that it cannot be made more similar, for nothing further can be made in matter once this soul stands out upon the very furthest threshold of the body. Indeed, it was necessary for some form in nature to be expressed that was most similar to God, if indeed the Divine Craftsman was to overcome matter in the way that <term>Plato</term> <note>the famous Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) whose work Ficino translated</note> handed down in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>Plato's dialogue concerning the creation of the universe</note>. He intends such a mind which is in the body to be a "tasting" or a fragment taken from the Mind that is outside of bodies, appearing like a certain face of that higher Mind reflecting in the mirror of more sublime matter.

Consider to what great similarity of itself fire raises matter, and by what degrees. The sphere of fire possesses a triple quality: **heat**, **light**, and **lightness** <note>the quality of rising upward</note> which presses toward higher things. That sphere moves the lowest bodies; into the thickest and most unrefined bodies it pours heat alone, as usually happens in stones. Into purer bodies it pours both heat and light, which it does easily in wood. Finally, into the thinnest bodies, beyond heat and light, it also draws that lightness toward the heavens. This it achieves in paper and linen, so that it immediately takes the substance of these things into itself as if they were most similar to it. Therefore, the form of fire in a stone is dark and unrefined, but in linen, it is bright and agile at the same time.

In almost the same way, the Divine Mind provides to inferior bodies **life** alone, as if it were heat; to more excellent bodies it also provides **sense**, as if it were light; and to the most excellent of all, it provides **intellect**, as if it were that lightness through which the soul rises into God. Thus, that Divine Ray, penetrating all things, is indeed in stones, but does not live; in plants, it lives, but does not shine; in brute animals, it shines, but is not folded back into itself, nor does it return to its source. In humans, it exists, lives, shines, and is folded back into itself. First, through a certain observation of itself, and then it is reflected back into God its source, by happily recognizing its own origin. Just as the ascent of fire has a certain end which it can attain—and this is rest in its own sphere—so the ascent of our mind, perpetually directed toward God, has a determined end...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind’s ability to understand abstract concepts proves it is independent of matter, placing it at the highest threshold of physical existence. He uses the analogy of fire's properties (heat, light, lightness) to explain the hierarchy of being, concluding that the human soul is unique because it can reflect upon itself and return to God.</summary>

...possesses, of which it may one day become a partaker; nor will that end be anything other than rest in God, which the soul will not achieve until it has departed from this life.

## The Objection of Lucretius and the Response: That the Mind can Operate without the Body. Chapter VI.

**T**wo impious men, Lucretius and Epicurus <note>Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC) and Epicurus (341–270 BC) were ancient philosophers who argued that the soul was material and died with the body.</note>, will disturb our discussion—as they are accustomed to doing—not with any reason, but with loud clamor. We, for our part, assert two main points here: first, that God creates the soul in His own likeness; and second, that He creates it in matter. Against the first point, Lucretius will object: if the mind is so divine, firstly, it is against its nature to be joined with a body to complete the species of an animal; and secondly, even if it is so joined, why does the mind never contemplate anything without the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia" — the faculty that produces and stores mental images based on sensory input</note> thinking as well? Against the second point, Epicurus will object thus: If God creates the soul in matter, it is therefore created *from* matter, and is consequently mortal. We respond to the first objection now (and will respond more extensively elsewhere) briefly in this manner: Since the lowest power of understanding in the universe is awakened to its own proper contemplation through the operations of the senses and the imagination—and since the senses and imagination act through bodily **spirits** <note>Subtle, vapor-like substances that Renaissance thinkers believed carried signals between the soul and the body.</note>—it follows that it is not against the nature of the mind to be united to this body to fulfill the human species on earth. This is especially true since our mind is said to be not a simple mind, but an **animating mind** <note>original: "animalis mens" — a mind that possesses the power to give life to a physical body.</note>, the lowest of beings and the one that gives life to bodies. Even if there is no inclination toward bodies in the general definition of a "mind," nevertheless, in the specific definition of this "lowest mind," such an inclination is included as something natural to it. This is because it was created on the boundary between higher minds and souls, and thus is inclined to give life to the nearest bodies. And because a thing operates according to the mode of its own substance—and the substance of the human mind is indeed entirely incorporeal, yet united to matter—it happens that while it does understand incorporeal things, as long as it inhabits the body, it often perceives them together with something that is in some way corporeal: that is, an **image** <note>original: "simulachro" — a mental representation or "ghost" of a physical thing.</note> of the imagination. Therefore, it usually requires such images. But when it has laid aside this body and been restored to itself, it will understand within itself. Yet the mind relates to these images of the imagination in one way before it conceives a universal concept within itself, and in another way afterward. Before, it needs them so that it may be stirred by their prompting to give birth to a **universal concept** <note>original: "universalem speciem" — the abstract idea of a thing (e.g., "Humanity") rather than a specific instance (e.g., "Socrates").</note>. Afterward, if it needs them, it needs them (as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> believe) as a foundation, or as a companion to the concept. Also, by the command of the intellect, a new image is often formed in the imagination that corresponds to that universal concept, in which that universal concept of the mind shines forth, just as a model shines in its image. However, perhaps the mind does not need the image of the imagination at all, as the **Platonists** believe, once it has produced the concept through the invitation of that image and retains it as its own. But such is the nature of twin eyes fixed in the same root, or hanging from a single hinge, that they open and close together and look at the same thing. In the same way, the mind and the imagination, which are the twin eyes of the same soul and very close to one another, open together and perceive things together, each according to its own mode. While the imagination thinks of "this man," the mind thinks of "Man" in general, and vice versa. And this is a natural concurrence. Nevertheless, with the help of the hand, one eye can look without the other; likewise, with a more burning zeal of study, the mind can be turned toward universal concepts even when the imagination ceases to act—just as it often happens through some disturbance that the imagination wanders intently through corporeal things while the mind is at rest. Furthermore, when the soul considers itself, it can then perceive its own act, power, and essence without any image of the imagination. This is especially true when it notices that it is understanding, and again understands that it notices this, and is folded back upon itself in a similar way without end. This is particularly true if, as some believe, it perceives its own intelligible concept and its own act through that very concept or act itself; in that case, it would certainly require neither an image nor a physical instrument. It can even judge the nature of an image itself without needing another image. If anyone should argue that the intelligence requires images of natural things while it considers their underlying principles, we might perhaps grant this for the sake of argument, because just as the fellowship with individual men accompanies humanity itself, so the thought of this or that man accompanies the understanding of humanity. However, we will not easily grant this in the case of divine things—such as when the angelic essences...

<summary>Ficino defends the soul's divinity and immortality against the materialist arguments of Lucretius and Epicurus, explaining that while the human mind is united to the body to "animate" it, it is capable of abstract thought and self-reflection independent of physical sensory images.</summary>

--- Page 264 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from Chapter VI, refuting the materialist view that the soul cannot function without bodily images. It then transitions into Chapter VII to address Epicurus’s specific objection regarding the origin of the soul from matter.</meta>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK X.<-

When we contemplate these things, are we always forced to look at bodily images? Since such divine essences do not incline toward this or that matter, so too our contemplations—by which we are made equal to them in some way through the act of knowing—are not necessarily bound to bodily images. For the mind does not properly borrow its knowledge of these things from bodies, but rather from **ideas** <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, perfect forms or patterns of all things, existing in the divine mind.</note> that are either innate—when the mind returns into itself—or infused—when it rises above itself. But who would say that the mind, in the exact contemplation of divine things, requires the support of mental images? In fact, by the meeting or intervention of such images, the mind is greatly hindered in this kind of speculation, and is often deceived; and if it does not wish to be deceived, it is compelled to scatter those images like clouds.

Perhaps, indeed, when the mind departs from itself through the senses, it reaches only sensible qualities. When it returns to itself through the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination that processes sensory data into mental images.</note>, it reaches the intangible **intentions** <note>original: "intentiones" — a technical term for the mental representations or concepts of things perceived by the senses.</note> of sensible images. When it returns into itself through reason, it reaches intangible principles that lean toward those intangible intentions. When it rises above itself through the intellect, like an angel, it reaches intangible principles already separated from imaginary intentions. 

What then? Does not the philosophical mind behold in the universe and in itself a certain angelic and divine knowledge that is free from mental images? First, it proves that such a knowledge must exist, and then it describes within itself what it belongs to, what kind it is, and why and how it happens. It even attains this knowledge according to its form, and experiences it while describing it. Surely such a description is a certain conception of the soul that is free from every mental image. For it is impossible to behold and define a knowledge free from images by means of an image. Next, the soul turns itself toward this very conception, acknowledging that it has now conceived it in this way. This "turning back" is much more absolute and free from images. Finally, it turns back toward this turning again and again, and always flies further away, step by step, from mental images. 

I pass over those more familiar points: namely, when the mind dismisses individual things and perceives not only the most specific species, but also the subordinate levels, the higher and highest genera, and finally the **transcendentals** <note>Concepts that go beyond the categories of being, such as "the Good," "the True," or "the One."</note>—dividing, composing, defining, and arguing. In these acts, the mind certainly strives not only to disregard images but is actually compelled to do so. It is furthermore worthwhile to notice that the lowest power of the soul is more joined to the body than the middle power, and the middle more than the highest. When the highest power of reasoning, through an act of human intelligence and will, firmly collects itself into itself, then the lowest power is for the most part separated from its bodily work. This is because the duties of ruling, moving, nourishing, digesting, and purging then usually lose half of their strength, or even the greater part. 

If this is so, it is necessary that the middle power must then be removed from matter by a much greater part, which is evident in men who are so abstracted during contemplation that they feel nothing at all. From this it follows that the highest power sometimes entirely leaves behind bodily things in this very act, and by its virtue, the remaining powers leave them more and more. Indeed, that which grows can eventually be fully completed, specifically when that thing is completed upon which it was growing. Therefore, the very abstraction of the soul from the body, which grows more powerful as the intensity of speculation increases, is also completely fulfilled when that intensity is fulfilled. It is fulfilled when, all other things being entirely neglected, only the First Truth and Good is loved and thought upon with the highest fervor of the mind. Then, therefore, the abstraction is completed; and the end of this abstraction, which separates us from mortal things, will not finally be a separation from life, but the attainment of the First Life. For things that accompany each other on a journey also accompany each other at the destination. Wherefore, the same harbor that receives the soul fleeing from the body also receives the soul in contemplation: this harbor is Truth itself. Truth is eternal; indeed, it is eternity itself. 

Let these things be said to Lucretius; let us proceed to Epicurus.

<margin>■</margin>
### The Objection of Epicurus and the response: that God does not make the mind except from Himself, and through Himself. Chapter VII.

<margin>■</margin>
**I**n what way, says **Epicurus**, does God produce this soul in matter, unless it is also *from* matter? But we ask him: in what way does the Sun produce light in the air, yet not *from* the air? Or a face produce an image in a mirror, yet not *from* the mirror? Or the mind of a speaker produce the meaning of a voice in the air, yet not *from* the air? Just as the Sun generates heat in the air *from* the air, but generates light not from the air itself (though it is *in* it); and just as the mind of a speaker generates sound from the air, but the *meaning* of the sound not from the air itself, but *in* it; so God draws other forms out from the bowels of matter, but the intellect...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind can achieve a state of contemplation entirely free from sensory images, leading to a "harbor" of eternal truth. He begins a rebuttal against Epicurus, using analogies like sunlight and mirrors to show how God can place the soul in matter without it being made of matter.</summary>
<keywords>contemplation, mental images, abstraction, Lucretius, Epicurus, divine intellect, First Truth, immortality of the soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book X against the materialist views of Epicurus. Having previously discussed how the mind can contemplate divine truths without physical images, Ficino now addresses the origins of the soul and the distinction between how God produces rational souls versus how nature produces lower forms.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

[God], who is the ultimate form, spreads [forms] over the face of matter; He does not drag them out from its depths. Epicurus should have considered that matter itself has no power to form itself (for nothing unformed forms itself). It does, however, have a "formable" power and preparation, which we call the **incipience of forms** and which the ancient theologians called **ancient chaos**. To this matter, as the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the universe by a divine Craftsman or Demiurge.</note> teaches, God applies a formative power—not as something belonging to the matter itself, but rather He adapts celestial and elemental influence as an instrument of God Himself for the influx of this formative power. Perhaps this divine influx flowing from God, penetrating the heavens, descending through the elements, and ending in the lower matter, is that very formative power which Plato calls the **reason of divine intelligence**. It is through the infusion of this reason that the "machine of the world" is established out of necessity and mind—that is, from matter necessary for bodies and from forms that reflect the divine mind and goodness in a most beautiful order. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> call this power sometimes the "instrument of God," sometimes "nature," and sometimes a **seminal power** <term>seminal power: the latent capacity within nature to produce specific forms of life, like a seed.</term>. That formable nature of matter is subject to this formative power. God, therefore, through a formative force of this kind diffused through the machine of the world, fits those forms to the formable power of matter itself—specifically those forms we have placed as "proximate" to matter and those we have placed as "intermediate."

On this point, every Platonist will observe a certain order in four levels of both forms and their subjects:

1.  **Rational souls** are ignited upon the pure face of indivisible matter through a pure ray of God.
2.  **Irrational souls** are drawn out into the light from the depths of matter—which is not yet extended in space—through celestial and vital influx added to that divine ray.
3.  **Familiar forms** of the elements and mixed bodies are led out from the "bosom of matter" (now extended through indefinite dimensions) through the familiar qualities of the elements.
4.  **Foreign forms** of the same are drawn out from the "womb of matter" (now extended through certain defined dimensions) through the additional foreign qualities of the elements.

We believe these forms—except for rational souls—are bound to matter because they have no operation at all in which the nature or instrument of the body does not somehow concur. They always propose the use of the body as their end, since they depend on the body while being fitted to the formable power of matter via celestial or elemental formative instruments. A sign of this is that none of them "turn back" toward God, as if God were not their proximate cause, but rather a distant one. 

However, we conjecture that the **rational soul** is made by God without any instruments primarily because it turns directly back toward God, which we shall declare in what follows. Therefore, instruments concur not for the production of the human soul, but for the preparation of the matter in which the human soul is to dwell. God produces the soul by Himself once that matter is prepared. Plato teaches this in his book *On Nature*, where he maintains that the rational soul is granted by the Craftsman of the world alone, while irrational souls are also granted by His ministers who assist in this work. Aristotle also followed his teacher in this, saying in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*:

> When a human is generated, the intellect is infused from without, and it alone is divine, for its operation is not carried out through anything corporeal.

It is as if the intellect is not squeezed out from the innermost bosom of matter, as he thinks other forms are. Therefore, God Himself infuses this without an instrument. You have an example of this in the light of the Sun and in the soul. The light of the Sun, using heat as a medium, clears the air by scattering the clouds, but then it illuminates the clear air by itself. The soul, through natural heat, prepares food for the form of life by "cooking" (digesting) it. Once the food is cooked and prepared, the soul grants the form of life not through heat, but through itself. Again, the soul breaks the air using the tongue as an instrument; the broken air sounds, and by sounding, it signifies. That sound is like a kind of "animal" composed of broken air as its body and the **signification** <note>The meaning or concept conveyed by words.</note> itself as its soul. This signification, like a soul, lies hidden in the words; it is like a kind of life that is not "heard" in the word that is heard. From where is such meaning given to the sound? From the soul of the speaker itself. But does the soul give meaning to the voice through the tongue? Not at all. For the tongue is a body and performs only a physical and sensible task. It gives no meaning by itself—as is evident whenever someone speaks by chance without the mind attending to the matter. Meaning is an incorporeal and invisible thing. Otherwise, anyone who heard the voice would immediately know what was signified by the voice. Therefore, meaning, which is something insensible, becomes like a soul in the voice (that is, in the broken air as its body). It is created, I say, by the thought of the soul alone, not through the [service] <note>original: "obsequium" — referring to the physical action or compliance of the tongue.</note> of the tongue.

<summary>Ficino argues that while physical forms and irrational souls are produced through natural "instruments" and celestial influences, the rational human soul is infused directly by God. He uses the analogy of speech to show that while the tongue creates the physical sound, only the incorporeal mind can provide the meaning (signification).</summary>

obedience. And thus, while you pronounce the name "Plato," the air, once struck, is divided into several parts: *Pla-to-nem* <note>The Latin accusative form of the name Plato, divided into three syllables.</note>, which run through three moments of time. However, the **meaning** is not divided into parts, because it is conceived in a single moment within the speaker’s indivisible mind before it is even pronounced. This meaning often signifies vast things, even though it cannot equal their physical mass in terms of size. It also often signifies motion and time without itself possessing motion or time. When it is pronounced as a sound, while a part of the sound is being uttered, the majority of it has not yet been grasped by the listener; nor is it perceived bit by bit. Instead, it is only after all the syllables have been pronounced that the meaning of the whole is immediately understood. This meaning often remains perpetual in the listener’s intellect even as the syllables perish, just as it existed in the speaker’s mind before he spoke. Therefore, the meaning produced directly by the speaking soul is incorporeal. The "soul" of the voice is simple and, in a way, immortal, while the sound—fashioned through the intermediary of the tongue—is dissipated into parts and dies. 

If the Sun and the soul can achieve something in matter without instruments, how much more can God transmit a form to matter with no intervening instrument? And this will be especially true for the **rational soul** <term>rational soul: the highest part of the human soul, capable of abstract thought and free will</term>, which thinks and chooses somewhat without an instrument. This would never be possible if the soul were manufactured through the work of a physical instrument. If it is made by God through no medium, it is made by Him only through His own nature. God is eternity itself. Therefore, the soul is made through eternity itself. That which is made through eternity is eternal. And that which is closest to the highest state of being is so stable that it is furthest removed from mortal change; for death is the ultimate change. Just as in other classes of things, besides that which is "such" by its own nature, there are others which are "such" through something else; so too in the order of eternity, beyond God, who is eternal by His own nature, there are many things which become eternal through Him. Indeed, that famous **Timaeus** <note>The speaker in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the world.</note> teaches that such things are those procreated by God without a medium. Therefore, the human soul will be both immortal and inserted into this body like a **meaning** inserted into the air by God the Speaker. If anyone observes this "meaning," he understands the mind of God who speaks it.

### Objection of Panaetius and the response: that the soul is from God without a medium. Chapter VIII.

**P**anaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 185–109 BC) who famously doubted the immortality of the soul.</note> will perhaps grant us that something can be created by God in matter without a physical instrument, but he will not concede that our soul is made this way unless we show this again by some clearer sign. For he believes that the soul of a newborn is generated from the soul of the parents, just as the body is generated from the body, because children are often born similar to their parents in both physique and character. But the conjecture of Panaetius seems to hold little weight, because children are often born dissimilar in body, and very often in mind. Those who follow their fathers' morals do so by absorbing them through habit rather than by birth. And if some do not acquire them through use but still imitate them, they do not imitate them because a soul is born from a soul, but because the soul from a tender age "flatters" its own body, in which certain similar impulses arise due to the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific mixture of physical humors or qualities inherited from parents</term> of the parents. However, as they age, they change their morals for better or worse by their own judgment. 

Thus, the conjecture of Panaetius must be rejected. Since he would demand a sign from us by which it is more clearly shown that the soul comes from God, our sign will be of this sort: Whenever any object occurs to it, the rational soul searches not only for what that thing is and of what sort, but also what its origin is. It never stops until it has found its cause. Nor does it stop at just any cause, but it always investigates the "cause of the cause," so that it does not rest until it has reached the **Supreme Cause**. Every thing rests in its own proper end. The proper end of a thing is its own proper cause. For it is there that a thing is perfected, and all things seek natural perfection as their end. If they seem to seek a common end, they do not adopt it unless it is congruent and accommodated to them, and becomes their own; it becomes such when it is received in a proximate, sufficient cause ordered from above. Air does not seek Venus or Jupiter, even if it derives its origin from there, but it seeks the "concave of fire," where its own proper principle and domestic place reside. Other things likewise do not seek just any cause of themselves. For no things would stop until they were transformed into God, who is the first principle of all. Or if they were never transformed into God, they would move in vain and recklessly. Therefore, they do not seek just any cause, but the proximate one. For it is enough for each thing that its own species remain incorrupt...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a direct, incorporeal creation of God by comparing it to the "meaning" of a word, which exists independently of the physical sounds used to speak it. He refutes the Stoic Panaetius's claim that souls are physically inherited, asserting instead that the soul's innate drive to find the "First Cause" proves its divine origin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book X of the Platonic Theology regarding the direct relationship between the soul and God. He is demonstrating that because the human mind finds no rest in any created thing, it must have been created directly by the First Cause (God) without any intermediary, and its ultimate "homing instinct" is to return to that source.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...to preserve it incorrupt and whole. This state of preservation is maintained by a thing's own cause, provided that cause is sufficient and of a higher order. A truly highest cause, however, would transform the nature of a thing distant from it into a more sublime nature; in doing so, that thing would cease to be what it was and would perish. But things do not desire this; they desire to remain unharmed in their own state. Insofar as they persist in that state, they achieve a similarity to the First Cause.

To what end is this argued? It is so that you may understand that any thing comes to rest immediately only when it has reached its proximate <note>The "proximate cause" is the most immediate factor responsible for a thing's existence or movement.</note> cause, and it searches no further. Therefore, the mind, which finds rest in nothing except the First Cause, has no proper cause except the First. A sign of this is that the human mind turns toward God without a medium. If things return to their cause in the same way they proceeded from it, then those things that proceeded through a medium return through a medium; those that proceeded without a medium return without a medium. 

The soul is reflected back into God without a medium when it looks up to God—not in any creature, nor in an image of sense or imagination—but as absolute and naked above all created things. It looks up to Him as such when it argues that God is so infinite that He surpasses by an infinite interval everything that can fall into thought; at this point, nothing created is interposed between God and the soul. But how could the soul's gaze be fixed on God without a medium, unless the power of gazing had also proceeded from Him without a medium? 

If it seems to some that the soul needs intermediaries to reach Him, because it ascends to God through the arrangement of the world and the orders of angels, know this: the soul does not use these intermediaries to gaze upon God in or through them (as one might look at the Sun reflected in water or through a glass), but rather as certain steps. These steps allow the soul—which once fell below its true self—to return to its own citadel. Having returned there, it sees God without a medium. Furthermore, it is invited by the arrangement of the world to set aside the "cult of the body" and return to its own reason. It is warned by the investigation or inspiration of angels to set aside the accustomed wandering of reason and betake itself to the light once divinely infused into it. Having turned back, it gazes upon God through the light of God itself, just like one who, through a ray of the Sun, no longer looks at the colors of bodies, but looks at the Sun itself. Of this, Zoroaster says:

> You must hasten toward the light and toward the rays of the Father, from whence a soul was sent to you, having put on much intellect. <note>original: "χρὴ σε σὺ σπύδῃ πρὸς τὸ φέγγος καὶ πρὸς πατρὸς αὐγὰς ἔνθεν ἐπέμφθη σοι ψυχὴ πολὺν ἐσαμένη νοῦν." These lines are from the *Chaldaean Oracles*, a collection of mystical verses Ficino attributed to Zoroaster.</note>

That is: You must ascend to the light itself and the rays of the Father. From whence the soul was infused into you, surrounded by the great light of the mind.

That the mind eventually reaches this state is something we can infer from the fact that it separates itself from all knowledge of created things; it asserts that the divine summit stands an infinite distance above every concept of a created thing, no matter how sublime. While it describes God in this way, it grasps God according to its strength. The soul, therefore, possesses a certain power capable of receiving God without a medium. This power is granted by God alone. For He who alone forms, He alone disposes. He who fills, He himself expands. It is just like the sight: it receives that innermost ray (implanted from its origin, by which it sees the light of the Sun most closely) daily from that same light of the Sun. Thus, the power capable of God needs no medium beyond God to receive God, just as the visual ray needs no medium to receive the solar ray, because ray comes from ray, and the power capable of God comes from God with no medium interposed. 

Thus far, we have proven our proposition chiefly through the **intellect** <term>intellect: the power of the soul to grasp universal truths and divine reality</term>. Now, we prove the same thing through the **will** <term>will: the soul's power of desire or "appetite" for the good</term>. Every appetite is filled by the possession of its cause. For the same thing that creates the thirst of desire by "making" a thing, extinguishes that thirst by "perfecting" it. The will can be filled only by the possession of the **infinite good**. The will desires the good only as far as the intellect offers it. The intellect finds the common nature of the good itself, separated from the narrow limits of all participating things; for this reason, the good remains infinite in itself. It is also diffused into infinity, since goodness can be communicated to innumerable things in infinite ways. 

If the will desires the good as far as the intellect offers it, and the intellect offers infinite good and infinite goods, it follows that the will desires just as much. Therefore, it is filled only by the possession of the infinite good. Furthermore, just as the object of the intellect is Being itself under the aspect of the True, so the object of the will is Being itself under the aspect of the Good. Because every power can be satisfied only by that in which the complete nature of its object is found, it follows that the intellect and the will can be satisfied by God alone, in whom alone is the complete nature of truth and goodness. And because the intellect always wanders from one truth to another, and the will is carried from some goods to others, it is clear enough that rest can be obtained only from that which embraces all such things. For a stable state [habitus] stops motion, and an infinite state stops a somehow unending motion.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is a direct creation of God because it can only find satisfaction and "rest" in the infinite. He uses the metaphors of solar rays and the Chaldaean Oracles to show that the soul returns to God without intermediaries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book X of the Platonic Theology. Having previously argued that the soul finds no rest in finite things, he now concludes that the soul’s capacity for the infinite proves it was created directly by God, making it immortal by nature.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK X.

## ## THE SOUL’S DIRECT RELATION TO GOD ##

Finally, a legitimate intellect is one that understands things as they truly are, and a legitimate will is that which desires things according to their true desirability. Now, things exist as they are ordered by God, and they are desirable insofar as they are ordered toward God. Therefore, neither the intellect nor the will can find rest in the things themselves. Instead, the intellect resolves things back into God, and the will refers them back to God. By a natural instinct, God alone is proposed to the intellect as the object to be beheld, and God alone is proposed to the will as the object to be loved. If only infinite goodness is capable of filling the capacity of the will, then surely only infinite goodness could produce the nature of the will—especially since the will sometimes joins itself to infinite goodness without any medium <note>In this context, "without a medium" means there is no intermediary or "middle-man" between the soul and God.</note>. It does this most clearly when the intellect no longer proposes "this" or "that" specific good to the will, nor shows it a mere heap of all goods gathered together, but rather reveals the very fountain of goodness itself, from which the harvests of such a heap first sprouted.

Furthermore, no effect extends itself beyond the reach of its cause. The human mind transcends any finite thing because, whatever finite truth or good you offer it, the intellect is capable of understanding more, and the will is capable of desiring further. Therefore, no finite thing can be the cause of the soul. This seems most strongly confirmed by the fact that a particular cause or mover cannot produce a power or inclination that tends toward the universal. Since there is in the intellect a power for universal truth, and in the will an inclination toward universal good, it is perfectly clear that the intellect and the will are not made or moved by any created thing. For whatever is created is merely a particular truth or a particular good. Can the mind not reject any particular good, even if it cannot reject the universal good? What does this mean, except that the soul is subject to the action and command of the universal good alone? 

Let us conclude, therefore, through the acts and turnings of the intellect and will, that the human soul came forth from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note> into the light, produced by God with no intervening medium. We conclude also that the infinite power of God, which produced the soul, is in a certain way so grafted into the soul itself that it becomes as if the soul's own natural power. Through this power, the soul turns itself toward God as often as it wishes. The Platonists <note>The "Platonists" refers to the school of philosophy following Plato, which Ficino spent his life translating and reconciling with Christianity.</note> believe that it requires no less infinite power for a person to betake themselves to the infinite God—and to recognize and love the infinite as such—than it does to create something out of nothing. By His infinite power, God created the soul from nothing; by that same infinite power, the soul reaches back to the very divine power that procreated it. Whether this infinite power was infused into the soul once and for all, or is rather continually poured in and preserved by God, it demonstrates that the soul is a participant in infinite power. It is "capable" of the infinite (so to speak) in such a way that it reaches the infinity of God through this very gift.

We know that the infinity of God is whole, entire, and exists all at once. By contrast, the infinity of time is something that vanishes continuously and is continuously restored; it has partly flowed away and will partly flow in the future, never possessing anything in the present except a single moment. A single moment is surpassed by a "whole" infinity an innumerable number of times. Thus, the infinity of God surpasses the infinity of time by an unimaginably infinite distance. Since the soul reaches the former (God's infinity), it towers far above the latter (time). For this reason, the soul exceeds all the limits of time and lives perpetually. This is further confirmed by the fact that if God does not create the soul through angelic or celestial powers, He certainly does not create it through material seeds. Therefore, the soul does not undergo the "pestiferous" <note>Ficino uses "pestiferous" here to mean "destructive" or "decaying," like a disease that rots the body.</note> change of death.

If, therefore, you desire to worship your parent, worship the Good alone. Do you seek a parent? The nature of the body is not your parent, O soul. Indeed, you are better in proportion to how much you obey your true parent; you are more excellent in proportion to how much you oppose the body. It is entirely good for you to be with your Father; it is, in a way, bad for you to be with the body. No other soul <note>original: "animus". Ficino distinguishes between the individual human soul (anima) and a general "mind" or "spirit" (animus).</note> begot you, O soul. The operation of a soul is mobile and changing. If you had been made by such a thing, you would have a completely changeable substance; you would stop your progress within that very mutability and would neither demand a stable nature nor think of anything above the soul. No "manifold" <note>A "manifold" intellect is one that deals with many complex parts rather than simple, unified truth.</note> intellect created you, for then you would never reach the highest simplicity, and the attainment of that intellect’s level would be enough for you. 

But as it stands, you ascend through understanding and loving—beyond any mere intellect—to life itself, to essence itself, to absolute being. Mere "understanding" is not enough for you unless you understand both *well* and the *Good*. Indeed, the Good itself is sufficient for you without doubt, for you seek nothing for any other reason than that it is "one" and "good." Therefore, the Good itself is your procreator, O soul—not a good body, nor a good mind, nor a good intellect, but the Good; the Good itself, I say, which exists in itself, infinite beyond the limits of any subject. It grants you an infinite life, either from age to age, or at least from a certain beginning into eternity.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul’s innate desire for universal truth and infinite goodness proves it was created directly by God, the only infinite cause. Because the soul can transcend time to reach for the eternal, it must be immortal and independent of the decaying body.</summary>
