MARSILIO FICINO'S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

### Third reason. As the object is, so is the power. Chapter IX.

**T**hese four things—essence, power, operation, and object—follow this order: power flows from essence, operation flows from power, and operation seeks an object. Thus, a specific kind of essence, through its own specific power, operates in a certain way regarding an object that is suitable to it. It should not be thought that any power flows from an essence other than one familiar to it, nor that any operation is produced by a power other than its natural one, nor that an operation deals with any object unless it is similar, appropriate, and convenient. For why would that natural power of an essence, in its operating, desire one specific object rather than another, unless that object were more familiar, fit, and suitable to it? If it did not agree more with one thing than with others, it would either desire nothing at all, or seek all things equally.

Thus, the innermost ray of the visual power perceives colored rays through the ray of the Sun. The innermost air of the ears draws in "broken air" <note>original: "aërem fractum." This refers to the classical and medieval theory that sound is created by the vibration or "breaking" of air particles.</note>—that is, sounds—through the external air. The sense of smell, born in the misty vapor of the air, perceives the fragrant vapor in an apple through a similar vapor diffused into the thick air from the apple. Taste, submerged in the moisture of saliva, reaches flavors—which are either naturally liquid or liquefied there—through the dissolving of food in the mouth. Touch, adapted to "earthy nerves" <note>According to the theory of the four elements, the sense of touch was associated with the element of 'Earth,' making it capable of perceiving solid, material qualities.</note>, easily feels earthy and solid things and very bodily qualities.

You see that objects always agree with their natural operations and powers. You are compelled to confess the same regarding the mind: that the mind is free from matter, because its object is free from matter. Such is the universal reason <note>In this context, "reason" (ratio) refers to the underlying logic or essence of a thing.</note> and <term>idea</term> <note>Ficino uses "idea" in the Platonic sense: the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing that exists in the divine mind, beyond the physical world.</note> of every thing. Both the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy.</note> and the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle famously walked about while teaching.</note> call this the "primary object," because it presents itself to the first and direct gaze of the mind. They judge the "adequate object" to be the entire breadth of being itself, because the intellect runs through the whole universe of being by abstracting, dividing, compounding, and defining. Being, however, is common to all things—both incorporeal and corporeal—and is infinite.

And lest anyone be so deceived as to say that the intellect perhaps matches universal reason in some other quality rather than in its separation from matter, we must consider that it matches most in what it necessarily does in order to understand. What, above all, does it do? Certainly, it segregates both itself and the idea from the passions of matter. Nothing hinders the mind from understanding, or a thing from being understood, more than union with passive matter.

Furthermore, if not only such a power seeks such an object, but the approach of such an object also makes the power much more like itself—just as sight, being naturally bright, both seeks light and becomes brighter when light approaches—it follows that the mind is not only remote from matter and "ample" <note>Meaning broad or expansive in its capacity.</note> because it naturally and constantly applies itself to remote and ample things, but also that it becomes much more remote and ample because those things which are remote and ample strike, seize, and occupy it. 

But how far can it be segregated from matter? So far, evidently, that it escapes the passions of matter. For it naturally longs for the reason and idea of both every individual thing and of being itself, absolute and free from these material constraints. It can, by its very nature, attain that which it is moved toward. And finally, that "ideal reason" which exists entirely in eternity, since it is in God, can lift the mind that raises itself toward it with all its might

->entirely above the limits of place and<-
->time.<-

# PLATONIC THE-
## ology, on the immortality of souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,
#### BOOK XI.

---

->*First reason. The mind is united with an everlasting object, and receives absolute species, and eternal principles. Chapter 1.*<-

The very absolute principle <note>original: "Ratio"; here meaning the essential logic or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> of a thing is that which is first, directly, and properly understood by us in its actual state. That which is actually understood becomes more "one" with the intellect through an intellectual species <term>species<gloss>In Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, a 'species' is not a biological category, but the mental form or 'image' through which the mind perceives an object's essence.</gloss></term> than that which is actually seen becomes one with the sight through a visible species; and it is more so to the extent that a tighter bond arises from purer things. This bond increases further because a visible thing is indeed outside the sight, but the intelligible principle itself is present both to all the matter of the world that can be formed by it, and to every place (since it does not look to a specific location). Without a doubt, it dwells in the inner chambers of the minds that are closest to it by nature, whereby they are always influenced by it and toward it. 

If a single thing is made from the understanding intellect and that intellectual species (or the principle signified through the species), and if that species and principle—as such—is separated from place, time, and the other sufferings of matter, then the intellect in this very act will be removed from those same things. An act of this kind is proper to the intellect itself. A proper act accompanies a proper essence, and vice versa. Therefore, the intellect will be separated from all contagion of matter, not only through its proper act but also through its proper essence. And just as that common principle, as far as it is in itself, encompasses all space and time (even though it sinks down toward space and time when it regards matter), so the mind, which is naturally suited to it, even though it restricts itself to parts of space and time when it regards the body, nevertheless encompasses both as a whole as far as it is in itself. This is especially true because a species cannot be absolute in its power of signifying if the mind, which is both its subject and its source, is not also absolute; for every subject receives qualities according to its own nature, and a source pours its own flavor into the streams flowing from it. 

From this, two things follow. One is that the substance of the mind is not produced from the hiding places of matter. The other is that it is immortal because it becomes one with that species and universal principle, which, insofar as it is universal, flees place and time. 

Regarding this same point, let us argue again as follows. The intelligible thing itself is the proper perfection of the intellect, which is why the intellect in its actual state and the intelligible in its actual state are one. Indeed, as long as the intellect has only the potential to understand, it is not yet joined with the thing that has the potential to be understood; but it is joined when it is actually understanding with the thing already actually understood. However, it is joined with it (as the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who often taught in the "Peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum.</note> maintain) because the form of that thing dwells within the mind. But those things which share one form are themselves one. Therefore, a unity is made from the understanding mind and the thing understood, since the form of this thing, as such, forms the mind. Therefore, whatever belongs to the intelligible, insofar as it is intelligible, belongs to the intellect insofar as it is intellect, because the perfection and that which is perfected are of one kind, and they are always bound together by a mutual proportion. 

But the intelligible, as such, is necessary and perpetual. Indeed, in the act of speculation <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to the highest form of theoretical contemplation or scientific study.</note> we value nothing that is corruptible, because we do not believe we know anything unless we hold a certain and necessary principle of the thing. Those things which are necessary are perfectly grasped by the intellect, while contingent <note>Things that can change or be otherwise, unlike "necessary" eternal truths.</note> things, as such, are grasped imperfectly. For when the intellect affirms contingent things, it is often deceived. If it does not wish to be deceived, it doubts; and both acts—being deceived and doubting—are imperfect. Rightly, therefore, when it thinks upon contingent things, it is accustomed to doubt, lest they be changed in the meantime, and it must judge them differently at different moments. For they are changed in every single moment. For example, while we say that "Plato is sitting," he may have stood up in the meantime. Universal definitions of things, however, are perpetual, such as "Man is a rational animal." The properties of the species which are properly defined are also eternal, such as "Every rational being is able to reason." For such definitions and properties are always equally true.

<summary>Ficino begins Book XI by arguing that the human intellect is immortal because it unites with eternal, universal truths (species) that exist outside of time and space. He asserts that the mind must share the nature of its objects, and since the objects of pure thought are necessary and perpetual, the mind's essence must be as well.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the opening argument of Book XI, which posits that the human mind’s ability to grasp eternal, universal truths (ratios) proves its own immortality. MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...even if no man breathed on earth. The intellect sees these principles clearly, holds them firmly, and asserts them without error or doubt. And if it understands any contingent things, it comprehends them primarily under these universal principles; when it thinks of corruptible things, it does so not as such, but as eternal. Therefore, the intellect is everlasting, for it is joined to eternal principles and perfected by them alone. If the intellect grasps them, and because it grasps them, it has some proportion with that which is grasped, then the intellect will certainly have a congruence with these principles. These have neither beginning nor end. But if the mind had both a beginning and an end, it would have no proportion with them, since it would be distinguished from them entirely by opposite conditions. Therefore, the mind either always was and will be like them, or if it began to exist at some point, it will nevertheless never cease.

---

->*Objection of the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, whose philosophy was often associated with the belief that the soul dies with the body.</note> and the response regarding the union of the mind with species <term>species<gloss>In this context, the mental "form" or essence of a thing, rather than its physical appearance.</gloss></term>, drawn from absolute and eternal principles. Chapter 11.*<-

**N**or should any Epicurean stun us here by objecting that the sun's light is received by the eye, yet the eye perishes while the sun's light remains unharmed. Similarly, they might say that the universal species—that is, a principle signifying universally—and the eternal principle are grasped by the intellect, yet the intellect perishes at some point while the species or principle remains. 

We respond that the sun's light is not received by the eye at all, because not even for a moment is it held by it; when the sun sets, the sight loses the light in an instant. If the eye had received any light, it would certainly retain some of it, even for a short while, just as water retains heat for some time after the fire is removed. Therefore, we can affirm that light is *present* to the eyes, but by no means *in* them or *received* [permanently]. 

The mind, however, is said to "receive" that species and universal principle of man and other things for the very reason that it retains it in memory even when the man [the object] is absent. Add to this that light itself, insofar as it is light and visible, does not obtain this from the eyes. For it is such by its own nature, and the eyes follow from it so that they may become bright and see. However, that universal species of "man"—the very fact that it is universal—does not come from individual human persons, in whom whatever exists is particular. Yet it is universal in the mind. Therefore, it is from the mind that it becomes universal. 

But how is this so? Especially as it pleases Aristotle <note>Ficino often reconciles Plato with Aristotle; here he uses Aristotle’s theory of the intellect to explain the soul's power.</note>, our mind has two powers: one active <term>agent intellect<gloss>intellectus agens; the part of the mind that actively creates concepts.</gloss></term>, the other capable <term>passive intellect<gloss>intellectus possibilis or capax; the part that receives and stores those concepts.</gloss></term>. The active power is that which creates universal species; the capable power is that which receives them once conceived by the active power. 

Therefore, when the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> gazes upon this specific image <term>simulacrum<gloss>A mental likeness or representation of a specific physical object.</gloss></term> of a man, such as Socrates, the light of that active power immediately strikes that image, not unlike a ray of the sun striking water. And just as this sunbeam, reflected from the water onto the opposite wall, produces a bright and trembling circle there, so the light of the active power, striking the particular image of a man conceived by the imagination and reflected from that image into the capable power of the intellect, produces a certain species within it. This species no longer refers to Socrates here in this place and time, but to the nature of man equally common to all persons, freed from certain limits of place and time. Here, both the species itself is universal, and the nature represented through it is universal. In this, the marvelous power of the intellect appears.

Surely, since the intellect creates a species free from matter, place, and time—and thus receives into itself something in a way eternal—through which it also apprehends a similar nature, why should it not itself be free from these same things and be everlasting? Finally, those things which the intellect reaches, being so separated [from matter]—if they are such by their own nature, then the intellect is also such. For when it reaches separated things, it is then where they are; therefore, it is also separated. But if those things are by nature enslaved to those passions [of matter], but the intellect frees them by its own power, it is much more and much earlier free itself, so that it may free the others. 

Tell me, why can the form of any thing not become one with the intellect before it is entirely separated from matter, unless because the intellect itself is much earlier and much more separated from matter? In what way it becomes one from that species and the intellect, the comparison we brought in about the sunbeam and the water teaches us. Indeed, that bright and trembling circle born therefrom is not sufficiently united to the wall, because the nature of that brightness and of the wall is too different. But if it falls upon a mirror, it will be more tightly united. Finally, if it returns to the light of the sun itself, from which that ray had been sent down which created the bright circle, it will unite entirely into one. But what is that species among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> which the intellect produced, if not a certain spark [produced] when the image of that which [comes] from things...

Ficino refutes Epicurean objections by distinguishing between fleeting sensory perception and the mind's ability to create and retain universal truths independent of matter.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 11.

...which the imagination had gathered, then what of that active power through which that mind gave birth? What then is our mind, but a certain spark <note>original: *scintilla*</note> of the higher mind? Therefore, that mental form is infused into our mind just as a spark of fire is a spark of a greater fire, and as that brilliant circle is infused by the light of the Sun by whose ray it was procreated. For this reason, the mind and that form become one, just as one flame is made from two joined sparks, or one light from the rays of two candles, or one splendor from that brilliant circle and the light of the Sun. Furthermore, that which is thus united to eternal things through a mental form becomes, without controversy, eternal, especially for this reason: that the intellect, in the act of understanding, is perhaps not only joined with the eternal thing understood, but is also itself the very eternal thing which is understood.

For it is in a sense the same ray that strikes the water from on high, which shines in the water, and which is reflected back into the air; where, having been poured back into itself, if it were to gain the power of sight, it would immediately see that very brightness of its own which overflowed from the water. It would do the same if it bounced back from gold or silver. For it will always see its own brightness, though affected in various ways according to the variety of objects from which it was reflected. 

If we desire a more suitable example of those two powers of the intellect and this union, let us consider the eye of a weasel (he means a cat, which the common people call a <term>catum<gloss>The Latin word *catus* is the root for the English "cat."</gloss></term>), in which there are two powers almost as there are in our mind: there is in it, on the one hand, a transparency, and on the other, a spark; the former is a receptive power, the latter an active one. The spark shines outward at night, draws the image of this or that color from the bodies placed opposite it, and impresses it upon the transparent power, which perceives the object through it. Indeed, perhaps it does not so much perceive the opposite body as its own ray, which was unfolded and then folded back; and when it was being folded back, it leaped back into the eye, now painted with the image of the body. Therefore, although it may seem to discern now this color, now that, it nevertheless always discerns itself in a certain way, but reflecting in a various manner from various colors. 

What prevents that active power, which is the ray of our mind, shining out in different ways upon various images of the imagination, from being reflected from there into itself, and seeing itself affected in a diverse manner according to the diversity of the images? In this case, that mental form or "reason" which we understand to be absolute and perpetual is perhaps nothing other than the ray of the intellect reflected back into itself. It notices itself easily when it directs itself toward images, just as a face does not see itself unless it looks into a mirror, from which it is also reflected back in different ways according to the variety of the mirrors themselves—just as the ray of the mind is reverberated back into the mind differently by various images. But concerning these things, we shall speak more fully in the following sections.

->Objection of Epicurus and the response, that the mental forms are innate to the mind.<-
### Chapter III.

**P**erhaps Epicurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose followers believed the soul was material and died with the body.</note> will deny that those forms which the intellect conceives daily are perpetual, because they both begin to exist when they are experienced and cease to exist when they are consigned to oblivion. We, however, following the opinion of our Plato, think it sufficient to say that if those forms are "born," they are produced by the perpetual principles of the soul, and they refer back to the eternal Ideas <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things.</note> above the soul. 

**The first reason.** Surely sensing and understanding, because they are vital operations, proceed from an intrinsic and vital principle—an active principle, I say. For there are certain operations common to both living things and those lacking life, such as generation, alteration, and change of place. Those things that lack life undergo such operations rather than performing them. For they do not in any way generate themselves, or alter themselves, or move themselves. Living things, however, perform these actions within themselves, because by nourishing and growing they alter themselves and generate something within themselves, and by judging and desiring they change their location. 

If nature ought to equip living things better for their own specific actions than for common ones—and that which is active is better equipped than that which is passive—and since nature has granted them an active principle for common operations, it has much more so disposed them for their own specific actions, namely sensation and intelligence, so that they might act through them rather than merely be acted upon. For this reason, neither the mind nor even the senses (as is pleasing to most Platonists) are formed by external bodies in order to perceive anything. But just as the life-giving part of the soul alters, generates, nourishes, and increases through implanted seeds, so the inner sense and the mind judge all things through formulas <note>Innate concepts or "mental blueprints" that exist in the mind from birth.</note> that are indeed innate, but are excited by external things. Nor is this judgment anything other than a trans-

the positioning of a form from potentiality into act. For no operation of an agent should transcend its limits. Therefore, a life-giving and internally remaining operation does not come from an external principle lacking life, but from one that is internal and vital. Indeed, a sign that the lower sense is quite effective is taken from this: that it composes, divides, moves through reasoning, and by its own affection turns the body into contrary qualities. A sign that the mind is most especially effective is taken from Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose *Consolation of Philosophy* deeply influenced Ficino's view on the soul's independence from the body.</note> against the Stoics <note>The Stoics believed the mind was a "blank slate" that only received impressions from the outside; Ficino, following the Platonic tradition, argues the mind is active and creative.</note> from the fact that, beyond those things which the sense does, the mind itself devises universal rules regardless of the nature of the objects; it descends by composing and ascends by resolving, and by referring back to itself, it refutes the false with the true. Finally, since different powers of the soul judge the same thing differently (for the imagination or phantasy judges one way, while reason judges another), it is consistent that the judgment itself follows the form and nature of the one judging, not the thing judged. And because the judgment exists as an act of the one judging, it is probable that each judge completes its work not from an external power, but from its own.

**Second Reason.** But let us return to the mind. Just as the images <note>original: *simulachra*</note> of individual things are not burned into the imagination by bodies—as we have also proven elsewhere—so the species <note>original: *species*—in this context, "species" refers to the "universal form" or "ideal type" of a thing, such as the concept of "Humanity" rather than a specific person.</note> of universals are not stamped into the mind by images. Instead, the mind produces them through its own power, just as the imagination fashions images by itself. For in what way shall an image (which is also called a phantasm) procreate something more free and more ample than itself? The image is indeed singular and bound to the conditions of matter, but the species is more free and more ample because it is universal. If this species, which is also called a universal, is not made from images, much less is it made from external things, which cannot form the mind through any other medium than through images. Again, for one spiritual species there must be one spiritual cause—or at least a unified cause ordered in a spiritual manner. But individual things which are outside are many and corporeal. And yet none of them, taken by itself, since it is strictly solitary and of a corporeal nature, will procreate an incorporeal species that signifies a common nature. But not even all the individuals joined together will achieve this. For they are scattered, and they do not have any such order that, being connected to others, they might arrange one series of causes. Therefore, just as a single simple thing is not made by the joining of stones, but rather a heap, so by a crowd of individuals there will perhaps be a certain confusion of images rather than one simple species. Furthermore, in any individual, three things are found: the nature of the species, the accidents which are not necessary to the species, and the thing itself composed of both. For example, in Socrates there is "humanity," which is called the nature of the species; there is whiteness and such-and-such a shape, which happen by chance to the species and are called "adventitious" <note>External or non-essential additions.</note>. From both of these the person of Socrates is composed. Is it from these persons that the common species—which is the equal likeness of all men—is imprinted on the mind? Certainly it is not imprinted from the accidents of persons (for it would then reflect the accidents of a man, not his substance), nor even from that nature which is subject to the accidents. For that is not the whole person of any man, but only a part of him. Therefore, such a nature is not predicated of any man. Who would say, "Socrates is humanity"? But we do say that Socrates is a man. "Man" is therefore predicated of Socrates—of the whole Socrates, I say, not of his humanity alone or his accidents. Similarly of the whole Plato, and of all others; where it appears that "man" himself, whom our mind commonly names, conceived within itself from all these whole persons, is much more ample than this or that nature of each person. Indeed, that which comprehends another and is more ample is not made by that which is both comprehended and is narrower, especially since that nature becomes singular in individual men. But what has been made singular does not create the universal. But is that species brought into us from all the whole persons together? Not at all. For that species looks upon as many as innumerable persons. But we have never inspected innumerable persons, nor have we received from certain persons that species which further comprehends infinite others. Nor can anyone safely enough prescribe a common rule from certain individuals; for whoever attempted this would be deceived, just as if someone, considering only the animals of the earth and seeing that they breathe, were to conclude that every animal breathes. Since, therefore, the species is generated neither from individual persons nor from their images, it remains that it is made by the intellect. The intellect does not generate it from a phantasm or in a phantasm. For a phantasm, because it is singular both in its being and in its signifying, if it were to become the matter or the location for the species, would likewise render the species singular. But it is doubtful whether the intellect generates it through the phantasm as if through a middle

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOULS. BOOK XI.

...positioned in the middle between the intellect and the species <note>original: "speciem"; here meaning the intelligible form or mental concept of a thing</note> to be generated. They think this cannot happen for this reason: because a middle cause, being closer to the effect, corresponds more with the effect than a more remote cause does. For example, in the generation of a human being—because the Sun generates a human through the medium of a human father—the generating human father corresponds more with the human child than the Sun itself does. Therefore, if the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty that processes sensory data into mental images</note> were the proximate cause of the mental concept, the concept would be born more similar to the mental image <note>original: "phantasmati"</note> than to the intellect. From this, two absurdities would follow.

First, that a concept born in this way would immediately choose the mental image and the imagination as its natural home (since they are more like it) rather than the intellect. Second, if the intellect did receive knowledge through such a concept, it would understand something singular <note>i.e., a specific, individual object</note> even more so and even earlier than it would understand the universal <note>i.e., the general category or essence of a thing</note>. This is because the concept would primarily report on the singular, being more closely related to the singular mental image.

Nor should we listen to those who place the mental image between the intellect and the concept as if it were some kind of instrument. Does not the active power of the mind correspond more with its own receptive capacity than a mental image does? In what way, then, will the active power form the receptive power through a foreign mental image? For an instrument of formation must be placed between the former and the thing to be formed; yet a foreign mental image cannot be placed between those two powers which are, in fact, siblings to one another.

Therefore, when the intellect creates that form, it produces it neither *from* the image <note>original: "simulachro"; a sensory likeness</note>, nor *in* the image, nor *through* the image. Perhaps it inserts some ray or power into the mental image of the imagination, through which that image—acting as a former for the mind—generates a form of this kind, which we call an "intelligible species." But we do not think this can happen either. Truly, that power received by the image would be bound by the same material conditions as the image itself. Thus, it would not generate an "intelligible form," which is free from those conditions.

And if someone says that the form is grasped by the intellect in an absolute <note>i.e., non-material or universal</note> way, even though the imagination itself did not create it as something absolute, we shall conclude from that very point (which we desire above all) that the intellect is not subject to the imagination like a thing being formed is subject to its former—since the intellect possesses forms in a more excellent way than the imagination is able to grant.

The result is that the intellectual form, if it is born, is born from the intellect alone, and without a medium. For if the mind generates that form and, by generating it, receives it into itself without a medium, it certainly produces it through itself, with no other thing intervening. From all this, it is concluded that **the intellect forms itself.** And since it could not form itself if it were entirely "formless," it is necessary that before those forms or notions (which it produces within itself at almost every moment throughout its life), there must lie hidden in the inner recesses of the soul other forms natural to the soul. These are as many in number as there are species of created things in the world, by which the soul is able to produce the intelligible forms of those species.

**Third Reason.** For certainly, things require specific seeds. Nature does not make just anything out of anything, nor does it make something out of nothing. Therefore, the essence of the soul—which is one and looks upon almost all things equally—cannot produce many and varied forms, some at one time and some at another, unless it does so through many implanted "formulas" <note>original: "formulas"; innate patterns or blueprints</note> that differ by species. Through these, it can create or bring forth one form at one time rather than another.

**Fourth Reason.** For the soul often brings these forms out into the light suddenly, by a certain natural instinct, without any prior deliberation or will. But effects that occur in the natural order display the same kind of form that their causes possess. For hot things are made by fire because it is hot; because a cause that produces something naturally from its own being makes the effect (albeit in a lower way) such as it is itself. Therefore, the mind, which by its own being naturally generates the universal forms of all things, seems to have obtained from its origin the universal forms of all things within its own essence, so that likes may be generated by likes.

For if there is one efficient cause of those forms (namely the intellect) and one subject (namely the same intellect), no reason can be given why many and different species are made, except that the intellect brings them forth as different through different "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; internal logical principles or essences</note> natural to itself. The diversity of sensory images is not sufficient to produce this variety; those images contribute nothing more to this construction than providing an occasion for work, as the mind is stirred to bring forth its forms by their presence. This, however, is nothing other than making those idle internal "reasons" more ready for action.

**Fifth Reason.** Furthermore, if the Divine Mind, which is full of all Ideas through its own essence, produces the soul directly <note>original: "absque medio"; without an intermediary</note> from that fullness, then the soul must flow forth from there full of Ideas. Truly, since God is hindered by nothing at all in the creation of the soul, He makes it as perfect...

It argues that the human soul does not enter the world as a blank slate, but rather possesses internal "reasons" or blueprints for all things, derived from its proximity to the divine.</meta>

->## MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...it makes it as perfect as it can be in such a genus. Certainly, the soul emerges more perfect if it descends into so difficult a task <note>original: "prouinciam," literally "province" or "jurisdiction," here meaning its earthly role or duty</note> full of notions rather than empty. From the beginning, it is capable of holding notions in that part where it corresponds with the angels. For just as it belongs to its temporal part to run about in continuous searching, so it belongs to its eternal part to have possessed them from the beginning—especially since the soul is closer to God than prime matter <term>Prime Matter: The most basic, formless substance from which all physical things are made; the "clay" of the universe.</term> is. Therefore, if matter receives all forms <note>original: "species"</note> from that source, and takes them as soon as it is prepared, it is necessary that the soul also receives them all. Indeed, the soul is prepared to receive all things as soon as it receives being from God. For its essence is simple and stable above time; therefore, it cannot be increased or made "more prepared" through the passage of time. Zoroaster <note>A legendary ancient sage whom the Neoplatonists believed predicted their philosophy.</note> sang of this thus:
> The paternal mind sowed symbols <note>original Greek: "σύμβολα πατρικός νόος ἐνέσπειρεν ταῖς ψυχαῖς"</note> in the souls.
And Orpheus as well:
> For the first nature deposited all things in Proteus <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἂν τὰ γάρ πρῶτα πρώτη φύσις ἐγκατέθηκεν"</note>.
Orphic theology calls the "third essence"—the seat of rational souls—"Proteus" <note>Proteus is a sea-god capable of changing into all forms; here he symbolizes the soul’s ability to take on or contain all knowledge.</note>. Also Archytas of Tarentum, in his book *On Wisdom*, says that man was born the wisest of all living things because God infused him with the Ideas <term>Ideas: In Platonic thought, these are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things existing in the divine mind.</term> of all things. Through these, the mind is able to generate notions of things, no differently than the mouth fashions the names of things through the tongue. So says he.

☙ **Sixth Reason.** Truly (to speak in the Platonic manner), the beginnings of all forms to be received lie hidden in matter. In nature too, through which matter is moved toward forms, the "seeds" of forms lie concealed. This is why within the natural constitution of a tree, the seed is enclosed to propagate a similar tree. In the seed, the whole tree to be generated is contained. The same happens in the natural constitution and seed of an animal. Therefore, in that part of the soul which nourishes the body and uses nature as an instrument to move and form matter, there exist—in a much more excellent way—the reasons <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the formative principles or spiritual blueprints</note> of all forms. Thus, from the "reason" of the head which is in the soul, that seed of the head which is in nature arises, and from this seed sprouts the form of the head which is seen in matter. And the same occurs in the chest, arms, and other limbs. If this lowest part of the soul is fertile, and it forms bodies itself and is not formed by bodies, and contains the principles for generating forms, will the mind—which is the highest part of the soul—be sterile? Or will it be formed only by bodies? Or will it lack the principles for producing species? By no means. Rather, just as the lowest part, which is closest to individual bodies, gives birth to individual and corporeal things through principles implanted in it from the origin, so the mind, which is closest to the incorporeal and entirely absolute minds, has principles implanted from there, through which it produces those species that are free from the passions <note>original: "passionibus"; here meaning the physical impressions or changes caused by the senses</note> of bodies.

**Seventh Reason.** For in this way the soul will hold the middle ground between divine and corporeal things, if it appears to share in both, and will possess within itself the principles of both types of forms: the intelligible <note>things understood by the mind</note> and the sensible <note>things perceived by the senses</note>.

**Eighth Reason.** Nor is it fitting for the soul to be inferior to bodies. Therefore, if bodies possess natural qualities before they acquire accidental <note>temporary or external</note> ones, the mind much more so has its own "formulas" in the intellect before it receives "foreign" ones from outside. A double community <note>shared nature</note> belongs to matter: natural and accidental. The natural is that nature in which individual things of the same species agree with one another—such as humanity, in which all individual humans agree. This community (as most believe) is perpetual and more excellent than any individual. The accidental community is that universal notion which the mind thinks about regarding that natural community, once all individuals have been excluded. This is "accidental" not only regarding matter but also regarding the mind. If matter possesses one natural community before this accidental one, the mind (being better than matter) likewise possesses the other before this one. For it is necessary that some common form in the mind be more excellent than it is in matter. Now, the natural is more perfect than the contingent <note>that which happens by chance or external influence</note>. Therefore, common forms must be present in the mind before those which it fashions upon the encounter with corporeal things. Often, however, while we are looking at our innate forms, we think through ignorance that we are looking at external or "adventitious" ones. This is no different than those who, due to sleep or some ailment of the brain or eyes, think they see things flying here and there outside their eyes, which are actually being moved and seen within.

**Ninth Reason.** Why is it that beasts, having inspected individual things, do not devise a common notion, whereas man does so from his own rational nature (by which he differs from beasts)? Unless it is because his own na-

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 11
->Q 3<-

...possess the seal of such figures? For if nature procreates forms through its own specific property and likeness, it surely procreates them through a natural matrix <note>original: "matricem," referring here to a creative womb or mold that shapes living things.</note>. Who would say that such a nature lacks distinctive characters?

**The Tenth Argument.** Furthermore, when we construct perfect demonstrations in the sciences, we are accustomed to demonstrate certain properties of specific things from higher and broader principles. However, among those notions that are newly fashioned by the mind, the broader a notion is, the further it is removed from actual substance; for this reason, the notion of a specific "species" is closer to substance than the notion of a general "genus." Thus, among these fashioned ideas, the one that is less common is judged to be more excellent. Therefore, there must be other notions in the soul besides these—notions that are both broader and more excellent at the same time—from which a true demonstration is constructed. 

Since a true demonstration proceeds not just from universals, but from universal *causes*, and since the notions innate to the mind are not the effects of a demonstrated cause, and since, conversely, forms within physical bodies cannot be universal, it follows that above both the forms in bodies and the forms in our minds, we must seek other forms in the Divine Mind, the creator of all things. These are the universal causes of all things, and the human mind possesses their "formulas" <note>original: "formulas," meaning the internal patterns or blueprints derived from the divine ideas.</note>, so that through these—acting as likenesses of the causes—it may refer its conclusions back to those divine causes by the process of demonstration. But more on the Ideas elsewhere.

**The Eleventh Argument.** This very process of demonstration always infers things that are less known to us from propositions that are better known, and those in turn from others, until it reaches certain principles that are known to the mind through itself <note>original: "per se nota," meaning self-evident truths that require no further proof.</note>. This is necessary so that the progression does not wander fruitlessly into infinity, and so that we do not weave a reckless circle by coming back to the same points. Those things which are self-evident to the mind shine upon the mind’s vision through the very nature of the mind. Furthermore, distinct demonstrations are made for each specific kind of thing from their own principles, and these vary across different fields of study. Therefore, according to these different species and fields, there are present in the mind principles of various teachings, known from the natural light of the mind. All subsequent knowledge is contained within these very principles. From this it follows that the soul, by its very nature, abounds with all teachings.

**The Twelfth Argument.** Just as trees and living creatures, and their limbs, sprout from their own seeds, so too sciences arise from internal beginnings. The mind should not be more sterile than nature, which brings forth its offspring from implanted seeds rather than pouring them out by accidental impulses.

**The Thirteenth Argument.** When we seek the truth among ourselves through questioning and answering, how could the reasoning which concludes the matter ever reach its goal unless something were first granted? But could anything be rightly granted if it were unknown? Thus this reasoning (as Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian philosopher whose work Ficino heavily integrated with Platonism.</note> says), unless it found something already known within us upon which to lean, could never lead us to the unknown; we would discern nothing at all through it. Therefore, there is within us, prior to the act of reasoning, a certain understanding from which reasoning takes its start.

**The Fourteenth Argument.** Is not our reasoning a mobile thing? While it investigates variety, it descends from one thing to another, and when it examines something it has found, it ascends from one to another. But every motion begins from rest (or something stable) and tends toward stability. Motion of this kind is a "complex" of notions. Every single thing has its own beginning and its own end. Therefore, because reasoning is a progression of notions, it is led back to notions; because it is mobile, it is led to certain stable notions. By their impulse, the soul seeks what it desires; by their signs, it finds what it sought; by their light, it examines what it found; and by their firmness, it rests in the things discovered. Thus, it begins from these notions in its seeking, and returns to them in its examining. There are, therefore, certain stable and perpetual notions in the mind, which are both the beginnings and the ends of reasoning.

**The Fifteenth Argument.** This applies not only to reasoning, but to any form of understanding. For just as the senses—which always know through "adventitious" <term>Adventitious: Coming from the outside; not inherent or innate.</term> forms called "accidents"—always deal with accidents (as the Platonists <note>The followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists like Plotinus and Proclus, who influenced Ficino.</note> believe), so conversely the mind, which defines the essences of things, understands through "essential" forms. And because the sense—which trusts in the deceptive and suddenly vanishing images of things—is often deceived and cannot distinguish a mere image from a true thing (requiring the judgment of reason for this), the mind must likewise lean upon essential "reasons" <note>original: "rationibus," here meaning the rational blueprints or definitions of things.</note> so that it too is not deceived, and does not require the judgment of some even higher power.

**The Sixteenth Argument.** Furthermore, if we know the angels, we cannot know them through species drawn from the senses; for since these sensory forms depend upon bodies, they do not represent angelic forms...

### MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...which do not decline toward bodies, it follows that we know them through implanted forms <note>original: "species," referring here to the mental concepts or "blueprints" used by the mind to recognize reality.</note>. For in what way do we judge that angels are natures that do not lean toward bodies, unless it is through forms that do not depend on bodies at all?

**The seventeenth argument.** Finally, intellectual knowledge is the middle ground between divine and sensory knowledge; therefore, it also possesses middle-ground conditions. God knows through His own unmoving essence; the senses know through moving qualities—that is, through external forms. For this reason, the mind must know through unmoving qualities, which are called **innate forms**. Ultimately, the order of the universe requires that, just as pure minds <note>Ficino refers here to angels.</note> look into themselves, while the senses look only at other things, the soul—which participates in both mind and sense—should look not only at forms outside itself, but also at those within itself. 

Where we are accustomed to say, in the manner of **Aristotle**, that the mind procreates new forms, we can more accurately say, in the manner of **Plato**, that innate forms are drawn out from the inner sanctuaries of the mind. It is the nature of "sisterly" powers <note>original: "Germanarum uirium," meaning powers that are closely related or born from the same source.</note> that they accompany each other in action just as they do in existence, and they mutually arouse one another to act. Smell and taste are sisterly powers; hence the soul is often invited to taste something by its scent. The power of desiring and the nature of anger are also sisterly; thus we are easily provoked to anger by lust. Even the "sisterhood" of the eyes causes them both to turn toward the same object at once. The sisterhood of sense and imagination ensures that when the sense is working toward something, the imagination works toward that same thing. 

Because of a similar sisterhood, when the imagination brings its own forms into action, the mind also leads its own forms out into the light. At that moment, the forms of the mind are not strictly "born," but rather those that were narrowly compressed open up more widely and bloom; those that were lukewarm become hot; and those that were shining by themselves only at the very peak of the mind begin to glow from a distance and shine brightly within the **reason** (which follows the mind), having now been made clearer. Therefore, what **Aristotle** would call a "creation" of forms, **Plato** would name a "shining forth" <note>original: "coruscationem," a flashing or glittering light.</note>, through which the awakened eye of reason is irradiated by the forms of the mind. That first flash in the mind is intelligence itself; the following irradiation is the very process of reasoning. Through intelligence, the essences of things are defined. Through reason, those defined essences are put together and arguments are constructed. But the mind cannot fashion true definitions of essences through the accidental images of things; rather, it builds them through the "reasons" <note>original: "rationes," here meaning the rational principles or logic underlying things.</note> infused into it from the origin of all things.

**The eighteenth argument.** Infused, I say, by the "reasons" of things which God possesses. These are in God as the very essence of God, understood by God Himself under various rational aspects. Therefore, the forms of all things are in God, and there they are nothing other than the essence of God itself, both in potential and in act <note>original: "habitu simul & actu," meaning they exist both as a permanent capacity and as a fully realized reality.</note> at the same time. 

All forms are also in the angel. They are not the very essence of the angel, but rather certain **essential reasons**—that is, those that always accompany the essence. There they thrive in both potential and act at once, because the angel understands all things simultaneously according to all those forms. Furthermore, all forms are in the human intellect. In this, too, they are called "essential reasons," all present in potential at once, just as in the angel; however, they are not all in act at once, because the human does not use them all at the same time. For this reason, the human intellect is called the "lowest" and is in some way similar to matter. Yet, because it is more excellent than matter, it possesses forms in an **effective potential** <note>original: "effectiuo habitu," a state where the soul has the power to bring the knowledge into use.</note>—which is not granted to matter—and this potential is called the "active power of the mind," because it brings itself into action. It is also a "receptive power," because it receives the perfection of the act. 

Finally, all forms are in matter. There they are also called "rational and essential," because they are "kindling" <note>original: "fomites," literally tinder for a fire.</note> or certain dispositions or regards toward forms that perpetually accompany the essence of matter. These are the "potencies" of forms—potencies, I say, capable of receiving forms but not producing them—and they are, in a way, the forms themselves, though imperfect. Hence, all forms are also in matter in a perpetual way according to potential, but not according to effective potential or act.

**The nineteenth argument.** Who would deny that the soul, from a tender age, longs for things that are true, good, honorable, and useful? Yet no intellect desires things that are unknown. Therefore, even before the soul seeks them, there must be certain notions within the soul through which—as if they were forms and reasons—it judges that those things ought to be desired. 

The same is proven by seeking and finding. If **Socrates** seeks **Alcibiades** <note>Ficino uses this famous pair from Plato’s dialogues to illustrate how we recognize truth.</note> in a crowd of men, and is eventually to find him, it is necessary that some image of Alcibiades exists in Socrates' mind, so that he knows which man he is seeking above the others, and so that he is able to distinguish the Alcibiades he has found from others in the large gathering. In the same way, the soul would neither track down those four things <note>Truth, Goodness, Honor, and Utility.</note>, nor ever find them, unless it had some notion of them—that is, of truth, goodness, honor, and utility—through which it might seek them with the intent to find them; so that whenever it finds what it had investigated, it may recognize it and distinguish it from its opposites.

<summary>Ficino argues that human knowledge is possible only because the soul possesses innate "forms" or "reasons" infused by God. He distinguishes the human mind's way of knowing from that of God, angels, and matter, and uses the example of Socrates recognizing Alcibiades to show that we must already "know" concepts like Truth and Goodness to seek them.</summary>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XI.
249

We prove this not only from our desire, our searching, and our discovery, but also from our judgment. For whoever judges someone to be a friend or an enemy is not ignorant of what friendship or ill-will is. In what way, then, would we daily judge many things to be true or false, good or bad, as we are accustomed to do—and judge them correctly—unless truth and goodness were somehow known to us from the beginning? Furthermore, how could many people, even those not trained in the arts, frequently and correctly approve or reject works of architecture, music, painting, and other arts, as well as the discoveries of Philosophers, unless some <term>form</term> <note>original: "forma," referring to an ideal blueprint or standard in the mind.</note> and rational principle of those things had been granted to them by nature? 

Comparison also shows us the same thing. For whoever compares honey to wine and pronounces one sweeter than the other recognizes what sweet flavor is. And whoever compares **Speusippus** and **Xenocrates** <note>Speusippus was Plato’s nephew and successor; Xenocrates was the third head of the Academy.</note> to **Plato**, and judges Xenocrates to be more like Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows the "figure" of Plato. In the same way, when we correctly judge from among many good things that one is better than another, and one appears better or worse than another by a greater or lesser participation in goodness itself, it is necessary that we are not ignorant of what goodness is. 

Moreover, since we often judge excellently from among many diverse opinions of Philosophers or others which is more like the truth and more probable, we must not lack some <term>intuition of truth</term>, so that we are not unaware of which things are more like it. For this reason, it is recorded that some in their youth, some even without a teacher, and most from only a few very basic elements of doctrine demonstrated by teachers, have turned out to be most learned. This could never have happened, as we said, unless nature helped them greatly. **Socrates** demonstrated this abundantly to the youths **Phaedo**, **Meno**, and **Theaetetus**, and taught that boys can answer correctly regarding individual arts if someone questions them prudently, since they are endowed by nature with the rational principles of all arts and disciplines.

->*Confirmation of the previous points, and furthermore concerning the Ideas.*<-
->Chapter IV.<-

**W**e can argue again in this way from those three books of **Plato**—the *Phaedo*, *Meno*, and *Theaetetus*—and additionally from the *Parmenides*, the *Timaeus*, and the *Symposium*. If one person is called "greater" and another "smaller" specifically and chiefly "by a head," that would be absurd. <note>Ficino is referencing an argument from Plato’s *Phaedo* (96d-101c) about "formal causes." He argues that physical things like "a head" cannot be the cause of abstract qualities like "greatness."</note> First, because a person would be both greater and smaller through the same thing. Second, because something would be placed in one category through a form belonging to another—for instance, through the form of a "head" into the form of "greater" or "smaller." It is better to call someone "headed" by a head than "greater" or "smaller." Finally, it is absurd to call something "greater" by means of something small <note>like a head</note>. 

Therefore, if a formal cause is to be asserted, a person will be called "greater" by **Greatness**. Similarly, we will not properly call the number ten "more" than the number nine by a "unit"—since we properly name a "one" from "unity"—but rather we shall say it is more by **Plurality**, and that another is less by **Fewness**. Likewise, we shall assert that the number two is created not by the division of one into two (since this state is sometimes claimed to happen by the joining of one thing to another), and in general one must not say that the same effect is produced by opposite causes. Therefore, we shall assert that the number two is created according to the Form, by the **participation** <note>original: "participatione," the Platonic concept where physical things "share in" or "reflect" an ideal Form.</note> in **Duality** itself. 

But let us leave these as lighter matters and proceed to weightier ones. If a color or a shape were **Beauty** itself, in what way could any color or shape be ugly? Likewise, by what logic would many subjects participate in one Beauty as a common thing, unless there were one common nature of Beauty that was both within the individuals and presiding over them—so that the beauty which is *within* depends on the Beauty which *presides*? 

Accordingly, **Goodness** itself is one thing, and the things that become good by participation in goodness are another. **Beauty** is one thing, and beautiful things are another; and it is similar for the other forms, which Plato calls **Ideas**. For there are many beautiful bodies, but Beauty itself is one. For everything that is primary and highest in any class of things is only one. Again, these beautiful things have two natures: first, the bodily matter which participates in beauty, and second, the quality of beauty. But Beauty itself is nothing other than Beauty, since whatever is primary of its kind in any category is nothing other than that kind. Likewise, these bodies are partly beautiful and partly ugly; for they are judged deformed by their very matter (which is something other than beauty), but Beauty itself does not admit ugliness. If opposites indeed flee from one another, beautiful bodies also change, and are now beautiful, and now...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 11 of the Platonic Theology. ## MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...on the contrary. **Beauty** is truly immutable for this reason: because it is nothing other than beauty itself, and insofar as it is beauty, it does not change. Thus, it neither turns into its opposite, nor is it ever deprived of its foundation and support, since it sustains itself. Add to this that all physical things can appear beautiful to some people but not beautiful to others; however, Beauty itself cannot be conceived as lacking beauty. Furthermore, beautiful bodies are divisible, but Beauty itself is indivisible. It is not "small," for then it could not form great bodies; it is not "large" <note>In the sense of physical magnitude or bulk.</note>, for then it would not fit small bodies. Finally, it is not corporeal, since it would then not be suitable for spiritual things. It is also not temporal, for then it would not exist in eternal things. 

However, Beauty exists much more in souls and minds than in bodies. But it is not "primary" in them either, both because souls are shapeless in themselves unless they are formed by the **Good**—whose splendor is Beauty—and because they desire Truth as something beautiful. Beauty itself, however, does not "desire" itself <note>Because it is already complete and perfect.</note>. Finally, this is because it is simply and commonly lovable not just to be an animal or an intellectual being, but to be well and to be good. Since the Good is the most alluring thing of all, it is the highest Beauty. Therefore, the <term>Idea</term> <note>original: "idea"; here meaning the divine, perfect blueprint or Form in the mind of God.</note> of beauties itself is above bodies, souls, and minds. It is one, simple, pure, immutable, indivisible, incorporeal, and eternal. 

The nature of all Ideas is the same, which we also prove here by another example. When a human being generates another human, he does not, strictly speaking, give birth to the specific "humanity" itself, which is considered commonly in both the parent and the child. If he did, he would also be giving birth to himself, who exists through that same humanity. Furthermore, a limited nature cannot generate an unlimited nature. Therefore, this individual man is not the cause of "humanity" existing simply as a concept, but rather he is the cause of it being propagated in that specific matter. It is necessary, however, that there be a common cause for the common human nature, and one that acts by its own power, as shown by its most orderly and stable composition. For this reason, above the particular agents acting within specific types of things, there must exist a **universal agent** that looks upon and directs the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem"; the essential form or "type" of a thing.</note>. This is also apparent in those things that are generated from visible, fertile seeds, as we have demonstrated elsewhere.

Many of the Platonists argue again from the objects of the mind in this way: Since our intellect naturally captures forms and understands <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes"; refers to the underlying logic or formal principles of things.</note> either as separate from matter or by separating them through thought, it follows that these common "reasons" of things, separated from matter, are the mind's natural objects. Since objects of this kind move, form, and perfect the intellect, they are established in a more excellent and truer grade of the universe. They are as far removed from mere fictions as possible, so that the mind—the judge of truth and the corrector of the senses—is not further from the truth than the senses themselves. For this reason, those "reasons" are rightly considered to be more sublime, truer, and more effective in nature than the intellects which are formed by them. 

But should those "reasons" in turn be called "intellectual"? Not properly so. Indeed, rational souls are "intellectual" according to their participation <note>Meaning they share in intellect but are not its pure source.</note>, while angels are "intellectual" according to their form. Finally, those "reasons" and Ideas are "intellectual" in terms of their cause, but they are <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibiles"; things that are the *objects* of thought, rather than the *subject* that thinks.</note> according to their form. For the "intellectual" relates to the "intelligible" almost as the one desiring, moving, and being formed relates to the desirable mover and the former. 

But where are they? Indeed, the Platonists generally place less common Ideas within more common Ideas. And finally, they place all classes of Ideas within **Being** itself, the first and most common of all beings and the most perfect, which they call the "supreme intelligible"—intelligible according to its form, but intellectual according to its cause. To this, they immediately subject the many minds that are intellectual by form, but intelligible by participation. To these, they subject the rational souls, which are intellectual by a certain participation, but in no way intelligible. 

Consequently, they judge that "Being itself" and the "Intelligible itself" are the same, since Being is the natural and adequate object of the intellect. Furthermore, they place the "Intelligible itself" below the first principle of all things. For the Intelligible is such that it can be grasped in some way, but the first principle cannot. They properly call the first principle **Unity itself** and **Goodness**. And because Unity represents an eminence and power set apart from all things, while the Intelligible represents a certain light already accommodated to intellects by a certain proportion, they think that Unity is something else, and higher than the Intelligible. Again, because minds desire both the act of understanding and the object of understanding (the Intelligible)—not simply, but to do so "well" and for the "good"—and because they desire the Good simply, for this reason also they place **the Supreme God** before Being itself (which is also the Intelligible).

## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS. BOOK XI.

->Q 5<-

I pass over the fact that the <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibile"; that which is capable of being understood by the mind.</note> relates to the intellect, whereas the **good** relates to the **will**. Therefore, the good is not only different from the intelligible, but even more excellent, for that which ravishes the will is more excellent than that which is merely grasped by the intellect. For this reason, they believe that "being" itself is perceived by the intellect according to its capacity, but that the **Good** instead draws the soul toward itself through the will, and once drawn, pours itself into the soul. And if the Good is "touched" in some way by the soul—which is already occupied in its own manner—it is properly touched through the "head" or the unity of the mind, which God (who is the leading unity of the universe) implanted in us from the beginning. 

However, to return to the subject: in the **Good** itself, the <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ideae"; the eternal, divine archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note> exist only as causes, distinguished from one another only by certain relative patterns. But in the **Intelligible** itself <note>The second level of reality, often identified with the Divine Mind or Logos.</note>, they exist properly through Form, and are further distinguished from each other by absolute forms. In the subsequent minds—whether they are separated from bodies or joined to them—these Ideas are more and more distinct through a certain gradual participation. In **Nature**, they exist as certain "lowest seeds" of the forms infused by the Ideas, and finally, in **Matter**, they exist as shadows. 

In his *Letters*, **Plato** calls the **Good** itself "God the Father," and the **Intelligible** itself "God the Son." **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the primary founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> also calls him "God from God," "Light from Light," and the "Reason" and "Word" of God. Again, in the *Epinomis*, Plato affirms that the sensible world was adorned by this kind of divine Reason, or Word (which he calls the "Intelligible World"). Because the Ideas are a single form in the first stage, but many forms in the second (for they do not believe there is absolute diversity of forms in the "First Form"), Plato—having contemplated how colors exist in light or how lines in a circle relate to the center—says in his *Letters* that the multi-form Ideas, which are absolutely distinct, exist *around* the first principle of things rather than *in* the first principle. Similarly, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, he says that the **Idea of the Good** (that is, the Good itself, in whose form all Ideas are a single form) is the cause of the "beautiful ideas"—namely, those which in the subsequent stages are many absolute forms, differing from one another.

**Plotinus** and **Proclus** <note>Another major Neoplatonist who systematized Platonic thought.</note> confirm the existence of these Ideas by the arguments above, and they place them differently (as they say) in the "First" than in the "Second." Certain others proceed toward the same conclusion in this way: In **Matter**, which is the lowest level, a shadow of the Ideas is reflected; but above matter shines the "face" of all the Ideas, whose fountain is God, the author of all things—as Plato’s *Timaeus* most clearly teaches, as well as the tenth book of the *Republic* and the *Parmenides*. For if the Mind and Nature are full of forms, and act through them (as is apparent in both natural things and man-made crafts), then surely **God**, who is the shaper of Nature and Mind, ought not to be formless. Therefore, He acts through forms, which we call **Ideas**. 

Plotinus and Proclus call these not only "exemplary" forms <note>Blueprints to be copied.</note>, but also "essential" forms. They believe that the Architect of the world uses no "deliberation" <note>original: "consultatio"; debating or thinking through a problem.</note> in fabricating the world. For they argue that such an operation would be imperfect; someone who deliberates about completing a work must have first conceived the work within himself in an imperfect way, and then sought out how to finish it. This is foreign to a perfect Mind. Furthermore, if the universe were arranged only by the shifting discourse of providence, nothing would ever be stable, nor would the motion of the world be perpetual and steady. Therefore, **God** creates and disposes the universe by His very **Being** (*esse*), especially since this kind of action is the first, most universal, and easiest of all actions. Thus, it must come from a first, most universal, and most blessed cause, wherever it may be, and it is most fitting for Him. 

Every cause that creates by its very "being" produces an effect in the next level that is like what the cause is in the first level. Since, therefore, the world is a connection of all species, it follows that the Architect of the world is—in a way more excellent than can be imagined—a connection of all species, and possesses the "exemplary forms" of all things, which are (to use their way of speaking) "essential" to Him. They confirm this again as follows: If **Art** imitates **Nature**, and produces works through the rational principles of those works, then Nature also possesses the rational principles of its own works. Again, since Nature lacks "reason" in itself <note>In the sense of conscious, discursive logic.</note>, and is moved and perfected by God, it receives its principles from the Ideas of the Divine Mind itself. And just as the principles of Nature are more internal to Nature than the principles of Art are to Art, so too must the Divine principles be at least as internal to God as the principles of Nature are to Nature.

They add that sensible forms are not entirely or truly what they are called. Certainly, equality and similarity everywhere participate in inequality and dissimilarity. True **Beauty** cannot exist in a subject that is in itself deformed and formless. True **Good** cannot exist where there is deficiency and a leaning toward evil. Furthermore, in the heavens...

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of Ideas, arguing that God (the Good) contains the blueprints of all reality. He asserts that God creates the world not through human-like deliberation, but by his very essence, acting as the ultimate "form" from which all nature and art derive their logic.</summary>

Here, he moves into a classic Platonic argument: that the perfect "blueprints" of things (Ideas) cannot exist in the physical, divisible world, but must reside in the Soul and in God.</meta>
