->MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

<meta>Catchword: ri do mi-</meta>

Philosophers refuse to admit that a true line, a true surface, or the true point of a center or a pole exists within physical matter. This is because the <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning the "rational principle" or "mathematical definition."</note> of these things is indivisible, and thus they cannot exist within a thing that can be divided. But our own soul possesses and gives birth to true forms; through these, it observes and proves how much other, "false" <note>Meaning physical objects, which are only imperfect shadows of the true forms.</note> things fall short of the true ones. For this reason, the **Soul of the Universe** <note>original: "anima uniuersi"; the Neoplatonic concept of a conscious force that animates and governs the entire cosmos.</note> possesses and generates the true rational principles of forms to an even greater degree. For where the power and intelligence are more excellent, there the conception and birth of forms are more distinct.

Finally, the **Architect of the World** <note>original: "mundi opifex"; referring to God as the Creator.</note> generates even more certain and perfect forms within himself; and (to use the words of **Proclus**) <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who deeply influenced Ficino’s thought on how the Divine Mind contains the blueprints of all things.</note> while God generates himself through the act of observing himself, he simultaneously generates all things within himself. Added to this is the fact that since the members of the universe harmonize with one another in a perpetual order, they are not joined and governed by chance, but by reason. That Reason which orders all things cannot be ignorant of itself. Otherwise, the "Highest Reason" would be irrational if it had no rational understanding of itself. Indeed, a reason that embraces itself through self-knowledge is more "rational" than one that abandons itself through ignorance. 

Therefore, that Reason understands itself as the ordainer of all things; from this, it follows that it always understands the principles and modes by which each individual thing is arranged. For this reason, the rational principles of all things exist within the **Highest Reason** of all. 

But did God know all things because he was *about* to make them? Certainly not. Otherwise, he would be directing his essential operation—his very turning toward himself—toward external things, and he would be dependent on something outside himself. Therefore, just as the **Sun** illuminates all things by shining within itself, so God, by understanding and willing himself, both knows and brings about all things. Who does not see that if, by seeing himself, he sees and makes all things, it follows that within his own substance there are **substantial forms** which are the archetypes and causes of all things? For in the very order of nature, it is always the case that an external action proceeds from an internal one. The resulting work is very similar to the action itself—just as the act of "illuminating" comes from "shining," and the "illuminated object" comes from the "illumination," being similar to both the illumination and the light.

Furthermore, plants and animals are generated from seeds. It is necessary, however, that the <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the underlying blueprints or "codes" that determine what a creature will become.</note> of the living being be present in some way within the seed, from which it is then rationally procreated. Yet, these are only present *potentially* in a physical seed. For a seed is uniform and almost formless, whereas that which is born from it is multiform and beautiful. Likewise, if a seed is divided, many whole things can grow from it, as if the whole things being generated were hiding within the parts. From this, it is clear that the **seminal power** <note>original: "uim seminariam"; the life-force or "program" within a seed.</note> hidden within the seed itself is, in a sense, incorporeal, and in it lies the principle of this movement and generation. 

It is necessary that the multiple blueprints of a complex living being exist within the multiple seminal powers, which we call **Nature**. For the "same," insofar as it is the "same," could not directly generate such great diversity. Moreover, it is necessary for these to be present *in act* <note>meaning "actually present" or "fully realized," rather than just a dormant possibility.</note>. For that which is merely "potential" is imperfect; it cannot be brought forth into something "actual" except by something that is already "actual" and more perfect. Therefore, there are individual blueprints for each of the specifically different parts of a living being, by which each is procreated in its own time, place, and order—and even recreated, if possible, if they are cut away. 

But are these seminal powers within the seeds of living beings the *ultimate* causes? Not at all. For the species itself is not created by any one of them; rather, a particular individual under that species is created, and each of those individuals takes its origin from another under the same species. Therefore, one must take refuge in **Universal Nature**, in which the universal blueprints of all their species exist. I speak of the "Nature of the Earth," the procreatress of all things of the earth—especially since physical seeds are often absent when plants and animals spring up spontaneously; thus, **incorporeal seeds** are needed for their production. 

To proceed in the proper order: let us refer each species of earthly things to the universal Nature of the Earth; likewise for the other elements. Then, let us refer the natures of the four elements directly to the **Nature of the Moon**, in which the blueprints of all elemental things reside; and the Nature of the Moon to the nature of the higher sphere, and so on in succession. Finally, let us refer all natures to the **Universal Nature** of the universe itself. In this, there must necessarily be the blueprints of both natural things and of all "natures"—blueprints, I say, that are both archetypal and effective, so that it may direct and lead all natures to certain ends by certain rules. 

However, "Nature" cannot be the highest reason and cause of things, both because it is inherently irrational (as is evident in our own nature), for it does not know other things, and because it is a cause mixed with its effect—just as if a carpenter were poured into the wood he was carving. For such a cause was necessary so that things moved by another external and common force might possess a certain familiar and internal power from a separate cause. Indeed, these things are not guided in a proper, distinct, and suitable way except through a power that is itself proper, distinct, and suitable to them—and finally, by a most excellent cause that operates purely and absolutely...

<summary>Ficino explains that physical reality is governed by "rational principles" or "seminal reasons" (blueprints) that exist in a hierarchy from individual seeds up to the Soul of the World and God. He argues that God creates and knows the universe perfectly by simply knowing Himself, acting as the ultimate intellectual source of all natural order.</summary>

<keywords>Platonic Ideas, Seminal Reasons, Universal Nature, Anima Mundi, Proclus, Divine Architect, Incorporeal Seeds, Rational Principles</keywords>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XI</header>

## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XI

[In the same way, the soul] which is to rule <note>This continues from the previous page's discussion of the soul's dominance over the body.</note> must be separate from the work itself in its essence, its existence, and its power, just as we see in the air that heat from the sun above is mixed in, but the light itself is not. <note>Ficino uses the sun as a metaphor for the divine: while its heat (physical influence) enters the air, its light (higher essence) remains distinct and unpolluted.</note> Furthermore, even if nature is irrational in itself, it must still possess the <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the structural laws or blueprints that guide how things grow.</note> of physical bodies. Through these, it can internally order, move, and shape individual things in appropriate ways toward a fitting end. Since nature is irrational in its own right, it must be led by that which is rational by its very nature, and it must be shaped by these rational principles. Indeed, it would be irrational to entrust the order of the entire universe to a nature that is itself irrational. Therefore, it is necessary that the principles of things exist so rationally within a higher cause that the cause itself, in noticing itself and its own attributes, possesses a certain and clear understanding of both itself and its principles. It would certainly be absurd if we were to possess the rational principles of ourselves, our works, and the universe, while the Cause of the universe possessed the principles of neither itself nor its own works. For this reason, if the Creator of the world knows all things, he certainly did not look at external things to perceive them; for his knowledge, by which those other things were produced, undoubtedly precedes the things themselves.

For who is ignorant of the fact that an external work follows an internal action? Thus, God, by looking into Himself, knows all things. It follows that the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the ideal forms or "types" of all things.</note> of all things are within Him, through which He knows and makes all things. And (to speak briefly) just as in this material world all matters are eventually reduced to one ultimate, internal matter, so—and even more so—in the formal world all forms are necessarily reduced to one ultimate, internal form. This can be argued again from the following: every level of life generates its own offspring within itself before producing it externally. The more excellent the life is, the more internal is the offspring it generates for itself. Thus, the vegetative life, both in trees and in animals, generates the seed—which is like a potential tree or animal—within its own body before it either casts it out or produces an external tree or animal from it. Likewise, the sensitive life <note>The life of the senses and perception.</note>, which is more excellent than the vegetative, gives birth through the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasiam"; the faculty that creates and stores mental images.</note> to a likeness and "intention" of things within itself before it fashions them in external matter. But that first offspring of the imagination is closer to the soul because it is within the soul itself, unlike the offspring of the vegetative life, which is in the body and not the soul. Likewise, the rational life, which is more excellent than the sensitive life, gives birth within itself to the "reason" of things and of itself—as a kind of offspring—before it brings it into the light through either speech or action.

That first rational offspring is closer to the soul than the offspring of the imagination. For the rational power is reflected back upon its own offspring, and through that offspring upon itself, which is something the imagination cannot do. In the same way, the angelic life produces the notions of itself and of all things within itself before it draws them out into the matter of the world. This offspring is more internal to the angel than human reason is to us, because it is neither stirred up by external things, nor does it change. For this reason, the Divine Life, which is the most eminent and fertile of all, generates this entire "Machine of the World" <note>original: "mundi Machinam"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the structured, functional cosmos.</note> within itself as its own offspring before it gives birth to it externally. Furthermore, this kind of offspring—which **Orpheus** calls **Pallas**, born from the head of **Jove** <note>Ficino identifies the Greek goddess Pallas Athena (Wisdom), who sprang fully formed from the head of Zeus, as a symbol for the Divine Ideas or the Logos existing within the mind of God.</note>—must be more intimate (if I may say so) to God than an angelic notion is to the angelic mind. Indeed, in an angel, since "being" is one thing and "understanding" is another, the notion generated by understanding is different from the angel’s own essence. But in God, because "being" and "understanding" are the same, the notion that God begets by understanding Himself—as a most exact image of Himself—is the same as God Himself. Since pleasure accompanies generation, **Plato** says in the ***Timaeus*** that God was wonderfully delighted with his own work. Moreover, in that most intimate offspring of God, which is the "universal seed" of the world, there reside the specific seeds of all the members that are born in this world as His external offspring. These seeds agree with one another in their essence, so that God is not a multiple substance; yet they differ in "reason," so that whatever is made in the world is not a single, uniform thing without any variety. Now, proceed further. Since God has infinite power, and the things that follow Him are all finite, the divine power is not limited only to doing those things for which finite resources can suffice. Rather, it can do countless other works, even incorporeal ones, without them. Therefore, does it not seem necessary to you that the forms of these works—which He can make without instruments or specific subjects—are at least distinct in their relationship, so that they have their own specific rational principle there? For since many things are not made from "the One" (insofar as it is absolutely one) without some medium or specific subject, there is no reason why such forms could be...

He uses the hierarchy of life—from plants to angels—to show that the higher the intellect, the more internal and perfect its creative conceptions are.</summary>

He is refuting the idea that nature acts randomly or that the forms of things are merely accidental.</meta>

...[diverse things] emanate, unless the wisdom of God were multiplex (if I may say so) and in a certain way multiform. Furthermore, whatever the remaining secondary causes do, they perform it all as instruments of the primary cause, and they act in such a way that they are regulated by it. They are regulated and led by God in certain ways toward generating certain forms in matter, through nothing other than the certain <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the structural blueprints or logical patterns in the mind of God.</note> of the forms which are in God, just as the instruments of art and nature are directed toward forms through the forms of the agent. And just as forms, both artificial and natural, are more clearly present in the agent than in the work or the instrument, so the forms of the whole world are, in their own way, more expressive in God than they are in the secondary causes and matter. For this reason, **Mercurius** <note>Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage associated with the "Hermetica."</note> thinks that the world is the "all-formed" image of the "all-formed" God. And **Plato** says in the *Timaeus* that the divine power, wishing by the grace of its own goodness to make the world as beautiful as possible, decreed to shape it according to that exemplar which is the most excellent of all. Therefore, He made the world in His own likeness, such that He shaped the parts of the world according to the forms of His own Ideas. From this, the madness of certain dogs is condemned—those who bark that Plato placed the Ideas outside the divine intelligence.

The single sky, full of stars, reflects a torrent of its own stars in images by night; these images are neither the stars themselves—though they may seem so to infants—nor do they remain, but are continually renewed by the flowing water, even though they are commonly thought to stay still. Similarly, the one God is the source of the Ideas, which are indeed reflections and not the true "species" <note>original: "species"; here meaning the essential forms as they exist in the physical world.</note> among the Platonists (though some physical scientists think they are the true ones), and they never rest, as **Heraclitus** says, while matter slides away, even if the ignorant think they are at rest. And this is the way through which temporal things, as **Parmenides the Pythagorean** <note>Ficino follows the tradition of viewing Parmenides as a Pythagorean philosopher.</note> wishes, become participants in the eternal Ideas. Truly, just as eternity—which is only a single moment remaining always the same and in the same way—measures all time which flows through innumerable moments while staying at rest, and just as a stable center measures the points of the running circumference, so any Idea, consisting eternally as one and the same, measures all those temporal things which are participants in one and the same Idea within the same species. What I say of one must be understood of all Ideas.

**Beauty** itself is the measure of all beautiful things, because by approaching the primary beauty and receding from it, subsequent things are judged more or less beautiful; and that which falls away from all beauty falls away from all essence, and that which possesses total beauty has total essence, because primary essence and primary beauty are the same. Whatever a human judges within a certain species, he judges by referring it to the species—for instance, when he judges the Sun or fire to be beautiful, he then refers two beautiful things to one species of beauty absolutely. And when he pronounces the Sun to be more beautiful than fire, he refers back to the same Idea, not absolutely, but by comparison. In both relations, he measures the beautiful Sun and the beautiful fire through the same Idea, but in the first he measures both through the whole Idea, and in the second he measures one of them through a different degree of the Idea. Nor should we listen to certain **Barbarians** <note>A common term Ficino used for Scholastic or Aristotelian thinkers who lacked what he considered proper Platonic refinement.</note> who think that beautiful things cannot be measured by their proximity to the pure act of beauty because that act is infinite, and therefore other things cannot approach more closely to it. They want such a measure to be devised instead by the distance or "recession" from the pure privation <note>original: "priuatione"; the total absence or lack of a quality.</note> of beauty.

For these people seem to err for this reason: if a pure act is infinite by affirmation, similarly a pure privation is infinite by negation. Nor does the comparison of beautiful things happen in relation to the divine essence which is entirely infinite, but in relation to the Idea of beauty itself, which is in a certain way finite insofar as it regards the creature, because it is a certain determination of divine perfection, made indeed by the divine mind and confirmed by the will. Those things approach it more closely which receive its likeness more purely. Those, on the other hand, recede. Rightly, then, the measure of beauty in beautiful things is taken from the source from which the beauty itself is received. But this is taken from the Idea, not from the pure privation of beauty. Finally, what could be more foolish than wanting to discern the possession of beauty through its absence, when both nature and reason compel the opposite? Therefore, let us confess without doubt that the human mind refers beautiful things to the rational principle of beauty itself.

However, since that which measures is more excellent than that which is measured, the human mind, insofar as it measures all temporal things through their relations to the Ideas, which are contained under them...

He refutes the notion that Ideas exist outside of God and explains that the human mind uses these innate concepts to judge and categorize the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the human soul's relationship with the Divine Ideas. While the previous section discussed how God contains the blueprints (Ideas) for all creation, this page focuses on how the human mind possesses "inner formulas"—shadows or reflections of those Divine Ideas—which allow us to judge and understand the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>233</page-num>

-> ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XI. <-

...than those things <note>referring to physical objects</note> because of the **Ideas**. And for that reason, the soul is closest to the Ideas, because it measures whatever follows them, inasmuch as it falls in the middle between the fountain of the Ideas and the streams flowing from it. But although the soul measures according to the Ideas, it does not measure through the Ideas themselves as if they were its own immediate means. For universal Ideas are not the private instrument of this or that particular human mind, nor do universal Ideas fall in between an individual mind and other individual things as a middle ground. However, because the soul cannot measure the individual <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulachra"; the reflections of divine archetypes found in the material world.</note> of the universal Ideas in any other way than through the **formulas** of the Ideas proper to the soul—which, as it were, lean down toward individual things—it is necessary that these formulas of the Ideas inhere in the mind. Through these, the mind compares the images to the Ideas; it approves those that match the formulas and rejects those that do not. 

But from where do these formulas come to the mind? Do they come from the images? From the soul's own imagination? Or perhaps from the Ideas? They do not come from the images, for the soul uses these formulas to measure the images; therefore, the formulas precede the images and are as much more excellent as they are closer to the Ideas. Indeed, if they were made from the images, they would not truly measure them, but would rather be measured by them. For a measure is an equalization. A cause equals the effect, but the effect does not equal the cause. Nowhere in physical bodies do we find the perfect <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the perfect, logical definitions of concepts like 'circle' or 'justice'.</note> of unity, goodness, or beauty. For it is necessary that these be unmixed with their opposites. In bodies, however, unity is mixed with a multitude of parts, goodness with vice, and beauty with deformity. Nowhere have we ever seen the perfect ratios of geometric figures in the matter of bodies, yet we hold them within ourselves. Otherwise, we would neither be able to speak of them, nor use them as a standard to rebuke the defects of physical forms. 

Therefore, we do not seem to have received them from bodies, for then they would be inferior to them. Nor should it be said that they are nowhere, because the mind cannot understand through itself that which is nothing at all. For even privations <note>the absence of a quality, like darkness being the absence of light.</note> are thought of through their positive states, and false opinions do not arise in us because we think of that which is absolutely nothing, but because we either join or disjoin things against their natural order. Truly, if the objects of the senses exist somewhere, then the rational principles—which are the objects of the mind—must also exist, provided that the mind is more noble than the senses, and that what is absolutely nothing neither moves the soul’s gaze, nor contracts it, nor defines it. 

Therefore, they are not invented by the soul. To be sure, fictions measure other fictions, but they do not measure true things. The soul's fictions follow actual things even more confusedly than shadows follow bodies. Bodies are not discerned by their shadows. Who, then, could gaze upon the essential definitions and hidden properties of beauty, scent, flavor, or heat through a fictitious and external image? Furthermore, a fiction of the soul is inferior to the soul itself. But those formulas are more excellent than the soul, because through them the soul even judges and corrects itself. Indeed, through the principles of unity, goodness, and beauty, the soul often judges itself—seeing how much it is divided into parts, or how much it is at odds with its own emotions. Likewise, it judges how much it fails by nature or is corrupted by vice. Again, it judges how much it was born deformed or has become base. Does it not, through the **seal** of beauty, pronounce that it is more beautiful than bodies, and that this part of itself is more beautiful than that, and this habit more beautiful than another? 

Indeed, these principles even seem to be more sublime than the angels, because our mind designates the angel through that same seal when it affirms that an angel is more beautiful than the soul, and one angel more beautiful than another, and God more beautiful than the angels. Yet, the soul does not "measure" God; rather, it leaves Him as the immeasurable measure. For just as wisdom does not "become" wise, and motion is not "moved," so the primary measure is not measured. Therefore, insofar as those formulas measure the angels—acting as rules expressed by the Ideas existing above the angels—they are certainly more sublime than the angels. And the soul, in this very act by which it measures the angels, is more excellent than that very nature of the angel which it designates within itself by measuring. Although an angel also measures the soul through rules that are, in a way, more direct, and by that very act the angel exceeds the soul more than it is exceeded by the soul's act. 

But in what way are these "seals"—which we also call formulas—invented by the soul if they are higher than both the soul and the angels? On the contrary, they are in the soul before every invention of the soul. For the soul compares all its discoveries to such seals. Indeed, by the seal of truth, it discerns which discoveries are true, which are truer, and which are false. Likewise, whatever is manufactured through the soul's new and temporal acts is entirely changeable. For what is made by motion is surely made changeable. But such seals are immobile. For they cling to the soul immovably, since we refer whatever occurs to the soul at every moment—or whatever is made by the soul at our will—to them as things firmly inherent. Furthermore, if those things also changed,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from the previous section. Having established that the soul possesses "formulas" of the Divine Ideas, he now argues that these inner standards must be "immobile" (unchanging) to allow us to judge the changing world. He shifts from metaphysical deduction to empirical "signs," such as the way even uneducated people recognize beauty.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>

-> MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY <-

...[if they] were moved, they would have to be referred to other things, and those again to others, and there would be no first principle of judging within us. The **seal** <note>original: "sigillum"; Ficino uses this to describe an innate mental archetype or "stamp" impressed upon the soul by God.</note> through which we pass judgment on the state of this thing, or the state of that, or even on eternity, cannot be movable. Indeed, in the seal is expressed the **rational principle** <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning the structural logic or essence of a thing.</note> of that which is signified by it. But the rational principle of stability and eternity itself is utterly foreign to the rational principle of motion. Furthermore, we define the stable and the eternal in no other way than under the principles of stability and eternity. Principles of this kind are devoid of all change, since stability precedes motion. That which is prior in nature is released from that which comes after. 

And yet, we possess these principles—through which we define such things—within ourselves. For the mind does not speak through things that are foreign to it. If these principles were outside of us, we would still require other principles of principles, as if they were intermediaries, through which we might draw out those principles by which we were to speak of stability and eternity. Those other principles would likewise be immobile, because they would be the principles of immobile principles. Therefore, wherever we walk, we will arrive at immobile principles that are innate to us. 

Plotinus, when he disputes concerning the age <note>original: "de æuo"; referring to 'Aion' or eternal duration.</note>, wisely says: *Do we speak of eternity as if bearing witness to external things, and dealing with things that are foreign? By no means. For we do not understand unless we touch, and we do not touch foreign things. Therefore, it is necessary that we be participants in eternity.* Thus far he speaks. 

Therefore, such seals are immobile. Indeed, even the seal of motions is immobile. For when we judge the motions of things, we compare them to the eternal **Idea** of motion through the seal of motions implanted within us. If this seal were also a motion or movable, it would have to be compared through another seal. For motion is not bound to eternity except through a competent medium that is neither motion nor movable. Likewise, if it were movable, we would not rightly judge motions through it. For a motion is then judged correctly when it is referred to boundaries and spaces that remain permanent. For if those do not remain, neither can motion exist, nor can the progression of motion be perceived. Even **time** itself, which is a certain property and duration of motion, is measured in no other way than if it be preserved through a stable memory, and circumscribed by a stable moment of eternity. If the seal of motion is stable, much more stable are all the seals of the remaining things. From all these points, two things are concluded equally: namely, that such seals are both inserted into the soul by the Ideas, and they cling to the soul itself immovably.

---

## Confirmation of the above through signs. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V.

**H**owever, we find many signs of this matter. First, that simple country people, who have never thought anything about the Ideas, and youths who have heard nothing of them, as soon as beautiful bodies encounter their senses—provided they use reason—they refer them to the Ideas in two ways (as we have said). 

One way is when they affirm that "this is beautiful," which they do only because the shape of such a body matches the **seal of beauty** born within them. The other way is when they affirm that "this is more beautiful than that," and "that more than another," according to how much one thing approaches closer to the seal than another. They did not previously acquire such a seal through teaching, nor through discovery, for they have neither thought anything about it, nor heard of it, nor even then do they collect it from individual beautiful bodies. Indeed, through the seal itself—which is not at all deceptive—they rebuke the deception and defect of individual things. 

Nor [do they collect it] from a certain common nature which is in individuals. For that which lies in deceptive things becomes deceptive itself, and produces a deceptive notion from itself. Furthermore, when they think more diligently about that seal, they find it to be, or to represent, something that is **one above the many**, subsisting in itself. For above that nature which is "one" in some way in many things, there must be such a nature which is "one" before the many, so that it may be equally common to the many. Because such a seal is in no way enclosed by the multitude of singular things, it is in no way collected from that multitude, nor is it even conceived by the machination of thought. For through the seal itself, we find that above the movable and manifold beauty of every soul, there is one beauty remaining in itself. Therefore, the seal raises its power higher above souls, whereas the "machinations" of the soul can fabricate nothing more eminent than souls. 

If, therefore, as soon as we use reason, we refer most things to seals of this kind—which we neither learned before, nor then collected or fashioned, especially since the sign of comparison must always precede those things which are compared—it follows that we possess them before any use of reason.

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XI.

The second sign is that both types of connections <note>likely referring to the mental associations or logical links mentioned previously</note> happen suddenly, often even without any preceding intention of the will or any discursive reasoning. This indicates that the mind does not need to acquire a rule for such connections recently or from the outside, but has possessed it internally for a long time, and is able to use it at will whenever it directs itself toward it.

The third sign is what everyone experiences within themselves: whenever they wish to find the definition and cause of a thing, they attempt nothing else but to penetrate the innermost depths of the profound mind, once all the obstacles of the senses and the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiae"; the faculty of processing sensory images.</note> have been removed. What they are hunting for then first shines most clearly once they have penetrated the secret shrines of the mind, as if the treasures of the sciences lay hidden within. Thus Pythagoras sang:

> But you, take heart, for the human race is divine,
> To whom sacred nature, bringing all things to light, shows each thing.
> <note>original: "ἀλλὰ σὺ θάρσει ἐπεὶ θεῖον γένος ἐστὶ βροτοῖσιν οἷς ἱερὰ προφέρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν ἕκαστα."</note>

That is to say: "But you, have confidence, since there is a divine lineage in men, to whom sacred nature shows all things by bringing them into the light." Should we then wonder that Homer, Didymus, and many others, who were blind either by nature or from infancy, wrote in such a way that they seem to have clearly seen everything? Shall we wonder that Zoroaster and other discoverers of wisdom produced knowledge of all things through long solitude alone, and solely by the turning of the whole soul toward the mind alone?

The fourth sign is taken from the concept of approval and disapproval. A **bodily temperament** <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, bile, etc.) in an individual.</note> that abounds in blood demands certain flavors for itself, as well as other uses of things, while a temperament of bile demands others, and phlegm yet others. When what is suitable is offered to each temperament, such a nature adopts the thing offered no differently than fire takes to sulfurous fuel. Hence, the **sanguine** person praises sweet things, the **choleric** sharp and bitter things, the **melancholic** sour things, and the **phlegmatic** soft and tasteless things. What we say of the sanguine person must be similarly applied to the others. The sanguine person does not know for what reason he approves of sweet things, because he does not commend them by deliberation, but by the natural instinct of his temperament. Surely, through natural instinct he also desires types of qualities: red and green to the sight, joyful things to the hearing, sweet to the taste, and tempered things to touch and smell. If he affects and approves of these five qualities through his temperament, it is necessary that within the very mixture of that temperament there reside five **seeds** <note>original: "fomites"; literally "tinder," used here to mean the innate triggers or foundations of these sensory preferences.</note> of these five approvals. For just as the internal logic of those five qualities differs from one another, so they are approved by such a temperament under different rational principles. Therefore, in every human being there are five natural "seeds" for the five qualities corresponding to the five senses. 

And because there are different temperaments of the humors in different men, the desires for bodily things are diverse among men. However, since there is one human species in all, and one species of mind, there is therefore a common approval of those things which pertain to the mind. Every mind praises a round figure as soon as it is considered in objects, yet does not know why it praises it. In buildings, it similarly praises a certain squareness of the houses, or the equality of the walls, the arrangement of stones, the opposition of angles, and the shape and placement of windows. It furthermore praises, in the same way, a certain **proportion** of human limbs, or a harmony of numbers and voices. It commends mortal gestures and behaviors as decorous. It commends the light of wisdom and the intuition of truth. If any mind whatsoever adopts all these things always and everywhere immediately—and does not know the reason why it adopts them, nor can it *not* adopt them—it adopts them by an entirely necessary and natural instinct. 

But because the rational principle of the things desired here differs among them, it is necessary that they be desired by the mind based on the different principles of its own nature acting as "seeds," and approved by them as if by formulas and rules, so that their opposites are rejected by those same rules. Indeed, as soon as their opposites are presented to us, they offend us by their very nature, even if we do not know the cause. Therefore, the **rational principles** <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the innate structures or "blueprints" in the soul.</note> of these and similar things are inborn in the mind.

The fifth sign is taken from the definition of **art**. Because every art ordains a work by a certain reason toward a certain end, it is a **rational faculty**. If a rational faculty is inborn in all irrational nature, it is much more inborn in every rational being. How skillfully do the elements seek their own proper place! With what great art of geometry do they maintain a straight line in their ascent and descent? With what great industry of architecture does the rain restrain itself into little spherical drops? How great—

...air, through its shrewdness, comes to the aid of nature's works so that no vacuum is left within her. The **constitution** <term>complexio: the specific balance of elements or qualities in a living thing</term> of plants and animals also employs a wonderful skill in the medicinal art for preserving or recovering their natural state. The souls of irrational animals themselves exercise specific arts within their specific species. Insects produce silken webs, spiders weave linen, swallows practice pottery, swans perform music, bees handle architecture, storks follow civil law, lions practice the art of war, and finally, foxes follow the art of the hunt. 

Now, who would say (considering these things) that only the rational nature was lazy, or was constituted from the beginning as irrational out of such laziness? On the contrary, if the seat of reason ought to receive a rational art much earlier and more fully than an irrational seat, then it is necessary that all arts be innate to the rational species of humans, since individual arts are innate to individual species of irrational animals. For almost all these arts are gathered together in the genus of irrational animals as a whole, but different types of arts are dispersed through different species of animals. Therefore, all these arts are collected in the single rational species of humans, even if they are divided among individuals. Again, all are united in the single angelic species, in which they are nonetheless divided according to forms, since the angel is multiform. Finally, all are united in the one, singular God, and through the single form of God. 

For this reason, arts are divided among themselves in the genus of irrational animals according to **disposition** <term>habitu: a state of being or potentiality</term> and **action** <term>actu: the actual exercise or practice of a skill</term>; for no species of "mute" <note>original: "mutorum"; referring to animals who cannot speak</note> creatures either practices all arts in action or possesses them all as infused traits. Instead, any one of their species uses and possesses a single art. Thus, it is necessary that arts be divided in the human species according to action—because different people focus on different things—but not according to disposition, because each individual possesses them all. Indeed, in the angel, all are united in both disposition and action. For any one of them can contemplate any of the arts, though they are divided in their execution, because different angels govern the world in different ways. All are united in God in every way, because He possesses, sees, and executes them all. For in all who work, as the **Theologian Paul** <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 12:6: "And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all."</note> says, *He works all things.*

The sixth sign is derived from the affection for the arts, which are attained not only by those who lack a teacher and find them on their own, but even by those who are said to have had masters, books, or men to guide them. For even those who learn by choice do not draw a spiritual and living knowledge from physical letters that lack life; rather, provoked by the letters, they give birth to it within themselves. And those who learn by hearing do not truly learn until they themselves reflect upon, examine, and approve what they have heard. Now, no examination or approval of truths occurs unless the rule of truth has first shone within. 

Furthermore, those who are said to "teach" do not simply pour the exact same knowledge they possess into another person. For by teaching others, they themselves would end up ignorant if knowledge passed from one mind to another like a physical object moving from one subject to another—which is not how qualities work. Nor do they generate another knowledge of a similar kind in the student through their own. For such generation belongs to physical qualities, not to human knowledge, the action of which is enclosed within and perfects the one working rather than external things. 

But in what way does a master instruct a student? There are two kinds of arts. Some are those whose matter (the material they work on) has no effective principle of work within itself, such as clay or stone; these seem to be subject to the potter and sculptor in such a way that they only wait for the hand of the artist, having nothing in their own nature to help complete the work. But there are other arts whose matter acts toward the work through a certain form and motion, which should be called natural rather than artificial. Thus the earth is subject to the farmer, and the human body to the doctor. Indeed, the fertility of the soil contributes much to the farmer in producing crops, and the constitution of the human body contributes much to the doctor in recovering health—so much so that often a field produces crops without cultivation, and the constitution of our body drives away diseases without the work of a healer. This signifies that the seeds of the crops are in the field by nature, and the seeds of health are in the constitution. 

Therefore, in the first kind of arts, that artist is called the **Lord and Master** of the matter; but in the second kind, he is the **awakener and servant** of nature. That the art of teaching belongs to this second kind is proven by the fact that the soul—which seems to be the "matter" subject to the teacher—sometimes foretells what is to be heard before it hears it, and after it has heard, returns what was heard more fruitfully and better. Often, even if it does not hear, it gives birth from itself, since it possesses the **seeds of knowledge** <term>semina scientiarum: the innate sparks of potential understanding within the soul</term> no less than a field possesses the seeds of crops.

Unde qui docet, minister est potius quàm magister. Quapropter Socrates apud

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 11.</header>

## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 11.

Plato, in the book on knowledge titled *Theaetetus*, says that he is the son of a midwife, and very much like a midwife himself. This is because, in educating men, he does not "induce" <note>original: *inducat* — to lead into or instill</note> knowledge, but "educes" <note>original: *educat* — to draw out</note> it, just as midwives bring out the children already conceived. Therefore, when a teacher strives to demonstrate something to a listener through many arguments, the listener is not shaped bit by bit—like clay by a potter or a stone by a sculptor—but rather, after many clues, he suddenly beholds the truth, even in the teacher’s absence. This happens once he has been sufficiently provoked, just as a field cultivated by a farmer produces its own fruit in its own time after long labor, even while the farmer himself is doing nothing. Who taught the eyes to see? Who taught the ears to hear? A doctor does not provide sight to the eyes; he either scatters the darkness poured over them or directs them toward an object. In the same way, a teacher does not pour knowledge into the mind, but purges its vision or directs its focus. No one grants hunting sagacity to dogs, nor the virtue of running to horses, nor warlike strength to elephants; yet men often compel these very virtues, lying hidden and dormant in their limbs, to wake up through practice. A teacher does the same for the mind, as Plato teaches in the seventh book of the *Republic*. For the mind possesses its own virtue (which is the intuition of truth) no less firmly and naturally than the senses or animals possess theirs. Socrates, the leader of teaching, provokes this virtue by searching; when the mind is asked correctly, it answers with the truth. It could not answer with the truth unless it already knew it. 

Furthermore, because things themselves are interconnected, and similarly the reasons <note>original: *rationes* — the underlying logic or principles</note> for things are joined together, one easily passes from one thing to many. It often happens that from a single footprint shown by a teacher, the sharp mind of a student hunts down a great many things in a long sequence using its own "nose." Add to this that the mind possesses no weaker a faculty for seeing the truth than the feet possess the power for walking. Socrates leads a child by an outstretched hand to show him where to step; he questions a youth to show him how to learn. He does not grant the child the power of walking, but provokes it and leads him more safely to the goal. He does not bestow intelligence upon the youth, but makes him more ready to achieve the effect of his own work. 

As for Socrates himself, if he is ever said to have acquired his knowledge as if it were new—either through discovery or through instruction—he acquired it in this way: if he discovered things by himself, he would never have used the things he found unless he had known the method of using them beforehand. One does not grasp the method of use if one does not grasp the nature of the thing itself. If, however, he heard it from another, he did not conceive knowledge from hearing it until he knew whether the teacher's reasons agreed with the truth. No one understands this except one who beholds the truth itself. Therefore, before he finds or hears anything, he is in possession of the truth. 

And Archelaus, who taught Socrates, either found it by himself or received it from Anaxagoras. Whichever it was, he knew it before. And even if Anaxagoras received it from Anaximenes, and he from Anaximander, and Anaximander from Thales—finally, Thales, or some other Egyptian priest or Persian Magus, lacked a teacher. He who lacks the teaching of man learns while nature teaches—or rather, he knows because God has been teaching him for a long time. 

For this reason, Socrates says in Plato’s book on wisdom <note>The dialogue *Theages*</note>: "Theages, no one ever learned anything from me, although many turned out more learned through my company, both by my encouragement and by the inspiration of the good spirit <note>original: *bono dæmone* — the *daimonion*, Socrates' famous internal divine voice</note>." You too, he says, will profit much in a short time if God is favorable. Furthermore, Socrates narrates in that same place how some, while they enjoyed his company and were near him, turned out sharper even when he was silent; but when they left him, they suddenly became duller. It was as if that power of genius belonged to a certain divine influx from God, penetrating through the spirit <note>original: *genium*</note> and mind of Socrates into the souls of his associates. 

And Orpheus says that the Muses are the daughters of Jupiter and Memory, because clearly knowledge lies hidden in deep memory, having been granted to us long ago by God. Indeed, he passed down these things concerning Memory:

> *Containing the whole mind, a dweller in human souls.*
> *Reminding all of the things which each person always keeps hidden in the boundaries of the mind, awakening the spirit in all.*
<note>Translated from the original Greek: πάντα νόον συνέχεσσα βροτῶν ψυχαῖσι σύνοικον. ὑπομνήσασα δὲ πάντα ὧν ἂν ἕκαστος ἀεὶ εὐνοίᾳ γνώμην κάθηται, ἐπεγείρουσα φρένα πᾶσιν.</note>

That is to say: "Containing the entire mind, a companion of human souls. You remind us of all the things whose notion each person always hides within the limits of the mind; you rouse the mind in everyone." 

We shall now conclude the present dispute, provided we first remind ourselves that when we hear that the "arts" are in us by nature, we should not understand them to be impressed by a celestial or physical nature, nor that they flow from the mere essence of the soul. (For beasts have them as impressions from such a physical nature, while God alone possesses them as flowing from His mere essence). Rather, we should understand that the **species** <term>species: here meaning the mental forms or "blueprints" of things</term> of things and the rules of the arts were infused into our minds as soon as they were born from God, as Plato teaches in the *Timaeus*, no differently than they are infused into angelic minds. There is, however, a threefold difference...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<sig>S i</sig>

between us and the beasts, as far as the arts are concerned. First, that we receive them from God without a medium <note>original: *sine medio* — meaning directly, without an intermediary force</note>. They receive them through the intervention of celestial nature. Second, that each of us receives all the types of arts that beasts possess, whereas they each only have one. Third, that beasts are driven to the use of their art at a certain time by a necessary impulse of nature, whereas we choose the use of one art, or many, by the free judgment of reason. We agree, however, with the angels and God regarding the species of things and the rules of the arts; we agree in several other things, but especially in this: that these rules exist within us in an absolute and clear way, almost exactly as they do in them. Therefore, the divine absolute ideas have impressed distinct images of themselves upon us as if upon mirrors, but they have impressed certain more confused shadows upon corporal nature—just as we, in the light, paint a clear image of our own body in a mirror, but cast only a shadow upon a wall. Where an idea shines in an absolute and clear manner, it does not only shine clearly, but almost in its entirety. For all the properties of ideas, which we described from Plato’s perspective at the start of this discussion, consist primarily in being universal and unconditioned <note>original: *soluta* — literally "loosened" or free from physical constraints</note>. That it is not the shadows of ideas, but clear images that dwell within us, is evident primarily because we distinguish the shadows from the images by right reason, and because the formulas of these ideas implanted in us represent the ideas themselves clearly to us and turn us toward them. The shadows of ideas in physical bodies do not reflect the ideas back to us until they are purified and reshaped by the formulas of our mind. Finally, if they shine in our minds through distinct images and in a complete and unconditioned way, they also shine in a way that is thoroughly immortal. If the natural subject <note>In philosophy, a "subject" is the underlying thing in which qualities exist.</note> of an immortal thing is itself immortal (for if the subject is dissolved, whatever clung to the subject is destroyed), then the mind of man is undoubtedly immortal, as it naturally and firmly receives the species of immortal ideas in an immortal way.

### Second Reason: The Mind is the Subject of Eternal Truth. Chapter VI.

**A**urelius Augustinus <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), whom Ficino viewed as the bridge between Platonic philosophy and Christian theology.</note>, a man of divine genius (none of the Latins expressed Platonic majesty more exactly in both wisdom and eloquence), built arguments of this sort upon the foundations laid by Plato. A true thing is one thing; Truth itself is another—just as a chaste person is one thing, and chastity is another. Truth is more excellent than a true thing, since every true thing is true because of Truth. When something that is called "true" perishes, Truth itself does not perish. Just as if a chaste person should die, chastity itself does not die. If this world will remain forever, it is true that it will remain forever; if it will not remain, it is true that it will not remain. What happens when it has perished, if it is destined to perish? Will it not then be true that the world has perished? For as long as it is not true that the world has died, it has not died. It is therefore a contradiction that the world has died and yet it is not "true" that the world has died. But something cannot be true where Truth does not exist. Therefore, Truth will exist even if the world perishes. What if Truth itself were to die? Would it not be true that Truth has died? But I do not think anything can be true if Truth does not exist; therefore, Truth shall in no way die. These are the words of Augustine. But where is Truth? Not in bodies, for it would change when the bodies change, yet Truth is eternal. From this follows that Platonic paradox: that bodies do not truly "exist," because Truth does not remain in them. Therefore, what we call gold—if it is not truly gold—is false gold. If this is so, it is not even gold at all. And so it is with the rest of the species of physical things. Furthermore, the state of a body does not remain exactly the same through two points of time, as we have shown elsewhere and show now in this manner. Just as stable and simple eternity is the measure of stable and simple things, so flowing and varying time is the measure of moving and manifold things. The points of time never remain the same, but always creep up on each other, one succeeding another. The moving body of the world has time as its own measure. If this is so, the arrangement of the heavens and their change surely matches the flow of time. Therefore, the arrangement of the heavens cannot be exactly the same in two moments of time. For if it remained the same through two moments, then in that little delay, time would have flowed from one moment to another, but the heavens would have rested in one. But flow does not agree with rest at all. That which does not agree cannot be measured. For how can motion measure rest, or a flowing thing measure something standing still?

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind must be immortal because it contains clear, universal "images" of divine ideas rather than the blurry "shadows" found in physical matter. He cites St. Augustine to prove that Truth is an eternal, unchanging reality that exists independently of the physical world.</summary>

in one. For this reason, in that brief delay, time would not have measured the heavens. But in truth, time always measures the heavens, just as eternity measures those things that are above the heavens. Therefore, just as those eternal things remain continually in eternity without any change, so the heavens run continually under the rule of time without any rest. If the configuration of the heavens never stays the same, much less do the tiny bodies <term>corpuſcula</term> <note>These are the fundamental "seeds" or atoms of matter in the sublunary world</note> which are beneath the heavens and are swept along by the heaven's swift force. For it is necessary that these things vary continually through influx and efflux, through condensation and rarefaction, through the tightening or loosening of qualities, through the harmony or discord of their physical constitution <term>complexionis</term>, and through all other movements.

Indeed, Plutarch and Proclus <note>Two major Neoplatonic philosophers who influenced Ficino's view of the soul and the cosmos</note> demonstrated this abundantly, and before them Heraclitus said: "Just as we cannot enter the same water of a rushing stream twice, or touch the same part of a spinning wheel twice in the same way, so we are completely unable to grasp a physical constitution or disposition of the body that persists through two points of time." If the state of no body persists as exactly the same and similar through two moments, then a quality begins and ends in that same moment. That which begins in nature does not yet possess a finished act of existing or operating; that which ends no longer retains such an act. 

Therefore, at that very point in which that quality is said to "be," it can also be said "not to be," since it has not yet completely departed from "not-being," and is already sliding back into "not-being." And because the speed of time exceeds the speed of the tongue, while you are pronouncing that it "is," it escapes while you are speaking, before you have finished uttering the word "is" from your mouth. And as Timaeus says <note>Ficino is referring to the character Timaeus in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which describes the creation of the universe</note>, it deceives the speaker, nor is anything ever truly pronounced or perceived concerning this world. It cannot be said to "be" any more than it "is not," since it both is and is not equally while the word is being uttered. 

Truly, since things that are continually changed are "becoming" only insofar as they are changing, and things that are "becoming" do not truly "exist" while they are becoming, therefore whatever changes and becomes in this way is not so much said "to be" as it is said "to seem to be." 

But what shall we say of time? It is always falsely said "to be," since its nature (if I may speak thus) is "not to be." Certainly, concerning any present moment, it is truly said: "this is not time," but rather the boundary <term>terminus</term> of time. Only the past or the future are affirmed to be time. Indeed, we think that a certain continuous succession is signified by time. But the past and the future do not exist. Therefore, we place the "being" of time, in a way, within "not-being." 

The moment, however, which is the boundary of time, turns into "not-being" even while we pronounce that it "is," and compels those speaking to lie. What we demonstrate concerning time must also be judged concerning temporal things: namely, that their "being" is held within "not-being" (so to speak). 

That Pythagorean saying agrees with this: "He who is called a man is more a 'non-man' than a man." For if you consider his innumerable parts, you could judge innumerably that "this part is not a man," and "that part is likewise not a man." Only once will you say of the whole, "this is a man." 

Hence, Timaeus, when discussing the elements, thinks there are two parts to an element: matter and form. Because of matter, it is not called fire or water; it is called so because of form—therefore, only according to a part. This thing is called "fire" only according to a part, and that "water." In reality, this is not "fire," but "fiery"; that is not "water," but "watery." 

Add to this that a "true such-and-such" is that which is "purely such-and-such"—for instance, "pure wine" is that which is purely wine. But the nature of any species, when it is in matter, first possesses an inherent potential for "not-being," as we proved in the fifth book. Then, it suffers many additions, and often contrary ones. Indeed, in the air there is often something fiery, and there is always some position or state that is outside the essential nature of air. In this or that human, there is often some constitution against his nature, and always some habit, or affection, or figure, or position beyond the necessity of the human species. The other species of natural things behave similarly. 

But since above all things that are "such-and-such" only partially and impurely, there must exist those things which are "such-and-such" according to themselves, entirely and purely. Timaeus thinks that above the stained and maimed forms of matter, there are other forms that are pure, whole, and separate. And he trusts most in the strength of that reasoning which argues thus: 

"Forms which are in another thing—namely, in matter—also come *from* another thing; yet they do not come from the formless nature of matter itself. Form must come from form, and ultimately from a Form that exists through itself <term>per ſe ſubſiſtente</term>. And just as all formable matter is reduced to one single Form-giver <term>formatorem</term>, so even if someone introduces many form-givers, they will never have a mutual order among themselves insofar as they are diverse, nor will they lead to a single work and end, except insofar as they are led by the one Form-giver of all. Therefore, it is necessary that forms are given to matter by a Mind <term>mente</term> that is full of forms, where the forms are the very essence of that Mind, and therefore they are the true Species. But because that Mind is the first Being, while matter is..."

<summary>Ficino argues that the physical world is in a constant state of flux and "not-being," using the fleeting nature of time and the instability of matter to prove that true, stable reality (the Forms) must exist in a higher, divine Mind.</summary>

Ficino is using the theories of Proclus and the dialogues of Plato to show that while divine things are stable and "actuality," material things are "potentiality" and constantly in flux.</meta>

-> MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY <-

...closest to nothingness; and since that [the Divine Mind] is pure act, and this [matter] is pure potentiality, it follows that matter is almost infinitely inferior to the mind. Whatever is received by something takes on the nature of the receiver. Therefore, the forms submerged in matter are so much inferior to the species <term>species</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "species" refers to the intellectual blueprints or "Forms" that exist in the Divine Mind</note> of the mind that they are shadows of them rather than images; they retain the names of those forms—falsely at that—rather than their true nature. Just as works of art are likenesses of natural things, so natural things are likenesses of divine things. However, works of art come closer to the truth of natural things (because they share the same matter) than natural things come to the truth of divine things. If, therefore, a painted horse falls so far short of a natural horse that it is not a "true" horse, then a natural horse falls so much further short of the "Divine Horse"—that is, the Idea and true reason of a horse—that it should be said to represent a shadow of the horse rather than its true form. And if the true essence of man or horse is the Idea itself of man or horse, and matter (being so far removed) does not preserve this essence, then we must conclude what Socrates said in the *Phaedo* and the *Republic*: namely, that "true men" and "true horses" are not found in matter. Matter deceives the ignorant "little souls" <term>animulas</term> <note>A term often used in the Renaissance to describe the human soul in its fragile, embodied state</note> with these shadows of Ideas, so that, like dreamers seeing likenesses of real things, they think they are looking at the things themselves. 

This agrees with a paradox by our Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonic philosopher whose works Ficino translated and integrated into Christian thought</note>. Things composed of the elements possess neither eternity nor stability. Pure minds possess both, and they grasp all their own attributes at once. Between these are the souls, which possess their own eternity within a certain motion. Indeed, souls closest to the minds admit motion only in their operation, while the souls that follow are also subject to motion in their power. Finally, the entire machine of the corporeal world—being inferior to the essence, operation, and power of souls—has obtained an essence so changeable that it is entirely temporal in every way. And just as a thing that is completely eternal always remains whole in the "One," so the machine of this world, being entirely temporal, at every moment of infinite time flows out from the divine world and immediately flows away and back again. This is much like how some believe light is always poured out from the Sun, moment by moment, spreading out all at once, then suddenly vanishing and being replaced. Truly, what is measured by an indivisible eternity must itself be indivisible. 

Therefore, that which has a divisible essence—constituted both from parts and from many natures, such as the machine of the world—does not harmonize with indivisible eternity. Instead, it aligns with divisible time, by which it is measured and with which it perpetually slides away. Furthermore, it is granted a power and action that is divisible by motion. For this reason, the mass of the world begins to be and ceases to be out of "nothingness" <term>ex non esse</term> all at once in every single moment, and then is born again, just as in motion and time (to which it is entirely subject) moments flow out and flow back individually and all at once. This is further confirmed by the fact that the perpetual motion of the heavens requires infinite power. Since the limited body of the world can neither possess this power from itself nor receive it all at once from another, it must draw it from its Maker and Mover gradually, moment by moment. I say "draw it" in a way that is momentary and quickly vanishing.

Since a temporal essence receives in a completely temporal way, a limited nature cannot be capable of eternity (whose power is infinite and exists all at once). Certainly, the nature of the world cannot receive infinity all at once. And since eternal infinity exists as a whole and is indivisible, it cannot be received by anything gradually.

Here Proclus distinguishes these things: He says that immobile essences come from God "all at once," so to speak, but are preserved by themselves through their own power. For since they exist there without motion and all at once, they can thereafter persist as stable through themselves, and by their own power they can proceed from certain of their potentials into their acts. For this reason, he calls such essences "self-subsisting" and affirms that they "produce themselves." However, he says the corporeal machine—flowing after the motion of the soul and time, and moving along with corporeal motion and time—has nothing stable and no power to preserve itself. Therefore, it is not "substantial" or "true," but entirely "shadowy" and "false." He labels it such in the manner of the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect who believed the physical world was made of darkness or evil; Ficino uses the comparison to highlight the world's lack of true reality</note>, as something perpetually slipping away and utterly in need of an influx from above to restore it, like the shadows of a body in rapidly flowing water. Hence that saying from the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>: We say that the intelligible world *always is* and *never becomes*, but the sensible world *certainly always becomes* and *never is*. Here Proclus adds that the intelligible world always exists as the same in number, whereas this sensible world is never properly one and the same in number.

but rather that it is one and the same thing in number, continually recreated. And as far as the body is concerned, it is always becoming and beginning; but as far as it depends on the divine mind, it is always made, and suddenly achieves its end. But let this paradox now have its end. Since, therefore, the whole machine of the senses is a kind of vanity, and daily causes vanity in the senses, therefore **Solomon** <note>Ficino quotes Ecclesiastes 1:2 to align Platonic philosophy with biblical wisdom.</note> cried out:
> *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.*
Truth, therefore, is not in sensible things nor (*as **Epicurus** held*) in that part of the soul which is sense, because it looks outside itself, and is compelled to feel with a certain passion, and is deluded by the frequent trifles of sensible things. For this reason, **Xenophanes**, **Parmenides**, **Zeno**, **Melissus**, and **Stilpo** <note>These are mostly Eleatic and Megarian philosophers who argued that the physical world of change is an illusion.</note> said that nothing of truth is grasped by the senses. Almost the same thing pleased **Anaxagoras**, **Empedocles**, and **Plato**. For even if someone should say that there are some sensible things that always remain the same way, and brings up for us the question of the **Sun** and stars—in which he might not be easily convinced that they deceive us by swift mutability—certainly no one can help but confess that there is nothing sensible that does not have a false likeness so similar that it cannot be distinguished. For, to omit other things, as **Augustine** says, all things that we feel through the body, even when they are not present to the senses, we nevertheless experience images of them just as if they were entirely present, either in sleep or in madness. When we experience this, we are completely unable to discern whether we are feeling them with the senses themselves or if they are merely images of sensible things. If, therefore, there are false images of sensible things that cannot be distinguished by the senses themselves, and nothing can be perceived unless it is distinguished from the false, then the judgment of truth is not established in the senses. 

And it may perhaps happen that the sense perceives some things truly, as **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle was more optimistic about sensory data than Plato, believing senses are generally reliable regarding their proper objects (like color for sight).</note> held, yet it never truly discerns whether it perceives truly or the opposite. Since the truth of natural things consists in their agreement with the reasons of the divine mind—just as the truth of artificial things consists in their agreement with the ideas of the craftsman’s mind—the sense does not recognize such a congruence, and therefore it has no test for truth. Again, since the truth of a knowing power arises when the power matches the things to be known, but is perfected when it is equated to the ideas, the sense—which notices neither that congruence nor that equation—lacks the judgment of truth. Add to this that the sense does not grasp the innermost and pure substance of a thing, or in what order any thing is arranged in nature (which entirely belongs to the truth of the thing itself), but is attracted by a sudden impulse of qualities to pursue or flee, in which it indulges the convenience of its own body rather than the grasping of the truth of things. 

Therefore, the judgment of truth is not established in the sense. It is, however, established in reason. For the privations <term>privations</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present, like darkness being the absence of light.</note> of things are known through their habits <note>original: "habitus," referring here to the presence of a positive quality or state.</note>: darkness through light, and silence through voices. The privation of truth is the false. Our reason refutes the sensible things and the senses as false, which it could not do except by the examination of present truth. Again, reason describes truth itself thus:
> *Truth is the pure integrity and integral purity of each nature.*
But truth is not defined except under the natural and proper reason of truth. Truth is in the very reason of truth. Therefore, truth is in the mind that defines truth, just as it is in the mind that refutes the false. Furthermore, it is in the mind that describes any thing. For the definition of a <term>species</term> <note>In this context, the "species" is the essential "Form" or blueprint of a thing that exists in the mind.</note> encompasses the very essence of the thing, both whole and separated from external accidents. If, therefore, the truth of things is in the species themselves, and the species is grasped by definition, and the definition by the mind, who would not see that truth is in the mind of man? 

If truth is immortal, it sufficiently declares that the mind in which it inherently and inseparably dwells is incorruptible. For a quality that dwells inseparably in some subject is destroyed if the subject is removed. But that truth dwells in us inseparably can be proven by the fact that—either continually or at least at our will—suddenly and solely by the mind’s collection of itself into itself, we both condemn many false things and define certain common natures, whether of natural things, or moral things, or crafts. Furthermore, the same is concluded from what we showed previously: that the clear reasons of the Ideas dwell stably in the mind. In these, indeed, the truths of all things are contained. Above all others, however, this is shown most greatly by the rational power itself, which is no less natural to man than flight is to birds or barking to dogs. Through this, **Socrates** is a man; through this, man is distinguished from other species of animals. We call the rational power, for the present, the very virtue of reasoning, which perceives consequences—that is, it notices step-by-step what follows from what, and runs through from preceding things to consequences in order. This is a kind of natural <term>dialectic</term> <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth.</note>, that is, the art of discourse,

Since the mind possesses these immortal truths inseparably, the mind itself must be immortal.</summary>
