# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

->**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XI**<-

<margin>The definition of reasoning.</margin> of reasoning <note>original: "differendi," referring here to the art of dialectic or logical dispute</note>, is implanted in humans from their very origin. Through this, even children and the most unlearned people defend their own positions with whatever conjectures and assertions they can. Indeed, every human speech, and the entirety of life’s action and consultation, is nothing other than a kind of argumentation. There is no one so insane that they do not infer one thing from another by arguing; and in this way, a broken mind argues from images to images in almost the same way a healthy mind runs through the things themselves. Therefore, the rational power is never separated from a human being. But if truth is not separated from this power, then truth will never be separated from the soul. 

Within this power of reasoning, there are two types of necessity: one according to its subject, and the other according to its use. The first necessity is that the faculty of reasoning itself is so deeply implanted in the entire human species that it cannot be removed. The second necessity, which is seen in its use, is twofold: absolute and relative. 

**Absolute necessity** appears in three areas: namely, in the principles of the disciplines, in definitions, and in properties. 
Principles are of this sort: 
*Whatever exists, exists either through itself or through another.* 
*Contraries by their own nature repel each other.* 
*Every whole is greater than its part.* 
*To each should be given what is his own.* 
These and many such principles are necessarily so, such that they are necessarily known, because they can never be otherwise, nor can they be ignored by anyone, however unlearned. 

There is also necessity in **definitions**, as when a circle is defined in this way: 
*A circle is a figure in which all lines drawn in a straight path from its center to the circumference are equal.* 
For although either such a joining of words in the mouth, or such a drawing in the dust, may be a matter of chance <note>original: "contingens," meaning something that could be otherwise or is temporary</note>, that truth is nevertheless necessary and eternal, because that is the very nature of a circle. 

A similar necessity exists in **properties**; for example, *the circle is the most capacious of all figures.* And, to omit other things, do we not run through numbers from necessary truth to necessary truth without end? *Two times two is four. Three times three is nine. Two times four is eight,* and so on. We do the same in the compositions and comparisons of geometric figures. Because if definitions and properties flow into principles (since they flow *from* principles), and principles are necessarily and always present in the rational power—from which it constantly reasons about something—it follows that these three necessary truths, which are all called **absolute**, are contained within the natural logic <note>original: "dialectica"</note> of human beings.

There remains **relative necessity**, which also has three parts. One is in position, another in condition, and another in demonstration. 
The first is like this: *Nothing can not-be while it is.* *An animal, while it lives, necessarily lives,* and similar things which are affirmed of the present time. From these, necessity is held for the past and the future: *What has been done cannot be undone.* *What is to be, cannot not-be.* 
The second is like this: *If the body lives, it necessarily exists.* *If an animal runs, it is moved.* 
The third is of this sort: *Every part is smaller than the whole. The head is a part of the human body. Therefore, that head is smaller than the human body.* 

This conclusion is entirely necessary because the two preceding propositions, joined together, are necessary. For it is necessary that the head be smaller than the body, both because a part is smaller than the whole, and because it is itself a part of the body. Therefore, in these three also—position, condition, and demonstration—there are three necessary truths. And if these three are in human reason when it disputes, then these three truths are also necessary within it. And because reason disputes always—even while we are silent and while we sleep (for the whole life of a human is a certain perpetual reasoning)—those truths are therefore always in the reason. 

Reason is always (if I may speak thus) both *truth-telling* <note>original: "veridica"</note> and *truth-making* <note>original: "verifica"</note>. It is truth-telling in the first three truths, which are necessary in themselves even if reason does nothing. It is truth-making in the three others, because reason imposes a certain necessity on them through positions, conditions, and demonstrations, or through any other modes of arguing. For it is a matter of chance that this animal lives; however, while it lives, it does not live by chance, but by necessity. It is a matter of chance that this man moves; yet if he runs, it follows necessarily. It is a matter of chance that this head is smaller than this body; but once those two prior propositions have been positioned by the mind, it is necessary—even though in the species of "head" and "body" themselves, that relationship is never a matter of chance. 

If reason captures necessary truth in some things, and creates it in others—and it always captures and creates—who will deny that there is perpetual truth within it? Indeed, who will deny that reason itself is necessary, since it receives those things which are necessary in themselves exactly as they are without changing them, and those things which are not such in themselves, it makes necessary by its own power? It is much more "necessary" than all those things which are made necessary by it through positions, conditions, and arguments. Therefore, reason itself is absolutely necessary, almost like those principles of the disciplines...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul possesses an innate and inseparable faculty of reasoning (dialectic) that contains eternal truths. He distinguishes between absolute necessities (like mathematical definitions) and relative necessities (logical deductions), concluding that the soul's constant use of these truths proves its own eternal and necessary nature.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XI #

...definitions and permanent properties. Therefore, human reason was either necessarily always present and will be so like those things, or at least it will necessarily always be. For what prevents reason from being perpetual? Its perennial action is nothing other than providing a relative eternity to any temporal and contingent things <note>Ficino argues that the human mind "anchors" the changing things of the world by connecting them to eternal, unchanging truths.</note>, derived from an absolute eternity remaining firmly within, and arranging one necessary and perpetual series out of both necessary and contingent things. If it will always be, it will also always live. For reason does not exist except as living, and within a living being.

->Objection of the Sceptics and response, that something certain can be known.<-
->Chapter VII.<-

**N**or should the Sceptics <note>A school of ancient philosophy that argued human beings can never achieve certain knowledge, but only "probable" opinions.</note> be listened to, if they deny that truth is in our minds because they seem to doubt individual things. For the mind does not doubt everything, as appeared in all those necessary truths we have listed, and similar ones. I know that this appears white to me. I know that this smells pleasant to me. I know that this touches my taste sweetly. Who would not know that the supreme good is that than which nothing is more excellent? And that it exists either in man, or outside of man; and if in man, it is either in the soul, or in the body, or in both. Who does not know for certain that God either exists, or does not exist? And if He exists, He must be one, or many; and if many, they must be either finite in number, or infinite? It must be that God is either corporeal <note>Physical or having a body.</note> or incorporeal. And if He is not corporeal, He is necessarily incorporeal. 

Likewise, the results declare many rules of astrology and medicine to be certain, to say nothing of arithmetic and geometry, than which nothing is more certain. And what is greater: if ever the mind doubts any matter, it is even then certain of many things. For it does not doubt that it is then doubting. And if it holds for certain that it is doubting, it holds that certainty from a certain truth. Indeed, he who understands himself to be doubting understands a truth, and concerning this thing which he understands, he is certain; therefore, he is certain about the truth. 

And everyone who doubts whether truth exists has a truth within himself from which he might not doubt. Nor is any truth true except by Truth itself. Therefore, it is not necessary for him to doubt truth who was able to doubt from any source at all, as Augustine says <note>Ficino is paraphrasing St. Augustine's famous "If I am mistaken, I am" (*Si fallor, sum*) argument, which predates Descartes' "I think, therefore I am."</note>, especially since he not only understands that he doubts, but notices that he understands this, and acknowledges that he notices it, and so on to infinity. Furthermore, he discerns a doubting mind from one that is certain. Nor is it hidden from him when it would be better not to doubt, and how ardently he desires the truth. He compares certainty with doubt, by which it happens that he is certain of both. He is, moreover, certain that he investigates, feels, lives, and exists. For indeed, no one doubts who does not exist, live, feel, and investigate. 

He is also certain that he is not the Primary Truth <note>The "Primary Truth" refers to God.</note>, since that Truth does not doubt through itself. He knows that Truth is not entangled in doubt and error. He knows that in judging, he must either be mistaken or not mistaken. He knows that whether he is mistaken or not mistaken while he judges, he is undoubtedly living. Finally, he is not ignorant that there is something else in nature outside his own mind that brings doubt to him. 

Certain truths of this kind are perceived even in doubt itself. By this we are warned not to fear Aristo, Pyrrho, or Herillus <note>Aristo of Chios, Pyrrho of Elis, and Herillus of Carthage—philosophers associated with various degrees of skepticism or different views on the "highest good."</note>, who, while they opine that nothing true is known by us, themselves undoubtedly know that this opinion of theirs must be either true or false. They know that if it is true, something true is understood by man. They know that if it is false, the opinion opposite to them is true—namely, that something true is indeed known by man.

---

->Objection of the Peripatetics and response, that truth dwells familiarly<-
->in the mind. Chapter VIII.<-

**B**ut should the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked (*peripateo*) while teaching.</note> be feared, who deny that truth dwells familiarly in the mind, because so few seem to be skilled in it, and whoever does know it has been unlearned for such a long time since infancy? Certainly they are not to be feared, as Augustine testifies where he explains the mind of Plato: 
> Either there is something in the mind which is not in its present thought, or the art of music is not in the musician when he is thinking only of geometry. But the latter is false, therefore the former is true. 

The mind does not feel that it possesses anything, however, unless it has come into thought. It is possible, therefore, for something to be in the mind which the mind itself does not feel is within it. For how long that is so makes no difference. For if the mind has been occupied with other things for a long time, although [it turns] its attention to things previously thought...

<summary>Ficino refutes the Skeptics by arguing that the very act of doubting proves the existence of certain truth and the reality of the self. He also uses an Augustinian argument to show that knowledge (like music) remains in the soul even when we are not actively thinking about it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Chapter VII of Book XI, where Ficino refutes the Sceptics by demonstrating that certain knowledge exists within the human soul. He is currently developing the Platonic concept of "recollection" (anamnesis), arguing that the soul does not "create" truth but rather "rediscovers" eternal principles already residing within its own nature.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO. PLATONIC THEOLOGY. #

...[that the mind] can easily reflect upon it, it is called forgetfulness or lack of skill. But when we either reason within ourselves or are correctly questioned by another, and we perceive the truths concerning certain liberal arts <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy) were considered the essential knowledge for a free person to master in the Renaissance.</note>, those things which we find, we find nowhere else but in our own soul. For this reason, the soul must withdraw into itself, leaving behind external things, in order to find these truths. Nor is "finding" the same as "making" or "begetting." Otherwise, the soul would beget eternal things through a temporal discovery—yet it often finds eternal things. For what is so eternal as the principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> of a circle, or whatever else in arts of this kind is understood to have never *not* been, and to never *not* be in the future?

From this, it is manifest that the human soul is immortal, and that all true principles are in its secret depths, even if, due to either ignorance or forgetfulness, it seems either not to have them or to have lost them. Imagine that you have forgotten something, and others wish to recall it to your memory. They ask, therefore: "Is it this, or that?" offering various things as if they were similar. You do not see that which you desire to remember, and yet you see that it is *not* what is being said. When this happens to you, does your forgetfulness seem total? Not at all. For that very discernment by which you do not admit what is falsely suggested is a certain part of the act of remembering. Such people do not yet see the truth, yet they cannot be misled or deceived, and they know well enough what they are seeking.

But if someone were to tell you that you laughed a few days after you were born, you would not dare to say it is false; and if the source is one to be trusted, you will not "remember" it, but rather believe it. For that entire time is hidden from you by a most powerful forgetfulness. This, therefore, differs greatly from that other kind of forgetfulness; this is a middle state. For there is another state closer and nearer to the truth for revisiting a memory. It is similar to when we see something and certainly recognize that we have seen it before, and we affirm that we know it, but we struggle to repeat and recall where, or when, or how, or through whom it came to our notice. As if it happened with a man, we might even ask where we knew him. When someone mentions it, suddenly the whole matter is poured into the memory like light, and we no longer labor to remember.

Such are those who are well-educated in the liberal arts. Since they have these arts buried within them by forgetfulness, they undoubtedly "dig them out" <note>Ficino refers to the Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, suggesting that learning is the process of the soul recovering knowledge it possessed before being joined to the body.</note> by speaking; yet they are not content, nor do they restrain themselves, until they gaze most broadly and clearly upon the whole face of truth, whose brilliance already gleams somewhat within those arts. But in these arts, certain false colors and forms pour their thoughts as if into a mirror, and they often fail and deceive those who seek, leading them to think that what they know or seek is the whole. These are those very images that must be avoided with great caution; they are caught being deceptive when they vary like a shifting mirror of thought, while the face of truth remains one and immutable. 

For although thought may depict for itself a square of one size or another, and place it as if before the eyes, nevertheless the inner mind, which wishes to see the truth, turns instead toward that principle according to which it judges all those things to be squares. What if someone were to tell us that the mind judges according to the same standard by which it is accustomed to see with the eyes? Why then does it say—provided it is truly educated—that a true sphere touches a true plane at a single point? What has it ever seen with the eyes, or can it see, of such a kind? Especially since nothing of this sort can be fashioned even by the imagination <term>phantasia: the mental faculty that produces images based on sensory data</term> of thought. Do we not prove this even when we describe the smallest circle in the mind through imagination and draw lines from it to the center? For when we have drawn two, between which a needle could scarcely be pricked, we can no longer draw others in the middle by that same imaginary thought so that they reach the center without any mixing; yet reason cries out that innumerable lines can be drawn, such that in every interval between them even a circle can be inscribed. Since that imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> cannot fulfill this, and the eyes themselves fail even more—since it was infused into the soul through them—it is manifest that imagination differs greatly from the truth, and that truth is not seen while this is being seen. The same happens when reason divides a line into infinity, which neither sense perceives nor imagination attains. From all these things, Augustine thinks it is established—as Plato also teaches in the *Epistle to the Syracusans* <note>Plato’s Seventh Letter, where he discusses the "spark" of knowledge that is lit in the soul after long study.</note>—that the truths of things themselves:

->dwell familiarly within our mind,<-
->and show that mind their own<-
->perpetual familiarity.<-

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY,
## on the Immortality of Souls
->by the same author, Ficino,<-
### BOOK XII.

*Many reasons and signs that the human mind is formed by the divine mind in the act of understanding. Chapter I.*

Plato, the father of philosophers, when discussing how to acquire wisdom in his letter to the Syracusans <note>This refers to Plato’s *Seventh Letter*, where he outlines his theory of knowledge.</note>, says that five things especially must come together for the knowledge of any subject: the name, the description, the image <term>idolum: a physical representation or likeness</term>, the formula <term>formula: an innate mental concept or "inner blueprint"</term>, and the Idea. Let us use the example of a circle, as he does, so that we may judge all other things in the same way. Our soul is often prompted toward the knowledge of a circle through hearing, when it hears both the name "circle" and a description of the circle such as this: "A circle is a curved figure, which is everywhere at equal intervals from a middle point." It is also prompted through sight, when it sees a circle either made of wood on a lathe or drawn on a wall; this is not a true circle, because it is not perfect, but rather an "idol" and a shadow <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of the true one. Having been prompted by these three things, the soul, greedy for truth, brings into action its own innate "formula" of a circle. Using this formula like a stamped character, the soul directs its sharp gaze toward the "Idea" of the circle itself which flourishes in the Divine Mind; indeed, this directing of the gaze is the very "knowledge" of the circle.

Plato shows in that letter that the soul, while enclosed in a body, cannot rise to the Idea without those four steps. Because the soul has long ago fallen far below itself, it must first return into itself through those three external steps, and then, through the formula which it holds within itself, ascend above itself to the Idea. For just as the forms of things are transmitted from the divine mind into physical matter through the lowest power of the soul—that is, through the "seeds of forms" <note>Ficino refers to "seminal reasons," the creative sparks that allow life to take shape in the physical world.</note> infused into this power—so too there is no passage from the perception of bodily forms into the Ideas of the divine mind except through the highest part of the soul. This happens through the innate formulas of the Ideas, so that we may transcend the forms of the body (which are entirely temporal because they change in both their essence and their qualities) and reach the forms of the divine mind (which are entirely eternal because they do not change in any part). This is achieved through the forms of the human mind, which are partly eternal and partly temporal: they are eternal because they remain the same in essence, but temporal because they turn from a state of potential habit into an active thought, and back again.

For a craftsman who is about to shape some material rightly prepares it first. Therefore, that Sublime Mind <note>God</note>, which is destined to form our mind daily through Ideas, long ago prepared our mind for this formation by means of the "characters" of the Ideas. It stamped us, as the Prophet sings: *The light of His face is sealed upon us* <note>A reference to Psalm 4:6.</note>, or, as he says elsewhere, *that we might see in His light.* This is so that through a formula awakened at the right moment, the Idea might be kindled in the mind no differently than fire is kindled in wood by sulfur, or than light is kindled in the air by a clear and serene nature. And just as nature relates to its own matter, so does God relate to His. Nature has adorned celestial matter (as some think) once and for all with all forms, but it adorns elemental matter in every single moment. Therefore, it is probable that God also filled "angelic matter" (so to speak) with all Ideas once and for all, but fills "soul-like matter" <note>the human mind</note> daily.

The opinion of Avicenna and Algazel <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Algazel (Al-Ghazali) were prominent medieval Islamic philosophers whose works heavily influenced Latin Scholasticism and the Renaissance.</note> seems in some part similar to this Platonic mystery. For they think that both elemental matter and the intellectual matter under the Moon are subject to a certain divine mind as a "former." They believe that bodily forms are its instruments for preparing elemental matter, but that the divine mind itself finally imprints the substantial forms upon that prepared matter. Similarly, they think the human mind is often prepared by the images of bodies received through the senses and the imagination, so that it turns itself toward that divine intelligence; and to the extent that it turns, it is daily formed by it. They argue that what we call "understanding" is nothing other than being formed by the divine intelligence. Furthermore, what we call "remembering" is simply having already contracted a habit by which we may easily turn toward the divine mind at our will. But let us leave the Arabs for now, though they are friendly enough to Plato. Let us return to Platonic matters. That we truly cannot know things unless we form them with Ideas is shown by these reasons:

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of how the human mind connects to the Divine Mind. On the previous page, he introduced Plato's five requirements for knowledge (Name, Description, Image, Formula, Idea) using the example of a circle. Here, he expands on why the first four are insufficient and why we must ultimately rely on the eternal "Idea" within God to truly understand anything.</meta>

<page-num>266</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

Plato seems to have convinced himself of the following. **First.** The name of a circle is changeable. For through the usage of different languages, a name can be varied or called something else. If this is so, the description is also changeable, since it is composed of names. The image <term>idolum: a physical representation or likeness</term> is also changeable. For a circle made of wood can be destroyed, and one that is painted can be wiped away. The formula <term>formula: the innate mental concept</term> is also changeable because it shifts from potentiality (a "habit" of the mind) into an active thought, and from an active thought back into a potentiality. However, that which is grasped through the true science of the circle is entirely immutable, because it is both universal and cannot be otherwise than it is. Therefore, an immutable Idea is necessary to grasp the immutable nature <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the circle.

**Second.** A circle that is made on a lathe or painted is not "pure," because it always has something of a straight-line figure mixed into it. Similarly, the phantasy <term>phantasia: the faculty of imagination that processes sensory data</term> which follows the sight of such an object does not reach the pure nature of the circle, which is entirely separated from its opposite figure (the straight line). Reason, too, if it listens only to the imagination, is deceived; it is necessary, therefore, that it recur to the pure Idea, through which it may perceive what is pure.

**Third.** True knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> of a circle consists in knowing *what* a circle is (its essence). 

However, those four previous things signify "quality" rather than "substance," because they are themselves qualities.

**Fourth.** The true and perfect mode of knowing follows the mode of being. Therefore, just as the circle—as well as the other species of things—is conceived and produced by the Divine Mind through the "Ideas of Ideas," so they must be known by the minds that follow <note>meaning human or angelic minds</note> through those same Ideas, so that all sciences may imitate the First Science to the best of their power. The truth of a created thing consists in this: that it corresponds to its own Idea in every way. Knowledge, however, consists chiefly in this: that the mind matches the truth. But the mind cannot square with the truth of the thing itself unless it also squares with the Idea, in whose harmony the truth is located; thus, through the Idea, which is the cause of the thing, the mind knows the thing, since true knowledge is knowledge through the cause. For this reason, the theology of John the Evangelist, which calls the Divine Idea the "Divine Reason" <note>original: "rationem diuinam," referring to the *Logos* or "Word" in the Gospel of John</note>, calls that very Reason "the Truth," because through it things both truly exist and are truly known.

**Fifth.** The intellect understands and judges any created things within their absolute "reasons" <term>rationibus: the eternal archetypes or blueprints in the mind of God</term>. And just as the same sensible objects are usually available by their nature to everyone who can perceive them—and those objects do not change even if the observers change—so the same intelligible "reasons" show themselves everywhere and always to all who use reason. They remain stable in themselves, while the souls of those reasoning approach them more or less closely. Reasons of this kind are superior to all created things, not only because all created things are tested or rejected by them as if by rules, but also because they are "prior" due to both their vastness and their simplicity. Therefore, they exist in God Himself, through which He Himself both discerns and arranges each thing. Consequently, when the intellect grasps reasons of this kind, it then grasps (in a certain way) both God, in whom they exist, and the things of which they are the patterns <note>original: "exemplaria"</note>. Yet, according to a certain natural origin, it grasps God (by whom they exist) before it grasps the things in which they do not reside, even though they are present to them. Nor should it seem incredible to anyone that any physical things are known through incorporeal patterns, rather than the other way around. For we perceive physical bodies through the spiritual images of sensible things—whether they are in the senses or in mirrors—and not the reverse. As for the fact that we are so deceived in this matter that, while we gaze upon the spiritual patterns of things, we often think we are looking only at the physical natures of things—is this any wonder? Even infants, when they see the incorporeal reflections of bodies in mirrors, and dreamers, when they think of spiritual images, believe they are seeing actual bodies. But this will be discussed more clearly in what follows. To these arguments, add two signs: one through the intellect, the other through the will. Through the intellect, in this way: in the knowledge of a natural species, such as beauty, we first devise some description of beauty common to all beautiful things. We immediately add certain properties of beauty deduced from that description.

We might perhaps grant that these notions could be thought out through a "formula" of beauty innate to the mind. But when we linger longer in this very consideration, we find that the nature of beauty which we have defined is infinite (because it is pure), and because it is infinite, it is God. Now, no one of sound mind would grant that an infinite nature—and God Himself—could be grasped through a limited formula which exists at a vast, indeed incomparable, distance below God. Therefore, the mind, through its own formula led forth from potentiality into act, [reaches] the Idea...

<summary>Ficino explains that human knowledge of physical objects is unreliable because physical things and mental images are changeable; true, immutable knowledge requires the mind to access the eternal "Ideas" or archetypes located within the Divine Mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from page 266 regarding how the human mind reaches true knowledge. He previously explained that the "formula" (our mental concept) is a mere ray of the divine "Idea." Here, he explains how that ray pulls the mind upward to unite with God, the source of all Truth and Goodness.</meta>

# ->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII<-

...and so, by a certain divine preparation, it is connected to that which is above; and once connected, it rises above itself. For no thing is ever raised above itself unless it is drawn by something superior. In what way does water fly into the air, unless it is lifted by the heat of the air? Moreover, by a certain easy and natural instinct, the **formula** <term>formula: the innate mental concept or "spark" within the human mind</term> itself, since it is a ray of the **Idea** <term>Idea: the eternal, divine archetype in the mind of God</term>, leaps back toward that Idea. It carries upward with it the mind into which this ray was infused. When this ray is led back to the Idea, it flows back into it as if into a fountain, just as a ray of light is reflected back to the Sun. Through this process—though not yet completely—a single thing is fashioned out of the mind and God. Hence Paul, the divine theologian, says:
> *He who adheres to God becomes one spirit.* <note>original: "Qui adhæret Deo, unus fit spiritus." 1 Corinthians 6:17</note>

This is signaled through the will; that is, the Mind, in the clear recognition of truth, is bathed in such wonderful pleasure that it exceeds every measure of human delight. The will desires such a state of life for its own sake alone, and all other things for the sake of it, as if such a state sits upon the highest citadel of nature, beyond which nothing remains to be desired.

For these reasons and others very similar, Plato seems to have convinced himself that nothing can truly be learned except when God is the teacher. Therefore, in the same letter <note>Ficino refers to Plato's Seventh Letter</note>, he says: *Divine mysteries cannot be taught with words.* But if someone dwells for a very long time with divine things and leads a life similar to them, suddenly—like a light flashing from a sparking fire—the light of truth shines forth in the soul and then nourishes itself. He rightly writes that this happened to him, because he had also written in his letter to King Dionysius that all the care of his mind was occupied in the investigation of divine things. Socrates believed that through the eventual purification of the mind, one would attain whatever investigation one desired. Therefore, having sometimes set aside his usual anxious searching, he fled to "mortal philosophy" <note>This refers to Socrates' "second sailing" or turning toward human ethics and definitions to find clarity</note> so that his mind, made more serene by the clearing away of bodily clouds, might suddenly catch the light of the divine Sun always and everywhere. Indeed, it seems that Socrates himself first attained this, and then Plato followed by imitating Socrates.

But let us return to the established order. In the seventh book of the *Republic*, when Plato had called God "Goodness itself," he added that it can scarcely be perceived; yet, if this is ignored, nothing can be truly known or rightly done, either publicly or privately. Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle</note> affirms that Socrates and Plato learned this from the Indian philosophers. Socrates declared this most openly to Theages: namely, that these things, as well as others, are learned from God alone, just as we narrated in the previous book. 

In the sixth book of the *Republic*, Plato compares God to the Sun (as we explained in our book *On Love*). Just as the highest thing in the realm of sensible objects relates to the senses and the things that can be sensed, so the highest thing in the realm of intelligible objects <term>intelligibilia: abstract truths or concepts that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term> relates to the intellect and the things that can be understood. The Sun creates the eyes that will see and the colors that are visible. It grants to the eyes their generation, their power of seeing, and the act of seeing, because without light we see nothing in actuality. It likewise gives to colors their generation and the power by which they can move the eyes, and the act through which they do move them. 

In this same way, God (as Plato writes) grants essence to minds, then the power of understanding, and finally infuses the intelligence itself. He also grants essence to the intelligible things, the power by which they can move the mind, and the act through which they do move it. Thus, God joins the act of the mind with the act of the intelligibles, just as the light of the Sun joins the act of the eye with the act of colors. And just as in seeing there is a threefold act—the movement of the color, the gaze of the eye, and the brightness of the light connecting the other acts to each other—so it is in understanding. There, the act of the intelligibles is called *Truth* by Plato, and the act of the mind is called *Knowledge*. According to Plato, the knot of both acts is God; indeed, He causes the mind to understand knowingly, and causes things to be truly understood—moreover, He causes Himself to be understood.

For this reason, John the Evangelist says that the Mind of God is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, and that no one proceeds to God except through it. <note>John 14:6. Ficino interprets the "Logos" or "Mind of God" as the intermediary</note> For He is the truth of the things to be understood, the life of the understanding mind, and the way through which the things themselves flow into the mind, and in which the mind meets the things. Therefore, he said elsewhere that only those can see the Spirit of Truth with whom and in whom God dwells. 

For if good things move the will under the rationale of "goodness," and therefore goodness itself moves the will through goodness toward goodness, and we desire nothing else in individual things except goodness itself; it follows that because true things move the intellect under the rationale of "truth," therefore truth itself, through truth, moves the intellect toward truth itself. The intellect understands nothing else other than truth itself. No one doubts that Goodness and Truth itself are God. 

Clear eyes see bright things by a common light; "airy" ears <note>Based on the ancient theory that the inner ear contained "pure air" to resonate with sound</note> hear sounds through the common air. Truth-telling minds understand and pronounce true things through a common truth. Likewise, good wills are moved toward good things by common goodness itself. And just as the eye, illuminated by the light of the Sun, gazes upon the colors and shapes of bodies within that light, and nothing else...

<summary>Ficino explains that the human mind can only achieve true knowledge through a divine connection, using the Platonic analogy of God as the "Sun of the Intellect" who provides the light (Truth) necessary for the mind to "see" spiritual realities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the "Divine Light." Having previously established that the human mind contains an innate "formula" or spark of the divine, Ficino now argues that all human knowledge is actually a perception of God’s own light, filtered through various forms, and explains why ancient philosophers always integrated worship with their studies.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...nothing is truly seen except light itself, although it may seem that various objects are being observed. This is because the light infused into the eye shines with various splendors as it is reflected into the sight from various bodies; and while the eye perceives this light reflected in bodies, it cannot endure the light itself in its own fountain-source. In the same way, our mind, illuminated by a ray from God, understands in that very ray the **reasons** <term>reasons: the "rationes" or eternal blueprints of things</term> of all things, whose fountain is God and which are God Himself. Therefore, it is only through the light of God that the mind knows light itself. Yet it seems to know diverse things because it understands itself under the various **Ideas** <term>Ideas: the divine archetypes</term> and reasons flowing from that source.

However, although we know all things daily through the light of God, and we perceive that very light step-by-step as it shines back under this or that figure of things, we will not see the pure light of God—absolute, free from all Ideas, and utterly infinite in its source—until we attain that state of the purest mind. In that state, we may behold the light itself in a single gaze, shining with the splendor of all Ideas at once. Then (as that distinguished herald of truth, John the Evangelist, says) **we shall see God as He is** <note>original: "uidebimus Deum sicuti est" — 1 John 3:2</note>, because we shall know God as God. For now, shaped by this or that Idea, we see Him as this or that species of things. 

Yet even in this life, according to John, theologians are children of God because they are daily reformed through divine Ideas. The series of these Ideas is called by him the **Word** <note>original: "ratio," usually translated as "the Word" (Logos) in John 1</note> of God, the life of all things, and the light of minds—not only of angelic minds, but also of human ones. Of all humans, I say, because He **illuminates every man coming into this world** <note>John 1:9</note>, so that whatever anyone understands, they understand in Him and through Him, even if dark minds do not comprehend Him because they do not recognize that they see all things through Him. Such minds indeed hear the voice of the divine spirit **breathing wherever it wills** <note>John 3:8</note>, but they do not know whence that voice comes or where it goes. 

When the ancient theologians recognized these things, they always joined the study of philosophy with religious piety. In the beginning, the philosophy of Zoroaster (as Plato testifies) was nothing other than wise piety and divine worship. The discussions of Hermes Trismegistus also begin with prayers and end in sacrifices. The philosophy of Orpheus and Aglaophemus is entirely occupied with divine praises. Pythagoras began his philosophical studies with the morning singing of sacred hymns. Plato commanded that in every single thing, one should begin from God, not only in speaking but also in thinking; and he himself always began from God. 

But I return for a moment to Pythagoras. When he had discovered that the longest side of that triangle which they call right-angled <note>The Pythagorean Theorem (a² + b² = c²)</note> was equal in power to the two remaining sides joined together, he sacrificed a hecatomb <note>A massive sacrifice, traditionally of 100 oxen</note> to God, as one who understood that nothing of truth can ever be seen without the light of the highest truth. Hence, finally, Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, is imagined to be born from the head of Jupiter alone. Hence also that saying: **From Jupiter is the beginning, O Muses; all things are full of Jupiter.** <note>original: "Ab Ioue principium Musæ, Iouis omnia plena." A quote from Virgil's Eclogues, echoing the Greek poet Aratus.</note>

## *The first question concerning the ascent to God: how the mind is*
## *raised into the divine Idea. Chapter II.*

**T**hree questions arise here. First, by what means the mind is raised into the divine Idea. Second, for what reason we do not notice that we are seeing God in 그 state. Third, by what means God continuously infuses this very intelligence into us, as Plato affirmed above. To the first, we answer thus for the present: When the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes sensory images</term>, excited by the figure of some man perceived through sight, is formed by a human likeness, then the **formula** <term>formula: the internal mental spark or concept</term> of the human species which lay hidden in the secrets of the mind flashes forth. It forms the focus of the mind or reason into an actual state, which it had previously formed as a mere habit. Such a formation is either a certain ambiguous understanding or the birth of understanding. After it is sufficiently formed in this way, the **Idea** of man is formed—that is, the "reason" through which God generates man. Thus, the mind, through the formula of the human, fits the divine Idea, just as wax that has been shaped by a ring matches its model when it is carefully applied to the ring. That very "fitting" is the true and distinct understanding of man. 

Therefore, Plato says in the *Symposium* that the soul, as a lover of divine beauty, when it touches divine reasons, no longer gives birth to mere images of things, but to true things; it nourishes what is born, becomes familiar with God, and is immortal above all others. But no one seems to have revealed this secret more clearly than John the Evangelist, who, when the mind of a man touches something true, does not say (as others are accustomed to) that it sees some [true...] <meta>catchword: ueram (true)</meta>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book XII of his Platonic Theology. Having discussed how the mind is illuminated by a ray from God, Ficino now explains how the human mind participates in divine Truth and why, despite seeing through God's light, we often fail to recognize the source of that light while in our earthly state.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII.

...true, but to **make the truth**, because he attains it in the thing itself; so that God, who is truth itself, is made as it were into his very form. For then the mind, clothed in an **Idea** <term>Idea: the eternal archetypes in the divine mind</term>, becomes the very truth of the thing—the "son" or product which was created through such an Idea. This is what all who contemplate do; regarding them, John says they "receive from the fullness of divine reason," <note>original: "de plenitudine diuinæ rationis accipere" — a reference to John 1:16</note> because whoever truly contemplates some species of things already receives into himself one of the number of Ideas, the fullness of which is divine reason itself.

Indeed, perfected theologians call the mind **fired gold**, because just as gold takes on the form of fire—through which it becomes hot, thinned, and glowing—so that mind, clothed in the Ideas of the divine mind, both shines with the light of truth and burns with the fuel of goodness. Paul the Apostle also affirms that the mind which contemplates divine things is both renewed daily, transformed into the same image as God, and becomes one spirit with Him. <note>referencing 2 Corinthians 3:18 and 1 Corinthians 6:17</note> **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition whom Ficino believed was a contemporary of Moses</note> similarly says that from a pure mind and divinity, a single spirit coalesces in a certain way. And all the Platonists prove that in contemplating the **reasons** <term>reasons: the "rationes" or blueprints of reality</term> of things, divine reason is touched by a certain substantial touch of the mind rather than an imagined one, and that the mind's own unity is coupled in an inestimable way to God, the unity of all things. Plato confirms this in the *Phaedrus*, in the *Epinomis*, and often elsewhere—especially in the *Phaedrus* when he says the contemplator of divine things is segregated from the rest, thoroughly purified, clings to God, and is filled with God; and in the *Epinomis*, that the soul perfected by contemplation emerges as utterly one alongside the divine unity. He holds the same view in the books of the *Republic*.

->Second Question. For what reason do we by no means notice that we see God in that state? Chapter II.<-

**T**o the second question, we can respond as follows. Just as the eye, formed through the **species** <term>species: here meaning the visual form or image</term> of a color, sees the color but does not discern the very species through which it sees; so perhaps the intellect, formed in some way by an **Idea**, immediately understands through this the natural appearance itself which was made through such an Idea. Yet it does not yet clearly behold the Idea itself; rather, it does not recognize it, even if it beholds it. 

Perhaps this happens in the beginning of contemplation and "squaring," but as one proceeds in contemplating and harmonizes more with it, one looks upon the Idea itself more clearly and recognizes it, though one does not yet discern where one is looking upon it. For just as children, while looking at their own reflections in that glare of the sun which surrounds the surface of water, think they see them not in the external light but in the bottom of the water; so the mind, while still unrefined, sees the reasons of things in the high God, yet thinks it sees them in itself or in other things. 

This is especially true since the reason of a natural thing in God—for instance, the "reason of air"—does not reflect God entirely as God (that is, as the absolute and free principle of the universe), but rather as the **exemplar** <term>exemplar: the perfect pattern</term> of air. The result is that when the mind is surrounded by the divine reason of air itself, it understands God not as God, but as "air"—for it sees a "watery" or "airy" God, that is, one circumscribed to the nature of air. 

The Angels, however, who are formed by all Ideas at once, perceive the fountain of all nature through that very gathering of all Ideas. For in this way, they insinuate themselves into the divine substance not from one part of it (as we do), but almost as a whole. Therefore, they notice *where* they see those things. The same will happen to us when we are thoroughly reformed into God. But now, almost all of us are deceived in this matter, no differently than common people who, seeing many things at night by the Moon, say they see by the light of the Moon—when nevertheless that is the light of the Sun, by which one sees even at night. 

So, ungrateful men affirm that they behold truths by their own natural light, which they actually behold in the common and divine light. But if the globe of the Sun itself either did not rise and set, or was never glimpsed by us in its own shape, no one would know from where this light is sent into the air by which we see all things. Just so, no one now knows from where light is sent down into the mind because we discern all things, for God—from whom that light descends—is hidden. 

It descends, however, in such a way that it is the beginning, middle, and end of our intelligence. The **beginning**, because just as the vision of the eye itself is produced by external light as a universal cause, and also by a certain interior spark ignited from it as a particular cause, so in us the act of understanding depends both on the vast mind of God and on our own. It is the **middle**, because in it we discern the eternal reasons which exist only in eternity. Finally, it is the **end**, because we only truly know Him. For the eternal reason of any thing, within eternity itself, is nothing else according to its essence than eternity. Here is revealed that divine [Plato...] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Platonis"</note>

<summary>Ficino explains that human knowledge of specific things is actually a partial perception of God's eternal Ideas, though we mistake this for our own natural light. He uses the analogy of moonlight (which is actually reflected sunlight) to show how we rely on divine light without recognizing its source.</summary>
<keywords>divine light, Ideas, contemplation, Marsilio Ficino, Platonism, Hermes Trismegistus, epistemology, reasons, archetypes, intellectual vision</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on how the soul attains divine truth, specifically referencing the teachings of Plato and the Neoplatonists regarding the ascent to the ultimate Principle.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...our **Plato's mystery**, which is read in the seventh book of the *Republic*. For he says that the Theologian <note>In Ficino's time, "Theologian" often referred to Plato himself or those who studied divine matters through his philosophy.</note> ascends through suitable foundations and steps of demonstration as far as the **Principle** of the universe, to touch it and to hold it, adhering always to those things which adhere to the Principle; indeed, he does not strive toward it by any corporeal steps of sensible things, but rather leans upon the **species** <term>species: here meaning the "Forms" or "Ideas"—the eternal blueprints of reality</term> themselves, through them and toward them, until he arrives at the **Species** which is the end of the universe.

A brief explanation of these words will be as follows: The Theologian, both by acting and by disputing, purges the soul from corporeal affections, segregates reason from the fallacious conjectures of sensible things, and invites the mind to betake itself by such steps toward the truth: by **species**—that is, by the formulas implanted in us from our origin; through **species**—that is, through the formation which comes to us from the **Ideas**; and toward **species**—that is, toward the consideration of the Ideas themselves and the species of natural things. He says that these species "adhere" to God, the Principle of the universe, for He is the fountain of Ideas; but the mind of the Theologian adheres to them—that is, it introduces itself to be formed by them. Through this introduction, he says, one "touches" God—that is, one is formed by the divine mind. 

He added "and to hold" God for two reasons (as I think): First, because once the mind has so begun, it perhaps never entirely interrupts such a state of life; second, because after our mind has been formed from many parts by the divine mind through long contemplation, it begins to be wise so far above the human level that it knows how to contemplate itself through God, and to contemplate God in God. 

Now, he calls God here by several names: **Principle**, **End**, and **Species**. 
*   **Principle**, because all things are from Him, and because intelligence takes its beginning from Him. 
*   **End**, because both intelligence and all things are terminated in Him. 
*   **Species**, both because He is the **Act** <term>Act: in scholastic philosophy, "act" is the state of being real or complete, as opposed to "potency" or mere possibility</term> which forms and makes all things as they proceed from Him as their Principle, and reforms and perfects those same things as they are turned back toward Him as their End; and because every mind is formed by Him when it understands the truth. 

He added a fourth name to God, namely the **Good** itself, or **Goodness** itself. It is proper to the Good that it diffuses itself, that it allures things, and that it perfects them. God diffuses Himself by producing things, allures them by converting <note>original: "convertendo" — in this context, turning things back toward their source</note> them, and perfects them by forming those things that proceed and reforming those that have turned back. 

Moreover, he places the **Good** itself above **Mind** and above **Essence**. Above Mind, certainly—that mind which is the invisible eye capable of truth and greedy for goodness. For God is not said to be "capable of truth" or "desirous of goodness," but is Truth and Goodness itself. However, according to a more excellent sense, He can be called "Mind," both because the divine truth is not ignorant of itself, and because many minds flow forth from a certain exuberance of divine goodness. God is also located above that **Essence** which is the subject of "being" itself. Indeed, He is even located above that "being" which is the **act of essence**. For such an act, because it is mixed with passive power, is impure and infinite. He is nevertheless called "Being" by the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who generally identified God with "Being" (Ens) or the "First Mover."</note> insofar as He is pure and absolute Act, through which all essences receive the act of being. 

However, **Plotinus** and **Proclus** <note>Two of the most influential Neoplatonic philosophers after Plato.</note> place the **One** and the **Good** above "Being" for these reasons: The influence of the One and the Good propagates itself more widely than the influence of Being. Indeed, formless matter and potentiality must be said to participate more in the One and the Good than in Being; for "to be" happens through **Form**, but matter is formless—yet matter is still called "one," and is greedy for the Good. And they seem to have received this argument from **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian (likely 5th century) whom Ficino believed was the biblical Dionysius and who synthesized Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>. 

Furthermore, just as a multitude is not the same as nothingness, so "Being" itself is not the same as the "One." Yet, they are not arranged equally—Being on one side and the One on the other—lest two principles of things be foolishly established. Nor again is Being above the One, for if it were, the One would become a participant in Being, and would no longer be "one," but "two"—that is, "one" and "being" together. It follows, therefore, that the **One** is above **Being**. 

Finally, as much as "Unity" signifies something simpler than "Being" (in which essence and being are enclosed), so much more does it suit the first Principle of things. Nor do they permit "being" to be segregated anywhere from "essence," lest the proper act be segregated from its proper power. Nor do they wish it to seem a wonder to anyone that they name the Principle of things "**Unity**." For they distinguish it thus: It must be named either Unity, or Multitude, or a Composite of both. But it is not a Composite, lest it be forced to depend on that which reconciled the diverse things into one. It is not a Multitude devoid of unity, because such a thing would lack all power, and the universe would lack all union. Again, in the Principle of all things, all power must exist. Therefore, if the Principle were Multitude itself, then to the extent that any part fell into multitude, it would become more powerful. But since things are more powerful to the extent that they approach Unity, and the opposite is also true, it follows that the Principle of things is properly **Unity**.

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's ascent to God using Plato’s Republic, defining God as the One and the Good who exists above Being and Mind. He argues that Unity is the most fundamental characteristic of the first principle of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Republic VII, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, The One, The Good, Being vs Essence, Plotinus, Proclus, Dionysius the Areopagite, Unity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's ascent to the divine. On the previous page, he discussed how the "Theologian" (Plato) uses the "species" or eternal Forms to reach the ultimate Principle. Here, he distinguishes between the One, the Good, and Beauty, explaining how the soul's deepest, pre-rational desires lead to a mystical union with God that surpasses intellectual understanding.</meta>

-># ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII.<-

...to be called. Finally, since each individual thing is properly created and preserved by a certain union, who would not see that unity itself is the cause that makes and preserves all things? Likewise, all things desire the Good simply; but they do not desire "being" (existence) simply, but rather "well-being" (existence in a good state). Perhaps if they were completely unable to achieve well-being, they would not even desire to exist, as <term>Olympiodorus</term> <note>Olympiodorus the Younger (c. 495–570 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher in Alexandria who wrote influential commentaries on Plato.</note> proves, since things desire to exist for the sake of the Good. Therefore, since the Good is the ultimate end, it is surely the first principle of all. If it exists above "Being" itself, it exists much more so above Life and Mind. 

When people speak of the **One** and the **Good**, they always mean the same thing. For just as in the order of things, "well-being" consists in union—since evil happens through discord and division—so too, above the order of the universe, the One and the Good are the same. Its splendor is **Beauty**, which is nothing other than the rational order of many forms shining out in the mind, the soul, nature, and matter. They prove that the One is above Beauty because Beauty is composite <note>In Platonic thought, the ultimate Source must be "Simple" or "One." Since Beauty requires a relationship between parts—symmetry, order, etc.—it is considered "composite" and thus one step below the absolute Unity of the One.</note>. Again, they prove that the Good is above Beauty because all things always desire the Good, but only those things which know Beauty desire it, and even then, only after they have come to know it. Furthermore, we desire Beauty for the sake of the Good, hoping it will be beneficial to us. Finally, we want to truly possess the Good, yet we are often satisfied if we merely see Beauty openly. 

Too blessed are those whom the beauty of the universe—the splendor of the Good itself—transforms into the Good through love. This is especially true because, while it transforms them into the Good, it likewise reforms them into the One, and thus joins them to the Good itself in unity. Indeed, the One and the Good, being the same, are spread through all things and over all things; they are desired by all things by a natural desire, even without conscious knowledge. Nor can they differ from each other as two equally ranked things, lest there be two separate principles of reality. Nor can the One be above the Good, lest something be called "better" and more desirable than the Good. Nor again can the Good be above the One, lest that which is called good cease to be "one" (unified). Therefore, the **One** and the **Good** are fundamentally the same, just as division and evil are equally shunned as the same thing. 

Blessed is he who is completely united with the Good. He is not united by intellectual power, strictly speaking. For since the intellect is manifold and located below the "intelligible" <note>The "intelligible" realm refers to the world of eternal Ideas. Ficino argues that God (the One) is even higher than these Ideas.</note>, it neither matches the nature of unity, nor can it reach that which towers over universal being. Add to this that since the One and the Good are desired by a certain instinct that precedes intelligence, it follows that they are reached by a certain "touch" above intelligence—a <term>unifying touch</term> <note>original: "tactu unifico"</note>, so to speak. This happens through our own inner unity, which surpasses our intelligence and joins the soul to the very unity and goodness of all things. This is not an imaginary link of the intellect, but a true union of the soul's very substance. From this follows not some light, external, or partial joy—like that of one seeing or hearing a good thing—but a powerful, internal, and universal pleasure is produced. It is like a taste or touch superior to the intellect, belonging to one who now deeply tastes and touches that sweetness which is superior to anything the mind can grasp. 

Truly, a natural thirst desires liquid before we recognize through our senses that we are thirsty; and after we have recognized it, we desire it again. The appetite that follows the senses is imaginary and more remote from our essence; the preceding appetite, however, is intimate to our essence. Similarly, it is not so much the desire that follows the mind's action, but rather the one that precedes it (as the starting point of motion), which enjoys the goal of that motion. It is this desire that completes the substantial bond and, therefore, it alone completely fulfills our deepest prayer.

***

### Third Question: In what way God continually infuses intelligence into us. Chapter 4.

**B**ut from here let us now descend to the third question. I believe this to be the sense of our <term>Plato</term> when he writes that both knowledge is infused into the intellect and truth into intelligible things by the Good itself. He means that this beneficial and life-giving act of all things, which is **God**, always encompasses His works and inserts Himself into all things. Most of all, by shining in the secrets of the mind, He continually cleanses, sharpens, illuminates, and inflames its gaze. He gives life to the "formulas" <note>Ficino uses "formulas" to refer to innate ideas or divine blueprints placed in the human mind by God at creation.</note> implanted in the mind, so that whenever we are free from cares and apply our soul to the investigation of truth, those formulas—made more lively by God’s life-giving power—burst forth more readily into the open...

<summary>Ficino argues that the One and the Good are identical and represent the highest principle above the intellect, reachable only through a mystical "unifying touch." He then begins explaining how God constantly illuminates the human mind and activates its innate divine ideas.</summary>
<keywords>The One, The Good, Beauty, Olympiodorus, mystical union, unifying touch, divine illumination, innate ideas, Platonic Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XII of the *Platonic Theology*. Having previously established that the One and the Good are the ultimate source, Ficino now transitions into an explanation of how human understanding is a direct reflection of divine light, using the metaphor of mirrors and musical resonance.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...and the sharpness of the mind, set ablaze by God's radiation, may behold more clearly and ardently. In this, God relates to the very act of understanding as the primary and universal agent; the <term>formula</term> <note>Ficino uses "formula" to mean the inner patterns or rules of logic and geometry that God places in the human mind as reflections of His own Ideas.</note> acts as the specific and secondary agent; the image acts as the stimulus; and the mind occupies the place of matter <note>In the sense that the mind is the "receptacle" that receives the form of knowledge.</note>. But let us consider this matter through an example, so that we may see more clearly by what means the act of understanding descends into us from God. If God, according to the Idea of the mind to be created which flourishes within Himself, tempers our mind in the act of procreation and shapes it as much as possible to Himself—just as motion and sound pass from one lyre to another similarly tuned—is it any wonder that when the divine mind "sounds" through the act of understanding, the human mind resonates in harmony? 

Imagine a craftsman who makes a thousand mirrors; once they are made and arranged in order, he presents himself before them. In a thousand mirrors, a thousand images of the craftsman result. Sometimes the craftsman moves himself in such a way that he turns his eye to look at his other limbs, and turns his limbs as best he can toward his eye. The images in the mirrors imitate these movements. At the movement of the living eye, all the imaginary eyes move; at the movement of the living limbs, the imaginary limbs move. Similarly, God procreates souls, and then presents Himself to them as if to mirrors; through this presentation, images of God are made in each of them. These images are the very "minds" of the souls, so that while the minds are many (because there are many souls in which they exist), they are also all one (because it is one God whom they reflect). Furthermore, each mind, through its power of understanding, reflects the power of God as He conceives the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The "Ideas" (Forms) are the eternal archetypes of all things existing in the Mind of God.</note>, and through its internal formulas, it reflects the Ideas themselves. From this, that prophetic saying which we touched upon above is also opened up:

> The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us, and in your light we shall see light. <note>original: "Signatum est super nos lumen uultus tui Domine, & in lumine tuo uidebimus lumen." A combination of Psalm 4:6 and Psalm 36:9.</note>

Truly, God, through His own fruitful power by which He conceives Ideas through discernment, provides and preserves a power for the mind through which it may reach the Ideas by understanding. Again, God, through the Ideas themselves already conceived and distinguished by reason, imprints and preserves the "formulas" of the Ideas in the mind. At God’s movement—that is, at God’s act—a continuous movement occurs in our minds. In what way? The power that is in God, which conceives the Ideas, turns itself in a certain way toward those Ideas, and the Ideas in turn reflect back toward that power. Meanwhile, by a certain harmonious tempering, it happens that the power of understanding in a person's mind (if it is unburdened and raised up toward God) turns itself toward the internal formulas, and the formulas are turned toward the power of understanding. And thus, the acts of the mind perpetually imitate the acts of God in a wonderful consonance. Truly, because a face in a mirror, when it seems to look at the face from which it flows, is actually being looked at rather than looking, the Apostle Paul says:

> When you have known God, or rather have been known by God. <note>original: "Cum Deum cognoueritis, imò cogniti sitis à Deo." Galatians 4:9.</note>

Thus, the "upper face" of our soul is called an imitation of the divine face by the Platonists—so much so that <term>Plotinus</term>, <term>Theodore of Asine</term>, and <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>Three major Neoplatonist philosophers who emphasized the soul's divine origin and its continuous connection to the higher realm.</note> judged that this mind of man, which is not merely human but divine, lives and operates continuously in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal truths, above the physical world.</note> through a continuous intuition of the Ideas. Now, two reasons especially moved Plotinus, Theodore, and Iamblichus to this conclusion. 

**First**, because the supreme mind of the Soul is an intellectual essence according to its own nature, it understands through its very essence—just as fire is hot by its essence and water is cold—even though the lower power of the soul's mind may not understand through its essence. Therefore, just as fire is always hot, so the mind is always understanding. The objects of this intelligence are the eternal species of things themselves. But the intellect, in the act of understanding, does not cling to the deceptive shadows of objects; rather, so that it may truly understand, it is united with the objects themselves. Therefore, the mind is always united with the eternal species, which is why it diligently inhabits the temple of eternity. This is what Iamblichus means: "The being of our intellect is nothing other than understanding the divine powers." For he thinks that just as it is the same act by which the Sun illuminates the Moon and the Moon is illuminated by it (reflecting the Sun with the likeness of its light), so too it is the same act by which the divine mind creates and illuminates our mind, and our mind is created and illuminated therefrom, being turned toward that source by a certain natural intuition. Similarly, an image in a mirror looks back at a face by the same act by which it is looked at by the face. And just as it is made by being looked upon, so it is preserved by looking back. Such is the soul's likeness to God.

The **second** reason is as follows. The rational soul is made by the divine mind and joined to the body, and it occupies a middle ground between the mind and the body. If it clung only to the mind, it would not grant life to the body. If it clung only to the body, it would understand nothing. Therefore, it clings to the mind and the body simultaneously—just as a line touches the center and the circumference at once, or as the light of the Sun is joined to the Sun while being diffused through the air. And yet, as the rational soul relates to the body, so the Mind relates to the rational soul. But corporal life itself is nothing other than a continuous act of the soul poured into the complexion of this body, without departing from the soul.

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's connection to God using the metaphor of a mirror, arguing that human thought is a resonant reflection of divine activity. He cites Neoplatonists to argue that the highest part of the human mind remains eternally united with God's Ideas, even while the soul animates the physical body.</summary>
<keywords>mirror metaphor, divine illumination, Iamblichus, Plotinus, intellectual essence, eternal species, rational soul, intelligible world, participation, resonance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XII of the *Platonic Theology*. In the previous section, Ficino used the analogy of mirrors and musical resonance to explain how the human mind receives light and "harmony" from the Divine Mind. Here, he explores the idea that our highest intellect is in a state of perpetual activity, even when we are not consciously aware of it.</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII.
S
<meta>Catchword: properly</meta>

Therefore, the life of the intellectual soul is nothing other than the perennial act of the divine intellect, joined to the soul and never severed from God. And just as God inserts the seeds of things to be generated into the soul's corporal life, so He kindles the little sparks of things to be known in the soul. Corporal life is a reflection <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of the rational soul. The life of the intellectual soul is a reflection of the divine life and mind. The lowest part of the soul, which is the power of nourishment <note>The "vegetative" soul responsible for growth and digestion.</note>, presides over corporal life. If this lowest part, which is joined to the body, acts always and operates in a certain way by its very being, then much more does the supreme power—which is stronger because it clings closer to its source—operate always, and operate in a certain way through its very being. Moreover, it acts around the mind, from which it flows most closely. For mind flows only from mind. The mind which is above us, because it is pure intellect, is fed by the pure intelligible—that is, it enjoys pure truth. This same mind of ours is fed continually if it reclines at the banquet of the higher mind. 

Nor do we wrongly place an essential and perpetual intelligence in the soul, because it exists in the soul for the reason that it harmonizes with the perpetual causes of its own essence. And just as there is an innate, perpetual, and essential appetite for the good in the soul, so too there is a natural and essential intuition—or rather a certain <term>touch</term> <note>original: "tactus." A Neoplatonic concept where the mind "touches" God directly, bypassing logic.</note>—of the truth itself, to use the words of Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and the soul's direct contact with the divine.</note>. This "touch," I say, is prior to and more excellent than all cognition and discursive reasoning. The divine Iamblichus confirmed such an opinion by this further reasoning: <margin>Just as we reach temporal and contingent things through temporal and contingent cognition, so we must reach necessary and eternal things through an essential and perpetual notion.</margin> This notion precedes our inquiry in the same way that a state of rest precedes motion. Conversely, temporal cognition follows inquiry in the same way that a contingent effect follows motion and time. 

Now, they believe that the divine act of the mind itself—which occurs through a certain intuition and a "touch," as it were, of divine things—is not actually interrupted within itself because of lower actions; however, as far as our **conscious awareness** <note>original: "animaduersionem." The act of the mind noticing its own operations.</note> is concerned, it may be interrupted in the lower powers. Meanwhile, the acts of the rational intellect (or the intellectual reason) which occur through step-by-step reasoning are usually interrupted because of lower operations, and vice versa. 

But why do we not notice such a wonderful spectacle of that divine mind of ours? Perhaps because we have ceased to wonder or notice due to the constant habit of seeing. Or perhaps because the "middle powers" of the soul—namely, **reason** and **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia." The faculty that processes and stores sensory images.</note>—since they are for the most part inclined toward the business of life, do not clearly perceive the works of that higher mind, just as when an eye sees something but does not recognize it. But when the middle powers are at rest, sparks of that intellectual speculation flow down into them as if into a mirror. From this, true reasoning is born from true understanding, and human understanding from the divine. 

Nor is it strange that something happens in that mind which we do not feel at all. For we notice nothing unless it passes into the middle powers. For this reason, although the power of desire often hungers and thirsts, we do not notice this until the intention of such a passion passes into the imagination. Does not the power of nourishment act continually? Yet we do not weigh its constant action at all; likewise, we do not weigh the perpetual intelligence of the mind. Nor is that intelligence weaker because we do not recognize that we are understanding; rather, it is even more intense. For often while we sing or run, we do not think at all about the fact that we are singing or running, and because of this, we perform the action more attentively. Indeed, the conscious awareness of an action distracts the soul’s focus and diminishes the action. Novices in any art cannot perform the works of that art without paying close attention, but veterans—even if they are not paying attention—operate by a certain habit and, as it were, by nature. What prevents the continuous intelligence of the mind from being like this? 

Since light joined to light harmonizes into one without confusion (for both are everywhere, yet one can be discerned from the other), it follows that the minds of men, joined to the divine mind, become in a way one with the divine mind and one with each other, yet without being confused among themselves. This is no different than many lines drawn from a circumference to a center; through their points, they touch the middle point of the circle, and there the point of each line becomes, in a way, one with the center point of the circle. Each individual point also becomes one with the others in a certain way; though location or time does not distinguish them, reason itself distinguishes them. This is the same way that many notions in the mind are joined both to each other and to the mind without any confusion. Truly, just as smaller spheres within a larger sphere touch the center of the larger sphere with their own centers, so our minds are like smaller spheres of the intelligible world, encompassed under divine goodness as if by a larger sphere, and revolved beneath it...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect is perpetually active and connected to God, even when our conscious awareness is distracted by the body or lower mental faculties. He uses analogies of light, geometry, and habit to explain how the soul can "touch" the divine without losing its individual identity.</summary>
