<page-num>274</page-num>

<meta>Catchword: Where</meta>

properly through their own centers—that is, through their own units <note>In Neoplatonism, the "unit" or "one" of the soul is its highest point, which allows it to connect directly with the Divine One.</note> which are more excellent than their own intellects—they join themselves to the divine unity as if to the center of the universe. And if by chance the circles are pulled apart, the centers are also pulled apart, seeing as they had been united rather than confused. But Plotinus never wishes them to be pulled apart, lest the eternal spheres of the minds remain less united with their own highest sphere than the temporal spheres of the visible world are with the greater sphere. But he himself shall see to this. Let us, however, return to the established order. From all these things which we have drawn from the fountains of Plato and Plotinus, it is concluded that the human mind, in its own act of understanding, is compared to the divine mind almost in the same way that **matter** is compared to **form**. 

Certainly, if our mind is daily formed by the ideas of the divine mind, and through them performs its own proper work, who does not see that our mind is subject to the divine, just as matter is subject to form? And that it relates to divine forms no differently than <term>prime matter</term> <note>materia prima: the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things.</note> relates to natural forms? Whence it ought to be no less immortal than that matter, especially because the more pure and simple the mind is compared to bodies and souls—and for this reason is more "one"—the tighter the bond that results from those two minds coming together into one than usually results either from any corporal things mixed together, or from souls running together, or from a soul uniting with a body. 

The knot of this bond is increased by the fact that God is unity itself and goodness itself. And through the power of unity, the bond of all things is united; through the power of goodness, attraction and approach happen everywhere. Nowhere does a more fruitful union result than where the mind breathes together with divinity. Likewise, if God—who is closest to the mind and perpetually flowing from it—glides inside it with an infinite thinness of purity, and fills it completely with an amplitude of power, and connects the parts of the mind like joints from within (just as a sinew connects them to each other and to the whole), and binds that whole essence to Himself like an intimate knot, then He is more interior to the mind than the mind is to itself. What wonder is it then that God is united to the mind in its own intelligence as a form? Especially after He has already been united in essence and life more than a form? 

The chief sign of that union is this: that through true intelligence the most intimate substance of a thing is always inspected, as if it had penetrated more deeply into the **idea** of the thing than either sight penetrates the appearance of color, or the imagination penetrates the image of color—since sense and imagination only touch the surfaces of things. Therefore, Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note> says that from the breathing together of divinity and the mind, one spirit coalesces. And the Theology of John <note>Referring to the Gospel of John or the Johannine tradition.</note> teaches that those who contemplate divine reason are so perfected into one with it, just as it is united to God. Truly, if in the genus of corporal things there is such a great union that matter (which is their furthest limit) is made into one thing not only with all the intermediaries, but even with the supreme of the corporal genus, who will deny that there is at least an equal union in the genus of intellectual things? Thus the human mind, although it is the furthest limit of those things, may nevertheless become one with all intellectual forms, and even with the supreme. 

However, a third nature does not arise from the soul and God (made by some third component joining both and directing both to a third act), as happens in the composition of natural things. Rather, because in the contemplating soul God is both the **prime mover** and the **ultimate former**, the entire act is God—by which act He Himself is always God, and the soul becomes, at least at some point, divine. And just as nature, through natural motion, hands over the order of forms to matter, so God, through divine and mortal life, hands over the clear possession of forms to the mind, so that a divine and immortal life belongs to the same mind to which a divine and immortal intelligence is suited. 

And just as matter, although it flows under inferior forms, nevertheless always rests in the sublime ones (as some think), so the mind of man, although it flows through sensible and imaginary forms, can nevertheless at some point rest forever under divine ones—which it even does now, as Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Theodorus wish. Thus, just as the boundless dimension of quantity always perfects matter, so the immense power of divine amplitude perennially forms the mind with eternal ideas through its light. And because every formation is effected through congruence, this subject cannot be mortal, since it is continually formed by eternal forms. If prime matter is incorruptible—into which certain everlasting forms penetrate, even though matter itself does not penetrate into them—will not the mind also be immortal, which is not only penetrated by those forms, but also penetrates them by knowing, and is reflected back into them by recognizing? Furthermore, where the **first mind** is, there is **first life**, since mind is the reflection of life into its own being.

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by comparing the human mind's relationship with God to the relationship between matter and form, asserting that the mind is "formed" by eternal divine ideas. He cites Neoplatonic authorities and Christian theology to show that the mind's ability to grasp the inner essence of things proves its divine and indestructible nature.</summary>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII<-

<page-num>275</page-num>
<sig>S 2</sig>

Where there is first life, there also is first being, since life is the first and most intimate motion of being itself. <note>original: "uita eſt primus & intimus ipſius eſſe motus"</note> Certainly, God is called **First Being** among many insofar as He exists through Himself and truly remains perpetually as that which exists. Insofar as He does not grow sluggish in idleness but works assiduously within Himself, He is called **Life**. Insofar as His act is of such a kind that it does not flow outside but flows back into Himself, He is called **Mind**. For by that reflection, He observes Himself. 

But since that which is highest in any genus contains nothing of a contrary genus—neither mixed in nor close by—it follows that the First Mind suffers nothing of unreason <note>original: "demens"; here meaning the absence of intellect or madness</note> either in itself or near itself; nor does the First Life suffer anything mortal; nor does the First Being suffer anything that will rush into nothingness; nor does the First Unity suffer anything dissoluble; nor does the First Goodness suffer anything subject to disease. Therefore, the mind which is joined to the Mind, just as it retains nothing of unreason in that union, so it admits nothing mortal, perishable, dissoluble, or subject to disease, because through the First Mind it is also coupled to the First Life, to First Being, and to similar Unity and Goodness. What wonder is it if the intellectual life remains immortal because of its encounter with the First Life, since the celestial bodies (as the Platonists maintain) are indeed dissoluble by their own nature—because they are both mobile and composed of many natures or parts—yet they endure undissolved because they are coupled to the immortal soul with no other body coming between them? Those things which are dissolved by another medium are of a different sort, such as bodies composed of many elements, which receive an immortal soul (as the <term>Magi</term> <note>The Magi: traditionally referring to the followers of Zoroaster, whom Ficino considered part of a "prisca theologia" or ancient lineage of wisdom leading to Plato.</note> hand down) through the medium of a celestial body.

# *First confirmation of the previous reasoning through sight.*
## *Chapter V.*

**A**lthough Plato discussed the idea that the souls of men transmigrate from bodies into other bodies and remember the arts of a previous life in subsequent ones, he did not do so according to his own judgment, but recounted it from the opinion of certain Egyptians; an opinion which <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian whom Ficino frequently cites to reconcile Plato with Christianity.</note> rejected. However, that the soul of man descends from its very Creator marked with the forms of things, and that it does not sufficiently comprehend the substances of things through these forms alone, but is able to comprehend them once they are reformed through these as if they were preparations for the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The Platonic Ideas: the eternal, unchanging patterns or archetypes of all things in the divine mind.</note>—this, I say, Plato often seems to have affirmed from his own mind, and Augustine highly approved. 

Therefore, walking in the footsteps of Augustine, let us strive again toward the confirmation of the previous sentiment. Let us proceed, however, by a triple path: by sight, by hearing, and by reason. First, by sight, in this manner: The soul by which bodies live is more powerful than all bodies, because it gives life to bodies. It is certainly more excellent than that which possesses sensation. But indeed, in the human soul there is something more outstanding—I do not mean that by which it senses sensible things, but that by which it judges concerning sensible things. Now indeed, it is easy to see that the one judging is more excellent than those things about which it judges and which do not themselves judge. 

Not only does the rational life judge concerning sensible things, but also concerning the senses themselves; for example, why an oar must appear broken in water when it is straight, and why it must necessarily be perceived that way through the eyes. For the sight of the eyes can report this fact, but it can in no way judge it. Therefore, the rational life excels the sensual. Thus, if reason judges according to itself, there is no nature more excellent. But because it is clear that reason is changeable—since it is found now ignorant, now skilled—it judges better the more skilled it is, and it is more skilled the more it participates in some art, discipline, or wisdom; thus the art itself must be sought. 

Nor do I wish "art" to be understood here as that which is noted by experience, but that which is tracked down by reasoning. For certainly it must be asked why it offends us if, when two windows are located not one above the other but side by side, one of them is larger and the other smaller, when they could have been equal? Yet if they were one above the other, and both were unequal even by half, that inequality would not so offend. And why do we not care much how much one of them is larger or smaller when there are only two, but in a group of three, the sense itself seems to demand either that they be not unequal, or that the middle one be between the largest and the smallest such that it exceeds the smaller by as much as it is exceeded by the larger? For in this way, nature itself is first consulted, as it were, as to what it approves. Where it is most especially to be noted how that which, when looked at alone, was less displeasing, is rejected when compared to something better. Thus it is found that "common art" is nothing other than the memory of things experienced and pleasing, with a certain use of the body and operation joined to it; if you lack this [operation], you can still indeed judge concerning the works, which is much more excellent than working [as a] craftsm— <note>original: "artifici-" catchword "cioſa" implies "artificiosa" (skillfully/craftsman-like)</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's immortality is derived from its union with the Divine Mind and demonstrates the soul's superiority over the body through its ability to judge sensory perceptions and aesthetic proportions.</summary>

->MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...you cannot be <note>original: "cioſa," likely the end of "preciosa" (precious) from the previous page</note> [precious?]. But since in all arts **harmony** <note>original: "conuenientia"</note> is what pleases—through which alone, when preserved, all things are beautiful—and this harmony itself seeks **equality** and **unity**, whether by the similarity of equal parts or the gradation of unequal parts, who is there who can find supreme equality or similarity in physical bodies? Who would dare to say, after careful consideration, that any body is truly and simply "one"? For all bodies are changed, either from one species to another or by moving from place to place, and they consist of parts occupying their own locations, by which they are divided into different spaces.

Furthermore, true equality and similarity, and that true and primary unity, are perceived not by any sense, but are seen by the mind when it understands. For from where would equality be sought in bodies (of whatever kind), or how would it be proven to differ so greatly from perfection, unless that which is perfect were seen by the mind? 

And since all things that are beautiful to the senses—whether produced by nature or crafted by the arts—are beautiful in specific places and times (such as a body or the motion of a body), that equality and unity known only to the mind—by which we judge physical beauty through the senses as messengers—is neither swollen <note>original: "tumida"; referring to physical extension or occupying space</note> by location, nor unstable in time. For it cannot be rightly said that a round temple is judged according to one standard, and a round vessel or a round coin is judged by another. Similarly, in the case of time and the motions of bodies, it is ridiculous to say that equal years are judged by one rule and equal months by another. Rather, whether something moves harmoniously through these vast spaces, or through hours, or through the shortest moments, it is judged by the same one and unchanging equality. 

Because if smaller and larger spaces of shapes and motions are judged by the same law of parity, similarity, or congruency, then that law is "greater" than all of them—greater in power, though in the space of place or time it is neither larger nor smaller. If it were larger, we would not judge smaller things according to the whole law; if it were smaller, we would not judge larger things according to it. 

Now, in truth, since a square market-place and a square stone are both judged by the entire law of "squareness," and if the movements of a running ant's feet and those of a walking elephant are judged to be in proportion by that same law of equality, who could doubt that this law is neither larger nor smaller than those intervals of space and time, since it surpasses them all in power? 

Since this law of all arts is entirely unchanging, yet the human mind—to which it is granted to see such a law—can suffer the changeability of error, it is clear enough that there is a **Law** above our mind, which is called **Truth**. Nor should it be doubted that the unchanging nature which is above the rational soul is **God**, and that the first life and first essence are there, where the first wisdom is. For this is that unchanging Truth, which is rightly called the Law of all arts and the Art of the Almighty Architect. 

Therefore, when the soul feels that it does not judge the appearance and motion of bodies according to itself, it must at the same time acknowledge that its own nature is superior to the nature it is judging [the body], but also that the nature by which it judges—and which it can in no way judge—is superior to itself. 

For I can say why the limbs of any body ought to correspond to each other on both sides: it is because I am delighted by a supreme equality, which I behold not with my eyes, but with my mind. For this reason, I judge those things which I see with my eyes to be better the closer they are, by their nature, to those things which I understand with my soul. But as to *why* those mental ideals are as they are, no one can say; nor would any sober person say they "ought" to be so, as if they could possibly be otherwise. 

And as for why they please us, or why we love them most vehemently when we are at our wisest, no one who understands them rightly would dare to say. For just as we and all rational souls judge lower things correctly according to Truth, so Truth itself alone judges us when we cling to it; but even the Father <note>referring to God the Father</note> does not judge Truth itself. For Truth is not less than He is. And therefore, whatever the Father judges, He judges through Truth. 

For all things that seek unity have this as their rule, or form, or model, since Truth alone has fulfilled the likeness of Him from whom it received its being. The Mind judges all things because it is above all things when it is with God. It is with Him when it understands most purely and loves what it understands with total clarity. Thus, as much as it can, it becomes that very Law and the very thing through which it judges all things, and which no one can judge. 

Just as in the case of these temporal [human] laws: although men judge them when they institute them, once they have been instituted and confirmed, it is not permitted for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but rather to judge *by* them. If the founder of temporal laws is a good and wise man, he should consult that **Eternal Law**, which no soul is permitted to judge, so that he may discern through its unchanging rules what should be commanded or forbidden for the time being. Therefore, the Eternal Law...

...it is permitted for pure minds to recognize [this law], but it is not permitted to judge it. To be sure, we can judge the soul and the body according to that law: "this action is less vigorous than it should be," or "this is less bright than it should be." But no one judges the law itself. For when someone says that eternal things are better than temporal things, or that seven and three are ten, no one says it *ought* to have been so; rather, he simply says it is so. In recognizing it, he does not correct it as an examiner, but rejoices in it as a discoverer.

But for many, human pleasure is the end, and they do not wish to strive toward higher things to judge why these sensible things please them. Therefore, if I were to ask a builder who has constructed one arch why he builds another similar to it on the opposite side, he will respond, I believe, that the parts of the building should correspond with their pairs. Furthermore, if I continue to ask why he chooses this very thing, he will say this is fitting, this is beautiful, this delights those who see it—he will dare say nothing more. For he rests his gaze downward <note>original: "inclinatus enim recumbit oculis"; literally "leaning, he lies back with his eyes," suggesting a person focused only on physical sight</note>, and does not understand where his judgment depends.

But I will not cease to remind the man who is "eyed" within <note>original: "intrinsecus oculatum"; a metaphor for the mind's eye or intellectual vision</note>, seeing indivisibly, to ask why these things please him, so that he might dare to be a judge of human pleasure itself. For in this way he is raised above it and not held by it, since he judges it rather than judging according to it. And first I will ask: are things beautiful because they delight us, or do they delight us because they are beautiful? Here, without hesitation, the answer will be: they delight because they are beautiful. Then I will ask: why are they beautiful? And if he wavers, I will suggest: is it because the parts are similar to each other and are brought into a single harmony by some connection? 

When he finds this to be true, I will ask whether they perfectly fulfill this **unity** <term>unity: the state of being one or undivided. Augustine argues that while physical things try to be "one," they are always divisible; perfect Unity only exists in the divine realm</term> which they are clearly striving for, or if they lie far below it and, in a sense, represent it falsely. For who, once prompted, would not see that there is no form and no body at all that does not possess some trace of unity? And yet, no matter how beautiful a body is, since it necessarily has one part here and another there across spatial intervals, it cannot achieve that unity which it follows. 

I will demand that he answer where he sees this unity, or from where he sees it. If he did not see it, how would he recognize it? What would the forms of bodies be imitating? What would they be failing to fulfill? Now, indeed, it is rightly said to bodies: "If some unity did not hold you together, you would be nothing. But again, if you were Unity itself, you would not be bodies."

From where, then, do you know this unity according to which you judge bodies? If you did not see it, you could not judge that they fail to fulfill it. If you saw it with these physical eyes, you would not truly say that although they are held by its trace, they are nevertheless far distant from it. For with these eyes you see nothing but bodily things; therefore, we see it with the mind. But where do we see it? If it were in the same place as our body, someone in the East judging bodies in this way would not see it. Therefore, it is not contained in that place. And while it is present everywhere, for the one who judges it is nowhere through the spaces of locations, and by its power it is nowhere absent.

When the soul is stirred by many illusions of phantasms <note>original: "phantasmatum"; mental images or sensory impressions that can deceive the mind</note> disturbing it from all sides, and yet it recognizes these to be false, where is the truth that is beheld by the mind? That light is true, through which you recognize that all these things are not true; through this light you see that "One" by which you judge that whatever else you see is "one," yet also that whatever mutable thing you see is not that "One."

Furthermore, ask what delights you in the pleasure of the body: you will find nothing other than **harmony** <note>original: "conuenientia"</note>. For if resistance or disagreement produces pain, harmony produces pleasure. Recognize, therefore, what is the supreme harmony. **Do not go outside. Return into yourself. Truth dwells in the inner man.** And if you find your nature to be changeable, transcend yourself. But remember when you transcend yourself, you are transcending a reasoning soul. Reach, therefore, toward that place from which the light of reason itself is lit. 

For where does every good reasoner arrive, if not at the truth? Since truth does not reach itself by reasoning, but is itself what reasoners seek. And when we both see through discussion that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true, where, I ask, do we see this? Surely neither I in you, nor you in me, but both of us see it in that unchangeable truth which is above our minds. There, indeed, we behold with the mind's eye the very form according to which these temporal things were made, and from there we hold the truth and knowledge of things conceived, like a word within us. 

See there a harmony than which none can be higher, and harmonize yourself with it. Confess that you are not what it is, since it does not seek itself. You, however, have come to it by seeking—not through the space of locations, but by the affection of the mind—so that the "inner man" may harmonize with his spiritual inhabitant with spiritual pleasure. Or if you do not perceive what I am saying and doubt whether these things are true, at least see whether you do not doubt that you...

This internal standard proves the soul's connection to a higher, immortal reality beyond the physical senses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the human mind recognizes eternal truths, continuing a long paraphrase and quotation of St. Augustine’s "On True Religion." ...you are disturbed. And if it is certain that you are doubting, seek where that certainty comes from. It comes from the light that **illuminates every man coming into this world**, <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:9, often used by Ficino to describe the "Intellectual Light" shared by God and the human soul.</note> which cannot be seen with these physical eyes, nor with those by which **phantasms** <term>phantasmata: mental images or impressions derived from the senses</term> are imagined. Rather, it is seen with those eyes by which it is said to the phantasms themselves: "You are not what I seek, nor are you that source from which I bring you into order." 

When I encounter something foul among you, I reject it; when I find something beautiful, I approve it. Yet that source from which I reject or approve is even more beautiful. For this reason, I approve that source even more, and I place it before not only you, but all those physical bodies from which I drew you. Where these things are seen, there is a light without the space of locations or times, and without any phantasm of such spaces. Could these things be corrupted in any part, even if every person who reasons were to perish? For reasoning does not create such things, but rather finds them; therefore, before they are found, they remain in themselves, and when they are found, they renew us. 

In this way the **inner man** is reborn, while the **outer man** is corrupted day by day. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:16; Ficino uses this to describe the soul turning away from the body toward the divine.</note> Between our mind, by which we understand that Father and the Truth (that is, the inner light through which we understand Him), there is no intervening creature. For this reason, let us worship that very Truth—which is in no way dissimilar in Him or with Him—which is the **form** of all things that have been made by the One and strive toward the One. From this, it appears that all things were made through this form, which alone fulfills what all things desire.

->A second confirmation through hearing, according to Augustine.<-
->Chapter VI.<-

**T**hus far, through those things perceived by sight and with Augustine as our guide, we have arrived at the point of finding that our mind is formed by the divine mind. Next, with the same guide, let us proceed through those things which are heard. In harmonious sounds there is a certain **number**; <term>numerus: in this context, "number" refers to rhythm, ratio, and musical proportion</term> from this, a certain number also arises in the act of sensing, because a rhythmic sound is sensed rhythmically. There is also a certain number in the very nature of the sense itself. For otherwise, the sense would neither be soothed by the harmony of sounds nor offended by their absurdity. Therefore, whatever that thing is by which we either grant our assent or shrink back—not by reason, but by nature—when something sounds, I call that the "number" of the sense itself. 

This power of approving and rejecting does not come to be in my ears only when I hear a sound. Indeed, the ears are open to good sounds no differently than to bad ones. See rather if these two things ought to be distinguished. For if any verse is pronounced now more quickly, now more slowly, it must necessarily occupy a different span of time, even if the same ratio of the "feet" <note>Metrical feet, the rhythmic units of poetry.</note> is preserved. Therefore, so that the verse may soothe the ears by its very kind, that power acts by which we adopt harmonious things and reject absurd ones. However, as for the fact that it is sensed in a shorter time when uttered more quickly than more slowly, it makes no difference except in how long the ears are touched by the sound. 

Therefore, this affection of the ears when they are touched by sound is in no way the same as if they were not touched. Just as hearing differs from not hearing, so hearing this voice differs from hearing another. This affection is neither stretched further nor restrained shorter than the measure of the sound that creates it. It is one thing in an **iamb**, <note>original: "iambo"; a metrical foot consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one.</note> and another in a **tribrach**; <note>original: "Tribracho"; a metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.</note> it is longer in a longer iamb, and shorter in a shorter one, and it is nothing in silence. If this occurs in a rhythmic voice, it must also be rhythmic itself, nor can it exist when its creator—the sound—is absent. For it is like a **footprint impressed in water**, which is neither formed before you press a body into it, nor remains when you have removed it. 

However, that natural and **judicial power** which is present in the ears does not cease to exist in silence; nor does the sound insert it into us, but rather the sound is received by it to be either approved or rejected. Who would deny that the power of numbers is in the soul, since the soul enacts these numbers which we find in the pulse of the veins and in the reciprocal breath? When I pronounce a verse, sometimes more quickly or more slowly, while still observing the law of timing (by which the feet correspond in a ratio of one to two), I do not offend your sense with any deception of judgment. And yet that sound, which is produced with shorter and, as it were, more fleeting syllables, cannot occupy more time than it sounds. If those **judicial numbers** were held by the bond of time in only as much space as those sounding syllables are arranged, they would not be able to reach a judgment of those sounding syllables which are poured out a little more slowly under the same iambic law. Therefore, that span of time does not hold those who preside over the judging. But if they were held by no time at all, they would nonetheless be employed for judging, no matter how much more slowly one produced iambic sounds (provided the intervals were fitting and responded to each other). But as it stands...

Using the example of music, he explains that the soul's ability to recognize harmony (numbers) is not created by the sound itself but exists as an eternal standard within the "inner man."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the soul's innate power to judge sensory information using divine or mathematical standards. Having discussed sight, Ficino (drawing heavily from Augustine's "On Music") now moves to the sense of hearing and the concept of rhythm or "number."</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII.

If I were to utter a single syllable with a duration as long as—to be brief—three steps of someone walking, and another syllable twice as long, and so on, arranging such long iambs in a ratio of one to two, that law of rhythm would still be preserved. Yet, we would not be able to use that natural judgment to approve of those dimensions. Therefore, those **judicial rhythms** <term>iudiciales numeri: the innate patterns in the soul used to judge harmony and proportion</term> are held within certain limits of temporal spaces, which they cannot exceed in their judging; whatever exceeds these spaces, they cannot manage to judge. Nevertheless, these rhythms regulate individual actions. For that which restrains and checks us from uneven steps when walking, or from uneven intervals of blows when striking, or from uneven movements of the jaw when eating, or even from uneven strokes of the nails when scratching—and which, in any focused act of the bodily members, silently commands a certain equality—is a certain "judicial" something. 

It is this which allows human beings to have a sense and a choice of beauty and decorum far more than beasts. For beasts are driven toward whatever incites them for the sake of calming a bodily passion; they are not attracted by the grace or desire for beauty. Hence, horses do not choose a more beautiful mare to love, but are drawn toward any of them with an equal fury. This "judicial" quality points toward God as the founder of the living creature, whom it is certainly right to believe is the author of all harmony and concord. 

Furthermore, rhythms—both those in sound and those produced in sensing—are offered to and judged by these judicial rhythms only insofar as memory can preserve their intervals. For rhythm, which consists of intervals of time, cannot be judged by us in any way unless we are aided by memory. Even with any short syllable, since it has both a beginning and an ending, the beginning occurs at one moment and the end sounds at another. Therefore, in hearing even the shortest syllable, unless memory aids us so that at the moment when the end (rather than the beginning) of the syllable sounds, that movement made when the beginning sounded remains in the soul, we could not say we have heard anything at all. This is why, when we are occupied with some other thought while people are speaking, we seem to ourselves to have heard nothing. 

Therefore, must we not think that those judicial rhythms—which cannot judge rhythms situated in time intervals unless memory offers them up like a servant—are themselves stretched through a certain space of time? For although we do not see spaces of time within them, they are nonetheless only employed to judge things that occur in spaces of time—and not even all of those, but only those that can be articulated by memory. When that verse is sung: *God, creator of all*, <note>original: "Deus creator omnium." This is a famous hymn written by Saint Ambrose, which St. Augustine uses as his primary example in "On Music."</note> we hear the rhythms of the verse itself through "sensing rhythms," we are delighted by "judicial rhythms," and we evaluate them by some other means. We evaluate this delight (which is like the verdict of those judicial rhythms) because we can deliver a more hidden but certainly truer verdict through other, higher rhythms. 

For it is one thing to be delighted by sense, and another to evaluate by reason. Indeed, it is one thing to approve or reject rhythmic movements—which happens in the delight taken in harmony or the offense taken at the absurdity of such movements—and another thing to evaluate through reasoning whether these things delight us rightly or not. And if it has seemed right to us that the sense of delight itself could in no way approve of equal intervals or reject disturbed ones unless it were imbued with certain rhythms, then it must also seem right that **reason**, which is placed above this delight, can in no way judge the rhythms below it without certain more "lively" rhythms of its own. 

Now, if you please, let those rhythms which rose up to claim the leadership be named **sensory rhythms**, and let those who have been found more excellent receive the name **judicial**, since it is more honorable. Come now, observe the force and power of reason as much as we can perceive from its works. For reason itself (to speak primarily of what pertains to the undertaking of this work) first considered what constitutes good **modulation** <term>modulatio: the art of rhythmic movement or measurement</term> and perceived it to be in a certain free movement, turned toward the goal of its own beauty. Then it saw that in the movements of bodies, there was one aspect varied by the brevity or length of time (depending on how much more or less lasting it was), and another aspect varied by the striking of local spaces at certain degrees of speed or slowness. Once this division was made, it followed how that which exists in the delay of time—articulated in a modest interval suited to human sense—produces various rhythms, as well as their types and order, even up to the measures of verses. Finally, it attended to what the soul (of which reason is the head) was doing in moderating, performing, sensing, and retaining these things. It separated all these **animate rhythms** <term>animales numeri: rhythms belonging to the 'anima' or soul/life-force</term> from bodily ones, and recognized that the soul itself could not have noticed, distinguished, or certainly counted all these things without certain rhythms of its own. It placed these above the others of a lower order by a certain judicial estimation, and now when...

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

[The soul] acts in this way by its own very delight, through which it weighs the moments of time and directs its own movements according to such rhythmic measures. What is it that we love in the many things we perceive through our senses? Is it anything other than a certain "parility" <term>parilitas: evenness or the quality of being equal</term> and equally measured intervals? Would a <term>pyrrhic: a poetic foot of two short syllables</term> foot, or a spondee, or an anapest, or a dactyl, or a proceleusmatic, or a dispondee delight us in any other way, unless it compared one of its parts to the other in an equal division? Furthermore, what beauty does the iamb, the tribrach, or the trochee possess, except that their smaller part divides their larger part into two equal halves? Now, as for the rhythmic feet of six "times" <note>In classical prosody, "time" refers to the duration of a syllable; a short syllable is one time, a long is two.</note>, do they sound more charming and festive for any other reason than that they are divided by both laws? That is, they are either divided into two equal parts possessing three times each, or into one single part on one side and a double part on the other—meaning the larger part contains the smaller part twice, and in that way is divided equally by it, with two times measuring and cutting the four times into two pairs. And it is the same in all other instances by a similar logic. We are delighted by equality to such an extent that we demand it not only in the intervals of voices, but even in the spaces of silence.

Reason therefore examines the soul’s carnal delight—which claimed the "judicial" role for itself—and asks: since equality in the number of temporal spaces soothes the soul, are any two short syllables it hears truly equal? Or is it possible that one of them is uttered a bit longer—not quite reaching the length of a long syllable, but exceeding its partner by some tiny amount? Can it be denied that this delight might fail to sense such a discrepancy, and thus rejoice in unequals as if they were equals? What is more foul than such an error and inequality? 

By this we are warned to turn our joy away from those things that merely imitate equality; for we cannot fully grasp whether they achieve it—indeed, we perhaps grasp that they *do not* achieve it—and yet, insofar as they imitate it, we cannot deny that they are beautiful in their own kind and order. That "Equality" which we did not find to be certain or permanent in sensory rhythms, but which we nonetheless recognized as shadowed and fleeting, the soul would surely never seek unless it were known somewhere else. This "somewhere else" is not in the spaces of places or times, for those swell and pass away; nor is it in the forms of bodies, which we can never call truly equal; nor in the intervals of time, where we similarly remain ignorant of whether something passes by slightly more or less than it ought in a way that escapes our senses. 

I ask where you think that Equality exists, which we look upon when we desire certain bodies or the movements of bodies to be equal, yet, upon more diligent consideration, we do not dare to trust them. I believe it is there where that which is more excellent than bodies reigns. But let us ask whether it is in the soul itself, or even above the soul. We believe that this rhythmic or metric art, used by those who make verses, possesses certain "numbers" <note>original: "numeros"; here meaning mathematical ratios or rhythmic principles</note> according to which they construct their verses. Whatever these numbers are, they do not pass away with the verses, but remain. We must agree, therefore, that fleeting things are constructed from certain remaining numbers. We consider this art to be nothing other than a certain disposition of the craftsman's soul. 

What if someone who never learned this art were questioned about everything pertaining to numbers? Do you not think he could know this art? These numbers will not pass from the one who teaches into the one who learns; rather, the learner will move himself internally within his own mind toward something from which these numbers are imprinted upon his mind. This creates that disposition called "art," and the learner will understand and answer that the things he is questioned about are true. Since these numbers about which he is questioned are unchangeable, they are therefore eternal, and there is no inequality in them. From where, then, must we believe that which is eternal and unchangeable is granted to the soul, if not from the one eternal and unchangeable God? Therefore, he who speaks when another questions him moves himself inwardly toward God, so that he may understand the unchangeable truth.

### *The third confirmation through the mind, according to Augustine.*

## Chapter VII.

We have investigated our proposition sufficiently, first through the evidence of sight, and then through the reminders of hearing. Now let us track it through the evidence of reason. Every person expresses his mind in speech in one way when he is attending to what is happening within himself. However, he defines the human mind through specific or general knowledge in a different way. Thus, when someone speaks to me about his own mind—whether he understands this or that, or does not understand, and whether he wants this or that, or does not want it—I believe him. But when he speaks the truth about the human mind specifically or generally, I acknowledge it...

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XII.<-

I acknowledge and approve of this. From this it is clear that one thing is what each person sees in themselves—which another person believes when they speak of it, yet does not see—while another thing is seen in the truth itself, which another can also behold. One of these changes through time, while the other subsists in unchanging eternity. For we do not gather a general or specific knowledge of the human mind by seeing many minds with our bodily eyes through some similarity; rather, we gaze upon the inviolable truth, from which we may perfectly define (as much as we are able) not what the mind of each individual man *is*, but what it *ought* to be according to eternal reasons. Furthermore, when the wicked think about <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "æternitatem"</note>, and rightly rebuke or praise many things in the behavior of men, by what rules do they judge these things, if not by those in which they see how each person ought to live, even if they themselves do not live in that same way? Where do they see these rules? For it is not in their own nature, since it is certain that these things are seen by the mind, and their minds are clearly changeable; yet whoever sees these rules in them sees that they are unchangeable. Nor do they see them in the "habit" <note>In this context, "habit" refers to a stable disposition or character trait.</note> of their own mind, since those rules are of justice, while it is clear their own minds are unjust. Where then are these rules written? Where does even the unjust man recognize what is just, where he discerns that he should have what he himself does not possess? Where, then, are they written, if not in the book of that light which is called Truth? From there, every just law is transcribed and transferred into the heart of the man who works justice—not by moving into it, but as if by being imprinted upon it, just as the image from a ring passes into the wax, yet does not leave the ring. But he who does not work justice, yet still sees what ought to be done, is the one who turns away from that light, though he is still touched by it. Because he does not see *how* he should see, he sins somewhat more excusably, for he is not a transgressor of an unknown law. But even he is sometimes touched by the splendor of the truth that is present everywhere, when, being rebuked, he confesses his fault. 

Finally, this higher <term>Aurelian discussion</term> <note>original: "Aureliana discursio"; referring to the arguments of Aurelius Augustine.</note> is concluded by four boundaries: namely, that the mind does not rise to the highest things unless it is drawn by the instinct of that which is highest; that it would not use eternal reasons for judging according to its will unless it could equal itself to eternity; that it would not grasp immutable things by immutable reason unless it touched the very rule of immutability; and that many souls would not grasp the same truth unless either there were one <term>human intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus humanus"</note> in many people (which is impossible), or at least many human intellects were plunging themselves into the same fountain of truth. It is as if some people are best going to understand the order of a craft when they have penetrated the single design through which the craftsman constructed the work. 

However, this opinion of <term>Augustine</term> is confirmed chiefly in two ways: first, through the common power of arguing, and second, through the common notions of truth, goodness, and being. Every intellect grasps the necessary consequence in things that are both contingent <note>Things that could be otherwise or are not guaranteed to exist.</note> and non-existent. For this consequence is necessary: *if <term>Plato</term> runs, <term>Plato</term> moves*, even though Plato, and his running, and his motion, are all contingent things. Indeed, even this is necessary: *Plato was speaking while he was debating*, even though neither Plato, nor his debate, nor his speech are present now. Therefore, the necessity of such consequences is not founded in those temporal things which either do not exist at all or are contingent; nor is it founded in the thoughts of the soul alone—otherwise, it would not be true necessity but a fiction, and it would not even be immutable, since our thought is changeable. It is founded, therefore, in the eternal and necessary series of things which the divine mind, the ordainer of all, contains within itself, where it grants things their mutual relationship. For this reason, every light of true reasoning is kindled by the first truth and is reflected back into the same, since every necessity of consequence is founded in the highest necessity of all nature. 

Common understandings of truth and goodness also teach this; we have proved in the previous sections that these exist in the minds of all, based on the fact that they constantly compare things that are true and good. But if truth itself and goodness is God, it follows that God shines into the minds of men as often as we judge true and good things through God as a standard. The notion of "being" itself, implanted in everyone, teaches the same. For all men judge that *this* thing in no way exists, while *that* thing exists, but in an imperfect way, and *this other* thing exists in a way closer to perfection. However, such a gradation in being is neither made nor known except by an approach toward the highest being (which is God) or a departure from it. But no one can see an approach toward Him or a departure from Him unless he sees Him. Moreover, more experienced men see Him in another way: namely, when they resolve all subordinate kinds of things into the most general ones, and those, in turn, into that which is called simple and absolute being. Such a being is either a false fiction, or it is God. It cannot...

<page-num>282</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

Moreover, [it would follow] that "being" itself is false, provided that anything in reality truly exists. If that comparison regarding the degrees of things, and this resolution <note>The process of tracing effects back to their ultimate cause.</note> does not occur except through the power of the highest and absolute <term>being</term> <note>original: "esse." In Scholastic and Platonic philosophy, "Being" (Esse) is the most fundamental act of existence, which Ficino identifies with God.</note>, then it certainly occurs through God, by whom the intellect is formed to both compare and resolve. Added to this is the fact that "being" itself shines so clearly that it cannot be thought of as not existing. For just as that which is called "nothing" strikes us as being entirely devoid of existence, so "being" strikes us as being entirely devoid of non-existence. Therefore, within it, there appears neither any potential at all for not-being, nor any defect of being.

From the first part, it is eternal; from the second, it is most full in the total perfection of being—that is, God. By this reasoning, "being" presents itself to us most evidently; and to those who observe correctly, it appears as God. This is further confirmed by two reasons. First, because "being" is so manifest that in every single thing that is known, "being" itself is also always known. He who calls something a "man" or "white" says that "being" exists in the species of man, and so on. Finally, the "mode of being" in individual things, through which individual things subsist, implies "being itself," just as "animal" is implied in every species of animal. The second reason is that all other things are known through "being" itself, but "being" is known through itself. Indeed, in the cognition that occurs through intuition, that which is called "non-being" is known through "being." <term>Being in potential</term> <note>Something that has the capacity to exist but is not yet real.</note> is known through <term>being in act</term> <note>A thing that is fully realized and currently existing.</note>. Being in act is known through the "act of existing." Such an act is "being itself." If every being is recognized through the "being" which is its specific act, it follows that all existing things are known through the "being" which is the act and origin of all things that exist. And if one were to place "being itself" simply above potential being and actual being—something that is neither potential nor act—then "being itself" would either be a fiction, or it would be God, or some sign of God, as the Platonists prefer. 

But God is the "Author-Act" of all existing things, and through the excellence of His action, He moves the one who is moving [the mind] more primarily, more powerfully, and more lastingly than any other things that are presented; indeed, other things move the mind only by His power. Therefore, absolute being itself—that is, the <term>pure act</term> <note>original: "purus actus." A philosophical term for a being with no unrealized potential; a state of perfect and complete reality, which can only be God.</note> who is the effector of all existing things, who is God—is the first thing that offers itself to our minds in a wonderful way: it flows in, it shines forth, it makes all other things visible. Although we possess the form and notion of this in ourselves in a somewhat perpetual way, and through it and in it we know all other things, we nevertheless do not notice it—just as the eye does not consider that it is continually seeing the light of the Sun and all other things through it and in it, nor does the reason notice that it is continually reasoning, even though it reasons almost constantly. For we are not accustomed to noticing things that have been familiar for a long time. For who considers the fact that he is breathing? 

Where the Platonists call the highest God "Being itself," they wish it to be understood not as the "being" that is an essence, but as the principle of this being—namely, a "being above being" <note>original: "esse super esse." This reflects the "Neoplatonic" idea that the Ultimate (the One) is beyond even the category of existence.</note>, which is conceived by its own specific rationale of being and grasped by some notion. For they properly call the highest God "Unity" and "Goodness," but they call the "following God" (God from God, <note>original: "lumenq; de luce," meaning "light from light," a phrase from the Nicene Creed applied here to the second person of the Platonic or Christian trinity.</note>) by the name of "Being," derived from the first Unity into three parts: namely, Essence, Life, and Mind. And because these three are present in each of the three in their own way, they produce the other three up to the number nine; from this it happens that in the angels, the number nine is to be observed, and a similar scale exists in happy souls. They say that the contemplating mind is indeed formed by the highest God through the "head of the mind" (unity), but by the "following God" through the intellect. But let them see to those matters; for us, it is enough that the soul is formed by divinity. 

From all the above, it is concluded that human reason, in considering the order of things, is always occupied with the divine reason that orders all things, no less than the spheres of the world revolve around the center point of the world. But if a revolution, which naturally and constantly moves around a perpetual center from its own self, is perpetual, it is necessary that our reason will be perpetual. Since reason, by understanding through God and in God, is reflected back into God without a mediator, it clearly testifies that it proceeded from God without a mediator. Who would deny that what is closest to eternity will itself be eternal? And furthermore, it sees the eternal form in God exactly as it is eternal, while it concludes by certain reasoning that it is eternal. Thus it sees in such a way that it looks up to it; it follows, therefore, that it receives it in an eternal manner. And because it receives it as it is—provided it receives according to its own nature—it follows that the soul itself is perpetual, since it receives in a perpetual manner. This reason of ours is nothing other than <term>intellectual life</term>. Therefore it will always live; indeed, it will also always understand, if it will always exist. But it is helpful here, as we often do, to wander a little more widely with Augustine. When we reason, the soul does it. For no one does this except one who understands. Neither the body understands, nor the soul [supported by the body...]<meta>catchword: ...assisting</meta>

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration that the soul operates independently of the body. Having established that the soul turns away from the senses to find truth, Ficino now argues that the soul’s connection to eternal Truth (God) grants it immortality.</meta>

<page-num>285</page-num>
->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.<-

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.

...the body assisting, because when the soul wishes to understand, it turns away from the body. For that which is understood is always of the same kind <note>original: "eiusdem modi," referring to the unchanging nature of Platonic Forms or universal truths</note>, and nothing of the body is always of the same kind. Therefore, the body cannot help the soul as it strives toward understanding; it is enough if the body does not hinder it. If the soul searches deeply and reaches the truth through reasoning, it certainly reaches the truth by itself. Wherefore it clings more closely to the truth itself—through which all things reached by understanding are made true—than it does either to sensible things or to their images <note>In Platonic thought, "images" are the mental shadows of physical objects, which are less real than the abstract Truth itself</note>, which it does not reach by itself but through instruments and other media. For the soul could not contemplate those truths through itself without the greatest union with Truth itself. Those things which are grasped by the senses are felt to be outside of us and are contained in specific places, which is why it is even claimed they cannot be truly perceived <note>Ficino follows the Platonic view that physical objects are too unstable and "outside" the mind to be objects of certain knowledge</note>. Truly, however, those things which are understood are not understood as if placed elsewhere than in the soul which understands them. For they are understood simultaneously as not being contained in any place.

Therefore, this union of the gazing soul and that truth which it gazes upon is either such that the soul is the subject and that truth is in the <term>subject</term> <note>In logic, a "subject" is the underlying thing in which qualities or "accidents" exist</note>, or conversely, truth is the subject and the soul is in the subject, or both are <term>substances</term> <note>original: "substantia." An independent reality that does not need another thing to exist</note>. If the first of these three is true, then the soul is as immortal as that truth and the supreme <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratio." Here used to mean the divine logic or logos that structures the universe</note> of things, which inseparably inheres in the soul and cannot exist except in a living thing. The same necessity exists in the second case. For if that truth, which is called reason, has nothing changeable about it—as is apparent—then nothing that exists within it as a subject can be changed. 

There remains, therefore, all the struggle over the third possibility. For if the soul is a substance and the reason to which it is joined is also a substance, someone might not absurdly think it possible that while reason remains, the soul might cease to exist. But it is manifest that as long as the soul is not separated from reason but clings to it, the soul must necessarily remain and live. By what force, then, can it be separated? By a bodily force, whose power is weaker, whose origin is lower, and whose order is more distant? In no way. By a soulful force, then? But even then, how could that be? Is there some other more powerful soul who cannot contemplate reason unless he separates the first soul from it? But reason is not lacking to any observer, even if everyone contemplates it at once. And since nothing is more powerful than reason itself—because nothing is more unchangeable—it follows that a soul not yet joined to reason can in no way be more powerful than one already joined to it.

It remains that either reason separates itself from the soul, or the soul is separated from reason by its own will. But there is nothing of envy in that divine nature to prevent it from offering itself to be enjoyed by souls. Furthermore, the more a thing exists, the more it makes whatever is joined to it also exist; and the opposite of "being" is "destruction." As for the will, who would say the soul is separated from truth by choice, when the soul never desires anything more greedily than to be joined to truth? What then? Must we now conclude that the soul is immortal? Or can it be extinguished even if it cannot be separated? Yet if that power of truth affects the soul by its very union (and it cannot fail to affect it), it surely affects it in such a way as to grant it "being." For Truth itself exists most fully where the highest and unchangeable <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia." The fundamental nature or "is-ness" of a thing</note> is understood. Therefore, whomever Truth affects by its own power, it compels to exist in some way. Consequently, the soul cannot be extinguished unless separated from reason; but it cannot be separated; therefore, it cannot perish.

That which introduces doubt, however, is that the foolish soul seems to be separated from reason itself and to exist in a certain state of "falling away," while the wise soul exists in a more certain and fuller essence. But if—as no one doubts—the soul is most wise when it gazes upon the truth that is always the same, and clings to it immovably, joined by divine love; and if all things that exist in any way come from that essence which exists in the highest and greatest degree, then either the soul exists because of that essence, or it exists by itself. But if it exists by itself, since it is its own cause of existing and never deserts itself, it never perishes. 

If, however, it exists from that [divine essence], one must diligently ask what thing could be contrary to it, which might take away from the soul the "being" that the essence provides. What is it, then? Is it perhaps falsehood, because that other thing is truth? But it is manifest and obvious how much falsehood can harm the soul. For it can do no more than deceive. But no one is deceived unless they are alive. Therefore, falsehood cannot destroy the soul. But if falsehood—which is the contrary of truth—cannot take away from the soul the "being" that truth gave it (for truth is thus most invincible), what else will be found that could take away from the soul that which makes it a soul? Nothing, certainly. For nothing is more powerful than its opposite for the purpose of taking away that which is created by its opposite. But if we seek the opposite of truth, not merely as it is truth, but as it is "being" in the highest and greatest degree—though it is that very thing insofar as it is truth (since we call that "truth" by which all things are true)—to whatever extent they exist, they exist to the extent they are true...

...even if these things are true, I would in no way shun that which more clearly supports me. For if no essence, insofar as it is essence, has any contrary, then much less does that first essence, which is called Truth <note>original: "ueritas"</note>, have a contrary insofar as it is essence. For the First is True. Every essence is essence for no other reason than because it *is*. To be, however, has no contrary except not to be. Hence, nothing is contrary to essence. Therefore, in no way can any thing be contrary to that substance which exists most greatly and primarily. If the soul possesses its very existence from that substance—for it cannot have this from elsewhere, since it does not have it from itself, but from that thing which is more excellent than the soul itself—nor does the soul have its being from any other than from Truth. Indeed, since from Truth alone the soul receives its "well-being" <note>original: "bene esse," a technical term for the soul's flourishing or state of grace</note>, it follows that there is no thing through which it might lose its being, because no thing is contrary to that through which it possesses it, and therefore it does not cease to be. Truly, because it possesses Wisdom through a turning toward <term>conversion: the Neoplatonic concept of "conversio," where the soul turns back toward its divine source</term> that from which it exists, it can lose it through a turning away <term>aversion: the opposite of conversion, where the soul turns toward material things</term>. For turning away is contrary to turning toward. But that which it has from that to which nothing is contrary, it has no means by which it could lose it. Therefore, it cannot perish.

# PLATONIC
## THEOLOGY, on the Immortality of Souls,
### by the same author Ficino,
### BOOK XIII.

->How much the soul dominates the body is shown by many signs, and<-
->first from the effects of the imagination.<-
->Chapter I.<-

Hitherto we have demonstrated the divinity of the soul through reasoning; henceforth we shall confirm the same almost similarly through signs. Four affects follow the imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes and stores sensory images</term>: appetite (desire), pleasure, fear, and pain. When these are most vehement, they suddenly affect their own body entirely, and sometimes even another’s body. How much heat does the desire for revenge stir in the heart, or the lust for pleasure in the liver—and even in the pulse? It was from the change of pulse that the physician Erasistratus recognized that Antiochus was captured by love for Stratonice <note>Antiochus, son of King Seleucus, fell in love with his stepmother Stratonice; Erasistratus diagnosed this "lovesickness" by observing the boy's pulse when she entered the room</note>. Again, how destructively does the desire to harm bewitch boys and other more delicate persons through a frequent gaze? How clearly does the craving of a pregnant woman infect the tender fetus with the mark of the thing she imagined? What various gestures and figures do parents imprint upon their children—and how unlike themselves!—on account of a vehement imagination of things by which they are affected by some chance while they are coupling? Thus it happens that men are much more different among themselves in figure, gestures, and character than any brute animals of any species are among themselves. How often is a malicious will said to have harmed men, beasts, and plants with its curses and sorceries? Add to this that some gluttons, thinking greedily of certain feasts, infect their own saliva with a similar taste. Boys also, and pregnant women, because of an excessive craving for a forbidden food or drink, melt away, waste away, and fall into ruin. These and similar things the appetite effects through many means. Great joy effects no less. It can suddenly destroy the body, and often relieve it of disease.

Did not Sophocles and Dionysius, the Tyrant of Sicily, both die suddenly upon receiving news of a tragic victory <note>Sophocles supposedly died of joy after winning a dramatic competition; Dionysius after winning at the Lenaia festival</note>? A mother, seeing her son returning from the Battle of Cannae <note>A disastrous Roman defeat against Hannibal; several legends tell of mothers dying from the shock of their sons returning alive when they were thought dead</note>, suddenly expired. No one is ignorant of what pain can do in contrast. Furthermore, the distress of a foul spectacle infects the taste and provokes nausea by sight alone. Boys, and even older people, when they see a bitter portion offered to someone else, immediately feel bitter saliva in their mouth, which a vehement imagination moves. In some, the bowels are even loosened by such a thought. And what is marvelous: for some, the teeth are "set on edge" both by a certain sight and by a sound. Does not mercy, which is a kind of pain, sometimes so affect the body of the one who feels pity...

...affects a person poorly when he sees the body of another affected? This is demonstrated by those who, at the sight of human blood, immediately fall as their spirit fails, and those whose elbow aches while they see or hear of another's elbow being wounded. What of fear? Do we not often grow dizzy and tremble out of dread when looking down at the earth from high windows? Do we not sometimes even turn red? Those who fear grow pale suddenly, just as those who are bashful blush. With sudden fear, the heart trembles, the hair stands on end, the voice sticks in the throat, and even life itself fails, or long-lasting illnesses follow. Yet sometimes fear even cures certain diseases, such as hiccups and <term>quartan fever: a malarial fever where paroxysms occur every seventy-two hours</term>. However, when the most intense fear coincides with the most intense longing, a marvelous effect sometimes results. Hence (as is found in Herodotus), when someone wished to kill King Croesus, the son of Croesus—who had previously been mute—suddenly loosened his tongue due to his great fear of his father's death and his desire to cry out, and shouted with a loud voice:

> O man, do not kill Croesus!

From then on, he was able to speak. Therefore, these four <term>passions: the four traditional emotions of Stoic and Platonic philosophy—joy, grief, desire, and fear</term> dominate the body completely, since they change it in every respect. These are, moreover, the movements of the soul itself. For in proportion to how much the soul judges something to be good or evil, it desires, rejoices, fears, and grieves. From this it follows that the nature of the body is entirely subject to the movements of the soul. Hence it happens that the human face bears both the clear signs of the soul's inclinations and the most certain evidence of individual passions. The former are understood only by <term>Physiognomists: scholars who judge character or future fate from facial features</term>, but even common people understand the latter. Who would not easily recognize a soul that is desiring, fearing, angry, rejoicing, or mourning? From this it happens, again, that man alone laughs and man alone weeps, because the movements of the soul have the greatest command over the body. 

From the fact that the body is entirely subject to the character of the rational soul, we conclude two things. First, that this soul is a most excellent form and is self-subsisting, because a form that exists only *through* the body cannot dominate the body. Second, that the human body yields most easily to its own soul. For that which is solid and hard because of an abundance of "earth" <note>original: "terrae," referring to the heaviest of the four elements</note> does not yield easily. Therefore, if our body is compared to other animals, it possesses the least amount of "earth" (and even that is of a refined sort) and as much as possible of the higher elements; for this reason, it is the vessel of a celestial soul. A proof of this matter may be that the most gifted men are oftentimes soft of flesh, slender, and of delicate health, and their bodies vary greatly with even the slightest of their movements—as we read regarding Aristotle, Pyrrho, Speusippus, Carneades, Chrysippus, and Plotinus. 

Plato sensed this in the *Timaeus* when he said that God could have made the human body so solid that it would be minimally harmed by external things, but He willed to make it softer so that it might be more ready for <term>speculation: the act of intellectual or divine contemplation</term>, as if we were born not for this earthly dwelling, but for celestial contemplation. He adds also that the motions of a most powerful soul can both weaken and dissolve its own body. This happens not only in passion, but also in the intensity of contemplation. He writes also in the *Charmides* that those <term>Magi: wise men or priest-physicians</term> who were physicians of the soul and body, followers of Zamolxis and Zoroaster, judged that all things of the body, both good and evil, flow from the soul into the body itself, just as the quality of the eyes flows from the brain, and the quality of the brain from the whole body. And just as it is impossible for the eyes to be healed unless the brain is healed, and the brain unless the whole body is healed, so the whole body cannot be well unless the soul is well. Truly, the health of the soul is cared for by certain "Apolline incantations"—that is, by philosophical reasonings. Socrates, moreover, recounted that it was common among the Thracians for those physicians to make some men immortal through such a healing. So great is the command of the soul over the body, so great its power. 

This "magical" opinion seems to agree with the sentiment of the Hebrews and Christians: that in the soul of the first parent, Adam, when it was healthy, all things were healthy; but afterward, when the soul became infirm <note>referring to the Fall of Man</note>, all things became infirm. Furthermore, concerning our movements, this must be carefully noted: that some, beginning from the body, do not penetrate to the soul; others do penetrate; some, beginning from the soul, do not overflow into the body; while others do overflow. The first kind are like this: when the most temperate air surrounding the body moves the body in some way, yet offers us a sensation of neither heat nor cold. The second are when it moves in such a way that we feel something. The third are when the mind tranquilly contemplates something, or the <term>phantasy: the faculty of the soul that processes mental images</term> moderately looks upon some light thing, for the body is not agitated by those thoughts. 

Finally, the fourth kind occurs whenever either the mind or the phantasy applies itself more vehemently to something,

aut <note>catchword: or</note>

...or considers it either very harmful, or very useful and pleasant. For then the body suffers something. Indeed, when certain movements overflow into the body through an emotion of the soul, they seem to descend into the body not through the force of the body, but through the command of the soul. For the body has no power of acting on its own, and it suddenly receives the motions brought upon it by the soul with no delay intervening. For the face suddenly turns pale when the soul feels fear, and it grows pale solely through the agitation of the soul. However, when the soul is distressed because the body has become excessively hot, a disturbance of this kind does not happen to the soul until it has both felt the suffering of the body and judged it to be harmful. 

To feel and to judge are acts of the soul. Therefore, the soul is disturbed properly through its own act, not by the violence of the body; and for that reason, it moves itself and is not moved by the body. This is clearly seen from the fact that the body is always agitated by a powerful thought or emotion of the soul, and the body cannot resist it; yet the soul is not necessarily cast down from its state by the suffering and torment of the body. 

Diogenes the Cynic <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 412–323 BCE) known for his extreme asceticism and rejection of social norms.</note> walked naked upon ice and snow in winter and upon burning sands in summer, and meanwhile he would laugh and joke. Polemon of the Academy, even while feeling the most rabid bites of dogs, did not even turn pale. Anaxarchus of Abdera, the philosopher, was ordered by Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, to be cast into a hollow stone and struck with iron hammers. But the philosopher, neglecting the punishment of his body, said: "Strike, strike the vessel of Anaxarchus, for you do not frighten Anaxarchus himself." <note>original: "tunde, tunde Anaxarchi uasculum, Anaxarchum ipsum nihil terres." By "vessel," Anaxarchus refers to his physical body as a mere container for his true self.</note> The tyrant then ordered his tongue to be cut out. Then Anaxarchus, having bitten it off, spat it into the tyrant's face. Innumerable others, and most of all the martyrs of Christ, are recorded to have done such things. 

From these examples, it appears that the soul's own judgment does not always follow its bodily nature, nor can the sufferings of the body penetrate the soul. Indeed, judgment does not always follow the nature of the body. For judgment varies according to the variety of conjectures, even while the same <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to determine health and temperament</term> of the body remains; and often judgment remains the same even when the complexion has changed. It is established, therefore, that the soul can oppose the body by its own power, but the soul itself cannot be harmed except by itself. Moreover, the harm that is brought upon it by itself is a kind of internal conflict rather than destruction. For nothing is destroyed by its own self.

## The second sign from the affects of reason,
### Chapter 11.
### Concerning Philosophers.

**W**e have sufficiently related that our soul is the mistress of the body from the affects of the imagination, and we have also begun to indicate the same thing partly from the affects of reason. Let us therefore follow this part more extensively. In this category, we place philosophers, poets, priests, diviners, and prophets. 

They say that Epimenides of Crete slept for fifty years—that is (as I believe), he lived removed from the senses; similarly, they say Pythagoras remained hidden for ten years, and Zoroaster for twenty. Socrates (according to Plato) stood from one sunrise until the next sunrise, unblinking, motionless, in the same tracks, with his face and eyes directed toward the same spot, deep in thought and abstracted from his body. Plato, having frequently withdrawn far from his body through the intensity of contemplation, finally departed from the bonds of the body entirely during that very state of abstraction. His disciple Xenocrates was abstracted from his body for a full hour every single day. Archimedes of Syracuse, intent upon his geometric figures, did not feel the tumultuous destruction of his falling homeland or the enemy looming over his head. 

Porphyry, the disciple of Plotinus, writes that Plotinus was often accustomed to withdraw from his body and change his expression; then he would discover certain wonders which he would later write down. Porphyry asserts that he himself was present for these miracles of Plotinus four times. He also affirms that he himself, when he was sixty-eight years old, was seized by the divine once while in the midst of contemplation. We read that Heraclitus and Democritus did the same many years before them. Both withdrew into solitude. One appeared sad in his look because of the intensity of his study; the other, when he began to call his mind away from the senses and found himself hindered by his eyes, blinded himself. <note>A common legend in antiquity that Democritus put out his own eyes so that the distractions of sight would not interfere with his internal reason.</note> 

What more is there to say? Whoever has discovered something great in any of the more noble arts did so especially when, having departed from the body, they fled into the <term>citadel of the mind: the highest, most rational part of the soul, isolated from sensory input</term>. Hence Plato writes in the *Phaedrus* that the minds of philosophers especially recover the wings with which one flies toward divine things, because they are, of course, always devoted to the divine. And in one place he calls them divine, while in another he calls them the sons of God,
