...shines, because they are in a certain way reborn from God. Because of this, Aristotle writes that all men who have been excellent in any of the arts were melancholic <note>In the Renaissance, "melancholy" was not just sadness, but a specific temperament associated with deep thought and the planet Saturn.</note>, whether they were born that way or became so through constant meditation. I believe this happens for the reason that the nature of the melancholic humor follows the quality of the earth, which is never spread out widely like the other elements, but is more tightly contracted into itself. Thus, the melancholic humor both invites and helps the soul to collect itself into itself. Conversely, if the soul frequently collects its own spirits into itself in this way, the subtle parts of the humors are dissolved through continuous agitation, making the physical complexion much more earthy than it was originally—especially since the soul, by collecting itself, renders the body’s condition one of compression. Such is the nature of the earth. 

I should also mention that such is the nature of Mercury and Saturn; while they collect the spirits into the center, they recall the sharp edge of the mind away from external things toward its own, and they fix it in contemplation, directing it to penetrate the very centers of things. Yet, neither the planets nor the humors of this kind act as "efficient causes" <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of a change; Ficino argues the stars provide the opportunity, but the soul does the actual work.</note> of this; rather, they provide the occasion or remove impediments, while the mind itself—both invited and unencumbered—perfects such things. Great indeed is the empire of the mind, which by its own power is released from the fetters of the body. Immense is the wealth of the mind, which, whenever it desires the precious treasures of God and nature, digs them out not from the bowels of the earth, but from its own breast. 

It appears most clearly how much reason dominates the body in those who, though they may have led a shameful youth, suddenly change their character—either through God’s inspiration or a man’s exhortation—so that from being intemperate they turn out temperate or continent. This is said to have been done instantly by Polemon <note>A Greek philosopher who famously converted from a life of debauchery to one of philosophy after hearing a lecture.</note> on the same day he heard Xenocrates disputing on modesty. The same happened to Diogenes when he heard Antisthenes discoursing on liberty. Nature usually abolishes what has grown over a long time only over a similar length of time. Therefore, to shatter a habit strengthened by long custom in a single moment is not the work of a physical nature, but of a higher and divine one.

### On Poets.

**F**urthermore, consider the Poets, whom Democritus and Plato affirm are seized by a certain divine frenzy <note>original: "divino quodam furore"; Ficino refers to the Platonic idea that poets are "possessed" by a higher power when they write.</note>. Two of Plato’s dialogues, the *Phaedrus* and the *Ion*, show this above all others. He brings forward three signs of this fact. First, that individual men can hardly master individual arts over a long period of time without God; yet true poets—such as he claims Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and Pindar were—have inserted into their works certain unmistakable signs and proofs of all the arts. 

Second, that while in a frenzy they sing many things, and indeed wonderful things, which they themselves do not fully understand a little later once the frenzy has cooled—as if they had not uttered them themselves, but God had cried out through them as if through trumpets. 

Third, that it is not the most prudent or those most learned from an early age who have emerged as the best poets, but rather certain "insane" ones—as is known to have been the case with Homer and Lucretius—or those who were more unrefined, as Hesiod testifies he was, and as Plato writes was the case with Solon and Tynnicus of Chalcis, who suddenly appeared as wonders in poetic matters without previous art. He adds that certain very inept men are seized by the Muses for this reason: because divine providence wishes to declare to the human race that noble poems are not human inventions, but celestial gifts. He offers this sign in the *Phaedrus*: that no one, however diligent and learned in all the arts, ever excelled in poetry unless he also possessed that more fervent agitation of the soul which we feel when "there is a God within us; we grow warm when he stirs. That impulse holds the seeds of a sacred mind." <note>original: "est Deus in nobis, agitante calescimus illo. Impetus ille sacræ semina mentis habet." Ficino is quoting the Roman poet Ovid (*Fasti* 6.5).</note> Let us come to the priests.

### On Priests.

**T**he writings of Saint Paul the Theologian and the deeds of his disciple show that he ascended to the three heavens of the celestial hierarchies in a divine abstraction of the soul. Certain Galileans <note>The Apostles of Jesus.</note> also once, through the sudden inspiration of God, turned from fishermen into the greatest theologians. Many priests before their time were accustomed to rave through the instinct of demons...

...all antiquity testifies that certain wonders were spoken. Aulus Gellius <note>A Roman author of the 2nd century AD, known for his "Attic Nights."</note> writes that the most chaste priest Cornelius was moved in his mind at Padua at the very time Caesar and Pompey were clashing in Thessaly <note>The Battle of Pharsalus, 48 BC.</note>, so much so that he saw the time, the order, and the outcome of the battle. Pliny also records that the soul of Hermotimus of Clazomenae used to wander after leaving his body and announce many true things from a distance, until his enemies—who were called the Cantharidae—burned his body while he was away, thus taking away the "sheath" <note>The body is often described by Platonists as a "sheath" or "vessel" for the soul.</note> for his returning soul. Maximus Tyrius the Platonist and Herodotus write that the soul of Aristeus of Proconnesus used to do the same. Augustine refers to a priest of Calama <note>Probably referring to Restitutus of Calama, mentioned in Augustine's "City of God."</note> who was accustomed to calling himself away from his body at his own will, especially when he was soothed by a plaintive melody. "He lay there," he says, "very like a dead man, without breath, and even when he was burned or cut, he did not feel it." Yet when he woke up, he said he had felt nothing except the melody itself and the voices of those speaking during that very abstraction. This signifies that the soul used to perform nothing in the body then, since there was no movement, sense of touch, or breath; yet it was doing something within itself, since it was contemplating the harmony heard before and perceiving voices. And that Cornelius, Hermotimus, and Aristeus, whom I spoke of above, would not have seen things so far off after they had withdrawn from the body, unless the soul, when it is released from this little body, lived more freely and wandered more widely; nor would the soul of the priest of Calama have withdrawn from the body of its own accord and acted apart from it, if it were entirely the body's handmaid. These things seem to be confirmed by these words of Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "He who rightly uses divine meditations," he says, "and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, alone truly becomes perfect. But being separated from human pursuits and always clinging to the divine power, he is regarded by the common crowd as if he were out of his mind <note>original: "extra se positus"</note>, but he is full of God and hidden from the crowd."

->On Soothsayers and Prophets.<-

**W**e have spoken of Philosophers, Poets, and Priests; now let us speak of Soothsayers and Prophets. I would be forced to be more long-winded if I were to commemorate the Augurs, Haruspices, Auspices, Mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" usually referred to astrologers who calculated planetary positions.</note>, and Magi. Their works certainly indicate very skilled minds. But those prophecies especially indicate divine minds which—as Plato wants in the *Phaedrus*—occur without art or deliberation. Such are the things which Plato relates concerning the prophetess Diotima, Socrates, and Epimenides; what Varro together with Plato relates concerning the Sibyls; what historians tell of the Pythian oracles, and almost all philosophers confirm (especially the Platonists); what everyone experiences concerning dreams; and what the Hebrews hand down concerning the divine Prophets. The minds of all these people then especially surveyed many places and embraced the "three times" <note>Past, present, and future.</note> into one, when they separated themselves from the body.

Therefore, when the human soul is completely joined away from the body, it will (as the Egyptians say) comprehend every place and every time. Indeed, by its very nature, such a soul is already almost everywhere and always. To look around at many and very remote places, and to recall all past time and anticipate the future, it is not forced to go outside of itself; rather, having left the body and returned into itself, it achieves this entirely. This is either because by its nature it is everywhere and always (as the Egyptians think), or because when it receives itself back into its own nature, it is immediately joined to the Divine Power, which encompasses all the boundaries of place and time. However, I will recount from a deeper source, if you please, the way in which prophecy falls into the soul. Three orders of things seem to belong to the human soul: providence, fate, and nature. Providence is a series of minds; fate is a series of souls; nature is a series of bodies. At the beginning, under God, we place those minds entirely released from the body according to Plato, whom Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian who wrote on the celestial hierarchy.</note> calls angels—namely, the purest intellects. We add a lower grade of minds: those which are already united to bodies and seem to be like certain angels, holding in a way the lowest grade of angels. In their number are all rational souls, whether of the world <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul.</note>, or of the worldly spheres, the stars, demons, or humans. In the third place are the globes of the heavens, the elements, and the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>. Accordingly, God is the head of the angels because, sending down His ray—endowed with the reasons for creating all things—through all the angels, He forms all things step by step, so that in each individual He describes the universal figure of the world. Nor does He thus adorn only those sublime intellects and purest angels...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical exploration of the soul's hierarchy. In the previous page, he discussed historical accounts of the soul's ability to leave the body (ecstasy). Here, he begins to systematize how the soul connects to the universe through three levels: Providence, Fate, and Nature.</meta>

<page-num>289</page-num>
->**ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.**<-

...but even through those higher beings <note>referring to angels</note> as intermediaries, He also passes that same ray into the minds of rational souls—which are like the lowest order of angels—endowing them with the same principles. This kind of arrangement of things, this divine law inscribed upon minds, is called **Providence**. 

**Fate** follows. Indeed, rational souls possess not only that power of understanding, through which they are angelic and counted within the order of providence, but also a life-giving and governing power over the body. This power nourishes the body while within it, perceives physical things through the body, moves the body through space, and rules it within that space. The Platonists call this power the **idol** <note>original: "idolum"; here meaning a "likeness" or "image" of the soul that acts as the intermediary between the pure mind and the physical body</note>, that is, the image of the rational soul. Within this "idol" are the seeds of all motions and qualities that the soul unfolds within the body. All rational souls—both our own and those that are above us—possess those powers of understanding. They also possess these life-giving and governing faculties over bodies. 

**Nature** follows. For in every animated body, there is a certain specific disposition or effective and vital **complexion** <note>the physical balance of elements or "temperament" of a body</note> which the life-giving power of its soul grants to the body. The Platonists intend for this to be the "nature" of bodies—a sort of footprint of the soul in the body, or a shadow. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino</note> wishes for this nature to be divisible along with the division of the body, full of "seeds," and the final thing flowing into the body from the life of the soul. 

Let us summarize it in this way: All minds—whether they are sublime and above souls, or lower and implanted in souls—are so connected to one another that, beginning from God their head, they proceed in a long and continuous series, and any higher minds distribute their rays to the lower ones. Let us see what arises from this. When someone strikes the top end of a straight piece of wood lying on the ground with their finger, even the slightest pulse resounds at the other end of the wood. The same happens in a stretched string; if its tip is touched, the whole thing trembles and sounds. If you stretch two strings on a lute at an equal interval, when one is struck, the other also trembles. If you tune two lutes to the same pitch, when one sounds, the other echoes back. 

What is the point of this? It is so we may understand that from the mutual and harmoniously tempered connection of all minds, the same thing occurs: the sparks of the first minds shine down into the middle ones, and those of the middle ones shine all the way into the lowest, and they are reflected back from the last ones through the middle back to the sublime. This mutual connection of theirs, and the continuous flowing of the infusion of sparks from the higher to the lower, we call **Providence**.

Let us set aside minds for the moment and consider the "idols," that is, the images of souls. Let the head of all be the idol of the **World Soul** <note>the "Anima Mundi," which Platonists believed animated the entire universe</note>; to this, let the twelve idols of the twelve souls that drive the twelve spheres <note>the celestial spheres of the planets and stars</note> be connected. Furthermore, since there are many souls in any given sphere, let the idols of these be bound to the one idol of the single, common soul that rules that entire sphere. And so, all the idols of rational souls hang from one supreme idol by a certain mutual **conspiracy** <note>original: "conspiratio"; used here in the literal sense of "breathing together" or harmony</note>, so that any nod of the first idol passes into the middle ones, and from the middle into the lowest, and the "seeds" of all physical things are transmitted from the first idols to the following ones. This kind of harmony and the hand-off of seeds is what we consider to be **Fate**. 

By the same logic, let us proceed through bodies. Let the complexions (or dispositions, or "natures") of the twelve spheres be joined to the one supreme nature of the world’s matter itself. Indeed, let the individual natures of every tiny body belonging to any sphere be similarly referred back to the universal nature of its own sphere. This dependency is called the **natural series**, in which the instinct of higher natures is poured into lower natures. 

Thus, all minds are reduced to one Mind like lights to a single light; all idols and images of souls are reduced to one idol of the Universal Soul; and all natures of bodies (which are like shadows of souls) are properly reduced to the common nature of the one Body, which is like the shadow of the one Soul. Our soul is joined to higher minds through its "head"—that is, the **Mind**; it harmonizes with the idols of higher souls through its internal power—that is, the **Idol** by which the body is ruled; and it is reconciled to the natures of worldly bodies through the **Nature** of its own body (into which the idol instills itself), as the nature of this body follows the nature of those others. 

Therefore, we are bound to the whole machine of the universe by these, as if by three cables: Mind to minds, Idol to idols, Nature to natures. This is no different than how a fetus in the womb is connected to the entire maternal body through continuous ligaments, whereby it also perceives the passions of the mother’s soul, body, and spirit through its own soul, body, and spirit. The soul, therefore, is **above Fate** through the Mind, existing only in the order of Providence as an imitator of heavenly things and a governor of lower things along with them. For the soul, as a participant in Providence, rules itself, its home, the city, the arts, and animals according to the model of divine governance. Through the Idol, it is in the or...

He uses the analogy of vibrating lute strings to show how divine influence flows through this hierarchy, allowing the human soul to transcend fate when it acts through its higher mind.</summary>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...in the same order of fate, but not subject to fate. For the **idol** <note>original: "idolum"; referring to the "image" or lower animating power of the soul</note> of our soul, by its own nature, joins with superior "idols" to form and move the body. By its nature, the body is indeed under fate, but the soul, while existing within fate, moves nature. Therefore, the mind is above fate within providence; the idol is within fate but above nature; nature is under fate but above the body. Thus, the soul is placed within the providence of fate and the laws of nature, not merely as a passive recipient, but also as an active agent. For this reason, Plato says in the *tenth book of the Republic* that the virtue of the soul is not a slave-like spirit guiding one’s life; rather, he says that the fortune of a life is chosen by us, not that we are chosen by a spirit or by fortune. The blame belongs to the one who chooses, not to God. Zoroaster also teaches this: 

> Do not increase fate. <note>original: "μηδ' γ' αὔξαν τὴν εἱμαρμένην"</note>

That is: Do not add to your destiny. It is as if it were in your own power to yield to fate or not to yield. While we are bound by those three parts <note>Mind, Idol, and Nature</note> to the order of things, there is a fourth part through which we are especially set free and belong entirely to ourselves. This is **reason** <note>original: "ratio"</note>, which we place in the middle, between the mind (the head of the soul) and the idol (the foot of the soul). For the "mind" exists in the soul not insofar as it is the soul proper, but insofar as it is angelic and occupied by higher intellects. Likewise, that "idol" of the soul—that is, the power that governs the body—is not the function of the pure soul, but of the soul as it already leans toward the body. 

But **reason** is placed between them; it is a certain power belonging to true souls, through which they run from the principles of things to conclusions in a temporal succession through universal concepts. They resolve effects back into causes and lead causes back into effects; they also run through particular concepts according to the pattern of universal reasoning. In this first and universal reasoning, it should be called **intellectual reason**; in particular reasoning, it is called **thinking and opining reason**. 

However, that "mind" which is the head and charioteer of the soul, imitating the angels by its own nature, attains what it desires not through succession, but in a single moment—or rather, as Plotinus argues, it contains all things simultaneously in a state of being and action. And rightly, after this stable mind of the soul which imitates the angels, there follows the mobile reason which is proper to the soul. Its attendants are those unthinking powers of sensation located in the idol—namely, the "confused phantasy" which follows natural instinct, and the "imagination" which gathers the five senses. Nature itself is the attendant of the idol. 

The Platonists compare our mind to our own internal "Sun," our reason to the "light" of this Sun, the idol to a "ray" of this light, and nature to the "reflection" of the ray (that is, to its brightness or, more accurately, its shadow). To return to the power of reason: they often say it relates to the mind in the same way that we see speech relates to the soul, moving in a perpetual and free motion. Finally, that rational faculty—which is the true nature of the soul—is not one single, determined thing. For it wanders up and down with free motion. Indeed, the first motion is that which is located in the soul’s own nature, since the soul itself is the **third essence** <note>original: "essentia tertia"; a central Neoplatonic concept where the soul sits between the eternal/divine realm and the temporal/physical realm</note>, whose power is inherently mobile. 

This "first motion" is not this or that specific movement; it is not carried only here or only there, but is a common motion that flows freely like a fountain of movement, gliding through all parts at every moment. Therefore, although we are in a way subject to the common order of things through the mind, the idol, and nature—subject to providence through the mind, to fate through the idol, and to universal nature through our particular nature—nevertheless, through **reason**, we are entirely our own masters. As if set free, we follow now these parts, now those. 

Sometimes reason clings to the mind, where it rises into providence. Sometimes it obeys the idol and nature, where it undergoes fate out of its own "love" for the body; while trusting in the senses, it is distracted here and there by the encounter with sensible things. Sometimes, leaving other things aside, it withdraws into itself, where it either investigates other things through argument or searches into itself. This middle power, which is proper to the soul, is so very free and restless. And when something strikes our outer parts—for instance, the mind, the idol, or nature—it is possible that the soul perceives it immediately in some way, yet it does not "notice" that it perceives it until the experience passes into the middle power <note>Reason</note>.

For since this is the middle power through which we are human—and indeed, which is what we ourselves are—whatever pertains to it most evidently pertains to the human being. Colors or voices often move the eyes or ears, and sight and hearing immediately perform their duty (the one sees, the other hears), yet the soul does not yet notice that it is seeing or hearing unless our middle power directs itself toward these things. This is obvious in those who do not recognize people they pass by while they are thinking intensely about something else. In the same way, superior minds <note>angels or divine intellects</note> always move our own mind which is attached to them, yet we do not notice an impulse of this kind because the middle power through...

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.

...it turns away from higher things by wandering through lower things. For the same reason, the idols <note>The "idols" are the lower, animating powers of souls that govern physical matter</note> of superior souls are always striking our own idol; yet we do not recognize this influence when that middle part of the soul <note>Reason</note> is focused more firmly on something else. Similarly, the natures of the larger bodies <note>The physical cosmos</note> continually provoke the nature of our own body, and very often we do not notice this instinct for the same reason. 

We have an example of this in the body. For often, provoked by no external thing, we become angry within ourselves; or, troubled by no evils, yet terrified by news or omens, we grow numb, mourn, and tremble; or, soothed by no good things, we are joyful within ourselves and sing. Where do these come from? Such new effects certainly have a new cause. This cause is surely the varying state of the body at various times—whether yellow bile <note>original: "crocea bilis"</note> seethes in the gall or liver, or black bile <note>original: "bilis atra"</note> boils in the spleen, or the heart overflows with bright blood. 

Such states and natures of the body—because they are close to the life-giving power contained in the <term>idol</term> <note>The lowest faculty of the soul that connects it to the body</note> (and which contains them in turn)—incite it with various pulses. They provide an occasion for the idol to act upon the body's complexion <note>The balance of humors</note> in a different and more passive way than usual. This operation, having become more agitated, tickles the sense of feeling contained in the same idol, or secretly pricks the <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of imagination or mental imagery</note> of that same idol, just as the stomach is pricked by natural hunger. That secret pricking and tickling does not pass to the middle part of the soul [Reason] when it is preoccupied with something else; however, it does pass through when the mind is idle. Then, through the thinking reason, we suddenly become somewhat angry, or mournful, or joyful. The intellectual reason notices these things, which is why it sometimes consents to them, and at other times flees from them or drives them away through counsel and remedies. 

In short, we are often struck by these emotions in a long sequence descending into us from universal natures through our own nature, and we are utterly ignorant of where they come from. If this is so, why should superior minds <note>Angels or celestial intelligences</note> joined to our mind not also strike it always? We do not notice this impulse when our middle part is so occupied with its own acts that the influence of the [higher] mind does not pass through to it. But when that part is idle, what prevents some angelic thought from creeping into our rational powers, even if we do not see where it creeps from? This is indicated by those who—without a teacher and solely through the focus of an empty reason, or even through tranquility—have often produced many magnificent things even while not seeking them, as if the light of the Sun suddenly poured itself into clear air. 

And although the arrangement of the world—which is inscribed all at once in the minds and reasons of supernal souls—offers itself entirely and simultaneously to our mind through a perpetual continuation, the temporal succession of worldly seeds <note>The causal chains of events</note> follows itself little by little in the idols and natures of those [higher] souls. In a similar sequence, it descends through the idols of all souls and the natures of all bodies until it reaches the idol of our soul and the nature of our body. 

For example: the reason for tomorrow's rain reigns today in the idols of the celestial souls and the natures of the heavens. This same reason flows down through the idols of the elemental souls and the natures of the elements until it strikes the idol of our soul and the nature of our humors. The striking of our idol comes from those [higher] idols; the striking of our nature comes from those [higher] natures and our own idol. 

When that influence of [higher] minds shows something to our reason—provided it is strongly idle or empty for the sake of the mind—it reveals things pertaining to the universal knowledge of eternal things or the governance of the world, such as God’s law, the orders of angels, the restoration of ages, or the changing of kingdoms. When the instinct of idols and natures strikes a completely empty reason and imagination, it portends something pertaining to the changes of times and the disturbances of elements, such as future rain, earthquakes, and similar things. 

By what path does this happen? That power of the supernal idols about to bring rain prefigures the wheels of the heavens toward rain; these dampen the air; the damp air moves our <term>pituita</term> <note>original: "pituita"; phlegm or the watery humor</note>, and the phlegm moves the <term>spiritus</term> <note>A subtle, vaporous substance that mediates between the soul and the physical body</note>, especially in that part where the spirit itself is watery. Since the spirit is a vapor of the blood, and the four humors are in the blood, the powers of the four humors and elements are also in the spirit. Therefore, that watery power of the spirit, irritated by the phlegm, goads the life-giving power of our soul in that part where the life-giving force possesses the seeds of watery things. This force rouses those images in the idle imagination and reasons pertaining to phlegm, so that we suddenly think of rivers, rains, snakes, eels, fish, and such things. In the same way, the power of the supernal ones [brings] heat and summer for the creature, [moving] through suitable means the <term>cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile</note>, that is, the bile in us and the **choleric** spirit...

<summary>Ficino explains how higher cosmic influences and internal bodily humors (like bile or phlegm) affect human thoughts and emotions through the "idol" and "spirit." He argues that when the mind is quiet or "empty," it becomes receptive to angelic insights or premonitions of natural events like rain.</summary>

...moves the habit, this one the life-giving power, and that one the fiery images lurking in the imagination and reason, so that we imagine fires and red and yellow colors.

->Seven types of withdrawal.<-

**T**ruly, when we are at leisure in such a way that we notice influences of this kind, there are seven types of withdrawal <note>original: "uacandi genera." Ficino uses "vacatio" (leisure or vacation) to describe the soul's withdrawal from sensory business to focus on its own internal life.</note>. We withdraw by sleep, fainting <note>original: "syncope"</note>, the melancholic humor, a tempered complexion <note>A "tempered complexion" refers to a perfect balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, solitude, wonder, and chastity. Since the soul fulfills its operations of moving and sensing in this coarser body through the spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle vapor that served as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note> closest to it, it follows that when—either because the spirit is exhausted in the external senses or because those passages of the brain are filled with vapors and humors—the spirits suitable for sense and motion are no longer transmitted to the limbs, then the soul collects itself in a certain way. It is then occupied neither in sensing corporal qualities, nor in ruling and moving the limbs of its body, nor in handling external business. This happens easily in sleep. Moreover, to the degree that the outer act is released, the inner act is intensified. 

The inner acts are the visions of the imagination <note>original: "phantasiae"</note> and the discourses of reason. But most often the imagination—by whose nod we lead much of our lives—is so intensified that it revolves its own images within itself with a very sharp intuition. Those revolved images shine back more sharply into that "common sense" which, in the Platonic manner, we call the <term>imagination</term> <note>Ficino distinguishes between "Phantasia" (the faculty that stores/generates images) and "Imaginatio" (the faculty that perceives them, often identified with the "common sense").</note>; from there they shine into the lower senses and the spirit. Indeed, an image shining in these senses and the spirit is usually asserted to be a real thing. For when they are awake, men say they see a man when they turn themselves toward the image of a man glittering in these faculties. Similarly, when they are asleep, they affirm they see a man when his image—preserved by the imagination itself—shines through into the sense and the spirit. 

However, those images shine out above all others to which the imagination is more strongly affected, whether a past thought or disturbance, or a present tumult of the dominant humors causes it. And these dreams <note>original: "insomnia"</note> are vain, and they offer nothing of prophecy, for they are born either from the remnants of waking hours or from the disturbance of the body. Men who are devoted to a life of pleasure are usually mocked by such dreams; they are vehemently affected by things that move the senses, and they afflict the imagination most sharply either to accept these things as good or reject them as evil, with the result that their remnants disturb the imagination in sleep. Furthermore, those weighed down by excessive food or drink never have a clear imagination in sleep. For because of the immoderate redundancy of humors and vapors, those images are often moved in the imagination which present spectacles of the earth. In these men, also, because the power of the genitals is incited by the heat of wine, images of a beloved person preserved by the imagination are moved, from which an embrace is imagined. 

From these reasons, Plato concludes in the ninth book of the *Republic* that reason is often so occupied in sleep that it does not freely perceive higher influences. He says, however, that it will perceive the truth as often as it is not disturbed. There are also many who despise a life of pleasure, yet are studious of civil affairs, or desirous of power and glory. In these men, while they sleep, even the imagination is sometimes lulled to rest, but then reason handles private and public business, and is mostly occupied by them. There are some who despise both pleasures and human glory, but are dedicated to the investigation of divine and natural things. In these men, during sleep, not only the imagination sometimes ceases, but also the acts of reason and anxious consultation. Instead, that accustomed investigation of speculative reason rises up, so that we seem either to measure the heavens, or divide the elements, or count the species of animals. 

Prophecy <note>original: "uaticinium"</note> does not commonly happen to any of those we have listed, although those last ones—the philosophers—truly reason even while sleeping; indeed, they sometimes find what they had sought for a long time and did not find while awake, because reason is then more tranquil. Something of this sort happened to Galen <note>The famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD.</note>, who writes that when he was sick around the diaphragm, he dreamed he would be freed if he let blood from the vein that is between the thumb and forefinger; he reduced the blood and recovered his health. And there are some—though very few such are found—who, having tamed pleasures and neglected civil affairs, so order their lives that they burn with a desire to attain the truth, yet they distrust that it can be investigated by human tracks (in which the ambiguous mind of natural philosophers usually trusts). Therefore, they give themselves to God and strive for nothing themselves. With open and purified eyes, they wait for what might be shown most clearly, which is also said to have been commanded...

He distinguishes between vain dreams caused by physical excess and the more significant insights or healing visions (like those of Galen) that occur when the mind is tranquil.</summary>

<header>BOOK XIII ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.</header>

...Socrates is said to have both said and done. These are called pious and religious men; the minds of these people are at leisure more than others during wakefulness, and are entirely at leisure in sleep, which is why a heavenly impulse is easily noticed by them. But there are two kinds of these men. Some frequently admire this temple of God—namely, the machine of the world <note>Ficino often refers to the physical universe as a "machine" (machina), meaning a complex, divinely engineered structure.</note>—while others more earnestly worship the divine power of this temple. When the minds of the former are quiet in sleep, the changes of the world are shown to them, especially those toward which they are more inclined, so that they may see future rain, war, plague, and the like. We have spoken above about the manner and order of this demonstration.

However, the interpretation of a dream is often difficult, and often it is also easy. It is difficult when—after a future rain has been expressed in the <term>phantasia</term> <note>In Renaissance psychology, the *phantasia* or "imagination" was the faculty that processed and stored sensory images.</note>—the power of the imagination does not commit the image of rain to memory carefully enough. Instead, being too swift and fickle, as soon as it is pushed, it runs smoothly through similar and subsequent images. Thus, from rain it might be moved to think of winds; from winds to the highest mountains; from mountains to snows. Having passed through these, the person wakes up, and once awake, remembers the last-seen snow more than the rain; hence, they predict future snow, not rain.

Therefore, an interpreter of dreams must be a most keen hunter, knowing how to track back from the nearest footprint to the remote one, and from there to another even more remote, seeing what follows most closely from each thing until reaching the first. We are accustomed to observing this in daily conversations: when we have moved from one topic to another, and then to another, we finally do not have the original topic ready at hand. Then we consider the very last words, and from which words those could best follow, and again from which those followed, until we recall the first topic most clearly. 

The skill of the hunter requires a swift and versatile wit, whereas the prophetic faculty—if it is to foresee things clearly—requires a peaceful and quiet mind. These, being somewhat contradictory, do not easily meet in the same person. Therefore, for the most part, the same people are not both clear prophets and interpreters; often those who prophesy do not know what they are prophesying most of all, and those who interpret are swifter to err in their own foreseeing. This is what Plato indicates in the *Timaeus* when he said that some are seers <note>original: "vates"</note> and others are interpreters of seers. 

But to return to the matter: those who, because of choleric and fiery spirits <note>In the theory of the four humors, "choleric" refers to yellow bile, which was associated with heat and speed.</note>, run too quickly through the course of the imagination, need an interpreter for their dreams. But for those in whom the imagination proceeds more deliberately because of a tempered or melancholic <note>A "melancholic" temperament was often associated with depth and intellectual focus in the Renaissance.</note> complexion of spirits, the foreseen things stick firmly in the memory and are not confused by new and various images; therefore, their prophecies do not need interpretation. 

And these are the prophecies of dreams that happen to those religious men who admire and are awestruck by this divine dwelling. Such a thing is said to have happened to Hippocrates: when he was going to treat Democritus—who was commonly reported to be insane—he received word from God during his rest that it was not Democritus who was insane, but the common people. By the same logic, Socrates predicted the future excellence of Plato from a dream. Enough on these. 

But for those religious men who worship the divinity of this temple rather than the temple itself, it happens that when they rest in sleep, their minds, being greedy for divine majesty, are struck vehemently by the divine power. A certain thought about God occurs to their minds, such as they were most accustomed to seek while awake—for instance, a desire to know the seat and operation of God. To the resting reason, an infinite and invisible light occurs, which is entirely everywhere and within itself, and which sees itself through itself without an eye. Here, if the imagination is slow to move, the notion remains flat and clear, which the soul, once awake, reveals to men as unpolluted as it was received. 

But if the imagination is swifter, it immediately begins its own work after the reason, as is its custom. It revolves its usual images and, having imitated reason to the best of its ability, it fashions an immense light of the Sun, shining everywhere to the eyes of all, and revolving in a perpetual circuit within itself. Here, then, there is a need for an interpreter, such as Joseph and Daniel were, who interpreted the dreams of kings. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus." A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed; Ficino translated many of these.</note> excelled in this divination, as is shown by his book *On the Power and Wisdom of God*, which we translated from the Greek tongue into Latin.

This kind of prophecy is indeed most suitable for religious men (as we have said). It also happens sometimes to others if they lie sober and free from cares, whether by some providence or by a stroke of luck. Thus, to King Alexander as he slept, a dragon showed a herb with which he might cure the gravely wounded Ptolemy. This happens especially near sunrise, when the crowd of vapors and external cares has settled a little. Although it is commonly said that morning dreams are truer, this does not happen solely because we are more sober (for we often go to sleep sober, yet clear visions do not occur then), but also because prophecy is strengthened by the approach of the Sun and Phoebus the seer <note>"Phoebus" is a name for Apollo, the god of prophecy and the sun.</note>, and the bloody...

->MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...sanguine and fiery spirits <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried life and thought through the body; "sanguine" refers to the blood and "fiery" to a hot, active temperament.</note> dominating at that hour contribute by their brightness to a clear vision, and (as we see) because we wake up immediately, we do not confuse the crowd of following images. What has been said about sleep is confirmed by these verses of Orpheus:

->*Messenger of things to come, greatest soothsayer for mortals,*<-
->*For you come with tranquility upon souls rejoicing in sweet sleep,*<-
->*Addressing the souls of mortals, having yourself awakened the mind.*<-
->*And yourself sending down the thoughts of the blessed during sleep,*<-
->*Silent to silent souls, foretelling things to come,*<-
->*To those whose mind, through divine worship, walks the good path.*<-
<note>original Greek: "ἄγγελε μελλόντων...". These are fragments of the Orphic Hymn to Sleep or a similar Orphic fragment common in Neoplatonic circles.</note>

That is to say: Messenger of things to come, greatest soothsayer for mortals, you approach souls soothed by the quiet of sleep, and addressing them, you awaken the mind. You suggest the thoughts of the blessed deities to them through sleep. Silent to silent souls, you foretell things to come—to those souls, I say, whose mind most rightly employs divine worship.

We have said enough concerning that leisure of the soul which occurs through sleep. Next follows the leisure which occurs through **syncope**, that is, through the falling of a half-alive body, when, due to a failure of the heart, the spirits are not sent to the limbs, and those that are in the limbs are withdrawn to protect the weakened heart; in which state, just as in sleep, prophecy occurs.

**Hercules** is said to have excelled in this, as well as many **Arabs** who were seized by the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy; called "comitial disease" in the text.</note>. Hence **Plutarch**, in his first book *On the Soul*, says: "Enarchus, recently ill, was left by physicians as if already dead, and after a short time brought back to himself, he said he had been dead and restored again to the body, and would not die of that disease; he said those spirits who had led his soul away were vehemently rebuked by their master. For they had been sent for Nichandas, not for him." Now, Nichandas was a tanner, and not unknown in the wrestling schools, who at the time Enarchus revived, fell into great fevers and died suddenly. Enarchus, however, lives and survives, dwelling most happily with us.

The third mode of leisure arises from the contraction of the **melancholic humor** <term>melancholy</term> <note>One of the four "humors" of ancient medicine. Ficino, following Aristotle, believed a certain type of melancholy was linked to genius and prophetic ability.</note>, calling the soul away from external business, so that the soul may be at leisure while the man is awake, just as it is sometimes accustomed to be while he is sleeping. Certainly, just as the most suitable instrument must lack its own motion—lest perhaps when the craftsman intends to move it to the right while working, it should meanwhile be carried by its own motion to the left—so it is necessary for that mind, which divine providence intends to use as an instrument for prophecy, to be quiet, as the melancholic often are. But even these, when they are seized by a divine power, become so much more agitated than others, just as dense bodies, if they are set on fire, burn more fervently than thin ones.

For this reason **Socrates**, whom **Aristotle** judged to be melancholic, foresaw many things by the inspiration of a familiar **daemon** <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, a "daemon" is a guardian spirit or a divine voice that guides an individual, not an evil spirit.</note>; Plato, Xenophon, Antipater the Great, and Apuleius are witnesses to this. Indeed, when Timarchus had departed from that banquet where Socrates was reclining, despite the prohibition of Socrates' daemon, he thereafter committed those deeds for which he was executed. Charmides competed at Nemea against Socrates' advice, and regretted having competed.

A certain small branch struck the eye of **Crito** while he was staying in the country against Socratic advice. Likewise, while Socrates was fleeing with several others from an enemy attack, when they came to a three-way crossroad, he refused to flee the same way as the others because he was deterred by his daemon. Then indeed those who had fled by the other way fell into the enemy cavalry. **Aristides** and **Thucydides** and many others, as long as they were near Socrates, profited greatly in the study of philosophy by the instinct of that daemon, even while Socrates himself was silent; and the further they withdrew, the more unfit they became for philosophy. When he was approaching death, as **Xenophon** writes, he predicted to Anytus that his son, who then seemed modest, would become most shameful, and so it happened.

There is also a fourth mode of leisure from a **temperate complexion** <note>A physical state where the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) are perfectly balanced.</note>; for such a complexion brings no tumult from any dominant humor that might stir the imagination toward any particular image. For men of this kind are moderate in their passions and actions, and thus have a mind so tranquil that even while awake they are subject to celestial influences—which is said to have happened to **Pherecydes of Syros, Pythagoras, and Plotinus**. I admire Plotinus above the others, who (as his disciple **Porphyry** relates) foresaw the character of men, their errors, and events; and when Porphyry himself was contemplating killing himself, Plotinus perceived it through divine insight and prevented it.

<summary>Ficino outlines the physical and psychological states—such as sleep, fainting (syncope), melancholy, and perfect health—that allow the soul to detach from the body and receive prophetic insights, citing famous examples like Socrates and Plotinus.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII

For this reason, as the younger Pliny writes, while Curtius Rufus was governing Africa, as the day was waning and he was walking in a portico, a figure of a woman appeared, larger and more beautiful than a human. <note>original: "curtio Russo". This story appears in Pliny the Younger’s *Letters* 7.27. Curtius Rufus was a Roman senator whose rise to power was supposedly foretold by this phantom.</note> She predicted that he would go to Rome, hold honors, and even return to the same province with supreme power, and die there. And all these things happened.

The fifth <term>vacation</term><note>Latin: *vacatio*. In Ficino’s philosophy, this is a "leisure" or "freedom" of the soul where it is unburdened by physical needs or sensory distractions.</note> seems to come from solitude, where the soul, distracted by no cares of human affairs, for a little while, by the influence of either deities or the heavens, contemplates daily the same things that the celestial deities contemplate doing. This is indeed what Zoroaster, the prince of the Magi, is said to have achieved through twenty years of solitude, where he wrote and did many things concerning the entire art of divination. The writings of Orpheus to Musaeus <note>Musaeus was a legendary polymath and poet, often called the disciple or son of Orpheus.</note> declare that Orpheus performed similar things in the deserts of Thrace.

The sixth vacation comes from admiration. When the Sibyls and the Pythian priests <note>The Sibyls and the Pythia were famous female oracles of the ancient world who delivered prophecies in a trance state.</note> withdrew into the cave of Jupiter or Apollo, where they believed the deity itself was present, they thought upon the majesty of the deity with such a stupor of admiration and veneration that the senses, the imagination, and the reason immediately ceased their own actions. Then the mind, exposed to the deity alone—whether it was a God or a <term>demon</term><note>Ficino uses "demon" in the classical sense: a spirit or supernatural being, not necessarily evil, that acts as a mediator between gods and men.</note>—felt the heavenly commands, especially those pertaining to the business they had recently deliberated upon. Aulus Gellius records that the priest Cornelius of Padua was similarly affected. And Orpheus introduces certain Corybantes of this kind. Albigerius of Carthage excelled in this type of prophecy. He would respond, by the inspiration of spirits, to almost whatever anyone had done or thought. Aurelius Augustine affirms that he was often present at his divinations.

The seventh and most excellent of all is that alienation of the soul which occurs through the chastity of a mind devoted to God, just as Orpheus teaches Musaeus in the *Hymn of All the Gods*. For such a mind is not just for a time, like the others, but almost always the peaceful temple of God, whose door (as John the Theologian says) God knocks at first, and once it is immediately opened He enters, dwells in it diligently, and feeds the man with <term>ambrosia</term><note>The legendary food of the gods, representing spiritual nourishment.</note>. Through this (as Aurelius Augustine reports) a certain rustic in his time used to withdraw from the body, and knew he was awake while yet seeing certain wonders with non-corporeal eyes. Through this, John the Theologian, the most divine of all, saw the entire order of the ages on Patmos. Through this, Ezekiel looked upon a field filled with the bones of the dead, and the bones later rising again. Through this, Isaiah saw God sitting, surrounded by Seraphim. But all these, just like those who dream, immediately covered whatever they perceived in the mind with the veils of imagination, so that the visions of the mind, obscured by the shadows of imagination, required an interpreter. Let us now conclude, through these seven types of prophecy, that the excellence of the human soul against matter is so great that even when the body is tamed, or asleep, or half-dead, it sees much more clearly and works much more excellently than when the body is functioning, as if it does not need the support of the body to accomplish any magnificent thing. Here it appears how great the soul's concord is with the celestial beings, and how great its kinship with God; for as often as it returns into itself, it becomes a participant in celestial secrets and divine providence.

### *The third sign, from the industry of arts and governance.*
#### *Chapter III.*

Other animals either live without art, or each with one particular art, to the use of which they do not apply themselves, but are drawn by a law of fate. The sign of this is that they make no progress over time in the industry of fabricating work. On the contrary, humans are the inventors of innumerable arts, which they execute by their own judgment. This is shown by the fact that individuals practice many arts, change them, and become more skillful through long-term use. And what is marvelous is that human arts fabricate by themselves whatever nature itself fabricates, as if we were not servants of nature, but rivals. Zeuxis painted grapes so well that birds flew toward them. Apelles painted a mare and a dog so well that passing horses neighed and dogs barked. Praxiteles expressed a Venus in marble in a certain temple of the Indians with such beauty that she could scarcely be kept safe and modest from the lustful gazes of those passing by. Archytas of Tarentum made a dove out of wood by mathematical discipline; he balanced it and inflated it with spirit so that it flew. The Egyptians, as Hermes records <note>original: "Mercurius". Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage central to the Hermetic tradition.</note>, constructed such statues of the Gods that they spoke and walked. Archimedes of Syracuse made a brass heaven, in which all seven

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...the movements of the seven planets were most accurately represented just as they are in the heavens, and the device itself revolved like the sky. I pass over the Pyramids of the Egyptians, the buildings of the Romans and Greeks, and the workshops of metals and glass. Finally, man imitates all the works of divine nature, and he perfects, corrects, and amends the works of lower nature. Therefore, the power of man is almost similar to divine nature, since man governs himself through his own counsel and art—being by no means restricted by the limits of a physical nature—and he emulates the individual works of a higher nature.

And he requires the support of lower nature so much less than the beasts, for although he was granted fewer physical protections by nature than the beasts, he himself constructs food, clothing, bedding, housing, furniture, and weapons from his own abundance. Therefore, since he supports himself by his own ability, he supports himself more abundantly than nature itself supports the animals. From this arises an unspeakable variety of pleasures, delighting the five senses of the body, which we ourselves devise through our own ingenuity. 

Beasts are confined within the very narrow boundaries of nature. Our soul does not only look to the needs of the body, like beasts enslaved to nature's command, but to various delights of the senses, like a kind of food for the imagination. Nor does the soul only flatter the imagination through various charms—while every day it delights the imagination through different games as if in jest—but sometimes the thinking reason acts more seriously, and eager to <term>propagate its offspring</term><note>Ficino uses the metaphor of "offspring" to describe the products of the human mind, such as inventions and art.</note> it shines forth and clearly shows how much talent it possesses through the various weaving of wool and silk, paintings, sculptures, and buildings. In composing these, it often considers no physical convenience, no sensory charm—since sometimes it even suffers inconvenience and trouble from them by choice—but rather the amplification of its own eloquence and the approval of its virtue. 

In these arts, one may observe how man handles all materials of the world from every direction, as if all things were subject to man. He handles, I say, elements, stones, metals, plants, and animals, and transforms them into many forms and figures, which beasts never do. Nor is he content with one element, or a few of them like the beasts, but he uses them all as if he were the Lord of all. He treads the earth, furrows the water, and climbs into the air with the tallest towers—to say nothing of the <note>original: "pennas Dædali uel Icari"</note> wings of Daedalus or Icarus. He lights a fire, and uses the hearth familiarly; he alone takes special delight in it. Deservedly, only a celestial animal delights in a celestial element. 

By celestial power, he ascends to heaven and measures it. With a super-celestial mind, he transcends heaven. Nor does man just use the elements, but he adorns them, which no beast does. How wonderful is the cultivation throughout the whole world! How stupendous the structure of buildings and cities! How artistic the irrigation of waters! He acts as the <term>representative of God</term><note>Latin: *Vicem gerit Dei*. This is a central theme in Ficino's work: man as the "Vicar of God" or "God on earth" because of his ability to govern and create.</note>, who dwells in all elements and cultivates them all; being present on the earth, he is not absent from the ether. 

And he uses not only the elements, but also all the animals of the elements—creatures of earth, water, and air—for food, convenience, and pleasure; and he uses the higher and celestial things for learning and magical miracles. Nor does he only use beasts, but he also commands them. It is possible that some beasts, using weapons received from nature, may sometimes attack man or flee his attack; however, man, using weapons he has made himself, both avoids the attacks of wild beasts, and puts them to flight, and tames them. Who ever saw any men held under the rule of beasts, in the way that we everywhere see herds of both the fiercest wild animals and gentle livestock obeying men throughout their entire lives? 

Man does not only rule beasts cruelly, but also governs, nourishes, and teaches them. Universal providence is proper to God, who is the universal cause. Therefore, man, who provides universally for all things living and non-living, is a kind of God. He is undoubtedly the God of animals, for he uses them all, commands them all, and instructs many. It is established that he is also the God of the elements, who dwells in and cultivates them all. Finally, he is the God of all materials, who handles them all, turns, and shapes them. He who rules the body in so many and such great matters, and acts as the representative of the immortal God, is undoubtedly immortal. 

But although arts of this kind shape the matter of the world and command animals, and thus imitate God the craftsman of nature, they are nevertheless inferior to those arts which, imitating the divine kingdom, take up the care of human government. Individual beasts are barely sufficient for their own care or the brief care of their offspring; man alone, however, abounds in such perfection that he first commands himself (which no beasts do), then governs a family, administers a republic, rules nations, and commands the whole world. And as if he were born to rule, he is entirely impatient of servitude. Add that for the public good... <meta>catchword: publici (of the public)</meta>

...undergoes death for the sake of the public good, which beasts do not do, inasmuch as he despises these individual mortal goods, trusting in the stability of a common and eternal good. Furthermore, arts of this kind might perhaps seem to some to belong to the present life, although such great care is not necessary for the present life alone, but rather looks toward imitating the providence of the divinity. Let us therefore consider those arts which are not only unnecessary for bodily sustenance, but are often even harmful to it, such as all the <term>liberal sciences|The "liberal arts" were the core curriculum of classical education, thought to be the studies worthy of a "free" person (liber), including grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</term>, the study of which weakens the body and hinders the comforts of life. These include the subtle calculation of numbers, the curious description of figures, the most obscure movements of lines, the <note>original: "superstitiosa"</note> meticulous harmony of music, the lifelong observation of the stars, the inquiry into natural causes, the investigation of long-lasting things, the eloquence of Orators, and the <term>frenzies of Poets|Ficino refers to the "furor poeticus" or divine inspiration, a Platonic idea that poets are possessed by a divine power rather than just using technical skill.</term>. In all these things, the human soul despises the service of the body, as one that is able at some point—and even now begins—to live without the body's help. This one thing must be noted above all: that no one can discern how a skillful craftsman’s work was artistically constructed, or by what logic, except for one who possesses the same artistic genius. For no one could discern by what path Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), the Greek mathematician known for creating mechanical models of the planetary orbits.</note> constructed his bronze spheres and gave them motions similar to the celestial movements, unless he were endowed with a similar genius. And he who discerns this because of a similarity of genius could certainly construct the same things himself once he has understood them, provided that the material was not lacking. Since, therefore, man has seen the order of the heavens—from where they are moved, where they proceed, by what measures, and what they produce—who could deny that he possesses almost the same genius (if I may put it this way) as the Author of the heavens Himself? And that he could, in a certain way, make the heavens if he obtained the instruments and celestial matter; for he makes them now, albeit from other matter, yet very similar in their order.

->*Four gifts of man in the arts.*<-

**I**n the human arts, four most excellent gifts of our soul shine forth: a most rapid ease of perception, a most ample and deeply indelible memory, a most sagacious prediction of the future, and the use of innumerable words. How divine an acumen do you think flourished in Homer, who, though both blind and poor, perceived so many and such great things, and sang so excellently, that Plato asserts all human and divine arts converged in him. How divine it was in Didymus of Alexandria, of whom Jerome writes that he was blinded from childhood, yet afterward drank in logic, physics, and theology beyond all others; and—what is a marvel—he turned out to be a wonderful geometer, accustomed to describing and teaching geometrical figures, and he also composed outstanding works of Theology. <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD) was a famous Christian theologian who lost his sight at age four but mastered the entire curriculum of his day through listening and memory.</note> Certainly, a divine light infused these men at their birth and revealed to them as they sought things that would have been impossible to find through human study alone. And although Plato and Aristotle write in their books on civil institutions that some regions are more suited for exercising genius than others, we have nevertheless found that not only in the east and south, but also in the west and north, many men have frequently been wonderfully famous in every art. If the diversity of regions and ages necessarily causes a great difference in the condition of bodies, it causes very little in geniuses; and even this we correct through counsel and study. Who does not see that the genius of man, by its nature, is not subject to places and times? There follows that indelible memory in which so many have excelled: Mithridates, king of twenty-two nations, administered justice for each of them without an interpreter. <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus (120–63 BC) was legendary for his linguistic abilities.</note> Cyrus and Lucius Scipio knew the names of all their citizens. Fabius Maximus and Lucullus held the histories of all nations in their memory. Seneca says that he could repeat two thousand names in the same order they were recited, and that he could recite two hundred verses pronounced by his students in reverse order. Augustine writes that in his time there was a certain man who had read many things and had never forgotten anything he had read. There was another in Rome who committed an entire comedy to memory while it was being recited. The capacity for so many and such great things, and such stability in those things that have been received, cannot be contained in a narrow corner of the brain, nor preserved in its fluid and failing matter, but requires the most ample and stable vessel of a divine soul.

There is also that prediction of future things in which the Chaldean and Egyptian mathematicians excelled. Certainly, that substance does not act in the future if its prophetic power does not anticipate the whole future, just as its remembering power recalls the whole past. Moreover, this substance is eternal, which in...

...collects the fleeting intervals of time into an eternal monument. Finally, the use of speech and writing, which is unique to humans, indicates to us that a certain divine mind is within us, which the beasts lack. Without speech, we would be able to live just as the beasts and mute humans do. Therefore, speech was granted to us for some more excellent work: namely, as the interpreter of the mind, the herald of infinite inventions, and an infinite messenger. Nor should <term>Epicurus|A Greek philosopher often associated by Renaissance thinkers with materialism and the denial of the soul's immortality.</term> dream that beasts possess reason just as we do, but merely lack the use of speech and hands through which they might signify the reason lurking within. For nature does not fail in necessary things, nor does she abound in superfluous ones. She did not give feet or arms to trees, for their earthy body is fixed in the soil, and they are nourished everywhere by earthy food. To the bodies of brutes, being somewhat less earthy, not every earthy food is sufficient everywhere; therefore, they are equipped with feet to seek out nourishment more conveniently. Their <term>imagination|Latin: *phantasia*. In Renaissance psychology, this was the faculty that processed sensory images into basic thoughts.</term> holds only a few confused concepts, and only those necessary for the use of the body, which can be sufficiently expressed by lowing, barking, neighing, chirping, snarling, roaring, or by gestures. But the human mind, the inventor of infinite and distinct things, is supported by the use of innumerable speech, as if by some worthy interpreter of itself. It is also fortified with hands as the most fitting instruments for manufacturing the innumerable inventions of the mind; nature would have given these same instruments to the beasts as well, if that same internal craftsman were within them to use such instruments. Therefore, the mind conceives within itself through understanding as many things as God makes in the world through His understanding. It expresses just as many in the air through speech. It writes just as many on paper with a pen. It figures just as many in the matter of the world by manufacturing. For this reason, it is clear that anyone who denies that the soul—which is the rival of God in the arts and in governing—is divine, is out of his mind.

### The fourth sign from the effect of miracles. Chapter IV.

**N**ot only in the shaping and figuring of matter through the reason of art, as we have said, does the human mind claim a divine right for itself, but also in transmuting the <term>species|The essential forms or types of things in nature.</term> of things through command. This work is indeed called a miracle, not because it is contrary to the nature of our soul (since it is an instrument of God), but because, since it is a great thing and happens rarely, it produces wonder. Hence we marvel that the souls of men dedicated to God command the elements, summon the winds, compel clouds into rain, drive away mists, cure the diseases of human bodies, and the rest. The <note>original: "Poëtæ canunt"</note> Poets sing of these things having been done openly in certain ages among various nations, Historians narrate them, none of the most excellent of our Philosophers deny them (especially the Platonists), and the ancient Theologians testify to them—<term>Hermes Trismegistus|Known here by his Latin name Mercurius; a legendary Egyptian sage thought to be a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom.</term> first of all, and Orpheus—and later Theologians have confirmed them by word and deed. 

You will perhaps wonder if I search for the reasons behind miracles. But listen. In the first book, it was discussed that the <term>third essence|In Ficino's hierarchy of the universe (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter), the Soul is the 'Third Essence'—the crucial middle link that binds the spiritual and physical worlds together.</term> is below the Angel and above the whole matter of the world, formed by the Divinity, and forming matter; it receives spiritual forms from the Divinity and gives corporeal forms to matter. In the third book, it was also established that the third essence is nothing other than rational souls—both our own and those superior to ours. From this, it is concluded among the Platonists and the followers of <term>Avicenna|A famous Persian philosopher and physician whose theories on the soul's power over matter influenced Western thinkers.</term> that every rational soul, through its essence and power, is positioned over the whole matter of the world and can move and form the whole, namely when it acts as an instrument of God for these things. 

Nevertheless, this is the order of things: all rational souls (as we have said) have an intellectual head, a rational middle, and a lowest <term>vivifying|Life-giving (Latin: *uiuificum*).</term> part. This middle force is the soul's own unique property. However, the intellectual force is a certain ray of the higher intellect sent down into the soul, and reflecting itself back again into the higher intellect. The vivifying force is an act of the soul overflowing into the body, and resulting from there back into the soul—just as the light of the Sun in a cloud is a "splendor" according to its own nature: as it looks toward the Sun it is a "ray," but as it fills the cloud it is a "paleness." The intellect looks up to what is intelligible and remains within itself. Reason "runs," but within itself. The vivifying force runs below itself as far as another thing, while it fills the body. Because, however, through this lowest part of themselves (or shadow), souls depart furthest from their own dignity by approaching bodies, it has happened that these types of governing forces of bodies are in a way weakened; or, that broad dominion which the soul possesses over the universe of bodies having been interrupted, they are distributed individually to individual bodies...

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.

...to which, while they are bound, they take care of their own bodies and almost neglect those of others. What binds them to these bodies? As **Plato** suggests, it is love—that is, the impulse of an overflowing life inclined toward giving life to the things closest to itself. Furthermore, different species of bodies are closest to different species of **rational souls**. Hence he argues that some rational souls are joined with certain bodies, others with the **celestial spheres**, others with the stars, and still others with different forms. Finally, some are joined with the bodies of men. And from certain dispositions of the innermost "seeds" <note>original: *seminum*; Ficino refers to "seminal reasons," the latent blueprints or formative powers within nature and the soul.</note> established by providence, some human souls are better suited to governing certain human bodies than others.

And, to speak briefly, that **life-giving power** <note>original: *uis uiuifica*</note> of every rational soul, because it belongs to the **third essence**, <term>third essence|In Ficino’s hierarchy of being (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter), the Soul is the "third essence" or middle term that connects the eternal and the temporal.</term> has an equal power over any body; however, through a certain amatory instinct, some souls accommodate themselves to moving certain bodies rather than others, with divine tempering clearly contributing to this. When one particular instinct ceases, that life-giving power becomes free, so that, affected by a new instinct, it may in some way rule and move another body. If this lowest part of the soul surpasses all the natures of bodies, how much more so do the middle and highest parts? 

The **Supreme** part—that is, the **Mind**—is so super-eminent that it never tastes anything corporeal, being greedy only for divine things, stable by nature, and possessing sudden intelligence. The **Middle** part—that is, the **faculty of reasoning**—is also more eminent than the lowest part; sometimes (as we have said elsewhere) it ascends into the Mind when, having received the principles of demonstration from the Mind, it investigates the universal reasons of natural things through argumentation. At other times, however, it declines toward the life-giving power when it trusts in **imagination**, <gloss>original: *phantasia*</gloss> listens to the senses, and flatters the body. It ascends into the Mind through a love of grasping higher things; it descends into the lowest power through a love of governing lower things. 

Rightly, since it is the middle of both, it loves both; and as it is more eminent than the lowest part—which rules only one body—the Reason itself moves and governs many things. For while the governing faculty of your body nourishes your body alone, and serves its nourishment through sense and desire, your **Reason** takes care of both your body and others, and fashions works of art in external matter. Since Reason is equally able to handle any materials, it approaches different ones at different times, wherever love draws it. When the love through which it carves stone ceases, it suddenly leaves the statue. When love draws it toward clay vessels, it takes up the potter's art. 

When we speak of handling bodies, we set aside for a moment that Mind which utterly despises bodies, and we speak more of **Reason** and the **governing power**. Although both of these have equal power over any bodies in the world because of the common nature of the "third essence," they act most powerfully upon that which they are most affected by, provided that the divine tempering of the "seeds" does not prevent it. The affections of those souls that are above us are more stable than ours, and they always weave the same order, proceeding in a constant tenor, since in them both the supreme power and the middle power turn upward, dwelling upon eternal contemplation. Only the lowest power varies its works, but it performs successions, and those are most orderly, so that stability appears even in change itself, while the same tenor is observed and the same things are woven back together in a similar way. 

But however it happens, the forms of things implanted in the three powers of those souls are the causes of the forms expressed in mundane bodies. And, so to speak, the **fatal imaginations** <note>In this context, "fatal" means "fated" or "determined by the laws of the universe."</note> which arise step by step from the images <gloss>original: *idolis*</gloss> of those souls are like the most vehement affections of pregnant women: whatever they imagine for themselves, they express in their spheres and the things that follow, as if in their offspring. Our soul also, being affected toward this body according to the order of its "seeds," shapes this body through the very governing power of the body. What provides this body with its certain **complexion** <note>The specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determines a person's health and temperament.</note> of the four humors, what gives the face its colors and features, if not the soul? 

The soul also drives a heavy body upward against its nature, and overcomes four opposing things <note>The four elements (earth, air, fire, water) or their qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that naturally conflict within the body.</note> in turn; yet no one wonders at this miracle. But how much that same power can do in forming the body through the imagination with more vehement affections, we have said above. Indeed, it produces different qualities in the limbs according to the diversity of the affections. **Anger** produces heat, redness, a bitter taste, and a flux of the bowels. **Fear** produces cold and paleness. **Grief** produces the moisture of sweat and a bluish-whiteness. **Anxiety** produces dryness and blackness. The affections of the soul themselves are certainly the authors of these qualities, because they often move toward such qualities as are contrary to our prior complexion. And, as **Hippocrates** teaches and
