<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the soul's "life-giving power" (uis uiuifica). He has just explained how the soul governs its own body and is now transitioning into how the soul’s internal states—specifically its imagination and emotions—can project outward to affect other bodies and even distant objects.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
<meta>catchword: And because</meta>

**Galen** <note>original: *Galenus*; a famous Greek physician and philosopher whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> says that a long-standing emotion changes the body's previous **complexion** <term>complexion|In medieval medicine, the "complexion" or temperament was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual.</term> and draws it into its own nature. This is the work of the **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*; in Ficino's psychology, the faculty that processes and stores sensory images.</note>. We have explained elsewhere what **reason** performs in the arts and in governance. Therefore, we have explained here what is produced in one's own body by the soul's governing power through the **life-giving virtue** and the emotions that serve it. Furthermore, something is produced by this power in *other* bodies that are near to it; for example, it sometimes digests food through natural heat and warms those who touch it. The maternal soul also acts upon an outside body when it nourishes a fetus in the womb, which it completes through the continuous bonds by which the fetus is tied to the mother’s body. 

Nor does the soul merely shape a nearby body, but sometimes even a distant one. For when the **semen** has been cast by a man into the womb, even a long time later when the man is absent, the formative power left in the seed thrives there and performs the role of the paternal soul in the seed, shaping a human body. This is just as when someone throws a stone far away: the "expelling power" <note>original: *uirtus expultrix*; the kinetic energy or force transmitted from the thrower to the object.</note> placed into the stone by the thrower drives the stone for as long as it rules over it, following that same strike of the air and toward that mark which the thrower intended. 

If that part of the soul suited for governing the body performs something upon an external and distant body through its life-giving power, why should it not also do so through the **sensitive power**, which is more eminent than the former—namely, through the emotions of the **imagination**? Therefore, the imagination shapes its own body like a life-giving virtue, as we have said, whenever it is agitated by sharp emotions. It also shapes the bodies of others through **fascinations** <term>fascinations|From the Latin *fascinatio*, referring to the "evil eye" or the ability to influence others through a gaze or psychological projection.</term> and spells. It is no wonder that the soul does such things through its emotions, if certain herbs or stones do so through their vapors (provided the **celestial souls** breathe upon them). 

Nor is the soul lacking a continuation of means through which it may carry out its action upon another body. Indeed, the hostile imagination of a sorcerer seeks to inflict a fever upon a boy in the child's tender little body. The imagination of the fever vibrates "feverish spirits"—that is, **choleric** ones—just as the imagination of sexual intercourse vibrates seminal spirits toward the genital members. That struck choleric and fever-bearing spirit rouses foul and feverish vapors if any exist in the sorcerer's body. As soon as these are stirred up, they rush forth together with the spirit like **arrows** toward the place where the malicious imagination had aimed, as if at a target. 

They flash forth most especially from the eyes of an elder and pass through the eyes of the boy as if through glass materials—just as rays pass through glass—and they infect the boy's spirits and humors. Those who are most powerful in these spells are those for whom, at birth, a malignant aspect of **Saturn**, a "terrestrial" seed from the parents, and a similar diet have forged a **melancholic** <term>melancholic|A temperament associated with the humor of black bile, often linked to deep thought, but also to gloom or malevolence if "burnt."</term> complexion abundant in foul vapors. Furthermore, the savage power of **Mars** adds the little fires of bile. When these people are in old age—a "terrestrial" and melancholic time of life—they are exceedingly peevish; they grow violently angry at whomever they encounter and curse them with a most hostile mind. Because of the "earthy" humor, they fix their imagination more firmly and effectively upon their desires. This humor, once ignited, burns most vehemently and is extinguished slowly, like a fire in thick wood or hard material. Nor do they lack malignant vapors through which, as if with arrows, they may hurl poison at an adversary. 

Do you wonder that the body of one person is defiled by the mind of another? Yet you do not wonder that a mind is harmed by a mind when, through habit, we drink in the vices of others. You do not wonder that your body is easily infected with disease by the vapor of another body, as **consumption**, **epidemics**, **leprosy**, the **itch**, **dysentery**, **pleurisy**, and **redness of the eyes** <note>original: *phthisis, epidimia, lepra, pruritus, dysenteria, pleuresis, oculorumque rubor*</note> indicate. Among the Western Ethiopians, it is said there were beasts called **Catoblepas** <note>A legendary creature mentioned by Pliny the Elder, said to kill with its gaze.</note> which killed men by their sight alone, just as **Basilisks** do in Cyrene. Such is the force in the vapors of the eyes. 

Why should your body be less subject to another's mind than to another's body? Why not rather *more* subject, since the mind is more powerful and does not lack the means through which to act? We read that people in **Illyria** and among the **Triballi** <note>Tribes in the Balkans noted in ancient texts for having the "evil eye."</note> used to do this; when they were angry, if they gazed at a man too long and intently, they would kill him—and these people even had double pupils in their eyes. Certain women in **Scythia** are said to have done the same. Such is the power of the imagination, especially when the vapors of the eyes serve the emotions of the soul. For that wonderful attention of the imagination increases the power no less than the **ostrich’s eye** fixed upon its egg <note>A common medieval belief that ostriches hatched their eggs simply by staring at them intensely.</note>. Indeed, while one emotion grows hot, another grows lukewarm. Therefore, in the intense focus of a sorcerous imagination, the soul's "natural" emotion (by which it is bound to its own body) is relaxed for a short time; thus becoming freer from its own body, it begins to transform the new matter toward which it is newly moved, as if it were its own fresh body. If a malicious imagination has such great power, how much do you think a **beneficial reason** will have? Surely at least twice as much.

He argues that the soul’s power is so great that it can project "spirits" or "vapors" through the eyes to shape or harm external matter.</summary>

Having previously discussed how the soul's imagination and biological "life-giving virtue" can affect its own body and those nearby, Ficino now elevates the discussion to how the higher faculty of Reason, when aligned with the Divine, can perform miraculous healings and even govern the material world.</meta>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.</header>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.

And because **reason** <note>original: *ratio*; the higher human faculty of logical and discursive thought.</note> surpasses **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*; the faculty that processes sensory images.</note>, and goodness surpasses evil, it follows that when reason is fixed upon some benefit with the soul's entire intention toward God, it sometimes affects the body it is concerned with—whether its own or another's—with a benefit. According to the Platonists, those who excel in this gift are those endowed with a balanced **complexion** <term>complexion|The specific physical temperament or balance of bodily humors (fluids) believed to determine health and personality.</term> and a heavenly disposition by a certain divine favor. Furthermore, they are nourished by pure and moderate food and raised with honorable and divine habits. These people are often the "physicians of the human race." If they ardently desire good things for a body they wish to help, directing their pious prayers straight to God, they provide that help instantly—especially if the soul of the person receiving the benefit is prepared. Hence Zoroaster <note>A legendary ancient sage and prophet to whom various mystical "Chaldean Oracles" were attributed in the Renaissance.</note> says:
> If you extend a fiery mind to a work of piety, you will also save the flowing body.
> <note>original: "ἐκτείνας πυρινὸν νοῦν ἔργον, ἐπ᾽ εὐσεβίας, ῥευστὸν καὶ σῶμα σαώσεις."</note>

Philostratus <note>A Greek writer known for his biography of the wonder-worker Apollonius of Tyana.</note> narrates that certain miracles of this kind were performed by the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana. Again, many Pythagoreans affirm that similar deeds were done by Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Philolaus. Moreover, Iamblichus writes that the Pythagoreans, whenever such miracles were recounted, were accustomed to believe easily that they were done by God through divine souls. In matters of this sort, they always had these verses of Linus <note>A legendary pre-Homeric poet and musician.</note> on their lips:
> One should hope for everything, since nothing is beyond hope; all things are easy for God to accomplish, and nothing is impossible.
> <note>original: "ἐλπέσθω χρὴ παντ᾽ ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐστὶ οὐδὲν ἄελπτον, ῥᾴδια πάντα θεῶ τελέσαι, καὶ ἀνήνυτον οὐδέν."</note>

But let us return to those souls through whom God performs miracles as if through instruments. How much does an excellent, balanced physical condition contribute to this? It makes their reason more unhindered, untroubled by the storm of excessive **humors** <term>humors|The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to regulate health.</term>. What does a moderate and pure diet contribute? It ensures the soul is not weighed down by the burden of its body. What of that honorable and pious education? It allows the soul to desire good for humanity and, being in some way similar to God, to be aided by God—or rather, to be led by God as an instrument. 

Finally, since reason is more eminent than imagination, when reason is devoted entirely to God and directed toward this one work of conferring a benefit, that prior natural attachment by which the soul is joined to its own body is greatly relaxed. Released from its own body, it acts upon another. For in these matters, it can easily be led by God as an instrument, since its nature is above all bodies. Although a certain attachment once snatched it away to govern a single body, it is like a most wise and powerful king whose providence and jurisdiction oversee all parts of a vast kingdom equally. He may neglect the other parts for a time, enticed by the charm of one area, but once his love for that part cools, he transfers his care to governing the others.

Our Plato seems to have touched upon all these mysteries: that "tyranny" of the imagination, and again this "empire" of pious reason in the *Timaeus*, where he discussed the power of the soul over the body. In the *Phaedrus*, however, he hints at something even more wonderful when he says that every soul has care for the entire universe, and that our soul, when it is free, wanders through the whole of heaven and governs the world together with the celestial souls, traveling about in different forms. 

He revealed when the soul becomes like this in the *Epinomis*, where he affirmed that the necessity of the mind and the joined soul overflows every other necessity, and that every decree for such a soul is "fatal" <note>Meaning "ordered by fate" or possessing the power of destiny.</note>. Furthermore, in the tenth book of *The Just* <note>Ficino's title for Plato's *Republic*.</note>, he called the intellectual soul "Necessity," between whose knees is a certain spindle around which the spheres of the world revolve. Why mention this? So we may understand that it can sometimes happen that a person’s soul—with the entire intention of its reason—is turned toward the Mind and its own "Head," just as we said it is sometimes turned toward imagination and lower reason. 

What kind of soul performs these things? One that commands the imagination to be silent and, burning with desire for the supreme divinity, does not rely on the usual wanderings of natural reason. It lives by the mind alone, becomes an angel, and receives God with its whole heart. Zoroaster signifies this when he says:
> The soul of mortals somehow draws God into itself; possessing nothing mortal, it is entirely intoxicated by the divine; for it glories in the harmony under which the human body was placed.
> <note>original: "ψυχή ἡ μερόπων, θεὸν ἄγξει πως ἐς ἑαυτήν οὐδὲν θνητὸν ἔχουσα, ὅλη θεόθεν μεμέθυσται ἁρμονία αὐχεῖ γὰρ, ὑφ᾽ ἧι πέλε σῶμα βρότειον."</note>

The Theology of Saint John <note>Referring to the Gospel of John, specifically the concept of being "born of God" (John 1:13).</note> says a soul of this kind is "born again from God." Indeed, the influence of the highest God, flowing through angelic minds down to the soul of man, urges it...

He argues that the soul’s higher reason can act as a divine instrument, potentially governing the physical world as envisioned by Plato and ancient sages.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from the previous page regarding the soul's miraculous power. Having established that the soul can heal the body through its alignment with the Divine, Ficino now explains how the soul can transcend its "animal" state to become "angelic," thereby gaining command over the very elements of the universe.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...daily the soul is immersed in the body, so that having shed the fleshy husk, it might lay aside its **animal** <note>In the sense of "anima" or "soul-driven" biological functions common to all living creatures.</note> powers and operations, and instead of a soul, it might become an **angel**—just as a ray of the Sun thins out vapors, draws them upward, and converts them into a fiery nature. He who commits himself entirely to this inspiration ceases to be a soul and becomes, through God’s regenerating power, a son of God, an angel. For this reason, Plato in the *Timaeus* called theologians the "sons of God." If the soul by its own nature exceeds the machinery of the world, and through its inferior powers performs wonders even in the bodies of others, what do we think it will do when it has risen to its own "head" <note>The "head" of the soul refers to its highest intellectual faculty, where it touches the divine.</note> and escaped into an angelic state? This must be possible at some point, since the soul so often becomes **brutalized** by the charms of the senses; surely the inspiration of God ought not to be any less powerful than the charms of the senses.

In that state, therefore, it will no longer merely fascinate or heal a single tender or sick person, but will command the spheres of the elements. For as long as it is devoted to this body, it agitates the elements of this "small world" <note>The human body as a microcosm.</note>—that is, it moves the four **humors** <term>humors|The four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</term> and induces in them heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and all colors and tastes, as was shown before regarding the vital act and the affects of the imagination. Therefore, when it emerges into the wide world, having been released and now filled with God, it moves the humors of this "greater living being" <note>The universe as a macrocosm.</note>—that is, the four elements of the larger world—as if they were its own. Indeed, it has now become, as it were, the **Soul of the World**, or at least of that part of the world toward which it is most inclined. 

And just as the same human soul which had ruled the tiny one-cubit body of an infant later rules a body of two cubits, then three, then four, and even ten (as is said of giants), so too if the body grew to a hundred or two hundred cubits, the soul would rule it just as easily. For that which, by the order and dignity of nature, precedes all physical bulk can fill and move the whole bulk just as easily as a part of it. If the life-giving force of the rational soul has power from God over the spheres of the world, it also has power over the affects of reason and the mind. Thus, by **affect alone**, under God’s guidance, it will summon the winds, bring clouds into a clear sky, and force them to turn into rain. Again, it will calm the winds and clear the air. That this can be done, or has been done, is confessed by Hippocrates of Cos, and by the Moorish and Arab theologians—Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Jewish philosopher and poet.</note>, the prince of the Moors, and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> among the Arabs. I pass over how many disturbances of the elements and storms the Egyptians and Platonists believe happen both from the conflicts of **daemons** <note>Spiritual beings intermediate between gods and humans; not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> and from the "falling" of souls into bodies—matters which Plutarch, Porphyry, and Proclus dispute most diligently. 

It is certainly the opinion of Plato and the Platonists that from the heavens down to the earth, different regions in all the spheres were distributed to different divinities from the beginning. Thus, when a region of the earth dedicated to certain divinities is influenced—either through celestial influx or primarily through the affections of souls—miracles appropriate to such divinities are often performed, either by the divinities themselves or by the souls occupied by those same divinities. But of these things we shall speak elsewhere; for now, let us relate a certain **Magical** opinion.

The Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, often associated with astrology and magic in Renaissance thought.</note> think that something else truly marvelous can be done by the soul: namely, that by pouring out rays into its own body, it may surround itself with light and, by the lightness of those rays, lift itself on high. Some report that their father Zoroaster did this very thing. For my part, if any reason for this miracle can be assigned, I think it is perhaps this: **First light** is in God, and there it is such that it surpasses the intellect; therefore, it cannot be called "intelligible light." But when that light of God is infused into an **angel**, it immediately becomes "intellectual light" and can be understood. When it is infused into a **soul**, it becomes "rational" and can be not only understood but also thought upon. From there it migrates into the soul’s **idolum** <note>original: *idolum*; the "image" or lower part of the soul that acts as a bridge to the body.</note>, where it becomes "sensitive," though not yet corporeal. From there it moves into the **ethereal vehicle** of the *idolum*, where it becomes "corporeal," though not yet manifestly perceptible. Finally, it enters the elemental body—whether simple and airy, or composite—which is the vessel for the ethereal, and there it becomes manifestly visible. 

And I believe this is that **Golden Chain** which Homer saw hanging from heaven and let down all the way to the earth, which men might grasp to lift themselves into the heavens. Truly, celestial souls abound with such divine light that a huge abundance of it overflows into their bodies, which we see in the stars. If at any time a human soul fixes its gaze so firmly upon God that it is filled and ravished by divine light, it then sparkles just as much, and pours the richest rays into its vehicle, and through the vehicle and airy body, into this body which is manifest to the eyes. Because that most full abundance of rays then shines forth, it thins the body and lifts it up—the ethereal vehicle and airy body contributing to this, like **tow** <note>original: *stuppa*; coarse, dry fibers of flax or hemp.</note> lifted up by a flame. By such a **fiery chariot**, the Magi and Platonists would say that Elijah and Paul were snatched up into heaven, and finally after...

He introduces a hierarchy of light—from God down to the physical body—to explain how the soul can literally illuminate and levitate the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s transition from a biological "animal" state to a divine "angelic" state. Having argued that the soul can heal and command the elements through its alignment with the Divine, Ficino now draws on the "ancient theologians" like Zoroaster and Hermes Trismegistus to explain how the human body itself might eventually be "glorified" or lifted beyond its material limits.</meta>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII.

...after the judgment of the world, the body—which our theologians call "glorified"—is to be similarly snatched away. This is why Zoroaster commands:

> Because the soul is a bright fire by the power of the Father,
> let the immortal depth of the soul be adored, and spread all your eyes
> upward; nor should you leave the dross of matter in the precipice.
<note>original Greek: ὅτι ψυχὴ πῦρ δυνάμει πατρὸς ἔσα φαεινὸν ἀγάσθω ψυχῆς βάθὸς ἄμβροτον, ὄμματα δ’ἄρδην πάντ’ ἐκπέτασον ἄνω μὴ δὲ τὸ τῆς ὕλης σκύβαλον κρημνῶ καταλήψῃς. This is a fragment from the *Chaldean Oracles*, which Ficino attributed to Zoroaster.</note>

That is to say: Since the soul becomes a splendid fire through the power of the Father, let the immortal depth of the soul rule within you, and lift all your eyes together on high. In doing so, you do not even leave the material body itself to fall into the abyss. He calls "fire" that very light with which God overflows by His own nature, and with which the soul—turned toward the Father by His power—abounds. And because God is unity itself above the mind, and the center of essences above all being, the soul is not joined to Him through the mind properly speaking, but through the **unity of the soul** <note>Ficino identifies a "spark" or "center" in the soul that is even higher than the intellect, which allows direct contact with God.</note>, which is the "head" of the mind and the center of the entire soul. 

Therefore, Zoroaster says: *Let the immortal depth of the soul lead you*—that is, that very unity which God once impressed upon the soul as a seal of divine unity. From this unity, and toward it, all other powers of the soul hang, like all the lines of a circle hanging from and leading to the center. *Let all your eyes follow*—that is, all the powers of the soul engaged in knowing. This is the goal of that saying: *Lift up your gates, O you princes, and be lifted up, you eternal gates* <note>A reference to Psalm 24:7, interpreted here as the soul's faculties opening to the divine.</note>, etc. *Together*—that is, collected into one mind, or into the unity that is the mind's head. Then the body, both celestial and earthly, will follow them. This is why he said the material body (the earthly one) is not then left in the precipice; for then the body itself will also be lifted on high, and will not be left in the lowest place of the world, which the Magi often call "the precipice."

Hermes Trismegistus also describes the power and effect of this miracle when he disputes with his son Tat regarding **regeneration** <term>regeneration|The spiritual rebirth or "deification" where the human soul transcends its mortal nature.</term>. Let this suffice regarding the miracle that the mind shows in its own body according to the opinion of the Platonists. But concerning those miracles it demonstrates within the spheres of the world, certain questions are raised among the Platonists, which I shall state and solve as follows.

---

## *Six questions and solutions concerning miracles. Chapter V.*

**Q:** When the human mind sheds its bodily cares, why does it still affect the passions of the elements? 
**A:** Because the divine soul—the child of the highest and common good—does not despise the public good. Therefore, like a god, it will providently move the elements for the benefit of animals and men. 

**Q:** Can it be lifted so far above its body that it touches the spheres of the world? 
**A:** It certainly can, if it is "everywhere," as some believe. Does not a light enclosed in a thick lantern shine out to a distance the moment the lantern is opened? It illuminates even the most remote things, yet does not leave the lantern. When the lantern is closed again, the light is gathered back into the corner without harm to itself; even though it previously filled a vast space, it was poured out without being dissipated. Such is the wondrous power of light. It rests in the narrowest place and fills the widest. It does this because light is, in a sense, incorporeal. The mind does the same, for it is a divine light. 

**Q:** Does this divine mind, in performing these miracles, withdraw from the body in all its parts? 
**A:** There is no need for it to entirely abandon its duty of reconciling opposites. The soul in the body, through its **idol** <note>The *idolon* or "image": the soul's lowest shadow or animating power that stays with the body even when the higher mind is in ecstasy.</note>—like the "hair" of a comet in a vapor—first reconciles the contrary elements into one. Then, if anything is dissolved, it restores it by nourishing; it also increases, rules, moves the body, and so on. We see very clearly that the work of moving and ruling the body is sometimes relaxed or interrupted. When the soul is seized by a more powerful **imagination** <note>Original: *phantasia*.</note>, the duty of increasing and nourishing is diminished because of the intense investigation of reason. This is why philosophers do not digest their food well; and the soul contemplates more sharply in an adult body than in a youth’s, being less occupied with growing the body. A sober body hinders speculation less when the soul is intent only on contemplating. 

Therefore, when such an abstraction of the soul occurs through the mind that even imagination and natural reason are suspended—which usually weaken the nutrition and governance of the limbs—what prevents the body from falling, or prevents it from nourishing nothing in the body? Perhaps only the duty of "reconciliation" will remain, by which the soul does not yet allow the fluids to dissolve and flee. But it will not then...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion of the soul’s highest states. On the previous page, he used the "Chaldean Oracles" (attributed to Zoroaster) to describe how the soul, as a divine fire, can lift even the material body toward the divine. Now, he explains the mechanism of this miracle: how the soul detaches from its lower functions to act through its "divine center," and why such miracles do not disrupt the natural order but fulfill it.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...such a reconciliation occurs through the <term>idolum<note>The *idolum* (from the Greek *eidolon*) is the "image" or "shadow" of the soul. In Ficino’s psychology, it is the lower part of the soul that animates the physical body and manages sensory perception. It acts as a bridge between the immortal mind and the material flesh.</note></term>, which completely abandons the earthly body when the soul tastes nothing of the earth. For then the *idolum* leaves behind the nature of the earth, just as the rational principle of earthly bodies leaves behind their physical images. I believe, therefore, that at that very brief moment when the mind is in an "angelic" state, the body of a man who is completely <term>abstracted<note>To be "abstracted" here means to be mentally and spiritually withdrawn or "pulled away" from material concerns and physical sensations.</note></term> is neither moved, nor sustained, nor even contained by the power of the *idolum* to which it was previously accustomed. 

If it is indeed moved, sustained, or contained, I believe this happens through that **center of the soul**, which we just called the "unity" of the soul granted by God. Through this center, the soul is reconciled to God—the center of all things and pure unity—and through it, the soul reconciles not only the elements of this body, but even the world itself. Zoroaster revealed that God can be reached through this center alone, saying:

->You must perceive the Intelligible with the **flower of the mind**.<-
<note>original Greek: ἐστὶ δ' τι νοητόν, ὅ χρὴ σε νοεῖν νόου ἄνθει. This is another fragment from the *Chaldean Oracles*.</note>

Zoroaster calls the very center of the soul the "flower of the mind," which Plato calls the "head of the mind." This opinion of ours seems to be confirmed by the divine theologian Paul, who said that a soul snatched up to God is neither clearly in the body nor outside the body; <margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin> obviously because it is not in the body through the *idolum*, but is present through its center.

How long does the soul perform these miracles? How long does it remain thus "abstracted"? It remains so only for a short time, for a certain natural affection of the lower power pulls it back to the care of the body, just as a stone thrown upward is said to stay in the air for a moment between its ascent and descent. But does the human soul throw the order of the world into confusion by performing miracles? Not at all. For, to speak in Platonic terms, such miracles are already prescribed in the universal law of things and in the perpetual series of causes that work toward the same end. 

The providence of the "minds" [angels/intelligences] beneath God, which conspire continuously down to our own mind, leads to this very thing. The divine "fate" of the soul-images flowing from the First Soul down to our own soul’s *idolum* contributes to this as well. Furthermore, a certain divine disposition of all "natures"—running from the affection of the First Nature down to the <term>complexion<note>In Renaissance science, the "complexion" is the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) that determines a person's physical and mental health.</note></term> of our own nature—concurs toward this end. Celestial signs often foretell the same to us; through these signs, the thoughts of the divine powers are signified as if through eyes or nods. *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1.</note>

Therefore, when that angelic soul desires to perform some wonderful work—for instance, to summon the winds—the higher causes do not suddenly favor this wish and desire new things simply because the soul has desired them. On the contrary, the soul desires it because the celestial powers have already decreed it. How so? The foresight of future winds rests in the higher divinities. This disposition (as we have said elsewhere) runs down through those three series—Providence, Fate, and Nature—to our souls: specifically through **Providence** into the mind, through **Fate** into the *idolum*, and through **Nature** into the complexion of our body. 

But the disturbed souls of men do not receive these impulses. A peaceful soul, however, receives these heavenly impulses from all sides; hence it begins secretly to think the same things that the higher beings think, and to will or not will the same things, being inclined by a natural—that is, divine and inward—instinct. To such a soul, all thoughts and affections succeed according to its wish, and it receives whatever it asks from the higher powers. Indeed, it asks for what they were already going to give; and because they were going to give it, they provoked the soul to ask. It is like a mother who holds an apple before her son’s eyes so that, being thus invited, the son asks for the apple. The son sees, asks, and receives. He receives, I say, not only because he asks, but he asks because he is destined to receive. The mother does not decide to give because the son wants to receive; rather, it is the other way around. 

Most of the time, we do not walk according to natural or divine desires, but according to those kindled daily by chance. For as different things meet our senses, we are affected in various ways. Occupied with contingent things, we rarely achieve what we desire, because we rarely (and only by luck) coincide with the will of the higher beings. But the angelic soul both agrees with them, because it lives peacefully, and commands the world, because of its own accord it is released from this little body (which is but a tiny particle of the world) and returns to its own most ample nature. 

God foresaw such a soul; a soul acting freely not only by divine help, but by its own will—which acts most freely when, setting aside external actions, it turns toward contemplating and loving itself and its own origin. God also chose such a soul to perform miracles. Avicenna in his *Metaphysics*, and Proclus and Iamblichus in their commentaries on the *Timaeus*, argue that the prayers of such a most holy man are not in vain, even regarding public changes in the world. They prove that the prayers of a most holy man, especially if with him...

He argues that the soul does not "break" natural laws, but rather acts as a conscious participant in a pre-ordained celestial plan.</summary>

ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 14.
305

...where the prayers of the people also join together, they unite souls with God in such a wonderful way that, in a sense, the operation of God and the soul becomes one; yet it is the operation of God as the craftsman, and the soul as the divine instrument. Regarding those miracles that God performs through Himself without an instrument, which are far greater, we are not treating them at present. Are miracles of this kind natural to the soul? They are natural in a certain way, as the Platonists believe, and yet also not natural. They are natural indeed insofar as the soul returns to its proper merit and becomes the <term>handmaid<note>Original: *pedissequus*. This suggests the soul follows closely behind God, acting as an attendant or servant to the divine will.</note></term> and instrument of the supreme God. They are not natural, however, insofar as the soul serves the use of only one body, by the love of which it is captured for a time; in that state, it neither unfolds the full breadth of its power nor becomes a partaker of the divine. But whenever the soul does unfold its power and becomes a partaker, it shows that it will never be dissolved by any blow to the body, since it somehow stands above all things and turns all things according to its will. But let the individual points we have discussed regarding miracles from the mind of the Platonists be affirmed by us only insofar as they are approved by Christian theologians.

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY,
# regarding the Immortality of Souls,

## by the same author, Ficino,

### BOOK 14.

->*Chapter 1. That the soul strives to become God, we show through twelve signs according to the twelve gifts of God.*<-

At the beginning of this dispute, we established two foundations for the signs pertaining to the immortality of the soul. In the first, we treated how much the soul rules over bodies, which we completed through four signs. In the second, we deal with the fact that the soul strives to become God. We shall treat this through twelve signs according to the twelve gifts of God. In this, the wonderful greatness of the mind will appear, for it is not enough for the soul to emulate God in those marvelous ways we have mentioned, unless it also actually becomes God. Hence Zoroaster exclaimed:
> O man, artifice of a most daring nature.
<note>Original Greek: *ὦ τολμηροτάτης φύσεως ἄνθρωπε τέχνασμα*. Ficino quotes from the *Chaldean Oracles*, which he believed were the work of the ancient prophet Zoroaster. The quote emphasizes the human soul's "daring" or "audacious" ability to reach for the divine.</note>

It is agreed among all <term>Theologians<note>Ficino uses "Theologians" to refer to a long tradition of "Ancient Theology" (*Prisca Theologia*) that includes figures like Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, and Plato, as well as Christian thinkers.</note></term> that God is the very first truth and goodness itself. He is the author of the universe. He is above all things. He is in all things. He is eternal. He provides for all. He administers justly. He perseveres strongly in His character while He administers. He handles things temperately and sweetly. He lives most opulently and most joyfully. He beholds, wonders at, and worships Himself as being so blessed.

All theology among all nations attributes these twelve gifts to God. Whatever men do everywhere, they direct toward the possession of these gifts; they seek and strive for nothing else but to acquire such gifts for themselves as fully as possible. God alone is the most complete possessor of these. Therefore, the entire effort of our soul is to become God. Such an effort is no less natural to humans than the effort to fly is to birds. For it is present in all humans, always and everywhere; therefore, it does not follow the accidental quality of any particular man, but follows the very nature of the species. 

Furthermore, a natural movement directed toward a certain end is determined toward that end rather than another for no other reason than a certain disposition of its nature. Through this disposition, it agrees with such an end more than any other; because of this agreement, it loves the end, and through that same agreement, it is able to reach what it loves. Just as air, which by its lightness agrees with the hollow of the sphere of fire, strives and moves toward it because of that very quality. Moreover, it is able to reach it and rest within it once it has reached it. Therefore, the human struggle, when intent upon God, can be fulfilled. For who planted this within our minds, if not that very same God whom we seek? Since He alone is the author of species, He implants the proper appetite within those species. For from the first principle of things—as if from the first good and desirable thing—every natural appetite is derived. That same first...

MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY.
306

...[God] is the first mover. He is also the ultimate end. Indeed, the order of ends follows the order of agents; just as the supreme agent moves the agents that follow it, so the ends of the remaining agents must be referred to the end of the supreme agent. For whatever the first agent itself does, it does for the sake of its own end. Moreover, the first [agent] leads and acts upon all the actions of all subsequent causes, moving them all toward its own action, and therefore toward its own ends. From this it follows that the ends of all lower agents are ordered by the first agent toward its own proper end. The first agent is God. The end of the divine will is His own goodness. For this reason, all subsequent things are necessarily ordered toward God as their end, especially because nothing tends toward anything as an end except insofar as it is good. Thus it happens that the good is the end, precisely because it is good. Therefore, that which is the highest good is, most of all, the end of all things. Add to this that the first good is the cause for all things to be good; therefore, it is the cause for them to be desired. If, however, He is the one for whose sake all things are to be desired, it follows that He Himself is to be desired by all things, and most of all. He is, therefore, the end of all things—yet in such a way that for minds He is the end according to the <term>form<note>In Platonic thought, "form" refers to the true essence or reality of a thing, while "shadow" refers to a faint, imperfect reflection of that reality.</note></term>, but for all other things He is the end according to the shadow. 

Therefore, He exists as the end for man according to the form, since nothing else satisfies [mankind]. Thus men desire the form of God in such a way that this kind of desire was granted by God. Nor is the desire by which we long for God ignited by God any less than the bodily appetite is lured by any object presented to the senses. Indeed, it is ignited all the more, the more the highest good is more powerful in its attraction than the smallest goods. Truly, as I discussed in my book *On Love*, the splendor of the highest good itself shines in individual things; and where it shines more fittingly, there it especially allures the one who sees it, excites the one who considers it, and seizes and occupies the one who approaches it. It compels him to venerate this kind of splendor above all others as if it were a <term>divinity<note>Original: *numen*. A Latin term for a local deity or a divine power presiding over a place or person.</note></term>, and to strive for nothing else than that, having set aside his former nature, he might become that splendor itself. 

This is evident from the fact that a person is not satisfied with the sight or touch of a beloved human being, and often cries out: "This person has something about them, I know not what, that burns me; yet I do not understand what I desire." Here it is clear that the soul is using a divine splendor that shines in a beautiful human being as if in a mirror, and being secretly captured by it, is pulled upward—as if by a hook—so that it might <term>turn out to be God<note>Original: *ut Deus euadat*. This refers to "deification" or *theosis*, the process by which the soul becomes united with God, sharing in the divine nature without losing its identity.</note></term>. 

God would be (if I may say so) an unjust tyrant if He commanded us to attempt things we could never fulfill. Yet He commands that we seek Him, while He inflames human desire for Himself with His own little sparks. He would also be an unskilled and overly reckless archer if He directed our desires—like arrows—toward Himself as a target, yet did not add feathers to the shafts so they might eventually reach the wood [of the target]. Finally, He would be unfortunate if His efforts, by which He pulls us toward Himself, never achieved their end. 

For this reason, our soul can eventually become God, since it naturally strives toward that end with God's encouragement. However, it does not become God unless it puts on the form of God, just as nothing becomes fire unless it receives the form of fire. Therefore, just as the matter of air (which was previously under the moisture and heat of air) casts off its moisture through the power of fire, retains its heat, and—having accepted dryness—is clothed in the form of fire; so the essence of the human soul (which now possesses a mind and lower powers) casts off its lower powers in a certain way as God strips them away. And with the mind—or rather, with the "head" of the mind’s unity being preserved—it puts on the divine substance like a fresh form. Through this, it almost becomes God; through this, it thereafter performs all operations as some kind of God rather than as a soul. 

It is necessary that this can eventually be fulfilled, so that it is not attempted in vain by a seeking human species, or rather, so that it is not attempted recklessly by a drawing God. The soul, enclosed in the dark dwelling-place of this body, never (or hardly ever, and then only for a moment) relaxes all its lower powers. Therefore, that miraculous work is not fulfilled in this body, and is hardly ever tasted by anyone. Truly, natural desires must be fulfilled in many people, and not through a momentary quality, but through a stable habit such as they desire. 

But if the mind is raised higher to contemplate spiritual things, it departs further from bodily things. The supreme limit which the intellect can reach is the very substance of God. It follows that the mind is finally able to enter the divine substance when it has been completely alienated from mortal senses. Therefore, the soul, released from the chains of this body and departing pure, becomes God in a certain certain way. Moreover, God and the eternity of God are the same. Therefore, by a similar reasoning, it becomes eternity, or rather, it becomes eternal. Indeed, the theologian John calls this state "becoming like God." Paul, however, calls it being "transformed into the image of God."

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS. BOOK 14. 307</header>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS. BOOK 14.

#### The fifth sign of immortality, based on the fact that the soul seeks the First Truth and the First Good. Chapter 2.

**I**ndeed, the previous reasoning will make us even more certain of our immortality if, by running through those twelve divine attributes one by one, we show that in seeking these things the soul naturally strives to equal God in some way.

Therefore, our mind conceives a general concept of truth and goodness, through which it seeks universal truth and desires universal good. In universal truth, all true things are contained; in universal good, all good things are included. From this, it follows that the soul naturally seeks all true things and naturally desires all good things. This is evident from the fact that once the truth of a particular thing is known, we do not rest, but seek another, and then another, as long as we believe there is any truth left to be known. The same is observed in the pursuit of good things. However, every truth and every good is God Himself, who is the <term>First Truth<note>In Ficino's philosophy, "First Truth" refers to God as the ultimate source and standard of all reality and knowledge.</note></term> and the First Good. Therefore, we desire God Himself. 

But what do we desire most in Him? To become like Him. For all things, according to the capacity of their nature, tend toward Him as their end, and they desire to become like Him in their own way: bodies lacking life seek Him through mere existence; living things through life; sensing things through sensation; and rational things through the intellect. We cannot be made like God through the intellect, however, except by understanding God; for the intellect becomes like whatever it understands, just as it transforms itself into the images of things when it grasps them. Our end, therefore, is to see God through the intellect, and to enjoy that vision of God through the will, because He is our highest good—the supreme object of our highest power, and the most perfect act regarding that power. Our highest powers are the mind (the "head" of the soul) and the will. The supreme object of these is universal truth and universal, complete good, which is God. 

Nor should any of the <note>original: "Arabum" (the Arabs). Ficino likely refers to Islamic philosophers like Averroes or Avicenna, who sometimes argued that human minds could only reach the "Active Intellect" or an angelic level, rather than God directly.</note>Arabs object that it is enough for us to enjoy the company of some angel. For there is a natural desire within us to always find the cause of every effect, and this inquiry does not cease until the <term>First Cause<note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical term for the original source of all existence—God.</note></term> is reached. Since we desire to see the cause of every effect we recognize, and our intellect recognizes "being" itself as a universal, it follows that we naturally desire to know the cause of "being" itself, which is God. We cannot be said to have reached our ultimate end until our entire natural desire is at rest. Therefore, the ultimate human end consists in the knowledge or possession of God alone, which alone brings an end to natural appetite. 

This is clearly apparent from the fact that the attainment of one's proper end brings the greatest delight. The soul rejoices in the possession of nothing else so vehemently, so purely, and so firmly as it does in even the smallest taste of divine contemplation. For the sake of this taste—if it is ever truly felt—all possessions, the whole world, and life itself are held in contempt. Whoever lives piously with God from time to time cries out that only then has he truly lived, apart from evils, and tasted something of the good, as if he had finally retreated into a safe harbor. This is the point of that passage by <note>original: "Platonis in libro de scientia" (Plato in the book on knowledge), referring to the dialogue *Theaetetus* (176a-b).</note>Plato in his book on knowledge:

> Evils cannot be entirely avoided. For it is necessary that there always be something contrary to the good. Among the gods above, however, it is impossible for evils to exist; rather, they necessarily revolve around mortal nature and this lower place. For this reason, one must flee from here to there as quickly as possible. 

To flee from here to there is nothing other than to make oneself as like to God as possible. And it is justice, holiness, and wisdom that make one like Him. Thus says Plato. He teaches this rightly. For where the Good of all goods flourishes, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. 

Nor should we believe <note>Panaetius was a Stoic philosopher known for his more earth-bound, practical ethics.</note>Panaetius when he says that we may desire divine things but will never reach the summit, because the full possession of the divine and a quiet life belong to angels, not the souls of men. Nature itself teaches us the opposite. Indeed, the elements which seek their natural places out of natural desire are carried more rapidly the closer they get to their destination and boundaries. For this reason, <note>referring to *De Caelo* (On the Heavens).</note>Aristotle shows that natural straight-line motion cannot wander into infinity; otherwise, in its progress, it would not be sometimes slower and sometimes faster. Therefore, something that moves more vehemently toward something later than it did before is not wandering into infinity but is heading toward a certain goal. We experience this in the very desire for knowledge. The more someone understands, the more ardently they burn to know the rest. Therefore, the natural desire for knowing is directed toward a specific, determined end. What is this end? The Cause of all causes, which once found, satisfies all natural...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...finishes every inquiry into causes. Nature gave to dense bodies a desire and inclination by which they might seek lower places; she furthermore provided them with gravity and cold as the means through which they might descend to their desired location. She gave to more subtle bodies an appetite for a higher place, and added lightness and heat as the means to achieve that desired end. She gave to the beasts the appetite for food and sex, and added members prepared for eating and mating. The Guide of Nature <note>Ficino uses "naturae dux" to refer to the Providential power or Creator who directs natural laws.</note> gave to the soul a vow for the universal and whole truth and good; this is indeed more natural than the appetite for food and sex, insofar as it is more continuous. For the body demands to eat only rarely, and to mate even more rarely. But we desire the true and the good at every single moment. Indeed, we are always eager for new things, imaginations, and reasons. We are always opening our eyes to whatever occurs, and we are exceedingly delighted by the longest and widest prospect—indeed, we are satisfied by the immense alone. We always perk up our ears to hear anything, which infants and adults do alike, the learned and the ignorant, and all craftsmen in any art, with nature as their guide.

Add to this that the lust for sex can be tamed, and the voracity of eating can be diminished, but the desire for the true and the good cannot be tamed at all; indeed, while those physical desires decrease with age, these spiritual ones increase. Add further that those bodily things are sought for the sake of something else, but these are sought for their own sake. Therefore, as much as the desire for the true and the good is more natural than the desire for food and sex, so much more has it been provided for by the Guide of Nature that it should thoroughly attain its end. Indeed, it is more natural for this very reason: because it is more ready to acquire its end.

Truly, if the property of each species is necessary and wisely arranged by its author, it follows that the effort of the rational species, which is directed toward the possession of the whole good as its end, should be able to reach what it strives for. For if the attainment of the ultimate end were impossible, then the entire species, as well as the actions pertaining to that species, would be accidental, fortuitous, and vain. The eye sometimes rests in the sight of a graceful appearance; the ear rests in a melody; and each sense is sometimes satisfied and filled by its objects. Nature has gifted the senses with such great happiness. But shall Reason, their queen—who, though inferior to the angels, is yet superior to the beasts—be so unhappy and so neglected by the Architect of Nature that she wanders forever and never rests?

Certainly, she never rests in this life. Nor should we listen here to any of the <term>Arabs<note>Ficino is likely referring to Averroes and his followers, who argued for a single "Universal Intellect" shared by all humanity rather than individual immortal souls.</note></term> imagining that the human intellect, which cannot reach its goal in individuals in this life, might at least achieve it in the whole of humanity. First of all, there is not one intellect in all people, who are utterly at odds with one another (as we shall show elsewhere); secondly, the soul never follows its desired habit even in all men simultaneously. And while it is blind to divine things in individual men, it is blind to them in almost the same way in all men. Finally, it is not permissible to imagine that we can comprehend the very substances of divine forms from natural substances as we wish. For these natural substances decline toward matter, but those divine ones do not. Moreover, the human intellect, as long as it inhabits this body, tends toward knowing physical things in a certain way. Furthermore, natural effects cannot equal or demonstrate the powers and substances of divine causes. Add to this that divine forms are much more distant from natural ones than natural ones are from each other. Therefore, if colors are not known through voices—as is apparent in the blind—much less are divine things ever comprehended through natural things, as <term>Plato</term> writes to <term>Dionysius</term> of <term>Syracuse</term>. <note>Referring to Plato's Second Letter, which discusses the difficulty of expressing the nature of the "King of All."</note> I pass over the fact that the divine substance and power, being infinite, cannot be perceived by us according to our wish until we are absolutely formed by it. This indeed cannot be perfected in a soul joined to a body affected in this way.

But to return to the proposed argument: the capacity and appetite of reason require not just some true or some good things, but all of them in their integrity. It seems she never attains them here because, as <term>Plato</term> says in the <term>Epinomis</term>, <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato (though its authenticity is now debated) which discusses the pursuit of wisdom and the afterlife.</note> the intellect is always ambiguous and the will is always anxious. Therefore, the soul will attain these things when stripped of the body. If it attains the universal good, it will in no way lack immortality, which is as great a good as death is an evil (since death deprives one of all goods). But the mind that will see all true things will enjoy no goods if it suspects it is going to die. Therefore, so that the attainment of the end may be secure and tranquil, it is necessary for the mind to be certain of the eternal possession of its end. <term>Aurelius Augustinus</term> confirms this in the thirteenth book of *On the Trinity*: "All wish to be happy, and therefore they do not wish to perish and be consumed, because they are happy. Nor can they be happy unless they are living. They do not wish to perish, therefore, because they live. Thus, whoever are truly happy, or desire to be so, wish to be immortal. For he does not live happily who does not have what he wants."

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul's unique and relentless desire for universal truth and goodness, unlike temporary physical appetites, proves that it must be destined for an immortal life where these desires can finally be satisfied. He refutes the idea of a collective human intellect and cites Plato and Augustine to assert that true happiness requires the certainty of eternal life.</summary>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIV.</header>

wants. Therefore, a truly happy life can in no way exist unless it is eternal. Thus says he. But lest the followers of Panaetius <note>Panaetius (c. 185–109 BC) was a Stoic philosopher who, unlike many other ancient thinkers, was rumored to have doubted the immortality of the soul.</note> doubt any longer that a truly happy life is suited to man, we shall conclude thus: Since it is characteristic of an intellectual nature to taste every good through knowledge, it is certainly also its characteristic to feed on every good—that is, the whole, perfect good—through its affection. Therefore, happiness <term>Beatitudo: the state of ultimate fulfillment or "blessedness"</term> is proper to an intellectual nature. Indeed, whatever kind of intellect one possesses determines the kind of happiness one can achieve. If one has a true and formal intellect <note>Ficino distinguishes between a "formal" or essential intellect, which grasps the true nature of things, and a "shadowy" one.</note>, one achieves a true and formal happiness. But if one has a shadowy intellect, one achieves a shadowy happiness.

Although the human soul is a certain image of a more divine intellect, it nevertheless possesses the true form of the mind within itself, which is proven by three signs. The first is that it understands many true things according to their true reason. The second is that it understands the true reason of truth itself. The third is that if our soul possessed only a shadow of an intellect, it would never definitively understand the form and substance of the intellect, but would only look upon its accidents <note>In traditional philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties, like color or size, as opposed to the "substance" or essence of a thing.</note> confusedly. Since, therefore, the soul possesses a power of understanding that is not merely shadowy—like that of some more clever beasts—but is truly expressed and formal, it can therefore eventually achieve a truly happy life. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that I propose one intellect is shadowy and another formal. Indeed, the Platonists—as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino’s attempts to harmonize Plato with Christianity.</note> argues—distinguish all types of things in this way, primarily unity and mind, soul and nature.

But let us set these aside for the moment and see by what reasoning Origen, in his books *On First Principles* <note>Origen was a 3rd-century Christian theologian; his "De Principiis" explored the nature of the soul, the cosmos, and God.</note>, confirms the above. When Origen considered that God, the craftsman of all things, took care in each detail not only for necessity and utility (both private and common) but also—and no less so—strove for the beauty of things and the wonder of those watching, he concluded thus: Just as a human craftsman builds things as beautiful as possible so that those looking on might be drawn to consider and admire the genius with which he built them, so God constructed the world as a most artistic work. From this he concludes that the inquiry into the reasons by which all things exist was inserted into the minds of all by the very reason of God the Craftsman, and is moved from there daily. Thus, our mind naturally desires these reasons no less than the eye desires colors and the taste desires food. He adds that we received such a desire from God on the condition that it could eventually be fulfilled, so that it would not have been implanted by God in vain.

Furthermore, whoever indulges this love with the zeal of their will—even if they achieve little truth in this life—is nevertheless prepared by this affection to grasp the fullness of truth in the future. And since such preparation occurs through God, the final formation will also happen through God. For acting causes do not arrange matter for any other reason than to eventually form it once it has been arranged. We briefly confirm Origen’s opinion in this way: namely, that insofar as we consider what the forms of the universe are in their effect, and whether they help or hinder us, we seem to be led by created nature and obey the life of the body, wishing to transform external forms into our own form as utility demands. But when we examine the reasons by which each thing was so created and ordered—an inquiry we naturally pursue—then we are drawn by the very reason of things toward that reason itself; we strive for eternal life and attempt to reform our soul into the all-encompassing form of the Craftsman. Hence the Apostle Paul says: "the inner man is renewed daily, while we contemplate the invisible and eternal things." Likewise, he says: "But we, beholding the glory of the Lord with an unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the spirit of the Lord."

### Sixth sign: because the soul strives to become all things. Chapter III.

**I**t has been shown that our soul, in all its acts, strives to the best of its ability to acquire that first gift of God, that is, the possession of the whole truth and the whole good. But does it seek that second gift? Does it strive to become all things, just as God is all things? It strives in a marvelous way. For it lives the life of a plant, insofar as it indulges in nourishing the body; the life of a brute beast, insofar as it flatters the senses; the life of a man, as it consults reason regarding human affairs; the life of heroes, as it investigates natural things; the life of daemons <note>original: "daemonum". In the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits between humans and gods, possessing higher knowledge of mathematics and the cosmos.</note>, as it speculates on mathematics; the life of angels, as it inquires into divine mysteries; and the life of God, as it works all things through the grace of God. # MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY

This soul experiences all things within itself in a certain way, though some differently than others. And so the human race strives to become all things, since it lives the lives of all things. In admiration of this, Hermes Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus is a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom a series of mystical and philosophical texts, the Hermetica, were attributed; Ficino was their primary translator into Latin.</note> said: "Man is a great miracle, a being to be venerated and adored, who knows the race of demons as if by a natural kinship, and who passes over into God as if he himself were God." Furthermore, whatever things exist are true to the extent that they exist. To the degree that they have been allotted a certain power, order, and use, they are also good. We have shown above that the mind seeks all true things and all good things. Therefore, it seeks all things. But what else does it seek, except to know all things through the intellect and to enjoy all things through the will? In both ways, however, it attempts to become all things. Just as a sense—for example, sight—does not perceive colors unless it puts on the forms of the colors and becomes one with them (arising from the power of seeing and the act of the visible form, just as one thing is made from air and light), so too the intellect does not know things themselves unless it is clothed in the forms of the things to be known. It must become one thing from the power of understanding and the act of the <term>intelligible form</term> <note>original: "formæ intelligibilis"; the mental concept or "blueprint" of an object that the mind grasps.</note>, a union accompanied by a single action. For there is one operation of understanding for both. Likewise, who would deny that from corporal matter and the form assigned to it, one thing is made, since one act and one motion proceed from that composite? 

But it is much more necessary (as pleases the Platonists and Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Almohad-era Muslim philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle; Ficino often engages with his theories on the intellect.</note>) that a single something be made from the power and the form of the thing to be understood. This is partly because a more stable composition often results from these (for they often remain together longer than corporal matter and its form), and partly because the intellect itself is a kind of form—a form, I say, gaping open toward a further form, much like matter. Therefore, it is more compatible with the form it is to receive than corporal matter is with its own form. For all forms descend from the supernal mind into the matters of the world; for this reason, they are much more compatible with our mind than with matter. Finally, just as the mind is more excellent than matter, so much more effectively does it adopt and unite to itself the form it desires. Nor should it be believed that the soul unites the things it grasps to itself any less than the body does. For the body turns food—even very diverse kinds—into its own substance through the soul’s "cooking" <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of digestion ("concoquente") to describe how the soul processes sensory information into intellectual knowledge.</note>. So also the mind turns what it receives—or rather, conceives—into itself, and much more so. Since the dimensions of bodies hinder mutual union in physical things, spiritual things are much better suited for union. Thus, the reasons <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the essential principles or definitions of things.</note> of understood things pass into the substance of the intellect more than food passes into the substance of the body, as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated and commented upon extensively.</note> maintains. 

Through these points, it is clear that from our mind and the form of the thing to be understood, a single thing is made. However, that which so takes on the form of another as to yield a single thing from itself, nearly turns into the very thing whose form it took. Who does not know that when the matter of air receives the form of fire, it becomes fire or becomes fiery? Therefore, the intellect becomes almost that very thing which it understands. It becomes, I say, that thing in act. For it was already the same thing in power, and in a certain way in habit, even before it understood, as Plotinus thinks. Surely the intellect understands a circle then, when it becomes, in act, the "reason" of the circle. Indeed, this becoming in act is itself the act of understanding. The intellect was already that same reason of the circle even before, both according to its power (regarding the substantial Idea of the circle itself) and according to habit (regarding the formula of the Idea familiar to us). Moreover, the truth of individual things consists in the very reason of their form. And so the mind becomes any true thing whenever it understands things themselves by converting itself into their perpetual reasons. But more on this elsewhere. 

It is enough for us at present that, since the intellect seeks to understand all things and is thoroughly clothed in their forms by understanding them, it follows that it seeks to become all things. Hence, it strives to become God (in whom all things exist) while it strives to become all things. Enough regarding the intellect. Our will desires the same thing, because it always affects to enjoy all good things. By enjoying things, it unites itself to the things it enjoys. But there is a difference between the intellect and the will. For both indeed become all things—the intellect all true things, the will all good things—but the intellect is united to things by transferring them into itself, whereas the will, conversely, is united by transferring itself into the things. In what way? Surely our intellect understands things in its own manner rather than according to the nature of the things themselves. Indeed, the forms of bodies, which are particular, immense in matter, divided, confused, imperfect, and mobile, it understands in a certain universal, absolute, simple, distinct, pure, and stable way. Conversely, it comprehends God and the angels, who are stable and simple, through a discourse that is for the most part mobile and manifold. Thus our intellect perceives those things that are below it, as well as those above it, in its own manner. For which reason it is said to transfer all things into its own nature. From this, that saying of Plato's also seems to be confirmed: that the mind understands through innate forms, since...

...after it understands according to the manner of its own nature. The **Will**, however, at first does not remain within itself like the intellect, but moves the soul and body to action so that they may approach the desired things. Furthermore, the Will does not desire things in that specific, internal way that they exist within the soul, but rather as they exist in themselves. To the intellect wishing to know gold, the universal and incorporeal "idea" of gold is sufficient; but to the Will, this is not enough. For as far as human life is concerned, the Will desires that particular and physical gold, just as it is in itself.

Let us conclude, then, that our soul flies toward God by means of the intellect and the will—as if by those twin **Platonic wings** <note>In his dialogue *Phaedrus*, Plato uses the metaphor of wings to describe how the soul can rise above the material world to contemplate divine truths.</note>—precisely because it flies toward all things through them. Through the first [the intellect], it applies all things to itself; through the second [the will], it applies itself to all things. Thus the soul desires, strives, and begins to "become God," making progress every day. Now, every motion directed toward a specific end begins first, then proceeds, intensifies gradually, and advances; surely, at some point, it is perfected. For it is intensified by the same faculty with which it began. It later advances by that same faculty by which it was intensified. Finally, it is perfected by that same faculty by which it advanced. For this reason, our mind will eventually be able to become all things in a certain way, and emerge as a kind of God.

### Chapter IV.

**O**ther attributes of God follow: the third is that He is the author of the universe; the fourth is that He is above all things. Our mind chases after these as well. We have said elsewhere how the soul emulates all the works of God through various arts, and thus, in the likeness of God, it produces all things. We have also said that man always contends to dominate himself and all others—both men and beasts alike. He is impatient with any kind of servitude. Even if he is forced to serve, he hates his Master, as he serves against his own nature.

He strives to overcome stubbornly in any matter, and he is ashamed to be surpassed even in the smallest things or the lightest games, as if being defeated were against the natural dignity of man. Indeed, the feelings of shame and modesty, which are unique to the human race, signify that some "majesty" <note>original: "nescio quid angustum" - literally "I know not what narrow thing," but in Ficino's context, it refers to the soul feeling "cramped" by its mortal limitations compared to its divine potential.</note> lies hidden within us which it would be a sin to violate and which is most worthy of veneration. Concerning this, I have written elsewhere. 

But as far as the desire for victory is concerned, one can clearly see the immense magnificence of our soul from this: that the empire of this world would not be enough for it, if, after subduing it, the soul learned there was another world remaining which it had not yet conquered. Hence, when **Alexander the Great** heard the philosopher **Anaxarchus** <note>Anaxarchus (c. 340 BC) was a philosopher of the school of Democritus who accompanied Alexander on his campaigns and taught that there were infinite worlds.</note> arguing that there were innumerable worlds, he exclaimed: "Woe is me, for I have not yet gained possession of even one!" Thus, man wants no superior and no equal, nor does he suffer anything to remain excluded from his empire. This status belongs to God alone. Therefore, man seeks a divine status.

We can clearly conjecture this from the fact that many philosophers and princes have sought divine honors for themselves. It was not enough for them to be considered good men, unless they were also considered divine. Indeed, they wished to be worshiped as gods. While countless men have attempted this, it is said that among philosophers, **Empedocles** <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC) was a Greek philosopher who famously claimed to be an immortal god in his writings.</note> especially desired it, and among princes, Alexander of Macedon. In short, all people desire the same thing; and if they hoped to succeed, they would attempt it, as if claiming divinity by their own right.

**G**od, moreover, is everywhere and always. Man, too, desires to be everywhere. For he uses the four elements, as we have said. He measures the earth and the sky, and searches through the deep hiding places of **Tartarus** <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment; here used to mean the deepest parts of the earth.</note>. To him, the sky does not seem too high—to use the words of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii"; Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage whom he identified with the Egyptian god Thoth and the Roman Mercury.</note>—nor the center of the earth too deep. Intervals of time or place do not stop him from running through all things, whatever they are and in whatever times or places they exist. No wall blunts or beats back his vision. No boundaries are enough for him. He strives to rule everywhere, and to be praised everywhere. And so he strives to be as God is: everywhere. 

He also strives to be "always," just like God. He seeks this in two ways. First, he strives to remain in the mouths of men through all future time, and he grieves that he could not have been present in all...
