[...to be] celebrated in past centuries, nor could it be honored in the future by all—not only by nations of men, but by types of brute animals. Everyone, both the young and the adult, the simple and the learned, strives for this with all their might and zeal; and they affect this more ardently the more they excel in talent. Now, what all men seek—and especially the more excellent ones—is desired by them by **natural law** as a "good." Therefore, it is not sought in vain, since there is no recklessness in the law of nature. It would be sought recklessly and in vain as a good if it were to be of no benefit to those seeking it. But praise that is not felt is of no benefit. For this reason, the human species **prophesies** <note>Ficino uses the term *vaticinatur* (prophesies/divines) to suggest a natural, instinctive premonition or "gut feeling" implanted by nature about the soul's survival.</note> that it will not lack sensation in future ages, since it often even despises its present life so that it may be celebrated by posterity. It also has the greatest care for its descendants throughout life, and especially at the end of life, believing that future centuries pertain to itself. We do not see these things done by beasts, as if their nature "prophesies" that there is nothing in them that is either worthy of veneration or endowed with eternal sensation. Indeed, a natural prophecy—especially of the most excellent minds—cannot go astray, just as **Plato** writes in his letter to Dionysius. <note>original: "Plato in epistola scribit ad Dionysium." Reference to Plato's *Second Letter*, where he discusses the soul's concern for the future and its reputation.</note> From this, he wishes it to be concluded that a sensation of human affairs survives for the souls of men, which he also confirmed in the *Laws* <note>Plato’s final dialogue, *The Laws*, where he discusses the soul’s immortality and divine providence.</note> as being from the order of **divine providence**.

The second mode by which our soul wishes to exist always—and indeed to live (since for the soul, to exist is the same as to live)—appears as follows. The human soul, and indeed every soul, contemplates a certain eternal life; as soon as it has contemplated it, it strives for it and always desires to exist. Entirely, the **appetite for being** <term>appetitus essendi: the intrinsic, natural drive toward existence found in all things</term> is natural, because it is present in all things as soon as they are born, and it is continuous. It does not come about by deliberation, because it is present in things at the very trace of their birth. Nor does it happen by chance, because it is in all things and is continuous. Assuredly, the elements, through the power of their natural qualities, resist things that attempt their corruption, lest their "being" be taken from them. Again, they most greedily seek places suitable for themselves and repel those things standing in the way of their motion, so that they may preserve their being. This appetite for being is called "natural" for this reason: because it follows the natural qualities of things. Plants also, by the instinct of their vital constitution, suck up more healthful moisture, extending their roots very far toward it so that they may preserve their being. Likewise, they turn away their small branches from shadows and entwine their supports with certain hooked twigs so that they do not lose their being. We call this appetite "natural" because it follows the natural constitution of life. Brutes, through natural desire, adopt those things which preserve their being, and through natural anger, they repel things that would destroy them.

Therefore, in these things, the appetite for being is similarly natural, because it does not follow deliberation or chance, but natural and innate powers. However, since the natures of these things do not have any power through which they might provide eternal being to their own proper subject and body, none of them desire to exist always in their own proper substance—for they would strive in vain—but they nevertheless desire, according to nature, to be eternal in their **species**, for which their natural powers sufficiently serve. Hence, they generate things similar to themselves in species, through which propagation that species of things remains perpetual in the world. Indeed, this appetite lacks cognition not only in elements and plants, but even in brutes. Truly, the power of generating, which serves this end, has no cognition at all. But if there are any bodies whose principles are sufficient to exist in their own proper substance, those things desire according to nature to be eternal—not only in species, but also in their own substance—such as, perhaps, the bodies of the **stars**. <note>Ficino, following ancient cosmology, believed the stars were composed of a "fifth element" or quintessence that made them naturally incorruptible and eternal in their physical form.</note> Let us return to our own affairs. Our soul desires to exist. But is this kind of appetite natural? Without a doubt, it is no less natural to our soul than the appetite for being is to other things. But it desires to exist *always*. Is this desire for being "always" just as natural as the desire for "being"? It clearly is. And let no **Epicurean** <note>Followers of Epicurus, who argued that the soul was composed of atoms and dissolved at death.</note> object to us that, although the soul naturally desires "being" itself (since even if it did not know it, it would desire it), it nevertheless longs for "eternal being" contrary to nature, perhaps because it first knew that eternity and afterwards desired it. For that knowledge does not prevent the greed for eternity from being natural. For our senses also know foods, which they nevertheless desire according to nature. After they have seen them, the wolf desires the lamb and the dog desires the hare; yet they desire them naturally, because from their natural constitution they are immediately so compelled to desire that they cannot *not* desire. And just as it is natural for the eyes to perceive such objects, so it is natural for the power of desiring to immediately strive for such things once inspected. By the same reasoning, it is natural for the intellect to know clear objects, and for the will to want those things which have been judged good. Whatever is clearly offered, the intellect naturally recognizes. Whatever...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book XIII. Following the previous discussion on how the soul’s desire for fame and posterity acts as a "prophecy" of its own survival, Ficino now delves into the metaphysical mechanics of the will and intellect. He argues that the universal human desire for eternal existence is not a random whim, but a "natural appetite" implanted by God, proving that immortality is the soul's natural end.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIII. #

Whatever is offered under the aspect of "the good," the will desires naturally. Therefore, it is natural for the intellect to know eternal being, and it is natural for the will to seek that known being as a good. Just as the irrational appetite <note>The basic instincts found in animals.</note> follows the senses, so the will—which is a rational desire—follows the intellect. Therefore, if the craving for food is natural because it is sudden and not born of deliberation, then the will for immortality is likewise natural, because it is a sudden act following the pure nature of the intellect and the will. For as soon as "eternal being" is offered to the mind, it is judged as something to be desired without discursive reasoning <note>Step-by-step logical deduction.</note>, and the appetite follows without any preceding deliberation. 

If this were pursued by chance or by careful deliberation, then not everyone, nor always the same people, nor all equally would seek it; instead, this desire would vary according to the variety of circumstances and the people deliberating. But as it stands, all people—both necessarily and suddenly—claim this for themselves by the impulse of nature, just as we necessarily want the "good" itself, whereas we do not necessarily or by nature want this or that specific thing. Thus, we do not naturally desire to be "of such a kind" or "here or there," but we desire absolute being itself, in which no deprivation of being is mixed, as nature draws us toward it. 

And just as we always dread the everlasting deprivation of life by the impulse of nature, so we love everlasting life as nature draws us. Moreover, the Architect of Nature <note>God, often referred to by Ficino as the *artifex* or craftsman.</note> tempered knowledge with essence, appetite with knowledge, and the attainment of the goal with appetite. Therefore, just as a beast knows only temporal being according to the capacity of its nature, and seeks temporal being according to its nature, so our soul, by the magnificence of its own nature, knows eternal being and naturally desires it. 

For being itself is desirable according to nature, and indeed desirable in the same way that it is naturally knowable. Thus, just as being is known by the nature of a beast only as something temporal and present, so it is desired by it in a limited way according to its nature. But by human nature, just as being itself is known as something perpetual, so it is naturally sought as something perpetual, so that what is known through its own intellectual nature alone is naturally desired through that same nature. Indeed, we shall attain what we desire through that same nature. For it is reasonable that we reach the goal in attainment through the same faculty by which we reach it in knowing and willing, so that the end of the motion is natural to the same thing to which the motion itself is natural. 

Therefore, for one who reaches eternal life through knowledge and will, I do not see why they should not reach it through life itself; since the power of that life surpasses temporal things, both the intellect and the will—which depend on it—carry themselves beyond temporary things toward the eternal. Furthermore, since a natural desire is not in vain, it follows that the human soul attains the perpetual being it naturally longs for. Perpetual being, I say, not only in its species <note>original: "in specie"; referring to the survival of the human race through children.</note>, but in its own proper substance, for it desires this. Rightly, because bodily things are born through propagation, they seek perpetual being through propagation; but the mind seeks the perpetual being of its own substance, because the mind also subsists in itself and is made by God; it does not lie within some subject of generation, nor is it produced by succession <note>The mind is created directly by God, not passed down like physical traits.</note>. 

But who naturally desires impossible things? For who naturally desires either to fly or to cross rivers with dry feet? To be sure, some vain boy, stirred by some sensory event, might occasionally wish for the power of such miracles; but not even boys do so often, and men never think of or desire such things. But we all desire eternal life, and we desire it always, even when we do not notice that we are desiring it. Therefore, the longing for it is not impossible. 

I think this should be noted most carefully: that life is more natural than knowledge, since life is prior, more interior, more continuous, and more substantial than knowledge. Therefore, the desire for true life is more natural than the desire for true knowledge. True knowledge is that which is so free of its opposite—that is, ignorance—that it neither has ignorance mixed in through deception, nor can ever fall into it through forgetfulness. True life is also that which is neither mixed with any death-dealing quality in its action, nor liable to death according to any inclination. 

Since, therefore, the desire for true (that is, eternal) life is much more natural than the desire for true knowledge, it follows that the attainment of eternal life is far more natural and possible than the attainment of true knowledge. On the contrary, since life is much more in harmony with eternal life than are intellect and will, if we attain eternal life through understanding and willing, surely we attain it much more through living. Indeed, if eternal life communicates itself to the later acts of the soul—namely, the intellect and will—certainly it must have communicated itself first to life itself, which is the prior act. Otherwise, the Author of Nature would not so vehemently [impel] us...

<summary>Ficino argues that the universal human desire for immortality is a "natural appetite" implanted by God, and since nature does nothing in vain, this desire proves the soul must be immortal in its own substance, not just through its offspring.</summary>

He uses a quote from Zoroaster to support the idea that everything proceeding from the divine "fatherly" source must be perfect and capable of reaching its goal, setting the stage for Chapter VI's discussion on the soul's drive to emulate divine virtues.</meta>

...daily hurries the soul toward a longing for this thing, just as it does not hurry it toward any other impossible things. For the divine Zoroaster <note>Ficino often cites Zoroaster, whom he considered a "pious philosopher" and a precursor to Plato, as the author of the Chaldaean Oracles.</note> said:
> For nothing incomplete runs out from the fatherly source, <note>original Greek: ὀυ γὰρ ἀπὸ πατρικῆς ἀρχῆς ἀτελὲς τι τροχάζει</note>
that is, nothing proceeds or rolls out imperfectly from the fatherly principle.

->*Signs 11, 12, 13, and 14: That we desire to attain the four virtues of God. Chapter VI.*<-

**T**here are four other gifts of God pertaining to the four virtues. For we call Him provident, just, courageous, and temperate. Who would deny that God surveys all things? That He governs through rightful and natural orders? That He remains immobile in His own state while He performs these deeds, and never grows weary? That He is tranquil, handling each thing sweetly and with moderation? Behold the human soul, which emulates this divine <term>prudence</term><note>The virtue of wisdom and foresight.</note>. How curiously it recalls the past—not only its own private affairs, but all public and worldly matters? How intensely it inquires into the present, even into things belonging to others and far away? How eagerly it gasps for the future? How diligently it anticipates future ages? What heavier insult can a man hear than to be called ignorant or improvident? Hence it happens that no one willingly confesses to ignorance of any matter or art; for, as nature shows, man judges that ignorance of anything is not proper to him, but rather that a mastery of almost all things belongs to him, just as it does to God.

Our mind also hunts after divine justice. Under how many laws does it subject its own body? How does it govern a family? How does it regulate a city? How does it manage even kingdoms? With how many punishments does it rage against sinners? How many good men does it affect with rewards? How heavily does it feel indignation toward the most wicked? How ardently are the most upright men separated from the evil? Finally, with what great order—almost celestial—is human society arranged? In every form of government, society is directed toward one elder and wiser leader, just as the whole world is directed toward the one God. Indeed, even thieves divide their plunder justly among themselves. And wicked men, if they inflict any injury, think they are inflicting it justly—either by avenging injuries received, or by removing harmful men from their midst, or by stealing what they themselves need while others have plenty—and they wish to appear as if they are perpetrating every act most justly. In all these things, it is clear that the human race wishes to claim for itself a justice no less than that which God Himself possesses.

We also strive to attain the <term>fortitude</term><note>In this context, courage combined with spiritual stability or "immovability."</note> of God. Truly, the fortitude of God is an immobile state. The wisest men acquire this state for themselves as best they can, because they resolve to live content with the goods of the soul, and to make nothing of the comforts or discomforts of the body and of fortune, as if such things do not pertain to them (who are the souls themselves). Those who neglect these shifting things remain immobile in soul. The less wise, however, desire the same stability of life but approach it by another path, thinking the matter will succeed more easily for them that way. What then? They fight and subjugate to their power all those who might seem able at some time to drive them from their seat and dignity.

Furthermore, who would not desire divine <term>temperance</term><note>Self-control and the moderation of passions.</note>? The wise study to moderate the movements of the soul so that they do not clash in any way; the unwise study to arrange their bodies and their affairs so that their souls are not disturbed. Both seek an unbroken harmony of their own minds. To the wise man, this succeeds eventually; to the unwise man, not at all. Finally, just as with all other things, the highest "reasons" or archetypes of these four virtues are in God, so much so that God is the highest Prudence, the highest Justice, and the highest of the rest. Men who are studious of these virtues seek the highest reason of them, wishing to lack nothing that pertains to their perfection. All men desire this, though some set out on different paths. All, therefore, seek God. But those seek God by the straightest path who first, through <term>civic virtues</term><note>The practical virtues used in social and political life.</note>, prune away the secondary passions of the soul; then, through <term>purifying virtues</term><note>virtutes purgatoriæ: virtues that cleanse the soul of worldly attachments.</note>, uproot them; thirdly, through the virtues of a soul already purified, they further moderate the primary passions. Once these are tempered, they are finally formed by the <term>exemplary virtues</term><note>virtutes exemplaribus: the perfect patterns of virtue as they exist in the mind of God.</note> which are in God. We can undoubtedly be formed by these exemplary virtues eventually. For preparation or disposition looks toward a form and a habit, and a specific disposition looks toward a specific habit. Therefore, the cause which [draws] a certain subject more and more by degrees...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human drive to master the four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—is evidence of the soul's innate desire to emulate God and achieve a divine state. He outlines a hierarchical path of virtue, from social conduct to spiritual purification, leading toward union with the divine archetypes.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Chapter VI, which discusses how God prepares the soul for divine virtues, and begins Chapter VII, which argues that the human soul's insatiable desire for wealth and pleasure is a sign of its orientation toward a divine state of being.</meta>

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XIV.</header>

...and prepares it more; for this reason He prepares it, so that He may introduce the substantial and primary form. Thus, just as that subject, according to the common order of nature, participates in that preparation, so also can it be made capable of the primary form. God, who is the <term>exemplary power</term><note>In Platonic thought, "exemplary" refers to the perfect "Forms" or "Ideas" in the mind of God that serve as models for everything in the physical world.</note> itself, influences the species of the human soul from the beginning with certain seeds and incitements of the virtues. Through these human virtues—namely, the <term>civil and purgatorial virtues</term><note>Ficino follows the Neoplatonic hierarchy of virtues: 'civil' virtues manage social life, while 'purgatorial' virtues cleanse the soul of earthly attachments to prepare it for the divine.</note>—purified souls are properly prepared for the exemplary and divine virtues. We infer that these three types of human virtues are preparations for the divine from the fact that they are brought into us and awakened by the divine; because their images are so clear that the divine virtues may be recognized through them; because they approach the divine more and more by degrees; and because they affect us in such a way that we do not rest in these human virtues, but are drawn toward the divine ones. Therefore, God must at some time form the species of the soul with the immortal habit of divine virtue, and the species of the soul is capable of being so formed.

### The fifteenth sign: that the soul seeks the highest wealth and pleasure. Chapter VII.

**W**e have established that the life of God is most wealthy and most pleasant. For He alone is the highest wealth and the highest pleasure, who is the source of all goods and in need of nothing. If, therefore, all men seek the highest wealth and the highest pleasure, they seek to become gods. A certain possession of some things or a specific kind of pleasure is not enough for a human being, as it is for other living creatures; rather, a person thinks he has achieved very little in these things as long as even the smallest thing remains to be acquired. For this reason, wise men, judging that the wealth and joy of God truly consist in the treasures of the intellect and of honesty alone, desire these things only, but to the highest degree. Unwise men, however, imagining that the divine majesty overflows additionally with bodily goods, desire bodily things as well, and to the highest degree. 

It is clear, moreover, that they do not seek such things merely for the sake of necessity or bodily convenience. Truly, even if they judge that they have as much as suffices for living, and as much as is needed to live pleasantly and abundantly, they still do not cease to accumulate treasures and to diligently seek out the most exquisite delights, as Midas, Sardanapalus, and Xerxes demonstrated. <note>Ficino uses these three historical/mythological figures as archetypes of excess: Midas for his legendary greed, Sardanapalus (a legendary Assyrian king) for his extreme decadence, and Xerxes (the Persian king) for his immense ambition and luxury.</note> The first accumulated treasures to an immense degree; the others offered the highest rewards to those who could discover new delights daily. These men do not serve the body; rather, they harm it, and they are not ignorant of the bodily damage they cause. They do not comply with the body, but, envious of divine happiness, they strive to prepare for themselves an immense abundance of that same state, both in the use of things and of pleasures. To achieve this, they destroy their own bodies, afflict their minds, and disturb their lives. 

Finally, neither the wise (though they come closer) nor the unwise in this life attain those vast treasures which they desire; therefore, they never rest here. Yet any thing whatsoever rests in its own place and natural state. How vigorously the elements seek their own places! How firmly they cling to them! A plant eagerly adopts the soil and site that are suitable and congruent for itself; how stably it remains there with all its strength! Likewise for the beasts. For the cattle and flocks seek the heart of the earth and the face of the ground, the fish seek the water, and they seek them most greedily, and linger in these places most willingly. Finally, all these things (to speak briefly) rest when they have obtained their natural place and state. 

Our body also indicates this: when it is in good health, well-fed, and reclines softly according to its wish, then neither its temperament nor its accompanying senses—indeed, the very beast within us—asks for anything further. But meanwhile, either the intellectual reason studiously inquires into the causes of things and anxiously consults about things to be done, or the <term>thinking reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio cogitatrix*. Ficino distinguishes between the higher intellect that grasps eternal truths and the 'thinking' or 'discursive' reason that deals with practical plans and sensory imagination.</note> fashions and demands new pleasures. It is stimulated by regret and made restless by suspicion. Anxiety of this kind is unique to the human being himself. Indeed, it arises from the powers of the soul proper to man, not from the powers of the bodily elements, nor from the powers of the beast, which have enough in us, as we have said. 

Wherefore man alone, in this present state of living, never rests; he alone is not content with this place. Therefore, man alone travels as a pilgrim in these regions, and cannot rest during the journey itself while he aspires to the celestial homeland which we all seek, although we set out by different paths on account of the variety of opinion and counsel. If, therefore, those things which are inferior to us rest once they have attained their natural state and their native seat, it is also necessary for us (as we have said elsewhere) to be able to attain these things at some time and to find rest. In [the present] life...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul’s perpetual restlessness and desire for infinite wealth and pleasure prove that its true home is not on earth, but in a divine, celestial state. Unlike animals that rest when their physical needs are met, the human intellect continues to strive, indicating that man is a "pilgrim" searching for God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the fifteenth sign of the soul's immortality: its insatiable desire for the highest good, which cannot be satisfied by earthly pleasures or temporary gains.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

is not given in the present life. For we rightly desire, as if it were our natural habit and our goal, that good which possesses three principal conditions: namely, that it be **pure**, **complete**, and **stable**. In this life, however, the possession of the good is neither **pure**—since a certain natural affection of the soul toward the body, and the very first movements of the senses themselves, distract and disturb the minds of even the most excellent men—nor is it **complete**. For it is necessary that everything in which there is naturally a power and an urge toward certain acts must eventually reach those very acts if it is ever to find rest. Since, therefore, there is in the human intellect a natural capacity and a striving to perceive and possess the **forms** <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, "forms" are the essential blueprints or spiritual realities of all things.</note> of all things, it will only then have attained its natural end when it has acquired them all. But because in this life it never acquires such a state, it never possesses a complete good here; nor is it **stable**, since our good consists in action that is unimpeded, secure, and continuous.

Every action of men living on earth, however, suffers some impediment, danger, and interruption. What of the fact that those things which require a longer time for growth usually endure longer once they are mature? Yet man strives strenuously until extreme old age to acquire the state of happiness, which he finally perceives only in part, and possesses in this life for the shortest possible time.

Therefore, so that the state which has been partially acquired may one day be fulfilled, and that which grew over a very long time may endure for a very long time, it is necessary that the soul outlast the body. Because the soul here "follows a fleeing Italy" <note>original: *Italiam sequitur fugientem* — a literary reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*, where Italy represents a promised land that seems to recede as one approaches it.</note> and does not reach its paternal harbor, it is continuously anxious and mournful. Furthermore, and this is wonderful, as often as we are at leisure, we fall into sorrow like exiles, even if we do not know the cause of our sorrow, or certainly do not think of it. From this it happens that man cannot live alone. For we think that through the society of other men, and moreover through a multiple variety of delights, we can expel this hidden and perpetual sadness. But alas, we are too much deceived.

Indeed, in the midst of the games of pleasure we sometimes sigh, and when the games are over, we depart more sorrowful. The same thing happens to us as to those who, with an empty stomach, eat in their dreams while sleeping; they are not filled, because the stomach did not desire the image of food, but the food itself.

We also offer to the mind—which thirsts for **nectar**, that is, the joy of the fatherly vision—the lethal waters of the **River Lethe** <note>In Greek mythology, the Lethe is the river of forgetfulness. Ficino uses it to represent earthly distractions that make the soul forget its divine origin.</note> while we employ the shadowy games of bodily pleasures. These are false pleasures, not only because they are very brief and full of anxiety, but because they are mixed with pain. For a desire that lacks its object is a kind of pain. Moreover, the pleasures of the body are perceived only as long as the want and the desire remain. Rightly, therefore, earthly delights do not fill the soul, but merely tickle it. For the soul affects true things and true joys, but bodily things are shadows of things, and their allurements are shadows of joy. For this reason, if neither the drinking of any temporal thing nor of all temporal things combined extinguishes the thirst of the mind, it does not thirst for temporal liquor, but for the eternal. And if a thirst kindled by the heavenly Sun must one day be filled, and is never satisfied by the River Lethe, it will one day be satisfied by an eternal draught of nectar.

But it is helpful again to confirm what has been said with these mysteries of the **ancient theologians** <note>Ficino refers to the *Prisca Theologia*, a lineage of ancient wisdom he believed included figures like Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, and Plato.</note> which I shall relate. For they affirm that souls in bodies are slumbering, and that whatever we seem to do or experience here is nothing other than dreams. They say that the thoughts of souls separated [from the body] differ far more from the thoughts of those joined to it than the thoughts of those awake differ from the dreams of those sleeping; and similarly, pleasures differ from pleasures. This is proved in this way: we experience in ourselves not only daily, but almost at every hour, that as often as a tiny bit of vapor—somewhat thicker and more humid, exhaling from the lower parts of the body—seeks the head itself and fills the passages of the brain, we are immediately weighed down by sleep and soon deluded by dreams and images. We also experience sometimes that if some vapor of "black bile," which the Greeks call <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: *melancholiam* — in medieval medicine, one of the four humors, associated here with profound depression or madness.</note>, has besieged and captured the citadel of the body, then immediately our queen—namely, reason itself—is, so to speak, cast down, and men are seized by manifest insanity. If a tiny smoke has such great power in us, if such a slight movement changes us so much, how much more must it be judged that the celestial and immortal soul—when it falls from that purity in which it was created at the beginning, that is, when it is shut in the dark prison of the earthy and dying body—is then (as the Platonists say) changed from its true state? For it is then [afflicted] not only by the smoke of one accustomed humor, but by all of them equally...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's persistent restlessness and dissatisfaction with earthly pleasures prove it is meant for an eternal, divine existence. He likens our earthly life to a dream or a state of exile, where physical pleasures are merely "shadows" that cannot satisfy the soul's thirst for divine truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the soul’s entrapment in the physical body and introduces the sixteenth sign of its immortality: the human capacity for self-veneration and the worship of God.</meta>

...and weighted down by the new vapors of all the humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note>, and thus burdened by an unaccustomed mass of fluids and limbs; furthermore, it is submerged in that formless matter, which is most different from the most beautiful form of the mind, as if in the River Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; here, Ficino uses it to describe how the soul "forgets" its divine origin upon entering the body.</note>. For this reason, the Pythagoreans and Platonists believe that during the entire time the sublime soul dwells in the lowest body, our mind is tossed here and there, up and down, like a sick person in a state of perpetual restlessness; it is always drowsy and delirious, and the individual movements, actions, and passions of mortals are nothing other than the dizziness of the sick, the dreams of the sleeping, and the delusions of the insane. Thus Euripides did not err when he called this life the **dream of a shadow** <note>original: "umbrae somnium"</note>. Therefore, since all are deceived, those tend to be less deceived who, meanwhile—just as sometimes happens in sleep—suspect and say to themselves: "Perhaps the things that now appear to us are not true; perhaps at present we are dreaming." Whoever is so disposed among the dreamers is certainly like Tiresias, of whom Homer says that in the underworld: "He alone is wise, while all others flit about like shadows" <note>Referring to the blind prophet Tiresias in the *Odyssey*, who retained his intellect even in death.</note>—or rather, they *are* shadows flitting about.

### Sixteenth sign, that we worship ourselves and God. Chapter VIII.

**I**t remains for us to speak of that twelfth attribute of God, through which He loves and worships Himself, which humans claim for themselves in two ways. First, because everyone not only loves and protects themselves—as all other creatures do—but they also greatly worship themselves and venerate themselves as if they were certain deities. The wise do this insofar as they subject external and bodily things to the mind as their ruler. They depend entirely on the mind as if on God. They also establish the August majesty of their own mind as something divine, considering it a sin to defile it with base thoughts and earthly filth. Indeed, this natural notion has bred shame and modesty in the human race, so that we revere not only the presence of other men as if they were divine, but also the conscience of our own mind (as Pythagoras commanded) as if it were the face of God. It constantly goads us with repentance for evil deeds, even if we do not fear punishment. Conversely, the memory of good deeds brings delight, as if the celestial soul always shrinks from the earthly stains of vice. The unwise do the same in a certain way, though they are surpassed by the wise in bringing this work to completion. Again, the most foolish men act similarly but differently, insofar as they are overly pleased with themselves, persist most stubbornly in their own opinion, and hold fast to their judgment as if it were a divine decree. Finally, all men honor the most excellent souls—those who have served the human race best in this life—as divine, and they adore them once they are released from their bodies as certain gods most dear to the Highest God, whom the ancients called **Heroes**. Such great reverence for oneself and one's kind does not appear in beasts—not even in the greater ones, let alone the viler ones.

And this is the first way in which men imitate divine worship: namely, because they worship themselves as gods. There is also a second way: because we alone of all living beings worship God. We alone honor God with affection, gestures, words, shrines, and sacrifices. Plato, in his *Protagoras*, wants this to be the greatest proof of our divinity: that we alone, as participants in a divine lot, recognize and desire God because of a certain kinship. We acknowledge Him as our Author, invoke and love Him as a Father, venerate Him as a King, and fear Him as a Lord. For just as the Sun is not seen without the Sun, just as the air is not heard without air, and an eye full of light sees light, and an ear full of air hears the resonating air, so too God is not known without God. But the soul full of God is directed toward God only insofar as it recognizes God, being illustrated by divine light, and thirsts for Him, being kindled by divine heat. Hence the soul is made into a temple of God, as Xystus the Pythagorean <note>Likely referring to the "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of moral aphorisms widely read in the Renaissance and often attributed to a Pythagorean philosopher.</note> believes. Indeed, he believes that the temple of the eternal God will never fall. The human mind moves God daily. The heart burns for God. The breast sighs for God. The tongue sings of Him. The head, hands, and knees adore Him. The crafts of men reflect Him. If God does not hear these things, perhaps He seems ignorant. If He does not listen, perhaps He will appear ungrateful—and in a way, cruel, if He forces us to cry out daily to someone who will not hear us. And let no one dare to say that God despises human affairs as if they were insignificant. Surely, a comfortable dwelling moves the builder as an **end** <term>Final Cause: the purpose or goal for which something is done</term>, just as it moves him as an **agent** <term>Efficient Cause: the person or thing that brings something about</term> to think of a certain form for the house, for which form he again seeks a certain material. Where the **end** moves the **agent**, the **agent** moves the **form**, and the **form** moves the **material**.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's divine nature is evidenced by its unique capacity for self-reverence and the worship of God, contrasting this spiritual reality with the "delirium" of physical life. He posits that the human mind acts as a temple for the Divine, implying a reciprocal relationship between the Creator and the created.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Sixteenth Sign" of the soul's immortality, expanding on the argument that divine providence, which governs even the smallest parts of nature, must logically ensure an eternal destiny for the human soul.</meta>

## MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY

The same happens in civil and military deliberations. Thus it follows that the end—the goal—is the **cause of causes**, and therefore precedes all other causes. Furthermore, all natural things are established for the sake of some certain end, since individual parts seem to lead toward specific, highly effective uses. For example, the shoot of a vine-branch (which they call a <term>tendril</term> <note>original: *capreolus*, literally "little goat," referring to the curling, horn-like shape of a vine's climbing shoot</note>) is born for this purpose: to bind the vine to the nearest small tree. This act of binding is the "cause" for which the shoot originated. But because that which does not exist in any way cannot be the cause of existence for any effect, nor can it set all causes in motion, it is necessary that an act of this kind existed both before the shoot and before all the other causes of the vine. However, it did not exist in physical bodies until the very last moment. Therefore, it existed in a certain incorporeal nature that governs bodies long before it appeared in the vine-shoot. Indeed, that nature—the "artisan of the vine"—shaped the form of the shoot in such matter by means of its own form, for the sake of such an act. 

But did this intended act exist in that nature according to the mode of nature, or according to a purpose of the will? Certainly, it was according to both. From the former, it was the same as a certain form of the agent and a model of its affection. From the latter, it was the end goal. Wherever there is a purpose of an artistic will, there is **mind**. For this reason, the Divine Mind presides over all bodies; it embraces the forms of all physical things in an intellectual way and, like an archer, directs individual things to their own ends, and finally, all things toward the One. 

This **Divine Farmer** <note>original: *Diuinus hic agricola*</note> tends the shoots, the tendrils, and the roots. For from where else do the shoots turn toward the sun while avoiding the shade? Or how are the tendrils stretched out like hands toward that part where a support is closest? Or why do the roots, fleeing dryness, spread out most toward moisture? This choice—which did not exist previously—is the work of artistic counsel, or rather, of the truest intellect. Yet a true mind is not *inside* the vines. Therefore, it is present *to* them. Furthermore, it is present to even the most lowly little beasts, which always choose the better options in their crafts. God tends the trees, and he leads and feeds the beasts, as the ancient Theologians also maintained. 

Would He then despise only human beings? Who alone on earth do not despise the Divine Majesty? Far be it! Indeed, if God does not neglect any parts of the world, even the smallest, He surely does not despise the human race, which is such a **precious** <note>original: *pretiosa*</note> part of the world; it stands in the middle of temporal and eternal things, and in so far as it grasps the eternal, it orders the temporal. It is so close to God that, by insinuating itself into the secrets of the Divine Mind, it recognizes this work of God—namely, the order of the world. The intelligence of the world’s order is, by that very fact, more excellent than the order itself. Indeed, such order was made and is ruled through intelligence. If our soul is more excellent than the world through its knowledge, it will also be more excellent through its life. By the power of this life, which is separable from the body, the soul possesses the ability to be separated from the body through its operation, and to transcend the world itself by the power of a "super-worldly" (so to speak) life. 

How much intelligence surpasses the order of the world is apparent from this: such order is dispersed through time, while intelligence possesses the whole simultaneously and in a stable manner. Again, order follows its cause but does not "catch up" to it; intelligence catches up to the cause of order when it finds God, its artisan. There, the soul receives such ample things from God that it thereafter regards the world as a mere shadow. One does not despise so great a thing unless he conceives of something even greater. If the human soul is so vast, why would it be neglected by God, the provider for even the smallest things? If the soul senses God, why should God not also sense the soul, especially since God gave this very power and action of sensing to the soul, and preserves and leads it? 

Hence David asks: *Does he who planted the ear not hear? And he who formed the eyes, does he not consider?* <note>Ficino is quoting Psalm 94:9.</note> Furthermore, if the soul ascends to God, why should God not descend in some way to the soul? If the mind asks for what is just from God, while seeking its paternal inheritance, why should God not hear it? What does this most dutiful son ask of his most indulgent parent? **Eternity**. He will certainly obtain it. For the eternal God can grant it, and the life of the mind can receive eternity, which its knowledge and will already grasp. For the soul does not will unless it knows, nor does it know unless it lives. Indeed, eternity must be given to the mind, which both transcends time and, for the sake of the eternal God, despises temporal things. This is done not only by the more religious, but even by the impious in some way. For those whom the love of God does not attract, at least the fear of Him terrifies. Those whom fear does not terrify, at least suspicion unsettles. Thus, many men—indeed, all men—certainly cast aside very many comforts of temporal life out of love for God, or suspicion, or fear. God, therefore, ought to grant eternal things in exchange for temporal ones. None of the other animals abstain from present goods because of a desire for future ones. It follows that man would be the most foolish and miserable of all animals if he enjoyed neither the present life nor the future one. And these...

his wretched foolishness and foolish wretchedness would arise from the fact that he trusted in the wisest and happiest God. But just as nothing can become extremely cold by approaching fire, so a human being—because he alone clings to the wisest and most blessed God—cannot become the most foolish and most wretched from this; rather, he becomes most blessed for this very reason: because he joins himself to the Most Blessed. He joins himself to Him by despising temporal things <note>things that exist only in time and pass away</note> and desiring eternal ones. If he becomes blessed by despising temporal things, he is only made so by the attainment of eternal things. Furthermore, if God is the first and highest life, the living being that clings most closely to Him lives the longest. However, we do not live longer in the body. If God is the highest wisdom, man is as much wiser than the other animals as he clings more closely to God. In this very approach, he judges himself to be immortal. Because a judgment of this kind is true—for it is made by the soul at the moment when it is wiser than other animals and other men—it is true that the soul is eternal. If the **First Truth** <note>original: *prima ueritas*, a name for God as the ultimate source of all truth</note> cannot deceive, then the hope of immortality will not be deceived, having been inserted into us by the **First Immortality** to such an extent that, even while all things among which we live are unwilling and crying out against it, we always retain such a hope. If the First Goodness is not malicious, the greed for the First Good infused in us by Him does not deprive us of temporal goods except to grant us eternal ones. If every opinion is truer the better it is, and better the more it makes those who hold it better, then the opinion of immortality is the truest of all; for more than others, it makes men best, most excellent, and therefore most happy. Who does not know that whatever leads most to human perfection is truest in human nature? If the intellect by its nature loves God as Truth and Goodness itself, and God both loves the intellect—especially the pious one, as it is most closely related to Him—and loves it back as a lover, it follows that there is a certain natural friendship between them. The end of friendship is the sharing of life. Therefore, the life of God can be communicated to the intellect, namely in that manner by which it is loved by Him. Since the end of friendship is of the same nature as the friendship itself, and vice versa. But it is loved and desired as perpetual. This seems to be confirmed by the fact that, since it is the property of the Good to draw all things to itself and to communicate itself to all, it is necessary that the **Infinite Good**, which is God, draws and communicates infinitely. Therefore, He communicates Himself to each according to their wish, because the very same God who communicates is the one who drew them. Moreover, the intellect desires the perpetual life of God by nature no less than it desires a certain understanding of Him. Finally, if God is beneficent—indeed, if He is Beneficence itself—He cannot lack the duty of gratitude. He cannot be grateful toward one who loses his present life out of love for divine worship, except after this life.

->That Religion is the most proper and true characteristic of the human race. Chapter IX.<-

**T**hat man is more excellent than the beasts is shown by his works as evident testimony, which Aristotle demonstrates in the twelfth book of animals <note>Ficino likely refers here to the *History of Animals*, though that work traditionally has ten books; he may be using a different medieval division or referencing the *Parts of Animals*</note>. Let us therefore ask by what principal gift he is most excellent. He certainly seems to excel in the ingenuity of the arts and of governance, especially because (as we have declared elsewhere) humans vary their crafts, inasmuch as they are themselves craftsmen, not merely the instruments of another craftsman. Beasts, however, do not vary theirs, because they are instruments of an artistic nature rather than possessing the art themselves. But although we excel other animals in the ingenuity of art and governance, this industry is nevertheless shared between us and the beasts. It is necessary, however, for the human species, once it is distinguished from the beasts, to have some distinct and proper perfection in which no beasts participate in any way. Will it be speech? But by gesture, cry, and song, beasts imitate speech. Will it be reason? Certainly reason, yet not every operation of reason. For even in beasts, active reason has certain traces, seen through signs of arts and governance. Even the reason that speculates on natural things seems to have something "imaginary" <note>based on mental images or instinct rather than abstract logic</note> in beasts. For they themselves heal their diseases by choosing certain foods and remedies, and as if they were foreseeing future storms, they display evidence of things to come, and change their locations to avoid the coming dangers of the seasons, although they are led to this by nature rather than leading themselves. What then remains that belongs entirely to man alone? The **contemplation of divine things**. For beasts show no sign of religion; thus, the lifting up of the mind toward God, the King of Heaven, is as proper to us as the upright posture of the body toward heaven is proper to us. And worship...

worship of the divine is almost as natural to humans as whinnying is to horses or barking to dogs. But if some curious person should assert that certain beasts also venerate the celestial bodies (which I do not believe in the least), the Platonists will respond that such beasts are doing something else entirely at the moment when they appear to honor the heavens. Or, if they perhaps do honor them, they do not know what they are doing. Or, if they do know, then they too must be participants in intelligence and immortality. But in truth, to return to our point, the most perfect living being <note>original: *perfectissimum animal*; Ficino refers to the human being as the pinnacle of the animal kingdom</note> excels in that property by which it is most perfect and most distinct from lower creatures—the property by which it is joined to the most perfect, that is, the divine. Furthermore, if the human being is the most perfect of mortal animals, then by the very reason he is human, he is most perfect through that specific gift which he alone possesses among them, and which is not shared with other animals. That gift is religion. Therefore, he is most perfect through religion. If religion were empty and false, he would, by contrast, be the most imperfect of all, since through it (as we explained just before) he would be the most insane and wretched. However, he cannot suffer such contrary things through the same part of himself—being both supremely perfect and supremely imperfect through religion. Therefore, religion is true. Or are we unaware that the prophecy <note>original: *uaticinium*; here meaning a natural instinct that predicts future events</note> which arises from an entire species of animal is true? Many reptiles crawl out from the depths of the earth when the sun rises, and a mist in the air follows. A great crowd of crows flies from a certain quarter of the sky in the evening, and winds are foretold. By the common prophecy of all humanity, religion is likewise true.

For everyone, everywhere and always, worships God for the sake of a future life. It is true, therefore, that there will be another life, provided that the most perfect species of animal holds a true judgment in that which is most natural to it. That this assertion of religion is such a natural judgment appears not only from the fact that it belongs to humans alone, but also from the fact that all human opinions, feelings, and customs—except for religion—are subject to change. When I say religion, I mean that very instinct common and natural to all nations, by which a certain Providence, the queen of the world, is everywhere and always acknowledged and worshiped. We are led to this piety chiefly by three causes. First, by a certain natural sagacity (so to speak) infused in us by Providence itself; second, by philosophical reasons that prove the providence of the Architect from the very order of the building <note>an early version of the "argument from design," comparing the universe to a well-built house</note>; and finally, by prophetic words and miracles. Regarding what I just said about the Prophet, it is worth confirming this next with arguments that both **Plato** in the *Protagoras* and **Avicenna** <note>a Persian polymath (980–1037 AD) whose works on metaphysics were influential in the Renaissance</note> bring forward in his *Metaphysics*.

Man (as they say) is a naturally social animal, for he lacks many necessary things that individuals cannot provide for themselves; but when all are gathered into one, they provide mutual services to one another in turn. Furthermore, speech—acting as a kind of interpreter of the human mind from one person to another—indicates that man is social; nature would not have given this to man unless he were intended to live in a community. For this reason, gathering together is natural to man. Truly, if they rush together without law, they will shortly be scattered by mutual injuries; once scattered, they will perish from the lack of many things and will be torn apart by wild beasts as if they were unarmed. Therefore, so that they may live, and live well, it is necessary for them to be gathered together. But again, so that they may remain in a community, there is an absolute need for law. I mean a law of such great authority that no one trusts that he can or should transgress it through violence or deceit. Such a law cannot exist unless the lawmaker is, and is believed to be, divine. Finally, for him to be and be held as such, he must be sent to men by divine providence with certain manifest miracles. This person, indeed, **Plato** and **Avicenna** call the Prophet, the divine leader of the human race. This is the point of that Platonic saying in the book *On Kingship* <note>original: *de regno*; referring to Plato's dialogue *The Statesman* (*Politicus*)</note>: just as beasts cannot be successfully led by a beast without a human, so too humans cannot be led by a human without God. Again, in the *Protagoras*, he says that humans could not live together without law, nor could they receive a law sufficient for this from *Prometheus* <note>representing "created providence" or human ingenuity</note>, but Jove himself, the creator of all, sent *Mercury*—that is, some Prophet and interpreter of the divine will, and the bringer of both divine and human law—to men along with the law. That God sends Prophets to such a duty in certain ages can be shown along with **Avicenna** in this way: If God provides most accurately for the human body, not only in things entirely necessary but even in those that are merely convenient—such as eyebrows, eyelashes, and the arch of the soles of the feet—how much more does He provide for the soul and the whole human race in the most important matters, and those most necessary for our good, especially since minor goods exist for the sake of major ones? Therefore, if minor goods are present to us from the very beginning, without doubt major goods are also present, which are able to be present and are the causes why...

->*Three objections of the Lucretians, and their solutions. The first.*<-

### Chapter X.

**O**ne should not believe the Lucretians <note>followers of the Roman philosopher Lucretius, who argued that religion was a product of fear and superstition</note> when they say that religion does not arise from natural judgment, but from a corruption of the bodily constitution <note>original: *complexionis*; the balance of humors in the body</note>, from the laws of social planning, or from the force of the heavens. Surely, I do not think it proceeds from a corruption of the constitution, because there is no constitution in men worse than that in beasts—especially regarding the judgment of truth and the choice of the good—and yet humans alone are diligently occupied with religions. Furthermore, even among humans, it is not specifically those with a depraved constitution who worship God. For not everyone has a corrupt constitution, yet all in some way worship God, and have always worshipped Him. Nor has human nature always been depraved, nor is it only the unrefined who adore Him; rather, the most gifted and wise do so as well. This was demonstrated by the Magi <note>the priestly caste of ancient Persia</note> of the Persians, the Priests of the Egyptians, the Hebrew Prophets, and the followers of Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato, as well as the ancient theologians of the Christians. All of these, beyond controversy, excelled in wonderful wisdom and an incorporeal holiness. <margin>❦</margin> Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, disputing about prayer, says that the most excellent men among all nations have devoted themselves to prayers out of a zeal for wisdom—men such as the Brahmans among the Indians, the Magi among the Persians, and similar figures among the Greeks and Chaldeans. This is what he says. Nor should we think that those men were faking it, for they confirmed the holiness of their speech through both their lifelong works and by risking their lives. There were also many other most learned philosophers—Barbarians, Greeks, and Latins—who, even if they did not excel in such great purity of life as those I mentioned before, nevertheless lived honorable lives and did not hesitate to support religion. It is possible, of course, that some of them were faking it to some extent, but I do not believe they all faked it, nor did those who faked it live entirely without any religion. <margin>❦</margin> For it is difficult to depart entirely from nature. It is handed down that Diagoras, Dicearchus, Epicurus, and Lucretius were impious beyond all others; yet even they were sometimes forced by nature to agree somewhat with religions, as their books testify. But just as those men published some things against religion with impunity, so too many other philosophers would have openly vomited the poison of impiety if the majority of people had been impious. It is one thing not to admit this or that specific religious cult (which many do), but it is another to fundamentally abolish all religion—which very few have attempted, and even they did so with suspicion rather than absolute assertion. Furthermore, if some gifted and learned men are found to be ambiguous in religion, it is not surprising. For Plato writes that two ages are especially religious: childhood and old age. Children suckle religion with their milk, and they remain in what they have imbibed until reason is awakened in adolescence. Reason, by its own nature, demands the causes and explanations of individual things. If, at this age, they either take up those studies or happen upon those discourses in which the causes of things are diligently sought, they begin to want to assert nothing except that for which they have perceived a reason. Then, for the first time, they cast religion mostly behind their backs, unless perhaps they commit themselves to the laws and the counsel of their elders; this is because the most hidden reasons for divine things are only perceived at long last, after a long time, with exquisite diligence, and with a purified mind. Those adolescents have not yet reached such reasons, and because they offer almost nothing <meta>catchword: offer</meta>

<meta>catchword: Epicurus,</meta>

They assert things for which they see no reason; if they rely solely on their own judgment, they neglect religion in a certain way. Some, established in this opinion, surrender themselves to **Aristippic pleasures** <note>original: *Aristippicis uoluptatibus*; referring to Aristippus of Cyrene, a Greek philosopher who taught that pleasure is the highest good</note>, eventually thinking nothing more of religion than if it were **old wives' tales**. Others, however, through a **Pythagorean cleansing** <note>original: *Pythagoreo risu*; literally "Pythagorean laughter," a metaphor for the joyful purification of the mind</note>, purge the mind from the senses through the disciplines of Ethics, Physics, Mathematics, and Metaphysics. They do this so that they are not forced to go blind—like those with bleary eyes suddenly directing their gaze toward the **divine Sun**—but rather, progressing step by step, they may clearly and healthfully perceive the divine light: first in Ethics as if in the **earth**, second in Physics as if in **water**, third in Mathematics as if in the **Moon**, and fourth in Metaphysics as if in the **Sun**. These, **Orpheus** calls the *legitimate Priests of the Muses*, who finally, in their more mature years, feel much better about religion. We read of this in **Plato**, in his *Letter to King Dionysius*, in the *Phaedrus*, in the first book of the *Republic*, and in the tenth book of the *Laws*. 

Plato warns young men not to pass judgment rashly on divine matters, but to trust the laws until age itself teaches them—either through those levels of study we described, or through experience, or through a certain separation of the soul from the body which a moderate old age brings. In that stage of life, the soul, seeing things separated from bodies as if from a close distance, discerns them more clearly than it was accustomed to. Therefore, when Plato had handed down certain divine mysteries to **Dionysius** (who was still a young man) under a kind of veil, he added first that he should examine them diligently, for no study could be more blessed than this. Next, he warned him to be careful lest these things fall into the ears of the unlearned, because among the common crowd nothing is more ridiculous, but among men endowed with good character, nothing is more wonderful and divine. He adds, moreover, that divine mysteries—after they have been examined frequently, or rather, always—hardly at last, with much labor, are purified and shine forth like **gold**. Thus, even many of the sharpest and most learned men, though they rejected such things as incredible when hearing them in their youth or even in their thirtieth year, later—by the benefit of a more mature age, a more diligent examination, or rather (as he says elsewhere) by **divine revelation**—conceded that such things are the most probable and manifest of all, while condemning the contrary views as false. This is what Plato says.

To this is added the fact that many men who excel in any art are either **Melancholic** <note>referring to the four humors; Melancholy was associated with "black bile" and was thought to produce both genius and profound sadness or doubt</note> by nature—such as **Heraclitus, Aristotle,** and **Chrysippus** were—or they become so, as happened to **Democritus, Zeno of Citium, the Arab Avempace,** and **Averroes**. This humor is cold, dry, and black; these three qualities are contrary to those three in which the vigor of life consists: namely, heat, moisture, and clear spirit. Such a humor, being contrary to life, takes away the hope of life and injects a suspicion into the mind against life itself. This is why they sometimes waver and lack confidence regarding the immortality of the soul. **Avempace** <note>a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> writes that this happened to him. They do not lack confidence because they are excellent in talent or learning, but because they are suspicious and fearful due to this "earthy" humor. Even unlearned and dull little men sometimes lack confidence themselves if they are oppressed by that same humor. 

Furthermore, distinguished men very often have the best hopes if they are not troubled by such a humor. Even those who are troubled by it from an early age—provided they have not been educated entirely perversely—easily cast off these vain suspicions and follow the **natural instinct of religion**. Such is the force and stability of nature itself. This is what **Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Varro,** and **Apollonius of Tyana** achieved above all others. Therefore, those suspicions have no weight in proving the "death" of souls, since they proceed neither from talent nor from wisdom, but from a disease. 

Moreover, those in whose birth **Saturn** and **Mercury** are most powerful are often sharper. For these stars invite contemplation because they contract the spirit toward interior things. These planets, if they are "direct" <note>moving forward in their orbit from the perspective of Earth</note> and well-disposed, increase talent and do not diminish religion. But if they are "retrograde" or poorly disposed, they make a man thoroughly fearful and suspicious everywhere because of their earthy quality, which is not sufficiently tempered by the aspect of other stars. This results in the person wavering and lacking confidence not only in religion, but in other matters as well. 

However, one must remember that an opinion or feeling does not have enough credibility if it follows either a Melancholic, sick temperament—which is in a way contrary to life—or an unseemly and harmful position of the stars. Such a position perverts the human constitution and brings a defect with it, not only regarding confidence in life, but also regarding the governance of human affairs. This is why ungodly men are most often either extremely lazy or cowardly, such as **Epicurus** is said to have been,

He argues that through mature study and the purification of the mind, the natural instinct for religion and the belief in the soul's immortality are eventually confirmed.</summary>

**Epicurus**, or the wicked, like **Aristippus**, or the insane, like their follower **Lucretius**, who while he was driven by insanity due to **black bile** <term>black bile: *atra bilis*, the humor associated with melancholy; in extreme cases, it was thought to cause madness</term>, first attempted to destroy his own soul with words in his third book *On the Nature of Things*, and then destroyed his own body with a sword. Therefore, just as one should not trust a sick person regarding the taste of wine, but rather a healthy one, so regarding the end of human life we should trust a healthy and natural human intellect rather than an insane one. I call a healthy and natural human **temperament** <term>temperament: *complexio*, the specific balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which was believed to determine a person's physical and mental health</term> "sanguine" and perfectly balanced. The **sanguine** <note>original: *sanguinea*; the humor of blood, associated with an airy, warm, and moist nature</note> temperament is airy, consisting of vital heat and moisture. A balanced temperament is like the heavens and does not disturb the judgment of truth. Such human temperaments are mostly suited for a healthy mind and prudence; while they do not themselves grant us religion (for this is a gift infused into the mind from the divine, when we are commanded to neglect all else for divine grace), they certainly do not hinder it, nor do they cast various suspicions into the mind.

Furthermore, what is found in the majority and the most perfect examples is considered "natural." What is found in the very few and the sick is considered "monstrous." Truly, what is natural tends to be truthful, while what is monstrous tends to be deceptive. Now, judgment favoring religion is found in the majority and the more serious of men, while the opposite is found in the very few and the most frivolous, by whose example others are also sometimes infected. In those few, this is not a judgment of reason, but a disease of the soul and a fearful suspicion proceeding from a depraved bodily temperament. This is clear from the fact that men of this sort often have reasons that favor the eternity of the soul, yet they remain suspicious—just as those whose reason judges that wine should not be drunk, but their lungs nonetheless thirst, or those whose reason judges there is nothing in the path to harm them, yet their senses shudder in the darkness.

Not only is an unequal temperament contracted from parents or the stars, but a quality induced by habit—as we indicated at the beginning—leads the human race away from religion. For men who are over-curious in any discipline, because of the excessive agitation of the brain, tend to go insane as the brain becomes "dried out." **Plato** writes of this in the ***Theaetetus*** against those who said nothing in the world ever stood still; these men, he says, affected by vertigo due to frequent turning, thought that everything was spinning when it was they themselves who were turning. Thus it is no wonder if men curious in the arts sometimes clearly rave in matters of religion and other things; their insanity is revealed both by their frivolous habits and by their overly ridiculous opinions on many subjects, as well as the contradictions between those very opinions. Therefore, it is not from a healthy constitution that religion is born, but from a corruption of the constitution that impiety arises.

Plato asserts in his *Letters to the Syracusans* that impiety is born not only from a depraved temperament but also from depraved morals. He says we must always believe the ancient and sacred oracles which assert that the human soul is immortal, that it has judges, and that it suffers the greatest punishments once it has been separated from the body. For this reason, it should be considered a lesser evil to suffer the gravest injuries than to inflict them. A greedy man or one lacking in mind might either not hear these things or mock them; or, devoted to pleasures, he might not see them like a blind man. Consequently, a maximum evil necessarily follows him as he lives impiously, and a wretched migration awaits him after death as well. All this is found there. Similar things are said in the ***Gorgias***, in the tenth book of the ***Republic***, and in the ***Laws***, where he adds that this opinion on the soul has been proven by necessary and "adamantine" <note>original: *adamantinis*; meaning unbreakable or rock-solid, a term Plato uses for his most certain proofs</note> reasons. **Cleombrotus** <note>A student of Plato who reportedly leapt to his death to reach the afterlife after reading the *Phaedo*</note> was so persuaded of this that he deprived himself of this life out of love for the other. **Demosthenes** also said he preferred to die honorably than to live basely, after he had heard Plato and **Xenocrates** debating the immortality of souls. Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that the **Platonists** usually attribute the greatest cause of impiety to the lowest class of **demons** <term>demons: *daemones*, in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits. Here, Ficino views them as malicious entities that tempt humans</term>. These spirits, through a certain silent persuasion, push you with all their might—either toward a false religion out of ambition, or toward no religion at all out of envy.

->Second objection and solution.<-

**W**e have refuted the first objection of the followers of **Lucretius**, by which it was said that the worship of God happens through a depravity of human nature. There it appeared that it is the Lucretians who are rather the depraved ones, for they judge the nature of men to be at its worst when it is joined to the best God. But what of the second point they bring forward: that the veneration of divine things arises from human counsels and civil institutions? Not at all. It cannot be said how quickly human inventions are changed—even true ones, let alone the false and faked. All human institutions are changed into contrary institutions in a short time. Also, contrary [institutions] at the same [time]...

At the same time, different nations have different laws, and what is considered shameful to some is deemed honorable to others. But what is older than religion? Or what is more widespread? Nor did the founders of laws invent this to restrain the masses. For before cities and homes, religion flourished in the world; scattered and wild men worshipped God, and those very lawgivers feared the deities. Plato confirms this in the *Protagoras* <note>A dialogue by Plato where the sophist Protagoras discusses the origins of human society and the virtues.</note>, saying that even before they gathered together, or spoke, or practiced any arts, humans immediately from the beginning—owing to a natural kinship—adored God, and established altars and sacrifices. Accordingly, men would have eventually rejected such a heavy yoke of religion, which is contrary to so many of life’s comforts, if it were a fiction and did not rest upon the stability of truth. 

But perhaps Protagoras will argue that religion is not natural, but only seems so because we "drink it in from our tenderest nails" <note>original: *à teneris unguiculis*; a Latin idiom meaning from earliest childhood.</note>. We shall respond to Protagoras thus: he learned to speak and drink from infancy; nonetheless, speech and drinking are natural. Everywhere and always humans speak and drink because it is natural. But in different times and places, they speak and drink in a different order, because the order of performance depends on opinion rather than nature. Similarly, God is adored among all nations in every age because it is natural, though not with the same sacrifices and modes. Since speech is natural, it reaches its end, which is to reveal the will of one to another. Drinking also reaches its end, which is to restore the body's moisture. I do not see why religion should not obtain its own end. Its end is to enjoy God; its desire is to enjoy Him forever.

->Third objection and solution.<-

**OR** are humans driven to religion by the stars, as the wicked object in the third place? Not at all. Certainly, the stars favor the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament</term> of the bodies. Religion, however, is an enemy to bodies <note>Ficino refers to the way religious practice often involves fasting or the denial of physical impulses.</note>. Nor can the heavens instill a desire higher than that of the celestial spheres, which a religious man even scorns. Add to this that religion condemns fate and asserts freedom. Since, therefore, it is the very thing that resists fate, how shall it have that resistance from the fates? Furthermore, a certain conjunction of planets provides fertility, but the opposite provides scarcity. This one brings plague, that one health; likewise war and peace. We see how quickly the gifts of the heavens are changed into their opposites. Thus, if a certain position of the stars forces one to worship God, a contrary position would shortly erase divine honors from the memory of men. Yet, there has never and nowhere been an intermission of religion, even though God is honored differently at other times and in other places. 

This variety has followed the counsels of human minds, which are by no means subject to the stars. Indeed, the human mind by its very nature, being divine, is led to perceive, worship, and fear God, just as it is led by its nature to love the good and avoid evil. Nevertheless, through the free choice of its own deliberation, it varies the ritual of worshipping God, just as it walks toward the good by various paths according to its will. From the preceding discussion, it is concluded that this common religion of all nations toward one God is entirely natural to the human species and a virtue proper to man, and therefore most excellent. Indeed, two acts of humans are most excellent: those, namely, which are in the most excellent part of the soul and are concerned with the most excellent object. Such in our mind are the knowledge and love of God. 

In this life, human love toward God excels human knowledge, because no one truly knows God. However, those truly love God—as He is known—who despise all things for His sake. Again, just as it is worse to hate God than to be ignorant of Him, so it is better to love Him than to know Him. Add that by investigating God, we make very little progress over a very long time; by loving Him, we make the most progress in the shortest time. For this reason, love joins the mind with the divinity more quickly, more closely, and more firmly than knowledge, because the power of knowledge consists more in discernment, while that of love consists more in union. Furthermore, it is more pleasing to God himself to be loved than to be scrutinized. For we contribute nothing to God by looking at Him, but by loving Him, we contribute whatever we are and possess. Therefore, God rewards those who love Him rather than those who investigate Him. Then, we can use the knowledge of God poorly—namely, for pride—but we cannot use the love of God poorly. And by loving God, we perceive a far greater pleasure than by investigating Him, and we are made better by loving than by inquiring. Indeed, just as it is not the one who sees the good, but the one who wills it, who becomes good, so the soul does not become divine from the fact that it considers God, but from the fact that it loves Him—just as matter, not because it takes light from the fire, <meta>catchword: capiat (takes/receives)</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that religion is a natural human instinct older than law or civilization, refuting Protagoras's claim that it is merely learned behavior and dismissing the idea that it is governed by astrology. He concludes that loving God is superior to merely knowing Him, as love leads to a faster and more profound union with the Divine.</summary>
