## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 14.

...it might grasp it, but because it is fire, it escapes the heat. <note>original: "sed quia calorem, ignis euadit." This refers to a metaphysical analogy: a thing that is essentially a quality (like fire is heat) isn't affected by that quality as an external force.</note> Hence that saying of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note>: the soul is made pure by seeking God, and by imitating God it becomes God. This was indeed taken from Plato himself, who said: divine light is not acquired by us little by little through inquiry, but rather it is suddenly kindled in us at last through divine power by a perfect union of life. Furthermore, by knowing God, we contract His greatness into the concept of our own mind; but by loving Him, we instead amplify our mind toward the immense breadth of divine goodness. In the former, we cast ourselves down into God; in the latter, we raise ourselves up into God. For we know as much as we ourselves can grasp, but we love both what we see and however much of divine goodness we prophesy remains beyond our sight. Nor is love content with human knowledge. For knowledge is created and finite. The will rests only in the primary and immense good. 

Since the whole of religion consists in this very love, humans possess nothing more divine than religion (as Plato testifies in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue often attributed to Plato or his pupil Philip of Opus, discussing the path to wisdom.</note>). This religion is as far removed from falsehood as other human pursuits are, to the extent that it joins us more closely to God, the highest truth. Therefore, its foresight is more true than the opinions of other faculties. Its foresight promises worthy rewards to the good and threatens punishments to the evil. A worthy reward is owed to the integrity of the most holy man. Integrity, confirmed through the highest habit, is an indelible good; even if he lived for a thousand thousand years, he would always act in the same way. Therefore, no reward is worthy of it unless it is indelible and eternal, especially since that is the most fitting reward of holiness, for the sake of which holiness does everything, and which can fulfill its desire. Such is that in which the whole reason for the good exists. His reward, therefore, is the everlasting possession of the immense good. 

Thus, the religious soul will live forever, so that it may receive a worthy reward. The impious soul will also live forever, so that it may pay the penalty for its impiety—one who sins infinitely whenever he forgets the infinite God for the sake of finite comforts, and contracts an indelible evil habit, through which he would sin for a thousand thousand years if he lived, since he once decided to sin for as long as he lives. He has already offended divine justice—to which future ages are present—for as long as he would sin if he were to live; thus an infinite punishment is owed to him who is already sinning infinitely. Add to this that if the reward for true virtue is eternal (for it looks to God, on whom it depends as its beginning, as its end), it follows that the punishment for vice—which fails both the eternal reward of virtue and the principle of life—must be everlasting. No such punishment exists in this very brief time of life; therefore, it will exist in the future. In this way, the adversities that happen to the good in this life, and the prosperity that happens to the evil, seem destined to be compensated, so that piety is not a loss to the good, and (as we read in the *Phaedo*) impiety is not a gain to the evil. Indeed, the good ought to be beneficial, and the evil harmful. In this life, piety is harmful, for it compels one not only to despise present goods but even to undergo labors and death for the sake of God and honor. On the contrary, impiety is often very beneficial. Therefore, lest the place of justice be missing, the sentence must be delivered elsewhere. 

Nor should it be thought that this part of justice, which concerns human affairs, does not belong to God, to whom the administration of the whole world belongs. In this world, if He does all things by understanding and loving them (as Plato wishes), it follows that in doing them He understands and loves each individual thing. And in caring for the whole, He does not neglect the parts (for if the parts are not cared for, the whole is not cared for). Plato says this in the *Laws*. Indeed, the human species is no small part of the world, and is itself an administrator of justice. If, therefore, divine justice—as the Orphic hymns sing—distributes the elements each to their own places, and if it doles out small gifts to each thing, even the smallest, according to its nature, why would it not also distribute places, rewards, and punishments to men according to their merits? 

God frequently leaves either the good untouched or the evil unpunished, so that by these signs He may show us that another life remains, in which justice, which cannot be deceived, may be fulfilled according to merits. But sometimes He punishes crimes, especially the most serious ones, even in this life, so that we may recognize His providence because of this. For the present, I pass over many examples of divine providence. Philo the Jew <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy, particularly Platonism.</note>, the Platonist, writes in his book *On Providence* that a law existed among the ancients that temple-robbers should be either burned, thrown from a height, or drowned. And when Philomelus, Onomarchus, and Phaylus <note>Leaders of the Phocians during the Third Sacred War (356–346 BC) who were notorious for seizing and looting the treasures of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> had despoiled the temple, a few days later, without the work of judges, by a certain divine fate, they fell into these three punishments. Plato, however, commands in the *Laws* that we should never doubt divine providence because unjust men often seem to depart from here unpunished, since we do not know by what reason and where—as it serves the order of the universe—each thing is repaid to each person. Again, in the final book of *The Republic*, he proves that the soul, through virtue, becomes like God...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's love for the infinite God necessitates an eternal reward, and since earthly life often lacks justice for the pious and the wicked, an afterlife must exist where divine providence balances the scales.</summary>

[...and becomes] a friend [to God], and therefore is so cared for by God that whatever happens is ultimately directed toward the good. Whether a person is placed in poverty, in sickness, or in some other calamity, each thing—either in this life or in the future—will eventually lead to the good. Nor should divine goodness be called harmful because it permits sins to be committed and punishes those that are committed. Indeed, rational nature holds its own rank in the kingdom of God. To this nature, **free motion** <note>Ficino uses 'motion' here to mean the 'movement' or 'activity' of the soul, essentially synonymous with free will.</note> is granted. It is given to such motion that it can progress toward the better, and to the good of nature, it can add the further good of will, action, and attainment—so that a nature of this kind is not only made good by another as a passive recipient, but also makes itself good as an active agent. 

Furthermore, it is given to such motion that it can cross over into the worse—not that it strips off its own nature, but that it puts on a foreign and inferior one. This infection is followed by punishment that is either harmful or purgatorial <note>Ficino distinguishes between 'harmful' punishment (retribution) and 'purgatorial' punishment (remedial/cleansing).</note>. This follows, I say, by a certain necessary and divine law, leading the sinner internally toward things similar to himself. And as Plato says in the tenth book of the *Laws*, the principle of motion is in the soul, by which it makes itself such or such according to its own judgment. But after it has turned out that way, it is soon transferred—not so much by its own judgment as by a certain fatal law of God—into a matching condition and place. 

Plato adds, as if with the **divine mouth of David** <note>original: "diuino Dauidis ore." Ficino is comparing Plato's philosophy to the biblical Psalms of King David, specifically Psalm 139: 'Whither shall I go from thy spirit? ... if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.'</note>, that whether you have penetrated to the center of the world <note>The center of the earth, often associated with the depths of the underworld.</note> or flown to the upper surface, you will not be able to escape the divine law. The point of that passage in the tenth book of the *Republic* is the same: since you can neither hide from nor escape the divine eyes and hands, take every care not to sin—that is, never to become more unlike God. For He hates souls that degenerate far from His likeness. Indeed, even if you were to obtain both the **ring of Gyges** <note>A mythical ring mentioned by Plato that granted its wearer invisibility, used here as a test of moral character.</note> and the **helmet of the underworld** <note>original: "galeam... infernalem." This refers to the Helmet of Hades, which also granted invisibility.</note>, you must flee far from injustice. 

But let us return to the *Laws*. He says in the same place that the world is full partly of good things and partly of bad, and that God has set over us certain gods and spirits <term>daemons<gloss>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or 'guardian angels,' not 'demons' in the modern evil sense.</gloss></term> like shepherds to guard the sheep, through whose providence we may avoid evils and pursue good things. He adds that those who, having seized many things unjustly, trust they can appease the gods with gifts, are just as mistaken as if those who tear sheep to pieces thought they could win over the shepherd by returning certain limbs of the sheep to him. 

Finally, everywhere Plato finds both that we sin by our own judgment and that we necessarily suffer after the sin. But let us now return to the established order. What then? If God both permits and punishes, in the permitting, the wonderful excellence of the human race shines forth; in the punishing, God’s power and immense goodness. If the mind is permitted to sin, who does not see that man is his own master and lord, acting in various ways by his own judgment? If God punishes faults, He carries out the good of justice within the very evil of the faults—a justice that would have no place unless there were wrongdoing. Without this, some part of virtue, so to speak, and of justice and the kingdom of God would seem to be missing. Here, His infinite power and goodness shine brightly, for against the nature of evil, He makes good things out of evil ones, so that the whole of nature is wonderfully ordered. In this nature, the magnitude of the good is so great that it shines in both good and evil things, and its power is tested in both. There is also such an observance of order that the mind, which by sinning seems to depart from the order, still walks within the very order of free motion even while departing; and by suffering, it immediately returns to the order of justice, as it suffers such things as are fitting for its sinful habit.

# PLATONIC THEOLOGY, on the Immortality of Souls,

->by the same author, Ficino,<-

## BOOK XV.

->*Five questions about the soul follow. First, whether there is one intellect for all men. It is not so.*<-

### Chapter I.

**W**e have already refuted many things that are usually brought against the soul in previous discussions. Five doubts remain (I believe) to be clarified. The first is that which the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle taught while walking about (peripatos).</note> Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval European thought. He famously argued for the 'Unicity of the Intellect.'</note> doubted: whether perhaps there is one single mind for all men and that it is eternal, while souls are many and mortal—so that the eternity of the mind itself would be of no benefit to human souls destined to perish. Second, a point which some doubt, is why souls, if they are divine, are joined to earthly bodies so low. Third, for what reason they are so greatly disturbed within these bodies. Fourth, why the righteous depart [from this life]. Fifth, what the state of the soul is before it enters the body, and what it is after its departure. 

Averroes, a Spaniard by homeland and an Arab by language, was devoted to the doctrine of Aristotle but ignorant of the Greek language. It is reported that he read the Aristotelian books in a "barbarous" tongue <note>Ficino likely refers to the Latin translations made from Arabic, which he viewed as inferior to direct translations from the original Greek.</note> after they had been perverted rather than converted <note>original: "peruersos potius quam conuersos"—a play on words suggesting the translation was a distortion.</note> from the Greek. Thus, it is no wonder if, in certain recondite matters, the mind of that very brief writer [Aristotle] was hidden from him. Plethon <note>Gemistus Plethon, a Byzantine scholar who reintroduced Plato to the West and influenced Ficino significantly.</note> and all the most skilled Greeks testify that this happened to him. And what is most significant, the Greek words of Aristotle themselves cry out against Averroes. Plethon himself says that Aristotle thought, without controversy, that human souls were many and everlasting. He adds that he does not wish to pervert Aristotle’s words, even if Aristotle perverted the words of Plato and the other philosophers. 

So it stands. Yet Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who argued that the soul was a physical "form" that died with the body.</note> seems to have perverted Aristotle's sense regarding the soul when he says Aristotle thought the soul was mortal. Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator who took a middle path, arguing for the soul's immortality.</note> explained Aristotle more fairly, saying that by him the **agent intellect** <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The active part of the mind that "lights up" concepts so they can be understood.</note> is considered to be unique, but the **potential intellect** <term>potential intellect</term> <note>The capacity of the mind to receive knowledge.</note> is multiple, and that both are perpetual. What Alexander himself thinks, he declares in his *Natural Questions*, where he says: Medicine, although it is a science, yet in its operation it appears as an art; in the same way, the soul, although it is immortal, yet when submerged in a mortal body it appears to be mortal. And again he says: The Maker of the world did not wish to bind the divine and celestial souls of men to earthly bodies without a certain suitable medium. Such a medium he calls "spirit" and "vehicle" in the manner of the Platonists. 

Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher of late antiquity.</note> affirms that not only the Platonists but also Aristotle posited an immortal soul. Themistius asserts it was posited for the same reason that Plato had posited it. And after he proved in the third book *On the Soul* that both intellects—namely the active and the receptive—are perpetual, he added that only this [composite], namely the one mixed from both, is of such a [mortal] kind, but the passive reason—that is, the **phantasia** <note>original: *phantasiam*; the faculty of imagination that processes sensory images.</note>—is not at all [perpetual]. For this reason, he concluded that we do not remember human affairs after death, because the recollection of these things usually occurs through a turning toward mental images [phantasmata] and because of an affection for bodily things. Therefore, when he says we do not remember, Themistius wants this to be added to indicate that souls live after death, and that there are many souls, but it is no wonder if they do not remember bodily things; for if he had thought souls perish, there would have been no reason to assign why they do not remember. But let us return to Averroes.

->An account of the opinion of Averroes.<-

**A**verroes, when he read frequently in Aristotle that the intellect undoubtedly has nothing of a corporal and mortal nature mixed in, took it in such a way that he concluded three things from it. First, that the intellect is not a body—that is, it is not composed of matter and form. Second, that it is not some quality divisible with the body, or...

He cites various Greek commentators to argue that Aristotle actually believed in the multiplicity and immortality of individual human souls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of the Arabic philosopher Averroes' views on the human mind. The text begins mid-sentence, completing the list of Averroes' propositions regarding the intellect's separation from the body.</meta>

...dependent on the body in any way. The third point is that the intellect is not the kind of form that is able to complete, give life to, and rule the body—nor is it so joined to the body that a single composite is made from the substance of matter and the substance of the intellect, sharing one single existence. We grant the first and second points to Averroes; the third, however, if we follow the ancient Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note>, we by no means concede. He <note>Averroes</note> denies that the substance of the intellect can be the "perfecting form" <note>The 'form' that brings a thing to its finished, functional state.</note> and the life-giving act of the body. His first argument for this is as follows: If the intellect were such an act of the body, a single composite would be born from it and the body, sharing a single existence. However, it cannot be joined with the body without itself becoming a partaker of the body. The mind, which reason shows to be absolute and free from bodies, does not admit such participation.

The second reason: If the mind were the form of the body, it would receive things in the same way that corporal matter receives them. For whatever is the form of a body receives nothing without its own matter. But whatever matter receives, it receives in a "divided" <note>Spreading out across space or time.</note> way; hence the forms of things in matter become temporal and particular. The intellect would also grasp things in this way, and therefore would never comprehend any universal nature through its forms.

The third reason: Matter does not "know" the forms it possesses. Thus, if the mind were joined to matter and, through its association, received things in the same way matter does, it would know nothing at all.

The fourth reason: It is impossible for there to be an infinite power in a body in any way. Yet the power of the mind is, in a sense, infinite. From this, he wishes to conclude that the mind has no commerce with matter.

But since there are many species <note>Types or categories.</note> of mind in nature, he wishes one particular species of mind to be the "human mind"—specifically, that which contemplates the order of things within us. This is because the "mode of understanding" <note>The way we think.</note> is the same in kind across all human beings, just as the soul is the same in kind, through which there is one life in kind and one shape in kind across all humans. Because the human mind is one "in kind" <note>term: *species* — meaning they all share the same essential definition.</note>, it must also be "one in number" <note>term: *numero* — meaning there is literally only one individual entity, rather than many separate ones.</note>; that is, unique and singular, not divided among individuals. For a form that is one in kind is not cut into many individuals except by the addition of matter. But how shall the human mind, which exists as one in itself, be divided into many, since it partakes of no matter?

Furthermore, if there were one intellect in me and another in you, it would be necessary that the "species"—which is the likeness of the thing to be understood—would be one in number in me and another in you, though they would be the same in kind. Since these forms of things to be understood exist in the mind as if in a subject <note>A container or foundation.</note>, there must be different and distinct species in different minds. Distinct, I say, in number, just as the minds are distinct in number. But species or forms that are many in number but one in kind are "particular" forms; these cannot contribute to true understanding, because that which is truly understood must be universal.

Add to this that when one person teaches another, the teacher seems to pour his own knowledge into the student. He either hands over the exact same knowledge he himself had, or another knowledge that is the same in kind but different in number. If he hands over knowledge that is the same in kind but different in number, he will be generating knowledge in the same way that nature is accustomed to generating its work. Truly, that which acts through nature produces its own form in another—a form matching most closely in kind, but differing in number. But this applies to things that correspond to each other in matter. Yet the mind, both of the teacher and the learner, is above matter, and knowledge itself is not an active quality like heat or such things. 

It remains, therefore, that the teacher communicates the exact same knowledge "in number" <note>The very same instance of knowledge.</note> that he himself possesses to the student. This can never happen unless there is a single, unique intellect in both of them; otherwise, the same quality of knowledge would have to pass from one subject to another, or the teacher, by teaching, would be forced to lose his knowledge. 

Furthermore, if our minds were different in number but identical in kind, the notions of things we know would be identical in kind but different in number. But things which, besides their diversity, agree in some "kind," certainly agree in some common notion. Both my intellect and yours would see this common notion, and gather those diverse notions toward it. Thus, we would both conceive this type of notion—I one and you another—also differing in number but agreeing in kind. Therefore, we would again have to reduce them to another common notion, and so on to infinity. But it is absurd to introduce an infinite progress in ordered things. In the species of things, an order is necessary.

By these reasons, Averroes concludes that the human mind, because it is without matter, is unique, and has always been, and will be; and that this mind is the lowest of all minds. And just as he attributes individual minds to each of the higher celestial spheres, so he attributes to this lower world one mind, which is not properly the mind of this man, or that man, or human...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Averroes's theory of the "Unity of the Intellect," specifically focusing on how the single, universal human mind interacts with the individual, perishable souls of particular human beings.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK 15.

...mind of the species, so that there is a single, unique intellect for the entire species in this lower world (as some interpret him), being present everywhere as a whole. He <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> believes that the human being we see consists of this body and what he calls the "sensitive soul," but by no means the intellect. He considers this sensitive soul to be the most perfect of all such souls, differing in species from those of the beasts. He claims there are as many souls as there are human bodies, and that they are born and die with those bodies. He calls the highest power of this soul the "cogitative power," which the Greeks call <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: phantasiam; the faculty of forming mental images or representations</note>. He adds that the souls of beasts have a certain "estimative power," through which they judge suddenly by natural instinct what is good or bad for them, and either pursue or flee it. 

Our soul, however, possesses that cogitative power which is not driven by the guidance of nature, but searches through reason, deliberates with a kind of counsel, and chooses according to its consultation; yet it perceives nothing universal, but only moves through individual things. For this reason, he calls this "particular reason," whereas he calls the intellect "universal reason." He locates this particular reason in the middle part of the brain, between imagination and memory. For he believes that in the first part is the "common sense," which collects within itself the operations of the five senses. In the second part is the imagination, the preserver of those images which the common sense had collected. In the third part is the cogitative power, the judge of those things which the imagination has stored. In the fourth part is the memory, the guardian of the judgments which the cogitative power has produced.

Therefore, the cogitative power is the queen of the middle part, which, among all lower things, is closest to the mind—so much so that the mind is present to it everywhere and fulfills its own understanding through its assistance, while the images of things shining in the cogitative power move the mind to understand. And this is the only communion man has with the mind; it is not because the intellect is a part or a life-giving form of this human being who is composed of a body and a cogitative soul. For the intellect is separated from the human being both in essence and in being. But because the intellect is present everywhere to the thought of this human being, and from this particular thought it draws a universal species, the human being provides the occasion for the intellect to speculate, just as colored light provides the occasion for the eye to see. 

Nor is a single thing made from this human being and the mind; rather, a single operation happens—namely, a single act of understanding—which nevertheless is not in the human being in any way, but in the mind alone; in the mind, I say, prompted by human thought. Nor does anything pass from that mind into the human being, but the whole process is completed in the mind. The human being does not understand anything through the mind; rather, in the human being, the mind understands. And the habits of the arts and sciences are in the mind itself. The cogitative soul is united to a child from his first origin, but the mind joins only much later, when the images in thought are so pure that they move the intellect. 

The <term>Averroists</term> <note>Followers of the philosophy of Averroes, often associated with the controversial idea that all humans share one single mind.</note> affirm that there are not only two powers, but two substances from which the intellect is composed. Indeed, they claim the "active power" is one substance, and the "capable power" is another. The former is by its nature luminous and form-giving; the latter is entirely dark and formable. From their eternal coupling, they constitute a single soul according to its being, just as a single thing in nature is composed of matter and form. They call the former the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>original: intellectum agentem; the active part of the mind that processes sensory data into abstract thoughts</note>, and the latter the <term>formable and capable intellect</term> <note>original: intellectum formabilem et capacem; the passive part of the mind that receives and stores those thoughts</note>. 

They judge the agent intellect—because it is an act existing through itself—to always understand itself by itself, so that by looking at its own essence, it sees itself and also the higher minds through itself. This kind of intellection is its very essence. Since its essence is always joined to the capable intellect, they believe it follows that through this same intellectual essence, the capable intellect always understands the agent intellect, of which that very act of understanding is the essence. Let it also understand the higher minds. This intellection is a single, stable, and eternal act in the universal intellect or soul. There is also in its formable part another intelligence—eternal indeed, but varying, temporal, and multiple—which it borrows from us. And because it clings closer to the agent intellect than to the phantasia <note>imagination</note>, and yet through its union with the temporal phantasia it receives temporal knowledge, they believe what we said a little earlier is clear: namely, that because of its union with that eternal intellect, it possesses an eternal intelligence, which is clearer the more familiar it is to the agent intellect than to the phantasia. In us, however, they believe that doubtful and changeable knowledge is hunted out individually, so that while <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>A famous ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> was living, through the images of things shining in <term>Pythagoras’s</term> thought, it gathered that "Pythagorean" knowledge; but when Pythagoras died and those images ceased, the in-

And because every day an innumerable multitude of men strives for the knowledge of all things, he argues that the intellect learns everything from this daily. From this "agent intellect," and from the higher minds, they believe this marvelous connection of things consists. For they say there are forms entirely absolute from matter, namely the angels themselves, among whom there are not many angels within a single angelic species, but as many as there are angels, there are just as many species of angels. There are, moreover, many corporal forms within the same species—for instance, the souls of animals and forms lower than those. Between these is placed this composite made of man and mind, of many human souls and one mind, like a certain huge monster composed of many legs and one head, where the absolute form joins with the corporeal, and the corporeal with it in turn. And as is fitting, that which is absolute remains unique in itself. That which is corporeal is manifold, while one mind suffices for innumerable souls. And indeed, they call that composite of the mind and each one of us the "intellectual man," but each of us separately from the mind they call the "cogitative man." And first, they affirm that the "intellectual man" understands something because a part of him—that is, the mind—understands, just as we are accustomed to calling a man "flat-nosed" because his nose is flat; but they say the other man <note>the "cogitative man," or the individual person without the shared intellect</note> understands nothing at all.

->Confutation of Averroes. That the mind is the form of the body is evident first from the order of nature. Chapter 11.<-

**G**reat was once the controversy among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>original: Peripateticos; the followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they studied</note> concerning the human mind, and the lawsuit is still before the judge. Dicaearchus used to say that it was a form, both of the body and corporeal. Of the body, because it gives life to the human body. Corporeal, because it is drawn from the heart of the body. Averroes, on the contrary, said it was neither a corporeal form, nor even a form of the body. Avicenna, the prince of Arabian theologians, and Alganteles <note>original: Alganteles; likely Al-Ghazali, the Persian philosopher and theologian</note> followed a middle path; they asserted that the mind is indeed the form of the body, but not a corporeal one. Thus, between forms which are of the body and corporeal, and forms which are neither corporeal nor of the body, there are certain middle forms, being as different as possible, yet agreeing in a certain way partly with the former and partly with the latter. 

Rightly, between entirely divine forms—which are so separated from matter that they cannot be joined—and entirely natural forms—which are so joined that they cannot be separated—middle forms are interposed. These are partly natural and partly divine; they are so separated that they can be joined, and so joined that they are able to be separated. This is indeed shown by their powers and actions, which are distinguished by such a difference between conjunction and separation. Finally, it is not without reason that between the sense—which is both in the form of the body and requires an instrument—and the angelic intellect—which is free from both—there is the human intellect, which is indeed the form of the body, but requires no bodily instrument. This opinion is both more probable according to the common judgment of men and most in harmony with the books of Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Themistius. We have already sufficiently refuted Dicaearchus together with the Epicureans in the preceding books; next, rejecting Averroes with all our strength, we have approved the interpretation of Avicenna and Alganteles—indeed, the very opinion of Plato and Aristotle. For from the foundations we have laid elsewhere, we shall show it is probable that among forms which are bound to the body only by giving it life, there is a middle form which both gives life to the body and understands, so that the image of the divine countenance does not succumb everywhere to matter, but conquers it in some respect. # ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

<margin>1</margin>The <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: Idearum; in Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal patterns in the mind of God</note> of divine things are like the shapes of a gold seal, and the things themselves are like the figures impressed into wax. If the impression in every piece of wax turned out blurry and confused, you would call the person who pressed the seal incompetent. In the same way, the divine mind—which moves matter because it yearns to see its own likeness reflected there—might perhaps seem incompetent if it never achieved its goal. But it will never achieve it unless forms of this kind appear in bodies, ruling over their own bodies almost as God rules the world, and reflecting back upon themselves and upon God through the power of understanding, just as God turns back toward Himself. Indeed, the divine mind, by stirring matter through the motion of the heavens, is said to generate or bring forth something—or rather, everything—even if it does not produce every single form through a change in matter or draw it out from matter itself. Since the very first starting point from which this universal generation or production begins is the divine mind itself, the final goal where such generation concludes must also be a kind of divine mind. <margin>1</margin>The ultimate goal of generation lies in that which is born, and that goal is its <term>form</term> <note>original: forma; the "organizing principle" or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is</note>. Therefore, there must be some divine mind that serves as the form of matter. For if the process of generation started by fire ends in the form of fire, and that started by a human ends in a human figure, why should the generation or production arranged by the divine mind not end in a mind? Generation does not end except in a form, which is the specific and most internal perfection of the thing generated. If an art, using its tools, finally grants to matter a form that is most similar to the form held within the mind of the craftsman; if the nature of the human body, in the process of generation, moves the seed first to the form of milk, then to blood, then to flesh, and finally to a man; if fire moves wood first toward a trembling, then to heat, then finally to fire itself; what is to stop the divine mind from moving the matter of the world first toward the forms of the elements, second to mixed bodies, third to plants, fourth to beasts, and fifth to the form of itself—that is, to a mind that is the form of the generated body, so that the face of the parent might shine forth in its most noble offspring? 

However, it moves matter toward the lower forms by "drawing them out" <note>original: educendas; a technical term meaning to bring a potentiality out of matter, like carving a statue out of stone</note> from the matter itself through change; but it moves matter toward the mind by "pouring it in" <note>original: inducendam; meaning the mind is added to the body from the outside by God</note> through a divine act. For if the mind were merely drawn out of matter, it could not truly be a "mind." This belongs to the divine order: that while the higher forms are neither drawn out nor poured into the rational soul, and the lower forms are both poured in and drawn out, the soul itself is poured in, not drawn out. And if the form of a mixed body is so valuable that it possesses the power and action of the elements, and the form of plants is so strong that it does whatever the lower forms do, and likewise the form of beasts, who could deny that the mind possesses the power and action of the lower forms? In this way, its very essence, while it understands, is also felt through the body and nourishes the body. <margin>1</margin>Indeed, since a higher nature both includes and surpasses the entire power of a lower nature, and will perform the same work as the lower nature as long as the same tools are supplied to it, that mind which sees within us must be able to perform the work of nourishing and sensing no less than the "thinking soul" does. Certainly, if the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: spiritus; a subtle vapor thought to connect the soul to the body</note> of our physical temperament is a sufficient instrument for the mind to serve its intelligence—as the <term>Averroists</term> <note>followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroes, who argued that the intellect was a separate entity from the individual person</note> believe—it will much more serve the substance of the mind for sensation and nourishment. And because nature does not abound in superfluous things, there is only one primary form within us, just as in other bodies, since higher forms contain the lower ones. 

We gather that the human mind is the lowest of all minds, both from the fact that it moves from rest into action and back again, and because it receives the opportunity for understanding from physical bodies. In this way, it is closest to bodies, which are brought from potentiality into action because of matter, are moved from the outside, and take their opportunity for operating from the outside. If it is the lowest of minds and is therefore joined to the highest body, and because of this proximity it draws from bodies its rest and external motion, then the human body (the most noble of all composite bodies) must in turn receive two things from the mind: namely, action and internal motion. Action is received from the form, and internal motion from the soul. <margin>1</margin>Therefore, the lowest mind is made into the form and soul of the highest body. Indeed, just as matter, which is the final limit of physical things, is not itself a specific body, so the human mind, which is the final limit of minds, is not some "separate" mind, but is joined to the body by nature. And because it needs the senses to begin its understanding—perceiving bodies through the senses and, as it were, drinking in their forms—nature ordained that there should be the greatest possible kinship between sense and intellect, so that this kind of "drinking in" could happen most easily and perfectly. But there can be no greater kinship, nor can it happen more easily or perfectly, than if they exist in the same substance.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind is the ultimate goal of creation and must be the "form" of the human body rather than a separate entity. He explains that just as lower life forms contain the powers of the elements, the human mind contains the powers of sensing and nourishing while also possessing the unique ability to reflect on God.</summary>

## MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...the soul possesses both mind and sense. And just as oysters, which are the lowest of all sentient beings, are so close to trees (which are the highest of all things lacking sense) that they are partly fixed to the earth like trees and partly use the sense of touch like sentient creatures, so too the human intellect—the lowest among all other minds—is joined to nature. It is joined to those <term>forms</term> <note>the "organizing principles" that give shape to physical matter</note> which are the highest among bodily things, so that it partly gives shape to the body as they do, and partly understands as the higher minds do. Justly so: for just as between fire and water, which are most distant from one another, there is air (which is hot like fire on one side and moist like water on the other), so between the angels and the souls of unthinking animals, which differ most widely, the **rational soul** is placed in between. It understands like the angels and it gives shape to the body like the animals. And if a form that is closer to matter is the "shadow" of one further removed from matter—just as the vegetative power is the shadow of the sensitive power, and the sensitive is the shadow of the intellective—it follows that the intellective soul is joined to matter through its own shadow, and therefore through its own life-giving act. 

A principal agent moves the agents that follow it. A principal goal compels all other goals. Principal matter supports all other types of matter. Therefore, the principal form gives shape to all other forms as much as possible. Since, therefore, in the order of natural things the mind is the principal form, it must in some way shape the other forms and take the place of them all. It could never achieve this unless it shaped matter that had been appropriately prepared beforehand by lower forms; then, as those lower forms cease their work, the mind experiences within itself the powers of the forms that follow. 

Furthermore, if natural motion reaches its goal, and if there is such an ascent in the hierarchy of forms that they strive more and more to transcend matter—yet the others do not transcend it—it is necessary that at least the final form of natural things reaches that goal. This form must not only shape matter but also, through some part of itself, entirely exceed matter. In that part where it exceeds body and time, it is joined to spirits and eternity through the act of understanding. The **Platonists** call such a form both "natural" and "divine," because it is the boundary between natural and divine forms. 

The minds that govern the celestial bodies are distributed in such a way that each one primarily moves a body, doing so from within and without any intermediary. Much more so should the human mind primarily move a single body, and stir it from within without any intermediary, since it is even closer to the body. Thus, it would seem contrary to the order of nature if that sublime mind were joined to the body without an intermediary, yet the lowest part were joined through a "thinking soul." 

Moreover, the order of nature requires that there be a pure good and an intellectual good: a pure intellect and an "animal" intellect, a pure soul and a bodily soul. The first is **God**, the second is an **angel**, the third is the **rational soul**. The **irrational soul** is the fourth. Therefore, unless there were somewhere a form that was partly intellectual and partly life-giving, the order of nature would be thrown into confusion. That order consists in this: God is pure Good; an angel is an intellectual good, but a pure intellect; the rational soul is an "animal" intellect, but a pure soul, because it sustains itself. The irrational soul is an "impure" soul because it requires the support of a body. 

Thus, because "being in oneself" precedes "being in another," and that which exists in itself overflows by its own perfection into something else, it has come to pass that there is Good in itself, good in the mind, mind in itself, mind in the soul, soul in itself, and soul in the body—just as the highest body of the heavens exists in itself, while all other things exist within it. If the entire genus of "soul" is more excellent than the entire genus of "body," then the genus of soul must be more extensive than that of the body. Thus, the lowest part of the animal genus surpasses the highest part of the bodily genus; and for this reason, the highest part of the animal genus surpasses the highest part of the bodily genus in a marvelous way. 

The result is that the rational soul not only enters the depths of the body by providing nourishment, but also surpasses the heights of the body by understanding. This is right, because that which is more excellent ought to depend less on that which is worse, rather than the other way around. Therefore, just as the lowest souls are, as it were, contained by bodies, and the middle souls are in a way both contained and containing, so the sublime souls entirely contain their bodies. They do not contain the body entirely unless they both penetrate it from within and surround it from without. And just as the soul receives intellectual life from above by surrounding the surface of the body, so it grants animal life to the lowest part by penetrating the body’s depths. While it surrounds the body (inasmuch as it comes from God), it is allotted the **active intellect**; while it resides within itself, it possesses the **potential intellect**. While it penetrates (inasmuch as it winds itself into the vital spirits), it feels and moves; while it immerses itself in the bodily fluids, it nourishes and sustains.

But let us return to the universal order of things. We can say that **God** is a form that neither adheres <note>to matter</note>, nor gives shape <note>in the way a soul shapes a body</note>, nor is shaped. The irrational soul, by contrast, is shaped, gives shape, and adheres. But an angel is indeed shaped by God, yet does not adhere...

<summary>Ficino describes the rational soul as the middle point of reality, bridging the gap between the eternal (angels) and the physical (animals). He argues that the soul "contains" the body rather than being "contained" by it, acting both as an intellect and a life-giving force.</summary>

...of matter, nor to form matter. Justly, therefore, between the <term>angel</term> <note>original: "angelum"; the OCR reads "angulum" (angle), but context confirms "angelum" (angel) is intended</note> and the irrational soul, we shall place the **rational soul**, which is endowed with such a nature that it does not remain stuck in matter, yet it is formed by higher things and gives form to lower things. Furthermore, that Platonic distinction found in the metaphysics of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian philosopher whose works on metaphysics deeply influenced Renaissance thinkers</note> seems highly commendable: namely, that in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>the realm of pure thought and spirit, as opposed to the physical world</note> one must proceed from the highest Intelligible toward many intellects, as if from a shaper to the powers that can be shaped from it. 

First, one proceeds from that Absolute Being to the absolute intellects, which do not decline from that state in any way. Second, one moves to those intellects that turn slightly toward sensible things—that is, things perceived by the senses—only for the purpose of governing them from the outside, so that such a duty seems to happen to them, as it were, externally. Third, one moves to those intellects which, as far as is possible in an intellectual nature, naturally decline toward sensible things—that is, they must govern them from within through life and motion. In no other way is the sensible world perfectly connected with the intelligible world, and the lower things disposed most beautifully and excellently according to the pattern of the higher things. From this, however, follows a certain fourth degree, though it is a "shadowy" one as some believe; it is the "knot" of minds with bodies—namely, the species of **irrational lives**—which the Platonists believe follow the minds like shadows proceeding through bodies.

But let us return again to divine things. No one denies that God exists, but the very "being" of God is not determined by any specific "kind" of being through which he becomes "this" or "that." Otherwise, God would be composed of a common nature of being and some added difference (that is, a specific property of being). Therefore, **Being Itself** is absolute, circumscribed by no limits; it exists as something utterly infinite, an immense root that contains and produces all those things that have "this" or "that" kind of being. For all composition flows from a simple source. 

Therefore, angels have being, but each of them has a "certain" kind of being—that is, with this or that property within one species of angel or another. For this reason, the being of an angel is not infinite like the Divine Being. It no longer contains the entire, untouched fullness of all being, nor does it exist as "all being," but is instead enclosed within one certain species of things, through which it is limited to a single mode of being.

For it is right that the Divine Being—which precedes the <term>Ideas</term> <note>the eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the mind of God</note> (that is, the species) and distributes being to things flowing from itself through those species—should itself be drawn into species, and therefore into different modes of being for different species. Thus, angelic being is limited within the angelic species. However, the **angelic species** (which we also call the <term>essence</term> <note>the "what-ness" or core nature of a thing</note>), which is the foundation of such being, is in a certain way infinite. It is not infinite in the way God is, but because it remains consistent with itself and preserves the entire integrity of its species; it receives nothing into itself beyond the species and the properties of that species, since it does not approach any lower nature by whose "contagion" it might be infected. 

But if this angelic essence did not differ from its being, its being would also be called infinite, since it would subsist in itself and through itself. However, to be infinite in both ways and to exist through oneself is a property of God alone. Likewise, if an angel's being did not differ from its essence, since "being" is an <term>act</term> <note>in philosophy, an "act" is the fulfillment or reality of a thing, as opposed to its "potential"</note>, then the angel would be pure act alone. But since participation only happens through <term>potential</term>, the angel would participate in nothing else and would be utterly simple in every way—which can only apply to God. Thus God is entirely infinite, because He exists as being alone, and as "the whole" and "all" of being.

The angel is finite according to its **being**, but infinite according to its **essence**; add to this that it is also infinite in a certain way according to its power and operation. For it is not hindered by the obstacle of any lesser thing, nor by care or anxiety, from always exercising its entire power (however great that may be) in its work. 

The **form of the body**, such as the **rational soul** is, because it exists in a certain species (just like the angel), also has a finite being. Its essence, however, is partly infinite and partly finite. It is **infinite** insofar as it never loses anything belonging to its species. For its nature is a vital and rational act, which it neither ever loses nor interrupts. But it is **finite** because it admits something beyond its species (or the principles of its species)—namely, this or that "affection" or inclination toward a specific habit of a human body. Through this inclination, it becomes the life-giving form of the body and is numbered among the multitude of bodies. Insofar as the essence of this soul is infinite, it exceeds the capacity of the body and leads an intellectual life. Insofar as it is finite, it has a proportion with the body and leads a corporeal life with it. In the former, infinite power and operation flourish; in the latter, by contrast, they are finite. Finally, the **corporeal form** is finite in every respect: according to being, essence, 

<margin>virtue,</margin>

...power, and action. It is finite in its **being** because its being is circumscribed by the limits of a certain species. It is finite in its **essence**, both because it receives many accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties, like the color of hair on a person, which can change without the person ceasing to be human</note> beyond its species, and because it does not preserve its own vigor entirely. Indeed, its nature is an effective or vital <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the realization of a potential</note>, yet it undergoes passions and destruction within the body. It is finite in its **power** and **action**, since its power is increased and diminished, and any operation extends only as far as the dispositions of its instruments and subjects allow. Such are all forms lower than the rational soul. 

It is necessary for these four grades of things to exist in nature so that we may descend gradually from that which is altogether infinite, through mixed intermediaries, to those things which are altogether finite. Indeed, this gradation could not be continued unless—just as in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>the realm of eternal truths and spirits</note> there is the infinite and the finite, namely God and the angel—so too in the sensible world there are two images of those: something that is in a certain way infinite, and something that is altogether finite, namely the **rational soul** and any lower form. The former is a form of the body but is not corporeal; the latter is both of the body and corporeal. 

Again, let us descend by these steps:
1. **God** possesses being from Himself, in Himself, and for Himself. 
2. The **Angel** possesses being not from himself (since he is from God), but in himself and for himself. 
3. The **Form of the body**, such as the rational soul, does not have being from itself (since it is made by another), nor does it preserve its being for itself alone (since it communicates it to the body), yet it has being **in itself**, because its being is founded upon its own essence, and the act of its essence is its own. Just as the soul of the Sun, according to the Platonists, shines in itself and illuminates the Sun, yet in such a way that it does not lose its own light. 
4. But the **Corporal form** has being neither from itself nor for itself, just like the soul. Nor, however, does it have being in itself. For it is so dedicated to matter that a composite is made from it and the matter, in which "being" itself is properly founded, and of which being is the act; however, its form is not the proper foundation of its own being. 

Nature must not lack this order. But it would lack it, were there not some form of the body that is not corporeal. Similar to this seems to be that distinction of our **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Elements of Theology" deeply influenced Ficino</note>. He says the "Divine" is to be called the Intelligible itself; "Pure Intellect," however, belongs to itself and is in itself. Then "Animal Intellect" <note>the soul</note> belongs both to itself, because it possesses its being in its own essence, and to another, because from its own rational life it pours out another life lacking reason—like an image—into the body. After these comes "Nature," that is, the vital complexion; like a shadow resulting from the life infused by the soul into the body, it is to be judged as belonging only to another, that is, to the body, with which it is extended and divided. Finally, the "Body," because of its diverse and thoroughly dissipatable condition, is properly called "the other." Here it appears that in the very order of things, the animal intellect, or the intellectual soul, holds the middle place. 

**Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a student of Plotinus</note>, following the mind of **Plato** in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, seems to bring forth a similar order, thus distinguishing the universe into six grades: he proves that some things only *are* (**being**), some only *become* (**becoming**), others both **are and become** simultaneously, and others **become and are** simultaneously. Besides these, he places something "above being and becoming" over all things, and he places something "below being and becoming" under all things.

Indeed, he says that "Being" is the whole latitude of minds, whether they are minds in themselves or minds in souls. On the other hand, he wishes "Becoming" to be the latitude of sensible things, whether they are elemental or celestial. The "Being and Becoming" simultaneously is the genus of souls. And in turn, "Becoming and Being" is the very nature of the universe that gives life to the whole, which is the summit of those things that "become." Insofar as it is distributed through bodies, it is said to "become." But insofar as it is not at all corporeal in itself, it is said to "be." Finally, over all things he places **The Good**, and under all things he subjects **Matter**. 

To what end is this? So that we may understand that the order of the universe cannot be continued unless there are intellectual forms that are simultaneously the givers of life to bodies; for only to these can it belong to be said to "be and become" at the same time. They "be" through a substance that is entirely indivisible and through the sudden intuition of the intelligence itself; but they "become" through the temporal discourse of their remaining actions. This Pythagorean reasoning persuades us that such a form must exist. It pleases **Timaeus of Locris** <note>a character in Plato's "Timaeus," traditionally considered a Pythagorean philosopher</note> that God the Father broods over Matter the Mother to generate forms as offspring. In the Father is the effective fecundity of all forms; in the Mother is the receptive fecundity of forms, especially corporeal ones. In the Father is the effective act of forms; in the Mother is the receptive power of forms. Offspring are born similar to the Mother: namely, the many forms that emerge from the depth of matter and are finally submerged back into the same, just as the shape of a golden vessel comes from the gold and returns into the gold. Again, it is necessary that some offspring be born...

<summary>Ficino uses Neoplatonic hierarchies from Proclus and Porphyry to define the soul as a middle being that both "is" (eternally) and "becomes" (temporally). He distinguishes the soul's self-founded existence from the matter-dependent existence of lower physical forms.</summary>

Ficino is distinguishing between "material forms"—which are heavily dependent on matter (the "mother")—and "rational souls," which derive more directly from the divine "father." The catchword "gitudine" from the previous page's footer likely refers to "multitudine" or a similar term, though the text here begins by contrasting the influence of the parental principles.</meta>

<page-num>335</page-num>
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV. ###

...none are very similar to the father, provided that the father has more influence than the mother in this union. Forms of this kind, leaping out from the father's **act** <note>In this context, the "father" represents the active, formative principle or God, while the "mother" represents passive matter.</note> onto the face of matter, and from there bouncing back into the father's act, are just as brightness reflects from the Sun onto gold and back to the Sun. Indeed, those forms more similar to the mother lie hidden, in a way, within the bowels of matter first, like the shape of a vase within the gold. They also lie hidden in the powers of the world’s souls and bodies, which are the instruments of the divine craftsman. God rescues them from the womb of matter through the motions of the world, and brings them into **being** <term>esse</term> <note>original: "esse"; the state of existence or being</note> according to the capacity of the matter. 

But to whom does this kind of being properly belong? To that **composite** body which is fashioned from this generation. Why? Because the instrument through which they are generated by God is itself a composite. If, therefore, the immediate cause is a composite, and the effect usually turns out very similar to the immediate cause, it follows that what is properly produced is that which is a composite. Truly, it is to that which is produced that "being" properly belongs. Therefore, that being is proper to the composite. For it does not arise from form or matter alone, but from the composite. 

Add to this that such forms cling to matter according to their potential, in a certain way, before they achieve being. And they are produced into being in the womb of matter at the very moment the being of the composite is completed. Because they truly come to be by clinging to the power of matter itself and receive their being there, they retain their being by adhering to that same matter in **act** <note>the state of being fully realized or functional</note>, and they exist for as long as they cling to it. They do not, therefore, exist through their own being—since they are made, exist, and remain by clinging—but through the being of that composite of which they are parts, and which is the goal of generation. And rightly, since they have no being of their own, they possess no power or operation of their own. 

Such are the forms that seem more similar to the mother than to the father. But those which are more similar to the father, such as **rational souls**, are brought forth from the pure act of God; therefore, they are suddenly led to the act of being. For this reason, they have being within themselves first, as it were, and are joined to matter afterward. They have being before they cling to the body, and they retain being before the body in the very order of nature, and after the body, they have their own being within themselves. They have a certain choice of their own within themselves, not shared with the body. They impart their being to the body in some part, and they perform certain operations in the body and through the body.

->How the mind approaches the body,<-
->Chapter III.<-

**B**ut in what way do they impart their being to the body? Do they mix with it? Not at all. For that which is mixed is ruined and confused. Do they touch the body? By no means. For touch is proper to two bodies. Are they enclosed within it? Not that either. For nothing is enclosed by a place except a body. What, then, do these forms do to the body when they communicate their being to it? They penetrate it everywhere with their **essence**, and they dedicate the power of their essence to it. 

Since being is drawn from essence, and operation flows from power, by joining their essence they impart being; by dedicating their power, they communicate operations, so that from the meeting of soul and body, one being of the living creature emerges, and one operation. This being indeed belongs to the soul itself through its essence, but becomes the body's through participation. The soul does not submerge its own being into the body, but raises the body up to itself. Nor does the body take in the whole fullness of that essence, but touches something of it according to its own nature; nor does the body sustain the soul, but is sustained by it. 

In what way a non-extended form might fill the mass of the body will be clearly understood by anyone who considers that even an extended form relates to the body in such a way that any part of it relates equally to any part of the matter, and vice versa. Thus, we can imagine any part of this form to be in individual portions of matter, and to form them in such a way that the whole is present at any point. But let us take away extension from this form, while meanwhile leaving the duty of forming the body. We can do this. For to "form" is something else, and more excellent, than to be "extended." Therefore, if matter is indeed extended but does not form, some form of matter can form and yet not be extended. Thus we shall see an indivisible form forming the whole at once—the whole matter and any part of it equally. And if that **Pythagorean** <note>Refers to the followers of Pythagoras, who used geometry to explain the structure of the universe.</note> saying is true, namely that a point by its motion makes a line, a line a surface, and finally a surface by a similar motion makes depth, we can easily imagine that the same point by its motion [spreads] itself, whole and indivisible, through the length...

<summary>Ficino explains that while material forms depend on the body for their existence, the rational soul has an independent being granted by God. He argues that the soul permeates the body without being "mixed" or "enclosed" by it, using the analogy of a geometric point to show how an indivisible spirit can animate physical matter.</summary>

Here, Ficino transitions into how the soul, as a point-like substance, interacts with the three-dimensional bulk of the body.</meta>

...[len]gth, width, and depth. Hence it happens that wherever you divide or touch [the body], you find a point. If this point were indeed an accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or attribute (like color or shape) that cannot exist on its own but must be "supported" by a substance.</note>, it would necessarily be supported by the bulk of the body. But if it were a substance, like the soul subsisting in itself, it will be present to the bulk, yet separated from the bulk, it will remain perpetually in itself.

## How the Mind is Present to the Body. Chapter III.

**I**s this soul, so excellent, joined to unformed matter without a medium? A more perfect form always contains less perfect forms within itself, just as a quadrangle contains a triangle. If the rational soul has the most outstanding power—that of understanding—it also possesses the powers of sensing, nourishing, and ruling. Therefore, within the power of the rational soul, the sensitive and nutritive souls are enclosed, as is the form of mixed bodies <note>Mixed bodies refer to physical objects composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) but lacking life, such as minerals.</note> that lack life. The rational soul approaches matter endowed with all these forms, and through its own form or power—which takes the place of mixed bodies lacking life—it clings most closely to unformed matter. In that matter, it establishes the temperament <term>complexio</term> <note>original: "complexionem"; the specific balance or "complexion" of the four elements and humors that constitutes a body's physical state.</note> of the four elements, while it binds the parts of matter into one and tempers the elements. Through its form which has the power of plants, it clings to the body composed of matter and temperament; it grants that temperament of elements movement toward any part of space, which is called life. Through the form proper to animals, it accommodates itself to them and generates the spirit <note>The "spiritus" was considered a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as the "instrument" or bridge allowing the incorporeal soul to move the physical body and receive sensory data.</note>, the instrument of the senses. Through the rational form, it commands the rest. Thus, through its lowest power it is the form of matter; through the second, it is the form of a mixed body; through the third, a plant; through the fourth, the form of an animal—indeed, it is the form of forms. From this it follows that the rational soul forms bodies more than other forms do, because it forms through more powers; and it forms more purely, because it touches unformed matter with its "foot" <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor: the soul's "foot" is its lowest faculty (matter-shaping), while its "head" is its highest faculty (intellect).</note> up close, but with its "head" it looks out from a distance.

Just as fire, out of the four degrees of its own heat, pours the first into cold wood, the second into wood already warm, the third into wood already heated by the first two, and adds a fourth on top of those three, through which it shines from above. So the essence of the rational soul is filled with four certain degrees: the mixed, the vital, the sensual, and the intellectual. It applies the first to matter; it employs the second to the first; it adds the third to the second; and adds the fourth to the third. Here it now seems to form matter according to its whole essence as well as according to all its degrees; although it forms in the same way according to the whole essence, yet it forms in different ways according to each degree. For the first is the form of matter; the second is the form of the mixed body; the third is the form of the vital form; the fourth is the form of forms of all corporeal things. Through three degrees the soul becomes particular <note>i.e., tied to a specific, individual physical existence.</note>; through the fourth, it remains absolute and capable of absolute forms. Is it any wonder if, in this most excellent degree, some power and operation appears very similar to divine things? This degree is closest to those divine things precisely because it is farthest from matter. We see this even in some forms of mixed bodies: due to a temperament agreeable to the celestial bodies <note>Ficino refers to the astrological and "natural magic" idea that certain physical mixtures can "tune in" to the powers of the stars.</note>, some power and action results that is foreign to the elements of which that body is composed, but is in harmony with the celestial things which it resembles in temperament. Nor should it seem surprising that the soul, although it is the form of the body, nevertheless has some power not shared with the body. Angels are not drawn out of matter either according to their essence or according to their preparation for essence; whereas irrational souls <note>Animal or plant souls.</note> are drawn out through both. Therefore, because rational souls are intermediate, their condition must be intermediate. They cannot sprout from matter through their essence, yet they do sprout from matter according to "preparation" <note>The physical body must be "prepared" or organized correctly to receive the soul, but the soul's essence is not created by the matter.</note>. Therefore, they will indeed gush forth according to preparation, but by no means according to essence. If power follows essence, then no power of an angel is shared with the body. But every power of beasts belongs to the soul and body together, because it is drawn from matter along with the essence. However, the power of the rational soul is in its essence alone, descending with it from on high. And since a soul of this kind exceeds the proportion of the body, and is not "in" the body, but rather the body is "in" it, the body does not encompass all its power. The body touches only a small part of that power, because the soul—which according to preparation depends in a way on matter—is affected by the body to such an extent that it [accommodates] its inner powers to it...

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchical relationship between the rational soul and the body, arguing that the soul contains the lower forms (nutritive, sensitive) within itself and acts as a "form of forms" that governs the body without being entirely dependent on it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous chapter regarding the soul's relationship to the body. While the previous page discussed the soul as a "point-like" substance, Ficino now moves to describe the soul as a necessary "middle" between purely spiritual beings and purely material ones, before exploring different analogies for how a non-physical mind can inhabit a physical body.</meta>

<page-num>337</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.</header>
<sig>Y</sig>
<meta>catchword: nature</meta>

...will accommodate <note>original: "accommodet"; this word continues from the previous page's catchword.</note> [the body] by a certain proportion, and through it and in it, the soul may freely operate. Nor should it be considered absurd for a rational substance to be joined to matter, because the order of nature cannot be preserved otherwise. For there is a certain spirit <note>Ficino uses "spiritus" (spirit) here to mean an incorporeal substance or life-force.</note> separated from matter, which is rational and incorruptible, such as an angel. There is also a spirit that is joined to matter, which is irrational and corruptible, such as the soul of beasts. These two are far apart. Indeed, they belong to the same genus of "spirit," yet they differ from each other by three distinctions. 

What then is the "middle" between these? It cannot be a spirit that is only "separated," for if it is separated, it must also be rational and immortal. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "rational," for such a spirit must additionally be either joined or separated. It cannot be a spirit that is only "incorruptible," because it would necessarily also have to be rational. It cannot be a spirit that is only "separated and rational," for it would then also have to be immortal. It cannot be a spirit that is only "separated and incorruptible," for if it possesses these two, it also possesses reason; since it exercises neither sense nor nutrition, its existence would be in vain unless it possessed the operation of reason. It cannot be a spirit that is only "joined and irrational," for such a thing is also mortal. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "joined and immortal," for that which shares an immortal life with the angels also shares their intelligence. Finally, it cannot be a spirit that is "joined and rational" yet "transient" <note>original: "caducus"; meaning falling or subject to death.</note>, because if it shares intelligence with the angels—which is a certain reflection of its own life back into itself—it must also share their life.

Therefore, there must be a certain spirit in the body that is the "middle" of these extremes, which is both rational and incorruptible. It should agree with both because it is a spirit. It differs from the angel because it is joined to a body; it differs from the beast because it is rational. It properly agrees with the angel because it is immortal; it properly agrees with the beast because it is joined. Indeed, since there must be a middle between those extremes that is in some way equally distant from both and an equal participant in both, it is necessary that there be a spirit which is partly separated, rational, and eternal, and partly joined, irrational, and transient. Such is especially the human soul: in its highest part are those first three conditions [separated, rational, eternal], in its lowest part are the following three [joined, irrational, transient], and in its middle part all six are mixed together and tempered by "musical ratios" (as Plato says) <note>Ficino refers to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the World Soul being composed according to harmonic and mathematical proportions.</note>.

### How the Mind is in the Body. Chapter V.

**B**ut in what way is the rational soul joined to the body? Not like one solid body to another solid body. For these solid bodies, which are joined by touch alone, are neither entirely "together" <note>original: "simul"; meaning occupying the same space or acting in perfect unison.</note>, nor do they act together, whereas the soul and body are entirely together and operate together. Furthermore, it seems most absurd to compare the soul—the most effective origin of vital motion—to dense and thick bodies. The more these are said to possess "corporeal properties," the less they seem to possess natural action and vital motion. For if they are divided, they remain scattered, nor do they immediately return to their union as purer things are accustomed to do. On the contrary, those things which have the least corporeal thickness easily avoid a blow when they seem to be struck by more solid things; when they are penetrated, they penetrate most effectively; and when they are divided, they return to their unity so swiftly that they hardly seem to have departed from it. 

Therefore, as we were saying, the soul is not joined to the body like one solid to another. Again, it is not like water in wine: for these "soft" bodies lose their former power through mutual mixing and cease to be what they were. Since the soul is incorporeal and does not have matter in common with this body, it cannot be mixed and confounded with the qualities of this body. 

Is it perhaps like the heat of fire in water? This way is better: for heat is not a body, and so it is more similar to the soul. But even this is not enough for us: for a part of the heat is in a part of the water, not the "whole in the whole." Perhaps it is like a voice in the air: for a voice is perhaps one and the same as a whole in any part of the air, since the whole is heard in every part. It moves the ears and announces something to the intellect, just as the soul is "whole in any tiny part" of the body. It rules the body while simultaneously understanding. But the voice has something fragile about it and is subject to "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon or changed by an external force.</note>. It is born from the "breaking of the air" <note>A traditional Aristotelian definition of sound as *fractio aeris* (the breaking/vibration of air).</note> and is pushed back by a light breeze. 

However, I have in the meantime something more similar: namely, the image of a color coming through the air to the eyes. This is spiritual <note>Here "spiritual" means non-material or light-like.</note>; it runs in a moment, reaches far, occurs as a whole everywhere, does not suffer the force of the wind, paints the air, and forms the vision. That is indeed very similar, but it differs in this: that it does not rule or govern the air.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is a unique "middle" substance connecting the eternal world of angels with the mortal world of animals, using various physical analogies to explain how the incorporeal mind can inhabit the body without being a physical part of it.</summary>
