<meta>This page continues Ficino's exploration of how the soul inhabits the body, transitioning from theoretical definitions to vivid analogies involving a ship's pilot and the sun's light.</meta>

<page-num>318</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...governs, <note>original: "nat"; continuing the word "gubernat" from the previous page.</note> just as the soul governs the body. But look: a pilot governs a certain ship, and he is in the ship. Is the soul related to the body in this same way? No, because the pilot does not "fill" the ship; he is not present to the whole of it, nor does he move it by his own self alone, but through the rudder. Yet now, in this rudder, I have found a "soul," since when the sailor rules the ship through it, the art of steering is not only in the sailor but also passes into the rudder. It becomes whole in the whole rudder and rules it; this very thing is the "soul" of the rudder. But this art contributes nothing of its own nature to the substance of the rudder; it merely agitates it while being agitated from the outside. The soul, however, contributes something to the body and moves it by its own nature.

I ask you, O Philosopher, lift your eyes to heaven! You seek a celestial soul on the earth or in the sea. Look up at the light of the Sun. This light is one and indivisible—so to speak—present as a whole in every part of the air. It illuminates the air and heats it, yet it takes nothing from the air, nor does it suffer any force from any source, nor is it stained by any filth. The air fluctuates with the winds, but the light remains, as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founding philosopher of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and heavily relied upon.</note> wishes. It comes from the Sun; in a moment, it passes into the air. It is not separated from the Sun again; it is even reflected back toward the Sun. Without the light, the air is "dead," since it is cold and dark, destitute of any form. 

Light has two qualities: brightness <note>original: "fulgorem"</note> and heat. It exercises its brightness in the air, yet does not give it over to the air; but it does grant heat to the air. Hence, when the Sun sets, the light is not extinguished (as Plotinus thinks), but the whole light suddenly withdraws along with the Sun, while the remnants of heat are left behind deep into the night—as if the air had become a participant in the heat, but not the brightness. But let it be, if you like, that it does not bestow brightness. What else is the "being" of that light than to shine? Without that light, the air does not shine; without the air, the light still shines. Indeed, the opinion of Plotinus is true: light does not depend on anything transparent in any way, but depends continuously on the Sun alone, and always accompanies it, insofar as it is a certain perpetual act of the Sun itself. 

But let us proceed to the rest. Light approaches the air; the light shines there just as it did before in itself; the air shines, which did not shine before. The light shines through itself; the air shines through the light. Is the "shining" of the light and the "shining" of the air through light two different things? Not at all; otherwise, the air would remain bright when the light departed. Therefore, there is one "shining" by which both shine; but it belongs to the light by its essence, and to the air by participation. Therefore, it is one thing that somehow belongs to both; yet the light is not "in" the air (though it is commonly said to be), but the air is "in" the light—if indeed that which is narrower and subject to being acted upon <note>original: "passioni"; meaning the capacity to receive external impressions or changes.</note> is contained by that which is more ample and incapable of suffering. 

Similarly, the soul of man is sent by God into matter; it passes into it suddenly, yet does not depart from God. Rather, it does both at once: it rules the body, and it also reaches the very truth of all things (which is God himself) in a certain miraculous way (as Plotinus argues) through the intellect. Again, just as light is reflected back to the Sun, so the soul is reflected back to God through the will, insofar as it always hungers for the goodness of all things, which is God himself. It fills the body without hindrance, as light fills the air, and it is similarly present "whole to the whole." While the body suffers, the soul does not suffer, but rather perceives and judges those sufferings. It does not flow away as the body glides toward decay, but stands firm. 

The soul has two principal powers: the judicial <note>The power of judgment and reason.</note> and the vital. It does not hand over judgment to the body, but performs it itself. It lends or grants life to the body, insofar as it communicates a certain "image-like" power of its own life to it. Hence, the soul alone judges, not the body. However, both the body and the soul "live." Therefore, when the soul departs, the sense-perception leaves immediately, but traces of life seem to remain in the body—namely, heat and motion. For the soul, "to be" is "to live," since the essence of the soul is life, through which the body formally lives. The "being" of a living creature is nothing other than "to live." Yet the "living" of the soul joined to the body is not one thing and the "living" of the composite being another; rather, just as both live through one and the same life (that is, the essence of the soul)—but the soul through its own life and the body through a borrowed one—so most people judge that they live through one life alone. Both are, and are called, "living things"—the soul by its own right, the body by another's. 

And, as we touched upon above, the soul is not "in" the body, although it appears so to those who, seeing the body but not seeing the soul, think the soul is hidden in the body as if in a little vessel. But those who look upon the soul entering the body from within, and from the outside stepping over it, embracing it, sustaining it, and moving this tiny dust, will undoubtedly confess that the body is in the soul. Who could doubt that the soul is ampler than the body, when in one part of itself it is equated to the body (namely, in its vital power), but in another part it exceeds it (namely, in its judicial faculty)? Thus the body, being narrower and unstable, is in the soul, which is utterly more ample and stable, just as that which is contained is in that which contains it. Therefore, although the whole soul is present to the body, the body is not present to the whole soul, but only to its lowest part—that is, the vital part. This seems to be confirmed by the fact that since the soul is by its power far 

->greater<- <note>original: "maior"; catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino uses the analogies of a ship's pilot and the sun's light to argue that the soul is not "contained" by the body, but rather that the body exists within the more "ample" and stable soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the body, moving from the analogy of light to the specific philosophical arguments for why the mind must be the "form" (the defining essence) of a human being.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

...greater than the body, and arises from the power of motion and amplification, it is necessary that the soul is not only present to the whole body, but also, as Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist who argued that the soul remains partially "un-descended" or superior to the physical realm even while animating it.</note> prefers, exceeds the body by its very presence. And because it is indivisible, wherever it is, it is there in its entirety. The body, however, just as it is not equal to the soul’s whole power, is also not equal to its whole presence. Plato sensed this in the *Timaeus*, when he said that the maker of the world placed the body within the soul. Again, in the tenth book of the *Republic*, where he says the body of the world turns "between the knees of Necessity"—that is, it is ruled and moved by the lowest part of the celestial soul. In the *Phaedrus*, he also affirmed that souls raise their heads above heaven.

But although the soul thus exceeds the body, it should not seem impossible to anyone that it draws matter to itself to such an extent that it creates a single composite thing. Since it is the proper nature of "forms" <note>In Platonic and Aristotelian thought, a "form" is the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> to perfect and bind matter to themselves, and to couple the parts of matter together, the more excellent a form is and the more it dominates matter, the more perfectly it can achieve this. If even the lowest forms do this, what prevents the sublime ones from doing so, provided they naturally desire it? If angelic minds do not do this, it arises from the fact that they have no inclination whatsoever to complete the species of any animal through their union. 

Yet all the Platonists and the ancient Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle.</note> maintained that this union is achieved by the higher minds. None of them can be found who did not affirm that the celestial spheres are animated by rational souls. Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus testify to this among the Platonists; among the Peripatetics, however, are Theophrastus, Avicenna, and Algazel <note>original: "Alganteles"; Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), the Persian theologian and philosopher.</note>. In this matter, Ptolemy, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note>, Zael, and Manilius, and the other principal authors of Astronomy seem to agree with us: they affirm that celestial bodies are endowed with divine souls and minds, and obey God himself, the ruler of all, like certain divine animals. 

And this is not without reason: for when they saw that certain things pertaining to human souls were foretold by the stars, they thought this could not happen unless the stars were animated, seeing future human actions and indicating them, in a way, by their own signals. Furthermore, just as the rays of those celestial bodies flow into our bodies, so the "rays" of their souls flow into our own minds. All things sent from those most orderly causes are ordered and good; yet they can be perverted by the diverse mixing of many causes around us and by the defect of matter. Thus, "Mercurial" prudence [from Mercury] is turned into malice, "Martian" magnanimity [from Mars] into ferocity, and "Venereal" charity [from Venus] into lust. It is similar for the rest, just as the rays of the Sun are sent as mild from their source, but here on earth are often received as scorching. But let us set these matters aside for now as superfluous to our present task.

->*That the mind is the form of the body is clear from human opinions and actions.*<-
->*First reason: because man is a rational animal.*<-

### Chapter VI.

**N**ot only does the order of natural things demonstrate that it is the same soul in man that both contemplates and feels (as we have declared in previous sections), but this is also shown by the opinion of the wise and by the nature of human operation. All philosophers have agreed in this opinion: that man is a specific kind of thing whose "proper difference"—the thing that makes him different from the beasts—is being "rational." Now, this "proper difference" must always be taken from the intrinsic form of the thing. For nothing differs in species from another except through its inner nature. 

However, "rational" is not derived from the "cogitative soul" <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic thought and processing sensory data.</note> alone, because in that there is only "particular reason" <note>Reasoning about specific, physical things.</note>; but man operates rationally toward the common good and honor through his words and deeds. Therefore, his defining difference is taken from universal reason, and this resides in the mind. The mind, therefore, is that form through which each of us is placed in the human species. 

If the mind were separated in its being from the man, a single species would not be made from the mind and this man together; and man would be more properly called "fleshy" because of his interior flesh, than "rational" because of an exterior reason. Nor should Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Andalusian philosopher who famously argued that there is only one "Active Intellect" shared by all humans, rather than each person having their own individual mind.</note> say that man is something assembled from a "cogitative animal" and a mind, and that the whole is called rational because of one of its parts—just as a body is called "snub-nosed" because the nose is snub. For first, the nose is continuous with the body, but the mind is by no means continuous with the cogitation. Second, a mind of this sort is a species separate from the cogitative animal...

He begins a specific refutation of Averroes, asserting that "rationality" must come from an internal human mind rather than an external shared intellect.</summary>

...this living being is a species unto itself, separate from the mind. The title of a <term>specific difference</term> <note>In traditional logic, a "difference" is the characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a broader group (genus). For humans, the "difference" is "rationality."</note> does not pass from one species to a separate species. And just as, according to Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was a Spanish-Muslim philosopher. His followers, the Averroists, argued that all humans share one single, eternal "Possible Intellect," a view Ficino strongly opposes here to protect the concept of individual immortality.</note>, the mind is not called "cogitative" or "sensual" because of the thinking soul it approaches, so too the thinking soul should not be called "rational" or "intellectual" because of the mind. Furthermore, the title of the "difference" will not pass to some third thing made from them. For one difference requires one specific species, and vice versa. But those two [the mind and the soul] do not form one species, because they do not come together into one essence or one way of being.

It is altogether ridiculous for a man to receive the "difference" by which he is human from a single, separate mind. For in that case, individual persons would be one single human being but many animals, and the nature of the species would remain universal, while the nature of the <term>genus</term> <note>A "genus" is a general category, like "animal."</note> would have been made particular. It is no less ridiculous to place the human species in such a "heap," because just as it would not be simply one, so it would not be (so to speak) a "being" in the simple sense, nor a substantial species of things, but a chance pile. This is especially true because one true thing does not naturally arise from two things that already exist as perfect species in their own right; rather, a "false" unity is formed, bound together by something else. For something that can exist entirely on its own does not throw itself into the lap of another, nor does it naturally admit another within itself when it is self-sufficient. On the contrary, since every thing is distinguished by its own actions, and action is the principle of separation, those things that exist in actuality resist being joined. But both Mind and the living being subsist in actuality, and they cannot be coupled by another, as we will show in what follows. 

However, Aristotle teaches in his book *On Ethics* <note>original: "de Moribus," referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> that there is a universal reason in the soul by which we feel and live, and that because of this, we are called "rational." In the first book, he says that the mind is in the soul just as sight is in the eye. Likewise, he says there are two parts of the soul: the irrational and the rational. He divides the first into two: the nutritive part, which never obeys reason, and the sensitive part, which sometimes obeys. Similarly, he divides the second part into "active reason" and "speculative reason." He places the moral virtues in the will and the appetite that obeys reason; the principles of the moral virtues in active reason; and the speculative virtues in speculative reason. He does the same in the text where he also asserts that the rational power is a part of the human soul, and that this power does two things: namely, it understands and governs human affairs through prudence and art, and it contemplates natural and divine things through wisdom, which is contained in intelligence and science. In his book *Problems*, he says: "Nature, our parent and the author of all, has inserted two instruments into us, whose work we can use instead of external tools. I mean that she gave the hand to the body and the mind to the soul." For the mind is also to be numbered among the things bestowed upon us by nature, truly performing the role of an instrument. Thus far Aristotle.

### Second reason: because man understands.
### Chapter VII.

**A**ristotle <note>Decorated initial</note> intends that man is a living being composed of body and mind. Indeed, in the first book of the *Ethics*, he decides to discuss the happiness proper to man, which consists in man’s own proper activity. In the tenth book, he says that man’s proper activity is "understanding" <note>original: "intelligentia"</note>, because it is according to the mind—which is more properly ours than the senses—since it is the highest part of the soul. He adds that we either *are* our mind, or we are the mind most of all, even though he intends for us to be composites. It is as if the mind were the most natural form of man. 

In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, he says it is better to say that a human understands *through* the intellectual soul than that the soul itself understands. There, Averroes admits that understanding, properly speaking, belongs to the whole composite, just as sensation does. Every person also experiences in themselves that they understand something, and they do not do this except through the intellect. Moreover, how would we ourselves at this moment investigate the nature of the intellect unless we ourselves understood? And since we use the intellect more by our own choice than we use the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>—which is often forced upon us from elsewhere—the intellect is more familiar and more natural to us than imagination. If the Averroists are asked what exactly it is that "understands" properly (since Aristotle and Averroes say that "man" properly understands), they will answer that it is not the mind; for according to them, the mind is not man, nor is the cogitative animal man, because it lacks the power of understanding. Rather, they would call it a kind of "heap" made of the mind and this kind of animal, and the action of the mind...

He emphasizes that "understanding" is the unique activity of a human being, which requires the intellect to be intimately joined to the person.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s refutation of the Averroist position. Having argued that a separate mind cannot provide a "specific difference" to a human, he now tackles the argument that the mind’s actions can be attributed to the whole person through a "link" with the imagination.</meta>

[the act] which is intelligence, is attributed to the whole itself because the action of a part is often ascribed to the whole. This is indeed foolish. First, because such a "heap" <note>Ficino uses "heap" (*aceruus*) to mock the Averroist idea that a human is just a collection of a body, a soul, and a separate shared mind, rather than a unified being.</note> is not in any one species or one genus, nor does it possess that unity through which it could agree in a single operation, such as intelligence is. Next, because the action of a part is only ascribed to the whole when that part is either continuous with the other in one essence—just as we say a man "sees" because his eye sees—or when it exists as a single being within it. For example, we say fire "heats" through the process of heating, which comes from the heat and the <term>form</term>, which is such a part of the fire that by forming the other part of the fire (the matter), it leads it to a single being. Or, [it is ascribed to the whole] in a single effect of movement, such as when we say the soul, together with the arm, "brandishes" a sword, because such motion passes from the soul into the sword through the arm.

The mind, however, according to those thinkers <note>The Averroists.</note>, is neither continuous with the living being in one essence, nor in one being (as is well known), nor even in a single effect of movement. This is because intelligence never leaves the mind so that it could be communicated to anything other than the mind, nor is it carried out through any instrument. From this, they are forced to admit—contrary to their leader *Aristotle*—that it is properly said that the *mind* understands, but it cannot be said that the *man* understands, except in an extremely improper and absurd way.

Nor should they bring up that common example of the heavens—that the heavens are sometimes said to "move themselves" because one part of them moves another, and thus a man "understands" because a part of him understands. The example does not harmonize. For motion passes from the mind of the heavens into the heavens, but intelligence neither passes from the human mind into the living being, nor vice versa. Instead, they will assert something equally ridiculous: that the heavens are affirmed by some to "understand," even though only a part of them understands alone. Although one rarely hears it said of the heavens that they "understand," but of man it is said always; nevertheless, whoever says it would speak falsely and foolishly, unless perhaps he thinks that the mind shares a single species with the heavens.

Accordingly, whoever says that all men understand through a single mind—and a mind separated from men at that—is no less delusional than those who would say that all people see individual things through the same eye, which is removed from everyone. Finally, when they are asked why *we* are said to act based on what a separate mind does, they respond: because although that mind is not the <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> from which we have our being, it is nevertheless that from which we have our action. This response is indeed ridiculous, because it proves the same thing by means of itself.

The **Averroists** assert a certain tighter "link" (as they think) between the mind and the <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: *phantasia*. In Renaissance psychology, this is the faculty that handles sensory images (phantasms) before they are processed by the intellect.</note> of this living being, through which a man becomes "one" and "intelligent." This is supposedly because the mind draws the **species** <note>In this context, an "intelligible species" is the abstract concept or mental "form" of an object.</note> through which it understands from the **image** <note>original: *simulachrum*. Often used interchangeably with "phantasm," the sensory data stored in the imagination.</note> which the imagination has formed for itself through the senses. If the species is the form of the mind, and the image is the true form of the imagination, they believe it follows that as often as the species is linked with the image, so often the mind coincides with the imagination. They claim this linkage happens as often as the species depends on the image, which occurs whenever a man contemplates something.

We do not think a link of this kind is sufficient. For in what way can an "intelligible species" be the knot by which the imagination is bound to the mind? Such a species is of a nature that as long as it clings to the images of the imagination (as if to particular foundations), it remains particular and separate from the mind; and as soon as it is made universal in the mind, it is already far removed from the images of the imagination. Therefore, the species will never bind our imagination to the mind, for it cannot exist in both at the same time.

Indeed, the act of understanding is in the mind alone, which no one denies; but the mind is accustomed to understand that of which it has the species and likeness within itself. Therefore, from the very fact that the mind receives the species (through which something is understood) from the images of the imagination, it in no way follows that the *imagination* understands anything. Rather, it follows that the imagination itself, or its images, or its objects, *are understood*.

Whoever, therefore, joins the mind with the imagination and claims to constitute a single "understanding thing" out of the two, achieves nothing more than trying to make one single "understander" out of the person understanding and the thing understood outside the mind—just as if one were to make a single "seer" out of the sight and the thing seen. Unless, perhaps, one wants to argue that just as a single "heater" is made from the fire that heats and the air heated by it (when the ignited air heats a hand), so too from the understanding mind and the imagination—whether it is understood or moved in any way through intelligence—a single act of understanding is produced again, by which both understand the thing placed outside the imagination. If that were to happen, then that sublime and separate mind would have communicated intellectual power to the imagination, just as fire communicates heat to the air before it communicates the external act of heating. Indeed, it would be even more so, since the act of understanding is always enclosed within the intellect and does not migrate...

outward, from which it follows that intelligence cannot be handed over to anyone without a mind. And thus the mind would be within the human body as its **form**, which is what we are currently investigating. However, that conjunction cannot occur, because intelligence is not fulfilled through a physical instrument. Finally, to prove that intelligence is common to that entire "heap" <note>Referring to the Averroist "composite" of body, soul, and separate mind.</note>, they bring forward a connection of this sort: when the imagination (*phantasia*) conceives some image of things, that same image is immediately received in the mind. In the imagination, it is called a "phantasm" and appears particular and manifold; in the mind, however, it is called an <term>intelligible species</term> <note>The abstract essence of a thing understood by the intellect, as opposed to a sensory image.</note> and appears entirely absolute and one. Since it is one and the same form which shapes both the mind and the imagination at once, it forges a single composite out of both, which is called "man." Furthermore, because intelligence follows the intelligible species, and the species is the form of the composite, intelligence is properly assigned to the composite.

They show an example of this connection in the eye: within it is the "visual spirit," while light, colored by the image of a color, works its way into that visual spirit. In turn, the spirit penetrates the light, where the image of the color—which is in the light—shines exactly the same within the spirit; therefore, it makes one thing out of the light and the spirit. 

We, however, will deny that it is possible for the exact same form to be received simultaneously in an eternal subject and a corruptible one. For all forms have modes of being as diverse as the subjects by which they are received. Therefore, the form will have a far different existence in the mind than in the imagination. Where there are two distinct ways of being, and very different ones at that, there are also two very different forms, which are the principles of that being. 

Furthermore, even if we were to grant that the same form exists in both, not even then would intelligence be common. Indeed, intelligence exists only where the proper and intrinsic principles of understanding are found. These are two: the intellective power and the intelligible species in an entirely absolute mode. In the imagination, however, there is neither an intellective power nor an absolute mode of the intelligible species. Therefore, that "knot" of yours will do nothing to help a man understand, just as the image of a color—even if it is the same in the light and in the spirit—will not make the light, or the combination of light and spirit, "see." For only that visual spirit sees, in which alone exists both the power of seeing and the image of the color according to the visual mode. 

Nor should they further object to us that this composite "understands" because the imagination offers to the intellect whatever the intellect becomes. For in that case, a certain animal would similarly be constituted from light and spirit, which would be called a "seeing animal," and the whole would be said to see simply because the light offers to the spirit what it might see. 

Let the Averroists <note>Followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), who argued for a single, shared human intellect.</note> therefore eventually come to their senses and agree with their own **Aristotle**: that the thing by which something exercises its proper action is its own form and the producer of its species. The proper action of man is intelligence, through which he differs in his operation from the actions of brutes; therefore, through the intellect—as his most intimate form—he differs in being from the souls of irrational animals. Does not Aristotle show from this that the soul is the form because the animal lives and feels through it, while man understands through it, and strictly through the intellect? Thus, in that inquiry where he searched for the principle by which we understand, he finally handed down the nature of the mind, saying that the intellective part of the soul is that by which we understand. 

Moreover, because he uses the plural number, he shows that it is not some separate thing, but that **we** properly understand. And within the human soul itself, he places the intellect, both the "active" and the "capable" <note>The Agent Intellect and the Passive/Potential Intellect.</note>. In the second book of *On the Soul* (*De Anima*), he says this definition is common to every soul:

-> "The soul is the act of an organic physical body having life in potentiality." <note>original: "Anima est actus corporis physici organici potentia uitam habentis."</note> <-

Or,

-> "The soul is the principle of living, sensing, moving from place to place, and understanding." <note>original: "Anima est principium uiuendi, sentiendi, secundum locum mouendi, intelligendi."</note> <-

Again,

-> "The soul is that by which we live, and by which we sense, and understand primarily." <note>original: "Anima est id quo uiuimus, & quo sentimus, ac intelligimus primò."</note> <-

From these two descriptions, he concludes the first, as if through a syllogism. Since a syllogism must not be made from ambiguous terms, it follows that the word "act" (*actus*) signifies the same thing everywhere—that is, the natural act of the body. He reveals this immediately when he adds the division of substance into matter, its form, and that which is composed of others. He says that every soul is that form which is the second part of the composite. Again, where the power of understanding is, there also are the powers of sensing and nourishing. And just as a triangle is within a quadrangle, so is the vegetative soul within the sensitive, and these are within the intellective soul. And although he says the power of understanding is "separated"—that is, distinguished and separable from the others as the eternal is from the falling—he nevertheless says further that the intellect is distinguished from the others either by subject (as the ancients thought, who assigned reason to the head, anger to the chest, and lust...

He maintains that intellectual activity belongs to the individual soul, which contains vegetative and sensitive powers like nested geometric shapes.</summary>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV

...magnitude to the liver they seemed to attribute, or rather to be distinguished by a certain reason, just as on the same surface the concave is distinguished from the convex. Furthermore, Aristotle praises those above all others who consider the human soul to be indeed incorporeal, but nonetheless "something of the body"—that is, such an <term>act</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the fulfillment or realization of a potential; here, the soul is what makes the body alive and human.</note> in a certain kind of subject. Hence, in the third book of *On the Soul*, he says: "Since the intellect is not separated from the body, it must be investigated elsewhere whether it can understand forms separated from the body." He reveals this most clearly in the second book of *The Natural Works*, where he maintains that the human soul is both natural and separated from matter, as well as joined to it. He says it is "joined" because it is the <term>end of human generation</term> <note>The final goal or result of the biological process of reproduction.</note>, but I believe he calls it "separated" because of its power of intelligence. 

These words, however, cannot be rightly understood as referring to a "thinking soul" or to a single, universal mind. Also in the twelfth book of *The Divine Works* <note>Ficino refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics* as "The Divine Works."</note>, where he denies that forms precede their matter but rather follow after it, he concedes only that form which becomes the intellectual soul, clearly declaring that our soul is the form of the body, beginning with the body, yet not ending with it. Nor can those words be understood as referring to the **Averroistic mind** <note>The philosopher Averroes argued that all humans share a single, eternal "Agent Intellect" rather than having individual immortal souls. Ficino spent much of his career refuting this.</note>, which would be numbered among "moving causes" rather than "formal causes"; such a mind would precede the human body and is not joined to our body from its very birth. This contradicts the order Aristotle uses in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where he applies the intellect to us from our very origin, even if it "descends from without." **Theophrastus** and **Themistius** also confess that the intellect is joined to us from the beginning and is innate to our soul. 

If one reads in Aristotle that "whatever is generated is subject to corruption," this does not apply to the soul, which is not generated through "motion" <note>Physical change or biological growth.</note> but is created in an instant. Indeed, let everything that had a beginning be corruptible according to Aristotle—so long as it is physical by its own nature—yet let it always be preserved by the power of God, because it proceeded from God without an intermediary. This entire view was discovered by **Pythagoras** and approved by **Plato**. If the generation of humans has always existed, then an innumerable multitude of souls would now exist, provided they are of the same species. However, infinite species cannot exist. Certain **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note> indicate that spiritual things of the same species can be innumerable based on the fact that innumerable images are produced in the air by heat and light. There are, nonetheless, some philosophers who do not believe the generation of humans has been eternal. I will pass over for now that Pythagorean doctrine: namely, that generation is everlasting, and that there is a fixed, eternal number of souls that simply change bodies.

->*Third Reason: because man moves himself freely.*<-
->Chapter VIII.<-

**P**latonists and Peripatetics all agree that man moves himself, and that human actions are so arranged that the man himself who acts is the master of his own operations. To act rationally is to act by reasoning in a certain way before carrying something out. One first accepts a **universal rule**, then joins to it a **particular opinion**, and thirdly draws a **conclusion** in this manner: "Every good thing should be chosen; this food is good; therefore, this food is to be chosen." 

The first part of this type of argumentation belongs to the mind alone; the second can also belong to the <term>phantasia</term> <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes sensory images of specific things.</note>; and the third similarly. And just as the universal rule for judging what is "good" exists in the mind alone, so too the universal will for desiring the "good" exists in the mind alone. In the imagination, there can only be a particular opinion and a particular desire. When they affirm that man moves himself freely, they do not mean the mind alone (in which "moving" is a matter of directing works rather than being moved), nor the animal nature alone (in which "being moved" is to be driven to a task rather than leading freely), but they mean both together. If both together produce a specific kind of thing and a single human person, the mind must be the life-giving **form** of the body. If it were otherwise, we would never find anything that moves itself freely; instead, a mind standing near an animal would force the animal into motion, much like the force imparted to a stone by a thrower pushes it upward. In that case, the name "freedom" would be a fiction, just as the "personhood" of man would be a fiction. 

Furthermore, if one posits a single mind for all (as Averroes wishes), whatever you answer to these questions will either be absurd or will fit us, but certainly not Averroes. For if that mind moves us by its nature, it will certainly move us continually and in the same way, just as an intelligence moves a celestial sphere; for they assign that mind to us in the same way they assign intelligence to the heavens. Or if...

...will, or it will compel us through that will, and thus we will never be free, and there will be nothing in the order of things that moves freely. Or, it will persuade us; but if that is granted, I ask in what way I—being a "thinking animal"—perceive that persuasion, which I cannot arrive at except through my intelligence? And so it will appear that intelligence is my own property, especially since it is necessary, if I am to move freely, that it be the same substance that persuades and moves, and which is persuaded and moved; otherwise, the name of "liberty" will be empty. 

But let us proceed again toward the same point by a different path. Since we have found that this living body is very often moved by the mind—especially in those operations which, through preceding counsel, lead in the most orderly ways to a rational end rather than a merely bodily one—we must ask whether the mind moves the body through a natural union of its substance with the substance of the body, or solely by command? It does not seem to do this by command alone, because it would only do so by persuading or ordering the <term>phantasia</term> <note>The "phantasia" or "imagination" was considered the faculty that processed sensory images and mediated between the senses and the higher intellect.</note> so that it might move the limbs of the body. And the phantasia would move them only if it consented. 

Now, however, the intellect frequently rouses the body against the inclination of the phantasia and the senses, while the appetite of the senses is struggling against it. Therefore, the mind moves the limbs through a certain natural union of its substance, and through its very <term>being</term> <note>original: "per esſe". Ficino argues the soul moves the body because it is the body's essential form, not just an external driver.</note> rather than by mere command. Furthermore, if the mind frequently stops or moves the limbs against the inclination of the phantasia, without the phantasia being in the least bit persuaded, and does so from within and in the same order in which the phantasia is accustomed to move them, who would not see that that "thinking soul" <note>Referring to the "vis cogitativa," which medieval philosophers often separated from the higher immortal mind.</note> then effectively ceases its work and is superfluous, since the mind usurps its functions? 

Truly, the mind moves in the manner of a natural form. Indeed, nature is the internal principle of motion and rest. And since the mind produces external motion in the limbs, it can much more easily produce internal motion in the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, which are more easily stirred. By stirring the humors, it will temper their qualities for the work of nutrition. Again, how much more will it be able to vibrate the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus". In Ficino's medical-philosophy, "spirit" is a very subtle, vaporous substance that acts as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>, which is moved by even the lightest breeze? While it tempers the spirit from within, it will exercise spirit within spirit. 

What need, therefore, do we have for twin souls—one intellectual and one thinking—when one is sufficient? Nor is the mind less capable of both understanding and sensing than the thinking faculty is of sensing and nourishing. Indeed, the mind can even nourish, since the <term>vegetative power</term> <note>The lowest level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> can not only act itself, but can also carry out the motions and actions of the elements. 

There is certainly a power in us that considers "being" itself, or "the thing," and reason itself, with a concept more universal than what is sensible or insensible. It can, at its own judgment, compare some intelligible thing to some sensible thing; indeed, it can compare each and every intelligible thing to each and every sensible thing, which results in this same power knowing all these things. But since the senses do not reach insensible things, nor perceive anything more universal than the genus of sensible things, and the phantasia is ignorant of universals, that power must be the mind alone. 

Therefore, in the substance of the mind, there will be a power capable of discerning all sensible things, just as in the phantasia; this could certainly be called a kind of "excellent phantasia" or an "intellectual sense." Where there is a power of sensing, there is also an act of sensing, provided the <term>spirit</term> is not lacking—the medium in which either the passions of the body are expressed or the images of qualities shine forth. Moreover, the "luminous spirit" is subject to the mind, facilitating the office of sensing. Therefore, that excellent phantasia which is in the substance of the mind, when infused into the spirit of the brain, thinks; when infused into the spirit of the eyes, it sees; while from one single source it pours out many powers. 

Truly, if in <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" (the idea that all humans share one single mind) Ficino is attacking.</note> the bodily phantasia provides service to the intellectual substance for the act of understanding, why should the spirit in our view—which accompanies the bodily phantasia—not also serve that same substance of the mind in executing the act of that "phantasia" which accompanies the intelligence? And if the earthy limbs of the body receive motion from the mind and transmit it to the outside, what prevents the "fiery spirits," illuminated by the presence of the mind, from offering the occurring images of bodies to the mind's phantasia? For this reason, the power of understanding, sensing, and nourishing is located in the same substance of the mind, in which also consists the entire power of operating and moving freely. For when we are about to do something through reason, that reasoning which we described above necessarily precedes within us. If this were scattered through many substances, as if through different persons, it would not result in action. For it is necessary to reduce every effect to one principal cause, in which the entire faculty and rationale for acting is gathered. The rationale of human action consists in that reasoning. Therefore, it is all concluded within the nature of the mind, which indeed the nature suffi-

He refutes Averroism by suggesting that the "spirit" acts as a bridge, allowing a single individual mind to govern all bodily and intellectual functions.</summary>

...[proportio]n will be a sufficient principle of human action, both because all reasoning is contained within it, and because the members of the body—the eye, tongue, hands, and feet—obey it alone so easily, so quickly, and so constantly that they perceive and follow almost every nod of the mind. Indeed, it would be incredible if the mind were not their own proper <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is; Ficino argues the mind is the "form" of the body.</note> and its intimate ruler.

### *The fourth reason: because the powers of the soul alternately hinder and move one another.*
### *Chapter IX.*

**W**henever a single nature possessing two different powers of acting is too intently focused on the action of one, it almost ceases from the action of the other. For this reason, it is hardly possible to listen keenly to a lyre and taste a feast at the same time. If the most intense tasting did not hinder the hearing, we would assert that these two powers did not belong to one substance, but to two different substances. However, the most intense acts of nourishing and sensing do hinder human intelligence, and intelligence hinders them. This signifies that the intellect is a power of that very same soul of ours which also possesses the power of nourishing and sensing. 

The followers of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century philosopher whose followers argued that the higher "Intellect" was a single, eternal substance shared by all humans, rather than being part of the individual soul.</note> will respond to this by saying that sense and <term>phantasia</term> <note>The "phantasia" or imagination is the faculty that processes mental images (species) from the senses.</note> are two powers of our soul, and therefore they hinder each other. They argue that when the act of the phantasia is weakened because of the excessive focus of the senses, the act of the mind is also weakened—not because the mind is in the same soul as the phantasia or the senses, but because the mind requires the service of the phantasia to create and view <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refer to the mental images or representations of things.</note>. 

However, it is not consistent for the Averroists to say that the phantasia is weakened by the focus of the senses, since they believe the phantasia is a motion produced by the senses. Nor is it likely that the phantasia is much weakened by the effort of nourishing; nevertheless, let us set aside nourishment and sense for now and consider the phantasia and the mind. I certainly experience this in myself: when the phantasia is too intent, human intelligence or reason is weakened, and vice versa. So much so, that the mind or reason is mostly vacant when the phantasia rules too much—even if it is a healthy and sober phantasia—and the same happens in reverse. Just as the sense, even if it is healthy, distracts the phantasia when it is more intently occupied with external things, and vice versa. 

Furthermore, in those who are dreaming, drunk, angry, in love, out of their minds, or delirious, when the phantasia revolves its images within itself with the soul’s total attention, is not every judgment of the human mind or reason put to sleep? Conversely, when in those who are contemplating, reason fixes its burning gaze on the consideration of divine things, is not the phantasia mostly silent? And if it interrupts at all, is it not immediately ordered by reason to be still? Is it not forbidden from being carried away too much by affects or from wandering further through its usual winding paths? 

Who then will deny that the mind and the phantasia are powers of the same soul, since they weaken each other by their respective intensity? Moreover, let us grant the Averroists that there is as much alternating motion between the mind and the phantasia as there is between the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was the faculty thought to unite the data from the five individual senses into a single perception.</note> and a particular sense. Just as the image of a thing shining in the eye reflects from there into the common sense—and similarly, the act of seeing overflows from the eye into the common sense—so do both images and actions continually reflect from the phantasia into the mind. 

Yet it seems to me that there is an even greater reciprocity between the mind and the phantasia than between the internal sense and the external sense, because both images and actions are reflected back from the mind into the phantasia. I do not clearly see how this happens from the internal common sense back into the eye, nor do they explain it. If they assert that this sometimes happens in dreamers, so be it. But I will find something else in which their reciprocity exceeds that of the senses. Indeed, between the mind and the phantasia there occurs a mutual exchange not only of images and actions, but also of affects and habits, such as never occurs between the common sense and the eye. 

Since, therefore, the mind has a much greater kinship and a more indissoluble bond with the phantasia than the common sense has with any other sense—and yet both the common sense and the particular senses are in the same soul—why should the mind and the phantasia not also be in the same soul? Why is the eternal mind almost always so affected toward the temporal phantasia that it obeys and flatters it, and when the phantasia grieves or rejoices, the mind "condoles" (if I may put it that way) and "con-rejoices" with it, unless a foundation of the same nature and substance underlies both? In what way could the finite power of the phantasia often accompany the somewhat infinite power of the mind in acting—so that as far as the mind speculates, the phantasia thinks along with it—unless the same substance equalized them both? There is never a sudden, easy, and complete exchange of qualities between two things unless [they share a common nature].

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind, imagination (phantasia), and physical senses must belong to a single, unified soul because their activities constantly interfere with or support one another. He refutes the Averroist idea of a separate intellect by pointing out the deep emotional and functional sympathy between our higher reasoning and our mental images.</summary>

...a common matter underlies them. Wherefore neither would the intellect ever become so easily **phantastic** <note>Used here to mean "pertaining to the imagination" or the faculty of forming mental images.</note>, nor the imagination ever turn out to be intellectual, nor would the former ever be made irrational at some point, or the latter rational, unless a common subject underlay both. For just as one wheel moves another because they rest on the same machine, so those two appetites—namely, the rational and the irrational—move each other in turn most easily, as much by impulse as by judgment, because they are in the same substance of the soul. Hence that Aristotelian saying in the third book of *On the Soul*: "Just as sphere moves sphere, so desire moves the will"; but desire could not move [it] unless it were either like a superior sphere drawing an inferior one—which no one would ever say—or a sphere connected to the same artifice as the mind.

### Fifth reason: because a separate mind does not need the imagination.
### Chapter X.

**A**ccording to <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to late medieval and Renaissance debates; he argued the intellect was a single, separate entity shared by all humans.</note>, the nature of the mind does not have a common existence with the body, nor does it communicate its own existence to it. It does not have its origin there, neither according to essence, nor according to its preparation for existing. It does not form any single <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to a specific kind of being or a shared biological/metaphysical classification.</note> with the body, nor is it numbered according to the count of bodies. Therefore, just as it has a mode of being entirely separate from this animal, so it will have a mode of cognition completely segregated from the body. Consequently, there is no reason that compels it to draw its <term>species</term> <note>Here, "species" refers to the "intelligible forms" or mental concepts the mind uses to understand things.</note> from the <term>simulacra</term> <note>original: *simulachris*; the mental images or "phantasms" derived from sensory experience.</note> of the imagination, or to require a temporal and moving discourse for the knowledge of things, especially eternal ones. 

Indeed, such a mind would be most similar to the celestial minds, and much closer to them than to the qualities of bodies. Therefore, it would understand those celestial things, and in their manner, more than these bodily things. This contradicts Averroes’ own leader, **Aristotle**, who writes that this mind understands nothing without <term>simulacra</term>. But simulacra belong to bodies, not to minds. 

I pass over the fact that since the primary and familiar objects of the human intellect are the common natures and principles of natural things—which are joined to bodies but separable from them—we can argue from a certain proportion between the power and its object that the human intellect is such that it is both joined to the body and capable of being separated from it. Because it is joined, it therefore almost always turns itself toward simulacra. Indeed, because it is joined, it turns toward things joined [to matter]. And because it is joined in a "separable" manner, it therefore turns itself in a separable manner: that is, by abstracting and separating. 

But minds that are not only "separable" but truly "separate" look upon things that are separate, and they do so in a separate manner. Therefore, to speak briefly, nothing seems to me to demonstrate more clearly that the nature of the human mind is a **mean** <note>A "middle point" or bridge between the physical and the divine.</note> than its natural inclination toward both realms. For whether through the intellect it begins from bodies and then soon transfers itself to incorporeal things, or if it sometimes begins from incorporeal things and in turn slips back to the simulacra of bodies. Or whether through the will it either desires eternal things while being deflected by an affection for temporal ones, or conversely, it desires temporal things and is in turn often restrained by a reverence for eternal ones. 

But let us now return to the Averroistic question. The Averroists will respond that this intellect indeed understands the celestial minds without the images of the imagination, but the natures of bodies not at all. To this we shall counter: In those celestial minds there are incorporeal "species" of bodies, through which they judge bodies. Therefore, if this intellect understands those minds, it receives the knowledge of bodies from them. There is therefore no need for it to receive that knowledge from bodies. 

Then they will assert that this intellect is the lowest [of all intellects], subsisting in itself while clinging to us. Insofar as it subsists in itself, it is compared to the superior minds as a transparent and glassy body is compared to light, and it sees through them. Insofar as it clings to us, it draws species from the simulacra and understands corporeal things. To this, we will say first that it is superfluous for an intellect, which always looks upon bodies within the [divine] causes of bodies, to also always see the same things in sensory images—and for one who possesses them in eternity to borrow daily from time. Next, it is not because it "clings" to us that it receives species from images, but because it takes them from here, it "clings." For as Averroes thinks, the intellect is joined to us only for this reason: that it is formed by the species received from us. Therefore, the intellect must be considered first as if prepared by a certain power to receive species of this kind before it clings to us. It is not, therefore, through this "clinging" to us that it is prepared for such species, unless perhaps he thinks it clings to us as far as...

<meta>catchword: nature</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind must be the soul's own form rather than a separate entity, as its ability to shift between eternal truths and sensory images proves it occupies a "middle" position in the cosmic hierarchy. He critiques the Averroist view that a separate intellect would need to rely on the body's sensory images (simulacra) to function.</summary>

Ficino is arguing that if the intellect were a separate, superior entity only temporarily linked to humans, it would not logically depend on human sensory perceptions (phantasms) for its knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>

pertains to the proximity of nature—that is, that the nature of that intellect is, by a certain degree, close to our soul. If this were the case, nothing further would follow than that a mind of this sort moves and forms our soul. For when a more worthy degree approaches an inferior one, it does not receive from it, but rather bestows upon it. The sphere of the moon moves the sphere of fire; it is not moved by it. <note>In the traditional geocentric cosmology, the "higher" celestial spheres influenced and moved the "lower" elemental spheres.</note> Why, then, does this mind borrow knowledge from the soul rather than lend it? Surely, if it is superior and as much more excellent as **Averroes** believes, it ought to possess wisdom through itself alone, while the soul should possess it through the mind—especially since this mind is joined to the body in the same way that the celestial mind is joined to the heaven, according to Averroes. Therefore, just as that celestial mind takes nothing from the heaven, so this mind should take nothing from the body.

Nor should the Averroists object to us that, just as the celestial body is full of its own forms, so its mind is full of its own [forms], while our mind always receives new forms just as our body continually varies its forms. This objection achieves nothing. Indeed, the action of a craftsman takes its character from his instruments only when it is carried out *through* those instruments, such as cutting and the like. But that action which remains solely in the mind of the craftsman, such as the deliberation of planning the work, does not take its character from the instruments. Therefore, it is not fitting to give the character of intelligence from the body itself, since the intelligence is not completed by the body.

We shall next ask Averroes: while the mind understands within us, does it become more perfect, more imperfect, or neither? If neither, this perpetual activity will be in vain, accomplishing nothing by its work. Indeed, it would not even work at all, for there is no movement toward an indifferent goal. If it becomes more perfect, then the perfection of an eternal mind will always depend on temporal <term>phantasms</term> <note>original: "simulachris." In this context, these are the mental images derived from sensory experience.</note>. That which is imperfect would always be perfecting that which is more perfect—especially since they claim it is moved and formed by our imagination no differently than a mirror is by a body. But if it becomes more imperfect, why is it always moved toward the imperfect? By what appetite does it assiduously strive toward a defect? And—what is even weaker—by what force does the lesser always infect that which is more excellent?

Does not Averroes himself, when he disputes concerning the separate minds, say that since they know eternal things through their own essence, they know no temporal things? Otherwise, as he says himself (to use his own word), they would become **vile** <note>original: "vilescerent." Averroes argued that for a superior intellect to focus on inferior, changing things would degrade its dignity.</note>. If this is so, it follows from Averroes's own opinion that temporal knowledge brings about a defect where knowledge is eternal. Since the human intellect (as he asserts) always knows eternal things, it is not only said to understand temporal things in vain (since it does not emerge more perfect from this), but it actually becomes more imperfect. I certainly think that mind, as a spectator of eternal things within us, would be more imperfect for the reason that it is always mocked here by false images and disturbed by cares. And this intelligence of its would be superfluous in the nature of things, because it contributes nothing and is established for the sake of no end.

Indeed, what does it bestow upon our souls from its own? Does not the human soul have by its own nature that particular power of reasoning through which, as Averroes thinks, it instructs that mind—or rather, often mocks and disturbs it? But the soul neither has universal discourse from itself, nor receives it from the mind. For the particular and mortal soul is not capable of universal and eternal reasons. If it were capable of them, it would certainly understand them, and would itself be an intellect, and would be everlasting. Therefore, a coupling of this sort confers nothing on our souls, unless perhaps you think it is useful to us that the presence of a mind draws us against our nature, involves us in false fables, and, while using a deceptive hope of divine things, deprives us of the pleasantness of present goods. But neither is it profitable to the mind, as we have said; since it is divine, it is not to be referred to this human being as if to an end—to a human being, I say, who is separated from its very being.

Again, since the mind sees the higher causes of things through its own essence (in which all intermediate causes and every effect are contained), and therefore perceives all corporeal things in them and through them, it has no need of our imaginations and senses to discern corporeal things. This is especially true because there is within it, according to Averroes, that **Agent Intellect** <note>The "Intellectus Agens," which Averroes and his followers described as a power that makes potential knowledge actual, often viewed as a single entity shared by all humanity.</note>. Since this is in eternal act, through which it can bestow an intelligible nature upon individual sensory things, it can—even more so and more primarily—fill the potential intellect with that same intellectual splendor. It can then both offer to the potential intellect the species of higher things innate to itself, and, through its own most efficacious power, lead those universal species down into particular concepts. For if it can fashion universals out of particular contingencies, it can also conceive any particulars out of universals, whether they be innate or divinely inspected—especially since its essence is superior to the potential [intellect] and it has already fulfilled this office from eternity.

<summary>Ficino argues that the Averroistic "Separate Intellect" is logically flawed because a superior, eternal mind would be degraded, not perfected, by relying on human sensory images. He contends that such a mind would already possess all knowledge through its own essence and the "Agent Intellect," making its connection to individual human imaginations unnecessary and even harmful.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s refutation of Averroës’ theory of the "Unity of the Intellect." Ficino argues that the intellect cannot be a single, separate entity shared by all humans, as this would lead to logical and ontological absurdities.</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>

Nor, again, should it be said that the mind and the animal <note>Referring to the "animal soul" or the sensitive part of a human being.</note> are joined for the sake of a composite made of both. For they are not joined in such a way that one thing is truly produced from both. Nor is it fitting to refer true parts to a false whole as if to an end goal. Perhaps they will say that this coupling contributes to the beauty and ornament of the world. But I do not think the world is adorned by this superfluous fiction—or rather, this **monstrosity**—which has a single head, and one that, although it is divine, nevertheless changes colors like a **chameleon** according to the variety of objects it perceives. Moreover, it has innumerable legs; the head remains, but the legs are always being cut off and then sprouting back again. Nor shall we tolerate them if they say that this monster serves to connect superior and inferior things. For in what way will that which is not only not a single thing in itself, but does not even receive any connection from elsewhere, connect other things? 

There must be one specific **form** in the world that knits superior forms to inferior ones. For it is the duty of unity and form to connect. And in that form, the properties of all forms must meet, so that the superior forms are in a way relaxed and lowered toward the inferior ones, while the inferior ones are stretched and raised toward the superior. But in that **Averroistic monster**, neither is a single common form found, nor do the extremes migrate into one another; instead, while each part keeps what is its own, they remain scattered. 

Finally, if they say the mind is everywhere "under the Moon," <note>In the geocentric model, the region "sub-lunar" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the realm of change and decay.</note> they place it in vain where there are never any humans—such as in the highest reaches of the air, the unnavigable sea, and the uninhabitable land. For there, the intellect never accomplishes anything, nor does it move anything. The **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> never designate divine minds anywhere except where they suitably govern and move something. But if they say the mind is only present where there are humans, two absurdities immediately follow. First, that it will be entirely in two men separated by a very long distance, and yet it will not be in the space between them, which nature does not allow. Second, that when the men move, the mind itself will move. Yet the Peripatetic school does not usually admit that a substance which is neither a body nor the specific form of a body can be moved, either by itself or by accident. Furthermore, by what reasoning will anyone explain how such a divine mind follows a little man—who wanders about and very rarely uses his mind—everywhere like a servant? Is it by natural necessity? But the mind is superior, and it seems to need the man neither for its existence nor for its well-being. It cannot be attributed to violence or to deliberation. Nor is it permitted to claim that it moves when the man moves because it is naturally adapted to the human species. For they do not adapt the mind to the man in any other way than they adapt the [celestial] mind to the heaven—yet they do not think that mind moves along with the heaven. Lastly, if they say the mind does not move when the man moves, they are forced to admit both that the mind sometimes lives far from the man, and that the man lives far from the presence of the mind.

## Sixth reason: because both intellects are a power in the soul. Chapter XI.

**A**s for their claim that the **agent intellect** <note>The "active" part of the mind that processes sensory data into universal concepts.</note> and the **capable intellect** <note>The "passive" or "receptive" part of the mind that receives those concepts; often called the "possible intellect."</note> are two distinct essences from which the unity of the intellectual soul is constituted, that is indeed superfluous and absurd. It is superfluous because one essence, equipped with two powers, is sufficient: one power to produce the species <note>The "intelligible species" or mental representations of things.</note> and the other to receive them. Just so, the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination or mental imagery.</note> draws certain intentions from images and receives them once they are drawn. The eyes of animals that see at night possess twin powers in the same essence: through one they draw out the images of colors, and through the other they receive them. Light itself both creates certain colors in the clouds or water and receives them. 

How, then, is a double power—both active and receptive—founded in the same essence? Clearly, from different principles or relations. Indeed, light produces colors insofar as it comes from the Sun; it receives them insofar as it exists, as it were, in itself outside the Sun. Thus the soul, insofar as it originates from God—who is most pure act—receives the power to manufacture species. But insofar as it is in itself below God, it becomes, as it were, passive, and is formed by receiving the species. Thus, that **Averroistic fiction** is superfluous. It is also absurd because a substantial unity is not constituted from two essences that both exist in "act." For two acts of existing are two beings, not one. There is no doubt that the **agent intellect** is, for them, a certain substance in "act" (since it acts upon something), and we do not fight against this. But when they add that the **capable intellect** is also another actual substance...

<summary>Ficino mocks the Averroistic concept of a single universal mind as a "monster" and argues that the active and receptive powers of thought must reside within the individual human soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical assault on the Averroistic interpretation of the soul. In the previous pages, he argued against the "Unity of the Intellect"; here, he specifically refutes the idea that the "Mind" (the intellect) is a formless, "pure potentiality" similar to physical matter. He argues that if the mind were truly as blank and formless as matter, it would be indistinguishable from it, leading to the absurdity that even stones could think.</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>

-># MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #<-

...and we have not proved it to be such that it is <term>pure potentiality</term> <note>original: *mera potentia*; the state of being able to become something without yet having a fixed form or "actuality."</note>, no differently than <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: *materia prima*; the most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe that receives physical forms.</note>. For if the mind, which is capable of receiving knowledge, were pure potentiality, it would not be distinguished from primary matter. And wherever there were matter, there would be intelligence, such that even stones themselves would understand. 

It is indeed certain that primary matter is pure potentiality. However, there cannot be more than one "pure potentiality" in nature, just as there cannot be more than one "pure act" <note>original: *merus actus*; a state of complete, perfected existence, usually referring to God.</note>, and vice versa. For if all things said to exist "in potential" are such through one common principle, and all things "in act" are similarly so, it is necessary to arrive at a single source of potentialities and a single source of acts. 

Again, if the first and common distinction in composite things is that which exists through potentiality and act, and many things do not arise from one except through a certain order of some things to others—and similarly, one does not arise from many except through this kind of order, in which one thing is related to another as potentiality is related to act—it follows that the multitude of things takes its beginning from the very mixture of potentiality and act. From this it happens that neither "pure act" nor "pure potentiality" is able to be manifold, since potentiality does not fall into number except through a mixture of act, nor does act except through a mixture of potentiality. From these points, it is concluded that the mind cannot be pure potentiality. 

And if it is said that the mind is also a simple potentiality, no less than matter is, and that it nonetheless differs from matter, one must ask by what reasoning it differs. Clearly not in the respect that it is "potentiality," both because in this very thing they agree, and because through potentiality, confusion and chaos reign; distinction, however, happens through **act**. Therefore, something beyond potentiality must be added to the mind, through which it may differ from the potentiality of matter, and that something will indeed be some "act." 

Now, if this act were infused into the bosom of the mind, it would ensure that the mind is not pure potentiality, since it has an act mixed in. But if the act weighs upon it from the outside, it will not make the mind differ from the potentiality of matter (insofar as that is potentiality) until, by acting upon the mind through its own proper act, it grants some intimate act to the mind, through which the mind may differ from "pure potentiality" as potentiality. For such a discrepancy does not occur except through some act, insofar as it is an act, and thus again the mind will not be pure potentiality.

The <term>Averroists</term> <note>original: *Auerroïci*; followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroës, who argued for a single "Possible Intellect" shared by all humans—a view Ficino spent much of his career refuting.</note> will imagine that the mind differs from matter because the mind looks toward one kind of act—namely, the absolute and universal—while matter looks toward another—namely, the concrete and particular. As if, indeed, these "lookings" <note>original: *respectus*; the relationship or orientation toward something.</note> were not themselves some kind of act! Surely, if the "looking" of the mind were nothing other than the potentiality of the mind itself, it would provide no difference. But if it were something else, it will be an act. 

Furthermore, if mind and matter exist before they look toward the forms they are to receive, and they "look" in accordance with how they are in themselves, then certainly because they are diverse in themselves, they look toward diverse acts, and not the other way around. Nor should it be thought that the mind looks toward a more perfect act than matter looks toward, except for the reason that the mind itself is more perfect. If this is so, the mind departs further from "nothingness" and approaches closer to the **highest act**, from which all perfection comes; therefore, it is not "potentiality" alone. 

Consequently, if matter holds the middle ground between act and nothingness, and that which is considered "below" matter is nowhere (since nothing exists "above" it that is not act or in act), we must ask where we should place the essence of the mind. Surely, if it is something, it will not be placed below matter. Or perhaps it will be established in the same grade of perfection as matter? By no means. For it would receive nothing more excellent than matter does. Added to this is the fact that, just as things which are equal in quantity are one in quantity, so things which are equal in perfection are one in perfection. Perfection is in the **form**, and through the form comes the **species**. Therefore, things that are one in perfection are one in form and one in species. Hence it happens that two different species of things cannot be equally perfect to one another. 

Therefore, since the mind is a different species than matter, it will not be placed in the same grade of perfection as matter; it must therefore be in a more excellent grade. If it is placed above matter, it will be an act, or at least "in act." And it is so much more "in act" than other natural forms, as it is many degrees further removed from matter than all of them, and closer to the divine act. If it is "in act," and is not placed in the category of sensible things, it will certainly have an act above the act of sensible things in general, and will have an act according to a certain species that is intelligible and intellectual. Moreover, in the category of things, it will have a **vital act**, by which it may give life to sensible things. 

But if it is said that the mind relates to "intelligible forms" <note>Forms that can only be understood by the intellect, such as mathematical truths or the concept of Justice.</note> just as matter relates to "sensible forms" <note>Forms perceived by the senses, like the redness of an apple.</note>, this example may be true in some way, but it does not force the essence of the mind to be devoid of all act. Perhaps some Averroist will think that the superior reasons mentioned above might be escaped, if he were to concede that...

<meta>catchword: potentia (potentiality)</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind cannot be "pure potentiality" like raw matter; it must possess its own "act" or form to be distinct from matter and closer to the divine. He contends that the mind's superior perfection and its ability to give life prove it occupies a higher ontological rank than physical substance.</summary>
