<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s complex metaphysical argument against those who claim the human mind is merely a blank slate (pure potentiality). He specifically targets the "Averroistic" view (named after the philosopher Averroes) which suggests that the "Active Intellect"—the part of the mind that actually thinks—is a single, separate entity shared by all humans, rather than a personal power of the individual soul.</meta>

<page-num>350</page-num>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

...that the nature of <term>pure potentiality</term> <note>the state of being able to become something without yet being it</note> is not compressed into a single point, but possesses within itself a certain "latitude" or range, through which it can be stretched or relaxed. In this way, its natural perfection would be more "intense" in the mind and more "relaxed" in matter. But not even by this argument can he escape. For just as a number is an "act" (a completed thing), and indeed a "highest act," so too is pure potentiality a "highest potentiality." Now, whatever holds the highest place in any category has a certain fixed limit (so to speak), beyond which that category does not extend; anything short of that limit is not yet the highest, nor is it "pure." 

*Indeed, a quality does not fall from the peak of its own kind except through some mixture of an opposite kind.* <note>original: "Quippe qualitas non aliter cadit à sui generis summitate, quàm per quandam oppositi generis mixtionem."</note> Furthermore, if the nature of potentiality is more perfect in the mind than in matter, then either the mind is not "pure potentiality" because of some added perfection, or if it is potentiality by its very self, then that potentiality is more intense in the mind and more relaxed in matter. This "intensity" must be either according to quantity or according to quality (being "better"). If the first is true, matter will no longer be the "extreme" of potentiality, since something else would be "more" potential; if the second is true, the mind will not be pure potentiality, because that which is "better" participates more in "highest goodness." And that highest goodness is "highest act." Since, therefore, the mind is not pure potentiality, it does not possess a "substantial" potentiality, but an "accidental" one. And because potentiality and act must match, the mind will be subject to an "accidental act," but by no means a "substantial" one. For this reason, a third substance cannot be formed from the mind and the substantial act of the <term>active intellect</term> <note>the power that "activates" thoughts</note>. For a "partial potentiality" (as the <term>Metaphysicians</term> <note>Aristotelian philosophers</note> say) cannot receive a "simple act." 

The followers of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>the famous Greek philosopher whose works on the soul were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought</note> think that the "receptive intellect" understands the universal patterns of natural things only when it has received their absolute and intelligible forms. But since these patterns are not such in themselves, and cannot become "actually intelligible" except through an intellectual and active nature, they introduced a certain "effective intellect" as the creator of these absolute forms. If the nature of this "active intellect" is a certain power planted in the same essence where the "receptive power" is also born, then what need is there for that <term>Averroistic</term> <note>referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), a 12th-century philosopher who argued for a single "Active Intellect" for all humanity</note> clumping together of two separate substances? 

But if it were some other substance more excellent than this one, which pours intellectual power through the substance of the "receptive mind" all the way down to the "images of the imagination," and provides those images with the power of effective intelligible forms (as the Averroists believe), it would much sooner and more greatly grant that same power to the substance of the receptive mind itself. That higher substance would grant it in a stable way, and this lower substance would receive it in a stable way, since both are eternal. Therefore, the very same substance that has the "receptive power" will also have the "effective power," and there will be no need for a union of two substances for these two duties of the mind. 

From this, the error of <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, an early commentator on Aristotle who denied the immortality of the individual human soul</note> is also refuted. He, through a forced interpretation of Aristotle, tried to strip all divinity from the human race. He asserted that receptive minds are indeed within us and distinct in number, but that the "active mind" is outside of humans and is a single entity—the sole location of the mind's divinity—which is the universal cause of intelligible forms. Truly, since in all natural things there are certain powers that produce their own movements, it is a sacrilege to say that the substance of the human mind (the most excellent of all natural things) is deprived of an "effective power." And because an operation proceeds from a power, the universal mind does not grant our mind the "act of understanding" before it first grants it the "power of understanding." 

Furthermore, if a universal cause is set directly against a particular effect—that is, as a cause to an effect and as a universal to a particular—it is necessary to place a "particular cause" between these two as a middle ground. For example, the universal power of the Sun does not produce *this* specific human (who is a particular effect) except through *another* human, acting as a particular and proper cause. By the same logic, that "universal active mind" would not produce this or that specific instance of understanding in the "receptive mind" without a certain "particular active mind" that lives within us. For just as we use the receptive mind as a kind of familiar "form" for understanding at our own will, so too do we manufacture ideas through an "effective mind" as if by an art that is our own and inborn to us. Wisely, Aristotle never called the "active" and "receptive" minds two different essences, nor did he place them above the soul; rather, he called them "parts of the soul," and said they were two different powers within the soul. If anyone, however, should call the Averroistic mind

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV #

->Solution to the Averroistic arguments regarding the separate mind. Chapter 12.<-

**F**rom all the arguments brought against Averroës, we conclude two things. First, that the soul in a human being is the same one that gives shape to bodily things and is itself shaped by incorporeal things. Only through this medium can the rays of divine things be transmitted down to the lowest levels—if indeed the same thing that is illuminated by the higher also illuminates the lower. Moreover, through this same medium, the lowest things are reflected back to the sublime, provided that the same entity that rules the lowest is itself ruled by the highest. We also conclude a second point: that human minds are numbered according to the number of individual humans. They are distinct either by species (as the <term>Magi</term> <note>Ficino uses "Magi" to refer to ancient Persian and Zoroastrian sages whom he believed held a "primary theology" that prefigured Christianity.</note> believe) or certainly by number (as the later <term>theologians</term> <note>Likely referring to Christian Scholastics like Thomas Aquinas.</note> assert). For as many human bodies as there are, there are just as many <term>vital complexions</term> <note>The "complexion" (complexio) is the specific physical balance of humors and qualities that makes up an individual body.</note>, just as many life-giving souls, and just as many minds belonging to those souls. Just as physical complexions are distributed according to the distribution of bodies, and lives are distributed according to these complexions, so too are minds distributed according to the number of life-giving souls, for minds are the powers of those souls. However, this distinction does not arise from the body as if the body were the cause of an incorporeal substance’s power; rather, it proceeds from the incorporeal Creator Himself. As for those arguments of Averroës, by which he denied from the start of the question that the intellect is the "form" of the body, they have no weight against us. They only prove that the soul is not a "bodily form" lacking its own existence and depending on the body for its very essence. We, however, do not want the soul to be such a form; we hold it to be something subsisting in its own being and the mistress of matter.

Furthermore, to refute several other "traps" with which the Averroists strive to catch the Platonists, we must remember that it is not against the nature of the human soul to be joined to a body. It is natural for this eternal soul to be forever with an eternal and celestial body, and to be with a temporal and earthly body for a certain time—just as it is natural for each planet to always be in its own sphere, but to be under this or that specific zodiac sign only for a time. Even after the soul has departed from the body, it is natural for it to be reconciled to it again, so that even when it remains apart from the body, it stays with a certain affection or "inclination" toward returning to that same body. In the same way, a stone stays intact even when placed high up, yet meanwhile, it inclines toward lower things according to its nature. A planet, leaving a sign, returns to it eventually by natural order. The Magi and Egyptians, along with the Platonists, agreed that the soul would eventually return to the dwelling of the same body, so that this natural affection would not be in vain for eternity. Otherwise, something "violent" (unnatural) would be eternal. 

Because the soul exists in itself through the act of God, but exists in the body through the qualities of the <term>complexion</term>, and because the act of God remains eternal while the complexion is eventually dissolved, the soul ceases at some point to be in the body, but it never ceases to be in itself. It subsists in its own being after it has been separated from the body. It subsisted similarly while it was present in the body, but it no longer communicates its being to the body as it once did. Nor should it seem miraculous that the soul, which inhabits the body for a time, can remain separate from the body without being destroyed, provided that the thing moved depends more on the mover than vice versa. The mind is the true "mover" of the body. Therefore, if certain bodies remain somewhat undecayed when separated from the soul—such as bones, nails, sinews, and hair, which seem to last a very long time, as do wood, stones, and especially balsam, honey, and oil, which almost never rot—should not the mind, the ruler of the body, be able by natural order to remain forever incorrupt without a corruptible body? The mind clearly shows that it is not corrupted during the progression of this life by the corruption of this or that part of the body, since the mind remains the same through every age, shedding old matter and putting on new, while the body is continually renewed by the "outflow and inflow" of matter. 

But let us proceed to the rest. When the soul approaches the body, an animal is produced through the generation of the bodily complexion and the <term>vital spirit</term>. When the soul departs, the complexion is dissolved, the spirit is released, and the "animal" is undone. This animal is not produced by some accident, but from the ordered convergence of all natural causes, and it is dissolved in the same way. However, <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> proves that this "evil" of dissolution does not pertain to the soul itself, because the soul did not mix itself into the body. Instead, remaining within itself, the soul did not create one irrational animal out of itself and the body, but rather out of the body and its own "vital image" (simulacrum) beneath it. But let Plotinus see to that himself. Whether the soul approaches matter through the mediation of quantity, it is not necessarily extended, just as a surface does not become "deep" within a deep body, nor a line "wide" in a wide space, nor a point "long" in a long space, nor the meaning of a voice...
<meta>catchword: and of color</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is an individual, subsistent entity that acts as the body's ruler rather than a dependent byproduct. He asserts that the soul's natural inclination to the body suggests an eventual reunion (resurrection) and compares the soul's permanence to the way physical matter (like hair or balsam) can persist after life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the Platonic Theology. Having established that individual human minds are distinct, Ficino now explores the relationship between the soul, the body’s physical dimensions (quantity), and how the soul remains a unified whole despite the body's division into parts.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

The image of a color in the wide air becomes large. For matter itself requires <term>quantity</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "quantity" refers to physical extension or size.</note> more than the soul does. If the soul precedes quantity, it is by no means subject to quantity when it arrives. Since the reception of form happens through potentiality and not through a physical act, quantity is received in the matter, not in the soul. This quantity is, I say, first indeterminate because of the infinity of matter itself, and then determined to a certain shape because of the presence of the soul, which certainly provides the origins of the species. No one doubts that matter naturally precedes quantity in a certain order. Natural causes, because they are subject to place and time, act locally and temporally; thus they transform a work little by little, part by part, in both time and space. Therefore, they cannot complete a work of this kind anywhere except in matter that is already extended. But because God surpasses all division, both local and temporal, He acts in an entirely <term>indivisible</term> <note>Meaning God does not act in "stages" or "parts," but all at once.</note> manner. He can grant an individual form to matter itself at that very stage where matter precedes quantity; this form, like all other forms, is accompanied by a determined quantity that resides in the matter, not in the soul.

Let there be in man a single common form of the whole, and a primary one—that is, the rational soul. Let there also be, as many like to believe, many particular forms of the parts that are distinct in species, which are obedient to the soul: forms of the flesh, the bone, the nerve, and the rest. From these, a certain "composite" is made, which is the subject of physical shape, division, and suffering. Let the soul be present to the shaped body, but let it not be shaped itself. Indeed, it is clear that the soul itself is not the subject of such a shape, because the shape of the body both precedes the soul and follows it. When asked about the "being" of the whole, some answer that through the "being" of the soul’s substance, the "substantial being" of the whole is created, which results from the joining of the parts. For they say the "being" of the soul is that by which the "being" of the whole exists, and by which the soul itself exists in itself. And this soul does not stop in a resting foot, but it stands in a moving hand; it moves, and perhaps is not moved itself. For just as in a physical body it does not undergo "place," but is present above place and within place, so in a moving body it does not undergo the movement of another, but is in a certain way immovably within the motion. And if it "runs," it runs with the running limbs by transferring them, not by being transferred itself. Therefore, when the hand is moved at the same time the foot is at rest, the soul—which is entirely in both—is not forced to be moved and at rest simultaneously. But if the soul is moved in the hand, as <term>Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Medieval philosopher and theologian.</note> argues, what forces it to rest in the foot meanwhile? Can it not be moved in the unmoving foot by the mind itself? Although just as it is not impossible for the same man to be moved by contrary motions at once—such as when he is carried in a ship toward the rising sun, but meanwhile is pushed toward the west by someone else or runs toward the west himself on the ship—so it would not be absurd, according to <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>The most influential Scholastic theologian (1225–1274), whom Ficino frequently cites even when he leans more toward Plato.</note>, for the soul to be at rest and in motion simultaneously in different parts, according to the state or motion of the other part.

The whole soul is in the arm; it is whole in the hand. If the hand is amputated, the soul is not "truncated" or cut; it does not remain in the air, nor does it condense itself back into the arm, nor does it flee in time (for all these are the sufferings of bodies). Rather, it now gives life to the arm alone, whereas before it gave life to both the arm and the hand. It ceases to be where it was, not through motion, but it ceases to operate in an instant where it used to operate. This is just as if a small portion of air is broken in the West and the light vanishes; that light, as <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD), whose works Ficino translated into Latin.</note> wishes, is whole in the East and whole in the West. When that portion in which it was whole is removed, the light is not "broken," but it ceases to illuminate the portion it previously illuminated; nor does it condense into itself by a temporal flow, just as it did not stretch itself out by thinning itself from East to West in a temporal flow. For in an instant it made itself present, and in an instant it makes itself absent. If the soul is everywhere whole throughout the body, and it alone understands, then it understands everywhere. Yet it does not understand "in" any specific member, because the soul is not in the limbs, but rather the limbs are in the soul. However, it seems to the common people that it understands in the brain, because <term>phantasia</term> <note>Phantasia, or imagination, was considered the faculty that processed sensory images before the intellect analyzed them.</note> mostly accompanies intelligence. This imagination is stirred by those <term>spirits</term> <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were thin, vaporous substances that carried signals between the soul and the body.</note> that are in the brain, just as the affections of the imagination accompany the stirring of those spirits that are in the heart or the liver: the spirits of the heart follow the affection of anger, and the spirits of the liver follow the affection of lust. If someone asks, "What is it that feels, or what is it that understands in a man?" the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> will answer, but in various ways. For they will say that "sensing" is an act of the "composite" <note>The "composite" is the unified whole of body and soul.</note>: first, because the power of sensing in the composite itself comes from the matter, the form of the mixture, and the soul; and second, it is an act of the soul, because sensation happens by its power. They also say that "intelligence" is an action of the whole composite. Although in the soul alone...

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul is an indivisible form that resides in the body without being limited by physical dimensions or "quantity." He uses the analogy of light and a ship passenger to show how the soul can be present in all parts of the body simultaneously without being divided or moved by the body's physical changes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the Platonic Theology. The previous page discussed how the soul, as an indivisible form, relates to the physical quantity and extension of the body. This page addresses how the intellect operates within the human composite and begins a rebuttal of the "Unity of Intellect" theory proposed by the commentator Averroes.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.<-

...[the soul] alone is intelligence, and therefore can remain in the soul when it is separated from the body; nevertheless, as long as the soul is the <term>form of the composite</term> <note>The "composite" is the human being viewed as a single unit of joined soul and body. In Scholastic philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> in such a way that it joins into one common existence, the whole being to which that existence belongs is said to operate through the form, just as it exists through it. This is the point of the <term>Aristotelian</term> <note>Referring to Aristotle (384–322 BCE), whose philosophy provided the framework for these debates.</note> maxim: *The intellect is the act of no physical organ.* And rightly so: for the intellect is not in the body in the same way that the senses are, but rather it is in the soul. Nor should we believe, as **Averroes** <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Andalusian philosopher who famously argued that there is only one "Active Intellect" shared by all humanity.</note> thought, that the intellect is separate from the human being, as if it were merely separated from a physical organ. Nor, again, should we explain it in the manner of **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (active c. 200 CE), a commentator on Aristotle who argued the soul was mortal and tied to the body's temperament.</note>, who held that while individual senses are assigned to individual instruments, the entire body is the instrument of the intellect itself. For we see that the most noble powers do not use just any instrument, but only the most noble; thus, while touch uses almost anything, the **imagination** uses a unique and distinct part. Therefore, the body as a whole will not suffice for the mind. 

Nor should it be said that a single harmony is created from the conspiracy of all the physical instruments, which the intellect then uses as its own instrument. For if that were the case, the intellect would need all the instruments, and it would be the most "organic" and physically mixed of all the powers; that Aristotelian maxim would no longer stand. Indeed, while the senses do not exist without the body, the intellect is separate and unmixed, using no organ whatsoever. For if it used organs, it would become restricted to this or that specific nature, and it would no longer be able to know all things. However, it is not so "separate" that it does not give life to the substance of the soul in which the body exists; otherwise, one could not say that a *human being* understands. It is "separate" because it is not in the composite in the way a sense is, but is in the very substance of the soul, which is separable from the composite. Nor does it use an instrument in the act of understanding. This was confirmed in the book *On Animals*, and *On Sleep and Wakefulness of Animals*, where it is said: *The powers of acting belong to those things to whom the actions belong.* Since sensing happens through an instrument, but understanding does not, the power of sensing belongs to the composite, while the power of understanding can be proper to the soul alone.

### *Solution to the Averroistic arguments concerning the single mind.* Chapter XIII.

**W**e have now resolved the arguments of Averroes and his followers, by which they thought they could demonstrate that the substance of the mind cannot be the life-giving form of the body. Let us next resolve those arguments by which Averroes tries to show that the mind is unique and single for everyone. He says that the numerical multiplication of forms within the same species arises from **matter**. But the mind lacks matter. Although this is the opinion of certain <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note>, many of the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists** believe that the nature of a species is poured into many individuals not because of external matter, but because of certain "modes" implanted within the form itself; when the form is brought into actuality, it becomes this or that individual. For they believe the "angelic species" exists in every angel, brought down to an individual angel without any mixture of matter. 

But to follow partly the Peripatetics and partly some of the Platonists for the moment, perhaps we might concede that the number of forms arises either from matter, or because of matter—or rather, because of the composite of matter and form. Indeed, just as bodily forms draw their essence from matter in a way, so they draw their number within the same species. However, forms that are not bodily, but are *of* the body—such as **rational souls**—do not have their origin in matter, and thus do not take their number from it. Yet, because Divine Providence established them not only for the contemplation of divinity but also for the governance of bodies, just as God willed there to be a certain number of different bodies (that is, composite human beings) for the "ornament" of His work, so He ordains a certain number of souls. But to speak with **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, what distinguishes **Plato’s** soul from **Socrates’** soul? It is that divine concept which first tempered the life-giving power of the Platonic soul toward the "clothing" of a certain celestial body, and through this, adapted it to generate and rule a certain specific complexion of the elements of the body. In the same way, He adapted the soul of Socrates to its own specific traits. Thus, He distinguished the life-giving powers of souls because of matter (or rather, because of the composite of matter) for the sake of the world's beauty, and He distinguished the intellectual powers of those same souls to distinguish the souls themselves. But for what reason? For the sake of different perspectives on divinity. Under various ideas, we can enjoy the divine mind, investigate it through various traces, and set out toward this goal by various paths. Truly, infinite goodness willed to communicate itself not only to physical eyes but also to spiritual eyes in infinite ways (so to speak), and to be seen as [innumerable] by almost innumerable eyes...

...to show the marvelous faces of himself. And so he tempered the intellectual eyes and affections of various souls in different ways, so that by a different path we might set out toward the various possessions of the manifold divine goods. **Proclus**, following the mind of **Plato** who says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s *Timaeus* (41d-42e) describes the Creator assigning each soul to a star as its "chariot" and guide.</note> that <note>original: "Deum animas hominum alias alijs ducibus stellisq; accommodasse"</note> God had assigned the souls of men to different leaders and stars, proves that the differences among souls do not arise from bodies or inclinations toward bodies, but from that very essential assignment made by God to different leaders and stars. From this, the difference of inclinations and actions arises, both for seeing eternal things and for governing temporal ones. 

Accordingly, just as **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) was a Franciscan philosopher who argued for the "thisness" or individual essence of things.</note> and his followers argue, every nature—except the First, which alone is <term>pure act</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "pure act" refers to God, who is fully realized and has no potential to change or be anything else. All other beings have "potency," meaning they can change or be multiplied.</note>—has a certain potentiality mixed in that is in a way unformed in itself and formable from elsewhere. This potentiality relates to several and singular modes of existing in the same way that matter relates to several forms. Therefore, just as there are human and equine species, so too can any intellectual species—whether of angels or souls—be derived into many individuals. 

Moreover, the number of minds within the same species contributes to completing the order of the universe entirely. Indeed, that order is full in which the higher things are ordered toward the lower, these lower things back toward the higher, and equals are ordered among themselves. We clearly perceive an order of this kind in corporeal things. But if incorporeal things have a fuller order, we are compelled to imagine a similar order—that is, a triple one—within them as well. However, there can be no order among equals unless several individuals are contained under the same species. Furthermore, the number of many minds in the same species leads to their perfect happiness. For these minds, gazing upon one another within themselves in a certain way, rejoice together with an equal and mutual (as naturally happens) recognition and familiarity. 

Finally, the universe is far more beautiful if there is a multitude everywhere below the level of species, just as there is above it. Above, indeed, it is characterized by a general and specific <unclear>infinity</unclear>; below, however, it is adorned by a certain numerous variety. Nor do they think the number of individuals serves only to preserve the species itself, because even in bodies there are far more individuals everywhere than would be necessary for the conservation of the species. 

Besides, we see that nature in individual species does many things not entirely for the sake of survival, but also for the sake of ornament, which we see clearly in colors, shapes, features, and a most ordered arrangement. Finally, the primary end for which God wills all things to be is not, properly speaking, that they simply *exist*, but rather that they exist *well* and are in a good state. And if they exist primarily for this reason, whatever they are, they certainly exist for the same reason, however many they are. Therefore, God did not want several minds to exist in the same species just so that the species itself might exist and merely be preserved, but rather that it might exist well and be in the best state. This kind of state consists in a beauty that is varied on all sides and a blessed action in various ways everywhere. 

If anyone, however, argues that the multitude of human souls contributes to the survival of the species, we shall grant it thus: namely, that such a number is necessary not properly for the species of the soul itself, but for preserving the species of the <term>human composite</term> <note>The "composite" is the human being viewed as a single unit of joined soul and body.</note>. For God wills many men to exist, perhaps because the human species is not preserved in a single one. But many men cannot be made unless there are also many souls. The number of souls seems to serve not so much the number of bodies as the number of composites and the whole species—indeed, the order of the entire universe. Nor should anyone think that souls differ among themselves because the differences regard the bodies. For they are different in themselves before they regard the bodies with a different principle. So say they.

Now let us return to the proposal. As for what **Averroes** <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Islamic philosopher who famously argued that there is only one "Intellect" for all of humanity, an idea Ficino is attacking here.</note> adds—namely, that if the acts of my intellect differ by number, the species of things to be known will similarly differ and will be particulars, yet those things which are to be understood must be universals—it is solved in this way: It is not so much singularity that opposes understanding, but rather the gathering of corporeal accidents. Indeed, individual intellects and their individual conceptions can be understood most conveniently. Add to this that just as the image of a color in the eye is not that which is properly seen, but that *through which* the color itself is seen, so the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental image or "intelligible form" that represents an object in the mind.</note> and likeness of things in the mind is not that which is properly understood, but that *through which* the universal principles of things are understood. Nor is that species in the mind so singular that it hinders the understanding of universal principles. For if a statue, which is singular and corporeal, represents to us in a certain way the common figure of men, how much more does that mental species represent the common nature? For it is in the mind, which is absolute from all "passions" <note>In the philosophical sense, "passions" are things acted upon or physical properties like weight and temperature that affect matter but not pure mind.</note> of bodies, and is therefore itself free from them, from where it also relates...

<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.</header>

to us a matter closed in neither a certain place nor time. One must remember, however, that most thinkers place this order among the species <note>The term "species" in this context refers to the mental "forms" or "images" that the mind uses to recognize and understand objects.</note>: that in the angels they are universal, both in how they represent things and, in a way, in how they exist; whereas in brute animals, they are particular in both ways. In the souls of men, they are indeed singular in their existence, because they exist within entirely singular essences, but they are universal in their representation, because they exist in essences freed from the limits of matter. But let those thinkers see to these matters themselves. He <note>Referring to Averroes.</note> furthermore brought up some point or other concerning the knowledge that a teacher passes to a student, which is easily resolved from those things we have discussed elsewhere regarding innate species. For indeed, that argument of Averroes is easily turned back against him. Surely, if the teacher's knowledge does not pass into the student, nor generate another instance of knowledge within him, one of two things follows: namely, that the very same intellect which is in both people either possesses the same <term>habit</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition, such as learned knowledge or a skill.</note> in both, or it generates one habit in the second person from the habit it possesses in the first, within itself. Neither can happen according to Averroes. Not the first, because since that mind of his would daily know all the arts in all men, and some would teach others all those arts in a certain perpetual succession of teachers and students, it follows that the habits of all sciences would always be exactly the same in that mind—which Averroes openly rejects. Not the second, because knowledge would then be an "effective quality" (which he denies), and innumerable mental qualities similar to one another would exist simultaneously in the same subject, which he would also by no means admit. For if anyone does not see how far that accidental heap of superfluous qualities is outside the purpose of nature—especially in an eternal and divine substance—then he himself is outside the purpose of nature. Finally, Averroes reasoned: If there were two singular species in two singular minds, it would be possible to reduce them to a universal one, and each mind would reduce it to its own, and in each mind again, each species would turn out to be particular. For which reason it would be possible to collect them both again into another without end. That is a vain argument: First, because the gaze of the mind is clearly excited by the species, yet it is not terminated in the species—as if the mind necessarily looked at the species as its object—but rather it looks *through* the species at the universal nature of the thing. Two minds look upon this nature as surely one and the same, and as a unity, through two different species, just as the eyes of two men see the same object through two different images of it. Therefore, minds do not intend to reduce their species to other species, but to see the natures of things through them. Even if they should sometimes intend this, they will not proceed to infinity, because their species have their own power and meaning. And so, it is not permitted to always resolve them as singulars into other things that are more common in reality; but let them proceed without end, if it pleases. For what prevents the mind, which has a certain infinite power, from wandering without end, provided it never completes this infinite course in actual practice? A similar argument can be made concerning notions and concepts, and the response is likewise very similar.

### Signs that there is not only one mind. Chapter XIV.

**A**fter we have responded to the reasonings of Averroes, it remains for us to bring forward those signs or arguments which most strongly argue against there being only one intellect in all men. First sign: If the mind is so divine that it has no commerce with matter, is one, and is without beginning or end, and is present everywhere beneath the Moon <note>In the traditional Aristotelian view, the region "beneath the moon" is the earthly realm of change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note>, it is not likely that it is so ignorant of itself that in almost all men (except for Averroes alone), it has always thought and continues to think that it is multiple in number. For I certainly not only understand, but I also understand that I understand, and similarly that I feel. Therefore, I who understand and I who feel am one and the same. One, I say, through a single being. Otherwise, it would not have been affirmed for so long both by me and by everyone else that the one who understands and the one who feels is exactly the same; rather, the "understander" would be clearly distinguished from the "feeler." For in what way is it likely that a separate, eternal, divine mind, knowing all things in eternity, would be so ignorant of itself that it always and everywhere thinks that it not only understands, but also feels, and moves, and nourishes itself—when, as Averroes thinks, it does none of these things? Second sign: The mind is the place of truth. Truth is the food of the mind, which results in them willingly inviting one another in turn. But since the human mind is either never, or only with great difficulty, made capable of accepting the Averroistic opinion, we can gather that this opinion is not true. Moreover...

Having previously discussed how knowledge is transmitted, Ficino now argues that Averroes himself was unsure of his own theory and that it contradicts the basic structure of human nature and logic.</meta>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<meta>catchword: be formed,</meta>

Even Averroes himself fell into this kind of opinion not by the free judgment of his own mind, but because he did not know any other way to interpret the books of Aristotle, which had been <note>original: "peruersos"</note> poorly translated into the Arabic language. Nor does he put forward a final sentence; rather, he is testing the strength of his own ingenuity. He affirms only this: that the mind is immortal. However, he does not affirm that the mind is one; he merely opines and remains in doubt. In fact, he says that he is only attempting to construct a theory and is leaving the opportunity for debate to those who come after him. And if any others support his doubt, they do so not so much from a sincere conviction of the soul, but rather out of a certain ambitious zeal, so that they might appear capable of defending paradoxes.

Rightly did <term>Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note> say that this paradox is so far from being probable to anyone that not even Averroes himself could have persuaded himself of it. It would have been much more probable—indeed, truer—if Averroes had followed <term>Themistius</term> <note>A 4th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> in introducing a single <term>active intellect</term> <note>The "intellectus agens" or Active Intellect is the part of the mind that processes raw sensory data into abstract thoughts.</note> that provides light, while many other intellects are partly illuminated and partly illuminating. Or if he had followed <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, whose sun-metaphor Ficino famously loved.</note> in positioning God as the Sun, placing beneath Him a single Intellect that is whole everywhere (like the light of the Sun), and then further placing many more intellects beneath that (like the rays of the light), and finally many souls beneath those (like eyes watching the rays). Or, at the very least, if he had followed <term>Avicenna</term> <note>An 11th-century Persian philosopher.</note> in making many minds subject to one Mind, as things capable of being formed are subject to a Form-maker. 

For anyone can easily grasp these ideas and confirm them with an example. But the "Averroistic invention" is entirely foreign to the capacity of any mind. Now, if human minds cannot grasp an invention, it is either because the idea is above them and divine, or because it is against them and false. Because the Averroistic invention concerns the mind, yet is not above the mind's level, it is therefore false. 

**The third sign:** Every time we think about the "unity of the mind" <note>The idea that all humans share one single consciousness.</note>, we naturally tend to hate the idea and desire a multitude of minds—provided that we desire to survive as individuals. Nor should we think that we hate the idea of a single mind merely through our imagination. For if there is any hatred in us toward this concept, the mind itself—which is capable of knowing its own unity—is also capable of hating it. It is not likely that a divine and most blessed thing would always despise, reject, and hate its own nature.

---

### Reasons why there is not one single mind. First, because seven redundancies follow from it. Chapter XV.

**T**he arguments shall be as follows: If the <term>active intellect</term> perfectly understands itself—which the Averroists admit—it cannot be ignorant of its own power and its natural, continuous operation. Therefore, it notices that it is continuously forming, by its own light, the clarity of the <term>receptive intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus capax," also known as the passive or potential intellect, which receives information.</note>. For if the receptive part often notices that it is being illuminated, I do not see why the active part would not notice that it is doing the illuminating, since it is not ignorant of how the receptive intellect is moved by <term>mental images</term> <note>original: "simulachris," often called "phantasms," the pictures the brain forms from sensory input.</note>. 

From this, it follows that it knows it governs individual men and, moreover, illuminates the mental images of men. Thus, it understands those images and whatever is signified by them—especially because while it descends to sensible things through its intellectual power, it also passes into them through that same cognitive force. Therefore, it understands those things not because it is formed by them, but because it forms itself within them, while it discerns its own natural form (or innate forms) within individual things through its own distinguishing light. 

If the receptive part, in a certain reflective way, receives through itself and reaches the images from which it seemingly received them, why would the active part—which actually creates the <term>species</term> <note>The mental "form" or "category" of a thing.</note>—not reach the images from which it creates them? Both parts must reach them in an intellectual manner, since by their nature they are nothing other than intellect. He who reaches them in this way gazes upon the sensible images. 

Since, therefore, the substance of the mind in this "active" part has the power to know both eternal and temporal things, what is the need to join that "receptive" part to it? Is it perhaps to prepare and execute the effect of this work? Not at all. For the active part prepares the receptive part and the images of the imagination, not the other way around. Nor does it need external matter to act, since it is capable of operating both within itself and from internal sources. Since there is already in the active part an effective power sufficient for understanding, the addition of a receptive power to form one mind out of two substances is <note>original: "superflua"</note> redundant. 

But even if we grant that the receptive power is joined to the active, this receptive part, being subordinate to the active, would again know both eternal and temporal things. This knowledge would also be redundant in the universal mind on the receptive side, since it is already present on the other side. Furthermore, this receptive power, formed by human images, knows temporal things in us which it already knew in the active part. Thus, this third instance of knowledge is likewise redundant. If the power of seeing through some "active sense" joined to itself always saw every individual thing, it would be said in vain that the eye requires a separate power through which it might be moved and formed by external objects.

be formed. Just as a redundancy <note>original: "superfluïtas"</note> arises from the words of Averroes regarding these three types of knowledge, so too does it arise in these three types of formation. If the <term>capable intellect</term> <note>The "intellectus capax," or possible intellect, is the passive part of the mind that receives and stores information.</note> is formed by the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The "intellectus agens," or active intellect, is the part that processes raw sensory data into abstract thoughts.</note> once through its essence—as Averroes himself thinks—it is redundant for it to be formed again and again by the images of all men at once, and redundant for it to be formed daily by the images of wise and happy men. All these redundancies follow from the sayings of Averroes which we recounted from the beginning. This clearly shows us that his opinion should be rejected as useless. 

Let him boast, then, that he has discovered a "divine mind" which, while being wise in itself, is always raving <note>original: "delirat"</note> within us. And since countless men consider the same thing every day and are often mistaken, that mind would consider the same thing a million times over at every single moment and would frequently be deceived. If the mind itself never notices this redundancy and the fallacies injected into it by <term>phantasms</term> <note>Phantasms are the mental images derived from sensory experience.</note>, then it is forever ignorant of itself. Yet we experience the opposite within ourselves whenever we refute our own errors. If it does notice them, yet does not turn its attention away from those wanderings into itself when it is able to do so, it is forever weak and forever lacking self-control. But the eternal mind is able to turn its face away forever from the trifles of temporal images. Indeed, the temporal soul often withdraws itself for a time from the trifles of the senses; nor can an affection for individual things—which are beneath mankind—detain that mind in those errors and whirlpools, for it is not even so affected toward human nature itself that it would conspire merely to manufacture appearances. In what way, then, will it concur with this living being in its innermost operations, unless it first joins with it in its very being? For even the form of fire communicates the very heating of external matter (which is an external operation), even if it has by no means communicated its own being; however, to be hot in itself (which is an internal operation), it only communicates after communicating its being.

->*Second reason: Because the mind preserves species, and by now it ought to be full of everything.*<-

### Chapter XVI.

**A**lthough in the previous book we proved, according to the opinion of Plato, that new forms do not come into the mind, let us nevertheless side with the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> for the present. Let us grant that new <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" are the mental forms or universal concepts of things.</note> are created in the capable mind by the power of the agent mind when images are present—provided that the image does not provide the efficient power to create the form, but rather the impulse of an occasion, as we have explained elsewhere. If the entire power of producing a universal species is in the agent, and the entire power of sustaining it is in the capable faculty, then surely the species will be preserved by those two even without the presence of images. 

But let it be granted, if it seems right, that the image has the efficient power to produce the species, as long as it plays the role of a tool, while the agent intellect acts as the craftsman. Therefore, the agent intellect, as the principal cause in which the entire power of subsequent causes is included, once it has impressed the species upon the capable mind, preserves it by itself. Indeed, species flourish in the mind even while the images lie dormant in idleness; and since in Averroes’ view these images relate to the species as external movers, they cannot preserve the species unless they are acting upon it and moving it. But they move only when they are in act, not when they are merely a <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) refers to a stored capacity or skill that is not currently being used.</note>. If species remain in the inner sense for a long time and proceed into action even if they are not preserved or stirred up by the external senses, how much more so should species remain in the mind without the need for images? 

The mind should not be compared to the external senses, which lose forms when the objects are absent. For the senses do not possess true forms, but merely images, and they do not contribute by their own power to the manufacturing of those images. The mind, however, possesses true "reasons" <note>original: "rationes," referring to the underlying logical principles or definitions of things.</note> through which it understands the true substances of things, and it fashions them for itself. Therefore, it can preserve them by the same power with which it fashioned them. Furthermore, if the species of the mind depended on images no differently than shadows depend on bodies, they would have nothing in themselves more excellent than the images. But if they have anything more sublime, that would be the gift of the agent power, by which they will be preserved even when the images are removed. That they do not depend on images like shadows can be proven by the fact that they are so radically fixed that they imprint a totally indelible habit. Nor should it be said that species have a meager essence because they refer to universals, and therefore always need the foundation of images to preserve them. First, because they contain and refer to more things, better things, and things more pertaining to the essence of reality than images do; therefore, they are...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument against the Averroist position that the human intellect is entirely dependent on bodily images. Here, Ficino transitions from logical critiques to a psychological and metaphysical explanation of how the Mind (mens) actually governs the Imagination (phantasia), rather than being its slave.</meta>

<page-num>359</page-num>
<header>## ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.</header>

and conversely, intelligence moves from being into non-being, and back again. Nor do the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" are the abstract formal qualities or "essences" of things that the mind perceives.</note> require images to be preserved. Indeed, even those who champion the use of <term>phantasms</term> <note>Mental images derived from sensory experience.</note> confess that although we need specific images to understand the common natures of bodies, we are never accustomed to using specific images to gaze upon divine forms. Instead, we use the "natures" themselves, which images merely accompany. From this it appears that these notions of divine things are preserved in the mind not by images (which flow together by accident), but by the mind itself, having already been prepared through prior speculation.

Furthermore, when we connect that Platonic series of Ideas—in which we place certain middle species before the final species, and again place subaltern genera before those, until by many steps we climb to the widest genera—we are also forced to transcend the genera. Reaching that nature which encompasses all genera from the outside, we are then compelled to let go of images. Such images wander only as far as the final species and cannot accompany that ascent, unless perhaps we were to arrange the entire universal order within every single image. That cannot actually happen; and even if it were imagined, it is not imagined by the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "phantasy" or imagination is the faculty that handles sensory images; the "mind" is the higher faculty of abstract reason.</note> but by the mind. For the mind occasionally innovates new notions beyond existing notions—even into infinity, if it pleases—whereas images do not innovate in this way. Nor does anything hinder the mind, as pertains to its nature, from flying thus "naked" of images into eternity.

Sometimes, however, as the mind resolves narrower things into broader ones, it paints images in the phantasy that correspond in a way to the species. In these cases, because the species themselves come first, they create and preserve the images, not the other way around. We perceive that the phantasy is formed by the mind from the fact that many things suddenly shine within it—the likes of which it had never received from the senses nor devised on its own. The mind also divides and composes images not without some logic, and it proceeds by imagining into infinity. Indeed, the phantasy is shaped by the mind without end. It even receives rational habits and characters. 

The phantasy is formed by the mind far more than it forms the mind. For if the phantasy ever "forms" the mind, it does so only because it has been struck by the senses and by the power of the mind. The phantasy cannot hand over an infinite number of forms, yet the mind forms the phantasy out of itself and without end. Occasionally, whether through deep affection or a certain divine inspiration, the mind can be provoked to understand without any images at all. This signifies (what we have often sought to prove) that even while the mind is present in the body, it sometimes operates without the body’s help. Therefore, when it has departed from the body, it will operate by itself all the more effectively.

If the <term>Averroists</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Averroes, who argued that the individual soul could not think without the body's sensory images.</note> argue here that those who have a particular physical <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the balance of bodily humors (blood, bile, etc.) which was thought to determine personality and health.</note> tend to be stronger in intelligence and memory because intellectual notions depend continuously on the senses, we can respond to these <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> that a certain physical state of the body serves the *senses* directly, but the *mind* only by accident. This is because while the mind is joined to the body, it crafts its own species through sensory images in a certain way; and as often as it turns toward its own species (which it made and preserved), it almost always turns back toward the images. It "turns back," I say, partly because of a certain kinship between them, and partly because of a habit conceived from the soul's condition of being coupled to the body. 

And although we see wit and memory in any variety of physical complexion—which forces us to admit these things proceed from a higher principle—let it be (if you like) that a "dry" nature is more mindful. This is true as long as dryness is the cause of memory *directly* in the senses, but in the mind only *by accident*. This is not only because the memory of the senses serves the mind, as we said, but also because the "dryness of the spirits" <note>The "spirits" were thin vapors in the body that carried signals; dryness was thought to make them less volatile and more stable for storing information.</note> does not hinder the soul when it contracts toward its innermost parts to collect itself. Thus, because of intense and constant thought, the intellect is sharpened and the memory is confirmed. Humidity, on the other hand, does the opposite.

To these points, the <term>Platonists</term> would say that there are as many "armies of souls" as there are stars, and that they take their nature and name from them. Hence, they say there are Saturnian souls, Jovian, Martian, Solar, and others likewise. From these stars, souls receive various gifts regarding wit, memory, will, character, arts, and fortunes. All these gifts, insofar as they come from that source, are good, although here on earth they often degenerate due to a multiple clash of causes. Furthermore, souls receive spiritual gifts from the *souls* and divinities of their stars (both those leading and those following), but they receive bodily and sensory gifts from the physical *bodies* of the stars. Therefore, if the Saturnian or Mercurial souls of men obtain help from that source for wit and memory, they also simultaneously receive a certain physical disposition in the body from the physical bodies of those same stars. This physical state is not the *cause* of the intellectual gift, but all these things happen together. Finally, from the intensity of the will and constant attention, a great...

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY

...from which the excellence of sharpness and memory largely arises. But we must not digress further here. Our point is this: let us reject that Averroist <note>The followers of the 12th-century philosopher Averroes, who argued that all humans share a single, communal intellect.</note> opinion which asserts that the absolute <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the abstract, universal forms or "blueprints" of things held in the mind.</note> of the divine mind depend upon the bodily images of the temporal imagination, like shadows depend upon bodies. Instead, let us place our faith in Plato, who says that what has truly been understood once can never be entirely committed to oblivion; rather, the "species" of the thing understood is turned into an everlasting <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitum"; a permanent disposition or state of being.</note> within the eternal mind. For it has no contrary whose approach could destroy it, nor is it ever abandoned by its subject.

Therefore, if the Averroist mind is said to draw the species of all things from the imaginations of all men at every single moment—through which it understands all things—and if this mind has no beginning, and the generation of mankind has also always existed, then surely for thousands of millions of years before us, it possessed all species and habits not just once, but countless times. Indeed, it never received its first species from anyone, if there was never a "first" man who understood. Thus, it did not fashion its species through anyone’s images; rather, its species are its very self, or the unfolding of its essence.

Aristotle would not have granted this; he would say that the mind receives species, and has received them all for a long time. Yet it preserves whatever it receives in an immovable way—provided it receives them intellectually—according to an intellectual reason. If it acquired every single thing infinitely long ago, and is full of all things and overflowing, what more does it seek? What is the meaning of this superfluous, endless receiving of forms? For this reason, the mind would understand nothing in us now, since it receives nothing from us.

Perhaps Averroes will answer that if the mind already possesses the species of some thing—say, gold—it does not receive another species of gold recently from my imagination while I am thinking about gold. Instead, he might say that the species of gold itself (which, as far as I am concerned, was in a sense "sleeping" in the mind) is awakened because of the image of gold in my mind. Thus, the mind recently looks back at my imagination and understands gold in me, just as it previously understood it in someone else.

If that were the case, the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that actively processes sensory data into abstract thought.</note> would no longer produce any species, nor would the "capacity" of the mind receive any, since all species have been possessed for a long time. This, however, contradicts Averroes and his followers, who want new species to be created and received daily. It also contradicts the Peripatetic <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> sect, which asserts that the intellect is like a **blank slate** <note>original: "tabellam cui nihil sit inscriptum"; literally "a tablet on which nothing has been written."</note> upon which nothing is written. Averroes, while defending his opinion, will never be able to explain this except in an inept and ridiculous way.

To us, however, it is not inconsistent. Led by Plato, we believe the intellect is not forced to generate a new species of "man" every time the imagination presents us with various images of different men; rather, the previously conceived species is instead "awakened." Just as Socrates’ imagination does not fashion a new image of Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates.</note> within itself every time he happens to see Alcibiades on the same day, but rather brings the latent image from within into action. The eyes would do the same, if they could preserve images.

### *Thirdly, because as often as two people understand the same thing, total absurdities follow.* Chapter XVII.

**M**y imagination is now thinking of gold, and yours is also thinking of gold. The Averroist mind, excited by our images, gives birth to the species of gold within itself and understands gold. We must ask: does it now receive one single species and one single understanding of gold for both of us, or twin species and twin understandings? Or perhaps one species and twin understandings, or vice-versa?

Some followers of Averroes follow the first part of this division. They are refuted by this reasoning: if the diversity of our images makes no diversity in the Mind, they prattle far too rashly whenever they assert that the Mind understands gold in me and in you—or rather, that "I" and "you" understand gold. For the Mind alone will understand, and only within itself while we are thinking. This would be just as Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato and head of the Academy.</note> sees within himself one common truth harmonizing with both Speusippus and Polemon <note>Successive heads of the Platonic Academy after Plato.</note> while he hears them disagreeing in words through ignorance during a dispute.

Furthermore, if the Mind understands gold in me now and in you with the same act of understanding, then as soon as it stops considering it in you, it must likewise stop considering it in me. But we experience the opposite. They will deny that this follows. They might say that just as in our case the same soul gives life to both the arm and the hand, and if the hand is cut off it stops giving life to the hand but not the arm; so too, they say, the Mind stops considering in your image but continues to consider in mine alone, whereas before it was considering in both at once. This example is not suitable. The act of giving life passes into the body, but the act of understanding does not descend into the images. Therefore, in two members...

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

->Z 5<-

In the different members of the body, different acts of giving life are received; yet the act of understanding in a single mind remains one. But this example is more fitting in this way: just as the soul lived through one life in both limbs, and afterwards lives through that same life in only one, so the mind, through the same act of understanding, considered things in both individuals, through which it afterwards contemplates in only one. But even this example does not fit well enough, because we can correctly say "to live here or there," but we can by no means say "to understand here or there." Indeed, understanding is completed by being set apart from any specific location.

Truly, if the eye, with the same gaze, sees both the right and left parts of a small surface at once, and meanwhile, the left part is removed, does that very same gaze—which was perceiving both—not remain whole? It simply ends at the one part, whereas before it ended at both. In the same way, does the same act of understanding look upon one <term>simulachrum</term> <note>original: "simulachrum"; a mental image or phantasm derived from the senses</note> which had previously looked upon two? This also fails to harmonize. First, because the eye does not properly "cease to see" while its vision remains whole; rather, that part of the surface which is broken away "ceases to be seen." But even if it did cease to see, what then? Is the gaze not directed toward localized parts of a surface? So that it might not be unreasonable to say it sees "here" as much as "there," and therefore perhaps it ceases to see here at some point, but not there. 

Intelligence, however, does not extend itself toward localized images, but toward a reason that is excluded from all space. Therefore, it is not correctly said to perish "here" and not "there," but either it perishes nowhere, or it ceases entirely everywhere. What, then, does that rash response mean: that intelligence looks at two images at one moment, and then only one? It is not because it looks at the images themselves, for it looks at something higher. Nor is it because it moves the images, because the mind does not properly understand from this; rather, it affects the images in such a way that they either understand, or move something else toward understanding. Or is it perhaps that the mind is moved by the images? If that were so, why did they not say the mind is "looked upon" by the images rather than "looking upon" them? 

But they might say: What does it mean for the mind to be "looked upon" by others? Does the mental <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the abstract form or concept of an object</note> depend upon the images like shadows depend upon bodies? Indeed, this is the "magnificent" discovery of Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose theory of a single, shared human intellect Ficino is attacking here.</note> himself! No more does it follow from this that the mind understands "in the images" than that the sense of hearing hears "in the voice," or the sense of smell smells "in the odor." On the contrary, because the images of gold have been set aside, the mind—through itself—enters into the absolute and single <term>species</term> of gold, and into the one and absolute reason of gold. Thus, it understands apart from us in the Idea itself through a single act; and if it ever ceases to understand, it ceases there entirely all at once and in a single moment. 

Those who assert that "species" are the shadows of images, and then claim that one species emanates from two images—and again that the same species which previously flowed from your image alone later flows from mine as well (both while you are present and after you cease)—are just as delusional as those who would claim either that a single shadow flows from two different bodies, or that the shadow of one body is preserved by another body after the first has been removed. 

Add to this that in the same moment, that one mind, through one species and one act of understanding regarding one piece of gold, would disagree with itself: it would judge in me that gold is to be despised and rejected, yet in you it would judge it precious and desire it. Such a great conflict in judgments and emotions cannot proceed from a single principle, insofar as it is one. 

They claim there is no diversity in the intelligence or the species; does it then come from the diversity of the images? Not at all. Certainly, a diversity of images would produce a difference in the species and the acts of intelligence before it ever produced a difference in judgments and emotions. Who, then, would agree that a single act of understanding could end in contrary judgments and conflicting emotions, as if the same motion could proceed toward opposite goals? 

Some of them flee to this explanation: that those two images create one species in the mind, but that this species, insofar as it proceeds from two images, produces two acts of understanding directed toward different ends. But who would say that the "truth" of the images (which is closer to the species than to the acts of intelligence) does not create different species, but does create different acts of understanding? Furthermore, if that species is given to the mind with different respects toward different things, it is not given as something entirely absolute, nor is it a sufficient principle for understanding. If it is not given as something different, it will not give birth to a difference in the acts of understanding. 

Add to this that no person of sound mind would ever concede that a single power of acting or knowing could, through a single form at the same time, produce multiple operations that are numerically different regarding the same object. Just as a single eye, looking at the same thing through a single image, does not produce two visions at the same time—for one is sufficient, and they cannot be different unless they come from different principles. Hence, if all men used the same eye for living, they would have only one vision of the sun at the same time through one image of the sun. Similarly, one intellect through one...

the appearance of gold, in a single moment, it has one understanding of gold. Nor do those two <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulachra"; these are the "phantasms" or mental pictures derived from the senses that the mind uses to think</note> bring about any difference here. Though they precede the act of understanding as certain preparations—or rather, as incitements—they never actually enter into the act, nor do they even necessarily concur with it. A similar comparison applies to the acts of the senses in relation to the imagination. Nor do I think there will be a lack of those who dare to assert that two images of gold provide two <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the "intelligible forms" or mental concepts</note> to the mind, yet only one act of understanding regarding that gold results from them.

We have rejected this because if a diversity of images has such great power as to produce a diversity in the species—even though the image and the species exist in different substances <note>The image is in the physical imagination, while the species is in the immaterial mind</note>—how much more will a difference of species produce a difference of understandings, especially since they exist within the same essence of the mind? Among such people, does not a single movement work toward contrary ends when, through one understanding, contrary judgments and contrary feelings are made?

What will they answer us when we ask: can either species, taken separately from the other, produce an act of understanding, or not? If it cannot, the mind will be unable to see anything unless the images of that thing are doubled in the mind, one of which will always be superfluous. If, however, it can, then each species performs its own act, and two acts of understanding arise from two species.

More recent followers of <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued that all humans share a single, communal intellect</note> admit that two <term>intelligible forms</term> <note>The abstract concepts that the mind "reads" from sensory data</note> of gold are produced simultaneously in the same mind from two images, which are followed by two acts of understanding. At first, one might mock them with the same reasoning Averroes used to mock us, as we have shown elsewhere. It is certain that these forms do not differ from one another in kind, since they both lead to the knowledge of one type of gold and are both intellectual likenesses of gold. But if they differ only in number within the same kind, they can—and indeed must—be resolved into another more common form, if understanding is to be fulfilled through them. 

Let them be resolved, then. We ask whether that more common form is entirely one within the mind in both me and you, or if it is different. If it is the same, the understanding is completed by this alone, and we could have posited only one from the start. If it is different, we resolve it similarly. And because we would wander into infinity, it is better to posit only one at the beginning. 

But let us set aside these quibbles. If intelligible forms follow images to the extent that they are created and preserved by them, and are counted by them, it is impossible that they would not be singular in the same way that the images are singular—just as the images of colors exist as singular things according to the singularity of the colors themselves. For whatever is so tightly bound is necessarily subjected to the singular conditions of those things. Nor will the mind grant them the ability to become absolute <note>meaning universal or independent of specific physical instances</note>. For just as the mind does not sufficiently provide them with a beginning in time or a persistence in time, so it will not sufficiently provide them with the absolute commonality of an eternal nature. And since commonality and "absoluteness" consist in unity, the mind—which cannot grant unity to the forms even though it is itself one, but is overcome in this by the images—will also not grant commonality. Instead, it will be overcome by the images that provide singularity. 

Hence, we will ask Averroes' followers about these two intelligible forms of gold: do they differ by themselves, or by the subject in which they exist, or by something added from outside? Not by themselves, otherwise, according to their own doctrine, they would differ in kind. Not by the subject, which they say is unique. Not by anything foreign.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; For this could be nothing else than some relationship, either to the images of gold or to the essence of gold itself. Certainly, they will not differ through the aspect pertaining to the essence of gold, since that essence is one. But neither will they differ through their relationship to the images of gold themselves.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; For a form contributes to understanding only insofar as it is freed from the looking upon images; it regards a nature that is entirely free from images—namely, a nature free from place and time. Therefore, as soon as the intellectual form is shaped, it ceases to look at the images. But suppose those forms do look at the images and differ by that relationship; certainly they do not differ by a simple relationship, but by a double one. Therefore, there will be two relationships in the two forms, not differing in kind, since they refer to the one nature of gold. They would thus differ only in number. But by what do they differ? Not by themselves, otherwise they would differ in kind. Not by the subject, for they are placed in one mind. Nor should they be said to be doubled because they are placed in double forms. For it was granted that the forms themselves are doubled by the relationships, rather than by something added from outside, since we would again have to add relationships to relationships and be tied down by the later ones just as by the former.

Again we ask whether those relations are founded in the forms or in the <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulachris"; these are the "phantasms" or mental pictures derived from the senses that the mind uses as a starting point for thought.</note>. If in the images, the forms will be looked back upon by the images rather than looking themselves. If in the forms, they do not pertain to the essence of the forms themselves—because they would introduce a difference into the forms according to species—but are added to the essences of the forms from the outside by the makers of those very images. From this it follows that such things are particular, because of the very singularity of the corporeal images. How much this hinders the purity of understanding, no one of sound mind is ignorant. Truly, since images are compared to forms like external agents, they will never cause one form to be distinguished from another; instead, individual images would apply certain conditions to individual forms emanating from them, by which the forms would differ among themselves in no other way than the images differ from each other. Thus, they will not be <term>absolute forms</term> <note>Universal concepts that are independent of specific material instances.</note> while they are contracted into the narrowness of the images. Moreover, it is entirely incredible that two absolute forms should be found in the same subject differing only by number. For by the very fact that they would differ neither by reason and essence, nor by subject, they would be forced to differ from each other through foreign qualities, and thus they would not be absolute. However, it is not impossible for them to be in two subjects. For they will be distinguished from each other at the same time because they will form distinct subjects, yet they will remain absolute because they will not be formed by the subjects, since the subjects are simple and free from impurities.
