### Fourth [Reason]. Because either knowledge is the same for many men, or qualities are superfluous. Chapter XVIII.

**A**ll qualities—whether [separated] from their limit or from an external conserver—that are one in species, if they concur in the same subject, also become one in number. For things that agree in species also agree in form. If, moreover, they agree in matter because of the subject, they are entirely one. For this reason, in a single drop of wine, there is sweetness and redness together; these two qualities are different in species, yet there are not two sweetnesses there, nor two rednesses. Although the images and splendors of qualities can exist in the same place, differing only according to number—such as the images of two eggs in the eye and the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of the soul that stores and processes sensory images.</note>, or even the two lights of two candles in the same air—this is because they depend continuously on external things, and therefore they follow the number of those things whose images or lights they are, rather than the number of the subject. However, those qualities which are both true and follow the nature of the subject rather than the object become one in number through the subject if they were one in species.

Now, the absolute form of the mind is its true and stable quality because it is not an image, shadow, or splendor of foreign accidents, but an offspring of intellectual substance, an exemplar of substances, and a rule of truth depending on the intellect, not on external things. Therefore, there are not certain absolute forms in the mind differing from each other only in number. Here one may disregard that <term>Averroistic objection</term> <note>Referring to the followers of Averroes (Ibn Rushd), who argued for a single, shared human intellect. They claimed that the multiplicity of individual sensory images allowed one universal mind to think different things for different people simultaneously.</note>. They say that the image is the principle of the intelligible form; therefore, as many images as occur at once, just as many forms are made, because any one of the images apart from the others can sufficiently effect the form.

We, however, say that the image is neither the principle of the form—provided the form is universal—nor the preparation of the capable mind to receive the form (lest it be in the mind before the form, or certainly be more like the mind), but it is a certain occasion for the incitement of the active power. This [the image] would never even accomplish if it were in one substance while the form was in another. But if they are in the same soul, as they certainly are, it provides an occasion in a certain way, as we have explained elsewhere. Therefore, when the image of gold presents itself, if the mind had never before received the form of gold, the mind itself produces it, having found the occasion to produce it. But if it has produced it at another time and possesses it, it does not produce another, but leads the one it possesses into act. Indeed, it produces and leads forth only one, even if a thousand images of the same species were to occur.

Do you not notice that when you look at a thousand men in a theater with your eyes, and afterwards you recall a thousand images of these men at once in your imagination, the mind meanwhile considers them thus: "Man is a beautiful animal, rejoicing in society, clever, and religious." Here the mind does not pronounce this about any one of those thousand, but about the one common nature of them all, about the common substance of the rational animal, and about the common definition of society, cleverness, and religion itself. This one judgment concerning the one [nature] of all...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind produces its own universal concepts (forms) using sensory images only as "occasions" for thought, rather than being shaped by them. He uses this to refute the Averroist idea that a single universal intellect could contain multiple individual thoughts.</summary>

Ficino is arguing that if all humans shared a single mind, our individual thoughts and learned "habits" (skills or knowledge) would be indistinguishably merged into one, which contradicts our experience of individual learning and personality.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
<page-num>364</page-num>

The mind cannot more conveniently grasp the nature of men or of virtues than through a single **species** <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning a universal concept or the essential form of a thing that the mind perceives.</note> and likeness. From this, it is apparent that the mind has drawn only one single "species of man" from a thousand images of men. It does the same always with all the images of the same species, however diverse they may be: from all the images of horses collected together, it draws one "species of horse," but it does not draw one species from the images of a horse and a man together, but rather two.

Whoever has ever understood anything experiences this within themselves. Therefore, when a hundred men see a horse, they collect a hundred <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulachra"; these are the mental pictures or "phantasms" derived from the senses.</note> in their individual imaginations. Truly, if there is only one mind for everyone, then being provoked by those hundred images, it conceives only one species of horse, which a single act of understanding follows. There will be, therefore, only one act of understanding among a hundred men. 

In what way then does one person cease to understand while another does not? Certainly, innumerable men succeeding one another could understand through that same act of understanding remaining within itself. From this, it would follow that the contemplation of temporal things is eternal—something that **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential and controversial in the Renaissance.</note> himself will not concede. The mind does not consider the horse as "this specific horse," but simply according to the universal nature of the equine species. This nature is one, even if there are a thousand images of a thousand horses in the soul of one man or many. 

Therefore, there will be only one consideration of a horse among many men. From such consideration, the **habit of knowledge** <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition or state of mind, such as being "learned" in a subject like grammar or geometry.</note> is contracted in the mind. In the mind, I say, not in the **imagination** <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty that processes sensory images; Ficino argues it is lower than the intellect and tied to the body.</note>, provided that the act of understanding is the disposition toward the habit, and where the disposition is, there the form must be—that is, the habit: a universal habit derived from universal acts and forms. But in the imagination, since according to Averroes it is bound to matter, there can be neither an act nor a habit according to a universal mode. 

There will be, therefore, one and the same habit of knowledge—as far as it regards the consideration of the equine species—among a hundred men. Indeed, since the intellect preserves these species and habits, any one of us who understands through this intellect, and whose understanding is that very same understanding of the mind, would right now understand everything that present and past men have ever known. 

Averroes will respond that we understand through the intellect only insofar as it is joined to us through our images. And because the images are not the same for everyone, nor are they affected in the same way, therefore what one person knows, another does not necessarily recognize. Such a response is not sufficient. For when the mind is already actually endowed with the species, it can meditate by itself, as **Aristotle** confesses. From this, we see that we can meditate on that which we have already learned whenever we wish, without being hindered by the absence of images. For if images are the "way" to the species, what need is there for the way after we have reached the goal? What need for preparation after we have obtained the habit? This habit is so far from needing images as its preservers that it does not even seem to further need those very acts from which it was most closely and properly created once it has been confirmed. 

Indeed, when it is already "grown up," it flourishes in the intellect by its own nature and no longer depends on images, nor does it look back at them. If this is so, the habits that exist in the Averroistic intellect are already equally perfected for everyone, since they are already absolute and do not look outward to this place more than that. Therefore, **Aristippus** and **Socrates** <note>Aristippus was a follower of Socrates but focused on pleasure, whereas Socrates focused on virtue; Ficino uses them as opposites to show the absurdity of their sharing the same mind.</note> would have been equally learned and equally good. And when **Plato**, **Simus**, and **Xenophon** learn grammar, they would both acquire a habit of grammar identical to each other.

There is one single principle for the most similar grammar; therefore, its habits, wherever they may be, are of the same species. Such a habit in Plato and a similar habit in Xenophon are one in species. But if the intellect in which they exist (as if in a subject) is one, then they are also one in number. For if any forms become one by the unity of the subject, such a thing is most especially a habit, which passes into the nature of the subject; indeed, it usurps the nature of the subject for itself, provides a certain inclination, and, being itself immobile, moves the subject. 

Therefore, if the mind is one, either the knowledge of two people will be entirely the same—two will think as one and cease to think as one—or else innumerable qualities of the same species will exist in the same subject. Daily, the intellect would receive many qualities identical in species to those it already has, as if honey were to receive, at every single moment, one sweetness after another, each most similar to its own. And in this, Averroes's opinion will greatly oppose itself, for in his books *On the Soul*, he repeated three times (following the opinion of Aristotle) that every subject must be empty of the species of that quality which it is about to receive. Furthermore, we experience in ourselves that the mind not only understands, but also notices that it understands, and moves from one thought to another, often similar, often even opposite...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that Averroes’s theory of a single shared human intellect is logically impossible because it would mean all people share identical knowledge, virtues, and thoughts simultaneously. He highlights the absurdity of individuals like Socrates and Aristippus possessing the same moral habits if they shared one mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s systematic refutation of the Averroistic "Unity of the Intellect." On the previous page, Ficino argued that if all humans shared one mind, our individual thoughts would be shared. Here, he continues that line of reasoning before moving into a new argument regarding the impossibility of holding contradictory beliefs in a single mind.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
<page-num>365</page-num>

...to transfer itself most easily in a moment, and to connect many things into **one**. Furthermore, it is undoubtedly a marvel that the **Averroistic mind** <note>The doctrine of Averroës, a 12th-century philosopher, which claimed all humans share a single, eternal intellect.</note>—which is supposedly unique, eternal, indivisible, uniform, and equally present to all—can catch many notions of a person who is disputing through the expression of a single word; and what is more, it can often perceive what another person holds in their **phantasy** <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of the soul that stores and processes sensory images (phantasms) before they are understood by the intellect.</note> (which is further removed from the mind). Yet, [under this theory], that mind would never notice in me what it understands in you, nor would it ever join what it gazes upon in you with those things it observes in another, nor would it ever predict by its own power what it thinks in one person while in the company of another. Nor is it permitted to flee to the "diversity of images" <note>original: "simulachrorum diuersitatem"; the Averroists argued that differences in human thoughts came from different individual sensory images, even if the mind was one.</note>, for these images are outside and below the level of the mind; moreover, many things are understood at a specific time when no image is intervening, nor accompanying the thought in a proper sense.

### Fifth argument: because contradictories would exist in the same thing. Chapter XIX.

**C**ontradictories oppose one another much more than contraries do, just as there is a greater repugnance between **being** and **not-being** than there is between being **this way** and being **that way**. Therefore, if contraries cannot meet in the same subject, much less can contradictories. Thus it happens that each of us experiences within ourselves that our mind never affirms and denies a thing entirely at the same time, nor does it fully will and not will something, even if many different **images** <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulachra"; mental pictures derived from the senses.</note> of that thing are present in our phantasy. 

Now, the Averroists should not bring forward the argument that the image of whiteness and blackness can be in the eye and the phantasy simultaneously, or that their **species** <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the intellectual form or concept of a thing.</note> can be in the mind at once (where there might also be knowledge of contraries simultaneously). For these kinds of forms, which are contrary when they exist outside the soul, are not contrary inside the soul because they lose their [physical] nature. They are transformed into a certain quality of the soul, and an "imaginary" one at that. But to assent and not to assent, to will and not to will, retain their contradictory force, because these are essential acts rather than imaginary ones, and they signify the **being** and **not-being** of that same act or affection of the soul. 

Therefore, although the species of whiteness and blackness are not contrary within the sense of sight, nevertheless, the vision of an object as white and the vision of that same object as black oppose each other in such a way that they cannot happen at once—even though those visions depend continually on different species and objects. In the same way, the affirmation of the **Divine Trinity** <note>original: "diuinæ Trinitatis"; the Christian doctrine of one God in three persons, often used in logic as a test for belief or denial.</note> and its denial cannot coexist in the mind at the same time, even if they are said to depend on different images and species. Surely, the diversity of the agents involved does nothing to prevent contrary affections from opposing and expelling one another. 

What is it, then, that makes the Averroistic intellect affirm in **Plato** that the "One" itself is above essence and the "Good" itself is above the mind, while in **Aristotle** it rejects this? <note>Ficino uses Plato and Aristotle here as examples of two different people who held opposing philosophical views.</note> Certainly, no variety of images causes this. For such high contemplation is only performed correctly when images have been set aside. Or what makes that intellect affirm in Plato that the heaven is made of fire, but deny it at the same time in Aristotle? Would the diversity of two images perhaps do this? It might, if the mind judged *within* images, or *through* images, or *about* images. But in truth, having taken the opportunity provided by those images, the mind immediately withdraws into itself and judges the common nature of "heaven" and "fire" through a common species within itself. It leaves the looking at images to the phantasy—and a very small part of it at that—which is weakened the more the mind's contemplation is strengthened, and vice versa. 

This is the clearest proof for what we were discussing above: namely, that the intellectual species is neither created by the image nor preserved by it. Could different species, conceived in the mind by the occasion of different images, produce those different opinions? Not at all: for the mind receives only one species from two different images of the same "heaven." But for the sake of argument, let us say it receives two. Even if there are two paths by which opposing opinions seem able to enter the mind, there are not two parts, or powers, or specific forms in the mind in which discordant opinions can be received; rather, they are all gathered into a single and indivisible center of intelligence. A single and most simple judge passes sentence there. One judge cannot so manifesty contradict himself at the same time. A duality of species can do nothing more than provoke the soul in different ways, if indeed they are different. But the intellect delivers its judgment by neglecting the weaker species and, through the command of the one prevailing species, it brings forth only one single opinion—just as the phantasy, though it may be agitated by various conjectures through various senses, produces only one...

<summary>Ficino argues that if all people shared one mind, that mind would have to believe and disbelieve the same things simultaneously, which is a logical impossibility. He uses the differing philosophies of Plato and Aristotle to show that a single intellect cannot hold contradictory "truths" at once.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s "Fifth Argument" against the Averroist doctrine of the Unity of the Intellect. Ficino is arguing that if all humans shared one single mind, that mind would be forced to hold contradictory beliefs and desires at the same moment—a logical impossibility.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
<page-num>366</page-num>

...yet it produces one judgment and one feeling. Anyone can experience this within themselves: that the mind does the same thing amidst various conjectures. But if that one mind were to hesitate between two ideas in two different men, being pulled here and there, since it is conscious of itself within itself, it would not be ignorant of why it was hesitating. Having weighed the conjectures, it would incline toward one side in a brief moment. 

And if it is absurd to say that heat and cold can be received at the same time in the same subject—even if these two are brought in by different causes, namely fire and water—would it not also be ridiculous for contrary opinions to fall into the mind, even if they are sent in from different causes? For whatever is received, is received according to the disposition of the subject. A single subject cannot be disposed in opposite ways at the same time to receive forms that are simply contradictory. 

Furthermore, the argument will be stronger if we argue about contrary **habits** <term>habits</term> <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning stable mental dispositions or acquired patterns of thought, like being "a mathematician" or "virtuous."</note>. Since confirmed habits no longer depend on images [simulachra] for their existence—and are now independent even (what is more) from their own actions—the **Averroists** <note>Followers of the 12th-century philosopher Averroës, who argued that all of humanity shares a single, collective intellect.</note> cannot say that contrary habits can coexist because of certain contrary agents (that is, the images). 

As for their claim that the mind, "clothed" in two **species** <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; mental representations or forms of things being understood.</note>, can act as two subjects in which conflicting things are held: we do not admit this. It does not belong to those who trust in "species" to think of them as mere shadows circling the surface of the mind. Furthermore, in their view, species hold the place of a foreign and temporary act, while the mind holds the place of substance and subject. Two subjects do not come into being because of two added forms; rather, something is received by reason of the subject, not the forms. Therefore, one mind is one subject, even if it receives two species; and by reason of itself (not the species), it receives whatever comes to it. 

How then could an entrance be open to contradictions? One cannot even imagine it, unless perhaps they add that the mind relates to a species as matter relates to quantity. Therefore, just as matter, extended through quantity, receives contrary qualities [in different parts of itself], so the mind, "clothed" in species, receives conflicting opinions. 

This example does not fit at all. They consider quantity to be inseparable from matter, but species to be entirely foreign to the mind. Furthermore, matter does not receive contrary forms through quantity until it is cut into different parts by extension. If Averroës were to grant that the mind is cut into different minds by these species, perhaps we would admit his point. Therefore, if matter—even though it is prepared by quantity—does not receive contrary qualities at the same point in itself, so the mind does not admit contradictions, even if it were affected by various species. By nature, it is a contradiction that they should dwell together. They cannot be together, even if someone tried to reconcile them through some medium. 

Add to this that if conflicting things are to be received through certain preparations, they require conflicting preparations. If preparations, in so far as they contribute to certain habits, match them in some proportion, they must likewise hinder diverse habits and disagree with their preparations. And if preparations for conflicting things are received by the same subject through other discordant affections, we will wander into infinity. But if no affection intervenes, that is indeed absurd; for conflicting habits could then be received without a medium, just like the affections. 

Therefore, if our mind were to be disposed toward the conflicting acts and habits of contradictories, there would first be a need for species that oppose each other, and even for discordant reasonings. These, excited by the disagreeing species, would take up clashing principles of reasoning and reach contradictory conclusions through discordant means. All this conflict, which distracts one toward contradictories, can no more be received by the mind without a medium than can the contradictories themselves. If a medium is sought, it will be sought without end. 

Just as we have disputed concerning contradictory assents, so we may speak of contradictory feelings. For example, when that [one shared] mind, in the person of Plato, wants some universal object, and at the same time, in the person of Aristotle, does not want it—such a feeling does not belong to the **phantasies** <note>original: "phantasias"; the faculty of the soul that deals with sensory images.</note>, which no more reach a universal thing by desiring it than by thinking of it. We also see contrary feelings in the mind when two men simultaneously reject two universal objects that disagree with each other, and when some rejoice in incorporeal things while others at the same time grieve. 

Finally, the same mind will be virtuous and wicked at the same time, wise and ignorant, certain and doubtful, happy and miserable. What will they say to this? That from conflicting acts and feelings, conflicting habits will grow together in the same mind—namely, contrary ones. This [is the conclusion of their theory].

<summary>Ficino argues that the Averroist theory of a single shared mind is logically impossible because it would require one mind to hold contradictory beliefs and emotions simultaneously. He refutes the idea that "mental species" allow the mind to function as multiple subjects, noting that a single substance cannot be in two opposing states at once.</summary>

...Furthermore, this is the most absurd of all because a **habit** <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable, acquired mental disposition, such as knowing a language or a science.</note> is not some imaginary thing, but rather takes the place of a natural form. Now, a natural form and its inclination is destroyed by the arrival of an opposing form and inclination. We have perhaps disputed longer than was proper about the mind with those people who deprive themselves of a mind when they separate it from the human species—a mind which is so familiar to the human species that we cannot even accept the mind without using the mind, nor can they reject the mind without using the mind. However, we believe that in the preceding arguments we have not only refuted Averroës, but also those **Moors** <note>Ficino refers to the North African and Andalusian Islamic philosophers who followed Averroës’s interpretation of Aristotle.</note> who think there is only one soul for all. For if there is a distinction among minds, there is a much greater diversity among living beings—both because human minds are more unified with each other (since they are more excellent) than souls are with each other, and because if a single soul were sufficient for governing our bodies, one mind would be even more sufficient for grasping the truth. 

Therefore, we must not believe those **adulterated Platonists** <note>Ficino likely refers to thinkers who misinterpreted Plotinus or other Neoplatonists to suggest a total pantheism or a lack of individual identity.</note> who assert that all living things live through a single **World Soul** <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima mundi"; the concept that the entire universe is a living organism with its own soul.</note>, because then we would not be guided by free movement and a variety of deliberation, but would be carried along by a sudden impulse, like arrows. And if we all breathed by some single soul of the world, we would also only contemplate by some single mind above the world. In fact, the very diversity and distinction of worldly bodies signifies a distinction of natures; the distinction of natures follows a distinction of souls; the distinction of souls accompanies a distinction of minds; and minds implanted in souls retain the number of those souls. 

One may also laugh at a certain barbarian, **David of Dinant** <note>A 12th-century philosopher condemned for pantheism, claiming God, mind, and matter were the same substance.</note>, and the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of a dualistic religion who believed human souls were fragments of divine light trapped in matter.</note>, who wanted our souls to be certain "portions" of God, or even God Himself. That this cannot be so is sufficiently declared from those five levels of reality arranged in the first book. For God can neither be torn apart into many souls, since the highest unity cannot be divided, nor can He become the "matter" of many souls (lest He become viler than the souls), nor can the Highest Act take the place of a subject. Nor can He, while remaining in His own form, change so frequently within us—since He is the stable center of all moving things—from truth to falsehood, from good to evil, from joy to sorrow, and back again. Finally, if God were the soul of all things, He would be as a mind in all things, which has already been refuted above.

But since **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century commentator who attempted to harmonize the views of Plato and Aristotle.</note> asserts that there was one single opinion held by Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus regarding the mind, if we wish to conclude this **Peripatetic** <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle.</note> dispute with a happy end, let us gather into one the Platonic and Peripatetic truth itself, which has been scattered across many interpreters. Let us accept from **Averroës** <note>A 12th-century philosopher whose "monopsychism" Ficino usually opposes, but here he extracts a specific point for his synthesis.</note> that the receptive intellect is immortal. Let us accept from **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century Aristotelian who argued that each person has their own individual intellect.</note> that receptive intellects are certain powers naturally implanted in our souls, as many in number as there are souls. We may then conclude that the souls of men are immortal. And this is the con-

->clusion of the Platonists, the Christians, and the Arabian<-
->Theologians, and it is most in harmony with the<-
->ancient Peripatetics.<-

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book XVI of the *Platonic Theology*. Having previously argued against Averroës regarding the "Unity of the Intellect" to prove each human has an individual, divine mind, Ficino now transitions to the next logical problem: if the soul is so divine, why is it trapped in a physical, "lowly" body?</meta>

# PLATONIC THEO-
## logy, on the Immortality of Souls,
### by the same author, Ficino,

-> BOOK XVI <-

-> The second question follows: why souls are enclosed in earthly bodies. <-
-> Chapter I. <-

**A**fter we have answered the first question and shown that the divinity of the mind belongs to our souls, let us answer the second: let us show why souls, if they are divine, are enclosed in such lowly earthly bodies.

-> First Reason: So that they may know individual things. <-

**T**he <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia"; the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a being.</note> of God—if indeed it should be called an essence—is not one specific <term>genus</term> <note>original: "genus"; a logical category or class of things.</note> of things. Otherwise, He would only act upon things of His own kind, just as water makes things wet but not dry, while fire, conversely, generates dry things but not wet. However, since God produces every genus of things through His own essence, and since that which He produces remains dependent on Him who is above all things that are made, God is not in any specific genus of things, but is above all genera. Therefore, when He contemplates His own essence—the origin and <term>exemplar</term> <note>The perfect "blueprint" or Idea of a thing existing in the divine mind.</note> of all—He contemplates every genus of things, every species, and every individual. For the essence of God is the beginning, the middle, and the end—not only of specific principles, but also of the individuals that wander under any given species.

Truly, since the divine essence contains nothing similar to matter (which usually clouds cognition), it is light and the highest form of perspicacity. For this reason, God—through His own essence—properly perceives individual things as if through an effective light that distinguishes between them. And since the essence of God is utterly absolute—not only from all matter and the properties of matter, but also from every fixed condition and relationship to this or that created thing—and since it is infinite, it therefore relates to all things indifferently (so to speak). Therefore, He either knows nothing besides Himself, or He knows all things. 

But to say He knows nothing is a wicked thing to utter, since He is the supreme reason of those who know, of things known, and of knowledge itself. Nor should **Averroës** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle often clashed with Christian and Platonic views on God's knowledge of particulars.</note> object to us that God is debased if He considers lower things. Surely, because He knows Himself to be all the things that are below Him, He therefore knows what it is to be "lower" from the perspective of the Principle; thus, He understands the ways in which they fall short. But while He recognizes the very logic of their defect, He Himself suffers no defect. If God, in considering the very foundation of imperfection (which is most foreign to Him), does not Himself become more imperfect, He certainly will not become imperfect in thinking about other things, even the most imperfect ones.

What more? Knowledge of oneself and others is desirable as a good; for it is a certain possession of oneself and of minds. However, one mode of knowing can be less desirable than another. Indeed, the mode by which the **external sense** <note>Sight, hearing, etc., which only perceive the surfaces of objects.</note> knows is imperfect. Less imperfect is that by which the **internal sense** knows, and even less so by which **reason** knows, and least of all by which the **angelic mind** knows. Therefore, that mode of knowledge by which God discerns individuals—since it is more perfect than the angelic mode by infinite degrees—certainly contains no imperfection, but rather encompasses all perfection. Such is surely the mode of divine knowledge, which exists through His infinite perfection. 

Finally, just as it is better for us finite beings to know certain finite things than to be ignorant of them, so it is more fitting for the infinite God to see infinite things than to see either nothing or only finite things. Indeed, He knows individuals everywhere distinctly; for he who perfectly understands the Cause of causes most perfectly possesses both all causes and each individual cause. And a distinct perspective, being much more perfect, is much more to be desired than a confused one. But let us not wander too far; let us proceed to the rest. The **Angel** also beholds all of God’s works and individuals. For if the object of our mind is being itself and the common truth, and the human mind therefore directs itself (albeit gradually) toward all existing and true things, it is right that the mind of an angel, which is more excellent than ours, should grasp all things and—as the **Platonists** wish...

<summary>Ficino begins Book XVI by arguing that God possesses perfect knowledge of all individual things because He is their source and exemplar. He refutes Averroës' claim that knowing lower things debases God, asserting that divine knowledge is an infinite perfection that encompasses all levels of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration in Book XVI of how the divine mind connects to the physical world. Having established that God contains the patterns of all things, Ficino now moves to the "middlemen" of the universe: the angels. He explains how these celestial beings gain their knowledge and how the hierarchy of reality descends from God's pure light down to human souls.</meta>

<page-num>369</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.</header>
<sig>Aa</sig>
<meta>catchword: fima [likely completing 'simplicissima' or 'simplici']</meta>

The Platonists say they see all things at once. But where does the angel look so that he may see all things? Does he direct his sharp gaze toward physical bodies? Not at all. Because the mind of an angel is stable and perceives all things simultaneously, he cannot learn about things from bodies, which, having been changed so often by their own movement, show one thing at one time and another at another. And if the mode of acting follows the mode of being, an angel—who is entirely free from a body in his being—will also be free in his understanding. Nor will he be formed by bodies, for he is more excellent than bodies and has no commerce with them. 

Or perhaps he will turn his intuition toward his own angelic <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of what an angel is.</note>? He will indeed turn it there, but in the angel he will only perceive the angel. For he will see in the angelic nature only as much as that nature extends itself. That nature exists only in the angelic <term>genus</term> <note>A logical category; here, the "class" of angelic beings.</note>. He will therefore see the angel within it, but he will not clearly discern the other kinds of things. Truly, if matter hinders knowledge, and a created essence possesses something similar to matter—something unformed and dark—it follows that no created mind, insofar as it looks into what is essentially a naked darkness, can achieve clarity of vision. It would be just as if the Moon looked at itself before it was yet illuminated by the light of the Sun.

Therefore, just as the eye does not discern colors except through the forms of the colors themselves, so the mind does not clearly see the kinds of things except through their own forms, since form is the principle of action. The essence of a single angel is the form of that angel alone, and even that is, in a way, dark. But the essence of God—indeed, His truth and goodness—is the form of all things: the purest light, the root, the reason, and the <term>exemplar</term> <note>The original "blueprint" or perfect Idea in the mind of God.</note>. Through this alone, as if through the Sun, all things can be seen. 

Will the angel then discern all things through the essence of God itself? Not through the absolute essence of God without a medium. For how can an infinite essence fit a finite mind as if it were a finite form, without some preparation coming between them? Nevertheless, the mind itself must have some form within it through which it acts in understanding. For this reason, the angel receives the forms and exemplars of things from the essence of God. Just as the eye receives the forms of colors and sees them through the light of the Sun (which produces all colors), so the mind of the angel receives the <term>species</term> <note>The mental "types" or categories of things.</note> of all things and understands them through the light of God (which produces all things). 

Rightly does God form the spiritual matter nearest to Himself—that is, the angelic minds—more early and more fully than He forms the matter of the world, which is most remote from Him. But there are many levels of minds, and many more than there are of bodies, as <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century Christian mystic whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" of angels were foundational for medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> Dionysius the Areopagite teaches. For the best Craftsman willed to establish more levels in His most excellent works than in His lowlier works. Thus, the City of God will be more glorious if there are more ranks of nobles and free men within it than of mercenaries and slaves. Such is the comparison of minds to bodies. 

Now, as to how many principal orders there are in the angelic ranks, we have discussed this sufficiently according to the mind of Dionysius, both in our book on religion and in our discussion on the <note>Refers to the biblical account of the Apostle Paul being "caught up" to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2).</note> Rapture of Paul. We have also indicated elsewhere the way in which the Platonists divide them into nine orders: namely, because the intellects of angels are certain beings gazing upon the supreme <term>intelligible</term> <note>That which can be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the senses.</note> itself, in which they behold essence, life, and intelligence. But there, in the "essence," both life and intelligence exist according to the mode of essence. Again, in "life," the other two exist similarly according to the mode of life. Likewise in "intelligence," the other two exist—that is, life and essence—according to the mode of intelligence. Therefore, in that realm, the supreme and one "intelligible" is divided into three, and then through those three it is multiplied into nine. By that same order, the intellects contemplating it are distributed into nine ranks. 

This is the way the Platonists divide those angels who are devoted solely to contemplation. However, as for those who also govern the world, some arrange them in groups of twelve and seven, primarily according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac and the seven Planets. Then to these they add other armies of angels, according to the number of stars in each sphere of the world, attending to specific duties. They also add as many crowds of <term>daemons</term> and <term>heroes</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" and "heroes" are not necessarily evil or mythological, but intermediary spirits that link the divine to the human.</note> serving the angels, and finally as many orders of particular souls who adapt themselves to the higher divinities. 

But let us set aside for now the armies of daemons and heroes; it is enough to have understood that the Platonists placed innumerable minds above us. In naming these, <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated theology and ritual into philosophy.</note> Iamblichus accepts from our own writers the names not only of angels, but also of archangels and principalities. He believes the divine light descends to us through all of them, as if through layers of glass. Because of this, through almost innumerable levels of mediating spirits, that divine ray—the shaper of minds—reaches all the way down to the lowest minds, which are the souls of men. 

Four things seem to be considered here: 
1. First, that divine ray.
2. Second, the species of things within it, which we call the reasons for creating things and Ideas. 
3. Third, the minds. 
4. Fourth, the powers of those minds. 

The ray, insofar as it is in simple—

He outlines the hierarchy of these spiritual beings, drawing from both Christian (Dionysius) and Platonic (Iamblichus) sources, showing how divine intelligence descends to human souls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XVI. Having previously discussed how angels perceive the universe through divine light, Ficino now shifts his focus to the human soul. He examines how the soul—occupying the lowest rank of "minds"—bridges the gap between pure divine ideas and the messy, sensory world of physical bodies.</meta>

<page-num>375</page-num>
# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI. #

->Aa 2<-

<note>original: "xat"</note> and to have universal [concepts]. Let us imagine the human soul just now flowing out from God and not yet clothed in a body, so that, being free from the occupation of the body, it directs its entire attention toward its own mind. There, according to its nature, it simply receives the influx of that divine ray perpetually standing by and inspiring it. What will the soul naturally grasp through a ray of this kind? As many <term>ideas</term> <note>In Platonic thought, "ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints of things in the divine mind.</note> as there are species of created things—one idea for each species. Through the idea of "human," what will it understand? Only the nature common to all humans; it will not see individual people within it. It will do the same through the idea of a horse, and all the rest. 

Therefore, the knowledge of this soul remains confused, since the distinct progression of species into individuals is hidden from it. Its natural appetite would be empty and its affection always restless, for it wishes to lack no truth and no good. But why is the human soul unable to clearly perceive individuals subject to the species in these ultimate ideas—just as it sees the species themselves—in the same way that angels see genera, species, and individuals within their own ideas? 

Because, as we have discussed elsewhere, it is the way of nature in every order of things that <term>action</term> <note>Active power or the ability to create/initiate.</note> at the highest point of that order is free from <term>passion</term> <note>From the Latin 'passio,' meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>, while passion at the lowest point is deprived of action, and in the middle, there is a middle composition. It is established that our souls are the lowest of minds. Therefore, as far as intelligence is concerned, God alone acts; the angel both acts and receives; but the soul receives through the nature of its mind alone and does not act. 

Indeed, God pours ideas out elsewhere and does not draw them from anywhere else. The first angel receives two (so to speak) ideas—that is, those two broadest categories of things—and in receiving them, he is in some way passive. But once these are received, because of his own inherent power, he penetrates the "innards" of those categories and clearly sees all the following species within them. He then fabricates for himself his own concepts of whatever species he chooses, which he also derives down to individuals. This is no longer passion, but action. 

The second angel does the same, and the others as well; yet a later angel always receives more ideas from above through passion and will fabricate fewer concepts of species for himself through action. Therefore, passion increases gradually while action decreases until one arrives at the lowest mind, which acts not at all, but is nourished by the ideas it receives and creates nothing new. Its intelligence is nothing other than the reception of ideas that is not hidden from itself. 

And since ideas are universal by nature, no mind can lead them down to distinct concepts of individual things without its own action. Therefore, the human soul—which, in the part where it is "mind," is the lowest among minds—understands only by being passive; it does not distribute universals into individuals. Nevertheless, in the part where it is divine, it possesses some action through its center (which is like the "character" or seal of God), by which it produces or draws out species, though it does not divide them. Furthermore, in the part where it is "soul," because it is not the lowest of souls, it is capable of animal and bodily operations. 

By divine providence, the human soul is located at such a grade that just as it follows immediately after the higher minds, it immediately precedes earthly bodies. Through this kinship, it is moved toward these lower things and inserts itself into them through a certain amorous affection. Hence, coupled to earthly bodies—the most excellent of all earthly things—it governs them. Through the vital power, it brings life-giving passions to them from within; through sense, however, it judges the "foreign" passions inflicted on the body from the outside. 

Because the human body consists of the four elements and is located in the middle of the world, it experiences the impulses of all the elements and all surrounding things through the five instruments of the senses. The soul discerns these impulses, brought in from individual things on all sides, one by one through the senses. Through its own animal power, it fashions images of them within itself by means of the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The imagination or the faculty that processes sensory data into mental images.</note> and preserves them in memory. Thus it happens that in a short time, the phantasy is full of individual forms for almost every individual thing. 

From here, reason is provoked. First, it brings forth universal species, and through them, with a simple intuition, it conceives common notions. But soon, from this intuition, it reflects back from the act of understanding toward the intelligible species, and through this, it looks back at the "simulacrum" (the mental image). Through that image, it perceives the individual—at first vaguely and indeterminately (thinking, for instance, "some honey"), and then determinately (namely, "this or that honey"). 

But after these briefer acts, reason is accustomed to run more widely in this manner: "What is this sweet and yellow body that the phantasy now offers to me? Why is it sweet? Is this sweeter than wine?" Here, reason seeks three things which, as it seems to the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, including Ficino himself.</note>, had been hidden from the phantasy: 
1. The **substance** of the thing, when it asks *what* this is. 
2. The **cause** of that quality, when it inquires *why* it is sweet. 
3. Its **order** in relation to others, when it asks whether it is sweeter than wine. 

After this, it answers three things to itself: First, "this is honey." Second, "it is sweet for this reason: because its moisture..."

<summary>Ficino explains that the human soul is the "lowest mind," meaning it is purely receptive to divine ideas rather than active like angels. To gain specific knowledge of individuals, the soul must join with a body and use its "phantasy" (imagination) and reason to process sensory data into complex understanding.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY #

...is fatty, and moderately cooked <note>original: "coctus." In Renaissance medicine, "coction" refers to the process of digestion or ripening by heat.</note>. Third, it is sweeter than wine, because its sweetness soothes the tongue more and for a longer time. These discursive movements of human reason, because they follow the impulse of the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "phantasy" was considered the faculty of the soul that stores and processes sensory images (phantasms) before the intellect analyzes them.</note>, are particular in nature and wander through individual things. Indeed, reason moves on to other questions. What is honey? What is sweetness? Now it asks no more about *this* honey than about any other; similarly, it asks about any sweetness whatsoever. And having set aside that specific image of honey which the phantasy provided, it investigates the common <term>ratio</term> <note>Here "ratio" means the defining essence or logical principle of a thing.</note> of all honey and all sweetness. This is a universal question. The answer also becomes universal, like this: "Honey is the juice of bees, hot in the second degree <note>A reference to Galenic humoral medicine, where substances were graded by their qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note>, cleansing in power, sweetest in flavor, and fatty to the touch." Again: "Sweetness is a flavor proceeding from a moderate coction of airy moisture." Reason sought these common definitions of honey and sweetness for a long time, and finally found them. 

If it sought them for a long time, it did not already possess them. For it received from elsewhere that which it arrived at through its discursive wandering. Where did it receive it from then? Not from the phantasy. For if the phantasy had possessed those definitions, it would surely have offered them immediately, just as it offered the sensory images—especially since the light of a universal definition is more illustrious and divine than sensory images, and should have shone all the more clearly upon the "eyes" of reason when they were turned toward it. Therefore, reason receives these definitions from the <term>mind</term> <note>Ficino distinguishes between "Ratio" (step-by-step reasoning) and "Mens" (the higher, intuitive intellect).</note>; and because reason is closest to the mind, it acquires that very power through which, having sometimes set aside particular questions, it may turn itself toward universal ones. And he who seeks definitions in a general way brings back universal truths from the mind. 

One might ask what benefit is derived from the body. A great deal, without doubt. To be sure, if the soul remains outside the body as it was when first created, it will indeed know universals, but it will not perceive individuals—either through its own power or through the divine ray contained within it—because its mind does not descend below the final <term>ideas</term> <note>The perfect blueprints of species.</note>, and its reason remains at rest in the intuition of the mind. However, in this body, because of the senses, reason becomes accustomed to running through individuals, applying individuals to common concepts, and deriving common concepts from individuals. It runs through individuals in this manner: "This is sweet and yellow, therefore it is honey." It applies individuals to common concepts thus: "This is sweet. All that is sweet is moisture moderately cooked. Therefore, this is moisture cooked in such a way." It applies common concepts to individuals like so: "Everything sweet and yellow is honey. This thing, because it is such, is therefore honey." 

Reason, having become accustomed to this, will—when the soul has been separated from the body—easily distribute the universal ideas of the mind into individual notions. This is because reason, just as it does here through its temporal wandering, provokes that divine and effective center of the soul and head of the mind to gradually lead the formulas <note>Latent patterns or blueprints.</note> hidden in the mind out into the light and translate them into reason. So there, through a sudden and continuous affection generated by long habit, reason will "set fire" to those formulas, so that they sparkle out from the mind into the reason as if struck from the sparks of individual things. 

<margin>What souls do after death.</margin> 
For this reason, Plato in his *Letters* and *Laws*, and also Plotinus in his book *On the Immortality of Souls*, grant that in separated souls there remains some sense and care for our affairs. Plotinus wishes this to be understood in this way: they notice human things only insofar as there remains in them some habit or affection leaning toward bodily things. Once this is finally removed, they apply themselves to divine things with such attention that they either do not see individual events happening among us, or (as is common for those thinking very intently on something) they do not notice that they see them. 

The reasoning regarding the remembrance of human things is almost the same. For Plato in one place grants that they remember, but in another says that Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, flows between the region of this life and the next. For they remember as long as they are affected by those things which they had sensed here, but after that, not at all. Furthermore, souls that glide into bodies forget divine things only to the extent that they immerse themselves in the body. When they first emerge, and to the degree that they emerge, they then first and only then remember. There are, however, many souls (as is pleasing to both ancient and our own <note>i.e., Christian</note> theologians) that govern these or those things, here or there, not out of affection, but by a certain providence distributed by God. Add to this that in the *Republic*, Plato writes that souls which knew each other here by some affection recognize each other there and are moved toward each other in a similar way. Avicenna also says in his *Metaphysics* <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian philosopher whose work deeply influenced Western Scholasticism and Neoplatonism.</note> that souls, both the blessed and the wretched, in the other life—as long as a certain habit contracted from sensory things persists for a time—can imagine those things which they previously imagined here with more vehement affection.

This "training" allows the soul to retain its connection to the human world even after death, until it eventually turns its full attention back to the divine.</summary>

Ficino argues that the human soul is the essential "bridge" that prevents the chain of existence from being broken.</meta>

ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.

### *The second reason: so that singular forms may be reconciled with universal forms. Chapter II.* ###

**T**his human reason is truly a wondrous power, belonging specifically to the rational soul, and it is through this power that we are human. It receives individual things from the **phantasy** <note>In Renaissance psychology, the "phantasy" was the faculty that stored and organized images gathered by the five senses.</note> and universal things from the mind, gathering both into one. Just as in a human being the mortal is joined with the immortal, so in this kind of reason, temporal images are linked to eternal **forms** <note>original: "speciebus." These are the "species" or "ideas" in the Platonic sense—the perfect, eternal blueprints of things.</note>. If this reconciliation did not happen somewhere in the world, the series of forms would remain broken. However, this cannot happen unless the rational soul is joined to an earthly body.

### *The third reason: so that both the divine ray and its formula may be reflected back to God. Chapter III.* ###

**I**n this regard, the soul performs another even more wondrous task. That divine ray, which is filled with **Ideas** <note>Platonic Ideas: the eternal, divine archetypes of all created things.</note>, descends as far as the soul. It passes through the soul’s life-force and through nature into the matter of the world. In that matter, it fashions certain final and shadow-like likenesses of the Ideas, just as light fashions the images of colors in a mirror, or rather, just as the shadows of bodies are marked out on the earth by light. Such likenesses or shadows depart very far from divinity itself. For they become impure from pure things when they are stained by their opposites; they become scattered from united things, individual from common things, and utterly unstable from stable things. 

If all things seek their own origin—whereby the ray of the Sun, after striking the earth, is reflected back toward the Sun—is it any wonder that these shadow-like likenesses of the Ideas also seek their original purity through a certain hidden instinct? And is it any wonder that the ray itself, which fashioned them, strives ardently to ascend again after it has descended? Will such a great effort be in vain? Not at all. Who will help? Not the souls of beasts, which gape only at individual images. Not those minds superior to ours <note>Ficino refers here to angels or celestial intelligences.</note>, for because they do not have bodies subject to all the storms of all physical things, they do not take in the particular passions and forms of any specific bodies. 

Only the soul of man remains. Because of its earthly body, the soul is, in a way, struck by the individual disturbances of every individual body. Through the senses, it takes in these likenesses of the Ideas that have been "infected" by the matter of the world; it collects them through the phantasy, purifies and refines them through reason, and then binds them to the universal Ideas of the mind. Thus, that celestial ray which had flowed down to the lowest depths flows back to the heights. The likenesses of the Ideas, which had been scattered in matter, are gathered in the phantasy, purified of impurity in the reason, and finally, having been individual, they emerge as universals in the mind. 

In this way, the soul of man restores a world that had already begun to fall apart; because by the soul's service, the world which was once spiritual and has now been made physical, is constantly purified and daily becomes spiritual again. Rays sent down from the wide circle of the Sun into a narrow hole in a very high wall form a cone by means of a <term>Pyramid</term> <note>In classical optics, light was thought to travel in the shape of a pyramid or cone with the source or the eye at the apex.</note>. They are slanted in that hole to such an extent that they are carried across it in a transverse way, and when they fall upon the floor below, they form a shining circle. This circle is larger the further the floor is from the hole, appearing as if it will eventually match the width of the Sun's globe if it falls as far from the hole as it had originally flowed from the Sun. 

This is exactly what happens in our eyes. The rays that are compressed into a narrow space in the pupil are carried through it into the soul. In the soul itself, they fulfill the magnitude of the Sun, for it is in the soul that the sun’s true size is judged. From this, it appears that the soul is as far distant from the eyes as the solar orb stands above the eyes. For this reason, according to the <term>Egyptians</term> <note>Ficino often cites "the Egyptians" when referring to the ancient wisdom of Hermes Trismegistus, whom he believed anticipated Christian and Platonic truths.</note>, there is also a celestial soul in heaven which stands as far above earthly eyes as the heaven itself does. 

Likewise, the influx of Ideas sent down from the higher minds into bodies becomes very narrow after being very wide; and while they emerge as entirely particular after being universal, they finally receive their original vastness when reflected from bodies into the human soul. From this, they clearly show that the human mind is almost as far removed from bodies as the higher minds are. Therefore, since the human mind is just as separated from mortal things as the divine minds are, it must be equally immortal—especially since it restores to eternity those forms that had fallen away from eternity into time and the parts of time.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is the essential cosmic connector that gathers scattered, "polluted" sensory data from the physical world and, through reason, restores it to its original, universal, and spiritual state. This unique role as the "reflector" of the divine ray back to its source serves as evidence for the soul's immortality.</summary>

## The fourth reason: so that the soul may become more blessed. Chapter IV. ##

**F**urthermore, the descent of the soul into the body contributes to the soul’s own **beatitude** <note>original: "beatitudinem." In this context, it refers to the state of supreme, divine happiness or "bliss" achieved in the presence of God.</note>. For if someone is of a duller wit and is always physically healthy, he will not know how much his good health is worth. He must fall ill at some point so that, by comparison at least, he may recognize the value of health, and having recovered it, enjoy it more sweetly. The human soul, being duller than all other minds <note>Ficino refers to "minds" or "intellects" here as the hierarchy of angels and celestial spirits, which are more perceptive than human souls.</note>, requires comparison for a full judgment of the greatest things. Therefore, having been tossed by the storms of the world, it will both prophesy more rightly here and discern more acutely there how quiet and sweet a harbor is found in God; it will cling to Him more intently and enjoy Him more sweetly. 

**P**lotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> seems to approve of this reasoning significantly, and even more so Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus who edited his works; he was known for his emphasis on the soul's purification.</note>, who says that the soul, having experienced these evils more often, finally clings entirely to its **Parent** <note>original: "parenti." Referring to God as the source or progenitor of all souls.</note>, never to return to these things again. Perhaps God Himself ordained that divine joys should fall to the higher levels of minds by their very nature, but should be earned by the lower order through labors. This way, there would be those who were made blessed by their birth and those who made themselves blessed by their living, so that neither the sublime spirits should be valued more than they are (since they obtain their bliss from elsewhere), nor the inferior spirits be looked down upon (since they are the authors of their own bliss). 

**W**hat if the angels—since they are further removed from time—earned their bliss in a single moment through a sudden turning toward God as soon as they were created, while we attain a similar happiness through a longer circuit? What is lacking in our nature is repaid by our industry. And while the endurance of honest and pious labor is balanced against the weakness of our origin, we in a certain way equal the angelic excellence and rewards. Thus, four levels of the "good" are found. God has His good from Himself alone; the body has its good from another alone; the angel and the soul have theirs not only from another (because they are from God) but also from themselves, because they provide good for themselves. However, the angel does this through an eternal act, and the soul through a temporal one. Nor should we wonder that the soul can not only stray toward the extreme evil, like the wretched, but also progress toward the highest good, like the angels. For a first and free movement has no limit anywhere except in the infinite.

## The fifth reason: so that the soul’s lower powers may proceed into effect. Chapter V. ##

**M**oreover, this habitation in the body serves not only reason and the mind, as we have explained, but also those three lower powers of the soul: the **phantasy** <note>The faculty that processes and stores sensory images.</note>, the senses, and the power of nutrition. These must be present in the soul no less than mind and reason, if indeed it holds the middle ground between angels and beasts. Truly, that power which never proceeds into action is vain and restless. There is no action for these three powers without a body—or certainly, it does not begin without a body. Without an earthly body, I say, they do not perform their operations, whether individually or as a whole. 

**A**dd to this what Plotinus says: that the soul clearly perceives its own powers and nature through its actions, and unless all these powers are brought forth, the soul will not know itself or its own things perfectly. Because the acts and effects of these powers are entirely mobile and temporal, it is only right that they should act for a certain time; so that what acts temporally may operate upon temporal things, a body of this kind is granted for a time. But since the operation of the mind and its handmaid, reason, can be continuous toward eternal objects, they rightly operate forever, while the other three powers are at times idle. 

**B**ut for what reason is the soul’s habitation here so brief? Plotinus answers: so that it may set out for better things more quickly once the burden has been laid down. A short age is enough to fulfill these duties for the sake of which it came here. But in what way is it fitting for the sempiternal soul to now descend to the earth, now ascend, as if playing a game, being now inside the body and now outside it? Perhaps, as Plotinus thinks, there is no need for the soul to be moved in place or time for these duties through descent and ascent. For just as it was born from God above space and time (which are sufferings of the body), so it remains outside the limits of space and time, hanging from God in no other way than light hangs from the Sun—the whole light being everywhere throughout the air. I believe Plotinus learned this from the Egyptians, who think the soul is a participant in the immense presence of God according to its essence.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's journey through the physical world is a necessary education that sharpens its appreciation for God and allows its lower sensory faculties to be exercised, ultimately making the soul "the author of its own bliss."</summary>

Having explained that the soul descends into the body to better appreciate divine bliss by contrast, Ficino now addresses the mechanics of this descent, the soul's "ethereal" vehicle, and why deceased souls do not typically return to our sight.</meta>

-># BOOK XVI ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS #<-

...is a participant, since according to its **power** and **activity** it becomes a participant in the immense divine intelligence and will through the unending intuition of unending truth and the affection for goodness. Therefore, according to them <note>The Platonists, whom Ficino is interpreting</note>, it should not be said that the soul now sits here, then passes there, but rather that it now gives life to the earth, and later does not, just as light—unchanged in its location—now illuminates an open eye, but does not illuminate a closed one. But let them see to this themselves. 

To what purpose is this "game" of granting life to the body and taking it away? We have said enough, I think. For the soul gives life so that it may fulfill those duties we have recounted. It takes it away, so that it might not be absent from better duties for too long due to the service of lower works. And just as the stars rise and set to our eyes to fulfill the office enjoined upon them by God, so too many spirits <note>original: "spiritus." These are the "daemons" or celestial beings that occupy the hierarchy between humans and angels.</note>, having often fashioned new bodies, now present themselves to our eyes, now withdraw; thus the souls of men sometimes appear in bodies and sometimes lie hidden. 

Here a threefold level of manifestation appears. The souls of the stars show themselves to the eyes of men always and continuously, though differently to different people. The souls of the following spirits show themselves always, yet not continuously—"always" because they do so in every age, but "not continuously" because they pause in between. Our souls show themselves neither always nor continuously. 

But if it is not against nature for something from the higher bodies to descend every moment to the lower ones and then ascend again (as with the rays of the stars and flames), it is also not against nature for some of the higher spirits to descend here daily, as it were, and ascend. Likewise, it seems agreeable to the Platonists that just as angelic lives are always separated from bodies, and those of **brute animals** are never separated, so there are two middle states: first, the happier souls, which are always partly separated and partly joined without any hindrance to their action; and second, the less happy souls, which are sometimes segregated and sometimes joined—joined, I mean, to an **elemental body** <note>The physical body made of earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, which in a way hinders intellectual activity. For according to the Platonists, they always possess an **ethereal body** <term>ethereal body: A subtle, luminous, and permanent "vehicle" of the soul, more refined than the physical body but less pure than the spirit.</term>, and according to the Christians, they will eventually possess such a body forever. 

I pass over the fact that the Platonists think not only our souls, but also the souls of many spirits, sometimes change their own bodies. Indeed, they believe that the divine goodness now pours itself out into other things, and now turns those things back to itself. From this, souls have the power to rule bodies, and from this, to betake themselves to the incorporeal; and those which can do both perfectly at once do not change their bodies, while those which are otherwise situated rightly exchange them. 

From this arises that common disbelief: "What is this? The dead do not return, they are not seen, they do nothing." The Platonists think they do indeed return under other forms. But in truth, what need is there for a veteran and retired soldier to return to the battle? If a return to the fight were according to nature, then surely all would return. If it is against nature, do not seek the return of anyone. It is certainly against nature for a return to be superfluous, if it was according to the laws of **providence** <note>Divine care and the logical order of the universe.</note> that those who fulfilled their duty should depart from here. The sphere of fire often ignites a flame in the air; a little later, the flame returns to the sphere. Do not seek a more frequent descent of that flame. That perpetual circuit with the sphere is natural to it; to descend again is against its nature. 

And although the soul, by the nature of the **third essence** <note>Ficino's term for the soul as the middle point of five levels of reality, linking the divine and the material.</note>, looks toward both—namely the corporeal and the incorporeal—like a **two-faced Janus** <note>original: "Iani bifrontis." The Roman god of gates and transitions, depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, nevertheless, because a wider providence is suited to higher minds and a narrower one to lower minds, and our soul is the lowest of all those minds, the narrowest providence is suited to it. Hence, it rules a celestial body for a short time and an earthly one for a short time. And when it looks upon the corporeal and the incorporeal equally and moderately, it performs both duties of the third essence equally. This is what happens in this life. But when after this life it dwells more attentively on the incorporeal because of its purity, then it looks after the corporeal more negligibly; or, because of its impurity, it is merged into the lowest bodies, and then it is deprived of the authority of human governance. 

Since human life is the middle between the divine and the bestial, while the soul acts in the middle, it also touches both extremes. While it declines toward one of the extremes (which it begins to do even now, and completes later when it has departed), it touches the middle state only a little, and the other extreme not at all. But why are the souls of the dead not seen? You do not see God, the angels, or the air, yet you do not deny their existence because of this. Why do they not do anything? God does all things, the angels act, and yet you do not notice their actions any more than you see them. What prevents souls, now released from the bonds of earthly bodies, from moving an ethereal or aerial body that is invisible to our eyes? What prevents them [from influencing] our reason and imagination...

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's relationship with various types of bodies, comparing the human soul's visibility to that of stars and spirits.
