<meta>This page continues Ficino's argument that souls remain active after death and explores the cosmological necessity of rational souls throughout the universe to ensure it is a "temple" of worship.</meta>

<page-num>376</page-num>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...our [souls] daily through thoughts, visions, and signs. Yet do we not sometimes remain ignorant of where these things come from? For the movements of invisible things are often themselves invisible. 

Avenzoar <note>original: "Auenzoar," referring to the 12th-century Arab physician Ibn Zuhr.</note>, also known as Albumaron the Arab physician, writes that he received the best remedy for his own ailing eye in a dream from a doctor who had recently passed away. Many things of this kind happen to us daily. Plato, in the ninth book of the *Laws*, teaches that the souls of those who have been killed often pursue their killers with hostility. From this, it perhaps happens that the wound of a murdered man, even while the corpse is lying there, may cast out blood again upon the one who had wounded him, provided that the killer stands near and looks upon the wound itself. Indeed, Lucretius <note>An influential Roman poet and philosopher.</note> affirmed that this sometimes happens, and judges have observed it as well. 

Posidonius the Stoic confirms Plato’s opinion with the story of two Arcadians <note>People from Arcadia, a region of Greece.</note>, close friends, who came to Megara. One turned aside to stay at an inn, the other with a host. When they had gone to rest after dinner, the one staying with the host saw his friend in a dream during the night, begging for help because the innkeeper was planning his death. At first, he woke up terrified by the dream; then, when he had collected himself and decided that the vision should be considered worthless, he lay back down. Then, as he slept, that same friend appeared to ask that, since he had not helped him while alive, he should at least not allow his death to go unavenged. He said he had been killed by the innkeeper, thrown into a wagon, and covered with dung; he asked his friend to be at the gate in the morning before the wagon left the town. Deeply moved by this dream, he was at the gate in the morning, ready for the ox-driver. He asked the driver what was in the wagon. The man fled in terror, and the dead body was unearthed. Once the matter was revealed, the innkeeper was punished. 

Some of the Stoics also infer that the souls of the deceased are mindful of kindnesses from the story of Simonides <note>A famous Greek lyric poet.</note>. When he saw the body of an unknown man cast out dead and had buried him, and later intended to board a ship, he was warned not to do so by the man to whom he had given burial. If he had sailed, he would have perished in a shipwreck. Simonides returned; the others suffered shipwreck. All these things teach us that the souls of the dead exert some influence upon us.

### Sixth Reason: That the world may be adorned and God may be worshiped. Chapter VI.

**B**ut so that we may conclude the preceding discussion with a fitting end: the divine architect <note>Ficino uses this term for God to emphasize the order and design of the universe.</note> willed to make the work of the world as similar to Himself as possible. Such a work is achieved if it is everywhere most full of reason. Surely, just as reason is in Him—simultaneously uniform and all-encompassing—so in His handiwork He willed there to be one rational soul, and many: specifically, one for a single sphere <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the universe was composed of nested celestial spheres or layers.</note>, and many for the many spheres. And because any given sphere imitates its whole, He also placed many souls in any given sphere, so that just as a sphere contains a sphere, so a soul might contain souls. 

Indeed, He established at least as many souls in the highest realm as there are stars. Since these stars imitate their own sphere, they each revolve around their own center and have obtained their own movers <note>Refers to the "Intelligences" or spirits thought to guide the movement of celestial bodies.</note> for their own motions. For it is probable that they have their own lives beyond the life of the sphere, provided they are more excellent bodies than those of earthly animals, which have obtained their own lives. I pass over the fact that each of the souls of the heavenly bodies has its own intellectual motion concerning intelligible things <note>Things understood by the mind rather than the senses.</note>, and a shared animal motion concerning corporate things along with the universal soul of the sphere. These twin motions of the souls are followed by twin motions in the stars: one specific and one shared. 

In this way, the smaller spheres perfectly imitate the larger ones, because they similarly contain many rational souls, which have both a shared condition in fate and a specific condition within themselves. Therefore, in every sphere of the world, beyond the common soul of each sphere, He established many rational living beings, as we have argued elsewhere. For this reason, it was necessary for there to be such beings in the middle seat <note>Meaning the Earth, which was central in this cosmic model.</note> of the world as well, so that there would be a great multitude of rational beings in all its members to adorn and worship this temple of God, and to sing to and praise God the creator. Other minds do this in the higher spheres; human minds do this on earth. Nor shall this mortal breast be future <note>i.e., destined for destruction</note>, which continually resounds with the eternal name of God. 

Let no one lose faith that there are many inhabitants in the spheres of the planets just because only a single planet is seen in each of them. Rather, because the numerical multitude of inhabitants always increases as one descends from the summit (as the Platonists believe), a single leader—that is, the soul of the sphere itself—is sufficient in the highest heaven for the number of stars themselves. But since more inhabitants live in the individual circles of the planets than in the highest, and they are of a lower order, there is a need for more leaders. Therefore, two leaders in each...

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.

...is the soul of the sphere, and God established the soul of the planet there. Inhabitants of this kind they call angelic, demonic <note>original: "dæmonica," referring to 'daimons'—spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans, not necessarily evil spirits</note>, heroic, and finally human, composed of a rational soul and a body appropriately suited to their sphere. These inhabitants are not seen, however, because they possess either less light or less solidity than the stars and planets. Nor is this surprising, since even the spheres in which they exist are not seen. They follow their own planet in nature, motion, and name, just as the planet follows the soul of the sphere, and the sphere follows the soul of the universe. Finally, they conclude that if there are many rational beings in the two extreme spheres of the world <note>The highest heaven and the Earth</note>, it is only right that there are many in the middle spheres as well. 

We, in turn, conclude that if God adorned the surrounding spheres with divine minds, He rightly adorned the middle one with divine minds as well. Nor should the habitation of the Earth be despised, for it is the central choir of the divine temple and the stable foundation of such great spheres. Nor should it be thought a small thing that the other spheres revolve around it as if around a hinge. What of the fact that the rays of all the celestial bodies, flowing together here, are mixed together and attain a marvelous power through a wondrous union? What of the fact that the green face of the Earth, varied like the sky, is wrapped in three transparent bodies—water, air, and fire—and, reflecting the rays of the stars, gathers them into a splendor? 

Therefore, if you were positioned on the Moon and looked out at this globe from there, it would perhaps appear to you just as the Moon now appears to you from the Earth; you would think that those who live here are celestial beings and that they inhabit some star. For this reason, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras</note> named the globe of the Earth—wrapped in its water, air, and fire as if in its own veils—a single sphere of the world and a kind of star. And Plato calls the Earth the most ancient Goddess of all the Gods who are within the heaven. He adds that vast regions of the Earth are inhabited much higher than ours, where the stones, metals, plants, and animals are far more excellent and beautiful than ours, and where men live for a very long time and are happily nourished by scents and refined foods. I pass over what Diodorus and Pliny <note>Ancient Roman naturalists and historians</note> relate elsewhere, that some men are nourished by scent alone. 

That which Olympiodorus the Platonist writes is certainly marvelous: that Aristotle saw a man who never slept and lived solely on air exposed to the rays of the Sun. These things are much like the accounts that in the divine gardens—as if in the Elysian fields <note>A paradise in Greek mythology</note>—men could have lived as immortals by merely tasting the Tree of Life. 

But to return to the established order, Timaeus <note>The speaker in Plato's Timaeus dialogue</note>, imitating Moses, says that in the beginning God created fire, heaven, and earth as the principal members of the world; and so that He might bind these two more fitly together, He soon interposed air and water, as if they were created not for their own sake, but for the sake of the others. If it were permitted to converse a little more broadly (as we often do) with our ancestors, I would indeed state that the chief and proper nature of fire is light rather than heat. 

**First**, because light is more divine. **Second**, because it acts more swiftly. **Third**, it spreads itself more widely. **Fourth**, it is not like heat which, when the fire departs, remains in a way in the heated object as if common to other things; rather, as something uniquely proper to fire and mixed with nothing else, light follows its fire everywhere. **Fifth**, because the more fire is mixed with foreign solidity, the more it boils and the less it shines. Conversely, the more it is restored to its own purity, the less it burns and the more it shines. 

To what end is this? So that we may understand that heaven is fire, whose property is indeed to shine in action, but to be warm in power. Thus it can be said with good reason that celestial fire is light, whose heating power is harmful to no one of itself, but is gentle and healthful to all. Whence also the ethereal fire below the Moon, following the celestial fire in a way, does not consume the nearby air. However, as for why the power which is only healthful and gentle in the supreme fire becomes "biting" (so to speak) in the case of the lower fire—which differs in species from the higher—it happens either because it is mixed with terrestrial harshness (where it burns more vehemently in more solid and drier matter) or because it is forced by a certain reflection, and as if suffering violence, it also inflicts violence. Therefore, in the freer air, it is gentle to everything it touches, but among concave surfaces that have been struck, it strikes back; and when reflected more violently by a concave mirror, it also reflects back more violently.

Although the whole heaven is described chiefly through fire, they nevertheless subjoin the other elements as well, but in a celestial mode. Therefore, fire prevails everywhere in heaven, but in some places together with a certain solidity of "celestial earth," which is evident in the more manifest stars; for because they resist the rays of the eyes with a certain solidity, they are clearly discerned even though they are most remote. In other places, however, the fire is subject to a certain property of "celestial water"...

### MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY
<meta>catchword: Third</meta>

...[it] flourishes especially in the Milky Way <note>original: "orbe lacteo"</note>, and therefore stars are seen there as much as the nature of water allows. Finally, fire reigns everywhere with an added airy transparency. The result of this is that in the spheres, it is mostly not seen, since it does not obstruct the eyes because of its own nature and that of the air. All astrologers confess that certain natures of the elements are in the heavens. From this come the Elysian Fields <note>The paradise of Greek mythology; Ficino identifies these mythical fields with the refined elemental regions of the heavens</note> mentioned by the poets. From this also comes the saying: *Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth*. From this, David and Moses pour waters through the celestial regions. 

Again, what is the point of this? So that we may conclude that if the elements are found in heaven in a certain celestial manner, then conversely, celestial things can likewise be found in the elements in a certain elemental condition. This is especially true in the globe of the Earth, which, besides heaven, is the other foundation of the world; in which, although earth prevails just as fire does in heaven, nevertheless air and fire are joined to it just as they are in heaven. Finally, fire reigns above the Moon, but earth reigns everywhere below. And even near the very center of the world, through earthly openings, the lights of fire, air, and water flow from all sides. 

For this reason, it should seem strange to no one that celestial souls are sent down to earthly things, and conversely, the wandering inhabitants of the earth are sometimes sent back to celestial things. Finally, whatever kind of earth this may be, man is its master. He is certainly a <term>god on earth</term><note>Ficino emphasizes the "dignity of man," a core Renaissance theme, suggesting that the human soul’s ability to govern the world reflects God’s own power</note>. Nor should the human soul be thought any less divine because it is surrounded by a fragile body; rather, it is most divine for this very reason: that even in the earthly dregs—if earth were indeed lowly—it performs such divine works against both the nature of its location and the burden of the body, so that while it governs lower things, it does not depart from higher ones. 

All the Platonists, with whom Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher who blended Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine</note> agrees, judge it the natural duty of divine minds to remain in their own nature, to proceed by providing and acting, and to turn themselves back toward their origin by knowing themselves and their source, while also turning the things that follow them toward that same source. Therefore the soul, as if divine, fulfills these three according to its powers. It is drawn to this governance of internal things not so much by an amorous affection due to affinity, but by a certain innate zeal for <term>providence</term> <note>Providence here refers to the soul’s protective and ordering care over the body and the physical world</note> due to the excellence of its nature. For all the most excellent things propagate themselves most widely through the abundance of their inner perfection. 

And as Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (3rd century AD)</note> says, the Good itself procreates the Intellect with poured-out splendor. The Intellect also, while it unfolds, expresses the rational soul. The soul itself, propagating itself, brings about life and corporeal form. From this, Dionysius the Areopagite says: "Certainly the divine unity, united to all things, in turn unites all things; while it gathers together those things that are equal among themselves into one by a certain mutual consent because of the similarity of quality, it turns lower things toward higher things because of their need through a desire for enjoyment, and it deflects higher things toward lower things because of their abundance through a zeal for providing, so that they may imitate divine providence." 

The Platonists argue that rational souls imitate divine providence in four ways:
1.  In the first grade, they place the **Soul of the World**, in which there is a universal providence over the world under God, through which it grants all things to everyone.
2.  In the second, the **souls of the twelve spheres**, in which there is a "universal-particular" providence, through which they distribute certain things to all worldly beings.
3.  In the third, the **souls of the stars** and of whatever spirits rule in any sphere of the world. Among these, they judge there to be a "particular-universal" providence, by which they grant individual things to several members of the world that correspond to them.
4.  Finally, in the fourth, **particular souls**—namely those that return from the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and divine ideas</note> to the <term>sensible</term> <note>The physical world perceived by the senses</note>, and back again. They believe the providence of these souls is so particular that they impart certain things only to certain individuals; furthermore, they fulfill through many courses of lives what the higher souls do in fewer periods, and what the first souls complete in a single circuit.

Indeed, Plotinus and Proclus <note>A major late Neoplatonist philosopher (5th century AD)</note> argue that just as one circuit of the world encompasses many—those of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, and others in sequence—so one inner circuit of the worldly soul contains many circuits of particular souls through its species, since a higher soul completes a longer orbit around intelligible things, and a lower soul a shorter one. ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.

# The third question: for what reason souls, if they are divine, are affected by
## disturbances. Chapter VII.

**I**t was asked thirdly, for what reason souls, if they are divine, are subject to <term>disturbances <note>original: "perturbationibus"; in Platonic philosophy, these are the irrational passions or emotions—like fear, lust, or anger—that "disturb" the soul's natural peace.</note></term>. But no one would ever wonder at this if we were to consider that no mind was ever granted a body more burdensome than the human one. Certainly, the minds of the spheres, the stars, and the <term>higher spirits <note>original: "dæmonum"; Ficino uses this in the classical sense of guardian spirits or intermediary beings between gods and men, not as "demons" in the modern sense.</note></term> preside over simple bodies. These bodies are so consistent in the unity of their similar parts that nothing of their own flows out, and therefore it is not necessary for anything new to flow in. Furthermore, by a natural agility, they are so inclined toward motion that they live and move at the slightest nod of those minds. By contrast, the human body is composed of the four <term>clashing elements <note>fire, air, water, and earth, which were thought to be in a constant state of conflict due to their opposing qualities of hot/cold and wet/dry.</note></term> and is slowed down by the weight of water and earth. Therefore, it is dissolved at almost every moment by the disagreement of its parts, and it falls downward by its own weight, becoming unfit for life and sluggish in its movement. Because of this internal disagreement in which the <term>humors <note>original: "humores"; the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note></term> expel one another, something is always flowing out of the body, and in turn, it is necessary that something flows back in.

Therefore, to regulate, move, and restore a body of this kind, the most intense attention of our soul is required. This is the point of that Platonic saying: *Sublime bodies approach sublime souls, and lower souls approach [lower] bodies*, because the former yield very easily to their souls, while the latter yield to these with the greatest difficulty. But if any of those higher minds were enclosed within the barriers of our body for a decade, perhaps it would be exhausted by the burden and troubled by care not much less than our own soul, and we would distrust its divinity just as we now distrust our own. But someone will say that the <term>World Soul <note>original: "mundi animam"; the vital spirit that Platonists believed animated the entire universe as a single living being.</note></term> has a body composed of the four opposing elements, and yet it is not exhausted by that care as our soul is by our body. This is clearly true; however, the elements themselves, which are the members of the world’s body, are not merely parts of other elements, but are whole, entire elements. They are not outside their natural places, but are each disposed in their own regions. They are not confused with each other everywhere, but are separated into their proper seats. They are not subject to external bodies, for no body exists outside the world. By contrast, the fire in our body is not "all" fire, but only some part of a greater fire. The same is true of the other three. Therefore, the elements of this [human] body are imperfect. They are also outside their own proper places; for this reason, the fire and air within us are always fleeing from here toward the heights, while the water and earth fall toward the depths. It is truly most difficult to perfect what is imperfect, to reconcile things that are fighting, and to detain bodies outside their natural place. Furthermore, those four elements are mixed within us in every tiny particle of the body, which causes the fight to burn more vehemently everywhere; in the world, however, they are in some way distinguished in different places and rest more peacefully. There are also many massive things outside of us which, looming over us from all sides, afflict the body. The Soul of the World is not oppressed by such burdens and labors, nor are the souls of the elements, for whatever enters or leaves their bodies has barely the weight of a single atom. Also, the restoration is balanced on all sides, and the natural harmony never clashes—a harmony, I say, that leads to the well-being of the spheres. Yet not even those souls, however divine they may be, can restrain the impetus of the spheres so much that the parts of the elements and composite bodies do not devour and destroy one another, or that floods of fire and water do not often disturb the world. And yet, such opposing qualities could not be produced and led by heaven in any way unless their powers were within it; nor would they be in heaven unless they were in the movers and the Creator of the heavens. But in God they are a single form, distinguished only by reason; in the angels, they are further distinguished by forms; in souls, by motion and time as well; in heaven, by place and simultaneously by power; and finally, below heaven, by their effect and opposition. To what end is this? So that we may understand that the souls of the elemental spheres do not have such great power that they can moderate and reconcile the qualities (which do not fight among themselves in heaven) so that they do not fight one another and kill themselves below heaven. There are those who say that the celestial substance reconciles them by its excellence, but that <term>matter <note>original: "materia"; the raw, chaotic "stuff" that lies beneath the elements.</note></term> which is beneath the elements is shapeless, unstable, and ineffective, and can neither contain them together nor reconcile them. However it may be, it appears that the souls of the elements, if they have souls, cannot entirely pacify them at the same time; even the World Soul cannot do this. So it is no wonder that our souls

He contrasts the heavy burden of the human soul with the World Soul and celestial spirits, whose bodies are simpler and more harmonious.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of why the human soul, despite its divine origin, experiences suffering and "disturbances." Ficino explains that the human soul's unique role is to bring divine reason to the physical earth, even though this requires inhabiting a heavy and complex body.</meta>

<page-num>380</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
<meta>Catchword: so that heav-</meta>

...our [souls] labor so much in tempering the <term>humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that Renaissance medicine believed controlled health and temperament.</note></term>, and sound with dissonance in the region of dissonance. In every way, however, the governance assigned to higher souls is as much easier as it is happier. If our soul presided over the controls of the world's body as they do, perhaps it would arrange things with the same happiness as they. But some divine minds had to be sent even into the small particles of the earth, so that the King of the World might be celebrated no less in the regions of the earth than in the heavens and the whole of the elements; this task fell to our souls. 

Hippocrates writes that sudden changes, especially those to the exact opposite, bring about the greatest and longest-lasting diseases. But Plato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, thinks that the soul falling into the body rushes suddenly from the highest light into extreme darkness, so it is no wonder that it remains blind and disturbed for a very long time. Its disturbance is increased (as <term>Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentaries on Plato deeply influenced Ficino.</note></term> argues in the *Timaeus*) because it falls from unity into a discordant multitude, and from a state of rest into a change almost entirely devoid of stillness; hence it is always pulled apart and, as if affected by vertigo, it stumbles and wavers. 

Nor does that <term>vital shadow <note>original: "uitalis umbra"; the lower part of the soul that animates the physical body and is most closely tied to its sensations.</note></term> of its own, naturally handed over to the body, easily permit it to emerge from so many floods and great storms. Toward this shadow the soul is affected by a vehement love, as if toward its own offspring, and as that shadow suffers daily, the soul itself suffers in its own way. Perhaps, indeed, as long as the soul does not notice itself at all, it thinks it is nothing other than a shadow appearing openly in the river of the body, just as Plato teaches in the seventh book of the *Republic*. Nor does it disturb itself differently when this shadow is troubled than do unrefined children who, when they see their shadows confused in water, lament greivously. 

The Platonists place such an order among souls: namely, some never descend into "generation" (that is, into a body that can be born and die), such as divine or near-divine souls; others indeed descend into generation and from a better life into a less good one, yet in such a way that they are by no means infected or undergo any evil—these they count among <term>daemons <note>original: "dæmones"; intermediary spirits that act as messengers between the divine and human realms.</note></term> and heroes; others descend and are at the same time somewhat corrupted, but can be purged again and transfer themselves back to better things. They add that in the highest souls, vice is found neither in their essence nor in their action, but in the lowest shadows of souls, it is found in both. In our souls, however, action can indeed be corrupted, but the essence by no means. 

Many think the difficulty of human life is increased further by this: that the movement and habit of the soul, insofar as it is intellectual and rational, ought to be a circuit [circular]. Similar too is the motion and shape of the <term>ethereal vehicle <note>original: "aetherei uehiculi"; a subtle, celestial "body" of light that the soul was thought to inhabit as it descended through the planetary spheres toward the physical world.</note></term>. But in the composite body, by growing, sensing, and moving forward, the soul undergoes a linear motion, as it were, having abandoned its circular path. The vehicle too is compelled to change its motion and shape. Even if it is not destroyed according to its substance (because, as some think, it lacks matter), it is nevertheless disturbed in its shape and motion. It will only recover these when the mind is raised up to its "head" (that is, the intellect) and is restored entirely to its proper habit. It seems to have lost this habit for as long as, through intemperance, it fixes its "head" (the mind) on the ground, but raises its "feet" (the lower powers of the soul) on high; indeed, no habit can be imagined more deformed or more laborious than this. 

But why was some airy body not given to us in which we might inhabit the earth and more freely contemplate celestial things? Because the air has its own spirits, and in this way, they would have been lacking to the earth. And if simple bodies are not lacking in reason, then some composite and earthly bodies must in turn possess reason, so that this corporeal world may be entirely rational, just as that spiritual world, according to whose model this one was made, is entirely reason. That best Father [God] willed that His priests, who sing to Him in the higher spheres, should remain there always as the same ones, because they lead their lives there without labor due to the happiness of the place. But on earth He did not want His priests to endure long delays, because perpetual or longer labor is not owed to those who diligently praise God. Therefore He sends them here daily and recalls them, so that through a succession of souls on earth, that which exists through the same life in the heavens may always happen here. I omit the fact that many think the souls of daemons and heroes even in the air change their bodies for the better, though more slowly. 

But, someone will say, let our soul have a body more burdensome than other minds, and therefore let it be anxious at times and prohibited from contemplation more than others; but why does it have a more fragile body than the beasts? It is not because it has a more fragile body that it should be thought less divine; rather, because it is more divine, it has a more fragile body. We have argued elsewhere that our body is the most tempered of all earthly things and most similar to heaven...

He argues that human bodily fragility is actually a sign of our high degree of "temperament" and divine nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of why the human soul struggles with its physical existence. Ficino explains that while the soul is divine, its role as the governor of a complex, balanced body requires constant effort, which manifests as physical and emotional disturbances.</meta>

<page-num>381</page-num>
### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.

...so that it may offer a more peaceful service to the gifts of the celestial soul. Yet this very **temperance** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "temperance" or "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> is necessarily followed by **fragility**. A constitution in which heat exceeds too much is hardly harmed by external heat or cold. For an immense heat overcomes lesser heats, so that by comparison they hardly appear, and it breaks the force of cold. And if cold excels in some constitution, not just any coldness applied from outside is felt, and heat is easily tolerated. Similarly where moisture or dryness prevails. 

But where these four qualities are moderate and mixed in a harmonious temperament, whatever new quality arrives forces one of those four qualities to exceed; when it exceeds, the harmony of the previous constitution perishes, and the natural state is dissipated. Therefore, because it was necessary for man to have the most temperate constitution of all earthly things, yet this is harmed by even the smallest offenses, it followed that the nature of the human body would be fragile. 

Nevertheless, the diligent industry of our arts assists this fragility, so that our temperament might persevere longer against the storms of the world. For the divine craftsman has balanced all things such that in beasts, he compensated for the weakness of the soul with the strengths or gifts of the body; in us, however, he compensated for the fragility of the body with the strengths of the soul. Thus he indicated that the souls of beasts are destined for the death of the body, but ours are dedicated to the life of a perpetual mind—though they must always labor while outside their homeland. 

For a temperate constitution—which is most natural to the human species, as we have said—is compelled to sound with dissonance from every side for innumerable causes, both from the beginning in many people and daily in individuals. Therefore, there is a continuous need for the most intense attention of the soul (even if we barely notice it) to restore the temperament of nature itself. This is the hardest and perpetual labor of the **vegetative power** <note>The *potentia vegetatrix* is the part of the soul responsible for unconscious biological life, such as growth, nutrition, and healing.</note>. It not only greatly relaxes and interrupts the focus of the mind—which is why we almost do not "use" our minds—but it also affects us with many hidden disturbances and agitates us as if we were dreaming. 

Indeed, while the soul operates under the burden of balancing these qualities or those, meanwhile using its own appropriate **seminal reasons** <note>original: "seminalibus rationibus" — these are the internal blueprints or governing principles the soul uses to shape matter.</note> for these tasks, it gradually rouses images and affections in the higher sense that pertain most to those physical qualities. Therefore, in processing **bile** <note>Yellow bile, associated with the element of fire and the emotion of anger.</note>, a hidden inclination toward anger arises. In agitating the **blood**, a vain joy. In **phlegm**, boredom and laziness. In **black bile**, fear and sorrow. Often indeed, images and affections of this kind grow so strong that, with reason entirely vacant regarding such matters, insanity follows. 

Furthermore, in many people, while the soul strives to thin out the coarser **spirits** <note>In this medical context, "spirits" (*spiritus*) are subtle, vaporous substances that serve as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical organs.</note>, it proves them to be very dull. While in others it strives to gather the looser spirits, it shows them to be unfit for the persistence of contemplation and memory. But if ever we say the soul "collects the dryness of the spirits," we wish it to be understood not as if the spirits act *upon* the soul, but so that the soul does not labor in gathering the spirits, whereby it would be forced to be diverted from contemplation. Finally, just as the external sense is offended while dealing with troublesome things, so too the internal sense, perceiving many intrinsic offenses of the spirits brought on by various humors and causes, rouses troublesome images and affections.

Enough now on the causes of burdensome governance. Regarding the vices of the soul, although we have said something, more must be said. Since the soul was created in the middle boundary between minds and bodies, it not only gasps for divine things but is also joined to matter by a natural providence and love; and in matter, through a certain **shadowy communion** <note>original: "umbratilem... communionem"</note> of its life, it arranges the animated body, and thereafter loves it as its own work and proper offspring. Natural love joined the soul to the body; natural love detains it in the body. This same love daily provokes the soul to the care of the body. 

I pass over what **Plato** proves in the *Laws* and **Plotinus** confirms: that since the soul precedes the body and rules it, it does not so much receive a corporeal affection from the body as immerse itself into the body through such an affection of its own. This opinion certainly agrees with **Zoroaster** and in some way with **Moses**, who say that evils come to the body from the faults of the soul. But however it may be, the soul indeed loves the body, yet the burdensome and fragile nature of the body demands that the vital power of the soul sustain and move it with the greatest effort. It demands that the senses and the **phantasy** <note>The *phantasia* is the faculty of the soul that creates and stores mental images, bridging the gap between raw sensory data and rational thought.</note>, which can benefit or harm the body, look around constantly and—for the sake of the body, as if for the soul's own son—desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve. From the very beginning, three powers of this kind undertake this kind of work, with such great intensity because of the construction of the new body, that there is almost no attention of the soul toward reason until, once the body is adult and the senses are purged, the intensity of this work relaxes.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is constantly distracted from contemplation because it must exhaust its energy maintaining the body's delicate balance of humors. This physiological labor creates involuntary emotions and mental "shadows" like anger or sorrow, illustrating the struggle of a divine mind trapped in fragile matter.</summary>
<keywords>humors, temperament, vegetative power, spirits, phantasy, Plato, Plotinus, Zoroaster, Moses, soul-body relationship, physiology of the soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the human soul’s descent into the physical body is a result of its natural role as a provider and governor. While the previous page focused on the fragility of the human temperament, this page explores the psychological struggle between the higher reason and the lower imaginative faculties, and how the soul can eventually emerge from this "sea" of physical corruption.</meta>

->### MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-
#### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVI.

But as soon as reason awakens, it weakens—with the greatest difficulty—the dominion of the **fantasy** <note>original: *phantasiae*; the faculty of the soul that processes sensory images into mental pictures</note> which has been established in the soul through long use; for it is indeed an arduous task to resist either nature or habit. In this struggle, one must fight both against a habit strengthened beyond nature and against natural affection. Nevertheless, the soul finally achieves this through diligent discipline. But in the meantime, reason itself—due to its natural knowledge and providence <note>providence here refers to the soul's "caring for" or "looking after" the body</note>—loves those three lower powers <note>the vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative faculties</note> as if they were sisters or daughters. Therefore, reason often yields to them. These powers naturally take care of the body. Thus, reason also declines toward the body through its love for them. From this long-standing decline, reason contracts a habit of inclining more easily. 

We call a habit of this kind a vice, or even a certain (so to speak) death. For as often happens in many species of animals <note>Ficino likely refers to silkworms or spiders here</note>, after the lower power has wrapped itself in natural threads while fashioning the body, the higher power often weaves the begun work with a more solid web, and finally, hiding itself secretly beneath that very hard texture, it loses itself; it shall not rise again into the light until that thickened texture is broken.

For this reason, the divine soul is not corrupted *by* the body, nor is it forced, but out of its own love for animating the body (which is both its work and its instrument), it voluntarily casts itself down from its own state so that it may lift the body up to itself. Nor are there lacking among the Platonists those who say—especially **Hermias** <note>Hermias of Alexandria, a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>—that there are certain "demons of generation" <note>spirits that oversee the process of birth and physical life</note> who naturally increase the soul's inclination toward the body. Certainly **Plato**, in his book *On Beauty* <note>The *Symposium*</note>, says—much like **Moses**—that a certain demon mixed pleasure with many evils from the beginning. I pass over the fact that in his *Letters*, he says a demon disturbed public affairs. But more on these matters in what follows. 

Let us return meanwhile to the soul’s providence. Since it is proper to all divine minds to gaze upon higher things and to provide for lower things, the same is also proper to our soul; it cares for and cultivates not only its own body, but also the body of all earthly things and the Earth itself. But the heavier this providence is—because it cares for things that are more fragile and less fit for maintaining order—the more it distracts the soul from contemplating higher things, though not entirely. For in every age, we seek all truth through the intellect, we love all good through the will, and through our actions, we worship God, who is truly the All-Good. These three duties of virtue signify that even in the midst of such a great storm on this sea, the soul always receives celestial things, and by receiving them, it is seized daily by a more vehement love for them. Through such love, the soul catches fire, and the love for the body—through which the soul had been corrupted—gradually cools, and the stains of vice are wiped away. 

Therefore, the soul is never forced from the outside, but by love it sinks into the body, and by love it emerges from the body. To this end tends that divine saying: *He who loves his soul in this world, loses it; he who hates it here, receives it into eternal life.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:25</note>. **Socrates** expresses what the soul becomes and how it appears in this "sea" in the tenth book of the *Republic*: 

*Just as if someone were to see the sea-god **Glaucus** <note>A mortal fisherman who became an immortal sea-god, but whose body became encrusted with shells and seaweed until he looked like a monster</note>, worn down and distorted by the waves over a long time, and moreover covered with rocks, seaweed, and oysters, he would judge him to be a wild animal rather than a creature of the sea; so too, when we see the soul distracted and surrounded by earthly affections and habits, we think we see something earthly rather than celestial. But if we were to strip the soul bare and consider it pure, and see it already emerging from this sea through the love of divine things, we would undoubtedly recognize that the soul—because it is kin to divine and eternal things—desires such things, and touches them as soon as it has completely escaped, and dwells with them in serene light, and through that fellowship, it turns out to be entirely divine.* 

Thus far Socrates. Therefore, when we say the soul is corrupted, we do not mean it loses its own nature so much as it admits foreign things—that is, lower things—into itself. A vice of this kind does not destroy nature, but occupies it. But lest any of us think our soul is bodily simply because it seems daily infected by bodily causes, it is worthwhile to hear the divine **Paul the Apostle** crying out: *Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against many crowds of demons, who dwell among us in this misty air.* <note>Ephesians 6:12</note>. The ancient theologians—as **Origen** and **Augustine** confirm—believe these demons are clothed in airy bodies, agile in motion, sharp in perception, and endowed with a miraculous knowledge of things. They believe that through their airy bodies, these demons slide deep into our own **airy spirit** <note>The "spiritus," a subtle vapor that Ficino believed connected the physical body to the immaterial soul</note>; and just as any men can, through external signs and great skill, guess at internal feelings, so these most sagacious demons guess not only through external signs, but even through the very movements of our spirits, which [arise] from **fantasy**... <meta>The catchword "tafia" completes the word "phantasia" (fantasy) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's struggle to free its reason from the "habit" of physical existence and sensory imagination. He uses the Platonic metaphor of the sea-god Glaucus to describe how the soul's divine nature is obscured by the "seaweed and shells" of earthly life but can be purified through divine love.</summary>
<keywords>reason, fantasy, providence, Glaucus metaphor, Plato, Socrates, St. Paul, demons, airy spirit, purification</keywords>

The opening word "tasia" is the conclusion of "phantasia" from the previous page.</meta>

### BOOK XVI ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS

<note>original: phan-tasia</note> imagination are more frequently incited to seek out more attentive daily devotions and sharper affections, through which the spirits themselves are properly moved. From this, it follows that they <note>meaning demons or spirits</note> most accurately understand by which path they are more easily able to disturb each person, and, being themselves affected by a certain perturbation, they disturb us daily. We judge that the movement of this perturbation happens primarily in this way: the aerial demons move the aerial spirit within us, and by its vibration, the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note> in the body are moved and images are excited in the imagination. 

But in what manner? Truly, in a **sanguine** <note>Associated with blood; usually cheerful or amorous.</note> body, by frequently stirring the blood and images that are in some way similar, they allure the soul to vain pleasures. In a **choleric** body, however, when the bile and corresponding images of bile are irritated, they stir up angers and battles. In the **phlegmatic**, while they increase the phlegm, they occupy us with sluggishness and torpor through matching images. Finally, when they incite the **black bile** <note>Latin: "atram bilem," associated with melancholy.</note> in melancholics, they strike in fear and sorrow, terrify the imagination with false shadows, and mock the soul with often false opinions. 

Serapion and Avicenna <note>Serapion the Elder and Avicenna (Ibn Sina) were highly influential medieval medical authorities.</note> report, according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers, that all this can be done by demons—especially through the incitement of black bile—and they themselves do not deny it. For it is not fitting that the divine mind should be so deceived and attacked by the senses in any other way than by demons striving toward that same end. The Platonists think that the violence of such envious and ambitious demons can be purged through philosophy and sacrifices, as the Orphic hymns demonstrate to us. 

**Christ**, however, the true physician of souls, prescribes that these things be done through **fasting and prayer**. If it were permitted to explain the oracle of God itself philosophically, one might interpret fasting as abstinence from those things which either increase a particular humor or move a certain image and affection. One might explain prayer, truly, as such a vehement conversion toward God that the soul does not notice the stings of demons, and the demons lose confidence that they can conquer a mind dedicated to God. 

But let us now conclude the discussion. Therefore, let no one say the soul of man is less divine because it is troubled in caring for the body or because it "visits" the body. For a much harder province <note>Latin: "prouincia," referring to a duty or sphere of administration.</note> is assigned to our mind than to the rest of the celestial minds. Nor is the soul corrupted by the body; rather, it vitiates itself by loving the body too much, just as it purges itself. Nor should it be thought that divinity is lacking in us because we live much more anxiously than the beasts. On the contrary, we are divine most of all for this reason: that having been deprived for a time of our heavenly home and habitation—that is, as long as we are God’s vicars <note>Representatives or deputies.</note> on earth—we are continually troubled (even if we notice this very little) by a desire for our heavenly fatherland; nor can any earthly delights console the human mind, which is greedy for better things, in this exile.

->**Fourth question: why souls depart unwillingly from bodies.**<-
->**Chapter VIII.**<-

The fourth question proposed to us was: if souls are celestial, why do they depart from the earth so unwillingly? First of all, not all depart unwillingly. For **Theramenes**, **Theodorus of Cyrene**, **Cleombrotus**, and absolutely all the students of **Hegesias of Cyrene** <note>Hegesias was a philosopher known as "The Persuader of Death" because his lectures on the misery of life led many to suicide.</note> departed spontaneously and most willingly. So too the **Gymnosophists** <note>The "naked philosophers" of India encountered by Alexander the Great.</note> of the Indians, and the **Getae**, a people of Thrace, among whom births were mourned and the newborn wept over, but funerals were festive and celebrated with play and song as if they were sacred rites. I pass over countless other soldiers, citizens, philosophers, and religious men; I pass over the first-fruits of the Christians <note>The early martyrs.</note>. I pass over the fact that not all who are dying mourn, but all who are being born mourn, and as if unwillingly, they inaugurate this earthly journey with tears, as if entering an exile. 

Furthermore, even in those who dread death, it is not the "whole soul" (so to speak) that is terrified. Inasmuch as that part of us which, by departing, proceeds toward something better, not only does it not depart unwillingly even once, but it even departs daily of its own accord. What else do we do through moral philosophy but separate the soul from the affection of the body? What else do we do through speculative philosophy but call reason away from the senses? This whole study of philosophy, as **Plato** says, is a **meditation on death**. <note>A famous Platonic maxim from the *Phaedo*.</note> 

Since death is the liberation of the soul from the body, death is not terrible to philosophers and their like, because it is familiar and domestic to them, nor is the future state of the pure soul after death hidden from them. For such it will be, as they experience it nearly every day at the highest peak of contemplation: tranquil, indeed, and serene, and surrounded by the formulas of the Ideas <note>The Platonic "Forms" or eternal truths.</note> as if by the rays of stars, and flashing with the splendor of the divine sun.

<summary>Ficino explains how demons manipulate bodily humors to disturb the soul and argues that the soul's true nature is found in its longing for its heavenly home, as evidenced by the philosopher's practice of "dying" to the senses.</summary>
<keywords>demons, humors, phantasia, melancholy, fasting and prayer, Hegesias, meditation on death, Platonic Ideas, contemplation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the soul's transition from the body. The previous page ended with the phrase "that is," which leads into the description of the soul gleaming as it departs.</meta>

<page-num>384</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...gleaming. Hence the Prophet Daniel says: "the learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many in justice, like stars for all eternity." <note>A reference to Daniel 12:3. Ficino uses this to illustrate the radiant state of the perfected soul after death.</note> But that part of the soul departs unwillingly which was assigned only for the nourishing and protecting of the body, since by departing it is vacated from its certain natural duty and deserts its friend. Furthermore, in most people, reason loves this lower part of the soul too much, with the result that it grieves in some way at its loss. 

**Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the primary founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> however, does not properly call this a "part" of the soul, but a certain shadowy <term>simulacrum</term> <note>An "image" or "likeness" that is not the thing itself; a phantom or reflection.</note> of the substantial soul. For he proves that a human being is the rational soul itself, which, remaining within itself, generates the "animal" below it. It does not properly compose a single "animal" from itself and the body, but rather from such a body and a certain vital image of itself infused into the limbs. In this animal, indeed, are those senses which perceive external bodies with a certain <term>passion</term> <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon or feeling a physical sensation, rather than just emotion.</note>, as well as the <term>phantasia</term> <note>The imagination or "spirit-image" that bridges the gap between physical senses and the rational mind.</note>, which is entirely confused and disturbed. 

But in the very substance of the rational soul, there is an **impassible** <note>incapable of suffering or being changed by external physical forces.</note> and universal sense, looking not toward sensible things, but toward the images and passions which are in the senses of that animal. There is also the **reason** which receives the **mind** <note>Latin: "mens." In Ficinian thought, "mens" is the highest, most divine part of the soul that perceives truth intuitively.</note>. And insofar as the soul is governed within itself and raised up into the mind, it profits and rejoices in its separation [from the body]. However, insofar as it both forms the animal through a gift of providence and looks back at what it has formed, it is delighted by a certain commerce with the body. 

But let us proceed to the rest. Some also fear the torture felt in departure more than the departure itself; yet **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue of the same name. Ficino refers to the passage (81d-e) describing natural death as pleasant.</note> teaches that this will be sweet, like the oppression of sleep, if it happens through a certain loosening due to the maturity of nature, rather than through a suffocation caused by lack of restraint. Very many, however, [fear] this departure because they do not think they have earned the **divine vision** by their works; hence it happens that they dread long-lasting or perpetual darkness of the mind. Add to this that very many find it difficult to leave behind the charms of this life in which they were ensnared from the beginning. 

There are also those who distrust their own divinity, because they have never looked upon the divine splendor of the **pure mind**, but only the mortal darkness of bodily images infused into the soul through the senses. And those who look sharply at the splendor of the mind with the eyes of reason—not yet purified by **Philosophy**—are struck back by its rays, grow dull, and waver. For since nothing is more present to the eyes of reason than the very substance of the mind, it is likely that it remains unknown to us not because of a lack of light, but because of its [overwhelming] greatness. Therefore, whoever looks upon both the pure mind and the purified eyes of reason will not only not distrust it, but will revere it as a god. 

But although some may distrust, very many nevertheless have confidence. And even those who seem to distrust simultaneously hope that they will be eternal. Nor can a hope of this kind ever be utterly uprooted from our soul, since it is naturally implanted in us. Those species of thought tend to be deceptive which take their origin from the senses by some chance or use; the opinion of eternity certainly does not have such an origin, since the sense perceives nothing except what is **failing** <note>Latin: "caducum," meaning fleeting, perishable, or falling.</note>, and it forces us to suspect at times that those who have departed from life may be nothing more, after they are seen nowhere. 

Therefore, the hope of **immortality** follows the natural instinct of reason, since the soul hopes for it not only without the help of the senses, but even against their will. Therefore, I usually marvel at nothing more than that each of us hopes for this, given that we are always occupied among perishable things; yet we do not cease to hope. This signifies that this hope stands firm by the strength of nature. I think this also should be considered: that it would not be strange if humans, even if they had more evident reasons for immortality than for all other things, would still distrust the reasons in this matter more than in others. For what we love much, we fear for much. We love nothing more than eternal life, for the primary reason that it is most natural to us. 

Entirely from the fear of death itself, we can conjecture that some sensation remains for us after death. For if the soul fears death because it hates perpetual darkness, and if hatred proceeds from a difference in nature, then the soul is **perpetual light**. Or at least, it discerns eternal darkness in no other way than through some eternal light; it is not able to behold this [darkness] without an immense light. If the light of the soul, which is its mind, is related to that light just as the life of the soul is related to life itself, and the light of the soul is reflected upon the immense light, then the life of the soul necessarily embraces **infinite life**.

Furthermore, since life agrees more with life than light with life, if the light of the soul in its own way—that is, by understanding—reaches immense life, much more so does the life of the soul in its own way...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino discusses why the soul feels reluctance to leave the body, distinguishing between the higher rational soul and the lower "animal" image. He argues that the universal human hope for immortality is a natural instinct of reason that persists despite the physical evidence of the senses.</summary>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

that is, by living, the soul attains an infinite life. Furthermore, he who dreads the darkness <note>In this context, "darkness" refers to the perceived nothingness or gloom of death.</note> deliberates with himself whether he is to live forever without the body or whether he is to cease to exist. This very deliberation signifies that the soul, having [mentally] left the body, already then returns into itself. For the body does not reflect upon itself, nor is it elevated into a life separate from the body. In that same deliberation, the soul judges how much more excellent eternal life, free from the mortal body, is than either the present life or the deprivation of life, and it desires that free and eternal life. It could not judge or desire in this way unless it first experienced such a life within itself. If a free life is vastly different from a servile one, and yet the soul, though shut in the body, experiences and exercises it, how much more will it be able to fulfill it when released from the body?

Furthermore, in the same deliberation, the mind debates whether it can do anything by itself once the body has been laid aside, or not. And if it finds that it can, it does not doubt that it will live apart from the body. Wherefore even now, although it leads its life with the body, it nevertheless performs something without it, when it judges what and of what sort that very thing is which is said to "operate without the body." For who could cast off every body <note>To "cast off every body" means the mental act of abstracting the mind from all physical matter to think about pure concepts.</note> through some body? Who could do this to all bodies while using the body? Who, by working with the body, could perform that operation which occurs without the body? Yet he who thinks out and forms that very operation performs, in a certain way, an operation that is without the body. For <term>excogitatio</term> <note>original: "Excogitatio." This refers to intensive mental reflection, contriving, or "thinking something out" through pure intellect.</note> is an act of the soul. If, while it is in the body, it performs something without the body, it will be far more able to act without it when outside of it.

And yet, what is wonderful is that the soul is so invincible that whoever declares war on its eternity is overcome by it. For whether the <term>Lucretians</term> <note>Followers of the Roman poet Lucretius, who argued for a materialist view of the world where the soul dies with the body.</note> fight weakly, the soul is not conquered; or if others fight vigorously, they fight bravely because they use the arms and stings of that same soul—indeed, the soul itself fights. Therefore, when the soul itself seems to succumb, it then triumphs most of all. For it excels to the highest degree. Even if it seems to destroy itself [in argument], it perceives that it is about to destroy itself. He who perceives anything still breathes <note>Ficino argues that the very act of a skeptic using reason to "kill" the soul proves the soul's vitality, as the intellect must be active to form the argument.</note>. From these things it is clear how, if the fear of death arises from a dread of darkness, in that very dread immortality is shown.

Perhaps he who fears death does not so much dread the darkness as he prophesies and fears either punishment or sorrow. This indeed I think is more likely. From which immortality is also declared. For just as no one desires those things which he does not hope will be beneficial, nor thinks they are beneficial unless they are perceived, so no one fears things he does not judge will be harmful, nor thinks they will be injurious unless they can be perceived. For desire looks toward pleasure in the attainment of good or the avoidance of evil; fear looks toward pain in the presence of evil or the absence of good. Moreover, pleasure and pain do not occur without cognition. Therefore:

->he who desires the state of life because of the pleasure with which he is<-
->filled during the time of life, also fears the state after death because of<-
->the pain which he is to<-
->perceive at that time.<-

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind’s ability to abstract itself from the body and its fear of post-mortem pain prove the soul's immortality, as these acts require a conscious existence independent of physical matter.</summary>

## ology, on the Immortality of Souls,

### BOOK XVII.

#### *The fifth question: what is the state of the soul before it approaches the body, and what is its state after its departure. Chapter I.*

**B**UT let us now approach the fifth discussion, through which that question may be resolved which asks: what is the state of the soul before it enters the body, and what is it once it has departed? In these matters pertaining to Theology, six supreme theologians <note>Ficino refers to the *Prisci Theologi* (Ancient Theologians), a lineage of sages he believed preserved a single, divine truth throughout history.</note> once reached a consensus. The first is said to have been Zoroaster, the head of the Magi; the second was Hermes Trismegistus, the prince of the Egyptian priests. Hermes was succeeded by Orpheus. Aglaophemus was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus. Aglaophemus was succeeded in Theology by Pythagoras, and Pythagoras by Plato, who encompassed, expanded, and illuminated their entire wisdom in his writings. But because all of them used to shroud the sacred mysteries of divine things in poetic veils <note>original: "Poëticis umbraculis." Ficino believed ancient sages hid truths from the "profane" or uneducated using allegory and myth.</note> so they would not become common to the profane, it happened that their successors interpreted Theology in different ways. Hence, the crowd of Platonic interpreters divided themselves into six Academies, of which three were Attic <note>Greek or "Athenian" schools.</note> and the rest were foreign. Of the Attic schools, the Old flourished under Xenocrates, the Middle under Arcesilaus, and the New under Carneades. Of the foreign schools, the Egyptian was under Ammonius, the Roman under Plotinus, and the Lycian under Proclus. However, although there were six schools of Platonists, those three Attic ones along with the Egyptian school took whatever Plato wrote about the circuit of souls <note>The "circuit" refers to the reincarnation or travel of the soul through different celestial and terrestrial states.</note> differently than the words seemed to sound; but the two following schools <note>The Roman and Lycian schools, which Ficino often found more reliable for literal metaphysical truths.</note> observed the face of the words themselves more carefully. Let us diligently review how these two schools explain the Platonic mysteries.

#### *The exposition of Plato concerning the soul according to the last two Academies.*
#### *On the composition of the soul. Chapter II.*

**P**lato, in the *Parmenides*, calls God "the infinite," but in the *Philebus* he names Him "the limit." <note>original: "terminum." In Platonic metaphysics, the "Limit" (the principle of order and form) acts upon the "Unlimited" (the principle of multiplicity).</note> He is called infinite, clearly, because He receives no limit from elsewhere. But He is called the limit because He limits all things by means of forms distributed everywhere like measures. From this, the Platonists argue that insofar as God, as the infinite, excludes every limit from Himself, a certain power hangs from Him like a shadow, which is, as it were, the material [aspect] that lacks any limit; it is formless by its own nature and, so to speak, indefinite. But insofar as God, as the limit, looks back upon His own shadow as if into a mirror, an image then results in that shadow, and that very infinity—that is, the most universal matter—is limited by forms in a most orderly way. They confirm the same thing in this way: If the power of making the universe is always in God, then deservedly there is always a potentiality for the universe to be made (so to speak) outside of God. For He could not always make all things, as they believe, unless all things could always be made. They call such a power "most universal matter"—that is, the force that receives all forms equally. By its own nature, this matter neither inclines toward being itself (otherwise it would not need a heavenly shaper), nor toward non-being (otherwise it would not obey the shaper); rather, it is equally inclined toward being and non-being. Likewise, it stands as a kind of medium toward this or that form, and is determined by the shaper. Let this matter also be one in all things—not in number, nor in species, nor in genus, but rather by a certain analogy and proportion. Specifically, because it depends on the One, it represents the infinity of the one God in whatever way it can, in a certain shadowy manner; just as "act" is also said to be one in all things in a certain way, because it comes from the one Limiter and imaginatively reflects the limitation of the One. And an act of this kind surpasses potentiality, for the reason that it flows from God, who is no longer fleeing [into infinity] but is now looking back upon matter.

He then begins a metaphysical discussion on God as the "Limit" and matter as the "shadow" or potentiality that receives divine form.</summary>

Ficino is discussing the metaphysical structure of created things, specifically how they are composed of "potentiality" and "act," and how this relates to the soul's place in the hierarchy of being between God (who is pure act) and matter.</meta>

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

This kind of power <note>original: "potentia." In this context, it refers to both a "capacity" and the "potentiality" to receive a form.</note> in spirits seems to possess something of the body, insofar as in minds it holds the patterns of bodies, and in souls it further contains motions, and in both it possesses a form-giving faculty. Conversely, in bodies it seems to have something of the incorporeal, because even as it precedes quantity, it appears indivisible, and always sustains certain powers that are, in a way, incorporeal. Out of this infinity and this limit—that is, from a receptive, formable power and a formal act—the Platonists believe all things under God consist. The Moor Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058), a Jewish philosopher and poet whose work *Fons Vitae* was highly influential on Christian scholastics, who often mistook him for a Muslim ("Moor").</note> perhaps signifies this in his book *The Fountain of Life*, and our own theologians confirm it briefly as follows: If every creature, both individually and collectively, receives its being from God, then certainly it does not exist of itself; and if it were abandoned by Him, it would no longer exist. For this reason, it is able to be, and able not to be. Therefore, it is not its own "being" <note>original: "ipsum esse." A technical distinction: the creature *has* being but is not *Being itself*.</note>; rather, it is a potentiality toward being. Truly, nothing is a potentiality toward itself, nor does it receive itself. For always an agent, while it acts, makes that which is such-in-potentiality into something that is such-in-act. For this reason, a creature is produced, not from the fact that a potentiality is impressed upon a potentiality (otherwise nothing would yet be brought into act), nor from the fact that an act is infused into an act, or that the same thing is joined to itself (otherwise that which is produced would exist before it existed). But in the production itself, the act is properly applied to the potentiality. And these two must necessarily be distinguished in the creature. Otherwise, the "being" of the creature, because it would subsist in itself, would be utterly infinite. Since, therefore, being differs from essence, does it then arise from the essence? Not at all. For nothing, as an efficient cause, can bestow being upon itself; and so it receives being from elsewhere. Hence, insofar as it receives, it is potentiality; but that which is received is called act. Therefore, whatever is produced is composed of potentiality and act—that is, of essence and being.

The Platonists refer essence and potentiality to "infinity," but being and act to "limit." <note>Ficino uses the Pythagorean/Platonic terms "Infinity" (*infinitas*) and "Limit" (*terminus* or *finis*) to describe the two basic building blocks of reality below the One.</note> Furthermore, in the *Sophist*, the *Parmenides*, and the *Timaeus*, five genera of things are numbered, from which (except for the First) they compose all things: namely, essence, the same, the other, rest, and motion. Essence clearly signifies the formal definition of each thing; it also implies "being" as the act proper to essence. "The same" is mentioned because everything agrees with itself first of all, and with others. Again, "the other" is added because it possesses a certain difference, both within itself and in relation to other things. Furthermore, there is "rest," since a thing retains its unity for some time. Finally, "motion" in this place signifies a certain transition from potentiality into act, whether by existing, or by acting in any way, internally or externally. For this reason, the infinity of things is subjected to the divine infinity, and the limit of things is subjected to the divine limit. Next, we refer three things especially to the infinity of things: namely, essence, the other, and motion. To the limit of things itself, we similarly reduce three things by distributing them equally: namely, being, the same, and rest. However, what is called "the one and the many" in the *Parmenides*, and "the indivisible and the divisible" in the *Timaeus*, must be understood such that the one and the indivisible propagate through their various genera according to "limit," while the multitude and the divisible propagate according to "infinity." Although they compose all individual things (except the First) from these as if from seeds and elements, they say that incorporeal things are fashioned from a more harmonious mixture of these seeds than bodies are. For this reason, they believe those things remain more indissoluble.

For the present, I shall set aside the mixture of other things, and I will soon explain the reasoning by which the Pythagoreans and Platonists mix the soul from these genera—provided I first give warning, lest we perhaps think that although most of these men say the soul has always existed, they believe it exists entirely of itself. For since the soul does not unfold its entire operation (through which it always operates) all at once, but rather little by little, it is clear that it does not possess this infinite power of always operating all at once. For if it possessed it all at once, it would also produce it all at once as a single act. For every operation of a power (as they say) is one act of one thing. Therefore, it always receives the power of always acting. For this reason, it does not act in the same way, but differently at different times; so that it can be said in summary that whatever acts temporally—whether body or soul—receives the power of operating continuously and little by little, but never possesses the whole of it entirely at once. For this reason, the soul is judged by the Platonists not only to "always be," but also to be "always being born" <note>original: "gigni semper." This suggests that because the soul acts in time, it is in a state of constant "becoming" or perpetual generation relative to God's eternal "now."</note>—specifically insofar as it draws its power little by little, and unfolds some forms from within differently than others, and continually varies its affections and actions. Therefore, insofar as the vital soul is the cause of its own motion, it supplies itself in a way with an essential and indeterminate life, and is thus judged "to be"; but insofar as it unfolds this in infinite time, and receives such power little by little from higher beings, it is indeed judged to be "perpetually born" from another. Added to this is the fact that the supreme principle of things is present to all things, so that individual things participate in the principle everywhere according to their nature; otherwise they would suddenly vanish.

He argues that because the soul acts over time rather than all at once, it is both eternally existing and "perpetually being born" as it receives its power from God.</summary>

This page picks up mid-sentence discussing why the Soul is distinct from the ultimate "One."</meta>
