...potentiality. <note>Completing the thought from the previous page: things are composed of potentiality and act.</note> However, Soul is not present in all things, for not all things are alive. Likewise, the first principle must be entirely the "One" itself; for if it were some kind of multiplicity, it would undoubtedly have a cause for its union above itself. This is because the act of uniting is the duty of unity, not of multiplicity. Indeed, to say that the first principle is a scattered multiplicity is a forbidden thought. Yet, every soul is a multiplicity. Furthermore, the first principle is conceived as being above all essence, since every essence allows for multiplicity within itself—at least of the kind we have enumerated in previous sections. Soul, however, is a specific essence: namely, a vital and life-giving one. Finally, the first principle can never be contaminated, nowhere and in no way; yet many souls are sometimes, somewhere, and in a certain manner "infected" <note>Ficino uses "inficiuntur" (infected or stained) to describe how souls can be tainted by their association with the material world or vice.</note>. For this reason, the soul necessarily has an essence composed by its own higher principle in a certain way.

Furthermore, in things composed by God that are above the soul, the gifts that look toward the "limit" <note>The "limit" (terminus) refers to the Platonic concept of *peras*, which gives form and definition to the "unlimited" (*apeiron*).</note> surpass the opposite types by a very long interval. In things that follow after the soul, however, the opposite occurs. But in the composition of the soul, God joins these types together as equals. Since the soul is the truest "middle" of all things composed by God, it is fitting that it was composed by reason of certain very equalized middle-points, as far as is possible. Therefore, in the soul—to pass over other details—the "partible" <note>original: "partibile." That which can be divided into parts.</note> is harmonically tempered with the "impartible" <note>original: "impartibile." That which is indivisible or whole.</note>, and "the different" with "the same," and "motion" with "rest," just as a sharp note is tempered with a flat one.

Indeed, in those things above the soul, three things are chiefly considered: essence, life, and intelligence. In those things below the soul, there are likewise three: quality, nature, and sense. In this scheme, sense is the likeness of intelligence, nature is the likeness of life, and quality is the final image of essence. In the higher things, the "impartible" surpasses the "partible" in terms of essence, life, and intelligence; "sameness" also exceeds "difference," and "rest" exceeds "motion." In the lower things, however, the opposite occurs entirely. But in the soul, as the middle of all things, a middle path is observed through all these aspects. 

Therefore, whether you compare the soul to the extremes of the world—judging it between Minds (which are essentially indivisible) and Qualities (which are entirely divisible in time and space)—it is judged to be the middle. Or, if you compare it to its own extremes—that is, to its own Mind on one side and to the life immersed in the body on the other—it is similarly considered the middle between the individual and the divisible. Finally, if you compare it to its own internal middle, which is Reason, even this Reason is called "impartible" when it rises toward the intellect and universals, but is called "partible" when it declines toward the senses and particular things. There it attains "identity" (if I may call it that) and rest; here, in turn, it undergoes "alterity" <note>original: "alteritatem." The state of being "other" or different, a core Platonic category.</note> and motion. And while it moves through the consideration of eternal things in a certain way, it mixes divisible motion within an undivided state. Conversely, while it remains in itself to some degree while touching upon temporal things, it tempers divisible motion within a certain undivided state.

Moreover, just as the World Soul, in moving the heaven which is called <term>ἀπλανὴς</term> <note>original: "aplanes." The "sphere of the fixed stars," which does not wander like the planets.</note> (that is, "inerratic" or fixed), shows "the different" within "the same," so too in moderating the planets (which are in a way "erratic" or wandering), it seems to preserve "the same" within "the different" through the very order of its motion. But so far, "the same" surpasses "the different." Finally, in governing the lower things, it permits "the same" to be surpassed by "the different." 

In a similar way, the human soul seems to relate to three "vehicles": the ethereal, the aerial, and the composite body. Now, therefore, one can sufficiently understand what Timaeus <note>Referencing the speaker in Plato's *Timaeus*, who describes the mathematical and musical composition of the World Soul.</note> means when he uses musical proportions in the composition of the soul. He means nothing other than that the soul is composed—both from the categories of things and from its own powers—in such a way that it fits most perfectly first with its own Idea, then with itself, and thirdly with other things.

The Pythagoreans are accustomed to using both mathematical figures and numbers in describing the soul, because just as mathematics are intermediate, so too souls hold the middle position between natural and divine forms. They therefore establish a triangle <note>This refers to the "Lambda" diagram from the *Timaeus*, where the numbers 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27 are arranged to show the soul's harmonic structure.</note> at whose apex Unity is located, from which three numbers flow on each side—even on one side and odd on the other. On one side, first two, then four, finally eight; on the other side, first three, then nine, finally twenty-seven. By these, they believe all parts, powers, and duties of the soul are designated. For those things above the soul are thought of as "united" rather than "numerous." Those things below the soul are indeed numerous, but are by themselves maximally dissonant. But the soul is first called "numerous" because, being closest to bodily multiplicity, it is understood to be manifold in both its motions and its powers. Secondly, since it is the closest principle of ordered motion and generation, it is concluded by probable reason that its "numerosity" is maximally consonant. From this consonance, the continuous consonance of the body—both celestial and elemental—depends, just as it does upon the soul itself in musical matters...

He uses Platonic and Pythagorean musical and mathematical theories to describe how the Soul's internal harmony allows it to govern both the stars and the human body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book XV of the *Platonic Theology*. Ficino is transitioning from discussing the soul’s essence as a multiplicity to explaining the specific Pythagorean and Platonic mathematical ratios that define its internal "harmony."</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

->Bb 3<-

harmony exists in the mind first, and then that harmony which is perceived in voices and sounds is accustomed to flow from there. Accordingly, when Philolaus <note>A Greek Pythagorean philosopher (c. 470 – c. 385 BCE) who was the first to write down Pythagorean doctrines.</note> had named God "Unity" in the Pythagorean fashion, he soon after named extended matter "Duality." This is because, just as duality itself is the first division among numbers, so the dimension of matter is the primary cause for forms becoming scattered among themselves and turning into opposites. Therefore, they think that the soul, while hanging from the divine Unity, pours itself into matter as if into Duality, not unlike how a triangle starts from a single top angle and ends in two similar angles at the base. Thus, in a composite body, the soul is always being pulled apart and disturbed. It is with good reason, then, that the soul is represented by the figure of a triangle.

Next, they apply seven numerical terms to this triangle. Truly, since we see that the generation of things is governed by the sevenfold number of the planets, and that Saturn—the highest of the planets—effects changes in human life every seventh year; and since the Moon—the lowest of the planets—induces a change every seventh day both in itself and in the bodily fluids <note>original: "humoribus". In ancient medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were thought to be influenced by the moon’s cycles.</note>, they are rightly judged to describe the soul, which is the origin of motion and generation, by the number seven. There are even those who believe that a fetus is perfected in the womb by sets of seven, and that once born, a person is guided through the stages of life in a similar way.

Furthermore, they provide numbers on both sides—both even and odd—to declare that the soul is composed of a divisible nature through the even numbers and an indivisible nature through the odd. Again, they add linear, surface, and solid numbers so that it might appear that the soul pours itself most easily through the length, breadth, and depth of the body. They choose only those numbers whose mutual proportions create musical consonance, to show that a soul composed harmoniously disposes and moves all things harmoniously. 

Indeed, between four and three there is a sesquitertian <term>sesquitertian: a ratio of 4:3</term> proportion, from which is born the harmony that the Greeks call the *diatessaron* <note>A perfect fourth in music.</note>. But between three and two is the sesquialter <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2</term> proportion; this produces the harmony that they call the *diapente* <note>A perfect fifth.</note>. Moreover, between four and two, or four and eight, there is a double proportion, which makes the *diapason* <note>An octave.</note> consonance. Between one and three, or three and nine, or between nine and twenty-seven, there is a triple proportion, from which the melody of the *diapason-diapente* <note>An octave plus a fifth.</note> is composed. Accordingly, between four and one, or two and eight, a quadruple proportion arises, which generates the *disdiapason* <note>A double octave.</note> harmony. Finally, between eight and nine occurs the *epogdous* <note>A ratio of 9:8</note>, which constitutes a whole tone. They call a sound smaller than a tone a semitone. 

For this reason, all the proportions we have described, which are especially necessary for the art of music, are made from those numbers described in the figure of the soul. Through these, it is signaled that the soul’s natural composition, as well as its natural motion and action, are more consonant and rhythmic than anything else. Nor are there lacking those who measure the sizes of the celestial spheres against one another—their intervals, motions, and the positions and aspects of the planets—by nearly similar proportions. They even arrange the vital spirit by a similar tempering of its qualities. I will pass over many things (not without reason) which many people in this area treat as lightly as they do with curiosity regarding the "powers" of numbers and shapes. 

This is the sum of the Pythagorean and Platonic mystery. I omit the fact that they are accustomed to call Intelligence "Unity," since it often functions through a simple intuition; but they call Knowledge "Duality," since it proves a conclusion from a starting principle; and Opinion they call "Trinity," because it additionally brings the opposite of the conclusion into the middle through a certain ambiguity. Finally, they call Sensation "Quaternity," because it seems to be mostly concerned with things composed of the four elements. 

I omit again that they call the soul a "chariot" <note>A reference to the famous allegory in Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is a charioteer driving two winged horses.</note> because it produces circular motions. Or that they place a certain "straight line" in it insofar as it moves and looks toward bodies. Then, they describe a certain lower circle, like the orbit of the planets, for when the soul returns into itself. They also describe a higher circle, like the orbit of the fixed stars, insofar as it turns toward higher things. They include two wings—namely, the instinct of the intellect toward the Truth itself, and the instinct of the will toward the Good itself. The charioteer is the Mind; the "head" of the charioteer is the divine Unity which is superior to the mind. The higher horses are "Sameness" and "Rest"; the lower horses are "Otherness" and "Motion." Likewise, there is a good horse and an evil one: namely, the nature of anger and the nature of desire <note>In Plato’s allegory, the "good" horse represents spiritedness (thumos) and the "bad" horse represents base appetite (epithumia).</note>. For the former seems closer to reason than lust is. 

Finally—to speak briefly—by this reasoning, all the Pythagoreans and Platonists believe that rational souls, both our own and those higher than us, are composed in nearly the same way. From this they conclude that the celestial souls produce an inestimable melody in the revolving of the spheres, and that our souls are wonderfully delighted by harmonies of this kind. However, between the celestial souls and our own, which are far distant...

->MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

they place three intermediate grades, composed in a middle fashion, which bind our souls to the divine in a certain way; they believe these grades proceed according to the proportion of essence, life, and intelligence. For they believe that angelic souls, shining forth most closely from the intelligible world, pour intelligible light into those that follow through the mode of permanent essence. Then come the demonic souls <note>In the Platonic tradition, "demons" (*daemones*) are not inherently evil but are intermediary spirits or "guides" between gods and humans.</note>, by way of an unending life and process. Finally, there are the heroic souls, according to the mode of the mind's turning <note>original: *conversionis*. This refers to the soul "turning back" toward its divine source.</note>. I should mention that they think angelic souls proceed from God according to intellectual power, and demonic souls according to craftsmanship and providence—and therefore they "fabricate" worldly things. Heroic souls proceed according to the power of turning back especially, and therefore perform the duty of purifying souls. All of these are harmoniously tempered and perform harmonious acts, and they are wonderfully delighted by harmonies. But we shall treat these kinds of souls more appropriately in the following sections.

### Species and Cycles of Souls according to the two last Academies <note>Ficino refers to the "last Academies," likely the Neoplatonic schools of Plotinus and Proclus, who expanded upon Plato's original teachings.</note>. Chapter III.

**F**our are the kinds of souls: there are divine souls, that is, the souls of the spheres of the world and the stars, which are called divine for this reason—that they are closest to God and exercise a common providence for the world in a perpetual region. There are profane souls, that is, the souls belonging to beasts, which are devoid of all divinity. But let us leave these aside for the present. Between these two extremes are two middle ones: namely, souls always following God, such as the souls of demons and of sublime heroes; although these are not properly called divine, they nevertheless never depart from God. In this first kind of soul, the principles are so arranged that here "essence," and there (so to speak) "identity" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Identity" (the Same) and "Difference" (the Other) are fundamental categories used to describe the soul's composition in the *Timaeus*.</note> somehow surpass the other principles. Beneath these are the souls that sometimes follow God and sometimes leave Him. In these, the principle called "the other" <note>original: *alterum*. Refers to the principle of "Difference" or "Otherness."</note> seems to somehow surpass the others. Such are the souls of lower demons and heroes, but more clearly the souls of men; since these are the lowest of all minds, they do not have the power by which they can perfectly fulfill two very different things at the same time—that is, to gaze upon divine things through human reason and to govern earthly bodies. Yet it is necessary for them to do both, since they were born for both. Therefore, they do in turns what they cannot do at the same time.

They use this alternation in three primary ways. First, they transfer themselves from the intelligible world to the sensible, and back again. Furthermore, within the intelligible world itself, they perform various types of contemplation in turn. Again, in the sensible region, they change through different modes of living. Plato describes these alternations often elsewhere, but especially in the *Phaedrus*, and more clearly there where he says that some souls are companions of some gods in heaven, and in contemplating the Ideas <note>The eternal, perfect forms or patterns of all things in the mind of God.</note>, they perform a mental journey similar to their own god according to their strength—contemplating step by step above the heavens regarding divine things, then in the heavens regarding celestial things, then below the heavens regarding natural things. And as far as they are able to imitate the gods, they remain among the higher beings. Likewise, when they repeat the many cycles from causes to effects and back again, he says that the soul which has gazed upon the "Idea" (which is the head of the cycle) does not fall in that cycle which is continued properly through that Idea; but it slips when the "bad horse"—that is, the power of desiring, incited by the power of generating—now growing strong in its own time, turns the soul away from contemplating toward generating. Then he enumerates nine lives, not because there are only that many, but because they slip down through the seven planets and fire and air; finally, he describes many transmigrations through lower things and the return to higher ones, where many things are undoubtedly poetic rather than philosophical.

Therefore, let us now turn to a more philosophical order. Indeed, many Platonists think there is something that has infinite life of itself, something that has it from another, and something that has it from neither. Again, that which has it from another either declines toward the highest or the lowest, or possesses a middle state entirely. Truly, God possesses the permanence of the infinity of life entirely of Himself; the angel also possesses it permanently, but received from God; then the divine souls, which are superior to ours, have an infinite life from elsewhere, but a "running" life—running, however, in a certain fixed order by coursing from species to species, devoid of all defect and forgetfulness. Finally, our souls have a similarly infinite life, but not only running,

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

<page-num>391</page-num>
<sig>Bb 4</sig>

but also inordinately, and from a better state into a worse one, and in turn a force mutable by both remembering and forgetting. They say that souls below our own in no way participate in infinite life. Here the followers of <term>Proclus</term> <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino’s views on the soul’s descent and ascent.</note> confirm their own view, namely that celestial souls also traverse through understanding. This is because between the gods—who receive intelligible things both always and by remaining still—and the particular souls—which receive those things only sometimes and by "running" <note>original: *currendo*. In Neoplatonic thought, "running" refers to the discursive process of the mind moving from one thought to another, rather than grasping everything at once in a single intuition.</note>—the celestial and sublime souls hold a fitting middle ground; they indeed always gaze upon the truth, but they do so by passing from one form to another. We have, however, recounted the opinion of <term>Plotinus</term> on this matter elsewhere.

Accordingly, they wish for there to be one "infinite" in both power and perseverance, followed by many "infinites" in perseverance rather than in power (this perseverance, I say, either possessing all its own things at once, or succeeding from some things to others, whether that happens in a greater or lesser order); finally, there are many things which are infinite neither by their own power nor by a perseverance received from elsewhere. They place such an order among spirits. In the sensible world, however, the pole, as far as it can, represents the first step of that order; the axis represents the second; the celestial sphere the third; the elemental sphere the fourth; and finally, the fifth step consists of those things composed of the four elements.

But having set aside this digression, let us return to our own souls. The soul of a human being will indeed always exist, because it longs for eternal things. And it has also always existed, as they say, because it would also have an end unless it lacked a beginning. The soul of <term>Pythagoras</term> was at some point free from an earthly body before the birth of <term>Pythagoras</term>, and afterwards it was enclosed when <term>Pythagoras</term> was born. There are two lives here: one free, the other corporeal. That life which was free received an end at the beginning of the corporeal life; therefore, it also must have had a beginning at some point prior. For that which ceases, began; and so, it was not always outside the body before <term>Pythagoras</term>, even if it was so at some point. And after it began to be in the body, it will not be in those bodies forever, because that which begins, ends.

From this it follows that, before <term>Pythagoras</term>, his soul must have been in an earthly body and outside of it countless times, and again after <term>Pythagoras</term>, it will be outside the body and in the body in turns. And just as all the spheres of the world vary their forms through their souls and finally repeat their own cycles (which we observe in the four seasons of the year and the four alternating phases of the Moon), so our souls, similar to the celestial spirits, are clothed in various forms of bodies, and in certain circuits of time, are wrapped in the same bodies as before. These cycles <term>Zoroaster</term> calls <term>palingenesia</term> <note>original: παλιγγενεσίαν</note>, that is, <term>regeneration</term>, about which <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> disputes at length with his son <term>Tatius</term>. And <term>Plato</term>, in his book *On the Kingdom* <note>Ficino is likely referring to the *Politicus* (The Statesman), where the myth of the reversing cosmic cycles is told.</note>, describes this resurrection as something that will happen at the end of the world’s revolution, by God’s command and with the demons ministering.

What the world completes through one life, our soul carries out through many. For the Platonic <term>Timaeus</term> relates that God, the craftsman of the world, cast all the seeds of things into a certain bowl, and tempered them with one another through musical scales (as we said above); from this tempering, he created rational souls distributed into three grades. Thus, in any soul, all seeds are inserted, so that since the soul is made from a mixture of all types of things, it can easily recognize all things through a certain kinship, move all things, and give life to all things, experiencing an "all-formed" life more easily. What else do we understand by "God’s bowl" but the "third essence," <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "Third Essence" is the Soul itself, which sits in the middle of the hierarchy of being, connecting the divine realm above with the material realm below.</note> intermediate between the divine and the corporeal, shimmering with the sparks of the divine and heavy with the seeds of the corporeal? From this source, three primary species of souls have flowed: Divine souls, those always following God, and those sometimes following God. To the first, the <term>Pythagoreans</term> assign wisdom; to the second, right opinion; and to the third, wavering opinion. From this it is gathered, as we have often said, that our soul is in a certain way "all things," and therefore contains within its own vitals the progressions of all living things.

Yet it does not unfold all of them individually. For the first souls perform more than the second, and these also perform more than the third. For this reason, although the human soul is adapted to all things, it seems destined for many progressions of lives. It is transferred from life to life neither by a certain violence inflicted from the outside, nor by a deliberate choice, but by a certain natural instinct, just as in this life teeth, hair, seed, and the rest come forth at their own time. For just as in the nature of the universe itself, so in the natures of particular souls, individual things are ordered by a certain eternal law, and they come forth into action in a way that is consistent both with themselves and with the whole of nature. Certainly, one single harmony is made from all the members of the world's living being, through which individual parts harmonize with other individuals and with the whole everywhere. Therefore, just as the World Soul itself produces certain things at certain times, so also particular souls are naturally inclined and disposed toward certain types of living at a certain time by the seeds implanted within them. And while, little by little, the affections and acts of a past life fade—

He describes the soul as a "third essence" that mediates between the divine and the material, containing the seeds of all life forms within itself.</summary>

<page-num>392</page-num>

...is traded, and in turn the attention of the following life is intensified, with the nature of the universe contributing to individuals everywhere. Yet it is necessary to remember that, as the tenth book of the **Republic** <note>Plato’s *Republic*, specifically the "Myth of Er" in Book X, which describes the afterlife and reincarnation.</note> teaches, souls descend by fate—that is, they desire generation, and they desire it at a certain time. This arises from a natural instinct joined to the order of the universe, but they choose such a life, or such another, by their own free will. For although they naturally lusted after a corporeal life before they thought about it, they nevertheless chose such or such a *kind* of life before they adopted it. He says they choose for the most part according to the habit and affections of their previous life, which habits and affections were once produced from free acts. Therefore, he says, the fault lies with the one choosing, not with God. <note>A famous line from Plato: "The blame is his who chooses: God is blameless."</note> A <term>daemon</term> <note>In this context, a *daemon* is not a "demon" in the modern sense, but a guardian spirit or guiding genius assigned to a soul for its lifetime.</note> does not choose you by lot, but you choose the daemon. For virtue is free. But after someone has chosen a life and a daemon, virtue can arrange and compose the chosen life rather than set it aside. For the certain circuits of the lot must be fulfilled. 

As for what is written in the same place—that the world is turned between the knees of the goddess **Necessity**—we have explained this elsewhere. For she is called the Necessity of the soul of the world because the universe is led by her fatal power. "Between the knees," I say, means through her lower power, which is adapted to the turning spheres. Indeed, she leans upon the divine with mind and reason; and though this lower power is one and universal, it is nevertheless given a threefold name. **Lachesis**, that is, the "lot-caster," because she inserts the individual lots. **Clotho**, that is, the "weaver" or "unroller," because she unrolls the lots belonging to each person from the beginning in certain orders and times. **Atropos**, that is, the "unchangeable," because she proceeds with immutable reason in unrolling the lots. 

Plato asserts that the soul, inclining toward lower things, goes to all these goddesses in this specific order: first, after Lachesis casts the lots upon it, the soul naturally lusts for an elemental life; then, after multiple examples of lives are proposed, it chooses a specific life and its guiding daemon by free choice; and then Lachesis confirms the choice. From there, it is led by that same daemon to Clotho, Atropos, and Necessity. Who does not see here that the soul, solely because of its affection for this body, soon falls into the full power of the fates, and finally to the river <term>Lethe</term> <note>Lethe is the mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>—the river of oblivion—which is to say, into this body, where it immediately forgets divine things? 

Accordingly, it signifies that the soul which has first drunk from that river—that is, which has adopted a body for itself with a more vehement affection—forgets higher things more deeply and remembers them more slowly; and conversely for the opposite case. But let us come now to the different species of living. Sometimes it leads an **angelic** life in the ether near that star to which it has been made closer either by nature or by habit, and then it simultaneously consents and concurs with the steady governance of the universe. But it can run up and down through all the spheres step by step, spending time in each life, governance, and contemplation appropriate to that sphere and star. Sometimes it leads a **demonic** life in fire, then a **heroic** one in the air, a **human** one on the earth, and even a **beastly** one. 

And often, while it leads the life of a human, a life like that of a horse, or a lion, or similar animals gradually springs up from its seeds into its natural instinct and imagination. This signifies the affections and character traits proper to such beasts that arise within us. Finally, having set aside the human form, it enters the body of that beast whose character it has shown itself most similar to—whether it introduces itself into a beast’s offspring and becomes the proper soul of the beast's body (as <term>Plotinus</term>, **Numenius**, **Harpocratius**, and **Boethus** believe), or whether it joins itself to the beast's soul and acts as a companion to the beast (as was pleasing to **Hermias**, **Syrianus**, and <term>Proclus</term>). 

But after it has migrated from one beast to another and has unfolded all those progressions of beastly life which it was more prone to unfolding, it brings forth human progressions again, then heroic ones, then demonic ones, and finally divine ones. Some souls live more or less in different places, insofar as they are variously disposed by fate, or fortune, or choice and habit. Plato designated these transmigrations and restorations by periods of a thousand years, three thousand, and ten thousand—more for the sake of discussion and example, as **Hermias** says, than because he thought they could be certainly numbered. For any of these numbers is not only very large but is also destined to be completed by a certain ratio, to show that souls require a long but certain time for perfect purgation; and those that have either sinned more lightly or have rather practiced philosophy will return to their fatherland sooner. 

However, it must not be understood that the soul will commonly return to the exact same human being in number unless the entire course of the world has finally been fulfilled, as is written in the book *On Kingship*. Astronomers calculate that this course (as we have said elsewhere) is fulfilled in thirty-six thousand years. Meanwhile, however, the soul is often said to return to the same thing—namely, into the same species of life and a similar way of—

He also details the various levels of existence a soul can inhabit, from angelic to animal, and the vast cycles of time required for spiritual purification.</summary>

...way of living, namely from the divine to the divine, from the human to the human, from the brute similarly to the brutal, just as the circuit of the world itself often returns to similar things in the meantime, until it finally returns to exactly the same things. Lest anyone think it absurd for the soul to transfer itself into such diverse species, they <note>The "they" refers to the Platonists or proponents of the soul's cycles.</note> bid us consider how many different affections and habits the soul often puts on even in this body—not only in different people, but in the same person—namely those of a planet, a brute, a man, or an angel. Again, lest anyone wonder why we do not remember those things we did in a previous life, they bid us notice not only how much of our infancy we forget in old age, but also how easily we forget the events of yesterday. These things they say to those who object with that prophetic saying: *In circuitu impii ambulant* <note>original: "In circuitu impij ambulant." This is from Psalm 12:8 (Psalm 11:9 in the Vulgate): "The wicked walk in a circle." Critics used this scripture to condemn the Platonic idea of reincarnation cycles.</note>. As if to say that those who introduce such circuits of souls should be judged as wicked.

### That Plato is more correctly explained in the manner of the four preceding Academies,
### especially the first and the fourth. Chapter IV.

The four Academies older than these <note>The "Academies" refer to the historical phases of the Platonic school, traditionally divided into the Old, Middle, and New Academies.</note> differed from them in this, while agreeing among themselves: they thought that the writings of Plato were entirely poetic. But they differed among themselves in that Carneades thought Plato both believed and treated all things in the manner of the **Skeptics** <note>The Skeptics of the New Academy argued that Plato was not a dogmatist and that certain knowledge was unattainable.</note> as if they were ambiguous, and that he held no preference in those matters. Arcesilas, however, believed that Plato held nothing as certain, yet held some things as likely and probable. Xenocrates as well as Ammonius affirmed that he held some things not only as likely and probable, but also as true and certain—and those were a few specific points regarding the providence of God and the immortality of souls. 

We, therefore, following in the footsteps of Xenocrates and Ammonius, do not deny that Plato affirmed certain things about the soul; but many things treated by him regarding its "circuit" we understand as poetic, in a way different from what the words seem to signify—especially since he did not invent such circuits himself, but recounted those of others. First, indeed, they were invented by the **Egyptian priests** under the figure of souls being purged; then they were sung in poetic verses by **Orpheus, Empedocles, and Heraclitus**. I pass over how **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician who was credited with the doctrine of metempsychosis (transmigration of souls).</note> inserted the transmigrations of souls into those accustomed fables and symbols of his. 

For this reason, we shall respond to the latest Academies in this way. They rely chiefly on two foundations: their own reasoning and Platonic authority. As for what they explain concerning the types of things and the **musical composition of the soul**, and again what they assume in their argument—that there are four species of souls—we admit this. Again, we grant that our soul can scarcely do both at once—namely, see divine things and rule bodies, especially those that are more unfit. We grant that too, but we do not think it necessary because of this for the soul to drive its innumerable powers up and down; it performs both duties sufficiently if, while it lives on earth, it sometimes cares for bodily things and sometimes cultivates itself and God; and when it has departed from here, it may more easily rule its vehicle <note>The "vehicle of the soul" is a Neoplatonic concept referring to a subtle, quasi-material body that carries the soul.</note> and apply itself more intently to divine things. 

We concede, moreover, that the soul is pregnant with the seeds of all lives, and therefore can perform the progressions of all of them—yet in such a way that those seeds are in this soul according to the manner of the human soul and species; and from them may sprout affections and habits congruent with other species, yet a true transmigration from species to species never occurs. For whether the soul is compared to the body as a specific form is to its specific matter, or as a specific art is to its specific instrument, any soul cannot enter any body. For who would dare say that the form of the Moon forms the matter of a stone, or that the art of music enters the tools of a potter? 

Rightly did the divine **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who argued against the idea that human souls could reincarnate into animals.</note> reject the transmigration of the soul from a human into beasts. **Porphyry** also rejected the infinite circuit, and allowed the soul to wander for certain ages only within the human species, and finally asserted that the purged soul of a man clings forever to the heavenly Father, never to return to the misery of this life; for it could never be blessed if it either did not know it was to return here (when it was eventually to return) or if it foresaw and feared future evils. This is indeed confirmed by the fact that an unstable good cannot fulfill a natural appetite, which properly recognizes and hungers for the eternal and infinite. Again, a soul enjoying truth with infinite power is neither torn away from it by violence, nor...

<summary>Ficino argues that Plato's descriptions of reincarnation should be read poetically or metaphorically rather than literally. He aligns himself with the interpretation that souls maintain their species and, once purified, remain eternally with God rather than cycling back to earthly misery.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where critics used the biblical verse "the wicked walk in circles" to attack the Platonic concept of soul-cycles. Ficino is now defending Plato by arguing that the philosopher may not have literally believed in the soul's "fall" from the divine or its reincarnation into animal bodies.</meta>

<page-num>194</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

deception does not move it, nor does that will turn it away. Not the will of God, whose nature it is to convert <note>In this context, "convert" means to turn something toward the good or toward Himself.</note> things; nor the will of the soul, which—since it never chooses anything except for the sake of the good—has nothing to choose outside of Him, in whom it acknowledges the total nature of the good. Nor does any change of life befall a soul living in eternity beyond time. Finally, to say that a soul enjoying its end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the soul's ultimate goal or highest purpose: union with God.</note> is sometimes separated from it is as if someone said that the earth could be diverted from its own center, or fire from the proximity of the Moon <note>In ancient physics, fire naturally rose toward the "sphere of the moon," which was its proper place.</note>, or iron from a massive magnet to which it clings.

Moved by these and similar reasons (as I believe), Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> felt ashamed to rashly tear the soul away once it was fixed in its center. Likewise, Syrianus and Hermias <note>Later Neoplatonic commentators from the 5th century who sought to reconcile Plato's myths with logical philosophy.</note> were ashamed to plunge a celestial soul into the bodies of beasts. And so that they might assign proper punishments to monstrous vices, they thought that sacrilegious souls were observed among the souls of beasts, yet they do not rule the bodies of those brutes. This is because if a soul passes into a brute, it will not be purged thereby, but rather entirely infected. For purgation does not occur except where some protest of the conscience reigns. 

Furthermore, regarding their denial that the soul will exist forever unless it has always existed—and how it might be condemned otherwise—we have spoken elsewhere and will speak again. Therefore, their reasons do not persuade us to give credit to the infinite errors and wanderings of souls, or to the absurd confusion of species. But lest they defend their position with the authority of Plato, we must remember that Plato learned the Pythagorean wisdom—which had flowed from Zoroaster—from Archytas, Eurytus, and Philolaus. After he had traveled the world and examined all the other opinions of the philosophers, he finally chose the Pythagorean sect as more plausible than the others, and he illustrated it with his writings. 

For this reason, he introduces Pythagoreans debating in his primary dialogues: Timaeus of Locri, Parmenides of Elea, and Zeno, from whom Socrates learns in Plato’s works so that he may repeat those lessons to others in Plato's other dialogues. Indeed, three signs especially seem most evident by which we can judge that he by no means affirmed those Pythagorean doctrines as his own. 

**First**, because he introduces those same debaters who had formerly said such things. **Second**, because he depicts Socrates as ambiguous, merely repeating what he had heard—Socrates, who used to proclaim that he knew nothing except this one thing: that he knew nothing. **Third**, because those things he had written about such matters he did not confirm in his old age. Indeed, in the books of the *Laws*, which he wrote in his seniority—the only books in which Plato's own persona speaks—he asserted no such thing. And in his *Letter to King Dionysius*, when he was quite old, he said that he had never composed anything about divine matters, nor was there any work of Plato’s concerning them, nor would there ever be, as if to say he had not revealed his own mind but had narrated the minds of others. In the *Letter to the Syracusans* as well, which he wrote later in his old age, he repeated the same things, adding that no one existed then, nor would exist in the future, who understood Plato’s mind regarding such matters. 

Rightly so, because he did not write it down. Does Plato, then, affirm nothing about divine things? Some things, undoubtedly: namely, that God cares for human affairs, and that He renders rewards or punishments for the works of the immortal soul. But he affirms nothing else. For these few things he asserts not only in other dialogues where other characters speak, but also in the *Laws* and the *Letters* where he speaks himself. 

He does not assert that the world has always existed, but he "generates" it in the *Timaeus*. He generates it, I say, from the beginning of ordered time, by almost the same reasoning used first by Moses and then by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage believed to be a contemporary of Moses.</note>, as Severus, Atticus, Plutarch, and many other Platonists have explained. Hence Numenius the Pythagorean exclaimed: **"What else is Plato than Moses speaking in the Attic dialect?"** <note>original: "nihil aliud esse Platonem, quàm Mosen Attica uoce loquentem." This is a famous quote suggesting Plato was a "Greek Moses" who had access to Hebrew wisdom.</note> although Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Proclus wish to interpret a "perpetual generation" of the world there in Plato. 

But if perhaps that text is to be explained that way, it will be the opinion of Timaeus the Pythagorean rather than Plato’s. Indeed, Plato himself says in the *Epinomis* that the stars will be either immortal or so long-lived that their own life suffices for them, and they lack nothing longer. This is consistent with what he says in the *Timaeus*: namely, that the stars would be dissolvable by their own nature because they were composed from a beginning, were they not preserved by the will of their Creator. Again, in the sixth book of the *Laws*, he says the human race has either existed always or arose many ages ago. There, he seems to have preferred a beginning rather than eternity. Aristotle also, where he disputes the nature of such questions, says the question of the eternity of the world is "neutral"—as if to say it is not so much a demonstrable certainty as an opinion that is in some way probable on either side. However, as for Plato's statement in the *Laws* that souls exist before bodies, he perhaps intends this so that it is attributed to the dignity of their nature rather than to time ->itself.<-

<summary>Ficino argues that Plato's more controversial ideas, like reincarnation or the eternity of the world, were often reports of other philosophers' views rather than his own beliefs. He highlights the "Attic Moses" connection, suggesting Plato's core truths align with Judeo-Christian revelation regarding God's providence and the soul's judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s defense of Plato against the literal interpretation of metempsychosis (the migration of souls into animal bodies). Following the previous discussion of Porphyry and Syrianus, Ficino now examines specific Platonic texts to show that "beastly" transformations refer to moral character rather than physical species.</meta>

<page-num>39</page-num>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV. ###

...is attributed. Although even some Christians believe that souls precede bodies for some brief interval of time. In the *Laws* <note>Plato’s last and longest dialogue, concerning ethics and law.</note>, Plato does not confirm that the souls of men pass into beasts. In the ninth book [of the *Republic*], however, he says that according to the myths of the priests, they go into other men. And in the seventh book, he declares how it should be interpreted if they are ever said to insert themselves into other bodies. There he teaches that he who ignores necessary doctrines will never be a God, or a <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a 'daemon' is a tutelary spirit or intermediary between gods and humans, not an evil entity.</note>, or a hero among other men. It is as if these things are said by way of comparison to other men—including those things he sometimes myths about the bodies of wild beasts—even though in the *Phaedrus* he does not say the soul of a man passes into the *body* of a beast, but into a "beastly life," and in the *Timaeus* into a "beastly nature," not into the body of a wild animal. In the final book of the *Republic*, he says the soul of Thersites <note>A character from the Iliad known for being ugly and scurrilous; Plato uses him as an example of a low-minded soul.</note> passed not into the body of an ape, but into an "ape." By these instances, it is understood that he means a transformation of habit and life rather than of species or body. Furthermore, in the *Phaedo*, after he recounted the passage of souls into wild animals in the manner of the Poets as punishment for sins, he added that it is not the mark of a wise man to confirm such things, but only that it can be asserted with prudence that they pay some penalties for their crimes. He adds that souls purified through legitimate Philosophy will live forever with God without bodies; he confirms this in the *Epinomis*, saying the pious soul, separated from the body, spends the remaining time in the contemplation of all the most beautiful things. In the *Gorgias* also, and the *Theaetetus*, and the tenth book *On Justice* <note>Another name for Plato’s Republic.</note>, he describes the perpetual punishments of the wicked for many sins that cannot be expiated; he asserts such punishments were instituted for the sake of justice and example rather than for a cure, where he rejects those inexplicable errors of souls. Through these points, it is clear that Plato, in the manner of Christians, signified an everlasting good and evil. 

As for what Christians call Purgatory, Plato understood it to be where he [God], intending to purify the soul, revolves it more frequently through lower things—specifically not so much through bodies as through the lives and dealings of beasts. Finally, once purified, he restores it to heaven. In the ninth book *On Justice*, he figures the human soul in this way: There is a certain heap of many heads of wild beasts, as if forced into a beastly globe; from this manifold heap of beastly heads, a certain trunk sprouts forth as if from roots, which trunk is a lion on one side and a dragon on the other. Upon this trunk a certain man is placed, holding a club in his hand, with which he beats the raging beasts. Finally, the skin of a human body surrounds all those things, through which it appears to be a single animal, which is a simple animal. <note>Ficino is summarizing Plato's famous allegory of the tripartite soul from Republic IX: the multi-headed beast (desire), the lion (spirit/anger), and the man (reason).</note> He intends the heap of many beasts to be the insatiable part of concupiscence <note>The drive for physical pleasures and desires.</note>. The trunk composed of the lion and the dragon is the force of anger. It is called a lion when it supports reason, and a dragon when it resists it. The man is reason. After this, Plato commands that we nourish that inner man rather than those beasts, lest because of hunger, the man failing, only the beasts remain within us. 

By these things, we are warned to accept the "transition of souls" not into various species, but into dispositions <note>original: *habitus*</note>. Thus, in Plato's view, he who is devoted to nutrition and remains sluggish day and night will be a "tree." He who lives by prey through concupiscence will be a "kite" <note>A type of hawk.</note>. He who serves excellently as a soldier will be a "lion." He who rages cruelly against the human race will be a "dragon." He who lives by civil reason will be a "man." He who investigates natural things will be a "hero." He who studies mathematics, a "daemon." He who studies divine things, an "angel." For the soul becomes such as the disposition it puts on; such, I say, in the body, and such outside the body. Socrates proves the same things in the *Phaedrus*, saying: "I therefore consider whether I myself am more complex than Typhon <note>A monstrous multi-headed giant from Greek mythology.</note>, or a more divine animal." And later in the same book, he places a charioteer in the soul, and twin horses—one good and one bad—representing, of course, reason, and the powers of anger and concupiscence. There it appears that both the "man" and the "beasts" are within the very powers of the soul. In the same way, Parmenides the Pythagorean in his book *On Nature* had figured the soul. Timaeus the Pythagorean, a most noble man, also says that the migration into beasts is falsely introduced to terrify wicked men. But Pythagoras himself signified the whole matter thus:

> If, having left the body, you come to the free ether, 
> You shall be an immortal God, undying, no longer mortal. 
<note>original Greek: "Ην δ' ἀπολείψας σῶμα ἐς αἰθέρ' ἐλεύθερον ἔλθῃς. / Εσσεαι ἀθάνατος, θεὸς ἄμβροτος, οὐκέτι θνητός." These are the final lines of the *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras.</note>

That is, if having laid down the body you ascend to the free ether, you will be an immortal God. Immortal, not further mortal. As if to say, you will be made an immortal God in such a way that, being entirely far from death in the future, you will never again return to mortal things. Orpheus also, in his hymn to the *Earthly Mercury*, says of Mercury:

> Inhabiting the house of Cocytus, the irreversible abode of Necessity. 
<note>original Greek: "Κωκυτοῦ ναῖον ἀνυπέστροφον οἶκον ἀνάγκης." Mercury (Hermes) acts as the Psychopomp, leading souls to the underworld from which there is no return for the wicked.</note>

<meta>catchword: id est, (meaning 'that is')</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that Plato's descriptions of souls entering animal bodies are allegories for moral dispositions rather than literal biological transformations, aligning Platonic thought with Christian views on Purgatory and the soul's ultimate divine destiny.</summary>

# THE PLATONIC THEO-
## logy, on the Immortality of Souls,
### by the same author Ficino, Book XVIII.

->*That Plato does not forbid giving faith to the Theology common to the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs; namely, that the world was created. Chapter I.*<-

---

Plato therefore seems to forbid nothing in giving faith to the Theology common to the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs <note>Ficino is referring to the three "Abrahamic" religions—Judaism, Christianity, and Islam—noting their shared belief in a created universe, which he seeks to harmonize with Plato’s "Timaeus."</note>—namely, that the world began at some point, that angels were created from the beginning, and that the immortal souls of men are created daily. To these things we are compelled by divine authority; to these we are led by reasons of this kind: The mass of the world cannot exist through itself in such a way that it does not depend on something else to establish it in its being; otherwise, it would in a sense be making itself. However, to "make" something does not belong to a body, because whatever a body seems to do, it carries out through a certain incorporeal power lying within the subject; rather, it belongs to essence itself, which remains entirely incorporeal within itself and is the origin of that power. Furthermore, a corporeal mass cannot contain itself. Indeed, it cannot "contain" unless by doing something, especially since it cannot contain without union. However, to unite seems to belong not to a divisible nature—which itself stands in need of union—but to a power that is, in the end, entirely indivisible. 

Again, this same mass cannot operate or move through itself, because if it cannot give being to itself, much less can it provide action for itself. Conversely, if it could act upon itself, it could also act through itself. But that it cannot operate through itself is also clear from this: that it cannot move itself, as we proved in the sixth book. We have shown elsewhere, moreover, that the perpetual and most orderly motion of the world requires infinite power, which a finite and determined nature of a body cannot have from itself. Therefore, the world—as if wandering and dissolvable of its own accord—borrows its indissoluble order from elsewhere. But from where does it borrow it? Surely, if the world can neither subsist through itself, nor contain itself, nor act and move through itself, it necessarily depends upon a cause existing through itself and containing itself—a cause, I say, that is altogether indivisible. This is so that the cause itself is not likewise dependent on another (namely, on parts or a gatherer of parts), nor contained by another (namely, by a unity connecting the parts together), nor insufficient (since it would need parts), nor have "non-being" mixed in (since a composite made of parts is none of the individual parts themselves). 

Furthermore, since the world is composed of dissimilar things, it is necessary to examine the cause of such a composition. For a body does not compose itself, since it is the principle of neither action nor union. Nor should it be said that the parts of the world flowed together into such a composition by some motion of their own, for bodies do not move through themselves. Nor should they be thought of as driven to it by some external force, or as driving each other. For what is it that drives? And what drives first? Again, it is a sacriety <note>In this context, "nefas" or "wicked/wrong" to suggest that chaotic impulses could result in such a perfect arrangement.</note> to commit such a marvelous order to impulses lacking order. In what way is such great order and ornament produced from ordered and unordered things, especially since the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "agent" or "doer" that brings something into being.</note> is always expected to be more excellent than the effect? 

Furthermore, if you say the parts of the world are the <term>material causes</term> <note>The physical substance or "stuff" from which something is made.</note> of this composition, we shall ask about the efficient cause. But if you say they are the efficient causes, we will again inquire how a rational work could be produced from things lacking reason. Therefore, if the world is composed neither from itself nor by chance, it certainly has a fixed cause of its composition. Nor let anyone assert that it has only a <term>final cause</term> <note>The purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists.</note>. For it certainly has that, since it moves rightly toward the Good as toward an end. But <margin>*</margin> since it is not moved toward that end in vain, it certainly attains something of the Good from it. It receives this according to its essence, since it desires and is moved according to its essence. Therefore, it receives its being from the same source from which it receives its essential goodness. Thus, that cause is as much the "efficient" as it is the "end." It is also the <term>exemplar</term> <note>The divine "pattern" or "blueprint" (Idea) used by God to shape the world.</note>: for if the world is carried toward the Good by a certain rational plan, certainly God continually directs it toward that Good by a certain rational plan, as if by an exemplar. 

But truly, since leading toward an end and seeking the good is the duty of the Will, it is no wonder that God moves the world by His will, just as He also composed it by His will. This same point is further confirmed as follows: That which is called "fortuitous" or "contingent" is usually posterior to that which is ordered or consists of determined causes. Therefore, the order of the world cannot have happened by some cause prior to it. And if anyone brings forward many causes of worldly effects, unless he reconciles them all under one, he will not be able to explain why the world, though it consists of diverse things, is both one and united. And by what reason would one whole be better than many parts, unless he finds one cause that is both common and more excellent than the many causes, by whose power all... 

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe is not self-sustaining or eternal but was created by a single, rational, and incorporeal God. He uses metaphysical logic to show that the world's unity, movement, and order require an "efficient cause" (God as creator) that acts with will and purpose.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY
<page-num>398</page-num>

...come together into one. For this reason, there is one cause of the union of the universe itself, to which all things are coordinated. If this cause were devoid of reason, then human beings, who use reason and know themselves, would be more excellent than the first cause, and the human work would be rendered more perfect than the divine work. Therefore, God moved His infinite goodness rationally—a goodness that can be propagated through all things. Hence it pleased His goodness to propagate itself through individual things, for it is the property of the "good" to please, and of the "sovereign good" to please in the highest degree. Indeed, by this affection of the rational will, all things were both procreated rationally and most excellently, and are continually disposed. 

That the world is disposed by divine reason and will is signified in the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>The Chaldean Oracles were a 2nd-century collection of mystical verses believed by Neoplatonists to be ancient divine revelations.</note>, which Proclus <note>A major late-antique Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the Oracles.</note> recites, in these words: "The Intellect of the father, emanating with perfect counsel, understands the all-formed ideas, all of which indeed have proceeded from one source. For from the father were both the will and the end. They were distributed by a certain intellectual fire, and then divided into certain other intellectual forms. For the King placed before the multiform world an unfailing intellectual figure, of which the second world is a footprint—hurrying along with the form—and a visible world endowed with all-formed ideas. A single source, from which break forth innumerable other divided ideas, producing things around the bodies of the world. These are carried in a certain circuit, rightly assimilated and turned in every direction; but in other places are other intelligences from the paternal source, like sparks from a watchful fire around the primordial ideas. For the first idea flowed from the father, as did the voluntary source." Thus far the Oracle, in which mention is made of the Father, Son, Spirit, ideas, angels, and the voluntary disposition of the world. 

But let us now return to the established order. Elements and plants, in whatever they do, operate by a certain necessary affection of their nature. That affection is only of one kind; therefore, each of them performs a single thing. Brute animals, moreover, operate through appetite, which—as it is provoked in various ways through the senses—attempts various things. And just as elements and plants act by innate necessity, so brute animals operate by an external necessity. The rational soul acts through the **will**, which is indeed moved to work not by the forms of things (as appetite is), but by the notions and counsels of the intellect. This is **free operation**, which is worthily suited to a perfect living being. Such an operation, above all others, must belong to God. Wherefore Plato in the *Timaeus* states that the beneficent will of God stood as the most certain origin of things. Mercurius <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage believed to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> also says that the world consists of the divine will, which all effects accompany. Orpheus, where he speaks of the supreme Jove [Jupiter], says this:

> For having hidden all things, he again brought them forth into the joyful light 
> from his sacred heart, performing wondrous deeds.
> <note>original Greek: πάντα γὰρ κρύψας, αὖθις φάος ἐς πολυγηθὲς. ἐξ ἱερῆς κραδίης ἀνενήκατο μέρμερα ῥέζων.</note>

That is, when he had hidden all things, he thereafter sent them out into the pleasing light from his sacred heart, performing his thoughts and wonders. In these words, Orpheus clearly declares that the world had its beginning of time from the divine will. Nature and appetite never attempt any new work unless when nature is variously affected and appetite is variously provoked; however, even in man, the intellect and will often begin a new work without any novelty in themselves. For example, in the morning Plato decides to summon Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato and later head of the Academy.</note> in the evening. The firm intention of the future calling stands until that hour calls Xenocrates. The change indeed occurs not in the mind and will, but in the mouth of Plato and the limbs of Xenocrates. 

The <term>world machine</term> <note>Latin: "machina mundana," a common Renaissance metaphor for the structured, functioning universe.</note> was always prescribed in the architect of the world, and the moment of its beginning was marked in the architect's will. At that very moment which He had pre-marked, the machine was begun, with no change intervening on God's part. God had completed the substantial world entirely within Himself from eternity. He permitted the shadowy world to emanate from there when it was better. It was better when the will of divine goodness—through which all things are good—decreed it. Indeed, we want things because they are good; however, they are good because God wants them. And in the manner He wants them to be, and when He wants them to be made, only in that manner and at that moment are they good. Similarly, we understand truly for the reason that we understand things as they truly are. On the contrary, they truly are so for the reason that God understands them so. Thus, the truth of things proceeds from the divine intelligence, and the goodness of things from the divine will. Where the first cause of things is, there is the supreme reason of things. 

Wherefore, things ought to have been made rationally, just as God understood and saw. God understood that they ought to emanate from Him temporally—that is, from the beginning of time—and He [designed] this shadow, whose nature is occupied in motion and time. And the motion of the worldly shadow ought to have been produced, and must be produced, from a temporal beginning to an end, whose time is simultaneously at the beginning and the end in individual moments. Nor should it be asked why the world began to flow out from that point rather than at a prior moment. For if it had begun a thousand years before, we would still ask why not earlier. Nevertheless, a beginning [must occur] at some point...

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe was created through God's rational will rather than necessity, citing the Chaldean Oracles, Hermes Trismegistus, and Orpheus to demonstrate that the physical world is a "shadowy" temporal emanation of a perfect, eternal divine plan.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the world’s creation, moving from the rational necessity of a first cause to addressing common misconceptions about the timing and location of the world’s beginning, drawing heavily on Platonic and astrological traditions.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

...when it ought to have had it. Add to this, that such a notion is a fallacy of the imagination <note>original: *phantasiae*; Ficino refers to the lower faculty of the mind that struggles to conceive of non-physical realities like eternity.</note>. There are no moments of time before the first moment of the world in which it ought to have been created earlier. Whatever is thought of before the world is the unique and stable point of eternity. Every sequence of temporal moments began with the world and as the world runs its course. Similarly, one should not investigate why the world is situated here rather than there. That, too, is a fallacy of the imagination. There is no physical place outside the world. Time measures the whole course of the world; the whole of physical space is filled by the world's vastness. And, as Plato’s *Timaeus* shows, time is equal to the course of the stars, and space is equal to the world's breadth. He who thinks of a physical place outside the world is deceived. He who imagines times before the world is deceived. And he will also be deceived who believes that something is added to divine perfection—or that it is even appropriate—whether the world flows from Him or does not, since the world is much less in relation to God than a shadow is to a body. Yet, nothing is ever added to or taken away from a body by its shadow.

Indeed, that spiritual world—the exemplar <term>exemplar</term> <note>The "exemplar" is the perfect, divine blueprint or world of Ideas upon which the physical world is modeled.</note> of this world and the first work of God—is a life equal to its architect. It was always with Him and will always be. The corporal world, however, which is the second work of God, departs from its maker in one respect, because it was not "always" <note>That is, it had a beginning in time.</note>. It retains the other respect, because it is to be forever. But composite bodies, which are the third works of God, lose every part of eternity. It is reasonable that the world is not made equal to God in terms of its life, just as it is not equal in terms of its substance. Nor is it infinite in every direction, so that it may yield to the divine infinity. It is also fitting that, just as all things have two acts—one internal and one external—and the former is a life equal to the agent, while the latter is subsequent to it, so too the Maker of things contains within Himself a "progeny" equal in life, but produces an "offspring" outside Himself that is subsequent, so that eternity, no less than other perfections, may be lacking in the effect. And just as this world is produced as something finite in power and size by an infinite God, so it seems likely that it is made "new" and circumscribed by a beginning by the eternal God. And just as a certain site is assigned to the world (because it is "here" in such a way that it does not exist through immense space), so a certain time is assigned to it (because it is in "this" time in such a way that it did not exist previously through an immense duration). It is as if God exceeds the substance of the universe by infinite degrees of perfection, and even more so, exceeds the duration of the universe by infinite degrees of duration.

For in any thing, substance is more excellent than duration. But whoever considers the parts of the world which are below the Moon—how they are changed from being this into that, and vice versa—and the parts of the same world which are above the Moon—how they pass in turn from being in one state to being in another—and because it changes everywhere, he sees they are needy and imperfect. And again, considering that the universe itself consists of some subject <note>or "matter"</note> and form, and the subject (which naturally precedes form) can both undergo such a form and not undergo it; likewise, that the world consists not only of parts of quantity but also of parts fighting amongst themselves; and finally, that the entire body exists in no way through itself, but entirely through another (that is, through every type of cause: efficient, final, formal, and material), and therefore according to itself it completely wavers—whoever, I say, considers these four things can clearly guess that the entire mass of the world, by its own nature, would be changeable from being into non-being. It would not be so unless it had at some point passed from non-being into being. Hence, the followers of Democritus, the Cyrenaics, the Stoics, and the Cynics were nearly all forced to admit that the world had a beginning in time. The Egyptians say that the first day of the world dawned in such a way that Aries was in the middle of the sky <note>the Midheaven or 10th House</note>, Cancer was rising, the Moon was in Cancer, the Sun in Leo, Mercury in Virgo, Venus in Libra, Mars in Scorpio, Jupiter in Sagittarius, and Saturn in Capricorn; and they say that each of the planets are the lords of those signs in which they were believed to be while the world was being born. The Chaldeans think that when the world was born, the Sun was in Aries. Both groups believe that the world was born at some point, and they call Aries the "head of the signs," either because the Sun was in it, or because it began to run through the middle of the sky. For this reason, astronomers judge the fortune of the entire year especially from the entry of the Sun into Aries, as if almost everything depends on that. I pass over the fact that the Egyptians assigned only Leo to the Sun and only Cancer to the Moon, but for the remaining planets, besides those signs in which they then resided, they joined the remaining five signs in such a way that a second order began from the end of the first order. Thus, just as Aquarius succeeds Capricorn, it hands over [rule] to Saturn, who had been last; then Pisces to Jupiter, who had been next to Saturn...

He supports the world's temporal beginning by citing its inherent changeability and the astrological "birth chart" of the universe (Thema Mundi) used by Egyptians and Chaldeans.</summary>

->MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...had been [assigned], Aries to Mars, Taurus to Venus, but Gemini to Mercury. But leaving these things aside, let us return to the main point. Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino’s understanding of how the divine relates to the physical world.</note> demonstrates that the world—since it possesses an extended and composite essence, and is therefore by its own nature scattered and liable to dissipate—is only held together by a certain indivisible power infused from divine unity. Furthermore, because it is always moved toward the good in an orderly way by a natural appetite, it has received the nature of such an appetite and the origin of its motion from the divine mind and goodness. This power, through which the world is connected and moved, must be infinite so that it can be connected and moved without end; yet the world, being finite, cannot possess this power from itself. Instead, it must always receive it from divine infinity, not all at once (for it cannot contain it), but rather according to its own temporal nature, drinking it in, so to speak, drop by drop <note>original: *guttatim*</note> at every single moment. He shows that this happens just as moments flow by suddenly; as it is drunk in momentarily during these moments, and always in this manner—as we have recounted elsewhere—the bodily world flows and is in a state of becoming <term>becoming</term> <note>In Platonic thought, physical things are always "becoming" (changing) rather than truly "being" (static and eternal).</note>, but it never truly *is*. It is like the shadow of a towering tree in a rushing stream, which, although it appears to be a tree, is not a tree; and though it appears for a long time, it remains only by being continually renewed as the waves are continually renewed. To whom, then, should it seem a wonder that the world proceeded from non-being into being at the beginning, once and for all, when according to some it is so shadow-like and unstable that it passes away into non-being and returns again at every single moment? But let Proclus see to these matters himself.

Plato, in his book on the generation of the world <note>Referring to the *Timaeus*.</note>, shows that the world was created by the grace of divine goodness. Such a work was not established for the purpose of making God—who is goodness itself—any better, but so that it might reflect the divine goodness. Just as parents do not generate children for any other reason than that their image may be seen in their children. The world especially reflects the goodness of God the Creator if it shows not only how generous He is, but also how excellent. It shows how generous He is insofar as it is always preserved unharmed by God; for if the world were left to itself, it would dissolve, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*. It testifies to how excellent He is insofar as it began to exist at a certain time; through this beginning, it is clearly perceived that the world is not from itself, but from God. It shows that God exceeds the world by an infinite interval—He who was (if I may put it this way) for an infinity before the world—and that He produced the world from nothing <note>original: *ex nihilo*</note> by infinite power, acting by freedom of will rather than by necessity of nature. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic, whom Renaissance thinkers often viewed as a contemporary of Moses.</note> taught such an origin of the world's generation more clearly. Nor should it seem a wonder that he knew such things, if this same Hermes was the same man as Moses, as the historian Artapanus <note>A historian of the 2nd century BCE who sought to identify Jewish figures with Egyptian and Greek heroes.</note> has shown through many conjectures.

### Angels and souls have not always existed. Chapter 11.

**W**e have established an order among bodies; let us now establish an order among spirits. There is that supreme spirit, who always was and will be: that is God. There are also the lowest spirits of the beasts, which neither always were nor will be. It is necessary that there be two types of middle spirits between these such differing extremes, which share part of that first spirit and part of the lowest spirits. In what way, then, shall we arrange these middle spirits? Shall we say they have always existed, but will eventually cease? Not at all. For whatever has always been has lived through infinite power into infinity. Infinite power is never diminished. Therefore, if they had always existed, they would always remain, and would be equal in duration to God, not "middle" spirits. Therefore, to be middle spirits in their endurance, they must have begun at some point but never cease; although they were made from nothing <note>original: *ex nihilo*</note>, they shall not turn into nothing. For that which we call "nothing" is neither the matter nor the maker from which they are formed during their creation, but perhaps the boundary from which they arise—and even that is not a boundary in reality, but only in name. They are not, therefore, compelled to follow the nature of "nothingness" itself, by which they would return to nothing, for they had already rejected that nature as soon as they came forth into being. Rather, they preserve the nature of their cause from which they received their essence, so that through that same infinite power they are preserved in being far from nothingness—the same power by which they emerged from nothing into being, leaving nothingness behind. It is not absurd to think that what is procreated directly by an infinite principle and an infinite end (that is, God) will have no end, since many things which proceed from a finite beginning and boundary are rightly considered to proceed without end. For thus number proceeds from unity, thus the mathematical line from a point, and thus future time from the present moment without [end]...
