# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XV.

...time without end, nothing prevents it from being thought of as progressing. But that something created should exist forever, especially the soul, is proven not only by religion but also by Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>Alganteles is a Latinization of Al-Ghazali (1058–1111), a Persian philosopher and theologian whose works were influential in the West.</note> speaking as philosophers. Therefore, while angels occupy one middle position between God and the beasts, human souls were assigned another middle position immediately after the angels. They agree with the angel in that they will always exist; they differ in that they have not existed throughout all time like the angels, who, having arisen from the beginning of things in a natural order before the course of heaven (whose companion is time), have existed throughout all time, even if they have not existed through all eternity. Our souls, born after the origin of time, are lower than the angels, yet they are not temporal. For God, through that very point of His eternity—which is always the same, stands above the universe, and encompasses the circuit of time—procreates human souls through the same power by which He procreated the angels. Therefore, human souls are made above the passions <note>In this philosophical context, "passions" refers to being subject to change, decay, or the external influences of the material world.</note> of time, although they are made after the origin of time. But the souls of brute animals are generated both after the origin of time and under the passions of time, because they are not made directly by God through His eternity, but through the revolutions of the heavens and the powers of souls; thus it happens that they do not live forever. For they are subject to the changes of time, being made under time through the motion of heaven. And if they have anything noble in them, it flows continuously from the very fountain of the <term>third essence</term> <note>In Ficino’s hierarchy of reality (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter), the Soul is the "third essence" that acts as the bridge between the eternal and the temporal.</note>, of which they are not streams, but shadows. For this reason, the Platonists think they are certain idols <note>original: "idola"; here used in the Platonic sense of reflections or phantom-images, not false gods.</note> of the World Soul, or of the soul of that sphere which they inhabit, and they place them between the third essence and the qualities of bodies; yet they reduce them to this essence as shadows. Hence Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated and commented upon extensively.</note> says: "Just as many images are diffused from one face through many mirrors, so from the soul of a sphere into the bodies of brutes many likenesses of a single soul are sent"—the bodies, I say, of brutes, in which human souls are not present. For where these human souls are, the irrational power follows the rational substance of our soul like a shadow.

---

->Souls are created daily. Chapter III.<-

**B**ut why are new souls created daily by God? Could God not have created all souls at once when the world was constructed, just as He procreated all the angels at the beginning of the world? It was not fitting: for if they had lived for a long time released from the chains of the body, they would have judged clearly how much more precious the free life is than the other, and would never have wanted to enter bodies, insofar as they are intellectual beings. Neither God nor an angel wishes to force the free will of the soul. For the mind is moved by nothing other than persuasion. Indeed, the soul would not even have known each individual body which it could choose, since it lacks knowledge of individuals before sensory experience. Thus, this middle part of the divine temple <note>Ficino views the universe as a sacred "temple" where every level of being, from angels to humans, performs a liturgical role of praise.</note> would lack divine priests and sacred hymns. Yet it is necessary that in each circle of this temple, its own choirs of priests should be led, singing to God. Furthermore, it is consistent with reason that just as the souls of the spheres (or angels) were not procreated through some delays of time before their own spheres, so neither should our souls be created before our own bodies. <margin>|</margin> Also, the soul is the form and the act <term>act</term> <note>Ficino uses "act" (Latin: *actus*) in the Aristotelian sense: the soul is the "actuality" or the functioning reality of a body that has the potential for life.</note> of the body. Although the "act" is prior to potency <term>potency</term> <note>Potency or potentiality is the capacity to become something; "act" is the realization of that capacity.</note> in the universe according to the order of nature, it is nevertheless posterior in time within the same subject, because movement is produced from potency into act. <margin>|</margin> For this reason, the seed (which is potential life) existed before the soul (which is the actualizing life). Additionally, it is natural for every form to be united to its own matter. Otherwise, that which is composed of matter and form would be a mere heap, contrary to nature. But that which belongs to a thing according to nature is granted to it before that which is contrary to nature. For what belongs according to nature is inherent in itself; what happens contrary to nature comes from some external accident. Therefore, for the soul—by its very nature as a soul—it is more fitting to be joined to a body than to be separated. How then could it have lived before the body? Add to this that if any superior mind (as some think) is both one in a single species and immortal, while any bodily form is both multiple in the same species and mortal, the soul of man—which follows those minds and precedes these forms—will participate in both, such that it is either a single soul in the single human species and mortal, or immortal and multiple. The first is impossible. For if a single soul took the place of the entire species of souls, it would encompass within its powers the innumerable souls that could be made under that species. Thus, it would be of immense power in some way, and immortal...

<summary>Ficino argues that human souls occupy a middle ground between eternal angels and temporal beasts, being created by God in time but destined to exist forever. He explains that souls are created daily rather than all at once to respect their free will and their natural role as the "act" or perfection of the human body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the middle nature of the soul. The previous page discussed how the human soul is situated between eternal angels and temporal beasts. This page explores why the soul, though one in its nature (species), is many in number, and how it remains immortal despite its connection to a physical body that begins in time.</meta>

<page-num>402</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<meta>catchword: shows,</meta>

...because the <term>species</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "species" or "Form" is the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note> of things are everlasting, and that which captures a whole species is itself everlasting. Furthermore, because the soul would have no communion with these bodily things, it would be quite far from destruction. Indeed, if it were such, it would preserve the sheer simplicity of its own species. That species is set apart from the decaying body. Therefore, it would remain in its own purity, foreign to mortal bodies, and would not provide life to them. From these points, it is clear that the human soul cannot be one single soul shared by all men; conversely, it cannot be both one and mortal at the same time. Therefore, it will be immortal and multiple. In its immortality, it will imitate the <term>minds</term> <note>Ficino uses "minds" (mentes) here to refer to higher angelic or purely intellectual beings that exist without bodies.</note>; in its multiplicity, it will imitate forms that are entirely bodily.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Perhaps it is consistent with the order of things that the first rank is held by the ideal species of things themselves, and the second by those things that receive these species. And among those that receive them, first are those that receive their own species in its entirety according to the capacity of the creature, and do so always. Second are those that do not receive it in its entirety, yet still receive it always. Third are those that receive it neither in its entirety nor always. We see this in the heavens: we place the <term>exemplar of lights</term>, that is, the Sun, in the highest position; in the second, the stars, each of which always receives its own full light from there; in the third, the Moon, which indeed always receives light, but not the whole amount, and though it seems to suffer eclipse, it nevertheless recovers it suddenly—and similarly with air and water. In the fourth rank are those things composed of the elements, which are in some way transparent and bright; these things desire light, but neither always nor in its entirety—to say nothing of their opposites, which admit light in no way at all. But from where does this one species of soul receive its multiple number? Perhaps not from the fact that it imitates the minds. It must be, then, from the fact that it imitates bodily forms. What are these forms like? They begin with the body and end with the body. If our soul were entirely like that, so that it began and ended at the same time as the body, it would not be "imitating" them, but would be of the same genus. And if it had neither of these traits (neither beginning nor ending with the body), it would not imitate them, would not fit them, would not cling to them, and would not give them life. Therefore, it must have one or the other: either it will begin with the body only, or it will end with the body only. The mind, which is directed toward immortal truth and goodness as its goal, cannot end with the body. For it does everything for the sake of this goal. Just as we form a conjecture about the beginning of things from their <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being; for Ficino, this is ultimately God.</note>, so we are accustomed to take a conjecture about the perseverance of things from their goal. If, therefore, the mind is properly directed toward an everlasting goal by a certain natural kinship, it is capable of everlasting perseverance. For a proper goal corresponds to a proper agent, and the perseverance of a thing directed toward a goal holds the middle ground between the two. Since the mind has an everlasting goal, it also has an everlasting agent, and for that reason, it possesses perpetual life and perseverance from both sides.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If it does not end with the body, but at least begins with the body, the soul of man certainly becomes multiple in many bodies. This is indeed signified by the diverse opinions and contrary passions of men. Such multiplicity does not come from its own species (through which it is one), but (as some think) in a way from bodies, or rather from God, the reconciler of souls and bodies. Not because it is divided within the body. Not because it is made of matter like the body. Not because it is born from the body. From where, then, if not because it becomes a companion of the body by divine will? When God grants a beginning to both simultaneously, He does not, however, grant the same principle of origin. Therefore, they have neither the same nature nor a similar end, but the same beginning, as we have said. From this, He also hands down the same number. Hence the soul’s affection for the nature of the body is increased, because it accompanies the body’s beginning. And in the creation of this soul, the change, which appears to be one, is actually threefold:
1. The change of the soul from nothing to being, made by God alone, is called **creation**.
2. The change of a non-living body to life itself, to be received from the soul, is called the **formation** of the body.
3. The result is called the **generation** of the animal.
The <term>term of creation</term> <note>The "terminus" or end-point toward which the action is directed.</note>, toward which the soul is directed, is within itself, responding only to the divine eternity, which is the "term" from which creation proceeds. However, the term of formation, toward which it happens, is the soul—not so much remaining in itself as in the body. The term from which it happens seems to be Nature. Finally, the term of generation is the "animal" composed of soul and body. The term from which it comes is likewise Nature—Nature, I say, not only particular nature, but also universal nature, by whose power particular nature prepares the body for the soul. Universal nature is called a certain power, or the instrument of the **Soul of the World** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a concept from Plato’s *Timaeus* suggesting that the entire universe is a living being with a soul.</note>. Therefore, Plato said in the *Philebus*: "If the world lacked a soul, from where would we have ours?" Not because our soul, in itself, comes from the Soul of the World, but because it exists in the body through its work. For the *Timaeus* [shows] that our souls are made by the same God, and from the same source, as all the higher ones...

<summary>This page argues that the human soul is immortal because it is directed toward eternal truth, but it is multiple in number because it begins its existence alongside a physical body by divine will. Ficino distinguishes between the soul's "creation" from nothing by God and its "formation" and "generation" into a living animal through nature.</summary>

--- Page 431 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 402 regarding the multiplicity and origin of souls. Ficino is specifically addressing the Platonic view of the soul's creation and responding to the theological concern of how a holy God can be involved in the creation of a soul during an act of human passion.</meta>

<page-num>403</page-num>
<header>->MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-</header>

shows. From this it is also shown what <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note> *Timaeus* says: namely, that the **rational soul** comes from God alone, but the **irrational life** <note>Ficino distinguishes between the immortal, thinking part of a human and the lower "animal" functions (growth, sensation) which he believes are influenced by the stars.</note> beneath it, which is enslaved to the body, depends upon the celestial gods by God's command. This is because they prepare the body for that life and strengthen our soul to infuse that life into the body. But let us set these matters aside as being unnecessary here.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Suppose someone says: "Let there be many souls, and let them even begin along with their bodies—this does not offend the ears; yet here one <term>scruple</term> <note>A "scruple" (scrupulus) was a small sharp stone; metaphorically, it refers to a nagging doubt or moral hesitation.</note> remains: in what way is it fitting for God to procreate individual souls at every single moment according to the lust of those lying together?" Sexual union is not an evil, since it was naturally instituted for a good purpose; rather, the evil is the lack of moderation in the minds of those lying together. Generation <note>Ficino uses "generation" (generatio) for the biological process of making a body, and "creation" (creatio) for God making a soul from nothing.</note> of the body does not arise from the lack of moderation, but from the union of the body.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To this generation, God distributes souls not according to the lust of those coupling, but according to the prescribed law of <term>providence</term> <note>The divine plan by which God guides all things in the universe.</note>, which sees the number and the times of those lying together from the beginning of things in <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "in aevo." Ficino refers to aevum, a state of "ever-abiding" time between human linear time and God's timeless eternity.</note>. In eternity, He has conceived of these souls long ago. Why then does God give birth to souls daily? Because bodies were to be generated not all at once, but through succession. Add to this that He continually illuminates the angels; and just as He never stops forming the higher minds, so He never ceases to procreate the lowest minds. In the higher realm, there is perpetual formation; here, there is perpetual procreation. Procreation, I say, is as constant as the **Sun**, God’s <term>vicar</term> <note>A representative or deputy. Ficino often describes the Sun as the physical representative of God's light and power in the visible world.</note>, which continually illuminates the higher bodies and continually generates the lowest. It befits the immense power of God to always show Himself powerful to the eyes of minds, so that they may see God—at the lowest grade of minds, because of the world's final place—continually procreating something out of nothing. Thus, through this continuous effect, they may more clearly recognize the altogether infinite power of God, performing an infinitely creation-act infinitely, if it so pleases Him. Let them worship Him as He illuminates in the heavens; let them marvel at Him (if I may say so) as He creates on the earth. Surely <term>creation</term> is a more excellent operation than <term>illumination</term>. Therefore, the former is more fitting for God than the latter; the latter is done continually by God, and thus the former is made continuous according to God’s will. The ministers of God move the heavens. By this motion, subsequent things are generated, while every <term>species</term> of things on earth does something, and in doing so becomes a minister of heaven. Shall God Himself alone do nothing, while all other things are performing some work? Far be it that the **First Act** should do nothing while others are acting. But you will say that He acts enough so long as He does not desert the other acting things but supplies them with the power of operating. That is not enough. For from this, the proper works of other causes follow, and their images are made in the world, not God’s. Why would you be unwilling for God also to busily perform His own works and His own images, by always procreating many things without a medium?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, since **creation** is God's own proper operation, while external **generation** is the proper operation of others, God will not cease to create something as long as others do not cease to generate something.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;God is the true **center of the world**, as we discussed in the book *On Love*; because He is one, simple, and stable, and resides in all things; and all other things, which are altogether many, composite, and mobile, perpetually revolve around Him through their natural desire for Him. Thus, God is the center of all, because He is so present in all things that He is more internal to each thing than it is to itself. He is also the **circumference of the world**, because existing outside of all things, He so towers over the universe that He excels the highest peak of every thing with His immense dignity. Likewise, as much as He is the smallest of all in quantity (if it is permitted to say so), so He is the greatest of all in power. As He is the center, He is in all things; but as He is the circumference, He is outside all things. In all things, I say, but not enclosed, because He is also the circumference. Outside all things, too, but not excluded, because He is also the center.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What then is God? He is, so to speak, a **spiritual circle**, whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. <note>This famous paradoxical definition was a favorite of Renaissance Neoplatonists, often attributed to the "Book of the Twenty-Four Philosophers."</note> But if that divine center should have some imaginary or clear seat of operation in any part of the world, He rules most powerfully in the middle of things, like a king in the middle of a city, the heart in the middle of the body, or the Sun in the middle of the planets. In the Sun, therefore—that is, in the third and middle essence of things—God has placed His tabernacle. A tabernacle, I say, for demonstrating His power more frequently. This seat is familiar to God, not so much because it is a type of soul, but because it is the middle of the divine city, the public treasury, and the harmonious moderation of the urban parts.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We have already frequently declared that the **human soul is the middle of things**. In this region, therefore, the principal operation of God will more frequently prevail. Such is creation. Therefore, He busily creates the souls of men. Indeed, because He is the stable center, He creates continually. Because He is the circumference which encompasses the circumference of the world, He creates them (as the Platonists would say) in a certain way in the circumference of the world. Again, because He is the center, He is the highest point of things. Because He is the highest, He pours out individual things, both individually once from the beginning...

->of things<- <meta>catchword: rerum</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that God continually creates individual human souls to match the physical generation of bodies, asserting that this continuous creation demonstrates God's infinite power. He famously defines God as a spiritual circle whose center is everywhere and circumference is nowhere, placing the human soul at the vital "middle" of this divine order.</summary>

<page-num>404</page-num>
<header>->MARSILIO FICINO: PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-</header>

of things, then all things in summary every day, just as in creating the soul, which is the midpoint of things, He pours out from His own bosom the universe, which is gathered together in summary in that midpoint.

## From where the soul descends into the body. Chapter IV.

**F**rom where then does the soul descend into the body? In truth, since God is present in every place without being confined by place, and since the soul is not enclosed by place but is created and present in an instant, one should not say properly that it "descends," nor should one ask from where it descends. For it is present to the body by flowing from God Himself—as I might say—just as a ray from the sun’s light is present to the eye. But it is pleasing at times to converse along with the ancients. Therefore, if we believe Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom the "Chaldean Oracles" were attributed; Ficino viewed him as a source of ancient wisdom.</note> and Mercurius <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of Hermeticism.</note>, it is sent down from the vast circuit of the world. And to bring their opinion into order: the lowest mind first adheres to the highest body—and not only does it adhere, but it is infused, through which, as a medium, it is coupled to thicker bodies.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A simple and immortal spirit is joined to a composite and mortal body in no other way than through a body that is itself simple and immortal. Nor is this done without justice, since the soul, through its own essence, provides life to the body. Its essence is eternal life. This eternal life, to whatever it first adheres, it adheres to forever, especially since the essence of the soul is immutable; thus, it follows that it vivifies the body closest to it immutably. For the proper act of perpetual life is eternal vivification. One might think that Aristotle thought something similar in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where, after he had proved that the intellectual soul is separable from the body because bodily operation does not share in its operation, he added shortly after that a certain body belongs to this soul which is separable from the body of generation <note>The "body of generation" is the physical, biological body born of parents.</note>. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From this, it also appears what we were seeking against Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose interpretation of Aristotle suggested that the "Intellect" was a single entity shared by all humans, which Ficino (the "Platonist") argues against here to preserve individual immortality.</note> in earlier sections: namely, that the intellectual soul is a "form" that gives life to the body. This is especially true because when Aristotle proved in that same place that out of the three souls—namely the vegetative, the sensitive, and the intellectual—this one alone is both from the outside and separable from the body (because its operation alone can be completed by itself without a physical instrument), he then added that all these, namely the three souls, are equally in the seed according to potentiality. But truly, if anyone considers these things diligently, he will find that there cannot be any power common to these through which the body produces three souls—provided it is in potentiality—unless it be a certain faculty by which it receives life and motion from the intellectual soul in the same way as from the others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But let us now return to the body closest to the soul. The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests/sages.</note> call this the <term>vehicle of the soul</term> <note>original: "vehiculum animae"; a Neoplatonic concept of a "star-body" or "spirit-body" that carries the soul between the material and divine worlds.</note>, a little ethereal body, received from the ether, the immortal garment of the soul. In its natural shape, it is round because of the region of the ether, but it transforms itself into a human likeness when it enters a human body, and restores itself to its prior shape when it departs. The Magi judge this to be necessary for this reason: because angels are such that they are separable in power and separated in act from bodies; irrational souls are neither separable in power nor in act. From this, it follows that rational souls, as intermediaries, ought to be such that they are always separable in power (because if bodies are withdrawn from them, they will not perish), but in act they are always joined, because they obtain a familiar body from the ether, which they keep immortal through their own immortality. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Plato calls this the **chariot** of both gods and souls in the *Phaedrus*, and the **vehicle** in the *Timaeus*. The souls of the spheres and the celestial souls use this vehicle in its purest form; the souls of <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> use it in a less pure form; and our souls also use it in a less pure form because of the mixture of the earthly body. For this reason, Zoroaster gives this instruction:

> Do not defile the spirit, nor deepen the plane. <note>original Greek: "Μὴ πνεῦμα μολύνῃς, μὴ δὲ βαθύνῃς τὸ ἐπίπεδον." From the Chaldean Oracles.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That is: Do not stain the spirit, nor increase the "plane" into a "depth." He calls the vehicle itself a "plane spirit," not because it is not a body and lacks depth, but because, due to its extremely thin and shining purity, it is as if it were not a body. He instructs, therefore, that you should not, because of too much affection for the elemental body, force this spirit to become filthy and heavy even after this life through the addition of a superior elemental darkness, which the ancient theologians called the "shadow of the soul." Nor, however, do they want the rational soul to adhere to the nearest vehicle as a part, but rather that the rational soul itself, insofar as it is rational and a companion of the celestial souls, pours out a life-giving act into the vehicle. This we have often called the **idol** of the soul; Plato calls this mortal species of the soul in his book *On the Generation of the World*

<summary>Ficino explains the "vehicle of the soul"—an immortal, ethereal "garment" that acts as a bridge between the spiritual mind and the material body. He synthesizes views from Zoroaster, Aristotle, and Plato to argue that the soul is never truly without a body, even if it is a celestial one.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "vehicle" (vehiculum) or subtle body of the soul. Ficino explores how the soul, though spiritual, interacts with the physical world through an intermediary "image" and various grades of celestial and elemental bodies.</meta>

<page-num>409</page-num>
<header>->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.<-</header>
<sig>Cc 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: alone</meta>

...not because it dies at any time, but because, if the vehicle were withdrawn, it would fall away, as some believe. For just as the moon’s splendor in a cloud produces a paleness from itself, so the soul in the celestial body emits an image <note>Latin: *idolum*; Greek: *eidōlon*. In Platonic thought, this is the "shadow" or lower reflection of the soul that interacts with the senses.</note>, like a comet's tail from a star. This would vanish if that celestial body vanished, just as the paleness is extinguished when the clouds are scattered. Yet because the vehicle is never withdrawn, Zoroaster says:

> Even for the image there is a portion in the place of clear light. <note>Original Greek: *Ἔστι καὶ εἰδώλῳ μερὶς εἰς τόπον ἀμφιφάδοντα.* From the Chaldean Oracles, suggesting that even the soul's lower reflection has a place in the divine realm.</note>

(That is, the image also has a place in the transparent region. This is because it returns to heaven along with the vehicle and the rational soul.) Plotinus, however, thinks that this image itself is simply mortal, even if the vehicle is not withdrawn. Similarly, he says that the sun's light in the air—or rather, present to the air—would not be extinguished even if the air were removed from between them. For it depends on the Sun alone as its perennial activity, and it is not a "passion" <note>An external effect or change suffered by a thing.</note> of the air or a quality proper to the air. Indeed, it is present or absent in a moment, and nothing of it remains in the air once the Sun is removed. Nor is it present only to the air, but similarly to everything transparent, even if the transparent natures are contrary to each other, as if it does not depend on a specific nature of the subject. Nor does it depend in any way on the transparent thing by reason of its being transparent; it is only present to it because it is not hindered from being present, just as it seems hindered from being present to what is opaque. For the Sun always emits this activity; it does not let it go, nor does it send it in. It happens by lot that what receives it—or rather, what *seems* to receive it—is placed beneath it. This activity, in turn, perpetually accompanies the Sun. The same holds true for a face in a mirror and the soul in a body. Thus says Plotinus. 

In this image, they believe there exists a certain irrational and confused fantasy <note>Latin: *phantasia*. In this context, the faculty that processes sensory images without rational judgment.</note>, and furthermore, senses of such a kind that one sees and hears equally through the whole vehicle. Very few men use these senses properly, and rarely. Yet through them, wonderful harmonies of the heavens are often sensed, as well as the voices and bodies of demons <note>Ficino uses "demons" in the Greek sense of *daimones*—spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans.</note>, whenever someone, having left the earthly body for a time, betakes himself into his celestial body. Therefore <term>Tatius</term> <note>Tat, the son of Hermes Trismegistus in the Hermetic texts.</note>, the son of Mercury, when he had been purified by his father's sacred rites and expiations, immediately cried out that he was then translated into an immortal body and beheld and heard wonders. Mercury himself relates that this also happened to him a little earlier during an abstraction of the mind. <term>Olympiodorus</term> the Platonist also reports that <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term> <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> was accustomed in this way to look out from the city of Rome at things happening in Egypt. 

I pass over the fact that many Platonists believe the soul uses three vehicles: the first immaterial and simple, which is celestial; the second material and simple, which is aerial; the third material and composite, which is constituted of the four elements. The first gives an irrational but immortal life; the second an irrational but long-lived life, which survives for a certain time in the simple body after the composite body is dissolved; and the third, finally, a life that is both irrational and destined to be dissolved along with the dissolved body. Furthermore, in the first life shared with the vehicle, the sense is common and impassible <note>Incapable of being changed or harmed by external forces.</note>; in the second, it is passible and common (that is, through the vehicle, the whole sense is equally universal); and finally, in the third, the sense is both divided and passible.

### Chapter V. In what part of heaven souls are created, and from where they descend.

**I**n what part of heaven souls are created—although it is foolish to seek a physical location for those things which are not enclosed by any location, and just as wherever the Sun shines, a ray is sent, so wherever God is present, a soul is sent—nonetheless it is pleasing at times to play poetically with the ancients. Therefore, as Timaeus says, souls are sown by the artisan of the world among different stars, which become the companions of the souls in life. The Platonists want this understood not as individual souls, but as legions of souls governed by individual stars and fates. He adds that God placed the souls on their vehicles and taught them the nature and laws of the universe. 

From what part of heaven do they descend? Especially from <term>Cancer</term>, as the Platonists say; and in turn they believe they ascend through <term>Capricorn</term>, which is opposite to Cancer. Hence they call the former the "Gate of Men" and the latter the "Gate of Gods." No one, however, should be so deceived as to take descent or ascent here according to physical location; but because the Moon, mistress of Cancer, is closest to generation <note>The process of being born into a physical body.</note>, while Saturn, master of Capricorn, is most remote, they say souls descend through Cancer (that is, through the lunar and vegetative instinct) and ascend through Capricorn (that is, through the Saturnian and intellectual instinct). For the ancients call Saturn the "mind," by which...

<vocab>vehiculum: the subtle "chariot" or astral body of the soul; Zoroaster: legendary Persian sage; Plotinus: the third-century founder of Neoplatonism; Tatius: a character in the Hermetic dialogues; Mercurius: Hermes Trismegistus; Olympiodorus: a Neoplatonist commentator; Apollonius Tyaneus: a famous Pythagorean sage; Cancer: the zodiac sign of birth/descent; Capricorn: the zodiac sign of ascent/divinity; Saturn: the planetary intellect.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul, in its descent from the celestial spheres toward the physical body, gathers qualities and "vehicles" (subtle bodies) from the planets. This process explains the diversity of human nature and talent.</meta>

<page-num>406</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...they seek only higher things. Added to this is the fact that the dry power of Capricorn and Saturn, while it contracts and gathers the spirit toward the innermost parts, constantly provokes one to contemplation. The lunar moisture, however, scatters and dilates the spirit, and distracts the soul toward sensible things <note>Saturn, being the furthest planet, represents the highest intellectual withdrawal, while the Moon, being closest to Earth, represents physical sensation and change.</note>. In the descent itself, the soul receives certain supports or incitements to better carry out its activities: from the divinity of Saturn through itself, and from the light of Saturn through the ethereal body and the image <note>Latin: *idolum*. The "shadow" or lower reflection of the soul that bridges the gap between the rational mind and the physical body.</note>. It receives similarly from the divinity and light of Jupiter for the governance of civil life; from Mars for magnanimity <term>magnanimity<gloss>greatness of soul, particularly in showing courage and endurance</gloss></term> in repelling injuries; from the Sun for the clarity of imagination and the senses; from Venus for charity; from Mercury for interpretation and eloquence; and from the Moon for procreation. And although these individual gifts are given as goods, they can nevertheless degenerate into evil when mixed with the earthly nature. 

A descent of this kind can occur almost as suddenly as the descent of rays from the Sun, which, though sent down to earth suddenly, are clothed in various colors during that very fall. However, some think that souls lead a life suited to each sphere for a certain time. For they receive their own vehicles <note>The *vehiculum* is a "spirit-body" or envelope made of celestial ether that the soul wears to interact with the material world.</note> from individual spheres and finally, after many centuries, descend to the elements, leading a demonic life in fire and air, and a human or brutal life on earth. Likewise, they return to the higher realms by similar steps. So they say. As for us, in all things we write, we wish them to be affirmed by us and others only insofar as they seem to agree with the assembly of Christian Theologians.

---

->**When the soul is infused into the body, and where it is led while it lives in the body.**<-
->**Chapter VI.**<-

**W**hen is the soul infused into the body? After the seed in the woman's womb—which had previously flowed from the man's whole body and carried with it the formative power from the man's soul—has been affected by this same power for about forty-five days. During this time, it is changed such that in the first six days it becomes milk, in the following nine blood, in another twelve flesh, and in the remaining eighteen it is fully formed; then the soul is created and infused <note>Ficino follows a traditional Aristotelian/Galenic timeline for embryology, where the physical body is prepared in stages before the rational soul enters.</note>. 

Those who think souls lived before entering the body say they naturally chose a demon <note>Latin: *dæmon*. In the Platonic sense, this is a "genius" or tutelary spirit, not an evil entity.</note> as a guide for life at the very beginning of the descent, before entering the body. Others say that after they began to exercise choice, they secretly chose a demon as a guide for life by the way they chose their character. Often the same demon is chosen by many. For many souls can use one *genius*, that is, one demon as a guide of their natural talent. Those who think they choose beforehand believe they receive these guides primarily from that crowd of demons which is suited to the same star to which the soul was assigned by the Artisan of the World <note>The Demiurge or Creator.</note> himself. For there are as many legions of demons and heroes as there are stars in number. And from such a crowd, a soul is allotted one guide above the others who most agrees with that chosen life and the "figure of the heavens" (the astrological arrangement) which is composed at that very moment of the descent. For these reasons, the greatest difference in human talents and fortunes arises. 

However, those who say souls acquire different geniuses after birth according to the changeability of their character also allow such guides to be changed when character is changed; they seem to attribute more to counsel than to fate or fortune. But however it may be, we need the perpetual protection of divinities. Indeed, since Plato says this in the *Symposium*, *Protagoras*, *Statesman*, and *Critias*, he proves it in the *Laws* as follows: namely, since we dwell among false goods and innumerable evils, from which perpetual deception and disturbance arise. Therefore, like sheep, we always need the wonderful protection of divine shepherds. He adds that since our own vice destroys us, while our own virtue—being small—cannot save us, we can be saved only by the power of superior guardians (of whose power our own virtue is a small image), especially since, as Hermias <note>A Neoplatonist commentator on Plato's *Phaedrus*.</note> says elsewhere in his exposition, malicious demons constantly twist us toward lower things with all their might. But those guardians who choose us are of one kind, and the demons we choose are another.

## Through which part of the body the soul enters, through which it exits, and by which guide it proceeds. Chapter VII.

<margin>In the *Phaedo*</margin>
**T**hrough which part of the body does the soul enter? Through which does it exit? The soul, which is the intermediary of all things, is first infused—by the command of God (who is the center of the universe)—into the central point of the heart (which is the center of the body). From there, it pours itself through all the members of its body, when it joins its <term>vehicle<gloss>Latin: *currum*, literally 'chariot.' In Neoplatonic thought, this is the 'astral body' or subtle envelope that carries the soul between the spiritual and physical worlds</gloss></term> to the natural heat, and through that heat to the <term>spirit<gloss>The 'spiritus' was considered a thin, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the heavy physical flesh</gloss></term> of the body. Through this spirit, it immerses itself in the bodily fluids, and through the fluids, it grafts itself into the limbs. Finally, when these intermediaries are dissolved by disease, the soul immediately collects itself (so to speak) with its vehicle and flows back into the heart, from where it had first flowed out. Once the heat of the heart is extinguished—which was the proper receptacle for that vehicle—it abandons the heart, with its vehicle finally accompanying it. Just as when the eye is closed, the light of the Sun that had flowed into it flows out entirely, with its own heat accompanying it. And, as Plotinus proves, it is not extinguished, but perpetually follows its own Sun. I will set aside for the moment the fact that the <term>genii<gloss>Guardian spirits or personal 'daemons' assigned to each person at birth</gloss></term> and their own spirits lead all exiting souls to the common judge; but once the sentence is passed, the spirits depart first. Violent and evil spirits drag away the wicked souls, while God peacefully leads the good ones. These things are found in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Hæc in Phædone." Referencing Plato’s dialogue on the soul.</note>.

## On the state of the pure soul, especially according to the Platonists. Chapter VIII.

**W**here is the pure soul when it departs from the dead body? Where the pure light of the Sun is when the eye is closed. For it is reflected back into the Sun as light. The ethereal vehicle of the soul is also reflected back into the <term>ether<gloss>The 'fifth element' that makes up the heavens; it is weightless, eternal, and pure</gloss></term>, once the earthly burden has been laid down. The soul, having once been born in the ether, breathes toward the ether, as Pythagoras says—especially if it has conceived in its mind a habit of living and thinking similar to the ethereal minds. For the soul is moved and acts by habit, just as nature acts by forms. This is clearly seen in those who, after they have acquired the habit of an art, operate almost naturally, without deliberation or focused attention (just as nature does). Plato asserts in the *Phaedo* and the *Gorgias* that habits—both of character and of learning, both good and bad—remain in the separated soul. This is proven by the reasoning that habit is converted into nature in such a way that an inclination proceeds from it just as it does from nature; this is most fully realized in souls set apart from this world of change.

But why do the souls of the <term>elements<gloss>The spirits or animating forces of the spheres of Fire, Air, Water, and Earth</gloss></term> and their vehicles not also strive toward a heavenly dwelling? I shall answer according to the opinion of the Platonists rather than my own: the duty assigned to them by God is to remain there forever. Souls yield to the divine will. Their vehicles also yield to the desire of the souls. Those souls do not lose a more excellent duty because of this service. Their vehicles maintain an unimpeded circular motion around their souls. And just as it is natural for the heavens to turn there around their souls, so it is here for these vehicles to turn around theirs. But our soul, having rightly performed the duty enjoined upon it for a time, chooses for itself that region of the ether above all others to which it was assigned at birth. It takes refuge in that star and deity <note>original: "astrum atque numen"</note>, as Plato says, to which it made itself similar while living. But let the Platonists see to these matters. Furthermore, just as on earth the soul proceeds in its consideration from individual things to common natural species, and from species to divine reasons (as if to the causes of natural things), so in heaven it turns itself in reverse: from divine reasons (that is, the Ideas) to natural species perfectly, and from these, in a certain way, to individuals. And whereas here it inspected individuals diligently, there it looks upon them effortlessly. Again, where it saw divine things obscurely, it perceives them there clearly. And what it saw here piece by piece through instruments in an external light, it sees there according to the species, through itself, in an intrinsic light. Indeed, as much as it was formerly turned toward the senses, so much is it then turned toward the mind, in whose eye the divine light shines. Although this light can be called intrinsic to minds, it nevertheless depends and is preserved by God Himself much more than a ray infused into the eye depends on the Sun; it is present, full of forms, just as the light of the Sun is full of colors. It shows the forms themselves and all things through the forms to the minds, insofar as the souls are turned toward Him, pure and burning. He reveals to those who are entirely turned toward Him at least as many species of things as He has created in the world. For it is not fitting to form the mind less than the matter of the world. Nor is it fitting to grant less to the mind than it naturally desires; and it desires to comprehend the order of the universe, by which it is itself comprehended, and which it has sought with long-standing admiration. In this, the soul itself obtains the duty of a certain providence. However, it looks upon individual and lowest things in that light only if it has... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at "siue præte-", likely "siue præterita" (or past things) based on the catchword.</note>

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul enters and exits the body through the heart, mediated by 'spirit' and a 'vehicle.' After death, pure souls return to the ethereal realm and their assigned stars, where they perceive the divine Ideas directly rather than through earthly senses.</summary>

<meta>This page follows Chapter VII of Book XVIII, continuing Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the soul's separation from the body. Having established how the soul exits the heart, Ficino now explains how the disembodied soul views earthly affairs and why its divine perception is clouded while bound to the flesh.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY.

...whether these things were past, present, or future, insofar as they are directed toward them either by a certain providence or by affection. Indeed, just as old men neglect or laugh at the games of children, and philosophers at the pursuits of the common people, and those who are awake at the dreams of those who sleep—unless necessity sometimes demands otherwise—so too, and much more so, do our <term>separated minds<gloss>Latin: *segregatæ mentes*, referring to souls that have departed the physical body</gloss></term> neglect these individual and contingent things. They do so unless a certain providence has been entrusted to them by the Father of all Himself (whose nature is providence itself, whose act is to provide, and whose office is to provide for all). <note>Ficino argues that the afterlife is not a state of total detachment, but one where the soul only cares for Earth when acting as an agent of God’s will.</note> **Plotinus** proves that such souls, according to the opinion of the ancients and by his own reasoning, care for their own people and often benefit the human race publicly through prophecies and other favors. But since their providence agrees with the divine will, they are not touched by any disturbance from our affairs, but govern these things easily and calmly.

But lest anyone should doubt that a separated soul can be raised to such great light—simply because we see it surrounded by such great darkness in the body—the **Platonists** command us to compare the intellect to sight, and the <term>intelligible<gloss>That which can be perceived by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses</gloss></term> to the visible. Sight never fully comprehends the light itself in the Sun, for that light always exceeds the proportion of the eye. Sometimes, hindered by a <term>cataract<gloss>Latin: *cataracta*. In ancient and Renaissance medicine, a cataract was thought to be a film or "suffusion" of fluid blocking the pupil</gloss></term>, it does not even see the light in colors. At other times, clouded by some vapor, whether red or saffron, it judges obscurely and differently than things actually are. At other times, either because of a contraction toward the internal imagination, it does not seem to behold external things; or, because of a distraction toward objects far apart from one another, it barely sees either one. And if it turns a little more attentively to one, it meanwhile turns more slackly or not at all to the other.

Similarly, the human intellect never fully comprehends that immense fullness of divine light overflowing in the absolute nature of God, since that light greatly exceeds the capacity of the mind. Furthermore, it can sometimes clearly perceive that same light of God, either determined in the <term>ideas<gloss>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the divine mind</gloss></term> of created things or already contracted in the angels—namely, when it has been so removed from the contagion of the body as they are. But while it is joined to the <term>elemental body<gloss>The physical body made of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire</gloss></term>, as it is now, its proportion to those things is so hindered by a kind of "cataract" that it cannot at all comprehend those ideal reasons and angelic substances which are separated far from matter. 

Therefore, as often as it thinks out certain of their properties according to its strength, it perceives them so involved in the images of the phantasy—like vapors and mists—that it is forced to see them either very obscurely or differently than they are, because it is joined to the <term>phantasy<gloss>The faculty of the soul that deals with sensory images and mental pictures</gloss></term>. Finally, even if for a little while it can dispel the clouds of the phantasy, nonetheless, because it is contracted to the difficult service of ruling the body and to the continuously impending rush of sensory images, as soon as it is distracted toward the intuition of intelligible things, it barely looks up at the supernal inflows. It almost fails to see them, or (as the Platonists believe) sees them only as if through a sudden flash that quickly vanishes.

For this reason, it should seem a wonder to no one that here we perceive neither the clarity of divine things nor that very sweetness which is tasted there, nor do we ever taste even a little of it ourselves. Indeed, because of <term>formless matter<gloss>Latin: *informem materiam*. In Platonic thought, matter is the chaotic, "ugly" substrate that resists the order and beauty of the mind</gloss></term>—which is most alien both to the mind and to divine things—the mind, not unlike a tongue paralyzed by phlegm, cannot taste the truth and pleasure of divine flavors. But then at last it will receive the healing taste of the nectarean liquor, when it has thoroughly purged away the lethal humors of the **River Lethe** <note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness; souls drink from it to forget their previous lives and divine origins.</note>. Moreover, it must have desired the divine fountain not only with a natural thirst (which is troublesome in itself) but also, by a certain habit of moral and pious thirst, it must have chosen that fountain as the thing to be desired above all others—indeed, as the only thing. 

By what manner of taste it feeds on these flavors, we have discussed elsewhere. This is the point of that Platonic saying in the ***Phaedrus***: that souls which have emerged from the waters of Lethe fly higher. There, they first perform a celestial circuit together with the celestial gods, and then a <term>super-celestial<gloss>Beyond the physical heavens; the realm of pure intellect and God</gloss></term> circuit with the super-celestial beings. This happens in such an order that some souls are moved in a circuit there with some deities, and they repeat circuits of this kind by turns. This means nothing other than that the souls, released from elemental bodies and restored in celestial <term>vehicles<gloss>Latin: *uehiculis*. The "astral body" or subtle envelope that carries the soul through the heavens</gloss></term> to their own proper circular shape, inhabit the celestial region. They then harmonize in a certain government of the world together with the stars and other heavenly inhabitants to whom they are more familiar by nature or habit, and they discourse similarly through the species of things by reason. Again, they suddenly agree with the super-celestial gods (that is, the angels) in the intuition of the ideas themselves, as if in a kind of circuit, and happily perform both tasks together with both groups.

<summary>Ficino explains that the human soul's inability to perceive divine truth while alive is due to the "cataract" of the physical body and the "phlegm" of matter. He describes the soul's eventual return to a celestial state where it regains its circular form and joins the gods and angels in governing the universe and contemplating eternal Ideas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s existence after death. On the previous page, he discussed how the separated soul views earthly matters. Here, he moves into the nature of the soul’s divine nourishment and its ultimate union with God, drawing heavily on the "Golden Age" myths from Plato's Statesman and the concepts of divine love in the Symposium and Phaedrus.</meta>

<page-num>409</page-num>

->ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.<-

[...to per]ceive. He adds that they feed there together with the higher beings on divine nourishments, namely <term>ambrosia<gloss>In Greek mythology, the food of the gods; here, Ficino interprets it as the soul's clear and sweet intuition of truth</gloss></term> and <term>nectar<gloss>The drink of the gods; here representing the soul’s participation in divine providence</gloss></term>. Indeed, he considers ambrosia to be the clear and sweet intuition of truth, while nectar is that excellent and most effortless providence. Here is also revealed that ancient secret celebrated by Plato in the book *On the Kingdom* <note>original: *de Regno*; this refers to Plato's dialogue *The Statesman* (Politikos)</note> above all others: that the current circuit of the world from East to West belongs to <term>Jupiter<gloss>Latin: Iouium. For Ficino, Jupiter represents the "World Soul" that governs the visible, physical order of the universe</gloss></term> and is governed by fate. However, there will eventually be another circuit opposite to this one under <term>Saturn<gloss>Representing the higher, intellectual realm of the angels</gloss></term>, moving from West back to East, in which men will be born spontaneously and proceed from old age back into youth; nourishments will be supplied to them freely and according to their wishes under an eternal spring.

They call Jupiter (as I believe) the "Soul of the World," by whose fatal law this manifest order of the visible world is arranged. Furthermore, he maintains that the life of souls in elemental bodies is "Jovian," dedicated as it is to the senses and to action. But Saturn represents the supreme intellect among the angels, by whose rays the souls are illuminated beyond the angelic level, set on fire, and continually raised according to their strength toward the intellectual life. Whenever souls turn toward a life of this kind, they are said to live under the "reign of Saturn" insofar as they live by the intelligence. Consequently, in that life they are said to be "born again" spontaneously because they are reformed into something better by their own choice. Again, they are said to grow young day by day—that is, day by day (if days can even be counted there) they flourish more and more. Hence that saying of the **Apostle Paul**: *The inner man is renewed day by day.* <note>2 Corinthians 4:16</note> Finally, nourishments are supplied to them in abundance under a perpetual spring because they enjoy the marvelous spectacles of truth itself, not through the senses or laborious study, but through an internal light and with the greatest tranquility and pleasure of life. The "scent" of such a life is sensed by the mind when it is separated as much as possible, but its "flavor" is tasted only when the mind is profoundly separated from the body.

He adds to these points in the *Symposium* that purified souls, which have loved divine beauty above all else, finally immerse themselves entirely into the very ocean of divine beauty; there, they do not merely drink the divine liquids but now pour them out from themselves onto others. He concludes the height of happiness in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato, though modern scholars often attribute it to his pupil Philip of Opus</note>, where he says that the most purified soul—once its mutability is steadied and its multiplicity gathered—betakes itself entirely into its own unity through a higher intellect. Through this, it is transferred into a divine unity superior to the <term>intelligible world<gloss>The realm of pure ideas and forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</gloss></term>, living for God rather than for itself, to whom it is certainly joined by a marvelous reason that transcends the intellect.

Plato maintains that this is not yet achieved except by a certain divine light, which does not shine in the mind in any other way than if it is transformed into God, having been completely set on fire by the love of God. This is why in the *Phaedrus*, he placed divine love far above all degrees of <term>divine madness<gloss>Latin: *divini furoris*; the four types of inspired "frenzy" (poetic, telestic/religious, prophetic, and amorous) that Plato believed could elevate the soul</gloss></term> and all goods of the soul. Here, in particular, the Platonic mysteries lie hidden, which I will briefly summarize in the few points that follow.

To be sure, when separated minds first turn toward themselves through a natural ray that is their own, they see a few things—just like animals that see at night—and even those they see as if through a cloud. This is because their own nature represents these things under limited species and formulas of things, almost as if they were without form. But afterward, turning themselves through their own ray into the light common to all species of sublime minds, they now see clearly through that light (as if by the light of day) all things created by the Author of this light himself. Yet they cannot attain the Light itself, which is the origin of this light—which they naturally crave and therefore do not desire in vain—simply by looking up at it. For they cannot entirely penetrate the light that is most intimate to God through the furthest light from God (insofar as it is external), nor can they comprehend the vastness of God with their own extreme narrowness. Indeed, that light, although vast in God, becomes narrow in the minds of men.

However, although they perceive the light only obscurely, by loving it ardently they are meanwhile profoundly set on fire by its heat. Being so ignited—which is the proper nature of love—they are transformed into light. Finally, being strengthened by this, they now obtain through love what they could hardly follow through sight; they now easily become that very light through love, which they previously struggled to pursue with their eyes. So great is the power of love, so great its ease, so great its happiness—or rather (to speak more correctly), so great is the power of the light that is loved. For the mind, by loving the light, does not so much set itself on fire and transfer itself, as it is ignited, transferred, and made to shine by the light itself, which softly allures, powerfully strikes, and deeply penetrates. Since the entire power of perception and enjoyment which is in the external senses is present much more in the imagination, and is again far more powerful in the mind (especially when it is unencumbered), and since the most exact reasons for sensible things and delights are in God, it follows that while the unencumbered mind possesses God, it enjoys the highest and most pure delights of all...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's discussion from Book XVIII of the Platonic Theology. Having previously described how the soul transitions from the physical world, he now details the specific "ranks" or "levels" of the soul's experience of God in the afterlife, blending Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY<-

...of the senses, the soul perceives most fully in its own wonderful way; not only with imaginary delight regarding God, as if by seeing, hearing, and smelling (for these senses alone cannot satisfy it), but it is also soothed by a certain substantial pleasure very similar to taste and touch. I say taste or touch, however, not of some external object as occurs in the physical senses, but of that which penetrates deeply and of being penetrated: penetrated, I say, by the whole and immense good, which brings with it a complete and immense joy.

## Nine levels in the heavenly home.

**T**herefore, nine levels of the blessed are arranged not only among the Christians, but also among the Platonists, both for the angels and for human souls. This is done for the reason (as I believe) that divine contemplation there achieves perfection in nine principal ways. Truly <insert>just as we, with what sagacity we can, hunt for the power, wisdom, and goodness of God from the power, order, and suitability of things, so they in turn recognize these same three things in objects from the divine goodness and wisdom, as if from the final, efficient, and exemplary cause of the universe. This is done in such a way that some consider the divine goodness chiefly in itself, others refer it primarily to things themselves, and others primarily refer things back to the goodness itself as if to their end, yet each individual gazes upon all things.</insert> Thus, therefore, a threefold intuition of divine goodness is fulfilled, through which the first three orders of the blessed are distinguished. In a similar way, power is contemplated in three ways, and wisdom in as many. From this, six additional orders of the blessed are counted. To these nine levels of the fortunate, the eight regions of the heavens and a ninth region devised above the heavens seem to be appropriately suited among the Platonists. Among the <term>Orphics<gloss>Followers of a mystical tradition attributed to the legendary poet Orpheus, which Ficino believed predated and influenced Plato</gloss></term>, however, there are the eight heavens and the ethereal fire beneath the Moon. Among the Christians, there are nine circles beneath the <term>empyrean<gloss>The highest part of heaven, believed in ancient and medieval cosmology to be composed of pure fire or light, serving as the dwelling place of God</gloss></term>. For anyone is carried to that region by a certain similar habit, as if by a natural lightness, to whose angelic inhabitants they made themselves most similar during life. Similarly, Christians also believe that rejected souls are cast down into nine levels of rejected <term>demons<gloss>Fallen spirits or malevolent entities who have turned away from the divine order</gloss></term>, to whom they made themselves similar by their way of living, falling by that very similarity as if by a natural weight. 

But more on these elsewhere. Indeed, that there are nine levels in blessedness is also proven (as I believe) by this reasoning. Surely we fear divine power, we seek wisdom, and we love goodness. Only the love of goodness transforms the soul into God. Therefore, love without inquiry and fear restores the soul to its heavenly home, whereas the opposite does not. But let us now arrange in order the levels themselves by which one ascends into heaven. 

In the first are those who chiefly love goodness, then fear power, and lastly seek wisdom. 
In the second are those who primarily love goodness, but behave equally regarding the remaining two. 
In the third are those who are similarly moved toward the good first, then search out wisdom, and lastly fear power. 
In the fourth are those who behave equally regarding all three. 
In the fifth are those who first love the good, and then greatly fear power. 
In the sixth are those who similarly love the good, but in the following level desire wisdom. 
In the seventh are those who love the good absolutely and simply. 
In the eighth are those whom power moves first, goodness second, and wisdom third. 
In the ninth are those with whom wisdom is primary, goodness second, and power third. 

I believe a mystery of this kind was signified in the Gospel where the divine oracle calls his followers "nine times blessed" <note>original: *nouies beatos*; Ficino is likely interpreting the Beatitudes from the Gospel of Matthew as a nine-fold ladder of merit to match the nine celestial spheres</note>, because by nine levels of merit, with God as guide, the nine heavens are blessedly sought according to the nine orders of contemplation. But behold, now the blessed commemoration of the Holy Gospel seems to warn us that, having dismissed philosophical ambiguities, we should seek blessedness by a shorter path along the way that Christian theologians lead, and Thomas Aquinas first of all, the splendor of Christian Theology.

## On the state of the pure soul, especially according to Christian Theologians.

**A**ny created mind—whether looking into its own essence (which there differs from its "being" and exists in a certain species infinitely distant from God), or into its own proper light, or into any light determined within it—cannot understand the divine substance. Since that substance is infinite, certainly what it is cannot be represented through anything finite. Only through those things which we have said do minds know both that God exists and what...

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.

...is rather what it is not, than what it is, and by what logic either it is referred to other things, or other things are referred to it. Plato proves this in the *Parmenides* <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of "The One" and the many.</note>. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 500 AD) whose "Mystical Theology" heavily influenced Ficino’s ideas on the soul’s ascent to God.</note> confirms the same in his *Mystical Theology*, concluding that minds at the highest level of natural knowledge are joined to God as if to one unknown, like an eye growing dim under the light of the Sun. In such knowledge, however, natural desire is not fulfilled. For whatever is imperfect within a certain species <term>species: here meaning a specific type or category of being or knowledge</term> desires the perfection of that very species. Such knowledge is judged imperfect in the very category of "knowing." For we are accustomed to rest in no mode of knowledge until we have known what the thing itself is according to its substance.

Furthermore, it is natural for reason to engage in a continuous discourse through various reasons until it reaches the supreme reason. Because this supreme reason is infinite, it alone can stop the discourse of reason, which would otherwise wander aimlessly without end. Indeed, the mind always devises something further beyond any finite limit. This is apparent in numbers, lines, shapes, and proportions. Thus, the mind is able to find rest only in the substance of God, which alone is infinite. 

This should be judged to happen because the sharp insight of natural intelligence, as well as the heat of the will, is a kind of ray infused from the divine light itself through its own light; it naturally springs back toward that same light and does not cease to move until it has finally restored itself to its own Sun. Accordingly, the closer something is to its natural end, the more violently it approaches that end. This is manifest in the movements of the elements <note>Ficino refers to the Aristotelian idea that objects accelerate as they approach their "natural place," such as a stone falling faster as it nears the earth.</note>. Truly, minds separated from the body become closer to God through natural knowledge than those joined to it. Therefore, since our minds are not content with the boundaries of their natural knowledge, those separated minds are certainly much less so. 

Because the natural appetite of any species is directed by universal nature and must not be entirely in vain, all minds must be able to see the divine substance, without which they see nothing perfectly. But since they cannot see that substance through any created image, yet they still require a form <term>form: the essential "shaping" principle that allows an intellect to perceive an object</term> through which they may see—a form, I say, proper to the divine substance, by which they may perceive it not through the imagination, but properly—it is necessary for them to be so coupled to the divine substance that they may now look upon it through itself. 

Something similar appears in sight, which perceives colors through their own images under light, but cannot see light through anything else except light itself. But lest anyone think it absurd to join God to the intellect as a form, one must remember that the perfection of the mind consists in the truth. Moreover, the truth, being, and the intelligible are the same thing. Whatever in this very category is composed of essence and being stands as a "being" and "truth" rather than as "being itself" or "truth itself." It cannot be the form of others in the same category, since that form is already contracted in itself to its own matter, as it were. 

Therefore, no created mind can become the form of the remaining minds; rather, God alone stands toward the genus of minds everywhere as the form, He who alone is "being itself" and the simplest truth. I say "as the form" not as a part of a composite thing, but as a principle of operation, by which the mind operates as God rather than as a mind—just as gold set on fire acts as fire rather than as gold, the kind of gold the Apocalypse of John <note>original: "Apocalypsis Ioannis". This refers to Revelation 3:18: "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined in the fire."</note> commands us to buy.

->*How the mind is joined to God.*<-

**F**or the mind to put on the divine substance as a form, however, it is not said to happen by its own power, but it is drawn by divine action. Indeed, an inferior nature cannot attain the property and form of a superior one without the action of that superior nature itself. This is manifest in the elements, in which air does not become fire unless fire is acting upon it. 

Furthermore, nothing can ever be led to a more excellent action unless the power within it is first strengthened. If it is to be led toward a familiar type of action, but one that is more intense, it will certainly be enough if the usual power is simply increased. For example, if air, which naturally heats at one degree, is eventually to heat at two degrees, it is enough to intensify the quality of its natural heat. 

However, if air is to claim for itself an action superior in kind and category—namely, if it is to give light, which is proper to the ethereal body—it must now receive a new form from that ether. To what purpose is this? So that we may understand that the mind cannot be raised to perceive the divine substance through itself merely by an increase of natural power and light, since such an operation differs from the natural operation of the mind by more than...

<summary>Ficino argues that human reason is naturally restless and can only find fulfillment in the infinite substance of God. He concludes that for the mind to truly "see" God, it must be supernaturally transformed by God acting as its "form," similar to how fire transforms gold.</summary>
