<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument in Book XVIII of the Platonic Theology. Following the previous page’s discussion of how the soul finds rest only in the infinite substance of God, Ficino here explains the specific "light" required for this union and addresses the philosophical problem of how a finite mind can relate to an infinite Creator.</meta>

...differs in kind, but requires a certain new power and a new light, descending from a higher principle. Indeed, they call this the **light of grace and glory**, by which the mind is illuminated, and much more, set on fire; it is then clothed in the divine substance—whose heat it now feels—like a flame. I say a flame, not such as the dry vapor lifted from the earth in a "hairy star" <note>original: "crinita stella." This refers to a comet, which was historically thought to be an atmospheric phenomenon of burning vapor.</note> as it nears the sphere of fire, though that might seem a very similar thing; rather, it is a super-celestial flame, shining healthfully and not burning. 

Someone might perhaps deny that the mind can be led to see God through any light at all. Their argument might be that if there is no proportion between sight and sound, then surely there is no proportion between the mind (or the light received by the mind, which is finite) and the immense God. We, however, shall respond that although God exceeds the faculty of the intellect, He is not as "alien" to the intellect as sound is to sight, or as something insensible is to the senses. This is because, as is pleasing to Christian theologians, God is the **first intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibile primum." The primary object that can be understood by a mind, acting as the very source of truth.</note>, and the beginning, middle, and end of all intellectual power and action. There is, therefore, a certain proportion between the intellect and God—not because there is any measurement between them, but rather a certain relationship, like that of "intellectual matter" to an "intelligible form," or an effect to its cause. 

Furthermore, even if that infused light becomes finite within the mind, it is nonetheless infused by God endowed with the power to couple the mind to the divine substance—not by a natural bond, but rather by an intellectual one. A natural ray of light cannot accomplish this, because from the start it has passed entirely into the nature of the receiver (which was previously formless in itself), and thus the ray itself becomes dim and weak. Nor can the mind, since it falls far short of divine simplicity, obtain its full perfection through that same natural ray. Therefore, the natural ray in the mind is one thing (through which it understands a few things according to its own species), but the divinely infused light is another. By the lifting power of this infused light, the mind is wonderfully elevated to a most eminent degree above itself—further than can even be imagined. 

Finally, the infinity of God does not signify a "privation of form" (the kind of infinity that belongs to matter, which, because it is ineffective and formless, is rightly judged unfit for knowledge); rather, it signifies **absolute excellence**, contracted by no subject at all. This "Sun" <note>Ficino often uses the Sun as a metaphor for God, following the Platonic tradition.</note> has this nature: by shining and illuminating in a wondrous way, it can move the intellectual sight most of all and be seen; and by the same power by which it exceeds the mind, it can elevate that same mind above its own natural strength. 

However, one must not think that the mind, though it understands what the divine essence is, actually **comprehends** <term>comprehend: here used in the technical sense of "to fully encompass or contain."</term> it. For the mind's power is limited, and the light within it is determined; when it enters the divine essence, it is not formed by the *entire* power of the divinity. What then? Does it see one part of the divine substance while not seeing another? Certainly, we must not say so, since God cannot be divided. Rather, we must believe that the mind looks upon God but does not fully "comprehend" Him—that is, it does not perceive God with as many reasons, or with as much certainty and perfection, as God is perceived by Himself. Added to this is the fact that it cannot see all that God sees and can do simply by seeing God. For God sees and can do infinite things beyond those that exist in nature (which we have proved elsewhere). If the mind does not encompass God's substance, it certainly does not encompass His intelligence and power. Therefore, it does not see everything that God understands and can do. Otherwise, since power is usually measured by what it can do, if the mind saw everything God can do, it would fully comprehend Him; it would equally encompass the power and substance of His living and acting. What more? The higher an intellect is, the more things (either in number or by reason) it ought to understand. From this it follows that the divine mind, gazing upon itself from every side, sees more things and through more reasons than any other intellect could see.

### All species of minds can be joined to God.

**N**o one should lose hope that human minds—even though they are the lowest in the category of minds—can be led to the contemplation of the divine substance itself. For even the angelic minds do not arrive there by some natural power, but are rather drawn by a divine and (so to speak) **supernatural** power. Now, a work that is performed by supernatural power cannot be hindered by a difference in nature, since nothing anywhere resists the immense power of God. Just as easily...

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.

The divine power moves the whole mechanism <note>original: "machinam." Ficino uses this term to describe the organized structure of the universe as a grand machine or work of art.</note> as easily as it moves the smallest part of the world. It heals a person who is seriously ill as easily as one who is only slightly sick. For this reason, by the same divinely infused power that the highest minds are raised, the lowest minds are also snatched up to the heights. Furthermore, God stands at an immense distance above all created minds; but the lowest mind differs from the highest by a finite interval, since both are finite. And it is judged that there is no proportion between this finite interval and that infinite one. 

But if adding something finite to the infinite brings no change (as it seems), what prevents God’s own power—which instantly traverses the immense space to the angel—from then embracing the tiny gap between the angel and the soul, so that both soul and angel are snatched up together? Finally, if the class of minds, by their very nature as minds, has a natural instinct to see the highest <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibile." This refers to anything that can be grasped by the intellect rather than the senses—specifically, the ultimate Truth or God.</note> clearly—which is what they search for in every act of seeking and desire in every act of wanting—it follows that such an instinct is as natural to the lowest minds as it is to the highest, and that the former may eventually reach their naturally desired goal just as the latter do. 

This natural desire itself shows us this, for since it draws us toward the infinite, it cannot be implanted, moved, or finally satisfied by anything other than the infinite itself. If the lower things moved by nature are not moved in vain, much less so are those led by the supreme power. The ray of this power, passing through all the orders of minds, both illuminates each so they may see and inflames them so they may love. Since fire and the Sun usually spread light further than heat, it is reasonable that wherever the ray of the divine Sun reaches to warm, it can reach even further to illuminate. Therefore, just as human minds, set on fire from there, daily desire the divine Good, so too, once illuminated, they will one day behold the divine Truth there, and by beholding it, they will happily enjoy the true Good.

->Different degrees in the heavenly home, and that all see all created things.<-

**P**ossunt <note>This "P" marks a decorative initial in the original text.</note> however, some minds can gaze upon the divine substance more clearly and fully than others, to the extent that they are prepared—like a transparent material for that light—under different degrees of perfection, whether they are prepared differently because of their nature or because of a diversity of acquired disposition. But the greatest variety in our minds arises from different degrees of love. To these degrees of love, different levels of vision and, much more, levels of joy appropriately correspond. 

Perhaps, although each mind sees all created things, as we shall prove, some nevertheless touch upon more than others among those things which are not created, and they grasp what they see through more numerous reasons; yet all see with a true understanding. And since joy corresponds to love as its goal, those who have loved more ardently are carried more closely (as is the way of love) and, clinging more deeply, are transformed into the Good, thus enjoying it more sweetly through the very habit of love. 

Therefore, if the goal of minds is to reach the divine substance, necessarily every desire of the minds is completely fulfilled there as in its goal. It would not be fulfilled, however, unless they grasped the entire order of the created universe from every side. Indeed, the usual study of the intellect is such that it resolves particulars into universals, all the way to the most common thing, and describes Being itself in an absolute sense, dividing it most distinctly through all its degrees, as if it were born for this purpose: to one day be shaped by the form of the universe. What prevents the intellect, while it beholds the source of the universe, from seeing the universe flowing out from it? Especially since the intellect is not hindered from other things by the highest object of thought (as the senses are temporarily hindered from feeling smaller things after experiencing an intense sensation), but rather is marvelously strengthened. 

Furthermore, the category of things that can be understood is broader than the category of things that exist in nature. For many things can be understood beyond those which nature makes. Therefore, whatever things are necessarily required to complete <term>natural being</term> <note>original: "esse naturale." The physical existence of things in the world.</note>, even more and many more things are required to complete <term>intellectual being</term> <note>original: "esse intelligibile." The existence of things as they are understood in the mind.</note>. But intellectual being is finally perfect only when the intellect has reached its highest goal, just as the perfection of natural being consists in the very constitution of all things. Therefore, whatever God has produced for the perfection of the universe, He also produces within the intellect joined to Him. Again, although one may see God more perfectly than another, each sees Him in such a way that their natural capacity is filled to their heart's desire. This capacity in any mind extends to all types and species of the universe, and moreover, to the individual things found everywhere within those species.

<summary>Ficino explains that the human mind is naturally drawn toward the infinite God and that this desire is not in vain, as God's power bridges the gap to elevate the soul. He describes the state of the soul in heaven, where different souls experience degrees of joy based on their love, yet all find total fulfillment by perceiving the entire universe within the divine source.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON PLATONIC THEOLOGY

Nor do we desire anything beyond this. Therefore, minds in God also discern individual things distinctly. Certainly, since a higher power can do whatever a lower power can—and even more excellently—and since souls joined to bodies know both universals <note>General concepts, like the idea of "humanity."</note> and individuals, it is consistent that minds joined to Truth itself <note>God.</note> should comprehend both through a single power and a single gaze. This is especially true since the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species." In this context, these are the divine "blueprints" or "Ideas" of things existing in the mind of God.</note> of things within them are most vast, and those minds attain a most effective power there, through which they derive the general categories and specific forms down to individual things. Truly, the forms of things reach the intellect in a certain order when it is joined to the body, and a different order when it is separate. In the body, the mind works by a kind of "resolution," separating the individual from the conditions of matter; but there, in the divine state, it works from a certain conjunction of the mind with the divine Form, which is the maker of all things and the judge of individuals. This Form is not something abstracted from individuals, but is the creator of every individual thing everywhere: not only of their form, but also of their matter, in which the origin of a thing’s individuality resides. For this reason, the forms flowing into the mind from that source represent not only common traits but also individual ones to the joined minds. This is further confirmed by the fact that if angelic minds move the celestial bodies through their intellect, they must necessarily not be ignorant of the very thing they move, nor of the positions which are changed by that motion. Our own minds can be led to the same kind of knowledge as the angels—especially regarding motion—particularly if they attain some office of governance there.

->The state of the soul with God is immobile.<-

**S**ince minds there see the forms of created things within the unique Form of God, it is consistent that they see all things with a single vision. If this vision is most perfect, it is possessed in a state of stability rather than sought through a succession of thoughts. For it is probable that minds, which desire rest rather than motion, will rest firmly once they have attained their goal—especially because if they know all the species of the universe there, and since countless individuals proceed under certain categories (whether by number, figure, or proportion), it seems to follow that they see species that are, in a way, infinite. But since it is not possible to travel through the infinite, they do not count them by passing from one to the next, but behold them while remaining still. Again, if the perpetual act of understanding is the very life of the one who understands, and if that understanding becomes a participant in eternity because of its stability, it follows that the blessed mind may rightly be said to have been translated into eternal life. And rightly so. Indeed, the human mind is placed in the middle, between eternal and temporal things. Therefore, just as its operation is accustomed to becoming temporal when it is joined to temporal things, so it becomes eternal when joined to eternal things. Finally, I do not see how that vision could be subject to change or movement, for there the power of seeing transcends time from the very start, and the object which is seen, as well as the form by which it is seen, is stability itself and eternity itself. From this it follows that souls, once they have cleared the path to God, will never depart from Him, provided they have now transcended motion and fulfilled their natural desire. Since this desire is founded on a stable substance and is naturally directed toward a stable object, it surely seeks no other end than a final, stable possession. Is it any wonder if the everlasting mind desires that which it wants—not for the sake of something else, but for its own sake—as something to be held forever? Furthermore, where a mind is not ignorant of any natural things beneath itself, it certainly is not unaware of what kind of possession it holds. Therefore, if it were going to lose it, it would foresee that loss and live unhappily, thinking that it would eventually—even soon—be deprived of such a dear possession. Add to this that whatever naturally adheres to an end is never torn away from it except by some external force. Since, therefore, the mind is naturally joined to God as the end most desired above all others, and the efficient cause of this union is God Himself, and no greater opposing force can occur to violently separate what God has freely joined, the mind is undoubtedly compelled by no one ever to depart from that place. Moreover, one cannot imagine how it would turn itself away, either from certain truth through a fallacy, or from the pure and total Good through its own will. Certainly, neither the substance of the mind is changed, nor does its clarity of understanding fail under a light that continually strengthens it; nor is the light ever withdrawn, which is poured from eternity into eternity; nor does the will ever withdraw from the possession of the Whole, whether due to the prodding of another or because of boredom with the company of that Object which, since it cannot be fully exhausted, is doubtless...

He concludes that once the soul is united with God, it enters a state of eternal rest and can never be separated from this ultimate happiness.</summary>

...and it always occurs as something new, and with the highest admiration; therefore, it is possessed with continuous desire. Finally, if something becomes more immobile the closer it is to the highest state of God, it is necessary that minds already formed by divine substance should emerge as entirely immobile.

->Each person satisfied in God.<-

HERE truly, individuals achieve whatever they seek. Philosophers, who are so studious of truth, here perceive all true things within Truth itself, the mother of all truths <note>original: "veritate veritatum procreatrice." Ficino refers to God as the source from which all specific truths are born.</note>. Here, civic-minded men devoted to governance and power become the most powerful governors alongside the omnipotent Governor of the world. Here, those greedy for victory and glory have now conquered all adversity. They know all things, and they are known by all the blessed. Here, the spectators of pleasures, if only they reach this place, shall enjoy total pleasure within the very cause of pleasures. For just as bodies are shadows of divine things, so too the delights of the senses are shadows of divine joy. For the mind is far more effective than the sense, and the true and total Good is more powerful—beyond what can be thought—and sweeter than any false good. Furthermore, the intellect is accustomed to penetrating its object from every side, since it distinguishes internal things from external, and what is its own from what belongs to another—something the senses never achieve. Likewise, because of the marvelous purity and power of the intellect, the <term>intelligible</term> <note>Something that can be understood by the mind alone, as opposed to something felt by the physical senses.</note> flows entirely into its innermost depths, which a <term>sensible</term> <note>Something perceptible by the physical senses.</note> thing cannot do for the sense. For this reason, the pleasure of the pure intellect regarding the highest intelligible is not only continuous and pure—unlike the senses—but also intimate and whole, and is grasped entirely at once. It surpasses the pleasure of the senses much more than the sweetness of flavors surpasses the empty allure of smells. We are usually flooded with pleasure when we are restored to our proper state, in whatever way that may happen. Truly, no greater restoration can be imagined than when the soul, which had degenerated from the <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic thought, the "Idea" is the perfect, divine blueprint of a thing. Here, it refers to the soul returning to its original, perfect form in God.</note>—indeed, from itself—is restored from every side to its own Idea, and thus to itself. There, it rejoices again in the very Idea of joy, and in one Good, it enjoys all goods. And since those things we desire delight us, yet we desire all things because they are good, we are there flooded with the highest pleasure; for since every good is there, we perfectly achieve whatever can be desired. However, different minds enjoy every good according to the essence of the Good primarily, but they enjoy the degrees of good according to various specific Ideas, insofar as they love different degrees of the total Good from the beginning and travel to that Good by various paths. Finally, to put it briefly, there is one thing altogether which all the blessed enjoy, although some enjoy it in different ways and reasons than others, as each person's own pleasure draws them, whether from their disposition or from the object's particular allure. Thus, as **Plato** says, all envy is absent from the divine chorus. For common charity in that chorus ensures that individuals congratulate each other on their happiness as if it were their own. Furthermore, where everyone achieves their wish—both what they loved, and by the means they especially chose, and as far as they desired—there everyone lives entirely content and full, without envy and far from its sting. For there, both natural and acquired capacity is completely filled, nor is a greater capacity desired by anyone. For his own things are naturally most dear to each. To this is added that nothing is more pleasing to the blessed, who burn with entirely divine love, than to will that very thing which they know God wills; and thus, to possess the beloved God in the measure they receive Him, by the reason they receive Him, and in the manner God exhibits Himself. And indeed, they know that their Good cannot be entirely comprehended there, and they are wonderfully delighted by this very fact, choosing that their treasure be infinite rather than finite.

### On the bodies of the blessed. Cap. IX.

A twofold happiness belongs to the pure soul: one from itself, which we have discussed, and another from the body, which among the **Platonists** is of this kind. It is better to think of this by a certain example. Your eye is indeed round, transparent, bright, very swift in motion, and it sees my eye with marvelous clarity; it perceives itself and its own state within mine; it shapes each of your soul's affections within itself and carries them over into mine, and in turn receives my affections through mine. Such are those "chariots" <note>A reference to the "chariot of the soul" from Plato's *Phaedrus*, here adapted to mean the celestial body or vehicle the soul inhabits.</note> of the souls, both within themselves and towards each other.

For each of them is entirely an eye, and behaves in almost all respects as we see eyes themselves behave. Therefore, they are like certain round eyes, transparent, brilliant, and swift in motion, surveying everything on all sides with total ease. They display the affections and thoughts of their own minds, and indicate them to other minds with a kind of nod, as it were, most easily. They also receive from others, in a similar way, indications of the feelings and thoughts of others. Not only do they see from all directions, at a great distance and most sharply, but they also hear. Similarly, all the stars and <term>demons</term><note>In the Platonic sense, "demons" (*daemones*) are not evil spirits but intermediary beings or guardian spirits between gods and humans.</note> easily form voices; and just as there are senses there without any suffering, so there are also voices, though of a different species and kind than ours. These are the views of Plotinus and Hermias <note>Hermias was a 5th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Plato's *Phaedrus*.</note>. Avicenna confirms this Platonic opinion in his *Metaphysics*, proving that the soul, when separated from the contagion of the body, exercises the function of imagination in heaven through a certain celestial instrument—as if received from the body of heaven itself—and through it. For he wishes (following Plato’s opinion) for the intellectual soul to preside over the entire mass of bodies by natural dignity and command. Finally, those chariots <note>Refers to the *ochema*, the "astral vehicle" or "spirit-chariot" the soul inhabits as it descends through the spheres.</note>, filled with the overflowing brilliance of their minds, shine wonderfully, and through them—as if by certain rays—the entire heaven is traversable. And as it pleases many Platonists, they sparkle especially in the Milky Way, no differently than the stars. Hence the ancient poets used to say that when happy souls flew back to the inhabitants above, new stars shone in heaven. But let them look to those matters. Added to this is what the followers of Zoroaster, Pythagoras, and Plato—especially Plotinus and Proclus—dispute: that when the same causes eventually return in their entirety, the exact same men will return. And Plato, in the book *On Kingship* <note>original: "de Regno." This refers to Plato's dialogue *The Statesman* (Politicus), where he discusses the cosmic cycles of the world.</note>, writes that after the present and fated course of the world, God will command and awaken the souls of men to receive again their bodies which they lost in this current cycle. Thus, just as under Fate human bodies once fell into the earth, so under the command of divine Providence they shall rise again from the earth and come back to life. These mysteries of the ancient philosophers do not differ much from the mysteries of the Hebrews and Christians, which are also confirmed by the followers of Muhammad. For the common opinion among these three Laws <note>The "three laws" refers to the three great monotheistic religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.</note> is that motion itself cannot truly be an end, because it always flows from one thing into another. This very thing—to tend toward something else—is utterly foreign to the nature of an end, especially the ultimate end. Therefore, the highest and last end of the universe, which the world must eventually attain (since even individual things smaller than the world eventually attain their own end), will not be motion, but a state of rest. For rest is more perfect than motion, and all things move for the sake of rest. Furthermore, the body of the world in that state, being most perfected, will be most beautiful. When the course of heaven is finally finished, by which all things are generated, nothing further will be generated; instead, they confirm first by divine authority the resurrection from the earth of the individual bodies of men, for whose sake all things were previously generated, at God's command. For they say God often predicted this through the Prophets and Apostles, and raised many dead people across various ages. Furthermore, they say that holy men, even after they have departed this life, have performed miracles and do so daily. I omit the rest, for they are innumerable. Certainly, in our own time, in the month of December 1477 and January 1478, certain relics of the Apostle Peter found in the city of Volterra displayed twelve miracles—and massive ones at that, manifest to all the people. These and similar things are the most powerful proofs of the resurrection, so much so that Avicenna asserts in his *Metaphysics* that one must believe the authority of the divine person asserting the resurrection. Although Avicenna does not attempt to bring any reason for such a great matter, Christian theologians persuade us by reasons of this kind. The first reason: because a single natural compound is made from the human soul and body, and the soul is drawn to the body by natural instinct. Therefore, it is clear that the soul is coupled to the body not only from the order of the universe, but also according to the order of its own nature; from which it follows that it is contrary to the order of both the universal and its own nature for the soul to remain apart from the body. However, they remain eternal after the destruction of the body. And since that which is against nature cannot be eternal, it follows that souls will eventually receive their bodies back.

The second reason: Individual souls are naturally inclined toward vivifying and ruling individual bodies. For so both nature and the providence of a life placed between eternity and time dictate—having an inclination partly toward eternal things and partly a natural one toward temporal things. But a natural inclination remains as long as nature remains. For this reason, souls separated from bodies will always be naturally inclined toward them. Moreover, a natural inclination...

Here, he provides specific "ratios" or logical arguments for why the soul must eventually be reunited with its body to achieve perfection and justice.</meta>

<page-num>417</page-num>

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.

<margin>Dd</margin>

...and [the soul's] inclination ought not to be always in vain. For that is most foreign to the order of the universe. Therefore, souls will eventually receive their own bodies, for which they always have a natural affection.

**Third Reason.** The soul is one part of the human species, and the body is the other. Therefore, separated from the body, in the state that it is a soul, it is imperfect, just as a part usually is when outside the whole for which it was established to constitute. For this reason, its natural appetite will never be at rest. No soul will ever be blessed unless it is returned to its whole by the resumption of the body, or at least hopes to be returned.

**Fourth Reason.** Worthy rewards are owed to virtues, and punishments to vices. Since these are not granted in this life, they are granted in the other. However, the body is a participant along with the soul in both virtues and vices. Therefore, so that it may likewise be a participant in rewards or punishments, it is finally restored to the soul. Nor should it seem absurd that souls, after they have departed from their natural state, should return to the same once more. Since planets both leave and seek again their natural domiciles. Particles of the elements, too, are often driven out of their proper site and separated for a long time, meanwhile they move continuously toward it on account of it, and finally return. Nor is it difficult for the infinite power of God, present everywhere, who created the whole from nothing, eventually to bind back together bodies dissolved into the elements, from the elements restoring them in turn. Indeed, the same body will be woven back together because there will be the same <term>form</term><note>In Platonic and Aristotelian thought, the "form" is the organizing principle of a thing; for a human, the soul is the "form" of the body.</note>, which was once that very soul, and also the same eternal first matter, which underlies all things. Finally, the same indeterminate dimension, the companion of matter, [will be there]. Furthermore, in this life any person is said to have the same body from childhood to old age, even though it flows out and flows back in continually. 

But the body will rise again entirely immortal. For from the beginning God so tempered the order of things that for the rational soul, which is eternal life and the natural form of the body, its own matter—that is, the body—should agree in this very thing: so that through the soul itself, always living and naturally desiring always to give life, the body itself might likewise be able to live always. A power of this kind is a certain good most consistent with the order of the universe. Therefore, when God who created from the beginning, and created such a thing that it could live always, when, I say, He shall <term>recreate</term><note>Ficino uses "recreate" (recreabit) to refer to the Resurrection.</note> it, He will undoubtedly fulfill what is most fitting, lest a power so good, as it is consistent with the universe, should always be in vain. Moreover, that creation made through God, once the motion of the world ceases (which was finally established for the sake of some peaceful perfection), will be directed toward something purely stable. Thus, the body will remain always joined to the soul. 

Again: the intention of nature in generating aims at least for the perpetuity of the species, and it has obtained this from God himself, in whom the first root of perpetuity flourishes. Wherefore the intention of God in <term>regenerating</term><note>original: "regenerando," here meaning the act of bringing to life again at the Resurrection.</note> is directed toward something perpetual much more than nature is. Therefore He will recreate man as incorruptible, not in species only (for that could be sufficiently fulfilled through customary generation), but also eternal in <term>number</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "in number" (numero) means the specific, numerical identity of an individual person, not just the "human type."</note>. Not according to the soul alone (for it had this previously), but also according to the body. Added to this is the fact that in daily generation the soul comes to a body already made, but in that regeneration, on the contrary, the body comes to the soul. Wherefore, just as the present life of the composite human follows the condition of the falling body, so that future life of the composite will in turn follow the condition of the immortal soul, so that deprivation may finally cease in a state of being, at least according to the most perfect species of natural things. And death, as if most weak, as the Prophets say, is swallowed up by life. 

Likewise, bodies rise again for this reason: so that rewards and punishments may be paid in perpetuity to bodies that have so deserved them. Therefore they will rise as eternal. Add that they are also raised up so that souls do not remain always imperfect. Since, therefore, the perfection of the soul itself is most especially consulted in this matter, such a body will be restored as fits the soul. To an eternal soul, an eternal body is fitting, such as sacred scriptures testify was granted from the very beginning of things. Which gift, though interrupted for a time by a certain disordered motion, will finally be restored by God ordering the universe as it is best. 

But that the state of the natural man was such from the beginning is shown from this: that by as much as man is more perfect than the brutes, by so much he ought to be able to attain his end more easily, more perfectly, and more often than they do theirs. But in the present state, the opposite happens. From which it is clear that men, precisely because they have departed from their first temperament, struggle toward their happiness with the greatest difficulty, and will only most easily attain it then, when they have been restored to their former state. Which opinion indeed seems most of all consistent with the mysteries of **Zoroaster, Mercury, and Plato**, and with the poets singing of the **Golden Age**. But let us now return to the resurrection. Finally, the immense power of God, effecting...

<summary>Ficino argues for the necessity of the resurrection of the body, asserting that the soul is naturally imperfect without its physical counterpart and that justice requires the body to share in the soul's eternal rewards or punishments. He reconciles this Christian doctrine with the ancient traditions of Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, and Plato, viewing the resurrection as a return to man's original, perfect state.</summary>

Ficino is concluding his philosophical arguments for the resurrection of the body, specifically how the soul's immortality eventually necessitates the eternal life of the body it inhabits. <page-num>418</page-num>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>

...is the cause of resurrection. Therefore, by the same infinity of life by which He raises the dead, He most appropriately preserves them free from death forever. For so great a miracle of coming back to life seems fitting only for a life that is eternal hereafter. In this matter, Almighty God renders bodies so entirely subject to the rule of their souls that the eternal life of the soul also overflows eternally into the body. This indeed naturally suits the most excellent form <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, the "form" is the organizing principle of a thing; here, the soul is the "form" of the body.</note> in relation to the matter subjected to it, and is most consistent with the order of nature. 

Furthermore, according to the order of merits—as the Theologians teach—this is also greatly fitting: that bodies should be thoroughly joined to the souls of men (which are themselves forms of life) not only in terms of life, but for pure souls, also in terms of qualities and actions, just as those souls are joined to God. Thus, the intellect, full of divine light, and the will, filled from there with incomparable joy and efficacy, completely transfer their splendor and efficacy to the body, moving it in a marvelous way. Just as those souls are raised to the clarity and virtue of celestial minds, so too are the bodies raised to the clarity and virtue of the celestial bodies. 

Nor should it seem strange to see the human body—which by nature is not unlike heaven due to its temperament—suddenly elevated entirely to the celestial region when it assumes a certain celestial form by a gift [of God], drawn, of course, by the soul. This soul is supported by the infinite virtue of God; while on earth and separated from God, it holds together, sustains, and raises the body against the nature of its elements, and then, joined to the super-celestial God, it can also raise the ethereal region up to the heights with it. Nor does that purest body—having now been made ethereal in virtue and quality—either strike the ether or be struck by it through penetration.

## The State of the Impure Soul. Chapter X.

**To** understand the state of the impure soul after death, we must observe the character and habits of the living. For as the character is in youth, so for the most part are the habits in old age, and such are also the dispositions of the dead. In the present life, virtue and vice are born. With virtue arises a reward; with vice, a punishment. In the future life, virtue and vice are perfected. There, reward and punishment are fulfilled. Virtue is the reward beginning; reward is virtue matured. Vice is punishment being born; punishment is vice completed. For the seed and the harvest are the same thing; so too the harvest and the fodder. Therefore, what we sow in this autumn, we shall reap in that summer. We shall be fed either in the Stygian marsh <note>The Styx, a river in the Greek underworld; Ficino uses this to represent a state of misery or Hell.</note> during the dark night, or we shall eat in the Elysian fields <note>The final resting place of the virtuous in Greek mythology; here representing Paradise.</note> on a serene day. 

Just as nature, the servant of divine providence, moves bodies internally upward by lightness and downward by heaviness, so providence leads all things by an internal law and a similar natural inclination. By this law, the higher minds and souls, which are implanted within them, govern the universe under the first governor. By this same implanted law, human minds lead themselves to the places appropriate to their life. And just as the humors in an animal have two principles of motion—namely, the natural and the animal—by the natural, light things often move upward and heavy things downward, but by the animal, they move especially toward those members that need them most, as the life of the living being requires; so souls possess two principles of motion within: one is their own impulse or judgment, the other is the law of divine providence entirely implanted in their innermost parts. 

By the former <note>free will and choice</note>, they move themselves into these or those habits; by the latter—once those habits are contracted—they are led by a certain internal and hidden inclination to the places, punishments, or rewards fitting for those habits. Plato most frequently approves this opinion received from the ancients. All the Platonists <note>The school of philosophers following Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists who sought to harmonize Plato with religious truth.</note> confirm this everywhere. Some, however, distinguish that law—which is always good and divine in itself—by calling it "grace" and a "good <term>daemon <note>A 'daemon' in the Greek sense is a guiding spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil 'demon' in the modern sense.</note></term>" when it returns good things for good merits. On the other hand, they sometimes call it "Nemesis" <note>The Greek goddess of divine retribution.</note> and "Fury" and an "evil demon" when it leads sinners to punishment. That law leads from within in the manner of nature, and so gently that no one feels violence from providence until they reach the end. Meanwhile, the universe, which would very often be discordant due to the first principle of the soul's motion <note>i.e., the erratic choices of human will</note>, is restored to its harmony everywhere through this second principle of motion <note>i.e., the divine law of cause and effect</note>, while each individual gradually obtains their merits by their own movement. Furthermore, we do not lack good spirits to help us, who are called "genii" <note>Guardian spirits assigned to a person's character or 'genius'.</note>, the constant leaders of our innate character <note>original: "ingenij duces"</note>, who lead not by force, but by persuasion.

<summary>Ficino explains how the soul's eternal nature eventually transforms the body into an ethereal state and discusses how the soul’s habits in life naturally lead it to its appropriate place of reward or punishment after death through a "law of providence."</summary>

Having previously discussed the physical resurrection and the soul's influence on the body, Ficino now transitions into the moral and metaphysical consequences of the soul's character. He explores how the soul's internal state determines its fate after death, drawing heavily from Plato's dialogues and the Hermetic tradition.</meta>

<page-num>419</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.</header>

There are also evil beings—not as naturally ordained leaders, but as foreign adversaries (so to speak)—whom the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who in the Renaissance often integrated these ideas with Christian theology.</note> believe can be driven away in this life through philosophy and sacred rites. But both Plato and Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage believed to be a contemporary of Moses.</note> say that after this life, wicked souls, having changed their guiding spirit <note>original: "genio." The 'genius' was a personal guardian spirit or daimon assigned to each soul at birth.</note>, fall into the power of an evil demon; specifically after they have been led by their own spirit to a judge who cannot be deceived. This is especially true since all things become visible in separated souls—both those things which were there by nature and those which arose from their passions. Hence, Socrates says in the *Gorgias*: "Leaving all other things aside, I consider how I may show the judge a soul that is as healthy as possible. For the greatest of all evils is to descend to the underworld with a soul stuffed full of sins." He adds both there and in the *Theaetetus* and the *Republic* that these things should not be mocked as if they were mere fables. Indeed, whoever denies such things always brings ridicule upon themselves. Therefore, he teaches that we must strive above all else to acquire the best character. For character, he says, is the path leading either to the underworld or to the heavens.

I believe it will be worthwhile to repeat more extensively what he writes about these matters in the *Republic* and in the book on knowledge <note>Referring to the *Theaetetus*, which discusses the nature of knowledge and justice.</note>. Surely, he says, those people are to be utterly mocked who think that justice should be pursued or injustice avoided merely for the sake of human rewards or punishments. Rather, that view is true which asserts that those are not the real rewards or punishments which occur occasionally or by chance, but rather those which follow virtues and vices by an eternal and necessary order. He adds in the book on knowledge: that God is justice itself, and nothing is more like Him than a just person, and nothing more unlike Him than an unjust one. Furthermore, true wisdom and power should be considered that which knows this and follows it by choice; whereas the contrary state should be judged as extreme ignorance and weakness. Accordingly, he places two extreme models in the universe: at the highest point, the most blessed divinity; and at the lowest, the opposite, which is devoid of divinity and most miserable. And he affirms that the unjust, because of their extreme ignorance, never notice that through their injustice they are becoming more unlike the most blessed and more like the most miserable day by day. Such unlikeness or likeness is the proper punishment for injustice, while the proper reward for justice is judged to be that very likeness to the most blessed and unlikeness to the most miserable. To this he adds that the unjust are received into the homeland of blessedness neither in this life nor the next (insofar as they are unlike it); rather, by a certain perverse habit, they are drawn back to the lowest place of misery (to which they have become similar), and they always wander through a malignant region, like themselves, among evil ones who are similar to them. He finally adds that these things are often mocked by certain ambitious men, but if they are forced to give and receive reasons for these things carefully, they eventually go away (as we indicated above) truly convicted and mocked like children.

But now let us return to character <note>original: "mores," which refers to moral disposition, habits, or character.</note>; by distributing these in order, we will understand by what logic rewards or punishments are distributed. Before we distinguish them, however, it must be remembered that good character only leads to happiness if it is sought primarily through love for God, the author of happiness. On the other hand, it is primarily those souls in which all love of God is extinguished that evil character plunges into misery. Hence that Platonic saying: "To a wise man, God is the law; but to a foolish man, lust is the law." Also: "He shall be blessed who humbly submits himself to the divine law, but miserable who proudly despises it." There are four types of character among the living. There is the man who is **temperate**, **continent**, **incontinent**, and **intemperate**.
*   The **temperate** man is he whose reason judges truly, and whose sensual appetite willingly obeys reason.
*   The **continent** man is he whose reason also judges truly, but whose appetite obeys with difficulty.
*   The **incontinent** man is he in whom, even if reason does not judge badly, bodily disturbance nevertheless prevails.
*   The **intemperate** man is he in whom reason is either asleep or corrupted by an over-dominant appetite, where everything is done at the command of the imagination, and reason does not oppose the appetite.

When we speak here of temperance or continence, we understand it in the Platonic rite <note>Meaning according to the Platonic tradition or method.</note> as composing or disposing the soul against all types of disturbances, so that the duties of all moral virtues are included in these. Furthermore, when we place the imagination in the separated soul, we understand it either in the Platonic rite as the "inner sense" which they place in both the ethereal and aerial vehicle <note>The "vehicle" (ocuhema) is a Neo-Platonic concept of a subtle, spirit-like body that allows the soul to interact with different levels of reality.</note>—though specifically with passion in the aerial one—or in the manner of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, especially Avicenna, as the disposition and habit of even the rational part which it conceived within itself by obeying the senses, declining toward bodily passions and dragging toward matter. Because of this, Avicenna says the soul is twisted toward the sensible in an intelligible way, as if by a certain nature even without choice or meditation, both here and in the next life. To return now to our purpose: in the temperate soul, only the...

Ficino is currently explaining how the soul's moral disposition during life—whether it was controlled by reason or enslaved by bodily passions—determines the speed and nature of its ascent toward the divine or its descent into a state of "dream-like" suffering.</meta>

<page-num>420</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<meta>catchword: lest the fury</meta>

While the power of nourishment cares for the body, the <term>Phantasy</term><note>The faculty of imagination that sits between the physical senses and the rational mind.</note> does not love it, and reason even hates it. Therefore, once the service of caring for this body is fulfilled, that life-giving power is satisfied, as if with its vehicle; whatever other powers of the soul remain, just as they were accustomed in a temperate person, they dedicate themselves to considering the truth of all things—and all the more fervently than before, as they have been made freer. All of them, therefore, suddenly return into the ether by a common effort and an ethereal chariot.

The soul of the continent person <note>One who struggles with desires but successfully masters them through reason.</note> is indeed carried into heaven, as he says shortly after, but not suddenly. For in such a person, the appetite of the phantasy was accustomed to barely obeying reason, due to the charms or terrors of the body. Therefore, in death, it leaves corporeal things with difficulty, and this distress occupies the edge of reason for a little while. But reason, which had become accustomed to conquering that phantasy, commands it to be silent. Once the complaint of the phantasy is settled and the darkness expelled, the celestial spark begins to shine, and with all the powers of the soul in agreement, the supernal fatherland is revisited. The incontinent person, however, is freed late from these prisons, and the intemperate person <note>Incontinent people know what is right but fail; intemperate people have lost the ability to even recognize what is right.</note> never. Indeed, the souls of these people, infected by corporeal passions, have fallen into such insanity in this life that they have rashly preferred the shadows of goods to the goods themselves; they have loved shadows and feared shadows. And after this life, they are similarly compelled to be insane—the former for a long time, the latter forever. Certainly, the insanity of the incontinent finds some remedy, because although the disturbance of the phantasy used to dominate, reason was still accustomed to opposing it sometimes during life. Similarly, after death, reason cries out against the insanity of a certain raging phantasy and grieves that it is deprived of the possession of sublime things. This outcry and repentance gradually weaken the power and action of that phantasy, especially since corporeal incitements that nourish such a phantasy are no longer present. And anyone would gladly listen to a doctor who is about to cure them, being affected by the weariness of a long-lasting illness; it becomes just as it is for one who is vexed by horrendous dreams: meanwhile, because he is not pressed by the deepest sleep, he says to himself perhaps that he is dreaming and being tortured by empty cares. Whence the fear and labor are diminished. The same thing perhaps happens in the underworld to the incontinent, and as much as the noise of the delusional phantasy is diminished, the command of liberated reason is increased. Thus, at last, the soul is unhindered and attains blessedness. In the intemperate soul, however, even while it increased the life of the man, reason slept entirely or was altogether obedient to emotion; whence it carries with it an indelible habit declining toward corporeal things as if it were its nature. Such is the habit of this soul, as Orpheus sang:

->The gates of Hades are unspeakable, and the people of dreams.<-
<note>original Greek: ἄῤῥητοί τ' ἀΐδαο πύλαι, καὶ δῆμος ὀνείρων.</note>

The gates of Pluto cannot be unbolted; the people of dreams are within. Plato says of this soul in the seventh book of the *Republic* that it sleeps deeply in this life, and departs before it wakes up, and after death is weighed down by a deeper sleep and disturbed by sharper dreams, which is properly designated by the name of Tartarus. It is carried, as Plato wishes, by an excessive love for the elemental body. Therefore, when the earthly body is dissolved, it weaves for itself another as soon as possible from the vapors of the elements. With only a sort of nod, it weaves it from easy matter. With only a single breath, it refreshes that constantly vanishing body daily, as if by breathing. He adds that such a soul revolves around the body and the elemental region toward which it had been inclined, with its affection persevering. Nor should it seem a wonder, they wish to say, that the soul forms a vaporous body as its own and perceives through it, since that is easier and closer to the soul. And in this body, through such a spirit, it provides life and sense to the body. If it is asked what the shape of that body is, we shall respond according to the Magi <note>Ancient Persian sages often cited by Ficino as part of a "perennial philosophy" that predates Plato.</note> that various likenesses of different animals are made from these sorts of vapors. For whatever animal's life it imitated in its habits, it makes itself into such a thing first, and such would its affection and disposition appear entirely if it were discerned by some sense; it also fashions such a shape in a certain way in its own shadowy body, provided that the light body can be colored and shaped by the vehement affection and habit of the soul. And just as it had felt the passions of the flesh in life, so it feels the passions of that body, and all the more sharply as the body is purer. But those senses are of another kind, and those of the flesh of another. And thus, perhaps, the transformation of men into beasts among the ancients is to be understood. Some truly say that the soul does not properly form such a body and feel through it, but rather, just as through the magic art certain statues adapted to certain demons are bound to those demons (which Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> confesses and Plotinus as well), so by divine law, souls that have surrendered themselves to bodies are enslaved to water or fire; and indeed so slavishly that because of this they are vehemently indignant and grieve. But however this may be, this suffering [is called] Tisiphone... <note>One of the Furies (Erinyes) in Greek mythology, whose name means "avenging murder."</note>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion of the soul's state after death, specifically focusing on how the "phantasy" (the faculty of imagination) becomes the instrument of punishment for those who lived according to their passions rather than reason.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII #
<note>The header in the original text says Book XVI, but this is a known typographical error in the early editions of the *Platonic Theology*; the content belongs to Book XVIII.</note>

->Dd 3<-

...from love. He <note>Likely referring to Plato or the "divine law" mentioned later.</note> applies two other furies to the soul to torture it through its emotions: **Megaera** <note>One of the three Furies of Greek myth; her name implies "grudging envy."</note> indeed on account of hatred and the fear of an imaginary evil; but **Alecto** <note>The Fury whose name implies "unceasing anger."</note> on account of the desire for an imaginary good. Plato says these furies are incited by avenging <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmonibus"; in the Platonic tradition, these are not necessarily "devils" but spiritual intermediaries or personified psychological forces.</note>, and Plotinus proves this, and Orpheus himself describes a great avenging demon in his own hymn. For the first disturbances of the soul are such as those experienced by people who are delirious with a fever-induced frenzy, or those terrified by a <term>melancholy humor</term> <note>In ancient medicine, an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause hallucinations and profound fear.</note>. Indeed, **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian polymath and philosopher (980–1037 AD).</note> confesses that this happens, and **Proclus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note>, when he says there are certain "irrational demons," signifies that it is no wonder if the souls of the wretched become irrational.

For when the actions of the five senses cease, the internal actions are greatly increased. And if you are accustomed to using reason most of the time, then you will contemplate most diligently. If you are accustomed to the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that stores and manipulates sensory images.</note>, then you will imagine most vehemently. This happens in sleep to such an extent that we believe images of things to be the real things themselves; we tremble, sweat, cry out, and jump up, terrified by horrible visions. Much more does the deception of terrifying images happen to the wicked in death and after death. For then the various duties of nourishing the body cease, as do the multiple actions of the external senses, the preoccupations of human affairs, and the comforts of physical things. There remains only (as the Platonists think) the rule of the raging phantasy or the "phantastic reason" <note>A state where reason is enslaved to the imagination.</note> over the wicked person. This phantasy, moved by the hatred and fear I mentioned, turns over within itself a long sequence of dismal images. Now it imagines the sky falling on its head; now that it is being swallowed by the deep chasms of the earth; then that it is being consumed by an onslaught of flames; then submerged in a vast whirlpool of water, or seized by the shadows of demons. 

And so, it tosses its "body" <note>Referring to the "astral" or "ethereal" vehicle the soul is thought to inhabit after death.</note> everywhere through the depths, wherever the impulse of the raging phantasy and the "evil demon" drives it. As **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius"; refers to the legendary author of the Hermetic texts.</note> and Plato say—who actually believe there are two demons in this matter, though people may not notice it—these are the ministers of divine law. And the wicked man will suffer this through Megaera out of hatred and fear. However, through Alecto, out of the indelible habit of love he had contracted toward corporeal things, such thoughts and feelings creep back in. Just as old men who lived lustfully in their youth are burned by a double penalty in their old age—namely, that they burn with the desire for pleasures and yet are deprived of all hope of obtaining them (unless they are perhaps delirious)—so the wretched in the underworld are troubled by their former habits, some by one human desire, others by another. For the most part, they do not hope they can achieve them, although sometimes, like madmen, they seem to themselves to almost reach their delights, only to be immediately driven away from them toward sharper punishments. **Sardanapalus** is driven far from an embrace, **Midas** from gold, **Tantalus** from the feast, and **Sisyphus** from the summit.

So great is the power of the phantasy, so great its impulse, when either it rules alone, or when a certain "phantastic habit" and emotion, contracted from long-standing commerce with the phantasy, rules alone within the reason. **Olympiodorus**, in his commentaries on the *Phaedo*, confirms the order we have set down above, identifying three types of vices according to Plato’s opinion. First are those that are easily curable, namely those which lack a settled habit. Second, he says, are those that can be cured only with difficulty, being committed out of habit but accompanied by some resistance and repentance. Third and finally are those that cannot be healed, which are perpetrated by habit and are entirely lacking in resistance or repentance. Therefore, the first are assigned to **Acheron**, the second to **Pyriphlegethon** and **Cocytus**, and the third to **Tartarus** <note>These are the rivers and regions of the classical Underworld.</note> among the Platonists, from which Plato says no one can ever escape. 

Just as many levels are distributed to the good in the *Phaedo*, where it is asserted that innocent and pious souls, though lacking in philosophy, live easily in the air with "aerial bodies"; but souls endowed additionally with "civil philosophy" <note>The virtue of a good citizen and leader.</note> are carried in heaven with "celestial and shining vehicles"; and finally, the most purified souls live most blessedly above heaven without bodies. **Orpheus**, however, distributes nine principal regions to souls. To the upright, he assigns either the eighth sphere, or the planets, or the ether below the planets. Indeed, there are nine spheres if you divide them more carefully into the nine degrees of contemplation, which we have discussed appropriately elsewhere. To those in the middle, he assigns the air, or the water, and the earth. Finally, to the reprobate, he assigns Acheron, Cocytus, and Pyriphlegethon, where additionally the ninefold-interwoven **Styx** <note>The river of "Hate" in the underworld.</note> hems them in. 

The number nine is chosen because they sinned either by a certain emotion, or by a changeable habit, or by an unchangeable habit; and in whichever of these ways they failed, they sinned either in thought, or even in speech, or additionally in action—from which nine degrees of faults and nine degrees of punishments are rightly calculated. Indeed, that oracle of **Virgil** <note>original: "Maronis"; referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> in the sixth book [of the *Aeneid*] is by no means to be despised as merely "poetic," in which, following partly Hermes and partly Plato, he describes four emotions which follow the four humors. Indeed, from fiery bile comes appetite, from aerial blood vo- <meta>Catchword: "sanguine uo-" completes to "uoluptatem" (pleasure) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains how the soul's imagination (phantasy) becomes its own tormentor after death, creating hellish hallucinations based on the sinful habits and "humors" formed during life. He aligns classical mythology and the geography of the underworld with Platonic philosophy to categorize different degrees of punishment and reward.</summary>
<keywords>Phantasy, Furies, Megaera, Alecto, Underworld, Acheron, Tartarus, Plato, Orpheus, Olympiodorus, reincarnation, punishment, nine spheres, demons</keywords>

He transitions from discussing the "phantasy" (imagination) to how the four classical elements and the legendary rivers of the underworld represent specific psychological and spiritual states of suffering.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGIAN #

<margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin>
...it seems consistent that pleasure is born from blood, fear from the earthy black bile, and pain and softness from the watery phlegm. Then he <note>Ficino is likely referring to a Platonic source or his own synthesis of humoral theory.</note> adds that from these four affections, four such habits are conceived in the soul which decline toward corporeal things; these the wretched carry with them after death to be purged near the four elements. In this purgation, he arranges four primary regions of the underworld in the Platonic manner, where one may hear the crashing and roaring of **Acheron, Cocytus, Phlegethon,** and **Tartarus**. It seems quite consistent with these to arrange four regions in turn in the **Elysian fields** <note>The final resting place of the heroic and the virtuous in Greek mythology.</note>—namely, the four "triplicities" of signs in the Zodiac—which correspond to the four kinds of virtues by which the four affections are conquered, so that the celestial light is received with a serene mind. 

But it is necessary to remember that those who think souls living in the spheres of the planets, in fire, and in pure air are among the inhabitants of the underworld are not to be admitted among the Platonists. For in what way are they assigned to the underworld if they are both among the blessed and in bodies so light and obedient to the command of souls that they are not distracted from the contemplation of divine things? Therefore, we ought to call only that region of the world where the tumultuous confusion of the elements clashes by the name of the "underworld," according to the Platonic view. 

Finally, to summarize the opinion of the ancient theologians regarding the state of the soul after death in a few words: they think that only divine things (as we have said elsewhere) truly exist, and the rest are images and shadows of true things. Therefore, wise men, who devote themselves to divine things, are more "awake" than others. But the unwise, who pursue other things, are entirely mocked by dreams as if they were sleeping; and if they die in this sleep before they have been awakened, they are tormented by similar and more piercing visions after their departure. And just as he who in life devoted himself to true things possesses the highest truth after death, so he who has pursued false things is tortured by extreme deception, so that the former is delighted by true things, while the latter is vexed by false phantoms. 

For this reason, **Christ**, the master of life, often commands thus: "Watch, I say, watch, lest the Lord find you sleeping." Again: "Rise now, and let us go from here." <note>Cf. Mark 13:37 and John 14:31. Ficino is harmonizing Platonic "wakefulness" with Christian scripture.</note> For what else is it to wake up than to recognize that one is "dreaming" through the senses? And what else is it to rise and go than to bring oneself to God by the mind itself? 

Nor do I think we should pass over in silence a certain cause of punishment—hidden indeed to those suffering, but most powerful—which Plato indicated in the *Timaeus*, *Gorgias*, and *Republic*, and which **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) heavily influenced by Platonism.</note> interpreted. God tempered the soul from its beginning with a certain harmony of spiritual parts, powers, and movements. This kind of tempering in intemperate and unjust men is gradually loosened, and it is mostly dissolved in the damned. It is necessary, however, that from this loosening and dissolution no small distress and pain arise in the soul, even if it does not know from where or for what sake it suffers—just as when the natural tempering of the corporeal spirits, humors, and members is loosened, pain necessarily follows, even if the sick person does not know the reason for their pain. 

Christian theologians will not entirely deny these things, but they will add (as I think) some punishment from a true judgment of the damned soul, since it will consider that it has been deprived of the divine vision forever. This is therefore the greatest punishment, because God is the "end" <term>final cause</term> for whose sake we were born, and for whose sake we all desire and do all things. And therefore, the natural thirst which is directed toward Him is much sharper than that which rouses a thirsty man toward drink. But just as if someone were stupefied by a sleep-inducing **opium**, although they might be dying of thirst, they would not feel the sting and detriment of the thirst; but when the opium is worn off, they will feel it thoroughly and be more violently vexed—so the soul that has gorged itself on the river of **Lethe** <note>The river of forgetfulness; original: "Lethæum... flumen."</note>, most different of all from God, being deeply occupied by a stupor regarding the sense of divine things, does not feel the torments of its natural thirst toward God. But when the stupor is finally expelled, it both feels most acutely and is most violently tortured. 

And as if we could somehow, against our will, think ourselves to be far from God, yet occupied by the comforts of life we notice this more rarely; and when we do notice it, we hope that we will soon return to the Father. But there, neither comfort nor any hope delights the wretched, which can also be called **Acheron** <note>Ficino implies a derivation from the Greek *achos* (pain/sorrow) or *a-chairein* (without joy).</note>. The punishment is increased because they judge themselves deprived by their own fault; therefore they are perpetually indignant with themselves, which can be signified by the name of **Styx** <note>Associated with the Greek *stygein*, to hate or loathe.</note>. To this is added the **Tartarean** habitation of vile or most foul places, and finally the tortures of this human body, which seem to be **Cocytus** <note>From the Greek *kokytos*, lamentation.</note> in the soul and the sensation of **Phlegethon** <note>From the Greek *phlegethein*, to blaze or burn.</note>.

### *On the Middle State of Souls, Especially According to the Philosophers.* ###

**IT IS** often customary to ask about the souls of those who departed from their bodies before the age of choice <note>i.e., infants and young children who have not reached the age of reason.</note>. Plato writes that **Er the Pamphylian** <note>original: "Herum Pamphilium"; the protagonist of the Myth of Er at the end of Plato's *Republic*.</note>, who rose from death, narrated many and wonderful things about the state of other souls, but about these children he recorded some other things not very worthy of memory...

<summary>Ficino describes the afterlife as a psychological state where the soul's lack of divine harmony manifests as the classical rivers of Hades. He argues that "hell" is the confusion of the elements and the loss of the divine vision, which is felt most acutely once the "stupor" of physical life wears off.</summary>
<keywords>underworld, purgation, Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon, Cocytus, Lethe, divine vision, Origen, Myth of Er, harmony of the soul, humoral theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the afterlife, moving from the physical purging of the soul to a philosophical exploration of the "middle states" of existence—specifically for those, like infants, who die before they can choose good or evil.</meta>

# ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, BOOK XVIII. #

<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, BOOK XVIII.</header>

->Dd 4<-

Avicenna, however, in his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "in metaphysicis"; Avicenna was a 10th-century Persian philosopher whose work deeply influenced Western thought</note>, states that those souls which have not yet contracted a habit of either good or evil receive some measure of good from the abundance of divine mercy. If we were permitted to engage in philosophical conjectures on this matter, we might perhaps say that, while the usual course of things suggests one fate, a different lot has befallen them—one that seems outside the apparent order, but is actually brought into a specific order by Divine Wisdom. This wisdom permits nothing anywhere to be entirely devoid of order, though this arrangement is hidden from us while being perfectly manifest to the higher beings. What if God—just as He always places several middle steps between any two extremes that are far apart—has likewise placed many intermediate levels between the lot of the most blessed and that of the most miserable? These levels would be as numerous in the hidden ranks of souls as they are in the visible ranks of bodies. Thus, there would be many who are most blessed, and many who are most miserable, but also others who are less blessed, others who are less miserable, and finally those in the middle who are neither properly miserable nor blessed. For a person is blessed who enjoys the divine flavors in God, but miserable who never senses any divine fragrance and is always hungry. One is "less blessed" if they enjoy fewer of those flavors, and "less miserable" if they hunger and suffer less. Finally, the "middle" person is the one who perceives certain fragrances of the Creator within created things and lives content with that scent.

For this reason, philosophers will perhaps say that the souls of infants <note>Ficino is addressing the theological problem of the "Limbo of Infants"—the fate of children who die before they can act virtuously or sin.</note> ought not to complain against divine justice; for if they are deprived of the capacity for the Highest Good, they are also freed from the danger of the extreme evil. Furthermore, it is probable they do not complain if the "Divine Sun"—which creates natural things—pours the fullness of its light of natural forms into the clarity of a soul that is unclouded by any bodily passions. This light, as Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato regarding the creation of the universe</note>, demonstrates the order of the universe to the soul, and reveals the Arranger within that order (to the extent that the order itself can contain the Arranger), and God commands and causes the soul to be content with this good. 

Therefore, just as in a human being there is a spirit between the heavy body and the soul; and in our feelings there is a state of "painless-ness" <note>Latin: "indolentia"; a neutral state between pain and pleasure</note> between pain and pleasure; and in reason there is "right opinion" between knowledge and ignorance; and in the universe there is transparency between the bright and the opaque—so too there seem to be among the separated spirits those who are blessedly formed in the heavens by both the "Lux" and the "Lumen" <note>Ficino distinguishes between *Lux* (the source/Infinite Light) and *Lumen* (the diffused/emitted light)</note> of God. Conversely, there are those around the earth who miserably lack both. Between these, however, in the purer air, are those in the middle, to whom the light itself does not belong, yet the "Lumen" (the diffused glow) still reaches. 

We must remember, as we have indicated elsewhere, that it is one thing for *Lux* to remain in the Sun, another for *Lumen* to flow from it and spread through all things, and another for a certain "Ray" <note>original: "radius"</note> to be naturally implanted in the eyes. In the same way, the Infinite Light in God is one thing, through which alone God enjoys Himself and the blessed minds enjoy the divine goodness. The "Common Light" <note>Lumen</note> is another thing, which spreads abundantly from there through all transparent minds; through this light, as if through something created and external, individual minds see all created things (provided they do not turn away), though they do not see the Creator Himself as He is, unless they are moved into the source-light by being kindled by that glow. Finally, the "Ray" is another thing, which is unique to each mind and made natural to them from the beginning, witnessing in them even when they turn away or depart from the source. 

In the first grade are the blessed; in the second are those who are neither properly blessed nor miserable, provided they live content in this state. In the third grade are human souls, whether bound to bodies or to bodily affections, and for this reason they are already almost miserable, happy only through hope. The most miserable of all are below this grade; for them, only the "Ray" remains, and even that is now dark and burning, destitute of any confidence in the pure light. 

Perhaps a Platonist would conjecture this: if God created minds for the sake of the First Light, and those minds are prepared to attain it through both the recognition and, most especially, the love of divine goodness—since the mind is formed by the light it recognizes, and reformed by the love it sends back—then it is likely that divine justice wills that no mind should ever be entirely without the capacity and opportunity to recognize and love God. However, because many die before the use of reason, and others are "dull-witted" <note>original: "stolidis"</note> from the beginning (both things being subtracted by the malignant necessity of fate), it would be consistent that such a capacity be repaid by divine providence—either in this life in some miraculous way, or at least in the next—so that no one, without their own fault, lacks the sight of the Great Beauty. For this reason, even if the souls of these people never found it here, once they are separated from their bodies and placed in that "Lumen" we mentioned, they may recognize the Creator through His creatures. They may be kindled by the love of the Creator step-by-step, until at a certain time they are prepared to reach the source-light. I say "at a certain time," because only angelic minds exist entirely in eternity and can progress or fall in a single moment. Human souls, however, move as if by nature...

<summary>Ficino explores the "middle states" of the soul after death, arguing that divine justice provides a neutral, painless existence for those like infants who could not choose God, eventually allowing them to learn to love Him through His creations.</summary>
