# MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY #
<page-num>424</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO, PLATONIC THEOLOGY</header>
<meta>catchword: MARSL</meta>

...declining toward temporal things, they carry out their work in time, but for a longer period while in the body, and a much shorter one outside the body; indeed, they perform it only for moments when they have first been translated into an almost angelic nature. And if souls established in purgatorial <term>purgatory: a state of purification after death</term> punishments—even though they are in a worse condition and place—nevertheless rise up to happiness, it should not seem strange that the souls of those placed in the middle region of "indolence" <note>original: "regione indolentiæ"; here meaning a state of neither pain nor pleasure, similar to Limbo</note>, which is closer to happiness, are able to progress all the way to bliss. This is what the philosophers would chiefly think concerning infants.

However, concerning those who are entirely stolid <note>original: "stolidi"; refers to those born with severe cognitive or intellectual disabilities</note> by nature itself, the question seems far more difficult than the one regarding infants. For if these people have lived for a long time, they contract some habit or disposition toward matter (which is the lowest part of the universe), a habit that usually turns away from God, who is the highest part of the universe. This habit, accompanying the soul even when it is separated from the body, perhaps still turns it toward matter and meanwhile turns it away from God. Now, happiness is judged to belong to none except those turned toward God. But if these people are miserable, even though they could in no way turn toward the Highest because fate prevented them, then they are miserable through no fault of their own; and God would have commanded those who were unable to do so to turn toward Him in vain.

Perhaps some Peripatetic <note>followers of Aristotle</note> will respond that in fools, because of the excessive intensity of the phantasy <term>phantasy: the faculty of the mind that processes sensory images</term> itself, reason was so vacant that it created no habit by failing to act. They might say that the habit proper to the phantasy (which is not so much in the soul as in the animated body) ceases immediately once the composite of body and soul is dissolved. The result is that the mind, with no natural ray of the body hindering it, is immediately turned toward God; receiving the divine light that is present everywhere, it is set on fire; then, being set on fire, it loves; and by loving, it turns itself more vehemently and, by deserving something in a short time, it attains happiness. 

The Platonists, however, who think that the habit remains in a way in the persisting phantasy, and is transfused into the reason that consents to it (if indeed the reason, even then under compulsion, consented to anything), will respond that the habit turning toward opposites must be entirely deleted before the soul can be raised upward. But they would say that in this deletion, both the power of the guardian spirit <note>original: "genij"; a tutelary spirit assigned to a person</note> and the power of God work miraculously. For under divine providence, minds are no less cared for and provided for than bodies. Therefore, just as in sick bodies, where nature cannot expel a disease and return to health by its own power, it is accustomed to expel it with the help of the art of physicians; similarly, in minds where the natural faculty for purging the bodily habit and returning to God is lacking, the omnipotent Physician performs both tasks happily, either by His own power alone or through the ministry of His blessed servants. 

Nor will they think this lacks order; rather, divine mercy—which is most praised in a ruler—shines most clearly here. For God condemns no one without their own fault, and he who is deprived of the faculty of merit for a time through no fault of his own is eventually restored to that faculty by divine power—a safe faculty, I say, which cannot go astray and which, with God’s help, may deserve much in a short time. This is their view. But lest we think childishly and foolishly about children and fools, it seems we must now conclude thus: the conjectural path of the philosophers leads us almost this far. But because human conjecture is often and greatly deceived concerning divine things, we judge it much better and safer to commit ourselves with obedient humility to the holier leaders among the Christians.

### Conclusion ###

**A**fter God has granted us a limit to life that is not the same as that of other living creatures—as we have shown first by common reasons, second by specific arguments, and third by both signs and the solutions to questions—I judge that we must take the greatest care not to prefer this uncertain moment of fleeting life to infinite ages. Let us remember, if we are wise, that we cannot exist well, live perfectly, or understand happily for eternity unless we are formed by His essence (by whose creation we received our existence) and live by His life (by whose breath we breathe and move). Let us understand Him through His own intelligence, and all things through Him, by whose daily illumination we both consider created things and seek the Creator. We shall reach this supreme level of nature, God leading us, if only we separate the affection of the soul as much as we can from matter itself (which is the lowest level of nature), so that the more we depart from matter, the more we approach God. Though we now live for the moment of this deceptive life, let us live as much as we can so that we may finally live by His life forever. Amen.

### The author’s protestation concerning his writings. In all things that are treated by me, whether here or elsewhere, I wish only as much to be asserted as is approved by the Church. ###

<header>THE LIFE OF PAUL</header>

# MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine on the Epistles of Saint Paul,
## The ascent to the third heaven, for the understanding of Paul,
### PREFACE.

> I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know, God knows—such a man was caught up to the third heaven. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows—that he was caught up into Paradise, and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a man to speak. <note>original: "SCIO hominem in Christo..." This is a direct quote from 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, where Paul describes his mystical vision.</note>

Venerable fathers in Christ and most beloved brothers in the cathedral college, Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, the Sun of the world, the vessel of election <term>vessel of election: a traditional title for St. Paul, meaning a person chosen by God for a special task</term>, the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, sang these mysteries which I have just recounted in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians as if they were oracles; indeed, when we come to the exposition of that Epistle, we shall endeavor, by God's inspiration, to explain them according to our strength. In the meantime, however, since we desire from the beginning to understand every word of him who was caught up to heaven, yet it is not permitted to us—while we live our lives on earth as mere men—to hear these things, we must strive as much as we can to transcend human limits. Above all, the exalted Paul must be entreated so that he himself, by his clemency, may lift us up with him to a certain heavenly and angelic level.

For there is an "earth" within us, and also, in a certain way, a "heaven," and that heaven is threefold. Earth is indeed the body and the senses, and the physical desires. Heaven, however, is right and true reason. But reason is threefold, just as there appear to be three heavens. The lowest is indeed the <term>practical reason: the mental faculty used for making decisions about daily life and ethics</term> devoted to the governance and providence of human affairs, both private and public. The middle reason, however, considers the order of the world through the faculty of physics <note>original: "physica facultate"; here meaning the study of the natural world or science</note>. Finally, the supreme reason, or the mind, contemplates divine things higher than the world through theological reasoning.

Therefore, as we are about to perceive the secret mysteries of the sublime Paul, we must set aside physical sensation and desire as if they were the earth; likewise, we must bypass practical reason as if it were a kind of first heaven, and again set aside physical reason as if it were a second heaven, so that we may lift ourselves with all our strength—under Paul's guidance—to the mind that contemplates divine things, as if to a third heaven and angelic state within us.

Yet, because the contemplation of the mind cannot reach divine things by its own powers of intelligence, we must again establish three steps within ourselves, like three heavens, or rather, they must be sought from God through Paul: Faith, Hope, and Charity <note>original: "Fides, spes, charitas"; these are the three theological virtues</note>, which are gifts of the Holy Spirit—especially Charity, which surpasses all knowledge and joins us with the Seraphic order <term>Seraphic order: the highest choir of angels, associated with burning love for God</term>. Here at last a threefold heaven will also meet us. For in seraphic charity, that ineffable fervor of the Spirit will be kindled within us. In this nourishing fervor, however, the light and wisdom of the divine Word will immediately shine forth. By these divine gifts, endowed with grace, we shall attain by incomparable power a gift from the Father, by which we may be able to perceive the mysteries divinely revealed to Saint Paul.

But what we were just signifying—that light is kindled within heat—seems to me to require more diligent consideration. It is the opinion of the philosophers that heat in physical bodies naturally proceeds from light. Just as in spirits, the will proceeds from the intellect. The Sun, therefore, like a kind of Lord of heaven, first pours light into transparent bodies everywhere (as they are similar to it) and from there produces heat. To earthly things, however, it grants heat first, thinning out the thick matter. Afterward, it immediately inserts light into the vapors rising from there. Similarly, God pours love through the intellect into minds that are separated from the body. But for souls enclosed by a dark body, love is necessary first, created from faith and hope directed toward God. Purified by this love and turned toward God, they will attain the light of understanding. Therefore we too, venerable fathers and most beloved brothers, relying on divine faith and hope, and burning with love, must set out to the understanding of divine things as Paul reveals them.

<header>ON THE LIFE OF ST. PAUL.</header>
<meta>Catchword: IN PRO. (In prologue)</meta>

# ON THE LIFE OF ST. PAUL.

**P**aul, of the tribe of Benjamin, was born in the town of Giscala <note>original: "Gestali"; a reference to Giscala or Gush Halav in Galilee. Jerome records a tradition that Paul's parents moved from here to Tarsus.</note> in Judea. When that town was captured by the Romans, he moved to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. From there, he was sent by his father to Jerusalem to study under Gamaliel for the sake of his education, where he cruelly persecuted the beginnings of the Christian law. Near the end of the year in which Christ suffered, while traveling from Jerusalem to Damascus for the sake of persecution, he was cast to the ground by a sudden flash of light and converted to Christ. After he received baptism from Ananias in Damascus, he set out for Jerusalem. There, while the Jews were accusing him before Felix the governor, he appealed to Caesar as a Roman citizen. Because of this, he was sent bound to Rome to Nero in the second year of Nero’s reign. At Rome, he preached Christ for two years in free custody <note>original: "libera custodia"; a form of house arrest where a prisoner was supervised but not kept in a dungeon.</note>. He then spent ten years in the West. Finally, having returned to Rome, he was crowned with martyrdom in the fourteenth year of Nero. For thirty-six years after his conversion, he labored for the glory of Christ.

### *Summary of the Epistle to the Romans.*

**R**ome was home to many faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, who had been instructed not by the Apostles themselves, but by Jews who had already converted. These groups were engaged in a proud struggle, each wishing to surpass the other in status or in the reception of grace. The Jews indeed boasted that they were the people chosen by God, liberated from Egypt by miracles, nourished by Manna in the desert, instructed in the Law through Moses, enriched by the Prophets, and worthy of the promise of Christ. They threw the worship of idols in the faces of the Gentiles, saying that because of such sacrilege, the Gentiles were unworthy to be compared with the people of God. The Gentiles, however, responded in turn: the greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the more you show yourselves guilty of a greater crime. For you have always been ungrateful for all these things; for having been liberated by God from the Egyptians, you again worshipped idols; the Manna was always a source of loathing to you in the desert; you murmured against the Lord; you destroyed the Prophets. You even killed the Christ promised to you, whom we, as soon as we knew of him, immediately believed in, although he had not been preached to us before.

The Apostle settles these disputes in such a way that he confirms neither of them has earned salvation by their own righteousness. He demonstrates that the Jews transgressed the law, and the Gentiles did not worship the God they had known but rather idols; thus, he shows that both have similarly obtained mercy and are equals. He also shows that it was predicted in the Law that both Jews and Gentiles were to be called to the faith of Christ. Therefore, humbling them in turn, he exhorts them to modesty and harmony. He wrote this letter, as Haymo <note>original: "Haimon"; likely Haymo of Halberstadt, a 9th-century scholar whose commentaries were popular in the Middle Ages.</note> says, in Athens; however, as Origen and Jerome say, it was in Corinth. Perhaps he began the Epistle in Athens but finished it in Corinth. The Epistle to the Romans was placed first in the collection because of the excellence of the city itself (as I believe), not because it was the first written by the Apostle. For Athanasius says that he wrote at least four others earlier: two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, and one to the Thessalonians. Jerome agrees with this. Indeed, Paul himself testifies that he wrote this while setting out for Jerusalem, after he had already exhorted the Corinthians and others by letter to collect the ministry <term>ministry: referring to the "collection for the saints," a fund raised by Paul for the poor Christians in Jerusalem</term> which he was to carry with him.

THE MESSIAH IN THE PAULINE EPISTLES.

# ON THE PROLOGUE OF PAUL,
## How Paul was called and set
### apart. Concerning the eternal and temporal Birth of Christ.
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>» » » » »</margin>
> **PAUL**, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his Prophets in the holy scriptures.) Following the custom of the Orators, he places a prologue before his narrative, in which he achieves three main goals. First, he describes his own office and briefly proves it with many reasons, making his listeners attentive and ready to learn. Second, he explains the condition of those to whom he writes the Epistle. Third, he wishes them happiness and, in the meantime, seeks to win their goodwill. After these things, however, he will begin to narrate, starting with the first point and those that follow.

He was called Saul among the Hebrews, but was named Paul in the common address of the Gentiles, specifically when his profession was changed <note>A reference to the tradition that Saul changed his name to Paul upon his conversion and his mission to the Roman world.</note>. Furthermore, the name of Paul is more consistent with the names of the Gentiles, to whom Paul was primarily sent; finally, this name of Paul belongs by right of victory to the Apostle, taken from the proconsul Sergius Paulus <note>original: "Pauli Sergij"; referring to the Roman proconsul converted by Paul in Acts 13.</note> whom he converted, just as the surname of Africa was granted to Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus, the Roman general who took his name from the territory he conquered.</note>.

He calls himself a **servant** of Christ because he serves not his own glory, but that of Christ, and he reached the dignity of the Apostleship from a state of servitude or a certain humble condition. Indeed, "he who humbles himself shall be exalted." An **Apostle** <term>Apostle: from the Greek 'apostolos', meaning 'one who is sent'.</term> is understood to be one who is "sent," specifically with divine power. This is the meaning of: "God will give the word to those who preach the Gospel with great power." Sent, I say, not by men, but by the Holy Spirit, as is clear in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is asserted that Paul and Barnabas were sent by the Holy Spirit. He was **called**, however, by men as time went on. For this reason, he says to the Corinthians: "I am not worthy to be called an Apostle," yet he was called by God from the beginning, when he was divinely chosen for the Apostolic duty. Regarding this, the Lord says to Ananias: "This man is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel." First, he was called to the faith when he was cast to the ground by a heavenly flash of light. But in the words just narrated, he was called to the Apostolic dignity, by which he would preach Christ to everyone—not only to the Gentiles, but to the Jews. This is also what the preceding words of Luke <note>The author of the Acts of the Apostles.</note> signify. But to the Jews, I say, not so much in Judea, but specifically among those living among the Gentiles.

For this reason, he added: **Set apart**. Partly indeed from the other Apostles and from Judea. Hence the saying in the Acts of the Apostles by the Holy Spirit: "Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them." Partly also set apart from the Jewish profession. Hence the saying to the Galatians: "But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb," that is, from the Jewish Synagogue, or even, that he destined me for this office from the very beginning of my birth.

But why did he separate Paul from the Apostles and Judea, and send him primarily to the Gentiles? Clearly because he was to be quite a threat to the Jews, having suddenly turned from their greatest protector into their most fierce attacker; and he was most acceptable to the Gentiles because of his intellect and eloquence. Indeed, Paul was by his very nature, sharpness, spirit, and eloquence the most excellent of all men. Because of this, he obtained the name of **Mercury** <note>In Acts 14:12, the people of Lystra called Paul "Mercury" because he was the chief speaker, referencing the Roman messenger god of eloquence.</note> among the Gentiles. God chose such a great man so that he might be judged not only to have miraculously instructed the unlearned, but also to have wonderfully converted the most talented and educated. Perhaps he also separated him from the other Apostles so that no one could suspect either that those fishermen were instructed and encouraged by Paul, or that Paul had received the Gospel teaching from them. Therefore he says, **set apart for the Gospel**, that is, for the good news and the promise, not from man, but from God. Thus he said, **the Gospel of God**, which not only David, as we said above, but also Isaiah foretold: "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, of those who preach the gospel of good things."

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

This was indeed no trivial or new discovery, but one promised by God long ago, not through a single witness, but through many—and not just any witnesses, but through Prophets; men who did not predict through human cleverness or demonic instinct, but by divine inspiration. Among the Platonists <note>Ficino, a key figure in the Renaissance, often blends Christian theology with the philosophy of Plato.</note>, predictions are said to happen in five ways: by chance, by art, by nature, by a spirit, or by being moved by the Whole. Only prediction made by divine power is certain and always truthful. Therefore, it was spoken through the Prophets, and not in words alone—lest their memory perish with the sound—but in writings; not just any writings, but those proceeding from the Holy Spirit. Thus it was spoken in the holy scriptures, such as that passage of Jeremiah:
> Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts. <note>original: "Ecce dies ueniunt..." quoting Jeremiah 31:31-33.</note>

Moses indeed entrusted the law to writings, but Christ entrusted it to minds. Truly, where the Prophet indicates that the law of Moses was impressed upon tablets, but the new law upon minds, he also implies that the new law is as much more excellent than the old as minds are superior to tablets. Thus, just as the light of the Moon gives way and is overtaken by the light of the Sun when it arrives, so the old law should give way and be overtaken by the new. I say "in the scriptures," not concerning just any subject, but concerning his Son. For from this, the Prophets predicted that the Gospel law would proceed. When it says "concerning his Son," it carries a specific emphasis, lest we perhaps understand Christ—along with Photinus <note>Photinus (d. 376 AD) was a bishop who taught that Jesus was a mere man who was "adopted" by God, rather than being God's natural Son from eternity.</note>—to be an adopted son of God rather than a natural one. Christ certainly has twin natures: namely, the divine and the human. Yet he is a single person—the divine person. This person is the Son of God, who is always with the Father, begotten from him from eternity. By this reasoning, Paul spoke of "his Son" to signify eternal generation. But to express his temporal birth, he added:
> Who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh.

He was not simply "made" <note>Ficino is distinguishing between being "created" as a creature and "becoming" man through the Incarnation.</note>, as Arius <note>Arius (d. 336 AD) taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father; his views were condemned at the Council of Nicaea.</note> thinks, but in a certain way "made man." Therefore, he is asserted to have been made "according to the flesh." This is the same as saying: it was divinely brought about that the Son of God should assume flesh, namely, a human nature. Meanwhile, through these two words—"made according to the flesh"—the Manichaean <note>Followers of Mani who believed that matter was evil and therefore argued that Christ could not have had a real physical body, only a "phantom" or "ghostly" one.</note> is refuted, who claims that God only showed a phantom body. "From the seed of David" means from the seed of the Virgin Mary, who was descended from David. And lest you think that an affection of this kind brought something new to God, he added:
> Who was predestined the Son of God—that is, decreed and ordained from eternity to be the Son of God.

This is not because the divine person proceeded from the Father through a voluntary "destination" (since he is begotten by nature), but because it was divinely decreed that the Son of God himself, at a certain time, would demonstrate himself to be man through the assumption of human nature. Justly, he did not say "predestined" before saying "made," so that he might show that only the connection and union of the human nature is included under predestination. God has never predestined anyone simply to evil, but rather to good; for infinite goodness does not decree that anyone will simply be evil or miserable, but establishes with a certain condition that *if* someone is evil, they shall be damned. Simply, however, he predestined certain men to be Prophets, or Apostles, or Teachers. Similarly, he predestined that human nature would one day be joined with the divine. But lest you perhaps think—along with Nestorius <note>Nestorius (d. 450 AD) was accused of teaching that Christ was two separate persons, one human and one divine, joined only by a sort of "dwelling" or moral union.</note>—that the Divine Word took up humanity only through some shared dwelling, he added:

<margin>» In power according to the Spirit of holiness through the resurrection from the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord.)</margin>
"In power," that is, in the same divine power; as if he were to say, "in the union of the person." That divine power was handed over to Christ is proved by the Apostle from this: that Jesus was born through the power of the Holy Spirit, forming the offspring in Mary and, so to speak, sanctifying it; and because Christ poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit upon his own followers for prophecy and miracles, especially after he rose from the dead. Through this power, he first raised several dead people and then himself from death. We can, however, explain this more simply and fittingly to the words: Jesus was destined in the presence of God, and declared by God to men as the Son of God. But by what means? Truly, in power. In power, I say, of miracles to be performed openly. Then through the "Spirit of holiness," which Jesus poured out more abundantly upon his own after he rose from the dead. This resurrection stood as the greatest pledge of divine power, and was declared by the manifest gift of the Holy Spirit, diffused afterward among his followers. He called the resurrection of Christ the "resurrection of the dead" because this [led to] a general [resurrection], as he says...

->COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL<-

as Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and a key Church Father who influenced Augustine.</note> says, he brings about the resurrection. » **Through which Christ, indeed, we have received grace and Apostleship for obedience to the faith among all Nations for his name's sake.** » Paul says that he received from the Father, through the Son, the very grace of the Holy Spirit for the full effect of his Apostleship <term>Apostolatus: the office and authority of an Apostle</term>. And he received this among all Nations, so that eventually all might obey the Christian faith. For this reason, Isaiah says: *It is a small thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to convert the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light to the Gentiles.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 49:6.</note> When he says: **Among whom you also are called of Jesus Christ**, » he also includes the Jews who are mixed among the Nations. For » in what follows, he also accepts that the Jews are to be converted. **Called of Jesus Christ**, that is, by Jesus Christ. Where he said above, "for his name’s sake," he completely excluded his own glory. Here, meanwhile, he professes that he was sent chiefly to the Nations, and shows that in Jesus alone is fulfilled what God himself had promised to Christ through the Prophets. Namely, that Christ would proclaim the worship of the one God—which until now had been narrow and restricted only to the Jews—to all Nations, and would destroy idolatry. **To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints.** » Moreover, he writes not only to the Romans, but to all who are in Rome, whether they be » Romans, Greeks, Jews, or any kind of Barbarian. To these, however—not just anyone—but to those who are converted. But by what power are they converted? By the divine calling through which they are made holy, by which God calls them out of his love. Meanwhile, he says they are "twice called" <note>original: "bis uocatis"</note>, so they might understand that they have progressed, or will progress further, only by the grace of the divine calling. **Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.** » Finally, for those so disposed, he desires and promises the chief gifts of the Holy Spirit: grace and peace. By "grace," he means divine love and efficacy. By "peace," he means reconciliation with God through the forgiveness of sins. And so that he may express the whole Trinity, he desires that these gifts of the Holy Spirit come to us from the Father through the Son. And when he named the Father, he not only named His natural Son, but also us as the adopted sons of that Father, where he spoke with great emphasis of charity and obedience, saying: **our**. To this end the Apostle points in what follows: *that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.* Likewise: *heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ.*

---
### On the Reasons for the Trinity. Chapter II.
---

**H**itherto we have explained the introduction to the Epistle, but before we come to the narrative, it will be worthwhile to bring forward something concerning the divine Trinity and the assumption of humanity through the divine Word. For Paul touches upon these mysteries both here and frequently elsewhere. I will, however, touch upon them briefly for the present, for in my book *On Religion* <note>Ficino refers to his own work, "De Christiana Religione" (1474).</note> I have treated these matters more extensively. If it is the nature of the good to propagate itself, and of a greater good to spread itself further, it follows that God's infinite goodness must produce an infinite offspring of itself. Since nothing outside of God can be infinite, it is necessary that the infinite offspring of God be entirely fulfilled within God himself: namely, the Eternal within the Eternal. There, therefore, is both the Begetter <term>Genitor: the Father</term> and the Begotten <term>Genitus: the Son</term>. And since both are infinite, the Son is always equal to the Father. And since an infinite nature, because of its exact capacity, cannot be double, it follows that the nature of the Father and the Son is one and the same. Although, because of the relative opposition of the one generating and the one generated, the person is twofold. Where the Father perfectly sees himself generating another according to his will—another, indeed, only in person, but truly the same in nature, specifically in a singular nature. Hence, therefore, everything that generates anywhere strives to generate something similar and equal to itself according to its strength, and at least the same in specific nature as if generating a second self; but only the unbegotten Begetter can truly make himself into another. Furthermore, since love everywhere accompanies the good, it is necessary that alongside goodness itself and its infinite offspring, an equally infinite love flourishes between them. But since the one breathing love and the one inspired by love are opposed to each other by relation, although their nature is the same, the person is judged to be another. Therefore we are compelled to confess that in the one simple, infinite nature of God, there are three persons equal to each other and most similar. But if perhaps you ask how this generation and inspiration occurs, we shall answer that these are fulfilled through a certain mode of intellect and will. Truly, the paternal fruitfulness, by perfectly understanding itself and all things in itself, conceives in itself a perfect notion of its whole self and of all things, which is indeed a concept equal to and full of God...

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

« ...so to speak, he is the image and the super-abundant archetype <term>exemplar: an original pattern or model</term> of the world. This divine concept is not merely imaginary, as ours is, but a natural offspring. Since the nature of God is intelligence itself, and intelligence is the same as being. Therefore, what is generated internally through intelligence, generated by way of nature, exists as a natural offspring. Perhaps Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek hero and musician, often cited by Ficino as a precursor to Christian wisdom.</note>—unaware how—called this Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, who in Greek myth was born fully formed from the head of Zeus (Jupiter).</note>, born from the head of Jove alone. Plato named this son of God the Father in his *Epistle to Hermias* <note>The Sixth Epistle attributed to Plato, which discusses a "governor and father."</note>. In the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue from the Platonic circle; Ficino treated it as an essential part of Plato's philosophy.</note> he calls him the *Logos* <term>Logos: the Greek term for 'Word,' 'Reason,' or 'Plan'</term>, saying that the most divine *Logos* of all adorned this visible world. In the seventh book of the *Republic*, he signifies the invisible Son alongside God, while openly stating that the Sun is also the Son of God, but a visible one. Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet; Ficino believed his teachings prefigured Christian truths.</note> also, along with Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, attributed an intellectual offspring to God. These men said what they could, and indeed they did so with God's help. However, God alone understands this, and those to whom God has wished to reveal it. Finally, God, knowing Himself as the infinite good through that eternal notion we have mentioned, breathes forth from eternity an infinite love within Himself through that same notion. « For this reason, the Father, the Son, and the loving Spirit are called three Persons by theologians; they are entirely united in divine nature so that there is one simple God, yet they differ by an unthinkable relation. Indeed, the Father differs from the Son by nothing other than the fact that He generates, and the Son from the Father by nothing else than that He is generated; both again agree in this very thing: that by one power and reason they equally breathe the Spirit as a mutual love, proceeding from the Father through the Son, coming as if from two persons, yet from a single principle. The Spirit differs from the Father and Son together by nothing else than that He is breathed by them, while they breathe; and from the Son by nothing else than that the Son is generated, while He proceeds by breathing. If any human mind understood itself perfectly, it would vehemently love itself as understood, and would possess within itself a more distinct image of the Trinity. But now we are forced to look up at the Sun, in which God *placed his tabernacle* <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4.</note>. For in the single nature of the Sun, three powers exist equal to one another: first, the natural fertility itself, from which the inward Light always flashes forth, and from these proceeds the internal warming power. That fertility represents the Father, the inward Light the Son, and the warming power the Spirit.

### Reasons why the Divine Word assumed humanity, and concerning the world. Chapter III.

**T**hat the end of the human mind is to enjoy God can be conjectured chiefly from this: that all people naturally desire this, and find rest nowhere else. However, they cannot reach this without a certain sure faith, a firm hope, and an ardent charity <term>charitas: the theological virtue of selfless, divine love</term>. But our minds, distracted by the senses and occupied with sensible things, are not strong enough to attain these three things toward God. For, always clouded by shadows of this kind, they cannot grasp the divine light even though it is present—a light which, though naked, is sufficient for the angels' turning of their affection. But it is by no means sufficient for us. Our mind seems to have two eyes, as it were: one to look upward, the other to look downward. But when one is opened too wide, the other is meanwhile closed. Therefore, the higher eye in us is closed as long as the lower eye distracts itself entirely through the senses, looking too intently at what is offered to the senses and loving it too ardently. Thus, divine goodness, providing for us most mercifully, decreed to offer His previously invisible light to our eyes when He clothed it in humanity. He did this so that we might believe more certainly that He is God on the testimony of the very sense to which we are devoted, and that we might hope to be able to reach Him and love Him more ardently—He who became man for man’s sake, so that man might eventually become divine. Truly, we cannot easily despise the precepts of this teacher, whom we believe to be both God and man alike. That He is man, human passions demonstrate; that He is also God, His miraculous works declare. We certainly ought not to deny that we can endure what He, as a man, suffered. It is not safe to neglect the commands of God. Therefore, no remedy was more appropriate for our salvation than this very thing which divine mercy has done: that the divine light should reach our eyes under a human appearance. John the Evangelist, contemplating these and similar things, after he had said: *The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it* <note>John 1:5.</note>, brought forth the testimony of John the Baptist concerning the light made manifest to the senses. Then the divine light...

-># COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL<-

the light and the word, he says, having put on flesh, showed its glory to our eyes and gave us the power to become children of God, reborn by the Holy Spirit. For God had already become man, and the Son of Man was born of man. In that great epistle <note>Likely referring to the Gospel of John or a major Pauline letter discussed previously.</note>, the ancient prophets seem to have sensed a certain word when they introduced some one of the Gods greeting and helping men under a human figure. Why God willed that His Son, having become man, should be sacrificed for men, we shall declare with Paul in the following sections. Our <term>Plato</term> <note>Ficino famously led the Platonic Academy in Florence and viewed Plato as a precursor to Christian truth.</note> also seems to have touched upon something pertaining to the humanity assumed by God in his *Laws*, where he says: "The measure of all things is not man, but God," and most especially if God becomes man. Furthermore, when asked how long one should abide by his laws, he is said to have replied: "Until someone holier than man appears on earth to open the fountain of truth to everyone, whom everyone may then follow." Finally, if it is asked how the humanity in Christ is joined to the divinity, <term>Athanasius</term> <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his defense of the Trinity and the Incarnation.</note> answers: in the same way and manner that the body is joined to the soul in any man. <term>Thomas Aquinas</term>, however, says it is as the tongue is in the person. For God does not become a certain natural "form" of humanity in a strict sense, as the soul is to the body. Rather, humanity becomes a personal and joined "instrument" for the miracles of God—that is, for performing God’s own proper works in a miraculous way. Nevertheless, just as with the power within the Trinity, no comparison in this kind of union is entirely satisfactory. Just as an increase or a decree of the body or the tongue does not strictly pertain to the soul or the mind—even though the soul communicates vital motions to the body, and the mind communicates motions of expression to the tongue—so too in Christ the sufferings of his humanity do not touch his divinity, even if the miraculous acts of his divinity are hidden in a wonderful way through the humanity joined to it.

---

### On the Summary of the Epistle. On Adoration, On the Spiritual Worship of God.
### On the Various Rites of Sacrifice.
### Chapter IV.

**F** irst, I give thanks, etc.) The summary of the Epistle is to show that all the faithful in Rome, ,,
whether Jews or Gentiles, have been called to faith by the grace of God, and are to be ,,
saved by grace. Neither the prerogative of knowledge among the Gentiles, nor the privilege of the Law and its observation among the Jews—both of which they boasted of—suffice for divine calling or salvation. Instead, both groups equally require the grace of God for both things. This is especially clear from the fact that both groups, despite their respective advantages, had fallen into horrific vices. Since Paul is about to rebuke these vices severely, he first softens his readers and shows his love toward them in many ways, capturing their goodwill so that they might later listen to his corrections more willingly. Thus, he begins his narrative from a prayer, and his prayer from an act of thanksgiving; and while he prays himself, he teaches us how to pray. For he advises us that we should first give thanks, and then make our requests. But what and how should we ask? Spiritual goods, certainly, with the spirit raised directly toward God, not only for ourselves but for others, and that with diligence. And this only on the condition that our vow is pleasing to the divine will. Even <term>Plato</term> instructs us in his *Epistles* to begin with God. In all things, the beginning of acting and thinking must be made from God. But let us arrange his words again. "First I give thanks to my God." For the fact that you believe proceeds from the grace of God itself. "To my God," in whom I have placed my whole good, "through Jesus Christ.") For ,,
the one through whom prayers are offered is the same one through whom thanks are given. For He is the mediator and conciliator between God ,,
and men for both purposes. "For all of you.") It is a sign of the greatest charity to rejoice in the good of another and in the public good as if it were one’s own. "Because your faith is announced in the entire ,,
world." Paul, a strenuous soldier of Christ, congratulates Him first on His glory. The faith of the Roman ,,
church was being preached throughout the whole world because Rome was the head of the earth, serving as an example to all. Notice that the faith of Christ was already spread everywhere. For "their sound has gone out into all the earth." "For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of His Son.") ,,
Here he calls God as a witness to his secret prayer for the strengthening of the Romans' faith.

->## MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES<-

To this very God the Apostle serves, not in the ceremonial observance of the Jewish law, but in spirit—not indeed by affection alone, but also by the effect of Gospel preaching. They call it the Gospel of the Son of God because it was revealed by the Son of God and treats of both his births, namely the eternal and the temporal.

> "That I make mention of you without ceasing always in my prayers.") <note>Original: "Quod memoriā ueſtri facio ſine intermiſsione ſemper in orationibus meis." This is from Romans 1:9.</note> Whenever I pray, I also pray for you. And in what way? In the same way as I pray for myself and my dearest friends, namely without ceasing—that is, with completely continuous attention for the very time I have designated for prayers. Similarly, he instructs the Thessalonians: *Pray without ceasing* <note>1 Thessalonians 5:17.</note>. That is, pray with the highest attention toward God, taking care meanwhile that you are not distracted.

> "Beseeching, if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will
> "of God to come unto you.") <note>Romans 1:10.</note> And in this remembrance, I beseech above all others that if it should please the divine will, I may come to you, at least after a long time, and by whatever means, even with labor—provided it is a "prosperous journey," that is, that I finally arrive and be of use. But primarily, if God wills it. For when the head helps, all the members are helped. Perhaps, indeed, on account of his vehement desire to visit this church, Paul, having been captured in Jerusalem, appealed to Caesar <note>Paul used his rights as a Roman citizen to appeal to the Emperor, which eventually brought him to Rome as a prisoner.</note>.

> "For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual grace, to the end you may
> "be established.") <note>Romans 1:11.</note> That is, to be comforted together in you by that faith which is mutual to both you and me. What does he ultimately desire? That the wonderful grace of the Holy Spirit be imparted to them according to their capacity, so that they may worship God not in material things, but in spirit. Speaking modestly, however, he says, *to the end you may be established*, as if they had already made no small progress without him. *To be established*, I say, in the faith through which mutual hope and charity are increased, leading to mutual consolation. Through the faith, I say, which is mutual—that is, common to both.

> "Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but
> "was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles.") <note>Romans 1:13.</note>
After he had said that he desired and moreover beseeched God to go to Rome, he now adds that because of his great desire, he had often attempted the journey. Therefore, a very grave cause must now be assigned for why he did not come. Indeed, no cause is graver than the divine. He says: *I was let* <note>In older English, "let" means "hindered" or "prohibited."</note>. Since he said above that he sought the sense of the divine will, and now signifies by a very grave cause that he was prohibited but does not disclose it, it is understood that he was prohibited by God, for God wished Paul to do something more opportune in the meantime. He did not say "impeded," lest you might think he was detained by a storm or by business. <term>Plato</term> writes that <term>Socrates</term> <note>Ficino frequently compares Paul’s divine inspiration to the "daemon" or inner voice of Socrates.</note>, when attempting various things, was often prohibited by his <term>genius</term> <note>A guiding spirit or divine sign.</note>, but was never provoked to act. Certainly, a more divine cause leads the Apostle, sometimes forbidding him, other times provoking him. He assigns again the cause of his vehement desire, namely *that I might have some fruit among you*—that is, that you might bear spiritual fruit and I might gather it. *Even as among other Gentiles*, as if to say: if I have helped the members, much more ought I to help the head of the world <note>Rome was considered the "head" or capital of the world.</note>, and you should hope for fruit from me which I have produced elsewhere. Nor do I seek the favor of my benefit from you, because I am a debtor to you and to everyone, by God's command.

> "I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise. So,
> "as much as in me is, I am ready to preach the gospel to you that are at Rome also.") <note>Romans 1:14-15.</note>
He has shown and captured their goodwill in many ways. But since he writes in Greek, he here calls everyone except the Greeks "Barbarians," according to the <term>Greek custom</term>. For God had commanded that he carry His name before all nations, kings, and the people of Israel. Thus he says to the Corinthians: *Woe is unto me if I preach not the gospel* <note>1 Corinthians 9:16.</note> to the wise and the unwise. He dares to teach even the learned and deigns to instruct the unrefined. If, however, I render to you what I owe to everyone, I ask for no favor from you. As far as it lies in me, regarding my will, whenever God shall will it, I am inclined to such a duty. He said in the previous sections that he serves God in spirit, because Christ said, *the true worshippers shall worship in spirit and in truth* <note>John 4:23.</note>. Since God is as spirit and truth, He is to be worshipped in spirit and truth. In these words, Christ and Paul either disapprove of material worship or approve of it least of all. <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term>, <term>Pythagoras</term>, and likewise the Platonists <term>Iamblichus</term> and <term>Porphyry</term> <note>These were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who sought to categorize levels of divine beings and the appropriate ways to worship them.</note>, argue that there are five kinds of worship for the five kinds of spirits who are worshipped. For they say the lowest spirits inhabiting the thick air are accustomed to be worshipped with sacrifices of crops and animals; but the spirits inhabiting the pure air are worshipped with vapors, sounds, songs, and lights. However, the ethereal deities [are worshipped] with prayers...

# COMMENTARY OF SAINT PAUL

...through prayers and lights <note>referring to visual elements of ritual</note> simultaneously. But he says that intellects separated from bodies <note>meaning angels or pure intelligences</note> are worshiped through the powers and movements of the intelligence. Finally, he says the Father of these is worshiped by a certain ecstasy of the mind and an ineffable affection of the will. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries; Ficino frequently synthesizes his ideas with Christian theology</note> meanwhile condemns the Egyptians because they employed material worship more than others and were cultivators of "aerial demons" <note>In the Platonic tradition, these were spirits inhabiting the lower atmosphere, often associated with material influence</note>. He places the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages/astrologers</note> above them, as they followed a more spiritual worship, primarily honoring the minds separated from matter and the Father of those minds. Let them see to those matters. We, however, should not wander too far afield. 

Returning to Paul, we say that the primary mode of worship and prayer is that which is perfected in spirit—that is, by the intelligence and the will raised toward God through <term>charity</term> <note>Latin: *charitas*; here referring to the theological virtue of divine, selfless love rather than mere almsgiving</note>. Where it is commonly translated as "that I may impart to you some spiritual grace," it may also be interpreted as "imparting some gift of grace." For "charisma" in the Epistle to the Corinthians signifies a gift of the Holy Spirit. Here, the Apostle shows that the Romans, beyond faith—which itself is a gift of the Holy Spirit—require two further gifts: namely, intelligence and charity. By these, as if by light and fragrance together, their faith may be confirmed—that is, established and strengthened—and may become visible and active. Thus, a faith that was hitherto somewhat dim, cold, wavering, and as if lifeless, might become living and effective. For he reproaches them as if they were still too devoted to ceremonies and material things, not yet burning with charity. 

Therefore, he desires to hand down to them certain deeper meanings of the Scriptures and a more divine form of worship, and to kindle a more ardent charity within them. Through these gifts of the Holy Spirit, which he himself had received freely, that wonderful effect of spiritual gifts might arise: <term>paraclesis</term> <note>from the Greek *paraklesis*, meaning "encouragement," "exhortation," or "consolation"</note> corresponding with the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>The Holy Spirit as the Comforter or Advocate</note>. This is a consolation that recreates and nourishes the soul with both light and heat, so that it is disturbed by no adversities. He promises that this will happen through the faith common to them both—begun in the Romans but then perfected—a faith, I say, directed in both parties toward God through a charity that works good for each other. 

Furthermore, if I did not fear being wordy, I would discuss the power of light and heat. Just as light shows all things to the senses and creates images of all things, heat recreates and generates all things. Thus, charity (as heat) is better than intelligence (as light) to the same degree that it is better to produce than to show, and better to generate the things themselves than to display their likenesses. Finally, it is much more desirable for us to be nourished by heat than to be delighted by light. For this reason, our Plato says in the *Symposium* that our mind, finally joined with the Divine Mind through love, does not merely look upon the "Ideas" <note>The eternal, perfect forms of things in Platonic philosophy</note> and virtues, but now generates them within itself. Indeed, the power of love exists as a unifying and generative force; but these matters must be discussed more opportunely when we treat charity in the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

->On the power of the Gospel, double faith, and charity. How doubt, opinion, knowledge, and faith differ;<-
->on the worship of the Gentiles, and on the Mosaic law. **Chapter V.**<-

<margin>» » »</margin>
**N**on enim erubesco Euangelium Christi, uirtus enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti Iudæo primum & Græco. <note>Original Latin: "For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Romans 1:16.</note> He had heard that precept of the Savior in the Gospel of Luke: "Whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of Man be ashamed." <note>Luke 9:26.</note> Three things seem to be able to hinder the preaching of the Gospel: dangers, labors, and ignominy <note>shame or disgrace</note>. Since Paul feared no dangers for the glory of Christ, nor refused any labors, he certainly did not blush out of any suspicion of ignominy. Indeed, he knew that the Gospel was not a weak or human thing, but was filled with divine power—namely, with the Holy Spirit fortifying the preachers of the Gospel through prophecies and miracles. Paul says similar things to the Corinthians: "We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumbling block, and unto the Greeks foolishness. But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God." <note>1 Corinthians 1:23-24.</note> Likewise, the "word of the cross," although it is foolishness to those who perish, is to us the power of God. Because it did not seem that he should be ashamed of Christ either as something useless or as something foolish, he therefore called Him "the power and wisdom of God." Now, the Son of God is named Wisdom, Light, and Truth because He is born by way of intelligence. He is also named Power because in this "conception" <note>referring to the eternal generation of the Son</note> the entire potency of the Father is expressed. Paul encompasses the whole of this when writing to the Hebrews, saying: "Upholding all things by the word of his power." <note>Hebrews 1:3.</note> Truly, what does the power of God, which breathes in the Gospel word as something living and effective, work in those who believe?

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the famous passage in Romans 1:16-17 regarding the power of the Gospel and the "righteousness of God." Ficino continues his characteristic effort to harmonize Christian doctrine with the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

...does it work? Divine grace and salvation. To the Jew first and to the Greek, that is, to everyone; for under the name of "Greeks" he encompasses all worshipers of idols. Indeed, the Greeks were the primary authors of this [idolatrous] worship. But he said "to the Jew first," not because grace and salvation would belong only or even primarily to the Jews—for there is no partiality with God as far as the ultimate goal or the things necessary for that goal are concerned—but he said "to the Jew first" because the Jews, due to the privilege of the Prophets and of Christ, ought to be the first to hasten toward salvation, serving as an example to all others.

-> For the justice of God is revealed in it from faith to faith, as it is written: the just man lives by faith. <-

The divine power in the Gospel leads toward salvation and happiness primarily through three steps: through a kind of "double faith" and through justice. For one must believe not only in the Prophets who predicted that Christ would come, but also in the Apostles who affirm that he has already come. One must believe in words, and similarly believe in works; nor should one hold faith alone and simply, but rather that faith which is made "living" <note>This refers to the Scholastic concept of *fides formata* (faith formed by love), which Ficino discusses below</note> and effective in action by the accompaniment of <term>charity</term> <note>Latin: *charitas*; divine love</note>. Therefore, the listener of the Gospel, endowed with this "double faith," is judged to have attained the very <term>justice of God</term> <note>Latin: *iustitia*; often translated as "righteousness" in modern Bibles, but Ficino treats it as a philosophical virtue of soul-harmony</note> that produces blessedness. This is not merely a human justice established by the decrees of mortals, nor is it that justice, I say, found among the Jews which is content with the observation of ceremonial laws; rather, it is the Gospel justice which consists of spiritual truth. 

The Mosaic Law, given divinely, led toward justice through its observance, yet not toward that supreme justice of God itself. For it was given to those who were like slaves, unrefined and rather stubborn, suited to their character and to a specific time, rather than being the ultimate will of God. Truly, the justice of God is revealed through the Law of the Gospel. The Prophet Habakkuk said of this: "the just man," made just by this faith and justice, "now lives a certain divine life." 

Sacred Scripture uses the term "justice" to signify universal virtue. This is what Aristotle called "Legal Justice" and Plato, in the *Laws*, called the "principal intention of the laws." For justice of this kind is the observation of laws, and the laws themselves look toward and command universal virtue. In the *Republic*, Plato confirms the same, saying: Justice is the harmony of the entire soul resulting from all the virtues together. Neither the Gentiles nor the Mosaic law fully perfected this justice. For the law of the Gentiles seems to have been promulgated according to the opinions of men, and the Mosaic law according to the nature and custom of the people. But the Gospel law leads to justice—that is, universal virtue—which is not merely "civil" <note>meaning social or political ethics</note> but "purgatory" <note>cleansing the soul</note> and even belonging to the soul already purified. It uproots the secondary movements of the soul and cuts away the primary ones as much as possible, doing all of this by the grace of God. 

These four things differ among themselves: doubt, opinion, knowledge, and faith. One who doubts wavers equally between two sides. One who holds an opinion leans toward one of two opposites, but in the meantime still inclines somewhat toward the other. Knowledge, however, agrees with one side through reason, beyond controversy. But faith is directed toward one side without doubt through authority. Faith, moreover, is considered "double," as I said: for it is either "in-form" <note>unformed/rudimentary</note> or "formed" by the fervor of charity; and even if "unformed" and "formed" faith might perhaps be the same thing, it is only a virtue if it is formed by charity.

Regarding what we said above—that idolatry originated from the Greeks—our Plato confirms this in the *Cratylus*. For in explaining the name of the gods, *Theos* <note>original: "Theus"</note> in Greek, he says they were called "runners" <note>original: "currentes"; from the Greek verb *theein*, to run</note> because the ancients from the beginning worshiped the stars, which are always moving, as if they were gods. Because they also worshiped demons in the air according to the order and naming of the stars, and additionally worshiped certain men born under a specific "influence" (as they believed) of stars and demons, they consequently dedicated certain statues and sacrifices to them; of these things, all idolatry consists. 

Likewise, that the Mosaic law was not entirely absolute, but given according to the capacity of those receiving it, was "emended" not only by the Lord in the Gospel, but also by Socrates and Plato. For where that law permits revenge equal to the injury because of the ferocity of the Jews, these philosophers—in the *Crito*, *Gorgias*, *Republic*, and *Epistles*—emend this, utterly disapproving of all private vengeance. Indeed, Socrates offered the other cheek to the one striking him. 

Paul did not say the Gospel was "from" divine power, but that it "is" the power of God. He confirmed this to the Corinthians as well, saying: "The word of the cross, the Gospel, is the power of God." He often calls Christ the "Power of God," as in "we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God." When, therefore, he calls the Gospel the "Power of God," he seems to be saying that the Gospel is Christ; for certainly Christ is the Word of God, clothed in humanity by the sanctifying Spirit. The Gospel also—whether in meditation, in voice, or in writing—is the Word of God, brought forth indeed by the breathing of the Spirit, but clothed in human meditation, or voice, or writing...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino interprets Romans 1:16-17, arguing that "God's justice" is a spiritual harmony of the soul and that the Gospel is not merely a message, but is Christ Himself (the Power of God). He aligns Paul's teachings with Platonic philosophy, citing the Cratylus and the Republic to explain the origins of idolatry and the superiority of Christian non-retaliation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on St. Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. Having previously discussed the "righteousness of God" and the power of the Gospel for salvation, Ficino now transitions to the second half of Romans chapter 1, focusing on Paul’s critique of the Gentiles (pagans) and the "wrath of God" revealed against those who ignore the natural knowledge of the divine.</meta>

# THE COMMENTARY OF ST. PAUL
### PAGE 435

...the way the Divine Word is joined with a body of this kind existed from the beginning, not only in the Apostles but also in the Prophets. Thus, all of Divine Scripture speaks of Christ through the Holy Spirit as if Scripture itself were Christ—living and breathing everywhere for all those who read, hear, and meditate upon it with a certain intense affection. For this reason, Paul seems to be quietly warning us here to approach the Gospel with the highest reverence, almost in the same way we approach the Eucharist.

---

->Against the Gentiles: How they were ungrateful to God, concerning their impiety, and how they knew God through divine light. Chapter 6.<-

<margin>»</margin>
**F**or the wrath, etc. <note>Romans 1:18: "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven..."</note>) Up to this point, Paul has offered greetings to the Romans and wished them good things, especially grace and peace. He has demonstrated a feeling of immense love toward them, a long-standing desire to live among them, the reason for his long delay, his firm commitment to the Gospel, and finally, the saving promise of the Gospel. Since he has now won their goodwill and has wonderfully comforted those who would obey these saving promises, he now approaches the stubborn with threats and terrors. First, he corrects the Gentiles, and afterward, the Jews. *For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness.* <note>original: "Reuelatur enim ira Dei de cœlo super omnem impietatem, & iniustitiam eorum hominum, qui ueritatem Dei in iniustitia detinent."</note> By "ungodliness," he means the violation of divine worship. By "unrighteousness," he means the universal depravity that results from it. By "the truth of God," he means the knowledge of God held through the divine light. By "unrighteousness," he means they suppress it through ingratitude, just as one might hide a treasure in the light. 

<margin>» »</margin>
Notice how consistently he matches each opposite to its counterpart. Specifically, he said above that divine power flourishes in the Gospel, bringing salvation to believers, while in that same Gospel the "righteousness of God" is revealed through a twofold faith—which is undoubtedly attained through piety. Here, however, he follows by stating that divine wrath is revealed in the Gospel, coming from heaven as an avenger; namely, against the ungodly and the unrighteous—those who fail in the works of faith and <term>charity</term> <note>Latin: *charitas*; divine love in action</note>. He speaks especially against those who suppress the truth of God through unrighteousness, that is, through ingratitude. These are the people who excelled others in talent, learning, and philosophical ability, yet were nonetheless ungrateful to God. Indeed, they did not return the <term>natural light</term> <note>Latin: *naturale lumen*; the innate human capacity for reason and moral intuition</note>—a philosophical gift granted by God—back to God as was right, being unrighteous toward Him. This is because they did not properly worship the God they had come to know through this light. Such were the Gentiles, and the Greeks in particular. 

He calls the "wrath of God" a heavy punishment—as if God were capable of anger, it would be inflicted with the greatest fury. God afflicts curable sinners like a doctor for the sake of their health; however, He torments the incurable in the manner of an angry man, so that He may destroy them. He says "from heaven" perhaps for two reasons: because Christ is promised to come from heaven for judgment, and because just as the order of the heavenly bodies showed the Gentiles that God ought to be more rightly worshipped, so too does the heaven finally reveal God as the avenger. More broadly, he signifies the daily judgment under the figure of the Last Judgment, so that he might further terrify the ungodly. 

Moreover, he says "all ungodliness," because there are many types of impiety, which <term>Plato</term> enumerates more broadly and strikes down with lightning in the tenth book of the *Laws*. <note>Ficino frequently harmonizes Paul with Plato; here he references Plato's famous argument against atheists and those who believe God can be bribed.</note> He calls those "ungodly" who deny that God exists, those who affirm God but take away His providence, and those who admit God exercises providence but think He is not so much moved to mercy by repentance and the purification of the human mind, as He is appeased by sacrifices and gifts. Plato judges these impious opinions to be least deserving of pardon; for even if they think so poorly of God through a certain ignorance, they themselves provided the cause for their own ignorance through negligence or through a certain "intoxication" arising from the soul's disturbance. For what is proper in divine matters is taught openly everywhere—not only by the inner light but also by civil and sacred laws and the distinguished schools of the philosophers. 

Therefore, just as nothing is more acceptable to God than worshipping divine things correctly, so nothing is more detestable than violating the very worship of the divine, in which the Gentiles failed most greatly. He says they "suppress" or "detain" it, because the light of nature implanted by God remains even in the ungrateful and the proud, so that what had been a guide later becomes a judge; what was healthy for pure eyes becomes harmful for the impure. But lest they should defend their violation by saying, "How could we celebrate things we could not even know?" the Apostle dismisses the objection: *because what is known of God is manifest in them, for God has shown it to them.* What he earlier called "the truth of God," he here calls "what is known of God"—namely, that which can truly be known naturally by men regarding divine matters, and which is sufficient for the proper worship of the divine.

<summary>Ficino explains Romans 1:18, arguing that God’s wrath is a just response to those who possess the "natural light" of reason but fail to worship God. He aligns Paul’s critique of pagan impiety with Plato’s philosophical arguments against atheism and improper worship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans 1:19-20. Ficino is explaining how the "knowledge of God" was available to the pagan Gentiles through natural reason and the "light" of the mind, bridging Christian scripture with Platonic philosophy.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES
### PAGE 436

it was certainly manifest to the Gentiles themselves; and so that he might bind them more closely to this kind of worship, he immediately added that God himself revealed it to them, rather than it being the result of mere human industry and labor. However, he says "not so much *to* them as *in* them," <note>original: "non tam illis quàm in illis"</note> in order to declare that a light sufficient for the knowledge of divine things was implanted in their minds from the beginning by God. "Who shows us good things? The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us." <note>Psalm 4:6. Ficino uses this to argue that human reason is a reflection of divine light.</note> In our *Platonic Theology*, we have demonstrated through Platonic arguments that all divine truth is opened up from within by a certain divine light, especially taking from the seventh book of the *Republic* where it is taught by Plato that, just as the eye sees "sun-like" things (that is, luminous things) by the benefit of the sun, so the soul perceives divine things by the very light of God. 

Hence also that Platonic saying in the *Epistles*: "From long meditation on divine things, suddenly at last, as if from a sparking fire, a light flashes forth in the mind and thereafter nourishes itself." <note>Plato, Seventh Letter, 341c–d. This was a crucial text for Renaissance Neoplatonists regarding sudden enlightenment.</note> Hence James says that every light of truth comes from above, from the Father of Lights; from the Father who enlightens, as John says: "every man coming into this world." <note>James 1:17 and John 1:9.</note> It is said, however: *God has manifested*, because God Himself had made the common knowledge of divine things manifest to the Gentiles through the Philosophers, just as He had revealed it to the Jews through the Prophets. 

Indeed, the result of this was that both the Jews frequently boasted of their Prophets and the Gentiles of their Philosophers; and in this epistle, Paul chastises the empty boasting of both. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and the divine origin of knowledge.</note> the Platonist also attributes the inventions of the liberal arts to the Gods. He followed Plato in the *Timaeus*, who says that philosophy is a gift of the Gods, and that the knowledge of the Gods and spirits <term>daemons<gloss>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</gloss></term> descended to us through the ancient Theologians; to these men, as if they were sons of God because of their familiarity with Him, God Himself granted knowledge of Himself. Many people despise all philosophers, as if they relied on mere opinion alone and possessed no true science. Paul, however, grants them much science, even of divine things, but he accuses them of pride and ingratitude.

->*How the invisible things of God are known through visible things. How the threefold cause exists with God, and concerning the triple divine knowledge, as if of a triple heaven.*<-

### Chapter VII.

<margin>”</margin> **F**or the invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made.)
If you should ask how God opened His truth to the Philosophers, and through the Philosophers to the Gentiles, Paul responds: in two primary ways, through the <term>intelligible light<gloss>The "light" of the intellect or pure reason, which allows the mind to grasp abstract truths.</gloss></term> and the <term>sensible light<gloss>The physical light of the sun and stars that allows the eyes to see the physical world.</gloss></term>. Through the intelligible light, I say, which is naturally implanted in minds and, as Plato says in the *Republic*, is even poured over them daily. Also through the sensible light, in which He offers to our minds through our eyes the most beautiful order of the world and its miraculous craftsmanship—the most evident testimony of divine things and of divinity itself—constituted especially in the astounding splendor and order of the heavenly bodies, by which "the heavens declare the glory of God." <note>Psalm 19:1.</note> I will pass over for now how even this light, manifest to the eyes, is something incorporeal and lasting, and how through this, as if by a certain footprint, one may proceed to find divine things and the one God. For we have treated this in our book *On the Sun and Light*. 

Truly, where Paul said "manifest in them," and where he says "understood," he seems to touch upon the first light (the intelligible); but where he says "likewise seen through the things that are made," he is thought to signify the second light (the sensible). But what "invisible things of God" does he mean? Perhaps the intellectual substances <note>Meaning angels or pure intelligences.</note> which are perceived by no sense, not even an internal one, and are the effects of God alone. Certainly the Platonists, and even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, came to know such substances through the motion and order of the worldly spheres. These physical things are called "made" because they are composed of matter, but intellectual substances are thought not so much "made" as "created" out of nothing; perhaps this is what is meant by "the firmament proclaims the work of his hands." 

Furthermore, the "invisible things of God" are called the <term>archetypes<gloss>The "ideals" or "blueprints" of all things existing in the mind of God.</gloss></term> of all things in God Himself, which entirely surpass both sense and imagination. Paul seems to signify this to the Hebrews: "We understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things were made." <note>Hebrews 11:3.</note> Truly, in the very concept of the divine intelligence, the <term>ideal ratios<gloss>The mathematical and logical principles underlying creation.</gloss></term> of all these things extend outward; for He made the heavens in the intellect. From these Ideas, as if from models, all visible things were produced, so that they themselves are rightly known by philosophers through these images. There are two "worlds" <note>original: "secula"</note>: eternity and time. The Word, therefore—that is, the divine reason, the artisan of things—so joined these worlds together that temporal things would depend on eternal ones, and likewise so that the images of the Ideas flashing in eternity might shine back in the temporal world. He says, however, "they are seen, being understood,"

He reconciles St. Paul's theology with Plato's "Republic" and "Timaeus," arguing that the physical world serves as a visible mirror for God's invisible, eternal archetypes.</summary>
