### COMMENTARY ON THE DIVINE PAUL
# PAGE 413

For the mind, as soon as it has been warned by sense and has contemplated the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Platonic Ideas are the eternal, perfect patterns or "blueprints" of all things existing in the divine mind.</note>, soon returns to these sensible things more diligently, and with greater admiration than before. These things are to be "clearly seen from the creation of the world," unless he had added "of the world," perhaps it might be interpreted as "by man," since in him is every creature, though that would not be quite fitting. But since he says, "from the creation of the world," we shall explain it more aptly: that from the very beginning of the world, philosophical minds have begun to thoroughly investigate the divine art (by which all these things are most beautifully arranged) through the craftsmanship of the world, which is everywhere to be marveled at, so that the knowledge of divine things is not new to men, but ancient. 

Our Plato argues in the *Protagoras* that before all arts, from the beginning of things, men—because of a certain kinship with divinity and an intimate notion—began to sense the presence of God and to venerate divine things. Furthermore, in the *Timaeus*, he investigated God from the "creature," that is, the making of the world, in almost this way: the world, since it certainly falls under the senses, therefore does not have a completely perfect essence. Deservedly, it depends on some higher cause, and this one work comes from one cause at last; the most beautiful work from the wisest cause, and the best possible work from Goodness itself; and since it is composed most skillfully, it comes from the highest art and an exact model existing within the cause. 

We, therefore, in our *Commentaries on the Timaeus*, track down three causes of the work within God from this craftsmanship. From the **magnitude** of the machine, its most rapid and perpetual motion, and the wonderful powers of almost innumerable things, we find an admirable virtue and **Power** in the cause. From the wonderful **order** and skillful beauty, we find **Wisdom** and a providence that is utterly incomparable. From the common **utility** of things and the direction of all things toward the good as if toward an end, we find a provident and wonderful **Goodness**. 

These three, therefore—Power, Wisdom, and Goodness—as is pleasing to the Theologians, seem to represent the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Indeed, we call Divine Power especially the *efficient cause* of the world; Wisdom, consequently, the *exemplary cause* <note>The "exemplary cause" is the model or pattern (the Ideas) after which something is made.</note> of this work; and finally, Goodness the *final cause*. 

Our Plato declared this threefold order of the cause within God to King Dionysius, expressing the model when he said: "All things are from him, and through him, and in him." <note>original: "ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipsum omnia." Ficino is likely conflating Romans 11:36 with the pseudo-Platonic Second Letter (312e).</note> He expresses to us the *efficient* cause in "from him," the *exemplary* in "through him," and the *final* cause in "in him." Wherefore, touching upon these three in the present passage, Paul first brings forward the exemplary cause, saying: **The invisible things of God**, that is, the intelligible Ideas of things, are conjectured through their visible images in the world. Then he brings the efficient cause within God, where he says: **his eternal power also**. Lastly, the final cause, when he adds: **and divinity**. 

**Eternal power**, that is, infinite power, which even the Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian</note> philosophers seem to investigate from the perpetual and all-forming motion of the vast machines. The Platonists also do so by many reasons, which we explain in our *Theology* and in our *Commentaries on Plato*. Paul seems to call the divine goodness—insofar as it is the end of all things and provides for all—**divinity**, because the highest cause of things is the end, as Plato proves, and the principal name of God is "the Good," from which "divinity" is named, that is, goodness; and "the good," as Aristotle says, is the common divine element. 

We certainly do not say that the philosophers found the **Deity** <note>original: "Deitatem"</note> itself from the works. For this is the very substance of God, unknown to them as of yet; but they found **divinity** <note>original: "diuinitatem"</note>, that is, the beneficent and provident diffusion through all things, and meanwhile its set-apart excellence. Hence we think there is a threefold knowledge of God, like a "triple heaven," as we write in the book *On the Rapture of Paul*. For either God is recognized in things, or things are known in God, or God is known in Himself. 

The philosophers seem to have possessed two modes, like two heavens. For they grasped both how much "divinity" is in the world, and by what ratio the "model" of the world is expressed in God. However, what God himself is in himself, even Plato confesses in the *Parmenides* is unknown. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whom Ficino believed was the convert of St. Paul mentioned in Acts 17:34.</note> confirms the same, and only Paul, "caught up to the third heaven," attained it. 

We must investigate more diligently why he said, **being understood, they are clearly seen**, for it seemed rather that he should have said, "by sight they are understood," for through the sight one arrives at understanding. But Paul seems here to touch upon what he also says to the Corinthians: "we see now through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face." <note>1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> Here, therefore, he seems to be explained thus: "being understood, they are clearly seen," that is, when they are understood here by us, they are known by way of a vision in a mirror; for "is clearly seen" <note>original: "καθορᾶται"</note> signifies this. Plato and Plotinus think that only the Ideas are true things, while the natural forms of true things are images of the Ideas, resulting from the influences of the invisible Ideas upon the matter of the world itself, as if reflecting in a mirror to the sense. By the sight of these images, you see that men are so deceived that they believe...

...they think [these appearances] are real, just as infants take the images appearing in a mirror to be entirely true things. Hence perhaps Solomon calls matter "unity"—a "displaying unity"—and "all is vanity," <note>Ficino refers to Ecclesiastes 1:2. The Latin "vanitas" implies both emptiness and a deceptive appearance.</note> that is, all things deceive and render judgment empty and false. Philosophers, however, and especially the Platonists, by considering the forms in the matter of the world, recognize that they are likenesses of the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic thought, Ideas are the eternal, perfect archetypes in the divine mind of which worldly things are mere shadows.</note>, just as men, by the images in a mirror, realize there are just as many real things behind them. Turning their faces toward these Ideas in the other life, they contemplate them clearly, as Paul says, "face to face," <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note> crying out almost like the Prophet: *Lord God of virtues, turn us. Let your face shine upon us, and we shall be saved.* <note>Psalm 80:19 (Vulgate 79:20). Original: "Domine Deus uirtutum conuerte nos. Illumina uultum tuum super nos, & salui erimus."</note>

### Chapter VIII.

->Inexcusable are those who, having known God, did not worship Him. How they became vain and foolish,<-
->and why and how they worshiped others besides God.<-

**S**o that they are inexcusable.) In addition to those three types of impiety that we described in the previous sections—which are condemned by the Platonic law—Paul pursues a fourth against the Gentiles, common among them and worthy of no pardon. For it is by no means permitted to defend this with the excuse of ignorance. Among these people, not only the Laws but also the Philosophers most aptly celebrate one God as the founder of all things, providing for each, the beginning and the end of all things. Thus, no one ought to have been ignorant of this, unless they were either utterly negligent by choice or voluntarily intoxicated by disturbances of the soul. A just Judge will forgive none of these, as they are essentially voluntary faults of our ignorance; therefore, he said these people are inexcusable. *Because when they had known God, etc.* <note>Romans 1:21</note> Indeed, they knew Him—not only the philosophers themselves, but even the common people who were instructed by the laws and the philosophers. 

They knew, I say, that if all things come from the First, then by the highest right, all things must be returned to the First. If they also tend toward the First as if toward an end, then all things are deservedly dedicated to Him. He is to be venerated in all things and above all things. For His sake, all things must be thought of, sought, and likewise acted upon. If every light of truth comes from Him, then the thanks for every true discovery must be referred back to Him. If all good things come from the same source, we must confess that we are indebted to Him alone, or most of all. 

For this reason, Paul most sharply detests the fourth species of impiety: when someone transfers the glory owed to the First to something else, either as if it were God or something divine. He asserts that this impiety is the highest injustice. For that which we owe entirely to the First, we take away from Him and hand over to others unworthily and undeservedly. Therefore he added: *They did not glorify Him as God, or give thanks.* That is, they did not worship Him with a specific obedience, as was fitting. Nor did they give thanks, either solely or primarily, for the divine light by which [the truth] was discovered, or for any good they received. 

And since we have just mentioned "light," we ought to remember that Plato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, proves that human minds receive a twin light from God, even in this life. The first is a private light, naturally implanted in each individual. The other is a light common to all, extended in any contemplation of the mind, by which they are able to understand both all true things and the very source of truths—just as the eyes have a twin light from the Sun: one internal and one from the day, by which they see other things and the Sun itself. Concerning these matters, we dispute extensively in the seventh book of our *Republic* commentary, our book *On the Sun*, and in our *Theology*. 

The Apostle therefore rebukes the Gentiles because they neither pursued the discovered God with due honor and affection, nor gave any thanks for the light by which they had found Him. Finally, the true worship of God is to think of God frequently, and to love Him ardently for His own sake. It is to give thanks and pray in all things, and to compose one’s whole life according to His will and imitation; this, the Gentiles did not do at all. External ceremonies are not the worship itself, but signs of worship. 

*But they became vain in their thoughts.* What is written in Latin as "thoughts" is held in Greek as <term>dialogismois</term> <note>Original Greek: διαλογισμοῖς. This term can mean "reasonings," "disputes," or "calculations."</note>, that is, inventions, or argumentations, discourses, and syllogisms. To "become vain" here means, so to speak, to become proud, to glory emptily, and to take delight. This whole concept is fundamentally opposed to the two things just proposed: for it is against that which is called "glorifying" and, again, "giving thanks." For philosophers generally, after they have embraced the order of the universe in their minds and from this have reached the one Orderer of all, have been accustomed to take marvelous delight in this discovery as if it were their own most beautiful offspring—loving it ardently and dwelling within it as if it were the ultimate end...

He aligns Paul's theology with Platonic concepts of Ideas and the intellectual "light" provided by the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans 1:21. The previous page discussed how philosophers recognized God through his works but failed to honor him. This page explores the psychological and spiritual mechanics of that failure—how pride leads to a "darkening" of the mind and eventually to the worship of idols and demons.</meta>

<page-num>419</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL</header>

...to rest entirely within [themselves], which indeed seems to represent that arrogant crime of Lucifer. For because of an excessive love and joy in their own conception, they have, as if forgetting, failed to venerate God or to give thanks to the author of such great discovery. Meanwhile, trusting in their own strengths, they acted as if they had sought and found [truth] by their own industry, rather than by the light and help granted from heaven. This is just as if someone, seeing what is under a full Moon, fails to recognize that he has perceived it by the light of the Sun. Perhaps this is what the verse intends: *Day unto day pours forth speech,* <note>Psalm 19:2 (Vulgate 18:3). original: "Dies diei eructat uerbum"</note> that is, the divine light dictates a discovery to the pious mind; *and night unto night shows knowledge,* that is, out of self-confidence, it suggests ingratitude—perhaps even through the "nightly" confidence of the devil, it increases our ingratitude and our own murky opinion of ourselves. *And their foolish heart was darkened,* <note>Romans 1:21</note> just as an eye turning away from the Sun becomes dark—deprived, evidently, of the Sun’s splendor—so the intellect, distracted from God by the love and joy of its own self, does not bring back that promised blessed light of grace and becomes dark; it is deprived of divine wisdom because of its opinion of human wisdom.

Indeed, anyone who places his love and joy not so much in God (once found) as in his own discovery, can never perceive the ineffable light and joy flourishing in God’s presence. He never tastes, nor sees, *how sweet the Lord is,* <note>Psalm 34:8. original: "quàm suauis sit Dominus"</note> nor does he grasp those treasures which God has hidden for those who love Him. For this reason, he is judged to be vain, empty, dark, and foolish. And if the Philosophers sometimes thought they possessed the light of intelligence—by which they see God—from a divine source, they nevertheless seem, like drunkards, to have forgotten the divinity and true worship because of their excessive joy and love in their own discovery. For even if they occasionally did so through some light imagination or words, they never seem to have pursued God Himself with thanksgiving or praise with their entire affection. *Claiming to be wise, they became fools.* <note>Romans 1:22. original: "Dicentes esse sapientes stulti facti sunt"</note> For from this very fact—that they gloried in their own contemplation as if it were some wise discovery of their own—they became fools, evidently having not attained divine light and wisdom.

Notice, meanwhile, the fitting sequence in Paul’s words. For what he adds—*claiming to be wise*—consequently pertains to what he had said: *they became vain.* Again, what he just added—*they became fools*—timely regards where he says: *their foolish heart was darkened.*

A ray descending perpendicularly from God Himself into the soul, if it finds the soul tilted or uneven, leaps away from it transversely; it does not demonstrate God, but is merely an empty flickering in the soul. I call it "vain" because it lacks the object from which it comes and the end for whose sake it comes. But if it finds a mind that is entirely level and balanced, it immediately bounces back to God, and happily carries the mind with it to grasp its object and its end. There the mind, finally enjoying God, also enjoys itself—that is, attaining its own self within the <term>Idea</term> <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, the "Idea" is the perfect blueprint of the soul existing eternally in the mind of God.</note>. However, the soul that first attempts to rest within itself, because of this injustice, neither reaches God nor enjoys itself, because it lacks the Idea which is the "true soul" and in which the soul is formed. Hence it is called dark, empty, and foolish.

That this impious person also immediately turned out to be a fool, the Apostle demonstrates by the outcome, through what follows: *And they changed etc.* <note>Romans 1:23: "And changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man..."</note> The leaders of the Gentile religion, who were both Philosophers and Poets, seem to have sinned not only through this pride and ingratitude toward God, but also to have fallen through an excessive love of worldly goods or fear of evils. For although they had found—under the highest God—not only intellects separated from bodies (whom they name "extra-mundane gods"), but also intellects joined to the heavenly bodies (whom they call "mundane gods"), namely the spheres and the stars, and also <term>daemons</term> <note>In the ancient sense, "daemons" were not necessarily evil, but intermediate spirits inhabiting the air.</note> in either the pure or thick air, they established and maintained adorations and sacrifices to these mundane gods rather than to the superior ones, and especially to the daimons among the mundane ones. They hoped, evidently, that by the worship of mundane powers they would obtain worldly goods and avoid evils. And so they accustomed the common people to be even more eager to make vows and sacrifices to daimons. Indeed, they even hoped to be heard by these nearby powers more than by the superior ones. This sacrilege seems to have grown quite strong from an excessive greed for riches, which serve the needs and lusts of life—things which daimons are believed to supply. Thus Paul rightly wished to call greed "the service of idols." Finally, what is judged not only impious but even ridiculous, they gave many animals over to be worshiped by the common people, animals which were (as they thought) subject to certain daimons. Now indeed, <term>Iamblichus</term> and <term>Porphyry</term> <note>Later Neoplatonic philosophers (3rd–4th century AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and the nature of Egyptian and Greek rituals.</note> disapproved of the sacred rites of the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, because [of their focus on] either bodily goods or evils...

While the previous page discussed the psychological descent into pride and "darkening" of the heart, this page (numbered 440 in the source) analyzes Romans 1:23, where Paul describes the transition from worshipping God to worshipping idols of men and animals. Ficino uses this to bridge Christian theology with Platonic and Hermetic philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

grace, they would worship corporeal powers rather than incorporeal ones; but let us now return to the context of the words themselves.
» (**And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents.**) <note>Romans 1:23</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Here he indeed calls God "incorruptible" in comparison to man. But elsewhere he says: **who alone has immortality** <note>1 Timothy 6:16. original: "qui solus habet immortalitatē"</note>, because He alone is immortal through Himself. Our Plato introduces something similar in the *Timaeus*, but observe, I pray, with what skill and with what great indignation at the same time the most powerful Paul suddenly casts the Gentiles down like a bolt of lightning from the highest to the lowest. For he remained silent about the fact that they brought the veneration of the highest God down to the stars and <term>demons</term> <note>In Ficino's Neo-Platonic view, *daemones* are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>—which indeed would have been less surprising—but he immediately brought in the fact that the glory due first [to God] was given to corruptible man. He also lamented that they did not even worship a living man, but a likeness; and not only of a man, but of brutes; and not only of the more noble ones, but even of serpents. Among these things, consider what was said concerning man: *into the likeness of an image of corruptible man.* For the Platonists and Homer, as well as Maro <note>Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>, called our body the "image of the soul." The Apostle, alluding to this, censures the Gentiles because they did not worship the soul of the man itself, nor even the animated body of the man, which is called the "image of the soul," but they honored a likeness of the body—that is, a statue or a painting. But should it be thought that the most learned priests of that religion worshipped such things as mere names? Not at all. Rather, they gave the common people the handles for such an absurd adoration. Certainly, just as we discuss in the *Commentaries on Plato and Plotinus*, and in the third book of *On Life* <note>Ficino's famous work *De vita libri tres*, specifically Book III, *De vita coelitus comparanda* (On Obtaining Life from the Heavens).</note>, the ancient sages arranged certain long "chains" <note>The "Great Chain of Being" or series of correspondences.</note> of the worldly gods (as they call them), demons, and the powers following them in order. Under a particular star they placed certain celestial inhabitants; under these, others in the air in succession; and then other demons, endowed with the same property and name as the ones above. <term>Saturnians</term> <note>People or objects influenced by the planet Saturn.</note> under Saturn, <term>Jovians</term> under Jupiter, and Martials and Phoebians <note>Those under Mars and Apollo/the Sun.</note>, and others similarly. Furthermore, under the Saturnian or Jovian demons, they placed Saturnian and Jovian men. Then animals (besides man) belonging to this or that celestial body, or inhabitant, or demon; and not only animals, but even plants, metals, and certain stones were thought to have at least the "imaginary" properties of the higher beings. And though I will set aside for now how the Magi, through the selection and composition of lower things, taught men to seasonably draw down certain higher things that are congruent with the lower. Certainly the priests of that religion, who were the same as the Magi, when they dedicated temples to the celestials, celestial inhabitants, and demons, also placed statues of men there, arranged in a certain series, whom they believed to have been born under a particular influence of such powers and endowed with their gift. And they called a man "Saturn" or "Jupiter," who was constituted under the celestial or aerial Saturn or Jupiter. They also employed animals, woods, metals, stones, and characters <note>Signs or talismans.</note>—images congruent with those same powers. Perhaps they especially used animals whose likenesses they had noted or fashioned in the sky <note>A reference to the constellations of the Zodiac.</note>. Concerning these things, however, we dispute more extensively in the third book of *On Life*. Furthermore, they wished, as I believe, to indulge the common people too much, who were greedy for lower goods and devoted to superstitions of that kind. By this indulgence, they subjected the blind and wretched common folk to the worship of the lowest things. Mercury Ter Maximus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> is a witness that the fathers of the Egyptian religion were accustomed to place statues in temples manufactured by magic art, and to "awaken" demons and the souls of the deceased into them. Now Orpheus, the great author of that religion, consecrated many hymns not only to the celestials, but also to demons and demonic men, and applied certain fumigations to certain ones. Moreover, many civil priests and poets introduced superstitions that were much more old-womanish, unjust, and foul, while at the same time fortune incited evil demons everywhere. This Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Important Neoplatonic philosophers who wrote on theurgy and ritual.</note> confess. Rightly, therefore, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar. His "three theologies" are a major theme in St. Augustine's *City of God*.</note>, where he describes the three theologies—the Philosophical, the Civil, and the Poetic—judges the latter two to be far inferior to the first. For this reason, since Rome, as the head of the world where all things flowed together, admitted all the superstitions of all peoples, and received in its temples the eagle from the Greeks, the ox and the crocodile from the Egyptians, the dragon from the Babylonians, and similar things from everywhere, Paul rightly, among the Romans, against these superstitions especially,

He uses both Saint Augustine and Plato to explain how God "gives over" the prideful to their own destructive passions.</meta>

<header>ON THE COMMENTARY ON PAUL</header>

### How the impious slip again from guilt into punishment, and from punishment into guilt, and how God gives them over to disturbances and yields them to demons. Chapter 9.

<margin>»</margin> (**For which cause He gave them over**, etc.) <note>Romans 1:24</note> No one sins more gravely or miserably than one who, like the rebel angel <note>Lucifer</note>, falls away from God—the creator and giver of all good things—through ingratitude and pride. For such a person, like that unhappy angel, sins and is punished perpetually. They fall, as if in a certain circle, from sin into punishment, and from punishment back again into sin. This is because in this circular succession, the punishment for a sin is often itself a similar sin, subsequently producing further sin and punishment. Hence the saying: *The wicked walk in a circle.* <note>Psalm 12:8 (Vulgate 11:9). original: "Impij autem in circuitu ambulant."</note> Therefore, Paul follows this remarkable sequence in a long series, frequently repeating the cycle of guilt and vengeance. First, you saw ingratitude and pride: *Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful.* <note>Romans 1:21</note> Immediately following this is a punishment that is also a sin: *But became vain in their imaginations.* After this comes another retribution which is equally a sin: *Their foolish heart was darkened.* Then follows further vengeance which is likewise a transgression: *Professing themselves to be wise.* <margin>''</margin> Following this is yet another penalty and a further crime: <margin>''</margin> *They became fools.* Because of this foolishness, they *changed the glory* <margin>''</margin> *of the incorruptible God*, and so forth. This exchange, as a detestable sin, deserves the subsequent punishments and crimes that follow in turn: *Wherefore God gave them up to the uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts.* <note>Romans 1:24</note> However, it should not be read as "gave them up *into* the desires," but rather "*in* the desires" <note>original: "non autē legēdum est, tradidit in desideria, sed in desiderijs." Ficino is making a philological point based on the Greek preposition *en*.</note>—that is, at the moment they were desiring these things, He gave them over to uncleanness. For so the Greek text has it. I say He "gave them over," not by instilling malice, but by withdrawing grace. It is only right that he who left God for the love of an inferior thing should be deserted by God and left under the condition of that inferior thing. Here I cannot pass over what our <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential North African theologian.</note> says: *It is manifest that God works in the hearts of men to incline their wills wherever He wishes, whether toward good things by His mercy, or toward evil things according to their merits, by His judgment—sometimes open, sometimes hidden, but always just.* But whether God only permits such inclinations, as we touched upon above, or whether He sometimes moves them in a certain way (as Aurelius [Augustine] testifies), in the case of the diabolical and the proud, sin definitely relapses into punishment, and punishment into sin. When Augustine says that God sometimes "moves the inclination toward evil," understand this not as the <term>evil of guilt</term> <note>original: "malū culpæ." The moral stain of the sin itself.</note>, but as the <term>evil of punishment</term> <note>original: "malū poenæ." The suffering or consequence resulting from sin.</note>; and if both are joined, it is moved toward the evil insofar as it is a penalty, not insofar as it is a sin. 

Therefore, God gave over such ungrateful and proud people to the desires of their heart—that is, He at least permitted and allowed that minds rebelling against Him should themselves feel the rebellion of their own senses, and succumb by a just penalty to often intolerable disturbances. And those who transferred the glory of God to beasts were themselves cast headlong into becoming beasts. He says, therefore, not "into desire," but "into desires" <note>Plurality of passions.</note>. Since the crowd of disturbances in the senses is like a "multiple animal" (as in the *Phaedrus*), or rather an "all-kind animal," as is taught in the ninth book of the *Republic* <note>Plato’s image of the soul's lower passions as a multi-headed beast.</note>. Indeed, he called this entire crowd of desire by the name of "love" <note>In the sense of misplaced or disordered love/lust.</note>. For just as from the love of divine things all tranquility and virtue are born, so from the love of mortals all disturbance and depravity occur. 

He pursues the lusts of the idolaters—having fallen through the abuse of nature—which the Philosophers also call "monstrous," using very open words. Like a writer of <term>Satires</term> <note>A reference to Roman satirical poets like Juvenal or Persius who used graphic imagery to provoke disgust at vice.</note>, he places the deformed and shameful face of such lusts before our eyes, moving our stomachs so that he may make them openly abominable; meanwhile, in the manner of a tragedy, he reveals into what a low and miserable lot those who have fallen away from the Highest through ingratitude and pride have collapsed. Socrates also, in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, condemns lusts against nature with longer and more open words. But, lest he be hindered by shame, he speaks with his head covered <margin>''</margin> so that the listeners may be warned how shameful it is to do these things, when even to name them is shameful. <margin>''</margin> Paul, however, does not blush, nor is he restrained by modesty. For just as blushing is becoming to a boy but unbecoming to an adult, so any sort of modesty might befit a man speaking from a merely human disposition. But into a mind divinely inspired, neither modesty nor any similar disturbance falls. 

It seems that Paul touches upon three "theologies" of the Gentiles. The **Civil** theology, by which the Priests arranged statues, sacrifices, and ceremonies in the temples, where he says: *and they changed the glory of God.* The **Poetic** theology, which the Poets introduced in the theaters, where he says: *and they changed the truth of God into a lie*, or, as the Greek text has it, *in a lie*. Which tends toward the same thing. Lastly, the **Philosophical** theology, by which...

<summary>Ficino explains the "vicious cycle" of sin described in Romans 1, arguing that God punishes pride by withdrawing grace and allowing the wicked to fall into increasingly degrading passions. He harmonizes Paul's harsh rhetoric with Platonic philosophy and Augustinian theology regarding the nature of divine judgment.</summary>

<page-num>442</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

The philosophers taught [the people] to worship the spheres of the world, the stars, and spirits <note>Latin: dæmones. In Ficino's Neoplatonic view, these are intermediary beings between humans and the divine, though here they are associated with the falling away from the true God.</note>. When Paul says, **and they worshipped the creature**, he means they served the created thing rather than the Creator; in this kind of worship, it can be said that the divine truth is changed into a lie. Indeed, the responses of spirits received from the stars are often lies, as even Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher often cited by Ficino.</note> admits. Furthermore, they are said to have turned into a lie that truth-telling light infused by God—through which they came to know some truths about Him—because they did not pursue it with a sincere and devoted affection. Consequently, led on by human conjectures and passions, they fell into certain lies concerning God: either thinking that He does not care for the smallest things, or that He does less good for humans without the intercession of intermediary deities. One may even call the idols worshipped by the Gentiles "lies." These practices seem to have been allowed and even encouraged by the philosophers. Indeed, Paul detests two things most of all in the worship of the Gentiles. One is that many, having forgotten the Creator, adored created things. The other is that many, because of greed and lust, transferred that supreme worship and mental affection due to the highest God toward certain worldly deities, especially those closer to them. And so, to declare that supreme worship must first be attributed to God alone, he said: <margin>»</margin> **Who is blessed for ever. Amen.** <note>Romans 1:25</note> Truly, he repeats three times: <margin>»</margin> **God gave them over**, and so forth. <note>Romans 1:24, 26, 28</note> Perhaps this is to warn us that God abandons the impious in three stages, according to three degrees of impiety. For when impiety is just beginning, God Himself also begins to withdraw His breath and influence. As it grows, He withdraws it more and more, degree by degree. Finally, when impiety is complete, He pulls back entirely and deserts them, granting the highest license and power over the impious to all manner of falling disturbances and spirits—for that is what it seems to mean to "give them over." Furthermore, He gives them over to be driven as if by three Furies <note>In Greek mythology, the Furies were deities of vengeance; here used as a metaphor for psychological torment.</note>: first by the sluggish disturbances of the senses, second by craftier ones, and third by a reason already perverted by malice. He gives them over everywhere to the "destroying angels," whom all the impious imitate and worship. If you seek an example to understand more clearly how the impious are deserted by God because of their own faults—without God Himself changing—consider how the Sun commonly pours out its light upon open eyes. But if eyes are squinting, it provides less and less light, degree by degree. To eyes that are completely closed, it imparts nothing at all, but rather "gives over" such eyes to darkness. Thus, the person who disdained the Sun began to see phantoms and grow blind gradually, until now, as is fitting, overwhelmed by darkness, he stumbles and falls everywhere as he deserves. The Platonists think a threefold light is divinely infused into souls, just as a threefold light is given to the eyes by the Sun. The first is the light natural and proper to each individual. The second is a common light poured over those who are contemplating. The third and final light is shown or displayed to the heavenly beings and to souls that have either already returned to heaven or are sometimes "abstracted" <note>Meaning pulled away from the body in a state of mystical ecstasy.</note> while still here. Plato speaks of the first two by the example of the Sun in the *Republic*. Regarding the third, he speaks in the *Symposium* and the *Phaedrus*; this light relates to blessed or abstracted souls just as the pure light of the Sun is thought to relate to the celestial eyes of the heavenly dwellers. Therefore, God does not take away the first light from sinners, but leaves it as a punishment. He denies the second light more or less, and denies it entirely to the lost. Lastly, He grants the third light eternally in the "fatherland" <note>A common theological term for Heaven.</note>, while outside the fatherland He reveals it through a certain flashing to human minds when they occasionally exceed their limits, and He proves human fallacies. *I said in my excess, "Every man is a liar."* <note>Psalm 116:11 (Vulgate 115:11). original: "Ego dixi in excessu meo omnis homo mendax."</note>

### How those who did not approve of having God in their knowledge slip into all evils. Chapter 10.

<margin>»</margin> **And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient.** <note>Romans 1:28</note> Where the Latin text says **mind** <note>original: "sensum"</note>, the Greek has **intellect**. It is right for the mind to be understood as the intellect, because they do not yet return to their senses, but fall into other outrages for the same fault. Paul likens the punishment to the sin: just as they sinned in their "sense" (knowledge) of God, so they are punished in their own "sense" (reason); and just as they do not perform duties that are fitting and consistent with the knowledge of God, so they collapse into outrages that are not fitting for the dignity of a human being. Now, they slip away from lusts that are not only human but monstrous—which were described above with indignation—into a manifold iniquity produced by the demonic malice of the spirit. But what does it mean that **they did not approve of having God in their knowledge**? Certainly, they showed by no works of theirs that they possessed the knowledge of God. Which they nevertheless [possessed]...

...Paul confesses they possessed. For they performed no duty consistent with this knowledge. In this matter, observe that Paul spoke with great weight of meaning when he said, "to have God in their knowledge," rather than merely "to have knowledge of God." For all those who dispute about Him with true reasons according to their own judgment have a "knowledge of God." But in this "knowledge of God," only those also "have God" Himself who, burning with divine love, are joined to God as if through this flame; they think little of all other things and emerge strong for the glory of God.

Indeed, a pious soul turning toward God proceeds fortified by three divinely granted graces: certain faith, firm hope, and fervent charity. It seems that the Son primarily offers the certainty of faith, the Spirit offers the heat of love, and the Father primarily offers the firmness of hope. Therefore, God enters the soul accompanied by these three graces: with a certain new light, an incomparable joy, and an invincible strength. The Son seems to bring the light especially, the Spirit the joy, and the Father the strength. The light of faith is primarily distributed, then the joy of hope, and finally the strength of love. These three are the most certain proofs of the very presence of God. But he who does not have these yet says he "has God" is surely lying to himself. Therefore, it was rightly said: *God rejoices in an odd number <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet." This is a famous line from Virgil’s Eclogues (8.75), which Ficino here applies to the Trinity.</note>, that is, the number three, both in receiving and in giving.* Hence the saying: *and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.* Similarly, those who perceive wine by sight and smell have some "knowledge of wine." But those who truly taste it now "have the wine itself in their knowledge." Only these people thoroughly feel the power and fruit of the wine. For this reason, those who are now more closely joined through loving affection with the God they have come to know can be said to "have God in their knowledge." Since God is love, he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. They can also cry out with the Prophet: *You shall give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure; we shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house.* Therefore, God hands over to a "reprobate sense" <note>Romans 1:28. Ficino is playing on the Latin words "probauerunt" (approved) and "reprobum" (reprobate/disapproved).</note> those who indeed know Him but do not "have Him as known"—that is, those who do not embrace Him with love. For it is just that if they did not "approve" of God, they should fall into what is "disapproved." But into what kind of reprobate state? First, into a reprobate sense—that is, an intellect by which they think of nothing except what is far removed from uprightness, and for this reason, they are to be "reproved" by God and by pious men. This is like a person with bleary eyes who flees the light, or a person with a corrupted sense of taste who rejects healthy things and craves harmful ones. Hence the Apostle's saying: *they will not endure sound doctrine.* Then, they fall into the cruel power of a "reprobate demon," as if into the power of Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of Hades in Greek mythology, used here to represent demonic entrapment.</note>. Wounded and utterly infected by his rabid bite, these impious men bite and infect others everywhere; they delight in their crimes against the very order of nature—if I may put it that way—and in the meantime, they are most truly tortured within this false delight.

<margin>»</margin> Therefore, the Apostle, having moved against them, says: *Being filled with all iniquity.*) Even Paul, who is usually brief, now appears more wordy, stirred by a longer indignation; in a kind of invective, and in the manner of those who drive a point home, he heaps up many of the poisonings and crimes of the impious. He does this so that everyone might be warned to flee far away with all their might from that poisonous and miserable impiety, which is oppressed by so many and such great crimes and punishments at once.

<margin>»</margin> When he says *filled with all iniquity and what follows.*) He exaggerates the wretched fault of impiety in two ways: first, because all vices exist within it and arise from it; and second, because each individual vice is present to the highest degree. As the Book of Wisdom affirms, the worship of unspeakable idols is the cause of every evil. By "iniquity," he means "injustice." For this is what the Greek text <term>adikia<gloss>injustice or unrighteousness</gloss></term> properly has, and injustice itself signifies every vice. Hence the saying of John: *all sin is iniquity.* Just as "legal justice" encompasses all virtues—as Aristotle also testifies—so "injustice" covers all vices. For that which is against the law is "unjust." And every sin is against divine, natural, and civil law. Injustice is a kind of turning away from God. This turning away is included in every single sin. Paul subsequently divides "injustice" into many sins, because of the various and all-unjust turnings toward created things. But first, he repeats things pertaining to the lusts mentioned above, though here they are treated more as crimes committed through contempt for the law or for the person. For among the ancients, "wickedness" <note>Latin: nequitia</note> is a kind of licentious wantonness that cannot restrain itself.

<margin>»</margin> *Fornication.*) *Fornication is any sexual intercourse prohibited by law.* Where the Latin manuscripts have "malice" <note>Latin: malitiam</note> after "iniquity," translated from the Greek <term>ponēria<gloss>wickedness or malice</gloss></term>, I more willingly...

<page-num>444</page-num>
-> ### MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES ### <-

I place "wickedness" <note>original: *nequitiam*</note> as a term more suited to the Greek word and consistent with the "fornication" mentioned just before it. Then we come to new crimes: "avarice," and "malice" or "depravity." For where "wickedness" <note>original: πονηρία (*ponēría*)</note> is translated from the Greek after "avarice," I prefer to interpret it as "malice" or "depravity." This is more in harmony with its etymology. In "avarice," indeed, we strive for money for the sake of satisfying our lusts. For we use craftiness and depravity to pursue both lusts and money. **Full of envy, murder.** He then piles up the crimes of injustice. It was not enough for such a person to acquire perceived goods for himself, unless he also thought to hinder others from having them; thus, he envies those who have or will have them, and because of this envy, he plots "murders." **Full**—this also increases the weight—**of strife, deceit.** The envious man, when he cannot destroy his neighbor, attacks at least with open "strife," or secretly with "deceits" and "malignity." If he is unable to rebuke or defraud him, he pursues him with the poisonous malignity of his will and with curses. **Whisperers, detractors.** For the malignant man, while he cannot vomit out his internal poison in any other way, vomits it out through words, either openly or in secret. 

**Hateful to God.** <note>original: *Deo odibiles*</note> For what is more contrary to the good gift of God than to take such delight in evil deeds? They are "hated by God" because while they want evil things, they do not want good things. If they do not want these, it follows that they do not want God, the principle of all good things. For this reason, and because of their pride and the heap of evils they commit, they are "hated by God" as "haters of God." From this point on, they are not human, but diabolical. **Insolent, haughty, boastful.** Not only do they speak ill of the absent, but they even resort to "insolence" in the presence of others. They are not content with words, but attempt to tear things apart through deeds against the law. They seek to exalt themselves while depressing everyone else. **Inventors of evil.** They perhaps consider common harms to be trivial. They strain every nerve of their intellect to devise new types of wrongdoing. **Disobedient to parents.** Thus far he has followed the affirmative faults of injustice, which consist mostly in *committing* acts; next, however, he pursues the negative faults, which consist mostly in *omitting* duties. And just as he began with God when describing the former, so he begins with "parents" in the latter, who are to us on earth as if in the place of God. It was not enough for these people to harm their neighbors, unless they also rebelled against their parents. **Foolish.** <note>original: *Insipientes*</note> They can rightly be judged so senseless as to be utterly devoid of parental or any other kind of discipline. **Disorderly.** <note>original: *Incompositos*</note> That is, far from composure, as if not standing by agreements and contracts. Nor is that surprising. If they have already broken parental laws, they are **without affection.** <note>original: *sine affectione*</note> **Without a covenant.** <note>original: *Absq; foedere*</note> If they do not love God, they do not even love their parents. Likewise, if they do not love their parents, how will they love others? If they love no one, by what "covenant" of society—that is, by what law or promise—can they be bound to anyone? **Without mercy.** Rightly so, since all charity has now grown cold and they have utterly stripped off all humanity; they provide no help even to a miserable man, nor are they even moved by the mind's mercy. Therefore, they are not even to be considered human. 

**Who, though they knew the justice of God, did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death. Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.** Through these words, it is clear that they are their own enemies, for while they say God is just, they do not concede that He punishes, while they trust that they themselves will go unpunished. This is now the sum of the preceding discussion, and a kind of epilogue. For Paul returns to the "justice" and "knowledge of God" placed at the beginning and the "inexcusable crime" brought up there. Since, therefore, they knew what is "just" toward God—what is owed to God, to oneself, and to one's neighbor—and yet because of "impious pride" they acted against all these laws, they are now worthy of no pardon. For they are so blinded by their own fault that they did "not understand"—that is, they did not want to consider—that God punishes sins, and that others who have perpetrated such things must be judged worthy of "death." For souls that desert God are worthy to be deserted by the body, namely by "temporal death," and furthermore to be deserted by God, damned by a certain "eternal death." For God is the life of the soul, just as the soul is the life of the body. Of course, not only those who committed the acts themselves, but even those who, through a defect of charity, failed to prevent them, are judged worthy of this punishment. Perhaps Paul is touching upon certain "Philosophers" <note>Ficino likely refers to the Stoics or Platonists who, though personally moral, did not stop the public worship of idols.</note> in his rebuke; though they themselves did not worship demons or idols, and were not polluted by their own personal iniquity, they nevertheless did not come to the aid of the Gentiles who were in error.

## Against both Jews and Gentiles: Regarding their unjust judgment, how they will be judged by God, and their stubbornness.
### Chapter 11 <note>Ficino uses his own chapter numbering for this commentary; this section covers Romans 2:1–3.</note>

<margin>»</margin>**Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judges.** After he proved that the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans.</note> did not achieve righteousness <note>original: *iustitiam*</note> through the mere knowledge of the truth—the very thing they boasted of most—and showed they were not worthy of pardon, he now shows that the Jews also did not attain righteousness through the many privileges received by divine grace, in which they were accustomed to insolently exalt themselves. The result of this is that the power of the Gospel’s grace is necessary for both groups to achieve salvation. First, therefore, he argues that the Jews did not obtain the perfection of righteousness from the Law, then not from their lineage, and third, not from circumcision itself. We must first consider how both the Jews and Gentiles, having now become Christians, still insolently judged one another regarding their former lives. For the Jews frequently reproached the Gentiles, saying they lived without God's Law as if they were profane, and sacrificed to idols. The Gentiles, on the other hand, daily reproached the Jews, saying they had by no means kept the Law they received from God and had been ungrateful for their divine privileges. Therefore, Paul first condemns both for their improper judgment, universally disapproving of human judgment while approving of the divine. <margin>»</margin>**Therefore you are without excuse, etc.** It is as if he says: because you Gentiles suppressed the truth of God in your injustice, and having known God were ungrateful, you lack an excuse and do not deserve pardon; and at the same time, you, O Jew, because of the Law you received, are not worthy of excuse or pardon. Therefore, in whatever way one judges and condemns the other, he is also secretly condemned by his own judgment. This is because he is caught in a similar crime. He says, moreover, **O man**, so that each may remember he is not divine, but human. Therefore, in judging, one can easily be deceived and is similarly liable to faults and judgment. Furthermore, he says **everyone** <note>original: *omnis*</note>. Although he began with the Gentiles, he soon included the Jews as well. He also encompassed them at the beginning, where he said: *In the Gospel the divine power is active, for the salvation of everyone who believes, to the Jew first and then to the Greek.* And in the progress of this argument, he mentions both the Jew and the Greek together. <margin>»</margin>**For in that you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge.** But how are they the "same," at least in effect or kind, if less so in manner and specific quality? If the Jew condemns the Gentile for ingratitude toward God because he was not grateful for his philosophical talent and the gift of knowledge, the Gentile will similarly accuse the Jew of being ungrateful because he was not at all grateful for the many prerogatives granted to him by God. Again, the Jew will undoubtedly call the Gentile a transgressor of the natural law. The laws of the Gentiles certainly permitted idolatry, but they seemed to overlook fornication <note>Sexual immorality.</note> rather negligently; the Law of the Jews, however, marked both with a more severe censure. Therefore, the Jew condemned the manifest idolatry and fornication in the Gentile. The Gentile, in turn, criticized the hidden version of these in the Jew. By a similar logic, they mutually condemned each other for faults that were in some way common to both, and each, while accusing the other, also condemned himself. <margin>»</margin>**But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.** The Apostle warns these quarreling people in this way: "This judgment of yours is based on opinion and is carried out through agitation. We Apostles, however, know and are certain that you are meanwhile being judged by a higher Judge, who looks into the truth, however hidden, and punishes those who, being subject to crimes, do not purge their own but rather rebuke the crimes of others—not for the sake of correction, but for the sake of pride." Moreover, what I said about opinion, Plato confirms in the *Timaeus* with these words: *Certain understanding of the truth belongs to God alone, but opinion belongs to men.* When he says **they do such things**, he does not only signify the other crimes, but this above all: that you judge and condemn others, especially when you yourself deserve to be condemned, and that you insolently usurp the office of judging, which belongs to God alone. <margin>»</margin>**And do you think this, O man, you who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?** If God, as I just said, judges according to truth—that is, he inspects the innermost truth and is not moved by agitation—you, O man (that is, an earthly animal), ought not to think that you can escape divine vengeance. Toward this point tends that prophetic saying: *Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell...* <note>original: Psalm 139:7–8. The text cuts off here with the catchword *infer-*.</note>

<summary>Ficino explains the opening of Romans 2, arguing that both Jews and Gentiles are hypocritical when they judge one another, as both have failed to live up to the specific gifts (Law or Reason) granted to them by God.</summary>
<keywords>Paul the Apostle, Romans 2, Jews, Gentiles, righteousness, Law, Plato, Timaeus, judgment of God, Gospel grace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans Chapter 2. Having established that neither Gentiles nor Jews have an excuse for their sins, Ficino now explores the nature of divine judgment, the omniscience of God, and the danger of human hypocrisy in judging others.</meta>

<page-num>446</page-num>
-> ### MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES ### <-

...you are present in hell <note>original: *in infernum ades*; a reference to Psalm 139:8</note>. Likewise, "there is nowhere for one to hide from his heat" <note>original: *nec est quo se abscondat à calore eius*; a reference to Psalm 19:6</note>. And that word of Jeremiah: *I am judge and witness* <note>Jeremiah 29:23</note>. The same is confirmed by Plato in the *Laws* <note>Plato, *Laws* 10.903-905</note>, saying that every single thing is inspected and noticed by divine judgment. Therefore, for sinners, there is no refuge either among the heavenly beings or among those in the underworld. But why have we overlooked what the Apostle says to the Hebrews <note>Hebrews 4:12-13</note>: that the divine word most effectively penetrates the innermost parts, and all things are naked and open to his eyes? 

Moreover, Paul says "O man" <note>original: *ô homo*; Romans 2:1 and 2:3</note> twice, so that when you attempt to judge, you also say twice, "I am a man." Say it once regarding the relationship between you and your neighbor, remembering that you are a sinner and capable of being deceived, and that he, as a brother, must not be harmed. Say it a second time regarding God, reflecting that you, an earthly animal <note>A common Renaissance term for humanity, emphasizing our physical nature in contrast to our divine intellect.</note>, ought not to usurp for yourself a divine office. For it belongs to Him alone to judge, who alone is the searcher of minds and the Lord of the universe, whose coming for judgment the Apostle commands us to await. *Do not judge and you shall not be judged* <note>Matthew 7:1</note>—specifically regarding this most serious crime, which is to arrogantly claim for oneself the divine gift of judging, which is a form of diabolical pride. Nothing should be easier than silence; nothing should be more difficult for a judge, who is often moved not by his own benefit but by sheer malice, as if he were moved by the devil. Perhaps, indeed, he who refrains from judgment will restrain himself from serious
<margin>
,,
,,
</margin>
matters and will not have to be judged. 

*Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering?* <note>Romans 2:4</note> Perhaps you do not so much trust in God’s ignorance as you rashly hope in His mercy. To the extent that you have already been sinning most grievously for a long time and experience no vengeance from Him, you err gravely. While you are under a judge so just and wise, you promise yourself an unmerited impunity; you err more gravely when you despise divine kindness, and most gravely of all when you abuse such long divine patience and tolerance. 

The goodness of God is indeed copious, for He does not take away natural gifts even from one who sins heavily; rather, He supplies good things daily, as if coaxing you to return to thanksgiving and repentance. His patience is exceedingly copious, sustaining those who commit so many and such great sins, at least for a time. Finally, His long-suffering <note>original: *longanimitas*; a technical theological term for God's "long-mindedness" or enduring patience.</note> is copious, waiting a long time for repentance. *Are you unaware that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?* God is so good and merciful that, not moved by your evils but relying on His own goodness, He not only refrains from punishing you for so long despite your wickedness, but even heaps blessings upon you, so that you may have the time for repentance and the opportunity for gratitude. But you, meanwhile—wicked as you are—insanely turn what is granted to you for repentance into a rash confidence in impunity. You do not listen to what Isaiah warns: *God waits for you,* he says, *so that he may have mercy on you* <note>Isaiah 30:18</note>. 

If the First Principle <note>A Neoplatonic term for God as the source of all existence.</note>, which is limited by nothing, possesses infinite power, then this power encompasses any imaginable amount of time and space; it exists everywhere and always without doubt. If by this infinite power—which is itself intelligence—He made and arranged every single thing, He certainly understands and rules every single thing. Therefore, no human actions or thoughts escape His judgment. Thus David cried out: *Lord, O Father, where shall I flee from your face*—that is, from the Son? *Where shall I go from your spirit*—namely, the Holy Spirit? <note>Ficino provides a Trinitarian interpretation of Psalm 139:7: the "Face" of God is the Son (the Image), and the "Spirit" is the Holy Spirit.</note> It is as if he said: "If I am your friend, paternal power will sustain me." Hence the saying: *Your right hand shall hold me.* But if I am an enemy, that same power will crush me. *It is a hard thing to fall into the hands of the living God* <note>Hebrews 10:31</note>. Likewise, if I am a friend, Your holy and joyful face will meet me. If an enemy, it will be terrible and fierce. Again, if a friend, the heat of the Holy Spirit will cherish and restore me. If an enemy, it will consume and burn me. *There is no one who can hide from his heat.* But His heat, coming into an open, free, and wide soul, warms it most sweetly. In a narrow and distorted soul, however, being confined, it burns. Truly, by a certain mystery, while he was alluding to the Sun, he did not say, "there is no one who can hide from its light," but rather, "there is no one who can hide from its heat." For the light of the Sun does not take hold of all things, but all things in some way receive heat. So, too, the darkness does not comprehend the divine light, but it perceives the fire.

Just as God turns evils into good for those who are patient and repentant, so He has determined for those who abuse divine patience that good things shall be turned into evil. Since, therefore, through divine long-suffering you do not...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans Chapter 2. Following the discussion on God’s omniscience, Ficino now distinguishes between the types of divine judgment and explains the nature of eternal punishment, the "sin against the Holy Spirit," and why Christ is the most fitting judge for humanity.</meta>

<page-num>447</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL</header>

...those who are not turned, heap up for themselves a more bitter vengeance to be inflicted on sinners on the day of divine judgment. Now, divine judgment is twofold: one is the universal judgment for all that will occur at the end of the ages. The other is the particular judgment to be revealed to each individual after the end of this present life. Paul seems to touch upon both judgments here, and both are said to be displayed "on the day" and "with revelation." It is "on the day" because everything is clearly open to the divine judge, who is himself called the "Sun of Justice." It is "with revelation" because the marks of all sins present themselves, as if by justice, upon the soul. 

Regarding the Divine Sun, Orpheus says: *He looks into all things, hears all things within, and distributes all things justly* <note>Ficino often cites the "Orphic Hymns" to show parallels between ancient "pagan" theology and Christian truth.</note>. And Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>Plato, *Gorgias* 523c–524d</note> seems to have touched upon this kind of day and revelation where he says: all souls will come naked to the divine Judge without an advocate, bearing the scars and innermost marks of their vices. The severe Judge, inspecting these thoroughly, will discern and judge them, nor will he have any regard or selection for persons or other conditions. And in the final book of the *Republic* <note>The Myth of Er in *Republic* X, 614b</note>, Plato demonstrates that souls approaching judgment carry their own works openly with them: the good ones hanging in front, and the bad ones behind. Thus he spoke. 

So, therefore, *God will render to each one in just judgment according to his works* <note>Romans 2:6</note>. But how does He render to each according to his works if He punishes one who sins in time perpetually <note>Ficino is addressing a common theological question: how can a finite sin committed in time deserve infinite punishment in eternity?</note>? Surely for this reason: since the man has sinned against the divine majesty, whose dignity is infinite. Therefore, a guilt follows that is worthy of a certain infinite punishment. Likewise, if the sinner had determined to live in that same crime forever, this sin will not be in the future to God, but present; therefore, he will be punished as if he had always been sinning. Finally, if the sinner entirely loses divine grace because of a notable fault—without which no one rises from guilt—then by persevering in sin, he is destined to persevere in punishment. 

Yet by divine bounty, an eternal reward is given for temporal duties of virtue. Therefore, when it is said that He renders "according to works," you should not understand this as an equality of works, as if the works were equal to the rewards. For the reward exceeds the merit. Instead, it must be understood according to a certain proportion: namely, that He will grant good things to the good, and evil things to the evil; better things to the better, and worse things to the worse. 

The hardness of an unrepentant mind, condemned above, our doctors call the "sin against the Holy Spirit," which is worthy of no pardon. So that this may be understood more clearly, pay attention for a moment. They are accustomed to attribute power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and kindness to the Spirit. Although these goods are equally common to all three, they have nevertheless been accustomed to attribute these individual traits to each person specifically, according to a certain reason of manner or gift. 

Therefore, he who is overcome by disturbances and fails as if through powerlessness and weakness, sins against the power attributed to the Father, and thus seems to have sinned against the Father. He who sins through ignorance, sins against the wisdom of the Son. But he who has transgressed the law through malice and wickedness is thought to have offended the kindness <note>original: *benignitatem*</note> of the Holy Spirit. And this appears especially in deep-seated hatred, in the effect of envy toward divine grace, in hardened pride, in crimes perpetrated through voluntary malice, in contempt for divine things, in the proud assault on truth, and in extreme confidence or despair regarding divine mercy, as well as in a hardness that admits no repentance. Such faults are almost diabolical; they can be forgiven not by their own nature, but by a certain miraculous mercy and operation of God within us. However, faults committed through ignorance or weakness can be corrected by applying discipline and chastisement; therefore, they seem able to be forgiven more easily. 

Moreover, they attribute the office of judging especially to the Son, according to that saying: *The Father has given all judgment to the Son* <note>John 5:22</note>, whom He appointed judge of the living and the dead. A fitting reversal of affairs is preserved if the Son, who was judged by men, should himself judge men. He is also a suitable judge of the human race, being one who is above men and yet a man who has experienced human things himself. Furthermore, judgment must be conducted by light and reason; and the Light and Reason of the Father is the Son. Finally, if we consider the attributes, it might perhaps seem terrifying to grant judgment to the Father's power, lest a more rigid sentence be expected. To grant it to the kindness of the Spirit might provide too much confidence in indulgence. But it seems fitting to look to Wisdom <note>The Son</note> to judge justly, together with equity. 

The Son himself will fully carry out the universal judgment. But the particular judgment he carries out through the angel who is each person's guardian and scout, appointed from the beginning. Hence Plato in the *Gorgias* considers that this judgment is managed through certain specific Divinities <note>original: *Numina*</note>.

He also reconciles the temporal nature of sin with eternal punishment and defines the sin against the Holy Spirit as one of deliberate malice rather than weakness.</summary>

### On the Retribution of rewards and punishments, on proud contention against God, and divine vengeance. Chapter III.

<margin>"</margin>
<margin>"</margin>
<margin>"</margin>
<margin>"</margin>
**T**o those who, according to patience in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption: eternal life. But to those who are from contention, and who do not acquiesce to the truth, but believe in iniquity: wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish. <note>original: "His quidem qui secundū patientiam boni operis..." This is a direct quote from Romans 2:7-8.</note>) Just as I have currently arranged it, the text of these words is commonly read among the Latins in a way that has a rather obscure meaning. This has fatigued and continues to fatigue the minds of commentators. However, we shall translate more clearly and more in keeping with the Greek if we speak as Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a Greek Church Father and major defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy.</note>, a most learned Greek writer, does: *To those, indeed, according to patient perseverance in good work, glory and honor, etc. But to those from contention, not acquiescing to the truth, but complying with iniquity, etc.* The Greek word <term>hypomonēn</term> <note>original: ὑπομονὴν</note> signifies both patience and perseverance. It means "patience" insofar as one is not separated from a virtuous duty by the terror of evils. It means "perseverance" insofar as one endures until the end, with no weariness or softness calling them back. Since, therefore, as Athanasius maintains, Paul wants both to be understood and observed here, I have translated it as "patient perseverance." In this way, what Paul intends is more easily understood: namely, that God promises glory to those who persevere in good work. From the common form of translation, however, it has happened that some have interpreted it as: *Whoever uses God's patience well for a good work, etc.* But to interpret it this way is, as it were, to do violence to Paul’s words. 

But what sort of "glory" will God give to those persevering in good work? A clarity and splendor of the mind, in a certain way in this life, but most fully in the next, to the point that it overflows even into the body. This is what they call the "glorious body." Hence that saying of Isaiah: *He will fill your soul with splendors.* <note>Isaiah 58:11</note> And David: *The saints shall exult in glory.* <note>Psalm 149:5</note> And from the Gospel according to Matthew: *The just shall shine like the Sun in the kingdom of their father.* <note>Matthew 13:43</note> And what "honor"? A certain gift of office and wisdom in heaven, and a certain hidden honor among men. Thus David says: *Thy friends, O God, are exceedingly honored.* <note>Psalm 138:17 in the Vulgate</note> Regarding "incorruption," God is eventually going to grant this even to the bodies of the impious. Why then does he promise it especially to the pious as a distinction? Because immortality in the bodies of the pious will be accompanied by honor and glory, while for the impious it will be the opposite; and because the blessed will enjoy an eternal and firm state of "goods" <note>In the Platonic sense, "goods" refer to virtues and divine blessings.</note>. The wretched, however, will not truly be able to experience an immortal condition. Instead, they will perhaps be vexed by a ever-changing succession of various perturbations and punishments. Paul added, *to those seeking eternal life*, in order to express the "end" <note>The *finis* or ultimate goal.</note> of piety. For perseverance in good works, even if enduring until the end, does not bring back eternal beatitude unless it was undertaken and perfected for the sake of eternal life—that is, for the sake of enjoying God and the divine.

<margin>"</margin>
<margin>"</margin>
**B**ut to those from contention.) In the preceding sections, he first set down the merits, then the rewards. The merits were where he said: *To those, indeed, according to patient perseverance in good work.* The rewards were where he added: *glory*, and what follows. Here, likewise, he first recounts the faults, and then adds the punishments. He lists three faults in particular. The first is pride, which persistently contends with God. The second is lack of faith, which does not acquiesce to the authority of divine truth. The third is self-confidence, which indulges in iniquity. Four punishments are then described: namely, indignation, wrath, tribulation, and anguish. 

First, notice with what great reason Paul says those rewards are bestowed by God himself. But these punishments are not; for where he says *indignation*, etc., it is understood that they "are" or "will be" for sinners, rather than being "bestowed" by God. <note>Ficino is making a subtle theological point: God is the direct source of good, but the "punishment" is a natural consequence of the sinner's own state.</note> But let us return to the first point. Would not a venerable old man rightly be indignant at a servant or a boy who refused to execute any command unless he first demanded every single reason for it—reasons he should neither seek nor could even understand? Especially if the servant, while the Master was exhorting him to a more honorable life with words and duties, always strove to resist stubbornly, immersing himself entirely in crimes. Thus, Paul here inveighs against men similar to this servant, who behave toward God in opposition to those others above, who, as if humble and spontaneously subject to God in "good work"—that is, in keeping the works of God's precepts—persisted with the highest patience. These lower men, on the contrary, because of pride, make themselves equal to God in a way, just as if they honored God himself only in a "likeness"—that is, as a statue or a painting. But should it be thought that the most learned priests of that religion <note>Likely referring to ancient pagan priests/philosophers.</note> worshipped such things as actual deities?

<summary>Ficino explains the rewards for "patient perseverance" (glory, honor, and incorruption) and the punishments for those who pridefully contend against God. He uses linguistic analysis of the Greek text and philosophical analogies to show that eternal life is the goal of piety, while suffering is the natural result of turning away from divine truth.</summary>

<keywords>perseverance, divine justice, Romans 2, Athanasius, glory, pride, contention, Marsilio Ficino, theology, biblical commentary</keywords>
