<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans 2. On the previous page, Ficino discussed the rewards of "glory, honor, and incorruption" for the faithful and the "wrath and indignation" for the contentious. He now concludes a brief digression into his own previous writings on Neo-Platonism and natural magic before returning to Paul's argument that God judges Jews and Gentiles with perfect impartiality based on their actions, not their status.</meta>

<page-num>449</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL</header>
<sig>Ff</sig>

...to have willed: Not at all. On the contrary, he gave handles <note>Ficino uses the word "ansas" (handles) to mean "occasions" or "opportunities."</note> for such absurd adoration to the common people. But just as we have treated in the *Commentaries on Plato and Plotinus*, and in the third book of *On Life* <note>Ficino refers here to his major works *De vita libri tres* (Three Books on Life), where he discusses how "natural magic" uses the alignment of physical things with celestial ones.</note>. Likewise regarding these matters—how the Magi, through an inferior selection and composition of things, taught men to opportunely draw down certain higher things that are congruent with inferior ones—this must be disputed in another place more opportunely.

<margin>God weighs works, not persons; He condemns Jews and Gentiles equally, although the former sin without the law, the latter with the law. Chapter II.</margin>

**B**ut glory and honor and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no respect of persons with God. <note>original: "Gloria autem & honor, & pax... Non enim est acceptio personarum apud Deum." Romans 2:10-11.</note>) He has concluded the discourse of this previous dispute, in which he rebukes Gentiles and Jews with threats and evils. Now, repeating a similar discourse of reproach to both, and intending to win goodwill from both at the start, he begins with promises and happy omens. Because he will later charge the Jews with a greater crime, he repeats "to the Jew first" according to his custom—and rightly first. For the best things were divinely promised to the Jews first. Others are said to have entered into their promises. We have explained "glory" and "honor" in the preceding sections. Where he previously spoke of "incorruption," here he seems to name "peace." Since peace and harmony in the powers and parts of the soul—and especially in bodies—is the concord of the human mind with God, it once promised the whole man to be immortal, and promises it again. This is the point of that Platonic saying in the *Charmides* <note>The *Charmides* is a dialogue of Plato concerning temperance (sophrosyne).</note>: "The perfected temperance of the soul can make the body tempered and immortal." Even if good things were promised to the Jews first, nothing prevents Gentiles from attaining them equally if they perform good works equally. Indeed, Jews do not attain them otherwise than by performing good works similarly. By this reasoning he said, "For there is no respect of persons with God." Paul frequently repeats "works" for this reason: to restrain the insolence of those Jews who commonly trust in their privileges, their laws, and their ceremonies—thinking that even without their own work or other grace, they will carry away impunity for their crimes and possess salvation above all others. Where "respect of persons" <term>acceptio personarum</term> <note>A technical term for partiality or showing favoritism based on status rather than merit.</note> is blamed, it is that kind of partiality that only considers the person or some proper grace of a single person; it gives more to one than another without any other dignity or reason, whether of good or evil, which both otherwise equally deserve by preceding works or deserve in no way. God has no such selection in the retribution of evils or goods according to merit. Perhaps He does have it in the "callings" <note>original: "inuocationibus," here likely referring to the "calling" or "election" of individuals by God.</note> made by grace alone. These must indeed be treated where predestination is discussed. In the present case, however, the discussion is on the just retribution for preceding merits, where God considers actions and wills and weighs merits. He does not consider the "person" as Greek or Jew. For whosoever have sinned without the law shall also perish without the law; and whosoever have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law. <note>original: "Quicunq; enim sine lege peccauerunt... & quicunq; in lege peccauerunt, per legem iudicabuntur." Romans 2:12.</note>) He declares that God does not consider persons in punishing, but weighs the weight of the fault: because He looks at the sins and faults of both the Jew and the Gentile, not their persons. The fault of the Jew is heavier because the Mosaic law, given divinely, does not permit the Jew to always excuse ignorance and renders him liable by a tighter bond. Thus, those among the Gentiles who were neither instructed nor bound by the Mosaic law will be punished more lightly. For these will perish by the transgression of the natural law alone. "Without the law," meaning the Mosaic law, that is, without the Mosaic law weighing them down. The Jews, beyond the fact that they will perish similarly for despising the natural law, would also be punished by the heavier judgment of the Mosaic law. Furthermore, lest the Jews trust that they will be perfect by the mere reading of their laws and the observation of ceremonies, needing neither works nor the grace of another, he added: For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified <note>original: "non enim auditores legis iusti sunt... sed factores legis iustificabuntur." Romans 2:13.</note>—namely, whoever shall have kept the precepts of the law, whether Gentiles keeping their own law (the natural law) or Jews keeping the law further given through Moses; and that indeed holds true up until the Evangelical law <note>The "Evangelical law" refers to the Gospel or the Law of Christ.</note>, which is necessary for the salvation of both. And lest you understand what Paul says here—that the doers of the law are justified—as a universal statement (that any kind of righteousness is obtained through any law whatsoever), he means it is obtained not through the hearing and reading of the law, but through the observance of the precepts. Nevertheless, perfect righteousness—that is, righteousness worthy of perpetual salvation—is obtained only through the Law and Grace of the Gospel.

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that God judges based on actions rather than ethnic or religious identity, equating the "peace" promised by Paul with the "temperance" described in Plato's Charmides. He distinguishes between the Natural Law (binding on Gentiles) and the Mosaic Law (binding on Jews), noting that while both require "doing" rather than just "hearing," ultimate salvation requires the Grace of the Gospel.</summary>

Having established that God is an impartial judge of both Jews and Gentiles, Ficino now explores the concept of "Natural Law"—the idea that even those without the written scriptures possess an innate moral compass granted by God. He bridges Christian theology with his own Platonic philosophy, arguing that human reason contains a "veridical light" that acts as an internal judge.</meta>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

### On the natural and written law, on the judge and judgment within us, and also on the common judgment. Chapter XV.

" **F**or when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law unto themselves." <note>original: "Cum enim Gentes, quæ legem non habent... ipsi sibi sunt lex." Romans 2:14.</note> Through these words, he confirms that those who act according to the law, even if they have not heard it read aloud, obtain a certain justice. The Gentiles did not receive the divine law written on tablets, as the Jews did; for as David says: "He has not dealt thus with any other nation." <note>original: "Non fecit taliter omni nationi." Psalm 147:20. Ficino uses the Psalms to show that the written Mosaic law was a unique gift to Israel.</note> But they possessed a law naturally engraved in their minds—that is, from the very beginnings of their life—granted by divine power.

We must remember, however, that the Jews received a twofold law from God through Moses. One part was primarily moral, contained in the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term>, which was intended to endure forever and was necessary not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles. The Gentiles, however, received this kind of law in their minds rather than in writings. The other part was ceremonial, to be observed by the Jews only until the arrival of the Gospel. After that time, it became harmful <note>Ficino follows the standard medieval view that continuing Jewish ceremonial laws after Christ was "deadly" to the soul</note>, and it was never necessary for the Gentiles at any time.

Regarding the observation or breaking of the law—and the subsequent judgment, condemnation, and justification—Paul mentions three times: the past, the present, and the future. These are: Before the Gospel; during the time of the Gospel; and at the end of the ages. Everywhere, he maintains that the moral law—whether it was merely infused into the Gentiles or additionally written for the Jews—can lead toward justice and salvation. This happens not by hearing the law, but by acting upon it, and this is equally applicable to both groups at any time. At the final judgment, only works will be the basis for liberation.

Likewise, now that the Gospel has been spread, he wants it understood that the works of the law which lead to justice and salvation are those founded on the Law of the Gospel and on grace. Finally, no law—whether natural or written—has the power to achieve justice and salvation unless divine grace moves both the intellect and the emotions; and it must move them in such a way that the precepts of the law are kept through the grace of God himself. 

"They are a law unto themselves," that is, they stand in place of the law, whenever they observe the law that was divinely written in their minds from the beginning, reading it there, so to speak. Truly, that "True Light, which enlightens every man coming into this world" <note>original: "lux illa uera, illuminans omnem hominem..." John 1:9. This is a central theme in Ficino's philosophy: that Christ, the Word, provides the light of reason to all humanity.</note>, infused a truth-telling light into the mind. Just as that True Light exists as the judge of the universe, so too this truth-telling light shining from it sits as a judge in the soul, holding the place of God within man. This truth-telling light in the mind, derived from that great Lamp, naturally brought the moral law with it.

From this, David believes that "good is shown to us through the light sealed within us." <note>original: "signatum." A reference to Psalm 4:6, "The light of your countenance is sealed upon us."</note> Hence it is said in the Epistles: "To the wise man, God is the law; but to the foolish man, his lust is the law." <note>original: "Sapienti uiro lex Deus est, insipienti uerò libido."</note> For those are considered wise who, according to their strength, turn the attention of the mind away from the senses and toward the intellect, where they listen to the divine law dictating just duties.

Indeed, just as God placed the principles of contemplation in the light of the intellect to guide our thoughts, so too he placed rules to preside over our actions and duties. Through these, anyone of sound mind—if they examine them diligently—can understand what is good, honest, proper, and just in acting or not acting, or what is the opposite. Likewise, one can know that God, the Lord of the world (known through a certain natural kinship to Him and confirmed by the consensus of all), is to be revered and worshiped above all others; that one must give each person their due; that honor must be shown to superiors; and that "what you would not wish to be done to you, you should by no means do to another," <note>The "Golden Rule."</note> and other things of this kind. 

These sorts of rules are, as it were, laws inscribed upon our intellect-judge through the truth-telling light infused by the True Light, the judge of the world. For the present, I will omit the Platonic arguments by which we have proven these things in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology).</note>. Those which the Apostle briefly touches upon here, I shall also briefly skim. 

"They show the work of the law written in their hearts," that is, they declare by the thing itself that they naturally know and are certain of which works and duties are in harmony with the natural and moral law. They discern these things by a certain natural judgment, approving some as just and rejecting others as unjust. They could in no way do this unless they possessed within themselves the known "form" or pattern of justice itself. By referring individual cases to this standard, they are able to discern and judge which things are just, which are more just, and conversely, which are to be deemed unjust or more unjust. 

"Their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts within themselves accusing or even defending them on the day when God shall judge the secrets of men through Jesus Christ, according to my Gospel." <note>original: "Testimonium reddente illis conscientia ipsorum... secundùm Euangelium." Romans 2:15-16.</note> Where the Latin manuscripts have the genitive case here...

<summary>Ficino explains the concept of natural law, arguing that God inscribed a moral compass into the human intellect at creation. This "inner judge" allows even Gentiles without the Bible to distinguish right from wrong, though salvation ultimately requires divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>natural law, conscience, moral law, ceremonial law, Decalogue, inner judge, True Light, Platonic Theology, justification, divine grace</keywords>

Having established the concept of the "Law of Nature" on the previous page, Ficino now delves into the mechanics of conscience and the different stages of divine judgment, blending Scholastic logic (Aquinas) with Platonic imagery.</meta>

<sig>Ff 3</sig>

...ought, and therefore I have used the ablative case <note>original: "ideo ablatiuos posui." In Latin grammar, the ablative case often indicates the means or instrument by which an action is performed.</note>, because it harmonizes better with both Greek usage and Paul’s meaning, and because the most learned **Athanasius** <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent Church Father known for defending the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> understands it this way. The moral law has been divinely imprinted upon our minds. Beyond the argument we have just established, the witness is **conscience**—a certain truthful power of the soul, an observing faculty flowing from that truth-telling light. As **Saint Thomas Aquinas** <note>The influential 13th-century theologian and philosopher who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> maintains, this is a certain application of knowledge for the purpose of judging whether a deed was done well or poorly. Therefore, from the fact that conscience testifies regarding good or evil, we infer that laws exist in the inner chambers of the soul. By the observation or violation of these laws, an act is judged to be either just or unjust.

Now, the power of conscience, arguing the case for or against the soul in the presence of the internal light—as if before a Judge holding the laws—brings forth witnesses: frequent thoughts and memories. These sometimes accuse us, presenting a reason why something was done poorly. At other times, other thoughts arise in defense, arguing by some other reason that the act should not be condemned. And so, they often struggle back and forth in a mutual debate, until the matter is settled under the presiding judge, while the conscience meanwhile reviews the case. Indeed, accusation, defense, and judgment cannot be carried out without some knowledge of a law.

Through these things, then, it is confirmed that the moral law is imprinted on our minds. By this law, a person who is more prudent and temperate may lead a somewhat just life even without written laws. But the laws of the Scriptures appear for the imprudent and the wicked; they are further armed to compel those who have neglected their own internal laws. For this reason, Paul writes to **Timothy** that "the law was not laid down for the righteous." <note>original: "legem iusto positam non fuisse." 1 Timothy 1:9.</note>

Furthermore, we must remember that there is a triple day of judgment. One is the universal judgment at the end of the ages. Another occurs suddenly after the end of each person's life. There is also a third, which is daily. The final universal judgment is represented in the particular judgment after life, and both are reflected in the daily judgment. Paul, therefore, beginning from the daily judgment, reaches toward the other two as well. Truly, as often as someone calls themselves back from external things to the innermost parts—as the proverb <note>Refers to the ancient Greek maxim "Know Thyself" (Nosce te ipsum).</note> commands—and examines themselves, so often are they pulled into a dispute of this kind, to be settled under the internal judge, who is the vicar <term>vicar: A representative or deputy acting in the place of a higher authority.</term> of the Universal Judge. And at this very time, when the person in a sense separates themselves from the body, they arrive at a judgment similar to the judgment of souls separated from the body.

But this daily judgment differs plainly from the others in that, in this one, the debate is conducted gradually and back-and-forth, as we have said. In the others, however, no doubtful controversy is conducted; rather, the entire controversy is brought forth into a sudden remembrance and sentence by the judge. This is as **Augustine** <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). Ficino is likely referencing "The City of God," Book 20.</note> declares in *The City of God*. Paul calls that time "the Day," expressing the certainty of the Divine Judge, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness. And, so that the wicked may be rightly terrified, he will discern and judge the secrets of men no less than the manifest things.

The Gospel according to **Matthew**, however, calls that time "the night," as it is uncertain to us: "At midnight a cry went out." <note>original: "Media nocte clamor factus est." Matthew 25:6.</note> Moreover, the judgment will be through **Jesus Christ**, whom Almighty God has appointed as the judge of the living and the dead. In the midst of this, the Apostle calls his preachings and letters "his Gospel." He does so because he did not receive this doctrine from man, nor was he compelled to read or hear the other Evangelists. For he, just like **John** and **Matthew**, had Christ as his teacher; but while they had Him speaking on earth, Paul had Him revealing from heaven.

From Paul's earlier words, one may understand that since souls now judge and condemn themselves in a certain way, they will do so much more in the next life, where they will perceive themselves more clearly and condemn themselves by their own judgment. This is also confirmed by what **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, whom the Renaissance believed was Paul’s Athenian convert. In reality, these are the writings of a 5th-century Neoplatonist (Pseudo-Dionysius).</note>, the disciple of Paul, says when writing to John the Evangelist: "The souls of the impious, at the very time of judgment, even with no one pursuing them, are driven away by their own powers from the presence of the Divine Judge." I believe they do this because of a terrifying realization of divine indignation. For this reason, turning further away from the Good by their own impulse, they fall into extreme misery. It is much like eyes suffering from *ophthalmia* <term>ophthalmia: A historical term for severe inflammation of the eye or conjunctivitis.</term> which flee the daylight; the light is healthful to the healthy, but harmful to the sick. By this flight, they plunge themselves into their own evil—that is, into the darkness. To this same point tends that saying of **Plato** in his book *On Science and Laws*: "The wicked, by their own inclination, seek places suited to their merits, just as fire

->is carried upward by its lightness, but the earth<-
->downward.<-

<summary>Ficino explains conscience as an internal courtroom that mirrors God's judgment, arguing that the moral law is naturally imprinted on the human mind. He distinguishes between daily self-examination and the final judgment, noting that the wicked ultimately condemn themselves by fleeing the divine light.</summary>

## On the privilege of the Jews, and how they abuse it.
### Chapter XVI.

<margin>”</margin> **But if you are called a Jew.** <note>original: "SI autem tu Iudæus cognominaris." Ficino begins his commentary on Romans 2:17.</note> Up to this point, he has shown that those who observe the law attain justice, even if they are not "hearers" <note>Those who have not heard the formal revelation of the Mosaic Law, referring to the Gentiles.</note>. This pertained especially to the Gentiles. Next, however, he demonstrates that "hearers" are not made just unless they are also "observers." This, of course, pertains to the Jews. At the start, he will describe the privilege of the Jews—that they alone received the law. Then, he will rebuke their vice—that they transgressed the law. He will arrange their privilege around three points. First, regarding the People subject to the law. Second, regarding the law itself. Third, regarding the effect of the law. Therefore, as far as the People are concerned,
<margin>”</margin> whose name is venerable, he says: **But if you are called a Jew.** On this point David says: *Judah became his sanctuary* <note>original: "Facta est Iudæa significatio eius." A reference to Psalm 114:2 (113 in the Vulgate).</note>. And John the Evangelist says: *Salvation is from the Jews.* Indeed, the Jews are named after the Patriarch Judah, as is declared in Genesis: *Judah, your brothers shall praise you.* For when the ten tribes revolted from **Rehoboam** <note>Son of Solomon; his reign saw the split of the United Kingdom of Israel into the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and the Southern Kingdom (Judah) around 930 BC.</note> during his reign and worshipped the golden calf, they are recorded as having been led away as captives by the Assyrians, as is told in the fourth book of Kings <note>Known as 2 Kings in modern Bibles.</note>. But the sacred writings make no mention that they ever returned; rather, their regions were occupied by foreigners, who were afterwards said to be called **Samaritans**. However, the remaining two tribes, tracing their origin from Judah and Benjamin, persevered in the jurisdiction of Rehoboam and in the worship of the one God. Although these tribes later underwent captivity in Babylon, they are nonetheless reported to have been finally restored to their homeland by **Cyrus** <note>Cyrus the Great (r. 559–530 BC), the Persian king who ended the Babylonian Captivity.</note>, the king of the Persians, as the history of Ezra relates. But because the tribe of Judah was larger, that entire People took its name from him. And not only the peoples descended from Benjamin himself, but many also returning from the other tribes, who surely 
<margin>”</margin> bound themselves to the tribe of Judah. **And you rest in the law.** He now follows up on the privilege of the Jews which pertains to the law. But in what way do you "rest" in the law? Because through the law 
<margin>”</margin> you think yourself made certain of what must be done or what must be believed. **And you glory in God.** Namely, in the 
<margin>”</margin> author of the law, and in the worship of God alone. **And you know his will.** 
<margin>”</margin> That is, the will declared by the law, for the knowledge of the law one has received is its fruit. Indeed, the Jews seem to claim a great privilege for themselves in this: that they have learned through the law what God himself wants them to do, and what he does not want; surely because of this knowledge, he adds: **You approve the more useful things, being instructed by the law.** <margin>”</margin> That is, you discern those things which are more in harmony with the divine will. This pertains especially to your own perfection. Furthermore, it also pertains to the instruction 
<margin>”</margin> of others: **You are confident that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having the form of knowledge and truth in the law.** From these words it appears that the 
<margin>”</margin> Jews thought the Gentiles were "blind"—that is, entirely captured in mind so that they could never attain anything of the truth—or even if not entirely deprived of the eyes of the mind, they were nonetheless groping as if in darkness due to the absence of light, or at least they touched upon the very minimum of wisdom. Or finally, that they did not possess a manly and mature prudence. Therefore, regarding the first, they boasted they were "guides to the blind." Regarding the second, they were "a light to those who hesitate and stumble in the darkness." Regarding the third, they were "instructors of the foolish." And regarding the fourth, "teachers of infants." Just as if the Jew alone possessed the form of knowledge, revealed by divine power through the law, by which he was able to educate not only himself but all the Nations. For he professed not only the truth of the law in actions, but 
<margin>”</margin> also the knowledge of the mysteries. **You, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself?** Up to this point, he has recounted the privileges of the Jews, in which they could partly glory by right, but partly they were boasting too arrogantly. Now, however, he follows up more plainly on the abuse and transgression of the law, and signifies that in many ways they are worse than the Gentiles. And, so it seems to me, he questions them with a certain indignation and refutes them with a kind of invective. First, regarding doctrine. For it was said how much they trusted in their knowledge of the law, and professed themselves guides and the light of the Nations, as if of the blind. Therefore, the abuse of doctrine and the law is mentioned to them consequently—namely, to restrain their pride. It is as if he were saying: "He who is not wise for himself is wise in vain." Why then do you neither teach nor amend yourself?

<summary>Ficino explains the historical and spiritual privileges of the Jewish people, such as receiving the Mosaic Law, while beginning a sharp critique of their failure to live according to that same Law.</summary>

Indeed, you may be able to teach and correct others. However, he subsequently proves that the Jew does not apply the teaching of the law to his own use or to his own perfect discipline. <margin>”</margin> (**You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal? You who teach that one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?**) These are indeed considered crimes against one's neighbor. But even more so, you sin against God. (**You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?**) For you abuse those things which are judged to belong to divine worship. They committed this first while the Law was reigning, as Malachi testifies: *you say the table of the Lord is defiled.* <note>original: "dicitis mensa Domini contaminata est." A reference to Malachi 1:7, where the priests are accused of offering defiled food on the altar.</note> Then, you cursed the Christ promised by the Prophets under this Law, when you proclaimed that he performed miracles by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. But soon Paul reproaches them, saying that they violently offend the divine glory. <margin>”</margin> (**You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God through the transgression of the law?**) For while you transgress the law—which you celebrate so much in words—with shameful deeds, you provide an opening for the Gentiles to despise and revile divine worship among you, as if it were useless for morals and actions. This is indeed nothing other than to dishonor God, that is, to defraud Him of His due honor. <margin>??</margin> (**For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.**) Because of your shameful acts, they think God is affected by the failure of your law, and they therefore disdain to receive the God preached by you, just as it is written; for Isaiah says: *Its rulers act iniquitously, and therefore my name is blasphemed all day long.* <note>Ficino is paraphrasing Isaiah 52:5.</note> And Ezekiel: *I will do this not for your sake, O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have polluted among the nations.* <note>Ezekiel 36:22.</note>

->Circumcision is twofold, bodily and spiritual. The first does not suffice for salvation.<-

### Cap. XVII.

<margin>”</margin> **C**ircumcision <note>The text begins with a decorative woodcut 'C'.</note> indeed is of value if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. <note>original: "Circuncisio quidem prodest..." quoting Romans 2:25.</note> Thus far he has argued that the law is not sufficient for salvation. Now, however, he proves that even circumcision does not satisfy the requirement. This is because the observance of the law has power even without circumcision. But without the observance of the law, circumcision is judged invalid. But in what way does circumcision benefit? Namely, for washing away original sin. He confirms this in Genesis: *The male whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised,* and what follows. <note>Genesis 17:14.</note> But for you as an adult, it is only then beneficial when you observe the commands of the law, just as one thinks a religious profession <note><term>profession</term>: Ficino compares the Jewish rite of circumcision to a monk taking his vows (profession) in a religious order; the ceremony only matters if the person actually lives by the rules of the order.</note> will benefit only the religious who fulfill their law. For circumcision was like a certain profession, binding the circumcised to the observance of the law; therefore he wrote to the Galatians: *I testify to every man who becomes circumcised that he is a debtor to the whole law.* <note>Galatians 5:3.</note> But as for what the Apostle says: *If you become circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,* he is speaking only of the time after the Gospel was made public. Here, however, he signifies the time before the passion of Christ, in which circumcision had power. <margin>”</margin> (**But if you are a transgressor of the law, etc.**) Here he now shows how circumcision is of no benefit. It is as if he says: if you, O adult Jew, are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision; it is worth no more to you than uncircumcision, because you do not keep at all what you profess through circumcision. Jeremiah confirms this as follows: *All the nations have a foreskin, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.* <note>Jeremiah 9:26.</note> Indeed, they are considered more liable and guilty because of this, since they do not fulfill their promises. <margin>”</margin> (**If therefore a Gentile keeps the requirements of the law, his uncircumcision will be counted as circumcision.**) Here he now compares circumcision to the Gentiles, insofar as it pertains to this: that the Gentiles, by observing the law, bring back its fruit. Truly, if circumcision is beneficial by the observance of the law, but without this it is of no benefit, it follows that if an uncircumcised Gentile keeps the righteousness of the law—that is, the just precepts of the law—his uncircumcision should be counted as circumcision. For he brings back the fruit of true circumcision; for for the sake of this, the outer man is circumcised in the body, so that it might warn him to circumcise his soul. <margin>”</margin> Hence Jeremiah says: *Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskin of your hearts.* <note>Jeremiah 4:4.</note> <margin>”</margin> (**And he who is uncircumcised by nature, fulfilling the law, will judge you, who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law.**) Again he compares circumcision to the Gentile, showing that the latter is preferred because of his observance of the law. He says, therefore, that the uncircumcised Gentile "completing the law"—that is, fulfilling the commands of the law—does so "by nature," through natural reason. For it was said above that "by nature" they do the things that are of the law; here, by comparison with himself, he will judge you, the Jew, showing that you are to be judged and condemned. <margin>”</margin> You who are a transgressor of the law, while you overstep its precepts. **Through the letter and circumcision**, namely, trusting in the mere hearing of the written law and in bodily circumcision, which indeed is not so much true circumcision as it is a sign of inward circumcision.

<summary>Ficino explains that external religious markers like circumcision are meaningless without moral obedience to the Law. He argues that a virtuous Gentile who follows natural law is superior to a Jew who possesses the written Law but violates it through hypocrisy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the final verses of Romans Chapter 2 and the beginning of Chapter 3. Ficino, a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, here blends Pauline theology with his characteristic focus on the internal spirit over external forms.</meta>

<page-num>454</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLE</header>

>> **For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh.** <note>original: "Non enim qui in manifesto Iudæus est..." Romans 2:28.</note>

He assigns the reasons for the previous statements here. First, he brings forward the reason why Judaism or circumcision is not profitable without the observation of the law, whereas the observation of the law is profitable even without circumcision or Judaism. Certainly, a circumcised man who is a transgressor of the law is regarded as if he were uncircumcised, and he is condemned by the uncircumcised man who keeps the law. For he is not a true Jew who is one "outwardly"—that is, in name and lineage only. This will also be declared in what follows, where it will be said: *For not all who are of the circumcision of Israel are Israelites, but those who are children of the promise.* <note>original: "Non enim omnes, qui ex circuncisione sunt Israēl..." A reference to Romans 9:6-8.</note> By the same reasoning, that is not true circumcision which is manifest in the flesh. For that is thought to be a kind of "sign." This is indeed declared in Genesis: *You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of the covenant.* <note>original: "Circuncidetis carnem præputij uestri..." Genesis 17:11.</note> However, a sign is not judged to be true unless that which is signified follows in a fitting manner. Therefore, if any Jew is a transgressor of the covenant, his circumcision will not be true. For this reason, he will be regarded as if he were uncircumcised.

>> **But he is a Jew who is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.** <note>original: "Sed qui in abscondito Iudæus est..." Romans 2:29.</note>

He assigns the reason here why an uncircumcised man who keeps the law should be considered as if he were circumcised, and why, by comparison, he judges and condemns merely bodily circumcision. This is because he is truly a Jew who is one "in secret"—that is, who holds the mandates of the law in the affection of his heart, which Jews often profess in name alone. By similar reasoning, true circumcision is that of the heart "in the spirit"—that is, performed through the Spirit, through which superfluous thoughts are cut away from the soul. Likewise, "through the spirit" means a spiritual understanding of the law, not a literal one. He says to the Philippians: 
>> **We are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit.** <note>original: "Nos sumus circuncisio..." Philippians 3:3.</note>
>> **Whose praise is not from men, but from God.**

He seems to confirm the previous reasoning here. Since divine judgment is to be preferred to human judgment in all things, those things which appear to us from the outside—whether it be Judaism or circumcision—tend to be praised by men. But those things which lie hidden in the inner chambers of our mind can be approved only by divine judgment. From this, it is concluded that internal Judaism and circumcision are to be preferred to the external; and this is exactly what he says: the praise of such internal circumcision depends not on men, but on God. That which he says to the Corinthians also tends toward this: *For it is not the one who commends himself,* and so forth. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 10:18: "For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends."</note>

---

## On the prerogative of the Jews, and how their faithlessness did not change the promises of God. Chapter XVIII.

>> **What then is more for the Jew, or what is the utility of circumcision? Much in every way.** <note>original: "Quid ergo amplius est Iudæo..." Romans 3:1.</note>

After the Apostle has demonstrated that Judaism (to which the receiving of the law and circumcision belong) does not suffice for salvation when it is far removed from the observation of the law—and that through such observation a Gentile without external Judaism (that is, without the written law and circumcision) attains the fruit of both—he now raises an objection to these points and answers them. Namely, if (as has been said) neither the true Jew nor true circumcision consists in ceremonies but in the inner affection, what more was granted to the Jew than to others? 

Nothing, surely, seems to be, yet more appears to have been conceded where the Lord says in Deuteronomy: *The Lord your God has chosen you to be a special people to Himself.* <note>original: "Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus..." Deuteronomy 7:6.</note> 
>> **Or what is the utility of circumcision?**
Namely, the external kind. Yet it ought to be useful, since God Himself commanded it. Isaiah, moreover, says: *I am the Lord teaching you useful things.* <note>original: "Ego Dominus docens te utilia." Isaiah 48:17.</note> Therefore, when he adds "much," he settles the question. First, he defends the prerogative of Judaism; then, he will protect the utility of circumcision by its own reasoning. 

Truly, more was granted to the Jew. Thus, to show its magnitude, he answers, "much." To encompass the number of benefits as well, he adds "in every way"—not only in the contemplation of divine things but also in the management of human affairs. David confirms the first: *God is known in Judea.* <note>Psalm 76:1.</note> He also confirms the second: *He has not dealt thus with every nation.* <note>Psalm 147:20.</note> They also have more in regard to the fathers, the promises, and the offspring. Paul will relate these in the following passages: that theirs is the adoption of the sons of God, the glory, and the covenant. 

And lest pride increase in the Jews because of the description or enumeration of so many and such great goods, he narrates nothing performed by the Jews, but only things attributed by God. He considers that the other gifts were granted to them by God for this end: because He had destined His Son to be, and His body was to be received from the Jewish lineage. However, He had decreed these things not because of the merits of the Jews, but by His own will. Through these things, the Apostle extols them, not so much for the time after the coming of Christ, as for their status before the temporal birth of Christ.
>> **First, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.** <note>original: "Primum quidem, quia credita sunt illis eloquia Dei." Romans 3:2.</note>
This word, "first," in this place does not strictly signify the beginning of a numerical list; for he does not later...

# COMMENTARY ON SAINT PAUL

[Paul] adds "second" and "third," but he signifies the principal prerogative before Christ. Specifically, because God trusted them and granted to them, as if already to friends, his oracles <note>original: "eloquia sua"</note>—that is, the mysteries contained in the Patriarchs, the Law, and the Prophets. **For what if some of them did not believe?**

<margin>,,</margin>**Will their unbelief nullify the faith of God? Certainly not.** <note>Romans 3:3. Ficino uses "faith of God" to mean both God’s own reliability and the faith directed toward Him.</note> Perhaps someone might disparage the prerogatives of the Jews, as if they had lost the dignity of the divine oracles because of their ingratitude. He responds to this objection, saying that their unbelief could not nullify the faith of God. The objection is of this kind: "But what if some of them did not believe? Is it not thereby proven that there is no further advantage for the Jew?" Moreover, they did not believe first in the lawgiver, as **David** says, "they did not believe his words"; then they did not provide faith to the Prophets. **Ezekiel** confirms this: "They are unbelieving and subverters with you." <note>A paraphrase of Ezekiel’s frequent descriptions of Israel’s rebellion.</note> Finally, they refused to assent to the Son.

<margin>,, :</margin>Therefore, where he says: **Will their unbelief, etc.** He solves an objection of this kind by a certain argument, led to an absurdity. <note>term: "reductio ad absurdum" (a logical method where you prove a point by showing that its opposite leads to a ridiculous conclusion)</note> For if, because of the unbelief of some, the prerogative of the Jews were taken away from their midst, it would certainly follow from this that the faith of God is nullified and destroyed by the infidelity of man. To say such a thing is a wicked impiety. It is as if he said: "Has the unbelief of those who did not believe nullified the faith of God?" This indeed has a double sense: for it either signifies the faith by which one believes in God, or the faith of God by which God is judged faithful in fulfilling his promises. From the fact that some did not believe at all, the faith of the rest of the believers did not vanish. Nor, again, from this very fact could the faithfulness of God in fulfilling his promises be diminished. Yet it would have been taken away already if, because of the unbelief of some, it happened that there was no further advantage for the Jew. For God promised to make that people many and great. This indeed is clear in **Genesis**: *I will multiply your seed.* <note>Genesis 22:17.</note> **But God is truthful, and every man is a liar.**

<margin>,,</margin>The Latin manuscripts have "they have" <note>original: "habent"</note>; the Greek is "let it be" <note>original: "esto"</note>, and **Athanasius** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for defending orthodoxy.</note> reads it thus. "Let it be," therefore, means "let it be openly affirmed by everyone." Now indeed Paul declares this to be absurd: that divine faith is destroyed because of human unbelief. For God is indeed truthful, and yet every man is a liar. *I said in my excess, every man is a liar.* <note>Psalm 116:11.</note> From this it is clear that the lie and infidelity of man does not cling to divine truth, nor does it take away divine truth and faith. Indeed, God promised something to the Jews absolutely, and something else with a certain condition: absolutely, indeed, the Law and Christ. These things, therefore, he firmly fulfilled just as he had promised, nor did he retract them on account of their treachery. For these are not given according to the dignity of those receiving them, but by divine decree; nor are they balanced by any merits. But he sometimes promised worldly prosperity with a condition—namely, if they remained firmly in faith and piety. Men sometimes merit goods of this kind. But where they failed to keep such a condition, God did not keep such promises. And meanwhile, he must nonetheless be said to have stood faithful and truthful. Moreover, that which is said, "every man is a liar," seems to be brought forward chiefly for this: so that it may appear that the divine promise was made and completed, not because of any dignity of lying man, but because of singular mercy, so that grace might be imparted even to the unworthy, and it might appear that these things exist by pure grace. God is indeed called truthful because of his immutable essence, certain intelligence, and firm promises. But by contrary reasons, man is a liar. As it is written: **That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.** <note>Psalm 51:4.</note> After the Prophet said: *Against you only have I sinned, and done evil before you*, he immediately added, **That you may be justified in your words, etc.** To one continuing the words of David but considering the sense too little, he might seem to say that he had sinned for this end: so that God might be justified in his words, which would indeed be absurd. Therefore, this part, "that you may be justified," etc. is to be continued with those prayers: *Have mercy, blot out, wash, cleanse me*, not only because "I know my iniquity," but also much more for your glory. This glory will also appear from this: if, after I am purged and justified, you are justified in granting pardon and fulfilling promises, etc. Therefore, God will be judged just, both because he kept his promises and because, even if not to one worthy, he granted it to one not entirely a stranger. Moreover, David will not be entirely a stranger to grace if God forgives because of his mercy, for he prepares himself for pardon. "I know my sin, I repent of my fault continually, because it is always before me." I weigh how grave it is, since I have sinned against you alone—that is, it is known to you alone how grave it is—and I have sinned before you, whose future son and the breathing of the spirit is in me. Finally, he adds: The most powerful cause for pardon, namely, the glory of God, consisting also in this, that he is justified in his words. For God had promised through the Prophet **Nathan** to David that he would confirm his kingdom in his seed forever. Which...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans 3, focusing on verses 4 through 8. Ficino is reconciling the fact of human sin (specifically David's) with the unwavering reliability of God’s promises.</meta>

<page-num>456</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES<-

...is read in the second book of the *Laws* <note>original: "secundo Legum libro"; likely referring to Plato’s *Laws*, as Ficino frequently synthesized Platonic philosophy with Christian theology</note>. After these things, however, David completely stained himself with the crimes of adultery and murder. Because of this, a suspicion could arise in many people that God would by no means keep his promises to such an unworthy man. To these concerns, David responds in this way: "Because of my sin, divine justice will not be changed, for it is the nature of that justice, above all, to fulfill promises."

<margin>» »</margin> **That you may be justified in your words**
<margin>» »</margin> **and prevail when you are judged.** <note>Quoting Psalm 51:4, which Paul cites in Romans 3:4.</note>
That is to say: so that from this, you may appear just in your words. Indeed, even because of my crimes, you are not going to frustrate these promises at any time. 

<margin>» »</margin> **And prevail when you are judged.** 
That is, when you are judged by men as being likely to change your promise and decree—as if you yourself were changed by my wicked acts—in this very matter you surpass human opinion. You do this by fulfilling, clearly, what mortal suspicion imagined would remain unfulfilled. The promise indeed made by God to David concerning Christ, who was to come from the lineage of David, had to be completely fulfilled. For it pertained to the <term>prophetic oracle of predestination</term> <note>A theological term for a divine decree that is fixed and certain to happen regardless of human action</note>. 

However, it is not strictly necessary for the threatening promises <note>i.e., warnings of punishment</note> delivered through the Prophets to be fulfilled. For they are foretold as things to be carried out according to one's merits; if those merits are changed in the meantime <note>through repentance</note>, the outcome of the threats does not proceed. Therefore, if the promise to David had not been fulfilled, divine justice might perhaps be blamed. If, however, the terrors of the threats sometimes do not occur, divine justice is not reproached; rather, it is the mortals who are considered to have changed.

### He resolves questions concerning God’s truth, justice, and grace. Chapter 19.

<margin>» »</margin> **But if our injustice commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath?** <note>Romans 3:5</note> If God, in his mercy, grants good things even to the unworthy, his grace appears all the more commendable in that gift. Someone might then suggest that God uses our malice as a kind of instrument to celebrate his own glory. This would lead to the conclusion that God is "unjust" when he punishes the very sins that contribute to his glory. Therefore Paul asks: "What shall we say if someone argues God is unjust when he punishes sins that lead to his glory?" It is as if he is saying, "How shall we avoid the absurdities that would follow from that?" He expresses the resulting inconsistency by saying: **Is God unjust who inflicts wrath** (that is, vengeance) **for sin?** For this seems to follow from what was said. 

But in truth, sin is by no means necessary to God for the sake of commending the glory of his justice. For if sin tended toward the celebration of divine justice by some path of its own, it would be worthy not of punishment, but of reward. And thus God would seem unjust while he punishes men for their crimes—which is a wicked thing to say. Therefore, through the following words, he excludes this profanity, saying: **God forbid** <note>original: "absit"</note>, namely, that we should judge God to be unjust. 

**I speak as a man.** <note>Romans 3:5</note> That is: "I have brought forth this suspicious logical consequence regarding a potential injustice in God not as my own opinion, but through the tongue of certain people who doubt in this way." Notice how much Paul turns away from even uttering the words of others that might offend God in any way. Similarly, **Socrates** in the *Phaedrus* and *Philebus* <note>Two of Plato's dialogues</note> says he is terrified by the greatest fear of all, lest he should perhaps offend against the divine names. Paul shows that this must not be said by adding the following: 

<margin>» »</margin> **Otherwise, how shall God judge this world?** <note>Romans 3:6</note> That is to say, if God is unjust—for just as it pertains to the Creator of the universe to be all-powerful, so it pertains to the Judge of the universe to be most just. Hence that saying of David: "He shall judge the world in equity." And when Paul says, "How shall he judge this world?", he wants to be understood as referring not only to the judgment of men, but to the universal judgment, by which God powerfully touches all things and disposes them sweetly. He arranges and dispenses those things which are in the heavens and those under the heaven in a certain wonderful order. Therefore, he who is most just in the common distribution of the entire world must not be thought unjust in the affairs of men alone.

<margin>» »</margin> **For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie unto his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner?** <note>Romans 3:7</note> If in my lie (that is, because of my lie, which is included in every sin) the truth of God (that is, his fair faithfulness) has abounded—specifically, openly to his glory, so that human falsehood properly contributes to God's glory—two absurdities follow. 

First, that a man ought not to be considered a sinner because of a lie, if indeed it properly contributes to God’s glory. Therefore, Paul takes on the persona of the sinner, asking: **why am I also still** (that is, why even now) **judged by men for a lie, as a sinner, and a sinner entirely?** 

The second absurdity is that we would grant an opening to the false Apostles to make accusations, as they are accustomed to doing against the true Apostles of Christ. For when the true Apostles preached that through the abundance of Christ's grace, the abundance of sinners was saved—just as the Apostle says, "Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more"—they <note>the false critics</note> used to snap at the Apostles, as if they were making it a common...

<page-num>457</page-num>
->ST. PAUL’S COMMENTARY<-

<margin>»</margin> they might spread abroad that men ought to commit evils so that good things may result from them. This would indeed follow if a man's lie truly enhanced God's grace and specifically brought glory to Him; therefore he said: **And as we are slandered.** That is, not if we ourselves say and feel this, but as certain people charge us, as if by slander, and as they falsely claim. **Let us do evil so that good may come.** Namely, so that God’s truth, grace, and equity may be commended, let us abound in sins so that grace may also superabound. For we do not speak or feel this way. **Whose condemnation is just.** Namely, the condemnation of those who do evil so that good things may happen. For just as we ought not to propose falsehoods to conclude truths, so we should not choose evils so that we might reach a good end through them. Furthermore, the damnation of those who brand the Apostles with such unjust marks of infamy is just. Nor is it an injury, for they who unjustly condemn God or God’s ministers are themselves justly condemned. And those who do not fear to bring divine justice into doubt experience that very justice condemning them and feel it tormenting them.

### *Invective against the Jews and Gentiles, and that the observation of the law is not sufficient for salvation. Chapter 20.*

<margin>»</margin> **W**hat then: are we better than they? Not at all.) Paul, numbering himself among the Jews, asks this: What then is to be said? Are we more excellent than the Gentiles? He asks differently here than in the earlier passages. There he asked, "Is there anything more for the Jew?" <note>Refers to Romans 3:1</note>—meaning, something granted by God—and he immediately confirmed that the words, mysteries, and oracles of God were entrusted to the Jew above all others. Now, in the person of the Jews, he asks: Are we more eminent than the Gentiles? That is, regarding human persons and actions. Therefore he answers, "not at all." And just as in the previous sections he listed the many and great vices of the Gentiles, so he next lists as many for the Jews and Gentiles alike, so that both may be judged equal in their conduct; meanwhile, the Jews are so much worse to the extent that they have abused a greater gift granted by God. For there was an <term>altercation</term> <note>A formal debate or dispute</note> between the Jews and the Gentiles converted to the faith as to who were more excellent. In this, the Jews especially exalted themselves by divine gifts and looked down on the Gentiles as being least fit for salvation. Therefore, both seemed to the Apostle to need restraint, but the Jews most of all. **For we have charged that all Jews and Greeks are under sin.** As if he were saying: we have accused them with reasons and charged both as being so subject to sin that they can only obtain justice and salvation through divine grace alone. Let neither the Greeks trust in philosophy or <term>natural law</term> <note>The moral law believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</note>, nor the Jews in their prerogative or the written law, but let both flee to evangelical grace. The Apostle indeed charged the Gentiles when he accused them of "holding the truth of God in injustice and impiety." He also charged the Jews when he argued that they, having received the law from God, had transgressed it and defrauded God of His honor. **As it is written.** Namely, written by David, who piled up many serious faults of the Jews and Gentiles. He will also cite Isaiah as a witness against them. In enumerating the sins, he first brings forward those of omission, and then the faults of commission. **There is none righteous, there is none who understands, there is none who seeks God.** No one is righteous with perfect justice, which indeed ought to be referred to God, and toward this end divine grace must strive. **There is none who understands.** Namely, with the exact reasoning by which actions must be directed toward God especially. **There is none who seeks God.** Because they do not investigate what pleases God or what does not, and how He is the ultimate end to be proposed for our actions. **All have turned aside.** Namely, from the right way. They rightly wander in their choice of paths and journey, since they have not looked toward the goal. **Similarly they have become useless.** They do not attain the subsequent ultimate end in which they might find rest, after they have erred from the beginning in the very establishment of the goal and the choice of paths. Hence every effort is useless. **There is no one who does good, no, not one.** Surely, since they have already erred in the principles of their actions, they perform no work that is absolutely good; and because all have similarly erred, no one can think to reach the good by their own power. Hence all are judged to be in equal need of grace. **Their throat is an open grave, with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully.** Now he approaches the sins of commission, and begins with the falsehood of speech, detraction, and cursing. For into these and any horrible sins fall all mortals who, wandering once from the beginning, wander everywhere deprived of divine grace. **They have dealt deceitfully.** Because they spread and devise not only true crimes or those done openly, but also false and secret ones. **The poison of asps is under their lips.** For malicious deeds poured out by the tongue spread a virus for a long time that will infect many. **Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.** He increases the severity when he says, "full." Cursing even against God, and of bitterness...

<margin>»</margin> while they even provoke others to this and infect them. **Their feet are swift to shed blood.** <note>original: "Veloces pedes eorũ ad effundendum fanguinem." quoting Romans 3:15 / Isaiah 59:7</note> He now brings forward the testimony of Isaiah, and after the faults of the tongue, he now attacks sins of action. He expresses, therefore, how prone they must be thought to be toward any crime whatsoever, since they are carried headlong even to the murder of the Prophets. **Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways.** <note>original: "Contritio & infœlicitas in uijS eorum."</note> After the feet, he consequently touches upon their ways, that is, their wicked movements and acts. In these, moreover, he places "contrition" <note>In this context, contrition refers to being "ground down" or crushed by the consequences of sin.</note> and misery—namely, the punishments for the worst words and deeds. For even in this life, they are ground down and tortured by their own outrages in passing, as if by stumbling blocks and brambles. In the future life, truly, they are weighed down by eternal misery. **The way of peace they have not known.** Because they did not know—that is, they did not choose—the straight and shortcut way to blessedness, in which alone peace and rest can exist. Consequently, having abandoned this way, which is the only one, they are pulled apart through many ways, wandering into paths leading to the worst habits and to unhappiness. **There is no fear of God before their eyes.** What he has placed here last is the beginning of all evils. For just as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and wisdom is the beginning of acting rightly and happily—which <term>Plato</term> also demonstrates in the *Euthydemus* <note>A dialogue by Plato where Socrates argues that wisdom is the only true good and the source of happiness.</note>—so not to fear God is the origin of ignorance, like a blindness that wanders greatly in its choosing. And indeed, from here is the origin of the crooked and unhappy journey. Moreover, he said **before their eyes**, as he warns us to fear God not lightly, but constantly and most truly, and to always have such a "fragrance" of God as both an indicator and a leader of all actions. **Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are in the law.** Some among the Jews interpret the above words of David as being spoken against Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, and his army. So be it then, and let Isaiah speak of the Gentiles if it pleases. Yet, because both prophets are founded in the Mosaic Law, they must be considered as speaking for the Law, having been divinely sent for the instruction of the Jewish people. Therefore, even if their words touch upon or encompass the Gentiles, they nevertheless strive everywhere to chastise the people over whom they were placed, and thus they speak chiefly to form those who are under the Law. And for that reason, if at any time they touch upon the Gentiles, they meanwhile include the Jews also under the Gentiles' name and example. **So that every mouth may be stopped.** What indeed is the intention of the Prophets when they detest all people equally? It is so that no one may further dare to boast of themselves as if they were wise or just. **And all the world may become subject to God.** That all may equally recognize their errors and weigh how little they are sufficient for themselves, and therefore always look for the grace of God. **Because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him.** Neither the Gentile by the works of the natural law, nor the Jew by the Mosaic Law, can attain the justice worthy of eternal salvation. Both, therefore, are compelled to flee to evangelical grace. Moreover, he said **before him**: because the observation of the law is indeed thought among men to be sufficient for salvation, but by no means so before God. **For through the law is the knowledge of sin.** For the law does not lighten one's faults and sins, but weighs them down. It does this in two ways: because through the natural and the written law, we are taught what must be done and what must be avoided, so that ignorance cannot excuse us. Likewise, the law binds us to observance. Hence, when we strive for what is forbidden, having set aside reverence for the law, we sin with a certain heavier damnation. There is need, therefore, of a certain more indulgent clemency, help, and grace from the Author of laws, so that He may redeem us from crime and guilt either through aid, or through pardon and grace.

***

### *What the justice of God is, and how it does not depend on the works of the law, but on the grace of God through faith in Christ, and concerning redemption. Chapter XXI.*

<margin>»</margin> **B**ut now, apart from the law, the justice of God has been manifested, being witnessed by the law and the Prophets. The Apostle has long been laboring to affirm that salvation cannot be had without the faith of Christ. Hitherto indeed he wished to show this through the defect of the law; hereafter, however, he will open the same to us chiefly through the perfection of Christian faith and grace. Furthermore, in the preceding sections, he recounted that the Jews and Gentiles before the coming of Christ were almost equal in guilt; hereafter, however, he will demonstrate them to be equal in the state of grace. At the beginning, he says that the **justice of God** depends not at all on the law. He calls that "the justice of God" especially which God Himself requires as sufficient for salvation, and by which the Father Himself justifies those believing in the Son. This justice of God, therefore, has now—that is, in the time of grace—been manifested, both through the teaching of Christ, and through His miracles, and also through the evidence of His work. For indeed it has been found that many are divinely...

so to speak, justified. And this indeed is apart from the law, that is, while the law of this kind did not bring about righteousness, just as he says to the Galatians: *You who are justified by the law have fallen from grace.* <note>original: "Qui in lege iustificamini, a gratia excidistis." cf. Galatians 5:4</note> Hence also Isaiah says: *My salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed.* <note>original: "Prope est salus mea, ut ueniat & iustitia mea, ut reueletur." cf. Hence Christ says in John: *If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me: for he wrote of me.* <note>original: "Si crederetis Mosi, forsitan & mihi crederetis: de me enim ille scripsit." cf. John 5:46</note> Furthermore, it is shown through the effect. Because since the law itself could not justify, it argued sufficiently that righteousness must be sought from elsewhere. Moreover, the Prophets testified to it by announcing it. Therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles it is said: *To him all the Prophets bear witness.* **The righteousness of God, however, is through faith in Jesus Christ unto all, and upon** ,, **all, who believe in him.**) <note>Romans 3:22</note> Indeed, the righteousness which satisfies God, by which the ,, soul is justified before God, is obtained through that very faith provided to Christ and the Gospel. Through faith, I say, that is living—that is, <term>charity that gives it form</term> <note>original: "charitatem formatam." In scholastic theology, "formed faith" is faith animated by love (charity), rather than a mere intellectual belief.</note> and is active. This faith indeed prepares us for grace. But by grace we are truly justified. He says **Unto all**. Since justification of this kind can apply equally to everyone. He says, **and upon all**. Since it exceeds the merits and powers of all. **Who believe in him**, namely, that he is the son of God. Previously, indeed, that he would come; afterwards, truly, that he has come. **For there is no distinction, for all have sinned, and are deprived of** ,, **the glory of God.**) <note>Romans 3:23</note> This seems to be confirmed through Isaiah: *all of us, like sheep, have gone astray.* He ,, says there is no distinction between the Jew and the Gentile. Because neither is led to salvation by their own law alone, and both have sinned so much that they are deprived of the capacity for God’s glory. Both, therefore, equally require the grace of God. And for this grace, they are to be equally prepared through faith. Through which grace, surely, they are thought to be equally justified. Therefore it follows: **Justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus.**) <note>Romans 3:24</note> ,, Since they attained righteousness neither by their own laws nor by merits, but by faith alone and the grace of God. But before we proceed further, you must be warned that it should not be read as the Latin manuscripts have it, *they need the glory of God.* <note>Ficino is correcting the Latin Vulgate's "egent gloria Dei" (they need/lack) by comparing it to the Greek "hysterountai" (are falling short/deprived).</note> For that neither agrees with the Greek words, nor does it preserve a mode of speaking consistent with usage. For we do not properly say, "they need glory," but "they need grace," and "they are deprived of glory," or "they lack it." So Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373), a Greek Church Father and Bishop of Alexandria.</note> also reads it: For on account of this very thing that all have sinned, they similarly lack glory, and equally need grace to attain glory. But let us return to the immediate point. Again, it should not be read "through his grace," as the Latin manuscripts have it, but by the "Greek truth," as I was saying above, **by his grace.** Otherwise, the context is ridiculous. The grace of God himself makes us righteous through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus—that is, through this medium, because he sent Jesus to redeem us from our faults, as if we were the guilty ones, by his own satisfaction for us. By satisfaction, I say, by enduring death for us. To which death, indeed, we were all liable on account of original sin. Truly, a satisfaction of this kind cannot pertain to us otherwise than through faith. By which faith we believe that our redeemer is Jesus Christ; therefore it is added: **Whom God set forth as a propitiator, through faith in his blood.**) <note>Romans 3:25</note> He set forth, that is, he predestined ,, and openly placed him before all as the reconciler of the human race with God, in his own blood—that is, by the marvelous sacrifice of himself, pertaining to us through faith alone. Moreover, where he says **propitiator**, he touches upon the Mosaic <term>mercy seat</term>. <note>original: "propitiatorium." The golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant where God’s presence rested; Ficino follows the tradition of seeing this as a "type" or symbol of Christ.</note> Which indeed, as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical interpretation.</note> says, was the cover of the Ark, distinguished by twin cherubim; as our writers explain, it is a symbol of Christ. He who protects both the Church and the Ark, and just as the Cherub is figured, he is human, and likewise divine. **For the showing of his righteousness, for the remission of former sins.**) <note>Romans 3:25</note> ,, He assigns the final cause of redemption and propitiation—that is, so that God’s righteousness ,, might be declared in many ways, so that divine justification might come to us. So that what was promised by God might be justly and faithfully fulfilled, so that the universal sin of the human race should not be entirely unpunished. Which indeed can only be expiated by the satisfaction of Christ—both innocent and divine—on our behalf. Therefore he said, the showing of divine righteousness could be achieved in the remission of former sins. **In the forbearance of God for the showing of his righteousness in this time.** Which sins indeed God had tolerated until now, so that he neither punished nor absolved them—especially concerning the <term>fathers waiting in limbo</term> <note>original: "patres expectantes in limbo." Referring to the 'Limbus Patrum', the place where Old Testament saints were said to wait for Christ's resurrection.</note>—but he had tolerated them so that he might finally declare that only in this time of Christian grace can sins be absolved. **That he himself might be just, and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ**, namely, to this end that God himself might appear entirely just, and moreover might render the believer in Christ just.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

It seems it would be worthwhile, before we approach the following discussion, to say something concerning the redeemer made manifest through Christ. We shall briefly bring here the arguments from our book *On Religion*. <note>Ficino refers to his work "De Christiana Religione" (1474), where he attempted to harmonize Christian theology with Platonic philosophy.</note> For there, we discuss this at greater length. The life of the body is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The order of nature requires that the body obey the soul, and the soul obey God. The order of justice requires that if the soul disagrees with God, the punishment of <term>retribution</term> <note>original: "talionis pœna." The "lex talionis" or law of retaliation (an eye for an eye).</note> shall cause the body to disagree with the soul, and the senses to disagree with reason. The soul of our first parent rebelled against God, and consequently, his body and senses rebelled against him. This first rebellion was sin. The second was a certain punishment of that sin, and its flavor, as it were, flowed into all people, just as little streams flow from a fountain. This is the <term>original vice</term> <note>original: "originale uitium," more commonly known today as Original Sin.</note> which is the origin of all other evils of the soul and body. The volumes of the Hebrews testify to this; their divinity is attested by their supreme antiquity above all others, the agreement of almost everyone, their spread through the universe, their tireless duration, their harmony, majesty, sobriety, and miracles. Hence comes that opinion of the Magi descending from Zoroaster: namely, that all evils of the body proceed from evils of the soul, and if the soul is cured, the other evils are avoided. Plato hints at this in the *Timaeus*, and declares it in the *Charmides*. <note>Ficino often cites Zoroaster and Plato as "ancient theologians" who prefigured Christian truths.</note> To return to the proposal: since a rebellion of this kind disparaged the majesty of an infinite God, it rendered mortals utterly unfit for infinite happiness, and it could not be set right except by an infinite God. Yet they had to be set right at some point, lest they should have been ordained by God toward happiness from the beginning in vain. Sin was committed through pleasure; it must be purged through the opposite of pleasure—pain. All of human nature sinned once, in a way, in that man who acted in the stead of all; similarly, all must suffer once, in a way, in someone who also acts in the stead of all, who agrees with God far more than that first man disagreed. Truly, after Adam, only he who was inwardly joined to God, the creator of all, could act in the stead of all. Therefore, he was both God and man at once. He was God so that he might embrace all and be able to wash away an infinite fault. He was man so that he might be able to suffer for the fault, and that a man might suffer just as a man had sinned. Thus, the punishment and merit of that man had a certain infinite power, insofar as he was truly joined to the infinite God. Moreover, a certain infinite punishment and merit was needed to utterly wash away an infinite fault. Furthermore, the Jewish Doctors agree that divine providence appropriately and often purges the evils threatening a wicked people through the punishment of one just man, who will freely satisfy for all, just as all members of the body are often cured through the <term>incision of a single vein</term>. <note>A reference to the medical practice of bloodletting to balance the body's humors.</note> Likewise, they agree that through the fault of Adam the human species was infected. And they agree that this contagion has not yet been purged, but must be purged in the time of the Messiah, in whatever way it is purged. We, however, conclude from their own principle that a purgation of this kind is achieved through the passion of the Messiah. For just as one who is to satisfy for many must be step-by-step more righteous, so for everyone he must be the most righteous of all. Such a one is the Messiah alone. Moreover, Paul proves in the *Letter to the Hebrews* how it was necessary for the Messiah to be both priest and sacrificial victim to expiate souls.

->*Not through the merits of legal works, but through Christian faith is the Gentile made just and saved, equally as the Jew. Chapter XXII.*<-

<margin>">>"</margin> (**W**here then is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No. But by the law of faith.) <note>Romans 3:27</note> For a long time now the Apostle has begun to repress the boasting of the Jews, insofar as they boasted solely or especially in the Law, and trusted that they were quite superior to the Gentiles in attaining salvation. Therefore, since Paul has already proven that the Jews exist as equals in guilt to the Gentiles, he has hinted that the Gentiles are equal to the Jews in receiving grace. Here, then, he continues his effort to repress the vain glory of the Jews. Listen, Jew: if you are equally liable to sins as the Gentile, and again, when he is justified equally as you are through the faith and grace of the Gospel, where then is your boasting? That is, in what law do you boast so much that you think you alone, or chiefly, have reached righteousness by the merits of such works? It is excluded, clearly, and hissed off the stage. Since, indeed, one law seems to be excluded, or declared, or corrected by another, he asks by which law especially their boasting has been restrained. One law is said to be the rule of works, namely the Mosaic Law: which indeed seems to be occupied not so much in uprooting disturbances of the soul as in arranging outward actions.

<meta>catchword: The other</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the infinite nature of original sin required an infinite, divine-human Redeemer (Christ) to restore humanity, a concept he aligns with both Platonic philosophy and Jewish tradition. He then returns to his commentary on Romans, explaining that Paul "excludes" Jewish boasting because the Law of works cannot justify as faith does.</summary>
