<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans, moving from a general philosophical defense of the Redeemer to a specific analysis of Romans 3:27 through Romans 4:2. Ficino focuses on the transition from the Mosaic Law to the "Law of Faith" and begins his famous treatment of Abraham as the model of justification.</meta>

# COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL

The other is called the law of faith, that is, the Gospel, which not only corrects and arranges external actions but also regulates every movement of the soul <term>perfectly</term> <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a classical idiom for finishing a piece of work with absolute precision.</note> and uproots disturbances. Through this law, indeed, the boasting of the Jews is removed. For by its gift, any Gentile may obtain divine justice and grace no less than the Jews. <margin>,,</margin> *For we reckon that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law.*) Truly, a living faith that works through charity, shown to Christ, offers perfect justice to anyone who believes in this way, even if they have not been practiced in the works of the law. However, it is necessary for one who believes in this way to subsequently perform lawful works, lest faith without works be judged dead. <margin>,,</margin> *Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also:* <margin>,,</margin> God, the creator of the universe, provides for everyone, not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles. Therefore, he has applied a means of salvation not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles, so that just as the Jew, raised under the Mosaic precepts, has an entrance to grace, so the Gentile, nurtured and taught under <term>natural law</term> <note>The "lex naturalis," or the moral code Ficino believed was inherent in human reason regardless of revelation.</note>, may have a path to salvation; and both, having obtained righteousness through Gospel faith, may achieve eternal glory before God. <margin>,,</margin> *Since it is one God who justifies the circumcision from faith, and the uncircumcised through faith.* God himself, providing equally for both by the gift of the same faith—namely, the Christian faith—approves both as righteous and deems them worthy of grace and glory. He says, however, that he justifies the Jews *from faith* <note>original: "ex fide"</note> and the Gentiles *through faith* <note>original: "per fidem"</note>. "From faith" applies to the Jews because their faith is the most ancient of all. It began in Abraham, proceeded through the other Patriarchs and Prophets, always awaiting the Christ who was to come. Thus, the Jew is born into this faith and fortified by it; it is from this faith that he is said to be justified before God. But among the Gentiles, there was no ancient faith concerning Christ; rather, through the preaching of the Apostles, they are judged justified by this new and sudden faith. <margin>,,</margin> *Do we then destroy the law through faith? God forbid; rather, we establish the law.* <margin>,,</margin> Lest anyone think from what was said above that Gospel faith is contrary to the Mosaic law, he adds: the Mosaic law is not destroyed by the Gospel law but, as the Lord says, it is fulfilled. For those things in the Old Testament which were ceremonial, acting as a sign of things to come, have found their truth in the substance of the Gospel. And those things which were once moral have received their desired end and vow. For they arranged the movements of the soul and cut them back as much as possible, so that they might finally be completely purified. This perfect purification and purity is what the Gospel law provides.

### Neither Abraham nor anyone else is considered righteous before God because of circumcision or any similar work of the law, but because of faith. Chapter 14.

**T**he Jews preferred themselves excessively over the Gentiles in the reception of salvation because of the privileges of the Law and circumcision. Therefore, since the Apostle has already frequently suppressed this kind of boasting concerning the Law, he proceeds next to restrain it regarding circumcision, repeating a certain previous question which says: *What then is the benefit of circumcision?* And since Abraham was the first to receive the mandate of circumcision, Paul rightly resumes the question about circumcision regarding Abraham’s person, saying: <margin>,,</margin> *What then shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh?*) <margin>,,</margin> It is as if he were saying: After we have said that both the uncircumcised and the circumcised are justified before God, what exceptional capacity for attaining divine justice did Abraham find or bring back *according to the flesh*—that is, the circumcised flesh—from the fact that he circumcised his own flesh and that of his family by divine command and performed similar works? It is as if he says: he did not achieve perfect justice through works of this kind, but through faith. For if any mortal man looks upon him circumcising by divine command and performing other legal works outwardly, he will judge him worthy of the glory of justice; and this is indeed a human judgment looking at external things. For man is not able to look into the innermost parts. Thus, Abraham will earn glory among men. However, he does not earn glory before God by this same reasoning—for God looks into the innermost parts and justifies because of faith and the intention of the goal, rather than because of external movements. These external movements indeed often lie and deceive a judge intent upon them; and even if they are lawful, as in the case of Abraham, God nevertheless deems Abraham (and anyone else working similarly) worthy of the glory of justice not because of them, but through faith and internal intention. Human justice, looking at human good, is commonly acquired through the habit of external works. But divine justice—that which is primarily accepted by God and desires the divine and ultimate good—does not have as much to do with actions...

<summary>This page explains how the "Law of Faith" fulfills rather than destroys the Mosaic Law, emphasizing that both Jews and Gentiles are justified by faith. It introduces Abraham as the primary example, arguing that his righteousness came from his internal faith and intention rather than the physical act of circumcision.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on St. Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, specifically Chapter 4. Ficino is expanding on the distinction between "external" justice (based on visible deeds) and "internal" justice (based on faith), using the biblical figure of Abraham as his primary example. This follows the previous page's discussion on the "Law of Faith" versus the Mosaic Law.</meta>

### MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

...proportion with external things so that it can be acquired from them; rather, it arises from faith raised toward God through <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the theological virtue of selfless, divine love, rather than simple modern almsgiving.</note> and divine grace. Thus it is rightly said that external favor resides among men, while those same people report their innermost intention and glory before God. Wherefore the Apostle adds:

> For if Abraham was justified by the works of the law, he has glory, but not before God.

It is as if he says: if you judge a man just because of the external works of the law, this would be a human approval rather than a divine one. By "works of the law," he means that he was circumcised, or that he offered sacrifices, and other things of that kind which the Mosaic law commands to be observed. Furthermore, civil and human justice is acquired from external works, which indeed holds glory among men, but not a similar glory before God; for external glory does not make a man worthy unless a great affection of faith and charity, fortified by divine grace, has approached and preceded it. One should consider that what has been translated into Latin as "he has glory," is more properly "boasting" in the Greek <note>original: "Græce haberi propriè gloriationē," referring to the Greek word *kauchema* (boasting/matter of pride).</note>. Here the specific sense is this: he has in himself that which he may boast of—that is, if he earned justice through the works of his own <term>free will</term> <note>liberi arbitrij</note> as if they were his own, he could rightly boast, not only before God but also within himself. This would mean he was justified not only by divine grace but by his own actions and merits. But if he becomes just not through external works, but through the offering of faith alone, he shall boast only in the grace and generosity of God. What the Apostle says of Abraham, he wishes to be understood similarly of all other men. For what does the scripture say?

> Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as justice.

Indeed, it is written in Genesis that Abraham believed God when He promised the multiplication of his offspring. And because of this kind of faith, not because of external things, he was judged just by God. Moreover, he believed God especially when He promised the Christ; from which it is confirmed that through perfect faith in Christ, justice is acquired. Truly, God willed to impress perfect justice upon us, not in a lowly subject—namely, in external writings and movements—but in the most intimate affection of the mind, in which affection it has its beginning. He says, however, "he believed God." For there is a triple act of faith: to believe *that* God is, to believe God’s word, and to believe *in* God. He believes **that God is** <note>original: "Credere Deum"</note> who, relying on authority, affirms that God exists and provides for all. He believes **God's word** <note>original: "Credit Deo"</note> who gives credit to and obeys divine revelations and precepts. Finally, he believes **in God** <note>original: "Credit in Deum"</note> who, applying charity to faith, refers all things to God as his ultimate end. The first act seems to contain the matter of faith; the second, the form of faith; and the third, its end. Thus, to express the very form of faith, he said, "he believed God."

> Now to him who works, the reward is not counted according to grace, but according to debt. But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited to him as justice, according to the purpose of God’s grace.

The Apostle explains and confirms that statement: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as justice." For since Abraham, having as yet performed nothing external, believed God perfectly, and because of this very faith was judged just by God, he seems to have received justice from God freely (by grace). Similarly, many others, although they have not yet had the time, opportunity, or faculty for working, have been gifted with justice because of faith alone and their affection toward God, just as if they had completed the works of justice. For what is said to be "credited" is understood to be given freely to someone who does not yet truly deserve it. These things are confirmed in what follows, where it is said, "with the heart one believes unto justice." However, he who has already practiced many works consistent with justice and conducive to its application—if he is held just by God—has obtained this reward (that is, justice) not only by a gift but also by his own duty. This is based on the following reasoning: what is handed over to someone working as a "wage" is not properly given by reason of grace, but is repaid under the condition of a debt. But perfect justice, of which we speak here, is granted by the bounty of grace. Therefore, it is not acquired through the works of the law. Furthermore, when he says "who justifies the ungodly," he strengthens the argument. For if God sometimes calls a man who does not yet believe to faith, and through faith and grace leads him to justice and salvation, how much more does He make just and blessed a soul that is already, in a sense, pious and believing. Moreover, regarding what he says about "debt," you should not take it to mean that temporal works are worthy of either eternal beatitude or the perfect approval of justice. Paul condemns this where he says to the Romans: *The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come.* And to Titus: *Not according to the works of justice which we have done.* For our works, through their own form and nature, merit neither perfect justice nor beatitude. But according to the divine influence by which they are wonderfully incited and led, they do seem to merit them. Certainly, faith itself clearly does not merit these things unless it is supported by divine grace.

<summary>Ficino explains Romans 4, arguing that Abraham was justified by his internal faith rather than external rituals. He distinguishes between three types of belief and emphasizes that true justice is a gift of grace, not a wage earned by human effort.</summary>

# COMMENTARY ON ST. PAUL

...is supported. Finally, what he added: *According to the purpose of the grace of God.*) This signifies that God, by His own abundance, has predestined justice and imparts salvation to those who truly believe. Just as David also says: *Blessed is the man to whom God credits righteousness without works.*) Latin manuscripts have "having been received" <note>original: "accepto." Ficino is noting a grammatical error in the Latin versions he was consulting—likely the Vulgate—where the word "accepto" (received) made little sense compared to "acceptam fert" (reckons or credits).</note>; this is faulty and has no meaning. When it is said that God "credits justice," it is a Latin way of speaking, and it has this kind of meaning: God considers justice as accepted from that man who has not yet performed the works of the law. 

But how does He have it as "accepted"? Because even if that man does not bring the works of the law to God, he already possesses faith. Either the man himself offered this faith to God in the first place, and afterwards God increased it by His abundance, or God provided the faith from the beginning while joining the man to it through some miraculous work. Therefore, He made him just and reckoned him so, as if freely, though he had not yet performed the strong works that lead to justice. Indeed, sometimes he even did the opposite works [sins]. Which the Prophet <note>Referring to King David as "the Prophet," a common title in medieval and Renaissance theology because of the prophetic nature of the Psalms.</note> declares where he continues: *Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.*) 

From these things it is clearly seen that a man often burdened with sins is miraculously called by God to faith; thus he is considered just, and having been freely gifted with justice through faith, he is prepared for <term>beatitude</term> <note>The state of eternal happiness or "blessedness" in the presence of God.</note>. Truly happy and loved by God beyond measure, and judged well-favored by David, is he who without works—that is, preceding duties—and without labor, has received a perpetual gift for free. 

Where he says "iniquities," he signifies offenses committed through malice. Where he says "sins," he declares those committed through infirmity [weakness]. Finally, where he says "sin" [in the singular], he wants the common and <term>original sin</term> <note>The Christian doctrine of the innate corruption of human nature inherited from Adam.</note> of all to be understood. Sins, again, are said to be "covered" from the divine sight; these God does not look upon in order to punish. Similarly, He "does not impute" sin—namely, for vengeance. Grace of this kind is said to be granted to a few through a certain <term>predestination</term>, as it was for Paul and similar men who were divinely compelled toward the good. But the remission of sins granted to one who already believes, even if they are not yet performing works, seems to have happened to many. 

*Does this blessedness then come only to the circumcised, or also to the Gentiles? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? In circumcision, or before circumcision? Not in circumcision, but before.*) A question is raised about this kind of grace, which is called the "justice of faith," through which sins are freely forgiven; sometimes through faith alone, with no merits of preceding works, it reckons and renders the believer just, and sometimes even calls and justifies one who has previously worked evil. I ask, then, does it apply only to the circumcised, or is it granted equally to the uncircumcised? The answer is: equally. Indeed, Abraham was not yet circumcised when faith itself was reckoned to him as righteousness without preceding works. This occurred before the birth of Ishmael, whereas the circumcision took place when Ishmael was nearly an adult.

->*Circumcision is not the cause of justice, but the sign of justice, which is through faith. Likewise, the promise was made to Abraham not because of the works of the law, but because of faith. Chapter 24.*<-

**A**nd he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the justice of faith, which exists in the uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all believers without circumcision, that faith might also be reckoned to them as justice, and that he might be the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith which was in our father Abraham before circumcision.) 

After it has been argued that this beatitude, which consists in the remission of sins, belongs equally not only to the circumcised but also to the uncircumcised—and this was proved by the example of Abraham, who attained justice and such blessedness through faith itself from God before circumcision—it remained to reveal what the ritual of circumcision means. This is so that it should not perhaps seem to have been introduced in vain, since it is not the cause of justice. Therefore Paul says that it was divinely instituted as a sign and a seal. It is a sign indeed of the future, that is, of the spiritual circumcision to be performed through Christ. And it is a <term>signaculum</term> <note>A "seal" or "signet," used here to mean a physical mark that confirms or authenticates an internal spiritual reality.</note>, or seal, of that very justice which Abraham obtained through faith. Now, it is a seal of Abraham's disposition in two primary ways: namely, in regard to what he believed, and in regard to the effect of the flesh. For he believed the promise concerning the propagation of his offspring. So it was fitting that he received the seal on the organ of propagation...

<summary>Ficino explains that justice is a free gift from God through faith, as evidenced by David's Psalms and the fact that Abraham was justified before he was circumcised. He concludes that circumcision is not the cause of righteousness but a symbolic seal of a faith already possessed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Romans 4. On the previous page, Ficino discussed how Abraham was reckoned righteous by God due to his faith before he performed any works of the law. Here, he explores the specific role of circumcision as a "seal" or "sign" rather than the cause of that righteousness.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES<-

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

...has received. Faith itself removes guilt, just as circumcision removes the superfluous skin from the member of lust <note>A literal translation of "membro libidinis," referring to the foreskin and the medieval/Renaissance view of the body's physical drives.</note>. Moreover, Moses declares in Genesis that circumcision was introduced not as a kind of substance in itself, but as a sign or a seal. *You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.* By this, indeed, the people of God are distinguished from foreigners, and it signifies the cutting away of lusts which separate souls from God. Those who, through spiritual circumcision, have finally uprooted their bodily affections and thus restored the covenant with God, are said to be reconciled with God. Jeremiah touched upon a mystery of this kind: *Be circumcised to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your hearts.*

Then, where he says *so that he might be the father,* etc., he certainly wants this to be understood: Since Abraham was already judged righteous by God through faith itself before his circumcision—and was circumcised only a long time afterward—it follows that he is the father not only of the circumcised, but also of all those who believe without circumcision. Furthermore, when the text says *likewise without circumcision,* it can signify two things. First, that Abraham, through what he possessed before circumcision (namely, through faith), becomes the father of all who believe in the same way, so that it may be credited to them as righteousness—that is, the fact that they believe—just as it had been credited to Abraham. Second, that he is the father of those who believe without circumcision. Just as he himself had believed without circumcision, he is also the father of circumcision—that is, of the circumcised who draw their origin from him and have received the circumcision. Hence the saying in the Gospel of John: *Abraham is our father.*

Up to this point, this is the common exposition. But the more proper explanation is of this kind: namely, that he is the father and author of both faith and circumcision. Of faith, I say, for all believers, even the uncircumcised. For faith before circumcision, and thereafter without circumcision, is sufficient for righteousness and salvation. Regarding circumcision, it is understood in a twofold way, whether bodily or spiritual. The bodily kind is clearly for the Jews. The spiritual kind, however, is not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles, namely through imitation, insofar as they properly follow the footsteps of the faith which was in father Abraham before he was circumcised by divine command. That is, they believe with the same certainty, love, and works with which he had believed. This faith is indeed sufficient for their righteousness and salvation, just as it was for his, even without circumcision.

Some people ask whether circumcision contributes to washing away the guilt of original sin. Those who follow Bede <note>Bede the Venerable (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> think that original guilt was remitted through circumcision in the Old Testament just as it is remitted through baptism in the New. However, our Thomas Aquinas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican philosopher and theologian.</note> seems to moderate this view, suggesting that circumcision, simply by the performance of the act itself <term>ex opere operato (from the work performed)</term>, neither confers grace nor has the power either to remove guilt or to establish righteousness. And unless it brings righteousness, it cannot remove guilt. For darkness is not expelled without the arrival of light. There is no such power in circumcision because grace itself is not within it, and without grace there can be no righteousness.

Hence Augustine, following the mind of Paul, argues this way to the Galatians: *If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died in vain*—that is, without cause. Similarly, we are permitted to argue: If grace proceeds from being justified by circumcision, then Christ died in vain. Which is indeed a wicked thing to say. Truly, the remission of sin never occurs without grace. Paul opens this up in what follows: *Having been justified, therefore, by his grace,* etc. Rightly, therefore, Paul placed almost nothing in circumcision except a sign and a seal. Thus, original sin was removed and the help of grace for acting rightly was provided not through the act of circumcising itself, but through faith in Christ, of which circumcision was a sign.

Insofar as circumcision was a sign of what was to come, it is rightly judged to have been changed. For the same sign is not suitable for the present, the past, and the future. Therefore, baptism is the sign of present grace. For this reason, it contains a more ample effect of grace. For the closer and more present the agent is, the more effectively he works. Furthermore, regarding the promise made to Abraham, faith indeed stood prior to the promise, but circumcision came much later. Likewise, circumcision is called a sign and image of faith, while faith is the archetype and living substance. From this it is clearly concluded that the cause of the promise itself was not circumcision, or any such work of the law, but faith itself, supported by grace and living through charity. Wherefore the <margin>>> Apostle adds:</margin>

> For the promise to Abraham or his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is abolished. For the law brings about wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression.

Next, from the very form of the promise, he confirms the circumcision already begun, namely...

## MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES

<margin>Signature: Gg</margin>

...that any external work similar to legal observance does not bring perfect righteousness. In Genesis indeed it is written that a promise was divinely made to Abraham: *that in his seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.* <note>original: "benedicentur omnes Gentes terræ"</note> Moreover, "in his seed" is to be understood preeminently as "in Christ." Hence the Apostle says to the Galatians: *The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed;* he does not say "to seeds" as if referring to many, but "to one," namely Christ, whom Paul also calls the "heir of the world," <note>Paul interprets the "seed" of Abraham as a single person, Christ, rather than many descendants (Galatians 3:16).</note> that is, of all nations, which was indeed the father's promise. And David foretells it thus: *Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.* <note>A reference to Psalm 2:8.</note> In a certain way, the promise also had to be fulfilled in the seed of Abraham through those so named by imitation—namely, in those who are spiritually called the "seed of Abraham" through the grace of Christ. Therefore Paul says in the following verses: *Those who are children of the promise are counted as the seed,* who are also heirs of the world through Christ.

Accordingly, in this promise he denies one thing but asserts another. He denies, I say, that the promise was made through the law, but asserts that it was made through the righteousness of faith. This was rightly not through the law itself, because the law had not yet been given, nor through the observance of the law at some future time, because the promise was not made on the condition that a future law—or anything external similar to the law—must be observed, but simply because of faith itself. The very words of the promise declare this. Therefore, the promise was not made in such a way that it was only to be fulfilled through the law. Hence Paul says to the Hebrews: *The law brings nothing to perfection.* <note>Hebrews 7:19.</note> He affirms, however, that the promise was made through the righteousness of faith, and finally that it would be fulfilled through the same, so that the end might agree with the beginning. For, as it is said to the Hebrews, *the Saints through faith conquered kingdoms.* <note>Hebrews 11:33.</note>

And again he confirms the same thing in this way: first, he will show that the promise was not to be fulfilled through the law, and afterward that it must be perfected through the righteousness of faith. The reasoning, which leads to a near impossibility <term>reductio ad absurdum|a method of proving a point by showing that the opposite leads to an absurd or impossible result</term>, is constructed in this manner: if the promise made to Abraham were to be fulfilled through the law, it would immediately follow that the faith of Abraham (who believed the promise) would be empty, because this promise would be abolished. Since such a consequence would be absurd, the premise is surely proven false. For who would say that God either does not stand by his promises or that he deceives someone who believes him?

In laying out the consequence, it is said: *For if those who are of the law are heirs, etc.* <note>Romans 4:14.</note> This must be understood as: if it were necessary to obtain the promised inheritance solely as a consequence of this observance of the law, then faith and the promise are made void. First, because the promise was made not only to the Jews, but clearly to all nations who did not possess such a law. Now, however, it would be conceded to pertain to the Jews alone. Second, because if it is through the law, then that faith in which the promise was founded appears to waver as if it were insufficient, and the promise along with it. Truly, if the promised inheritance is to be rendered not by reason of the promise but by reason of future legal observance, such a promise becomes empty, insofar as it is rendered not because of itself, but because of something else far in the future.

Finally, as our Saint Thomas <note>Refers to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential medieval theologian whom Ficino frequently cites.</note> explains, if the promise is said to be fulfilled through the law, and the law in some way hinders or delays the effect of the promise, it will indeed be hindered while it is seen as a matter of command. The Apostle proves that the law at least incidentally hinders the attainment of the promised inheritance from this: *the law brings wrath,* <note>Romans 4:15.</note> that is, it increases divine indignation and vengeance upon sinners. *For where there is no law, there is no transgression.* Therefore, those who live by natural law alone sin more lightly than those who are additionally subject to written law. Since, therefore, such a law increases the guilt of the transgressors but does not bring with it the aid of helping grace—which is the specific gift of Christ—it consequently happens that it hinders or delays the effect of the promised inheritance. This is especially so because the excuse for sins is diminished through the knowledge given by the law, and because of our greed for liberty and license, "we strive for what is forbidden." <note>original: "nitimur in vetitum," a famous quote from the Roman poet Ovid, suggesting that humans are naturally inclined to want what they are told they cannot have.</note>

And this disadvantage through the law occurs in moral matters. It also occurs very much so in ceremonies, with which the Mosaic law bound its people (innumerable and very difficult to observe) at least until the Messiah. From this, transgression happened very frequently. It would also be more serious if such a curious attachment to legalism were to continue after the Gospel has been spread. Hence that saying of Paul to the Corinthians: *The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.* <note>2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> Because, as he will affirm in what follows, the spirit inwardly helps our weakness. From all these things it is concluded that the promise of the inheritance as the [greatest...]

<summary>Ficino explains that the promise to Abraham was based on faith, not the Mosaic Law, because the law actually increases human guilt and transgression by making the "letter" of the command more clear without providing the spiritual "grace" to follow it.</summary>

...made from the best, is not founded upon that which is in any way a cause of evil or an impediment to achieving what has been promised. Therefore, it is not founded in the law. Otherwise, it would not possess stability.

### How the promise to Abraham, which is not to be fulfilled through the law, is to be fulfilled through faith and grace. Chapter 25.

> Therefore it is of faith, so that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise might be firm for all the seed. Not to that only which is of the law, but also to that which exists from the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: "Because I have made you a father of many nations" before God, whom you believed, who gives life to the dead, and calls those things which are not as though they were. Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: "So shall your seed be," like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. <note>Original: "Ideo ex fide, ut secundum gratiam..." This is Ficino’s Latin rendering of Romans 4:16–18. The comparison to the sand of the sea is a common biblical expansion on the "stars of heaven" metaphor from Genesis.</note>

After he showed that the promise proposed by God to Abraham and his seed is not to be fulfilled through the law, he subsequently shows that it must be fulfilled through faith. He concludes this from a certain logical choice in this manner: This promise seems to be fulfilled either through the law or through faith; certainly not through the law, otherwise it would waver and vanish. Therefore, we attain the promise through faith, so that we may thus be heirs of the world. John confirms this in his epistle: *This is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith.* <note>Original: "Haec est victoria quae vincit mundum, fides nostra." A quote from 1 John 5:4.</note>

However, he sets down the opposite of the previous foundation of proof in the present case. For as he had said in the earlier parts—and indeed the earlier foundation stood—if the righteousness and the promised inheritance were by the power of the law, faith and the promise would vanish. But now the foundation is of this kind: if it exists from faith, that is, if it is founded in faith and proceeds through it, the promise remains firm. This is specifically because of the power of divine grace bringing righteousness to us. 

But so that this proof may proceed by its own steps, I have decided that Paul's words should be arranged as the <term>Greek codices</term><note>Greek codices: Ficino is referring to original Greek manuscripts of the New Testament. As a Renaissance Humanist, he compared the Latin Vulgate to Greek sources to find the most accurate meaning.</note> have them, so that the sense is of this kind: the promise exists from faith, so that it may come to us chiefly according to grace; and that for this reason, the promise may remain firm. Firm, I say, both in itself always, and to be equally provided to all the "seed" of Abraham. 

Truly, if what was promised were ultimately granted to our legal duties, it could certainly seem to be granted to human merits rather than to divine grace and bounty. This would both diminish the estimation of divine mercy and beneficence, and increase human arrogance. But if it proceeds to us through faith itself and the most intimate affection of the mind, it will undoubtedly be attributed entirely to divine grace. This indeed seems to contribute greatly to the wonderful glory of divine goodness and power. 

Moreover, this view is to be preferred for another reason: if the promised inheritance consisted in the observance of the law, it would depend both on the future and on our highly unstable actions, and therefore it would utterly waver. But if it has made its foundation in stable divine grace, it will itself stand stably. Added to this is the fact that such observance of the law pertained only to the Jews. The promise, however, was clearly made for all nations. Therefore, so that it may have stability in all, it seems it will proceed not from a law observed by a few, but rather from a faith equally common to all. 

Therefore, when he said "to all the seed," he touched upon the twofold seed of Abraham: both the bodily, I say—that is, the Jewish—and the spiritual likewise—that is, the whole human race which, just as Abraham believed, is destined to believe. The Gospel touches upon a seed of this kind: *God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones,* <note>A reference to Matthew 3:9 or Luke 3:8.</note> that is, from the Gentiles to make imitators of Abraham and, as it were, adopted sons. 

After this, where he says, "who is the father of us all," he confirms what he had just posited: namely, that the seed of Abraham is not only the Jewish people, followers of the law, but also any nation simply believing in the manner of Abraham. For he is the father of us all—that is, of any believers, whether Jews or Gentiles. He confirms this same thing by the authority of Genesis: *I have made you a father of many nations.* Hence that similar passage in <term>Ecclesiasticus</term><note>Ecclesiasticus: Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the biblical Apocrypha/Deuterocanon. Ficino uses it here to bolster Paul's argument.</note>: *Abraham was the great father of a multitude of nations before God, whom you believed.* This was added to express that what is future to us stands present to divine providence and is, as it were, already placed in His sight. Abraham also believed God’s foretold future so perfectly that he perceived it as if present and already done. *Who gives life to the dead,* namely the Jews, who were as if dead by the crimes of <term>transgression</term><note>Transgression: In Latin "praevaricatio," referring to the breaking of the Mosaic Law.</note> and ingratitude. *And calls those things which are not...*

<summary>Ficino explains that the promise to Abraham's descendants must be based on faith and grace rather than the law, because human actions are unstable while divine grace is firm. This allows Abraham to be the spiritual father of all nations (Gentiles) rather than just the physical father of the Jews.</summary>

# ST. PAUL’S COMMENTARY #

That is, he calls even the Gentiles to grace and salvation, who until now were as if they did not exist in God’s sight, if compared to the privileges of the Jews. Just as those who *are*, that is, equal to the Jews, who were already adopted and chosen. From this comes that which follows: "I will call those who were not my people, 'my people,'" and so on. <note>Original: "Vocabo non plebem meam, plebem meam." Ficino references Romans 9:25 and Hosea 2:23 to show how the "non-existent" Gentiles are brought into the promise.</note> Thus, through a calling of this kind, the promise of Abraham belongs also to the Gentiles. It fits the literal meaning most aptly to say that God "gives life to the dead," that is, he raises Abraham and Sarah—who were sterile and worn out by old age—to produce offspring. And also to choose and predestine the future progeny that did not yet exist, as if it already existed. In this sense the Apostle speaks to the Ephesians: "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world." <note>Ephesians 1:4</note> Likewise in what follows, it is said not from works, but from His will, that "the elder shall serve the younger." <note>Romans 9:12, referring to Jacob and Esau.</note> Now, intending to praise the faith of Abraham, he added: "who against hope believed in hope," <note>Romans 4:18</note> namely, against natural hope and natural power, since Abraham and Sarah were sterile and worn out by age—for he had completed his ninety-ninth year, and she her ninetieth year and was sterile, as related in Genesis. Yet he believed God who promised him a progeny. Therefore he believed in the hope offered by God, rather than in the life of nature. Divine hope is of such a kind. "I have made you a father of many nations." Likewise: "So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea." <note>Genesis 15:5 and 22:17. Ficino views these metaphors as representing both the quality and quantity of the faithful.</note> In these words, he determines that the succession of Abraham—whether by nature or by imitation—belongs to every kind of human. Through the comparison to the stars, he declares the excellence and divinity that many would have in this succession; through the sand of the sea, he declares a truly innumerable multitude. Since, indeed, his hope was not only intense and swift, but also firm, he added:

> "And he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body already dead (since he was nearly a hundred years old), nor the dead womb of Sarah. In the promise of God he did not waver through distrust, but was strengthened by faith, giving glory to God, knowing most fully that whatever God promised, He is powerful enough to do. Therefore it was credited to him as righteousness." <note>Ficino's Latin rendering of Romans 4:19–22.</note>

Truly, it was a firm faith that did not distrust at all despite natural impediments. In the hundredth year Isaac was born, as is handed down in Genesis, but he was promised nearly a year before. As for his begetting sons by Keturah after the death of Sarah, this is also thought to pertain to the same strength of Abraham, restored by divine power. Keturah was indeed young, but Sarah was sterile and decrepit, and Abraham was already naturally powerless. Pythagoras strongly approved of such ease and firmness in receiving divine matters, and frequently had this gentle sentiment on his lips: "one ought to believe all things, since nothing is incredible; all things are easy for God, nothing is impossible for God." <note>Ficino, a key figure in the Renaissance, often blends Christian theology with the "ancient theology" of Pythagoras and Plato.</note> Furthermore, Plato in the *Phaedrus* and the *Laws* detests a man who is incredulous regarding divine things. But since Paul had said, "he was not weakened," or "did not waver in faith," why then did he add: "In the promise of God he did not waver through distrust"? Because, clearly, just as he believed God who promised a progeny, so he gave ready faith to God who portended the excellence and exaltation of the future generation. For after God predicted: "I have made you a father of many nations," etc., He added: "Your seed shall possess the gates of your enemies, and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." <note>Genesis 22:17-18</note> The comparison to the stars also, as I said, signifies excellence. Moreover, in saying "he did not waver through distrust," he criticizes the distrust of Zechariah, who is said to have hesitated at the divine promise, and for this distrust was deprived of his senses for a time. <note>original: "uisu ad tempus orbatus"—literally "deprived of sight," though the biblical Zechariah in Luke 1:20 was actually struck mute. Ficino may be using "vision" metaphorically or referring to his temporary sensory isolation.</note> As for Abraham exclaiming, "Do you think a child shall be born to a hundred-year-old man?" <note>Genesis 17:17</note> Such a voice was not that of one doubting, but of one marveling at an unusual thing, and equally exulting. Perhaps with a similar feeling, the Virgin Mary cried out at the voice of Gabriel: "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" <note>Luke 1:34</note> As if she were saying: "I know for certain that this will happen, but express the manner of it more clearly yourself, since it is not a human way, but surely a divine one." Therefore, since Abraham did not waver by his own impulse—which is expressed where it is said: "Against hope he believed in hope," likewise, "and he was not weakened in faith," and again, "he did not waver through distrust"—it was rightly added: "but he was strengthened by faith," that is, he was additionally helped in this from above. Noticing this, Abraham gave glory to God, namely, attributing both the firmness of his faith and the promised gift not to his own merits, but entirely to divine goodness, and considering that what was promised would undoubtedly come to pass, since God is truthful—nay, Truth itself—and likewise almighty. However, he who is inspired by God, or instructed in any way, yet still wavers in faith, distrusting divine providence, or truth, or power, detracts from the divine glory. Hence, since he said from the beginning...

After he recounted that Abraham’s faith was accepted by God as righteousness, and subsequently described the nature of that faith, he concludes that it is not just any faith, but one that is ready, certain, stable, and giving thanks with love <note>The Latin "charitate" refers to "caritas," the highest form of Christian love or charity.</note>, tending everywhere toward the glory of God—just as Abraham’s faith stood—which is accounted by God as righteousness. 
<margin>»</margin> **It was not written for his sake alone, that it was credited to him for righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it will be credited as believers in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was handed over for our sins and rose again for our justification.** <note>Original: "Non est autem scriptum tantum propter ipsum..." quoting Romans 4:23-25.</note> Paul says in the following sections: 
<margin>»</margin> **Whatever things were written, were written for our instruction.** <note>Romans 15:4</note> Similarly, in the present passage, he teaches that God established in Abraham, the supreme Patriarch of believers, a model for the entirety of this discipline. And perhaps with great significance he introduced earlier that phrase: **I have made you the father of many nations before God, in whom you believed.** <note>Romans 4:17</note> That is, I have established you as a Patriarch, a model, and a leader for all nations who are primarily destined to believe, just as you believed—and indeed in the sight of God. This means not only within the providence of God but also, as Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a major Church Father known for defending the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> says, as an image of God, so that he might be as it were a kind of divine power, the author for all of pious belief and living well. 

And according to his likeness, pious faith is credited to us also as righteousness. What kind of faith, I ask? The same kind that he possessed, as we described above. And furthermore, just as he believed with holy devotion that his own deadened body <note>Ficino refers to Abraham's advanced age and sterility as a "dead" state from which life was miraculously produced.</note> would one day be raised up by divine power, so we too should believe that Christ both died and was raised up by divine power. May a faith of this kind be credited to us for righteousness just as it was to him—namely, to us who believe that Christ has come in the same way that he believed Christ would come. 

Since, in truth, the power and manifest operation of the Father and the Son are the same, just as it is said the Father raised Jesus, so it is often said that Jesus rose from the dead. Again, as he says in the following sections, **God did not spare his own son, but handed him over for us all.** <note>Romans 8:32</note> So also to the Ephesians, **he handed himself over for us.** <note>Ephesians 5:2</note> Regarding what is said here, **he was handed over**, it can be understood as being handed over by the Father, by himself, and by the Jews. Moreover, it is said that **he rose for our justification**, so that by rising he might justify us—that is, make us worthy of that righteousness by which we ourselves might rise again. As for the fact that he was handed over to death for our sins, this signifies that by his death, as if by a certain sacrifice made for us, he in some way atoned for our faults.

->*How divine grace is acquired. Also, which evils it avoids and which goods it confers—namely, righteousness through faith. Also hope, love, and the divine inheritance. Also how constant divine hope is.*<-

### Chapter XXVI.

<margin>»</margin> **Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus, through whom we have access in faith into this grace, in which we stand and boast in the hope of the glory of the children of God.** <note>Romans 5:1-2</note> Hitherto the Apostle has proved how necessary Christian grace is for salvation, chiefly by showing that neither the knowledge of truth and philosophy for the Gentiles, nor circumcision or the observation of the law for the Jews, was sufficient for salvation or of much use without the grace of Christ. Hereafter, however, he will discuss the power of grace, intending to show which goods we obtain through grace and, because of that same grace, which evils we avoid. First, however, he will prescribe the way and the manner by which one arrives at grace. 

Since it has been said how faith will be credited to everyone as righteousness—namely, to those who believe in the resurrection of Christ as the foundation of our righteousness—he rightly adds: 
<margin>»</margin> **Therefore, having been justified by faith.** Insofar as through that very faith in the resurrection, we obtain its effect, which is justification. 
<margin>»</margin> **Let us have peace with God.** This little phrase can indeed be read in two ways: "we have" <note>Original: "habemus"</note> and "let us have" <note>Original: "habeamus"</note>, but the ultimate meaning is the same. For we cannot be reconciled to God in any other way than through righteousness, founded upon faith and Christian grace. By this reasoning, we who are so affected already have peace with God. As for the expression "let us have," it perhaps suggests that we should hold firmly to that kind of peace which we thus possess, and never suspect that it could be held or obtained in any other way. We have, I say, or let us have it through our Lord Jesus Christ. For he himself is our peace, as it is written to the Ephesians. <note>Ephesians 2:14</note> Because he himself led us to that kind of peace, which peace he here calls a "certain grace," because it is not granted for our merits...

He then transitions into Chapter 5, discussing how justification through faith brings peace with God and the necessity of grace over philosophy or the Law.</summary>

is distributed to us, but freely—not indeed by our own power, but by divine help—therefore he adds:

<margin>»</margin> **Through whom we have access into this grace.** <note>Quoting Romans 5:2.</note> For by whose power we approach this grace, we ought to hope that we both hold it and are able to hold it only by the protection of that same one. Appropriately, therefore, in the letter to Timothy, he is called the mediator between God and men. <note>1 Timothy 2:5</note> And to the Ephesians: **Through him we both have access in one spirit to the Father.** <note>Ephesians 2:18</note> Moreover, he says **in faith**, that is, in the very firmness of the Christian faith. In Greek, it does not read *through faith*, as is commonly said in Latin, but *in faith*, and that more correctly. <note>Ficino is noting a grammatical nuance: the Latin Vulgate often uses "per fidem" (through faith), but he prefers the sense of being grounded "within" faith (Greek: *en tēi pistei*).</note> Otherwise, if it were said "through faith," faith might perhaps seem to be some kind of cause of grace. But our <term>Thomas</term><note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> asserts the contrary—namely, that grace is the cause of faith. For by divine grace we obtain the ability to believe rightly and firmly, as is read in the letter to the Ephesians: **By grace you have been saved through faith**; <note>Ephesians 2:8</note> he intends, however, that faith is the first effect of coming grace, and therefore it is rightly said that we reach grace through Jesus. To which we have access—that is, entrance and admittance—**in faith**, as if in the first light of grace itself. This faith is certainly followed in turn by the remaining gifts of grace: vision, <term>charity</term><note>From the Latin *charitas*, referring to divine, selfless love.</note>, constancy, joy, and glory.

Where he says, **in which we stand**: <note>Romans 5:2</note> It must be understood that we have this by the power of grace, so that we have not only been raised from guilt as if from death, but we also stand firm in an approved disposition, looking straight up toward God, relying on such great hope of future glory that we can boast in this above all else. All these things are indeed the gifts of grace. The glory, I say, of the children of God; that is, we shall be regarded as children of God, having been made so through adoption just as Christ existed so by nature—and thus again at the end of the ages, just as the angels were at the beginning of the ages.

Truly, how excellent a companion of grace such hope is appears most clearly from this: that we do not hope for something brief or light, but for an eternal and divine good. Furthermore, we do not only boast through this hope and exult in the expectation of the highest goods, but we even take delight in all adversities which we endure for the sake of this profession and the testing of hope, and we consider that they will in some way lead toward future glory. For this reason, the Apostle adds:

<margin>»</margin> **Not only that, but we even boast in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience produces testing, and testing produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.** <note>Romans 5:3-5</note>

Thus the text continues: not only do we boast in this—that we hope to attain the glory and happiness appropriate to the children of God—but we even boast and rejoice in the very tribulations undertaken for the sake of this grace. Not merely opining, or suspecting in the manner of other mortals, but knowing for certain that **tribulation produces patience**, etc. That is, in tribulations we are trained toward an unconquerable habit of patience, specifically with God helping, by whose grace we endure in adversity.

<margin>»</margin> **Patience produces testing.** Just as gold is tested by fire, so a constant soul is tested by adversity. For he can be approved as a believer and lover of divine things who, for their sake, willingly sustains all the hardest things. **And testing produces hope.** Indeed, he who has endured in present adversity can undoubtedly hope for future happiness.

<margin>»</margin> **And hope does not put us to shame.** <note>Original: "Spes autem non confundit." In this context, "confundit" means to be disappointed or let down by a false hope.</note> It is never deceived nor does it fail, so that it might happen that the one hoping would eventually suffer blushing and ignominy, or be touched by regret for having hoped. Hence the Psalm: **In you, O Lord, have I hoped; let me not be put to shame forever.** <note>Psalm 31:1</note> But why does hope of this kind persevere so strongly or attain its end so happily? Because, clearly, it is nourished by love: by the love, I say, of a mind raised toward God, which love is surely ignited in the mind by the love of God himself.

Hence <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term><note>A 5th-6th century mystical theologian whom Ficino translated and heavily influenced his Neoplatonism.</note>, following <term>Hierotheus</term><note>The legendary teacher of Dionysius.</note> as his authority, calls divine love a kind of circular motion <note>The OCR reads "cucularem," but this is almost certainly a typo for "circularem." Ficino is referencing the Neoplatonic idea of the "divine circle": love flows out from God and returns to Him.</note>, beginning from divine goodness itself, proceeding into the soul, and from there returning into the divine good. For the motion of the soul tending toward the infinite good, since it cannot set out from the soul's finite power, undoubtedly receives its impulse from that same infinite good, so that the end finally corresponds with the beginning. If our love for God takes its beginning from God's own love toward us, then appropriately those things necessary for love—namely faith and hope—also proceed from the same divinity. Since God does not move anything in vain, and the common and persistent impulse of the mind itself should not be made entirely empty, it follows that faith, hope, and love both endure strongly and eventually achieve their result. That the impulse toward divine things in us proceeds from divinity itself is also confirmed by this: that all mortal things on earth surrounding the soul produce in us a contrary impulse, so that the soul, overwhelmed by mortal things, cannot prevail except through divinity...

<summary>Ficino explains that faith and hope are gifts of grace, not human achievements, and that suffering (tribulation) serves to refine the soul's character. He uses Neoplatonic concepts of "circular motion" to describe how divine love originates in God, enters the human soul, and leads it back to the divine.</summary>
<keywords>grace, faith, hope, tribulation, Thomas Aquinas, Dionysius the Areopagite, divine love, circular motion, patience</keywords>

In the previous section, he established that hope does not disappoint because it is rooted in divine grace rather than human effort. He now transitions into a deep mystical and philological analysis of how God’s love is "poured out" into the human heart, drawing parallels between Christian scripture and Platonic philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>470</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

...to emerge entirely toward divine things. Now, in Greek it is said, <term>the love of God is poured out</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκκέχυται</note>, which carries a particular emphatic quality. It is as if he were saying that from divine love, as if from a fire, love is thoroughly kindled within us like a flame by way of a sparking fire. And this is indeed expressed abundantly. Truly, Plato seems to have touched upon this in his letter to the Syracusans <note>Referring to Plato’s Seventh Letter, where he describes the "spark" of divine knowledge that suddenly ignites in the soul after long familiarity with the subject.</note> in this way: from the long-standing commerce of our soul with divinity, suddenly at last, like a sparking fire from that place, a light shines forth in the soul, and henceforth nourishes itself. But the Apostle seems to speak specifically where he says, *through the Holy Spirit*, as if by God’s breathing upon us, an amatory fire is kindled within us. 

Altogether, he confirms the firmness of hope with a double argument. In the present moment, he does so from the gift of the Holy Spirit itself. In what follows, however, he does so from the death of Christ. Meanwhile, he touches upon both types of love: both the love by which God loves us, and that by which we love God. He considers both loves to have been branded into our wills by the Holy Spirit. We, however—to speak with our <term>Thomas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, whose Scholastic definitions Ficino often harmonizes with Platonic thought.</note>—explain it thus: for the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son, to be given to us, means that we are brought to a participation in that love, which is the Holy Spirit itself. By this participation, we are made lovers of God himself. Now, from the fact that we love him, we have proof that he loves us. It is not as if we first loved God, but because he first loved us, as the major epistle of John declares. <note>1 John 4:19</note> Moreover, the love by which God loves us is said to be "poured out" in our hearts because it diffuses widely within us. From both understandings of these words the same conclusion is reached: namely, that hope of this kind is never deceived. For because God loves us, he will not deny himself; and because we love God, we can easily hope that he will give us eternal goods.

> <margin>»</margin> **For why did Christ, while we were still weak, at the opportune time die for the ungodly? For scarcely will anyone die for a just man. Yet perhaps for a good man someone might dare to die.** <note>Romans 5:6-7</note>

Regarding what is read in Latin as "according to the time" <note>original: "secundum tempus"</note>, most understand this to mean those three days that Christ’s body lay in the tomb; this does not particularly please me, nor did it please <term>Athanasius</term> <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria and champion of orthodoxy.</note>, who was most learned in the Greek language. For the word Paul uses is <term>kairos</term> <note>original: καιρὸν</note>, which does not simply mean "time" itself (for that is called <term>chronos</term> <note>original: χρόνος</note> in Greek), but rather signifies a "favorable time" or an "occasion"; it properly designates a seasonal opportunity and fitness. 

Furthermore, since Paul wishes to express Christ’s immense love toward us, he would not be expressing it if he said Christ experienced death for us for only a "short time." Rather, he expresses it by showing that Christ observed a time that was not only fitting for himself, but also opportune for us—foreknown entirely by divinity and, in a certain way, even destined, as Athanasius says. The Gospel often signifies this: *My hour has not yet come.* Likewise: *The hour has come.* And again: *Your hour has come, and the power of darkness.* Indeed, if you look to the divine will, the death of Christ is considered a predestined sacrifice. But if you look to the impulse of those who killed him, it is a foreknown homicide. 

Truly, a sacrifice that is at once salvific and a homicide that is utterly wicked concur at the same time by a certain miraculous occasion. The diabolical instigation among wicked men did not prevail to bring about this event at any other time than when the divine will both foreknew the homicide and predestined the sacrifice itself—God working so that such a sacrifice would be celebrated at a certain opportune time. The prophet <term>Habakkuk</term> seems to have foretold it thus:
> **O Lord, your work in the midst of the years, bring it to life. In the midst of the years you will make it known. When you are angry, you will remember mercy.** <note>Habakkuk 3:2</note>

"In the midst of the years" perhaps signifies in the middle of the world’s course. For some wish to believe that the course of the world is completed in ten thousand years <note>Ficino refers to a theory of "Great Years" or world cycles often found in Neoplatonic and astrological thought.</note>—granted that motion was established for the sake of rest—and that in the middle of this world-course, God showed himself to men so that his coming would be equally distant from both extremes of the ages. This was so that neither the expectation of his future coming would be too protracted, nor the memory of his past coming be entirely abolished. But God, the fountain of eternity and the producer of time, has seen to the times himself. 

Perhaps, indeed, the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who Ficino believed were part of a "Golden Chain" of ancient wisdom leading to Plato.</note> call the "Good" itself "Opportunity" <note>The Greek *Kairos*.</note>. For it provides for all things opportunely, and every single nature is at its best when it chooses, or obtains, or approaches what it has desired at the opportune moment. For in this consists prosperity and happy fortune, proceeding from a higher influx and, finally, from heavenly providence. But let us return to the sequence of the Apostle’s words. Through this questioning, therefore, he signifies that Christ willed to die for us because of an incomparable love toward us, so that from this we might both firmly hope for all good things from him, and suffer...

<page-num>471</page-num>
<header>ST. PAUL'S COMMENTARY</header>
<sig>Gg 4</sig>

# ST. PAUL'S COMMENTARY

For that same reason, we owe every misfortune <note>original: "mala omnia"; Ficino suggests that because of our debt of sin, we deserve all the "evils" or sufferings that come our way</note>. Truly, our debt is increased by the fact that we were **weak**, that is, we were sinners against Him, and burdened with the guilt of no light crime, but with **impiety** <note>godlessness or lack of reverence</note>. One does not find anyone else who would wish to die for his unjust enemy, or even to labor for him in the slightest degree. One is scarcely found who would despise his own safety for the safety of some **just** person. Perhaps, indeed, such a person might be found somewhat more easily, yet rarely is there one who would wish to undergo death for a **good** man—that is, for a man who is liberal toward everyone and more beneficent than others, and to whom one owes a great deal because of his kindness. 

Here, he seems to call **"Just"** <term>iustum</term> the man who harms no one, does not seize the property of others, and renders to each his own, even if he distributes nothing from his own private goods. But the **"Good"** man <term>bonum</term>, as I have said, is a generous sharer of his own goods. For this is considered the defining characteristic of goodness. We, however, were neither just toward men, nor toward God; nor can we ever be "good" toward God—that is, beneficent—for He has no need of our goods. In this, the marvelous love of Christ toward us shines forth, confirming our hope for us and kindling a mutual love within us. 

<margin>»</margin> *But God proves his love toward us, in that while we were still* <margin>»</margin> *sinners, Christ died for us.* <margin>»</margin> What he expressed a little earlier through a question, he now declares through an affirmation without a question. It is just as if he had said: by this especially is the immense love of God toward us demonstrated, because His son Christ wished to undergo death for us, who were sinners against Him, as if the will of the Father and the Son were the same.

<margin>»</margin>
**N**ow indeed, just as in the previous sections the Apostle showed the love of God the Father toward us primarily through the fact that He poured His Spirit into us, so in the present section he finally demonstrates it through this: that He gave up His Son for us; and he provokes us on both counts to a reciprocal love toward God. Indeed, God emphasizes His love in two ways: first, because He gave His Son to suffer for our salvation, and then because He did so for His enemies—that is, for sinners and rebels. 

All of this is confirmed in a similar way in the second chapter of the letter to the Ephesians: *God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our sins, made us alive together with Christ, etc.* <margin>»</margin> *Therefore, much more* <margin>»</margin> *now that we have been justified by his blood, will we be saved through him from the wrath.* <margin>»</margin> Thus far he has asserted how God, on account of His incomparable love toward us, satisfying the debt on our behalf through the sacrifice of His Son, made us just from being unjust—specifically, those of us believing in Him. 

Next, he describes how He grants justification and salvation. First, the salvation by which we are freed from **wrath** <term>ira</term>, that is, from misery. Then, that we may also be received into a happy life with God. For if we have received from Him that which was more difficult—namely, to be made just from being unjust—surely we shall also be able to obtain that which is easier and follows from it: that, being now justified, we should be freed from wrath, that is, from the vengeance which injustice deserved. And since, while making us just from being unjust, He also made us friends from being enemies, He rightly makes His own goods common to us as if to friends, while by a certain marvelous liberality and communion He makes us participants in His own blessed life. Therefore he adds: <margin>»</margin> *For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of* <margin>»</margin> *his son, much more, having been reconciled, will we be saved by his life.* <margin>»</margin> 

In the meantime, several **antitheses** <note>Direct opposites used for rhetorical effect, a common tool in both Paul's letters and Ficino's philosophy</note> are to be noted here, arranged in a certain order. God Himself makes the unjust just by **justifying** them. He makes enemies into friends by **reconciling** them, specifically on account of their injustice. Those liable to wrath He frees from wrath, namely by admitting us into His own life through the death of His Son. <margin>»</margin> *And not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom* <margin>»</margin> *we have now received reconciliation.* <margin>»</margin> We do not only boast in the hope and expectation of the glory to be with God at some future time through the justification and reconciliation offered to us, but we boast even now in God Himself—that is, in a certain marvelous union with God through the faith and love already forged, with Jesus Christ naturally mediating this through his teaching, his power, and his sacrifice. 

It follows from what was said above that it is a greater thing to justify the unjust than to grant salvation to the one already justified. This is because in the former case, there is no "proportional principle" <note>A Scholastic concept meaning there is no inherent quality in a sinner that "fits" or "matches" God's justice; the change must come entirely from outside the person</note> in the man for obtaining divine justice, but the whole thing is perfected by **grace alone**. However, in the one already justified by divine power, the gift of the Holy Spirit already dwells, which, by moving the free will toward action, brings it about that he thus merits salvation.

<margin>»</margin>
**T**herefore, just as through one man sin entered into this world, <margin>»</margin> *and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all* <margin>»</margin> *have sinned.* <margin>»</margin> Someone will perhaps ask: why then was it necessary to be justified through Christ...

<meta>catchword: to be reconciled</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the logical progression of Romans 5, distinguishing between a "Just" man and a "Good" man to highlight Christ's extraordinary love in dying for sinners. He argues that if God performed the difficult task of justifying enemies, He will certainly perform the easier task of saving those who are now His friends.</summary>
<keywords>justification, reconciliation, grace, divine love, friendship with God, Scholasticism, logic of salvation, Romans 5</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the Pauline Epistles, specifically transitioning from the mechanism of reconciliation in Romans 5:11 to the comparison between Adam and Christ in Romans 5:12.</meta>

<page-num>471</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPISTLES</header>

...mortals might be reconciled: He answers thus. For this reason, I say, namely, it was necessary. Then, intending to explain the cause, he begins from a deeper point in this manner, which the present text sets forth by means of a certain hidden comparison. Moreover, it agrees with the first epistle to the Corinthians, where it is said: *Just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.* Thus, the fall into sin and death—which indeed possesses the condition of an evil far removed from order—nevertheless undergoes a certain order once established; much more so does the return to justice and life preserve an order. 

But that fall seems to admit at least as much order in that, through it, a great multitude is led back to the unity of its principle <note>The "principle" here refers to the single source or origin of the human race, namely Adam</note>, from which it is drawn down by a certain wondrous transmission. For from one first father, as if from the principle of the species, the entire human species was produced as a certain single common nature, and thus emerged as a sharer in one original inclination and fault; for that reason, it was made subject to death. What wonder is it, then, that the human species is restored by a certain order to original justice and life, starting similarly from one—namely, from one principle of salvation and grace? And just as from one beginning of generation fault and death flowed down into all, so from one beginning of regeneration, justification and life-giving power flow forth into all. 

Truly, as I warned above, Paul minimizes such a comparison here and signifies it secretly—for he wishes it to be understood by implication—but he touches upon it more openly afterward. If, however, the present words of Paul were arranged otherwise than I have arranged them, we would fall into an extremely long **hyperbaton** <term>hyperbathon</term> <note>A rhetorical figure where the natural word order is disrupted, often separating words that belong together</note> in the speech, and we would not easily strike upon the word which the grammarians call the "principal" verb. 

It may be asked why he said that sin and death entered into the **world** through sin, rather than merely into the human race. Perhaps it is because when our soul first, and then our body, lost their higher order, external things also in some way went out of orbit <note>original: "exorbitaverunt"; suggesting that the fall of man caused a cosmic misalignment or disorder in the physical world</note> along with us, especially for our sake. Indeed, death follows sin—not only the death of the soul, namely the deprivation of divine happiness, but also the death of the body. Our Plato touched upon this Mosaic mystery in the *Charmides*, as I have narrated elsewhere, following the opinion of the Magi, signifying that the imbalance and death of the body proceed from a certain intemperance of the soul. For he asserts that if the soul recovers its temperance, its immortality will overflow even into the body; for the goods and evils of the soul flow forth into the body, just as an outflow occurs from the whole body into the brain, and from the brain into the eye. He asserts, moreover, that temperance is recovered through certain philosophical and secret reasons, as if by certain **incantations** <term>praecantationibus</term> <note>Ficino, a Neoplatonist, often interpreted Plato's "incantations" as beautiful, philosophical discourses that heal the soul's harmony</note>. 

Accordingly, concerning <term>originale peccatum</term> **original sin**, which flowed from Adam into all, there would be need for a longer dispute at present, had I not discussed many things concerning this in the book *On Religion*; it will suffice, therefore, to touch upon this briefly. The Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve salvation through free will without divine grace, denying inherited original sin</note> indeed deny this, saying that the sin of the first parent pertains to his descendants not by original succession, but rather by a certain voluntary imitation—namely, insofar as they imitate the injustice of their parents. Aurelius Augustine argues against them thus: If the progress of Adam’s sin into all were said to be by imitation rather than through Adam, then all transgressors would most especially be said to imitate the Devil, the first transgressor; moreover, this is confirmed by that passage in the Book of Wisdom: *Through the envy of the devil, death entered into the world.* 

Furthermore, just as we receive justice and salvation from Christ—not principally because we imitate Him, but because we receive virtue from there through grace and the satisfaction offered to us by Him—so from Adam a certain original injustice, the origin of death, flows into us, not so much by our imitation as by a certain **propagation**. For if it happened by imitation alone, the comparison introduced here by the Apostle would not be fitting. Moreover, the Apostle declares to the Ephesians that it flows as if naturally: *We were by nature children of wrath.* Likewise David: *For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother conceive me.* 

Now, he calls this original vice the "sin of nature." Just as a daily fault (which they also call "actual" sin) is usually called a "sin of the person," this original sin is in a way voluntary, just as the actual sin is; for just as the latter is committed through the will of the person sinning, so the former is believed to have been perpetrated through the will of the **principle** of human nature. Truly, just as various members of the body are parts of one human person, so individual persons are members of human nature. Therefore, just as the movement of the hand or foot has the character of the voluntary and of fault through the will of the personal principle, so through the will of the principle of the human species, similar inclinations of individual men are judged voluntary and liable to punishment.

-> Nothing more could be found. <-

<summary>Ficino explains the transmission of original sin from Adam to all humanity, contrasting it with the Pelagian view of "imitation" and using Platonic philosophy to show how the soul's disorder affects the body and the world.</summary>
<keywords>Original Sin, Adam vs Christ, Pelagianism, St. Augustine, Plato's Charmides, propagation, human nature, temperance, cosmic order</keywords>
