# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine, his Preface to all his Preachings.

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Nourishing God, the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you. <note>original: "Adspira nobis precor Alme Deus, uia, ueritas, uita, Trinitas, unus Deus. In medio Ecclesiæ laudabo te. In conspectu angelorum psallam tibi."</note>

**T**HIS single homily of ours, most beloved brothers, will have three principal parts, so that it might be accepted as one by the unique Trinity. Each part, by a similar reasoning, will contain three parts, forming a ninefold number <note>The number nine was sacred in Neoplatonic and Christian thought, representing the nine choirs of angels</note> that will imitate the heavenly number of the angels, who kindly reconcile us to the high God. The first <term>Hierarchy</term> <note>Ficino uses the system of Dionysius the Areopagite, which ranks angels into three hierarchies of three orders each</note> indeed [will be addressed]. The second will show the way to the true life. The third, finally, will place the highest truth of life before our eyes. See, I pray, my brothers, how opportunely we have arrived, with God as our leader, at that ladder of the Patriarch Jacob. On this ladder, surely, the heavenly angels both ascend and descend at once. They ascend indeed while contemplating the God of Gods in Zion. Meanwhile, they descend to provide for men. They descend, I say, to take hold of the hands of men. They ascend again to lead us, once grasped, to the heights. O estimable ladder, O steps altogether incomparable, O ineffable ascent, and wonderful descent! The heavenly angels do not ascend at one time and descend at another, after the manner of men and animals, but they accomplish both wonderfully in the same moment. Just as rays striking the earth from the Sun return to the Sun in a moment. Nor do the angels only ascend at the same moment they descend, but also by the same reason they are elevated by divine contemplation; perfected and strengthened from that source, they prepare themselves to confer benefits upon us, truly overflowing with the fullness of the divine.

But let us return to where we have already progressed a little too far. We shall entrust the first part of our discourse to the lowest Hierarchy, in which part there will be three steps, entrusted to the angels, archangels, and principalities. The second part of the discourse we shall dedicate to the middle Hierarchy, also having three steps, entrusted to the powers, virtues, and dominions. Finally, we shall designate the third to the third Hierarchy, similarly containing three steps, through which—may the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim lead us to the heights! But so that what we wish for you may now become more manifest in all our preaching: First, indeed, we shall treat the Immortality of the soul. This will pertain to "Life." And we shall confirm it by three reasons, or persuasions, or modes, as you please. Second, they will speak concerning the firmness of the Christian faith. This will surely look to the "Way" that will finally lead us to the true life. And this again we shall bring forth in three similar modes. Third and finally, we shall declare the true sense of the Gospel, pertaining to the "Truth"—that is, a threefold sense: historical, moral, and allegorical. <note>These represent the standard medieval layers of biblical interpretation</note>

-> *The first part of the preaching on the immortality of the soul. Preaching the first.* <-

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Nourishing God, the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**L**ET us approach the first part of the preaching with the help of the first Hierarchy of angels. In every natural thing, we are accustomed to investigate the property of its nature through its continuous and natural inclination; for example, through an inclination toward descent, we infer that there is gravity in any body. Similarly, through an inclination toward ascent, we find lightness to be present. If, therefore, we find a certain body to have an inclination toward both, we will think it possesses both properties. To what end is this? Truly, we see the <term>brutes</term> <note>Non-human animals, which Ficino views as lacking rational souls</note> are hurled only toward perishable things. However, we consider that angelic intellects raise themselves only toward eternal things. Wherefore, we conclude that on the one hand there is only a perishable nature in the brutes, and on the other hand only an eternal nature in the angels. Since, therefore, our soul is commonly and assiduously inclined toward both—both the temporal and the eternal—we infer that it has, as it were, both natures: an eternal nature through the intellect, and a temporal nature through the senses. Furthermore, if man (as is confirmed by many reasons) is the most perfect of animals, he is most perfect especially through that part and faculty which he alone possesses, while other liv-

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces his collected sermons, structuring them around the ninefold hierarchy of angels and Jacob’s Ladder. He begins his first discourse on the immortality of the soul, arguing that because the human soul is inclined toward both temporal and eternal things, it must possess an eternal nature.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>Catchword: lectui</meta>

...not shared with other living creatures in any way. This is religion alone. For even the shrewder beasts seem to possess certain traces of reason, yet they have no judgment of religion. Moreover, man would not be perfected by religion if he were deceived by it, and if he were cheated of present goods by the hope of future ones. Likewise, as Plato proves in the *Protagoras*, religion was the first thing to happen to man—not only before all the arts necessary for food, but even before speech and social commerce. Since it is the most common and firm of all things, it follows that it is the most natural of all. And because it was inserted into raw, unpolished men at God’s instigation, it is not only most natural, but also most divine. Truly, the natural judgment of a species cannot be deceived, nor does natural instinct fail. Much less does God—the supreme truth and goodness—fail when promising eternity through religion, even while stripping us of present goods and afflicting us with evils for the sake of such hope. Hereafter, we shall approach the second part, entering the path toward eternal life through the proof of faith, by the grace of the second Hierarchy.

### *On the proof of faith. The second part of the preaching.*

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Nourishing God: the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you. <note>original: "Adspira nobis precor Alme Deus, uia, ueritas, uita, Trinitas, unus Deus. In medio Ecclesiæ laudabo te. In conspectu angelorum psallam tibi."</note>

**I**F the disciples of Christ had intended to introduce a fiction for the sake of deceiving people, they certainly would have had some reason for an easier persuasion. But they did the opposite. For they undertook a matter most difficult of all to believe and to observe. Add to this how many ways it was difficult if you consider the times, the places, and the persons. Namely, they spoke in learned times, in the grandest cities full of every kind of doctrine, and against the powerful, the many, and the learned; they themselves were most weak, destitute of all things, unlearned from the start, and very few. They would not even accept the Ceremonies from the Jews, nor the many Gods from the Gentiles. If they had admitted such things, we would have found that everyone would have suddenly become Christians. Listen to Paul speaking thus to the Corinthians: "See your calling, brothers. For not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong. And the ignoble and contemptible things of the world God chose, and those things which are not, to destroy those things which are." <note>A translation of 1 Corinthians 1:26-28</note> Likewise, if they had been pretenders, they could not have persevered with such great harmony among themselves amidst so many and such great difficulties. Yet they did persevere. Otherwise, they would have obtained nothing. Paul, for the glory of Christ, endured thirty-seven years by the grace of innumerable torments. Peter likewise for as many. John for sixty-eight years. And the others similarly throughout their entire lives. Nor did they hope for or desire any reward for such great labor in this life. Rather, they utterly despised all the gifts of life, and life itself. Hence Paul says: "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more miserable than all men." <note>1 Corinthians 15:19</note> Furthermore, they did not whisper in corners, but boldly spread their doctrine openly to the common people. Indeed, Paul, even with his neck bound in a chain, preached publicly. Hence he says to the Philippians: "The things which happened to me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the Gospel, so that my bonds in Christ are made manifest in all the Palace, and in all other places." <note>Philippians 1:12-13</note> And to the Colossians he says: "The Gospel has now been preached to every creature which is under heaven." <note>Colossians 1:23</note> Likewise, none of these things were done in secret <note>original: "in angelis," likely a scribal error for "in angulis" (in corners/secret), matching the previous sentence's context</note>. And to the Corinthians: "Not corrupting the word of God, but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. But if our Gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the God of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious Gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them." <note>2 Corinthians 4:2-4</note>

### *The third part of the preaching: concerning the Gospel.*

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Nourishing God: the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**B**UT having progressed successfully this far through the way of proven faith, let us proceed now to the Gospel truth, invoking the third <term>hierarchy</term> of angels. First, the <term>Thrones</term> will open to us the historical sense of the Gospel. Second, the <term>Cherubim</term> will reveal the moral sense. Third, the <term>Seraphim</term> will disclose the allegorical sense. Just as each one of us is ruled by a certain angel and persuaded toward the good, while being incited toward evil here and there by certain evil spirits, so Jesus was ruled by the Holy Spirit. Who, after appearing to his eyes and ears at his baptism, soon appeared to his understanding...

<summary>Ficino argues that religion is a unique, natural human instinct and defends the historical truth of the Gospel by highlighting the suffering and sincerity of the Apostles. He organizes his theological levels of interpretation—historical, moral, and allegorical—according to the angelic orders of Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s sermon series. On the previous page, Ficino was discussing the soul's relationship with the divine hierarchy. The text here begins mid-sentence, following the catchword "intellectui" (to the intellect) from the preceding page, as he explains how the intellect is led toward spiritual purification through the example of Christ's withdrawal into the desert.</meta>

...persuaded the intellect <note>The catchword from the previous page was "lectui," completing the word "intellectui" (to the intellect).</note> to go into the desert, leaving behind the harmful commerce of men, to devote itself to fasting, prayer, and contemplation, so that it would no longer fight against flesh and blood, but against the demons of the misty air <note>original: "caliginosi aeris dæmones." This refers to the Pauline and Platonic concept of the "lower air" being the realm of demonic spirits.</note>. By overcoming them through fasting, prayer, and contemplation, he might provide us an example that danger from demons looms over us even in a state of perfection, and that they can be conquered, and by what defenses. The Platonists also confirm the temptations of demons, and how they are expelled by the same remedies.

### *The Second Sermon.*

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Holy God: the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**F**ollowing the order established from the beginning, we shall observe the triple and ninefold number <note>Ficino uses a "ternary" (3) and "nonary" (9) structure to mirror the nine choirs of angels described by Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> in the parts of our speech as something angelic, both now and in the future. This is not without reason, since we speak in the sacred temple of the angels. There, always mindful of that oracle, **I am the way, the truth, and the life**, we shall distribute the first part of the sermon to life itself, the second to the way, and the third to the truth. Thus, from the first we may obtain faith to believe in eternal life; from the second, hope to receive its goods with God; and from the third, charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *Caritas*, or divine love.</note> toward God, the giver of immortal goods. And so, from faith through hope to charity, we shall ascend as if to the third heaven, with Paul as our guide, so that we may either hear the secrets of God (insofar as a man may) or at least taste the mystical fruit of charity which surpasses all sense—namely, a certain ineffable joy.

### *On the immortal life of the soul, the first part of the sermon.*

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Holy God: the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**N**othing can, of its own accord, oppose its own origin. Otherwise, it would naturally be carried toward its own destruction, which necessarily follows once the origin is lost. Furthermore, whatever an effect does, it does by the power and help of its cause. Therefore, if the soul fought against its cause, in that struggle the cause would be entirely opposed to itself. But the soul often opposes our body—indeed, all bodies. Therefore, it does not take its origin from any body. For it often abstains from bodily prompts for the sake of honor, or truth, or religion. When our Plato chose to inhabit the Academy—a healthy spot in Attica—for the sake of taming the body, was not his mind opposing the body? When Xenocrates, the beloved disciple of Plato, and Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar. Tradition claims he castrated himself to ensure his purity, an act Ficino uses here as proof of the soul's war against the body's desires.</note>, their follower, burned away their virile parts to utterly extinguish the fires of lust, did not the infused soul declare war on the members of the body? Before these, the Persian Magi, the Egyptian Priests, and the Pythagorean philosophers abstained from wine and meat to weaken Venus <note>A common metaphor for sexual desire.</note> and remain sober for contemplation. But the holiness and martyrdoms of Christians testify much more to the victory of the mind over the body. Certainly, we all daily abstain from bodily prompts for a specific reason, according to our strength. And even if we never broke the impulses of the body, the struggle itself, which is continuous within us, would be enough to show that there is another substance in us besides the corporeal, one that opposes bodily things—both the humors <note>The "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were believed to govern physical and mental health.</note> and even the celestial influences that move the senses through those humors. If the soul frequently obeys the body, it is not led to this by violence, but by love; it is moved toward corporeal life much like a mother toward her offspring. When the body flatters too intensely, the soul is not consulted, not even slightly. This reason has been assigned thus far from the fact that the soul opposes the body in its conduct. A second reason must soon be assigned: that the soul rises above the body, which proves it does not depend on the body. Daily, the images of sensible things deceive the senses in many ways. The intellect corrects this deception by means of reason. Insofar as it thinks of or desires something incorporeal, the intellect undoubtedly raises itself above the body. Truly, no thing can transcend the powers and order of its cause. The internal sense, when the external senses report to it, can imagine nothing more excellent than a vast light affected by various colors, smells, sounds, and wonderfully pleasing tastes. When the imagination is questioned about God, it offers nothing more sublime than this to the reason. But the reason, from the highest watchtower of the mind, looks out upon and corrects the deceptions of the phantasy <note>Phantasy (imagination) was considered a lower faculty dealing with sensory images; Reason was the higher faculty that could grasp abstract truths.</note>. It describes God in a very different way, as we declare most extensively in our Theology.

<summary>Ficino argues for the immortality and independence of the soul by demonstrating how it naturally opposes the body's desires through asceticism and intellectual reasoning. He draws on both Christian martyrs and pagan philosophers like Plato and Xenocrates to prove the mind is a substance distinct from the physical body.</summary>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

we declare. The third argument is brought forward in this manner: If the rational soul <note>Latin: "rationalis animus." Ficino distinguishes between the biological life-force and the higher human intellect.</note> drew any part of its origin from the body, then the more closely it clung in union to the body, the better off it would be. For every thing is preserved and perfected by its own origin. Yet now, the opposite occurs. There are two principal parts of the rational soul: the intellect and the will. When we are occupied with bodily matters, the intellect either perceives nothing at all, or it does not discern purely, being deceived by the senses and by imagination <note>Latin: "phantasia." In Renaissance psychology, this refers to the faculty that processes sensory images, which can cloud pure thought.</note>. Socrates clearly proves this in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the immortality of the soul.</note>. The will is afflicted while it is vexed by many cares from that source. On the other hand, when the soul despises bodily things—when the senses are stilled and the clouds of mental images are driven away—and the soul contemplates something by itself without the body distracting it, then the intellect discerns purely and shines most brightly. This is also apparent in those who prophesy, whether through the quiet of sleep or some other alienation <note>A "stepping out" or ecstasy where the soul is temporarily detached from physical constraints.</note> from the body. Therefore, as Plato says in the *Crito* and the *Apology*, some people predict the future when they are near death. It is as if they then see those things prescribed among the celestial spirits, to whom the soul is joined by its own nature, provided it is separated from the body. Not only does the intellect, by calling itself away from the body, see what it desires more clearly and become divine—and thus find itself in a better state—but the will is also no longer afflicted by disturbances; rather, it rejoices exceedingly in divine things as if in things similar to itself. From this it follows that the body is not the origin of the rational soul, since the further the soul departs from the body, the more perfect it becomes. It also follows that if the more the mind is immersed in this body, the more it fails, and the further it departs, the more it profits, then the mind will be most perfect when it has flown entirely out of this body. Destruction does not come from that which brings the highest perfection. Instead, it is the fullness of life, to such an extent that it is perpetual. For the soul will never fail through any change, since it does not perish by exiting the body—and certainly no greater change than that can happen to it.

## On the proof of faith. Second part of the preaching.

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Holy God: the way, the truth, and the life; Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**I**t is clear that the **A**postles were led to preach by no hypocrisy or ambition, since they did not seek their own glory, but the glory of Christ. Hence that saying of Paul to the Corinthians: *For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus.* Likewise: *Among you one says, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollo." Are you not worldly? For what is Apollo? What indeed is Paul? Nothing but ministers of him in whom you believed.* And to each as the Lord gave. *I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase. So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. Now he who plants and he who waters are one.* Therefore, let no one glory in men; for all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollo, or Cephas <note>The Apostle Peter.</note>, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come—all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s. For this reason, in the Acts of the Apostles, when a certain Cornelius wanted to worship Peter, he was forbidden by Peter. Furthermore, when the people of Lycaonia <note>The residents of Lystra who mistook Paul and Barnabas for Zeus and Hermes (Acts 14).</note> wanted to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas as if they were gods because of their miracles, they were not permitted to do so by them; John also in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> forbade himself to be worshipped. But what is more manifest than this from Paul? *Far be it from us to glory in anything other than the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.* Added to this is the fact that they bore tortures for Christ not unwillingly, but spontaneously and gladly. Hence Paul to the Romans: *We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience trial, and trial hope, and hope is not confounded. Because the charity of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us.* Likewise to the Corinthians: *I abound with joy in all our tribulation.* Again to Timothy: *In this we labor and are cursed, because we hope in the living God. It is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, because Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all patience, for the instruction of those who are to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever.* Again to the Colossians: *Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up those things that are lacking of the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for his heart, which is the Church.* Likewise Luke in the Acts: *The Apostles, having been beaten by the Jews, went out rejoicing because they were [held]...* <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

**T**hat which is naturally bound to a body, whose nature is determined <note>Term: *determinata*. <meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the Christian faith and the immortality of the soul. Following the previous discussion on the steadfastness of the Apostles under persecution, Ficino now moves into a philosophical comparison between animal instinct and human reason to demonstrate human free will, before returning to a historical list of learned early Christians to prove that the faith was not merely a product of "unlearned fables."</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

<page-num>478</page-num>

...swallows for building a nest, bees for hives, and spiders for webs. For this reason, all animals of the same species always build their works in the same way. They neither learn at any time, nor do they ever vary. This is because the natural instinct <note>original: "species naturalis," referring to the innate blueprint or drive within a species.</note> by which they are led is present from the beginning and remains the same. Humans, however, both learn and constantly vary their works. Yet they possess one and the same nature from the beginning. Therefore, they are not drawn to act by nature alone, but they move themselves by their own counsel, acting differently at different times. 

From what then do we think this arises? It is because elements, trees, and beasts never err in their specific motions, choices, and arts. But man errs very often. This is not because they possess a more perfect intellect than man—indeed, they possess no intellect at all—but because they are drawn by the Divine Intellect and its instrument, Nature, which never errs; whereas man is led by his own intellect, which is capable of error. Yet if the human intellect ever rests from its own particular actions for a time, then it too is led by God and does not err. This is made clear through prophecies and miracles. And if man were always led by God, just as other things are, he would err as much less than they do as he is a more perfect instrument. 

Conversely, if other creatures led themselves as man does, they would err more frequently, insofar as they have been allotted a less perfect nature. Finally, if our choice were carried along by a certain necessity, we would never act otherwise than as the passion of the body and the immediate imagination, stirred by the senses, entices us. This is exactly what all beasts do, and what the "beast" within us <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the lower, irrational parts of the human soul.</note> does. On the contrary, however, though we are often first moved in such a way, we soon deliberate and choose against the provocations of such incitements. This is because we prefer the freedom of the soul, its virtue, and its eternal happiness over mortal things. This is most apparent in philosophers and religious men, who—for the sake of finding truth or entering into divine grace—choose a way of life that is not only repugnant to the senses, but undoubtedly harmful to the body. In this very matter, the human mind declares its free action and its command over the body and bodily things.

# The testimony of the Apostles for Christ is most strongly confirmed by this: that they neither intended to deceive anyone, nor were they themselves deceived.

To this point tends that word of Peter: *Be ready always to satisfy every man that asketh you a reason of that hope and faith which is in you.* <note>original: "Parati semper estote..." 1 Peter 3:15.</note> Likewise: *For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known to you the power and presence of our Lord Jesus Christ, but having been made eyewitnesses of his majesty.* <note>original: "non enim indoctas fabulas sequuti..." 2 Peter 1:16.</note> Likewise, Paul to the Corinthians: *I therefore so run, not as at an uncertainty: so I fight, not as one beating the air. But I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.* <note>original: "Ego sic curro non quasi incertũ..." 1 Corinthians 9:26-27.</note> Hence Paul and Apollos, everywhere debating the mysteries of Christ with the learned, brought forward the volumes of the Prophets. Paul often commands his disciples, especially priests, to apply themselves diligently to the deep understanding of the Prophets. Origen, in his work *Against Celsus*, says that Paul would reproach those who believe rashly. Indeed, it is the custom of Christians to draw their listeners toward their certain conviction. 

Furthermore, those who testified to us of this faith with their own blood were men of the most prudent judgment. And if they were not all highly learned from the beginning, they were certainly so shortly thereafter, as their deeds and writings confirm. Among these were many thereafter: John, Paul, Hierotheus, and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, traditionally considered a philosopher-convert of St. Paul.</note>—all supreme philosophers—as well as Justin, Pantenus, Quadratus, Agrippa, Aristides, Luke, and Mark, who were also philosophers. Likewise, Thomas and Apollos, who were most skilled in the Jewish law. Also Timothy, Titus, Clement of Rome, Barnabas, John the Elder, Hegesippus, Papias, Melito the philosopher of Asia, the wise Ignatius, Polycarp the distinguished teacher of Asia, Dionysius of Alexandria, and very many others excelling in wisdom. We enumerate these in a long list in our book *On Religion*. Among the innumerable, I cannot remain silent regarding Origen, a most famous philosopher and martyr. 

Finally, if dialecticians, orators, or poets had laid the first foundations of this religion, we might suspect that the common people had been deceived by cunning and eloquence. If all the learned had always rejected it, we might judge it perhaps worthy of contempt. If princes had entirely favored this law either from the beginning or shortly after, we might think the weaker had been coerced by the more powerful, and that successors, as happens, had sucked in that law with their mother's milk. Therefore, Divine Providence willed that the simple truth of His religion should take its first origin from men who were at first unrefined, simple, and few, so that the cunning, the learned, and the many might be caught by them, like fish by fishermen, in a happy and miraculous way. He permitted, moreover, His religion to be cruelly attacked by the powerful in every nation for more than three hundred years. This was so that the number of learned witnesses and the faithful might be greater, and the authority of the matter itself might be truer, more certain, and firmer. For it is easy to keep faith in prosperity, but difficult in adversity.

<summary>Ficino argues that human free will is proven by our ability to act against instinct and bodily harm, unlike animals. He further defends Christianity by listing the many philosophers and scholars who joined the faith, arguing that its humble origins and survival through persecution prove its divine truth.</summary>

<keywords>free will, animal instinct, reason vs nature, Apostolic testimony, early Church fathers, Divine Providence, Christian philosophers, Origen, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

# SERMONS

<meta>catchword: may</meta>

The intellect reaches a thing understood by true reason through the act of understanding. When, therefore, it comprehends an indivisible substance with certain reasons, it touches an indivisible thing with its own indivisible part and understands it. Otherwise, a divisible thing would touch an indivisible one. This same indivisible intellect is sufficient for understanding; the intellect itself exists as the only thing that understands itself. Since, therefore, intellectual substance is entirely indivisible, it can never be dissolved. Especially because this intellectual substance is not only impartible <term>impartible: incapable of being divided into parts or sections</term> but also subsists in itself—namely, it does not depend on the body. Otherwise, it could not reflect back upon itself. As we prove in our Theology by the reasoning of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Elements of Theology" deeply influenced Ficino’s synthesis of Platonism and Christianity.</note>. It turns back upon itself when it observes its own action, its power, its essence, and its cause. But if its action, being free, returns inward, much more so is its essence released from bodies. Furthermore, there must be a proportion between the nature that knows and the nature that is known, just as there is between sight and light, or between hearing and sound. Much more so between the intellect and its own proper "intelligible" <term>intelligible: a concept or object that can be grasped by the mind rather than the physical senses</term>. For the intellect penetrates the intelligible by defining and distinguishing—something the senses never achieve regarding sensible things. But the characteristic of the intelligible is the universal and specific "ratio" <note>original: "ratio," here meaning the essential definition, conceptual structure, or logical blueprint of a thing.</note> of the thing known. Since, therefore, this ratio is absolute, separated from place and time, the intellect is rightly freed from these same things and is everlasting.

Human laws are not admitted from the start, or propagated after they have been admitted, except by the usual, common persuasions of human and natural reasons, or by some imperial authority, the force of arms, or the ease and convenience of living and the allurements of pleasures. Furthermore, the disposition of the stars can never introduce such laws among men by any other instruments. Therefore, since I have recognized that the Christian law among people of sound mind—both having arisen at some time and quickly spread very widely, while the probable arguments of many opposed it, while the weapons of the powerful raged against it everywhere, while all use and hope of human pleasure were clearly taken away from it—we will necessarily conclude that a law of this kind is neither human, nor depends on celestial fate, but is entirely divine, proceeding from some super-celestial power. What of the fact that many centuries before, all these individual things were predicted in a long succession by many Prophets and Sibyls <note>The Sibyls were ancient Greco-Roman prophetesses who, in the Renaissance, were believed to have foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note>, as we shall show in what follows? What of the fact that Christ, the master of life, predicted both his own death, the persecution against his disciples that would be everywhere, and the spreading and immutability of his religion? He also predicted the miserable ruin of the Jews that was coming soon, the conversion of the Gentiles, and the stubbornness of certain Jews that would last until the end of the world—which he both predicted himself and inspired his disciples to say. And what is wonderful is that Christ predicted the siege would happen on the Sabbath, and the destruction by hunger and sword to be brought by the Gentiles, along with unheard-of slaughter and captivity. Moreover, he prescribed the scattering of the Jews among all nations beforehand, exactly as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Jewish historian whose account of the Siege of Jerusalem in "The Jewish War" was used by Christians as proof of fulfilled prophecy.</note> wrote after the ruin. Finally, if purity is the most characteristic trait of religion, this is certainly the most divine, which admits neither the base superstitions of later Jews and the most filthy delusions of the Talmud <note>Ficino reflects the common Renaissance-era polemic that contrasted the "pure" Christian gospel with the complexities of the Jewish Talmud.</note>, nor the obscene and wicked fables of the Pagans, nor the abominable license of the Mohammadans and the absurdities of the Quran. This law promises neither earthly rewards, as other laws do, but celestial ones. It does not command the enemies of its law to be killed, as the Talmud and Quran commanded, but either to be taught by reason, or converted by prayer, or tolerated with patience. Nor does it ardently practice virtues for the sake of ambition or pleasure or human tranquility, but for the grace of God alone, and it tramples this whole world underfoot and holds it as nothing, in order to attain the other world. To this also belongs the purity and simplicity of its speech, and its unusual majesty and harmony, and a certain hidden power implanted in its words.

### On the five loaves. Luke Chapter 9.

> Breathe upon us, I pray, O Holy God, the way, the truth, and the life; the Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you.

**F**rom five loaves and two fish, he satisfied five thousand men. It is asked how that bread received its increase. This could have been achieved in four ways: by Creation, by Rarefaction <term>rarefaction: the thinning or expanding of matter to occupy more space</term>, by Generation, or by the Attraction of magnitude of foreign matter. He did not create new matter there by Creation; for since Creation is the most noble of all actions—

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality based on its indivisible nature and proves the divinity of Christianity by its survival against persecution and its fulfillment of prophecy, unlike other religions. He begins a theological analysis of the miracle of the five loaves, examining the physical nature of the bread's increase.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, Proclus, Christian law, prophecy, Sibyls, Josephus, Talmud, Quran, miracle of the loaves, Luke 9, metaphysics</keywords>

This page picks up with the final syllable of a word (likely "but") and moves into the mechanics of divine creation and the specific miracle of the loaves and fishes.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

<page-num>480</page-num>

...but <note>Original: "ma", likely the conclusion of a word like "anima" (soul) or a conjunction like "but"</note> He uses the most noble works in the production of the world, of angels, and of souls. If He had only thinned out <term>rarefecisset: the process of rarefaction, where matter becomes less dense/thinner</term> the present matter, He would have nourished nothing further. It would be just as if someone were to stretch out marrow into a larger space. However, He could probably apply a greater quantity to the present matter, not indeed by thinning out what was already there, but by generating other matter endowed with a similar density. For even from the first beginning of the world, He procreated matter that was not yet quantitative <note>Ficino refers to "prime matter," which in Aristotelian philosophy has no size or form until God acts upon it</note>. Soon He applied quantity—not indeed to thinned-out matter, which was not yet quantitative. For "rarefied" is a certain state pertaining to a thing that already has quantity. 

He could also probably have inserted into the bread a wonderfully attractive power, which most effectively drew in air from all sides and the vapors of water. These, being immediately condensed and "cooked" within the bread, would suddenly cause an increase. Similarly, the grain of a beech tree, by its attractive and digestive power, sucks in air and moisture, whence it swells; from a tiny thing it becomes large and tall; from one come many, and from the misshapen comes the beautiful. Nature accomplishes this over a long time; a Spirit <note>Original: "Dæmon". In Ficino’s Neoplatonic view, these are intermediary beings or "daemons" who can manipulate natural forces faster than nature but slower than God</note> accomplishes the same in a short time. God alone does it in a moment. God also does many things by His will, producing forms even without motion. A Spirit, however, joins things that are in a specific place by moving them, from which forms result. 

Jesus arranged twelve tables in a row in the meadow, and He ordered a hundred to sit at each table, namely fifty on each side. After this set of twelve tables, He added another set of twelve lengthwise, and another thereafter, up to five sets of twelve. Therefore, there were sixty tables and six thousand people—namely, five thousand men, five hundred children, and as many women. He blessed the bread, saying:
> Grow, loaves, and fill the faithful people.

He did the same with the fish, after first removing the bones. There were five pounds of bread, and likewise of fish; and while He blessed them under the Sun, the shadow of five fingers resulted upon the fish, and likewise the shadow of another five fingers upon the loaves. From this, each was increased separately up to twenty-five pounds. Then He broke each loaf with a stroke of His open palm and fingers over the bread—the bread yielding to His raised fingers. From this, six mouthfuls resulted. He drew His hand across it again, and thirty-six mouthfuls were made. From the five loaves thus multiplied, one hundred and eighty pieces were made. Jesus gave to each of the twelve Apostles fifteen pieces in their lap—that is, a portion for each. But the fish He carried whole Himself. He distributed them little by little, proceeding among the tables in breadth through the side paths, while the twelve Apostles proceeded through the twelve paths lengthwise. Finally, when they were filled and the fragments collected, He blessed a spring, so that they might drink more safely and pleasantly, saying:
> Let the spirit of the Lord be carried over the waters. <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2</note>

We categorize things as the corporeal body, the spiritual body, and the spirit. In the first class are Earth, Water, and mixed Air. In the second are pure Air, Fire, and Heaven. In the third are the Soul, the Angel, and God. Indeed, God and the Angel are simply spiritual. But the Soul is spiritual insofar as it acts through the intellect. It is also called "animal" <note>From "anima", meaning the breath of life</note> when it exercises the works of life and the senses in the body. It is also called "corporeal" when it acts while the intellect is doing nothing—which is what remains of the soul. For in this state, it takes on a corporeal affection and habit. Here the soul is handed over to the conditions of the body—that is, so that it becomes susceptible to suffering, dark, slow, and dull. 

Therefore, the body can sometimes be drawn back to the nature of the soul, so that it becomes impassible <note>impassible: incapable of suffering or being harmed by external force</note>, bright, agile, and spiritual. This happens, I say, when the whole soul emerges as intellect, absorbed by the divine intellect. Nor is this surprising, for we have seen earth become water through thinning, and this water likewise become air, and this air likewise become fire. Fire, if you take away its matter, will be "heaven." If you subtract dimension from heaven, it will be spirit—that is, light released from matter and dimensions. Thus you see the corporeal ascend to a spiritual nature. Just as you can imagine spirit being made corporeal: first by adding dimension to light, then matter; by adding corporeal affection and habit to the soul; and by applying condensation to fire, air, and water.

***

### *On that passage of Paul: Colossians 3*

<margin>"</margin> **B**rothers, if you have risen with Christ, etc.) The congregation of the faithful, according to Paul, is one body, of which Christ is the head. The head, according to Plato, is the "whole man." For it is round like the heavens. It has seven passages, like the seven planets; two eyes, like the Sun and the Moon. It contains all the senses which are not in the rest of the body. It has seven powers of knowing: the five senses, imagination, and reason. According to Galen <note>Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was a prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium</note>, the head holds the sovereignty in the body, and from it is derived the power of life into the body...

# SERMONS.

...life, sense, and motion. The rest serve this as the instruments of man. Therefore, brothers, if Christ is our head in heaven and we are his members insofar as we are on earth, we—like severed limbs—lose motion, sense, and life, except insofar as we remain bound to him by faith, hope, and charity, as if by <note>Ficino uses the anatomical metaphor of "nerves" to describe the theological virtues that connect the human soul to God</note> three nerves. Let us seek, therefore, by ascending higher, to be more tightly bound to Christ, who is above, lest we perish utterly. Let us be wise and "taste" the things that are above. Let us flee the earthly baits prepared everywhere by the Devil; for with the "flavor" of these things, he ensnares us as if with a hook, and holds us fast with a long-lasting taste, so that we do not fly away to Christ. Therefore, be wise regarding the things that are above. Indeed, the animal and diabolical man that was within us has already died through the passion and resurrection. Meanwhile, we live as the spiritual man, until the glory of life is manifested in us—that glory which is now hidden from us and reserved in Christ with the Father.

> Hence that saying of John: We are the children of God <note>original: "Filij Dei sumus"</note>, as if already born, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

But when Christ, in whom the glory of life is preserved for us, appears in judgment, then we also shall appear, and we shall shine together with him through the splendor of glory forever. For our intellects shall be illuminated by the light of his intellect, and our bodies shall shine forth as if by the rays of his own body. Whence our images shall be seen within one another, and the image of Christ shall be seen in all, and the images of all shall be seen in Christ; and every eye within us shall be blessed—namely, the eye of the mind and the eye of the body.

> Hence that saying of John: This is eternal life <note>original: "Haec est uita aeterna"</note>, that they may see you, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent; may God by his mercy lead us to such a life.

The Platonists <term>Platonici: followers of Plato, specifically the Neoplatonists like Plotinus whom Ficino translated</term> hand down the idea that the soul is the seedbed of the body. Therefore, the form of the body is like a certain soul degenerating into a material nature. Thus, it is probable that, in turn, the bodily nature may one day be led back to the nature of the soul itself. Similarly, a grain of wheat swells into a blade of grass, and the grass returns to a seed. Fire is condensed into earth, and earth returns to fire. Once this matter has returned [to its source], from being immobile, dull, and obscure, it becomes mobile, agile, clear, and penetrating without dispersing. Therefore, when the nature of the body is led back into the nature of the soul, besides what it will obtain from the soul in terms of <term>impassibilitas: the state of being unable to suffer or be harmed</term> invulnerability, clarity, and agility, it will possess from the soul the power to penetrate solid things—neither dispersing nor being dispersed—just as the soul penetrates this solid body everywhere without being dispersed. For the soul meanwhile gives life to the body, and not only does it not disperse it, but it even binds together conflicting elements. Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated into Latin</note> proves that a solid body cannot penetrate another solid without breaking, not indeed through a fault of the materials—which, since they are indivisible in their primary nature, can easily come together—nor through a fault of their dimensions. For these, being effective, neither break nor resist; rather, it is through the fault of solid hardness. But hardness and solidity are a certain quality. Therefore, if such a quality is removed, bodies immediately instill themselves into other bodies without any breaking. Liquids into liquids, just as fire into air, or air into water. Likewise, liquids into solids, like oil into paper or wood, or fire into iron. What then? Does the glorified body, which has now been led back to the nature of the divine soul, lack all solidity? By no means; for He says,

> Touch, and see, etc. <note>original: "Palpate, & uidete"</note>

How then does it penetrate wood while solidity remains on both sides without mutual breaking? Because this quality [of hardness] is quite lowly, belonging as it were to the earth; where solidity or hardness does not threaten, it does not have such power to cause breaking or to prohibit penetration as the faculty of the animal body has now, both for effective and penetrating motion. For such is the power of the soul and of divinity: both for the connection of bodily parts, and for creating and preserving them. Truly, if it is the office of the soul to bind together the conflicting parts in the body and to preserve them bound together, it performs this perfectly when the soul itself is absorbed into divinity, and the body into the soul. The clarity of the glorified body is further in nature from the eye than the clarity of the Sun. For although the Sun holds the highest place in the whole category of bodily things, it nevertheless does not transcend the category. But the glorified body, insofar as it has already ascended to the condition of the divine soul, so far does it transcend both the limits of the Sun and the faculty of the eye—which, as long as it is simply earthly, is less able to look upon the glorified light than the light of the Sun. But just as it is placed in the will and judgment of the soul to demonstrate itself, both to the ears through words and to the eyes through nods, so the glorified man has it in the judgment of his will to show his now-spiritual body, or to hide it. But how? Not indeed by altering himself. For that is not fitting; nor by affecting the imagination of youth (for he would be deceiving), but either by restraining his rays, lest they flow out too abundantly, or to be gazed upon...

...by strengthening the rays of the eyes <note>Ficino refers to the ancient "extramission" theory of vision, where the eyes emit rays to perceive objects; the glorified Christ can strengthen these human rays to allow them to see his divine light</note>. He is also able to shape the surrounding air on its surface however he pleases, and in this shaped form, he presents himself to those looking on. Thus was Christ seen in glory on Mount Tabor. Thus, after the resurrection, he was seen by his mother, specifically through a tempering of his rays. But by the shaping of the surrounding air, he appeared to the women and the disciples: in the gardens as a gardener, to those traveling as a fellow traveler, and to those fishing as a fisherman. He broke the bread with the lightest touch, for the power of the divine hand takes the place of a sword <note>This suggests that Christ's spiritualized body does not require physical force, but his "touch" carries a penetrating, sharp power</note>. For even a simple man, insofar as he has a hand, seems to possess all instruments. He inflamed the hearts of those hearing his words with a certain more burning breath. For since they were still, as earthly men, unsuited for the light, he began under simple faith to frequently warm the soul with charity, so that by this heat it might be purified and transferred to the light of intelligence. 

Furthermore, the Angel who descended to the tomb was from the order of the <term>Virtues</term> <note>In the traditional celestial hierarchy, 'Virtues' are the choir associated with miracles and strength</note>, who rule the sphere of death. He came, therefore, to terrify the guards, appearing in the form of lightning and with the wondrous effect of an earthquake, things which seem to belong to the planet Mars. Two other, grander angels were from the order of <term>Dominations</term>, who lead Jupiter, and <term>Powers</term>, who lead the Sun. Although that first angel also had a silver garment to comfort the women, just as he had previously terrified the soldiers through the lightning.

### On the two disciples in Emmaus. Luke 24.

> Breathe upon us, I pray, nourishing God—the way, the truth, the life, the Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the angels I will sing to you.

**T**he two disciples were going to Emmaus, and because they lacked firmness of faith, the Devil held their eyes back so that they would not recognize their father, Jesus. He did this by summoning a certain vapor to the eyes, which both scattered the pupils and tinted them with a reddish hue, so that the image of Jesus appeared both larger and ruddier. We derive these reasons from a certain foundation in Augustine. Therefore Jesus, in order to restore their clarity of sight, uses an explanation of the Scriptures to bring them faith, so that once this was applied, charity might also be kindled. Little by little, faith began to rise again. Charity also began to burn. Hence that saying: *Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?* <note>original: "Cor nostrum erat ardens, dum nobis loqueretur in uia"</note> 

Truly, just as faith was not enough unless charity was added, so charity in "affection" (feeling) was not enough unless charity in "effect" (action) was added. Therefore, Jesus finally revealed himself when they received him with hospitality and a feast. There, he not only offered himself to be clearly seen, but also to be tasted in the sacrament of the Eucharist. Indeed, he blessed and broke the bread. In that moment, by the communion of Christ, the Devil—who had brought on the blindness—was expelled. Therefore, we must approach Jesus with charity of both affection and action, if he is to say to us: *Taste and see how sweet the Lord is.* <note>original: "Gustate me, ac uidete, quàm suauis sit Dominus"</note> 

For he, out of the love of charity, approached the creation of the world and descended to redeem mankind. From this it follows that all things are moved to generate and to work by love; this is evident not only in living creatures, but even in the elements and the heavens. And (as we have said elsewhere), the best in any order possesses the specific sign of amorous charity. The <term>Seraphim</term> among the angels, the <term>Empyrean</term> among the heavens, and so on. The Seraphim, under the Trinity (to whom the Empyrean heaven is attributed), rule the <term>Crystalline sphere</term>; and rightly so, since they burn with charity, they touch the Empyrean—the fiery heaven—with their head. 

The <term>Cherubim</term>, in whom there is the fullness of knowledge, rule the <term>Firmament</term>, which is the fullness of stars. Whence Daniel says: *The learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament.* The <term>Thrones</term>, who are seats, rule the sphere of Saturn, signifying stability. The <term>Dominations</term> preside over Jupiter, the signifier of lords. The <term>Virtues</term> lead Mars, for both that planet and this order signify manliness. The <term>Powers</term> dominate the Sun, which signifies magistrates. The <term>Principalities</term> belong to Venus, whose love is the principle of affections and motions. The <term>Archangels</term> belong to Mercury; rightly do the primary messengers preside over the principle of messengers. The <term>Angels</term> (that is, the "messengers") preside over the Moon, which announces to lower things the influences of the higher. 

The Thrones refer to the Father, the Cherubim to the Son, and the Seraphim to the Spirit. Likewise, the Principalities refer to the Father, the Archangels to the Son (the first messenger), and the Angels to the Spirit (who messaged second). Again, the Firmament refers to the Father, the Crystalline to the Son, and the Empyrean to the Spirit. Saturn refers to the Father, Jupiter to the Son, and Mars to the Spirit. The Sun refers to the Father, Mercury to the Son, and Venus to the Spirit. The Moon refers to Christ, who by its light [reveals] his divinity...

...his humanity with his darkness. Again, just as three persons in God agree in one Divinity, so the Sun, Mercury, and Venus always meet closest in a certain common splendor. Finally, there is one substance in the Sun under the aspects of form, light, and heat, just as there is one divine nature in the three persons.

->On the labors and hardships of the Apostle Saint Paul.<-

> I went out to sow your seed, O Lord. Your seed is indeed good; help us because of your great mercy, so that I also may sow well, and your people here may receive your seed well, and bring forth a hundredfold fruit from it.

<margin>,,</margin>The great Jesus from on high, through Ananias, thundered these words to Saul of Tarsus: "I have chosen
<margin>,,</margin>you today, Saul, as my most choice vessel of all, so that you may carry the
<margin>,,</margin>seeds of my word to all nations, by which you may propagate Gospel fruits everywhere.
<margin>,,</margin>You will indeed suffer many things while sowing for my name's sake, but your
<margin>,,</margin>tears will become bread—I say, heavenly bread. For you will sow on earth mourning, but you will gather
<margin>,,</margin>a hundred for one in heaven exulting. Arise therefore, go eager, mindful of what I promised through David to the
<margin>,,</margin>sowers: *Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going they shall go and weep, casting their seeds, but coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.*" <note>original: "Qui seminant in lachrymis..." referencing Psalm 126:5-6</note> Paul very briefly narrates in the Epistle to the Corinthians how many and how great things he subsequently endured among all nations—for fourteen years now, day and night, by land and sea, from men, from beasts, in body and soul—while he sows the Gospel. Furthermore, how many labors he suffered over thirty-five years could never be told without great labor. I will explain just one thing which is somewhat obscure. He relates that besides being beaten with rods three times and stoned once, he was lashed five times by the Jews—that is, at five separate times, and each time he received thirty-nine stripes. For the Mosaic law was that if anyone sinned against the law but was not worthy of capital punishment, he should be afflicted with lashes, no more than forty. <note>Deuteronomy 25:3. Jewish tradition limited this to thirty-nine to ensure the biblical limit of forty was never accidentally exceeded.</note> But the interpreters of the law, led by equity, decreed to beat with much fewer lashes. But they judged Paul more harshly than others, that is, to be tortured with only one subtracted <note>original: "una tantum subtracta," meaning 39 lashes</note>. Paul recounts his labors, hardships, and many vigils, hunger, thirst, many fasts, cold, and nakedness, and constant cares for all the churches, and revelations from time to time, to confirm the authority of his Apostleship. Once this is confirmed, the Gospel truth preached by him to the nations is established. Let it be established, I say, against the snares of false Apostles, who, having set out from the Jews for baptism, contended to mix legal ceremonies with the Gospel law. And when Paul introduced the Gospel, as one freed from external ceremonies, he was an object of hatred to them. Hence they calumniated him, as if he were not a true Apostle. But he confirms the truth of his Apostleship from his passions and revelations, against those who both lived in pleasures and were not worthy of revelations. For Jesus had proclaimed: "If anyone wishes to be my disciple, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." The end finally is that the Gospel truth may be whole and firm. Having told the revelation, he confirms how much care God has for him as a legitimate servant, such that He willed him to be tortured often by an iliac passion <note>A historical term for severe abdominal pain or intestinal obstruction, which Ficino interprets here as Paul's "thorn in the flesh."</note>, lest perhaps he be puffed up by divine gifts and think himself something more than a man; but from the pain of his belly, he recognizes himself as truly a man, and preaches Christ, not himself. That the "thorn in his flesh" was not the heat of lust is testified by his life full of innumerable and continuous labors, his most meager diet, hunger, nakedness, and constant labor. And the providence of God proves virtue more suitably and safely through bodily pain than through lust. Nor should it disturb you that he calls it a "thorn of the flesh": for he was accustomed to call whatever pertains to the body and matter by the name "flesh." Likewise, regarding what he says about the Devil goading him, remember that demons often move the humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, etc.) believed to control health and temperament.</note> to cause diseases. This is confirmed by Serapion and Avicenna <note>Serapion the Elder and Avicenna (Ibn Sina) were highly influential historical medical authorities.</note>. Thus instructed by revelations, and amid labors and dangers, he disseminates the word of God in the whole world. This is what God himself sows in today’s Gospel, and while he sows, some falls by the way, etc. Since he calls it "his seed," he declares by "his" that God himself is the one who sows; moreover, he sows in human souls, both the intellectual rules of conscience from the beginning, and daily the truths...

Ficino uses Neoplatonic and Scholastic theories to explain the mechanics of spiritual vision and the structure of the celestial and angelic realms.</meta>

# PREACHINGS.
<sig>Hh 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: by that. For-</meta>

...and when the spirit is withdrawn to the innermost parts, it deserts the outermost; when it is expanded again, the soul is likewise present to them. God was therefore able to expand such a spirit even as far as the third heaven. With the spirit stretched out that far, the very substance of the soul was present in heaven, while meanwhile being present to the earthly body at the same time. For the soul makes itself present as a whole everywhere to the extent that the spirit is expanded. For the soul’s presence governs a Giant just as it governed a tiny infant. But by what means could the spirit itself be expanded so far? It certainly could, since even a ray of light is expanded that far. Indeed, the spirit is a certain **radiant vapor**, <note>Ficino refers to the "spiritus," a subtle medical and philosophical substance believed to bridge the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> and is extended from a base into a cone just like a ray. Add to this that the Holy Spirit of God, insofar as it drew Paul’s spirit toward heaven at great length, likewise contracted the air surrounding Paul’s body from all sides, and by its heat suddenly refined it within Paul’s body to replenish the spirit. For even in us, the spirit is refreshed by the air we constantly draw in. Therefore, in the meantime, Paul’s soul quickened his solid body with only the "vegetative" life of a plant, <note>In medieval philosophy, the "vegetative" power is the lowest level of soul, responsible for basic life functions like growth and nutrition, separate from sensory or intellectual powers.</note> while it also gave life to a spiritual body; and touching the third heaven with that spirit, freed from the various duties of the physical body, he perceived the secrets of God. Thus the mind, insofar as it touched the highest things, was neither properly in a solid body, nor entirely outside the body. Because he dwelt in a spiritual body, and by what means this happened, he confesses is unknown to man. 

We, however, even if we do not know, nevertheless have an opinion. He was "rapt," <note>original: "raptus," meaning seized or snatched up; the theological term for Paul's ecstatic experience in 2 Corinthians 12.</note> not proceeding by his own power, but led by divine power into the third heaven—specifically the corporeal heaven, that is, the **empyrean**. For the first heaven is the entire starry region, containing both the wandering stars (planets) and the fixed stars. Some philosophers, especially the Jews, have said this is one single mass, not only by contact but by continuity, and that it has twin motions, and those being opposite to one another. One motion is its own, from the West; the other is foreign to it, from the East. For a single nature cannot have two opposite motions that are equally its own. For this reason, one ascends from this starry region to the **Crystalline heaven**, which has a single, constrained motion which the starry heaven imitates. Furthermore, since the motion in the starry region is manifold and diverse, and its quality is also manifold—being both transparent and luminous, and shining in various ways—we rightly proceed to the Crystalline heaven, where there is a single motion and a single quality. Again, because stability must exist above what is mobile (as a sign of perfection), and an active light must exist above a transparent quality (which is in a way passive), surely above the whiteness and motion of the Crystalline is the light and stability of the **Empyrean**. Therefore, let the first heaven be the starry; the second, the crystalline; the third, the empyrean. There, Paul saw the light which always illuminates the things following it (which are not luminous of themselves), and illuminates mobile things in a non-mobile way. From this, he contemplated the very goodness of God, which is altogether eternal and endowed with infinite power. Again, in that infinite goodness, and therefore in an infinitely propagable nature, he found an infinite and most inward offspring. For two things cannot be equally infinite. He also found in that infinite goodness a love toward itself that was likewise infinite. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Where Paul, after the third corporeal heaven, also found a triple divine heaven: the **Father**, the **Son**, and the **Holy Spirit**. After this, he also descended through a triple angelic heaven. For he saw how the divine nature, the fountain of intelligence, created not only the corporeal heavens but also the intellectual ones when He procreated the **Angels**, who revolve perpetually around God just as spheres revolve around a pole. He saw this angelic nature similarly distributed into a triple heaven. For just as the one nature of God is wonderfully derived into three persons, so he recognized the one general nature of angels as being divided into three **hierarchies** (that is, sacred princedoms). The first hierarchy is attributed chiefly to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Spirit. In the first, the **Seraphim** consider the Father chiefly in Himself; the **Cherubim** consider the Father chiefly as He governs the Son; the **Thrones** consider the Father with the Son producing the Spirit. In the second, the **Dominations** contemplate the Son chiefly in Himself; the **Virtues**, the Son as begotten by the Father; the **Powers**, the Son as He produces the Spirit together with the Father. In the third, the **Principalities** contemplate the Spirit chiefly in Himself; the **Archangels**, the Spirit as proceeding from both the Father and the Son; the **Angels**, the Spirit as flowing from both the Son and the Father. Though each group contemplates all things, they do so in different primary ways. Indeed, the blessed souls are distributed through these same nine numerical grades of angels.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; There is also another distribution of the angels according to **Dionysius**. <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, the primary historical source for the nine choirs of angels.</note> For the first hierarchy is devoted entirely to contemplation, and by contemplating, it illuminates those that follow. The **Seraphim**, as **Blessed Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas.</note> explains, consider the very order of divine providence chiefly in the divine goodness, as if it were the end goal. The **Cherubim** consider the same chiefly in the divine essence, as if it were a kind of form or exemplar. The **Thrones** consider it chiefly in...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's sermon on the Apostle Paul's ascent. Having established how the "spirit" (the bridge between body and soul) could be expanded, Ficino now details the specific celestial hierarchies Paul encountered and provides a roadmap for how the soul can follow this same path through faith, hope, and charity, and through the cultivation of Neoplatonic virtues.</meta>

<page-num>486</page-num>

# OF MARSILIO FICINO

...by Him. Perhaps the **Seraphim** <note>The highest order of angels, whose name means "the burning ones," associated here with divine power and providence.</note> contemplate more how powerfully He provides; the **Cherubim**, how wisely; and finally the **Thrones**, how beneficently. The second hierarchy reaches action through contemplation. But the **Dominations**, like architects, impose the general rules of providence upon those that follow. The rest then carry these out. Indeed, the **Virtues** govern by moving the heavens, and they concur with God as instruments for performing miracles. Meanwhile, the **Powers** drive away those things that might seem to hinder the order of providence. The third hierarchy now descends further to govern lower things. The **Principalities** care for public affairs, namely princes and cities. The **Archangels** direct each person toward divine worship and are present at sacred rites. The **Angels** arrange smaller matters and assist as guardians to each individual. 

Thus far, Paul inspected the "face" of the divine heavens appearing in the three physical heavens and the three angelic heavens. These angelic heavens he specifically called **Paradise**. <note>original: "Paradisum"</note> Thus far, it is as if he is "seeing," while he views the exterior of God through the heavens shining on both sides. Furthermore, he is said to have "heard": for through hearing we come to know interior things. Then he knew the secrets of God, insofar as God Himself revealed to him—beyond the **Ideas** <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, "Ideas" are the eternal, divine blueprints of all things in the mind of God.</note> of the Angels and the heavens—the Ideas of other things which He can create, provided He wills it. Truly, the knowledge of these secrets cannot be perceived by a human being unless they are among the blessed. Therefore, it was not permitted for Paul to speak of these things to men, for they would not have perceived them in the least. 

It profits us nothing, O brothers, merely to know that Paul climbed to the highest places and then brought his disciples there with him, unless we also offer ourselves as such to Paul, so that he might also lead us to the heights. Heavy things cannot be carried to the highest points. Let us therefore, brothers, lay down all the weights of earthly vices; being purified and light, let us approach Paul and pray to God that He might stretch out His holy hand to his suppliants. He will stretch it out immediately through His kindness, and will easily elevate the light ones on high. There we shall recline at the feasts of the Angels. We shall look down upon the earth, where mortals, like swine, are constantly rolled in the mud and nourished by filth. Meanwhile, among the Angels, we shall feed upon the infinite flavors of the sweetest **Manna**, <note>The miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert, here used as a metaphor for spiritual nourishment.</note> and from the tree of life, we shall drink eternal wine with **Christ**. 

Having spoken of what he saw—that is, the faces of the physical and angelic heavens—to his disciples, **Luke, Barnabas, Clement, Timothy, Titus, Dionysius, and Hierotheus**, <note>Ficino lists the traditional companions of Paul, including Dionysius the Areopagite, to whom the most famous book on the Angelic Hierarchy was then attributed.</note> whom he led into the third heaven through three specific steps (just as he himself had ascended and descended by three), he then addressed them thus: 

"Receive, O sons, the **Faith** <note>original: "fidem"</note> by which you may believe that the **First Good** <note>A Neoplatonic term for God as the ultimate source of goodness.</note> is to be loved by you above all else; from Him all things have the quality of being lovable, and you have the power to love. **Hope**, <note>original: "Sperate"</note> sons, that if you love Him, you are without doubt loved back by God. For unless you were first loved by Him, you would not be able to love Him. **Love**, <note>original: "amate"</note> sons, with your whole mind the **Whole Good**, and by loving it, grasp that **One** in which all good things are one. Having grasped this, you comprehend all things, because in Him you possess neither yourselves nor other things as separate. 

Thus, through the first heaven of **Faith**, you proceeded to the second heaven of **Hope**, and from this to the third heaven of **Charity**; <note>The three "Theological Virtues": Faith, Hope, and Charity (Love).</note> inflamed by this, you burn for God, you shine from God, and you rejoice in God, just as those who have reached the heaven of **Venus** (the third and amorous heaven) reach entirely to the Sun as if it were God. 

Again, O sons, being entirely inflamed by the love of God, drive far away the love of mortals. You have in your soul both the 'first' and 'second' movements of the mind regarding mortal things. The **First Movements** are certain incitements of the senses and the emerging judgment of reason. The **Second Movements** are those which persist even after the judgment of reason, and are the assents of reason itself. Therefore, first cut away these 'consents' and make them more moderate, from which **Civil Virtue** <note>The first level of virtue in the Neoplatonic scale, dealing with social and moral conduct in the world.</note> will arise in you. After this, root out such consents entirely, and there will be in you **Purifying Virtue**. <note>original: "purgatoria uirtus"; the second level of virtue, where the soul detaches from physical impulses.</note> Finally, cut away even the first movements to the best of your strength. Thus, by the integrity of a soul already purified in this way, you will perceive **Exemplary Virtue** <note>The highest level of virtue, existing in the divine mind as a model for all others.</note> in God, as if in a third heaven. 

It is just as one who, passing through **Mars** (the planet of the cutting sword) to **Jupiter** (the sign of equity) and to **Saturn** (the significator of the segregated or contemplative mind), comes from there to a third heaven, reaching the **Milky Way**, <note>The "Lacteus circulus," which in ancient cosmology was sometimes considered the path of souls or the boundary of the physical world.</note> which is most richly hidden with stars, like God. Saturn himself seems to reach this through **Capricorn**, his own domicile. 

Finally, sons, leave this visible world behind; proceed to the **Imaginable World** as if to a second heaven; and from this to the **Intelligible World** <note>The realm of pure intellect and eternal truths, beyond physical form or mental images.</note> as if to a third—that is, to the principles of the universal order. If you contemplate these without the matter of the world, you will immediately possess the mind of the **Worldly Architect**. For the order of the worldly craft, once matter is subtracted, is the very mind of the Divine Craftsman. 

Thus, through the third heaven, you will now reach God for the third time—just as one who has correctly perceived the **Zodiac** as the visible world, will reach the **Crystalline Sphere** as if it were the imaginable world (in which the imaginable signs are placed), and from this to the **Empyrean**, <note>The highest, fire-filled heaven, the dwelling place of God.</note> as if to the intellectual heaven and intelligible light, from whence he shall ascend to God..."
