...God, so that from the light—which is both dispersed and trapped in matter—he may finally arrive at the light that is at once unified, everywhere whole, and free from all matter.

### On the Passion of the Lord

**W**e are all blind, O Lord; have mercy on us through the merits of your passion. Look upon us, most merciful Lord, so that we may look back at you and see you joyfully. Today, my brothers, the Christian people are occupied everywhere with vain bacchanals <note>original: "bacchanalibus"—Ficino is referring to the Carnival celebrations (Mardi Gras) that preceded the solemn season of Lent, which he views as a pagan-like distraction from the suffering of Christ.</note>; meanwhile, Christ, the savior of the people, foretells in the Gospel of Luke to his disciples the sorrows of his future passion. He endured these because of the guilt of our "bacchanals." He suffered them most willingly to free us from perpetual tortures. 

Moreover, he foretells his passion to inspire them to patience and martyrdom. He also predicts his resurrection so they are not terrified by any evils. He warns of all things so they may recognize his divinity—that he was not conquered by human force, but was to suffer by his own choice. Lest they abandon him during the passion, he even confirms each detail with the oracles of the Prophets. This is apparent through Isaiah, Daniel, and others. Isaiah says: *I offered my shoulders to the stripes, my cheeks to the blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.* <note>Isaiah 50:6</note> Hence also that regarding the cross: *He handed over his soul to death and was counted among the wicked.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> And regarding the resurrection, David says: *You will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.* <note>Psalm 16:10</note> 

He foretold that he would suffer under the Gentiles and the Jews, because of Pilate and his attendants. Truly, the disciples did not understand—namely, the mysteries of the Prophets. Likewise, they believed he often spoke allegorically, signifying something else under the name of his passion and death. For they had already conceived him to be so divine that he could not be killed. Soon after, he gives sight to a blind man, confirming his divinity through a miracle, lest the coming passion detract from his divinity. He illuminates the blind man, but one who asks, and asks again, and overcomes the obstacles of the worldly crowd that pulls one away from God. 

Perhaps he is first enlightened in his mind before his body. For the blind beggar, perhaps ignorant of the Prophets, calls him "Son of David." Jesus, loving his perseverance, moves him away from his own state. He asks what he wants, so that he might confess his wish before everyone and openly show those present that he is blind. Nor does he ask for money, but for light, when he says: "Lord." He was already enlightened in his mind through the very presence of Christ. When he says, "that I may see," he desires the light of the eye. Jesus, by a movement of his tongue or his eyes, illuminated him—just as the Sun, by the appearance of its rays, makes us seeing—when he said, *Look up*, namely at me, because your faith toward me has made you worthy of salvation. Recognize me as the giver of salvation. When he said *Look up*, he challenged him to turn his eyes toward him. Immediately he illuminates him with his gaze while he speaks five words: *Your faith has made you whole.* 

The man, as one grateful, follows him, praising God in Jesus, and challenges others to praise him. In the blind man begging on the road, note human blindness in this life, which is needy of salvation. In this blind man enlightened immediately after the narration of the Lord’s passion, note that Christ's passion was necessary for human salvation. Of Christ passing through the way of Jericho (which signifies the Moon <note>In the Renaissance, "Jericho" was often etymologically linked to the Hebrew word for Moon, *Yareach*. Ficino uses this to symbolize Christ descending into the changeable, material world.</note>, that is, descending from heaven), it shows that the work of achieving salvation happens in a moment, when persistence overcomes obstacles. Finally, the light of understanding must be sought from God. Hence that saying of David: *Give me understanding, and I shall live.* <note>Psalm 119:144</note> 

In this, as John cries out: *The charity of God appeared among us when God sent his only begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him.* <note>1 John 4:9</note> God so loved the world that he gave his Son for our sins. Charity is to love God for his own sake, and everything else for the sake of God. For since every multitude of things is from the One, and is therefore referred back to the One, surely all good things must be referred back to the one and first Good. They are from him as if from an <term>efficient cause: the agent or force that brings something into being</term>; they are in him as if in a model; and they are toward him as if toward an end <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</term>. 

For the first maker of things and their mover acts and moves all things for his own sake. Since, therefore, all things are good through the first Good, and are loved insofar as they are good, we seem to say two things regarding him. First, that these things have some image of him. Second, that by loving these things, we love him in all things. But for whose sake? Only so that we may please him. But why should we please him? Is it so that we may avoid evils or obtain comforts? Not at all: for if you loved that first principle not for its own sake, but for the sake of other things and for your own favor, it would be against the order of wisdom...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s sermon or discourse, shifting from the specific details of Christ's Passion to a broader philosophical and theological exploration of divine love (charity) as the governing principle of the universe and the primary path to God.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO
<page-num>488</page-num>

...you might place the first and ultimate end beneath the things that follow, and refer it elsewhere; thus far then.

Finally, let your resolution be to please God; and if anything must be added as to why you wish to please Him, add: "for the glory of God," so that His empire may be more glorious. This very thing is <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitas"—In Ficino’s Neoplatonic Christianity, charity is the highest form of love, a divine force that connects the soul directly to God.</note>, because of which you strive to please Him not only for the glory of God, but also so that others may please Him, namely for the sake of amplifying the divine glory. For God Himself, out of love for Himself—that is, out of the love of amplifying or communicating His own goodness, as <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on the "Divine Names" deeply influenced Ficino’s view of God as the "Good" that overflows into creation.</note> says—procreated all things. Now, love consists in the will. Therefore, <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage whom Ficino believed anticipated Christian truths.</note> and **Plato**, together with our own theologians, confirm that the divine will procreated all things out of the love of His own goodness. Therefore, the universe—which is so great and of such a kind, and was brought into being at that time—receives its lot specifically from the divine will and charity. For it was made as great, of such a quality, and at such a time as God willed. For as far as power and wisdom are concerned, it could have been made at another time and in another way.

Since, therefore, all things were made out of divine love, all things are preserved and moved by that same love. Thus, individual things, led forth from there, are moved and act by a certain love of their own propagation, which imitates the divine propagation. Likewise, they pursue a love of their own preservation, by which they imitate the divine eternity, and they flee from its opposite. Without love, they would neither act at all, nor achieve anything by acting. Likewise, by a mutual love of the parts, the whole is saved, and the parts are preserved. Finally, by a love common to all things among themselves, the universe is perpetually preserved; and every love of this kind is called **charity**. For when it is implanted by God, it calls all things to divine imitation and law.

Perhaps only those beings who possess intellect are able to stray from this end through the movement of their **free will**. Yet, because of this gift of free movement, they owe far more to God than the rest of creation. Therefore, God demands charity much more from them, by which they may love God for the sake of God, and love themselves together with all other things for His sake. 

How much value God places on charity is clear not only from the fact that He made, preserves, and moves all things through charity, and preserves His kingdom over His subjects through the charity of those subjects, but also from the fact that He has established the symbol—that is, the sign and image of charity—in the highest places everywhere. Among the **Angels**, the order of the **Seraphim** <note>The highest rank of angels, whose name means "the burning ones," associated by Ficino with the heat of divine love.</note> is the first. It is the first image of the Holy Spirit and of divine charity. Among the spheres of the heavens, the first is the **Empyrean**, the symbol of charity. Among the planets, the **Sun** is the lord, whose heat is the property of charity. Among the elements, the highest—**Fire**—is the sign of charity. Finally, the generation of things and of life consists in a heat very similar to charity.

After all, what use is food to the body unless heat cooks and digests it, and translates non-living things into the form of life? Similarly, all things and actions are dead to us, nor do they nourish the soul, unless they are touched by the heat of charity and referred back to the very life of the soul, which is to say, to God Himself. All the seeds of things lie as if dead beneath the earth unless they are quickened and sprout by the vernal warmth of the Sun. Once born, they possess dead colors and shapes unless they are illuminated by the light of the Sun. Similarly, whatever are called "virtues" by men lack life unless they are formed by charity. In charity there is both heat and light: heat, insofar as it hungers for God; light, insofar as it is delighted by Him. Both are summarized in the one name of divine love and charity. Just as our solar power made all things alive, so too, in the manner of salt, it preserves them. 

But why does charity alone make it so that the other virtues are truly virtues? Because it directs them toward happiness—that is, toward the ultimate end. Because it is the first principle of all things, it makes other things good for us, insofar as it refers them to the **First Good**. For it is by participation in the First Good that they are good; therefore, when sought apart from Him, they are bad. Finally, by charity alone can we attain God. For since He is immense, we cannot grasp Him unless He gives Himself to us. He does not give Himself except to a soul that gives through charity. 

Therefore, by the way of the intellect, we progress over a very long time; by the way of loving, we progress the most in the shortest time. Also, very few are able to reach toward God by their genius, but all are able to approach Him through charity. Therefore, lest anyone should be able to complain, God established charity as the way of happiness, equally common to all, which leads us back to our fatherland. And there, according to the diverse degrees of loving, He arranges the degrees of joys; and by the seasoning of love itself, He ensures that eternal fullness lacks any weariness. For the soul is not only delighted by fullness through love, but in the meantime, it hungers for it; and therefore it is perpetually delighted. It hungers, I say, not to obtain it, but to hold it. Therefore, it desires to retain the good with the same love with which it had striven to attain it. Just as light objects strive to remain on high with the same lightness by which they had striven to set out. Finally, the soul becomes **God** not by knowledge, but by charity. Just as wood [does not become fire] because [it takes in] light...

<summary>Ficino argues that charity (divine love) is the fundamental force of creation, preservation, and salvation, acting as a "shortcut" to God that is accessible to all people regardless of their intellectual capacity. He uses cosmic analogies, such as the Sun's heat and the Seraphim, to illustrate how charity gives life and "flavor" to all other virtues.</summary>
<keywords>charity, divine love, Neoplatonism, Dionysius the Areopagite, Seraphim, free will, Sun analogy, path to God, happiness, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

...not because it takes its fire from an external source, but because it escapes the heat of the fire. Thus the soul becomes God <note>original: "fit Deus"—Ficino uses this in the Neoplatonic sense of "deification" (theosis), where the soul achieves a state of union with the Divine through love.</note>, not through the external light of knowledge, but through love for God, and from within it shines as God.

### Concerning the star of the Magi, by whose guidance they reached Christ, the king of Israel, already born.

> Breathe upon us, I pray, Nourishing God; show us your star today, which you once showed to the Magi, so that just as it once led the Magi to Christ, the same star may lead us to the mysteries of Christ.

**A** star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall rise out of Israel <note>original: "Orietur stella ex Iacob, & consurget uirga ex Israël"—A quote from Numbers 24:17.</note>. Through these words in the Book of Numbers, Balaam predicts the Messiah who is to be born. At that time, a certain star arose in a miraculous way around Judea. Now, Balaam lived in the Eastern region toward Jerusalem, where the <term>Magi</term> <note>original: "Magi"—The priestly class of ancient Persia, famous for their expertise in astronomy and astrology.</note> were, among whom were priests highly skilled in astronomy who also ruled the people. These men, being most curious about celestial signs, had noted what Balaam had predicted would be signified by the miracle of a star. Finally, when Christ was born, a certain wonderful <term>Comet</term> <note>original: "Cometa"—In the Renaissance, comets were often seen as portents of major historical shifts; here Ficino identifies the Star of Bethlehem as a unique comet.</note> shone in the heights. 

That it was judged to be a comet by learned men is testified by **Origen** in his work *Against Celsus*, saying that he had read in the book of <term>Chaeremon</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest of the 1st century AD.</note> the Stoic concerning comets that sometimes prosperous and healthy things are signified by them. Such was the one that shone at this very time of Augustus Caesar. He explains the history of this from Chaeremon himself, adding that the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A term often used in antiquity to refer to Babylonian astrologers and sages.</note>, when they had considered this and noticed that their own demons had recently been weakened, went to Judea to worship someone more excellent than their own demons. 

Our Platonist **Chalcidius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Plato's *Timaeus* who provided one of the few pagan accounts of the Star of Bethlehem available to Renaissance scholars.</note> testifies to the same, bringing forward various stories about stars. While these are rarely seen, they portend great calamities. Then he adds: "There exists also another holier and more venerable history, which relates that by the rising of a certain star, not diseases and deaths were announced, but the venerable descent of God for the sake of human salvation and mortal affairs, which he testifies was observed by the Chaldeans, who worshipped the newly born God with gifts." Thus says Chalcidius. **Suetonius** <note>A Roman historian; Ficino is referencing his "Life of Vespasian" where Suetonius mentions a messianic expectation in the East.</note> is also a witness in these words: "An old and constant opinion had spread throughout the whole East that it was in the fates that at that time those proceeding from Judea would gain mastery over all things; and because of this, the Jews rebelled against the Romans and perished." 

From this, it is gathered that the Eastern astronomers judged by the rules of <term>Astrology</term> <note>original: "Astrologia"—In Ficino's time, astronomy (calculating movements) and astrology (interpreting meanings) were largely the same discipline.</note> and by portents somehow consistent with their rules that a King was born at that time who would reform the world for the better with miraculous authority. For where they judge a comet to be prosperous and healthy, they recognize it to be from the nature of the **Sun, Jupiter, and Venus**. They pass down that where a leaden color appears, it is a Saturnian comet and signifies pestilence and poverty. But where the color is fiery, it is of Mars, portending battles and fires; and most comets are such. For the fiery and moving force of Mars draws vapors upward from the earth through many regions to the high area of the air touching the fire, and there they are immediately inflamed. They also judge various events from comets based on the signs and planets in which they rise and set, whether they move from the South toward the North or vice versa. 

Perhaps, therefore, when the Eastern astronomers saw a comet arise in the month of December at the beginning of **Sagittarius**, they judged it to be a healthy portent because it showed rays that were both golden from the nature of the Sun, silver from the nature of Jupiter, and mixed from the nature of Venus. Perhaps also Jupiter was then in the beginning of Sagittarius. If we measure correctly, the Sun then occupied the middle of the sign of Sagittarius. Venus, always close to the Sun, easily occupied the end of Sagittarius; it is probable that such was the figure of the heavens afterward, at the birth of Christ in the month of December, if he was born after midnight. For we read in the Gospel that he was born while the shepherds kept their nightly watches, and it is said by the angel, "today he is born." 

From this position of the heavens, both great wonder and controversy fell upon the astrologers: for from Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus, they judged he would be a most just, most bright, and most merciful King. Yet from the Sun’s position, they judged he could not be particularly wealthy. How then will he be a great King and yet poor? Furthermore, from Jupiter in the angle of the ascendant, they thought his lineage would be very fruitful, but from the new Moon occupying the "face of the Virgin" <note>This refers to the astrological decan or face within the sign of Virgo.</note>, they thought the birth would be sterile, and that a certain **Virgin** would be exalted rather than one who had conceived in the usual way. From these judgments of the astrologers, and also from the predictions of Balaam and the other Prophets, the news spread...

<summary>Ficino explains the Star of Bethlehem through a synthesis of biblical prophecy, Roman history, and complex astrological calculations, arguing that the heavens themselves signaled Christ's divine nature and paradoxical poverty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discourse on the Nativity, transitioning from the symbolic meaning of the star to the specific astrological and angelic circumstances of Christ's birth and the journey of the Magi.</meta>

MARSILII FICINI

There was a common opinion throughout the whole East that a King of justice—because of **Jupiter**; of truth—because of the **Sun**; and of grace—because of **Venus**, was at that time risen or designated. However, the place where he was born was unknown to those in the East. Indeed, the Comet led them for perhaps two months, according to the two hours of the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time; here, Ficino links the duration of the comet's visibility to astrological timings.</note>, and although it moved toward the South toward Judea, it did not designate a certain place. Furthermore, up to that point, because of such controversy, it was not known whether he who was born, or about to be born, was sent from the heavens or rather from the Divine. 

Until the Comet showed itself again after two years—representing, as it were, those two months—no longer in the highest part of the atmosphere, but now in the lowest air. Then we recognize the earlier Comet of the <term>Magi</term> <note>original: "Magi"—the Persian priest-astronomers.</note>; they followed its motion, and with it as their leader, they reached Jerusalem in forty-one days. They were no longer seeking a human King, but a divine one. For they saw that the manner and motion of the Comet could not be natural. 

Moreover, that the Magi came and announced the birth of such a great King and the time to Herod can be witnessed not only by the Gospel, but also by Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer. This famous pun relies on the similar sound of the Greek words for "pig" (*hys*) and "son" (*hyios*).</note>, who says: 
> When Augustus had heard that among the boys in Syria whom Herod, the King of the Jews, ordered to be killed, his own son was also slain, he said: "It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son." 

We therefore believe that the Comet was not natural, but divine, moved by the **Angel Gabriel**, and furthermore illuminated by him. For he who had announced John, the precursor of Christ, to Zechariah, and who announced Christ to Mary, the same one portended the birth and place of Christ to the Nations, and through the Nations he also convicted the Jews. And under the form of a star, he taught those who were students of the stars; through the light of the star received from the Sun, he led them to the Sun. 

The Astronomers carried gold to the newborn King because they considered him "Solar"; through fragrant Frankincense, they designated the grace of **Venus**; through Myrrh, which knows nothing of decay, they portended a "Jovian" <note>Related to Jupiter (Jove), often associated with kingship and immortality.</note> life. But meanwhile, these things were converted into another mystery. For with the **Gold**, they helped the poor man. With the **Myrrh**, they strengthened the tender body. With the **Frankincense**, they seasoned the stable. They offered Gold to the King; Frankincense to the Priest; and finally, Myrrh to God. 

It is truly probable that that Comet was an Angel, so that just as an Angel in human figure directed the journey of Tobias, so an Angel in the form of a star directed the Astrologers to Christ. For, as **Moses the Egyptian** <note>original: "Moses Aegyptius"—The Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> testifies, the most learned of the learned Hebrews, the highest knowledge of the stars led **Abraham** to the point where he alone, and the first in his age, understood that there was one first cause of the heavens, and he humbly adored it. From this it resulted that he subsequently obtained from God the light of grace and prophecy. 

But let us return to the Comet. In this very event in the Gospel of Luke, where our Christ is born, the **Angel of the Lord** shone around the Shepherds with light and announced to them great joy, saying: 
> Today the Savior of the world is born. 

And he rightly said "today," as if on this day, although perhaps it was the middle of the night. Because the light of the Comet itself then presented the day; hence that saying of David: 
> And the night shall be illuminated as the day. <note>original: "Et nox sicut dies illuminabitur"—Psalm 139:12.</note>

Thereafter, the Angel suddenly brought this light toward the East to the Persians, to lead the Magi from there to Christ. Hence that saying of Isaiah: 
> Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon it, etc. And the Nations shall walk in your light. <note>Isaiah 60:1-3.</note>

For when the Lord was born, this light appeared around Jerusalem. Then the Gentile Magi walked in this light. Because just as it first proceeded from Judea into the East, so in turn it returned from the East into Judea, bringing the Magi there. Moreover, that this Comet was the same Angel who had declared great joy to the Shepherds, we conjecture from this: because when the Magi saw such a star again, they rejoiced with great joy; and it says "exceedingly," because when they had first seen it at the beginning, they had rejoiced with great joy, just like the Shepherds. But now "exceedingly," because a most welcome good is accustomed to happen to you which you have tasted at another time and receive again after it was interrupted. 

Indeed, the same Angel who, under visible rays, had led the Magi to Christ, soon, under hidden rays, admonishes the minds of the sleeping Magi not to return to Jerusalem, and warns Joseph to flee with the boy into Egypt. The Angel, at the death of Christ, in the very form of the Moon, subjected the full Moon to the Sun above the powers of nature in a moment, and turned the day at noon into night—he who also, at the birth of Jesus, under the form of a Comet, turned the middle of the night into day. Hence that saying of David: 
> As is its darkness, so is its light, <note>Psalm 139:12.</note> 

since both were fulfilled by the ministry of the same angel. And both similarly in the middle space, whether of night or of day. But in what way did the Angel amass the Comet? Standing immediately in the middle of the air, he gathered a thousand <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> of the air poured around him into a somewhat narrower space, and the whole of it, just like a soul

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the Nativity, moving from the physical nature of the angelic light to the specific timing of the Magi’s visit and the astrological symbolism of the Virgin. # SERMONS.

He bound the body to himself with wondrous power and separated it from the remaining elements. Just as by the power of <term>rennet</term> <note>original: "uirtute coagulí"—the substance used to curdle milk into cheese.</note>, a great deal of milk is condensed into a smaller space and separated from the water. And why did the Angel condense the air? So that the light which he was to exhibit in this air might appear to the eyes of men. For things that are very thin and dispersed escape the sharpest sight. But from where did the Angel apply light to this body? Clearly from the very light of his own intelligence. For that intellectual and invisible light which is in him, if it is somehow transferred into the air, becomes visible; indeed, it becomes conspicuous to the blessed in thinner air, but in denser air, it is seen by others as well. 

We said in the previous sections that the Magi came to Jerusalem on the twenty-first day after the birth: at the time when, the period of purification already being completed, Mary offered her Son in the temple. Therefore, on the same day that Simeon and Anna recognized Christ, the Magi were also preaching of the still-unknown Child in Jerusalem. On the following day, however, they arrived in Bethlehem. Furthermore, since Joseph was commanded to take flight with the boy upon the arrival of the Magi, and therefore it is not probable that he brought the boy into the temple after receiving the divine commands, it seems likely that the Magi greeted the boy after the purification. 

Besides what we said regarding <term>Sagittarius</term> <note>The Archer zodiac sign.</note> based on the calculations of some, it would be said more probably, in my opinion, regarding the **Virgin**, and regarding the middle of the night. It was certainly necessary that when Christ rose, a sign from one of the twelve [zodiac signs] should likewise arise. I do not know what sign I should find more fitting for one born of a Virgin than the **Virgin** itself. And specifically, the "first face" of this sign. For every sign has three <term>faces</term> <note>Also known as "decans," these are ten-degree divisions of a zodiac sign.</note>. In the first face of the Virgin, as **Albumasar** <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer whose work was highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> testifies, the Indians and Egyptians alike contemplated a certain image which represented a virgin girl, very beautiful, sitting and nursing a boy. Most of all, the rising of this "face" fits the boy rising from the Virgin, and for one calculating correctly, such a face is born in the middle of the night in the month of December. 

This, moreover, was the "face" in which the Comet is believed to have shone—not as the *cause* of Christ, but as a *sign*. For if those stars had any power to bring about the birth from a Virgin, they would surely have done so more often over so many centuries. In truth, celestial bodies cannot create a law that would cause one to disregard heaven and instead adore and hope for something *above* heaven. In short, a celestial fate cannot be read favorably by a faith that denies fate itself. The light which is spread from the Good itself through all spirits is beneficial. Therefore, it provides movement and rest around the Good; that is, it brings it about that you love the Good and delight in the Good, whatever kind of good it may be, insofar as it possesses the image of the Good itself. He who among men does not have charity—especially one who suffers from envy—already begins to fall gradually into the <term>outer darkness</term> <note>A biblical reference to being cast away from God's presence.</note>, that is, outside the gifts of the beneficial light. For he hates the good and grieves at the good.

->**On the Song of Simeon, and the true peace of the faithful.**<-

> *Breathe upon us, I pray, nourishing God, the way, the truth, the life, the Trinity, one God. In the midst of the Church I will praise you. In the sight of the Angels I will sing psalms to you.*

**C**onsole us, O Lord, always in our weakness. Just as you once consoled Simeon in his old age. Simeon, a wise priest, when he had learned from the observation of the Scriptures that Christ was to come in that age, beseeched God that he might live long enough to see the birth of Christ. He received a promise from the Holy Spirit, therefore, that he would see Him in his own lifetime. But as the advent was delayed and his strength failed due to old age, he said in his prayers: *My eyes have failed looking for your word, saying: When will you console me? Be mindful of your word to your servant, O Lord, in which you have given me hope.* Meanwhile, the Lord answered him: *I will fill you with a multitude of days, and I will show you my salvation.* 

With this confidence, therefore, the pious Simeon, full of the charity of the Holy Spirit, waited a long time for the coming of Christ, and considered Him with his whole mind—not only for his own consolation, but for the common consolation of the people of Israel. And because he hoped with charity, he today attains what he expected; and with that same love with which he hoped, he embraces Jesus in the very arms of love. O fortunate old man, who so easily embraces Him who encompasses the world in his fist! O truly blessed old man, who rules and sustains Him who both rules you and sustains all things! Simeon, therefore, wonderfully transformed into joy from his long-lasting desire, cries out: *O Lord,*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s sermon on the recognition of Christ in the Temple, specifically focusing on the Song of Simeon (the *Nunc Dimittis*). It transitions from the theological meaning of "peace" to a new philosophical discussion on the creation of matter.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

Lord, where he confesses Jesus to be God: **"Now for the first time you release me, and every one of your servants, in peace."** <note>This refers to the *Nunc Dimittis* (Luke 2:29), the canticle sung by Simeon upon seeing the infant Christ.</note> You do not "release" us in the sense that you are fleeing from us—for you are always everywhere—but you allow us to depart from this life. For you did not wish, as you promised, for me to leave this place before I saw your eternal Son—whom I had previously seen only with my mind—now born in time and seen with my eyes. 

I depart indeed now in peace, which has been made between men and God through your Son, once the sins of men were removed. Without this, peace could not have existed among men. I understand that peace is prepared as soon as I have seen your **salvation**, born here for the common health of the whole world. That saving Word of yours was indeed in the world before, but hidden from us. Now, however, having taken on a body, he will be revealed before the face of all peoples together. Therefore, he will truly be a **light to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.** 

The Jews, indeed, possessed some light even before this through the Prophets, the Law, and the <term>Figures</term> <note>Symbolic types or shadows in the Old Testament that prefigure the New Testament.</note>. The Gentiles, however, lacked such light; but they receive light from the Apostles. This light is for the glory of Israel—I do not mean the whole [ethnic] people, but especially *yours*: that is, the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, and chiefly Christ and God the Father. 

At Christ’s birth, a multitude of Angels announced this light, this glory, and this peace. For splendor appeared in the heights, and the Angels cried out: **"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will."** <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis Deo, & in terra pax hominibus bonæ uoluntatis."</note> The total glory and the entire effect of our salvation comes from God through Christ, born at that time. From this, peace was made for men, with Christ acting as the mediator between them and God. For men, I say, "of good will"—that is, those who join their own will with the divine will, just as the Angels join their will with the divine. Thus, "your will shall be done on earth as it is in heaven." Therefore he exclaims: **"My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you; not as the world gives, but as my Father who is in heaven gives."** 

Tell me, I ask you, my brothers, what peace or concord can you find in the world, which is entirely composed of discordant things? In our own bodies, <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in ancient medicine to determine health and temperament through their balance or conflict.</note> continually fight against humors. The senses rebel against reason, and within reason, opinions contradict opinions. Shall we find peace outside ourselves in things "below the Moon," <note>The "sublunary" sphere, which in ancient cosmology was the region of change, decay, and conflict, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note> which are furthermore in disagreement among themselves? Cold things fight hot; dry fight moist; heavy fight light; rare fight dense; soft fight hard; black fight white; and finally, bitter fight sweet. 

Let us at least seek peace and concord in the heavens, since we cannot find it below the heavens. But alas, we cannot find concord and peace even in the celestial body itself. For even there, astronomers have found manifold conflict. They teach that signs are contrary to signs, planets rebel against planets, and the movements of the heavens are carried out in opposition to one another. Rightly, therefore, the Author of Peace says that peace is given to us, not indeed from the heavens, but from the Father of all, who commands the heavens: from the Father, I say, through the Son, by the exhortation of the Spirit, who is called the Spirit of peace and love. As the Apostle also says: **"Hope is not confounded, because the love of God is kindled in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us."** 

Wherefore, most beloved brothers, glowing with the love of the Holy Spirit, let us enter the temple today. There we shall immediately find the only-begotten Son of God; we shall see him with wonder, and our eyes will rejoice. We shall touch him with fear, together with Simeon, and our heart will then rejoice. We shall embrace him with reverence, just as 그 (that) holy old man did, and our joy will be full. We shall sing: **"Our eyes have seen your salvation,"** and we shall find full peace in him, and no one shall take our joy from us. For God, who possesses and preserves all things for everyone, will be with us forever and ever.

***

->On the creation of things.<-

**A** potter first prepares clay for himself, as a kind of matter in which he may fashion the forms of vessels that he holds in his mind. In one mind, I say, he holds many forms, and similarly he fashions many forms in one clay, while he extends the unformed clay (previously made shapeable by him) and shapes it by extending it. Similarly, from the beginning, God created one **matter**, utterly unformed, of which Moses says: *Darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* In the first moment of its creation, this matter had neither form, as I said, nor even magnitude. For by the order of nature, matter is first that which it is in itself, before it is beautiful or large.

He then begins a philosophical explanation of creation, using a potter's analogy to describe how God shaped unformed matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse from the previous page regarding the nature of creation, then transitions into the formal dedicatory preface of Marsilio Ficino's famous work, *De Vita* (On Life). The previous page concluded a sermon on Simeon and the infant Christ, moving toward the physical properties of the created world.</meta>

<header>SERMONS.</header>
<page-num>495</page-num>

Nor could matter have become beautiful unless it first possessed some magnitude. In the first moment of creation, therefore, God made matter so that it might simply exist, though it was not yet a body. In the second moment, He extended it into three dimensions: namely, length, width, and depth. Matter thus extended immediately became a body, though it was not yet able to perform any action itself. In the third moment, God shaped this body—that is, the extended matter—into many forms, specifically those of the elements and the heavens; and in the heavens, He established it with the forms of the stars. Beneath the heavens, in addition to the forms of the elements, He shaped it into the forms of vapors, stones, metals, plants, and animals. Matter is indeed one and the same everywhere, though clothed in all these various forms. All the motions and actions of things, however, are brought about through the forms of the things themselves. For heavy things descend by gravity <note>original: *gravitatem*; in this context, it refers to the "form" or quality of weight that compels an object downward, rather than the modern Newtonian force.</note>, not by matter. For the matter in light things is the same as in heavy ones. Similarly, light things ascend through the quality of lightness. Hot things do not provide heat through their mass, but through the form of heat; and cold things through cold. Gravity, lightness, heat, and cold are all forms.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Florentine Physician and Philosopher,
->Dedicatory Epistle on the book *On Life* to the magnanimous<-
->Lorenzo de' Medici, savior of the fatherland.<-

The Poets sing of Bacchus as the highest presiding priest, twice-born. Perhaps they signify that a future priest must be reborn immediately upon initiation, or that the mind of a perfect priest, being deeply intoxicated by God, already appears reborn. Or perhaps, in a humbler sense, they mean that the wine—the offspring of Bacchus—is generated once on the vine (as if from Semele <note>In Greek mythology, Semele was the mother of Bacchus/Dionysus who perished when Zeus revealed his true form.</note>) when the clusters ripen under the sun <note>original: *Phœbo*; referring to Apollo/the Sun.</note>, and is regenerated a second time after the "lightning" of the harvest in its own vessel, like pure wine in the thigh of Jove <note>Referring to the myth where the infant Bacchus was sewn into the thigh of Jupiter/Jove to complete his gestation.</note>. But we must not speak of sacred mysteries at present, as we are soon to provide physical aid to the weak instead. Nor should we proceed with a style enslaved to gravity, but rather one that is free and playful, since we have somehow begun with Father Liber <note>original: *Libero patre*; "Liber" is a name for Bacchus, but also the Latin word for "free" and "book." Ficino is punning on his own freedom of style and the subject of his book.</note>.

And rightly, I say, "somehow": for perhaps a more prudent man would have inaugurated his medical work with Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, the first of physicians, rather than with Bacchus. But what of it? If there is any omen—and not a vain one—it is that my mouth happened to speak of Bacchus just now. For he, with a certain nourishing wine and most joyful sense of security, heals perhaps more healthily than Phoebus does with his herbs and songs. In whatever sense you take those stories, Bacchus, that leader of priests, is said to have had two mothers. But Melchizedek, that highest priest, had hardly one mother and hardly one father <note>original: *uuam uix matrem, unum uix patrem*; a reference to the biblical Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:3) who is described as being "without father or mother" or genealogy.</note>. 

I, the least of priests, have had two fathers: Ficino the Physician <note>Ficino’s biological father, Diotifeci d’Agnolo, was the personal physician to Cosimo de' Medici.</note> and Cosimo de' Medici. From the former I was born; from the latter I was reborn. The former commended me to Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note>, who was both a physician and a Platonist; the latter consecrated me to the divine Plato. And Cosimo, just like my father, destined Marsilio for a medical career—Galen indeed for bodies, but Plato as the physician of souls. For a long time now, I have practiced the health-giving medicine of souls under Plato; after translating all his books, I then composed eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness, thus satisfying my father the Physician to the best of my ability. Then, thinking I must next satisfy my "Medici" father <note>A pun on the name "Medici," which means "physicians."</note>, I composed a book on caring for the health of scholars. Scholars then desired not only to be well at certain times, but to live a long time in good health. To them, therefore, I then gave the book *On Long Life*. But they distrusted earthly medicines and remedies in so great a matter. I have now added this book *On Life*—concerning a life both vigorous and long, to be obtained from the heavens—so that from the living body of the world itself, a more vigorous life might flow into our body, as if...

<header>E P I S T L E</header>

...[a certain] member of the world, as if it were propagated from a vine. Pray, most indulgent Lorenzo, forgive these books of medicine if, while I wish to be a Physician <term>Medicus; a doctor of medicine</term>, I am also somehow—even if unwillingly—a Poet <term>Poëta</term>, though often not a good one. For Phœbus <note>original: "Phœbus"; another name for the god Apollo, who in classical mythology presided over both the healing arts and music/poetry.</note> is both the discoverer of medicine and the master of poetry; he bestows his life upon us not so much through herbs as through the lyre and song. Furthermore, even Venus, according to the astrologers, brings forth the Musician and the Physician alike.

But until now, while I have looked after the lives of scholars and similar citizens with great care, I have neglected the health of my own books, so long as I allowed them to remain separated from one another. Therefore, showing duty toward them now for the first time, I join them into one body. Now that its limbs have been joined into a single form, let life be present at once. However, this physical work—this "body" of mine, so to speak—cannot receive life unless it is my own. Such a life depends entirely on my soul. But that soul, magnanimous Lorenzo, my patron, has already lived in your presence for a long time, especially in that grandest part of your palace where, alongside Plato, my work *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>original: "de animorum immortalitate"; this refers to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*, his major philosophical work dedicated to Lorenzo years earlier.</note> is kept, having been dedicated to your name long ago.

Yet that soul of mine, though it leads its life in your presence as if in a blessed homeland, is nevertheless restless (as the theologians <term>Theologi</term> maintain) until it receives this physical work as its own body. Receive therefore, best Lorenzo, after those books on the Soul, these books on the Body as well <note>The "books on the Body" refers to the text this letter introduces: *De Vita libri tres* (Three Books on Life), which focuses on the physical and psychological health of scholars.</note>; and with the same breath of inspiration with which you once favored the former, look fortunately upon these. For thus shall this body live through its own soul under your
->spirit, and our soul in turn<-
->shall rest, now united with its body within your<-
->household.<-

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the first book of Marsilio Ficino’s *De Vita Libri Tres* (Three Books on Life). Following the previous page’s philosophical dedication to Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino now addresses the practical health concerns of the "literary" class, positioning himself as the first physician to specifically treat the ailments caused by intellectual labor.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Florentine Physician and Philosopher,
### most celebrated, on the protection of the health of scholars, or of those who devote their effort to letters, for the preservation of good health.

-> BOOK I. <-

-> *On the Nine Guides of Scholars. Chapter I.* <-

Whoever enters upon that rough, steep, and long path, which indeed finally leads to the lofty temple of the nine Muses with constant labor, seems to stand in need of exactly nine guides for this journey. Of these, the first three lead us in heaven, the following three in the mind, and the last three on earth. First, in heaven, Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, associated here with the initial spark of inquiry and investigation.</note> either impels or exhorts us to set out on the investigation of the Muses' path; for the entire duty of investigation is attributed to Mercury. Next, Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbus"; another name for Apollo, the sun god, who provides the light of clarity and understanding.</note> himself so illuminates both the searching minds and the things sought with most abundant splendor that what was being sought is clearly found by us. Then comes the most gracious Venus, mother of the Graces, and with her entirely nourishing and joyful rays she so seasons and adorns the whole matter that whatever was sought by the instigation of Mercury and found with the guidance of Phoebus, having been bathed in a certain wondrous and healthy beauty by Venus, may always delight and be of use. There follow three guides of this journey in the mind: namely, a burning and steady will, sharpness of wit, and a tenacious memory. The last three on earth are a most prudent head of the household <note>original: "paterfamiliâs"; referring to the provider or manager of domestic affairs who allows a scholar the leisure to study.</note>, a most esteemed teacher, and a most skilled physician. Without these nine guides, no one has been or ever will be able to reach the temple of the nine Muses itself. The first [six] guides God Almighty and Nature have granted to us from the beginning, but our own diligence must provide the final three. However, the precepts and duties which pertain to the head of the household and the teacher regarding literary studies have been treated by many ancient and wise men—especially our Plato, both frequently elsewhere and most diligently in his books on the *Republic* and the *Laws*. Then Aristotle in the *Politics*, and also Plutarch and Quintilian have done so excellently. But until now, only a physician has been missing for scholars of letters, one who might stretch out a hand to those who go, and assist with healthy advice and medicines those whom neither heaven, nor the mind, nor the head of the household or teacher has failed. I, therefore, pitying their most laborious lot—those who travel a difficult path for the sake of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom. Ficino suggests that intense study "weakens the nerves" or drains the body's physical vitality.</note> who weakens the nerves—step forward first as a physician for the weak and the infirm, but would that my ability were as complete as my favorable will. Arise now, young men, be eager with God as your guide. Arise, youths and men, whom an overly burning zeal for Minerva exhausts too much. Approach the physician willingly, who, with God showing and favoring the way, bestows upon you healthy advice and remedies for the perfection of your purpose.

-> *How Diligent Care Must Be Taken of the Brain, Heart, Stomach, and Spirit. Chapter II.* <-

In the first place, just as runners are accustomed to take care of their legs, athletes their arms, and musicians their voices, so scholars of letters ought to take at least as much account of the brain, the heart, the liver, and the stomach—indeed, even more so, insofar as these members are more excellent than those, and scholars use them more frequently and for more important things than the others do. Besides this, any skillful craftsman cares for his instruments with the greatest diligence: the painter for his brushes, the ironsmith for his hammers and anvils, the soldier for his horses and weapons, the hunter for his dogs and birds, the lute-player for his lute, and everyone else similarly for his own. Only the priests of the Muses <term>Musarum sacerdotes; a poetic way to refer to dedicated scholars or philosophers</term>, only [priests] of the highest good...

<summary>Ficino introduces the "nine guides" necessary for a scholar's journey, identifying a lack of medical care for intellectuals as a major problem he intends to solve. He argues that scholars must care for their vital organs—the brain, heart, liver, and stomach—with the same diligence a craftsman shows for his tools.</summary>

ON SCHOLARS

<page-num>496</page-num>

...good hunters of truth are (oh, the shame!) so negligent and so unfortunate that they seem to utterly neglect that instrument by which they are able, in a sense, to measure and grasp the entire world. An instrument of this kind is the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle bodily fluid that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> itself, which is defined by physicians as a certain vapor of the blood—pure, subtle, warm, and clear. Procreated from the subtler blood by the very heat of the heart, it flies to the brain, and there the soul uses it continually for the exercise of the senses, both internal and external. For this reason, the blood serves the spirit, the spirit serves the senses, and finally, the senses serve the reason. Furthermore, the blood is produced by the "natural power" which flourishes in the liver and stomach. The thinnest part of the blood flows into the fountain of the heart, where the "vital power" flourishes. From there, the created spirits ascend to the brain and—as I might put it—to the "heights of Pallas" <note>An allusion to Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, representing the brain as the seat of intellect.</note>. In these heights, the "animal power"—that is, the power of sensing and moving—holds dominion. Therefore, contemplation is almost always of the same quality as the service of the sense itself. Moreover, the sense is of the same quality as the spirit; the spirit of the same quality as the blood; and those three powers we mentioned—namely, the natural, the vital, and the animal—are of such a quality as those things from which, through which, and in which the spirits themselves are conceived, born, and nourished.

### *That scholars are prone to phlegm and black bile.*
### Cap. III.

**N**ot only must men who are greedy for letters care most diligently for those members, powers, and spirits, but they are also commanded to most cautiously avoid <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture.</note> and <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor associated with melancholy.</note> always, no differently than sailors avoid <note>The classic "between a rock and a hard place" metaphor from Homer's Odyssey, referring to two sea monsters on opposite sides of a strait.</note> Scylla and Charybdis. For as much as they are idle in the rest of the body, they are that much busy in the brain and mind. Because of this, they are compelled to produce phlegm (which the Greeks call <note>original: "phlegma"</note> *phlegm*) and black bile (which the same people call <note>original: "melancholiam"</note> *melancholy*). The former often dulls and suffocates the intellect; the latter, however, if it should abound too much or become inflamed, vexes the person with constant care and frequent delusions, and disturbs the soul and judgment. Thus, it can be said not without merit that scholars would be exceptionally healthy if phlegm were not troublesome, and the most joyful and wisest of all, if they were not often forced to lose their wits—sometimes through sorrow, sometimes through the fault of black bile.

### *How many are the causes by which scholars are or become melancholic.*
### Cap. IIII.

**T**here are three principal kinds of causes that make scholars melancholic. The first is celestial, the second is natural, and the third is human. The celestial cause is such because <term>Mercury</term> <note>The planet Mercury was thought to govern the initial spark of curiosity and communication.</note>, who invites us to investigate doctrines, and <term>Saturn</term> <note>The planet Saturn was associated with deep, long-term focus, but also with the "heavy" temperament of melancholy.</note>, who causes us to persevere in investigating doctrines and to preserve what is found, are said by astronomers to be in a certain way cold and dry. Or, if by chance Mercury is not cold, he is nevertheless often very dry due to his proximity to the Sun. This dryness and coldness is the same as the "melancholic nature" among physicians; and Mercury himself and Saturn impart this same nature to students of letters—their followers—from the beginning, and they preserve and increase it daily. 

The natural cause will be evident because, to achieve especially difficult sciences, it is necessary for the mind to withdraw itself from external things to internal ones, as if from a certain circumference to the center; and while it speculates, it must remain most stably in the very center (so to speak) of the man. To collect oneself from the circumference to the center, and to be fixed in the center, is most characteristic of the Earth itself, to which black bile is very similar. Therefore, black bile provokes the soul so that it may both collect itself into one and stay in one, and contemplate continually. And black bile itself, being like the center of the world, forces one to investigate the center of individual things, and carries one toward comprehending the highest things, since it agrees most with Saturn, the highest of the planets. Contemplation itself also, in turn, draws together a nature very similar to black bile by a certain constant collection and, as it were, compression. 

The human cause, however, is from ourselves: because the frequent thinking of the mind intensely dries out the brain. Therefore, when the moisture is largely consumed (which is the fuel of the natural heat), the heat also is usually extinguished; from this, the nature of the brain becomes dry and cold, which is called the earthy and melancholic quality.

<summary>Ficino explains the physiological connection between blood, spirits, and the brain, arguing that scholars are naturally prone to melancholy and phlegm due to planetary influences (Saturn/Mercury) and the intense mental "compression" required for study.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physiology of the scholar. On the previous page, Ficino established the relationship between blood, spirit, and the senses. Here, he explains how intense mental activity physically alters the blood, leading to the condition known as melancholy, and introduces the classical idea that genius is often linked to this state.</meta>

# ON THE PRESERVATION OF HEALTH, BOOK I.

Furthermore, because of the very frequent movement of inquiry, the moved <term>spirits</term> <note>These are the "animal spirits," a subtle vapor that Renaissance doctors believed carried signals between the brain and the body.</note> are also continually dissolved. It is necessary for these dissolved spirits to be restored from the more subtle parts of the blood. For this reason, since the thinner and clearer parts of the blood are frequently consumed, the remaining blood is necessarily rendered dense, dry, and black. Added to this is the fact that nature, being entirely intent upon the brain and heart during contemplation, abandons the stomach and the liver. Therefore, because the food—especially if it is either too abundant or too hard—is poorly digested, the blood produced from it becomes cold, thick, and black. Finally, due to the excessive idleness of the limbs, superfluities are not expelled, nor are the sticky, tenacious, and dark vapors breathed out. All these things tend to produce a melancholic spirit and a mournful and fearful soul. Indeed, inner darkness occupies and wears down the soul much more than outer darkness does. Truly, of all scholars, those most oppressed by <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bile"; one of the four bodily humors, believed to cause a "melancholic" temperament when in excess.</note> are those who, sedulously devoted to the study of philosophy, call the mind away from the body and bodily things and join it to incorporeal things. This is partly because the more difficult work requires a greater intention of the mind, and partly because, insofar as they join the mind to incorporeal truth, they are compelled to disjoin it from the body. Hence, their body is sometimes rendered as if half-alive and melancholic. Our Plato signifies this in the *Timaeus*, saying: a soul contemplating divine things very often and very intensely grows so much on such nourishment and becomes so powerful that it exceeds what the nature of the body can endure; by its own more vehement agitations, it sometimes either escapes the body in a way or seems, at times, to dissolve it.

### Chapter V: Why the gifted are melancholic, and which of them are so, or otherwise.

It should suffice to have shown thus far—by first celestial, second natural, and third human reasons—why the <term>priests of the Muses</term> <note>Ficino's poetic term for scholars and intellectuals.</note> are either melancholic from the beginning or become so through study. Indeed, Aristotle confirms this in his book of *Problems*.
<margin>For he says that all men who have been outstanding in any faculty were melancholics.</margin>
In this matter, he confirmed that Platonic saying written in the book *On Science*: namely, that gifted people are usually very excited and "furious" <note>In this context, "fury" refers to a state of divine inspiration or intense intellectual agitation, rather than simple anger.</note>. Democritus also says that no men can ever be great in talent except those who are stirred by a certain fury. Our Plato seems to prove this in the *Phaedrus*, saying that the doors of poetry are knocked upon in vain without fury. Although he perhaps wishes divine fury to be understood here, nevertheless, according to the physicians, such fury is never incited in any others except melancholics. Next, however, we must assign the reasons why Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle assert that some melancholics occasionally so far excel everyone in talent that they seem not human, but rather divine. Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle undoubtedly asserted this, but they do not seem to explain the reason for such a great thing sufficiently. Yet we must dare (with God showing the way) to investigate the causes. Melancholy—that is, black bile—is of two types: one is called "natural" by physicians, while the other happens by <term>adustion</term> <note>The "burning" or overheating of humors, which was thought to change their chemical and psychological effects.</note>. That natural type is nothing other than a certain denser and drier part of the blood. The "burnt" type is distributed into four species: for it is conceived by the combustion of either natural melancholy, or of the purer blood, or of yellow bile, or of "false" phlegm. Whichever is born from combustion harms judgment and wisdom; for while that humor is kindled and burns, it usually makes men excited and Raging—which the Greeks call <term>Mania</term> <note>A state of frantic over-activity or madness.</note>, but we call "fury." But when it is already extinguished, the thinner and clearer parts being dissolved and only a foul soot remaining, it renders them dull and stupid. This condition they properly call "melancholy," as well as "madness" and "faint-heartedness." Therefore, only that black bile which we called natural is conducive to judgment and wisdom for us. Yet not always. To be sure, if it is alone, it obscures the spirits with its too-black and dense mass, terrifies the soul, and blunts the talent. If, however, it is mixed with simple phlegm, since the cold blood stands around the heart, it brings on sluggishness and torpor through a certain thick coldness; and as is the nature of every very dense matter, when melancholy of this kind cools, it is stretched to the peak of coldness. In this state, nothing is hoped for, all things are feared, and it is a weariness to behold the vault of heaven. If black bile, whether simple or mixed, putrefies, it produces quartan fever, tumors of the spleen, and many things of the same kind. Where it overflows too much, whether it be alone or joined to phlegm, it makes the spirits thicker and colder, continually affects the soul with weariness, dulls the edge of the mind, "nor does the blood leap around the heart in Arcadian fashion" <note>A poetic way of saying the person lacks spirit or vitality, referencing the ancient Greek region of Arcadia.</note>. It is necessary, moreover, that black bile neither...

He explores the classical link between this "black bile" and genius, distinguishing between "natural" melancholy (which aids wisdom) and "burnt" melancholy (which causes madness or stupor).</summary>

-> MARSILIO FICINO ON THE HEALTH OF SCHOLARS <-

...be so few that the blood, yellow bile, and <term>spirits</term> <note>The "animal spirits" or subtle vapors that act as the medium between the soul and the physical body.</note> lack a bridle, so to speak, which would result in an unstable intellect and a fleeting memory. Nor should it be so abundant that we appear to drowse and require spurs, weighed down by too much mass. Therefore, it is necessary that it be as refined as its nature allows. For if it is thinned out as much as possible according to its nature, it can perhaps even be abundant without causing harm—even so much that it seems to equal the yellow bile at least in weight. Let <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor responsible for melancholy.</note> abound, therefore, but let it be very refined; let it not lack the surrounding moisture of a more subtle <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor.</note>, lest it dry out completely and become excessively hard. However, it should not be mixed entirely with phlegm—especially not with the colder or more abundant kind—lest it grow cold. Rather, let it be mixed with yellow bile and blood in such a way that one body is made from the three, composed in a ratio of double the blood to the other two. Where there are eight parts of blood, there should be two parts of yellow bile and two portions of black bile. Let the blood be kindled a little by those two parts of black bile, and once kindled, let it shine rather than burn; otherwise, like a harder material when it boils too much, it might burn and agitate too vehemently—and when it cools, it might likewise become cold to the extreme. For black bile is like iron: when it is inclined toward cold, it is extremely cold; when, on the contrary, it turns toward heat, it is extremely hot. Nor should it seem strange that black bile can be easily kindled and, once kindled, burns more fiercely. Indeed, we see that <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calcem"; quicklime, which reacts violently with water.</note>, which is similar to it, boils immediately when water is poured over it and burns away. Melancholy has such power toward either extreme because of the unity of its stable and fixed nature. Such an extremity does not happen to the other humors. When it is extremely hot, it provides the greatest boldness—indeed, ferocity—but when extremely cold, it brings extreme fear and sluggishness. Yet when it is infected in varying degrees between cold and heat, it produces various affections, not unlike how pure wine—especially strong wine—is accustomed to bring various moods to those drinking it, from drunkenness or from partaking a bit too freely. Therefore, it is necessary that the black bile be appropriately tempered. When it is moderated as we have said and mixed with yellow and red bile, because it is dry by nature and, by condition, as refined as its nature allows, it is easily kindled by them; because it is solid and very tenacious, once kindled, it blazes for a very long time; and because it is most powerful in the unity of its tenacious dryness, it heats up more vehemently. Just as a log among straws, if both are kindled, heats and shines more and for longer. Moreover, from long-lasting and vehement heat come great brilliance and vehement, long-lasting motion. This is the point of that saying of Heraclitus:

> A dry light is the wisest soul. <note>original: "Lux sicca, anima sapientissima." A famous fragment suggesting that the soul is most intelligent when it is not "wet" with bodily passions or dull humors.</note>

### How black bile makes men gifted. Chapter VI.

**P**erhaps someone will ask what kind of body is formed from that humor made of those three humors in the proportion we have described. In color, it is much like the gold we see, but it turns somewhat toward purple. And when it is kindled, whether by natural heat or by the motion of the body or mind, it heats and shines almost like glowing, red gold mixed with purple; and like a rainbow, it draws out various colors as the heart blazes. Someone may ask again: In what way does such a humor benefit the intellect? Truly, the spirits created from this humor are, in the first place, refined—not unlike that water which they call the **Water of Life** <note>original: "aqua Vitæ"; high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy, used medicinally in the Renaissance.</note> or **Water of the Vine**, and "burning water," whenever it is expressed from thicker pure wine by a certain distillation over fire, as is usually done. For the spirits, compressed under the narrower passages of such black bile, are refined to the highest degree by a heat that is more vehement due to its unity; and being pressed through narrower passages, they burst forth more refined. Secondly, they are similarly hotter and, by the same logic, more luminous. Thirdly, they are agile in motion and most vehement in action. Fourthly, emanating continually from a solid and stable humor, they serve the work for a very long time. Relying on such service, our mind investigates vehemently and perseveres longer in its investigating. It easily finds whatever it has sought, perceives it clearly, judges it purely, and retains what it has judged. Add to this that, as we indicated in the previous sections, the mind—by means of such an instrument or stimulus, which in a way corresponds to the center of the world and (if I may say so) collects the mind into its own center—always seeks the center of all things and penetrates to their innermost secrets. Furthermore, it corresponds with **Mercury** and **Saturn** <note>Ficino blends medicine with astrology: Mercury rules the clever intellect, while Saturn rules deep, solitary contemplation and melancholy.</note>; the latter of these, the highest of all the planets, carries the investigator toward the highest things. Hence, singular philosophers emerge, especially when the mind is thus called away from external movements and its own body, and becoming as close as possible to divine things, it is made an instrument of the divine. Wherefore, filled from above with divine influxes and oracles, it always devises certain new and unusual things and predicts the future. This is something not only Democritus and Plato affirm, but

...even Aristotle in the *Book of Problems*, and Avicenna in the *Book of Divine Things* and the book *On the Soul*, acknowledge this. Why so much talk about the humor of black bile? So that we might remember how much <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor responsible for melancholy.</note>—or rather, a "shining" bile of this kind—must be sought and nourished as the best, and how much that other kind, which is its opposite, must be avoided as the worst. For it is such a dreadful thing that Serapio said its force is incited by an evil demon, and the wise Avicenna did not deny it.

### Chapter VII: The Five Chief Enemies of Scholars: Phlegm, Black Bile, Sexual Intercourse, Overindulgence, and Morning Sleep.

**B**ut to return to where we digressed some time ago, the path that leads to truth and wisdom is a very long one, filled with heavy labors on both land and sea. Whoever undertakes this journey, as some poet might say, is often endangered on land and sea. For whether they sail the sea, they are continually tossed among the waves—that is, between two humors, namely <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor.</note> and that harmful melancholy—as if between Scylla and Charybdis. Or if they travel by land (so to speak), three monsters immediately present themselves. First, the earthly Venus <note>Symbolizing sexual desire.</note>; second, Bacchus and Ceres <note>Symbolizing wine and food/gluttony.</note>; and third, the nocturnal Hecate <note>Symbolizing the night and, by extension, late-night study and the resulting morning sleep.</note> frequently opposes them. Therefore, Apollo must be called from the ether, Neptune from the sea, and Hercules from the earth, so that Apollo may pierce these monsters—enemies of Pallas Athena—with his arrows, Neptune may tame them with his trident, and Hercules may crush and tear them with his club.

The first monster is sexual intercourse, especially if it exceeds one’s strength even slightly; for it suddenly exhausts the <term>spirits</term> <note>The subtle "animal spirits" or vapors that act as the medium between the soul and the physical body.</note>, especially the more refined ones, weakens the brain, and undermines the stomach and the heart. No evil can be more adverse to the intellect than this. Why else did Hippocrates judge intercourse to be similar to the <term>falling sickness</term>? <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; epilepsy. Hippocrates famously described the act as a "minor epilepsy."</note> Except that it strikes the mind, which is sacred, and is so harmful that Avicenna said in his book *On Animals*: if any more <term>semen</term> <note>original: "spermatis".</note> is discharged through intercourse than nature can bear, it is more harmful than if forty times as much blood had flowed out. Thus, the ancients did not without reason wish the Muses and Minerva to be virgins. This relates to that Platonic story where Venus threatened the Muses that unless they performed the sacred rites of Venus, she would arm her son against them. The Muses replied: "O Venus, threaten Mars with such things; for your Cupid does not fly among us." Finally, nature has separated no sense further from the intelligence than the sense of touch.

The second monster is overindulgence in wine and food. Indeed, if the wine is either too much, or too hot and potent, it will fill the head itself with the worst humors and fumes. I pass over the fact that drunkenness makes men insane. As for excessive food, it first calls all of nature's power to the stomach for the task of digesting. Because of this, one cannot focus on the head and on contemplation at the same time. Furthermore, if it is poorly digested, it dulls the sharpness of the mind with many thick vapors and humors. Even if it is sufficiently digested, nevertheless, as Galen says, a soul suffocated by fat and blood cannot perceive anything celestial.

The third monster is staying awake late into the night, especially after dinner, which forces you to sleep even after the sun has risen. Since many scholars err and are deceived in this matter, I will explain more extensively how much it harms the intellect, and I will bring forward seven principal reasons. The first is derived from the heavens themselves; the second from the elements; the third from the humors; the fourth from the order of things; the fifth from the nature of the stomach; the sixth from the spirits; and the seventh from the imagination.

First, three planets, as we said above, greatly favor contemplation and eloquence: the Sun, Venus, and Mercury. These, running with nearly equal steps, flee from us as night approaches, but as the day either approaches or is already rising, they rise again and revisit us. But after the rising of the Sun, they are suddenly delivered into the <term>twelfth region of the sky</term> <note>In traditional astrology, the 12th House is known as the "House of Imprisonment" or "Hidden Enemies." Ficino suggests the planetary energies become trapped or weakened here after dawn.</note>, which is assigned by astronomers to prison and darkness. Therefore, it is not those who rise for contemplation and writing either at night when the planets flee us, or during the day after the Sun has risen when they enter the house of prison and darkness—but rather those who rise when the planets are nearly seeking their rising or are already rising—who alone perceive most sharply and write and compose their discoveries most eloquently. 

The second reason, namely from the elements, is this: when the Sun rises, the air is moved, thinned, and becomes clear; when it sets, the opposite occurs. The blood and the spirits are necessarily compelled by nature to follow the movement and quality of the surrounding air. The third reason, which is drawn from the humors, is of this sort: In the morning...

<summary>Ficino identifies five major enemies of the scholar's health and intellect, focusing specifically on the biological and astrological dangers of sexual excess, gluttony, and improper sleep cycles. He argues that the scholar must align their habits with the rising sun and the movement of the planets to maintain the clarity of the "animal spirits."</summary>
