<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the "five chief enemies" of the scholar. The previous page ended mid-sentence, calling upon Apollo to help the scholar navigate the dangers of the humors, specifically mentioning the dawn (aurora) as the time when the body begins its daily cycle.</meta>

In the **dawn**, the blood is moved and begins to rule; through this motion, it becomes thinned, warmed, and cleared. The <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, these are subtle, airy vapors that act as the bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note> usually follow and imitate the nature of the blood. But as night approaches, either that thicker and colder <term>melancholy</term> <note>The humor of black bile.</note> or <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor.</note> becomes dominant, which undoubtedly renders the spirits completely unfit for contemplation.

The **fourth reason**, drawn from the order of things, is this: the day is granted for waking, and the night for sleep. For when the Sun approaches our hemisphere or moves above it, it opens the passages of the body with its rays and expands the humors and spirits from the center toward the surface, which indeed excites and leads us toward waking and action. Conversely, when the Sun recedes, everything is contracted; by a certain natural order, this invites sleep, especially after the third or fourth part of the night. Therefore, whoever dozes in the morning when the Sun and the world are waking up, yet stays awake late into the night when nature commands us to sleep and rest from our labors, is without doubt rebelling against both the order of the universe and himself. He is disturbed and pulled apart by two contrary motions at once. Indeed, while he is being moved by the universe toward the exterior, he is moving himself toward the interior. And conversely, while he is being drawn by the universe toward the interior, he meanwhile withdraws himself toward the external. Therefore, by this perverse order and these contrary motions, both the whole body and the spirits and the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "ingenium"; the natural talent or mental capacity.</note> are utterly weakened.

In the **fifth place**, we argue from the nature of the stomach in this way: the stomach, by the long-lasting action of the daytime air, is greatly dilated as its pores are opened, and it is finally much weakened as the spirits fly out. Therefore, as night comes on, it requires a new supply of spirits to be nourished. For this reason, whoever begins long and difficult contemplations at that time is striving to pull those very spirits back to the head. These spirits, being thus distracted, serve neither the stomach nor the head sufficiently. It is especially harmful if, burning the midnight oil after dinner, we apply ourselves too intently to such studies for a long time. For the stomach then requires more spirits and much heat to cook the food. Yet these two things are diverted to the head by such late-night study. The result is that there is enough for neither the brain nor the stomach. Add to this that the head, because of this motion, is filled with the thicker vapors of the food; and the food in the stomach, deprived of heat and spirit, becomes <term>undigested</term> <note>original: "crudescit"; literally "becomes raw," referring to the medical condition of *crudity* or indigestion.</note> and rots, which in turn fills and harms the head. Finally, in the morning hours when one should rise so that every limb may be purged of all the excrements retained during sleep, then (what is worst of all) the person who had utterly interrupted their digestion by studying at night is compelled to further hinder the expulsion of excrements by sleeping in the morning. All physicians judge this to be extremely harmful to both the intellect and the body.

Rightly, therefore, those who use the night for the day against nature, and conversely the day for the night, are like **owls**; they imitate owls even in this, perhaps unwillingly: just as the eyes of owls grow dim under the light of the Sun, so too the "eyes" of their minds grow dim under the splendor of truth.

In the **sixth place**, the same is proved from the nature of the spirits: by the fatigue of the day, all the most subtle spirits are eventually dissolved. At night, therefore, only a few thick spirits remain, which are most unfit for the study of letters. A mind relying on these "maimed" spirits can no more fly than can **bats** or **horned owls**. On the contrary, in the morning after sleep, when the spirits are refreshed and the limbs so strengthened that they need very little support from the spirits, many subtle spirits are present to serve the brain. They can obey more quickly because they are very little occupied with nourishing or governing the limbs.

**Lastly**, the **seventh reason** is deduced from the nature of the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The faculty of the mind that processes images and sensory data.</note>. The phantasy—whether it should be called imagination, thought, or by any other name—is distracted and disturbed by many long and contrary images, thoughts, and cares during waking hours. This distraction and disturbance is entirely contrary to the subsequent contemplation, which requires a tranquil and serene mind. Only by the quiet of the night is that agitation finally settled and pacified. Therefore, we approach our studies with a mind always disturbed as night comes on, but usually with a tranquil mind as it recedes. Whoever tries to judge things while the mind is too agitated acts no differently than those suffering from vertigo, who think everything is spinning (as **Plato** says) when they themselves are spinning.

For this reason, **Aristotle** wisely commands in his *Economics* to rise before light, asserting that this is most beneficial for both the health of the body and the study of philosophy. But this must be understood such that, by a quick and modest dinner, we most diligently avoid "morning crudity" (indigestion). Finally, that sacred prophet **David**, the trumpet of the omnipotent God, never says he rises to sing to his God with the lyre and psalms in the evening, but always in the morning and at daybreak. We ought to rise in mind at that hour, and soon after in body, if only it can be done conveniently.

### Which hour is more suitable for beginning studies, and what the method of continuing them should be. Chapter VIII.

**F**rom those things which have been discussed above, it is now sufficiently clear that we should begin our studies at an opportune time, either exactly at sunrise, or at least one hour—or two at the most—before the Sun rises. But before you get out of bed, rub your whole body for a little while, gently, with your palms; then your head with your nails, but a little more lightly. On this matter, let <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> provide advice. For by friction, he says, if it is vigorous, the body is hardened; if light, it is softened; if much, it is reduced; if moderate, it is filled out. When you have risen from bed, do not apply yourself immediately to reading and meditation, but allow at least half an hour for any necessary <term>expurgation</term> <note>In this context, cleansing the body's wastes (going to the bathroom) and clearing the senses.</note>; soon after, gird yourself diligently for meditation, which you shall extend for about one hour according to your strength. Then you shall relax the focus of your mind for a little while, and in the meantime, diligently and moderately comb your head with an ivory comb, drawing the comb forty times from the forehead toward the neck. Then rub the neck with a rougher cloth; finally, returning to meditation, dedicate two additional hours, or at least one hour, to study. Studies can, however, sometimes be prolonged until the hour of noon, provided some intermittent breaks are made. Furthermore, sometimes—though rarely, unless we are forced to take food in the meantime—they may continue for about two hours after noon. For the Sun is powerful around its rising, and powerful in the middle of the sky. In that region of the sky which closely follows the middle, which astronomers call the <term>Ninth House</term> <note>In Renaissance astrology, the Ninth House is the "House of Wisdom," associated with long journeys, religion, and higher learning.</note> and the House of Wisdom, the Sun rejoices most. Since all the poets hold <term>Phoebus</term> <note>Apollo, the god of the Sun, medicine, and the Muses.</note> to be the leader of the Muses and the sciences, it is rightly so that if something deeper must be thought out, it should be contemplated during these hours. If the Muses are to be sought, let them be sought during these same hours with Phoebus as the guide. For the remaining hours seem better suited for reading the works of the ancients and others, rather than for thinking out new things of one's own. We must always remember, however, that at any hour, the focus of the mind must be relaxed at least once for a short time. For since the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle vapors believed to animate the body and mind.</note> are dissolved because of such focus, you will naturally become sluggish if you never cease to stretch them. While you labor with the mind, let the body rest in the meantime. Weariness of the body is bad, that of the mind is worse, and that of both at once is the worst of all, distracting a person with opposite motions and destroying life. Finally, let meditation proceed no further than there is pleasure in it—indeed, rather stop just short of that.

---

### Precepts for avoiding phlegm. Chapter IX.

**I**t seems worthwhile to briefly repeat those things which we said were harmful to scholars and to apply remedies to each. Therefore, lest <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor that can cause sluggishness and "brain fog."</note> increase too much, exercise should be used twice daily on a nearly empty stomach, yet never so laborious that the sharp spirits are dissolved; excrements must be most diligently purged from all passages. Grime must be thoroughly wiped away from the skin of the whole body, especially the head, both by washing and by rubbing. Avoid foods that are too cold, and—unless <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis" or melancholy.</note> stands in the way—avoid moist foods, and all those that are fatty, virulent, viscous, oily, gluey, or those that are prone to rot easily. If the stomach is cold, either by nature or by age, the drinking of water must be either abandoned entirely or certainly reduced. Food should be moderate, but drink more moderate still. The dwelling should be high up, very far removed from heavy and cloudy air; humidity must be expelled by the use of both fire and warm scents. Cold must be kept away from the head, but especially from the neck and the feet; for it hinders the intellect greatly. A moderate use of spices in colder dishes is beneficial, especially nutmeg, cinnamon, and saffron; also preserved ginger in the morning on an empty stomach, which is also extremely beneficial for the senses and the memory.

---

### By what means black bile should be avoided. Chapter X.

**T**hese things increase that most wretched <term>black bile</term> which we detested in previous sections. Thick and turbid wine, especially black; foods that are hard, dry, salty, bitter, sharp, old, burnt, roasted, or fried; the meat of beef and hare; old cheese; salted meats; legumes—especially beans and lentils; eggplants, <note>original: "melangia."</note> arugula, cabbage, mustard, radish, garlic, onion, leek, mulberries, carrots, <note>original: "cariotę"; likely referring to carrots or possibly dates.</note> and whatever heats or cools while simultaneously drying; and all things black. Anger, fear, pity, grief, idleness, solitude, and whatever offends the sight, smell, and hearing—especially darkness. Furthermore, excessive drying of the body, whether born of long periods of staying awake, or much agitation of the mind, or worry, or frequent sexual intercourse, or the use of [hot] things...

...of very hot and dry things, or by an immoderate discharge and purging, or by laborious exercise, or by hunger, thirst, heat, a very dry wind, or cold. Since, however, **black bile** <note>Also known as melancholy, one of the four humors; in excess, it was believed to cause sadness and intellectual blockages.</note> is always very dry and also cold—though not equally so—this must certainly be resisted with things that are moderately warm, but especially moist. Use boiled foods constantly, which digest easily and produce subtle and very clear blood. 

But in the meantime, so that consideration may be given to the stomach and <term>phlegm</term> <note>The cold, moist humor; Ficino is balancing the need to moisten the dry melancholy without making the stomach too sluggish.</note> as well as the black bile, let the feasts be seasoned with cinnamon, saffron, and sandalwood. Pumpkin and cucumber seeds, and washed pine nuts, are beneficial. Meat from birds and chickens, or suckling four-footed animals, are suitable; especially soft-boiled eggs; and from animal parts, the brain; sweet apples, pears, peaches, melons, Damson plums, and the like; properly cooked gourd; and moist herbs that are not sticky. But cherries, figs, and grapes, I do not praise at all. 

I strongly loathe nausea and over-satiety. Nothing, however, is more powerful against this plague than wine that is light, clear, sweet, and fragrant—the most fit of all for generating translucent <term>spirits</term> <note>In Ficino’s medical theory, "spirits" are a thin vapor in the blood that links the body to the soul.</note>. For as it pleases **Plato** and **Aristotle**, this humor is softened, sweetened, and brightened by this wine, no differently than lupins soaked in water or iron ignited by flames. Truly, as much as its use benefits the spirits and the intellect, its abuse causes just as much harm. 

Furthermore, it is agreed that it is beneficial to infuse gold or silver that has been intensely heated, or to put their leaves in cups or in the broth itself, and to drink from a gold or silver vessel and take food from them. Likewise, it is very useful if the juice of <term>liquorice</term> is often swallowed on an empty stomach, as well as the juice of sweet pomegranate and sweet orange. 

Sweet odors—especially temperate ones—confer no small benefit: if cold reigns, they should lean toward the warm; but if heat dominates, they should press toward the cold. They should therefore be tempered from roses, violets, myrtle, camphor, sandalwood, and rose water, which are cold; and again from cinnamon, citron, orange, cloves, mint, lemon balm, saffron, aloe wood, ambergris, and musk, which are warm. Spring flowers are especially beneficial, as are the leaves of citron or orange, and fragrant apples, and especially wine. Odors of this kind, as they suit each person, should be inhaled through the nostrils and applied to the chest and stomach. However, we do not approve of odors that are very hot and dry, if they are used alone and continuously. 

A <term>hyacinth</term> <note>original: "hyacinthus"; here referring to the gemstone (zircon or sapphire), which was historically believed to have medicinal properties when held in the mouth to cheer the heart.</note> should be held in the mouth, for it greatly cheers the mind. **Hierobatana**, that is, wild clary, is also beneficial both in food and scent. Again, bugloss, borage, lemon balm, and the water of these three; also lettuce, endive, raisins, and almond milk should be very familiar at the table. 

Air must be avoided if it is wild, or too icy, or cloudy; but temperate and clear air should be admitted most freely. **Mercury**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato** command that a discordant or grieving mind be composed and uplifted by the lyre and song—as constant as it is harmonious. Moreover, **David**, the sacred poet, used to free Saul from madness with the psaltery and psalms. I myself also (if one may compare the lowest things to the highest) frequently experience at home how much the sweetness of the lyre and song can prevail against the bitterness of black bile. 

We praise the frequent sight of clear water, of green or red color, the use of gardens and groves; we strongly approve of strolling beside rivers and through pleasant meadows, as well as riding, being carried, and gentle sailing; and above all, variety—easy occupations and various non-burdensome business, and the constant company of gracious people.

### On the treatment of the stomach. Chapter X.

**I**t follows that we should take care of the stomach as diligently as possible, lest over-satiety bring on nausea or indigestion and offend the head. Food should be taken twice daily, moderate and light, seasoned moderately with cinnamon, mace, and nutmeg. Yet dry food should always exceed softened nourishment in weight and movement, unless perhaps we greatly fear the dryness of the black bile. Let food wait for hunger (if it can be done conveniently) and drink for thirst. Let a desire for both remain at the end of the meal. Let loathing and over-fullness be far away. 

One must abstain from those things which, because of excessive moisture or a virulent, oily, and viscous substance, weaken the stomach by relaxing it, or are even cold or very hot, or are digested with difficulty because of hardness. And such things as these, which for a long time after the meal return a rather troublesome taste to the palate, or cause bloating, or fill the head with many vapors; especially from all things that easily rot either outside or inside the belly. 

Sweet tastes or sharp ones, if they are alone, we approve of in no way; but we want sweet things to be tempered by something sour, or sharp, or dry. **Mastic** and dry mint, fresh sage, raisins, cooked quinces preserved in sugar, chicory, rose, coral, washed capers preserved in vinegar, are very friendly to the stomach. Furthermore, pomegranates...

...pomegranate with a flavor between sour and sweet, and generally whatever is moderately acidic and somewhat harsh, which doctors call <term>styptic</term> <note>Astringent substances that contract tissues; thought to "bind" the stomach and help digestion.</note>, or those that are somewhat sharp, salty, or aromatic. **Myrobalans** <note>A type of dried plum-like fruit from India, highly prized in the Renaissance for balancing the humors.</note>, however, surpass all others. Red wine is also better than white, with a slightly bitter taste; unless heat or a "distillation" <note>A discharge of fluid or a cold.</note> demands otherwise, it is best to drink it undiluted in small amounts. Generally, liquid dishes should be taken before harder ones. After a meal, coriander, quince preserved in sugar, pomegranates, harsh pears, medlars, dried peaches, and similar things are suitable. One must chew each item thoroughly before swallowing. If the stomach needs external comfort, use mastic, rose, mint, and coral. 

Care must be taken not to apply ourselves to difficult thinking or diligent reading for the next two or three hours after a meal. Perhaps four hours of leisure will be necessary if the food or drink was more abundant, or the food harder to digest. It is bad to distend the belly with food or drink; it is worst to think about difficult things while the stomach is so distended. One should not sleep after a midday meal unless absolute necessity compels it, and then not before staying awake for two hours. At night, however, after dinner, staying awake for one hour (it seems) is enough. Sexual intercourse is harmful to the stomach, especially if you lie together immediately while full or while hungry. The stomach mourns in idleness and rejoices in exercise, except when it is full of food. Immediately after taking food, one should walk moderately, but then sit down.

### *On those things which nourish the principal members and the spirits. Chapter XII.*

**B**ut now, to make it worthwhile, let us bring forth from the physician's workshop several things that either keep the strength of the stomach, heart, brain, <term>spirits</term> <note>The subtle vapors that Ficino believed connected the soul to the body.</note>, and intellect intact or restore them; and if <term>phlegm</term> or **black bile** <note>The cold, dry humor associated with melancholy and intellectual burnout.</note> increases, or nausea threatens, they drive it far away. All doctors have agreed without controversy that nothing is more healthful than <term>theriaca</term> <note>A complex ancient "universal" medicine and antidote containing dozens of ingredients.</note> for nourishing and strengthening both individual members and powers, as well as the spirits and the intellect. 

We will use this primarily at half a drachm, or at least a third of a drachm, twice a week in winter and autumn, but once in summer and spring, either alone or, if you like, in cold and damp weather with a little clear, sweet wine; but in hot and dry times, especially if your nature or age is hotter, with two or three ounces of rose water, specifically on an empty stomach six or seven hours before a meal. If **theriaca** is missing, we will give <term>mithridatum</term> <note>A similar complex medicine, named after King Mithridates, used as a tonic and antidote.</note>. 

But when we take **theriaca** or **mithridatum**, we must completely abstain from everything hot on that day, and if it is summer or spring, use cold things. In second place for the same cause, all approve of **aloes** properly selected and washed: Take two drachms of Chebulic **myrobalans**, and one drachm each of purple roses, red sandalwood, emblic myrobalans, cinnamon, saffron bark, citron fruit, behen <note>A medicinal root.</note>, and lemon balm (that is, *citraria*); and twelve drachms of properly washed, select aloes. From these, make pills with excellent undiluted wine, which you should use once every week at dawn, in a weight that suits your nature—with rose water in summer, but with wine at other times. 

On days when you take neither the theriaca nor the pills, use a confection of this kind morning and evening, two or three hours before food: Take four drachms of the finest cinnamon, two of Chebulic **myrobalans**, and as many of emblic ones, half a drachm of saffron and roses, two drachms of red sandalwood, one drachm of similar corals, and as much of the whitest sugar as is sufficient. Dissolve the sugar in rose water and the juice of citrons or lemons in equal portions; cook gently. Then add a third of a drachm of musk and as much ambergris. Finally, make solid morsels—which they commonly call <term>morsulos</term> <note>original: "morsulos", meaning "little bites" or lozenges.</note>—and wrap them in gold leaf. 

We ourselves have experienced these three things in the use we prescribed: the **theriaca**, the aloes tempered as we described, and that confection; we found them to benefit every member, the powers and spirits, to sharpen the senses and intellect, and to confirm the memory. Also, <term>phlegm</term>, bile, and **black bile** are easily led out or corrected by those pills. Furthermore, the three things we mentioned are judged very familiar to every age and nature.

### Remedies for Catarrh and Distillation, the Common Plague of Studies.

When the head is tossed about by "distillations" <note>The "dripping" of fluids from the brain, similar to a head cold or sinus drip.</note> due to phlegm, we will sometimes give some of the pills we have just described at the hour of sleep. Furthermore, we shall command the patient to frequently chew frankincense at that hour and at others, for it wonderfully assists the distillations, all the senses, and the memory. Again, nutmeg and <term>theriac</term> <note>An ancient multi-ingredient "universal" medicine, often used as an antidote or general tonic.</note> held in the mouth are approved. Marjoram also, which they call *amaracus*, or its water, may be applied to the nostrils or infused. After a meal, however, we shall restrain the vapors of the food with coriander and quinces.

### On Headache. Chapter XV.

If the head frequently aches, weighed down by a cold humor, in addition to those things we have related, we shall command the patient to hold in the mouth that confection which they call *diambra* <note>A costly aromatic powder containing ambergris.</note>, or *diacorī*, or *plirisarcoticon* <note>Complex medieval medicinal pastes used for strengthening the body.</note>. Moreover, they should frequently chew mastic. Furthermore, smear the forehead, temples, and neck with the leaves of marjoram, fennel, and rue, thoroughly diluted together with rose oil and rose water.

### A Remedy for Dimming Vision. Chapter XVI.

When the eyes grow dim but do not redden, nor show any other sign of heat, then surely an eyewash made from the water of fennel, marjoram, celandine, and rue—with saffron and antimony added—is beneficial. But such water must first be squeezed through a thick cloth. However, you should apply nothing to the eyes unless you have first frequently purged with "Pills of Light" <note>original: *pilulis Lucis*, a specific medicinal formula believed to clear the eyesight.</note>. But if the dimming eyes are red, purge them immediately with pills composed of fumitory. Presently, an eyewash made of rose water and sugar is useful. Sometimes, indeed, help is most readily found by adding egg white, tutty <note>A form of zinc oxide used for eye ailments.</note>, and milk. Generally, however, the daily use of fennel preserves and sharpens the sight. Indeed, one ought to frequently keep its seeds in the mouth and eat its leaves. The *Triphera minor* described by Mesue is excellent. It is best to take a candied Chebulic myrobalan <note>A dried fruit from India used as a tonic and digestive.</note> daily on an empty stomach, and with it some bread made of sugar and powdered fennel; this, moreover, is wonderfully beneficial to the intellect and for prolonging life. The use of eyebright is also a singular protection for the eyes. In every case of either headache or dimness of the eyes, vapors must be diverted backwards by means of friction and cupping. And if heat is the cause and blood is abundant, we shall apply leeches <note>original: *hirundines*. While this literally means "swallows," it was a common orthographic variant for *hirudines* (leeches) in medical contexts involving bloodletting from the neck.</note> to the neck and shoulders.

### On Restoring the Sense of Taste. Chapter XVII.

The stomach of those devoted to literature often loses almost all sense of taste. If this happens through a fault of phlegm—which a sour taste in the mouth or much sticky saliva indicates—after you have moved the bowels with the medicines we described above, use aromatic rose-sugar; specifically, rose-sugar mixed with rose-honey and cinnamon, or even ginger alone, or mint syrup, but primarily theriac. If, however, it happens perhaps due to an abundance of bile—which a bitter mouth usually demonstrates—likewise after a purging of prepared aloes as we have said, or rhubarb, take either *triafandalum* <note>A compound of three types of sandalwood.</note> or *oxysaccharum*—composed of sugar, white vinegar, and the juice of sharp pomegranate—or peaches or pears, whether preserved or made into a syrup as Mesue teaches, or our own confection of this sort, which is most healthy for the taste: Take four ounces of rose-sugar, two ounces of cherry preserve, the same amount (two ounces) of quince jelly, half an ounce of Chebulic myrobalans, the same amount of emblic myrobalans, and half a drachm each of red sandalwood and red coral. Pour over this three or two ounces of syrup made from citron or lemon juice. But if the stomach is weak and cold, add two drachms of cinnamon. These should be used two hours before food. Quince jelly and the use of capers with vinegar always remove nausea arising from either humor.

...with vinegar; likewise, a moderate drink on an empty stomach of white rose vinegar, if it is mixed with double the weight of sugar. Again, syrup of mint and of wormwood. Likewise, mint either preserved in vinegar or diluted and sprinkled with the tart juice of a pomegranate.

### Most Exquisite Remedies for Black Bile. Chapter XVIII.

**B**ut let us now set aside these matters as being somewhat lighter, and let us return to that which is most dangerous: to black bile <term>atra bilis</term> <note>Also known as melancholy, this humor was believed to be cold and dry. When it became "burnt" or excessive, it was thought to cause depression, anxiety, and even madness.</note>, namely, which as often as it abounds and rages, weakens both the entire body and, most especially, the spirit <note>The "spirit" (spiritus) was a subtle vapor in the blood that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note>—which is the instrument, so to speak, of the intellect—and the intellect and judgment themselves. The first precept in curing it, as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated medical thought until the 17th century.</note> taught, is that we should not strive to draw it out suddenly, lest by chance, when its more liquid and subtle part is withdrawn, the much denser and drier residue remains; rather, it should be softened little by little, digested in equal measure, and then drawn out. Second, that in the meantime, the head and the whole body should be moistened to the utmost of one's strength, partly with more humid foods, partly with sweet and moderate baths and similar ointments. This must be done with caution, however, so that neither "distillation" <note>Catarrh or sinus drainage.</note> is provoked, nor the stomach or liver destroyed, nor the passages of the body obstructed. Third, and indeed this is most necessary, that the heart be continually cherished and strengthened with suitable things, partly taken internally and partly applied externally to the chest or the nostrils. Furthermore, let those things be seen, heard, smelled, and thought of which bring delight, while contrary things should be kept far away.

### Syrups That Will Be of the Greatest Benefit to Melancholics. Chapter XIX.

**M**any people have composed mixtures against this humor. For the present, however, I shall bring forward three choice and safest kinds of remedies from among many: first received from the ancients, then confirmed by more recent authors, and sometimes adapted by us for our own use. In the first kind is the composition of an excellent syrup. In the second, most proven pills. In the third, most healthful <term>electuaries</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note>. When these three are applied opportunely, the melancholic humor is softened, digested, and dissolved; the spirits are sharpened and brightened, the intellect is cherished, and the memory is strengthened. The syrup is of this kind:

Take of borage, bugloss <note>Plants traditionally used to "gladden the heart" and purge melancholy.</note>, and the flowers of both, lemon balm, maidenhair fern, endive, violets, dodder, polypody <note>A type of fern used as a mild purgative.</note>, senna, and dodder of thyme <note>original: *epithymum*</note>—a handful of each; twenty damson plums, ten fragrant apples, one ounce of raisins, half an ounce of licorice, three drachms <note>A drachm is roughly 1/8th of an ounce.</note> each of cinnamon, red sandalwood, and citron peel, and half a drachm of saffron. Let all be cooked in water, except for the dodder of thyme and the aromatics, until a third part is consumed. Afterward, let the strained decoction be cooked again moderately with sugar and the dodder of thyme. Finally, let the aromatics be infused, namely the cinnamon and the saffron. Let three ounces of this syrup be drunk, warmed, at dawn, together with two or three ounces of bugloss water; and together with these, at least two or more of the following pills ought to be taken, according as it suits each person—namely, in such a way that the bowels are moved a little every day.

### Pills for Softening and Purging Corrupt Humors. Chapter XX.

**A**s far as the present purpose is concerned, there are two kinds of pills: some suit the delicate, others the more robust. The first may be called "Golden" or "Magical," partly in imitation of the Magi <note>Likely referring to Persian or Eastern physicians/sages.</note> and partly by our own invention, composed under the very flow of Jupiter and Venus <note>Ficino was a priest and astrologer; he believed medicines were more effective if prepared when the planets Jupiter and Venus—the "benefics"—were in a favorable alignment.</note>. These pills draw out phlegm, bile, and black bile without distress; they strengthen the individual members and sharpen and illuminate the spirits. They dilate the spirits so that, when constricted, they do not produce sadness, but rather rejoice in dilation and light. Again, they stabilize them so that they do not vanish through excessive extension. 

Take, therefore, twelve grains of gold—especially the leaves of it, if they are pure—and half a drachm each of frankincense, myrrh, saffron, aloeswood, cinnamon, citron peel, lemon balm, raw crimson silk <note>Silk was often used in heart tonics in the belief it helped generate pure blood.</note>, mint, white behen, and red behen <note>Behen (or Been) roots were highly valued as tonics for the heart and spirit.</note>; one drachm each of purple roses, red sandalwood, red coral, and the three myrobalans <note>Astringent plum-like fruits from India: Emblic (Amla), Chebulic, and Indian (Black) myrobalans.</note> (namely the emblic, chebulic, and Indian); and as much properly washed aloes as the weight of all the rest combined. Fashion the pills with the choicest unmixed wine. 

There follow pills for dissolving melancholy that are somewhat stronger, yet not at all violent: Take of peony, myrrh, Arabian stoechas <note>A type of lavender.</note>, lemon balm, frankincense, saffron, the three myrobalans (namely the emblic, chebulic, and Indian), and roses...

...one drachma of each; three drachmas each of troches of agaric, polypody, epithyme, senna, and properly washed and prepared lapis lazuli and Armenian stone; two ounces of washed aloes; and form these into pills with a fine wine. If a manifest heat dominates alongside the melancholy, the cold ingredients in this composition should be increased by an additional third of their weight. 

I have composed these pills for students of literature by imitating the Greeks, Latins, and Arabs. However, I did not wish to mix in stronger substances, such as hellebore <note>original: "veratrum," a powerful and potentially toxic purgative used in antiquity for madness.</note>, which the fanatical Carneades <note>Carneades (c. 214–129 BC) was a Greek skeptic philosopher; legend says he purged himself with hellebore to sharpen his mind before writing.</note> used. For I advise only literary men, or those slightly more robust, for whom nothing is more destructive than violent treatment. Therefore, I have omitted the "Indian pills," the well-known pills of lapis lazuli or Armenian stone, and the composition they call *hieraglogidion* <note>A complex purgative electuary containing bitter herbs and often scammony.</note>. 

Finally, if it is appropriate to provide a simpler composition, such as I use for my own household: Take one ounce of washed aloes; two drachmas each of myrobalans <note>An astringent fruit used in Ayurvedic and medieval medicine to purge humors.</note>, both emblic and chebulic; two drachmas of mastic; and two of roses, especially the purple ones; and make pills with wine. Furthermore, no one should ever use these pills—either the former or the latter among those we have approved—on their own, lest they by chance become excessively dry. Such dryness is indeed the worst thing in melancholy. Instead, take them together with the syrup we described above—following partly Mesuë <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician.</note> and partly Gentile da Foligno <note>A famous 14th-century Italian doctor who died during the Black Death.</note>—or with one, two, or three ounces of light, fragrant wine, as suits each person. Or use them with honey-water, raisins, and licorice. Or, if heat dominates anywhere, with violet julep and rose water. 

I entirely advise all scholars who are prone to black bile <term>atra bilis</term> to use this purgation twice every year—namely in spring and autumn—for fifteen or twenty consecutive days; specifically, taking the pills with the syrup and similar liquids. Those who are somewhat less subject to this ailment will find it sufficient to take the first or last pills throughout the year, once every week: in summer with the julep, as we said, and at other times with wine.

### The Use of Certain Other Medicines for Healing. Chapter XXI.

**I**t is necessary to remember that when a very great danger of drying out is imminent, yet necessity compels a purging, it is worthwhile to pause the pills. Instead, when it is time to purge, one should sometimes infuse an ounce (or at least half an ounce) of *diasenna*, *diacatholicon*, or Persian *triphera* <note>These are all names of compound electuaries or soft pastes used as gentle laxatives.</note> into the syrup itself, or a similar decoction made in bugloss water. 

But if the body is more robust, or the bowels more restricted and hard, add one or two drachmas of the electuary *hamech*. Cassia is also useful here, and manna is even more useful. These do not suit every type of melancholy, but especially that which is created by adustion <note>The "burning" of humors due to excess heat, making them toxic.</note>. If, however, the melancholy is natural <note>Ficino distinguishes between "natural" melancholy (a temperament) and "adust" melancholy (a pathological state caused by heat).</note>, they are indeed suitable, but especially if a double or triple portion of polypody is added to the syrup, along with saffron-colored licorice and raisins. Likewise, let two ounces of liquid honey of roses be added to the medicine. 

We have stated in the preceding sections how often the syrup should be taken. But the medicine should be taken with it for sixty days. However, if no humor <note>The physical fluid of black bile.</note> appears in the melancholics, but only a melancholic complexion—that is, a cold and dry quality of the limbs—remember that it is not at all expedient to move the bowels or let blood. Rather, do only those remaining things which we have said (or will say), especially whatever pertains to moderately warming the body, greatly moistening it, illuminating the spirits as much as possible, and soothing the limbs. 

But where the humor of black bile itself overflows, we do not only moisten the body and the humor, but we also loosen the bowels with the caution we mentioned—and now even more vigorously. Indeed, Plato warns us in the *Timaeus* <note>referring to Plato's dialogue on the nature of the physical world and human biology.</note> that a long-term disease, such as melancholy, should not be provoked with weak and annoying drugs or troublesome medicines.

### The Rules for Bloodletting. Chapter XXII.

**T**here are some who are rather bold in bloodletting, whom wise physicians greatly detest. For blood is the balancer of black bile, the fuel of the spirit, and the treasure of life. Only when an abundance of blood is indicated—either by excessive laughter, great boldness and confidence, a red color, or swelling of the veins—should we let blood for literary men. When the situation demands it, we should take it from the veins of the left arm with a wide incision: four ounces in the morning and as many in the evening. Then, after a few days—at least seven—at the highest...

He also introduces the cautious use of bloodletting, viewing blood as the essential "treasure of life" that should only be drawn under specific symptoms of excess.</summary>

...at most fourteen [leeches], to irritate the hemorrhoids <note>original: "mariscas," literally "fig-like" growths, used here to refer to hemorrhoidal veins.</note>, either by a somewhat rougher friction or by applying the "swallows" which they call bloodsuckers <note>original: "sanguisugas," or leeches. Ficino uses the term "swallow" (hirudo) as a classical synonym.</note>, so that three or four ounces of blood may trickle out from there. Both of these treatments seem suitable only for the more robust patients. For the weaker ones, if necessity demands it, one should only irritate the hemorrhoidal veins as we have taught. However, it is not permitted to loosen the belly with medicines, nor to draw blood, unless you have first softened and smoothed the path with fatty and mild enemas <note>original: "clysteribus."</note>. And let this be a common rule for the melancholic nature: care must be taken so that, if necessary, the lower belly is always lubricated and purged through the frequent use of such enemas.

### On Electuaries and Confections. Chapter 24.

**E**lectuaries <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey, syrup, or sugar.</note> follow next, among which I certainly praise the one that Rhazes <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925) was a Persian physician and one of the most influential figures in medieval medicine.</note> called "the exhilarating one." There are also those that Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the famous Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> composed in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*, but I much prefer the one Mesues <note>Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Assyrian physician; many recipes in the Middle Ages were attributed to him.</note> describes as follows: Take one pound of raw silk recently dyed a scarlet color <note>original: "coccineo," dyed with kermes, which was thought to have heart-strengthening properties.</note>; submerge it in the juice of sweet and sweet-smelling apples, along with bugloss juice <note>A plant used to treat "black bile" or melancholy.</note> and rose water, one pound of each. After twenty-four hours, cook all of this gently until the water turns red. Then remove the silk and squeeze it out thoroughly. Soon after, pour in one hundred and fifty drachmas of the whitest sugar and cook it again until it thickens like honey. Then remove it from the fire and, while it is hot, pour in six drachmas of raw amber <note>Ambergris, a rare substance from the sea used as a perfume and medicine.</note>, finely chopped, and allow the amber to melt. Finally, add this powder: take six drachmas each of raw wood of aloes and cinnamon; thirteen drachmas of properly washed lapis lazuli <note>A blue gemstone believed to purge the body of melancholy.</note>; two drachmas of "unions," which are white pearls; one drachma of true gold; and half a drachma of choice musk. One or two drachmas of this are given with wine, morning and evening, three or four hours before a meal. This recipe pleases me above all others. Nevertheless, I also approve of Mesues’ "sweet musk" compound and his "composition of gems," provided they are taken with rose water. I would also wonderfully praise the one devised by the great philosopher Pietro d’Abano <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1315), an Italian physician and astrologer.</note>, except that he himself feared that its excessive use might cause too much dilation and exhilaration of the spirits <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to the subtle vapors that carry life and thought through the body.</note>. 

For this reason, I have additionally devised two very safe ones, most suitable for any time, age, or nature because of their balanced temperament, in which "the useful is mixed with the sweet." These nourish as much as they warm and strengthen. Furthermore, they are as suited for stabilizing the spirit and the intellect as they are for sharpening and illuminating them: Take two ounces of sugar cooked with bugloss flowers, one ounce of candied citron peel, two ounces of candied chebulic myrobalan <note>A dried fruit used as a digestive and tonic.</note>, one drachma of choice cinnamon; half a drachma each of sandalwood and red coral, as well as raw and chopped scarlet silk, saffron, and pearls; a third of a drachma each of gold and silver; and two grains each of amber and musk. Melt them all together with citron or lemon juice cooked with sugar. 

Another confection follows, somewhat more healthful and certainly much sweeter: Take four ounces of sweet almonds; two ounces each of pine nuts (washed for the duration of a day) and cucumber seeds; four ounces of the hard sugar they call "Candy" (that is, white candy); and one and a half pounds of another very white sugar. Melt all these in rose, lemon, and citron water in which glowing gold and silver have been quenched, and cook them together gently. Finally, add one drachma each of cinnamon, red behen <note>A root used in traditional medicine to strengthen the heart.</note>, red sandalwood, and similar coral; half a drachma each of the brightest pearls, saffron, and raw scarlet silk ground very fine; twelve grains each of gold and silver; and a third of a drachma each of hyacinth <note>A gemstone, likely zircon or garnet.</note>, emerald, sapphire, and carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, such as a ruby or garnet.</note>. 

If anyone lacks gold, silver, amber, musk, or precious stones, these confections will still be very beneficial without them. Of these, I chiefly choose three: the one by Mesues which I recounted, and my two which I just described. We have already sufficiently explained above how they should be used. But if someone desires something simpler and suited to everyone, let him thoroughly crush a perfectly ripe, whole citron fruit and cook it with plenty of sugar and rose juice. Once cooked, season it with a little cinnamon and saffron, or with a "rose-scented aromatic" <note>A standard pharmaceutical preparation of the time.</note>, and use it tempered thus: Take one ounce of the rose aromatic, and two ounces each of rose sugar and "diabugloss" sugar <note>Sugar infused with bugloss flowers.</note>, or mix in a musk compound in a similar way. For although these two are not simple, they are nevertheless easily obtained.

### Remedies for Emaciating Insomnia. Chapter 24.

**I**t often happens to melancholic people, especially the learned, that they are wasted away by long periods of wakefulness due to the brain becoming excessively dried out. Because nothing increases the evils of black bile more than long bouts of insomnia, this great evil must be countered with every effort. Therefore, let them eat lettuce after other foods along with a little bread and a tiny bit of saffron; let them sip pure wine after the lettuce, and let them not work by lamplight <note>original: "lucubrent," referring to late-night study by candlelight.</note> for more than an hour. When they go to sleep, let them take a confection of this kind: two ounces of white poppy seed, one ounce of lettuce seed, half a drachm <note>A drachm is an ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> each of amomum <note>original: "amomi," an aromatic spice related to cardamom.</note> and saffron, and six ounces of sugar. Dissolve and cook all of these together in poppy syrup. Let them eat two drachms of this, and at the same time taste a little poppy syrup or wine. You should smear their forehead and temples with oil of violets and water-lily <note>original: "nenufare."</note> with added camphor. Likewise, use milk, almond oil, and violet oil. You shall bring the scent of saffron, camphor, and the rinds of sweet fruit <note>likely oranges or citrons.</note> to their nostrils. Use a little vinegar as well, but plenty of rose water. For the elderly, use the leaves of cooling plants. You shall soothe the ears with sweet songs and sounds. You will often moisten the head with washes of this kind: namely water in which have been cooked poppy fruits, lettuce, purslane, mallow, roses, vine leaves, willow leaves, and reed leaves, with chamomile added. Also, the shins, arms, and often the whole body should be moistened with sweet baths made from similar things. Furthermore, drinking milk mixed with sugar on an empty stomach is most beneficial, provided the stomach can tolerate it well. These moistening things are wonderfully helpful for the melancholic, even if they sleep enough. Remember that almond milk should be a very familiar sight at the table.

### Remedies for Dull Memory and Forgetfulness. Chapter 25.

**I**t happens sometimes that for scholars—either because they read or write with their heads diligently bowed, or because they grow sluggish from too much idleness—a certain viscous phlegm <note>original: "pituita."</note>, occupying the head along with excessively cold melancholy, makes it heavy and renders them dull and forgetful. Therefore, the head must be unburdened for these people with those remedies which we have elsewhere said are suitable for phlegm. If those are not sufficient, flee to the "Indian pills," the "cocchiae" pills, and "hieralogodion" <note>These are specific compound medicines from the medieval pharmacopeia used for purging the head.</note>. Furthermore, turn to the "holy" remedy <note>original: "iaram," likely a corruption of "hiera," a class of sacred bitter medicines.</note> of colocynth, or those of Archigenes, Andromachus, or Theodotion, or to the "Jewish pills" which Mesue <note>A famous Persian physician often cited by Ficino.</note> describes in the chapter on headaches. But if the nature or age of the patient is colder, and it is not summer, use that "Anacardina" confection after purging, which Mesue calls the "Confection of the Wise" in his book of remedies. Again, use that "Anacardina" which he records in the chapter on forgetfulness according to the opinion of the son of Zacharias. Give one drachm early in the morning, but let whoever takes it abstain entirely that day from anger, sexual intercourse, drunkenness, labor, and hot things. These things are indeed most powerful against dullness and forgetfulness. But if the patient prefers more familiar things, give candied ginger mixed with a little frankincense, which greatly benefits the senses and memory, especially with these things added: namely, honey of the marking nut <note>original: "melle anacardi."</note>, honey of chebulic myrobalans, sweet flag, nut grass, ambergris, and musk. Also useful are "diambra," "pliris sarcoticon," and "diacoron" <note>Various aromatic electuaries.</note>; but these should be held in the mouth for a long time, and even infused into the nostrils and ears. The scent of frankincense, marjoram, fennel, nutmeg, rue, and cloves also helps not a little. Remember, however, that theriac <note>original: "theriacam," a famous ancient universal antidote and tonic.</note> must never be placed second to any remedy in these and similar cases, as we said from the beginning. Furthermore, for the dull and forgetful, rub the temples and the back of the neck with an ointment of this kind: take one ounce of elderberry oil, two ounces of oil of ben <note>original: "olei de been," derived from the Moringa tree.</note>, half an ounce of euphorbium, and the same amount of castoreum <note>A yellowish secretion from the scent glands of beavers.</note>; you shall rub the arms, legs, and neck vigorously. And if necessary, you shall apply cupping glasses <note>original: "cucurbitulas."</note> to the neck. Moreover, you shall cover and warm the crown of the head with crushed marjoram, frankincense, and nutmeg.

### We Must Be Intent on the Guarding of the Spirits. Chapter 26.

**I**f men who are hungry for truth must care for the corporeal spirit <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "spirit" is a thin, vaporous substance that links the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> with such great medical diligence—lest perhaps, if entirely neglected, it becomes an obstacle or serves poorly those seeking the truth—then it is fitting to cultivate the incorporeal spirit, that is, the intellect itself, much more diligently with the instructions of moral discipline. For truth itself, being incorporeal, is captured by the intellect alone. For it is not right to cultivate only the servant of the soul (the body) while leaving the soul (the lord and king of the body)...

He emphasizes the use of cooling plants like poppies and memory-enhancers like the marking nut, concluding that physical health is the foundation for intellectual and moral growth.</summary>

<page-num>509</page-num>
<header>ON PRESERVING HEALTH. BOOK I.</header>

...and to neglect the king <note>Referring to the soul as the ruler of the body.</note>, especially since it is the opinion of the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and philosophers often cited by Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> and of Plato that the whole body depends so much upon the soul that unless the soul is well, the body cannot be well. For this reason Apollo, the author of medicine, judged Socrates to be the wisest of men, rather than Hippocrates, even though Hippocrates was born of Apollo's own lineage. This is because Hippocrates studied the healing of the body as much as Socrates studied the healing of the soul—though what they both had attempted, only Christ truly achieved. 

Accordingly, we are commanded by Socrates to cultivate our minds with the best morals, so that we may more easily attain the light and truth sought by our natural instinct with a serene mind. How much more is it right to worship divine truth itself, primarily through holy religion? For the created mind was made for seeking and grasping this truth, just as the eye was made for perceiving the light of the Sun. And, as our Plato says, just as the sight perceives nothing visible anywhere except in the splendor of the supreme visible thing—that is, the Sun itself—so too the human intellect grasps nothing intelligible except in the light of the supreme intelligible thing, which is God, who is always and everywhere present to us. In that light, I say, which *enlightens every man coming into this world* <note>original: "illuminat omnem hominem uenientem in hunc mundum," a reference to the Gospel of John 1:9.</note>. In the light of which David sings: *In thy light shall we see light* <note>original: "In lumine tuo uidebimus lumen," from Psalm 36:9.</note>. 

Truly, just as his splendor is suddenly poured into cleansed eyes looking toward the light itself, shining abundantly with the colors and shapes of things, so when the mind is first cleansed of all bodily disturbances through moral discipline, and directed toward divine truth—that is, God himself—by a certain religious and burning love, suddenly (as the divine Plato says) divine truth flows into the mind. It happily unfolds the true reasons which are contained within it, or by which all things consist; and by as much light as it surrounds the mind, it simultaneously pours a blessed joy into the will.

->END OF BOOK I.<-

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence on the
## Second Book, On Prolonging Life, an Epistolary
## Preface to Filippo Valori.

### P R E F A C E

**A**lthough our Plato lives by his own <term>Genius</term> <note>In this context, "Genius" refers to a protective spirit or the innate divine nature of a person, rather than just high intelligence.</note>, and shall live, as I believe, as long as the world itself lives, my own Genius nevertheless always impels me toward this: that after divine worship, I should look after the life of Plato before all things. For a long time now, the <term>Medical House</term> <note>original: "Medica domus." A clever pun on the name of his patrons, the Medici family, and the Latin word for "medical" or "healing."</note> has aspired toward this very thing more than any other. You too, my dear Valori, conspire toward the same end; you are the dearest friend of doctors and a devoted student of Platonic glory and discipline. Therefore, the same life that I always desire for Plato, I also wish for Doctors, and the like for Valori. 

For this reason, I urge and beseech you, my Valori, that with as much effort as you always favor Platonic glory, you should at some point read and observe these precepts of ours on prolonging life with equal diligence. By living long through these, you may be able to patronize the recently reborn discipline of Plato for a longer time, together with the great-hearted Lorenzo de' Medici. Farewell.

<summary>Ficino concludes his first book by arguing that physical health is impossible without spiritual health and moral discipline, using the Platonic analogy of God as the sun. He then introduces Book II with a dedication to Filippo Valori, framing the preservation of life as a way to protect the "reborn" Platonic philosophy under the Medici patronage.</summary>

ON PROLONGING LIFE. BOOK II.
515

Even though the entire discussion of the previous book contributes greatly to the prolongation of life, such a great matter seems to require its own specific care, which I will summarize as briefly as possible in what follows.

#### *How heat and moisture are to be tempered, by a certain counsel of Minerva.*
### Chapter III.

**M**oreover, while we handle this rich oil—so necessary for our fiery vigor—with a "fat Minerva" <note>original: "pingui Minerva," a Latin idiom for plain common sense or unrefined wisdom, here punning on Minerva’s association with the olive tree and its oil.</note>, Minerva the olive-bearer herself, the source of vital oil born from the head of nourishing Jove, laughs at us. For while we clearly see the quantity of her gift, we have not yet sufficiently seen its quality. Laughing, then, she says: "I have given you oil in abundance, not only enough to nourish the flame, but I have also poured into your lamp an oil pure and free of dregs." So she spoke. But we, wandering as we spoke, stumbled because the lamp was "a word unto our feet" <note>An allusion to Psalm 119:105; Ficino often blends Neoplatonism, classical mythology, and Christian scripture.</note>, yet not yet heard by us. From this lamp, therefore, let us learn that oil must be continually supplied to the flame, with such diligence that we neither overwhelm the light with a sudden flood, nor again delay giving drink to the thirsty lamp. 

But these two matters we think have been sufficiently discussed above. Two others remain for us, one of which we seem to have touched upon lightly, and the other hardly at all. Meanwhile, touching Pallas <note>Another name for Minerva.</note> in such a way that she, who is never accustomed to laugh, laughed at us. What then? First, we shall consider that the flame, even a small one, is entirely devouring; therefore, that lamp shines longer in which the flame is so tempered to the wick—that is, the match—that it does not gulp down the oil, but sips it. And so, in our entire diet we will take care lest at any time, especially in youth, the innate fire—by its very nature voracious—becomes too strong. It will be enough to ward off both flooding moisture and piercing cold. 

Next, we will consider that the lamp is frequently extinguished when the oil poured in is not pure, but (as I might say) full of dregs <note>original: "amurcosum," referring to *amurca*, the bitter, watery sediment found in unfiltered olive oil.</note>. From these dregs, shortly after, "fungi" <note>The carbonized, mushroom-like growths that form on a lamp's wick and dim the light.</note> grow thick and extinguish the light. Now, we have received this oil from Pallas as a foster-child—namely one that is very airy, pure, and tenacious and firm with a certain natural viscosity. Therefore, what is supplied to replace what is gradually consumed must not only be equal to it, but similar. That it may be similar, it must not only be airy and rich, but thoroughly separated from dregs—that is, from a certain refuse gathered from thicker earth and water. To avoid this gathering and refuse, let us flee such foods, as well as idleness, indigestion, and filth. Meanwhile, let us cultivate Minerva with such moderation that she may increase the "head" from which she herself was born <note>Minerva was born from the head of Zeus; Ficino uses this to represent the intellect.</note>, but not diminish the nerves and the stomach.

#### *Causes of the drying up of natural moisture and the overflowing of foreign moisture. And how necessary perfect digestion is for life. Chapter IV.*

**N**atural moisture is quickly dried out by these things: a profuse flow of blood, violent loosening of the bowels, long-term diarrhea, excessive sweating, widely opened pores, sexual intercourse to the point of weakness, panting thirst, agonizing hunger, long vigils, use of very hot as well as dry things, laborious movement of mind and body, anxiety, anger, pain, a drier and hotter air—especially when heated by fire—and a wind that is dry, violent, and constant. 

The opposites of these things increase moisture beyond measure. Frequent drunkenness does both: for it dries out the drunkard with too much heat, and then suffocates him with moisture. Nothing, however, is more harmful to both than indigestion <term>original: "cruditas," literally rawness; the state of food that has not been "cooked" by the stomach's heat</term>. For when food is not cooked <note>Renaissance medicine viewed digestion as a "concoction" or cooking process powered by the body's internal heat.</note>, there is a lack of what should irrigate the natural moisture on one hand, and on the other, putrefied remains are left over which, overflowing, overwhelm the natural heat. For this reason Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in the Renaissance.</note> says that blood is corrupted when digestion itself is corrupted, and following Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, he calls digestion the "root of life." 

Therefore, this rule of Galen's is the best, and almost the only one: to care for digestion above all else everywhere. For what seems to be the greatest precept—namely, to use healthy things—will be of no use unless you digest them. Indeed, a harmful humor flows from healthy foods just as from their opposites if they flow into the limbs "raw." From foods that are even less praised by the culinary art, a less bad nourishment is often received if they are more vigorously digested. Let us therefore most diligently avoid indigestion as a heavy cause of both dissolution and suffocation, by using a quantity of food and drink suited to us. We must also attend to quality, simplicity, preparation, thorough chewing, and fasting—which calls back hunger—and if necessary, even by an external poultice for the stomach, and by certain styptic <note>Substances that contract tissues or check secretions, often used to "close" the stomach after a meal.</note> things taken internally after meals.

<summary>Ficino uses the metaphor of an oil lamp to explain how life is sustained by a balance of innate heat and vital moisture, emphasizing that digestion is the "root of life." He lists lifestyle factors that deplete or overwhelm these natural humors and stresses the importance of "concoction" (digestion) over the mere quality of food.</summary>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE HEALTH OF SCHOLARS</header>

And let us take diligent care that food does not exceed drink, nor should the food be too liquid, or too hard, or significantly cold in its actual temperature; nor should the nourishments be of widely different kinds, nor should we add raw food to raw food. For these things greatly hinder concoction <note>original: "concoctionem," the process by which the body "cooks" or digests food using innate heat.</note>. Furthermore, let us take the greatest care that we do not impede digestion either by sexual intercourse immediately after a meal, or by frequent and unnecessary midday sleep, or by staying awake at night, or by any untimely labor of the mind or body, or by any other means. Indeed, I speak of digestion not only the first, which occurs in the stomach, but also the second, which occurs in the liver; furthermore, the third in the veins; and finally, the fourth which is performed in the members <note>Ficino follows the Galenic model of four stages of digestion/transformation of food into tissue.</note>. These require a long interval of time, and if hindered in any way, the fuel is not supplied to the humor. Therefore, just as with digestion, it is primarily necessary for life to assist in the purging of excrements. It is also necessary to wipe away filth from the skin. Physical movement is as necessary—provided it is continuous, tempered, and varied—as the movements of the heavens, the air, the fire, and the water, provided that the necessity of concoction and sleep is preserved, and exhaustion and wasting away are avoided. Furthermore, we acquire decay and rot in the shade; we live under the open sky and in the light. This was a saying frequently in the mouth of my father, Ficinus, a distinguished physician. But to carry these things out successfully, it would be worthwhile to have accustomed the body from a tender age not so much to city affairs as to certain rural exercises and similar pursuits. Occasionally, one should have maintained a somewhat varied type of nourishment and life. That wise man <note>referring again to his father</note> often used to warn me of this. For those who live with a certain most elegant fastidiousness at every age often live less safely. But those who did not accustom themselves as youths should at least do so as adults, attempting it cautiously and by degrees.

->*Blood and humor suited to life should be airy, tempered in quality,*<-
->*of a medium and tenacious substance. Chapter V.*<-

**A**ll the Greeks, among the precepts most necessary for a long life, command that we be nourished by *euchymia* <term>euchymia: a Greek medical term meaning "good juices," referring to the production of healthy humors through proper diet</term>. We call "euchima" those healthy nourishments which bring good nutrition, that is, good blood. We call blood "good" when it is not cold, not dry, not turbulent, but warm, moist, and clear. Warm indeed with a heat that is not sharp; moist with a humor that is not watery; and clear, yet not meanwhile too thin. For blood that is too fervent both sharpens the natural heat and dries up the humor, and the humor or heat which it introduces is made easily dissolvable and fleeting. Furthermore, blood that is too moist and prone to wateriness blunts the natural heat; it either dulls the natural humor or drives it to melt under the heat, or it suffocates the heat with its moisture. And entirely, if any portion of the natural humor is drawn from watery blood, it both putrefies easily and quickly flows away and dissolves. From this it follows that those who eat softer fruits and herbs—unless perhaps they take them rarely, and then as a medicine to soften the bowels—soon fill their veins to the brim with raw juice prone to putrefaction. And lest that happen, it is safer for nourishment if they are either cooked or at least mixed with bread. Therefore, let the blood be neither fiery nor watery, but airy <note>original: "aerius," corresponding to the element of Air, which is warm and moist.</note>. Not like thick air, lest it be too prone to wateriness; nor like the thinnest air, lest it easily catch fire; but it should maintain a medium substance in which the middle air holds the most dominion. Let the other elements be present only insofar as they are adapted to the command of the air. Let its substance not be too thin, lest it generate an unstable humor and a volatile spirit subject to dissolution. Let it not be too thick, for otherwise it will not serve the intellect at all, and it will hardly be transformed into natural humor and spirit; it will obstruct the passages and give cause for suffocation. And the spirit which is finally and with difficulty created from such thickness is, by its very density, poorly suited for life, and it suffocates the natural heat just as thick smoke immediately compresses and extinguishes a flame. I omit the fact that it is at least so dark that I wish it did not cause a mournful character, or worse. Above all, however, as it seems to me, it is advantageous for a long life to have blood that, along with a truly airy substance that is not too thick, has within itself some glutinous and tenacious humor—almost like the quality olive oil has alongside its thinness, or the humor of a fat yet thin eel, or oil drawn from turpentine by a certain sublimation. You, therefore, diligently choose foods and all other things which, according to your strength, produce such blood and humor. For such blood and humor is the fuel for the vital heat, just as oil is to a flame, and along with thinness, it also possesses firmness. For the precept...

# THE EXTENSION OF LIFE. BOOK II.

**Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925 AD), a Persian physician whose works were central to Renaissance medicine.</note> recommends for the preservation of youth the use of things that draw the blood toward the chest <note>original: "praecordia," the region around the heart and diaphragm.</note>, gathering it there and warming the heart. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037 AD), another foundational medical authority for Ficino.</note> approves of this, instructing that watery and unstable blood must be avoided.** However, one must take into account the differences between bodies. For where the body is denser, one should avoid all remedies that lead to thinness of blood; where it is rarer <note>meaning more porous or less compact</note>, one should avoid those that lead to its thickness. Where there is a medium physical constitution, we go more safely by a similarly middle way. We should never, however, attempt to uproot the natural constitution of the body, for otherwise we would uproot life itself. It is also useful to remember that when we greatly fear thinness of the blood, and the stomach is meanwhile not very strong by nature, we must approach thickness by smaller degrees. When we strive to nourish a slender man with thicker foods, we must meanwhile warm the stomach and encourage sleep. Physical exercise should be increased according to one's strength, while mental exercise—which very often harms many people—should be decreased.

But if the stomach cannot bear foods that are too sticky <note>original: "viscosa"</note>, hard, or very cold, we shall finally achieve that firmness of blood and humor by using corals, sandalwood, roses, coriander, myrobalans <note>a type of astringent fruit used in medicine</note>, quinces, quince preserve <term>diacydonion</term> <note>a thick, marmalade-like medicinal paste made from quinces</note>, rose-sugar, and astringent things; this achieves the same result that we cannot safely reach here with overly "gluey" foods. Indeed, those who cannot digest the "viscous limbs" <note>referring to connective tissues or gelatinous parts</note> of larger animals will be most conveniently nourished by pine nuts, pistachios, licorice juice, and starch, with sweet almonds added, along with their oil, quince seed, and sesame oil, together with the whitest sugar and rose water. We will also grant them the extremities of hens or kids, as well as tortoises, snails, and testicles <note>considered in this period to be highly restorative and "generative" foods</note>. We shall give them wines that are not white, but red and astringent, and somewhat slightly bitter, tempering the wine with water in which iron has been quenched or with mastic-water. We will also lightly soothe the skin with oil of mastic and quinces. Meanwhile, we shall avoid things that make the blood thin or "boiling," unless perhaps we pour a little saffron or cinnamon into the stickier dishes so they are more easily digested and, once digested, transferred through narrow passages to the limbs. For it is difficult to lead sticky or slightly firmer foods from a stomach that is not very strong all the way to the third and fourth stages of digestion, unless they are carried by such <term>vehicles</term> <note>substances that help "carry" nutrients or medicines through the body's channels</note> and, moreover, encouraged by gentle rubbing. When you perform these rubbings, do them with softer hands, and remember to moisten the hands with a fragrant wine in which you have boiled chamomile, myrtle, and roses.

***

->On the common rule of eating and drinking, and the quality of meals.<-
->Chapter VI.<-

**B**UT let us set aside for now those extremely dull or very thin human bodies and come to a common way of living, suited to a common and middle physical constitution. Beware lest by any means the passages of the body are either open beyond measure or too obstructed. In the former case, there is danger of exhaustion <note>original: "resolutione," the thinning or dissipation of the vital spirits</note> and injury from external forces; in the latter, there is danger of rot and suffocation. Although I do not restrain you with the tightest bridle of rule—which Hippocrates condemns—I do not relax the reins to the point of license. Take moist herbs and fruits sparingly. Even more sparingly take milk and fish, and eat both with honey. Use mushrooms most sparingly of all, and only with aromatics and pear seeds. Similarly, drink pure water only in small amounts. Season things that are moist or fatty with sharp aromatics; otherwise, they bring much foreign and putrid humor to the limbs. Even if they provide a humor necessary to nature, they offer one that is subject to very swift corruption. This is no different than how watery wine is quickly disturbed and spoiled. From this comes swift graying of hair, paleness, and the wrinkles of old age. Meat, too, if eaten daily—especially if the weight of it approaches the weight of the bread eaten—brings swift putrefaction. For this reason Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who advocated for vegetarianism</note>, relying on the authority of the Pythagoreans and the ancients, detests the eating of animals. Have we not heard that the long-lived men before the Flood spared animals? Although doctors do not so much forbid the use of meats as the abuse. Finally, flee moist things as being liable to rot, keeping in mind that the moist and the fat age and die more quickly. This is what Hippocrates says, and the reality of the matter declares it. Conversely, take very dry things moderately, or at least temper them with a freer amount of drink. You will be safe choosing the middle...
