# ON THE EXTENSION OF LIFE. BOOK II.

...in Egypt, a friend of the heart. And hellebore <note>A poisonous plant used in antiquity as a purgative to treat madness; Anticyra was famous for it.</note> is taken without harm in Anticyra, but elsewhere it is a poison. **Aristotle** chooses a high dwelling place facing the South and the East, under thin air that is neither damp nor cold. And **Plato** found long-lived people in very high and temperate regions. Indeed, it is most harmful to fertilize fields with dung, or to fail to drain stagnant waters from the fields. For all things born there are more quickly subject to corruption. For this reason, I cannot help but criticize those who criticize the wise **Hesiod** <note>An ancient Greek poet whose work *Works and Days* deals with farming.</note> for omitting the manure-pile in his agricultural writings. But that prudent man looked to health rather than fertility. He believed a field could be sufficiently enriched by turning over the leaves of lupines and beans at the proper time. However, if we are compelled to inhabit damp and unclean regions and consume food that will not last, let us observe the diet that **Physicians** have commanded under pestilential air. We have dealt with this sufficiently in our book *Against the Plague*.

In summary, we shall use sweet and somewhat warm scents, and we shall be purged often and gently with properly prepared <term>aloe</term> <note>Aloe was used as a mild laxative to "cleanse" the system of corrupt humors.</note>. We say it is "properly prepared" if it has been washed with rose water or the juice of roses, or if it has been perfectly mixed with fresh, crushed roses. Then let <term>myrobalan</term> <note>A dried fruit used in medieval medicine, thought to purge bile and strengthen the organs.</note> be added to it, along with <term>mastic</term> <note>A resin from the mastic tree, used to strengthen the stomach.</note>, and perhaps rose. This medicine is, without controversy, wonderful for long preserving **a healthy mind in a healthy body** <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano"</note>. Furthermore, we shall rouse the body and use a hearth at the appropriate time. 

We shall season our feasts with this powder: take a quarter ounce of <term>emblic myrobalans</term> <note>Indian gooseberry, prized for its cooling and restorative properties.</note>, half an ounce of sandalwood, a full ounce of cinnamon, and an eighth of an ounce of saffron. Thus, with this powder—and at the same time avoiding sharp, imminent, and putrid foods—we may perhaps be able to inhibit corruption in such places. Let us remember that where many perish from putrefaction, suffocation, and <term>resolution</term> <note>A medical term for a dangerous weakening or "melting" of the body's strength or humors.</note>, there we must most strongly resist putrefaction and suffocation. Where the opposite occurs, one should in turn use aromatic seasonings and, as we said, somewhat <term>styptic</term> <note>original: "austeris"; substances that contract tissues and stop secretions.</note> scents. At any time, anointing with oil prevents putrefaction; baths of water and oil prevent the injury of cold; and they prevent the "resolution" that looms from labor or hot weather. 

Similarly, one should often rinse the mouth with water and hold <term>liquorice</term> juice or crystalline sugar in the mouth. One should pour plenty of rose water and a little rose vinegar over the hands and face, and use similar scents. Every seven hours, one should be refreshed with modest food, and the body and mind should rest together in their accustomed warmth. 

It is of the greatest importance what kind of wine and wheat we eat regularly. These should be such that they remain intact beyond a year, and preferably up to three, if we are to hope for incorruptible nourishment from them. Whether the wine is white or red, let it be clear, sweet, styptic, fragrant, and such that it requires water—unless you happen to find a wine that is both light and durable, which is very rare. **Isaac the Philosopher** <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 850–950), an influential Jewish physician and Neoplatonist.</note> says that a stronger wine is "vinous," cooked by the sun and purified by the winds; he orders this to be tempered with pure spring water some time before we drink it, so that it may be perfectly mixed. He warns that watery wine, or wine that is weak or sour, must be avoided, as it quickly becomes acidic within the veins and limbs, or otherwise putrefies. Indeed, if watery wine subject to putrefaction is cooked while its substance is preserved, it will at least be useful—otherwise it is not praised, because it will create corruptible humor; however, its sharpness must be tempered with chosen water. 

But wine of the kind we have approved, **Isaac** says (following the opinion of the ancients), is very similar to the "great <term>theriacs</term>" <note>A legendary universal antidote and cure-all.</note>. This, as we said, when tempered, warms a cold constitution of the body, cools a hot one, moistens a dry one, and dries out a damp one; and (as **Galen** says) it restores the natural humor, fosters heat, and tempers both. 

Mixing such wine with water is more necessary for young people than for the elderly, and for cold old men, it is least necessary of all. For cold and hard old age (as **Plato** says) glows and softens with pure wine, just as iron does with fire, or a lupine with water. Know also that the things we said are achieved through wine—doing opposites and tempering disagreements—can also be done through liquorice, though more weakly. It can also be done through rose oil, but applied externally. Let these things be familiar to you. Nor should you doubt that whatever is tempered in its quality and powerful in its virtue can temper the rest, just as cold can make other things cold; this belongs primarily to the **temperament of Jupiter**, through which things are most healthy. But these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE [HEALTH] OF SCHOLARS<-

## Diet, Sustenance, and Medicine for the Elderly. Chapter 9.

**T**hose who have already completed their seventh "septenary" <note>The seventh seven-year cycle, meaning those reaching age 49.</note>, reaching their fiftieth year, should consider that **Venus** <note>The planet associated with youth, sex, and moisture.</note> signifies the young, while **Saturn** <note>The planet associated with old age, coldness, and dryness.</note> signifies the elderly, and among astrologers, these stars are the most hostile of all to one another. They should therefore flee the act of Venus <note>Sexual intercourse.</note> for the sake of Saturn, as it takes away much life even from the young. For it does not care for those already born, but for those yet to be born, and it even dries out plants as soon as the seed is produced. Furthermore, they should consider cold and the night air to be lethal to them, and they should maintain a diet from which they can hope for the most blood and the most <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "spirit" was a subtle vapor in the blood that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note>. This comes especially from fresh egg yolks and wine that is somewhat sweet, very fragrant, and of high quality. For this yolk specifically restores the blood of the heart, and wine especially restores the spirit. They should use the finest meats that are very easy to digest, and in short, follow a diet that increases both heat and moisture. They should constantly refresh the spirit with scents, especially of wine. They should avoid wakefulness, fasting, and thirst, as well as labor of body and mind, solitude, and sorrow.

They should return to music if they have happened to stop, for it should never be interrupted. They should recall certain games and habits of their past childhood, as far as is becoming. For it is very difficult (so to speak) to grow young again in body unless you first become a child again in your mind. Thus, in every age, it is greatly conducive to life to retain something of childhood and to be always occupied with various delights. Yet one should avoid long and profuse laughter, for it dilates the spirit too much toward the exterior.

But let us return to the elderly. If they are cold, they should seek aromatic and warm fomentations <note>Warm, moist medicinal compresses.</note> that are also moist. They should remember that it is not childish to use that "childish" fomentation of **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text.</note>, which was indeed first used by **David** <note>A reference to the biblical King David, who in his old age sought warmth from a young maiden, Abishag. Avicenna interpreted this medically as the transfer of vital heat.</note>, though perhaps used too late.

->A Wonderful Fomentation for the Elderly<-

The crumb of bread that is still warm and fresh, soaked in <term>Malmsey</term> wine <note>A sweet, fortified Greek wine.</note> with powder of mint, applied to the stomach and often held to the nose. For even the scent of such crumbs alone kept the spirit of **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who, according to legend, extended his life by several days just by smelling hot bread to reach a festival.</note> within him when he was already about to expire, holding back the fleeting breath for as long as he pleased. Furthermore, they should use light massages, or sometimes baths that draw nourishment to the extremities.

Above all, they should make a habit of eating washed pine nuts. Indeed, the ancient physicians approved of this nourishment as most suitable for the elderly. For it is warm, moist, and fatty; it smooths every roughness and simultaneously (which is wonderful) while it increases natural moisture, it dries out superfluities and purges putrid humors. There are those who give the elderly one <term>drachma</term> <note>A measurement of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of such nuts to eat daily after meals. I would also give another drachma to the elderly on an empty stomach, or a fresh, warm, "golden" pine-nut preparation.

I would also compose an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> in this manner: Take four ounces of cleaned sweet almonds, the same amount of pine nuts, two ounces of pistachios, one of cucumber seeds, one of cleaned hazelnuts; crush them and cook together with the whitest sugar, to which you have added one drachma of fresh preserved ginger, half a drachma of saffron, a third of musk, the same of amber; melt the sugar with lemon balm water (that is, *citraria*) and rose water, and add many gold leaves to these. By the daily use of this, the elderly attain a stronger and longer life. They can take this at the table, or many hours before a meal. Their complexion will be improved if they drink a bit of white, fragrant wine along with such a confection.

In warmer times, rose sugar together with gold leaves and preserved <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A dried fruit used in medieval medicine to balance the humors, particularly to purge "black bile" associated with old age.</note> will prolong the life of the elderly. No one doubts that <term>Theriac</term> <note>An ancient "cure-all" compound containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> is suitable for the same moist persons and times, concerning the use of which enough was said in the previous book. No one will deny that the roots of <term>elecampane</term> and <term>ben</term> roots <note>Often referring to *Moringa* or *Behen* roots, used as tonics.</note>, both white and red, are very beneficial to them, especially when fresh—the former for nourishment, the latter as a spice—and simply everything that is warm, moist, and aromatic at the same time, and also styptic <note>Astringent; substances that contract tissues.</note> and fatty.

It is certain that the elderly should habitually use choice juice of licorice. For they say that licorice is very similar to the heat and moisture of the human body, and furthermore, it helps with various diseases of the elderly. Almond milk and starch foods should also be familiar, as well as sugar and raisins. **Rhazes** <note>A Persian physician (865–925 AD) known for his clinical observations.</note> highly approves of a <term>triphera</term> <note>A type of electuary or preserve, often containing myrobalans.</note> made of Indian, Emblic, and Belleric myrobalans. Likewise, Indian myrobalans preserved in sugar are highly recommended not only for preserving but also for retarding old age. **Avicenna** praises the "greater" and "lesser" triphera of myrobalans. Again, it is pleasing to eat a confection of iron scales, but especially of gold, daily, and myrobalans, especially the "chebulic" kind <note>A specific variety of myrobalan (*Terminalia chebula*).</note> properly preserved, to delay the inconveniences of old age.

He includes specific recipes for electuaries containing gold leaf and exotic spices to prolong life and delay the decay of Saturnian old age.</summary>

->ON PROLONGING LIFE. BOOK II.<-

### *On the necessary natures of aromatics and cordials, and again on the diet of the elderly.*
#### Chapter IX.

Know that varied virtues reside in **myrobalans** <note>The dried, plum-like fruit of various tropical trees, highly prized in Renaissance medicine for balancing the "humors" or bodily fluids.</note>. First, one which wonderfully dries out superfluous moisture, which is why it prevents gray hair. Second, one that gathers the natural moisture and protects it from both corruption and inflammation at the same time, which is why it extends the use of [the body's] functions for a long time. Third, one which, by its astringent and aromatic power, gathers, nourishes, and strengthens the natural and animal <term>virtue and spirit</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the subtle vapors that carry life and thought through the body.</note>. Because of this, someone might perhaps think that the myrobalan was the Tree of Life in Paradise. Gold, silver, coral, <term>spodium</term> <note>original: "spodium"; likely refers to zinc oxide or the ash of burnt ivory, used for its cooling properties</note>, and precious gemstones do nearly the same thing, although they bring a power of brightening in place of aromatic virtue.

But you must remember that aromatics are most beneficial to us for life (as we indicated above) when they are equally moist and hot with a certain aromatic vigor, and possess a fatty viscosity suitable for growth—such as, in particular, the roots of the **white behen** <note>A type of campion or sea-lavender root</note>, as well as the red ones, especially when fresh. Or at least when, along with a certain subtle, fragrant, and sharp virtue, they have a dense substance and a strongly astringent property, such as the composition found among the **cold cordials** <note>Medicines intended to cool an overheated heart</note>, first in myrobalans and in **amber** <note>original: "succino"; refers to fossilized yellow amber</note>. Next, in roses, and in the juice and seeds of the citron. Thirdly, in sandalwood and coriander, as well as myrtle and other similar things.

Among the **hot cordials**, however, [this property] is found in **zedoary** <note>A root similar to ginger</note>, agarwood, citron peel, and cloves, nutmeg, mace, frankincense, mastic, and **leopard's bane** <note>original: "doronico"</note>, as well as the quality we experience in **sage**. They say that **ambergris** <note>original: "ambra"; a fragrant substance produced by sperm whales</note> and **musk** possess an astringent virtue. **Ginger**, moreover, because of its particular moisture—especially when fresh and preserved—is often beneficial for the elderly. But this and the clove, because of the intensity of their heat, must be taken cautiously. Zedoary should also be taken cautiously, even though it is judged similar to **theriac** <note>A famous ancient "universal" medicinal paste made of dozens of ingredients</note> and has a nature that is both astringent and fatty, which is most suitable for the elderly.

Ambergris, because of its nearly temperate heat, is taken quite safely; and because of its viscosity mixed with a subtle astringency, it has a special privilege for life in strengthening the limbs and spirits. Furthermore, if a water is made from it and the skin is washed, it restores the <term>fourth digestion</term> <note>The final stage of nutrition where food is transformed into the actual substance of the organs and tissues</note> and expels the diseases arising from its failure. 

Those aromatics, however, which have an extremely subtle substance—such as **cinnamon** and **saffron**—must be mixed with cold and harder cordials. For if aromatics are only hot and subtle and are taken alone, they excite the natural heat too much and dissolve the moisture. Yet they are necessary, both for digesting colder and moister meals, and for transporting the hard cordials to the heart. For it must not escape you that the moisture necessary for life itself has its primary seat in the heart, and in its arteries and veins, as **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus, a highly influential 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher</note> clearly teaches and as **Avicenna** <note>The Persian polymath and "Prince of Physicians," author of the *Canon of Medicine*</note> proves; this moisture is frequently irrigated and nourished by the natural moisture of the other limbs. 

Therefore, care must be taken that the moisture of any limb does not dry out by some chance, and much more, that the moisture of the heart is not diminished. And so that nutrients, or fuels, and all cordials may be carried most widely through the narrow passages to the heart, insert **saffron** into them. To make them stay there, however, use **myrobalans**. But to achieve both, take musk and ambergris among the hot things, and roses and myrtle among the cold things.

Remember that sweet **fennel** <note>original: "marathrum"</note> will benefit the elderly. For it both spreads nourishment through the limbs and, by the same faculty as milk, increases the natural moisture. Hence **Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> says that snakes cast off their yearly old age with fennel. We also approve of **sage**, for it temperately warms and strengthens the virtue of nature and drives away paralysis. We also approve of the moderate use of preserved ginger, for it possesses fatness along with heat.

### *On gold, golden foods, and the restoration of the elderly.*
#### Chapter X.

Everyone approves of **gold** above all things, as being the most temperate of all matters and safest from corruption. Indeed, it is consecrated to the **Sun** because of its splendor and to **Jupiter** because of its temperance; therefore it can wonderfully temper the natural heat with moisture, keep the humors from corruption, and insert a Solar and Jovial virtue into the spirits and limbs. Nevertheless, one must make the very hard substance of gold more subtle and very easy to penetrate. For they know that cordials [are] then most [effective]...

# MARSILIO FICINO: ON THE HEALTH OF STUDENTS

...to restore the hidden power of the heart, since nature labors very little in absorbing them. To ensure that nature is not fatigued, these remedies should be administered either in a highly refined state or alongside other subtle substances. They believe it would be best if **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary alchemical life-extender where gold is made into a drinkable liquid</note> could be made without any other mixtures. If that is not possible, they wish it to be taken crushed and reduced into fine leaves. You shall have what is essentially "potable gold" (so to speak) if you do the following:

Collect flowers of borage, bugloss, and lemon balm—which we call *citraria*—and when the Moon enters Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, and looks upon the Sun or Jupiter <note>Ficino was a practitioner of "astrological medicine," believing that the influence of the planets could be "captured" in medicines prepared at specific times.</note>, cook them with white sugar dissolved in rose water. For every ounce, carefully insert three **gold leaves**. Take this while fasting with a certain "golden" wine. Likewise, take the water distilled from a capon <note>A castrated rooster, favored in Renaissance diets for its "temperate" and nourishing meat.</note>, either over a fire or otherwise consumed, together with a rose **julep** <note>A sweet medicinal drink, usually made of sugar and water</note> in which you have previously crushed several gold leaves. Furthermore, extinguish glowing gold in the clearest spring water, and crush gold leaves into that same water. Temper a "golden" wine with this, and eat a fresh egg yolk along with a drink of this kind.

Indeed, you will easily preserve the moisture in the whole "tree" of the body if you preserve it in the roots. Take, therefore, the heart, liver, stomach, testicles, and brain of chickens, young pullets, and capons; cook them in a little water with very little salt. When cooked, crush them—using all the meat and all the broth—and with sugar and an added fresh egg yolk, make a **cake** <note>original: "placentam"; in this context, a flat bread or medicinal loaf</note> seasoned with a little cinnamon and saffron, and gilded with gold leaf. Eat this when hungry at least once every day, and eat it alone, using a clear wine for your drink.

->On the use of milk and human blood for the life of the elderly. Chapter XL.<-

**O**ften immediately after the age of seventy, and sometimes after sixty-three <note>Ficino refers to "septenaries," cycles of seven years which were thought to mark major transitions in human life and health.</note>, the "human tree" gradually withers as its moisture dries up. Then, this human tree must first be watered with a human and youthful liquor so that it may turn green again. You shall choose, therefore, a healthy, beautiful, cheerful, and temperate young girl, and while you are hungry, suck her milk when the Moon is waxing; immediately afterward, eat a little powder of sweet **fennel** <note>original: "marathrum"</note> properly mixed with sugar. The sugar does not allow the milk to curdle or spoil in the stomach, while the fennel, being both subtle and "friendly" to milk, will spread it to the limbs.

When elderly "hectic" fever <note>A wasting disease or chronic fever associated with the drying out of the body's radical moisture.</note> consumes a person, diligent physicians strive to restore them with the liquor of human blood, which has been distilled over a fire with sublime art. What, then, prevents us from occasionally refreshing those who are already nearly worn out by old age with this drink? There is a common and ancient opinion that certain old hags—commonly called **striges** <note>A legendary screech-owl or witch said to suck the blood of infants.</note>—suck the blood of infants to grow young again through their strength. Why should our elderly, who are destitute of all other help, not suck the blood of a youth who is—I say—willing, healthy, happy, and temperate, whose blood is of the best quality but perhaps too abundant? Let them, therefore, suck like **swallows** <note>original: "more hirundinum"; Ficino may be referencing a folkloric belief about how swallows feed or restore themselves, or it may be a slip for "hirudo" (leech).</note> one or two ounces from a vein in the left arm that has barely been opened. They should then immediately take an equal amount of sugar and wine; they should do this while hungry and thirsty when the Moon is waxing. If the blood is "raw," it is digested with difficulty; let it be cooked first with sugar, or let it be moderately distilled with hot water and mixed with sugar, and then drunk.

To warm the stomach with pig's blood is also a present help; one should soak a sponge in blood flowing from a pig's vein, moistened with warm wine, and immediately apply it warm to the stomach. Galen and Serapio <note>Two of the most influential authorities in medieval and Renaissance medicine; Galen was Roman, Serapio likely refers to the Arabic physician Ibn Sarabi.</note> say that the bite of a rabid dog is cured by drinking dog's blood. They did not choose to assign a reason for this. I, therefore, having sought a reason for two days, finally believe that the poisonous saliva of the rabid dog, impressed upon the injured foot of a man, ascends gradually through the veins to the heart like a poison, unless something distracts it in the meantime. If, therefore, the man drinks the blood of another dog in the meantime, that raw blood floats in the stomach for many hours, as the stomach is about to cast it out through the bowels as something foreign. Meanwhile, this canine blood diverts the canine saliva—which was previously grasping at the upper limbs—to the stomach before it can reach the heart. For in canine blood there is a power to attract canine saliva, and in the saliva, in turn, a power to pursue similar blood. Thus the poison, removed from the heart and absorbed by the blood floating in the bowels, is led down through the lower parts together with the blood, leaving the man unharmed.

Why do I mention this? First, so that I might reveal a supporting cause for such a hidden matter during this discussion. Second, to warn that blood can be drunk—and indeed healthfully—and that in human blood there is a power which attracts and mutually pursues human blood. Perhaps you should not doubt that youthful blood drunk by an old man can be drawn to the veins and limbs, and there be of the greatest possible benefit.

He justifies this through the medical principle of "like attracting like," citing ancient authorities and the treatment of rabies.</summary>

# ON PROLONGING LIFE. BOOK II.

### On the diet, residence, and lifestyle of the elderly. Chapter XII.

**I**t is beneficial for the very elderly to remember that their weak nature must not be burdened by the weight of too much nourishment, nor distracted by too great a variety of dishes. Indeed, even a youthful age becomes old quickly through this vice. Therefore, let them divide their meals, and refresh their nature not so much with a large amount of food as with frequent nourishment, provided an interval is given for digestion. For often, even after the stomach itself has cooked the food, if the liver has not also processed it, taking in more nourishment distracts and fatigues nature; when this weariness is frequently repeated, untimely old age flies toward us. In winter, the elderly should seek sunny spots like sheep; in summer, let them revisit pleasant places and streams like birds. Let them frequently spend time among green and sweetly-smelling plants; for these, being alive and breathing, breathe together with the spirit of man to increase it. Let them retreat to places generally friendly to bees, and taste honey in the winter. For honey is a food primarily friendly to the elderly, except where one fears the "fire" of yellow bile <note>In the system of the four humors, yellow bile was considered hot and dry; honey, being "hot," could exacerbate a bilious temperament.</note>. Very fresh cheese is a friend, as are dates, figs, raisins, capers, sweet pomegranates, jujubes, hyssop, scabious, and betony—but pistachios are much more so. Pine nuts, however, are the greatest of all, as we have said. From these they will receive the most help if they keep them in slightly warm water for twelve hours before eating them. In this way, they will not harm the stomach. Furthermore, it helps if, while using these, they also spend time among pine and olive groves and vineyards, or at least take in the vapor and scent of the pine. Likewise, let them often anoint the body with the gum and "tears" <note>Resin or sap</note> of the pine mixed with oil or wine. For it is probable that trees endowed by nature with long life—especially those that stay green in winter—may benefit you toward a long life through their shade, fresh vapor, fruit, wood, and any timely use. We have spoken of long-lived animals above. Now, it will perhaps also be conducive to the same goal if you live mostly among those who are healthy, similar to you in nature, and friendly—and perhaps even more so if they are a little younger. But as to whether and how the frequent company of adolescents might be able to delay old age for a little while, the modest Socrates <note>A reference to the Platonic idea that the elderly can "draw" life or inspiration from the beauty and vitality of the young.</note> must be consulted.

### What supports the elderly receive from the Planets to foster all their members. Chapter XIII.

**B**ut instead, you anxious old men, consult Apollo, who judged Socrates the wisest of the Greeks. Consult Jupiter, and Venus as well. Apollo <note>original: "Phœbus"; Ficino uses Phoebus Apollo as the patron of medicine and the Sun.</note> himself, the inventor of the medical art, will give you nutmeg to foster the stomach. Jupiter, along with Apollo, gives mastic and mint. Venus gives coral. To foster the head, again, Apollo gives peony, frankincense, and marjoram, and with Saturn, he gives myrrh. Jupiter gives spikenard <note>term: "spicam nardi"; an aromatic essential oil from the Himalayas, highly prized in antiquity.</note> and mace. Finally, Venus gives sweet fennel and myrtle. To foster the heart, you shall receive from Apollo lemon balm <note>original: "citrariam"; an herb used to lift the spirits.</note>, saffron, aloe wood, frankincense, amber, musk, leopard's bane, a small amount of cloves, lemon peel, and cinnamon. From Jupiter, the lily, bugloss, basil, and mint, and alkanet roots <note>original: "beenias"; likely referring to the roots of Behen or Alkanet, used in cordials.</note>, both white and red alike. From Venus alone, myrtle, sandalwood, and rose; and together with Saturn, coriander. Store these things away diligently. And those things which are for the stomach, prepare with quince oil in the form of a wax salve. Those for the head, pour over with spikenard oil and rub onto the neck, temples, and forehead. Finally, those for the heart, sprinkle with "golden" wine and rose water, and apply them externally to the region of the heart. But the liver, which is primarily necessary for creating blood—I know not how we overlooked it. Apollo will always help this organ with agrimony and balsam of Gilead. Jupiter with pistachios and raisins; Venus with liverwort, endive, *spodium* <note>original: "spodio"; a medicinal powder made from burnt ivory or metal oxides, used as a cooling agent.</note>, and chicory. Finally, to foster the spleen, that Saturn of yours, along with Jupiter, will give you capers, hart's-tongue fern, and tamarisk. Just as Jupiter with Venus cures the bladder with pine, licorice, starch, cucumber seeds, mallow, marsh-mallow, manna, and cassia. Do not flee so much from Saturn, O elderly men, even though he is to be feared by many. For just as he is a stranger to the young, he will be a domestic friend to you. Therefore, so that he may invigorate and strengthen your whole body according to his powers, you shall sometimes take—when he is reigning, and likewise from Apollo—mummy <note>original: "muniam"; Mummia was a substance made from bitumen or ground-up ancient remains, believed to have intense preservative powers.</note> along with the flesh of a roasted goose. Anoint these with a little goose fat, pound them diligently, cook them with the honey of Chebulic and Indian myrobalans <note>original: "Myrobalanorum chebularum"; a type of astringent fruit from India used in Ayurvedic and Renaissance medicine.</note>, and season them with amber, musk, and saffron, believing that there is true faith in medicines that contribute to life. By this, you may hope that God will breathe upon you as you pray, and that the things created by Him—especially the celestial ones—will undoubtedly work toward increasing or preserving...

## On the conversation of old men under Venus through green meadows.
### Chapter 44.

**B**ut from these heavier deities <note>referring to the restrictive influences of Saturn or the sternness of Jupiter mentioned in previous chapters</note> I call you old men back for a little while to Venus, through gardens and green meadows. I summon you all to nourishing Venus—not playing with you, exactly, but joking. She pours out this playful oracle for you, I say, and for me, now an old man: "I, children (if you do not know), gave you life through pleasure and movement. Therefore, through a certain pleasure and movement, though not of the same kind as in your youth, I will preserve your life. Liber <note>another name for Bacchus, the god of wine and freedom</note>—the sower of the vine and propagator of life—will also preserve it through liberty. Liber himself always hates slaves; and the long life he promises to the living, he fills with free leaves <note>original: "foliis liberis." Ficino is making a Latin pun on "Liber" (the god), "liber" (free), and "liber" (the inner bark of a tree or a book).</note>. To my life as well as my mind, when Saturn was reigning, 'diminished mint' <note>original: "diminuta mentha." Ficino puns on "mentha" (mint) and "mens" (mind). He suggests that a "diminished mind" or perhaps a specific preparation of mint was once useful, but now more is needed.</note> once was beneficial, and it pleases daily: but for you, 'greater mint' is beneficial for the mind and life; 'diminished' harms. Gather laughter from my gardens; disregard the fig. But when you pluck these violets, consider that you are plucking lilies; and when grasping the lily, understand you are grasping the saffron. Jupiter himself, having obtained saffron from Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god</note>, propagated it into the lily. I, receiving the lily from Jove, transformed it into these violets you see here. Finally, let the rose be your Morning Star, and the myrtle be your Evening Star."

After this oracle, we must consider her command: that the nature of green things—insofar as they are green—is not only alive, but even youthful, overflowing with a thoroughly healthy moisture and a certain vivid spirit. Therefore, through their scent, sight, use, and frequent habitation, a youthful spirit flows into us from them. While walking among green things, let us meanwhile seek the reason why the color green nourishes the sight above all others and delights it healthily.

We shall find at last that the nature of sight is luminous and a friend of light, yet volatile and easily dissipated. Therefore, while it expands through its friendly light, it is sometimes completely snatched away by an excessive surplus of light and dissolved by violent dilation; however, it naturally flees darkness as an enemy, and thus retracts its rays into a narrow space. The eye wishes to enjoy light in such a way that it is indeed amplified by this friend of its, but not meanwhile dissipated. Now truly, in whatever color there is much more darkness or blackness than light, the sight does not expand, and thus the ray of sight is not dilated as it desires. Where, conversely, there is much more of a brilliant color than black, the sight is spread too wide, distracted by a certain harmful pleasure.

For which reason the color green, tempering black with white most of all, provides both benefits: delighting and preserving alike. Moreover, with its soft and still tender quality—just as water resists the rays of the eyes without offense—it prevents the rays from perishing by wandering too far. For things that are both hard and rough break the rays in a way; while things that are very thin and porous open a path to dissolution. But things that have some solidity and a smooth uniformity at the same time, like mirrored bodies, neither break the rays nor allow them to be dispersed further. Finally, things that in addition to these benefits are also tender and soft, like water and green things, flatter the liquid rays of the eyes with their softness. 

Ultimately, the ray of sight is a certain light naturally kindled for us within the water of the eyes, and it requires a tempered light in a "resisting water," so to speak. Therefore, the eye rejoices in water, is delighted by mirror-like things, and is charmed by green things. In these green things, truly, the indwelling light of the Sun still possesses a spring-like moisture within itself, and a subtle water full of a certain hidden light. From this it also happens that when the color green is thinned, it is resolved into saffron yellow. 

To what end is this? So that we may understand that the frequent use of green things—since such use refreshes the spirit of sight, which is in a way the foremost part of the <term>animal spirit: the subtle substance in medieval physiology that mediated between soul and body, specifically governing sensation and movement</term>—also restores the animal spirit itself. And let us also remember: if the color green, because it is the middle and most tempered among the grades of colors, benefits the animal spirit so much, then those things which are most tempered in their qualities will much more benefit the natural and vital spirit in our nature, and be extremely profitable for our life. Nothing in the world is more tempered than the heavens; almost nothing beneath the heavens is more tempered than the human body; nothing in this body is more tempered than the spirit. Therefore, through tempered things, the life remaining in the spirit is refreshed. Through tempered things, the spirit is conformed to the celestial heavens. 

Finally, let us learn from the temperance of green—which, by illuminating, equally gathers and expands the animal spirit and therefore helps it most—that we too, in choosing, compounding, and using heart-remedies, should choose aromatic, subtle, and sharp things which have the power to extend or even illuminate the spirit...

He provides a physiological explanation for why green is the most healing color for the eyes, being a perfect "tempered" balance between light and dark.</summary>

ON PROLONGING LIFE. BOOK II.

...usually illuminate, which is what saffron and cinnamon do. These should always be mixed with aromatic, styptic <note>substances that contract or tighten tissues</note>, and binding agents, such as myrobalans <note>a type of dried medicinal fruit used as a tonic</note> and similar things, and vice-versa. Nor should one overlook those things which, even without an aromatic sharpness, accomplish both effects at once: they dilate the spirit somewhat, while also binding it firmly and illuminating it greatly. We have spoken of these elsewhere; such effects are produced by gold, silver, spodium <note>a medicinal powder made from burnt minerals or ivory</note>, coral, amber, silk, and precious gemstones—among which the hyacinth stone <note>the jacinth or zircon gem</note>, even if just held in the mouth, is highly recommended due to its Jovial <note>relating to the planet Jupiter</note> temperament. For since these most beautiful and almost celestial things could not be created under the earth without some supreme benefit from the heavens, it is probable that such things contain wonderful heavenly virtues.

Indeed, a composition of this kind, which equally binds the spirit while dilating and illuminating it, delights the spirit inwardly and refreshes it, just as the sight of greenery refreshes the eyes from the outside. In the elderly, it preserves a certain natural "greenness" for a very long time, much like a laurel, olive, or pine tree that stays green even in winter. It achieves this all the more because it works internally, especially if such a composition glows with an aromatic scent and entices with its flavor. 

Just as the body, composed of the thicker parts of the humors, is refined into a "fifth form" <note>the quintessence, or the purest substance beyond the four elements</note>, so the spirit, formed from the most subtle portions of those same humors, naturally possesses a fifth form that is most tempered, lucid, and therefore celestial. It must be preserved in this very form so that it remains subtle yet firm, as we have said. Let it be entirely bright, but also somewhat solid. Furthermore, it should be continually fostered with fragrant, firm, and bright things if we desire to preserve the life that flourishes in the spirit and to claim these celestial gifts for ourselves. Having contemplated these things thus far by the command of Venus, let us now imagine we have heard from Mercury himself.

---

### The Personification of Mercury advising the elderly regarding pleasure, scents, songs, and 
### medicines. Chapter XV.

**I**n the meantime, while Venus herself was conversing among the old men—quite pleasantly so far, though perhaps she was about to prattle on too long—Mercury, the author of speeches, interrupted this conversation with these words: "What business do you old men have with this 'eternal girl' Venus? And again, what has Venus to do with serious discourse? Are these speeches not mine as much as yours? Is your reason not the same as mine? Listen to me now with the same attention you gave her—indeed, with much greater attention than you gave Venus. 

You know there are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Learn now that there are also (so to speak) five reasons. For while your soul is daily filled through the five senses and conceives the reasons of things from them, five notions and habits for judging things result, like five types of reasoning. Furthermore, just as there are five senses on one hand and five reasons on the other, so the tenor of life is arranged in five stages concerning sense and reason. From this, five ages of man are counted. 

The first age is drawn by sense alone. The second is attracted more by sense than led by reason. The third is driven equally by the alternating persuasions of reason and sense. The fourth is led by reason rather than sense. The fifth, finally, ought to be governed by reason alone. Therefore, let the first and second ages, as subjects of Venus, listen to Venus speaking if they wish; but let the remaining ages listen to Mercury. 

I address all the rest of you, therefore, not only for myself, but also for this Diana whom you see at my left: for since she is speechless <note>referring to the moon or the silent nature of the huntress</note> and I am 'double-tongued' <note>referring to Mercury's role as the eloquent messenger and translator</note>, I rightfully speak for her, since I possess her tongue. 

Truly, Venus has instilled in you one harmful pleasure, by which she might harm you while benefiting future generations. She gradually drains you through a kind of hidden pipe, filling and procreating another life with your colors, finally leaving you on the ground like the discarded, exhausted skin of a cicada <note>original: "spolium cicadarum." Ancient Greeks and Romans believed cicadas shed their old age with their skins</note>, while looking out for the more tender cicada. Do you not see that Venus generates something fresh, living, and endowed with sense out of your very substance? She steals youth, life, and sense from you—from your whole body, I say, through the pleasure of the whole—in order to make a whole life from it. 

Meanwhile, warned by the quality of that matter which remains after the fourth digestion <note>in Galenic medicine, the final stage of nutrition where food is turned into the body's actual tissues</note>, I advise you that foods cooked by a fourth digestion are of the greatest help to your life. Namely, when it is fresh, whole, and able to be sipped, together with sugar and a little saffron: human milk, or...

...pig's or goat's milk taken with a little honey. And these two are more healthful when they still glow with their own natural heat. Although an egg seems to require another brief cooking, especially for a less robust stomach, it should be cooked only lightly. But, to return for a moment to Venus <note>Here, Venus represents sexual desire and physical pleasure</note>, if you have ever seen Venus, you have seen her as quite youthful, and polished as if with a harlot’s cosmetics and ornaments. She, who is always new, always affects new things; she hates old things and destroys what has been made so that she may build what is to be made. She again—if it is right to say so—is like a harlot who is not content with any one man; she loves the crowd and (to speak in the language of logic) she favors the "face of the species" more than the individual.

Now, she does not only cast you down through touch, but she also deceives you daily through taste and destroys those she has tricked. For those flavors you perceive in things, which are pleasant due to a certain moderate temperament, were handed down by Diana, Apollo, and Jove <note>Representing the balanced forces of nature, light/reason, and kingly order</note>. But those wondrous lures of flavor, by which you wretched men daily lose your lives like captives in secret, are fashioned by the treacherous Venus. Why then do you accuse Mars? Why Saturn? Mars, indeed, harms you quite rarely and does so openly. Saturn also more often professes himself an enemy by his face; he harms more slowly and denies no one time for remedies. Only Venus comes openly as a friend, yet arrives as a secret enemy. Accuse her instead, if it is permitted to accuse anyone among the gods. Against her manifold traps, equip yourselves with the eyes of Argus <note>A giant with a hundred eyes from Greek myth</note> and arm yourselves with the shield of Pallas <note>Athena, goddess of wisdom</note>. Plug your ears against her flattering promises as if against the lethal songs of the Sirens. 

Finally, accept from me this flower of providence, by which you may avoid the sorceries of this Circe <note>The enchantress from the Odyssey who turned men into beasts</note>. She promises you—and barely even grants them—two pleasures, and lethal ones at that; but I, by the benefit of my father and brother <note>Mercury is speaking; his father is Jupiter and his brother is Apollo</note>, promise you five. I provide five that are pure, perpetual, and health-giving: the lowest is in smell, the higher in hearing, the more sublime in sight, the more eminent in imagination, and the highest and most divine in reason. The more pleasure is perceived in touching and tasting, the more frequent the damage to life. Conversely, the more pleasure you derive daily from smell, hearing, sight, as well as imagination and often reason, the longer you extend the threads of your life. 

But just as I warned you to beware of the subtle Venus in the allurements of touch and taste, so beware of Saturn in that more secret and excessive delight of the contemplative mind. For there, he himself frequently devours his own children <note>A reference to the myth of Saturn eating his children, interpreted here as the way deep study can "consume" the scholar</note>. For those whom he snatches away with the lures of his sublime contemplations, and recognizes there as his own, he meanwhile cuts away from the earth with a certain sickle (if they stay their step there too long) and often steals away the earthly life of the unwary. In this at least he is more indulgent than Venus: for while Venus gives the life she takes from you to another, restoring nothing to you for your loss, Saturn—in exchange for the earthly life from which he is separated and from which he finally separates you—restores to you a celestial and eternal life. 

In this very way, Venus and Saturn seem similar to each other; for Saturn, who rejoices in Aquarius just as he reigns in Libra <note>Astrological references to the signs where Saturn has dignity</note>, vexes men with the lust for procreation, and harms those he vexes so that he may benefit posterity. But she [Venus] makes the body fertile and stimulates the fertile one; he [Saturn] urges the mind, pregnant with its own seed, toward birth. You, therefore, mindful of the proverb—*Nothing in excess* <note>original: "Ne quid nimis"</note>—must restrain the lust of both "birthing" processes with the constant reins of prudence. Although he [Saturn] harms much more quickly and severely those whom he weighs down with weariness, lethargy, sorrow, cares, and superstition, than those whose bodily strength and mortal character he raises to the heights. 

I advise you to observe above all what the just Jupiter taught Pythagoras and Plato: that human life is preserved in a certain equal proportion of the soul itself with the body, and that both should be nourished and exercised by their own specific foods and movements. If anyone eventually makes one much stronger than the other through their upbringing, he causes no small loss to life. Therefore, whoever chooses from among the things praised by the art of the Physicians those that benefit both the body and the intellect at once, claims for himself the greatest aid to life. In their number, consider wine, mint, myrobalans <note>dried medicinal fruits</note>, musk, ambergris, fresh ginger, frankincense, aloe, hyacinth <note>the gemstone</note>, and similar stones or herbs, which are prepared by Physicians for the utility of both. But having sometimes cut through these longer wanders, I, also a Physician, have come to this point: if flavors taken from things no longer living, and scents from spices already dry and void of life, are judged to contribute much to life, why do you doubt that scents from plants and roots still clinging to their own soil and living will accumulate the strengths of life in a wonderful way? Finally, if vapors...

If vapors exhaling from merely vegetable life <note>referring to the use of plants and herbs mentioned on the previous page</note> greatly benefit your life, how much do you think the songs of the air will benefit you? These are indeed made of an entirely airy <term>spirit</term>, harmonic for the harmonic part of ourselves, still warm and living for the living part, endowed with sense for our sensory part, and conceived by reason for our rational part. Therefore, I hand over to you this lyre, crafted by me, and with it the song of <term>Phoebus</term> <note>Apollo, the god of the sun, music, and healing</note>, as a solace for your labors and a pledge of long life. For just as things that are perfectly balanced in quality and aromatic at the same time can harmonize the humors with each other and the natural spirit with itself, so do such odors harmonize the vital spirit, and so, in turn, do similar harmonies harmonize the animal spirit <note>Ficino divides the "spiritus" into natural, vital, and animal types, governing different bodily and mental functions</note>. Therefore, while you tune the strings on the lyre and the sounds in your voice, consider that your internal spirit is being harmonized as well. And lest I seem more stingy than Venus, who "freezes without Bacchus" <note>A reference to the proverb *Sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus*—without food and wine, love grows cold</note>, receive through me this nectar from Father <term>Liber</term> <note>another name for Bacchus, god of wine</note> himself. Those among you who are especially cold should take two ounces of local wine or sweet Malmsey on the same hours every fourteenth day, along with one "ounce of peace" <note>likely a metaphorical instruction to remain in a tranquil state of mind</note>, three hours before a meal. Also, once take one drachm of "sublimated water" <note>aqua vitae or distilled wine</note> distilled from wine with half an ounce of rose julep. Indeed, they can also very conveniently rub this liquid on the skin and use it for smelling. And so that I may bring you <term>Ambrosia</term> <note>the food of the gods</note> as well after such nectar, I grant you this additional medicine received from <term>Jove</term> <note>Jupiter</note>. Take four ounces of Chebulic myrobalans <note>a dried fruit used in medieval medicine as a purgative and tonic</note>, three of rose sugar, and of candied ginger one ounce in winter, but half an ounce in summer. Cook these three gently with Emblic honey, and decorate them with seven leaves of gold. Take a bolus of this on an empty stomach four hours before lunch. Take it daily for at least a full year, so that from it your youth may be renewed like the Eagle's. Let us consider that Mercury has spoken thus far.

## *A confirmation of the above, and precepts on avoiding sexual intercourse and constant thinking.*

### Chapter XVI.

**A**strologers say that <term>Venus</term> and <term>Saturn</term> are mutual enemies. Since there can be no hatred in heaven, where all things are moved by love and where there is no defect, we interpret them as "enemies"—that is, different in their effects. Let us set aside other matters for the present. See how <term>Saturn</term> has placed pleasure for us in the center, while <term>Venus</term> has placed it at the circumference. Pleasure is, in a way, the bait for the <term>spirits</term>. Therefore, from opposite sides, <term>Venus</term> and <term>Saturn</term> hunt for the flight of our <term>spirit</term>. She, through her pleasure, lures it toward external things; he, meanwhile, through his own, recalls it to the innermost parts. Thus, they distract the spirit if they move it at nearly the same time, and they dissipate it. For this reason, nothing is more pestilential to a contemplator or a seeker of knowledge than the sexual act; conversely, nothing is more foreign to one pursuing such acts than care and contemplation. We count the natural and religious contemplator in this same category, and in a similar degree, anyone who is deeply thoughtful in their business affairs and subject to heavy cares. From this it follows that if we wish to relieve and otherwise console someone who is either too occupied by Saturnine contemplation or weighed down by care, and we attempt to do so through sexual acts, games, and jokes—treating them as remedies from a far distance—we strive in vain and even with loss. And conversely, if we wish to moderate someone lost in sexual work or loosened by games and jokes, we cannot easily correct them through Saturnine severity. The best discipline is to use the studies and similar remedies of <term>Phoebus</term> and <term>Jove</term>, who are in the middle between <term>Saturn</term> and <term>Venus</term>, to call back toward the middle those men who are leaning toward one or the other extreme. But let us finally act as physicians. Just as a flame is commonly extinguished in two violent ways—either as if blown out by winds, or conversely as if crushed by ashes—so we dissipate the spirit quickly by the sexual effect, or we gradually suffocate it by the Saturnine effect, and often squeeze it out by compressing it, and resolve it equally. The spirit, flying frequently to the outermost parts, renders the internal parts either empty or foreign to life. But when it is often forced to the innermost parts, it renders the other surrounding members less fit for life. Therefore, <term>Venus</term> brings on swift old age to our internal parts, and <term>Saturn</term> to our external parts. <term>Venus</term> especially does so when the body is easily weakened and totters from any movement of hers. <term>Saturn</term> also does so most of all when the powers of the mind and body are undermined by any duty of contemplation, or care, or labor—even though someone born for contemplation or for lust is usually naturally very strong for their respective duty. For nature often joins power together with pleasure and ease. Therefore, let each person know himself, and be the moderator and physician of himself.

Those who intend to engage in frequent sexual intercourse should consult others on the matter. I, however, have already provided counsel for those who exercise their intellect in the previous book. Ultimately, they must employ every diet and every remedy by which the limbs, the <term>spirit</term> <note>In Ficino’s medical system, the "spirit" is a subtle, airy substance that links the physical body to the immortal soul</note>, the senses, the intellect, and the memory may be strengthened. They should revisit their thoughts at intervals and not wait for even the slightest exhaustion from thinking. This is especially true as they first begin to turn gray, although there are some who produce gray hairs not so much from a weakness of nature—namely while they are still young—as from some preceding sickness or disease, or even from a likeness to their parents, specifically if they were conceived when their parents were already turning gray.

## Medicines for the elderly, and again regarding housing and diet. Chapter XVII

The rule of the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologer-priests famous for their wisdom and longevity</note> should perhaps be approved for the recovery of youth: to gradually purge the foreign humors absorbed by the body, both the internal ones through suitable medicines, and the external ones through rubbing, baths, and the induction of sweat; and meanwhile, to gradually fill the body with healthy and enduring nourishment. There are those who, by means of certain lozenges made from vipers <note>original: "uipera"; viper flesh was a common ingredient in Renaissance "Thierica" or cure-alls</note>, or prepared hellebore, promise to lead out all old and putrid humors. Once these are purged and a most healthy humor is restored by beneficial nourishment, they claim youth is returned. Those who are more cautious feed hellebore to chickens, and then feed the man with those chickens. I judge that this kind of treatment is dangerous in youth and should instead be attempted in old age, lest we perhaps experience that "youth" promised by <term>Medea</term> to the elderly Pelias <note>In Greek mythology, the sorceress Medea tricked the daughters of King Pelias into cutting him up and boiling him by promising it would make him young again; he simply died</note>. For Hippocrates asserts that young men who are purged with exquisite medicines age quickly. But where diet does not suffice, you may safely use a clyster, or manna, or especially washed aloe. If your bowels are more constricted, take manna with capon broth and the power of <term>myrobalan</term> <note>A dried, plum-like fruit from India used as a gentle laxative and tonic</note>. If not, you will preserve yourself as a young man even in old age with this purgative:

Take one ounce of washed aloe, two drams of emblic myrobalans, the same amount of chebulic myrobalans, two drams of purple roses, and the same amount of mastic. Form these into pills with Malmsey wine <note>original: "maluatico uino"; a sweet Greek wine highly prized for medicine</note> when the Moon is happily situated and enjoys a favorable aspect with <term>Jupiter</term>, especially if either the Moon or Jupiter possesses fixed houses <note>A reference to "Fixed Signs" in astrology (Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius), which were thought to grant stability and longevity</note>. For these conditions contribute greatly to the duration of life. You can also usefully combine rhubarb here with the aloe, specifically half a part of aloe and half a part of rhubarb; as often as necessary, take one pill in the morning, up to three or five, and drink a little wine afterward. But where you fear phlegm more, you can conveniently take a third part of agaric <note>A type of mushroom used in medicine</note> lozenges in these pills, along with two thirds of aloe, omitting the rhubarb. 

But for many years now, I have found that first composition of pills to be the safest for every age. Make a confection of the same sort at the same hour: Take one ounce each of emblic, belliric, Indian, and chebulic myrobalans; two ounces of cinnamon; one ounce of zedoary <note>original: "doronici"; a root similar to ginger</note>; one ounce of purple roses; two ounces of red sandalwood; one dram of saffron; a third part of a dram of musk, and the same of amber. After this, melt white sugar with rose water and citron juice, cook it, and form it into boluses, and wrap them in gold leaf. We have found by experience that taking and giving this four hours before lunch is useful for strengthening the vital power, and for brightening and firming the spirit. It will be especially beneficial if you drink a little "golden wine" <note>likely a reference to a light, amber-colored wine or wine infused with gold</note> afterward. 

It will also be beneficial to frequently soak heated bread in golden wine and rose water, and season it with a little cinnamon and plenty of sugar. Frequently mix these two with almond milk and a little bread, for such mixtures reflect a <term>Jovial nature</term> <note>Pertaining to the planet Jupiter, which Ficino associated with life, growth, and a balanced temperament</note>. Beyond all that we have explained or at least indicated above, all city-dwellers must diligently beware of heat, frost, any cold following heat, or night air, mists, and winds—whether blowing from a marsh or rushing through a narrow space. Likewise, avoid places where the air is either moved too violently or not moved at all. Beware of any damp habitation, stench, sorrow, and lethargy. The followers of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Scholars and intellectuals, who are ruled by the planet Mercury</note> must be more diligent in this, and the elderly most diligent of all. Furthermore, after they have lightly rubbed the whole body in the morning, they should soothe it against the discomforts of air and labor with warm oil or some slightly bitter wine, into which they have previously infused myrrh, rose, and myrtle. Let them frequently keep sage in their mouths, as it is most friendly to the nerves and teeth. And when they are forced by the defect of their teeth to return to liquid foods like infants, let them beware of things that are too soft. Let them indeed return to milk, but mixed with moderate wine.

Having previously discussed physical purging and the restoration of youth, he now concludes the rules on fire and sunlight before transitioning to a groundbreaking theory on how the "spirit"—the vital link between soul and body—is nourished by scents, air, and music.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
->ON PROLONGING LIFE, BOOK II.<-

They should use fire only as a medicine, specifically as much as the necessity of expelling cold and stirring up innate heat requires; otherwise, like a gluttonous thing, it will dry out the natural moisture. They should follow the sun, however, as long as it is pleasing, as if it were food—avoiding the dripping of humors <note>original: "destillatione"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to catarrh or the "dripping" of excess fluid from the brain</note> and similarly shunning intense heat. They should love gentle movements, which are quite necessary for stirring up heat. But they should hate heavy labors of the body, and much more those of the mind, as well as prolonged thirst, fasting, and wakefulness.

### On the nourishment of the spirit, and the preservation of life through odors. Chapter XVIII.

**W**e read that in certain hot regions, fragrant everywhere with many scents, many people with slender bodies and weak stomachs are nourished as if by odors alone. Perhaps this is because the very nature of the place reduces the fermented juices of herbs, fruits, and trees into odors, and then dissolves the humors of the human bodies there into <term>spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus" is a subtle, airy substance that connects the physical body to the soul</note>. Therefore, since both odor and spirit are a kind of vapor, and "like is nourished by like," surely both the spirit and the "spiritual man" <note>Those whose lives are governed by intellectual or "airy" pursuits</note> receive a great deal of nourishment from odors. Indeed, nourishment through odors—or at least a restorative fomentation—is especially necessary for the elderly and the slender, so that we may somehow compensate for the lack of more solid and abundant food. 

Some, however, tend to doubt whether the spirit is actually nourished by odors. I believe that it is perhaps only nourished in this way: unless the thick foods are finally expanded into vapors through digestion, the spirit itself (which we have said is vapor) receives no nourishment from them. Therefore, wine full of aroma suddenly refreshes the spirit, which other things can barely restore in time. We call that vapor into which cooked foods are finally transformed "odor," because odor is everywhere a kind of vapor. This vapor drawn inward from food, unless it pleases the spirit with a certain scent, offers hardly any nourishment to the spirit. 

For this reason, we strongly approve of our <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose work was foundational to European medicine</note> when he says that the body is nourished by sweetness, but the spirit by a certain (to use his words) "aromaticity." Since the thickness of the body cannot grow except by a thick nature, such as is found in sweetness, the thinness of the spirit cannot be restored by anything other than a certain smoke and vapor in which aromaticity itself thrives. We call the "aromatic quality" that which is fragrant, sharp, and in a way styptic <note>Astringent or contracting</note>. 

Accordingly, because the liver provides nourishment to the body through the blood, it is greatly increased by sweetness. But the heart, because it both creates the spirit and produces nourishment for the spirit, rightly desires aromatics. It is useful, however, to season aromatics for the heart with sweetness, and to mix sweet things for the liver with aromatics, while avoiding excessive sweetness in the meantime. 

What more? <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> himself, following <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, thinks the spirit is nourished not only by odor, but by air. Air, I say, not simple air, but rather air suitably mixed. If we believe them, we will judge no choice of food or anything else more necessary for life than air that is adapted to us. For the air—always affected by the qualities of both the lower and celestial things, surrounded by an immense (so to speak) breadth, and penetrating us from all sides in perpetual motion—wonderfully reduces us to its own quality. This is especially true of the spirit, specifically the <term>vital spirit</term> flourishing in the heart, into whose inner chambers the air constantly flows; it suddenly affects the spirit according to how the air itself is affected. Through the vital spirit, which is both the matter and origin of the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The spirit responsible for brain function and sensation</note>, it likewise affects the animal spirit. 

The quality of this air is of the greatest importance to the ingenious <note>Scholars and those with high intellectual capacity</note>, who labor heavily with such a spirit. Therefore, the choice of pure and luminous air, odors, and <term>Music</term> <note>Ficino believed music resonated directly with the "spiritus" to heal the mind</note> pertains to no one more than to them. For they judge these three to be the principal restoratives of the animal spirit. 

Indeed, "chosen" <note>specifically selected or purified</note> air is most powerful for life. For those born in the eighth month in <term>Egypt</term> live very long lives, and some in the temperate regions of <term>Greece</term> are very healthy by the benefit of the air, as <term>Aristotle</term> relates and Avicenna confirms. But surely, just as the body is composed of various parts and must be nourished by various foods, so the similarly composed spirit must be delighted and cherished by a certain variety of always-chosen air. It must be refreshed daily by a similar variety of chosen things. For air and odor seem to be like a kind of spirit. 

Now indeed, <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> and <term>Nicolaus</term> <note>Nicolaus of Damascus</note>, the Peripatetics, along with Galen, conclude that the vital and animal spirit is nourished both by odor and by air, because both are mixed and of a similar nature; and both, once inhaled, penetrate into the chest, where they are "cooked" and tempered for life, and diffused through the arteries. Where both...

<summary>Ficino argues that the "spirit"—the vital bridge between body and soul—is primarily nourished by vaporous substances like odors, pure air, and music rather than solid food. He explains that while the liver thrives on sweetness, the heart and the scholarly mind require "aromaticity" and temperate air to maintain vitality and prevent the decay of aging.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s medical advice on how to prolong life by nourishing the "spirit," the thin vapor that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immortal soul. He has just established that because the spirit is airy and vaporous, it can be fed by things of a similar nature, such as odors and fine air.</meta>

<page-num>526</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE CARE OF SCHOLARS<-

Once digested <note>original: "coctus"; literally "cooked," referring to the internal heat of digestion</note>, it nourishes both kinds of spirit (as they say), but especially the **animal spirit** <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul) was a refined vapor responsible for brain function, thought, and sensation</note>. They also say that the air we breathe benefits us not only by cooling our internal heat, but also by providing nourishment. For even very cold animals must breathe. They add that a thicker air is more suitable for the **natural spirit** <note>The spirit associated with the liver and nutrition</note> because it is more bodily; however, a subtle, pure, and clear air is better for the **vital spirit** <note>Associated with the heart</note>, and most of all for the animal spirit. Nor should it seem strange that a spirit so thin is nourished by thin things. Indeed, many small fish are nourished by the clearest water, and **basil** <note>original: "ozimum"</note> lives, grows, flowers, and smells sweet in similar water. I will pass over those elements upon which they say the chameleon and the salamander are fed <note>Ancient lore claimed chameleons lived on air and salamanders on fire</note>. Let us return to our own subject. It certainly matters a great deal what kind of air we breathe and what odors we inhale. For such does the spirit within us become. 

Indeed, the soul animates us through life only insofar as the spirit preserves a harmony that holds the soul and body together. The spirit within us is the first to live, and the most alive—it almost lives alone. Does it not often happen that by some sudden accident or emotion, life, sensation, and motion suddenly desert the limbs because the spirit has retreated to the innermost parts of the heart? And often these senses return immediately to the limbs through rubbing and odors, with the spirit returning there—as if life resided in that volatile spirit rather than in the humors or the limbs. Otherwise, because of the thick tenacity of the limbs, life would approach and depart from them quite slowly. 

Therefore, whoever desires to prolong life in the body, cultivate the spirit above all. Increase it with nourishments that increase the blood—specifically temperate and clear foods. Foster it always with chosen air, nourish it daily with sweet odors, and delight it with sounds and songs. But meanwhile, beware of smells that are too hot, flee those that are too cold, and choose those that are temperate; balance cold smells with hot ones, and dry with moist. 

Know that every odor, because it is the most subtle part of a body, possesses some heat. You should expect more nourishment from the odors of things that are themselves nourishing—such as the aromatic pear, the peach, and similar fruits. Even more nourishment comes from fresh, warm bread, and especially roasted meats, and most of all from wine. Just as flavor, which is wonderfully pleasing, provides abundant and rapid nourishment for the body, you should think of odor in the same way for the spirit. 

It pleases me to mention to you again **Democritus**, who, when he was just about to die, in order to comply with his friends, kept his spirit alive for four days by smelling warm bread; he would have preserved his spirit even longer if he had wished <note>A famous anecdote where the philosopher delayed his death to avoid mourning during a festival</note>. There are also those who say he did this with the smell of honey. I believe that if he used honey, he poured honey dissolved in white wine over the warm bread. For the smell of honey is not to be despised. Honey is the "flower of flowers"; it nourishes not a little by its very sweetness and, by its own quality, protects substances from decay for a long time. Therefore, if anyone knows how to eat honey as food so that it does not clog the passages with too much sweetness nor increase the bile with its heat, he will have a sure aid for a longer life. At least, use this condiment for those of cold and moist temperaments. 

But to recall you to odors: whenever you fear a "suffocation" or excessive compression of the spirits—which frequent sorrow and lethargy portend—love diffused odors. But where you fear the flight and exhaustion of the spirits, take odors infused into your food instead. And if you take any odors externally, apply them like a shield only to the left ribs <note>The area over the heart, the source of vital spirit</note>. Do you not see how suddenly the **womb** <note>original: "matrix"; refers to the medical theory of the "wandering womb" which was thought to move throughout the body in response to pleasant or foul smells</note> itself flings itself up or down toward odors? Or how swiftly the spirit flies to the mouth and nostrils, enticed by the bait of a sweet scent? 

When the spirit is found to be either meager or very "flighty"—which faint-heartedness often shows, along with bodily weakness occurring for small reasons—entice, or rather feed and retain it, not so much with odors applied externally as with those taken internally. Choose the odor of wine above all others. For the odor exhaling from wine nourishes the spirit greatly, coming from a substance that nourishes the body most quickly and affects the senses with pleasure. Such wine is especially warm, moist, fragrant, and clear. Sugar is also said to be such, if it gives off a scent. Cinnamon is similar, as are leopard's bane <note>doronicum</note>, anise, and sweet fennel, if they were to add more sweetness to their sharpness. 

But what balance nature has not made, create for yourselves. As often as you fear the scattering of the spirits, apply to the hotter and sharper substances those things which are able to restrain the flight of the spirit for a while and bring it to a halt: such as toasted bread, rose water, rose vinegar, rose, myrtle, violet, sandalwood, coriander, quince, and citron—combined with saffron, cloves, and cinnamon. Indeed, use camphor with barley when one must act against graying hair. I always love fresh mint, for the mind...
