<page-num>517</page-num>
<header>ON PROLONGING LIFE, BOOK II.</header>

...as well as healthful and most safe for the spirit. Lastly, remember that all things contrary to poison are very beneficial to life, not only in taste but also in smell—especially **theriac** <note>original: "theriacam"; a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "panacea" or universal antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note>. We have described these in the book against the plague, and we will describe them again in the following book. Among these, lest anything remain hidden from you, we also count wine. For just as hemlock is a poison to man, so wine is a poison to hemlock—not if drunk at the same time, but shortly afterward. And so that I do not entice you here with scents alone, I command you to prepare an <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> to be tasted every morning, sweet in smell and taste, and very healthful for life.

Take three ounces of **chebulic myrobalans**, one of **emblic**, one of **Indian**, and one of **belleric** <note>original: "chebularum... emblicarum... Indarum... belliricarum"; these are various types of medicinal fruits from India, highly prized in Renaissance pharmacy for balancing the "humors"</note>, half an ounce of **leopard's bane** <note>original: "doronici"</note>, two ounces of **cinnamon**, one drachm of **costus** <note>an aromatic root used in incense and medicine</note>, a third of a drachm of **ambergris**, and the same amount of **musk**. Grind them diligently and add as much **rose-sugar** as satisfies the taste. Add enough **red sandalwood** for color, and likewise as much honey of emblic or chebulic myrobalans as is needed to make the soft form of an electuary. Add as many sheets of **gold leaf** as there are ounces of the aforementioned ingredients. 

However, where a complex composition is too difficult, we have found through experience that this simple one is best: namely, one made of chebulic myrobalans, **sweet fennel**, and sugar liquefied in rose water, taken both on an empty stomach and after dinner. Remember, moreover, that **preserved myrobalans** are better; if you have dry ones, soak them for at least an entire day in oil of sweet almonds or cow’s butter before mixing them. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text</note> also approves for you a confection made from emblic and Indian myrobalans with honey of **anacardium** <note>the marking nut or cashew</note> and cooked butter. Likewise, chebulic myrobalans with **ginger** and scales of **iron**, or preferably **gold**. **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "Petrus Aponensis"; a 13-century Italian physician and astrologer</note> also approves a composition of **saffron**, **mace**, and **castoreum**, taken in equal parts, ground and mixed with wine. From this, he affirms that life is accustomed to being prolonged even for those who are nearly dying. Finally, **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note>, an excellent astrologer and physician, asserts that by the use of **triphera** <note>a class of electuaries, usually containing myrobalans</note> and similar things, life is made longer. In every triphera, the myrobalan is the foundation; but they improve upon this with certain subtle and soft things, especially where the myrobalan is drier, so that it may penetrate and neither block the passages nor dry out or constrict the bowels too much. Furthermore, we use it most conveniently with wine, but in moderation, lest it cause distress. As for Peter’s composition which I just mentioned, if it is indeed useful, I judge it to be more useful by smell than by drink.

### The Medicine of the Magi for the Elderly. Chapter XIX.

**T**he **Magi** <note>The Three Wise Men or Kings from the Nativity story</note>, observers of the stars, came to Christ, the leader of life, guided by a star, offering the precious treasure of life: **gold**, **frankincense**, and **myrrh**—dedicating three gifts for the three planetary lords to the Lord of the stars. Gold, indeed, for the temperament of **Jupiter**, which is the most balanced of all. Frankincense for the **Sun** (specifically Phoebus), burning with both heat and fragrance. Finally, myrrh, which firms and strengthens the body, for **Saturn**, the firmest of all the planets. 

Come here, therefore, all you elderly men, to the wise Magi, who bring gifts that will also prolong your life—gifts with which they are said to have once venerated the Author of life. Come, I say, you elderly who endure old age with difficulty. Come also you others, whomever the dread of approaching old age disturbs. Receive, I pray, these life-giving gifts with alacrity. Take two ounces of frankincense, one of myrrh, and half a drachm of gold beaten into leaves; grind the three together, melt them, and mix them into pills with a certain golden pure wine. Prepare this at an opportune time, when **Diana** <note>the Moon</note> enjoys a favorable aspect with **Phoebus** <note>the Sun</note> or **Jupiter**. After this, at any dawn, take a small portion of this great treasure and wash it down with a small drink of pure wine—unless perhaps the summer heat has grown intense, for then it is better to drink rose water. If any among you fears heat more at any time, let him add an equal weight of chebulic or emblic myrobalan to the combined weight of the frankincense, myrrh, and gold. This will undoubtedly protect the natural moisture from putrefaction. This will push away the dissipation of moisture for longer. This will nourish the three spirits within you: the **natural**, the **vital**, and the **animal**,

->senses, sharpen the wit, and<-
->preserve the memory.<-

## On avoiding the dangers that loom in every seven-year cycle of life.
### Chapter XX.

**S**ince astronomers have distributed the individual hours of the day to the planets in succession, and similarly the seven days of the week, and have even assigned the duties of the planets to the months during gestation, why should we not also arrange these by years? Just as **Saturn** ruled the infant hiding in the womb in the first month and the **Moon** in the last, so once born, with the order now reversed, let the **Moon** lead in the first year of life, **Mercury** in the second (if you wish), **Venus** in the third, the **Sun** in the fourth, **Mars** in the fifth, **Jupiter** in the sixth, and **Saturn** in the seventh. From there, the same order is repeated throughout life. Therefore, in every seventh year of life, a very great change occurs in the body, which is consequently very dangerous, since **Saturn** is generally "foreign" <note>original: "peregrinus"; in astrology, a planet is peregrine when it has no essential dignity in its current position, often making its influence more unpredictable or difficult</note> to us, and the governance then passes immediately from him, the highest of the planets, back to the **Moon**, the lowest of the planets. The Greek astronomers call these the **Climacteric years** <note>critical turning points in life, thought to occur every 7th or 9th year</note>; we call them "ladder-like," "step-like," or "decisive" years. Perhaps in illnesses, the planets even rule the movement of the humors or of nature itself through the days in that same order, which is why every seventh day is called "Judiciary" <note>or "critical days," used in ancient medicine to predict the turning point of a disease</note> for the same reason—and the fourth day as well, since it holds the middle position in a set of seven.

Therefore, if you desire to extend your life into old age, uninterrupted by any such "steps," consult an astrologer carefully whenever you approach any seventh year. Learn from where the danger looms over you, then either go to a physician or summon your own prudence and temperance. Even **Ptolemy** <note>the most influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer and geographer of antiquity</note> admits that the threats of the stars can be prevented by these remedies. He even adds that the promises of the stars can be increased, just as a tiller of the fields increases the strength of the earth. **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "Petrus Aponensis"; a famous 13th-century physician and astrologer</note> proves through many arguments and the testimony of **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and **Haly** <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician</note> that the natural end of life is not determined exactly to a hair’s breadth from the beginning, but can be moved further or closer. He asserts this based on both the stars and on physical matter. He concludes, following these authors and reasons, that even a natural death can be delayed, both with the "engines" of astrology and the protections of physicians. 

Therefore, we are not working on these precepts in vain. Do not be reluctant to ask physicians what your natural diet should be, and ask astrologers which star favors your life; when that star is well-positioned and the **Moon** is moving toward it, assemble those things you have learned will be beneficial. Do not be ashamed to listen often to those who seem to have attained a prosperous old age not so much by luck as by virtue. Furthermore, Ptolemy and the other professors of astronomy promise a prosperous and long life through certain images <note>astrological talismans</note> made of specific stones and metals under a certain constellation. Regarding these images, however, we are composing a commentary on **Plotinus** <note>this refers to Ficino's third book of "On Life," titled "On Obtaining Life from the Heavens"</note> concerning one part of them, and for the rest, concerning celestial favor. We believe that book should be added to this work next, just as we wished this to be written after the book we composed on caring for the health of men of letters. But as for that celestial favor I just mentioned for the sake of a long youth—speaking as much as a poet is allowed and acting as much as a physician is allowed—we shall seek it from **Phoebus** and **Bacchus**.

->To Phoebus and Bacchus alone belongs eternal youth,<-
->For unshorn hair becomes both gods.<-

**Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the sun god</note> and **Bacchus** <note>Dionysus, god of wine and vitality</note> are always inseparable brothers; both are almost the same. Phoebus is the very soul of that celestial sphere, while Bacchus is the sphere itself; indeed, Phoebus is the whole circuit of the sphere, while Bacchus is that flaming circle within this circuit. Or rather, Phoebus is the life-giving light in this flaming globe, while Bacchus is the health-giving heat arising from that light. Therefore they are always brothers and companions, and almost always one and the same. And what of this? If the Sun in Spring is indeed Phoebus, awakening the songs of birds with his own song and tempering the seasons with his lyre, then in Autumn the same Sun exists as Bacchus, the creator of wine. That father **Liber** <note>another name for Bacchus</note>, who loves the hills, brings us three things to preserve youth: first, these sunny hills; then, on these hills, especially the sweetest wine; and within the wine, a perpetual freedom from care. **Phoebus**, the brother of Bacchus, bestows three things with equal kindness: first, the daily light; under the nourishment of that light, sweet-smelling herbs; and in the shadow of this light, the lyre and perpetual song. By these "weights," and especially by these threads, **Clotho** <note>one of the three Fates (Parcae) who spins the thread of human life</note> will no longer be a "Sparer" <note>original: "Parca"; Ficino is making a pun on "Parca" (the Fate) and "parcitas" (frugality or being sparing)</note> but will draw out for us the long threads of life. Almost all the poets sing of the three **Fates**. We, though not poets, also sing of three. A prudent **restraint** in all diet begins a long life for us; a constant **restraint** in undergoing cares prolongs that life; but a negligent **restraint** in enjoying the heavens cuts life short. **Pythagoras** celebrated temperance above all things...

...celebrates, we also celebrate three things at present. Maintain **temperance in your emotions**, maintain **temperance in your entire diet**, and observe the **temperateness of the air**. # MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine, on the third book,
### On Obtaining Life from the Heavens; an epistolary
#### PREFACE
### addressed to the Most Serene King of Pannonia <note>original: "Pannoniæ"; refers to the Kingdom of Hungary, specifically King Matthias Corvinus (reigned 1458–1490), a great patron of the Renaissance</note>.

**M**ost happy King of all, the ancient philosophers most diligently investigated the powers of the celestial bodies and the natures of lower things. Since they considered that a man is wise in vain who is not wise for his own benefit, they rightly seem to have directed their entire investigation primarily toward **obtaining life for themselves from the heavens**. They judged (as I believe) that both the elements and the things composed of them would be known to them in vain, and that the movements and influences of the heavens would be observed with too much secondary concern, unless these things, once known and joined together, should eventually lead them toward life and happiness. 

Furthermore, such contemplation was of benefit to them, first in this present life. For **Pythagoras**, **Democritus**, and **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>original: "Apolloniusque, Theanæus"; a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, and whoever else applied themselves especially to this, attained prosperous health and a long-lived life through the use of the things they had learned. It contributed, moreover, to their future life—both through the propagation of their glory among posterity and by being enjoyed with God in eternity. For indeed, from the wonderful order of the whole world, they finally came to know its Ruler, and loved Him, their kinsman, above all things. 

To you, indeed, your high-mindedness, magnificence, and victory promise a glory that will endure through all ages. Divine mercy also promises a life blessed for eternity with God in exchange for your singular piety and justice. Finally, the happy stars have decreed for you a prosperous life among mortals and one long in years (as far as I have been able to conjecture from certain signs). However, your own diligence and the care of your physicians and astrologers can undoubtedly ensure that what the stars promise, they actually provide with the firmest faith, and even extend with a fuller abundance. Indeed, all the most learned astrologers and physicians confess that this can be achieved through science and prudence. 

Therefore, while I had recently composed a commentary among the books of **Plotinus** <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher whose works Ficino translated and interpreted</note> destined for the great **Lorenzo de' Medici**, specifically on the book by Plotinus regarding the drawing of favor from the heavens, I decided to select that particular piece now from among our other commentaries and dedicate it specifically to your Majesty, with the approval of Lorenzo himself. I hope that while I consult the prosperity of your life, I shall meanwhile consult the life and splendor of our age and of the human race. And so that these writings of ours might more powerfully benefit the King's health and prosperity, I thought they should be sent by way of **Valor** himself <note>original: "Valorem"; Ficino is punning on the name of his friend Filippo Valori, who delivered the manuscript to the King</note>. I pray, most merciful King, that you embrace this "Valor" of ours. For your nature, virtue, and authority are so powerful that without you, even **Valor** <note>meaning both the messenger Filippo Valori and the concept of "strength" or "worth"</note> itself cannot be strong. 

July 10, 1489. Florence.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S
## exhortation to the Reader of the
### following work.

**G**reetings, ingenious guest. Greetings again, whoever you are that are eager for health <note>original: "salutis"; Ficino plays on the Latin word *salus*, which means both "health" and "salvation," as well as "greeting."</note>, you who approach our threshold. I pray, eager guest, see first how hospitable I am. It was certainly the duty of the one entering to immediately offer a greeting to the household. But I, anticipating you with a greeting, have already commanded you to be well as soon as you were in sight. I received you most willingly as you entered and were still unknown. To the one who lingers with me, I will give the promised health (if God breathes upon us). You have therefore found a hospitality that is friendly to all, and now full of love toward you. If by chance you bring anything with you contrary to love, or if you hold any hatred, I pray you lay it down before you touch these life-giving medicines. For love and the pleasure of your parents gave you life. In turn, hatred and grief take life away. Therefore, for the person whom hateful grief vexes, there is no place left anywhere for life-giving medicine. For this reason, hereafter I address you not only as a guest, but as a friend.

The workshop <note>original: "officina"; Ficino envisions his book as a laboratory or pharmacy where he prepares spiritual and physical cures.</note> of your Marsilio is somewhat larger than can be confined by these railings alone which you see here. For it is not circumscribed by this following book alone, but also by the two preceding ones. Truly, in summary, the whole work is a kind of medicine intended to help life according to its powers, so that your life may be strong and long. And it strives for this everywhere through the help of physicians, aided from heaven. Indeed, this workshop of ours brings forth various antidotes, drugs, poultices, ointments, and remedies according to the different temperaments and natures of men. If some things perhaps please you less, let those go, but do not reject the rest because of them.

Finally, if you do not approve of **astronomical images** <term>imagines astronomicas; talismans or amulets engraved with celestial symbols intended to capture the influence of specific planets or stars to heal the wearer</term>, which were otherwise invented for the health of mortals—and which I myself do not so much approve of as describe—you may certainly discard these with my permission, and even, if you wish, my advice. But do not neglect those medicines strengthened by a certain heavenly support, unless by chance you have neglected life itself. For I have found by frequent and long experience that there is as much difference between medicines of this kind and others made without an expert astrologer as there is between pure wine and water. This is so true that even an infant born in Florence in the eighth month from conception, in the month of March, with the night ascending and **Saturn retrograde** <term>retrogrado; the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky, which in traditional astrology often signified a weakened or Malefic influence</term>, appearing half-dead, might seem through this kind of diligence to be returned to life by us—or rather by God—instead of merely preserved; and he has now completed nearly three years in good health. Now truly, if I relate more things of this same kind, I shall speak the truth. I shall assert this not boastfully (which is entirely foreign to a philosopher) but rather by way of encouragement. But we have now addressed you enough, partly winning you over, and partly encouraging you. Next,

->therefore let us speak with Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino's Book III is largely a commentary on a specific passage from Plotinus regarding the "World Soul."</note>, so finally<-
->for you more diligently<-
->consulting.<-

# MARSILIO FICINO
## of Florence, on Obtaining Life from the
### Heavens, composed by the same author among his
### Commentaries on Plotinus.

->In what consists, according to Plotinus, the power that attracts favor from the heavens; namely, that the soul of the world and the souls of the stars and demons <note>Ficino uses the term "demons" (daemones) in the classical Greek sense: intermediary spirits or protective powers that bridge the gap between gods and men, not necessarily evil entities.</note> are easily drawn by the appropriate forms of bodies. Chapter I.<-

**I**f there were only these two things in the world—here Intellect, and there Body—but Soul <note>original: "anima"; specifically referring to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, which Neoplatonists believed animated the entire universe.</note> were absent, then neither would Intellect be drawn to Body (for it is entirely immovable and lacks the impulse of motion, being as far distant from Body as possible), nor would Body be drawn to Intellect, as it is by itself ineffective and unfit for motion, and far removed from Intellect. But if a Soul were placed between them, conforming to both, an attraction would easily occur from both sides to both sides. First, the Soul itself is most easily led, since it is the primary moving thing, and is mobile from itself and of its own accord. Furthermore, since (as I have said) it contains all the middle levels of things within itself in its own way, it is related to both sides by a close connection. Therefore, it is joined to all things—even equally to those things which are distant from each other, provided they are not distant from the Soul itself. For besides the fact that it conforms on one side to divine things and on the other to transitory things, and inclines toward both by affection, it is meanwhile entirely present everywhere at once. 

Added to this is the fact that the Soul of the World possesses at least as many <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales"; these are the generative spiritual "seeds" or blueprints within the World Soul that correspond to the eternal Ideas in the Divine Mind.</note> of things by divine gift as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind, and by these reasons it fashions as many species in matter. Thus, every species corresponds to its own Idea through its own seminal reason, and through this reason it can often easily receive something from that Idea, since it was created from it through this very reason. Therefore, if it should ever degenerate from its own proper form, it can be reshaped again through this closest medium, and through that medium it can be easily reformed by the Idea. Indeed, if you correctly apply many things which are scattered but still conform to a certain Idea to a specific species of thing or to an individual within it, you will soon draw a unique gift from the Idea into this matter which has been so opportunely prepared—drawing it, clearly, through the seminal reason of the Soul.

For it is not Intellect itself that is properly drawn, but the Soul. Therefore, let no one think that certain divinities <note>original: "numina"</note> who are completely segregated from matter are attracted by specific materials of the world, but rather demons, and the gifts of the animated world and of the living stars. Again, let no one wonder that the Soul can be, as it were, allured through material forms. For the Soul itself created such baits <note>original: "escas"</note> suitable for itself in which it might be allured, and it always and willingly dwells in them. Nor is there anything found in the entire living world so deformed that Soul is not present to it, or that the gift of Soul is not within it. 

Therefore, Zoroaster called such harmonies of forms with the reasons of the World Soul "divine lures," which Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop who wrote on dreams and the spirit.</note> also confirmed were magical enchantments. Finally, one should believe that at a certain time, all gifts are drawn from the Soul into a specific species of matter, but only the gifts of the specific "seed" from which that species sprouted, and of similar seeds. Thus, a human being, by applying only human things, does not claim for himself the proper gifts of fish or birds, but rather human and similar gifts. By applying those things which belong to a certain star and its demon, he undergoes the specific influence of that star and demon, just as wood prepared with sulfur is ready for a flame that is present everywhere. 

And this influence is received not only through the rays of the star and the demon themselves, but also through the Soul of the World, which is present everywhere. In the Soul, the reason of every star and demon flourishes—partly as a seminal reason for generating, and partly as an exemplary reason for knowing. For according to the ancient Platonists, the Soul, by its own reasons, built figures in the heavens beyond the stars, and parts of them such that they themselves also become certain figures; and it impressed properties upon all of these. In these stars, figures, parts, and properties, all the species of lower things and their properties are contained. For the universal figure, it established eight and forty...

...sixty, namely twelve in the zodiac and thirty-six outside of it. Likewise, there are thirty-six in the zodiac corresponding to the number of "faces" <note>Also known as decans, these are ten-degree segments of the zodiac signs, each associated with a specific celestial power.</note>. Again, in that same place, there are three hundred and sixty corresponding to the number of degrees. For in every degree there are many stars, from which the images there are composed. Similarly, he divided the images outside the zodiac into many figures according to the number of their faces and degrees. Finally, he established certain relationships and proportions between these universal images and the universal forms <note>Ficino is describing a "ladder" of reality where physical shapes on earth reflect geometric patterns in the stars, which in turn reflect divine ideas.</note>, which themselves exist as images there. Indeed, figures of this kind each have their own continuity arising from the rays of their stars meeting one another, joined by a certain peculiar property. From these most orderly forms depend the forms of lower things, which are clearly organized from that source. These celestial forms, although distinct from one another, proceed from the "reasons" <term>rationes</term> <note>These are the "rational principles" or blueprints within the Soul that guide the formation of matter.</note> of the soul which are joined together, and are in a way changeable things proceeding from stable ones. But insofar as these celestial forms do not comprehend themselves, they are referred back to the forms in the Mind—either the animal mind or a higher one—which do comprehend themselves; these, though manifold, are reduced to the most simple One and the Good, just as the celestial figures are reduced to the pole. 

But let us return to the soul. When, therefore, the soul generates the specific forms and powers of lower things, it effects them through its own "reasons," with the assistance of the stars and celestial forms. However, the singular gifts of individuals—which are often as wonderful in certain people as they usually are in entire species—it provides through "seminal reasons" <note>The *rationes seminales* are the latent "seeds" or creative potentials within the World Soul that unfold into specific physical realities.</note> in a similar way, though not so much through the help of celestial forms and figures as through the position of the stars, the habit of their motions, and the aspects of the Planets, both among themselves and in relation to the stars higher than the Planets. 

Indeed, our soul, beyond the specific powers of its members, brings forth a common virtue of life everywhere within us, but most especially through the heart, which is like the fountain of the fire closest to the soul. Similarly, the World Soul, thriving everywhere, unfolds its common virtue of life throughout all things, especially through the Sun. Hence, some people place the soul—both in us and in the world—entirely in every member, but primarily in the heart and the Sun. Always remember that just as the virtue of our soul is applied to our limbs through the spirit <note>In Ficino’s medical theory, "spirit" is a subtle, vaporous substance that links the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note>, so the virtue of the World Soul is spread through all things by the **fifth essence** <note>The *quinta essentia* or quintessence: the celestial "ether" that fills the universe and acts as the spirit of the world.</note>, which thrives everywhere like a spirit within the worldly body. This virtue is most especially infused into those things that have drawn in the most of this spirit. 

Furthermore, this fifth essence can be taken into us more and more if one knows how to separate it when it is mixed with other elements, or at least if one frequently uses those things which abound in it—especially the purer sort, such as choice wine, sugar, balsam, gold, precious stones, and myrobalans <note>A type of dried fruit used in Renaissance pharmacy for its astringent properties.</note>. It is also found in things that smell most sweet and things that shine, especially those which possess a warm, moist, and clear quality in a subtle substance. Besides wine, this includes the whitest sugar, especially if you add gold to it, and the scent of cinnamon and roses. Moreover, just as food properly taken into us—though not alive itself—is reduced by our spirit to the form of our life, so too our bodies, when properly adapted to the worldly body and spirit (namely through worldly things and through our own spirit), draw as much as possible from the life of the world. 

If you wish for food to take on the form of your brain, liver, or stomach above all else, take food as similar as possible—that is, the brain, liver, and stomach of animals not far distant from human nature. If you desire your body and spirit to receive virtue from some member of the world—namely from the **Sun**—seek those things which are primarily "Solar" among metals and stones, and even more among plants, but most of all among animals, and especially among men. For things more similar to you undoubtedly confer more. These things are to be displayed outwardly and taken inwardly as much as possible, especially on the day and hour of the Sun, and while the Sun is ruling in the figure of the heavens. 

"Solar" things include all stones and flowers called **heliotropes** because they turn toward the Sun. Also gold, orpiment <note>A yellow mineral (arsenic trisulfide) used as a pigment.</note> and golden colors, chrysolite, carbuncle, myrrh, frankincense, musk, amber, balsam, yellow honey, aromatic reed, saffron, spikenard, cinnamon, aloeswood, and other spices; the Ram, the Hawk, the rooster, the swan, the lion, the beetle, the crocodile; and men who are blond, curly-haired, often bald, and magnanimous. These can be adapted for use partly through foods, partly through ointments and fumigations. These things should be sensed and thought of frequently, and above all, they should be loved. Much light must also be sought. If you suspect the stomach is deprived of heat from the liver, draw the faculty of the liver to the stomach, both by rubbing and by warm applications using things that agree with the liver...

Similarly, so that your body is not forsaken by Jupiter, move your body during the day and hour in the reign of Jupiter, and meanwhile make use of Jovial things <note>items associated with the planet Jupiter</note>: silver, hyacinth, topaz, coral, crystal, beryl, zinc oxide, sapphire, airy and green colors, wine, white sugar, honey, and thoughts and feelings that are mostly Jovial—that is, constant, balanced, religious, and law-abiding. ## *On the harmony of the world, and on the nature of man according to the stars. How attraction is made from each individual star.* Chapter 11.

No one ought to distrust that we, and all things around us, can claim celestial gifts for ourselves through certain preparations. For these things were made by the heavens, are continually ruled by them, and were prepared from the beginning primarily for that purpose. And what is most important: the world is a living being <note>the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul</note>, more alive within itself than any other animal, provided it is the most perfect animal. Therefore, just as in us the quality and movement of any member—especially a principal one—pertains to the others, so the acts of the principal members in the world move all things; the lower members easily receive from the higher ones, which are prepared to give of their own accord. For the more powerful a cause is, the readier it is to act, and thus the more inclined it is to give. Therefore, a small preparation applied by us is sufficient for capturing the gifts of the heavens, provided that each person accommodates himself especially to that to which he is chiefly subject. 

But before the specific nature of each of us, we must consider the specific nature of the human species. The Arabic astrologers <note>likely referring to scholars like Al-Kindi or Albumasar</note> agreed that this nature is Solar. I conjecture this to be true from man's erect and beautiful stature, the subtlety of his humors, the clarity of his spirit, the perspicuity of his imagination, and his pursuit of truth and glory. I even add to this a Mercurial property, on account of the strenuous movement of man's versatile intellect. And since the human race—born naked, unarmed, and in need of everything—procures all these things for itself by its own industry, this is the hallmark of Mercury. I also add a Jovial property on account of the temperate complexion of the body and our laws. And since we receive life in the second month [of gestation], when Jupiter rules, and are born in the ninth, when he again receives dominion. 

Thus, the human species will finally be able to claim even more ample gifts from these three [the Sun, Mercury, and Jupiter] if it accommodates itself to them more and more every day through Solar, Mercurial, and Jovial things. But what of the others? Saturn does not easily signify the common quality and lot of the human race, but rather a man set apart from others, whether divine or beastly, blessed or crushed by extreme misery. Mars, the Moon, and Venus represent affections and acts common to man and other animals alike. 

Let us return, therefore, to the Sun, Jupiter, and Mercury. We have mentioned some Solar and Jovial things, but somehow we passed over Mercurial things; they are of this sort: Tin <note>original: "Stannum" – though usually assigned to Jupiter, Ficino follows a tradition here linking it to Mercury</note>, silver (especially quicksilver), silver marcasite, the agate stone, porphyry glass, and things that mix saffron-yellow with green, the emerald, and lacquer. Wise and ingenious animals that are also strenuous: monkeys and dogs. Men who are eloquent, sharp, versatile, with long faces and hands that are not fat. 

These things pertaining to a planet are to be sought and put into practice while that planet is ruling (as we said) in its day and hour; if possible, also when it is in its own house, or its exaltation, or at least in its triplicity, term, and angle of the sky <term>dignities</term> <note>These are technical terms for positions in the zodiac where a planet's power is strengthened</note>, direct and outside of "combustion" <note>not too close to the Sun</note>, and more often in the east if it is superior to the Sun, likewise in its apogee <note>original: "Auge"</note>, and when it is regarded by the Moon. If anyone seeks a benefit from the Moon herself or from Venus, he must observe similar times. From Venus, one seeks through her animals which we mentioned, and through carnelian, sapphire, lapis lazuli, yellow and red copper, coral, and all beautiful and varied or green colors, flowers, harmonies, and sweet odors and flavors. From the Moon, one seeks through white, moist, and green things, through silver, crystal, pearls <note>original: "uniones"</note>, and silver marcasite. Because Saturn indeed grants stability and perseverance...

...threatens. Mars, on the other hand, is the planet of effectiveness of motion; we are sometimes compelled to request patronage even from these planets for the sake of such motion, provided that the [astrological] times are similarly observed. From the former [Saturn], we seek favor through certain materials that are in a way earthy, dark, and leaden, such as dark Jasper, the Magnet <note>the lodestone, used for its magnetic properties</note>, the cameo-stone <note>original: "camoium," likely referring to sardonyx or stones used for cameos</note> and chalcedony, and in some part through gold and golden Marcasite <note>original: "Marcassitam," iron pyrite or "fool's gold," often used in Renaissance alchemy</note>. From Mars, however, we seek favor through fiery red things, red brass, all sulfurous things, iron, and bloodstone <note>original: "lapidem sanguineum," or hematite, believed to stem the flow of blood</note>. Nor is it that Saturn does not possess something of gold; for he is thought to possess it because of its weight. Furthermore, just as gold is similar to the Sun, so it exists in all metals just as the Sun exists among all the planets and stars.

Now, if anyone should suspect that Saturn and Mars are harmful by nature—a thing which I myself have never believed—nevertheless, even these must be used, just as Physicians sometimes make use of poisons, which Ptolemy proves in his *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy</note>. Therefore, the power of Saturn will sometimes be beneficial if taken cautiously, just as physicians use things that are astringent and binding, or even those that induce stupor, such as opium and mandrake. The power of Mars may be used as well, like Euphorbium <note>a caustic plant resin</note> and hellebore. Indeed, the most cautious in this matter seem to have been the Brahman Magi and the Pythagoreans, who, because they feared the tyranny of Saturn due to their diligent pursuit of philosophy, clothed themselves in white garments and daily used Jovial or Phoebaean <note>referring to Jupiter or the Sun/Apollo</note> sounds and songs, and lived mostly under the open sky.

Everywhere, indeed, remember that through the affection and pursuit of the mind, and through the very quality of our spirit, we are most easily and suddenly exposed to the planets that signify that same affection and that kind of pursuit and quality. Very often, therefore, we are subjected to Saturn by withdrawing from human affairs through leisure, solitude, and constancy, or through Theology and the more secret philosophy, superstition, Magic, agriculture, and through sorrow. We are subjected to Jupiter through civil and ambitious business, through natural and common philosophy, through civil religion, and ancient laws. To Mars through anger and contests; to the Sun and Mercury through the study of eloquence, song, truth, glory, and skill; to Venus through joy, music, and festivities; to the Moon through a way of living similar to that of plants <note>referring to a simple, vegetative existence or a specific diet</note>. 

But keep this difference in mind: the exercise of a more public and broad genius belongs to the Sun, while the private and technical kind belongs rather to Mercury. Furthermore, grave music belongs to Jupiter and the Sun, light music to Venus, and that which is in between to Mercury. A similar reasoning applies to the fixed stars. This indeed is the general rule for the human species. But it shall be a specific rule for each individual to explore which star and what good things it promised in their nativity <note>the individual's birth chart</note>, and to demand grace from that star rather than another. And from each star, one should expect not just any gift, or what belongs to another, but what is its own—unless perhaps you then receive many general gifts from the Sun, as if from a general leader of the heavenly things, and from Jupiter in a nearly similar way; and likewise all worldly things from the soul and spirit of the world. That this world is animated like any other animal, and much more effectively so, is proven not only by Platonic arguments but also by the testimonies of the Arab Astrologers. There they also prove that from a certain application of our spirit to the <term>spirit of the world</term> <note>spiritus mundi: a subtle substance that bridges the physical world and the divine soul</note>, performed through the physical art and through affection, celestial goods are channeled into our soul and body. This happens on one hand through our spirit as the medium within us, which is then strengthened by the spirit of the world, and on the other hand through the rays of the stars acting fortunately upon our spirit, which is similar in nature to those rays and then adapts itself to the heavenly things.

->*That between the soul of the world and its body there is manifest its spirit, in whose power are the four elements. And that we can draw this through our spirit.*<-

### Chapter III.

**C**ertainly the worldly body, as far as appears from its motion and generation, is everywhere alive; the Indian Philosophers prove this from the fact that it generates living things from itself everywhere. Therefore, it lives through a soul present to it everywhere and perfectly accommodated to it. Thus, between the world’s body—which is tangible and in part perishable—and its soul itself, whose nature is too distant from such a body, there exists everywhere a spirit, just as there is between the soul and body in us, provided that life is always communicated everywhere by the soul to the thicker body. For such a spirit is necessarily required as a medium by which the divine soul may both be present to the thicker body and bestow life deeply upon it. However, every body easily perceptible to you, being suited to your senses, is thicker, and from the soul...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's exploration of the "World Spirit" (spiritus mundi), a vital substance that bridges the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul. Having discussed specific planetary materials on the previous page, Ficino now moves toward a more general theory of how life and "spirit" permeate the entire universe.</meta>

<page-num>535</page-num>
<header>COMPARISONS. BOOK III.</header>
<sig>LI 4</sig>

The most divine soul, when far removed from its source, degenerates. There is a need, therefore, for the support of a more excellent body that is almost not a body at all. Furthermore, we know that all living things—plants as well as animals—live and generate through a certain **spirit** <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, "spirit" (spiritus) is not a ghost, but a subtle, vaporous substance that acts as a bridge, allowing the immaterial soul to communicate with and move the heavy, material body.</note> similar to this one. And among the elements, that which is most "spiritual" <note>meaning most vaporous or airy</note> generates most swiftly and is moved perpetually as if it were alive. But meanwhile you may ask: if elements and living beings generate something similar to themselves by their own spirit, why do stones and metals not generate, since they are midway between elements and living beings? It is because the spirit in them is confined within a thicker matter. Yet if that spirit were properly separated and kept apart, it would be able to generate something similar to itself like a "seed-like power," provided it were applied to some matter of the same kind. Physicians <note>here referring to alchemists or natural philosophers</note> diligently separate such a spirit from gold by a certain sublimation over fire, and when they apply it to any other metal, they will produce gold. Such a spirit, properly drawn from gold or another source and preserved, the **Arabian Astrologers** call the **Elixir**. 

But let us return to the **World Spirit**, through which the world generates all things, since all things also generate through their own spirit. This World Spirit we can call both the "Heavens" and the **fifth essence** <note>term: "fifth essence" (quintessence). Beyond the four physical elements (earth, water, air, fire), this was believed to be the pure, celestial substance of the stars.</note>. This is almost the same thing in the body of the world as our own spirit is in ours. There is this primary exception: the World Soul does not draw this spirit from the four elements as if from its own humors, as our soul draws ours from our humors. Rather—to speak in a **Platonic** or **Plotinic** <note>referring to the philosopher Plotinus</note> manner—the World Soul procreates it directly from its own generative power, just as you procreate a thought. Together with this spirit, it procreates the stars, and immediately through it, it gives birth to the four elements, as if all things were contained within the power of that spirit. 

The spirit itself is a most thin body, almost not a body, and almost already a soul. Likewise, it is almost not a soul, and almost already a body. In its power, there is a minimum of the nature of earth, but more of water, more still of air, and again even more of fire, and the greatest amount of the "stellar fire." The very sizes of the stars and elements have emerged according to the measures of these levels. This spirit thrives everywhere in all things as the immediate author and motion of all generation, of which that famous poet <note>Virgil, in the Aeneid (6.726)</note> said: *The spirit nourishes from within.* <note>original Latin: "Spiritus intus alit."</note> It is entirely luminous, hot, moist, and life-giving by its own nature, having obtained such gifts from the higher gifts of the soul. **Iarchas the Indian** testified that **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker from the 1st century AD.</note> had drunk deeply of this spirit, saying: 
> No one should wonder, O Apollonius, that you have attained the knowledge of divination, since you carry so much of the **ether** <note>the pure upper air or celestial spirit</note> in your soul.

---

-> *That our spirit may draw in the World Spirit through the rays of the Sun and Jupiter, and to what extent it becomes "Solar" and "Jovial." Chapter IV.* <-

**Y**ou will therefore strive, first and foremost, to introduce this spirit into yourself. By this means, you will bring back certain natural benefits, both from the body of the world and from its soul, and even from the stars and the **daemons** <note>term: "daemons." In the Platonic tradition, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences that exist between humans and the divine.</note>. For the spirit itself is the middle point between the thick body of the world and the soul, and within it—and through it—are the stars and the daemons. For whether the body of the world and worldly things are directly from the World Soul (as **Plotinus** and **Porphyry** prefer), or whether the worldly body as well as the soul is directly from God (as our own theologians prefer, and perhaps **Timaeus the Pythagorean**), the world certainly lives and breathes, and we are permitted to draw in its spirit. 

It is drawn in properly by a human through his own spirit, which is conformable to it by its own nature, especially if it is made even more related to it by art—that is, if it becomes "celestial" to the highest degree. It becomes celestial if it is purged of filth, and entirely of those things which cling to it that are unlike the heavens. Indeed, if such filth exists—not only within the viscera, but even in the mind, on the skin, in clothing, or in one’s dwelling and air—it frequently infects the spirit. 

Finally, the spirit will be made celestial if it creates "spheres" for itself through the circular motion of the mind and body. It will become celestial if, through the frequent sight and contemplation of light, it begins to glow. It becomes celestial if those things similar to heaven are applied to it, using that same diligence with which **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note> treats the spirit in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*, and which we ourselves strove to treat in our book *On Caring for the Health of Scholars*. In that work, first, the clouding vapors are separated from the spirit, even through purging medicines. Second, it is illuminated by shining things. Third, it is cultivated in such a way that it is simultaneously thinned and strengthened. Lastly, it will become most celestial—as much as present reason dictates—if the rays and influence of the **Sun** (which rules among the celestial bodies) are applied to it above all. And so, through this spirit as a middle-ground within us, celestial goods will overflow into our body and mind: all celestial goods, I say, for all things are contained within the Sun. Moreover, the Sun will properly contribute to making the spirit "Solar" when it is in the sign of **Aries** or **Leo**.

->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE<-

...the Moon looking upon him <note>Original: *ipsum* refers to the Sun</note>, especially in **Leo**, where he so enlivens our spirit that he fortifies it to repel the poison of an **Epidemic**. This is clearly seen in **Babylon** and **Egypt**, and in regions belonging to the sign of Leo, where the Sun entering Leo settles an epidemic for the very reason we have stated. At that time, therefore, you should also compose exquisite **Solar** remedies everywhere. Then begin to use Solar things, though with the caution that you diligently avoid drying out under the heat. However, the Solar spirit cannot easily escape unless it is very abundant. For **abundance** <note>Original: *amplitudo*—referring to the fullness or "breath" of the spirit</note> pertains most of all to the Sun. Indeed, much will be achieved both by diligence—cherishing the heart with **cordials** <note>Medicines or foods believed to strengthen the heart</note> both internally and externally—and also by a diet of subtle foods that are nonetheless very nourishing, easy, and healthy. Frequent and gentle movement is also beneficial, as is timely rest, and thin, serene air removed from heat and frost, and above all, a **joyful mind**. Again, the spirit will not be Solar unless it is warm, subtle, and clear. You will make it subtle and clear if you avoid sad, thick, and dark things. Use bright and joyful things, both inside and out. You should receive much light by day and night. Expel filth, idleness, and lethargy. Above all, **avoid darkness**. 

However, when you are about to lead the spirit toward the heat natural to the Sun, take care not to lead it to the third degree of heat and dryness. For the heat of the Sun itself does not naturally dry things out; otherwise, the Sun would not be the Lord of life and generation and the author of growth. Rather, it happens that things dry out when his rays are trapped in the hollows of dry matter. Therefore, you should apply and preserve a subtle moisture for that heat—the kind that is Solar, and especially **Jovian** <note>Related to the planet Jupiter</note>—within the spirit, through the use of such things, if you intend to produce a Solar effect; otherwise, you might perhaps lead it toward a **Martian** <note>Related to the planet Mars</note> nature instead of a Solar one. They say that **Mars** is similar to the Sun in a few ways—and these are obvious and not particularly excellent—and meanwhile, he is an enemy. But we know that **Jupiter** is most similar to the Sun in many excellent gifts, though they are more hidden, and he is a most dear friend. Hence **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer</note>, where he discusses **consonance** <note>The harmonic relationship between planets based on their positions</note>, says that Jupiter consonates most perfectly with the Sun above all others, and Venus with the Moon; and all Astrologers attribute a universal beneficence to the Sun just as they do to Jupiter. However, the Sun acts more effectively in these matters, and Jupiter acts under the power of the Sun. In both, heat flourishes and overcomes moisture. But in Jupiter it overcomes it moderately, while in the Sun it overcomes it excellently; in both cases, it is beneficial. 

Since they consonate so well, you can easily make your spirit Solar and Jovian at the same time, and you can rightly mix Solar and Jovian things together, especially if you compose them with each other and apply them to the spirit when Jupiter looks at the Sun in **trine** or **sextile** <note>Astrological aspects: a "trine" is 120 degrees apart (harmonious), a "sextile" is 60 degrees (favorable)</note>, or at least when the Moon proceeds from the aspect of one to look upon the other. Especially when she moves from the aspect of the Sun toward a **conjunction** with Jupiter. Separately, you will specifically make a spirit Solar or Jovian when you observe the Moon’s aspect toward the Sun or toward Jupiter. Even so, once you have attained the nature of the one, you will soon easily attain the nature of the other. Understand a **sextile** aspect to be when two planets are distant from each other by the space of two signs. A **trine**, however, is when they differ by an interval of four signs. They measure a **conjunction** or the aspect of the Moon to others by twelve degrees before and as many after.

### *That the three Graces are Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus, and that Jupiter is the middle of the twin Graces, and best suited to us.*
### *Chapter V.*

**Y**ou will find Jovian compositions and treatments, as well as Solar ones, in our book *On Long Life*, and in the book *On the Care of Scholars*. There we also mixed in many **Venereal** <note>Related to the planet Venus</note> things. For in the case of scholars, we fear the dryness which Venus resists. And Venus herself is most friendly to Jupiter, just as Jupiter is to the Sun; they are like the **three Graces** <note>In mythology, the Charites (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia), who represent charm, grace, and beauty</note> in harmony and joined together. From these three Graces of heaven and from stars of the same kind, Astrologers both hope for and diligently seek out favors, and they believe and arrange for them to be transmitted through **Mercury** and the **Moon**, as if they were messengers; they believe this happens easily and commonly through the Moon. Indeed, they think the Moon joined with Jupiter or Venus is more fortunate than if she looked through a sextile or trine. Nevertheless, if she is "received" by them while looking through a trine, they consider it almost as if she were in conjunction. Similarly, if she is seen by the Sun and at the same time received. If we wished to run through all the powers and effects of these three and of similar stars one by one, we would be undertaking a long work, difficult to search out and most difficult to observe...

->COMPARING THINGS. BOOK III.<-

...observed. If we turn ourselves specifically to **Venus**, we will not easily possess the **Sun**. If specifically to the **Sun**, we will not easily possess **Venus**. Therefore, so that we may embrace the three Graces <note>In this context, the "three Graces" refer to the combined beneficial influences of the Sun, Venus, and Jupiter</note> at once in a single being, we shall finally take refuge in **Jupiter**. He is the medium between the **Sun** and **Venus** in both nature and effect, being extremely tempered in quality. Whatever is hoped for from **Venus** or from the **Sun**, he delivers in his own particular way—more magnificently and honorably than **Venus**, and more temperately than the **Sun**. In all things, he is most consistent with human nature. 

We shall therefore utilize **Jupiter** when both he and the **Moon** possess dignity <note>In astrology, "dignity" refers to a planet being in a position of strength, such as its own zodiac sign</note>, whether natural or accidental, and are either together or look upon each other favorably. If this cannot be achieved, mix **Solar** and **Venereal** things together; in this way, you will create a "**Jovial**" composite from both. This is done specifically when the **Moon** moves from a conjunction with **Venus** toward a sextile aspect <note>A harmonious 60-degree angle</note> with the **Sun**, or vice versa. 

In composing things that cherish and strengthen the heart and the spirit, remember that the **Moon** contributes most of all, especially if, along with these gifts, she travels through the airy signs—most importantly **Aquarius**, which is considered the most airy of all. Or, if she is in her own domicile <note>Cancer</note>, or her exaltation <note>Taurus</note>, or in the house of **Jupiter** or the **Sun**. Wherever she may be, she should occupy one of those twenty-eight mansions <note>The "Mansions of the Moon" are 28 divisions of the lunar cycle used in ancient astrology</note> that is suitable both to herself and to the work at hand.

### On the natural, vital, and animal powers, and which planets help or hinder each, especially through their aspects.
#### Chapter VI.

**T**he primary discipline is to correctly understand which spirit, which power, and which matter these **Planets** chiefly signify. The **Moon** and **Venus** signify the <term>natural spirit</term> <note>The "natural spirit" was believed to reside in the liver and govern nutrition and growth</note> and the generative power, as well as things that increase them. **Jupiter** signifies the same, but more effectively; he also rules the liver and stomach. He has no small part in the heart, the spirit, and the <term>vital power</term> <note>The "vital spirit" was believed to reside in the heart and govern life-force and heat</note>, insofar as he agrees with the **Sun** by his own nature—and even in his own right, otherwise the heart would not specifically receive the vital spirit in the month of **Jupiter**. For this reason, the Greeks call Jupiter "life" <note>Original: *Zēn*</note>, and "the one through whom there is life" <note>Original: *Dia*</note>. 

Astrologers also testify that he has power over the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul) was believed to reside in the brain and govern thought and the senses</note>, saying that **Jupiter** contributes to philosophy, the discovery of truth, and religion. **Plato** also says that philosophers proceed from **Jupiter**. **Homer** indicated this as well, following the opinion of the ancients, saying: "Such is the mind in men as the father of men and gods <note>A traditional title for Jupiter/Zeus</note> brings it daily." Indeed, he never gives such a title to any deity except **Jupiter**. 

The **Sun** signifies the vital spirit especially, and the heart; he also has a significant role in the head because of sensation and movement, of which he is the Lord, nor does he lack natural power. **Mercury** signifies the brain and the instruments of the senses, and therefore the animal spirit. 

Consequently, the safest path will be to do nothing without the favor of the **Moon**. For she frequently and easily sends celestial things down to the lower realms. They call her a "second **Sun**," as she creates the four seasons of the year every single month. In her first quarter, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> believe she is hot and moist. In the second, hot and dry. In the third, cold and dry. In the fourth, cold and moist. Her light is undoubtedly the light of the **Sun**. She rules the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined health</note> and generation, and she measures all the changes of the fetus in the womb by her revolutions. Whenever she is joined to the **Sun**, she receives life-giving power from him, which she pours into the humors; there, she also receives from **Mercury** the power that mixes the humors. **Mercury** brings this power through his transformations into all things and his many-layered orbits. There, she also soon receives from **Venus** the power that assists in forms suitable for birth. 

It will be worthwhile to remember that the daily course of the **Moon** is distributed into four quarters. In the first, she rises from the East to the mid-heaven; during this time, she increases the humors and the natural spirit. In the second, she seeks the setting point from the mid-heaven and produces the opposite effect in us. In the third, she goes from the setting point to the point below the mid-heaven, and again increases that spirit and humor. In the fourth, she falls from there toward the rising point and decreases them in turn. This is most apparent on the shores of the Ocean, where the sea visibly ebbs and flows according to this course, and the vigor of the sick follows the same order. It is also probable that the **Sun**, through his own similar quarters, increases or diminishes natural heat and the vital spirit—and the animal spirit as well, insofar as he has **Mercury** as his companion. 

Once these things are understood, the physician will be able to observe more opportune times for restoring the humors, natural heat, and any spirit. But enough about the **Moon** for now. Nor does the physician teach us to leave out **Jupiter**, in whose month...

->MARSILIO FICINO ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS<-

From the former [the Sun] we have received life, while from the latter [Jupiter] we were born into a shared and more fortunate existence. Jupiter is the one who stands in the middle—in both quality and effect—between the **Sun** and **Venus**, and likewise between the **Sun** and the **Moon**; therefore, he embraces all things. I believe it is wicked and dangerous to overlook the **Sun** itself, the Lord of Heaven, unless perhaps one says that he who possesses **Jupiter** already possesses the **Sun** within him, for there the Solar power is perfectly tempered for human beings. Not only **Iamblichus** and **Julian**, but all authorities affirm that all the virtues of the heavenly bodies are present in the **Sun**; and **Proclus** <note>Ficino cites several Neoplatonic philosophers: Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), the Emperor Julian (331–363 AD), and Proclus (412–485 AD).</note> says that at the sight of the **Sun**, all the virtues of all the celestial beings are gathered and collected into one. No one will deny that **Jupiter** is a kind of **Sun** tempered specifically for us. 

Nor should you neglect the **Moon** when she is tempered toward **Venus**, for she greatly aids a strong and prosperous life. Since **Venus** makes a human being fertile and joyful, you should observe her influence. However, if you rightly mix the **Moon** (who is similar to **Venus**, being entirely equal in moisture and only slightly less warm) with **Jupiter** or the **Sun**, you already essentially possess the power of **Venus**. 

What then? To walk the safest and most convenient path of all, observe the **Moon** when she looks upon the **Sun** <note>An "aspect" in astrology—the angle between two planets.</note> and is joined with **Jupiter**, or at least when she looks upon both **Jupiter** and the **Sun** at the same time, or certainly when, shortly after looking at the **Sun**, she proceeds to a conjunction or aspect with **Jupiter**. At that very time, assemble for yourself or apply **Solar**, **Jovial**, and **Venereal** things together. But if necessity or business urges you to take refuge in just one of the great powers, flee to **Jupiter** himself, or rather to the **Moon** and **Jupiter** together. For no star cherishes and strengthens the natural powers within us—and indeed all powers—more than **Jupiter** does; likewise, none promises more prosperity and abundance. It is lucky to receive his influence everywhere, whereas receiving the **Sun** is perhaps not safe in every situation. For the former always helps, while the latter often seems to harm. **Venus**, on the other hand, is somewhat weak. Therefore, **Jupiter** alone is called the "beneficent father." 

**Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> confirms this when he says:

> A medicine hardly moves nature at all unless the **Moon** is joined with **Jupiter**. 

To such an extent does he think the entire nature of the universal body is strengthened from that source. I have also found through experience that when the **Moon** is joined with **Venus**, medicine hardly works. Although we should observe the **Moon** in relation to the **Sun** especially when we fear **phlegm** <note>term: pituita (phlegm), one of the four humors believed to cause sluggishness and coldness.</note>, and in relation to **Venus** when we fear **bile** <note>term: bile, specifically yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness.</note> and similar drying conditions, nevertheless, directing the **Moon** toward **Jupiter** contributes to all these things in some way. It is especially helpful for expelling **black bile** <note>term: atra bilis (black bile), the humor associated with melancholy and depression.</note> and for restoring and strengthening the common **complexion** <note>term: complexion (the unique balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual).</note> of men. Just as licorice, rose oil, and wine (which also moistens what is dry and dries what is too moist) cool down things that are too cold, so too is **Jupiter** suited to human heat, much like wine, rose oil, chamomile, and licorice. Therefore, when you hear **Albumasar** <note>The Latin name for the 9th-century Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note> saying:

> There is no life for the living, except through God, save through the **Sun** and the **Moon**.
<note>original: "Non est uita uiuentibus, præter Deum, nisi per Solem & Lunam."</note>

Understand this as far as it concerns the common influx belonging to everyone. But the influx most proper and best suited to man comes from **Jupiter**. There are, in the nature of the body, powers of attracting, retaining, **digesting** <note>term: coquendi (literally "cooking"), the internal heat used by the body to process food and mature the humors.</note>, and expelling. **Jupiter** aids all of these, but especially the virtue of digestion, as well as generating, nourishing, and growing, because of his abundant, airy moisture and his ample heat, which moderately governs that moisture. 

Truly, through the rays of **Jupiter** which are always diffused everywhere, the **Sun's** own light is most greatly tempered for the health of men, with the rays of **Venus** meanwhile constantly contributing to the same end, and the **Moon** transferring them similarly. The rays of **Venus** and the **Moon**, being somewhat more moist, require a tempering force, just as the **Sun's** rays, being hotter, require the tempering of something more moist. The rays of **Jupiter**, however, require no tempering. For what else is **Jupiter** but a kind of **Sun** that was tempered from the beginning specifically for the health of human things? What is he, again, but a **Moon** or **Venus** made warmer and more powerful? Therefore, astrologers predict a fertile, strong, and healthy year starting from **Jupiter**, and from him they hope for remedies for imminent diseases. And **Empedocles**, where he assigns specific duties to each of the planets, names **Jupiter** alone as the prince of generation, following **Orpheus**. 

Besides **Jupiter**, they teach that the **Moon** must be carefully observed in all works, as she is a fitting medium between celestial and earthly things. Thus, the **Moon** should be in a degree, position, and aspect suitable to the desired work. She should not be in the eclipse line, nor "under the rays" <note>An astrological term for a planet being too close to the Sun to be seen, thereby losing its power.</note> of the **Sun** within twelve degrees on either side, unless by chance she is in the same minute as the **Sun** <note>term: in unitate Solis (Cazimi). A planet within 17 or 16 minutes of the exact center of the Sun was thought to be fortified rather than burned up.</note>. Indeed, many believe all planets will be strong when they stand in the "unity of the Sun." They measure this unity as thirty-two minutes, so that sixteen are counted before and sixteen after. She should not be hindered by **Saturn** or **Mars**, nor should she

### ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF CELESTIAL THINGS. BOOK III.

...descends. In southern latitude, when she passes beyond those twelve degrees mentioned. Let her not be positioned opposite the **Sun**, nor let her light be decreasing, nor let her be slow in her course—that is, when she does not travel twelve degrees in a single day. Let her not be in the <term>Combust Way</term> <note>original: "via combusta"; a specific, traditionally unlucky area of the zodiac spanning the end of Libra and the start of Scorpio</note> from the twenty-eighth degree of **Libra** to the third of **Scorpio**; nor in the eighth house, nor in the **Ascendant**, nor in the <term>terms</term> <note>original: "finibus"; specific sub-divisions of zodiac signs ruled by different planets</note> of **Mars** or **Saturn**. Some authorities even wish the **Moon** not to be in the sixth, twelfth, ninth, or fourth houses. However, they approve of her in the other regions of the sky. Where you cannot encompass all these conditions, at least wait for **Jupiter** or **Venus** to be in the **Ascendant** or the **tenth house**, for in this way they assist the **Moon’s** detriments.

Nor would it be out of place to remember that as the **Moon** increases in light, not only our moisture but also our spirit and virtue are increased, and these are expanded toward the periphery, especially in her second quarter. When she is decreasing, however, the opposite happens, especially in the last quarter. Her first <term>trine</term> <note>an aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered very harmonious</note> to the **Sun** takes precedence over the second. This is preceded by the first <term>sextile</term> <note>an aspect of 60 degrees</note>, and followed by the second sextile. As the **Moon** is filled with light, so she is filled with heat. It seems, therefore, that some do not observe how the **Moon** looks at the **Sun** (for she always looks at him) so much as they ensure she has the most light, especially while she is waxing. Meanwhile, let her look upon **Jupiter** or **Venus** by trine or sextile.

Accordingly, fiery things help the <term>attractive virtue</term>, earthy things help the <term>retentive</term>, airy things help the <term>digestive</term>, and watery things help the <term>expulsive virtue</term>. If you wish to assist all of these in a matter, you will strengthen the attractive virtue most especially through fiery things when the **Moon**, positioned in fiery signs or stations—namely **Aries**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius**—looks at **Jupiter**. The retentive virtue is helped by earthy things, most effectively when she gazes at the same planet while placed in earthy signs or stations: **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**. The digestive and generative virtues are helped through airy signs—namely **Gemini**, **Libra**, and **Aquarius**—whenever she looks up at or enters under **Jupiter** in airy signs. The expulsive virtue is aided through watery signs: **Cancer**, **Pisces**, and **Scorpio**, when she herself is placed in the waters and illuminated by the rays of **Jupiter**. You will most effectively achieve your desires in all these things if **Jupiter** occupies the same or similar, or at least not dissimilar, signs or mansions.

If you are about to purge the bowels with solid medicines, choose **Pisces**; with liquid ones, **Scorpio**; with moderate ones, **Cancer**. If you intend to purge through the lower parts, use **Pisces** and **Scorpio**; through the upper parts, **Cancer**. You shall avoid the harsh aspect of **Saturn** or **Mars** to the **Moon**. For the former afflicts the stomach, while the latter dissolves the intestines. You shall avoid **Capricorn** and **Taurus**, for they bring on nausea. You know that a limb must not be provoked <note>meaning: treated with invasive medicine or surgery</note> when the **Moon** occupies the sign assigned to that limb (for she moves the humors), but rather it should be soothed. Let these things said regarding the natural virtue and spirit—which dominate chiefly in the liver and are divided into the four offices we have described—be sufficient.

What then do we advise regarding the <term>vital virtue and spirit</term> <note>the spirit responsible for life and heat, centered in the heart</note> flourishing in the heart? This has already been mostly indicated. For these are aided primarily by fiery parts and, in a way, simultaneously airy parts, when the **Moon** looks upon **Jupiter** in similar houses or mansions, especially if she embraces **Jupiter** and the **Sun**. You can also strengthen the <term>animal virtue</term> <note>the spirit responsible for thought and sensation, centered in the brain</note> ruling through sense and motion in the head primarily through airy things, with fiery ones added, when the **Moon** looks upon **Jupiter** in similar houses or seats, especially if she almost embraces **Jupiter** and **Mercury**.

Here, however, I warn you not to think that **Mercury** is watery or earthy (as I myself once suspected, otherwise he would not contribute to the movements and speed of the intellect), but know that he is in some way airy. For this same reason, he is so mobile, so easily changeable, and contributes so much to the intellect, especially when positioned in **Aquarius**, which is very airy. The moisture in him is tempered, and the heat is slight. Placed under the **Sun**, he is said to dry things out. But when he is made more distant from the **Sun**, he is thought to moisten. In the former case, he heats much from the nature of the **Sun**; in the latter, he heats very little and moistens more by his own nature. In heat, perhaps, he does not yield to **Venus** and surpasses the **Moon**, but in moisture, he yields to both. **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel (965–1050), an influential Arab astrologer</note> proves that **Mercury** mixes the qualities of the heavenly bodies because he is very easily changed, both into the quality of the "term" he enters and into the nature of the star he looks upon. Therefore, I think he is so easily changed because he has neither the excellent power that **Jupiter** has, nor an exceeding quality like most celestial bodies, through which he might resist alteration.

Finally, it is probable that **Mercury**, the constant <term>Achates</term> <note>original: "Achatem"; a reference to the loyal companion of Aeneas, meaning Mercury is the Sun's loyal attendant</note> of the **Sun**, possesses many of his powers, and therefore certain solar things can be hoped for from **Mercury**. Sometimes, however, they say that **Mars** imitates the **Sun** in certain duties, and that **Venus** bestows those things which pertain to the **Moon**. Remember these things, therefore, in your work. And never neglect the "terms." For they say that the planets perform opposite things in different terms, as if in light or dark places. Finally, where **Mars**...
