->THINGS COMPARED TO THE HEAVENS. BOOK III.<-

### On the power of the heavens, on the strength of rays, and from where images are thought to gain their power. Chapter XVI.

**T**he almost immeasurable magnitude, power, and motion of the celestial bodies ensure that the rays of every star—which, as all astronomers admit, easily and instantly penetrate to the very center of the Earth's mass (itself like a mere point compared to the heavens)—reach their destination. There, as the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who held that the Earth was a sphere and that numbers governed the universe</note> and **Platonists** believe, these rays are strongest, both because they touch the center from every direction and because they are all gathered there into a narrow space. By their intensity, the dry matter of the Earth located there, far removed from moisture, is set on fire; once ignited, it is thinned out and dispersed through passages in every direction, breathing out fire and sulfur alike. But they believe this fire is very dark and like a blaze devoid of light, just as in heaven there exists a light devoid of heat; however, the fire between the celestial and the infernal realms joins light with heat. They believe, moreover, that the fire standing at the center is the **Vestal fire** <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; Ficino identifies her here with the Earth's internal life-force</note>. Indeed, they thought Vesta was the life and divinity of the Earth. For this reason, the ancients used to build the Temple of Vesta in the middle of cities and place a perpetual fire in the center. But lest we wander too far, let us now conclude: if the rays of the stars penetrate the entire Earth so quickly, it cannot easily be denied that metals and small stones, when they are engraved with images, are suddenly penetrated by them, and you can impress upon them wondrous powers, or at least some degree of power. After all, they generate the most precious things deep within the Earth. 

But who would deny that rays penetrate through these things? For air, its quality, and sound—which is less effective—suddenly pass through solid objects and affect them with their own specific quality. Now indeed, if hardness stood in the way of penetrating rays, light would pass through air much faster than through water, and through water much faster than glass, and similarly through glass much faster than crystal. But since light pierces all solid things in the same moment as it does liquids, it is clearly evident that hardness in no way resists the rays. Therefore, they will say it should not be denied that metals receive the rays and influences of the celestial bodies and even preserve them for a time—a time destined for them by the heavens. They preserve, I say, a certain virtue created from the contact of these converging rays. Indeed, what if a harder material, by the very fact that it seems to resist a powerful cause, exposes itself more to the blows? Thus a sword cuts the wood beneath the wool, while the wool is not cut. Thus that lightning bolt sometimes dissolves the metal within leather without the leather being harmed. 

Since, however, the celestial nature is incomparably more excellent than this fire of ours, we must not think that the office of a celestial ray is merely the kind of work we see a fiery ray perform—namely to illuminate, heat, dry, penetrate, thin out, and dissolve (things very well known to our senses). Instead, we must believe they have many more and more wonderful powers and effects; otherwise, inferior matter and the falling senses would be entirely equal to the divinity of heaven. But who does not know that the **occult virtues** <term>occult virtues</term> <note>Hidden properties of objects that cannot be explained by the four elements (hot, cold, wet, dry) but come from the heavens</note> of things, which are called "specific" by doctors, are not produced by elemental nature, but by the celestial? They can therefore (as they say) impress occult and wonderful powers upon images beyond the known ones, just as they insert them into other things. For they are not inanimate, like the rays of a lamp, but living and sensual, as if flashing out from the eyes of living bodies; they carry with them marvelous gifts from the imaginations and minds of the celestials, as well as a most vehement force from their strong emotion and the very rapid motion of their bodies. They act properly and most especially upon the **spirit** <term>spiritus</term> <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "spirit" is a subtle, airy vapor that links the physical body to the immaterial soul</note>, which is very similar to celestial rays. 

They act, moreover, even upon the hardest bodies, for all these things are very weak compared to heaven. Furthermore, in various stars there are various powers, and therefore in their rays, they vary among themselves. Besides, different virtues are born in the strikes of rays falling in one way or another. Finally, in the mutual encounters of rays, different powers suddenly arise here or there, at this time or another, much more and faster than in various mixtures of the elements and elemental qualities—much faster even than in tones and numbers harmonizing in one way or another with a Musician. If you consider these things diligently, perhaps you will not lack confidence when they say that by a certain sudden cast of rays, powers are impressed upon images, and different powers from different casts. Is it then done so quickly? I pass over the "fascinations" <note>original: "fascinationes"; the power of the "Evil Eye" or enchanting someone with a look</note> performed by a sudden glance. And the most piercing loves kindled instantly by the rays of the eyes—which are themselves certain fascinations, as we prove in our book *On Love*. I pass over how quickly a red eye infects the one looking at it, or a menstruating woman looking into a mirror. Did not certain families among the **Illyrians** and **Triballi** <note>Ancient Balkan tribes mentioned by Pliny the Elder as having the power to kill with a gaze when angry</note> reportedly kill men with a look when they were angry? And certain women in **Scythia** <note>An ancient region in Central Eurasia</note> were accustomed to do the same?

**T**he **Catoblepas** <note>original: "Catoblepas" — a legendary African beast said to have a heavy head always looking down; its gaze or breath was lethal</note> and the **basilisks** <note>original: "reguli" (little kings); legendary serpents that kill with a glance</note> kill men simply by the casting of rays from their eyes. The **electric ray** <note>original: "Torpedo marina"</note> also, by touch—even at a distance through a stick—suddenly numbs the hand. The **remora** <note>original: "Echinus"; though usually meaning a sea urchin, Ficino refers here to the "Echeneis" or ship-holder fish</note> too, a tiny fish, is said to stop a great ship merely by its touch. Furthermore, the **tarantulas** <note>original: "Phalangia"</note> in **Apulia** <note>A region in Southern Italy famous in the Renaissance for "tarantism," a dancing mania supposedly caused by spider bites</note> change a person’s spirit and mind into a sudden stupor by some bite, even a hidden one. What does a rabid dog do, even when the bite is not apparent? What about a broom, or even the strawberry tree? Do they not stir up poison and madness with the lightest touch? Will you then deny that the celestial bodies, with the rays of their eyes—with which they look upon things and touch them at the same time—immediately perform wonders? Now, a pregnant woman, by a mere touch, immediately marks a limb of the child about to be born with the sign of the thing she desired. Will one truly doubt that rays, touching in one way or another, produce different effects? For even when you are gathering the herb **hellebore**, whether you pull the leaf downward or upward, by this sudden touch, you are the cause for the hellebore to either purge humors downward or upward. At the beginning of the generation of any thing, do not the celestial <term>influences</term> <note>original: "influxus"; the "flowing in" of power from the stars</note>, through the cooking and perfect digestion of matter, bestow miraculous gifts—not so much over time as in a single moment? Under the favorable countenance of heaven, do not innumerable frogs and similar living creatures often leap forth from the sands in an instant? So great is the power of heaven in prepared materials; so great is its speed. Finally, if fire has the property of doing in the shortest possible time what others do in a long time—chiefly because it is most similar to heaven—who could doubt that heaven performs great things in a mere moment, even in less-prepared matter, just as a greater flame is wont to do?

Why then, they ask, do you doubt that heaven acts in a nearly similar way in the construction of an **image** <note>A talisman or astrological figure</note>? You will say, I suppose, as I myself used to say, that there are natural steps of alteration underlying this. This deficiency certainly diminishes the celestial gift, yet it does not seem to take it away entirely. For <term>Natural Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Physici"; scientists/physicists of the era</note> do not want an image to be fashioned from just any metal or stone, but from a specific one. In such a material, the celestial nature has already begun a virtue naturally for this very purpose which is desired, and has, as it were, almost perfected it—just as fire is latent in sulfur. This virtue is finally perfected only when this material is violently stirred by art under a similar celestial influence, and through that stirring, it grows warm.

Thus, **Art** arouses the power that was begun there, and while it reduces the material to a shape similar to its own celestial figure, it then exposes it directly to its **Idea** <note>The Platonic archetype or formal cause in the divine mind</note> there. Once it is so exposed, heaven perfects it with that power with which it had begun, just as it provides a flame to sulfur. Thus, a certain power to attract chaff was given to **amber** <note>original: "succino"</note> from heaven; it is somewhat weak, but often made stronger through friction and heating, it suddenly seizes the chaff. **Serapio** <note>Likely the Arabic medical author Ibn Sarabi</note> writes that a similar power was given to the **Albugedi** stone, which is like a **jacinth**, but it does not attract chaff until hairs are rubbed against this stone. Likewise, that Jovian <note>Pertaining to the planet Jupiter</note> **Bezoar stone**—that is, "liberating from death"—which we described in our book against the plague, received power from the beginning against poison from Jupiter; yet it is not so strong that it can pass the same power to other materials to be exercised. But as soon as it receives the figure of that celestial one under the influence of the celestial **Scorpio**, it is thought to suddenly carry back a perfected power against scorpions, which it is then able to communicate to mastic or incense. 

The same reasoning must be held concerning the jacinth, topaz, emerald, and the rest: that the fashioning of figures has no efficacy elsewhere than where the material agrees in effect with the star from which the craftsman hopes to receive this power. And furthermore, where this very material is already from the beginning such as you intend to make it through the figure. They advise, therefore, to use the materials of no one for images unless they are these very ones which you know already possess nearly the same power you desire. They command us, therefore, to investigate most diligently the powers of little stones and metals, and meanwhile to remember that among stones, the **Carbuncle** glowing in the dark and the **Pantaurus** <note>A mythical solar stone mentioned by Philostratus</note> are chiefly under the **Sun**; the **Sapphire** is under **Jupiter**; the **Emerald** under **Venus**, **Mercury**, and the **Moon**. Furthermore, they say that metals, besides gold and silver, have hardly any power for these things. A safer reckoning in these matters would be if you relate pure gold to the Sun and Jupiter—to the former because of its color, but to the latter because of its tempered mixture, for nothing is more tempered than Jupiter and gold. Relate pure silver to the Moon, but at the same time to Jupiter; and Venus to silver when it is mixed. Furthermore, the image will be more effective if the elementary power in its matter agrees with the special power naturally implanted in it, and this, moreover, with that other special power to be received from heaven through the figure. Finally, you will learn that lower figures and forms are conformed to celestial ones from the fact that (as they say) **Perseus**, with the severed head of **Medusa**, is accustomed to portend a future decapitation for some; and they do not doubt that many similar things, as well as the Moon and other **Planets** under certain **Signs**, stir certain memories within us.

<meta>catchword: Quam (Than/How)</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that just as animals and plants possess "occult" powers triggered by touch or rays, man-made talismans can capture celestial virtues if crafted from materials that naturally correspond to specific stars. He emphasizes that "Art" (human skill) does not create these powers but rather "arouses" and perfects the dormant potential already placed in stones and metals by the heavens.</summary>

He argues that while material qualities (heat, cold) dominate the Earth, mathematical forms (number and shape) dominate the heavens and influence our world through resonance.</meta>

<header>COMPARING CELESTIAL THINGS. BOOK III.</header>

## What power shapes have in heaven and under heaven.
### Chapter XVII.

**B**ut lest you perhaps distrust shapes <note>original: "figuris" — refers here to both geometric shapes and the specific configurations of stars or talismans</note> too much, they will bid you remember that in this elementary region under the Moon, elementary qualities—namely heat and cold, moisture and dryness—can do a great deal in a transformation tending toward something elementary. However, qualities that are less elementary or material—namely lights (which are colors), numbers, and likewise shapes—perhaps have less power toward such material things, but are thought to have great power toward celestial gifts. For in heaven, lights, numbers, and shapes are almost the most powerful of all, especially since there is no matter there, as most **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripatetici" — followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who generally held that the heavens were made of a fifth element (aether) rather than the four earthly elements</note> believe. For in this way, shapes, numbers, and rays, since they are not supported by other matter there, seem to be almost substantial. And since in the order of things mathematical forms precede physical ones—being simpler and less "needy" <note>original: "minus egenæ" — in Platonic thought, higher, simpler forms are more self-sufficient than complex material ones</note>—they rightly claim the greatest authority for themselves in the preceding levels of the world, that is, the celestial levels; thus, no less is accomplished there by number, shape, and light than by some elementary property. 

A sign of this authority is found even under the Moon. For highly material qualities are common to many species of things, and when these are changed in some way, the species are not always completely altered. However, the shapes and numbers of natural parts possess a property inseparable and peculiar to the species, as they were destined from heaven together with the species themselves. Indeed, they have the greatest connection with the **Ideas** <note>original: "idæis" — the archetypal forms in the Divine Mind</note> in the Mind, the queen of the world. And since these shapes and numbers are certain species designated there by their own Ideas, they certainly obtain their own powers from that source. Therefore, not only are the species of natural things bound to certain shapes, but also their motions, generations, and mutations are bound to certain numbers. 

What truly shall I say of light? For it is the act or the image of intelligence. Moreover, colors are certain kinds of lights. Therefore, when **Astrologers** <note>original: "Astrologi"</note> say that lights (that is, colors), shapes, and numbers have the greatest power in our materials prepared for celestial things, you ought not rashly to deny these things, as they say. You are not ignorant that **harmonies** <note>original: "concentus" — musical consonance</note> through their numbers and proportions have a wonderful power to stop, move, and affect the spirit, soul, and body. Furthermore, proportions constituted from numbers are like certain shapes, or as if made from points and lines, but in motion. Similarly, celestial shapes behave in their motion toward acting; for these shapes, through their harmonic rays and their motions that penetrate all things, secretly affect the spirit every day just as powerful Music is accustomed to affect it openly. 

You know, besides, how easily the shape of a mourner moves many to pity. And how much the shape of a lovable person immediately affects and moves the eyes, the imagination, the spirit, and the humors; no less living and effective is a celestial shape. Does not the merciful and cheerful face of a prince in a city gladden everyone? Does not a fierce or sad one suddenly terrify? What then do you think the faces of the celestials—the lords of all earthly things—can do against these? Especially since even those coming together for offspring are often accustomed to impress upon the children to be born long afterward not only such faces as they themselves then carry, but even such as they imagine. 

By the same reasoning, celestial faces immediately infect material things with their own marks, in which, if they sometimes seem to lie hidden for a long time, they then emerge in their own times. Now, the "faces" of heaven are celestial shapes. You can call the shapes that are more stable there "faces," and those shapes that change more often "aspects." You can also call the **aspects** <note>original: "Aspectus" — the angular relationships between planets, such as a square or trine</note> between the stars, created by their daily motion, "faces" as well as shapes. For they are called **hexagons** and **squares** <note>original: "hexagoni, tetragoni" — the sextile (60°) and square (90°) astrological aspects</note>. 

"Let it be so," someone will say, "let celestial shapes be most powerful for acting as you please, but what has this to do with shapes of images made by art?" 

They will answer that they do not contend for this most powerful thing—that our manufactured shapes should be most powerful for acting through themselves—but rather that they should be most ready to receive the actions and powers of celestial shapes, insofar as they are made opportunely while those stars are ruling and are modeled exactly according to them. For that shape requires this shape. Does not one **lute** <note>original: "cithara"</note> resound when another is sounded? This happens only if it also has a similar shape, and is placed in view, and the strings placed upon it are similarly tuned. What is the obstacle here, so that a lute suddenly suffers from another lute, except for some placement and a certain conforming shape? The shape of a mirror—smooth, concave, and shining—is congruent to heaven; because of this very quality, it properly receives such a great gift from heaven that the 
->rays<- <note>original catchword: "radios"</note>

...it completely gathers the rays of **Phoebus** <note>original: "Phœbi" — another name for the Sun</note> into itself, and suddenly burns every solid thing located at its center out of sight. Therefore, do not doubt—as they say—that a certain material for making an image, which is otherwise very suited to heaven, can through a shape similar to heaven given by art, both conceive a celestial gift in itself and then pass it on to someone nearby or to the one wearing it. Indeed, not only the shape, but also the permeable disposition, which he calls the **Diaphanous** <note>original: "Diaphanam" — refers to the Aristotelian concept of transparency, the medium through which light travels</note>, is something ineffective and passive by its own nature. Nevertheless, because a permeable disposition in heaven is the proper receptacle of light, wherever this quality exists naturally under heaven, or is prepared in some way, the present celestial light is suddenly acquired and also preserved. This happens where, along with this transparency, there is either fiery heat (as in a flame), or something airy or watery that is also "sticky" (as in glow-worms <note>original: "noctilucis"</note>, creatures that see in the dark, **carbuncles** <note>original: "carbunculis" — gemstones, like rubies or garnets, once believed to emit their own light</note>, and perhaps in some way in **Camphor**). Consider for yourself what follows from that regarding images.

### What kind of celestial shapes the ancients used to imprint on images, and concerning the use of images. Chapter XVIII.

**S**omeone, however, will ask which celestial shapes they were most accustomed to imprint on images. For there are forms there in the heavens very conspicuous to the eyes, and depicted by many as they are—such as **Aries**, **Taurus**, and similar shapes of the zodiac, and those which are clearly outside the zodiac. There are, moreover, very many forms there, not so much visible as imaginable through the **faces** <note>original: "facies" — also known as decans, these are 10-degree subdivisions of each zodiac sign, each associated with a specific symbolic image</note> of the signs observed, or at least devised, by the Indians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans. For example, in the first face of **Virgo**, a beautiful maiden sitting, having two ears of corn in her hand, and nursing a boy. And the rest, such as **Albumasar** <note>a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> and several others describe. Finally, there are certain **characters** <note>original: "characteres" — sigils, symbols, or magical shorthand</note> of the signs and Planets designated by the Egyptians. They wish, therefore, for all these to be engraved on images. 

If someone expects a specific benefit from **Mercury**, they ought to place him in **Virgo**, or at least the **Moon** there with an aspect to Mercury, and then make the image from tin or silver, in which is the whole sign of Virgo, along with its character and the character of Mercury. And if you are going to use the first face of Virgo, you should also add the figure which we said was observed in that first face. And similarly for the others. 

Indeed, the most recent authors of images accept their entire form as round, in imitation of heaven. But the older ones, as we read in a certain assembly of the Arabs, preferred the shape of the **cross** above all, because bodies act through power upon a surface already spread out. Now, the first surface is described by a cross. For in the first place, it has length and width. This is the first figure, and the straightest of all, and it contains four right angles. Indeed, the effects of celestial things result especially through the straightness of rays and angles. For the stars are greatly powerful when they hold the four angles or rather **hinges** <note>original: "cardines" — the four most important points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note> of heaven: namely the east, the west, and the two points in the middle <note>the points directly above and below</note>. When arranged thus, they cast rays into each other in such a way that they form a cross. 

Therefore the ancients used to say that the cross was a shape made by the strength of the stars, as well as a receptacle for that same strength; they believed it had the highest power in images and received the forces and spirits of the Planets. This opinion was either introduced or greatly confirmed by the Egyptians. Among their characters, one cross was distinguished, signifying "the life to come" <note>Ficino is referring to the Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life</note> in their custom, and they used to engrave that figure on the breast of **Serapis** <note>a Graeco-Egyptian deity associated with healing and the afterlife</note>. 

I, however, believe that what existed among the Egyptians concerning the excellence of the cross before Christ was not so much a testimony to the power of the stars as a prophecy of the power it would receive from **Christ**. But the Astrologers who lived immediately after Christ, seeing miracles performed by Christians through the cross, yet not knowing or not wishing to attribute such great things to **Jesus**, attributed them to celestial things—although they ought to have considered that miracles are not performed through the cross itself without the name of Jesus. That it is suitable for images, because it reflects the strength of the Planets and all the stars, is perhaps probable; yet it does not have great power for this reason alone, but can do something when joined with the other necessary things, perhaps toward the prosperous health of the body. 

But let us return to relating the opinions of others, as we began. The ancients used to make an image of **Saturn** for longevity of life in the stone **Feyrizech** (that is, **Sapphire** <note>original: "Feyrizech, id est, Saphyro" — likely a reference to the Persian 'firuzaj', usually turquoise, but Ficino follows a tradition equating it with sapphire</note>), in the hour of Saturn, with Saturn himself ascending and fortunately positioned. The form was an old man sitting on a high throne or a dragon, his head covered with a certain linen cloth...

They said all kinds of fevers were cured by this. An image of the **Moon** with the first face of Cancer rising, for growth. 

**The Form of Mercury:** A man sitting on a throne, wearing a traveling hat and crested, with eagle's feet, holding a rooster or fire in his left hand, winged, sometimes on a peacock, holding a pen in his right hand, in a multicolored garment. 

**The Moon:** A girl with a horned head <note>representing the crescent moon</note> atop a dragon or bull, having snakes above her head and under her feet. 

To cure stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, pains of the genitals, and to staunch blood, [they made] an image in the hour of **Saturn**, with the third face of Aquarius rising with Saturn. Likewise, they would imprint a **Lion** on gold, with a stone in the shape of the Sun rolling under its feet, in the hour of the Sun, when the first degree of the second face of Leo was rising. They believed this would be beneficial for expelling diseases. They did something similar for diseases of the kidneys when the Sun was in the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "corde Leonis" — the star Regulus</note> occupying the **midheaven** <term>midheaven</term> <note>The highest point in the sky that a planet or sign can reach.</note>. I heard from the famous physician **Mengo** <note>Mengo Bianchelli, a contemporary of Ficino</note> that such an image, made with Jupiter joined there with the Sun, freed **Giovanni Marliani** <note>A celebrated 15th-century mathematician</note>—a singular mathematician of our age—from the fear he used to feel during thunder. Furthermore, to strengthen health and avoid sorcery, he fashioned an image from silver in the hour of Venus, with the Moon occupying the **angles** <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses, the most powerful positions in a horoscope</note> and Venus looking on favorably, provided that the lord of the sixth house <note>the house of illness</note> looks at Venus or Jupiter with a **trine** <term>trine</term> <note>A harmonious astrological aspect of 120 degrees.</note> or opposite aspect. And Mercury must not be unfortunate. 

They did this in the last hour of Sunday, so that the lord of the hour held the tenth region of heaven. **Pietro d'Abano** says that a physician can cure a sick person through an image. Provided that in crafting it, he observes that the angles of the rising, the midheaven, and the setting are fortunate, as are the lords of the rising and, by the same reasoning, the second house, but the sixth house and its lord should be unfortunate <note>meaning weakened, so as to weaken the illness itself</note>. He also says that health will be firmer and life longer than it was originally ordained if, after examining the **nativity** <note>birth chart</note>, an image is made in which these factors are placed fortunately: namely, the significator of life, the givers of life (both the signs and the lords), and especially the **ascendant** and its lord. Also the midheaven, the place of the Sun, the **Lot of Fortune** <note>original: "pars fortunæ" — a calculated point in a chart representing prosperity</note>, and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>the New or Full moon</note> occurring before birth. Let the evil and unfortunate factors "fall." He concludes that no astrologer doubts that such things contribute to prolonging life. 

It would be tedious to relate which **faces** the ancients observed for each sign, and which **stations of the Moon** <note>also called Lunar Mansions, 28 divisions of the lunar cycle</note> they kept as necessary when making images. For in the station of the Moon from the seventeenth degree of Virgo to its end, they made images against disease and hatred, and for a successful journey. In the station from the beginning of Capricorn to the twelfth degree, [they made images] against disease, discord, and captivity. In the station from the twelfth degree of Capricorn to the twenty-fifth degree, against weakness and imprisonment. In the station from the fourth degree of Pisces to the seventeenth degree of the same, for curing diseases, for profit, partnership, and for increasing harvests. And in other cases, they similarly devised other things, often through **vain curiosity**. 

But I have reviewed only those which savor not so much of the Mage as of the Physician. For I suspect that medicine of this kind is largely vain. However, for other more legitimate medicinal preparations, I think these mansions of the Moon should be chosen, as well as the sixth degree of Aries, and again the nineteenth degree and 26 minutes. Also in Gemini the tenth degree and 51 minutes. In Cancer the nineteenth degree and 26 minutes. In Libra the sixth degree and 34 minutes. In Capricorn the nineteenth degree and 26 minutes. In Aquarius the second degree and 27 minutes, and in the same sign the fifteenth degree and 8 minutes. Furthermore, the opinion of **Haly** <note>original: "Haly" — Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> should be kept in mind: that any sign, as long as the Sun is in it, becomes "alive" and dominates the others, its effect...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of astrological talismans and their timing, transitioning from specific planetary images to a philosophical and theological defense of their efficacy, citing authorities like Porphyry, Albertus Magnus, and Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

<page-num>558</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO, ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS<-

...[as] happens with the others, that you should direct the Moon there to receive from that place her own gift for medicines. To that place, I say—that is, to the sign and the **face** <term>face</term> <note>Also called a decan, this is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note>, and especially the degree—so that if you seek the benefits of **Jupiter**, you raise the Moon directed to or joined with these, as long as the Sun illuminates a place of this kind where the Jovian property flourishes. And similarly for the others. Truly, it would be curious to relate, and perhaps harmful, which images they used to make, and how they joined or separated souls among themselves, for the purpose of securing happiness or inflicting calamity, whether on a single individual, a house, or a city. I, indeed, do not affirm that such things can happen. But astrologers think they can, and they teach how; such things I do not dare to recount.

**Porphyry**, where he describes the life of his master **Plotinus**, confirms that such things can happen. And he relates that **Olympius the Mage** and an Egyptian astrologer attempted such things against Plotinus in Rome, while trying to "strike" Plotinus <note>original: *siderare Plotinū* — to strike with the influence of the stars, usually implying a curse or blight</note> through images or things of that kind; but the attempts were turned back upon their author because of the exalted soul of Plotinus. **Albertus Magnus** also, a professor of both Astrology and Theology, says in his *Mirror* <note>The *Speculum Astronomiae*, a text influential in the Middle Ages</note> (where he says he distinguishes lawful things from the unlawful), that images duly established by astrologers acquire power and effect from the celestial figure. And immediately after, he relates their wonderful effects, such as **Thabit**, **Benthorad**, **Ptolemy**, and other astrologers promise. And he describes images for bringing calamity or prosperity to someone, which I deliberately omit. And meanwhile, he confirms that they can have an effect, although as a good man he condemns the abuse of the art, and as a lawful theologian he detests the prayers and **fumigations** <term>fumigations</term> <note>The burning of incense or herbs as a ritual offering to spirits or stars</note> which certain impious men have used in making images. 

Yet he does not reject the figures, letters, and words imprinted on images for this purpose alone: that they may receive some gift from a celestial figure. That this can indeed be obtained through images, **Peter of Abano** confirmed. Indeed, he even affirmed that some region or other was destroyed by that image which Thabit relates was made by the astrologer Phidias. But **Thomas Aquinas**, our leader in Theology, is more fearful of these things and grants less to images. For he thinks they acquire only as much power from the heavens through their figures as is usually produced by the heavens through herbs and other natural things. Not so much because there is a "figural" quality in that material, but because such a composite is already placed in a certain species of craftsmanship that agrees with heaven. 

He says these things in his third book *Against the Gentiles* <note>Summa contra Gentiles</note>, where he laughs at characters and letters added to figures. But he does not mock the figures themselves so much, unless they are added as certain signs for summoning demons. Also in his book *On Fate*, he says that constellations give the order of being and enduring, not only to natural things, but also to artificial ones; therefore, images are made under certain constellations. But if anything wonderful happens to us through them beyond the usual natural effects, he attributes it to demons, the seducers of men—which is clearly evident in the book *Against the Gentiles*, but especially in his booklet *On the Hidden Works of Nature* <note>De occultis operibus naturae</note>, where he seems even to think little of the images themselves, however they are made; and I too shall value them at nothing, insofar as he himself has commanded. 

However, to attribute certain wonderful effects of images to the deception of demons is not alien to the Platonists. For **Iamblichus** also says that those who, neglecting supreme religion and holiness, rely only on images and hope for divine gifts from them, are very often deceived in this matter by evil demons, who meet them under the pretext of good spirits. Nevertheless, he does not deny that certain natural benefits result from images constructed according to the lawful reasoning of astrology. Finally, I think it safer to trust oneself to medicines than to images, and that these reasons can have efficacy themselves. 

For it is probable that if images have any power, they do not acquire it so much recently through their shape as possess it naturally through the material being כך affected. And if anything is newly acquired while it is being engraved, it is obtained not so much through the shape as through the heating that comes from a certain striking <note>original: *contusione* — pounding or striking with a tool</note>. This pounding and heating, done under a celestial harmony similar to the harmony that once infused power into the material, excites and strengthens that very power, just as a breath does a flame, and makes manifest what was previously hidden—just as the heat of a fire brings into view letters written in onion juice that were previously concealed. And letters written on stone with goat's fat, entirely hidden, come forth if the stone is submerged in vinegar, and stand out as if engraved. Indeed, just as the touch of a broom or a wild strawberry tree <note>or arbutus</note> rouses a sleeping madness, so perhaps a certain striking and heating alone brings forth a power lying dormant in the material, provided it is done at the opportune time. Which celestial opportunity is useful in medicines...

<summary>Ficino explores the theological and philosophical legitimacy of astrological talismans, citing authorities like Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas to distinguish between natural celestial influence and forbidden demonic magic. He concludes that while talismans may have some natural efficacy through their materials and the timing of their creation, it is safer to rely on traditional medicines.</summary>

...to be used in completing [preparations/reflections]. Or if someone perhaps wishes to handle metals and stones, it is better only to strike and heat them than to shape them into figures. For besides the fact that I suspect these figures are empty, we should not rashly admit even the shadow of idolatry. Likewise, one should not rashly use even beneficial stars to expel diseases very similar to them. For they often increase these diseases, just as harmful stars sometimes diminish diseases unlike themselves, which indeed **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational figure of Western astronomy and astrology</note> and **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> clearly teach.

### On Constructing a Figure of the Universe. Chapter 19.

**B**ut why then do we permit a universal image—that is, an image of the universe itself? From which, nevertheless, people seem to hope for benefit from the universe. A follower of those people will perhaps engrave, if he wishes, some archetypal form of the whole world in bronze, which he may then at the right time stamp onto a gilded silver plate. But when specifically should he stamp it? When the **Sun** touches the first minute of **Aries** <note>This marks the vernal equinox, the astrological beginning of the year and, symbolically, the "birthday" of the world</note>. For from this point, as if from the revolution of its own birthday, astrologers forecast the fortune of the world impending for at least that year. 

He will therefore stamp the figure of the entire world on this very birthday of the world. But do you see how beautifully, while discussing this, the argument that the world was once born occurs to us? Since it is reborn every year. Do not astrologers, in the very birth of a man, first measure in which sign, which degree, and which minute the Sun was located? And there they lay the foundation of the whole figure. And in each subsequent year, as soon as the Sun enters that same minute, they consider the man as if reborn, and from that they predict the fortune of the year. Just as, therefore, they would not be able to do this for a man unless he were as if reborn, and he could not be as if reborn unless he had once been born, so too one can conjecture that the world was once generated. Namely, with the Sun then positioned under the first minute of Aries, since through that same position every year, a certain lot of the world being as if reborn revolves again. 

Then, therefore, he fashioned the figure of the world. He will take care, however, not to engrave or stamp the figure on the Sabbath, the day of **Saturn**. For on this day, God, the craftsman of the world, is said to have rested from His work, which He had begun on the ideal day of the **Sun**. For as much as the Sun is suited for generation, so much is Saturn unsuited. But He had finished the work on the day of **Venus**, signifying the absolute beauty of the work. But concerning the principles of the worldly fabric, our **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** has recently expressed further the divine mysteries of **Moses** regarding the genesis of the world <note>A reference to Pico’s *Heptaplus* (1489), a mystical commentary on the Creation</note>. 

Therefore, to return to the plan: he will not engrave his first world on the day or hour of Saturn, but rather on the hour of the Sun. He will stamp it on the world's birthday, especially if the fortunate **Jupiter** and **Diana** <note>The Moon</note> are present then. They will think it best, however, to add colors to the work besides the outlines. There are truly three universal and at the same time singular colors of the world: green, gold, and sapphire-blue, dedicated to the three **Graces** of heaven. Green is dedicated to **Venus** and the **Moon** alike; being moist, it is appropriate for moist things and those being born, and it is also suited for mothers. No one doubts that gold is the color of the **Sun**, and it is not foreign to **Jupiter** and **Venus** as well. Finally, we dedicate sapphire-blue especially to Jupiter, to whom even the sapphire stone itself is said to be consecrated. 

Hence **lapis lazuli**, endowed with this color, has a prerogative among physicians because of its Jovian virtue against the black bile <term>black bile</term> <note>Melancholy, the humor associated with Saturn</note> proceeding from **Saturn**; and it is born with gold, marked with golden spots; thus it is a companion of gold just as Jupiter is a companion of the Sun. The **Armenian stone** <note>Azurite, often used as a blue pigment</note> has a similar power, possessing a similar color along with a certain greenness. Therefore, they will judge it expedient, in order to seize the gifts of the celestial Graces, to gaze very frequently at these three colors especially, and in the model of the world which you make, to insert the sapphire-blue color into the spheres of the world. 

They will think it worthwhile to add golden stars to the spheres in the very likeness of heaven, and to clothe **Vesta** or **Ceres** (that is, the earth) in a green garment. A follower of those people will either carry such a model or gaze upon it placed before him. It will be truly useful to look at a sphere endowed with its own motions, such as **Archimedes** once made, and recently a certain Florentine of ours named **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo della Volpaia, who constructed a famous planetary clock for Lorenzo de' Medici</note> fabricated. And not only to look at it, but also to reflect on it in the mind. Accordingly, in the innermost parts of his house, he will construct a bedroom built into an arch, decorated with figures and colors of this kind, where he may spend most of his time awake and asleep. And when he leaves the house, he will look not so much with attention at the spectacles of individual things, as he will perceive the figure and colors of the universe. 

But let those fashioners of images see to these things. You, however, shall fashion a more excellent image within yourself; for when you know that nothing is more orderly than heaven, nor can anything be imagined more temperate than Jupiter, you will hope to obtain the benefits of heaven and Jupiter only if...

He suggests decorating one's living space with these colors and figures to internalize the order and temperance of the heavens.</summary>

<meta>catchword: rather</meta>

...rather through your thoughts, affections, actions, and diet, you will present yourself as most orderly and temperate. But since we have fallen into a mention of celestial <term>temperance</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "temperance" refers to a perfect balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, it might be opportune to remember that there is no excess of elemental quality in heaven—to speak in the manner of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>. Otherwise, if it were so composed, it would have dissolved after so many centuries; or if it were simple, it would at least have destroyed other things by its great magnitude, power, and motion. But indeed, as the most moderate of things, it moderates all things and mixes diverse things into one.

Furthermore, both by this very temperance of its own and by the excellence of its form, it has earned its life from the divine. For we see that composite things only finally attain life when a perfect blending of qualities seems to have broken the previous opposition between them, as in plants. Next, a more perfect life is found in animals, insofar as there is in them a <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and mental constitution of a person based on their humors</note> further removed from opposition than in plants. In humans, for the same reason, life is more perfect again, and in a certain way, already celestial. Indeed, the human complexion has already approached celestial temperance, especially in the <term>spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus" was considered a thin, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note>, which, beyond the subtlety of its substance and the tempering qualities in which it agrees with heaven, has also obtained celestial light. 

Here, moreover, where such a spirit is most especially celestial, it has obtained celestial life from the divine above all others. And insofar as it makes and keeps itself such in all its diet and law of life, it brings back singular gifts from the celestial beings. But when we say there is no excess of elemental quality in heaven, we mean either that there is no such quality at all—but rather the temperate productive powers of those qualities—or if there are any similar qualities there, they are held in a sort of airy balance. 

And when we name certain things there "cold" and "dry," we accept this according to Platonic reasoning; that is, so that "cold" is what is called the cause of the least heat, and "dry" is that which offers us the minimum of moisture. Thus the astrologer **Abraham** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer highly respected by Ficino</note> says that **Saturn** leaves our body in a certain way cold and dry because it bestows a heat and moisture less than our own. By the same reasoning, the meat of an ox or a hare is warm and moist in itself, yet to us, it is cold and dry. 

From this induction, take two corollaries. First, if bodies that are more temperate live more, then heaven, being most exactly temperate, possesses the most absolute life in itself; one may conjecture that insofar as other things approach its temperance and life, they obtain a more excellent life. Second, that life is a form perfect in itself, completing the body and presenting the principle of motion. A principle, I say, that is intimate, and of a motion both driven from within and unhindered through every part from without. If, therefore, this very thing is life, consider him to be captured by madness who does not recognize that such a form exists in heaven—the most excellent body, always in perfect circular motion, giving life to all things, and more so to those things by degrees which have either naturally approached its likeness or daily expose themselves more aptly to its influences.

### ->*How much power images are thought to have over the spirit, and the spirit over them. And about the disposition of the user and operator. Chapter 20.*<-

**W**e have found that if anyone uses **hellebore** <note>A plant used in ancient medicine as a powerful purgative to treat madness and melancholy</note> rightly and bears it strongly, it changes in some way the quality of the spirit and the nature of the body through its exquisite purging and its occult property; it even changes the movement of the soul, so that the person seems almost to have been reborn. For this reason, they say that **Medea** and the **Magi** <note>Legendary sorcerers and practitioners of ancient Persian magic</note> were accustomed to restoring youth with certain herbs, whereas myrobalans <note>A type of dried fruit used in medieval medicine</note> do not so much restore youth as preserve it. 

Astrologers think that favorable images have a similar power, through which they change the nature and morals of the wearer in some way and restore them for the better, so that he turns out as if he were someone else, or at least they preserve prosperous health for a very long time. Harmful images, however, are thought to have the power of hellebore used without skill and power against the wearer—that is, poisonous and pestilential. But against someone else, for whose calamity they were made and intended, they have the power of a bronze or concave mirror so placed that, with the rays collected and struck against the opponent, it burns them nearby, but at a distance compels them to grow dim. From this arose the history or opinion that through the "engines" of astrologers and the "poisonings" of magicians, humans, cattle, and plants can be struck by stars and waste away. I myself, however, do not sufficiently understand that images have any power over a distant thing. But I suspect they have some power over the wearer, though I do not think it is of the sort many imagine; rather, it is by reason of the material...

<header>COMPARISONS. BOOK III</header>

...rather than figures, and as I have said, I place medicines far above images by a long interval. Although the **Arabs** and **Egyptians** attribute so much to statues and images fashioned by astronomical and magical art, they believe that the spirits of the stars are included within them. <note>original: "spiritus stellarum"</note> Some understand the "spirits of the stars" as the marvelous powers of the heavens, while others understand them as demons, or even as attendants of this or that star. They believe, therefore, that the spirits of the stars—whatever they may be—are drawn down into statues and images, much as demons are accustomed to sometimes occupy human bodies, and through them to speak, move, be moved, and perform wonders. They believe the spirits of the stars do similar things through images. They think that demons, the inhabitants of worldly fire, insinuate themselves into our bodies through fiery shoulders, or through ignited spirits and similar affections. <note>Ficino is referencing a theory that spiritual entities interact with the "spiritus" or vapors within the human body</note> Similarly, they believe the spirits of the stars can be inserted into suitable materials for images through opportunely received rays, <term>fumigations</term> <note>The use of incense or smoke to attract celestial influences</note>, lights, and powerful tones, and that these can perform wonders upon the one wearing or approaching them. We, however, believe these things can happen through demons, who are not so much constrained by specific matter as they are delighted by worship.

But these things are discussed more carefully elsewhere. The **Arabs** report that our spirit, when we properly fashion images, if it has been most attentive to the work through imagination and emotion, is joined at the stars with the very <term>spirit of the world</term> <note>The "spiritus mundi," a universal channel of life connecting the heavens to the earth</note> and with the rays of the stars through which the world spirit acts. Thus joined, the human spirit is also a cause, so that from the world spirit, through the rays, some spirit of a certain star—that is, a certain living power—is infused into the image, most of all in harmony with the spirit of the person then performing the work. Such work is also aided by fumigations suited to the stars, insofar as such fumigations affect the air, the rays, the maker's spirit, and the material of the image in this way. 

I, however, consider that odors—as they are very similar in nature to the spirit and the air, and when they are lit, are also in harmony with the rays of the stars—if they are **Solar** or **Jovial** <note>Related to the Sun or Jupiter</note>, they powerfully affect the air and the spirit so as to capture the gifts of the Sun or Jupiter, which are then ruling opportunely under the rays. The spirit thus affected and gifted can, through a more powerful emotion, act not only upon its own body, but also upon a nearby body that is naturally similar but weaker, and affect it with a similar quality. I believe that the harder material of an image can hardly receive anything at all from odors and the imagination of the worker; however, the spirit itself is so affected by the odor that one thing is made from both. This is evident from the fact that an odor does not act further upon the sense of smell once it has acted enough. For the sense of smell, like anything else, suffers nothing from itself or from something very similar. But of these things elsewhere. 

Therefore, I consider the intensity of the imagination to have power not so much in the fashioning of images or medicines, but in the application and reception of them. If someone wearing a properly made image (as they say) or certainly using a medicine in a similar way, powerfully desires help from it, and believes and hopes most firmly without doubt, then surely a very great heap of assistance will be added. For where either the power of the image (if there is any) penetrates the flesh when warmed by contact—at least the natural power in its chosen material—or certainly the vigor of a medicine taken internally glides into the veins and marrow, bringing a **Jovial** property with it, the spirit of the man is transferred into that Jovial spirit by emotion, that is, by love. For the power of love is to transfer. Faith and unwavering hope then thoroughly and firmly fix the spirit of the man, now thus moved, within the Jovial spirit. 

If, as **Hippocrates** and **Galen** <note>The two most authoritative Greek physicians of antiquity</note> teach, the love and faith of a sick person toward the physician contribute greatly to health (indeed, **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician and philosopher, known as Ibn Sina</note> says this confidence does more than medicine), how much should we think the emotion and faith we have toward a celestial influx, already implanted in us, acting within, and penetrating the organs, contributes to celestial aid? Indeed, love itself and faith toward a celestial gift are often the cause of celestial support; and conversely, love and faith perhaps sometimes proceed from this: that the mercy of heaven already favors us for this very thing.

Thus, for two people to be reconciled by a most burning love, an image [is made] under a Moon joining with **Venus** in **Pisces** or **Taurus**...

<page-num>563</page-num>
<header>COMPARISONS. BOOK III.</header>

If one were to observe the daily movements of the stars and explore which specific speeches, songs, movements, dances, habits, and actions most people are usually incited to under their influence, you might then imitate such things to the best of your ability in your own songs. These songs would please a similar part of the heavens, and you would receive a similar celestial influx. Remember that song is the most powerful imitator of all things. For it imitates the intentions and affections of the soul, as well as words; it also represents the gestures and movements of the body, the acts of men, and their characters. It imitates and acts upon everything so vehemently that it suddenly provokes both the singer and the listeners to imitate or act out those same things. By this same power, when it imitates celestial things, it miraculously provokes our <term>spirit</term> <note>In Ficino's philosophy, the "spirit" (spiritus) is a subtle, vaporous substance—a bridge between the physical body and the immortal soul—that can be tuned like a musical instrument.</note> to the celestial influx, and draws the influx down to our spirit. Furthermore, the very material of harmony is much purer and more like the heavens than the material used in medicine. For the air itself is warm or lukewarm, still breathing and in a sense living. It is composed of its own "joints" and "limbs" like a living creature; it does not only carry motion and display emotion, but it even carries a meaning like a mind, so that it might be called a kind of aerial and rational animal. Therefore, harmony is full of spirit. If it happens to correspond to this or that star—whether according to its meaning, its structural "joints," the form resulting from those joints, or the emotion of the imagination—it transmits no less power into the singer (and from him to the nearest listener) than any other medicinal composition. It does this as long as the song maintains its vigor and the spirit of the singer, especially if the singer is by nature *Solar* <note>original: "Phœbeus," referring to the qualities of Phoebus Apollo, the god of the Sun and music.</note> and possesses a powerful vital spirit in the heart and an animal spirit in the head. For just as the natural power and spirit, when at its strongest, immediately softens and liquefies the hardest foods and turns bitter things sweet, and even produces offspring outside itself through the production of seminal spirit—so too the vital and animal power, when it is most effective, acts powerfully upon its own body through the conception and agitation of its spirit in song. Then, through its effusion, it moves those nearby, affecting both its own spirit and that of others with a certain "sidereal" or star-like property, which it has conceived both from its own form and from the chosen opportunity of the hour. Indeed, for this reason, many Easterners and Southerners, especially the Indians, are said to have an admirable power in their words, as they are for the most part made of spirit. I am not speaking of a supernatural force, but of a vital and animal force that is nearly the most powerful of all, as is found in those in other regions who are especially *Solar*. A song conceived with this power, timing, and intention is effectively nothing other than a "second spirit," recently conceived within you by your own spirit, which has become Solar and acts both upon you and your neighbor with Solar power. If a vapor or spirit sometimes emitted through the rays of the eyes (or otherwise) can fascinate, infect, or otherwise affect a neighbor, how much more powerful is the spirit that flows more abundantly and fervently from the imagination and the heart simultaneously? It is more powerful in its movement, so that it is not at all surprising that certain diseases of the mind and body can sometimes be taken away or brought on in this way—especially since this kind of musical spirit properly touches and acts upon the spirit that is the medium between the body and the soul, affecting both with its own emotion. You will surely grant that there is a wonderful power in the aroused spirit of a singer if you grant to the *Pythagoreans and Platonists* that the heaven itself is a spirit, disposing all things by its movements and tones. Remember, however, that all music proceeds from **Apollo**. **Jupiter** is musical only insofar as he is in harmony with **Apollo**. Furthermore, **Venus** and **Mercury** derive their music from their proximity to **Apollo**. Likewise, harmony belongs only to these four; the other three planets have "voices," but not "songs." We attribute slow, deep, hoarse, and complaining voices to **Saturn**. To **Mars**, we attribute the opposite: fast, sharp, harsh, and threatening voices. We give the middle voices to the **Moon**. As for harmonies, we ascribe to **Jupiter** those that are deep, intense, sweet, and steadily joyful. Conversely, to **Venus**, we ascribe voluptuous songs filled with playfulness and softness. Between these two, we place the songs of the **Sun** and **Mercury**. If they are venerable, simple, and intense, combined with grace and sweetness, they are judged to be *Apollonian*. If they are somewhat more relaxed and pleasant, yet vigorous and complex, they are *Mercurial*. You, therefore, shall reconcile each of these four to yourself through your songs, especially if you use the appropriate sounds, so that when you call out by singing and playing opportunely in their manner, they will seem to answer immediately—either like an echo or like a string on a lute that trembles whenever another string, tuned similarly, is plucked. And as *Plotinus* and *Iamblichus* would have it, this happens naturally...

->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE<-

In a similar way <note>original: "liter," likely an abbreviation for "similiter" (similarly)</note>, this will happen to you from heaven, just as a resonance or tremor comes from a lute <note>original: "cithara"</note>, or an echo is made from an opposite wall. Certainly, through frequent use, when Jovial, Mercurial, or Venereal harmonies are made while these planets are ruling, your **spirit** <note>Ficino defines "spirit" as a subtle vapor in the blood that links the body to the soul.</note>—singing most attentively to this very thing and shaped by the harmony—emerges as Jovial, Mercurial, or Venereal. Meanwhile, it becomes Phoebean <note>Pertaining to Phoebus Apollo, the god of the Sun and music.</note>, since the power of Phoebus himself, the leader of music, flourishes in every consonance. And in turn, by becoming Phoebean yourself through Phoebean song and sound, you meanwhile claim for yourself the power of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury. Again, from the spirit affected within in this way, you similarly affect the soul and the body. 

Remember, however, that a prayer <note>original: "orationem," which can mean a formal speech or a prayer</note> composed fitly and opportunely, full of emotion and meaning and performed with vehemence, has a power similar to songs. It is not expedient to report how much power Damis and Philostratus <note>Damis was the companion and Philostratus the biographer of the ancient miracle-worker Apollonius of Tyana.</note> claim certain Indian priests have in praying, nor even with what words they affirm Apollonius summoned the ghost of Achilles. For we are not speaking now of worshiping deities, but of a certain natural power of speech, song, and words.

Indeed, that there is a Phoebean and medicinal power in sound, and a certain potent one at that, is clear from the fact that in Apulia, those bitten by the <term>tarantula</term> <note>original: "Phalangio." This refers to "tarantism," a phenomenon in Southern Italy where victims of spider bites were said to fall into a trance cured only by specific, frantic music.</note> all become dazed and lie half-dead until each one hears his own certain sound. For then he dances fitly to the sound, plays from then on, and recovers. And if after ten years he hears a similar sound, he is suddenly moved to dance. I gather from the evidence that that sound is Phoebean and Jovial.

### How we may adapt ourselves to the seven celestial ways, and for whom Saturn is harmful and for whom he is favorable. How Jupiter defends against Saturn. How heaven acts upon the spirit, body, and soul. Chapter XXII.

Since the heaven is composed according to harmonic principle and moves harmonically, and effects all things through harmonic motions and sounds, it is rightly through harmony alone that not only men, but all these lower things are prepared, according to their capacities, to receive celestial things. We distribute this harmony capable of receiving higher things through seven levels of things:
1. Through **images** (as they think) harmonically constructed.
2. Through **medicines** tempered by their own certain consonance.
3. Through **vapors and odors** created with a similar symmetry.
4. Through **musical songs and sounds**, to whose order and power we wish to relate the gestures of the body, dances, and rhythmic movements.
5. Through the **concepts of the imagination** and graceful motions.
6. Through the **congruent discourses of reason**.
7. Through the **tranquil contemplations of the mind**.

For just as we daily expose the body to the light and heat of the Sun through its own harmony—that is, through timely position, habit, and shape—so too we expose the spirit to the hidden powers of the stars. This is done by preparing it through its own similar harmony: through images (as some believe), and certainly through medicines and harmonically composed odors; and finally, through the spirit thus prepared for the higher things (as we have often said), we expose the soul and body to them. 

I say the **soul**, insofar as it is inclined toward the spirit and body by its affection. In the soul we now place the imagination, the reason, and the mind. Our **imagination** can be disposed, composed, and strengthened toward Mars or the Sun, either because of the quality and motion of the spirit, or through our own choice, or even through both, so that it becomes immediately a proper receptacle for a Phoebean or Martial influx. Similarly, the **reason**—either through the imagination and spirit together, or through deliberation, or both—can adapt itself to Jupiter by a certain imitation; thus, because of its dignity and proximity, reason itself receives Jupiter and the gifts of Jupiter much more than the imagination or spirit does. In the same way, the imagination and spirit receive celestial things much more than any lower objects or materials.

Finally, the **contemplative mind**, insofar as it withdraws itself not only from those things we perceive, but also from those things we commonly imagine and argue through human customs—and calls itself back through affection, intention, and life to the "separated" things <note>The "separated" things are the Platonic Forms or divine Ideas, existing apart from matter.</note>—exposes itself in a certain way to **Saturn**. To this mind alone is Saturn favorable. For just as the Sun is an enemy to nocturnal animals but a friend to diurnal ones, so Saturn is hostile to men living a common, public life, or to those who flee the customs of the common crowd but do not yet let go of common affections. For Saturn granted the common life to Jupiter, but claimed the "separated" and divine life for himself. To the minds of men who are truly withdrawn from here, he is in a way a friend, as if to his own kin. For to those spirits inhabiting the sublime air, Saturn himself...

<header>THINGS TO BE COMPARED, BOOK III</header>

Satur<insert>n</insert>us <note>original: "nus"; the word Saturnus is split from the previous page</note> (to speak in a Platonic way) stands for Jupiter, just as Jupiter is the "helping father" to men who lead a common, everyday life. Indeed, no version of Saturn is more hostile than the one encountered by men who merely pretend to lead a contemplative life without actually practicing it. For Saturn does not recognize these people as his own, nor does Jupiter—who serves as the tempering influence of Saturn—help those who flee the common laws, customs, and commerce of men. For Jupiter claimed these social duties for himself (as the myths say) once Saturn was bound, while Saturn kept the things that are set apart and secluded. For this reason, those Lunar peoples whom Socrates describes in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and the afterlife.</note>—who inhabit the highest surface of the earth, living above the clouds—are very sober, content with the fruits of the earth, and devoted to the study of secret wisdom and religion. They taste the happiness of Saturn and lead a life so prosperous and long-lived that they are considered not so much mortal men as immortal **daemons** <note>In the ancient sense: intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note>, whom many call heroes, a "golden race" enjoying a certain Saturnian age and kingdom.

I believe this is perhaps what the Arabic Astrologers intended when they say that beyond the equinoctial line to the South, there are certain most refined inhabitants—daemons—who seem neither to be born nor to die, and that Saturn and the "Tail of the Dragon" <note>A point in astrology (the descending lunar node) often associated with endings or spiritual release.</note> hold power there. Albumasar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> certainly seems to confirm this in his book *Sadar*, saying that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and that the people there are very long-lived, mostly passing away only in extreme old age. He assigns the reason for this as being that Saturn does not harm his own household, only outsiders.

You, however, should not neglect the power of Saturn. For the Arabs say he is the most powerful of all; they say that while other planets take on the strength of those they approach, all planets instead approach him, and planets joined to him act according to his nature. Among the planets, he is the head of the widest sphere. To be sure, any planet is the head, heart, and eye of its own sphere, but Saturn is also closest to the innumerable fixed stars and is most similar to the **Prime Mobile** <note>The outermost moving sphere in the ancient model of the universe, which drives all others.</note>; he is said to have a long circuit. He is the highest of the planets, which is why they call a man "fortunate" if Saturn breathes upon him favorably. 

And although men mostly fear him as being alienated from common life, they nevertheless believe he can be appeased even for common life, provided he has great power and dignity in the **ascendant** <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note>, or if his own Jupiter looks upon him favorably, or receives him excellently within his own boundaries. Otherwise, his influence, when received unseasonably—especially in "thick" or heavy matter—becomes like a poison, just as an egg becomes poisonous through rot or excessive heat. From this, certain "unclean" people are born or escape: the lazy, the sad, the envious, and those exposed to unclean spirits. You should flee their company far away! For the poison of Saturn lies hidden and dormant in some places like sulfur kept away from a flame. But in living bodies it often flares up, and like ignited sulfur, it does not only burn but also fills everything around it with a noxious vapor, infecting those who come near.

Against his influence, which is usually foreign and somewhat dissonant to most men, Jupiter arms us—both by his own natural quality and by his specific foods and medicines, and (as they believe) even by his images, as well as by the habits, business, studies, and things properly belonging to him. However, it is not only those who flee to Jupiter who escape the harmful influence of Saturn and undergo his favorable one, but also those who betake themselves with their whole mind to that divine contemplation signified by Saturn himself. The Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Platonists believe that the malice of fate can be avoided in this way. Since they do not want the celestial bodies to be empty shells, but rather divinely animated and, moreover, ruled by divine minds, they certainly believe that many things pertaining to the body and spirit proceed from there to men, but also many goods that "overflow" into the soul—not from the bodies of the planets to the soul, but from their souls. Even more of these things flow from the higher minds above the heavens.

Among these matters, if you wish to assign all the reasons that led Moses to mandate the rest of the **Sabbath** <note>The day of rest, Saturday, which is "Saturn's Day."</note> for the Hebrews, you will perhaps find—beyond a more sublime and secret allegory—that the day of Saturn is unsuited for civil and military actions but fit for contemplation; therefore, on that day, divine protection should be implored against dangers. Abraham, Samuel, and many Hebrew astrologers confess that this protection against the threats of Mars and Saturn can be obtained through the elevation of the mind to God, and through vows and sacrifices. They confirm that precept of the Chaldeans: "If you raise your mind, burning with a work of piety, you will also preserve your frail body." It is worth considering that saying of Iamblichus: that the celestial, worldly deities have certain higher powers within themselves and some lower ones. Through the lower ones, they bind us to the effects of fate, but through the higher ones, they in turn release us from fate—as if they held the keys (as Orpheus says) for opening and closing.
