# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE
<page-num>566</page-num>

...moreover, the divinity higher than the world redeems us from fatal necessity. It is also very worthy of investigation what that Hebrew practice says: that in the sacrificing of animals and the dispersing of our possessions in sacrifice, the evils threatening from the heavens are deflected from us onto our belongings. <note>Ficino refers to the concept of the "scapegoat" or sacrificial substitution, suggesting that material losses can satisfy malefic planetary influences that might otherwise harm the person.</note> But we leave these things to be explored by our Pico. <note>original: "Pico nostro"; referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), Ficino’s friend and colleague who studied Hebrew Kabbalah.</note>

Finally, whenever we say that the gifts of the celestials descend to us, understand that the qualities of the celestial bodies come into our bodies through our rightly prepared spirit, and these same gifts also first flow through their rays into the spirit naturally, or in whatever way the spirit is exposed to them. Then also the goods of the celestial souls partly leap forth into that same spirit through rays, and from there overflow into our minds; and partly they reach the minds of men exposed to them from the souls of the celestials and from angels. Exposed, I say, not so much by some natural contract as by the choice of free will or by affection. In short, whoever imitates the benevolence, action, and order of the celestials through their vows, study, life, and morals, you should consider them more similar to the higher beings and thus they receive more ample gifts from there. However, those men who are artificially dissimilar and discordant to the celestial disposition are both secretly miserable and finally turn out to be publicly unhappy.

---

->*That you may live and act prosperously, above all know your natural talent, your star, your Genius, and the place suited to them; dwell here, and follow your natural profession. Chapter 23.*<-

---

**Q**uicever is born of sound mind and in control of himself is naturally instituted by heaven for some honest work and way of life. Therefore, whoever desires to have heaven favorable should, above all, undertake this work, this kind of life, and pursue it diligently. For heaven favors its own undertakings. You were made by nature for this very thing above all others: that which you first do, speak, imagine, adapt to, dream of, and imitate from your tender years; that which you try more frequently, which you perform more easily, in which you profit most, in which you delight above others, and which you leave behind unwillingly. This is surely that for which heaven and the Ruler of heaven begat you. To that extent, therefore, heaven will favor your undertakings and breathe upon your life, insofar as you follow the auspices of your parent [the star] itself—especially if that Platonic doctrine is true (in which all antiquity agreed) that every person at birth has a certain <term>daemon</term> <note>daemon: In the Platonic and Renaissance sense, a guardian spirit or "genius" that guides an individual's destiny, rather than an evil spirit.</note> as the guardian of their life, destined by their own star. This spirit also assists in this very duty to which the celestial powers assigned the newborn.

Whoever, therefore, through the arguments we just mentioned, has scrutinized his own natural talent, will find his natural work and will simultaneously find his star and <term>daemon</term>; following their beginnings, he will act prosperously and live happily. Otherwise, he will experience adverse fortune and feel heaven to be an enemy. There are, therefore, two types of unfortunate men above others. One is of those who, professing nothing, do nothing. The other is of those who undertake a profession alien to their natural talent and contrary to their <term>Genius</term>. <note>Genius: A Roman concept nearly identical to the Greek daemon, representing a person’s guiding spirit or innate character.</note> The former are sluggish with idleness, while heaven, always active, is meanwhile inciting them to action. The latter, while they do things alien to their celestial patrons, labor in vain, destitute of higher protectors. The first point is confirmed by the ancient proverb: "The gods help those who act, but are hostile to the idle." The second is confirmed by a similar proverb: "Do nothing against the will of <term>Minerva</term>." <note>Minerva: The goddess of wisdom; the proverb "invita Minerva" means acting against one's own natural inclination or talent.</note> For this reason, I believe, Jupiter is entreated in the <term>Pythagorean poems</term> <note>Referring to the "Golden Verses," a set of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras.</note> either to relieve the human race of so many evils himself, or at least to show us which <term>daemon</term> we should use as a guide.

Therefore, it will be worth the effort to investigate to which region your star and your <term>daemon</term> have designated you from the beginning for habitation and cultivation; for there they breathe upon you more. That place is indeed the one in which your spirit, once gone forth, is somehow recreated; where the senses remain more vigorous, where the constitution of the body is stronger, where most people favor you, and where your prayers succeed. Experience these things, choose this region, and cultivate it happily. If you leave from here, you will surely be unhappy unless you are to return or go to similar places. But meanwhile, exercise yourself in this region with frequent movements, and engage in certain circles after the fashion of the celestials: for being born from such motion and circuit, you will be preserved by similar things. Furthermore, as far as habitation is concerned, you will usefully remember this: just as the countryside supplies the city with the necessary food for life, but the city consumes it, so too life itself is greatly increased by frequent stay in the country (where boredom should least seize you), but is worn away by both urban leisure and urban business. Regarding both habitation and profession, that teaching of the Eastern <term>Astrologers</term> <note>Likely referring to Arabic or Persian astrologers like Albumasar or Al-Kindi, whose works were central to Renaissance astrology.</note> is by no means to be despised: namely, that by a change of name, profession, clothing, diet, and place, the celestial influence upon us is changed, sometimes for the better and sometimes for the worse. <term>Daemons</term> also or...

<summary>Ficino explains that human prosperity depends on identifying one's innate talent and "Genius" (guardian spirit), then aligning one's profession and location with that celestial destiny. He argues that resisting one's natural inclination leads to misery, while choosing the right environment—specifically the countryside—replenishes the spirit.</summary>

-> ### COMPARISONS. BOOK III. <-

<page-num>367</page-num>
<header>COMPARISONS. BOOK III.</header>

...to be changed, or the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who believed in a hierarchy of spirits and the soul's connection to the stars.</note> will judge that we relate to the same things differently here and elsewhere. The astrologers <term>Astrologi</term> agree with the Platonists that the guardian spirit <term>Daemon</term> <note>original: "Daemonem"; here meaning a protective spirit or "genius" assigned to a person, not an evil entity.</note> of each individual can be twofold: one specific to their birth <term>genitura</term> <note>one's astrological nativity or birth chart</note>, and the other to their profession. And whenever one's profession agrees with their nature, the same spirit—or certainly one very similar—is present for us both, and from that, our life will be more concordant and tranquil. But if the profession is at odds with one's natural character, the spirit acquired by art <note>the "professional" daemon</note> is discordant with the natural spirit <term>genius</term>, and life becomes laborious and full of anxiety.

For those wishing to find what kind of spirit presides over each person from the moment of birth, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "Personal Daemon."</note> seeks a rule from the planet that is the master of the birth. Julius Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer and author of the *Mathesis*.</note> says the master of the birth is either the planet that has the most dignities there, or, according to a firmer opinion, the one whose domicile the Moon is about to seek immediately after the sign it already holds at the person's birth. But he thinks the spirit is not to be investigated by that same rule, but rather, according to the opinion of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers famous for their technical precision.</note>, from the Sun or the Moon. Specifically, from the Sun toward the Moon in a daytime birth, and conversely from the Moon toward the Sun in a nighttime birth; so that once the interval between these has been calculated, you may traverse an equal space descending from the degree of the Ascendant, and notice at which point you end. They believe that whichever star's limit that point falls upon, the spirit belongs to that same star. In short, they are accustomed to weigh the course and fortune of life from the master of the birth and the spirit together. I have added "fortune" because some calculate the "Part of Fortune" <term>pars fortunae</term> by nearly the same method.

The ancients hoped that their own spirit had descended to them from one of the "pivots" <note>the four angles of the horoscope: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note> of the sky—namely from the East, the West, or the Midheaven on either side—or at least from the eleventh or fifth regions. The eleventh region indeed follows the Midheaven above our heads and is nicknamed the "Good Spirit" <term>bonus daemon</term>; it gazes upon the degree ascending from the East from a sextile aspect <note>an aspect of 60 degrees, considered harmonious.</note>. The fifth region follows the Midheaven of the antipodes <note>the Imum Coeli or bottom of the sky</note> and is called "Good Fortune" <term>bona fortuna</term>; it beholds the ascending degree from a trine aspect <note>an aspect of 120 degrees, considered very beneficial.</note>. In the third place, they hoped for a spirit that came—if it must come from a "falling" <term>cadenti</term> region—at least from the ninth or the third. For the ninth is called "God" <term>deus</term>, and the third "Goddess" <term>dea</term>. The former gazes upon the descending degree <note>Likely referring to the 1st or 7th house; the 9th trines the 1st house.</note> from a trine, and the latter from a sextile. They dreaded the falling twelfth and sixth regions, nicknamed the former "Evil Spirit" <term>malum daemonem</term> and the latter "Bad Fortune" <term>malam fortunam</term>.

But we, considering it pointless to wish for things already past <note>i.e., your birth chart is already set</note>, advise that those same regions which they hoped for regarding spirits and fortunes be observed for the purpose of choosing planets and stars for a work to be accomplished. Let them be in the angles, or in the two "following" <term>succedentibus</term> regions we mentioned <note>the 11th and 5th houses</note>, or at least in the two falling regions we just named <note>the 9th and 3rd houses</note>. For it is not without reason that they say the Sun rejoices in the ninth, the Moon in the third, Jupiter in the eleventh, and Venus in the fifth. These houses look upon the ascending degree.

But let us return to the plan. Whether from that experience and diligence I spoke of earlier, or from this art I have just reviewed, let us first investigate the instinct of nature and the spirit. We shall judge that person to be unfortunate who professes no honorable duty. For he who does not undertake an honorable work truly lacks a leader of his profession, and he has scarcely any natural leader either. Since the duty of the stars and spirits—or rather the leader-angels <term>angelorum ducum</term> divinely disposed for our protection—is to act always, excellently and most widely. Furthermore, as we said above, he is unfortunate who, through a profession contrary to his nature, undergoes a spirit different from his natural Genius.

Remember, however, that more noble spirits (or, if you prefer, angels) are received step-by-step according to the dignity of one's profession—and even more noble ones in public governance. It is possible to adopt a craft and a way of life that is not contrary to one's Genius and natural talent, nor far different, even if one proceeds to more excellent things. Remember again to enter into the familiarity of those upon whom the Graces <term>Gratiae</term> <note>The three goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity.</note> breathe. You shall weigh this from the goods of the mind, body, and fortune: for just as a scent comes from musk, so something of the good exhales from a good man into his neighbor, and often remains infused there. Moreover, a gathering of three fortunate people would be miraculous, or of two who wonderfully overflow into one another.

Finally, remember to flee far from the unbridled, the impudent, the malignant, and the unhappy. For these people, full of evil spirits or rays, are harmful; and like lepers and the pestilential, they do not only harm by touch, but even by proximity and sight. Indeed, the very proximity of living bodies is thought to be a form of contact, because of the effective exhalation of vapors flowing outward from heat, spirit, and emotion. The familiarity of the shameful and the cruel will be especially pestilential—if it is true that after the vegetal life is infused into us in the month of Jupiter <term>Iouis</term> (that is, the second), the sensual soul <term>sensualem animam</term> is thereafter infused in the month of Mars <term>Martio</term> (the third)...

He also warns that the company we keep can spiritually "infect" us through the transmission of celestial rays and vapors.</summary>

...enslaved to disturbances. For those who are carried away by such disturbance, being full of Mars <note>Influenced by the planet Mars, associated with anger and conflict.</note>, they infect those near them with a **Martial contagion**. Conversely, frequent association and close dealings with the fortunate and the excellent is, as we have said, customarily and wonderfully beneficial. They say that **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD.</note> discovered an old man in Ephesus under whose form a demon was hiding, who by his mere presence was contaminating the entire city with a plague. On the other hand, **Xenophon** and **Plato** testify to how much **Socrates** benefited many by his presence alone.

### By what means scholars may recognize their own nature, and follow a lifestyle agreeable to their spirit. Chapter XXIIII.

**S**ince I am speaking to students of letters, I want each one to remember that anyone captured by a love of literature is, first and foremost, **Mercurial** <note>Under the influence of Mercury, the god of speech and commerce</note>, and furthermore, **Solar** <note>Under the influence of the Sun</note>, insofar as Mercury himself is Solar. This is a condition common to all of them. Specifically, however, beyond a Mercurial nature, whoever excels in the grace, charm, dignity, and beauty of eloquence should recognize **Apollo** and **Venus** within themselves. He who is more inclined toward law, or toward natural and common philosophy, should not be unaware that he has **Jupiter** as his patron. But he who is driven to investigate the most secret things with deep curiosity should know that he is not only Mercurial, but **Saturnine** <note>Under the influence of Saturn, associated with deep thought but also melancholy.</note>. Under Saturn’s lordship also are all those who remain in any study until the end of their age, especially those who are negligent of divine matters. Finally, if it is true—as many natural philosophers and astronomers <term>Physici, quam Astronomi</term> claim—that the soul endowed with intellect descends into the human conception in the month of the Sun (that is, the fourth month), then those who live mostly by the intellect are primarily Solar from the beginning and become more so every day. 

Therefore, these men must seek the favor of these planets. Medicines must be fashioned under their breath <note>original: "spiraculo"; refers to the celestial influence or "breathing" of the planets.</note>. They must dwell in their regions. But above all, I call upon you, O scholarly worshippers of the **Muses**, to look to Apollo, the leader of the Muses. Therefore, whoever among you, most beloved brothers in the love of the Muses, are much stronger and longer-lived in mind than in body, they should certainly know that in their birth, the Moon <note>original: "Phoebe"; referring to the Moon as the provider of material substance.</note> supplied very little matter, but the **spirit of Apollo** <note>original: "Phoebeum spiritum"; referring to the Sun's vitalizing power.</note> infused a great deal; indeed, every day they resolve the humors and nourishment in the body into spirit for the most part. Each of you, therefore, is almost entirely **spirit**. You are, I say, a certain **spiritual man** <term>spiritalis homo</term> <note>Ficino uses "spirit" (spiritus) to mean the "pneuma," a thin, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note>, masked by this little earthly body, exhausting the spirit before others through a certain perpetual labor. Thus, for such a person, the spirit must be refreshed more assiduously than for others, and in old age (in which it commonly becomes thicker), it must be recalled to its proper refinement. 

You certainly know that the thick body is nourished by the four thick elements. Know then that the **spiritual body** is nourished by its own four refined elements. For the spirit, **wine** stands in for Earth; the **odor** of the wine itself takes the place of Water; **song** and **sound** act as Air; and **light** represents the element of Fire. By these four, therefore, the spirit is chiefly nourished: by wine, and by its odor, and by song, and likewise by light. 

But I know not how, having begun with **Apollo**, we have soon fallen upon **Bacchus**. And rightly so, for we have come from light to heat, from ambrosia to nectar, from the intuition of truth into the burning love of truth. Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> and Bacchus are certainly brothers and inseparable companions. The former brings you two very powerful things: namely, **light** and the **lyre**. The latter likewise brings two: **wine** and the **odor of wine** to refresh the spirit, by the daily use of which the spirit itself finally becomes "Phoebian" and free. For this reason, prepare yourselves daily to receive the light of the Sun, so that—insofar as it can be done by a certain distillation and drying out of the deity—you may live as frequently as possible under the light, or at least in the sight of light, whether from afar or up close, whether covered or in the open, tempering the power of the Sun everywhere for your vital use, and in the night reflecting the Sun with **fire**, not forgetting the **cithara** <note>A stringed instrument like a lyre.</note> and song in the meantime. Always breathe, both while awake and while sleeping, living air—air that lives with light. 

Likewise, you ought to behave toward the pure gift of **Bacchus**, which was brought forth by the favor of Apollo. Therefore, receive wine in the same proportion as you do light. Receive it abundantly, provided that no distillation, nor drying out (such as I have described), nor drunkenness occurs. And besides the substance of the wine, which is taken twice daily, you should inhale the odor more frequently, partly by rinsing the mouth with pure wine when the spirit needs refreshing, partly by washing the hands with the same, and partly by applying it to the nostrils and temples. We have talked enough now, brothers, and we have drunk enough. Therefore, farewell.

### *Concerning Astronomical diligence in procreating children, in preparing feasts, in buildings and dwellings, and also in clothing, and how much it is permitted to care for such things. Chapter XXV.*

**B**UT it is also helpful for a moment to address the stern priest of religion. Come now, tell me, what specifically do you condemn in the use of the stars, priest? You will say: "Whatever takes away from our free will, and whatever detracts from the worship of the one God." I not only join you in condemning those same things, but I also strongly detest them. I know that you even curse—and I moreover shudder at—those who, when they wish to entreat God, flee to Jupiter in the midheaven as he enters that vast **head of the dragon** <note>original: "draconis caput." In astrology, the Dragon's Head refers to the North Node of the Moon, considered a point of increase. Ficino here sarcastically connects it to the biblical dragon/Lucifer to appease the priest.</note>; they are as wretched as they are foolish, destined to be devoured by that very dragon who once fell from heaven, dragging a third part of the stars with him <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation 12:4.</note>. 

But will you concede that one may choose opportune hours for carrying out contracts, marriages, conversations, journeys, and similar works? I see you will not easily assent to these things, fearing some threat to our free will. Therefore, although that Great Theologian **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and saint who argued that the stars influence the body but not the soul's free will.</note> would grant these things, and although reason itself might dictate that through the very act of choosing (which belongs to our will), celestial things are subjected to the use of our prudence just as herbs serve the Physician—nevertheless, for the present, I will believe you instead. And as with such difficulty you now permit them, I shall just as easily let them go. 

However, you have (I believe) long since permitted the observation of the Moon, and thus of other stars, for curing diseases and consequently for preparing remedies. It has also been conceded by you, and moreover approved, that when the Moon is waxing and increased in light, and not otherwise **unfortunate** <note>In astrology, a planet is "unfortunate" if it is in a harsh alignment with "malefic" planets like Mars or Saturn.</note>, one may scatter seeds in the fields and plant vines. Why then, in "planting" a human (to speak bluntly), should we not use the benefit of the Moon, Jupiter, and the Sun? For we always use the service of Venus for these duties. But I should have said more correctly: "others always use it." For to me, Venus herself is **Diana** <note>Diana was the goddess of the hunt and a virgin; Ficino is humorously asserting his own celibacy as a priest.</note>. 

What also shall we say of diet? Will it not be permitted and beneficial to produce wine in autumn, and daily bread and feasts, under a fortunate star? And if we are unable to wait for specific alignments of the stars in preparing these, it will at least be helpful to catch the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon when they are **ascending** <note>Rising on the eastern horizon at the start of an undertaking.</note> or otherwise in the **angles** <note>The four most powerful points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, or Bottom of the Sky.</note>. For in this way, all things that we use, being happily influenced from the heavens, will happily influence us. 

Up to this point, I see you would concede without controversy, unless perhaps you say that in this way our life would be nothing other than perpetual servitude. To this I would reply that mortals will serve in vain the piling up of money and honors, to which they are perpetually enslaved, unless in the meantime they accumulate more days of life for themselves through **natural diligence** <term>diligentia physica: The careful application of natural science and medical-astrological timing to maintain health.</term>. Either, therefore, let them serve God alone—which is indeed the most important thing—or if they are going to serve anything else, let them serve a life that is both strong and long, rather than indulging in vain money and honors. 

Therefore we are in agreement. But should they then lay the foundations of houses at random, or live in ill-omened ones? For a certain contagious disaster of a building infects the inhabitant much like a poisonous vapor of pestilence preserved in a wall for even two years—just as the vapor of an epidemic lurking in a garment infects and destroys the unwary user long afterward. 

But since we have stumbled onto the mention of clothing here, will you forbid me, pious father, when making a garment or first looking upon it, to diligently hunt for a "breath of Venus" <note>An astrological timing where Venus is prominent, intended to imbue the object with grace and health.</note>? By this, the garment is made "Venereal," as it were, so that it might similarly affect the body and spirit with a certain prosperous quality. Do not Physicians forbid the skins of foxes, but approve those of lambs? Perhaps a star affects garments daily as they are "born" <note>Ficino treats the moment a garment is completed or first worn as its "birth" or inception.</note> no differently than it affects those born once and for all at the beginning. That garments and other works of art receive a certain quality from a star is confirmed by **Thomas Aquinas** in his book *On Fate* <note>Ficino cites the most authoritative Catholic theologian to prove that even artificial objects can hold "occult" or celestial properties.</note>. You, therefore, will surely affirm it. Indeed, that infected clothes infect the user is witnessed by both the itch and leprosy. Finally, if you care for the life of the people (as I think you do), you will permit these things. And with your permission, I shall advise that they be observed. 

But if you do not exactly disapprove of such care for this dying life, but rather advise that it should be neglected, I for one shall neglect it—relying on my faith in a better life—and I advise others to do the same. Farewell.

<summary>Ficino argues that using astrology to time daily activities like cooking, building, and making clothes is a legitimate form of "natural diligence" rather than a violation of free will. He justifies these practices to a hypothetical religious critic by citing Church authorities like Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas.</summary>
<keywords>astrological timing, free will, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, medical astrology, planetary influences, natural diligence, clothing, agriculture</keywords>

<page-num>570</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS</header>

### How higher things are drawn down through lower things exposed to them; and how worldly gifts are especially drawn through worldly materials.

-> Chapter XXVI. <-

**B**UT lest we wander too far from that which we established at the beginning while interpreting Plotinus, let us briefly summarize it thus: The world was made as good as it could possibly be by the Good itself (as Plato, along with the Pythagorean Timaeus, teaches). It is, therefore, not only corporeal, but also a participant in life and intelligence. For this reason, besides this body of the world which is familiarly manifest to the senses, there lies hidden within it a certain spirit-body <note>original: "spiritus corpus quoddam." Ficino refers to the *spiritus mundi*, a subtle, vaporous substance that acts as a bridge between the physical world and the immaterial Soul of the World.</note>, exceeding the capacity of our fleeting senses. Within this spirit thrives the soul; within the soul shines the intelligence. And just as below the Moon air is not mixed with earth except through the medium of water, nor fire with water except through air, so in the universe there is a certain "bait" <note>original: "esca." Ficino often uses fishing or trapping metaphors to describe how physical objects "catch" celestial influences.</note> or fuel for joining the soul to the body; this is the very thing we call the spirit. The soul is also a kind of fuel in the spirit and body of the world for attaining intelligence from the divine, just as the highest degree of dryness in wood is prepared to be penetrated by oil. The oil soaked into this wood is food for fire—I mean for heat, most closely. Heat itself is the vehicle of light, as if this wood were of such a kind that it might shine in the presence of fire without being consumed, such as we have sometimes seen. Now, by this example, we shall see whether a human being, or something else below the Moon, can—through certain preparations, partly natural and partly sought through art—receive in an opportune way certain vital and perhaps even intellectual goods from above.

However, that which pertains to religion here we shall discuss elsewhere, when Plotinus brings these matters into the open. But as for what pertains to natural influences, of whatever kind they may be that come from above, know that they can only be matched to us and our materials through time when nature suggests "fuels" for them within us and our things, and when the heavens have conspired more opportunely toward them. Does not nature itself, the architect of the fetus, when it has affected and shaped the little body in a certain way, immediately draw down the spirit from the universe by this very preparation, as if by a kind of bait? And through this spirit, as if through fuel, does it not drink in life and the soul? And finally, through a certain form and disposition of the soul, is the body thus living not at last worthy of the presence of the Mind <note>original: "mentis," referring to the *Nous* or Higher Intellect.</note> already gifted from the divine?

Therefore, everywhere "nature is a magician," as Plotinus and Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neoplatonist bishop who wrote on dreams and the spirit-body.</note> say; namely, by enticing certain things everywhere with certain "foods," not otherwise than how she draws heavy things to the center of the earth, light things to the concavity of the Moon, leaves by heat, roots by moisture, and other things similarly. The wise Indians <note>Ficino likely draws this from reports of Gymnosophists or Hermetic texts claiming the world is a single living creature.</note> testify that the world is bound to itself by this attraction, saying that the world is an animal that is everywhere male and at the same time female, and everywhere it couples with itself through the mutual love of its members, and thus it stands firm; the bond of the members, moreover, exists through the mind implanted in it, which, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mixes itself with the great body. 

Hence Orpheus calls nature itself and the worldly Jupiter both male and female <note>original: "marem... & foeminam." This refers to the Orphic concept of the *Androgynous Zeus*.</note>. To such an extent is the world everywhere greedy for the mutual marriage of its parts. Indeed, that the masculine sex is everywhere mixed with the feminine is declared, on one hand, by the order of the signs, where the one preceding is always masculine in order, and the following one is feminine; and on the other hand, by trees and herbs, which, just like animals, possess both sexes. I pass over the fact that fire holds the place of the male toward the air, and water toward the earth as the female, so that it is no wonder that the members of the world and all its joints desire mutual marriage among themselves. The planets also conciliate this, being partly male and partly female, but especially Mercury, who is both male and female, the father of Hermaphroditus. 

Truly, observing this, agriculture prepares the field and the "female" for celestial gifts, and through certain graftings propagates the life of the plant and leads it to another and better species. The Physician, the Natural Philosopher, and the Surgeon perform similar things in our body, both for our own nourishment and for matching ourselves more abundantly to the nature of the universe. The Philosopher also, skilled in natural things and the stars, whom we are properly accustomed to call a **Magus** <note><term>Magus: A practitioner of "natural magic." Unlike "black magic" which deals with demons, Ficino's Magus is a scientist-priest who uses the hidden properties of plants, stones, and timing to harmonize human life with the cosmos.</term></note>, does the same, applying celestial things to earthly ones by certain allurements, and doing so quite opportunely, not otherwise than a farmer skilled in grafting inserts a fresh sprout into an old trunk. Ptolemy strongly approves of this, affirming that a wise man of this kind can assist the work of the stars just as a farmer assists the power of the earth. The Magus subjects earthly things to heavenly ones—indeed, lower things everywhere to higher ones—so that they are like appropriate females everywhere to be fertilized by their males: like iron to be drawn by the magnet, like camphor to be dissolved by the burning air, like crystal...

<summary>Ficino explains the "natural magic" of the universe, arguing that the world is a living, hermaphroditic organism where higher celestial influences are drawn down into lower physical objects through specific "baits" or preparations, much like a farmer grafts trees.</summary>

<page-num>571</page-num>
<header>COMPARISONS. BOOK III.</header>

...just as a crystal is to be illuminated by the Sun, or sulfur and sublime liquid <note>Likely referring to alcohol or "aqua vitae."</note> are to be ignited by a flame; or as an empty eggshell filled with dew is to be raised up by the Sun, or even as the egg of a hen is to be brooded upon. Furthermore, just as some who brood over eggs—even without animals—bring life to them from the universe, and by opportunely preparing certain materials often procreate animals without eggs or manifest seeds (such as a scorpion from basil, bees from an ox, or from sage a creature similar to a blackbird), thus drawing life from the world into specific materials at opportune times. So too that wise man, when he has learned which materials (whether partially begun by nature or perfected by art) can receive a specific heavenly influence even if they have been scattered and then gathered, collects these things especially while that influence is reigning. He prepares them, applies them, and through them claims celestial gifts for himself. For wherever a certain material is thus exposed to the higher beings, like a looking-glass to your face or a wall opposite a voice, it suddenly suffers an effect from above—namely from that most powerful agent, from a power and life that is wonderfully present everywhere—and it carries back a virtue from that experience, not unlike how a mirror represents an image from a face, and a wall represents an Echo from a voice. 

Plotinus himself uses almost these same examples where, imitating Hermes <note>original: "Mercurium." Ficino uses the Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, he says the ancient priests, or Magi, were accustomed to observe something divine and wonderful in statues and insensible sacrifices. He wishes to clarify, along with Trismegistus, that it is not properly the divine spirits entirely segregated from matter that are received through these material things, but only "worldly" spirits, as I said from the beginning and as Synesius approves. "Worldly," I say, meaning a certain life or something vital from the Soul of the World, and from the souls of the spheres and the stars; or even a certain motion and a vital presence, as it were, from the <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>; indeed, that sometimes the daemons themselves are present in such materials. 

Hermes himself, whom Plotinus follows, says these are aerial daemons, not celestial ones (let alone higher ones). Hermes himself composes statues from herbs, trees, stones, and aromatics that have in themselves (as he says) a natural power of divinity. He adds songs similar to the celestial ones, by which he says they are delighted, and thus stay longer in the statues and either benefit or harm men. He adds that the ancient Egyptians, who were also priests, when they could not persuade the people by reason that there were gods—that is, certain spirits above men—devised this illicit Magic by which, luring daemons into statues, they might declare them to be divinities. 

But Iamblichus condemns the Egyptians because they did not merely accept daemons as certain steps toward investigating the higher gods, but worshipped them greatly. He prefers the Chaldeans to the Egyptians, as they were not occupied with daemons. By Chaldeans, I mean the leaders of their religion; for we may suspect that the Astrologers, both of the Chaldeans and the Egyptians, attempted in a certain way to draw daemons into clay statues through celestial harmony. 

The astrologer Samuel the Hebrew <note>Possibly Samuel ibn Abbas or a similar medieval source.</note> seems to signify this, relying on the authority of David the "Bilastrologer," <note>original: "Bilastrologi." Likely a reference to a specific medieval astrological authority.</note> namely that the ancient fashioners of images made statues that pronounced the future. He teaches that the harmony of the heavens was accommodated to these. He says to melt the metal into the form of a beautiful man on the day of Mercury at the third hour (which is the hour of Saturn), when Mercury comes under Saturn in Aquarius in the ninth region of the heaven <note>The "ninth house" in astrology, which governs prophecy and religion.</note> to designate prophecy. The constellation of Gemini rises, signifying Prophets (as they say); Mars is <term>combust</term> <note>A planet is "combust" when it is too close to the sun, weakening its influence.</note> by the Sun and does not look at Mercury; the Sun, however, regards the place of that conjunction; meanwhile Venus occupies some angle and is Western and powerful; the Moon regards the ascending degree from a <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious.</note> aspect, and Saturn does likewise. These are his words. 

I, however, think first according to the opinion of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] that if they indeed made speaking statues, it was not the simple influence of the stars itself that formed the words there, but daemons. Secondly, if it happened that they entered such statues, I do not think they were bound there by celestial influence, but rather obeyed their worshippers voluntarily, ultimately intending to deceive them. For a higher nature is sometimes won over by a lower one, but it cannot be constrained. And that disposition of the stars described a moment ago can perhaps never actually occur. Although daemons may be included in statues by astronomical reasoning, Porphyry says that when they were present through the worship offered to them, they gave oracles according to astronomical rules, and for that reason they were frequently ambiguous. And rightly so, since Iamblichus proves that true and certain prophecy does not suit evil daemons, nor human arts or nature, but comes from divine inspiration to purified minds. But let us now return to Hermes, or rather to Plotinus. Hermes says the priests received a fitting power from the nature of the world and mixed it. Plotinus, following him, thinks the whole thing can easily be accomplished within the reconciling Soul of the World, insofar as that Soul [contains] the forms of natural things through the seed-like...

<meta>catchword: ...reasons which</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic theory of how "animated" statues and talismans work, citing Plotinus and Hermes Trismegistus. He reconciles these magical practices with Christian thought by citing Thomas Aquinas, arguing that while celestial timing can attract spirits, true prophecy requires divine purification.</summary>

<page-num>572</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE</header>

...[the Soul of the World] generates and moves certain principles <note>Latin: "rationes"—these are "seminal reasons" or internal blueprints that govern the growth and form of things.</note> divinely implanted within itself. It even calls these principles "gods," since they are never abandoned by the Ideas of the supreme mind. Therefore, through such principles, the Soul of the World easily applies itself to materials which it formed from the beginning through those same principles, whenever a Magician or priest, at the opportune times, has applied the forms of things properly collected. These materials properly regard this or that principle, just as a Magnet regards iron, Rhubarb regards bile <note>original: "cholera"; in medieval medicine, rhubarb was used to purge yellow bile.</note>, Saffron the heart, Agrimony <note>original: "Eupatorium."</note> and Spodium <note>A technical term for metallic ash or residue, often used in ancient pharmacy for its cooling properties.</note> the liver, or Nard <note>original: "Spica."</note> and Musk the brain. It can indeed happen at times that when principles are applied to forms in this way, even more sublime gifts descend, insofar as the principles in the Soul of the World are joined to the intellectual forms of that same Soul, and through them to the Ideas of the divine Mind. Iamblichus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy (divine magic).</note> also approves of this when he treats the subject of sacrifices. We shall dispute this matter more opportunely elsewhere, where it will also appear how impure the superstition of the Gentile people was, and on the contrary, how pure the Evangelical piety was—a task we have already largely performed in our book *On the Christian Religion*.

->**THE END.**<-

# MARSILIO FICINO’S
## Apology, in which Medicine, Astro-
## logy, and the Life of the World. Also concerning 
## the Magi, who greeted Christ 
## immediately upon His birth,
## are treated.

**M**arsilio Ficino the Florentine sends three and fourfold greetings to his brothers most beloved in the study of truth: the three "Peters"—Nero, Guicciardini, and Soderini <note>Francesco Nero, Girolamo Guicciardini, and Paolantonio Soderini were prominent Florentines and friends of Ficino.</note>. I might perhaps have more rightly said "Triple-Peter" [Tripetro] rather than "three Peters." For just as where there is one palm, the several fingers on it do not make several hands, so your three bodies as friends seem to prevent nothing from one will creating a single "Peter." Christ, that craftsman of the celestial fatherland, created so great a rock <note>A pun on the name "Peter" (Petrus) and "Rock" (petra).</note> that this one rock was sufficient for the founding of this immense edifice of His Church. I also, by a certain divine fate, have obtained such great rocks that three of them now suffice for my own quite arduous building. Now to you, friends, now—if you do not know it—that citadel of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; her citadel represents a place of intellectual defense.</note> seems necessary, by which we may ward off the cruel attack of impious giants far from us. For this reason, I have decided to fortify the "Life" of my three books—which come to the aid of the public life—with your citadel, first constructed of three rocks. 

You know (as I believe) that I composed a book *On Life*, divided into three small volumes. Of these, the first was inscribed *On the Healthy Life*, the second *On the Long Life*, and the third *On the Celestial Life*. Therefore, the bait of so sweet a title will entice many to taste it. But in such a great number, many (as I believe) will be ignorant, and not a few will be malicious. One will say: "Is Marsilio not a priest?" He certainly is. "What business then do priests have with medicine? What, moreover, with Astrology?" Another will say: "What does a Christian have to do with magic or images?" Another, indeed—himself unworthy of life—will envy a life drawn from heaven. Finally, all those so affected will be far too ungrateful for our benefit to them, and they will not be ashamed to be cruel toward our charity, by which we consult the prosperity of the public life according to the capacity of our talent. This labor, therefore, will be common to us; but so that it may be in some way lighter, since you are three against three enemies, undertake a distributed battle. Nor will you (for I know your character) refute an invective with an invective, but rather (such is your wonderful sweetness) you will overcome the bitterness of another's gall with the sweetness of your honey. 

First, most candid Nero, I shall respond to the first critics: that in ancient times the most ancient priests were also physicians, as well as Astronomers <note>Likely a printer's error for 'Astronomers' [Astronomos].</note>. Certainly, the histories of the Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians testify to this. Furthermore, the duties of singular charity pertain to no one more than to a pious priest, which indeed shine most brightly in the greatest benefit of all.

<summary>Ficino concludes his third book of "De Vita" by explaining natural sympathies and then begins his "Apology," defending his right as a priest to write about medicine, astrology, and natural magic.</summary>

Having just finished the third book, which dealt heavily with astrological influences, he now addresses his friends and critics to justify the union of medicine, astrology, and natural magic.</meta>

<page-num>593</page-num>

# APOLOGY #

It is, without a doubt, a truly most excellent duty—as well as a most necessary one, and one especially desired by all people—to ensure that men have **a sound mind in a sound body.** <note>Latin: "mens sana in corpore sano," a famous phrase from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> However, we can only truly fulfill this duty if we join medicine to the priesthood. But since medicine is quite often useless, or even harmful, without celestial favor (as both Hippocrates and Galen <note>Ancient Greek founders of Western medicine.</note> admit, and as we ourselves have experienced), it follows that **Astronomy** <note>In Ficino’s time, "Astronomy" and "Astrology" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of celestial influences.</note> belongs to that same priestly charity to which we have said medicine belongs. Holy Scripture <note>Referring to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1: "Honor the physician for the need thou hast of him."</note> commands that a physician of this kind be honored, since the Most High created him out of necessity. And Christ himself, the giver of life, who commanded his disciples to heal the sick throughout the whole world, will also command his priests that—even if they cannot heal with mere words as the disciples once did—they should at least heal with **herbs and stones.** And if these substances are not sufficient on their own, He will command the priests to infuse them with a certain opportune "breath" from heaven <note>Latin: "afflatus," a divine or celestial influence.</note> and apply them to the sick. For He Himself, by that same celestial breath, everywhere incites animals to find their own medicines, so abundantly does He provide for the lives of all. Thus, by a divine instigation of celestial instinct, serpents heal their eyes with **fennel**, <note>Latin: "marathro." Ancient lore claimed serpents ate fennel to clear their sight after shedding their skin.</note> and swallows heal theirs with **celandine**; <note>Latin: "chelidonia," from the Greek "chelidon" (swallow). It was believed swallows used this plant to restore sight to their young.</note> and eagles, when troubled in giving birth, found by divine providence the **eagle-stone**, <note>Latin: "aetitem," a hollow stone with a smaller stone loose inside, believed to assist in childbirth.</note> by which their eggs might immediately and successfully be brought forth. Therefore, if God Himself, through the heavens, incites every kind of animal toward medicines, He surely permits priests to expel diseases using medicines strengthened by the heavens—not for profit, I say, but out of charity. To these points, you may henceforth add even more with the sharp stings of your own wit, if it should be necessary.

Rise up after this, you vehement Guicciardini, <note>Francesco Guicciardini, a prominent Florentine statesman and friend of Ficino.</note> and respond to those with "curious" minds: tell them that **magic and images** are not "approved" by Marsilio, but are merely "narrated" while he interprets Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note> himself. My writings clearly declare this, if they are read with a fair mind. Nor is a single word asserted here concerning that **profane magic** which relies on the worship of demons; rather, mention is made only of **natural magic**, which captures the benefits of the heavens through natural objects for the sake of the body's prosperous health. This faculty, surely, ought to be granted to those who use their wits legitimately, just as medicine and agriculture are granted by right—and even more so, since this industry is more perfect, coupling celestial things to earthly ones. From this workshop, the **Magi** <note>The "Wise Men" from the East in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> were the very first of all to adore the newborn Christ. Why, then, do you fear the name of "Magus" so dreadfully? It is a name pleasing to the Gospel, which signifies not a "sorcerer" or "poisoner," but a **wise man** and a **priest.** What does that first Magus, the worshiper of Christ, profess? If you wish to hear: he is like a sort of "farmer," or rather, a **"cultivator of the world."** <note>Latin: "mundicola," a play on "agricola" (farmer/earth-cultivator).</note> Nor does he adore the world because of this, just as a farmer does not adore the earth. But just as a farmer, for the sake of human food, tempers his field to the air, so that wise man, that priest, for the sake of human health, tempers the lower parts of the world to the higher parts; and just as a hen's eggs, he opportunely subjects earthly things to the heavens to be "brooded" upon. God Himself always does this, and by doing it He teaches and urges us to do the same: that the lowest things may be generated, moved, and governed by the highest. Finally, there are two kinds of magic. One belongs to those who reconcile themselves to **demons** through a certain worship; relying on their work, they often manufacture portents. This was utterly exploded when "the prince of this world was cast out." <note>A reference to John 12:31.</note> But the other kind belongs to those who opportunely subject natural materials to natural causes, to be formed in a certain wonderful way.

There are also two species of this latter art. One is "curious," <note>In the sense of "prying" or "superstitious curiosity."</note> the other is "necessary." The former invents superfluous prodigies for the sake of ostentation, such as when the Persian Magi <note>Ficino often contrasts the "good" Magi of the Bible with the "bad" sorcerers of Persia.</note> supposedly generated a creature like a blackbird with a serpent's tail from saliva putrefied under dung (while the Sun and Moon occupied the second face of Leo and held the same degree). They then reduced it to ash and poured it into a lamp, whereupon the house immediately seemed full of serpents. This sort of thing is to be shunned as vain and harmful to health. However, the **necessary species** must be kept, which joins **Astrology with Medicine.** But if anyone should stubbornly press further, deal with him thus, Guicciardini: let him not read these things, nor understand them, nor remember them—let no man use them, if he is a man utterly unworthy of such a great benefit. There are many other things besides which you, with your wit, will be able to bring forward against ungrateful ignorance. And what are you doing, our vigorous Soderini? <note>Paolantonio Soderini, another of Ficino's influential Florentine patrons.</note> Will you tolerate certain superstitious and blind men—I know not who—who see manifest life in even the most abject animals and the lowliest herbs, yet do not see it in the heavens, nor in the world? Now truly, if these little men grant life to the smallest particles of the world, what madness is this, what envy, to neither know nor wish the **Whole** to live—**in which we live, and move, and have our being?** <note>A quotation from Acts 17:28, here applied by Ficino to the "World Soul."</note> Indeed...

<summary>Ficino defends his work by distinguishing "natural magic" (using celestial timing for medicine) from "demonic magic." He argues that because God gave animals natural remedies, priests should be allowed to use astrology and herbs to heal the body as well as the soul.</summary>
<keywords>Natural Magic, Medicine, Astrology, Priesthood, Plotinus, Magi, World Soul, Guicciardini, Soderini, Christ the Healer</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the "Apology" (Ficino’s defense of his book *On Life*) and begins a new letter regarding the psychological requirements for a healthy life. Ficino continues his argument that the universe is a living organism and calls upon his famous humanist friends—using mythological nicknames—to help defend his work against "superstitious" critics.</meta>

<page-num>574</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS</header>

Aratus <note>A Greek poet (c. 315–240 BCE) whose work on stars was famous in the Renaissance.</note> sings of this, clearly signifying Jupiter as the common life of the world's body. Quite opportunely, I seem to have stumbled upon these words of Aratus. I remember that Luke the Evangelist and Paul the Apostle freely used these words, <note>Ficino refers to Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said."</note> in which those wise men did not shudder at the "life of the world." But indeed, a certain superstitious person will object to these things, claiming it cannot easily be proven from such words that Paul agrees that the world has a soul, but only that it is subject to God, and that we live in this very God.

So be it, then: let us not name a "soul" in the world, since that does not please you. Let the name "soul" be considered profane. But will it not at least be permitted to speak of some kind of "life"? Let us say that God himself, the craftsman of the world, mercifully inspires this work of his—so happily completed—with life, since He is not stingy toward even the most useful living things, and daily provides life most abundantly through the heavens and the many things within them. Tell me, I pray, do you not see that oxen and donkeys (O you ox, O you donkey!) are alive, they who generate living things from themselves by a certain touch? If, therefore, these creatures also generated certain living things from themselves merely by their *sight*, would you not judge them to be much more alive? 

The Heaven is the husband of the Earth; it does not touch her (as is the common opinion), and it does not copulate with the Earth as a wife, but with the rays of its sun and stars—as if with eyes—it illuminates its wife from all sides. By illuminating her, it fertilizes her and procreates living things. Does the Heaven, then, while bestowing life even by a mere glance, possess no life of its own? To think that the life and life-giving gaze God gave to the ostrich is far better than the Heaven itself! Having finally brought these points into the open, unless you can persuade that superstitious fellow, I leave him half-dead—or rather, not alive at all.

Furthermore, so that we may plead our cause with more advocates, add, my dear Pietro Nero, <note>Pietro del Nero, a member of the Platonic Academy of Florence.</note> our "Amphion," <note>In myth, Amphion moved stones with his music; here Ficino refers to the orator and poet Cristoforo Landino.</note> Cristoforo Landino, the orator and poet. Our Amphion, with wonderful sweetness, will quickly soften the stony hearts of our enemies. But you, my dearest godfather Guicciardini, <note>Piero Guicciardini, father of the famous historian Francesco Guicciardini.</note> go now, go swiftly and summon "Hercules" Poliziano. <note>Angelo Poliziano, the brilliant poet and scholar. Ficino likens him to Hercules for his strength in intellectual combat.</note> Formerly, when a more dangerous battle was to be fought, they used to call upon Iolaus; <note>The nephew and charioteer of Hercules who helped him slay the Hydra.</note> you now similarly know Hercules, because the "Hercules" Poliziano has attacked, torn apart, and slain the barbarian monsters now devastating Latium, <note>Central Italy; Ficino refers to Poliziano's defense of refined Latin against "barbaric" medieval styles.</note> and he fiercely fights them everywhere and safely defends us. He will immediately crush with his club, and burn with flames, even the hundred heads of the Hydra threatening our children. 

Come now, my sweetest Soderini, <note>Paolo Antonio Soderini, a prominent Florentine statesman.</note> arise, go and greet "Phoebus" Pico. <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous philosopher. Phoebus is another name for Apollo, god of wisdom and light.</note> I often call this man my Phoebus, and he in turn calls me Dionysus and Liber. <note>Both names for the god of wine and inspiration.</note> Therefore, we are brothers. Announce to my Phoebus that a venomous Python <note>The dragon slain by Apollo; here representing Ficino's critics.</note> is now emerging from the swamp against us. Beseech him, I pray, to draw his bow. Let him hurl his arrows at once. He will aim them immediately—I know what I am saying—and he will kill the whole poison at once with a single death. 

Farewell now happily, my most beloved brothers, worthy not only of good health, but of happiness itself; take care of the health and happiness of my children <note>Ficino often referred to his books as his "children."</note> now being brought into the light.

September 15, 1489. In the fields of Careggi.

->THE END OF THE APOLOGY.<-

# THAT SECURITY #
### and tranquility of mind are ###
### necessary for life. ###

**M**arsilio Ficino to his brothers, most beloved in the hunt for truth: Bernardo Canigiani, Giovanni Canacci, and Amerigo Corsini, greetings. Since I had established a certain "hunt" in these first words, we perhaps rightly and immediately employed "dogs" and "runners." We have aptly called those practicing philosophy "hunters," as they are always laboring in the breathless tracking of truth. But have we also aptly called them dogs? Socrates says in the *Republic* that this is most apt. For those practicing philosophy are either legitimate or spurious. Both are dogs. The former investigate truth itself sagaciously and hold onto it firmly once found. The latter, however, bark, bite, and tear for the sake of mere opinion. Indeed, dogs claim so much for themselves among philosophers that they have not only inserted themselves into a particular sect, but even established their own sect under the name of "Cynic" <note>From the Greek 'kyon', meaning dog. The Cynics were a school of philosophy known for their rejection of social conventions.</note> at one time.

<header>LETTER.</header>

### LETTER.

The Academy even has its own dogs. Therefore, I call upon you, the sagacious dogs of the Academy; I call upon you as the swiftest of runners. For there are three. <note>original: "Treis enim est" - likely a typo for "sunt." He refers to the three books of his work *De Vita* (On Life).</note> Therefore, I pray you, defend my three children, who are still quite tender and who, I fear, will immediately step out among wolves. Run, I say, with alacrity, for I am now assigning you desirable business, not worries. You know my George Benignus Salviati, <note>Juraj Dragišić (c. 1445–1520), a Franciscan theologian and member of Ficino's circle.</note> who long ago sagaciously attained that truth whose tracks you are now hunting far and wide. He, like the Sun, being greater himself, illuminates his younger brothers. Therefore, if you hear any howling of wolves, report it to him. That most brave George will easily put all wolves to flight—he who once even transfixed a vast dragon. <note>A play on the legend of Saint George, the namesake of George Benignus.</note> He, therefore, will relieve me of anxiety and you of care at the same time.

For some among you is accustomed to say, and indeed quite often, that nothing is experienced as more healthful for life than to "swallow down time" with great security. The others, hearing this, immediately smile. But come, tell me, Canacus, <note>Likely a nickname for one of Ficino's students.</note> what is this of yours so often repeated: "to devour time"? What, finally, do you mean by it? Not to *be*, you will say, but rather to drink; not to chew or grind, but to engorge with full throat. For time itself is by nature a certain liquid thing (if I may put it so) and prone to slipping away. Indeed, this is the condition of liquid things: if you constrain them into a narrow space, you suddenly lose them. For when forced together, they flow away and quickly escape. If you happen to squeeze water that has been soaked into a sponge, you press it out and immediately scatter it. If you hold it more loosely, you will retain it; and much more so with air, fire, and the ether.

Hence, among the Poets, they struggle in vain who strive to grasp the vast phantoms of the gods or the spirits of the dead in their arms. <note>A reference to classical scenes where heroes try to hug ghosts (like Aeneas and Creusa), but their arms pass through them because the spirits are "thin" and "wide."</note> Very wide things must be received very widely. Liquid and very vast things must be possessed in the vastest way. Then certainly distress presses heavily upon us when we reduce the soul itself, and its naturally vast movement, into a narrow space. Whoever weighs their studies and business with extreme precision, and always grinds themselves down most exactly into every tiny detail, meanwhile—alas!—those miserable ones secretly wear away their own life.

Therefore, Pythagoras seems to have commanded rightly: "Take care lest you are ever perhaps confined in a narrow space." <note>A philosophical maxim advising against mental rigidity or excessive focus on trivialities.</note> Nothing is vaster than heaven; nothing is more vital. Conversely, the earth, being the narrowest, has the least life in the world. Finally, if we live by heaven and by time, the more widely we absorb these, the longer we live. Therefore, live joyfully far from narrowness, O friends. Live joyfully. Joy created you through its own heaven, which it declares by its own "smile"—that is, by dilation, movement, and splendor—as if exulting. Your own joy will preserve heaven for you. Therefore, live joyfully every day in the present. For anxiety over present things snatches the present from you and steals away the future. Curiosity about future things quickly drags you into the past. Therefore, I pray again and again: live joyfully. For the fates permit it, as long as you live without care. 

But so that you may truly live without care, do not take up even this one care: that you should ever be anxiously concerned with what particular diligence you might escape cares. For this one care, alas, wears away miserable mortals with every other care. Therefore, neglect diligence, but love negligence—and even love this negligently, as much as is permitted to you, I say, and as much as is becoming. I command these things to you not so much as a priest, my friends, but as a physician. For without this one thing, which is like the life of all medicines, all medicines applied to prolong life die away.
September 16, 1489. In the fields of Careggi. <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino's Academy met.</note>

## ANDREAS LENNIUS to students 
## of medicine, Greetings.

It seemed to us not without purpose to attach to these books *On Life* an "antidote to epidemics" <note>A treatise on the plague.</note> as a sort of finishing touch <term>crown<gloss>from the Greek 'coronis,' meaning a curved line at the end of a book or the final flourish</gloss></term> by the same author, which he had written in his own mother tongue—that is, Tuscan—at the request of his friends. But now this treasure of life has been channeled into the Roman colony <note>Meaning it has been translated from Italian into Latin, the language of Rome.</note> by Girolamo Riccio of Pavia, so that if you measure profit along with pleasure, it should not be despised. In it are handed down not only the definitions of the disease and the causes producing the sickness, but also the signs, as well as the <term>prophylaxis<gloss>preventative treatment</gloss></term> and the cure for the present evil, touching upon remedies adapted to various and different bodies with marvelous brevity and ease. Relying on these defenses, you may enter into a plan for life and health, and persuade yourself:

->For a man, to be healthy is the best thing, as it seems to me.<-

# THE ANTIDOTE AGAINST EPIDEMICS
## By Marsilio Ficino,
->the most renowned Florentine Physician and Philosopher, translated from<-
->the Tuscan language into Latin by Girolamo Ricci.<-

### P R E F A C E

**I** have deemed it worthwhile, driven by a sense of duty toward my homeland, to write down certain counsels against the disease of the plague. However, so that everyone may be able to grasp its meaning and put its care into practice, I have decided to reject all subtle and lengthy disputes. For it will be enough that whatever I am about to hand down at present—even if no more can be said in so brief a composition—is both proven and handed down through sufficient reasoning and the authority and experience of many authors, both ancient and modern. I especially rely on my father, M. Ficino <note>Marsilio’s father was Diotifeci d’Agnolo, a prominent physician to Cosimo de' Medici.</note>, a leader among doctors, who restored many infected by this blight to their former health. We therefore implore God, the Best and Greatest, the giver of human life and the revealer of true and health-giving medicines, that He might disclose to us effective remedies against the dangers of the plague, and that He might preserve His gift of life for us, to His own praise and glory.

->*What the plague is, and of what sort it may be. Chapter 1.*<-

**P**lague is a certain poisonous vapor created within the air, an enemy to the **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit (a subtle substance believed by ancient doctors to be the primary instrument of the soul, carrying life-force from the heart through the arteries)</term>. It is not an enemy because of any elemental quality (such as being too hot or too cold), but rather by a specific property of its own. Just as **Theriaca** <note>A famous ancient medicinal "polypharmacy" compound containing dozens of ingredients, used as a universal antidote</note> is a friend to the body—not because it is hot, cold, dry, or moist, but because a certain form results from its entire composition that is suited to the form of the vital spirit—so too is that pestilential vapor an enemy to nature. This is not because of its heat, coldness, moisture, or dryness, but because its proportion is, as it were, exactly contrary to the proportion in which the vital spirit consists within the heart. And just as poisons are continually born in the earth, so a poisonous vapor is often born in the air; however, it is not as potent because it is more widely dispersed. Nor can it take hold in pure air, for such air is conformed to the spirit and to fire, which by the power of its own nature does not receive the mixture of another nature; hence it does not take on any putrefaction. Thus, pure air, by receiving no mixture, can by no means rot.

Furthermore, a poisonous vapor of this kind attaches itself only to a human body in which there are **humors** <term>humors (the four primary fluids of the body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term> suited to fever, such as those disposed toward rot and inflammation. Indeed, if the vital spirit is more powerful than the vapor, it drives it far from itself; but if it is weaker, it flees from it as its own contrary. Therefore, it is useful to seize, purge, and strengthen the air, the humors, and finally the heart. It must be noted (so that you may understand correctly) that when I say this vapor is poisonous, you should not believe it to be so according to its form and entire nature, for then everyone would be infected by it. Rather, it is of such a quality that it very easily passes into the nature of a poison. It properly becomes a poison when, through it, the humors in a human body rot and simultaneously boil to a certain degree. This usually happens on the third day, and sometimes sooner, especially where one abounds in superfluous humors, particularly blood and **cholera** <note>original: "cholera" — here referring to yellow bile, one of the four humors, rather than the modern bacterial disease</note>. And when it has already taken on the nature of a poison, it receives a quality like that of lime or arsenic, the effect of which is to rot, corrode, and burn both within and without. It is, therefore, of the highest necessity...

<summary>This page introduces Ficino's treatise on the plague, defining the disease as a "poisonous vapor" that attacks the heart's vital spirit. Ficino explains that the plague targets those with imbalanced humors and emphasizes the need to strengthen the heart and purify the air.</summary>
<keywords>plague, medicine, vital spirit, humors, Theriaca, yellow bile, pathology, Florentine medicine</keywords>

...so that we may resist these three effects, especially internally, with all the industry we can.
