### *The causes of the origin of the epidemic, and which bodies are especially liable to this evil.*
#### Chapter II.

**A** vapor of this kind is created in the air at the time of a more universal plague from certain malignant **constellations** <note>In the 15th century, physicians believed the alignment of stars and planets directly influenced the "subtle air" and human health.</note>, especially from a significant conjunction of Mars with Saturn that impacts human affairs, and from eclipses of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refers to the Sun and the Moon.</note>. Such is the present plague in this year of 1479, and such it also was in the year 1478; and this especially harms human beings. It rages in those places that have an unfortunate **horoscope** <term>horoscope (the configuration of the planets at a specific moment, believed here to determine the vulnerability of a specific geographic location)</term>, or its own "ascendant," due to the aforementioned celestial aspects.

In more particular <note>original: "particularibus," referring to localized outbreaks rather than global pandemics</note> pestilences, however, the aforementioned poison is known to arise from winds and malignant vapors from pits and sewers, and likewise from earthquakes. But whatever the cause of these may be, the plague always reigns most powerfully in thick air—in marshy, foggy, and foul air. When it spreads into thin and subtle air, it penetrates and kills more swiftly; however, it reigns more frequently and for a longer duration in thick, hot, moist, and foul air. 

Some learned men assert that pestilential putrefaction occurs first in thin air and only later in thick air, but that it is much more curable in the thick. I do not know by what reasoning or foundation I should adhere to the first part of that opinion, since experience shows us the contrary. Furthermore, reason dictates to us that since a pure element cannot rot—only a mixed one can—it follows that the less "mixed" an element is (as is the case with subtle air), the less apt it is for putrefaction. Therefore, subtle air does not take on such rot except through the constant influence of a pestiferous celestial alignment. But just as thicker, mixed, and stagnant water is usually easier to rot, so too does thick and foggy air receive putrefaction without difficulty.

**Raymond** <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a 13th-century polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were highly influential in Ficino’s time.</note> gives this precept: that if the plague is stirred up from below, one must seek higher and thinner air; but if it arises from above, one must first flee for two months downward to thickish, cold, moist, and pure air, where the infirmity is usually rare. In the following two months, one should move to the middle region of the air, and thereafter to a slightly higher region—namely, dry, cold, and subtle air—always fleeing that which is hot, moist, and foggy. Humans in such air are like fish in murky waters. Moreover, pestilential air does to humans what dark and rotting waters do to fish. 

But what is poison to humans need not always be so to other living creatures, because of the diversity of celestial signs and animal species. Hence it arises that I am entirely uncertain what to say of the opinion of those who assert that when a pestilential poison begins in the air, the small birds that usually live on high descend to the depths and inhabit the plains. But when it arises in the earth, they say that worms and snakes emerge from the bowels of the earth, and the small birds whose habit it is to fly and live near the ground seek the heights and head for the mountains. They add further that when the poison is ignited first in the air and then in the earth, the animals sometimes flee from on high to below, and then back again to the heights. This is why it is commonly said that vultures or kites yield to pestilential air, and those places which such kites occupy are not subject to pestiferous air.

We have often heard that this contagion has passed from humans to pigs. This could perhaps happen through some similarity, not of the spirit, but of the flesh. In these most recently passed days, cats and dogs have carried the plague-sickness from one house to another once or twice, yet they themselves were not harmed in any way by this contagion. Let no wonder seize you because of this—that sometimes a human or a beast may receive the aforementioned vapor and yet infect others without suffering any harm themselves. For a glowing iron consumes tow <note>Coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp.</note> and straw, but the iron itself is not consumed. This arises from the disposition of the receiving subject, in which, according to **Aristotle, Galen, and Avicenna** <note>The three primary authorities of medieval and Renaissance medicine: a philosopher, a Roman physician, and a Persian physician.</note>, the effect of a thing chiefly consists. 

So it was in these recent days that a two-year-old boy in our household stayed a whole day with an infected boy of about seven years; he often ate food that had been chewed by the more infected boy, yet he contracted no stain of the disease from him—though others who were a considerable distance away were seized by it. Do not have too much confidence in your own constitution, thinking that you are of such health that this contagion is not to be feared; rather, [seek] this physical...

<sig>Oo</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...remedy (ficum)</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the causes of the plague, citing both astrological alignments (like Mars and Saturn) and terrestrial miasmas (like sewers and stagnant air). He also discusses how the disease can be carried by animals without them falling ill, emphasizing that individual susceptibility varies.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, Mars, Saturn, miasma, air quality, contagion, animal transmission, susceptibility, Raymond Lully, Aristotle, Galen, Avicenna</keywords>

--- Page 601 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the plague vapor interacts with physical matter. The previous page ended while explaining that some learned men believe certain people are more prone to infection than others based on their physical makeup.</meta>

...observe this "dry" rule <note>original: "siccum obserua canonem." A "canon" in this context is a fundamental medical rule or principle.</note>. When the material is highly prepared, the active cause—however weak it may be—quickly produces an effect. In this way, a tiny spark ignites tinder and sulfur because of the recipient's readiness. Conversely, a cause that is extremely powerful will act even upon material that is not prepared. And although sulfur receives the action of fire more quickly than wood, and dry wood that is finely cut catches more easily than other wood, a burning furnace nevertheless instantly sweeps even thick and green logs into flame, because the supreme power of the agent quickly prepares and shapes them. Often, a pestilential vapor of this kind becomes extremely powerful by the force of its own causes, and you cannot know exactly when this happens. Even if such a predisposition is not present at one time, it will be in another.

---

### *In what way and in what temperaments the plague spreads most swiftly through contagion.*
#### Chapter III.

**T**his poisonous vapor is often so subtle that it cannot be discerned by sight. Sometimes it dissipates, but it is easily regenerated from that point as long as the disposing influence remains. And although it may be small at the beginning, it expands from place to place with a much faster course than sulfur when it is ignited. It is far more opposed to the **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit (in medieval medicine, a subtle substance refined from the blood in the heart that carries life-force through the body)</term> of the heart—which is a vapor from refined blood—than sulfur is to the nose. 

A vapor of this kind is ignited by the infected air only in bodies predisposed to it; but once it has been ignited, it spreads all around with marvelous speed and ease—just like ignited sulfur—even more than before. This is especially true when it is ignited in a "subtle" <note>In this context, "subtle" means thin or refined rather than thick and heavy.</note> humor and in the thin air of summer, where it scatters and leaps from one body to another. It ignites most powerfully where there is a greater similarity of nature, and in a body full of **waste** <note>original: "recrementis," referring to the body's undigested or un-expelled waste products</note>, along with foul vapors both inside and out, and in foods and "superfluous" humors that are prone to inflammation and rot. It also thrives where the matter is hot and moist, or where the body has been weakened by **sexual intercourse** <note>original: "coitu." Traditional medicine warned that sex depleted the vital spirits and opened the pores, making one vulnerable to the plague.</note>. 

Likewise, it thrives in a body exhausted by the passions of the soul, or one that is excessively hot, or accustomed to baths, or whose pores are too open or greatly assisted <note>meaning the pores are dilated and thus vulnerable to admitting the poisonous air</note>. This was indeed the opinion of **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>Galen (2nd century) and Avicenna (11th century) were the two most authoritative medical figures for Renaissance doctors.</note>. Children and women are very prone to the plague because their "thin and soft" matter is easier to transform, they are full of humors prone to rot, and their lives are lived outside of a strict or moderate order. 

Just as a hot and thick wind disturbs and spoils wine, so this pestilential vapor infects and forces everything toward the heart—first the spirits, then the humors, which then bubble up as they rot. This **bubbling** <term>ebullition (a medical term for the "boiling" of humors that causes the heat of a fever)</term> is the fever itself, which is then scattered throughout the entire body. It bubbles or swells more than other fevers because the poisonous matter is so great that nature tries to expel it immediately from the principal members with all the strength it can. 

This vapor can stain every humor, but most of all the **sanguine** <note>The humor associated with blood.</note>, second the **choleric** <note>Yellow bile.</note>, third the **phlegm**, and fourth the **melancholy** <note>Black bile.</note>. Thus it happens that those of a sanguine temperament are more subject to this danger; those of a choleric temperament a little less; then the phlegmatic; and the melancholic less than the others. This is because a cold and dry humor is unfit for inflammation and rot, and especially because they have narrow channels <note>original: "meatus," the internal passages of the body</note> through which the poison must pass. For this reason, the elderly are less liable to the pestilential disease, although the plague of this year has not left even the seniors untouched. The reason for this was perhaps that, beyond other adverse planetary alignments, **Saturn retrograde** was the "Lord of the Year" <note>In astrology, the "Lord of the Year" is the planet with the most influence over that year's events. Saturn is traditionally associated with old age and chronic illness.</note>. 

It is a wonder to say that, although almost the entire population has fled from our city of **Florence**, nevertheless about one hundred and fifty people have died every day.

---

### *Concerning the signs and indications of the plague.*
#### Chapter IV.

**A**s for which signs indicate and clearly reveal a fever to be the plague, no one can show this easily because of such a great variety and deceptiveness of symptoms. Indeed, the entire assembly of Doctors testifies to this, especially **Avenzoar** and **Rhazes** <note>Avenzoar and Rhazes were influential medieval Islamic physicians.</note>. For sometimes the urine will be clear because the humors do not reach the liver, and a slight fever will appear because the poison is not in a hot humor; but because of this, the poison does not spread to the outside, and so the patient dies immediately.

-> It will appear <-

### ANTIDOTE

At times, the patient will seem to be recovered, because nature—in its first encounter—has driven the poison away from the heart. However, shortly thereafter, the patient will be left without breath <note>original: "destituetur spiritu." This refers to the failure of the "vital spirit," the life-force believed to be generated in the heart.</note>, because nature will not be strong enough for a second attempt at repelling the threat. This happens once the body is exhausted by the first conflict, and because the poison has either multiplied, mutated into something more malignant, or moved closer to the heart than before. Nearly everyone seems to trend toward improvement in the beginning, because at that time, a more robust nature gathers all its strength against the enemy; yet, in other less severe illnesses, such a sudden and massive effort is not induced. 

Furthermore, the patient will appear to maintain a strength of virtue <note>original: "uirtutis robur." In this context, "virtue" refers to the body's innate healing power or "medical virtue."</note> because the aforementioned poison is not as contrary to other members of the body as it is to the heart; but when it attacks the heart itself, it kills instantly. Therefore, in these times, it is by no means appropriate to delay by examining the signs of the disease, for you will be deceived; nor will nature wait for you, unless you hurry to administer remedies. For this reason, when you see a fever present in these times, presuppose that it is the plague (or that it could quickly become so), and administer the care for a pestilential fever. This is especially true because as long as the poisonous influence of the air lasts, every **superfluous humor** <term>humor (one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health in Galenic medicine)</term> is easily infected. Any infirmity whatsoever can easily transform into the plague, especially "furious" and continuous fevers. Hence, it commonly happens that in this sickly time, no illness appears except the plague. But if other and various illnesses do appear, then the plague is diminishing and ceasing. 

There are several signs of a pestilential fever: namely, a continuous fever without a regular and manifest decline, accompanied by great distress of the breath and chest, a sudden weakness of the pulse, a heaviness of the entire body (especially the head), delirium <note>original: "phrenesi," referring to "phrenitis" or inflammation of the mind</note>, anxieties, shivering, thirst, and blood-colored spots in many places. The urine will be thick, turbid, and like that of pack animals <note>original: "iumentorum." Comparing human urine to that of beasts of burden was a standard diagnostic marker for severe internal putrefaction.</note>. Remember, however, that signs can be deceptive. 

Observe furthermore, that any child who suffers from an infestation of worms at that time can be said to be infected by the plague, because that material is prepared for the plague just as sulfur is for fire. Physicians, as if ignorant of this, have often been cheated of their desire to help. Beyond the cloudiness of the air and the abundance of animals born from rot <note>referring to the theory of spontaneous generation, where insects were thought to be born from decaying matter</note>, the primary signs of an approaching plague are:
*   A multitude of worms
*   Smallpox and measles
*   Continuous and "enclosed" fevers
*   Turbid urine
*   Redness of the eyes
*   Sores on the palate
*   Delirium

In general, any fever in which the **humor** frequently directs itself toward the heart indicates that the human temperament is predisposed to the plague. Know also that when a pestiferous vapor persists in the air for a long time, it infects the water and the fruits of the earth. Therefore, it is safer to boil your water, or to prepare "iron-water" <note>original: "ferratam aquam." This was water in which red-hot iron had been quenched, believed to have strengthening, astringent properties.</note>, and to dilute your wine with it. Pure wine is not suitable, as it is "smoky" <note>original: "fumosum," meaning it sends vapors to the head</note>, according to the opinion of <term>Avicenna</term> and <term>Rhazes</term> <note>Two of the most influential historical medical authorities; Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was Persian, and Rhazes (Al-Razi) was a celebrated physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>. It is also helpful to correct the foods you eat with pleasant-smelling things and with salty or vinegary flavors, especially when the plague arises after an earthquake. It is also of no small benefit to use "dry" things in fragrant, elevated places, and to inhabit mountains and hills.

---

->**Prophylactic care through diet and lifestyle in a state of plague.**<-
->**Chapter V.**<-

**A**BSTINENCE must be practiced during a time of plague from things that cause inflammation or are too "opening" <note>meaning they open the pores of the skin or the channels of the body</note>, because they make the body more ready to receive the poison. Specifically, one must beware of external heat from the Sun, as well as heat from fires and heavy clothing. Internally, one must avoid salt, hot spices, and medicines, as well as herbs of intense heat. One should avoid the frequent use of sharp things, except for onions, chicory, or radish with vinegar, because these resist the poison. Likewise, avoid wine that is too "smoky," and exercise after eating (especially in hot weather), and avoid sweating, because it alters the humors. In infected air, one should not expose oneself to the air much, nor engage in excessive exercise under the open sky, because by heating the body and opening the pores, it immediately receives much of the infected air. Similarly, one must abstain from things that cause blockages <note>original: "oppilationem"</note> and rot, because they provide the material for pestilential fever; such things are viscous, cold, and humid, especially when they take on some accidental or external heat. Also avoid things that are viscous, hot, and humid, where the humidity outweighs the heat and is poorly digested—to put it briefly,

# MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS

-> Humidity is the mother of decay. <-

And what is difficult to preserve outside of us will also not be easily preserved within us. Therefore, fish are to be avoided as much as possible; among their kind, small little fish are less harmful, specifically those from a river that is clear, rocky, and flowing. These should be fried in oil with salt and immersed in stavesacre <note>original: "staphisagria," a plant used in ancient medicine, though here possibly used in a culinary context or as a preservative</note>, or vinegar, or orange juice with salt and a moderate amount of pepper or cinnamon. Milk and all recooked foods must also be avoided. But if you wish to use it, let it be the first of your foods and in a small quantity with a little sugar. 

All fruits are to be avoided, except for almonds, sour cherries, "gold-apple" pears <note>original: "pyris chrysomelis"</note>, peaches, quinces, hazelnuts, dried plums, sloes, medlars and cornelian cherries, lady apples, pomegranates, and hard-shelled fruits. Truly, do not use other fruits at all, or do so rarely—indeed, very rarely. However, you may use cold, dry, and acidic or somewhat bitter fruits and herbs for a longer duration. But when using hot and moist fruits, such as figs, grapes, mulberries, and sweet cherries, make sure they are consumed in small amounts, and immediately afterward eat an orange with salt. Furthermore, if you use cold and moist things, such as melons, soft and tender fish, or fatty plums, take some fennel and orange with salt afterward, washing it down with a little good, fragrant wine. 

You must also avoid mushrooms and moist herbs, purslane, squash, and all moisture, as well as anything that is prone to decay. You shall also beware of fruits and things that are too sweet, and moist herbs; I permit you lettuce mixed with mint or cinnamon. You may also correct the lettuce with basil and very finely ground cloves that tend toward a reddish color and have the scent of cloves: for this is most pleasing to the heart. I also allow you squash and the herb called *Selbastrella* <note>original: "Selbastrella," a Tuscan name for salad burnet, often used to flavor wine</note> in the Tuscan tongue. 

Again, take heed that the opinion of Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis," a famous 9th-century Persian physician</note> does not deceive you; he allowed cold and moist vegetables and fruits during very hot weather because he lived in Egypt, where there is extreme dryness and where such fruits and vegetables are perfectly ripened by nature. Therefore, be cautious not to take such liberty in regions that are not similar to Egypt.

It should be noted, moreover, that acidic, harsh, and sharp things are to be administered in both a preventative and a curative regimen, because the danger chiefly looms in heat and moisture and the decay depending on them, in the dissolution of the spirits, and in the approach of poison to the heart. Thus, things of the aforementioned flavor resist all the said evils, for they cool, dry, preserve, strengthen, constrict, and unite. It is worthwhile to remember here that things that are too sharp, where a tightening of the chest or weakness of the stomach is feared, are to be tempered with sugar, salt, almond milk, cinnamon, pepper, fennel, saffron, eggs, and a small amount of fat. 

I highly recommend bread made of spelt or barley, and dishes prepared from these. Likewise, biscuits, rice, and raisins tending toward acidity, and bread made of the best grain, sufficiently baked with a little salt. Use capers with vinegar frequently, and occasionally that kind of cheese which the Florentines call *Marzellino* <note>original: "Marzellinum," likely Marzolino, a sheep's milk cheese from Tuscany</note>. Very fatty or salty cheese must be avoided. I do not praise cabbage for you, nor legumes, except for lentils. Above all, I forbid kidney beans, nor do I much praise turnips or spinach. I allow you parsley and parsnips. However, I forbid rocket, carrots, boiled wine-must, mustard, watermelons, melons, bean pods, fresh chickpeas, cucumbers, sweet and soft cherries, grapes, sweet figs, and mulberries. 

Do not fill yourself with too much wine, meat, and eggs, lest you multiply blood, yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, decay, and inflammation. Use eggs with verjuice <note>original: "agresta," the tart juice of unripe grapes</note>, vinegar, and oranges. Meats should be light and dry, well-cooked: chickens, small birds, castrated kids, young pigeons, turtle doves, and wild birds. If you use moist meats, let them be roasted, but see to it that they are well-filled throughout with sharp and acidic seasonings, with a little pepper, cinnamon, coriander, and salt. 

Cloudy wines are entirely harmful, especially new wine <note>original: "musta"</note>. Be more sparing than usual in food and drink; let the food be somewhat more abundant than the drink. However, I do not want you to endure excessive thirst or hunger. Take care not to let the stomach become nauseated, but preserve it with moderation in food and drink, with exercise and fasting, and with appropriate evacuations. 

Abstain from sexual intercourse and excessive passions of the soul, unless perhaps you find yourself entirely burdened by the abstinence from intercourse. Recall to mind the saying of Avicenna <note>original: "Auicennae," the influential Persian philosopher and physician</note> in the third book of *On Nature*, that the excessive evacuation of seed through intercourse harms a man more than if he were to lose forty times as much blood. Hippocrates said that intercourse is a species of the disease of epilepsy. Beware of air that is very cloudy, thick, enclosed, and moist, and know that air which does not move and refresh itself frequently...

# ANTIDOTE

<margin>Page 585</margin>

-> Where neither wind nor sun penetrates, nor cleanses, it easily takes on a mixture and poisonous putrefaction, just like stagnant water. <-

Remove yourself from the crowd of men, especially when you are fasting, and when heat succeeds humidity, or humidity succeeds heat. Also, turn away from air that is too hot, because it opens the pores and weakens the body too much. Your dwelling should be spacious and dry, continuously receiving dry air, and during the summer, fresh air from time to time. Take care when you have become very hot that you do not immediately expose yourself to the cold, or to damp, foggy air, or to hot and humid winds—especially in infected places or when coming from an infected place. Avoid every wind blowing from the aforementioned places, unless it is very distant or broken by rains. 

However, a wind that cools, dries, and clears the air is by its nature healthful, provided you receive it with moderation; it is the **principal physician** against a poison of this kind. Take great care to avoid winds coming from stagnant pools or marshes; flee foul waters, rotting vegetation, soaking flax <note>The process of "retting" flax in water to separate fibers produced a notorious stench believed to carry disease</note>, and any foul odor. Stay far away from the smells of cabbages or nuts, and from stinking herbs. Likewise, one must abstain from baths, from afternoon naps, and from close and crowded company. Flee from the crowd quickly and far away, and return slowly, because this poison is accustomed to lasting a long time and is extremely ready to cause harm. 

Eat dry foods of the best flavor—sharp and acidic—avoiding broth, fat, sweets, and viscous things. Use subtle, clear, fragrant wines that are slightly "smoky" <note>likely referring to aged or robust wines</note> but little acidic, not sweet, and diluted with very clear and thin water. In short, at all times beware of things that generate either too much blood, or watery, thick, and turbid blood, and likewise anything that harms the stomach. 

This is the rule for food and drink. In my judgment, it is useful for everyone to sprinkle the following composition of spices over their food: 

*   Take half an ounce of red sandalwood, 
*   Three and a half drachmas of choice cinnamon, 
*   And half a drachma of saffron. 

**Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian physician who wrote extensively on the plague</note> uses these spices at all times: 

*   Take half an ounce of cinnamon, 
*   One and a half drachmas of manna, 
*   Half a drachma each of cloves and white and red *been* <note>original: "been," referring to the roots of the Behen plant, used as a heart tonic</note>, 
*   One drachma of red coral, 
*   Two drachmas of cardamom, 
*   Half a drachma of saffron, 
*   And sugar equal to the weight of all the ingredients. 

Likewise, some have another description, which is as follows: 

*   Take two drachmas of pearls, 
*   Half a drachma of white and red coral, 
*   One scruple each of roses and <term>spodium: a powder made from burnt ivory or minerals, used for its cooling properties</term>, 
*   One drachma of cinnamon, 
*   And one scruple of saffron. 

Another: Take half an ounce of cinnamon, half a drachma of cloves, two scruples of red coral, half a drachma of saffron, and sugar to the weight of all. 

For the first meal, it is useful (unless the heat bothers you) to take figs, rue, and nuts with salt, especially in cold or humid weather. It should be noted that very hot spices—such as the fourth composition we described—should only be used in dishes that are very moist, cold, and acidic; the others, however, we can use in everything. After a meal, prepared coriander seeds are a great help, even according to **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037), whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard text in Europe</note>, who highly praises them for this purpose on an empty stomach. 

When your stomach is empty, use vigorous rubbing (friction), comb your hair, purge all superfluity from the body, and keep the entire body clean. In the morning, prepare a moderate fire, and occasionally during the day, especially in damp times. Frequently fumigate the house with good odors, and your clothes as well. You should move toward your nose, and also keep in your mouth where it is most opportune, some <term>theriaca: a famous poly-pharmaceutical "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients</term>. In other places or times, use citron peel, zedoary, or a little incense; you can even carry a "citrus apple" in your hand as mentioned above. 

*   Take one drachma of laudanum <note>here referring to the resin of the Cistus plant, not the later opium tincture</note>, 
*   Two drachmas each of white and red *been* and red roses, 
*   One scruple of liquid storax, 
*   One drachma each of myrrh, mint, and cloves, 
*   And half a drachma each of white and red sandalwood and camphor. 

Make a "scent ball" (pomander) with musked rose water. Hang around your neck a **unicorn horn** <note>usually narwhal tusk, believed to neutralize poison</note>, a hyacinth stone <note>likely zircon or garnet</note>, a topaz, or an emerald, so that it touches the chest; these may also be held in the mouth. Avicenna said it would be necessary for the hyacinth and similar stones to be warmed by our natural heat, which brings their virtues into action so they may work within us. Also carry with you in your hand fragrant fruits to smell, especially citron, lemons, oranges, etc. Frequently wash the opening of the throat and your hands with vinegar, and sometimes with strong wine. Do not omit the scent of mint, lemon balm, germander, rue, red violets, and myrtle. Use "cold" scents, which you should temper with "hot" ones, though let the cold ones predominate, especially in hot weather.

Above all, take care to do this: namely, mix equal parts white rose vinegar and rose water with a potent white wine and a small amount of zedoary <note>A root related to ginger, used as a stimulant</note> or citron peel. I truly do not know whether I ought to speak of this at present, or rather pass over it in silence: that some doctors are often accustomed to give a drink of a boy's freshly passed urine or lye <note>Lye-water, often made from wood ashes</note> on an empty stomach. I pray that this remedy be granted as one suited specifically for the peasants <note>Ficino reflects the class-based medicine of his time, suggesting harsher or "baser" remedies for the poor while reserving expensive spices for the elite</note>.

### *The Preservative Cure for the Epidemic. Concerning preservative pills and powders.*
## Chapter VI.

**T**heriac <term>Theriaca: A famous "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium, believed to cure all poisons</term>, the very queen of all compositions and handed down from heaven, is necessary for us twice a week. Indeed, so that you may recognize true theriac: it should leave a long-lasting taste in the mouth and cause an astringency <note>A drying or puckering sensation</note> in the stomach; it ought to be between four and twelve years old, and before use, it should be tested on venomous animals. Theriac, chosen according to the opinions of Galen and Averroes <note>Influential Greek and Arabic medical authorities</note>, renders a man safe from every poison and venomous disease. It is even permitted during the pestilential fever itself. Galen says that he found theriac to be more effective than all divine things in preserving and curing. Moses the Egyptian <note>The philosopher and physician Maimonides</note> said that a wonderful experiment was performed with it during the plague at Antioch. Nor do I think I should pass over Galen’s metaphor in silence, where he says: The plague is a dragon with an aerial body that breathes poison against man, and theriac is a kind of purgative that cleanses the poison and tames the dragon. 

It should be taken nine hours after food, and six or seven hours before food. He who cannot swallow it should at least apply it to the heart, the stomach, the nose, and the pulse points. One <term>drachma</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> should be given frequently to adults; to others, either one drachma or one <term>scrupulus</term> <note>A smaller unit, roughly 1.3 grams</note>. Those of a hot temperament, having taken the theriac in the summer time, should drink a third of a cup of rose water with a little rose vinegar; others of a different constitution or in a different season should take it with white wine mixed with water of scabious <note>A herb often used for skin conditions and the plague</note> and lemon balm. But if theriac is not available, or is not suitable for your nature, take mithridate <term>Mithridatum: A complex semi-solid paste used as an antidote, named after King Mithridates VI</term>. On other days of the week, take pills against the disease at least four or five hours before food—namely one, or two, or more, according to your constitution—drinking a little white wine with scabious and balm water afterward in cold weather, or with rose water and rose vinegar in the summer. 

These are the older pills: Take one ounce each of myrrh and saffron, and two ounces of aloe. But because these open [the pores], heat, and dissolve the spirits too much, some people wash the aloe and add "sealed earth" <term>Terra sigillata: Medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, stamped with a seal to guarantee authenticity</term> or Armenian bole <term>Bolus Armenus: A red medicinal clay used as an astringent</term> in a dose equal to the myrrh; however, Armenian bole is more desirable. Some compose them thus: Take six drachmas of aloe, three drachmas of myrrh, two scruples of citron seeds, half a drachma of tormentil <note>A herb used as an astringent</note>, one drachma of saffron, two drachmas of rhubarb, one scruple of cloves, one drachma each of agaric <note>A type of medicinal mushroom</note>, citron peel, and red sandalwood, two scruples of citron seeds, one and a half drachmas of sorrel seed, one and a half drachmas of red coral, three drachmas of Armenian bole, and two grains of camphor; mix with syrup of citron. Avicenna and Averroes say: He who uses aloe, myrrh, and saffron will never be in danger from the plague. The aforementioned compositions temper the qualities of these ingredients and increase their power. But the compounds of Nicolaus <note>Likely referring to the "Antidotarium Nicolai," a standard medieval text on pharmacy</note> are much better, according to which these are the true pills: Take one drachma each of myrrh, saffron, Armenian bole, amber, and red coral, two drachmas of emblics <note>Indian gooseberry, a fruit used in Ayurvedic and Greek medicine</note>, and washed aloe equal to the weight of all the others; let the pills be made with fragrant white wine. I believe they would be more noble and better suited to the purpose if "sealed earth" were put in place of the emblics...

# ANTIDOTE

...two drachms of sealed earth <note>original: "terra sigillata," a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, stamped with an official seal to guarantee its purity</note> and three drachms of Armenian bole <note>original: "bolus armenus," a red medicinal clay used as an astringent and antidote</note>; let pills be made with the sour juice of citron, and let them be taken with white wine, rose water, or rose vinegar. In other cases, however, let him follow the aforementioned composition. 

Take care that the **aloe** <note>Aloe resin was a staple of medieval medicine, used here to purge the body of "corrupt" humors</note> be bright, light, somewhat reddish, delicate, fragrant, easily broken, becoming oily, and when you breathe upon it, it should become moist. Let the **myrrh** also be clear, and the **coral** delicate; without theriac <note>A complex ancient "wonder-drug" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium</note> and the said pills, a proper preservation cannot be well achieved. Therefore, above all others, use the two aforementioned things: namely, theriac on two different days, and at least three of the pills, because by drying out excess moisture, they preserve the body from putrefaction. They also strengthen the heart and narrow the passages so that the poison cannot find a path to the heart, and they drive it away from there. 

It seems to me that the aloe in the aforementioned pills should not be washed when the weather is humid and cold, nor when the person’s temperament <note>original: "complexio," the balance of the four humors</note> is similar; but in other times and temperaments, it is better to take the pill composition in powder form only when there is a need for haste. It can also be taken three or four hours before dinner, just as before lunch. You may also take it once a week, or twice if needed; however, when the pills might cause discomfort (though they are of no harm) in winter and humid weather, you may take in place of the pills a **dried fig** with half a walnut, a little rue, and a bit of salt, drinking a little rose water or rose vinegar afterward. But if even this should bother you, use in its place—taking nothing else—a bit of toasted bread dipped in potent white wine, with a bitter orange soaked in rose vinegar and sprinkled with cinnamon. 

There are some who give these kinds of pills in the evening or morning, one at a time: Take half a drachm of aloeswood <note>original: "ligni aloes," the fragrant heartwood of the Aquilaria tree, distinct from the bitter aloe resin</note>, two scruples of tormentil, one scruple of white dittany, half a drachm of zedoary <note>a root related to ginger</note>, one drachm of saffron, half a drachm of barberry, two scruples of burnt stag’s horn, one scruple of red sandalwood, one drachm each of sorrel seed, red coral, and Armenian bole, two scruples of camphor, half a drachm of the gems from which the "electuary of gems" is made <note>A luxury medicine containing crushed precious stones</note>, one drachm of pearls, and half a drachm of hyacinths <note>likely referring to zircons or blue sapphires</note>; prepare this with syrup of redcurrant or lemons. 

I, however, am accustomed to give these kinds of pills at all times, even in hot weather: Take one scruple each of zedoary, aloeswood, agrimony, saffron, round birthwort, white dittany, gentian, citron peel, and citron seed; one drachm each of prepared coriander, tormentil, red sandalwood, red coral, red roses, spodex <note>likely zinc oxide or burnt ivory</note>, and emblic myrobalans; two drachms of sealed earth; four drachms of Armenian bole. Make pills with the sour juice of citron, which you should administer with white wine, white rose vinegar, and rose water. 

I place much faith in this composition of ours, taking it when one does not take the pills composed with aloe. Furthermore, after the operation of the aforementioned pills, one may add to the composition: ambergris, musk, hyacinth, emerald, topaz, pearls, and **unicorn horn** <note>Usually narwhal tusk, believed to sweat in the presence of poison</note>, one scruple of each. It will be even better, and highly praiseworthy, to drink these with an acidic wine or white vinegar, along with rose water, sealed earth, and Armenian bole, with a small portion of emerald, hyacinth, and topaz, or at least with pearls and corals. These things are greatly commended by **Galen** and **Avenzoar** <note>Galen was the foundational Greek physician of antiquity; Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr) was a celebrated 12th-century Arab physician</note>. 

Others give the peels and seeds of citron and lemons with wine or rose vinegar and rose water. I, however, frequently give this simple confection—which is indeed most effective and safe—with white wine or rose vinegar and rose water: Take two drachms of Armenian bole; one drachm each of sealed earth and red coral; half a drachm each of citron peel, zedoary, and saffron; six ounces of rose sugar made from red roses; ten ounces of citron juice; and make an electuary <note>A medicinal paste or jam</note>.

Also: take half a drachm of ambergris, one scruple of musk, and six grains of camphor. Also: take equal parts of emerald, hyacinth, and topaz; let them be ground and washed just as **Mesue** <note>An influential 8th-9th century Persian physician</note> washes lapis lazuli; make pills with the juice of wood-sorrel. They can also be placed upon wounds, bites, and poisonous pustules. They also use this composi-

# THE ANTIDOTE OF MYREPSUS <note>Nicolaus Myrepsus was a 13th-century Byzantine physician whose "Antidotarium" became a standard pharmaceutical text in the Renaissance.</note>

...hyssop, scabious, cinquefoil, capers, lemons, watermelons, and oranges—specifically those we call **golden apples**—and generally all acidic things and those that possess a certain bitterness. Know that the small blossoms of the grapevine are very beneficial if you accustom yourself to using them in food, drink, and electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note>; likewise, the water of scabious, as well as lemon balm, is wonderful in all these things which are administered to both the healthy and the sick, because it dries out poisonous moistures. And where there is a need for great cooling during the drying process, one should rather use the waters of endive, roses, plantain, rose vinegar, or the water or juice of wood sorrel, juice of lemons, citron, oranges, chicory, pimpernel, and fumitory. However, when it is necessary to use temperate remedies, take the water of borage and bugloss, and in each decoction add damson plums, myrobalans <note>A dried plum-like fruit from India used as a laxative</note>, and tamarinds. And keep this in a mindful heart: how well these four things agree in all remedies—namely, white wine, white rose vinegar, and rose water, all in equal weight, with a very small quantity of saffron. Where it is necessary to act without delay and with a certain ease, you shall administer what is appropriate in a thin and liquid form, or give the aforementioned things to be drunk afterward.

*Raymond* <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully, a major figure in medieval alchemy and medicine</note> says that if it can be delayed long enough for the composition of the aforementioned pills to be made, it is better for the pills to be administered than the powders. This is because such a composition is better fermented, and through this fermentation, it acquires a specific power beyond its temperament <note>original: "complexionalem," referring to the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note>; also, by remaining in the stomach, it preserves, strengthens, and comforts more effectively, and spreads better through the more remote parts of the body, provided one drinks a little of some liquid substance afterward and practices much abstinence. Yet we do not wish the pills to be excessively dry and hardened; indeed, if they are such, they should be remade.

**Bloodletting** <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> is suitable for sanguine people—namely, to draw blood so that they may be preserved, if they otherwise have no natural flow of blood. By "sanguine," I mean those who are decently fleshy, red in color, hairy, and robust, who have large veins and who eat foods of great nourishment. For these, I say, let blood be drawn from the **right basilic vein**; then, after a two-month interval, let the cutting be done again from the left basilic vein. Do not exceed the weight of one pound at a single time. Let it also be done during temperate seasons of the year, and while the Moon is in a good and fortunate aspect.

Pure blood is diminished at sunrise, **choleric** blood at noon, **melancholic** at sunset, and **phlegmatic** in the middle of the night. *Raymond* therefore wishes that, according to the order of *Avicenna* <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> and based on the four types of blood mentioned, those four hours should be observed in the extraction. Moreover, these types are recognized first by their signs, and then according to the four ages of life in which they dominate, following the aforesaid order. And where a great abundance of blood does not appear, he wishes that no cutting be done at all, neither for the sake of preservation nor for cure. And when you wish to draw blood, take care that a clyster <note>an enema</note> is administered the day before, and that some non-laxative medicine is given. Nor do I think it should be overlooked that where the blood declines much toward other humors, it should by no means be evacuated. Remember **Galen** and **Avicenna**: the more they practiced the art of healing, the more timid they always became toward bloodletting, because bloodletting draws more from the natural and good [blood] and from the spirits than medicine does, and it grants less time to discern the bad blood from the good.

For infants and children, those things that are effective against worms are beneficial, as the danger of these is most imminent at these times; once a week, administer to them in a drink one drachm of **dittany** with a somewhat styptic <note>astringent or mouth-drying</note> wine, or with wine from a decoction of wormwood and nigella, or wormseed <note>original: "feminis sancti," likely a corruption of "seminis sancti" or Santonica</note>. Also, let the stomach, navel, throat, and chest be anointed with bitter oils and herbs and the like; sometimes you shall also provide rhubarb pills. But because a very moist and very hot temperament is dangerous in a time of **plague**, there is a need for cooling, drying, and frequent evacuation, which are indeed done with moderation according to the opportunity. 

Wear this **sachet** applied to the heart: Take two drachms of red roses; one drachm each of red sandalwood, red coral, and spodium <note>a medicinal powder made from burnt ivory or minerals</note>; half a drachm each of zedoary, aloeswood, cinnamon, cloves, citron peels, and saffron. Be diligent that every superfluity is purged, and take care that the belly does not remain bound <note>constipated</note>, and that it is not slow to release its usual purgings—whether it be the flux of hemorrhoids, scabs, natural and customary sweats, old open wounds through which humor flows without trouble, tears, blood flowing from the nostrils, the usual and ordinary universal drops, and the like—since these mentioned purgings render one more secure from the disease. I advise...

# ANTIDOTE

...as quickly as you can, immediately anoint the pulses of the temples, hands, and feet, as well as the nostrils, the back of the head, the throat, the chest, and the area around any blister or swelling <note>original: "bulla & apostema"</note>, if one should appear, with scorpion oil and theriac <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal" antidote made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh</note>. The true composition of the oil is as follows: Take eight ounces of fifty-year-old olive oil and add fifty scorpions; boil them together with the oil until they sink to the bottom. This should be done in summer, and especially in the month of August. Keep it and use it, for it is a marvel against poisons. But if the stomach is heavy with food, vomiting should be easily provoked with warm water, vinegar, and oil, or even with radish, also trying to provoke it with a feather; and immediately afterward, administer an enema <note>original: "clystere"</note>. Every day you shall renew a decoction of mallows, "mother of violets," beets, barley, lettuce, chamomile, violet honey, red sugar, one ounce of senna or cassia, two drachmas <note>A unit of weight, roughly 1/8 of an ounce</note> of laxative rose juice, and a sufficient amount of common salt and violet oil. When this is done, you shall apply a poultice <note>original: "epithema"</note> to the heart made of "cordial" substances—those that are somewhat cooling in their primary nature. Take two drachmas each of the waters of roses, bugloss, wood sorrel, and water lily; one drachma each of lemon balm water, pomegranate juice of medium flavor, and the acidity of citron; one ounce of quince juice; two drachmas each of white, red, and yellow sandalwood; half a drachma each of spodium <note>Likely zinc oxide or burnt ivory</note>, ivory shavings, citron seeds, and sorrel seeds; six grains of dyer's grain <note>Kermes, used both as a red dye and a medicinal astringent</note>; and half a drachma of camphor. Let all these be well ground together and warmed in a clean glass vessel; then, with a cloth dyed in scarlet <note>original: "panno de Grana," referring to cloth dyed with kermes</note> and moderately warm, apply it to the chest, renewing it every three hours. Likewise, for the stomach, keep this composition in a small bag to revive and strengthen its spirits: Take one handful each of wormwood and mint; half a handful each of lemon balm and wood sorrel; one ounce of red roses; three drachmas each of citron peel and rice; two drachmas of prepared coriander; one drachma each of red coral, mastic, and red sandalwood; half a drachma each of mace and clove leaves; and four cypress nuts. Compose these with quince juice. Likewise, you shall administer this remedy under the armpits: Take roses, chamomile flowers, melilot, myrtle flowers, cypress nuts, and sandalwood, all in appropriate quantities; let them boil in water, in which a sponge or some lint <note>original: "stupa"</note> should be dipped, then squeezed out and applied moderately warm. Renew this frequently, for it is marvelous.

->The use of cupping glasses, and the method of curing through bloodletting.<-
->Chapter VIII.<-

**H** AVING done these things and administered them duly as described, if a blister or sign has not yet appeared on the legs, immediately apply two cupping glasses <note>original: "ventosas"</note> to the buttocks, and likewise two to the back of the thighs. The ancients held that bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> should be performed after the removal of such cupping glasses. If the usual blister or sign has not appeared, let blood be taken from the common vein <note>The median cubital vein in the arm</note> on the right side, to prevent the poison from reaching the parts of the heart. Even if such a sign or blister has appeared, the blood should be drawn from that same side so that the poison does not extend and spread—as it is always prone to do—through all the veins and parts of the body. If the sign appears around the ears or the neck, blood should be let from the cephalic vein <note>A vein in the arm associated by medieval doctors with the head</note> on the side where the sign is, near the thumb of the hand. If it appears under the armpits, the hepatic vein <note>Also called the basilic vein, associated with the liver and torso</note> in the arm of that same side should be evacuated. If it appears in the groin, bloodletting should be done from the saphenous vein—that is, below the ankle of the same side. Finally, as a general rule, whenever such a sign appears from the base of the throat up to the head, the bloodletting should be from the cephalic vein on the side of the sign. If it appears from that part down to the navel, whether in front or behind, the bloodletting should likewise be from the hepatic vein. If from the navel downward, the saphenous vein should be used as described above. And bloodletting must be performed as quickly as possible, at least when the swelling <note>original: "apostema"</note> first begins to appear. You may fearlessly have a good quantity extracted, unless the patient happens to have very little blood; after extracting about two ounces, stop for a moment so it can be judged whether the blood is good or not. If it is "bad" <note>Dark, thick, or discolored</note>, you may extract more copiously; if "good," more sparingly. In weak patients and those without much blood, an extraction of two ounces is sufficient. However, you must never do this during the shivering stage of a fever. While the bloodletting is happening, the patient should taste or hold an orange or something acidic in their mouth, and vinegar should be applied to the nose, forehead, and the pulses of the temples, for this is the common manner of bloodletting. The "Thunderous" Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno, a famous 14th-century physician known as "Speculator" or "Fulmineus" for his prolific writing</note> highly praises what we shall now say...

# MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS
<lang>English</lang>

...we shall speak as of something proven by experience. If a visible swelling <term>apostema; a swelling or inflammatory tumor, often a "bubo" in plague contexts</term> should appear near the shoulder blades, cupping glasses should be applied where the shoulder blades meet: however, the bloodletting should be done from the median vein <note>original: "mediana"</note>, which is usually called the *common and black vein*. If it appears in the neck or head, the cephalic vein <note>The "head vein" in the arm, thought to drain the upper body</note> should be bled near the thumbs of the hands. If it is under or in the right arm, the person should be bled from the "lung vein" <note>original: "uena pulmonis"</note>, between the middle and ring finger of that same side. If it is around the arm or the left side, from the *salvatella* vein <note>A vein on the back of the hand near the little finger</note>, between the ring and little finger of the right hand. If it is in the groin, or in the left side, the bloodletting must be performed from the "paralytic vein" between the hollow of the knee and the next closest vessel on that same side. If it appears in the shin or the right foot, it is done from the vein called the *Woman's vein* <note>original: "Vena mulierum"; likely the saphenous vein at the ankle, so named because it was frequently used to treat "women's complaints"</note>. 

Spanish and Catalan doctors usually perform phlebotomy on the first or at least the second day after administering an enema, in two staggered sessions. For robust, bloody <note>Sanguine temperaments</note>, and middle-aged men, they do it this way on the first day: first, they draw blood from the opposite side [of the swelling], because the humor <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health</note> is still in motion and has not yet become poisonous. If a swelling appears under the left arm, they immediately draw six or four ounces from the right hand, or three ounces from the left ankle. Then, after six or eight hours, when the patient is refreshed and rested, they draw six, four, or three ounces from the left arm, according to the pressure and strength of the thicker vein, since that vein shows itself to require phlebotomy more opportunely. They do the opposite when a swelling appears in the groin: first, they bleed from the arm of the same side, and secondly from the foot of that same side from the *saphenous* vein <note>The large vein of the leg</note>. 

But if the patient is not very robust, nor overflowing with blood, yet possesses a decent natural vigor and constancy of strength, or if it is already the end of the second or the third day—at which point it is likely that the matter itself has begun its course and motion and is already infected with poison—they evacuate two or four ounces from the side of the swelling, in a place as close to the swelling as possible. If it appears behind the ears, they bleed from the cephalic vein of the same side. But if this cannot be easily reached, let it be done in the median vein which shares in the whole body. If even that is not accessible, let it be done in the same hand from the vein that is between the thumb and the index finger. 

They do similarly from the middle of the second day to the following days; but from the beginning to the middle of the second day, they would perform phlebotomy from the opposite side, and likewise from the first to the middle of the second. If the swelling is under the arm, it should be evacuated from the vein of that same arm, and from the common vein, or at least from the hepatic vein <note>The "liver vein," usually the basilic vein of the arm</note>, or from the same hand below the middle finger and the one next to it. If at that same aforementioned time the sign itself is in the groin, you should cut the vein below the knee of the same side, or below the ankle of the same foot. If the sign tends toward the buttocks, draw blood from the thicker and more visible vein on the top of the foot of the same side. The method for these cases is that around the middle of the second day, they mostly begin on the opposite side. 

But let us turn to our universal rules. Because a disease of this kind is either in the blood itself or in the humors mixed with the blood, it seems to me that blood should be drawn from everyone, from age fourteen up to sixty; I judge it to be much better that the poison should breathe out <note>original: "expiret"</note> through the opening of a vein than that the patient should be greatly tormented by the outflow of blood. Draw it in repeated turns with a six-hour interval. For robust bodies and those with much blood, draw one pound <note>original: "libram unam"</note> at most. For the moderately robust and those with moderate blood, up to eight ounces; for the weaker, if the pulse is steady, four, three, or two ounces, or at least one. However, where a dominance of choler <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and dryness</note> prevails, the extraction should not exceed two ounces. 

Many recommend drawing blood until the person, though not yet weak, becomes weakened. This pleases me very little, since it dissolves the spirits <note>The "vital spirits" believed to carry life through the body</note>. Where the pulse falters, nothing at all should be drawn. My greater concern is that the swelling appears first; even afterward, hemorrhoids should be provoked, with frictions made with rough things and onion juice, along with cupping, scarification <note>Making small incisions in the skin</note>, and leeches. Where blood is abundant, you shall do the same after a second vein-cutting. But where
->there is a small amount of blood, at least<-
->you shall do this.<-

<header>ANTIDOTE</header>

# On medicines that dissolve poison and draw it outward.
## Chapter IX.

Certain people apply a topical compress <term>epithema; a liquid-soaked cloth applied to the body, particularly over the heart or liver</term> as soon as blood has been evacuated once. However, the wiser physicians do this from the very beginning and renew it frequently—specifically every three hours—applying it moderately warm with a **scarlet cloth** <note>Scarlet-dyed wool was often used in medical treatments because the color was thought to stimulate the blood and heart</note>. We have described one above, and here is another: Take half a pound each of rose water, endive water, bugloss water, and lemon balm water; two ounces of vinegar; three drams each of sandalwood, roses, and coral; two drams of spodium <note>original: "spodij"; often referring to ash or burnt ivory used for cooling</note>; one scruple each of pearls, hyacinths <note>The gemstone zircon, often used in ground form</note>, and sapphire; half a dram each of white and red behen <note>Roots of the Centaurea behen, used as a tonic</note>, the bone from a deer’s heart <note>A small, cross-shaped bone or cartilage found in the hearts of older stags, highly prized as a heart tonic</note>, and citron seeds; half a scruple of musk; and one scruple each of camphor and saffron. If you notice an unusual heat in the patient, ensure the liver and the region of the kidneys are anointed with sandalwood ointment twice a day.

Then, after four hours (following the usual manner and order), two drams of the "powder against the disease" should be administered, either with white wine and endive water, or with squill vinegar, along with two drams—or at least one—of **theriac** <term>theriaca; a famous, complex "cure-all" paste containing dozens of ingredients including opium and viper flesh</term>. After this drink, assist nature in producing a sweat using warm cloths and fumigations. A physician would not be in error to administer theriac alone, yet it is more common to give it with the powders. Some add vinegar, which does not displease me; I also prefer that it be administered frequently. Water of scabious and lemon balm are also useful alongside theriac, provided there is not excessive heat present.

The **ancient description** of such a powder against the disease is as follows:
Take one ounce each of white dittany, white coral, tormentil, Armenian bole <term>bolus armenus; a medicinal red clay thought to counteract poison</term>, and gentian; and half an ounce of *terra sigillata* <term>sealed earth; a clay from the island of Lemnos, stamped with a seal to guarantee its authenticity as an antidote</term>.

The **more modern** version is this: Take equal parts of tormentil root, agrimony, aloeswood, Armenian bole, valerian, dock, and red sandalwood; mix with a weight of scabious root equal to all the other ingredients, combined with the blood of a bull that has been dried in the sun and distilled.

**Another description:** Take four drams each of spodium, white dittany, gentian, tormentil, juniper berries, citron seeds, and carline thistle; and two ounces of strawberry tree leaves.

**A third description:** Take one dram each of tormentil, white dittany, burnt hartshorn <note>Deer antler</note>, and zedoary <note>A root similar to ginger</note>; and two scruples each of pearls and red coral.

**A fourth description:** Take two drams each of tormentil, white dittany, Armenian bole, camphor, pearls, red sandalwood, burnt hartshorn, round birthwort, and white sugar.

**A fifth description:** Take two drams each of tormentil and dittany; three drams each of sorrel seed and citron seeds; one scruple each of white ginger, cinnamon, and saffron; two and a half drams each of Armenian bole and *terra sigillata*; and two ounces of sugar. This powder is highly effective (so it is said) against poison, whether administered before or after exposure.

**A sixth description:** Take two drams of tormentil roots; one dram each of red sandalwood, fresh white dittany, burnt hartshorn, pearls, Armenian bole, and round birthwort; half a dram of camphor; two drams of white sugar; one dram each of pimpernel, myrrh, and zedoary; two drams each of sandalwood and *terra sigillata*; one scruple each of citron seeds and saffron; and half a dram of hyacinth gems.

These powders provide vigor to the heart and assist it in expelling poison from itself; they dry up putrid humors, block the paths to the heart so the poison cannot reach it, and frequently expel the poison through sweat. It has been found by experience that the first description (the **ancient** one) and the last of the **modern** ones are much more effective than the others.

There are some who, after inducing vomiting (if necessary), and after an enema and anointing, first administer the powders and the compress, and only after these have worked do they perform bloodletting. They do this when the patient has a great deal of blood, and perhaps they are not wrong. But where blood cannot be drawn, or due to a lack of blood, they administer medicine in place of phlebotomy—but the powder is given first. 

After the sick person has sweated, or the proper time for sweating has passed, one must not wait for the "digestion" <note>The maturation or "cooking" of humors in the body</note> of the humor, because there is no time or opportunity to allow for it. Indeed, when necessity is imminent (for necessity itself is not subject to the law), the usual distinction of times and days should not be observed. Nor should one trust in some hope that nature is striving toward evacuation on its own; nature's actions are irregular here because of the lack of digestion and the violent force of the poison. Truly, when nature is oppressed, it acts as best it can, which is more than it ought.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s instructions on treating the plague. Having previously discussed compresses (epithemata), he now addresses the timing of bloodletting versus internal purging and the specific herbal formulas used to draw the "poisonous vapor" away from the heart.</meta>

<page-num>590</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EPIDEMIC</header>

After a suitable time for sweating, you should either reduce the blood, if it is in excess, or, if it is not abundant, you should administer a purgation—though using substances that do not disturb the stomach. For a violent bout of vomiting causes the pathways of the chest to dilate, which allows the poison to race toward the heart and draws it toward the brain. For this reason, those who prescribe goat’s rue <note>original: "capraginem"; *Galega officinalis*, often used as a febrifuge or to induce sweating, but here criticized as too harsh</note> and similar emetic and poisonous substances are in error. Indeed, nature can scarcely resist even a single poison.

Perhaps someone might challenge us, asking why physicians are accustomed to inducing vomiting in those who have been poisoned. I say that the condition of these poisons is not the same. Other poisons have more physical matter and are better suited for removal through vomiting, as they sit in the stomach; this plague, however, is a certain poisonous vapor located in the regions of the chest. Therefore, let no medicine be present that can violently induce vomiting. While I would not at all condemn a vomit that occurs without violence, I would still more strongly approve of a diversion of the poison through the lower parts <note>i.e., through the bowels</note>.

The medicine you give should be dissolved in white wine and the waters of scabious, endive, roses, plantain, bugloss, and lemon balm, or in rose vinegar, in which a decoction has been made of Damask plums, myrobalans <note>A dried plum-like fruit from India, used as a laxative in medieval medicine</note>, and tamarinds.

However, if the disease attacks someone with a full stomach, what should be done according to the order of the Moderns? Ensure that after anointing with oil of scorpions and <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium</note>, they vomit easily using warm water, vinegar, oil, and radish juice—even attempting to provoke it with a long feather. Afterward, you shall administer a clyster <note>An enema</note>, then a compress, and then the powders mentioned before. Later, at a time when the patient is quieter and restored, perform <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>bloodletting</note> if they are of a sanguine temperament; if not, administer medicine. 

If you extract more than four ounces of blood during bloodletting, abstain from medicine until twelve hours have passed since the procedure. And even if you have performed the bloodletting, do not place your hope in that alone, especially in a plethoric <note>Over-full of blood or humors</note>, sanguine, and robust body. Indeed, even in others from whom you have extracted little blood, medicine must still be offered at the proper time, according to the quality of their complexion and strength. Similarly, if you have given medicine first, you should not be content with that; if the body is plethoric and the patient’s strength allows, enjoin bloodletting as well in the proper manner and time. 

You shall make this distinction: when it is both possible and convenient to administer both, if blood is abundant, let bloodletting come first and be more copious. But where blood is not abundant, let the medicine come first and bloodletting follow—and let it be modest, for the sake of "venting" <note>original: "eventuandi"; a medical concept of allowing trapped vapors to escape rather than just reducing blood volume</note> rather than diminishing. After the third day, no extraction of blood should be done unless a great multitude of blood compels you to it.

Whenever you administer medicine, bloodletting, or vomiting, you must ensure that the poison does not return inward from the "sign" <note>The "sign" refers to the physical manifestation of the plague, such as a bubo or tumor</note> due to the agitation. If the sign is visible, ensure that during such a commotion you place cupping glasses and leeches above and below the sign, and apply cold compresses over the heart. Both before and after, you shall offer things that defend against poison through those means: namely <term>theriac</term>, <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>A medicinal red clay used as an astringent and antidote</note>, emeralds, hyacinths, topaz, or at least other types of gems or corals mixed with the juice of anti-poisonous herbs.

When you perform a purgation, offer the medicine with a little saffron in the decoction mentioned above. The primary and safest medicine, according to the Persian physicians and Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a famous 9th-century Persian Christian physician</note>, is one ounce of <term>Persian trifera</term> <note>An electuary (medicinal paste) made of myrobalans and other ingredients</note> with two drams of <term>electuary of hamech</term> <note>A specific purgative paste intended to cleanse black bile</note>. Or at the very least, half an ounce of the trifera and one dram of the electuary of hamech with three drams of the same. The Persians administer this with cold water, or the juice of nightshade or endive. I have heard of this often and made a successful trial of it this very year. 

Where the trifera and electuary of hamech are missing, you shall offer <term>diasenna</term> <note>A senna-based laxative</note> in place of the trifera, and <term>diamanna</term> <note>A preparation of manna, the sweet sap of the flowering ash</note> or rose juice in place of the electuary of hamech in the manner described. I have experimented with this and found this composition to be of great utility and safety:

Take:
*   Persian trifera and pulp of cassia: half an ounce each
*   <term>Rhubarb</term>, <term>diamanna</term>, or electuary of hamech: one dram

But where the nature is strong and the belly is "stiptic" <note>Constipated or bound up</note>, you shall give two drams of diamanna or the electuary of hamech, tempered with the waters of bugloss and endive, and the decoctions and waters mentioned before. 

I myself keep the rhubarb in white wine and endive water with a little spikenard for an hour, which I give in substance by mixing everything together; often I also add an ounce of <term>manna</term> afterward. <term>Pills of fumitory</term> <note>original: "pilulae de fumo terrae"; used for skin diseases and liver cleansing</note> and "aggregative" pills <note>Pills designed to purge multiple humors at once</note> in equal parts are also suitable: one full dram for the robust, but half a dram for others, followed by a drink of white wine with endive, rose, and scabious waters. These same aggregative pills alone, at any time, especially when it is less hot...

<unclear>................................................................</unclear> dram.

...one drachm, or half a drachm. It should be noted that if the fever clings to subtle and hot humors <note>In medieval medicine, "subtle" humors are thin and move quickly, often associated with yellow bile or heat</note>, there will appear a vehement thirst, dryness of the throat, blackness of the tongue, a sharp color in the head, frenzy <note>original: "phrenesis"; a state of delirium or mental agitation</note>, or similar horrific symptoms. However, if it clings to thicker and less "furious" humors, the fever will appear slow and the aforementioned symptoms will be milder. Consider signs of this kind, and you should know that in whatever humor is present, <term>trifere</term> <note>A type of complex electuary or paste, often used as a carrier for other medicines</note> is suitable with <term>agaric</term> <note>A fungus (*Laricifomes officinalis*) used as a powerful purgative</note>, and **aggregative pills**, either alone or with pills of fumitory. Also, a **solutive syrup** <note>A laxative syrup designed to "loosen" the bowels</note>, which we will describe below, is suitable if the matter is "furious," as is <term>diaphoenicon</term> <note>A date-based purgative electuary</note> with **electuary of hamech** <note>A famous, bitter purgative compound used to treat "black bile"</note> or rose juice. Likewise, cassia with rhubarb; also manna with "diamanna" in cold decoctions. If the matter is thick, cold, and moist, two scruples of the stronger aggregative pills and one scruple of agaric pills are suitable. For weaker patients, however, one ounce of **diacatholicon** <note>A "universal" laxative made of senna, rhubarb, and tamarind</note> with two drachms of diaphoenicon, or with one or a half drachm of troches of agaric. Likewise, regarding the pills against the disease mentioned above, one or a half drachm; and perhaps pills of this kind are suitable for any humor.

Note that agaric, when well-prepared and made into troches <note>Small medicinal lozenges or cakes</note>, is exceptional in this case, regardless of the humor or body part. Therefore, when I am certain of its preparation, I would use it in every medicine, giving two drachms, or one, or a half, according to the potency of the medicine and the constitution of the person. And where I might doubt its preparation, I would infuse it in **oxymel of squill** <note>A mixture of honey, vinegar, and sea onion (squill) used as an expectorant or to cut through thick humors</note> with rock salt, and afterward, by straining, I would place it over the medicine without pressing it. Likewise, it should be noted that the aggregative pills are appropriate, and in their place, "Si quibus" pills ought to be administered to those who are less robust. And you should know it is better to give liquid medicine than pills in this case. If "diamanna" can be had, it is better and stronger than rose juice. And the electuary of hamech is better than both—namely, both diamanna and rose juice. Finally, in every humor, this solutive syrup is wonderful in place of medicine, at least one ounce and at most two, with rose water and white wine.

Take two drachms each of: citrus rinds, caper roots, barberry, red sandalwood, and spodius <note>Ash or mineral residue, often used as an astringent</note>.
Take one handful each of: clove-scented herb <note>likely *Geum urbanum*</note>, lemon balm, bugloss, borage, and chicory.
Take one and a half handfuls each of: sorrel, horehound, and liverwort.
Take two drachms of: wild endive.
Take one handful each of: seeds of pumpkin (namely melons, watermelons, and cucumber) and violets.
Take two drachms each of: thyme, dodder of thyme, agaric, rhubarb, senna, and polypody <note>A type of fern root used as a laxative</note>.
Take six drachms each of the juices of: wormwood, fumitory, dwarf elder, and plantain.
Take one drachm of: chebulic myrobalans <note>A dried fruit from India, often called "black myrobalans"</note>.
Take half a drachm of: yellow myrobalans.
Take two drachms of: scammony <note>original: "diagridij"; a potent resinous purgative</note>.
Take two pounds of: white sugar.
Make a syrup with quince vinegar.

This syrup is called **divine** by the Doctors in both preserving and curing, because it immediately cuts away the humors prone to putrefaction, strengthens the principal organs, and drives poison outward; many successful experiences of it have been seen. Among other Doctors, **Peter of Tossignano** and **Gentile of Foligno** <note>Famous 14th-century Italian physicians known for their works on the plague</note> commend it in a marvelous way, and it seems to me to have been made with the intent of the "Persian trifera," but more solutive; it pleases me greatly for persons who are not extremely weak and do not have an overly loose belly. It should be taken once a week by the healthy and the sick alike. 

Note that after the operation of the medicine, or bloodletting, if you have not administered medicine the following day, one drachm of **theriac** <note>The most famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical antidote, containing dozens of ingredients including viper flesh and opium</note> should be drunk with one ounce of rose water and a little rose vinegar. Do not fear the heat of the theriac, because such a small portion can provide little heat; for an "elemental quality" (such as heat and the like), being very material, does not act much except with much matter. But a "specific virtue"—insofar as it is a celestial gift and almost spiritual—acts greatly, according to **Galen**, even with little matter. Theriac, moreover, acts against poison by its specific property, and besides this, it scarcely reaches the second degree of heat; therefore, it is far more powerful at expelling poison than at heating the body. Since pestilential fever is much more poisonous than it is hot, theriac should be given with rose water; and in other matters, one should strive toward a certain coolness so that you may use this very thing. **Mithridatum** <note>A precursor to theriac, named after King Mithridates VI</note> can also be given in place of theriac, but much more powerful experiences have been seen from theriac. Therefore, **Moses the Egyptian** <note>The philosopher and physician Maimonides (1135–1204)</note> says it was told to him by a certain wise physician that while he was practicing the art in **Antioch** during a time of plague, he found by experience that all other remedies were weak; but only those who, by his advice, took theriac, escaped safe and surviving, while the others did not.
