If another course is taken, let him take something by mouth; you should create a solution either with an enema or a suppository. Then, at the fourth hour, you will administer some nourishment, which we discussed a little further above.
The wine should be white, light, fragrant, and diluted with **iron-rich water** <note>original: "aqua ferrata"; water in which hot iron had been quenched, believed to have strengthening and astringent properties</note>, at least equal to a recently prepared portion. However, **golden water** would be better, in which glowing gold has been extinguished; or indeed, gold can also be extinguished in wine. Do not allow the patient to suffer thirst, nor the mouth to become parched, but have him continually gargle with well-diluted white wine. He should keep moist and cool things in his mouth; let him frequently drink equal parts of **citron juice** <note>original: "acetositas citri"</note> and **rose julep** <note>A sweet, medicinal syrup made with rosewater and sugar</note> with pomegranate wine and the water or juice of **wood-sorrel** <note>original: "acetosella"</note>. Simple syrup of sorrel with iron-rich water is useful, as is the juice of citron or lemons, or squeezed oranges; you shall give these with water and sugar, or perhaps better with barley water or iron-rich water. Likewise, **sugared roses** or <term>diamenatum</term> <note>A confection likely made with mint</note> or <term>diaprunis</term> <note>A plum-based purgative electuary</note> and <term>diacydonites</term> <note>A quince-based digestive aid</note> dissolved in water, strained and pressed; or roses, sour cherries, **myrobalans** <note>Astringent plum-like fruits used to balance humors</note>, tamarinds, plums, quinces, and dried peaches, crushed and infused in water, then strained, pressed, and presented with sugar and fresh water, are all useful. White vinegar with iron-rich water and sugar is suitable for both the sick and the healthy alike. **Compound oxysacchara** <note>A medicinal syrup of vinegar and sugar</note> made with white vinegar, sour pomegranate juice, and sugar is also beneficial. Also helpful is pomegranate juice of a mild flavor, or the juice or wine of sour pomegranates with a little sugar, and barley water with pomegranate wine. It is good to rub **golden rings** in water for so long that they are somewhat worn down by the water. Likewise, it is good to boil water with gold and use it in food and drink. According to **Gentile** <note>Likely referring to Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous physician who wrote extensively on the plague</note>, it can perhaps be managed so that gold is reduced to a liquid form suitable for drinking, in this manner: Take one ounce of gold and two ounces of **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, mix them, and let them remain mixed until the gold is dissolved. Then place it in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A chemical distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note> over a slow fire, just enough so that the quicksilver leaves the alembic. Afterward, take the gold from the bottom of the alembic and add forty-seven ounces of **bugloss water** <note>Water distilled from the bugloss plant, used to "gladden the heart"</note>; place it in a glass alembic, well-sealed. You will continue the fire under it for three days and nights—a well-proportioned fire, I say. In the end, if you are skilled in the art, you will find the water hardly consumed and the gold liquefied; and this is **potable gold**, most heart-strengthening, and it can be digested. Gold in any other form is of little use because it can by no means be digested. You shall administer twice a day on an empty stomach from these syrups: namely, half a drachm each of citron juice, lemon, chicory, and **fumitory** <note>original: "fumo terrae"; a plant used to "cleanse" the blood</note>, with one ounce each of **lemon balm** water and wood-sorrel juice. Likewise, syrups of **verjuice** <note>original: "agresta"; the juice of unripened grapes</note>, of currants, barberry preserves, of quinces, of mild pomegranate, and of pomegranate with endive and bugloss waters. Likewise, syrup of endive with endive waters and citron juice, with wood-sorrel juice and sour pomegranate wine; also, the squeezed juice of lemons, or citron, or oranges should be presented with water and sugar. It would not be displeasing if, in place of water, you administered a chicken broth, which is commonly called **peppered broth** <note>original: "piperata"</note>, or partridge cooked with verjuice and endive, then strained, to which some of the aforementioned juices are mixed, tempering the sour with sweets, just as nature does in pomegranates of mild flavor. Also, sour pomegranates with wine and their own juice alone, or even with other juices—let all be well seasoned. Likewise, rose juice, myrobalans, tamarinds, sugared roses, and <term>diamarenatum</term> <note>A cherry-based confection</note>, <term>diaprunis</term>, and <term>diacydonites</term> dissolved in water, strained and pressed, are to be drunk with fresh water. Likewise, **oxysacchara** with rose julep and iron-rich water. Also, rose juice and citron juice with pomegranate wine. Note: syrup of sorrel is useful in whatever syrup it is found. Where citron juice is not available, squeeze lemons or oranges and temper them with sugar; where there is greater heat, you shall give a greater quantity of the sour things, and where there is less heat, less. And where sour syrup is not available, you shall give vinegar, water, and sugar mixed together. White vinegar is better than red. Also, this excellent syrup: Take three ounces each of the purified juices of lemon balm, borage, and bugloss; one and a half ounces each of rose water and white vinegar; half an ounce of citron and lemon juice; and one pound of white sugar. From this, you will offer two ounces to drink, with two and a half ounces of bugloss and wood-sorrel waters; use from these as you please. And at the same time, give two **camphor troches** <note>Lozenges or tablets containing camphor, used for their cooling effect</note>. Some of the wise give this potion in place of a syrup: Take one pound of rose water, half a pound of fragrant white wine, and [half a pound] of finely powdered **Armenian bole** <note>original: "bolus armenus"; a medicinal red clay used as an astringent and to counteract poison</note>...

...you should occasionally apply rose water with rose vinegar to the forehead. Unless you fear excessive sleepiness, you may add a little camphor. Take care that the sick person does not fall into too deep a sleep; five or six hours throughout the day and night are sufficient, since too much sleeping draws the poison back inward. **Cupping glasses** <note>original: "ventosae"; suction cups used to draw blood or "humors" to the surface</note> placed on the back, along with rubbing and bandages around the extremities, help with both <term>phrenesy</term> <note>A state of delirium or fever-induced mental confusion</note> and lethargy. Likewise, a suppository made of hard soap with a little rock salt is helpful. A moderate amount of sleep at the beginning of the illness is useful, but one should not stay awake so long that the "spirits" are dissipated as a result.

The room should be aired out by opening and closing windows often, for this refreshes the air; however, it must be aired in such a way that the patient does not feel it or suffer any chill. Linen cloths soaked in vinegar should be stretched along the sides of the bed. Sprinkle the walls and floor of the chamber with vinegar mixed with water; let it be scattered here and there, and in the corners and on the walls, place green branches, vine shoots, reeds, willows, roses, small plants, cucumber leaves, and any other greenery, little flowers, and fragrant apples <note>In the medieval and early modern periods, pleasant smells and greenery were believed to "purify" the air of miasma or infectious vapors.</note>. 

You shall make a **fumigation** <note>A medicinal smoke or incense</note> from sandalwood, roses, myrtle, camphor, turpentine, frankincense, citron peels, pomegranate peels, and common apples, adding a few cloves and saffron. Above all, take care that every six hours you change and renew the patient’s shirt and all their cloths, linens, and fumigants, along with the vessel used for the fumigation. If it can be done conveniently, you should change the bedding and the room every twenty-four hours. Before the patient is brought in, however, the room must be well cleaned and fumigated with good scents as is appropriate. Otherwise, the clothing, bed, and dwelling become infected with the poison. 

Nor do I wish to pass over in silence that where unusual heat, redness of the stomach, and a lack of intestinal pain appear, **Rhazes** and **Johannitius** <note>Rhazes (865–925) and Johannitius (809–873) were foundational Persian and Arab medical authorities whose works were central to European medicine.</note> were accustomed to giving a large quantity of fresh, cold water to drink just once. But for me to act more safely, I would give three pounds of fresh barley water with three ounces of sugar. And perhaps I would also give half a pound of cucumber juice mixed well with an ounce of sugar, followed by an ounce of orange or pomegranate juice and one <term>drachm</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</note> of sugar. 

A certain countryman of ours, a robust man, as soon as this disease attacked him, immersed himself in cold water and stayed there for two hours; upon coming out he was cured. Nevertheless, this is a most deceptive experiment. Perhaps it would be safer to sit in lukewarm water that does not reach the chest, since these parts should not be opened, nor should the humors be provoked toward them. Some in this case have taken "antidotes," especially those of a cold nature, and perhaps even those of a hot nature, before or after **theriac** <note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients</note>, or **sealed earth** <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay often stamped with a seal to prove its origin</note> with **Armenian bole** <note>A red medicinal clay used as an astringent</note> and vinegar mixed with water, and similar things which act against poison. Among these, a certain physician was cured. Yet to me, the matter seems quite dangerous.

---

### On the cure through the art of surgery. Chapter 11.

**I**n this case, one must not wait until a swelling or a blister appears. Instead, once the purging or bloodletting is done, be swift and ready to extract the poison by making a <term>ruptory</term> <note>A caustic application designed to break the skin and create a discharging sore to "draw out" toxins</note> with yeast and **Spanish fly** <note>original: "cantharides"; a beetle used in medicine to cause blistering</note>, or another of those things we shall describe below. Apply it to the muscle of the right arm below the inner elbow, or where the pulse is usually felt (though not directly over the pulse itself). You shall do the same on the right ankle, four fingers' breadth inward, so that a blister forms; open it and keep it open. 

If the usual sign appears, and the inconvenience or shortness of time prevents the standard order from being observed, let bloodletting and purging be done. Once these are finished, or at least the bloodletting, make a ruptory and apply it to the same side at a distance of six fingers from the "sign" <note>likely referring to a plague bubo or localized swelling</note>. There are those who do not trust the variability of the timing, but regardless of the order, they apply remedies as best they can, both before and after. The order of some modern practitioners is such that, when nothing else helps, the patient is first purged with enemas, powders, bloodletting, and medicine. Afterward, the ruptories should be applied as we said (even if no sign appears). Indeed, it is safer to apply the ruptories and the other things appropriate to this disease immediately, whether a sign appears or not. If a sign is visible, do as follows: if it appears near the ears, suddenly apply a ruptory to the back of the neck on the same side as the sign. If it is under the arm, let the ruptory be placed on the muscle of that same arm, or near the pulse, but not directly upon it.

If [the swelling] is in the groin, place [the treatment] near the ankle—that is, above the heel bone of the same side. When it appears elsewhere, apply a **ruptory** <note>original: "ruptorium"; a caustic substance used to blister the skin and "break" an abscess or draw out toxins</note> six finger-breadths, or two inches, away from the sign, ensuring it is never placed upon the chest, regardless of the circumstances. And if it is in the throat, specifically in the front part, the ruptory should be placed at the back—that is, on the neck. If, however, it is in the back part of the same location, it should not be applied to the front, but rather beneath the site of the sign. You should leave the ruptory there until it has formed a blister; then open the blister and apply butter and cabbage leaves, as well as a sponge soaked in this decoction:

Take one handful each of chamomile, wood-sage, melilot, and scabious; boil these in half a pound of water until it is reduced by half. Because this draws out the poison, renew it and keep it applied frequently until the end of the cure.

### A description of simple ruptories.
### Chapter XII.

**T**hese are the ruptories: swallow-wort, vitriol <note>Sulfates of metals, used here as a corrosive</note>, flower of copper, rancid nut, cardamine, arsenic, quicklime, counter-poison, dodder, lime mixed with fuller’s soap, "aura" <note>likely a reference to a specific volatile mineral or resin</note>, hound’s-tongue, leaven with lye, galbanum, horsetail, spurge, pigeon dung, hawk dung, goose dung, duck dung, watercress, live snails (either crushed or with their shells), a skinned and roasted frog, calamint, hart’s pennyroyal, birthwort, radish, mistletoe, knotgrass, costus root, pepper, sea-sponge stone, crushed spearwort, nettle, white mustard, wild mint, scabious, hemp, hemp-seed, Spanish fly <note>original: "cantharides"; a beetle used as a powerful, often dangerous, blistering agent</note> and rock salt, chewed grains, pellitory, yolk of egg with much salt, and comfrey. Scabious, when crushed between two stones, is wonderful. The said ruptories must be applied quickly, as I have said, and perhaps even directly upon the appearing sign. For delicate persons, milder ones should be used, and for others, stronger ones. It is safer to place them below the sign rather than above it, or if placed above, let them be less strong, while those below should be stronger.

### The reasoning, methods, and conditions for curing the aposteme.
### Chapter XIII.

**T**his sign is called an **aposteme** <note>A general term for a swelling, abscess, or tumor; in this context, a plague bubo</note>. When it appears before the onset of fever, it indicates that the heart is strong and powerful enough to expel the poison; in such a case, the fever is merely an accident of the aposteme. The opposite is true when it comes after the fever. Now, this aposteme is of two kinds: one is a blister and is called **anthrax** or a carbuncle; the other is a swelling and is called a **bubo** or a gland. The blister usually emerges through the <term>emunctories</term> <note>Traditional medical term for the "cleansing" organs or nodes (like lymph nodes) where the body was thought to expel waste</note>, and the further it is from the vital organs, the less dangerous it is. A black one is the worst of all; a green one is second and slightly less evil; a gray one is third; and a red one is fourth. The drier it is, the worse it is. Swelling usually occurs in the emunctories—that is, the cleansing points of the vital organs, of which there are three: behind the ears, under the arms, and in the groin. The brain dismisses its poison through the emunctories behind the ears and into the neck. The heart sends it under the arms. The liver sends it to or around the groin. For this reason, a swelling is worse than a blister, since it shows that much of the poison has flowed toward the vital organs. And the closer the swelling is to the heart, the more dangerous it is. 

The cure for both—the blister and the swelling—is nearly the same. There are some who, when an aposteme appears before the fever and far from the heart, immediately apply bandages between the place of pain and the heart, and apply cold, dry things on top to repel the matter. But upon the site of the pain itself, they place warm, moist, and dissolving things. Others, as soon as the aposteme begins to appear, apply cupping glasses (as we have said) both on top and to the side, along with ruptories, immediately administering this medicine:

Take half a dram each of prepared black hellebore, senna, and cinnamon, and half a scruple of <term>diagridium</term> <note>A preparation of scammony resin, used as a potent purgative</note>. Let these be infused in four ounces of pomegranate wine and one ounce of sugar. It would be better if it stood in the infusion for many hours; afterward, strain and press it out, to be given when the aposteme appears and before the patient sleeps. They prepare the hellebore in this way: they cut it lengthwise into small pieces and place it inside an apple wrapped in <term>tow</term> <note>Coarse flax or hemp fibers</note> previously soaked in rose water, and so they cook it under hot ashes. ### Rules and methods for applying ruptories.
### Chapter XIV.

When the circumstances do not allow for blood to be drawn with cupping glasses <note>original: "uentosis"; suction cups used to draw blood to the surface</note> or leeches <note>original: "sanguifugis"</note>, and the flesh cannot be cauterized with fire, ruptories <note>original: "ruptoria"; caustic substances applied to the skin to create a chemical burn or blister</note> should be applied either below or above the site, or in both places at once, using the compositions mentioned before and those I will describe below. You should apply these—if it seems there is enough time—after blood has been drawn and the patient has rested a little, or at least after they have taken their medicine and it has finished its work. If no surgeon is present to operate by hand, give the powder; if you do not have that, give the medicine. If you have no medicine, apply the ruptories without delay above and outside the "sign" <note>The "sign" refers to the bubo or plague swelling</note> with moderation and in the proper order. If time is pressing and nothing has been done yet, administer the purgation and the ruptories at the same time. Never cease the administration of remedies, and do not delay in the hope that you will do everything later with more convenience. 

Take care not to place things that are so cold or styptic <note>original: "stipticas"; substances that shrink or constrict tissues</note> upon the sign that they drive the poison back inside. Use things that are well-suited for drawing out and dissolving, such as warm substances. These should be tempered somewhat at times if you are going to continue using them alongside cold things, so that excessive inflammation is avoided, yet not so cold that they constrict the area. Do not fear the pain too much, since it draws the poison to the extremities. However, I do not wish for you to tolerate excessive pain, as that would add strength to the poison, increase the fevers, and weary the patient's nature too much. I do not want you to allow the site of the ruptory to heal completely through medical art until three months have passed; when you do finally close it, repeat the purging of the body. 

A certain fellow Florentine of ours truly "hit the mark" <note>original: "incidit bullam"; perhaps an idiom for striking the core of the problem, or a play on words regarding the "bulla" or swelling</note> regarding this: though he was so liberated from the disease that he seemed no different from a healthy man, very soon after he healed the wound, forty days later, he was re-infected by the disease and died within two days. This happened primarily because he had closed the wound without purging. For you should know this: anyone who dies after the seventh day does so more because of poor care than because of the nature of this disease. Know that after the poison has flowed into the abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> so that the vital organs are relieved, unless you draw it out well and continuously, and rectify and purge it, the internal poison of the abscess becomes more aggravated; once contracted, it vaporizes inward and kills. Therefore, continually fortify the body by closing its internal and external paths [to keep in strength], evacuate the humors often, and cleanse and purge the poison from the wound. Do not trust their hope for health if it is contrary to reason; indeed, do not cease remedies even for a moment because of it, especially if the seventh day has not yet passed.

### Compound ruptories and certain strong plasters.
### Chapter XV.

There are many kinds of compound ruptories that are powerful at drawing the poison outward. We shall describe many so that you may conveniently use whatever help is available according to the opportunity. Take figs, iris <note>original: "ireos"</note>, and crushed wheat grains in equal parts; this ripens the swelling quickly and breaks it. Also, leaven with oil and salt. Also, pitch with raisins <note>original: "passulis"</note> and honey. Also, sparrow dung with pig lard <note>original: "axungia porci"</note>. Also, powdered glass with turpentine. Also—if it were not so disgusting—human dung is very effective both before and after the skin breaks, by placing breadcrumbs soaked in boiling oil over it. Also, oil boiled with ashes. Also, ten Spanish flies <note>original: "cantharides"; a toxic beetle used to cause severe blistering</note>, with one ounce of raisins, one and a half ounces of leaven, and one ounce each of scabious, hound's-tongue <note>original: "cynoglossæ"</note>, greater comfrey <note>original: "consolidæ maioris"</note>, and counter-poison <note>original: "antipharmaci"</note>; let these be incorporated with lily oil. ### On temperate plasters. Chapter XVI.

**T**he aforementioned ruptories and plasters are very strong, both for breaking the skin and for quickly drawing out the poison. However, they should not be continued for long, as they would cause too much inflammation; nevertheless, one can use them more when the abscess <note>original: "apostema"; here referring to the plague bubo</note> is not very green, red, or black in color, and also where there is not much corrosion. I will now provide certain tempering and more suitable applications for cases where there is fear of great inflammation. Take two ounces of marshmallow root, one head of white lilies, and one and a half ounces of linseed flour; let them boil in common water, and let them be crushed with yeast and old lard <note>original: "axungia ueteri"</note>; apply it warm. Likewise, take two handfuls of bran not entirely purged of flour and let it be cooked in vinegar. Likewise, columbine with vinegar and rose oil. Likewise, barley flour with the juice of water dock or comfrey. Likewise, onions cooked with butter, adding later dried figs and yeast; it can be sweetened with chamomile oil (if necessary due to the intensity of the odor) by adding cooked apples, or marshmallow and mallow and their mucilages. If even greater soothing is needed, take cooked onions and cooked apples with butter and chamomile oil. Likewise, a handful each of mallow, marshmallow root, and scabious; let the herbs boil in common water, with which the flour should be incorporated. Let the herbs be crushed and everything seasoned together with one ounce of chicken fat, an equal amount of chamomile oil, and half a drachma of saffron <note>original: "croci"</note>, for it is a most delicate plaster. Likewise, scabious, pigeon's foot <note>a type of geranium</note>, chicory, and great comfrey. After these, a plaster of celery, water dock, and vetch flour with the juices of the aforementioned herbs is suitable, and according to some, even with theriac <note>original: "theriaca"; a famous ancient multi-ingredient compound used as a universal antidote</note>. Likewise, a plaster of opopanax <note>a medicinal gum resin</note> crushed with raisins. Likewise, asafoetida, rue, and nitre with honey. Sometimes it is good to be anointed with theriac, with cooked onions and mallows placed on top. Some also place orange flowers and crushed leaves with lard and mallows on top. As for the theriac itself, some believe that nothing should be placed on top of it, because it might drive the poison back inward.

### Very temperate plasters. Chapter XVII.

**W**hen the blister <note>original: "bulla"; likely a carbuncle or plague sore</note> is very black and burning beyond measure, and when it ignites, corrodes, and spreads very quickly, the treatments you administer must be tempering: drying with a certain coolness, and a temperate, resolving heat. For example: take plantain and galls cooked with vinegar; likewise, lentils mixed with bread and the siftings of bran. Likewise, take sour and medium-flavored pomegranates, cut into four parts and cooked in vinegar until they dissolve; let them be ground and applied. But do all things with moderation, as is quickly necessary for internal purging.

## On the method of mitigating pain around the abscess itself. Chapter XVIII.

**T**he things treated in the previous chapter are confirmed to be effective for blisters that are very black and corrosive; however, in other cases where the inflammation is not as great, be more moderate and more mature <note>that is, more cautious or gradual</note> in repelling the humors. If you strive to soothe the burning and pain—stemming partly from the disease and partly from the "ruptories" <note>the corrosive medicines used to break the skin</note> or from the inflammation—place warm crumbs of fresh bread, straight from the oven and soaked in vinegar-wine or plantain juice, around the mark. Likewise, cook the aforementioned bread crumbs and also lentils in vinegar; apply this and change it frequently, and so the plaster does not dry out, immediately place plantain leaves over it. When you remove the plaster, let the surface of the wound be washed with astringent wine <note>original: "uino ponco," likely "uino ponto"</note> or vinegar, and apply barley flour with honey. I understand, however, that these things ought to be placed not *on* the wound, but *around* it; although according to Pietro da Tossignano <note>original: "Petrum de Tussigniana"; a famous 14th-century physician</note> and other learned and experienced men, these things we have mentioned do not repel the humors much, but rather drive out the heat, comfort the site of the pain, and dissolve the humors with a certain moderate heat. Afterward, heal the remaining wound with those things which pertain to poisonous and corrosive sores.

## On the method of cutting away the rotten flesh of the abscess itself. Chapter XIX.

**W**hen the wound has become necrotic <note>dead tissue</note>, take care immediately that the "rope" of dead flesh falls away. Take one ounce each of bear’s breech <note>original: "brancæ ursinæ"</note>, marshmallow root, periwinkle herb, and mallow leaves; let them be cooked, crushed, and mixed with unsalted pork lard and old butter. Let them sit together for three days, then let them be strained and pressed out, adding a little wax and mastic <note>a resin from the lentisk tree</note> to the strained liquid; save this for use. Let it form a proper scab on the wound, which you may afterward pull away easily once you have used the said plaster and anointed it with butter and oil. Do not remove the scab with any violence (for that would be very harmful); wait until nature begins to do it by itself, which you may afterward assist with the things mentioned above. Meanwhile, lest the poison corrodes and runs through the healthy parts of the body, it is necessary to help in this manner: have a large cupping glass <term>ventosa<gloss>a glass vessel used in "cupping" to create a vacuum on the skin</gloss></term>, so that when it is applied it surrounds the whole wound in this way: namely, that when placed on top it touches only the healthy flesh all around, so that the wound cannot be touched by the cupping glass from any side. Therefore, apply this cupping glass to draw out the poisonous blood from the depths and to prevent it from returning back inside.

## On the method of cleansing the wound. Chapter XX.

**O**nce the abscess has been ruptured and the matter of the poison extracted, things that are both binding and cleansing should be administered. Take barley flour with honey and a little salt; place cabbage leaves over it. Likewise, take powdered sarcocolla <note>a Persian tree resin traditionally used to "glue" or heal wounds</note> and an equal part of honey; if you want it stronger, first cook the honey itself, and afterward add the sarcocolla.

### On the method of regenerating good flesh. Chapter XXIII.

**W**hen the sore has been cleansed, to regenerate healthy flesh, take the leaves of basil, well crushed. Also take yellow-flowered plants <note>original: "xanthos"</note>, greater centaury, the herb cinquefoil <note>original: "penetaphyllon"</note>, and equal parts of greater comfrey; let them be distilled in spring through an alembic <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, or make a juice from these herbs, and allow them to sit together until they are well mixed. Afterward, add a fifth part of water of life <note>original: "aquæ uitæ"; distilled alcohol or brandy</note> to them and save it for use; for you will find this wonderful for regenerating flesh. Likewise, the "beard of the asphodel"—that is, burdock <note>original: "lappa"</note>—boiled with wine dregs is helpful for this. Also, a plaster made of green coriander with honey and raisins.

### On various ways of extracting blood from the "sign." And the method of cauterizing by fire. Chapter XXIIII.

<margin>◯</margin>
**A**ll the aforementioned care regarding the "sign" <note>original: "fignum"; the physical mark of the plague, such as a bubo or carbuncle</note>, as we have narrated before, is performed with simple and compound ruptories <note>corrosive substances used to break the skin and drain the infection</note>. However, the opinion of all the Italian doctors would be more praiseworthy if we followed the method I will now describe, setting aside those ruptories and acting thus: Place cauteries <note>tools for burning the skin</note> at a distance from the "sign" as we have already said, and at the same time place a large cupping glass <note>original: "uentosam"</note> over the "sign." Once the glass is removed, prick the area in various places with a scarifier and a small lancet; then replace the cupping glass to draw out the blood, and remove it once the blood ceases to flow. Next, apply three well-cleansed leeches. When these are full and removed, cut young roosters, pigeons, or doves through the middle, and apply them warm, one after another. After this, according to some, the area should be anointed with theriac <note>original: "theriaca"; a complex ancient medical concoction used as an antidote to poison</note>, and then you should allow the patient to rest. Some people, in place of this, pluck the area around the anus of a rooster and take one ounce of soap (of a somewhat dark and almost green color) and half a scruple of opium; they pound these well and, with white salt and powdered dung, they make a suppository for the rooster, and apply the whole bird over the wound. Once this is finished, restore the patient's strength, and afterward cauterize him gently. I do not mean with wax or boiling oil, because these cause blockages, but with glowing gold, silver, or iron. The instrument should have a round, flat surface at its tip in the shape of a fairly large coin, and in the middle of this flat surface, a sharp point or edge in the shape of a diamond, though not too sharp. After the burning, anoint with butter and cover the place with a cabbage leaf, and allow the patient to rest. This is much more preferable to using ruptories, because it works more quickly, drives out the poison more effectively, and furthermore leaves the limb in better condition. After this, they use the same things to be placed over the wound that we mentioned above to be administered after a ruptory, and in the same manner. Some people suffering from the pestilential disease show no other "sign" than spots, like measles, scattered across the skin of the body. These patients should be wrapped in a warm scarlet cloth and kept from the cold. Two large, warm sponges should be applied to the back over the kidneys and to the chest, soaked in a decoction of melilot, chamomile, and lentils, and well squeezed; these should be changed frequently while the stomach is empty. You shall also give him a drink of a decoction of dried figs, dyed lentils, and saffron.

### On the cure according to the custom of the Spanish and Catalans. Chapter XXV.

...of the followers of Gentile <note>original: "telanorum", likely "Gentilianorum" referring to followers of Gentile da Foligno</note>, we shall consider these medications. Therefore, according to them, a clyster <note>an enema used to clear the bowels</note> should be administered immediately; afterward, if there is an abundance of blood, phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is performed. If not, medicine is administered according to the quality of the offending humor. At the beginning, they apply a compress <note>original: "epithema"</note>, then once some evacuation has been achieved, at least with the clyster, they proceed to the care of the abscess <note>original: "apostematis"; a swelling or bubo</note>. Also, following their custom, nothing should be placed over the abscess from burning inflammations, because they induce spasms, ignite fevers, and make the poison more malignant, especially if the abscess is in the emunctories <note>original: "emunctorijs"; the lymph nodes in the armpits, groin, or neck, thought to be the body's drainage points</note>. They also say that highly maturing and softening agents should not be applied at the start, because they bind, block, cause putrefaction, create a reservoir, and push the poison inward. They also say cold things should not be administered, nor anything that desiccates, neither with a sponge nor with a cloth, because they trap the vapors inside and tighten the area. But truly, using clean wool or hemp tow is praiseworthy.

The present decoction is most familiar, especially for those who are delicate by nature, and also for use on the emunctories. Take chamomile flowers, melilot, and maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillos Veneris"</note>; let them boil in water, soak the wool or hemp, wring it out with your hands, and apply it lukewarm or slightly warm; renew it every hour until it resolves or opens. However, after it has opened and the fifth day has passed, use maturing agents and those things which cleanse and regenerate. 

To safely break blisters <note>original: "bullis"</note>, apply crushed scabious, either alone or with old salted pig lard <note>original: "axungia"</note>. If the blister is green or black, but is not in the emunctories, you should open it suddenly in various parts with a lancet <note>original: "lanceola"</note> or a razor, so the poison may exit quickly. Then wash the blister with salt water so that no clotted blood remains there, and apply leeches <note>original: "sanguisugas"</note>. After it has been ruptured and purged of poison, and after the fifth day has passed (as mentioned above), apply maturing, cleansing, and regenerating agents. 

Beyond these things (unless the patient is of a very tender age), a large cupping glass <note>original: "uentosa"</note> should be placed not directly on, but beneath the blister at a distance of six fingers. Afterward, an opening should be made with a lancet or razor, and the cupping glass applied again to draw out the blood—specifically two or three ounces, or even more, according to the strength and endurance of the patient. 

<note>Warning for practitioners</note> Take note: when the sign is in the emunctories, apply the cupping glasses to the proper mark, but do not cut, nor disturb it too much by frequent cupping, because in this way a spasm may be provoked, hot humors are drawn in great numbers, the poison is made worse, and many perish by doing so. Truly, if such a sign appears around the ears or in the throat, apply the cupping glass behind, under the vertebrae of the neck, not directly on or in the parotid glands <note>original: "parulis"</note>. If it appears under the arms, apply the cupping glass on the same side, but slanted downwards. If in the groin, apply the cupping glass on the thigh, or behind under the buttocks. In any of these cases, do this: place the cupping glass at a distance of six fingers from the sign, as we said, and by scarifying <note>making small surface incisions</note> draw blood with the cups or leeches. But over the sign itself, place the aforementioned decoction, so that it may gently soothe and resolve. 

Along with the decoction, it would be good if you could apply some stone that draws out poison, either powdered or whole, such as emerald <note>original: "smaragdus"</note>, hyacinth, or topaz. However, according to some of these doctors, we can apply leeches and sometimes even cupping glasses directly to the sign. Even if it is in the emunctories, nothing should be done with violence, and afterward it should be washed with salt water. This is done when the sign is extremely swollen or of an evil heat; and when the sign is open, after the fifth day has passed, they use maturing agents. If this decoction has very little effect, you may reduce it to the form of a "gout-drop" decoction. 

When the abscess is more swollen than usual, some, after the third day, cut it deeply along the length of the limb in which the sign appears, specifically avoiding the veins and arteries in the spaces between. And if the blood flows too much, one should counter it with hemp tow dipped in egg yolk and rose oil, but not in the white of the egg, because that is cold and viscous. At that time, they comfort the patient with cordials <note>heart-strengthening medicines</note> both internally and externally. Truly, the wiser among them do not approve of this incision, judging it to be of the greatest danger, especially in the emunctories. 

After the fifth day, if the fever is not severe and the sign is not very poisonous, black, or green, and if it is close to rupturing, the body being well purged, begin with maturing agents to ripen the abscess. Take half a pound each of marshmallow root <note>original: "barbæ maluauisci"</note>, lily root, elecampane <note>original: "enulæ campanæ"</note>, squirting cucumber <note>original: "cucumeris asinini"</note>, and onions; one ounce each of fat figs <note>original: "caricarum"</note>, fenugreek seed, and linseed; one handful each of marshmallow leaves, bear's breech <note>original: "brancæ ursinæ"</note>, and violet herb. Let them be boiled vigorously in water and well crushed. If for...

<meta>This page continues the specific instructions for treating plague-related swellings, transitioning from gentle compresses to stronger "maturative" agents (designed to bring an abscess to a head) and "ruptive" agents (to break the skin and drain the poison). # MARSILIO FICINO ON THE PLAGUE

For delicate patients, this maturing agent may be prepared: let the aforementioned ingredients be gathered, cooked, crushed, and pressed. Afterward, add one pound—or as much as is sufficient—of fresh, melted, strained lard <term>axungia porci; pork fat used as a base for ointments</term>. Some add snails well-crushed together with their shells; this is appropriate where the skin is very dense, such as in the groin and behind the ears. Others add two ounces of coarse bread leaven, more or less according to the need for drawing and breaking, which is more suitable for buboes <note>original: "bullis"; the characteristic inflammatory swellings of the bubonic plague</note> than for inflammations of the emunctories <note>the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin, seen as the body's "drainage" points</note>. There are also other lighter maturing agents, such as wheat flour boiled with oil and water until it reaches a certain stickiness, or with the crumb of bran bread and fatty figs cooked together and then crushed. We can also whip olive oil or sweet almond oil with fresh lard. If such lard were old and salted, this plaster would be useful for gently breaking the buboes. We can also add fresh chicken fat; if a plaster is made from such fat, lard, fresh butter, violet oil, and cooked lily roots <note>original: "barbis liliorum"; literally "lily beards"</note>, it is pleasing to delicate patients.

Maturing agents of this kind (as we said before) ought to be applied after purging, once the fever has ceased, and after the sore <note>original: "signum"; the "sign" or mark of the plague</note> has opened and the poison has been cleared out, specifically after the fifth day has passed. Then they use cleansing agents, afterward regenerating agents, and finally agents to close and heal the sore. If the bubo is black or green and corrosive, and is not located in the emunctories, lance it deeply with a small blade or a lancet <note>original: "rosario"</note>. Afterward, you shall administer a "douche" with somewhat warm salt water, lest the blood (as we mentioned) should clot; then apply a cupping glass, leeches, or the plucked rear of a rooster <note>a common folk remedy where the vent of a live, plucked bird was applied to the sore to "draw out" the venom</note>. Some apply a living snail, others a living frog; this can be done when the sore is not in the emunctories. Afterward, apply some simple "ruptive" agent which we described above, or even this one:

Take the yolk of an egg with a modest amount of salt—not too strong, for it might make the bubo malignant—and let this be changed frequently. But if even this disturbs the bubo too much, use salted lard, or both together. There are certain very strong rupturing agents that should not be placed over the emunctories, nor where a heavy fever is present; for even if they are applied where the patient is strong, they are of very little benefit. Take raw figs and leaven. Likewise, if this is not effective, they make it stronger, though observing the method and order already described: take well-ground Spanish flies <term>cantharides; a toxic beetle used to cause blistering</term> and a third part of lard; place this over the malignant bubo three or four times. Surgeons say this has been frequently tested. When they wish to have something even stronger, they add a fourth part of fuller’s soap, which they say works miraculously on a malignant bubo in a robust man.

Also, another strong remedy for buboes: take half an ounce of well-powdered nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, one ounce of wheat grains crushed or chewed by the teeth <note>saliva was thought to have medicinal properties</note>, two egg yolks, one drachm of saffron, and one ounce of turpentine; let them be well mixed and applied with clean flax fibers. Others apply quicklime with soap. But because these kinds of burning and violent things frequently make the abscess and fevers more malignant, it is safer to take care before the ulceration <note>the breaking of the skin</note> lest the matter turn back inward, or lest it be made "rabid" by these sharp fevers, especially in those with weak or very choleric constitutions. Therefore, for these purposes, it is useful to apply the plaster of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated medieval medicine</note> over the entire limb. Take plantain, lentils, and bran bread in equal parts; let them be cooked in water until they reach a certain solidity; apply it to the place of pain and for a wide space around it. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the 11th-century Persian physician</note> adds gallnuts where more thin blood appears than thick. Likewise, a plaster of sweet and sour pomegranates cooked in vinegar and water is useful for this, especially where the matter appears inflamed. But after the burning begins to cease, the plaster of Avicenna is suitable, made from fatty figs, raisins, nuts, and barley flour, cooked together for maturing and breaking. After the rupture has been made, let the wound be cleansed with the juices of celery, wormwood, and plantain, with honey of roses and flour, cooked with a little washed turpentine; then it is healed according to the order of other wounds, and an ointment of Armenian bole <term>a red medicinal clay</term> and rose oil is placed around it.

Some, at the beginning, for the sake of strong "attraction" <note>drawing the poisonous humors away from the heart</note>, place crushed "flammula" herb (that is, dodder) between the muscles of the shins, or the arm, or upon the shoulder blades; this, by creating an ulcer, draws the humors toward itself from the emunctories and the principal organs. This remedy is useful in robust bodies and where no fever is present, but not otherwise.

# THE ANTIDOTE TO THE PLAGUE

...elsewhere and not otherwise. Some apply an actual cautery <term>cauterium; a hot iron used to burn tissue</term> over the "sign" <note>original: "signum"; the external mark of the plague, such as a bubo or carbuncle</note> with a glowing iron, which indeed is more suitable for robust patients and where there is no high fever. Raymond <note>likely Raymond Lull, a 13th-century polymath and alchemist often cited in medical texts</note> says that theriac <term>theriaca; a complex ancient herbal "universal antidote"</term> and Armenian bole <term>bolus armenus; a medicinal red clay believed to absorb toxins</term> do not draw the poison to themselves but rather drive it away. Therefore, he says they should not be taken by mouth after the second or third day when the matter is already poisonous and has reached the heart itself, unless the body has been well-evacuated <note>purged of harmful "humors"</note> and corrected. Likewise, he forbids them from ever being placed directly on the "sign," nor does he want them applied unless the "sign" is outside the emunctories <note>the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin</note>, and even then, before the third day and in the surrounding area, not directly on top. Armenian bole can be administered even after the seventh day, once the wound has been purged of poison, by anointing the surrounding area. Thus, it is appropriate on the third day before the wound becomes poisonous, and it is appropriate after the seventh day once the wound is purged of poison; however, the surrounding area should be anointed with rose oil, rose vinegar, and rose water to protect the limb. Hitherto we have related the opinions of the Spaniards and Catalans along with the corrections of Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician</note> and Raymond, singular physicians. It is a true matter, and Raymond is of this opinion: namely, that the sick person ought not to be purged with phlebotomy <term>phlebotomia; bloodletting</term>, medicine, or vomiting when the abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> is very full and poisonous—that is, after the second day has passed—lest the poison be turned back inward by such motion. This opinion indeed seems in need of correction according to others, and thus one should be purged if necessary (with the aforementioned precautions) even after the second day, provided that while the person is being purged, you apply cupping glasses and leeches below and above the "sign," and that the heart be protected inside and out with cold cordials <note>heart-strengthening medicines</note>. This method is also not entirely foreign to the intention of the aforementioned Raymond.

### ->On the protection of those attending the sick, who manage the infirm.<-
### ->Chapter XXIV.<-

**H**aving discussed what was said at the beginning regarding protection (namely theriac, pills, and the like), those attending the sick, unless they are free of an excess of blood, ought to draw a little blood from the common vein after performing a good purging with one dram (or at least half a dram) of the aforementioned pills. It is useful for them to frequently take powders and medicine against the disease, as was said previously, and to do so in the morning or as far away from the sick person as possible, especially when they are fasting. The living quarters should be aired out often, and fumigations should be made, as said above, never omitting turpentine <term>terebenthina; a resin used for its aromatic and medicinal smoke</term>. They should carry glowing torches in their hands and well-kindled coals smoking with good scents. They should wash the entire body with warm vinegar twice a day, namely morning and evening. One should change garments frequently and very often renew the fumigations, especially with frankincense, turpentine, juniper, myrtle, sandalwood, roses, and camphor, or rosemary, laurel, and the like. One should hold in the hands oranges <note>original: "arantium"</note> and a bunch of rue or wood sage <note>original: "querculæ maioris"</note> and mint and lemon balm with myrtle and fresh blossoms. One should always be well-purged of every excess humor and food. Again, repeat that health-giving scent with rose water, rose vinegar, Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, potent wine</note>, zedoary <term>zedoaria; a root similar to ginger</term>, or citrus peels; above all, wash the hands and face frequently with these. One should also drink a little of this composition and even hold a sponge dipped in this same mixture to the nostrils, tied to a stick of ash wood <note>original: "lignum fraxini"</note>. For the ash tree has such power against poison that no venomous animal dares to approach its shadow or its scent; indeed, such a creature would sooner give itself up to be burned by fire than stay near this tree. They should quite frequently make fires and hearths throughout the entire house, especially with fragrant wood and materials. Nor should anyone who has been once freed from this disease think that they cannot perish from it thereafter; for in the present year, this disease attacked one of our Florentines three times; having been perfectly freed the second time, he could not escape death the third. In the same year, in the month of September, I cured a certain poor woman of the plague; she was indeed healthy, like others who had remained safe, but when she moved among the sick, she was infected again after eighteen days and died. No one is to be trusted in the belief that they are stronger or healthier than others, since poison kills the strong just as it does the weak. Indeed, this poison harms them more than others...

->MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS<-

[He] shows that those of a <term>sanguine; the temperament dominated by blood, characterized by a ruddy, warm, and vigorous nature</term> and robust disposition are vulnerable because the passages of their chest are open. They have a very strong heart and much warm, moist blood; therefore, the very heat of the heart draws in much of the destructive air through these open channels, and indeed draws it in suddenly, before it can be tempered by the passage. For the heat of the blood is very quickly ignited and inflamed. Immediately, the moisture undergoes putrefaction and is turned into poison. Indeed, just as a greater quantity of wine in a vessel—and the more potent it is—turns into a greater and sharper quantity of vinegar, so too a powerful poison is produced in greater abundance the hotter the blood in the chest is. Since the blood itself becomes the poison, it is very easily transformed into the same substance by even a small contact with it. For the parts, once they have touched each other, mutually convert into poison.

And let it not escape you, O you who care for the patient, that the closer you are to them—whether by kinship, or by similarity of <term>complexion; the specific balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile)</term>, nature, or astrological constellation—the greater the danger of contagion you face. This is because there is a certain readiness in the quality of the transmission, so that a transformation of like to like can be fulfilled, just as fire moves to air, or as this air moves toward the earth. And when two lutes or two small stringed instruments are tuned to the same pitch, the movement resonates, and the voice of one sounds in the other. 

If you ask, however, through which paths the poison enters? I answer: through all the pores of the body, especially those that are most open. It strikes more quickly when it enters through the nose, the mouth, and through the pulses <note>meaning the arterial points</note>; and it strikes much more strongly if it finds paths open in warm, moist, and thin <term>humors; the primary fluids of the body</term>, and especially if it proceeds from similar humors. Thus, the influence of Mars occurs in a diverse and contrary way, whereas with the influence of Saturn, it shows itself more slowly. Often the poison lingers for a long time in clothing and on the skin, in the open paths and veins near the heart, without anyone seeming to be burdened by it, because it is a very small and light vapor. It does not have the same opposition to other parts as it does to the heart; but as soon as that tiny bit becomes contiguous to the heart, it causes manifest, not hidden, harm. Similarly, the poison of a rabid dog, and indeed other poisons, may reveal their injury even a long time later.

I would have you know this finally: that the poison remains in persons for a space of two months. Walls, iron tools, and vessels made of wood—unless they are corrected with washings, fumigations, and fires—perhaps retain their poisonous quality for a year or more. Woolen clothes and that sort of material, unless they are aired out, washed, and frequently fumigated, or placed by the fire, in the wind, or in the sun, remain infected for three years and beyond. You surely know the musty smell of a spider in a small box where it has rotted can be preserved for many years. Similarly, the scent of musk remains for a long time in the cotton it was first placed in. Indeed, just as oil is to fire, so wool is the nourishment of this poison; and indeed this wool so nourishes the poison that it not only preserves it, but also increases and strengthens it at the same time. One must not use the vessels of those who are infected for the arrangement of food or drink, nor should anything that has clung to them be touched.

You must live joyfully, because gladness shapes the <term>vital spirit; the subtle vapor believed to sustain life and bridge the gap between soul and body</term>. Live continently and soberly; indeed, sobriety and continence are of such great value that by these alone, the philosopher Socrates kept himself unharmed in the midst of many and truly heavy plagues that occurred in Athens.

Aristotle and Galen say that the disposition in pure bodies is such that they almost never feel the plague, or even if they are infected, they at least do not perish.

See, I now hand over two singular things for your preservation. Prepare an emerald <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> so that it can be drunk, touched, held in the mouth, and hung from the neck; its virtue against poisons is so great that, according to the testimony of Rhazes, Avenzoar, and Serapion <note>famous Persian and Arabic medical authorities whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance medicine</note>, the eyes of vipers and <term>buboes; the inflammatory swellings of the lymph nodes characteristic of the plague</term> fall out of their own accord at the mere sight of it. To the poor, I am accustomed to give wild radish; let it not inflame the blood too much for those nearby, for it has such efficacy against poison that it causes a scorpion to burst at its touch. Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> says that if its seed is crushed with vinegar and used to wash the hands, serpents can do no harm when touched.

The bezoar stone <term>lapis bezoar; a stone-like mass found in the gastrointestinal tract of certain animals, highly prized as a universal antidote</term> (if anyone is able to have it) is above all things powerful against poisons. Although in the Persian language everything that has the property and virtue of repelling poison is traditionally called "bezoar" by the ancients, nevertheless, according to Serapion and Rhazes, the name "bezoar" is principally given to a certain stone that resists all poisons—both hot and cold—and all poisonous diseases or ulcers by its own virtue. It is beneficial whether taken by mouth, held in the mouth, hung from the neck, or finally, applied externally in any way.

# ANTIDOTE

India is in the regions of the East, and it is diverse, having three different colors. For some are sea-green and dark, some are sea-green, dark and green, while another is white and somewhat bluish—namely, similar to the color of a clear white wine. This last one is the best among the rest: light, delicate, soft, without flavor, and shining like light. The dose of it, when taken by mouth, is twelve grains. <term>Rhazes; a famous Persian physician and scholar (865–925 AD) whose works were fundamental to medieval medicine</term> and <term>Serapion; likely refers to Serapion the Younger, an influential 12th-century author on medicinal simples</term> testify that they frequently found in their own times that this most precious stone, by its own inherent quality, surpassed all medicines—whether simple or compound—and even the complex <term>theriacs; an ancient and medieval "universal antidote" made of many ingredients, often including viper flesh</term> in resisting poisons. <insert>Hahamed says</insert> let it be bound in a ring, and let the image of a scorpion be engraved upon the stone when the Moon is in Scorpio, while observing the ascendant. When this is done, let frankincense be sealed with it while in the sign of Scorpio. If you later give a proper amount of this powdered incense in a drink to someone poisoned, it will be as effective against the poisons as the stone itself. <insert>Abdallahamarac says</insert> that he saw this stone, which he says the son of Mamari purchased, and that he gave the palace of Córdoba in exchange for the solution of the stone. Serapion says the same stone works wonders not only in humans, but also in certain other animals; first, that by touching a scorpion's stinger with this stone, it loses its power to sting. Furthermore, he asserts that when ground and mixed with water and placed in a snake’s mouth, it kills it.

->Flee quickly, far away, and return slowly.<-
<note>original: "Fuge citò, procul, ac tarde reuertaris." This was the standard medical advice for the plague in the Renaissance: flee the infected area as fast as possible, go a great distance, and do not return until the danger has long passed.</note>

## Chapter XXV.

**I**t seemed appropriate to reserve for the end of the book the declaration of the principal rules regarding this matter. Flee as much as you can from the company of men, and especially when you are fasting. Be always distant from a companion by at least the space of two <term>cubits; an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches, the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term>. In an open place, or when speaking with an infected person, stay at least six cubits away, under the open sky or in a well-ventilated area, and take care that the wind does not blow from him toward you. Let the Sun, a fire, sweet smells, or a wind blowing toward him be between you; for narrow places and crowds of people together are extremely dangerous. I also remind you that the morbid contagion is multiplied by the enclosure of walls and the contact and continuity of houses. Above all, I advise that you flee quickly and far from those places where the plague is imminent, and return slowly.

I said "quickly"—that is, as soon as the signs of the approaching plague appear. These signs are: when the air of that place seems to be outside its natural disposition, leaning toward heat and humidity; when it appears foggy, with thick clouds and dust; when the winds are heavy and lukewarm; and also when the waters and fields smoke and smell. Likewise, the fish are of bad taste and odor. When many animals born of putrefaction appear upon the earth, along with an abundance of mushrooms and rotting weeds; when the fruits of the earth and animals are tasteless and do not keep well; when urine becomes turbid; and when many animals of both the earth and air leave that place. Unusual fevers arise—hidden, furious, continuous, and deceptive—with anxiety of the chest, a collapsing pulse, <term>phrenesis; a state of delirium or mental frenzy believed to be caused by inflammation of the brain</term>, turbulent urine, ulceration of the palate and intestines, redness of the eyes, worms, <term>measles; here referring generally to skin eruptions or "morbilli"</term>, many disturbances among women, rabid anger, quarrels, dire wars, monsters of nature, and wonderful signs from either nature or from God, which are much-hated and rare. For these things we have mentioned are the omens of an approaching plague. 

Flee then, before you become one of the twelve thousand marked. This can happen in two ways: either because you will already be caught by the contagion of the infected, or because you have already received the dismal quality of the infected air. In that case, the air gradually becomes "familiar" to you, so that your nature does not resist the air, nor the air your nature. But if you suddenly seek a different atmosphere, the first air will depart; nature will resist it, and it will resist nature, and that is where the origin of the plague comes from. I also advise you to flee "far away"—namely, so that you move to places where neither things, nor people, nor sounds, nor noise, nor any rumors of the infected place can reach you. Be so remote that high mountains stand in between to block the passage of vapors, so they cannot touch you by the blowing of the winds or the spreading of the air. Consider the layout and site of the place to which you run; namely, that it is not similar in any way to the pestilential air—such as in heat, cold, humidity, dryness, clouds, rain, or winds. Finally, let it be established in such a place that the winds...

...winds, clouds, and rains may not be able to breathe, expand, or move from there toward you. Nor should it escape your notice that the horoscope or <term>Ascendant; the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, believed by Renaissance thinkers to influence the fate of cities and the spread of disease</term> of some infected city or castle often spreads the plague to all those places which were subject to that city or castle from the beginning, and which have some conformity with that Ascendant. 

Thirdly, we say that you should return late <note>Ficino advises waiting a significant amount of time before returning home after fleeing the plague</note>, because even a tiny remaining infection of the past disease is powerful enough to very suddenly stain all those who began their flight even at a timely hour. Indeed, those who return to an infected place after having previously fled are in greater danger than those who always remained in the same place (provided they acted with caution), because nature poorly tolerates sudden and new <term>accidents; in medieval medicine, this refers to external conditions or symptoms affecting the body</term>. 

Furthermore, these qualities of the disease remain for a very long time (as we have said before) in walls, timber, clothes, and all kinds of fabrics and other things. As far as the condition of the air alone is concerned, one <term>angaria; a term originally meaning a period of forced labor or a post-stage, here used to describe a specific cycle of time or trial</term> is sufficient, so that where all people who are present have remained immune from this disease for three months, one can judge the air to already be purged. 

But be most cautious in approaching and touching those things which retain the poison longer than the air. The surfaces of furnaces in walls keep the poisonous heat longer than wood does; but purify them (as we have often said) namely with fires, washings, airings, fumigations, scents, and the rest. 

Humans are generally purified in a space of fourteen days. 
Houses, timber, and other such things in twenty-one. 
Fabrics, garments, and the like in a space of twenty-eight days. 

During these times, keep separate vessels for drinking and eating, as well as all bedding; or at least, if you cannot manage the rest, purify the other linens with washings and fumigations. Horses, money, furniture, small bundles, and such things, unless you act very cautiously, are accustomed to preserve the poison for a long time. Therefore, be a watchful, cautious, and prudent

# THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO
## Of Florence,

-> BOOK I. <-

-> PREFACE TO THE LETTERS. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence to all his letters at once, Greetings. <-

> **AS OFTEN** as my letters, at my command, give greetings to my friends, give immortal greetings to your most dear Girolamo Rossi <note>original: "Hieronymo Rossio." Rossi was a friend of Ficino and likely a patron or editor who facilitated this publication</note>. For I had fathered you as mortals, and destined, by I know not what fortune, to die shortly. However, Girolamo, a man distinguished by his piety, has recently regenerated you, making you now (I hope) immortal. For a long time you lay hidden, longing for the light, yet no one until now rescued you from the darkness—perhaps because Fate or your <term>Genius; in Roman religion, a guardian spirit or innate guiding force of a person or thing</term> was not yet willing. But our Rossi—or rather, a <term>Roscius; a reference to Quintus Roscius Gallus, the most famous actor of ancient Rome, suggesting Rossi has "staged" or presented the letters with great skill</term> for you—has happily followed that same charity toward you as an inheritance, just as he always conducted himself with piety toward your father Marsilio. He has seen to it through both diligence and labor that your countenances, which were just about to be utterly crushed, were clearly expressed <note>Ficino is likely referring to the transition from messy handwritten manuscripts to the clarity of the printed press</note>. Therefore, greet this learned and pious restorer of yours, who was sad until now but is now joyful; and for this immense gift of immortality, give him immortal thanks. December 15, 1494. Florence.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Of Florence, Preface to his Letters, specifically
### to the First Book, dedicated to Giuliano de' Medici, a Magnanimous Man.

-> Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Giuliano de' Medici, a Magnanimous Man. <-

> **THE GREAT** Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the founder of the Medici political dynasty and Ficino’s primary patron</note>, magnanimous Giuliano, your grandfather and patron, often had that Platonic saying on his lips: that nothing is more convenient for conducting great affairs than the goodwill of prudent and learned men. He believed there was no surer proof of one's own justice and prudence than if such friends are present, nor of injustice and imprudence than if they are absent. This is a golden precept of our Plato. Cosimo proved this in reality even more than in words throughout his entire life; he was certainly a man wealthy in money beyond others, but far wealthier in men, and wealthiest of all in prudence and justice. And—what is most rare and wonderful—he left his son and grandsons as heirs to this entire treasure. Thus it happens that in my Giuliano, I recognize that old man upon whom, after God, my sole safety depended. There is no one, therefore, whom I wish more to be well than Giuliano, and indeed I pray and beseech God for this daily. To declare the vow and affection of my mind to you more certainly, I have decided to dedicate the first volume of my letters to my friends to you, the king of friends. By this, all friends may be referred back to one principal friend, and as you read them, as often as you read a "greeting," you may understand that Giuliano is being greeted by Marsilio.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## On the Desire for Happiness.

*Cosimo de' Medici to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, sends greetings.* <note>original: "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting.</note>

**Y**esterday I retired to my estate at Careggi <note>Careggi was the site of the famous Medici villa where the Platonic Academy met.</note>, not for the sake of tilling the field, but for tilling the soul. Come to us, Marsilio, as soon as you can. Bring with you the book of our Plato on the *Highest Good* <note>original: "Summo bono." This likely refers to Plato's Philebus, which discusses the nature of pleasure and the good.</note>, which I believe you have by now translated, as you promised, from the Greek tongue into Latin. For I desire nothing more ardently than to know which path leads most conveniently to happiness. Farewell, and do not come without your Orphic lyre <note>Ficino was famous for performing "Orphic hymns" on a lyre as a form of musical therapy and spiritual practice.</note>.

---

->What the way to happiness is.<-

*Marsilio Ficino to Cosimo the Great, sends greetings.*

**I** shall come to you as soon as I am able, and most gladly. For what could be more pleasant than to dwell in Careggi—that is, the "field of the Graces" <note>Ficino is making a pun on the name "Charegium" and the Greek word "Charis," meaning Grace.</note>—together with Cosimo, the father of the Graces? In the meantime, receive in these few words the path which the Platonists consider most suited to happiness. And although I think it unnecessary to show the way to one who has already nearly reached the finish line, I nonetheless decided that your desire must be obeyed, both in my absence and my presence. All men wish to do well, which is to say, to live well. Now, they will live well if they possess many goods. These things are called "goods": riches, health, beauty, strength, noble birth, honors, power, and prudence; and besides these, justice, fortitude, temperance, and above all others, wisdom <term>Sapientia; in the Platonic sense, this is the highest form of knowledge, connecting the human mind to the divine</term>, which indeed encompasses the entire power of happiness. For happiness consists in the successful attainment of a desired end, and wisdom provides this to every individual faculty. Indeed, skilled flute-players best achieve whatever the use of flutes requires; and learned grammarians achieve what pertains to both reading and writing letters; so too do wise pilots reach a prosperous harbor of navigation better than others; likewise, a wise leader of war manages military affairs more safely; and a wise physician leads the body better to its desired health. For this reason, wisdom makes us masters of our wishes in every human task to the best of our ability; it never wanders, nor is it ever deceived—otherwise, it would not truly be wisdom. Since wisdom is the cause of attaining one's end, it is necessary that it has total power over happiness. Furthermore, only those who possess many goods are called blessed. Yet, they are not blessed until those present goods benefit them; nor do they ever benefit them unless they use them. For the mere possession of a thing has no weight regarding happiness. However, even use is not enough, for one can use a thing badly, from which it happens that he is harmed rather than helped. Therefore, just as we add use to possession, so it is fitting to add rectitude to use, so that we do not merely use a thing, but use it rightly. Only wisdom provides us with the ability to use each thing rightly. This can be seen in the arts, where only those who are skilled in the art use both the material and the tools correctly. By this same reasoning, wisdom ensures that we use riches, health, beauty, strength, and the other things called "goods" rightly. Therefore, in every possession, use, and operation, the cause of acting prosperously and well is knowledge. For he who possesses and uses many things without a mind is harmed more the more he possesses, because he has more things to misuse. Truly, the foolish man errs less the less he acts. Erring less, he acts badly less often. And he who acts badly less often is less miserable. Certainly, he acts less if he is poor than if he is rich, if he is weak than if he is strong, timid than bold, lazy than vigilant, slow than swift, dull than shrewd. Therefore, none of those things which were called "goods" above are goods in themselves. For if ignorance presides over them, they are even worse than their opposites, since they can provide the wicked leader with more abundant tools for crimes; but if prudence and wisdom preside over them, then finally they are better. Yet they are not in themselves either good or bad; for to a wise man, both adversity and prosperity turn out well, as he uses both rightly, but to a fool, it is the opposite. Therefore, of all our concerns, wisdom alone is a good in itself, and foolishness alone is an evil in itself. Since we all wish to be happy, and happiness cannot be had without the right use of things, and knowledge provides the right use of things, everyone—setting all other things aside—ought to strive with both the fullness of philosophy and the zeal of piety to become as wise as possible. For in this way our soul becomes most like God, who is wisdom itself; and Plato judged that the highest degree of blessedness consists in this very likeness.

### Imitation is more useful than reading.
->Marsilio Ficino to the Magnificent Amerigo Benci,<-
->sends greetings.<- <note>original: "S. D." abbreviated from "Salutem Dicit," a formal greeting.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
**I** received today in your name the Greek Dialogues of our Plato, a gift certainly magnificent, worthy of your spirit, and most welcome to mine. I give you great thanks. And may the celestial Graces <note>In Greek mythology, the Charites or Graces are the goddesses of charm, beauty, and gratitude.</note> one day return immortal thanks to you. In this matter, I believe you wished to imitate the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino’s primary patron and the founder of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>, as you do in many other things; for in days past, he adorned my library with a Greek Plato. I indeed praise your gift, Amerigo, and I approve of your imitation. For imitation is a path better suited to virtue than reading, just as harmony affects us more powerfully when it glides into our ears in the present than when it is merely thought of as something past; and just as a battle moves one more sharply when it is witnessed than when it is narrated. Thus, the distinguished works of living heroes inflame us toward virtue more ardently, and form us more exactly, than the words of ancient philosophers disputing about morals.

### Medicine for the body, Music for the spirit, Theology for the soul.
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Musano of Cesena,<-
->sends greetings.<-

<margin>C</margin>
**A**s soon as our tertian fever <note>A "tertian" fever (likely malaria) was characterized by paroxysms occurring every third day.</note> was expelled by our medicines, and you—together with Giovanni Aurelio—had greeted our Academy as if it were your physician, you demanded from us the sound of the lyre and the singing of hymns, and you obtained them. Then, you read many scattered passages in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>. Do not wonder, Francesco, that we mix medicine and the lyre with the study of Theology. You ought to remember, since you are dedicated to philosophy, that nature has joined within us the body and the spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle, airy vapor in the blood that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immortal soul</term> with the soul. The body is indeed cured by the remedies of medicine. The spirit, however—which is an airy vapor of the blood and a kind of knot between the soul and body—is tempered and nourished by airy smells, sounds, and songs. Finally, the soul, being divine, is purified by the divine mysteries of Theology. Among the Egyptian priests, there was one and the same faculty occupied with drugs, strings <note>i.e., musical instruments like the lyre.</note>, and mysteries. If only we might attain this natural and Egyptian skill as successfully as we pursue it earnestly and gladly. But enough of these things for the present. Yesterday you requested that I transcribe for you that proverb of mine inscribed everywhere on the walls of the Academy. Here it is: *All things are directed from good toward good.* Be joyful in the present. Neither value your wealth, nor seek after status; flee the high places, flee business, and be joyful in the present. Farewell.

### A Theological Dialogue between God and the Soul.
->Marsilio Ficino to Michele Mercato of San Miniato, his beloved<-
->fellow philosopher, sends greetings.<-

<margin>S</margin>
**W**e have often philosophized together about moral and natural matters, beloved Michele, and even more often about divine things. I remember, however, that you were often accustomed to say that mortal things are to be acquired by use, natural things are to be sought by reason, and divine things are to be asked of God through prayer. I have also read in our Plato that divine things are revealed because of the purity of one's life, rather than being taught by doctrine and words. Therefore, when I was thinking diligently on these and similar matters, I began at times to grieve in my soul. For I had already lost confidence in reason, and I did not yet have confidence in revelation. From this arose a certain intimate dialogue between the soul and God. Listen to this, if you please, although I think you perhaps already speak to God more closely than I do.

> **GOD.** My wretched soul, why do you grieve so much? Put an end now, O daughter, to your tears. Behold, I am here with you, your Father; I am here as your medicine and your salvation. **SOUL.** Oh, if only my Father would breathe upon me! Ah, if I thought such a great gift could fall to me—ah, how much joy...
