...[that I] should be mad with <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "tristitia" (sadness) or "stultitia" (folly).</note> sadness: Now indeed I do not see by what means that might be possible; for he who is present to me only from the outside is not my highest Father. If that craftsman of nature, as I believe, begot me as his offspring within, rather than just his nature, and he who is only within is not my highest father—since he indeed is greater than I, but he who is within me is undoubtedly less than I. But how anything can be both inside and outside me at once, I do not know. This, whoever you are, guest, this troubles me deeply: that I do not wish to live without my father, and I despair of being able to find him.

**GOD.** Put an end, O daughter, to your tears; do not afflict yourself, O daughter. It is no guest who speaks with you, but a member of your household more intimate to you than you are to yourself. I am indeed present to you and within you at once. I am present to you because I am within you; I am within you because you are in me—for unless you were in me, you would not be in yourself; indeed, you would not exist at all. Put an end, O daughter, to your tears; behold your parent. Your parent, as much as he is the smallest of all in mass, is the greatest of all in power; and since he is the most narrow, he is within all things; since he is the most vast, he is outside all things. Behold, I am present to you, both inside and outside—the greatest narrowness and the smallest breadth. <note>Ficino is using paradox to describe God's transcendence and immanence: God is "narrow" enough to fit inside the smallest soul but "wide" enough to encompass the universe.</note> Behold, I say, do you not see? I fill the heaven and the earth, and I penetrate and contain them. I fill, and am not filled, because I am fullness itself. I penetrate, and am not penetrated, because I am the very power of penetrating. I contain, and am not contained, because I am the very faculty of containing. I am not filled, lest I be unworthy, because I am abundance itself. I am not penetrated, lest I cease to be, I who am being itself. I am not contained, lest I cease to be God, I who am infinity itself. 

Behold, do you not see? I enter through all things without being mixed, so that I may also transcend them, I who am excellence itself. I transcend all things without being disconnected, so that at once I may enter, and enter deeply, and unite—I who am union itself, through which all things are made, through which they stand firm, and which all things desire. Why do you despair of finding your parent, O mad one? It is not difficult to find where I am, since in me they exist, from me they are made, and through me all things are preserved, always and everywhere. And by infinite power, I am expanded through an infinite interval. Rather, in no way can it be found where I am not; for through me this very place exists, and is said to be "everywhere." Through me as leader, through me as light, whatever anyone does, they act and seek, and they seek it somewhere; nothing is desired anywhere except the Good; nothing is found anywhere except the True. I am all Good, I am all True; seek my face, and you shall live. But do not be moved so as to touch me, I who am stability itself; do not be distracted by various things so as to grasp me, I who am unity itself. Stop the movement, collect the multitude <note>A Neoplatonic instruction to "collect" the fragmented thoughts of the many into a single point of focus.</note>, and you will immediately reach me, who have already long since reached you deep within.

**THE SOUL.** Do you abandon me to this so quickly, O my salvation? Why do you so suddenly abandon your thirsty daughter? Go on, act further, go on, I pray, venerable divinity; tell me, I beseech you by your majesty, if it pleases you, more plainly—ah, make it so it pleases you!—tell me then, because it will have pleased you, more plainly: what are you not, my father, so that I may come back to life? What are you again, my father, so that I may live?

**GOD.** It is not the nature of a body that is your parent, daughter. For you are better in proportion to how much more you obey your parent; however, you are more excellent in proportion to how much more you oppose the body. It is good for you to be with your father; it is bad for you to be with the body. No mere spirit <note>original: *animus*. In Ficino's hierarchy, the *animus* is often the rational mind, which is lower than the pure *intellectus*.</note> begot you, O soul <note>original: *anima*</note>, otherwise you would think of nothing beyond the spirit, and you would stop your step in the very mutability of the spirit, nor would you require a completely stable nature. No multiplex intellect created you, for you would not reach the highest simplicity, and the attainment of that intellect itself would suffice for you; but now, through understanding and loving, you ascend to life itself, to essence itself, to absolute being itself above any intellect. Nor is intelligence enough for you unless you understand both well and the Good. Indeed, the Good itself is undoubtedly enough for you; for you do not seek anything for any other reason than because it is good. 

Therefore, the Good itself is your procreator, O soul—not a good body, not a good spirit, not a good intellect, but the Good itself. The Good which indeed consists in itself, infinite beyond the limits of any subject, and it grants you infinite life, either from age to age or at least from a certain beginning into eternity. Do you desire to gaze upon the face of the Good? Behold the entire universe, full of the light of the Sun. Behold the light in the matter of the world, full of all the forms of all things, and revolving; subtract the matter, leave the rest. You have the soul: an incorporeal light, all-forming, changeable. Remove change from this again, and you have now attained the angelic intellect: an incorporeal light, all-forming, unchangeable. Take away from this that diversity through which any form is different from the light, and from elsewhere...

is implanted in the light, so that the essence of light and of each thing’s destiny is the same, and light itself forms itself, and through its own forms, it forms all things. This light shines infinitely because it shines by its own nature, and it is neither stained by the mixture of another thing nor contracted; it is through all things because it is in nothing—it is in nothing in a proprietary sense, so that it may shine equally through all. It lives from itself and provides life to all, especially since its shadow—which is this light of the Sun—is the only thing among corporeal objects that gives life. It perceives everything and bestows sensation, if indeed its shadow excites all senses in all beings. Finally, it loves each individual thing, if indeed all individuals are most truly its own. Therefore, that which is the light of the Sun is the <term>Shadow of God</term> <note>original: "Vmbra Dei"; a central Neoplatonic concept where the physical sun is a metaphor for the divine intellect</note>. Therefore, what is God? God is the Sun of the Sun; God is the light of the Sun within the body of the world; God is the light of the Sun above the angelic intellects. Such is my shadow, O soul, that it is the most beautiful of all corporeal things. How great do you think my own light is? If my shadow shines so much, how much does my light blaze? You love light everywhere above all other things—nay, you love it alone. Love me alone, O soul—me, the infinite light—love me, I say, infinitely; then you shall shine and be delighted infinitely.

**THE SOUL.** O wondrous thing, which surpasses admiration itself! What unusual fire now burns me? What new Sun is this for me, and from where does it begin to glow? Who, and from where, is this great and so sweet a spirit that now pricks and soothes my marrow, bites and licks, goads and tickles? And this is a bitter sweetness: who could imagine even a bitter sweetness that melts me entirely and draws out my very core? In comparison to this, those things which were previously taken up seem bitter to me, or even those things which were sweetest. How sweet is this bitterness, which binds me together and restores me after I have been torn apart, and through which even the most bitter things become sweet to me. How necessary this will is, since I cannot *not* want the Good itself, and I am better able to avoid or delay anything else rather than the greed for the Good. For even if I should wish to avoid this, I would only attempt to avoid it because I judged that avoidance itself to be good; thus, this necessity is of a voluntary kind. Since nothing is more voluntary than the Good, for the sake of which I want all things—nay, which I want in all things everywhere—and I want it so much that I further wish to be unable *not* to want it. What a living death this is, let whoever can imagine it, through which I die in myself and live in God, through which I die to death and live for life, and I live by life and rejoice in joy. O pleasure above sense! O gladness above the soul! O joy above the mind! I am indeed now outside my mind, yet not mindless, because I am above the mind. I am in a frenzy again, an exceeding frenzy, yet I am not cast down, because I am lifted on high. I exult now everywhere and totally, and I overflow, yet I am not scattered, because <note>original: "Deus unitas unitatum"</note> God, the Unity of Unities, gathers me with You, and lives me with You. Exult now with me, therefore, all you whose exultation is God. My God has come to meet me. The God of the universe has embraced me. The God of gods now glides into my very marrow. Now, now God Himself nourishes all of me, and He who begot me, regenerates me. He had begotten a soul; He reforms it into an angel; He converts it into God. What thanks shall I return to you, O Grace of Graces? You yourself teach me, Grace of Graces, teach me I pray, and provide it. Finally, let God himself be God as a grace unto yourself.

### Law and Justice.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Ottone Niccolini and Benedetto d'Arezzo, men of counsel, and to Piero <-
-> Pazzi and Bernardo Giugni, Knights, sends greetings. <-

**Y**ou have persuaded me to make the Greek *Laws* of Plato into Latin ones; the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), Ficino's primary patron and the de facto ruler of Florence.</note> also exhorted me toward the same. And so I have done it now, and all the more willingly because I judged that the city had more need of excellent men of counsel than of good merchants or doctors. And Minos <note>The legendary lawgiver of Crete.</note> profited the Greeks as much more than Galen <note>The famous Roman physician of Greek origin.</note> as the soul is more excellent than the body or the spirit, and eternal life more than temporal. For trade seems to be the body of the city, medicine its spirit, and law its soul. And although many laws appear to exist in the city, there are not, however, many souls of the city. For just as many arts and various ranks of citizens do not make many cities, but one, if they proceed toward the same end by a similar reason; so, although there are many constitutions of magistrates in the city, there is nonetheless one single public law—namely, the common rule of living rightly, leading toward public happiness. God and nature prepare us for this law, constitutions exhort us to it, and finally, the one God forms it. For from the divine law proceeds both the law of the stars and the law of men. For this reason, all founders of laws—partly imitating Moses like apes, as he was the truest author of divine laws, and partly compelled by truth in some way—[derived their laws] from...

<sig>43</sig>

claimed to have received their laws from God under various fictional guises. The Egyptians' lawgiver Osiris claimed to have them from Mercury <note>original: "à Mercurio"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>; Zoroaster <note>original: "Zautrastes"</note> among the Arimaspians <note>a legendary people of northern Scythia</note> from a good spirit; Zalmoxis among the Scythians from Vesta; Minos of Crete and Solon of Athens from Jupiter; Lycurgus the Spartan from Apollo; Numa, king of the Romans, from the nymph Egeria; Muhammad, leader of the Arabs, from the angel Gabriel. Our Plato begins his books on the *Laws* with God, whom he calls the common founder of all laws. He also confirmed this in the dialogue titled *Pythagoras*, saying that those arts pertaining to physical sustenance were handed down to us by Prometheus—that is, by human providence. However, the law for living well and happily was granted by Jupiter—that is, by divine providence—through Mercury, which signifies angelic inspiration. I could not help but admire the laws of this best of friends. Indeed, some order and harmony of law is necessary in the elements of the world, in the humors of a living creature, in the diet of beasts, and even in a band of thieves; for even they cannot associate with one another without some just order. What shall we say to this: that although no other virtue exists among those in the underworld, law and justice are not lacking there, so that they may punish the wicked according to their deserts? And although those moral virtues—which help mortals calm the disturbances of the body and senses—are no longer necessary among the blessed (from which those enjoying the blessed life are already freed), law and justice nevertheless flourish among them. These grant eternal rewards to each according to their worth and preserve the blessed. Farewell.

### On Divine Madness.
->Marsilio Ficino to Peregrino Agli, greetings.<-

**O**n the third day before the Kalends of December <note>November 29th</note>, my father Ficino the physician brought two letters in your name to me at Figline <note>the Ficino family's hometown</note>. One was written in prose, the other in verse. Truly, reading them caused me to congratulate our times for producing such a youth whose fame and glory might illuminate them. Indeed, my sweetest Peregrino, when I consider your age and the works that proceed from you daily, I not only rejoice in the great talents of my friend, but I also marvel greatly. I hardly know—to set aside more recent men—who among those ancients whose memory we venerate achieved so much at the age you have reached. I ascribe this not only to art and study, but much more to that <term>Divine Madness</term> <note>original: "diuino furore"; in Platonic philosophy, this is a state of inspired "frenzy" or heightened consciousness where the soul transcends human reason to reach divine truth</note>, without which Democritus and Plato deny that any man was ever great. That you are inspired by this—and, so to speak, thoroughly seized by it—is evidenced by the very ardent movements and emotions expressed in your writings. The ancient philosophers intended this very agitation, which occurs through external movements, to be the greatest proof that there is a certain divine power in our souls. But since I have mentioned "madness," I will relate the opinion of our Plato on this matter in a few words, with the brevity required by a letter, so that you may easily understand what madness is, into how many parts it is divided, and which God presides over each type. I trust this will be of both great pleasure and utility to you. He believes, therefore, that our soul—before it fell into bodies—existed in the celestial seats (as Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Heraclitus had also argued earlier), where it was nourished and rejoiced in the contemplation of truth, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. And since those philosophers I mentioned a moment ago had learned from <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto"; the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of Egyptian wisdom</note> (the wisest of all Egyptians) that the supreme God is a certain fountain and light in which the patterns of all things shine forth—which they call <term>Ideas</term>—they thought it necessary for the soul, while constantly contemplating the eternal mind of God, to also look more clearly upon the natures of all things. Therefore, says Plato, the soul saw justice itself, saw wisdom, saw harmony, and a certain wonderful beauty of the divine nature. He calls all these "Ideas," "divine essences," and "primary natures" which exist in the eternal mind of God; human minds are happily nourished by a perfect knowledge of these for as long as they dwell there. However, when the souls are weighed down into bodies due to the thought and desire for earthly things, then those who were previously nourished by ambrosia and nectar—that is, by the knowledge of God and perfect joy—are said, in that very descent, to drink from the <term>River Lethe</term> <note>original: "flumen lethæum"; the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology</note>, which is the forgetting of divine things. Nor do they return to the higher realms, from which they had fallen by the weight of earthly thoughts, until...

# BOOK I OF THE LETTERS

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing a thought from the previous page.</note>

...had disturbed them, to fly back once they have begun to recognize those divine natures that they had forgotten. That divine philosopher <note>referring to Plato</note> believes we achieve this through two virtues: specifically, the one pertaining to morals and the one pertaining to contemplation. He calls the former by the common name "justice" and the latter "wisdom." Therefore, he says that the soul flies back to the heavens on twin wings—understanding these virtues as the wings—and Socrates discusses in the *Phaedo* <note>one of Plato’s dialogues concerning the immortality of the soul</note> how we attain these through the two parts of philosophy, namely the active and the contemplative. Hence, in the *Phaedrus*, he says that only the mind of the philosopher recovers its wings. In this recovery of wings, the soul is drawn away from the body by their power; filled with God, it is pulled toward the heavens and strives vehemently. 

Plato calls this withdrawal and striving <term>Divine Madness</term> <note>original: "divinum furorem"; a state of inspired alienation from the mundane world</note>, and he divides it into four parts. For he does not think men ever remember divine things unless they are stirred by certain shadows and images of them perceived through the senses of the body. Thus, Paul <note>the Apostle</note> and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note>, the wisest of Christian theologians, assert that the "invisible things of God" are understood through those things which have been made and are seen here. 

Plato maintains that human wisdom is an image of divine wisdom. He considers this very harmony, which we create with voices and musical instruments, to be an image of divine harmony. Furthermore, he judges that the "comeliness" and "loveliness" resulting from the most fitting composition of the body's parts and members is an image of divine beauty. 

However, since knowledge <note>scientific or certain knowledge</note> is present in no men, or certainly very few, and cannot be grasped by any bodily senses, it follows that the likenesses of divine wisdom among us are very few, and these are hidden from our senses and utterly unknown. For this reason, Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* that the image of wisdom can in no way be seen by the eyes; for if it were seen, it would stir up marvelous loves for that divine wisdom of which it is an image. 

But we do see the likeness of divine beauty with our eyes, and we notice the image of divine harmony with our ears. Plato considers these senses to be the most piercing of all those acting through the body. Consequently, through certain "simulacra" <note>images or representations</note> present in bodies and taken into the soul through the bodily senses, we remember, in a way, those things which we knew before when we were established outside the prison of the body. 

By this <term>recollection</term> <note>original: "recordatione"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul remembering its pre-birth knowledge of the Forms</note>, the soul catches fire and, flapping its wings, gradually cleanses itself from the thoughts and filth of the body, becoming utterly affected by divine madness. Two types of this madness are stirred by those two senses I mentioned just now. For, by the appearance of beauty offered by the eyes, we recover a certain memory of true and intelligible beauty, and we long for it with an inexpressible and hidden heat of the mind. 

Finally, Plato calls this "divine love," defining it as a longing to return to the contemplation of divine beauty, which is sparked by the sight of a physical likeness. Furthermore, it is necessary that he who is so affected not only long for that celestial beauty but also be greatly delighted by the sight of the beauty open to the eyes. For it is so ordained by nature that whoever desires something is also delighted by its likeness. 

However, Plato thinks it is characteristic of a coarser wit and a corrupted nature if someone lusts only for the shadows of that true beauty and admires nothing else besides the appearance offered to the eyes. He says such a person is affected by that love whose companion is petulance and lewdness; he defines this as an irrational and insolent desire for the pleasure perceived by the sense regarding the form of the body. He defines this love elsewhere as a heat of the soul "dying in its own body and living in another's." Hence he says the soul of the lover leads its life in a foreign body. 

Marveling at this, the Epicureans <note>followers of Epicurus who held a materialist view of the world</note> define love as a certain striving of "little bodies"—which they call atoms—to pour themselves entirely into the person from whom the images of beauty were drawn. Our Plato says this kind of love is born from human diseases and is full of care and anxiety; it belongs to those men whose minds are so overwhelmed by darkness that they think of nothing high, nothing excellent, nothing at all beyond the fragile and fleeting image of this little body. Nor do they look back at the breezes, being enclosed in darkness and a blind prison. 

But those whose talent has been drawn away and released from the "mud" of the body are such that when the form and loveliness of any body is presented to them, they are delighted by its first appearance as a likeness of divine beauty. Indeed, from this image, they immediately bring back into memory that divine beauty which they admire above all and truly desire, and by whose most burning desire they are snatched away to the heavens. And this is the first attempt at flying out...

<summary>In this letter, Marsilio Ficino explains the Neoplatonic concept of "Divine Madness," detailing how the soul uses the physical senses of sight and hearing to remember the divine beauty and harmony it knew before birth. He distinguishes between noble "Divine Love," which seeks the creator, and base lust, which remains trapped by physical shadows.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Divine Madness, Neoplatonism, Plato, Socrates, Divine Love, Reminiscence, Beauty, Harmony, Soul's Wings, Phaedrus, Epicureans</keywords>

--- Page 633 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter on "Divine Madness." Having previously discussed the first type of madness (the desire for beauty inspired by sight), Ficino now transitions to the second type: the musical or poetic madness inspired by hearing and the Muses.</meta>

Plato calls this striving "divine alienation" and "madness." These remarks seem sufficient regarding that madness which we said occurs through the eyes. Through the ears, however, the soul drinks in certain harmonies and most sweet numbers; by these images, it is warned and excited toward <term>divine music</term>, which is to be considered by a sharper and more intimate sense of the mind. 

Among the interpreters of Plato, divine music is twofold: they believe one kind consists in the eternal mind of God, while the other exists in the order and motions of the heavens, through which the celestial globes and spheres produce a certain wonderful harmony. Our soul was a participant in both of these before it was enclosed in a body; but in these shadows, it uses the ears as if they were small cracks or crevices, and through them it receives the images of that incomparable music, as we have often said. 

By these images, the soul is led back to an intimate and silent recollection of that harmony which it enjoyed before. It burns entirely with desire and longs to enjoy true music again, wishing to fly back to its proper home. Since the soul realizes it can in no way achieve this as long as it is walled in by the dark dwelling of the body, it strives at least to imitate that music to the best of its ability, since it cannot possess it here. 

Among men, this imitation is twofold. For some imitate celestial music with the rhythms of voices and the sounds of various instruments; these we certainly call "light" and almost common musicians. But some others, imitating divine and celestial harmony with a graver and firmer judgment, arrange the sense and notions of their inner reason into poetic feet and meters. These are the ones who, inspired by a divine spirit, pour forth most weighty and excellent songs with a "round mouth," as they say <note>original: "ore rotundo"; a classical idiom for eloquent, well-turned speech</note>. 

Plato calls this more serious music "Poetry," the most effective imitator of celestial harmony. For that lighter kind, which we mentioned just before, merely soothes with the sweetness of voices; but poetry—which is also characteristic of divine harmony—expresses most weighty and, as a poet would say, <term>Delphic</term> <note>meaning oracular or prophetic, referring to the Oracle at Delphi</note> meanings more ardently through the rhythms of voices and movements. Thus, it not only charms the ears but also provides the mind with a most sweet food, very similar to celestial ambrosia, and therefore it seems to approach closer to divinity. 

Plato believes this poetic madness arises from the Muses. He judges that anyone who approaches the gates of poetry without the instinct of the Muses—hoping that he will turn out to be a good poet by some sort of technical skill—is himself empty, as is his poetry. He believes those poets who are seized by celestial inspiration and power often bring forth such divine meanings, breathed into them by the Muses, that they themselves, once they have stepped out of their madness, do not fully understand what they have produced. 

And as I think, that divine man <note>Plato</note> intends "the Muses" to be understood as celestial songs; therefore they say they are called *Canorae* and *Camenae* from the word for song <note>Ficino is using a traditional, if linguistically debated, etymology linking the Muses' Latin name "Camenae" to "canere" (to sing)</note>. Whence divine men, stirred by the Muses—that is, by celestial powers and songs—meditate on poetic modes and rhythms in imitation of them. 

Thus, in the *Republic*, when Plato treated the rotation of the celestial spheres, he said that individual <term>Sirens</term> sit upon individual circles, signifying that a song is presented to the divine powers by the motion of the spheres, as a certain Platonist says. For "Sirem" is correctly expressed in Greek as "singing to God" <note>Ficino offers a creative etymology here: "Seirēn" from "seira" (chain) or "seirein" (to bind/sing), interpreting it as a song directed toward the divine</note>. The ancient theologians also wanted the nine Muses to be the musical songs of the eight spheres, and one greatest harmony which is composed of all of them. 

By this reasoning, therefore, poetry proceeds from divine madness, madness from the Muses, and the Muses from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. For the Platonists frequently call the soul of the whole world "Jove," who nourishes from within the heaven and the lands, the liquid fields, the glowing globe of the Moon, and the Titan stars; infused through the limbs, he agitates the whole mass and mixes himself with the great body <note>This is a paraphrase of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the "Spirit of the World"</note>. 

From this it follows that from Jove—the spirit and mind of the whole world—the musical songs of the spheres arise, which he calls Muses, just as he moves and rules those spheres. Wherefore that most famous Platonist said: "From Jove is the beginning of the Muse; all things are full of Jove" <note>original: "Ab Ioue principium Musæ, Iouis omnia plena"</note>. For that soul called Jupiter flourishes everywhere and fills all things; and shaking the heaven like a certain lyre (as Alexander Milesius the Pythagorean says), he produces celestial harmony. 

Thus Orpheus, 그 divine prophet, said: "Jupiter is first, Jupiter is last, Jupiter the head, Jupiter the middle; all things are born from Jove. Jupiter is the foundation of the earth and the starry heaven. Jupiter came forth as the male, Jupiter the incorruptible bride. Jupiter is the spirit and appearance of all things. Jupiter is the root of the sea, Jupiter the motion of unwearied fire. Jupiter is the Sun and Moon. Jupiter is the king and prince of all; hiding the light, he sent it forth again from his holy heart, working his thoughts." 

From these things it is understood that Jove, infused in all bodies, contains and nourishes all things, so that it was not undeservedly said: "Jupiter is whatever you see, whatever you are moved by" <note>original: "Iupiter est quodcunque uides, quodcunque moueris"</note>.

<summary>This page explains the second type of divine madness, poetry, which is triggered by the soul's memory of celestial harmony (the Music of the Spheres). Ficino traces the source of this inspiration through the Muses back to Jupiter, defined as the World Soul that animates and harmonizes the entire universe.</summary>

The previous page detailed the first two types of madness—the amorous and the poetic—describing how the soul responds to beauty and harmony. Here, Ficino transitions into the religious and prophetic forms of inspiration.</meta>

LETTERS, BOOK I.
Qq 4
<meta>Catchword: noli</meta>

Following these are the remaining types of divine madness, which he divides into two parts: he considers one to be concerned with mysteries and the other with the outcome of future events, which he calls prophecy. First, he defines <term>madness</term><note>Latin: *furor*. In the Platonic sense used here, this is not "insanity" but a state of being "possessed" by a divine power that elevates the soul.</note> as a more vehement agitation of the soul in performing those things pertaining to the worship of the gods, religion, expiation, and sacred ceremonies. However, the state of mind which falsely imitates this kind of madness he calls <term>superstition</term>. 

The final nature of madness, in which he places prophecy, he considers to be nothing other than a foreknowledge inspired by divine breath; we have named this by the more specific terms "divination" and "prophecy." If the soul burns more sharply within that very divination, he calls it madness—a state where the mind, drawn away from the body, is stirred by divine instinct. If, however, someone foresees the future by human skill and sagacity rather than by divine infusion, he judges such a foreknowledge to be called <term>providence</term> or <term>conjecture</term>. 

From all of this, it is now clear that there are four species of divine madness: Love, Poetry, Mysteries, and Prophecy. That common and utterly insane mother of the masses falsely imitates divine Love; a lighter music (as we have said) imitates Poetry; superstition imitates the Mysteries; and conjecture imitates Prophecy. In Plato’s writings, Socrates attributes the first madness to Venus, the second to the Muses, the third to Dionysus, and the last to Apollo. 

Furthermore, I chose to be more long-winded in describing the madness pertaining to divine love and poetry for two reasons: because I have recognized myself to be vehemently moved by both inspirations, and so that you may remember that the things you write are inspired by Jove and the Muses—with whose spirit and divinity you are filled—and do not originate from yourself. Therefore, my dear Peregrino, you will act justly and piously if you recognize (as I believe you have done until now) that neither you nor any other man is the author of the greatest and best things, but rather that the immortal God is their author and principle. Farewell, and be assured that nothing is dearer to me than you. Florence, December 1, 1457.

## *An excuse for prolixity.*

->Marsilio Ficino to the Great Cosimo, Greetings.<-

**L**orenzo of Pisa, a priest, is explaining Solomon’s *Song of Songs* for your sake; if I remember correctly, he has already composed eighteen books for the explanation of that one little book. If you wonder, Cosimo, why Lorenzo speaks so prolixly when Solomon spoke so briefly, I answer that Lorenzo is forced to be prolix for this very reason: because Solomon was so brief. For the more entangled Solomon's knot is, the more "machines" are needed to untie it. Niccolò Fulginate, the distinguished philosopher, praises Lorenzo’s writings; I also approve of them, though I usually recoil from wordiness. Yet that work does not seem too large to me, because I find almost nothing of greatness in Theology that he has not gathered there. But let me not become even more wordy while excusing wordiness. Farewell.

## *On divination and the divinity of the soul.*

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Matteo Corsini, fellow<-
->philosopher, Greetings.<-

**M**y mother Alexandra was born to her father Giovanni and mother Angela. Alexandra was from Fighine; Giovanni was from the town of Figline, and Angela was from Florence. Angela wrote to Giovanni and Alexandra saying she was well and would return the following day. After reading the letter, they fell asleep at night, and they both saw Angela at the same hour. She appeared to Alexandra in the vestibule of the house; and when the daughter congratulated her mother as if she were returning, the mother, fleeing her daughter's embrace, said: "Farewell, and see to it that the priests pray to God for me." To Giovanni, however, she said: "Oh, how much I grieve for your fortune, my Giovanni; farewell, and command that prayers be offered to God for me." Suddenly, having seen these things, both woke up and cried out, judging her to be dead. They sent word to Florence. It was reported back that she had departed from this life that very night. 

If you marvel at these things, Corsini, hear another equally marvelous thing. My mother gave her son, immediately after he was born, to a country nurse; seventeen days later, while sleeping at noon, she seemed to herself to be weighed down by a great anxiety of heart, and to be raised up by her own mother who had died long ago, who said: "Do not... <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "noli" (do not); the story continues on the next page.</note>

...“Do not afflict yourself, daughter,” but on the following day the peasants brought back to her the son who had been suffocated by his nurse. ## A manner of praise without flattery.
->Marsilio Ficino to the theologian Francisco Castiglione, sends greetings.<-

**I** have read your expositions regarding the mysteries of the Prophet David. I wish to exclaim, Francisco, that just as God found David to be a man after His own heart, so has David found you to be a man after his own heart. But where we might suspect a reputation for adulation, it is better to hint at a thing than to explain it fully. Greet Giorgio Antonio Vespucci, a man distinguished for his humanity and learning. **Farewell.**

<margin>The utility of the solitary life.</margin>
->Marsilio Ficino to the priest Gregorio Epifanio, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.<-

**G**od is stable unity and a unique state of being. These matters are subtly disputed by our Platonists, as you well know. Whoever, therefore, wishes to attain God should avoid the "multitude" and movement to the best of their power. Let us withdraw then, my Gregorio, into that unique and stable <term>watchtower of the mind</term><note>A metaphor for the highest state of intellectual contemplation, removed from the distractions of the physical world.</note>; there the invisible light will shine forth to us immediately, as Plato says. 

But so that we may more conveniently achieve and continue this in these times, I have decided to spend some time at <note>original: "montem Vechium"</note> Montevecchio, that estate given to me by the Great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino’s patron</note>; you shall be there with me. You have heard the proverb: "The possession of no good thing is pleasant without a companion." I do not know what companion I could have in these times more pleasant than you. **Farewell, and fly to us.**

## On modesty in composing.
->Bessarion, Cardinal of Sabina, to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, sends greetings.<-

**E**xcellent and learned man, our friend: in previous letters we promised that we would send you our recently published work, produced with great effort in defense of Plato. We do this both because of your immense and extraordinary devotion to Platonic doctrine, and so that you may easily see and read for yourself what we have drawn from that fountain. 

For if anything in this industry of ours—whether eloquence or knowledge of the liberal arts—has shone forth, or if we have achieved anything at all, we willingly allow and desire it to be thought that we either received it all from him <insert>Plato</insert>, or that he himself supplied it in his own defense. This also seems to pertain somewhat to his praise: that he pleaded the cause for himself by his own strength and greatness, did not need outside help, and left only the place for a patron’s voice and effort. We have given this book to you through those physicians who handle such affairs here. By sending it, we believe we have satisfied our promise and your own studies and disposition toward Plato. Fare well, and let us know if you have received the book. From the City <note>Rome</note>, on the Ides of September, 1469.

...excellent both in character and in letters, yet he emerged somewhat obscured, wrapped in darker thoughts; and as if smeared with a certain earthly covering, he remained hidden from those men who do not possess lynx-like eyes. <note>The lynx was legendary in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for its supposedly "piercing" vision that could see through solid objects.</note> For this reason, some lesser <term>Philodoxi</term><note>From the Greek: "lovers of glory" or "lovers of opinion," as opposed to "philosophers" or "lovers of wisdom."</note> were once deceived by the external soil; because they could not penetrate to the inner parts, they looked down upon the hidden treasure. Those times have come, Bessarion—they have now come!—in which the spirit of Plato rejoices, and his divinity, and all we of his family greatly congratulate ourselves. **Farewell.**

# Exhortation to Knowledge.
## Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Pazzi.

**L**orenzo de' Medici praises two things in you above others: magnificence and sharp wit; I too praise them. But Antonio, while you can match others in the use of magnificence, you can match *yourself* in the exercise of your wit. If you devote yourself as much to the study of doctrine as you have long indulged in generosity, I do not doubt that you will shortly be the most learned of all, just as you are now the most magnificent of all. Come, I pray, my sweetest Antonio, entrust yourself to yourself, just as you have others entrusted to you. Our Lorenzo says that you are not only magnificent toward the learned, but also abundantly learned yourself. I believe it, and I congratulate you. But you will not have done enough for me until you excel as much in knowledge as you do in greatness of soul. If the most learned men please you above all, take care that you please yourself above others. Therefore, whatever you are worth in all things—rather, your total worth—I beg you to set aside four hours daily for yourself; give the remaining time, however you please, to your friends. Fare well, but do you wish to fare well? Learn well; and I pray, learn today; he who learns tomorrow, never learns. 
->November 7, 1473.<-

# Consolation on the death of someone.
## Marsilio Ficino offers consolation to Sigismondo della Stufa.

**I**f each of us is primarily that which is greatest in us—which remains always the same, and by which we understand ourselves—then certainly the soul is the man himself, while the body is the man’s shadow. Whoever, therefore, is so delirious as to think that the shadow of a man is the man, dissolves into wretched tears like Narcissus. <note>In Greek mythology, Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection and wasted away; Ficino uses this as a metaphor for being obsessed with the physical body rather than the soul.</note> You will stop weeping, Sigismondo, when you cease seeking your Albiera Albizzi <note>Albiera degli Albizzi (1452–1473) was a famous Florentine beauty whose early death was a major event in the social and literary circles of the Medici.</note> in her black shadow, and begin to follow her into the white light of her own self. For then you will find her as much more beautiful than you were accustomed to as she is more removed from the deformed shadow. Withdraw into your own mind, I pray; there you will possess her most beautiful soul, most dear to you. Indeed, betake yourself from your mind into God; there you will contemplate the most beautiful <term>Idea</term><note>For Platonists, "Ideas" are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things existing in the Mind of God.</note> through which the divine craftsman had created your Albiera. And as much more beautiful as she is in the form of the Creator than in herself, so much more blessedly will you embrace her there.
->Farewell, August 11, 1471.<-
->Florence.<-

->The Praise of Truth.<-
### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric poet, sends greetings.

**I**t is whispered about, as you say, that certain letters are circulating in my name that are, as it were, "Aristippean" <note>Aristippus of Cyrene was a Greek philosopher associated with hedonism; Ficino is being accused of writing letters that are too focused on worldly pleasure.</note> and partly "Lucretian" <note>Referring to Lucretius, the Roman poet of Epicureanism and materialism, whose views often conflicted with Ficino’s spiritual Platonism.</note>, rather <gloss>than</gloss> Platonic. If they are mine, Angelo, they are not of that sort; if they are of that sort, they are certainly not mine, but forged by my detractors. For from my tender years, as no one is unaware, I have followed the divine Plato. But you will easily distinguish our writings from those of others by this sign: in my letters, there is always a certain idea—according to the strength of my wits—that is either moral, natural, or theological. But if sometimes there is something somewhat amorous within them, it is surely Platonic and honorable, not Aristippean and lewd. Moreover, my praises are true and of the kind that exhort and advise, rather than flatter; and there are almost no superfluous words. For I determined from the beginning of my studies always to write as briefly as I could. Indeed, in such a short span of life, to speak superfluous words is the mark of a philologist <note>In this context, a "lover of words" or a pedant.</note> rather <gloss>than</gloss> a philosopher. And since there are very few people to whom many things are known, those who speak many things often speak either falsehoods, or superfluities, or both. All these things are foreign to the dignity of a man, and most foreign to the profession of a philosopher. Farewell.

->How useful it is to support the learned.<-
### Marsilio Ficino to the Great-Souled Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

**A**lmost all other rich men nourish servants; you nourish the priests of the Muses. Continue, I pray, my Lorenzo; for those others will turn out to be slaves to pleasures, but you will be the delight of the Muses. Homer, the supreme priest of the Muses, has come into Italy under your leadership, and he who until now was a wanderer and a beggar has finally found a sweet and open guest-house at your home. You nourish in your house that Homeric youth, Angelo Poliziano <note>Poliziano was a brilliant prodigy in the Medici household who gained fame for translating Homer’s *Iliad* from Greek into Latin hexameters.</note>, who expresses the Greek persona of Homer more broadly in colors. He expresses it already, and what is wonderful, he expresses it at such a tender age that unless someone knew Homer had been Greek, he would doubt which of the two was the natural Homer and which the painted one. Continue to delight in these "painters," Medici, as you have begun; for other painters decorate walls for a time, but these illustrate the inhabitants <note>Ficino likely means the "inhabitants" of the soul or the residents of the household throughout history.</note> for eternity.

->The praise of the maker comes not from words, but from the work.<-
### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici, sends greetings.

**A**ccept with a joyful spirit, O Medici, the poem of Naldo Naldi of Florence <note>A humanist poet and close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note> and the declamations of Benedetto Colucci of Pistoia. One is the delight of Apollo, the other a companion of Mercury. I do not wish to praise them sparingly, since they seem worthy of being praised beyond measure. Yet I do not wish to praise them much, lest by praising my own admirers, I seem to extol myself. I shall therefore be silent regarding the virtues of these "painters"; look upon the tablets yourselves with care. The painting will speak; when the painter speaks, he speaks poorly, but when the painting speaks, it speaks well. Vain is the craftsman who expects honor from another rather <gloss>than</gloss> from the work itself; the virtue of a work does not depend on the judge, but the work commends the artist to the judge. Farewell.

->On the civil, purifying, and exemplary virtues of the purified soul.<-
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Lapaccino and Migliore Cresci, sends greetings.

**T**hose men seek God by the straightest path who first, through the "civil virtues," <term>civil virtues</term> <note>These are the social or political virtues (like justice and temperance) that allow a person to function well in society.</note> somewhat prune the excessively luxuriant passions of the soul. In the third place, through the virtues of a soul so purified, they extirpate those passions by the roots as far as their strength allows. Once these are eradicated as much as is possible for a man, they are finally formed by the "exemplary virtues," which are in God. For those three kinds of virtues are certain steps by which we gradually approach the divine virtues. Moreover, every natural...

->On the wise and happy man.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Seraphico <note>Antonio degli Agli (1400–1477), a bishop and fellow philosopher from San Miniato who shared Ficino's interests in Platonism.</note>, his fellow philosopher from San Miniato, sends greetings.

**I** consider the man to be wise and happy who, because he depends on God alone, lives joyfully in the midst of calamities. He is one whom neither fear disheartens, nor pain tortures, nor desire corrupts, nor lust inflames. He is the one who gathers soft and beautiful flowers among the thickest thorns; who pulls and digs pearls out of the dung; who sees through the deepest darkness; who, though weighed down by shackles and bound by chains, runs as if free and unhindered; and upon whom, finally, the celestial spirit has breathed. Therefore, continue as you have begun: imitate Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, who practiced philosophy no less by their actions than by their arguments, even when fortune was against them. While so many practice philosophy only with their tongues, they themselves cherished it with their whole hearts. He who is not wise for himself is "Seraphic" <note>A play on Antonio's name "Seraphico." Ficino suggests that true spiritual wisdom must be internalized to be effective.</note> in wisdom in vain. Farewell, and persevere in your way of life.

->It is better to write good things than many things.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant Renaissance poet and scholar, famously called "the Homeric poet" by Ficino for his mastery of Greek and his translation of the Iliad.</note>, the Homeric Poet, sends greetings.

**W**hy do you ask so often for the titles of my books, Angelo? Is it perhaps so that you may praise me in your poems? But praise lies in the choice, not the number; and the good lies in the quality, not the quantity. Or is it rather so that you may have everything of mine with you? Since all things are common among friends, however it may be, receive what you asked for. From the Greek language into Latin I have translated:
*   The physical and theological elements of Proclus the Platonic;
*   The four books of Iamblichus of Chalcis on the Pythagorean sect;
*   The mathematical works of Theon of Smyrna;
*   The Platonic definitions of Speusippus;
*   The Platonic *Epitome* of Alcinous;
*   Xenocrates’ book *On the Consolation of Death*;
*   The verses and symbols of Pythagoras;
*   The book of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurij Trismegisti"</note> on the *Power and Wisdom of God*;
*   All the books of Plato.

I have also composed:
*   A commentary on the Gospels, on the *Sovereign Good*;
*   A commentary on Plato’s *Symposium* concerning love;
*   A work on *Physiognomy*;
*   The *Declarations of the Platonic Discipline* dedicated to Cristoforo Landino <note>A prominent Florentine humanist and commentator on Dante.</note>, which I later revised;
*   A compendium on the *Opinions of the Philosophers regarding God and the Soul*;
*   *Economics*;
*   *On Pleasure*;
*   *On the Four Sects of Philosophers*;
*   *On Magnificence*;
*   *On Happiness*;
*   *On Justice*;
*   *On Divine Frenzy*;
*   *On the Consolation of Parents upon the Death of a Son*;
*   *On Appetite*;
*   A *Theological Prayer to God*;
*   A *Theological Dialogue between God and the Soul*;
*   The *Theology on the Immortality of Souls* <note>Ficino's masterpiece, the *Platonic Theology*, written to reconcile Plato with Christian doctrine.</note> divided into eighteen books;
*   A work *On the Christian Religion*;
*   *Disputations against the Judgments of Astrologers*;
*   *On the Rapture of Paul into the Third Heaven*;
*   *On Light*;
*   An *Argument for the Platonic Theology*;
*   *On the Life and Doctrine of Plato*;
*   *Five Questions on the Mind*;
*   A volume of *Philosophical Letters*.

I only wish, Angelo, that we had written as well as we have written much, so that our works might please others as much as you please me, and yours please me. Farewell.

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Albitio <note>Niccolò degli Albizzi, a member of a powerful Florentine family and a student/patron of the humanities.</note>, sends greetings.

**Y**ou have heard that proverb, my Niccolò: "Nothing is sweeter than profit." But who among men actually profits? He who acquires that which will be his own. What we know is truly ours; all other things belong to fortune. Let little men envy the rich, whose chests are wealthy but not their souls. You, however, should emulate learned and good men, whose minds are like God. Warn your fellow students to beware of Scylla and Charybdis <note>In Greek mythology, two sea monsters on opposite sides of a strait; here used as a metaphor for the dangerous and seductive traps of worldly pleasure.</note>—namely, the pestilential allurements of pleasures.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

## Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de’ Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>, a Magnanimous man, sends greetings.

<margin>God is the author of wonders, not man.</margin>

**W**hat I should do at present I do not know, Lorenzo. Your wonderful letters compel me to wonder in a wonderful way, yet my philosopher’s modesty forbids me from crying out. Your singular humanity and magnificence urge me to give you innumerable thanks, but your letter again discourages it. Permit me at least, my Lorenzo, I pray, to give thanks to the highest God because he has decided in our times to join a most humble spirit with an exalted mind in a fortunate citizen; prudence with power in a private youth; abstinence with license in a powerful man; and wisdom with eloquence in a most busy one. Great things are in you, Lorenzo, without a doubt, great things. And lest anyone perhaps suspect the vice of flattery—which ought to be most foreign to a man who is both a philosopher and your dearest friend—I have said these "great things" are *in* you, not *from* you. For almighty God alone performs wonders. You are an instrument of God, O good man, well-suited—I know what I am saying—for performing magnificent deeds. You shall therefore successfully carry out wonders for as long as you obey the divine Artisan. Moreover, you will obey him perfectly, believe me, if you pray to him often, so that he himself may show you the way in which you are to obey. He will surely show the one who asks—he who, even before you ask, stimulates you to the asking, and shows both what and in what manner you should ask. Farewell, happy hope of our fatherland. But before I make an end, I beseech you, my Lorenzo, both for the sake of the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, an informal circle of scholars sponsored by the Medici.</note> which flourishes through you, and for this your fatherland which is dearer to you than all else, that you take care of your good health; for unless you are well, I do not think that in these times either the Academy or the fatherland can be well.
January 21, 1473. Florence.

---

->Wonderful praises of Lorenzo de’ Medici.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527), a trusted secretary to the Medici and a devoted student of Ficino.</note>, a true man, sends greetings.

**H**ow difficult it is, my Niccolò, oh how difficult it is now not to be struck by envy! Perhaps, Niccolò, if Lorenzo’s qualities were not also mine, I would not be able to keep from envying such great, numerous, and mature virtues in a young man. Tell me, friend, I ask: who speaks more elegantly? Who proves a point more sharply? Who soothes more sweetly? Who rouses more vehemently? You poets long ago yielded to "The Laurel" <note>A pun on Lorenzo's name, *Laurentius*, and the laurel tree (*Laurus*), the symbol of poetic excellence.</note>; you orators have just now yielded; and now, right now, let us philosophers yield. By Jupiter! These idle veterans are surpassed so quickly, so easily, and so greatly by that most busy "recruit." Let others envy the things of others and be burst by gnawing jealousy. I, however, marvelously rejoice in and enjoy what is mine: for Lorenzo is mine, on account of his incredible humanity. I also belong to Lorenzo, on account of the singular gifts of his mind; he bought me at a great price—that is, with himself. As God may love me, I speak, Niccolò, what I feel: no one was more familiar to the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), Lorenzo's grandfather and Ficino’s first patron.</note> than I, no one dearer. I recognized in that old man a virtue not merely human, but heroic. I now recognize in this young man, deep within, I recognize that whole old man; I see a phoenix in a phoenix, and light in a ray. That "Cosimian" splendor already shines forth from our Lorenzo in many ways every day: a light for the revelation of the Latin peoples <note>original: "lumen ad reuelationem Gentium Latinarum" — a paraphrase of the "Nunc Dimittis" (Luke 2:32).</note> and the glory of the Florentine Republic. So much for these matters. Furthermore, Lorenzo asked in his letter whose "Graces" those were for which I had thanked him. Were they mine, or another’s? Respond to him in my name: they are God’s. I also wish that those three Graces <note>The Charites (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia), who in Neoplatonism represent the unfolding of divine benefit.</note> described by Orpheus be favorable to our "Doctor" <note>original: "Medici nostro" — a play on the name Medici, which means "doctors."</note>: namely, Splendor, Joy, and Vitality. Splendor, I say, of the mind; Joy of the will; Vitality <note>original: "uiriditatem" — literally "greenness" or "flourishing."</note> of the body and of fortune. These Graces already breathe upon Lorenzo from on high, and they will continue to breathe as long as he acknowledges that he has received these graces solely from God alone. Farewell. January 21, 1473. Florence.

But who would have believed this? Which I myself can hardly believe, even though I have seen it clearly. I have sent two letters to you; you have sent barely one to us, and that one of so few... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence here; "paucorum" likely refers to "a few words."</note>

...of words, so that if you take away the first greeting and the final note of the place and day, almost nothing remains. But it does not befit a philosopher to be talkative. Yet it does not befit him to be silent either. For Terence <note>Publius Terentius Afer (c. 185–159 BC), a Roman playwright. Ficino refers to a famous maxim from his play *Andria*.</note> teaches us what he is said to have been taught by the Greeks: **Nothing in excess.** <note>original: "Vt ne quid nimis." A fundamental Greek principle of moderation (*miden agan*).</note> But even from these passages I see the reason why I am absent from your thoughts. For since you always have before your eyes Saint Christopher <note>This likely refers to Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a fellow scholar and member of the Platonic Academy. Ficino is jokingly suggesting that Landino’s physical or intellectual "size" is blocking Lorenzo's view of others.</note>, to whom your house is dedicated, his body is of such great size that it completely takes away your view of all other things, and in a way creates a sort of eclipse between you and us. I wonder at this, yet I truly cannot find the words to accuse you. For no word is so harsh or so insulting that "Marsilian silence" <note>Ficino often joked about his own tendency to go silent or be slow in replying, which his friends called "Marsilian silence."</note> would not be much worse—a silence by which you have failed both your own promise and our friendship. 

I grieve not a little that you have broken your word and brought such an injury upon our friendship. But what happens to be even more distressing to me is this: while you have frustrated our love, you have so alienated us from the goodwill of other men that no one remains whom I might hereafter trust. For nothing seemed so perfect, so constant, or so true as our friendship, which had grown from God through both your virtue and the passage of time; if it has somehow withered away, nothing remains in which we can safely trust. Therefore, know that we are wonderfully angry with you. Yet we are not so angry that, if your most pleasant letters were delivered to us, they could not—with their incredible sweetness—soothe all the harshness and indignation of our soul. For since you hold the spear of Achilles <note>The spear of Achilles (the spear of Peleus) was said in mythology to have the power to both wound a person and heal the very wound it made.</note> in your hands, know that your slowness in writing is the point with which you wound, but your letters can heal the wound in such a way that they can remove and blot out not only the wound itself but every last scar. 

Farewell at Pisa.

->Amatory matters: how each person should be loved, and how praised.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, a magnanimous man, sends greetings.<-

**T**hat you love me, Lorenzo, I have known for a long time from many very clear proofs. That you are "in love," I have recently learned from this one thing especially: that like a jealous man <term>zelotypus (jealous)</term>, you grow angry at the slightest and most false little offenses. Be angry as you please; be angry, you jealous man, provided that in the meantime you burn with love. The fire of anger and love is similar: for when I grow angry with you, as I often do, I am then burning most with the fire of love. You too are burning not a little; I know what I am talking about. But if ever we seem to grow lukewarm, even then this lukewarmness of ours burns more fervently than the love of others. 

Behold now, my Lorenzo, this anger of yours seems milder to me than the gentleness of others; that bite of yours is sweeter than a kiss <note>original: "suauio" (a lover's kiss).</note>. Oh, how sweetly you bite! How sharply you kiss! You mix a wonderful sweetness with sharpness, and sharpness with sweetness, as nature is wont to do in the most delicious flavors; and as often as your sharpness turns more strongly sour, it smells sweeter than sweetness itself, like Malmsey vinegar <term>aceti maluatici (Malmsey vinegar, made from a sweet Greek wine)</term>. 

But what do you accuse me of, you sharp accuser, you most sharp lover? Brevity? But you are the cause: for that I am brief is due to your busy affairs; that I seem very brief is due to the magnitude of your love for me. You accuse me of silence, suspecting it comes from forgetfulness, and forgetfulness from absence. You ought to remember that Marsilio is not absent from there if Lorenzo is not absent, in whom Marsilio dwells—if, indeed, the soul is everywhere at the same time, which you yourself confirmed in your letter the other day. What then does Saint Christopher <note>A continued reference to Cristoforo Landino.</note> prevent me from seeing you? Especially since he is transparent and clear, and in Christopher himself I behold Lorenzo, since through Lorenzo I see and embrace Christopher himself. 

Finally, do you want me to tell the truth? It is not the "opposition" of Christopher that brings on an eclipse through which I am either blinded or silent. Rather, you compel me to be darkened, stunned, and entirely mute by your lightning and thunder. Wicked youth, you rejoice too much in victory, however honorable. What more is left for you or for the rest of us? For you, perhaps to conquer yourself? For others, to suffer being conquered with a calm mind. Certainly, to speak of myself first, I rejoice in being overcome by you almost as much as you rejoice in overcoming me and others. But what shall I say of the others? The morning sun gathers the clouds. The midday sun scatters them. Youthful virtue excites envy; mature virtue settles it, and finally tames the spite which previously surpassed all opinion.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK I</header>

### ->A challenge to write.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

**F**riend, why have we been competing in silence for so long? In the end, what gain will come to the victor, or what loss to the defeated? I have truly decided that it is better for me to be defeated by you in this stubborn silence, so that I might win in a contest of speaking. Thus, from now on, the first place in keeping silent shall be given to you, and the first place in speaking shall be given to me. Will you always need spurs in the race? Will you never run of your own accord? Why are you so harsh with me? Perhaps I seem to joke too sharply with you, my dear Giovanni. But you act most sharply of all; so, respond most sharply too, if you please—provided that you do respond. If that pleases you less, then be sweetly silent. Certainly, believe that beneath this sharpness of my words lies a heart's affection sweeter than honey. Farewell, and stay away as long as your business requires. For it is enough for me when your business is being done. October 7th <note>original: "Nonis Octobris"</note>, from Careggi <note>The Medici villa outside Florence where Ficino spent much of his time translating and writing.</note>.

---

### ->That letters among friends are necessary.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

**S**ince I thought you would return to Florence shortly, I sent you no letters, hoping soon to hear and return true words in person. But now this perpetual serenity of the sky—if I may call it that—threatens me with your longer delays in the Trebbia hills <note>The hills around the Trebbia river, likely where Cavalcanti was staying at a family estate.</note>. But who would not be captured by the sweetness of Trebbia? Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine; Ficino implies the area is famous for its excellent vineyards.</note> certainly loves these hills, and my Giovanni has been captured by them; this is surely the reason why I have not written until now. But why do you write nothing? "I have nothing at all to write," you will say. Write that very thing—at least that you have nothing—though a subject for letters is never lacking between friends. For what is dearer to a friend than the life of a friend? Therefore, in turn, one must often indicate how one's health is. I cannot declare my own health unless I first know yours. Indeed, I am well if you are well—or rather, if I understand that you are well. Farewell, from Careggi. October 14th <note>original: "XIIII"</note>.

---

### ->The loss of time is heavy.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

**T**he care of my own body and that of my father is burdensome to me, as is your absence. Both must be endured with a level mind, lest they become heavier through impatience. If you have any human kindness in you, do not weigh me down with a third burden when I am already pressed by a double load: you burden me too much unless you send the books back to me. For the loss of time goads me to demand them more often. There is no loss heavier than that of time. Alas, I demand more boldly those things which perhaps I would prefer not to receive; yet the one whom I would truly wish to receive, I do not dare to ask for. It is fitting for me to have those books; it is necessary for me to be without this friend for the present. It is more prudent to be without him then, for it is fitting to fulfill one's duty, and then to do voluntarily what is necessary to the best of one's ability. It is in your interest to fulfill that duty, and in mine to strive for it. Farewell, and while you tend to the affairs of others, tend to yourself for your own sake among those others.

---

### ->That the letters of friends are joyful.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

**W**hat then shall I do? Shall I be the first to write to you? Or shall I wait for your letters? Indeed, since I am accustomed almost never to write to others unless provoked, I am nonetheless compelled to come to meet you and be the first to enter the contest. Nor will I allow you to be silent any longer. For you cannot be silent without causing me to waste away. An immoderate heat <note>This could refer to the summer weather or, in Ficino's Neoplatonic language, the "heat" of his affection or melancholy.</note> drove me here—which does not escape you—and an old, intolerable heat draws me back there, so much so that I can hardly restrain myself today from flying straight back to the city. You can, however, keep me here for a few—and indeed very few—days with your letters; for while I am entirely intent on reading your words, I shall neither feel the blasts of the winds nor hear the lightning and thunder. Thus it happens that words are able to calm the winds and drive away storms. Greet Ugolino Verino <note>Ugolino Verino (1438–1516), a celebrated Florentine poet and member of the Platonic Academy.</note>, your priest of the Muses. Farewell, August 30, 1478. From Marciano <note>Marciano is a locality near Cascina or perhaps refers to a specific estate where Ficino was staying to escape the heat or plague.</note>.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->No one should be slandered, because God takes vengeance.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

**H**omer, it is said, was deprived of his eyes because of his slandering of the divine Helen; because he never recognized his error, he is said never to have seen again. For the same reason, Stesichorus was struck with blindness, but he understood his mistake and sang a "palinode" <note>original: "palinodiam," a poem retracting a previous sentiment.</note>—that is, a contrary song—saying: "That speech was not true; you did not go in the well-decked ships, nor did you reach the towers of Troy." <note>Stesichorus was a 6th-century BCE Greek poet. Legend says he regained his sight after writing this recantation.</note> By these words, he immediately recovered his lost sight. Furthermore, when Socrates had slandered the God of Love, he was seized by his familiar "daemon" <note>Socrates' *daimonion* was an internal divine voice or spirit that warned him against errors.</note> while crossing the river Ilissus; before he suffered any adversity, he purified himself and praised Love once more, which he had previously slandered, and so escaped unharmed. Thus, Stesichorus was more prudent than Homer, but Socrates was wiser than both.

I have certainly been more careless than Socrates, though I hope I am not more unfortunate than Stesichorus. What is the point of this? Simply that on the fifth of this month <note>original: "mensis huius nonis," October 7th.</note> I wrote a letter to you in the morning, intending to rebuke your long-lasting silence, in which I accused you of being untamable and nearly the harshest of all men. By evening, I was overcome by ill health, and I have not yet recovered. For this reason, fearing lest some misfortune hang over me because of my slander of my "Hero," <note>original: "Herois." Ficino frequently refers to Cavalcanti as his "Hero" in a Platonic sense—a person of noble soul.</note> I decided to write a palinode, however brief, for the sake of expiating my crime. Therefore, I assert not that my Hero is harsh, but rather that I am soft, and that to a soft man, a constant man often seems fierce. Let this be my palinode; let it be a song contrary to the previous one, and let it also be a contrary request. For I was praying that you would send very sharp letters, if it pleased you, rather than none at all. Now, on the contrary, I ask for none rather than sharp ones; for a sick mind needs consolation, not instigation. Farewell. Florence, October 15 <note>original: "Idibus Octobris"</note>, 1468.

->Man is the soul. The soul of the lover is in the beloved.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

**I**, Giovanni, have often sought myself. First, I felt my chest with my hands; then, I often gazed at this face of mine in a mirror. But I could never assert that I had touched myself there, nor seen myself here. For when I seek myself, I certainly seek no one other than the very one who is seeking, where the Marsilio who is sought and the one who seeks are entirely the same. Who, then, seeks? He who desires to find. Who desires this? He who judges that it must be sought. Who judges? The soul alone judges. Therefore, I seek only the soul when I seek myself, since I myself am only the soul. I am confident that this soul can neither be touched nor seen. For we would not doubt its nature so stubbornly if it were open to these senses. Therefore, I have at times turned the sharp edge of my mind back upon itself, to see if perhaps I might perceive myself in this way; but even so, I did not entirely achieve what I desired. Indeed, in this interior intuition of mine, I am neither sufficiently delighted nor at rest. But he who attains what he investigates immediately rejoices and rests; therefore, I do not find myself within myself. But if I am to seek myself in another, how shall I grasp myself? If I do not possess myself, through whom alone I can grasp whatever I am able to grasp? Return, therefore, and give yourself—or rather me—back to me. Since I am unable to do it, return today and do not put it off for hours that are always "about to come." I beseech you, do not allow more of our days to be marked with a black pebble. <note>original: "nigro numerari lapillo." In antiquity, a black stone was used to mark a day as unlucky or bad.</note> For as many bright days as you spend there, just as many cloudy and black days we spend here. Farewell.

*Serious matters to Giovanni. The soul understands after death, and much more clearly than in the body.*

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

**I** have written several letters to you, best of friends, in which I attempted a somewhat "amatory" <note>In the sense of the Platonic tradition of "spiritual love" between friends.</note> style of writing, which indeed seems to suit our intimacy and is not foreign to that honorable freedom of Socrates and Plato. Now, however, after these amatory jests—for such are the Platonic introductions—let us come to serious matters in the manner of the Platonists. Hear now what I once discussed concerning the mind with Bernardo Giugni and Bartolomeo Fortini <note>Bernardo Giugni (1410–1473) was a high-ranking Florentine diplomat and magistrate; Fortini was also a respected citizen.</note>, citizens of excellent justice. There are two principal doubts among mortals concerning the mind. The first is whether the intellect can be separated from the body...
