<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical discourse to Giovanni Cavalcanti. Having established the soul's superiority over the body in the previous page, Ficino now addresses two specific questions regarding the soul's existence after death: whether it can function without a body and how clearly it perceives reality once freed from physical constraints.</meta>

<page-num>627</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK I.</header>

...[whether the soul] can exist and work after the body has been laid aside. Second, if it understands anything then, whether it understands clearly or not. We shall respond to these questions now as briefly as we can. For these and similar matters are argued at great length in our *Theology on the Immortality of Souls*. <note>Ficino refers here to his magnum opus, *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*, written between 1469 and 1474.</note> We concede that the intellect thinks of many incorporeal <note>original: "incorporalia," things that do not have physical bodies, such as thoughts or spirits.</note> things: namely God, angels, souls, virtues, the proportions of numbers, and the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the perfect, eternal patterns of which all earthly things are merely shadows.</note> and universal reasons of things. Just as we cannot see invisible things through sight, we cannot think of incorporeal things through any bodily instrument; nor can we seek, search for, find, or preserve things that are absolute—free from matter, place, and time—through a nature that is restricted to the body, place, and time. And if the mind, even while it rules the body, sometimes so withdraws into itself that it contemplates something by its own power, it follows that once separated from the body, it would be much more able and find it easier to contemplate by itself. If it can work by itself, it will also be able to exist and live by itself.

And to descend to the second question: the soul will then discern whatever is offered internally to be understood more clearly than the senses now perceive what is offered externally to be felt. It will be at least as much clearer as sight is sharper and faster than hearing and the rest of the senses. It will also be as much clearer as the mind is more excellent than the senses, and as the object of the mind is more excellent than the object of the sense. Anyone who uses the mind’s power does not doubt that the mind is more excellent than sense; for he sees that the mind is the judge of the senses, and being more precious, it is granted to fewer people and exercised more slowly and rarely. This also shows that the objects of the mind are more sublime than the objects of the senses: for the former are <term>universals</term>, <note>General concepts like "humanity" or "beauty" as opposed to specific humans or beautiful things.</note> vast and eternal, while the latter are particular, narrow, and mortal. 

Added to this is the fact that the more the outer sense is strained, the more the inner sense is relaxed, and vice versa. For he who looks or listens too intently can hardly imagine anything in the meantime; and he who imagines intensely hardly sees or hears what is then offered from the outside. The same proportion exists between imagination and the intellect. The soul in this body has two greatest obstacles of all: first, it is distracted into many operations and disturbances, and various operations hinder and weaken each other—for it is very difficult to apply oneself to different things at once. Second, because of the condition of this lowest dwelling place, and because of the bodily service assigned to men for a time, the soul exercises its lower actions far earlier, more attentively, and more often than the higher ones. 

Hence it happens that when we wish to contemplate incorporeal things, we usually work feebly and look as if through a certain mist. But when the actions of nourishing, growing, sensing, and imagining are either entirely omitted or greatly relaxed, then the gaze of the mind will be so sharpened that it will discern whatever it sees more clearly than this light. Truly, the soul will then perceive through itself that intelligible light <note>The light of the intellect or God, which allows the "eye of the mind" to see truth.</note> more piercingly than it now sees this sensible light through the glass windows of this bodily prison. For it will look calmly through its own clear serenity at the most excellent objects in the light of the divine Sun—a light so bright that the light of this physical sun is like a shadow to it. And because it is the clearest light, it is most hidden from impure eyes, but most manifest to the pure. 

The soul will not look at these things as if they were painted images, but as true things, of which all other things are but images. When during sleep the operations of movement and the outer senses cease, the imagination (which feeds on the remains of the senses) is so strengthened that it paints images within as if they were representing real things. What then will the intellect do—which is far more effective than the imagination—when it has escaped, much more free from obstacles than the imagination of a dreamer, and when Reason beholds the true reasons of all things in the highest Truth? It will surely then paint all true things within itself most exactly; or rather, it will be painted by all true things from elsewhere. But by whom most of all? By the Mind—the Mind, I say, the Light of lights. 

And how easily will this happen? Most easily indeed, and suddenly. For due to a certain natural kinship, visible light illuminates a clear physical body as soon as it is serene and pure, and it forms that body with its own form, and through its own form with the forms of all visible things. Similarly, the intelligible and more-than-intelligible light, which is God, forms the intellectual clarity as soon as it has become serene; it forms it, I say, with His own form (that is, the divine form), and through it with the forms of all intelligible things. And it immediately affects the soul with as much vital warmth and joy as the brilliance it has already bestowed; and so it hands over a life free from death, just as it pours in a light far removed from darkness. Beyond any limit of time, it pours light into the mind, by which now, from the changing of time to...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...it ascends to the state of eternity. It feeds on goodness according to its desire always, and by filling the soul, it attracts the appetite with beauty, and fills it by attracting it. There, there is fullness without satiety <note>original: "saturitas est absque satietate," meaning a state of being completely satisfied without ever becoming bored or "fed up."</note>, where there is good without evil, and through the infinite good, the capacity of the soul also becomes infinite. Therefore, the infinite good and beautiful—the source of all countless good and beautiful things—attracts and fills the soul equally forever.

---

->*Against Averroës: namely, that there is not a single intellect for all human beings.*<-
<note>Averroës (the Latin name for Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an Andalusian philosopher who argued that all humans share a single, universal "active intellect." Ficino strongly opposed this because it denied individual immortality.</note>
->*Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.*<-

**A**verroës was of the opinion that there is a single intellect for all human beings, and that through it, all people understand whatever they understand anywhere. Some people, more greedy for new things than for true ones, say this opinion is quite natural. And I confess it, but I call it "natural" only for this reason: because, just as natural things tend to be, it is highly changeable and is destroyed by its own opposite. For by the very fact that someone affirms the opposite, Averroës’s opinion is suddenly undermined. Since opposites cannot exist in the same thing at the same time, if the intellect in a certain philosopher—say, in Averroës—and in a Platonist simultaneously feels opposite things about itself (while in the former it says it is unique, and in the latter it says there are many intellects, not just one), it is clearly established that there is not one intellect in them, but many. Is there not, in those matters pertaining to the intelligence and the will, the greatest diversity among men at the same time? For at the same time, some affirm the same thing while others deny it; some want it, and others do not. 

What, moreover, shall we say about conflicting habits? The intellect is most learned in one person, unlearned in another; in this one it is just and upright, in that one unjust and wicked; in this one happy, in that one miserable. Therefore, the same intellect cannot exist in everyone. If the intellects are diverse, the souls are much more diverse. Add to this that if the intellect is unique, and always has been, as Averroës says, it is not likely that it would be so ignorant of itself that in almost all men—except for Averroës alone—it has always thought and still thinks itself to be multiple in number. What is more natural to the mind than knowledge of itself? Why then, when the mind thinks about the opinion of Averroës, can it either never or only with difficulty grasp it, except because it is a false opinion? 

Finally, as often as we contemplate the unity of the mind <note>The idea that we all share one mind.</note>, we are usually moved to hate it and to desire a plurality of minds, provided that we desire to survive after death. Truly, that same mind would hate its own unity—if indeed it can feel hate—since it is the only thing that can know itself. It is not likely that an eternal and even divine thing would always despise, reject, and hate its own nature. Why do I draw out this speech further? We have disputed these matters more than enough with each other in your field at Regnano <note>Regnano was a villa belonging to the Cavalcanti family where Ficino often stayed.</note>, while your guest Marsilio was composing that great volume of *Theology* <note>original: "Theologiæ uolumen," referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*.</note> there. Farewell. April 16th, Florence.

---

->*Theologians are awake; the rest are dreaming.*<-
->*Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.*<-

**S**ome wonder why we follow Plato with such great devotion, as he always seems to move among paradoxes and wonders. But they will cease to wonder, I believe, if they consider that only those things which are divine truly exist, because they are neither infected by the contagion of a foreign nature, nor are they ever changed from their state. Bodily things, however, do not truly exist at all, but only seem to exist, since they are infected by opposites and are constantly changing; therefore, they are not true things, but images or shadows of true things. 

Since nearly all other philosophers, devoted only to the study of natural things, were dreaming in these images as if they were true things, our Plato, dwelling upon divine things, was either the only one awake, or the most awake of all. Therefore, I think it is as much better to follow Plato the Theologian than the other philosophers, as it is better to entrust oneself to awake pilots than to sleeping ones.
->Farewell.<-

->The Truth of God is Splendor, Beauty, and Love.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.<-

**H** <note>The letter "H" is a large decorative drop-cap in the original.</note> This was the primary pursuit of the divine Plato, as the dialogues *Parmenides* and *Epinomis* <note>The *Parmenides* is a challenging dialogue about the nature of the "One," while the *Epinomis* is a later work often attributed to Plato's circle discussing astronomy and wisdom.</note> indicate: to show that there is one principle of all things, which he named "the One" as its primary title. He also maintained that there is a single truth of this very "One"—that is, of God—which is a light infused into all minds and forms; a light that both presents forms to minds and joins minds to those forms. Therefore, whoever wishes to profess the Platonic study must cultivate this unique truth: the single ray of the One, namely God. This ray passes through angels, souls, the heavens, and the rest of the physical bodies. And, as we discussed in our book *On Love*, its splendor shines in each thing according to its nature, and is called grace and beauty. Where it shines more fittingly, there it especially allures the one looking upon it, excites the one considering it, and ravishes and occupies the one approaching it. It compels him to venerate this kind of splendor above all others as if it were a divinity, and to strive for nothing else than that—having set aside his former nature—he may himself become that splendor. This is clear <note>original: "patet," though the OCR suggests a typo "pater" in the print.</note> from the fact that when a lover is not content with the sight or touch of a person, he sometimes cries out: "I do not know what this person has that burns me, and I do not understand what I desire." Here it is certain that the soul is burned by the divine splendor which shines in a beautiful person as if in a mirror, and being secretly ravished by it, <margin>marginal squiggle</margin> is pulled upward as if by a hook so that he may become a god. Therefore, anyone must be considered insane and miserable who, while being provoked by God through sight toward sublime things, instead plunges himself into the mud through touch. When he could have become a god from a man by contemplating that divine beauty through human beauty, he instead turns himself from a man into a beast by preferring a corporal and shadowy form over the spiritual and true beauty.

### That Ideas according to Plato are in the divine mind.
->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.<-

**P** <note>The letter "P" is a large decorative drop-cap in the original.</note> Our Plato, in the *Timaeus*, imitating and approving of Timaeus the Pythagorean, asserts that the world was born from God. He introduces a three-fold cause for this generation: the efficient, the end, and the exemplar. For he maintains that the world was created by the power of God, for the sake of His goodness, according to the exemplar <note>The "exemplar" is the perfect blueprint or model used by the Creator.</note> of divine wisdom. And just as there are exemplars of the whole building and its parts in the mind of an architect, so too in a certain divine intelligence above the world there are exemplars of this entire world and its parts. He calls that world "intelligible" and eternal, but this one "temporal" and sensible. He calls the models of this world in that one <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the eternal, non-physical blueprints of all things in the physical world.</note>, and the likenesses of those in this world "images" and "shadows." On account of this, one may—and indeed should—laugh at certain envious people who commonly proclaim Plato to be as foolish as they are unfair, claiming he positioned Ideas and the universal "reasons" of things as being separated both from bodies and from the divine intelligence, and from each other, like little clouds scattered through the air by the wind. But since we have brought many arguments against them in those books which we composed while staying with you in the fields of Regnano <note>Regnano was a country estate where Ficino often wrote and studied.</note>, let it suffice now to bring forward only the testimony from Plato’s *Timaeus*. First, he says, "Let us consider what is usually investigated before all else in a question about the universe: whether this universe has always existed without any beginning of generation, or whether it was created, taking its start from some beginning." It is certainly seen and touched and is a body; all such things move the senses, and things that move the senses are perceived by opinion through the senses. It is established that such things are born and have been created, and we assert that whatever is born must necessarily be born from some cause. Indeed, to find the maker and father of the world is difficult, and when you have found him, to proclaim him to the common people is impossible. Again, it must be considered whether the craftsman of the world imitated an exemplar—that which is always one, the same, and similar? Or that which we call "created"? But if the world is beautiful and the maker of the world is good, he preferred to imitate the eternal example; otherwise—which is a sin even to say—he followed a created exemplar instead of an eternal one. Since the world is the most beautiful of all created things, and its author is the best of all causes, there is no doubt that he followed the eternal example. Thus, that which was created was made according to that which can be grasped by reason and wisdom alone, and remains immutable. From which it follows that it is necessary that this world...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical defense of Platonic thought, transitioning from the abstract nature of the "One" on the previous page to the specific way God (the Architect) created the world as a single, living reflection of the Divine Mind. It concludes with the start of a new, more moralistic letter to his friend Giovanni Cavalcanti regarding the soul’s struggle in the material world.</meta>

<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...while the other is an image. And a little later: *Let us say for what reason the author of things established generation and this whole universe. He was good; and he who is good is never touched by any envy regarding any matter. Therefore, since spite was most foreign to Him, He willed all things to become as similar to Himself as they possibly could.* If anyone receives this primary cause for the birth of the world from wise men, he will certainly receive it most rightly. And after a few words: *It must be said that this world is a living being* <note>original: "animal"; in the Neoplatonic sense, this means a "souled" or "animated" being, implying the universe itself possesses a World Soul.</note>*, and an intelligent one, truly established by divine providence; having posited this, let us see what follows. After the likeness of which living being did God establish the world? We do not think He made it similar to any one specific species of animals. For if it had been made similar to an imperfect living being, it certainly would not be beautiful; rather, we consider it to be most similar to that Living Being of which all other animals, both individually and generally, are parts.* For that Being embraces within itself all living things that are perceived by the mind alone <note>These are the "Platonic Ideas" or "Forms"—the eternal blueprints of all things existing within the Mind of God.</note>, just as this world contains us and the other animals that are seen. Thus, wishing to make this world most similar to the most beautiful and altogether absolute of all things that can be understood, God made it a single living being visible to the sight, containing within its own limit all animals matching its nature. Did we rightly say the world is one? Or would it have been more correct to say there are many or innumerable worlds? Surely one, since it was formed according to the likeness of the One; for that which contains all living things that are understood cannot have a second companion. For again, there would have to be another living being that contained these two, of which these two would be parts? And this world would be more correctly called an image not of those two, but of this third one. Therefore, so that this world might be most similar to the absolute Living Being, in that it was alone and one, for that reason neither two nor innumerable worlds were procreated, but one world was made, only-begotten <note>original: "unigenitus"; Ficino uses the same word used in the Creeds for Christ to describe the uniqueness of the created universe.</note>, and so it shall be. 

But hear Timaeus the Pythagorean <note>A character in Plato's *Timaeus* whom Ficino treats as a historical teacher of Plato.</note>, who stood as Plato’s teacher and who, in similar words, placed the Ideas in God. *The world,* he says, *is the best of those things that have been generated, because it was generated by that best author, who looks not upon man-made models, but upon the Idea and the intelligible substance. To which model, indeed, that which is made should be exactly and perfectly most beautiful and beyond correction. But it is perfect above all fruitful sensible things, because that exemplar of it, which contains all intelligible living beings within itself, left nothing else outside, since it is the most absolute limit of intelligible things, just as this world is of sensible things.* Thus he spoke. 

We have heard that the Ideas of all things exist in a certain living and eternal exemplar, which is the most excellent of all intelligible things, and so absolute in every way that nothing intelligible is outside of it. This, however, can be nothing other than God. But what is clearer than this: when Plato had said that God made all sensible things after the likeness of the intelligible, he added that He made all things similar to Himself. As if the exemplar and God were the same. Truly, because there are as many species of created things in this world as there are Ideas—that is, intelligible reasons—in God through which all things are created; and because the created species are in matter which is not living of itself, they either do not live or barely live. But the Ideas, because they are in God who lives of Himself, live in God. Plato says in the same book: *As many and of what kind the mind beholds the Ideas in the Living Being itself, so many and of such kind he thought to fashion the species in this world.* John <note>Referring to St. John the Evangelist. Ficino famously argued that the beginning of the Gospel of John—"In the beginning was the Word"—matched Plato's theory of Ideas.</note> felt this, as does Plato, as you hear. This was felt by the predecessors and successors of Plato. Believe Marsilio: he who feels otherwise departs from the truth.

### The Cause of Sinning, Hope, and the Remedy.

->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.<-

**W** <note>The letter "C" (for "Cur" or "Why") is a decorative initial in the original.</note>hy do souls, since they are divine, live so profanely? Because they inhabit a profane house and region. Others fall into sin because of negligence or ignorance, and that is not surprising as long as we dwell in these dark dregs of the world; others because of an excessive love for the body, and that is also not surprising, for the body is the companion and offspring of the soul; others because they distrust either immortality or divine mercy—and what wonder, since they lead their lives in a place of death and malice? Others because they trust more than is right in either divine mercy or tomorrow's correction; both distrust and excessive confidence are dangerous—the former torments, the latter deceives. It is, therefore, the highest wisdom always to use the present moment as best we can. The only refuge is to commend oneself to God very frequently. There is excellent hope when, having done these things, you remember that it is not hidden from God how hard or how dangerous a province <note>Ficino uses the Roman term "provincia" (duty or administrative region) to describe the difficult "assignment" of living in a human body.</note> we...

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.

**Y**esterday in the fields of Novoli <note>A village near Florence where the Cavalcanti family had a villa.</note>, we renewed the sacred solemnities of Saint Christopher and Saint James. I said "sacred," Giovanni, but I certainly would have added "festive" if you had been present, for without you nothing is festive for me. See, therefore, how dear you are to your Marsilio, for whom not even heavenly things—if it is right to say so—are dear without you. And rightly so; for He who joined James and Christopher in the sacred rites <note>These two saints share the same feast day, July 25th.</note> also joined Marsilio and Giovanni in life. The same, or surely a very similar <term>genius</term> <note>original: "genius"; in the Renaissance, this referred to a tutelary spirit or a person's innate divine nature.</note> presides over us both. I believe God ordained that we live on earth with the same will and similar character, and in heaven under the same <term>Idea</term> <note>The eternal "Form" or blueprint of a soul in the Divine Mind.</note> and with equal degrees of happiness. Farewell, the <term>Achates</term> <note>The legendary faithful companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid.</note> of our voyage, and finally, the harbor and the seasoning of my life.

->The lawgiver is more excellent than the sophist.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.

**T**he Greeks once marveled at the power of speech, memory, and sharp wit in Carneades <note>A Greek philosopher and head of the Academy known for his persuasive but often skeptical rhetoric.</note>. Your companions, as you say, praise these same qualities in Giovanni Guidi, and because of a certain resemblance, they often nickname him "Carneades." You, however, call him a follower of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> because of his invention of laws. You ask, furthermore, which praise is more excellent: to be like Carneades or like Lycurgus. Carneades introduced disputes through arguing, but Lycurgus resolved them. The subtleties of Carneades are more often useless than useful; and when useful, they are so to few people and rarely. The discipline of Lycurgus is supremely useful, everywhere, and necessary for everyone. Finally, just as it is better to live well than to speak well, and to be happy than to seem so, the faculty of Lycurgus is that much more excellent than that of Carneades. But learn from Herodotus <note>The Greek historian.</note> how great the excellence of a lawgiver is; for he writes that when Lycurgus first entered the temple of Apollo, the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The priestess and oracle at Delphi.</note> poured forth these verses:

> Beloved of heavenly Jove and all the dwellers 
> Of heaven, Lycurgus, who comes to our rich temples, 
> I doubt whether I should prophesy that you are now a man or a God, 
> But I hope rather that you are a God, Lycurgus.

Read this letter to our friend Priori Pandolfini; I know he will confirm these things, for he knows the nature of the new man. Farewell. And persevere in your goodwill toward Giovanni Guidi.

->The lawful limit of love is fellowship.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.

**Y**ou ask what cause chiefly led me to devise several love letters. There are, Giovanni, very many who, when speaking or writing of matters of love, wander far from the law of love. An error of this kind is as harmful as it is common. Right affection is as manifold as the many people who love. Indeed, all men love—I said "men," Giovanni, for he who does not love a man is not a man. Therefore, not only in the book I composed *On Love* <note>Ficino's famous "De Amore," a commentary on Plato's Symposium.</note>, but also in my letters, I have set a limit for lovers as to how far they should proceed. He who transgresses this limit, since he is a true enemy to himself, cannot be a true friend to others. Only he will keep the lawful limit in speaking or writing who has first kept it in his thoughts; and he will keep it in his thoughts who has recognized what true beauty is, and what is not true beauty, but only a likeness of the truth. The lawful limit of loving is <term>fellowship</term> <note>original: "consuetudo"; implying a deep, habitual, and spiritual intimacy or shared life.</note>; this consists of three things: thought, sight, and hearing. For (as all philosophers define it) love is nothing other than the desire for beauty. The beauty of the body lies not in the shadow of matter, but in the light and grace of form; not in a dark mass, but in a certain luminous proportion; not in sluggish and unsuited weight...

But why do I consult the crowd for so long in the manner of our Socrates and Plato, rather than consulting myself? Perhaps the more I strive to prevent the common folk from loving shamefully, the more that insane and ungrateful crowd will suspect that I love too much—which is also said to have happened to those divine heroes, our leaders Socrates and Plato. Therefore, let enough and more than enough have been said of these things for now. Farewell.

-> Neither is love without religion, nor religion without love, praised. <-

### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Contronio of Lucca, sends greetings.

**I** am sending you the [treatise on] love that I promised. I am also sending [the one on] religion, so that you may recognize both that my love is religious, and that my religion is full of love. Truly, nature has so arranged things that love is not honorable unless it is religious, nor is religion true unless it is undertaken through love. Angelo Mametti—son of the orator Giannozzo and heir to his father’s virtue—sends you his greetings.

## On Enduring Injury.

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.

**Y**ou say that one of your household was recently affected by insult and injury from certain impudent men. He who commits an injury, Giovanni, does it to himself. For he disturbs his own soul and infects it with the mark of an evil habit. Infamy, hatred, danger, and inconveniences follow. He who receives an injury receives it not from the one inflicting it, but from himself. For the rational soul itself, which is the man himself <note>Ficino follows the Platonic view that the "true man" is the rational soul, not the physical body.</note>, is not offended unless he judges that injury to be an evil for him. A judgment of this kind is placed within our own choice. Since, therefore, no one is harmed except by himself, no one should complain about another when he should instead complain about himself. Let him who complains think not how to punish another, but how to punish—that is, to chasten and correct—himself. Have you ever seen certain puppies who bite the stone thrown at them, even if they were not hit by it? Since they were not harmed by the stone, they harm their own teeth with their bite. Imprudent men do the same; for often, when kicked by a donkey's hoof, they strike the donkey—or rather themselves—with their fist. Truly, the unwise receive many injuries into themselves by their own opinion, which by their nature usually bounce back like balls upon the thrower. 

You will say perhaps that it is difficult not to desire revenge. Do not doubt: even if men forgive, soon after the most just God will avenge. What is more convenient, what more glorious, than to have God as one's patron and avenger? And to merit at least as much good from Him by waiting as the injurious man wished to inflict evil, and in this way to turn evil into good. O, what a precious good is tolerance! Socrates, the wisest of the Greeks, practiced this alone; Christ, the master of life, practiced this above all other virtues. For it is said He descended to men almost for the sole purpose of practicing this. Impatience is as much to be blamed as patience is to be praised. Let us skip the rest. Impatience disturbs the mind, destroys past goods, infects the present, and hinders the future. Nor should one give ear to the rumors of the vile commoners if they invite one to revenge. What is the common crowd? A certain <term>polypus</term> <note>original: "polypus"; literally an octopus or polyp, here used to mean a multi-footed animal without a head, signifying a mindless, chaotic mob.</note>, that is, a multi-footed animal without a head. It is the mark of a great-souled man, because of his own greatness, to think little of things that are small. All temporal things are small and very brief; that which is past is no more, that which is future is not yet, and that which is present is indivisible, beginning at the same moment it ends. 

He is not strong who succumbs to injuries, but he who overcomes them. But he overcomes who so resists that he is not moved from his state by their force. Read these things to your household member; tell him also to seek a remedy from reason, and not to wait for it from time. For time is a harmful doctor; daily he deceives the sick person with the expectation of the future, and before he expels old pains he adds new ones to the old, piling up evils daily so that he leads one with a false hope of life toward death. But one must live today, for he who lives tomorrow never lives. If you wish to live today, live for God, in whom yesterday and tomorrow are nothing other than today. Farewell. March 30, 1474.

### On acquiring constancy against fortune.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

Socrates, in that book by Plato titled *Theaetetus* <note>original: "Theætetus"; a dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge and the role of the philosopher</note> regarding science, armed his friend Theodorus the Geometer to bravely repel the blows of fortune—not with iron weapons, as most people are accustomed to do, but with golden ones, in this manner. He said, "It is impossible, Theodorus, to utterly uproot evils. For it is necessary that there always be something contrary to the good. Among the higher beings <note>referring to the divine or celestial realms</note>, evils cannot exist; but they necessarily circle this mortal nature and the lower region. Therefore, one must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. Now, we say that 'fleeing' means making oneself as similar to God as possible, according to one's strength. And <term>Prudence</term>, <term>Holiness</term>, and <term>Justice</term> <note>these are the three central virtues Ficino identifies for spiritual ascent</note> render a person similar to God." 

Now, you shall hear briefly how this divine precept of our Plato should be understood. Just as God is the creator and likewise the governor of our souls, so the world is the parent and governor of our bodies. Truly, because the soul is a son of God and the body is a member of the world, our soul is led mercifully and sweetly by God as if by a father according to the laws of <term>Providence</term>. Our body, however, is dragged by the forces of <term>Fate</term> from the body of the world—like a small particle pulled by a violent impulse from the whole mass. The force of Fate does not penetrate our mind unless the mind first plunges itself of its own accord into the body that is subject to Fate. 

Therefore, let no one trust so much in his own counsel and strength that he hopes to entirely avoid the diseases of the body and the loss of possessions. Let every soul withdraw itself from the plague of the body and collect itself into its own mind; then fortune will exhaust its force upon the body, but it will not pass into the soul. The wise man will not fight in vain against Fate; rather, he will resist it by fleeing. Adverse things cannot be put to flight, but they can be fled from. Therefore, we are commanded by Plato to flee from here to there—that is, from the love of the body and the care for external things to the cultivation of the soul; for otherwise, evils cannot be declined. 

He adds "as quickly as possible," I believe, for this reason: so that we may begin to separate the soul from its commerce with the body from a tender age, before it is submerged by long-standing habit. Certainly, through this flight, the soul is not undeservedly rendered similar to God, since it emerges free from the contagion of the body, just like God. We attain this kind of freedom chiefly through three virtues: Prudence, Justice, and Holiness. <term>Prudence</term> recognizes what we owe to God and what we owe to the world; <term>Justice</term> grants to the world what is its own; <term>Holiness</term> attributes to God what is His. And so, the prudent man concedes his body—as a member of the world—to the revolution of the world itself, to be driven about however it happens. But he separates the soul—as a son of God—from commerce with the body, and commits it to divine Providence to be governed according to His will. If we follow this golden precept of our Plato, my sweetest Giovanni, we shall sail happily, safely, and unharmed to the port through this boiling whirlpool of fortune, with the heavenly breeze breathing upon us. Farewell.

### That stable friendship which is forged by God.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

The Platonic philosophers, my best Giovanni, have most excellently defined true friendship as a stable union of the lives of two people. Truly, we believe that "one life" exists only in those men who walk by one work toward one end—as if by the same path to the same destination of the journey. We also think that their society will finally be stable when that which they have proposed for themselves to pursue through a certain common duty is not only one thing, but also stable and firm. 

But since every pursuit and commerce of men usually strives toward that which is thought to be good, and there seem to be three goods for mortals—I mean goods of the soul, of the body, and external goods—either virtue of the soul is sought by them, or pleasure of the body, or abundance of riches. Of these, surely the first is certain and perpetual, while the other two are fleeting and mortal. For this reason, a stable union of life—which is true friendship—can exist only among those who set out neither to accumulate riches nor to satisfy the lusts of the body (all of which are fluid and fleeting), but to grasp and cultivate the one and stable virtue of the soul with a certain common zeal and with the whole fire of the mind. Our Plato, that master and leader of all philosophers, wished for the virtue of the soul to be called <term>Wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapientiam"; the text breaks here as it continues to the next page</note>. Wisdom...

Indeed, he <note>referring to Plato, continuing the thought from the previous page</note> believed it to be the knowledge of divine things. Furthermore, in his books on the *Republic*, he demonstrates that divine things can only become known to our minds by God illuminating us, just as the forms of bodies are seen by the eyes only when the Sun illuminates them. Therefore, the same God whom we desire to see is the one who illuminates the sharpness of the mind so that we are able to perceive, and who finally shows Himself to the brightened mind, delighting it by that showing; God is likewise for us the Way, the Truth, and the Life. He is the Way, certainly, because He turns us toward Himself, leads us, and carries us away by His own rays. He is the Truth because He shows Himself as true to us who have turned toward Him. Finally, He is the Life because He perpetually feeds and delights our soul—the contemplator of Himself—with that blessed vision.

Therefore, it is necessary that all those who desire to taste the sweetest liquids of wisdom thirst for this perennial fountain of all wisdom. Indeed, it is necessary that all who desire to attain virtue of the soul pursue wisdom. From this it follows that whoever resolves to cultivate their soul is compelled to worship God. Now, we defined "friends" earlier as those who strive toward virtue with a similar and equal zeal, and who cultivate their souls with mutual favor. The cultivation of the soul consists of virtue alone; virtue is wisdom; wisdom is the knowledge of divine things. Divine light grants us knowledge of this kind. Therefore, the cultivation of the soul is the worship of God Himself. Since friendship strives with the consent of two people to cultivate the soul through virtue, it clearly seems to be nothing other than the highest concord of two souls in worshipping God.

Moreover, whoever worships God with a pious mind is loved by God. Therefore, friends are never merely two; there are necessarily three: namely, two human beings and one God. God, I say—<term>Jupiter Hospitalis</term>, <term>Jupiter Amicabilis</term>, the Savior of human life <note>Ficino uses these names for the Roman god Jupiter to describe attributes of the one Divine Creator: as the protector of guests (hospitality), the patron of friendship, and the savior of life</note>. Plato always worshipped Him, and Socrates always honored Him; He is the leader of human life, He reconciles us into one, and He is the indissoluble knot and perpetual guardian of friendship.

Because they had this God as their reconciler, those ancient <term>Theologians</term> <note>original: "Theologi"; Ficino refers to the "Ancient Theology" (*prisca theologia*), a lineage of wisdom he believed started with figures like Zoroaster and Hermes Trismegistus</note> whose holy memory we venerate, are said to have entered into the bond of friendship among themselves. Among the Persians, Zoroaster is said to have taken Arimaspes as his constant companion in the religious mysteries of divine philosophy, by the inspiration of the divine power. Likewise, Hermes Trismegistus among the Egyptians took Aesculapius. In Thrace, Orpheus took Musaeus. There also, Aglaophemus took Pythagoras. At Athens, Plato first took Dion of Syracuse, and then, after Dion’s death, Xenocrates. To such an extent did these wise men judge that both God as leader and a human as companion were necessary to complete the celestial journey safely and calmly.

Although I have very little confidence that I can follow their footsteps impressed upon the regions of heaven from above, I nevertheless seem to have achieved this one thing abundantly: that in the study of sacred Philosophy, in the exercise of virtue, and in the investigation of truth, I do not lack the advantageous and pleasant society of an excellent man. For I believe the intimacy of Giovanni Cavalcanti and Marsilio Ficino should be placed in the number of those friendships we commemorated just before; and with God as our Leader—who happily established and fused this bond for us—it will greatly profit both of us in our affairs, in the tranquility of our lives, and in the investigation of divine matters.

->Poetic frenzy is from God.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Pelotto and Baccio Ugolini, sends greetings.

**W**hen I, along with my close companions Antonio Calderini and Bindaccio Ricasoli, were reading what both of you composed in praise of Carlo Marsuppini, that foster-child of the Muses <note>Carlo Marsuppini (1398–1453) was a famous humanist and Chancellor of the Florentine Republic</note>, we agreed that the opinion of our Plato is most true: that Poetry proceeds not from art, but from some kind of frenzy <note>original: "furore"; referring to "divine madness" or inspiration</note>. And although there is no need for arguments when the matter itself is obvious, I will nevertheless state what Platonic reasoning persuades.

Plato discusses divine frenzy in the *Phaedrus* and the *Ion*, for which he brings forward three signs in particular. First, that individual men hardly master individual arts over a long period of time without God. Yet legitimate Poets—such as he maintains Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and Pindar were—inserted certain signs and proofs of all the arts into their works. Second, that while in a frenzy they sing many things, and indeed wonderful things, which they themselves do not sufficiently understand shortly afterward when the frenzy cools down—as if they themselves had not spoken, but God had cried out through them as if through trumpets. Third, that the best poets did not turn out to be the more prudent men or those more highly educated from an early age. Rather, they were some who were "insane," as it is well known Homer and Lu- <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page with the name Lucretius</note>

<margin>Care for fatherland, family, and friends.</margin>
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Tedaldo, greetings.

**B**artolo Tedaldo, your uncle, a learned and prudent man, often had that Socratic saying on his lips: that two things above all other human affairs must be cared for, namely the fatherland and the family. And rightly so, for the family is a member of the fatherland, and the fatherland is the body. Why then, our Francesco, why do you travel abroad so much and for so long? In this way, you neither cultivate your country nor sufficiently cultivate your family. One must not think so much about leaving many goods to one's children, as much as making them very good; the former you can perhaps achieve outside the country, but the latter certainly within the country. I believe you trust in the diligence and honor of your son, Lactantius. I myself certainly do not distrust him. But what shall I say of friends? You must sometimes comply with them if you want them to comply with you; comply with your friends—indeed, with yourself today. Give tomorrow’s compliance to your enemies, if you have any. Let there be, I pray, at least a care for me in you, to whom you are as dear as that which is dearest. Farewell. March 5, 1474.

->Who is to be called a true man.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bartolomeo Fonzio and Alessandro Baccio, pupils of the Muses, greetings.

**I**f you wonder why I call Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Nicolaus Micheloctius, a prominent Florentine diplomat and secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici</note> by the specific name of "a true man," I answer because I find nothing effeminate in that man, nothing deceitful, nothing that does not display the power of virtue and carry it within itself. Where do you think this proceeds from? From the fact that no one can be found anywhere who can detract even the slightest bit from Niccolò. Why is he praised without exception? Because he is loved without pretense. And from where does that come? Because he loves without pretense and lives without lies. Farewell, but take care that Niccolò does not read this letter. I decided to praise him while he was absent, lest I should seem to praise a "true man" with less than the truth. Greet our friend Pietro Cennini, a man adorned with piety and letters. April 6, 1474.

->On humanity.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Tommaso Minerbetti, a humane man, greetings.

**W**hy are boys more cruel than old men? Why are infants more foolish than the prudent? Why are the dull more so than the gifted? Because they are, so to speak, "less human" than the others. Hence, those who are cruel are called inhumane and feral. For those who stand far off from the perfected nature of man—either because of a defect of age or because of an adverse disposition of the stars—these people for the most part either hate or neglect the human species as something alien and foreign. Nero <note>The Roman Emperor, used here as a classic symbol of tyranny and lack of empathy</note> was not a man, so to speak, but a kind of monster in a human skin. For if he had truly been a man, he would have loved other men as members of the same body. For individual men, under one Idea <term>Idea: In Platonic philosophy, the perfect, eternal form or archetype of a thing</term> and in the same species, are one man. For this reason, as I believe, the wise have called that one virtue out of the whole number of virtues by the name of man himself—that is, *humanity*—which loves and cares for all men as if they were brothers born in a long line from one single father. Therefore, most humane man, persevere in the duties of humanity. Nothing is more pleasing to God than charity. There is no surer sign of madness or portent of misery than cruelty.

<margin>The folly and misery of mankind.</margin>

### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Vanni, Cherubino Quarquatio, and Domenico Galeti, greetings.

**Y**ou have seen the sphere of the world painted in my study <term>gymnasio</term> <note>While *gymnasium* usually means a school, Ficino used it to refer to his personal study or his 'Academy' where he taught and wrote.</note>, and on this side and that, Democritus and Heraclitus <note>Democritus and Heraclitus were often paired in art and literature as the "laughing" and "weeping" philosophers; the former laughed at the absurdity of human life, while the latter wept for its tragedy.</note>. One indeed laughing, the other truly weeping. Why does Democritus laugh? At that which Heraclitus mourns: namely the common crowd, a monstrous animal, insane and wretched. 

Mortals daily ask for good things from God, but they never ask that they might use them well. They wish that fortune might follow their desires, but they take no care that their desire should follow reason. They strive for even the smallest household items to be as beautiful as possible, but they almost never strive for the soul to be made beautiful. They diligently seek out cures for bodily diseases, but they neglect the diseases of the soul. They believe they can have peace with others, yet they themselves are constantly at war with themselves. For there is a perpetual struggle between the body and the soul, between sense and reason. 

They trust they can acquire a faithful friend from among the number of others, yet none of them keeps faith with himself. What they have approved, they reject; what they wanted, they do not want, and vice versa. They arrange the parts of buildings with a carpenter’s rule <note>original: "ex amussim"</note>, they tune the strings of a lyre to perfection <note>original: "ad unguem" – literally 'to the fingernail,' a Roman idiom for high precision</note>, but they never try to make the parts and movements of the soul harmonious. They make stones resemble living beings, but living beings they make like stones. They despise the wise themselves, but they venerate the statues and names of the wise. They profess to know the affairs of others while they are ignorant of their own. 

What else shall we say to these things, friends? Magistrates forbid homicide, yet everywhere they permit the instruments for the slaughter of men to be manufactured. They wish for the finest harvest of men, yet they do not sufficiently cultivate the sowing of men—that is, childhood. Today men always live badly, hoping to live well only tomorrow. For the sake of ambition they contend with each other in wrongdoings; it would be a more convenient way to glory to compete in mutual benefits. Since they always speak ill, they hope they will hear good things; though they act wickedly, they hope to receive good things. We do not declare ourselves to be the authors of good things, but we call God the author of evils <note>Ficino critiquing the human tendency to take credit for success while blaming God or the stars for failure.</note>. We cast our faults upon the stars. 

How many will you find who value a man as much as money? Who cultivate themselves as they cultivate their fields and other things? Who bring up their family with as much diligence as many raise horses and dogs and birds? Who consider how heavy is the loss of time? In spending money we are most frugal; in giving away time we are prodigal beyond measure. How many will you provide who recognize the poverty of their own soul? Every man thinks himself to abound in wisdom but to be lacking in money. 

Alas, the pain! We seek the greatest things in the smallest, the highest in the lowest, good in evils, rest in fleeting things, peace in conflicting things, abundance in poverty, and finally, life in death. Let us seek, friends, I beseech you, these same things which we already seek. But let us not seek them further where we have been seeking them. He is too insane and wretched who trusts he will find a thing's opposite in its opposite. Farewell.

---

<margin>The folly and misery of mankind.</margin>

### Marsilio Ficino to Cristoforo Landino, a man of singular goodness and learning, greetings.

**A**ristotle introduced "problems" concerning the nature of things. I now raise problems with you concerning the nature of men. Tell me, why do men boast that they are rational, and yet they live by chance? They desire or fear many things before they know well enough whether they should be sought or feared; or on the contrary, they prefer the shortest and smallest things to the eternal and immense. Why do they wish neither to obey a man nor to submit to a wise person? Yet they most willingly serve beasts and vices. Why do we strive to rule over others, when we do not rule ourselves? Why, through the zeal for ruling, do we fall daily into slavery? And we strive to obtain honors more than we strive to be worthy of those honors? 

Furthermore, since we see that beasts cannot be rightly ruled without the guardianship of a man, in what way do we judge that men can be successfully governed by a man without the counsel and help of God? What is it that makes us complain and feel needy in such a superfluous abundance of things? What makes us envy many people, when the condition of mortals is worthy of pity rather than envy? Why do we so easily forget good things, but never the bad? And since opposites are driven out by opposites, why do we try to cure evils with evils? Why do we often hope to arrive at glory? We admire virtue in another, but we strive to *appear* admirable ourselves rather than to *be* so. The vice of another is displeasing, yet we hardly think about how we might not be displeasing to ourselves and others.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino writes to his colleagues about the inherent contradictions and follies of human life, contrasting the care people take for external objects with the neglect of their own souls. He uses the classical figures of Democritus and Heraclitus to illustrate the absurdity and tragedy of the human condition.</summary>

We close our ears to the truth, and we lay them open to lies. What shall I say of those who, captured by the love of someone or something—whether a person or an object—hold themselves in hatred, and desert themselves to pursue something else? O madmen, o wretched ones! Since you cannot grasp things belonging to others except through yourselves, by what means will you ever grasp external things if you have lost your internal ones? Why do you seek good things far away among strangers, when they are near, or rather, when they are within you? 

And I am often also accustomed to marvel at this, Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a famous humanist scholar and member of Ficino’s Platonic Academy.</note>: for what reason do we fear only one death—namely, that which is the end of dying—but do not fear our daily deaths at all? Certainly, at every moment the temperament of the body is altered, and the past life ends <note>Ficino refers to the Heraclitean idea that we are constantly changing and "dying" to our former selves every second.</note>. Finally, as it seems to me, because we practice virtues falsely but practice vices in reality, for that reason, as much as it is within us, we turn out to be falsely happy but truly miserable. Democritus laughed at these things, Heraclitus wept for them, Socrates wished to cure them, but only God can cure them. Oh, what a miserable animal man is, unless he eventually flies up above "man"—that is, unless he commends himself to God, loves God for God's sake, and loves all other things for the sake of God. This is the only solution to those problems, and the only rest from evils. Farewell.

### An exhortation to modesty and the study of literature.
### Marsilio Ficino to the high-minded Giuliano de' Medici, greetings.

**A**lthough my love toward you is such that I cannot be a perfect judge in your affairs—or rather, *our* affairs—I will nevertheless say what I feel, Giuliano, since you ask. First, I praise your prudence, because you do not rely on your own natural talent, but you consult an elder. For you know how much each person pleases himself because of natural self-love. Next, I praise a certain natural sweetness in your letter. You seem to me like certain painters: just as you always express the beauty of your eyes and the charm of your face through your gaze and your tongue, so now you have expressed them with your pen. Proceed, therefore, most sweet Giuliano! Proceed, I pray. Diligently survey the gardens—the Tusculan ones <note>original: *Tusculanos*. A reference to Cicero's "Tusculan Disputations." Ficino is encouraging Giuliano to study Cicero’s philosophy.</note>, as you have already begun. For if you graze upon the "Tullian flowers" <note>original: *Tullianos flores*. "Tullian" refers to Marcus Tullius Cicero. Ficino uses the metaphor of a bee gathering nectar to describe studying Cicero's elegant prose.</note> with annual practice, you will eventually pour forth honey. If it were permitted for me to commend your own people to you, I would most highly commend Andrea Cambini <note>A Florentine historian and associate of the Medici.</note> to you. Farewell.

### That a friend exists within the friend.
### Marsilio Ficino to the high-minded Giovanni de' Medici, greetings.

**C**ome now, Giuliano <note>Although the letter is addressed to Giovanni in the heading, Ficino addresses "Giuliano" in the text; these letters were often shared among the Medici brothers, or this may be a clerical error in the original edition.</note>, I pray you: if someone watched diligently over your affairs while you were sleeping, would you be angry with him because he did not wake you up at an inconvenient time? Or should you rather be indebted to him? You will certainly be indebted quite a bit. You are indebted also to me, who, while you were lying down, meanwhile took part in your serious business, consulted on it, and favored it. But you will say, "Why did you not summon me?" Even if I had been able to, and even if I had thought you were absent from there, I would not have summoned you, lest perhaps I be more troublesome to you. But in truth, my great love for you has long since impressed your image upon my soul. And just as I sometimes see myself outside myself in a mirror, so I very often see you inside me, in my own heart. 

Furthermore, your brother Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo the Magnificent (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note> was present then—your "other self" both by nature and by will. Therefore, since I saw this Giuliano of mine clearly, both inside and out, I could not think that he was absent from that place. It was not through any negligence, therefore, but through too much love that it happened that I did not call you then to conduct your affairs, nor did I inform you afterwards of what had been done. Do you wish to be summoned at other times, sweetest Giuliano? You must take care to be loved less. That is a difficult thing indeed, and perhaps impossible. For you would first have to take care not to be Giuliano. You will only strip away my love when you strip away yourself. What, then, shall I do in the future? Shall I call you at other times? Not at all, I think. Desire has already, for a long time, sufficiently called us both to each other and to itself. Farewell.

### The health of a friend from a friend.
### Carlo Marsupini to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, greetings.

**G**reetings, my only health <note>original: *Salue solus mea salus*. Marsupini is playing on the Latin word *salus*, which means both "health" and "salvation," as well as the greeting *salve*.</note>. For I am healthy and safe only so long as I am with you. And only then do I seem to myself to live, when I live with you. As often as I am away, so often have I perished. See to it then, my Marsilio, lest by deserting me you lose a man—or rather, kill a friend. You are always running about here and there. Now you take care of bodies here below; now you [take care of] souls above...

...you guard our souls. Meanwhile, I, a soldier, perish. If you have such great charity as you certainly have, why, I ask, do you not care for your dear Carlo by staying here? For his mind is sick from your departure, and his body is ill; his only salvation is that you return. This is now the fourth day since you left; when you have doubled the four <note>Meaning eight days total.</note>, keep your promises. Farewell.

->*A divination concerning a friend.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his friend Carlo Marsupino.<-

**Y**ou too, three and four times greetings. I seemed to myself to be reading a certain very brief oration in my sleep this dawn, in which there was such a context of words and thoughts as I have always observed to the best of my ability; thus I was unsure whether I was reading my own words or another's. A little after rising from bed, your letter was delivered to me, from which I suddenly knew in reality what I had argued in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, the *Theologia Platonica*, where he discusses the soul's ability to transcend the body during sleep.</note>: that morning dreams often contain something of prophecy. See, Marsupino, Marsilio in your own eye today, more beautiful than Marsilio himself <note>original: *in tua pupilla hodie Marsilio pulchriorem*. This is a play on the word *pupilla*, which means both "pupil of the eye" and "orphan/ward." In Neoplatonic thought, a friend sees their own soul reflected in the eye of the beloved friend.</note>. But let us dismiss these things for now. In short, your letter is such that it compels me to respond with my feet rather than my hands, and with my voice rather than letters <note>He means he would rather walk to see him and speak in person than write back.</note>. Greet Taddeo Ugolino, a religious man.

---

->*How much the longing of friends can do.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.<-

**T**heologians measure moments by eternity, natural philosophers measure motion by time, and lovers measure time by affection. For they believe that the greater the desire, the shorter the time of possession appears, but the longer the time of expectation. Therefore, you have declared how much you love me especially in your letter, in that you called the silence of a single day a "long-lasting silence," and called my letters, which flew to you most swiftly, "most long-awaited." In turn, I wish it to be known how much I love you: your letter, though I have read it ten times now, appears so brief that in almost the same moment it bids me "be well" and "farewell" <note>original: *salvere iubeat, & ualere*. In Latin, *salve* (be well) is a greeting, while *vale* (be strong) is the standard word for goodbye. Ficino is playing on the fact that he doesn't want the letter to end.</note>. These two things are contradictory in love. When others are told to "farewell," they are understood to be safe; but when lovers hear "farewell," they hear it badly—indeed, as an evil. Therefore, you make me rejoice when you say "be well," but at the same time you make me grieve when you command me "farewell." Yet you seem to command both at once. I would certainly write more, perhaps even better things. But distracted for your sake by these clashing emotions, I can neither write more at present, nor write better. May you both be well and farewell. March 21, 1474. Florence.

---

->*It is better to praise benevolence than genius.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric poet, sends greetings.<-

**A**ngelo, I had taken up my pen to extol your "Homeric Muse" <note>A reference to Poliziano’s famous Latin translation of the *Iliad*.</note> to the heavens with wonderful praises as much as I could, but suddenly Cupid interrupted me thus: "What are you doing, foolish Ficino? Will you always be occupied with praises of the Muse? Praise me, Philosopher, if you wish to praise without suspicion of flattery. If you celebrate the Polizian Muse, you celebrate Angelo alone; if you celebrate Cupid, you celebrate Angelo and Marsilio together. For I am the love common to you both; I cherish both, and am cherished by both." These things that god said to me, Angelo; but I said to him: "The Polizian Muse is truthful; she has never compelled me to lie. But you, perjured Love, force me to lie every day. Yesterday I so loved Poliziano’s delights that I swore I could not love them more vehemently in the future; yet today I love them so much again that I swear I did not love them enough yesterday, and I affirm that I cannot love more ardently tomorrow than today—and that 'tomorrow' deludes me similarly every day." My love is always full-grown—who would believe it?—and yet always a youth; let it grow young as it pleases, provided it does not grow old. But listen, Cupid: Venus is not the mother of love, but Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry; Ficino argues that their friendship is born from their shared love of literature and poetry.</note>; the Muse fosters this love diligently, it grows constantly; let it grow with this fuel forever, even if it be perjured. This is not a vice in love. Thus, Angelo, I both ought to and wish to cherish our common love and your Muse together. You, adore the Muse herself, the mother of love and glory. March 21, 1473.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->Whom love deceives, and whom it does not.<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to that true man, Niccolò Michelozzi.<-

**T**oday, Niccolò, I wrote letters to Lorenzo de' Medici and Angelo Poliziano <note>Poliziano was a brilliant poet and scholar in the Medici circle; Michelozzi was Lorenzo the Magnificent's private secretary.</note> that were, I know not how, quite amorous in nature. It should be no surprise if they seem rather foolish, for love itself is a foolish thing. Do you wish me to play the fool a third time? You wish it, and so I am willing, but I shall be brief. For me, Niccolò, nothing is greater than the fact that I love, and nothing is better than the fact that I am loved, especially by men most worthy of love. Perhaps, on account of love, I might occasionally speak with less than total truth, but concerning love itself, I can speak nothing but the truth. Love does not deceive me when I have exercised judgment before I began to love. Love that follows judgment does not blind; it is only the love that precedes it that does so. Love sometimes sees nothing, and sometimes sees too much. To what end do I say this? You understand. For you are especially skilled in matters of love, being the most affectionate of all men. Commend me and my dear Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino’s closest friend and the "hero" of his *De Amore* (Commentary on Plato's Symposium).</note> to Lorenzo de' Medici. And look after his health with the greatest diligence, for his is a life that belongs to the public. Farewell. 21 March 1478. Florence.

->A recommendation based on poverty and merit.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Matteo Palmieri, the Theologian.<-

**A**lthough I know for certain that men of letters require no recommendation to win the "palm of the Muses" <note>A play on words with the recipient's name, Palmieri.</note> from you, nevertheless, to satisfy the duty of friendship, I most highly recommend to you Luca of San Gimignano. He was once my teacher, along with Comando, in the study of grammar. I owe him as much as the ability to speak with excellence through art is superior to merely pouring out empty words by chance. You ought to favor him for two reasons: because he is in need, and because he deserves it. To do good for the needy is the duty of the merciful; to do so for the deserving is the duty of the just. I know that you are accustomed to being both merciful and just. Farewell.

->Since all things are well-governed by God, everything should be accepted for the better.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Bishop Campano, the poet.<-

**D**o you too, Campano, ever laugh at the arrogance of mortals? How often I both avoid it and rebuke it before God. Neither do children grasp the counsel of old men, nor do peasants reach the thoughts of the wise. Yet man, a mere animal, often dares to hunt for the reasoning of the divine nature more pridefully than is fitting, and to speculate upon the ends of His providence. What is worse, any mortals at any age—even amidst feasts and harlots—discuss divine mysteries quite licentiously. Pythagoras rightly forbade anyone from speaking of such things without the divine light. No one, Campano, perceives divine things unless he is himself divine. For the Apostle Paul said rightly: *No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.* <note>original: "Quæ Dei sunt nullus nisi spiritus Dei cognouit." A quote from 1 Corinthians 2:11.</note> Again, no one lies more regarding divine matters than he who measures them "to the fingernail" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to measure with excessive, pedantic precision.</note>. For thus says God in Isaiah: *I will catch the wise in their own craftiness* <note>Ficino is blending Isaiah 29:14 with 1 Corinthians 3:19.</note> and elsewhere, *The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are vain.* <note>Psalm 94:11 or 1 Corinthians 3:20.</note> It ought to be enough, therefore, for a man to know that this most beautiful machine of the world depends upon and is governed by a certain single, most wise Architect. And since He is Goodness itself, nothing can proceed from Him except the good; and those things which proceed from Him cannot be governed by Him in any way other than well. Therefore, all things are to be accepted as being for the better. He who thus understands and loves divine things is divine by nature, good by art, joyful in hope, and happy in his reward. Farewell, be happy, and love me.

->On the folly of men, and what constitutes true knowledge.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Panteo Pandolfini.<-

**O**ur friend Angelo Poliziano has today "condemned" his friend Panteo to the discipline of Marsilio—or rather, to the discipline of Plato. For my part, although I am accustomed to perform a Comedy for new friends and a Satire for old ones, I shall perform a Satire for Panteo. For I wish our friendship to be born and perfected at the very same time. Consider, my Panteo, how perversely we behave. We do not easily listen to the infamous; yet we, though wicked, hope to be heard by God. We live as madmen, and we unjustly try to change God rather than changing our own morals. We wish to persuade others of good things, yet we do not persuade ourselves. We carry the good in our mouths, but evil in our hearts.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK I.</header>
<sig>Ss</sig>

Speaking of virtue, we have not heard our own sound, much like a lyre <note>Ficino often used musical metaphors; here he suggests that many talk about virtue without actually "sounding" it out or practicing it themselves.</note>. We imitate bad doctors, who do not provide for themselves the health they promise to others. Lend me your ears for a moment, dear friend, I pray. I will teach you oratory, music, and geometry both for free and in few words. Persuade yourself of what is honorable, temper the movements of your soul, and measure your strength and your actions. And you will say that is too difficult. It will not be difficult in the manner of Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher whose work on duties influenced Cicero.</note>, if you desire to live well as greedily as you desire simply to live.

### Praise of liberality, praise of alms-giving.
## Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, a Magnanimous man,

**I** shall say, my Lorenzo, what I feel, even if it perhaps seems shocking to say; but in truth it is not shocking because it is true: for nothing is more sacred than truth. I shall therefore speak what I feel freely. God, Lorenzo—God himself is for sale. But with what coin is God most especially bought? With that which he himself buys others: that is, by a certain liberal charity toward the poor. For God, with immense love, bestows all things freely upon all, and gives only to the poor. For everyone, however wealthy they may seem, are entirely destitute before God. Deservedly, by this virtue alone we buy God: since by this alone we most truly imitate him. No one who is wise, or brave, or temperate boasts that they emulate God. These virtues are but shadows of divine virtues; only the person liberal toward the poor exactly imitates Him. For the liberality of man and God in giving is the same. O most happy merchant, who for a small price redeems himself from his enemies—that is, from his vices—and at the same time buys both men and God! He will never be poor who is rich in men and in God. He who, in the midst of great wealth, often considers what it is to be poor, will never end up at the bottom; he who, established at the top, mercifully looks upon the lowest things. A small man never achieves anything better than when he humbly ascends to the heights. A great man does nothing greater than when he magnificently descends to the depths. Other virtues for the most part benefit only the one practicing them; liberality benefits the practitioner as well as others, and it is judged more excellent insofar as it spreads its duty more widely than the other virtues. For the more expansive a good is, the more divine it is. And if a wicked deed is the worst thing because it is against the nature of the good and against the society of the human race, we necessarily judge a kind deed to be the best. Other virtues are sometimes thought to stir up envy; this one alone always both kindles love and utterly extinguishes hatred and envy. It truly fulfills its duty most when it assists a person, both because of the misfortune of the needy and because of the merit of the virtuous. Sow, therefore, my Lorenzo, sow—I say—happy farmer, as you have already begun to do, with good spirit in this dry human earth, which for you will at last overflow not only with crops, but even with milk and honey. For although "man" is said to be derived from "earth" <note>original: "homo, dicatur ab humo". An etymological pun common in Latin literature.</note>, the nature of man and the earth in bearing fruit is different. He who throws seeds into barren earth suffers a loss of seeds. But he who sows in a needy person certainly sows usefully. And as He who does not lie has promised, he receives a hundred for one, and—what is more precious—one God for a hundred seeds. To what end is this? When I heard that in these holy days you had distributed many things mercifully to the poor, as you are abundantly accustomed to do—and even more than usual—I did not wish to be too sparing in praising charity, in the exercise of which you have stood out as liberal and, so to speak, lavish. 12 April 1474. Florence.

->No virtue is more lovable than kindness.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi, a true man, S. D. <note>S. D. stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "sends greetings."</note>

**I**f weeping belongs to women, Michelozzi, I confess myself to be more womanly than others. Thalia <note>The Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, associated here with a gentle or "soft" disposition.</note> gave us a soft nature. But our Laurel <note>original: "Laurus". A poetic pun on Lorenzo de' Medici's name.</note> has rendered it softest of all. I weep indeed, whether from a certain tender joy or some other wondrous affection, as often as I consider—and I consider often—how pious our Lorenzo is toward God, how merciful toward the poor, and how beneficent toward all. But the more beneficent he is to others, the more he is, in a way, "maleficent" to his Marsilio—if indeed by these benefits, or rather "harmful" deeds of his, he daily fascinates and ensnares me, poor as I am, in wondrous ways. And while he removes tears from others, he stirs up tears in me. And when he is most ardently loved by me, then he departs further away. Advise that most affectionate man, the Laurel, that he should love the things he has loved. And as soon as it is permitted, let him approach as near in presence as he has approached in love.
