<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

## Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous man Giuliano de' Medici, sends greetings.

When in recent days you provoked your friends to repentance for their sins and to tears with a certain moral speech during the nocturnal rites, some began to wail, and others beat their breasts with their palms. However, Antonio the Tuscan Poet <note>original: "Antonius autem Poëta Tuscus"; likely Antonio Pelotti, a poet in the Medici circle.</note> is said to have fallen down as if bloodless and lifeless. Shortly thereafter, you suddenly betook yourself to the Mugello mountains, so that just as you had nearly destroyed that Antonio by your presence, so you might destroy your Marsilio here by your absence. Ha! You are a man of little duty; once you spared your most cruel enemies, but now you do not spare your friends. Perhaps you have decided to live in the country for a few days so that you might return to us more greatly missed, and after your stay in the country, you might appear more sophisticated <note>The Latin "urbanior" plays on "urbs" (city), suggesting both being "more of the city" and "more refined."</note>. For you are one who knows that desire usually proceeds from lack, and admiration from novelty. 

But there is no need for this medicine, O crafty Medici <note>Ficino frequently puns on the name "Medici" and the Latin "medicus" (doctor) or "medicina" (medicine).</note>, for either you or me. For what can be seen as more sophisticated than your sophistication? What, if I may say so, do I desire more than the one I already desire? Send away these remedies, I pray, which are very troublesome to the sick and unnecessary for the moderately healthy. Let those men, my friend, be more greatly missed because of absence who, because of their constant presence, are missed less day by day. For us, however, this thirst of ours is not so much extinguished by your "false liquor" as it is inflamed. At least while you drag out your delays there with our Angelo <note>Referring to Angelo Poliziano, who often accompanied the Medici to their country villas.</note>, keep your Marsilio on your lips. Either lick him, Giuliano, or chew him. I would rather be bitten by Giuliano than spat out. Farewell.

->That the rich man is more likely to be unjust than just.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric poet, sends greetings.

God willed that the whole of the water be common to each aquatic creature, and the earth to the creatures of the earth. Only Man, an unhappy animal, has separated what God had joined. He has confined his empire, which by nature had been wide, into a narrow space. He introduced "mine" and "thine" <note>The concept of "meum et tuum" (mine and thine) was a standard legal and philosophical shorthand for the invention of private property, which many humanists viewed as the source of social strife.</note>, the beginning of all dissension and evil. For this reason, not without justice did Pythagoras decree that among friends, and Plato among citizens, all things should be held in common. 

Therefore, those rich men must be considered utterly unjust who, because of pride, forget God, the giver of all riches. They also make themselves the masters of the poor, and call themselves the "possessors" of money, when they are themselves possessed by money. On the contrary, those are just and happy who, established in the greatest riches, consider themselves the ministers of God, the guardians of the poor, and the distributors of money. You are a very fortunate youth to have recently obtained such patrons. I have had such patrons for a long time. And you will wonder, Angelo, if I say that I am most sorrowful because of the abundance of my Giuliano. Truly, unless Matteo Franco <note>Matteo Franco (1447–1494) was a priest and poet famous for his wit and "salty" humor.</note> now seasoned me with his salts <note><term>salibus</term>: A Latin pun on "sal" meaning both literal salt and "wit" or "humor."</note> during Giuliano's departure, as if I were tasteless, I would either not smell quite right to myself, or certainly I would suddenly fly toward the sweetest flowers and scents of Giuliano de' Medici. But in any case, Poliziano, I will hardly restrain myself here for three days.

->The goodness and dignity of the legal scholar.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Nicolini, son of the distinguished legal scholar Otto, and distinguished heir to his father’s art, sends greetings.

A painter who uses his art wrongly is not necessarily a bad painter on that account, but a bad man. Therefore, a good painter is not the same thing as a good man. This is because there is a great difference between moral goodness and the art of painting. And it is the same way in the other arts. But indeed, a legal scholar <note><term>iurisconsultus</term>: A professional expert in law; a jurist.</note> who uses the law in a way that is not legitimate is both a bad legal scholar and a bad man; therefore, a legitimate legal scholar is a good man and a legitimate citizen. So great is the affinity between skill in civil law and virtue in both respects. 

He who adulterates a coin—a thing truly most useful, dug from the bowels of the earth—is punished with the severest censure by the command of human law, as you know. Therefore, he who adulterates the law itself—a most precious thing sent from heaven—with what great severity is he punished by divine law? I approve of you, therefore, my Angelo, because you use the law legitimately. Proceed, I pray. Despise threats and allurements with a high mind; Almighty God, the author and teacher of the law, its end and its reward, will not desert you. Proceed, my friend, do not doubt; you will heap up riches that are incorruptible before God. Great also is the dignity of the legal scholar among men. He is a public... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "ciuium" indicates the sentence likely concludes "public [servant] of the citizens."</note>

### The dignity of the priest.

Marsilio Ficino to Pace Sacerdote <note>original: "Paci Sacerdoti"; Pace Sacerdote was a professor of Canon Law and a friend of Ficino.</note>, professor of Canon Law, sends greetings.

**O**ften I and Richard Angelleri <note>original: "Ricciardus Angellerius"; a noted theologian and contemporary of Ficino.</note>, a distinguished theologian, have discussed together the dignity of the priest. We concluded, finally, that just as nothing is better than a good Angel after God, and nothing worse than a bad one, so nothing on earth is more beautiful than an honorable priest, and nothing more foul than a base one. The former is the salvation of religion and of men; the latter is a plague. What is a legitimate priest but a mind dedicated to God? An Angel acting in the place of God among men. A living temple of God. He who rightly considers the dignity of the priesthood will not abuse the priesthood. Let us reflect, therefore, on what it is to be a legitimate priest. For it is almost this: to be a God. Indeed, a priest is a kind of temporal God, while God is the eternal Priest.

### Holy orders are not to be given to just anyone.

Marsilio Ficino to Martino, Bishop of Cortona <note>Martino Ghini, Bishop of Cortona from 1455 to 1477.</note>, sends greetings.

**S**ebastiano Salvini <note>original: "Bastianus Saluinus"; Ficino’s cousin and a dedicated student who helped transcribe his works.</note>, our kinsman, comes to you having requested the third mystery of holy orders and, as I believe, being about to receive them. But you, who do not know the man and know that what is sacred must not be given to dogs, will perhaps say: "O Marsilio, it is necessary that he who is to perform such a great office be literate, pious toward God, and just toward men. Who will testify or stand surety that this young man will be such a person?" I answer you, venerable father, with that saying of Socrates: "As a vessel is known by its sound, so is a man." And so, to a certain person passing by who was silent, he said: "Speak, stranger, so that I may see you," as one who judged that the soul alone is the man. Furthermore, if you possessed the art of Zopyrus <note>A famous physiognomist of antiquity who claimed to be able to judge a person's character from their physical appearance.</note>, I would perhaps add that you should consider his natural disposition. But the Master of Life forbids a man to be judged according to his face. Do you seek a guarantor? You have Marsilio. Do you wish for one more substantial? The Bishop of Volterra <note>Filippo Sacramoro, then Bishop of Volterra.</note> stands as surety. The young man was educated in the household of both.

### No harmony delights more than that of heart and tongue.

Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous man Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

**S**ebastiano Foresi <note>original: "Bastianus Foresius"; a Florentine poet and friend of the Medici circle.</note> sends to you his poem on the triumph of virtues over vices, a work worthy of such a great title. Read the poem, Lorenzo, and choose the poet: for in his soul, too, the virtues triumph over the vices. No dissonance offends more, nor does any harmony delight more, than that of the heart and the tongue.

### On the duty of a citizen.

Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero <note>original: "Petro Hero"; Pietro Nero was a member of a prominent Florentine family and a student of Ficino.</note>, sends greetings.

**T**ell me, Pietro, why, when a fever invaded your uncle Bernardo, did it suddenly approach me? Or is it perhaps because we are so close that the Dog Star <note>Sirius, associated with the "dog days" of summer heat and fever.</note> could not vomit its flames into one without setting the other on fire? May he recover quickly, so that Marsilio may recover—indeed, so that Florence may be better off. If she always had such Doctors as she has in him and in the Medici <note>Ficino here plays on the name "Medici" and the Latin "medicus," meaning doctor.</note>, she would never be seriously ill. For these men rightly perform the duty of a citizen, without which the good health of the fatherland is not preserved. Moreover, it is the duty of a citizen to consider the city as a single animal, constituted of citizens as its parts. And the part ought to serve the whole, not the whole the part. For when only the benefit of the part is sought, the benefit of both—that is, the part and the whole—is utterly lost. But when the good of the whole is sought, the good of both is preserved. Therefore, a citizen ought to remember that nothing, whether good or evil, can happen to any member of the city without pertaining to the other members due to a certain connection, and to the whole; and again, nothing can happen to the whole body of the city without soon pertaining to the individual members of this animal. Therefore, let no one in this urban family say, "this is mine" and "that is yours": for everything in this huge animal...

...are in some way common. But let him call this or that "mine" not by personal possession, but rather by affection and concern; let each man love and honor his country as he would a parent. As a private citizen, let him obey the ancient and proven laws as if they were God. For laws of this kind are not established without God. Let the magistrate remember that he is no less subject to the laws than the private citizen is to the magistrates. Let him understand that when he judges, he is being judged by God. Let him always keep Plato’s precept <note>original: "Platonis præceptum"; referring to the principle in Plato's *Republic* that a ruler must seek the good of the whole state rather than a faction or themselves.</note> before his eyes: that he should look not to himself, but to the city; not to some part of the city alone, but to the whole. Finally, let him know that the best place in the heavenly homeland is reserved for the one who has, to the best of his ability, arranged his earthly homeland according to the heavenly model. For nothing is more pleasing to the common King of the world than the common good. I believe you know these and similar things pertaining to a legitimate citizen, and I hope you will observe them, since you do not lack learning or prudence, and moreover you have a teacher in this matter at home who is sufficient—about whose virtues I shall speak elsewhere. Our Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>original: "Ioannes Caualcantes"; Ficino’s closest friend and "unique soul," who often acted as a patron and intermediary for his work.</note> commends himself to you.

### What it is to live well.

->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Girolamo Pasqualino <note>original: "Hieronymo Pasqualino"; a Venetian jurist and associate of the Platonic Academy.</note>, sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou ask what it means to live well. Nothing more useful can be asked. To live well is to understand the truth, to deliberate well, to will the good, and to perform good deeds. The first belongs to wisdom, the second to prudence, the third to justice, and the fourth to perseverance. The first is from God; the second is from the first; the third is from God and man together; and the fourth is from the third. Those who live this way live as humans; those who live otherwise live as animals. Farewell, and live as a human.

### Vows are not to be despised.

->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher, the excellent Francesco Marescalco of Ferrara <note>original: "Francisco Marescalcho Ferrariensi"; a courtier to the Este family and a friend of Ficino.</note>, sends greetings.<-

**I** have not yet finished my book *On the Christian Religion* <note>original: "de Christiana religione"; Ficino's major apologetic work defending Christianity through the lens of Platonism.</note>, Francesco, because while I was revising it this August, I fell into a fever—specifically, a daily one. Perhaps Saturn was threatening me this year; he was in Aquarius, the ascendant of my birth, from the start, and during these times he is in Cancer, the sixth house of my birth <note>Ficino refers to his astrological chart: the "sixth house" traditionally governs illness and health.</note>. Let us set aside celestial matters for now, for there are those who think little of such things; let us come to super-celestial matters. Listen, then, to what happened to me during this illness: I sank at one point into such weakness, Marescalco, that I almost despaired of my health. I therefore meditated upon all the great things I had read over thirty years, to see if anything might occur to me that could console a sick soul. Human writers, with the exception of the Platonists, contributed absolutely nothing; but the works of Christ <note>original: "Christi autem opera"; referring to the Gospels and Christian scripture.</note> consoled me much more than the words of the philosophers. Furthermore, I made vows to the Blessed Mary and asked for some sign of recovery. Suddenly I breathed a little easier, and in my dreams I received a clear message of health. Therefore, I owe my soul and body not to Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine; it was traditional to sacrifice a cock to him upon recovery.</note> by a cock, but to Christ and his Mother. Everything should always be interpreted for the best, Marescalco. What if God wished to warn me through this sign during my illness to confirm the doctrine of Christ with sharper wit and study hereafter? Especially since a few days later, I was also freed from a burning in my urine by a similar vow. Listen, if you please, to another thing, both marvelous and true. My father, Ficino the surgeon <note>original: "Ficinus chirurgicus"; Diotifeci d'Agnolo, the personal physician to Cosimo de' Medici.</note>, who was singular in his age at Florence, was once led by a certain peasant named Pasquino to treat his son, Thomas, whose head had been most seriously wounded. The physician, having inspected the incurable wound and thinking the boy would undoubtedly perish shortly thereafter, withdrew from there as if not intending to return. The parents of the sick child, abandoned by the physician, humbly begged the Blessed Mary for their son's health. Therefore, at the very hour they were praying, a certain woman appeared to Ficino while he was on his way, sitting under an oak tree—either yawning or certainly sleeping very lightly. She was of a truly venerable appearance and addressed him thus: "Why are you ungrateful toward God, Ficino? Those things which you have received freely from Him, you do not give freely." He replied, "I give bread daily to beggars." She added, "Lavishly bestow the gifts of your art also upon the needy." After three days, that peasant returned to the physician, praying that he would return to treat his son. Ficino was greatly amazed by this, for he thought the boy had died. He went for free, prompted both by the past dream and by the vow of the parents. For the peasant told him what vows he had made, and at what hour. Finally, the boy recovered his health beyond the physician's expectation or his art of healing. From that time on, Ficino often [acted] for their health...

### *The nobility, utility, and practice of medicine.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Thomas Valerius <note>Tommaso Valori, a Florentine statesman and close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note>, an distinguished physician, greetings.<-

**I** read in Homer: "A physician is worth many other men," and rightly so. For the sacred Hebrew scriptures teach that the faculty of healing is a gift of God rather than a human invention: "Honor the physician, for the Most High created him for necessity" <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1.</note>. Furthermore, the Gentiles <note>A common term for the ancient Greeks and Romans in this period.</note> maintain that the authors of this art were gods. These same people honored Apollo, Aesculapius, and exceptional physicians with divine honors; for they dedicated shrines to Chiron, Machaon, Podalirius, Hippocrates, and Hermagoras. Hippocrates confirmed this in his Letter to the Abderites, saying that medicine is a gift of the gods and is free, and that he never accepted payment for its use. In his Letter to Philemon, he also says: Medicine is close to prophecy; for these two arts have one parent, namely Apollo, who is our progenitor; he both predicts future illnesses and cures those who are afflicted with ill health. For this reason, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Apollonius of Tyana are said to have cured diseases not so much with herbs as with songs <note>original: "carminibus"; this refers to incantations or rhythmic chants believed to have therapeutic effects by harmonizing the spirit.</note>. And the Magi <note>Referring to the ancient Persian philosopher-priests.</note> believed that the soul of the sick person must be purged with sacred reasonings and prayers before the body. This is because an art of this kind is both received from God and practiced by divine power. Since the soul depends on God, the body depends on the soul. Do not the Hebrews believe that the Archangel Raphael practiced the work of this art? Setting aside the rest, Christ himself, as the Physician of the human race, cured the sick and infirm—as many as were presented to him—and handed the power of healing to his disciples. Therefore, because this art is most noble, kings in former times by no means disdained to study and practice it. Such were Shapur <note>original: "Sabor"; likely Shapur I or II, Sassanid kings of Persia.</note> and Ginges, kings of the Medes, Sabid the king of the Arabs, Mithridates the king of the Persians, Hermes the king of the Egyptians, and Mesue <note>A famous name in medieval medicine, referring to the Persian/Syriac physician Masawaih.</note>, the grandson of the king of Damascus. Some also believe that Avicenna was a Prince of Cordoba. Democritus, Timaeus of Locri, Plato, and Aristotle—most illustrious philosophers—wrote on this art, as did countless other noble philosophers.

As much has been said regarding the nobility of medicine as a letter almost allows. But how great its utility is, we perceive from the fact that the arts directed toward living well seem to be of little use without its help. For we cannot live well unless we are alive, nor can we progress much in any faculty in this very short span of life unless we are in good health, nor can we easily deserve much from men or God unless we live a long and sober life. Indeed, the diligence of medicine provides every such capacity. However, one must use this art with the highest piety toward God and charity toward men. Just as Luke the Evangelist, and the divine physicians Cosmas and Damian <note>Saints Cosmas and Damian were famous "unmercenary" physicians who healed for free.</note> taught us by their example. For God is the author of all good things, and a legitimate physician is like a certain god among men. For he restores them to life from death, and is honored like a god even by kings and wise men when they are sick. 

All confess that a physician needs sharp wit, learning, and experience; no one doubts that he also needs gravity and diligence in deliberation. But once a consultation has been maturely held, no art—as Hippocrates says to the Abderites—can be more harmed by delay than this one. Yet it is no less, and indeed more dangerous, as Galen says to Glaucon, to anticipate and hinder nature. For he says that many are lost daily through this error—that is, the rashness of physicians who either impede or rush nature. Indeed, he who does not trust in his own genius will more easily avoid this error. For Hippocrates writes to Democritus that although he was already in old age, he had not yet reached the end of medicine. Galen also says that when he was ninety years old, only then did he finally grasp the nature of the pulse. Above all, the physician must remember that God is the author of health, Nature is God's instrument for effecting and preserving health, and the physician is the servant of both—just as a craftsman prepares not the strength, but the material for the artisan, and removes obstacles. If the physician should want to move or stop the material prematurely, he often handles both poorly and hinders nature, which would have executed both well. But let us hear our divine Plato speaking on this matter in the *Timaeus* from the perspective of the Pythagoreans: "Of all movements, the best is that which occurs in itself..."

<summary>In this letter to Tommaso Valori, Ficino argues for the divine status of medicine, tracing its lineage from Greek gods and Hebrew prophets to Christ himself. He emphasizes that the physician's role is to serve as a humble assistant to God and Nature, warning against medical arrogance and the dangers of rushing the natural healing process.</summary>
<keywords>medicine, physician, Apollo, Hippocrates, Galen, divine healing, nature, Thomas Valerius, soul and body, medical ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the letter to Thomas Valerius regarding the nature of health and medical practice, transitioning into a personal letter to Lorenzo de' Medici about the value of time and the importance of self-care amidst political duties.</meta>

...comes from oneself. For it is most closely related to the motion of the mind and to the movement of the entire being. However, that motion which is brought about by another is inferior. The worst motion of all is when a body, lying still and at rest, is moved by others limb by limb. Therefore, the purging and regulation of all the body's constitutions that is achieved through gymnastic exercise is the most healthful. Closely following this is easy transport, whether it is performed by boat or any other vehicle. The third kind of disturbance is useful only when extreme necessity demands it; otherwise, a man of sound mind should in no way undergo that medical purging which is usually done with drugs—that is, with loosening remedies <note>original: "solutiuis medelis"; referring to laxatives or purgatives used to balance the humors.</note>. For illnesses, unless they are very dangerous, should not be provoked with drugs. 

For every constitution of diseases is, in a way, similar to the nature of living creatures. Indeed, the composition of animals is bounded by specific cycles of time from the very beginning of their generation. This same principle applies to the entire species, and every individual animal contains within itself a fated span of living from its birth, excepting those afflictions that are forced upon it. For the triangles—that is, the proportional qualities <note>Ficino is referencing Plato's *Timaeus*. In this theory, the body's physical elements are composed of geometric triangles. Health consists of these triangles being sharp and well-fitted; aging and disease occur when these triangles wear down and can no longer hold the body together.</note>—possessing power from the very beginning of each individual, hold together sufficiently for the use of life until a certain time; beyond that, life is extended for no one. This same pattern of constitution applies to ailments. If anyone contends to cut these short with drugs before the fated course of time, small illnesses usually become huge, and few become many. Therefore, diseases must be corrected and governed with diligence in diet, as much as leisure allows each person, and a troublesome evil should not be easily instigated with drugs. 

These are the words of Plato. The Florentine people often praise our Galen because he followed this rule. I also highly praise Lorenzo Marcellinus <note>Lorenzo Lorenzi (Marcellini), a prominent Florentine physician and professor who was a close friend of Ficino.</note>, a true physician, for this reason. I would also highly praise Thomas Valerius, were I not writing to him. Farewell, and give my best regards to Antonio Benivieni <note>A famous Florentine physician (1443–1502) and a pioneer in the use of autopsy to determine the cause of death.</note>, a good doctor. Our companion Girolamo Amati <note>A member of Ficino’s inner circle, known for his interests in both medicine and music.</note> greets you; he is a great delight in his devotion to both medicine and the study of the lute <note>original: "citharae"; Ficino used "Orphic" music played on a stringed instrument as a form of psychological and spiritual therapy.</note>.

->Time must be spent sparingly.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.<-

**G**reetings a thousand times, my health and salvation after God <note>original: "mea post Deum salus"; Ficino uses "salus" to mean both physical health and spiritual safety, acknowledging Lorenzo as his protector.</note>. I thought it a sin that as soon as my hand could guide a pen, I should write to anyone else before my sole Patron. What, then, should I write most especially? I would certainly write more serious things to you now, if it were permitted, than I am accustomed. "Not always do the orchards and humble tamarisks delight" <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (4.2), signaling a transition to a more elevated or serious topic.</note>. But what stands in the way, Marsilio, of it being permitted at this present time? Since you are about to write to him who not only permits it, but has already commanded it of you in his own letters. 

Lorenzo, in this illness of mine, nothing afflicted my mind more sharply than the memory of time spent uselessly; on the other hand, nothing remained to console me even a little except the memory of those things I had learned, though I have not learned much. For the divine mind is truly delighted, nourished, and increased by the divine food of truth alone. Other delusions of fleeting trifles do not fill the immortal mind, which by a certain natural instinct demands things eternal and immense. 

I beseech you, therefore, my dearest Patron, by the eternal God, to spend the most precious and tiny moment of this very brief time sparingly and prudently, lest you one day regret your extravagance and irreparable loss in vain. The loss of time frequently brought Theophrastus <note>The successor to Aristotle, who famously lamented that humans die just as they begin to become wise.</note> to tears when he was eighty years old; the loss of time often forced the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici the Elder (1389–1464), Lorenzo's grandfather, who provided Ficino with the villa at Careggi and the resources to translate Plato.</note>, when he was over seventy, to sigh heavily in my presence. 

Against empty cares, unnecessary games, and non-essential business, I pray you cast that Socratic saying: "Get far away from here, you sacrilegious enemies! Depart as quickly as possible, you thieves of my soul, lest I be forced to depart from myself!" These things gradually steal you from yourself and lead a great man captive—a man born to command. Redeem yourself, I beg you, from this wretched captivity while you can; you can only do it today; today, for the first time, be under your own jurisdiction. Believe me, it is not the mark of a wise man to say, "I shall live [tomorrow]." Tomorrow's life is too late; live today. 

What I ask is easy, Lorenzo. It is not difficult to spend one hour rightly and usefully. I pray you, use one hour well every day—that is, to nourish the mind with liberal disciplines—and for that tiny bit of time, live happily for yourself. For the rest, if you wish, live for others; for, as you know, you must often live for others if you wish to live for yourself. But do both by the grace of God. Indeed, you were created first for the grace of God, and then for your own sake and the sake of others. Indulge only rarely and briefly in games and jokes.

# LETTERS. BOOK I.

For I know whereof I speak: God has ordained you for greater, or rather, for the greatest things. And false delights of this kind vanish as quickly as a flash of lightning; as soon as they are seen to rise, they turn into their opposite. But do not promise me "tomorrow" any longer; you promise what you neither possess, nor know if you will ever have. If you were only to eat or drink tomorrow, friend, would you not perish within three days? Let that "tomorrow" perish today; let it perish as soon as possible, lest you yourself perish. Nothing is more deceptive than that "tomorrow"—it has deceived all men whom the earth has ever brought forth. 

Alas, what are you doing, foolish Ficino? Behold, either Lorenzo will knit his brows, or he will laugh. Either is an evil. Rather, both are good. For I know the character of physicians: from a good man, nothing proceeds but good. However, I warn not so much Lorenzo as Marsilio <note>Ficino is referring to himself in the third person here, a common rhetorical device in his letters.</note> and all other mortals in this letter. We all suffer most severely from this disease: "It will happen tomorrow." We barely possess the present time; for we hold it so lightly that we are unable to retain it even for a moment. But the future is nothing; therefore, no one possesses the future. O madmen, O wretched ones! We cast our hopes into nothingness, and we always misuse the treasure we actually possess. Yet we wish to use rightly that which we do not possess at all. Thus nearly all of us are sick unto death. Therefore, one should not seek Galen or Hippocrates <note>The most famous physicians of antiquity; Ficino implies that physical medicine cannot cure the soul's procrastination.</note>, but Aesculapius and Apollo <note>The gods of healing and light; a transition to spiritual and divine remedy.</note>. 

Fare well today; if you fare well only tomorrow, you will never fare well. But I wish this letter to be sealed with this seal: neither listen to flatterers, nor ever heed detractors, with whom every great house abounds. The former try to tear out the eyes of your mind; the latter try to cut off your hands—that is, your friends. God himself will finally destroy the lie, but he will protect the truth. Trust in God alone, Lorenzo; I too trust in God. Again, fare well today.

->*A human being without religion is more unhappy than the beasts.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Benedict Collucius of Pistoia, Rhetorician, Greetings.

**Y**ou urge me to continue diligently in the defense of religion, just as I have begun. I will indeed attempt this to the best of my strength, Benedict. Not because religion needs defenders of this sort—for it stands forever against its unwilling enemies under the guidance of God, who wishes to be honored among all nations—but because only then do I seem to myself to live happily, nay, only then to live at all, when I write, or speak, or think about divine things. 

Indeed, I believe that if divine worship were removed, the human race would be more unhappy than all the animals. I set aside the constant and manifold care of this defenseless, weak, and always-ailing little body; I speak of the very inquiry of reason, which is seen to make us superior to the beasts. This reason itself, I say, because of repentance for the past, fear of the future, anxiety for the present, the contemplation of evils, and the insatiable desire for innumerable things, would undoubtedly render us more wretched than the beasts if divine hope were taken away. Blessed are the heavenly beings, who know all things as if in light. Secure are the beasts, who understand nothing at all, as if in darkness. Anxious and wretched are men, who dwell in a kind of middle mist; they stumble and are troubled. Only the divine light, by the merit of piety and the gift of mercy, can bestow truth and blessedness upon us.

->*Response to the letter concerning the frugal spending of time.*<-

### Lorenzo de' Medici to Marsilio Ficino, Platonic Philosopher, Greetings.

**Y**our letter was most delightful to me; it rebuked the loss of past time in us in such a way that it did not seem our leisure was entirely useless. For it has happened that, through the private loss of a small amount of time, those precepts have flowed from you which can benefit not only us, but all those who suffer from the same disease. You had indeed often declared your mind toward us. But within myself, I have often considered that this letter of yours seems to have surpassed every other duty of friendship in its goodwill—whether because you hold the first place in love toward us and far excel others in friendship, or because you are able to provide those gifts of friendship abundantly which others cannot. 

Others, to be sure, who pursue us with benevolence, can help either with riches, honors, or pleasures—all of which are established in the power of Fortune, so that we have nothing firm, nothing more constant than their weakness and volatility, as you have often taught and we have even more often experienced. But you abound in these precepts, and you deal with us in such a kind of friendship that it easily appears that, just as you yield to none of your friends in virtue, so you surpass the rest in love. You do this indeed through a certain natural beneficence of yours. You do it, moreover, because it does not escape you, under this condition...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

virtues have been given by the immortal God to men under the condition that they help as many as possible, and you cannot be led to abuse this divine generosity. I rejoiced wonderfully that you have recovered your former health. I would rejoice much more if I could achieve through your letters the restoration of my own former mental health—which I certainly do not despair of, both because of your very serious precepts and because, as you know, I wander <note>original: "deliro"; Ficino often uses this to mean wandering from the path of reason or focus</note> not out of malice, but rather out of a certain natural ease and habit. But your role is that of the Apostle: to reprove, rebuke, and exhort; <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 4:2, "reprove, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching."</note> and since you understand that I am moved by things of this kind, do not cease to use all those stimuli with us by which you think our prostrate mind can best be raised. This one thing I strive for from you and expect: that no one wishes it for you more gladly, nor advises you more wisely. I congratulate you again, and myself, that the immortal God has restored you to us safe and sound. I was no less warned by the danger to your life than you were. For the same fate would have snatched the darkness from your eyes and the light from ours. Indeed, nothing can illuminate our life more than your most serious and loving admonitions and your most pleasant company. If these were extinguished, the other part of our life would be utterly extinguished—and indeed that part without which whatever remains is not worth a trifle. Warned by this danger, I shall enjoy you more gladly and more often; and since the human condition is such that it is moved more by examples than by reasons, I shall use both you and time by this law: time, as if having no tomorrow; and you, as a man for whom not even a moment of time remains free from the fear of death. Farewell, and take care of your health. Florence, October 10, 1474.

->To no one who rightly wills is the path to the good entirely closed.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi, <term>a true man</term> <note>original: "uero uiro"; a play on "vir" meaning both man and one who possesses "virtus" (virtue/courage)</note>, greetings.

**M**ichelozzi, those who confute someone usually do so by contradicting them. However, when Lorenzo de' Medici agrees with me most, he then most strongly confutes me. Namely, while he most skillfully praises my letter—in which I reprove his past waste of time—it seems he has not spent even a moment of his life unprofitably. But if our patron, Niccolò, is such in his negligence that he seems to have been diligent, how do you think he will turn out if he wishes and is able to be more diligent? I pray that he may indeed wish this; and I beseech God that he may be able. Although, there is not so much need to beseech God that he may be able as that he may wish it. Firstly, because to no one who rightly wills is the path to the good entirely closed. Secondly, because God listens to an honorable will rather than to the entreaties of words. Farewell, and exhort Lorenzo to diligence, so that in a short time he may surpass the Latins in learning as much as he surpasses his fellow citizens in authority without controversy.

->Imitation is better than reading.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.

**J**ust as harmony, while it glides into our ears in person, affects us more vehemently than when it is thought of as past, and as a battle moves us more sharply when it is watched than when it is narrated: so the outstanding works of illustrious men inflame us more ardently toward virtue, and shape us more exactly, than the words of orators and philosophers disputing about morals. For nature is so arranged that things themselves have much greater power than their names. And the truth of things itself moves the soul more effectively than what is merely probable or false. For this reason, the imitation of Socratic manners has instructed more people in virtue, and more truly, than Aristotle's discipline concerning morals. And Christ alone, by his example, has benefited more people more greatly toward an honorable and holy life than all the orators and philosophers have with their words. I praise you, therefore, my Lorenzo, that you do not despise moral reading. Yet, you should far prefer imitation to reading, as a living thing; especially since you long ago set before yourself that old man to be imitated—the one judged by a decree of the Senate to be the <term>Father of the Fatherland</term> <note>original: "Patrem patriae"; a title bestowed on Cosimo de' Medici in 1465, modeled on the Roman title given to Cicero and Augustus</note>. I speak of the Great Cosimo, your grandfather, my patron, a man prudent above others, pious toward God, just and magnificent toward men, temperate in himself; very diligent in his private affairs, and much more accurately circumspect in the Republic; who lived not for himself alone, but for God and his country; in whose soul, among men, nothing...

Ficino also discusses the stewardship of time with Lorenzo's secretary, Niccolò Michelozzi, praising Lorenzo's inherent virtue while urging continued diligence.</summary>

...nothing more humble, yet nothing more exalted. I, Lorenzo, spent more than twelve years happily philosophizing together with him <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Lorenzo's grandfather and Ficino’s patron.</note>; he was as sharp in disputation as he was prudent and strong in governing. I owe much indeed to our Plato, but I confess I owe no less to Cosimo. For the <term>Idea</term><note>Ficino uses "Idea" in the Platonic sense: the perfect, eternal form of a virtue.</note> of virtues which Plato had shown me once, Cosimo practiced every day. I pass over the other good qualities of this man; Cosimo was as greedy and frugal with his time as Midas was with his money. And since he spent his days most sparingly and counted his hours with great care—a man most greedy for moments—he frequently lamented the loss of hours. Finally, imitating the philosopher Solon <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, known for his wisdom and for saying he learned something new every day until he died.</note>, although he had philosophized excellently throughout his whole life even in the midst of the highest affairs, he philosophized most of all during those days in which he passed from this shadow into the light. And so, after we read Plato’s book on the single principle of things and the highest good—as you know, for you were present—he died shortly thereafter, as if he were already about to possess in reality that very Good which he had tasted in discussion. Farewell, and just as God formed Cosimo according to the Idea of the world, so may He shape you, as you have begun, according to the Idea of Cosimo.

->Endure, and save yourselves for favorable times.<-
<note>original: "Durate, & uosmet rebus seruate secundis"; a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.207), a famous exhortation to perseverance.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Salviati, Archbishop of Pisa, greetings.

**I** sent a letter to you last summer in which I urged you greatly to have confidence, affirming that you were not born for small or mediocre things. At that time, you possessed things that were small in relation to your merit, though great in spirit. Behold, now by God’s favor you have attained "mediocre" things. For those things which appear greatest to almost everyone else are but mediocre to my Salviati. Therefore, great things await you hereafter, if any faith is to be placed in Marsilio, or rather in God. It is still both pleasing and permitted to prophesy in this way. Truly, when divine providence created you Archbishop of Pisa, it declared me a prophet. I am uncertain, therefore, which of us is more to be congratulated: you as the Archbishop, or me as the prophet—perhaps both equally. For since all things are common among friends, whether I prophesy for you or you rule, I rule along with you. Farewell, be happy, and I pray you care for your health most diligently; for thus I see that the Florentine Priesthood, which has long been lifeless, will soon breathe again. How vehemently and how frequently our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and a member of the Platonic Academy.</note> congratulates me on this matter a letter cannot contain; grasp it in your mind. Again, farewell and be happy.

### The divinity of the soul from its power of discovery.

**H**itherto I have spoken quite religiously in a certain temple of the Christian religion with you, most religious Lorenzo. And I spoke through God in such a way that I did not notice the need for a letter. Today, for the first time after the sacred discourses were finished and I left the temple, I recognized that I now stand in need of a letter’s help. Rise up then, my letter, rise up. Be present; today you must carry pious greetings to him through whom Florence is safe.

## Marsilio Ficino to his dear Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.

**O** truly wonderful thing, or rather, too absurd! How can this be, best Lorenzo? I began a little while ago, as it seemed to me, quite beautifully. Now, suddenly after the greeting, all my focus fails. Perhaps, Marsilio, this is the highest "health" <note>original: "salus"; Ficino plays on the double meaning of "salus" as both "health/salvation" and the "greeting" at the start of a letter.</note>: to find nothing at all beyond health itself. But truly, it is not health, I think, to be deprived of <term>invention</term> <note>original: "inuentione"; in rhetoric, the art of "finding" or "discovering" what to say.</note>. Will you then carry nothing further, you destitute letter? Nay, I want a few more things from you. For behold, I have meanwhile found something else to be carried, though perhaps this very thing is ridiculous: namely, the fact that I find nothing. Halt your step, letter, and take this as well. I have found a third thing: that I just now recognized my power of discovery was failing because I am usually accustomed to finding many things. But do not hurry; take a fourth point if you please: that from abundance, poverty is often recognized, just as a privation is known by the habit of its opposite. Do you want a fifth? Turn the tables of Logic: for from poverty, as if from a privation, the appetite for abundance arises and is increased. But behold, a sixth point sprouts somehow in my presence: that since appetite draws its natural origin from poverty, it is always poor. Yet—and this can be called the seventh—the human soul is never truly destitute, for it generates abundance even from poverty, and weaves a discovery out of the very lack of discovery.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...from the shadowy ends of the earth, he digs out the brightness of silver and the radiance of gold. This is surely the "land of the living" <note>original: "terra uiuentium"; a common biblical and philosophical metaphor for the realm of eternal truths or the soul's true home</note>, in which the goodness of God is seen; the eternal land of the soul, I say, whose fruit is never-failing and whose motion is perpetual. Therefore, this letter asks us a thousand times to cultivate this land. It will provide us with the most abundant, incorruptible, and sweetest fruits. But I do not wish to weigh down the little back of this letter with a heavier burden. Farewell now, you cheeky letter. And after you have given my greetings, bid the Medici <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note> to be well and happy, and ask him to return.

### A new work pleases its maker too much.
#### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, greetings.

> This letter to Lorenzo was just being born, and immediately upon its birth, it began to flatter me too much, as usually happens. But a little later, after I had considered it further, it pleased me less. Yet, whatever its quality, it belongs to the Medici. I, however, as a just man, return to each what is theirs. If anything particularly terrible from the writings of schoolmasters should come into your hands during these years, read that to Lorenzo first; then, immediately after, read him my letter, so that when compared to the worst, it may cause less offense. But hey, I beg you, read it elegantly—partly with a sweet voice, partly with a "well-rounded mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo"; a classical rhetorical term meaning polished or eloquent speech</note>—so that perhaps, deceived by such a veneer, he might praise it a little. Or at least he might say: "At least Marsilio sent something; I prefer foolish servants to lazy ones, and even lazy ones to none at all." As for your recommendation of Giovanni Pietro of Padua to me, I accept it gladly. For Philosophy herself also recommends him to me, since he wishes to be a philosopher as much by nature as by study. Farewell.

---

### On perseverance.
#### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Alvito, greetings.

> Those who seize us by the neck or the hands drag the body; those who catch us with their eyes drag our senses; but those who catch us by our ears and hearing drag our soul and mind. You have just now captured my soul through my ears. For such great things concerning your elegance and constancy have sounded in my ears through the words of our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and frequent character in his dialogues</note> that I have neither been able nor willing to restrain myself from loving and esteeming you greatly. Let this letter be a sign of our love for the present; let it approve of your constancy and exhort you to perseverance, for one cannot exist without the other. Among the prudent, no man is seen as sufficiently proven if fortune has not yet sufficiently tested him. Nor is he proven enough by fortune unless he has persevered right to the end. How great a good perseverance is can be seen by this: that while other virtues promise good things, perseverance delivers them. Indeed, the more difficult it is, the more it is to be praised above the rest. But do not let the difficulty frighten you, for all the labors of human virtue are very brief, while the reward is eternal. Add to this that the burning purpose of a clear mind illuminates dark things, warms cold things, softens hard things, and tames the untamable. Farewell.

---

### It belongs to the wise man to desire nothing except the health of the soul and good health of the body.
#### Marsilio Ficino to his friend Andrea Cambini, greetings.

> There are many mortals, Andrea, who are so greedy that they desire many and various things daily—indeed, they desire innumerable things like insatiable men. My friend Cambini, however, as one who is prudent and moderate, desires (I believe) nothing other than the health of the soul and the good health of the body. Therefore, "be healthy" <note>original: "Salue"; also means "be saved" or "greetings"</note> and "farewell" <note>original: "Vale"; also means "be strong" or "be healthy"</note> at the same time.

---

### On Music.
#### Marsilio Ficino to the learned and prudent Antonio Canisiano, greetings.

> You ask, Canisiano, why I so frequently mix the studies of Medicine and Music together. "What business," you say, "do drugs have with the lyre?" The astronomers, Canisiano, would perhaps attribute these two to the alignment of Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus—believing that medicine proceeds from Jupiter, and music from Mercury and Venus.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s collection of letters. The previous page ended with a letter to Angelo Poliziano regarding a message to Lorenzo de' Medici. This page contains a profound philosophical defense of the relationship between music, medicine, and the soul, followed by a short personal note to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini.</meta>

# LETTERS, BOOK I.

Our Platonists, however, refer everything back to one God, namely Apollo, whom the ancient theologians considered the inventor of medicine and the king of the striking of the lyre. In his book of *Hymns*, Orpheus considers that this god grants health and life to all things through his vital rays and drives away diseases. Furthermore, he tempers all things with his tuneful strings—that is, by his own motions and powers—producing winter with the *hypate* <note>original: "hypate"; the lowest-sounding string in the Greek lyre, associated here with the gravity of winter</note>, that is, the deep tone; summer with the *neate* <note>original: "neate"; the highest-sounding string, associated here with the sharpness of summer heat</note>, that is, the high tone; and spring and autumn with the Dorian modes <note>original: "Dorionibus"; the middle tones or "Dorian" musical mode</note>, that is, the middle voices. Since, therefore, the same god is the leader of Music and the discoverer of medicine, it is no wonder that both arts are often practiced by the same men. Added to this is the fact that the soul and the body harmonize with one another in a certain natural proportion; likewise, the parts of the soul harmonize with each other, as do the parts of the body. Indeed, the harmonic cycles of fevers and humors <note>The "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which Renaissance medicine believed governed health</note>, and the very movement of the pulse itself, seem to imitate this harmony. As Plato and Aristotle assert, and as we ourselves have often experienced, deep music preserves and restores the harmony of the parts of the soul. Medicine, in turn, restores the harmony of the bodily parts. Since, therefore, the body and soul agree with one another—as we have said—it can easily belong to the same man to care for both the harmony of the parts of the soul and the parts of the body. 

Hence Chiron <note>The centaur from Greek mythology who was a master of both music and healing</note> practiced both faculties. Hence the Prophet David is said to have cured the soul and body of the raving Saul with his lyre. Democritus and Theophrastus affirmed that this can indeed happen in other diseases of both body and soul. Moreover, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and the physician Asclepiades demonstrated this through actual practice. Nor is this surprising: for since song and sound proceed from the thought of the mind, the impulse of the imagination, and the affection of the heart, they strike—along with the fashioned and tempered air—the "aery spirit" <term>spiritus (spirit)</term> <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "spiritus" is a subtle vapor that acts as the physical link between the immaterial soul and the material body</note> of the listener, which is the knot of the soul and body. It easily moves the imagination, affects the heart, and penetrates the innermost chambers of the mind. It also stops and moves the humors and limbs of the body. Timotheus demonstrated this when he roused King Alexander with sounds into a fury, and then calmed him. I pass over the miracles of Pythagoras and Empedocles, who suddenly restrained lewdness, anger, and fury with a more solemn music. Conversely, they roused sluggish minds with other melodies. I also pass over what they tell of Orpheus, Arion, and Amphion. 

But to return to our purpose: the first music consists in reason, the second in imagination, the third in speech. Song follows speech, the movement of fingers in sound follows song, and the movement of the whole body in gymnastics or dance follows sound. We see, therefore, that the music of the soul is led down step by step to all the members of the body. Orators, poets, painters, sculptors, and architects also imitate this music in their works. Since there is such a great communion between the music of the soul and the body, what wonder is it that both the body and the soul are tempered by the same man? Finally, one who has learned from the followers of Pythagoras, Plato, Hermes Trismegistus, and Aristoxenus that both the soul and body of the world—and of individual animals—consist of musical ratios; and one who has received from the sacred letters of the Hebrews that God "disposed all things in number, weight, and measure" <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20</note>; such a person will neither wonder that almost all animals are captivated by harmony, nor will he accuse Pythagoras, Empedocles, or even Socrates for playing the lyre in their old age. Instead, he will admit that the famous Themistocles, who refused the lyre when it was offered at a banquet, was poorly educated. 

Our Plato shows in the dialogue *Alcibiades* that music belongs to the learned who are cultivators of the Muses, saying that the Muses are the leaders of music and that music is named after them. However, Plato everywhere rejects plaintive or frivolous melody because it renders the soul either broken or lewd and wrathful; he chooses only the solemn and constant kind as the most healthful medicine for the spirit, soul, and body. As for me—to say something about your Marsilio—I frequently apply myself to more solemn strings and songs after the study of theology or medicine for this purpose: so that I may utterly neglect the other pleasures of the senses, expel the troubles of soul and body, and lift my mind as much as possible to sublime things and to God. In this I rely on the authority of Hermes and Plato, who say that music was granted to us by God for taming the body, tempering the soul, and praising God. I know that David and Pythagoras commanded this above all others, and I believe they achieved it. Farewell.

->That praise is most true, which is itself worthy of praise.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini, many greetings.<-

**Y**ou praise our lyre, my Aurelio, with poems worthy of praise. In turn, I shall praise your poems with the lyre. But let them be worthy of praise. Just as you speak true things, so I shall sing; let each of us praise our own most truly. For that praise is most true, which is itself worthy of praise. Farewell.

->Happily<-

->He is loved happily who is loved by one most worthy of an extraordinary love.<-

# Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, Orator of the Venetians, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S. D."; an abbreviation for "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends health/greetings." Bernardo Bembo was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo.</note>

**I** used to think, Bernardo, that I loved Marsilio <note>Ficino often refers to himself in the third person in his letters to emphasize the philosophical "self."</note> in such a way that I could never love him more. This is because every man loves individual things for his own sake, and in all things loves himself, and loves himself above all. But yesterday, this opinion of mine—happily enough—deceived me. For then, for the first time, I began to love myself more ardently than I was accustomed to, as soon as I recognized with absolute certainty that I am loved ardently by you—a man most worthy of love above all others. Indeed, I grant so much to Bernardo that I value myself as much as I understand I am valued by him. Who, therefore, can ever please me more than he through whom I please myself more every day? May I always please you, Bernardo, so that I may displease no man of wisdom. What gratitude shall I return to you for this love for me? Love itself. Other things are for the most part acquired at a price belonging to someone else. But since love is born freely from a free will, and is therefore free, it is never bought or sold for any price except within itself. Farewell. Be happy. March 7, 1474. Florence.

-> On law and justice. <-

# Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>

**I** promised on the Nones of March <note>March 7th.</note>, if I remember correctly, to Lorenzo as he was returning from Pisa to Florence—since he was then traveling to the Pisan countryside—that I would write something to him. Therefore, I who am always accustomed to write to friends because I *wish* to, am going to write at present because I *ought* to. It is just to keep one's promises. For so it is commanded by law. Receive, therefore, a "just" and "lawful" letter. Or rather, to speak more correctly: as often as I wish, so often also I ought; but by the law of love, again, when I ought, then also I wish—but by the love of the law. Hence you receive today a letter that is both voluntary and just. To separate the voluntary from the just, or the just from the voluntary, is neither permitted to anyone, nor is it pleasing to friends. Behold, Marsilio, you both ought and wish now to write something to the Medici. But what will you write above all, and relying on which divine power? O Justice, the salvation of men and queen of the world, you have long since given me the cause for writing; I pray you now suggest the material, so that what I had freely promised with you as my witness, I may fulfill happily with you as my helper. 

That **Divine Law**, by which the world consists and is governed, kindles in our minds while they are being created the inextinguishable light of that **Natural Law**, against which the test of good or evil is measured. From this natural law, which is a certain spark of the divine, the **Written Law** proceeds, being a ray of such a spark. Now, these three laws—divine, natural, and written—teach every individual what justice is, so that almost no room for excuse is left for those who sin, as if they appeared to have failed entirely through ignorance. Indeed, these three lights show to the eyes of the mind that justice is nothing other than a habit of the will, so directed and strengthened by reason that, having despised base enticements, it resolves to act in no other way than that which divinity, nature, and civil life have dictated. 

What does divinity command, except that we refer the whole sharp focus of our thought, the movement of our will, the power of our operation, and our meritorious works back to God, from whom we have everything? What else does nature teach, except that we subject money to the body, the body to the soul, the soul to reason, and reason to God? Finally, civil life <note>original: "civilitas"; refers here to the duties of citizenship and living in a structured society.</note> seems to warn us that individual citizens should remember they are certain members of the state. Therefore, it is fitting to love the fatherland as the "universal body" of them all, and the citizens as the members of that same body. For this reason, he will be held as a just man without controversy who worships God as Father and Lord with incomparable piety. He will moderate his own affections and impulses most diligently; he will love men with brotherly charity; he will love himself in God, and love men in himself; he will cling to God with all his strength, and bring others with him to divinity as much as he can. 

Furthermore, it is the duty of the just man to give each his due: honor and reverence to elders, a certain domestic familiarity to equals, and help and counsel to inferiors. Moreover, when he is placed in the magistracy <note>Holding public office.</note>, he should always have the law itself before his eyes like God. He should consider himself not the master of the law, but its faithful interpreter and most diligent servant. In administering it, he should punish crimes with a certain equity and without agitation. He should return rewards for virtues according to merit without envy. Let him not think of his own interest, but the common good. Nor should he trust in his own intellect, but consult old, pious, and wise men in all things. Let this also remain stored deep in his mind: *You, to whom the ruler of the sea and land has given great power of death and life, set aside your inflated and swollen expressions; whatever fear dreads from you...* <note>original: Ficino is quoting Seneca's tragedy *Thyestes*, lines 607–612, reminding rulers that they too are subject to a higher power.</note>

<summary>This page contains two letters: one to Bernardo Bembo celebrating the reciprocal nature of friendship and self-worth, and a second to Lorenzo de' Medici outlining the philosophical hierarchy of Divine, Natural, and Written Law as the foundation of Justice.</summary>

the Lord threatens you with a greater [punishment] than this: every kingdom is under a heavier kingdom. <note>original: "omne sub regno grauiore regnum est." This reflects the Renaissance view of a cosmic hierarchy where earthly rulers are subject to divine law.</note> What justice is, who is just, and what the duty of a just person is has been sufficiently stated. How great, moreover, the fruit of just action is, is clearly declared by this: that no house, nor city, nor army, nor any commerce whatsoever—whether of good men or of bad—can stand without just distribution according to merit. Indeed, if justice is so necessary to the machine of the world <note>original: "mundi machinæ"</note> that, were it removed, the world would utterly collapse, then certainly it cannot be said how necessary it is to the life of men. For if it is lacking to men, whether they are gathered together they are quickly destroyed by one another, or if they live apart, they will be torn apart everywhere by wild beasts. O perpetual bond of the human race, O most health-giving medicine for our diseases, O public soul of the city: justice is the blessed life, justice is the celestial life. Mother and queen of the Golden Age. Sublime Astraea <note>The virgin goddess of Justice in Greek mythology, said to have been the last immortal to leave the earth as the Golden Age ended.</note>, who dwells in the starry thrones. Divine one, we beseech you, do not desert your earthly seats, lest we wretches fall into an Iron Age. Dwell among us, we pray; dwell always, heavenly power, making us citizens of the heavenly homeland, so that we may imitate the life of the celestials as much as possible in the present, and fully attain it in the future. Farewell.

## On the Soul.

->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Francesco Tedaldi, sends many greetings.<-

**L**actantius Tedaldi—a close friend as dear to me as he is a son to you—has delivered a small work to us in your name, in which the disputes of the Western Philosophers <note>term: "Western Philosophers" (Occidentales Philosophi). Ficino likely refers to the Scholastic thinkers of the Latin tradition, who were heavily influenced by Aristotle.</note> concerning the soul are recounted. At length, it is asked what Marsilio Ficino thinks on this matter according to those men. Although it is not my place to settle such great disputes among them, my books *On the Immortality of Souls*—which I have composed and which will be sent to you shortly, I hope—will explain what I think at great length. Meanwhile, I will respond very briefly to that part of the dispute which they most desire to know. First, I know that my soul is a substance; otherwise, I could not perfectly comprehend and define "substance." I would not be able to be anything more excellent than an "accident," <note>term: "accident" (accidens). In Aristotelian philosophy, an accident is a quality (like color or height) that cannot exist on its own but must exist in a substance.</note> nor could I judge or measure how much an accident falls short of a substance. I know it is not corporeal and mortal; for I would not grasp incorporeal and immortal things, nor distinguish them from corporeal and mortal ones. I know it is rational; otherwise, I would not know how to provide reasons concerning it and other things. I know that although it participates in reason, it is not—as some think—Reason itself. For if it were, I could not wander from the truth in assigning reasons for things, nor wander from reason in doing things. Therefore, he who affirms that the soul is Reason wanders further from reason than he who denies it. Furthermore, reason is either a substance or a quality. If it is a substance, then reason is, according to its essence, the highest absolute and utterly infinite thing. Such a thing is not the soul, but God alone. If it is a quality, it is an accident, and it seems to be a power of the soul rather than the soul itself. But as for the soul—which freely rules the substance of the body by forming it, moving it in opposite directions, and stopping it, and which can take on contrary qualities in turn—no one would dare to affirm that it is a quality or an accident. For in what way can it be called an accident <note>A pun in the original Latin: "accidens" (an accident/falling upon) vs "occidens" (setting/perishing).</note> or "perishing" when it runs equally through all types and species of both substances and accidents? It also reflects upon itself both through affection and cognition, and therefore also through life; since it clings to itself and not to a subject, it touches and chooses incorporeal things so many times without a bodily instrument, and rightly distinguishes them from corporeal ones. It often resists bodily inclination and does not find rest in the body. Finally, the further it removes itself from the body, the more effectively it understands, and the better and more happily it conducts itself. The soul, therefore, is an incorporeal, rational, and immortal substance, suited for ruling the body. Many among the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato, whom Ficino championed.</note> believe that the soul precedes the body. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note>, on the contrary, think otherwise. However, I believe those "Western Philosophers" whom you praise (though you do not name them) are Peripatetics. For, as you say, they disputed about the soul after a feast, as if they thought the body must be refreshed before the soul could be brought forth. Even though I have brought forth the "little soul" <note>original: "animulam," a diminutive and affectionate term for the soul.</note> of this letter after my own meals, I nevertheless agree with them regarding the order of creation. Farewell, and see to it that you are frequently present at those disputes; for in this way you will cultivate both the body and the soul at the same time. Our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti commends himself to you. Please commend me to those philosophers.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

## Consolation on the death of a friend.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, Envoy of the Venetians,<-
->Sends Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. D." or Salutem Dicit, a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

**C**ome now, Bernardo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend of Ficino and a devotee of Platonic philosophy.</note>, if I may ask, why do you mourn at the death of a friend? Is it death you mourn, or the dead man? If it is death, Bernardo, mourn your own. For just as certain as you are that he has died, you are just as certain that you yourself will die. Indeed, you are dying even now. For in any given moment, the life that has passed has perished. If you mourn the dead man, was he a bad man or a good one? If he was bad, it is good for you to have lost such a companion. But you ought not to grieve for your own good. If he was good—as I rather believe, since he was loved by one so good and prudent as yourself—it is certainly good for him to live apart from the continuous death of the body. One should not envy a friend such great benefits. Perhaps you grieve because you will no longer see your friend as you were accustomed to. Was your friend not simply the one who loved you? And who loved you, if not that very soul which knew you? Indeed, you did not see that soul any differently then than you do now; nor do you see it any less now than you did then. Perhaps you will blame his absence. But since souls do not occupy space, they are present not so much by location as by thought. When you do not think of him, you cannot grieve; but when you do think of him—which you are doing now—you call him back into your presence immediately at your own will. Therefore, you should never complain of absence, unless perhaps you object that the company of that liberated soul does not suit your own soul while it is currently locked in a body. Separate your mind from your body, Bernardo, if you can. Believe me, you will suddenly be in harmony. But if you cannot, do not doubt that, whether you wish it or not, you will be in harmony a little while from now. For this life we live, if compared to our will, is very short; if compared to the age of the world, it is a mere point; if compared to the age of God, it is even less than a point. Farewell, and live for God, who, since He alone is infinite life, alone drives death and the sorrow of death far away from His worshippers.

## The parts of a legitimate Jurist.

->Marsilio Ficino to Pierfilippo of Perugia, illustrious Jurist,<-
->Sends Greetings.<-

**A**strologers attribute the faculty of the Law to Jupiter and the Sun, than which nothing in the heavens is more beautiful. What, then, is more beautiful on earth than a fair interpreter of equity and the laws? Conversely, what is baser than an unfair one? You desire, I believe, to gaze upon the image and nature of a legitimate jurist. Oh, what a beautiful sight, how marvelous! His soul is the worship of God; his spirit is the care for the law of the fatherland; his brain is clear judgment; his eyes and tongue are learning. His chest is a tenacious memory. His heart is an upright will. His hands are the effects of that upright will. His feet are perseverance. His whole being is equity and gravity. But why do I fashion the Idea <note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal form or archetype of a thing.</note> of a jurist with words? While Pierfilippo, in the manner of painters, paints himself into his student Francesco Soderino, he will achieve a true likeness of that very Idea in reality. Indeed, although a suspicion of flattery forbids me from asserting it, truth nevertheless compels me to confess that Pierfilippo is such a man. His teacher strives that Soderino will also be such a man. The nature and beginnings of the student indicate it. His father, Thomas Soderino, a most distinguished knight, ardently desires it. Our friend Girolamo Amadei, who is most fond of him, undoubtedly promises it. Marsilio Ficino hopes in God for the things he prays for.

## That which is ardently desired is quickly acquired.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Altoviti, Sends Greetings.<-

**Y**our soul ardently desires, as you write, to fly to us. If it does not have wings, it can neither fly, nor should it desire what it cannot do. If it has wings—as I rather believe—it flew here as soon as it desired to, for with eternal and spiritual wings, neither time nor place can stand in the way. Therefore, unless my reasoning fails me, you already have what you were seeking with your whole mind. But let what you have be as great to me as it is easy for you to acquire and dear for you to possess, so that Marsilio may possess it no less in reality than Giovanni does in his estimation. Farewell. Our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and often described as his "unique friend" (unicus amicus) and the dedicatee of his commentary on Plato's Symposium.</note> commends himself to you.

->*We ought to follow the springs rather than the rivulets.*<-

**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Pietro of Padua, sends greetings.**

**T**here are many in our age who are not philosophers, but "philopompi" <note>original: *philopompi*. A Greek-derived pun by Ficino, meaning "lovers of processions" or "lovers of display," contrasted with "philosophers" or "lovers of wisdom."</note>, who most arrogantly claim to hold the mind of Aristotle. Yet they have very rarely heard Aristotle himself speaking—and then only briefly—and even then, he was not expressing his own thoughts in his native Greek, but rather babbling the ideas of others in a barbarous tongue <note>Ficino is criticizing scholars who only read poor Latin translations of Aristotle rather than the original Greek.</note>; for this reason, they have understood him not at all. When these men chatter among boys in the marketplace, they seem to the common folk to know something. But if you were to question them intelligently at home, you would find they know little of Physics, even less of Mathematics, and least of all of Metaphysics. Men of this sort are still children even in their seventieth year; they are devoid not only of eloquence but of basic Grammar. They do not think deeply about natural or divine things, but rather obsess over certain "barbarous" terms <note>A jab at the technical, often clunky jargon used by late medieval Scholastic philosophers.</note>, which they then clumsily mix and confuse with one another. Thus, these shallow Sophists bring before the public things worthy only of a circle of schoolboys, rather than a crown of men. They speak in such a way that you would despise philosophy for their speech; they live in such a way that you would condemn philosophy for their life. For this reason, our Plato rightly called them not the husbands of philosophy, but its adulterers, from whom are born not legitimate children but absurd opinions among philosophers. I approve of you, therefore, my friend, for not emulating the childish follies and vain pursuits of these men, who do not drink from the springs but merely lick the rivulets, and who foolishly follow the shadow of opinion rather than the light of truth. Know that you will only truly draw near to the truth if you most diligently avoid the footsteps of those who wander. Commend me to our friend Bernardo Bembo, the most distinguished envoy of the Venetians. Farewell.

---

->*The Peripatetic desires money not as a Philosopher, but as a human.*<-

**Marsilio Ficino to the great-souled Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.**

**I** would recommend Oliverio Arduino, a distinguished <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle's philosophy. The name comes from the Greek word for "walking," as Aristotle famously taught while walking about.</note>, to you in no small measure, were it not that his own Aristotle recommends him to you most highly. If Aristotle—who judged that money was necessary for happiness—had been able to compose his books without coins, then this Peripatetic too would be able to interpret the Aristotelian works without them. You understand, then, what Oliverio wants; he is a Peripatetic, not a <term>Cynic</term> <note>A school of philosophy that practiced extreme poverty and rejected social conventions; Ficino is joking that unlike a Cynic, a scholar of Aristotle needs financial support.</note>. But you will say, "it is not the part of a Philosopher to desire such things." Let it be so, indeed. Yet he does not ask for these things insofar as he is a Philosopher, but insofar as he is a human. Whether it is truly the part of a Philosopher to seek money, we shall debate after you have granted it. Farewell. Lorenzo Bonincontri of San Miniato, the astronomical poet and poetic astronomer, sends you his greetings.

---

->*A recommendation based on formerly happy fortune, innocence, and knowledge.*<-

**Marsilio Ficino to Donato Carlo, sends greetings.**

**I** recommend the Marsupini family to you most highly. They were once men of quite fortunate circumstances, but now, alas, they are all too unfortunate; yet never, I believe, were they unjust. Above all others, Carlo is recommended to you from on high by his father, Carlo the Poet <note>Carlo Marsuppini (1399–1453), a famous humanist scholar and Chancellor of the Florentine Republic.</note>. Listen for a moment, I pray, and if you are able, hear his plea: he beseeches you, both by your wisdom and humanity, and indeed by divine mercy, at least not to abandon this learned and entirely innocent youth today—the sole hope of his father. It is not right for the Muse to become a beggar, or for innocence to be made miserable. Bring help, therefore, Patron of the Muses, to this foster-child of theirs, who will perish without your aid. April 14, 1474. Florence.
