...indeed, I have always urged you to recognize that you have all things from God, to give Him thanks, and to commend yourself to Him diligently. I exhorted you to persevere; for the beginning belongs either to the will or to luck, but perseverance truly belongs to virtue. ->No one speaks well of love without love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Nicolaus Michelottus, a true man.

**Y**ou wrote a lover’s letter to me, Nicolaus, and almost more than a lover’s letter. No one, Nicolaus, writes such beautiful love letters unless he is a lover. Let that whole book which I once composed about love <note>original: *de amore*. This refers to Ficino's famous "Commentary on Plato's Symposium," written a few years prior.</note> respond for me. Perhaps I write too little now, because during this time of penance <note>original: *poenitentia*. Likely referring to the Lenten season, as the letter is dated just before Easter 1474.</note> I think of too many things. I have greeted your friends as you ordered; they do not quite accept these greetings. They prefer to be saved by your penance rather than greeted in your name. <note>Ficino is playing on the Latin *salutatio* (greeting) and *salus* (health/salvation). He suggests his friends are more interested in Nicolaus’s spiritual well-being than a formal "hello."</note> 

Farewell. 16 April 1474. Florence.

->Precepts for the memory.<-

### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Banco the Arithmetician.

**I**f you wish to be strong in the remembrance of good things, take care to forget evil things; it is worthwhile to plunge base things into the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> so that you may retain precious ones. Flee, Banco, the onset of disturbances; flee the tumult of thoughts arising from manifold business. Do you wish to think usefully? Think of very few things, and those which very few men think of. This is that saying of Pythagoras: "Avoid the public paths" <note>original: *populares uias declinato*. A Pythagorean maxim suggesting that the philosopher should avoid common opinions and seek deeper truths.</note>; follow the byways instead. Why should thoughts wander aimlessly? There is a need for sagacity and selection; the hare hides in a small patch of grass. Evils lie open everywhere, but that which is good is reduced to a narrow space. 

Do you wish to be powerful in the memory of good things? Take diligent care that you understand the certain reason <note>original: *rationem*. Can mean reason, proportion, or rational principle.</note> of what is to be learned. For the response <note>original: *responsio*. Likely referring to the "answer" found through dialectical inquiry.</note> is the indissoluble bond of truth and memory. For this reason, perhaps, our Plato says that what has once been well understood can never be entirely handed over to oblivion. Those things must also be committed to memory which are not only useful but also pleasant. For foods that bring the sweetest flavor pass more easily into our nature and are transformed within us. And the more greedily something is drunk down, the longer it is retained. 

Add to these things what Aristotle and Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos was the legendary inventor of the "Method of Loci," a mnemonic technique using spatial organization.</note> think must be observed: that a certain order should either be present in what is learned or at least devised. Order consists in a certain proportion and connection. In those things which are arranged in an ordered series, if you take up one thing, the rest follow immediately by a certain necessary continuation of either nature or art. The intention of the mind itself, if directed toward one thing or a few things as if they were one, acts more powerfully; if distracted among many things, it weakens. But the continuation and order of parts leads both the whole itself and the intention of the mind into a single focus. 

Furthermore, it must be observed that we should frequently meditate on what we have learned: for thus the food of the soul is digested and, as it were, converted into the substance of the soul. It also helps very much if one often reviews what has been committed to memory with elegant speech and sweet song. For pleasure is the seasoning of things, the bait of love, the incentive of genius, the food of the will, and the strength of memory. Wonder <note>original: *admiratio*. A technical term in philosophy; the "beginning of wisdom" that focuses the attention.</note> also contributes much: for because of it, the mind becomes more attentive and burns the marks of things deeper into its innermost recesses. For this reason, since children wonder more because of the novelty of things, they also retain them longer. Perhaps they also think of fewer things than men, and moreover, their thoughts are much more tranquil. But more of this elsewhere. 

If any trust is to be placed in physicians in this matter, the brain should often be purged with aloe and comforted with the scents of cinnamon and marjoram. Indeed, I do not find fault with this, but I approve much more of the purging of the soul. For the soul must first be purged of evils so that it may be filled with goods. 

Farewell—which is to say, nourish the soul well. <note>A pun on the Latin *vale* (farewell) and *ale* (the imperative of *alere*, to nourish).</note> You will nourish it well not by feeding it as many things as possible, but rather the most select.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK I</header>

### *The definition, duty, and end of virtues.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino, sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou often ask me now, Antonio, to define the virtues for you; perhaps you expect from me those very minute definitions <note>original: *petitiones*</note> used by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their systematic and detailed classifications.</note> and the Stoics. Calderino, our Platonists are not accustomed to doing things that way. Indeed, the power of virtue consists in unity rather than in division. For this reason, the Pythagoreans believed that unity belonged to the good, while multiplicity belonged to evil. I shall, therefore, define them very briefly, especially since it is better to practice the virtues in measure than merely to know them. Virtue is a habit of the mind <note>original: *habitus animi*</note> that contributes to happiness through choice.

There are two kinds of virtues. Some reside in the intellect. Others reside in the appetite, whether it be the rational or the irrational appetite. The former are called speculative virtues, the latter are called moral virtues. They are called speculative because they are acquired by contemplating <note>original: *speculando*</note> and, once acquired, they are occupied with contemplation. The latter are called moral because they are acquired through custom and habit <note>original: *more & consuetudine*</note>, and once acquired, they consist in the practice of character and deeds. In the speculative category are wisdom, the contemplation of divine things, science (which is the knowledge of natural things), prudence (that is, the knowledge of things to be managed rightly in private and public life), and finally art, which is the correct rule of works to be performed. 

In the other category are justice, which freely gives to each his own; furthermore, fortitude, which makes one more ready for honorable deeds and casts away from us the hindrance of fear; and finally temperance, which repels the softness of lusts, which is the other hindrance to honorable things. Moreover, liberality and magnificence are the companions of justice, and other virtues are similarly companions to others. To put it briefly, speculative virtue is nothing other than an acquired clarity of the intellect; moral virtue is nothing other than a steady fervor of the appetite kindled by that clarity of the intellect. 

One must remember, however, that in human virtues nothing is more precious than choice <note>original: *electione*; referring to the conscious decision to act rightly.</note>, for the sake of buying which Plato, in his books on the *Republic*, judges that all other things should be sold. For all things hinder, and nothing profits, the man who does not know how to discern good from evil, and to separate evil from good. If we wish to obtain the faculty of choice, let us consult elder and more proven men in all things. Therefore, let us consult Time above all others. For what among temporal things is more ancient and more proven than Time? We shall consult Time if we frequently and deeply consider the events of the past. For the past is the teacher of the present and the future. The consideration of the future also teaches us about the present. For it is most difficult to manage the present rightly unless you have considered the end and the outcome of every action. Think as much as is proper, and leave the rest to God. Whatever follows, approve of it as having been done by God. For he who disapproves of divine governance is rejected by God. Since, truly, God is the beginning and the end of all things, and since we were born for God and not for ourselves, the things related above are virtues only insofar as they are practiced for the sake of worshiping, imitating, and attaining God. Therefore, the worship of God is the virtue of virtues. The attainment of God is the reward of the virtues.

### *The nature and duty of the soul, and the praise of history.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Giacomo Bracciolini, son of the orator Poggio and heir to his father’s art, sends greetings.<-

**T**he ancient Platonists used to renew the city-based celebrations of Plato's birthday every year. The New Platonists <note>The members of Ficino’s own Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>, Bracciolini, have celebrated both city and country festivals in our own times. The country celebrations at the estate of the high-minded Lorenzo de' Medici in Careggi are recounted in our book *On Love* <note>original: *de amore*; Ficino's commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note>. The city celebrations in Florence were held at the royal expense of Francesco Bandini, a man excelling in talent and magnificence. You were there, as were Bindaccio Ricasoli and our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti and many other academicians; I also took part. And out of the many and various things we discussed at that banquet, I often meditate on this one in particular, which I shall gladly recount to you today: what we concluded before the feast regarding the nature of the soul. 

For nothing pertains more to man than the discussions concerning the soul. In this way, that Delphic precept "Know Thyself" <note>The famous inscription at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note> is fulfilled, and all other things—whether they are above the soul or below the soul—are investigated more sagaciously. For in what way can we grasp other things abundantly, unless we grasp the soul itself, through which all other things must be grasped? Does a soul not misuse itself if it does not strive to look upon that through which, and for the sake of which, it desires to look upon all things? As we all agreed there, the rational soul is placed on the horizon <note>original: *orizonte*; a key Neoplatonic concept where the soul is the "middle point" of the universe.</note>, that is, on the boundary of eternity and time, since between eternal and temporal things...

<page-num>658</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...and temporal things, the soul possesses a middle nature. As a middle point, it possesses rational powers and actions that rise toward eternal things, while also possessing powers and operations that incline toward temporal things. Justly so, since different inclinations arise from different natures; by the very fact that we see the soul turning now toward the eternal and now toward the temporal, we know it is constituted of both natures. Our Plato <note>Ficino frequently refers to Plato as "noster" (ours), signaling his role as the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy.</note> placed that higher part of the soul in the kingdom of Saturn—that is, in the realm of the mind and providence—but the lower part in the kingdom of Jupiter—that is, in the realm of life and fate. 

For this reason, the soul now seems to have a twin face like Janus <note>original: *bifrontis instar*. Janus was the two-faced Roman god of transitions.</note>: one golden and one silver. With the former, it looks toward the things of Saturn; with the latter, it looks toward the things of Jupiter. By looking, it judges and desires. It is better to love eternal things than to judge them; they are judged well only with great difficulty, but they can never be loved badly, provided they are loved ardently—for they are never loved too much, but rather never enough. It is far better to judge temporal things than to cherish them. They are generally judged well enough, but for the most part, they are cherished in a base manner. Indeed, the judge transforms the form of the thing being judged into himself, but the lover transforms himself into the form of the thing loved. It is better to raise lower things to us by judging them than to cast ourselves down to them by loving them. Farewell. 

But before I make an end, I ask you, my dear Bacciolino, that you do not cease from your begun study of composing histories. For the historians praise the style of your speech, and the subject itself is exceedingly necessary for life—not only for providing pleasure, but even more for the instruction of morals. Inasmuch as things which are mortal in themselves attain immortality from history; things which are absent become present through it; old things become young again. It quickly grants a young man the maturity of an old man. And if an old man of seventy years is considered prudent because of his experience of events, how much more prudent is he who fills a lifespan of a thousand or three thousand years! Indeed, each person seems to have lived as many thousands of years as the years of deeds he has learned from history. Farewell again.

---

### Three guides of life, and the one best rule of life.

->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Francesco, sends greetings.<-

**T**here are three guides for human life. The first is reason, long and diligently examined. The second is experience of things, confirmed by long-standing habit. The third is the authority of the ancients—specifically those who were such that they could not easily be deceived by another, nor do they seem to have wished to deceive others themselves. For one must pay more attention to what each person has done than to what he has said; to speak well belongs to many, but to act well belongs to few. 

The best rule of living, however, is that you think and strive, as much as you possibly can, to live according to the mind. This does not mean always living "happily" <note>Ficino distinguishes between worldly "happiness" (luck/fortune) and the inner peace of the mind.</note>, for stability and tranquility are found in the mind; he who falls from the mind slides down to the lower depths. Do not strive stubbornly to live long in the body, for nothing is "long" in corporal matters if you compare it to eternity. Add to this that in the life of the body itself, we are surpassed by many of the lowliest creatures. The life of the body is a punishment, and should be called the death of the soul. Strive for this one thing above all others, which our Plato commands in the *Gorgias*: that you live as well as possible during that time assigned to you here by God. In this way, the punishments of eternal misery are avoided, and the foundations of an eternal and happy life are laid by a certain divine help.

---

### The method of teaching, praising, and blaming.

->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Lippi the Rhetorician, sends greetings.<-

**S**ince you have read the Greek and Latin rhetoricians, I think you should so instruct your students that they always remember that the audience ought to be persuaded not by what is pleasing, but by what is permitted. For he who advocates for what is just persuades more easily and successfully, since he has justice as the patroness of his cause. Let them remember that they themselves must be just. For the speech of one whose life is not approved is itself rejected. 

Deeds move people more powerfully than words; he moves others most who is himself most moved. However, he altogether offends the ears who sings one way with his mouth but strikes the lyre another way. Divine Music <term>Musica: for Ficino, music was a mathematical and spiritual harmony that should reflect in one's character</term> is the correct harmony <note>original: *concentus*</note> of thoughts, words, and actions. Let them remember, when they are about to praise or blame someone, that the nature of things, places, and times is vast; therefore no one can so...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s ethical and philosophical instructions, moving from the internal psychology of the soul to the practical duties of a teacher (addressed to Laurentius) and the metaphysical importance of self-knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>659</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK I.</header>

...so wise and good that another could not be found who is even wiser and better. Conversely, no one is so foolish and so bad that there is no room for someone even more foolish and worse; therefore, praise should be given sparingly, and blame even more sparingly. Furthermore, in praising others, let them <note>This "them" refers to teachers or advisors mentioned in the preceding context.</note> encourage and advise. There is no murderer more deadly than a flatterer <note>original: "Nemo pestilentior homicida q̃ adulator"</note>, who, as much as it lies within him, kills the soul. Therefore, let them praise virtues and God, the giver of virtues, rather than the persons themselves. The former is the way of the pious philosopher, while the latter is the way of the flatterer. Let them blame vices and not the persons. The former is the act of a friend, the latter of an enemy; let them hate not the man, but the vices. Therefore, let them consider not how they might harm the man, but how they might dissolve the vices.

Let them strive more to be good than to be learned; for knowledge breeds envy, while goodness kills envy. Goodness is both more useful to men and more pleasing to God than knowledge; it is also more stable, for we more quickly forget some fact which we learned in a short time than we lose the character which we have acquired through laborious and long-lasting habit. Learning by itself contributes little for a short time, but goodness lasts for eternity and leads toward reaching God. Therefore, counsel your disciples in the Socratic manner <note>The Socratic manner refers to a method of questioning that clears away false beliefs to reach the truth.</note> to use human teachings to drive away the clouds of the senses and to clear the soul. For then, from the divine Sun, the ray of truth will shine upon the mind—but otherwise, never. This is the only useful study. He who acts otherwise labors in vain and in misery. In this way, your pupils from the Lippi family <note>Likely referring to the family of the painter Filippo Lippi or a specific student of that name.</note> will honor you. It was not books, but disciples, that made those divine teachers, Pythagoras and Socrates, famous. Or rather, they were indeed books, but living ones; for a book is a disciple lacking a soul, but a disciple is a living book.

Lorenzo <note>original: "Laurenti"; likely Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron, though here addressed in the context of teaching.</note>, what you have learned freely from God, the teacher of all truth, teach freely. It is a crime for knowledge, which is free by nature, to become mercenary. I praise the man who, without the blush of shame, has learned many things and teaches them without envy. Whatever overflows in the disciples reflects back upon the teacher. Teach, I beg you, willingly. For we have as many children of the soul as we have disciples. If parents generate children of the body with pleasure, why should the learned not also procreate children of the soul with pleasure? Present yourself as an example of good character. Holiness of life makes teaching venerable; younger men easily drink in the habits of their elders. They should be considered sacrilegious who infect the souls of the young—or indeed of anyone—with their words or habits. Finally, imitate Pythagoras and Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher often compared to Pythagoras for his asceticism and wisdom.</note>, who, after the fashion of the Indian philosophers, admitted into their discipline not just any youths, but those who were well-born and excellently raised. For it is not fitting for the Muses to become either the servants of decadence or the weapons of injustice. Farewell, and greet Albertinus of Cremona, a true philosopher—that is, an exemplar of learning and integrity.

### Knowledge and reverence of oneself is the best of all things.

->**Marsilio Ficino sends greetings—that is, the knowledge and**<-
->**reverence of oneself—to the Human Race.**<-

**K**now thyself, O divine race clothed in mortal dress! Strip yourself, I beg you; segregate yourself as much as you can—and you can do as much as you attempt. Separate, I say, the soul from the body, and reason from the affections of the senses. You will see at once gold purified from the filth of the earth; you will see the air clear once the clouds are scattered. Then, believe me, you will revere yourself as an eternal ray of the divine Sun. Nor will you dare, in your own presence, to further attempt or even think anything shameful or base. Nothing at all can be hidden from God, through whom alone whatever is open anywhere is made manifest. Nothing of yours is hidden from the living mind of God, which is everywhere the living statue of God. If the sight of a venerable ancient king produces modesty, revere always and everywhere the admirable presence of God, the King of all, and of the soul, the queen of bodies.

Rightly, therefore, did the divine Pythagoras command: *revere yourself*. He who does not blush to think base things in his own presence, and allows his soul—divine by nature—to serve its slave, the body, and drowns this divine pearl in the mud, certainly seems to be ignorant of his own value. Nor has he considered that divine oracle: *You have made him a little lower than the angels* <note>original: "Minuisti eum paulò minus ab angelis"; a quote from Psalm 8:5.</note>, and what follows. Again: *I said, you are gods, and you are all children of the Most High* <note>original: "ego dixi Dii estis & filij excelsi omnes"; a quote from Psalm 82:6.</note>. Alas, your minds are too ignorant of yourselves; alas, your hearts are blind! Rise up now, I pray, from this deep sleep; come to your senses at last, I beseech you. For if you come to your senses, you will breathe happily. Why do you look at things of this sort for so long? O divine beings, look up to heaven, you citizens of a heavenly fatherland, who are currently inhabitants of the earth! Man is indeed an earthly star surrounded by a cloud; but a celestial star is a man. You are something great, O soul; small things do not satisfy you. You are also the best, if evil things displease you; the most beautiful, if you shudder at the foul; and eternal, if you value temporal things little. Since you are such, if you re- <note>The text breaks off; the catchword indicates the word "perire" (to perish) or "resipiscere" (to recover one's senses).</note>

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s exhortation to the soul to recognize its higher nature and includes two letters: one to Francisco Bandino regarding the soul's divinity, and another to Antonio Agli offering consolation upon the death of his brothers.</meta>

<page-num>660</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

If you desire to perish, I pray you seek yourself there where such things belong. Truly, great things are only found there where no location imposes a limit or an end; where the best things are found, where nothing adverse happens; the most beautiful things, where nothing is out of harmony; and the eternal, where there is no deficiency. Therefore, seek yourself outside the world. But so that you may both seek and find yourself outside, fly outside—or rather, look outside. For you already embrace the world from the outside. But you think you are in the lowest place of the world because you do not perceive yourself flying above the heavens, but only see your shadow, the body, in the depths. It is just as if a boy, standing over a well, thought he was at the bottom of the well; while he turns his gaze upon himself, he sees his own reflection as if at the bottom. Or as if a bird flying in the air believed it was flying on the ground while it saw its shadow on the earth. Therefore, leaving behind the narrowness of this shadow, return to yourself; for thus you return to what is vast. Know that there is an immense vastness in the spirit, but in the body there is an infinite—so to speak—narrowness. You can see this from the fact that numbers, which are close to the spiritual nature, increase without end, yet they do not decrease without end <note>Ficino refers to the Pythagorean idea that numbers can grow to infinity but are bounded at the bottom by the "One" (Unity), which cannot be divided further. Conversely, physical matter (magnitude) cannot grow infinitely but can be divided infinitely.</note>. Physical magnitude, on the contrary, has a limit to its growth, even though it has no limit to its decrease.

### On the divinity of the mind and religion.

->Marsilio Ficino to Francisco Bandino, greetings.<-

**O**thers, when they are about to write to Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti was Ficino's closest friend and "unique Achates," a reference to the loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>, his unique companion, write two letters; seeing two bodies, they think two wills must also be present. But Bandino, who looks inward with "lynx-eyes" <note>original: "linceis oculis"; a common Renaissance metaphor for exceptionally sharp or penetrating sight.</note>, so to speak, wrote a single letter to a single person. In it, he calls Marsilio immortal and divine, as one who does not fix his gaze upon the flesh (which is but the garment of this man), but looks upon the <term>interior man</term> <note>The "interior man" is a Platonic and Pauline concept referring to the rational soul, which is the "true" self as opposed to the physical body.</note>—that is, the soul itself, which was granted to men by the immortal and divine God. Oh, how perceptive you are, Bandino, to perceive in a sudden intuition what I first spent ten years investigating through long wanderings, and then spent five years composing eighteen books on the subject! The beginning of those books—which you already seem to understand—begins to signify the divinity of the soul with these words: "Since the human race, on account of the restlessness of the mind, the weakness of the body, and the lack of all things, leads a harder life on earth than the beasts, if nature had granted them the same end of living as the other animals, no creature would be more unhappy than man." But because it is impossible for man—who, through the worship of God, approaches closer to God (the author of happiness) than all other mortals—to be more unhappy than everyone else, and since he can only become happier after the death of the body, it seems necessary that some light remains for our souls as they depart from this prison <note>Ficino is quoting the opening of his own masterpiece, the *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology).</note>. But enough of this. Continue, Bandino, to look deeply into individual things as you do, as much as you can; for in this way you will never be deceived. He who looks only at the surface sees only shadows and dreams. Moreover, you are the hinge of affairs and substance <note>meaning he is a man of essential importance</note>. You promise to honor us as soon as you are able, but you have already for a long time magnificently honored the divine Plato and his followers. You honor us now even as you promise; for a truthful man such as Bandino performs his duty even as he makes the promise. Farewell.

### Consolation on the passing of someone.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Agli, Theologian and Bishop of Volterra,<-
->sends divine consolation.<-

**I**f it were permitted to console one who is able and accustomed to console others, I would write you a consolatory letter now regarding the passing of your brothers. Therefore, I will not console Antonio, but I will pray. I beseech you, venerable father, by God himself, the life of the living, that you do not think so much on the earthly death of your kin as on their celestial life. Do not follow your own will so much as the divine will; to agree with that will is the only true piety, true wisdom, and highest happiness. Things that happen to others as necessary and adverse become voluntary and prosperous for him who agrees with the will of the Governor of all. But why do I, unskilled as I am, offer medicine to Hippocrates? <note>Ficino uses the famous physician Hippocrates as a metaphor for the Bishop's own wisdom; it is like "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note> Physician, heal yourself—rather, commit yourself to be healed by God. For there is no remedy, as you yourself know best, against the poison of earthly death, except a fervent love and frequent consideration of the celestial and super-celestial life. Farewell. April 28, 1474. Florence.

## Against lying and impious detractors.
### Marsilio Ficino <note>original: "S. D." (Salutem Dicit) — a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends greetings."</note>

**Y**ou know that your brother is a source of the greatest disgrace to you, because he is held by everyone to be a liar and unstable. I cannot deny that he is a liar, one who so impiously and insolently wields his venomous tongue and pen against divine majesty, which is the infinite truth itself. Therefore, men proclaim nothing truer about him than that he is a liar. But why do I not find this man "unstable," since he is so stubbornly stable in his purpose that he has already grown old in his very instability and malice? Either correct your brother’s faults if you can (though curing such an old disease is most difficult, and so wicked a vice is perhaps impossible—for never has a demon risen again who is said to have fallen once he rebelled against God), or at least bear it with an even mind, since even God tolerates his insults; perhaps because God knows this man does not know what he is babbling. Your brother’s vices do not obscure your virtues, my friend; rather, they illuminate them, for your whiteness <note>The Latin word "albedo" suggests purity or brilliance, contrasted here with the "blackness" of the brother's character.</note> shines forth more brightly because of his blackness. Therefore, do not be less stable in good character than your brother is in evil, so that you may perform good deeds as well as he performs bad ones.

---

## Against lying and impious detractors.
### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Rucellai <note>Bernardo Rucellai (1448–1514) was a Florentine humanist, diplomat, and relative by marriage to the Medici family. He was a close associate of Ficino.</note>, an eminent man, sends greetings.

**D**o not be overly disturbed, Bernardo, if that man barks so foully against everyone; for that dog barks according to his nature and habit. A rabble-rouser of that sort will cease barking only when he ceases to live—unless, perhaps, even after death he accompanies Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of Hades in Greek mythology.</note> with his barking. But tell me, I pray, Bernardo: what harm can his barking do to anyone? On the contrary, it makes men more vigilant and cautious. And since it is common knowledge that he is accustomed to disparaging honest men—either out of envy or because of his own dissimilar nature—will not that man be considered most proven who is most condemned by him? I certainly would prefer to be defamed by a wicked man in words rather than in reality. Indeed, a wicked man defames "in reality" the one whom he praises in words, for he is then judged to be a friend and like unto him. Every detractor necessarily disparages himself before he disparages others, for he takes upon himself the crime of being envious and slanderous. 

Oh, how greatly he misuses his tongue who uses it for evil! Let the slanderous pollute their own mouths with curses; let us not, in turn, pollute ours. If we loathe foul smells, we ought to know that nothing smells worse than filth in the mouth; foul speech is the sign of a rotting mind. We must, therefore, be diligently on guard lest we be infected by the contagion of the wicked. We should not care what "little men" <note>original: "homunculi" — a diminutive used to suggest people of small moral or intellectual stature.</note> say about us, but what "men" say; and not so much what men say, as what Truth itself speaks. If any falsehood is cast against you, despise it, trusting in the truth; if anything true is cast, use your adversary’s insults for your own improvement. Do not turn toward any side, whether favorable or adverse, at the lightest breeze of common gossip. A divine soul ought to depend on no other reality than God. 

But you strive in vain to correct that ruined man; being insane, he neither hears nor listens to reason. That impious man will never spare honest men, who has never spared God. In what way can a madman who hates God love any humans, who are the images of God? You ask me to correct him by whatever reasons I can; you are ordering me to "plow the shore" <note>A classical idiom meaning to engage in a useless or impossible labor.</note>. No one attacks divine things more infectiously, and again, no one attacks them more foolishly, than this little man whom you ask me to correct. This Thersites <note>A character from Homer's Iliad known for being the ugliest and most foul-mouthed of the Greeks.</note> ought to be punished rather than merely scolded. Oh, the wickedness! He has vomited many invectives from his venomous mouth against God with impunity. But with what mouth? That which was created by God himself for the sake of praising God. I have nothing for which to accuse this age of ours, Bernardo, except that it has produced this impious little monster. A glorious war is said to have once been declared against Jove by the Giants; in these times, an ignominious war is declared against the highest God by Pygmies <note>Ficino contrasts the legendary "Gigantomachy" (War of the Giants) with the current situation, which he deems pathetic by comparison.</note>. You might commend this miserable little monster to my teaching; and certainly, if he had a brain and strength, he would be very harmful to the human race. Hercules would have passed over this creature out of contempt; Marsilio rejects him because of the stench. Farewell, be happy, and command me to do lighter things at other times.

# MARSILIO FICINO

## *What happiness is, that it has degrees, and that it is eternal.*

->*Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, a high-minded man, sends greetings.* <note>original: "S. D." (Salutem Dicit) — a standard greeting.</note><-

**S**ince you and I recently disputed many things regarding happiness back and forth at the estate in Careggi <note>The Medici villa where Ficino’s Platonic Academy met.</note>, we finally arrived at the same opinion, led by reason. On that occasion, you subtly discovered certain new reasons why happiness consists in the act of the **will** rather than that of the **intellect**. It pleased you then that you should compose that dispute in verse and I in prose. You have already fulfilled your duty with an elegant poem <note>Ficino refers to Lorenzo’s poem *L'Altercazione*, which captures their philosophical debates.</note>; I, therefore, with God’s breathing upon me, shall now perform my task as briefly as possible. Three kinds of human goods are enumerated: namely, the goods of **fortune**, of the **body**, and of the **soul**. The goods of fortune are money, honor, goodwill, and power. And to begin with the first: money is not the highest good <term>highest good<gloss>In Latin, "summum bonum," the ultimate goal of human life.</gloss></term>, as Midas believed; for it is not acquired for its own sake, but for the sake of the comforts of the body or the soul. Neither are honor and goodwill the highest good, as Augustus used to say, because they depend on the judgment of another and are often not felt by us; very often they are both bestowed and lost without merit. Nor is power the highest good, as Caesar wished, since the more people we rule, the more we are vexed by sharp cares, the more dangers we undergo, the more men and businesses we serve, and the more enemies we have. The goods of the body are strength, health, and beauty. Strength and health are not the highest good, as Milo of Croton <note>A famous ancient Greek wrestler, used here as an example of physical prowess.</note> seems to have thought, for we are subject to the smallest injuries. Nor is beauty the highest good, in which Herillus the Sceptic boasted; for no one, however beautiful he may be, lives content with this alone, and beauty is a good for others rather than for the beautiful themselves. 

As for the goods of the soul, some belong to the irrational part of the soul, others to the rational part. Those of the irrational part are the sharpness of the senses and their pleasures. Aristippus <note>A philosopher who founded the Cyrenaic school, which taught that pleasure is the highest good.</note> judged the highest good to be in both. We, however, believe happiness consists in neither: not in sharpness, both because we are surpassed in this by many beasts, and because a sharp sense usually offends us no less than it helps us. Nor does it consist in the pleasures of the senses, for heat precedes them, suspicion accompanies them, and repentance follows them; one brief pleasure is bought with many long sorrows. And the intensity of this kind of pleasure lasts only as long as the body's need lasts—for instance, the sweetness of a drink lasts only as long as the thirst; and all need is a kind of distress. Therefore, the pleasure of the sense, because it is often mixed with its opposite (that is, pain), is neither a pure nor a true pleasure, nor is it sufficient. And if anyone should say there are some pleasures of the senses that do not follow a need, I respond: they are so weak that no one would place blessedness in them. Nor would anyone dare place blessedness in a certain state composed of sharpness and the delights of the senses, for such a state is deceptive, fleeting, and restless. Vile delights do not fill the soul, which seeks higher things by a certain natural instinct. 

Other goods of the rational part of the soul are called "natural," such as wit, memory, and a ready boldness of will. Happiness does not consist in these, for they are good to those who use them well, but bad to those who use them poorly. Other goods of the rational soul are "acquired," such as the moral and speculative virtues. Is happiness found in morals, as the Stoics and Cynics <note>Philosophical schools that emphasized virtue and self-control as the path to happiness.</note> believe? By no means; for the operations of the moral virtues, such as temperance and fortitude, are full of business and labor. In labor, however, there is not that "end" which we seek, but rather restlessness; for we do business so that we may have leisure, and we wage war so that we may live in peace. Furthermore, morals are never sought for their own sake, but are applied like certain medicines for the purging and tranquility of the soul. Yet the ultimate end is not found in the "tranquility" of the Epicureans. For the tranquility of the soul is directed toward the contemplation of truth, just as the serenity of the air is directed toward the light of the Sun. Does blessedness, then, dwell in the speculative virtues, such as the contemplation of truth? Certainly, in those very things. But there is one kind of contemplation that is (so to speak) sub-celestial <note>Concerned with things on Earth.</note>, another of celestial things <note>The stars and planets.</note>, and another of super-celestial things <note>Divine or spiritual realities.</note>. Democritus placed the end in the first kind of speculation. Anaxagoras did not wish to rest in that, because celestial things are more excellent than sub-celestial ones, but he was not willing to be content with the speculation of the celestial. From this, he said that he was born for the contemplation of those things, and affirmed that the heaven was his first home. This Aristotle indeed rejected, because the consideration of super-celestial things seems far more worthy. Thus, blessedness would be the highest act of the highest power regarding the highest object. But there is one consideration of these things which the soul can achieve while enclosed in the body, and another when it is released. Aristotle thought the man who possesses the first kind is happy; our Plato denied it, because the consideration of divine things in this life involves ambiguity of the intellect and anxiety of the will...

<summary>Ficino addresses Lorenzo de' Medici, arguing that true happiness (the highest good) resides not in fortune, the body, or the lower soul, but in the rational soul's contemplation of divine truths.</summary>
<keywords>happiness, highest good, summum bonum, Lorenzo de' Medici, moral virtue, speculative virtue, contemplation, Plato, Aristotle, Careggi</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical treatise addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici regarding the nature of the highest good. The previous page established that happiness does not reside in external goods like money or honor, but in the soul.</meta>

<page-num>661</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK I.</header>

...always has [some bitterness] mixed in. Therefore, according to Plato, true happiness belongs to the soul when it is separated from the body and contemplating divine things. Among the class of divine things are placed the angels and God. Avicenna and Algazel <note>Two influential Islamic philosophers whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance scholasticism.</note> seem to affirm that the soul will be happy in the contemplation of angels. The Platonists refute this with two reasons. 

The **first reason** is of this kind: our intellect has this innate condition, that it seeks the cause of every thing, and in turn seeks the cause of that cause. Therefore, the inquiry of the intellect never ceases until it finds that cause of which there is no cause, but is itself the cause of causes; and that is God alone. 

The **second reason** is as follows: The affection of the **will** is satisfied by no good, so long as we think another good remains beyond it; therefore, it is satisfied only by that good beyond which there is no further good. What else is this but God? Wherefore, in God alone can the inquiry of the intellect and the affection of the will find rest. In God alone, therefore, does the happiness of man consist. This indeed follows from the fact that no thing can find rest anywhere except in its own cause. And because God alone is the soul's own cause, the soul rests in God alone. But we have discussed these things more broadly in our theological work *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>Ficino refers to his masterpiece, the *Theologia Platonica*.</note>.

Furthermore, there are two acts of the soul concerning God. It **sees** God through the intellect, and it **rejoices** in the known God through the will. Plato calls vision **ambrosia** <note>The "food of the gods" in Greek mythology, used here by Ficino to represent intellectual nourishment.</note> and joy **nectar** <note>The "drink of the gods," representing the sweetness of the will's delight.</note>; he calls the intellect and the will the **twin wings** with which we fly back to God as our father and our fatherland. Therefore, he says that pure souls, when they have flown up into heaven, feast upon ambrosia and nectar at the divine table. 

Joy in that state of happiness is more excellent than vision. For just as we deserve more in this life by **loving** God than by **inquiring** after Him (to the extent that we are closer to Him), so in that life a greater reward is given to love than to inquiry. We deserve much more by loving than by investigating for many reasons:

**First**, because no one in this life truly knows God. But one truly loves God, however He is known, if they despise all other things for God’s sake. 

**Second**, just as it is worse to hate God than to be ignorant of Him, so it is better to love Him than to know Him. 

**Third**, we can use the knowledge of God badly—namely, for pride. We cannot use His love badly. 

**Fourth**, he who looks upon God contributes nothing to God by this; but he who loves Him gives both himself and whatever he possesses to God. Therefore, God gives Himself to the lover rather than to the seeker. 

**Fifth**, by scrutinizing God we progress only a little bit after a long time; by loving, we progress most in the shortest time. For this reason, love joins the mind with the divinity more quickly, more closely, and more firmly than knowledge, because the power of knowledge consists more in distinction <term>distinction<gloss>In Latin, "discretione," referring to the analytical process of separating and identifying individual truths.</gloss></term>, while the power of love consists more in **union**. 

**Sixth**, by loving God, we not only perceive a greater pleasure than by scrutinizing, but we are also made better. 

By these reasons we can conclude that the reward owed to love is greater than that which is granted to human inquiry. It is fitting for the lover to enjoy and rejoice in the thing loved, for that is the end of love. But it is fitting for the seeker to see. Therefore, joy in the happy man surpasses vision. Furthermore, we seek to see so that we may rejoice, but we do not seek to rejoice so that we may see. We can assign a reason why we wish to see, but we can assign no reason why we wish to rejoice other than joy itself. It is desired as if for its own sake. We do not desire to see simply for the sake of seeing, but to see such things and in such a way that we may rejoice. 

Nature itself never rejects any joy, yet it sometimes rejects certain knowledge—indeed, even if we judge it will be very troublesome—so that delight is a seasoning not only for knowledge but for life itself; if it is removed, all things seem tasteless. Joy is fuller than knowledge; for not everyone who knows also rejoices at the same time, but whoever rejoices necessarily also knows. Just as nature considers it worse to suffer pain than to be ignorant, so it is better to rejoice than to know. And just as it always and everywhere flees pain for its own sake, and all things because of it as the highest evil, so it follows pleasure for its own sake, and other things for its sake as the highest good. 

Since the power of knowledge, as we said above, consists in a certain distinction, and the power of love in union, we are more closely united to God through the joy of love, which transforms us into the beloved God, than through knowledge. It is not the one who sees the good, but the one who **wills** it, who becomes good; thus the soul becomes divine not because it considers God, but because it loves Him, just as matter [becomes fire] not because... <note>The sentence is interrupted by the page break.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding whether the intellect or the will is the primary faculty for reaching the "Highest Good" (God). The previous page ended with the catchword "tio," completing the word "intellectio" (intellection or understanding).</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

[Intellec]tion is established by the good itself, rather than the notion of the intellect which remains within. For the intellect grasps the object in a certain <term>imaginary way</term><note>In Renaissance philosophy, "imaginary" (imaginario) refers to the use of mental images or "phantasms" to process information, rather than something "fake."</note>. The will, by an essential instinct, strives to transfer itself into the object. Appetite is founded in the essence and is most broad and perpetual; for whatever things exist always desire something. Cognition acts through received images, belongs to the few, and is intermittent. Therefore, the possession of the good through the nature of appetite is more substantial than through the intuition of cognition. 

If God were to separate the mind from the will and preserve each nature separately, the mind might perhaps seem to retain its prior form. For it would still be a kind of rational form. The will would perhaps change its form; for it would be an appetite lacking the choice of reason. But the mind would no longer enjoy any good whatsoever; for it would be like an animal without taste: nothing would please it, it would approve of nothing, and it would assent neither to another nor to itself. Yet the will would still enjoy its own certain goods according to its strength. Therefore, enjoying the highest good seems to belong to the will rather than the intellect. 

Deservedly, the end of movement—that is, happiness—belongs to the will, since the beginning of movement pertains to it. For the intellect, since it is known according to the nature of things, and understands the things themselves according to its own nature, seems in a certain way to attract things to itself; therefore, it is not properly said to move the soul. The will, since it desires to attain things in the way they are in themselves, draws the soul to external things. Therefore, the will is the beginning of movement. Moreover, the end of universal movement is external, which finally joins itself as a kind of form to the soul. The soul enjoys this end most greatly through the will. 

Because a reward is owed to the one who labors. Indeed, care and the stimulus regarding the attainment of good or the avoidance of evil is in the effect. The will enjoys God more, not only because it deserves more from God than the intellect does, but also because the distinction of <term>blessedness</term><note>Latin: beatitudo. This refers to the state of supreme spiritual joy or "the beatific vision."</note> belongs to it. For as much as someone loves more ardently, so much more blessed do they become; therefore, the substance of happiness itself pertains to the will. What shall we say to this: that since many more people can love God ardently than can know Him clearly, the way of love is infinitely safer for men toward the infinite good—which wishes to impart itself to as many as possible—and is far more accommodating. Therefore, attainment belongs to the will. 

What again to this: that the movement of rational souls is free, and because it is free, it can proceed beyond any finite limit so far in merit that it can even surpass the blessedness of some angels. We are able to surpass them by loving and rejoicing rather than by understanding. Furthermore, by knowing God, we contract His magnitude to the capacity and concept of our mind; but by loving Him, we amplify our mind to the immense breadth of divine goodness. In the former, we almost cast God down into ourselves; in the latter, we raise ourselves up to God. For we know as much as we grasp. But we love both as much as we behold, and as much as we prophesy—beyond our clear intuition—that the remainder of divine goodness survives. Where we look upon the abyss of divine infinity loosely and obscurely, we nevertheless love intensely and ardently, and likewise rejoice. 

Vision is not, as some think, the measure of joy; for one who sees little can love much, and vice versa. Finally, that is the highest good of the soul by which the soul is contented. But the soul is not properly contented by the vision of God itself: for the vision which is received in the seeing soul is a created thing and finite in its degrees of perfection, just as the soul is. But the soul is never contented by any created and finite good. Therefore, vision is not the highest good. Rather, the soul is contented by the God who is seen, rather than by the vision of God. 

The enjoyment of the good in the sense does not properly consist in the good moving the sense, but in the sense reflecting, turning, and diffusing itself into that good which is offered. This spiritual turning and diffusion is nothing other than pleasure, as we discussed in the book *On Pleasure* <note>original: "de Voluptate". Ficino's 1457 treatise where he explores the Epicurean and Platonic definitions of joy.</note>. So in the separated mind itself, the enjoyment of God (if I may speak thus) does not properly consist in God showing Himself to the mind—this is more God's act than ours—but in the mind turning itself into God, which is joy. Nor should it be thought that the soul turns itself into the vision of God so that it may rest in it, but into the God who is seen. For it wants the vision for the sake of the one seen, who is joined to it as a form. Just as taste does not expand into the tasting of a flavor, but into the flavor tasted. For it desires the tasting for the sake of the thing tasted. No appetite seeks an imaginary thing, but a substantial one; otherwise, the memory and imagination of an absent good would suffice for the one desiring. But the vision of God in us is an imaginary thing and, as I said above, finite. Wherefore, the act of the will—which is a turning and substantial diffusion into the infinite God—has more of the nature of infinity than the act of understanding, which is the notion of God.

<summary>Ficino argues that the will (love) is superior to the intellect (knowledge) in achieving union with God, because love expands the soul to meet God's infinity, whereas the intellect merely fits God into its own finite capacity.</summary>
<keywords>will vs intellect, divine love, beatitude, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, highest good, De Voluptate</keywords>

--- Page 680 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the soul attains happiness through the will's union with God. The previous page ended mid-sentence, arguing that the intellect understands things according to its own nature, while the will reaches toward the thing itself.</meta>

...let there be certain things granted according to the capacity of the mind. God, therefore, is the highest good. Happiness, moreover, is the enjoyment of God; we enjoy Him, therefore, through the will. For through the will, by loving, we are indeed moved toward God, and by rejoicing, we are expanded and transformed into God. Furthermore, different souls enjoy different <term>virtues and Ideas</term><note>In Neoplatonism, "Ideas" are the eternal forms or divine blueprints of all things existing within the mind of God.</note> of God. For each person possesses primarily that virtue which they loved above others in this life and imitated to the best of their strength. 

Yet all enjoy the whole of God. For He is whole in each individual Idea. But those who behold Him in a more excellent Idea possess the whole God more excellently. Since each person possesses the whole God according to their own capacity and enjoys Him in the manner they had loved Him, therefore—as Plato says—<note>original: "liuor adeft" (likely a typo for *abest*). Ficino is quoting Plato's *Phaedrus* or *Timaeus*: "Envy is absent from the divine choir."</note> envy is absent from the divine choir. For since it is the most pleasant thing of all to possess the object loved, anyone lives content and full in possessing what they had loved. Indeed, if two lovers should obtain their delights, each will rest in the possession of their beloved, nor will they have any concern whether another might possess a more beautiful beloved. Add to this that although some there are more capable than others, nevertheless each overflows to the very peak of their own capacity, so that they require nothing further. Add also that by a certain amorous affection, every soul there yields most willingly to the will and distribution of divine justice. 

Moreover, a blessed soul can never be removed from God. For it must be said that this cannot happen by force; for from where could violence be brought against a soul held by the infinite power of God? Nor can it happen by choice; for since the will is not moved toward anything except by reason of the "good," once it has clung to that in which the entire reason of the good resides—and recognizes it as such—it is never moved from there toward anything else. And because it is the nature of the good to apply the power of desire to itself, it follows that it applies the infinite good without end. Again, because the will rests in something only insofar as it is judged to be good, it rests without end in the infinite good. And if the soul, while involved in the motion of the body, chose a happiness free from all change, it will do so much more when it is above motion. Nor can the lower parts of the soul turn the higher parts away from there, for they have yielded to them forever once the soul turns itself toward the infinite state of God. <margin>||</margin> Finally, if the soul were ever to be separated from that state—if it were ignorant of this, it would not be blessed, for it would be lacking knowledge; if it knew, it would not be blessed, for it would be fearful and distressed. Therefore, one who enjoys God once, enjoys Him always. 

Read happily, fortunate Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, the ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron.</note>, these things concerning happiness which your friend Marsilio Ficino has briefly touched upon here—things largely discovered by you. For such is the requirement of a letter, but these matters are treated most extensively by him in his books *On Love* and in his *Platonic Theology*. Farewell.

# *A Theological Prayer to God.*

## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Rucellai <note>Bernardo Rucellai was a Florentine diplomat, scholar, and close friend of the Medici circle.</note>, an outstanding man and sweet friend, greetings.

**N**othing is sweeter to me beyond the realm of men than to speak with God. Nothing is sweeter to me among men than to speak with you; God, the leader of my life and the conciliator of our friendship, always hears what I speak with you. What I often speak with God, you yourself shall now hear. I use this prayer, Rucellai, to God daily, so that God may shine upon my mind and favor my will. You too should use it sometimes, unless perhaps you have something better; for there is no one for whom I more desire God's favor than for you. I have sometimes heard our Lorenzo de' Medici singing things similar to these to the lyre, moved, as I believe, by a certain <term>divine frenzy</term><note>Ficino's term for a state of inspired madness (poetic, religious, or amorous) that elevates the soul to the divine.</note>. But hear the prayer now.

> O immense light seeing itself, seeing all things in yourself; O infinite sight shining by your own light, illuminating the universe; O spiritual eye, by whom alone and whom alone spiritual eyes see; O immortal life of those who see; O every good of those who live. O Good that completely fills the desire of those who love, you alone, God, kindle in us the desire for the whole good, you who alone are the whole good. I beseech you, purest light, through your very self: purge, I beseech you, the misty vision with which I perceive you, you who inflame the cold heart with which I thirst for you. Enlarge the narrow eye with which I behold you, you who raise the humble pupil that I may look up. For you penetrate my innermost depths, O depth of depths; you also raise up my heights, O height of all heights. What penetrates my depths? What lifts my summits? Surely the wondrous rays of your wondrous goodness and beauty, diffused everywhere wonderfully through minds, through souls, through bodies. With these, therefore, you affect me even without my knowing; with these, I say, you allure me, you compel me, you burn me. As much as a singular beauty, behold, now, behold I hasten to you, gasping, O unique beauty. But he limps—ah, too much this lover of yours—he limps, alas, wretched man; reach out, I pray, a pious hand to the limping one, O my hope.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s ecstatic prayer and philosophical meditation on the soul's ascent to God. Having previously discussed how the will finds its end in the Divine, Ficino now addresses God directly, pleading for the soul's return from its earthly exile to the source of all goodness.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

<meta>Catchword: That (Quod)</meta>

Lead, I pray, the one you allure; receive the one you compel; cool the one you burn; delight the one you distress. You will delight this man of yours wonderfully now, I hope—O wondrous joy, O fountain of all joys. I know indeed that in you alone—or rather that you alone are—whatever we desire anywhere. If this good pleases us, or if that good pleases us, it is not because it is *this* or *that* specifically, but because we truly desire the quality of goodness in individual things. If the life-giving liquid, diffused everywhere through individual things, flows from the unique fountain of goodness which flourishes in itself, overflowing above all things, then without doubt we long to drink from the fountain of goodness itself. O perennial fountain of all goods, we thirst for you, and you alone, everywhere. 

And therefore this or that individual good does not quench our thirst, nor again this and that together, insofar as we rightly prophesy that the <term>Good itself</term><note>In Neoplatonism, "The Good" is the supreme principle or God, which exists above all specific, participating goods like "a good meal" or "a good person."</note> exists above *this* good and *that* good. You, then, our God, you alone will quench this burning thirst; you, I say, are the Good of every good. Do not allow all your people to be compelled to thirst so much and for so long in vain. O primal Mind, far from all madness; O primal Wisdom without any folly, from whom nothing is hidden of those things which you wisely perform. You who despise nothing of those things which you perform with a benevolent will—and you perform all things. Do you care for even the smallest earthly things? Entirely so, even those which do not care for you. Do you care for the smallest things, and feed and fill them? But do you look down upon us alone, who are the only ones on earth who do not look down upon your majesty? Do you permit us alone, I say, to wander always restless, we who alone trust that we can find rest in you alone? Let such harmful ingratitude be far from the highest beneficence! 

Let deception be far from the highest Truth. You surely deceive us—alas, you deceive us wretches—if you compel us, wounded by your stings, to sigh anxiously for you every day and yet never heal us; if you command us to leave behind temporal things for the sake of worshipping you, and yet do not repay eternal things in exchange for temporal ones; if you have ordained that these diligent worshippers of yours lead a life on earth more miserable than the beasts, and yet do not preserve a more blessed life for them in the future. 

But you do preserve it for us, as we all constantly hope, O Savior of the world, O unique salvation of the human race and unique refuge, with whom every good belongs to man, and without whom nothing is good. Indeed, just as your most clear intelligence and burning charity illuminates and kindles our understanding and will to behold and love you, and forms the soul into that very likeness and unites it to yourself, so your eternal life perpetually gives life to our life within itself. And for those to whom the understanding of immortal things is granted, and a <term>capable will</term><note>Ficino argues that since the human will can desire infinite/immortal things, the soul itself must be capable of surviving death to reach them.</note> that commands mortal things, immortal life is much more fitting. By a certain power of the soul joined to eternity and separated from the passions of time, the eternal mind grasps what is eternal, just as its affection dominates temporal things. 

Thus, every act of the soul reaches eternity in its own way: the will by willing, the intelligence by understanding, and the life by living. And eternity itself, which communicates itself to the later acts of the soul, has already communicated itself to the prior act, which is life. Therefore, Best Father, you will one day make us partakers of your bliss, both by hereditary right and by the gift of your beatitude. Make us partakers even now in your presence; perform this also, if it pleases you—perform it, we pray. 

But if it does not yet please you because we do not yet deserve it, grant at least that we are not ensnared by the deceitful allurements of this world, nor succumb to its threats and blows. Have mercy on us, most indulgent Father; have mercy on your children. Cherish your own, and recreate those whom you created, for we are born from you alone, since you alone can fill our intellect and affection with your complete truth and goodness. Therefore, have mercy on your children wandering as exiles far from the heavenly homeland in this <term>forest full of miseries</term><note>original: "sylua." In Platonic thought, the "forest" or "wood" (hyle) often symbolizes the material world or chaotic matter where the soul feels lost.</note>. 

Have mercy on your people, we beg, who sigh for you everywhere day and night as for their Father and their homeland. Where the homeland is, there is rest, there is the true good; where exile is, there is restlessness, there is the false good, and there is the true evil. We truly seem to ourselves to live only for a little while and to be removed from evils, tasting something of the true good and rest, when we cling to you for a moment, whether by the focus of the mind or by the affection of piety. 

Drive far from us, Kind Father, whatever separates us far from you: distrust, despair, and lukewarmness. Give us in return those things that join us to you, Kind Father: true faith, firm hope, and most burning charity. Lest by chance, separated from you—the Life of lives, the Light of lights—and left to ourselves, we immediately slip away like the dead into the <term>outer darkness</term><note>original: "exteriōres tenebras." A reference to the biblical "outer darkness" where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, here used to describe the state of a soul separated from the Divine Light.</note>. But so that we may live piously for you as much as possible, and having lived diligently for you, let us also live and shine through you always. Let us shine and glow, burn and be delighted at the same time. Let us rejoice happily without an end to our desires, which are entirely infinite. Let us infinitely love your infinite beauty without anxiety. Again, let us enjoy the infinite good for eternity without any satiety.

# LETTERS, BOOK I

<meta>Catchword: Education (Institutio)</meta>

### *That one must trust and serve virtue and God alone.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Salviati, greetings.

If anyone thinks the cause of my long silence has been forgetfulness, they are mistaken; for I confess I owe you so much that I could not forget you before I forgot myself. I knew indeed that it was not fitting to write about every little thing to a man occupied with many affairs. I was therefore wishing for something great in your circumstances—and expecting it daily—as a reason to write a congratulatory letter to you. I do not yet see anything having happened that is worthy of my wish and your merit. 

Have faith in God, Salviate <note>Francesco Salviati was a high-ranking cleric, later famous for his role in the Pazzi Conspiracy against the Medici.</note>; I know you were not born for small or mediocre things. Therefore, be of good and, as you usually are, great courage. For you will have already attained great things if you remain of great mind. Most certainly, the most merciful God does not frustrate the hope of the pious. 

But why should I lament the death of our Cardinal Pietro? <note>Pietro Riario, a powerful Cardinal and nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, died in 1474 at the age of 28.</note> The Immortal God will certainly not desert us, even if a mortal man has. The younger Pietro departed in prosperity, as I reckon, lest he perhaps die more miserable in old age. Even if the extension of life sometimes brings an amendment of character, it is often an annulment or diminishing of past prosperity. He has lived much, Salviate, who has deserved much from God for as long as he lived among men. He who has not yet made enough progress in intellect and virtue, though he may have completed a hundred years, has not yet lived enough. Finally, to settle the matter in a few words: no one lives long or happily unless he lives for eternal beatitude. 

Farewell, my dear Francesco, and always be mindful of that which God has already often warned you: that one must not trust in fortune or in man, nor must one serve anyone except Him who serves no one, who never wishes to deceive nor can be deceived, who lacks nothing, and who never allows His own people to lack anything. Farewell again. Our friend Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and "unique soul," often mentioned in his correspondence.</note> commends himself to you.

***

### *What sort of imitation ought to be.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to Baccio Martelli, greetings.

I have read that oration by the rhetorician Bernardo Nuthius <note>Bernardo Nuzzi, a contemporary Florentine notary and orator.</note> to the learned and magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Our Nuthius seems to have long ago drunk deeply of and digested <term>Tullius</term><note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher who was the gold standard for Latin prose in the Renaissance.</note>. In that oration, a certain wonderful reciprocity is perceived; for there Nuthius is Ciceronian, and Cicero appears "Nuthian." A similar reciprocity seems to have existed between Homer and <term>Maro</term><note>Publius Vergilius Maro, better known as Virgil.</note>, and again between Aristotle and Theophrastus. Persist, therefore, in your intimacy with our Bernardo; for he is a distinguished rhetorician—and, I might add, the best kind—for the things he teaches others to be persuaded of, he has already persuaded himself. Farewell.

***

### *Praise that is brief is often great.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to Bartolomeo Scala, the Envoy, greetings.

I have read the *Camaldolese Disputations* by Cristoforo Landino <note>A famous philosophical dialogue set at the monastery of Camaldoli, featuring Lorenzo de' Medici and Leon Battista Alberti.</note>. In those books, he penetrates the depths of Virgil; he imitates the dialogues of Cicero <term>to the fingernail</term><note>A Latin idiom (ad unguem) meaning "perfectly" or "with the utmost precision," referring to a sculptor checking the smoothness of a joint with their nail.</note>; he crafts a happy man most happily. Read them yourself; I know you will feel as I do. Farewell. 

But why, Marsilio, are you so brief in praising Cristoforo? Because he possesses something indescribable that I cannot express. Farewell again.

***

### *He who favors the good, favors himself.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.

I will consider myself in your debt if you favor Pacio, a learned and good priest; you will be favoring me as well. For when it concerns the business of a good man and a friend, it is our own business. Farewell.

***

### *What constitutes a just petition and recommendation.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.

Many ask you for things of which they are unworthy; Gregorio Epiphanius <note>A Greek scholar who assisted the Florentine humanists with translations.</note> is far more worthy than the things he requests. Although he is a very dear friend to us, I recommend him to you more because of his virtue than because of our friendship. For it is on account of his virtue that he is my friend. Farewell.

# MARSILIO FICINO

### A Brief Instruction for a Bishop.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Niccolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings. <-

**I** remember when you were still a boy and, together with your most learned teacher Cherubino Quarquaglione, you visited our Academy, I advised you that as soon as your age allowed, you should take up the study of divine literature and law, and then be initiated into holy orders. I often asked the same of your father Otto, a distinguished jurist and knight. I did so because <term>astrology</term><note>Ficino frequently integrated astrology into his Neoplatonic world-view, believing celestial configurations influenced human character.</note> showed me you would be a great man in religion, and <term>physiognomy</term><note>The practice of assessing a person’s character or fortune from their outer appearance, especially the face.</note> showed me you would be a legitimate priest in both learning and character. Behold now, what is most rare: in the twenty-fifth year of your age, you have been appointed Archbishop of Amalfi by royal favor and under happy auspices. Therefore, my dearest Giovanni, I congratulate you as a true Archbishop, and myself as a kind of prophet—not so much because you fulfilled the judgment of astrology, but because you fulfilled that of physiognomy. Through the former, one may approach God’s vicar <note>original: "Dei uicarium" — referring to the Pope.</note>; but through the latter, one may approach God Himself. It remains for you to carry out successfully what you have so prosperously attained at such a tender age with God's help. 

You will achieve this at last if you always remember that you are a man; that those things you could not obtain without God, you cannot rightly govern or happily possess without God; if you diligently commend yourself to Him with a pious mind and the best works; if you consult older and proven men in all things; and if you choose not whatever pleases you, but what is permitted—not what irrational emotion falsely flatters you with, but what most diligent reason measures out. Remember that a true pastor must be so outstanding in virtue that he serves as a model of all virtues for the flock subject to him. Otherwise, the vices of the pastor infect the flock, and the vices of the flock redound to the infamy and ruin of the pastor. But what need is there for Marsilio to instruct an Archbishop? As your learning and character declare, the epistles of Paul the Apostle have instructed you sufficiently in this matter. Farewell, and be happy.

-> An oratory, moral, dialectical, and theological praise of Philosophy. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, jurist and knight, a Venetian orator distinguished in learning and authority, sends greetings. <-

**Y**ou ask why, since I have praised many things and arts here and there, I have nowhere pursued the praise of Philosophy, to the study of which I am always devoted. My "Achates" <note>original: "Achates" — a reference to the faithful companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid; here referring to his close friend Giovanni Cavalcanti.</note> Giovanni Cavalcanti happened to ask the same thing a few days ago. I answer, first, that the inventions of men can sometimes be praised by men according to their worth, but Philosophy, being an invention of God, far surpasses human eloquence. Second, in celebrating individual things and arts, I have celebrated Philosophy, the inventress of all things and mistress of the arts. Indeed, we only praise individual things worthily by her power and orations, and we judge any faculty to be worthy of praise only insofar as it participates in the virtue and dignity of Philosophy. But since this mother and nurse of ours seems to rightly demand a declamation from us at some point, let us begin here, if it pleases you.

-> Oratory Praise of Philosophy. <-

**O** Philosophy, guide of life! O seeker of virtue and expeller of vices! What could not only we, but the life of men in general, have been without you? You gave birth to cities; you called scattered human beings into the fellowship of life; you joined them together first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the communion of letters and speech. You were the inventress of laws, the mistress of character and discipline. But how insolently I have overstepped: I was beginning, I know not how, a sort of Ciceronian <note>original: "Tullianam" — referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> oratorical chant. This kind of melody is certainly sweet; but because we ought to sing of Philosophy—which is the rule of every song as well as the subject to be sung—in no other way than philosophically, let us repeat this play from another starting point.

-> Moral Praise of Philosophy. <-

**I**f everyone defines philosophy as the love and study of truth and wisdom, and Truth and Wisdom itself is God alone, it follows that legitimate Philosophy is nothing other than true religion, and legitimate religion is nothing other than true Philosophy in the proper sense of the words.
