<header>LETTERS, BOOK I</header>

...[propri]ety <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "-tas," likely completing the word *proprietas* (propriety or property) from the previous page.</note> is derived partly from the nature of things and partly from the nature of concepts—a point which Plato, Aristotle, Varro, and Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, who integrated Platonic philosophy with Christian theology.</note> discuss with the greatest subtlety. Certainly Philosophy, the investigator of things and the inventor of concepts, gave birth to Grammar, the rule of speaking and writing correctly. If Philosophy alone, or more than any other discipline, understands the nature of minds, the power of their operations, the form of their works, the arrangement of places, and the fitness of times, then she surely taught orators what to persuade, by what means, to whom, and when. She also taught poets how to describe things, move the emotions, and delight the mind; it follows also that historians could not have preserved their dignity without her help. She delivered a soul to cities when she devised earthly and human laws in the likeness of celestial and divine laws. She birthed and increased the body of the city when she provided agriculture, architecture, medicine, military skill, and all other faculties pertaining to sustenance, adornment, or defense. Finally, she removes misery from mortals more than anything else and bestows happiness, since she discerns good from evil. She shows how we may either cautiously avoid evils so they do not harm us, or bravely endure them so they harm us less. Furthermore, she demonstrates how we may more easily attain good things, and by what reasoning we may rightly use those goods—whether given by nature or fortune, or acquired through industry—so that they may be beneficial. I wished, my dearest Bernardo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian statesman and close friend of Ficino.</note>, to put an end to this letter now, lest I be more wordy in your presence than is my custom. For you yourself know how much prolixity displeases us, except in our Plato, that fountain of celestial eloquence. But look, the divine matron <note>Lady Philosophy, often personified as a noble woman since Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note> whom we venerate above all others cries out against it. Therefore, if you please, listen to the speech she still requires of us—or rather, the one she offers to us.

->*Praise of Philosophy, Dialectic, and Theology.*<-

**P**hilosophy uses the instruments of <term>Dialectic</term><note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth through reasoned argument.</note>, crafted by her own hand, to investigate the true in the contemplation of things, the honorable in the use of things, and the good in both. From this, she hands down many principles for contemplation, many precepts for action, and many institutions common to both. Of these common elements, the one that seems most important to me is this: The end <note>The "goal" or "purpose" (Latin: *finis*).</note>, as a master, is more excellent than those things which, as servants, are directed toward that end. And those things which are more excellent are always the ends of the others. It is therefore right and fitting that external and mortal things serve the body, the body serve the soul, the senses serve reason, active reason serve <term>speculative reason</term><note>In Neoplatonism, "speculation" (from *speculum*, mirror) refers to the intellectual reflection on divine truths.</note>, and speculation serve God. From this it follows that all arts pertaining to external things, the body, the senses, and action must yield and be obedient to contemplation as if to a queen. And rightly so. For this kind of operation belongs properly to God. It requires no specific instrument or place; it does not serve external things; and it is the most continuous of all things—indeed, it is perpetual. It embraces its eternal object, which is present everywhere, at will. And if life is a kind of act, and where there is more act there is more life, then surely the act of contemplation—the most excellent of all in both dignity and perseverance—is a certain greatest and most eminent life; add to this that it is the sweetest of all. For it does not, like the senses, borrow impure, false, and fleeting delights from the outward images of things; rather, possessing within itself an abundance of the true and eternal reasons and natures of things, it is nourished and rejoices purely, truly, and stably in things that are pure, true, and stable. It rejoices, I say, in the utterly infinite, infinitely; for what is greatest is that this kind of life, being closest to the life of God, is transformed into His most exact image. God, therefore, is at once the light and the eye of human contemplation, while contemplation is the light and eye of action. And if this "eye" seems to be at rest, nevertheless without it, all things are badly idle or even more badly busy, and are entirely dark and wretched. But at its nod, we perform every single thing successfully. This life, situated at the highest summit of things and being without controversy the most blessed, wise Philosophy points out to mortals, both with her own eye and with the finger of her Dialectic. She also leads us to it, as I believe, by four principal steps: the moral, the natural, the mathematical, and the metaphysical. The divine Plato thinks that the celestial and immortal soul dies, in a sense, when it enters the earthly and mortal body, and revives when it departs. Yet it may depart through a certain zeal for meditation before it departs by the law of nature, when Philosophy—the medicine for human diseases—purges and awakens the little soul buried in the pestiferous mud of vices with moral remedies. Then, lifting it from the depths with certain natural machines, she leads it through all things composed of the four elements, and through the four elements themselves, all the way to heaven.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains how Philosophy serves as the foundation for all human arts and sciences, ultimately leading the soul toward God through contemplation. He outlines a Neoplatonic hierarchy where the physical and active life must serve the intellectual and contemplative life.</summary>

<header>LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

leads. She <note>Philosophy personified.</note> provides a gradual ascent to the highest spheres of heaven by means of mathematical ladders. Finally—and this is more wonderful than can be described—she lifts the soul with metaphysical wings <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings to glimpse the realm of true Being.</note> beyond the very peak of the heavens to the Architect of heaven and the entire world. There, through the gift of Philosophy, the soul not only becomes happy, but as it happens—if I may say so—it becomes God, and in a way, becomes happiness itself. There, all mortal affairs, arts, and business cease; from the entire number of human pursuits, only holy Philosophy remains. There, true blessedness is nothing other than true Philosophy, since Philosophy—as defined by the sages—is the "love of wisdom." We believe that the highest blessedness consists in a certain movement of the will: a love and joy regarding divine wisdom.

We can surmise that the soul, through the benefit of Philosophy, can eventually become a kind of God from this: while under her guidance the soul’s intelligence grasps the natures of all things bit by bit, it puts on the forms of those things it apprehends. Furthermore, through its will, it partly enjoys and partly dominates individual things, thus in a way becoming all things. And while it becomes all things in this manner, it gradually becomes God, who is the source and Lord of all. Truly, God perfects the universe both within Himself and outside Himself. The mind of a man practicing legitimate Philosophy, like a kind of God, also conceives the true and eternal notions of all things within itself.

But shall we say the human mind can create individual things outside itself? I will pass over how the Philosophical genius—through thought, words, and letters—accurately imitates and expresses the hidden works of Almighty God using various instruments and materials. Instead, I think this one thing should be primarily noted: any person cannot discern how or in what manner the work of a skilled craftsman was constructed, unless they possess nearly the same artistic genius. For no one could discern the way that famous Philosopher Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE), the ancient mathematician famous for his mechanical inventions.</note> constructed his bronze spheres and gave them motions similar to the celestial movements, unless he were endowed with a similar genius. And he who discerns the work because of a similarity in genius could certainly build the same things once he understood them, provided that he did not lack the tools or the material. 

Therefore, since the Philosopher has seen the order of the celestial spheres—where they are moved from, where they proceed to, by what measurements, and what they produce—who could deny that he possesses nearly the same genius as the Author of the heavens? And that he could, in a way, make the heavens and the things within them if he obtained the tools and celestial material? For he makes them now, albeit from different material, yet very similar in their arrangement.

> O too-wonderful intelligence of the celestial Architect! O eternal wisdom, born from the head of supreme Jove <note>Jupiter; used here by Ficino as a poetic name for God the Father.</note> alone! O infinite truth and goodness of things, sole queen of the entire world! O truth-telling and benign light of intelligence! O healing fire of the will! O beneficial burning of our heart! Enlighten us; enlighten and inflame us to such an extent, we pray, that we may burn inwardly with the love of your light—that is, the love of truth and wisdom. For this alone—O Almighty God—this alone is to be truly wise; this alone is to live most blessedly with God and as God. Whoever wanders far from your rays, since they never discern anything clearly, are everywhere deceived and terrified by the treacherous shadows of things, as if by certain horrific dreams, and are miserably tormented everywhere under perpetual night. But whoever lives diligently with you, since they alone perceive, love, and embrace things that are true, eternal, and immense under your rays, they consider whatever is confined by time or place to be a mere shadow or a dream. Thus it happens that they cannot be cast down from the high citadel of celestial happiness by either the desire for or the fear of earthly things.

I think, my dear Bernardo <note>Bernardo del Nero (1424–1497), a prominent Florentine statesman and close friend of the Medici and Ficino.</note>, that your Marsilio has declaimed enough for a single letter. Farewell then, happy patron of Philosophers. And as you have done until now, live continuously in the blessed arms of holy Philosophy. Live also, I pray, continually mindful of the heart of Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino's closest friend and "unique soul," often mentioned in his correspondence.</note>, which belongs to Marsilio.

***

-> *The Grace of the Jubilee.* <-

### Francis Cardinal of Siena to Marsilio Ficino the Florentine,
### Platonic Philosopher, Sendeth Greetings.

**M**arsilio, most illustrious, greetings. Mindful of you and desiring the eternal salvation of you and yours, we have obtained from the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Sixtus IV.</note> the Grace of the Jubilee <note>original: "gratia Iubelei"; 1475 was a Jubilee Year in the Catholic Church, a time for special spiritual graces and pilgrimages.</note> for you and your aged parents. Therefore, give praise to God, and with your elderly parents, take hold of these incomparable gifts of divine grace with your whole mind. And pray for us. Farewell, best of men, and be mindful of us. Rome, the 4th day of December, 1475.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK I</header>

### An Expression of Thanks.

Marsilio Ficino of Florence gives immortal greeting for an immortal gift to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena. <note>Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini (1439–1503), who later became Pope Pius III. He was a significant patron of the arts and humanities.</note>

**W**HEN I, along with my parents, read your happy letter, in which you signify that a favor has been obtained for us from the Pope by your commanding grace, we were moved with no less joy than those who are destined to hear that most blessed voice:
> Come, you blessed of my father. <note>A quotation from Matthew 25:34, often associated with the Final Judgment and the welcome into Heaven.</note>
Therefore, my father suddenly exclaimed before all others:
> Now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word. <note>The "Nunc Dimittis" from Luke 2:29, the song of Simeon upon seeing the Christ child.</note>
As you are a magnificent giver, you also seem a just and prudent collector; you grant eternal things, not temporal ones, and you do not demand temporal things from us, but eternal. Indeed, you command that we pray to God for your health; you certainly command most justly, for we owe even much more than you command. You also command most prudently, for before you commanded us to pray, you took care that we should not pray in vain. We shall, therefore, fulfill what you command, venerable father, as long as we live. And without a doubt, you have bestowed this singular and divine gift as gladly as we have received it. Know that we consider and openly confess that we owe much more of our temporal life and all temporal things to him to whom we owe our eternal life. Farewell, and be happy in God, the author of happiness.

-> Leisure nurtures utility. <-

Marsilio Ficino to Andrea Cambini, <note>A friend of Ficino and a Florentine official who served as the provveditore (overseer) of various fortresses.</note> guardian of the fortress, sends greetings.

**W**HILE I was walking in the forum together with our distinguished friend Francesco Casato, your elegant letter was delivered to me. In it, you indicate that you have now established a life of leisure while guarding that fortress, and that in this state of life, while all other things are present according to your wish, only divine things are missing. For that reason, you ask that we send our *Religion* <note>original: "religionem nostram." This refers to Ficino's major theological work, *De Christiana Religione* (On the Christian Religion).</note> to you by way of the son of Francesco Berlinghieri, a young man adorned with both letters and good character. 

First, I indeed approve of what you say: that you have found leisure at the summit of a fortress; for truly, only in the highest watchtower of a serene mind is that Elysian and happy tranquility found. The lowest valley of the senses is tossed on every side by the waves of <term>Acheron</term>, <term>Styx</term>, <term>Cocytus</term>, and <term>Phlegethon</term>. <note>In Greek mythology and Neoplatonic allegory, these are the four rivers of the underworld, representing woe, hatred, lamentation, and fire, respectively. Ficino uses them here to represent the turbulent world of sensory experience.</note> However, as for what you add—that in such leisure human things are supplied to you in abundance, but divine things not at all—I cannot help but marvel at this. For other things, as you know, since they are placed both outside us and only in specific places, are sought through movement, business, and labor. Divine things, however, since they are both within us and everywhere, are grasped through rest, leisure, and tranquility. 

Therefore, if you are truly at leisure as you say, you possess nothing less than human things (which are all excessively busy), and again, you possess nothing more than divine things. Their immense light, shining everywhere, reflects into the clear and perceptive eye of the mind as often as the mind rightly turns toward it. Moreover, the mind turns toward that light by its very nature, as something divine, as soon as it is not turned away from it by the disturbances of human affairs. Perhaps, indeed, to be turned toward the Sun of the Divine is nothing other than not to be turned away. 

Why then do you seek our *Religion*, my dearest godparent? You are already religious enough, I think, if through leisure you are released from the cares of the lowest things and are naturally "re-bound" <note>Ficino is playing on the etymology of the Latin word *religio*, which he (following Lactantius) derives from *religare*, meaning "to bind fast" or "to bind back" to God.</note> to the tranquility of the highest. But behold, while I am writing, it occurs to me what my godparent desires. No one is ignorant of why beautiful people are delighted by mirrors more than the deformed. Therefore, our Cambini, seeing as he has already emerged as abundantly religious, yearns for our book treating divine matters as if it were a mirror, in which he may gaze upon his own religion as if it were his own image. I will send this mirror of mine as soon as I can. Or rather, to name it more correctly, I will direct this pupil of my eye toward you, in which, by looking, you may clearly discern yourself. For those who live with one heart see also with one pupil, and are seen in that same pupil. But lest I be much longer for the present than is my custom: Farewell. 

Yet I see that you, as one most fond of Marsilio, do not wish to say farewell so quickly so that you may fare better. <note>A play on the word *Vale*, which means both "farewell" and "be well/strong."</note> Do you desire the letter to be a little longer, as those who love from afar usually do? Then receive a greeting from our common friend, that you may fare even better. Paolo Saxia, a learned man, bids you hello. And so, now, fare thee well.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

### On Perseverance.

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Soderini, sends greetings.<- <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524) was a Florentine diplomat and bishop who studied law and became a significant political figure.</note>

**T**ell me, my sweetest Soderini, what should I write? Shall I praise your character, your morals, and your learning at great length? By no means, for there is no need for witnesses in a matter manifest to everyone. Should I perhaps urge you more vehemently toward the most precious study of civil law? Not even that, for he who goads one who is already running of his own accord does not, I think, give instructions, but rather causes a stumble. Therefore, I will not urge you to run faster, but rather I will pray that you continue. Truly, the prize for runners is not located at the starting gates, but at the finish line. Any person, even the most sluggish, can begin a race; but truly, only a few reach the end. At the beginning of sowing, thorns and rocks threaten; in the middle, the most charming flowers smile; at the end, the sweetest fruits are gathered. It is not the one who sows, but the one who tends and reaps the crop who should be called a happy farmer. I believe that our Soderini will soon be a happy farmer. The hard labor of sowing has long since passed for him, as has the harsher winter; a flowery spring has long been underway, and a fruitful summer approaches day by day. Therefore, take diligent care of your health, so that you may be strong enough to enjoy the sweet fruits of your agriculture most pleasantly. Farewell. But why do I write so little at present to him whom I love so much? Because even while we seem to be apart, we converse much with one another day and night because of our mutual love. Furthermore, your Girolamo Amati <note>Girolamo Amati was a humanist scholar and a friend to both Ficino and Soderini.</note>—and because he is yours, he is therefore mine—the knot of our shared benevolence, who is setting out for the University of Pisa, will tell you many things in person. Again, farewell.

---

->*Only the divine physician can cure the diseases of the soul.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena, sends greetings.<- <note>This is Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini, to whom the previous page's letter was also addressed.</note>

**R**ecently, Venerable Father, I was weighed down by heavy sorrow due to the loss of an excellent friend, and neither the Muse Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry and eloquence; here representing the soothing power of music and poetry.</note> with her lyre—often my sweet relief in labors elsewhere—nor Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> could console me in my grief; somehow, she had even forsaken me. For unless she had moved her untamed shield away for a little while, the weapons of either rigid Saturn or savage Mars <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic astrology, Saturn represents melancholy and Mars represents strife or sudden blows of fate.</note> would never have wounded this wretched man. Only Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light, healing, and prophecy.</note> remained—that is, the divine physician—who seemed able to cure the disease of the soul. To what end is this? Truly you, Venerable Father, divining this unfair lot of mine—for you could not have known it otherwise—sent very opportunely to your Marsilio a letter full of love and grace, in which you forbade thanks to be given to you for the greatest benefits received from you. And, to speak more truly, you did not reach out a letter, but rather a most healthy and divine medicine: manna, nectar, and ambrosia. Refreshed by this medicine, or rather nourishment, my soul has revived, breathed again, recovered its senses, and grown strong. Therefore, hereafter you shall be my Phoebus; my lyre shall always sing of you, the singular author of my soul’s tranquility. The philosopher Democritus <note>A Greek philosopher often associated with the pursuit of cheerfulness and peace of mind (*euthymia*).</note> valued this tranquility so highly that they placed both divine and human happiness in it alone. And indeed, this tranquility is usually least present in those who perform great deeds, because they themselves are very small in the midst of great things; but to my Phoebus, the harbor of tranquility, great things are fitting and the greatest things remain, since he is greatest in the midst of great things.

### Where the Reciprocity of Love is Born.

->Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, sends greetings.<- <note>Amerigo Corsini (1452–1501) was a Florentine poet and member of Ficino’s Platonic Academy.</note>

**T**hat proverb, Corsini—"if you wish to be loved, love"—from where do we think it receives its greatest power? If we ask the reason for this proverb from Love himself, perhaps he will answer that he is so free and precious that he neither wishes nor is able to be bought or sold for any other price than himself. If, however, we ask a man who is truly a lover and a friend, he will answer, I think, in this way: Whoever loves intensely takes himself away from himself, in a sense, and gives himself to the beloved. Therefore, the beloved—provided he is of sound mind—cares for the lover as if he were his own property. For his own things ought to be most dear to everyone; he knows also that, to return like for like, a man is owed for a man, and a will is owed for a will. It is added that he who loves carves the image of the one he loves into his own soul; thus the soul of the lover becomes...

<header>LETTERS, BOOK I.</header>

...as a kind of mirror in which the image of the beloved is reflected. Therefore, when the beloved recognizes himself in the lover, he is compelled to love him in return. If we ask nature for the truth of that proverb <note>The proverb "Like attracts like."</note>, perhaps she will teach us this: Likeness always gives birth to Love. Likeness, however, is a certain nature that is the same in many; for if one person is like another, the other is necessarily like the first. Therefore, the same likeness that compels the one to love the other also leads the other to love the one. For a similar tuning, either in twin strings or in two lutes, has this effect—as we experience every day—that whenever one is struck, the other is moved as well. 

If teachers of this kind either do not satisfy us or perhaps explain too little, let us now turn to the philosophers, my dear Corsini, and let us hear what cause they primarily offer for this mutual affection. Astrologers believe there is mutual goodwill between those in whose birth chart an exchange of "lights"—that is, the Sun and the Moon—has occurred: for instance, if at my birth the Sun was in Aries and the Moon in Sagittarius, while at your birth the Sun was in Sagittarius and the Moon in Aries. Or for those whom the same sign, or at least a similar one, and the same or a similar planet was ascending, or if favorable planets looked upon the angle of the East in a similar way. Or if Venus was positioned in the same house of the nativity and at the same degree. The Platonists add those whose life is guided by the same, or certainly a similar, spirit <note>original: "daemon". In the Neoplatonic sense, a guardian spirit or guiding genius assigned at birth.</note>. Physicians and world-watchers, however, wish the cause of similar affection to be a likeness in complexion <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) in the body.</note>, nutrition, education, habit, and counsel. Finally, where many causes concur, there mutual goodwill is found to be more vehement; where all are present, there the affection of Pythias and Damon, or Pylades and Orestes, rises again. 

What more? This kind of reasoning, Amerigo <note>Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512), the famous navigator, who was a student of Ficino's uncle and a member of this intellectual circle.</note>, has for a long time joined Giovanni Cavalcanti and Marsilio Ficino in a certain divine love; the same reasoning now happily joins Amerigo to us as well. What shall I say of Bernardo Bembo the Venetian? <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note> Not only a certain reason of this kind, but even divine providence has joined him to us.

---

->True poetry is from God to God.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Alessandro Bracci, Priest of the Muses, sends greetings.<- <note>Alessandro Bracci (1443–1503) was a Florentine poet and diplomat.</note>

**O**ur Plato, in the dialogue titled *Ion*, thinks that only those songs are divine which are infused into poets by divine music and the frenzy <note>original: "furore". Refers to *divinus furor* or "divine madness," the Neoplatonic idea that the soul must be "rapt" or inspired by God to create true art.</note> of the Muses—songs which, when they are sung by human music, stir both the singer himself and the listeners into a kind of frenzy. My lyre <term>cithara<gloss>A stringed instrument similar to a lute or lyre used by Ficino to perform "Orphic" hymns.</gloss></term> soon proved Alessandro's poems, written to Marsilio yesterday, to be of such a kind before many listeners; they were also proved a little later by our close friend Giovanni Battista Boninsegni, a man exceptionally learned in Latin and Greek literature. 

For this reason, Bracci, you owe this poetry of yours not so much to your own diligence (which is nevertheless not small) as to the inspiration of the Muses. Therefore, from now on, I pray you, my friend, leave mortals behind; since you sing by the inspiration of God, sing of God. Not only Moses and David and the rest of the Hebrew Prophets, but also Zoroaster, Linus, Orpheus, Musaeus, Empedocles, Parmenides, Heraclitus, and Xenophanes clearly advised us of this in their religious poems. Furthermore, Pythagoras and Plato advised it. They expelled Homer and Hesiod from the company of men to the underworld because they partly translated divine things to men as if they were ungrateful, and partly translated human things to the gods as if they were impious. Accordingly, if (heaven forbid) you should happen to sing only of men—as if ungrateful to God—you will mostly sing of ungrateful and shifting things; but whenever you sing of God (which I hope you will rather do), 
->Echo will accompany your song<-
->sweetly and happily.<-

<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->One’s own things are to be sent to us.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Soderino, most distinguished in letters and character, sends greetings.<-

**M**y sweetest Soderino, I have often wished to send my very own original manuscript <note>original: "archetypum"</note> to those who requested my letters from me, but this book of mine immediately objected with a great deal of complaining: "I beg you, do not send me where you yourself are not, my father." Yet, when I just now commanded it to set out to Peter, it objected not at all; for it seemed to understand that when it set out to Soderino, it would not truly be departing from Marsilio. Go forth then, go my book, without whom I go nowhere. But you ask now for some travel provisions <term>viaticum | funds or supplies for a journey</term>, I see; however, I find no provision more precious at present than Paulo Antonio, the most dear brother of my Peter. Carry his name with you, therefore, as a sweet provision for the road. And as often as he might happen to look upon you within his own home, bid him greetings many times in the name of Marsilio.

->**The end of the first book.**<-

# MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine to Federico, Duke of Urbino, ever unconquered, and especially wise and merciful, sends greetings.

### PREFACE.

When I was distinguishing my letters, collected from all quarters, into books, it pleased me to separate those which pertained to Platonic Theology <note>Ficino's masterwork was the *Theologia Platonica*, and he categorized his correspondence similarly, separating philosophical/spiritual matters from "human" or mundane ones.</note> above the rest—as if they were divine by their very subject matter—from other letters that are, as it were, human, and to gather them into one. And since I wished to place a truly divine head upon this body which is divine in its matter, I gladly enrolled Federico, Duke of Urbino, above all others. His divine virtue—to speak in the Platonic manner—has so filled the very "Idea" <note>The "Idea" refers to Plato's Theory of Forms: the perfect, eternal template of a thing as opposed to its imperfect earthly manifestation.</note> not only of an absolute man but also of a perfected prince, that if that famous Diogenes <note>Likely Diogenes the Cynic, who famously mocked Plato’s theory of Ideas by saying he could see the table and the cup, but not "tableness" or "cupness."</note> were to behold him—he who denied that Ideas could even be conceived—he would now undoubtedly confess that they can not only be understood by the mind, but even perceived by the eyes.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine’s Letters,
### BOOK II.

Five questions on the mind. First: Whether its movement is directed toward a specific, certain end or not? Second: Whether the goal of its movements is further motion or a state of rest? Third: Whether it is something particular or a universal thing? Fourth: Whether it is able to eventually achieve its desired end? Fifth: Whether, after it has attained its end, it ever departs from there?

->Marsilio Ficino to his Fellow Philosophers, Greetings.<-

Wisdom, born from the highest head of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis" — Ficino uses the Roman name for the king of the gods to represent the supreme Divine Creator.</note>, the creator of all things, commands her lovers—the Philosophers—that if they ever desire to possess the thing they love, they should always seek the highest "heads" <note>Ficino plays on the word "caput" (head), meaning both the physical head and the source or primary principle of a thing.</note> of reality rather than the lowest footprints. For Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, famously born from the head of Zeus/Jupiter.</note>, that Divine offspring sent down from high heaven, herself dwells in and has established the high citadels. She shows us, moreover, that we cannot reach the highest principles of things unless we first ascend into the "head" of the soul—which is the mind—leaving behind the lower parts of the soul. She promises, finally, that if we gather ourselves into that most fruitful head of the soul, we shall there undoubtedly procreate a mind by means of that very head (that is, the mind). A mind, I say, that is both a companion to Minerva herself and a nursling of supreme Jupiter. Therefore, my excellent fellow philosophers, I shall now bring forth into your midst what sort of "mind" I recently created with my mind during a night's study on Mount Coelano <note>A location where Ficino spent time in philosophical retreat.</note>, so that you, who are far more fruitful than Marsilio, might be provoked by a kind of rivalry to give birth to an offspring more worthy of the sight of Jupiter and Pallas.

<margin>The motion of every natural species, because it is driven by a certain order, is therefore recognized to proceed from a certain principle and be directed toward a certain end.</margin>
Every movement of a natural species proceeds by a certain definite reason. For one species moves differently than another, and every species always keeps the same course in its movement, so that it always progresses and returns from one point to another, and from that to the next, in a most fitting manner. We ask: from where does it chiefly receive the order of such movement? Among the Philosophers, there are two boundaries of movement: the point "from which" it flows, and the point "into which" it arrives. From these boundaries, it acquires its order. For this reason, it does not wander from the uncertain and disordered into the uncertain and chaotic; rather, it is directed from a certain and ordered nature into something certain and ordered, which agrees with the nature from which the movement began. For everything recurs to its own nature rather than to something foreign; otherwise, dissimilar species of things would sometimes move in similar ways, and similar species would often move dissimilarly, and the same species would act in different ways at different times, and diverse species would often be driven in the same way. Add, furthermore, that the succession of movement would be taken away—that process by which it flows forth step by step through many suitable stages and fitting forms at a certain time, and flows back in certain cycles of time. Add, finally, that no specific mode of movement would be directed toward a particular region, quality, or substance rather than any other.

<margin>The most ordered movement of the world is directed toward a certain end by divine providence.</margin>
If individual movements are carried out according to a certain wonderful order, then certainly the universal movement of the world itself does not lack the perfection of order. For just as individual things are "from" the universe and "toward" the universe, so they receive their order from the order of the universe and are referred back to the order of the universe. In this common order of the whole, all things—however diverse—are reduced into one by a certain agreement and reason. Therefore, all things are led by a single Orderer who is most full of reason. Since a supremely rational order comes from the highest...

He argues that all natural movement is directed toward a specific end by a rational, divine order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's inquiry into the nature of the human mind. Having established that all things in the universe are directed by a higher reason, he now contrasts the physical goals of elements and animals with the spiritual goals of the human intellect. The catchword "animus" (soul) from the previous page suggests a focus on the soul's inner life.</meta>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

...flows from the highest reason and wisdom of the mind, in which individual ends <note>original: "fines" — here meaning goals, purposes, or finishing points</note> are necessarily prescribed, toward which it directs each thing. A common end for the entire universe is also prescribed, toward which these individual ends are led.

### What boundaries the movement of elements, plants, and animals has.

**W**e do not doubt what limits the movement of the elements, plants, and irrational animals <note>original: "brutorum" — referring to animals that lack human reason</note> has. Indeed, some elements descend toward the center of the world by a certain weight <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea of "gravity," where heavy things like earth and water naturally move toward the center of the universe.</note>. Others ascend toward the hollow of the upper sphere by lightness <note>original: "levitate" — the opposite of gravity; light elements like fire and air move upward.</note>. The movement of plants, proceeding from the power of nourishment and generation, is terminated once the plant has sufficient food and has produced another plant like itself. The same happens to that power which we and the animals have in common with trees. The movement of irrational animals, which properly pertains to the senses, proceeds from a perceptible form and a natural need, moving through those things sensed externally to fulfill the needs of the body. The same occurs for that part of nature which we ourselves have in common with all animals. All these motions which we have just described are known to arise from a particular power because they tend toward a particular thing. And in these boundaries we have mentioned, they find sufficient rest, and are perfected as much as their nature requires.

### Five questions regarding the movement of the mind.

**I**t remains for us to inquire about the movement of the human mind. First: Whether it tends toward some end or not. Second: Whether the end of its motion is further movement or a state of rest. Third: Whether this good it seeks is a particular thing or the universal. Fourth: Whether it is able to eventually attain its desired end, that is, the highest good. Fifth: Whether, after it has achieved its perfect end, it ever departs from there.

### The movement of the mind looks toward a certain end.

**I**f all other things do not wander here and there by wise chance, but are directed by a certain rational order toward that which is most their own and most fitting—by which they are entirely perfected—then how much more does the mind, which is the receptacle of wisdom, look toward an ordered end by a natural instinct? For the mind understands the order and ends of natural things; it rationally orders its own affairs daily toward a certain end; and it is more perfect than all those other things we mentioned. It must, I say, look toward an end so that it too may be perfected according to its desire. This is especially true because just as the individual parts of life—that is, deliberations, choices, and faculties—are referred to individual ends (for each of these looks toward its own end as a "good"), so too the whole of life is similarly directed toward a universal end and good. Since any parts serve the whole, it follows that the order within the parts exists for the sake of their relationship to the whole itself. Furthermore, the order of those parts regarding particular ends depends on a certain common order of the whole, which contributes chiefly to the common end of the whole. Truly, if every mover moves for its own sake, it is consistent that the mind leads its various parts to their own ends for no other reason than that they should lead to the common end and good of the mind itself. Finally, who is so lacking in mind as to think that the mind strives—both by nature and by purpose—to show order to individual and diverse things toward a single point, unless the mind itself also had a certain order toward the One? For indeed, the final and common end everywhere moves all the rest. For the first thing desired is that for whose sake all other things are desired. If that final and common end were entirely absent, the rest could not exist. For unless the absolute form of the entire building is first prescribed by the architect, the various workmen will never be moved to their diverse tasks in an order that serves the whole. Indeed, they would never be sent to their pre-defined duties by one who did not himself first have the common limit of the entire work defined.

### The end of intellectual motion is not more motion, but a state of rest.

**I**f the end of intellectual movement is movement itself, then surely it moves in order to move, and moves again so that it may move thereafter without end. From this it would follow that, persevering perpetually in motion itself, it would never cease to move, and therefore never cease to live or to know. Perhaps this is that perpetual motion of the soul by which it is said to always act and live...

<summary>Ficino argues that just as elements and animals move toward specific physical goals, the human mind must have a supreme, universal goal (the Highest Good) that results in a state of rest rather than eternal wandering.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical exploration of the human soul. On the previous page, he distinguished between the limited physical goals of animals and the higher goals of the human mind. Here, he argues that the mind naturally seeks a state of stability and eternity, rather than constant motion, and that its ultimate goal is to encompass the entire universe of truth and goodness.</meta>

->LETTERS, BOOK II<-

...the soul is considered by some Platonists. I think, however, that since the mind recognizes and judges a stable state to be superior to change, it naturally desires that state beyond movement, seeking its own good in a certain stable condition rather than a mobile one, and finally achieving it. An indication of this is that the mind profits more in a state of rest than in motion. Furthermore, its familiar objects are the eternal reasons <note>original: "rationes æternæ" — these are the "Ideas" or "Forms" in Platonic philosophy, the unchanging blueprints of reality.</note> of things, not the shifting passions of matter. It follows that just as the power of life—namely intelligence and will—advances beyond the boundaries of moving things toward those that are stable and eternal, so life itself certainly attains its goal and its good in eternity, beyond any temporal change. Otherwise, the soul could never, either by understanding or by desiring, cross the boundaries of moving things, unless it were able to surpass them by living. Finally, motion is always imperfect and tends toward something else; but the nature of the "end" itself <note>original: "finis" — the goal or ultimate purpose</note>, especially the highest end, is such that it is neither imperfect nor does it progress toward anything else.

### *The object and goal of the mind is the universal truth and good.*

**B**ut is some specific truth and good called the goal of intelligence and will? Or is it the universal? Certainly the universal. For the intellect conceives a most ample notion of that which the Philosophers call "being," "truth," and "good." <note>These are the "transcendentals" in medieval philosophy—properties that belong to everything that exists.</note> Under this notion, whatever is, or can be, is thoroughly understood. This very thing which is called "being, truth, and good," containing all things, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking (peripateō) while teaching.</note> consider to be the common object of the human intellect. For just as the object of sight is the "sensible" (that which can be sensed), the object of the intellect is called the "intelligible" (that which can be understood). The intelligible, in its vastness, encompasses all things. Again, the intellect is naturally inclined to understand the entire magnitude of being; it sees all things within that notion, and in turn, it inspects "being" itself within the notion of all things. Furthermore, it understands all things under the aspect of the "true," and desires all things under the aspect of the "good." The Peripatetics refer both of these back to the concept of "being." Whether the "good" is broader than "being," as the Platonists believe, or not, seems to have no bearing on the present question. Let us therefore use these three names for now—being, truth, and good—as if they signify the same thing, for we have discussed these matters more diligently in our commentaries on the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of pleasure and the "Good." Ficino wrote a famous commentary on it.</note>. It seems we must first ask whether the intellect can clearly reach whatever is included under "being." It certainly can. For it divides being into the ten most general categories <note>original: "genera decem" — Aristotle's list of the ten ways something can be described (e.g., substance, quality, quantity).</note>, and again divides those ten categories step-by-step into many subordinate classes beneath them. Then it places certain final "species" <note>The most specific level of classification before reaching individual things.</note> under those subordinate classes. Finally, it subjects individual things to these species, so to speak, without end. If the intellect can describe "being" itself as a kind of whole, and divide it step-by-step into all its members, and compare those members most diligently both to each other and to the whole, who cannot see that it is by nature capable of the entire universal being? For he who sees the whole itself in its form, and perceives its boundaries and the steps through which it spreads everywhere, can without doubt understand the individual things contained within those boundaries. Much more so, then, since among the Platonists the mind can conceive of the "One" and the "Good" which are above being, it will be much more able to traverse its entire breadth on all sides. Certainly, after the notion of being—a word we have now repeated often—the mind even thinks at its own will of that which can be imagined as most different from it, namely, "non-being." If it can travel from being to that which is infinitely distant from it, it can much more easily travel through any things contained between them as intermediates. Hence Aristotle says: just as matter, which is the lowest of natural things, can take on all physical forms and thus all physical things can come to be, so the intellect—which is (so to speak) the lowest of supernatural things and the highest of natural things—can receive all the spiritual forms of all things, and become all things. Just as the universe under the aspect of being and truth is the object of the intellect, so under the aspect of the good it is the object of the will. What does the intellect seek, except to transform all things into itself by depicting them all within itself in its own way? What, in turn, does the will strive for, except to transform itself into all things by enjoying them all in the manner of all things? The former strives so that the universe may become, in a way, the intellect; the latter strives so that the will may become the universe. Therefore, the natural effort of the soul tends toward this: as Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and philosopher (c. 980–1037) whose work deeply influenced Western Scholasticism and Renaissance thought.</note> says in his *Metaphysics*, that the soul itself may become, in its own way, the whole world...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect and will are not satisfied by specific, changing things, but naturally seek the universal "Being, Truth, and Goodness." He describes the soul as a microcosm that strives to encompass the entire universe within itself through understanding and desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical exploration of the human soul. On the previous page, he argued that the soul’s orientation toward eternal and stable truths suggests that its ultimate goal lies beyond the shifting world of time and matter. # MARSILIO FICINO

...escape. For we see that every soul, by a natural instinct and a continuous effort, strives to know all true things with the intellect and to enjoy all good things with the will.

->*The origin and end of the soul is the infinite truth and good alone.*<-

**I**t is necessary to remember that the "universal" itself, which we call the goal of the soul, is entirely infinite. For we consider the primary and proper "end" <note>original: "finis" — here meaning the ultimate purpose or goal toward which a thing moves.</note> of any thing to be that which each thing specifically and most intensely desires as its highest good. It is for the sake of this good that the thing seeks and does all other things; in this good it finally rests entirely, so much so that it places a limit on the strivings of its nature and its desire. This condition is innate to our intellect: that it seeks the cause of every thing, and in turn, the cause of that cause. Therefore, the inquiry of the intellect never ceases unless it finds that cause which has no cause of its own, but is itself the "cause of causes" <note>original: "causa causarum" — a philosophical term for the First Cause, or God.</note>. This is God alone, who is boundless. Likewise, the affection of the will is satisfied by no good as long as we think there is another good remaining beyond it. Therefore, it is satisfied only by that good beyond which there is nothing more. And what else is this but the boundless God? Thus, whatever truth or good is offered to you that has certain fixed degrees—no matter how many—you still seek more through your intellect and desire more through your will. Hence, you can rest nowhere except in the boundless truth and good, nor can you reach your goal except in the infinite. Since every thing rests in its own origin—from which it is made and where it is perfected—and since our soul is able to find rest only in the infinite, it follows that the infinite alone is its proper origin. Properly, this should be called "Infinity" and "Eternity" itself, rather than merely "something eternal" or "something infinite." Since the effect closest to a cause turns out to be most similar to the cause itself, it follows that the soul is in some way an infinite and eternal power; otherwise, it would never properly incline toward an infinite goal. This is why there are some among men who are not content to live beneath the heavens or to be filled with temporal riches.

->*The soul can eventually attain its desired goal and good.*<-

**T**he rational soul can indeed eventually reach its perfect goal. For if those things which are less perfect in nature attain their natural perfection in the state of the goal they seek, how much more so the soul, which is both the most perfect thing and the goal of all natural things. If things that do not prescribe a goal for themselves or for others sometimes attain a suitable one, how much more so the mind? The mind hunts for its own goal, and having found it, establishes goals for many other things, foretells the goals of many, and sees the goal of all things. If natural power is not in vain even in the smallest things, it is certainly not in vain in the soul, which is so great that it can precisely measure the vast interval by which the smallest things are exceeded by the greatest. Furthermore, the soul would by no means naturally follow a certain goal unless it were also able to reach it. For by what power is it moved toward that goal, if not by the power through which it can also arrive? We see, moreover, that when the soul strives intensely, it makes great progress in such movement. By the same power that it makes progress, it is also eventually perfected. Finally, we see that it moves more and more vehemently as it goes, just as any physical element <note>Ficino refers to the Aristotelian idea that elements move faster as they get closer to their "natural place," such as a stone falling faster as it approaches the Earth.</note> moves more quickly the closer it gets to its natural boundary. Therefore, just as an element does not move from one thing to another forever without a destination, neither does the mind progress in vain; rather, it eventually reaches the goal it has desired for its own sake. <margin>bracket annotation</margin> There are, in both natural and human things and actions, certain principles and certain ends. It is against nature itself and the logic of a "principle" <note>original: "principium" — meaning a starting point or source.</note> to ascend from one beginning to another forever without a first principle. It is against the logic of a "goal" <note>original: "finis"</note> to descend from one goal to another in succession without a final end. Every action takes its origin from a supreme agent; every desire takes its origin from a supreme goal. For whatever things are "such-and-such" for the sake of something else must necessarily be traced back to that which is "such-and-such" for its own sake. Therefore, if the highest points are missing on either side, no action will begin at all, and no desire will be incited. Finally, since a "mover" moves for its own sake, wherever there is a supreme mover, a supreme goal is found as well. This is true in any order of things, and similarly in the order of the universe. But it is helpful to explain the above reasoning concerning the mind a little more broadly. If anyone should ask us

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul's restless search for ultimate truth and goodness proves its origin and destination are God, the infinite and eternal cause of all things. He asserts that this goal is attainable because nature does nothing in vain, and the soul’s increasing drive indicates an approaching final destination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letters, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of the human soul. The previous page established that the soul’s ultimate goal is the infinite God; this page transitions into a comparative analysis between the intellect and the physical senses to prove the intellect's superiority and divine nature.</meta>

## BOOK II OF THE LETTERS

...asks which of these is more perfect: the intellect or sense, the thing that can be understood or the thing that can be felt? We shall promise to show him what he desires at once, provided that he first answers this one thing for us. Be, O friend who asks me, something within yourself that has some knowledge of both—knowledge, I say, of the intellect itself and of sense, and again of the intelligible <note>original: "intelligibilis" — things that can only be grasped by the mind, like math or justice.</note> and the sensible <note>original: "sensibilis" — things perceived through the five senses, like color or sound.</note>. For the same power that compares these things to one another already sees both in some way.

Answer then: do you wish such a power to be the intellect or the sense? Answer, I pray, freely. So that by this answer of yours, I may soon answer that question of yours. Now I hear you answering thus: "Such a power is not the sense." For we all use our senses constantly, and we use them most especially and intently. If, therefore, the sense could see itself and those other things, then all people—or at least very many—would easily and clearly perceive the power itself of feeling and understanding, as well as the objects of understanding and the objects of sense. 

But since there are very few who know all these things, and even those few do so with difficulty, and do not know them through a brief moment of intelligence but through long reasoning, it is certain that the sense in no way knows either itself or the intellect and the intellect's objects. Rather, it is established that all these things are known by the intellect. Furthermore, that power which searches into both is the same as that which, by reasoning, finds these things and concludes by reason which of them is more perfect. Now, that which seeks by reasoning and assigns a reason is the "ratio" <note>The faculty of Reason, which processes logic and arguments.</note>, not the sense.

Therefore, it is the intellect alone which knows all these things. Thus, I respond to your first question in this way: the intellect is at least as much more perfect than the sense as its power is more widely and perfectly spread in its action. The sense, as you yourself were showing, can recognize neither itself, nor the intellect, nor the intellect's objects; but the intellect knows both. 

There is also another degree of perfection. Indeed, when the intellect compares itself, the sense, and other things according to their degrees of perfection, it already has the very "form of highest perfection" <note>The Platonic idea of an absolute standard of perfection against which all things are measured.</note> before its eyes, as it were. Comparing both to this form, it judges that whichever comes closer to it is the more perfect. If it reaches the form of highest perfection, it undoubtedly reaches it from a certain highest proportion to it. Therefore, it is not only more perfect than sense, but is even, almost after perfection itself, supremely perfect. 

I see, moreover, a third degree of perfection in the intelligence; for while it seeks and judges itself, it is certainly reflected back upon itself. Whatever is of such a nature also exists and remains within itself; it is, moreover, entirely incorporeal <note>Having no physical body or matter.</note> and simple <note>In philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts, and therefore cannot be broken apart or destroyed.</note>. Finally, since it proceeds from itself toward itself in a circular motion, it can certainly be moved eternally—that is, it can always act and live. 

I pass over the fact that the intellect, as something more perfect, is common to fewer people, and is exercised later and more rarely, and is granted as an "end" <note>A final goal or purpose.</note> after the use of the vegetative power <note>The basic biological functions like growth and nutrition.</note> and the sense. It gives the rule and laws to the sense and prescribes its goal; it leads itself to action by its own will when it reasons and deliberates. The sense, however, where reason does not resist, is always driven by the instinct of nature. 

I pass over how reason often chooses differently than what the sense and the use of the body require, clearly because the principle of choice does not depend on the body; otherwise, its goal would always look toward the body. That reason is in no way subject to bodies in its movement is perceived from this: that in contemplating it transcends bodies, in deliberating it extends itself to diverse and opposite things, and in choosing it often fights against the inclination of the body. Therefore, it is much less subject to any bodies in its essence and life. 

What of the fact that the sense seems to grow dull in some way as age advances, while the intellect does not? It can, however, be turned away from the intensity of contemplation when it is too occupied in caring for and tending to the body. What of the fact that whenever the object of the sense itself is too powerful, it suddenly harms the sense, and after that encounter, the sense cannot immediately discern weaker things? Thus, an excessive brightness offends the eye; thus, a louder noise offends the ears. The mind, on the contrary, is never harmed or confused by the most excellent of its objects. Rather, having known that object, it simultaneously discerns lower things more clearly and truly. This indeed signifies that the nature of the mind is supremely spiritual and excellent. 

What of the fact that the sense is limited only to bodily objects, whereas the intellect, according to its innermost action, emerges from all bodies, seeing that it is not submerged [in matter] according to its essence and life? It separates bodily forms from the "passions of matter" <note>The limitations and changes that physical matter undergoes.</note>; it also discerns those forms which are entirely incorporeal by themselves from bodily forms, since it is itself separated from the passions of matter and from the conditions of bodily form. Furthermore, the sense is content only with particular objects. But the familiar objects of the intellect are the "universal" and "eternal" reasons of things, which it [seeks] normally through a certain principal [affinity] to them...

<summary>Ficino argues for the superiority of the intellect over the senses, noting that the intellect is self-aware, deals with universal truths, and is independent of the body's physical decline.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the human soul's nature. Having established that the soul compares the intellect and the senses, Ficino now argues that the intellect’s ability to grasp eternal truths proves its own eternal nature, and he addresses the paradox of human suffering through the myth of Prometheus.</meta>

<page-num>610</page-num>
<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

the intellect can familiarly touch upon these proportions, from which it appears that the intellect itself is also absolute and eternal. This is especially true because it reaches these sorts of principles <note>original: "rationes" — the underlying rational structures or laws of reality.</note> through certain forms <note>original: "species" — mental images or categories through which we perceive things.</note> which it both creates and receives. It is necessary that these forms be free from the "passions" or influences of matter; otherwise, they would not be able to reflect those higher principles and ideas. Furthermore, unless the intellect itself existed free from the passions of matter, it would be able neither to create nor to receive forms of this kind in such a way.

### *The mind is able to achieve its desired end more so than the senses.*

**R**eason is indeed proper to us, for God did not infuse it into the beasts. If He had, He would have likewise given them speech as the interpreter of reason, and hands as the minister and instrument of reason; moreover, we would see in beasts some signs of deliberation and truth-seeking. As it is, however, we see that they never act otherwise than by the impulse of nature; they are driven solely by the necessity of the body. All spiders weave their webs in the same way; they do not learn to weave, nor do they improve their weaving over any length of time. Finally, if they possessed reason, there would appear in brute animals certain signs of religion and works of worship manifest to everyone. For where the intellect is present—which is like an eye positioned toward the intelligible light—there also shines the intelligible light which is God, and He is looked up to, loved, and worshiped. Inasmuch as the intellect is more perfect than sense, man is at least that much more perfect than the brute; and he is more perfect precisely because of that which he has as his own, which is not shared with the beasts. Therefore, he is judged more perfect solely on account of his intelligence. This is especially true since, through the gift of intelligence, he may approach that infinite perfection which is God through affection, contemplation, and worship. The chief perfection of anything consists in the possession of its appropriate goal. The attainment of this goal is easier and more complete in proportion to the richness of one’s innate perfection. For where that perfection which is born within us from the beginning prevails in its forms, there—by the order of nature—that final perfection is granted more abundantly, easily, and happily; for the latter follows the former, and arises from its service. From this it is concluded that reason is much more easily able to achieve its fitting and desired end than sense, and man more than the brute.

### *The immortal soul is always miserable in a mortal body.*

**W**e experience within ourselves our "beast," that is, the sense, very often achieving its goal and its good—namely, when it is completely filled by the attainment of a sufficient object, as far as the sense is concerned. But we do not experience our "human," that is, the reason, achieving its desired end. For even in the greatest pleasures of the body, when the sense is entirely filled as far as it is able, the reason is still vehemently troubled and agitates the sense. Whether it wishes to obey the senses, it is always suspicious and schemes for new delights; it continually seeks I-know-not-what beyond. Or, if it strives to resist the senses, it makes life laborious. In either case, therefore, not only is the reason itself not happy, but it even thoroughly disturbs the happiness of the sense. If it has already tamed the sense and collected itself within itself, then, driven by its own nature, it searches for the principles and causes of things. In this search, it often finds what it does not want, or fails to find what it does want, or perhaps does not comprehend as much as it desires and is capable of holding. It certainly always wavers, vacillates, and is in anguish. Since, therefore, it is nowhere at rest, it is certain that while it is so affected, it neither enjoys its own desire nor permits the sense to enjoy its goal, even when that goal is present. Indeed, nothing more irrational can be imagined than that man—who through reason is the most perfect of animals, and indeed of all things under heaven (most perfect, I say, in terms of that formal perfection granted to us from the start)—should, for that very same reason, be the most imperfect of all in terms of that final perfection for the sake of which the first perfection was given. This man seems to be that most unhappy <term>Prometheus</term><note>Ficino uses Prometheus as a symbol for the philosopher whose reason "steals" divine fire but leads to the "torment" of endless questioning while trapped in a mortal body.</note>, who, being instructed in the divine wisdom of Pallas and having obtained celestial fire in his reason, is judged for this very reason the most miserable of all. He stands upon the highest peak of the mountain—that is, in the very fortress of contemplation—suffering the continuous bite of a most rapacious bird: the sting of inquiry. This lasts until he is carried back to that same place from which he once received the fire; so that, just as he is now incessantly goaded toward the Whole by that one little ray of heavenly light, he may then be filled completely by the whole light.

->Just as it is difficult for a person placed outside their natural state to pursue happiness, so they achieve it easily once they are restored to that natural state.<-

**T**he arguments concerning the happiness of human felicity, which were brought forward by us earlier in the first part, appeared to show the truth itself clearly in a certain natural order. Why is it then, as experience teaches, that such great difficulty opposes us as we strive for blessedness? We seem to roll that great stone of Sisyphus <note>Sisyphus: A figure from Greek mythology condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down each time.</note> upward through the steep parts of a mountain. Is it any wonder? We seek the highest peaks of Mount Olympus <note>Olympus: The highest mountain in Greece, legendary home of the gods; here representing the heights of spiritual perfection.</note>. We inhabit the abyss of the lowest valley. We are weighed down by the baggage of a most heavy body. While we pant for the heights, we often suddenly slip back into the precipice, as much by our own weight as by the sheer cliffs on every side. What of the fact that from there, very many stumbling blocks and obstacles hold us back? From there, the harmful charms of certain meadows delay us. Thus, alas, for us miserable people, thus bound outside our sublime fatherland in the lowest depths, hardly anything is offered that is not difficult; nothing occurs that is not miserable on every side. What then shall we respond to such an ambiguity? On one hand, logical argument promised the greatest ease; on the other, experience equally shows the greatest difficulty. Finally, only the Mosaic <note>original: "Mosaica" — referring to the teachings of Moses in the Book of Genesis regarding the Fall of Man.</note> teaching will settle such a great dispute for us. We have been placed outside the order of our original nature; we act and suffer, alas, contrary to the order of nature. Just as easily as the first man, having turned entirely toward God, could receive happiness, so easily did he then lose that ease by turning against it. Therefore, all the offspring of the first parent, being placed outside the order of their prior nature, receive blessedness with the same difficulty as they would have received it with ease had they been restored to that very order. 

But what will the Philosophers say to these things? The Magi indeed, followers of Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster: An ancient Persian prophet; Ficino viewed him as one of the "ancient theologians" who prefigured Christian truths.</note> and Hostanes <note>Hostanes: A legendary Persian sage and magus often associated with alchemy and ancient wisdom.</note>, will bring forward something similar. For they say that because of a certain ancient weakness of the human mind, all things happen to us as weak and difficult. But if anyone were to restore the balance <note>original: "temperationem" — a balanced state of the soul's humors or qualities.</note> of the soul, all things would then be well-ordered. Nor is that view of the Pythagoreans and Platonists discordant with this: namely, that the soul is afflicted by so many evils in the sensible world because, being too enticed by the greed for sensible goods, it imprudently lost the goods of the intelligible world. The Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note> will perhaps say that man, rather than the beast, wanders from his own proper end because he is moved by free will; from this, he can go astray here and there as he uses various conjectures in his deliberations. However, the irrational animal is not led by itself, but by the providence of nature itself, which never errs, toward an end suitable to itself—directed like an arrow to a target. Yet, that error and transgression of ours, since it does not proceed from a defect of nature but from a variety of reason and a crookedness of counsel, by no means destroys our natural power, but rather disturbs it through the will. And just as in an element placed even outside its own proper place, a force and natural inclination toward its own proper boundary is preserved along with its nature—by which it can eventually seek its own region again—so in man, even after he has wandered from the right path, they believe there remains a natural power both to seek the path and the destination. 

Finally, the most exact examination of the Theologians concludes the whole matter briefly thus: No inclination toward any motion can be greater than the mover <note>original: "motor" — in Aristotelian physics, the force that initiates movement.</note>. Since, therefore, the inclination of the soul verges chiefly toward the infinite, it clearly depends solely upon the infinite. For if the soul’s motion proceeded most closely from some determined cause below God, it would only verge toward a limited end. Indeed, although the power of moving is infinite in the infinite principle, nevertheless in the subsequent cause, which is determined, it is limited. And motion follows the quality of the immediate mover rather than the remote one. For this reason, the mover itself who properly turns the soul toward the infinite is only that same infinite power, which moves the mind according to the free nature of the will in a certain way to choose paths most freely. 
<margin>10.</margin> 
Again, in accordance with the infinite power of the mover, it incites the soul to desire the end to such an extent that it cannot *not* desire it. If a motion of this kind cannot reach that toward which it is directed, then certainly no motion can. Where infinite power flourishes, there infinite wisdom and goodness also rule. These move nothing in vain, nor do they overlook any good for anyone that can and ought to be received. Accordingly, since man—both on account of the use of reason and contemplation—approaches much closer to the most blessed angels, and on account of divine worship approaches much closer to God, the fountain of blessedness, than the beasts do, it is necessary that he be able at some time to be much more blessed in the possession of his desired end. As one who is more similar to the heavenly beings, both in the ardor of his will and the light of his intelligence, he is likewise more similar in the happiness of his life. For from the power of life, the power and excellence of understanding and willing proceed. But now, in this body, both on account of...

Therefore, just as the heavenly and immortal soul continually pursues its happiness with difficulty in an earthly, unbalanced, and perishing body, so it achieves this happiness easily, whether free from the body or within a balanced, immortal, and heavenly body. Moreover, the natural end <note>The "natural end" refers to the "telos" or ultimate purpose of a being, which according to Ficino is the fulfillment of its design.</note> does not seem to exist except in a natural state. The most natural state of the eternal soul seems to be that it should live in its own body, which is now eternal. From this, it is concluded by necessary reason that the immortality and brightness of the soul can and must eventually shine forth into its own body. In this state, indeed, the highest happiness of man is fulfilled. ->The mind, once it has attained happiness, never loses it.<-

**W**hen the soul reaches its infinite end, since it reaches it chiefly by that reason by which it is affected, drawn, and led from here, it reaches it surely without end. If it was able at some point to rise up from a certain finite degree, which is infinitely distant, toward the immense, it is also able to remain infinitely in that very immensity. This is especially true because the same infinite power, which had drawn the soul so far toward itself, retains it more vehemently within itself than can be explained. In the infinite good, no evil can even be imagined; and whatever good can be imagined or desired is found there in its fullest. There, therefore, is eternal life, the clearest light of intelligence, a state lacking change, a condition free from deprivation, a secure and safe possession of the whole good, and joy full on every side.

->The end of the five questions concerning the mind.<-

->*Above sense is the intellect. Above the sensible <term>sensibile: objects perceived by the five senses</term> is the intelligible <term>intelligible: truths or forms understood by the mind alone, such as mathematics or justice</term>. Above our minds are other minds; above bodily forms are incorporeal forms.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his fellow-philosophers, Greetings.<-

**W**e seek and find daily, by reasoning and consulting, what may be truer or better in both natural and human affairs. In this discourse, indeed, we use certain common and incorporeal rules of truth or goodness. And we refer those things being discussed to the incorporeal, common, and highest form of truth or goodness by way of comparison. Thus, that which appears to approach more closely to the degree of that highest form among other things is judged to be truer and better than the rest. However, we do not do all of this by sense, but by reason; for only reason exists in men, which assigns the reasons <note>Ficino plays on the word *ratio*, which means both the faculty of "reason" and the "underlying principle" or "explanation" of a thing.</note> for things, and by reasoning compares individual things to the common form according to common rules. From this, two things are chiefly concluded. First, that reason exists as something much truer and better than sense, since reason alone brings us to the highest truth and goodness, as much by discourse as by affection. And when we deal with the truth and goodness of sense itself, whatever that may be, it is not sense that accomplishes this in any way, but reason. Second, that in so far as reason is truer and better than sense, at least the objects of reason are that much truer and better than the objects of sense. This is especially so because whenever the truth or goodness of sensible things is sought, this cannot be investigated or found in any other way than by a certain power and light of intelligible reasons and forms. Therefore, these intelligibles, which are called the objects of the intellect—that is, the incorporeal reasons of things and the forms released from the passions of matter—are truer and better, and therefore they seem to exist more in the nature of things than the forms of bodies which are offered to the senses. Added to this is the fact that just as the sensible moves the sense, so in a certain way the intelligible moves the intellect. If we cannot perceive those things which are below us unless we are moved by them in some way through certain species <note>original: "species" — In this context, mental images or representations of external objects.</note>, much less can we conceive anything above us unless we are so moved by it that the mind, pregnant with its seed, may give birth from there to an offspring similar to a more excellent substance. For the mind, by its own power alone, would never produce anything unless it were either inferior or equal. Therefore, when the mind [turns] toward that...
