the intelligible rises, and because it is necessarily truer than the sensible—just as it is often more excellent than the mind itself—it must, by its own power, raise the mind completely to itself and above the mind's own nature. If this <term>intelligible</term><note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "intelligible" refers to things that can only be understood by the intellect, such as mathematical truths or divine ideas, as opposed to "sensible" things perceived by the physical senses.</note> were nothing, or if it did not exist more truly than the sensible, it certainly could not move the intellect more truly than a sensible thing moves a sense. But now it moves it far more truly, since it leads the mind much further toward the truth as well as toward the <term>reason</term><note>original: "rationem" — Here meaning the underlying principle or logic of a thing.</note> of any truth. For we perceive what is true by its own principle, and what the principle of truth is itself—and in turn the truth of that principle—not by sense, but by reason. 

If anyone should say that the mind is not moved to understanding by foreign or external things, but that it conceives its own <term>species</term><note>original: "species" — In this context, mental forms or representations of things.</note> and objects for itself by its own miraculous power, we shall say it follows from this that the mind is entirely incorporeal and eternal; for if it is moved by nothing else but itself, it conceives by its own power incorporeal and eternal species or reasons. For the true reason of anything, since it can never be otherwise than it is, is everlasting. 

Furthermore, we shall add this: if there is no lack of a certain most simple and perfect form in the most simple mind—rather, it is present, and through it the mind speaks of the simplicity and perfection of all things, concluding that it is itself simpler and more perfect than many things, and that many other things are simpler and more perfect than itself—if, I say, such a form is not lacking to the mind but is present, it is much less lacking to the universe; indeed, it is much more truly within it. And the mind receives from that form the power by which it is moved toward it. 

We shall add besides, that the human mind is indeed the highest in the genus of natural forms, because it conceives or receives forms that are purer and more perfect, in comparison to which it thinks nothing of natural forms. Yet it is not the highest in the order of minds, because it is not the "truest"—that is, the most supremely truthful—since, at least through the fault of the harmful body, it often doubts and is deceived. But that mind is seen to be the truest which never admits anything false, and nothing at all ambiguous. 

Since, indeed, whatever is truer exists more greatly and more powerfully, it follows that there are other minds above our mind which are truer in their manner, and which are further removed from falsehood than ours. Finally, above all, there is a certain supreme and truest Mind, in which the mind is nothing other than Truth, and understanding is nothing other than Being, and acting is nothing other than Willing. Since this Mind is most fecund—indeed, Fecundity itself—it procreates, preserves, and illuminates as many minds as possible, as if they were daughters. 

Truer minds also possess truer reasons of things, and the Truest Mind possesses the truest reasons. From this it is concluded that the incorporeal reasons of things, which are thought by human reason at its pleasure, are not mere fictions—as might perhaps seem to those who live and judge things by their senses rather than by reason—but rather, above us in a certain divine mind, as if in a supracelestial Sun, the truest lights of all reasons shine most clearly. From there, the true rays of these reasons are sent down into other minds (which seem to be intermediate between that Mind and ours) as if into superior and in a certain way immutable stars, and even into our mind, as if into the now-mutable Moon.

->The mind is eternal, because it uses a ray received from above to reach the heavens.<-

**S**ince, indeed, the edge of the mind does not act through such rays—that is, it does not see and desire—differently than the substance of the mind itself has received them, we therefore conclude by the clearest light of true reason that the eternity of its own life has been granted to all grades of minds, even the lowest, by the first Mind, or rather by the supreme Light of minds; for to all is granted a certain recognition, desire, and veneration of natural eternity.

->The mind understands created things by a reflected ray of God, and the Creator by a direct ray.<-

**T**his Moon of ours—that is, the mind—accordingly as it is turned more or less, or in one way or another, toward its Sun, or turned away from it, is varied by a diversity and succession of light and certain shadows. It is never deprived of the entire capacity for receiving light. Yet it never shines totally on all sides, for the part lacking reason, being in some way denser—that is, more unsuited—does not reflect the light. This Moon of ours, I say, receives rays by which it perceives the supracelestial stars (that is, the angels) and discerns by a certain reason that they are far more excellent than celestial bodies, and loves and worships them more vehemently; rays, I say, of this kind from the very stars of heaven, which can raise neither the intellect nor the affection higher than to themselves,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's relationship with divine light. In the preceding sections, he likely established the soul as an incorporeal entity that moves toward truth. Here, he deepens the metaphysical comparison between the physical Sun and God as the "Intelligible Sun," a hallmark of his Neoplatonic theology.</meta>

## MARSILIO FICINO

...can have, it could not have had from them. It can, however, have received them from the angelic stars—or rather, from the supercelestial Sun through the angelic stars. Every light of the stars, as common opinion holds, is from the Sun and toward the Sun. Every light of minds is likewise from God and toward God. When this Moon of ours <note>Likely referring to the human soul or mind, which reflects divine light as the moon reflects the sun.</note> looks upon the divine Sun in such a way that it perceives Him to be infinite, and clearly beholds by what principle He is so, and because He is infinite, asserts that He precedes the angels by an utterly infinite interval, and considers the angels themselves as nothing in comparison to Him—certainly, it did not receive from the angels that kind of ray by which it both progresses infinitely above the angels and holds them as nearly nothing. Nor, again, did it receive it from God Himself *through* the angels. For while a ray passes through a determined <term>angel</term><note>In Ficino's hierarchy, angels are "determined" or "finite" beings compared to the infinite God.</note>, it is itself determined, and thus it cannot raise either its sight or its affection to the proper view of the immense <term>insofar as it is immense</term><note>original: "in quantū immensum est"</note>. For there is need of a properly infinite power for that motion which, tending toward a properly infinite goal, proceeds without end in such a way that it can only find its end in an infinite goal. Therefore, it is the pure ray of the immense God alone by which we recognize that God is immense; unless we knew this, we would always be searching further beyond. It is also seen to be the flame of the immense God alone, by which we so burn for the immense that no liquid besides the immense could extinguish—or rather, to speak more correctly—<margin>•</margin> fulfill our thirst.

Perhaps it will be worthwhile to explain that likeness of the **Platonic Sun**, just as we have explained very broadly in the book *On Love* <note>Referring to Ficino's *De Amore*, his commentary on Plato’s *Symposium*.</note> and in the *Theology*, here also somewhat more broadly than above. Among all the instruments of the senses, the eye is the purest. Among all the powers of the soul, the intellect is the purest. In the visible world, the highest visible thing is the Sun. In the intelligible world, the highest intelligible thing is God. Therefore, just as sight relates to the visible, so almost does the intellect relate to the intelligible. Sight discerns all visible things (that is, colors) in the glow of the highest visible thing (that is, the Sun). The intellect beholds all intelligible things and all truths in the light of the highest intelligible and of Truth itself. And any intellect has a greater need for such light than sight does for its own, by as much as every intellect and any intelligible thing depends more upon the supreme and infinite Intelligible than sight and any visible thing depend upon the Sun itself, which is finite and is produced and preserved by higher causes. 

Whatever is seen anywhere—whether by the eyes of certain animals which see at night by a certain innate small ray, or by others by the light of fire or stars—all of this is seen by the splendor of the Sun itself. For just as every warm thing is made and preserved by that which is supremely warm, so every bright thing is made and preserved by that which is supremely bright. Preserved, I say, because even if "equal causes" (that is, those in the same species as the effect) are not necessary for the conservation of the effect once it is generated, nevertheless, higher causes are necessary even in preserving the effect. By the same logic, whatever is understood anywhere—whether by a certain implanted and natural light as if by a familiar ray of the eye, or by the rays of the lower angels as if by fire, or by the lights of the higher angels as if by stars—all this is understood by the rays of that infinite and intelligible Sun. This is especially true because a Sun of this kind flourishes everywhere as a whole and fills all things from within; and from that source all things depend more, both in being preserved and in being born, than images in mirrors depend upon bodies. 

Indeed, we can discern other things by the ray of the Sun reflected through various other objects. But we are not able to receive the Sun itself except by a certain direct ray of its own and by a direct gaze into it. And yet, by this ray which flows out from the Sun (and by which the eye is therefore mixed and diminished in some way), the eye cannot discern how pure and how great the Sun is. But if we recognize its purity and magnitude, we do not measure it with these eyes, which are far deceived, but with reason. However, it was necessary for the eye to have been so established by nature that it might adhere as closely as possible to the globe of the Sun itself, so that it might perceive its proper purity and magnitude. 

Thus, the ray which, emanating from God, is infused into created things, properly shows us only created things; but God shows Himself more to us when the ray is directed into that mind which is truly directed toward God. <margin>•</margin> Nevertheless, since He is perceived by the mind according to the quality and capacity of the mind, that ray cannot demonstrate the purity and infinity of God. And therefore, through it, we could never think of God as an act entirely pure and infinite. For we have nothing within us above the mind that could refute the fallacy of the mind. Yet, by certain reason, we consider the abyss of divine purity and infinity, and we notice the "reason of infinity" and, in turn, the "infinity of reason." Also, when we proceed through innumerable degrees of perfection above the highest angels, moving more and more step-by-step, by what reason the divine act [continues its] progress...

<page-num>685</page-num>

### BOOK II OF THE LETTERS

...of this nearly infinite sort, we think it infinitely exceeds us. For this reason, not only is the ray of the divine Sun present in the eye of the mind, but even the divine Sun Himself is present under the very principle of His infinity (so to speak), through which the mind may see and desire both the truest principle of infinity and the infinity of that principle itself. He is present, I say, everywhere and always. For whenever minds are unencumbered and lean more attentively toward this body, they consider the divine act as infinite by this principle: because it is not confined by the limits of any <term>subject</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, a "subject" is the underlying thing in which qualities exist; Ficino argues God is not "contained" by anything else.</note>, nor is it tainted by the mixing of quality, nor surpassed by the excellence of a superior cause, nor exceeded by intervals of time or spaces of place, nor bounded by any number of degrees of <term>virtue</term><note>Here meaning "power" or "potency."</note>, however many they may be. Perhaps it is not even bounded or surpassed by the mind, which proceeds without end beyond any number and limit, both in imagining and in desiring. The mind sees that beneath the infinite act of God lies an infinite <term>passion</term><note>original: "passionem"; in this context, it refers to the capacity of matter to be acted upon or shaped.</note> of matter (so to speak). It sees time as somehow unending, motion as always equal, space as immense (if I may put it that way), and a somehow perpetual succession of generation, as well as the untiring discourse of the mind. It sees pure nothingness itself as being considered infinitely through negation, and an immense evil imagined there. It sees pure <term>being</term><note>original: "ens"</note> itself (as I might say) as being infinitely affirmed through reasoning, and that it is a completely immense good, because it is an immense power. For any power is one thing, and number and measure are another. And any power is prior to measure in a certain order. Therefore, whenever number or measure is added to power, it happens from the outside and as a later occurrence. The power of God Himself admits no such thing. Therefore, He who perfects all things by number and measure possesses neither number nor measure Himself. If He does not admit it within Himself, neither does He suffer it around Himself. Therefore, just as He replicates Himself infinitely within, so He unfolds Himself infinitely without. From this it follows that He is everywhere and always, that He does all things with the greatest ease and perfects them, and that He is present and inherent in all things most easily. For just as an infinite dimension, if it existed, would occupy immense space, so if there is an infinite power, it diffuses itself everywhere without end, and also lives forever without beginning or end. The <term>Platonic</term><note>Followers of Plato, whose ideas Ficino translated and revitalized in the Renaissance.</note> philosophers think that where the highest visible thing is, the highest sight exists in that same place. For this reason, they attribute to the globe of the Sun not only life, but also the most piercing and certain power of seeing of all. In this, they seem especially to imitate <term>Orpheus</term><note>The legendary poet and prophet; Ficino often cited "Orphic" hymns as ancient theological sources.</note>, who calls the Sun the "eye of the world," by which the eyes of all see and which they look upon. They think that the Sun and the life-giving stars, being alive, inspect whatever is contained in the world by the rays they cast through all things.

->*God sees and cares for all things.*<-

The <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they discussed philosophy while walking.</note> think that the highest intellect and the highest <term>intelligible</term><note>Something that can be understood or grasped by the mind, as opposed to something felt by the senses.</note> are entirely the same. Certainly, the highest intellect possesses the highest mode of understanding; therefore, in understanding, it does not look outward, but inward, nor does its intelligence depend on anything other than itself. That the highest intelligible is also the highest intellect is clear from this: that there must be a certain maximum proportion between the intellect and the intelligible. Since, therefore, that which is separated furthest from the "passions of matter" becomes the most intelligible, that which is most abstract is also the highest and truest intellect. Furthermore, it would not be the highest intelligible unless it were also such to itself, and were understood by itself. Finally, if "intelligible" signifies a certain excellence over common intellects—for it moves, illuminates, forms, and perfects them—nothing is found in the intellect according to participation or form of the good that is not found in the highest intelligible itself according to its cause and acting power. Therefore, rational souls are said to be certain intellects according to participation; angels, however, are considered intellects according to form. The highest intelligible, that is, God, is intellect according to cause—an intellect, I say, above all thinkable intelligence. An intellect infinitely more excellent than any other intellect. If the light of the Sun, by which the eye sees the Sun, possessed an eye, certainly while our eye saw it, it would in turn look back at our eye—and much more clearly, because all clarity emanates from it. And do we still doubt whether that divine eye—by which the eyes of our minds see most closely, and which they see everywhere—sees our eye in return? Unless He Himself saw us, He who by continually seeing us, always illuminates...

<page-num>686</page-num>

# MARSILIO FICINO

...and by illuminating, it bestows upon us the power and the act of seeing; surely, otherwise, we would see nothing anywhere. For we certainly understand nothing except through the light of the highest <term>intelligible</term><note>The "intelligible" refers to things that can be understood by the mind alone, rather than perceived by the physical senses.</note>, which is full on all sides with the reasons of every understandable thing. Just as we do not see anything except the light of the Sun, which is depicted with the colors and shapes of all things.

And do we still doubt whether that immense goodness loves us or provides for us? It fosters us even without a medium, just like children, and embraces us everywhere and always. And do we still doubt whether we discern the sublime rays of forms from the lowest darkness of matter by some tiny and corporeal spark, or rather by the incorporeal and heavenly light? Let us argue for higher things, and everywhere let us refute lower things; let us measure how small are earthly things, how great are heavenly things, and how immense are the things beyond the heavens. No one seems to lie more everywhere than he who trusts to measure the greatest things with the tiny finger of bodily sense, rather than with the greatest measure of the mind. No one falls more deeply into the shadows, either slipping away secretly or being cast down unwillingly, than he who, being proud toward God and himself, becomes ungrateful to the heavenly Sun—so much so that he claims to see light without the light of Him to whom all light belongs. It is just as if someone believed they could see the heavenly lights only by the ray of their own eye, and not by the celestial splendor. 

Here the Apostle Paul exclaims against certain prouder philosophers: <note>original: "Qui cum Deum cognouissent, non sicut Deu͂ glorificauerunt..." — quoting Romans 1:21–22</note> *Because when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor were they thankful; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; and professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.* The minds of these men seem to have suffered an eclipse when they fell away too proudly from God—or rather, quite miserably from themselves. For we ourselves fall away unhappily whenever we foolishly abandon Him without whom we cannot exist in any way. Alas, whoever miserably leaves this guardian does not leave Him entirely; for at the same time, he falls back into the hands of the same one, but as an avenger. Alas, whoever scorns the Father when He shines kindly, meanwhile experiences the same Father as a burning judge. Thus, in the same light where he neglected to venerate his own infinite good, he may feel his own infinite evil—unless he eventually learns to love what he neglected. And because of the impurity of his eyes, he may always grieve under the ray of that light, having failed to purge his eyes and lift them up so that he might always rejoice in the total light. 

When the minds of impious philosophers imprudently fell away from God, then the senses in them imprudently fell away from the mind. Although the body followed the senses willingly, it did so powerlessly; from this arose certain most monstrous opinions, and from that, the most savage customs of all. From this comes a life that is wretched on all sides. Conversely, no one has more probable opinions, more proven customs, or a more blessed life than those who philosophize legitimately—that is, piously—who always join the study of science and truth with religious and true piety. This seems to be nothing other than being unwilling to separate the love of the truth that must be found from the love of the truth that must be honored.

->*The elements are moved changeably.*<-
->*The celestial spheres are moved stably.*<-
->*Souls stand changeably.*<-
->*Angels stand stably.*<-
->*God is stability itself.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Francesco Ippolito, <term>Doctor of Both Laws</term><note>original: "utriusq; Iuris Doctori" — a degree in both Civil and Canon (Church) law.</note>, most distinguished Count of Gazoldo, greetings.

**W**e see the elements being moved changeably from the earth all the way to heaven. I say "changeably" because they seem to be moved away from the straightest rule of motion in some way, either due to an impediment or some other cause. However, the celestial bodies are indeed moved, but "stably," for they persevere continually in their own natural motion. Accordingly, <term>stability</term><note>original: "status" — referring to a state of rest, permanence, or unchanging condition.</note> is judged to be far more perfect than motion. For motion necessarily needs stability, but not the other way around. Therefore, if as we now ascend from lower to higher things, a more perfect motion meets us step by step, and that motion is more perfect which is more stable, then much more should stability itself meet us as something more perfect than motion. 

Thus, just as stability increased in the elements all the way to heaven—to the point that a mode of "standing stably" has been found—it must increase so much more above heaven that some substance of stability itself is found. There, then, will be something that stands always, albeit "changeably." These are the rational souls, whose substance is always the same and suffers no motion, yet their affection and action vary. But since any change signifies a certain need—because of which that which is moved tends to run toward what it does not possess—it is necessary that above that which is unworthy, there is something which is full...

<page-num>903</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II.</header>

## LETTERS, BOOK II.

...by which moving things are sustained and governed, and to which others return so that they may be fulfilled. Therefore, angels are placed above souls; they truly stand forever, and they stand firmly, because in them, substance and action are always the same. Bodies are the shadows of spirits; spirits, conversely, are the lights of bodies. There are three types of bodies, and therefore there are three types of spirits. A body composed of the elements <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> changes from its state both in its whole and in its parts. The spheres of the elements, even if they change in their parts through a cycle, nevertheless remain incorruptible as wholes. Finally, the celestial spheres <note>The planetary and stellar spheres above the elements.</note> remain indissoluble both in their parts and in their whole. Spirits, perhaps by reason of a vacuum <note>Ficino refers here to a lack of substance or a potentiality for change.</note>, might change entirely. However, **rational beings** <note>original: "Rationales"; referring to human souls.</note> remain permanent in their entire substance and principal action, even though they are changed by a certain cycle according to specific particles—that is, according to their lowest powers and actions. Angelic spirits remain the same and similar in both respects. Or rather, to express it more correctly: if many bodies are found which, although they change in their arrangement, always remain the same in substance—and these are the ones whose proper motion is a circuit <note>Referring to the circular motion of the heavens.</note>—then it is much more certain that many spirits exist which, even if they are changeable in some arrangement, are nonetheless entirely immutable in substance.

Such indeed are those who, endowed with reason, perform a certain <term>rational circuit</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "circuit" is the process where the soul goes out of itself to understand the world and returns to itself to understand God.</note> from themselves into themselves internally, whenever they observe and care for themselves. They act externally again: first, by deliberating from the end of things to be done back to the principles, and vice versa; then, by arguing from certain propositions to conclusions, and back again; then, by contemplating from the effect to the cause, and again from causes to the effect. Again, they act when they resolve particulars into universals themselves, and in turn divide universals into particulars by composing them. 

Every power directed toward a circuit is judged to be eternal, both because it does not depart from itself through its own center, and because, if necessary, it returns to itself through its own circumference; at any point, it always begins a beginning from the end. This is especially true where there is a spiritual circuit, for there the circumference is joined to the center. A simple substance of this kind folds its power back upon itself and increases it by that folding. Relying upon itself, it preserves itself. 

One must remember, however, that where the discourse of reason takes place, there are certain innate, stable principles of reasoning—that is, certain <term>common and manifest notions</term> <note>original: "communes quasdam manifestasque notiones"; these are innate ideas or "seeds of truth" that Ficino believes God planted in the human mind.</note>. Starting from these as if from rays of light, we may judge those things which are more unknown to us, comparing the things we have found to these principles. Furthermore, it is proper to remember that because those principles are necessary and eternal, the power of the soul which is the subject of those principles is likewise eternal. We possess that discourse of reason as something proper to our nature. However, the foundations of that discourse are common to us and the angels. In that part, we are heavenly; in the other, we are <term>super-celestial</term>.

There are two extremes of the worldly body: namely, the Earth and the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest heaven, believed to be composed of pure light or fire and the dwelling place of God.</note>. Both seem immobile, but for different reasons. The Earth is immobile because it has not attained any power for a circuit. The Empyrean heaven is immobile because it has already attained every power of bodies. The middle spheres, by a certain eternal but moving power, seek something further, something permanent and eternal. What we have said about these three levels, understand to be said exactly the same way regarding sense, reason, and mind; and again regarding beast, man, and angel. 

Because the elements are not only bodies but are also composed of the lowest matter, they are tossed about in a mobile fashion. But the celestial bodies, because they lack such matter and are, as it were, "non-bodies," therefore run their course stably and evenly; by their own order, they seem to restrain the "errors" <note>The word "error" here refers to the wandering or erratic movements of the lower elemental world compared to the perfect circles of the stars.</note> of the elements. Yet, because they are carried by opposite and contrary motions, if they are carried by their own natures, it would be necessary for contrary natures to be within them. Nevertheless, there is no dissonance of contrary qualities where all destruction and all transgression are absent. They are moved, therefore, by a certain tempering, by which the higher cause itself rules powerfully and leads them sweetly. 

Nature is "uniform" because it brings so many things into one; it is also "omni-form" because it reduces those things to all-shaped ends and dispositions. It is not, however, a corporeal form; otherwise, it could not be uniform and omni-form at the same time. Furthermore, every corporeal thing is necessarily changed while it moves; therefore, it cannot be the most perfect mover. And because it does not remain stable while moving, it cannot by its own power alone maintain a permanent tenor in motion. For this reason, the celestial globes are moved by a certain spiritual and rational substance, one possessing an eternal and tireless power, by which it is able to roll such great masses so evenly and swiftly, and to complete a wonderfully rational and most beautiful order.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the hierarchy of the universe, arguing that the human soul’s ability to reason using eternal principles proves its immortality. He describes the celestial spheres as being moved by rational, spiritual substances (angels or world-souls) that maintain the perfect order of the cosmos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the ontological hierarchy—the ladder of being—moving from the movement of the rational soul to the absolute stability and unity of God. It bridges a philosophical treatise on the nature of being with the beginning of a letter to his Hungarian and Florentine associates.</meta>

<page-num>618</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

Since rational souls are in no way bodies, but already incline toward bodies by a certain natural affection, they indeed remain always the same in essence and life, but in a mobile way. Truly, they are moved by an innate and proper power. But since angels are neither bodies, nor do they incline toward the vivifying of bodies, they stand firm and stable, as we have discussed in the preceding sections. Just as all moving things are necessarily led back to one primary motion and time, so all stable things are necessarily led back to one first state <note>original: "statum"; referring to a condition of rest or immutability</note> and eternity, as if to a hinge or a center. Upon this center, all things that "stand" or remain stable lean with all their strength; around it, all things that move revolve; and through union with it, things so many and so diverse produce a certain single harmony. Motion and time are almost the same; stability and eternity are entirely the same. For those things which appear separate in the lower realms are miraculously joined in the higher ones. Whatever is said to "stand," whether in itself or in another, first stands by stability itself. Then, in a certain way, it takes on some composition. But above that which is in some way composite, there necessarily exists something most simple, upon which the rest depend, and by which they are united and composed. This is especially true because that which is first in nature, since it receives nothing beyond its own primary being, cannot be thought of as being composed from elsewhere in any way.

Thus, therefore, above the sluggish nature of the movable, and above the wandering movement, there is a more constant motion; above a stable condition, there is a stable substance with a certain changeable condition; and above this nature is Stability itself, the simplest of all. Where there is the highest simplicity, there is the highest unity; therefore, there exists one God, who is in truth absolute unity, and, as the Platonists like to say, is also in a way the unity and hinge of the mind, just as the mind is the hinge and unity of the soul, and the soul the unity and hinge of nature, and finally, nature the unity of bodies. Just as God is pure stability lacking change, so He is pure unity devoid of imperfect multiplicity. Because His stability is pure, He is therefore swifter than all motion; for from eternity He is Himself within Himself all that which the whole of motion achieves only in part, and by degrees, and through the whole of time. And whatever divided motion does for a divided nature in a divided interval of time, that whole thing indivisible Stability perfects in an indivisible moment of indivisible eternity, just as He wills. For where the most constant power dominates, there the swiftest action of all is produced. But where an unstable nature wavers, the motion becomes slower.

Again, since God is pure unity—the principle of infinite multiplicity—He is therefore infinitely more powerful than an infinite multitude of things. If an innumerable number can emanate from Him throughout everlasting time, He is already in act an innumerable number, or rather, infinite unity and immense power. And whatever things are infinitely dispersed and, so to speak, infinitely weakened, He powerfully gathers into the immense through His own immense unity. Since, indeed, there is no difficulty of action where the measure of power is absent, and since a measured nature cannot resist Him, He therefore perfects all things infinitely more easily and happily than can be imagined; so much so that by His stability He effects all things at once—He who is all things at once, upon whom as a center all individual things depend like lines and points, so that by one stable nod He can move <note>original: "vibrare"; literally to vibrate or brandish, here meaning to give life and motion</note> individual things according to the nature of each.

->*A corporeal form is divided and moved by another. The rational soul is not divided, but moves of itself. An angel is neither divided nor moved, but is filled from elsewhere. God is a single, simple, and immense fullness.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Miklós, Bishop of Vác <note>Nicolaus Bathory (1435–1506), a leading figure of the Hungarian Renaissance</note>, and Francesco Bandini <note>A Florentine humanist who acted as a link between Ficino and the Hungarian court</note>, greetings.<-

# A
form which exists as such from itself and primarily <note>original: "primoque"; meaning in a fundamental or first-principle sense</note> must be most fully of that kind within its genus. For that which is hot and bright from itself and primarily, is exceedingly hot and bright. Whatever, therefore, is not perfectly of such a kind depends on some other higher thing. <margin>* Corporeal form.</margin> Every form which is divided along with matter or dimension, and is changed by another, is the most imperfect of all forms. For it requires the support of the dimension of its subject, since it does not exist from itself, given that it is not found either in itself or with itself. Nor does it arise chiefly from the subject, which by its own nature is judged to be formless, nor again from quantity, which does nothing through itself but through quality; moreover, because of extension and dispersion, that form becomes weak, and finally, because of motion, it appears needy. Therefore, it neither acts nor is moved by its own power, since it does not possess an intact force, and by its own power it is neither sustained nor does it subsist. <margin>* The Soul.</margin> Wherefore

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the ontological hierarchy—the ladder of being—moving from the movement of the rational soul to the absolute stability and unity of God. It explains why the soul must be a self-moving, incorporeal substance and how it seeks "Fullness" through the higher ranks of angels toward God.</meta>

<page-num>689</page-num>

### LETTERS BOOK III.

[The soul] depends upon a certain more excellent form, which can exist in itself without a subject <note>In philosophy, a "subject" is the underlying matter or substance that carries qualities. Ficino argues the soul doesn't need a body to exist.</note> and with itself, without physical dimensions. This is the <term>rational soul</term> (original: *anima*), which is moved in a certain way by itself because it precedes qualities that are entirely changeable; yet it is not divided by matter or quantity in any way. This is especially clear because the soul itself clearly distinguishes individual forms from divided ones and joins them within itself, and because it **turns back into itself** <note>This refers to self-consciousness or reflection, a key ability of the incorporeal soul.</note>, which a divisible form cannot do. For where one part is distant from another, a turning of the whole back into itself has not yet occurred. 

That the rational soul moves freely by its own power is most apparent when it understands bodily things by its own light rather than theirs, and when it frequently chooses, by its own <term>free will</term> (original: *arbitrio*), to act against the impulses of those bodily things. It constantly directs its movements toward many opposing parts, as one who is not dragged along by a determined quality of nature or an object, but is led rather by the variety of its own counsel. 

However, because it moves in a certain way, it is judged to be somewhat "in need," since no thing usually seeks through motion what it already possesses. Therefore, above the soul is the **immobile angel**. I say immobile because the angel is already full in every respect. Just as one ascends from that which is not at all full toward that which is most full, so one ascends toward **Fullness itself** from that which is "fullest." This is because a descent occurs in a certain order from Fullness to that which is less full, passing through the "fullest." 

Indeed, the intention of every cause in acting is to generate something as similar to itself as possible, and the more powerful a cause is, the more easily it achieves this. From this it follows that the Cause, than which no more powerful can be imagined <note>Ficino is using a variation of St. Anselm’s definition of God.</note>, generates something for itself so similar that nothing more similar can be imagined. Such a similarity is not found anywhere except where the substance of the generator and the generated is entirely the same. But let us set aside for the present what God generates within Himself <note>A veiled reference to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, and consider what He procreates outside Himself. 

For here too it is consistent that God procreates certain most similar things, and then step-by-step things that are less similar, so that no rational order in the degrees of being can be considered by us which was not first both considered and fulfilled by the Supreme Reason. Truly, from such an order of God, natural causes preserve this kind of order in producing their effects, and minds, in their reasoning, similarly maintain a skillful order, discovering both the natural and the divine. 

From these points we conclude: that souls are not yet "fullest," that angels are already "fullest," and that above the angels, who are being filled, there is a **Fountain** from whose waters they are filled. Many can and should be "fullest," so that in the most perfect work of God, the most perfect parts may abound everywhere. But Fullness itself is simple—it is that by which all full things are full, and because they are filled, they are called "composite" <note>In Neoplatonism, anything created is "composite" (made of parts), whereas the Source (God) is "Simple" (one single thing).</note>. 

Supreme Fullness, I say, can only be one. If someone were to introduce two supreme fullnesses, we would ask whether they differ entirely within themselves, or agree in every part? Or rather, do they partly agree and partly disagree? If both are similarly and entirely "fullness," they cannot differ. If they are said to agree entirely, they are one, not two—which is what we wish to prove. If they agreed in one part and disagreed in another, first of all, both would be composite, depending on their parts and on some simple component. Secondly, neither would be that very "Fullness" we are seeking. For that in which one differs from the other would not be found in the other. Add to this that in the Supreme Fullness, nothing ought to be (so to speak) "not full." But if it had diverse parts, no part would be the same as another, or the same as the whole; therefore, no part would be "fullest." 

For this reason, to repeat the same point often, Fullness must be unique, entirely indivisible, and also infinite. Indeed, just as in that which we call a "pure vacuum" or emptiness itself, nothing that is "present" can be imagined; so in **Pure Fullness**, which must exist as the total opposite of pure vacuum, nothing can be imagined into infinity that is not present. 

From where else does the primary matter of the world, and the entire course of the universe, and the discourse of every mind obtain this quality—that they naturally strive to be filled beyond any limit—if not from Fullness itself? It overflows beyond every limit and draws minds, the world, and matter beyond their limits. Since, however, immense Fullness cannot draw things into a vacuum, we rightly prophesy that the effort of matter, the course of the world, and the discourse of the mind will one day be entirely filled by that Supreme Fullness itself. Then the stability of the world's center will communicate itself entirely to the circumferences of the spheres, and the clarity of the pure circumference will spread itself all the way to the center. The entire machine of the world will be clothed in the **harmless flames of the Empyrean heaven** <note>The Empyrean was the highest heaven in medieval cosmology, associated with light and fire.</note>. Bodies and the natural senses of rational souls...

## Compendium of the Platonic Theology by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.

->The ascent from corporeal substance to the incorporeal, namely to souls, angels, and God. Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosophers, **sends greetings.**<-

**S**ince substance is the foundation of every <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidentis"; in philosophy, an 'accident' is a property that can change without destroying the thing itself, like the color of a shirt.</note>, it is prior to the accident by a certain order of nature. Since it is prior and does not lack the power of form, it can exist somewhere without an accident—specifically, I mean, without a bodily accident. For a physical accident, when added to the common definition of substance, brings not so much progress as it does defect. Truly, if a substance exists without a bodily accident, it will be truer because of its purity, and more powerful because of the very simplicity and unity of its individual nature. For this reason, there is already in reality a certain substance separate from the division of quantity and the mixing of bodily quality; otherwise, that potential—so rational and so good—would always be in vain in the universe, or that nature, which is considered truer and more powerful than any bodily substance, would be entirely false or altogether weak. The first level of incorporeal substance is a certain kind of life, that is, the soul. Moreover, that incorporeal substance seems to be the same as a certain kind of life. Indeed, the property of life is a certain power, truly marvelous, for penetrating, uniting, and moving a body. A substance that is entirely incorporeal possesses such power in the highest degree. Lives of this kind already exist in the order of things. For a living body depends more upon the life joined to it than life depends upon the body. For the body is formed, sustained, ruled, and moved by it. Therefore, just as below this union of body and life certain bodies are found—namely stones, metals, and others of the same kind—which can remain without life, so also, and much more likely, there exist even more lives which can sustain themselves without any support from a body: these are partly rational souls, and partly angels. Above souls are angels. But is it necessary for angels to be above bodies and souls? It is certainly necessary. Indeed, the nature of the intellect itself, insofar as it is intellect, seems to be this: that it lives apart from the body rather than in the body. For it understands by a certain abstraction of forms from the individual passions of bodies. And the more it is abstracted from them, the more clearly it discerns, the more effectively it acts, and the more blessedly it lives. It is as if that were the most natural habit of the mind; to join the mind to a body, however, might perhaps be nothing other than to separate it far from its own origin. But what is more natural exists, for the most part, in the very order of things. Therefore, above those intellects that are present in bodies—that is, the rational souls—there are certainly many minds separated from the commerce of bodies. Just as the property of the pure intellect itself is to live apart from the body, so the nature of pure sense is to be with a body. Therefore, the spirit in which there is only sense with life lives only in the body, it seems. But the spirit in which there is only intellect leads its life only outside the body. But where intellect and sense are joined—which is the case for a human—that kind of spirit is endowed with such a nature that it can live both in the body and outside it. But since the intellect in this case is a certain part of the soul, which contains other parts besides, it is also ambiguous; it runs through things by a certain spiritual motion, understanding one thing after another <note>This refers to 'discursive' reasoning, where the human mind moves step-by-step, unlike an angel who knows things instantly.</note>. For that reason, it is necessary that a more perfect mind exist above it, which is neither contracted to the capacity of the soul, nor mixed with lower parts, nor distracted in its action by time, but is absolute and pure in itself, clear on all sides, performing its action not by running through things, but by remaining still.

->Above the mind in the soul is the mind in itself; above that is God.<-

**T**hat Platonic reasoning contributes to the same point: If the soul, according to its own form and reason, were the Intellect, then certainly the entire soul would be nothing but Intellect—and indeed, the most absolute Intellect. And every soul would appear to be a master of intelligence. But since the matter stands otherwise, it is clear that the soul is not, according to its own properly principal form...

He establishes a ladder of existence where the human soul, being "ambiguous" and discursive, sits between the purely physical and the purely intellectual minds of angels and God.</summary>

<sig>Xx 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: tur; some ghosting from verso</meta>

...not as a participant in the whole, but possessing intelligence according to a certain <term>participation</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "participation" refers to the way lower things reflect or share in the qualities of higher, perfect "Forms" without being the Form itself—like many mirrors reflecting one sun.</note>. Just as above the minds of souls—which are called "minds" because they participate in intelligence—there are many minds according to their <term>form</term> <note>original: "secundum formam"; these are the Angels, whose very nature is pure intellect, unlike humans who must strive to use reason.</note>, that is, angels; so above these formal minds there is one single Mind according to its efficient cause and its powerful virtue, which is God.

->*Human intellects are many, angelic intellects are many, but the divine intellect is the only one.*<-

**T**hat there are many intellects according to participation is clear from the fact that rational souls are very numerous. Furthermore, within the minds of different men at the very same moment, there appear opinions, feelings, and habits that are utterly in conflict with one another. We have already declared in the previous sections that there are also many intellects "according to form" in the higher realms, when we said it is more in keeping with the nature of the mind itself to live separately from the senses and the body than to live with them. 

We prove that there is a single Intellect—the Cause above all minds that are "minds by their form"—by the following: since the spiritual multitude of individual minds is more ordered and united than the multitude of physical bodies, it is necessary that such a union proceeds from one specific cause. For diverse things—whether they are physical or otherwise—cannot harmonize into one work, or one order, or one end, by the very fact that they are diverse. They can only do so insofar as they share something in common. And this very thing which is called "common" does not originate from any one of them individually (for then it would be private to that one, and not common to all). Nor does that common quality arise from all of them together acting out of their own varied powers. For things that are diverse, as we have said, do not produce union simply because they are diverse. 

But does this nature, which is common to all, exist entirely by itself? Not at all. For it is a greater thing to "exist out of oneself" than to "subsist in oneself." Since a nature of this kind does not subsist in itself, but rather in a "crowd" <note>original: "turba"; refers to the multitude of different beings.</note> of individuals, it certainly cannot exist out of itself. Therefore, that union of all things proceeds from a certain Unity which subsists in itself above the count of all things. And because that sublime Unity belongs to no single thing, just as numerical unity is present everywhere in all numbers, and a point is present in all lines, so too this Unity remains indivisible while being present to all spirits and bodies alike, equally binding the universe together. These things, by this very mutual agreement, are led toward the One because they are led *by* the One. Just as all the bodies of the world are brought back to one supreme Body <note>Ficino refers here to the "Primum Mobile" or the outermost sphere of the heavens in ancient cosmology.</note> that contains and moves everything, so all spirits are brought back to one supreme Spirit that embraces all things, and which gives life and motion to bodies through the spirits subject to Him.

->*Things are not confused in a circle, nor are they reduced to several equal principles, nor do they progress upward without end.*<-

**H**ere, it seems, three primary errors are excluded: First, the error of those who say all things depend on one another in a circle, so that just as this depends on that, so that in turn depends on this. In such a case, the same thing would be compared to itself as both cause and effect, prior and posterior, higher and lower. 

The second error is of those who introduce several "principles" <note>In this context, a "principle" (principium) is a fundamental source or beginning of reality.</note> side-by-side. If this were true, there would be a certain number of principles composed of a common nature and individual properties. Thus, none of them would truly be a "principle," because none would be perfectly simple, and they would all have to proceed from a higher Unity that binds the individuals together. 

The third error is of those who always ascend upward without end from one principle to another. But while they seem to pursue innumerable principles with great curiosity, because they never find a "First," they actually reach no principle at all. They really ought to consider that whatever depends on another depends by its own nature; and unless it is supported by something else that does *not* depend on anything else, it will completely waver. Therefore, if all things depend on others without end, everything will waver everywhere. It would be as if liquids were to cling to liquids, and nowhere were there any solid things to hold the liquids in place. There would be no stability in things, no order, no cycle, no perseverance, and no restoration. There would be no thing more excellent than another, since where there is no...

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchy of the universe, arguing that the diversity of human and angelic minds must be unified by a single, self-existing Divine Mind (God). He refutes the philosophical errors of circular logic, multiple starting principles, and infinite regress, using the analogy of liquids needing a solid container to find stability.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument regarding the hierarchy of the universe. Having established that the divine intellect is the single source of all other intellects, he now argues that this progression of causes cannot be infinite and must lead back to a single, supreme point of Truth and Goodness.</meta>

<page-num>692</page-num>
<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...the highest. In that realm, some things do not approach the summit more closely than others. But we see clearly that in nature, some things act and others are acted upon; the former precede in dignity, while the latter follow. Furthermore, a multitude and breadth of causes produce a corresponding number and magnitude of effects. Therefore, if one were to ascend from cause to cause without end, one would similarly descend from effect to effect without limit. There would be no extremes, but everything would be a middle point, and everything would be infinite. Indeed, if any given thing received its power from innumerable predecessors and was able to give power to innumerable successors, the "uncountable" would be "infinite." This is absurd. Every single thing would appear equal to every other thing. This is likewise judged to be absurd. Nowhere would we find the lowest body, which is the earth; nowhere the lowest matter, which is a single, pure <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; in Aristotelian terms, matter without form is "pure potential," waiting to be shaped into something real.</note> capable of receiving forms. 

Unless there is a supreme spirit, unless there is a supreme form, a <term>pure act</term> <note>original: "actus purus"; a philosophical term for God, who is fully realized and has no "potential" to change or improve because He is already perfect.</note>, and a fountain of forms, no effects would ever begin to be made. This is because intermediate causes would never begin to act, as they do not act until they are moved by all those above them. If the beginning of motion is expected to come from an innumerable series across an immeasurable interval, it will never be received. There would be no knowledge of any effect, because there would be no way to comprehend an infinite number of causes. What more? Every single movement in human and natural affairs is directed toward certain ends because they are governed by a certain principle; for if they were not governed from that source, they would never be directed toward that end. Therefore, since the movements of the whole universe are more orderly than the individual movements that relate to its order, the universe directs itself all the more toward a certain end—that is, toward the good and beautiful common to all things. It is necessary, then, that it proceeds from one certain principle, which is Goodness itself and the highest Beauty.

### Truth is above the mind.

**B**ut perhaps, while we strive to cut away this infinite progression, we might ourselves foolishly wander an almost infinite distance from the purpose of our discussion; let us now, if you please, return to the mind. What the eye is in the body, and sight is in the eye, the intellect is almost exactly that in the soul. Again, what the light of the Sun is to sight, the light of truth is to the mind. The light of the Sun is one thing, and the eye is another; similarly, Truth itself is one thing, and the intellect is another. Otherwise, every truthful effect and every thing participating in the truth would likewise participate in intelligence. Your eye, because it is a part of another thing—that is, the body—neither sees all things clearly nor sees all its own objects at once. If your whole body were made into a single eye, it would see all things from all sides at once. Yet, even then, the eye and the light would not be the same thing. Similarly, your mind, because it is a part of the soul, understands things neither clearly nor all at once. If your whole soul were to become a single intellect, it would turn from a soul into an <term>angel</term> <note>Ficino follows the Neoplatonic idea that angels are "pure intellects" who don't have to reason things out step-by-step like humans do.</note>; it would perceive all things clearly, and would no longer hunt for this or that through the passage of time, but would gaze upon all things clearly and simultaneously. Yet even then, Truth itself would be one thing, and the mind itself another; for the mind is nothing other than a spiritual eye meant to perceive the light of truth and the heat of goodness through the intellect and the will.

### Truth and goodness are the same.

**N**ow it seems we must investigate whether truth and goodness are one and the same? Let us set aside the schemes of the <term>dialecticians</term> <note>Logic-choppers or formal debaters.</note>. If, in the order of things, being false and being bad do not differ from one another, it follows that in the same order, being true and being good—truly existing and existing well—do not actually differ. Therefore, above the order of all things, Truth and Goodness are the same in substance. This is especially true because the empire of Truth extends exactly as far as the empire of Goodness, and vice versa. For whatever is found to participate in the true, participates in the good as well, and the reverse is also true. Yet this very thing, which is called Truth and Goodness, towers above every mind: because the mind does not find rest in its own nature, but in the possession of the true and the good. And the traces of truth and goodness spread themselves more widely than intelligence does. For even where no gift of intelligence appears, something of the true and the good seems to lie hidden. What then shall we say...

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe must have a single First Cause (God) to avoid the absurdity of infinite regression. He further explains that Truth and Goodness are identical, supreme realities that exist above the level of the individual mind.</summary>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK II.</header>
<sig>Xx 3</sig>

...we shall say: God places all things into their own proper and pure <term>species</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "species" is the essential form or "idea" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> according to the <term>exemplar</term> <note>A divine blueprint or pattern in the mind of God.</note> of His own art; then, according to the exemplar of His own bounty, He benignly distributes to all things a certain order and use toward some purpose. In the first act He makes all things true; in the second, He makes them good. Again, when God shines for the intellect, He is called Truth; when He warms the will, He is called Goodness. In the former, the intellect is enlightened and grows; in the latter, the will is gently attracted and filled.

### *God surpasses the mind by an immense interval.*

**M**oreover, let us measure—if it can be measured—since God surpasses the mind, by how great a distance He surpasses it. Ah, what immense madness it is to try to measure the immeasurable! For He is distant from the mind in dignity by as much space as lies open to the mind’s own reasoning as it runs step by step from the clearer to the even clearer, and to the will as it aspires from the better to the even better. Indeed, that path lies open until something truly immense meets us, which, by its own infinity, imposes a limit upon a progress that would otherwise be infinite.

### *God is certainty itself, and joy itself.*

**A**lthough it may seem the height of madness to wish to comprehend with the mind that which insurmountably exceeds the mind and the mind's stimulus (that is, the will), it is by no means the act of a madman to wish at least to be most fully comprehended by Him. For perhaps to "comprehend" that which is incomprehensible is nothing other than to be happily comprehended by it. What then? Do we wish to be most clearly comprehended by the supreme and uncreated form—which has until now embraced us in secret—so that this very fact is not hidden from us? Let us apprehend as much as we can of those things which, in the category of created forms, appear highest to us. The highest among these are those which can turn themselves without a mediator toward the supreme and uncreated form, for the very reason that they proceeded from that same form without a mediator. All types of minds appear to be of this kind. Indeed, all minds are able daily to seek, consider, and worship the supreme divinity—not only in other things, but even setting all other things aside—in its own (so to speak) specific excellence. Therefore, the highest things in the universe, after the supreme principle of the universe, are minds, acting as mirrors of the Highest. Let us take what is highest in the mind, which is the intellect and the will; and again, what is highest in the intellect and will. In the intellect, the supreme act is understanding; in the will, it is desiring. But what is the further supreme point in understanding? What, again, in desiring? In the former, it is the highest clarity—that is, the most exact certainty of all true things. In the latter, it is the fullest joy—that is, the complete and secure enjoyment of all good things. We can neither imagine nor desire anything further. What, therefore, is God? Certainly, as much as shines forth from Him in the mind, which is His mirror: God is the clearest and most certain truth, the fountain of all true things. The truest clarity of all clarities. Again, He is infinite goodness, which while it enjoys itself, enjoys innumerable goods. He is also immense joy, being good through Himself, and through Himself making it so that there are other goods in which one can rejoice.

### *Certainty or clarity itself is the same thing as joy itself.*

**W**hen we say God is clarity or joy, we do not place clarity or joy within the will <note>Ficino is arguing that these are not just feelings or states *inside* us, but are the very essence of God Himself.</note>, but in themselves. Nor do we wish clarity to differ from joy in that realm where truth does not differ from goodness. Therefore, it is a rejoicing clarity and a clear joy. Clarity, I say, not rejoicing in joy as if it were some other thing, but in itself. Joy, not clear by any other clarity than itself.

### *Just as light does not need the eye, so truth does not need the mind.*

**T**he eye is one thing, a certain little ray inborn in the eye <note>Ficino refers to the ancient "extramission" theory of vision, where the eye was thought to emit a small ray of light to meet the light of the sun.</note> is another, and the most ample light of the Sun is yet another. That little ray is the eye's own clarity and exists within the eye; but that light of the sun is the common clarity of all things—a clarity not belonging to the eye, though the eye was created to perceive it. Similarly, the mind is one thing, its own...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical letter from the previous page, where he began arguing that God, as the first cause, must possess the perfections of the mind (certainty and joy) in an infinite and supreme degree.</meta>

clarity, that is, a ray implanted in it from the beginning. God is something else: the supereminent clarity of clarities, a clarity not properly requiring a mind, which seems to have been created specifically to perceive that clarity. He is the joy of all joys, which any will feels; a joy not requiring a will by which it might rejoice, since indeed every single will rejoices only by means of Him.

->To supreme certainty, nothing is uncertain.<-

**I**f the light of the Sun were not only the cause of sight and of the visible object itself, but also the cause of all causes, and if sight itself were the Sun's most excellent and closest effect—since perfection cannot be granted by a defect, but rather there is a need for a perfect sight to generate a needy one—certainly, whatever appears in sight as good and especially desirable would be found in its entirety, and much more excellently, in light. Truly, the best and most desirable thing for the eye is that light should neither be hidden from it, nor, when it appears, should it offend the eye, but rather it should greatly delight it. Therefore, even if light did not have an eye, nevertheless in its own way—that is, by itself as a more sublime sight—it would see itself clearly, and would behold all colors in itself as the source of eyes. It would also see that it is that which all eyes see; and seeing all things through itself, it would also see itself everywhere. I pass over for now the fact that the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato, whose philosophy Ficino was instrumental in reviving during the Renaissance.</note> think light sees all things. Now God is the total and immediate cause of the mind, and the mind is the highest work of God. Therefore, whatever is to be supremely desired by the mind as its "best," all this God already possesses in a manner more excellent than can be expressed. For what is more desirable to the intellect than the certainty of all truths? Or to the will, than a joy rejoicing in all goods? It would not be enough for the mind (ask it yourself)—it would not be enough for it to possess the whole of truth if that truth itself, which it possesses, were hidden from it. All good is not enough, unless it provides what is pleasant and rejoices in everything. Therefore divine clarity, although it does not properly "use" an intellect <note>Ficino means God does not need to reason or think through things step-by-step like a human intellect.</note>, is nevertheless not hidden from itself. Nor is anything hidden from it anywhere, since all things are open everywhere through it. For what could be certain to anyone, if to certainty itself—through which all things are made certain—it were not certain?

->Where the chief end of minds is, there also is their beginning.<-

**B**ut repeat the previous points in this way: any effect, by the impulse of nature, seeks its cause, so that where it is made, there also it might be perfected. It properly seeks its immediate cause—if such a cause is one that collects the duties of all remote causes in itself—and it seeks the remote cause under the form of this immediate one. For it receives its own distinct form from the immediate cause rather than from the remote one. Therefore, in that immediate cause from which it had its own beginning, it also places its own end. Just as fire reaches its natural limit in the <term>concave of the Moon</term> <note>In the Aristotelian and Ptolemaic cosmology of Ficino's time, the "sphere of fire" was located just below the sphere of the Moon. Elements were thought to seek their natural home.</note> rather than in the Sun or Mars; and air in the sphere of fire, not in Venus or Jupiter. Since, therefore, any mind—with nature as its guide—has established its own chief end only in that supreme certainty of all things which rejoices supremely, or in that supreme joy of all things which is supremely certain, as in its immediate cause; who would not see that God himself, who is the immediate cause of minds, is that supreme certainty and highest joy? A certainty, I say, not *of* something, or *in* something, or *toward* something, but of itself in itself and toward itself. Otherwise it would neither be pure and simple, nor supremely high. Since, therefore, it receives no limit or measure from any part, it is left immeasurable. Wherefore it admits nothing at all of the uncertain. Therefore nothing, whether in it or outside it, can ever be or even be imagined which is uncertain to certainty itself. Which, while it surpasses all things, is all things surpassingly. Nor does it depend on anything else in being and acting, but others depend on it in both. In which, since its very being is not different from its being certain—or rather, its being certainty itself—surely while it is of itself, it is similarly certain of itself; or rather, to speak more correctly, it is certainty. And while it is certain of itself—which embraces all things by a wonderful power—it is undoubtedly certain of all things, or rather, the certainty of all things. Accordingly, light, which is seen by all, is nothing other than a certain spiritual amplification of a pure and effective form. Where, therefore, the purity and efficacy of form is least limited, where infinite light buds forth, from there an entirely immense light emanates. Truly, what transparency is in bodies...

this is perspicacity <note>The quality of having keen mental perception or insight.</note> in spirits: just as visible light is in bodies, so perfection is in spirits. For this reason, those things which approach closer to the spirit shine more easily or more abundantly. And conversely, things that shine on their own propagate a spiritual quality from themselves. Therefore, in the supreme spirit, light thrives, and perception is at its highest. In Him, clarity and perception are the same thing. I do not say that God is a certain power for perceiving that requires an act of perceiving, nor again do I call Him that which is named "to perceive," lest He seem to be either a straining toward something else or a composite being. But by the very name of "act," I call God "perception-itself" <note>original: "perspicientiam." Ficino uses this noun to describe God as the essence of perception rather than a being who performs the action of perceiving.</note>, existing through itself, and not perceiving itself by any clarity other than itself. But what did I just say regarding "perceiving"? For who would not speak improperly if they said "vision sees" or "wisdom is wise"? Yet wisdom is not foolish, nor is vision blind. Similarly, "perception-itself" should not properly be said to perceive anything, nor again should it be said that anything exists anywhere that is not clear and perceived by it. For just as specific things are perceived by this or that perception, so all things are clear and perceived by that supreme and infinite perception. In that same place, supreme joy also abounds where supreme clarity flashes forth, which is the spiritual origin of joy. Indeed, in that place, clarity and joy are the same. For nothing else is exhilaration—whether in the eye, which appears most spiritual within the body, or in the spirit itself—than either clarity itself or a fitting illumination. Who doubts that all joy reigns there, where all good is found? Since joy is desired most of all as the best thing, and it is both the splendor and grace of the Good itself pouring around, and a certain amplification of the surrounding power concerning the Good.

->*God is the lightest clarity and the clearest joy.*<-

**W**here, therefore, we wish to speak most correctly, we do not properly name God "intellect," lest He require an act of understanding; nor do we call Him "intelligence" itself, lest He remain within a certain intellect and be filled by some other light. Rather, [He is] clarity itself, wonderfully joyful, and the clearest joy, which all intellects seek, just as all the stars seek the Sun. A clarity, I say, seeing all things by the rays of its own certainty and making them so that they may see; moreover, by the flames of its own joy, as the mother of all pleasure, making each thing, cherishing what has been made, by cherishing in turn giving life, moving the living by sense, drawing the moved by reason, then steadying the captured by the mind, and finally filling those things that stand firm with the truth and goodness of itself.

->*God makes and moves things by willing, rather than by understanding.*<-

**B**ut it delights me, I know not how, to ascend again from that which is most beautiful in bodies to the best spirit by a certain similarity. Therefore, just as the Sun, the image of God, shines in itself with that same light and is warm in its own way, and by that same ray illustrates and warms each thing; yet it makes and moves things more by warming than by illustrating. So God Himself, the archetype of the Sun, is both clear to Himself in His own understanding by that same clarity, and rejoices in Himself in His own way by His own willing. Furthermore, by the rays of that same clarity—to speak for a moment in human terms—He understands and wills all things. Truly, He does not procreate so much by understanding as by willing. Hence it seems to be granted to all animals and natures that they generate things similar to themselves by a certain appetite according to the nature of each, and even by pleasure. We must remember, however, that just as God, by understanding Himself, understands other things (which are certain rays of His own intelligence), so by willing Himself—that is, by rejoicing in Himself—He wills other things at the same time as those and rejoices in them, which are certain affections <note>In this context, "affections" refers to the results or impacts of his will.</note> of His effect. And a kind of action of this sort, namely the voluntary, is most perfect and suits God, the most perfect of agents. For what acts by free will acts more excellently than what is driven to act by a necessary impulse of nature. Certainly, that action is most happy in which the author is the master of his own action, so that he may prescribe the end, the mode, and the measure of acting: and may establish for his works their own end and certain paths. Indeed, if God were to act by a natural quality, just as fire warms by heat, He would be a composite of the highest degree, since He would procreate innumerable things from His natural forms distinct from one another—especially those things which can be produced by creation alone, namely <term>matter</term> <note>The underlying substance of all physical things, which in Neoplatonism is the lowest level of reality.</note> itself, and <term>forms</term> <note>The essential blueprints or natures of things, which can exist either within matter or separately as pure ideas.</note>, whether separated from matter or separable.
