<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<meta>catchword: but</meta>

Moreover, He does not distribute individual things through some sequence or turn, but pours forth all things at once—or rather, blends them together. Add to this that, since His act is immeasurable, He would suddenly compel all things and agitate the spheres of the world in an instant. He would leave nothing in the universe as contingent <note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to things that happen by chance or could have happened differently, as opposed to things that must happen by necessity.</note>, and would take away the freedom of deliberation. But in truth, because He accomplishes all things through liberty, He therefore creates, moves, and establishes things specifically by the measure that He wills. He understands the whole of the universe without difficulty, for in Him, to understand is the same as to be. He creates and cares for individual things without difficulty, for in Him, to do is the same as to already will to do. He understands all true things while He understands Himself as every truth. He also wills all good things while He wills Himself, who is every good. The logic of the divine intelligence and will is of one kind, while human logic is of another. A human truly understands the underlying principles of things only when he understands them primarily as they are. But these things are true precisely because they are as God understands them—He who is truth itself, through whom all things are true and are understood truly everywhere. The human will desires individual things because they are good. But individual created things are good because God Himself wills them—He who is goodness itself, through whom things are good and through whom we rightly desire individual things.

->*God provides for all things, especially for minds, because they are procreated directly from Him.*<-

<margin> { </margin>
**F**rom this it is established that the First Cause, through the benevolence of His will, provides for all things because all things are His to the highest degree. Certainly, since He is the primary cause in the highest sense, He is the cause of their preservation and perfection just as much as He is the cause of their creation. Supreme Providence belongs especially to the Supreme Good. This Providence is nothing other than the diffusion and preservation of what is good. It is further established that subsequent causes <note>Ficino is referring to "secondary causes," such as nature or human agency, which follow the "First Cause" (God).</note>, while they receive from the First Cause their fertility and inclination for generating, also receive from that same source their diligence in providing. Indeed, if anyone were to deny that the world is governed by both the most skillful reason and the most benevolent will, he seems to me to have considered neither the rational and most beautiful order of things in themselves (and toward one another, and toward the whole), nor the marvelous convenience of individual things everywhere serving one another most aptly, nor the mutual use of things. Truly, a comfortable dwelling moves the builder as an "end" <note>The "end" or "final cause" is the purpose for which something is made; in this case, the purpose of having a home motivates the builder to start work.</note>, acting as an agent cause, so that he may devise a certain specific form for the house, for which form he in turn seeks specific materials. In this, the end moves the agent, the agent moves the form, and the form moves the matter. The same happens in civil and military deliberations. Thus it happens that the "end" is the "cause of causes," and therefore precedes all other causes. Moreover, all natural things are established for the sake of some certain end, since individual things are seen to lead to specific uses. For example, the little tendril of a vine shoot, which they call a *capreolus* <note>original: "capreolum." Literally "little goat," used here for the vine's climbing tendril because it "leaps" or clings like a goat.</note>, was born for this: to bind the vine to the nearest small tree. This act of binding is the cause for why the tendril grew. But because that which in no way exists cannot be a cause of being for any effect, it is necessary that such an act moved all causes and existed before all other causes of the vine. However, it did not exist in physical bodies until the very end. Therefore, it existed in some incorporeal nature that directs bodies long before it existed in the vine shoot. This nature, the craftsman of the vine, for the sake of such an act, shaped the form of the tendril in such a material through its own form. But did such an act exist in that nature according to the mode of nature, or according to the purpose of the will? Certainly, according to both. From the former, it was the same as a certain form of the agent and a pattern of its own disposition; from the latter, it was the "end" or purpose. Where there is a purpose of a skillful will, there is Mind. Therefore, the Divine Mind presides over all corporeal things, embracing the forms of all physical things in an intellectual way. It directs individual things to their own ends, and finally all things toward the One. But above all, God cares for and loves minds—not only angelic ones but also human ones—as if they were daughters procreated directly from Him. For since they are indivisible and separable from matter (or already separated), they cannot be made from a preceding part or material; but to create something out of nothing—which seems to be infinitely distant from "being" itself—is a work belonging only to infinite power.

->*All minds are indivisible, separable from matter, and eternal.*<-

**T**hat minds are indivisible and separated (or separable) from matter is evident from this: they reach the very "reason" <note>Here, "reason" refers to the "ratio" or the essential, abstract definition/logic of a thing.</note> of a thing, which is indivisible and entirely separated, through which many things are indivisible and separated and are known. I say they reach that reason properly, insofar as it is individual and separated. Just as...

<page-num>697</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II.</header>

...Indeed, just as the indivisible center of lines is reached only through their own indivisible point, so we can only attain the indivisible and secret nature through an indivisible and secret power. God, by producing existence, grants temporal existence to some, and by His providence, He procures their temporal well-being. But to those to whom He has granted eternal existence by His incomparable generosity, He directs their well-being not so much for a time, but for eternity. Hence, He disposes things for them in time in such a way that—although these things may not seem good to those who do not see eternity itself—they are nevertheless always the very best in the eyes of Him who knows exactly how time serves eternity.

That He has granted everlasting life to minds <note>Ficino often uses "minds" (mentibus) to refer to human souls or angelic intellects.</note>, we shall now demonstrate briefly by the light of reason and by the light of clarity. First, from **Reason**, in this manner: If the logic <note>original: "ratio"</note> of any thing—which is shown by the specific definition of its species—cannot be otherwise, then whoever doubts whether the supreme Logic of all logics could be otherwise either does not use reason or abuses it. Therefore, Supreme Reason is eternal, or rather, it is eternity itself. This Reason weaves itself into all minds everywhere, so that wherever they please, they may reason according to their will. And it grants a certain property of its own eternity to the extent that, under the gift of reason itself (that is, by the act of reasoning), the eternal principles of things are grasped insofar as they are eternal. But the eternity of reason, and the reason of eternity, is comprised by its own definition.

Then, from the **Light**, in this manner: No one doubts that the light of the divine Sun is inextinguishable, just as they observe that its shadowy image shining in the celestial Sun is never extinguished. Indeed, in the supreme and pure act of any activity, no suffering or deprivation can be imagined—just as there is no act in the lowest potentiality, nor any habit in mere deprivation. That super-celestial light is spread far and wide through all minds thinking of super-celestial things, like stars, according to the nature of each. It preserves that inextinguishable property of its own insofar as that which cannot be extinguished is discerned from that which can by a certain light of reason; and by that reason, it is demonstrated why this thing becomes extinguishable or that thing inextinguishable. Surely, that light is granted under the logic of an inextinguishable property wherever the inextinguishable logic of any nature is perceived. And the supreme source of every nature and light is sought, loved, and raised up by a certain proper natural thirst.

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, on the rapture of Paul to the third heaven, and the immortality of the soul.

**I**t is not permitted for us, my dear Giovanni, in these times because of the suspicion of an epidemic <note>Ficino refers to the plague outbreaks that frequently forced scholars to flee Florence for the countryside.</note>, to live our lives together familiarly on earth as we were accustomed to do. But what, meanwhile, prevents us from dwelling in heaven, where no fear of plague disturbs us? Therefore, come, friend, let us now fly away to heaven. But, you will say, perhaps to which one specifically? Certainly to that one by whose rays we have been inflamed for so long while living a heavenly life together on earth. Do you not remember, Giovanni, when our most esteemed friend Bernardo Tenere <note>Bernardo Canigiani, a friend and student of Ficino.</note> was dining with us in your house, how we discussed the rapture of Paul into the third heaven? <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where the Apostle Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven."</note> Let us renew that banquet today, so that we may live together in it despite the epidemic.

### Dialogue between Paul and the soul: that one does not ascend to God without God, and on faith, hope, and charity.

->MARSILIO<-

**T**ell me, I pray, most blessed Paul—if it is permitted for a man to speak—how you ascended into heaven, and why into the third? PAUL: May such proud impiety be far from us, Marsilio, far indeed, that we should say we "ascended" there. For I do not wish to glory in myself in revelations of this kind; all my glory is that King of Glory alone, God. I did not ascend, Marsilio, but I was snatched <note>original: "raptus sum," the root of the word "rapture."</note> into heaven. The heavy elements of the world do not seek the heights unless they are lifted up by the high. Earthly inhabitants do not climb the steps unless the heavenly Father has drawn them. MARSILIO: I beseech you, Paul, teach me this also: by Him who snatched you, whom does He snatch most of all? PAUL: Are you ignorant of this, which no one who either snatches something or is snatched can be ignorant of? He snatches him above all others whom He loves more ardently. He ardently loves the one who loves Him. That most kind snatcher wants nothing else from you, so that you may be happily snatched by Him, except that you should wish, even if only slightly, to be snatched—but even this you would never wish, unless He had willed it first.

On the previous page, he argued that the soul possesses an eternal quality because it can grasp eternal principles through reason. Here, he shifts from the faculty of Reason to the higher virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity, using a dialogue between himself and St. Paul to explain the "third heaven."</meta>

<page-num>698</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...had been. Just as the Moon does not shine back upon the Sun unless it has first been lit by the Sun, so you do not love the Lover himself unless you have been set on fire by that very Love <note>original: "amore ipso"</note> loving and acting within you. Again, you do not call upon Him like an echo unless He has first called you; you do not take hold of Him as if He were in a place unless He first takes hold of you. You can, for the most part, grasp finite things even if you are not grasped by them; but to grasp the Infinite is nothing other than to be grasped by it. And just as an image in a mirror does not look back at a face unless the face itself looks at the mirror—indeed, even when the image seems to look at the face, this is nothing other than the image being looked at by the face. Again, just as action and motion do not measure time for us unless time itself truly measures them, so the soul neither looks back at God unless He is already looking at it, nor does it judge unless He is already judging. 

**MARS.** <note>Marsilio Ficino, the author, addressing St. Paul.</note> But come now, O man so dearly beloved by God, teach us for a third time why you were raised specifically into the "third heaven," so that you might see that invisible thing which is everywhere, as if it were in the third? For if it is anywhere, it is surely rather in the highest heaven.

**PAUL.** <note>The Apostle Paul, whom Ficino depicts as a Neoplatonic guide.</note> Not so, O too-earthly man, not so are super-celestial things understood! Put away the clever subtleties of the second heaven invented by Mercury <note>Ficino associates the sphere of Mercury with rhetoric and dialectic.</note>. Put away the laws established, as you say, by Jupiter in the sixth heaven. Put away the Philosophy given to men by Saturn in the seventh heaven. Those things do not reach Truth itself, which is the mother of Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn. Do you wish to reach the Sun running in the fourth heaven, where that King of the world has placed his tabernacle? Come then, climb the back of the third heaven which touches the fourth. There, Venus <note>The sphere of Venus represents Love.</note> will immediately grant you, as much as she is able, what the others could not provide. 

Common folk say that Venus gives "common love." But certainly, an angel increases that distinguished charity <note>original: "charitatem." In this context, Charity refers to Divine Love, the highest of the three Christian virtues.</note> in distinguished men. I speak of Charity, which flows from the triple heaven above the heavens into the third heaven and its angel, and then into our soul. For the Holy Spirit of God first burns this into the Seraphim. Secondly, they enjoin this principal mystery and service upon the Principalities <note>Seraphim and Principalities are ranks in the celestial hierarchy of angels.</note>. These, ruling the third sphere, set fire to the angel of Venus there, from which the charity planted in you by God is continually nourished, grows, and is perfected. 

Why say more? Do you wish to leave behind these circuitous paths and reach the Sun of the Sun by a shorter track? First, let **Faith** be your heaven, by which you firmly believe that He is to be loved by you above all else—He from whom you have this very power to love whatever you love, and from whom the things that are loved receive the very fact that they are lovable. Second is **Hope**, through which you undoubtedly and ardently expect to be loved in return by Him; for you could not love Him unless you were first loved by Him. Third is **Charity**, which both compels you spontaneously and lures you of necessity—all other things being utterly cast aside—to embrace Him. For if He alone is cast aside, you possess nothing; but if you possess Him, there is nothing among all things that you have lost. Without His arms, you have the strength to embrace neither yourself, nor other things, nor Him. 

It was here, O too-wandering soul, here alone that I penetrated the most precious inner chambers of God. Unless they are opened by the Master of the House, they are not seen. The house of almighty Olympus <note>A classical poetic name for Heaven.</note> is not opened except to minds seeking this very thing through Faith, asking through Hope, and knocking through Charity. For Charity is the end and the perfection of all other things. Set on fire by its little sparks, Elijah was once snatched up to heaven in a chariot of fire. By its flames, I too was snatched up to heaven. Finally, let this remain stored deep in your mind: Cold depends on darkness, and darkness on death. But heat depends on light, and light depends on life. Therefore, cold leads to darkness, and darkness leads to death. But heat leads to light, and light leads to life.

---

->*By the chariot of Faith, Hope, and Charity, one ascends seven times into the third heaven. First, indeed, through the*<-
->*civil and purifying virtues of the purified soul.*<-

By this triple heaven, as if by a certain vehicle—that is, by right Faith, firm Hope, and most ardent Charity—you shall traverse the triple heaven seven times. There you shall see again the sweet Father and the fatherland, from which you will emerge three and four times—that is, seven times—blessed. First, by the merits of these three, three kinds of virtues will also be granted to you by divine gift: the **Civil Virtues** and the **Purifying Virtues** of the purified soul <note>Ficino uses the Neoplatonic classification of virtues: "Civil" (social/political), "Purifying" (detaching from the body), and "Exemplary" (the divine archetypes).</note>. These indeed act so that you do not know whether you are in the body or out of the body. Shaped by these, you will finally reach the **Exemplary Virtues**, which are nothing other than God. For you will see yourself drawn by the Spirit of the Lord from "glory to glory" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18.</note> in these three kinds, as the essence of virtue progresses more by degrees. You will recognize that this cannot happen except by a closer and ever closer approach to that divine and supreme Idea of virtue, so that you may be transformed into that same image.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marsilio Ficino and St. Paul regarding the soul’s ascent. On the previous page, Paul began explaining the "third heaven," a concept from the New Testament (2 Corinthians 12:2). Here, Ficino outlines five distinct ways to understand this "third heaven" through various lenses: astronomy, psychology, intellect, spirit, and theology.</meta>

<page-num>699</page-num>
<header>BOOKS OF LETTERS. BOOK II.</header>

### Second, one goes to the third heaven through the region of the planets, through the star-bearing heaven, and through the crystalline heaven.

**S**econdly, you will pass through the region of the seven planets—which is, as it were, the first "wandering" heaven—to the eighth sphere, which is the most orderly <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, believed to be the most stable part of the physical universe.</note> of stars, whose motion is single and simple. There, the "waters which are above the heavens" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:7; medieval cosmology often placed a "crystalline" or "watery" heaven above the stars.</note> praise the name of the Lord. From the summit of this, immediately in the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest, fiery heaven, which Neoplatonists like Ficino viewed as a realm of pure light and divine love rather than physical fire.</note>—which is entirely a most healthful burning—you will recognize that vital light of God, by whose overflowing goodness such a great and healthful ardor is kindled. You will see most clearly that divine light and truth itself dwell in that burning (that is, in love) as if in the **tent of the Sun** <note>original: "tabernaculo Solis." A reference to Psalm 19:4, symbolizing where God's light is most concentrated.</note>, and that this ardor is born from and flourishes in that light.

### Third, the third heaven is climbed through the visible world, through the world of the imagination, and through the intelligible world.

**T**hirdly, you will pass through the entire body of the world as if it were one heaven visible to the eyes. Then you will betake yourself to its image, painted by the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "world of imagination" or "phantastic world" refers to the mental faculty that stores and manipulates sensory images.</note>, as if to a second heaven. Finally, leaving behind both the universal visible body and the imaginary image of the body, you will proceed to nature itself (on which it necessarily depends) and to the reason by which it is defined by the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure ideas and intellect, beyond physical matter or mental images.</note>. This will be the third heaven for you in the mind, above sense and imagination; here, suddenly, the divine intelligence shines upon your own intelligence. For what else is the "reason" of the universe and its parts but that eternal art by which its architect arranged it? For if you subtract the matter from a corporeal craft, leaving the design behind, what remains is the mind of the craftsman, now visible to your own mind.

### Fourth, the third heaven is sought through irrational, rational, and intellectual spirits.

**F**ourthly, let the first heaven be for you every spirit below your own <note>i.e., the "irrational spirits" or souls of animals.</note>. Let your own spirit be the second, by virtue of the gift of reason, through which it judges irrational things but is not judged by them, being far superior to them. The third is the angel, who is like a most clear eye, for whom those things you hunt for through a temporal sequence of thought are known in a stable, instantaneous moment. Constantly behold God in the angel, like light in a clear eye, and eternity in a stable moment.

### Fifth, the third heaven is reached through the three angelic hierarchies.

**F**ifthly, know that just as in you—who are a world in miniature <note>A "microcosm."</note>—there are three "spirits": the natural in the <term>liver</term>, the vital in the heart, and the animal in the brain <note>Ficino uses the medical theory of Galen, where three "spirits" (vapors) govern digestion, life, and thought.</note>, through which alone you perceive a finite light; so around this larger world there are three hosts of divine spirits, like three intelligible spheres, constantly revolving around the divine center. Some govern the region of the world subject to the Moon; others rule the celestial spheres; and others fly above the summit of heaven.

### Bright darkness, dark light, pure light. The nine choirs of angels.

**I** too fly here and there at will, lifted on the wings of the <term>Seraphim</term>. And though I find nothing anywhere outside of the immense Good—which fills the universe within and surrounds it infinitely without—nevertheless, whatever I find that is not the Good itself, I see to be composed of a certain **bright darkness** and a certain **dark light** <note>Ficino is using the mystical language of Pseudo-Dionysius, where God is a "darkness" that is actually an excess of light.</note>. I know that darkness cannot illuminate itself, nor can light encompassed by darkness shine of its own accord; otherwise, it would flourish in itself and shine most purely and fully. I observe, therefore, that it shines from that Light itself in which there is no darkness at all. Therefore, when it shines in the darkness, the darkness does not grasp it. This is the absolute Good itself, encompassed neither by the limits of a subject, nor a cause, nor degrees, nor place, nor time. But since all things desire the Good by natural instinct as their end, by which alone they are perfected, I conclude that the same Good is the principle from which all things are made. Since it creates and perfects all things out of itself and its grace, it certainly arranges all things according to its own pattern as the intermediary. It is therefore the beginning, the middle, and the end of all. And because it is entirely invisible, it is contained in each of the three, and so on. Now, the end moves actions in a certain way.

<summary>Ficino explains the "third heaven" through five different frameworks: astronomical spheres, the hierarchy of the mind (senses, imagination, intellect), the types of spirits (irrational, rational, angelic), and the angelic hierarchies, concluding with a mystical meditation on God as the absolute Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the "third heaven." Having previously discussed physical and intellectual ascents, he now details the angelic hierarchy and the theological structure of the divine realm, culminating in the mystery of the Trinity.</meta>

<page-num>700</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

is in some way the principle for acting. The Principle moves the exemplar and the form of the work. Toward this, all the blessed spirits continually direct the eyes of their minds. Each of them gazes upon these three—<term>Beginning, Middle, and End</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, all things proceed from a source (Beginning), remain in their essence (Middle), and return to their goal (End).</note>—but different orders do so in different ways. In these, they behold the true <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes." These are the divine blueprints or "Ideas" of all things in the universe.</note> of all things that exist in the universe.

The **Seraphim** contemplate the End itself more closely and intently than the rest. The **Cherubim** contemplate the Beginning within the End. The **Thrones** observe the Middle within the End. The **Dominations**, however, gaze upon the Beginning itself. The **Virtues** see the End within the Beginning. The **Powers** see the Middle within the Beginning. The **Principalities**, although they admire all things, nonetheless gaze upon the Middle more closely and, if I may say so, more gladly. The **Archangels** see the End within the Middle. The **Angels** contemplate the Beginning within the Middle. 

Blessed souls—according to the various merits of their pious lives and the similarity of their characters to the various angels—follow these nine orders of angels within the nine spheres of the <term>heavenly homeland</term> <note>original: "sphæris patriæ." A common Renaissance term for Heaven.</note>. I gladly pass over the unhappy souls who, beneath the Moon under a foul darkness where the **Styx** <note>In Greek mythology, the river of the underworld; Ficino notes it "flows between nine times" (original: "nouies stix interfusa"), referencing Virgil’s description of the underworld's geography.</note> flows between and hem them in nine times, accompany the nine crowds of malignant spirits.

### The light of God shines in the ardor of the Empyrean heaven.

**W**hen the spirits of darkness were dismissed, suddenly an immense light flashed upon me from the highest watchtower of the shining spirits. There I saw the Seraphim burning with immense love. In such a burning, the infinite light of the Infinite Good shone back at me. Often before this <term>rapture</term> <note>original: "raptum." A mystical state where the soul is "caught up" or snatched away from the body to behold divine truths.</note>, I had wondered whether the "Good" itself is an object of the will or of the intellect; it would follow that the soul enjoys the Good more through the fire of the will than through the clarity of the intelligence. There, in the midst of my rapture, I immediately recognized that I had thought the truth, when I saw that it was not the knowledge of the Cherubim, but rather the <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitatem." Here meaning divine, selfless love.</note> of the Seraphim that is closest to God. Justly so, since the nature of the Good is such that it is desired; and the very reason it is desirable is that it is the Infinite Good itself. Most closely following the Good—and suddenly resulting from it—is a most blazing love.

### Sixthly, one takes refuge in the third heaven through the three persons of the Trinity.

**C**ome now, follow me in this sixth way as much as you can, O mind—a mind truly greedy for the Infinite Good itself, truly the daughter of the Infinite Good. Ah, hurry, and let it not weary you: for you are able, O good mind, to do as much as you will. For where one proceeds and profits by the will alone, there "following" is nothing other than "willing to follow." Therefore, be of good heart. 

Truly, the End toward which you are moved (without end, in a way) is properly the Infinite Good; and necessarily the Beginning from which you are moved is the Infinite Good. Since this Good is the origin of all things from itself and for its own sake, it certainly moves all things from itself and for its own sake. Especially and properly, it moves the spirit—and most especially this spirit which properly desires it. Your Father is so good that, since He did not give you this desire wickedly (that is, in vain), so that you would naturally wish to follow this kind of Good so much, He simultaneously granted that you would one day be able to reach it and obtain it. 

In the order of things, as you know, all things are good, primarily because they are ordered beautifully and usefully, and they naturally desire the Good. If all good things in the order of the world meet in one certain common nature of "the Good," in which all good things are one single Good, then necessarily, in the hands of the Orderer of things, one Good is all good things. That healthy nature, common and one, which lies within the multitude of all things and is contained by all, emanates from one certain Form which is in itself above all multitude and contains all things. 

But go further: if you call that which you imagine *below* the order of things "infinitely evil," why do you not also confess that which stands *above* the order of things is "infinitely good"? If propagation belongs to the Good—for whatever things are more perfect, the more they seem to propagate themselves—then without a doubt, infinite propagation exists within the Infinite Good. An *internal* propagation, I mean. For nothing truly infinite exists outside of it. There, therefore, is the **Father and the Son**. Alongside the infinitely good Father and the infinitely good Son, an infinite **Love** flourishes. 

If each of the three is equally infinite, they are also equal to one another and most similar. If there is an infinite nature and fullness, since it leaves nothing of itself outside itself and comprehends the whole within, it can only be one. There is one substance of the three, and it is most simple. It must be most powerful, for power consists in union, just as weakness consists in division. 

Now, therefore, O soul—three and one, a single spirit consisting of **intellect, will, and memory** <note>Ficino uses the traditional Augustinian "Psychological Analogy," where the human mind's three faculties mirror the Holy Trinity.</note>—you have climbed with me the one unique ether and the threefold heaven.

<summary>Ficino describes the celestial hierarchy of angels and their specific modes of divine contemplation, concluding with a philosophical defense of the Trinity and the soul's mirroring of the divine nature.</summary>

LETTERS, BOOK II.
701

Within the heavens, you saw three things in one Sun that are equal and similar to each other: its form, its figure, and its light. You judged that the Sun was not triple in these three, but unique. Above the heavens, in the one nature of goodness itself, you found from eternity an offspring and a love propagating outward. Nor did you recognize three natures in these, but a single nature, propagating itself without separation, loving most fully and similarly. And what you have looked upon here by divine means, it is by no means permitted for a man to speak of otherwise than as three persons and one God.

### *Seven sevens concerning the soul.*

**S**eventhly, consider with me, O soul—purified from the <term>seven capital sins</term> <note>Also known as the seven deadly sins: pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath, and sloth.</note> and free from the seven malignant spirits—how the gifts of the seven planets adorn you from without so that you appear happy; how the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit imbue you from within, and how the seven Angels surrounding the throne of God lead you so that you are truly happy. Consider with me this seventh day of light, in which you shall truly rest—namely, at the seventh hour of the day, when you shall see most clearly—so that you may be seven times blessed in that light, which promises to forgive you seventy times seven while you live in misery.

### *Thirdly, the mind reaches the third heaven while it considers God in creatures, creatures in God, and God in Himself.*

**C**onsider with me the one and triple <term>super-celestial heaven</term> <note>In Ficino's cosmology, this is the realm of pure intellect and divine presence, existing beyond the physical stars.</note>: first, namely, God your Father in the things created by Him; second, the created things in God; and third, God Himself in Himself. Into this third heaven I was once most excellently <term>snatched</term> <note>original: "raptus sum." Ficino is echoing the language of the Apostle Paul, who was "caught up" to the third heaven in 2 Corinthians 12:2.</note> so that I myself might no longer be most wickedly snatched away; and so that anyone who is most miserably snatched away on earth I might lead with me to be most blessedly snatched up there.

### *The Trinity of the Creator is found in nine trinities of creatures.*

**D**ivine Trinity you will recognize in all things while you consider nine trinities in them, which the nine orders of angels imitate. Namely: in the single machine of the heavens, you find figure, light, and motion. In any spirit above the heavens: substance, power, and action. In every number of spirits: three hierarchies, and in each hierarchy three orders. In any composite thing beneath the heavens: matter, form, and virtue. In all things: measure, number, and weight. Again: power, order, and utility. Furthermore: beginning, middle, and end. In yourself: memory, intelligence, and will. In the sciences: the natural, rational, and moral faculty. In each trinity, the first element represents the power of God and the Father; the second, wisdom and the Son; the third, love and the kind Spirit. Thus, the invisible things of God are seen and understood through those things which have been made.

### *Definition and divinity of the soul.*

**H**ere, while you find God in things as if they were divine, you also find yourself. Indeed, if you find spirit in bodies, light in darkness, good in evil, life in death, eternity in time, and the infinite in finite things, remember that you are an incorporeal spirit, luminous by nature, and good—immortal and capable of eternal truth, stability, and immense good. Up to this point, let this be the first heaven for you, from whose summit you have recognized both God and yourself in all things.

### *That created things are found in the Creator through divine reasons and ideas.*

**A**pproach, I pray, the second heaven, so that from there you may look upon all things in God. Anyone discerns all the works of God in God who considers the arrangement and form of a house in the mind of the master of the house, of a kingdom in the king, of a craft in the craftsman, or of the sciences in the wise man. Always remember this, however: that whatever these men meditate upon and perform with time and labor, that eternal truth and infinite power accomplishes in a moment, as it wills, and most easily—especially since, in God, to understand is nothing other than to be, and to act is nothing other than to will.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains how the Trinity is reflected throughout the cosmos in groups of three, such as memory, intelligence, and will in the human soul. He describes the soul's journey through different "heavens" of understanding to see the relationship between the Creator and the created world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s theological argument from page 701, where he leads the soul through an ascent of the mind. Having discussed the Trinity and the "super-celestial heaven," he now explains how the mind perceives the divine archetypes (Ideas) and finds proof of its own immortality through this intellectual vision.</meta>

<page-num>702</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...to will. Just as all natural forms are gathered in one matter, so all their <term>principles</term> <note>Latin: *rationes*. In Ficino's Platonism, these are the divine "blueprints" or "rational patterns" of all created things, residing in the Mind of God.</note> are gathered in one craftsman. But behold, I see a certain common mass in the structure of the world. I observe diverse forms within that mass. I know that the formed mass is one thing, and the forms that do the forming are another; and because I understand this mass to precede the forms in a certain order like a foundation, I separate the mass from them in my mind, and I imagine it either dispersed into the abyss or gathered separately into a point. I preserve the forms, however, as best I can. But in what do I preserve them? In a certain essence common to all. For all things commonly agree in the fact that they "are." In this indivisible essence, I say, I see the forms as entirely indivisible. We have already separated dimensions from all of them. Moreover, I wish for one single form of every species of thing to exist here. And just as all natural forms—which are such-and-such by a certain participation—are gathered in a single subject that is by its nature infinitely passive (that is, in <term>prime matter</term> <note>The formless, underlying substance of the physical universe.</note>), so I wish for all forms that are such-and-such by their very essence—that is, the principles of forms—and I see them in a single source that is by its nature infinitely active.

->*God is the infinite life of lives, and the light of lights.*<-

**W**here act is infinite, there is also life, and that life is indeed utterly infinite. For life is the innermost and absolute act of essence. In infinite life, there is nothing that does not live most perfectly. Therefore, *what was made by him was life in him* <note>original: "Quod ergo factum est ab eo in ipso uita erat." A reference to the Gospel of John 1:3-4.</note>. Moreover, where perennial act and immense life flourish, there the most absolute light of intelligence exists. For intelligence is the perfection of life and its reflection upon itself. Therefore, *this life is the light of men, which shines even in the darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it* <note>A paraphrase of John 1:4-5.</note>. The light of day is pleasant to healthy eyes, but most troublesome to the sick. The ray of God comes as a blessing to a good mind, and is called "Father" and "Grace." But to a bad mind, it is a rigid judge and a fury. Through this true light, which *enlightens every man coming into this world*, you have just now seen all things in God, and God himself. For whatever is in the most simple God, is God himself. That series of <term>Ideas</term> <note>Latin: *dearum*. Ficino uses the feminine plural here, likely referring to the Platonic Ideas as divine "Goddesses" or archetypes.</note>, therefore, which you perceived in God, is the divine wisdom itself, which is the Word of God with God, and is God himself, and through him all things were made. Thus God himself is found in all things, and all things are found in him.

->*The mind finds its own eternity in the eternity of principles and ideas.*<-

**Y**ou have also just now found your own immortality. For in what way could you have separated mortal conditions from the forms of the world, and conceived immortal principles from them, and traced these principles back into the eternal life and intelligence of God—making that act of thought, so to speak, the "maker of the maker"—unless you yourself were immortal and capable of the eternal life and intelligence of God? Let the most wicked men doubt their immortality; their poor souls, seeking life only in the region of death, have been dead for a long time, buried in the mud of their vices.

->*Confidence in immortality received from the four stages of contemplation.*<-

**B**ut you, O heavenly soul, trust with me—you who, while you contemplate the true and eternal principles of all created things in God, grasp in a way the eternity of each principle, the principle of eternity, and the truth of eternity.

### The four stages.

**I**ndeed, you sense the eternity of a principle when you judge that the principle and definition of anything are so certain that they could never be otherwise. For instance, that "man is a rational animal," and that "a circle is a figure turned back on itself, from whose center to the circumference all straight lines drawn are equal"—this was necessarily always true, and always will be true. You understand the principle of eternity when [you understand] the <margin>nature</margin> of eternity...

<summary>Ficino explains that the human mind proves its immortality by its ability to perceive eternal, divine "principles" (Ideas) in God. He describes God as the infinite life and light that sustains all things and outlines how intellectual contemplation leads to the realization of the soul's eternal nature.</summary>

While the previous page focused on the "principles" or "blueprints" of forms within the Mind of God, this section moves toward a formal definition of Eternity and provides a logical proof for the soul’s immortality based on its ability to grasp eternal truths.</meta>

<page-num>701</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II.</header>

You define its nature in this way: Eternity is a moment, or a point always stable through itself, which no point precedes and no point succeeds; thus it is the measure of rest, just as time is the measure of motion. You recognize the truth of eternity when you prove that true eternity exists only in that which, from itself and in itself, rests without beginning or end. You perceive the eternity of Truth when you argue that Truth neither ever began nor will ever cease. Otherwise, Truth would have existed before itself, or would exist after itself. Truly, if it were said to have "begun" at some point, it was already true from eternity that Truth would one day exist—and it could only be true through Truth itself. And even if it were thought to "cease," it would thereafter be true for eternity that Truth once existed—and it would only be true through that very same Truth.

->*The immortality of the soul based on its proportion to immortal things.*<-

**P**ay attention, soul thirsty for the eternal liquid. Remember that you could not touch an eternal object at all unless there were some proportion between you and it. Therefore, if you have not existed from eternity, you shall at least live for eternity. Nor do you merely "touch" eternal things when you argue that they exist and what they are like; rather, according to your nature, you penetrate them when you distinguish their intimate nature into its various parts and powers. Indeed, you even seem to encompass them in a certain way when you define them. I pass over the fact that it might seem to some that if the mind encompasses an eternal <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: *rationem*. Here meaning the divine logic or "Idea" behind a thing.</note>, it must be greater than that reason and therefore eternal; let it suffice if, by grasping it in its own way, the mind must at least be equal to it in some fashion. Whether it is already equal by nature, or becomes equal by the act of grasping—being continually expanded by a certain mutual love from God, the fountain of reasons—it is sufficiently shown that the mind is everlasting. God made the soul from the beginning equal to eternal reason (so to speak) in terms of its essence and life, since every day He renders it equal to that reason in terms of intelligence and love, as far as can be achieved. Finally, whatever power grasps something, it grasps it according to its own nature and draws it back into its own way of thinking. If, therefore, you were mortal, you would never have conceived of eternal things insofar as they are eternal, nor could you have grasped the <term>reason of eternity</term> under the logic of eternity. But just as all things appear red to bloodshot eyes and bitter to a bitter tongue, so all things would be judged as mortal by a mortal soul. But in fact, so far is it from the case that eternal things are thought to be fleeting when properly contemplated, that the contemplating mind separates the conditions of mortality even from individual mortal things, and perceives them under a universal logic. The mind could never separate these from matter and corruption unless it were itself far removed from them. You grasp your own eternity, therefore, in this fertile heaven, when you grasp the eternity of any reason here to the best of your strength in God, the immense fountain of reasons.

->*The mind sees God in Himself; yet because of His excessive splendor, He cannot be seen entirely.*<-

**F**urthermore, do you not see God Himself in Himself, encompassing that which remains for you as the third heaven, in which I myself saw those secrets which it is not permitted for man to speak? <note>A reference to St. Paul's vision in 2 Corinthians 12:2-4.</note> You perceive the light of the Sun in the elements, and you look up at it in the stars; you cannot look at it in itself. And yet, if you are wise, you are content that your Sun is so great that it exceeds the capacity of the eyes. Similarly, you recognize the Divine Light in the things created by it, and you recognize it in the "reasons" of created things. But you cannot endure it as it is in its absolute self. Yet you rejoice that your treasure is so great that it is entirely <term>innumerable</term> <note>Meaning beyond counting or calculation.</note>—innumerable, I say, not because you lack the art of counting (which is there most full within you), but because He exceeds the highest level of that art by the degrees of His power. Nevertheless, you seem to have "counted" enough when—having numbered all things that can either exist or be understood—you calculate by right reason that God Himself is nothing of the sort, and when you understand *how* His power is innumerable. You see enough when you see truly *how* He is invisible. You comprehend enough when you understand *how* He is incomprehensible. For you never understand Truth itself more clearly than when you rightly understand the way in which it is above all understanding. Where there is the highest light, there is the highest darkness; and where there is the highest darkness, there too is the highest light. Hence, nothing is better known than this, yet nothing more unknown; nothing more present, yet nothing more absent; nothing more visible, yet nothing more invisible. Because of this, David exclaims: *Night is my illumination in my delights.* <note>Psalm 138:11 (Vulgate numbering). Ficino uses this to describe the "Divine Dark," where God's light is so bright it appears as darkness to the human mind.</note>

<summary>Ficino defines eternity as a stable point beyond time and argues that the human soul must be immortal because it has the capacity to contemplate eternal truths. He concludes by describing the vision of God as a "divine darkness" caused by the overwhelming brightness of the supreme light.</summary>

<keywords>eternity, immortality of the soul, divine reason, Neoplatonism, apophatic theology, divine darkness, Marsilio Ficino, nature of truth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical discourse on the soul's ascent and its relationship with the Divine. Following the previous page’s discussion on how the soul "touches" eternal things, Ficino here explores the "via negativa" (the way of negation) and the superiority of love over knowledge in reaching God.</meta>

<page-num>704</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->*We speak more correctly of God by denying and relating, than by affirming.*<-

**B**ut truly, what you see thus in this heaven <note>A reference to the "third heaven" mentioned by St. Paul, representing the highest state of mystical contemplation.</note>, you cannot speak of; that is, you cannot pronounce absolutely and affirm. Whenever you deny other things of God, proceeding in this way—"God is neither any body, nor a quality of a body, nor an angel, nor anything else that might be more highly conceived"—you deny truly. Whenever you relate other things to God, comparing them in this way—"God is the principle <note>Latin: *principium*, meaning both the beginning and the foundational source.</note>, because all things flow from him; God is the end, because all things flow back to him; God is life and intelligence, because through him souls live and minds understand"—you also relate truly. But if you were to affirm, "God himself in his absolute nature is this very thing which I have either discovered or thought," you would be greatly deceived. Indeed, if that highest Author of all is greater than you, he cannot be that which is confined by your intelligence—for what is so confined is less than you. If the principle of principles and the end of ends is infinite, he is not any of those things which, having been discovered and comprehended by you, now appear finite.

---

->*The blessed soul is content with this very thing: that its good is incomprehensible. Nor would it be content if it were comprehensible.*<-

**W**hat then, O soul, do you live contentedly because you do not fully comprehend and define your life, since it is infinite? Rather, I know you rejoice in this very fact: that your life and your good are without end. It is enough for you to be happily grasped by the Incomprehensible, and nothing suffices for you unless it is incomprehensible. For whatever truth or good is offered that has certain limits—no matter how many there are—your intellect still requires more, and your will desires further. Thus, you can find rest nowhere except in a truth and good that is immense <note>original: *immenso*, meaning "immeasurable" or "without boundaries."</note>, nor can you find an end except in the infinite. Indeed, you depend upon the infinite alone, and from it you possess a power that is in some way infinite by reason, through which you tend toward and progress toward the infinite.

---

->*The will enjoys God more than the intellect.*<-

**B**ehold, I see where the intellect fails in a way, the will suffices. Behold, love <note>original: *charitas*, referring to divine or sacrificial love.</note> penetrates where knowledge cannot penetrate at all. You look upon the infinite, though not most clearly; you love it most ardently; you rejoice in it most vehemently. You see, indeed, as much as is visible to you; but you love both what you see, and that which you see is so overflowing that it cannot be fully seen by you. And this very thing pleases you most: that without any anxiety or satiety <note>A state of being "fed up" or over-filled; Ficino argues that divine joy never becomes boring or exhausting.</note>, you enjoy a good which, since it is infinite, is both infinitely available to you and infinitely delights you. Even if the light of the intellect does not discern this immensity by an entirely infinite reasoning, nevertheless, the infinite will is affected by immense love and joy while it enjoys that good. And if the will is full—to which it belongs to be satisfied—then the whole soul is entirely content.

---

->*The mind measures its own immortality in its object, which is without measure.*<-

**W**hile the soul in the third heaven measures how immense God is (so to speak) much more precisely than in other states, it recognizes at the same time how much its own life exceeds the measure of nature and of any time. For the soul would not reach the reasoning of the infinite—or rather of infinity itself—if its life were destined to have an end. Nor would it be more delighted by contemplating an immense object than by contemplating limited ones, if it were itself within the limit of natural and temporal forms. The powers of such forms are delighted not by the greatest objects, but only by moderate ones that are congruent with them in a certain proportion. If the power of life, such as intelligence and will, proceeds without end in understanding and loving beyond any limit of place, time, or degree offered to it, then certainly that life itself is not constrained by the boundaries of place, nor ended by the limits of a certain time, nor overwhelmed by the degrees of a contrary quality, nor filled up by the presence of a determined truth and good.

<summary>Ficino explains that God is best understood through what He is not (negative theology) and argues that the soul’s infinite desire for joy and truth proves its own immortality, as only an eternal soul could crave the immeasurable.</summary>
<keywords>via negativa, divine infinity, immortality of the soul, will vs intellect, Neoplatonism, third heaven, Marsilio Ficino, mystical theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's relationship to God. While the previous page focused on the "unknowability" of God through negation, here Ficino shifts to the "Mirror of the Mind" and the "Circle of Light." He uses Neoplatonic metaphors of light, reflection, and optics to prove the soul's immortality and its role as a bridge between the temporal and the eternal.</meta>

<page-num>705</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II</header>

### *Celestial light is perceived by celestial light; super-celestial by super-celestial.*

**T**ell me then, by what light do you behold the celestial light? Surely by the celestial. Tell me therefore by what light you just now saw the super-celestial. That light of the world manifest to the senses is a certain quality; therefore, diverse bodies do not receive it except through a single nature implanted in them and suited to light. A nature of this kind is called <term>perspicuity</term> <note>original: *perspicuitas*. In Renaissance optics, this refers to the transparency or clarity that allows a medium or organ to receive light.</note>. Because truly this perspicuity in the eye is more closely related to sensible light than it is in these other bodies—for there is a sensory perspicuity within it—for that reason, after the light has been infused into the eye, it is in a certain way reflected back into itself, specifically when the eye perceives it. In this, it is seen that the eye does not only suffer from the light while receiving it, but also in some way acts upon it while judging it in its own manner.

### *The soul sees its own immortality when it sees the ray of intelligence being infused into itself by God and reflected back into God.*

**B**y the same reasoning, spiritual light is a single thing—that is, Truth itself. Diverse spirits do not receive this except through a certain spiritual perspicuity innate to them. Because truly in spirits endowed with reason, a perspicuity of this kind exists that is more similar and closer to this light, it happens that spirits not only receive it, but also judge it, and thus are reflected back into the light itself. Here it is seen that this spiritual and <term>intelligible light</term> <note>Light that is grasped by the intellect rather than the physical eyes.</note> first flows into the intelligence without at all deserting itself; then it flows back into itself without abandoning the intelligence. 

And just as the light of the Sun, insofar as it remains in the Sun, is invisible, but as it flows out from the Sun into colors, it is visible—and insofar as it flows into the eye and becomes natural to it, it becomes the power of sight, and when it reflects from there back toward the Sun, it is then made a "seeing" thing—so the light of God, insofar as it gathers itself absolutely within Him, is above the intelligence. Insofar as it unfolds from there into the <term>ratios of things</term> <note>original: *rationes rerum*. The divine blueprints or archetypes of all created things.</note>, it is intelligible; insofar as it is infused into the intellect and becomes natural to it, it becomes "intellectual." Truly, when it flows back into God Himself, it is "intelligent." 

Therefore, a certain <term>circle</term> <note>A central concept in Ficino's Neoplatonism: the *circulus spiritualis* where divine energy flows from God to the world and returns from the soul back to God.</note> is formed here, shining marvelously from the divine Truth itself into the intellect, and from the intellect back into Truth; the beginning and end of this circle is God. The intellect is the middle. If the first and last boundary of this circle is eternity, as eternity, then certainly the middle is eternal, which is indeed a participant in those boundaries. For in what way could the splendor flowing from eternity into the mind flow back again into eternity through the intelligence (which seizes the object) and through the will (which passes into the object and is seized by it), unless it preserved its own power and eternity within the mind? By the same reason that the mind receives this light, it also acts through it. For it cannot act through it more excellently than it has received it. It acts truly through it in a certain absolute and eternal way, since by its rays—raised above place and time—it reaches the indivisible and eternal ratios of things, and insinuates itself into eternity itself in wondrous ways.

### *The mind is the mirror of God.*

**O** most sagacious hunter, who tracks and finds the most hidden footprints of God in this deep forest of the world! O most sharp-witted reasoner, who finds the reasons of things in the highest Reason of all! O most piercing searcher, who penetrates in a certain way the sanctuaries of God in His abyss! And, to put it briefly, in performing all these things, the mind contemplates God in itself as if in a mirror, and beholds itself in God as if in the Sun—O most divine mirror of the Divine Sun, both illustrated by rays and Kindled by flames! Truly, by the rays of Truth itself, it discerns true things everywhere, and in all true things (and above all things) it discerns Truth itself. By the flames of the Good itself, it burns for and thirsts for all good things everywhere, and in all good things (and above all things) it hungers for the Good itself.

### *Bodies are shadows of God, but souls are immortal images of God.*

**Y**ou see, O my mind, you see that you are the mirror of God when the rays of your intelligence, sent into Him, bounce back from Him. If you are His mirror (as you are without doubt), since you contemplate Him in yourself and yourself in Him, it follows that what is below you from God is merely a certain footprint and a <term>shadow</term>, while that which is in you is the image of God and a more express likeness—so that it is rightly said that you were created "in the image and likeness of God." A shadow does not distinctly represent the body to the viewer, but an image, expressed according to the likeness of the body...

<meta>Catchword: expressed</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's immortality through the metaphor of a "spiritual circle," where divine light flows into the mind and reflects back to God, arguing that the mind acts as a divine mirror rather than a mere shadow of the physical world.</summary>

expresses the expressed more clearly. The machinery of the world, like a shadow of God, does not show you God himself unless you bring its order back to yourself and dispel the shadow by your own clearest examination. Then at last, within yourself as an image of God, the world is transformed from a shadow into an image; and in yourself, as a true likeness of God, you truly recognize God when you prove that He is the very eternal truth and true eternity. Time, however, is His shadow, and all temporal things are shadowy. Since you are a true image of eternity above the shadow and shadowy things—seeing as you, being in the middle, distinguish these from that—you are certainly eternal, circumscribed by no limits of place or boundaries of certain time. Otherwise, you would not be able to run through immense space or time in thought, or pass beyond these to an indivisible and eternal nature.

->The mind, because it is an image of the divine countenance, must always look up to God.<-

**O** Image of God in the mirror of the mind: as long as you are in a riddle <note>original: *in ænigmate*. A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in aenigmate]; but then face to face."</note>—that is, the shadow of the body—you know through a mirror, but outside the shadow you shall see face to face. O image of the divine countenance in the mirror, behold your own face. To behold it is almost nothing other than to be beheld. Since the ray of His eye is that very thing which inspects, and is that very thing which is reflected back by itself, know yourself, O mind, you who are so desirous of knowing other things. Tell me, what are you, O mind? You are the exact image of the universal exemplar, the legitimate daughter of the Father of all, the everlasting ray of the super-celestial Sun, continually reflected by nature back into the Sun. God, therefore, most willingly gazes upon you as His own image; He loves you entirely as a daughter; He shines upon you as His own ray, and joins you to Himself. Therefore, now through your character and piety, conform yourself to your exemplar, by which you may be most purely reformed. Love above all that Father by whom you are happily generated, and more happily regenerated. Rejoice only in the light, without which you can never rejoice in others, nor in yourself. Darkness is terrible above all things, because life consists in light and light in life; and the more internal the darkness, the more terrible it becomes. Darkness outside the body is horrible to all; it is more horrible within the body to the melancholic <note>original: *melancholicis*. In Renaissance medicine, those suffering from an excess of "black bile," often associated with profound intellectual focus but also deep despair.</note>; it is most horrible in the soul to the wretched. Therefore, the light of the air is pleasant to all, because it is most akin to the vital spirit, and it delights and teaches through the variety of innumerable things; more pleasant is the light in the sanguine spirits of the body; but most sweet is the innermost light of the blessed mind.

->God is joy itself. Only through Him do we rejoice; in Him alone do we rejoice blessedly.<-

**I**f all people do all things for the sake of avoiding pain and attaining joy, and if they reject life itself without joy, then clearly joy is the end of all things; it is therefore also the principle, for it is that toward which they are moved and flow. What then is joy itself other than God? The Good of goods, the Joy of joys. Since you rejoice so much in these goods and those, tell me—if it can even be said—how much do you rejoice in that Good or in that Idea of Joy <note>Ficino uses "Idea" in the Platonic sense: the perfect, eternal form of a concept from which all earthly examples are derived.</note> without whose allurements, without whose form, you would rejoice in neither these goods nor those? In this Good and in this Idea, all those who rejoice in anything—even the ungrateful—rejoice continually. But they do not rejoice well or blessedly unless they are grateful, to whom this joy comes much more weightily than to the ungrateful. Therefore, if you wish to rejoice in the Good itself and in Joy itself in the best and most blessed way, remember in all things that please you, that nothing else pleases you but Him.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Argument for the Platonic<-
->Theology to Lorenzo de' Medici, savior of his country.<-

**I** have decided, Magnanimous Lorenzo, before I publish that great volume of *Platonic Theology* dedicated to your name—in which there still remains some work requiring examination—to publish, if it pleases you, the Argument. I do this not so that, having been practiced by an argument of this kind as if by a prelude to Theology, you might approach the "game" more promptly—for you seem to me to have already won the prize of the game itself—but so that, being reminded meanwhile by this pledge, you may remember (as I remember I owe you) what I had long ago rightfully promised, and that I wish eventually to pay what I acknowledge I owe. Especially since I do not owe this thing so much because I promised it, but rather I promised it because I owed everything.

<sig>Yy 2</sig>

# The three stages of Platonic contemplation.

**T**here are indeed three principal stages of Platonic contemplation. The first ascends from the body through the soul to God. The second consists in God Himself. The third, finally, descends back to the soul and the body. Our argument likewise contains these three stages.

### The first stage of contemplation is the ascent to the Soul, the Angel, and God. Concerning divine intelligence and love. The heavens are form without matter, as it pleases some.

**I** was recently and diligently considering that paradox of Aristotle: the heavens lack matter. I was also meditating on the reasoning of Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Al-Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> by which he proves this Aristotelian paradox. He argues that because matter is by its own nature formless—and therefore relates to any form equally and is capable of receiving all forms in turn—it flows continuously from one form into another. From this, it follows that whatever consists of matter can eventually lose its form. The heavens, however, cannot lose their own form, both because there is no contrary quality found anywhere within them (just as no motion is found contrary to their circular motion), and because their motion is always equal and untiring without any departure from its path, returning into itself and beginning its starting point again where it seems to end. From these points, Averroes concludes that the heavens are a certain form existing by itself without matter; although they do not require a subject of matter, they are nevertheless subject to <term>quantity</term> <note>In this context, "quantity" refers to mathematical extension or physical dimensions, such as size and volume.</note> and motion according to place. He wishes this kind of form to be a middle point between physical forms and metaphysical forms. For natural forms exist with a certain quantity and are within matter. But forms that are entirely above nature lack both quantity and matter. He argues there must be a middle form so that one does not pass from one extreme to the other without a midpoint; this middle form, though it has quantity, does not have matter. He believes the celestial substance is of this kind. Proclus the Platonist <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers and a head of the Neoplatonic Academy.</note> also thinks that the celestial vehicle of the soul is a body, yet possesses no matter.

### Form can exist without quantity more than it can exist without matter.

**H**aving directed these steps of Aristotle, Averroes, and Proclus toward the heavens, I have attempted with all my strength to ascend *above* the heavens. Certainly, since the genus of forms is able to free itself from matter in some place—as has just appeared to us in the case of the heavens—it can also, and even much more so, absolve itself from quantity. For if it depended on one or the other, it would depend more on matter (by which a substantial form is often sustained) than on quantity (which a substantial form perhaps sustains no less than it is sustained by it). This is most clearly seen in the heavens, as Averroes prefers, where such a form sustains the dimensions of quantity. Add to this that form agrees much more with matter than with quantity in a certain order of genus and nature. Therefore, if it can exist without matter, it can much more easily consist without quantity—especially that form which is a <term>substance</term> <note>A "substance" is something that exists in itself, whereas an "accident" (like color or size) must exist in something else.</note>. For since an accident is added to a substance, a substance can exist somewhere without quantity, which is an accident.

### Form can exist without quantity more than it can exist without mass.

**J**ust as the order of forms progresses toward the better from the elements into the heavens while being liberated from the shadow of matter, so too above the summit of the heavens it progresses into something far better when, in souls and angels, it is also absolved from the mass of quantity. Having laid aside the weakness of division, it gains strength because of the unity of its indivisible nature. It is finally perfected above these in the Best [God], when in God it is also liberated from quality and the lack of accidents. Moreover, it can be preserved more easily from quality than from mass. For substantial form everywhere in nature sustains qualities, but is never sustained by them. Yet in some places, it seems to lie within quantity. This is clearly seen in the lowest forms of nature.

<summary>Ficino explains the stages of spiritual ascent, arguing that just as the heavens are "pure form" without heavy matter, the soul and angels are even higher forms that exist without physical size or "mass," eventually reaching God who is free of all limitations.</summary>

### The heavens are either a certain visible life, or a nature most close to life.

**T**he heavens indeed, since they are without matter, seem to the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, which Ficino helped revive in the Renaissance; they emphasized the spiritual and ideal over the material.</note> to be something spiritual in a way, rather than corporeal. What, then, are the heavens? They are circular light and a luminous circle without matter, just as their opposite—the lowest depths of the earth—is matter without light. Therefore, as the Platonists believe, the heavens are either a kind of life that is not hidden like the soul, but manifest to the eyes because of its dimensions; or at least, since it is a nature closer to life than other bodies, it lives with a life far more familiar to itself than others.

---

### The difference of light in the heavens and the elements according to the Platonists and Peripatetics.

**B**ut it is helpful to ascend step by step from light back to light. We see in the elements that where the nature is less thick, light is more easily present. And the more that ignited matter is thinned and rarefied, the more purely it shines through. For this reason, since the heavens shine most brightly, they are proven to lack matter; and for this very reason—because they lack matter—they shine most intensely. If anyone should say that the denser parts of the heavens shine more than others, the Platonists will respond that the rarer parts actually shine more, but cannot be seen because of their extreme fineness and light. The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (ether) and that light behaved differently there than on Earth.</note> will respond, in turn, that it is one thing to glitter from oneself and another to glitter from another source. Therefore, because the elements receive brightness from elsewhere, those that are rarer receive it more easily. But celestial things, which shine from themselves, reflect more abundantly the denser they are. However, let us set aside questions of this kind. Let us leave the heavens for a moment, lest we be utterly deluded by bodily splendor.

---

### When we purify celestial light, we first find the soul, then the angel.

**C**ome now, if you will, leave behind the light and motion of the celestial nature and subtract the dimensions of quantity—for it is possible to subtract these in thought, as the light and motion of the heavens are one thing, and dimension is another. The form that remains is a certain spirit which is as much more luminous and swift than the heavens as the heavens are more luminous and swift than the elements; this incorporeal substance appears to be the rational soul. Subtract motion from this again, and leave light and quality—for you can subtract it. For light and quality are one thing, and motion is another. The form that then remains is an angel, far brighter and swifter than the soul. For the angel neither scatters its light through motion nor distracts its own action through time, as the soul does.

---

### It is better to ascend to a substance in which power is nothing other than the substance itself.

**H**owever, we do not yet seem to have purified the nature of things enough. There remains for us still, unless reason deceives me, the task of separating the <term>accident</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color or speed) that exists in a "substance" but is not the substance itself.</note> from the <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying reality or essence that carries properties.</note>. For an angel possesses both substance and quality. But we must first ask whether it is better to do this, and then whether it is possible. It is certainly better. For where substance is one thing and quality another, a substance of this kind is formless and imperfect by its own nature; it is formed and perfected from elsewhere, and in receiving and sustaining quality, it is in some way passive <note>original: "patitur"; meaning it is acted upon or affected by the quality rather than being the source of it.</note>. Moreover, that quality, because it is a form in another subject, cannot sustain itself, and much less can it exist of itself. It therefore lacks both a cause and a subject, and is not entirely whole or full since it is received only according to the capacity of the subject. From this, it necessarily follows that there must be a higher form which—lest we wander without end—is self-sufficient and most full within itself, and is a power infinite in every way, since it is neither exceeded by anything higher nor limited by any receiver. Add to this that everything composed of substance and quality is weakened in its power because it is divided into parts. And because it is composed, it depends both on the parts and on that craftsman who reconciled those parts into one—parts which, being diverse, would not have come together of their own accord. Therefore, since such a composite is not the "best" either in its parts or as a whole, there must be something better: a substance that is not distinct from its own quality, and a quality that is nothing other than its own substance, so that at last a certain act is found that is entirely pure and immense. Who can doubt it is better that above that which...
