...from that which is composed of substance and accident, let us ascend to that which is better.

### *Many reasons why it is necessary for there to be a pure and infinite act.*

**I**t is better, then, to ascend to this point, but is it possible? Perhaps you ask if it is possible? Since it is already necessary for it to be so, as we have proven. But if you require another reason, a logic of this kind leads to the same conclusion: because substance is the foundation of an accident, it is prior to the accident; and because that which is prior does not depend on that which is posterior, substance can exist somewhere without any accident. And this is a better state, as we have shown. Therefore, lest this kind of power at the beginning of all things be so good in vain from eternity to eternity, it seems worthwhile that it should already exist in "act." <note>In this philosophical context, 'Act' or 'Actuality' refers to a thing being fully realized or 'in motion,' whereas 'Potentiality' is the mere possibility of being something.</note> Especially since where there is the highest act and the highest perfection, there "potentiality" and "act"—the *ability* to be and the *fact* of being—are one and the same. And if in lower and less good things—namely mixed elements, plants, and animals—nature has already provided for their parts and the rest to exist in the way that is best for them, how much more so in things that are vastly better? In the highest peak of nature, whatever is proven to be better already exists, and exists more truly. Furthermore, things judged to be better in the universe are not considered better for any other reason than that it is agreeable to true reason, it contributes most to the order of things, and it is especially fitting for the Orderer of things. Truly, it would be a sin to say such a thing is impossible or false.

Again, potentiality and truth are naturally desired as "goods." And this very fact that they exist means they are either goodness itself or derived from goodness. Therefore, that which is more possible and more true in the nature of the universe is also better; and conversely, what is judged better for the universe is also more possible and more true. Likewise, that which is better partakes more in the "Good." It is therefore not impossible. For that which is impossible is judged to partake in no good at all. Added to this is the fact that if the Pure Act <term>Pure Act (Actus Purus): A theological concept describing God as complete perfection, having no potential to change because He is already everything He can be.</term> and infinite act, which we have conceptualized through debate, is infinitely better than an angel, and better than the universe of which the angel is a part (since the whole universe is limited), then it is necessarily infinitely more powerful in its existence. For power is a good, and goodness is power. Indeed, since to exist truly and actually is a good, and nothing of the good is lacking in the immeasurable Good, the Immeasurable Act is already more truly "in act" than all other things. If infinite power, through an infinite duration, has not yet come into act, no other power ever shall. Indeed, if that infinite act (which is the same as that power) is not always in act, certainly no other shall be. If a certain power, which by its own nature lacks all things and is infinitely passive—that is, matter—is always in act, then without doubt that power which is "Total Act" and is infinitely effective is also always in act. It is from this active power that passive potentiality exists and is able to be acted upon.

But why do we inquire so curiously and ineptly whether it is possible or true for an immense good to exist in the universe or not? For nothing is more possible or more true than that which nothing more powerful can be imagined. <note>Ficino is echoing St. Anselm’s famous 'Ontological Argument': that God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived.'</note> It would not be an immense good unless it contained within it whatever is judged better to exist. Our mind, through thought and affection, progresses through degrees of goodness without end; it would exceed the nature of the Supreme Principle if some good could be thought of that was not in it, or unless that Principle were immense. Why say more? If in the highest Beginning and End of all things, where whatever is desirable is found in the highest degree, there is the highest Goodness; and if that highest Goodness is exactly the same as the highest Power and Truth, it follows that whatever is judged better regarding it will be more possible—indeed, it is already more true. In all things, one must remember that a potentiality capable of some good is in reality something, and is founded on some true thing; furthermore, it depends on something else which already possesses that good in "act." Again, that which possesses a good in act proceeds from another which is itself "Goodness" and the "Act of every act."

### *Concerning the light of God, and the shadow of matter.*

**B**ut perhaps it will seem to someone that this nature—in which quality is not distinguished from substance—exists without form or light. But let him remember that we have proven we must ascend to a "Form existing in itself"; therefore, that substance is Form. Truly, just as in the lowest of things—that is, primary matter—to exist is the same as to be formless and dark, so in the Highest, to exist is the same as to be beautiful and bright; indeed, it is to be Form and Light itself. For matter, according to Moses, is the abyss of darkness <note>original: "Materia enim apud Mosem, tenebrarum abyssus est"</note> and the formless subject of forms. God is Light, the abyss of lights, and the Form that is the fountain of forms. Matter is an infinite [power] of suffering...

<summary>Ficino argues that God must be "Pure Act"—a state of perfect, infinite existence where potentiality and reality are one. He contrasts God as the "Fountain of Forms" and infinite light with matter, which he describes as an "abyss of darkness" and formless potential.</summary>

This page explores the metaphor of Light to explain how God interacts with the human mind and will.</meta>

<page-num>710</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...potentiality. God is the infinite power of acting; or rather, He is infinite **act**. <note>Ficino uses 'Act' (actus) to mean a state of total reality or completion, as opposed to 'Potentiality' (potentia), which is the mere possibility of being something.</note> Therefore, that power is the power above all powers that are involved in undergoing change. This is the "Act of acts." And just as it is truly said of matter that it is *only* matter—being neither this form nor that—so of God it is said innumerably and truly: God is *this* form and *that* form. One matter is the lowest shadow of shadowy things. One God is the highest light of lights. Matter is unknown because of its excessive darkness; God is unknown because of His excessive light. For if light is that which is more pure and more luminous, then surely God—since He alone is pure act—must be called the only true light. If light consists in a certain form of the whole, more than in a subject, then beauty consists in light. True light exists only there where the form exists without the contamination of a subject. <note>In Platonic thought, a 'subject' is the material thing that 'carries' a quality. Ficino argues that God is 'form' without the 'weight' or 'impurity' of matter.</note> True beauty exists only where there is only true light and true form. Therefore, every form and light that is either seen by the eyes or grasped by thought is merely a shadow compared to the form and light of God, because it is finite. God is rightly called infinite act because He is not restricted by the limits of a subject or a cause, as we have said. From this it is clear that He is a light beyond measure.

### *As much as the light of God towers above the surface of the intellect, so much does the heat of God penetrate the center of the will.*

Since heat takes its origin from light, there is also an immeasurable heat—a heat infinitely beneficial in the infinite good. We reach this heat through the ardor of the **will** rather than through the "spark" of the mind. For as much as God towers over us by the light of His intellect, He burns into us by the ardor of His goodness, so that nothing is higher than God, and nothing is deeper. The broader His light is, the more unknown He is naturally to our intellect; the more vehement His heat is, the more certain He is (so to speak) to our will. Therefore, in the highest peak of intellectual cognition, God is in some way a kind of "night" to the intellect. But in the highest love of the will, He is certainly "day" to the will. This is why Orpheus <note>original: "Orpheus". Ficino refers to the mythical poet Orpheus, whom the Neoplatonists believed was a real ancient theologian who taught that God is both hidden darkness and manifest light.</note> calls God both Night and Day. Nevertheless, when the divine splendor arrives in the souls of the blessed and is called "night," it is far brighter than any temporal day. And by this divine gift, it is nearly as much brighter as God is (so to speak) more luminous than the Sun, and the soul is purer and clearer than the air.

### *Light in the elements, the heavens, the soul, the angel, and God.*

Light in the elements is easily perceived by the eyes, whose composition consists of elements. Light in the heavens, although more ample, is nonetheless seen with more difficulty, for the quality of the eyes is further removed from the heavens. Light in the soul is not seen at all—just as the light of the Sun is not seen by an owl—because it is too great, nor does corporal sense have any proportion to it. Instead, it is thought of through the reasoning of the rational soul. Light in an angel is neither seen nor even thought of, for it is beyond the proportion of the senses and beyond the capacity of temporal reasoning; nevertheless, it is *understood*. It meets in the soul with the angel in a certain stable intelligence of its own, rather than in the shifting reasoning of thought. Because the light in God exceeds even the limits of the intellect, it is not understood at all by the natural intelligence of man, but is rather believed and loved; and having been loved, it is seen through a grace poured into us. Indeed, the soul, set on fire by love for Him, shines the more clearly the more ardently it burns; it discerns more truly and enjoys more sweetly. Hence Plato asserts that the divine light is not pointed out by the "finger of reason," but is captured by the clear serenity of a holy life.

### *What the heaven, the soul, the angel, and God are, and the difference between visible and invisible light.*

So that we may finally gather the windings of our dispute into a few words: we say that the **heaven** is a certain light that is in a way a "body without matter." The **soul** is a great light without quantity. The **angel** is a very swift light without motion. **God** is the best and most powerful light without quality, whose heat we experience through the will sooner, more certainly, and more vehemently than we experience His light through the intelligence. In this, invisible light differs most from visible light: visible light—whether in fire or in the heavens—coming from the outside, illuminates before it heats. However, invisible light, acting from the inside, in a way heats before it illuminates. Therefore, in the former, we move from sight to touch; in the latter, as if by a kind of touch, we proceed into the "unseen" itself.
Human...

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchy of light from physical elements to God, arguing that while God's light "blinds" the intellect (becoming a "divine night"), His goodness "heats" the human will through love.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical discussion of God as "Pure Act" and "Infinite Light" to the specific Platonic definitions of God as the source of all reason, truth, and craftsmanship. It bridges the gap between God's essence and His role as the architect of the universe.</meta>

Human beauty is seen before it is loved. Divine beauty, however, is loved so that it may be seen. But in the former, he who sees is miserably possessed by hope. In the latter, to see is nothing other than to possess happily. Therefore, anyone who believes they will possess God without a singular love and worship of Him labors in vain and entirely against the order of nature, or hopes to find Him before they have begun to love Him.

->*The second level of Platonic contemplation consists in God. The uniform and omniform craftsmanship depends on a uniform and omniform art.*<- <note>Ficino uses "uniform" (uniforme) to mean having a single, simple nature, and "omniform" (omniforme) to mean containing the patterns of all possible shapes and things.</note>

**T**he common opinion of all believes, and the diligent reasoning of the wise proves, that this craftsmanship of the world—which is artistically and rationally arranged and driven according to its own nature and motion—is governed by a certain rational art and artistic reason. Indeed, as much as can be conjectured from craftsmanship of this kind, which is both one and universal, and which is established and driven throughout the whole and its parts with such wonderful reason that scarcely any human reason can grasp it, and no reason at all can fully imitate it: without doubt, we argue along with Timaeus <note>original: "cum Timeo" — referring to the character in Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, who describes the creation of the universe by a divine craftsman.</note> that the art which effects the world is a certain reason that is both one and universal, uniform (so to speak) and omniform. A Reason, I say, of the whole world, encompassing within itself all the reasons of all the parts of the world.

->*God is named art, reason, substance, nature, life, sense, intelligence, certainty.*<-

**I**f this reason is most absolute and is the source of all reasons, from which all substance, nature, life, sense, and intelligence are entirely produced and drawn, no one ought to be so irrational as to deny that a reason of this kind is the most stable substance, the most fertile nature, eternal life, the most piercing sense, and the most lucid intelligence. Most lucid, I say—that is, most certain. For what light is in the body of the world—the source of lights and of those who see—certainty is in the creative reason of the world. This certainty is as much more lucid than physical light as it is more certain; a certainty, surely, that is certain of itself from itself, certain of all things within itself, and which through itself makes all things clear and certain to serene minds.

->*God is truth, the source of all true things, the cause of the truth of things and of the mind.*<-

**W**hence also He is named the highest truth of every truth, by whom all true things are made, through whom true things are tracked down, and in whom true things are discerned. Investigators of things consult this truth whenever they wish concerning true matters; they search for truths through its naturally implanted spark; they discern found truths from false ones by its rays poured through all things. By its examination, they compare and judge truths already discerned among themselves; and when they understand the "species" <note>In this context, 'species' refers to the essential forms or 'blueprints' of things.</note> abstracted from individual things—in which the truth of each thing consists—they understand nothing but truth itself, that is, God, who is the gathering and source of all abstract things, that is, the Ideas, just as the light of the Sun is the source of colors.

->*Common descriptions of God according to the Platonists.*<-

**W**hat, then, is God? The reason of reasons, the source and craftsman of all things, the uniform and omniform form, the immovable substance moving all things, stillness in motion, eternity in time, the container in space, depth in the heights, the summit in the depths, unity in multitude, power in weakness. The most fertile nature of natures, the most natural fertility of fertilities, the eternal life of living beings and of lives. The light of sensible things, indeed, and the keenness of the senses. A sense perceiving the marrow <note>original: "medullas... in corticibus" — literally the pith or marrow inside the bark/husks. This is a metaphor for seeing the inner essence of things within their outer physical appearance.</note> of sensible things within their husks, and the husks within the marrow. Also an intelligence of such a kind that it is itself the goodness of things to be understood, the truth of every intellect, and the joy of the will.

He describes God as the source of all Ideas and the ultimate certainty that allows the human mind to distinguish truth from falsehood.</summary>

### *Many reasons why the joy of the contemplator surpasses the pleasures of the senses.*

**J**oy, I say, born from the truest goodness and the highest truth, is itself the highest and truest joy. Hence the divine Plato <note>Ficino frequently refers to Plato as "divine" to signal his belief that Platonic philosophy was a precursor to Christian revelation.</note> says that from those things offered to the senses—because they come from the outside and do not truly exist, but are impure and brief—there arises a certain external titillation around the "skin" of the body and soul, a pleasure that is false, mixed with pain, and fleeting. However, from those things which insinuate themselves deeply into the mind from within—because they are innermost, true, pure, stable, and supreme—an innermost, true, stable, and supreme pleasure is infused into the very marrow of the soul. Furthermore, the sense and the sensible object are so related to one another that, because of their density and weakness, they cannot entirely penetrate each other. But the intelligible object <note>term: intelligible object — In Platonic thought, this refers to a reality that can only be grasped by the intellect, such as a mathematical truth or a divine Idea, rather than something seen or touched.</note>, by its own thinness and miraculous power, glides into the inner reaches of the intellect, and the intellect, by its own subtlety and virtue, penetrates the intelligible object on all sides. Otherwise, the mind could not separate the nature of the thing to be understood from foreign elements, nor distinguish it into its parts, nor compare its innermost qualities with its outermost. Thus it happens that the pleasure of the mind, if it is ever truly perceived through proper contemplation, becomes more interior and more vehement than the delights of the senses. If we are accustomed to being greatly delighted when we have recovered the natural state of the body through opposites—such as when we are cooled after being too hot, or when we are replenished after being emptied—how much pleasure do we think drenches that man who, having lost the natural state of his mind to darkness and malice, now resumes it through light and goodness, and is entirely reformed according to his own Idea? <note>term: Idea — For Ficino, the "Idea" is the perfect, divine archetype of a thing that exists in the mind of God.</note> And if a greater and greater delight is born step-by-step from things that are more and more fitting, and if nothing is more fitting to a human being than the very Idea of humanity (which is the true man), what could be sweeter than both to embrace that Idea within oneself by understanding it, and to be restored to it by loving it? Moreover, in loving all beautiful and good things, we truly love nothing else (though we are perhaps unaware of it) than beauty and goodness itself, from which and out of which each beautiful and good thing exists. It is just as if one were to say that a plum or wine pleases a palate hungry for sweetness, not because it is a plum or wine, but because it is sweet; and therefore, nothing else is desired in these things but sweetness itself, and through sweetness, goodness. Therefore, if it is the most pleasant thing of all to possess the things you love, what can be thought more pleasant than to possess Him who is goodness itself? For nowhere else do we possess the thing loved, but only its shadow. There, then, our Idea pleases us, for everyone is most dear to himself. There alone are we most fully delighted, where alone we most truly find ourselves. In our Idea, all Ideas please us. Beauty delights us in all things; all things in goodness fill us. And according to our own form, we there properly rejoice in the very Idea of joy. Thus it happens that we rejoice there only in the full plenitude of joy. If one person or another rejoices where this or that good is found, then surely where Goodness itself is, there is Joy itself. If no one truly lives or is wise unless he properly lives by Life itself and is wise by Wisdom itself, then without doubt no one truly or fully rejoices unless he properly rejoices in Joy itself. Finally, since we rejoice in a finite beauty and good in a finite way, we surely rejoice infinitely in the infinite beauty and goodness of the fountain of innumerable forms and goods.

### *The taste of the soul, infected by the bitter humor of the body, tastes the flavor of divine things either not at all, or only with difficulty and very rarely.*

**B**ut of this great joy, alas, we miserable ones are scarcely and quite rarely participants on earth. Even now, our sick minds perceive only a certain meager shadow of it, passing by in a moment. The natural taste of these minds—O, the grief!—is too much infected by the bitter humor <note>term: humor — In medieval and Renaissance medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note> of this body. From this it results that that celestial and most healthful flavor is either not felt, or it offends at times, or it delights only lightly and briefly. Those among us sometimes taste more sharply and are delighted more vehemently and longer who, through the study of morals and contemplation, wipe away the filth and stain of the body from the nature of the mind; but they are the "few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom glowing virtue has carried up to the heavens." <note>original: "pauci quos æquus amauit Iupiter, aut ardens euexit ad ætherea uirtus" — A quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 129–131.</note> Who indeed are these, O friend? These are surely they to whom it is said by the divine teacher:

> I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice. Your joy shall be full, and it shall never be taken from you. <note>original: "Iterum uidebo uos..." — This is a translation of John 16:22 from the New Testament.</note>

### *The third level of Platonic contemplation. Why the soul in the body knows divine things with difficulty, and that it is immortal.*

He laments that bodily existence and its "humors" usually dull this spiritual taste, making divine joy a rare experience reserved for those who purify themselves through virtue.</summary>

### The first obstacle of the mind in perceiving the light of intelligible things: its union with the body.

**F**iery is their vigor and celestial their origin <note>original: "Igneus est ollis uigor & cœlestis origo"; these are lines from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, where the poet describes the divine origin of souls.</note>, so far as harmful bodies do not slow them down, nor do earthly limbs and mortal members dull them. Hence they fear and desire, they grieve and rejoice; nor do they look back at the breezes of heaven, shut up as they are in darkness and a blind prison. Let us see what our Virgil <note>original: "Maro"; referring to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> intended in these Platonic verses. The soul, enclosed within the dark prison of this body, scarcely perceives the wonderful light of truth and the true things that shine miraculously within it, because it has so little proportion or alignment with that light. This lack of proportion arises from three causes. The first is that the soul is a "form" <note>term: form — in this philosophical context, a "form" is the organizing principle or essence of a thing. The soul is the "form" that gives life to the body.</note> joined to a body. That light, however, is a form entirely separated from the commerce of bodies. This is the point Aristotle makes in his *Metaphysics*: our intellect relates to those things which are clearest in nature just as the eyes of a nocturnal owl relate to the light of the Sun. Along the same lines, Avicenna <note>A Persian philosopher and physician whose works on the soul were influential in the Renaissance.</note> writes in his *Metaphysics*: Just as the tongue of a paralytic, weighed down by a certain humor <note>term: humor — an old medical term for bodily fluids believed to influence health and temperament.</note>, loses the ability to taste certain flavors, but regains that taste once the humor is purged, so the human intellect—because of its union with the mortal body—is like a paralytic; that is, it is deprived of its natural "sense" regarding those things which are entirely incorporeal and eternal. And just as the humor of the tongue takes away the *act* of tasting but not the *power* of taste itself (which is evident when the person is healed), so the body disturbs the action of the intellect regarding spiritual things, but does not destroy its underlying potential. We can infer this because the further the mind calls itself away from the body—both through the cultivation of morals and the frequent practice of contemplation—the more clearly it discerns incorporeal things. And together with these, it even discerns itself, for the soul is also incorporeal, since through its own action and a certain innate affection, it sometimes transcends the order and power of physical bodies.

### The second obstacle to the intelligible light: the mind’s attachment to the body.

**T**he second cause that hinders the proportion we mentioned from the beginning is this: since the soul is joined to the body in such a way that it moves and acts naturally within it, it surely turns its natural affection first toward bodily things. Such an affection leads it far away from things that have no body.

### The third obstacle to the intelligible light: the mind turns its gaze toward bodies.

**T**he third cause is that the mind frequently turns the "edge" of its vision toward the senses and sensible things, and toward their images stored in the imagination <note>term: phantasia — the faculty of the mind that stores and manipulates images of physical objects gathered by the senses.</note>. These images, like certain clouds, overshadow the mind's vision to such an extent that it cannot discern the wonderful light of intelligible things, since it looks for their splendor not within itself, but mostly within these "clouds." In this state, the mind sees itself degenerating and becoming almost like a physical thing; because of this, it sees nothing clearly or truly, but only what is blurred by the darkness of images. This condition of the mind is like eyes suffering from red ophthalmia <note>A general historical term for inflammation of the eye.</note>, to which the light does not appear clear as it truly is, but red, and colors in the light do not appear as they are, but red. There are even some whose minds are so darkened by the contagion of the body and the mists of physical things that they never see the rays of spiritual things at all, like an eye suppressed by a cataract. However, when these physical "filths" are washed away in some measure, incorporeal things are seen by the soul a little bit; but when they are completely dissolved, suddenly the intelligible light—full of the rays of all intelligible things—pours itself entirely into the eyes of the intelligence. This light is indeed everywhere, and by its nature it illuminates the intellectual eye as soon as it has been purified, just as visible light illuminates the sight. And all sensible things shine much more clearly in that intelligible light, as if in their primary source, than they do in physical light, which is in truth but a shadow of the former. One must remember, however, that while the soul is occupied in building and ruling the mass of the body, and distracted or disturbed by various actions, it turns its gaze toward spiritual rays either not at all, or most often in a neglected, light, and slanted way. Indeed, even when it looks a little more attentively as much as it can, because it is joined to the body, it most often bends itself back toward those things it is joined to—that is, toward the clouds of bodily images flying about in the imagination.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains how the human soul's union with the physical body acts as a "prison" that obscures divine truth, using medical and optical analogies like cataracts and owls' eyes to describe the intellect's limitations. He identifies three specific obstacles: the soul's structural union with the body, its emotional attachment to physical life, and the distracting "clouds" of sensory images in the imagination.</summary>

The imagination <note>term: Phantasia — the faculty of the soul that creates and stores mental images based on sensory input. Ficino sees it as a bridge (and often a barrier) between the body and the pure intellect.</note> also clothes the rays of spiritual things with the images of physical bodies as soon as they begin to glimmer in the mind. For this reason, the mind either does not see at all, or sees only with great difficulty and through a veil. But when the mind is both separated from the body and cleansed from bodily stains, it turns its entire focus solely toward incorporeal things. Then, it shines with an abundant light according to its desire. It discerns all things clearly within that light, as if they were both most clear in themselves and most intimate to the understanding. It achieves this when "the completion of a cycle of time has removed the ingrained stain, leaving the ethereal sense pure and the fire of the simple air." <note>original: "perfectio temporis orbe... auræ simplicis ignem"; Ficino is quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid* (VI.745–747), describing the purification of the soul after death.</note>

## *An argument for the immortality of the soul: since it understands incorporeal things without a bodily instrument, it reaches separated forms and separates those that are joined.*

**F**or the present, let it suffice to understand that our soul can be separated from the body according to its substance, and can thereafter remain within itself, because the intellect acts without any bodily instrument. This occurs when the intellect, traversing through all the genera and species <note>term: genera and species — logical categories used to classify everything in the natural world, from "Animal" (genus) to "Human" (species).</note> of physical things, ascends from there to the order of spiritual things and distinguishes them into their own categories. However, through a physical instrument—which is by its nature particular and limited—the soul would not be able to comprehend anything except physical and particular things. If it can act without the body, it can also live and understand apart from it. 

Furthermore, according to its action (which both comes from its substance and remains within its substance), the soul not only reaches things that are separated and eternal—proving even against the deceptions of the imagination that such things must exist in the order of the universe—but it also, by its own power, separates forms from matter. It does this when it distinguishes the nature of each species from individual objects in the natural world. <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated from Greek to Latin.</note> and <term>Proclus</term> <note>original: "Proculus"; a major late-antique Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino’s views on the soul’s hierarchy.</note> say that since the essence of an action is both its principle and its foundation, the mind—which calls itself away from the body in the act of abstracting—is much more capable of living apart from the body according to its essence. <term>Themistius</term> <note>A 4th-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> considers it more difficult to separate natures that are joined together than to perceive forms that are already separated; from this he concludes that the intellect can certainly reach separated forms <note>note: "Separated forms" refers to Platonic Ideas or purely spiritual beings that do not have physical bodies.</note>, since it separates joined natures at will.

## *An argument for the immortality of the soul from its proportion to separable forms, and from its access to separated ones.*

**N**atures of this kind are the natural and familiar objects of the human intellect as long as it inhabits this natural body. For it understands them continuously and by a certain natural instinct by separating them from individual things. Hence, it is necessary that no small proportion exists between the intellect and these forms. From this, it is concluded that the intellect is joined to the body in such a condition that it remains separable—indeed, it is already separated in a way, since its "domestic" objects are species which, though joined to individuals, are not treated as joined, but rather as separable and separated. 

Indeed, the common mode of understanding is this: when the imagination envisions "this man" or "that man," the intellect disregards the mortal accidents <note>term: accidents — qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as hair color, height, or location.</note> of the man, and disregards this specific place or time. Instead, it directs itself toward "Humanity" itself, which is common to all individual men and flourishes everywhere and always. It does the same with other species. But it appears most "separated" when, occasionally exceeding the condition of its life here, it resolves those species of natural things entirely into the very Reasons and Ideas <note>note: In Platonic thought, "Ideas" or "Reasons" (Rationes) are the eternal, perfect blueprints of all things in the divine mind.</note> that are above nature and completely free from all matter. And just as it previously proceeded by a natural intuition from an image found in the imagination to a species by abstraction, it then proceeds by reasoning from that species to the entirely eternal Reason of the species. This is because it is necessary that a nature which is "one" across "many" individuals must proceed from a single Form that stands above the multitude.

## *An argument for the immortality of the soul: because it understands something for which a specific mental image is sometimes not necessary.*

**C**ertainly, since action proceeds from essence, the condition of acting is always the same as the condition of being, and vice versa. Therefore, because our soul is now joined to the body in such a way that it may one day be separable and remain separated, it begins its process of knowing from the individual forms of things entirely joined to matter, regardless of the local conditions. Nevertheless, it then proceeds to species that are joined in effect, but are separable by their own nature and the power of the intelligence. Thirdly, having by its own power briefly moved past the images of the imagination... 

<meta>Catchword: toward the reason (ad ratio.)</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is immortal because the intellect can perform abstract tasks, like defining "Humanity" or understanding eternal Ideas, without using physical organs. He concludes that if the soul's highest actions are independent of the body, its existence must also be independent and eternal.</summary>

<page-num>715</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II.</header>

toward reasons <note>term: Rationes — these are the rational principles or "blueprints" of things that exist in the mind, independent of physical matter.</note> that are already separated from matter. The mind could never conceive of these reasons existing as entirely absolute within the order of things, unless it could expel the clouds of phantasms <note>term: Phantasmata — mental images or impressions derived from the physical senses that can cloud pure intellectual thought.</note> from its line of sight, at least for a very brief moment. But soon, due to the nature and habit of this earthly region, those clouds gather again and block the clarity of heavenly things. However, from that sudden abstraction <note>The act of drawing the mind away from physical sensations to focus on pure thought.</note>, metaphysicians conclude that the intellect is able to understand at some point without phantasms. From this, it follows that it can live apart from the body and understand with the greatest clarity.

### *The soul in the body, according to the Platonists, proceeds in knowing from particulars to species, and from species to ideas. Outside the body, it proceeds in reverse: from ideas to species, and from species to particulars.*

**B**ut when the soul is separated, it proceeds differently than it does while in the body. For in the body, the soul passes from individual things to species <note>The general category or essence shared by individuals of the same kind.</note>, and from species to reasons. When separated, however, it is the opposite. Naturally beginning from the things familiar to it at that time, it sees the species within the divine reasons by a natural intuition; then, within those species, it looks upon individual things as if by a sudden argument, yet in an instant. From this, a circle is made by the soul from time to eternity, and from eternity back to time. Therefore, just as it was joined to matter in such a way that it was separable and could eventually exist apart, so it then exists apart in such a way that it can be joined again, and at some time be bound. Powers proceed from natures; natures are indicated by powers. For the soul is ruled by infinite power, wisdom, and goodness. Therefore, these natural powers are not in vain. The Platonists can perhaps use this argument to suggest the everlasting circuit of souls. The Hebrews, Christians, and Muslims <note>original: "Hebræi, Christiani, Mahumetenses"</note> seem to be able to use this same argument most truly for the resurrection of human bodies.

### *That which the soul understands obscurely in the body, it understands as clearly as incorporeal things outside the body.*

**C**onsequently, while the soul leads its life in matter and, in a sense, under the rule of time, it sees natural forms in the shadow of the lowest matter. It sees supernatural forms, for the most part, under the "eclipse" of natural ones. But when it leads its life outside of matter and above time, it then perceives supernatural forms in the light of the Highest Form <note>God or the Supreme Good.</note>. It looks upon natural forms beneath the rays of the supernatural. Then, therefore, it sees all things clearly; here, it sees all things obscurely, since it perceives temporal things in no other way than through images drawn in by the senses and, as it were, filtered within them. For there is no other proportion between these physical things and the soul. Yet, as long as it is occupied with the immortal body <note>Ficino likely refers here to the "astral body" or the soul's attachment to physical life.</note>, it turns toward eternal things only with difficulty and very little; and when it does turn, it is very often dazed and deceived by the interference of bodily images. Hence that mystery of our Plato in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the philosopher's preparation for death.</note>: The soul living in another (namely, in the body) and looking through another (namely, through the windows of the senses and phantasms)—looking, I say, at things that are on high, that is, both the species within individuals and the individual forms in matter—discerns nothing clearly anywhere. But when it lives in itself and looks through itself, and looks at those things which are in themselves—that is, the reasons of things <note>term: Rationes rerum — the eternal principles of things as they exist in the Divine Mind.</note> which exist in themselves while they are in the supreme reason of all—then it perceives all things most clearly. This is because they are both most intimate and most clear; they shine all the more brightly in themselves as they are purer, truer, and more powerful than these earthly things.

### *Sense in the imagination is more excellent than external sense; sense in the mind is far more excellent than in the imagination.*

**B**ut does the soul comprehend those things through senses? Certainly, through certain senses—namely, the "sense of senses." For besides those senses which the Platonists believe are exercised in the ethereal vehicle <note>term: Vehiculum — the "astral body" or subtle spirit that serves as the intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note> of the soul, there are also several much clearer senses which the mind can use even without a body. To be sure, the five senses exercised in the nerves and spirits flow from those that flourish in the imagination <note>term: Phantasia — the faculty that processes sensory data into mental images.</note>. But in the imagination, those five senses are a single sense, broader and more piercing than the physical ones; add to this that it is more stable, for it preserves what the physical sense does not. Again, there is a single sense in the mind that is broader, more stable, and more piercing than in the imagination, just as the mind is more excellent than the imagination. If it is broader, it surely reaches beyond the categories of things comprehended by the senses and imagination. If it is more stable, it also preserves things longer than the imagination. If it is more piercing, it sees more certainly, clearly, and splendidly than the senses or the imagination. It sees, I say, sometimes through the senses and through the imagination, both images and individual things, whenever it turns itself toward them.

<meta>catchword: It sees</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul's true intellectual power is found when it separates from the "clouds" of sensory images, allowing it to move from universal divine ideas down to specific particulars. He argues that the mind possesses a "higher sense" far superior to physical sight or the imagination, which allows it to perceive eternal truths clearly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s independent life. Having established that the soul can understand without physical images, Ficino now describes how the soul experiences spiritual senses and turns to the nature of Platonic friendship and the internal structure of the human soul.</meta>

<page-num>716</page-num>
<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

The soul perceives by itself, awakened by that form <note>Referring to the "Idea" or divine blueprint mentioned on the previous page.</note>, and more clearly because it is closer to the source. It looks into itself at itself when it reflects upon itself; it can reflect upon itself if it loves, seeks, and understands itself. In this state, it appears utterly indivisible and subsisting within itself. For a form that is either divisible or necessarily dependent on something else can never reflect upon itself. Finally, the soul discerns reasons <note>term: rationes — the underlying rational principles or "blueprints" of things.</note> most clearly when, from within itself, it looks toward the highest Reason of all. In that Reason, the vision of the mind sees the principle and power of light and colors—a light and color so much more radiant in its Idea than it is in the physical bodies formed from it. In that same Reason, the hearing of the mind hears a sound more resonant and harmonious than all the sounds that either the ear can hear or the imagination can conceive. The same logic applies to the other senses of the intellect. Whoever wishes to enjoy these most sweetly must take care to use the bodily senses indeed, but not to place their ultimate enjoyment in them.

## As love is, so is friendship.

->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Alamanno Donato, sends greetings.<-

**S**ince friendship—as no one doubts—takes its power and its name from love (for friendship is nothing other than mutual love confirmed by a certain stable, that is, honorable habit), it is fitting that whatever the nature of the love is from which friendship is derived and named, such also will the friendship always be. What kind, then, shall we say ours will be, Alamanno? Certainly, since it began from nowhere else than Platonic love, we shall never call it anything other than Platonic. Indeed, while recently explaining our commentaries on Plato’s *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuium" — Plato's famous dialogue on the nature of love.</note> concerning love, we began to love each other in such a way that we seem to have already fashioned and perfected within ourselves that very "Idea" of true love which Plato describes there. From this very Platonic love, a certain Platonic friendship is born, which is conceived, nourished, and increased in the nurturing lap of the Muse Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy and Heavenly Love.</note>. Since it takes its origin from the Muses, it never smells or tastes of anything except what is musical, harmonious, and elegant. More trust is to be placed in this one goodwill (as it says in Plato) than in any necessity or blood kinship. Why then do you hesitate further, Alamanno? Do you wonder whether our Plato meant for there to be more than one soul in one body? So far is it from many souls being in one body, that often the opposite seems to happen: we see one single soul existing in the many bodies of friends through the constancy of Platonic love. But enough on these matters for now. I come now to the things you asked about.

## According to Plato, there is one soul in a human, but three powers in the soul.

**Y**ou ask whether one should trust those Peripatetics <note>term: Peripatetics — followers of Aristotle, who often criticized Platonic theories.</note> who do not hesitate to slander Plato by claiming he placed several souls in man—namely the rational, the spirited <note>original: "irascibilem" — the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and "fire."</note>, and the desiring <note>original: "concupiscibilem" — the part of the soul associated with physical appetites.</note>. I answer that there is indeed only one soul, through whose many powers we perform all these functions. Just as the single body of fire acts sufficiently in three ways through its three qualities: by light it shines and illuminates; by lightness it ascends swiftly; by heat it warms and burns. And in every tiny particle of fire, these three qualities flourish equally; they exist in the same place at once, yet are distinct from one another by their specific properties. In the same way, the substance of the soul, being one and the same, seems able to sufficiently carry out three duties through its three powers. Specifically, by reason—like a kind of light—it discerns the true and the good from the false. Furthermore, by appetite—like lightness—it moves itself most easily toward those things which please it. Again, by spiritedness and the heat of anger—like a certain warmth—it is carried away to either consume or repel those things which seem sometimes able to hinder it from attaining what it seeks. What prevents one soul from being equipped with three powers? Although they differ from one another in their specific properties, they are nevertheless everywhere together in the same soul, wherever the soul exists as a whole. But it is worthwhile to hear Plato himself arguing about this matter in the fourth book of the *Republic*. He holds it as certain that the substance of the soul is one, but the powers in the soul are many. For he says: "One and the same thing can never act or suffer contrary things at the same time in the same respect and toward the same object." If something seems to move and stand still at the same time, it is moving through one part of itself and standing still through another—just as if someone were to move one hand while the other remains still. Or certainly, it will be moved by one principle, but by another not at all...

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul possesses spiritual senses superior to physical ones and defines Platonic friendship as a single soul inhabiting multiple bodies. He also defends the unity of the soul against Aristotelian critics, using the analogy of fire to explain how one soul possesses three distinct powers: reason, appetite, and spirit.</summary>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK II</header>
<meta>Catchword: regina</meta>

Just as a sphere does not change into a straight line, but meanwhile rotates in a circle while remaining fixed around its center. Therefore, it stays at the center, while the circumference revolves. But let us now come to the nature of the soul. The soul of a thirsty person, insofar as it thirsts for nothing else, desires only to drink, and is driven solely toward that because it is parched. If, therefore, something meanwhile draws the thirsty soul back, there will certainly be something else in the soul itself besides that power we called thirst, which pulls it away from drink as if it were a <note>original: "bestiam"</note> beast. For a thing, as we said above, being one and the same, never performs opposites at the same time through the same part of itself regarding the same object. For in what way could the single hand of a single archer stretch a single bow and release it at the very same moment? 

However, we see that some thirsty people sometimes do not wish to drink; therefore, the souls of these people have something within them that impels them to drink, and again something else that forbids and hinders the drink. The former we are accustomed to call <term>concupiscentia</term> <note>desire or appetite</note>, and the latter <term>ratio</term> <note>reason</note>. For this reason, desire and reason appear to be distinct from one another. Also distinct from one another are the powers of desiring and of <term>irascendi</term> <note>spiritedness or anger; the part of the soul that feels indignation</note>. For reason often commands things from which appetite shrinks—as is apparent in taking medicines, or undergoing labors and dangers—but the vigor of spirit is sometimes aroused (since it then takes up arms on behalf of reason). It finally brings it about that, being indignant at slothful desire for what reason had commanded, we act and endure even against the will of desire. 

Furthermore, when reason commands us to fight for our country, but appetite in the midst of battle—provoked by sleep, hunger, or thirst—calls us back from the fight to softness and feasting, spirit, while it is carried against the enemy, drags us to battle against the will of desire. Moreover, who that is possessed of reason could doubt that the power of spirit is one thing and reason another? Surely, while there is anger in beasts, there is no reason. Again, in children, anger seethes almost immediately from birth, but we employ reason only later in life. Furthermore, anger often drives us to take revenge, but reason forbids it. Since both anger and lust differ from reason, lust nevertheless seems to depart further from the dignity of reason than anger does, both because it twists us toward viler things and because anger, being indignant against the vile impulse of lust, often helps reason. Lust, however, never seems to favor reason against anger. Thus says <note>Ficino is summarizing Plato’s "Republic," Book IV.</note> Plato. From these things it is clear that Plato did not posit three souls, but three powers in the one soul of man.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine: What Light is in the Body of the World, in an Angel, and in God. To Phoebus the Venetian, most illustrious Orator.

**G**reetings always in the light of life, our Phoebus. <note>“Phoebus” was a nickname for the sun-god Apollo; Ficino uses it here for his friend Phoebus Venetus (Domenico Zane) to play on the theme of light.</note> Greetings, celestial Phoebus, most famous not by external light, but by an inner one. When in days past the mind of your Marsilio, pregnant with the rays of the Platonic Sun as if with certain seeds, was striving to give birth to a "Sun" from them as best it could, it—unhappy through I know not what sterile weakness of nature—gave birth to a "Moon" in place of a Sun, a moon in need of borrowed light. Therefore, I shall dedicate this child of the Platonic Sun, obscured by my own darkness, to the Platonic Phoebus as soon as possible, so that it may at least be illuminated by his rays. Receive freely, most famous Phoebus, what is yours. And because they are rightfully yours, I pray that you return them clearer by your own immense splendor.

### Each sense reaches only the object suitable to itself.

**O** God, greatest of all, I dislike the darkness through whose fault everything that displeases me does so—either because they exist with that darkness, or because, slipping away from it, they fall back and are weighed down toward it. I love light above all things, for the sake of which I love all else—either because they exist with it, or because, flowing toward it, they flow back and are led back to it. Therefore, tell me, my senses, you who report almost innumerable other things to me: tell me, I pray, what is light? 

Hearing answers: "I am of the air; let it be enough if I report airy sounds to you." Smell also answers: "Indeed, I am not so bright; I am of vapor, so learn of vapors from me. Why do you seek foreign things from me?" Taste says: "I was born indeed in liquid; I indicate liquids to you." "Do not," says Touch, "extort from me what I cannot do; I am corporeal, I report corporeal things. Seek light higher up."

### A description of visible light.

**H**aving been thus warned, I shall now ascend from the lowest point where I had fallen to the highest parts of my body, so that from there I may receive a light swifter and higher than all the rest. Come now, oh my eyes, shining through that light, I pray you, by which you are delighted above all others—nay, by which alone you are delighted—now judge...

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s faculties, transitioning from the psychological struggle between reason and desire to a metaphysical investigation into the nature of Light. He uses a dialogue between Reason, Sight, and Mind to define light not just as a physical phenomenon, but as a spiritual bridge to the Divine.</meta>

<page-num>718</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...to your queen, Reason, what light is. A splendid sight suddenly responds: I am a spirit and a spiritual splendor; therefore, since you rightfully demand my own duties from me, I grant as much as I have most willingly. Light <note>original: "lumen"</note> is a certain spiritual, sudden, and most wide-reaching emanation from bodies, coming from their nature without any loss to themselves. It is a brightness, as it were, from <term>diaphanous</term> <note>transparent or translucent</note> things, but it is color from their opposites <note>opaque objects</note>; it is the source of quantity, shape, and motion from all things. Gather all kinds of colors into one category: what will this whole be but a certain multi-colored light—or rather, a light made opaque in the more solid and darker matter of the earth? Separate the earth that is mixed with it, and what will remain but a certain quality—or better, the clarity and the very act of the transparent, just as heat is the act of the opaque? Indeed, heat is an opaque light, but light is a clear color—or rather, it is a certain flower and vigor of the transparent body and of colors, being as it were of a single color in its act, but of every color in its power.

->Nothing is clearer than light and God, and nothing is more obscure.<-

This is a sketch, O my eyes, rather than a painting. I have never heard anything defined more obscurely. O, most marvelous thing! In what way can it be that nothing is more obscure than light? For nothing is clearer, since through it all things are made clear and revealed. Therefore, I shall ascend from here to the sublime mirror of the Mind, so that I might at least see this one thing from there—beyond which I can see nothing else anywhere. O Mind, you who rightly measure all things, tell me: could it be that light is God himself, than whom nothing is clearer, and nothing more obscure? Nothing is clearer than that God exists, and that he is supremely powerful, wise, and good; for everything created by him proclaims this to our ears, so that no one is more deaf than he who does not hear such a great sound and roar of all things. On the contrary, nothing is more obscure than *what* God is, so that no one is more in the dark than he who imagines this to be perfectly clear to himself.

->Intelligible light is the cause of things understood; visible light is the cause of things seen.<-

The Mind responds that God is the "Father of lights," with whom there is no change by which he might be extinguished or diminished, nor any "shadow of turning" <note>A reference to James 1:17</note> by which he might undergo night or suffer an eclipse. It responds again that God is the light in which there is no darkness at all. He is the Form in which nothing is unformed, and Beauty in which nothing is deformed. Surely God—as the Mind, which is his ray, demonstrates—is invisible light, infinite truth, and the cause of every truth and of all things. This visible light is his splendor—or rather, his shadow—and it is the infinite cause of visible things. Truly, because it is the nature of light and truth to declare other things truly to the rest, all things are truly and clearly visible to God through himself. It is just as if the visible light, being the fountain of colors and visible things, were to look upon itself as if it were all colors, and thus see in itself all colors and all sensible things.

->Visible, rational, intelligible, and divine light.<-

But the Mind warns that one must not leap forth so suddenly to such a sublime speculation, but must ascend step by step, lest we be forced into dimness and blinded by too much splendor. Do not, Reason, trust in the senses. Sight does not report enough to you, and the other senses not at all. Sight, because it is a sensual light, receives and gives only a sensible splendor. And conversely, because it receives and gives sensible splendor, you recognize this to be a certain sensual light. Beyond this, however, one may not go during the day. But learn this from me: first, that I (the Intelligence) am a certain intellectual light, since my object is that <term>intelligible</term> <note>perceptible to the intellect rather than the senses</note> light which I both seek in anything to be sought and find in anything found. For the light of each thing and its truth are the same. Truth is the innermost light, the light of truth pouring itself out to the outermost parts. Learn then that you (Reason) are a certain rational light and a shining reason, since you seek the "reason" <note>or principle</note> of light as your origin with such great greed through your reasoning. But do you wish to attain the principle of light more conveniently? Seek it in the leader of every reason. There is the principle of light where the principle of all things resides: in the highest truth, which is itself the highest certainty and clarity, you will find the truth and clarity of light. Indeed, the clarity and truth of this light which you seek are the same. What is light in God? The immense exuberance of his goodness and truth. What is it in the angels?

the certainty of intelligence flowing from God and the overflowing joy of the will. What is it in the heavenly realms? An abundance of life from the Angels, an unfolding of power from the heavens. The laughter of the heavens. What is it in fire? A certain vital vigor from the heavenly bodies, a cheering of the spirit itself in sentient beings, and a vigor of the senses. In all things, it is the luminous outpouring of an innermost fertility. Everywhere, it is the image of divine truth and goodness.

<margin>At the joy of the deities, their celestial eyes laugh; they rejoice in splendor and motion.</margin>
**P**ost-reflecting on this, we see that from the celestial rays—which descend to us from the super-celestial realms through the heavens as if through certain panes of glass—perfection, life, sensation, certainty, grace, and joy are given to all. It is necessary that light in the spirits above the heavens be the perfection of their form, the fertility of their life, the sharpness of their senses, the clearest and truest certainty of their intelligence, the abundance of grace, and the fullness of joy. The splendor of the heavens is the image of all these things; indeed, it is like a shadow compared to their clarity, because the body of the heavens can no more exactly imitate the clarity of the spirit than the earth can imitate the brightness of the heavens. At the wonderful joy of the celestial spirits, the heaven—acting as if it were their body, or rather their eye (for Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek poet and prophet; Ficino often cited "Orphic" hymns as ancient wisdom</note> calls the Sun an eye)—laughs with splendor and exults in its motion. In contrast, the earth, being furthest removed from them, mourns in darkness and grows numb in its place and through idleness. Nor should one think that the heaven is moved by any force or defect. Its motion is perpetual by nature and it never leaves its natural place. Its substance is also most absolute, from which nothing of itself departs; rather, it moves from a certain excess of joy, because of which, in its rejoicing, it knows not how to remain still. At the song of the joyful <term>numina</term> <note>Divine powers or deities</note>, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in the "Harmony of the Spheres"</note> believe, they call the dances of the spheres. From this, through most ordered and varied movements, they produce a wonderful harmony. At the laughter of the stars—which is indicated chiefly by their rays—all things that are under the heavens and upon the earth laugh. At the darkness, as if at sadness, all things mourn. For we are accustomed to congratulate those who laugh and to feel sorrow with those who weep.

<margin>The laughter of heaven proceeding from the joy of the deities—that is, light—fosters and delights all things.</margin>
**Q**uite clearly, if light is the laughter of the heavens proceeding from the joy of the celestial spirits, humans indicate this as well: whenever they rejoice in spirit and laugh with their face, they certainly shine within and are expanded in spirit; they also seem to shine in their face, especially in the eyes, which are the most "celestial" parts of us and which, in laughter, produce a circular motion like that of the heavens. In those who mourn, on the other hand, everything is darkened, extinguished, and numbed. But the rays directed from the laughing stars—like the eyes of divine minds—most kindly and joyfully foster and generate the seeds of things, not otherwise than the gaze of an ostrich upon its egg <note>A common Renaissance belief held that the heat of an ostrich's gaze was sufficient to hatch its eggs</note>. For by their power, natural heat is inserted into all things. From this, life arises, is nourished, and increases. This is why all things seek by their will, because they are generated not only by earthly pleasure, but also by celestial joy. Who then would deny that the deities move and beget all things with a certain joyful affection? Since we see that by the nature of animals and by art, all things are procreated and perfected through pleasure.

<margin>Light is one thing. Heat is another. And light precedes heat.</margin>
**Q**uite clearly, brightness is one thing and heat is another. For things shine or glisten which are not hot, including many cold things. Many things are also hot which are dark; the heat of fire often penetrates where splendor does not pass, and splendor is propagated much further and faster than heat. Anyone who considers it will find that heat comes from light, just as in spirits the clarity of intelligence precedes the affection of the will in its origin, and in the machine of the world, the rays of the Sun are the origin of the heat that follows.

<margin>Light is as if a certain spiritual thing. And spirits are certain lights.</margin>
**Q**uite clearly, light is a certain spiritual thing rather than a physical one, because it is propagated everywhere without time <note>instantly</note>. It fills transparent bodies without injury. It surrounds itself with filth without being defiled. Furthermore, it bestows itself more easily upon those bodies that are further removed from heavy, physical mass. Hence the purest bodies of heaven and fire, as the Platonists believe, shine in themselves. Air and water shine from them. The interior parts of the earth neither shine of themselves, nor from the others. On the surface of the earth, light—infused into different mixtures of the four elements, especially the earthly ones—takes on the forms of different colors, as if they were little bodies, of which light-rays are like certain little souls...

<summary>Ficino explains light as the "laughter of heaven," a spiritual emanation of divine joy that organizes the cosmos, distinguishes it from physical heat, and identifies it as a bridge between the material and spiritual worlds.</summary>

Having previously discussed light as an expression of divine joy, he now examines how light descends through the cosmic hierarchy—from God to the human eye—and how the physical body obscures the soul's natural radiance.</meta>

the sparks of light infused into them. If you were to separate and preserve those sparks from those material mixtures, you would perhaps see the true nature of rational souls when they are separated from their bodies. For souls are certain lights that were once more clouded within bodies, but once restored to their own nature, they become most brilliant. In this way, the body—which is entirely different from the soul—casts a kind of eclipse over it, just as the Moon does when joined with the Sun; or rather, just as a terrestrial mixture, being most foreign to the heavens, renders celestial light opaque and creates color out of light, so the body surrounding the soul turns intelligence into sense.

->Light in God, in the angel, in reason, in the spirit, and in the body.<-

**B**ut to return to where we turned aside: although the heaven shines and exults within itself, it does not do so from itself, but from the clarity and joy of the higher realms. It is like an eye that shines from the clarity of the spirit <note>In Ficinian psychology, "spirit" is a subtle, warm vapor that acts as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note> and the gladness of the soul. The spirit, moreover, rejoices most in its own clarity and that of the Sun; the soul rejoices in the clarity of the spirit and the mind. It appears that this light is the mind itself shining through the body—as if through a transparent vessel—and thus becoming visible. However, the mind as light within itself is entirely invisible due to its excessive abundance and refinement. Furthermore, light in the mind is truth and a joy that rejoices in the truth. Thirdly, the light from the mind present in bodies is a certain declaration of the truth of sensible things; it is the flower of beauty and the delight of the senses. But let us review this more precisely: in the divine mind, light transcends intelligence. From there, that same light, infused into the angelic mind, is rendered according to intelligence, but remains above the limits of reason. This divine and angelic light, when it enters the minds of men, now proceeds according to reason. Yet it surpasses the phantasy <note>original: "phantasia" – the mental faculty that processes sensory images</note>; in the spirit, it operates according to phantasy, above the level of the senses. In the body, however, it becomes familiar to the senses—chiefly through the eyes, which are like the soul's celestial stars—but it does not belong to matter itself. In all minds, light is an overflowing life; it is a clear and certain truth and a full joy. From there, in bodies, it is the unfolding and outpouring of divine life, the declaration of the truth of things, the grace of form from the Author, and an incitement to pleasure. Empedocles and Zeno <note>Ancient Greek philosophers</note> held that just as a flame relates to a coal, so light relates to a flame; they believed a flame is like dense light, while light is a most refined flame and the life of all things. Plotinus and Proclus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who deeply influenced Ficino</note> judge that light is a certain vision and gaze of the deities, sent forth from afar through the rays of the celestial eyes; they believe it is a certain divine spirit that both sees all things and, as much as it is within itself, is seen by all. They add that a spirit of this kind is never extinguished but follows the stars.

->Light is the shadow of God; God is the light of light.<-

**F**inally, light is like a certain deity in this worldly temple, reflecting the likeness of God. So much so that our Plato, in his books on the *Republic*, called it the son of the Good itself. For like God, it is to be venerated above all things in sight; it is a certain sudden and most wide expansion that, without detriment to itself, most willingly and happily bestows itself upon all due to its exuberant goodness and generosity. It is the cause, preservation, and awakening of all things that are born. Accordingly, it lifts other things toward the life, truth, and joy from which it descended. Without its presence, all things seem to die; yet by its presence, they seem to revive. It is the best divine thing remembered by the human race, so that neither the impious dare to deny that God exists—since nothing is clearer to the senses than His image—nor may the wicked trust that they can hide from His eye or escape His hand. His image is clarity itself, and more swiftly than can be said, it expands through all things in a moment. God is One in all and above all; light is One in all and around all. Light in things made by God is a certain splendor of divine clarity. And (if I may speak thus) it is God as if limiting Himself and accommodating Himself to the capacity of His works. But God Himself is an immense light consisting in Himself, existing through Himself in all things, and beyond all things throughout the immense. He is that fountain of life in whose light, as David says, we see light. <note>A reference to Psalm 36:9</note> He is also the eye by which all eyes see, as Orpheus says—the eye that inspects all things within individuals. <note>Ficino refers to the "Orphic Hymns," which he believed contained ancient theological truths</note> And in truth, He beholds all things in Himself while He perceives that He Himself is all things. Farewell, and be happy together with your divine senate, most illustrious Phoebus. <note>Likely a reference to a specific person addressed by a classical nickname</note> Greet, in the name of Marsilio and all men of letters, Bernardo Bembo <note>A Venetian diplomat and scholar, father of the famous Pietro Bembo</note> the Venetian—or rather, the Florentine and the delight of our people.

He concludes by defining light as the "shadow of God" and an ever-present reminder of the divine that sustains life and prevents the wicked from hiding.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine prophesies to Matthias, the most fortunate King of Pannonia <note>Pannonia: A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans; here referring to the Kingdom of Hungary</note>, security in peace, victory in war, and eternal glory in victory.

## PREFACE TO BOOK III.

### An exhortation to war against the Barbarians <note>original: "contra Barbaros." In this context, Ficino refers to the Ottoman Turks, who had captured Constantinople in 1453 and were threatening Central Europe.</note>.

**O**ur Plato, the father of philosophers, most fortunate King, used to advise his beloved disciples Xenocrates and Dio—holy men indeed, but a little more severe and somber than philosophers should seem—to perform sacred rites to the Graces <note>The Charites (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia), who represented charm, beauty, and creativity</note> most diligently, so that they might be rendered more gracious and pleasant. What our Plato once had to do for his two disciples, I see that I must now do for these twin books of my Letters, as if for my own children. I seem, pregnant as it were with a certain cold seed, to have given birth to these children somewhat more severe than letters should be. For who in these iron ages and regions could ever produce works of gold or silver? Therefore, in the Platonic manner, I now command them not only to sacrifice to the Graces, but even to vow themselves to them with their whole minds, so that they may emerge more gracious and more urbane. 

Behold now, therefore, do you not see? Suddenly, by some divine power—or rather, I know for certain, by some happy spirit—they have been snatched up and are journeying toward your lofty palace as if to the Graces' own temple. They hope (I believe) to be surrounded by the most pleasing splendor of the three Graces in your presence alone—that is, the splendor of a just Jupiter, a nourishing Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and wisdom</note>, and a lovely Venus—whereby, having immediately changed that somber expression, they may henceforth appear much brighter and more joyful to those looking upon them. I pray, most fortunate King, that as these Marsilian sons suppliantly enter that sacred temple, you will look upon them with the joyful and vigorous rays of your eyes, as you are accustomed to do with all things. Thus, they will owe it to me merely for their existence, but to your Royal Majesty for the fact that they are beautiful. 

And I shall seem to have satisfied my guide Plato, who commanded that only that prince should be venerated in whom excellent wisdom is joined with supreme power. Nor shall I have satisfied Plato alone by this veneration of the unconquered King Matthias, but also the rest of the Greek philosophers—indeed, even the poets, orators, historians, and all writers without a doubt. For while all these once sought nothing other than true glory and light with the greatest zeal, now, after many centuries of light, they are falling into darkness under the savage Turks—alas, what grief!—stars, I say, falling into darkness under ferocious beasts. 

Alas, the celestial lights of the liberal doctrines and arts have lain for a long time in limbo <note>A state of neglect or "the edge of hell"; Ficino uses the theological term to describe the suppressed state of Greek learning under Ottoman rule</note>; or rather, in a place far darker than limbo. And just as those ancient Saints once lying in limbo called upon the Messiah, so these wise men cry out to Matthias as their Messiah; the wretched call "Matthias!" with a perpetual shout, so that he might restore them from limbo, or rather from the underworld, into light and life. Not only the men of letters I have mentioned, but also very many nations in Asia and Europe, miserably serving under the monstrous Turks like the Jews under the impious Pharaoh, continually cry out for Matthias as a second Moses, for whom God might divide the Red Sea and wonderfully open any path that is impassable, to deliver the chosen sons of God from extreme slavery and misery. 

Again, beautiful Italy and holy Religion herself, the mother of all good things, call out to Matthias with constant shouts, hoping to escape the monstrous hands of the Barbarians only through his hands. Therefore, these two children of mine, having entered the nourishing temple of the Graces in your presence, now pour out suppliant prayers to you for the common safety of all in such words: "Rise up, Matthias! Act again under the most fortunate auspices!" Just as...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

In this way you have often risen happily elsewhere. Rise, we pray, O victorious Hercules <note>Ficino frequently addresses King Matthias Corvinus as "Hercules," casting him as a legendary defender of Christendom against the Ottoman "monsters."</note>, while time remains, against these dire and monstrous beasts. They so wickedly depopulate the fields, destroy towns, and devour men; they not only impiously trample under their filthy feet the disciplines of all laws and liberal arts, and—what is most wretched—holy religion itself, but they also, as much as they are able, erase them from all human memory. You, Hercules, have wonderfully conquered and tamed such monsters through virtue alone many times before. But now a new victory—we know beyond doubt what we say, indeed, what we prophesy for you—a new victory is sent down to you from high heaven. For you, who will fight bravely on behalf of the whole race of men and virtues, and on behalf of God himself, the whole world will favor, the entire heavens will do battle, and the winds will come in conspiracy to your trumpet calls. To you alone Almighty God has given empire without end. That highest God, who established the Sun in the heavens <note>original: "in Deo." Likely a typo in the original for "in caelo" (in the sky) or referring to the Sun's divine placement.</note> as the King of the stars and the sky, also established Matthias alone under the Sun, to bound his empire by the Ocean and his fame by the stars. <note>This is a paraphrase of Virgil’s *Aeneid* (1.287), "imperium Oceano, famam qui terminet astris," originally written to praise Augustus Caesar.</note>

-> October 1st, 1480. <-
