### *That human prosperity is deceptive.*
### *Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a prominent Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous humanist Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend of Ficino.</note>, Venetian Orator and most distinguished Knight, sends greetings.*

**I** have just taken up my pen, most distinguished Bembo, on the condition—or perhaps by chance—that I should write to you whatever first came to mind. But perhaps this occurred to me first: to speak of and wish for true health <note>original: "salutem." In Latin, this word means both "health" and the standard "greeting" at the start of a letter.</note> to a friend and a man who is the truest of all. I would consider the beginning of true health to be this: never to hope for true health from that which is a liar and false. Otherwise, my dearest Bernardo, if we have caught one of our servants in a manifest lie ten times, and yet we easily believe him again and again, shall we not be judged worthy—on account of our own imprudence—to be deceived by him at great risk and loss as often as we place further trust in his words?

Two things especially have been perpetual liars from the very beginning of things. First, the evil Demon <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic Christian worldview, this refers to the fallen spirit or tempter who lures the soul away from truth.</note>, that first rebel against the truth. Second, human prosperity, which is a false happiness and an impediment to true happiness. We cannot easily refute the lies of the Demon. But earthly prosperity is proven to have lied most openly to the human race as many times as moments have flowed in the entire course of time from the beginning of the world until our own day. Indeed, such moments are considered by the Philosophers to be innumerable. Add to this that at any point of time, with a feigned smile, with pestilential allurements, with poisonous charms, and with false promises, prosperity deceives countless men everywhere. Thus, it can rightly be said that the lies of such prosperity appear infinitely more numerous than the infinite points of time. 

Because it is of such a nature, it should no longer be called a "liar," but rather "lie" itself, and an most obvious one at that. Let us then believe rashly, let us still believe easily (as we are accustomed to do) in falsehood, so to speak—so that we may be truly miserable, we who so imprudently still have faith in a most false happiness. A happiness, I say, that has made men miserable infinitely more often than it has infinitely deceived them. Who is so blind that he should not finally see clearly that this unhappy "happiness" of mortals is actually at its weakest when it shows itself to us as if it were most firm? 

For it is not called "happiness" by us until it has reached the very peak of its course. But in that very moment in which it seems at its peak—and because it appears at the peak, it is judged to be happiness—it suddenly slides back into the opposite without delay. Thus, what is named "happiness" by us is instead a certain beginning of unhappiness. And in truth, what appeared at first glance to be honey because of a similarity in color turns out to be gall to our inner taste. 

Someone will perhaps ask for what reason this has been so arranged by nature, or perhaps granted by fate. Four causes for this are primarily numbered among the Philosophers: divine, celestial, natural, and human. First, divine providence decreed that earthly prosperity should be volatile and fleeting so that it could not hold us for long far away from divine blessedness, since it cannot be held by us for even a single moment. And also so that we might be compelled by frequent troubles to remember the Heavenly Physician more often. Furthermore, we are to remember that we have not been established in this restless region as if in our homeland, but have been relegated to it as if in a kind of exile.

# BOOK III OF THE LETTERS

The fatal law of the stars is so moderated by divine providence that, in the perpetual course of the heavens—which is devoid of all rest—as soon as the planets reach the highest point of either their altitude or their direction, they <term>retrocede</term><note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky, which in astrology often signals a shift in influence.</note>. Furthermore, they glide most swiftly from the <term>sextile</term> or <term>trine</term> aspects<note>Astrological angles of 60° and 120°, traditionally considered harmonious or "salutary."</note>, which are judged to be healthy, into the <term>square</term> or <term>opposite</term> aspects<note>Angles of 90° and 180°, traditionally considered difficult or "noxious."</note>, which are held to be harmful. Following this, the four elements are arranged beneath the heavenly bodies in a certain natural order, so that when either heat or cold, dryness or humidity, is stretched to the highest degree proper to its nature, finite nature then neither permits it to proceed further, nor allows it to remain there even for a moment, due to the condition of perpetual motion. Therefore, when qualities of this kind seem most intensely strained, they are suddenly relaxed. 

The humors and <term>complexions</term><note>The specific balance of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined an individual's temperament.</note> of our four bodies follow this same rapid change. Hence, as it is found in Hippocrates <note>original: "apud Hippocratem." Refers to Aphorisms 1.3: "In athletes, a perfect state of health is precarious."</note>, the highest health of the body is judged to be the most deceptive. Indeed, in the realm of nature, a descent almost immediately follows the ascent itself. And those things which flourished quickly also wither quickly. Finally, a more abundant breeze of vain prosperity puffs up the vain souls of mortals, rendering them swollen and sick. From this point, like sick and delirious men, they become forgetful of themselves; thinking their lot is higher than the human condition, they believe everything is permitted to them and that no danger threatens. 

This is roughly what is said to have happened to King Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note>. Therefore, they become unrestrained within themselves through a looser license, quite negligent regarding their own affairs, and arrogant, injurious, and insulting toward other men. Others, in turn, stirred by hatred and envy against them, both engineer plots and prepare for battles. For this reason, our prosperity is very easily disturbed for many causes that anyone can easily understand. And just as a stone thrown into the air, when it seems to have ascended highest, then suddenly descends without any interval of time, so Fortune, having carried someone to the highest peaks of affairs, immediately and without delay either orders him to descend of his own accord as if from a mountain, or she herself casts him down headlong. 

Certainly, a heavier fall threatens the greater men, and a deeper ruin threatens those who are higher. Most often, after the flattering breezes and sweet west winds, a screeching gale from the North suddenly strikes the sail and lifts the waves to the stars. On account of this, King Philip of Macedon <note>The father of Alexander the Great.</note>, on the day he reported victory both in the Olympic games and on the battlefield at the same time he received his firstborn Alexander, feared the contrary wind in such a favorable breeze of abundant prosperity. He said, "O <term>spirit</term><note>original: "dæmon." In the classical sense, a presiding spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, repay such a great good with the smallest possible evil." And a little while later, he was blinded in one eye by a certain arrow. 

We too, if we are wise, if we wish to be well, should fear in a similar way. Or rather, to speak more correctly, so that we may never be compelled to fear in such a way, let us not believe in lies, let us not hope in what is invented, nor let us chase after fleeting or flying things, nor love things that are hostile and harmful to us. But let us eventually believe in the truth, we who have believed in lies so easily and for so long. Let us believe, I say, in the divine truth, which never lies, which does not deceive, and which daily warns us in many ways never to trust in unfaithful Fortune, nor to follow her, who is blind, as the leader of our life. 

Rather, with all our strengths granted and preserved for us by the Infinite Good, let us pursue that same Infinite Good. Indeed, it not only never flees—since it fills the universe with immense power—but it even runs to meet those who follow it with the immense kindness of its nature. And what is greater: it even runs ahead of those who are about to follow, while it both makes all things and, by a certain natural instinct, always entices all things to follow. And when it commands us to follow it by virtue—since Wisdom commands nothing in vain—it also leads those who go, and brings those who persevere to the end. He is the beginning, the ruler, the guide, the path, and the goal.

->Prose should be adorned with poetic measures and rhythms.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Bartholomaeus Fontius the Rhetorician, sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou ask most elegantly, Fontius, by whose command especially I am compelled, or upon whose authority I rely, when I occasionally interweave poetic measures and rhythms into prose. To respond briefly to such a sharp man: heaven commands this of me, and the heavenly Plato teaches the same. For if you look up at the sky, you see there Mercury, the master of the virtue of eloquence and simultaneously the craftsman of the lyre. If we were ever permitted to hear him speaking to us, we would frequently hear him mixing some melodies of his lyre into his words. Especially since he is always a companion both to Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note>, the father of more serious music—that is, of poetry—and to

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<meta>Catchword: Slanderers</meta>

...to Venus, the mother of light music, let it either be joined completely, or at least cling as closely as possible. Whether you listen to the celestial Plato, you immediately recognize his style which—as Aristotle says—flows midway between prose and song. You recognize that Platonic speech, as Quintilian says, rises far above prose and pedestrian speech, so that our Plato seems inspired not by human genius, but by some Delphic oracle. Indeed, such a mixture or tempering in Plato so pleased Cicero that he said: "If Jupiter wished to speak in a human tongue, he would speak in no other language than the Platonic." I pass over the fact that Moses, Job, Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, and nearly all the other Prophets among the Hebrews; Hermes <term>Trismegistus</term><note>The "thrice-great" Egyptian sage, whom Ficino believed was a contemporary of Moses and a precursor to Plato.</note> as the wisest of the Egyptians; likewise in Greece, Gorgias, Isocrates, Herodotus, Aristotle, and many others; and finally among the Latins, sometimes Cicero, frequently Livy, Apuleius, the divine Jerome, and Boethius the supreme philosopher, all adorned their prose with certain poetic rhythms. They did so with this purpose: that the speech, because it is "loose" <note>original: "soluta", referring to prose (oratio soluta) as opposed to "bound" verse.</note>, might reach its goal more easily and quickly by proceeding with a freer foot; yet, because it is rhythmic and poetic, it might delight, charm, and seize the listener with musical harmonies and figures. For by a certain natural instinct, individual things—since they are born of music—are wonderfully seized by music as well. I would rather follow these men with unequal steps than not follow them at all. 

Therefore, my friend, you will forgive a "Platonic" or even an "unfit" writer, and you will grant him this mixed style of speaking, which nature herself first implanted in him at birth, which a continuous reading of the poetic Plato then increased, and which the frequent use of the <term>lyre</term><note>original: "cithara". Ficino was famous for performing "Orphic hymns" on a lyre to accompany his philosophical meditations.</note> further confirmed. Nevertheless, I do not break out into poetic sounds by chance, but especially where there is some poetic subject matter or form. For such a tone and such strings seem appropriate. Indeed, all antiquity teaches us to mix the poetic with the philosophical; before Aristotle, they did this most of all for this primary reason: so that the sacred mysteries of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom.</note> might be both venerable and beautiful to all, yet shared only with the few, and indeed the pure. Divinity itself teaches us the same, for everywhere it delights in certain poetic figures: it has adorned the heavens with lights as a meadow is with flowers, and it has so modulated the diverse circuits of the spheres that they create a wonderful harmony and melody through congruent accords. Furthermore, beneath the Moon, that same God—similarly delighted by poetry—has arranged the discordant forms of things into a most beautiful harmony. Finally, the earth, which seemed the most shapeless of all things, he decorated in various ways with the wondrous shapes and colors of metals, gems, plants, and animals, and he willed the fruits of the earth to be covered with leaves and adorned with flowers. What more? He has tempered both the individual parts and the whole universe with musical numbers and poetic measures.

->Only he loses no dear one to whom all are dear in Him who is never lost.<-
<note>A quote from St. Augustine's "Confessions," IV.9, referring to finding stability by loving others in God.</note>

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, Greetings.

**I** cannot say with how much weariness I am affected, my sweetest Giovanni, because on account of this suspicion of the <term>plague</term><note>original: "Epidemicæ suspitionem". Outbreaks of the plague were frequent in 15th-century Florence, often causing the elite to flee to country villas.</note> I am forced by my father's command to be without you for these few days; and yet, in the meantime, I am with you more constantly than can be imagined. And by God, unless I were with you in this way, being without you would surely not be so painful. You alone are my care, Giovanni; you alone are my solace. I pray you, comfort your Marsilio with your most longed-for letters. Whenever they come to us, they will indeed arrive most happily. 

I am writing this letter to you under the <term>opposition</term> of the Moon to the Sun, and in a way also to Mercury and Saturn, and also under the <term>square</term> aspect of Mars to the Sun and Moon; at this time, almost nothing is more unhappy according to the Astronomers. Nevertheless, I know I shall write most happily. For our friendship was joined to us from our earliest years not only by the conducive stars, but by the decree of God, the leader of the stars. It pleases me now for a little while, as I am often accustomed to do both secretly and openly, to cry out together with our leader, the most divine Aurelius Augustine: *Only he loses no dear one to whom all are dear in Him who is never lost.* My Giovanni, you are now in your thirtieth year, if I count correctly; do not, therefore, be a prodigal in spending that which is irreparable, but weigh out your days more sparingly each day, as fewer of them remain for you to spend hereafter.

-> Slanderers should be despised. <-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

**T**he laws so dread infamy and hate slanderers that they strictly punish even those who speak ill of shameful things. Indeed, we have seen and approved this being publicly observed in our Florence two or even three times this summer. However, I ask no such thing from the laws today; for I do not wish the laws to be armed on my behalf against fleas <note>original: "pulices"; Ficino uses this disparagingly to refer to petty, stinging critics.</note>, which will be crushed at the first arrival of winter's cold. Let him, therefore—let that impious man touch your "anointed ones" <note>original: "Christos tuos"; a daring use of the biblical term for "anointed" kings or prophets to refer to the Medici and their circle.</note> with impunity, he who has for a long time been permitted to touch Christ himself. Let the common crowd be the judge of learning everywhere, though it is scarcely known to more than a very few. Let these little men, who have no judgment of their own, pass judgment as they please upon my life, which is known to God alone. I either care nothing for these and similar things, along with Socrates and Zeno, or certainly very little, along with Aristotle and Theophrastus. Indeed, I have learned from Heraclitus and Thales that all mortal things, whether good or bad, seem to die even as they are seen to rise. I have learned from Pythagoras and Plato that the soul sleeps in the body, and that whatever we seem to do or suffer here is nothing other than dreams. I have learned from the Teacher of Life <note>A reference to Jesus or the Gospel.</note> that the "whole world is set in wickedness" but that for a good man, all things return to good. Therefore, the very high walls of sacred Philosophy keep all such trifles far away from you. Nevertheless, Philosophy herself warns me of one thing today: that I should signal the matter to you so that you may perform your duty, just as you have most diligently performed it in our affairs at other times. That is, that you might show by even the slightest nod that what displeases God above all else also displeases you: namely, to give what is holy <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6: "Do not give what is holy to dogs."</note>—and your holy things at that—to be torn apart by dogs, or to be gnawed at by the fleas of dogs.

-> Slanderers should be despised. <-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Giuliano de' Medici, Greetings.

**T**hat that "dog" continually barks against me, just as he has always been accustomed to do against good and learned men, and against the soul and God, does not surprise me in the least. For he is so disposed by both nature and habit that he cannot help but bark. Nor do I care, for he is the sort of man who cannot disparage anyone except by praising them, nor praise anyone except by disparaging them. Let him bark as much as he likes among those above and those below <note>original: "apud superos, & apud inferos"; meaning among the living and the dead, or in heaven and hell.</note>, provided it is clearly understood that his barking does not please the Medici.

-> Congratulations on a public office. <-

### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero, Greetings.

**M**y dear Pietro, my great affection of mind and heart commands me to write many things, but what I am about to write at present, I do not know. For our domestic and more than familiar habit does not allow me to act too seriously, yet the supreme dignity of the magistracy <term>magistratus</term><note>A high-ranking administrative or judicial office in the Florentine Republic.</note> in which you have been placed does not permit me to joke, as we often do between us. What then shall I do? Certainly what God first advised and what the matter itself most urgently required. Therefore, first I pray and beseech the Ruler of Heaven, without whom nothing on earth is done happily, that He may direct your will to His own, and lead the outcome of your office and the city to your heart's desire. Then, I congratulate the office itself most highly, because it will be managed rightly by a pious and learned man. And I congratulate my Pietro, not so much because he has recently attained this dignity, but because he has long since been so established by God that he is worthier than any mortal dignity. Therefore, give thanks to Him diligently, and commend yourself to Him humbly. Farewell.

->Truth is defended by its own power, rather than by that of another.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Pietro of Piacenza, Apostolic Commissary, sends many greetings.

**T**he Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Sixtus IV.</note> has sent you as a vigorous leader to prepare arms against the enemies of divine wisdom. However, it is not so much the soldiers of Mars <note>The god of war.</note> as the priests of Pallas <note>Minerva, the goddess of wisdom; Ficino argues that intellectual and spiritual "warfare" requires scholars, not soldiers.</note> who are suited for defending wisdom. God has forbidden me from serving under deceitful Mars and has commanded me to follow the camps of invincible Minerva. Would that I might follow her as successfully as I have long followed her willingly. Therefore, I send these "arms" <note>Ficino refers to his writings and philosophical arguments as his weapons.</note> to you, with which I continually fight with all my strength against the enemies of truth. You, indeed, as a devoted foster-child of Pallas and patron of the Muses, will see to it that I may be able to build other such engines of war in the future. He who attacks the detractors of truth with spears fights however he can, but he who approaches them with true reasons always truly conquers.

->Venus tames Mars, Jupiter tames Saturn.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Rinaldo <note>Rinaldo Orsini, the Archbishop of Florence.</note>, Archbishop of Florence, sends many greetings.

**I**n recent days, Pietro of Piacenza, the most distinguished commissary of the Pope, has very kindly not only promised but also written down—both through a letter and especially in words spoken in your name—whatever I had requested regarding a matter of public burden. Then, while I was wishing to thank you in person for the benefit granted on your account, ill health has detained me for several days now. Finally, the day before yesterday, while I was attempting it more resolutely, my breath failed me so much in the middle of the journey that I could scarcely return home on foot. Soon after, it was announced to me that this gift of yours had been thrown into confusion. I wondered at this in a most extraordinary way, and having very diligently searched for the cause of the disturbance, when I could not find it on earth, I finally found it in heaven. You wonder at this, venerable father. Did not Thales of Miletus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who, according to legend, fell into a pit while looking at the stars; Ficino uses this to justify looking to the heavens for explanations of earthly events.</note>, having fallen on earth, rise in heaven so that he might inspect there what he had not seen here? Therefore, I observed what recently hindered my arrival, and I found that a square and malignant aspect of Saturn toward the Moon had done it. From this, I concluded that the benefit had been intercepted through the snares of some "Saturnian" man <note>In astrology, a person influenced by Saturn was thought to be cold, obstructive, or melancholic.</note>. At first, I lost almost all hope of a remedy, when I considered that Saturn is perhaps as powerful among the planets as he is high in the sky. But then it came to mind what the ancient sages fabled, not without the highest reason, concerning Saturn and Jupiter, and Mars and Venus: namely, that Mars is bound by Venus, and Saturn by Jupiter. This signifies nothing other than that the benevolence of Jupiter and Venus restrains the malice of Saturn and Mars. I believe, therefore, that the wound which was perhaps inflicted by some Saturnian person can best be healed by someone "Jovial" <note>Meaning a person under the influence of Jupiter, characterized by benevolence and authority.</note>. And I find no one at present in Florence in whom I recognize every image, power, and gift of Jupiter more than in you. Someone will perhaps mock a priest for observing astronomical matters. But I, relying on the authority of the Persians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans, used to think that while earthly things pertain to others, celestial things pertain to the priest alone—yet in such a way that a place is left for human counsel, and the highest authority is referred to the Ruler of heaven. But do you wish us to set aside celestial matters now? Let us set them aside. What, then, shall I ask? This one thing: since in other matters you are superior to Caesar himself, do not allow yourself to seem inferior even to Pilate in this one thing. Rather, let it be that what was written in the Commissary’s hands in your name from the beginning while I was present in my case, "remains written" <note>original: "sit scriptum"; a reference to Pontius Pilate's biblical phrase "What I have written, I have written" (John 19:22), suggesting the Archbishop should stand by his original promise.</note>. This, venerable father, is what I ask for the sake of philosophical leisure; nevertheless, your will be done.

->Happy is he who is content with his lot.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Valerio, Scribe of the Roman Prince <note>Likely the secretary to the Pope or a high cardinal.</note>, etc., sends many greetings.

**I**f those whose virtues are obstructed by "narrow circumstances at home" <note>original: "res angusta domi"; a quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal (3.164) referring to the difficulty of succeeding while poor.</note> do not easily rise, certainly they emerge with much more difficulty whose progress is blocked by "no circumstances at home." Usually, those who are blocked by nothing lack nothing. But our disciple, who just now greeted you, for this very reason lacks everything...

<meta>This page continues the third book of Marsilio Ficino’s letters. It concludes a letter regarding the virtues of moderation and the dangers of excessive wealth before moving into a playful exchange with Giovanni Cavalcanti and a philosophical discourse on the nature of praise addressed to Antonio Seraphico.</meta>

...will proceed, because nothing at home stands in the way. But what shall I say about the whole matter? An abundance of all things hinders the human race just as much as a lack does. A moderate possession of things and a temperate state of fortune is not only safer, more pleasant, and more stable, but also better suited for Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom; here representing intellectual pursuits.</note> and the Muses. Just as we highly approve of those poor people who are rich in that very poverty and sublime in their low lot, so we admire those wealthy men even more who live soberly even in the greatest abundance, and are humble and prudent in high fortune. 

Many, since they seem to possess everything, think that everything is permitted to them; having forgotten the human lot, they judge themselves to be something above men, when often they are less than men. Let them learn from Alexander the Great, Caesar, Nero, and Domitian; let them learn either to attribute less to their personal spirit, or to indulge their natural talent <note>original: "ingenio"</note> less, or to trust fortune less, or to despise men less. But while I say many words about these things, I perhaps seem to make much of those whom I truly believe should be made little of. Fortunate is he to whom a moderate lot has fallen; happy is he who is content with his lot. November 1, 1474.

### Virtue makes the legitimate citizen.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his one-and-only friend, sends many greetings. <-

**W**hen, after the nightingales, you sent us turtledoves, I promised too rashly and in vain that I would write something about them at another time. For nothing at all subsequently comes to mind in this matter. But if turtledoves are far more lusty <note>original: "salatiores," suggesting both fertility and saltiness/wit.</note> than nightingales, why did those nightingales produce something for us long ago, while these doves produce nothing? Is it perhaps because Philomela <note>The nightingale of Greek myth.</note> is consecrated to the Muses, but the turtledove to Venus? Our house, however, is not dedicated to Venus, but to the Muses. 

But come, let us try for a little while if perhaps at least Tommaso Minerbetti—for whom an elegant wife recently bore a clever son—might "bear" something for us. Since Tommaso chose me as godfather <note>original: "compatrem"</note> for the newborn, did he not make me his peer <note>original: "comparem." Ficino is playing on the Latin words for "godfather" and "equal/peer."</note>? It is a great thing, my Giovanni, to be made equal to great men. It is also best to be compared to the best. How much I value Minerbetti making much of us is not hidden from you, who know how much I have always valued his judgment. For that "Idea of the best citizen" which we read daily in our Plato, we have now recognized almost entirely in this man. Public cares are as much a concern to him as private matters are to others; in him, singular magnanimity and incredible gentleness contend with each other for equality. In him is a most generous prudence and a most prudent generosity; in him is such kindness combined with gravity that as many as see him, love him, and as many as know him, love and revere him. September 17, 1476.

### What the true praise of praise is.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Seraphico <note>Antonio degli Agli, a bishop and fellow humanist.</note>, his fellow philosopher, sends many greetings. <-

**O**ther craftsmen are accustomed to work more easily and more accurately the smaller and lighter the task they undertake. Add to this that they are praised all the more, the more their workmanship surpasses the material. On the contrary, those skilled orators who deal in praise behave differently in these three ways. Indeed, they praise great things more easily and more truly than small things, and that praise is usually most approved by the wise which maintains such a balance that it seems, in a way, to be surpassed by the person being praised. 

But why is there such a difference between the craftsman and the orator? Unless it is because man-made works do not have their power from the object being fashioned, but from the craftsman. For an action is powerful not when one undertakes a massive machine, but when there is great virtue in the artist. Praise, however, on the contrary, does not truly receive its strength so much from the speaker as from the person praised. And although it often acquires a certain appearance of truth from the dignity of the praiser, yet the praise will be true only if true virtue exists in the one whom we praise. 

But by some unhappy negligence, I had omitted here, Seraphicus, a fourth point—and indeed the greatest of all—which if I skip even for a moment, my Seraphicus, I feel a religious scruple. Other craftsmen only express what they intend with precision when they look at nothing else than the form of the work to be made. Praisers, however, on the contrary, only praise rightly when they refer the excellence of the praised man to something else: namely, to God. From where do we think this proceeds? Surely because men have their well-being from the very same source from which they have their being. And just as human art in a certain natural mat-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bastianus Salvianus, his cousin, sends greetings.

**G**reetings, our Salvianus. Your letter has fulfilled my longing, not because it praises Marsilio, but because it seems to me worthy of praise itself. I desire in letters a clear brevity, an elegant sharpness, and a charming gravity. You write—what was already known to me—that I hold great influence and authority with Thomas Minerbettus <note>Tommaso Minerbetti, a Florentine official and diplomat.</note>, a man outstanding in virtue. Indeed, I value having influence with a man of no small authority among all people as much as if I myself had authority among all. I recommend his noble children to your diligence a thousand times over. This is your business, Salvianus. No gain is greater, and no possession on earth more precious, than men. You gain such noble parents through their children, and you gain such high-born sons through teaching. Thomas’s children are growing up for you, my Salvianus, if they grow up in the liberal arts <note>term: "liberaliter" (liberal arts education), referring to the education befitting a free man, such as grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note>. From the field of Careggi, September 27, 1476.

-> *What the elegance of the earthly banquet is like, the splendor of the heavenly banquet, and the super-heavenly bliss.* <-

### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

**T**oday, my unique patron, those sacred and solemn rites of the divine Cosmas <note>St. Cosmas, the patron saint of the Medici family. The feast day is September 27.</note> return. We have been accustomed to celebrate them every year for a full cycle of Saturn now: first under the Great Cosimo, then under the Pious Piero, and finally under the Magnanimous Lorenzo. There, beautiful Apollo used to play the lyre <note>original: "Chelim" (from the Greek 'chelys', a lyre made from a tortoise shell).</note> sweetly; the sweetest Muses sang; the Graces performed their most pleasing dance; the playful nymphs frolicked; wicked Venus joked charmingly; Jupiter gave the laws; and Mercury discoursed. Happy was Marsilio—far too happy!—to whom it was granted by your kindness to sit at the feasts of the gods for so many years. 

Nothing in this autumn, nothing on earth, acts more infectiously than the suspicion of a pestilential epidemic <note>A reference to the plague outbreak in Florence in 1476, which forced many to flee the city.</note>, which disturbs that blessed banquet. But I see that what is now interrupted among mortals is being fully restored among the beings above. Look up now, heavenly Lorenzo, look up to heaven! There, in the Milky Way <note>original: "orbe lacteo"</note>, the Great Cosimo receives his heavenly companions at a banquet of nectar and ambrosia. Behold, the Galaxy provides them with perpetual milk, and he places before them the Jovian fish <note>The constellation Pisces.</note> and the lunar crab <note>The constellation Cancer.</note>; to these he adds the young goat, the bull, the lamb, and the heavenly birds. He tempers the bowls of Father Bacchus <note>original: "Liberi patris"</note> in the constellation of Aquarius; Diana gladly bestows her prey, and the most bountiful Ceres distributes her fruits. 

Furthermore, the rainbow <note>original: "Iris"</note> encircles them on all sides nine times with wondrous variety—a rainbow reflecting from the rays of Apollo upon the dew of manna, shining among the stars of the zodiac and mixing sweet scents from the Elysian fields. A new song of the heavenly Sirens soothes them, and the lyre, sounding in harmony with the motions of the spheres and stars, delights them for eternity. Oh, thrice and four times blessed are those to whom the heroic virtue of the Sun has rendered life joyful, and whom the Fates <note>original: "parcæ"</note> now spare. Those who, far from the storms of Aeolus, the waves of Neptune, and the mists of Pluto, feed in the Elysian fields on the serene breeze of highest Jupiter. 

How happy is that banquet, Lorenzo! In which one food is all food. A greed that is always satisfied, and a satiety that is always greedy. How marvelous are those nuptials, in which to love is the same as to enjoy; to see is nothing other than to embrace; to embrace now is the same as to embrace always. How just and how pleasant is that commerce, where law instructs the will, and the will establishes the law. Nothing is pleasing except what is permitted, and whatever is pleasing is always permitted. There, happiness is easier and fuller than can be imagined; there, every pleasure follows the will infinitely more easily and fully than our will follows pleasure here. Oh, fortunate are those whose fortune is already completed! We are called from one fate to another. We wretches follow a fleeing Italy in vain. But if anyone follows a fleeing Italy in vain, it seems necessary that only...

...let that man rightly follow his own Italy and happily attain it—he who follows one who does not flee, but remains. Remain happy, therefore, my Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>, in the love of the ever-remaining God. ## The wise person despises no one as useless.

->Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Michelozzi <note>Niccolò Michelozzi (1447–1527) was a devoted secretary to the Medici family and a close friend of Ficino.</note>, a true man, sends greetings.<-

**I** have often wished, Niccolò, during this stay of mine in the country, to write something to the magnanimous Lorenzo, our sole patron, as was proper; but I know not what faint-hearted and timid affection stood in my way until this day. But today, during the sacred rites of Saint Cosmas <note>The feast day of St. Cosmas (September 27), the patron saint of the Medici family.</note>, the "Great Cosmas" <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the grandfather of Lorenzo and Ficino’s first great patron, who had died and is here imagined as a heavenly guide.</note> from heaven provides a certain daring and confidence, just as he was accustomed to do while on earth. He does so chiefly for this reason: that a good man is not to be feared, for he knows not how to harm anyone, and by the kindness of his nature, he always strives to be useful even to the ungrateful. Therefore, having driven away my timidity, I wrote to the Medici today.

Truly, in that letter, it seems to me that I have somehow raved. Perhaps it is because I rashly put my sickle into another’s harvest <note>A classical proverb meaning to meddle in someone else's business; here, Ficino refers to writing poetry.</note> and, unaccustomed, knocked at the doors of the poets. Indeed, all poetry leads to madness through its cups. For Aristotle writes in his book of *Problems* <note>Aristotle, *Problemata* XXX, 1, a famous text in the Renaissance linking genius and "melancholy madness."</note> that those who philosophize are also, in a way, insane. But whatever the case, my Niccolò, one should only demand from individuals as much as they are able and know how to provide. The rest must be overlooked. 

God uses the wise for governing, but the insane for divining. A skilled craftsman uses various instruments as the task requires. A good leader of war loves the cavalry, but does not neglect the infantry. A wise father of a household, who has vessels of gold, silver, and bronze at hand, does not despise any other vessel, however flimsy or humble; for he knows that almost nothing in a large house is entirely useless. A learned physician collects various herbs, even the thorny and poisonous ones. For the grace of light, the black and dark colors necessarily serve the painter. God uses formless matter for every form of nature; He uses deformed things for a certain number of degrees and necessary uses, for the adornment of comparison and variety; finally, He uses even the evil demon for the good of examination, trial, and justice.

## To perverse minds, all things are adverse.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio degl'Agli <note>Antonio degl'Agli (1400–1477), a humanist prelate and Bishop of Volterra.</note>, Bishop of Volterra, sends greetings.<-

**M**any report that the <term>tax burden</term> <note>original: "rem onerariam" – likely referring to the *decima* or other clerical taxes being levied at the time.</note> against the priests is seething again and again, and that nothing can be found anywhere more "boiling" than this. Indeed, it seethes as much with frost as with heat. Some add that there is no need for it to seethe any further, for the priesthood has long since <term>boiled away</term> <note>original: "decoxisse" – a pun meaning both to boil down/exhaust and to go bankrupt.</note> entirely, and they claim to have seen this calamity of the Church depicted in the Apocalypse. Some assert the cause of this misery is Saturn in Leo and Jupiter in Pisces, being in retrograde. Others are of the opinion that not the stars, but the retrograde minds of men are the cause. 

But what do we think? Surely, Antonio, we think that both the stars and the minds of men are adverse only to those who interpret these things with a perverse mind. We believe that subjects are governed justly by just princes. We know that by the Infinite Good, all things are ultimately turned to good for good men. We learned from Christ, the master of life, to pay tribute willingly. We learned from Paul, the principal herald of Christ, to obey princes. 

But to come now to our own matter: my fortune, venerable father, is thin and humble in the judgment of the common people—as it is almost always accustomed to be for those who philosophize—but it is fat and sublime enough for my thin desire and humble spirit. If I do not commend this to my ancient patron, I shall perhaps seem to neglect the matters entrusted to my care and protection. If I do commend it, I shall seem to have too little confidence both in justice toward everyone and in your benevolence toward me. One thing alone, therefore, will suffice to mention: a long-lasting and continuous illness, even though it may seem light at the beginning, is nevertheless judged to be very grave in a slight condition of the body.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->The Graces and the Muses are from God, and are to be referred back to God.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a prominent Venetian diplomat, scholar, and father of the famous Pietro Bembo. He was a close associate of the Florentine Platonists.</note>, Venetian knight and illustrious jurist, greetings.

**Y**ou ask what the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, the informal circle of scholars and patrons led by Ficino under Medici sponsorship.</note> is doing, my Bernardo? It loves Bembo. What else? The Academy venerates Bembo. All the men of letters among us agree on this: that he is to be especially loved and venerated, whose breast is a temple of the Graces, and whose mind is a fountain of the Muses. Rejoice, therefore, Bernardo, in your own goods. In "your own," I say, because they are within you, not because they originate from you. Indeed, let it not escape you that you hold these individual goods from the very Good of all goods <note>Ficino uses "the Good" (Latin: *bonum*) as a Platonic name for God.</note>. But he alone both uses these things prosperously and enjoys that Good blessedly, who does not seek to enjoy these [individual] things, but simply to use them.

->Neither can he truly please himself who displeases the Truth, nor can he truly rejoice in good things who, in loving them, neglects the Good itself from which they are made good.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s most beloved friend and "unique" soulmate, to whom many of his letters and his commentary on Plato’s *Symposium* were dedicated.</note>, his unique friend, greetings.

**I** cannot endure that your people should return from the marketplace of Figline <note>Ficino’s family home was in Figline Valdarno, near Florence.</note> to you empty of our merchandise. For I think it a sin that, while they bring the belongings of others to you, they do not bring back your own. They carry, therefore, three letters from us: one corrects what I had hastily dictated to our boy when my brother arrived; the others are copies of those I had written some time ago to Antonio Agli <note>Antonio Agli (1400–1477), Bishop of Volterra and a humanist scholar.</note> and long ago to Piero Nero. I did not have anything from today at hand. I have given you external things. "You are a rustic, Corydon; you send tasteless little apples to a very sharp palate." <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (2.56–57). Ficino is modestly comparing his own writings to "tasteless apples."</note> Nevertheless, trust that Alexis might taste the little fruits a bit, for they are his own. Farmers are usually more pleased by their own fruits, even if they are less good, than by those of others. And perhaps no way seems more convenient for reaching a certain human happiness than that, for the most part, each person’s own things please him. I said "a certain" happiness, Giovanni—that is, a shadowed one. For if nature willed this to be a kind of solace for mortals, especially in the poverty of things and talent, yet there would be no true happiness in this, since in these things which please us, we would displease the Truth. Because he who does not please the Truth cannot truly please himself. Indeed, a little later, he who already displeases the Truth truly displeases himself. But which of men is most loved by Her [the Truth], if not he who loves Her most of all? Where, oh friend, where is such a lover? Let mortals at some time be ashamed: let them be ashamed, I say, while for no other reason than that they love mortal goods, they neglect in loving them that eternal Good itself, from which these things have their very nature as goods. All things are indeed good in themselves, because they are from Him. Again, they are good to us insofar as they are referred back to Him. But bad and bitter things do not unjustly befall us, because with a certain supreme injustice we pursue these things while abandoning Him—things which are necessarily in Him and are preserved by Him. Oh, how wonderful it is, my Giovanni, or rather how miserable, that those very things which are intimately joined to Him should utterly separate us from Him. Unless they bore Him within them in some way, they would not have the power to join us to themselves; if they were not in Him, they certainly would not be in themselves, and would not exist at all. Farewell. But do you notice anything, my Cavalcanti? Something I myself, to whom it just happened, hardly noticed. After I had said I had nothing from today to send, suddenly I know not what from "today" has sprung up for us. Sown, clearly, by Him for whom there is no tomorrow, nothing external, for whom whatever exists is the same moment. And therefore He alone can sow and reap in the same moment; and as often as He wishes, He reaps by sowing and sows by reaping.

->No one is happy except he who truly rejoices; no one truly rejoices except he who rejoices in the Truth.<-

**S**ince my brother said at this moment that he would be passing your way, and I could find nothing to give him for you, I suddenly thought to give that very thing which is neither to be found elsewhere nor to be sought. Which, even if all mortals seek it, yet no one who seeks it in a mortal way finds it. I was just now reading this [definition] of happiness...

...the definition in the *Confessions* of our [Saint] Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose work Ficino synthesized with Platonic philosophy.</note>, whose divine footsteps I follow as frequently as I can. To live blessedly is nothing other than to rejoice in the truth. And this very joy concerning the truth is happiness itself. Live happily, my best Giovanni, but so that you may live happily, rejoice truly; and that you may rejoice truly, rejoice in the truth. Absolute truth is the light of God in itself. The truth of things is the splendor of God within them. Therefore, if you wish to rejoice in the truth, love, seek, and consider God for his own sake, and all other things for the sake of God.

*He who loves the eternal form enjoys it at least as easily and securely as he who loves the temporal form enjoys it with difficulty and anxiety.*

### Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti send greetings to Giorgio Antonio Vespucci <note>Giorgio Antonio Vespucci (1434–1514) was a prominent Florentine scholar, a Dominican friar, and the uncle and tutor of the explorer Amerigo Vespucci.</note>, a most learned man.

**Y**our short letter, sweetest Vespucci, though not short on affection and learning, brought us long-lasting pleasure. For it showed how well you have been in spirit for a long time, and how beautifully you now fare in body. Happy, then, is our Vespucci, who possesses what seems most to be desired: a sound mind in a sound body <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano," a famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal's Satires.</note>. For him, health of the soul depends neither on deceptive fortune nor on the insane health of the body—which is lost daily against our will—but flows from that fountain of life which only he loses who lets it go of his own accord. Whoever has truly thirsted for this for a long time seems already to have drunk. For the price at which this liquid is bought is the thirst itself; and the thirsty soul has that very thing for which it thirsts from a certain libation of the source, from which, drinking more fully, it reaches a state where it thirsts for nothing further. 

He is a truly fortunate hunter who has resolved to pursue the Sun with all his strength through the suns <note>Ficino uses the "Sun" as a metaphor for God or the One, and "suns" likely refers to the various intellectual or earthly reflections of divine light.</note> everywhere available to him. Indeed, even before he seeks it, he most easily finds the one whom he only sought after being kindled by that same heat. For he would not have recognized what he found unless he had been illuminated by its light. Blessed is he who sometimes loves, to the extent of his powers, the Form <note>In Platonic terms, "Form" (Idea) refers to the eternal essence of Beauty or Truth.</note> which alone can never truly be loved enough. For this immense form is the measure of every other form; it is always vast, shining everywhere; out of love for infinite goodness, it shows itself uniform and constant to its immense lover. And the lover, by immediately loving such a beloved as far as his arms can reach, embraces the One who embraces all things, and securely possesses his own Possessor. 

Truly, the vow of a man who strives for something other than love is often frustrated by the outcome; but he alone who loves nothing besides love itself, attains it suddenly by desiring it, and always desires it by attaining it. Furthermore, if no one can do anything without power, or know anything without wisdom, so no one loves without love. But that power and wisdom, and love itself, are inwardly the same thing and are God—this the powerful do not dare to deny, the wise know, and the lovers feel in their essence. 

To this it is added that just as nothing is beautiful without beauty, so there is no lover without love. But among mortals, any finite beauty is one thing, and the desire for this beauty is another. Therefore, among us, human love burns in one place, and beauty shines in another. However, since infinite beauty allows nothing foreign outside of itself, it is even less likely to leave anything of its own outside itself. Therefore, it possesses its own love within itself. From this it follows, conversely, that wherever the love of that Beauty burns, that Beauty must also necessarily shine. For just as the furthest darkness coincides with the furthest cold, so the highest light conspires with the highest heat. Perhaps, best Vespucci, we will seem to some to wander too far in these matters. Yet it delights us to discourse at length about divine love with a pious man who is also a very dear friend. For what limit can there be to immense love? Meanwhile, let some ridiculous person laugh at us for treating such things so often and at such length. We, however, shall mourn the one who laughs. Farewell.

->*God turns all things to good for the good.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti, greetings.

**G**iovanni, write sometimes what you have done in the matters common to you and me, or what you wish for me to do—if only at present you yourself know what you want, my best Giovanni. I, however, in these times, do not know in a way what I want. Perhaps I do not want what I know, and I want what I do not know. Nevertheless, I believe it is clear to you now by the benevolence of your Jupiter, directed in Pisces <note>In astrology, Jupiter is the "ruler" of the sign Pisces; "direct" motion (as opposed to retrograde) is considered strong and positive.</note>, while for me these days it is not so, due to the malignancy of my Saturn, retrograde in Leo <note>Ficino frequently blamed his melancholic temperament on Saturn. Here he notes Saturn is in Leo (a sign where it is weak) and "retrograde" (moving backward), which he interprets as a period of personal difficulty or indecision.</note>...

...and the end. Indeed, I praise this most of all in myself: that by his [God's] eternal gift alone, I am least of all desirous of mortal goods. Yet, because I am too fearful regarding evils—a trait for which you sometimes reproach me—I blame a certain melancholy <term>melancholy: In Renaissance medicine, one of the four temperaments, associated with the element of earth and the planet Saturn. While it caused sadness, Ficino followed Aristotle in believing it was also the temperament of genius.</term> complexion. This is, it seems to me, a most bitter thing, unless it were somehow softened and made sweet for us by the frequent use of the lyre <note>Ficino famously practiced "astrological music therapy," playing a lyre decorated with a picture of Orpheus to counteract his depressive tendencies.</note>. Saturn seems to have impressed this nature upon me from the beginning, being positioned almost in the middle of my ascendant, Aquarius; and with Mars also in Aquarius, the Moon in Capricorn, and both the Sun and Mercury in Scorpio—occupying a new quarter of the sky—looking on from a square aspect <note>A "square" is a 90-degree astrological aspect, traditionally considered tense or challenging.</note>. Perhaps Venus in Libra and Jupiter in Cancer resisted this melancholy nature somewhat. But since I have slipped into speaking rashly: I see you will rightfully force me to sing a second "palinode" <note>A poem or song retracting a previous sentiment.</note> to Saturn. What then shall I do? I will indeed turn back and say either that a nature of this kind does not proceed from him—if you prefer—or, if it must proceed from him, I shall agree with Aristotle, who says that this very temperament is a singular and divine gift.

-> No one ascends to God, unless God himself has somehow descended into them. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, <-
-> Sends Greetings. <-

**A**lthough I promised you three old letters some time ago, nevertheless, because I think you would rather taste new wine <note>original: "mustum"</note> than old these days, I am sending new things. In these last three days, I have composed three short theological works concerning the triple ascent of the mind to God. To this height, no one ascends unless He has first somehow descended into them—He who can be moved nowhere since there is no space outside of Him, as He fills all things entirely from within and embraces all things infinitely from without. I am sending the little preface to the third work, which has not yet been edited. October 28, 1476.

-> The common crowd feeds on trifles. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, <-
-> Sends Greetings. <-

**I** am leaving our farm at Cella <note>Ficino's family property at Figline, though he also spent much time at the Villa di Careggi gifted to him by the Medici.</note> at this hour, heading for Florence. I am carrying with me five short theological works composed by us during this final period of our rural stay, concerning divine providence, the names of God, and the joy of contemplation. These cover the ascent from the matter of the elements to the heaven without matter; to the soul without quantity; to the angel free from change; to God, a substance without accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of the thing (like hair color). God, being perfect, has no such temporary qualities.</note>; concerning the rapture of Paul to the third heaven <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where the Apostle Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven."</note> and how the soul sees God’s eternity and its own there; concerning the mind's hindrance by the body and its immortality; and concerning light, which in the divine beings is a rejoicing brightness and a bright joy, while in the machinery of the world it is a kind of laughter of the heavens proceeding from the joy of those divine beings. These works are brief in words, as I clearly see myself; whether they are also brief in their thoughts, or long, others shall see. If, however, those who once used to gather our leaves and flowers do not now disdain to collect these fruits, whatever they may be—yet I know not how it is that May arrives more welcome to mortals every year, even though it almost lacks fruit, than does September. I am going now to the city; you come too, Giovanni, so that we may at least be urban companions, even if we were not rural companions this summer. Farewell. November 10, 1476.

But why have I said not a word now about this third girl <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti’s daughter.</note> born to you recently? Because you said not a word to me. Do you want me to confess the truth? I will not say a word on this matter until I have found out whether I should be congratulating you or consoling you <note>A wry comment reflecting the Renaissance preference for male heirs, though Ficino softens this in the next sentence.</note>. Rejoice, however, in whatever way it may be, in the gifts of the Great King [God]. For nothing from the Great is small or to be despised.

...carries. He belongs to the number of the many who pursues many things; he is unique who pursues one. It is the mark of a childish and weak mind to attempt different things at every moment. It is also the mark of rash ambition to profess many things daily. Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher (6th century BCE) who believed that numbers were the ultimate reality; he associated "The One" (Unity) with the divine and the good.</note> teaches us that unity looks toward the good, while diversity looks toward evil. Just as the natural power in the liver and the vital power in the heart, when they are pulled in two directions, are weakened in both, so the animal power <term>animal power: From the Latin 'anima' (soul). In Renaissance medicine, this referred to the 'animal spirits' produced in the brain which governed sensation and movement.</term> in the brain does not suffice for us when directed toward diverse things. Furthermore, everyone performs more aptly that for which they were better suited by nature. One thing is suitable to one person. One thing, therefore, is necessary: for many things cause disturbance. One thing, I say, which is honorable in itself and more suitable to the doer than all others. Finally, if God is always the same and acts in the same way, a person is further from God the more they are prone to diverse things. December 10, 1474.

### How envy may be punished, mitigated, or uprooted.

->Marsilio Ficino to a man who fears envy. Greetings.<-

**D**o you wish to take revenge for the injuries inflicted by the envious? Take care that they envy you more and more every day. For if punishment is an evil, then the punishment for the evil is certainly within the evil itself. Do you wish to mitigate that spite in some way? Be more kind than others. Indeed, while other good qualities usually irritate spite, kindness alone softens it. Or perhaps you desire to uproot envy entirely? This is the task, this is the labor <note>original: "Hoc opus, hic labor" — a famous quotation from Virgil's Aeneid (6.129), referring to the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>. You must turn out to be so excellent and of such great standing that no one can hope to equal or surpass you. December 10, 1476.

### Love everyone, but choose and love one alone. Trust in God alone.

->Marsilio Ficino to a man. Greetings.<-

**I** hear you are grieving because you were deceived by a friend. Believe me, you cannot have been deceived by *a* friend, but rather by *friends*. A unique friend is another self who does not deceive. However, many people appear as if they were a "self," yet they very often deceive. Therefore, if you are ever deceived, do not blame "the friend," but rather "friends"—or rather, do not even blame friends, but yourself, who loved before you judged most diligently. Either you loved too much, or you trusted too much in the human lot. Love everyone, choose and love one alone, and trust in God alone. December 10, 1476.

### Favors poorly placed, I judge to be ill deeds.

->Marsilio Ficino to Marsilio Ficino.<-

**D**o you think that favors poorly placed are bad deeds? And do you grieve that you have done wrong because you did good to evil and ungrateful men? I will not tell you not to grieve. Indeed, because of a certain very great error, you are to be judged worthy of grief—and the greatest grief at that. And since you did a good thing poorly, you are worthy of ill. Therefore, grieve as you do, and be tormented by repentance as is fitting. But do not blame the ingratitude of others or your fortune, but rather your own lack of prudence. Men are justly ungrateful to you, to whom you yourself did not give justly. Have you yourself never been ungrateful toward another—either toward a man or certainly toward God? Ingratitude is punished. Have you studied so long under the mistress of Philosophy to discern so many foreign things that you forget your own? O, what a wondrous thing! You philosophers, while you follow wisdom without enough wisdom, are often prone to folly. What then? Should you have handed nothing over to anyone? Far be it from you! Do not let yourself be ungrateful to God, the giver of all things, from whom you received everything for free, just because you strive to escape the ingratitude of others. Far be it, while evil men displease you, that you yourself either become evil or become less good and thus displease the good. Those are forced to perish from hunger who, for this very reason, no longer endure to sow because the greatest part of their past seed withered. Therefore, you should have tested the character and life of a man through a long—at least fifteen-year <term>fifteen-year: Ficino uses the term 'trilustri,' referring to three 'lustra.' A lustrum was a five-year period in the Roman calendar.</term>—examination before you gave anything. Or if perhaps the matter urged you to help more quickly, you should at least have given, in the manner of Aristotle, not to this specific man,

> but to humanity; or rather, in the manner of Plato, not to this man,
> but to God. December 2, 1476.

->There are three stages of Platonic contemplation.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

**I** have decided, Magnanimous Lorenzo, before I publish that great volume of *Platonic Theology* <term>Platonic Theology: Ficino's masterpiece, *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum*, in which he sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</term> dedicated in your name, in which there still remains something needing examination, to publish an introductory outline if it pleases you. I do not do this so that you, practiced by such an outline as if by some prelude to Theology, might approach it more ready for play—since you seem to me to have almost already achieved the palm of the game itself. But I do it so that, reminded by this pledge in the meantime, you may remember—and remember that I ought to remind you—what I had rightly promised for a long time, and that I wish to eventually pay what I know I owe. Especially since I do not owe this so much because I promised it, as I promised it because I owed everything to you.

Indeed, there are three principal stages of Platonic contemplation. The first ascends from the body through the soul to God. The second consists in God. Finally, the third descends to the soul and the body. Our introductory outline also contains these three stages.

->Where the foundation itself wavers, whatever you build upon it will collapse.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Paolo of Florence, an excellent priest and his fellow philosopher, Greetings.

**Y**ou ask, my Paolo, for what reason I write nothing to you. It is because where speech is perpetual, there is no need for letters. I speak with you, my Paolo, as long as I speak with myself; I say this because I love you. I do not love because I speak. A friendship that stands only on letters or words falls by silence. One which is contracted by brief utility or pleasure is dissipated in a brief time. Where the foundation itself wavers, whatever you build upon it will collapse. Therefore, the knot of our goodwill is indissoluble. It is a knot which no light or brief cause connects, but the arms of eternal Philosophy bind together. The book on the Providence of God, which you ask for, I will send at the time when God has provided that I would send it. However, I will send it freely, because He also provided this very thing: that I would send it freely.

->Where charity glows, there God shines, there grace sparkles.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Alberto Parisio, distinguished in learning and morals, Greetings.

**G**od Himself is charity; he who remains in charity, remains in God, and God in him <note>A direct quotation of 1 John 4:16.</note>. Almighty God sang these things through the divine mouth of John the Evangelist. Where, therefore, charity glows most of all—since God shines there especially—truly the splendor of grace and the grace of splendor shines forth. Since truly nothing has ever been more pleasing to me than to be where grace of this kind shines, certainly my heart has for a long time lived together with yours. However, so that where my heart lives by loving, my mind may also live by disputing <note>original: "disputando." In a Renaissance context, this refers to formal philosophical debate or logical reasoning.</note>, receive today in the book I am sending my mind, dear friend, reasoning with all its strength concerning divine faith and hope. Deservedly, since the vehicle of faith and hope is accustomed to carry one toward charity—which both philosophers and theologians believe—it now carries my mind to your mind, which is both burning with charity and reflecting with grace.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->All the goods of the world are evils to him who lives uncleanly in the world.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to the human race, sends greetings.<-

**W**hy do you, O man, disparage the world for so long as if it were entirely unclean and evil? The world is certainly arranged and led in the most beautiful and best way by a most beautiful and best Reason; yet to you it is unclean and evil, because you live uncleanly in the world and as an evil person within the good. The first origin of worldly evils for you is the excessive desire for worldly goods. You love the small world <note>Ficino likely refers to the "microcosm" of the individual or material objects.</note> more vehemently than the large one. You also admire this large world which you see more than the immense world which you understand—in which the large is contained almost as the small is contained within the large. 

O celestial mind, you love your earthly shadow—that is, the body—more than your own celestial splendor, more than the super-celestial light. Since love is the principle of every motion, whether natural or animal, as long as you ardently love the body, you desire or fear all things for its sake; by desiring you are made anxious, and by fearing you grieve. Ah, why do you, O mindless mind, love these things with such passion—things which can easily be hindered before you obtain them, and can be taken away just as easily after you possess them? Alas, why do you so anxiously pursue that which flees from you, while you yourself flee from that which follows you? 

Miserable one, why do you strive in vain to hold onto these fleeting earthly things as if they were "goods"? Indeed, holding them can keep you far from the True Good, yet they themselves cannot be held by you by any means. Why do you so rashly trust your footing to the swiftest motion? Why try to fill yourself with a vacuum? Why try to quench the wind with a fist? Do you wish to utterly extinguish this burning thirst that vexes you so much? Drink the true water while awake, not the image of water in a dream. 

Know that only those things truly exist which belong to the intellect, the judge of truth. Those things which belong to the senses—which are ignorant of truth itself—are only "truth-like," not true. Do you wish to be wealthy in a short time? Strive to take away as much from your greed as you have hitherto strived to add to your heap. Live, I pray, according to the law of nature, which is content with a few tiny things, not according to opinion, which always thinks you are poor. Necessity is confined within narrow boundaries; opinion has none. 

The things necessary for us are laid out and prepared everywhere; we labor for the superfluous. Necessity provides a useful and convenient travel-allowance for the wayfarer; opinion provides a useless weight and labor. If you desire rest, do not seek rest through motion, but stop the motion. If you desire command, command yourself through reason. If you desire liberty, serve reason. If you wish to avoid pain, flee pleasure, the bait of evils; "pleasure bought with pain is harmful" <note>This is a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 1.2.55).</note>. That pleasure of the body which seems greatest of all produces the greatest pain. 

The art and experience of medicine teaches that nothing creates more bile <term>bile: in Renaissance medicine, 'yellow bile' was one of the four humors; an excess was thought to cause bitterness, anger, and physical illness</term> than honey. The sweeter the nourishment, the more bitter the gall it creates. Why has it been ordained by nature that by laughing profusely we often weep, yet by weeping we laugh not at all? It is to remind us that there is more true pain in the senses than pleasure. Indeed, pain is felt within pleasure more than pleasure is felt within pain. 

If you desire to please yourself, see to it that you please not the common crowd, but the wise—or rather, Wisdom herself. It will be necessary for you to be displeased with yourself if you wish to please anyone beyond what is rational. If you wish to live prudently, remember that there is such a cycle of good and evil that neither should these goods be taken up without fear, nor should evils be endured without hope. One should therefore rejoice moderately in good things, and grieve even more moderately in bad ones. Learn the present from the past. In present matters, look around at every detail as much as you can. From these details, look toward the end. Never approach present things, whether to be said or done, unless you have looked toward the future to the best of your ability. Neither do nor say anything for which you cannot give a probable reason. Finally, when you have humbly commended yourself to God in every detail, and have done each thing as much by the examination of reason as by the counsel of the wise, live with a tranquil mind, and accept whatever follows as being for the better.

### *On the sufficiency, end, form, matter, manner, seasoning, and authority of the banquet.*

### *Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, most distinguished knight and legal consultant, sends greetings.*

**W**hile I was thinking about writing something philosophical regarding the true magnificence and elegance of the banquet, Bernardo Bembo first occurred to me as the person to whom I should write on this matter—he is a dear foster-child of philosophy and a man of singular magnificence and elegance. Accept therefore with a willing mind, my Bernardo, these things which the "Fat Minerva" <note>original: "pinguis Minerva." A Roman idiom referring to common sense or plain, unrefined wisdom, here used with self-deprecating humor by Ficino.</note> has dictated to your Marsilio regarding a banquet that is not very "fat" <note>Ficino plays on the word "fat" (pinguis) to mean both a lack of luxury and a lack of intellectual pretense.</note>.

### *No human delight is more sufficient than the banquet.*

**I**t is the common opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> and of physicians that a human being is composed of body and soul. The body consists on the one hand of a thicker part, that is, the limbs and humors, and on the other hand of a more subtle part, that is, certain vapors of the blood and spirits <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>. The soul, moreover, is composed of sense and reason. Just as the humor relates to the spirit, so the sense relates to reason. Nor can anyone ever live contentedly in human affairs unless all these parts of the human being have been satisfied, at least for a little while. All other things which are considered "goods" among men seem to belong to only one or two of these parts we have mentioned; only the banquet, however, encompasses them all. I speak of the "legitimate" banquet, which—to count the parts individually—refreshes the limbs, restores the humors, recreates the spirit, delights the senses, and fosters and excites the reason. The banquet is a rest from labors, a release from cares, the food of genius, a proof of magnificence and love, the bait of benevolence, the seasoning of friendship, the fuel of grace, and the solace of life.

### *The end of the banquet is the sweet communion of life.*

**F**urthermore, so that it may be more clearly seen what a legitimate banquet is, let us see what the "end" <note>In the philosophical sense of "purpose" or "goal."</note> of the banquet is, what its form is, and what its matter is. The "end" of this seems to be indicated by its name: not "gorging" or "heavy drinking" as it is among the Greeks <note>Ficino contrasts the Latin "convivium" (living together) with the Greek "symposion" (drinking together) or "commessatio" (revelry).</note>, but the sweet communion of life; so that just as we eat the common nourishment of the body within it, so we may enjoy the same good of the mind and life with a common will.

### *The form of the banquet is the fitting number and quality of guests, conversation, and the lyre.*

**T**o the form of this belongs especially the number and quality of the guests. In this matter, we strongly approve of that rule of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar.</note>: that there should be no fewer than the three Graces, and no more than the nine Muses. From this commerce of Graces and Muses, it also appears clearly enough what sort of people they ought to be: for it is necessary that they be gracious, musical, and literate. Care must be taken, therefore, that no one who is contentious or who flares up in anger quickly be easily admitted, unless perhaps he is the kind of person who can be softened by the first cup or by a single little word. Let the Melancholics <note>Those suffering from an excess of the "black bile" humor, seen as sour or depressed.</note> and the bitter also be utterly exiled from there, unless they are like Zeno the Stoic and Xenocrates the Platonist, who—just as lupines <note>A type of bitter legume that was soaked in water to remove its bitterness.</note> lose their bitterness in water—would become sweet when drenched in unmixed wine. If something regarding divine matters must be treated, let the sober ones postpone it; if they dispute about natural things, let it be when the table has been cleared. During the feast, however, let the speech be varied and pleasant: a brief history, a very brief story, or a somewhat longer fable. Let them imitate Nature, the craftswoman and mistress of life, so that what she achieves in the sweetest flavors, they may achieve in their speech: let them mix sweetness with sharpness, wit with gravity, the useful with the sweet. Let them be witty, sharp, and clever, but not annoying or bitter. The banquet tolerates vinegar, but not wormwood; we do not admit a buffoon at all if he is too troublesome. We utterly detest the obscene and the filthy...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino writes to Bernardo Bembo defining the ideal "convivium" (banquet) as a holistic exercise that nourishes both the body's humors and the soul's reason through moderate social interaction.</summary>
