<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s letter to Bernardo Bembo regarding the ethics and spiritual significance of the banquet. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, discussing the importance of inner character over outward display.</meta>

<page-num>746</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO<-

For wise men are offended much more by what you show in your mind, your speech, and your face than by your clothes and your equipment. Therefore, so that my lyre does not sound out of tune, but remains harmonious, I pray: be present, O glory of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of music and light.</note>, at my solemn calling, and you, O tortoise-shell lyre, welcome at the feasts of supreme Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>, O sweet solace of labors. Let long-haired Iopas <note>A singer mentioned in Virgil’s Aeneid who performs at Dido’s banquet.</note> certainly be present with his cíttern at the table of the Graces and the Muses.

### *The necessary substance of the banquet consists of the fruits of Bacchus and Ceres.*

**A**s far as the substance of the banquet is concerned, we think first that sadness is the poison of life, and gloom is likewise the poison of the table. Indeed, the <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "thiriacam." A famous ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote against poison.</note> for sadness and gloom is a sweet and clear wine. Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine.</note> equates its power to the strength of the gods. Our Plato also asserted that the intellect and the physical powers are wonderfully nourished by the moderate heat of wine. But lest I be accused of praising wine too much, like Homer, I shall now leave Bacchus behind and flee to Ceres <note>The goddess of grain and agriculture.</note> and the guardian of the gardens. We by no means desire the fatty and overly greasy feasts of Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for his decadent luxury.</note>. We do not want, by any means, to be without <insert>the fruits of</insert> Pythagorean crops, vegetables, and orchard fruits <note>Pythagoras was famous for advocating a simple, largely vegetarian diet.</note>. For no table is easier, and none more blessed, than that which the most generous Nature prepares for you.

### *The manner and seasoning of the banquet.*

**J**ust as we do not greatly praise a completely meager banquet, so we utterly detest a luxurious one; for this is "dying together" rather than "living together" <note>Ficino makes a pun on the Latin "convivere" (to live together/to banquet) and "commori" (to die together).</note>. We do not require the height of elegance and splendor, lest there be a servile difficulty where we easily seek freedom. We certainly desire what is clean and pure; we shudder at the filthy and the sordid. Finally, lest anything among us be tasteless or unsalted <note>The Latin "insulsum" means both "unsalted" and "witless."</note>, and lest anything be sordid or obscure, everything ought to be seasoned with the salt of wit and illuminated by the rays of the mind and character, so that just as was said of the dinner of Plato and Xenocrates, our banquet may smell sweeter and last longer the following day.

### *The authority of the banquet derived from Philosophy, the Heavens, and God.*

**I**f anyone should perhaps marvel that we celebrate the banquet to such an extent, he ought to remember that Plato, Xenophon, Varro, Julian, and also Apuleius and Macrobius the Platonic did the same. Did not Themistocles, Socrates, Empedocles, and many other philosophers frequent banquets? Do not even the inhabitants of heaven often recline at table among the ancient heroes? The sky also has a "Milky Way" <note>original: "lacteum... orbem."</note>. It has the "Mixing Bowl" <note>original: "craterem." Referring to the constellation Crater.</note> of Father Bacchus, it has the "Jar" <note>The constellation Aquarius.</note>, the "Crab" [Cancer], the "Fish" [Pisces], and the "Birds" [Cygnus], as well as the "Lamb" [Aries], the "Kid" [Auriga], and the "Bull" [Taurus]. I pass over what kind of banquets Muhammad promises to the blessed. But who does not know that Christ, the master of life, frequently took part in banquets? That he showed his first miracle there, when he is said to have turned water into wine? Furthermore, that in that greatest assembly he satisfied many thousands of men with a few loaves and fishes? What else does the honeycomb signify? Or the broiled fish? Or the breaking of bread? Did he not sing the chief mysteries of divine things to his disciples at the Supper? This is also the goal of that wonderful sacrament of the Eucharist. To this also tend whatever things are often read concerning divine foods and drinks in the sacred writings of the Hebrews and Christians. Why so many words about the banquet? Clearly so that we, who do not live without distress when apart from one another, may live together most pleasantly as one. And let us remember that the true nourishment of man is not so much the plant or the beast as it is man himself. Also, the complete nourishment of man is not so much man as it is God. Only by His nectar and ambrosia is human thirst and hunger continually stirred and increased, and finally filled so wonderfully and happily, that there alone is always the greatest pleasure joined with the greatest fullness.

Farewell happily together with your most happy senate, most illustrious Bernardo; the whole Academy commends itself to you a thousand times. You, however, commend our "obscure Moon" <note>Likely a humble reference to Ficino's own work or soul.</note> again and again to the "shining Phoebus" <note>A reference to Bembo or a higher intellectual light.</note>.

LETTERS, BOOK III

->*How pleasing the sight of a friend is, how necessary, and how voluntary love is.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti. Sends Greeting. <note>The Latin abbreviation "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard formal greeting meaning "says health" or "sends greetings."</note><-

**S**ince I was forced to linger a long time in bed today, and was thinking of some remedy against the boredom of a prolonged reclining, the first—indeed the only one—who occurred to me to counter the looming boredom was my Cavalcanti, my singular physician. Greetings, therefore, and greetings again, O my salvation, driver away of my ills, seasoning for all my good things. My dear Giovanni, you indeed demonstrate many other things daily, but especially that Aristotelian saying: namely, that nothing in human affairs is more pleasing than the presence of an outstanding friend. I received the truth of this Aristotelian sentiment from you long ago, and I have learned its reasoning. Truly, he who—as much by my longing for him formerly as by the absence of his body recently—completely took me away from myself, now in turn restores me by a certain mutual affection and the presence of his mind. It is hidden from no one how gladly even "little men" <note>original: "homunculi." Ficino often uses this diminutive to refer to the humble or limited state of mortal humans.</note> gaze at their own image in mirrors. A friend, however, does not look at just his own image in a friend, but at himself. Certainly, even if I am, as it were, a "pretty little man" in myself, thin and short, yet in the heroic mirror of him whom I have loved for five <term>lustra</term> <note>A lustrum is a period of five years; Ficino is referring to twenty-five years of friendship.</note> now, I see myself as a tall man of high standing, not a little man. 

You will receive, therefore, a letter perhaps more necessary than voluntary, since I seem to have been compelled to dictate this for the sake of avoiding boredom, as I said. Alas, I have just failed—I know not how, my Giovanni—I have failed too much against the heroic genius and the Platonic divinity. Behold, now Plato reproaches me more sharply from on high, crying out: "Marsilio, why do you separate what is voluntary from what is necessary in a lover? A lover’s letter, O Marsilio, is as voluntary as it is necessary. No necessity is more voluntary, and no will is more necessary, than that of love." For what is more voluntary than love? It is the first, highest, and perpetual affection of the will, and it brings it about entirely that we do not wish *not* to love. Again, what is more necessary than love? It is burnt into the unwary heart secretly by the rays and flames of the celestial powers. And the lover experiences the full-grown flame before he has even felt the ray or the spark. He cannot help but burn, if he burns by a celestial fate. He cannot help but burn, since even while he seeks relief, he always kindles the heat by the very drink with which he somehow vainly trusts he might extinguish it. Whence comes such a wonderful mixture of necessity? It is because God is both the highest necessity and the highest liberty; and we all desire the Supreme Good to the highest degree, nor can we not-will it, nor do we wish to be able to not-will it. Almost the same thing usually happens to anyone who is gently enticed, secretly snatched away, and vehemently kindled by that warmer splendor of the divine ray which shines out wonderfully to us in beauty. **January 30, 1476.**

->*Man is a wolf to man, not a man.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the most learned man Jacopo Bracciolini. Sends Greeting.<-

**A** wolf is a sad thing for the stables. <note>A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues (3.80): "Triste lupus stabulis."</note> A little fox is a sad thing for the chicks of the hens, but man is a sadder thing for men. For man is both a wolf and a fox to men; just as the best of animals is—if he is ever found—the best man, so the worst animal is the worst man. He is most prudent, my Bracciolini, who is most cautious. Moreover, the most cautious of all is he who diligently guards against man. But here there is need for a <term>Lynceus</term> <note>An Argonaut famous for having sight so keen he could see through stone or into the earth.</note> and an <term>Oedipus</term> <note>The mythical figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx.</note>; here there is need for an <term>Argus</term> <note>A giant with a hundred eyes.</note>. Only he will hold onto the character and counsel of a man who remembers that it can be held either by no means at all, or certainly only very rarely and with the greatest difficulty.

...to try to enumerate them, there is something in each that you would not approve of. As it is written in Homer and Plato, God has given all things to no one. I want you to remember that you are a human being among humans, and while others displease you, you also displease others. Only the first <term>Good</term> <note>Latin: "bonum." In Ficino's Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the One or God, the source of all perfection.</note> is that in which there is no defect. In the heavenly bodies indeed some defect may appear, but not evil. In these things which are subject to the Moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, which in ancient and medieval cosmology was the realm of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) and subject to change, decay, and imperfection, unlike the eternal heavens.</note>, both defect and evil are found. All things except the First, because they proceed from the Good, are in a certain way good; but because they are not the Good itself, they either seem not entirely perfect, or even evil. Since therefore all things are mixed, he who gathers the evil from each eventually turns out the worst, but he who chooses the good, the best. For each person becomes like the food they consume. Farewell. And so that others may bear with you, bear with others.

### The method of learning and speaking.
-> Marsilio Ficino to his secretary Luca Fabiano, sends greeting. <note>original: "S. D." for "Salutem Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "wishes health."</note> <-

**N**ature grants us many instruments with which we may learn—eyes, ears, nostrils, taste, and touch. But she has given only a single instrument by which we may teach, namely, the faculty of speaking. She certainly advised us that we should use the service of learning just as much more often than the duty of teaching, as she handed over more instruments for learning than for teaching. No wordy and talkative person, therefore, can be wise, for he has always taught but never learned. Whoever lacks wisdom and letters <note>meaning literacy or education</note> is to be judged not only poor but also blind and mute. Be, I pray, swift and diligent in hearing and seeing, but slow to believe, slower to judge, and slowest to speak. So that you may speak good things, hear good things; so that you may also hear well of yourself, you too speak well of others. For it cannot happen that he who speaks ill does not hear ill. In speaking, however, beware of a lie no less than a sailor avoids a reef. For the light of truth is immense, its power immense. It quickly uncovers a lie and destroys the liar. Remember that flattery is a slavish vice—indeed even much viler than slavish. For no one can flatter so aptly that he is not surpassed by far by little dogs. Remember moreover that reckless or rigid rebuke is either dangerous or altogether useless. Our Plato <note>Ficino often refers to Plato as "ours" because he dedicated his life to translating and teaching his works.</note> commands that we either speak only the truth where we might be of use, or keep silent. If anyone has been a disciple of the Apostle Paul’s prudence, life, and purpose, he alone will be able to persist as urgently as he does opportunely. We must take total care lest, while we rebuke the morals of others with words, our own morals in the meantime refute our words. You have begun well, as I hear; proceed therefore on the path you have started. And so that you may make your journey successfully, do not cease to restrain your horse—that is, your senses—with reins and a bit.

### The pursuit of revenge is nothing other than receiving an injury again.
-> Marsilio Ficino to a man impatient of injuries, sends greeting. <-

**A**re you grieving that you received an injury, O friend? I concede indeed, but you seem not so much to have been harmed because someone did something bad to you, but because you judged what he did to be an evil. To an evil man, indeed, all things, even good ones, turn into evil. But to a good man all things, even those which seem the worst, are finally converted into good. Are you thinking of taking revenge? I warn you carefully to beware, for if you attempt to take revenge, you will suffer a second and third injury, and in your zeal to destroy another, you will destroy yourself. The smallest bees, when provoked by an injury, sting, and in stinging they leave behind their life. I do not force you to forget entirely—for perhaps it is worthwhile to remember so that at least at other times you may beware of the malicious. For he who has harmed once usually never forgives. Forgive freely, I pray, lest you both afflict yourself and he harm you again and again. His own evils necessarily await him. For fortune leaves nothing untouched, nor does fortune leave anything unhurt, nor does God leave anything unavenged.

# LETTERS, BOOK III.

->*He who undertakes many things errs much.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to a man who is curious and busy, sends greeting.<-

**I** see you, my friend, more anxious than I would wish. You are handling not only your own business, but even the business of others, as if you had already properly settled your own. Since we are tripped up and err in almost every single moment, there is no way more convenient for either attaining tranquility or avoiding errors than to think about a few excellent things, to speak even fewer and more select things, and to do the very fewest things—and those indeed as possible as they are honorable. They err and labor much who undertake many things by thinking, speaking, or doing; but most of all those who speak and do more than they have thought through.

->*He never satisfies art, he who is always satisfied by his own artifice.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to a vain craftsman, sends greeting.<-

**W**hatever you have said or done satisfies you very much, O too idle a craftsman. <note>The Latin "iners" implies a lack of skill or laziness in the higher sense of artistic striving.</note> Do you wish me to tell you the reason, by your kind leave? Because, of course, your mind perhaps grasps nothing more than what your tongue or hands have expressed. Oh, what a tiny mind it is, to which the tongue or hands are equal! Truly, wherever the mind (as is proper) surpasses its instruments and material, the work never satisfies the maker; indeed, he never satisfies art, he who is always satisfied by his own artifice. <note>Ficino expresses a core Renaissance idea: the artist's internal "idea" should always be more perfect than the physical object they produce.</note>

->*Love is the sole guardian of life, but love if you would be loved.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to a man seeking power, sends greeting.<-

**D**o you wish to live safe and secure? Beware lest men fear you too much, or utterly envy you. We have as many enemies as those who fear us, and as many as those who envy us. He whom many fear must fear many; he also serves very many, whom many serve. Any subject serves one; the master serves all. Love is the sole guardian of life, but love if you would be loved.

->*The loss of money seems heavy, but the loss of people is the heaviest.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Andrea Cambini, <note>Andrea Cambini was a Florentine historian and a close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note> his excellent fellow-countryman, sends greeting.<-

**W**hat is there to wonder at in love? Not being loved in return. What is impious? To love for one's own sake that which ought to be cherished for the sake of another, and conversely, to cherish for the sake of something else that which should be loved for its own sake. What is most foul? To hate one whom you had loved. In this we offend greatly: while we will not leave other things, however light, unless compelled by a heavy cause, yet we often both abandon and pursue a friend—that most precious treasure—induced by the slightest cause. Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who emphasized the sacred bond of friendship.</note> commands that we should not easily lose a friend for any reason, but rather bear with them as long as we can; and we can do so until we are forced to leave them entirely against our will. The loss of money seems heavy, but the loss of people is the heaviest. In human affairs, nothing is either more rarely acquired, more preciously possessed, or more unhappily and dangerously lost, than a friend.

->*Little should he be believed, who believes too much.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Salviati, Archbishop of Pisa, <note>Francesco Salviati (1443–1478) was a high-ranking cleric who was later famously involved in the Pazzi Conspiracy against the Medici.</note> sends greeting.<-

**V**enerable father, you ask why I trust so little in some who dwell among us? Because these men, venerable father, believe too much. The reasoning behind loving and trusting is very different: for we easily love a man much who easily loves much. However, we hardly place trust in one who hastily offers his trust to any man or judgment. Just as he falls more quickly who moves more quickly, so he is easily deceived who believes easily. But as it is rash and dangerous to suddenly believe too much in either the authority and words of anyone or in some thin piece of evidence, so it seems just as dangerous and irrational to reject a probable reason without a more certain reason. Finally, it is as impious, wicked, and miserable to be unwilling to believe in God without the assertion of reason. For God is reason itself, and there seems to be no need for another reason by which we should utterly assent to Reason itself.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO / On Duties.</header>

# MARSILIO FICINO

## On Duties.

->Marsilio Ficino to Cherubino Quarquallio, a most learned man, sends greetings.<-

**E**ven if I am sometimes perhaps less dutiful than is fitting, as is often the case for those occupied with philosophical studies, I cannot restrain myself at present from writing something about duty to the most dutiful of all men. If I were as dutiful in my arguments as you are in your actions, one would miss neither the subtlety of Panaetius <note>original: "Panetij"; Panaetius was a Stoic philosopher whose lost work "On Duty" served as the primary source for Cicero’s famous treatise of the same name.</note> nor the abundance of Cicero in this matter. I shall proceed, therefore, with a "thick Minerva" <note>original: "pingui Minerva"; a Latin idiom meaning to speak plainly or with common sense, rather than with polished or subtle refinement.</note>, since I can do no other for now. And so, to fulfill my own duty at last, I shall send these "duties of all" to the most dutiful of friends.

Duty is the proper action of each individual, preserving what is decorous and honorable, just as the matter, person, place, and time require.

The virtue and duty of the **Priest** is a certain wisdom burning with piety, and a piety shining with wisdom.

Of the **Prince**, it is circumspect providence, merciful justice, a highness that is humble, and a humility that is high.

Of the **Magistrate**, it is to remember that he is not the master of the law but its servant and the public guardian of the city; and furthermore, that he himself is judged by God while he judges men.

Of the **Private Citizen**, it is to obey the commands of the magistrates so willingly that he seems led by his own will rather than compelled by the necessity of the law.

Of the **Citizen**, whether he be a magistrate or a private person, the duty is a care for the public interest as diligent as his great love for his own.

Of the **Knight**, it is indeed fortitude in war, but magnificence in peace.

Of the **Merchant**, it is truthful faith and diligence in nourishing the city with external provisions while also sustaining himself.

Of the **Craftsman**, it is to justly distribute the provisions received from the merchant to the individual members of the city. Merchants and artisans and others should seek money in such a way that they harm no one. For whatever rises from evil eventually falls back into evil. They should also be so liberal that they do not seem to have sought gain in vain, nor merely for the sake of hoarding it. They should spend in such a way that they can spend for a long time, and be proven to have spent honorably and usefully.

Of the **Farmer**, it is to consult the weather and elder farmers regarding the timeliness of cultivation. Furthermore, he should offer the fruits of the field to his guests with as much faith and liberality as the field returns those fruits to him with interest.

Of the **Master**, it is to serve law and reason, so that he may rule his servants legitimately and rationally. He should consider that the servant is a human being just as much as the master. He should always mix humanity with dignity.

Of the **Servants**, it is to consider their life as belonging to the master, and the reason of the master as their own.

Of the **Husband**, it is to love his wife as if she were his own body and sense, and to lead her most carefully.

Of the **Wife**, it is to honor her prudent husband as her own soul and reason, and to follow him most willingly.

Of the **Father of the family**, it is to cherish his sons as offshoots of his own life, and to rule them like members of his body by his own best example.

Of the **Sons**, it is to follow the parent as their root and head, and to venerate him as a second God.

Of the **Brother**, it is to be moved toward his brother as if toward another self.

Of **Blood relatives**, it is to love one another as members of the same body.

Of **In-laws**, it is to remember that they are joined by law as if by a kind of nature, so that they ought to share their wealth and labor with one another.

Of **Friends**, it is to seek the truth through shared counsel and to pursue the good through shared help.

Of the **Teacher**, it is to procreate a learned and good student through his own teaching and goodness, as if he were a son of his mind. I desire, if it were permitted, to warn teachers not to forget that Aristotle kicked back against the divine Plato. <note>Ficino refers to the famous intellectual rivalry where Aristotle diverged from his teacher Plato's theories.</note>

Of the **Student**, it is to honor the preceptor as the father of his intelligence. He must take care, however, not to secretly soak up the master's vices.

Of the **Lawyer**, it is that he should be the most serious of all men, and should know that he who corrupts the sacred law must be punished with a more severe judgment, as a sacrilegious man, than he who counterfeits money.

Of the **Physician**, it is to consider, whenever he approaches the sick, that a life is at stake, so that he dares attempt nothing without reason and nothing without counsel.

Of the **Orator**, it is to have already persuaded himself of what he is about to persuade others.

Of the **Poet**, it is to have seen both nature and morals so that he may have the power to paint them.

Of the **Musician**, it is to imitate grace in sound and the elegance of speech in song. He should also remember that the movements of the soul ought to be in harmony much more than voices. For a musician is unrefined and a stranger to the Muses if his mind is in discord while his voice and lyre are in harmony. David and Mercury <note>King David (the biblical psalmist) and Hermes/Mercury (the mythical inventor of the lyre), whom Ficino often synchronized as figures of divine music.</note> command that, since we sing with God moving us, we should sing of God.

Of the **Philosopher**, it is to seek divine things more diligently so that he may enjoy them, and to examine natural things so that he may use them. He should be present for human affairs but not entangled in them. A singular philosopher should not blush for the sake of his country... <note>Ficino here references the differing political stances of Plato and Aristippus regarding the philosopher's duty to the state.</note> even the risk of his life is not forced by Plato and Aristippus, which indeed pleases me as well, because a philosopher becomes a philosopher even in an unwilling city that resists him...

<header>LETTERS, BOOK III,</header>

...and is a child of heaven, not of earth. Add to this that it seems entirely impious and wretched to lose a man who sees everything for the sake of the safety of the blind, who perhaps can never be saved.

The **Man** should beware lest he become in any way womanish. The **Woman** should strive to be, in a sense, manly <note>original: "uirilis"; here meaning possessing the strength of character or "virtù" associated with men in the Renaissance</note>, but especially modest. For as much as high-mindedness suits a man, so much does modesty suit a woman. The **Old Man** should see that he does not act childishly; let him remember that he was once young. The **Youth** should take care to be like his elders <note>original: "sit similis"; implying he should emulate the gravity of the old</note>, believe that he can grow old, and honor his seniors. It is the duty of the **Native** to cherish his fatherland as the father of his father and the mother of his mother, and whenever he must deal with foreigners, he should consider that he himself will one day be a traveler. The **Inhabitant and the Stranger** should know that they are alone, honor everyone, and hardly touch—let alone manage—the affairs of others. The **Fortunate Man** should know that the goods of fortune are only good for a good man, and that rains follow a clear sky. The **Unfortunate Man** should consider that the evils of fortune are only evil for an evil man, and after rainy days, he should expect clear ones. For we see that spring returns the leaves to the trees which winter took away. **Man** should consider—since he can never live contentedly among earthly things—that he is indeed a citizen of heaven but a mere inhabitant of the earth, so that he may strive to think, speak, or do nothing that would seem unbecoming for a citizen of the heavenly fatherland.

->*He who, placed at the summit, looks down upon the depths both sharply and mercifully, never falls to the lowest depths.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Cardinal Jacopo of Pavia.<-

**W**hile I was writing a certain philosophical letter on duties to our friend Cherubino Quarquagli, Cherubino himself, an exceptionally dutiful man, stood before me unexpectedly. "Behold, a messenger of health <note>original: "nuncius salutaris"; a play on the Latin "salus" which means both health and a greeting</note>," he said, "venerable father, he bids Marsilio be greeted again and again in your sacred name." Your messenger greeted us today with such good omens that he not only announced future health but granted it. Greetings, therefore, O my health and safety; may you always fare well under God, the eternal author of health. You seem to me to surpass both Argus <note>a giant from Greek myth with a hundred eyes</note> in his eyes and Lynceus <note>an Argonaut known for sight so sharp he could see through stone or underground</note> in his vision (if I may say so), you who from such a height have looked so far upon Marsilio, who is so humble and so small. I wish, venerable father, that just as you clearly see me, you might also see me as "illustrious" <note>original: "clarum"; playing on the double meaning of "vividly seen" and "famous/bright"</note>. Then I would be as well-known to all as all things are known to you. But so that both you and anyone else may see me as illustrious, I pray you look upon me favorably, as you have begun. Indeed, the astrologers claim that men are born and turn out fortunate by the favorable aspect of a lucky star. What can I give back for such a great favor of grace? I have nothing else at present except to add this, following the duties of individuals I have described step by step according to my talent. It is also the duty of Marsilio Ficino to love the Cardinal of Pavia ardently as a temple of the Graces, and to venerate him singularly as a fountain of the Muses. And having performed this one duty, I shall consider myself to have handled the subject of duties most dutifully. Furthermore, if you ever hear anything from your high place about this lowest little man, you have heard this one thing most of all (which is the greatest thing in him): that Marsilio Ficino is the oldest foster-son of the Medici house. Therefore, the Medici—both Castor and Pollux <note>the twin "Dioscuri" of myth, here used to refer to the leaders of the Medici family as Ficino's twin patrons</note>, my patrons—humbly commend me to you. And they believe that while I am commended to the Cardinal of Pavia, I am commended to all who are great, upright, and learned. February 8, 1476.

Our friend Cristoforo Landino <note>a famous humanist scholar and colleague of Ficino</note>, a man of singular learning and goodness, commends himself to you.

->*The ease of a life of vice is followed by difficulty; the difficulty of a life of virtue is followed by ease.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero, a most sincere man.<-

**J**ust as it is much more difficult to walk by a certain reason than to wander by chance, to ascend than to descend, to attempt new things than to handle the familiar, to hit the single center-point of a circle than to fall upon any of its other innumerable points, or to strike the target itself (that is, the mark) with an arrow than the things surrounding it; just as it is harder to keep to the path and the furrow than to stray this way and that, and to hold exactly to the straight line than to slip into the oblique—so much more difficult it is to act rightly than to transgress, and to be good than to be evil. The evidence of this fact is that we all err daily, while rarely and few of us act honorably and justly. Nevertheless, the divine law pays back two benefits for this great difficulty of virtue. First, that virtues [are] so... <note>the sentence continues on the next page</note>

...they are linked together, so that he who attains one, follows and attains them all. Vices, however, on the contrary, are so repugnant to each other that they cannot all exist in the same person at once. For how can someone be both a miser and a spendthrift at the same time? Or both more bold and more fearful? Secondly, that supreme ease and pleasure of life follow that first difficulty of budding virtue. And a brief struggle leads to an everlasting reward. The ease of vice, however, is soon followed by the difficulty of a miserable life and perpetual pain. Hence that symbol of Pythagoras: *Do not touch the animal with the black tail.* <note>A Pythagorean "symbolon" or riddle. Ficino interprets it as a warning against the dark consequences of vice which "blackens" the soul.</note> That is, flee vice, which is followed by the blackness of the mind and the affliction of the will. Farewell, most brilliant Nero. And since you have already attained virtue through difficulty and ease of life through virtue, so that you may gain happiness from there, remember how arduous and laborious it is to retrace your steps from the vast precipice of vices and to escape to the upper airs <note>original: "superasque evadere ad auras"; a famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid (VI, 128-129) regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>, so that no one is able to ascend here, unless he whom impartial Jupiter has loved, and whom burning virtue has then carried up to the heavens.

->*Just as beauty naturally begets love, so love, through opinion, regenerates beauty.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to Jacopo, Cardinal of Pavia. <note>Jacopo Ammannati Piccolomini (1422–1479), a prominent humanist and cardinal known as "Il Papiense."</note>

**A**t the very moment Cherubino Quarquagli <note>A close friend and frequent messenger for Ficino's correspondence.</note> greeted me in your name the other day, that letter of ours flew to you at almost the same instant. For the most burning affection of my heart, suddenly set ablaze by the rays and flames of your name, drove my hand to write before my mind could dictate what I should chiefly say. So it is no wonder if what we wrote so quickly appears very slight. Indeed, the logic of nature is one thing, and the logic of speech another: for nature, the lighter something is, the faster it moves; but in speech, on the contrary, the faster it is, the lighter <note>Ficino plays on the double meaning of "levis"—meaning both physically light/fast and intellectually slight/trivial.</note> it seems. But remember, venerable father (I know what I am saying), that you recently received a letter from me that was not the daughter of counsel, but of love. Since it is not hidden from you that anything should be received in the same spirit it is sent, you received it, I believe, not so much with counsel as with love. Especially since you created it from the beginning with a certain immense love toward me. Water produced the fish; water catches them. A plant grows with the same moisture from which it sprouted. Our letter was born long ago from love; your love, which created it, now embraces it; in embracing it, it wonderfully nourishes it; and in nourishing it, it regenerates its beauty for you. Truly, just as beauty naturally begets love, so love in turn, through opinion, actually regenerates beauty. But indeed, Marsilio, in what way do you think your writings are read with love rather than counsel by that man who is himself (so to speak) counsel? Because, clearly, if he is Counsel itself, he is also Love itself. Therefore, as much as he looks into what is offered to him with the rays of his mind, so much does he penetrate it from every side with the flames of his heart; as sharply and acutely as he perceives, so sweetly and kindly does he always interpret. Just as cold accompanies darkness, so heat follows light everywhere. Again, sweetness follows heat when it is surrounded by a sharp flavor. In nature, sweetness overcomes sharpness when perfected by heat; in a man perfected by virtue, indulgence overcomes judgment. Hail, therefore, my counsel. Hail again, my love. I pray that you freely give counsel to your Marsilio (where there is need). Love your friend everywhere. Marsilio will consult you like an oracle in more serious matters. In every single thing, he will honor you. February 9, 1476.

->*Pious things befit the pious.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to the poet Naldo Naldi, greetings. <note>Naldo Naldi (1436–1513) was a Neo-Latin poet and a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>

**A**lthough I can give nothing old to him to whom I have long ago given all my things along with myself, I now give you a new little gift: this is the volume recently composed by me concerning the pious faith <note>original: "de pia fide"; likely referring to Ficino's major work "On the Christian Religion" (De Christiana Religione).</note>. Not that I think there is any need for these pious words for a man who abounds in pious works, or for this kind of faith of mine for a man who is powerful in knowledge. But lest, while I discourse on faith and piety, I myself should seem less faithful and pious, if in the meantime I should be unmindful of a pious and faithful friend. February 13, 1476.

## Pious things befit the pious.
->Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti send greetings to Amerigo Corsini,<-
->a man most distinguished in letters and character.<-

**W**e send to you, our friend—more faithful than faith itself—our volume *On Pious Faith*. <note>original: "de pia fide uolumen." This refers to Ficino's work *De Christiana Religione* (On the Christian Religion), which he often circulated among friends.</note> We do this not because we judge that a man who already excels in faith and charity has need of such disputations, but so that in this book, as if in a mirror, you might most pleasantly contemplate the beautiful countenance of your own faith and love.

## *If we clearly perceived how ugly and how sick a depraved soul is, we would not sin.*
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the magnanimous Giuliano de' Medici.<-

**Y**ou remember, sweetest Giuliano, while we were keeping watch together this past night, that we happened by chance upon these words: how ugly is a head without hair, and how ugly is a face without a beard. From this, a little later, a certain "Lenten declamation" <note>original: "declamatiuncula... quadragesimalis." A light-hearted reference to the style of sermons preached during Lent, which often focused on the themes of repentance and the ugliness of sin.</note> arose in me, perhaps suited to these current days. I only wish it may seem as well-groomed and "bearded" to you as you seem beautiful to me, both inwardly and in your very skin. Just as deformity is more hideous in the face than in the hand, and a disease in the heart is more pestilential than in the feet, so too the foulness and sickness in the souls of wicked and shameful men is more abominable and foul than the collective deformity and plague of all bodies. If we were able to perceive with our eyes, or even fully imagine in our minds, the filthy and horrendous image of a wicked mind, we would certainly sin only very rarely and lightly, and we would flee nothing more distantly than the sight of an evil mind. 

The comparison between the beauty of the soul and the beauty of the body is nearly the same. For if that inner beauty were perceived even for a moment by the eyes or the mind, it would allure more charmingly, seize more greedily, and delight happy lovers more vehemently than any singular physical beauty could entice lost and miserable lovers. Why did the wise men inscribe "Know thyself" <note>original: "noſce teipſum"; the famous Delphic maxim (Greek: Gnothi Seauton).</note> upon the temple of Apollo? It was so that you might look up at your pure mind as an eternal ray of the true Phoebus <note>Apollo as the sun god.</note>—that is, the super-celestial Sun—enveloped in the cloud of the body; and so that you might recognize that the brightness of the cloud depends on the ray, and the splendor of the ray depends on the Sun. Thus, you should praise the body within the soul, but honor the soul within the body. Again, you should love and cherish the soul in God. Indeed, you should love and venerate God in the soul, but wonder and be struck with awe at Him in Himself. When our leader and teacher Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> came to know himself and God within himself, he immediately exclaimed: "Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new; late have I loved you." <note>original: "Sero te amaui pulchritudo tàm antiqua, & tàm noua, ſero te amaui." A famous passage from Augustine's *Confessions* (X, 27.38).</note>

---

## *Nothing is more shameful than a man who has everything beautiful except his soul.*
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the Human Race.<-

**I**f any farmer, not only without any reward but even to his own great loss, should cultivate the fields of others while neglecting his own, he would undoubtedly be judged most foolish and miserable by everyone. Therefore, those minds are exceedingly insane and wretched which always expend all their effort in this: that the body and external things be as well-off and as highly decorated as possible, while they utterly neglect to ensure that they themselves are good and adorned. Oh, how bad is the man whose dog and horse are better than his soul! Oh, how deformed is he whose shoe, as far as it is in his power, is more beautiful than his soul! Truly nothing is good or beautiful to this man, in whose eyes everything except himself—that is, except his soul—appears good and beautiful. 

If some Cynic philosopher <note>Ficino likely refers to the anecdote of Diogenes of Sinope, who reportedly spat in a wealthy man's face because the house was so clean he could find no other "filthy" place to spit.</note> were to enter the highly decorated house of such a man and were compelled by necessity to spit, he would certainly spit in the man's face, because he would see that everything there was clean and adorned except the man himself. Nothing is poorer or emptier than he whose granaries are full, but whose soul is empty. We are accustomed to call those who are "outside their mind" demented. <note>A play on words: "de-mente" literally means "out of mind."</note> But how a soul can be "in" a demented person when it has long since been "in the serving-dishes," <note>original: "in patinis." A Latin idiom for being obsessed with gluttony or physical luxury.</note> I do not understand. Tell me, I pray, oh unhappy soul—as curious about the affairs of others as you are negligent of your own—tell me, I say, to which of men are all things healthy, except to the healthy? Why then, insane one, do you wander so anxiously here and there outside yourself, and labor so much and so much in vain?

<meta>The catchword "Da ope" (Give help) indicates the start of the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page contains three short philosophical letters by Ficino emphasizing that moral and spiritual health are far more important than physical appearance or wealth. He uses the metaphors of the mirror, the sun's ray, and a clean house to argue for the cultivation of the soul over the body.</summary>

<keywords>soul, beauty, virtue, Neoplatonism, Giuliano de' Medici, St. Augustine, self-knowledge, Delphic maxim, Amerigo Corsini, moral philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the moral reflections of Marsilio Ficino, transitioning from general advice about the soul to a specific philosophical letter addressed to the Venetian diplomat Bernardo Bembo regarding the nature of Fortune and Divine Providence.</meta>

Take care that you are good and beautiful, and suddenly all things will be good and beautiful to you. But you will only fulfill what I command if you desire to become good and beautiful as much as you strive for your smallest pieces of furniture to be of the best quality and to appear most ornate. If, while we feed our bodies, our dogs, and our birds, we did not meanwhile let the human being itself—that is, the soul—perish from hunger, surely everyone would live as content and full as no one is content now. But now, who would wonder if the soul is never filled, if it is always afflicted, when it abandons itself? Its only care is to fill its own beast <note>Ficino uses "beast" to refer to the lower, animalistic appetites of the human body.</note>, which becomes more voracious in its very fullness, and becomes more savage and robust against its master, who, through his own negligence, is utterly starving and bloodless.

### For the bad, good fortune is bad; but for the good, bad fortune is good.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to Bernardo Bembo,<-
->the most distinguished Venetian knight.<-

**T**ell me, steadfast man, for what reason does fortune hate and often depress the one whom the people deservedly love, while on the contrary she more often loves and extols the one whom the people rightly hate? Is it perhaps because fortune is not only opposed to reason, but has also been an enemy to the people from the very beginning of the world? Whence the people are always unfortunate and miserable. Perhaps she is also ambitious. And so that any great deed may be ascribed not to the virtue of men or their race, but to herself alone, she extols in wondrous ways the one whom as many men as possible rightly want brought low; but the one who is sublime, she casts down into the depths. What if she is blind, as they say, or a rival of nature? Since nature ordained that you live as an animal before you live as a human—for you feel before you understand—Fortune, likewise, affects to make a "great man," but first she makes a "huge beast" swollen with poisonous pride. 

Whence a <term>tyrant</term> <note>In the Renaissance sense, a tyrant is one who rules by passion and self-interest rather than law and reason.</note> is born in character and countenance before he even gains his tyranny. These men, placed in positions of dignity beyond their worth, ensure that those very dignities are no longer worthy of honorable men. They even cause it to be believed at times that neither divine providence governs the world, nor human prudence governs the human race, but rather chance. Truly, however, <term>Divine Providence</term> <note>The belief that God actively guides the universe toward good, often contrasted with 'Fortune' or random luck.</note> sometimes, contrary to all favor of fortune, suddenly casts others down from the highest peak to the bottom. Others, against the malignant impulse of fortune, it wonderfully raises to the heights. 

But if Providence permits the proud to stand for a long time, or the humane to fall for a season, it also permits the former to have a mind as dejected and miserable as their fortune is perhaps high; and the latter to have a mind as exalted as their fortune is humble and abject. Indeed, for the bad, good fortune becomes bad, but for the good, bad fortune becomes good. Truly, if the choice were given to me, I would rather be <term>Hercules</term> than <term>Sardanapalus</term>. <note>Hercules represents the life of virtuous struggle and labor, while Sardanapalus, a legendary Assyrian king, represents the ultimate extreme of luxury, decadence, and effeminacy.</note> As much as the one crushed monsters, the other was oppressed by monsters; the one, having overcome wild beasts, emerged as a God; the other, overcome by beasts, was made worse and more miserable than a beast. 

Where there is the most wisdom, there is the least need for luck; where there is the least wisdom, luck dominates the most. And if sometimes fortune is joined to wisdom, they do not both rule at once. For either luck is in no way joined to reason, or it serves it. For this reason, luck, envious of honorable men, resists with all its strength so that right reason may not rule anywhere—seeing as, if reason were ruling, luck would lose both its glory and its empire. Often luck endows much to the one whom nature or virtue has endowed little. Nor does it easily enrich the one whom nature or virtue has enriched. There are in certain ages some great and powerful men, like certain human gods and divine men—rarer than the <term>Phoenix</term>—whom not fortune, but divine providence makes great. These are discerned by a certain sign. For they are such that they attribute nothing of their prosperity to luck, and very little to human virtue, but as much as possible to divine virtue. And they are as humane in countenance toward all as they are divine in mind above all. 

If where there is swelling there is no health, surely no one who is "puffed up" is sane; no one who is insane and profane is not beast-like; no one who is divine is not humane; and no one is most humane who is not divine. Certainly, the divine man does not want fortune as his leader, for she is blind and often falls by chance. He does not rejoice in the promises of fortune, for she is unfaithful even to her own, whom she has raised to the highest peak of dignity beyond their merit. Indeed, she rejoices in a reciprocal game between the highest and the lowest, and delights in alternating turns. He also does not fear the threats of fortune, for they are vain. Nor can she do more against us than we wish her to be able to do, "when we make you, Fortune, a goddess and place you in heaven." <note>Ficino is quoting the Roman satirist Juvenal: "If we had wisdom, you would have no divinity, Fortune; it is we who make you a goddess and place you in heaven."</note> No one is more miserable than he who places true happiness in fortune... 

<summary>Ficino writes to Bernardo Bembo to explain why "Fortune" seems to favor the wicked, concluding that true happiness and greatness come from Divine Providence and a virtuous soul, which can turn even "bad" luck into a benefit.</summary>
<keywords>Fortune vs. Providence, Bernardo Bembo, Hercules, Sardanapalus, Virtue, Tyranny, Neoplatonism, Human Soul</keywords>

--- Page 761 ---
<meta>This page continues the conclusion of a letter to Bernardo Bembo (addressed here as "Aeneas") regarding the mastery of Fortune through virtue, and introduces a new philosophical letter to Lorenzo de' Medici concerning the soul's hunger for eternal truths.</meta>

...tune. No one is more fortunate than he who does not judge accidental prosperity to be truly happy. He who either laughs at the ridiculous weeping of fortune along with Democritus <note>The "laughing philosopher" of Greece, known for mocking human follies.</note>, or weeps at her mournful laughter with Heraclitus <note>The "weeping philosopher," known for his melancholy view of the changing world.</note>, is judged wise by Hippocrates. He who tramples upon the childish game of fortune with Socrates is judged wise and divine by Apollo. Finally, he who, like Aeneas <note>Ficino often addresses his friends with classical nicknames; here he compares the recipient's struggles to the epic journey of Virgil's hero, Aeneas.</note> in times of adversity, alone preserves himself for favorable things like Aeneas, looks up at the serene days after the rain, and at last takes possession of the longed-for Italy: Therefore, my Aeneas, *do not yield to misfortunes, but go against them more boldly* <note>original: "ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito" — a famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid.</note>. Therefore, *every fortune must be overcome by enduring it* <note>original: "superanda omnis fortuna ferendo" — another Virgilian maxim.</note>. Farewell more joyfully, my Aeneas. For you will one day enjoy as many good things in a safe harbor as you have bravely overcome storms at sea.

---

->*The soul of mortals is not filled, because it seeks eternal things.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.

**I**f I now recite to you, Lorenzo, a certain little Lenten declamation <note>Ficino refers to a "quadragesimalem," a short sermon or reflection suitable for the forty days of Lent.</note> which my mind declaimed to me this dawn, behold, what will it be worth? Perhaps only to move you to as much laughter at my follies in the present as the most skillful preachers usually squeeze tears from the common people in these days. Nevertheless, I shall recite it just as it seems to me, Lorenzo. For I know that a man distinguished by piety, although he might perhaps sometimes laugh at words of piety in a certain way, cannot truly mock piety itself.

"Marsilio, he who thirsts for wine extinguishes his thirst, as you see, with wine. And more so if he drains two cups than if he drains one. To such a man, the image of wine—whether seen or thought of—incites rather than settles the thirst. For it is the nature of the image to allure, and of the substance to feed. Therefore, the image of wine nourishes thirst just as much as wine itself nourishes a thirsty man. This is indicated to us by the punishment of Tantalus <note>In myth, Tantalus was punished with eternal thirst and hunger; water and fruit would recede whenever he tried to reach them.</note>; or rather, by our own punishment, for we are all Tantaluses. We all indeed thirst for true goods, but we all drink dreams. While we gulp down the lethal waves of the river Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> with full throats, meanwhile we barely lick a certain shadowy taste of nectar and ambrosia <note>The food and drink of the gods, representing divine wisdom.</note> with the tips of our lips. Whence a panting thirst continually burns us miserable Tantaluses. If we were to take possession of such things as the mind can grasp, surely in the taking, the soul would eventually be filled, either entirely or for the most part. But since the more we possess of mortal things everywhere, the more the soul's appetite is inflamed, it is clear enough that the mind seeks not mortal things—which are but images of the eternal—but the eternal things themselves. Therefore, the soul is eternal and not perishable, since its true nourishment is eternal. In a perishable body it dozes deeply and grows sick; in this body, drinking dreams through the senses, it nourishes its thirst by drinking, but not itself. The soul, sick because of its passions, rests nowhere in its misery, but wanders restlessly and in vain everywhere. Where it trusts it might lie down softly, it falls deeply; where it hopes for a more healthful medicine, it drains a more deadly poison. O miserable lot of mortals, more miserable than misery itself! To where, then, shall we poor wretches flee? Certainly nowhere, unless we flee from the lowest things to the highest—unless we flee to those things which never flee away. What then must be done, so that we may both wake and be well? Our life must be turned exactly to the opposite. We must unlearn what we have learned from the common crowd—through the learning of which we have hitherto been ignorant of ourselves. We must learn what we have neglected—for while these things are unknown, we cannot know ourselves. We must love what we neglect, and neglect what we love; we must endure what we flee, and flee what we follow. We must weep for the laughter of fortune, and laugh at the weeping of fortune. For thus neither the filth of the common crowd will defile us, nor will the neglect of the immortals harm us, nor the curiosity of mortals torment us. Neither will softness cast us down, nor pleasure dissolve us. Nor will fortune ensnare us when prosperous, nor kill us when adverse. But the more purified we are, the more serene we shall be; and the more serene we are, the more we shall shine. Then first do we emerge full of true forms <note>In Platonic thought, "Forms" are the eternal, perfect archetypes of reality.</note>, when first we are emptied of dreams."

# MARSILIO FICINO

->Not the husk, but the marrow nourishes.<- <note>A favorite metaphor of Ficino’s, suggesting that the inner spiritual meaning of a text is more important than its outward literary form.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the most distinguished Francesco Guasconi.

**I** give to you our *Religion* <note>original: "religionem nostram" — Ficino refers to his book *De Christiana religione* (On the Christian Religion), likely a recently completed copy.</note>, a pledge of religious love. I do so not to instruct a man already distinguished by his piety, but because I believe that with this one gift I shall satisfy Piety herself more than with all my other disputations. If by chance this *Religion* of ours seems very poor to you, remember that the Christian religion was founded in poverty. Remember, furthermore, that among us there are not so much "presses" <note>original: "expressores" — a play on words regarding the newly invented printing press (from *exprimere*, to press out/print).</note> of books as there are "oppressors." Yet, whatever its quality may be, since there is nothing in a beloved thing that does not please the lover, it will seem beautiful and rich enough to its lover, Guasconi. May 20, 1475. Florence.

---

->*Those things which are truly good are better the greater they are.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Bonincontri, Astronomer and Poet, sends greetings.

**I** cannot say with how much pleasure I was affected in reading your letters, most distinguished Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Bonincontri (1410–1491) was a famous wandering scholar, poet, and astrologer who taught in Florence.</note>. In them, I certainly find nothing to criticize, even though you offer many excuses for them. But what did I just say, my Lorenzo? Rather, I criticize nothing where every single detail pleases me exceedingly. Therefore, to speak more correctly, nothing in your letters pleases me more than that which you most suspect might please me less. I mean your prolixity <note>Verbosity or long-windedness.</note>, my friend, or rather, your sobriety. For those things which are truly good are better the greater they are. You bring to us a most weighty judgment between three powers: namely, between Providence, Fate, and Liberty <note>The classic philosophical problem of how God's plan (Providence), the stars/destiny (Fate), and human Free Will (Liberty) interact.</note>. You have heard that the judgment between three goddesses was once brought to Paris. I, however, would not wish to offend such powers in so great a conflict. *The judgment of Paris remains stored deep in the mind, as does the injury to her slighted beauty* <note>original: "Manet alta mente repostum iudicium Paridis spreteq; iniuria formae" — a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* regarding Juno’s grudge against the Trojans.</note>. But perhaps no further danger remains. You yourself seem to have delivered a most cautious opinion on these matters. For you did not foolishly separate these powers, as some are accustomed to do, but joined them together most aptly. We confirm your opinion more extensively in our book *On the Astrologers* <note>Ficino refers to his work *Disputatio adversus astrologiam divinatricem* (Disputation Against Divinatory Astrology).</note>.

---

->*Many things cannot be firmly joined together in that thing which is itself mutable and diverse.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Lottieri Neroni, sends greetings.

**I** embrace your learned and pious letters, Lottieri, with a certain supreme joy, especially in that part where you kindly embrace me in that Good which encompasses all things. You have often read that <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle.</note> principle: *Whatever things are the same as a certain third thing, are also the same as each other.* This, however, seems to me to be fulfilled only when that "third thing" is inwardly identical to itself—that is, individual, simple, and permanent. Otherwise, it could not join together and firm up the things that return to it. But let us explain what we mean with a clear example. As long as lines remain in an individual and immobile center, they each stand within themselves as undivided and unmoving, and they are either entirely the same as one another or joined together. But when they are drawn out from the center toward a divisible and moving circumference, they gradually become more divided and mutable within themselves, and are rendered disjoined from one another. If, in turn, they are folded back from that circumference into the center again, they will immediately be seen to recover their prior unity and stability. We ought to consider God in the center, the heavens and the elements in the circumference, and finally, souls and minds in the lines. Why then does the common crowd boast daily of a false benevolence? "I have been entirely yours for a long time," says one; "I, in turn, will always be yours," says another; yet another dares to say, "I and you are entirely one and the same." Oh, how false men are, how deceptive! Truly, while they themselves, falling from the stable unity of God, plunge entirely into the mutable, manifold, and divisible machinery of the world, and thus do not retain natural stability and unity within themselves, they nonetheless—insanely and shamelessly—promise to others that which they have lost and miserably squandered. Let them cease, therefore, to profess a mutual benevolence for one another...

The very same thing both happens and remains, so long as those who love are not themselves as they boast to be to others, and do not love in that thing which is also not such. It never gathers, nor fixes souls for themselves and others, except for unity itself—that simple and immovable eternity which most greatly embraces all things, inasmuch as they are most especially its own. ->Cupid persuades more even by remaining silent, than Mercury does by pleading or Phoebus himself by singing.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Domenico Galletti, sends greetings.<-

If the Muse supplied me with as much material as the love I have for you, my Domenico <note>Domenico Galletti was a poet and secretary to the Pope.</note>, stimulates me daily to write, you would certainly read "Greetings, Galletti" in our name as often as you yourself desire to be well. However, the material that the envious Muse has long denied us is now suggested by Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s closest friend, often described as his "unique friend" and the interlocutor in his *De Amore*.</note>, that sweet nursling of the Muses. He confesses that he owes you much because of our friendship, since I, having loved you first as one older than him, learned through that to love him both ardently and steadfastly. But if my love were as great in its power to perform services as it is in its feeling, you would in turn recognize that you owe a great deal to Cavalcanti. Truly, since he meets us everywhere as someone most similar to you and most loving, it results that in loving him, I do not unlearn how to love Domenico. Therefore, that God <note>Likely referring to Love/Cupid in a Neoplatonic sense, or the Divine generally.</note> commends Cavalcanti’s cause to you, without whom nothing is ever commended anywhere either quickly or successfully. Heavenly Galletti, you—as a soldier of Cupid—often experience that he persuades before he even urges. Moreover, he persuades much more vehemently even by remaining silent than Mercury does by pleading or Phoebus himself by singing. Is this any wonder? For those gods pour "flying words" from the outside at the doors of the mind's ears. But he, from within, brands the very heart with the indelible marks of burning thoughts. But I leave these amorous matters to you poets. I come now to the cause common to our Giovanni and ourselves.

->T H E   E N D.<-

# THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO
## of Florence,
### BOOK IV.

->There is no one who could be envied by a man who is able to see how we are all driven, within and without, by the Furies.<-

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Lorenzo Francesco, son of Domenico, sends greetings.<-

Pythagoras commanded his disciples "not to eat the brain or the heart." <note>A famous Pythagorean "symbolon" or cryptic maxim. Ficino provides an allegorical interpretation here.</note> That is, they should not consume their brains with superfluous thoughts, nor burn their hearts with immoderate cares. If all things happen by fortune, those who strive to define and arrange with certain reason those things which happen beyond reason in innumerable ways labor in vain. If all things arrive by fate, those who struggle to avoid the inevitable necessity of this fate fall into it all the more heavily, for they add their own labor to fate. Finally, whether our affairs are said to proceed by fortune or by fate, Divine Providence arranges irrational fortune into a rational order, and even tempers harsh fate most sweetly toward the good, so that all things turn out ordered and good for those who willingly consent to the Divine Will. For these people alone, internal and external things are in harmony; for all others, both are everywhere in discord. These people alone make voluntary that which is necessary, and make good those things which seem evil. Just as—

<page-num>752</page-num>
# MARSILIO FICINO

Just as the pure mind rejoices in the universal good, so the impure mind is afflicted by all evils. As the greatest light draws all lights to itself, so the greatest evil on earth—that is, the evil man—draws all evils to himself from every side. Indeed, he inflicts much more upon himself than he receives from elsewhere. Just as we are insatiable for what is good, so, in some strange way, we are almost insatiable for what is evil. We do not so much feel present evils as we increase them; we repeat those of the past, we anticipate those of the future, and we imagine those that will never be. I will pass over the perverse mind with which we endure adversity; do we not also so abuse prosperity that our very happiness becomes most unhappy for us? The success of external things is nothing other than the excess of reason and law.

Furthermore, what is health of the body to us but the insanity of the mind? <note>Ficino often argues that physical health and vigor can distract the soul from spiritual contemplation.</note> Every form of beauty and strength in the body often becomes the deformity and weakness of the soul. O, how deformed we are whenever we rush, ourselves deformed, into those things which God makes beautiful! Alas, how ungrateful we are to God, the giver of all good things, whenever we condemn His works and His governance. And the more our barns overflow with His good harvests, the more we produce thorns and tares within ourselves, carrying them both at home and abroad. And although we produce and sow these evils, we are nevertheless surprised if we ever reap the worst from them; yet we do not blame our own "agriculture," but the stars or God. <note>original: "agriculturam, sed astra Deumue culpamus." Ficino frequently defends the idea of human free will against a strict belief in astrological determinism.</note> 

There is no one, therefore, who could be envied by one who is able to see how much we are all driven by furies, both within and without. It is difficult to discern in one's own country who among others is the happier; it is even more difficult to discern abroad who is the more miserable. The measure is nearly equal in both places: there, individuals rejoice to the highest degree; here, we individuals grieve to the highest degree. Unless we are altogether blind, we ought to see clearly from this that our seed, <term>sementem</term> <note>seed: here referring to the Neoplatonic idea of the divine spark or "rational seeds" implanted in the soul by God.</note> since it fares so poorly on earth, is not earthly but heavenly; and if it is rightly cultivated, it will produce heavenly fruits.

->*When you have satisfied reason and counsel, consider that you have satisfied everyone.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher.

**I** hear you are much disturbed because the things you know you have done with certain reason are condemned by many. Do you value yourself so highly, my friend? Do you wish those who do not spare God to spare a man? What can be done that is more beautiful or better than those things which are done by God, who is the highest Reason? Yet, divine works are everywhere disparaged. We shudder at demons, we accuse the stars, we condemn the seasons. We also disparage the forms and powers of plants and animals; we criticize men and complain incessantly about our lot. The things we have received freely from God displease us; the things we have done ourselves please us to such an extent that we displease God. 

I pray that you strive as follows: as much as your new works—being your own offspring <note>original: "fœtus proprij." Intellectual works were often described as the "children" of the author's mind.</note>—suddenly flatter you, so much should you obey reason and submit to counsel. Once you have satisfied diligent reason and the approved counsel of prudent men, consider that you have satisfied all men. For in this way, you have satisfied Truth itself, which is greater than all. But if, even then, the things you have thought, said, or done by such reason are disapproved of somewhere, remember that it is a sign of good food to displease a foul palate, and a proof of bad food to please a foul palate. Farewell, and once your will has followed right reason, do not be disturbed if anything follows beyond your will.

->*He is wise in vain who is not wise for himself.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to a Moral Philosopher without Morals, sends greetings.

**H**ow absurd is a cobbler with a coat torn everywhere, or how unskilled a doctor who is always sick? How annoying is a musician whose lyre is out of tune with his voice? Just so base is a moral philosopher who is "un-moraled." <note>original: "Moralis Philosophus non moratus." Ficino is making a pun on "moralis" (the study of morals) and "moratus" (having good character/manners). He is criticizing a teacher of ethics who has no personal ethics.</note> He who speaks well but acts badly speaks good things in vain, whether to men who do not believe him, or to the powers above who will not grant him good things.

### The medicine for worldly evils is the worship of the super-worldly God.

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, the most illustrious Venetian knight. Greetings.

**S**ince the celestial father of men established that heaven would be our homeland, while we dwell upon the earth—a region most remote from our homeland—we can never be truly content. This lot is common not only to humans but indeed to all created things: that they may find rest nowhere except in their own place of origin. For the sake of rest, they strive to reach the end where they had their beginning. Thus water and earth descend to the depths, while fire and air seek the heights; thus moles and similar creatures hide themselves in the womb of the earth. Many other creatures tread upon the back of the earth. Fish, born of water, swim in water. But the souls of men, by a certain common and natural instinct, continually yearn for heaven, and further still for the King of Heaven, from whom they are created. Since this natural desire for God, infused in us by God, must not be in vain—lest the highest Reason, which does nothing without purpose, should have infused it in us fruitlessly—it follows that the minds of men are eternal, so that they may eventually reach the eternal and divine good desired by their nature.

From what we have said, it follows that since souls are never filled by earthly nourishment, nor can they feast upon celestial banquets while they gorge themselves on earthly things, they should strive in this life to cling to the King of Heaven with all their strength. For they are stained less by the bitter flavors of the earth and refreshed more by the sweet liquids of heaven the more greedily they are drawn toward the super-celestial fountain of sweetness. The closer we approach the Lord of the world, the further we depart from worldly slavery. However, just as we cling to Him in our homeland by seeing and rejoicing, so outside our homeland we do so by loving and adoring.

Therefore, no sufficient medicine is found anywhere against earthly diseases except for divine love and worship. And this is not without reason. Surely in any sickness, when the medicine does not overcome the quality of the "bad humor," it is converted into that humor itself, disturbs the body, diminishes strength, and increases the weight of the illness. Since, therefore, all our infirmity and adversity is bodily and worldly, whoever attempts to assist such an evil with bodily and worldly medicines undoubtedly labors in vain. Believe me, there is need here for a much stronger medicine—a medicine, I say, which is both spiritual and above the world, so that it may be able to expel bodily and worldly diseases. If we suffered only from this or that specific ailment, perhaps this or that physician would suffice for us. But our plague is "every evil." Therefore, our <term>theriac</term> <note>original: "tiriaca"; an ancient "universal" medicinal ointment or potion used as an antidote to poison, here used metaphorically for a spiritual cure-all</note> is "every good." Our disease is an insatiable appetite and continual disturbance; therefore, our physician is the immense Good and eternal tranquility. If anyone denies that our medicine is the true worship of God, no remedy for evils remains for him, and all hope of health is taken away. But he who truly trusts in divine remedies recovers as soon as he trusts.

->*We ought to consider not what anyone gives, but with what spirit they give it.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Giorgio Antonio Vespucci, an excellent and most learned citizen. Greetings.

**I** give to you my volume on true piety—not to instruct a man distinguished in piety toward piety, but because I think that by this one gift, more than by all my disputations, I shall satisfy Piety herself. I shall also satisfy my pious friend, as I believe, who, since he always burns with pious affection, measures that affection in all things rather than the effect. For he knows truly that in external things there is nothing great. Again, he knows that in a great affection, nothing is not great. He also knows that nothing great is ever given by one who never wished to give anything greater than what he gave. Conversely, he knows that nothing small is given by one for whom, compared to his desire for something greater, whatever he bestows is small. Finally, he knows that one must look not so much at the hand as the heart of the giver. And as much as the one desires to bestow, so much the other confesses he owes. For even if it is not received by the hand immediately, it is nevertheless accepted by our soul as soon as whatever the friend desired to hand over becomes known to us. He who can give new things every day never bestows anything excellent; only he gives the most excellent things to whom nothing remains to give anew...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...must be attributed, since he has once given himself and all his own things along with him. To put it briefly, we either give nothing, or we give everything. He who gives us some object but not his soul <note>original: "animum"</note> does not offer a gift; he either commends a deposit to our care, or he buys us, or perhaps he is hunting us. But he who gives the mind—which possesses all things—bestows everything all at once. **Farewell.**
