->*Just as it is shameful to love money, so it is honorable to love a human being, and so it is also necessary and blessed to love God.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Piero Guicciardini <note>Piero (1454–1513) was a prominent Florentine statesman and the father of the famous historian Francesco Guicciardini.</note>, most distinguished in letters and character. **Greetings.**<-

**J**ust as it is shameful to love money, so it is honorable to love a human being who is most worthy of love. No one doubts—provided they have ever loved anything—that a lover takes himself away from himself and gives himself to the beloved. Money can certainly receive the person who loves it, but it can never give him back to himself. Thus it happens that a lover of this kind possesses neither the money nor himself. However, he who loves a person who loves him back receives himself back in return just as much as he gave himself to the other while loving. Indeed, to speak more accurately, he receives himself back twofold; for in this way, he who had given one soul <note>original: "animum"</note> receives two. Again, just as it seems honorable and useful to love a man worthy of goodwill, so it is necessary and blessed to love God, the first origin of love and beauty. Without His heat, no one can love anything; without His splendor, nothing can be loved. Farewell, be happy, and commend me to your father Jacopo, a most illustrious citizen. March 1st, 1476. Florence.

---

->*As each person is in himself, so are the things which he receives.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini and Giovanni Pietro Cortusio of Padua, his fellow philosophers. **Greetings.**<-

**I**t is not an evil to fall into those things which are commonly called "evils," unless you are worthy of evil things. For no one suffers evil except an evil man. It is not a good to possess those things which are called "goods," unless you are worthy of good things. For no one enjoys good things except a good man. Internal things do not depend on external ones, but rather external things depend on internal ones. As each person is in himself, so are the things which he receives. We cannot complain so much about luck <note>original: "forte," often translated as "fate" or "fortune"</note> as we can about our own choice. We think of evil things continually, and so evils agitate us on every side. We follow evil things daily, and so evils deservedly follow us. We practice cruelty a great deal, and cruelty in turn "exercises" us. We flee from mercy, and mercy also flees from us. The more we voluntarily flee from human justice, the more divine justice pursues us against our will. Punishment for a crime is found within the crime itself; the reward for a good deed is in the good itself. If we only do good things tomorrow, we will receive good things tomorrow; if we do evil things today, we suffer evil things today. We are all out of harmony <note>original: "dissonamus"</note> with ourselves, and in turn, all things are out of harmony with us. If you rightly temper the movements of your soul—as the **Magi of the Persians** <note>Ficino often cites the Persian Magi (like Zoroaster) as ancient sources of wisdom who understood the harmony between the soul and the cosmos.</note> teach—then you have already tempered all things for yourself: the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> of the body, the seasons of the year, the plants, all animals, and the heavens. You will undoubtedly temper them if you arrange your soul with as much diligence as architects arrange stones, as painters arrange colors and lines, as musicians arrange voices, or as poets arrange words. And to speak briefly, nothing in you will seem disordered if you arrange your brain—which is covered by hair—as carefully as anyone arranges their hair. Fare well, and so that you do not cultivate other things in vain, cultivate yourself above all.

---

->*All worldly things are composed of discord; all things are opposed by discord both to themselves and to others.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino wishes peace <note>original: "pacem," a pun on the recipient's name, Pace.</note> to his friend Pace, but fears war. **Greetings.**<-

**Y**ou wrote to me recently, my dear Pace <note>likely referring to Pace Bombace, a scholar and friend of Ficino.</note>, quite elegantly and in a friendly manner as you usually do. However, I was not writing anything back to you because I thought peace existed nowhere, since I believed all things were utterly occupied by discord. But I have now found my "Pace" [Peace] there, where I have for a long time found my peace. Jupiter—as those who know celestial matters say—is the author of human peace. Rainaldo Orsini <note>Rainaldo Orsini (d. 1450) was a member of the powerful Orsini family and Archbishop of Florence; his relatives were major patrons of the arts and Ficino's circle.</note>, a protégé of Jupiter, nourishes both my Peace and yours. I will humbly commend you, as you request, to this protégé of Apollo. You, in turn, I pray, commend me to this protégé of Jupiter. But before I put an end to this letter, I wish to [discuss] with you—unless perhaps it is ridiculous...

<page-num>755</page-num>
<header>BOOK IV OF THE LETTERS</header>

...it might seem a slight thing to philosophize a bit about war starting from the name of "Peace" <note>original: "ex pacis nomine" — Ficino is punning on the surname of the addressees, the brothers of the Pace family</note>. Unhappy demons are set against happy angels, celestial signs against signs, planets against planets, and even elements against elements, plants against plants, and animals against animals. Furthermore, motion is opposed to rest, privation to habit, light to darkness, the bright and white to the black, sound to silence, and high pitch to low; the sweet-smelling is opposed to the foul, the salty to the tasteless—as the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on empirical observation and the physical world.</note> believe—and the bitter or sharp to the sweet; heat to cold, moisture to dryness, the light to the heavy, the dense to the rare, the rough to the smooth, and finally, the hard to the soft. Fortune and fate are opposed to the body, the humors of the body to other humors, and limbs to limbs; the body itself is opposed to the soul, sense to reason, emotion to emotion, vice to virtue, vice to vice, opinion to opinion, and finally, one wish to another. Of all things, only the virtues, if they are found anywhere, are truly in accord with one another, so much so that he who attains one attains them all. All other things, however, are in accord in nothing else more than in discord itself. Therefore, why should it be a wonder that the human race is shaken by continuous discord among itself? All things are composed of discord; all things are opposed both to themselves and to others. Things harmonize externally only when nothing is discordant within. But nothing is discordant within where either pure truth reigns, or the splendor of such truth overflows, or the heat of such splendor glows. The first indeed is God; the second is the contemplation of God; the third is the love and worship of God. Nor can those "Peaces" <note>The Pace family</note> give us that peace which the world, full of discord on every side, cannot give. But let me stop, lest while I dispute too long about war, I seem to have declared war upon your eyes or ears with a rambling discourse. **Farewell.** April 13, 1478. Florence.

---

->To change your lot for the better, change the shape of your soul for the better.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the human race, **Greetings.**<-

**W**hile searching today for the chief reason why men lead such a continuously laborious life on earth, there came to my mind a game of sorts, in which some people walk with their legs extended high while moving on their palms and the crowns of their heads. Furthermore, they try to look around at all earthly things with one eye, and all heavenly things with the other. Then, whatever they encounter on the ground, they strive to grasp with their nostrils, lips, and fingers. Conversely, if anything hangs over them from above, they try to touch and pluck it with their feet, and whatever they touch, they take up to carry. O most foul spectacle! O miserable monster! These are not men; they are not even animals. They seem to me like <term>Stygian trees</term><note>Trees associated with the River Styx in the underworld; here meaning hellish or death-like trees.</note>, whose leaves are most bitter, and which bear no fruit among their leaves. What can be imagined more monstrous? What more laborious and burdensome? We are all nearly such "friends" to ourselves—nearly all of us, alas, wretched ones! We foolishly subject the head (the reason of the soul) to the senses (which are the soul's feet). Consequently, with the mind thus pressed into the dirt, we trust ourselves to know heavenly and earthly things at the same time. We try in vain to reach the highest things of nature with the lowest soles of the soul. and while we strive to claim everything for ourselves, we carry around the burden of all things. Alas, in the meantime, with what insane misery, with what miserable insanity do we labor? Why do we weep for our lot or our fortune? Why do we think to change fortune by chance? Why try to bend fate? Change, I pray, this "game" of the soul; turn this shape of yours right-side up. For in this way, you will have changed your fortune and bent your fate, and you will suddenly turn the very shape of the world into something better for yourself.

---

->Do not seek pure things in an impure way, nor, after you have found them, make them common to the impure.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, **Greetings.**<-

...rather than out of a desire for plainer learning, you require a clearer interpretation of my letter. Therefore, you clever man, you are now demanding a kind of amorous prolixity <note>Ficino often uses "amatory" language to describe the intellectual bond between friends</note>, not clarity. However, so that I may satisfy both you with a longer speech and another who might truly require an interpretation in plainer words, the summary of that old letter will be as follows. I always strive with all my might to do that which prudent counsel and diligent reason have persuaded me is good. Nor do I refer this pursuit to any external fruit, which would be both fleeting and brief, and placed in the judgment of men or of fortune, but first indeed to that true joy which is perceived in the action of the good itself. This good and joy, if it can be called "temporal" because it is not continuously exercised and felt in the same way, is nevertheless a beginning, and situated in our own will. Indeed, such a good pleases both in the present and in eternity. I do not say this because I now fully enjoy eternity itself, but because I understand it is for no other reason than because it agrees with the <term>Idea</term><note>In Ficino’s Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" is the eternal, perfect form of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note>, that is, the eternal reason of God and the art of the Almighty; it agrees with the mind and pleases it. Therefore, just as I referred 그 good to inward joy, so I refer joy to the Idea, so that clearly for that reason the good pleases me, so that I myself may most please God—the Good of every good—without whom nothing can please me. "I do not possess present happiness," you say, "but I wait for the future one." Wait for happiness, Docteri, as one who is clearly going to be happy in the present—that is, the eternal—happiness, rather than the future one. For if there is any future happiness in you, it is happiness precisely because it exists in that happiness which touches neither the past nor the future. Farewell. April 15, 1478.

-> Nothing is either more wonderful or more lovable than learning joined to uprightness. <-

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Marcus Aurelius, the most distinguished Orator, sends greetings.

**W**hen singular learning, Marcus Aurelius, is joined together with a certain excellent uprightness, such a great splendor from learning and such warmth from uprightness immediately shine forth from this meeting—as if of the Sun and Jupiter—that with rays and flames of this kind stretching from the east even to the west, the minds even of the most remote nations, incited and kindled, are both most charmingly enticed and most vehemently carried away. By this means, therefore, Marcus Aurelius <note>This refers to Marco Aurelio, a contemporary diplomat and scholar, not the Roman Emperor</note> used to entice his Marsilio Ficino when he was a youth; he carries him away even now that he is more mature in age. Behold, now all this prey of yours hastens to you, Marcus: your Marsilio, both the youth and the mature man. Here, then, he offers you six little declamations, of which those first two, on the praises of philosophy and medicine, were born to him long ago in his tender years; but the following four, on the principal institutions of the human race, are truly born to him now. Born happily indeed, if they are continually nourished in your presence.

### Marsilio Ficino’s oration in praise of Philosophy.

**M**y mind is currently pulled in opposite directions, most distinguished men, just as it is accustomed to happen to those about to speak on these more serious matters. For both the ancient custom of this sacred gymnasium <note>original: "gymnasij" — here referring to a place of higher learning or a university academy</note> and the grave authority of the fathers—two things which rightly have the greatest power over me—compel me to speak today on the praises of philosophy. But when I consider the force and nature of this faculty within myself, it seems so remarkable to me, and so excellent, that I distrust whether it can be grasped by the human mind or explained by the tongue. And not only does the sublimity of the subject on one hand and the humility of my talent on the other deter me from speaking, but even your venerable sight now does so. And so, I was just now wavering whether to be silent or rather to speak. I shall speak, nonetheless, outstanding men, as best I can, judging it better that the subject itself of which I am about to speak should seem less than Marsilio's abilities, than that Marsilio should in no way obey the precepts of his elders. Therefore you will grant me pardon if I am unable to express its extraordinary praises in any way according to its dignity. And you will attribute everything whatsoever that is said by me to the divine light, by whose light we observe, by whose rays we comprehend, and by whose splendor we explain. It is an old opinion of theologians, outstanding men, confirmed by the reasons of many philosophers, by which we are certainly taught and instructed, that for each individual thing in the [nature... <note>The sentence continues on the next page with "nature of things"</note>]

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the divine nature of knowledge. While the previous page discussed the "Idea" and eternal joy in a personal letter, this page transitions into a formal oration or treatise regarding the "Prisca Theologia" (Ancient Theology) and the tripartite division of philosophy as it relates to the Christian Trinity.</meta>

<page-num>758</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

...in nature, things seem more perfect and more worthy as they approach the perfection and dignity of the first principle of all things, and as they more closely and more clearly embrace its image within themselves. Indeed, the Ancient Theology <note>original: "Prisca Theologia," a term Ficino used to describe a single thread of divine truth shared by ancient sages.</note> of the Egyptians and Arabs handed down that God is the principle of existing, of knowing, and of acting. From this source, Pythagoras, Heraclitus, and Plato, transferring that Theology into Greece, argued that from that very same God comes the principle of nature, the truth of doctrine, and the happiness of life. This is testified to by Plato’s books: the *Republic*, the *Parmenides*, and the *Timaeus*, as well as the *Theology* of Iamblichus and Proclus. Following those ancients, Dionysius the Areopagite—first a Platonist and then a Christian—disputed the same most extensively in his books. Much later, Hilary and Aurelius Augustine, the leaders among the Latin theologians, observed this as well. Thus, Augustine himself, in his books *On True Religion* and *On the City of God*, calls God the maker of all things, the illuminator of truth, and the giver of happiness. He confirms that this had been treated by various Platonic philosophers many centuries earlier, albeit in different words. 

Furthermore, in these three titles for God, which were first introduced by the ancient philosophers, the Christian Trinity is also contained in a certain way. Moreover, the three species of philosophy discovered and distributed by Plato correspond in all their parts to this trinity of nature. Thus, that faculty of philosophizing which speaks of the causes and progressions of things <note>Natural philosophy or Physics.</note> agrees with God as the principle of things. The second part, which treats the origin and method of discourse <note>Logic or Dialectic.</note>, is suited to God as the illuminator of truth. The final part of philosophy, by whose precepts and institutions we lead our lives and direct ourselves, our families, and the state toward achieving happiness <note>Ethics and Politics.</note>, is compared in a certain way to God as the giver of happiness. From this, it can now be sufficiently clear that philosophy agrees in every part with the whole and perfect (if I may say so) divinity, and contains a full and absolute image—as much as is granted to us—of the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 

By this it happens that no human faculty appears closer or more similar to divinity than philosophy; and therefore, nothing among us, except God himself, seems more perfect or more excellent than Philosophy. For this reason, Mercurius <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, the wisest of the Egyptians, seems to have explained it divinely when he said that men become Gods by the light of philosophy. Pythagoras sang the same in his *Golden Verses*, and Plato, in his books on the *Republic*, established ceremonies and mysteries of the Gods for philosophers who have finished their lives. 

Empedocles of Agrigentum, however, said that philosophy is a gift of the gods, which, to whomever it befalls, renders him such that he despises all moving things with a high mind, is illuminated by divine rays in the innermost edge of his mind, and hopes for future happiness with a firm conviction. But what is more excellent than what was said by Aristotle: Though other arts, terrified by the magnitude and difficulty of things, departed far from the inquiry into truth, Philosophy alone fled from no laborious work, nor did she think herself unworthy of the best things, but considered the knowledge of them <margin>-</margin> to be suitable and kindred to her. And since it would be impossible to approach the celestial seats with a corporeal mass, the soul, having obtained intelligence as its guide by the gift of Philosophy, transcends the nature of all things through contemplation. This is what Aristotle says. 

Finally (to speak briefly), since Philosophy <margin>-</margin> is a celestial gift, she puts to flight earthly vices, most bravely tames fortune, miraculously mitigates fate, and most certainly makes use of mortal gifts: she bestows immortal gifts according to one's prayer. O treasure most precious of all, by no means brought forth from the bowels of the earth or of Pluto <note>The god of the underworld and wealth.</note>, but descending from the highest peak of heaven and the head of Jove <note>A reference to Minerva/Athena, goddess of wisdom, springing from the head of Jupiter.</note>, without the possession of which we can neither rightly use other treasures, nor possess anything happily. O safest <margin>-</margin> guide of human life, who first utterly defeats the monsters of vice with the club of Hercules. Then, with the shield and spear of Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva.</note>, she avoids or overcomes the perils of fortune. Finally, lifting human souls upon the shoulders of Atlas, she both frees them from this earthly exile and restores them most truly and happily to the supernal fatherland. So that it was not undeservedly said by Plato that once, when wisdom reigned, a golden age existed, and again, if ever Philosophy shall reign, the golden age will return. 

But what are we doing, O excellent men? Why do we attempt to measure eternity in vain in a mere moment (so to speak) of time? Not only the day, but many years would fail us if we were to attempt to pursue all the praises of holy Philosophy. Therefore, nothing else remains to be said or done, except that with our whole mind and an ardent soul, having left behind all shifting and empty things in which nothing but certain shadows and phantoms are found, we should apply ourselves to the study of this divine gift.

<summary>Ficino argues that philosophy is a divine gift that mirrors the Christian Trinity and traces its lineage from ancient Egyptian and Greek sages to Church Fathers like Augustine. He concludes with a rhetorical exhortation to pursue philosophy as the only path to the "Golden Age" and true spiritual liberation.</summary>

### Marsilio Ficino’s Oration on the Praises of Medicine.

**P**hilosophers of the Pythagorean and Platonic schools, who flowed from <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto." Ficino viewed this legendary Egyptian figure as the "source of philosophy" and a contemporary of Moses.</note> as the source of philosophy, believe that nothing can be sought or found by the human mind in any way without that Principle from which the mind itself and those things which are to be learned proceed. They also held that the light for inspecting all things is that very same God by whom all things were perfected. For just as the spark of the eyes discerns the sparks of colors within the light of the Sun itself—the author of both colors and eyes—so the truth-telling mind perceives the truth of any matter within the supreme Truth, which is the progenitor of every mind and truth. Therefore, since today we are about to treat the praises of medicine (which is said to have descended from Apollo), led by both ancient custom and the command of the fathers, we turn the gaze of the mind from darkness toward the light and suppliantly adore the rays of the true and highest <term>Apollo</term>, <note>Ficino often used "Apollo" as a metaphor for the Christian God or Christ in his role as the "True Sun" and Healer.</note> so that, purified by His salutary heat, we may pursue the perfection of purification and its praises, either according to its own dignity or at least according to the strength of our own talent. There are three primary things among philosophers, distinguished men, by which they are accustomed to judge the perfection of any doctrine: namely, the end, the origin, and the matter. The origin of medicine, whether you follow the Hebrews and Arabs, or the Greek and Egyptian theologians, flowed from divinity itself. For the Hebrews and Arabs assert that <insert>Adam</insert>, the first parent of the human race, obtained that wisdom by divine light. But others have handed down that <insert>Apollo</insert> received that power for the safety of the human race from <insert>Jove</insert>, <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> the parent of men and gods; he then revealed it to <insert>Aesculapius</insert>, from whom <insert>Podalirius</insert> and <insert>Machaon</insert>, outstanding physicians, were born. Then, many centuries later, <insert>Hippocrates of Cos</insert> brought into the light those things which had been handed down by the ancients wrapped in obscure parables. And all these whom I have mentioned so far are said to have been admitted into the council of the Gods by the universal religion of the Gentiles. Why should I mention <insert>Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Diocles, Carystius, Erasistratus, Praxagoras, Chrysippus, Herophilus, Serapion, Apollonius, Glaucias, Heraclides, Themison, Plistonicus, Galen</insert>, or those most excellent and outstanding of the Greek philosophers, <insert>Plato</insert> and <insert>Aristotle</insert>? We have found that all of these were both the most acute philosophers and published many books on the art of healing. Why mention the <insert>Egyptians</insert>, the oldest of all nations, whose priests were all outstanding physicians, as <insert>Homer, Euripides,</insert> and <insert>Plato</insert> testify? Why mention the <insert>Magi of the Persians</insert>—that is, their priests—<insert>Zoroaster, Ostanes, Abstroficon, Gobryas, Paxates, Sinicariondas, Damigeron, Hismos, John, Apollonius, Dardanus</insert>, among whom almost innumerable volumes are said to have been found in this art, which protect our health by the movements of the stars, by words, herbs, little stones, and vapors? Was it not also that <insert>Mithridates</insert>, the King of Pontus, who was master of twenty-two languages, who spent long labor on the studies of this discipline? <insert>Shapur</insert> also, King of the Medes, and the divine <insert>Avicenna</insert>, and many Arabs brooded over this wisdom with burning effort: <insert>Serapion</insert> and his son <insert>John</insert>, and furthermore <insert>John Mesue, Abumeron, Avenzoar, Rhazes, Averroes, Albucasis, Isaac, Haly</insert>, and many other most excellent sages of the Hebrews and Arabs. I pass over the <insert>Latins</insert>, of whom <insert>Cornelius Celsus, Apuleius, Quintus Serenus, Columella, Pliny, and Lactantius</insert> were the first to compose books on the care of health, both in prose and in verse. Those who followed them are found to be almost innumerable and are so well known to you that they require no longer a narration. For can the origin of any faculty be found not only more outstanding than this birth of medicine, but even equal or similar? Since it proceeds from God, heroes, kings, leaders, Magi, philosophers, and indeed the most ancient and wisest of all. The matter subject to this art, around which it turns, and whose principles and properties it investigates, is <bold>Man</bold>, whom Hermes Trismegistus valued so highly that he said that after the first God, he was almost the greatest of the gods. The Stoics also and the Peripatetics [held] all things which...

<meta>This page concludes the oration on the dignity of medicine and transitions into a personal letter from Ficino to the astronomer-poet Lorenzo Bonincontro regarding his work on St. Paul’s mystical experiences. It continues the argument that the health of the body and the soul are inextricably linked.</meta>

<page-num>760</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...[all] things that are moved beneath the sphere of the Moon are made and moved for his <note>Referring to man, as established in the previous page.</note> sake. The Hebrews, Arabs, and Christian theologians also hold that the world itself was constituted for the sake of man. From this, who cannot see that the man with whom our faculty deals is nearly the most excellent of all things flowing from God? And therefore, the doctrine of curing man must be judged the most perfect of all. Nor should any doctor say that his art is concerned only with the human body. Indeed, Phoebus <note>The god Apollo, associated with both healing and the sun.</note>, as we read in the *Epistles of Hippocrates*, considered the cure of the soul and the body to join as one. For this reason, among the Egyptians and Persians, the same men were both priests and doctors. 

Plato writes in the *Charmides* that those Magi—the doctors of soul and body and followers of <term>Zamolxis</term> <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Thracians, often viewed as a god or a student of Pythagoras.</note> and <term>Zoroaster</term>—believed that all things of the body, both good and bad, flow from the soul into the body itself, just as the quality of the eyes flows from the brain, and the quality of the brain from the whole body. And just as it is impossible for the eyes to be cured unless the brain is cured, and the brain unless the whole body is cured, so the whole body cannot be well unless the soul is well. Indeed, the health of the soul is cured by certain "Apollinean incantations," that is, by philosophical reasonings. Socrates, moreover, recounted a common saying among the Thracians: that those doctors were accustomed to making some men immortal by such a cure—so great is the empire of the soul over the body, so great is its power. 

This "magical" opinion seems to agree with the sentiment of the Hebrews and Christians: that when the soul of Adam, our first parent, was healthy, all things were healthy; but when it became infirm, all things became infirm. <term>Cornelius Celsus</term> <note>An Encyclopedist and author of "De Medicina," the primary source of medical knowledge in the Roman world.</note> also wished for the art of medicine to be understood as complete and perfect only when one was able to protect a man’s health through the mutual knowledge of the soul and the body, in which two things both natural and moral contemplation, as well as their practical use, are contained. For even <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe.</note> judged that the quality of the body can affect the soul in either direction to the highest degree, and that the affections, movements, and images of the soul itself have the greatest power over the body's health, whether for good or ill. 

Furthermore, who does not see the goal of doctors? For by their care and diligence, being itself, living, and—above all—living well are preserved. What can be added that is better than these, or more desirable? What is closer to nature, or more agreeable to it, than to protect and preserve what it has itself brought forth? None of you are ignorant, most illustrious men, that human prosperity consists not in the possession of things, but in a certain pleasant use of them. But truly, no one of sound mind is ignorant that without health, no use of things is pleasant to us. Hence, <term>Orpheus</term> <note>The mythical poet and musician, central to Ficino's "Ancient Theology."</note> sang thus in his *Hymn to Health*: "Without you, all things are useless to men." <note>original: "Absq; te cuncta sunt hominibus inutilia."</note> 

Therefore, since medicine either protects or restores health, it seems to preserve and return all goods at once. For this reason, the sacred scriptures of the Hebrews rightly commanded that the doctor be honored, and Homer says correctly: "A man who is a doctor is worth many others." <note>original: "Vir medicus pretio multos æquauerit unus." A reference to the Iliad, Book 11.</note> Wherefore, I strongly exhort all of you, my friends, that you spare neither time, nor money, nor labor in any way, so that you may embrace with all your strength this most wholesome art, the preserver of human life. Thus, you may protect your own life and prosperity, and that of your kin and all others, and you may assist the other liberal arts, which cannot be learned or practiced without health. And finally, you may happily command all nations, and even the greatest kings, who all surrender themselves into your hands.

### Marsilio Ficino to Laurentio Bonincontro, 
### Astronomer and Poet, sends greetings.

**I** was recently looking for a friend among many whom I might most especially consult as to whether I have disputed truly regarding the <term>rapture of Paul into the third heaven</term> <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, where St. Paul describes being caught up into paradise. Ficino wrote a specific treatise on this event.</note>. There occurred to me, first and foremost, Laurentio Bonincontro: a poet of astronomical things, and an astronomer of poetic ones. For a long time now, his own <term>Atlas</term> <note>The Titan who held up the sky; here used to symbolize Bonincontro's mastery of astronomy.</note> has lifted him into the heavens upon his high shoulders as an astronomer, and in turn, Father Phoebus himself has sung celestial things to him with a "round mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo" — a Horace reference meaning eloquent or polished speech.</note> as to a prophet. Therefore, I shall only then think I have expressed a true image of divine things when my Laurentio—who has seen their face both with Atlas as his guide and Apollo showing the way—has fully approved of them.

BOOK FOUR OF THE EPISTLES.

# BOOK FOUR OF THE EPISTLES.

### *It is better to bear bad health well, than to bear good health badly.*

->Marsilio Ficino to his friends, sends greetings.<-

**W**hy do you, my friends, ask so often how I am doing? Ask rather whether I have finally recovered. Others, indeed, seem born for this: to be in good health. I, on the contrary, seem born for this very thing: to be continually in poor health. For by a certain weakness of nature, it was granted to me from the beginning that I have never experienced a single whole day of firm physical health. But by a most generous gift of God, I repay the losses of an envious nature, so that I bear my bad health almost as well as some people waste their good health. Therefore, as much as they owe to the grace of nature for the sake of prosperous possession, so much do I owe for the sake of its very use. Since God himself is our strength, we cannot be weak in all respects. For then the strength of the mind is perfected by the weakness of the body. For me, truly, it is good to cling to God. Since (as <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose Christian Neoplatonism deeply influenced Ficino.</note> says), if I do not remain in him, I shall not even be able to remain in myself. Stand therefore, O friends, stand in God, who is not moved, and you shall stand. Rest in him, who is not troubled, and you shall live in peace.

->*He who has given himself has given all things at once.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to <term>Bernardo Bembo</term>, most distinguished man of Venice, sends greetings.<-

**I** had scarcely given a letter for you to <term>Jacopo Lanfredini</term> <note>A Florentine diplomat and close associate of the Medici family.</note>, in which I desired to be made more certain whether you had received all those things of mine (or rather, yours), when your letter was delivered to me, filled with weight, charm, and affection. What truly shall I say of your wonderful gratitude? Others, when they have received the things of another for free, finally and with difficulty give thanks. Our Bembo, however, gives thanks because he has received what was his by right, and most abundantly indeed. I, my sweetest Bernardo, can for a long time now give you nothing new; I once gave you all things at once when I gave you Marsilio. And if a possession of that sort is light—for I am not so great as to fulfill your merits—it is nonetheless not a light thing that you have seized everyone else, no less than myself, by your character and letters. For you are the desire of all these people. You are the delight of our people. April 26, 1477.

### *On the nature, training, and practice of Platonic philosophy.*

->Marsilio Ficino to <term>Giovanni Francesco Ippolito</term>, Count of Gazoldo, most distinguished man, sends greetings.<-

**I** wrote a certain letter to <term>Bernardo Bembo</term> <note>A Venetian statesman and father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he was a key patron and friend to Ficino.</note> of Venice a long time ago, somewhat lengthy, concerning the praises of Philosophy. Recently, I also wrote something on the same subject to the most distinguished orator, <term>Marcus Aurelius</term>. It seems remaining that I should write something concerning the nature, training, and practice of <term>Platonic Philosophy</term>. This is so that it may appear more clearly by what path that most precious treasure of Philosophy may best be found by us, and once found, by what reason it may be lawfully possessed and dispensed. Since Philosophy is defined by everyone as the "love of wisdom" (as the name itself, introduced by <term>Pythagoras</term>, maintains), and wisdom is truly the contemplation of divine things, certainly the end of Philosophy is the knowledge of the divine. Our <term>Plato</term> <note>Ficino frequently refers to Plato as "ours" to signify his role as the philosopher's primary Latin translator and interpreter.</note> testifies to this in the seventh book of the *Republic*, where he says that true Philosophy is an ascent from those things which flow, arise, and pass away, to those things which truly exist and always remain the same. Philosophy therefore has as many parts and serving faculties as there are steps by which one climbs from the lowest things to the highest. These steps are built partly by nature, and partly by the diligence of men. For (as Plato teaches in the sixth book of the *Republic*), whoever is to be a philosopher must be so fashioned by nature itself that, in the first place, he is easy and ready toward all kinds of learning. Second, that he be truthful by nature, and utterly foreign to every lie. In the third place, that having despised all things which are subject to corruption, he applies his mind to those things which always remain the same. It is also necessary that he be magnanimous and brave, fearing not death, nor desiring empty glory. Furthermore, it is necessary that he be tempered in some way, and that he receive from nature those parts of the soul which are accustomed to be carried away by passions, now tamed.

<page-num>783</page-num>
# MARSILIO FICINO

Whoever is greedy for truth and turns his mind toward the contemplation of divine things despises the pleasures of the body. Furthermore, it is necessary for a **Philosopher** to be of a liberal spirit. Indeed, the valuing of worthless things is adverse and entirely contrary to the man who intends to contemplate the truth of things. Moreover, his will shall love justice, since he is a great seeker of truth, temperance, and liberty. Most of all, it seems he has need of sharpness of wit, memory, and <term>magnanimity</term> <note>Literally "greatness of soul," a virtue involving the pursuit of great honors while maintaining a noble character.</note>. Yet these three natural gifts—namely sharpness of wit, memory, and magnanimity—when a decent discipline and education is applied, produce a man perfect in virtue. But if they are neglected, they are said by <term>Plato</term> to be the causes of the greatest crimes. 

Therefore, the highest human diligence must be applied to this nature, so that he who is so naturally inclined may learn letters from his very childhood, as well as the elements of all the sciences. Furthermore, through the use of the <term>cithara</term> <note>A stringed instrument like a lyre, used in Greek education to harmonize the soul.</note>, his discordant soul must be composed. The body must be exercised with gymnastic games so that, by its good condition, it may provide suitable service to the studies of Philosophy. Meanwhile, the institutes of the laws of the best men should be brought to his ears. The mind of the youth must be so formed by honorable exhortations that it is rendered moderate and peaceful. This moral education they call **Ethics**. 

When the mind, through those things we have mentioned, has been freed from the disturbance of appetite and has begun to be loosened from the body, the knowledge of mathematics must soon be added to it, which deals with numbers, planes, figures, solids, and their many motions. Since numbers, figures, and the ratios of motions pertain to thought rather than to the exterior senses, the mind is separated by the study of these things not only from the appetite of the body, but also from its senses, and betakes itself to interior thought. This is indeed to "practice death" (which Plato writes in the *Phaedo* is the duty of one practicing philosophy), through which we are also rendered similar to God, as is learned from the *Phaedrus* and the *Theaetetus*. 

Among the Platonists, there is this order in perceiving these things: that **Geometry** follows **Arithmetic**, **Stereometry** <note>The study of three-dimensional layers or solid geometry.</note> follows Geometry, **Astronomy** follows this, and finally **Music** follows Astronomy. For numbers are prior to figures, and plane figures are prior to solids. Solid bodies exist before they are moved. Order and the ratios of voices <note>Or "sounds" / "tones".</note> follow motion. Therefore, let Arithmetic, which deals with numbers, precede; let Geometry, which treats plane figures, follow; let Stereometry, which considers solids, succeed this; and let Astronomy hold its place, which takes up the motions of solid bodies, that is, the spheres. Last is Music, which investigates the order of voices arising from motion. 

Once these are perceived, Plato hands down **Dialectic**, that is, the science of demonstrating truth. But he intends Dialectic to be not only that logic which teaches the first and smallest rules of reasoning, but also a profound artistry of the unencumbered mind, for comprehending the true and pure substance of every thing—first by physical, then by metaphysical reasons—so that an account can be given of anything, and finally, the light of the mind may be perceived above the nature of senses and bodies, and the incorporeal species of things, which we call **Ideas**, may be understood. From these, the **One** itself—the fountain of all species, the origin and light of minds and souls, the beginning and end of all (which Plato calls the **Good** itself)—may be inspected. The inspection of this is **Wisdom**; the love of it is most rightly defined as **Philosophy**. 

After the soul of the one practicing philosophy has first contemplated the Good itself, judging from there what things in human affairs are good, what are evil, base or honorable, harmful or useful, he disposes human things according to that exemplar; he leads away from evil, directs toward good, and by this **Prudence** of governing, he administers private, domestic, and public affairs, and teaches the laws and reasons of administration. From this, the laws had their beginning. For this reason, in the *Timaeus*, Plato asserts that Philosophy is a gift of God, than which nothing more excellent has ever been granted to us by God. For the Good itself, which is God, could bestow nothing better on man than a complete likeness of His own divinity, as far as is possible. 

Who would doubt that God is truth, free from the body, providing for all things? The Philosopher, however, through moral institution and that first erudition (which we mentioned), frees the soul from the appetite and sense of the body; through Dialectic he attains the truth; through civil doctrine he provides for men. Thus it happens that Philosophy is both a gift of God and a likeness, and a most happy imitation. If someone is endowed with this, by his likeness to God, he will be on earth the same as God is in the heavens. Indeed, the Philosopher is a mediator between God and men: a man toward God, a God toward men. He is an intimate of God’s truth, a possessor of his own liberty, and a leader of the rest of men by civil prudence. By which...

under a leader, and they say the golden ages once existed and will one day return, as **Plato** prophesied, when power and wisdom shall coincide in the same soul. According to Plato, the souls of those practicing philosophy—having recovered their wings through wisdom and justice—immediately fly back to their heavenly homeland once they have departed from the body <note>Ficino refers here to the famous myth in Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings to return to the divine realm.</note>. They perform the same duties in the heavens as they did on earth. They rejoice in truth with God, congratulate themselves on their liberty, provide for men through their piety, and, as interpreters and prophets of God, they complete there what they had begun here. They turn the souls of men toward God and interpret the secret mysteries of God for human minds. For this reason, the ancient theologians rightly honored the minds of philosophers—once released from the body—just like those thirty thousand "demons" of **Hesiod**, as if they were demigods, heroes, and blessed spirits <note>Hesiod, an early Greek poet, wrote of thirty thousand "daemons" (spirit guardians) who watch over mortals; in the Renaissance, these were often equated with angels or noble souls.</note>. Philosophy, therefore (to summarize in a few words), is the ascent of the soul from lower things to the highest, and from darkness to light; its beginning is the instinct of the divine mind, its middle path is the faculties of the disciplines we have described, its end is the possession of the highest good, and its fruit, finally, is the correct governance of men. I have shared these things with our friend **Francesco Berlinghieri** as a fellow philosopher, and you likewise shall share them with our friend **Giuliano Borgo**. Farewell.

->On the Life of Plato.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Francesco Bandini, Greetings.<-

**I** have endeavored in recent days to paint the "Idea" of a Platonic philosopher in colors. But if I had brought Plato himself into our midst, I certainly would not have shown you some painting of that Idea, but rather I would have pointed out the Idea of the true philosopher itself with my own fingers. Therefore, let us look upon our Plato, and we shall see the philosopher, philosophy, and the Idea itself all at once.

### The Genealogy and Birth of Plato.

<margin>
I had previously mentioned Plato's horoscope in my book *On Love*. But now I shall provide it as **Julius Firmicus**, the astronomer, describes it, whose opinion in this matter I consider more accurate. It is as follows: In the Ascendant, **Aquarius**, with **Mars**, **Mercury**, and **Venus**. In the second house, the **Sun** in **Pisces**. In the fourth, the **Moon** in **Gemini**. In the seventh, **Jupiter** in **Leo**. In the ninth, **Saturn** in **Libra**.
</margin>
**P**lato the Athenian, son of Ariston and Perictione (or Potone), traces his lineage from **Neptune** on both sides. For **Solon** <note>The famous lawgiver of Athens.</note> descended from Neleus and Neptune. Solon’s brother, Dropides, fathered the elder Critias, from whom Callaeschrus was born; he had two sons, namely the younger Critias (who was one of the thirty governors of Athens) and Glaucon, the father of Charmides and Perictione. Perictione, having married Ariston, gave birth to Plato, Adimantus, Glaucon, and also a daughter, Potone, who married Eurymedon and gave birth to Speusippus. Furthermore, Ariston, Plato's father, descends from Codrus, the son of Melanthus, who also (like Solon) traces his origin back to Neptune. They say it was well known in Athens that Ariston attempted to lie with Perictione while she was most beautiful, but his efforts were in vain; he saw **Apollo** in a dream and, commanded by him, kept himself pure from marital union until she gave birth. Both Laërtius and Policrates write of this. He was born in Athens (or in Aegina) 756 years from the capture of Troy, 333 years from the founding of the city <note>Referring to the founding of Rome (Ab Urbe Condita).</note>, and 433 years before the coming of Christ. As for Plato’s horoscope, which I...

MARSILIO FICINO

### *The education, character, learning, and sobriety of Plato.*

**I**t is said that while he was still in his cradle, bees poured honey into the infant’s lips—a prophetic sign of his future eloquence. They say that **Socrates** saw in a dream a young swan grow feathers in his lap, which immediately took flight into the heights with outstretched wings and sang the sweetest songs; the next day, when **Plato** was brought to him by his father to be tutored, Socrates said that this was the very swan he had seen. In his youth, he flourished in a poetic style. He composed elegies and two tragedies, which he personally committed to the flames as soon as he first applied his mind to philosophy. He was first instructed in basic literacy by his teacher **Dionysius**. Later, he listened to Socrates at the age of twenty; after the death of Socrates, he aligned himself with **Cratylus**, a disciple of **Heraclitus**, and **Hermogenes**, who upheld the philosophy of **Parmenides**. At the age of twenty-eight, he went to Megara to see **Euclid** along with other followers of Socrates. From there, he set out for Cyrene and listened to the mathematician **Theodorus**. From there, he traveled to Italy to meet the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who combined mathematics with mystical philosophy.</note> **Philolaus**, **Archytas of Tarentum**, and **Eurytus**. From these men, he withdrew to Egypt to visit the prophets and priests. He had decided to proceed to India to see the <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia/the East, associated with wisdom and astronomy.</note>, but he abandoned the plan because of the wars in Asia. Returning finally to Athens, he lived his life in the **Academy**, a place in Attica said to be unhealthy, which he reportedly chose—as **Saint Basil** and **Jerome** also confirm—so that the excessive vigor of his body might be pruned back like the over-abundant growth of a vine. For he possessed a most beautiful and robust physical build. It was for this reason—his broad shoulders, wide forehead, and the excellent condition of his entire body, as well as the richness of his speech—that he was called <term>Plato</term> <note>original: "Plato"; the name is derived from the Greek *platos*, meaning "breadth."</note>, though he had previously been named **Aristocles**. There was nothing unattractive about him, except perhaps a somewhat thin voice and a slight protrusion at the back of his head which somewhat marred his appearance. Due to living in the Academy, he suffered from a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms every fourth day.</note> for eighteen months, but through his sobriety and care, he recovered his strength to be even more vigorous after the fever than before.

### *The three military services and voyages of Plato; the first voyage.*

**H**e served in the military three times: first at Tanagra, second at Corinth, and third at Delos, where he also secured a victory. He sailed to Sicily three times: first to see the island and the volcanic wonders of Mount Etna. He was then forty years old, at which time **Dionysius** (the son of Hermocrates) urged Plato to speak with him. When Plato discussed the nature of tyranny, saying that a ruler does not perform well by doing only what is useful for himself unless he also excels in virtue, they say the offended and angry tyrant said: "Your words are those of idle old men." To which Plato replied: "And yours smell of tyranny." At this, the indignant tyrant first wished to kill him, but being pleaded with by **Dion** and **Aristomenes**, he did not do so. Instead, he handed him over to **Pollis** the Lacedaemonian, who had come to him as an ambassador at that time, to be sold. Pollis took him to Aegina and sold him. At that time, a man named **Charmander** accused him as one guilty of a capital crime; indeed, according to a law they had promulgated, it was a capital offense if any Athenian set foot on that island. However, when someone argued that the philosopher had landed there for the sake of learning, and that the law spoke of men and not of philosophers (who are above men), they released him unharmed. They decreed he should not be killed, but sold. By chance, **Anniceris of Cyrene** was present, who ransomed him for twenty <term>minae</term> <note>An ancient unit of currency; twenty minae was a significant sum, roughly the price of several high-skilled slaves.</note> and sent him back to his friends in Athens. The story goes that Pollis was later defeated by **Chabrias** and subsequently drowned at Helice, with a <term>daemon</term> <note>A guiding spirit or divine messenger.</note> announcing to him that he suffered such things because of his treatment of the philosopher. Nevertheless, Dionysius did not rest; when he learned what had happened to Plato, he wrote to him, begging him not to hurl insults at him. Plato wrote back to him that he did not have so much leisure time left over from philosophy that he would even remember Dionysius. To certain detractors who objected that Plato had been abandoned by Dionysius, he replied: "On the contrary, it was Dionysius who was left behind by Plato."

->EPISTLES, BOOK IV.<-

## The Second Voyage.

**S**econdly, he set out to visit **Dionysius the Younger**, having been summoned by him and **Dion** for the sake of practicing philosophy. Led by this hope, he believed he could use his counsel to transform the government there from a tyranny into either a **Republic** <note>In this context, a "Respublica" refers to a balanced, constitutional state rather than a specific modern republic.</note> or a kingdom. He hoped to see what he had long and vehemently desired: a truly philosophical government, in which either **Philosophers rule, or those who rule practice philosophy**. For he thought that cities could not otherwise avoid misery. He desired all of this to be achieved not by force or trickery, but by persuading **Dionysius** through philosophical reasoning. However, about four months after **Plato's** arrival, **Dionysius**, driven by false slanders, expelled **Dion** on the pretext that he was plotting against the tyranny; yet he continued to embrace **Plato** warmly. Eventually, **Plato** returned to his homeland. He visited a third time to reconcile **Dion** with **Dionysius**, having been entreated again by both of them. He was also asked by **Archytas**. On that occasion, **Dionysius** sent an adorned <term>trireme</term> <note>An ancient galley with three tiers of oars.</note> to meet him, along with **Archidamus** the <term>Pythagorean</term> orator and many noblemen; he even received him in a chariot drawn by four white horses as he disembarked. **Plato** demanded the promised restoration of **Dion**, and furthermore, land and men who might live according to a **Republic** established by him. Although **Dionysius** had promised this, he refused to fulfill it. When **Plato** openly rebuked **Dionysius** for breaking his word—both regarding the restoration of **Dion** and the safety of **Heraclides** (requested by his friend **Theodotus**)—he found **Dionysius** to be hostile thereafter. Consequently, he lived in extreme danger of being killed by the soldiers. But **Archytas of Tarentum** sent **Salmuscus** <note>Likely a transcription error for Lamiscus, a Pythagorean associate of Archytas.</note> as an envoy to **Dionysius** with a ship, requesting that he release **Plato**. The tyrant dismissed him and provided provisions for the journey; **Plato** then returned to his homeland. Shortly thereafter, **Dionysius** was driven from his tyranny by **Dion** and the citizens, thus paying the penalty for the crime committed against Philosophy. **Plato** was received in his homeland with extraordinary honor. When called upon to take part in the government there, he refused to do so because the common people had become accustomed to wicked morals.

## To whom Plato gave laws.

**I**t is said that the **Arcadians** and **Thebans**, having founded a city of honorable size, asked him to establish a **Republic** for them. However, when he understood that they were unwilling to follow the principle of equality, he did not go. But he did give laws to the **Syracusans** after the tyrant was expelled, and he wrote laws for the **Cretans** for their newly founded city, **Magnesia**, arranged in twelve books. Among his close associates, he sent **Aristonymus** to the **Arcadians** to establish laws; **Phormion** to the people of **Elis**; and **Menedemus** to the **Pyrrhaeans**.

## The restraint, gravity, and courtesy of Plato.

**H**e lived a celibate life, was extremely sober, and (as **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian who admired Plato's ethics.</note> asserts) stayed chaste. It is even said that in his old age he "performed the rites of nature" <note>original: "sacra naturae fecisse." This phrase is ambiguous; it often refers to fulfilling the debt of nature (dying), but here Ficino implies a ritual or act intended to prove he was not sterile to the public.</note> so that he might clear himself before the common people of the charge of sterility. As a youth, he was so modest and composed that he was never caught laughing except moderately. No one ever saw him angry. Hence, a boy educated at **Plato's** house, upon returning to his parents and seeing his father shouting, said, "I never saw this at **Plato's**." Only once was he secretly a little angry at a boy who had committed a serious fault, but he said to **Xenocrates**: "You beat this boy, for I cannot, because I am angry." He ate only once a day, or if twice, very sparingly. He slept alone. He strongly criticized a life of the opposite sort. He seemed perhaps a little more prone to loving young men, just like his teacher **Socrates**. Truly, however, both were as restrained by reason as they were inclined by their senses. How divinely they loved, and in what manner, is explained by what they spoke concerning love, which we have sufficiently discussed in our book *On Love* <note>Ficino's own famous work, *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note>. He hoped to leave a memory of himself either in books or in friends. And although he was of a <term>melancholic</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "melancholic" temperament was associated with deep thought and genius.</note> and profound genius, as **Aristotle** writes, he nevertheless employed many jokes. He very often advised the more severe **Xenocrates** and **Dion** to "sacrifice to the **Graces**," <note>A classical metaphor meaning to cultivate charm, politeness, and the social virtues.</note> so that they might be rendered more pleasant and agreeable. Thus, courtesy was mixed with **Plato's** gravity.

### *The Principal Disciples of Plato.*

**H**is disciples were Speusippus the Athenian, Xenocrates of Chalcedon, Aristotle the <term>Stagirite</term> <note>A person from Stagira, Aristotle's birthplace.</note>, Philippus of Opus, Hestiaeus of Perinthus, Dion of Syracuse, Amyelas, Heraclides, Erastus and Coriscus of Scepsis, Timolaus of Cyzicus, Euaeon of Lampsacus, Pithon, and Heraclides of Aenus, Hippothales and Callippus the Athenians, Demetrius of Amphipolis, Heraclides of Pontus, and many others. Along with these were two women, Lasthenia of Mantinea and Axiothea of Phlius, who used to wear men’s clothing. They also say that **Theophrastus** was a listener of his, as well as the orator **Hyperides**, Chamaeleon, and Lycurgus; **Demosthenes** too was a student of his, and Menesistratus. Inscribed upon the vestibule of the Academy was: *Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.* By this, he wished it to be understood that one must possess the proper measure not only of lines, but also of one’s emotions.

### *The Books of Plato.*

**H**e wrote a book on holiness, the *Euthyphro*; the *Apology of Socrates*; the *Crito*, concerning what he discussed with Socrates in prison; the *Phaedo*, on the immortality of the soul; the *Cratylus*, on the correct nature of names; the *Theaetetus*, on knowledge; the *Sophist*, on that which exists; the *Statesman*, on kingship; the *Parmenides*, on the one principle of all things and on the Ideas; the *Philebus*, on the highest good; the *Symposium*, on love; the *Phaedrus*, on beauty; the *First Alcibiades*, on the nature of man; the *Second Alcibiades*, on prayer; the *Hipparchus*, on the desire for gain; the *Lovers*, on philosophy; the *Theages*, on wisdom; the *Charmides*, on temperance; the *Laches*, on fortitude; the *Lysis*, on friendship; the *Euthydemus*, which is contentious; the *Protagoras*, on morals; the *Gorgias*, on rhetoric; the *Meno*, on virtue; the *Greater Hippias*, on beauty; the *Lesser Hippias*, on lying; the *Menexenus*, on the antiquity of Athens; ten books on the *Republic*; the *Timaeus*, on the nature of the world; the *Critias*, on the antiquity of Athens; the *Minos*, on law; twelve books on the *Laws*; and the *Epinomis*, or the *Philosopher*. He also wrote thirteen *Epistles*. We ourselves <note>Ficino refers to himself here, as he was the primary translator of Plato's works into Latin during the Renaissance.</note> have translated all these books of Plato from the Greek language into Latin. There are three types of Platonic dialogues: for he either refutes the sophists, exhorts the young, or teaches adults. Those things which Plato spoke with his own mouth in the epistles or in the books of the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*, he wishes to be held as most certain; however, those things which he disputes through the mouths of Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides, or Zeno in the other books, he intends to be held as likely truths.

### *The Eloquence, Wisdom, and Authority of Plato.*

**T**he style of Plato (as **Aristotle** says) flows midway between prose and poetry; its sweetness and abundance are so great that **Cicero** called Plato the most weighty author and master of both understanding and speaking. He added that if **Jupiter** <note>The king of the Roman gods, equivalent to the Greek Zeus.</note> had wished to speak in a human tongue, he would have spoken in no other language than that of Plato. Indeed, the learning in him was so vast that while before him all the illustrious Greeks had traveled to foreign nations for the sake of wisdom, after Plato's time, all other nations flocked to Athens. Even **Aristotle**, endowed with such a marvelous intellect and most eager for new doctrines, when he had come to Plato as an almost grown man, listened to him for twenty continuous years. Add to this that he was already advanced in letters before he approached Plato. Thereafter, he had Plato as his only teacher. I pass over what is written by **Cicero**: *I would rather err with Plato than think correctly with others.* <note>original Latin: "malo cum Platone errare quàm cum cæteris rectè sentire"</note> Furthermore, along with **Panaetius** <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 2nd century BCE.</note>, he calls him the "God of Philosophers." I also pass over that remark of **Quintilian**: "Who could doubt that Plato is supreme either in the sharpness of his debating or in a certain divine and Homeric faculty of eloquence? For his speech rises far above prose—what the Greeks call 'pedestrian' speech—so that he seems to me to be inspired not by human talent, but by some Delphic oracle." He seems to have acquired for himself a wonderful authority through divine wisdom and integrity, even in his own fatherland, which is something that happens very rarely. When Plato returned from Sicily with...

<header>OF LETTERS, BOOK IV.</header>
<meta>catchword: your head</meta>

When he had arrived at that most magnificent celebration of the Olympic Games, which was like a gathering of the entire world, he was received with such joy by everyone he met that he seemed like a God sent down from heaven to mortals. Seeing the games deserted, the spectacles of the athletes left behind, and the boxers ignored, and—what is more wonderful—seeing that those who had come to the Olympics across such long stretches of land and sea for the sake of feeding their eyes, ears, and minds, had forgotten every pleasure to seek out Plato and gaze upon him. In Plato they found rest, as if in a most pleasant inn. When a certain tragedy was being performed and no one was present except Plato, some people objected that it was a disgrace to the performer that no one was there but one man. He replied: "This one man is worth more than the entire Athenian people."

->The Charity, Magnanimity, and Holiness of Plato<-

<margin>if they were to dance</margin>
**H**ow great and constant his spirit was, especially in the cause of his friends, is shown by his letters, his contempt for the tyrant <note>Dionysius the Younger, the ruler of Syracuse</note>, and his defense of Dion. He often boldly rebuked the tyrant for governing unjustly or for deceiving his friends, even in the presence of witnesses; so far was he from being a flatterer. I pass over smaller matters, such as when Dionysius ordered at a banquet that everyone put on purple robes; Aristippus danced immediately, but Plato refused, saying that "womanly garments do not suit a philosopher." Furthermore, when the wicked Crobylus had accused the most brave general Chabrias and sought a capital sentence against him, and while Chabrias was abandoned by the rest of the citizens for fear of danger as he ascended to the citadel, Plato alone was always present to offer him aid. Indeed, when the slanderer Crobylus, in order to deter him from providing patronage, leaned in and said: "You come to provide a defense for others, ignorant that the poison of Socrates awaits you as well," Plato himself replied: "Long ago, Crobylus, when I fought for the dignity of my fatherland, I was not slow to face intolerable dangers; now, for the sake of duty and the safety of a friend, though you sharpen your sword and fire with threats, I refuse no trial." When Socrates was most unjustly shut in prison, Plato gathered money to ransom the innocent man, and while the trial was being conducted, he ascended the platform and began to speak thus: "Though I am younger, O Athenians, than all these who have ascended the tribunal..." But the judges, fearing the tyrant and afraid that he might move the citizens with his authority and eloquence, suddenly interrupted him and shouted: "Step down!" Plato went home. For as much as they suffered from a disease of a wicked mind, he was then suffering from a disease of the body. Indeed, the persecutors of Socrates paid the penalty shortly thereafter. When a certain fellow student was driven by envy because Xenocrates was so pleasing and acceptable to Plato, he tried to stir up enmities against him, reporting many insults supposedly said by Xenocrates against Plato. Plato, rejecting the accusation in mid-speech, refused to listen. The detractor persisted, affirming the crime with a severe face, and finally calling all the Gods and Goddesses to witness. Plato, to free himself from the man's persistence, said: "So be it; but Xenocrates possesses such faith and gravity that unless he had judged it useful to speak so, he would never have said those things." That Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, imitated the gravity and magnanimity of Plato is evidenced by the *Life of Xenocrates* in Diogenes <note>Diogenes Laërtius, the biographer of philosophers</note>, which is indeed a model of fortitude and holiness. Plutarch is witness that Dion also imitated him. Furthermore, Philicus, describing the life of the orator Lycurgus, says: "Lycurgus was a great man and many things were performed by him excellently, which no one could have done who had not been a listener of Plato." When Demosthenes was fleeing Antipater and Archias promised with flattering words that he would save his life, he replied: "Far be it from me to prefer to live basely than to die honorably, after I have heard Xenocrates and Plato debating the immortality of the soul." The same man, writing to a certain Heracleodorus, a fellow student of his, and rebuking him because after he had heard Plato he neglected the liberal arts and led a life of little honor, said: "Are you not ashamed to neglect those things which you received from Plato?" Dionysius, writing to Speusippus <note>Plato's nephew and successor at the Academy</note>, said: "Plato indeed taught those who crossed his threshold for free, but you exact tributes and take from the willing and unwilling alike." Laërtius also criticized the same man because he did not, like Xenocrates, imitate the chastity, fortitude, and gentleness of Plato. Truly, concerning the fortitude of Xenocrates, I cannot remain silent about the fact that when Dionysius said to Plato, "Your head..." <note>The text cuts off here, likely leading into a story where Dionysius threatens Plato with execution.</note>

## Sentences and Proverbs of Plato.

### Plato used to say these things about Aristotle and Xenocrates.

**A**h! What a horse and what an ass I have yoked together! Aristotle indeed needs a bridle, but Xenocrates needs spurs. Among his students was a young man who was overly elegant and very devoted to grooming his skin <note>likely a reference to excessive vanity or physical pampering</note>, whom Plato asked: "How much longer will you continue building a prison for yourself?" Whenever he saw a man entangled in love, he would say: "He is dead in his own body and lives in someone else's." He added that he who abandons himself for the sake of another is the most miserable of all, for he no longer possesses himself, nor the other. A learned man, an acquaintance of Plato, begged him to lend his ears for a moment while he read a small book he had published. When Plato subsequently asked what the title of the book was, he replied, *There is no such thing as contradiction* <note>original: "contradicendum non esse"</note>. To which Plato said: "Why then do you do this very thing yourself? Why do you contradict those who contradict? Why do you confer with me, if you forbid contradiction for yourself?" Leo, a powerful citizen, was criticized in an assembly because he had made loud and immoderate shouts in the senate. Plato said: "This is what it truly means to be a Lion <note>a play on the man's name, Leo</note>." To Diogenes the Cynic, who said that he could see these human things, but by no means "Ideas" <term>Ideas: the perfect, eternal forms in Plato's philosophy that exist beyond the physical world</term>, he replied: "Is it any wonder? For you have and use eyes with which these physical things are seen, but you do not use the mind, by which alone those Ideas are perceived." When his disciples were wondering why Xenocrates, who was serious throughout his whole life, had said something that provoked laughter, he said: "Why are you surprised that roses and lilies sometimes grow among thorns?" He used to say frequently to the living: "Prefer labors to leisure, unless by chance you think rust is better than brilliance." He would most often guide the youth toward a blessed life by this reasoning: "Observe the contrary natures of virtue and pleasure; for the momentary sweetness of the latter is followed by sudden repentance and perpetual pain, while the brief labors of the former lead to eternal pleasure." When he had seen someone playing at dice, he rebuked him; and when the man said, "How small a thing you find fault with!", Plato replied: "But habit is no small thing." He used to advise the drunk and the angry to look at themselves diligently in a mirror, for they would immediately turn away from such foulness. He greatly detested drunkenness and excessive sleep. He said it mattered most in educating childhood that children become accustomed to rejoicing only in honorable things. Otherwise, he said that pleasure was the bait for evils. He added that the health of the soul is true philosophy. But other faculties seem not so much to be philosophy as they are ornaments. Nothing is sweeter to a healthy mind than speaking and hearing the truth, for nothing is either better or more durable than truth. When some asked what kinds of possessions should ideally be provided for their children, he said: "Those which fear neither hail, nor the violence of men, nor even Jove himself <note>referring to divine or natural disasters like lightning</note>." To Demoncus, who was consulting him about the education of his son, he said: "The same care that is used in planting and directing young trees ought to be used in begetting and training sons. In the former there is labor, in the latter pleasure; but we must take care lest we seem asleep in the one and overly watchful in the other." To a certain Philedonus who was criticizing Plato because he was no less studious and diligent in learning than in teaching, and who asked how long he wished to be a student, he replied: "As long as I do not regret becoming better and more skilled." Asked what the difference was between the skilled and the unskilled, he replied: "The same as between the doctor and the sick." He used to say that for princes there is no more excellent type of estate than the friendship of those men who cannot be bought and sold <note>literally "who cannot play the innkeeper"—meaning men of integrity who do not treat their loyalty as merchandise</note>. Wisdom is no less necessary for a prince than the soul is for the body. Republics would be most blessed if either philosophers rule, or at least those who govern happen to philosophize by some divine lot. For nothing is more pestilential than power and audacity when they are accompanied by ignorance. Subjects also tend to be such as their princes appear to be. A magistrate must think not of his own good but the public good; not
->only a certain part of the city, but the<-
->whole is to be cared for.<-

<header>LETTERS, BOOK IV</header>

->*How much Plato neglected human affairs, and how much he loved divine things.*<-

**H**e repeated daily that only eternal things are truly real, while temporal things are merely likenesses. He believed that the soul sleeps within the body, and that the things the senses desire or fear are nothing more than dreams. Therefore, all these earthly things should be utterly despised, and to avoid the evils with which the world is filled, one must flee toward the eternal; for he believed there was no other way to escape them. He himself fulfilled the very things he taught. For while he was destined to be a leader in the republic both by a certain hereditary right and by the favor of the citizens, he utterly rejected all civil status. Though he was very wealthy by inheritance, he bestowed everything upon his brothers, except for a small suburban estate which they called the Academy <note>The site of Plato's famous school in Athens, originally a grove or garden.</note>. Content with this alone he lived, and although he stood as a teacher and friend to princes, he nevertheless accepted no riches from them. King Dionysius used to say: "Aristippus <note>A philosopher known for seeking luxury and royal favor.</note> always asks for money; Plato always asks for books." Additionally, he never took a wife, nor did he live in the city, being free from all things and serving truth alone. Hence Saint Jerome says: "Plato traveled with great effort through Egypt, and to Archytas of Tarentum, and that coast of Italy which was once called Great Greece <note>original: "Magna Graecia," referring to the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy.</note>. Thus he, who was a powerful master in Athens and whose doctrine made the gymnasia of the Academy resound, became a traveler and a disciple, preferring to modestly learn the things of others rather than impudently thrust his own ideas upon them." Finally, while he pursued letters as they were seemingly fleeing across the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold into slavery; he even obeyed a most cruel tyrant as a captive, bound and a slave, yet he remained greater than the one who bought him because he was a Philosopher. These are the words of Jerome.

->*The Piety and Gratitude of Plato.*<-

**H**e was grateful to God, from whom he said the beginning of thinking, speaking, and acting in all matters must come, and he always acted accordingly. Furthermore, he gave thanks to God daily: first, that he was born a human and not a brute animal; second, that he was a Greek and not a Barbarian; and third, that he lived in the time of Socrates. How grateful he was to his teachers and all his friends is evidenced by his dialogues, in which he honors them all wonderfully and attributes his own books to Socrates. For not only does he introduce Socrates as the speaker in nearly all the dialogues, but he also writes that all things composed by himself were not his own, but belonged to Socrates.

->*The things Plato affirmed, and those who confirmed him.*<-

**I**n those matters which are subject to the senses, he upheld the views of Heraclitus. Furthermore, in matters pertaining to the intellect, he most closely followed Pythagoras. In civil matters, however, he embraced his teacher Socrates. These are the things he asserted everywhere: That God provides for all things. That the souls of men are immortal. That there will be rewards for the good and punishments for the evil. Augustine, in his book *Against the Academics*, says that the authority of Christ is to be preferred above all; however, if one must deal in reasons, he says he found among the Platonists that which is not repugnant to the sacred writings of the Christians. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian traditionally identified with a judge of the Athenian Areopagus converted by St. Paul.</note> indicated the same. Later, Eusebius and Cyril declared this more extensively. Hence Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*, says: "The Platonists, with a few things changed, would become Christians." And in his *Confessions*, he relates that he found nearly the entire prologue of the Gospel of John among the Platonists. For this reason, in the second book of *The City of God*, he says: "Labeo the Theologian thought that among the Gentiles, Plato should be numbered among the demigods, just like Hercules and Romulus." He places demigods above heroes, but situates both among the divinities. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this man whom he calls a demigod should be preferred not only to the heroes, but even to the gods themselves. Whence Augustine says that he chose the Platonists above others because they felt much more correctly about divine and human matters than the other philosophers. This was also the judgment of Marcus Varro before him; and Apuleius made Plato not only superior to heroes, but equal to the gods, clearly because he penetrated the secrets of divine things. Plato was endowed with such modesty that, although he had acquired an amazing authority above all others, nevertheless, when asked by someone to what extent his precepts should be obeyed, he replied: "Until someone more sacred appears on earth, who may open the fountain of truth to all, and whom all may then follow."
