everyone. He added that he had discovered nothing by his own light, but only by divine light. However, what he felt in philosophy we have sufficiently treated in the book *On Love* <note>original: "de amore"; Ficino's commentary on Plato's Symposium.</note> and in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia"; referring to Ficino's major work, "Platonic Theology."</note>.

### Plato’s return to his heavenly fatherland and his praises.

He died on his birthday and completed his eighty-first year without any decline. Therefore, the Magi who were then in Athens sacrificed to Plato, believing his lot to have been higher than the human condition, because he had completed the most perfect number, which nine multiplied by nine produces <note>The number 81 was considered significant by Pythagoreans and Platonists as the square of nine.</note>. And what is wonderful, even at that age and on that very day he was writing. Concerning which Cicero says: "There is also a peaceful and light old age of a life spent quietly, purely, and elegantly, such as we have heard of Plato, who died while writing in his eighty-first year." Seneca also affirms that this happened to Plato by the benefit of his sobriety and diligence. Some say he returned to the gods while writing; others while reclining at a wedding feast after the dishes were removed, in the midst of a discussion. Aristotle dedicated an altar and a statue to Plato in a temple with this epigram: "Aristotle dedicated this altar to Plato, a man whom it is a sacrilege for the wicked to praise." Aristotle added: *“He who alone, by his life, teaching, character, and speech, admonished all and gave monuments, so that by virtue they might lead a happy life. No future ages will bear such a man.”* Other wise men also added many poems in praise of Plato, but three epigrams are foremost. The meaning of the first is this: He excelled all in temperance and justice, but so far surpassed them in wisdom that he overcame all envy. The sense of the second is this: Plato was translated into the number of the gods. Distant nations honor him because he himself knew the divine life and showed it to others. The meaning of the third is as follows: Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and healing.</note> begat Asclepius <note>The god of medicine.</note> and Plato, so that the former might heal bodies and the latter might heal souls. Furthermore, Mithridates, King of the Persians, placed a statue of Plato in the Academy inscribed thus: "Mithridates, son of Rodobates, a Persian, dedicated this image of Plato, the work of Silanion <note>original: "Silianiani"</note>, to the Muses." From all these things Plato achieved this: that the Greeks called Aristotle 'daemonic' <note>term: dæmonium; in this context, possessing an extraordinary or intermediate spirit between human and divine, though less than 'divine' itself.</note>, but called Plato 'divine.' This is clearly because the former was most human in life and natural in science, while the latter at once in both science and life turned himself chiefly toward divine things.

### A defense of Plato’s character.

I would now put an end to my words, if I were to add a few more things. There are certain plebeian versifiers who undeservedly usurp for themselves the name of Poets; these men, provoked as much by the difference in their characters as by the malice of envy, play most impudently against every excellent man. To whom a certain extreme license is granted against the good rather than against the bad, especially in this age of ours. But I would not wish to remember our times, which are as unfit for attaining virtue as they seem fit for pursuing it. Such petty poets once did not hesitate to bite at the divine Plato—judged by the Greeks to be the son of Apollo—and Socrates—judged by the Greek Apollo to be the wisest of men. Diogenes Laertius greatly detests their impiety. And as he himself declares, Aristippus of Cyrene, a most wicked man and an adversary of every best man of his time, even increased the ridiculous insults of the comic playwrights. Just as he slandered many other most modest and learned men with a certain fictional history, so he also slandered Socrates his teacher and his fellow students Xenophon and Plato. He forged certain lewd poems about harlots and boys in their names. Clearly, he did this so that he might obtain for himself a freer license for sinning by the false example of great philosophers. But Aristotle, to whom truth was a closer friend than even Plato <note>A reference to the famous maxim "Amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas" (Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend).</note>, could not endure such false slanders against a holy man; for in his elegies to Eudemus, he sang those things about Plato which we mentioned above, attributing this especially to him: that the profane should not only not disparage Plato in any way, but should not even dare to name his holy name with a profane mouth under the pretext of praise. Nor was he content with an elegy, but also, as Olympiodorus relates, he composed a noble oration in praise of Plato. Therefore, let the dogs of hell be silent among the gods above, and let them accompany Cerberus with their barking among the shades below. Let us, however, venerate the life and wisdom of Plato, most approved by the judgment of the wise, and let us freely proclaim along with Apuleius of Madaura: *“We of the Platonic family know nothing except what is festive, joyful, heavenly, and sublime.”*

->*As much as astronomers measure, so much do astrologers lie.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a prominent Venetian diplomat, jurist, and the father of the famous poet Pietro Bembo. He was a close friend and patron of Ficino.</note>, most illustrious jurist and knight, sends greetings.

**G**reetings a thousand times, my Bernardo—no, that is too little—greetings as many times as you draw breath, sweetest Bernardo. I write many things to you daily, but I transcribe few. For it seems to me that when I have written the original draft, I have in some way satisfied my love; however, I would by no means satisfy my duty even if I were to transcribe them. But to inform you now of our present studies: I am composing a book on the providence of God and the freedom of human choice <note>original: "de prouidentia Dei atq; humani arbitrij libertate"</note>, in which I refute, to the best of my ability, those judgments of the astrologers <term>Astrologorum iudicia</term> <note>Ficino refers to "judicial astrology," the practice of predicting specific human events and fates based on stars, which he argued interfered with the concept of free will.</note> which detract from providence and freedom. Indeed, just as diligently as astronomers truly measure the heavens, so much do the empty astrologers lie concerning human affairs. Farewell. But why do you, my most sluggish hand, pass over for so long that extraordinary Thomas, who was once the Achates <note>original: "Achaten"; a reference to the loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, used here to mean a devoted friend.</note> of Bernardo, the orator of the Venetians, whom my soul gladly embraces and my tongue celebrates? Therefore, Bernardo, as often as you see him, bid him greetings in the name of Marsilio. June 14, 1477.

->*You commend someone most when you show they belong to the one you are commending them to.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Marco Aurelio <note>Marco Aurelio was a Venetian diplomat and humanist who served as a secretary to the Venetian Republic.</note>, most illustrious orator, sends greetings.

**I**f it were permitted for me to commend your own things to you, I would most highly commend my close friend Nicolaus, who is endowed with both letters and fine character. That he is indeed yours is proven to us by your name, which sounds most frequently from his lips.

->*When love is kindled by the breath of the divine spirit, the other always loves back when one loves; often, when one thinks, the other thinks the same.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most illustrious jurist and knight, sends greetings.

**I** received a certain letter today, Bernardo, from our friend Marco Aurelio. In its very form, it was entirely Mercurial <note>Relating to Mercury, the god of messages, eloquence, and speed.</note> and very much like its father, but born, I believe, while Saturn was rising. For indeed, walking with heavier steps, although it departed from you in fair Venice on the sixteenth day of May, it finally reached our shores on the nineteenth of June. Embracing this letter with the greatest joy, I said in congratulation: "You have come at last, and your devotion has overcome a misfortune-filled journey." Even though this letter, as if born under Saturn, was somewhat slower in its movement, nevertheless, as if conceived by Mercury, it seems to have been most swift in its effect. For that which it asks of us today, it already fulfilled long ago while it was being born. 

In truth, on those same days of May in which the golden <note>A pun on the name "Aurelius," which comes from the Latin word for gold, "aurum."</note> Aurelius wrote to me, I—stirred by some hidden and almost divine instinct, whether of his letter or his Muse—dedicated a certain short work to Aurelio. Unless that work itself has also been Saturnine <note>Saturn was associated with slowness, melancholy, and gravity in Renaissance astrology.</note> in its gait, I believe it has already reached you. Observe, Bernardo, the wonderful power of our guardian spirits. While that Marco was giving himself freely to me, I in turn was giving the whole of myself to him by right, and I was embracing him as he was wonderfully embracing me. And so, by a certain celestial breath blowing us together, we conspired as one, almost without knowing it. I believe indeed that either Mercury himself in Taurus, or Phoebus in Gemini, tuned the twin lyres of Aurelio and Marsilio so similarly that when one sounds, the other resounds in turn. And from both let that sweet name of Bembo re-echo—a name musical to the Graces and most pleasing to the Muses. Farewell happily. But I see my Bernardo (for I know the man's nature) can neither wish to be, nor be able to be well without his delights. Cristoforo Landino <note>A famous Florentine humanist and professor, best known for his commentaries on Dante’s Divine Comedy.</note>, the glory of Minerva and the Muses, and Giovanni Cavalcanti <note>Ficino’s closest friend and the man to whom he dedicated many works.</note>, our fellow philosopher, are doing well. Therefore, fare you well. June 19, 1477.

->*When love is kindled by the breath of the divine spirit, the other always loves back when one loves; often, when one thinks, the other thinks the same.*<-

<meta>The previous page introduced Marsilio Ficino’s correspondence with Bernardo Bembo, discussing the providence of God and the deceptive nature of judicial astrology. This page shifts toward a systematic overview of Platonic philosophy, detailing the education and character required of a philosopher.</meta>

<page-num>782</page-num>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-

For whoever, eager for the truth, turns his mind toward the contemplation of divine things, values the pleasures of the body little. Furthermore, it is necessary for the philosopher to be of a noble <note>original: "liberali"; meaning a free or generous spirit, characteristic of a "liberal" education</note> mind. Indeed, the valuing of worthless things is adverse and entirely contrary to a man who intends to contemplate the truth of things. Moreover, his will shall love justice, since he is a great student of truth, temperance, and liberty. But most of all, he seems to need sharpness of wit, memory, and greatness of soul. And indeed, these three natural gifts—wit, memory, and magnanimity—when proper discipline and a decent education are applied, produce a man perfect in virtue. But if they are neglected, they are said by Plato to be the causes of the greatest crimes. 

Therefore, the highest human diligence must be applied to this nature, so that he who is so naturally disposed may learn letters from his very childhood, as well as the elements of all the sciences. Furthermore, by the use of the lute <note>original: "Cytharæ"; the cithara or lyre, used in Greek education to instill harmony in the soul</note>, his unharmonious soul must be composed. The body must be exercised by gymnastic games, so that by its good condition it may provide a suitable service for the studies of philosophy. Meanwhile, the institutions of the best laws must be placed in his ears. The youth's mind must be formed by honorable exhortations so that it is rendered moderate and peaceful. This moral education they call <term>Ethics</term>. 

When the mind has been freed from the disturbance of appetite through those things we have mentioned, and begins now to be released from the body, the knowledge of mathematics must soon be added to it, which deals with numbers, planes, figures, solids, and their numerous movements. Since numbers, figures, and the ratios of movements pertain to thought rather than to the exterior senses, the soul is separated by the study of these not only from the appetite of the body, but also from its senses, and betakes itself to interior thought. This is indeed "to practice death" <note>original: "mortem commentari"; a famous Platonic concept from the *Phaedo* (67d) where philosophy is described as a preparation for the soul's release from the body</note> (which Plato writes is the duty of the philosopher), through which we are also made like unto God, as is said in the *Phaedrus* and *Theaetetus*. 

Among the Platonists, the order in perceiving these is such that Arithmetic is followed by Geometry, Geometry by <term>Stereometry</term> <note>the study of three-dimensional figures or solid geometry</note>, this by Astronomy, and finally Astronomy by Music. For numbers are prior to figures, and plane figures are prior to solids. Indeed, solid bodies exist before they are moved. Order and the ratios of voices follow movement. Therefore, let Arithmetic, which deals with numbers, precede; let Geometry, which treats of plane figures, follow; let Stereometry, which considers solids, succeed this; let Astronomy hold the fourth place, which undertakes the movements of solid bodies, that is, the spheres. Let the last be Music, which investigates the order of voices arising from motion. 

Having perceived these, Plato hands down <term>Dialectic</term>, that is, the science of demonstrating truth. He intends Dialectic to be not only that logic which teaches the first and smallest rules of reasoning, but also a deep artifice of a free mind, for comprehending the true and pure substance of each thing—first through physical, then through metaphysical reasons—so that a reason can be given for anything. Finally, the light of the mind may be perceived above the nature of senses and bodies, and the incorporeal species of things, which we call <term>Ideas</term>, may be understood. From these, the One itself—the source of all species, the origin and light of minds and souls, the beginning and end of all (which Plato calls the Good itself)—may be inspected. The inspection of this is Wisdom, the love of which is most rightly defined as Philosophy. 

After the philosopher's soul has first contemplated the Good itself, judging from there what things in human affairs are good or bad, shameful or honorable, harmful or useful, he arranges human affairs according to that exemplar; he leads away from evil, directs toward good, and by this <term>Prudence</term> of governing, he administers private, domestic, and public affairs, and teaches the laws and methods of administration. This is where laws had their beginning. Wherefore in the *Timaeus*, Plato asserts that Philosophy is a gift from God, than which nothing more excellent has ever been granted to us by God. For the Good itself, which is God, could grant nothing better to man than the complete likeness of His own divinity, as far as is possible. 

But who would doubt that God is truth free from the body, providing for all things? The philosopher, however, through moral instruction and that first education which we mentioned, frees the soul from the appetite and sense of the body; through dialectic he attains the truth; and through civil doctrine he provides for men. Thus it happens that Philosophy is both a gift of God, and a likeness, and a most happy imitation. If anyone is endowed with this, by his likeness to God, he will be the same on earth as God is in the heavens. For the philosopher is a mediator between God and men: a man toward God, and a God toward men. He is familiar with God’s truth, a possessor of his own liberty, and a leader of other men through civil prudence. With which indeed <note>original: "Quo quidem"; catchword for the next page</note>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK IV.</header>

Indeed, under [divine] governance, they say golden ages once existed, and Plato prophesied they would return whenever power and wisdom meet in the same mind. According to Plato, the souls of those who practice philosophy, having recovered their wings through wisdom and justice, fly back to their celestial homeland as soon as they depart from the body. They perform the same duties in the heavens as they did on earth. They rejoice in the truth with God, congratulate themselves on their liberty, care for <note>original: "prouident"; likely meaning to look out for or provide for</note> humanity with piety, and acting as the interpreters and prophets of God, they complete there what they had begun here. They turn the souls of men toward God and interpret the secret mysteries of God to human minds. For this reason, the ancient theologians rightly worshipped the minds of philosophers—once freed from the body—just like those thirty thousand spirits of Hesiod <note>The Greek poet Hesiod wrote of 30,000 "daimones" or guardian spirits who watch over mortals</note>, as if they were demigods, heroes, and blessed spirits. Philosophy, therefore (to summarize briefly), is the ascent of the soul from lower things to the higher, and from darkness to light; its beginning is the instinct of the divine mind, its middle path consists of the faculties of the disciplines we have described, its end is the possession of the highest good, and finally, its fruit is the righteous governance of men. I have shared these common themes with our friend Francesco Berlinghieri as a philosophical companion, and you likewise shall share them with our Giuliano Borgo. Farewell.

### Marsilio Ficino to his friend Francesco Bandino, Greetings.

**I** have attempted in recent days to paint the "Idea" of a Platonic philosopher in colors. But if I had brought Plato himself into our midst, I would certainly have pointed out not just a painting of that Idea, but the very Idea of the true philosopher with my own fingers. Therefore, let us look upon our Plato, and we shall see the philosopher, philosophy, and the Idea itself all at once.

<margin>On the life of Plato.</margin>

### The Genealogy and Birth of Plato.

**P**lato of Athens, the son of Ariston and Perictione (or Potone), traces his lineage on both sides back to Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon; Plato's family claimed descent from the sea god through the early kings of Athens</note>. For Solon descended from Neleus <note>OCR: "Nereno"</note> and Neptune. Solon’s brother, Dropides, fathered the elder Critias, from whom descended Callaeschrus, who had two sons: the younger Critias (who was one of the thirty governors of Athens) and Glaucon, the father of Charmides and Perictione. Perictione, having married Ariston, gave birth to Plato, Adeimantus, and Glaucon, as well as a daughter, Potone, who married Eurymedon and bore Speusippus. Furthermore, Ariston, Plato's father, descended from Codrus the son of Melanthus, who also (like Solon) trace their origin back to Neptune. It is a famous story in Athens that when Ariston attempted to lie with Perictione, who was very beautiful, his attempts were in vain; he then saw Apollo in a dream and was commanded by him to keep his wife pure from marital intercourse until she gave birth. Both Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, the 3rd-century biographer of philosophers</note> and Polycrates write this. He was born in Athens or in Aegina, 756 years from the capture of Troy, in the 334th year from the founding of the city [of Rome], and 434 years before the coming of Christ. I previously described Plato's birth chart <note>original: "genesim"</note> as I had heard it in my youth in my *Book on Love* <note>Ficino's famous commentary on Plato's *Symposium*</note>. But now I shall present it as the astronomer Julius Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer</note> describes it, whose opinion in this matter I consider more accurate. It is as follows:

<margin>
I indicated Plato's birth chart as I had heard it in my youth in the book *On Love*. But now I shall present it as Julius Firmicus the Astronomer describes it, whose opinion in this matter I consider truer. It is thus:
In the Ascendant: Aquarius, with Mars, Mercury, and Venus.
In the second house: The Sun in Pisces.
In the fifth: The Moon in Gemini.
In the seventh: Jupiter in Leo.
In the ninth: Saturn in Libra.
</margin>

<margin>
Julius Firmicus asserts that this birth chart signifies a man who prevails with wonderful eloquence and, with a celestial genius, approaches all the secrets of divinity.
</margin>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK IV.</header>

->The Second Voyage<-

<note>Drop cap S</note>
**S**econdly, he set out to visit Dionysius the Younger <note>Dionysius II, the ruler of Syracuse in Sicily</note>, having been summoned by him and by Dion for the sake of studying philosophy. Led by this hope, he believed he could bring it about through his counsel that the state there would be transformed from a tyranny into either a Republic or a kingdom. He hoped to see what he had long and vehemently desired: a truly philosophical government, in which either philosophers rule or rulers philosophize <note>original: "uel gubernēt Philosophi uel gubernatores philosophentur"; a reference to Plato's famous "philosopher-king" ideal in the Republic</note>. For he thought that cities could not otherwise avoid misery. He desired all this to be achieved not by force or deceit, but by persuading Dionysius through philosophical reasoning. But nearly four months after Plato's arrival, Dionysius, driven by false slanders, expelled Dion on the grounds that he was plotting against the tyranny, though he continued to embrace Plato's presence. Eventually, Plato returned to his homeland. He traveled there a third time to reconcile Dion with Dionysius, having been pleaded with by both again. He was also asked by Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher and statesman</note>. On that occasion, Dionysius sent a trireme <note>an ancient warship with three banks of oars</note> to meet him, as well as Archidamus the Pythagorean orator and many noblemen; Dionysius himself received him as he stepped out from a carriage drawn by four white horses. Plato demanded the promised restitution of Dion, and furthermore, land and men who might live according to the Republic he had established. Although Dionysius had promised this, he refused to fulfill it. When Plato publicly rebuked Dionysius for breaking his word—both regarding the restoration of Dion and regarding his friend Theodotus's plea to protect Heraclides—Dionysius became hostile toward him. Consequently, Plato lived in the greatest danger of being killed by the soldiers. However, Archytas of Tarentum sent Lamiscus as an envoy to Dionysius with a ship, requesting that he release Plato. He released him and provided supplies; Plato then returned to his homeland. Shortly thereafter, Dionysius was driven from his tyranny by Dion and the citizens, thus paying the penalty for the crime committed against Philosophy. Plato was received with wonderful honor in his homeland, and though he was called to participate in the Republic <note>the government of Athens</note>, he refused to go because the common people had become accustomed to wicked habits.

---

->To whom Plato gave laws<-

<note>Drop cap F</note>
**I**t is said that the Arcadians and Thebans, having founded a city of respectable size, asked him to establish a Republic there. However, when he understood that they were unwilling to follow equality <note>the principle of equal distribution of goods or status</note>, he did not go. But he did give laws to the Syracusans after the tyrant was expelled, and he wrote the laws for the Cretans for the recently founded city of Magnesia, organized into twelve books. Among his close associates, he sent Aristonymus to the Arcadians to establish laws, Phormio to the people of Elis <note>original: "Ilios", though likely referring to Elis or a specific colony</note>, and Menedemus to the Pyrrheans.

---

->The self-restraint, dignity, and courtesy of Plato<-

<note>Drop cap V</note>
**H**e lived unmarried and was extremely sober and (as Aurelius Augustine asserts) chaste. For this reason, even in his old age, he is said to have performed the sacred rites of nature <note>original: "sacra naturae"; likely referring to rituals intended to prove his vitality or address his lack of children</note> so that he might clear himself before the common people of the charge of infertility. As a youth, he was so modest and so composed that he was never caught laughing, except moderately. No one ever saw him angry. Hence, a boy educated at Plato's house, upon returning to his parents and seeing his father shouting, said, "I never saw this at Plato's." Only once was he secretly a little angry with a boy who had committed a serious fault, but he said to Xenocrates <note>one of Plato's students and later head of the Academy</note>, "You beat this boy, for I cannot do it because I am angry." He ate only once a day, or if twice, very sparingly. He slept alone. He greatly disparaged a life of the opposite sort. He seemed a little more inclined toward the love of young men, just as his teacher Socrates was. But both were as restrained in their reason as they were inclined in their feelings. How divinely they loved, and in what manner, is explained by what they said about love, and we have treated this sufficiently in our book *On Love*. He desired to leave a memory of himself either in books or in friends. And although he was of a melancholic temperament and of the deepest genius (as Aristotle writes), he nevertheless employed many jests; he very often advised the more severe Xenocrates and Dion to "sacrifice to the Graces" <note>an ancient idiom meaning to adopt a more pleasant or charming manner</note> so that they might be rendered more pleasant and agreeable. Indeed, courtesy was mixed with Plato's dignity.

### *The Principal Disciples of Plato.*

**H**is disciples were Speusippus the Athenian, Xenocrates of Chalcedon, Aristotle the Stagirite, Philip of Opus, Hestiaeus of Perinthus, Dion of Syracuse, Anicles, Heraclides, Erastus and Coriscus of Scepsis, Timolaus of Cyzicus, Hebeon of Lampsacus, Pithorus, and Heraclides of Aenus, Hippothales and Callippus the Athenians, Demetrius of Amphipolis, Heraclides Ponticus, and many others. Along with these were two women, Lasthenia of Mantinea and Axithea of Phlius, who were known to wear men's clothing. They also say that the philosopher Theophrastus was one of his listeners, as were the orator Hyperides, Chamaeleon, and Lycurgus; Demosthenes and Menestratus were also said to have been his devoted students. Upon the entrance of the Academy <note>The school founded by Plato in Athens, located in a grove dedicated to the hero Academus</note> was inscribed: "Let no one unskilled in geometry enter here." <note>original: "Nemo huc geometriæ expers ingrediatur"</note> Indeed, he wished this to be understood not only regarding the measurement of lines, but also regarding the proper measure of the passions.

### *The Books of Plato.*

**H**e wrote a book on holiness called *Euthyphro*; the *Apology of Socrates*; *Crito*, concerning what he discussed with Socrates in prison; *Phaedo*, on the immortality of the soul; *Cratylus*, on the correct reasoning of names; *Theaetetus*, on knowledge; *The Sophist* <term>sophist</term> <note>professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion over truth</note>, on that which exists; *The Statesman*, on kingship; *Parmenides*, on the single principle of all things and on the Ideas; *Philebus*, on the highest good; the *Symposium*, on love; *Phaedrus*, on beauty; the *First Alcibiades*, on human nature; the *Second Alcibiades*, on prayer; *Hipparchus*, on the desire for profit; *The Lovers*, on philosophy; *Theages*, on wisdom; *Charmides*, on temperance; *Laches*, on courage; *Lysis*, on friendship; *Euthydemus*, on contentious reasoning; *Protagoras*, on morals; *Gorgias*, on rhetoric; *Meno*, on virtue; the *Greater Hippias*, on beauty; the *Lesser Hippias*, on falsehood; *Menexenus*, on Athenian antiquity; ten books of the *Republic*; *Timaeus*, on the nature of the world; *Critias*, on Athenian antiquity; *Minos*, on law; twelve books of the *Laws*; the *Epinomis* (or *The Philosopher*); and thirteen *Letters*. I myself <note>Marsilio Ficino, the translator of this volume</note> have translated all these books of Plato from the Greek language into Latin. Truly, there are three types of Platonic dialogues: he either refutes the sophists, exhorts the youth, or teaches adults. Those things which Plato spoke in his own voice—in the letters, the books of the *Laws*, or the *Epinomis*—he wishes to be held as most certain; however, what he disputes through the mouths of Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides, or Zeno in the other books, he wishes to be held as probable truths.

### *The Eloquence, Wisdom, and Authority of Plato.*

**T**he style of Plato (as Aristotle says) flows midway between prose and poetry; its sweetness and abundance are so great that Cicero called Plato the most venerable author and master of both understanding and speaking. He added that if Jupiter had wished to speak in a human tongue, he would have spoken in no other language than that of Plato. Indeed, there was such great learning in him that while before him all the illustrious Greeks had traveled to foreign nations for the sake of wisdom, after Plato's time, all other nations flocked to Athens. Even Aristotle, endowed with such miraculous talent and most eager for new doctrines, when he came to Plato as a nearly grown man, listened to him for twenty continuous years. 

Add to this that before he even came to Plato, he was already advanced in letters; yet afterward, he held Plato as his only teacher. I pass over what is written by Cicero: "I would rather err with Plato than be right with the others." <note>original: "malo cum Platone errare quàm cum cæteris rectè sentire"</note> Furthermore, along with Panaetius, he calls him the "God of Philosophers." I pass over that saying of Quintilian: "Who could doubt that Plato is supreme, whether in the sharpness of his debating or in a certain divine and Homeric power of eloquence?" For his speech rises far above ordinary prose—which the Greeks call <term>pedestrian</term> <note>original: "pedestrem"; referring to language that stays on the ground rather than "flying" like poetry</note>—so that he seems to me not inspired by human talent, but by some Delphic oracle. Through his divine wisdom and integrity, he seems to have acquired for himself a marvelous authority, even in his own homeland, which is something that happens very rarely. Upon returning from Sicily, Plato...

<page-num>767</page-num>

When he had arrived at that most magnificent celebration of the Olympics—as if to an assembly of the whole world—he was received by such joyful gatherings of everyone that he seemed like a God sent down from heaven to mortals. They saw the games deserted, the spectacles of the athletes abandoned, and the boxers left alone; and what is even more wonderful, those who had come to Olympia across such long stretches of land and sea for the sake of feeding their eyes, ears, and minds, forgot all pleasure and went to Plato, gazing upon him. They rested in Plato as if in the most pleasant of inns. When someone was reciting a tragedy and no one was present except Plato, and some people objected that it was a disgrace to him that no one but one person was there, he responded: "Even this one person is worth more than the entire Athenian people."

->*The Charity, Magnanimity, and Holiness of Plato.*<-

With how great and constant a spirit he was, especially in the cause of his friends, is indicated by his letters, his contempt for the tyrant, and his defense of Dion <note>Dion of Syracuse, a disciple of Plato who attempted to reform the government of Syracuse</note>. He often boldly rebuked the tyrant <note>Dionysius II, the ruler of Syracuse</note> because he governed unjustly or because he deceived his friends, even in the presence of witnesses; so far was he from flattering him. I pass over those smaller matters, such as when Dionysius had ordered at a banquet that each person should put on purple garments <margin>and dance.</margin> Aristippus <note>A philosopher and contemporary of Plato who favored pleasure and luxury</note> danced immediately, but Plato refused, saying that womanly things did not befit a philosopher. Furthermore, when the wicked Crobylus had set a day for the trial of the most brave general Chabrias and had intended a capital judgment against him, and when Chabrias was abandoned by the rest of the citizens for fear of danger as he ascended to the citadel, Plato alone was present at that time to offer help. Indeed, when the slanderer Crobylus, in order to deter him from the defense, said threateningly: "You come here to offer defense to others, ignorant that the poison of Socrates awaits you as well," he responded: "Long ago, Crobylus, when I was a soldier for the dignity of my fatherland, I was not slow in the face of intolerable dangers; now, for my duty and the safety of a friend, though you threaten with <unclear>sharpened</unclear> iron and fire, I refuse no trial." When Socrates was most unjustly shut in prison, Plato collected money to ransom the innocent man; and while the judgment was being carried out, ascending onto the platform, he began to plead thus: "Since I am the youngest of all these Athenians who have ascended the tribunal..." But the judges, fearing the tyrant and fearing that he might move the citizens with his authority and eloquence, suddenly interrupted him and shouted: "Get down!" Plato went home. For as much as they labored under a disease of a wicked mind, he was then laboring under a disease of the body. However, the persecutors of Socrates paid the penalty a little later. When one of his fellow students was incited by envy because Xenocrates was so pleasing and acceptable to Plato that he stirred up enmities against him, he reported many of Xenocrates' insults against Plato. In the middle of the speech, Plato rejected the accusation and ignored it. The detractor insisted, affirming the crime with a severity of face, finally calling all the Gods and Goddesses to witness. Plato, so that he might free himself from the man's persistence, said: "So be it; but Xenocrates is so strong in faith and gravity that unless he had judged it to be profitable, he would never have said those things." That Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, imitated the gravity and magnanimity of Plato is testified by the *Life of Xenocrates* by Diogenes <note>Diogenes Laertius, the biographer of ancient philosophers</note>, which is indeed an example of fortitude and holiness. Plutarch is witness that Dion also imitated him. Furthermore, Philiscus, describing the life of the orator Lycurgus, says: "Lycurgus was a great man and many things were performed by him excellently, which no one could have done who had not been a listener of Plato." When Demosthenes was fleeing Antipatrus and the latter promised to save his life with flattering words, he said: "Far be it from me that I should prefer to live basely rather than die honorably, after I have heard Xenocrates and Plato debating on the immortality of the soul." The same man, writing to a certain fellow student named Heracleodorus and rebuking him because, after he had heard Plato, he neglected the noble arts and led a life of little honor, said: "Are you not ashamed to neglect those things which you received from Plato?" Dionysius, writing to Speusippus, says: "Plato indeed taught those treading his threshold for free, but you demand tribute, and you take it from the willing and the unwilling alike." Laertius also carps at the same man because he did not, like Xenocrates, imitate the chastity, fortitude, and gentleness of Plato. Truly, I cannot remain silent regarding that instance of the fortitude of Xenocrates: when Dionysius said to Plato, "Your head <margin>is at risk</margin>..."

->The Maxims and Proverbs of Plato.<-
->Plato used to say these things regarding Aristotle and Xenocrates.<-

**W**hat a horse and what a donkey I have taken to be yoked together! Aristotle indeed needs a bridle, but Xenocrates needs spurs. <note>Plato meant that Aristotle was too quick and impulsive, while Xenocrates was too slow and hesitant.</note> Among his disciples was a youth who was overly refined and extremely devoted to pampering his skin; Plato asked him: "How long will you continue building a prison for yourself?" Whenever he saw a man ensnared by love, he would say: "That man is dead in his own body, but lives in another’s." He added that he who abandons himself for the sake of another is the most wretched of all, since he no longer possesses himself, nor does he possess the other. A certain learned friend of Plato’s begged him to lend his ears for a moment to hear a short book he had published. When Plato asked what the title of the book was, the man replied, "That one should not contradict." To which Plato said: "Why then are you doing exactly that? Why do you contradict those who contradict? Why do you consult me, if you forbid yourself from being contradicted?" Leo, a powerful citizen, was being criticized in a gathering because he had engaged in loud and immoderate shouting in the senate. Plato said: "This is what it truly means to be a 'Leo' <note>A pun on the name Leo, which means Lion</note>." To Diogenes the Cynic, who said that he could see these human things, but could not see the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect forms of things—like "the concept of a chair"—which Plato taught were more real than physical objects</note> at all, Plato replied: "That is no wonder; for you have and use the eyes by which these physical things are seen, but you do not use the mind, by which alone those Ideas are perceived." When his disciples were marveling that Xenocrates, who was serious in all aspects of life, had said something that provoked laughter, Plato said: "Why do you wonder that roses and lilies sometimes grow among thorns?" To the living, he was frequently accustomed to say: "Put labor before leisure, unless perhaps you think that rust is better than splendor." He often guided the youth toward a blessed life with this reasoning: "Observe the contrary natures of virtue and pleasure; for the momentary sweetness of pleasure is followed by sudden repentance and perpetual pain, while the brief labors of virtue are followed by eternal pleasure." When he saw someone playing with dice, he rebuked him; and when the man said, "How small a thing you find fault with," Plato replied, "But habit is no small thing." He was accustomed to advise the drunk and the angry to look at themselves diligently in a mirror; he believed they would immediately abandon such foulness. He greatly detested drunkenness and sleep. He used to say that it was of the greatest importance in educating children that they be accustomed to find joy only in honorable things. Otherwise, he said, pleasure was the "bait of evils." He added that the health of the soul is true Philosophy. He viewed other skills not so much as Philosophy, but rather as ornaments. Nothing is sweeter to a healthy mind than to speak and hear the truth, for nothing is either better or more durable than truth. When certain people asked what kinds of possessions should be especially prepared for one's children, he said: "Those which fear neither hail, nor the violence of men, nor even Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note> himself." To Demoncus, who consulted him on the education of his son, he said: "Just as care must be taken in planting and directing young trees, so must care be taken in begetting and instructing sons. Here is the labor, there the pleasure; we must be careful, however, lest we appear asleep in the former and more than awake in the latter." To a certain Philedonus who criticized Plato because he was no less studious and diligent in learning than in teaching, and who asked how long he wished to be a student, Plato replied: "As long as I am not sorry to become better and more skilled." When asked what the difference was between the skilled and the unskilled, he replied: "The same as between a doctor and a sick man." He used to say that for princes, there is no more excellent kind of property than the friendship of men who do not know how to haggle. Wisdom is no less necessary to a prince than the soul is to the body. Republics would be most happy if either philosophers should rule, or at least if those who govern should, by some divine fate, practice philosophy. For nothing is more pestilent than power and audacity when they are accompanied by ignorance. He also said that subjects tend to be of the same character as their princes. A magistrate must not think of his own good, but the public good; he must care not only for a certain part of the state, but for the whole.

# LETTERS, BOOK IV.

->*How greatly Plato neglected human affairs, and how greatly he loved divine ones.*<-

**H**e used to repeat daily that only eternal things are true, while temporal things are merely "likenesses of the truth." <note>original: "verisimilia," referring to the Platonic idea that the physical world is a shadow or imitation of the higher world of Ideas.</note> He believed the soul sleeps within the body, and that the things the senses desire or fear are nothing more than dreams. Therefore, all these things should be utterly despised; to avoid the evils with which the world is filled, one must take refuge in eternal things, for they cannot be avoided any other way. He himself fulfilled what he preached. For while he was destined to be a leader in the republic by both hereditary right and the favor of the citizens, he utterly rejected all civil dignity. Although he was very wealthy by inheritance, he bestowed everything upon his brothers, except for a small suburban estate which they called the Academy. <note>The "Academia" was a grove or garden outside Athens where Plato established his school.</note> Content with this alone, he lived his life; and though he stood out as a teacher and friend to princes, he accepted no riches from them. King Dionysius used to say: "Aristippus is always asking for money, but Plato is always asking for books." Add to this that he never took a wife, nor did he live in the city, being free from all things and serving the truth alone. Regarding this, Saint Jerome says: "Plato traveled with great labor through Egypt, and visited Archytas of Tarentum and that coast of Italy which was once called Great Greece. <note>original: "Magna Graecia," the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy.</note> Thus he, who was a powerful master in Athens and whose doctrines echoed through the gymnasiums of the Academy, became a pilgrim and a disciple, preferring to learn the ideas of others with modesty rather than to impudently thrust his own upon them." Finally, while he was pursuing learning as if it were fleeing across the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold; he even obeyed a most cruel tyrant as a captive, bound and a slave, yet he remained greater than the one who bought him because he was a Philosopher. These are the words of Jerome.

->*The Piety and Gratitude of Plato.*<-

**H**e was grateful to God, from whom he said the beginning of thinking, speaking, and acting in all things must come, and he always practiced this himself. Furthermore, he gave thanks to God daily for three things: that he had been born a human and not a brute animal, that he was a Greek and not a Barbarian, and that he lived in the time of Socrates. His dialogues bear witness to how grateful he was to his teachers and all his friends, for in them he honors them all wonderfully; he even attributed his own books to Socrates. For not only does he introduce Socrates as the speaker in nearly all his dialogues, but he also writes that all the things he composed were not his own, but belonged to Socrates.

->*What Plato Affirmed, and Those Who Confirmed Him.*<-

**I**n those things which are subject to the senses, he defended the views of Heraclitus. Furthermore, in those things pertaining to the intellect, he most closely followed Pythagoras. However, in civil matters, he embraced his own teacher Socrates. These are the things he asserted everywhere: That God provides for all things. That the souls of men are immortal. That there will be rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked. Augustine says in his book *Against the Academicians* that the authority of Christ is to be preferred above all; however, if one must proceed by reason, he says he finds among the Platonists that which is not repugnant to the sacred writings of the Christians. Dionysius the Areopagite indicated the same. Later, Eusebius and Cyril declared this more extensively. In his book *On True Religion*, Augustine says: "The Platonists, with a few changes, would become Christians." And in his *Confessions*, he relates that he found nearly the entire prologue of the Gospel of John among the Platonists. <note>Augustine famously noted that the Greek philosophers grasped the concept of the "Logos" or Divine Word, though they lacked the concept of the Incarnation.</note> Therefore, in the second book of *The City of God*, he says: "Labeo the Theologian thought that among the Gentiles, Plato should be numbered among the demigods, like Hercules and Romulus." He places demigods above heroes, but situates both among the divinities. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this man whom he calls a demigod is to be preferred not only to heroes, but even to those very gods. Whence he says that he chose the Platonists above others because they felt much more correctly about divine and human matters than the other philosophers. This is what Marcus Varro had judged before, and Apuleius made Plato not only superior to heroes, but equal to the gods, because he evidently penetrated the secrets of divine things. Plato was endowed with such modesty that, although he had acquired a marvelous authority above others, when asked by someone to what extent his precepts should be obeyed, he replied: "Until someone more sacred appears on earth, who shall open the fountain of truth to all, and whom all shall finally follow." <note>Renaissance scholars often interpreted this "sacratior" (more sacred one) as a pagan prophecy of the coming of Christ.</note>

<summary>This page describes Plato's ascetic rejection of wealth and politics, his deep gratitude for his teacher Socrates, and his philosophical alignment with Christian doctrine as noted by Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the biographical sketch of Plato by Marsilio Ficino, focusing on the philosopher's death, the honors bestowed upon him by his successors, and a defense against those who slandered his moral character.</meta>

<page-num>770</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...everyone. He added that he discovered nothing by his own power, but only by the divine light. As for his philosophical views, we have discussed them enough in our book *On Love* and in our *Platonic Theology*. <note>Ficino refers here to his own major works, which sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>

->*Plato’s return to his heavenly homeland and his praises.*<-

**H**e died on his birthday, completing eighty-one years without any decline. Therefore, the Magi <note>original: "Magi," referring to Persian priests or wise men who were said to be in Athens at the time.</note> who were then in Athens sacrificed to Plato, believing his lot to have been greater than human because he had completed the most perfect number, which nine multiplied by nine produces. <note>The number 81 (9x9) was considered significant in Pythagorean numerology as a "perfect" square of a sacred number.</note> And what is marvelous, he was still writing at that age and on that very day. Concerning this, Cicero says: "There is also a peaceful and mild old age for a life spent quietly, purely, and elegantly, such as we have heard was the case with Plato, who died while writing in his eighty-first year." <note>A quote from Cicero's essay "On Old Age" (De Senectute).</note> Seneca also affirms that this happened to Plato by the benefit of his sobriety and diligence. Some say he returned to the heavens while writing, others while reclining at a wedding after the tables had been removed, amidst conversation. Aristotle consecrated an altar and a statue to Plato in a temple with this epigram: "Aristotle dedicated this altar to Plato, a man whom it is a sin for the evil to praise." Aristotle added: "He who alone, by his life, teaching, character, and speech, admonished all and gave us monuments so that through virtue they might lead a happy life. No future ages will bring forth such a man." Other wise men joined in many poems in praise of Plato, but three epigrams are foremost. The meaning of the first is this: "He excelled all in temperance and justice, but surpassed them so much in wisdom that he utterly overcame all envy." The sense of the second is this: "Plato has been translated into the number of the gods. Distant nations honor him because he knew the divine life himself and showed it to others." The meaning of the third is of this sort: "Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo.</note> fathered Aesculapius and Plato—the former to heal bodies, the latter to heal souls." Furthermore, Mithridates, King of the Persians, placed a statue of Plato in the Academy inscribed thus: "Mithridates, son of Rodobates, a Persian, dedicated this image of Plato, a work of Silanion, to the Muses." From all these things, Plato achieved this: that the Greeks called Aristotle "daemonic," <note>original: "dæmonium," meaning possessing a powerful, intermediate spirit or intellect; not "demonic" in the modern sense.</note> but called Plato "divine." This is clearly because Aristotle was most human in his life and most natural in his science, while Plato turned both his science and his life primarily toward divine things.

->*A defense of Plato’s character.*<-

**I** shall now bring my words to an end if I add a few more things. There are certain common versifiers who undeservedly usurp the name of Poets; these men, provoked as much by the difference in their character as by the malice of envy, most impudently mock all the best people. In our age especially, a certain great license is granted to them against the good rather than the bad. But I would not wish to remember our times, which are as unfit for pursuing virtue as they seem fit for attacking it. Thus, such "poetasters" <note>original: "Poëticuli," a derogatory term for minor or inferior poets.</note> of old did not hesitate to bite at the divine Plato (judged by the Greeks to be the son of Apollo) and Socrates (judged by the Greek Apollo to be the wisest of men). Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> greatly detested their impiety. And as he himself declares, Aristippus of Cyrene increased the ridiculous insults of the comic writers—a most wicked man and an adversary of the best people of his time. Just as he slandered many other most modest and learned men with a fictional history, so he also slandered his teacher Socrates and his fellow students Xenophon and Plato. He forged certain lewd poems in their names addressed to harlots and boys. Clearly, he did this so that, by the false example of great philosophers, he might obtain a freer license for himself to sin. But Aristotle, to whom the truth was a closer friend than even Plato, <note>A reference to the famous saying: "Plato is my friend, but truth is a better friend."</note> could not endure such false slanders against a holy man; for in his elegies to Eudemus he sang those things about Plato which we mentioned above, granting him this especially: that the profane should not only not disparage Plato in any way, but should not even dare to name his holy name with a profane mouth under the pretext of praise. Nor was he content with an elegy, but also, as Olympiodorus relates, he composed a noble oration in praise of Plato. Let the hounds of hell, therefore, be silent among those above, and let them accompany Cerberus with their barking among those below. Let us, however, venerate the life and wisdom of Plato, most approved by the judgment of the wise, and let us freely proclaim along with Apuleius of Madaura: "We of the Platonic family know nothing but what is festive, joyful, heavenly, and sublime."

### LETTERS, BOOK IV

->*As much as Astronomers measure, so much do Astrologers lie.*<-
<note>original: "Quantum Astronomi metiuntur, tantum Astrologi mentiuntur." Ficino makes a sharp distinction here between "Astronomy"—the mathematical study of planetary movements—and "Astrology"—the practice of making specific predictions about human life, which he often criticized when it threatened the concept of free will.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished jurist and knight, greetings.<-

**A** thousand greetings, my Bernardo; I have said too little—greetings as many times as you draw breath, my sweetest Bernardo. I write many things to you daily, yet I transcribe few. For I seem to myself to have satisfied love in some way once I have written the original draft; but even if I were to fulfill the duty of informing you by making a copy, I would hardly be satisfied. However, to inform you now of our present studies, I am composing a book on the providence of God and the freedom of human choice, in which I refute, to the best of my ability, those judgments of the Astrologers which detract from providence and liberty. Truly, as diligently as the Astronomers truly measure the heavens, so much do the empty Astrologers lie concerning human affairs. Farewell. But why has my most idle hand for so long passed over that excellent Thomas, once the "Achates" <note>Achates was the famously loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid; here, Ficino uses it as a term for a devoted friend or secretary.</note> of Bernardo, the Venetian ambassador? My soul gladly embraces him, and my tongue sounds his name. Therefore, Bernardo, as often as you see him, bid him greetings in the name of Marsilio. June 14, 1477.

->*You commend someone most greatly when you show that person belongs to him to whom you commend them.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Marco Aurelio, most distinguished orator, greetings.<-

**I**f it were permitted to commend your own people to you, I would most highly commend my familiar friend Nicolaus, a man gifted in both letters and character. That he is indeed yours is proven to us by your name, which sounds most frequently from his lips.

->*When love is kindled by the inspiration of the divine spirit, the other always loves back when one loves; often, when one thinks, the other thinks the same.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished jurist and knight, greetings.<-

**I** received a certain letter today, Bernardo, from our friend Marco Aurelio. In its very form, it was entirely "Mercurial" <note>Mercurial here refers to eloquence, speed, and intelligence, associated with the god Mercury.</note> and very like its father, but born, as I judge, with Saturn rising. Truly, proceeding with heavier steps, since it departed from you in the Venetian territory on the sixteenth day of May, it finally landed on our shores on the 19th of June. I embraced this letter with the greatest joy and said in congratulation: "You have come at last, and your devotion has overcome the unfortunate journey." Although this letter appeared somewhat slower in its movement, as if born under Saturn, nevertheless it seems to have been most swift in its effect, as if conceived by Mercury. For that which it asks of us today, it already fulfilled long ago while it was being born. Indeed, on the very days in May when the "golden" Aurelio <note>A pun on the name Aurelio, which derives from the Latin "aurum" meaning gold.</note> wrote to me, I—driven by some hidden and almost divine instinct, whether of the letter or of his muse—dedicated a certain short work to Aurelio. Unless that work also proved to be "Saturnine" in its gait, I believe it has already reached you.

Observe for a moment, Bernardo, the marvelous power of our guiding spirits. While that Marco was giving himself freely to me, I in turn was giving the whole of myself to him by right, and I was wonderfully embracing him as he embraced me. And so, by a certain blowing of the heavenly spirit, we conspired together into one, almost without knowing it. I believe indeed that either Mercury himself placed in Taurus, or Apollo in Gemini, has so similarly tuned the twin lyres of Aurelio and Marsilio, that when one sounds, the other resounds in turn. And from both echoes that sweet name of Bembo, a name musical to the Graces and most pleasing to the Muses. Farewell happily. But I see my Bernardo—for I know the man’s nature—can neither be, nor ever wish to be, truly well without his "delights." <note>Ficino likely refers to Bembo's literary interests or his circle of friends.</note> Cristoforo Landino, the glory of Minerva and the Muses, and Giovanni Cavalcanti, our fellow philosopher, are well. Therefore, fare you well. June 19, 1477.

**Y**our most elegant letter was delivered to us yesterday, most learned Marco, a letter sweeter to me than honey and more precious than gold. But what am I doing? I am not permitted now to enter into praises concerning this...

to proceed further regarding this, lest I perhaps appear too vain, if I myself were to attempt to praise that letter sufficiently, which praises me more than enough. Therefore, let us begin again from another point, if you please. When love is kindled in our minds by a certain celestial spirit breathing upon us, whenever one person loves, the other always loves in return; often, while one is thinking, the other thinks the same thing in a similar way. For the celestial Author, since he embraces both as the common cause of all things, creates a mutual affection between lovers; and the affection of the lover, which depends on heaven through man, creates a reciprocal "Echo," striking both the face of plain humanity and the hollows of heaven. Greetings, therefore, my celestial friend; greetings always in God, the author of our benevolence. Neither the distances of lands, Marcus, nor any intervals of time seem to have been able to interrupt this celestial and perpetual love of ours, whether as it was rising or once it had arisen, or to delay it from the fact that as soon as one loved, the other by some divine chance loved in return; and while one was thinking and writing, the other at almost the same moment both thought and wrote the same thing. I believe you noticed, Aurelius—if only you have received that little work of mine recently sent to you—that at the very same time you were writing to me, I was also writing to you in turn. Moreover, that both of us then signified and requested exactly the same thing. To me, indeed, nothing in human affairs is more fortunate than to have emerged as an equal through that affection to him whom I hear is superior to no one in virtue. Nothing is more precious than to happily possess such and so great a possessor of myself. I have, therefore, with my whole mind, what I was seeking. But I grieve in a certain way for this one thing: that I am by no means the whole of what you yourself were seeking. My Aurelius, if you cannot have what you wish, at least wish to have what you can. Receive your Marsilio, Marcus, as a whole, however small he may be. I pray you, do not look further at that image which you had fashioned from the beginning, for Ficino is but a certain member of that image. Look rather, friend, at what you possess, than at what you imagine. Thus, certainly, you will recognize that you possess not a part of someone, but a whole something. For it is better to enjoy some whole pygmy than the limb of a vast giant.

->Nothing is weaker than human love, nothing firmer than divine love.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished jurist and knight, sends greetings.

**Y**ou write to us an oratory, poetic, and amatory letter, but I know not why you excuse yourself in vain for what absolutely no one accuses you of. Beware lest, where love is perfect, you think even the slightest offense could ever occur. In this one way alone, perhaps, you can offend charity: if you think that it can ever be offended. Human love is indeed a thing full of anxious fear, but divine charity <note>original: "charitas." Ficino distinguishes between "amor" (human love) and "charitas" (divine, selfless love), drawing on the Greek "agape."</note>—if we listen to Paul—believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails; or if we listen to John the Evangelist, fear does not dwell in charity, but perfect charity casts out all fear. Hence our Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> exclaims: "He alone loses no dear one, to whom all are dear in Him who is not lost." But I know not how I had just now begun a certain homily, as they say. And so I was delivering the duties of charity to that man whom the Florentine people admire, as if he were a certain image of charity and an exemplar of humanity.

->In vain do we excessively affect our own sufficiency in these things which are in no way sufficient for themselves.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to the human race, sends greetings.

**Y**ou seek sufficiency <note>original: "sufficientia." This carries the sense of self-sufficiency, contentment, or being "enough."</note> everywhere with the purpose that, after you have found this one thing, you will seek nothing further. Yet you always seek as many things as possible for this very reason: because you never attain this one thing. Do you want me to tell you the reason why you never attain sufficiency? Perhaps because you seek it outside of yourself. If, therefore, mortal riches cannot suffice for an immortal soul, take care that the soul itself at least suffices for them. Pay attention to what I say: I do not say that the soul should satisfy itself—for how can that which is both made and perfected by another satisfy itself? In vain indeed, alas, we wretched ones seek our sufficiency in these things which are in no way sufficient for themselves. Truly, only that which is enough for itself satisfies everyone entirely. But nothing can be enough for itself, except—

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical discourse on the nature of the "Immense Good" (God) and transitions into a formal letter to Riccardo Anghieri, where Ficino translates and discusses Plato's famous Allegory of the Cave to explain the difficult transition between worldly affairs and divine contemplation.</meta>

<header>LETTERS. BOOK IV.</header>
<sig>Ccc 3</sig>

...through the immense good which is from itself and toward itself. Here then alone, here, I say, let us seek what will satisfy us. Let it not be wearisome; no one ever follows the good in vain, who follows it well. For the good itself, because it is immense, flourishes everywhere and overflows from all sides; and our success in following it well is undoubtedly something good. But he alone wills well and follows the good, who follows individual goods everywhere for the sake of that supreme goodness itself, through which all individual things are good and are preserved.

->*A sudden transition from the smallest light to the greatest, and from the greatest to the smallest, hinders the sight.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Riccardo Anghieri of Anghiari, a distinguished theologian, sends greetings.<-

**M**en of civil life often rebuke philosophers, because they seem, for the most part, inept at the governance of human affairs. Philosophers, on the other hand, often disapprove of civil men because they are most inept at the contemplation of divine things. What, then, shall we say to these things? It is not for us to settle such great disputes between them. But our Plato <note>Ficino refers to Plato as "ours" because he spent much of his life translating and reviving Platonic thought in the West.</note> must be called here as arbiter, whom God himself fashioned for both human and divine matters. He, therefore, judges that both civil men and philosophers were intended from the beginning to fulfill both duties—provided only that they do not pass suddenly from one extreme to the other, but walk by proper steps. It is better to translate here word for word the Greek words of Plato himself from the seventh book of the *Republic*. After this, contemplate our nature with respect to education and its lack through such an image as this. Imagine in your mind a certain cave under the earth, whose entrance opens toward a beginning of light and lies open throughout the whole cave. In it are men who have been raised from childhood with their necks and legs so bound that they are forced to remain immobile and to look only at what is in front of them. Their heads are so restricted by chains that they cannot turn them around. Behind their backs, however, a light from a fire is suspended high up and far off. Between the fire and the bound men, a raised path lies open, along which a small wall has been built. Just as screens or curtains are often placed before the eyes of spectators by jugglers <term>praestigiatoribus</term> <note>Latin: *praestigiator*—a conjurer or performer of "miracles" or illusions.</note> creating marvels, over which they show their wonders. Think again of men behind the wall carrying various vessels and artifacts that rise above the wall—stone statues of men and other animals, and wooden images fashioned in various ways. And as is likely, those who carry these things are partly silent and partly speaking. These people are like us; for first of all, do you think those people see anything of themselves or the men near them besides the shadows that fall from the fire onto the opposite part of the cave? And what of those things being carried—nothing but shadows? If, therefore, they were permitted to speak to one another, would they not think they were speaking of these very things they saw before them? And if an echo resonated from the opposite part of the prison, as often as someone passing by spoke, do you think they would believe anything else was speaking except the passing shadows? Altogether, therefore, such people would judge nothing to be true except the shadows of manufactured things. On the contrary, notice now what their release from chains and the cure of their ignorance would be like. Certainly, if one of them were released and forced to stand up suddenly, turn his neck, walk, and look at the light itself, he would suffer immediately; and because of the brightness, he would be unable to look at those things whose shadows he saw before. Then, if someone were to tell him that he had previously looked at trifles, but was now closer to true things and was looking more truly—and showing him each of the passing objects, asked him what it was—do you not think he would be at a loss and believe the things he saw before were truer than what is shown now? And if he were forced to look at the light, do you not think his eyes would suffer? And that he would turn his eyes back to those things he had easily seen before, thinking them clearer than what is suddenly presented? But if someone were to drag him by force up the rough and steep ascent, and not let go until he had dragged him out to the light of the Sun, do you not think he would be distressed while being dragged? And when he has been brought out to the light, his eyes being filled with brightness, he would be confused and see nothing of these things which are now considered true by men. Therefore, habituation is needed first, if he is to behold things above; and first he will look at shadows more easily. After these, he will see images of men and other things in water; then the things themselves; afterwards he will more easily contemplate the things in the heavens and the heaven itself at night, while looking at the light of the stars and the Moon, than if he were to look at the Sun itself by day and the brilliance of the Sun in—

<page-num>774</page-num>
<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

<note>This text continues the description of the prisoner who has escaped Plato's cave and is now adjusting to the light of the sun.</note> And thus at last he will look upon the Sun itself; he will no longer look at its reflections in the water or in a foreign region, but will contemplate the Sun by itself in its own place, and will be able to recognize its true nature. Finally, he will realize that it is the Sun that regulates the seasons and the years, which governs all things under the heavens, and is in a certain way the author of all those things which they had previously seen in the cave. What if he then recalls his former dwelling, the "wisdom" of those people, and their chains? Do you not think he would consider himself blessed by the change of place and feel pity for them? 

Furthermore, if honors, praises, and prizes were shared among them there—given to the one who most sharply perceived the passing shadows and remembered best which of them came first, which later, and which usually moved together, and from these observations could best predict the future—do you think he would still long for these things? Would he consider those who are honored and hold power among them to be blessed? Rather, he would choose what Homer says: to become "a serf to a poor laborer in a foreign land" <note>original: "in alieno, scilicet rure conferui hominis mancipium effici" — Ficino quotes Achilles' speech from the Odyssey, expressing that it is better to be the lowest servant on earth than a king in the underworld of shadows.</note> and to suffer anything else rather than be mocked by those opinions and live in such misery. 

If this man should descend again and take up the same seat he held before, would he not find his eyes filled with darkness, having suddenly left the Sun? And if he were required to distinguish those shadows once more and debate about them with those who are oppressed by perpetual chains—and a judgment had to be rendered at the very time his eyes were hallucinating before his sight was cleared (which would not happen quickly)—would he not provoke laughter? It would be said by everyone to his disgrace that after he ascended, he returned with ruined eyes; they would say that one should never strive for the heights, and if anyone attempted to loose them and lead them upward, if he were caught, he should be killed immediately. <note>This is a thinly veiled reference to the trial and execution of Socrates, Plato's teacher.</note>

This whole image, oh friend, must be related to what was said above. This prison represents the visible world seen by our eyes; the light of the fire in the cave represents the power of the Sun. Finally, if you relate the ascent to the heights and the contemplation of them to the soul's ascent to the <term>intelligible region</term> <note>The realm of "Forms" or "Ideas" that can only be understood by the mind, not the physical senses.</note>, as I indeed hope, you will not go astray. This is my opinion, which you desired to hear; God alone knows if it be true. 

The things that appear to me tend toward this: namely, I think that in the intelligible order itself, the Idea of the Good exists as the supreme thing, though it is scarcely seen. If it is seen, however, one must conclude that it is the cause of all things right and beautiful for everyone. In the visible world, it created light and the author of light <note>The physical Sun.</note>; in the intelligible world, it reigns itself, producing truth and mind. It is necessary for anyone who wishes to act with a sound mind, whether in private or in public, to know this Idea. 

Consider this also, and do not be surprised that those who descend here are unwilling to deal with human affairs, but the sharp edge of their minds is always directed toward the heights; this is indeed probable, since it follows the pattern described above. What of this? Do you think it a wonder if someone, falling from divine spectacles to these human evils, seems inept in action and is laughed at? Especially if, before he is accustomed to the present darkness and while still troubled, he is forced in the courts or elsewhere to contend about the "shadows of justice," or about those statues of which these are but shadows, and to argue about the judgments of those who have never seen Justice itself. 

But if anyone has understanding, he will remember that the eyes are usually troubled in two ways and for two reasons: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we go from darkness into the light. He will realize that the soul is affected in the same way whenever he sees it troubled and too dull to perceive something. Therefore, he will not break out into laughter thoughtlessly, but will diligently inquire: is it a soul descending from a more luminous life that is overwhelmed by new darkness? Or is it a soul rising from great ignorance to a radiant spectacle, failing under an excess of flashing splendor? He will approve the state of the former and judge its life blessed, while he will pity the other. And if he should happen to laugh, he would not laugh at this one as ineptly as he would at the one who fell from the supernal light. These things the divine Plato said; to these, nothing should be subtracted, nor can anything be added. Therefore, Farewell.
