# LETTERS, BOOK IV

...no one would ever strive to resist the body in even the smallest matter. We would be filled with earthly wealth at all times. Either all, or certainly the vast majority of people, would rest in this middle region of the world as if it were their natural origin and homeland. Now, however, since our circumstances are far different, I believe—and it is no empty faith—that our lineage is divine. But if we are divine, why do we often lead a life similar to a beast? Because the condition of this natural region has been so established that we use our senses, like brute animals, long before we use reason like human beings. Furthermore, many more and more obvious stimulants present themselves to our senses than to our mind. Lastly, there is only one human being within us, but many beasts. It is worthwhile to contemplate that image of ours which Plato paints in the ninth book of the *Republic* <note>In Republic 588b-589b, Plato describes the soul as a composite of a multi-headed beast, a lion, and a human being.</note>.

Let us imagine a figure of the soul like those ancient natures mentioned in myth—the Chimaera, Scylla, and Cerberus—and many others in which various forms are said to have grown together into one. Picture, then, a single form of a multi-colored beast <note>original: "bestiæ uariæ"</note> possessing many heads all around it: heads, I say, partly of domestic animals and partly of wild ones, and let it be able to change and produce all these things from itself. Next, join to these a single form of a noble lion. Above this, add a single form of a man; let the first part be the largest, the second smaller, and the third smallest. Now join these three so that they grow together into one. Around them, place on the outside the image of a single human being, so that those who cannot see the interior, but look only at the outer covering, see only one animal: a man.

Let us say, then, to anyone who asserts that it is profitable for this man to act unjustly and not at all profitable to live justly, that he is asserting nothing other than that it is profitable for the man to feed that multi-headed beast and the lion, and to make that lion stronger, while allowing the human being to perish of hunger and wasting away—to the point where, due to weakness, the man is dragged wherever those other creatures pull him. Nor does he tame them or reconcile one with the other, but instead lets them tear each other apart with bites and devour one another in their fighting. Therefore, if someone says that just duties are profitable, he will advise that these things be done and said so that the inner man of this kind of animal may achieve the greatest power. Like a farmer, he should take care of that multi-headed beast, nourishing and watering the domestic heads, while immediately cutting away the wild ones. In this, he accepts the nature of the lion as a helper, cares for all things in common, and reconciles them to himself through mutual goodwill. By every reasoning, then, he who praises just things speaks the truth, while he who praises unjust things lies. For whether regarding pleasure, honor, or profit, the praiser of justice speaks the truth; the critic, however, offers nothing of substance and does not even know what he is disapproving of. Thus far, Plato.

In this figure of our soul is contained that distribution which is read in Plato's *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue where Plato discusses the physical and metaphysical creation of the universe and the human body.</note>. There, he divides the soul into three powers or parts: the nature of reasoning, of anger, and of desire. He assigned the rational power to the head as if to a supreme citadel and queen, especially because the head seems to work more than all else in contemplation, and all the senses flourish there most strongly. Furthermore, he placed the power of anger in the chest <note>original: "præcordijs" — the area around the heart and diaphragm, often associated with spiritedness or the "irascible" soul.</note>, since these parts are most excited in anger, boldness, and fear. Finally, he gave the nature of desire to the liver because a natural vigor resides there for both digesting food and increasing lust.

Accordingly, in the *Phaedrus*, he calls Reason the charioteer, since by a certain natural order it is the leader of the remaining parts. He joins to it twin horses: one white and the other black. As far as our purpose is concerned, the horses are the powers of the heart and the liver, because they must obey Reason as the charioteer. But high-mindedness, which is assigned to the heart, is called the white horse, for it is closer to Reason. The desire of the liver, however, since it is further removed from the excellence of Reason, is the black horse. Reason, in turn, is named Hercules within us. He slays Antaeus <note>A giant in Greek myth who was invincible as long as he touched the earth. Hercules defeated him by lifting him into the air.</note>—that is, certain monstrous phantoms of the imagination. This happens when he lifts him from the earth into the heights; that is, when he moves himself away from the senses and bodily imagination. He also tames the lion—that is, he restrains anger. He cuts off the Hydra sprouting many heads on all sides—that is, he amputates the power of desire. This power is not carried toward just a few things, but toward innumerable things, like an insatiable whirlpool, even greater than anger. But while our internal Hercules cuts off the Hydra of the liver with iron, the heads suddenly sprout back because the fuel <term>fomes: literally 'tinder' or 'kindling,' used here to describe the innate material tendency or 'root' of desire</term> itself is left behind. However, when he consumes it with fire—because he utterly extirpates the fuel—nothing is reborn from there. Plato commands...

## *The Principal Disciples of Plato.*

D isciples of his were Speusippus of Athens, Xenocrates of Chalcedon, Aristotle of Stagira, Philip of Opus, Hestiaeus of Perinthus, Dion of Syracuse, Anicles, Heraclites, Erascus and Doriscus of Scepsis, Timolaus of Cyzicus, Hebeon of Lampsacus, Pithorus and Heraclides of Enos, Hippothales and Callippus of Athens, Demetrius of Amphipolis, Heraclides of Pontus and many others. Along with these were two women, Lasthenia of Mantinea and Axiothea of Phlius, who were known to wear men's clothing. They say that Theophrastus was also his listener, as were the orator Hyperides, Chamaeleon, and Lycurgus; Demosthenes and Menesistratus were also said to be his devoted students. Inscribed upon the vestibule of the Academy was: **Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.** <note>original: "Nemo huc geometriæ expers ingrediatur." This famous motto emphasized that the study of abstract mathematics was a necessary preparation for philosophy.</note> This he wished to be understood not only regarding the measurement of lines, but also regarding the proper measure of the emotions.

## *The Books of Plato.*

L isted here are the books he wrote: *Euthyphro* on holiness, the *Apology of Socrates*, the *Crito* concerning what he discussed with Socrates in prison, the *Phaedo* on the immortality of the soul, the *Cratylus* on the correct reasoning of names, the *Theaetetus* on knowledge, the *Sophist* on that which is, the *Statesman* on kingship, the *Parmenides* on the one principle of all things and on the Ideas, the *Philebus* on the highest good, the *Symposium* on love, the *Phaedrus* on beauty, the first *Alcibiades* on the nature of man, the second *Alcibiades* on prayer, the *Hipparchus* on the desire for gain, the *Lovers* on philosophy, the *Theages* on wisdom, the *Charmides* on temperance, the *Laches* on courage, the *Lysis* on friendship, the *Euthydemus* on disputation, the *Protagoras* on morals, the *Gorgias* on rhetoric, the *Meno* on virtue, the *Greater Hippias* on beauty, the *Lesser Hippias* on falsehood, the *Menexenus* on Athenian antiquity, and the *Republic* in ten books. He also wrote the *Timaeus* on the nature of the world, the *Critias* on Athenian antiquity, the *Minos* on law, the *Laws* in twelve books, the *Epinomis* (or *The Philosopher*), and fourteen *Letters*. All these books of Plato we ourselves have translated from the Greek language into Latin. <note>Ficino published the first complete Latin translation of Plato's works in 1484, a monumental achievement for the Renaissance.</note> There are truly three types of Platonic dialogues: for he either refutes the sophists, or exhorts the youth, or teaches the adults. Those things which Plato spoke in his own voice in the letters, the *Laws*, or the *Epinomis*, he wishes to be held as most certain; but those things which he disputes through the mouths of Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides, or Zeno in the other books, he wishes to be held as likely truths.

## *The Eloquence, Wisdom, and Authority of Plato.*

S tyle, according to Aristotle, flows in Plato as a middle ground between prose and poetry; such is its sweetness and abundance that Cicero called Plato the most weighty author and master of both understanding and speaking. He added that if Jupiter had wished to speak in a human tongue, he would have spoken in no other language than that of Plato. Indeed, there was such great learning in him that while before him all illustrious Greeks traveled to foreign nations for the sake of wisdom, after Plato's time all other nations flocked to Athens. Even Aristotle, endowed with such miraculous genius and most eager for new schools of thought, when he approached Plato as a nearly grown man, listened to him for twenty continuous years. Add to this that before he approached Plato, he was already advanced in letters; thereafter, he had Plato as his only teacher. I pass over what is written by Cicero: **I would rather go astray with Plato than think correctly with the rest.** <note>original: "malo cum Platone errare quàm cum cæteris recte ſentire." From Cicero's Tusculan Disputations.</note> Furthermore, he, along with Panaetius, calls him the **God of Philosophers.** I pass over that remark of Quintilian: "Who could doubt that Plato is supreme, whether in the sharpness of his debating or in a certain divine and Homeric faculty of eloquence?" For his speech rises far above prose (which the Greeks call "pedestrian" speech), so that he seems to me to be inspired not by human genius, but by some Delphic oracle. Through divine wisdom and integrity, he seems to have acquired for himself a marvelous authority even in his own homeland—a thing which very rarely happens. When he had arrived at that most magnificent celebration of the Olympic Games, which was like a gathering of the whole world, he was received with such joyful greetings by everyone that he seemed like a God sent down from heaven to mortals. People saw the games being deserted, the spectacles of the athletes abandoned, and the boxers left alone; and what is even more remarkable, those who had come to the Olympics across such long stretches of land and sea for the sake of feeding their eyes, ears, and minds, forgot every other pleasure and flocked to Plato, gazing only at him. They rested in Plato’s presence as if in the most pleasant of lodgings. When someone was performing a tragedy and no one was present except for Plato, and certain people mocked him for the disgrace of having no audience but one, he replied: "Even this one man is worth more than the entire Athenian people." <note>This anecdote emphasizes the weight of Plato’s intellectual authority; in the eyes of the performer, the approval of one philosopher outweighed the applause of a mindless crowd.</note>

->The Charity, Magnanimity, and Holiness of Plato.<-

**O** How great and constant a spirit he possessed, especially in the cause of his friends, is indicated by his letters, his contempt for the tyrant, and his defense of Dion. <note>Dion of Syracuse was Plato's student and friend who attempted to reform the government of the tyrant Dionysius II.</note> He often boldly rebuked the tyrant—even in the presence of witnesses—for governing unjustly or for deceiving his friends; so far was he from being a flatterer. I pass over smaller matters, <margin>that they should dance.</margin> such as when Dionysius had ordered at a banquet that everyone should put on purple garments and dance. Aristippus danced immediately, but Plato refused, saying that womanly clothing did not befit a philosopher. <note>Aristippus was a fellow student of Socrates known for his hedonistic lifestyle and ability to adapt to royal courts, often contrasted with Plato's more rigid dignity.</note> Furthermore, when the wicked accuser Crobylus had brought formal charges and a capital trial against the very brave general Chabrias, and when Chabrias was abandoned by the rest of the citizens out of fear and retreated to the citadel, Plato alone was always present to offer him aid. When the slanderer Crobylus, wishing to deter him from providing defense, said threateningly: "You come here to offer a defense for others, not knowing that the same poison that killed Socrates awaits you," Plato himself replied: "Long ago, Crobylus, when I fought for the dignity of my fatherland, I was not slow to face intolerable dangers; now, for my duty and the safety of a friend, even though you threaten me with sharpened steel and fire, I refuse no trial." 

When Socrates had been most unjustly shut in prison, Plato gathered money to ransom the innocent man; and while the judgment was being carried out, he ascended the platform and began to speak thus: "Although I am younger than all these men of Athens who have ascended the tribunal..." But the judges, fearing the tyrant’s power and that Plato might move the citizens with his authority and eloquence, suddenly interrupted him and shouted: "Come down!" Plato then went home. For as much as those judges suffered from a disease of a wicked mind, he was at that time suffering from a disease of the body. <note>A reference to the tradition that Plato was too ill to be present at the final moments of Socrates' death, as mentioned in the *Phaedo*.</note> However, the persecutors of Socrates paid the penalty shortly thereafter. 

When one of his fellow students was driven by envy because Xenocrates was so pleasing and acceptable to Plato, and tried to stir up enmity against him, he reported many insults that Xenocrates supposedly said against Plato. Plato, rejecting the accusation in mid-speech, refused to listen. The detractor persisted, affirming the crime with a severe expression; finally, when the man called upon all the Gods and Goddesses as witnesses, Plato—in order to free himself from the man’s persistence—said: "So be it; but Xenocrates possesses such faith and gravity that, unless he had judged it useful to speak so, he never would have said those things." 

That Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, imitated the gravity and magnanimity of Plato is testified by the *Life of Xenocrates* in the works of Diogenes, which is indeed a model of fortitude and holiness. <note>Refers to Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> Plutarch is witness that Dion also imitated him. Furthermore, Philticus, describing the life of the orator Lycurgus, says: "Lycurgus was a great man and many things were performed by him excellently, which no one could have done who had not been a listener of Plato." When Demosthenes was fleeing Antipater and Archias promised him with smooth words that he would save his life, he replied: "Far be it from me to prefer to live basely than to die honorably, after I have heard Xenocrates and Plato debating on the immortality of the soul." <note>Demosthenes, the famous orator, chose suicide over capture by his political enemies.</note> The same man, writing to a certain Heracleodorus, a fellow student of his, and rebuking him because after he had heard Plato he neglected the liberal arts and led a life of little honor, said: "Are you not ashamed to neglect those things which you received from Plato?" Dionysius, writing to Speusippus, says: "Plato indeed taught those who crossed his threshold for free, but you demand tribute, and take it from the willing and unwilling alike." Laertius also criticized the same man because he did not, like Xenocrates, imitate Plato’s chastity, fortitude, and gentleness. I cannot remain silent regarding that story of the fortitude of Xenocrates: when Dionysius said to Plato that

->*How much Plato neglected human affairs, and how much he loved divine things.*<-

**H**e repeated daily that only eternal things are true, while temporal things are merely semblances of truth. <note>original: "uerisimilia." In Platonic thought, the physical world is a "likely story" or shadow of the true, eternal Realm of Forms.</note> He believed the soul sleeps while in the body, and that the things the senses desire or fear are nothing other than dreams. Therefore, all these things must be utterly despised; and to avoid the evils with which the world is full, one must flee toward eternal things, for they cannot be avoided any other way. He himself fulfilled the very things he taught. For while he was destined to be a leader in the republic by a certain hereditary right and by the favor of the citizens, he rejected all civil dignity entirely. Although he was very wealthy by inheritance, he bestowed everything upon his brothers except for a small suburban estate, which they called the Academy. <note>The Academy became the famous school founded by Plato c. 387 BC.</note> Content with this alone, he lived his life; and though he stood as a teacher and friend to princes, he nevertheless accepted no riches from them. King Dionysius used to say: "Aristippus always asks for money; Plato always asks for books." <note>Aristippus was a contemporary philosopher known for his hedonism and pursuit of luxury.</note> Furthermore, he never took a wife, nor did he live in the city, remaining free from all things and serving truth alone. Hence Saint Jerome says: "Plato laboriously traveled through Egypt, to Archytas of Tarentum, and that coast of Italy which was once called Great Greece <note>original: "magna Græcia"</note> so that he, who was a master and a power in Athens, and whose doctrine made the gymnasia of the Academy resound, might become a traveler and a disciple, preferring to modestly learn the ideas of others rather than shamelessly thrust forward his own." Finally, while he pursued learning as if it were fleeing across the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold; he even obeyed a most cruel tyrant as a captive, bound as a slave. Yet, he remained a philosopher greater than the one who purchased him. These are the words of Jerome.

->*The Piety and Gratitude of Plato.*<-

**H**e was grateful to God, from whom he said the beginning of thinking, speaking, and acting must be sought in all matters—and he always practiced this himself. Moreover, he thanked God daily that he had been born a human and not a beast; a Greek and not a Barbarian; and that he lived in the times of Socrates. How grateful he was to his teachers and all his friends is evidenced by his dialogues, in which he honors them all wonderfully and attributes his own books to Socrates. For not only does he introduce Socrates as the speaker in almost all his dialogues, but he also writes that all things composed by himself are not his own, but belong to Socrates.

->*What Plato asserted, and those who confirmed him.*<-

**I**n those things subject to the senses, he defended the views of Heraclitus. <note>Heraclitus taught that the physical world is in a constant state of flux ("Panta Rhei").</note> Furthermore, in those things pertaining to the intellect, he mostly agreed with Pythagoras. But in matters of civil life, he embraced his beloved Socrates. These are the things he asserted everywhere: That God provides for all things. That the souls of humans are immortal. That there will be rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked. Augustine, in his book *Against the Academicians*, says: "The authority of Christ is to be preferred above all; however, if one must proceed by reason, he finds himself among the Platonists," because they do not contradict the sacred writings of the Christians. Dionysius the Areopagite signaled the same, and later Eusebius and Cyril declared it more extensively. Concerning this man, Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*: "The Platonists, with a few changes, would become Christians." And in his *Confessions*, he relates that he found nearly the entire prologue of the Gospel of John among the Platonists. Therefore, in the second book of *The City of God*, he says: "Labeo the Theologian <note>Cornelius Labeo, an ancient Roman scholar of religion.</note> thought that among the Gentiles, Plato should be counted among the demigods, like Hercules and Romulus." He places demigods above heroes, but situates both among the divinities. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this man, whom he calls a demigod, is to be preferred not only to heroes, but even to the gods themselves. Hence Augustine says he chose the Platonists above others because they felt more rightly about divine and human matters than other philosophers. This was also the judgment of Marcus Varro before him; and Apuleius made Plato not only superior to heroes, but equal to the gods, because he had clearly penetrated the hidden things of divine matters. Plato was endowed with such modesty that, although he had acquired a marvelous authority above others, when he was asked by someone to what extent his precepts should be obeyed, he replied: "Until someone more sacred appears on earth to open the fountain of truth for all, whom everyone then should follow..."

As for what he believed regarding philosophy, we have treated that sufficiently in our book *On Love* <note>Ficino refers to his famous commentary on Plato's *Symposium*, titled *De Amore*.</note> and in our *Platonic Theology*.

### *Plato's Return to his Celestial Homeland and his Praises.*

**H**e passed away on his own birthday, having completed exactly eighty-one years. Therefore, the Magi <note>Ficino refers to Persian priests/astrologers visiting Athens; in the Renaissance, they were seen as seekers of ancient wisdom.</note> who were then in Athens sacrificed to Plato, believing his lot to have been more than human, because he had completed that most perfect number which nine multiplied by nine produces. And—what is marvelous—he was still writing at that very age and on that very day. Concerning this, Cicero says: "There is also a peaceful, pure, and elegantly spent old age, such as we have heard was Plato's, who died while writing in his eighty-first year." <note>original: "est etiam quiete & purè atque eleganter actæ ætatis placida ac leuis senectus..." from Cicero's *De Senectute*.</note> Seneca also affirms that this happened to Plato through the benefit of his sobriety and diligence. Some say he died while writing; others that he returned to the gods above while reclining at a wedding feast after the tables had been removed, in the midst of a conversation. Aristotle dedicated an altar and a statue to Plato in a temple with this epigram: "Aristotle dedicated this altar to Plato, a man whom it is a sin for the wicked to praise." Aristotle added: "Who alone, by his life, teaching, character, and speech, gave warning to all and left monuments so that they might be able to lead a happy life through virtue. No future ages shall bring forth such a man." Other wise men also added many poems in praise of Plato, but three epigrams are the most notable. The meaning of the first is this: He excelled all in temperance and justice, but surpassed them so much in wisdom that he utterly overcame all envy. The sense of the second is this: Plato has been translated into the number of the gods. Distant nations honor him because he knew the divine life himself and showed it to others. The meaning of the third is of this kind: Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note> fathered Aesculapius and Plato—the former to heal bodies, the latter to heal souls. Furthermore, Mithridates, King of the Persians, placed a statue of Plato in the Academy inscribed as follows: "Mithridates, son of Rodobates, a Persian, dedicated this image of Plato, a work of Silanion, to the Muses." From all these things, Plato achieved such renown that the Greeks called Aristotle "daemonic," <note>In this context, "daemonic" refers to a genius intermediate between human and divine, particularly in natural sciences.</note> but called Plato "divine." This was because the former was human in life and supreme in natural science, while the latter directed himself toward divine things in both his science and his life.

### *A Defense of Plato's Character.*

**I** shall now put an end to my words, if I add a few more things. There are certain common versifiers who undeservedly usurp the name of "Poets"; these men, provoked as much by the difference in their character as by the malice of envy, play most impudently against every good man. A certain great license is granted to them to attack the good rather than the wicked, especially in this age of ours. But I would not wish to recall our own times, which are as inept at pursuing virtue as they seem apt at persecuting it. Such petty poets of old did not hesitate to bite the divine Plato (judged by the Greeks to be the son of Apollo) and Socrates (judged by the Apollo of the Greeks to be the wisest of men). Diogenes Laertius <note>An ancient biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> greatly detests their impiety. And as he himself declares, Aristippus of Cyrene—a most wicked man and an adversary of every excellent person of his time—increased the ridiculous insults of the comic playwrights. Just as he slandered many other most modest and learned men with a kind of fictional history, so he also slandered his teacher Socrates and his fellow-disciples Xenophon and Plato. He forged certain lewd poems in their names addressed to prostitutes and boys, clearly so that he might obtain for himself a freer license for sinning by the false example of great philosophers. But Aristotle, to whom truth was a greater friend than even Plato was, could not endure such false calumnies against a holy man; for in his elegies to Eudemus he sang those things about Plato which we mentioned above, granting him this especially: that the profane should not only not be allowed to slander Plato in any way, but should not even dare to name his holy name with a profane mouth under the pretext of praise. Nor was he content with an elegy, but also, as Olympiodorus relates, he composed a noble oration in praise of Plato. Therefore, let the hounds of hell fall silent before the gods above, and let them join Cerberus in his barking among the shades below. As for us, let us venerate Plato’s life and wisdom, which are most highly approved by the judgment of the wise; and let us cry out freely with Apuleius of Madaura: "We of the Platonic family know nothing but what is festive, joyful, celestial, and supreme."

# BOOK IV OF THE LETTERS.

->*As much as astronomers measure the truth, so much do astrologers tell lies.* <note>original: "Quantum Astronomi metiuntur, tantum Astrologi mentiuntur." Ficino uses a wordplay here between *metiuntur* (measure) and *mentiuntur* (lie), a common Renaissance distinction between mathematical astronomy and predictive astrology.</note><-

## Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished lawyer and knight, greetings.

**G**reetings to you a thousand times, my Bernardo—no, I have said too little—greetings as many times as you draw breath, my sweetest Bernardo. I write many things to you daily, though I transcribe few. For it seems to me that when I have written the original draft, I have in a way satisfied my love; however, even if I were to transcribe it, I would hardly satisfy my duty. But to make you more certain of my current studies: I am composing a book on the providence of God and the freedom of human will, in which I refute, to the best of my ability, those judgments of the astrologers that take away from providence and freedom. Truly, just as diligently as the astronomers truly measure the heavens, so much do the empty astrologers lie concerning human affairs. Farewell. But as for that excellent Thomas, the "Achates" <note>Achates was the famously loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's *Aeneid*. Ficino uses the term to describe a devoted friend or secretary.</note> of the late Bernardo, orator of the Venetians, whom my soul gladly embraces and my tongue celebrates: why does my most sluggish hand pass him over for so long? Therefore, Bernardo, as often as you see him, bid him greetings in Marsilio's name. **June 14, 1477.**

## Marsilio Ficino to Marco Aurelio, most distinguished orator, greetings.

**I**f it were permitted to recommend what is already yours to you, I would most highly recommend my close friend Nicolaus, a man endowed with both letters and fine character. Indeed, your own name is the testimony to us that he is yours, for it sounds most frequently from his mouth.

## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished lawyer and knight, greetings.

**I** received a certain letter today, Bernardo, from our friend Marco Aurelio. In its very form it was entirely "Mercurial" <note>Mercury was associated with eloquence, speed, and intelligence.</note> and very much like its father, but born, I believe, while Saturn was rising. Truly, proceeding with quite heavy steps—since it departed from your fair Venice on the sixteenth of May—it finally reached our shores on the nineteenth of June. Embracing it with the greatest joy, I said in congratulation: "You have come at last, and your dutiful devotion has overcome the unfortunate journey." Although this letter seemed somewhat slower in its movement, as if born under Saturn <note>Saturn was associated with slowness, gravity, and melancholy.</note>, it seems nevertheless to have been most swift in its execution, as if conceived by Mercury. For what it asks of us today, it already fulfilled long ago while it was being born. Indeed, during those very days in which the "golden" <note>A pun on his name, "Aurelio," from the Latin *aurum* meaning gold.</note> Aurelio wrote to me, I—stirred by some hidden and almost divine instinct, whether of the letter or of his Muse—dedicated a certain short work to Aurelio. Unless that work too has been "Saturnian" in its pace, I believe it has already reached you. 

Observe for a moment, Bernardo, the marvelous power of our guiding spirits. While that Marco was giving himself to me freely, I in turn was giving my whole self to him by right, and I was wonderfully embracing him as he embraced me. And so, with a certain celestial spirit blowing us together, we conspired as one, almost without knowing it. I believe indeed that either Mercury himself positioned in Taurus, or Phoebus <note>Apollo/The Sun.</note> in Gemini, tuned the twin lyres of Aurelio and Marsilio so similarly that when one sounds, the other resounds in turn. And from both echoes that sweet name of Bembo, a name musical to the Graces and most pleasing to the Muses. Farewell happily. But I see my Bernardo—for I know the man's nature—can neither be well, nor ever wants to be well, without his "delights." <note>Likely referring to his friends or his literary pursuits.</note> Cristoforo Landino, the glory of Minerva and the Muses, and Giovanni Cavalcanti, our fellow philosopher, are well. Therefore, fare you well. **June 19, 1477.**

->*When love is kindled by the breathing of a divine spirit, when one loves, the other always loves in return; often, when one thinks, the other thinks the same thing.*<-

**Y**esterday your very elegant letter was delivered to us, most learned Marco; a letter sweeter to me than honey and more precious than gold. But what am I doing? I am not permitted now in this praise...

# MARSILIO FICINO

...to go further regarding this, lest I seem perhaps too vain, if I myself were to attempt to praise sufficiently that letter which praises me more than enough. Therefore, if you please, let us begin again from another starting point. When love is kindled in our minds by a certain breathing of the celestial spirit, the one loved always loves in return, and often, while one is thinking, the other is thinking the same thing in a similar way. For even the heavenly Author <note>original: "coelestis author," referring to God as the creator of the harmony between souls.</note>, since He embraces both as the common cause of all, creates a mutual affection between lovers; and the affection of the lover—which, depending on heaven through man, resists both the flat face of humanity and the hollows of heaven—in turn produces an Echo.

Greetings, therefore, heavenly friend; greetings always in God, the author of our benevolence. Neither the spaces of the earth, Marco, nor any intervals of time seem to have been able to interrupt this heavenly and perpetual love of ours while it was rising, or to delay it once it had arisen; rather, as one was loving, the other soon loved by a certain divine fate. While one was thinking and writing, the other, at almost the same moment, both thought and wrote the same. I think you have noticed, Aurelio—if you have lately received that little work of mine sent to you—that at the very time you were writing to me, I was also writing to you in turn. Furthermore, both letters then signified and requested exactly the same thing. To me, indeed, nothing in human affairs is more fortunate than to have emerged as an equal through that affection, than which I hear none is superior in virtue. Nothing is more precious than to happily possess such and so great a possessor of myself. I have, therefore, in my whole mind what I was seeking. 

But I grieve somewhat over this one thing: that I am by no means that whole which you yourself were seeking. My Aurelio, if you cannot have what you want, at least want to have what you can. Accept your Marsilio, Marco, as a whole, however small he may be. I pray you, do not look further at that image <note>original: "simulachrum." Ficino suggests Aurelio has an idealized mental image of him that the real Ficino cannot fully match.</note> which you had fashioned from the beginning, for Ficino is but a certain limb of that image. Look rather, friend, at what you possess, than what you imagine. In this way, you will truly recognize that you possess not a part of someone, but something whole. For it is better to enjoy some whole pygmy than a limb of a vast giant.

->*Nothing is weaker than human love, nothing firmer than divine love.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo, most distinguished lawyer and<-
->knight, greetings.<-

**Y**ou write to us a letter that is oratorical, poetic, and amatory, but you excuse yourself in vain for I know not what, which absolutely no one accuses; take care that where love is perfect, you never think even the slightest offense can happen. In charity <note>original: "charitate." In Renaissance Latin, this refers to *caritas*, or selfless, divine love, as opposed to *amor*, which can be more worldly.</note>, you can perhaps offend in this one way alone: if you think that it can ever be offended. Human love is indeed a thing full of anxious fear; but divine charity—whether we listen to Paul—believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails; or whether we listen to John the Evangelist—fear does not dwell in charity, but perfect charity casts out all fear. Hence our Aurelius Augustine exclaims: "He alone loses no dear one, to whom all are dear in Him, who is not lost." <note>A famous quote from Augustine's *Confessions*, Book IV, Chapter 9.</note> But I have somehow begun a certain homily here, as they say. And I was delivering the duties of charity to that man whom the Florentine people admire, as if he were a certain image of charity and an exemplar of humanity.

->*In vain do we strive too much for our own sufficiency in these things which are in no way sufficient for themselves.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the human race, greetings.<-

**Y**ou seek sufficiency <note>original: "sufficientiam," meaning a state of being satisfied, fulfilled, or self-sufficient.</note> everywhere with the purpose that, after you have found this one thing, you will seek nothing further. However, you are always seeking as many things as possible for this very reason: because you never attain this one thing. Do you want me to tell you the reason why you never attain sufficiency? Perhaps because you seek it outside yourself. If, therefore, mortal riches cannot suffice for an immortal soul, see to it that at least the soul itself suffices for them. Pay attention to what I say: I do not say that the soul should satisfy itself—for how can he who is both made and perfected by another satisfy himself? Too much in vain, alas, do we wretches strive for our sufficiency in these things which are in no way sufficient for themselves. Truly, only that which is enough for itself satisfies all things entirely. Moreover, nothing can be enough for itself, except...

# LETTERS. BOOK IV.

...besides the immense good which is from itself and toward itself. Here, then, alone—here, I say—let us seek what may truly satisfy us. And let no one be weary; no one ever follows the Good in vain who follows it well. For the Good itself, because it is immense, flourishes everywhere and overflows from every side; and our own success, for one who follows well, is undoubtedly something good. Moreover, he alone wishes to follow and does follow the Good well who, for the sake of that supreme Goodness itself—through which individual goods exist and are preserved—follows individual goods everywhere.

->*A sudden transition from the smallest light to the greatest, and from the greatest to the smallest, hinders the vision.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Ricciardo Angelerio of Anghiari, the distinguished theologian.<-

### C
ivic men <note>original: "Civiles uiri," referring to statesmen or those involved in political and public life.</note> often reproach philosophers because they seem, for the most part, unsuited for the governance of human affairs. Philosophers, on the other hand, more often disapprove of civic men because they are most unsuited for the contemplation of divine things. What, then, shall we ourselves say to these things? It is not for us to settle such great disputes between them. But our Plato must be called here as an arbiter, whom God Himself fashioned for both human and divine affairs. He, therefore, judges that both civic men and philosophers were originally intended to execute both duties—provided that they do not pass suddenly from one extreme to the other, but proceed by the proper steps. It is better to translate here, word for word, the Greek words of Plato himself from the seventh book of the *Republic*. <note>Ficino here begins his Latin rendering of Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, a foundational text in Western philosophy regarding education and the nature of reality.</note> After these things, you may contemplate our nature, in regards to its education and its lack of it, by such an image as this.

Imagine in your mind a certain cave under the earth, whose entrance lies open toward a light that begins and passes through the whole cave. In it are men who have been nourished from childhood, with their necks and legs so bound that they are compelled to remain motionless and to look only toward what is in front of them. Their heads are so restricted by bonds that they cannot turn them around. Behind their backs, however, let the light of a fire be suspended far above. Between the fire and the bound men, let there be an elevated path, along which a low wall has been built. Just as screens or curtains are often placed before the eyes of spectators by puppeteers <note>original: "praestigiatoribus," meaning magicians or illusionists who perform marvels.</note> who fashion miracles, over which they demonstrate their wonders.

Think again of men carrying various vessels and artifacts behind the wall, which project above the wall: stone statues of men and other animals, and wooden images crafted in various ways. And, as is natural, let those who carry these things be partly silent and partly speaking. These people are similar to us; for first, do you think they see anything else, either of themselves or of the men next to them, except the shadows which fall from the fire onto the opposite part of the cave? And what of the things being carried past—do they not see only the shadows? If, then, they were able to speak to one another, would they not think that they were speaking of those things which they saw before them? And if an echo resounded from the opposite part of the prison whenever one of the passersby spoke, do you think they would believe anything else was speaking except the shadows of those passing by? Altogether, then, such people would judge nothing to be true except the shadows of manufactured things.

Observe now, on the other hand, what their release from bonds and the cure for their ignorance would be like. Certainly, if one of them were released and compelled to suddenly stand up, turn his neck, walk, and look toward the light itself, he would immediately feel pain, and because of the brightness, he would be unable to look at those things whose shadows he had seen before. Then, if someone were to tell him that he had previously looked at trifles, but that now he was closer to true things and was looking more truly—and, pointing out each of the passersby, were to ask what it was—do you not think he would be at a loss? Would he not think that the things he saw before were truer than the things now being shown to him? And if he were compelled to look at the light, do you not think his eyes would suffer? And that he would turn his eyes back to those things which he had previously seen with ease, thinking them more certain than the things suddenly being offered to him?

But if someone were to drag him violently up the rough and steep ascent, and not let go until he had dragged him into the light of the sun, do you not think he would be distressed while being hauled along? And when he had been brought out into the light, with his eyes filled with brightness, he would be hesitant and would see nothing of those things which are now considered true by men. Therefore, there is first a need for habituation if he is to look at the things above. First, he will more easily look at shadows. After these, he will see the images of men and other things in the water; then the things themselves; afterwards, he will more easily contemplate the things that are in the sky, and the sky itself by night, while he gazes at the light of the stars and the Moon, rather than looking at the Sun itself by day and the brilliance of the Sun:

<meta>catchword: looks at:</meta>

<summary>Ficino introduces a translation of Plato's Allegory of the Cave from the Republic, using it to mediate the conflict between active political life and the contemplative life of the philosopher. He describes the initial state of the prisoners in the cave and the painful process of being forced toward the light of truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s presentation of Plato’s "Allegory of the Cave" from the previous page. Having described the prisoner's ascent from the darkness of the cave to the light of the sun, Ficino now concludes the allegory with its philosophical interpretation and the difficulties of returning to the world of shadows.</meta>

<page-num>774</page-num>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...and protect him. And thus, at last, he will look upon the Sun itself; he will no longer behold its images in the water or in a foreign region, but will contemplate the Sun according to itself in its own seat, and will be able to recognize its true nature. Finally, he will perceive that it is the Sun which regulates the times and the years, which rules all things beneath the heavens, and which is, in a certain way, the author of all those things which they had previously seen in the cave. What if he then recalls his former dwelling in his memory, along with the "wisdom" of those people and their chains? Do you not think he would consider himself blessed by this change of place and feel pity for those others?

Furthermore, consider the honors they used to bestow upon one another, the praises and rewards given to the one who could most sharply discern the passing shadows and remember most clearly which of them usually came first, which followed, and which moved together—and from these observations, could best predict the future. Do you think he would desire these things? Or that he would consider those who are honored and hold power among them to be truly blessed? Or rather, as Homer says, would he not choose "to be a servant to a landless man on a farm" <note>original: "in alieno... rure conserui hominis mancipium effici." This is a famous reference to Homer's *Odyssey*, where the ghost of Achilles tells Odysseus he would rather be a lowly servant on earth than the king of all the dead.</note> and endure anything else rather than be mocked by those opinions and live in such misery?

If such a man should descend again and take up the same seat he held before, would his eyes not be struck by darkness, having suddenly departed from the Sun? And if he were required to distinguish those shadows once more and debate about them with those who have been pressed by perpetual chains—and a judgment had to be rendered at the very time his eyes were swimming before his vision was purified (which would not happen quickly)—would he not provoke laughter? It would be said by everyone to his disgrace that after he ascended, he returned with ruined eyes, and that one should never even attempt to reach the heights; and if anyone tried to release them and lead them upward, if they could catch him, they would surely kill him. <note>This is a poignant reference to the trial and execution of Socrates, Plato's teacher, who sought to "awaken" the citizens of Athens.</note>

This whole image, oh friend, must be applied to what was said above. This prison is indeed the visible world that we see with our eyes; the light of the fire in the cave is the power of the Sun. Finally, if you relate the ascent to the heights and the sight of those things to the soul's journey into the intelligible region, you will not go astray—at least, so I hope. You desired to hear my opinion; God knows if it be true.

What appears to me, therefore, points to this: I believe that in the intelligible order itself, the Idea of the Good exists as the supreme principle, though it is hardly seen. But if it is seen, one must assert that it is the cause of all things right and beautiful. In the visible realm, it created light and the author of light <note>The physical Sun.</note>; in the intelligible realm, it reigns as the mistress that produces truth and mind. It is necessary for anyone who intends to act with a sound mind, whether in private or in public, to know this Idea.

Come and consider this as well: it is no wonder that those who reach this height are unwilling to involve themselves in human affairs, for their mind's eye is always directed toward the heights. Indeed, this is probable if it follows the image described above. And what of this? Do you think it marvelous if someone, falling from divine spectacles to these human evils, appears clumsy in action and is laughed at? Especially if, before he becomes accustomed to the present darkness and while he is still stumbling, he is forced to contend in the courts or elsewhere about the "shadows of justice," or about those statues of which these are mere shadows—debating the judgments of those who have never seen Justice itself?

But if someone possesses a mind, he will remember that the eyes are troubled in two ways and for two reasons: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we emerge from darkness into the light. He will consider that the soul is affected in the same way whenever he sees it troubled and hindered from discerning something. Therefore, he will not break out into laughter thoughtlessly, but will diligently inquire: Is the soul overwhelmed by new darkness because it is descending from a more luminous life? Or is it failing under a too-vibrant splendor as it rises from great ignorance toward a glowing spectacle? In the former case, he will approve of the condition and judge that life to be blessed; in the latter, he will feel pity. But if he should happen to laugh, his laughter would not be so foolish as the laughter directed at the one who has fallen from the supernal light. These are the words of the divine Plato; nothing should be subtracted from them, nor can anything be added. Therefore, farewell.

**I**f a divine vigor and a celestial origin of our mind were not within us, we could in no way recognize the deficiency of mortal things. We would never even be able to conceive of or desire anything whatsoever above the order of corporeal things...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of Platonic philosophy. While the previous page focused on the "Allegory of the Cave," this page shifts to Plato's descriptions of the human soul's internal struggle between reason and the passions, drawing from the Republic, Timaeus, and Phaedrus.</meta>

<page-num>779</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK IV</header>
<sig>Ccc 4</sig>

...no one would ever strive to resist the body, even in the smallest matter. We would be filled at all times with earthly riches. All, or certainly as many as possible, would rest in this middle region of the world as if it were their natural origin and homeland. But now, since our circumstances are far different, I truly believe—and it is no vain faith—that our race is divine. But if we are divine, why do we so often lead a life similar to a beast? It is because the condition of this natural region is established such that we use our <term>senses</term> <note>original: "sensu," referring to the physical senses and animal instincts</note> like brutes long before we use <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratione," the higher human faculty of logic and morality</note> like men. Furthermore, far more numerous and obvious stimulants present themselves to us regarding the senses than regarding the mind. Lastly, there is only one "man" within us, but the "beasts" are many. It is worthwhile to look upon that image of ours, which **Plato** paints in the ninth book of the *Republic*.

->Let us fashion an image of the soul such as those natures of old said to have existed: the **Chimera**, **Scylla**, and **Cerberus**, and many others in which various forms are said to have grown together into one. Shape, therefore, a single figure of a beast, multifaceted and having many heads all around—heads, I say, partly of domestic beasts and partly of wild ones—which is able to change and produce all these things from itself. Additionally, join to these one form of a noble lion, and above this, one form of a man. Let the first part be the largest, the second and third narrower. Join these three together so they cohere into one. Then, place around them from the outside the image of a single man, so that those who cannot look inside, but see only the outer covering, see a single animal: a human being.<-

Let us say, then, to him who asserts that it profits this man to act unjustly, and that living justly is of no use at all: he asserts nothing else than that it profits the man to feed that manifold beast and the lion, making the lion stronger, while allowing the human part to perish of hunger and be weakened, to the point that he is dragged wherever those other parts snatch him. He does not make one part tame or reconcile them to each other; rather, he allows each to tear the other apart with their behaviors and devour one another in their fighting.

Therefore, if someone says that just duties are profitable, he will advise that these things be done and said so that the "inner man" of this kind of animal may obtain the highest power. Like a farmer, he should take care of that multi-headed beast, nourishing and tending the domestic heads while immediately cutting off the wild ones. In this, he accepts the nature of the lion as an ally and cares for all parts together, reconciling them to one another with mutual goodwill. By every logic, he who praises just things speaks the truth, while he who praises unjust things lies. For regarding pleasure, honor, and benefit, the praiser of justice speaks truly; the critic, however, asserts nothing of substance, nor does he understand what he disapproves of. Thus far **Plato**.

In this figure of our soul is contained that distribution which is read in **Plato’s** *Timaeus*. There, he divides the soul into three powers or parts: the nature of <term>reasoning</term>, <term>anger</term>, and <term>desire</term>. He assigned the rational power to the head, as if to a supreme citadel or queen, especially because the head seems to work most of all in contemplation, and all the senses flourish there most abundantly. Furthermore, he placed the power of anger in the <term>precordia</term> <note>The area of the chest around the heart; considered the seat of "spiritedness" or thumos.</note>, since in anger, boldness, and fear, these parts are most agitated. Finally, he gave the nature of desire to the liver because a natural vigor exists there for both digesting food and increasing lust.

Accordingly, in the *Phaedrus*, he calls reason the **charioteer**, because by a certain natural order it is the leader of the remaining parts. He joins to this twin horses: one white and the other black. As far as our purpose is concerned, the horses are the powers of the heart and the liver, which must obey reason as their charioteer. But <term>magnanimity</term> <note>High-mindedness or greatness of spirit.</note>, which is assigned to the heart, is called the "white horse," for it is closer to reason. The desire of the liver, however, because it is further removed from the excellence of reason, is the "black horse."

Reason, again, is named **Hercules** within us. He kills **Antaeus**—that is, certain monstrous phantoms of the imagination. This happens when he lifts himself from the earth into the heights; that is, when he moves himself away from the senses and bodily imagination. He also tames the **lion**, which is to say he restrains anger. He cuts down the **Hydra** sprouting many heads on all sides—that is, he prunes the power of desire. This desire is not carried toward just a few things, but toward innumerable things with an insatiable abyss, much like the many heads of the Hydra. But while our "inner Hercules" cuts the Hydra of the liver with iron, the heads suddenly sprout back because the <term>kindling</term> <note>original: "fomes," a technical term for the "tinder" or root cause of passion/sin.</note> itself is left behind. However, when he consumes it with fire, he extirpates the kindling entirely, and nothing regrows from there. As it is commanded in Plato...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino interprets Plato’s allegories of the soul, describing the internal conflict between the "inner man" (reason) and the "beasts" of anger and desire, concluding with an allegorical interpretation of Hercules as the rational mind taming physical passions.</summary>

<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<meta>catchword: Many</meta>

[In the same way] Socrates [argues] in the *Phaedo*, do not abstain from one bodily pleasure for the sake of another bodily pleasure; otherwise, many [vices] suddenly spring up again in place of one. Rather, he commands that we strive to abstain from pleasures for the sake of **reason**, for he says that only in this way can vices be fundamentally rooted out. I shall now bring an end to this letter, if I may first offer this one reminder: namely, that we should remember that if there are many beasts within us, it is no wonder that in **Plato's** works, souls are said to transmigrate from man into beasts. Certainly, we possess from the beginning certain "kindling-wood" <note>original: "fomites," often used in a theological sense to describe the "tinder" or inclination toward sin</note> and the passions of beasts within us. When we have nourished these recklessly for a long time, reason is either lulled to sleep in a way, or it stays awake only under the appearance of wrath and lust. Wherefore, under the very skin of a man, the man himself sees that he has passed over into the nature of beasts. Hence Socrates says to **Phaedrus**: "I consider myself indeed, O Phaedrus, whether I am some beast more multifaceted, more burning, and more furious than **Typhon** <note>In Greek mythology, a monstrous giant with a hundred dragon heads; here representing the chaotic, multi-headed passions</note>, or whether I am a more peaceful and simple animal, a participant in a certain divine and mild lot—that is, of a tranquil intelligence." July 1st, 1477.

->He alone possesses all things, who is possessed by none except God.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Pasqualino, his dearest<-
->companion, sends greetings.<-

If you desire to possess as many things as possible, take care that nothing at all possesses you. For unless you possess yourself—the one through whom you are to possess other things—you will have nothing at all. Hence it happens that all men are always in want, and all are continually grieving. This is because everyone has long ago recklessly lost and wasted himself and everything with him, having been secretly captured himself while he was openly striving to capture [external things]. He alone can belong to himself and to another at the same time who has given himself to that one alone, who to God alone is the possessor of all, because He alone is all things. When someone finds all things in Him, he also finds himself—as much more perfect than himself as He is more perfect than he. Just as one who serves a slave is a slave most foul and wretched, so one who serves the <term>Lord of all</term> <note>original: "omnium domino," referring to God</note> becomes, in a way, the lord of all. He alone seems to serve freely who obeys infinite liberty. There, servitude is free where immense liberty—that is, God—expels far away whatever can be thought of as slavish or violent.

->As soon as we strive to oppose fate, we overcome it.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Marescalco of Ferrara, sends greetings.<-

You ask four things, my excellent fellow-philosopher. First, indeed, how am I doing? I am doing well indeed, Marescalco, just as I wish, after I began to wish to be well in the way that I am able to be well. Second, however: by what method do I philosophize? I philosophize chiefly by this method: that since things themselves do not follow my <term>will</term> <note>original: "voluntate"</note>, I at least follow things with my will; for in this way, things obey a will that follows them. Third, how much do I love you? If there is any limit to love, or any certain measure of free will, measure your love toward me, Francesco, and in that way perhaps you will measure mine toward you. Fourth, what am I composing? I am composing a book on the **Providence of God** and the **liberty of human choice**. In this work, I argue against the necessity of the stars and the <term>fate</term> <note>original: "fatum," the idea of predetermined destiny controlled by the planets</note> of the Astrologers. 

But perhaps someone might say that it is the mark of a fool to want to fight against unassailable fate. I, however, respond that this can be attacked so easily that whenever anyone wishes to attack it, then first, by that very fact that he so wishes, he overcomes it. Surely the motion of the celestial spheres can never lift the mind higher than the spheres themselves. But now, he who disputes against them seems already to have transcended them and to have reached God Himself and the free choice of the will. It is as if he were not compelled by celestial fate, but led both by super-celestial Divine Providence and by the liberty of the mind. Furthermore, since any opposing and (if I may say so) decisive action usually proceeds from one contrary to another, let no one dare to confess that the will itself and the disputation repugnant to the feigned violence of the stars proceed from the violence of the stars; rather, let us understand that they flow from Providence and liberty itself, for the sake of which we have spoken against fate.
->July 28, 1477.<-
->Florence.<-

# LETTERS, BOOK IV.

->He who serves many, has many servants.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the Venetian Bernardo Bembo, greetings.<-

<margin>112</margin>
**P**hoebus Capella, Francesco d'Este, and Pamphilus the physician <note>These were members of the humanist circles in Venice and Ferrara who were eager to read Ficino's new Latin translations of Plato</note> are asking us for our books of Plato, all of which we have long since translated from the Greek language into Latin. If you happen to encounter these distinguished men anywhere, bid them greetings in our name, and tell them the translations cannot be sent this month. You see, Bernardo, with what liberty I deal with you. I seem, in some way, to have just given an order. But you, my Bembo, are the cause; for you show yourself such a man to each person that whoever does not use the greatest liberty and confidence with you would undoubtedly seem the most servile and distrustful of all. Indeed, while you most willingly serve others, in the meantime you most greatly rule them. But others, when they seem to rule you most, then serve you most willingly. There is no rule easier, more excellent, or more secure than that of love. No action is more pleasant, and no service more happy, than that which is voluntary. The Calends of August <note>August 1st</note>, 1477.

->Friendship among men cannot be forged unless God inspires it.<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Hermolao Barbaro the Venetian, greetings.<-

<margin>121</margin>
**I** wrote a certain letter in recent days briefly discussing true friendship. I directed it not to any one of my friends in particular, but to all friends equally without a specific title. A little later, your elegant and most "Latin" <note>original: "latinissimè," meaning written in a very pure, classical style</note> letter was delivered to me, Barbaro. This is indeed the true bait of love—that is, love itself—which captures me, and once captured, provokes me to love, and to love in such a way that you alone now possess what was meant for many. Since you have suddenly claimed for yourself alone our discussion on true friendship, which was just about to greet all my friends, what was to be inscribed to everyone shall now be inscribed to Hermolao alone. Therefore, just as recently while writing to everyone I was led to write primarily to one, so hereafter in loving all my friends, I shall love this one man foremost.

->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosophers, especially Hermolao Barbaro, greetings.<-

<margin>122</margin>
**E**veryone, by a certain common notion, defines friendship as a union. Since union cannot exist except toward "the one," it seems we should rightly ask: what is that one thing toward which two people, in agreement, become and are called friends? Is it necessarily those who hold the same opinion who are friends? Not at all. We can hold the same opinion in many matters, both human and natural, and yet hate one another. Or perhaps does goodwill consist not in opinion, but in the will? Suppose that only those who want the same thing are called friends? Not even that; rather, it is for this very reason that enmities arise—because we want the same thing. Often those who seek the same treasure, or the same rank of dignity, or the same honor in an art, envy one another, grow angry, and fight. Someone might say that discord of this kind arises among men because they desire certain finite goods; when one possesses these, the other possesses them either not at all or not equally. If, however, some are found who desire the same good that is infinite—since that can never be hindered from overflowing everywhere into the immeasurable—they are agitated by no enmities among themselves. And friendship exists between those who want the same infinite good. But indeed, not even that seems to me to suffice for goodwill; for everyone, by a certain natural instinct, desires a good of this kind (whence we all wish to be happy), yet we do not all love one another. Where then shall we find goodwill itself, which is nothing other than wishing for the good, unless we find it around the Good itself which is every good—that is, God? Certainly nowhere else. Moreover, the human will can be affected toward God in two primary ways, as far as our purpose is concerned. For it either desires to receive from Him, or to give. The first instinct is common and natural to all, since we all desire and ask as many things as possible from God; but we do not, for this reason alone, love God or men. The other instinct does not seem to belong to just anyone, and quite few are found who surrender themselves and all they have to God—or rather, to speak more correctly, who *return* them to God. For we are nothing and possess nothing that we have not received from Him. Whoever returns himself to God—that is, every affection of thought, every effort of action... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

<meta>This page continues the letter to Hermolao Barbaro the Venetian regarding the nature of divine friendship. Ficino is explaining that true love is directed toward God, and all other things are loved through Him.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

and turns it back toward Him; this person loves God for the sake of God alone, and loves all other things for the sake of God. Indeed, a vain lover of physical form loves a painting of a beautiful body for this very reason: because he loves the form and substance of the body itself. In the same way, a true and pious lover loves created things for no other reason than that they are either images or shadows of God the Creator, whom he loves. The more similar they appear to Him, the more he admires and praises them. Truly, those minds most dedicated to God are the most similar to the Divine Mind. For this reason, such minds are moved toward God and toward one another with an inestimable fragrance and sweetness of love; they surrender themselves freely to Him as to a father, and most willingly give themselves to one another as to brothers. Other relationships which are called "friendships" among men are nothing other than robberies. True charity, as the Apostle Paul says <note>1 Corinthians 13:5: "Love... seeks not its own."</note>, seeks not its own, but the things of another. Even if we magnificently boast every day with honorable words of friendship, nevertheless each of us is generally such that he does not look out for anyone else, but only himself. For such a man does not truly give himself to the other, but rather strives to receive from him either some pleasure or some utility, whether it pertains to external things and the body, or to the soul. 

Finally, to speak briefly, only that man is to be called a true and legitimate lover who understands that in all the good things which are offered to him and please him, nothing truly pleases him except that Divine Good itself, from which and through which all things are good. Therefore, in all these things he loves Him, and in Him he loves all things, so that he does not even love himself except in Him through whom he has this quality of being lovable. He cares for all men according to his strength, as if they were created by the same Father as himself; but some he chooses above others as being more similar to that Father, with whom he may lead both a heavenly life on earth and a super-heavenly life in the heavens. Between these alone is there true friendship—that is, a friendship made true by the one and only God. Indeed, a true and stable union among many cannot be achieved except through eternal Unity itself. Moreover, true and eternal Unity is God Himself, who alone is true simplicity and immense power. Therefore, these men alone seem able to cry out freely with the Prophet: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one." <note>Psalm 133:1</note>

-> *Fortune can neither do good for the wicked, nor do evil for the good.* <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Ivani of Sarzana <note>Antonio Ivani (1430–1482) was a humanist and chancellor of Sarzana who corresponded frequently with Ficino.</note>, greetings. <-

**If** you saw someone suffering from an incurable disease of the body and tortured by various pains in different limbs, would you envy him his delicate feasts, his crowd of servants, his soft bedding, his purple robes, or his gilded chamber? Certainly, unless you were as sick in your soul as he is in his body, you could not be envious. Truly, whoever serves pleasures, money, glory, or the desire for power is oppressed by a certain incurable disease of the soul and manifold pain. Therefore, whoever envies these people sees nothing. For this reason, those people seem to me the blindest of all who consider Fortune <note>The Roman goddess Fortuna, often depicted as blind or unpredictable.</note> to be blind because she either "does good" to the wicked (for whom, in reality, nothing is good) or "does evil" to the good (for whom, in the end, nothing is evil). For as each person is within himself, so are the things he receives. Only those among men are seized by the "eyes of reason" <note>The intellectual capacity to see beyond appearances.</note> who do not see by what wonderful reason the individual parts of the world are arranged and moved; they alone seem subject to a certain fortune—if I may put it that way—and to the highest injustice. While the most exact order of things indicates the infinite power, wisdom, and justice of the Author, they themselves either think that irrational Fortune rules, or they complain about divine governance as if it were less than just.

-> *In Praise of Marriage.* <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Pelotto, poet and excellent friend, greetings. <-

**Regarding** the fact that you have for a long time applied your mind to marriage, my Pelotto, I cannot but highly approve. Thus, a man, as a divine being, preserves the human species through a certain perpetual succession. As a grateful being, he returns to nature what he had received on loan, and often with interest. As a happy and true sculptor, he carves a living image of himself in his children. Furthermore, he attains a dear partnership in life and a faithful guardianship of his affairs by this means alone, or at least primarily. He possesses, moreover, a domestic Republic in which he may exercise the steering-oars of prudence and the strengths of all the virtues. He also prepares a great protection for old age, which [he may spend] either in the bosom of a beloved wife or in the arms of children and grandchildren...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino, likely part of a letter to Antonio Calderini or a similar associate, transitioning from the nature of divine love to the practical and philosophical merits of marriage and domestic life as a mirror of civic duty.</meta>

# LETTERS, BOOK IV.

...or considers it safer in the performance of duty toward his relatives. Finally, a wife and a family are either a sweet consolation for our labors, or at least a supreme exercise of <term>Philosophy</term><note>Ficino views daily life as a training ground for the soul, not just an abstract study.</note> for mortal life. For this reason, *Socrates* confessed that he had learned much more moral discipline from his wives than he had learned of natural science from *Anaxagoras* or *Archelaus*. Who does not know that when man was first created, nothing was commanded or instituted by God as more ancient or prior than matrimony? And that it is numbered among the sacred mysteries and celebrated with the highest regard among all nations? The powerful have always honored it, and the wise have not despised it. For they saw that it was conducive to the conduct of affairs. Furthermore, if you live temperately and spend your time sparingly, it does not hinder your studies. Our own *Plato*, because he somewhat neglected marriage in his youth, was finally led by repentance in his old age to make sacrifices to the Goddess of Nature, so that by this act he might absolve himself before the common people of the crime of both omitting marriage and of sterility. He even established in his laws that whoever did not take a wife should be excluded from all public offices and honors. Moreover, he decreed they should be weighed down by public burdens more heavily than other citizens. *Trismegistus* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure whom Ficino believed was a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom.</note> says that such men are judged most unhappy by human law, and by divine law are seen as sterile and withered trees. 

From this law, however, only two kinds of men seem to be exempt: either those who, due to a certain weakness of nature, are entirely unfit for it, or those who have uniquely devoted themselves with pledged faith to *Minerva* <note>The goddess of wisdom; here representing a life of pure intellectual or celibate study.</note> as their wife. Nature herself excuses the former; as for the latter, the chaste *Minerva* would perhaps accuse them if they were to follow *Venus* <note>The goddess of love and physical desire.</note>. As for our friend *Pelottus* <note>Likely referring to a member of Ficino's inner circle, possibly a Latinized name for a contemporary friend.</note>, if he had perchance neglected marriage, Nature—which produced him strong and handsome—would surely have disapproved. And if *Minerva*, whom he has long served, should perhaps try to blame him for mixing *Venus* with the Muses, *Apollo* and *Mercury* will immediately defend him. Indeed, they will say that *Pelottus* dedicated more and better "posthumous" <note>original: "posthymenea" — a play on words combining 'hymeneal' (wedding songs) and 'posthumous' or 'after-songs.'</note> sacred songs to the Muses than he did before. Finally, they will command him to lift his gaze to the sublime stars. There, *Phoebus* (the leader of the Muses) and *Mercury* (their companion) lead *Venus*—the mother of love and music—in their midst; they walk with her at an almost equal pace, so to speak, and never depart far from her. 

But let us leave the stars for now and return to men. I see you, *Antonio*, hereafter often declaiming in this manner among your friends in favor of marriage. Man is either the only social animal, or the most social of all, as the philosophers say, for to him alone has nature granted the faculty of speech and the making of laws for this very purpose. Thus, whoever lives alone should understand that he is either perhaps something greater than a man, or undoubtedly something less; for he who transcends human strength among men is rarer than a phoenix. Therefore, he who enters into a continuous, domestic, and indissoluble society will fulfill the duty of humanity above all others. Through the commerce of this relationship, he strives to preserve the public society of the human race itself and learns how to govern it. Indeed, just as a city is made of houses, so the skill of the Republic is established from the discipline of the household. He will not know how to rule a city who has not learned to govern a home. He will not love his fatherland who considers that neither its good nor its evil pertains much to him. He will perhaps not care to imbue himself with more serious morals if, living alone, he does not have to provide an example of good morals for a family. Through leisure and a certain license, anyone not occupied in household affairs will turn out more negligent and worse every day. He will not truly or steadfastly know how to love anyone if he does not experience the true and indissoluble love of a wife and children. He will not learn to endure things abroad and overcome them by bearing them, unless he has had a domestic teacher of patience. He will not learn to pity men if he has never heard a wife or a son lamenting. For "the mind not ignorant of evil learns to help the wretched." <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid, Book 1: "Non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco."</note> What is worst of all, he who has no need to provide for his own, nor needs to call upon God often for the safety of his family, will for the most part neglect human laws, men themselves, and divine worship. Finally, it will be most difficult not to strip away our humanity unless we put on the legitimate cloak of marriage. Therefore, if you wish to be human friends and legitimate children of God, increase the human race legitimately, and—being similar to God—procreate children similar to yourselves:

->nourish, rule, and govern them. Remember, moreover, that in governing your<-
->household most diligently, you cultivate yourselves, learn<-
->the skill of the earthly Republic, attain dignities, and<-
->deserve the duties of the Republic.<-

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that marriage and domestic life are not distractions from philosophy, but essential training for virtue, civic duty, and understanding divine love. He cites Socrates, Plato, and Trismegistus to support the idea that governing a household is a prerequisite for governing a state.</summary>
