### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Disputation against the Judgment of the Astrologers.

#### Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the most distinguished man, Count Francesco Ippolito Gazolti.

**I** have written a book against the vain judgments of the Astrologers; I am sending you the Preface, and I will send the rest as soon as our scribe has copied it. Those who affirm that every single thing happens by necessity because of the stars are themselves entangled in three especially ruinous errors, and they entangle the common people as well. For, as much as lies in their power, they take away from the highest and omnipotent God His own <term>Providence</term><note>Ficino argues that astrology suggests a mechanical universe, which would mean God does not actively care for or intervene in human affairs.</note> over things and His absolute rule over the whole world. Indeed, they strip justice from the Angels—who, according to them, move the heavens in such a way that all human crimes, all evils for the good, and all good things for the wicked proceed from there. Finally, from men—who, it seems to them, are driven here and there no less than beasts—they take away liberty and deprive them of all tranquility. 

For if they promise good things (which they are accustomed to do rarely, barely, and very obscurely), they usually entangle those promises in the greatest difficulties, from which it follows that they benefit us very little; but if sometimes—and that most rarely—they announce things will come without great labor, we are rendered vain, proud, and negligent by it. And if by some chance it happens as they promised, the long-awaited pleasure is less gratifying. If instead they threaten evils, which happens much more often, we either long anticipate evils destined for the distant future, or, being wretched, we imagine and suffer by imagining evils that will never come. 

Finally, if the fates cannot be avoided, they are foreseen and predicted in vain; if they can be avoided by some means, then the "necessity of fate" is falsely defended by the Astrologers. Perhaps they will say (as I think they will) that this too is in the fates: that something out of many things is sometimes foreknown and avoided. Thus there will be a controversy among the <term>Parcae</term><note>The three Fates of Roman mythology who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note>, so that one determines to wound a man while another protects him. But let us grant them this for now, if you like, lest we seem perhaps too stubborn to anyone; yet we will never concede that it also consists in the decrees of the Fates that many people do not believe them, and many more contradict them. 

For how does fate now compel Marsilio to resist fate with the strength of his intellect? He who certainly is not driven by the force of fate itself, but rather by the power of some contrary or at least superior thing, now attacks fate. For necessity itself cannot at all oppose itself, so as to deny that necessity exists, and destroy itself by its own instinct and stings. What does that most common saying mean: *We are driven by the fates, believe in the fates.*? <note>original: "Fatis agimur, credite fatis." A common Stoic-leaning sentiment in Latin literature.</note> But if we consider the matter more carefully, we are not so much driven by the fates themselves as by the fatuous <note>A pun in the original Latin: *fatis* (fates) vs *fatuis* (fools/fatuous ones).</note> proclaimers of the fates. You will not yield to me, "believe in the fates," if you do not believe in the fatuous ones, who wrap not truths in obscure things (as is said of the <term>Sibyl</term><note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses whose oracles were famously ambiguous.</note>), but falsehoods. And they do not predict things specific to individual men, but things common to everyone. 

These most talkative men bring so much into the open that it is no wonder if, among many lies, they occasionally stumble upon some truth by chance. They wish to be wise for others, when they are not at all wise for themselves. It is worthwhile to consider how destitute they themselves are, how filthy, how unfortunate in their own business, how imprudent and inept in handling affairs. If by chance they practice trade, they foresee the outcome of trade much less than other merchants; if medicine, they perceive the course and end of a disease less than other doctors, and they treat bodies worst of all; and since they profess divination, they seem to live and fall everywhere by chance.

Arise then, O Philosophers, I pray; arise all who are most precious lovers of liberty and tranquility! Come now, gird yourselves with the shield and spear of <term>Pallas</term><note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, representing the use of reason against superstition.</note>; a war now looms against those wicked little giants who both try to equal themselves to the utterly immense God in the foreknowledge of future things, and, by their defense of celestial fate, try to take away free rule from the super-celestial God, who is supreme liberty. But those who strive so proudly to ascend to the heavens will be wretchedly cast down to the depths. Reach out Your hand to us from on high, Almighty God; supply strength to Your soldiers to defend this, Your empire. Now we begin; hasten to help, O divine powers who turn the ethereal circles; hasten to help those who will excuse your justice against impious enemies, who accuse you of a certain extreme injustice. You favor...

He mocks astrologers as incompetent in their own lives and calls upon philosophers to defend the soul's liberty against these "wicked little giants."</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Florentine, Letters,
### BOOK V.

-> Divine laws, faith, and science are confirmed. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his most reverend associates, greetings. <-

Human laws are accepted from their beginning, or propagated after they have been accepted, in no other way than either by the customary and common persuasions of human and natural reasons, or by a certain imperial authority—whether by the force of arms, or by the ease and convenience of living and the allurements of pleasures. Furthermore, the arrangement of the stars can never introduce laws among men by any instruments other than these. For this reason, if we understand any law among men of sound mind to have both arisen at some time and to have been most widely propagated while those probable arguments of the many opposed it, while the arms of the powerful everywhere raged against it, and while the use and hope of human pleasure were openly and utterly taken away from everyone by it, we shall necessarily conclude that such a law is neither human, nor depends on celestial <term>fate</term><note>Ficino distinguishes between "fate" (the mechanical influence of the stars) and "providence" (the direct will of God).</note>, but is entirely divine and proceeds from a certain super-celestial power. 

Moreover, that which is concluded by necessary proof is, without doubt, grasped by certain <term>science</term><note>In this context, "science" (scientia) refers to demonstrable, certain knowledge gained through reason, rather than the modern experimental method.</note>. Therefore, whoever believes in such a law by this kind of reasoning will possess both science as the mother of faith, and faith confirmed by science. He who does not consider such things is unable to consider himself. Truly, he who does consider them in some way but does not believe, believes nothing at all. What others may choose, I do not know; for my part, I certainly prefer to believe divinely than to know humanly. Inasmuch as divine faith is far more certain than the wisdom of men, that belief is always confirmed by true science. This science sometimes wavers through unbelief. Therefore, so that we may be able to believe anything of the truth anywhere, let us now believe in Truth itself; for since it admits nothing of ignorance or falsehood, it certainly ignores or deceives no one. Furthermore, so that we may be able to discern anything of the good anywhere, let us hope in the Good itself; because, as it does nothing of evil and suffers nothing of injustice, it never frustrates those who discern it, nor abandons those who love it. It has both enlightened them so that they might hope, and likewise inflamed them so that they might love. For movement toward the Good itself can neither depend on anything other than the Good itself, nor flow back there by any other means than that by which it first flowed forth.

---

-> Nothing can be one's own where the mind is shared. <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Naldo the Poet. <-

I recently returned to <note>original: "Cellanum"</note> Cellano <note>Likely a reference to a rural retreat or villa near Florence.</note> to visit my—or rather, our—Naldo, for nothing can be one's own where the mind is shared. On the second day of my stay in the country, I composed a very brief <term>argument</term><note>An "argumentum" here acts as a summary or introductory abstract for a longer work.</note> for our book on religion <note>Ficino's "De Christiana Religione" (On the Christian Religion), a central work of his career.</note>. And when I was addressing it to my friends, <note>Naldo Naldi (1436–1513), a prominent humanist poet and a member of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> Naldo came first to my mind—he who was the first of all to be loved by us. The others owe even this very fact—that they are steadily loved by me—entirely to him. Indeed, it was in loving him first that I learned to love the rest. I am sending the summary, therefore. I have written to Naldo what I have done. You, too, write what you are doing and how you are faring. But why, I ask, have I written, and why have I asked you to write? Let those who love only moderately be content with letters; but truly, I know that neither Naldo (of whom I speak) nor Marsilio will be content with a mere exchange of letters.

<summary>In this opening to his fifth book of letters, Ficino argues that Christianity's spread against all worldly opposition proves its divine origin and reconciles faith with reason. He also shares a personal note to the poet Naldo Naldi regarding his recent work on religion.</summary>
<keywords>divine law, faith vs science, Naldo Naldi, De Christiana Religione, Neoplatonism, Florentine Academy, providence vs fate</keywords>

The first section concludes a meditation on finding refuge from human misery in the "Good" (God), while the second section begins a letter to his close friend Giovanni Cavalcanti regarding the struggle between his own melancholy temperament and his divine calling.</meta>

<page-num>789</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK V.</header>

O miserable lot of mortals, a lot more miserable than misery itself! Where then shall we poor wretches flee, so that we might finally escape our misery? To Philosophy—that most meddlesome craft of the sophists? Or to power? Or to pleasure? Alas, we have already fled to these so many times in vain. For that more arrogant Philosophy entangles us in the most troublesome questions. Power, moreover, oppresses us with a certain extreme and most dangerous servitude. Finally, pleasure—brief and false—infects us with true and long-lasting pains. Perhaps wealth will be a worthy prize if we wish to attain what we pursue, so that we may flee only to those things which never flee from us; but surely nothing can flee except that which moves, while that which moves nowhere, since it fills the universe, cannot flee. But what need is there for us to move toward that which does not move anywhere, which is present everywhere to every individual? Let us not move, then, nor be distracted by many things, but let us remain as much as we can in unity. Clearly, we attain eternal unity and one eternity not by movement or by a multitude of things, but by stillness and union. But what is this thing? Speak, friends, oh tell me, what is it? Is it not the **Good** itself, which fills the universe? For nothing can be found that is good except by the presence of the Good itself. This is the very thing—do you not see? This is the very thing that all things desire, because all things are from it. And therefore, individual things are perfected through it, insofar as they strive to cling to it. 

But to the Good, as it seems to me at least, we can cling by no other means than by the love of the Good. Since this is the very condition of the Good: that it is desired, and that its desirability makes it the Good. And that which is best for us, as soon as we love it, we are joined to it. Indeed, since love is a certain good most close to the Supreme Good, it is, as it were, the flame of the Good. Wherever the flame of the Good burns more ardently, there the light of the Good also shines more clearly. What else is there to say <note>original: "Quid epistola," literally 'What of the letter,' a rhetorical transition.</note>, if God is the Good itself, the very light of the Good, and the very love of the shining Good? Let us love, O friends, let us love, I beseech you, before all other things, the luminous Good and the benevolent light. For in this way, we shall not only love our God, but by loving Him, we shall enjoy Him; since God is Love itself, and Love itself is God. Therefore, let us first glow with Him, without whose heat nothing is warm. Let us shine with His benevolent light according to our prayer, for without His splendor nothing shines. Come, friends, let us remain in Him who never recedes, and we shall remain forever. Let us serve the Sun, the Master of all, who serves no one, so that we may serve no one else, but master all things. Let us enjoy Him if we can—and we can if we wish, for by wishing we enjoy, and by enjoying we wish. Let us, I say, enjoy that which alone overflows through the immense, and thus alone shall we be utterly filled; thus alone shall we truly and fully rejoice. For where the Good flourishes without failing, there pleasure is felt without pain, and there joy is full on every side.

-> *God did not create humans for small things, but for great ones.* <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, **health.** <-

**L**ogicians <term>dialectici</term><note>Ficino refers to practitioners of Dialectic, the art of logical discussion and the investigation of truth through reasoned argument.</note> are accustomed to say that the condition of a contradiction is such that if someone already leans toward one side of it, they cannot at the same moment lean toward the other. But my mind <term>ingenium</term><note>While 'ingenium' often means 'genius' or 'talent,' in Ficino's psychology it refers to the natural disposition or character of one's mind.</note> is so distracted this autumn that I neither wish to speak, nor to be silent; again, I can neither act, nor not act. Perhaps this is because I am somehow double, though I seem to be single. But let me be both double—as Plato suggests in the *Phaedrus*—and even triple, as he discusses in the *Timaeus*, provided that what draws me toward honorable business always overcomes what pulls me back toward lazy leisure and sluggishness. Behold, that which invites me to act and to speak now overcomes; and so I speak as best I can, and I act. 

Yet, somehow, a deeper question immediately rises within us. For I wished to joke for a little while (as I often do) and at least write something witty to my friend Cavalcanti. And although I took up my pen with this purpose primarily in mind, I find myself writing more rigid things; and while I attempt lyrics or comedies, I end up performing elegies or tragedies. Shall I tell you why, my friend? I believe <term>Saturn</term><note>In Renaissance astrology, Saturn was the planet of melancholy, associated with deep, "rigid" intellectual labor but also with sorrow and heavy burdens. Ficino famously considered himself a "child of Saturn."</note> has chosen me as his only subject in these times, in whom he may test all the strengths of his own rigidity. But you do not wish for this (as I see), my dear Giovanni, nor do I wish it. What then shall we say, O friend? That God wishes His priests to be the most serious of all men, and that light matters should not be handled among sacred things, but only grave ones. Perhaps for this reason <term>Pythagoras</term><note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose "symbols" or maxims were often interpreted allegorically by Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> commanded his disciples in his symbols that they should not cut their nails during a sacrifice. **God did not create humans for small things, but for great ones—those who are not filled by small things and have known the great; indeed, He created them for the infinite alone, for they alone on earth have discovered an infinite nature, and nothing finite, however large it may be, can ever fully satisfy them.**

<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

# *No one who lacks self-control can be wise.*

->Marsilio Ficino to the Philosophers and <term>Sophists</term> <note>In Ficino’s Renaissance context, "sophists" refers to those who argue for the sake of cleverness or vanity rather than for the truth.</note>, greetings.<-

**A**mong all the powers of the soul involved in the process of knowing, the highest are the intellect and reason, while the lowest are taste and touch. The latter descend toward the most corporeal nature, whereas the former ascend toward an incorporeal and divine substance. Whoever strives to serve all of these at once will surely strive in vain. For no one who is entirely immersed in the darkness of the lowest things will be illuminated by the rays of the highest. Nor will someone who has tasted the true joys and goods of the highest things listen to the ridiculous charms of the lowest. The soul will not reach the truest <term>reasons</term> <note>Ficino uses "reasons" (rationes) here in the Platonic sense of the "Forms" or eternal blueprints of things.</note> of things, which are separated from bodies, unless it has first separated itself from the body through both the purification of morals and the intensity of contemplation. He who already possesses heaven itself and measures (so to speak) eternity itself will think nothing of those things on earth that are subject to time.

I pass over the fact that just as eyes suffering from a certain red inflammation <note>original: "ophtalmia"</note> perceive nothing but red, or a bitter tongue nothing but bitterness, so the soul—which has become almost corporeal through long-standing love and service to bodily things—will either think divine things do not exist at all, or will judge them to be merely physical. I pass over how much free and long-lasting leisure is needed to investigate the most hidden reasons of things. Nothing more slavish, nothing more busy and anxious can be imagined than the troubled life of one who serves the senses as if they were masters—and masters who are many and insane. While such a person is enslaved to these foolish tyrants, he nonetheless professes to be a servant of wisdom. 

Therefore, whomever you find foolishly serving the body, you shall deny they are wise. But those whom you know to be wise, you shall judge not as slaves to their bodies, but as their masters. Those who serve only the pleasures of the body certainly live anxiously; but much more anxious are those who try in vain to join the lowest pleasures with the highest. For since they labor too much on both sides, they enjoy the pleasures of neither the mind nor the body. God rejects none more than those who expect to drink nectar and ambrosia <note>The legendary drink and food of the gods, symbolizing divine wisdom.</note> from the filthy vessels of vice. He approves and loves none more (as Aristotle argues) than those who primarily cultivate a mind most similar to God and separate it far from the dissimilar stain of the body; those who strive not to overwhelm the divine light with the clouds of vice, but to perceive it with the pure serenity of the mind.

This reasoning, I believe, led Socrates to present moral discipline to men first, and Pythagoras to drive the profane far from his sacred schools. For just as a foul vessel makes any liquid poured into it—even the sweetest—stink by its own contagion, so knowledge received by an evil mind produces malice, not wisdom. Furthermore, just as air is to the light of the Sun, so the mind is to the light of truth and wisdom. Therefore, neither the air nor the intellect ever grasps its own rays while it is cloudy; yet both grasp them suddenly as soon as they become pure and serene. To this point tends that saying of Plato in his *Letter to the Syracusans*:

> "That which is divine," he says, "cannot be learned like other things that are learned; but from long-standing familiarity with the divine itself and a similarity of life, a light suddenly shines out in the soul, as if from a sparking fire, and it then nourishes itself." <note>original: "Quod diuinum est... disci non potest... sed ex diuturna circa diuinum ipsum consuetudine... subitò quasi ab igne scintillante lumen effulget in animo, seipsum iam alit." This refers to Plato's Seventh Letter.</note>

Why then do you lean over so many late-night studies, O Philosophers? Why is there need for such long labyrinths of debate, O Sophists? Do you not see? Our only path to the light itself is serenity. Alas, you often trust in vain that the impure can touch the pure (which Socrates condemns). Come, learn from the <term>Platonic Galen</term> <note>Galen was an ancient physician; Ficino calls him "Platonic" because he believed physical health and the "vapors" of the blood affected the soul's ability to think.</note> that it is impossible for a soul smothered by blood and fat to contemplate anything heavenly. Learn again from Pythagoras and Plato that the wisdom of the mind is nothing other than the light of the Highest Good itself, diffused everywhere through truly good souls as if through the purest mirrors. 

Therefore, as soon as you have fully become good, you will shine with the splendor of the Highest Good itself, which is wisdom. The celestial Sun, which generates the eyes of animals and the colors of things, shows those colors to eyes that are open and pure. The super-celestial Sun—that is, truth itself—procreates true things and minds; that same Sun reveals true things to minds that are pure and turned toward it. Purify the eyes of reason from all the filth of this harmful body; turn the gaze of the mind away from the lowest shadow of matter; turn the vision of your inner intelligence toward the light of the supernal form itself. From there, matter already sufficiently prepared is suddenly formed by corporeal forms; from there the

->*Philosophers, while they learn to dispute too curiously, often meanwhile unlearn how to deliberate.* <note>original: "Philosophi sæpe dum discunt curiosius disputare, interim consultare dediscunt."</note><-

### **Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.**

**W**hat do you say, O man, you who are so very sensitive in our affairs? Do you complain that you are being overwhelmed these days by the abundance of our letters? Ah, what are you doing, my Giovanni? Bear these lighter burdens, I pray, with an even mind if you can, since we ourselves bear much heavier ones. Why do I disturb you with such a number of letters? Because, clearly, I am myself confused by an excessive crowd of thoughts. This is the way of those who, given over to too much leisure, become the most "busy" of men. It is better to be busy while leisure weighs upon you than to be at leisure while business presses upon you. Consult with that fellow-philosopher of ours about what he should most especially do in his own case. Forgive your friends who are philosophers; for often philosophers, while they learn to dispute too curiously, meanwhile unlearn how to deliberate.

---

->*For philosophers, solitude is not, and should not be, a relaxation of the mind, but its intensification.* <note>original: "Solitudo philosophis, non remissio mentis, sed intentio esse solet & debet."</note><-

### **Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, greetings.**

**I** withdrew on the <term>Nones</term> <note>The 5th day of September in the Roman calendar.</note> of September to our Mount Celano <note>Ficino often referred to his villa in Careggi as "Mount Celio" or "Celano," evoking the hills of Rome to suggest a place of sacred retreat.</note>, far from the city, for the sake of relaxing—or rather, for the sake of intensifying—the mind. For among those who practice philosophy, solitude is not so much a relaxation of the mind as it is, and ought to be, an intensification. Here, Bernardo, on the day I received your most eagerly awaited letter, I had written shortly before—I know not what—to my close friends, perhaps something more tragic than philosophical. But whatever it may be, it would have been written to my friends in vain unless it were first transcribed for my Bembo. Indeed, whatever is said to Bembo, we consider also said to Phoebus Capella and Marcus Aurelius <note>Humanist friends and associates of Bembo and Ficino.</note>. When I return to the city, where I left another volume, those ten arguments of ours shall be transcribed in it. If I commend myself to you now, my Bernardo, understand that our "hero" Giovanni Cavalcanti is also commended under the name of Marsilio. If I say "Farewell," understand that a wish for your prosperous health is sent to you by that same hero through the words of Marsilio. Take care of your health. But I see that my Bembo is neither able nor willing to be well without his "delights." Bernardo, your friends Landino and Bracciolini <note>Cristoforo Landino and Poggio Bracciolini, prominent Florentine scholars.</note> are doing well for you; therefore, fare you well.

---

->*Wisdom is not granted to the profane.* <note>original: "Prophanis sapientia non conceditur."</note><-

### **Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo Bonincontri, Astronomer and Poet, greetings.**

**Y**ou are often accustomed to say, Lorenzo, that impious men can never turn out to be true <term>Astrologers</term> <note>In the 15th century, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of celestial influences on human life and the physical movement of stars.</note>. This indeed seems to me also to be most true. For if the heaven is the temple of God himself, it is consistent that profane men should be driven far away from the heaven and from celestial secrets. Furthermore, our Plato and the rest of the wise men of the Greeks confess without doubt that not only astronomy, but even all wisdom, descended from the <term>Barbarians</term> <note>Ficino uses this term in the classical sense to mean non-Greeks, specifically referring to the ancient Egyptians, Persians, and Chaldeans, whom he believed held the original "Ancient Theology" (*Prisca Theologia*).</note>. Indeed, we have found that among the Barbarians, only the Priests handled the physical, mathematical, and metaphysical sciences. They were those who knew that wisdom, the principal gift of God, neither should nor can be granted except to the most sacred and divine minds. For this reason especially (as I believe), Christ the master of life said that the sacred mysteries are given to the common crowd in a veiled way, but are revealed to the chosen disciples. But why do I now proceed further in this matter again? Read, if you please, what we wrote in recent days to the Philosophers and <term>Sophists</term> on this same opinion. My friend, provide a reader for these things if you find anyone who has joined learning with integrity above all others. Tell me, I pray, Lorenzo, whom do you most think of bringing to read these things now? Is it Angelo Manetti?

->I see you are thinking of him, and I myself just now<-
->thought of him before all others.<-

<header>THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

# MARSILIO FICINO

->He has won every vote who has mixed the useful with the pleasant. <note>original: "Omne tulit pūctum, qui miscuit utile dulci." A famous quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note><-
->Marsilio Ficino to Bastiano Foresi, his dearest kinsman, greetings.<-

**N**o one among all my friends, my sweetest Foresi, is there with whom I speak more deeply and sweetly than with you. For to others I speak only with my tongue or my pen, but to you I often speak with both plectrum <note>A small pick used to pluck the strings of an instrument.</note> and lyre; otherwise, the plectrum is silent to me without you, and the lyre is mute without you. Come, I pray, my Foresi: whenever you sing to the lyre, you must sing with me as well. But I see that while you are too intently fashioning that other cithara <note>A stringed instrument similar to a lyre; here, Ficino likely refers to a physical instrument Foresi was building or a metaphorical "composition" of his life.</note>, you meanwhile neglect the song and sound of the first. Among the dwellers in heaven, Bastiano, Apollo strikes the cithara but does not build it, while Mercury builds it but does not strike it. Therefore, let no one on earth trust that they can exercise both faculties—of building and of playing the cithara—equally well. If someone should object to us that those who busy themselves too much with the lyre are "dallying" <note>original: "delitare," a play on "delirare" (to be mad/delirious).</note> too much, you will respond in turn, I know, that we "lyre" for this very reason (if I may put it so): so that we do not "delirare" (go mad). Those who always handle heavy matters are surely weighed down by the very weight of that gravity. Those who are continually occupied with light things are deservedly driven here and there by any light breeze. We must mix gravity with levity (as nature teaches us), so that gravity may be relieved and uplifted by a certain modest levity, and levity may be steadied by the stability of gravity. But why do I speak of our music as if it were a light thing? I have demonstrated its dignity—or rather its divinity—elsewhere in a long letter, as you well know. But lest we seem to indulge too much in music, let us conclude briefly thus: nothing is weightier than a heavy harmony, nothing lighter than a light one, and nothing more balanced than a tempered one. Therefore, may the moderate cithara always be safe for us when we call upon it rightly. May you also be safe, provided you often greet our "eyes," Giovanni Cavalcanti and Piero Nero.

I, Lucas, Marsilio’s scribe, who transcribed this letter, commend myself to you. And I pray, if I seem worthy of such a great gift to you, that you love me as much as I see you are loved by Marsilio himself. My patron, Foresi, loves you as much as you yourself love to be loved. Farewell.

---

->No remedy for misfortunes is more suitable than patience.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Bastiano Salvini, his nephew, greetings.<-

**T**here is a common proverb, Bastiano, that nothing is more difficult than patience. We, however, feel the opposite: that nothing is particularly difficult which is not very laborious, nor is anything laborious that does not require great effort, and it does not seem to require effort where no "work" is needed. But in what way is "work" needed there, where one is not so much required to act as to endure? For patience does not command you to act, but to suffer. Just as it is more difficult to act than to suffer, so is it more difficult to act well than to suffer well. Indeed, all other virtues are concerned with acting well, but patience alone consists in suffering well. And what is suffering well other than not increasing one’s suffering through evils? And what shall we say this is? Unless it is the will to suffer that which you must suffer even if you are unwilling? For unless you suffer willingly, you will certainly suffer against your will; and unless you allow yourself to be led, you will be dragged and snatched away more violently. Oh, the wondrous power of patience! Other virtues fight against fate in a certain way, but patience alone—or most of all—conquers fate. For those things which fate has decreed to be immutable and necessary, patience, by consenting to the will of divine providence, changes them in such a way that it turns necessities into voluntary acts. Just as one who acts badly turns good things into evil for himself, so he who suffers well turns evils into good for himself; for in enduring evils, he himself becomes good. As gold is proved by fire, so is a man proved and made bright by adversity; like a veteran soldier, he becomes both skillful and fearless through the frequent exercise of danger; like one who has already tasted bitter things, he thereafter tastes sweetness more sharply, uses it more wisely, and enjoys it more pleasantly. A man does not rightly estimate the value of a good who has not experienced evil. He will never know how to enjoy good things who has never learned how to use bad ones. No one’s prosperity is weaker than his to whom all things seem to have happened prosperously.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK V.</header>
<sig>Ddd 3</sig>
<meta>Catchword: you wrote [original: "scripsisti"]</meta>

It is the mark of a wise man to expect rain even in clear weather, and in the rain to expect clear skies; indeed, in this dark life, one should consider nothing to be clear unless it is under a clear mind. A continuous storm strikes us from the outside; tranquility must be sought by us only from within. Where there is heat, from there comes serenity; where there is heat, from there comes light. However, light proceeds not from the shadow of matter, but from the light of the mind. They err in their speech, my friend, who say that many passions <note>In this context, "passions" (passiones) refers to things experienced or suffered, rather than just emotions.</note> befall the life of men from many evils. It would be said much more correctly that life itself is a kind of passion, pressing upon the wretched without any intermission. Remedies should be applied to continuous diseases not merely to act for a time, but to be of use continually. We are not always able to deliberate, to fight, or to resist, but we are always able to endure well; we do endure, and by enduring we are taught to endure. We are certainly always able to do that whose power consists in the will itself. As soon as we wish to endure well, we do endure well, if indeed to endure well is nothing other than to wish to endure. If we act badly, we will undoubtedly suffer evils, and suffer them badly. If we endure well, we act well. If we fight immoderately, my friend, we shall be exhausted, and by that very exhaustion we shall be utterly conquered by ourselves. If we yield at the right time, we shall undoubtedly conquer. The most fluid air yields to the blows of hard bodies; the air suddenly returns into itself just as it was before. But hard bodies are utterly dashed together and broken. The most flexible and soft things endure unbroken, and they bind the hardest things; because the hard do not know how to yield, they are compelled to be beaten, broken, and bound. Therefore, my dear Salvino <note>Likely Jacopo Salviati, a friend and patron of Ficino.</note>, conquer fortune by enduring it, and—as you have begun—conquer yourself so that you may conquer all else. Remember also that in this malignant region of the world, nothing escapes untouched by evils; yet under a just judge—or rather, under Justice herself as judge—no good can lack its just reward, and no evil its due punishment. Indeed, patience is a good so perfect that without it, the other goods of men cannot be perfected. For those things which are begun by other virtues are perfected by patience. Farewell, most beloved brother, and just as others bear with you, bear with others. Certainly, as often as I see things in a man that offend me, I remember that I too am a man, and therefore I have something that may offend others. By this reasoning, I bear with many daily, so that many may bear with me. Bear also patiently with the rigidity and length of this letter of ours. Let it not be that I have disputed about patience in vain, or that you seem to have heard to no purpose those things which, through your wisdom, you already began long ago both to learn and to observe.

-> Only the temple of Minerva protects men against the storms of fortune. <note>Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom; Ficino uses her temple as a metaphor for the refuge found in philosophical study.</note> <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings. <-

**T**hat friend of ours has already complained to me in two letters about his fortune, or rather, his fate. In this one letter, I advise him to flee to the temple of Minerva, by which alone we are protected against the storms and lightning bolts of fortune. I do not know through whom this letter might more conveniently ascend the Mugello mountains <note>A region north of Florence where many noble families, including the Medici, held villas.</note> than through you. Read it if you wish; send it if you can. Farewell. But what were you thinking just now while you read "read it if you wish"? Did you perhaps think I was permitting him to read your letter rather than you reading his? In the end, do as you please. Truly, I would not wish our writings to please anyone unless they have first pleased that man who pleases me above all others.

-> Old friendship does not need external duties. <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend: <-

**A**nswer, I pray you, Giovanni—if I ask a just thing—why do you not respond to so many of my letters? Do you not know that the flavor of your words brings the sweetest seasoning to our people? What is sweet to me in the midst of bitter things? Giovanni. What, again, is sharp in the midst of sweeter things? Giovanni. Or do you perhaps think that as soon as you have read our letters, you have responded, especially since you always respond to my words with affection and deeds? And often, before I say anything, you yourself have performed everything. It is indeed so. But I know you have proceeded further, for you first thought of responding, and even what you would especially say in response. See from this—what you had already seen before—that Marsilio is closer to your thoughts than your own tongue or hand. Therefore, the ministry of the tongue and hand cannot intervene between your mind and mine. You divine quite rightly, and I divine rightly too. For you also, by thinking...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

You wrote, Giovanni, and I read by meditating even while you were writing. But so that others may also be able to read these things of yours—the response you gave me—I will now transcribe them myself. Giovanni to Marsilio, greetings.

Our old habit of friendship, Ficino, has already ensured that you can no longer bring anything new to me. I have known your genius for a long time, Marsilio; I have a sense of your every thought, and I hold your words in my heart. I erred just now in my phrasing. For it was not so much the long duration of our habit as the very beginning of it that brought this about. Indeed, from the very start of this divine love, you did not impart your soul to me piece by piece, or one part after another, my Marsilio, but you poured the whole of it into me at once, entirely and uniquely. And only so much of this gift is poured out onto others who are loved by you as I myself pour back into them. What, therefore, do you try to give us further? You have nothing at all that he who possesses you does not already have. Therefore, the frequent duty of writing and replying—which among others is a sign of more perfect benevolence—would be an indication of *less* perfect benevolence between us, if it were applied strictly to our case. You err much more in our friendship by speaking, perhaps, than I do by staying silent. For you seem to suspect I know not what kind of division <note>original: "numeri," literally "number," implying a separation into two distinct entities rather than a single unity.</note> or absence between us. But I confirm our simple unity and continuous presence as it truly is, just as you most greatly desire it to be confirmed. What then? Shall mutual letters never be carried between us? Far be it that nothing should ever flow out from the most affluent abundance of our innermost fountain, or that nothing should overflow outside. Far be it that what burns within should never shine without. But for this reason, we have written and will write back and forth frequently: so that those things which our minds—or rather our single mind—thinks in turn, and speaks with itself by thinking, others also may sometimes understand through the use of letters. But you desire me to be well, which certainly you desire above all things. Farewell.

->Those who abuse the Muses bring back gall, not honey, from their spring.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Manetti, Distinguished Citizen, Greetings.

**S**ome writers, my friend, both Latin and Greek, compare men who are very studious of literature to bees. This is because, like bees, they collect from many scattered authors (as if from flowers) material which is then stored in the capacious hives of memory. Once digested by a certain meditation, this material produces the honey-sweet liquid of doctrine and eloquence. If anyone should deny that such a comparison is confirmed by the best authors, he will seem to me worthy of bringing back gall <note>Gall (fel) refers to bile or extreme bitterness, often contrasted with the sweetness of honey.</note> rather than honey from the very spring of the Muses. 

I, therefore, will not take away anything from this similarity, but rather add to it. You have heard, I believe, my friend, that when bees lick very many flowers of wormwood <note>Wormwood (absinthium) is a plant famous for its bitter taste.</note>, they very often produce honey there which, when tasted with the tips of the lips, seems somewhat sweetish; yet when swallowed by the throat, it proves to be not at all sweet, but almost as bitter as gall. We have found that almost the same thing often happens to certain gluttons of literature and "book-devourers" who have neither moderation nor selection. Indeed, the more greedily they seem to drink the sweetest waters of the Muses, the more they meanwhile conceive something bitter in their hearts. This, perhaps, the Latins call "bile" and the Greeks "melancholy" <note>original: "melancholian"</note>—a disease which, as Aristotle proves, is peculiar to diligent scholars. 

For this reason, Solomon calls the study of literature a most burdensome occupation, and added sadness as a companion to knowledge itself. What, then, shall we say to that saying of Aristotle? "The tree of knowledge," he says, "has indeed bitter roots, but the sweetest fruits." Certainly we will grant this to Aristotle, but we will add that fruits of this kind are perhaps peaches <note>original: "poma Persica," literally "Persian apples," the common Latin term for peaches.</note>, beneath whose sweetness lies a bitter pit. 

What then? Shall we detest the Muses? Far be it from us to think that the fountain of heavenly nectar and ambrosia pours out Stygian <note>Referring to the River Styx in the underworld; dark and hateful.</note> and bitter streams. We praise the use of the Muses as much as we condemn their abuse. Who, then, abuses the Muses most? None other than he who either follows their tracks rashly and out of season, or imprudently mixes vulgar Venus <note>In Platonic thought, "Vulgar Venus" represents base, physical lust, while "Celestial Venus" represents the divine love of beauty and truth.</note> with them, or separates them from their leader, Apollo. Diminutive men do not grasp knowledge when they tastelessnessly seize wisdom itself. The Muses <note>original: "camenae"</note> do not sing rightly, but rather are silent or screech, when the petulant son of Venus <note>Cupid, representing distracting passions.</note> interrupts. The choir of the Pierides <note>Another name for the Muses.</note> does not dance aptly—rather it limps and wavers—when the leader of the choir, Apollo, is far away. Accordingly, he who trusts himself to perceive the light of the sun without the help of the Sun, deservedly falls into darkness and does not rise into the light; he who seeks this truth and that truth separately from the Supreme Truth, undoubtedly does not fall upon the true...

->We never truly suffer adversity, except when we suffer perversely.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.<-

**O**ur beloved cousin <note>original: "Amitinus," likely a term of endearment for a close associate or relative</note> tells us again in a long list how much adversity we suffer daily. But I, as one who has long experienced this within myself, write now to him—and indeed to myself—a certain letter on the ease and happiness of patience, acknowledging that I have truly suffered more adversity when I suffered it perversely <note>Ficino implies that suffering is only "adversity" when our attitude toward it is "perverse" or poorly aligned with reason</note>. In reading this, there might perhaps be a need for the patience of the reader and the listener; read this patiently, my excellent Giovanni, and if you think it worthy to be sent, send it yourself.

->Perfect friendship does not need words or letters.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena, greetings.<-

**A**s often as I take up the pen, venerable Father—which I indeed attempt every day so that I might write something to my patron, through whose efforts (or rather, through whose business) I have obtained the leisure to write many things daily—just as often my patron himself interrupts me with these very welcome shouts: "I am here, the one you seek, in person; put down your pen, Ficino. What need is there for any letters where one is allowed to hear and return true voices continually?" Letters may make those who seem absent from one another present at times. But on the contrary, letters might show those to be absent who are actually present to each other everywhere. Therefore, do not separate yourself with a pen from the one to whom you are always joined in your heart. What shall I do here? I do not know, my patron. While you do certain things contrary toward me, I meanwhile suffer two contrary things in turn. You indeed urge me with spurs to run more frequently, and yet at the same time you restrain me with a bridle so that I may rest. I, however, if I do not move, seem lazy and ungrateful; if I do move, I seem insolent and inept. But while you are thus distracting my mind, and I am mutually distracted, this letter meanwhile—I know not how—breaks out from my hands, with this purpose: not indeed to speak to you (with whom I speak at will without a letter), but rather to the people, so that everyone may realize how much the patron and his humble client <term>clientulus</term> <note>A diminutive of "client," used here by Ficino to express humility within the social hierarchy of Renaissance patronage</note> agree in all things. I see that our Cavalcanti would have commended himself to you by a letter just now as if he were absent, had he not seen his Giovanni <note>Ficino's closest friend, Giovanni Cavalcanti</note> standing there in your presence as soon as the letter first greeted you.

->Rightly does he who voluntarily lacks God—who is all good—unwillingly lack every good.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Leone Michele, Venetian Peripatetic, greetings.<-

**I**f any of us loved the Good itself—which is every good—with as much heat as we all love these worldly goods daily (and those things which are not good without the Good itself), we would certainly feel at least as much good and joy as we all now continuously feel evil and pain. Indeed, the joy of that Good would be nearly as much more powerful than our true pain, and sweeter than false pleasure, as the substance of the Good itself is both mightier than evil and truer than the image of goodness; and as the pure mind is more clear-sighted than the impure. Now, however, what wonder is it if all evils follow us, while we ourselves, having abandoned the first Good—that is, God—wrongly follow individual things as if they were goods, all of which are evil without the first? Justly do we fall unwillingly into every evil as often as we fall voluntarily from Him who is every good. Why do we wander, insane and unhappy, for so long here and there? Truly, while we follow only individual things, we meanwhile flee the One itself, which is all things. But he who follows only the One itself soon attains all things in Him. Surely the mind can attain all things if it depends only upon Him who is above all things. From this, certainly, man alone among the animals has received the power to achieve whatever he wishes, provided that in the very thing he wishes, he also wills to do whatever he can. I approve of you, therefore, great-souled Leone <note>Leone Michele was a Venetian philosopher of the "Peripatetic" or Aristotelian school</note>, because you are no longer disturbed by many things, but (as Carlo Valgulio <note>A scholar and translator close to Ficino</note>, a most reliable witness among us, testifies) you have long since chosen that best part, which since it [is] not only from its whole...

### *Since God is love itself, whoever attempts to love something without God, attempts to love without love.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Locterius Neronio, greetings.<-

**I** wrote, my best Locterius, this past summer a certain letter to my friends about true friendship, which perhaps would have been written in vain to true friends unless it were read by those who are friends to us in that very One <note>Ficino refers to God as the "Very One" in whom all true friendships are anchored</note>, without whose heat no one can love anything, without whose splendor nothing can be loved, and without whose love—since we attempt to love outside of love itself—whatever we seem to love, we are forced to hate rather than to cherish. Without His friendship, all things are the more hostile to us the more they seem to be friendly. Oh, what a wonderful union of goodness itself, and beauty, and love! For where the goodness of good things shines, the beauty of beautiful things also gleams, and in that same place, the love of loves also burns. Indeed, beauty follows the very light of the Good like a splendor, while the heat of love follows the rays of beauty like a reflection of those rays.

### *Only he who rules over the willing, rules happily.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco, Cardinal of Siena, many greetings.<-

**T**ell me, I pray, with what words I might best invoke you at present, my most kind patron. The great dignity in which you are placed seems to demand that I begin with "Reverend Father in Christ," but your far greater clemency and supreme humanity entice me to invoke you more familiarly. Greetings, sweetest friend. And lest the patron's own name, most sweet to the client's mouth, be omitted: greetings again, my Francesco, sweeter than sweetness. Since I struggle with this kind of ambiguity now, what should I do? Truly, where the rank of dignity is surpassed by the affection of humanity, we are accustomed to speak with certain worthy and proud titles; but where a singular kindness exceeds the power of dignity, we ought to begin with human and familiar names. Especially for those of us who are not guests and strangers to you, but rather, by your kindness, members of the household. Clients, sweetest friend, are usually most pained when patrons seem likely to give nothing; I, on the contrary, rejoice most in this very thing—that my patron is to give me nothing further, since he has left nothing of himself for himself, but has long since given himself and all his things to us and with us. Live happily, my most lovable patron. Your friends cannot help but live happily while you live happily, you who live entirely for your friends. To whom all your household serves most closely for this very reason. No service is either tighter or more pleasant than the voluntary; no rule is safer and easier than that of love.

### *The herd disapproves of the excellent; God approves of them, with whom there is gratitude and liberty.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.<-

**R**eceive, Giovanni, copies of two letters which I devised at dawn today for the cause of our friend, and gave today to those priests whom you know. I do not know by what fortune [they will be received], and indeed that is not my care. I only wish I knew by what Muse <note>original: "qua musa"; Ficino refers to the poetic or intellectual inspiration behind the letters</note>. I am no mercenary. I know the reward of the mercenary is to be well-paid, but the end of a liberal art <note>term: "liberal art" (ars liberalis). In the Renaissance, these were studies like philosophy and rhetoric, practiced by free men for their own sake, rather than for profit</note> is to have done well. Whatever it may be, I will at least bring our friend back to memory; perhaps you will say it is better to seek oblivion than memory, and to lie well-hidden than to be exposed poorly. But let others forget him, if oblivion pleases some. He, however, cannot forget his own. We have found it to be true that no great man was ever known by his own people. What wonder is this? Truly, the excellent do not fit with the herd. Opposites are not loved by opposites. Envy takes the place of veneration. Weak eyes grow dim in too much splendor. They do not grasp...

...those who are filled with small things grasp great things. But perhaps you will grieve with me in this one thing, my dear Giovanni: that perhaps our greatest [friend] is unknown to his homeland, not because he is so great, but because he is considered so small. Let us not grieve, friend, as long as he is pleasing to us, and we are pleasing to Him—He who discerns small things just as well as great ones, and encompasses great things just as well as small ones. No one will be considered "least" who is approved by Him, for whom, in comparison to His own magnitude, even the greatest things are infinitely less than the smallest. Nowhere shall he be obscure who shines in Him, who shines in all things, and in whom all things shine. Nothing is easier than to please Him, for whom to please is nothing other than to *will* to please. Therefore you see, marvelous as it is, that these "least" goods are much dearer than the Infinite Good; for the former are acquired only with great labor and cost, while the latter, if it is bought at all, is bought with the will. But why is this so, friend? Perhaps because He overflows immensely and because His price is within Himself. Other things we buy, but He in truth buys us of His own accord: He buys us, I say, both by the goodness of His will toward us, and by the will of our goodness toward Him. Therefore, since this is enacted by goodness on both sides, and goodness itself is God, the "price" is on both sides. Nor are we ever entirely free until we have freely sold ourselves to infinite liberty. As soon as we belong to Him, who alone belongs to Himself, then only do we belong to ourselves. Children are nowhere more free or empowered than in their father’s house. No parents obey anyone more willingly than they do their children. But lest I seem to wander too far from where I began, I shall make an end in Him, for whom to wander toward is nothing other than to return.

### That Philosophy does not teach, but rather forbids, living and conversing with princes.
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends many greetings.

**I**n that book which I composed this year for Bernardo Bembo, the Venetian orator, concerning the praises of Philosophy, I attempted to assert through many reasons that Philosophy teaches all things. I should have excepted this one thing: that she does not teach us to spend our lives with princes. For if she forbids it entirely, as she certainly does, she in no way "teaches" it. Indeed, she forbids it utterly, it seems to me, since she commands the opposite; namely, she desires tranquility of mind through the love of finding truth, and freedom of life. However, in the courts of princes, it is not truth that dwells, but lies, simulations, dissimulations, slanders, and flatteries. Not tranquility of mind, but care, anxiety, envy, and finally every kind of disturbance. Not freedom, which is dearer than all gold, but rather a misery of servitude so great that it never spares either the subjects or the princes themselves, and its end is either slavery or ruin. 

Let no one object to me the case of Aristippus the Cyrenaic <note>Aristippus (c. 435–356 BCE) was a pupil of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school, which emphasized pleasure. He was famously comfortable in the courts of tyrants.</note>—not a Philosopher, but a <term>Phidolosum</term> <note>original: "Phidolosum," a play on words meaning "lover of pleasure" rather than "lover of wisdom."</note> and a <term>Philosomatum</term> <note>original: "Philosomatum," meaning "lover of bodies."</note>—who once lived so gracefully with Dionysius, the tyrant of the Syracusans. For he first stripped off Philosophy (if he had ever been clothed in it before under Socrates) the moment he "clothed" himself in Dionysius. Yet he eventually regretted wearing that garment. For he discovered that while a sword hung over the head of Dionysius, that same sword and Dionysius himself hung over the neck of Aristippus. 

Much more prudent in this matter, or certainly more fortunate, were Democritus, Heraclitus, Socrates, Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates, Xenocrates, Apollonius of Tyana, Plotinus, and many others, who far preferred a free and most rich poverty to the servile and most poor riches of kings, and a most sweet sobriety to the most bitter delights of tyrants. It is worth considering those great Philosophers whose memory we venerate, who would have lived much more happily than other men with princes and kings if only Philosophy were able to teach men how to do so. 

I pass over the fact that the young Octavian, ungrateful for benefits received and led by no great cause, handed over his own Cicero—a philosopher of no small renown—to be killed by a nefarious enemy. Nero, without cause, condemned his holy teacher, the Philosopher Seneca, to death. Alexander, King of the Macedonians, is said to have thrown the Philosopher Callisthenes, his own master, to be torn apart by lions for the sole reason that he was surpassed by him in a debate. 

But who would not marvel greatly that those "gods" of the Philosophers, our Plato and Aristotle—men the most serious of all, who knew all things that are, that have been, and that are to come—dealt so unhappily (I will not say imprudently) with tyrants? They were frequently brought into the highest peril of their lives for the slightest reasons: for when they "clothed" themselves in the prince, they did not "strip off" the Philosopher. Perhaps Xenophon, the follower of Socrates, was forced to strip off the philosopher at the court of the Persian king Cyrus,

<meta>This page continues from the previous page's discussion on the trials of the wise. The opening syllable "nophon" completes the name of Xenophon, the Greek philosopher and soldier, who was mentioned at the very end of the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>794</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

[Xeno]phon. <note>The text continues from the previous page naming Xenophon, who lived in exile.</note> O, the all too wretched lot of Philosophers among the powerful! The divine Plato was sold into slavery twice—oh, the grief! Three times he underwent the danger of death under Dionysius the Elder and the Younger, partly on account of a certain book <gloss>A theological work, written by Dionysius as if from the mind of Plato, and in a certain way revised by Plato; but mostly because Plato, as their teacher, would instruct them daily and exhort them toward a more just way of governing.</gloss> Alexander of Macedon expelled that great man of wisdom, Aristotle, his own teacher and tutor, in an altogether too shameful manner; later he even persecuted him cruelly, either because of Callisthenes the Aristotelian, or because Aristotle had published the secrets of nature to the common people after having previously entrusted them only to Alexander. For the most trivial reason, the state of Croton—or rather, its tyranny—destroyed the heavenly Pythagoras when he involved himself as a teacher to the aristocrats. For a slight reason, Zeno of Elea, a man of singular metaphysics, was destroyed under Hiero; and likewise Anaxarchus under Nicocreon. 

And lest I move from philosophers to poets for the moment, I will pass over the unjust exile of Ovid; I will pass over how Nero, on account of a musical contest, held his own Lucan in hatred for a long time and finally killed him. I will pass over how Domitian, driven by I know not what petty ambition, slew his close friend Statius during that famous "fly-catching" game of his. <note>The Roman Emperor Domitian was said to spend his leisure time catching flies and stabbing them with a sharp pen.</note> But, to conclude my speech regarding Philosophers: let no one be so ignorant of human nature as to trust that he can philosophize rightly and freely while simultaneously leading a secure and safe life among princes.

->*Only in loving and praising is he never deceived for whom the law of loving and praising is God.*<-

->*Marsilio Ficino to Georgius Cyprius, a legitimate physician, Greetings.*<-

**W**ho serves most basely? He who serves a slave. Who serves most miserably? He for whom the wages of servitude is punishment. Therefore, he is most base and miserable who serves the body. Again, what kind of man is he who serves the rumors of the common crowd? Vain, restless, and unfortunate. And what of him who enslaves himself to those who seem "distinguished" to the common people? He is hardly prudent. 

Truly, men are to be loved, not adored. But they must be judged by a long-lasting examination—at least fifteen years <note>original: "trillustri" - a lustrum was a five-year period</note>—and loved most diligently before you fully commit your affection; otherwise, love deceives the judgment, and the outcome frustrates the love. Very few, however, are to be praised, and these only when they are fully mature and long-advanced in years, and even then, most moderately. Otherwise, by praising others we are ourselves reproached, and we often repent having given praise. Only he is never deceived for whom the law of both loving and praising is God: so that he may worship God alone for His own sake, love men in God, and praise God in men. Why do I say this? Surely because I am discussing the chief institutions of character with a man already trained in moral precepts. Farewell.

->*Faith begets hope, hope charity; the fire of charity brings clarity of understanding.*<-

->*Marsilio Ficino to Lord Bernardo Bembo, Venetian Patrician, lawyer, and most illustrious knight, Greetings.*<-

**T**he Apostle Paul, that most elect vessel of divine wisdom, when he was caught up into the third heaven—from whence celestial love is kindled in the minds of those on earth—suddenly beheld that invisible Sun. No one can look up at its splendor unless he is first kindled by its flames with a certain divine love. But only he is fully kindled by such flames who always applies true faith to the rays that illuminate all things, and who most firmly places all hope in the heat of that same Sun which most kindly nourishes all things. 

Since, however, I did not sufficiently understand how much light recently shone upon me from that Sun, most illustrious Bernardo, I called upon Giovanni Cavalcanti as a judge in this matter. But since he, like me, seems to be in the dark, we have both by the same decision appointed our friend Bernardo Bembo—who is gifted with the eyes of a lynx <note>A common metaphor for someone with exceptionally sharp intellectual or physical sight.</note>—to be the judge in this matter.

->*Nothing is weaker than human love, nothing stronger than divine.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Amatio, sends greetings.<-

How different is the nature of love from almost all other things, my dearest Amatio? For while other things are judged to be firmer the larger they are, love and favor seem weaker the greater they appear. Indeed, a massive love is often offended by more frequent and more trivial causes than a moderate one. Either the heat of its own passion incites a "fiery bile" <term>In ancient medicine, "yellow bile" was associated with fire and a quick temper.</term> which, with a small breath of air, sometimes surges into a great tide of anger; or, fixed contemplation produces "black bile" <term>Also known as melancholy, this humor was thought to cause fear and obsessive thoughts.</term>, making one fear even when all is safe. Or perhaps it is the greed of the one who thinks he has given his whole self to another, and therefore demands the whole in return from the beloved, yet never fully possesses what he sought with his whole mind. But a perverted mind deserves to suffer these adversities—a mind either entirely soft or mercenary—which, since it feeds only on earthly winds, swells up rather than grows when it seems most mature; therefore, the larger it appears, the more fragile it truly is. Human love, then, is a thing full of anxious fear. But divine charity, set ablaze by the flames of the virtues and celestial rays, seeks again all the sublime peaks of heaven, where no dread of earthly evils ever causes anxiety. Such is our mutual love, my dear friend. Therefore, as certain as you are of your love toward me, be just as certain of my love toward you. Far be it from us that a human heart should not respond to a human heart that calls to it so often; for even musical strings seem to respond to other strings tuned like them, and one lute echoes another when it sounds, and a faithful Echo sometimes resounds back to those who call.

---

->*No one truly serves unless they serve willingly; no one truly rules unless they rule those who are willing.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of St. George.<-

After I departed from you yesterday, I could not restrain myself from feeling a sharp envy toward your household staff for enjoying your company, which is—if I may say so—sweeter than ambrosia and nectar <note>In Greek mythology, ambrosia and nectar were the food and drink of the gods, granting immortality and delight.</note>. Therefore, lest I perish from envy, I return quickly today to those who are permitted to recline at the feasts of the gods (if it is lawful to say so). And lest I be forced to leave there again and be tortured once more by spite, I return to you now with a guide who never departs far from you, and from whom I myself never depart—one who commands me and obeys you. "Who is this?" you will ask. You shall hear who it is shortly, if you wish. For yesterday’s journey, my guide was the most beautiful Venus in Taurus <note>Ficino is referencing an astrological alignment; Venus is considered "at home" and particularly strong in the sign of Taurus.</note> with the Moon accompanying her and occupying the middle of the sky. This, Pierleone the physician and excellent mathematician <note>original: "Petrus Leo physicus & Mathematicus"; he refers to Pierleone Leoni, the personal physician to Lorenzo de' Medici and a close friend of Ficino.</note> will confirm for you, I believe. For today’s journey, however, that most graceful celestial child of Venus, Love himself, shall be my leader. Therefore, receive your lover Marsilio with a certain amorous affection, if you will. For I hear that by a wonderful kindness of nature, you love even those who do not love you. See, venerable father, with what liberty—or rather license—I deal with you. I have just called myself your "lover"; perhaps I should have said your "servant." Alas, I have erred. But you yourself are the cause, my lord. For you show yourself to be such a man to everyone that he who does not use the greatest liberty and confidence with you would undoubtedly seem the most slavish and distrustful of all. Perhaps I did not err after all. For I confessed myself a servant enough when I declared myself a lover. No one truly serves unless they serve willingly; no one truly rules unless they rule those who are willing. Oh, how marvelous is the empire of Venus and Love! For (as the poets tell us) neither the most ferocious Mars nor almighty Jupiter himself can tame Cupid. Rather, all the deities among the poets are either burned by the flames of Love himself, or they shimmer and shine with his hooked rays and splendor.

# BOOK VI OF THE LETTERS.
<page-num>797</page-num>

[When individual things are] arranged and adorned at home in a certain order, you yourself will be delighted by a composed mind, by decorous words, and by good character. Your music will be the tempering of the affections of the soul and of all your actions, so that while everything outside harmonizes, the soul alone does not sound a discordant note. Let your recreation also be the frequent reading of the most select writers, lest perhaps in the midst of the greatest wealth, the soul alone should appear impoverished. Let your hunters and fowlers be certain men near you who are most proven and learned, who, by their wonderful prudence and humanity <term>humanity (humanitas)</term> <note>In the Renaissance, *humanitas* referred to the development of human virtue through the study of the "liberal arts"—literature, history, and philosophy.</note>, may acquire for you the favor and goodwill of all. Humanity alone is the bait by which men are caught; only through the favor of men are human affairs conducted prosperously. Nothing is more dangerous in a prince than if many people despise him, or hate him, or envy him too much. Contempt is avoided through knowledge, gravity, and integrity. Hatred, indeed, is softened by innocence and humanity. Envy, finally, is settled by munificence, liberality, and magnificence. Since all men are equal in appearance and free in their will, they bear servitude with an most resentful spirit, unless perhaps those who rule—to the same degree that they exceed their inferiors in loftiness—equal them in humility, and appear to excel far more in wisdom than in fortune. Nature gave the power of touch alone to the members lower than the head, but adorned the head alone with the powers of all the senses. In this matter, nature seems to have warned those who strive to preside over others as the head: they ought to surpass the rest in wisdom as much as the head itself surpasses all the limbs in sensation. No great man at all ought to trust that his character can remain hidden. For the greatest things are the most visible, and are those which everyone envies, least forgives, and most disparages. Let the prince see to it—since he himself can only with the greatest difficulty remain hidden from others—that nothing remains hidden from him at home or abroad. First, let him be an Argus <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, representing a watchman who sees everything.</note> himself, then let him nourish a certain lynx <note>The lynx was proverbially said to have sight so sharp it could see through solid objects.</note> near him, and (if it can be done) let him not lack an Oedipus <note>Oedipus was famous for his intellect in solving the unsolvable riddle of the Sphinx; here, it refers to a clever advisor who can solve complex problems.</note> as well. It is extremely dangerous in great matters to despise small ones; a small, neglected spark often excites a massive fire. It is neither fitting nor safe for him to give himself over entirely to sleep, for he must keep watch on behalf of many, and many in turn keep watch over him; nor is it fitting for the "head" of many men to be enslaved to a beast—that is, to serve the belly and lust. It is best and safest never to be angry; for what else is it to boil with anger than to become a drunkard and a madman? When anger has shaken off the bridle, the tongue must be restrained by a bit until the wrath cools down. And just as is done with the insane, the hands and feet should be bound, lest in that very fury something be said or done. The disciples of Pythagoras <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician who emphasized self-discipline and harmony.</note> were never able to detect a sign of anger in him. His associates had no other evidence of an angry Socrates <note>The Athenian philosopher known for his patience and search for truth.</note> than his silence. Plato, the father of philosophers, once somewhat angry with a delinquent boy, said to Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato and the third leader of the Platonic Academy, known for his stern and serious character.</note>: "You beat this boy yourself, for I cannot do it while I am angry."

Let your mind be equally humble and lofty, your gravity mixed with courtesy, your life sober, and your tongue truthful but very sparing. Let your hand be most generous, your promises not reckless, your faith firm, your observation full, your counsel long-lasting, and the opinions of the wise diligently examined. Do not let many deceive you easily every day, and do not yourself believe many people nor believe them easily. Let neither a flattering persuasion nor any light conjecture move you, but only certain reason. Do not approach a beginning unless you have first looked forward to the end itself, seeing it as both excellent and certain. Avoid evil and infamous ministers, lest you yourself be considered an evil master. But why have we passed over so quickly, and as if with blinking eyes, that which is of the greatest importance? The poets paint Love as blind for this reason: because a lover is very often deceived when he judges either himself or the thing he loves. Since men love no one more vehemently than themselves, they are certainly deceived by no one more than by themselves. Therefore, do not believe yourself in anything, and do not commit yourself entirely to a single counselor; rather, have many, and indeed those who are quite elderly, whom long experience of things has taught, whose character the most constant fame commends to you as the best, and whom reality itself most clearly proves. Whenever you deliberate with your elders on a weightier matter, take care that they do not perceive your own will, lest perhaps they follow your desire rather than utility and dignity in their advice.

Above all, however, proclaim daily to your people that the gift of truth (from wherever it is offered) will be as pleasant to you as the most precious gifts are usually pleasing to greedy tyrants. Open your ears, I pray, to those who advise you, lest you be forced to open your heart itself to the arrows of fortune. Shut your ears entirely to flatterers, as if against the wicked songs of the Sirens <note>Creatures from the *Odyssey* whose beautiful songs lured sailors to their deaths; a common metaphor for dangerous flattery.</note>. Remember that you are a man. Therefore, remember that you always have within you some things that could be rebuked.

<summary>Ficino provides a series of moral precepts for a ruler, emphasizing the need for self-control, the avoidance of anger, and the importance of surrounding oneself with wise, elderly counselors rather than flatterers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's moral and philosophical advice to a high-ranking person (specifically Cardinal Raffaele Riario), transitioning from the internal governance of the soul to the external management of one's household and the avoidance of flattery.
