# MARSILIO FICINO

For this reason, whichever of your household, without any exception, praise you, they are either blind themselves or wish for you to be blind. If the laws most severely punish as poisoners those who either fascinate the eyes with their gaze, or capture the ears with certain songs, or infect the body, what indeed do we think should be done to those who blind the eyes of the mind and seize the ears through sycophancy and flattery? Therefore, if you wish to see, to hear, and to live, remove all flatterers and ministers of pleasures far away like enemies. As for those who occasionally accuse others before you, what shall we say? These should perhaps sometimes be heard briefly, but never fully listened to. <note>The Latin distinguishes between *audiendi* (hearing) and *exaudiendi* (listening with belief or granting a request).</note> If ever they are heard by you, let them make you cautious rather than an avenger. Be content with this single kind of vengeance: if you show that you are able to take revenge, but do not. Truly, drive out backbiters, the foul-mouthed, and the envious from your threshold no differently than dogs infected with rabies.

Finally, let your home be a temple of God, the eye of Prudence, the scale of Justice, the seat of Fortitude, the rule of Temperance, the model of Honor, the splendor of Charity, a fountain of graces, a choir of Muses, a gymnasium for orators and poets, a sanctuary for philosophers and theologians, a senate of the wise, a nourishment for talents, a reward for the learned, a table for the poor, a hope for the good, a refuge for the innocent, and a protection for the wretched. If you observe these and other things of this kind to the best of your strength, you will finally hear that most happy voice: *Upon this rock I will build my church.* <note>A reference to Matthew 16:18, here applied metaphorically to the moral and intellectual foundation of the Cardinal's household.</note>

I commend to you Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, through whose mouth I have spoken the above things to you.

->*Only then should we congratulate a man who has obtained a dignity, when he appears worthy of that dignity.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to Cardinal Riario.<-

**U**nless Truth herself had commanded you in recent days to block your ears to flatterers, I would now pursue your letters with wonderful praises. How great they are, O Almighty God! But look, even as I begin a certain "praiseworthy song" (so to speak), although Truth does not refute it, the most modest Riario (as I hear) interrupts. You do not wish to be praised to your face, venerable father. So be it, indeed; but permit at least that I may praise at my own discretion this very fact—that you forbid yourself to be praised. Or perhaps you forbid that too? Lest a sharper sting of glory, which did not prick you from the front, should strike you from behind. I will indeed obey the master. But in the meantime, you will grant me this small favor: that if I congratulate you less, I may at least congratulate your dignity itself, because it has finally decided to adorn that man by whom it now seems almost equally to be adorned. Then I shall rejoice in my fortune because, being a lover of truth, I have recently found a patron whose own patroness is Truth herself. I shall also congratulate the happiness of Truth itself, which, although she came forth unarmed and naked, found not enemies, but friends. Yet she, venerable father, has often reproached me in these days, not because I sent her unarmed, but uncultivated. Who could deny that she went out from our threshold uncultivated? Since she was by no means accompanied by Religion herself, who contains all the cultivation <term>cultivation (cultum)</term> <note>original: *cultum*. Ficino plays on the word *cultus*, which means both "culture/care" and "religious worship/veneration."</note> of truth. Therefore, lest Truth complain further about me, or with me, or before you, I am sending Religion moreover as her attendant to you, but similarly unarmed and naked. Yet I do not think that either Truth, or her companion Religion, will be in any way "uncultivated" in the presence of our Cardinal, who is a diligent cultivator of both.

->*Truth makes a man worthy of dignity.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino gives greetings to Francesco Soderini, most skilled in civil law.<-

**T**ruth herself, sweetest Soderini, having been entreated by our prayers, visited our Cardinal Riario in recent days. However, she does not seem to have satisfied my wish through my prayers unless she also visits Soderini, a most true friend. But anyone errs who thinks that this Truth has come to you later; for indeed, she who approaches Riario *after* he attained dignity, proceeds to you *before* your dignity with this purpose: that she may either make you, or at least declare you, already worthy of that dignity.

# LETTERS, BOOK V.

->He has won every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet.<-
<note>original: "Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci," a famous maxim from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* regarding the ideal balance in writing and life.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo the Venetian, sends greetings.<-

**W**hen I consider the letters of my Aeneas, <note>likely referring to Aeneas Galotti, a student or associate of Ficino who served as a messenger</note> most distinguished Bembo, I seem to behold his mother Venus joined with Jove. Indeed, our Aeneas now dictates heavy laws with Jove, now sings of love with Venus. <note>Ficino uses astrological metaphors here: Jove (Jupiter) represents gravity, law, and authority, while Venus represents grace, love, and beauty.</note> He appears brilliant everywhere; he meets us kindly wherever he is. If by chance you ask why light spirits should have commerce with heavy ones, the very nature of things will immediately answer: Beneath the heavens, light elements are mixed with heavy ones, and flowers and leaves with fruits. In the heavens, the swift are tempered by the slow, and the moving by the fixed. There is also a supreme harmony of qualities between Mercury and Saturn, and between Venus and Jove. Therefore, he has won every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet. Fare happily, my sweet and useful Aeneas.

---

->I prefer that my letters be answered by the mind rather than by the hand.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the singular Peripatetic Giovanni Pietro Apollinari, sends greetings.<-
<note>"Peripatetic" refers to a philosopher of the Aristotelian school.</note>

**W**hether the same cause can produce contrary effects in the same subject is a great controversy among philosophers. Our friend Amatius recently settled this dispute for us, showing that it can be done, not with words—as the logicians usually do—but through reality itself. Indeed, he led us into contrary emotions at the very same time. He praises Giovanni Pietro, the singular philosopher, most wonderfully, and loves him ardently. But while I hear him praising you so, I am utterly driven to write something; yet when I see how ardently he loves you, I recognize the beloved philosopher as present in the lover, and so I am called back from writing, thinking that friends who are present do not need letters. What then shall I do? Shall I write? I will certainly write, so that I too might pull you in different directions of feeling, so that you might simultaneously not respond and yet respond. Believe me, distinguished man, however lukewarmly I write, I love you just as ardently. Therefore, respond to me, who writes clumsily, with nothing from your pen; but to me, who loves fittingly, I pray you respond with love. And if you love us, care for your health most diligently. For in these times of philosophy, it is impossible for philosophy to be well unless you yourself are well.

---

->No one has greater love than this: that a man lay down his soul for his friends.<-
<note>A reference to the Gospel of John 15:13.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.<-

**G**reetings, our magnanimous Medici, our best physician. <note>Ficino frequently plays on the name "Medici," which means "physicians" in Latin.</note> Truly you alone perform the office of a heavenly physician; for He sent down His eternal Son from heaven to earth as a healer of human diseases. You also, of your own accord, sent your most dear son to us yesterday to heal our very sick minds. He did not spare his son for the sake of the human race; you yourself also did not spare your son for our consolation. For this common suspicion of an epidemic <note>a reference to an outbreak of the plague in Florence</note> did not stop you from consoling your mourning friends with the presence of your noble son, so that you might fully fulfill that divine precept: "No one has greater love than this: that a man lay down his soul for his friends." Lorenzo, while you look out for our safety on all sides, you draw everything of ours to yourself, so that we now live in you rather than in ourselves. Thus it happens that we cannot repay you in kind; we would certainly lay down ourselves and our souls for you if we had them, but you, Physician, have these already. Therefore, lay these down wherever it pleases you. Fare happily, my sole patron until now, and now my sole father.

### *Material for writing is never lacking for those who love.*

->**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, the Venetian Jurist and most distinguished knight, sends greetings.**<-

**I** have long been searching for a legitimate excuse to offer you for this long silence of ours, and for that reason I remain silent even longer in the meantime, because I cannot find a sufficiently great cause to bring forward for the silence. Nevertheless, I am writing at present for this very reason, best Bembo, because I cannot find anything particularly important to write; writing this very thing, namely, that I have nothing to write. What indeed are we doing, sweetest Bernardo? Do you see what harm expectation does to us? Truly, while I expect your letters any day now, and you expect mine, neither of us sends the most-expected letters, and neither receives them. Therefore, let us strive hereafter to anticipate one another with letters. Especially since we should not have to wait for what the Muse might wish to dictate to our writings; for those people must wait for the inspiration <term>afflatus</term> <note>A Latin term for a divine breath or sudden inspiration from the gods or Muses.</note> of the Muses who are not inspired by love. But for those whose hearts burn continually with the breath of love, the power of invention always shines by that same light.

### *It is better to give superfluities than to deny what is due.*

->**Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone da Spoleto, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.**<-

**Y**our letter, my fellow philosopher, seeks Platonic mysteries from us, and at the same time treats of Platonic matters itself. It seeks them so beautifully that I do not know how to deny the one who asks; it treats them so well that I am unable to send anything. Indeed, I have absolutely nothing that I might send to him who already possesses all things. Therefore, what shall I do? Shall I be stingy to one who asks so graciously? Or rather a redundant giver to one who possesses everything? But I prefer to sometimes give what is superfluous, rather than risk denying what is owed.

### *Natural grace persuades more than acquired eloquence; humanity conquers things more than violence.*

->**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Marco Aurelio, most distinguished orator, sends greetings.**<-

**J**ust as all things seem to mourn when the Sun sets, but rejoice when it rises, so when Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a powerful Venetian diplomat and a close friend of the Florentine humanists.</note> formerly departed from here, all this people clearly grieved with him; now that he is finally returning, they congratulate one another. It pleases me to speak briefly here to the Venetian Senate. If ever you should wish, divine Senate, either to stop rivers or move stones, you will not call upon an Orpheus or an Amphion, but rather Bernardo. For he, by his silence, persuades no less through a certain marvelous grace than those men did by their singing. If it should be necessary to subdue distant or rebellious nations, you will not send Caesars or Pompeys, but rather Bernardo. For he captures more people, and more easily, through humanity and love than commanders do with arms. Why do I say these things to you, best Marco? So that you yourself may understand, and signify to your close friends, how much your choice in this matter is approved by everyone; and that you might ask Bernardo himself, especially in the name of our men of letters, to take his journey both swiftly and cheerfully. And let him, by his happy arrival, restore me to myself, for he quite easily snatched me away from myself when he departed.

### *An excuse concerning a book of Astronomy returned quite late.*

->**Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Benivieni, the legitimate physician, sends greetings.**<-

**T**he book of the stars, which you kindly gave to me quite a while ago, I finally restore to you. As for the fact that it returns to you rather late, do not cast the blame on me (who am usually more hurried), but on the stars themselves. For all of them, Antonio, decided to finish their own course first before they would return home. <note>Ficino is making a scholarly joke: the book about the stars could not be returned until the actual stars had completed their celestial cycles.</note>

# MARSILIO FICINO

### An Excuse for the Long Silence.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of Saint George, sending Greetings.<-

**D**id you ever think, venerable Father, that such a long silence could fall between us? But you will cease, I think, to wonder at this one thing, if only you diligently consider the common lot of all things in these times. A prodigious—do you not see?—a prodigious year is passing. Daily so many new, so many unheard-of things occur, that one must daily repeat that word: "I had not thought it." <note>original: "non putâram," a Latin phrase used to express shock at unexpected disasters or political shifts.</note> But, to leave aside public matters and come to my own: I had long desired to find and follow some prince who would please me entirely, and whom I myself would please equally. I found him at last; I was summoned a thousand times; I did not follow. I would never have thought this possible—ha! how often have I cursed that "impossibility," so to speak. You indeed, my Raffaele, were first commanding the impossible when you beseeched me to follow in your footsteps. For not only the private causes which I cited, but also certain public and very powerful ones which I could not declare, held me back. <note>Ficino likely refers to the political tensions between the Medici in Florence and the Papacy in Rome, which made it dangerous or impossible for him to join the Cardinal's court.</note> But I, a few days after your departure, both affected by weariness of myself and inflamed by longing for you, similarly wished for the impossible: namely, that I had not only come but even preceded you. And again I was held back, wretch that I am, by those same causes.

But what the cruelty of Mars and Saturn <note>In Renaissance astrology, Mars and Saturn are "malefic" planets associated with war, hardship, and separation.</note> had attempted either to tear asunder or dissolve, the kindness of Venus and Jupiter, <note>Venus and Jupiter are "benefic" planets associated with harmony, love, and restoration.</note> meanwhile striving to mend it on all sides, has repaired. It suddenly brought back to Florence our Archbishop of Amalfi, <note>Rinaldo Orsini, a mutual friend of Ficino and Riario.</note> a very close friend to me indeed, but to you most devoted above all others. Since I am able, as I wish, to speak of my Raffaele as often as my burning affection urges me to do so, and since I have in him a reciprocal praiser of you, he has stood out as the chief physician of my illness; he has restored my Raffaele to me. For indeed, "wherever two are gathered in your name, there you yourself are present." <note>original: "ubique sunt duo in tuo nomine congregati ibidem ipse ades," a playful adaptation of Matthew 18:20, suggesting that when Ficino and the Archbishop talk about the Cardinal, the Cardinal is spiritually present.</note> You remember how often and how much I praised the judgment and integrity of the Archbishop to you. If you ever come to know the presence of Amalfi himself, you will affirm that I have praised him truly indeed, but most sparingly. His brother Pietro Niccolini, an excellent man, will commend his cause. Your Marsilio, if he had ever deserved anything well from you, would commend him to you for all his merits; but since there are no merits—which is a matter of great grief—at least on account of your kindness and the virtue of Amalfi himself, he commends his business to you again and again.

---

### Patience Cannot Be Had Without Religion.

->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Coccio, the distinguished Jurist, sends Greetings.<-

**P**atience, as it seems to me, commands three things in particular. First, that you should be willing to suffer evils gladly, which nature itself commands you not to suffer. Second, that you should make voluntary for yourself what fate has decreed to be necessary. Third, that you should turn any evils into goods—which is the duty of God alone. In the first, it commands one to resist nature; in the second, to conquer fate; in the third, finally, to make oneself equal to God. It was once far easier for Hercules to obey the commands of Eurystheus and to tame those wild monsters than it is for us to obey the precepts of patience itself. <note>In Greek mythology, the hero Hercules was forced by fate to serve King Eurystheus and perform twelve near-impossible Labors.</note> And how much difficulty we struggle with is shown most especially by this: that in other matters, whatever we handle most frequently, we usually eventually perform best and most easily. But indeed, I do not easily see how much the common people profit in the duties of patience. Surely the whole life of men in this malignant region of the world, contrary to heavenly minds, seems to be nothing other than a certain perpetual disease and pain. Nevertheless, although we suffer evils constantly, we almost continually suffer them poorly. And to the other evils, which are innumerable, impatience itself is added—the greatest of evils, which is so evil that without it nothing is an evil to us, and with it nothing is a good. For impatience alone causes the adversities, which might pertain only to external things and the body, to pass over into the soul as well. It causes us, moreover, to enjoy very little the goods provided by nature or fortune; patience...

<meta>catchword: seems</meta>

Indeed, by bearing evils well, one transforms them into good; and by using goods well, one enjoys them most happily. Certainly, just as poorly—that is, with difficulty and unhappiness—as we bear evils when we are separated from the Highest Good, so well—that is, easily and happily—do we endure them when we are joined to the Highest Good. For where all good is found, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. We are joined to it, moreover, when we most willingly consent to the very will of God, the governor of all things. Finally, we consent if we love; or rather, if in loving individual good things, we recognize that we truly love nothing else but that Highest and Divine Good itself. It is from this Good that individual things possess the quality of being good and lovable, and that we ourselves possess the quality of being both worthy of love and capable of loving.

Let us recognize, therefore, my friend—I pray, let us finally recognize—that since nothing pleases us anywhere except because of the image of God itself, then nothing in these things that please us truly pleases us except God Himself, from whom these individual things receive the very quality that makes them pleasing. And just as in all things to be loved, we shall notice that it is God Himself who is loved by us, so shall we willingly consent to His will. Thus joined to God, we shall happily overcome fortune, nature, and fate. Truly we understand that just as individual things which are either hot or bright are necessarily referred back to the highest heat and light, so too whatever things possess any portion of good—that is, all things disposed well and wisely within the single order of the world—are clearly led back to the one supreme goodness and wisdom. Since this wisdom lacks nothing of the good, eternal life is fully present there: the highest intelligence of all things, the highest kindness, complete benevolence, and perfect happiness. And since all things are disposed from that source as well as they possibly can be, we shall always receive whatever happens as being for the better. In this one thing the entire power of patience consists: that we endure well, as if it were a good, whatever happens under the governance of infinite goodness.

->*Patience is the only medicine for evils.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, Jurist and most 
## illustrious knight, envoy of the Venetians, sends Greetings.

**A**s often as I take up the pen in these times—which I do frequently—it occurs to me to write something about patience. These iron ages <note>Ficino uses "iron age" to describe the period of war and civil strife in Italy during the late 15th century.</note> bring us nothing but evil. The Muses bring us nothing else but patience, the virtue for enduring such evils. Now there is a need for that metamorphic alchemy which turns iron into gold; so that these worst of ages, which come to us as "iron" because of suffering <note>original: "ob passionem." Ficino plays on the word "passio," which means both suffering and the passive experience of being acted upon by fortune.</note> itself, may at least be turned into "golden" ones by the gift of patience. 

Receive, therefore, most patient man, the copies of three letters briefly discussing patience.

->*Nothing is more either necessary or voluntary than love.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Antonio Vinciguerra, most learned 
## man and secretary of the Venetians, sends Greetings.

**R**ead happily, together with our friend Bembo, my book *On the Christian Religion*. And live always mindful of your Marsilio—or rather, to speak more correctly, of Bernardo Bembo. Into him that "Magical God" <note>Ficino refers to Love as a "magician" because it transforms the lover into the beloved, a common Neoplatonic theme.</note> has long since transformed me; He who alone among the divinities holds power over free wills. Celestial love, most beloved Antonio, alone often makes the will necessary—for I love in such a way that I cannot *not* love. And in turn, love sometimes makes necessity itself voluntary, when I love in such a way that I neither wish not to love, nor wish to be able to be unwilling. 

Therefore, whether you choose to call him "Marsilio Bembo" or me "Bernardo Ficino," you will name both of us quite correctly. You too, do you not notice, are bound by the same logic with us. A threefold cord, Antonio, is difficult to untie <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12: "A threefold cord is not quickly broken," symbolizing the bond between Ficino, Bembo, and Vinciguerra.</note>, but in all things we must look to our friend Bembo. Yet perhaps in this one area he should sometimes be avoided. Shall I say it? I shall certainly say it, for where love overflows, there also pardon abounds. Bernardo seems to be an Averroist in a certain way, rather than a Platonist. <note>Averroës was a medieval philosopher whose followers were often accused of heresy for believing in a single "Intellect" shared by all humans. Ficino is making a joke: Bembo's friendship is so powerful that he makes several people share one single will, "proving" the heresy through charm rather than logic.</note> Indeed, he alone persuades us of that Averroist heresy by his silence much more than all the Averroists do by their arguing. Namely, while by a certain wondrous grace and fusing love he creates one will among many, he also signifies—as it is in Averroës—one...

...in which I know not what bitterness and, as I might say, something of Saturn <note>In Renaissance astrology, Saturn was associated with melancholy and bitterness; Ficino often struggled with his own "Saturnine" temperament.</note> which my birth-chart either sowed in me or philosophy added to me, might at some time be softened by the sweetest commerce of some Jupiter <note>Jupiter represents the "temperate" and joyful planet that balances Saturn's gloom.</note>. You therefore, so that you might one day grant my wish, have given yourself entirely, Niccolò, to Rainaldo Orsini, a pupil of Jupiter himself. Indeed, you knew that wherever the Amalfitan <note>Rainaldo Orsini was the Archbishop of Amalfi.</note> is—who is my "other self"—there I am present as well. You wish me to be well; greet him frequently, and commend Marsilio to him as often as you greet him. Farewell happily. But tell me, I pray, did you think that our Quarqualius <note>Antonio Quarquagli, a member of Ficino's inner circle.</note> had now slipped from my memory? Whoever thinks me forgetful of my Quarqualius should also think me forgetful of myself. I am writing to him, therefore, something philosophical from that same workshop—but I hope it is something good.

-> Prosperous fortune in fate, true happiness in virtue. <-

-> Likewise to Sinibaldo, son of Pino, Lord of Forlì. <-

-> Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, greetings. <-

**I**ngense love for you, noble Lorenzo, has long commanded me to give you immense gifts. The contemplator of the heavens thinks nothing great among all that he sees with his eyes except the heaven itself. Therefore, if I give you heaven itself today, Lorenzo, look, what will be its value? But I would not wish to mention a price now, for love born of grace gives and receives everything freely, nor can anything beneath the heaven be weighed in equal balance for heaven itself. Astrologers say that he is born the most fortunate of all whose celestial signs fate has so tempered that the Moon first looks upon Mars and Saturn not badly, then looks upon the Sun and Jupiter, Mercury and Venus, well. As much as astrologers make one fortunate whose fate has well disposed the heavens, so much do theologians make one blessed who similarly tempers these same things for himself. 

But truly you will say this is far too great a thing. It is great indeed; yet approach it with good hope, noble Lorenzo; He who made you is far greater than heaven, and you yourself will be greater than heaven as soon as you decide to approach it. For these things are not to be sought by us anywhere outside ourselves; indeed, the whole of heaven is within us, we in whom there is a fiery vigor and a celestial origin. In the first place, what else does the Moon signify in us besides that continuous motion of our soul and body? Mars then signifies speed, but Saturn slowness. Furthermore, the Sun signifies God, Jupiter the law, Mercury reason, and Venus humanity <term>humanitas: the complex of virtues including kindness, culture, and refinement</term>.

Come, gird yourself now, noble youth, and in this manner temper the heaven for yourself along with me. Let your Moon—that is, the continuous motion of soul and body—avoid the excessive speed of Mars or the slowness of Saturn; that is, let it handle individual things maturely and opportunely, neither hurrying faster than is right nor delaying later than is proper. Moreover, let this Moon in you continually look toward the Sun, that is, God Himself, from whom it always receives nourishing rays, so that everywhere you may worship Him above all others from whom you have your being, so that you yourself may be worthy of honor. Let it also look upon Jupiter, that is, divine and human laws, which it should never transgress. For to depart from the laws by which all things stand is nothing other than to perish. Likewise, let it direct its sharp gaze toward Mercury, that is, toward counsel, reason, and knowledge; do not undertake anything without the advice of the prudent, nor say or do anything for which you cannot give a probable reason. Again, let one consider a man devoid of knowledge and letters to be in some way blind and mute. 

Finally, let it fix its gaze on Venus herself, that is, Humanity. By which, clearly, she warns us to remember that nothing great can be possessed by us on earth unless we possess men themselves, for whose sake all earthly things were created. But men are captured by no other bait whatsoever than humanity. Beware lest you ever despise it, perhaps thinking that humanity was born of the ground <note>Ficino plays on the Latin words 'humanitas' and 'humus' (ground/earth).</note>. For Humanity itself is a nymph of outstanding body, born of celestial origin, beloved by the ethereal God above all others. Indeed, her soul and spirit are love and charity. Her eyes are gravity and magnanimity. Her hands, moreover, are liberality and magnificence. Her feet are courtesy and modesty. Finally, the whole is temperance and honesty, beauty and splendor. O distinguished form! O beautiful spectacle! My Lorenzo, a nymph so noble is placed entirely at your disposal; if you join her to yourself in marriage and dedicate her as your own, she will bring you all sweet years and make you a parent with beautiful offspring. Finally, to say it briefly, if in this way you prudently temper for yourself the celestial signs within you...

->*The heavens promise good things, but Virtue provides them.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to his Giorgio Antonio Vespucci, and likewise to Naldo, greetings.

I am writing a letter to the younger Lorenzo regarding the prosperity of fate, which we mostly receive from the stars outside of us, and also regarding free happiness, which we acquire by our own choice from the stars that are within us. You shall interpret it for him (if it be necessary) <note>Vespucci and Naldo Naldi were the young Lorenzo's tutors; Ficino relied on them to explain his Neoplatonic theories to the boy.</note>. You will also advise him to learn it by heart and keep it stored deep in his mind <note>original: "alta mente repostam" — a reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, suggesting a memory held in the highest part of the soul.</note>. The great things we promise to that boy, he will provide for himself in equal measure, provided he reads them with the same spirit with which we wrote them.

---

->*Concerning the salvation of the philosophers before the coming of Christ.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Ivano of Sarzana, greetings.

The Mosaic commandments are distinguished by theologians into two kinds. Some pertain to natural and moral law. Others to ceremonies and judicial rulings. The first were given by God to Moses and the people. The second Moses himself established, divinely inspired. Furthermore, the first are commanded to be observed by all types of men forever. The second bind the Jews alone, specifically until the coming of the Messiah himself. These first ones we mentioned are so common that they could have been known even to someone with a less liberal education, or by natural judgment alone. For what else is contained in them except the worship of the one God and a moral life?

Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, and other similar worshippers of the one God, trained in the best morals, avoided the underworld by means of this Mosaic or natural discipline. However, they could not earn the celestial realms without the grace of the heavenly Christ. For this reason, they were brought into a middle region, where in Limbo <term>Limbo: from the Latin 'limbus' (edge), the theological concept of a place for the souls of those who lived virtuously but died before the Resurrection of Christ.</term> they were made most certain of the Messiah's coming, either through the Prophets—who were similarly kept in that same place—or through angels. Hence the Gentiles as well as the Jews sought the heavens, first under the hope of Christ himself, and then through the presence of Christ. You have read what we recently wrote to the Pope regarding peace during the war itself. Read again what we once wrote to "Peace"—a certain secretary of the Archbishop of Florence—concerning war during a time of peace, a few days before the war. I am transcribing a copy of that letter for you.

---

->*An Exhortation to Respond.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Phoebus Capella of Venice, a most distinguished orator, greetings.

Phoebus, unless you give me answers sometimes when I call you so often, perhaps we shall deny that you are Phoebus <note>Ficino is playing on his friend's name, Phoebus, which is an epithet for Apollo, the god of the Delphic Oracle who "gives answers."</note>, whose chief duty is said to be giving answers. Perhaps, you will say, "Marsilio, you are not so great that Phoebus himself should answer you." But come now, my Phoebus, just answer me, for suddenly I shall be so great. Oh, if only I could say, "Phoebus himself once answered me," oh, how great I would be!

---

->*He is happy who truly rejoices; only he truly rejoices who rejoices in the truth alone.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Capponi, son of Niccolò, greetings.

I have composed a certain short declamation <term>declamatiuncula: a brief formal speech or essay used for moral instruction.</term> addressed to the human race, briefly discussing the conduct of life. I shall only think I have treated such a great matter well when I seem to have correctly instructed the human race in your eyes—you who are most rightly instructed yourself. I have transcribed a copy of it for you; read it happily. But I will have said too little unless I add this one thing besides: live happily as well. For what else is happiness but true joy? It is for the sake of this that all people do everything. Therefore, so that you may live happily, rejoice truly; but so that you may truly rejoice, rejoice in the truth alone.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK V.</header>

->*A picture of a beautiful body and a beautiful mind.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his close friends: Again to Lorenzo de'<-
->Medici, and likewise to Bernardo Bembo, greetings.<-

**P**hilosophers argue much, orators declaim much, and poets sing much to exhort men to a true love of virtue. I, for my part, praise and admire these efforts. Otherwise (unless I praised what is good) I would not be good myself. But I believe that Virtue herself (if she were ever brought out into the open) would exhort everyone to embrace her far more easily and effectively than the words of men. You praise a girl to a youth’s ears and describe her with words in vain—trying to strike him with the stings of love—when you could instead offer the very form of the beautiful girl to the youth’s eyes. Point out the beautiful woman with your finger (if you can); you have no further need for words here. For it cannot be said how much more easily and vehemently beauty itself provokes one to love than words do. Therefore, if we bring the marvelous appearance of Virtue herself into the sight of men, there will be no further need for our persuasions; she will persuade more quickly than can be imagined.

Imagine a man endowed with the most vigorous and sharp senses, a robust body, prosperous health, a graceful form, a fitting breadth of limbs, and a becoming height. Imagine him moving promptly and skillfully, speaking elegantly, singing sweetly, and laughing graciously; you will love no one anywhere, you will admire no one, if you do not love and admire such a man the moment you see him. 

Come then, so that you may more easily contemplate the divine appearance of the soul from the fitting likeness of a beautiful body, let us match each part to each. For the body is the shadow of the soul itself; the form of the body, as far as it is able, reflects the form of the soul. For this reason, let that vitality and sharpness of sense in the body reflect, in a certain way, the wisdom and prudence of the soul. Let the strength of the body signify the soul's fortitude. Let the health of the body—which consists in the tempering of the humors <note>The "humors" refer to the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) which Renaissance medicine believed had to be perfectly balanced for health.</note>—signify the temperance of the soul. Let beauty, which is established by the order of the limbs and a becoming color, show us the order and splendor of justice. Let physical breadth signify liberality and magnificence, and height signify magnanimity <note>literally "greatness of soul."</note>. Let that dexterity signify urbanity and courtesy, and ornamented speech signify the art of oratory. Let sweet song represent the poetic faculty. Finally, let that most pleasing laughter represent the perfect joy with which virtue itself drenches us, and the secure happiness of life. 

Collect now these individual members and gifts of virtue that we have described into one, and you will clearly see a spectacle suddenly worthy of veneration and admiration. Oh, how lovable, oh, how wonderful is this form of the soul, of which the form of the body—so widely loved and wondered at—is but a certain shadow! Indeed, as much as virtue itself would immediately allure everyone to herself with a most pleasing appearance if she were discerned by the eyes, so much, without doubt, would vice (if clearly discerned) immediately terrify and put them to flight with its deformity. Come then, O friends, let us always keep this divine Idea <note>original: "ideam" — a reference to the Platonic "Ideas," the perfect, eternal forms of which worldly things are mere reflections.</note> and form of virtue before our eyes. This grace of splendor will allure us at once; the sweetness of its order and harmony will continually delight us; and a bounty of good things will fulfill us entirely.

->T H E   E N D.<-

# OF MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine, On His Letters,
### BOOK VI.

->A prayer of the Christian flock to the Pastor Sixtus, entreating him to say to his sheep, "Peace be with you."<-
->The Christian flock humbly commends itself<-
->to Sixtus, its most Blessed pastor.<-

**I** find it hardly easy now, O best of pastors, to decide where I should primarily begin. On one hand, I am moved to praise you by the wonderful virtues of your holiness; on the other, I am pulled back to complaints by the lamentable evils of my own misery. What, therefore, shall I do in the present moment? Shall I recount your praises? Or shall I rather enumerate our hardships? But (as it seems) we gain nothing by praising you. For singular excellence does not grow through common praises. It is better, therefore, to reveal our wounds to our physician—who is most likely to heal us for this reason—than to vainly count his most famous and innumerable praises. And if, compelled by a certain wretched necessity, we beseech him more importunately, yet we hope—trusting in his mercy rather than in our own entreaties—that he will utterly expel every plague from his sheepfold.

If I were entirely made of tongue, most blessed father, I could not explain how great a calamity now weighs upon me, or with how much pain I am consumed. It cannot be said with how great a joy I was once filled when God himself appointed you as my pastor. I had heard, indeed, that you were the phoenix of Philosophy, possessing the very citadel of Minerva <note>Roman goddess of wisdom and war</note> above all others. This is indeed so manifest to everyone that it cannot be denied. Truly, I hoped that when supreme power was joined to supreme wisdom, that Golden Age would return which Plato once prophesied would come when power and wisdom should coincide in the same person. Finally, just as the things I had long ago heard about your wisdom were true, so the things I hoped for regarding my own happiness were almost entirely false. I fear lest someone, perhaps too reproachful or lacking patience, might eventually dare to cry out: "Alas, how much my own opinion has deceived me in this hope, wretched as I am; my joy has been turned into mourning." Not a golden age (which I hoped for), but an iron one under a most wise Pontiff—who would have believed it? The iron ages have returned; I see nothing anywhere except weapons forged for my destruction; I hear nothing but the sound of arms, the clatter of horses, the thunder of cannons <note>original: "bombardarum," referring to early artillery</note>; I feel nothing anywhere but weeping, plundering, fires, and slaughter. Add to this that I am choked by hunger, and I am consumed day by day more and more by the plague. And as if these things were not enough to exhaust me from within without end, there constantly looms over my head a most voracious wolf, a roaring lion, a vast elephant, a pestilential Dragon, and Teucer <note>original: "Teucer," a classical reference to the Trojans, here used to denote the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II, the "Great Turk," who had recently invaded Otranto in 1480</note>—that monstrous enemy of the Church—who is even now about to devour this poor little flock of yours, and you especially, unless you are present to help. The whole Christian state hangs upon you alone as its head; upon you alone falls the weight of either the highest glory or the deepest infamy; for you, the greatest of all men, there remains either a reward or a punishment. Therefore, lest any such misfortune occur or impatience lead to complaints, consult first for yourself, most holy father, and look out for us. Save yourself first for us, we pray, and preserve us for yourself in turn, most blessed father. Forgive your sons, we beg, most indulgent father and fount of indulgence, if—partly driven by pressing evils, and partly moved by our own charity and relying on yours—we attempt to advise your holiness, "like a pig teaching Minerva" <note>A Latin proverb, "sus Minervam," meaning an ignorant person attempting to instruct an expert.</note>. Charity believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails, and the highest kindness cannot receive anything but kindly.

Remember that you are the Vicar of the most gentle and merciful Christ; forget (as you were once accustomed to do) injuries, the memory of which is nothing else for a man than the forgetting of himself. Lay aside whatever hatred you have against your own people, so that you may receive back your usual, if you have lately lost it, immense...

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VI</header>
<sig>Eee 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: Not</meta>

You cannot lose your gentleness without losing yourself. Therefore, keep that former charity (*for we know what we are speaking of*), which you shall retain, lest you be compelled to lose that pious spirit of yours. You will not allow anyone to rage any further against your flock using your own weapons, lest you yourself, through the fault of another, either turn into a wolf instead of a shepherd, or at least be thought of as one. Whoever takes up arms against your people undoubtedly wounds you before all others. For no one is a shepherd without a flock, and he who either denies or loses some part of the flock ceases to be the shepherd of the whole. If you belong to no particular group, you shall belong to all. If you belong to some specific faction, you shall belong to no one. Christ granted you, above all, a divine authority—not primarily of weapons, but of souls. Furthermore, he gave you keys, not a helmet or a sword. These are the keys with which you may close the doors of <term>Janus and Pluto<note>Janus was the Roman god of beginnings and war (whose temple doors were opened in wartime); Pluto was the god of the underworld. Ficino is asking the Pope to end war and death.</note></term>, but open the gates of the heavenly kingdom. Three times he said to you: *do you love me? Do you love me?* Then he added: *if you love me, feed my sheep.* If any have wandered seventy-times-seven times, forgive them. Leave for a time the ninety-nine who are obedient, so that you may redeem the hundredth who is less obedient; and when you have redeemed that one, rejoice more over this one than over all the others. He did not say: pursue that sheep with any curses, but pursue it kindly with prayers. He did not give you any rod with which to strike the straying sheep, but rather gentle words with which you might kindly call them back to the fold, and keys with which you might most safely guard them. A hireling, indeed, sometimes harshly strikes the straying sheep of another, but a shepherd always forgives and looks out for his own. The Lord did not appoint you a hireling, but a shepherd.

BUT I see what you will accuse; you will say that it is one thing to wander from the shepherd’s path, but another for a ram to strike the shepherd with its horn. And so, perhaps you complain to us about some "Ram." We have looked around everywhere, good shepherd, and we find no such ram among us. Does that soul lack the strength—I know not why you are so angry with the ram—that you nearly lose or throw away your entire sheepfold? Somehow your flock lies hidden from your eyes, O shepherd, scattered among the woods and rocks. O, if only you would look upon them for a little while, for you could not look upon such a great slaughter of your own people with dry eyes. Alas, your flock is vexed on every side by all manner of diseases and evils. Everywhere the shepherd is accused; everywhere he is disparaged. Meanwhile, wretched as I am, distress presses upon me from all sides. On one hand, I grieve for your ill-repute; on the other, I mourn my own misery. If the ears of Fame itself were offered to you for even an hour, through which you might hear both your own infamy and my weeping, surely you would bewail your own lot no less than I bewail mine. O my shepherd, unfortunate in this matter (if I may speak thus), O utterly unhappy flock—shame! Do you not hear it? Harsh and biting <term>satires<note>A reference to the political lampoons and criticisms being circulated against Pope Sixtus IV in Italy at the time.</note></term> are being armed against you, Supreme Pontiff. Against me, however, more mournful tragedies weigh down. No sharper satire shall be read anywhere, however false it may be. No tragedy was ever truer or more sorrowful; if you take away the matter of the tragedy, you take away the material for the satire at the same time. Delete your name from the book of infamy—your name which has long been written by God in the Book of Life. Rise up, our guardian, at last; rise up now as a lawful guardian; say, together with your Lord, say—I pray you—*peace be with you.* He spoke, and it was done. There will be peace and glory for you and yours. *A golden age will be led by us together with you.* Let the iron weapons from your sheepfold be turned against the barbarian wolves <note>A reference to the Ottoman Turks, who had invaded Otranto in 1480, threatening all of Italy.</note> under the <term>militia of Constantine<note>Likely referring to the duty of Christian rulers to act as the "secular arm" protecting the Church, as Emperor Constantine did.</note></term>. Without a doubt, the shepherd will be praised as much then, when the wolves are slaughtered or tamed, as he is now disparaged everywhere while the lambs are cast down. A thousand armed men shall fall at your side, though you are unarmed, and ten thousand at your right hand; God the Almighty himself will fight for you.

BUT BEHOLD, you accuse the ram again; accuse him once more (if he seems to you to deserve accusation), but let your accusation be Christian rather than hostile; let it not lead to any destruction, but rather to salvation. Your Lord did not come to destroy anyone, but to save. He wanted you to be a physician, not an executioner. But I would not wish to have uttered that harsh word "executioner" before your most holy majesty—a vice which no executioner would dare suspect in your piety. Almighty God gave weapons to you (as the Apostle Paul says): *not carnal, but rather spiritual and divine.* He ordered you indeed to provide for and spare the sheep subject to you, but to defeat the proud wolves—that is, the barbarian enemies of the faith—through the hands of Constantine; not for the sake of war, but for the sake of peace. *So that with the wild beasts tamed and the livestock saved, there may finally be one fold under one shepherd.* But spare your own first, O Nourishing Pastor: spare your own, lest while we contend among ourselves over wool and grass, the wolves in the meantime more easily and fiercely attack the very life of the sheep and the shepherd.

He urges the Pope to end the internal conflicts within Italy and instead turn his spiritual and secular authority against the invading Ottoman Turks.</summary>

I am this to you, just as each person is to themselves. You are to me what two eyes are. Fare well and be happy. But why have we just now passed over our Cristoforo Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498) was a famous humanist scholar and a close friend of Ficino. He is best known for his commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy.</note>, the Phoenix of the Muses? Because when I named Ficino in the greeting itself, I thought I had already named Landino.

---

->*He who loves ardently grasps nothing besides the beloved.*<-

### **Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to Raphael Riario, Cardinal of Saint George.**

**A**t this hour of the night when the supreme creator of nature—without whom nothing is born, God made man—was born for men, so that men might be reborn divine for God <note>Ficino is writing this on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day.</note>, this letter to Raphael is also born for me. But as I wondered with what nourishment I might especially foster and feed the newborn letter, I know not what spirit, from among those who sang the divine word to the shepherds on that same night, said: "What do you seek to write, Marsilio? Penetrate now the individual inner chambers of the soul; you will find a mind entirely empty of all other things, full of Raphael Riario <note>Raphael Riario (1461–1521) was a powerful cardinal and great-nephew of Pope Sixtus IV.</note> alone. Therefore, you will not be able to write anything to Raphael except Raphael himself. He has made you so empty of all others here, since he made you full of his own presence; for he is as great to you as he is dear, so that you cannot grasp anything else while you grasp him. Do you wish, then, to express most fittingly whatever you have, whatever you think, and whatever you say of Raphael? Come, with that same art of painting with which you have long painted him in your mind, now paint him on this tablet." Indeed, that spirit said this to me of Raphael. But I cannot paint it with my hands. Imagine it yourself in your mind. But where is it? Where is our Amalfitan <note>Giovanni Nicholino, the Archbishop of Amalfi, who served as an intermediary between the Florentine scholars and the Roman Curia.</note>? For a long time now, I have been searching for him here and there (as I am commanded) to greet him, but in vain was I seeking him outside of you, whom I could not find except within you.

---

->*It is neither your place to accuse princes, nor is it right to accuse fortune.*<-

### **Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Master Giovanni Nicholino, Archbishop of Amalfi.**

**I** hurried just now to my writing tablets with a certain plan, venerable Father, to write many things certainly to him whom I love and honor as much as possible. But when I took up the pen, immediately all invention fled, so that I seem to have received not a pen but a catastrophe of invention <note>original: "non calamum, sed calamitatem." Ficino is making a pun on the Latin words for "pen" (calamus) and "disaster" (calamitas).</note>. Even now I am in such doubt as to what I should write. Since I wish to write nothing of evil, and can write nothing of good, for nothing of good offers itself to us among these innumerable evils <note>Ficino likely refers to the ongoing wars and political instability in Italy.</note>. What shall I do? Shall I accuse Fortune, who is too much an enemy in these times? Or shall I rather cry out against the faults of men? Neither, finally; for that is not fitting, nor is this permitted. I shall have said enough if you reflect upon whatever things we once said together. I am writing to that most kind patron of ours, the Cardinal of Saint George; deliver the letter yourself. I would ask you to commend me to the most esteemed Lords of Pavia and Siena <note>The Cardinals of Pavia (Ascanio Sforza) and Siena (Francesco Piccolomini, the future Pope Pius III).</note>, if I did not know that as often as you commend yourself, you commend Marsilio together with you.

---

->*Among evils, he whom God protects is harmed less.*<-

### **Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Raphael Riario, Cardinal of Saint George.**

**Y**ou neither write to your little client, nor do you write back anything, my unique patron. And indeed, he bears that with as calm a mind as he suffers equal things. Since he denied his feet to you as you were leaving here <note>Ficino refers to his inability to physically accompany the Cardinal when he departed Florence.</note>, you also in turn rightly deny your hands to him as he writes; although perhaps one denies it willingly, while the other certainly denied it unwillingly. But an unhappy exchange of such a denial is justly repaid by a happy exchange of affirmation. For just as he gave his soul to you long ago, so you in return gave your soul back to him for his own, with great interest. Truly, in this common misery of the human race, which the mind shudders to recount, in which every one of us is miserable, he alone is less miserable, concerning whom the most merciful God has commanded his angel...

his own, so that he might guard him in all his ways <note>A reference to Psalm 91:11, "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways."</note>. ->*We ought to approve of ourselves only when we are approved by those who are most proven.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Domenico Boliani, the Venetian Jurist, sends greetings.

**I**f my friendship with the most illustrious patrician Francesco Michele, contracted long ago, required any further safeguards, I would entreat you by the very divinity of Love to maintain me in his goodwill with all your zeal. Indeed, I cannot explain how much I value being loved by men who are worthy of love. For unless I am pleased with myself, nothing else can please me; yet I am only truly pleased with myself when I feel I am approved by the most proven of men.

->*No one is more unfortunate than he who neither sees for himself, nor sees the one who sees.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Cocchi, distinguished Jurist, and likewise to Francesco Berlinghieri, and Pietro of Arezzo, and Master Georgius Cyprius, and Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger.

**I** wrote some time ago a certain letter resembling a prophecy to the Pope, but I wish it had been "pontifical" <note>Ficino puns on the word "pontifical," wishing his letter had the authority or effective power of the Pope himself.</note>. Nor would it be so divine among others as it is "divining" among us; certainly, it would drive far away the internal and external destruction even now hanging over the necks of the Christian flock. I call God to witness, my friends, that in this matter I have fulfilled my duty to the best of my strength; let others who remain see to the rest—those to whom eyes were given that they might see first of all, and ears that they might at least hear. Otherwise, even if they are perhaps forced at some time to cry out, "Alas, I did not see," it will never be permitted for them to say, "I did not hear." 

The Ides of January <note>January 13th.</note>, 1478 <note>In the Florentine calendar, the year changed in March; this likely refers to 1479 in modern reckoning, shortly after the Pazzi Conspiracy.</note>.

->*Know other things so that you may know yourself. Know yourself so that you may know God.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Lord Giovanni, son of the Most Serene King, Cardinal of Aragon.

**I** have written in the past three days three declamations, venerable Father—Platonic rather than Tullian <note>Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the standard for Latin eloquence. Ficino is signaling that his style is more philosophical (Platonic) than purely rhetorical (Ciceronian).</note>—by which I might deter my associates from vices and exhort them toward virtue as much as I could. The first describes a certain miserable shadow of a wicked life; the second reflects a happy image of an upright life; and the third, finally, expresses a divine model of goodness itself. I decided to send these three items to you as if they were mirrors, because I knew that all those who are most beautiful are greatly delighted by mirrors. 

Look at yourself for a moment in these, venerable father. In the first, you will immediately recognize what kind of person you once were; in the second, what kind of person you emerged as long ago; in the third, what kind you are now. And you will rejoice in your good qualities in no small measure. But so that you may rejoice happily in your goods, give thanks in all things to God, the giver of all good things. For why did God command "Know thyself," unless so that in knowing yourself, [you might know] whatever you...

->The Spirit breathes where it wills.<- <note>John 3:8</note>

### To Pope Sixtus IV, Marsilio Ficino of Florence and all his fellow philosophers together, proclaim a heavenly victory.

**W**e entreat you by Him who always hears all people, even those who do not speak, and very often listens to those who do not call out, that you might listen for a short while with a kindly mind to the voice of your sons, most kind father of all. For Almighty God, whom all things obey—and indeed, to obey Him willingly is nothing other than to reign—God Himself commands us to cry out in your presence and commands you to listen. Moreover, if you listen to us patiently, not only will you not repent of it, but also (as we hope) it will be helpful to have heard.

In the past year, most blessed father, on the very birthday of Christ the Almighty, certain relics of the Apostle Peter in the city of Volterra showed twelve immense miracles in a single month, manifest to all the people. Stirred by these new signs, four of us fellow philosophers <term>conphilosophi</term> <note>Literally "co-philosophers" or members of Ficino's Platonic Academy.</note> came together, being equally students of both prophecy and astrology. First, by an examination of prophetic mysteries, we agreed that it was portended by those miracles of Peter’s relics that Sixtus, the successor of Peter, would one day perform miracles most well-known to all peoples and nations. Then, turning ourselves to astrological matters, we diligently considered that past and future conjunction of Saturn and Mars in Virgo. Again, we studied the Sun’s upcoming entry into Aries, as well as the beginnings of the four quarters of the whole year. Furthermore, we looked at the future eclipses of the Moon in Aquarius and of the Sun in Leo, and again other eclipses of the following year; and finally, the discordant mixing of Mars with Jupiter, and many other things besides. From these, we concluded that the coming two-year period would be so miserable that it would be commonly thought that the final destruction of the world was imminent—namely, a shared and extreme calamity of the human race, pressing upon us through war, plague, and famine. We foresaw the death of many princes of every kind. Then, a new heresy would rise up under a false prophet. The mind shudders to relate what follows: that soon (may it be averted!) the Little Bark of Peter <note>original: "Petri nauiculam"; a traditional metaphor for the Catholic Church.</note> would be tossed upon the waves of the Tiber. Finally, that barbarians would lay waste to Italy. Since Mars was the leader there, and Saturn the author of plague, famine, betrayal, and heresy in all those celestial dispositions we have described, we agreed that all the remaining evils would arise from war itself. Here, then, wondering at one another, we said: Where, then, are those health-giving "Sixtine" miracles? Those miracles that were portended to us by the miracles of Peter, if—as we judge, and as the other astrologers of the whole world believe—such dire slaughter under his Pontificate shall everywhere vex private citizens, princes, and the Church?

At last, a long discussion led us by certain reason to this conclusion: namely, that the virtue of doctors and pilots is proven by diseases and storms. Therefore, divine providence permitted that during the care and governance of Sixtus, the stars and elements should for a time conspire together, both for the common destruction of the human race and especially against the Christian Ship, which is to be tossed by very cruel waves. This was so that Sixtus, like a Neptune rising in the middle of a storm with the trident of his own power, wisdom, and kindness, might temper the wrath of Aeolus <note>The ruler of the winds in Greek mythology.</note>—that is, the raging winds—and calm the swollen sea. Thus, with a virtue more than celestial, he might command the celestial movements and, by his wonderful kindness, tame fierce Mars and rigid Saturn. And indeed, not only the oracles of the Prophets but also certain celestial signs clearly demonstrate that Sixtus will do this shortly.

Here, therefore, all the Christian peoples will proclaim: "Who is this man? Who is he, that the elements so easily obey him, and the stars follow his command?" This is truly that legitimate Vicar of the most merciful Christ, who, having received the keys from Christ, closes the doors of Janus <note>original: "Iani Pluronis hostia." Janus was the Roman god of beginnings; his temple doors were closed to symbolize peace.</note> at the times appointed by Him, and opens the temple of Bounteous Peace to his children. For since he understands that it is no great victory to overcome the smallest things, and that nothing on earth is great since the whole earth itself is a mere speck, he has resolved, having now left the earth behind, to overcome the heavens—and not so much to conquer his own people by war, as to conquer war itself.

<meta>This page continues the prophetic address to Pope Sixtus IV by Marsilio Ficino and his fellow Platonists, which began on page 813. The previous page established that the philosophers had observed signs portending that Sixtus would perform "miracles" of peace and leadership.</meta>

<page-num>814</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

**SIXTUS**, the sublime Phoenix of Theology, possessing the high citadels of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom.</note> beyond all others, consults the divine oracle there in every matter; he does not rely on human counsel in administering divine affairs, but rather on the divine. Furthermore, from that height, he looks up to God Almighty, who performs all things through goodness and makes all benefits subject to Himself. Therefore, he himself likewise rejoices in a now-beneficent victory at the times appointed by God—he who well conquers all people while he binds the hearts of everyone to himself through kindness. Indeed, he understands that he to whom command over beasts is entrusted obtains an anxious servitude rather than a true empire. For the bodies of men—which alone are taken from us by violence—are truly nothing other than beasts; but surely souls, which are free by nature, cannot be conquered otherwise than by a certain liberal beneficence. The magnanimous Sixtus no longer rejoices in a restless ministry over beasts, but in a command over men themselves—that is, over souls. Our Sixtus, distinguished by his piety, in the manner of a father of pious parents, kisses his sons more gently after fatherly threats and rebukes; he cherishes them in a favorable bosom and embraces them in nurturing arms. And just as a short while ago a certain ill-will falsely seemed to follow his sons, so now, in truth, a great beneficence follows them. Hear now, everyone, hear the favorable voice of our shepherd. Look more closely at the joyful face of the shepherd, which clears all things in blessing—do you not see it? He opens his mouth, about to proclaim his fame to his sheep together with his Lord.

**PEACE BE UNTO YOU**, O sons, in this new spring. Do not be afraid; I am not a wolf, but a guardian; I am not a hireling, but a shepherd. A shepherd sent into the world by Him through whom the world was made, who was in the world and was sent into the world, not to lose His sheep, but to save them, and to lay down His life for His sheep. The Savior of the world sent me to you, so that I might preserve you for Him without whom nothing is preserved. Indeed, He willed that I should come to you, but not depart from Him; for to depart from Him through whom we exist is nothing other than to perish. In the name of Him who is always with us until the end of the age, I give my peace to you again, O sons, in this new spring—a peace sent to Sixtus by Him who moves and sustains the world, even though the world is unwilling. God is a clear light, in which there are no shadows. God is a shining love, in which there is no hatred. He who remains in clear light and shining love remains in God, and God in him. Therefore, sons, love one another just as I have loved you. My sons, let us love one another in Him, without whom no one ever has the quality of being loved. No part of the world can stand without harmony, since the world itself consists solely of harmony. No one in the world can please Him without harmony, for He made and preserves the world through harmony itself. Therefore, so that we may be truly blessed, let us truly love one another. But you, depart from my people, O cruel fates; depart from my people who obey God, who overcomes fate. Depart far away, cruel fates, you who will hereafter test your strengths elsewhere upon fools. Move suddenly from here, away from my sheepfold, you fierce weapons; turn yourselves now against the barbarian wolves <note>A reference to the Ottoman Turks, often called "Teucri" or "barbarians" by Renaissance writers.</note>. Hurry, I say, while the summer flourishes, before the wolves more fiercely invade both me and my sheep together. Against the Turks <term>Teucros</term>, the enemies of divine law, God Almighty Himself will fight for us. The heavens will do battle for us, and the winds, called together, will come to the trumpet blasts. A thousand shall fall at our side, and ten thousand at our right hand <note>A reference to Psalm 91:7.</note>. Briefly, there shall be one sheepfold under one shepherd. The Iron Age will soon be turned into a Golden Age. Indeed, once Mars is subdued—who was threatening the Christians with battles, plunder, fires, and slaughter—Saturn will also be subdued, who was plotting plague, famine, betrayals, and false heresies from that quarter.

**SIXTUS SPOKE**, and it was done; at that most kind voice of the shepherd, "Peace be unto you," all the sheep shall cry out: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. Sing to Sixtus a new song today, the Pontiff of our souls. Sixtus establishes the Church in peace. Sing, O poets, "Sixtus: the gates of war shall be closed." Sing, O Prophets, to the legitimate Vicar of the Messiah, "In his days there shall be an abundance of peace." Come all and see the works of the Lord, what wonders He has placed upon the earth. Taking away wars even to the ends of the earth, He shall crush the bow and break the weapons; He shall burn the shields with fire. Be still and see, for I am God; I shall be exalted among the nations, and I shall be exalted in the earth. The Lord of virtues is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.

**MOST MERCIFUL** God, who looks down upon the humble from on high, and grants high things to the humble; Almighty God, Savior of the world, who by the same power restores and preserves...

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine and his fellow philosophers together humbly commend themselves to Sixtus, the most holy Father in Christ.

**T**here has been among us until now, most Blessed Father, the Prelate Nicolini, a man full of grace and truth <note>original: "plenus gratie & ueritatis" — a direct reference to the description of Jesus in the Gospel of John 1:14.</note>, a man recently sent there from God, whose name is John <note>Giovanni Nicolini, Archbishop of Amalfi. Ficino is playfully comparing the Archbishop to John the Baptist.</note>. He came to Rome as a witness, to bear witness to us from that place regarding the name of Sixtus, and how our Sixtus embraces his daughter, Florence, with a gracious mind. For indeed, at his first arrival, he most mercifully embraced a man most dear to the Florentines. O legitimate successor of Peter the Apostle! O true fisher of men! (If it is permitted to say so), in this one casting of the nets he seems in some way to have surpassed Peter himself. For he did not catch merely one hundred and fifty-three fish <note>A reference to the miraculous catch of fish in John 21:11.</note>; rather, he caught almost as many as the Arno <note>The river flowing through Florence.</note> and the Pisan sea can claim. Sixtus, surely the legitimate Vicar of Christ, remembers that when his Lord Christ was about to choose disciples, he chose many of the first and most important from the number of fishermen, telling them that he would eventually make them fishers of men. He then gave them three principal baits and three nets with which they might fish successfully in this deep sea of the human race.

The first bait was unique piety and religion toward God. The second was sobriety of life and integrity of character. The third was both the good example of deeds and the true doctrine of words toward men. He also added three nets. The first net was burning charity, by which they might always love all others in God no differently than themselves. The second was supreme intelligence, through which they might as willingly forgive all people—as if they were children, should they ever be thought to have erred—as easily as they themselves hope their own errors are forgiven by our Father who is in heaven. The third net was a beneficence so abundant that he would do good not only to those doing good, but even to those doing evil. And those whom he considered to be less than good, or even enemies, he would overcome with a certain goodness and benevolence, imitating the Heavenly Father, who abundantly bestows the nourishing Sun and timely rains equally upon everyone, even the unjust, so that they might be seen as friends. Christ himself once commanded his disciples to entice everyone with this triple bait and to entangle them with these three nets; and we know that Sixtus—like Christ—has himself decreed the same, so that his Lord may one day meet him with joy and congratulation, saying: "I am coming, Sixtus. Come, I say, blessed son of my Father, enter into the joy of your Lord." 1 December 1478. Florence.

-> People rise from the mud every day to snatch our dinner from us. <note>original: "Surgunt è coeno quotidie, qui rapiant nobis coenam." Ficino is making a pun on "coeno" (mud/filth) and "coenam" (dinner/supper).</note> <-

### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Giovanni Nicolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings.

**I** write many things to you but few to the Pope; you, however, should conversely say few things about me but many things as a suppliant to the Pope. You cannot tell many stories of my good qualities. However, you perhaps ought to—and certainly can—pray with many words regarding my misfortune. O, how many things my soul urges me to speak about myself here! But a letter cannot contain them. Therefore, grasp them in your mind. I would be foolish if I tried to commend your own interests to you; it does not seem fair that the name of "Florentine" should hinder me among those people in times of adversity, if only that which never profited me in times of prosperity can now hinder me. Others, more fortunate—not to say happier—rejoice in our things. We are but a number, born to consume the fruits of the earth <note>A quote from Horace, Epistles 1.2.27: "Nos numerus sumus et fruges consumere nati."</note>; I said "fruits," provided that the fruits do not run out. Farewell. 

But before you go, it pleases me to speak briefly here to our Cardinal Riario <note>Raffaele Riario, the nephew of Pope Sixtus IV.</note>. You, my Lord, remember your servant now, if he seems worthy of any memory. For you have come into your kingdom; alas, how unwillingly I am now forced to ask, driven by the malice of the times, for things which I never otherwise thought should be sought by those practicing philosophy. Shall I say it? Perhaps it becomes the philosopher less, but it certainly befits the needy man. By Hercules, I shall be damned if I do not say it: People rise from the mud every day to snatch our dinner from us.

->*Nothing is more hidden than the human will.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Nicolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, Greetings.

**I** am sending a certain Prophecy to the Pope. The spirit blows where it wills <note>original: "Spiritus ubi uult spirat" — a reference to John 3:8</note>. I have been moved neither by any man’s desire nor by human agitation, but compelled by I know not what spirit, and by a love I recognize. If it were read with the same mind with which it was written, it would certainly offend no one. Indeed, divine truth joined with love ought to offend no one. Most philosophers claim that the truth of things is the most obscure matter of all. I, however, think that the human will is far more obscure. Indeed, the truth of things is sometimes tracked by its own footprints and can be discerned by certain judgments, since it depends on a determined cause and always remains the same. But the human will, because of its freedom, has no fixed cause and changes at any moment; it can be tracked neither by footprints nor by certain signs. This is especially true since, through pretense and concealment, it often displays signs contrary to itself. Therefore, before you publish this, consult both yourself and especially those who are most dear to the Pope. Let it finally be read to the Pope and others only if it is judged that it can be read with as much good favor from everyone as the good will with which it was composed by us. If not, keep it to yourself. For my part, where nothing can benefit me, I wish for nothing to harm me. God gave me a humble lot. Fortune once gave me a thin, and now a very thin, means of support. I obey God, I yield to Fortune, I agree with my means; I am content with a small lot, provided it is safe. Fortunate is he to whom a moderate fortune falls. Happy is he who is content with his own lot. I am certainly content with few things for this reason, even if I am often content with many people; for these "many" are contained within a few, and many must be restrained. Blessed are the poor in spirit; Blessed are the peacemakers <note>Ficino quotes the Beatitudes from Matthew 5 to emphasize his humble stance during the political tensions between Florence and the Papacy.</note>. The year passed so far has been portentous; a more portentous one looms. Daily you will say, daily you will hear: **"I had not thought it."**

### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Giovanni, Cardinal of Aragon, son of the most serene King Ferdinand.

**K**ing Alfonso, your most blessed grandfather, venerable father, recently poured forth an oracle from on high in an angelic tongue to your most blessed father, King Ferdinand. Marsilio Ficino, caught up by I know not what spirit, was present; he heard it and preserved it. That oracle, then pronounced by Alfonso in an angelic tongue, he has today translated into human language for you. He did this with the intention that first (if it please you) you may read it yourself, and then send it to your most serene father. Thus, what he previously perceived of Alfonso only with the eyes and ears of the mind, he may now, through our labor, receive also with the ears and eyes of the body. Let no one wonder that an oracle of this kind, though it is to appear in the exalted sight of a Royal Cardinal and the most serene King himself, nevertheless walks without any human ornaments. For that which is clothed in the splendor of the divine Sun—that is, of heavenly truth—I believe to be nothing else than to try to dress it in human clothes: to surround the pure light of the Sun itself with a certain thick darkness of clouds.

I would commend to you and your father our Archbishop of Amalfi, who is by far the most worthy of all commendation, did I not know that he is deservedly of such great authority among you that he himself is likely to commend both his Marsilio and many others to you often. **The day before the Calends of March, 1478. Florence.** <note>February 28, 1479, by modern calendars, as the Florentine year began in March.</note>

### The Oracle of King Alfonso to King Ferdinand, first pronounced among them in an angelic tongue, and then translated into human language by Marsilio Ficino.

**K**ing Alfonso, most blessed, congratulating his most blessed son King Ferdinand—formerly the preserver of peace, and now its author—prophesies true health, a certain and complete victory, and full joy in that very peace.
