### The descent of souls.

**W**hy are you so stunned? O son, why do you tremble? I fly here as easily and as graciously whenever I please, as easily and graciously as the rays of the stars and the Sun continually descend to you. Neither do the rays of the stars abandon their own heavenly bodies when they are sent down to you, nor do the higher minds <note>Ficino uses "higher minds" here to refer to celestial spirits or souls in the divine realm.</note> leave the heights when they breathe their influence upon you. Observe, I pray you, my sweetest son, how much the heavenly citizens rejoice in peace as if it were celestial nourishment. Truly, as soon as you began to think about reconciling peace (which for a long time now had been disturbed by a certain envious fate), I suddenly arrived here, enticed by this thought of yours as if by the sweetest bait for the beings above. Therefore, having driven far away all wonder and horror, stand by with attentive ears, and preserve what you hear from heaven as if it were an oracle stored deep within your mind.

### How pleasing peace is to the heavenly beings.

**I**n the beginning, most beloved son, you have perhaps heard nothing of my fate until now, nor have you ever fully understood your own. But today, as you have become not only a preserver of peace (as you were before) but even its greatest author, you are now judged worthy by the heavenly citizens to have the house of almighty Olympus <note>The Latin "Olympus" is used here by the Christian Platonist Ficino as a poetic name for the highest Heaven.</note> opened to you, where the most beautiful order of Providence itself and the harmonious series of fates flowing from it shall be revealed.

### The divine mind.

**C**ome now, Ferdinand, turn your mind back into itself, leaving the senses behind, through a certain circular observation of yourself. You will immediately see, when your mind is turned into itself and the body is cast down, that it is a certain incorporeal sphere, whose circumference—that is, intelligence and will—revolves through incorporeal things. Its center, however—that is, its life and substance—does not rest upon the axis of any physical body.

### God, Angels, Souls.

**C**ome again, and with that brighter circle of your mind, as if in a mirror, contemplate. In your contemplation, reach out to the spherical intellect and the intelligible sphere <note>A Neoplatonic term for the divine realm of Ideas.</note> that is everywhere in the world and everywhere outside the world, "whose center is indeed everywhere, as it infinitely penetrates the universe, but whose circumference is nowhere, as it infinitely towers above the universe" <note>original: "cuius centū quidem sit ubiq;... sed circumferentia nusquā" — Ficino is quoting a famous Hermetic definition of God.</note>. Contemplate that divine form, the fountain of all forms, the uniform form that contains all forms. This is the form that meets all minds everywhere, especially pure minds, as if they were mirrors. Here, that God of Gods flashes before you, besides whom there is no true God. Here overflows the eternal goodness of all good things, entirely devoid of evil. Here shines the immense light of lights and the Sun of all other minds. Toward Him, almost in the same way as stars revolve around the sun, the angels and the souls revolve from every side like the Moon toward the Sun.

### The immortality of souls.

**T**he human minds are certain everlasting rays of this eternal Sun, surrounded by the dark cloud of the body, yet reflecting themselves back toward their own Sun by thought and affection at their own will. Thus they truly leap back, just as they first leaped forth from their beginning. Therefore, since they are able at some time—once any middle obstacle is removed—to flow back into their Sun through both right contemplation and right love, they undoubtedly flowed out from there without any intermediary; that is, they are surely everlasting, being closest to eternity itself. They then reveal their immortality more clearly when they value mortal things as trifles, especially for the sake of eternal things. Furthermore, they grasp immortal things insofar as they are immortal, and they perceive immortality itself—that is, God—under the very reason of immortality through a certain certain reasoning.

### The Providence of God.

<insert>1</insert>
**G**od provides before all things for those who see Him seeing all things. Certainly, if God is (as He surely is) the cause of all, He is undoubtedly above all and is all things. If He is most simple—which His supreme power demonstrates—certainly there is nothing else in Him...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

to see than to be; therefore, because He is all things, He discerns all things within Himself most easily. If He is the best—which no one rightly doubts—then to see in Him is nothing other than to provide. For this reason, by seeing all things, He perfectly provides for the universe. He provides especially for those minds that see Him within individual things and worship Him above all else.

->*Fate and Free Will*<-

**B**ut to return at last to our own lot: that God of Gods, besides whom there is no true God, alone granted me a mind—a mind that turns itself toward God by its own free choice. My body, however, which is the shadow of that bright mind, was added by Capricorn (at God’s command), while Saturn, the lord of Capricorn, infused the spirit <term>spirit: in Ficino's philosophy, a subtle vapor that acts as a "knot" or bridge connecting the immaterial soul to the physical body</term> which is the bond between mind and body. The Genius <note>A personal guardian spirit or guiding divinity assigned to a person at birth.</note>, a companion of the "Thrones" <note>The third highest rank of angels, traditionally associated with the sphere of Saturn and divine justice.</note>, ruled and led me insofar as I obeyed God. I lived among mortals once, caught always between labor and glory. Ardent desire for rule brought about that labor (as usually happens), while a singular magnificence and incomparable greatness of soul brought about the glory. Finally, with a wonderful piety toward God and clemency toward men—like two wings—and with my Genius as my guide, I flew back to my heavenly fatherland. There, happily restored to the Father of myself and of all, I lead a blessed life somewhat similar to the Thrones, who especially adorn the sphere of Saturn.

->*The Celestial Paradise*<-

**H**ere, among innumerable spirits, it is granted to us to sit at the banquets of the gods, feeding on ambrosia and nectar. Here, although a specific star seems more familiar to each individual, the entire universe is nonetheless open and transparent to each of us by our will, much like looking through rays of light. Do you think, O blind men, that you see the sky itself and the stars from the earth through your thick air, any differently than if fish thought the same from beneath the vast depths of the sea? O how much this ridiculous opinion of yours deceives you! Surely the fish at the bottom see not the sky itself, but the water; they see not the pure lights of the heavenly bodies, but only certain faint images of them, already dimmed in the perpetually murky water. The same happens to you, O miserable ones, under your thick air, and yet you marvel greatly at the heavenly things that have been made earthly for you. Just as the light of day surpasses the darkness of night, and as the circumference exceeds the center point, so much clearer and larger are the ethereal things to us than they are to you. What shall I say to you of the multitude of innumerable stars unknown to you? What of the marvelous diversity and order of movements unknown to you? What of the inestimable sweetness of that harmony <note>The "Music of the Spheres," a Pythagorean and Platonic concept that the movement of celestial bodies creates a divine, harmonious sound.</note> produced by the various movements of the spheres and the consonant blending of all the globes?

->*The Super-celestial Paradise*<-

**B**ut why do I praise the celestial things to you at such length? They are almost as much shadows of the "super-celestial" things as earthly things are shadows of the celestial. O true light above the heavens, light so true that it cannot be truly expressed! O Truth shining wonderfully above the sky, so miraculously transparent that no one can ever sufficiently admire it according to its worth, since it wonderfully surpasses admiration itself. Here, O son, here, I say, one lives most truly, most clearly, most excellently, and most joyfully, where all life is nothing other than truth, clarity, goodness, and the fullest joy. Here, in that immense light of lights, we behold all the lights of the Ideas <term>Ideas: the eternal, divine archetypes or "blueprints" of all things in the mind of God, according to Platonic philosophy</term>, and in those lights, we most clearly contemplate every true thing. It is just as if someone were to look into the Sun and see all the rays flowing from it, and within those rays, see every individual color created there. Though I wish to show you things at this moment, my son, that are infinitely greater and more beautiful than the heavens, your human weakness of sight prevents me. Therefore, lest you be forced to go blind from too much splendor, I will not show you any further the more than marvelous light of the divine kingdom and the infinite Sun. Let it be enough to have indicated how blessed your Alfonso is, and how blessed you yourself will be, if only you are willing. Therefore, congratulate your father’s happiness now, my sweetest son; congratulate your father’s happiness greatly, rejoice in your own, and now joyfully listen to your own fate, which until now has been unheard of.

->*Fate and Liberty*<-

**T**he same Father who created my mind created yours and those of all others; for He alone procreates the mind, who alone recreates the mind, who is perceived by the mind alone, and who alone feeds and fills the mind. However, Aries—the head of the stars <note>Aries is the first sign of the zodiac, marking the vernal equinox and the "head" of the celestial year.</note>—once wove that body of yours for you, and Mars, the lord of Aries, ignited your burning spirit <term>spirit: in Ficinian philosophy, the 'spiritus' is a thin, vaporous substance that bridges the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</term>. A Genius <note>A personal guardian spirit or guiding divinity assigned to a person at birth.</note> was granted to you by God as the primary guardian of your life—a Genius from among the number of those who specifically accompany the angelic choir of the Virtues <note>The Virtues are the seventh rank of angels, believed to govern the movements of the celestial bodies and bestow grace and valor.</note>. You too live, my son, continually between labor and glory. Rigid Saturn himself threatens you with labor and crisis. Yet, that wise Mercury, the attendant of the Sun, promises you glory. From the former, a certain harshness can sometimes be a hindrance; from the latter, on the other hand, a wonderful prudence is beneficial.

->*The Nature of Saturn and Mars*<-

**T**wo among the planets especially and constantly plot dangers for men: namely, Mars and Saturn. Yet each of them, as experience teaches you, usually spares his own: Saturn spares the Saturnians, I say, and similarly Mars generally does not know how to harm the Martians. Certainly, when I was once a companion of Saturn, as often as I spared my own—that is, the Saturnians—so often did Saturn favor me. Conversely, he never favored me in anything else. Therefore, my Ferdinand, companion of burning Mars (if you desire to reign happily), spare your own. Who among all people are specifically yours is shown to you by that fiery quality of Aries, with whom Leo and Sagittarius also agree <note>These are the three "Fire Signs" of the zodiac, which were thought to share a common nature.</note>. Therefore, consider all sons of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius as your brothers. Furthermore, forgive, indulge, and yield (if it pleases you) to my people as well. Do you ask who mine specifically are? Those, clearly, who are ruled by either Capricorn or Aquarius, the seats of Saturn.

->*A Moral Admonition*<-

**B**y all means, be content within your borders. Believe me, Fate will give you far more and greater gifts of its own accord than when it is provoked. For as many as you pursue with violence, just as many will surely flee from you, and (heaven forbid) if they ever are able, perhaps they will put you to flight. But as many as you pursue with beneficence, just as many will follow you willingly and obey. You will conquer well as often as you conquer through kindness. You will dominate most securely for as long as you dominate over those who are willing. You will easily move all people (wherever it pleases you) if you yourself are never moved. In short, as you know, the highest prudence enters into a contest with deceitful Fortune either never, or certainly only when compelled. Where Mars rages most, there Fortune both rules the most and deceives most easily.

->*Divination*<-

**L**et it suffice for now that a most provident father has warned his dear son with paternal affection. Now it is pleasing to prophesy for a moment to my fortunate offspring. I see that you will quickly accomplish what I have advised. For I foresaw through your prudence that you would do so long before I predicted it. A distinguished victory awaits you in peace alone, full of safe triumphs; and in victory, tranquility; in tranquility, piety and the worship of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, representing the intellectual side of Ferdinand's Martian nature.</note>. Listen now, I pray, more attentively: listen, I say, with your whole mind, Ferdinand, to what follows. If you decorate your crown especially with three gems—that is, divine faith, hope, and charity—then surely at some time from the third heaven itself, where the angelic Principalities <note>The seventh rank of angels in the traditional hierarchy, often associated with the sphere of Venus.</note> adorn the gracious globe of Venus, the three Graces, breathing happily upon you, will put to flight the three Furies from your threshold and appease the three Fates. And when you have completed two cycles of Saturn <note>A cycle of Saturn is roughly 29.5 years; two cycles suggest Ferdinand's later life or a reign of about 60 years.</note>, then especially your sons, Ferdinand, will shine before you with the splendor of sublime power, both by the happy aspect of the Sun to Jupiter and by the conjunction of the Moon with Jupiter—or rather, by the greatest gift of Almighty God. But after you have fulfilled your father’s years, and moreover have added many circuits of Mars—deservedly known only to us, that is, the powers above—finally, on the same wings with which your father Alfonso here [flew], namely, both by piety toward God and clemency toward men... (ge- <note>The text breaks off; the catchword "genitus" or "genere" likely follows.</note>

### A Vow, an Oracle, a Miracle.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, Doctor and Knight,<-
->The most illustrious Orator of the Venetians, sends greetings.<-

**O** heavenly and divine friend, greetings forever. While chance brought some friends to me and my own choice gave others, heaven joined Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a prominent Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous scholar Pietro Bembo. He served as the Venetian ambassador to Florence.</note> with me from the beginning, and divine providence then wonderfully confirmed it. Heaven, I say, because we were born in the same year and on the same day under the same star. Furthermore, I assert that divine providence bound us together because in that year when you first came to Florence as an orator—almost four months before your arrival—when I was gravely ill, immediately after a certain vow was humbly made for my health to God and the Virgin Mary, you appeared to me in a dream. Though previously you were entirely unknown to me, you seemed to promise a swift and prosperous recovery. Having woken up, I was almost healthy and recovered shortly thereafter. Five months later, on the day I fully fulfilled my vow, and at that very hour, you visited our school <term>gymnasium: Ficino refers here to the Platonic Academy of Florence, his circle of students and fellow philosophers.</term> of your own accord with a large retinue. You greeted me in that very form I had previously seen by divine favor in my sleep; and many things were then said and done between us in exactly the same way I had seen while dreaming. In that same year, as if restored to life by religious vows, I composed a book on the Christian religion <note>original: "de Christiana religione". This refers to Ficino's major work, *De Christiana Religione* (1474), which sought to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>. Now, therefore, read happily, O heavenly and divine friend. Surely heaven itself bound him to us from the beginning, and then religion—loftier than heaven—bound him faster. Your Marsilio wrote this with his own hand. July 15, 1479.

### A true friend foresees what a friend will desire and anticipates the one who is about to ask.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Georgio Cyprio, distinguished Physician, sends greetings.<-

**I**f Love is a god, as both poets sing and theologians confess, then he is divine; if he is divine—or rather more than divine, since he is God—then he divines <note>Ficino is making a wordplay on "divinus" (divine) and "divinat" (prophesies/divines), suggesting that divine love grants a kind of psychic intuition.</note>. Therefore, a true friend foresees what a friend will desire and anticipates the one who is about to ask. Such a one indeed is our Georgio Cyprio toward us, born there where Venus herself is worshipped, the mother of twin loves. Indeed, unless I feared I might offend our more-than-intimate friendship with words, I would give great thanks for your promises. But truly, if one treats intimacy itself less intimately, he is no longer to be considered an intimate friend. We are then most grateful toward a very gracious friend when we receive as gratefully as he either gives or promises graciously.

### He who gives words instead of things gives leaves instead of fruits.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cocchi, most adorned in letters and character, sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou give me fruits, I send leaves; would that these were at least as beautiful as those are good. Read, together with our fellow philosopher Francesco Castiglionese, our letters concerning peace to the Pope and to the King, and recommend me to him. Fare happily.

**B**lessed are the heavenly ones, who never feel anything but good; those approach them most closely who, although placed in the worst region <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the material world or "sublunary realm" was considered the "worst region" due to its instability and distance from the divine Source.</note> and necessarily feeling evils from every side, nevertheless do not consent to evils anywhere, since they never disagree with the highest good. Those hold the third place who, after a fall, thus sometimes...

<meta>This page concludes a theological discussion on the nature of evil and the "Highest Good" (God), transitioning into a new letter addressed to Bastiano Foresio. ...they rise again to the highest good, so that they may recognize that it was an evil thing—specifically, to have yielded to evils. Let them recognize then that they yield to evils only when they themselves choose for greater goods to be displaced by lesser ones within themselves. Let them recognize that where the Good of all goods is found, there alone is the remedy for all evils discovered. Finally, those must be considered the lowest and most wretched who have closed their eyes to the rays of the highest good shining everywhere, so that they never see—within that very light, outside of which nothing good is seen—how great an evil it is to be always without Him, without whom whatever is felt is evil. Surely these people do not look up at the divine splendor to see how great the misery is outside of divine happiness, lest by looking up they become blessed; rather, they suspect and feel it in their own darkness through certain small rays of that light, like people hallucinating, so that by suspecting and feeling it here, they are miserable. The world (as Christ says), the teacher of life, is placed in the power of the evil one <note>original: "in maligno positus est." A reference to 1 John 5:19.</note>, chiefly for this very reason: because it is placed as smoke—nay, smoke in the world of the evil one. To the unhealthy and the restless, nothing seems healthy and nothing quiet. Why do we so often unjustly blame the "iron ages"? Since man first preferred iron to gold and became "iron-hearted" himself, the age which before had been golden by nature deservedly turned entirely to iron for him. What wonder is it if all evils follow us from every side, while we ourselves, having left the first Good, that is, God, follow individual evils as if they were goods—all of which are evil without the first Good. It is not without justice that we so often fall unwillingly into every evil, as often as we voluntarily fall away from Him who is the All-Good. Therefore, it is not permitted for us ever to complain about the ages; rather, it is permitted for the ages themselves to complain most vehemently about us. Let us therefore buy for ourselves, let us buy with all zeal that "ignited gold" <note>A reference to Revelation 3:18, "gold tried in the fire."</note> which the celestial eagle shows, that is, the pure light of truth, glowing with the very love of goodness. But we shall not easily buy the glow by the splendor, but rather the splendor by the glow. For gold itself does not glow when it is struck by the rays of fire from a distance, but it shines forth when it is occupied by the heat of the fire up close. Nor is it properly "ignited" because it shines with fire, but because it seethes with fire. In this way alone, if we ourselves are first set ablaze by the love of the Good (that is, of God alone), we shall suddenly shine with His splendor and become divine. God is light; God is love <term>Charitas</term>. To the one for whom God is dear above all things, God shines above all things. To the one for whom that Sun shines—through whom all things shine—all things easily shine back everywhere. Furthermore, all things become wonderfully sweet to him who tastes nothing anywhere except in that very Sweetness, without whose flavor nothing can be made or felt to be sweet. Why do I say these things? So that, as much as I am able, I might respond to the reader in these "Theological Letters" of yours. For you yourself recently stirred me to look up at these matters with your most splendid letters. Receive these, then, gladly; for they are yours, such as they are. I return them to you. The Calends of August, 1489. In the countryside of Careggi.

->*One is not harmoniously composed, who is not delighted by harmony.*<-
<note>original: "Non est harmonice compositus, qui harmonia non delectatur."</note>

## Marsilio Ficino to his dearest fellow countryman Bastiano Foresio, sends greetings.

**O**ur Aurelius Augustine writes in his books *On Music* that he who is not delighted by harmony is not harmoniously composed. Nor is that claim made without justice. Truly, since pleasure is usually produced by a certain similarity, it must be that he who is not delighted by musical concords is, in some way, devoid of concord himself. This man (if it is right to say so) I will say is not "composed" by God, who composes all things in number, weight, and measure <note>A common Renaissance reference to Wisdom 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>. I will say, moreover, that he is not a friend to God, who rejoices in consonance to such an extent that He seems to have created the world for this very reason: so that the individual members of the world would harmonize with each other and with the whole, and the whole itself would harmonize with the intelligence and goodness of its author as much as possible. Add to this that He himself arranged the spheres and tempered their movements with one another so that (as the Pythagoreans and Platonists believe) they produce an inestimable harmony and melody <term>Music of the Spheres</term>. We have discussed many things on this opinion elsewhere. One thing further it will be helpful to have mentioned, which I have indeed observed quite carefully: many talented people are found every day who are scarcely moved by nature toward these or those pleasures and pursuits of the other senses, but we have never found anyone endowed with talent who was not carried away by musical melodies. We also know that none of those who are *not* so carried away excel in sharpness of mind or judgment. The cause of this matter is chiefly twofold: one physical, the other mathematical. The physical cause is that the middle part of the brain, which...

...looks more closely at it, it seems to serve the judgment of the ear as a kind of instrument or incentive. When this harmony is perfect, it lacks no consonance <note>In this context, consonance refers to the pleasing combination of sounds or ideas that agree with one another.</note>, and is grasped by all the senses. But when it is composed in a truly harmonious way, the listener is wonderfully charmed by the harmony, as if by something similar and congenial to their own nature. 

Regarding mathematics—since Mercury <note>The Roman god Mercury, associated with the Greek Hermes, was viewed by Renaissance Neoplatonists as the patron of intellect, eloquence, and the inventor of the lyre.</note> is the giver of wit (as the poets learned from the astrologers) and the maker of the lyre—we see that those upon whom Mercury does not look kindly at their birth usually appear like the proverbial "donkey at the lyre" <note>original: "asinum quendam & ad lyram." On the other hand, those who are kindly regarded by Mercury, the master of both the lyre and literature, possess a natural affinity for both. 

Farewell happily, my dear Foresi; though blind Fortune may have looked upon you less, that most sharp-sighted Mercury has nonetheless regarded you with favor. Indeed, my Foresi, just after I wrote "Farewell" to you just now, I rose, hurried, and took up my lyre. I began a long song from the poetry of Orpheus <note>Orpheus was the legendary musician whose music could charm animals and gods; Ficino often performed "Orphic hymns" on a lyre to improve his health and spirit.</note>. You too, in turn, after reading this second "Farewell" (if you are wise, get up!), rise immediately and gladly take up the lyre, that sweet consolation for our labors. 

September 8, 1489. In the fields of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa outside Florence where Ficino lived and worked.</note>.

> ->An abusive person cannot hurt you in any other way than by making you<-
> ->abusive in return.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cocchi, sends greetings.

**Y**our enemy disparages you for no other reason than to make you appear publicly worthy of blame and to disturb your soul. If you allow yourself to be moved and break out into insults in return, he has achieved exactly what he sought against you with his whole mind. For he has already rendered you evil, abusive, and infamous. 

Our Plato, acting prudently, not only refused to speak ill of his abusive enemies, but did not even think of them, teaching us to imitate nature, which thrusts its opposite far away from itself. We shall do the same if we expel our enemies from our speech and our mind. Furthermore, if everyone else behaved toward our enemies with the same reasoning, those enemies would be utterly erased from human memory. 

But Christ (the master of life) instructed us much more divinely, commanding that we most willingly return a blessing for insults and good deeds for evil ones. For in this way, we ourselves remain unconquered and we subdue the enemy. We also thus imitate nature itself, which heals through opposites, tempers things with their opposites, and overcomes evil with good. Moreover, we follow God, who does good freely to all, even to His enemies—that is, the impious and the unjust—commanding His sun to rise and His rains to fall upon the wicked just as upon the good. 

Whenever I have strayed from this path, I have been filled with regret. But whenever I have followed it completely, then everything has turned out successfully for me. I believe you will follow these same precepts, and I congratulate you as if you were already following them.

> ->Since truth itself is unchanging and eternal happiness, only those live<-
> ->truly, stably, and blessedly who spend their lives in the study of truth.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to his friend Bastiano Salvino of Amitinum, sends greetings.

**I** received your letter, which argues in an unchanging way about the mutability of things—or rather, I should say it argues "mutably," which is to say, truly. For I believe that immutability itself is nothing other than truth. Indeed, truth itself is so unchanging that even the "truth of motion" is unchanging. For what else is the truth of motion? It is nothing but the very rational principle <note>original: "ratio." In this philosophical context, it refers to the essential definition or governing logic of a thing.</note> of that motion, which is grasped by its true definition. This principle is such that it can never be otherwise. 

Therefore, truth is always present; it does not pass from the past into the present, nor from the present into the future. Truth is so present that even the truth of the future and the past exists as a "present" reality. Indeed, by the same truth it is true in the present that this or that either is, or was, or will be; just as it was true from eternity that this or that would eventually be, and it will be true for eternity that this or that once was. Truth is so everlasting that even if it were said to have begun at some point, it would certainly have been true from eternity—and true only through that same truth—that truth itself would one day exist. And even if truth were imagined to end, it would then be true for eternity [that truth had ended]...

...and it will not be true that truth once existed except through truth itself. If truth is unmoving within motion, if it is present in the past and the future, if it is in the beginning without a beginning, and similarly in the end without an end, then surely it is nothing other than immobility itself and eternity. Therefore, the mind, being by nature capable of truth, is a participant in immobility and eternity. The will also, by nature greedy for truth, can be made the master of its own desire in an unmoving and eternal way. That life which is dedicated to the choice, study, and worship of truth alone lives most happily in an unmoving and eternal fashion. Certainly, whoever impiously and ungratefully departs from truth—the fountain of true blessedness—consequently falls miserably away from blessed eternity. But those who approach truth, the origin of true happiness, with all their strength, rise again blessed into a blessed eternity. Therefore, as you have begun, live happily in the study and worship of truth. For only those live truly and blessedly who live in the fountain of truth itself, which is true blessedness. Only those, moreover, can one day live in truth itself who always, as far as possible, live for the sake of truth.

->Where the Good of all goods flourishes, there alone is found the medicine for all evils.<-

### Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti to Leonardo of Colle, legitimate <term>Professor of Civil Law</term><note>The title "Iuris Civilis Professor" indicates Leonardo was a recognized expert in Roman law, likely teaching at a university like the Studio Fiorentino.</note>, Greetings.

**O**ur soul, as it is understood among the Platonists, occupies a certain middle region between eternal and temporal things. <note>Ficino frequently describes the human soul as the "center of nature" (*copula mundi*), capable of rising toward God or sinking toward matter.</note> And as a participant in both, it turns toward either one according to its own will. When it plunges itself into temporal things, it seems at first to feel a certain brief and false sweetness, but soon it is utterly overwhelmed by a long and true bitterness. But when it raises itself to eternal things, it experiences the opposite. For after a certain brief and false bitterness, it is drenched in true and lasting sweetness. This is because truth—which is the nourishment of eternal intelligence—is not temporal, but eternal. Most other human pursuits, for the most part, separate us from divine things or join us to mortal ones; religion, however, does the opposite: it loosens us from mortal things and "re-binds" <note>original: "religat." Ficino is playing on the etymology of the word "religion" (*religio*), which was thought by some to come from *religare*, meaning "to bind fast."</note> us to the divine, where, having driven far away the bitter tastes of the Styx <note>In Greek mythology, the Styx is the river of the underworld; here it represents the bitterness of earthly or hellish misery.</note>, it drenches us in nectar-like sweetness. If ever there was a time to indulge in religion, it is especially in this season, for as you see, this is an age of all evils. Only with God, where the Good of all goods flourishes, can the medicine for all evils be found. November 28, 1489. Florence.

->As the beauty of the body decreases, the beauty of the soul increases.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet and scholar in the Medici circle and a close associate of Ficino.</note>, his fellow philosopher, Greetings.

**I**f I say now, Poliziano, that I admire the sharpness and eloquence of your letters more than a little, someone might perhaps think me too full of wonder, since novelty usually produces such admiration in others, whereas I seem to admire even those things in Poliziano that have long been very well known to me. But in truth, I do not marvel at the old things in you now, but at the new. For my Poliziano has grown up so successfully in a very short time that, with his form changed, he now appears to me as someone else and entirely new. Therefore, he who pleased me more than a little—even a great deal—as a youth, pleases me the absolute most as an adult. Justly, as his form grew day by day, his grace grew as well. And that was made even more pleasing for this reason: because I often prophesied that it would be so. Proceed, therefore; I beg you, do as you have begun, and make yourself divine, so that you may simultaneously make me a true diviner. As for the fact that you extol "Marsilian" things everywhere with such great praise, I am not surprised; for who would not be passionate in singing their own praises? Who would not be set on fire? Who is so lacking in taste that his own things do not please him most of all? <note>Ficino is playfully suggesting that because he and Poliziano are so close or "of one mind," Poliziano praising Ficino is like Poliziano praising himself.</note> Francus reported to us what you have been doing on our behalf with all the learned men, especially with Hermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian humanist and diplomat known for his work on Aristotle.</note>, and what you ask me to do. I will certainly do it gladly—and I hope, beautifully. Certainly, I act beautifully and well whenever I do anything with my friend Bernardo Bembo <note>A Venetian statesman and father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he was a close friend of the Florentine humanists.</note>. Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino, another prominent member of the Platonic Academy.</note> and Cavalcanti overwhelm you in turn with countless greetings.

Naldo, our poet, asked me on your behalf for the *Rapture of Paul* <note>original: "Pauli raptum"; this refers to Ficino's work *De raptu Pauli*, a mystical interpretation of the Apostle Paul’s vision of the "third heaven."</note>. ->*An Orphic comparison of the Sun to God, and an explanation of the Ideas.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Cavalcanti to their fellow philosopher Lotterio Neroni, Greetings.<-

The entire sphere of the Sun (as the <term>Orphic</term><note>Referring to the mystical and philosophical tradition attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus, which Ficino believed predated and influenced Plato.</note> followers pass down) possesses a soul far more excellent than the other spheres. This soul exercises life and motion throughout the entire body of the sphere and diffuses them from there through all things. Through the globe of the planet itself, it exercises intellect especially, and sight. It exercises intellect through a certain <term>intelligible light</term><note>A concept in Neoplatonism where "light" is not just physical, but a form of divine knowledge or truth that the mind "sees."</note> in the very center of the Sun, ruling there as if in the head. It exercises sight through an invisible light in the whole circuit of the Sun, shining through as if through an eye. There, certainly, visible light arises from the intelligible light, and sight also arises from the intellect. For there, intellect is nothing other than that same intelligible light, and sight is nothing other than that same visible light. To be is no different for it than to shine; to shine is no different than to see; and to illuminate is no different than to create all things and to preserve what has been created. Just as easily as it shines inwardly by its own nature through being, so easily does it illuminate outwardly by shining; and just as easily by illuminating does it create and preserve all its things. 

But let us set aside for the present the Sun’s other duties and consider only its most intimate and visible Light—that is, sight itself. In that place, sight is as supreme as the "supreme visible thing." It is the sight through which all other sights see, and the visible thing through which all things are seen. Toward what, then, does that sight primarily direct itself to see something, if not into itself? In seeing itself, it looks upon all other things as far as they are able to be seen. But what does it see especially when it sees itself? Truly, it sees visible light, the fountain and origin of all visible things and colors. If the supreme sight and the supreme visible thing are there, surely there is supreme and perfect vision. And those things which we count as three in number by distinguishing them are in reality one and the same. For if such sight and the visible thing are one (as we have said), it follows that the vision—which is thought of as a kind of middle action between both—is the same as both. 

Furthermore, if that light sees itself perfectly, it certainly looks deep within to see both how much it can do in itself and how many things it can create from itself. To omit other things, which are innumerable, it certainly both creates and preserves all colors. For as it diffuses itself in various ways here and there through various subjects, it produces various colors everywhere. Therefore, it sees all colors in itself while it sees itself. But if that light is most simple and (so to speak) of a single color, in what way will it be so manifold and of all colors? Surely for this very reason: because it is the most simple in its genus, it is both the first and the most universal of all. If this is so, it deservedly embraces all the grades of its genus within itself. For only that form in any genus is entirely <term>all-forming</term><note>A Platonic concept where a single "Idea" or "Form" contains the potential for all the specific variations seen in the physical world.</note> which is all-forming in that same genus. And the multitude of forms, which brings about composition and diversity in subjects formed from elsewhere, signifies in the forming cause an eminent abundance and power, and a most unified (if I may say so) and strongest virtue.

But lest we wander too far, as many as there are species of colors in composite things, just as many <term>Ideas</term><note>In the Platonic sense, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal patterns or blueprints of all things existing in the divine mind.</note> of colors does that light behold in itself. For according as it sees itself first as a mere gra—

# OF MARSILIO FICINO

the most communicable grade is the Idea of the color black; at Grade II, the Idea becomes dusky <note>original: "fusci"; a dark, brownish-grey or tawny color.</note>; III, yellow; IV, blue-green; V, sky-blue and glaucous <note>original: "glauci"; a pale sea-green or grey-blue color.</note>; VI, a fuller red; VII, a brighter red; VIII, saffron; IX, white; X, clear or shining; XI, splendid; and finally Grade XII, splendor itself. Grades of this sort, which are many when found in various objects formed from elsewhere, are in their single formative cause one and the highest grade. This is no different than how innumerable numbers are a single unity in their own origin, and how innumerable lines are one and indivisible in a single individual center. Nevertheless, that Light, while it gazes upon its own highest grade, likewise perceives how that same highest grade can be diffused throughout the many subsequent grades, and how many species of colors can be procreated from it. The cause of colors is threefold: efficient, exemplar, and final <note>A classic Aristotelian and Scholastic division of causes: the "efficient" brings it into being, the "exemplar" is the model or pattern, and the "final" is the purpose or goal.</note>. It is the efficient cause insofar as it produces them out of itself and its own power; the exemplar cause insofar as it expresses them according to its own likeness; and the final cause insofar as it raises and leads them back to itself, and they themselves—by a certain natural instinct implanted in them—strive to reach its likeness as much as their own species allows. Colors are indeed divided in physical objects by quality, position, and time; but in their Cause, they are entirely united in these three ways. Furthermore, in objects they are confused and mixed together by contrariety; but in the Cause and the efficient power, they are distinct without any confusion, as much by the clarity of a sense discerning each one in turn as by the will of one choosing many. Finally, in objects they are imperfect because they are everywhere tainted; but in the Cause, they exist as entirely perfect, insofar as they are most pure and most full. Therefore, just as they are more divided among themselves in objects, so they are more truly themselves in the Cause, because there they suffer no deprivation of their essence or nature. 

You will perhaps ask: in what way are they distinguished in the Cause? I respond for the sake of example, still following that Orphic mystery <note>Referring to the "Orphic Theology," a body of mystical teachings Ficino believed originated with the mythical poet Orpheus and influenced Plato.</note>, that colors are considered in the Light itself in three ways. First, according to its disposition and will. Through absolute essence they are not divided at all, for there all colors are one pure light. They are distinguished from one another through vision and will, because the Light both sees and wills that the one light be diffused into many objects in many ways. Does that light therefore become a composite or a manifold because it sees that many things can be made from itself and wills them to be made? Not at all. Certainly, it does not see many things through many forms, but through one: namely, through the one Light which is the origin and exemplar of varying colors. Nor does it use multiple visions or choices to perceive and select many things; rather, it discerns many with a single vision and chooses them similarly with a single will. Therefore, they seem to be discerned only by reason—that is, by a far-reaching clarity that discerns many things and a will that deliberates upon many. I do not mean by the "reason" of our eyes, which look upon those things from the outside, but by the reason of its own eye, which contemplates and deliberates upon them within itself. For this reason, those respects by which the Ideas of colors are discerned from one another are not created by these colors or these eyes, but rather by the Light itself—which is as most piercing in sight as it is supremely clear—referring itself to the diverse species of colors. For there are as many "respects" as there are things thus perceived and chosen. Such a multitude in the one perceiving and choosing does not stand in the way of the simplicity of its own nature. 

But enough, now, enough, my dear Lotterio! We have fixed our gaze upon the celestial Sun according to our strength, like the eagle. Therefore, lest we be forced to go blindly into shadow, let us now turn our sharp sight back toward our own things—to our own, I say, which is to say toward our Idea and that supercelestial Sun <note>Ficino identifies the "Supercelestial Sun" with God or the Divine Intellect, the source of the physical sun’s power.</note>, which does not allow its burning lovers and contemplators to go wretchedly blind. For as much as it flashes in their eyes, so much does it confirm and strengthen their sight. Wherefore, if we do not wish to confess that Orphic mystery to be true, let us at least imagine it as true for a little while: that by looking up at the celestial Sun, we may look forward into it—as if in a mirror—to that supercelestial one, "who has set his tabernacle in the Sun" <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4 (18:5 in the Vulgate): "In sole posuit tabernaculum suum."</note>. 

December 19, 1479. Florence.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo, the Venetian Ambassador, Hearty Greetings.

**Y**ou ask, most refined Bembo, why that Neapolitan friend of ours <note>Likely a reference to a specific mutual friend or a scholar living in the country to avoid the war.</note> wishes to be a rustic for so long? It is because, evidently, one cannot be "Urban" <note>A pun on "Urbanus" (refined/city-dwelling) versus "rusticus" (country-dwelling/unrefined).</note> in these times. If he were even able, Bernardo, he would make known the immense grief which the condition of that city—once happy, now nearly miserable—presses upon him, or at least he would know...

<page-num>827</page-num>

if he were not cautious to keep silent, he would never flee far from the sight of that city which loves its own Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian statesman and father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note>. Truly, in such great misfortunes of the fatherland, he cannot help but grieve deeply. It is not granted to him to bring aid—I will even say it is not permitted—he does not wish to feign indifference, so he chooses to be absent. But perhaps you will say that such labor belongs to those Philosophers, and that such care disturbs those who are at peace; indeed (if given the choice), he would rather, along with Democritus, laugh at the insane Abderitans <note>The citizens of Abdera, whom the "laughing philosopher" Democritus viewed as foolish.</note> from some high mountain peak far from the city, than mourn the perishing Ephesians from a tower's watchpoint with Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was known as the "weeping philosopher" for his melancholy view of human folly.</note>. Yet he is the very one who imitates Jesus in this one thing at least, by a certain nature: Jesus weeping on the mountain over the wretched fate of the city of Jerusalem. He follows again now Pythagoras, now Plato, now Aristotle, who once fled far from the deformed face of Athens. Finally, so that he does not become a Socrates, he strives to be an Aristotle (if I may put it that way). You know, I believe, for what reason Aristotle, after the death of Socrates, left Athens and took himself to Chalcis. June 1, 1480.

---

->Happy is he who truly rejoices; he truly rejoices who rejoices in truth alone.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Joannes Franciscus Hippolitus, <term>Doctor of both Laws<note>A title indicating the recipient had mastered both Civil and Canon (Church) Law.</note></term>, Count of Gazoldo, a most illustrious man, sends greetings.<-

**F**rancesco Berlinghieri <note>A Florentine humanist and diplomat, author of a famous verse geography.</note>, our close companion, most distinguished in letters and character, delivered your letter to us. In it, you write that you have the first book of our letters and desire the rest. There are five remaining; I am sending the second, which is entirely devoted to the contemplation of Platonic mysteries <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic philosophical concepts he was reintroducing to Europe.</note>. The four that follow, just like the first one you have, consist of very short and varied letters. However, I will send those to you after I have received this second one back from you; I beg you to return it most diligently. For this was the only copy of this book in our possession. But you, by your letter full of great love toward me, have so suddenly bound me to you that I thought even my only copy should be entrusted to your faith and diligence. Furthermore, I wanted there to be a proof of my mutual love toward you: the second letter of this book, which I had long ago decided to address to friends under a certain common title (as I often do), I have recently inscribed to you. For I have now bestowed upon you alone a goodwill equal to the goodwill of all others. Read happily, and live happily; but so that you may live happily, rejoice truly; and so that you may rejoice truly, rejoice in truth alone.

---

->Public affairs cannot be governed rightly and happily without divine aid.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Berlinghieri, sends greetings.<-

**J**ust as most people are accustomed to congratulate friends who have attained magistracies and honors, so I am accustomed in this matter both to make vows to God and to hope for divine grace for my friends. Indeed, I have learned from Plato that those arts which concern private goods can sometimes be sufficiently governed by human prudence; however, in that faculty which cares for the public good, one must confess that the governor is God himself. To Him belongs the providence of all things, but especially of common and public affairs. Human prudence in such a faculty is not the governor, but rather the attendant and servant of divine governance. This is the point of that Platonic mystery in the *Protagoras*: that Prometheus—that is, human foresight—discovered all arts except for civil industry <note>Referring to the political art or the ability to live in a state.</note>. For this, he says, is supplied to us daily by Jove <note>Jupiter or God.</note> through Mercury—that is, from divine providence through angelic inspirations. This is also the point of that Platonic comparison: just as beasts cannot be led rightly and happily by a beast without a human, so too humans cannot be led by a human without God. What else does that prophetic saying mean: *The heart of the king is in the hand of God, and He turns it wherever He wills* <note>original: "cor regis in manu Dei"; a reference to Proverbs 21:1.</note>? And what of this Gospel and Apostolic word: *You would have no power unless it were given to you from above* <note>original: "Non haberes hanc potestatem nisi tibi data esset desuper"; Jesus' words to Pilate in John 19:11.</note>? Again, *there is no power but from God. Those that exist are ordained by God* <note>original: "non est ulla potestas à Deo. Quæ uerè sunt, à Deo ordinata sunt"; from Romans 13:1.</note>. For this reason, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher whose works were central to Ficino's synthesis of Platonism and Christianity.</note> set archangels over human leaders, as masters and guides. Hence David tempered the controls of his kingdom with the Psalms, as if with certain reins. For he knew that *unless the Lord keeps the city, he who guards it watches in vain* <note>original: "nisi Dominus custodierit ciuitatem, frustra uigilaturum, qui custodit eã"; from Psalm 127:1.</note>.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

## MARSILIO FICINO

Hence Solomon introduces divine wisdom crying out in this way: 
> By me kings reign, and the makers of laws decree what is just. By me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice. <note>original: "Per me reges regnant..." quoting Proverbs 8:15-16. Ficino uses this to argue that all legitimate authority derives from God.</note>

Hence the religion of the Romans also commanded that nothing public, whether in peace or war, be attempted without prayers and auspices. For this reason, Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus (236–183 BCE), the Roman general who defeated Hannibal. He was noted for his habit of praying at the Temple of Jupiter before business.</note> would not undertake public business until he had devoted himself to divine prayers. Orators and poets skillfully say that those who are in charge of public duties are like the pilots of ships; and as if they are always navigating among reefs, waves, and storms, they perpetually require the protection of the divine powers. Therefore, just as I am accustomed to feel toward other friends who have obtained magistracies, so I am moved now toward you, my dearest friend: indeed, first I make a vow to God for your prosperity, then I do not so much congratulate you as I wish—I wish, I say—for divine help, so that you may lead and complete this and all other magistracies piously, prudently, justly, mercifully, and finally, successfully. Indeed, I hope you will achieve this, for I know your character (by divine grace). Farewell.

->*He is not a common Father, who does not have a common care for his sons.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Bernardo Bembo, Jurist, Knight, and most distinguished Ambassador of the Venetians.<-

**I** have written nothing to you for a long time, my dear Bembo, because the malignancy of the times suggested nothing at all to me, whether listening or thinking, except evil. Moreover, although I have not forgotten how to write poorly, I have not yet learned how to write about "evils." But recently I heard this one thing, which I would approve of provided it is true: namely, that the Supreme Pastor <note>A reference to Pope Sixtus IV. This letter likely concerns the lifting of the interdict/excommunication against Venice during the Porphyry War or Ferrara War.</note> (relying on heavenly counsel) did not wish to segregate the Venetians from his flock. On the contrary, what could have been heard or thought more profane than that this Republic—which of all those on earth that are or have been, is now deemed divine by the very Vicar of God <note>The Pope.</note>—should be either attacked or deserted? Therefore, I will finally approve of everything when all others feel the same about the Venetians, and when the Pope himself feels about all others—that is, about all Christians—nearly what he feels about the Venetians. Namely, that he has considered and shown himself to be the father of all Christians, as judged by the divine oracle. For in truth, he is not a father who has no sons, nor does he truly have sons who does not treat his sons as sons. Indeed, I not only wish for this out of my charity toward all, but I even hope that the Pope himself, in his piety, will do it.

->*Only that favor does not grow old which arises from things that do not grow old.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Domenico Galletto.<-

**I** was just now thinking quite diligently to myself by what reasoning I might best entreat and implore you to help our essential fellow-philosopher Sebastiano Salvini <note>Sebastiano Salvini was Ficino's cousin and a frequent scribe and scholar in his circle.</note> in his legal case (if you are able in any way). At first, friendship presented itself to me, and when I had already decided to write thus: "I ask you by our friendship, my dear Galletto," and so on, Virtue itself suddenly interrupted me, saying: "Do not, Marsilio, entreat by friendship, which follows me—that is, Virtue—but by Virtue itself, which leads and sustains friendship." Therefore, Galletto, having changed my plan, I have decided to ask you, both in this matter and in all others, not so much through our love as through that Virtue which is the conciliator of our love. Truly, favor owes a great deal to virtue, since because of virtue, favor becomes immortal. You have heard, I believe, that proverb: "Nothing grows old faster than a favor," <note>original: "nihil citius senescit, quàm gratia." A common ancient sentiment, often attributed to Aristotle or Menander.</note> specifically that favor which arises from things that eventually grow old. But that which is born from ever-green Virtue never withers. 
What else does that poetic saying mean? "Eternal youth belongs only to Phoebus and Bacchus." <note>Phoebus (Apollo, god of light and order) and Bacchus (Dionysus, god of wine and joy). Ficino interprets them allegorically as the "light" of the mind and "joy" of the soul.</note> For favor itself is nothing other than splendor and joy. Among the poets, splendor received the name of Phoebus, while joy took the name of Bacchus. Virtue brings both splendor to the mind and joy to the will, ever living and ever green. Farewell happily, my Galletto, and just as you always shine by virtue alone, so always rejoice in virtue alone. Furthermore, whomever you encounter who rejoice in virtue alone, these...

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VI.</header>

Bid them greetings in the name of Marsilio, as if they were already known and dear to me. I do not wish for others to be sent; for I have no desire for the safety <note>original: "saluos." Ficino is punning on the Latin "salus," which means both "health/safety" and "salvation."</note> of those who do not wish to be safe themselves. And truly, whoever does not desire virtue—without which they cannot be safe—does not truly desire their own safety. Moreover, the beginning and the end of human virtue is to remember that human virtue does not exist without the grace and love of divine power. Farewell once again.

### Recommendation of a friend.

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ and his Lord, Raffaele Riario, Cardinal of San Giorgio. <-

**I**T has now become a firm opinion throughout Florence that Marsilio Ficino is dearly loved by Raffaele Riario <note>Raffaele Riario (1461–1521) was a powerful Italian cardinal and a major patron of the arts during the Renaissance.</note>. This opinion was born long ago from our personal intimacy, but it has been confirmed by my letters, which are circulated everywhere as witnesses of my reverence toward you. For this reason, many people ask me daily to recommend their causes to you. However, so as not to be a burden to you, I have undertaken the cause of only one man to be recommended during this entire time: namely, the priest Francesco Petrucci. You know, I am sure, the son of Cesare; I could not fail to recommend him to you, both because of the close bond I have with his family and because of his own virtues. Now, although you predicted at your departure that unless I came to join you there, you would never respond to me either by letter or by messenger, you did not, however, threaten that you would never respond at some point with your affection and assistance. Therefore, lest you become a perjurer—if indeed you bound yourself by that oath—do not respond with anything in letters or messengers; but so that you do not seem to have abandoned your natural character, you will respond eventually with a pious affection and with deeds. This is the way of great-hearted men, who abound as much in substance as others do in words. We recognize their affection in the effect rather than in the speech. Indeed, if I had been able to obey your commands in the past as much as I desired, you would certainly be writing nothing to this friend of yours as if he were present, just as you now write nothing while he is absent. So it seems to have been ordained by a certain fate (if I may put it that way), that I should receive no letters from you at all, and that you should give your Marsilio no words, but give him your services. Would that everyone gave services instead of words.

> My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. <note>original: "Auxilium meum à Domino..." quoting Psalm 121:2.</note>

-> Marsilio Ficino to Master Bernardo Bembo, Venetian jurist and most distinguished knight, sends greetings. <-

**A**FTER my long stay in the country, I was finally driven by heavy business from Badi <note>A rural area near Florence where Ficino often retreated.</note> back into the fever-stricken city. Here, on the first of July, cruel Mars <note>Mars, the planet associated with heat and fever, but also a play on the summer heat.</note> hurled twin flames at me and suddenly brought me into the peril of my life. Distinguished physicians arrived: Stefano of Milan, George of Cyprus, Antonio Benivieni <note>Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502) was a famous Florentine physician often called the "father of pathological anatomy."</note>, and several others, all of whom intended to try the arts of Apollo <note>Apollo was the Greek and Roman god of healing and medicine.</note> upon me with great diligence to see if there was any way I could endure it. But since I knew for certain that the extremely weak nature of my poor little body could neither bear two fevers—especially in the month of July—nor sustain the necessary aids of the doctors, I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence my help shall come. My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Therefore, by the breathing of divine mercy, a celestial breeze blew upon me, and just as both flames were increasing, they were utterly extinguished in a single moment, contrary to all medical reason. The doctors were stunned, my friends marveled, and the members of my own household cried out: "Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things." <note>original: "Cantate Domino canticum nouum..." quoting Psalm 98:1.</note> You remember, my dearest Bernardo, how long ago Almighty God gave me to you, when He forged our friendship in that miraculous way (which you know). Behold, the same God returns Marsilio to Bembo once again, while He restores him to life. We owe it entirely to God, therefore, that we live, that we live happily, that we love, and that we love happily. Live happily, love happily. July 23, 1480. Florence.

<meta>This page continues the sixth book of Marsilio Ficino’s collected letters. It concludes a philosophical letter to his close friend and disciple Giovanni Cavalcanti concerning the nature of true greatness and the role of the teacher, before transitioning to an urgent astrological warning addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

<page-num>83</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK VI.</header>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a discussion on how those with true wisdom rule over others.</note> ...rule over others. Furthermore, mortals are so insane that whenever they obtain some great thing, whether by chance or through some flaw, they suddenly believe they have become great themselves. It is just as if a madman, upon putting on a longer robe or entering a spacious house, were to boast that he had become taller or larger because of it. I, however, assert the opposite: surely those alone are great men who perform great deeds with an equally great virtue, and are not overcome by greatness, but either overcome it or equal it. 

Finally, those who have been raised to the highest peaks of affairs are accustomed to regard others as inferior and much smaller—indeed, as nothing at all. It is as if someone were so deluded that after climbing a very high tower, he thought he had become as tall and towering as the tower itself, and imagined that whatever he looked down upon from the tower was truly as tiny as it appeared to him from on high. But in my judgment, those who are truly the highest are the ones who, because of the very height of their soul, are established as if on the peak of Olympus, where the clouds of disturbances <note>original: "perturbationum nebulæ." In Stoic and Platonic philosophy, "perturbations" or "passions" were seen as storms that clouded the mind's clarity.</note> cannot reach them. They look down upon all others on the ground as the lowest of the low. Lastly, I judge that those see most sharply and judge all things most correctly who judge individual things not by how they appear from a distance to an observer on the outside, but by how they truly are within. I am also accustomed to prize those men as being of great soul and judgment who do not value things based on how they happen to appear from the outside, but rather on the value those things possess by their own virtue. 

I, (my sweetest John) <note>This refers to Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509), Ficino’s most beloved friend and student, to whom he addressed many of his philosophical works.</note>, against the wishes of the common crowd, give birth to such sons for myself as you hear; in this way also do I nourish my pupils. Indeed, by this reasoning, I separate them from the lamentable blindness and misery of the crowd. By this path especially, I carry my own people—removed far from the Lethean <note>Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; here Ficino uses it to mean the ignorance of the uneducated masses.</note> darkness and the Stygian storm—happily toward the heavenly light of Phoebus <note>The sun-god Apollo, representing reason and divine truth.</note>, to Elysian tranquility, and to the immortal food of Ambrosia and nectar-like sweetness. 

Nor have I ever demanded, nor will I demand, any other payment from my followers for such a happy gift than only two coins <note>original: "nummos." Ficino is speaking metaphorically here.</note>. The first is that they be as willing to receive gifts from me as I am to give them. The second is that they should give thanks not so much to me for Philosophy (which is the love of truth), but to Wisdom <term>Sophia</term><note>Sophia is the Greek word for wisdom; Ficino distinguishes between the human "love of wisdom" (philosophy) and "Wisdom" itself (the divine truth).</note> herself—that is, to the highest and divine truth, which I love. For she, I say—that truth—fills me with eternal light, just as the Sun fills the Moon. You, however, my sons and pupils, see those things which I show you everywhere most sharply only when you correctly discern them being shown by me as if by the Moon, through the rays of the Sun itself—that is, the rays of truth—even if they are reflected. Surely, sons so disposed will one day, in the full light of day, gaze upon the divine Sun itself, those things which you now see as if through the night in the Moon.

To what purpose is this? So that you may remember, my sweetest John, that I have for a long time gladly embraced you as a son; remember that from the beginning I have educated you as I am accustomed to educate my own. Nor shall I ever exact more coins from you for that education than those two I mentioned just before. Farewell. And live happily in the blessed arms of this, your mother Philosophy.
August 20, 1480. Florence.

-> The pious man shall rule the stars. <- <note>original: "Pius dominabitur astris." A famous Renaissance maxim suggesting that while the stars influence human fate, a virtuous and godly person can transcend astrological destiny.</note>

# Marsilio Ficino to the high-minded Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

Today and tomorrow, Lorenzo, watch yourself carefully; for Mars, running through your Capricorn ascendant <note>Lorenzo the Magnificent was born with Capricorn as his rising sign; Mars entering this sign was considered a volatile and aggressive influence.</note>, is seen today to look upon Saturn, and tomorrow upon the Sun, in a "square" aspect <note>original: "quadrato aspectu." In astrology, a square aspect (90 degrees) is considered a point of high tension and potential conflict between planets.</note>. Furthermore, Saturn itself, the Lord of your ascendant, has not yet entirely escaped the rays of the Sun. For this final reason, I too had to be cautious; I was coming to you in recent days to predict these same things, but it occurred to me in passing that it was better to delay until this hour, lest I weigh you down with longer fear and distress. For we are often accustomed, by our predictions, to anticipate evils that are far in the future, or sometimes to imagine things that will not happen at all. Since all those who must fear something at some time are considered miserable, surely those are less miserable who are troubled by a shorter duration of fear. I hope indeed—and my faith is not in vain—that the same King of stars and men, who has thus far miraculously saved you both from the threats of the stars and from the monstrous hands of men, will similarly save you in the future according to His mercy.
September 26, 1480.

->Great things befit great men.<-

**Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra.**

**I** write frequent letters (as happens daily) to many people, but listen, venerable father, to what has been happening to me for a long time in this matter, and indeed it is undoubtedly quite strange. My genius <note>original: "genius." In Ficino's Neoplatonic view, the "genius" was a personal guiding spirit or daimon that prompted thoughts and actions.</note> never urges me to copy out for my friend Soderini—a man certainly of very few equals—the things I write to the many. Yet, as often as I undertake some work for great princes and prelates, for Cardinals, for the Pope, or for kings, that same genius immediately commands and impels me to send the same gift to Soderini, as if it has long foretold and desired some great destiny for my Soderini. Perhaps it also warns me for this reason: that I should not think I will ever truly satisfy the "great" unless I have first satisfied this one man, who is truly worthy of great gifts, to the best of my ability. Read, therefore, this letter of ours which I am sending to Matthias, King of Hungary <note>original: "Mathiam Pannoniæ Regem." Matthias Corvinus (reigned 1458–1490), a famous patron of the arts and a frequent correspondent of Ficino.</note>; I wish it were truly "kingly." Take diligent care of your health, and preserve yourself for favorable times. November 30, 1480.

---

->Nothing encourages us toward the love of virtue more than the very appearance of virtue itself.<-

**Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, sends greetings.**

**W**hen I wished in recent days to exhort my close friends to a burning love of true virtue with words as brief as I could manage, I attempted to paint the image of a beautiful mind from a fitting likeness of a handsome body, using certain Platonic colors (as I often do). But while I was trying to express the image of a beautiful soul and body together, during the painting—owing to my lack of skill and my clumsiness in the art—the image itself did not emerge as I had hoped; instead, a shadow resulted. Indeed, it is so certain that every shadow is compelled to follow the very thing it is a shadow of, that if anyone were ignorant of this, he alone would seem not to be a real man, but the shadow of a man. Therefore, a shadow of this kind (to repeat the same point again), as soon as it arises among us, is compelled to leave Florence and follow the footsteps of Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519) was a Venetian diplomat and father of the famous Pietro Bembo; he served as the Venetian ambassador to Florence.</note> as he departs from here for Venice. If Bembo ever turns around and notices it following at his back, he will suddenly recognize himself in it, as much as can be discerned from a shadow. Furthermore, on account of a certain similarity, he will suddenly be reminded of Hermolaus Barbarus <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian humanist and scholar.</note>, and I believe he will not have forgotten our Girolamo Penci in the meantime. November 4, 1480. Florence.

->No ordinary recommendation; no ordinary training of a citizen.<-

**Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Gentile, Bishop of Arezzo.**

**W**hoever understands, venerable father, how ancient and yet how ever-green our friendship is, would think that Marsilio had long ago recommended to his friend Gentile more than a thousand various causes of his friends and relations; yet, until now, he has recommended none. It is as if he, by some instinct or spirit, foresaw that he would one day recommend the cause of Giovanni Maria, his uncle and the most beloved of all his relations, and that he was already setting aside for this uncle whatever weight might have been found in ten thousand recommendations. If, therefore, you grant this one favor to this one man, consider that you have certainly granted me ten thousand favors. And yet, I do not ask this of my Bishop—and a most just one at that—so that on account of our friendship (which began and remains in justice itself), he should ever do anything that might seem less than just to anyone. Far be it, venerable father, far be it from us to please man while in the meantime we displease God; for without His splendor or grace, we cannot please others, nor others please us, nor can we please ourselves, nor finally can we in any way please God. But enough of these things. It cannot be said how much I approve of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence.</note> having dedicated his firstborn son, Piero <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" de' Medici (1472–1503).</note>, to the discipline of Gentile, his former teacher. For I hope that by such an education, this boy will shortly emerge as an elder, even in his very childhood. Our Plato considers nothing more ancient <note>In this context, "ancient" carries the sense of "venerable" or "important."</note>, nothing more necessary than this for those who [rule] the helm of the republic <note>original: "gubernacula." The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "bernacula" on the previous page confirms the word is "gubernacula."</note>...
