<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

will happily receive <note>The text begins mid-sentence from the previous page, likely referring to those who receive domestic or political instructions.</note> their own. (And this is not without justification.) Indeed, if any art, even the smallest, must be learned by you from childhood itself and practiced according to your strength, then surely public governance, the mistress of all arts and the most difficult, must be learned from tender little nails <note>original: "ā teneris unguiculis." A Latin idiom meaning from earliest childhood.</note> as much as age allows. Thus, so that a very short time may suffice, according to one's strength, for a very long art and discipline, a faculty of this kind must be begun together with one's very breath—with life itself, so to speak. One must strive above all that those who are to be the head of others, as if of limbs, should surpass the rest in wisdom and prudence at least as much as the head itself surpasses the limbs subject to it in the abundance and sharpness of its senses—to say nothing for now of reason itself, which rules in the head alone. Let them also always remember that we never think with our feet or our hands, but with the head alone. Therefore, those who strive to be the head must necessarily—in order to be able to think and provide for themselves and all others—never be empty of prudent thoughts, but always be full of them. Otherwise, whoever thinks to set aside the weight of thoughts as if it were too difficult (while he himself is the head) is necessarily compelled to set aside his head at the same time. But why do I say these things? Why so many words concerning the faculty of governing and prudence to a man who not only understands these things more prudently than Marsilio, but also puts them into practice? Therefore, farewell.

## An uncommon recommendation.

->No one is to be loved more ardently than he who ardently loves the Muses.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, the Homeric Poet, sends greetings.

**O**ur Alamanno Donati <note>original: "Alamanus Donatus." A Florentine humanist and diplomat close to the Medici circle.</note> has for a long time now been sounding in our ears with that "well-rounded mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo." A phrase from Horace's *Ars Poetica* referring to eloquent, polished speech.</note> of yours, Poliziano—you know the man—more deeply in this manner: "I pray you, Marsilio, by your kindness, recommend me; I beseech you by that sacred love of yours for me, than which no plea is more holy, recommend your Alamanno as soon as possible to Poliziano." But when I diligently seek from him the reasons for such an ardent and persistent request, he simply repeats again: "Recommend me as soon as possible." He has yet to explain any cause for a recommendation so greatly desired. I, therefore, recommend to you the cause of one who brings forward no cause for his petition, likewise without a cause. But beware, Poliziano, lest you think this present recommendation is very light for the very reason that it seems to lack a cause. For on the contrary, I wish it to seem most weighty to you for that very reason; for among philosophers, that which is supreme in any genus of things is that which has no cause within that same genus, as if it depends on nothing else but itself. For this reason, let this present recommendation, for which no cause is brought to you besides itself, be judged by you as the greatest of all recommendations. If Alamanno himself (as those who are moved by any excitement are often won’t to do) merely shouts, and repeats the same shout more often now in our ears, and cannot clearly explain the reasons for his shout because his tongue falters under the most rapid emotion of his heart, I nonetheless, led by certain signs, believe that he is now entirely on fire, kindled by a certain mad love for some most beautiful Muse. And he vehemently desires, at least by the favor of Poliziano, the priest of the Muses <term>priest of the Muses: a common humanist title for a scholar or poet who "serves" the arts.</term>, to enter into friendship, so that with such a mediator, the lover may eventually more easily possess the beloved Muse. May he spend all his years in such studies with her, and may she "make him a parent with beautiful offspring" <note>A poetic allusion, likely to Virgil’s Aeneid (I.75), suggesting that Alamanno's studies should produce "children" in the form of literary works.</note>. Farewell; but before I seal this letter, I declare to this Alamanno, with you, Angelo, as my witness: if ever he should seem less dutiful or grateful for this great service of mine (which God forbid), he shall be thus reproached by me: "O too ungrateful man," I shall say, "did you not think I had done enough for you if I had reconciled you at least to a priest of the Muses? But when I reconciled you to my Poliziano, I seem to have recommended you not so much to a priest of the Muses as to the Muses themselves (which is much greater)."

## *A picture of a bad mind and one not good, likewise of an ignorant and a learned one.*

## Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger,

**I** have heard, Lorenzo, for a long time now, that men imbued with bad habits greatly displease you; I have also heard recently that for this reason especially you please good men, because the wicked displease you. In the former, I certainly approve of you; in the latter, however, I greatly congratulate you. For there is no shorter way to the good, no more convenient way, than to hate the evil. No more certain...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s moral and philosophical exhortations, likely addressed to the younger Lorenzo de’ Medici, following his earlier discussion on the necessity of wisdom in leadership. ...a more certain judgment of a healthy taste than to despise those flavors which are harmful to health. There is no life more fertile, nor glory more firm, than to be loved by good and prudent men. For those whom upright and prudent men love, even the wicked are eventually compelled to honor. However, so that evil men might be not only an object of hatred to you, but even of horror, I desire (if it pleases you) that you attend for a little while, so that I may point out to you with my finger <note>original: "digito demonstrare." A Latin idiom meaning to point something out clearly or vividly.</note> the most foul and miserable life of the shameful. Such, Lorenzo, is a soul infected by perverse habits: like a forest rough with thorns on all sides, terrifying with savage beasts, infested with poisonous snakes; or again, like a swelling sea, tossed by contrary winds or cruel storms and waves; furthermore, like a human body that is as entirely deformed on the outside as it is tortured on the inside by the great pains of its various members.

On the other hand, a mind adorned with the best habits is almost like a cultivated and fertile field, like a calm and peaceful sea, and like a human body that is as beautiful as it is strong. We have seen, friend, first a certain shadow of a bad mind, then the contrary image of a good mind. When we first perceive the former clearly, we cannot help but shudder violently; but we cannot help but wonderfully love and venerate the latter. For what else is it to turn out as a good man, than to both resolutely follow this image and, at the same time, utterly shrink back from that one?

But tell me, I pray, best Lorenzo: just as we considered the evil and the good soul a little while ago, do you wish next to look more clearly with me upon an ignorant mind, and then upon a learned one? Indeed, you desire it vehemently (as I judge), and likewise I desire to show it to you briefly. Such certainly is a mind ignorant of the truth: like the Moon when the Earth is positioned between itself and the Sun and it suffers an eclipse—that is, it is deprived of the Sun's splendor; or again, like the nightly, cloudy, and cold air; and finally, like a human body with blind eyes, deaf ears, and a mute tongue.

On the other hand, we think that a mind endowed with the knowledge of things and powerful in its abundance of words is no different than either the Moon full of the Sun's light, or the daytime air, serene, abundantly glowing, and moderately warm; or finally, a body with sharp senses and a ready tongue. Whoever sees the ignorant mind, once its most foul image or shadow is seen, will surely flee at once. But whoever does not ardently follow the learned mind when it appears—I see nothing anywhere for him to follow.

Proceed therefore, my Lorenzo, proceed I beg you; flee (as you have already begun for a long time), alas, flee far from that land and that miserable image of a wicked and ignorant mind. Come, pursue with all your strength (as you are doing) more and more every day the bright and blessed appearance of a good and wise soul. Thus, by as much as nature at the beginning and fortune thereafter enriched you, you may at least enrich yourself by your own industry. Lest by chance, when nature as well as fortune have supplied everything else to you according to your wish, you might one day seem to someone to have been so greatly lacking to yourself. And while everything around you—your fields, houses, furnishings, clothes, and finally the members of your body—each shine almost like stars, may you also seem to shine with the rays of your mind, character, and letters <note>meaning "literary studies" or "learning"</note>, appearing no differently among all these things than the Sun itself shining among the stars.

### A noteworthy recommendation of men of letters.
-> Marsilio Ficino to Jacopo Lanfredini, a lawful citizen, sends many greetings. <-

**I**f I were to write to my Jacopo in the common tongue <note>original: "uulgari... lingua," referring to the Italian vernacular.</note>, I would undoubtedly err twice. Indeed, I would be sending common things to a man and a friend who is anything but common. Therefore, I shall write in Latin, however I am able, provided that I am not a Barbarian <note>meaning someone who speaks or writes poor Latin</note>; for I prefer to be a Latinist rather than a Florentine. But what, then, should I chiefly write? If I were to commend my own affairs at present, perhaps I would seem too distrustful in friendship, and certainly less confident in my private business. But I prefer to trust my private business too much than to distrust a friend in any way.

Therefore, this letter will not offer a petition now, but a congratulation—not, however, to my Lanfredini, upon whose shoulders (however robust) the Senate recently placed a huge weight, but rather to the men of letters <note>original: "literatis," referring to scholars and the educated elite.</note>. For upon those same shoulders with which Atlas supports the heavens fitted with burning stars, our Jacopo will surely support men devoted to the contemplation of heavenly things. Truly, since he himself was first nourished by the Muses, and then dedicated his son Antonio to be nourished by the life-giving Muses from a tender age—and since they have happily nourished the son for the father—it is no wonder that, as one pleasing to the Muses, he will gladly recognize all their foster-children as brothers everywhere, and will preserve them with all zeal and labor.

### *Love should be answered with loyalty, not with words.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Lanfredini, greetings.<-

**I** received letters from your father Jacopo and from you at the same time, which were full of both elegance and love. Since I often hear Jesus crying out, "I and the father are one," <note>John 10:30.</note> I shall therefore respond to both father and son at once with just this one letter. All love, best of friends (as the proverb goes), demands loyalty. Therefore, I have decided to respond to your great love toward me with the greatest loyalty I can muster. If even a common, perfect loyalty requires witnesses, certainly this letter of mine will bring with it the greatest testimony of my loyalty toward you: that very volume composed by you concerning true faith. <note>Ficino plays on the double meaning of the Latin "fides," which means both "loyalty/trust" between friends and "faith" in a religious sense.</note>

### *He writes in vain who writes so that he is understood by no one.*
->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Bernardo Rucellai, greetings.<-

**W**hen I recently composed my book on *Caring for the Health of Scholars*, <note>This refers to the first book of Ficino’s famous work *De vita libri tres* (Three Books on Life).</note> and had discussed many new things concerning the humor of black bile <term>black bile: or "atra bilis," the substance thought in ancient medicine to cause "melancholy."</term> with all the subtlety I could, some of my close associates objected. They claimed I had discussed this humor at such length in vain for two reasons: first, because it seemed no one would be able to grasp these matters deeply; second, because that "blessed" tempering of the melancholic temperament—which I was sketching out rather than merely describing—could be found nowhere, just like the famous "Stoic Sage" of Zeno, or Plato’s "Republic," or Cicero’s "Orator." <note>Ficino refers to famous philosophical ideals that were considered perfect but perhaps impossible to find in reality.</note> And so, my dear Bernardo, I could not help but feel a heavy grief that this diligence—or rather, curiosity—of mine might be utterly useless. But yesterday our friend Pietro Guicciardini, son of the most illustrious citizen Jacopo, easily refuted those objections and freed me from the distress I had felt. Indeed, he read through our book in a single breath (as they say) and grasped every point so suddenly, and retains them so well in his memory, that he has shown these things can indeed be understood. Furthermore, he clearly demonstrated that the "blessed temperament" we hoped for already exists in him, a man who understands and remembers so clearly. And if this one most reliable witness is enough for me to show that I have not composed useless things, nevertheless, because a judge usually requires at least two witnesses in a case, I beg you also to read our book, my excellent Bernardo. If you do, I hope a second witness for my cause will soon be found. Farewell.

### *How unclean this world is, how false, and how deceptive.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni, his fellow philosopher, greetings.<-

**F**or a long time now, my own true and truthful genius <note>original: "genius." In the Platonic sense, a "genius" is a personal guiding spirit or daimon that inspires a person.</note> has been commanding Marsilio to write something to Lotterio Neroni—a most refined man and the truest friend of all—that is truly the most "true" thing among human affairs. But as I searched for something of that kind which could be proven as most true, and not finding it easily enough, that same genius showed me that among these lower things, nothing truer could ever be found (since they are in fact false) than this one thing: to believe that all these things, just as they are, are undoubtedly false. For in what way can anything "worldly" (if I may put it that way) be true in the world? Since the world itself is false, given that it is "unclean." <note>Ficino is making a pun on the Latin word "Mundus," which means "World" but also means "Clean." Therefore, the world is "unclean" (immundus).</note> Perhaps when God created this globe like a rounded apple—the kind we commonly call a "bad apple"—and saw it was too "unclean" (as if it had been drawn out of the most "unclean" chaos, as a poet might say), He immediately began to clean and purge it from the very surface of the world-apple. But the rinds <note>original: "putamina," meaning husks, shells, or waste-peels.</note> fell by their own weight into the very center to us miserable creatures. If, therefore, there are any "clean" things in the universe, they are granted only to the celestial beings. To us, however, as is fitting, there fell not clean things, but (so to speak) certain dregs and rinds. Hence that Christian saying: "Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has fallen to you, raging with anger." <note>Revelation 12:12.</note> Again: "Woe to the world because of scandals, for it is necessary that scandals come." <note>Matthew 18:7.</note> Hence also that Platonic saying: "It is necessary that there be evils contrary to the good; but since evils cannot exist among the gods above, they necessarily circle this lower region." <note>A paraphrase from Plato’s *Theaetetus* 176a.</note> No...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's letters, moving from specific advice for his friends to a broader philosophical and theological meditation on the nature of the material world and the human soul’s condition within it.</meta>

<page-num>837</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK <gloss>VI</gloss></header>

No other remedy is granted to us but to flee from here to there as quickly as possible, by a certain most pure likeness to the divine life. For, as it is written in Hesiod: "The earth is full of evils, and full too are the reaches of the sea." <note>Hesiod, *Works and Days*, 101. Ficino uses this classical quote to support the idea that the physical world is inherently troubled.</note> But the Platonists do not even consider the celestial bodies to be perfectly pure if they are compared to those things which are above the heavens. For those things which are above the heavens surpass the celestial things in purity far more than those celestial things surpass these objects placed below them. Therefore, even if it is not permitted to agree entirely with the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were followers of a dualistic religion that viewed the material world as inherently evil; while Ficino as a Christian priest cannot fully accept their heresy, he sympathizes with their dim view of earthly existence.</note> concerning the world, let it at least be permitted to cry out against it alongside them: O most foul world, which defiles and stains most deeply those who attempt to embrace it most greedily and tightly! O most false, deceitful, and ungrateful world, which—since it is entirely "settled in wickedness," as Jesus says <note>1 John 5:19; Ficino attributes the sentiment to Jesus directly.</note>—lies to them quite often, deceives them more, and harms them most of all who place their faith, hope, love, and service in it above all else. Like a certain eel, or rather a slippery snake, it glides through the palms of those grasping it too tightly faster than can be described, and flying into their faces, it bites them instantly and flees; and though absent, a little later it destroys the one who is also absent with its venomous bite. But lest certain bolder, or rather foolish, declaimers seem to be speaking, let us set aside these rhetorical flourishes for the present and bring forward with that brevity required of a Letter the specific reasons and the particular authorities upon which we rely in holding this opinion concerning the foul machinery of this lower world.

->*The soul sleeps, dreams, raves, and is sick within the body.*<-

**W**e experience within ourselves not only daily, but almost every hour, that as soon as a tiny bit of vapor—somewhat thicker and more humid—exhaling from the lower parts of the body seeks the head and fills the passages of the brain, we are immediately weighed down by sleep and soon deluded by dreams and images. We also sometimes experience that if a vapor of black bile <term>black bile: one of the four "humors" in ancient medicine, associated with the earth element and thought to cause "melancholy" or depression when out of balance.</term> (which the Greeks call <note>original: "melancholiam"</note> melancholy) occupies and captures the citadel of the body, our queen—reason herself—is immediately overthrown, so to speak, and men are seized by manifest insanity. If a tiny smoke has such power within us, if such a slight movement changes us so much, how much more must we think that the celestial and immortal soul is changed from its state (as the Platonists say) when it falls in an instant from that purity in which it was created? That is, when it is shut in the dark prison of a transitionary and earthly body? For then it is weighed down not by one usual smoke of some humor, but equally by all the new vapors of all the humors, and moreover by the unaccustomed mass of the limbs and humors themselves. Furthermore, it is submerged as if by a river in that formless matter, which is utterly different from the most beautiful form of the mind. For this reason, during all that time which the sublime soul spends in the lowest body, our mind is tossed here and there, up and down, like a sick person with a certain perpetual restlessness; it is always drowsy and always raving. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed in the transmigration of souls and the mathematical harmony of the universe.</note> and Platonists believe that every single motion, action, and passion of mortals is nothing other than the vertigo of the sick, the dreams of the sleeping, and the ravings of the insane; so that Euripides did not call this life "the dream of a shadow" without cause. <note>A famous tragic poet of Athens; the phrase "shadow of a dream" is often attributed to Pindar, but Ficino associates the sentiment here with Euripides.</note> Therefore, although all are deceived, those are usually less deceived who meanwhile sometimes suspect—as occasionally happens in sleep—and say to themselves: "Perhaps these things which now appear to us are not true; perhaps we are dreaming at this present moment." Whoever is so affected among the dreamers is surely to others as Homer says Tiresias <note>A blind prophet in Greek mythology; in the *Odyssey*, he is the only ghost in the underworld who retains his intellect.</note> is among those in the underworld: "He alone," he says, "is wise; the rest flit about like shadows"—indeed, they are flitting shadows. Here the divine David exclaims in an excess of mind: "Every man is a liar." <note>Psalm 116:11.</note> Hence the most wise Solomon, having woken up a little before the others and come to his senses, cries out: "Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity." <note>Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note> Hence Jeremiah warns the "wise" fools: "God saw that the thoughts of men, even the wise, are vain." <note>Cf. Psalm 94:11 and Jeremiah 10.</note> Hence Christ, the master of life, says: "My kingdom is not of this world." <note>John 18:36.</note> Though Christ himself was the eternal King of all things—inasmuch as all things were made through him and for him, and he was thus appointed heir of all things from eternity—nevertheless, whatever things flow without any stability under the most rapid turning of the heavens, and by a certain adverse mixture of contraries...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's discourse on the deceptive nature of the material world, moving from his own philosophical warnings to a detailed exposition of the Platonic Allegory of the Cave to illustrate the soul's entrapment in sensory illusion.</meta>

<page-num>838</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...they are confounded and utterly infected. Such things, I say, Christ denied were his own, as if such things are not truly real but only appear to exist falsely to us—namely, to those who are sick, sleeping, and delirious—since these temporal things are by no means the realities themselves, but rather mere shadows of things, namely, of eternal things. Whoever indeed accepts these images in place of the things themselves is, without a doubt, mocked by shadows and dreams, like one who is drunk, insane, or sleeping. These people, surely:

*They went wandering through the gloom under the lonely night through the shadows,*
*And through the empty houses of Dis <note>Dis: another name for Pluto, the god of the underworld.</note> and the void kingdoms.* <note>original: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras / Perque domos Ditis vacuas et inania regna." A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the journey into the underworld.</note>

Orpheus says that Pluto rules over the "people of dreams" in the underworld. Furthermore, the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras; in Neoplatonism, they often represented the tradition of mathematical and mystical philosophy.</note> especially call the entire region below the Moon "the underworld." Our Christ did not wish (as I believe) to be similarly called the king of dreams and delusions. Therefore, by the best right, rejecting the empty kingdoms of this world, he seems to sound in our ears thus: "O minds of mortals, all too mad; O blind hearts, where are you rushing? Why do you frantic minds shrink away from here so fearfully? Why do you rejoice so anxiously there? Alas, miserable ones, do you not see? An insane madness agitates you everywhere. On one side, false shadows of evils terrify you; on the other, vain shadows of goods snatch you away; and everywhere you are tossed between mockeries and bugbears. Nor does the vain desire for 'good' things trouble and weary your hearts, inflamed by furies, any less than the dread of false 'evils.' Indeed, the only medicine for so many and such great diseases is to believe the divine physician, or to wake up entirely and remain ever watchful—or at least to consider those who are sleeping to be precisely that: sleepers. Therefore, rise up at last from such deep sleep, you miserable ones; rise up, I say, fortunately from your unfortunate sleep. Breathe at last, my children; watch with me, my children; look back now and be wise with me, so that you too, according to your strength, may eventually enjoy the same most happy light and truth that I enjoy. Or at least, in the meantime, while you are waking up, say this to yourselves occasionally while sleeping: 'Perhaps these things we encounter are not true; perhaps we are dreaming.' For in this way, your dreams—even those that seem good—will deceive, inflame, and exhaust you less; and those that appear evil will certainly terrify you less."

->Real things are in the invisible world, but in the visible world are the shadows of things.<-

I think it would be worthwhile now to confirm the mysteries we have narrated above using the words of <term>Plato</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BCE) whose works Ficino translated into Latin, sparking the Renaissance Platonic revival.</note> himself, translated from the seventh book of the *Republic*. Imagine, he says, a certain cave beneath the earth, and in it men raised from childhood with their necks and hands bound behind their backs and their feet tied to certain columns, so that they can neither move anywhere nor see anything except what appears in their line of sight on the opposite side of the cave. But behind their backs, let a lamp be lit high up, and between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk about and speak to one another, carrying in their hands various images of trees and animals. Those who are thus bound will never truly see either themselves or any of those other things we have described, but only the shadows of themselves or of the other things which, because of the fire lit behind them, are reflected before their eyes onto the opposite part of the cave. For this reason, they will think themselves to be nothing other than their own shadows, and they will judge other things to be nothing but the shadows of those objects; they will even suppose that light itself is nothing other than that meager reflection appearing there. 

If, however, one of those who are bound should by chance be released and suddenly be forced to turn around and look at the lamp and the other things following beneath it, he will immediately grow dizzy and feel pain, and because of the brightness, he will be unable to look at the very things whose shadows he had seen shortly before. And this evil would happen to him much more if he were suddenly dragged upward from the cave toward the celestial and daylight. Therefore, he must be led not suddenly, but gradually by fitting steps, from the shadows of things to the things themselves, and likewise from the image of light to the light itself. Thus, he should first see those things which are in the cave as reflected in water, before he looks at them in themselves. Again, those things which are outside the cave among us, he should first look at by night in the water by the light of the Moon, then the earthly things themselves, and likewise the celestial things in heaven at night. Afterwards, however, by day, let him look at the Sun itself and the things seen under the Sun—first in the water, then in the things themselves, and finally look up at the Sun in the heaven. By this method especially, he will discern each thing purely and easily, and he will realize that he had been blind, deceived, and miserable when he was occupied with the meager shadows of things while bound in the cave. Therefore, whatever comparison there is of that cave to this world which we call visible, the same comparison exists between this world and that which we call invisible and divine.

<summary>Ficino explains the deceptive nature of the material world as a realm of shadows, concluding with a detailed paraphrase of Plato's Allegory of the Cave to illustrate the soul's journey from sensory illusion to divine truth.</summary>
<keywords>Allegory of the Cave, Plato's Republic, Neoplatonism, material world vs. divine world, shadows, spiritual awakening, Virgil, Orpheus, Pythagoras</keywords>

--- Page 858 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the Platonic Allegory of the Cave, specifically focusing on the soul's disorientation as it moves between the "invisible world" of truth and the "visible world" of bodily sensation and illusion.</meta>

# LETTERS, BOOK VI.

For here, the wretched souls, enclosed within the darkness and the blind prison of the dying body, truly see nothing else; neither do they see the true Sun, but rather the shadows of themselves and others, and a certain thin image of the true Sun. For true minds, true things of every kind, and the true Sun exist only in the invisible world; if we attempt to gaze upon these suddenly, without the appropriate stages of education and discipline, we are immediately blinded and pained. But when we are led through the proper stages of morals, doctrines, and time, we clearly discern and judge those blind and wretched ones who are deceived, occupied, and weighed down by the false shadows and images of this world.

Nevertheless, when the soul descends from the immense light of the invisible world into the dark body to rule and move it, overwhelmed by new darkness contrary to its nature, it is compelled to be half-blind, to hallucinate, and to stumble for a long time. Add to this that, because of a sudden and massive change for the worse <note>Ficino is referring to the "descent of the soul" into matter, a core Neoplatonic concept where the soul loses its clarity upon entering a physical body.</note>, it is forced to be sick for a long time, and is affected almost like those who are mocked and troubled by false images due to madness, sleep, or drunkenness. Or certainly, it is no different than if someone were suddenly cast down from the light of the Sun into that cave which we described. For they will be so overwhelmed by the new darkness that they will be able to discern those shadows only with great difficulty—or not at all—under the meager light of the cave. Furthermore, because of that dissolution and change for the worse, the soul will fall into various diseases of both the senses and the body.

Thus far, Plato. <note>original: "Hactenus. Plato." Ficino frequently marks the end of a summarized classical authority.</note>

Therefore, let mortals rejoice—let them rejoice rashly and excessively without envy—when on the stage they, though poor themselves, are clothed in the roles of the rich, or even while they are slaves, they nevertheless represent the majesty of kings. Let them also grieve in vain, but not without a certain pity; let them grieve too much when in a tragedy they are sometimes commanded to act out the gestures of the wailing and wretched—though they themselves are perhaps not wretched—and to wear the masks of the sick. 

But if we were to consider those people entirely vain and wretched who are so deceived that they exult or lament at stage plays as if they were true goods or evils, we would certainly judge all mortals to be much vainer and more wretched. Deep in a profound sleep, they accept shadowy likenesses of good and evil as true, especially since they truly suffer and are tortured for a very long time by these false and fleeting evils—which is quite miserable. And they suffer deservedly, since they are so foolish as to allow themselves to be deceived, believing that this anxious habitation of the celestial and immortal soul in the earthly region of death is true life—even though they clearly see it beginning with weeping and wailing, and followed perpetually by complaint and extreme misery. 

On the contrary, when the immortal soul, released from the mortal body, comes back to life, people think it undergoes death. They think this quite falsely, for only then—after the frequent death has finally died—does the true and eternal life rise again. For this reason, not without cause, among the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and for "going naked." Ficino views them as part of a lineage of ancient wisdom.</note> (the philosophers of the Indians) and also among the Getae (a people of Thrace), births were mourned and the newborn were wept for, while funerals were festive and celebrated with play and song as if they were sacred rites. 

This seems to be confirmed by the philosophers Hegesias and <term>Plotinus</term> <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note>, who believe that it is best for minds not to enter the dying body, or failing that, to exit immediately after they have entered. But more on these things elsewhere. Meanwhile, yet another error arises: people either foolishly believe that this anxious and laborious pilgrimage is their true homeland, or if they have learned they are pilgrims, they hope to find some rest during the journey. Yet they could and should be sufficiently warned by the very rapid turning of the heavens that they cannot rest for even a single moment under that swift celestial course, since the machine of the world itself naturally never has a moment of rest. Therefore, let wretched mortals recognize that they wander far from the truth, and let them cease. For in this way, they will undoubtedly cease to labor. Let them begin at last—or rather, as soon as possible—to live wisely, for only then will they truly begin to live...

->...and happily. Farewell. December 3,<-
->1480.<-

<meta>This page transitions from Ficino’s philosophical discourse on the soul’s descent into the body to a celebratory rhetorical piece. Having discussed the "cave" of the physical world, Ficino now presents a personification of Florence welcoming the soul of Dante Alighieri back from the "shadows" of exile and death, facilitated by the scholarship of Cristoforo Landino.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

->*Marsilio Ficino, the Florentine, imagines Florence congratulating Dante—through the pious work of Cristoforo Landino—now restored to life, returned to his homeland, and crowned.*<-

**F**lorence, for a long time mournful but at last joyful, congratulates her Dante Alighieri after nearly two centuries, now restored to life, returned to his homeland, and finally crowned. You once prophesied, my Dante, while settled in exile, that a time would come when <term>piety</term><note>Here, "piety" (*pietas*) refers to both religious devotion and the dutiful love of one's country and ancestors.</note> overcoming impiety would happily restore you to your fatherland, and would crown you with Apollo’s laurel in the exalted temple of John the Baptist. <note>Dante famously expressed this hope in the opening lines of Canto XXV of *Paradiso*, hoping to return to the "fair sheepfold" of Florence and receive the laurel crown at his baptismal font.</note> Your omen was not in vain, for your parents taught you well. Indeed, recently your father Apollo, taking pity both on my long weeping and your long exile, commanded Mercury to glide straight into the pious mind of the divine bard Cristoforo Landino. <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498) was a humanist scholar whose 1481 commentary on the *Divine Comedy* was seen by the Medici circle as Dante's intellectual "homecoming."</note> Clothed in Landino’s features, Mercury first woke you from your sleep with his life-giving wand, then brought you within the Florentine walls, carried by the rowing of his wings, and finally wreathed your temples with the laurel of Phoebus Apollo. Today, by divine will, the command of Phoebus, the labor of Mercury, and the pious work of Landino have at last been fulfilled: the prophecy of Dante, the vow of Florence. You have come at last, with Minerva showing the way, Mercury as the guide of the path, and a most brilliant troop of all the poets accompanying you. Finally, as you entered, the Graces received you happily; the <term>Muses</term><note>original: "Pierides," a common classical name for the Muses.</note> and the Nymphs gave you embraces and kisses. 

"You have come at last, and your expected piety has prevailed for your parent. The hard journey is conquered; it is granted to behold your face, my son, and to hear and answer your familiar voice. Indeed, I was lead to believe in my mind and thought it would be so, counting the hours, nor has my longing deceived me." <note>Ficino is quoting and adapting Virgil’s *Aeneid* (Book VI, 687–691), where Anchises greets his son Aeneas in the underworld. He likens Florence to a parent and Dante to the returning hero.</note> Oh, how much more beautiful and more blessed do I receive you now, sweet son, than when I lost you? That former mortal face of yours has been changed into one immortal and divine. The night of your Florence has been turned into day; all the sorrow of your Florentines has been turned into joy. Rejoice and exult, all you most happy citizens, for whom a twin Sun now rises wondrously in place of one—not with flames, however, but with doubled rays. Today, heaven itself (do you not see it?) most openly congratulates your happiness. Look up for a moment, O citizens, look up at the sky! Behold now, behold, while our Dante here is crowned, the house of almighty Olympus is opened wide. The flames of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term><note>The highest, fiery level of heaven in medieval and Renaissance cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>—seen by no others—flash clearly for us today, offering congratulations to the crowned Dante. Furthermore, who do you think this is, who fills our ears with such a new, such a sweet sound? Truly, the sound of the spheres and the nine Muses, heard in no other ages, today openly applauds the coronation of Dante. Listen again to the sweet songs of the Dominations from the globe of Phoebus; listen to the marvelous hymns of the Archangels singing from the globe of Mercury. Glory in the highest to supreme Apollo; glory always to the Muses; glory to the Graces; peace, joy, and happiness to the Florentines, who now rejoice in a twin Sun.

->**T H E   E N D .**<-

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine’s Letters,
### BOOK VII.

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò, most distinguished in letters and character, sends greetings.<-

### P R E F A C E:

The seventh book of our Letters has as its opening a Letter discussing the care of the health of scholars. From this letter, as if from the best and greatest of all, the book begins its journey. Where that letter leads, I myself most willingly follow. At present, it leads primarily to the one for whom the <term>Academy</term><note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, a circle of scholars and patrons led by Ficino under Medici sponsorship.</note> especially desires prosperous health. Greetings, then, my excellent Francesco; greetings as many times as not only this book, but all the books of my Letters bid my friends to be well. But receive this greeting in such a way that you realize you have received it not from Marsilio alone, but from the entire Academy, which is most fond of you. All things among us are held in common (after the <term>Pythagorean manner</term><note>Ficino frequently cites the Pythagorean maxim "friends hold all things in common" to describe the intellectual and spiritual bond of his circle.</note>). What I wish, everyone wishes; what each individual desires, I also greatly desire. Nor should this seem strange, for we are all one in Him who is truly the only One. We all stand in Him who alone remains by His own power; we all love one another in Him who alone is to be loved for His own sake. If there is anyone through whom all individual things are lovable, and for whose sake they must be loved, those who love each other in this One can, together with the Prophet, cry out: <note>original: "ô q bonum, ô q iucūdum habitare fratres in unū." A quote from Psalm 133:1.</note> "Oh, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity."

->Marsilio Ficino to the Reader, sends greetings.<-

I was just promising, reader, that the opening of this seventh book would be a Letter discussing the health of scholars. However, this letter subsequently grew so large for us that it no longer wished to be the head of such a small body, but desired to be an entire body of its own. Therefore, it has now withdrawn for a better purpose, having successfully matured into the <term>Book on Life</term>.<note>Ficino is referring to his famous medical-astrological treatise, *De Vita Libri Tres* (Three Books on Life), which began as a letter in this collection but expanded into a major independent work.</note>

<margin>Wisdom comes from God alone.</margin>
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends greetings.<-

Dear friend, please return like for like. Since I have barely written these words, you should barely read them. Yet, whatever kind of writings they are, read them anyway, however you may read. Indeed, during these days I have often taken up the pen with the intention of writing a few things to a man who thinks many things. But it suddenly occurred to me that I would be writing in vain to a man who would not read. In the end, I preferred to speak in vain rather than say nothing. It is heard. There are many types of fictions among the poets. But why do I now interrupt a pious man with these trifles of mine—one who is communing with God alone while commenting on <term>Augustine’s Soliloquies</term>?<note>St. Augustine’s *Soliloquia*, a dialogue between Augustine and Reason focusing on the knowledge of God and the soul.</note> I set aside poetic matters, therefore, and give only this warning for the present: remember that when we form speech, it is not so much the tongue (which is moved from elsewhere) that usually speaks, but the mind itself, which both moves the tongue and distinguishes sounds, and forms words at its own discretion according to its own model. What the tongue is to the mind, the religious mind is, in a sense, to God. Thus, it is not so much your mind speaking to God now, as God speaking to you through your mind. Therefore, my Giovanni, when you think you are speaking to God, you are in truth hearing God. Remember, then, that you frequently hear the Divine Majesty, and demonstrate to us through a life most wisely ordered—and confirm (as you have begun)—that you have listened to Divine Wisdom itself as a disciple. I wished here (as you see) at this third hour of the day to bring an end to the letter, so as not to disturb that divine Soliloquy of yours any longer; but as soon as I had put down the pen, it came back to mind that it is not fitting to spit out a completely fasting letter on a completely empty stomach.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Book VII, following the preface to Francesco Berlinghieri. It concludes a reflection on the nature of the Highest Good and transitions into personal letters to Bernardo Bembo and Giovanni Battista Boninsegni, maintaining the theme of spiritual health and Platonic friendship.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

But, so that my heart might bring forth a good word <note>original: "eructet cor meum uerbum bonum" — a reference to Psalm 45:1</note>—a good one indeed (as I believe)—I shall briefly confirm that higher opinion regarding the <term>Highest Good</term><note>The *Summum Bonum*, or the ultimate goal of human existence, which Ficino argues is found in God alone.</note>. All the sacred scriptures among the Jews and Christians proclaim that wisdom cannot be learned unless God is the teacher. Therefore, it must be sought from Him alone through faith, petitioned through hope, and knocked for through charity. When our Plato observed this, not trusting in his own studies, he often requested wisdom from God alone in his daily prayers to God. On this matter, Orpheus spoke most beautifully in myth, singing that wisdom was born from the head of supreme Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> alone. The Muses also have their beginning from Jove, for all things are full of Jove.

But you, if you were able to obtain this wisdom from everyone, perhaps you might—if not perfectly, then at least conveniently—attain it from that close friend of yours. Yet by what means will you obtain wisdom from one whose mind is always unhealthy because his body is never healthy? Recently, when he was suffering no small amount from weakness, first of the soul, then of the stomach, and finally of all his limbs, he changed his climate <note>literally "changed his sky"</note> but did not change his soul. Since he seeks strength from the air—the weakest of the elements and of all things—he has deservedly sought it in vain until now. You, meanwhile, cry out together with your <term>Aurelius</term><note>Saint Augustine (Aurelius Augustinus). The following quote is from his *Confessions* (4.16).</note>: "O Almighty God, when our strength is You Yourself, then alone is it truly strength; but when it is our own, it is weakness." I, too, shall finally achieve the same.

---

->*Where wisdom is greater, speech is shorter.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Lord Bernardo Bembo, the Venetian, sends greetings.<-

**T**hose who have been silent for a long time are accustomed, when they finally break their long-lasting silence, to burst forth more abundantly, and (as it were) like those who have been in labor for a long time, to eventually give birth to a weightier offspring of thought. Your Marsilio, however, does the opposite; for he does not conceive longer works after a long time of silence. Inasmuch as the longer he thinks to himself in silence, the more sharply he discerns that it is better for us to be silent than to speak. And there are very few things which we either know how to express worthily, or ought to express honestly, or are able to express safely. Therefore, I will respond to your letters only very briefly for the present. First, I rejoice in your prosperity—or rather, ours—and I wish you happiness. Next, I give great thanks for the little jar of <term>Theriac</term><note>A famous ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote and restorative.</note> you sent; I shall certainly give enormous thanks when you send a large vessel instead of a little jar. Although, I confess that even in this small, health-giving jar, I have received no less from Apollo himself than from you. Finally, regarding your request for <term>Alcinous</term><note>Likely referring to a specific manuscript or a person nicknamed after the Platonic philosopher Alcinous; here noted as staying with Giovanni Cavalcanti.</note>, know that he is staying in the country with our friend Cavalcanti at this time. As soon as he returns to us, he will return to you (as is right).

---

->*Though one may at times be absent in letters, one is never allowed to be absent in spirit from friends.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino and Giorgio Antonio Vespucci to Giovanni<-
->Battista Boninsegni, sends greetings.<-

**P**lato, the divine mediator of our friendship—or rather, of our kinship—has for a long time commanded that we never wish to be absent from our friend Boninsegni, with whom he has always wished us to be. Therefore, so that we might satisfy both Plato and our kinship to the best of our ability, we have already prepared ourselves many times to write. But as often as we took up the pen, that mediator of ours restrained us, openly advising that we should not interrupt Boninsegni with our letters while he is speaking diligently with Plato. What then shall we do, while our Plato both commands and forbids at the same time? Certainly, so that we may fulfill whatever he orders, we shall always speak to your soul with our soul; and simultaneously, to avoid whatever he forbids, we shall remain silent with mouth and pen. But let it be permitted to interrupt just a little now, since Plato has granted it this once, while we approach you from Athens while you are staying in the country in his own <term>Academy</term>, and we greet you in the name of all Platonists. Furthermore, we commend ourselves to your father Roberto, the distinguished presiding official there.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VIII</header>

### He who loves a shadow is transformed into a shadow.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Bernardo Bembo the Venetian, greetings.<-

**I** have a certain friend who is like a second self <note>original: "alter ego"</note> to me, a man of such a strange disposition that while he desires nothing in human affairs other than friends, he meanwhile takes no care at all to be a friend to his own self. Indeed—and this is as marvelous as it is miserable—he is like a Pamphilus <note>A character from Roman comedy known for being a "friend to all."</note> to others but a Timon <note>The famous Athenian misanthrope who hated mankind.</note> to himself; out of his love for others, he always hates himself. And like another Menedemus <note>The title character of Terence’s play "The Self-Tormentor."</note>, he seems born for the sole purpose of assiduously racking himself with pain. Toward others he is truly sweeter than Venus herself, but against himself he is fiercer than Mars and more rigid than Saturn. I have often rebuked him in this way, though so far in vain: "Whom do you flee, miserable Narcissus? You flee your own self, oh madman, so that you may follow another who flees from you even faster—one whom you will never be able to catch, once you have lost yourself. Alas, whom are you destroying, mad Narcissus? You are utterly destroying yourself so that you may pursue a shadow—certainly a fleeting shadow which you, in your misery, cannot embrace. But since love is accustomed to transform the lover into the beloved, by loving a shadow, Narcissus, you will shortly be turned into a shadow yourself." I often say this to him; you also, my Bernardo, should admonish him similarly, whether by word or by letter.

---

### On the best kind of living.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Antonio Ivani of Sarzana, greetings.<-

**Y**our letter was delivered to me, dearest Ivani, in which you gather many thoughts in few words concerning the best kind of living. Truly, I think you judge that to be the best kind of life which is removed as far as possible from this "dead life"—that state in which the mortal part lives, and the immortal part in a certain sense dies. This happens for as long as the celestial soul is not only joined to the earthly body by nature at the beginning, but is also enslaved to it daily by its affections. The result is that the only person who truly lives is the one who, at least in his affections, lives furthest removed from this false life. Just how false and deceptive this life is, this Platonic letter will discuss with you; I wrote it to Lotterio Neroni in recent months, and have now gladly transcribed it for you as well. Farewell.

---

### An excuse for when a friend is not greeted.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, greetings.<-

**I** wanted to spend this autumn in the countryside <note>original: "rusticari"</note>, Giovanni; I know well with what affection I desired it, but I do not quite know by what reasoning. I was afraid, however, that for the first time, you might not wish for what I wished. Therefore, departing for the country, behaving already like a countryman, I did not say, "Farewell, friend." I feared that you, by some less-than-good omen, might perhaps reply, "May you not fare well." For you know how superstitious <note>original: "auguriosus," referring to one who looks for omens or auguries.</note> I am at times (as the common saying goes). I could hardly have hoped that I might ever be well if the Hero <note>Likely referring to Lorenzo de' Medici, whom Ficino’s circle often addressed with semi-divine titles.</note> once forbade me from being well. Fare you well. And permit me to stay in the country for several more days for the sake of firmer health.

---

### Agriculture and the study of letters are happily joined together.

->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, the Magnanimous, greetings.<-

**W**hen at sunrise today I sought the highest peaks of the ancient mountain—the mountain, I say, called "Old Mountain" <note>Monte Vecchio, where Ficino had a villa.</note>, which Cosimo himself entrusted to his Marsilio to be cherished—and while I was wandering here and there in this wood, gazing upon the palaces of Careggi <note>The primary country villa of the Medici family.</note>, it suddenly came to mind that the feast day of Cosmas and Damian <note>The patron saints of the Medici family (as "Medici" means "doctors").</note> had already dawned, which used to be celebrated with great spirit by Cosimo himself and by his sons and grandsons. Here, indeed, I could not help but grieve when I saw no citizens from any direction flocking to the "Cosmic" solemnities (as is usually done). Suddenly that Jovian <note>Jupiter-like</note> Cosimo—to whom Jupiter, now that Juno is reconciled, has given a civil empire without end—breathing favorably upon us from a high oak tree, consoled our mourning with oracles of this sort. He said, "Marsilio, today the pious Lorenzo indeed restores my sacred rites in the city, but you..."

<page-num>343</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK VII</header>

...to be loved more ardently, is signified. Therefore, you, now like a <term>dialectician</term> <note>A practitioner of dialectic, the art of logical discussion and investigation of truth through reason.</note>, will clearly conclude that if honor and love produce faith, which of the two of you I would rather keep faith with. Add also another argument on top of this. In what way is it likely that I, a follower of Platonic Philosophy, ever thought to violate my faith toward you—to whose faith I was meanwhile committing all my affairs (as even you will not deny) and was clearly planning to commit them in the future? Since these things are so, what then was the reason that in the chapel of Novoli <note>The church of Santa Maria a Novoli, where Ficino held a benefice as a priest.</note> now one and then another minister of sacred rites could be under me, rather than my dear Albert? 

At first, I thought that some earthly <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a 'daemon' is a spirit or intermediary power, not necessarily an evil 'demon' in the modern sense.</note>, envying the heavenly friendship between us at that time, had disturbed that service established between us. For which reason, fleeing to the deities of the learned—namely Minerva and Apollo—I prayed that she with her spear and he with his arrows might pierce that Pythian spirit. But then, that guardian <term>genius</term> <note>A personal tutelary spirit or divine spark that guides an individual.</note> common to both me and you corrected me as I wandered in error. "No spirit," it said, "Marsilio, has attempted to separate you from Albert. Rather, you yourselves, who are by nature one work of the heavens, were being in some way cut apart by a certain grafted condition. Know that Saturn, the lord of Aquarius, infused almost a single spirit into both of you, since both were born with Aquarius ascending; from this, he gave you a heavenly friendship without end. For indeed, those things which Saturn, the highest and most stable of all planets, builds, no one (as the Astronomers say) either dares to destroy or can. But you yourselves must now acknowledge and recognize your error. For if friendship is a kind of equality, what can be more opposed to it than inequality? Therefore, when the heavens willed you to be friends, they also decreed that you would always be equals among yourselves. 

But you, as if ignorant of this heavenly mystery, were establishing a certain service and commerce between you, in which one of you would seem to be under the other in the future, as if you were unequals. But let disparity be far from heavenly friendship (as heaven commands); let domination and servitude be far away. Let friends truly be equal among themselves; let them always be both free and equal, and let them love one another freely." Thus spoke the genius. As for you, my most beloved Albert, fare you well happily. And remember that the "service" <note>The original Latin 'ministerium' implies a formal service or subservient role.</note> which did not please the powers above was rightly not permitted to us. And, in turn, that the mystery which pleases them ought to please us entirely as well. 

October 20, 1481. From the fields of Careggi.

->On the three Graces and the Genius.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, Greetings.<-

**W**henever in these times I take up my pen, Magnanimous Lorenzo <note>This refers to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici (1463–1503), the cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent and a major patron of the arts.</note>—which indeed I do daily to write to you—I seem to myself to have suddenly become quite fertile, and I am in labor with many things. But truly, as soon as I have written only these two words, "**Marsilio to Lorenzo**," I, who just now was about to give birth to many things as if most fertile, soon bring forth nothing, as if I had now become completely sterile. For this reason, I am often stunned beyond measure and I blame the powers above. For I see that what was abundantly supplied to us by both nature and art a little while before we were about to write to you, the same thing, a little while later when we are actually writing, cannot be inhibited by anything other than the powers above. 

Wherefore, as I said, I frequently blame them: sometimes as if they were envious, because perhaps they envy a heavenly friendship and pleasure on earth; and sometimes as if they were stingy, because where both nature and art are so prodigal, the divinity seems in some way (if it is right to say) parsimonious. Finally, Minerva, the leader of Philosophers, spoke today so that I might no longer be sterile toward you, nor sin so gravely against the deities: "Do not," she said, "impiously accuse the heavenly ones, who meanwhile, in turn, accuse and condemn you for your unjust rashness. You are ignorant, O impious one, you are ignorant! Nothing is ever either commanded or prohibited by the powers above without the highest reason. Therefore, learn (as I teach you in a few words) by what reasoning they now often forbid you from writing to the Medici with these words (namely, **Marsilio to Lorenzo**)."

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

### The Three Graces and the Three Planets

**I**n the beginning, those whom our poets depict as the three Graces—three young girls, as it were, embracing one another—are actually three primary planets in the heavens: Mercury influenced by Jupiter <note>original: "Mercurius Iouius." This refers to Mercury when it is positioned favorably in relation to Jupiter, combining quick intellect with a sense of justice and growth.</note>, Phoebus <note>A common name for Apollo, representing the Sun.</note>, and Venus, who are mutual and favorable companions to one another in their celestial circuit. Likewise, those three names of the Graces—namely, Greenness, Light, and Joy—correspond most aptly to these same stars. These stars, through their influence among the celestial bodies, are particularly favorable to human talent <term>talent</term> <note>original: "ingenium." In the Renaissance, this referred to a person's innate intellectual power and creative character.</note>. For this reason, they are called the Graces not of just any animals, but of humans alone; nor are they truly the handmaidens of Venus, but rather of Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic war.</note>. If you ever hear that Jupiter is the first of the Graces, you should not understand him simply as Jupiter, but as Mercury-in-Jupiter—that is, Mercury aided by some aspect or gift from Jupiter. For Mercury, through his vital and ready mobility, urges you to search out those very powers with tireless effort. The Sun, meanwhile, reveals every discovery to you as you seek with his light. Finally, Venus always adorns whatever has been found with her most pleasing beauty.

### The Genius—the daemon leader of talent—proceeds from the three Graces.

**T**herefore, these three planets, by a certain common consensus among themselves, distribute "geniuses" <term>Genius</term> <note>A "Genius" was understood as a personal guardian spirit or divine spark assigned at birth that governed an individual’s nature and destiny.</note> at the very moment of birth to various men. These are daemons <note>original: "dæmones." Not evil "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits between gods and humans in Platonic thought.</note> who serve as leaders of talent, varying according to which region of the sky they observe as people are born day by day. To follow these as leaders, more or less, is for the most part placed within your own free will. However, if the planets look down upon two people from the exact same region of the sky and in the same way, they bestow upon them the same Genius, or certainly one very similar. Where the same or a similar Genius presides, the same or a similar talent follows. Often, your own will joins in this spontaneously. Finally, wherever there is one or a similar mind, and one will, even if they appear to be two living beings, the man inside is actually one. 

For this reason, Marsilio, cease now to sin against the gods above—indeed, against yourself. Acknowledge at last your own birth chart and that of the Medici; you will recognize immediately that the Jovian Mercury, Phoebus, and Venus looked upon both of you similarly at your births from exactly the same part of the sky. This is the Ninth House <note>The "Ninth House" in astrology is traditionally associated with religion, philosophy, and wisdom. Ficino notes the astronomers call it the "Joy of Phoebus."</note>, which astronomers call the house of faith, religion, talent, and wisdom, and the joy of Phoebus. The result is that not only a similar Genius, but one and the same Genius was granted to both from that source—namely, an Apolline daemon. Since Apollo rejoices in the ninth dwelling of the ether, he sends down Apolline geniuses to men from there. From the number of these daemons, Phoebus himself has placed one in charge of you, with the approval of Venus and Mercury. From this, a single mind has followed in you both. To this end, a single will has also brought itself together from both sides. If, where these individual things are one, the man is also always one, then—lest you perhaps further separate with words those whom heaven and reason have joined—remember that whenever you write to your Medici, you ought to address it thus: (*Marsilio to Marsilio, Greetings*). And so at last, with the gods above breathing favor upon you, the vein of discovery will flow forth most abundantly for you.

Thus far Minerva has spoken. And so it is, my friend, my other self: it has often happened to me in these times, as I was saying. Then that leader of philosophers, Minerva, gave this counsel. And I myself, just as she moved me, will henceforth always ensure that our power of discovery does not run dry. Farewell. But why did I just say "farewell," as if one were leaving the other? No, let them fare well—or rather fare ill—all those who seek discord between us. For us, we should not say "farewell" [go well], but "stay well." Therefore, stay well. But lest this present letter, while it disputes concerning the Graces and the Genius, be perhaps less than "graceful" to our own Genius, we bid Vespucci <note>Likely referring to Amerigo Vespucci or a member of his family, who were close associates of the Medici and Ficino.</note> health now, and a thousand times health again—a man most pleasing of all to our Genius.

->October 18, 1481.<-
->At the estate in Careggi.<-

He identifies their shared strengths as originating from Mercury, Apollo, and Venus located in the Ninth House of their horoscopes.</summary>

### An Apologue. *A divine nature is nourished by divine food alone.*
### Marsilio Ficino *on the Apologue: what it is, where it comes from, and where it leads.*

**V**enus was once gathering various flowers and fruits in the Pythian gardens of Apollo when Mercury, wounded by love, began to pursue her. Finally, with Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and prophecy.</note> acting as both his witness and guide, Mercury successfully caught her under a certain laurel tree and knew her, much to the pleasure of both. From their union was born a child of great skill and beauty. In this child, anyone could easily recognize the piercing intellect of Mercury, the pleasing charm of Venus, and the brilliance of Phoebus. Therefore, after the name of his father Mercury—whom those above call *Logos* <note>original: "Logum." In Greek, *Logos* signifies reason, word, or divine intellect.</note>—his patron Apollo named him *Apologus* <note>The Apologue, or allegorical fable.</note>. Apollo commanded that as the boy ran about everywhere, he should benefit the human race with a certain healthy delight, just as much as his brother Cupid <note>Eros, the god of desire.</note> might harm them with the hook of noxious pleasure. However, being ignorant of the world, while the Apologue wandered outside the Pythian gardens in the nearby woods, he happened upon some shepherds. Wonderfully delighted by the boy’s divine form and character, they kept him among them for a long time, and fed the refined Apologue with rustic foods—that is, with acorns, chestnuts, and other things of that sort. For this reason, his beauty would have eventually been corrupted, and he would have turned from a refined creature into a boorish one, had not his patron Apollo recently reached out a favorable hand and successfully led him back from the woods to the Pythian gardens (which the Florentines today call the Pincian gardens <note>original: "Pinthios." Ficino is likely drawing a parallel between the classical site of Apollo’s oracle and the gardens of his Florentine patrons, the Medici.</note>). The Apologue teaches that a divine nature can only thrive on divine nourishment.

### *A philosopher must especially avoid three things: lust, greed, and ambition.* An Apologue.

**M**inerva, whom the ancient sages call *Sophia* <note>The Greek word for Wisdom.</note>, when she realized she had been born from the head of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note> alone, considered this a divine work—namely, to give birth from the head alone. She prayed as a suppliant to her father, and finally persuaded him, that she too, as a rival to her parent, might give birth from her head at least once. Thus, she gave birth to a daughter very much like both her grandfather Jove and her mother Minerva. Indeed, by her very nature, she immediately displayed a certain ancestral equity in her soul, as well as dignity in her face and her entire body. Furthermore, she reflected both the strength and the modesty of her mother in her thoughts and gestures. Her grandfather wished her to be named *Philosophy* <note>Literally "Love of Wisdom."</note> after her mother, Sophia. He commanded Philosophy that just as she had her origin from Sophia (who herself arose from the highest head of all things), so she should always keep the highest principles of things open to her, setting aside the lowly plants of the world. He ordered that she should never have any commerce with the "Lower Venus" <note>Ficino distinguishes between "Celestial Venus" (divine beauty) and "Common/Lower Venus" (physical lust).</note> or her poisonous son, Cupid. Otherwise, instead of eternal Philosophy, she would immediately turn into a temporary *Philocalia* <note>original: "Philocaliam." Literally "love of [physical] beauty." Ficino uses this to mean a superficial or worldly obsession.</note> in both reality and name. He added that she should even more strictly avoid all intimacy with the lowest Pluto <note>God of the underworld and wealth.</note> and his followers. Otherwise, having lost her ambrosia and nectar, she would carry back the waters and weeds of the Stygian marsh, upon which alone she would then unhappily feed. Finally, he warned her never to follow ambitious Juno <note>Queen of the gods, often representing worldly power and political ambition.</note> as she flies through the thicker air, lest she should accidentally trade her clear sky for darkness, her tranquility for storms, or the stars for clouds.

### An Apologue. *The impure never attain the Muses or the Graces, but only magpies and furies.*

**O**rpheus <note>The legendary musician and prophet.</note> once entered the Delphic groves to consult the oracle and immediately encountered Apollo, looking as if he had just been purified. But when he saw at Apollo’s right hand the Muses and the three Graces following closely, while on the left—though following at a distance—were magpies <note>original: "picas." In myth, the Pierides challenged the Muses and were transformed into magpies as punishment for their vanity.</note> and furies, he cried out in great wonder: "O, how different, and how opposed, are the armies that follow this leader!" "But do not wonder, O poet," said Phoebus. "To be sure, people sacrifice to me every day so that they may obtain the gifts of the Muses and the Graces from me. But to whoever performs the sacred rites with pure hands, the Muses from us...

<summary>Ficino uses mythological allegories to define the "Apologue" as a divine tool for moral instruction and warns that true Philosophy must avoid the worldly traps of lust, greed, and ambition.</summary>

## *An Apologue. Power does not rule without wisdom.*

**P**rometheus, when he had ascended into heaven and learned many mysteries from Jove himself, the author of all things, asked one question with particularly curious humility: for what reason had Jove decreed from the very beginning of things that the Sun and Mercury, more than the other planets, should be such close and constant companions in their celestial circuit? Jupiter replied: "So that whoever sees the Sun, the lord of the stars, walking nowhere in heaven without the wise Mercury, may clearly understand that on earth, power should never be granted without wisdom—or, if granted, it cannot long prevail." <note>Ficino uses the astrological proximity of the Sun and Mercury to argue that political or spiritual power (the Sun) is unstable and illegitimate without the guidance of intellect and reason (Mercury).</note>

---

## *An Apologue. On the translation of the book on love sent by Alamanno Donato to*
## *Lorenzo de' Medici.*

**W**hile Alamanno <note>Alamanno Donati (1459–1510), a Florentine humanist and student of Ficino.</note> was recently walking among the Laurels <note>original: "Lauros." A pun on the name of Lorenzo de' Medici (Laurentius), whose name derives from the laurel tree.</note> (as he often does), he frequently stumbled upon Cupid flying about the trees, and at last he caught him. The pious youth, gently handling the tender boy with light hands, began to arrange him; he adorned the now-recognized God with garlands and flowers, and while so adorning him, he asked: "What new breeze, beautiful Cupid, has directed your wings here? You have Paphos and Idalium; you have high Cythera." <note>Places in the Mediterranean sacred to Venus, Cupid's mother.</note> Then, sighing, the boy replied: "Alas, I have long been anxiously searching everywhere for my mother. Neither Paphos nor Idalium returns her to me, nor does high Cythera. Yet at last Apollo, taking pity on my long wanderings, warned me with these words: 'Cupid, your mother once used to delight only in light songs and dances; but having later become more ambitious, she began to envy Homer his Achilles and Virgil his Aeneas. She desired for herself a similar poet, who might sound forth her arts and praises upon a grander lyre. Finally, after many centuries, Venus found such a poet named Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici.</note> singing among the Laurels in the Tuscan land, in the very field of the Graces called Careggi <note>original: "Charegio." The location of the Medici villa where Ficino's Platonic Academy met.</note>. There she is now soothed by the sweetest song of her own praises, and forgetting all others, she rests most delightfully. There alone, among the chaste Muses, does your Venus now reside. Therefore, betake yourself there also, to live forever with your mother.' So Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note> once advised me, Alamanno. Thus, having left Cyprus and neglected the ivy and myrtle, I have long and anxiously sought this Careggi and these Laurels. If you yourself will lead me there to my mother, I will breathe upon you more favorably than all others, and I will unite you to my mother in a perpetual bond." Then Alamanno said, "Divine Cupid, you have flown into my hands at the most opportune moment. Indeed, the path that leads to Careggi is well-trodden by my feet. O happy me, into whose hands this most happy boy has flown today! Come then, divine boy, spread your light wings. Under the auspices of Apollo, let us both seek Careggi through the orchards of Faenza—I by walking, but you by flight."

## *An Apologue. Why Lucilia (that is, the soul) fares poorly when she departs from Phoebus (that is,*
## *from God).*

**P**hoebus <note>Apollo, acting here as a symbol for God or the Divine Intellect.</note>, the light of life and the author of vital medicine, once gave this command above all others to his daughter Lucilia <note>A name derived from "Lux" (light), representing the human soul.</note>: that she should never depart from her father’s side, for if she did, she would fall into various and most grievous diseases. At first, Lucilia obeyed her father’s commands, compelled as if by the bitterness of the approaching winter. But later, trusting in the prosperity of the now-smiling springtime, the girl began to wander further from her father’s hearth. She roamed freely here and there through the beautiful gardens of lovely Venus and the painted meadows. Lured there both by the soft charm of the grass and the beauty and sweet scent of the flowers, she wove for herself not only garlands and crowns, but even entire garments out of ivy, myrtle, lilies, roses, and other violets. Soon, plucking sweet fruits and ripe apples from every side, she did not merely taste them, but gorged herself with her throat full...
