...and insolently wanton with hunger in her new finery, and utterly forgetful of her parent (since she had escaped), the girl, more vain than boastful, approached the nearby cities. But meanwhile, along the way, snakes hiding in the grass bit the dancing girl’s feet, and bees entwined in her flowers and garlands stung her neck, cheeks, and hands; furthermore, her belly, swelling from excessive and harmful food, was most unpleasantly distended. Wherefore the ungrateful Lucilla, who had previously been enticed by the lures of pleasure and had neglected her physician father, is compelled by a certain extreme torture to return home, to acknowledge her father, and to implore her father's help with these very words: "Alas, help Lucilla now, Father Apollo <note>Ficino identifies the father as "Phœbus" (Apollo), the god of both light/truth and medicine, representing the divine source of wisdom.</note>; hurry, I beseech you, most merciful father, bring aid to your little daughter now perishing without your help." But Apollo said: "Why, empty Flora <note>Apollo addresses her as "Flora" (the goddess of flowers and blossoms) rather than Lucilla to mock her vanity and her preoccupation with fleeting, superficial beauty.</note>, do you call me your father? Cease now, wicked one, cease; I never fathered you, most vain Flora. Go away from here to your Venus, O profane Flora, go far away as soon as possible!" But when Lucilla as a suppliant had persisted longer and beseeched Apollo with many prayers—that he, who alone had given the girl life, should alone redeem her from death—and promised moreover that she would never in the future neglect her father's commands or counsel, then at last the indulgent father both scolded and warned her: "I shall not take you back for healing until you have cast off those Cupid-like dyes and Venus-like ornaments. Learn now, rash girl—learn while you wander far from your father’s hearth—how much long-lasting and heavy pain is bought by brief and light pleasure; learn how much gall it brings, whenever you despise the commands of the true physician, however little honey there may be."

### *Divine law cannot be created by heaven, but perhaps signified.*

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Federico, Duke of Urbino, ever unconquered,<-
->Sends Greetings and wishes for Happiness<-

**T**he same star that today successfully led the Magi, the supreme astronomers of the East, to Christ, has also led me into that contemplation by which I might easily and briefly reconcile the legitimate astronomers with the Christians. Today the Magi, having opened their treasures, as suppliants offered myrrh to Christ as God, frankincense as priest, and gold as king. Marsilio, however, offers to Duke Federico—ever unconquered, and especially wise and merciful—a certain small gift from the treasures of philosophy itself, at once theological, astronomical, and physical; he intends to give more ample gifts at another time when God permits.

### *The Christian religion is not from the stars.*

**T**he very nature of religion—than which nothing in human affairs is more common or firm—no astrologer ever thought could be created by celestial motion or arrangement. For they know that whatever things are created by motion must necessarily be changeable, and those which are created by a certain fixed arrangement of the stars are eventually dissipated by a contrary position. But the nature of religion itself, by which God is acknowledged and worshiped by the human race as the governor of the world, remains alone among all the studies and works of men most firm everywhere and always.

### *Common religion is not from the stars.*

**T**ruly, if any astrologer should say that the Christian law arose after some conjunction of Saturn with Jupiter—in which conjunctions certain astronomers <note>Ficino is likely referring to the theories of Albumasar and Pierre d'Ailly, who linked the rise of religions to the "Great Conjunctions" of these two planets.</note> place the greatest power for establishing laws—we shall respond briefly for the present, as far as a letter requires. Elsewhere we have disputed about these things more extensively and subtly. First, Saturn and Jupiter are joined every twentieth year, and in any such conjunction the power of the conjunction itself is thought to extend over as many years as possible; from which it follows that whenever a divine law is given to us by God, it is equally permitted for astrologers to feign some celestial power as either the author or at least the signifier of such a law. I pass over the fact that types of religion are rarely changed, even though those planets frequently run together. Furthermore, since they perpetually return to the same conjunctions every nine hundred and sixty years, and in that same interval are joined four times in any given sign, it is wonderous that the divine law—that is, the Mosaic and the Christian—so many...

<page-num>850</page-num>
# MARSILIO FICINO #

<meta>Catchword: especially</meta>

...of the ages of the world, it either would not have emerged earlier, or at least by now, after so much time, it would have been destroyed. This is especially true since many contrary planetary conjunctions have already passed. Furthermore, those astrologers who lived closest to the time of Christ could have judged the fate of the Christian law much better (if it were indeed subject to fate) than those who came later. Yet those men wandered so far from the truth that they too rashly affirmed that it would undoubtedly fall as soon as it completed three hundred and sixty-five years <note>This refers to a late-antique pagan belief that Christianity was a temporary magical sect destined to last only a solar year of years.</note>. In this matter, even the oracle of Apollo itself is proved to have lied. Indeed, iniquity lied to itself, yet divine truth did not lie; for truth inspired many Prophets and Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by Renaissance scholars to have predicted the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note> who were unskilled in astronomy from the very beginning of things, so that they might divinely foresee and preach the Christian law. Then, after Christ, He provided countless martyrs as witnesses to the Christian truth; among these, very many were highly learned in all the liberal arts and especially in astronomy, yet they most willingly endured all evils and finally death for the glory of Christ.

But let us now return to the astrologers. Truly, it seems much more difficult to be able to judge things that pertain to counsel, the mind, and God, than those things which pertain to the affections of the body, actions, passions, and physical works. Yet regarding matters of this kind, they judge with extreme difficulty and very often falsely. This is evident not only from experience itself but also seems confirmed by those reasons which I will briefly touch upon here (for I discuss these more diffusely elsewhere). **Plotinus**, following the opinion of **Plato**, and **Avicenna** <note>A significant Persian philosopher (Ibn Sina) whose views on providence and the soul influenced Ficino.</note> argue most subtly that each and every thing is contained under divine power and providence, specifically in such an order that incorporeal causes—namely God, the angels, and the souls of the celestial bodies—are the craftsmen of natural things. Physical causes, however, are the instruments of those higher craftsmen. Next, they show that whatever earthly things happen on earth proceed from a certain common concurrence of all causes, both higher and lower, acting together. Since, however, no one is ever able to comprehend all of these, it follows that no one can deliver a certain judgment regarding any matter of this kind. 

The astrologers, however, having cast aside both the divine and the lower causes and dispositions, look only at the heavens as best they can—and not even at all of those, but only a very few. They grasp the power of those few through a certain experience that is remote, rare, and deceptive, rather than through any solid reasons. Furthermore, they can only with great difficulty grasp the certain moment of our birth; the moment of conception is even more difficult; and finally, they cannot predict the infusion of the soul <note>The theological point at which God is said to place the immortal soul into the developing body.</note> at all. They do not understand the complexions <term>complexions: the specific balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, bile) that determined a person's temperament</term> of the parents or ancestors of the child being born; nor do they care to have—or even if they studied most diligently, could they ever fully attain—any account of nutrition, education, residence, habit, discipline, or counsel. 

Yet **Ptolemy** <note>The most famous astronomer/astrologer of antiquity; Ficino cites him to show that even the "master" acknowledged the limits of the stars.</note> commanded all these things to be diligently considered for this reason: he knew that the power of higher causes is not received by us except through the subsequent causes, and also through the way we are disposed by matter and habit. Hence, he says, the effects of the stars are often changed and hindered among us due to the different disposition of changeable matter. Indeed, he saw that every day, at the same moment, things are born that are different from one another in genus, species, number, and form, as well as in fortune and outcome; thus we can in no way sufficiently judge anything from that single moment of earthly birth or celestial conjunction alone. This is especially true since, beyond the specific lot of individuals, the common fortunes must also be considered and more diligently compared with one another. For these two are sometimes a hindrance and sometimes a help to each other. But no one can encompass all these things we have mentioned. For this reason, **Ptolemy** undoubtedly confesses that the judgments of astrologers are concerned with common and confused matters rather than distinct ones, and with the possible rather than the necessary. Therefore, let us finally return to where we digressed: if astrologers see visible things so obscurely (if I may put it that way), how obscurely will they see invisible things?

->Religion can perhaps be signified by the heavens.<-

**B**UT, lest we seem too persistent, let us grant that they see something, provided they see it through certain signs more often than through causes—and see those things which are ambiguous and most difficult to know. And then they can finally discern something when...

<summary>Ficino argues that Christianity is not subject to astrological fate, citing the failure of past predictions and the inherent limitations of astrology, which fails to account for divine providence, free will, and physical circumstances.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the stars are signs created by God, rather than the causes of spiritual events. He focuses on the distinction between celestial "signification" and "causation," specifically regarding the origins of the Mosaic and Christian religions.</meta>

<page-num>851</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK VII.</header>

...especially from the different strings of the world-lyre <note>The *cithara mundana* or "world lyre" is a Neoplatonic metaphor where the universe is seen as a musical instrument tuned by God; the planets are like strings that produce a cosmic harmony.</note>, they understand—or rather, to speak more truly, they prophesy—either a harmony or a dissonance. Plotinus the Platonist <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and heavily relied upon.</note> teaches that almost all effects below the Moon are signified by heaven, yet not all depend on the celestial body. For only corporeal things can be produced by a celestial body—or rather through a celestial body, as if through an instrument—by the movers of heaven themselves. If, however, there are things among us that entirely exceed the corporeal genus and approach the mind and divinity, these proceed only from the divine mind and the minds that follow it. Indeed, the counsels and wills of these minds can often be indicated by celestial figures and movements, as if by their own eyes and nods. But to clearly perceive those signs is the work of a man who is exceptionally wise and divine. This is what Plotinus says. For this reason, the Mosaic and Christian religion, being entirely spiritual and divine, could in no way be produced by the heavens nor through celestial bodies. This is especially true since those celestial movements are accustomed to producing their works on earth only through earthly aids. Yet the divine law not only lacked earthly help everywhere, but for many centuries it was everywhere disturbed and afflicted by every kind of impediment. Perhaps, however, it seems that it could be signified in some way through the stars, by that very same God—moving and tempering the spheres to designate that time—who foresaw and decreed that His law would exist in such a way and at such a time. Avicenna <note>An influential Persian polymath and philosopher (c. 980–1037) whose work *Metaphysics* bridged Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought.</note> confirms this in his *Metaphysics*, affirming that moral and divine laws are instituted in certain ages, sent and inspired through the souls of the Prophets by the providence of God alone; meanwhile, the entire order of the universe under the divine Mover and His ministers is so arranged that the very body of the prophetic soul is stationed somewhere on earth, and its arrival is signified equally in the heavens and on earth. Perhaps David intended this with these words: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands* <note>original: "Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annuntiat firmamentum." (Psalm 19:1).</note>. Perhaps also Albumasar <note>An 8th-century Persian astrologer whose works were vital to Western medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> points toward this in some way when he says that the Egyptians and Indians, in the first "face" of the constellation Virgo, observed a certain beautiful virgin sitting and nursing a boy, whose name among certain nations Albumasar thinks is "Jesus." Truly, that image which is imagined in that sign—or rather, made up rather than seen—if it were the proper *cause* of Jesus himself, certainly it would have produced either Jesus himself or someone very much like him many other times both before and after the time of Christ. Therefore, if such an image exists there, it is a certain *sign* of the Christian law, not its cause.

---

->Many things are signified through heaven which are not made by heaven.<-

---

# **M**oreover, that many things are indeed signified by heaven, yet not produced by it, is evident again from the fact that evils and experiences of disorder cannot proceed from those things which are the best and most ordered. Yet they are often predicted through celestial things—that is, as through signs, not as through causes—no differently than in augury and auspices, where many things are thought to be portended by birds, which nonetheless are not produced by birds. Therefore, Plato in the *Timaeus* did not say that the stars *make* the future, but *pronounce* it. However, they do not do so for everyone, but only for those who can attain this through reason. Furthermore, astrologers, in considering the birth-chart <term>genesis</term> <note>The *genesis* here refers to a nativity or natal horoscope—the positions of the stars at the moment of birth.</note> of anyone, are accustomed to judge many things pertaining to the country, parents, grandparents, brothers, spouses, servants, friends, and enemies, whose lot in no way proceeds from the birth-chart of another, but is rather indicated by it. This is also clearly seen in those "interrogations" <note>A branch of astrology (horary astrology) where a chart is drawn to answer a specific question.</note> which are made and handled regarding past events. Indeed, just as we daily foresee through someone's eyes, gestures, and words that they are about to do something—though they accomplish what they chose not by those signs, but by their will—so things are often portended through the "nods" of the celestial spheres. They are produced neither by those celestial bodies nor through them, but by the divine minds that rule and move those globes; they are signified through celestial things as if through their own faces, but by their own counsels they are either arranged in a most orderly fashion, or reduced to order, or at least foreseen from above by the gods as about to proceed from human causes, and are demonstrated to us through certain celestial signs. In this matter, Ptolemy <note>The 2nd-century author of the *Almagest* and *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational texts of Western astronomy and astrology.</note> also, as well as Albumasar, Zahel <note>Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century Jewish astrologer and mathematician.</note>, Manilius <note>A 1st-century Roman poet and author of the *Astronomica*.</note>, and the other principal authors of Astronomy seem to agree with us. Namely, when they affirm that celestial bodies are endowed with divine souls and minds, and like certain divine animals, they obey God himself, the ruler of all. Nor is this claimed without justice, since Ptolemy himself confesses that human wisdom [is subject to] another's work, that is...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that divine matters, specifically the life of Christ and the Christian religion, transcend celestial influence. While stars can act as signs (signification), they are not the causes (causation) of spiritual truths. Ficino is moving from general philosophical principles to historical "proofs" from both sacred and pagan sources.</meta>

<page-num>852</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<meta>catchword: and us</meta>

...to rule over the stars to such an extent that, by his own industry, he can often resist their threats and find favor in their promises. It would indeed be strange if Divine Wisdom allowed its own work <note>Meaning humanity, the pinnacle of God's creation.</note> to be entirely dominated by the stars. Hence that saying of Avicenna: *Heaven is an animal obedient to God.* <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was an influential Persian philosopher. Ficino cites him to show that even Islamic philosophy agreed that the heavens are subjects of God, not independent masters.</note> Since all these thinkers understand that every single thing here is created and governed by Divine Providence, they very rarely say that the celestial bodies *do* this or that when they speak of their power; rather, they most frequently assert that they *signify* such-and-such a thing. And just as they believe that false or merely human laws are portended by the stars, so too are the true and divine laws often signified.

->*Signs and testimonies concerning the divinity of Christ.*<-

**P**erhaps for this very reason, the Magi—the wisest of all in the study of Astronomy—set out from the East to Jerusalem at the time Jesus was born. They arrived asserting that they had been warned by a star that a boy had been born at that time and in that region who was to be the King of Israel and worthy of adoration. The fact that such great men came such a long way to worship a helpless infant clearly demonstrates that the Magi believed there was a divinity in the boy proceeding from a higher principle than the heavens—especially since they were led by a certain star that was miraculous rather than natural. <note>Ficino distinguishes between "natural" stars (planets/fixed stars) and the Star of Bethlehem, which he views as a supernatural sign created for a specific purpose.</note> Calcidius the Platonist <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato; Ficino uses him as a "pagan" witness to Christian truth.</note> cites various histories regarding stars which, when they appear rarely, portend great calamities. Then he adds: *There is also another holier and more venerable history which reports that by the rising of a certain star, it was not diseases and deaths that were announced, but the venerable descent of God for the sake of human salvation and mortal affairs.* He testifies that this was observed by the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" was a common term for ancient Babylonian astrologers/astronomers.</note>, who worshipped the newly born God with gifts. So says Calcidius. Nor should it seem surprising that the Magi noticed this, for in that same eastern region—and as some say, in the same city where the Magi lived—the Prophet Balaam flourished long before them. He predicted that the Messiah would arise like a rod out of Israel when a new star of Jacob arose, specifically in these words: *A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall rise out of Israel.* <note>Numbers 24:17. Ficino is linking Jewish prophecy with pagan astrology.</note> Moreover, that the Magi came to Jerusalem to worship Christ is evidenced for us by that cruel slaughter of the infants under Herod. Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer.</note> asserts that the Emperor Augustus was informed of this event, writing as follows: *When Augustus heard that among the boys under the age of two whom the King of the Jews ordered to be killed in Syria, Herod's own son was also slain, he said: "It is better to be Herod's pig than his son."* <note>original: "præstat Herodis porcum esse, quàm filium." This is a famous pun: in Greek, the words for "pig" (hys) and "son" (huios) sound very similar. Since Herod followed Jewish law, he would not kill/eat a pig, but he famously murdered his own family members.</note> Suetonius also writes that there was an old and constant opinion throughout the entire East that it was in the Fates that, around the time of Nero, those departing from Judea would gain mastery over all things. Josephus <note>A 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> writes that this same oracle was found in the sacred scriptures before the siege of Jerusalem. Indeed, this seems to fit no one more appropriately than the Apostles. For in these oracles, the Jews are designated as the Apostles were: those who, having gone out from Judea, would give laws everywhere to all the Gentiles. Even the Cumaean Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses of the ancient world; Christian humanists like Ficino believed they had foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note> seems to have described the same thing at that time: *By whom a great order of ages would be born anew, and the Virgin would flourish, and a new progeny would be sent down from on high.* Therefore, there was an old and constant opinion, consistent across the whole East, in the prognostications of astrologers, and in the sacred scriptures—namely in the Prophets and the Sibyls—concerning the divinity and the time of Christ.

->*The Christian Religion depends on God alone.*<-

**B**ut we dispute more broadly concerning the divine oracles of the Sibyls and Prophets in our book *On Religion*. In this letter, however, we shall briefly conclude regarding the divine law as it pertains to the question at hand. If anyone should object to us that Christ performed miracles by some fate of his birth <term>genesis</term> <note>Meaning a birth chart or horoscope.</note> or by some conjunction of stars favoring his birth, we will ask: by what means did innumerable holy men among the Christians, born at different times and places long after Christ, perform many miracles and continue to do so daily? Furthermore, that eclipse of the sun which occurred at the death of Christ, happening outside the order of nature, most clearly declared that Christ was born from a higher order than the celestial one. <note>A solar eclipse cannot naturally happen during a full moon (Passover); therefore, this "darkness" was seen as a divine miracle by theologians.</note> That there was indeed an eclipse is proven by the fact that it would not have been possible for Christ’s disciples, preaching such a portent everywhere, to lie about such a manifest matter. Moreover, Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History."</note> asserts that he read the same thing in the histories of the Gentiles themselves; and before Eusebius, Lucian of Antioch and Tertullian said the same. Phlegon, the writer of the *Olympiads*, also recorded the prodigious failure of the sun at the same time...

<summary>Ficino argues that the stars are signs of divine will rather than causes, citing the Star of Bethlehem and various pagan witnesses—including Calcidius, Macrobius, and the Sibyls—to prove Christ's divinity. He concludes by refuting astrological determinism by pointing to the "unnatural" solar eclipse during the Crucifixion.</summary>

<page-num>853</page-num>

<sig>Hhh 3</sig>

...and time confirms for us that it happened. That Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 1st-century judge of the Areopagus in Athens converted by St. Paul. During the Renaissance, he was believed to be the author of highly influential mystical texts (now attributed to "Pseudo-Dionysius").</note> and Apollophanes the philosophers, walking together near Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in Egypt.</note>, saw it clearly with their own eyes as a wonder and proved it through subtle disputations. We read of this in Dionysius’s letter to the wise Polycarp. We also infer from this what no one doubts: that according to the Law, the Jews always celebrated Passover at the full moon, and that at that very same time Christ's life flowed away on the cross. From this, it is understood by the most certain reasoning that the sun then failed <note>original: "defecisse," meaning an eclipse.</note>, and failed contrary to every order of nature. <note>A solar eclipse is impossible during a full moon; therefore, Ficino argues this event was a divine miracle rather than a natural astronomical occurrence.</note> This was so that the heavens might bear witness to the dying Christ with a new darkness, just as they bore witness to Him when He was born with a new light.

# Conclusion on the Divinity of the Christian Law.

**B**ut to return to the proposal: who would wonder if the Creator of the world so tempered the individual parts of the world that, in both the wondrous arrangement of the stars and in the supreme peace of the whole world, He greeted men in human form? Especially since, long before, He had commanded celestial things to retreat against their nature through His Prophets. Dionysius recounts that the Babylonians and Persians recorded such wonders in their annals as divine works. We read similar things in Plato’s book *On the Kingdom* <note>Ficino is likely referring to the *Politicus* (The Statesman), where Plato discusses the reversal of the motion of the universe.</note>.

The poets, as they are wont to do with everything, transformed this history into the fables of Phaethon <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon was the son of the Sun-god who lost control of the solar chariot, causing the earth to burn; Ficino views this as a distorted memory of a real celestial miracle.</note> and other similar tales. Finally, divine law and established religion do not originate from the lower or upper bodies of the world, since through the grace of the incorporeal and Good God, it despises all bodily things in life and transcends them in affection and thought. Nor does it depend on fate in any way—a fate which it always denies and condemns—nor is it born from human nature or prudence, which either neglects it or is lifted up by it across an immense space toward the immense God. But without doubt, it proceeds from the sole infinite Principle, and seeks only the infinite End. 

But it is pleasing to seal our letter with a Platonic seal. Our Plato, in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman*, posits two principles of religions: in one, religion was born immediately at the very beginning of things; in the other, it was confirmed after many centuries. Indeed, he teaches that religion was not so much an instinct as something implanted in souls flowing from God. Because of this knowledge, when they were first enclosed in bodies created or raised from the earth by divine power, they suddenly recognized and worshiped God as their Father. But the divine law was confirmed when eventually God alone, out of His sole mercy, sent it to men through a messenger chosen by Himself. Farewell. January 6, 1481. <note>Jan 6 is the Feast of the Epiphany, which commemorates the visit of the Magi—a fitting date for a letter about celestial signs of Christ.</note> Florence.

# Philosophy and Religion are Kindred.

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Antonio Ziliolo Sophronio of Venice, greetings.<-

**I**f anyone were to have a vast and wondrous workmanship <note>original: "opificium," referring to the created universe as a product of a craftsman.</note> always before his eyes—constructed and moved with both marvelous reason and manifest art—and if it were also perfectly suited to the use of the spectators as they desired, yet he did not notice that such a workmanship was made and moved by some supreme power, reason, and goodness, would we not think him blind in the eyes of his reason? Or if perhaps he did notice it occasionally, yet never feared, venerated, or worshiped the architect of such a great, beautiful, and useful work, must he not be considered worthy of extreme hatred, both by other spectators and by the architect himself? 

Truly, of all human arts and faculties, only pious Philosophy provides with every effort that we do not fall into such wretched blindness or incur such heavy hatred. For there is no other duty for a true philosopher than to always contemplate and teach the individual reasons and causes of both the parts and the universe. Then, in assigning the reasons and causes of things, he must finally ascend to the supreme Reason and Cause of all; furthermore, he must lead others toward the heights with him according to his strength. And while he shows with how much wisdom the world is ruled, he simultaneously demonstrates with certain reasons of providence how much it is guided for the benefit of the human race. So that we may recognize...

<summary>Ficino concludes his argument on the miraculous nature of the crucifixion eclipse and asserts that true religion and philosophy both lead the soul back to God, the supreme Architect. He cites Plato's views on the origins of religion and defines the philosopher's duty as the study of divine providence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of "learned religion," arguing that the great philosophers of antiquity—such as Plato, Pythagoras, and Hermes Trismegistus—viewed the study of wisdom as a form of worship. It concludes a letter to Antonio Ziliolo and begins two short letters to Phoebus Capella.</meta>

<page-num>854</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...that we might know and love God; the whole world cries out from every side, and the philosopher, the true interpreter of the world and of God, demonstrates this diligently and exhorts us to it. Indeed, unless we are utterly deprived of all sense, we ought now to recognize most clearly that in such a great order of the universe, nothing is entirely accidental—unless perhaps those people alone are "accidental" who believe that so artistic a work of craftsmanship could be a matter of chance. 

Therefore, a philosopher must be called wise while he raises us to the contemplation of God, and pious and religious while he inflames us with the love of divine goodness. For this reason, the entire philosophy of the Ancients is nothing other than **learned religion**. I shall pass over other examples for the present, for they are innumerable. Plato, imbued with the divine mysteries of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived by Ficino as a contemporary of Moses and the founder of the "Ancient Theology" (*Prisca Theologia*) that led to Plato.</note>, disputes in the *Republic* and often elsewhere that unless one has somehow seen the light and recognized the goodness of God Himself, one can neither see anything else that is true nor ever do anything well, whether in public or in private. He holds that the divine Sun is perceived only by its own light, and finally, that this light is usually poured only into a serene mind. For this reason, Plato himself, in the Socratic manner, always purified his own mind and everywhere taught others to purify theirs. 

Consequently, he commanded that in every single thing, one should begin from God—not only in speaking the truth but also in thinking—and he himself always began from God. For the sake of such purification, Pythagoras, imitating Orpheus, practiced an exceptional sobriety of life and, moreover, sang sacred hymns to the powers above to the accompaniment of the lyre every day at sunrise. He persuaded Empedocles and his other followers to do the same, so that they might imitate the celestial spheres which are always singing to God. Furthermore, when he discovered that the square of the longest side of a right-angled triangle is equal to the squares of the other two sides joined together <note>A reference to the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, he humbly sacrificed a hecatomb <note>A grand sacrifice, traditionally of one hundred oxen.</note> to God. This was because he understood that nothing of the truth can be seen anywhere without the light of the highest truth. If he sacrificed such a grand victim for the knowledge of so small a matter, do you not think he dedicated himself to God for the knowledge of his own self? And again, for the contemplation of the universe, that he also dedicated the universe itself in prayer to the Creator of the whole? 

What shall I say of Hermes Trismegistus? All of his disputations begin with prayers and end in sacrifices. What of Zoroaster? His philosophy (as Plato testifies) is nothing other than wise piety and divine worship. Finally (to speak briefly), that Saturnian and golden discipline of the Ancients <note>Referring to the "Golden Age" ruled by the god Saturn, a time of primordial wisdom.</note> seems worthy of being called not so much "Philosophy" as **Philothea** <note>term: Philothea (Greek: "Love of God") as opposed to Philosophia ("Love of Wisdom").</note>, and their every discourse is an oracle rather than a speech. 

These things I have said concerning the bond between wisdom and piety: first, so that we may remember how much we owe to those golden centuries of sacred philosophy; second, so that you yourself may understand by what reasoning Marsilio, a follower of antiquity, joins religious matters with philosophical ones to the best of his ability—not only in that one book on religion which you seek, but in all his writings. Finally, may you recognize that he now gladly embraces both you and Antonio Ziliolo <note>A Venetian lawyer and friend of Ficino.</note> as his fellow-philosophers in that philosophy which encompasses both wisdom and piety. Farewell.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Phoebus Capella <note>A Venetian statesman and humanist.</note>, sends fondest greetings. <-

**I** gave birth to a certain light long ago; that light immediately returned to its own Phoebus <note>A play on words: Phoebus is a name for the Sun god (Apollo), as well as the name of the recipient, Phoebus Capella.</note>. I also recently fathered a certain star; this star, similarly, as soon as it was born, happily sought out its own Phoebus again.

-> Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished Phoebus Capella, <-
-> sends fondest greetings. <-

**S**ince our friend William has often asked me to recommend him highly to my Phoebus, I have finally transcribed for him the letter which I wrote in recent days to Federico, Duke of Urbino <note>Federico da Montefeltro, the famous mercenary captain and patron of the arts.</note>, concerning the Star of the Magi. I gave it to William with these words: "If you wish, friend, to be recommended to Phoebus, come now and greet Phoebus with this Mercurial star as your guide. This will (I hope) successfully win him over to you." Go therefore, go swiftly, and do not be reluctant. For this is not one of those stars which might occasionally be seen as foreign in the temple of Apollo. Indeed, Mercury is, above all others, a member of Phoebus’s own household. Farewell. Florence, February 6, 1481.

->*That the Platonic discipline is pious.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Niccolini, Archbishop of Amalfi, sends greetings.<-

**N**umenius the Pythagorean <note>original: "Eumenius Pythagoricus." Ficino refers to Numenius of Apamea, a 2nd-century philosopher who sought the Eastern origins of Greek thought.</note>, whom Origen ranks above all other Pythagoreans, after he had read the books of Moses and Plato, judged that Plato was nothing other than "Moses speaking in the Attic tongue." Furthermore, Aurelius Augustine writes that we are led toward the truth by a twofold path: namely, by authority and by reason. Regarding authority, he places that of Christ above all others; but as for the reasons which most especially harmonize with this authority, he finds them only among the Platonists. He even claims that almost the entire Prologue of the Gospel of John can be gathered from their writings. Finally, he affirms that the Platonists would become Christians with only a few changes to their views, and that he chose them above all other philosophers for this reason: that because they think more rightly about divine matters than the rest, they seem rightly preferred above all others. 

Therefore, led first by the authority of the divine Augustine, and then confirmed by the testimony of many holy men among the Christians, I judged it would be worth the effort—since I was to philosophize—to do so chiefly in the **Academy** <term>Academy: The school founded by Plato; for Ficino, it represents the tradition of philosophical inquiry that leads to spiritual truth.</term>. I did this so that the Platonic doctrine—which relates to the Divine Law (that is, the Mosaic and Christian law) just as the Moon relates to the Sun—might shine forth more widely. To this end, I have translated all the books of Plato from the Greek language into Latin. Furthermore, lest anyone’s eyes be dimmed by the sight of this new light, I composed a volume as a commentary, divided into eighteen books <note>This refers to Ficino's magnum opus, *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum* (Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls).</note>. In these, the Platonic mysteries are explained to the best of my ability, so that we may follow his mind rather than merely his words; and, having removed the poetic veils, we may reveal the Platonic sentiment which is in total harmony with the Divine Law. 

Indeed, I believe—nor is this a hollow faith—that it was decreed by divine providence that those sharpest wits, who do not easily yield to the sole authority of the Divine Law, should at last yield to Platonic reasons which strongly support religion. Why do I say this? Venerable Father, read these things to your household, so that they may cease to wonder why Marsilio (since he is a priest of Philosophy) devotes himself so frequently to these studies. Farewell.

---

->An Allegory. Marsilio Ficino on Plato’s book on Kingship, to Federico, Duke of Urbino.<-

**J**upiter, the Greatest and Best, wishing to see at some time on earth such a kingdom as he always beholds near himself in heaven, sent down to earth long ago a certain royal and divine soul, modeled after the very idea of a divine king. Having summoned the heavenly inhabitants, he commanded that they all support this future king. The gods above already named him "Orbinate" <note>A pun on *Orbis* (the world/orb) and *Urbinas* (of Urbino).</note> from the "orb" of his royal faith and the empire of the world, while men, by changing a few letters, were to call him Federico, the Duke of Urbino. All the deities assented to Jove except for Juno; for Juno alone, the ambitious queen of the lower, thicker air, has until now envied the earth a heavenly kingdom. But Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom.</note> and Mercury, with the favor of the others (and Truth as a witness), have long since most gladly bestowed the royal crown and scepter upon this same man to whom Jupiter also gave them. Since the Academy everywhere worships and follows Pallas and Mercury, and since the divine Plato himself describes the kingdom and Monarchy of the whole world, he most happily grants it to Federico, Duke of Urbino, who is most deserving both by the judgment of Jove and the testimony of Truth.

---

->Marsilio Ficino’s Allegory to Federico, Duke of Urbino, regarding the book of Geography by Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò, dedicated to the same.<-

**T**o him whom almighty Jupiter, Lord of the whole world, created for the empire of the earthly orb, and whom Pallas and Mercury, the children of Jove, have long since deemed worthy of such great power—to him, the Academy, which is the devoted follower of these gods, rightly dedicates the Platonic form of the earthly kingdom. To him also our fellow Academician Berlinghieri <note>Francesco Berlinghieri (1440–1501), a pupil of Ficino who wrote the *Seven Days of Geography*, a verse translation of Ptolemy dedicated to Federico da Montefeltro.</note> grants the entire map of the earthly orb at a time when republics, leaders, and kings again and again concede to him—the master of the Italian war through happy auspices—both the spear of Pallas and the club of Hercules. And while many powerful men wish Italy to obey the ever-unconquered Duke Federico in war, in the meantime, both the Academy and the Academician subject the entire world to him in peace as much as in war.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

->Let the sacrilegious not touch sacred things.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Carlo Astoro, sends many greetings.

**O**ur pious Plato was being transcribed these days by a certain impious German, who recently shed sacred blood before the altars with his sacrilegious hands. That soldier—that "killer of the sacred" <note>original: "sacricida." A play on "homicide," referring to the man killing a priest.</note>, if I may call him that—took flight after slaying a priest. By that very flight, he seems to have committed a second sacrilege, for he left the sophisticated Plato <note>original: "urbanum Platonem." Ficino contrasts the "urban" or refined Plato with the "rusticos" or unrefined peasants.</note> wandering among the rustics. Moreover, he is likely to commit a third sacrilege if he should ever return and dare to touch the sacred Plato with his blood-stained hands. Therefore, I beg you, excellent man, to see to it that Plato does not wander too long in the woods, or—what would be even more cruel—be polluted again by the contaminated hands of that profane man.

---

->In God alone is salvation.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, sends many greetings.

**G**reetings, my most beloved Bandini; greetings, I say, a thousand times—indeed, always—in God, the eternal author of salvation <note>original: "salutis." In Latin, *salus* means both "health" and "salvation," a common pun in Ficino's greetings.</note>. I would have added "and in Plato," if salvation were to be sought in a man after God. We are doing well, which I know you desire to hear above all. We have recently heard the same of you and hope to hear it daily. I have dedicated two books of our letters to Matthias, the invincible King of Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniae Regi." Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490), a major patron of the arts and Ficino's work.</note>, which are now being transcribed by the labor of Francesco Iunio. Our other books, which you desire, are already in the hands of the printers; when they have been pressed out, they will come to you as ambassadors, happily expressing our mind to you. Meanwhile, this letter commends to you three friends especially dear to us among the Muses, to be greeted again and again: the Bishop of Kalocsa, the Bishop of Vác, and the learned Garasda <note>Nicolaus Garasda, a Hungarian humanist poet.</note>. Farewell, and be happy. May 9, 1482.

---

->We can only prove ourselves to the extent that we are approved by those who are proven.<-

### Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Pietro Molino of Venice, sends many greetings.

**O**ur Antonio <note>Likely Antonio del Pollaiuolo (c. 1432–1498), the famous Florentine painter and sculptor.</note>, the distinguished painter and sculptor, when he greeted me and my household in your name yesterday evening, so painted your features upon our faces and so sculpted your affections into our own feelings, that it did not seem so much that your greetings were being told to us by him, but that they were being delivered clearly by you in person. Therefore, we all rose up suddenly, recognizing no longer the Florentine Antonio, but the very presence of Molino himself, and we honored you with heads uncovered, as is fitting. Greetings to you, most learned Pietro; by this "salutary" presence of yours, restore us to health as frequently as you have begun to do. We shall truly consider ourselves worthy of honor only so long as you honor us. Our city will please us only as much as we know it pleases you. Would that our affairs please you more every day, so that we may more vehemently please ourselves. Farewell.

---

->An honest justification for a long silence.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Cavalcanti, his unique friend, sends many greetings.

**W**hen at dawn today I was applying myself entirely to finishing the work of *Sacred Theology* <note>Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, his magnum opus attempting to prove the immortality of the soul.</note> which I have been laboring on for a long time, and no one—not even my closest friends—dared to interrupt me, I was nevertheless interrupted by you, my unique friend, quite boldly with these reproaches: "Marsilio, you are usually accustomed to greeting your Giovanni with letters during the first days of your stay in the country, but now you have long abstained from your usual greetings. Do you not see, you sacrilegious man, how much you detract from our sacred friendship by this silence of yours?" To these words, Plato seemed to respond on our common behalf in this manner: "See, Giovanni, how great a power resides in your words. For among others, to say one thing is different from doing it; but you, by the very act of speaking, perform the deed. For with the same words by which you call Marsilio sacrilegious, you actually make him sacrilegious—if indeed a man who interrupts a sacred and public work for the sake of a private, however singular, friendship, is to be considered sacrilegious." Such a controversy, as I was saying, befell us this dawn. But you have won at last.

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VII.</header>

...as you are accustomed, and with the Platonic mysteries set aside for a little while, you now bring back the usual greetings from us. Do you wish to bring them back again? And to surpass Plato again? Respond, my friend, I pray. Respond—not, I say, as you are accustomed, but rather as you are *not* accustomed. But if you do not wish to respond to me, at least respond to Plato. Yet behold, while I look at you as you speak, I suddenly see a double countenance there—a marvel to behold—where just now I saw only one. And if I recognize the faces of friends correctly, I seem to see the welcome face of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici, Ficino's primary patron.</note> in your own (as if in a mirror), and I seem to be rebuked by him almost as much as by you. Therefore, since your countenances are now doubled, those greetings are doubled for me in turn; and what I said a little while ago to two people as if they were one, let it now be said to one as if they were two.

### A response regarding a birth chart, showing that such judgment is highly fallible.
->Marsilio Ficino to Zenobio the Roman, many greetings.<-

**A**lthough I do not have those instruments here with me now by which the celestial bodies are usually examined and weighed with precision, nevertheless, so that I may act for the present with a bit of "rough wit" <note>original: "pingui Minerva." A Latin idiom meaning common sense or a plain, unrefined approach.</note>, that figure of the heavens does not please me much, in which Mars holds the midheaven, Saturn occupies the sixth house, Jupiter is combust <note>term: combust. In astrology, a planet is "combust" when it is so close to the Sun that its influence is said to be weakened or burned away.</note>, and the Sun aspects the Moon in a square <note>term: square. An astrological aspect of 90 degrees, traditionally considered a position of tension or difficulty.</note>. But it is neither helpful to prophesy evil, nor is it fitting to believe much in this. For since judgment is often fallible in nearby and daily matters, it is certainly most fallible in the most remote things—especially since our affairs depend on many other causes besides the stars: on birth, nutrition, location, education, counsel, and chance. This is clearly evident from the fact that people are carried and born at the same moment, yet they differ most widely among themselves in genus, species, number, quality, fortune, and their end. Farewell.

### Divine things are not lost when they are sent.
->Marsilio Ficino to Lotterio Neroni, his fellow philosopher, many greetings.<-

**G**iovanni Cocchi, our fellow academic, met me yesterday evening in his usual manner, like a character from Terence <note>Publius Terentius Afer, a Roman playwright whose characters were known for their witty and colloquial dialogue.</note>. "I bid you greetings, our Marsilio," he said, "in the name of our Lotterio. But do you bid any greeting to be sent back to Lotterio? For I am flying to him (as you see)." When I, in turn, vehemently desired you to be well, I said, "You shall carry the same greetings back to Lotterio." Then Giovanni said, "But if you give back the same greetings to a friend, you will seem to reject by chance what he had sent." To this I replied: "If my left hand gives back to my right what it received from the right, I have not kept it as a miser would, but rather preserved it through a kind of exchange. Certainly, Lotterio and Marsilio are the right and left hands of the same man." By chance, a certain dialectician <note>A practitioner of formal logic; Ficino often contrasted the dry, hair-splitting "dialecticians" with spiritually-minded "Platonists."</note> was present and objected: "Even if the same man possesses whatever either hand possesses, that which he has already given back to the other is no longer in the first hand." Then I responded thus: "If a mutual exchange of money were made between us, what you object would certainly follow according to logic. But if it were a ray of light, it would not follow at all. For a ray is accustomed to leap forth from a bright body into a mirror and leap back again. This ray does not leave the body from which it flashes when it is emitted, and in turn, when it leaps back by reflection, it is not lost. Therefore, whatever a ray seems to wound by a certain striking, it warms; it cannot be broken by anything, but by mutual reflection it appears rather to be doubled. You do not know, O Dialectician, you do not know that Marsilio is greeted by Lotterio through rays sent in divine light, and in turn, the latter is re-greeted by the former through rays sent back. Furthermore, nothing here is struck down, but rather warmed; nothing is broken, but rather doubled. Therefore, Dialectician," I said, "farewell in your wretched darkness. You will only be happy when you gratefully look back at the light which always looks upon you freely." But you, Giovanni, carry those indivisible rays of divine salvation between me and Lotterio without any fear of division, and bring them back happily.

### A skillful petition and recommendation.
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, many greetings.<-

**I** recently sent several things from this workshop of ours, which have been ready for a long time, to Matthias, the invincible King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus, the King of Hungary (Pannonia was the Roman name for the region). He was a great patron of the arts and humanism.</note>. I sent them, Bandini, primarily with the hope and confidence that those things which I had made "Saturnine" <note>Ficino associated his own melancholic, scholarly nature with the planet Saturn; he hopes the King’s "Jovian" (regal and happy) influence will transform the work.</note> in some way, he might make "Jovian" by his own splendor. Which indeed I [hope] easily...

# MARSILIO FICINO

...I hope to achieve this, if you will eventually deliver with your "mercurial" <note>original: "Mercuriali." Referring to Mercury, the messenger of the gods, implying eloquence and speed.</note> mouth (as you are accustomed to doing) those "Ficinian" things which we sent to the King. My cousin-brother <note>original: "Amitinus frater meus." Sebastian was actually Ficino's cousin, but he refers to him as a brother and "another self."</note>, Sebastian, a legitimate professor of Theology and almost my other self, copied this out. While he was reading and transcribing the letter in which I was responding to you at length—saying that I could not easily satisfy your desire by my own arrival there—he could not restrain himself. Like some sort of "half-poet," he immediately thundered into my ears: "I will not suffer it, O Marsilio; I will never suffer you to be unable to do what you wish, so far as I am able. What then? I have found a way, Ficino, a way pleasing to those who have found it, which will return you to such a great friend." To which I said, "And by what way will you accomplish that, Salviati?" <note>Sebastian's surname was Salviati.</note> He replied, "If I go there as a second Ficino, you will at least have arrived in me as you desired." 

Thus, I have decided to set out for Pannonia <note>The Roman name for the region including modern-day Hungary.</note> under happy auspices. That is to say, on the safe feet of our friend Bandini, who himself has set out happily. Indeed, my Francesco, I would praise him to you and commend him to you most highly, if it were either proper to praise myself anywhere or necessary to commend myself to myself. Farewell happily. Live happily. Love me (as you do) and write what the friends greet. Greet our friends. I commend you to the royal court; commend us to the King. From the estate at Careggi. 20 September 1482.

---

### *In what respect the Platonic discipline especially surpasses the Peripatetic.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow Platonist, sends greetings.<-

**Y**our elegant letters have indeed filled me with great pleasure, because they prove you are now clearly eloquent in our judgment. They bring even greater pleasure because they signify you have turned out to be a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>original: "Peripateticum." A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for the "walking" (peripatos) style of his lectures.</note> as well. Finally, they bring the greatest pleasure of all because they promise, beyond a doubt, a Platonist; you seem to have cultivated your singular and fortunate genius as best as possible. 

Truly, after your studies in human eloquence, you tracked down the reasons for natural things among the Peripatetics, and now you betake yourself to the divine mysteries of our Plato. For while the Peripatetics indeed dispute most diligently with what great reason natural things are arranged everywhere, the Platonists show—beyond these things—how much further we are indebted to Him who arranged these things in number, weight, and measure <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>. For this reason, the former easily make us learned, but the latter make us, in addition, wise and blessed. Therefore, my excellent Giovanni, proceed happily as you have begun. If you should need our effort in such a noble purpose (as you say), I promise I shall not be found wanting. Farewell.

---

### *A pious greeting and a request for books.*

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Giovanni Francesco Ippolito, Count of Gazoldo, sends many greetings.<-

**L**actantius Tedaldus <note>A Florentine diplomat and friend of Ficino.</note> bids us greet you again and again in your name and that of Laurentius Bonincontrius. But with what sort of "health" or "salvation" <note>The Latin "salus" means both physical health and spiritual salvation.</note> specifically? Surely that by which, if it is preserved, nothing in us can be unsafe. Therefore, may you always be healthy/saved in God the Savior, and love us in that same love. Furthermore, may you be well, and may the little books of our letters return to us eventually. They have been guests of Hippolytus long enough now—quite enough; therefore, let them now return home safe. 22 December 1482.

---

### *An honest and vigorous demand for the return of entrusted books.*

->Marsilio Ficino to his "Sweet" Dulci, the distinguished Lawyer, sends many greetings.<-

**G**reetings, my most persuasive Dulci <note>Ficino is punning on the recipient's name, "Dulci," which means "Sweet."</note>. May you, with your sweetness, temper my bitterness—if you can, and would that you could. I, as you know, have never fathered any children, except for my books; but no one is ignorant of how dear children are to their parents. Since the children of the mind are as much closer and more excellent than those of the body, they are held that much dearer. To what end is this? Truly, that unconquered leader of yours <note>Likely Federico da Montefeltro, the Duke of Urbino.</note> asked me vehemently, both by letter and by voice, to entrust my books to Vespasiano <note>Vespasiano da Bisticci, the famous Florentine bookseller and manuscript producer.</note> to be sent to him at Urbino. Indeed, I entrusted them as willingly as he desired them vehemently. Vespasiano then handed them over to hired couriers to be delivered. But those men, although they received the books, did not receive their payment, and have been holding them captive away from me for a long time now. Meanwhile, I burn with the most ardent longing for them, and I fear a thousand dangers for them daily. I beseech... <note>The text breaks off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VII.</header>

I beseech you by the Muses, my Dulces, and I beseech your masters by the Graces, that they do not allow me to suffer such a heavy loss while I strive to obey the leader’s will and intend, moreover, to honor them. Farewell.

## *A busy man should not be interrupted without good reason.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Rucellai, <note>original: "Bernhardo Oricellario." A prominent Florentine statesman, historian, and brother-in-law to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> Orator of the Florentine Senate, many greetings.<-

**I**t is the opinion of wise men that a man occupied with weighty business should not be interrupted without a grave cause. For me, however, the "Platonic gravity" <note>A play on words: "gravity" meaning both seriousness and the weight of the work.</note> will now be a sufficiently serious reason to interrupt you; it is certainly enough that, as I believe you will easily admit, this Academy or library of ours is daily giving birth to a "Latin Plato," conceived long ago from Greek seed. But it cannot easily be born without the hand of a midwife; therefore, my Bernardo, apply the midwifery hands of the printers, so that they may now bring forth the offspring more maturely and shape what has been expressed. Farewell.

## *Friends do not exist unless one depends on the other.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, many greetings.<-

**Y**our letter, my Bandini, indicates your prosperous health to me, and indeed confirms my own. In turn, I respond for that reason: so that while I indicate my health to you, I may also confirm yours. Not without merit does one friend depend on the other, since one is truly within the other. Regarding our Bishop of Vác, <note>original: "Vaciensi." Referring to Miklós Báthory, the Bishop of Vác in Hungary, a patron of humanist learning.</note> what shall I say? Indeed, I have said enough just now when I spoke of us; accordingly, if I wish to explain my love toward him, I shall be very long-winded to others, but to myself, most brief. Therefore, lest others be weary of prolixity or I myself regret it, I shall be content only with the affection of brevity, since I cannot express it in speech.

## *Solitude is necessary for the learned.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Nero, <note>A member of the Florentine circle and an associate of the Platonic Academy.</note> a most candid man, many greetings.<-

**Y**ou yourself, along with our other friends, complain (as I suppose) that I have now been away from the city for a long time; but cease your complaining, for I am never less absent from the Academy than when I am absent from the city. Urban matters often distract me from you all, but rural ones restore me; here I am entirely yours and unburdened. For whether I walk about, I flourish everywhere for you and for myself; or if I sleep, your presence always brings our dreams back to me. Farewell, and give greetings to—but to whom? Indeed to no one specifically, for I would name everyone at once as "Academics." Again, fare well. April 1, 1483.

## *They do not truly love each other who do not constantly think of each other.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, <note>A wealthy patron and close friend of Ficino who funded the printing of Ficino’s Plato translation.</note> many greetings.<-

**Y**ou see, Filippo, that when I was about to write to a "Valori," I almost wrote to "Tarduccio." <note>Ficino is playing with names, likely referring to a shared identity or close association between friends.</note> What wonder is this? Truly, both are one to each other, and each is one to me. Thus it happens that whether I strike the lyre or sing songs, the one strikes and the other sings along. But hey, Valori, had we not decided to "rusticate together" <note>original: "corrusticari." A term Ficino used for scholarly retreats in the countryside to tend to the soul.</note> during these sacred days, not for the sake of cultivating the field, but for the sake of cultivating the soul? And by now we would have given each other our word, except that those who always live together cannot help but "rusticate" together. But here is the difference: with you as my guide, I was going to seek the fields of Maiano; <note>The location of a Rucellai villa.</note> but now, on the contrary, with myself as your guide, you have sought Careggi. <note>The site of the Medici villa and the heart of Ficino's Platonic Academy.</note> Since, however, there is a change in all things, soon I shall seek Maiano with you as leader. But let nothing be hidden from you: where you read "I," understand it as if under a larger "I" I meant Berlinghiero. <note>Berlinghiero Berlinghieri, another member of their circle.</note> I desire to return to you here laden with many greetings, which you may then pour out everywhere to our fellow Academics: to my fellow-godfather Boninsegni, to my fellow-godfather Guicciardini, and finally to all the brothers. Farewell.

Praise [to God]

# MARSILIO FICINO
## In Praise of the Platonic Philosopher.
### ->Marsilio Ficino to Pier Leoni, <note>Pier Leoni of Spoleto was a famous physician and a devoted member of Ficino's Platonic Academy; he later served as the personal doctor to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> his distinguished fellow-Platonist, many greetings.<-

**I**f the term "sophist" <note>In this context, a "sophist" is someone who uses clever but fallacious arguments, as opposed to a "sophos" or true wise man.</note> is derived from "wise man" by a certain lessening of the word, it is more just for the sophist to follow the wise man than the reverse. Therefore, my wise friend, do not seek the sophist any further; for he will soon (as is fitting) follow you. Farewell.

---

## All pains are born from the soul’s love for the body.
### ->Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, <note>A close friend and correspondent of Ficino, from a prominent Florentine family.</note> his most beloved, many greetings.<-

**T**hey say that Apollo, the fountain of medicine, fathered two sons in particular: Aesculapius and Plato—Aesculapius to heal bodies, but Plato to heal souls. The physicians who follow Aesculapius are accustomed to apply poultices and certain ointments to bodily pains, which they call *anodynes*, <term>anodyne: from the Greek "anodynos," meaning "without pain"; a medicine that relieves suffering.</term> that is, pain-relievers. The Academy, studious in the medicine of Plato, is also accustomed to apply a drug of this kind, like a pain-relieving poultice, to grieving souls; indeed, I use this above all others. I share this with my dearest friends, and if with my dearest, then certainly with Amerigo, the dearest of all. Where there is pain, there is love. Cast off love, and you will cast off pain. Cast off, I say—not the love of the Good itself, for far be it from me to command something either evil or impossible. Indeed, it is an evil not to love the Good itself, and it is impossible not to love that which you love by the necessity of nature. Therefore, I command you to cast off the love, not of the Good itself—which is the first, highest, and total Good—but of those individual things which are judged to be "goods" among men. Truly, to turn toward these things by loving them is nothing other than to turn away from the Good itself. To the extent that we turn away from Him (through whom alone these things are made good) and turn toward these things (which without Him are evils), to that extent are we plunged into evils. Again, where there is love, there is pain: specifically the love of these "goods" which can be delayed or taken away. If the possession of what we desire is delayed, pain burns and troubles us. If we possess what we know can be taken away in the meantime, pain distracts us; if what we sought and possessed is taken away, pain overwhelms us. Therefore, so that we are not compelled to suffer, let us love only the Good itself for its own sake, which alone is good through itself. Because of its infinite nature and power, it is never absent and thus cannot be delayed; it never fails and thus cannot be taken away. It never deserts any except those who desert it; it never leaves any except those who leave it. The seeking of the Infinite Good is not very laborious, for it is sought and found by the will alone. <margin>]</margin> Its possession is neither anxious nor suspicious, for it is retained by the same will by which it was sought and acquired. In loving and possessing this one thing, we embrace all things as "good"; but if this one thing is abandoned—by which alone all other things become good—all things everywhere turn into evils for us. Let us therefore cast off, let us cast off the affection that twists wretched men toward lower things, and let us put on the affection that lifts us to sublime things. <margin>1]</margin> For this will free us from evils, this will rescue us from pains, fill us with every good, and affect us with every joy: <margin>2]</margin> a joy, I say, that shall never be taken from us. These things, my dearest Amerigo, are applied briefly by us to the languors of the soul; the same are treated more broadly and elegantly by Plato, and more powerfully and divinely by the Sacred Scriptures. Farewell.

## An allegorical explanation of the Golden Age and others.
### ->Marsilio Ficino to Jacopo Antiquario, <note>Jacopo Antiquario was the influential secretary to the Duke of Milan and a noted patron of humanists.</note> Ducal Secretary, many greetings.<-

**O**thers, Jacopo, call you only "Antiquarian," but the Academy calls you both "Antiquarian" and "New-quarian," <note>original: "Antiquarium pariter & nouarium." A play on his last name, suggesting he doesn't just study the old (antiquity) but makes it new again.</note> as an innovator and cultivator of antiquity. What else do we think it means to "renew the ancient" than to recall those Golden Ages, happy under the former reign of Saturn? What, then, is Saturn among men? Or what is Jove? <note>original: "Iouem" (Jupiter).</note> Truly, since the Platonists distinguish the soul into three primary powers—namely, the power of understanding, of anger, <note>original: "irascendi." In Platonic psychology, this refers to the "spirited" part of the soul associated with courage and will.</note> and of desire—they divide the first power into two: that is, into a mind devoted primarily either to contemplation or to action. The contemplative mind they signify by the name of Saturn; but the mind occupied in actions they call Jove. Then, they judge the soul that is harder in its anger to be Mars, or softer in its pleasure to be Venus. Furthermore...

...they believe that under the first leader <note>original: "sub primo duce." Ficino is likely referring to Saturn, the ruler of the mythical Golden Age.</note> life is led both publicly and privately in a golden way—that is, it is precious, shining, and eternal. Under the second leader, life is silver; for just as silver follows gold in value, so too should action follow contemplation, like a handmaid observing her mistress. Furthermore, under the third leader, they believe life is led in an iron fashion, due to the harsh cruelty of arms. Finally, under the fourth, it is leaden; for lust and pleasure are like lead—softer, yet by their own weight they sink down to lower things. 

Just as those most empty-headed men commonly called Alchemists <note>Ficino often used alchemy as a metaphor for spiritual transformation while remaining skeptical of literal gold-making.</note> are as often deceived by their own opinions and frustrated by fortune as they attempt to smelt inferior metals into gold, so too for those who—to the best of their strength—subdue lust, anger, and action to contemplation, the matter itself succeeds daily according to their wish. Thus, in place of other metals, they bring back "gold"—that is, the most precious things in place of the useful, and eternal things in place of the fleeting. 

Proceed then, happy James, as you have begun: a cultivator of golden antiquity and Platonic contemplation. Favor the ancients as you do, favor the "golden" ones, and thus you shall be "golden" to us instead of merely an Antiquarian. Farewell happily, you who are dearer to the Academy than gold.

## Marsilio Ficino to Matthew of Forlì, Commissary of the Pope, sends greetings.

**T**he poets tell us that Jupiter once took the empire from his father Saturn. I, however, believe that in these times Mars <note>Mars represents war and conflict.</note> has usurped the kingdom of Jupiter <note>Jupiter represents law, order, and religious authority.</note> as if he were Saturn’s avenger. For, as the Astronomers say, religious men are signified and ruled by Jupiter. Yet daily, the goods of religious men are being transferred to "martial" men. But I wish that the celestial empire would change in turn, so that just as Jupiter long ago yielded to Mars, so too might Mars eventually be compelled to yield to Jupiter. Surely, only when Jupiter alone reigns can we hope that pious men will (so to speak) rule. 

And perhaps, unless astronomical reasoning deceives us, a great conjunction of the planets <note>original: "coniunctio Planetarum magna." This refers to the significant alignment of Jupiter and Saturn in 1484, which many Renaissance thinkers believed heralded a new era or religious shift.</note> will either accomplish this or, to speak more accurately, signify it within two years. Meanwhile, you commissaries, to whom the care of the pious flock is entrusted, keep that flock commended to you—a flock no less commended to you by God. We desire this from others, but from you, a man of remarkable piety, we now truly hope for it. Farewell. June 15, 1484.

## Marsilio Ficino to the most distinguished Lord Matthew of Forlì, Commissary of the Pope, sends many greetings.

**I**t is the opinion of our Plato that those souls especially which are more prone to love are able to recover the "wings" with which one flies back to heaven. <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as growing wings through the experience of beauty and love.</note> If it were permitted in a letter to assign reasons more accurately in the manner of those debating, I would indeed bring forward four reasons for this Platonic opinion at present. But truly, if even a lover is allowed to "swear falsely" <note>A play on the common poetic trope that the oaths of lovers are not punished by the gods.</note>, let a man speaking of love also be allowed to wander in his discourse. 

Therefore, the first cause of this matter is human, the second natural, the third celestial, and the fourth divine. It is human, I say, because love itself is the true foundation of friendship. Indeed, the power of friendship is so great that by this alone, even without any laws, the human race could live tranquilly and happily; yet if this is taken away, neither laws nor the other pursuits of men can make life blessed. I will pass over how sharp in invention, how powerful in eloquence, how manageable, pleasant, refined, and faithful love makes men in their reasoning and social habits. 

The natural reason is of this sort: certainly, a certain similarity is everywhere the cause of love. This is clearly seen in the stars, the elements, plants, and animals. Whoever, therefore, is most prone to loving men is surely judged to be the most similar of all to the very <term>Idea: In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" or "Form" is the eternal, perfect pattern in the divine mind upon which all earthly things are modeled.</term> of the human race, according to which the divine craftsman created mankind. Conversely, whoever is most alienated from love is both most unlike the divine Idea and most remote from the human species. 

The third reason, the celestial cause, we receive from the astronomers thus: men are usually more inclined to love when, in their birth chart <note>original: "in genesi."</note>, Venus and Mercury are so disposed that, on account of their mutual aspect or...

...entrance, reception, or end, they may take up the rudders of the mind with a harmonious will. Then, truly, Mercury—the master of wit and eloquence—transfers both to Venus, and Venus herself, the mother of grace, beauty, and faith, seasons that wit and eloquence with charm, adorns them with elegance, and forms them with truthful faith. For this reason, none are truly more acute or more elegant than lovers. 

However, we wish for it to be hidden from no one that lust, which pursues touch, is one thing; while love, which the Platonists judge to be content with sight, hearing, and contemplation, is quite another. Finally, there is a fourth divine reason, which the divine Plato proves extensively in the *Phaedrus* and the *Symposium*. Since the exemplary forms of all things exist in the divine mind, and certain shadows of them appear among us, nothing reflects the beauty of the Creator himself more expressively to us than created beauty. Nor does Plato think we can investigate divine wisdom and the other virtues of God through human wisdom or any other of our virtues as easily as we can find divine beauty through human beauty—and, once found, love it. 

Indeed, while the likeness of the other virtues in God may be compared to the Sun for our minds and perceived by them alone, the image of divine beauty pours itself through all things, and is clearly seen not only by the mind, but also by the eyes, which are the most piercing of all the senses. Hence, he considers that divine love arises from human love. Accordingly, he defines love as nothing other than the desire for beauty, and beauty as nothing other than grace; a grace, I say, implanted by the three Graces <note>In Greek mythology, the Charites (Graces) represent charm, beauty, and creativity. Ficino links them to specific planetary deities.</note>—that is, a grace primarily arising from three things and coming similarly from three deities. 

For Apollo <note>Associated with the Sun and music.</note> allures those who hear through the grace of musical harmony. Venus, however, ravishes those who look through the grace of color and shape. Finally, Mercury <note>Associated with the intellect and communication.</note> turns observers toward himself primarily through the wonderful grace of intelligence and eloquence, and inflames them with the love of divine contemplation and beauty. Because, in truth, it is not so much intelligence that tends to transport us into the thing we understand, as it is love that transports us into the thing we love. Therefore, our Plato thinks that by this very desire for divine beauty, rather than by the study of science or any other virtue, the mind—having received its wings—flies back to its homeland. 

What is the purpose of all this? To be sure, it is so that while you read this, you might not only understand our mind on this matter, but also that you might behold your own image in this description of the perfect lover, as if in a mirror. For while I am depicting both the legitimate lover and the pious friend, I wish to have expressed my Matthew <note>Matthew of Forlì, a friend and correspondent of Ficino.</note> to the best of my ability. Farewell.

->*An entreaty that the books of Plato, translated by us into Latin, be redeemed from the hands of the one who had hidden them.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Girolamo Cantiano,<-
->Orator of the Duke of Urbino.<-

**A**nniceris of Cyrene redeemed the divine Plato from slavery when he was sold in Aegina, and Archytas of Tarentum delivered him from destruction when he was placed in the greatest danger of his life in Sicily. But the "children" of Plato <note>Ficino is using "children" as a metaphor for his Latin translations of Plato's works.</note>, having left Greece when it was occupied by barbarians <note>A reference to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and the subsequent Ottoman rule.</note> and brought themselves into Italy, were by chance cast into prison, and (O, the wickedness!) they have been held in chains for two whole years. But look! Even now, Girolamo Cantiano—a man distinguished by his piety—will loosen them from their shackles and restore them to the light. Therefore, as much as Greece once owed to the Cyrenean and the Tarentine on behalf of Plato, so much will Italy owe to you, Cantiano, on behalf of Plato's books.
