<meta>This page concludes the current sequence of Ficino’s letters in Book VII. It follows a discussion on the Platonic view of beauty and love as the primary pathways to the divine. Here, Ficino shifts toward a more theological and mystical tone, interpreting the Psalms through a Neoplatonic lens to argue that the human "will" (love) rather than "intellect" (knowledge) is the true gate to God.</meta>

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VII.</header>
<page-num>863</page-num>

If God had made all things purely by a kind of naked intelligence, perhaps all things would both understand and would never stray from right intelligence. For by the very same property through which effects proceed from a cause, they represent their cause continually and stably, like an image impressed upon them by that cause. But since all created things possess knowledge, and those that have it often stray in their knowing—yet all things possess a natural affection <note>original: *affectum*; here meaning a natural drive, inclination, or "feeling" towards a goal</note> and do not stray in that very affection—it follows that all things were created by the Creator not so much through intelligence as through his will. 

This is indeed confirmed by the fact that just as things proceeded from their cause, so too are they turned back toward it. Since, therefore, all things are turned toward the good through affection and not through knowledge, it follows that all things proceeded from the Good through affection; and just as they proceeded by his affection, so they are everywhere turned back by that same drive. For what we call "appetite" <note>the natural desire or striving for fulfillment</note> in things signifies nothing other than a "passion"—that is, a pull or attraction inflicted upon all things by the First Cause itself. 

But those who see things being carried along but do not see the One who is drawing them are as deceived as those who might think iron seeks a magnet of its own accord, simply because they cannot see the magnet anywhere. From this it is clear that the divine will is the gate through which minds go out while they are being created, and again the gate through which those same minds return while they are being recreated. 

Therefore, to the musical Psaltery of David, the sacred poet, that true and almighty Phoebus <note>original: *Phœbus*; the Greek name for Apollo, the god of light and music, here used as a metaphor for God</note> from on high thunders to our minds: *Lift up your gates, O you princes, and be lifted up, you eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter.* <note>A reference to Psalm 24:7</note> O princes—O minds that are the princes of bodies, princes of the animals whom I have made a little lower than the angels, whom I have crowned with honor and glory, whom I have placed forever over the works of my hands—lift up your gates! Lift your wills upward! O eternal gates, O eternal wills created from eternity and capable of eternal things: do not open yourselves to receive lower things, whose entry would infect you; open yourselves to receive higher things, which will refresh you by their entry. 

Then, surely, I will enter through you as the King of Glory—the King, I say, of both light and joy. I will mark the light of my countenance upon your intellects, but I will give you my joy. I am the gate through which whoever does not enter is a thief and a robber. My will is the gate through which you all went out; your will is the gate through which you will all return to me. I am a fire that consumes and perfects. I consume matter but I perfect form; I consume material deformity but I perfect spiritual beauty. 

Consider what fire does everywhere: fire illuminates and it warms. But that which is illuminated by fire does not become fire simply because it receives the fire's light, but because it receives its heat. Similarly, like a fire, I illuminate intellects and I ignite wills. You do not escape into divine power simply because you seek my light through the faculty of understanding alone, but because you seek my heat through the burning of the will. 

Acknowledge therefore the greatness of love! For I created you by my love, and you too, by your love—love for me, I say—will recreate yourselves in me. I, by love, made you into "minds"; but you, by the love of God, will one day remake yourselves as "Gods." Then I shall say: *You too are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.* <note>A reference to Psalm 82:6</note>

->T H E   E N D.<-

# THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO
## the Florentine, to Filippo Valori,
### a Magnificent Man.

#### PREFACE.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Filippo Valori, the most noble<-
->heir to the virtue of Valori.<-

Since I had often attempted, my dearest Valori, to place a "head" <note>original: *caput*; Ficino is punning on the word, which can mean a "head," a "chapter," or the "completion" of a task</note> upon the eighth book of my letters, and was in no way able to do so, I finally as a suppliant besought the Divine Power to supply me with at least enough "valour" <note>original: *valoris*; here meaning strength, worth, or power</note> as would suffice for adding this "head." It was certainly a most fortunate prayer. For indeed, while I was wishing for "valour" to apply the "head," Valori himself has meanwhile become the "head" for me. 

Greetings, therefore, most sweet head of my book—or rather, of my child <note>original: *liberi*; a common Latin pun where *liber* means "book" and *liberi* means "children." Ficino viewed his writings as his offspring</note>—by whom my book is led and by whom it lives; or rather, by whom many of my children now live. Most opportunely, the House of Medici has long breathed life into them, and now the House of Valori breathes life into them as well. For indeed, these families desire exactly the same things everywhere, and Valori himself immediately follows the "medical" help <note>original: *opem medicam*; another pun on the name of the Medici family, who were Ficino’s primary patrons</note> with the gift of "prosperous health." May Almighty God always breathe upon the happiness of both families and preserve this ancient concord. Read happily, and live happily together with your most elegant brother Niccolò; and pray, invite the excellent academician Antonio Lanfredini to this reading, not merely as a reader, but as a judge.

# THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO
## the Florentine,
### BOOK VIII.

#### A thanksgiving for the Platonic books redeemed from an occupier by Girolamo.
->Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo, Ambassador of the Duke of Urbino, sends greetings.<-

I was just thinking, Girolamo, of giving you thanks through a letter because you have liberated the divine Plato from a certain long-lasting prison and harsh shackles. But the guardian spirit <note>term: *genius*; the protective spirit or divine spark associated with a person or their work</note> of Plato himself rebuked me with almost these words: "Do you truly, Marsilio, value your own eloquence so highly, and my liberty so little, that you trust you can increase the thanks owed to Girolamo for my liberation?" I myself shall greet my Girolamo; I myself shall both give thanks and return the favor. For I shall number him among my own academicians, and I shall now name him as my third liberator, after Anniceris and Archytas <note>Anniceris and Archytas were historical figures who famously rescued Plato from slavery and political imprisonment in Sicily</note>. Thus, Girolamo, hear now the spirit of Plato sounding to me in this volume as if in his own body.

#### Love does not suffer absence.
->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Pietro Compagni, sends greetings.<-

I only first began to suspect you were absent from here when I was reading your letter, in which you asked when I was going to set out to see you. Truly, I would have arrived there long ago if I had sensed you were away from here. At the moment, I set out to visit others because I love them less; I do not set out to the academician <note>meaning Pietro himself</note> because I love him too much—and so I embrace him that I do not allow him to leave. Farewell.

# LETTERS, BOOK VIII

### Preface to the Fables.

->Marsilio Ficino to Georgius Cyprius, his dearest fellow-godfather and most excellent physician, sends greetings.<-

**W**hen several learned men were talking at your dinner table about the fables <note>original: *Apologis*; these refers to the *Apologi*, a collection of short fables or moral tales written by Bartolomeo Scala</note> of our most elegant writer, Scala, they demanded a judgment on them from me especially, since I had recently read them. I said, "Every fable of our Scala seems to me both elegant and masculine." At this, they both smiled and mocked me. They smiled at "elegant," as if it were an elegantly expressed thought, but they mocked "masculine," as if the word were used improperly. I, therefore, (with you as my judge) affirm that I called Scala’s fables "masculine" not only properly, but most truly. For who could rightly deny they are masculine, when they, with a single breath, rendered me—who was previously sterile in such matters—so fertile that I gave birth to many "fable-children" in almost the same labor? This is further confirmed by the fact that after those men departed from our home, no more fables have been born among us. Those, however, which were born to us then, I commend to you—as if they were quite weak due to my prior sterility—to be nurtured by you as a fellow-godfather, and to be cherished and strengthened by you as a physician. Farewell, my dearest fellow-godfather and best physician, and may you read with joy.

---

### A lover's excuse for silence when we do not respond to the letters of friends.

->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, sends many greetings.<-

**W**e received your letter some time ago, my dear Valori—a letter shared not only with me, but also with Pietro Nero, Filippo Carducci, and finally all the members of our Academy. Thus, it is no wonder that none of us has yet responded to the letter, while each day we assumed one of the others was about to respond. To this is added the fact that a certain dialectician <note>a philosopher specializing in logic</note> from the Academy, hearing us being reproached because we seemed to think little of our Valori’s letter (which is full of "valour") <note>original: *ualoris plenam*; Ficino is punning on the name Valori and the Latin word *valor*, meaning worth, strength, or value</note> by such a long silence, began to argue in roughly this manner: "It can easily be shown, friends, that not we, but Filippo himself has been the cause of this long silence; wherefore he rather than any of us should be reproached. Surely, if Filippo is 'Valori' [our Worth], he is certainly our 'valour' [strength]. Again, if he himself is our strength, then he is surely our ability to act. But if he is our 'Valour,' it follows that while he is absent, we ourselves have no 'valour' [strength] at all. Therefore, let 'Valour' return, and our voice will suddenly return. He gives us our talent, and he takes it away." When the dialectician had concluded these points, all the others immediately agreed with most joyful applause. Only one man, a bit more curious in his arguing, began to challenge not the love for you (which is shared by all and held by each), but the very form of the argument. But all the others, turning to him and imposing silence, concluded that "lover’s conclusions," no matter how or from where they are derived, must not be dissolved but must be confirmed with all one's might. Therefore, fare well, our Valori [our Strength], and fly back to us.

---

### How individuals have guardian angels.

->Marsilio Ficino to Philippus Callimachus.<-

**I**t is the opinion of the Platonists, my dear fellow-Platonist Callimachus, that there are as many legions of daemons <note>original: *dæmonum*; in the Platonic tradition, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or "genius" guides that connect the divine to the human</note> around the earth as there are gods (that is, stars) in heaven. They hold that each legion contains as many daemons as there are stars in the sky, and that there are twelve princes of daemons just as there are twelve signs in the Zodiac. Furthermore, they believe some are Saturnian, others Jovian, others Martial, or Solar. Similarly, they classify and name various daemons according to both the name and the power of the other stars. They add, moreover, that there are as many orders of human souls as there are stars and legions of daemons, and that different souls receive the nature, duty, and name of different daemons and stars. These daemons they call "genii" <note>the *genius* was the personal protective spirit of a person</note>—the noble leaders of our natural talent <note>original: *duces ingenij*; Ficino puns on the shared root of *genius* and *ingenium* (inborn talent)</note>—assigned to individual souls by the law of fate (that is, by the divine law itself) at the moment when the souls descend into the bod-

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Marsilio Ficino. It concludes a letter to the scholar Filippo Callimachus (Buonaccorsi) regarding the nature of guardian spirits, follows with a brief commendation to the Venetian ambassadors to the Pope, and begins a significant philosophical letter to Braccio Marcello regarding the harmony between the teachings of Moses and Plato.</meta>

<page-num>866</page-num>

# MARSILIO FICINO

...into the body, by the disposition and influence of all the spheres, they are accommodated to us. So long as our minds do not obey certain lower <term>demons</term> <note>Ficino uses 'demon' in the classical sense of a *daimon*—a mediating spirit or guardian, rather than a purely evil entity.</note> and their fetters, our minds are led daily by a kind of easy and hidden persuasion, almost in the way that ships are steered by a pilot. But enough of these matters for now. For here this letter calls me back, whose humanity and humility hardly admit such sublime contemplations. You admit these things in words (as I hear), my dear Callimachus, as a follower of our Plato; but, as I see, you do not confirm all these things in actual fact. For you do not sufficiently affirm that each person has but a single good demon, since you yourself quite clearly have many good ones. At one time, he prefers an Apolline demon for poets, at another, a Mercurial one for orators. At another time, he prefers a Saturnian one for Philosophy, and at another, a Jovian one for gravity. Always, he prefers a Martial one for magnanimity, and a Venereal one for humanity and refinement, so that we might rightly nickname our Callimachus "Polidaemon" <note>original: *Polidæmon*; Greek for "one of many spirits."</note>. Greetings, then, and greetings again, Callimachus Polidaemon! Indeed, greetings as many times as you, by obeying good demons, meanwhile master the evil ones; and as many times as you, fighting nobly—as the name **Callimachus** <note>original: *Callimachus*; Greek for "noble/beautiful fighter."</note> sounds—also conquer nobly. What wonder is it that you bring back victory from every contest? For if Ulysses by a single demon (namely a Mercurial one), Achilles by a Martial one, and Aeneas by a Venereal one escaped safe from many dangers, you will surely go most safely everywhere under the faithful guardianship of many.

->Marsilio Ficino highly commends himself to Sebastiano Badoer and Bernardo Bembo,<-
->most illustrious Ambassadors of the Venetians to the Supreme Pontiff.<-

**S**o that you may approach the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> under more certain auspices, intending to strengthen the public concord of all Italy in his presence (which he desires), carry with you the concord between the divine law and the most excellent philosophers among the Gentiles. And humbly commend your Marsilio, a most devoted servant, to the Supreme Pontiff.

->*The Concord of Moses and Plato.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Marcello, most adorned in letters and character, sends greetings.<-

**N**umenius the Pythagorean, whom Origen places before not only the Pythagoreans but almost all philosophers, having read both the books of Moses and the Platonists, said that he recognized Moses in Plato, and that Plato was nothing other than another Moses speaking in the Attic language <note>The dialect of ancient Athens.</note>. Therefore, those who call you, best Braccio, to the Academy, do not exhort you so much to the Platonic discipline as to the Mosaic law. For when you first enter the Academy, **Parmenides** will meet you, who will demonstrate that there is one God containing or producing the **ideas** <note>The eternal forms or blueprints of all things in the mind of God.</note> of all things, that is, the exemplars and reasons, in the most eminent degree. **Melissus** and **Zeno** will meet you, to demonstrate that only God truly exists, while other things only seem to exist. **Timaeus** will come to meet you, showing that the world was created by God for the sake of His own goodness, and that God created the heaven and the earth from the beginning, then poured the airy spirit over the waters, and that all these things shall remain so long as it pleases the divine will. He will show that God made man so much in His own likeness that He established him as the sole worshiper of God on earth and the master of earthly things. In that same place, the **Statesman**, **Protagoras**, **Menexenus**, and **Critias** will present themselves to you, discussing how men were created from the earth at the beginning of things by the power of God and placed under the perpetual guardianship of divine spirits; how they received the law from a certain sole messenger of God, and finally, after the course of the world, shall rise again from the earth at God’s command.

There **Philebus**, **Theaetetus**, the **Phaedo**, the **Phaedrus**, and **Socrates** teach that our happiness lies in the likeness and enjoyment of God alone. You will hear a certain **Athenian Elder** <note>The 'Athenian Stranger,' the main speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> asserting that the world was disposed by the Word of God, and that God is the measure of all things—especially if God should become man—striking down the proud as rebels against God, but approving the humble as most dear to God; finally, proclaiming to all that whether they descend into hell or ascend into heaven, they will find the divine judge everywhere. You will hear **Hermias**, **Erastus**, and **Coriscus** being taught there that God [is the cause] of all things...

<summary>Ficino argues for the "Perennial Philosophy," claiming that Plato’s teachings are essentially a Greek version of the Mosaic law and Christian theology. He maps various Platonic dialogues onto biblical themes such as creation, the Word (Logos), and divine judgment.</summary>
<keywords>Platonism, Moses, Numenius, Polidaemon, concord, creation, divine judgment, guardian spirits, Athenian Stranger, Logos</keywords>

It develops the "pious philosophy" argument, attempting to show that the major tenets of Christian theology—the Trinity, the immortality of the soul, the fall of man, and the necessity of a Savior—were prefigured in the writings of Plato and his followers.</meta>

# LETTERS, BOOK VIII.

...that the leader and cause of all things is at once the Father and the Son, and that the highest good is established in the singular love of Him. You will be taught, moreover, in the writings to **Dionysius** <note>Ficino refers to the *Letters of Plato*, specifically those addressed to Dionysius of Syracuse, which were highly regarded in the Renaissance as mystical texts.</note>, that all things exist around the King of all for the sake of His grace, and that He is the cause of all good things. Further, you will learn that the blessed spirits are distinguished in this order: some reflect the power of God or the efficient cause, others His wisdom as the exemplar, and others His goodness as the end of all things. Finally, the **Syracusans** are taught that divine mysteries cannot be grasped by reason, but that through purity of mind we are at last made most like unto God; so that, like a light suddenly flashing from a sparking fire, a light may shine in the soul and henceforth nourish itself.

Next, you will behold **Er the Pamphylian** <note>A character from the "Myth of Er" at the end of Plato's *Republic* who returns from the dead to explain the afterlife.</note> rising from the dead by divine command, to report the secrets of souls to the living. He will lead you through the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the dwelling place of the blessed; Ficino identifies this with the Christian Paradise.</note>, which our people signify by the name of **Paradise**. He will also point his finger to the underworld, the cave of **purgatory**, and **Limbo** <note>original: *Lymbũ*; Ficino is mapped Christian geography onto Plato’s underworld.</note>. **Socrates** will confirm these same things for you there with many arguments, teaching that we must have much more care for eternity than for time. He teaches that fleeting things are to be despised so that we may attain eternal ones, and that it is better to suffer even the gravest injuries than to inflict them. Nothing else is to be sought or striven for, except that we may offer a most pure soul to the Judge who sees all things. Therefore, he will prove that confession and the voluntary repentance of sins are necessary above all for the salvation of men; but he will command that one must hasten toward this especially, lest an old disease of the soul should become altogether inseparable. Finally, he will warn us to be carried across the sea of this life upon the very ship of exact reason, until at last we are conveyed more safely and happily by the **Divine Word**. There, **Laches** <note>A character from Plato's dialogues, here associated with moral discipline.</note> will also exhort us to frequent confession of faults and to repentance.

But why had I passed over the noble **Charmides**? For he will reveal to you, **Braccio**, that all the inconveniences of both the body and of fortune proceed from a certain ancient intemperance of our souls. He will add, in turn, that if that original purity of souls were restored, immortality would also be restored. Finally, **Critias**, in the very inner sanctums of the **Academy**, will proclaim like a **Mosaic oracle** <note>A reference to Ficino's belief that Plato was a "Moses speaking Greek" (*Moyses Atticus*).</note>: that when God had at last created man as the inhabitant of the world (as **Protagoras** also said), He made him on earth most like Himself and filled him with a certain nourishing grace. As long as this grace remained, man would perpetually enjoy all the goods of the soul, the body, and fortune; God placed him in His gardens under a perpetual Spring, where he would prolong a happy life by the tasting of a small amount of wholesome fruit. He moreover fenced in the gardens lest anything foreign should enter. 

But when man turned aside little by little from divine things to fleeting ones, and obeyed the paternal laws less and less every day, that divine grace departed. Therefore, he fell into a shameful habit of soul, diseases of the body, the anxieties of life, and labors; and at last, he was translated from those gardens to regions that were utterly dissimilar. **Timaeus**, **Phaedrus**, and **Diotima** will testify in the Academy that this unhappily occurred through the ambush of a certain evil **demon** <note>Here used in the sense of a malevolent spirit or tempter, mirroring the Serpent in Eden.</note> under the bait of an insolent pleasure. But, to return to **Critias**, he will conclude for you that when God at last utterly disapproved of this human handiwork of His—since it had gradually turned from divine to profane—in order to both purge its malice and restore its purity, He washed the earth with a vast flood of waters.

Nor indeed should that golden sentence of **Plato**, the leader of the Academy, be omitted, where he says one should acquiesce to his precepts only until someone more sacred than man appears on earth to open the fountain of truth to all, whom everyone should then follow. Thus far Plato, and those who speak with the tongue of Plato. 

Furthermore, **Plotinus** and **Philo** command that the Divine Intellect be worshipped as the **Son of God**, flowing from God the Father Himself, either as a word from a speaker or as light from a light. Indeed, **Iamblichus** confirms this by the testimony of the **Egyptians**, most openly naming God the Father and the Son of Himself. He counts the angels, archangels, and principalities, which **Proclus** also distributes into a ninefold number <note>The "Nine Choirs of Angels," a classification commonly attributed to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, and he brings forward the **Chaldean Oracles** in which the paternal power in God, the intellect flowing from the Father, and a fiery love are expressed. 

But what shall I say of **Amelius**? He admires and gathers the whole of that prologue of the **Gospel of John**—which is read daily in the sacred rites—into a few words. Such are their views. But you, **Martello**, after you have entered the Academy and received these mysteries from these heroes within, as well as many more and greater things than a letter can hold, perhaps you will cry out with the voice of **Peter**:

->It is good to be here; let us make three thousand<-
->tabernacles.<- <note>A playful expansion of Peter's words at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:4), suggesting the vast number of "dwelling places" or truths found in the Platonic/Christian synthesis.</note>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that Platonic philosophy mirrors Christian truths, including the Trinity, the Garden of Eden, the Fall of Man, and the Great Flood. He presents the Neoplatonists and Plato himself as witnesses to the eventual coming of Christ, the "Divine Word."</summary>

# Confirmation of Christians through Socratic Matters.

->Marsilio Ficino to Paolo Ferobanti, distinguished theologian, sends many greetings.<-

**U**nless I feared, most excellent Paul, that there would be some who—either through the perversity of their nature or a lack of judgment—might interpret our words in a sense other than we intended, I would demonstrate in detail that Socrates (if not in the exact figure of John the Baptist) perhaps prefigured Christ, the author of our salvation, by a certain foreshadowing. I would do this primarily to confound that detractor, **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD) was a Syrian satirist known for mocking both traditional Greek religion and the early Christians, whom he viewed as gullible simpletons.</note>, who, after slandering everyone else, did not spare the good Christians. He dared to mock the martyrs of our faith because, being "too simple," they willingly lost all that men hold to be good, and like "unfortunates," they voluntarily exposed themselves to torture and slaughter. To Lucian, who mocks the simple, we must present Socrates—the wisest of all men, judged so both by the testimony of great philosophers and by the **Oracle of Apollo** <note>The Pythia at Delphi famously declared that no man was wiser than Socrates.</note>. Yet he, not out of some crude simplicity, but through a singular excellence of mind and (as Plato and Xenophon testify) a certain innate divinity and prophetic power, preferred eternal goods to fleeting ones throughout his whole life. He voluntarily endured physical hardships—especially hunger and nakedness—and all the misfortunes of fate. He was terrified only by the evil of the soul and eternal loss, intent solely on the duty of piety and charity. Indeed, neglecting his own comforts and held back by no danger, he applied himself everywhere within his fatherland to the purging of men’s minds, like a **physician of souls** <note>original: "animorum medicus"</note>. He detested pride above all else, while approving of gentleness, charity, and religion more than anything. He professed only the pursuit of true love and charity, and excluded the ambitious profession of the sciences. He relied everywhere upon divine testimonies and clung to them with firm faith, content with pious and just morals. And what is most marvelous: he hoped for no human reward for such a laborious duty, but subjected himself to certain danger and death because of it. Truly, he asserted that he was sent by God for this one purpose, and said that he preferred to obey God rather than men.

But let us hear Socrates himself for a moment, crying out thus before his unjust judges: *That I am such a person as to have been granted to the city by God, you may perceive from this: it does not seem humanly possible that I should have utterly neglected all my own affairs, and remained in this neglect of my household and in poverty for so many years, always intent on your good, meeting each of you like a father or an older brother, persuading you to take care for virtue. If I were receiving any payment for my duty, there would be a human explanation for it.* <note>Ficino is paraphrasing Socrates' defense from Plato's *Apology*.</note> Thus he spoke. And so, while he rebukes sinners, and—having been struck with a heel—he greets the one who struck him, and being struck on one cheek, he offers the other. Finally, he brought such hatred upon himself for the sake of the truth that he was accused of impiety by the very people to whom he had openly preached the duty of piety. What shall I say of the fact that, when he could easily have defended himself in court, he did not, nor did he excuse himself, but rather accused the judges? And when he could have left the prison, he refused, and sustained an unjust death most willingly, destined to give examples of the highest constancy and patience to posterity.

I pass over for the present the **price of thirty coins** <note>original: "triginta nummorum precium." Ficino is drawing a direct parallel between the fine proposed at Socrates' trial and the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas.</note> placed upon Socrates, and Socrates’ own prophecies, and the divine vengeance that followed immediately after his death. I pass over the **Washing** <note>original: "Lotionem." Socrates bathed before his death to save the women the trouble of washing his corpse; Ficino likens this to Christian ritual or the Last Supper.</note> performed by Socrates in the evening shortly before his death, and his exhortation to piety at the hour of supper. What of the fact that in that same hour mention is made of a **cup** <note>The cup of hemlock.</note> and a blessing, and at the moment of death, mention of a **cock**? <note>Socrates’ famous last words were "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius." Ficino likely links this to the rooster of St. Peter or a symbol of the resurrection/healing.</note> I pass over, moreover, many things both done and said by Socrates, written down not by himself but by his four principal disciples, by which the Christian faith is greatly confirmed against Lucian. For there are many things—and indeed the greatest things—recorded concerning the divine power infused in him, the abstraction of his mind from the body, and even a certain **transfiguration**. <note>original: "transfiguratione"</note> But a letter could not easily contain these things, nor would some people perhaps receive them kindly, thinking perhaps that Socrates

->is now being compared as a rival, rather than<-
->as a defender.<-

<summary>In this letter, Ficino argues that Socrates was a "foreshadowing" of Christ, comparing his poverty, his role as a "physician of souls," and the specific details of his trial and death to the Gospel accounts to defend Christianity against pagan critics like Lucian.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Jesus Christ, Lucian of Samosata, prefiguration, martyrdom, Apology of Socrates, 30 pieces of silver, last supper, pagan-Christian synthesis, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

### *In which praise consists of principles.*
## ->Marsilio Ficino to Galeotto, Prince of Faenza, sends many greetings.<-

**M**y friend Alamanno <note>Alamanno Donati, a close friend and student of Ficino.</note> recently asked me to set out for Faenza, a journey I am already inclined to take of my own accord. Indeed, for a long time now—at the command of **Plato**—something has been prophesied to me from on high. That which Plato failed to achieve during his third journey to Sicily <note>Plato famously traveled to Syracuse three times to attempt to turn the tyrant Dionysius II into a "philosopher-king," but the mission failed disastrously.</note>, I shall attain immediately upon this, my first journey: I shall find a man who is a prince of himself before he is a prince of his people; a man who is not so much a lord as he is the father of his country. He is one who inhabits not only the citadels of **Mars** <note>The god of war.</note>, but also those of **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>; who reflects Mars among his soldiers, yet acts as **Apollo** <note>The god of music and poetry.</note> among the Muses. O happy city! O truly named **Faenza**! <note>Ficino is making a pun on the name *Fauentia* and the Latin word *fauere* (to favor). He suggests the city is "Favored" because God has looked upon it with favor by providing such a prince.</note> God has looked upon you with such miraculous favor that He has made you happy through the favor of a most happy prince.

### *An excuse for a service not rendered.*
## ->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow Platonist, sends greetings.<-

**F**or the same reason that you desire to receive the Platonic books from us, we are currently compelled to keep them. If ever the opportunity to comply is granted, I shall do so most willingly and of my own accord. I grieve indeed—believe me—because of our singular and mutual love, both that you often desire things I cannot provide, and that I am not always able to provide what you desire. Farewell.

### *He who commends everyone should be commended by everyone.*
## ->Marsilio Ficino to Bandini.<-

**I**f anyone deserves to be honored by everyone, it is undoubtedly the man who himself honors everyone. Therefore, all men owe honor to the poet **Verrino** <note>Michele Verino (1469–1487), a brilliant young poet and student of Ficino who died at the age of 17.</note>. For he is so grateful and so gracious that he honors with great gratitude those to whom he is indebted, and honors freely even those to whom he owes nothing. He favors the good, exalts talent, adorns the learned, brings renown to princes, cherishes the saints, and venerates God in all things. What more can I say? You should hear him for yourselves. For he who praises everyone will himself be praised in everyone. Unless you feel a sense of recommendation for a man to whom all upright men are commended, I do not know whom you could ever hold in high regard. Farewell.

### *Praise of Charity.*
## ->Marsilio Ficino to Hermolao Barbaro of Venice, sends greetings.<-

**C**harity <term>Charity (Latin: *caritas*): In this context, it refers to the highest form of Christian love—selfless, divine, and communal—rather than merely giving alms.</term> seeks not its own, but the things of another; charity believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity thinks no evil, charity never fails; finally, in charity there is no fear, but perfect charity drives out all fear. <note>original: "Charitas nō quærit, quæ sua sunt...". Ficino is quoting directly from the Apostle Paul’s famous passage on Love in 1 Corinthians 13.</note> These things the high priests of our divine religion proclaim with simple words but with a certain immense mystery. You, most kind **Barbaro**, perhaps observe all these things toward me just as you do toward yourself, so that I do not doubt that this very charity—which the fathers of Christian piety desire above all else—burns brightly within you. 

Truly, my most beloved Hermolao, I call God Himself to witness—Who is Charity itself—that you have so expressed the very **Idea of Charity** within yourself and placed it before my eyes, that I, who hitherto loved you as much as I could as a free man, am now compelled to love you beyond my strength and by necessity. Until now, I was able not to love you [so intensely] and to endure your absence. But from now on, I cannot help but love you, and I cannot bear your absence with a calm mind as I used to. I hope, however, that God, who has wonderfully joined our souls, will eventually join our eyes in person as well. 

Nor do we wish anyone to think that Hermolao and Marsilio are or will be any less joined simply because one [Hermolao] appears to favor **Aristotle**, while the other [Ficino] favors **Plato**. For we are one in the same cultivation of truth and virtue, in which Plato and Aristotle themselves could not fail to be one. Continue, therefore, most Latin and most **Attic** <note>Refers to the pure, elegant style of ancient Athens.</note> Barbaro, as you have begun: strenuously rescue the "Attic Aristotle" from long-standing barbarism. <note>Hermolao Barbaro was a humanist scholar famous for translating Aristotle directly from the Greek, attempting to strip away the "barbaric" (clunky or inaccurate) Latin translations used by medieval Scholastic philosophers.</note> I, for my part, shall [rescue] our Plato...

<header>THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...from a certain forgetfulness of Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld. Ficino often uses this image to describe the "sleeping" state of ancient wisdom before the Renaissance.</note>, or rather, I have been awakened from sleep with all my strength. It has been so divinely ordained that, through my labor and yours, the Latin people may now, for the first time, hear **Plato** speaking and **Aristotle** speaking in Latin.

### One should not demand more from a friend than he possesses.
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini, sends many greetings.<-

**D**o you think, most just Aurelio, that I have done enough for you if I am yours as often as I am my own? I certainly think it is enough. For I know your fairness and modesty, and that you will demand no more of me than I have of myself. Until now, I have not been under "Marsilian law," but rather "Platonic law" <note>Ficino puns on his own name, Marsilio, suggesting he has not belonged to himself but has been a "subject" or "slave" to the work of translating Plato.</note>. Having been long devoted to the interpretation of this man, yesterday at last (with God’s help) I completed the Platonic work. Now, having first been returned to myself, I am likewise restored to my friends. You sent many poems to us last spring, composed partly by you and partly by your friends, in which I praise the human art, marvel at the Apolline fury <note>term: Apolline fury. In Platonic thought, this is *divine madness* or poetic inspiration granted by the god Apollo.</note>, and greatly approve of your piety toward the deceased. I give you immense thanks for this immense gift.

### Commendation of the Platonic books.
->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, sends many greetings.<-

**O**ur Plato finally comes to you through the pious efforts of Filippo Valori; and certainly, without a singular "valor," <note>Ficino is making a pun on his patron’s name, Filippo Valori, and the Latin word *valor*, meaning worth or courage.</note> he would never have been able to travel across such vast stretches of land. Therefore, come now, my fellow Platonist Bandini: as much as I love you, and as much as you love me, honor Plato as you usually do. And if Plato, as a traveler once again, has need of hospitality, be his host. Again, if he has need of a herald because he is little known in that place, be his herald. If, finally, he should need protection while trembling among adversaries, be his patron.

### An excuse for when a shorter response is given to friends.
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino, sends many greetings.<-

**N**o one looks upon the letters of friends more joyfully, or responds more eagerly, than Marsilio, to whom nothing is pleasing without friends. However, as to why I have only now barely returned one letter for your two, that great Platonist **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus was a 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino translated his works after finishing Plato's.</note> is the cause. Since he recently learned that his master Plato had arrived in Italy (with me as his guide, or rather, his translator), he urges me diligently day and night not to allow Plato to wander among the Italians any longer without his "faithful Achates" <note>note: original: "fido Achate". In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Achates was the famously loyal companion of the hero Aeneas. Ficino views Plotinus as the necessary companion to Plato's philosophy.</note>. I am therefore applying myself so vehemently to this great work that I sometimes scarcely remember myself. As soon as Plotinus restores me to myself, he will restore me to my friends.

### An excuse for when a shorter response is given to friends.
->Marsilio Ficino to Callimachus, sends many greetings.<-

**I** have received your letters, Callimachus <note>Filippo Buonaccorsi, an Italian humanist who took the name Callimachus and lived in Poland.</note>, which dispute subtly and elegantly concerning demons <note>term: demons (*daemones*). In the Neoplatonic sense, these are not necessarily "evil" spirits, but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>, and these letters are indeed quite "demonic" <note>A pun meaning both "about demons" and "inspired by a genius spirit."</note>. But see how demonic you are, my friend—or rather, how divine. For while you contend that a man cannot be occupied by a demon, you demonstrate in the meantime that you yourself are most occupied by a demon, and a divine one at that. I would most gladly discuss this matter with you at greater length, if our Plotinus did not call me back to his interpretation at every moment. Therefore, while Plotinus detains me, let Plato—having set out to you by our labor—speak with you in Latin; let him also give you great thanks for your gifts, while I myself remain immortally grateful. Farewell.
->April 18, 1485.<-

### That we must proceed by whatever way God leads.
->Marsilio Ficino to Francisco Bandino, sends many greetings.<-

**I** believe the **Plato** you requested, Bandino, has already reached you before these letters; therefore, read him happily in the meantime, while I give my effort so that, once you have read Plato, you may have **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino viewed him as the primary interpreter of Plato’s hidden mysteries.</note> to read. Our Plotinus, easily the leader of the Platonists along with his own Plato, composed fifty-four divine books. At this very hour (God breathing upon me), I have set the final hand to his thirtieth book. Thus indeed Almighty God commands; by this way Divine Providence leads us, and therefore by this way let us follow.

---

### Doubt: Whether philosophical works are governed by fate or providence.
->Ioannes Pannonius <note>original: "Ioannes Pannonius" refers to Janus Pannonius (1434–1472), a famous Hungarian poet and Bishop of Pécs who studied in Italy.</note> to Marsilio Ficino the Platonist, sends many greetings.<-

**I** have read at Buda, in your letter to Bandino, as well as in your preface to Plato and the preface to your *Theology*, how much you attribute to providence what someone else might suspect belongs to fate. First, I do not see to what purpose this renewal of the ancient Theology serves providence; furthermore, I remember once when I had set out for Italy to be instructed in Latin and Greek literature at Florence, I heard from two of your astrologers that, because of a certain position of the stars, you would renew the ancient opinions of the philosophers. Although I heard this position of the stars, I do not recall it well enough, but I think you remember it—indeed, that you discovered it yourself. Those astrologers also brought forth to confirm their judgment the fact that at a fated time you restored to the light the ancient sound of the lyre, and the singing and Orphic poems <note>term: Orphic poems. Mystical hymns attributed to the legendary Orpheus, which Ficino famously sang while playing a "lyre" decorated with an image of Orpheus.</note> previously consigned to oblivion; soon after, you also translated the most ancient **Hermes Trismegistus**, and many Pythagorean works. Likewise, you explained the poems of **Zoroaster**, and before I returned here from Florence, you had laid your hand to translating Plato—under those same astronomical auspices (as I indeed suspect). Moreover, there is also this argument that these things are done by you not so much by providence as by a certain fate: that before all these things, while still a youth, you lightly promoted a certain ancient philosopher or poet, whom you afterwards suppressed, relying on better counsel, and (as I hear) you withdrew him with all your might. Nor had that been a gift of divine providence, which you yourself, having become more prudent with age, rightly judged should be condemned. Indeed, friend, I warn you to be careful lest this renewal of the ancients be perhaps a certain curiosity rather than religion. <note>Pannonius is referring to Ficino’s early interest in the Roman poet Lucretius and Epicurean philosophy, which Ficino later renounced and allegedly burned his commentaries on because they were atomistic and denied the immortality of the soul.</note>

---

### That divine providence ordained the renewal of ancient things.
->Marsilio Ficino to Ioannes Pannonius, sends many greetings.<-

**I**f you had understood our writings which you say you read, you would not now doubt by what primary reasoning this renewal of ours of the ancients serves divine providence. To begin with, we should not require the highest Christian truths from those who preceded the coming of Christ, nor should we trust that the sharp and, in a way, philosophical minds of men can ever be enticed and led toward perfect religion by any other bait besides philosophy. For sharp minds commit themselves to reason alone, and when they receive religion from a certain religious philosopher, they immediately and gladly admit the common faith. Once imbued with this, they are more easily led to the better form of religion contained within that genus. Therefore, it was not without divine providence—which wishes to recall all people to itself wonderfully according to the capacity of each one’s mind—that a certain pious philosophy was born once among the Persians under **Zoroaster**, and among the Egyptians under **Hermes**, consistent with itself in both places. It was then nourished among the Thracians under **Orpheus** and **Aglaophemus**. It soon grew to adulthood through **Pythagoras** among the Greeks and Italians, and at last was brought to completion by the divine **Plato** at Athens. It was the ancient custom of the theologians to cover divine mysteries both with mathematical numbers and figures, and with poetic fictions. At last, **Plotinus** stripped theology of these veils, and he was the first and only one (as Porphyry and Proclus testify) who divinely penetrated the secrets of the ancients. But on account of his incredible brevity of words and the weight of his sen...

# THE LETTERS, BOOK VIII.

->*An Apology for Silence.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, many greetings.<-

**I** certainly told your brother Filippo—an upright and learned man—that in these times I am not permitted either to write anything to friends absent from the city, or to greet those who are present. For Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino was currently translating his massive "Enneads" from Greek into Latin.</note> the Platonist claims me entirely and utterly for himself. Because of this, Amerigo, you immediately accuse Plotinus—with a vehement speech and a most sharp poem—of envy; you argue that he himself belongs to no one, and that he strives to ensure that I, who am usually at the service of almost everyone, shall belong to no one. But I, in turn, am now working so that Plotinus may belong to everyone. While I diligently devote myself to this one man who will soon belong to all, I seem, in the meantime, to be devoting myself to everyone. Farewell.

->*Prophets and Interpreters of Prophets.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow Platonist Domenico Benivieni, many greetings.<-

**Y**ou were asking in recent days (and with great subtlety, as is your custom) by what power, above all, the reading of Plato remains so vital after so long a time, since your first reading of our Plato seized your soul and suddenly transferred it entirely into Plato himself. Unless our Plato were alive, my dear Domenico—indeed, unless he lived far better than we do—surely while we were being transferred into Plato, we would meanwhile slide into death. But since he once lived a life of eternal character among men, it is only right that, now living an eternal life, he does not turn his readers toward death, but more happily converts them toward life. For the moment, I set aside the arguments for such a great gift. Let us deal with what is now at hand.

Tell me, I pray, who might now heal our wounds—which the <term>Hebrew Doctors<note>Original: "Hebræi Medici." In the circle of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, this referred to Jewish scholars like Elijah del Medigo and Abraham Farissol, who were often trained in medicine but engaged in rigorous philosophical and theological debate.</note></term> inflict upon us daily—if not our Plato, the Physician of Souls? You yourself were present at the disputations which have often been conducted, and are still conducted, in the home of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A brilliant young philosopher and friend of Ficino who sought to harmonize all systems of knowledge.</note> (who is to be admired above all others), where Elijah and Abraham, Hebrew Doctors and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, argue against Guglielmo the Sicilian <note>Guglielmo Raimondo Moncada, also known as Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert to Christianity and a scholar of Hebrew and Arabic who taught Pico.</note>. They contend that the oracles of the Prophets do not pertain to Jesus at all, but were spoken in some other sense. They turn everything around and strive to wrench the arguments from our hands with all their might. Nor does it seem they can be easily refuted, unless the divine Plato comes forward into the judgment hall as the unconquered patron of our holy religion.

Let us therefore hear him, and let us consider diligently what he said on this matter in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most influential dialogues, dealing with the creation of the world and the nature of the soul.</note>, and what he might now bring to our attention. "Some," he says, "are prophets; others are the interpreters of prophets." For those who foretell often do not know what they are foretelling, and those who interpret quickly may err even more in their foresight. The cause of this is that the "hunting" skill of the interpreters requires a swift and versatile intellect. However, if a faculty is to perceive something beforehand, it requires a peaceful and quiet mind. Since these qualities are, as it were, repugnant to each other, they do not easily run together in the same person.

From this opinion of our Plato, we can therefore gather that the certain foreknowledge of the future resides in God alone; the divine mind speaks of future things through the Prophet as if through a tongue, while the mind of the prophet does not understand what the tongue is doing in the meantime. Nor is it without merit that they are called "Prophets"—that is, "foretellers"—and "soothsayers"—that is, "tellers of fates"—yet they are not called "foreknowers" or "foreknowers of the soul," as if it were not their duty to understand, but only to pronounce the things foreknown by the divine mind. 

If they are said to "presage"—that is, "to sense beforehand"—that very presage seems to pertain not to the mind and reason, but to the sense and the imagination. If, therefore, there is a prediction of the future in the tongue of prophecy, let there be a certain imagination of the future in the prophet's sense. But the certain reason and the end of that future resides in the divine mind. Nor does the Prophet speak entirely at random; for while he thinks he is imagining one specific thing and hopes to say that, he may meanwhile announce something else—similar, perhaps, but ultimately different. This is distinctly known beforehand by God, who blows into the prophetic trumpet, and it is finally discovered by the interpreter after the event to have happened exactly as the Prophet had uttered it (even if beyond his own expectation) and as God Himself had foreknown. The Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel of John (11:49–51).</note> did not fail to notice that the prophecies of those foretelling are of such a kind, where he says that Caiaphas the High Priest prophesied, saying: "It is better that one man should die for the people, than that the whole nation should perish." The Evangelist indeed admits these words as being among the prophecies...

...with him there will be need only of a sign, not prayers; yet a simple modesty <note>original: "subrusticus uerò pudor"</note> has often held me back, but perhaps a letter or a friend will blush less. Farewell. Florence, January 17, 1485.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Marco of Venice, Cardinal of San Marco, many greetings.

They say Mercury (as you well know, venerable Father) used not only to announce words, but also to interpret the mind of the sender. They also attribute to Mercury the timely gift of remembrance, and not without reason; for just as they attribute the movement of the body to the Moon, so they attribute the movement of the soul to Mercury. Therefore, when he moves the senses in the soul, he seems to announce; when he moves reason, he interprets; but when he stirs the memory, he rouses remembrance. What is the point of this? Our friend Calderinus <note>Antonio Calderini, a close associate of Ficino who often acted as a messenger to Rome.</note> seems to perform the complete office of Mercury between us. For not only does he deliver your letters to me like a messenger and bring back your words, but he also interprets your mind toward me. Finally, I say, he does not teach me love, but rather calls it back to my memory. For I have known for a long time that I am vehemently loved by you, not indeed through any other sign, but only by the reporting of my own inner consciousness. 

Venerable Father, we learn other human matters through external clues: for instance, that someone is learned, or handsome, or powerful and wealthy. But external signs do not teach us that someone truly loves us—for external things are very often deceptive—rather, it is the soul itself, affected by love for that person, that teaches it most certainly. For by the same likeness of character by which I have loved you for a long time, I do not doubt that I am loved by you in return (for the likeness is mutual). Therefore, our "Mercury," who recently performed his duty for us in your name, will in turn perform it for you in our name. Yet even so, he will not be able to express how much I value your judgment, and how wonderfully I honor your singular virtues. But what even Mercury himself (so to speak) cannot explain, let Apollo at least bring forth through prophecy, and finally let Jupiter happily fulfill the duty.

### Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderini, many greetings.

Greetings, our Calderini, and may our letter be safe as well. Since you departed from us during an eclipse of the Sun <note>Ficino often interpreted astronomical events as having direct effects on daily life or correspondence.</note>, who would wonder that our letter also suffered an "eclipse" at that time? Indeed, two concluding clauses were somehow missing at its end, perhaps because two quarters of the Sun’s light failed. Phœbus <note>The sun god, Apollo.</note> has suddenly resumed his light; so our letter has now resumed its end.

### Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Martelli, a man most distinguished in letters and character, greetings.

When I was staying in recent days with Filippo and Nicola Valori <note>The Valori family were prominent patrons of Ficino; their villa at Maiano served as a retreat for the Platonic Academy.</note> at their estate in Maiano, and was investigating the nature of <term>daemons</term> <note>From the Greek "daimon." In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense of evil spirits, but intermediary beings or "spirits" that bridge the gap between the divine and the human.</note> in a certain secluded spot there, Plotinus was suddenly present and poured out for us a divine oracle concerning these spirits, wrapped in words that were both very brief and very obscure. It seemed worthwhile, therefore, to summon Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was the student and biographer of Plotinus who edited his works.</note>, who was both a disciple of Plotinus and most devoted to scrutinizing spirits, so that he might easily unroll for us the "daemonic" shroud of his teacher. 

Porphyry arrived then, called forth both by his master Plotinus and by his own spirits, and he opened up to us what his teacher had felt. He confirmed what Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who incorporated Platonic concepts into Christian thought.</note> had argued concerning spirits. Porphyry indeed spoke with us in Greek words, the sum of which I shall interpret for you in Latin <note>In this translation, English.</note> words. If you read this summary alongside the letter I dedicated to you regarding the concord between Moses and Plato, you will see that regarding the contemplation of the Platonists, not only Plato but also the later Platonists agree with our religion. Farewell.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<meta>Catchword: subject to [obnoxiū]</meta>

->*The Platonists sacrifice nothing to God and the soul of the world except contemplation; however, to the stars that move the souls, they sacrifice flowers as well as the fruits of the earth and trees.*<-

**T**he first God, since he is incorporeal, immovable, and indivisible—contained by nothing, not even by himself—needs nothing external. Neither does the Soul of the World <term>Anima Mundi; the Neoplatonic concept of an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things in the universe</term> require external things, for it possesses and contains that very thing which is extended in three dimensions. It possesses a faculty that moves naturally, and by its own nature it has decreed that the body of the world be moved in a well-ordered and beautiful way according to the highest reasons. It has received the body into itself and embraced it, though the Soul itself remains incorporeal and free from all passion. However, to the other gods—both the world itself and the planets <note>original: "errantibus," referring to the "wandering stars" or planets</note> and the fixed stars, which consist of soul and body and are manifest to our eyes—sacrifices should be made, but only of inanimate things.

->*The spirits beneath the Moon, which are not seen, the ancients called "daemons," and they thought that every single daemon could sometimes help us and sometimes hinder us.*<-

**T**here remains the invisible multitude of those whom Plato called "daemons" <term>daemons: from the Greek 'daimones,' these are not "demons" in the modern evil sense, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</term> without distinction. Truly, some of these have been named by men and have attained honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among individuals. Others, however, for the most part, are not named, but receive a name and worship in a certain secret way from people in various villages or cities; the rest of the crowd is simply called by the common name of daemons. Indeed, there is a fixed belief among all people that these spirits will certainly harm the human race if they become angry because they are neglected or do not receive their lawful worship. Conversely, they believe they will do good to those humans who win them over with vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other fitting tributes. Since, therefore, this opinion concerning daemons is confused and contains much slander against them, it is necessary to distinguish their nature through reason. For they say it is perhaps necessary to declare the source from which this error regarding them has fallen upon men; thus, we must distinguish them in this manner.

->*All daemons are certain souls proceeding from the "Total Soul"—that is, from the very Idea of souls. They also possess a "spirit"—that is, a thin, subtle body. But the daemons who most rule over their own bodies are good and beneficent; those who are least in control of their bodies are evil and malicious.*<-

**T**herefore, whichever souls sprout from the Total Soul and govern large regions of the places beneath the Moon <note>The "sublunary" realm, or the Earthly world subject to change and decay</note>—resting upon or adhering to a "spirit" <term>spiritus: in Ficino’s medicine and philosophy, this is a "vaporous" substance that links the immaterial soul to the physical body</term>, yet surpassing that spirit according to reason—these are surely to be judged as good daemons. They provide all things for the utility of what occurs, whether they preside over certain animals, or certain fruits, or other things ordained for their sake, such as rains, moderate winds, clear air, the tempering of the seasons, and other things contributing to all these. Among us, they also oversee the arts, the discipline of music, medicine, gymnastics, and similar pursuits. It is not their primary nature to bring about harm when they are the ones who consult for the utility and convenience of things. Among these should be numbered the daemons who, as Plato says, "transfer and announce" human things to the gods and divine things to humans. While they carry our vows to the gods as if to judges, they bring back the commands and warnings of those gods to us, along with prophecy. However, whichever souls have the least command over their joined spirit, but instead yield to it for the most part, these are clearly led and carried away excessively by it when the anger and desires of the spirit grow strong. These souls are also daemons, but they are rightly called "malicious." Moreover, both these and the others we have mentioned are invisible and not entirely manifest to human senses, for they are not clothed in a solid body. Furthermore, they do not all have a single form; rather, they are marked by many figures and shapes which stamp their spirit. Sometimes they appear, and other times not at all. Sometimes they even change their forms—those, of course, who are of the worse kind. Their spirit, by the very reason that it is a certain type of body, is...
subject to passion <note>continued on next page</note>

He distinguishes between good daemons, who govern nature and human arts, and malicious ones who are enslaved by their own passions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the nature of daemons (intermediary spirits), specifically contrasting the orderly bodies and actions of good daemons with the chaotic, deceptive nature of malicious ones. It follows the previous discussion on the hierarchy of the universe and how these spirits interact with the material world.</meta>

<meta>catchword: plotting [machinan]</meta>

is subject to decay and dissolution, but because it is so bound by souls, its form can endure for a long time, though it is not eternal. For it is consistent that something always flows from it and is nourished. The body of good spirits consists in harmony, just like the bodies of the beings manifest to us; but the bodies of malicious daemons <term>daemons; in the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits between humans and gods, inhabiting the air. They are not all inherently "demonic" in the modern sense, though Ficino here focuses on the "malefic" or evil ones</term> are unstructured and, being subject to passions, inhabit a place near the earth. There is therefore no evil they do not dare to commit, for they have a wholly violent and insane nature, being devoid of the guardianship of better daemons. From this, they plot and rush forth in many sudden and violent ambushes; and while they carry out their incursions, they partly try to hide and partly inflict violence. For this reason, the sufferings they inflict are sharp and swift.

However, cures and corrections from better daemons seem to be slower. For every good thing is easy and steady in its governance, proceeding in an orderly fashion and not overstepping what is appropriate. If you think thus of daemons, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion by which you might think that evil comes from the good or good from the evil. Nor is this discourse merely absurd, but many, conceiving the worst opinions of the gods from this source, have spread them among many men. This is one of the greatest harms inflicted by malicious daemons: that while they themselves are the authors of the unfortunate passions falling upon earthly things—such as plague, famine <note>original: "penuriae"</note>, earthquakes, heatwaves, fire, and the like—they meanwhile persuade us that those who are rather the authors of the opposites (that is, of fertility and prosperity) are the ones who cause these things. Thus they try to absolve themselves from the very cause of the calamities.

And first, they strive to hide their own injustice from us. Then, they turn us toward supplications and sacrifices appropriate for seeking favors, as if the gods were angry with us. They do these and similar things, striving to lead us away from the right knowledge of the gods and toward themselves. For they take great delight in all things done thus unjustly and discordantly. And assuming the masks of other gods, and thus relying on our lack of prudence, they take the crowds into their fellowship. And due to such human lusts, they inflame minds with loves and desires for riches, power, and pleasures. Again, they involve us in new opinions from which seditions, wars, and other things of the same kind are born. 

What is most serious to the soul is that they persuade it that similar things are done by those above, so much so that they even subject the Greatest God <note>original: "Deum maximum"</note> to such accusations. They claim He throws everything into turmoil, high and low. This happens not only to unrefined men, but to many who are students of Philosophy. When this mutual error proceeds and is confirmed—for the philosophers who never separated themselves from the common filth have fallen into the same errors as the common people—the crowds, hearing opinions similar to their own from praised writers, are even more confirmed in this view of them. 

For poetic art has even more sharply excited such suspicions in men, because it uses an eloquence that is powerfully suited to astonishment and a kind of magical attraction, easily able to soothe and entice minds, and therefore to bring us to believe in things that are utterly impossible. But indeed, it must be firmly believed that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever benefit. For it is not the nature of heat (as Plato says <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, Book I, 335d</note>) to make things cold, but of its opposite; thus it is not the nature of the just to harm. Divinity itself is naturally the most just of all things; otherwise, nothing would be lasting. 

Must we not, therefore, distinguish this power and lot of the beneficent daemons? For that which is naturally ready to harm is contrary to the beneficent, and contraries never naturally occur regarding the same thing. While such daemons harm mortal nature in many ways, even sometimes in great matters, the certain good daemons never meanwhile abandon their duties, but they signal the dangers threatening everywhere from evil ones according to their ability—showing them now in dreams, now through divinely inspired minds, and through many other ways. But if someone could discern the signs, he would detect and avoid all the plots of the wicked; for these spirits give signs to all, but not everyone knows the signs, just as not everyone can read what is written, but only he who has first learned his letters. 

Through these contrary daemons, all sorcery <term>ueneficium; here referring to harmful magic or the "evil eye" rather than simple poisoning</term> is accomplished. For those who inflict evils through sorcery are accustomed to honor these daemons especially, and their leader; these daemons indeed abound in all kinds of figures and images, and they strenuously deceive with the machinery of wonders. By their work, the unfortunate plot love potions and amorous sorceries;

...plot. For all lack of self-control and the hope for wealth and glory grow strong through these spirits, especially deception. For lying is the particular characteristic of such spirits. Indeed, they wish to be seen as gods, and the power that presides over them wishes to be held as the Greatest God. These spirits are the ones who are satisfied only by libations and the smell of roasting meat; for their spiritual body is accustomed to grow fat from these things. For this body lives on vapors and fumigations, and as is fitting, assumes strength through various means and through the smell of blood and meat.

->*Those who sacrifice animals secretly attract evil spirits to themselves; however, to the good spirits—that is, the angels—we ought to consecrate only inanimate things with a purity of mind.*<-

**A** wise and temperate man will therefore take care to avoid using such sacrifices, by which he might attract such spirits to himself. Instead, he will strive to perfectly purify his soul. For they never attack a pure soul because of its total lack of resemblance to them. Furthermore, if it should happen to be necessary for cities to reconcile these spirits to themselves, such a practice has nothing to do with us. For in a city, wealth and external or bodily advantages are considered "goods" among citizens, and their opposites are "evils." They have almost no concern for the perfection and purity of the soul. We, however, shall not need the "advantages" that spirits might bring as much as possible; instead, through the soul and through external things, we will strive with all our effort to become similar to God Himself and those close to Him. This is truly achieved through tranquility of mind, a distinct comprehension of the truth of things, and a life entirely focused on these goals. We must become unlike wicked men and spirits, and unlike everything that delights in the mortal. Therefore, following what Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; Ficino frequently cites him in discussions of natural philosophy and piety.</note> has handed down, we also shall offer sacrifices in the manner agreed upon by the Theologians <note>Ficino often uses "Theologians" to refer to the "ancient theologians" (Prisci Theologi), including figures like Orpheus, Hermes Trismegistus, and Plato, who he believed shared a unified divine truth.</note>—recognizing that to the extent we neglect to purge the soul of disturbances, to that extent we are joined to wicked power. Thus we are rightly compelled to further appease this power; for as the Theologians hand down, those who depend on external things and do not yet rule over their internal disturbances are forced by this very condition to repel the onset of such an attack from themselves, otherwise they will never be able to cease from their labors.

->*Purity and abstinence protect us from evil spirits, to whom contemplatives ought to sacrifice nothing.*<-

**W**herefore, if ever the Theologians permit the slaughter of animals to wicked spirits for the sake of avoiding the evils they might inflict, they forbid the tasting of such sacrifices. Furthermore, they command that before you sacrifice in this way, you must purify the soul with fasting and especially with abstinence from animals. For they believe that the holy purity of the soul is like a symbol and a divine mark by which you are guarded, so that you suffer nothing from those you approach while reconciling them through sacrifice. For when you are disposed in a way opposite to those for whom you perform sacrifices, and you are purer and thus more divine, you remain unharmed in both body and soul, fortified by pure holiness as if by a citadel. For this reason, even to casters of spells and sorcerers <term>veneficis; literally "poisoners," but in this context referring to practitioners of dark or harmful magic</term>, such caution seemed necessary so that they might be safer from danger, yet they can never be entirely safe, for they are accustomed to summon wicked spirits for the sake of wantonness. Therefore, purity and holiness are not the proper domain of sorcerers and enchanters, but certainly belong to divine men and those contemplating divine things. Indeed, chastity and abstinence everywhere protect their observers against evil spirits through divine intimacy. Thus, if spell-casters had resolved to use these things fully, they would certainly never dare to cast spells at all, since they would have been called back by this purity from the lust for those things for whose sake they pollute themselves with impiety. Therefore, full of disturbances and hardly abstaining even a little from impure foods, and thus being entirely impure themselves, they pay the penalty for their unjust transgression against the universe—partly under the spirits whom they themselves provoke, and partly under divine judgment, which looks upon all the works and plans of mortals.

->*The wise person will abstain from both the food and the sacrifice of animals, for through these, evil spirits are summoned to us.*<-

**A** divine man will fortify his soul—first through the wisdom of divine matters, then through abstinence from those foods that incite disturbances in men, and finally through a likeness to God Himself. He will consider the soul to be an uncontaminated temple of God, specifically within this universe which is the temple of God the Father. Furthermore, since every physical body perceivable by the senses brings us certain "outflowings" of material spirits <note>original: "demones" – in Ficino’s Neoplatonic view, these are invisible entities that bridge the gap between the physical and spiritual worlds</note>, it is certain that alongside the impurity of nourishment drawn from flesh and blood, a demonic power is present. This power is easily attracted and enticed to such things because of a strong natural similarity and shared property. For this reason, all right-thinking theologians have applied themselves first and foremost to the study of abstinence. Remember, therefore, that while evil spirits delight in the victims of animal sacrifice, God has no need for such victims. He looks instead upon the character of those who worship Him, considering a correct understanding of divinity to be the greatest sacrifice. For in the eyes of God, the best offering is a pure mind and a soul free from disturbances. Hence, Plato says that while it is fitting for a good man to perform sacrifices and take part in divine rites, it is in vain for a wicked man to involve himself in sacred things.

### *An apology for silence to a friend.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandino, sends many greetings.<-

**Y**ou will say, my dear Bandino—indeed, I see you have been saying for a long time—that Marsilio writes to his friends rarely and too briefly, contrary to what a frequent and long-lasting love demands, which often requires much. But I, in fact, always feel as though I am writing much to my friends, since I am constantly writing many things for my friends and others to read. For a long time now, Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher whose works Ficino was the first to translate into Latin in the Renaissance</note> has been speaking in the Latin tongue, as I promised, in fifty-four books; but beyond these, he demands commentaries from us. We have already finished eight, and, trusting in God, we are eagerly proceeding to the rest as if on a journey. Commend us to Matthias, the unconquered King of Pannonia <note>King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, a great patron of the arts and Ficino’s work</note>. But tell him that he cannot truly hold Marsilio as commended unless he first holds our dear Giacomo Azzaroli <note>A Florentine diplomat and friend of Ficino</note> as commended.

### *A respectful demand from a friend.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a most learned man, sends many greetings.<-

**G**reetings. While others might press you for the sake of various things, I did not wish to press you by sending "Mahomet" <note>Likely a Latin translation of the Quran or a text about Islamic law that Pico had borrowed</note> back to us. However, I fear that if he stays away from his "homeland" <note>Ficino’s library</note> any longer, he will grow old, and we will eventually be unable to bring about his return. You will therefore see to it, in your humility, that he returns at the appropriate time. But if you intend to keep this guest at your house for a few days more, at least send Avicenna <note>The famous Persian philosopher and physician</note> immediately, who by divine promise is to be discussed right after Mahomet; for this discussion is now especially necessary for me. You will find this at the end of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note> or shortly thereafter.

### *An apology for brevity in writing to a friend.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandino, sends many greetings.<-

**S**ome time ago, I gave a letter for you to Giacomo Azzaroli, a true friend and an elegant man; remember to commend both him and me often in my name to Matthias, the unconquered King of Pannonia. I had written that I had already finished the commentaries on the eighth book of Plotinus. Now I am meditating on the commentaries for the twelfth book, and because of this constant labor, it happens that my friends receive only very rare and brief letters from us. And truly, when you receive such short ones, others perhaps receive none at all. I am finding wonderful mysteries in Plotinus and—what is even more marvelous—they are very frequent. I only wish I could explain them in words as well as I seem to perceive them in my mind. But farewell for now, my sweetest Bandino; Plotinus, meanwhile, summons me.
