# LETTERS, BOOK VIII.

## A recommendation of a friend in the name of a Philosopher.

**G**reetings, my most beloved Bandini. <note>Domenico Bandini, a Florentine diplomat and close associate of the Medici and Ficino.</note> I am now writing to you for the third time on behalf of our close friend, the priest Vincent. I pray that, if you are able, you might recommend this cause at a favorable moment to the invincible King Matthias <note>Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary (r. 1458–1490), who was a great patron of Ficino and the Platonic Academy.</note>; and furthermore, do so in my name, if indeed you believe the name of a Philosopher carries any weight with Kings. For such is usually the humble lot of the philosopher: he may have some influence among the lowest, but very little among the greatest. And perhaps we are content with this, provided we are true philosophers—that is, so long as we at least possess great power within ourselves. Yet I do not deny that I have sometimes had some influence with Matthias, nor do I doubt I shall have it again, since he is renowned not only for power but also for wisdom. Farewell.

## An Oration of Marsilio Ficino on charity, delivered in the college of the Florentine canons to the people, dividing the speech into three chapters.

**L**ift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of Glory shall enter. <note>A quotation from Psalm 24:7, often used in liturgy.</note> Lift up your ears, O uplifted minds; the living and effective word of God shall enter into you; and together with the word of God, charity, which is salvific above all things; and with charity, immediately, God the King of Glory. For God is charity <note>original: "charitas" — the Latin term for divine, selfless love, often translated as "charity" or "caritas."</note>, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him.

### That God is charity. Chapter I.

**T**hat God is indeed the highest charity, venerable and most beloved brothers, is not only proclaimed by the Apostolic trumpet <note>Referring to the New Testament writings, particularly those of St. John.</note>, but the entire nature of things cries it out. For the whole nature of things was created and is preserved because God the Creator Himself willed it from the beginning and continues to will it. But the will in God is, without doubt, nothing other than charity and God Himself. Will, I say, in God is not any kind of longing, but joy—a joy perpetually rejoicing in its own goodness. For since we can consider two main things in the will, namely desire and gladness, and since in the First Good there can be no stimulus for desiring <note>God, being perfect, lacks nothing and therefore does not "desire" in the sense of needing something He does not have.</note>, the will and charity there differ in no way from joy. For just as light and heat, which are two distinct things in a fire, are ultimately one in the Sun, so desire and gladness are two things in us while we are away from our fatherland <note>original: "extra patriam" — a common Platonic and Christian metaphor for the soul's exile on Earth, away from its true home in Heaven.</note> seeking a finite good; but in the presence of the Infinite Good, all will is pleasure itself. Furthermore, in the elements beneath the heavens, the motion of elements toward a place is one thing, and their rest in that place is another; but in the heavens, the motion and the rest of celestial bodies are exactly the same, as they rest within a perpetual revolution. Similarly, above the heavens, that same heat is charity and joy joined as one.

### He who remains in charity remains in God. Chapter II.

**W**hile divine charity rejoices in its own good, it loves and cares for the common good of all. Human charity, in turn, insofar as it rejoices in the common good of all, brings back a personal good for itself from that source. Therefore, he who remains in charity remains in God, and remains always in joy; both because God Himself is charity, and also because while the soul is ardently moved by the flames of charity—loving God the Most High in Himself and loving men in God—it is wonderfully affected by God Himself, who is charity, and is made God-like. <note>original: "Deusque efficitur" — literally "and is made God," referring to the theological concept of deification or theosis, where the soul becomes like God through love.</note> For just as any matter does not usually become fire because it receives light from fire, but because it receives heat, so the soul sometimes becomes divine, not so much because God shines upon our intellect, but because our will glows with the burning of divine love. Meanwhile, your Apostle cries out to us in this way: "Prophecy shall eventually cease for you in the fatherland, where the past and future end. Knowledge shall also cease for you, where reasoning ends and the manner of seeing is changed; but charity alone shall never cease." <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 13:8.</note> Indeed, the condition of loving, under the nature of rejoicing, will always remain the same.

### And God in him. Chapter III.

**B**y this reasoning, therefore, charity alone remains, and he who remains in charity remains in God; but in what way does God remain in him? In a finite soul, I say, God Himself, who is immense

->*An excuse for not having written for a long time.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Marco of Venice,<-
->Cardinal of Saint Mark, many greetings.<-

**P**ythagoras and Plato valued the precious treasure of divine mysteries so highly that they judged they should be entrusted not to fragile papers, but to eternal minds, and specifically those minds worthy of eternity. Therefore, they did not write down the highest secrets of divinity, but taught them by voice. <note>Ficino refers to the "unwritten doctrines" or the "Pythagorean silence," a common Renaissance belief that the highest truths were shared only orally among initiates.</note> I also value the fact that I am recommended to you so highly that I commend myself to you daily not so much through light letters, but through the weighty souls and conversations of friends. Therefore, whether friends writing from there to me write, "Marsilio, greetings," or those setting out from here for Rome say, "Ficino, farewell," I immediately add: "If you wish me to be greeted or to fare well, greet in my name the Cardinal, my unique patron, and humbly commend me to him as one most devoted." Thus, while I seem to have been silent with you for a long time now, I am never silent; and if some indeed fulfill my requests with words less than perfectly, I meanwhile fulfill them with my mind. This mind of mine, many others—and especially that man Calderinus, <note>Antonio Calderini, a scholar and frequent messenger between the Roman Curia and the Florentine Academy.</note> acting as a kind of Mercury for us—can very easily interpret and express.

->*On the same matter.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his Antonio Calderini, many greetings.<-

**I** have for a long time now been engaged in the commentaries on Plotinus, <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino’s translation and commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads was one of his most massive intellectual undertakings.</note> which we have translated; I am now explaining the twentieth book, and thirty-four remain. Because of these occupations, it is not permitted for me to travel; otherwise, I would have long ago greeted our patron the Cardinal in person, whom I greet assiduously in my mind. For there is no one whom I judge more worthy of greeting. I pray that you visit him frequently and (if it can be done) commend me to him even more frequently. Farewell.

->*One must be generous even to the ungrateful.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Miniato, many greetings.<-

**T**hat you love me, Miniato, <note>Miniato Pitti (d. 1511), a Vallombrosan monk and friend of Ficino.</note> you do both justly and as a friend: justly, because you love one who loves you; as a friend, because you honor me by loving. Furthermore, that you follow the Platonic discipline everywhere with public praise, you fulfill the duty of divine piety. For divine providence established that for the common salvation of intellects, especially those of philosophers. This is indeed what I have been striving for a long time; this I work out diligently, gathering daily in the manner of those who draw water, so that I may scatter and pour it out for the grateful and ungrateful alike, even for those who would gladly obscure me if they could in any way. But I know for certain that as Plato comes forward into the light, a legitimate friend of Plato cannot be obscure. Finally, as to your complaint that you recently received bad things for good from a certain Hugo, this is a complaint common to you, to me, and to many. Therefore, you shall console your own loss with the common loss, if it is permitted. Especially because God, the avenger, sees all things.

->*An excuse when you do not greet in person, but through letters.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Marco of Venice,<-
->Cardinal of Saint Mark, many greetings.<-

**P**arents are sometimes accustomed to imprint their own image upon a son so effectively that he who sees the child has also seen the parent. I indeed wish this were now granted to me by divine power: that I might procreate in my presence a letter with my mind so similar to myself that I might seem to have come to you while the letter approaches; otherwise, I shall undoubtedly be impious unless I suddenly convey myself to my patron, who is now so much nearer to us. If I have ever desired anything ardently, I desire this most ardently now, thinking I can achieve it. For among all the works of the arts, the book alone is called by the name "son" <note>original: "liberi tanquam filij nomine". Ficino plays on the Latin word 'liber' meaning both 'book' and 'child/free person'.</note> because it alone comes forth most similar to its author—certainly more similar than a painting. For a painting reflects only the shadowy figure of our person, since Plotinus thinks that men themselves—that is, souls—enter into this worldly tragedy wearing bodies as masks. <note>A reference to Plotinus's Enneads III.2.15-17, where life is compared to a play and the body to a costume.</note> A book, however, expresses the whole man, since...

...explains the whole soul. But what am I doing? While I slowly demand a letter very similar to me, I return one quite dissimilar. For it will not be similar to the humble Marsilio, but will have lifted its head higher. Now therefore I humbly commend myself to you. Farewell. From Florence, June 26, 1487.

->*Many things that the stars signify, demons persuade, and we perform.*<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Nicolaus Batoreus, Bishop of Vác, many greetings.

**Y**ou write that Matthias, the invincible King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490), the King of Hungary, who was a great patron of the Renaissance and invited many Italian scholars to his court.</note>, desires our presence, as do you and several others, for the sake of explaining the Platonic mind. You ask that if I am unable to come myself, I at least send one of my people to you who might satisfy your desire in this matter. I will indeed strive with all my strength to ensure that our cousin Sebastian <note>Sebastiano Salvini, Ficino's cousin and a frequent messenger/scholar in his circle.</note> comes to you; or, if he is unable due to his own occupations, another of my associates shall make the journey. 

As for me, it would be a marvel if I changed my ancestral home—whether Saturn ascending in Aquarius for us prohibits the move (as an astrologer might perhaps judge), or whether some genius of that kind forbids it (as a Magus might think), or if a little body unfit for labors hinders the path, or a mind always intent on contemplation commands me to rest. I have assigned ambiguous causes to this matter. For the Platonists think that human events are sometimes signified by the stars, but frequently incited by demons who are, as it were, the attendants of the stars, and finally carried out by humans, according to the condition of the things closer to us. Farewell.

### *Consolation on the death of a son.*

## Marsilio Ficino to Ugolino Verino the poet, many greetings.

**T**he opinion of the ancient sages, confirmed especially by Plotinus in his book *On Providence*, is that humans—that is, souls—descend into this life from God as if into a comedy or tragedy, where everything commonly thought to be adversity is purely fictional: feigned riches and poverty, feigned kings and slaves, and similarly feigned births and deaths. That Platonic saying perhaps points to this: "the human race on earth is God’s plaything." <note>original: "humanum genus in terris est Dei ludus." A reference to Plato's *Laws* (803c).</note> God himself is the author of this game and play, and he is also the father of souls; he sends them down from on high into this game like actors. The nature of the world itself provides them with their masks <term>persona|In Latin, *persona* refers both to the character role in a play and the physical mask worn by actors.</term>, with the union of male and female serving to minister this. 

Certainly, he departs more happily from the play who returns to the author, God, more accepted than before, having more obediently performed the acts assigned to him. Most fortunate of all is the one to whom more honorable and shorter acts have been given. For a longer tragic play usually inserts more comic elements. Will you then, Verino, weep for that noble youth <note>Ugolino Verino's son, Michele Verino, a promising young scholar who died at the age of 17.</note>, complaining that your son has migrated from a tender life? Was he your son? He was not procreated by you, but by God. You only adorned him with a certain mask when he was sent by God to play for a short time; yet even so, you instructed him for this game as best you could. He has not left life, but has returned from a kind of "play of life" into the very substance of life. Since he performed the learned, honorable, and pious duty of this play vigorously, he returned joyfully to the father before he could turn his comedy into a tragedy, destined to receive an eternal reward for a brief game.

### *The pursuit of riches and dignities hinders the study of letters above all else.*

## Marsilio Ficino to Piero Soderini the Academic, many greetings.

**A**ncient astronomers found two dwellings for Jupiter among the heavenly beings: Pisces and Sagittarius; and likewise two for Mercury: Virgo and Gemini. Since Virgo is opposite to Pisces, and Gemini is opposite to Sagittarius, we rightly judge that we are warned from heaven that nothing is more opposed to talent and the study of letters (which are attributed to Mercury) than the immense pursuit of riches and power (which are attributed above all to Jupiter). Furthermore, since Leo, the house of the Sun, is furthest distant from Aquarius, the house of Saturn; and again, Aries, the "exaltation" of the Sun, is most remote from Libra, the "exaltation" of Saturn—and the Sun signifies kings, while Saturn signifies philosophers and contemplatives—who, understanding these things...

[...diligently] ever hoped that either philosophers would become kings, or kings would be philosophers. Certainly, this can only be achieved by divine means, and our Plato <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic* 473d, where he famously argues that societies will only find peace when philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers.</note> earnestly desired it as if it were a divine gift. Indeed, I know this is your opinion, my Peter <note>Pietro Leone da Spoleto, a physician and close friend of both Ficino and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>. For I know the excellence of your talent and the preeminence of your mind. I have therefore decided to discuss these things with you, so that I might confirm you in this opinion of yours with celestial reasons. Farewell.

### *He is to be commended above all others who seeks wisdom throughout the whole world.*

**Marsilio Ficino to the Illustrious Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, many greetings.**

**G**reetings. Roberto Salviati, a faithful and vigorous friend, read your letter to me yesterday evening, in which you refute the slanders of your adversaries there with certain arguments. We agreed, therefore, that I should report these things to the magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and patron of the Platonic Academy.</note>, so that if he had previously received anything false from the city of Rome regarding the dictates of your adversaries, he might be convinced otherwise. I therefore took up the task gladly, and he listened willingly. From this, we gather that no hatred lurks in his mind toward you, but rather love. First of all, it had to be asserted that those men were thrown into prison not for your sake, but for their own; for the opposite had been rumored here until now. Your letter sufficiently declares that they were seized by their own fault, and Pietro Leone was a witness for me, who had heard that they had spoken out against the Pope too rashly and arrogantly. Meanwhile, our magnanimous Leone <note>Pietro Leone da Spoleto.</note> is departing from here, eager to travel the world, seized by the love of truth. Although he has already attained as much of it as is permitted to a man among us, he pursues it even more intensely, intending to bring back, if God favors him, a divine fruit instead of a human one. It is our duty, therefore, to provide such a great friend of the Divine with protection through religious prayers and vows amidst the various dangers of an uncertain journey. May he fare well and happily, and may you also fare well and happily.

### *An expression of thanks, congratulation, and recommendation.*

**To the most serene King of Pannonia, Matthias, forever invincible. Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself.**

**W**e received by the same messenger the news that you have recently, by the grace of God, bravely gained a victory, and that you have mercifully released our friend from prison by our favor. I therefore congratulate you as much as possible, I congratulate my friend, and finally I rejoice for myself, because I recognize that I have such influence with so great a king. I indeed give thanks to God for your happy victory, and to you also, after God, not a little but very much for the freedom of my friend, and for my authority with you. I also wish for you far greater victories hereafter, and for my friend, ever greater benefits. Since you have granted him freedom, the greatest of benefits, do not disdain to grant lesser ones as well, if the occasion should demand it.

### *The knowledge of the divinity of the soul is necessary before all things.*

**W**hat does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul? <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 16:26.</note> You labor in vain, O Philosopher, while you try to comprehend all things, unless you apprehend the soul through which you are to comprehend the rest. What does it profit you, O Theologian, to attribute eternity to God, unless you also claim the same for yourself, so that through your own eternity you may be able to enjoy the divine eternity? Therefore, philosophers and theologians alike, come, I pray you all, and hear the Prophet marvelling at how great things God has done for our soul. Why do you cry out, O Prophet, when you say "come"? Why again do you marvel when you say "how great"? Finally, what do you portend when you add "God"? I indeed cry out, I marvel, I portend that God himself has given divine things to our soul. If you believe the Prophets less, O brothers, then seek, ask, and knock <note>Reference to Matthew 7:7.</note> as much as is permitted to God, our parent. Therefore, you, good Jesus, who hang there for the soul—did you wish to suffer for a corporeal soul, or to die for a mortal soul? Look, O brothers, listen I pray you, do you not see him open his mouth and answer? "Far be it from me to have exchanged a most precious thing for a most vile one; rather, for the divine soul of man, God became man; for the immortal soul, I have died." Let our enemies, therefore, be ashamed, troubled, and confounded very quickly, since our God has done great and wonderful things for us. Our enemies are not those who snatch money from us—for money is not ours, but belongs to Fortune—our enemies are not...

...who kill the body; for the body is not so much ours as it is the property of fortune, nature, and fate. Our true enemies are those who destroy the soul, for the soul alone is truly ours—it is our very self. However, those who preach that the soul is corporeal and mortal are the ones who truly murder it. Therefore, let the followers of Aristippus <note>Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–356 BCE) was a pupil of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school, which emphasized pleasure as the highest good.</note> blush with shame; let the Epicureans be troubled; let the followers of Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), the Roman poet and philosopher whose work *De rerum natura* defended Epicurean physics and the mortality of the soul.</note> be confounded. Let them blush if they are indeed philosophers for relying on no reason; let them be troubled if they are men of any distinction for being deceived by the common habits of the masses. Finally, let them be confounded by the Platonic arguments that will follow.

### *Platonic Philosophy should be read as sacred among sacred things.*
### The Oration of Marsilio at the beginning of a Lecture.

**B**reathe upon us, I pray, nourishing God; I will tell of your name to my brothers, in the midst of the Church I will praise you, and in the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you. <note>original: "narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis..." This is a paraphrase of Psalm 22:22, commonly used in Christian liturgy to signify the proclamation of divine truth.</note> Dearest brothers, those who in former times obtained the fruits they longed for from God more abundantly were accustomed to return the first fruits to God. Truly the Pythagoreans, whom our own Platonists followed, would return to God the wisdom they had desired and received from the divine, and they would meditate upon and teach the sacred mysteries of philosophy in temples. Therefore, following the footsteps of the ancient sages to the best of our ability, we shall pursue the religious philosophy of our Plato in the midst of this Church. In these seats of the angels, we shall contemplate divine truth. But, O dearest brothers, let us enter these seats with entirely pure minds—seats which Almighty God recently filled with brighter angels and restored for those who had long since fallen into darkness, through the patronage of a citizen distinguished for his piety whom you all know and venerate <note>Likely a reference to Lorenzo de' Medici or perhaps a specific patron of the church where Ficino was lecturing.</note>. Furthermore, so that you may have a more certain hope that our souls can one day fly up more sublimely into those angelic seats, come, hear, and see how great things God has done for our soul. Now, if we have entered this angelic temple to behold the wondrous God and, having seen God, to enjoy Him sweetly—and since the command "know thyself" <note>The famous Delphic maxim, *Gnothi seauton*, which Ficino and the Neoplatonists interpreted as a prerequisite for knowing God.</note> is given to those who enter—we must first recognize our own soul, through which, as if through a venerable mirror, we may happily behold the face of our Parent.

### Congratulations.
### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandino, many greetings.

**P**andolfo of Pesaro, a distinguished man, has overwhelmed me with countless greetings in your name. But he spoke a truly true greeting to me when he said that you are well, and exceedingly well, and that you have been honored with great embassies by the unconquered King of Pannonia <note>original: "rege Pannoniæ." This refers to Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary (r. 1458–1490), a great patron of Renaissance learning.</note>. I rejoice greatly, Bandino, in your prosperity, for this redounds both to your friends and to your fatherland. Fare you better every day, and again, better still.

### *Jupiter and Venus tame Mars.*
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

**O**ur Roberto Salviati reports to me, while I was ardently occupied with my public lecture, that you have arrived safely in Bologna. I congratulate you indeed that you have been made closer to us, and I rejoice that you have escaped unharmed from the hands of the unjust. Last October, while Mercury was being burned by Mars <note>An astrological reference to "combustion," where a planet's influence is weakened or "scorched" by proximity to the Sun or, in this metaphorical case, by the aggressive influence of Mars.</note>, the "Matthiasite" peoples <note>original: "Mattiæ Gentes." This likely refers to the detractors Pico faced in the court of Matthias Corvinus or among the religious authorities.</note> raged against you, and the people plotted vain things, whom He who dwells in the highest immediately mocked. For in the meantime, at the hour of Jupiter and Venus, supported by the patronage of the magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, we stood in the way so that Mercury would not be burned even on earth. I pray that God may stand in the way of our adversaries and slanderers in the future. Farewell, be happy, and love me, who loves you.

### *An exhortation to friends, that they might cast off everything corporeal to perceive God.*

**T**hose are to be considered profane, as Plato says in his book on knowledge <note>Referring to Plato's *Theaetetus* or perhaps the *Sophist*, where materialism is criticized.</note>, who think that nothing exists except what can be grasped with the fist. O insolent Epicurean, grasp dust in your hand with all your might; it immediately escapes you. Constraint water, it slips away; check the air, it flows out; restrain fire, it flies away. O mad Epicurean, you cannot constrict fire, nor air, nor water, nor dust in your fist; can you therefore...

<page-num>887</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK VIII.</header>

...to embrace with a fist <note>The "fist" here represents the limited human imagination trying to grasp the infinite.</note> Him who himself embraces the entire universe with a single fist. If you wish for God to be a body, let Him be the most excellent body. Therefore, let Him be fire. Approach this fire; it possesses light equally alongside heat. Clench the light with your hand (if you can); you will carry back not light, but darkness. Grasp the heat with your fists; you will immediately be dissolved. God is a consuming fire <note>original: "Deus ignis consumens est," a reference to Hebrews 12:29.</note>; you cannot grasp Him with fists—that is, with the imagination—but rather with the affection of mortals. You can perceive Him even if you have delayed, yet with no fist of the imagination will you perceive the light of divine truth. For you will immediately slide back into the darkness of falsehood. There is need, therefore, for <term>dialectics</term> <note>dialectica: In the Platonic tradition, this is the highest intellectual method for stripping away sensory illusions to reach pure truth.</note> to dissolve all the clouds of the imagination. Again, even if you are a master of dialectics, you cannot healthily enjoy the vital heat of God if you are weighed down by mortal affections; for He dissolves whatever matter He finds. However, that which presents itself free from matter, He stands beside and wins over to Himself. Lay aside, therefore, earthly affections, and you will immediately and healthily enjoy the divine fervor.

---

### *That we must begin from the love of God, so that we may understand God.*

**G**od is love; he who remains in love, remains in God, and God in him. <note>original: "Deus charitas est..." a quote from 1 John 4:16.</note> But if love is a craving of desire, a sting of need, and God is in need of nothing but is the sum of all good, in what way is God Himself love? In love there is fervor, there is light, and there is also joy. God is therefore love; but the fervor of this love is indeed kindled in the soul, while the light flourishes in God, and the joy is in both. It is just like a ray of the Sun near a concave mirror: in itself it is light, but there in the wood it becomes heat, and from that heat, light is produced in the same place. He, therefore, who remains in the fervor of love, immediately remains in the light of God itself, and immediately divine joy remains in him. Indeed, a celestial body communicates light to transparent bodies (which are very similar to it) before it communicates heat; but to earthly bodies, which are very dissimilar, it imparts heat before light. Once these earthly things have been purged by the heat and made most similar to heaven, they immediately receive light from there. Therefore, the soul, surrounded by an earthly body, must begin from the love of God so that, being purged by love, it may then obtain divine light, and in that light, joy.

---

### *An introduction into friendship.*

->*Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Scali, Secretary to the King of Naples, greetings.*<-

**W**hile I was dining at the house of my friend Filippo Valori, I received a letter from my friend Nicolaus Valori, in which he indicates how ardently you love me and with what great praises you honor my works. He adds, furthermore, that you are the kind of man whom I ought to have loved vehemently of my own accord, even if you did not love me back. I, therefore, knowing for certain that the testimony of my friend Valori is most powerful, not only love you in return (you who have loved me for a long time), but I wish that I had anticipated you in love first. I cherish you in an extraordinary way, and I give you immense thanks that you have deemed me worthy of your goodwill and your praises. For in this way, I judge that I have been made worthy of the love and praises of all excellent men. What, then, shall I repay you for such a great gift? Even if it is not as much as I owe, it shall at least be as much as I am able; and perhaps I shall be able to do not a little, insofar as I have much influence in the house of Valori. This family has flourished with nobility, authority, and justice from the very beginning of the city of Florence. Farewell. Florence, the 14th day of December, 1487.

---

### *An exhortation to defend a just cause.*

->*Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Vittorio of Siena, the distinguished legal scholar, greetings.*<-

**S**ebastiano Salviano, a doctor of Theology and our learned friend from Amiternum, needs your patronage in his legal case, which is indeed a very just one. Truly, just as Justice is strong in heaven, her homeland, she becomes so weak outside her homeland on earth that she continually requires support. Only a just man, such as they say you are (and which I easily believe), is able and willing to sustain Justice, his own mother. I hope, therefore—and I desire this vehemently—that you will easily take up the most just cause of our close friend, and that you will dispatch it as quickly and successfully as possible. Farewell.

### Recommendation of a friend to the king.

->Marsilio Ficino to Matthias, King of Hungary, always unconquered, sends greetings.<-

**I** wish, most serene king, to send you letters almost worthy of your majesty, but I am forced to write in great haste. This is partly due to the priest Vincentius <note>Vincentius (Vincenzo Fondi) was a priest and a close associate of Ficino who traveled to Hungary.</note>, my close associate, who is urgently requesting this recommendation, and partly due to the messenger who is about to depart at any hour. You will therefore receive letters not of the kind usually produced by leisure and freedom, but of the kind that a more pressing necessity brings forth. Accordingly, if I seem perhaps too bold in my request, it is your usual kindness toward me that has granted me such great liberty. I therefore more willingly entreat you that, having once of your own accord freed him from prison for my sake, you might now, at my request, grant him this additional benefit: that he might eventually recover his lost money there (if it can be done). Truly, I give you thanks that I have such great influence with you so often, and I rejoice for my own sake. Finally, I pray to God that He may always breathe favorably upon you.

---

### Why great dangers loom over great men.

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, sends greetings.<-

**A** few days ago, I was consoling Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note> with friendly words (as is customary) regarding the recent death of his daughter. Although he is a high-minded man who needs no consolation, I nevertheless confirmed my consolation—even if it were superfluous—with necessary reasons and examples from the Old Testament. In the course of our conversation, we soon came upon Moses, whose life and deeds from the beginning we recounted (at Lorenzo's request). Having heard these things, Lorenzo said: "Do you see, Ficino, how many and how various and how great were the dangers that stood in the way of Moses' future greatness? This was not only from his infancy throughout his whole life, but even at his very birth and before his birth. Indeed, we have found it to be true that immense dangers often loom everywhere for great undertakings and for men who are destined for greatness. This happens either because great-souled men attempt grand, hard, and arduous things, or because adverse fortune, when frequently attempted and overcome, makes men most brave and most prudent. Or perhaps it is because common envy and the ambition of many always oppose excellence. Or perhaps divine providence has so tempered the lives of men with comforts and discomforts for the sake of our salvation. Or perhaps there lies hidden, besides these, some cause lower than God but higher than man, mixing human affairs in such a way—though to investigate this is for those with more leisure and perhaps sometimes for the curious." 

But wherever it comes from, it certainly happens this way. And so that I do not now recount past examples (which are innumerable), he added—for there were many of us present—"You see how certain the proofs of singular greatness are in the man of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher whose "900 Theses" led to conflict with the Church.</note>, which are not only signs of future greatness, but almost evidence of it in the present; and you see by what heavy dangers this young man is being tossed about." Finally, he praised you wonderfully, and the others voiced their approval. A little later, turning to me, he said: "But you men of leisure, have you found any more hidden cause for these things?" 

To this I replied: if the configuration or harmony of the heavens portending a secure ease of life is so different from that which promises excellence of virtue and glory, they can very rarely coincide, or perhaps they cannot. To this is added the fact that there are <term>daemons</term> <note>daemones: In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the evil sense, but intermediary spirits that inhabit the air and influence human affairs.</note> in the air, acting like secondary stars in this heaven closest to us. Among these, like the stars, there are higher daemons and lower ones; both are "shepherds" of men. The higher ones look after the excellent, while the lower ones look after the common herds. Certainly, the lower daemons are moved by human-like passions, and they are especially touched by the sight of superior things and by envy. Therefore, they grieve that men commended to the more sublime daemons are openly judged to be more excellent than their own, and for that reason, they do not want them to rule, to set out, or to prevail. They therefore stir up many people against them from everywhere out of their own "herds," and they even set beasts and the elements against them. 

These things were said there. But has not that high Saturn—the lord in the birth chart of each of us—decreed from the beginning that the bond of Platonic teachings would be something great? Saturn is also the lord in the chart of Plato. Therefore, Saturnian daemons especially rule the bond between these men. But meanwhile, Martial daemons <note>Spirits associated with the planet Mars, the bringer of war and conflict.</note> are everywhere plotting to dissolve this bond. Indeed, Mars itself has entered into the three charts I mentioned as an enemy. Finally, this bond, destined by powerful origins, will overcome the powerful adversaries it has endured thus far, by as much as Saturn is superior to Mars—Saturn, who once, when I was being born, was touching his own Aquarius with his head, and thirty years later, as you were coming forth into the light, was returning to the same spot. Toward this end (as I judge), Lorenzo, the most excellent among the Saturnians, both protects me and supports Pico toward Florence...

->*Where the friend goes, you go also.*<-

### To the Platonist, greetings.

**L**est you say that Marsilio, who was first in your friendship, has come to you last, look, he comes. Contemplate (if you please) the face and gestures of the one who now greets you. But meanwhile, look more closely at what lies hidden behind the mask. Will you ask, "Should I contemplate these youthful features in place of Marsilio?" But that suppliant Pico (if you did not know) recently obtained a request that his youth be renewed like the eagle’s <note>A reference to Psalm 103:5, "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's."</note>. He has indeed obtained it. But what of his gestures? By what means has he just now been made younger and yet more grave? Oh, with what heavy and friendly prayers is youth finally obtained in exchange for old age, so that it is no wonder that a man praying so gravely should emerge both younger and more grave at once. He has indeed emerged, but why has he specifically put on the face of Filippo Valori? <note>Filippo Valori was a close friend and financial patron of Ficino who helped fund the printing of his Plato translations.</note> I leave aside for now, Pico, which form love—that God who is the architect of such works—has chosen; certainly that spirit who fashions amorous transformations, using a marvelous "valor" [power] of nature and affection in the transforming, has expressed the form of Valori in this work. You have now recognized well enough with whom you are speaking as a friend. Farewell; love Valori.

->*The last shall be first.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Probus, Commissioner of the Pope, greetings.

**S**ince we read in the Gospel concerning the banquet that the last shall be first, sit down, most proven Probus <note>Ficino puns on the name "Probus" and the Latin "probatissime," meaning most excellent or proven.</note>; though last today at this table, you are first in my mind. However, I do not dare to demand that I be first in your mind; I shall consider it sufficient if I obtain second place with you, for from that I shall augur a favorable second fortune <note>Ficino puns on "secundum," which means both "second" and "favorable."</note> for myself. Moreover, he who is second to Probus will eventually have to be "probed" <note>Another pun on the name Probus and the Latin "probandus" (to be tested or approved).</note>. Indeed, many of us men of letters have approved of the Pope for entrusting us to be judged by a man so exceptionally learned. For when men of letters encounter an unlearned man, they fall; but when they find a learned one, they rise again. Finally, having found one who is both learned and upright, they rise, never to fall again. Farewell.

->*A joke regarding the fact that he who was about to greet did not greet.*<-

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, the Platonic Philosopher, greetings.

**H**ail, father of the Platonic family. It is now beyond all controversy that the star of Saturn is both harmful and ill-omened, and that you, my dear Ficino—though perhaps for your own good, certainly for my ill—were born under Saturn. For just as that planet is very much retrograde <note>original: "regradarius." An astrological term for a planet that appears to move backward in the sky, here used to tease Ficino for failing to arrive for a visit.</note>, so you too are endowed with a similar nature; having now come toward me twice, you became retrograde and twice retraced your steps. And what is worse, you did so while the sun was setting, so you cannot say you were revering the light of Phoebus <note>The sun.</note>. But tell me, I pray, what was the cause of this repeated retreat? Was it your Saturn? Or rather our fates? But whatever it was that took you from me—that is, took myself from me—act in the future, I beg, so that he who once joined us does not separate us. Never believe that you will come to me as one merely destined to come <note>Pico makes a complex pun here between "faturum" (one who is about to be/speak) and "Saturnus."</note>, for I always hunger and thirst for you, the solace of my life, the delight of my mind, the shaper of my character, and the master of my learning. Farewell, and come, so that your Saturn—that is, your vow of what is to be—may also return me to what I should be. Farewell again, or rather, greetings now that you are arriving.

->*The planets revere the sight of the Sun.*<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.

**A**s for why I came to you much later last month than I am accustomed, the cause was Saturn, who was also retrograde last month after he began to look from Capricorn toward the Sun in Taurus through a trine aspect <note>A "trine" or triangle aspect occurs when two planets are 120 degrees apart, usually considered a harmonious or powerful alignment in astrology.</note>. As for why yesterday I set out for you twice, both morning and evening, and twice retraced my steps: if there is any fault among the powers above, let the fault be Jupiter’s. For yesterday Jupiter began to be retrograde, as one who was similarly coming into a trine aspect with the Sun. For from Pisces he was already looking upon the Sun sitting in Cancer. Moreover, it is the custom and nature of the higher planets, as soon as they come into the very sight of the Sun...

### Relentless labor conquers all.
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, **S. D.** <note>S.D. abbreviates "Salutem Dicit," a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends greetings."</note><-

**G**reetings to the only salvation of the Muses. But for this very reason—that you may be safe <note>Ficino begins a complex pun on the name of their mutual friend, Roberto Salviati, and the Latin words "salvus" (safe/healthy) and "salus" (health/salvation).</note>—nothing in human affairs seems more expedient than that our friend Salviati should wish you to be safe. Therefore, as much as I always desire you to be healthy, I desire Salviati to desire health for you, now and always. Indeed, besides him, I know no one who immediately achieves whatever he wishes. For whether men obtain their desires through the power of prayer alone, he alone, with all his soul and spirit, continually effects whatever he chooses; or if instead they complete their undertakings through diligent work and care, he alone ardently pursues whatever he follows to the very end. Thus, it seems he alone might portend the saying: "He alone who perseveres to the end shall be saved" <note>A reference to Matthew 24:13.</note>; he alone shall be safe. Perhaps our friend even possesses that grain of mustard seed by which mountains are moved. For only yesterday, he moved a giraffe <note>original: "cameleopardum." A famous giraffe was gifted to Lorenzo de' Medici in 1487; Salviati was likely involved in its transport or care.</note> through the eye of a needle, leading an animal through pathless ways for which it was utterly unfit. Why then do we need those hundred reasons of Nicolaus <note>Likely Nicolaus Leonicenus, a scholar who wrote against the certainties of astrology.</note> which we are now reading together to refute the astrologers? Let this one reason be enough for us instead of a hundred: namely, since our friend quickly completes the hardest tasks with a certain burning zeal—even when Saturn is retrograde and denying him success in his duties—we have proof enough from this that our affairs are carried out by our own zeal and by a heavenly instinct rather than by the stars. The soul will be recognized to possess a wonderful power, if only it uses its power to the full in its work. Farewell. July 6, 1488. Florence.

---

### On the three Graces and Harmony.
->Marsilio Ficino to Roberto Salviati and Girolamo Benivieni, **S. D.**<-

**M**any writers are accustomed to address Pico as the "Count of Harmony" <note>original: "Concordiae comiti." Pico was the Count of the territory of Concordia, but Ficino plays on the word "Concordia" meaning harmony or peace.</note>. Thus far, he has been called "companion of harmony" quite rightly, as one who himself sought harmony and gladly followed harmonious men. Hereafter, however, he must be called not merely a companion, but the Leader of Harmony beyond all controversy. For now Harmony itself follows him as its leader. Indeed, just as clouds are scattered by the approach of the Sun, so at the arrival of Pico, all discords flee far away. Suddenly, harmony follows the leader everywhere, so much so that he alone is able to do what some once dared to try, and he does it continually: to reconcile the Jews with the Christians, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> with the Platonists, and the Greeks with the Latins. And rightly so, since those three Graces <note>In mythology, the Graces represent charm, beauty, and creativity.</note> who once accompanied their Venus, immediately upon Pico’s birth, left Venus and now follow Pico at the command of Jupiter, Phoebus, and Mercury. The first Grace shaped his mind from the beginning; the second strengthened his soul’s state and his body; the third finally commands his fortune to obey his counsel. And because she cultivates the soul, she bestowed three graces especially upon his mind: wisdom, eloquence, and probity; for so Phoebus, Mercury, and Jupiter decreed. Therefore, if (as the Furies bring forth discord) the Graces produce harmony, then Pico, whom the Graces accompany, is rightly followed everywhere by Harmony as his leader.

---

### How friends speak even while silent.
->Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone, his fellow Platonist, **S. D.**<-

**I** do not know by what plan, or rather by what fate or chance it happened, that when you left Florence yesterday, you did not say—even through a messenger, as you usually do—"Ficino, farewell." This I know for certain: it would have been proper for you to do so, if not for any other necessity, then at least by the law of friendship, if you were able. Nor would it have been done in vain. I truly desired, as I even signaled, to talk with you at greater length. But while I was forced to delay my conversation for three days, this unexpected departure of yours frustrates my "fable" <note>original: "fabulam." Ficino puns on the word for a story, a conversation, or a play.</note>. Thus this long-invented story leaves me, while the great-souled Lion <note>original: "Leo." A pun on his friend's name, Pierleone.</note> departs from here—a real lion, not a fable. I have just erred. For an invented story cannot vanish if it has not yet been told. What then? If my guiding spirit and yours judged winged words unworthy to be entrusted with an eternal...

...the meaning of this story might be entrusted. And so, if he has somehow disdained living voices, by what reason will he deign to notice letters that are not alive? Therefore, what I did not entrust to voices, I shall not entrust to letters either. My own Genius <note>In the Platonic sense, a 'Genius' is a guiding spirit or the higher intellect of a person.</note>—who is never absent nor ever departs from yours—is even now beginning this intimate conversation, speaking to yours and continuing it forever. Through these internal conversations, no envious or dark demons <note>Ficino uses 'demons' (dæmones) in the classical sense of spiritual influences, here specifically the 'black' demons associated with melancholy or malice.</note> encountered from the outside shall insert themselves further. A thousand shall fall at my side, and ten thousand at your right hand <note>original: "Cadent à latere meo mille & decem millia à dextris tuis." A quote from Psalm 91:7, suggesting divine protection.</note>. Fare happily; practice philosophy even more happily; destined to return one day most fortunately to the City of Flowers <note>original: "Florentem Vrbem," referring to Florence.</note>, which is so friendly to you. August 11, 1488. Florence.

### According to Orpheus, all things are to be resolved into fire.
->Marsilio Ficino to Callimachus the wise poet, greetings.<-

**T**hey say that Orpheus and some others have sung that, since all things are composed of four contrary materials <note>The four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, and since fire is the largest and most powerful of all and, by its perpetual motion, gradually wears down the rest, everything must finally be resolved completely into fire <note>The concept of 'ekpyrosis' or world-conflagration, a Stoic and Orphic doctrine.</note>. What then? If the divine Intellect, the moderator of all, has granted so great a dissolution to the world, then just as the world is compacted into a most beautiful form while it stands firm, so too, when it is finally dissolved, it is reduced to the most beautiful matter. If we believe this, we bear this great destruction of the universe with an even mind. Likewise, my dear Callimachus <note>Filippo Buonaccorsi (1437–1496), known as Callimachus Experiens, a humanist who fled to Poland after a conspiracy against the Pope.</note>, we shall magnanimously bear the recent fire at your house with an equal mind. Furthermore, you were seeking light from books; instead, those wise books have been turned into light for you and snatched up into heaven—contrary to how Prometheus snatched wisdom from heaven along with fire. What then do we omen for you from this, my friend? In the end, you will shine more by your passing than by your life. August 15, 1488. Florence.

### One must consider the style in which one writes.
->Marsilio Ficino to Hermolao Barbaro of Venice, greetings.<-

**T**he legal case of Matthias Cinus is being handled before you (as I hear); he manages the affairs there for a certain very dear friend of mine. Unless he had asked me, I would not be commending his rights to you, for I think it is superfluous to commend justice to a man so prudent and just. This cause, Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro was a high-ranking Venetian diplomat and one of the era's most meticulous Greek scholars.</note>, has compelled me to write something to you after a long silence. I would certainly write more often if I could write more elegantly. For I hear that nothing but the most exquisite things please your most refined ears. You are blessed, my friend, who have attained the first rank of eloquence. Yet I am not wretched, for I am content with the tenth. Farewell, and love me very much, as I love you. Our friend Giovanni Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola.</note>, who is now philosophizing excellently in Florence, commends himself to you. September 14, 1488. Florence.

### On the flight of Fame. And that each person's own things are dearest to them.
->Marsilio Ficino to Paolo of Florence, the Theologian, greetings.<-

**Y**our letters were most welcome to me, through which I understood both that you are well and that I am "flying." For since (as you write) I have already brought all of Europe into amorous servitude to myself, I was not able to do this by approach; therefore, I did it by flight. But you have added wings to this flight by the spirit of your praise, or rather, your public proclamation. You, then, be my Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman; Ficino jokes that Paolo’s praise gives him wings.</note> (provided I am not an Icarus to you), although I am very dear to you, and rightly so, since your own things ought to be most dear to you. Your things are also so dear to me that this noble youth, commended to you before all others, is also most welcome to me. Especially because he is already becoming an old man (as you say) in learning and judgment. Truly, nature often repays the changes of things in this way, since there are also many old men who are mere children in their wits. Finally, as much as I am my own, I am yours, my Paolo, and I am also this youth's. Farewell.

->*Nothing hinders the study of letters more than civic ambition. This is proven through Astrology.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Hermolao Barbaro, the most illustrious envoy of the Venetian Senate, sends many greetings.<-

**I** have heard from many people this year—and recently from Pedro Alamanni, who, having performed his embassy there, greeted me in your name yesterday—that in your current diplomatic mission, you have applied yourself to letters no less than usual, and (what is even more marvelous) you are philosophizing even more sharply than is your custom. People are usually inclined, my dear Barbaro, when they conduct public affairs—or even as soon as they first touch them—to interrupt their literary studies. This is partly because a busy life takes away the leisure <note>original: "otium." In the Renaissance, *otium* was not mere laziness, but the productive "holy leisure" required for study and contemplation, the opposite of *negotium* or "business."</note> for letters, which is the work of a free mind. It is also because the closer we approach Jupiter, the lord of governance and command, the further we depart from Mercury, the prince of letters. For the Moon and the other celestial bodies are never further separated from the houses of Mercury than when they enter the seats of Jupiter. Indeed, the very Architect of the world placed Pisces opposite to Virgo, and Sagittarius opposite to Gemini <note>In astrology, Mercury rules Virgo and Gemini. Jupiter rules Pisces and Sagittarius. These signs sit 180 degrees apart in the zodiac, representing fundamental opposition.</note>. Furthermore, do they not think that the Sun signifies princes and honors, while Saturn signifies Philosophers? Yet in the heavens, the kingdom of the one is opposed to the kingdom of the other, and their houses are contrary. Who, therefore, will ever philosophize as a prince? Or who as a Philosopher will rule? But since you achieve things that neither the heavens seem to promise nor mortals are accustomed to provide, we shall say that your soul—just as the Magician Olympius said of the soul of Plotinus—is more powerful than both human and celestial nature <note>Plotinus was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher. Ficino refers to a story from Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* where a rival's magical spells were turned back by the sheer spiritual strength of Plotinus's soul.</note>. Rejoice, therefore, in such great power. Your friend congratulates you for it. Farewell. October 11, 1488.

---

->*Few join public business with the study of letters.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Gaddo, Envoy of the Florentine Senate, sends greetings.<-

**I** am writing to Hermolao Barbaro, praising him because, amidst civil and turbulent affairs, he seeks his accustomed leisure for literary studies, and what is more wonderful, he even philosophizes more ardently. The more Jupiter weighs upon his head with public cares, the more he himself presses upon Minerva, who was born from the head of Jupiter <note>Ficino uses the myth of Athena (Minerva) springing from the head of Zeus (Jupiter) to show that wisdom can be found even within the heavy responsibilities of leadership.</note>. Few are those whom "just Jupiter has loved"—not the Planet, but the Creator of the Planets—few join together these two things so far apart from one another. Only those born of the gods were able either to pursue both at once, as Hermolao does, or, while pursuing one (which is the study of philosophy), to complete in a moment what others could scarcely do in a long time. Our friend Pico <note>referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous "Phoenix" of the Renaissance known for his incredible memory and vast learning.</note> achieves this second feat, for his is a fiery vigor and a celestial origin. Water transforms wood into water in barely a thousand years; fire converts it into fire as if in a moment. Theologians call Saturn "the most voracious" <note>In myth, Saturn (Cronus) devoured his own children. Ficino turns this into a metaphor for Pico's "devouring" of books.</note>. Just as Saturn was born, so Pico, like that Saturn devouring his children, daily devours entire great books—not indeed to reduce them to ashes, as our fire does, but to bring them into the light, as celestial fire does. Therefore, you, our most beloved Francesco, imitating Hermolao Barbaro, shall meanwhile not cease to philosophize during your embassy. You will greet him when your business allows in the name of Marsilio and Pico. You will indicate that as much as our "smoke" <note>A humble term Ficino uses for his own works or presence.</note> belongs to both of them, so much are they both ours. When I name "both," I wish for Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the great poet and scholar, who was a close friend to both Ficino and Pico.</note> to be understood as well—the indissoluble bond of them both. Farewell. October 11, 1488.

---

->*One truly lives only there, where one lives by the intellect.*<-

->Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Marco the Venetian, Cardinal of Saint Mark.<-

**D**o you not see how clever our friend Calderinus is? He devised long ago a most easy and safe travel-provision <note>term: "viaticum" — originally money or supplies for a journey; here, it refers to the spiritual and social "protection" provided by the Cardinal's favor.</note> by which he might always travel safely to Florence and return to Rome. For he always supports and arms himself with your greetings, by which he may go safely through spears and through fires, and may return his friend safe, and report himself safe to you also. Your greetings <note>The Latin *salutatio* means both "greeting" and "wishing health/safety."</note> indeed, whether they go from you or return to you, make this man (whom I just now called "clever") truly "prudent." For other men of that same brave sort mostly sleep at the doors of the foolish, but our friend meanwhile keeps watch there at the doors of the wise, so that he may draw health and safety from the Lord, which he also imparts to his friends. Indeed, he does this so that he may find life; for he hopes to live only there, where one lives most of all by the intellect; since he both reads and remembers the verse: *Give me understanding, and I shall live.* <note>original: "intellectum da mihi & uiuam." A quote from Psalm 119:144.</note> Live happily, therefore, above all others, venerable patron, and keep our clients commended to you.

# MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine to Martinus Uranius
## Of Constance, his unique friend, Greetings.

### P R E F A C E.

**T**he ninth book of our Letters—so that it may feel and be moved throughout—has long been calling for a "head," the citadel of the animal virtue <note>original: "uirtutis animalis." In Renaissance physiology, the "animal virtue" or "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul) was the highest of the three spirits, located in the brain and responsible for sensation and movement.</note> and the origin of sense and motion. While I was deliberating on choosing a "head" for this book, my own guardian angel presented himself as the head of the book, commanding me to follow this number nine. For the nine orders of angels have been accepted not only among Christians, but among the Hebrews and the Platonists. Under such a great head and leader, therefore, we ask: whenever the book or the man whom the angel guards wanders here and there, does the angel likewise wander? Not at all; for the angel, whom they call the "good demon" or "genius" <note>A "genius" was considered a personal protective spirit assigned to a person at birth, guiding their character and fate.</note>, is thought by Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>Three major figures of Neoplatonism who wrote extensively on the hierarchy of spirits and the soul’s ascent.</note> to either be always everywhere, or to be present wherever he wishes as easily and swiftly as a ray of the Sun, reaching here in a moment and reflected from here to there and everywhere in that same moment. Indeed, he is much faster and easier, for the ray is an act of a luminous body, while the angel exists by his own right. Or, he governs like one's own star, not descending but through an influence diffused everywhere. 

We seem to have said enough already about why we have begun the book with an angel. But why do we dedicate it specifically to Martinus Uranius? <note>Martin Prenninger (c. 1450–1501), a German humanist and jurist who took the name "Uranius" (meaning "Heavenly").</note> Because my book, having now been made "genial" <note>A play on words: "genialis" refers both to the "genius" (the angel) and to a pleasant, festive nature.</note>, has by its own right become the property of this man, who shares the same "genius" with me. Receive, therefore, with pleasure, and read with success, my heavenly friend Uranius, the letters of Martin and Marsilio alike. Farewell happily, my other self. July 4, 1480. Florence. <note>original: "M. CCCC. LXXX." Historical scholarship often suggests the 1480s or 1490 for this book; the presence of Pico della Mirandola, who arrived in Florence in 1484, suggests the date in this printed edition may be shorthand for 1489 or a typographical error.</note>

# The Letters of MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine,
## B O O K IX.
### A description of a healthy villa.

**W**hen in recent days I and our Pico della Mirandola—a man of admirable virtue—were wandering through the Fiesole hills, or rather the foothills of Fiesole, we were looking out over the entire settlement of the city of Florence spread out before our eyes. It is certainly a happy place, if only two inconveniences are carefully avoided: the mists of the central river Arno, and the sharp winds of the opposite mountain. We were imagining, therefore, a house on the hill at the roots of the Fiesole mountain, so that we might avoid the fog on one side and the North Wind <note>original: "Boream," the personification of the cold north wind.</note> on the other. Yet we did not want it situated in a hollow, so that it might catch the breeze more abundantly during the heat. Furthermore, we desired it to be placed equally between cultivated fields and groves, and abounding everywhere with springs, and that it should face toward the South and the East. This is exactly what Aristotle prescribes for buildings when he discusses domestic affairs. But while we were walking (and while we were imagining such things), we suddenly saw exactly such a place. Here Pico exclaimed: "Now, my Ficino, what we were just now vividly imagining and wishing for, we soon seem to see..."

...we seem to see. This happens daily to those who dream. Or perhaps, by the power of the imagination, have we fashioned such a form as we were engineering in the mind? Or rather, did a wise man once build such a thing? Exactly as the correct and physical method of building prescribes. Then I said: "Pico, that wise man Leonardo Bruni <note>original: "Leonhardus Aretinus." Leonardo Bruni (c. 1370–1444) was a famous humanist, historian, and chancellor of Florence.</note> is said to have constructed this very house, and almost in this very spot where you see it, Giovanni Boccaccio <note>The famous author of the *Decameron*.</note> lived; later, our friend Pier Filippo Pandolfini, a man of great family and name, chose it as a happy place to live, surely with the same wisdom as those men." "O happy man," said Pico, "to whom it happens that, when withdrawing from public business, he inhabits a sacred temple; I said 'temple,' for it is placed near this sacred grove, and twenty houses of the gods <note>original: "diuorum." Likely referring to local shrines or villas named after saints.</note> stand around it. Therefore, the place is sacred above others and especially suited for oracles. Hence, Pandolfini <note>A prominent Florentine family.</note> seems rightly named; for if we interpret this name from the Greek, it signifies 'entirely Delphic' <note>Ficino is making a pun: Pan (all) + Delphic (referring to the Oracle of Apollo). He suggests the name Pandolfini implies the family is full of prophetic or divine wisdom.</note>." These things, my Valor, were then discussed and approved among us; you will report these same things to your most distinguished fellow citizen <note>Likely referring to a member of the Pandolfini family.</note>, so that he may hereafter more willingly and more frequently inhabit a seat so healthy and divinely dedicated to him. Farewell. October 29, 1488.

### *A complaint and consolation on the death of friends.*
->*Marsilio Ficino to Amerigo Corsini, his fellow philosopher,*<-
->*sendeth many greetings.*<-

**I** was lamenting yesterday, my dear Corsini, together with Giovanni Canacci and Bindaccio Ricasoli, our brothers in Plato, over the far too cruel death of Alamanno Bonati, the "Mars" of the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence.</note>. I call him the Mars of our Academy for this reason: because the high-spirited and eloquent youth most sharply defended every one of us against envious detractors. Therefore, this Mars of ours was yesterday struck down and immediately removed from our midst by a far too cruel accident—Mars, coursing through Leo in conjunction with the Moon, dashed him against a rock after he fell from a mountain. I blame Mars above the rest (if it is lawful for us to blame any of the heavenly beings), since he himself, with the Moon, then occupied the Lion <note>The zodiac sign Leo.</note> which was once ascending at Alamanno’s birth. And now, having been struck, he holds the "eighth house" <note>In astrology, the eighth house is the house of death.</note> in the heavens. But in the same hour in which he, alas, miserably fell and perished, Saturn was rising from the east in Capricorn. Pitying the heavy fate of the Philosopher—for Saturn himself loves philosophers—he received his soul through Capricorn, the <term>gate of the gods</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, Capricorn was considered the portal through which souls ascended back to heaven, while Cancer was the portal for descent into birth.</note>, and numbered him among the angelic thrones there. And although that ought to be enough to console our sorrow, I was nevertheless weeping (as I said) for the premature death of the noble youth. To this they said, "Our Marsilio, alas, Mars has not only caused this one loss to the Academy, but it has also recently lost the learned and religious man Lottieri by death; thus we have need of a double consolation, if we proceed to mourn these things." Amidst these words, it was announced to us, Amerigo, that the highest magistracy of the Republic has been entrusted to you today. Wherefore we immediately obtained the double consolation we needed: both because a friend is honored by this office, and also because the office is honored by such a man. Therefore, the Academy congratulates you on this magistracy, and the fatherland rejoices. You too, our Corsini, prosper, not only by this present office but also by happy auspices. For now the Sun, in a most happy <term>Trine aspect</term> <note>An astrological aspect of 120 degrees, considered highly favorable and harmonious.</note>, looks upon Jupiter as it now moves directly forward, promising happier things for the future. These he will finally provide when God himself, the moderator of the stars, shall will it. October 29, 1488.

### *The position and aspect of the Planets contributing to talent.*
->*Marsilio Ficino to Hermolao Barbaro, greetings.*<-

**F**riends are frequently accustomed to write to one another that the minds of friends are not separated by mountains. In saying such things, they more often lie, or certainly are deceived. For minds are far disjointed when one is entirely ignorant of the other's <term>genius</term> <note>In this context, *ingenium* or genius refers to a person's natural talent, intellect, and spiritual character.</note>. You, therefore, are a true man—and in this, as in your other affairs, a teller of truth—if ever it happens that you write the same to us as you perhaps wrote to others; you recently sent to...

<header>LETTERS, BOOK VIII.</header>

...these as a certain formula of your intellect, and a beautiful one indeed. If only Mercury, the giver of intellect, inhabiting his airy domicile as the twins <note>original: "geminos habitans." This refers to the zodiac sign Gemini, which is the "domicile" or home of the planet Mercury.</note>, provides an ample mind. And perhaps more charmingly and elegantly than in a maiden <note>original: "uirgine." Referring to Virgo, Mercury's other zodiac sign.</note>, and looking from there toward Jupiter rising in Aries in a sextile aspect <note>A "sextile" is an astrological aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious.</note>, he adds integrity and humanity to beauty. And while he also looks from there at Saturn reigning in a trine aspect in Libra, and occupying (as I judge) the angle of the west—just as Jupiter occupies the east—he decrees for your intellect a gravity and a study of ancient wisdom, and that indeed firm and perpetual. And so your spirit, my Hermolaus <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a Venetian humanist and diplomat.</note>, has come to us, but so far without its body; it dwells with us naked, until we receive from you the rest of the heavenly figure <note>A "figure" or "scheme" refers to a complete astrological birth chart.</note>, by which the form of the body may be distinguished and more fully expressed. You are so humane, my Barbaro, that you could not endure your friend’s spirit to be without its own soul any longer. Will you then be so inhumane to your own spirit now as to allow it to long for its body any longer? Far be it from you to permit that. For if you perform what we vehemently desire, you will be entirely with yourself, Hermolaus, and equally entirely with us. To this is added that, once your birth chart is finally examined, we shall write something to you not useless for your health. We hope that while we care for your life, we look forward to the life of our age. Farewell happily, and that you may fare more happily, be entirely yourself everywhere. November 12, 1488.

### ->On the efficacy of speaking and the reason for joking.<-
### ->Marsilio Ficino to Pierleoni, a singular Philosopher, or rather a Poet, Greetings.<-

**D**eny now, at least, that you are a poet. If indeed you have just now become a shaper of fate <note>original: "fator." A pun on the verb "fari" (to speak) and "fata" (fate).</note> by speaking, this your letter certainly testifies, right in the introduction with these words: "I am," you say, "so difficult in writing," and what follows. What else do you attempt with these words, except to speak of the difficulty of writing? Meanwhile, you create this very difficulty by saying it—a difficulty, I say, not only of writing, but moreover of reading. These words are full of such grand and artistic erasures <note>original: "lituris." Referring to corrections or ink blots in the manuscript.</note>. Therefore, you are both so truthful and so effective, that what you say, you meanwhile bring about. But why do I now joke with a most grave Philosopher? Yet truly, I do not joke as a Philosopher with a Philosopher, but as a friend with a friend; but however I joke, what then? Does not Mercury himself now joke in the heavens, and play within us? He is accustomed to speak seriously when with Saturn or Jupiter, but to joke when with Venus. Therefore, at this hour, conjoined with Venus and the Moon, and now ascending, he rejects serious things and rejoices in the ridiculous. However, let us set aside these ridiculous things for a moment (if we can). As for the fact that you are spreading my Platonic works everywhere, I am as grateful as I am delighted by the light. For with such a man singing our works, just as if Apollo were illuminating them, we cannot remain obscure. You expect Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> from us. Expect Proclus and Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), a Syrian Neoplatonist.</note> together—that divine Iamblichus, wonderfully answering the many and most grave questions of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), student of Plotinus.</note>, and meanwhile revealing the divine mysteries of the Egyptians and Assyrians. We shall soon compensate for the slowness of our promises with the abundance of the gift (God helping). Meanwhile, farewell happily. But after I said farewell, our Pico della Mirandola, a man certainly to be wondered at, touched and read this letter. And he read it so beautifully, and judged it so sharply, that I would not say it was so much mine as his. What then? If by touch and sight together he has so affected it that he made it his own in an instant, yet meanwhile it does not cease to be mine. For which reason, when he said "farewell," I had to say: Ficino and Pico wish you a speedy recovery. January 3, 1490, just after sunrise.

### ->He writes enough to one friend, who writes to all friends at once.<-
### ->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Bandini, many Greetings.<-

**I** have written nothing to you for a long time, my dearest Bandini, because meanwhile I am writing many things both to you and to everyone. Would that they were as good as they are many. You have already heard that I have long since made all the books of Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism. Ficino's Latin translation was a massive undertaking.</note> Latin, and [I have written] commentaries on them...
