...begun to write [the commentaries] soon after, we have now brought these to the halfway point. Perhaps I would have finished them already, had I not been forced during my commenting to translate additionally into Latin the Platonic Michael Psellus’s *On Demons*, and Synesius’s *On Dreams*, and in part Porphyry’s *On Abstinence*, and also the divine Iamblichus’s *On the Theology of the Egyptians and Assyrians*, and finally Priscianus Lydus, who carefully interprets the thought of Theophrastus regarding the mind. Among these tasks, Filippo Valori—a man full of valor and grace, and most devoted to all your royal affairs—is transcribing the texts and commentaries of Plotinus for the King in a royal volume. Thirty-three large quires <note>A "quire" (quinternio) is a gathering of parchment or paper sheets; thirty-three quires represents a substantial portion of a massive manuscript.</note> have already been completed. Farewell. January 6, 1489. Florence.

### A friend within a friend. Likewise, an excuse for the journey not undertaken.
### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine Platonist humbly commends himself to the most serene King of Pannonia <note>Pannonia was the Roman name for the region comprising modern-day Hungary.</note>, Matthias, forever undefeated.

**S**if the wondrous power of friendship can bring about what the Pythagoreans promise—that the soul of a friend dwells within his friend—then surely my soul is now within Filippo Valori, who has recently traveled to Pannonia primarily to salute Your Majesty. Thus, when you hear him saluting you Humbly, you may consider that you have heard Marsilio himself. Indeed, I have long desired to visit Your Majesty, having been missed by many there, but I feared that my strength would not be sufficient for such a long journey. I decided at last to come in the person of Valori, especially since I have brought with me "provisions for the way" <note>original: "uiaticum." Ficino uses the term for travel funds/supplies as a metaphor for the intellectual nourishment of books.</note> full of the health-giving food of the mind, which would serve as both nourishment on the road and a vehicle for me. You will therefore read with pleasure the philosopher Priscianus Lydus, who carefully interprets the mind of both Theophrastus and Aristotle regarding the senses, imagination, and the intellect. I have not only translated this from the Greek, but have also explained it with brief notes. In reading this, you will clearly recognize what Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek rhetorician and philosopher known for paraphrasing Aristotle.</note> also asserts: that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus regarding the mind is the same. They held that there is one <term>Divine Mind</term> common to all men, illuminating human minds everywhere (which the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> call the "Active Intellect"). Yet there are as many individual minds belonging to men as there are souls, and these are likewise immortal (which they were accustomed to call "Possible Intellects," meaning they can be formed by the Divine Mind). Through these explanations, you will understand that Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, who argued the soul was mortal.</note> and Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued for a single collective human intellect.</note> are refuted, and you will fully recognize the divinity of our soul. Furthermore, you will not disdain to read the book by Michael Psellus on demons, which I have translated briefly; it reconciles the Platonists with the Christians regarding the nature of demons. After this, you will see the laborious work of Plotinus, a portion of which has now been brought to Pannonia (so that the whole may be shown to you in part). It remains for me to most strongly commend my friend Valori to your most happy Majesty, and myself within Valori. February 6, 1490.

### Preface to Theophrastus on the Soul.
### Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, greetings.

**H**e who commanded "Know thyself" <note>The famous inscription at the Oracle of Delphi.</note> seems to admonish us to know the soul. Since the soul is the center of all things, it is surely everything; therefore, once it is known, we shall easily know all things. I, therefore, (in order to first grasp the soul, through which I might attain all things) have for a long time studiously turned to the philosophers—not those of the common sort, but the most excellent. However, when I anxiously questioned the Platonists on one side and the Peripatetics on the other, and their answers seemed to disagree with each other, I despaired from the start of ever achieving my wish. But not long after, Themistius offered me the best hope, affirming that such great philosophers do not actually disagree in their opinions, but only in their words. He claimed that the view of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus regarding the soul is the same, despite the different terms used. Finally, by some divine chance, I fell upon a book by Theophrastus on the soul, explained briefly but diligently by a certain Priscianus Lydus, using the same reasoning employed by Plutarch, Iamblichus...

...eminent Platonists and Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they walked and talked.</note> had explained Aristotle's opinion on the soul. Therefore, when I noticed in reading them that the Platonists and Peripatetics were in agreement, I held in my mind almost everything I was seeking. And so that others might have it as soon as possible, we have translated this book from the Greek language into Latin. Furthermore, we have added certain brief expositions devised by us during the reading and translating. However, I did not think I should labor too much on this matter for the present, or wander too far afield, for our Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—a man certainly to be wondered at <note>original: "uir certē mirandus" — a witty play on his title "Mirandola".</note>—is already attending to this highest goal, where he most diligently discusses the minds of all philosophers on any given subject, and marvelously demonstrates that Plato and Aristotle are in agreement regarding the soul. Truly, I decided this book should be dedicated especially to you, my dear Valori <note>Filippo Valori, a close friend and patron of Ficino.</note>. For you, along with me, have for a long time been vehemently affected by the philosophers' views on this matter. Our physicians, however—to whom we are accustomed to give or rather return everything as if to patrons—will undoubtedly agree that this one little gift out of many be dedicated to my Valori, a man most friendly above others to the Medicean house, and always the most ready assistant for Platonic works. Moreover, although we found only a single Greek manuscript, and a faulty and fragmented one at that, you should nevertheless read it and offer it to others to be read in this state. For I have studied to correct and unlock it most diligently. And our Angelo Poliziano, a man of the sharpest judgment and great learning, has approved of this diligence of ours. Farewell. March 25, 1488.

### Preface to Iamblichus.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to the Reverend<-
->Father in Christ, Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal of the<-
->Holy Roman Church.<-

**W**hen I had decided to write a letter to you to congratulate you on the Cardinal’s dignity recently conferred upon you, and was thinking to whom I should best give it to be delivered to you—someone who would make our congratulation much more pleasing—I suddenly betook myself to the Academy. I hoped that in its innermost sanctuaries, at least, some greeter most acceptable to you would not be lacking. There, by a certain divine chance, I first encountered Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his interest in theurgy and ritual.</note> among the Academics, surnamed "The Divine," and a great Priest there. To whom I said: "Greetings, Iamblichus, great Priest. There is a man in Florence sent by God, whose name is Giovanni, born of the heroic Medici stock; he has come as a witness, to bear witness before everyone regarding the supreme authority of his magnanimous father, Lorenzo." I pray that you, too, will bear witness to him of my singular love toward him. You will make our congratulation—otherwise meager—fuller with your divine words and mysteries for this new priest of the Christian religion, who is even now about to bear the Cardinal's hat. He granted my prayers, and with this sentiment addressed to you, Giovanni, great Priest, that great Priest Iamblichus comes. Therefore, receive such a greeter joyfully, and after the first greeting, after the letter has been read, listen more attentively (if it please you) to what that Divine man says. For he promised that he would speak words equally worthy of his persona and yours, expressing to you in brief what the Egyptian and Assyrian Priests felt regarding religion and divine matters.

---

### Summary of the book.

**P**orphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major figure in Neoplatonism.</note>, who among the Platonists is called "the Philosopher" on account of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to the priest Anebo, full of various and weighty questions pertaining to all parts of philosophy, especially regarding God and angels, demons and souls, providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his pupil, responded to Porphyry's questions. Indeed, he introduces Abamon the Egyptian Priest responding to Porphyry on behalf of his disciple Anebo, to whom Porphyry had sent the letter. Therefore, of this entire inquiry and response—which is truly divine—I have translated nearly every sense rather than just the words, as if I were still too occupied with Plotinus. Thus it should not be thought a wonder if the speech seems disjointed in places, especially among the principles of the debate themselves, or by a lighter movement of words; for hereafter the context of the words will appear more continuous. I have been forced at times to add some word of my own, either for the sake of continuity or understanding...

### Preface to Proclus and Porphyry.

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, the Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. <-

**A**lmighty God seems to have once promised to Giovanni Bicci de' Medici <note>Giovanni di Bicci (1360–1429), the founder of the Medici fortune.</note>—a man of distinguished piety and, as far as civic life allows, a saint in the opinion of all—the same promise He made to a certain Abraham, as far as it is right to compare them: "Your offspring <note>original: "Proles" — Ficino is likely making a wordplay on "Proclus," the philosopher he is introducing, and "Proles," meaning offspring.</note>, O John, shall shine upon your age like the stars of heaven. The peoples shall bless your seeds. In your seed, finally, all nations shall be blessed." These were God's words to him. Truly, the "seeds" of Giovanni, whom the people bless, were first Cosimo, then Piero the son of Cosimo, and thirdly the magnanimous Lorenzo, born of Piero. But the "seed" of the same Giovanni in whom all nations shall be blessed is Giovanni, born of Lorenzo, upon whom—while he was still a young youth—divine providence miraculously conferred the dignity of the Cardinalate <note>Giovanni de' Medici was appointed a cardinal at age 13; he later became Pope Leo X.</note>, an omen of the future Pontiff, in whom indeed all nations may be blessed in the place of Christ. Therefore, to this family, chosen by God long ago as the best, every best man of letters ought to consecrate all his own works (if I may put it that way), and indeed those works that are most choice. 

As for Marsilio, a long-time protégé <term>alumno</term> <note>Literally "nursling" or "foster child," indicating Ficino's deep, lifelong dependency on Medici patronage.</note> of the Medici house, it was not permitted by his age to dedicate anything to Giovanni Bicci; it was permitted first to destine several things for Cosimo, then for Piero, and thirdly for Lorenzo. Now, by a fourth step and with God’s breathing favor, it is permitted to offer to Giovanni—the beacon <note>original: "Faro"</note> of the flower of the Medici house—flowers gathered from the meadows of the Platonic philosophers. I offer these indeed with happy omens, so that my books (or rather my "children") might also become participants in the blessing when the nations are finally blessed in you. You recently received, venerable Patron, the flowers I had gathered from the meadows of Iamblichus; now, receive happily those I have plucked from the fields of Porphyry and Proclus. Once you have tasted these in the manner of a bee, you may fashion them into honey in the gardens of the Academy.

### Preface to Synesius and Psellus.

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to the Magnanimous Piero de' Medici. <-

**A**lthough you read many things daily that are better than ours, I nevertheless judge that almost none please you more than ours—if only because one's own things usually please a person most. And those things are most especially "one's own" which have been possessed for the longest time. Certainly, the "Marsilian" works have been possessed by you for the longest time; I hope, therefore, that these will always be most dear to you. Even if I send you dreams, let these be held as true among you first, and through you, let them be held as true among others as well. Since I desired that the book of Synesius the Platonist *On Dreams*—which we recently translated from the Greek—should have authority and trust especially with the first reader, and through him with others, I have sent it specifically to you. You are now the fourth generation after the great Cosimo to read our works. I hope that through your approval, on account of your excellent learning and authority, these works will be approved by everyone. I have joined to the book *On Dreams* the book of Michael Psellus the Platonist *On Demons*, and not without reason, since the ancients judged that dreams are sent by demons <note>The word "demons" (daemones) here refers to intermediary spirits or guiding entities in the Neoplatonic sense, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. Farewell. April 15, 1489.

-> Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his best compatriot, Andrea Cambini. <-

**F**or many reasons and for a long time now, my dearest compatriot, I have owed you much, but for this very reason I owe you the most: that today you have lightened our mind, which was weighed down by some unknown weariness, of its troublesome burden. For you gave us three orations of your close friend Francesco Pucci to read. The reading of these delighted me so much that I am scarcely able to express this pleasure in even as many speeches as those of Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an Early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant Latin style.</note>. For those things are accustomed to delight most which...

## Response to one seeking Platonic instruction and a list of books.

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Martin Uranius Prenninger, sends greetings. <-

**T**he divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized ritual and theurgy alongside philosophy.</note>, following the mind of the Egyptians, describes two paths to happiness: one is Philosophical, the other Priestly <note>original: "sacerdotiam." This refers to theurgy, or divine ritual.</note>. The former is the more open path for finding happiness, but the latter is the shorter way to attaining it. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> and similar philosophers chose the first path above all. The religious people walk mostly in the second. Our Plato joined both lives together in a wonderful way into one, and he is everywhere equally a religious man and a philosopher: a subtle debater, a pious priest, and an eloquent orator. 

For this reason, if you follow the footsteps of the divine Plato for a long time, as you have begun, you will both find happiness, with God as your guide, and you will attain the same, with God as your leader. This is especially true because our Plato, together with Pythagorean and Socratic reasonings, follows the Mosaic law and prophesies the Christian law. Since you ask, your way to Platonic understanding will be led by our *Arguments* <note>Ficino wrote short "argumenta" or summaries for each of Plato's dialogues.</note> on his books, and the books of ours which you already have, titled specifically *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>Ficino's masterpiece, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>, which nevertheless encompass the whole of Platonic thought. Likewise, Alcinous <note>An author of a handbook on Platonism from the 2nd century AD.</note> has been sent to you today. Furthermore, and much more so, the divine Iamblichus, recently translated by us, is to be sent to you at another time. 

But most of all, the fifty-four books of Plotinus will lead you into the inner shrines of all wisdom; these we have both translated and now, for the most part, interpreted with commentaries. You will perhaps be able to receive these in the new Spring. You ask, moreover, what books I have either translated or composed besides these. I have indeed translated Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the "Hermetic" tradition.</note> *On the Divine Mind* and *On the Crafting of the World*, Synesius *On Dreams*, Psellus *On Demons*, and some works of Porphyry *On the Soul and Intellect*. Also some of Proclus *On the Alcibiades*, and the Platonic commentaries of Priscian on the books of Theophrastus *On the Soul*. 

I have composed works *On Pleasure*, and *On Caring for the Health of Scholars* <note>Ficino's *De Vita Libri Tres*, a famous medical and astrological self-help guide for intellectuals.</note>, which you will receive now; eight volumes of our letters; a commentary on the *Philebus*, not yet finished; *On Love*; and *On the Christian Religion*. I have also attempted certain other things rather than fully composed them, such as a book *Against the Plague* in the Tuscan tongue <note>The Italian vernacular.</note>. 

You ask which Platonic books are found again among the Latins: everything by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian once thought to be a disciple of St. Paul, but now known as "Pseudo-Dionysius."</note> is Platonic; many things of Augustine; Boethius's *Consolation*; Apuleius *On Demons*; Calcidius's commentary on the *Timaeus*; Macrobius's exposition on the *Dream of Scipio*; Avicebron's *Source of Life* <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, a Jewish philosopher.</note>; Al-Farabi *On Causes*; and many things in Henry of Ghent, Avicenna, and Scotus <note>Duns Scotus.</note> smack of Plato. Read also, in whatever translation, Proclus’s *Elements of Theology*, and his *Theology* itself, and the book *On Providence and Fate*. Likewise, we have also translated, in some fashion, Hermias on the *Phaedrus*, and Iamblichus *On the Pythagorean Sect*. There exists, moreover, a *Defense of Plato* made by Cardinal Bessarion of Nicaea. Also certain speculations of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa. 

But I seem to myself to have answered your questions well enough so far. However, as for the love toward Marsilio in your Martin—which I know for certain is singular—I trust I can never respond to it even with countless letters. But lest I be entirely ungrateful for your truly singular love, I respond, believe me, with a similarly singular love, and I embrace your soul, which burns toward me, with a similar ardor of mind. These rewards of your lover, Prenninger, you shall first carry from us. But I wish I could give some gift, or at least suspect a gift, to "Uranius"—that is, "The Heavenly One"—that is celestial, or nearly celestial. I truly wish, my Uranius, and I also hope, that before you return to your heavenly fatherland, you will be a sharer in happiness and blessed in heaven. Florence, June 11, 1489.

# MARSILIO FICINO

### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Pierleone, sends greetings.

**A**s much as you yourself desired to visit Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) whose works Ficino translated and admired.</note>, so much did I desire to send him to you. For those who share the same will, there is surely an equal and similar desire. Why did I not do so sooner? His hour had not yet arrived; it arrives now, though somewhat late, for him to depart from here. May he not reach you too late; he will certainly arrive as a good guest whenever he comes. Practice philosophy happily, my most esteemed friend, and if you desire anything from us, ask for it, but with such trust that you may receive it more quickly hereafter. Our Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous polymath and close associate of Ficino.</note> philosophizes excellently and loves you dearly. Farewell. August 11, 1489.

### *A Slight Recommendation.*
### Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Nesi, sends greetings.

**G**reetings. Bernhard the priest has asked me to recommend him to you regarding the vacancy of a certain small church that is nearly at hand. I therefore recommend him to you; however, there is no need to provide reasons for this recommendation. For he is better known to you than he is to me. It will therefore be a matter for your kindness to assist a friend, provided he is well-deserving. Fare well. August 8, 1489.

### *A Study on Long Life.*
### Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, sends greetings.

**O**n the day you departed from here, I completed the little book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "de Vita cœlitus cõparanda." This is the third book of Ficino's famous medical and astrological treatise, "De vita libri tres" (Three Books on Life).</note>. Yesterday, however, I opportunely happened upon a certain book by Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> on delaying old age, which I have long desired, but which was difficult to read and most difficult to understand due to the faults of the scribes. Meanwhile, the owner of the book is pressingly demanding its reading; therefore, this difficult and somewhat hurried reading on delaying old age delays your arrival to me. But I believe we shall endure this with a calm mind, provided that this diligence might one day delay old age for you. For my part, I must think not so much about delaying old age, but rather about retaining it. Meanwhile, while we are kept apart and treat separate things, we are doing the same: we emulate Prometheus, we fashion man, just like the soul; I fashion the body, you lead the soul divinely, I receive the body from the heavens. How beautifully—immediately after the world was wonderfully demonstrated by you in your sevenfold mirror <note>A reference to Pico's work "Heptaplus," a sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis.</note>—we now compose, by our joint labor, man the observer of the world. Farewell. August 8, 1489.

### *On the Poetic Style in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates.*
### Marsilio Ficino to the noble physician Antonio Faentino, sends greetings.

**Y**ou gave your letters to us perhaps on the day or hour of Saturn, or while Saturn was ascending, or at least while the Moon was entering a fixed house. For they reached Florence from Ferrara in scarcely four months; nevertheless, that Saturn of yours gave birth to a Jupiter: a letter full of humanity and elegance. If the speech of the gods and the style of oracles is song, and Hippocrates was once held to be a God, and his *Aphorisms* were oracles, you have translated them into verse quite rightly indeed. But perhaps, lest what you have done well might seem poorly placed somewhere, you seek a Maecenas <note>A historical Roman patron of the arts; here used as a general term for a wealthy protector or sponsor.</note> for your poem. There is no longer any choice among Maecenases, my dear Antonio, for there is scarcely one such as you name. Let him, therefore, be the patron of your verses. It will be very pleasing to me to read your lines. It is already most pleasing to be loved by you. For what is more lovable than to be loved by one who loves with judgment and is himself worthy of veneration? Our commentaries on Plotinus have been interrupted by Theophrastus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and certain others, they themselves also desiring to travel from Greece into Italy through us at some time. But I have recently returned to Plotinus, intending to follow through with the commentaries on him assiduously. Farewell happily, you who are most desired to return to us eventually. August 15, 1489.

# LETTERS, BOOK IX.

-> An astronomical omen for the book on long life. <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, sends greetings. <-

**J**ust as our Plato, provoked by Lysias, or invited by Timaeus, Zeno, and Parmenides, wrote down the very things they themselves had written; so have I now been led by Arnold the Philosopher <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist whose works on hygiene and the "retardation of old age" deeply influenced Ficino.</note> to compose a small book on delaying old age. Because I knew I was undertaking a task beyond earthly strength, I began the little work under the auspices of the heavenly bodies: specifically, with Mercury happily pursuing the right path in his own Virgo; with the Moon again entering Taurus and joining there with Jupiter; and from there looking upon Phoebus <note>The Sun.</note> through a Trine <note>term: Trine (an astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered very harmonious).</note>, and likewise upon Venus and Mercury. This was done so that our composition, born under vital planets while Mercury was reigning, might contribute to the life of those practicing philosophy—especially to you, most beloved Pico, who are the most worthy of life among all philosophers. Indeed, so that it might benefit you, the most diligent of men, I observed today Phoebus playing with Taurus, just as you yourself fortunately obtained at your birth. Finally, the work was completed as Diana <note>The Moon.</note> came to a trine with Saturn, thus caring for Pico, the son of sublime Saturn, above all others. This is especially so because Saturn meanwhile sits victoriously in Capricorn and holds the great Head of the Dragon <note>term: Head of the Dragon (the North Node of the Moon, considered a point of increase and good fortune).</note> in his right hand, and, full of glory, gazes upon Apollo <note>The Sun.</note> with the three rays of his eyes. By this very aspect, he is about to confirm the promises of the heavens for his own people with a truly firm treaty—if only (as is to be hoped) that supreme Jupiter, with the Head from which he gave birth to Minerva, favors the worshippers of Minerva <note>A metaphor for scholars and philosophers.</note>. August 24, 1489.

-> A response to one desiring his birthday and other matters. <-
-> Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius Prenninger of Constance, sends greetings. <-

**I** am sending you Iamblichus, whom you first requested, and Proclus besides, as well as Synesius; for you now claim our works by such a right that more must always be sent to you than you ask for. I will also soon allow the booksellers to copy the eight books of our letters which you desired. You sent the first [payment] for the first, and then truly the second. Indeed, I have decided at this dawn to dedicate a new work, now almost finished, specifically to your name. For charity and your virtue demand this and more from us. Furthermore, you ask for my birthday; and although our Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, who famously refused to allow his portrait to be painted or his birthday celebrated.</note> never granted this to friends who frequently demanded it, I am nevertheless so moved by your great love toward me that I shall never deny you anything, except perhaps what has been denied to my own ability. My birthday, then, was the nineteenth day of October <note>original: "Nouus ergo suprà decimum Octobris dies," literally the ninth above the tenth.</note>, specifically in the year of our salvation 1433. As for the hour of the day, although it was not recorded by my father Ficino the physician, we have nonetheless gathered from his and my mother’s words that it was the twenty-first hour <note>note: In the Florentine system of time-keeping, the 21st hour would be roughly three hours before sunset.</note>. I believe that nearly the middle of Aquarius was rising then, together with Pisces; that Saturn then held the angle of the East in Aquarius, with Mars in the same; that the Twelfth House, the "Prison," held [the North Node]; the Sun was in Scorpio, and Mercury in the ninth house; the Moon in Capricorn; Jupiter in Leo in the seventh. In that same place, Venus was in Virgo, and Fortune was in Aries. You have my birthday, such as it was. You have the man born, such as he turned out to be. And if my fortune was never grand or lasting, and a certain weakness of body always stood in the way of either writing or publishing my books, I have nevertheless perhaps never ceased from the duty decreed to me. Indeed, in this eighth seven-year cycle of my age <note>note: Ficino was 56 years old in 1489, entering his eighth "septenary" (7 x 8 = 56).</note>, you yourself have provided me the cause for a new edition, or rather, a new composition. For when you requested from us this year the book on "Curing the Health of Men of Letters" (composed in our seventh seven-year cycle, in which we published the books of Plato), your spirit indeed aroused my own spirit to compose a book on "Prolonging the Life of the Gifted." This was so they might not only be healthy as long as they live, but also live for a long time in good health. Therefore, we have now finished this book on prolonging the life of the studious, God favoring us; and to this we have then added a small work on "Obtaining Life from the Heavens," composed so that by remedies and medicines not just haphazardly put together, but crafted by the observation of the stars, we might promise prosperous health and long life to the gifted—if only God himself, just as he breathed upon me as I wrote, will breathe upon those who read and use it in the future. Fare well, fare well long. Fare happily. August 29, 1489.

# MARSILIO FICINO
### *An artful commendation of a learned man.*

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to the most serene King of Hungary, Matthias, ever invincible. <-

**U**ntil now, I did not think it possible for the same man to exist in two places at once, especially places so far apart from one another. Now, however, I not only think this can happen, but I indeed know it, hear it, and see it. I know for certain that our remarkable Theologian Nicolaus <note>Likely Nicolaus de Mirabilibus, a Dominican theologian who moved between Florence and the Hungarian court.</note> recently traveled from Italy to Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniam," the Roman name for the region comprising modern-day Hungary and surrounding areas.</note>. Yet, I still hear the same man speaking in Florence, as he was accustomed to do, in the public gymnasia, in the forum, and in the churches. I hear him reading frequently and disputing with diligence. We see him daily crowned with honor in the very circles of those practicing philosophy. Thus, your Nicolaus now lives among you, while in the meantime our Nicolaus breathes among us; he still calls out in the schools, and the echo resounds from the very walls. In this way, therefore, he has deceived my previous opinion, but he has satisfied my longing. For we used to miss the presence of such a great man so much that he should never have to be missed as if he were absent from us. 

Perhaps he will deceive you as well in another way, unless I warn you. Actors on the stage are usually accustomed to hide their own persons under a foreign mask. Nicolaus, however, hides a foreign person under his own. Therefore, when you listen to his disputations, know that you are looking at Nicolaus, but you are not hearing him. For you will rather hear that blessed Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> speaking, living now in Nicolaus’s own breast and crying out from his mouth. For either Aquinas was reborn in this man at his birth—as some Platonist might believe—or at the very least, the sublime Thomas breathes favor from heaven upon him as he speaks. Therefore, honor that Thomas of Aquino in Nicolaus, as if in a living statue. **September 6, 1489. In the district of Careggi.** <note>Careggi was the site of the Medici villa where Ficino’s Platonic Academy met.</note>

---

### *A playful expression of thanks.*

-> Marsilio Ficino to Roberto Salviati, sends greetings. <-

**T**he poets sing of Atlas, the Prince of Astronomy, who reached the heavenly heights not only through a perpetual observation of the stars, but also through a wonderful tallness of body. You also seem to me to have recently reached a star by some similar logic. For at the very moment when Jupiter from on high tasted the kisses of his daughter <note>Likely a poetic reference to an astrological conjunction of Jupiter and Venus.</note>—at which union he is usually unable to deny anything to the one who asks—you yourself gave me a letter. For this reason, my dear Roberto, I do not wish to deny you anything, although I cannot even return what you have given. Now, if I owe a man more in proportion to how much more I have received, then certainly I owe no one more than I owe you, most magnificent Roberto. 

Do you laugh at that word "magnificent"? Perhaps this grandest of words comes to our lips at an inopportune time, for what you gave, and what I owe, is immense. Indeed, you have presented me with the whole world at once, when you sent that "world" to us, divinely described by Giovanni <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494). The "world" refers to his work *Heptaplus*, a sevenfold explanation of the six days of creation.</note>. I was reading your letter at an opportune time, just as I was contemplating the gift with my eyes in that chapel of Saint Christopher <note>St. Christopher is traditionally depicted as a giant carrying the Christ child, who holds a globe representing the world, across a river.</note> which fell to us long ago and which we tend. I was looking over that globe with my eyes—the one he supports on his shoulders like Atlas—to see if perhaps anything equal or similar to your virtue might occur to us in the whole world to pay you back. 

Meanwhile, that Saint said to me: "Why, foolish Ficino, do you seek under heaven something equal to heaven? Have you not recently received the whole world from a friend? And meanwhile, your friend has made you more than a Prophet. A Prophet once saw a new heaven and a new earth; you, by the work of your friend, have not only seen these things but have even held them in your hands. In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth in the abyss of darkness, whom He had previously begotten in the abyss of light; He recreated them once in the wisdom of Moses, and He has recreated them recently in the spirit of Pico, in the word of Mirandola. Roberto gave this to you as a gift along with his letter. You can never equal such a gift; even I, as large and tall as I am, can scarcely equal it. Farewell from afar, Marsilio, and let your friend fare well from afar." These things, my Roberto, the Saint seemed to say to me. Therefore, with this very "long" health, may you fare well and happily, provided you frequently greet our fellow-Platonist Pico in my name. But hey, I should say, ought I not to have called him Democritus <note>term: Democritus (the "laughing philosopher" who proposed an atomic theory of the universe). Ficino is joking about Pico's role as a "maker" of a world.</note> at least in these days, rather than a Platonist? The Maker of the world rested on the Sabbath from all his works. But Pico, now that the world is finished... <meta>The sentence continues on the next page with the catchword "iam mundi".</meta>

Does he then, together with Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world was made of infinite atoms in a void.</note>, establish new worlds? But while writing, it fortunately comes to my mind what our friend is especially laboring upon. He does not now follow that solitary Democritus through the empty voids, counting innumerable atoms, but rather Him whom we hear daily crying out: *My Father works even until now, and I am working* <note>original: "Pater meus usq; modo operatur, & ego operor." Therefore, through these worlds, one already having been perfected, our Pico, a contemplator of the soul, follows Christ and not Democritus.

### *Preface to the book on a long life.*
-> Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, a most excellent and noble citizen, greetings. <-

**A**lthough our Plato lives by his own genius, and will live, as I believe, as long as the world itself lives, my own genius always impels me to provide for all things concerning the life of Plato after my divine worship. For a long time now, the House of Medici <note>original: "Medica domus." A clever pun by Ficino: the name "Medici" means "doctors," and they are supporting his work on "medical" matters and health.</note> has aspired toward this very thing before all others; and you too, my Valori, conspire toward the same, being the most friendly of "doctors" <note>Ficino is likely referring to Valori's support of the medical/Platonic arts.</note> and quite studious of Platonic glory and discipline. Therefore, just as I always desire life for Plato, I desire the same for the Medici, and a similar life for Valori. For this reason, I exhort and beseech you, my Valori, that with as much effort as you always favor Platonic glory, you might at some time read and preserve with equal diligence these precepts of ours concerning the prolongation of life. By living long through these, you may be able to patronize the recently reborn discipline of Plato for a longer time, together with the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Farewell.

### *Irony regarding his book against a Grammatical detractor.*
-> Marsilio Ficino to Tideo, royal procurator, greetings. <-

**T**he day before yesterday, I gave to Antonio the bookseller, at your request, the Platonic Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher; Ficino translated his work "On the Mysteries."</note> to be transcribed. If by chance, while reading, a certain continuous order does not occur to you in the book, know that I have expressed this book not word-for-word, but according to the sense. This was not so much because I was entirely occupied in my commentaries on Plotinus, but because there is only a single manuscript among us, full of errors, and what is worse, full of fragments. Furthermore, if our style there does not satisfy your judgment, O Tideo, since it does not please you, just send it back—or at least accept the meaning. For sometimes silver lies hidden under bronze, just as often bronze is covered by silver; but let not some severe Grammarian, that arrogant judge of philosophers, accuse me of arrogance because I seem here to claim "silver" for myself in a way. I concede "gold" to that man most willingly, if by any means I might appease so rigid a judge against me with such a great gift. And so that I may gratify him even more lavishly, I shall indeed call him the "source," and myself the "cistern." <note>Ficino is being humble/ironic here, suggesting the grammarian has the "pure gold" of perfect language, while Ficino only collects the "water" of the meaning.</note> Farewell, and be happy. I commend myself to you, and you also commend me to the great King.

### *A jest against a long silence.*
-> Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone, his fellow philosopher, greetings. <-

**O**thers are usually accustomed to purge the crime of long-lasting silence with a certain "Apology," and often a long one at that; but you, a new Orator—if indeed he who remains silent is an Orator—wash away the accusation of silence with silence itself. You are certainly a "new Physician" acting contrary to what others are accustomed to, curing like with like <note>original: "similibus similia curans." This refers to an ancient medical principle that a disease can be cured by something that produces similar symptoms.</note>. For a long time now, all of us friends have been condemning you because, neither of your own accord nor even when provoked, do you write anything to any of your people. But Proculus, having recently set out from you to us in Florence, imposed silence on our reproaches against you by your commands—though without your letters—bidding us to bear the longing for your letters of such long duration with an even mind. Surely, since such a great man and so great a friend to you could not obtain a short letter from you upon departing, it ought not to seem a wonder to us, he says, nor a thing done rashly by you, that we have not obtained for a long time now the letter which he himself did not receive. Thus you always not only say, but do, certain wonderful things in a friendly way: you defend silence with silence, you cure like with like, and you even persuade by being silent. But do not, I pray, again [return the] book, or free... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

...that book of yours, which long ago set out for Lorenzo de' Medici, behaves toward us with that same silence <note>original: "silentio". The OCR "filētiō" is a likely transcription error for "silentio," given the context of speaking and silence.</note> of yours. ->*On the book "Three Books on Life."*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Paolo of Florence, a distinguished theologian in the eminent flock of the Servants of Mary.<- <note>The "Servants of Mary" refers to the Servite Order, a mendicant religious order founded in Florence.</note>

**I** send to you our books *On Life* <note>original: "de uita". Ficino’s famous medical and astrological treatise on the health of scholars.</note>, my most life-worthy Paolo, not so much so that you might read these little aids to life, but so that you might preserve them. For while I greatly desire life for all my friends, I long for it most especially for you. For in your Orphic cry <note>A reference to the Orphic hymns; Ficino often compared powerful Christian preaching to the legendary music of Orpheus.</note>, a sacred declamation breathes everywhere, and the very walls of the temples come alive. December 15, 1489. Florence.

->*On the book "Three Books on Life," following the books on dreams and demons.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Piero de' Medici.<-

**I** and my friend Valori <note>Filippo Valori, who funded the printing of Ficino's works.</note> sent to you long ago the *Dreams* of Synesius the Platonist and the *Demons* of his fellow Platonist Psellus <note>Synesius of Cyrene and Michael Psellus were authors of Neoplatonic works that Ficino translated.</note>. But at the very threshold of your gates, by I know not what fate, the dreams immediately vanished and all the demons suddenly disappeared; I hope that this *Life* of ours, which we send now, might at least appear before you. The loss of dreams and demons is perhaps light, but the loss of life is truly not light. Go now, therefore, you who are dearer than life, and enjoy a better fate. Go now with spirit to Piero de' Medici, our glory; in his hands, you shall live more happily. December 15, 1489.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine’s Letters, to Niccolò Valori, most adorned in letters and morals.

### P R E F A C E .

->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to his twin friend Niccolò Valori.<-

**W**hen I had already finished twelve books of my letters and was revising them, I discovered that the tenth and eleventh books still lacked a specific dedication. And so, as I was thinking to whom I might best dedicate this twin work, you came to mind first of all, my Valori, a "twin" friend yourself. Until now, your excellent brother Filippo and you were the twin preservers of my works, like Castor and Pollux <note>In Greek mythology, the inseparable twin brothers who were transformed into the constellation Gemini.</note>. But now, since Filippo has recently passed away, you yourself remain for me as a twin, who surely, while you offer yourself to me—as you do daily out of your kindness toward me—you also bring back to us that Filippo who was loved by us beyond compare. And as much as the most heavy loss of our Filippo distresses us, just so much does the sufficient compensation through you console us. It also consoles the hopeful Marsilio with the firmest hope that his books will be no less commended to Niccolò hereafter than they once were to Filippo. Read happily, and live long and happily, both as a diligent observer of Platonic wisdom and a long-standing preserver of my studies.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine’s Letters,
### BOOK X.

->*Regarding the book "On Life" sent to a friend.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to Giacomo Martini, legal consultant.<-

**I** would have composed the book *On Life* <note>original: "de Vita". Ficino’s famous medical-astrological treatise on the health and longevity of scholars.</note> to benefit my friends in vain, unless it benefited my Giacomo especially, who is most dear to me of all friends. Therefore, lest I have written in vain, receive gladly this life of ours which I send; read it diligently, hold it in memory, and observe it with care. Live long as you wish, and happily. December 16, 1488.

---

->*Regarding the same.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the outstanding citizen Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger.<- <note>This is Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici (1463–1503), the cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent and a major patron of the arts, including Botticelli.</note>

**W**e desire our book *On Life* to be of benefit to all our literate and good friends. But especially to those whose life will benefit so many, and who have chosen the best way of living; these are most worthy of life of all. Read it then diligently, my most beloved Lorenzo, and live long and happily. December 16, 1488. Florence.

---

->*Jests.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to Bernardo Michelozzi, who, though perhaps his rival, is nevertheless most beloved.<-

**L**ast summer I dedicated to our Piero de' Medici the book by the Platonist Synesius on dreams, and the short work by the fellow-Platonist Psellus on demons. After Piero received the book, he immediately read the preface; having read it, he set it down. A little later the book itself was taken by I know not whom. Since then it has been sought for a long time and has not yet appeared, so that indeed it seems that as soon as they touched the inner chambers of the House <note>The Medici Palace in Florence.</note> or of some sacred shrine, the demons disappeared and the dreams vanished completely. I pray you, my Bernardo, search most accurately to see if these dreams or these demons have flown your way. If you find it to be so, I warn you to purify yourselves and drive them back to us. Finally, I suspect that either the Cardinal <note>Giovanni de' Medici, the future Pope Leo X.</note> or Gregorio took this book to read. If by chance they have it, let them send it back to us once read. At least let me know if they do not have it, so we may search more diligently elsewhere. Commend me to the venerable Pandolfo della Luna <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, a diplomat and writer.</note>. But why have I passed over the Sun? Commend me then first of all to our Cardinal, the Sun; then to Pandolfo, the Moon—and fully so <note>original: "plenè". Likely a pun on a "full moon."</note>—so that having begun here, we may follow the catalogue of the heavens. You shall also commend me to Giovanni Battista, as if to Jupiter on account of the laws; and even to Gregorio, our Mercury. But tell me, I ask you, where shall we place Venus? Let Matteo be Venus. But since Venus is helpless without Desire <note>original: "cupidine". A play on the name of the god Cupid.</note>, you yourself shall play the part of Cupid. Otherwise, my Bernardo, you will hardly be loved today. As for Saturn and Mars, joy and kindness drive them far away from your festive company. Farewell. December 21, 1488.

---

->*Preface to the books first sent to Lorenzo’s sons and Valori, then to Lorenzo de' Medici.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, savior of the fatherland.<-

**S**ynesius and Psellus, along with Iamblichus, Porphyry, and Proclus the Platonists, having entered your most grand house some time ago, greeted your noble sons. Up to now, they seem to have done quite rightly. But because they left you ungreeted, they have neither acted prudently nor turned out happily. Recognizing their own imprudence at last, so that they might eventually be more fortunate, they now revisit your threshold to know the Father, and in turn to recognize the sons along with the father, thus to live more happily from now on. For they have recently learned that not even our books *On Life* wished to live without your patronage. Moreover, the philosophers Priscian of Lydia and Theophrastus accompany these others. For since these have long said "hail" to my Valori <note>Niccolò Valori, a close friend and later biographer of Ficino.</note> and have ardently desired...

# BOOK X OF THE LETTERS

## Commending a legal case to a lawyer.
### Marsilio Ficino to Leonardo the Lawyer, sends greetings.

**W**e consider it redundant to commend our case with many words to such a dear friend. It is likewise unnecessary to commend a just case to a just Patron. What then? We shall use a notification rather than a recommendation with you. The Hebrews call Jupiter *Sedech* <note>original: "Sedech". From the Hebrew *Tzedek*, meaning righteousness or justice.</note>, that is, justice. This is because when Jupiter is dominant in a birth chart, it signifies a just man who will fight vigorously for justice; and in the conduct of legal cases, if Jupiter looks down powerfully from the heavens <note>A reference to astrological "aspects," where the positions of planets relative to each other influence earthly events.</note>, it portends that the judgment will be just. Since, therefore, you are not only exceptionally learned and eloquent, but also "Jovial" <note>In Ficino’s system, a "Jovial" person is one influenced by the planet Jupiter, embodying justice, authority, and balance.</note>, and are to fight for our case tomorrow while the Sun happily gazes upon Jupiter, we hope—provided you stretch the nerves of your intellect—that you will utterly defeat the unjust quibbles of our adversaries. Farewell.

---

## On friendship and the immortality of the soul.
### Marsilio Ficino to Girolamo Donati, most illustrious Ambassador of the Venetian Senate, sends greetings.

**A**ntonio Pelotti, the Apollo-like charm of our Academy <note>Antonio Pelotti was a poet and member of Ficino’s circle; "Apollinus" refers to Apollo, the god of light and poetry.</note>, a man otherwise incapable of deception, deceives me daily—and I am a willing victim. Indeed, I always thought yesterday that I owed so much to Pelotti that I would deny being able to owe him more in the future. Yet, with every subsequent occasion, he binds me more closely to him by some even greater service. Thus, he immediately proves me wrong for my previous thought. Today, at last, he has bestowed the greatest benefit of all upon me, when he made us friends who were previously just lovers of one another. For truly, my most beloved Girolamo, each of us has long loved the other ardently. Hitherto, however, neither was a friend, as it seems, because neither knew he was loved in return. But our poet Antonio, now performing the office of a poet—that is, of a maker and transformer—has fashioned a friendship between us, and transformed lovers into friends by revealing to each not only that he is loved by the one he loves, but that he was loved first and for a long time. Truly, the friendship of men who practice philosophy seems to be of no less importance among mortals than the gathering of the happy Planets is among the inhabitants of heaven.

Furthermore, Pelotti indicated to me how much you yourself desire to visit me. I certainly have long desired to see you, my Girolamo. And if I seem frequently to hear and see your noble soul and countenance in the countryside, it is not only in your most elegant letters, but also in the speech and face of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Angelo Poliziano, who act as your harbingers. You, for your part, will see me—as much of me as there is—approaching you in my own "Valor," that is, in Francesco Valori <note>A pun on the name of Francesco Valori (1439–1498), a Florentine statesman. *Valor* in Latin means "worth" or "value."</note>, the Ambassador of the Florentine Senate. I love and admire this man above others, for in his face, speech, and soul, he brings back that great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the patriarch of the Medici family and Ficino’s primary patron.</note>, whom I so venerated as a youth when he was an old man. Therefore, as soon as you look upon him, you will immediately look into Marsilio, living happily within his Cosimo. But you will not see me in my Valori merely as I am; rather, as if looking through a glass, you will see me made greater in him. Finally, however small I am in myself, or however great I am in him, I am yours, my best Girolamo. A great love would urge me to write much more, were it not for Niccolò Valori <note>Francesco's nephew and Ficino's future biographer.</note>, the nephew of the Legate—a truly elegant youth and remarkably mature for his age—who is coming to you and will speak many things with you in my name. Farewell.

---

## On love and friendship, and the commendation of a friend.
### Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Bembo of Venice, sends greetings.

**S**ince the singular love between us, my Bernardo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian diplomat and the father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note>, was created not from a mortal cause, but rather from an immortal and heavenly one, I have rightly decided to commend the memory of it not to just any book, but specifically to my books on immortality—commending, as it were, one immortal thing to immortality itself. A witness to such great love has long been the sixth book of my *Platonic Theology* regarding immortality. A further witness is the recently completed divine book of Plotinus on immortality, in the summary of which we wrote today the following words: "You desire, great-souled Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent).</note>, a brief summary at last of the long dispute regarding immortality—a dispute, I say, that has been drawn out at length both in the *Theology* and in the present work..."

# MARSILIO FICINO

**O**ur friend Bernardo likewise desired this when he, as the Ambassador of the Venetian Senate here, heard us disputing at great length on this matter—Bernardo Bembo, I say, a man of foremost learning, a patron of the learned, and my own brother in star and spirit <note>Ficino often spoke of "astrological brotherhood," where friends shared similar planetary influences in their birth charts.</note>. Therefore, for you and for him alike, this will be the summary, divided into four chapters. First: that the soul is able to rule over fleeting things and resist the incitements of the body. Second: that it frequently contemplates many things separate from bodies, whether it reaches those separate things through itself, or separates them itself. Third: that it naturally desires eternal things, and often neglects temporal ones through its trust in the eternal. Fourth: that it worships the eternal God for the sake of everlasting life. Finally, the whole of religion, which is natural to man, is the firmest foundation of immortality.

---

### Solar demons as Physicians. Also, a commendation of the book "On Life."

->Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone the Physician, sends greetings.<-

**G**reetings, my most beloved Pierleone; greetings again, great Lion. But lest you think that by the nickname "Lion" you are now judged inferior to a man, I speak of the celestial Lion, not the earthly one. Unless, perhaps, we read of an "earthly man" who descended from heaven to earth; for we read in the poems of Zoroaster <note>Ficino refers to the "Chaldean Oracles," which were attributed to the ancient prophet Zoroaster in the Renaissance.</note> that twelve rulers preside over the twelve signs of the Zodiac. Where he names the one who presides over Leo as the "Lion-Leader" <note>original: "Leonduchus". A term from the Chaldean Oracles referring to a guardian spirit of the constellation Leo.</note>, and adds that if he is rightly summoned, he will appear on earth in an immense form and occupy the whole world. The Chaldeans named the demons subject to him "Lions," who also occasionally present themselves to our eyes in various human forms at their will, intending to practice the arts of Apollo, healing with both herbs and words. If I now nickname you alone "Lion" from among these, the truth will not be indignant, nor should you, therefore, disdain it. But enough of these things. Our magnanimous patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, brings to you his own life along with mine. Since, therefore, he entrusts his own life to you, he also commends mine; here, I pray, act as the physician to both: care for his life with herbs, but care for and adorn mine with words. You will understand what I wish more clearly if you ever hear our Bernardo—a youth of excellent character and a man of outstanding virtue—reading our works.

---

### Those whom the Sun favors at birth are called Sons of the Sun; the Sun in Leo in the ninth region of the heavens.

->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici the Younger, sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou have rightly requested the "Oration to the Sun" delivered by Julian the Platonic <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), a Roman Emperor who attempted to revive Neoplatonism and solar worship.</note>, in which he recognizes the Sun as his own father through certain arguments; for you too, unless you are ignorant of your own birth, trace your lineage from Phoebus <note>A poetic name for Apollo, the sun god.</note>. For as you were being born, he immediately looked upon you from his royal throne with his own joy. You imitate that parent through the splendor of your virtue and your poems.

---

### Commendation of one man of letters to another.

->Marsilio Ficino to the venerable Father Joachim, General of the Preachers, sends greetings.<-

**S**ince I am about to commend a learned youth, endowed with a natural talent for virtue, to a most learned man of outstanding virtue—my friend to my dearest friend—I shall be brief for the time being. For I hope I shall easily persuade you: Domenico the Florentine, son of Giovanni, who is making his profession to the holy Dominic under you as Father, requests your patronage, and I ask it for his sake. Farewell.

---

### Regarding the book "On Life," on a gift received.

->Marsilio Ficino to Martinus Uranius of Constance, sends greetings.<-

**O**ur book <term>On Life</term><note>Ficino's *De vita libri tres*, a famous treatise on health, longevity, and astral magic.</note> has been printed. I received one from the printers these past few days to send to you. And this one you shall receive not for a price, like the others, but for free; or rather, it has already been bought by you, and indeed at a great price: for when you gave your soul to us through love, you claimed our life for yourself beyond controversy. I recently received in your name a knife-case decorated with handles of gems and gold, a gift not only philosophical but royal, and truly worthy of your royal mind. To me, it was most welcome.

...most welcome, especially since I clearly perceived through this gift that the same guiding spirit <term>Genius: In Roman and Neoplatonic thought, a personal protective spirit that oversees a person’s destiny</term> presides over both me and you. For since I had discovered that Chalcedony is subject to Aquarius (especially the middle of the sign), and Jasper to Saturn, the Master of Aquarius, and since Saturn ascended for me at that same degree, I was ardently wishing for both stones. Therefore, my vow, which was known to my own guiding spirit and then suddenly known to you, declares that we are governed by the same spirit. What of the fact that I began to desire such things last Autumn? You, meanwhile—as I guess—were deliberating at that same time about sending a gift to us. If anyone is ever to give thanks to himself, Marsilio certainly now gives great thanks to Martin. He can surely give thanks to himself, provided he is a twin. Each of us is a twin, my sweetest Martin <note>Ficino often spoke of "astrological brotherhood," where friends who shared similar planetary alignments in their birth charts were considered spiritual "twins."</note>. By the same reasoning, the constellation of the Twins in heaven will be, as I hope, a common lodging for our souls. Farewell happily. The books of letters are being copied for you daily. We will put the finishing touches on Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino spent years translating and commenting on his works.</note> very soon, and you will have it suddenly as soon as it is printed. You certainly always have me. April 1490. In the field of Careggi <note>Careggi was the site of the Medici villa where Ficino lived and worked.</note>.

->Approval of the book through the validation of Doctors.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Matthew of Arezzo, his close physician, sends greetings.<-

**I** composed the medical book *On Life* <note>original: "De vita." This was Ficino's famous three-part treatise on health, longevity, and the astral influences on scholars.</note> during the last spring and summer among the flowers in the field of Careggi—would that it were Flourishing! <note>original: "Vtinam Florentem." A pun on the city of Florence (Florentia) and the Latin word for blooming or flourishing.</note> Only then was I to approve it, when I learned it had been validated by physicians. Indeed, I received your letters in recent days, full of such spirit that by their sudden breath, my life—which having already been published had, so to speak, expired—immediately breathed again for me, and was approved in my eyes by your approval. See then, my Matthew, how much you please me, in which I also please myself. Continue, I pray, and as you already love us, always love us, and recommend us to the physicians. You ask, furthermore, if I have published anything recently. I recently gave seven books of the Platonists to the Great Lorenzo de' Medici to be transcribed at his discretion; when he writes back you will be able to have them, and not long after, the books of Plotinus and our commentaries on them. Farewell happily. 29 April 1490. In the field of Careggi.

->Commendation of the Peripatetic Academy.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio of Faenza, equally a Peripatetic and a Platonist, sends greetings.<-

**C**ontinue, I pray, Antonio, strenuous soldier: help the rising ancient Academy <note>The "Platonic Academy" revived by Ficino in Florence.</note> with all your strength, as you have long been doing. As a Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of Aristotle; named after the covered walkways (peripatos) of the Lyceum in Athens</term> soldier—nay, a leader—you will happily aid the Platonists. God himself will fight for religious Philosophy, for piety. If God is for us, who is against us? <note>A quotation from the Bible, Romans 8:31.</note> I have attempted an entrance for a friend, as you advised; an honorable place in the public gymnasium <note>A university or school, likely the Studio Fiorentino.</note> will, I believe, open up eventually. I will diligently see to it; I will not abandon the cause. I will reveal the whole matter more extensively elsewhere. Farewell. 30 April 1489. In the field of Careggi.

->On worshipping God in the Confessions of Augustine.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.<-

**H**e alone is everywhere safe, to whom God is present. "The Lord is near," says David, "to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth." <note>Psalm 145:18.</note> In truth, only a man at once wise and holy is the first to call upon God. We do not doubt that Saint Augustine was such a man. Therefore, together with Augustine, my Lorenzo—equally teacher and patron—let us suppliantly adore God. Thus, without a doubt, God himself will be present at our prayers. For he is mercifully present even to those about to pray, and he brings it about that we pray in truth. By what means we, worshipping God in truth, shall obtain our requests, the Prophet himself teaches. Who, after he says, "The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth," adds: "He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him; he also will hear their cry." <note>Psalm 145:19.</note> Furthermore: "The Lord preserves all who love him." <note>Psalm 145:20.</note> Finally: "My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord." <note>Psalm 145:21.</note> In which words he admonishes us that we should always fear, love, and praise God, if only <insert>seeking</insert>...

...seeking, we desire to be heard. Now indeed, what is most important to seek in prayer, he similarly reveals in these same words. For since these three things—fear, love, and praise—bring it about that we obtain our requests, it is right that these same three should seem to be asked for by us while we adore. Namely, that God grant us to fear Him rightly, love Him ardently, and praise Him properly. In short, David teaches how to adore and obtain requests where he says: *delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart* <note>original: "delectare in Domino, & dabit tibi petitiones cordis tui" — Psalm 37:4</note>. But now let us hear Aurelius <note>Likely referring to Saint Augustine (Aurelius Augustinus), whom Ficino deeply admired as a bridge between Plato and Christianity.</note> praying. For in this way, you yourself will be built up as a divine temple for the same person to whom you recently built a royal temple. 12 May 1490. In the fields of Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy met.</note>.

### A Daily Prayer.

->Marsilio Ficino to Hermolao Barbaro, his Amphion, Hercules, and<-
->Apollo, sends greetings.<-

**G**reetings, most kind and elegant Barbaro; greetings, always my primary safety after God. When you departed from here recently, you entrusted your life to our prayers before God. In turn, entrust my life to the Vicar of God <note>The Pope, as the representative of Christ on Earth.</note> with your own words. Truly, my Hermolao, what I once promised you, I perform three times every day. For I have now for a long time sung that Psalm daily to God: *I will extol thee, my God, O king* <note>Psalm 145 (144 in the Vulgate). Ficino emphasizes the rhythmic, "musical" nature of prayer.</note>. And after you reminded me, I sing it always mindful of you. All the teachers of the Hebrews have agreed without controversy that whoever praises God with this Psalm in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, will be an heir of eternal happiness. Indeed, you will understand what you are to do in turn for our life out of your kindness when you read our books *On Life* <note>Ficino's "De Vita Libri Tres," a medical and philosophical treatise on the health of scholars.</note>, especially the "Apology" added to the books, where when you hear Amphion, Hercules, and Apollo called together, you will understand Hermolao to be the advocate everywhere. 15 May 1490. Florence.

### On behalf of the book *On Life*.

->Marsilio Ficino to his most dutiful friend, Antonio Calderini,<-
->sends greetings.<-

**Y**ou will give the books *On Life* to Hermolao Barbaro in the name of Valori <note>Filippo Valori, the patron who funded the printing of the work.</note> and Marsilio, along with this letter; to the others, however, you will give these monuments in your own name. Whoever reads our works with a healthy judgment rather than a disturbed mind will clearly perceive with what sincere counsel, with what pious mind, and with what great veneration for religion I have written them. Furthermore, all men of letters will recognize how much they ought to favor our books, which most diligently look after the lives of the literate. Farewell. Also, most frequently commend us to the most Reverend Cardinal of Saint Mark, our patron. And give him great thanks for the sake of the patronage he has shown us. 24 May 1490. Florence.

->Marsilio Ficino commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ,<-
->Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra.<-

**I** received your most kind letters in recent days, through which I clearly recognized—or rather, acknowledged what was already known to me—how helpful you are not only in my affairs, but also in those of my friends. Therefore, I give you great thanks that you so willingly patronize our friends, but much greater thanks because you have presented your most reverend patron, the Cardinal of Aleria <note>Ardicino della Porta the Younger, who assisted in defending Ficino's work against charges of magic at the papal court.</note>, as a patron for me as well. For I learned through the letters of our Antonio Calderini that this man, formerly your master and recently mine, has vigorously protected us against a certain slanderer. I attribute this not to any merits of my own toward him, but both to your recommendations to him and also to his own piety and mercy. It will be your duty hereafter, or at least of your love, most excellent Soderini, by the same means you won such a patron for me, to perpetually preserve him, and to give, hold, and return the great thanks which I can scarcely express, and finally to signify to me if there is any way I can please this Father and Lord of distinguished piety.

# LETTERS, BOOK X.

## An expression of thanks for the protection offered to us by a Prince.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Marco, Cardinal of St. Mark, sends greetings.

You desire to see the great Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated from Greek into Latin.</note>, venerable Father, as our friend Antonio Calderino recently and most dutifully informed me. You shall indeed see Plotinus shortly, as I hope, once our commentaries upon him are finished. But so that you may understand in the meantime what sort of man, or rather hero, you are about to see, hear, I pray, what Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and biographer.</note> records in his description of the Master’s life. "And truly," says Porphyry, "Plotinus himself possessed from the beginning something greater than others by his very nature." For a certain Egyptian priest, arriving in Rome and becoming suddenly known to Plotinus through a mutual friend, wished to display his own wisdom in Rome. He persuaded Plotinus to come with him so that he might immediately behold his own "companion spirit" <note>term: companion spirit <gloss>original: "familiarem dæmonem". In the Platonic tradition, a 'daemon' was a guardian spirit or higher guiding intellect, not a 'demon' in the modern sense.</gloss></note> when the priest summoned it. Plotinus easily complied. 

The invocation of the spirit was performed at the Temple of Isis; for the Egyptian said he found this to be the only "pure" place in Rome. But when the spirit itself was called forth into view, instead of a minor spirit, a God appeared—one who was certainly not of the lesser rank of spirits. Thus the Egyptian suddenly exclaimed: "Blessed are you, O Plotinus, who have a God for a companion spirit, and have not been allotted a guide from a lower rank!" These are the words of Porphyry. 

But how opportunely have we now stumbled upon this story? For just as a God is said to have appeared to the Egyptian priest of old when he was invoking a spirit, so to me, recently calling upon "Hercules" and "Apollo" <note>Ficino likely refers here to his human patrons, such as Hermolao Barbaro and Rinaldo Orsini, using mythological names.</note> in my *Apology*, their father Jupiter himself seems to have appeared. This happened when the Venetian "Hinge" <note>term: Hinge <gloss>original: "cardo". A pun on the word 'Cardinal', derived from the Latin 'cardo' meaning 'hinge'.</gloss></note> of the Church, sent from heaven by Saint Mark, stood by me as a most safe Protector. That he was sent to earth from the very order of Jupiter is proven to us by his fortune, which is great, and his virtue, which is even greater. For the astronomers have named Jupiter the "first fortune," and the Jews, in their common tongue, call him *Sedech* <note>original: "Sedech" — the Hebrew word 'Tzedek' (צדק), meaning 'Justice' or 'Righteousness', and also the name for the planet Jupiter.</note>, which is to say, Justice. 

Greetings, and farewell happily, you who are a saving Jupiter to us on earth—heralded indeed by the celestial Jupiter, but created by the Higher One. As for me, I shall be forced to play the part of Mercury <note>The god of eloquence and messengers.</note> if I am to give thanks worthy of your service. 

**26 June 1490. Florence.**

---

## An expression of thanks for the protection offered to us by a Prince.

### Marsilio Ficino to Rinaldo Orsini, Archbishop of Florence, sends greetings.

Hail for a long time, hail forever, good Shepherd, the health of the sheep. A good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that he may both feed them and protect them from wolves. In this way, you recently and most piously snatched your lamb, Ficino, from the voracious jaws of wolves. And when Saturn <note>In astrology, Saturn was associated with malice, obstacles, and the "heavy" accusations Ficino was facing.</note> was already attacking us severely, you stood in opposition like Jupiter. 

I seem indeed to have prophesied that "Jovial" <note>term: Jovial <gloss>meaning 'of the nature of Jupiter'—magnanimous, protective, and just.</gloss></note> prelates—that is, the high-minded and truth-telling—would patronize me in my peril, for when I was disputing about the planets and stars, I so often placed Jupiter before the rest. Truly, I called you "Jovial" long ago, even before I examined your birth chart; and when I did examine it, I affirmed exactly the same thing. For I found Cancer <note>The zodiac sign Cancer is considered the 'exaltation' or a place of strength for the planet Jupiter.</note> rising (the kingdom of Jupiter), and Jupiter himself happily situated in the eleventh house <note>The 'eleventh house' in astrology is the house of friends, hopes, and patrons.</note> in his own joy, looking upon his Cancer from a hexagonal aspect. 

But we believe all good things ultimately proceed from the highest celestial Jupiter, the Creator of Jupiter. Since His Vicar, the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent VIII, who eventually cleared Ficino of the charges of magic.</note>, has begun to breathe favor upon us through your efforts, I pray that he might not only breathe upon us, but also continue to breathe for a long time. Therefore, if I could understand his birth chart and the condition of his body, and what disease the doctors fear most for him, I would diligently devise a confection or some medicine that would be profitable for a long life and prosperous health. This is the least thanks I wish to return to you; for even Venus herself, the leader of the Three Graces, would not be able to return a favor equal to yours. 

**26 June 1490. Florence.**
