# LETTERS, BOOK X.

I demand nothing, for I do not claim so much for myself; rather, it will be enough for me if I have not given anything. I recently retreated to the seclusion of Mount Vecchio <note>Montevecchio, a retreat used by Ficino.</note> so that the frequent visits and greetings of friends would not interrupt this work on Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose works Ficino was translating and commenting upon.</note> to which I am now entirely devoted. But, what is far more troublesome, it is not my friends who interrupt me—whom I now actually miss—but rather every day wicked tax-collectors disturb and, to speak more truly, extorters harass me. Shortly after those tithes were collected, they came in the name of the University of Pisa, separating a Florentine man, who is certainly most devoted to study, from his long-standing work on Dionysius. Fortune is an enemy to the studies of a lion <note>original: "lionis", likely a pun or specific reference to his own name or a patron's heraldry</note>; she agitates me with many injuries of this kind to prevent me from completing this divine work, and meanwhile afflicts me with frequent bodily ailments. But it is better to cut short this growing complaint here. I hope at last, by God’s favor, for prosperous health and an immediate easing of my cares, with Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent."</note> coming to my aid. Farewell happily, my best Bernardo, and bring what help you can.

---

*An apology regarding infrequent greetings.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Pandolfo of Pesaro, the Florentine Governor, sends greetings.<-

**I** would indeed have greeted you frequently, my most beloved friend, but the great Plotinus intercepted my earlier greetings, and now the even greater Dionysius the Areopagite intercepts those that followed. We shall endure such great interceptors with a calm mind, for even if they hinder formal greetings, they neither can nor wish to remove the mutual health <note>Ficino puns on 'salutatio' (greeting) and 'salus' (health/well-being).</note> of our souls, which are always speaking to one another. Wherever I am occupied among my books, I am certainly never absent from my most learned Pandolfo. Farewell.

---

*An allusion to a name, declaring that the goods of the soul are true riches.*
->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Bernardo—called "Dovizio" in the common tongue, but "Divitius" in Latin—sends greetings.<-

**S**ince the common people call you "Dovizio," my Bernardo, but the Latin language calls you "Divitius" <note>term: Divitius <gloss>from the Latin 'dives', meaning wealthy.</gloss></note>, someone might perhaps prophesy from this that you will be wealthy, not through common skills, but through Latin ones. But Latin skills are, as you well know, Latin letters: the liberal arts and the humanities, and above all, humanity itself. I do not merely prophesy that you will one day be wealthy in the possession of these riches; I testify that you are so already. But, lest I further separate those whom God himself has joined, consider that what I just said to you, my Bernardo, is also said to your older brother, Pietro. By the abundance of these riches, both of you have long been accepted by that great-souled man <note>referring to Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, who is by this measure the wealthiest of all. Glory and riches are in his house, and his justice endures forever and ever. <note>A quotation from Psalm 112:3.</note> October 25, 1490. In the district of Careggi.

---

*On fate and fortune, and each person’s own guardian spirit.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Giorgio "The Shield" of Alexandria, an eminent physician, sends many greetings.<-

**P**lato proves in the *Timaeus*, the *Phaedrus*, and the *Symposium* that love is the beginning of all disturbances. He proves again in the *Phaedo* that pain always follows pleasure, and often vice versa. I find this to be more and more true every day. And recently, my most beloved George, I experienced it beyond doubt during your departure. I had at last found, as the saying goes, a man after my own heart. Therefore, as much as I loved your presence, I was just as much driven by grief by your absence. And in turn, almost as much as your departure afflicted me with pain, your letters yesterday delighted me. For they restored your presence to me, and I believe you shall never depart again. You shall remain, then, singular friend, at least within me here in Florence. Where, as you yourself say, the fates do not wish you to be otherwise, with fortune even consenting to the fates. For among the Platonists, fortune agrees with fate—that is, with the series of celestial causes—because the leader of our fortune is the very <term>guardian spirit</term> <gloss>original: "daemon". In Platonic philosophy, this is a guiding spiritual entity assigned to a person at birth, not an evil spirit.</gloss> destined for each person at birth according to the celestial harmony. This spirit, most sagaciously and powerfully collecting the various causes scattered among us, leads them toward a single outcome, often beyond our own counsel, and for that reason, it is called "fortuitous." To such fortune, and to this spirit, the Platonists primarily [attribute...]

# LETTERS, BOOK X.

->Give thanks for what has been received before you ask for new things.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Gentile, Bishop of Arezzo, sends greetings.

**A**lways health to you, O Bishop most worthy of eternal salvation. Since I am soon to commend to you the case of a close associate <term>necessarius</term><note>A term often referring to a relative or a very close member of one's household/circle.</note>, I preferred first to give thanks in my own name rather than to ask a favor for someone else. First, therefore, I give you immense thanks, because in the matter of Mount Martiano <note>Likely referring to a property or jurisdictional matter in Montemartano.</note> you particularly, and of your own accord, yielded to me and gave me timely advice. I wonder indeed, and not a little, at your modesty, kindness, and mercy; though you owed me nothing, you conducted yourself so toward me that you have turned a friend into a devoted servant <note>original: "mancipium," literally a bondservant or someone legally bound to another.</note> who will henceforth owe you everything. I shall now explain the case of my associate through the courier.

---

->On Adoration.<-

## Marsilio Ficino to Bindaccio Ricasoli, a noble and learned man joined to him by singular affection, sends greetings.

**I** have long promised, my most beloved Bindaccio <note>Bindaccio Ricasoli was a Florentine nobleman and a member of Ficino's Platonic Academy.</note>, to write something concerning the power of divine adoration. But I cannot fulfill my promises without the beneficial power of Him who is to be adored. Therefore, so that we may happily begin this sacred discussion on divine adoration: Breathe upon us, I pray, O nourishing God.

Having thus begun fittingly, we lay the foundation of this sacred building with that divine saying of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>: "The investigation of divine things purifies the soul, but their imitation makes one a god." <note>original: "Inquisitio quidem diuinorum, purgat animum, imitatio uerò facit Deum."</note> This is what he says. We believe, therefore, that people truly seek God when, first loving God as He is known in any way possible, we diligently track Him through all His works and testimonies as if following footprints. Thus we may more truly venerate Him when He is found; such is that scrutiny by which the soul is thought to be purified, first from all disturbances and then from clouds.

But imitation, which is thought to make the soul "a god"—that is, as divine as is possible—is of such a nature that one is present to individuals while remaining "separated," in order to please God, who provides for all while remaining "separated" <note>Ficino is using the technical Neoplatonic sense of "separated" (segregatus/separatus) to mean transcendent—existing on a higher plane while still exerting influence below.</note>. Indeed, we cannot emulate divine power or wisdom, for we are always weak, always wavering, and frequently uncertain whether we have attained the truth. Yet it is possible instead to imitate divine Providence. For if anything is known to us concerning God—which is certainly established both by reason and by testimony—it is chiefly this: that God is a certain power and wisdom, so ruling all things that He is not mixed with the conditions and passions of the things He governs, but is utterly "separated" from them.

In this state, being exalted and separated does not prevent Him from being present to individuals and providing for them; rather, it is thought to contribute to this very thing. Conversely, the most diligent care for all things does not disturb the state of His transcendence. Therefore, so that you may, according to your strength, imitate Him "who dwells on high and looks down upon the humble in heaven and on earth" <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 113:5-6.</note>, you will strive first that you yourself, separated from earthly disturbances and vices, may benefit and provide for men everywhere with as much charity as possible, as if for brothers. By this very "separated providence," you shall imitate God and please Him most of all, who Himself provides for all while being separated from all.

This, then, is the imitation of God, which is thought to make the soul like a god. Socrates once attempted this according to his strength, and after him Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>. Christ, the Master of Life, fulfilled this. All those have followed this path who at last, through the duties of such a life, are said to have performed certain miraculous works as if they were already divine. The Highest God hears only their prayers, as being those of divine men, for their will runs together as one with the divine will. And God frequently uses souls so affected as instruments or subjects for performing miracles.

Finally, since by divine ordinance any matter, when most ready under certain causes, suddenly receives an influx from those causes as if joined to them; so, rightly, the minds that have already become divine through the imitation of God, and which draw closer to God through love and prayers, soon receive a certain divine effect. They are thought to transfer this effect into their own bodies, their affairs, and their neighbors—especially those who are similarly inclined. Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>Two major Islamic philosophers and polymaths whose works on the soul were influential in the Latin West.</note> seem to confirm this when they say that such souls, by their own prayers, often move not only their own bodies but even the elements of the world in a miraculous way. Furthermore, Damis and Philostratus <note>Philostratus was the biographer of Apollonius of Tyana; Damis was reputedly Apollonius's companion and source.</note> narrate, with Apollonius confirming...

<meta>This page continues the letter to Bindaccio Ricasoli concerning the power of divine adoration. It transitions into two introductory prefaces (proœmia) for collections of works Ficino is sending to his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

...they tell of certain wise and holy men among the Indians, called the <term>Oxidrachi</term> <note>A people of ancient India mentioned in classical histories of Alexander the Great; they were noted by Greek writers for their wisdom and for living in a "holy city."</note>, who defend their cities from enemies not with hands, but with prayer. For they say that when God is humbly entreated by them, He puts the enemies to flight with thunder and lightning. Moreover, our own Thomas Aquinas proves that God hears the prayers of holy souls by this reasoning: since every "mover" moves things in some way toward its own likeness, and therefore the movement of those who vow themselves to the good—being directed toward the Good itself—depends upon that very Good (which surely does not move anything in vain), He undoubtedly leads those whom He moves to desire it to their desired end. With the same power through which He first moved them by impressing a faculty upon them, He aids them so that they may persevere, and He also brings it to pass that they finally attain it. For in the movements of nature, He has established a similar rule and faculty of inclination and attainment. 

Furthermore, those things which are closer to their mover are moved by it more effectively. The First Mover moves all things; however, rational natures are much closer to Him than corporeal ones. Since, therefore, corporeal natures are moved by a natural appetite toward their various ends and do attain them, much more so do rational substances—who are moved by the First Good in their vows toward the good—attain the good they have desired, insofar as they are moved by Him. They are stirred by Him insofar as they proceed with desire and prayers both rightly and toward the true Good. To that extent, therefore, prayers are heard and the desired outcome occurs. 

These things are confirmed by a certain opinion of the divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) whose work on theurgy and the soul deeply influenced Ficino.</note>: just as the Sun has impressed upon solar things, and the Moon upon lunar things, and the hollow of the Moon upon light things a property by which they are moved toward the Sun, the Moon, or that hollow, so God Himself has infused into souls an instinct by which they might turn toward God through prayer; and this instinct is by no means in vain. For nature itself gives nothing and moves nothing in vain, being guided by the divine. Finally, if it belongs to a friend to comply with the honorable desires of a friend, the Divine Mind—to which our own minds are made friends by a likeness that is partly natural and partly acquired—certainly satisfies the legitimate desires of those minds. It belongs to His utterly immense goodness to bestow good things most widely everywhere, especially upon minds that have been divinely urged toward the specifically divine Good. We have already treated the remaining matters concerning Adoration in the argument on the *Timaeus* <note>Referring to Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the universe.</note>.

September 20, 1490. Florence.

### Preface to the books composed in youth, but finally collected and sent to Lorenzo.

->*Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends many greetings.*<-

**A**ll my books have come to you long ago, dearest Patron. My children, I say, whom I fathered in my youth or in a slightly more mature age. And those which I am giving birth to even in my old age come to you daily. But those which were born to me when I was once a youth, having become wanderers, still roam about by that same fortune—I might even say by recklessness. However, I have recently called these wanderers home and ordered them to flee straight to you, so that they might all recognize the same Patron of mine at once, and thus live more happily. And I, likewise, would be entirely present with him whom I have always loved with my whole self through every stage of his life—as a youth, a man, and an old man. Receive your own books gladly, best Lorenzo. Read them with favor; live happily, the certain happiness of our fatherland. Love Marsilio Ficino, who is entirely yours. 

October 27, 1490. In the countryside at Careggi <note>The site of the Medici villa where Ficino and his circle often met for philosophical discussion.</note>.

---

### Preface of Marsilio Ficino to the book entitled "On Man," addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.

**T**he <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on the physical and biological composition of things.</note> compose man out of soul and body. Christians teach that the soul of man is created as soon as the body is brought forth. Behold, our "Man" <note>Referring to the title of the book he is presenting.</note> comes to you, most humane Lorenzo, constituted of soul and body. First, indeed, you will look upon the body, where we discourse like doctors on the healing of the body; then you will look within at the soul, where, like theologians, we turn the soul from the care of the body toward the contemplation of God. There, indeed, in five little books, we ascend as if by steps to divine contemplation on a Platonic ladder. The sixth book then leads to God who has now been made man—that is, to Christ—along with the Magi, guided by the star. In the seventh, finally, the Apostle Paul, caught up to the third heaven, carries the mind away with him, to rest with God on the seventh day.

October 30, 1490. Florence.

# THE LETTERS, BOOK X.

->*Through which regions of the heavens souls descend and ascend.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Lorenzo de' Medici, greetings.<-

**T**he day before yesterday, you investigated with great diligence—as a Platonist, as is your custom in all things—the reasons why souls fall into bodies. However, as I recall, you omitted due to the shortage of time the specific region of the heavens through which they primarily descend. If, therefore, you also desire to know this, receive it in few words. The ancient theologians said that souls pass to the lower realms through Cancer, the home of the Moon. Since they come into this region subject to <term>generation</term> <note>The process of being born into the physical world of change and decay.</note> through a longing for generation, they rightly thought that souls make their way through the region of the Moon, which favors generation. For this reason, the ancients called Cancer the "Gate of Mortals." But they named Capricorn, which is opposite to it, the "Gate of the Gods," for they believe that souls, once finally purified, fly back through this gate to their heavenly fatherland. For just as they descend by the sting of the desire to generate, so they ascend in turn through the zeal of contemplation. All astrologers, in agreement with the Platonists, have held that <term>Saturn</term> <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, Saturn represents the highest intellectual and contemplative faculties, though it was often feared as a "malefic" planet by others.</note>, the lord of Capricorn, is the author or at least the signifier of divine contemplation. Therefore, this Gate of the Gods lies open to you, Lorenzo—a man distinguished by piety and a sublime contemplator—open, I say, to you who were born under such happy omens. Astronomers consider the head of the <term>tropic circle of Capricorn</term> <note>The Tropic of Capricorn, the southernmost point where the sun appears overhead; here used as a symbolic turning point for the soul's ascent.</note> for this reason: because that circle touches this sign, and the Sun, the lord of the heavens, reaching Capricorn, immediately seeks its ascent. But it seems we have happened upon the mention of this circle quite opportunely during our discussion. For it intersects that most beautiful path in Capricorn which astronomers have named the "Heavenly Way," called <note>original: "Galaxiam"</note> the Milky Way in Greek, but the "Lactic" path in Latin. Along this way, as they say, many small but frequent stars create little dwellings dedicated to the blessed souls. They assert that Capricorn is the head of this happy way and of these humble but heavenly homes. Now, golden Lorenzo, you are constructing a similar path in an age that is now nearly <term>Saturnian</term> <note>Referring to the "Golden Age" of Saturn, a mythical time of peace, justice, and plenty which Ficino and his contemporaries often claimed was returning under Medici rule.</note>. It is certainly a path of piety, consecrated with houses of charity and dwellings of love. May this path, as you rise happily, being born under Capricorn, finally lead you to Capricorn, the head of the heavenly way and the Gate of the Gods.

->*The lover's care is carefree.*<-
->Marsilio Ficino to the elegant Paulantino Soderonio, greetings.<-

**W**hen, on a previous night, we heard Lorenzo de' Medici—like a second Apollo in the tranquility of <note>original: "Mammolæ"</note> Mammola <note>A villa or estate belonging to the Medici where the Platonic Academy often met.</note>—singing of divine mysteries regarding love as if in a choir of the Muses, I and a certain other friend from the same company debated late into the night whether Mammola admits love and lovers, or not. He, indeed, denied it for this reason: because a gathering of that kind, desiring tranquility above all else, drives all cares far away; but love is a certain care, indeed the heaviest of all, and the wretched lover is constantly tormented in an intolerable way. I, however, not easily conceding to this reasoning, immediately objected in this manner: just as a great light utterly extinguishes smaller lights, so love, the most burning care of all, drives all others far away. Since, therefore, other mortals are oppressed by innumerable cares, all of which the lover has set aside at the command of Love, no one lives more <term>securely</term> <note>Here used in the Latin sense of "se-cura," meaning "without care" or "carefree."</note> than the lover. Therefore, no one comes more welcome into the pleasant company of Mammola. Then he replied, "Rather, he comes full of cares, whoever burns with the care of love, the sharpest of all cares." But I said, "Mammola does not reject the lover for this reason. For if the lover has long since been transformed into the beloved person, and has transferred his cares to where he has transferred himself, the lover enters Mammola already carefree." Finally, if you should happen to be convinced that he cannot be carefree as long as he loves: so be it, let the lover care for something, and indeed as much as possible, if you wish. But he no longer cares for human things, as I judge, but for divine things. Now, Mammola does not forbid caring for the divine, but only for the human. For as much as the pursuit of mortals is disturbed, so much in turn is the worship of divine things everywhere tranquil. Moreover, our Platonists are accustomed to infer from this that the soul, wounded by love, does not ultimately desire anything human, but rather the divine: because the fire of love is settled by no sensation or use of a beautiful body whatsoever. It is as if it seeks something else besides...

### *The fates will find a way, and Apollo will be present when called.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Filippo Pandolfini, most illustrious<-
->Ambassador of the Florentine Senate, greetings.<-

**I** have described for you the individual days of the coming year one after another, which I have observed through these late-night studies of the great birth. Indeed, I omen happy days for you and abhor unhappy ones; I pray for the former, but I pray against the latter. That helping Father and signifier of priests, Jupiter, stepped back into your Gemini on the seventeenth day of last September, and having retreated as far as Taurus, he will finally direct his step forward on the tenth day of this January; and thereafter, walking in a straight path, he will happily return to your Gemini at the end of February. And so he will proceed happily toward Cancer until the 20th of October. Therefore, at this time when Jupiter walks straight, and especially through Gemini, <note>original: "fata uiam inuenient, aderitq; uocatus Apollo"</note> the fates will find a way, and the sun-god Apollo will be present when called. Then, therefore, <note>original: "Carpe manu, namq; uolens, facilisq; sequetur: Cum te fata uocant. Antea non uiribus ullis Vincere, neq; duro licuit conuellere ferro." Ficino is quoting Virgil's Aeneid regarding the Golden Bough.</note> Pluck that golden branch of the tall tree with your hand, for it will follow willingly and easily when the fates call you. Previously, it was not permitted to conquer it by any strength, nor to tear it away with hard iron. But do you not see that Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> joined the judgment of our action together with fate when he says, "Pluck it with your hand"? He shows that religion also rules over fate when he says: "Apollo will be present when called." Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> himself confirms the same, saying, "The wise man will assist the work of the stars, just as the farmer assists the nature of the earth." Farewell; be fortunate in the heavens indeed, but blessed in the ruler of the heavens. December 26, 1490. Florence.

---

### *Lorenzo ordered Plato's books to be printed.*
->Marsilio Ficino to Braccio Marcello, greetings.<-

**A**stronomers report that Mercury, by breathing a vital force into the fetus, primarily shapes the spirit for human life. Poets also sing that Jove, intending to lead souls back from the underworld, commands Mercury to touch the souls to be awakened with his <term>caduceus</term> <note>The staff carried by Hermes/Mercury, often depicted with two snakes winding around it.</note>. For which reason, if Lorenzo de' Medici is as Jove to us in resurrecting Plato—he who shakes the world with his nod—it will have been enough for him to have signaled once with those eyes with which he often brings serenity to our private and public affairs. To you, my vigorous Braccio <note>A pun on the recipient's name; "Braccio" means "arm" in Italian.</note>, your arm will be the caduceus, with which, like a second Mercury, you may touch the work where our Jove signals; so that Plato has finally risen, not half-alive, but now as a living Plato, my dear Braccio—loving the beautiful Eurydice as much as Orpheus loved her; <note>In this allegory, Eurydice represents the vastness of wisdom or "breadth of judgment."</note> Eurydice, I say, specifically in the breadth of his judgment. But while Orpheus indeed descended to the underworld to see Eurydice again, Plato, as we hope, will shortly ascend to the heavens to see her; he is undoubtedly destined to live more happily in Florence than in Athens. For that Eurydice whom he once desired to visit there, he will now visit for the first time in Florence, and he will possess in his whole mind what he used to seek. You know that broad judgment is only found where contemplation conspires with public governance—where, evidently, the governor himself practices philosophy. It belongs to a noble <note>original: "Augusti," referring to the Emperor Augustus.</note> mind to follow one without the other; it belongs to the unfortunate to obtain either one without the other; but it belongs to the most happy to embrace both equally. Live happily, therefore, under the broad shade of the Medici Laurel <note>A pun on Lorenzo's name; "Laurus" is Latin for Laurel.</note> together with us and with Plato. January 20, 1490.

# BOOK X OF THE LETTERS.

-> *The harmony of Jupiter and the Sun; the harmony of colleagues.* <-

-> **Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Niccolini and Filippo Valori, distinguished citizens in the Florentine Republic.** <-

**P**tolemy, the prince of astronomers, says that in the harmony of the heavens, Jupiter accords most of all with the Sun. This harmony sounds most happily for men whenever those celestial bodies look upon each other in a <term>trine aspect<note>An astrological position where two planets are 120 degrees apart, generally considered the most harmonious and favorable alignment.</note></term>. Yesterday, they finally conspired into this very aspect. By aligning, they immediately graced you with a distinguished magistracy, and at the same time declared that one of you is Jovial <note>Under the influence of Jupiter, associated with justice and authority.</note> and the other is Solar <note>Under the influence of the Sun, associated with excellence and clarity.</note>. And just as the Sun and Jupiter are in accord in the heavens, you both will undoubtedly be in harmony in this office. I therefore congratulate you, not so much because you have been decorated with such a great gift, but because you were successfully established in dignity under a most happy star and the most fortunate auspices, at nearly the same time the happy star led the Magi to Christ. January 20, 1490. In the fields of Careggi.

---

-> *An expression of gratitude for an immense benefit.* <-

-> **Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.** <-

**Y**ou recently performed two almost divine miracles for my friend: you restored him to life, and you returned this mute man to us. For as soon as he revived through your inspiration, he conceived such a great thanksgiving in his mind for your immense benefit that he could not give birth to it through his mouth. Therefore, as David says, "Let praise be silence." <note>original: "Laus... esto silentium." A reference to the Vulgate text of Psalm 64:2, often interpreted as "silence is praise to Thee."</note> January 20, 1490. Florence.

---

-> *An allegory of how Mercury, the smallest of the heavenly bodies, signifies wisdom, the greatest of the virtues.* <-

-> **Marsilio Ficino to the noble and learned Bindaccio Ricasoli, sends greetings.** <-

**N**oble Bindaccio, you ask quite subtly, as is your custom in other matters, why God wished wisdom—the greatest of the virtues—to be signified by Mercury, the smallest of the heavenly bodies. To answer a brief question briefly: God warned us in this matter that we should remember that wisdom is very small among men, since it is promised by the smallest of the stars. He taught, moreover, that wisdom is not established by the size of the body, nor does it proceed from the mass of matter. Sometimes men who are smallest in body, audacity, or fortune are greatest in wisdom. Finally, the Sun represents God himself, while Mercury represents the wise man. Therefore, Mercury, who never departs from the Sun, signifies that only that soul will be wise which never departs from God. Furthermore, the Sun is thought to signify princes; since the Sun has no star closer to it in its path than Mercury, it warns that princes should have no closer connections in their familiarity than wise men. Moreover, because this same Mercury promises both wisdom and eloquence, he commands students of letters to join the study of eloquence with the study of wisdom. "He has carried every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet." <note>original: "Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci." A famous quote from Horace's "Ars Poetica," suggesting that the best work both instructs and delights.</note> February 14, 1490.

-> *Pallas, Juno, and Venus: the contemplative, active, and pleasurable lives.* <-

-> **Marsilio Ficino to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, sends greetings.** <-

**N**o one living by reason doubts that there are three lives: the contemplative, the active, and the pleasurable. This is because men have chosen three ways to happiness: wisdom, power, and pleasure. By the name of "wisdom," we understand any study of the liberal arts and religious leisure. Under the title of "power," we think of authority in civil and military governance, as well as an abundance of wealth, the splendor of glory, and busy virtue. Finally, under the designation of "pleasure," we include the delights of the five senses and the avoidance of labors and cares,

[...perfection], we do not doubt is contained. First, therefore, the poets named Minerva, second Juno, and finally third Venus. These three once contended before Paris for the golden apple—that is, for the palm and the victory. While Paris consulted with himself which of the three ways was most suitable for reaching happiness, he finally chose pleasure; but since he rejected wisdom and power, he rightly fell into misery while foolishly hoping for happiness. Only two are said to have appeared to Hercules: namely Venus and Juno. Hercules, neglecting Venus, followed a spirited virtue under Juno; yet he was not for that reason happy among mortals, being perpetually vexed by the labor of his struggles, but victory finally followed him to heaven; to him, at last, the overcome earth grants the stars <note>A poetic way of saying his earthly trials earned him deification or eternal fame.</note>. Two also met a certain Philebus <note>Referring to the protagonist of Plato's dialogue *Philebus*, which discusses the conflict between pleasure and wisdom.</note>: pleasure and wisdom. And by his judgment, Venus seemed to have overcome Pallas <note>Pallas is another name for Minerva, goddess of wisdom.</note>. But a little later, as Socrates judged more rightly, Minerva carried off the victory. Yet Venus and Juno, having been rejected, finally hounded Socrates under false judges and condemned him to death. Finally, our Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent).</note>, taught by the oracle of Apollo, subordinated none of these higher powers. For he saw all three, and adored all three according to their merits. On which account he received wisdom from Pallas, power from Juno, and from Venus he received the graces, poetry, and music.

### Congratulation on a new dignity, with astronomical auspices.
#### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord Hermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, sends greetings.

**P**oets say that Jupiter was often accustomed to send Mercury, and sometimes the Eagle. But at your birth, he sent both; for he himself, sitting in the citadel of the Zodiac in the eastern region, commanded the starry Eagle to fly through the summit of heaven under Capricorn, while Mercury entered the Gemini <note>original: "Dioscuros," the "sons of Zeus," Castor and Pollux.</note> in a certain hexagonal figure <term>sextile aspect<note>An astrological aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious.</note></term>. Moreover, he commanded his own Chiron <note>The centaur Chiron, associated with the constellation Sagittarius.</note> to inhabit the ninth region of heaven, which is consecrated to sacred things and wisdom. Therefore Jupiter—who is the author, or at least the signifier, of both the common religion and your own—when he first revisited his Gemini, from where he once sent Mercury down from on high, declared you a sacred prelate and set you over Aquileia <note>Ficino is making a pun on "Aquileia" and "Aquila" (the Eagle).</note>, commending the "Eagle's house" to your recent care and providence. But setting aside for the moment the stars and the portents of the heavens: I truly wish that this dignity may be happy for you, my dear Barbaro, and I pray to God, the founder of the heavens, for this; I also congratulate the dignity itself. For it shall surely be as much honored by you as most men are accustomed to be honored by their dignities. Finally, I rejoice for myself and for our age, because we have long seen learning joined with integrity of life, and now perhaps we shall see power breathing together with wisdom—a thing which our Plato especially desired. Such a great good, even if signified by the heaven, we believe was made by the ruler of heaven himself. Farewell, be happy, and keep your Marsilio in your good graces.

-> March 12, 1491. Florence. <-

### The life of heroic men is indeed laborious, but glorious.
#### Marsilio Ficino to Pierleone the Platonist, sends greetings.

**O**ne may perhaps conjecture from this that Hercules is, among the poets, a certain specifically Solar hero: for both the name of Hercules signifies the "splendor of glory" <note>A traditional (though philologically debated) etymology: Hera (glory/queen) + Kleos (fame).</note>, which pertains most of all to the Sun, and Hercules himself overcame twelve monsters, just as the Sun completes its course by passing through the twelve animals of the Zodiac. Therefore, hard labors celebrate the Solar hero. To him, at last, the overcome earth grants the stars. Also, the Apolline Spirit, being about to publicly celebrate our "Lion" <note>Pierleone Leoni, a famous physician and scholar whose name means "Lion."</note> of the Sun, decided not to test him in a single contest (that is, a duel), but to lead him everywhere into a crowd of enemies, so that from this his exalted virtue might finally carry off a broader victory. Therefore, under these auspices, O magnanimous Pierleone, you have successfully contended everywhere in the public schools <note>gymnasijs.</note>. Thus, finally, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered" <note>A biblical reference (Revelation 5:5), here applied to Pierleone's academic or philosophical successes.</note>. And so, it was first necessary for us to write to each other when there was cause for thorough congratulation. Until now, however, your frequent occupations have provided the cause of a long silence, not only for you but for me as well. As for what you ask—what I am working on at present—I am rereading the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian Neoplatonist whose works Ficino translated and commented upon.</note>, having begun these last summer. As soon as I had put an end to the commentaries on Plotinus, Dionysius alone remained for me to explain...

->Preface to the Fables on Pleasure.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to his friend Martin Uranius, given to him by heaven, sends greetings.<-

**T**he ninth book of our letters took its beginning from Martin; now the tenth book reaches its end in Martin. For the Martinian spirit and the Marsilian spirit <note>Ficino often played on the similarity of his name, Marsilio, and his friend’s name, Martin.</note> are entirely the same: the number nine claims it for itself, while the singular perfection of our love demands the number ten—which is, of course, the number of perfection. Truly, since love desires nothing other than pleasure, this tenth book, consecrated to love, rightly finds its end in pleasure. I speak of pleasure that is *Urania*—that is, heavenly pleasure—since it is dedicated to Uranius. <note>A pun on his friend's name, Martin Uranius, and "Urania," the name for heavenly or celestial love and pleasure.</note> You will therefore read here, my "other self," at the close of the tenth book, several <term>Fables</term> <note>original: "Apologos"; short stories or allegories intended to convey a moral or philosophical truth.</note> on pleasure. They are dedicated to you today, though they were devised by us long ago while we were commenting on Plato’s *Philebus*. That commentary was intended for Lorenzo de' Medici; however, as soon as the opportunity arises, it must be transcribed for you, for at this moment our copyists are busy transcribing letters to you.

### Fable: The evil demon draws us toward the false through a likeness of truth, and toward evil through pleasure; but God leads us toward the true and the good through these same things.

**G**od is truth and goodness; therefore, He composed all things from truth and goodness. Any thing is called "true" insofar as it remains in the uncorrupted purity of how it was made by God. Insofar as it is useful to others for some purpose, it is called "good" for those others. Likewise, insofar as one part of it is useful to another part within itself, it is called "good" for itself. Furthermore, God impressed upon things a <term>likeness of truth</term> <note>original: "verisimile"; something that appears to be true or has the "air of truth."</note> as a sign, and He infused goodness with pleasure as a "bait." This was so that the hidden truth of each thing might be tracked down through its visible likeness, and ultimately, through the truth of all things, the truth of God might be found. Again, it was so that through the bait of pleasure, individual things might be lured toward the "good" that is hidden within them, and through all good things, toward the Good of God. 

But the envious demon, seeing that God draws all things to Himself—partly by signs of likeness and partly by the bait of good things—tried to draw everything to himself in a similar way. Thus, he fashioned a "likeness of truth" and a "bait of goodness" in imitation of that divine expression. But he employed the former falsely and the latter wickedly. The result is that through that likeness, he draws minds toward the false, and through this pleasure, he draws the affections toward evil, and finally toward himself. For since he is a rebel and most estranged from divine truth and goodness, he is himself a kind of falsehood and malice. For this reason, in the *Timaeus*, Plato calls pleasure the "bait of evils."

### Fable regarding goods and evils.

**O**nce there were only two things: Good and Evil. As long as Good was generating things, Evil was not at all provoked to generate anything, out of pride, thinking it alone could resist the Good. At last, Good began to generate "goods." Then Evil, fearing for itself from the Good and the "goods," conceived a desire to generate "evils" against them. But because it was sterile and could not bring them forth from itself, it invoked its lot, Fortune. With Fortune’s favor, it began to generate evils, but in a manner contrary to how the Good generates goods. 

For Evil saw that "goods" refer back to the Good and contribute to it; that they possess virtue; that they preserve that in which they exist; that they agree with one another in their own health; and that they have pleasure following behind them. Against these, Evil threw their opposites: namely, degeneracy, hindrance, a disorderly crowd, and an impatience with that which sustains the Good. Likewise, it threw unfitness and goods that are simultaneously harmful. Finally, Evil placed pleasure at the *front* of the evil, mocking the Good itself—along with <term>Momus</term> <note>The Greek god of satire and mockery.</note>—for having hidden the "bait" of the good. Evil placed it *behind* the goods, whereas perhaps it would have been more rightly placed in front. But the Good itself, lest its kingdom be dissolved by the evil, decreed first indeed that it should endure evils...

...not only does it destroy another evil, but it also destroys itself. For whether it occurs through a lack or through an excess, it eventually destroys the foundation by which it is supported, apart from which it cannot stand alone. From this, it follows that evil is not able to be infinite in power, whereas good is able. This is what Pythagoras meant when he said: "Abstain from the animal with the black tail," <note>original: "Ab animali caudam habente nigram abstine." ## A Fable: Concerning Pleasure, which conquers the ambitious, but is conquered by Pallas.

**P**leasures once heard that they were being slandered everywhere by ambitious preachers. Conspiring together for their own defense, they chose Impudence as the patron of their cause, speaking these words: "Look, Impudence, at how ungrateful everyone is toward us! Indeed, since their entire happiness is situated within us, yet they dare to publicly condemn us." Then Impudence said, "I marvel at your laziness; for since you possess those very men and their homes, you do not even dare to occasionally show your faces to the people from the windows and gates. By doing so, everyone would understand that you are held in high delight by them, and that they only slander you so that no one might steal you away from them." After this, the pleasures—relying on the advice and further help of Impudence—opened their faces through the windows. From this it happened that the ambitious slanderers of pleasures lost all credit and authority among the people; and those who had slandered pleasure were in turn slandered everywhere by pleasure itself.

But after they had conquered their vain and false enemies, it remained for them to defend themselves against their true and legitimate enemies: the Philosophers. Since the philosophers prefer <term>Minerva</term> <note>Also known as Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> to pleasure, the judgment—with <term>Rashness</term> <note>original: "temeritate"; often personified as a blind or impulsive force.</note> recently called in as an advocate—was transferred to Jupiter. When they had come before Jupiter, Rashness, acting as the orator for the cause of the Pleasures, said that it was only right for Minerva to be summoned to judgment, since her followers prefer her, beyond what is divine law, to Pleasure, the mistress of all things. 

Pallas, having been summoned, appeared. Suddenly, Rashness objected: "Not even your Pallas, O Jupiter, according to the mouths of the Philosophers who value pleasure as nothing, boasts that she is your daughter. But I respond that Pleasure itself was born from you under the name of Venus, and that Minerva is the daughter of Pleasure under the name of Wisdom, whom all Philosophers follow for the sake of a certain pleasure. What more? Venus was born from you; but if Pallas boasts that she sprang from your head, we shall assert that she too was fathered by you along with Pleasure."

To these things Pallas replied: "But I affirm, O Pleasure, that you arose from me: both within Jupiter, who rejoices in himself through the benefit of wisdom, and among men, arising from me as the inventor of various delights—or rather, from my image among those practicing philosophy. For these men are delighted and carried away by a certain image of my splendor." 

Then Rashness said, "Let us set aside these <term>dialectical</term> <note>Logic-based or argumentative subtleties.</note> quibbles. Pleasure, being simple and innocent, does not arm herself with such thorns. Look around, Jupiter, at how vast the empire of Pleasure is! Behold Venus, behold Cupid, her attendants; behold the Graces, her handmaidens; and the God of the Gardens <note>Priapus, the god of fertility and gardens.</note> himself, her servant. In the kitchen is Ceres <note>Goddess of grain/food.</note>, and in the pantry is Bacchus <note>God of wine.</note>. Upon her nectar and ambrosia all the heavenly beings feed. Why should I mention Mars, the fiercest of the gods? Why yourself, Jupiter? Why the others who are everywhere ensnared by the allurements of Venus? And what the others finally achieve with difficulty through violence, and barely retain, she alone successfully fulfills with a single nod—dragging no one, but leading all who are willing, and retaining them gladly. She leads not only those who live on earth, but those in heaven, and those who guide the heavens. She carries away not only living things, but even non-living things toward their own specific pleasures. Furthermore, lest Pallas or Diana or Vesta boast of their own sterility and escape the empire of Pleasure: Pleasure herself, O Jupiter, commands Pallas to be delighted by her bows, Diana by hunting, and Vesta by the hearth-fires."

Indignant at this, Pallas said: "O Jupiter, you will soon see how 'strong' this Pleasure is, who so insolently boasts of an empire over all. Summon here <term>Dread</term> <note>original: "pauorem"; personified fear or terror.</note>, the most abject of all things, not just of the gods." Jupiter cried out: "Ho there, Dread!" Immediately upon the name of Dread being called, all the Pleasures, trembling along with Rashness, took to flight. Then all the inhabitants of heaven laughed and condemned that vile flight with a ridiculous judgment. 

Finally, Pallas sealed the matter with the sentence of the gods: "What is more worthless than Dread? For he is created from that which is not, whenever he arises from the image of an absent evil. He is again killed by that which is not, whenever he is destroyed by the image of an absent good. Yet Pleasure is even more worthless than such a vile Dread. For she is put to flight not only by him, but by his shadow—since she suddenly flees not only when Dread is present, but even when she is merely thinking of it. Indeed, to speak more truly, she perishes; and so that she might perish with greater ignominy, she does not even turn into anything similar..."

->*A Fable. Concerning Pleasure: that one must not contend with her, nor hope for her on earth.*<-

**W**hen Jupiter realized that souls were not returning to heaven because they were being held on earth by Pleasure, he sent Mars and Vulcan, as the strongest and most armed, to kill Pleasure. But they, being young men, were trapped by the charms of Pleasure at the very first encounter and laid down their arms. He then sent Pallas <note>Pallas is another name for Athena or Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.</note>, armed and wise, thinking the others had succumbed due to their rashness. To her, Pleasure said: "Are you not ashamed, O Pallas, a goddess clothed and armed, to fight with me, who am human, unarmed, and naked?" She replied, "It pleases me to fight you in this way, so that I may overcome you." To this, Pleasure answered: "Since you have no regard for either glory or utility in this struggle—for you will gain neither if I am defeated—it is clear that you are overcome by the mere pleasure of victory itself, fighting with no regard for glory or profit." Then Pallas, convicted by these words, broke out into blows and repeatedly directed her weapon at her. But Pleasure, whose nature is yielding, pervasive, and most subtle, immediately dodged the strikes. Therefore, Pallas stretched out her wide shield over her head, but Pleasure penetrated the shield; indeed, she is so powerful at penetrating that she pierces both body and soul. After this, Pallas called upon Pain <note>original: "dolorem"</note>, so that she might destroy Pleasure by means of a contrary enemy. But since opposites do not receive one another, Pain did not rush into the face of Pleasure, but instead took up a position right by her side. Then Pallas, together with her companion Vulcan, took up bellows and attempted to thin out and dissolve Pleasure. Yet she could not thin her, since she is already the thinnest thing, nor dissolve her into anything further, since she is the ultimate end. For when it is asked why someone does this or that, one does not answer "because of that" [beyond pleasure]. Again, it is asked "why that?" and the answer is "because it pleases." If one asks again "why does it please?", no other answer will be given than "because it is pleasing." They say that Pallas then returned to Jupiter, pale with grief because she had not conquered Pleasure. Then she, more hurried as if by her own flow of energy, approached Jupiter and said: "O son, now you will recognize that you have need of the counsel of old Saturn, from whom you have until now taken the kingdom and shut away in the inner chambers of the palace." <note>This is an allegory for the "Active Life" (Jupiter) which often displaces the "Contemplative Life" (Saturn).</note> Therefore, the doors were unlocked and Saturn was called to consultation. Then he said: "There are two principles of motion: Pleasure, for the sake of pursuing; and Pain, for the sake of fleeing. Indifference <note>original: "indolentia", literally "freedom from pain"</note> does neither. Therefore, Pleasure must not be destroyed; otherwise, souls will not seek heaven if pleasure were extinguished even here. Instead, Pleasure must be drawn up to here, and Pain must be left among men, so that from there everyone may flee to this place." The old man's counsel was pleasing. The demons who are the attendants of Mars and Vulcan were sent to seize Pleasure. For it was feared that the gods might indulge in her beauty and yield, but it was certain that the demons would have no regard for beauty. But the demons could never hold Pleasure in their hands; in her slippery softness, she wonderfully surpassed even eels. For her softness is reinforced by the constant use and habitation of soft and sweet things. Finally, Pleasure overcame both gods and demons, such that no one dares to contend with her. For she is to be fled rather than attacked. But lest we offend divine names any longer, let us admit that there is a "Minerva" on earth and other "gods" on earth—that is, human wisdom and power, which are mostly overcome by pleasure, but are surpassed by divine wisdom. For Saturn, together with Minerva, deliberated again that they should attempt to seize Pleasure not through violence opposed to her, but through a friendly grace. Therefore, they sent Mercury, Apollo, the Muses, and the Graces to lure Pleasure upward. Mercury, giving the first speech to her, dissuaded Pleasure from lingering on earth among her enemies: fear, pain, anger, hatred, envy, labor, poverty, and disease. Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> also soothed her with his lyre, the Muses with songs and melodies, and the Graces with dances and choruses. Enticed by these, Pleasure joined the singing Muses and, stretching out her hands, entwined herself with the Graces as they played charmingly. And so, accompanied by these deities as they returned to heaven singing and playing, Pleasure was carried into the heavens. The Earth was deserted by Pleasure; therefore, one must depart from here to go there—provided, however, that in departing you do not turn back, lest in the manner of Orpheus you lose your reward. But when did Pleasure flee into heaven? At the same time as the original Astraea <note>Astraea was the goddess of Justice, the last of the immortals to leave the earth at the end of the Iron Age.</note>, namely Justice, when Adam sinned. But lest mortals, deprived of pleasure, perish among—

since so many adversities afflicted and ruined them, Jupiter took pity on our misery. While he took away Pleasure, he multiplied our Hope. But the hope of attaining pleasure here is deceptive—that is, the hope of bringing it back from mortal things. For Pleasure has been transferred to Minerva <note>Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom</note>, led there by Mercury, Phoebus Apollo, the Muses, and the Graces. For this reason, we can only achieve full Pleasure in the presence of divine wisdom, though we may also find a certain delight in the liberal arts <term>liberalibus disciplinis: the traditional academic subjects like grammar, logic, and music</term>.

After this, Pluto, the king of the earth, seeing that the "bait" used to keep souls in the underworld had been taken from him, thought at least to fashion a bait similar in appearance to Pleasure. Therefore, having taken the clothes and the dyes left behind by Pleasure—which she used to wear while on earth (for she departed into heaven pure)—he decided to prepare and substitute another in place of Pleasure. He did not, however, prepare demons, for they are merely necessary ministers; nor souls, for they have already been judged. Instead, he prepared one of the Furies. It was not Anger, nor Envy, nor Hatred, Fear, or Grief; for the clothes and shoes of Pleasure did not fit these, as they were too different. Rather, he prepared Loss <note>original: "iacturam," meaning ruin, sacrifice, or financial loss</note>, whom he knew to have always been most intimate with earthly Pleasure. From this we are warned to flee far from Pleasure; otherwise, under the pretext of Pleasure, we will immediately fall into hidden Loss.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Of the Florentine’s Letters,
### BOOK XI.

->A letter concerning the gift of a silver cup.<-
->Georg Herwart of Augsburg <note>Augsburg was a major German banking and humanist center</note> to Marsilio Ficino<-
->the Platonist, sends greetings.<-

Whenever I recall—and indeed I recall it daily, or to speak more truly, every single hour—that fortunate and joyful day which brought me the beginning of your sweet acquaintance and friendship, I judge it worthy of the same celebration with which a birthday is usually honored. I mark it, as was the custom of the ancients, with a white pebble <note>A Roman custom signifying a lucky or happy day</note>. For that was the day which made known to me your eminent genius, your extraordinary virtues, and that honey-flowing abundance of speech which flourishes so richly in you. I value all these things so highly that I have given and dedicated my whole self to you, who are adorned with them. Nor do I hold anything more important than that an opportunity might be given so that I may be able to please you in all things, and that you might wish to use my labor, care, and talent—whatever they may be—wherever I am. I ask you most earnestly, again and again, to do so. I am sending to you now a silver, or as I might call it, a "little pot"—a truly frivolous and childish little gift. Indeed, your virtues are such that they deserve to be rewarded with more magnificent gifts. But since you are most kind, you will call it not "lesser," but rather a pledge and testimony, in some part, of our newly begun friendship and of your kindness toward me. And so you will believe that I send it to you with that spirit. Farewell, and love me. Given at Venice, on the Ides of April <note>April 13th</note>, 1491.

### How someone might encounter themselves under another person's mask while thinking.
->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow-Platonist Pierleone, sends greetings.<-

**I** received your letter, Pierleone, full of love and grace, and—to praise it in a single word—truly Platonic. In it, you write that whenever something Platonic occurs to you, Marsilio soon "succors" <note>A wordplay in Latin between *occurrit* (occurs/meets) and *succurrere* (to run to help/come to mind)</note> you; but take care that an external image does not perhaps deceive you. Indeed, I suspect that Pierleone himself lies hidden there under the persona <term>persona: literally a "mask" worn by actors in antiquity; here meaning a character or outward appearance</term> of Marsilio. For if any human form offers itself to you while contemplating Platonic matters, it is probable that the most "Platonic" form would offer itself above all others. And what in human affairs is more Platonic than the "Great Lion," the dwelling place of the Platonic Sun? <note>Ficino is punning on his friend's name, Pierleone: *Leo* means Lion. In Ficino's solar philosophy, the sun represents the divine intellect</note> Perhaps, therefore, like Narcissus, you imagine you are looking at another while looking at yourself. This is especially true of Marsilio, whose image a burning love has caused you to put on. 

But since we have happened upon the subject of images, you surely know that reason is the middle ground between imagination and the intellect. From one side, the images of natural things flow into reason from the imagination; from the other, the forms of divine things flow into it from the intellect. For this reason, it often happens that a certain divine form takes on a kind of natural image within human reason, so that what is divine within often appears as something natural to the eyes of reason. What if, by a similar logic, Pierleone is frequently and freely met under the figure of Marsilio? Thus it seems to me so far. 

Regarding Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 5th-6th century) whom Ficino and his contemporaries believed was the direct disciple of St. Paul mentioned in the Book of Acts</note>, you seem to me to judge quite rightly: certainly, no form of knowledge is more pleasing to me than the Platonic, and this form is nowhere more to be venerated than in Dionysius. I love Plato in Iamblichus, I admire him in Plotinus, but in Dionysius I venerate him. I often suspect that the Platonists older than Plotinus—Ammonius and Eunomius, or perhaps those before them—read the books of Dionysius before they were hidden away by some unknown calamity of the Church. I suspect that from those books, the truly Platonic sparks of Dionysius were poured into Plotinus and Iamblichus, from which the whole fire was kindled. 

Enough regarding Dionysius; Galen’s work *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato* will be very welcome to me. Words are often spoken of you in the presence of Lorenzo de' Medici. He truly loves you wonderfully and, as is his custom and as is right, he respects you greatly. May 12, 1491. In the countryside of Careggi.

---

### It belongs to the great to confer benefits even upon the undeserving.
->Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend<-
->Father in Christ and Lord, Raffaele Riario,<-
->Cardinal of San Giorgio.<-

**A**lthough there are perhaps no merits of mine for which I ought to obtain anything from you, I nevertheless dare to ask for a certain favor; not trusting in any merits, but relying on my respect for you and your mercy toward all. To provide a benefit to the deserving is just, and indeed human; but to grant it even to the undeserving is most merciful and divine. Great and divine things are especially becoming of a great and holy prelate.

# On the four types of divine madness. Likewise, true praises of Lorenzo de’ Medici.

->Marsilio Ficino to Pietro Divizio, most distinguished in letters and character, sends greetings.<-

Since you have for a long time heard our Plato disputing most extensively about love in the *Symposium* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the nature of love</note>, and since you moreover desired a certain brief summary regarding the opinion on love, I gave you a booklet to read on this matter, composed by us in our youth with a certain poetic flair, addressed to a foreign youth. I remember indeed how wonderfully you were delighted to hear that love itself is not in truth lust, but a certain madness <note>original: "furor"; here meaning a state of being "possessed" or inspired by a god</note> divinely incited in excellent minds. Furthermore, that divine madness, like a general category, contains four species within itself: Love, Poetry, Prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note>, and the Mysteries <note>original: "Mysterium"; referring to sacred religious rites or secret divine knowledge</note>. And indeed, Love proceeds from Venus, Poetry from the Muses, Prophecy from Apollo, and the Mysteries from Dionysus. Finally, I explained by what reasoning different human temperaments are stirred by different divine powers and various madnesses. It remained, most ingenious Pietro, to investigate whether the same mind could be inspired, so to speak, by several gods at once, being stirred by various madnesses from then on. 

Now, indeed, the question regarding love and poetry does not seem particularly difficult. For we do not doubt that Homer, Pindar, Callimachus, Sappho, and Virgil <note>original: "Maronem"</note> were all stirred by a simultaneous poetic and amorous instinct. Furthermore, Epimenides and the Sibyl were inspired by prophecy. But beyond these, only those who are (as they say) born of the gods could be inspired by the mysteries—such as the Gentiles say Orpheus was, and as our people pass down regarding David. 

We have also known in our own century a mind most blessed, which has obtained these four gifts of madness equally from the four divine powers. Truly, he conceived a poetic and amorous spirit under the Muses and the heavenly Venus long ago in the very flower of his youth. This is indeed echoed everywhere by his most sweet songs and his altogether wonderful poems. But as an adult he drew prophecy from Apollo, by which—certainly through a certain miraculous sharpness of mind implanted from heaven—he frequently foretells future dangers, both private and public. He applies a healing hand to these perils and immediately cures them with the power of Apollo <note>original: "Phoebęa uirtute"; Apollo, as Phoebus, was the god of both prophecy and medicine</note>. Finally, as he approached maturity, he happily attained the mystic madness from Dionysus. Ancient theologians defined Dionysian intoxication as a transcendence of the mind <note>original: "excessum mentis"</note>, which, once separated from mortal affairs, penetrates the secret mysteries of divinity. "Bacchus loves the hills" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics*</note>. In the hills of Ambra and Agnano <note>Two of Lorenzo de' Medici’s favorite villas and estates</note>, that Apollonian Lorenzo, intoxicated everywhere by Dionysian nectar, revels in divine frenzy. Then indeed, inspired from on high, he pours forth from an eloquent mouth <note>original: "ore rotundo"</note> heavenly songs above the reach of man, the profound meanings of which it is never permitted for anyone to penetrate, unless they are seized by a similar kind of madness. 

Indeed, that Patron of ours <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note> sometimes sweeps along with him some who are listening more attentively and successfully; he overflows into them, more than others, with the richness of his madness. By what reasoning he, being himself stirred by the divine power, is able to excite others in almost the same way, our Plato teaches in the book titled *Ion*. There, he places a small iron ring beneath a huge "Herculean stone" <note>a magnet</note>, which is soon easily snatched up; then he connects a second ring to the first, a third to the second, and a fourth thereafter. He creates a chain of rings hanging from the magnet, through which the power of attraction is suddenly poured from the first into the next in succession. By the same reasoning, he thinks a Muse is seized by Apollo, a poet by the Muse, and those listening are similarly seized by the poet. Virgil perhaps imitates this mystery in these verses: "What the almighty Father foretold to Apollo, and Apollo to me, I—the greatest of the Sybils <note>original: "Suriarum"; likely a variant or wordplay on 'Sybils' or 'Furies'</note>—disclose to you." But I would not wish to have named the Sybils at present, where we are treating not of the madness of the Sybils, but of the Graces. 

Abounding in this madness, happy Pietro, our Patron immediately affects both you and me equally, as well as his other observers; he seizes those he has affected, occupies those he has seized, and soon drenching those he occupies with a certain incomparable pleasure. Therefore, having been affected by so great a benefit, let us persevere in our most ardent love for him, in 

->loving whom singularly, we carry back a<- 
->divine instinct daily. June 8,<-
->1491.<-

<summary>Marsilio Ficino writes to Pietro Divizio, arguing that Lorenzo de' Medici embodies all four Platonic "divine madnesses" (Poetry, Love, Prophecy, and Mystery). Ficino uses the metaphor of a magnet to explain how Lorenzo’s divine inspiration is transmitted to those who follow and listen to him.</summary>

### Preface to the Foundations of Plato.
### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Valori, greetings.

**I**n the year of human salvation 1456—at which time I was indeed twenty-three years of age and you were born—I inaugurated the first fruits of my studies with four books of foundations <note>original: "institutionum"; these were Ficino’s early introductory manuals to Platonic philosophy</note> for the Platonic discipline. Cristoforo Landino <note>A famous humanist scholar and friend of Ficino</note>, my dearest friend and a most learned man, encouraged me to compose them. When either he or Cosimo de' Medici <note>The patriarch of the Medici family and Ficino's first great patron</note> had examined them, they certainly approved, but they advised that I should keep them in my own possession until I was educated in Greek literature and could finally drink from the Platonic sources themselves. For I had completed those early works partly by a certain accidental discovery and partly assisted by reading certain Latin Platonists. 

Afterward, having approached Plato and the Platonists in Greek, I gradually corrected those "Foundations" in the books that followed. Nevertheless, I did not wish to destroy the book itself, which I had fathered as my firstborn child in the year you were born. To me, you are certainly a son in respect and a patron in your constant favor; therefore, my most beloved son Valori, I pray that you embrace this book, your brother, with brotherly love. It is destined to live in the home of the Valori—a family close to me since my youth—by the truly desired Merit <note>A pun on the name "Valori" and the Latin "Valore," meaning value or merit</note> of your name. Farewell. November 1491.

---

### An Expression of Gratitude.
### Marsilio Ficino to Martin "Uranius" Prenninger, a unique friend, greetings.

**Y**our friend Joannes Streler, who is now almost one of our own, read me today a part of your letter to him, which was full of the most burning love toward us. In it, you also indicated that you celebrated our birthday with both a gathering of learned men and magnificent expense. I, therefore, cannot sufficiently repay such devotion of yours toward us unless I love you as much as I love myself. Moreover, of my incomparable love for you, my sweetest Martin, not only our letters will be witnesses, but also certain books to be published by us in the future. Live happily then, my Martin, always no less dear to me than my own life. 

I am sending to you the remainder of our commentary on the *Philebus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on pleasure and the highest good</note>, consisting of four quires <note>A quire is a set of leaves of paper/parchment folded together</note>. The printing of Plotinus’s books will be finished (as I judge) by this coming March, at the magnificent expense of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron</note> and in a royal format <note>original: "forma Regia"; refers to a large, high-quality book size</note>; he has decided that our books of Plato should also soon be printed with the same dignity. I, for my part, will take care with all my strength that the second printing is more correct than the first. Furthermore, I shall divide individual books into many chapters and sub-chapters, and I will clarify them with the most certain headings, as if with formulas. The books of Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, whose mystical Christian-Platonic works Ficino translated</note>, which you began long ago, will be finished somewhat later because of occupations of this kind. Farewell. November 24, 1491. Florence.

---

### On the book "On Life" given as a gift.
### Marsilio Ficino to Mazingo, the distinguished physician and inseparable friend, greetings.

**H**ail, curator of our health (with God as the author), a truly inseparable friend. In the first place, perhaps it is a wonder why I should call you an inseparable friend rather than something else. It is because, evidently, those whom heaven has joined, earth shall by no means separate. For in what way could the lowest earth of the world divide our souls by a distance of places, when the highest of the planets <note>referring to Saturn</note> joined us in his own dwellings with love? With a love, I say, as durable as Saturn himself is stable. Let this "Life" <note>referring to Ficino’s book "De Vita" or "On Life," which deals with the health of scholars and astrological influences</note> of mine in your possession be a pledge of such firm benevolence. Nor do I entrust this "Life" to you for approval and care without merit, for long ago I already
->entrusted this life of mine and my people to your care.<-

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

*Philosophical minds reach Christ through Plato; this occurred in the case of Aurelius Augustine.* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) famously wrote in his Confessions that reading the "books of the Platonists" prepared him to accept the Christian faith.</note>

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

**Y**ou write to me, my friend, most excellently—and nothing is more pleasing to me—that you daily persuade many, and have already convinced several, to leave behind Epicurean impiety <note>The philosophy of Epicurus, which in the Renaissance was often synonymous with the denial of the soul's immortality</note> and set aside the opinions of Averroes <note>Averroes was a medieval Islamic philosopher; "Averroism" in this context refers to the belief that all humans share a single intellect, which challenged the idea of individual personal immortality</note> in favor of the pious views of our Plato regarding the soul and God. By this path, which is truly a kind of "middle way," they may finally attain Christian piety. Hail, therefore, true fisher of men! For those who persuade common minds seem to catch fish, or rather little fish; but those who persuade the excellent are judged to be fishers of men. Perhaps the Gospel calls these "the great fish," for whose capture the net is not even torn. Indeed, our "Mirandulan net" <note>A pun on Pico’s title "Prince of Mirandola"</note> is now Platonic reasoning, which, if it is drawn correctly under Christian truth, is not torn but remains whole while it is filled. You have read that in ancient times no philosophers except the Platonists took up the Christian religion. Justly, therefore, do you fish for all the highest minds for Christ with these (if I may say so) "Platonic nets." I wish at least three such fishers of religion were present, so that no large fish would be left in the sea. But alas, we are miserable, or rather unfortunate: the harvest is indeed great, but the laborers are few. Therefore, my Pico, since we are few, we must work more frequently and more vehemently. Farewell.

---

->Recommendation.<-

### Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra, greetings.

**M**artin Prenninger <note>Original: "Martinus Vranius," a German humanist and jurist who was a close friend and correspondent of Ficino</note> has come from Germany to Rome, intending to carry out and (as I hope) complete the mandates of his prince with all his strength, provided you offer your counsel and effort. I desire this to be provided so intensely that I currently strive for nothing more ardently; his own marvelous virtue will recommend him to you if you get to know him. Therefore, let our great goodwill recommend him while he is yet unknown. Indeed, he is so dear to me that I cannot express it otherwise than to say: he is my "other self" <note>original: "alter ego"</note>. Since I have so far recommended none of my friends to you in vain—such is your incredible humanity and kindness—I hope now, or rather I know for certain, that Martin (or rather Marsilio himself) will be successfully recommended to you. April 1, 1492.

### Marsilio Ficino to his friend Filippo Valori, greetings.

**Y**ou remember, my Valori, how ardently our Martin Prenninger loves us, so much so that he even named his son Marsilio after me, and established my birthday as a day to be celebrated. I do not doubt that he is greatly loved by you. He will greet you, reveal his plan, and ask for help. If you remember how often I am accustomed to say of Martin, "he is my other self," I do not doubt that you will have him marvelously recommended in all things. I have written nearly the same things to our venerable Soderini. Therefore, recommend this Marsilio—who is, as you know, my twin—to him with redoubled prayers.

### Marsilio Ficino humbly commends himself to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal.

**S**ince the fourth degree is considered the greatest by the Medici <note>A play on medical terminology and the Medici family name</note>, and you are the fourth patron to me from the noble Medici family since Cosimo, you are without doubt the greatest. I clearly perceive this from the fact that you do not give me the things of others, but your own. For a long time now, you have honored me with your canonry. Now you have suddenly gifted me with the Church of San Martino <note>original: "Aede Martiana"</note>, which was granted to you as a gift. For this reason, despite the death of our magnanimous Lorenzo, I am not permitted to bewail my own fortune, seeing that I am henceforth so greatly commended to such a patron; nor can I pity his lot, whom we know to have been translated to the heavens by many evident proofs. <note>Lorenzo de' Medici died on April 8, 1492. Ficino refers to the lightning strike on the Florence Cathedral and other omens that supposedly preceded his death.</note>
