...we recognize. You have read, I believe, in Hesiod, <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet; this refers to a passage in his *Works and Days* where he describes 30,000 immortal spirits who watch over mortal affairs.</note> that thirty thousand beneficial spirits <note>original: "daemonum". In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary guardian spirits.</note> care for human affairs through the high air. These the ancient rulers of men called "scouts." Furthermore, they believe that the most excellent leaders among men, after their passing, migrate to such rulers, as if they were to be their colleagues hereafter in the governance of human affairs. The Platonists think, therefore, that those spirits congratulate the happy souls flying thither. Indeed, these congratulations give signs to men in the form of wonderful portents: thunder, lightning, flames, the collapse of structures, <note>original: "machinarum ruinas". This likely refers to the lightning strike on the lantern of the Florence Cathedral (the Duomo) on April 5, 1492, three days before Lorenzo’s death.</note> oracles, and dreams. These prodigies seem to signify partly the majesty of the migrating soul, partly a loss to the world of people, and partly the succession of ancient power to the heirs. They assert that this happened beyond controversy at the passing of Romulus and Caesar. And now, in the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent, a man almost divine, this was manifest to nearly the entire population of Florence. Live therefore most happily, my patron, content with the divine will, rejoicing in your father's happiness, and trusting in divine help. April 15, 1492. In the fields of Careggi. <note>Careggi was the location of the Medici villa where Lorenzo died and where Ficino often stayed.</note>

### An expression of thanks.

->Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini,<-
->Bishop of Volterra, greetings.<-

**G**rammarians indeed have nothing beyond the superlative degree, but orators and poets add something to it. Perhaps that line of Virgil’s tends toward this: *O thrice and four times blessed.* <note>original: "O ter quaterque beati" from the Aeneid. Ficino is playing with the idea that "blessed" is not enough to describe his gratitude.</note> "Thrice blessed" are indeed the most blessed. "Four times," however, is even more than most blessed. Hitherto, I clearly perceived that I was most dear to you, and I did not think I could ever be dearer. But now I see without a doubt how very dear I am. For you strip your own favorites <note>original: "chariffimos". Can also mean "most dear ones."</note> in order to clothe me. Therefore, the greatest thanks which I am usually accustomed to give you for many benefits, I now give as the "greatest possible" thanks, and I confess myself to be most devoted to you. Moreover, I owe no small debt to that member of your household who, I hear, having been asked by you, soon granted himself to us with no reluctant mind. April 25, 1492. In the fields of Careggi.

### The causes of the prodigies occurring at the death of a prince.

->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, the Florentine ambassador<-
->to the Pope, greetings.<-

**A**s I was thinking about the causes of the prodigies occurring at the death of excellent men, especially princes, it first came to my mind that these things happen neither by luck (for they have an order) nor proceed from nature (for they are diverse among themselves, so they cannot be referred to a single natural influence proceeding in one way, and they have in themselves mysteries altogether superior to nature). Then it occurred to me that if portents of this kind proceed neither from luck nor from nature, they undoubtedly proceed from some divinity—that is, from some sublime intelligence surpassing the powers of nature. But lest we reduce every minor thing to the Primary Mind <note>God</note> without some intermediate order, these things seem (to speak in the Platonic manner) to be referred to three powers especially. There is the *Genius* of the person, a spirit familiar to the man, whom our theologians call the "Guardian Angel"; there is also the *Genius* of the place, the protector of the house, city, or kingdom, whom they call a "Principality"; <note>In the Dionysian hierarchy of angels, Principalities are the protectors of nations.</note> and there is, in addition, a sublime order and choir of divinities or spirits or angels, into whose number and lot an excellent soul is about to migrate through similarity of office, as if to its own star, to be as a colleague in that same office there. Just as there are three authors of prodigies, so there seem to be three kinds of portents. That sublime choir kindles comets, <note>original: "crinitas" (hairy stars).</note> stirs up thunder, hurls lightning, and fires falling stars. The power presiding over the province shakes and destroys structures, pours out oracles, moves auguries and omens, and signifies the tides. The personal guardian, however, arouses dreams and all such things, and the barking of dogs, as if driving away evil spirits from there. Furthermore, you will seem to desire an end: for whose sake are these things done? First, those signs signify that most excellent souls are not extinguished or neglected, but reign with the beings above after death. Second, they foretell the calamity of a people deprived of such a great man, and they warn them to beware of imminent dangers. Third, they both admonish the dying man and indicate to his family that celestial favor does not die even though he is dying, but [remains] for the fami-

# MARSILIO FICINO

...and his family <note>original: "liæ suæ", likely "familiae suae"</note> will aspire to follow after him. Certain Platonists add that between the sublime eternal spirits <note>original: "daemonas", referring to intermediary beings, not necessarily evil spirits</note> and short-lived humans, there are certain intermediate spirits who are very long-lived. They believe that more powerful men are entrusted to the care of the more powerful among these spirits. Thus, when one of those spirits dies after many centuries, it is said that a great leader entrusted to him immediately falls ill and departs from this life. Furthermore, they say the air is disturbed and new and marvelous things happen when the airy bodies of these great spirits are dissolved, and when friendly spirits take the fate of both the great spirit and the leader quite hard. Farewell. April 25, 1492.

## On the solitary life, and how much a friend should be valued.
->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.<-

**D**o you ever hope to remain hidden, my dear Mirandola? <note>Pico della Mirandola was a famous philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man." He often sought a life of private study.</note> Small and obscure things can indeed be easily hidden, but great and famous things cannot. You certainly strive to always live well in private so that you may live well, but meanwhile, the more you become an object of admiration to the people, the more you are known. Hence, whatever you attempt, various rumors are immediately stirred up. What then? Will you always look around at the common crowd and, looking far ahead to what they might gossip about, become their slave? Or will you rather be content with your own profession and value the judgment of the common people as nothing? I certainly know your character. See then if I seem to see what you are doing. You do not value these things as absolutely nothing, but you value them as little. Yet you will highly value the judgments of the prudent. But enough of these matters. Truly, my dearest Giovanni, I grieved all the more heavily at your departure because you suddenly deserted me when I was placed in the deepest sorrow on account of the death of two friends at once, <note>One friend is certainly Lorenzo de' Medici; the other may be Enrico Eruli or another member of the Platonic Academy who died near that time.</note> hoping as I was that you alone would be my consoler and healer. But I hope you will return shortly; relying on this hope, I shall even console our friends. Farewell, and return happily. April 27, in the district of Careggi. <note>Careggi was the location of the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy met.</note>

---

## Praise of a friend, namely Bindaccio Ricasoli.
->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, Florentine ambassador, Greetings.<-

**T**he long-lasting illness of Lorenzo de' Medici, together with the injustice of the times (as I believe), was the reason that I too have been quite seriously ill. But from that long infirmity I have now recovered quite well, obviously by the inspiration of God. No one, however, lightened the weariness of my long languor more for me than our close friend Bindaccio Ricasoli—a man certainly most noble by nature, most proven in virtue, and most dutiful in his actions. He often greeted me of his own accord, and often also in your name. Moreover, he indicated that he owes you a great deal. Therefore, love him above all others, my dear Valori, as he loves you especially and is most worthy of everyone's love. Martin Uranius, <note>Martinus Uranius was the Latin name for Martin Prenninger, a German scholar and pupil of Ficino.</note> my other self, returned to us today and told us how kindly and how magnificently you received him. You have done indeed as you usually do, and you could have done nothing more pleasing to me at this time. June 26, 1492.

---

## Praise of the Legitimate Prince.
->Marsilio Ficino to Eberhard, Duke of Württemberg and Lord of Montbéliard, many greetings.<-

**W**e have for a long time now heard much from many people regarding the singular excellence of your virtues. We have recently received even more from our friend Martin Uranius, a most rich witness and guarantor to us, and a herald of your praises most worthy of trust among all. Therefore, the immense splendor of your admirable virtues—shining toward us like the brilliance of stars—has already kindled in us an incredible passion to vehemently love, cherish, and especially venerate you. I have indeed long desired what our Plato used to proclaim he hoped for: to know a prince in whom, as in Pallas <note>Athena/Pallas, the goddess of wisdom and war</note>, wisdom is seen equally alongside power; and in whom, as in Caesar, magnanimity joins with clemency; and as in Scipio, gravity concurs with courtesy. In whom, furthermore, there might flourish both the justice of Minos and the religion of Numa, and under whom that famous peace of Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar, the first Roman emperor</note> might return. One who, finally, would prefer the studies of peace to the business of war, would found temples, and would establish public schools of literature. One whom his subjects do not so much fear as they love, observe, and admire. Such is indeed the idea of the legitimate prince, and the longed-for...

...and once wished for by Plato, and desired by us in the first place, and (as constant rumor holds) is especially great in you, so that it is no wonder that I now, and all my fellow Academics, inflamed by the rays of your many virtues, honor and venerate you before other princes as a kind of heavenly divinity. But beyond this, we are compelled by a certain incredible love to beseech you (so that you may also love us) as ones who love you singularly; and always hereafter, remember (as you already do) that just as all light hangs from on high, so the splendor of your virtues depends on God himself, the Father of Lights. May that supreme author of all good things confirm your probity as well as your happiness for the future, and may he increase that confirmed disposition, even as you consider and follow the daily courses and aspects of the heavenly bodies.

<margin>
† Here the end of the Letter to the Duke of Württemberg is missing. This is the beginning of the letter to the one from Baden.
</margin>

† I certainly approve, my dearest [Margrave of] Baden <note>Original: "Bandaci/Bindaci." This likely refers to Christoph I, Margrave of Baden (1453–1527), a patron of humanists.</note>. However, if you should ever take up that branch of astrology by which too-certain judgments of the future are promised in vain, I do not approve of it at all. For the man I hold as my closest friend, I desire also to be the most fortunate. Yet we have all discovered that those who gape too curiously at predicting the future turn out to be, or become, the most unfortunate of all men. We believe the causes of this adversity are either manifest or hidden. 

The manifest causes are certainly that, by an infinite and entirely uncertain zeal for future things, they are always compelled to neglect all their own present affairs. Moreover, for the most part, they are either relying on the promises of an imminent fate or terrified by its threats; and while they themselves do nothing, hanging entirely upon fate, they fail in what their own judgment deems necessary. I think the hidden causes of this matter are that Divine Providence—to which nature, fate, and fortune are subject <note>Ficino argues that God's plan (Providence) sits above the mechanical laws of nature or the stars (Fate).</note>—does not give all things to all people, but dispenses to each his own justly. Therefore, to those to whom it has granted the future (and to those who desire it), it rightly denies the present. For since the present things, if you compare them with the future, are very few and very small, if you lack such things, provided that you possess the future things (which are most numerous and greatest), you ought not to complain to Providence about your lot. 

But perhaps Fortune—which seems to be opposed to Fate in this at least, that Fate asserts a necessary order of things while Fortune rejects such an order—is rendered hostile and adverse to the diviners of the future, as if they were the spokesmen and assertors of Fate. Perhaps also those who boldly anticipate things to come, which the Heavenly Father has placed in his own power, insolently usurp for themselves what belongs to God himself. Therefore Jupiter, being indignant at these men, strikes them down with lightning as if they were those Giants puffed up with too much pride. 

I will pass over for now the astrological points that occur to me. Namely, that searchers into hidden things and things far distant from the present immediately fall into the sphere of Saturn, who holds all things most hidden and remote. And since Jupiter has granted the present goods of fortune, such searchers are left content only with things to come and most secret. Therefore (to conclude everything briefly), my dearest [Margrave of] Baden, since we fall far short of managing even present things alone, let alone being sufficient for future ones, that which Paul divinely commanded must always be kept in a mindful soul: *Do not seek to know more than is appropriate to know, but be wise unto sobriety.* <note>Original Latin: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere, sed sapere ad sobrietatem." A quote from Romans 12:3. Ficino uses it here to warn against the "intoxication" of seeking forbidden or occult knowledge.</note> Farewell.

->On the opinion that should not be rashly publicized. Also, the songs of Orpheus.<-

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his friend Martinus Uranius, many greetings.

**T**he *Argonautica* and the *Hymns* of Orpheus, as well as those of Homer and Proclus, and the *Theology* of Hesiod—which as a youth (I know not how) I translated literally for myself alone, as you, my recent guest, saw at my house—it has never pleased me to publish. This was lest I should seem to recall readers to the ancient <term>Priscus</term> <note>Meaning "ancient" or "primitive." Ficino refers to the *Prisca Theologia*, the ancient lineage of wisdom he believed ran from Hermes Trismegistus through Orpheus to Plato.</note> worship of gods and demons, which has for a long time now been deservedly rejected. For as much as it was once a concern to the Pythagoreans not to publish divine matters to the common people, so it has always been my concern not to publicize profane ones. So much so, that I did not even spare my short commentaries on Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, a Roman poet whose work *De rerum natura* promoted an atomic, materialistic view of the world that denied divine intervention.</note>, which I commented upon while still a boy (I know not how); for these, just as Plato did with his tragedies and elegies, I gave to Vulcan <note>Meaning he burned them. Vulcan was the Roman god of fire.</note>. 

For a more mature age and a more exquisite examination (as Plato says) often condemns those things which youthful levity either rashly believed or at least did not know how to reject (as was proper). It is more dangerous (as Plato also says) to drink in harmful opinions than to spread the worst poison. For just as a good thing is the more divine the more widely it is spread, so a very widespread evil is most pestilential. I promised, however, to send you certain safer songs of Orpheus; behold, I send them.

<summary>Ficino warns the Margrave of Baden against the spiritual dangers of predictive astrology and explains to Martinus Uranius why he suppressed his youthful translations of pagan hymns and his commentaries on Lucretius to protect Christian readers.</summary>

### Orpheus’s verses concerning God.

**E**usebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop.</note> in the thirteenth book of his *Preparation for the Gospel* speaks thus: he asserts that even Orpheus, in the songs which he inscribed concerning the sacred word, claimed that all things are governed by divine power and that all things are produced by God, in the manner read in the book which Aristobulus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Hebrew Bible with Greek philosophy.</note> wrote to Ptolemy.

<margin>Against those of you who despise holy laws: flee from here, and far from here, oh wretched ones, go far from here, you profane! <note>original: "Contra qui sanctas leges contemnitis, hinc uos Effugite, & procul hinc miſeri, procul ite prophani."</note></margin>
**Y**ou who cultivate virtue, apply your ears and direct your minds only to my words. But you, who contemplate divine things and grasp the voices of the Muses <term>Muses: the nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences</term> with a high mind, embrace those things as well, looking with sacred eyes, and keep them beneath your breast. Having entered upon this path, look up only to that one great author of the world, who alone is free from destruction. We teach in the present discourse who he is. There is one perfect God, who created all things, nourishing all things and bearing himself above all; he who is grasped by the mind alone, and seen by the mind. He never brings any evil upon mortals. Besides him there is no other; you shall see all things here, so that you may better discern him on earth. For here I see his traces, here I see his lot and his hand; yet I am in no way able to discern who he is himself, for he sits upon the high clouds. No one has seen him, except a certain man born of Chaldean blood <note>original: "Chaldæo de ſanguine." Likely a reference to Abraham or Moses, suggesting that Orpheus learned from Hebrew wisdom.</note>, whom the sublime and golden seat of the heavens holds, whose right hand stretches to the ends of the ocean; from whose deepest roots the shaken mountains tremble, nor are they able to bear his weight, however immense they may be. He who dwells in the high summits of heaven is nevertheless never absent from the earth. He is the beginning, the middle, and the same is the end.

Likewise, in the third [part], he introduces these words of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note>.

The wisdom of the Greeks is to be admired, for they, judging Jupiter to be the mind of the world, which produced the world by containing it within itself, have handed down these things about him, proceeding from the theology of Orpheus.

### Orpheus’s poems.

**K**ing of the starry house and Jupiter himself, the beginning and the source, the truth, one power and one God, and one almighty being in whose royal body all individual things are placed: the earth, the wave, the fire, and the air, night together with day, wisdom and the first origin, and pleasant love—all these are in this great body of the high king Jupiter. For looking up at the neck of heaven, you will see great and upright reverence. This golden-haired head, the rays of the stars shine from the yellow crown; from there the head spreads two golden horns <note>These "horns" often symbolize the rising and setting points of the sun or the dual nature of celestial power.</note>, most like the head of a bull; one is the rising, and the other is the setting itself. But the eyes are the shining Phoebus <term>Phoebus: an epithet for Apollo, the sun-god</term> with his vast light, and the Moon wreathed with the radiant color of Phoebus.

<summary>Ficino presents Latin translations of Orphic fragments, sourced from Eusebius and Porphyry, which describe a monotheistic and pantheistic vision of God (Jupiter) as the creator and sustainer of the universe. The text emphasizes the "Ancient Theology" tradition, linking Orpheus to Hebrew wisdom and Neoplatonic thought.</summary>

The mind, foreknowing what is to come, remains the royal ether,
From which no clamor, nor force, nor rumor is hidden.
It can reach the secret, and as a conqueror penetrates through all things.
Moreover, his invincible body, without end or measure,
Is spread out; the great shoulders and broad chest,
Are the air, and he possesses wings made of the wind.
With these, flying to all things, he is swifter than the East Wind itself.
Then, his sacred belly swells from his ancient mother, the earth,
And a vast belly rises up from the high mountains,
Which a weight in the middle duly girds with resonant sounds.
Furthermore, the ultimate boundaries of the lands and the foundations
Of the wide globe, and the raging depths of Tartarus <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment and suffering.</note>
Are known to be the soles of the feet of the great ruler of Olympus.
He, while he had hidden all things beneath the earth, then
Bringing them back from the depths, brought them forth into the nourishing light.

### Porphyry’s exposition. <note>Porphyry (c. 234 – c. 305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus who sought to reconcile pagan mythology with philosophy.</note>
### The Image of Jupiter.

**T**he whole world, therefore, is Jupiter: a living being composed of living beings, a God established from gods. Jupiter, moreover, represents the intellect from which all things are produced, and who creates all things by the act of understanding. Therefore, for theologians who perceive Jupiter in this way, it is impossible to fashion an image of him exactly as the poems have described. One must believe Jupiter to be a providential and life-giving power, which they signify by a sphere and round figures. They establish the likeness of a man for him because he is the Mind, which produces all things through seminal reason. He is depicted sitting to express a stable and unchangeable power. His upper parts are naked and open, because he is visible to the higher intelligences; however, his lower parts are covered, because he is hidden from lower creatures. He holds the scepter in his left hand, because in these parts of the body, the most spiritual dwelling-place of life is found. For the Creator is the intellect of things and the life-giving spirit of the world. In his right hand, he holds out either an eagle or a Victory: the former because he is the lord of the other Gods, just as the eagle is of other birds; the latter because all things are subject to him. June 9, 1492.

### He exhorts his friends to favor Plotinus as he comes forth.
### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Carduccio, greetings.

**G**reetings, my Carduccio, most zealous cultivator of the Academy. See how true that proverb is: "there is a change in all things." Our divine Plato once gave birth to the great Plotinus. <note>original: "Diuinus Plato noster quondam magnum Plotinum peperit." Ficino views the history of philosophy as a genealogy of divine wisdom.</note> Now Plotinus is in labor with Plato, soon to give birth. Plato gave light to Plotinus; he will return the light to Plato when he himself first comes forth into the light. He has indeed already been edited by us, but as of yet (I know not how) he lingers at the threshold. Come, rise up, Carduccio, most ardent of all our friends! Push forward the lingering Plotinus, and exhort all our people and the rest to take him up eagerly with their hands, so that as he comes forth immediately into the light, he may in turn return the light to all who behold him. July 12, 1492.

### Regarding the book "On Life" sent to a friend.
### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Giovanni Canacci and Bindaccio Ricasoli, many greetings.

**I**f any of my close associates hold my mind, you two, certainly the most intimate of all, possess it entirely. It is therefore not hidden from you what purpose I followed, or what hope and confidence I relied upon when I wrote the books *On Life* <term>On Life: Ficino's "De Vita Libri Tres," a famous treatise on health, longevity, and astral magic written for scholars.</term>, so that I might benefit all gifted men, but among them, much more my friends, and most especially those citizens primarily necessary for the health of the fatherland. I did not doubt, for my part, that I would once be of use to as many as possible—indeed to all—if I [could help] those especially...

...that I might preserve the thread, O guardians of the public health <note>original: "salutis publicae seruatores." Ficino often played on the dual meaning of "salus" as both physical health and political/spiritual salvation.</note>. My part, thus far, has been to compose these books with this intention and diligence. It is your part, in turn, to give your constant effort, lest perhaps my opinion deceive me and I have labored too much in vain. Therefore, as often as you greet our friend Paolantonio Soderini <note>A prominent Florentine statesman and supporter of Ficino.</note>—a man most worthy of both frequent greetings and perpetual health—remember to remind him above all others to reread and observe the *Books on Life*. For we desire a long life and perpetual health for him most of all. Indeed, he is both highly gifted and a most dear friend, joined to the great Medici, our patrons, not only by a necessity of nature but certainly by the greatest necessity of goodwill; moreover, he is very necessary to the public well-being. If that man were as strong in physical vigor as he prevails in counsel, he would no more need the remedies of physicians to be well than he now needs the advice of anyone to live well. Indeed, if he ever took as much care for his own health as he daily looks out for the conduct of affairs, the interests of his friends, and the prosperity of the republic, I would by no means urge you to warn him about caring for the health of his body. Finally, fare well. And greet our Paolantonio frequently (as is your custom), intending to warn him daily to cultivate his health more diligently, so that he may live at least as long for his son Tommaso—that distinguished youth—as his own father, Tommaso, that most famous knight, lived for him.

July 22, 1492.

### Catalogue of close associates and students.

->Marsilio Ficino of Florence sends greetings to his unique friend, Martin Uranius<- <note>Martin Uranius (Prenninger) was a German scholar and jurist who acted as a key contact for Ficino in Germany.</note>

**Y**ou could have asked nothing more just of me than what you now frequently request through Johannes Streler, your fellow countryman: namely, a catalogue of our friends. I do not mean those who flow together from any sort of business or shared lodging, but specifically those meeting in the very communion of the liberal disciplines. Since I neither ought to be, nor wish to be, anywhere without the presence of my friends—and since I am not only in Italy within myself, but also in you in Germany—I rightly desire my friends to be present with me here, and there with me as well. Know that all of them are proven in both talent and character. For I have determined never to have any friends except those whom I judge to have joined letters together with honesty of character, just as one might join Mercury with Jupiter <note>In Renaissance symbolism, Mercury represented eloquence and learning, while Jupiter represented wisdom, justice, and authority. Ficino suggests that learning without character is incomplete.</note>. For our Plato says in his letters that true philosophy consists in integrity of life, while he calls letters a kind of external ornament of philosophy. The same author says in his letters that philosophical communion exists as something more excellent and stable than all other forms of not only goodwill, but even necessity.

But to come soon to the catalogue, receive all these friends as being praised in summary. Yet if I wished to narrate the specific praises of each one individually, I would be undertaking a far too lengthy work. If I should pass over any as not being equally praised, it would be utterly invidious. It would indeed be altogether absurd if, while I attempt to arrange my friends in order, I should meanwhile disturb everything with comparisons, ultimately carrying away hatred instead of goodwill.

The first and highest place among my friends, our patrons the Medici claim for themselves by the best right: Cosimo the Great; the two sons of Cosimo, those outstanding men Piero and Giovanni; and the two sons born to Piero: Lorenzo the Magnificent and the illustrious Giuliano; and the three children of Lorenzo: the magnanimous Piero, Cardinal Giovanni <note>The future Pope Leo X.</note>, who is most venerable, and Giuliano, endowed with an extraordinary nature. And lest I pursue the praises of each at length, I shall embrace all the Medici in one common praise: a heroic lineage.

Beyond our patrons, there are two kinds of friends for us. For some are not exactly "auditors" <note>term: auditores (listeners/students). In a Renaissance context, this refers to those who attended a master's formal lectures.</note>, nor entirely disciples, but close associates in familiar custom—if I may speak thus—conversationalists, and mutual communicators of counsels and liberal disciplines. Others, in addition to these things I have mentioned, have at some time heard us reading and, as it were, teaching; and if they were indeed like disciples, they were not truly disciples. For I do not Arrogate so much to myself that I would claim to have taught anyone or that I am teaching; rather (in the Socratic manner), I question everyone and exhort them, and I constantly provoke the fertile talents of my associates to give birth <note>Ficino refers to "Socratic maieutics," the idea that a teacher acts as a midwife to help the student bring forth the knowledge already within their soul.</note>. In the first class are: Naldo Naldi, close to me from our very earthly age <note>meaning: from early childhood.</note>; after him, in our youth, Pellegrino Agli, Cristoforo Landino, Leon Battista Alberti, Pietro Pazzi, Benedetto Accolti of Arezzo, Bartolomeo Valori, Antonio Canigiani; and a little later, Giovanni Cavalcanti, Domenico Galletti, Antonio Calderini,

Girolamo Rossi, Amerigo and Tommaso Benci, Cherubino Quarquagli of San Gimignano, Antonio Seraphico, Michele Mercati (both from San Miniato), Francesco Bandini, Loretto Lippi of Colle, Bernardo Nuthi, Comando, Baccio Ugolini, and Pietro Fanni the Priest. Many of these—except for Landino, Battista Leone, and Benedetto Accolti—occasionally heard our first lectures <note>original: "leones nostras," which likely refers to his early academic lessons or the "lion" imagery associated with Florentine intellectual pride.</note>. In my mature age, however, they are close associates, not students. Antonio Allio, Ricciardo of Anghiari, Bartolomeo Platina, Oliviero Arduino, our Sebastian Salvini of Amitina, Lorenzo Bonincontri, Benedetto Biliotti, Giorgio Antonio Vespucci, Giovanni Battista Boninsegni, Demetrius of Byzantium, Giovanni Vittorio Soderini, Angelo Poliziano <note>The famous poet and scholar Poliziano.</note>, Pierleone of Spoleto, and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>The renowned philosopher and author of the "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note>. In the second class, that is, in the rank of students, are Carlo Marsuppini, the five Nerli brothers, Guicciardini, Soderini, Compagni, Patenti, the two Philippos—namely Valori and Carducci—the four Giovanni Canacci, Nesi, Guicciardini, and Rosati. The four Bernardos: Vittorio de' Medici, Canigiani, and Michelozzi. The four Francescos: Berlinghieri, Rimicini, Gaddi, and Pietrasanta, Amerigo Corsini, Antonio Lanfredini, Bindaccio Ricasoli, Alamanno Donati, Niccolò Michelozzi, Matteo Rabatta, Alessandro Albizzi, Fortuna the Hebrew, Sebastian the Priest, Angelo Carducci, Andrea Corsi, Alessandro Borsi, Biagio da Bibbiena, Francesco Diacceto, and Niccolò Valori.

### Preface to the Compendium of Proclus.

->**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his unique friend, Martinus Uranius <note>Also known as Martin Prenninger, a German jurist and humanist scholar.</note>, Greetings.**<-

**A**fter your departure from Italy, many books, selected from a great many, were soon brought from Greece to the magnanimous Piero de' Medici <note>The son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, who took over the patronage of the Platonic Academy.</note> by the very elegant Greek collector Lascaris <note>Janus Lascaris, a scholar who traveled to the East to recover lost Greek manuscripts for the Medici library.</note>, for that royal library long ago happily established by the great Lorenzo. But I, among many things, (as is my custom) always read the <margin>Platonic [works], and first</margin> Platonic works first, and foremost among these the commentaries of Proclus on the six books of Plato’s *Republic* and <margin>the beginning of the seventh.</margin> the beginning of the seventh. Therefore, those little flowers which I have gathered while wandering here and there through these most pleasant meadows, smelling of holy religion above all else, I send to you, a man distinguished in religion.
<margin>August 11, 1492.</margin>

### Excerpts from Proclus on Plato's Republic by Marsilio Ficino: The Three Properties of Each God.

**P**lato in the *Laws* defines the nature of God through three properties: namely, through goodness, power, and knowledge; and through three similar ones in the *Republic*: namely through goodness, immutability, and truth. Indeed, immutability is characteristic of power, while truth is the perfection of knowledge. Every God is said to be truly good. This is both because no evil is mixed with His goodness, and because goodness in Him is not some habit added to His essence, but His very essence itself. For He is not first God and then becomes good; for by His very essence, He is formally and equally both God and good. Thus, every God is called good by His very nature, just as the first God is Goodness itself. Proclus proves the same in the *Elements of Theology*, that every God is formally a certain essential goodness, just as the first is the Good itself above essence <note>A reference to the Neoplatonic idea that the ultimate Source (The One/The Good) is "beyond being" or essence.</note>. Likewise, these three formally pertain to Divinity itself: pure goodness, unimpeded power, and knowledge uncertain of nothing.

### God is the Cause of No Evil, Never Changes Form, and Deceives No One.

**P**lato in the *Republic* sets down three theological dogmas. First, if every God is truly good by His nature, He is always the cause of good things, and never of any evil. Second, if He is truly powerful, He is utterly immutable. Third, if immutable power, truth, and goodness pertain to God, He never deceives anyone with any fictions or lies. Regarding the first, it is questioned from where evils come. If God does nothing toward evil...

<meta>This page transitions from the list of Ficino’s associates into a philosophical defense of Neoplatonic theology. Ficino is addressing common challenges to the nature of the divine, specifically focusing on how an unchanging God can interact with a changing world, the origin of evil, and the nature of divine visions.</meta>

-># THE WRITINGS OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

Regarding the second point: if God is in no way changed, how do the gods appear of their own accord, sometimes with form and other times without? For unless we admit these things, we would utterly destroy the entire discipline of sacred rites and the works of the <term>priests</term><note>In this context, Ficino refers to the 'theurgists' or practitioners of divine rites in the Neoplatonic tradition.</note>, as well as those very visions in which the gods spontaneously offer themselves in various forms. Regarding the third point: how is it that oracles sometimes give false responses? Indeed, many lies are discovered in the oracles.

The response to the first point is as follows: Evil has no proper "procession" <note>original: "processum" — a technical term in Neoplatonism referring to how lower realities emanate or flow from higher divine principles.</note> among existing things, neither from God nor from any other single cause. In truth, it is impossible either to posit an "Idea" of evils or to say that matter is the cause of evils. For all <term>Ideas</term><note>Ficino uses the Platonic sense: the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things in the divine mind.</note> are, as it were, intellectual and divine <term>species</term><note>original: "species" — here meaning forms or types.</note>. They exist as the archetypes both of essences and of the perfections belonging to those essences. 

Matter, however, was produced by God as something necessary for the world, and it is not inherently wicked, since it contributes to the generation of the universe. Nor is it "the Good" itself, since it is the lowest of all things, yet it holds its place within the order of necessary things. For whatever exists, exists for the sake of something. Therefore, it is wrong to posit any specific or material cause for evils, nor any single cause for them at all. But as he <note>Ficino likely refers to Proclus or another Neoplatonic authority he is summarizing.</note> says, we must say that it is *particular* and *dispersed* things that bring about evil. 

"Particular" things, indeed, because no universal thing—such as the Intellect, the Soul, or the Body—is the cause of evils. "Dispersed" things, because no single thing is the cause of evils, but rather (as he says) other occasions for evil must be sought. In the body, evil—that is, disease—occurs because of various elements flowing together without mutual proportion, while each part strives to overcome the others. Evil also occurs in the soul because of the different types of life and the contrary parts fighting among themselves. While these parts are in conflict, evil happens to some because of others, with each part acting according to its own nature. 

It was necessary, however, for the body to be such a thing—namely, composed of contrary and rebelling parts—so that there might be something perishable in the world. In this way, the world is made perfect, being constituted of all things. It was also necessary for souls to have a mixture here, so that these regions of the world would not be devoid of rational animals. Nor should rational lives be planted in bodies without a middle ground; rather, they should act and suffer the conditions of irrational things, and desire, feel, and imagine such things. For these are necessary for mortals, if they are to remain in these regions for even a short time. 

Therefore, while any things act according to what is their own, they "cut off" evils, and they do so for no other reason than for the sake of the Good. When these events occur, the Universe uses them opportunely, and they turn out for the good through the very power of the One who uses them. For this reason, there is no "pure evil" anywhere, but everything is in some way a participant in the Good. Thus, evil can even be said to depend on the divine in a certain way, insofar as it is in some way good. But meanwhile, from many other particular agents, it falls upon this world as if by chance—it "happens," I say, to many diverse things.

Regarding the doubts about apparitions, we shall respond as follows: While the higher beings remain immutable and do not change, certain divine visions leap forth from them, which take on their formation in the space surrounding us. For since the spectators use bodies, while the gods are incorporeal, the spectacles emanating from the divine—plainly in the presence of those worthy to see—possess something from the higher beings who produce them, but also something akin to the spectators. 

For this reason, they appear, yet not to everyone. And to those whom they do appear, they are seen only through certain <term>shining envelopes</term><note>original: "perfulgida animarum inuolucra" — the 'astral body' or 'vehicle' of the soul that allows it to perceive or project spiritual realities.</note> of the souls. Because of this, they are frequently seen even with the eyes closed. Insofar as they are extended and appear in some other medium of this kind (that is, the air), they become akin to the onlookers. But insofar as they are filled with divine light, possess efficacy, and represent the powers of the gods through their image, they depend continuously on the deities producing them through these very "clear symbols" (that is, signs), as if suspended from them. 

For this reason, the ineffable sacraments and mysteries of the gods are figured through such things, while they offer various forms to those who look upon them. Sacred eloquence <note>original: "eloquētia sacra" — likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles or similar divinely-inspired texts.</note> testifies to this, addressing the priest thus: *All divine things are indeed incorporeal, but bodies are employed for our sake. For you are unable to perceive incorporeal things in an incorporeal way, because of that corporeal nature in which you all exist.* 

These things, therefore, both appear and disappear according to the will of the gods; but the gods themselves are hidden, remaining meanwhile as they are by nature, neither receiving nor losing anything through these shown things. Just as those intellectual species (that is, the Ideas) do not become corporeal, or composite, or formed, while such things are produced through them—plainly, they are not such things themselves. Thus every God remains...

He also defends divine apparitions as symbolic "envelopes" of light necessary for corporeal humans to perceive the incorporeal divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of divine appearances and the reliability of oracles. It addresses how a formless, unchanging God can be perceived in various forms by human observers and explains the difference between true divine spirits and deceptive ones.</meta>

-># OF THE LETTERS. BOOK XI.<-

...remains unformed, even though it offers itself as if spontaneously formed. For there is no such form within the divine itself, but rather it proceeds from the divine; since the observer is unable to see that which is without form except as having form, he looks upon the unformed according to his own capacity through a specific form. To the third doubt, we respond thus: Falsehood is not found in the higher beings who respond, but in those who receive the responses, who, because of their own infirmity, receive the oracle perversely. And this very deception does not happen without the will of the gods <note>original: "numinum" — divine powers or deities</note>, who wish only the worthy to obtain what they desire. There are also some for whom it is not appropriate to know the pure truth itself as it remains with the Gods, but rather to experience what is appropriate through a deception occurring within themselves. Therefore, the gods are neither ignorant of the truth nor do they confuse it; rather, when confusion occurs among us due to our own unfitness, they use it for our benefit. Indeed, the history of oracles testifies that a false response occurs because of the place, the time, the manner, or some other error of the questioner. 

When Plato says in the *Republic* that not only everything divine, but also everything <term>daemonic</term><note>In the Platonic sense, 'daemons' are intermediary spirits between gods and mortals, not necessarily evil.</note> is always truthful and never lies, this must be understood as being said of the true and natural daemon, not of that spirit so called by a certain habit, which undergoes many changes and seduces those to whom it has become a friend. But that which belongs to the essence of the daemons, since it is rational, is entirely truthful. In the irrational, however, it is indeed incapable of truth; it is deceived and deceives as something false, and is considered a deceptive kind which, as history records, often deceives—whether it enters into oracles, listens to invocations, or meets people of its own accord. All of this is not a daemon by nature, but by habit. 

The whole of religion, the works of the priests, history, and the common report of men agree that the gods appear to the senses and offer many forms and various figures. Sometimes they project a light that is unfigured, and at other times figured; sometimes in human form, and sometimes in another. Meanwhile, the divinity remains everywhere unmoved. For the very simplicity of the Gods appears manifold to those who look upon them. This is not through any change or deception on their part, but because of the condition of nature, which defines the properties of the gods according to the capacities of the participants. For although God himself, who is participated in, is one and simple in himself, the <term>intellect</term><note>The highest part of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition.</note> participates in him in one way, the intellectual soul in another, the <term>phantasy</term><note>The 'phantasia' or imagination, which creates mental images from abstract thoughts.</note> in another, and the senses in yet another. For the intellect perceives indivisibly, the intellectual soul through a revolving motion, the phantasy through forms, and the sense through <term>passion</term><note>original: 'passiue' — meaning the sense is a passive recipient of external impressions.</note>. That which is participated in is uniform in its substance; however, through participation it becomes multiform. It is immutable, yet appears mutable because of our weakness. And although it is in no way heavy, yet while it fills us, it seems to weigh us down—just as the poets relate concerning Pallas <note>Athena, whose divine presence was often described as physically overwhelming to mortals.</note>. For the thing received must necessarily appear according to the nature of that which receives it. 

Therefore, when some of the Gods meet us as guests or in some other way, it must not be thought that any change is present in them, but rather that a varied imagination results from the indifferent receivers. This is one way in which the poets introduce the Gods—who are immutable in themselves—as if they were mutable to us. There is also a second way: when the divine itself, possessing many powers within it and being full of all <term>species</term><note>original: 'specierum' — here meaning the eternal forms or archetypes of all things.</note>, presents various intelligible spectacles to those who contemplate it. For then they say that the divine itself, containing these powers within, changes the demonstrated variety of powers into various forms, bringing forth now one and now another; it always acts according to all its powers, yet appears as something different to the transitory intelligences of souls because of the multitude of forms it contains within itself. 

In this way, that famous Proteus is said to change his own form for those who watch him, appearing now as one thing, then another. Therefore, Proteus—who is a certain divine intellect, full of all powers and species, and counted under the <term>series of Neptune</term><note>In Neoplatonism, a 'series' or 'chain' is a hierarchy of beings descending from a specific major deity.</note>—is constantly contemplated by the particular souls who are named "seals" <note>original: 'Phocæ' — based on the Odyssey where Proteus herds the seals of Neptune.</note> under that same series. Now they behold certain species, then others; and applying the future progression of their thoughts to Proteus, they suspect a change of form within Proteus himself. Thus he seems to become all things to those who watch him, as many as inhabit the earth, the water, the air, or the fire. For as many species as he contains within himself—or rather, as many eternal species as he *is*—he seems to become by turns because of the constantly alternating perception of those who watch him. 

The third mode of varied appearance is when the different visions of one God do not arise from the perceptions of the subjects, nor from the variety of divine powers, but when the same God proceeds according to different orders, and descends, as it were, to the lowest things, multiplying himself in number and declining into lower orders. Then again, the fables...

He uses the myth of Proteus as an allegory for how the divine intellect contains all forms and appears to change as the human mind moves through different thoughts.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO

...they hand down that the divine is changed from above into that very appearance toward which it has made its procession. For this reason, they say that Minerva made herself like Mentor, Mercury like a gull or a chatterer, and Apollo like a hawk. They show, of course, the more excellent orders of these Gods, into which they have proceeded from the whole. Therefore, when they describe divine appearances, they strive to keep them without form or figure. Just as when Pallas <note>Pallas Athena</note> revealed herself to Achilles alone, but not at all to the army present. Where they assert angelic appearances, they present the Gods clothed in foreign forms, but in these universal ones. In the same way, they sing that they have descended into a certain human appearance common to man and woman, and not proper to any specific human. But when they narrate <term>daemonic</term><note>In Ficino's Neoplatonic context, daemons are intermediary spirits, ranging from high rational beings to those closer to the material world.</note> processions, then they do not fear to assert changes into certain individual and particular things and a descent into brutes. For the last of the following orders of the Gods are declared through figures of this kind. Now indeed it is worth considering how clearly such things agree with the order of things. For the simple itself is suitable to the divine, the universal to the angelic, and finally the particular to the daemonic. And to the first belongs the intellectual, to the second the rational, and finally to this third a certain irrational genus. For in the very order of daemons, such a life is also intertwined.

->*The three habits and states of separated souls: Contemplative, Active, and Voluptuous.*<-

**T**he habits of souls are different even when separated from the body. Similarly, the places of the universe which they inhabit are different. It is necessary, therefore, for souls thus segregated from mortal instruments—so that they have no disposition toward worse things, nor are full of mortal disturbances and trifles—to carry with them <term>envelopes</term><note>original: "involucra" — the subtle, "astral" bodies that wrap the soul.</note> that were once radiant and are still pure as they were before, neither disturbed by material vapors nor solidified because of a terrestrial nature. But for souls not yet perfectly purged through Philosophy, but inclined toward an affection for the thick body and still desiring a life in common with it, it is necessary to see their <term>vehicles</term><note>original: "vehicula" — the Neoplatonic concept of the "chariot" of the soul, a subtle body that carries it through the spheres.</note> suspended for them, to show them to those who are able. These are clearly shadowy, material, and falling back with weight, carrying much of a mortal and solidified nature with them, which is clearly narrated in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul’s immortality and its journey after death.</note>. Furthermore, there are many differences among these souls still inclining themselves toward this life. For those who have led a great practical life <note>The "active" life of politics and social affairs as opposed to the "contemplative" life of the mind.</note>, and have not yet ceased from a life of that kind, rightly love an instrument suitable for practical actions; and segregated from this, they greatly desire intercourse and prefer this life of ours to the separated life, inasmuch as they cannot act according to that life, being more fit for the practical life. But those who, because of a shameful life, long for the fleeting body and think that life with it differs not at all from the life led within it, it is fitting for them to be carried down into a dark and ultimate place of the universe. Homer, just as Plato, distinguishes the soul from its <term>idol</term><note>original: "idolo" — the Greek *eidolon*, an image or phantom of the self that remains after death while the higher soul moves on.</note>, and the intellect from those things which are the soul's own; and he says the soul uses the idol, but the intellect is more divine than both. And he says the idol and the soul are in some way known even in this body. In which, and apart from which, the soul has care and providence for the body and naturally desires it, but the intellect is not comprehended by our <term>phantastic</term><note>Related to "phantasia" or the faculty of imagination/images.</note> and formable movements. Accordingly, just as the instruments of souls ascending into heaven emit a harmonic voice and display a rhythmic movement, so the sound of those descending beneath the earth and now less rational is similar to a lament, bearing only an image of an affectionate and phantastic life. Furthermore, one must not think that the places of the lower world and the judicial states beneath the earth at the rivers which Homer and Plato describe are vain imaginations and only fabulous terrors; but just as many and various places are distributed there according to merits for souls seeking celestial things, so it must be thought that for souls needing punishment and purgation, places are arranged beneath the earth, having various flows from the elements surrounding the earth. These flows they have surely called rivers. Finally, there are different orders of daemons set over this work: some indeed are avengers, some punishers, some purgers, and some judicial. It is consistent that souls are terrified there by the imagination of the presiding daemons, and by a state and habit that is varied and confused according to their merits, and segregated from the upper rays of the Sun.

->## *The three lives of the soul: divine, human, and beast-like.*<-

**W**e can summarize the threefold life of the soul in this way. The first life is indeed the best and most perfect, by which the soul is joined to the gods; there it leads a life most closely related to the beings above. On account of a certain supreme likeness, this life is already united with them—not belonging to its own authority, but to that of the gods—while it submits to its own intellect. Meanwhile, it awakens an ineffable gift and a <term>character</term><note>Here, "character" refers to a divine mark or seal impressed upon the soul by a higher power.</note> of that uniform substance of the higher beings. By joining like to like—namely, its own light to that Light, and its own uniform essence to the One itself which stands above all essence and life—it achieves this state as much as possible. We place the second degree of life in that state where the soul descends from the divine life into itself. It establishes the mind and knowledge as the leaders of its action, where it unfolds a multitude of reasons, gazes upon the all-formed differences of the <term>species</term><note>In Neoplatonic thought, "species" refers to the ideal Forms or archetypes of things.</note>, and gathers and represents within itself both that which understands and that which is understood. As if through an image, it expresses the intellectual essence, comprehending the intelligible nature within a certain unity. Finally, we consider the third life to be that which enters into commerce with the lower powers and acts with them; it uses irrational imaginations and senses and is entirely filled with these inferior things.

## *The distinction of things into four kinds; also concerning images and shadows.*

**P**lato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, compares the order of things to a line through a continuous connection of things, which indeed proceeds from mutual likeness. Truly, likeness is a certain unity in things arising from that absolute Unity which is the principle of the universe. This Principle, wishing to make the whole as similar to itself as possible—yet not being able to make it simply one—at least made it "most one" in its likeness. Even the very goodness of the Principle contributes to this union. For since it is the nature of the Good itself to, as it were, diffuse itself through all things through a process of outflow, and in turn to call all things back to its own unity through desire, it rightly renders the universe uniquely one to the highest degree. 

Furthermore, the Platonic line is divided into two primary parts: the <term>insensible</term><note>Meaning "intelligible" or "beyond the reach of the physical senses."</note> genus and the sensible genus. The first is far broader than the second, for it contains the second within itself. The first is further divided into things that are <term>intelligible</term><note>Pure ideas or divine forms.</note> and things that are <term>cogitable</term><note>Forms that can be reasoned out, like mathematical truths.</note>—that is, into divine forms and mathematical forms. The sensible genus, however, is divided into things that are substantial and things that are imaginal. The "substantial" things are bodies, while the "imaginal" are images and shadows of those bodies. 

Indeed, images and the reflections of bodies in mirrors require a subject <note>A "subject" here refers to the physical surface or medium, such as a mirror or water.</note> possessing three conditions: density, smoothness, and brightness. There is a need for density so that the flowing appearance, if it falls upon a subject that is too porous, does not suddenly flow through it, preventing the image from becoming a single thing from many flows. There is a need for smoothness so that roughness itself—due to some parts sticking out and others being deep—does not cause inequality in the composed image. There is also a need for shining brightness so that the image, which otherwise possesses a faint form, may become visible. For in this same way, even the smallest particles in the air of a house are often visible to the eyes in rays of light penetrating through small windows and cracks. Otherwise, on account of their thin nature, they are hidden from us.

Therefore, it must be said according to the Platonic opinion in the *Sophist*, that "apparent images" are certain substances of certain likenesses fabricated by a kind of <term>daemonic</term><note>In this context, Ficino refers to "daemonic" as a technical process of spiritual or natural "machinery" that bridges the gap between the material and the immaterial.</note> machinery. Now, even shadows—which he mentions alongside images as if they were related—possess a nature of this kind. For they too are images of bodies and shapes, and they have a great deal of "sympathy"—that is, a shared feeling and agreement—with those very things from which they fall. This is demonstrated by whatever arts of the Magi proclaim and promise regarding the making of idols and shadows. 

Truly, what shall I say of the powers of images and shadows, through which many things often happen in irrational animals that surpass all reason? For they say that if a hyena treads upon the shadow of a dog sitting high above, it will immediately cast the dog down from the height and devour it. And Aristotle says that a woman in the period of her menstrual blood stains a mirror placed before her with a certain blood, and the image... <note>original: "imaginem." The text cuts off mid-word; Ficino is referring to the medieval belief that a menstruating woman's gaze could tarnish a mirror.</note>

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's three levels of existence (divine, rational, and irrational) and outlines Plato's hierarchy of reality (the "Divided Line"), concluding with the quasi-magical and physical properties of images and shadows.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of reality, moving from the nature of images to a detailed Neoplatonic explanation of Plato's "Allegory of the Sun" from the Republic, focusing on the nature of the Good.</meta>

<page-num>942</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

Plato confirms that images are indeed certain kinds of substances when he says: just as <term>objects of thought</term><note>Latin: *cogitabilia*; in the Platonic "Divided Line," these are mathematical objects or things known through discursive reason.</note> relate to the objects of the intellect, so <term>objects of the imagination</term><note>Latin: *imaginalia*; things perceived as mental images or reflections.</note> relate to visible bodies. Objects of thought—that is, Mathematicals—are certain forms and species in themselves; similarly, images, since they are natural "out-flows" from natural things, also possess their own nature.

### *How the Good is above essence, and how it may be known.*

**P**lato, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, compares divine things in this way: he compares the Sun to the **Good** itself, the light of the Sun to the **Truth** flowing from the Good, and the colors which depend on that light to the **formal and ideal reasons** of things, which depend on the Good under the governance of Truth. He compares the eyes—both generated and illuminated by the Sun—to **intellects**, which relate to the Good in a similar fashion. He adds further: just as the Sun stands above the generation of lower visible things, so the Good stands above **being and essence**. Likewise, just as the Sun and its light surpass colors and sight, so the Good and the truth of the Good (which is light) are above ideas, beings, and minds. Finally, just as the Sun is the cause of action and perfection for our visible things and our eyes, but also the cause of their generation, nature, and power, so the Good is the author of all things, both for the <term>intelligibles</term><note>Things that can only be perceived by the mind, such as abstract concepts or Forms.</note> and for the intellects. Therefore, the Good is higher than all these. 

Since the Good itself is higher than the intelligibles, the intellect, and truth, it cannot be known by the same logic as the intelligibles; rather, it is known by a certain **divine intuition**. This is a perception that does not exceed understanding, but is what Plato calls an **illumination of the soul**. This occurs when the soul is divinely illuminated, after it has separated the Good (through negation) from all the things that exist after the Good, and has compared them all in a proper order. By this reasoning, the soul reflects and raises itself toward the Good, having now become <term>upward-turned</term><note>Latin: *resupina*; literally "lying on its back," but used here metaphorically to describe the soul looking up at the heavens instead of down at the earth.</note>, whereas until now it had been downward-facing. Among worldly things, the Sun appears "unbegotten" because it loses nothing of its own, nor does it admit anything foreign from the outside. All other things always receive new rays from it, while the Sun revolves in its own center and thus illuminates the celestial realms and those below. Therefore, in the way that the Sun is such a thing, it rules over all mundane things; however, insofar as it is a body and a moving thing, it is subject to a higher power—namely, that which is called the **sphere of identity**<note>A reference to the "Circle of the Same" from Plato's *Timaeus*, representing the uniform, fixed motion of the highest heavens.</note>, which follows a regular circuit. From this sphere the Sun is carried, and that sphere in turn is referred back to the most wise circuit, which is the **Mind**. Amidst all this, remember: just as there is an indivisible thing (such as unity or a point) among divisible things, so there is something incorruptible among corruptible things.

### *The three levels of the Good: in us, in the Idea, and above the Idea.*

**P**lato considers three grades of the venerable Good. One is found in all things: a certain state of life properly mixed from **intelligence and pleasure**. Another is found among the **Ideas**, and the last is **above the Ideas**. Among the Ideas, some constitute and define the essences of things, while others apply their perfections to those essences. Among the former, the first is **Being and Essence**. This is the <term>genus</term><note>A general category or class.</note> for all other "essential" Ideas—that is, those pertaining to the building of essences, such as the Idea of Animal, the Idea of Man, or the Idea of Horse. 

Among the Ideas pertaining to the perfections of all things, the first is not the "Simply Good," but the **Ideal Good**. This is the genus of all Ideas relating to the perfections of things in any way, such as the Idea of Beauty, the Idea of Justice, Wisdom, and similar things. Therefore, just as the essences of things precede their perfections in their origin—for "to be" naturally precedes "to be well"—so Being and Essence precede the Ideal Good in the hierarchy of Ideas. But the **Simply Good** is ultimately higher than Being; it is the **unparticipated Good**. For while the Good among the Ideas can be shared (participated in), it exists alongside essence or under Being. Finally, in us, the Good is both under essence and is a **participated good**. 

Now, the common consensus of all people defines the Good as "that for whose sake all things exist and which all things desire." This seems to prophesy that the Good itself exists for the sake of nothing else, nor does it desire anything else. It is necessary, therefore, that the Good is not merely "something good" within a being. For every essence desires the Good—that is, to exist according to its nature and to exist well...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains Plato’s Sun allegory, identifying the Good as the supreme author of both the intellect and the intelligible world, standing above essence and being. He also outlines a hierarchy of the Good, distinguishing between the participated good in humans and the unparticipated "Simply Good" that transcends all categories.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Republic, Allegory of the Sun, The Good, Essence, Being, Ideas, Hierarchy of Being, Illumination of the Soul, Neoplatonism</keywords>

### On demons.

-> Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Carducci, greetings. <-

**S**ince I am translating the commentary of Proclus the Platonist <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek Neoplatonist philosophers; Ficino's translations of his work were foundational for the Renaissance.</note> on Plato's *Alcibiades* from the Greek language into Latin—not so much word-for-word as sense-for-sense—and remembering that you desired a summary of the Platonic opinion on <term>demons</term><note>Latin: *daemones*. ### Philosophy is joined with fortune and riches.

-> Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, envoy to the Pope, a Florentine, greetings. <-

**"A** man’s enemies are those of his own household." <note>A reference to Matthew 10:36.</note> Indeed, those of my own household—who are many and very troublesome to me—frequently object that because they are neither philosophical nor content with a philosophical lifestyle and its simple furnishings, the other clients and minor dependents of the house of Medici <note>The powerful banking family and rulers of Florence who were Ficino's patrons.</note> have received a great deal from them in a few years. They complain that I, however, despite being the most long-standing and (if I may say so) the most "client-like" member of this family, have not brought back much after many years. But listen for a moment, my dear Valori, to this <term>apology</term><note>A formal defense or justification of one's position.</note> of mine to my people. 

The other friends have not yet received from the Medici as much as they wanted; I, however, have as much as I would have wanted, if only I had asked—and I certainly have as much as I want. They have theirs mostly by begging; I have mine freely. Likewise, the Medici gave to others things that belonged to others; to me, they gave of themselves. Thus we prove our case very well to our household. But they (which is most annoying to me) do not approve. For it should have happened long ago that either my people became philosophers along with me, or I should not have been a philosopher at all. 

But it seems to be fate from the beginning of things that no philosophers will ever be rich, nor again will rich men easily be philosophers. For it is said that Minerva has no commerce with Juno <note>Minerva is the goddess of wisdom; Juno is the goddess of riches and worldly power.</note>. Nor do Jupiter, Phoebus, and Venus favor the same people as Mercury and Saturn. Nor does Fortune, the mistress of affairs, easily agree with Wisdom, the contemplator of things. Furthermore, one thing is necessary: where you intend your focus, your talent prevails. Therefore, talent and fortune hold a divided empire within us; the former dominates mostly in the cultivation of the soul, while the latter dominates mostly in external matters. Hence these are called "goods of fortune." But in the body, perhaps both have equal power. But the letter is not permitted to philosophize further now, for another business is pressing.

---

### Where there is more fortune, there is less wisdom, and vice versa.

-> Marsilio Ficino to the excellent citizen and his most beloved Bindiaccio Ricasolano, many greetings. <-

**T**hat Aristotelian saying—where there is more intelligence, there is less fortune; and vice versa, where there is more fortune, there is less intelligence—is perhaps accepted by many in this way: that the wisest men and those who philosophize are the least fortunate. This is proven by the Pythagorean verses and confirmed by reality itself, as well as by astrological reasoning. They think that Philosophy is signified chiefly by Mercury and Saturn, but that these have no shared business with Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus, which signify an abundance of things. 

Finally, the legitimate contemplators of truth both neglect the goods of fortune and are themselves neglected by the most fortunate; they please neither princes nor the common crowd. So it is no wonder that they have the least amount of fortune. Conversely, the most fortunate usually neglect wisdom and live mostly in a reckless and improvident way—as if by the breath of fortune rather than by counsel. I do not at all reject the above interpretation, yet I would interpret that Aristotelian saying in a more useful and divine way. For since we have found that the more prudent men are, the less they live by chance...

### *Preface to the comparison of the Sun to God.*

-> Marsilio Ficino to the illustrious Eberhard, Duke of Württemberg and Count of Montbéliard, many greetings. <-

**O**ur friend Martin Uranius <note>original: "Uranius, id est, coelestis". Martin Prenninger (c. 1450–1501), a German jurist and scholar who took the name Uranius, meaning "Heavenly."</note>—that is, "Heavenly," and indeed a contemplator of heavenly things—has spoken with me at great length, saying that just as the Sun is among the stars, you are, beyond controversy, the same among all the princes of Germany. Inflamed by these praises, which are like rays of your virtue, I sent you that little letter some time ago as a pledge of my immense love for you. But it was not (as it should have been) a sufficiently great pledge. Therefore, to satisfy both your supreme dignity and my own desire somewhat more fully, I am now sending to the "Sun of Germany" <note>Referring to Duke Eberhard.</note> the Platonic and Dionysian Sun <note>Ficino refers to his treatise *De Sole* (On the Sun), which blends the solar allegories of Plato with the Christian mysticism of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, which will declare my great love for you everywhere with its splendor. Just as Mercury transfers the gifts of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun-god.</note> to the minds of men, so Johann Streler—who is like another Mercury to us—will bring this Phoebus-like gift of ours to you. You will read happily, then, O Sun-like prince, those things concerning the comparison of the Sun to God which Plato and Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century theologian whom Ficino and his contemporaries believed was the Athenian judge converted by St. Paul. His work was central to Ficino's attempt to bridge Platonism and Christianity.</note> partly treated, and which I partly interpret and comment upon. Live happily in this shadow of life, destined to enjoy the perpetual Sun at last after this one. Farewell.

### *Praise of our age as if it were golden, by golden minds.*

-> Marsilio Ficino to Paul of Middelburg, distinguished physician and astronomer, many greetings. <-

**W**hat the poets once sang concerning the four ages—lead, iron, silver, and gold—our Plato, in his books on the *Republic*, transferred to four types of human minds, arguing that a certain lead is naturally implanted in some minds, iron in others, silver in others, and gold in yet others. If, therefore, any age is to be called "golden" by us, it is undoubtedly that which produces golden minds everywhere. And that this age of ours is such, no one will doubt who considers the illustrious inventions of this century. For this age, as if golden, has brought back to light the liberal disciplines that were almost extinct: grammar, poetry, oratory, painting, sculpture, architecture, music, and the ancient singing of poems to the Orphic Lyre <note>Ficino was famous for performing "Orphic hymns" on a lyre as a form of musical therapy and meditation.</note>. And this happened in Florence. And what had been venerable among the ancients but was now almost destroyed, it has joined wisdom with eloquence, and prudence with military skill. This was most clearly shown in Federico, Duke of Urbino <note>Federico da Montefeltro (1422–1482), the archetypal "Renaissance Man" who was both a fearsome mercenary commander and a sophisticated patron of the arts.</note>, as if in Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of both wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>, and it has made his son and brother heirs of that virtue. In you also, my dear Paul, it seems to have perfected astronomy; moreover, in Florence, it has recalled the Platonic discipline from darkness into the light. In Germany, in our times, the instruments for printing books <note>Latin: "imprimendorum librorum inuenta sunt instrumenta." Ficino correctly identifies Germany as the source of the printing press.</note> were invented. Furthermore, there are the tables <note>Astronomical or ephemeris tables used for calculating planetary positions.</note> by which—in one hour, so to speak—the entire face of the heavens is opened for a whole century, not to mention the Florentine machine <note>Possibly a reference to a complex astronomical clock or an orrery.</note> that tracks the daily movements of the heavens. Now, our friend Michelozzi brings back to you the German tables, diligently printed, to be dedicated to your illustrious Duke. A celestial gift indeed, worthy of a celestial prince, and worthy besides (as I judge) to be approved by you, a contemplator of heavenly things, and finally worthy of our recommendation to you. Farewell. September 13, 1492.

## THE END.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
## Florentine Letters, to Girolamo Rossi, his Most Beloved.

### PREFACE.

-> Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Girolamo Rossi, sends many greetings. <-

When I had brought the twelfth book of my Letters to a close, and was considering to whom I should primarily address it, I judged it would be consistent with reason to dedicate the conclusion of this long-lasting work specifically to you, for whom I have long intended the work as a whole, as if to a final destination. Furthermore, so that the entire study of my letters may finally find rest in you, I have decided at this conclusion that however many letters I may write hereafter shall belong to this twelfth and longest book, and shall be summarized under the title of "Rossi"—or rather, "Roscius" <note>Ficino often Latinizes names; here he plays on the name Rossi by referencing the famous Roman actor Roscius, a common humanist pun.</note>. Read happily, and live most happily, for you are certainly loved by us with a happy heart.
