# MARSILIO FICINO'S
## Florentine Letters,
### BOOK XII.

> No one can completely root out evils and cares.

-> Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Vittorio Soderini and Francesco Diacceto, his fellow philosophers, sends many greetings. <-

You ask what that Gospel saying means: *It is necessary that scandals come.* <note>original: "Necesse est ut ueniant scandala." From Matthew 18:7. In this context, "scandals" refers to stumbling blocks or inevitable moral obstacles.</note> It means precisely the same as that Platonic saying: that evils cannot be entirely rooted out, but necessarily revolve around this mortal region <note>A reference to Plato’s *Theaetetus* (176a), where Socrates argues that evil is a necessary counterpart to good in the material world.</note>. I will set aside for now how many evils are sown among us by fate, nature, fortune, the elements, men, and animals. Far more serious, certainly, are those which we imprudently bring upon ourselves. Indeed, it should not seem surprising that men who are either devoted to a life of business or enslaved to their lusts are crushed by innumerable evils. For since they subject themselves everywhere to fate and fortune, they frequently run into disturbances as if by their own will. Yet it is certainly less surprising that men who have neglected the pleasurable and active life to dedicate themselves entirely to contemplation are also agitated by disturbances. For they seem to have avoided the usual causes of anxiety. However, they are often troubled by more serious cares than either the pleasure-seekers or the men of action. For contemplatives, having spurned human affairs, betake themselves either to religion and holiness or to Philosophy. In both cases, they fall into Scylla while desiring to avoid Charybdis <note>A classical metaphor for trying to avoid one danger only to fall into another.</note>. For the holy, in fleeing the delusions and trifles of mortals, run into demons who tempt them; "For their struggle is not against flesh and blood," as Paul the Apostle says, "but against certain wicked spirits, the tyrants of the dark air." <note>Ephesians 6:12.</note> Thus it happens that while God exercises the saints, demons vex them. But what shall I say of the Philosophers? Do they not, in rejecting either the business of Jupiter <note>The active, political life.</note> or the delights of Venus <note>The life of physical pleasure.</note>, often fall into the weariness, sorrows, and black bile <term>atram bilem: the humor associated with Melancholy and the planet Saturn; Ficino believed it was the "occupational hazard" of geniuses.</term> of Saturn? Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle all consider the most gifted men to be subject to this great evil, so that they seem to pay those same penalties which the contemplative Prometheus paid on Mount Caucasus for his celestial theft <note>Prometheus stole fire from the gods, symbolizing the philosopher stealing divine knowledge; his punishment (an eagle eating his liver) was often allegorized as the "gnawing care" of intellectual labor.</note>. To such an extent, indeed, do both types of contemplatives...

-> *That the Sun is not to be worshiped as the author of all things.* <-

-> Marsilio Ficino sends many greetings to the illustrious Eberhard, Count of Württemberg <-
-> and elder of Montbéliard. <-

**S**ocrates, while in the military camps, often stood under the open sky looking up at the rising Sun; he remained astonished in those same tracks, with limbs unmoved and eyes unblinking, in the manner of a statue, until he might greet the Sun rising again. Induced by these Platonic signs and similar evidence, people will perhaps say that Socrates, led by some Phœbean <term>Phœbean: relating to Phœbus Apollo, the god of the Sun and prophecy</term> spirit even from his very childhood, was accustomed to venerating Phœbus himself above all else. By that same reasoning, the wisest of all Greeks was judged so by the oracle of Apollo. For my part, I shall for the present pass over what ought most certainly to be affirmed regarding Socrates's spirit—whether it be called a genius, a spirit, or an angel. This much, certainly, I would dare to affirm: that Socrates, in that state of mental ecstasy, did not admire this visible Sun, but another. For to whomsoever novelty alone is accustomed to bring admiration, why would Socrates be so stunned in his admiration of this Sun, which he sees every day, and whose every motion and power he had already long since understood by both mathematical and physical reasoning? This Sun (witnessed by Plato) he called not the first God, but the son of God—not the first son of God, I say, but the second, and one already visible. For the first son of God is not this Sun manifest to the eyes, but another, far superior to this one: namely, the First Intellect, contemplatable by the intellect alone. Socrates, therefore, being sometimes reminded by the heavenly Sun, and sensing therefrom the super-celestial Sun, contemplated the majesty of the latter more attentively, and was astonished as he admired the incomprehensible goodness of that Father. James the Apostle called him the "Father of lights"—of lights, I say, both more than heavenly and heavenly. <note>original: "patrem luminum." From James 1:17.</note> With Him there is no change, nor any shadow of turning. For he considers even those super-celestial things to be naturally changeable, and he does not doubt that the heavenly things are overshadowed daily by the turns of the nights. For this reason, he judges that every "best gift"—namely, that which is naturally implanted in the mind—and every "perfect gift"—namely, that which is added after the natural endowments—descends not from this Sun and the worldly stars, but from higher up, from the Father of lights himself. For relying on the powers of intelligence, as if on certain steps received not from the heavens but from above, we ascend above the heavens, and there we recognize, love, and worship many things more excellent than the heavens, and we venerate the builder of the heaven itself above all things. Nor, however, could we understand or love anything incorporeal and better than the heaven by our intelligence, if we possessed intelligence only from the heavens. Now indeed, lest anyone should worship the Sun, Moon, and Stars too much, and venerate them as the authors and fathers of the number of intellectual beings, he [James] prudently warned that this Sun is not the principle of the universe. For the present, I shall set aside the arguments by which we affirm in our Theology that the principle of the universe is neither a body, nor a soul, nor an intellect, but something far more exalted. From this principle the heavenly Sun is so far distant that it should be judged to be a certain shadow of it, rather than an image. I shall briefly touch upon the arguments which James reaches here. Since the state [of a thing], as a principle, ruler, and end of motion, is more perfect than all motion,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument about the Sun’s limitations compared to God, then transitions into a new letter to Martin Prenninger (Uranius) regarding the intrinsic connection between the study of Law and the study of Philosophy.</meta>

# LETTERS, BOOK XII

<page-num>947</page-num>

certainly God himself, the beginning and the end and the ruler of all, cannot be subject to change, yet the Sun is in a state of constant motion. Furthermore, the power of the first principle [God], being as it were immense, reaches all things mightily and can never be restrained. The power of the Sun, however, acting through its rays, is hindered here and there; its rays are blocked, it suffers an eclipse when the Moon is in the way, it is often hemmed in by clouds, it is repelled by the density of the earth, and the Sun itself is weakened by the distance of its location—indeed, it is even a tiny particle of the world, held in a narrow seat. It is pulled by its sphere and pulled back again. Contrary to the impulse of its own sphere, it is revolved by a sphere that is always higher. It is hindered by opposing signs and stars, and sometimes weakened by the aspect of "malific" <note>In astrology, "malifics" usually refer to the planets Saturn or Mars when they are in a position that exerts a negative influence.</note> planets. Finally, the principle of the universe [God] works everywhere, always, and in all things. The Sun, however, does not create the globes of the world itself, nor can it by its own power produce anything cold, moist, dense, or similar. Nor do similar powers in the heavens derive any origin from the Sun. Nevertheless, although the Sun is distantly removed from the Author of the world, all celestial things seem to have been divinely reduced to the single Sun as a ruler and measure in the heavens. By this we are directly reminded that all things in heaven, under heaven, and above heaven are likewise referred back to the one principle of all things, considering at last that they should venerate this very principle with at least the same reverence with which the celestial bodies venerate the Sun.

-> *The union of Philosophy with laws; namely, that a Philosopher is made from a nobleman.* <-
-> *Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius Prenninger, his friend, sends many greetings.* <-

<margin>P</margin>hilosophy has always been my pursuit, yet I have never applied myself to the laws; nevertheless, two professors of law are my very dear friends: in Italy, Giovanni Vittorio Soderini, and in Germany, you especially, my excellent Martin. Both of you have joined a wondrous zeal for wisdom with a distinguished faculty for the law. Someone might ask: what kinship is there between laws and Philosophy? It is the same necessity as that between Jupiter, the author of laws, and Saturn, the leader of Philosophy—that is, the relationship between a son and a father. I will pass over for now the astronomers who claim that when Jupiter is joined with Saturn, he brings forth new laws, especially whenever they are joined at the very "cardinal points" <note>The four most important points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> of heaven and the heads of the <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note>. Did not the ancient poets and the theologians of old imagine Saturn as a contemplator in hidden places, devising laws and rights after long contemplation? He then handed these to his son Jupiter, the leader of actions, to be observed by the citizens he would command. Homer also says that King Minos, the founder of laws, used to withdraw into the cave of Jupiter for nine years, and there receive the laws from Jupiter. Yet no one skilled in the ancient mysteries would ever dedicate a cave—which is always public—specifically to Jupiter. This, therefore, seems to be nothing other than the hidden dwelling or shrine of Saturn himself, in which Jupiter, established as a colleague with Saturn, instructs King Minos in the laws before they are to be formed for the people. But having dismissed the duty of laws for now, let us pursue the study of wisdom. Indeed, I have exhorted many through my letters to take this up with all their might. Since you both have already advanced far in this very thing, I will not exhort you now, but rather confirm you in it. For we either consider ourselves, or we look up to God, or we look around at other men. If we look at ourselves, wisdom alone allows us to finally know ourselves and to live with ourselves alone, always content with our own riches. If we look toward God, wisdom alone makes us like God and his friends—specifically as we diligently contemplate the things God himself has made, and venerate him as the recognized author of all good things. If, however, we look to men, wisdom alone establishes the wise man as a king over peoples and kings, and finally as a kind of divinity to be produced. Since, therefore, the study of wisdom makes the soul truly happy, does it not furthermore make a man noble, or declare him so? If we are to believe Plato, the race of Philosophers is surely the most noble. For he says it is of gold, and truly proceeded from Jupiter himself, the craftsman of the entire world. If you give credit to the Stoics, you will recognize the nobility of Philosophers from their posterity; for they assert that they alone will be immortal. Finally, it would be a sin not to believe the prophet Daniel. He says: "The learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many in justice shall be like stars for all eternity." <note>original: "Fulgebunt, docti, sicut splendor firmamenti. Et qui multos erudierint ad iustitiam tanquam stellæ in perpetuas æternitates." A quote from the Book of Daniel 12:3.</note> By "firmament," he signifies not only the eighth heaven, but the entire mass of the spheres.

# MARSILIO FICINO

<page-num>949</page-num>

...it seems to signify the firmament of all the stars and planets. This firmament, however, also shines by its own nature, somewhat apart from the stars and planets, but with a certain rarer, scattered, and white light, and for that reason is less obvious to the eyes. In this same kind of light, truly learned and holy men will shine, both here and in their heavenly homeland <note>original: "patria" — often used in Neoplatonic and Christian contexts to refer to the soul's true home in heaven.</note>, even if they themselves have never taught anyone. But those who have not only contemplated divine things for themselves but have additionally taught others openly, and have given laws for the observance of justice, will shine with a brilliance more manifest than the others, sparkling most clearly like the stars. And this will not be for a fixed time, but through all time—not merely through the duration of this world, but through the very enjoyment of a more divine eternity, never interrupted, but utterly perpetual and continuous. For it seems just that those who were authors of a public and divine good and will always benefit humanity, and who did not hide the light given to them from heaven but brought it forth for the common good, should be gifted by God with a certain eternal splendor and goodness. Farewell.

---

->Why I always handle the same and ancient things.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori, the Florentine ambassador to the Pope, sends greetings.<-

**Y**esterday evening I had already said farewell to our friend Franco, and at that time a letter was intended for our Valori. But soon (I know not how) I was compelled to add a morning letter to the evening ones. This is something lovers are often accustomed to doing, not being content with single letters. Franco, therefore, (as I might put it) announced my health to you in our previous letter. But the present little letter will report to you the account of our studies, which Franco could not receive then due to his business. You ask (I see) what I am doing now. Indeed, I have been doing the same thing for a long time, my Valori. By some fate (I know not what), I always revolve back to the same point. Saturn, ascending in Aquarius, has been our "significator" <note>An astrological term for the planet that represents the subject of a horoscope.</note> from the beginning—I might even say our leader—as you know. Therefore, we are perpetually retracting Saturnian and ancient things. Long ago, when Saturn first returned to Aquarius, we translated the ancient works of Plato once under the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), Ficino’s first great patron.</note>. Now Saturn has returned to that same place again, and we also return to the same thing; we are translating Plato again after the "Laurentian" Plotinus <note>Refers to Ficino's translation of Plotinus, which was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici ("The Magnificent").</note>. But, as is fitting for a great work, we are explaining it with even greater commentaries. The "Little Commentary on the Timaeus," which was composed at your estate in Maiano, is now growing larger for us, and soon we shall approach the *Parmenides* in similar fashion. That great patron of ours, Piero de' Medici <note>Piero di Lorenzo de' Medici (1472–1503), who succeeded his father Lorenzo.</note>, has given us firm hope that he will again breathe life into the rising Plato. And indeed, he inspires so thoroughly now that our Plato, who has been a wanderer until now, is now about to found his Academy upon this "Rock" <note>original: "super hanc Petram" — Ficino is making a pun on Piero’s name (Petrus/Peter), which means "Rock," echoing the biblical phrase from Matthew 16:18.</note>. Therefore, while he is there with the Pope, please give him as many thanks as possible in our name for this matter during your leisure. Near him, as if near your Jupiter, you will recognize your "Dioscuri" <note>The Gemini twins, Castor and Pollux; here referring to two close associates.</note>, the Bibienas, Castor and Pollux; commend us to them as well, after him. I will make an end, not to a "little letter" as I said, but now to a full letter, if I first signify to you that the "Martian" cause <note>Likely referring to a legal or property matter involving the Marsili family.</note>—or rather a "Saturnian" one because of its lateness—is now finished through your efforts, in addition to the Medici authority. November 7, 1492.

---

->The similarity of Mercury with Saturn.<-
->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Filippo Carduccio, sends greetings.<-

**S**ince all the letters composed by me have now been transcribed for you and are almost ready to be brought to you by the courier, I decided that a "Mercurial" work should be delivered to a "Mercurial" friend, not without Mercurial auspices. To see if celestial things have any power in such business, so that the work might reach you more quickly and be read more swiftly, and furthermore, so that it might be considered through long re-reading, I have additionally added Saturn to Mercury, whether as a companion or a leader. I read again today in the tenth book of the *Republic* that Mercury and Saturn are very similar to each other in color, that is, in the light of all celestial things, so that it is no wonder they are also so similar in the light of intelligence. Thus, one indeed exhorts to wisdom, while the other—with God breathing more deeply upon him—leads one through to it. Indeed, the Sun is the image of God...

->EPISTLES, BOOK XII.<-

...they wish. God himself is the first author of wisdom. The signifiers of wisdom, Mercury and Saturn, as companions of the divine image, depart the least of all from the Sun; for Mercury almost always moves within the Sun's splendor, and Saturn seems to stray the least of all from the Sun’s ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the circular path on the celestial sphere that the Sun appears to follow</term> path. Astronomers believe these two are similar in a certain nature, and that Mercury rejoices in the houses, boundaries, and aspect of Saturn. From this, (in my opinion) it happens that almost all who begin their journey and profession under Mercury, end in Saturn alone. I wish that you, my Carduccio, might also eventually arrive from Mercury at Jupiter <note>Ficino uses planetary movement as a metaphor for life stages: Mercury represents study and youth; Saturn represents old age and contemplation; Jupiter represents justice, success, and the pinnacle of a well-ordered life.</note>. Farewell. November 14, 1492.

### *Apology for his book On the Sun and Light.*

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Filippo Valori, the Florentine ambassador to the<-
->Pope, sends greetings.<-

**I** was keeping the book *On the Sun*, intended for the most illustrious Piero de' Medici, at home for a long time now; and, contrary to the Gospel precept, I was almost impiously hiding a lamp—or rather the Sun—under a bushel <note>original: "sub modio" — a reference to Matthew 5:15: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel."</note>. But that Pietro Nero, whom we have frequently called the most "candid" <note>original: "candidissimum" — literally "whitest" or "brightest," but also meaning sincere and honest.</note> in our letters, thought it would be a pious thing for this light to shine forth to as many people as possible, as God commands. Therefore, I most willingly obeyed this most candid man, to whom the care of light and brilliance especially pertains. And beyond the mystery entrusted to the magnanimous Piero de' Medici, I allowed the book to be openly set in type by printers through the efforts of Pietro Nero. 

Look then, my Valori, dearer to me than light itself: this Sun of mine, such as it is, now rises openly. But perhaps it is soon to be struck by rising clouds, or even to be troublesome to certain owls and bats <note>These nocturnal animals represent critics who cannot handle the "light" of truth or Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>. The clouds indeed the winds will immediately scatter, or the Sun itself, when it has ascended higher, will thin out and dissolve. As for the bats, who grow dim and blind under the light, I purposely advise them—if only they are capable of taking advice—not to trample upon a light that is healthy for others. Instead, let them flee this splendor in their usual way and (as is fitting) stay hidden, being unworthy of the light. 

Indeed, with good hope, I challenge my Valori to this contest; I say that Valori will fight most valiantly, like a Hercules, not only against the owls, but even against empty monsters. For the Suns frequently have on their lips that Boethian saying spoken for Hercules: *The earth, once conquered, grants the stars* <note>original: "Superata tellus sydera donat" — a quote from Boethius’s "Consolation of Philosophy," meaning that overcoming earthly trials leads to heavenly reward.</note>. The ancients introduce Hercules, a man who was a foster-child of the Sun, undergoing the twelve labors—the twelve signs of the zodiac—for the sake of true glory and the splendor of truth, which are the Sun's own proper gifts and duties. 

Go now, my Valori, eager for battle; for there (I know what I am saying) you will have at least three invincible defenders. I mean the Herculean Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the great humanist poet and scholar.</note>, the Phoebus-like Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), known for his brilliance (likened to Phoebus Apollo).</note>, and the Amphion-like Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino (1424–1498), a senior Florentine humanist and commentator on Dante.</note>. Just as they have fought strenuously for my life these past three years, they will hereafter fight just as successfully for this splendor of mine, such as it is. January 11, 1493.

### *There are often twins in the heavens. Likewise, two Suns.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Martin Uranius the German, his unique friend,<-
->sends greetings.<-

**I**t brings joy, my Uranius, as a man of the heavens, to treat of heavenly things together with you. Not only are those Dioscuri <note>The twins Castor and Pollux (the constellation Gemini).</note> "twins" in the firmament, but there are also brothers among the planets. For Mercury is like a younger brother to Saturn; for they shine with a similar light (as Plato says) and both preside over the intellect. Kind Venus is the sister of Jupiter, as Diana is of Phoebus Apollo. Mars, however, being somewhat more arrogant and devoid of fellowship, does not so much accompany the Sun as rival him. For besides his own heat, which rivals the Sun's, he pours a certain light (I know not what) into the Moon, which has been observed by very few. 

After these things, the eternal air is like another Jupiter, the brother and husband of the following air, which is like Juno. But let us return to the Sun. What wonder is it if there are twin Suns in heaven, that twin Suns were also born to me: first a larger one, and then a smaller one. You saw the smaller one yourself last summer while you were with us in Florence, just as the ambassador was departing for the Pope; it followed closely behind you as you left for Germany, to your most illustrious prince, Eberhard... <margin>Eberhard I, Duke of Württemberg</margin>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...about to greet him. But the other Sun, which has now grown larger among my Platonic commentaries, Piero de’ Medici <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" de' Medici (1472–1503), son of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> rightfully claims for himself; and since he rightfully claims all things Platonic for himself, a similar light, O my Uranius, has shone for me as a twin between my household gods <note>original: "lares" — Roman household deities, here used to mean Ficino's home or study.</note>, one smaller and one larger. The smaller indeed has long since shone for Phoebus Capella <note>Scipio "Phoebus" Capella, a scholar and friend of Ficino.</note>, but the larger now shines for the most illustrious Piero de’ Medici. Therefore, O celestial man, contemplate both happily. You will contemplate them happily if, by the likeness of this light, you commit to memory this Platonic mystery concerning divinity which follows. We are accustomed to perceiving things that have very little light by searching for them here and there as we approach closer. But when we are about to see the Sun, we are not so much forced to seek the Sun—which meets us of its own accord and is the most open of all things—as we are to purge our eyes, open them, turn them, and according to our capacity, adapt them to it. Similarly, we are compelled to track down the small truths of other things through arguments, like tiny sparks. But we are not able to attain the immense light of God in this way; rather, we are prepared for it both by the loving turn of the will and the serenity of the mind, provided we are prepared for that light which happily flashes out of its own accord. Hence that Platonic saying: **Divine things cannot be taught with words and reasons like other things that are learned, but from constant familiarity regarding the divine itself and a communion of life, a light finally flashes forth in the soul, just as if from a sparking fire, and then it nourishes itself.** <note>This is a famous passage from Plato’s Seventh Letter (341c), a foundational text for Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note>

### On the book *On the Sun*, sent to him.
->Marsilio Ficino to his fellow philosopher Lorenzo, the priest of the Laurentian church.<-

**W**hile I was composing a book *On the Sun and Light* during these past days—small indeed, but written with great pleasure—you meanwhile, though unaware of my current midnight labors, quite opportunely discovered through astronomical calculations that our entire study of wisdom pertains chiefly to the Sun. This is because that "Lot," which the Egyptians call the "part of wisdom" in a nativity <term>nativity: a birth chart or horoscope</term>, had arrived at the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "cor Leonis" — the star Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo, considered highly auspicious.</note>. The Sun, as the Lord of that sign, held that subtle region of the heavens destined for wisdom. Opportunely again, immediately upon the completion of the book *On the Sun and Light*, you brought that astronomical calculation to us yesterday. Therefore, by the same opportunity, I in turn send the book itself to you today. I hope that this light of ours does not seem to bring forth the Moon, but the Sun. February 18, 1493.

### Love itself, being God, commands the lover to be loved in return.
->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the distinguished Julian, professor of Theology,<-
->not the least of the Order of Friars Minor, sends many greetings.<-

**T**here is no reason, my dearest Julian, why you should make excuses to us for your silence. For even if you have spoken to us rarely, you have nevertheless spoken of us frequently. And if anything was perhaps lacking in words, you compensate for all of it with your immense love toward us. Indeed, I have here a maximum proof, beyond a doubt, of your burning love toward me: that I, in your absence, embrace you daily with a love that grows more burning. As for that proverb, "If you wish to be loved, love," I have explained it with many reasons in my book *On Love* <note>Ficino's "De Amore," a commentary on Plato's Symposium.</note> and in various places in my *Epistles*. But the greatest of all reasons seems to be the one that just occurred to me while writing, unless a sudden opinion deceives me. But so that it may deceive me somewhat less, let us converse a little. The ancients used to depict Apollo and Cupid as archers, the latter indeed shooting flames, and the former shooting lights. Just as Apollo shoots light into both eyes simultaneously, so that by the same light with which I see you, you also see me in return; so Cupid shoots flames, so that with the same flame by which one already burns, the other may soon burn as well. Indeed, Plato proves that Love is a God, and all antiquity testifies to it, and our own Theologians place the Holy Spirit (which is the first Love) before the Seraphim—that is, the "loving" angels—and they set the Seraphic angels everywhere in charge of true loves. Therefore, the power of love, the friend of mutual charity and of Juno <note>In Roman mythology, Juno was the goddess of marriage and community bonds.</note>, when it inflames someone with love, immediately reflects the burning rays from this love as if from a mirror into the beloved by a certain hidden and miraculous power; so that the beloved, though absent or unaware, is miraculously inflamed and loves the lover in return. For a just deity does not allow a lover, moved as they are by a heavenly instinct, not to be loved in return. But even concerning...

->LETTERS, BOOK XI.<-

...love enough. You complained moreover in your letter that the books of Plotinus <note>Ficino's massive translation and commentary on the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, printed in 1492.</note> had not reached you at all, almost accusing me of slowness. The books themselves were completed by the printers this past May. But those who were commanded by the Medici to distribute them at least through Italy have thus far been slow, and even with urging, they remain slow. I have not yet published the new translation of Plato, though it is now more than half finished. You encouraged me more than anyone to do this—perhaps with the Angels encouraging you meanwhile, in whose church you persuaded me of this during dinner. At that time, after our declamations, you used to pray there frequently in the assemblies. I am sending to you to read the little book *On the Sun and Light* <note>original: "De Sole & lumine"</note> recently published by me, so that where our heat has long glowed, there light may also shine. **February 21, 1492.**

---

### On the book "On the Sun."
### Marsilio Ficino to Marinus the distinguished Physician, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

**A**ll astronomers (as you well know) believe that the Moon rejoices in the third region <note>The "Third House" in an astrological chart, traditionally associated with short journeys and siblings.</note> from the rising point of the heavens, leading a short journey of minor religious significance. But they believe the Sun rejoices in the ninth <note>The "Ninth House," associated with long-distance travel, philosophy, and religion.</note>, the ruler of a longer journey and of great religion—or, to speak more safely, at least the signifier of such things. Since you are therefore soon to undertake a long and religious journey to the shrine of Loreto <note>The Basilica della Santa Casa in Loreto, a major site of pilgrimage in Italy.</note>, I rightfully hand over to you now a certain "sun" that has recently risen for me. It will be (as I hope) an omen of clear air and an easy journey.

---

### On the book "On the Sun."
### Marsilio Ficino to Georgius Cyprius, the distinguished Physician, greetings.

**S**ince everyone agrees that Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo, the god of both the Sun and healing.</note> is the author of medicine and the father of physicians, I rightfully send to you—an old physician of our family—the "Phoebus-like" book *On the Sun and Light* recently published by us to read. Phoebus, therefore, will be a truthful witness to you of my perpetual love for you. "The sun will give you signs," (as our Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil; the quote is from his *Georgics*.</note> says), "Who would dare to call the sun false?" **June 14, 1494.**

---

### On the book "On the Sun" having been sent.
### Marsilio Ficino to Baccio Ugolino, greetings.

**S**ince Phoebus and Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine. Ficino often balanced the "sober" wisdom of Apollo with the "divine frenzy" of Bacchus.</note> are brothers, the one rightfully greets the other. But which one approaches the other first? Not Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus.</note> approaching Apollo, perhaps fearing he might bring back only words. But Phoebus himself approaches Bacchus, hoping to bring back pure wine. **June 15, 1493.**

---

### Happy omens for Philosophy, from Mercury, Saturn, and the Sun.
### Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Nicola Valori, greetings.

**N**one of our circle has begun to practice Philosophy under happier omens than you. I will not recount at length for now how much that conjunction of Mercury with Saturn in Aquarius is thought to contribute to the study of Philosophy. This was imminent when I was composing the book *On the Sun and Light*, and you were already beginning your first steps in Philosophy—and indeed from the Sun itself, just like a second Orpheus from Apollo rather than from the Muses. You immediately looked upon this Sun with eagle-like eyes, as was fitting for such great omens. After this, indeed, you set out with a certain marvelous speed toward the higher Sun, the author of celestial things who rules among the heavenly bodies, and you have quite happily undertaken *Platonic Theology* <note>Ficino's major philosophical work, *Theologia Platonica*.</note>. In this work, you see every day into the deepest mysteries as clearly as it is right for one to see who looks upon individual things not under the Moon, but under the Sun itself. Continue, I pray, my Valori, with that same eagerness with which you began; with me as your companion everywhere and Apollo as your guide, you will shortly attain the highest splendor of truth and glory.

MARSILIO FICINO

### ->The signs of a true Platonist, and on the Ideas.<-
#### ->Marsilio Ficino to Francesco Diacetto <note>Francesco da Diacceto (1466–1522) was Ficino's closest disciple and eventual successor at the Florentine Academy.</note>, his fellow Platonist, greetings.<-

**T**hose who think that the Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripateticam" — referring to the school of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> discipline is contrary to the Platonic are entirely mistaken. Indeed, a path cannot be contrary to its destination. Anyone who considers the matter correctly will find that the Peripatetic doctrine is the path to Platonic wisdom, for natural things lead us to the divine. From this it follows that no one was ever admitted to the more secret mysteries of Plato unless they were first initiated into the Peripatetic disciplines. 

There are three symbols of the perfect Platonist by which such a priest of wisdom is distinguished from other philosophers and sages. The first is a sublime mind, always turning itself from lower things toward the higher; the second is religion; the third is eloquence, and this of a quasi-poetic sort. The first pertains to Saturn <note>In Ficino's system, Saturn represents the highest contemplative intellect.</note>, the second to Jupiter <note>Jupiter represents law, justice, and religious order.</note>, and the third to Apollo <note>Apollo represents harmony, prophecy, and the arts.</note>. Thus, only he is a legitimate Platonist who walks the path we have described, endowed with these symbols and commended by these (so to speak) divine powers. 

Therefore, let us philosophize together, Francesco; I congratulate you as a legitimate Platonist and I rejoice for our Academy. As for my response to your question about the Ideas <note>The Platonic "Forms"—the eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the divine mind.</note>, according to the brevity of a letter, take it thus: You do not think that the specific ideas of individuals are distinguished within the First Mind absolutely in themselves, but rather by a certain relationship. I do not believe this is at all foreign to your friend Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino had recently published his translations of Plotinus's works.</note>, as I explain briefly in my commentaries on him. Proclus <note>A later Neoplatonist who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note> also denies in his commentary on the *Parmenides* that there are specific ideas for individuals—that is, ideas that are absolutely distinct. This is undoubtedly most consistent with Plato, who says in the *Timaeus* that the ideal Model is eternal, signifying that what is expressed through it and by it shall be everlasting. 

From this it is gathered that the species of natural things are expressed from that source entirely—as they are indeed everlasting—but individuals are not expressed in the same way; rather, they are distinguished from one another at the very end by the sequence of following causes. Nevertheless, this distinction does not escape the First Intellect, the founder of the universal order. Hence in the *Timaeus*, the elder gods and daemons <note>original: "dæmones" — intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, at the command and arrangement of the Architect, pursue the construction of individual things beneath the Moon. Therefore, so that there is neither an extreme multitude within that which is supremely unified, nor that the one who makes and perfects all things through intelligence should be ignorant of the many, the ideas of entirely mutable individual things are not naturally disjoined from one another in reality there; rather, they are distinct by the rational power of the same Intelligence applying itself in different ways. You have thought well on this, my Francesco. Farewell. **July 11, 1493.**

---

### ->An excuse for a long silence.<-
#### ->Marsilio Ficino to Filippo Valori <note>A Florentine diplomat and close friend of the Medici and Ficino.</note>, envoy to the Supreme Pontiff, greetings.<-

**Y**ou will perhaps ask the cause of this long silence; to answer briefly, it is nothing other than an uncertain cause for writing. For what should I write above all? Perhaps how I am faring? I am always in doubt whether I am faring well or ill. Shall I signal what I am doing? By Hercules, I am in doubt about this too! Indeed, I know what I want and what I am attempting, but what I am actually achieving I do not yet know. I even doubt whether to think of you as present with us or absent, since the daily company of your brother Niccolò <note>Niccolò Valori, a student of Ficino and biographer of Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, who philosophizes with me, renders you so present that I do not notice a need for letters. Grateful men are accustomed to send at least longer letters after a long silence. I, however, shall be so ungrateful now that I trust I might compensate for a very long silence with perhaps a very short little note. Not at all—rather, a great love provides confidence and does enough for duty. Farewell. **June 15, 1494.**

---

### ->On the Book "On the Sun."<-
#### ->Marsilio Ficino to Antonio Calderino, greetings.<-

**T**he Sun, the Lord among the heavenly bodies, excels the other causes of natural things most especially in this: that it does all things by its heat, but demonstrates all things by its light. For my part, even if there is no need for me to use the heat of the Sun to warm Calderino—whom I have found to be most fervent everywhere in managing and defending my affairs—I nevertheless decided that I must use the light of the Sun, so that I might now openly declare to everyone, with Apollo as my witness, our burning love which has long been confirmed by many testimonies. **July 15, 1494.**

LETTERS, BOOK XII.

### *Light is wonderful, for it is the image of wisdom. Also, how marvelous is the union of wisdom with power.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to Ramberto Malatesta, Illustrious Prince of Sogliano, sends greetings.

**I**t is the common and certain opinion of all—and as it were the very voice of nature—that nothing is more beautiful to the sight, nothing more lovable, and nothing more wonderful than light. And though everyone admits this beyond controversy, yet if you were to ask the cause of such a great and manifest thing, not everyone would find the reason. Only he will respond plausibly who perceives that this light, manifest to the eyes, is nothing other than the clearest light of intelligence <note>original: "intelligentiæ lumen" — In Ficino's philosophy, physical light is a visible manifestation of the divine intellect.</note>. Indeed, our Plato prophesied in the *Phaedrus* that if wisdom could ever be seen with interior eyes, it would excite much more ardent loves than this light, which daily stirs lovers when it appears in beautiful bodies. 

For this light, so clear to the sight, has not gained such great grace and admiration among us because of its own nature as light, so much as from that more secret light of which it is the image—from that light, I say, of divine wisdom. Therefore, divine wisdom has everywhere given primacy to light as if to its own deputy. Of our body, the eyes alone are the leaders, for among the members they are the ones possessing light, which is a kind of wisdom. Among all the powers of the soul, the mind alone reigns, clearly shining with the gifts of wisdom. Furthermore, among the elements and similar bodies, fire alone is the Lord, being as it were the "wise" element among them because it is endowed with light. Similarly, in the heavens, the Sun itself, the sole fountain of light, rules over all. Among astronomers, the Sun signifies both power and wisdom, rejoicing in the ninth region of the heavens <note>original: "nona cæli plaga" — In astrology, the 9th House is associated with philosophy, religion, and wisdom; Ficino notes it as the "Temple of Minerva."</note> as if in the Temple of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note>. By its proximity, Mercury also seems to have obtained the name of "the wise." 

Why say more? Finally, the kingdom of the whole world is not claimed by the violence of any heat or cold, nor by the force of certain motions, nor by any crowd of fluctuating bodies or vast mass; rather, it is claimed by Prime Wisdom, which, as it sees all things, is also powerful over all things. Just as it provides for each thing everywhere, so it is again the Mistress of each. This Wisdom, therefore, seems rightly to have commanded us to join wisdom with power according to our strength, just as she herself has manifesty joined them in the universe. For this reason, I believe it was divinely brought about that the light of the Sun, which effects all things as a power, should similarly show all things as a wise guide, and indeed should help and delight all things as a "good." By this we are always reminded to couple not only wisdom with power, but also goodness. Poets sing of such a venerable and truly blessed union having existed once during the reign of Saturn <note>The mythical "Golden Age."</note>, and our Plato desired to see it above all else. And we, his followers, desire above all else to love those who have joined the study of singular wisdom and uprightness of character with a noble lineage and princely rule. At this point, the suspicion of flattery and vanity—which is quite foreign to philosophers—prevents me from explaining what I feel more widely; but let it be permitted to speak at least briefly. In Ramberto Malatesta, Prince of Sogliano, I now have everything I sought with my whole mind; I love him with my whole mind, and as the law of friendship commands, I make all my things common to him.

***

### *How Venus through desire mixes lovers together. Friendly Jupiter through Mercury fuses friends.*

#### Marsilio Ficino to Ramberto Malatesta, Illustrious Prince of Sogliano, sends greetings.

**T**he ancient theologians of the nations valued friendship so highly that among the other deities—and indeed often above the others—they worshiped "Jupiter the Friendly" <note>original: "Iouem amicabilē" — likely referring to Zeus Philios, the protector of friendship.</note>, who was placed in charge of reconciling goodwill and friendships everywhere. Among these ancients, just as kindly Venus through Cupid both kindled loves and (if I may say so) joined lovers together, so "Friendly Jupiter" through Mercury brought forth more serious goodwill and fused friendships. If we may be permitted today to name Jupiter and Mercury, we would surely say that this friendship of ours was not joined by some human cause, but by the gift of Friendly Jupiter, especially since Minerva herself, the conciliator of our goodwill, is said to have been born from the head of supreme Jupiter. But shall we say he achieved this for us through Mercury? Through Mercury certainly, not only...

...through a more hidden and celestial means, but also through one more familiar and human to us. Since Petrus Martellus <note>Piero Martelli (1468–1531), a Florentine statesman and scholar who was a member of Ficino's circle.</note>, a most dear friend to us both who joined us as one, possesses not only a Mercurial wit, but even seems to present the very image and character of Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, associated with communication and intellect.</note>. I had indeed sensed this, as if by some prophecy of my own, even before looking at his horoscope; and once it was inspected, I was confirmed in my augury. Therefore, just as he has acted as a Mercury under Jupiter in binding our friendship, so hereafter he shall be a Mercury in both directions, indicating and interpreting our mutual counsels. August 4, 1494.

### The Sun as the Image and Deputy of God.

### Marsilio Ficino to the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord Francesco Soderini, Bishop of Volterra <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524), a high-ranking Florentine prelate and diplomat.</note>, sends greetings.

**L**ately, I sent the book *On the Sun* <note>original: "De Sole"</note>, dedicated to the magnanimous Piero de' Medici, to you also as his kinsman, to be read. But so that the whole book might seem inscribed to you, my other patron, I dedicate this summary of the whole work to you. Theologians attribute three principal things to God: power, wisdom, and goodness. The Sun, therefore, as the image of God, accomplishes all things among us as one who is powerful; it further distinguishes and demonstrates individual things to the eyes every day as one who is wise; and finally, it helps and delights us as one who is good. They say it is proper to God alone to work miracles. Thus the Sun, as God's deputy <term>vicarius</term>, seems to perform three things that are especially marvelous. Beneath the heavens, it brings back to life in Spring and Summer many things that were nearly dead through Winter. In the heavens, it illuminates, moderates, and rules all celestial things. And those things which are above the heavens—invisible not only to eyes but even to our minds—the Sun (so to speak) makes visible, while it warns us by the marvelous spectacles of the celestial realms to contemplate the super-celestial. Contemplate happily, sacred prelate, this Sun of ours and its light—you who are most worthy of the soul-nourishing light above all others. September 8, 1494.

### Preface to the Letters.

### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to all his letters at once, sends greetings.

**Q**uickly, as my letters say "greetings" to my friends (at my bidding), so many times shall you say "everlasting greetings" to our dearest friend Hieronymus Rossius <note>Girolamo Rossi, a physician and friend who helped prepare Ficino's letters for the printing press.</note>. For I had fathered you as mortals, and by some fate destined to die soon; but Hieronymus, a man of distinguished piety, has recently regenerated you—now, I hope, as immortals. For you were lying hidden for a long time in dark places, nor was anyone yet rescuing you from the shadows. Perhaps fate or your guardian spirit <term>genius</term> <note>A personal tutelary spirit or guiding force.</note> was not yet willing. But our Rossi—or rather now your Rossi—has followed you with the same piety with which he always bore himself toward your father Marsilio, now with a certain hereditary love. With both diligence and labor, he has seen to it that your features, which were just now being suppressed, should be fully expressed <note>This personification refers to the transition from manuscript to the printed edition, which "rescues" the letters from obscurity and grants them "immortality."</note>. Therefore, greet this learned and pious restorer of yours, once with sadness but now with joy, and give immortal thanks for the great gift of immortality. December 15, 1494. Florence.

### For the book On the Sun, likewise on the Star of the Magi, on the Feast of Epiphany.

### Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Niccolini <note>Angelo Niccolini (1450–1495), a Florentine lawyer and diplomat.</note>, illustrious citizen and legal expert, sends greetings.

**H**oday the Magi (observers of the stars, led by a marvelous star) greeted Christ, the author of the stars, with three principal gifts: gold, myrrh, and frankincense. Today Christ, with the Holy Spirit flashing from heaven, is said to have been bathed by John in the water of the Jordan. Today Christ, the creator of waters and wine, miraculously changed water into wine at the wedding feast. Therefore, distinguished and pious Angelo, you also solemnly celebrate this day—famous for three great miracles—with a threefold yearly honor: with a banquet, with music, and with reading. To this reading, held sacred in your house, I consecrate the book *On the Sun and Light*, composed by me lately for this reason: so that by the comparison of the Sun and visible light...

->*Regarding a gift of Bacchus. Also concerning the Gospel theme of water turned into wine.*<-
->*Marsilio Ficino to Mazino <note>Mazino de’ Mazini, a Florentine physician and friend of Ficino.</note>, the distinguished Physician, sends greetings.*<-

**I** was frequently reminded during the morning readings within the Octave of the Epiphany, and today I was reflecting in my mind on that Gospel account: wine made from water. I wondered whether, beyond the mystical and moral allegory, it might also have a physical <note>original: "physicum"; here meaning natural or medical.</note> sense, since Christ changed water into wine in a moment, whereas nature usually takes a long time. Indeed, the physical sense, pertaining especially to the physician, investigates why Christ wished this to be the first of his miracles. Perhaps it was to show that wine would be the first and greatest support of our life. But why "good wine"—that is, strong wine? Why was a Cretan or Oriental vintage <note>original: "merum"; undiluted wine.</note> reserved until now? Why did that Teacher of Life choose not to bring this wine to the first table, but delayed it so long? Perhaps he wished to warn us that wine, thriving with heat and power, should by no means be granted to burning youth, but rather should be saved for the restoration of colder old age. Finally, why did he change not just a part, but all the water into wine? Clearly, so that good, undiluted wine might be drunk, especially in old age. 

And so, while I was meditating on these things around noon, I began to desire and even search for wine of that sort, with which I might comfort both my own old age and the senility of my mother. For this past autumn, she completed her eightieth year, and I my sixtieth. But you, like a prophet, sent divine wine to me at that very same hour! A physician of Apollo <note>Ficino often associates medicine and the sun with Apollo.</note> surely—such as my Mazino is—suits both prophecy and the gift of Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine.</note>, since the same Phoebus Apollo is called both the first physician and the author of prophecy, and is the brother of Bacchus, joined to him in the sacred rites. Finally—and this I value highly—along with the most choice gift of Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus.</note>, you gave me a Galenic <note>Referring to Galen, the ancient Greek physician whose theories dominated Medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> letter, providing healthy counsel for life, so that you might in a friendly manner join advice with assistance. I, therefore, am and always shall be joined to you in love, as much as a prognosis is joined to medicine, or Bacchus to Phoebus. January 13, 1494.

---

->*Regarding the printing of the book "On Life." Also an immortal omen of friendship.*<-
->*Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Menchen <note>Johann Menchen (or Menken), a scholar from Cologne.</note>, priest of Cologne, distinguished professor of Canon Law, and Secretary to the great Prelate of Cologne, sends greetings.*<-

**O**n the eighteenth of January <note>original: "Quintodecimo Calēdas Februarij"; the 15th day before the Calends of February.</note>, near sunrise, I seemed in my dreams to greet a man previously unknown to me, endowed with a noble appearance, clothing, and retinue. After a physical <note>medical/scientific</note> discussion, he showed me his foot as if it needed to be cured. On that very same day, you arrived in Florence, about to set out for Rome as the legate of the great Prelate Hermann <note>Hermann IV of Hesse, Archbishop-Elector of Cologne.</note>. Since you could not come to us on account of a bruised foot, you signaled your desire for a visit. I came to you, as was not only proper but also fitting. Thus, as soon as I saw you coming toward me, I recognized you immediately as the heroic man I had seen in my sleep. 

After our first greetings, we happened upon the subject of our work *On Life* <note>original: "De Vita"; Ficino's three-part treatise on health, longevity, and astral influences, first published in 1489.</note>, and we discussed many things in turn pertaining especially to medicine. During our talk, so that whatever I had foretold while sleeping might be fulfilled, you showed me your bruised foot. Thus, I do not seem to have seen a mere dream, but to have received an oracle from heaven—an omen (as I judge it) that our friendship shall be divine. Since divine things are also immortal, I sensed (as I just related) the divinity of our friendship; you, meanwhile, devised its future immortality. For you have decided to take care that our books *On Life* be printed <note>original: "exprimendos"; referring to the printing press.</note> again, so that our life might be more widely propagated from that place, and that posterity may understand by this service of yours toward us how much you loved us, being loved by us in return. Thus, may this divine friendship of ours become immortal among posterity. Live happily, my John, propagator of our life, and most worthy of life. Farewell happily. January 17, 1494.

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

### A brief recommendation in a just cause.

-> Marsilio Ficino to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Francesco Soderini, <-
-> Bishop of Volterra, sends greetings. <-

**I** shall be brief in recommending the Monastery of Settimo <note>The Abbey of San Salvatore a Settimo, a significant Cistercian monastery near Florence.</note> to you regarding the legal case in Modena. Indeed, I know how much you love those monks, who are truly pious men. I do not only love them, but I revere them. I believe that, as just men, they are making just demands; you are a most fierce protector of justice. Finally, whatever service you bestow upon them, I shall consider it bestowed equally upon me, their devoted observer. The monk who is the procurator of this case, who is named Just <note>original: "Iustus"; Ficino is making a pun on the monk's name and the "just" nature of the case.</note> in both deed and name, will diligently report everything to you. I also recommend myself to you as much as possible. Farewell, and be happy. January 25, 1494.

-> *Plato said many things in agreement with Christians. Many Platonists imitated Christian teachings.* <-

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Jacopo Ron- <-
-> dono, Bishop of Rimini, sends greetings. <-

**A** holy brother of the order of Saint Dominic, a distinguished professor of Theology, greeted me in your name and asserted with many testimonies that I am ardently loved by you. Although this has been clear to me for a long time, I nevertheless longed for a report of your prosperous health, such as I have now received after a long wait. Philosophy, the mother of all human goods, long ago gave birth to our friendship—a bond which (as Plato says) should be placed before all other relationships and which will not perish with time. But surely these matters are too certain to require witnesses or words. He reported to us, moreover, that some brother (I know not whom) insolently asserted in a public speech that the divine mystery of the Trinity among Christians exists in Plato himself, and that Christians first received these familiar ideas from there. You, however, expect a judgment from me on this matter, as if the works of Plato were well known to me. I therefore assert without controversy that the secret of the Christian Trinity is never in the books of Plato themselves. However, there are some things similar in words, though not in sense. Truly, more similar things are found in his followers who flourished after Christ: in Numenius, Ammonius, Plotinus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and Proclus. <note>These are the "Neoplatonists." Ficino argues they didn't anticipate Christianity, but rather borrowed from it to bolster their own philosophy.</note> Since they had all read the Gospel of John, and some had even read the books of Dionysius the Areopagite, <note>A figure believed in the Renaissance to be a direct disciple of St. Paul, though now identified as a 5th-century author known as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note> they willingly adopted many things similar to the Trinity and took up the orders and names of angels, as if these were highly consistent with their master Plato, who was a follower of Moses. <note>A common Renaissance belief held that Plato had traveled to Egypt and learned the wisdom of Moses (the *prisca theologia*).</note> For this reason, Aurelius Augustine, once a Platonist and then deliberating on the Christian profession, when he had happened upon these books of the Platonists and recognized that Christian truths were approved by them through imitation, gave thanks to God and was rendered more inclined to receive Christian teachings. How much the Platonic teachings are similar to the Christian ones, you will be able to understand briefly from the letter I wrote long ago to Braccio Martelli on this subject. I am now sending a copy of it to you. Farewell, and love me (as you usually do), who loves you vehemently. February 11, 1494.

---

-> *Something must always be done, and as far as possible, one must persevere in it.* <-

-> Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Callimachus, <note>Filippo Buonaccorsi, known as Callimachus Experiens, a prominent Italian humanist active in Poland.</note> the most learned man and best friend, sends greetings. <-

**S**ince this entire universe, of which we are in a sense parts, is always in motion, we certainly neither can nor ever should be free from action and movement—especially since the first and perpetual motion (as the Platonists believe) is natural to the soul itself. Life is nothing other than the motion and act of the soul, so that it is as necessary for it to move and act as it is for it to live, and it is equally to be desired. But am I not being foolish in the meantime? It would perhaps have been more opportune, after a long silence, to give you an account of our affairs and news of our health immediately through a letter, rather than to suddenly begin philosophizing. Certainly, it would have been more opportune, my dear Callimachus. But the cause for my philosophizing so importunately is both our long-standing habit and my own Genius. <note>original: "Genius"; refers to one's guiding spirit or natural inclination.</note> You also are accustomed to philosophize with us often through letters, but always in a timely and fitting manner. Let us proceed therefore for a little while (as we have already begun), and may we not be foolish: there are three principal motions in the universe according to place...

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>LETTERS, BOOK II</header>

Some things indeed revolve perpetually around the same center in the same way; others truly change their place and position continually; still others imitate that circular motion in part, and in part this straight motion. Men also pursue different movements. But to speak now of my own movement, not another's, it has certainly been granted to me that I always revolve around the same thing. What does Marsilio do today? The same as yesterday. What will he do tomorrow? Again, the same as today. Always, (as you see) I am turned within the walls of the academy <note>The Platonic Academy in Florence, centered at the Villa Medici at Careggi.</note> around the same center, and I revolve again. However, what I have done, redone, and woven again in this long-standing circuit, you will understand from the catalogue of my books, which I send to you to be read together with my book *On the Sun*, so that our friendship may shine forth to those present and to posterity by the most clear testimony of the gift of Phoebus <note>Apollo, or the Sun; Ficino often uses solar metaphors for intellectual clarity and divine gift.</note>. Moreover, I send a triple volume on the Sun and Light, so that I may not only please you, but that you also may be able to please two of your friends. Therefore, you yourself will perceive from these what things are being composed by us. I have indeed heard from your Octaviano and the Fedaldi that you have now settled your affairs, which has happened to me as a most welcome thing. Farewell happily. April 11, 1494.

->*The wise are the children of Minerva; she gives birth to Philosophy, and Philosophy to Philosophers.*<-

->*Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved brother, Germain de Ganay, sends greetings.*<-

**P**oets celebrate Minerva as a perpetual virgin; yet she brings forth among the gods or men no greater children, while her perpetual virginity is meanwhile preserved. Indeed, she herself was born from the head of supreme Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus; according to myth, Minerva (Athena) was born fully armed from Jupiter's forehead, symbolizing her nature as the goddess of wisdom and intellect.</note> alone, and in a similar way she generates from the head alone; she generates, I say, in place of the extinguished giants, wise men as if they were heroes greater than the giants. Philosophy also, a perpetual virgin and daughter of Sophia—that is, of Minerva—brings forth Philosophers from her crown <note>original: "uertice"; the top of the head.</note> on behalf of the wise. Greetings therefore again, my most beloved Germain <note>Germain de Ganay (d. 1520), a French high official and patron of humanists who sought Ficino's guidance in Platonic studies.</note>, whom our common mother Philosophy has truly fathered as a "germane" <note>Ficino plays on the name "Germanus" and the word for "blood brother" (germanus).</note> brother to me; since she never wished her sons to be separated from one another, she drew you (as you write) into a love for me by the light sent there, and she in turn has seized me into a love for you by the heat transmitted here from that very light. Since, truly, all things of friends—especially of brothers—ought to be common, I have decided that all my things shall be common to you according to your wish. Therefore, I shall first send to you the books of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whom Ficino and his contemporaries believed was the Athenian convert of St. Paul.</note>, whom many Platonists have already transcribed for you, which you have requested for a long time. Then, the commentaries on the *Parmenides* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of "The One" and the "Many."</note>, which are being transcribed daily for your sake. These will perhaps be followed by the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and the *Sophist*. Indeed, the *Sophist* is already rushing toward the end <note>original: "ad calcem"; literally "to the heel," a common idiom for the finish line.</note>; meanwhile, the letters are also being transcribed and revised like the rest. For I had perceived that you had Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino had published a massive translation and commentary on Plotinus in 1492.</note>, but recently you do not write that you have him. If you wish him to be sent, let me know. Farewell.

->*For the book "On the Sun."*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Lord Bernardo Bembo of Venice, sends greetings.<-

**V**ulgar love is often accustomed to grow cold, or even to be entirely erased, because of long absence and protracted silence. But that our love—being singular as it is—can neither ever be abandoned nor obliterated because of these things, let Phoebus himself be a pledge by his heat and a witness by his light. The 19th day.

->*For the book "On the Sun."*<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Lord Antonio Cronico of Venice, sends greetings.<-

**T**he ancients used to worship a certain "Friendly Jupiter" <note>original: "Iouem... amicabilem"; likely referring to Zeus Philios, the protector of friendship.</note> as the reconciler of friends and the preserver of friendship. But in what regions of the world does this Jupiter chiefly dwell? Perhaps he has placed his habitation in the Sun. For indeed, friendship (*amicitia*) is named from and derived from love (*amor*). Love, moreover, is a certain heat. But the love of a lover proceeds from knowledge and is fathered by beauty. Yet Apollo <note>The god of the Sun, often associated with intellectual light and physical heat.</note> above all others is the author of heat, of knowledge, and of beauty. Let the friendly Jupiter in this Apollonian gift <note>Referring to the book "On the Sun."</note> be a pledge of our friendship. August 19, 1494.

He employs solar metaphors to describe intellectual kinship and the divine origin of wisdom.</summary>

# What he thinks about Astrology.
## Marsilio Ficino to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

**A**gainst many Astrologers, who in the manner of the giants <note>Referring to the Gigantomachy, the mythological battle where giants tried to overthrow the Olympian gods.</note> strive to snatch heaven from Jove as fruitlessly as they do impiously, both Pico, the foster-son of Pallas, and you, a Herculean soldier, often and successfully do battle. Indeed, Orpheus sings of Pallas <note>Athena</note> as the expeller of giants, and many poets tell of the giant Antaeus being lifted by Hercules from the earth and from life at once. But what of me? Truly, just as I am of one mind with you in every aspect of life, in this study also I conspire with you; and if perhaps I do not fight as strenuously, yet I judge just as clearly. Other Platonists, to be sure, mention the celestial images which the Astronomers describe when the opportunity arises, neither reproaching them nor, on the other hand, striving to approve them. But Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated.</note> laughs at such things beyond any controversy. I too, in my commentaries upon him, as his interpreter, mock them equally—partly trusting in his authority, and partly because I have no certain proof of that kind. Furthermore, in that same work, I bring many of the rules of the Astrologers into question by similar reasoning. 

But in my book *On Life* <note>Referring to *De vita libri tres* (Three Books on Life), where Ficino discusses how scholars can use astral influences to maintain their health.</note>, where I profess medicine and seek out remedies for life, whatever and of what kind they may be, I diligently search everywhere. I do not utterly despise those images, nor do I reject all the rules. For even if I think there is no certain reason in them, yet as a most studious curator of human medicine, I pursue remedies that are not only certain to the wise, but also probable to many, so that I may accumulate aids from all sides that might be profitable in any way. Finally, lest I should leave anything untried that might seem to anyone to be of use to life in some way, I nonetheless interweave some firmer things, and also gather many things here and there which, even if I perhaps have less hope for them, I nonetheless wish to be helpful. 

As for what I seem to say at the beginning of the third book—that images were placed in the heavens by the older Platonists—I do not actually mean that. For it is not my intention there to affirm that the Platonists were supporters of celestial images, about which they say little or nothing. Rather, it was the opinion of certain Platonists that the Soul of the World produced celestial bodies for itself, and created the stars along with the heavens, and beyond the individual stars (if indeed there are any images there), it also produced images of that kind. I describe there the arrangements of the signs and images not as you would find among the Platonists, but as you would observe among the Astrologers. Now, as to how much I believe in these images—whether celestial or made by art—the progression of the book declares. 

Furthermore, in my book *On the Sun* <note>*De Sole*, a work blending astronomy, theology, and Neoplatonic light metaphysics.</note>, I do not teach Astronomy so much as I seek out moral and divine allegories through these things. Finally, in the books *On Life* as well as *On the Sun* and *On Light*, mixing poetic things with philosophical ones, I have sometimes wandered quite freely and perhaps even licentiously. I deal more sparingly and severely with Plotinus, so that in the end it will not be ungrateful to me that the astrological portents have been singularly refuted by our friend Pico della Mirandola <note>Pico's massive work *Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem* was a major attack on judicial astrology.</note>. For those things which I nowhere affirm—indeed, which I mock along with Plotinus—I rejoice to see exploded by Mirandola. I congratulate you, Poliziano, that the superstitious vanity is being extinguished by him like the Pythonic poison <note>original: "Pithonicum uirus"; a reference to the serpent Python slain by Apollo (the Sun god).</note> by Phoebus. For you have always, in this cause (as you are accustomed to do everywhere), acted the part of Hercules. Indeed, for a long time now you have been accustomed to hunt down these prodigies of the Astrologers, like other monsters, so fiercely that you—a most brave Hercules—have conquered monsters not only on earth, but even in the heavens. May the stars at last grant you, as they did Hercules, a place among them once the earth is overcome; meanwhile, live long upon the earth. Farewell happily. 

The 20th of August, 1494.

# For the book *On the Sun*.
## Marsilio Ficino to Bernardo Rucellai, son of Mariotto, Greetings.

**S**ince I both wish for light for my friends and desire to reveal them by means of light, I have for a long time now taken care that my books *On the Sun* and *On Light* should be in the hands of all my friends. Surely you also, my sweetest Bernardo <note>Bernardo Rucellai, a prominent Florentine statesman and scholar.</note>, come now to be presented with this gift—recently loved by us because you were recently known, yet to be loved not only now but always. Moreover, that I love you vehemently is due not only to your elegant talent and integrity, but also because you are very dear to Girolamo Rossi, who is the dearest of all to me and, above all others, most worthy of light. But so that [I may say] something with you regarding light...

If at any point during your reading you should hesitate where we say the Sun or light was created first, I ask you to take care: perhaps you should not understand that the Sun, or the light of the Sun, was made in the very first moment or stage of creation, since Moses himself says: <note>original: "In principio creauit Deus coelum & terrā."</note> *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. ### *Recommendation of a client to a Magistrate.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Benino, a man gifted in letters and character, Greetings.<-

**I**t was certainly my duty, from the very start of your term in office, to congratulate you greatly—given our significant friendship—not only because you have been honored with this dignity, but even more so because you are the kind of man who will conduct this office with dignity. I also ought to have congratulated my friends and clients; for if they were innocent, they would find a protector in you, and if they were guilty, they would at least find a certain indulgence and clemency. For I know your nature. I know for certain that you will (as God himself commands by his actions) rightly join justice with clemency. Furthermore, if one may speak somewhat playfully regarding Jupiter in this matter, the Hebrews call him <term>Sedech<note>Ficino refers to the Hebrew word 'Tzedek' (צדק), which means 'Justice' and is the Hebrew name for the planet Jupiter.</note></term>, which means "Justice," and Astronomers grant laws and statutes to their Jupiter. The poets sing of the same Jupiter as being full of indulgence—to say nothing of that poetic line which leans more toward license than indulgence: *Jupiter decreed that whatever was helpful was pious.* <note>Ficino is likely paraphrasing Ovid, suggesting that in some poetic interpretations, Jupiter's "clemency" is actually just doing whatever feels good, which Ficino distinguishes from true judicial mercy.</note> Let it suffice among the Astrologers that Jupiter brings or signifies clemency along with the laws; in this, God truly seems to have warned men from heaven that they should mix both equally in their magistracy. But these things you know well enough through your own natural talent (as I believe). Fare well and happily in Florence. August 31, 1494.

### *Giving thanks for the mercy obtained for a client.*

->Marsilio Ficino to Niccolò Benino, a man gifted in letters and character, Greetings.<-

**S**ince good and evil are opposed to one another, and therefore undergo opposite conditions, it seems likely that if "the good" is so fertile, "the evil" should by contrast be sterile. Indeed, as much as a crime is an evil, so much is clemency a good; therefore it is necessary that merciful indulgence be far more fertile than the crime or offense. For this reason, if my client’s offense gave birth to my first letter to you, much more so ought your liberal and gentle indulgence give birth to a second letter in return—and one much better and greater. The first was (if I may say so) "Jovian," <note>Relating to Jove/Jupiter, the planet of law and justice.</note> relying on a comparison with Jupiter; the second, therefore, shall surpass the first, or at least equal it, if it is "Apollonian." <note>Relating to Apollo, associated with the Sun, which Ficino considered superior to Jupiter in his Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> For only the Sun can surpass Jupiter. Therefore, so that this letter may sufficiently fulfill my duty to you under Apollonian auspices, I send it to you as a companion of Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo as the sun-god.</note> and a handmaid of the Sun. Read gladly our book *On the Sun* <note>Referring to Ficino's "De Sole," a treatise on the physical and spiritual properties of the Sun.</note> which is given to you as a gift, and live happily. September 3, 1494.

### *On Friendly Jupiter and Apollo, regarding the book "On the Sun."*

## Oration of Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Jean Matheron, the illustrious envoy of the great King of the French.

**T**he ancient theologians first, and then the poets, worshipped "Friendly Jupiter" among the other divinities, as the father of chaste love and of the firmest friendship. He received this name "Friendly" from both love and friendship alike. Since our Plato also mentions this divinity from time to time, I have often asked myself while commenting on him by what other name I might more clearly call this God. Finally, after long meditation, it came to mind that I should call this most clear God "Apollo"—the source of light, heat, harmony, and knowledge. For indeed, we never love things that are unknown, nor do we know anything without light, nor are we ever provoked to love without a certain heat. Furthermore, a certain harmonic congruence is necessary for love and friendship. Again, for love, beauty of the body is often desired. For friendship, they always seek...
