...inner beauty is desired; however, both <note>Refers to inner beauty of the soul and outer physical beauty.</note> seem to be nothing other than a certain splendor. Apollo is the author of this splendor. Therefore, all lines of reasoning compel us to name Apollo as the chief source of love and friendship. If, for the sake of conversation, we perhaps accept the number of the Gentile <note>original: "Gentiliũ"; referring to the non-Christian, Greco-Roman gods.</note> gods in the ancient manner, we shall say that Phoebus is a certain god or divine power set over the Sun, a king among the celestial bodies; but if we rely instead on serious reason, we shall assert that Phoebus is the High God, of whom the celestial Sun is the image. Therefore, that Phoebus is the author of honorable love and firm friendship, while the Sun is the signifier. Since, therefore, I am singularly inflamed by a certain "Phoeban" splendor of your wisdom and virtues, I love you ardently, and I desire to forge a friendship out of that love; and so I come to you under the auspices of Apollo. Greetings.

->It is to be highly valued to be praised by a man who is himself praised.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Germain de Ganay, <note>original: "Germano Ganiensi"; Germain de Ganay (d. 1520) was a French high official and patron of humanism.</note> a man of outstanding virtue, sends many greetings.<-

**W**hat I had long ago heard from many people regarding your excellent virtue and dignity, Cosimo de' Pazzi <note>original: "Cosmus Saffectus"; Cosimo de' Pazzi was the Bishop of Arezzo and a student of Ficino.</note> and Lorenzo Spinelli have recently confirmed for me with much testimony—both noble men and certainly the most reliable witnesses in this matter. They told me, moreover, how much you value me and how ardently you love me. Truly, I value it most highly to be approved and loved by you, who are most worthy of praise and love above others; therefore, as much as it is a pleasure for you to look upon our affairs, so much is it desirable for us to gratify you entirely. You will soon see (I hope) some of our "Platonists" <note>term: <term>Platonicos</term>; here referring to Ficino's translations or commentaries on Plato's works.</note> coming to you from here. You would also have seen the Areopagite, <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whom Ficino and his contemporaries believed was a direct disciple of St. Paul and the "pinnacle" of Platonic philosophy.</note> the very summit of the Platonists, at the same time, if he could have arrived now in the dress that was fitting for both him and you; but the negligence of the scribe and the book-binder hindered his arrival. He will come in a few days (I hope) with letters. The commentary on the *Parmenides* has already been copied for you. Every day, the commentary on the *Timaeus* is being rewritten. Farewell, be happy, and (as you have begun) my dearest Germain, I pray you love your Marsilio, who is your "brother" <note>A pun in the original: "Marsilium germanum... tuum." "Germanus" means "brother" or "true," playing on Germain de Ganay’s name.</note> under Plato and who loves you ardently. October 16, 1484.

->An apology for a late greeting, on behalf of the book *On the Christian Religion*.<-

->Marsilio Ficino to Giovanni Stefano, <note>Giovanni Stefano Castiglione, the Milanese ambassador to the Florentine Republic.</note> most illustrious knight and Milanese ambassador, sends many greetings.<-

**E**ven if your virtue and dignity, as well as my great love for you, have long demanded that I should greet you of my own accord and frequently, the crowd of your business affairs prevented me from interrupting you except for some necessary matter. Now, therefore, since I think you may perhaps have less business, and our own situation requires it (as has long been fitting), I greet you. May you always be well in God himself, the author of eternal salvation, <note>original: "salutis"; in Latin, this word means both "health/well-being" and "salvation." Ficino is playing on the dual meaning.</note> O man most worthy of the well-being of all. Indeed, I did not wish to approach a man full of virtue and dignity empty-handed, nor to come to the renowned ambassador of the most illustrious Duke without a guide. Therefore, Christ, full of truth and grace, leads me in this presence, as I bring with me a book treating the Christian religion. I pray that the humble and poor appearance of the book does not offend you, since the Christian religion both teaches humility above all else and gladly tolerates poverty. Entirely, however, a book composed with Christian piety befits you, a man distinguished for piety. Furthermore, perfect love seems to desire two things most of all: I mean ardor and firmness. Certainly, how ardently I love you can be testified to by that Sun of ours that is with you, the source of light and heat; but how firm our love for you will be, this present book on religion shall be a proof and a pledge in your hands. For nothing is firmer than religious piety; "charity never fails." <note>A quote from 1 Corinthians 13:8.</note> Farewell, be happy, and I pray you love me, who have long loved you ardently. November 4, 1484.

### Oration of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Charles the Great, <note>Referring to Charles VIII of France (r. 1483–1498), who invaded Italy in 1494.</note> King of the French.

**Y**our exalted majesty, O King Charles, ever unconquered, is sometimes accustomed to say (as many have) that you are sent by divine providence on this expedition. Which we, and this entire Florentine people of yours, undoubtedly believe, firmly hope for, and vehemently celebrate. For it is likely both that a Most Christian King of the French is sent by Christ, and that a King Charles, <note>Ficino likely draws a parallel here between Charles VIII and his ancestor Charlemagne (Carolus Magnus).</note> distinguished above others for piety, should be led by Christian piety, especially since you have undertaken so great a journey and work with the intention of [delivering] Holy Jerusalem from the most cruel...

...occupied by barbarians, and finally redeem it for the supreme redeemer of the human race. Indeed, we hope that you will easily redeem that holy kingdom. Having first received your hereditary kingdom <note>Referring to the Kingdom of Naples, which Charles VIII claimed by dynastic right, sparking his Italian campaign.</note> for the sake of the journey, you may then follow the footsteps of Christ everywhere on this path according to your strength. Christ, the peaceful king, often promises peace to those who desire it; you also, the most Christian king endowed with singular piety, promise the same, (as we hear and as we hope) and you will certainly provide it. Indeed, you shall in truth do that which was once commanded by the father <note>Anchises, in Virgil’s Aeneid.</note> to pious Aeneas and the race of the Aeneadae:
**To spare the subjected, and to war down the proud.** <note>original: "Parcere subiectis, & debellare superbos." A famous line from Virgil's Aeneid (6.853), defining the Roman imperial mission.</note>
Wherefore, since you shall be the author of peace for all who desire it, you will show yourself peaceful especially to your own—that is, to us. You will visit your city of Florence with wondrous piety—Florence, named for the flower, that is, for the lily, and full of lilies everywhere. <note>The "lily" (fleur-de-lis) was the symbol of both the French monarchy and the city of Florence (the giglio).</note> You shall come unto your own, and your people will receive you with their whole mind. You, however, imitating your leader Christ, will cry out to the people: **Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.** <note>original: "Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam uos." A quote from Matthew 11:28.</note> Therefore, the people of the present and the future will forever celebrate the gracious King Charles—named for charity and grace—with these voices: **Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.** <note>original: "Benedictus qui uenit in nomine Domini." A traditional messianic greeting from Psalm 118 and the Gospels.</note> Charles, dear to us, exalted, the peaceful king. **This is the day the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.** <note>original: "Haec est dies, quam fecit Dominus..." from Psalm 118:24.</note> These things, I say, the Florentine people of the present and future will proclaim concerning your splendor. Moreover, the whole world and the common history of all men will (as I judge) soon recount what I say: Charles, the unconquered King of the Gauls, so far surpassed that Caesarean saying—great in word, but greatest in deed—**I came, I saw, I conquered**, <note>original: "Veni, Vidi, Vici"; the famous boast of Julius Caesar.</note> that he can now rightly say: "I have not yet come, nor yet seen, but I have already conquered." He has even surpassed that Hercules so celebrated among all men; for Hercules is said to have fought with hands, fire, iron, a club, and great labors. But Charles the Great, <note>Ficino punningly links Charles VIII to "Carolus Magnus" (Charlemagne).</note> not indeed with so many machines, but almost like Jove, shakes the world with a mere nod (if I may say so), so that he seems worthy of being called at some time the Lord not only of Gaul, but even of the world. For the exalted Charles seems to have been sent by divine providence to tame the Turks, and to vindicate holy Jerusalem from manifest enemies, just as Almighty God himself liberated the human race from hidden enemies.

### Why providence permits adversity. Also concerning prophecies and the remedies for evils.

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Cavalcanti, <note>Giovanni Cavalcanti (1444–1509) was Ficino’s most intimate friend, often called his "unique friend" (amico unico) and the dedicatee of many of his works.</note> his unique friend, sends many greetings.<-

**I**t is often asked by the Platonists why divine providence always permits men to be agitated by innumerable evils, the just and the unjust alike? They are accustomed to respond to these things briefly. First, indeed, that it is unknown to mortals whether these things are evils or goods. For human affairs are like shadows, and thoughts like dreams. To this point tends that Prophetic saying: **All is vanity. Every man is a liar.** <note>A combination of Ecclesiastes 1:2 and Psalm 116:11.</note> Again they respond that even if it were established that the things which seem evil are in some way actually evil, ultimately evil is permitted by the highest good itself only for the sake of the good. For difficult and adverse things purge a curable vice, while they punish an incurable one. In the former case, the good of purgation shines forth; in the latter, the good of justice. Furthermore, good men are discerned from the wicked in adversity, and are exercised and proven. Moreover, proof, progress, and constancy are a good. It is worthwhile, besides, to carefully consider that Platonic saying in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul and love.</note> concerning the poisonous craftiness of the evil demon. A certain demon immediately from the beginning mixed pleasure into vices, which he mingled with many things. These things Socrates says there, warning that the chief study of evil demons is to detain souls longer in this exile, separated from the heavenly fatherland and forgetting the supernal father, and to devise long delays with earthly enticements and delights. By these delights, indeed—as if by the cups of the sorceress Circe <note>In Greek mythology, Circe turned men into beasts with a magic drink.</note> or the sleep-inducing songs of the Sirens—the souls are soothed so that they never, or certainly only much later, return to the heavenly fatherland. Against these demonic snares, the beneficial providence of God ordained that bitter flavors be mixed in with these lethal flavors, lest we be captured by that kind of pleasure (which the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos.</note> calls the "bait of evils") like fish by a hook. The Platonists, especially Plotinus and Synesius, <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Synesius of Cyrene was a Neoplatonist philosopher who became a Christian bishop.</note> think for the most part that this is the reason why divine providence wished for souls on earth to be vexed by so many and such great perturbations. To this point tends that Platonic saying in the book on knowledge <note>Referring to Plato's *Theaetetus*.</note> (consistent with the Gospel) which I wrote to you long ago, my dearest Giovanni, and briefly declared. He says, "It is impossible, Theodoretus, <note>Ficino likely means Theodorus, the interlocutor in the *Theaetetus*.</note> for evils to be utterly rooted out; for it is always necessary..."

Ficino shifts from his political address to King Charles VIII to a letter addressed to his close friend and "intellectual twin," Giovanni Cavalcanti, attempting to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christian theology regarding why God allows suffering and how prophecy functions.</meta>

<page-num>962</page-num>
<header>->MARSILIO FICINO<-</header>
<meta>Catchword: of wisdom</meta>

...as being through something sub-contrary to the good <note>original: "per aliquid bono subcontrarium esse." In logic, "sub-contraries" are opposites that can exist together; here, Ficino argues that evil is not a primary force but an opposition that only appears in the lower, material world.</note>; certainly, evils cannot exist among the higher beings. But they necessarily revolve through mortal nature and this lower place. For which reason we must strive to flee from here to that place as quickly as possible. To flee to that place, however, is to make oneself similar to God according to one's strength; and justice, holiness, and **prudence** <note>original: "prudentia," referring to practical wisdom or moral discernment.</note> make us similar to God. Plato declares these things, stating that we meditate on this flight from here to God for this primary reason: so that we may escape the evils which necessarily afflict us here, so that from this mortal evil we might bring back that everlasting good. 

Indeed, no one recognizes the arrival of the doctor unless they are vexed by disease, nor do sailors admire the **prudence** of the pilot unless they are tossed by the waves. Mortals are surely so dull that they do not recognize the good from any other source than the comparison of evils; they are so ungrateful that they do not easily worship God, the giver of all good things, unless they are oppressed by evils. Therefore, tortured by frequent diseases and disturbances, they are compelled to flee to God himself as if to a doctor and a helper. They are also forced to recognize that the earthly province where they are constantly distressed and never truly at rest is not their homeland, but rather the celestial one. 

Indeed, no better cause can be assigned for why God permits evils and adversity than the <term>Evangelical reason</term> <note>Referring to the Gospel of John 9:3, where Jesus explains that a man was born blind so "the works of God might be displayed in him."</note> which teaches that the blind and the mutilated are sometimes born so that the admirable power and goodness of God may be declared to men—namely, that He will heal those who are incurably ill among men. Just as not every disease or wave, but only the most severe ones, usually testify to the supreme doctor or pilot. Often, therefore, men both privately and publicly are so constrained on all sides by extreme narrowness that no exit is open, and no human safety is now hoped for; yet the divine goodness and power, extending a propitious hand from on high to His children who are humbly entreating with a pious mind, declares that God alone is the savior in extreme calamities. 

And He demonstrates this more clearly when He has predicted through some Prophet that such great dangers, which are coming, would occur long before they arrived. It is the duty of a human doctor, even if he cannot provide health, at least to always provide a **prognosis**. It is the duty of the Divine, however, to embrace both equally. And although many examples of these things can be brought from the sacred scriptures, which are ready at hand for everyone, it is my intention at present—as it has always been—to bring to light things that are less known, and to confirm **Christian mysteries** through **Platonic** ones as much as I can. 

Listen then, my Giovanni—a worshipper of divine things as much as a student of Platonic ones—to the words with which Socrates, in Plato's writings, confirms the divine plan regarding the remedies for human evils and the Prophets; for thus he speaks in the *Symposium*: 

> <insert>The priestess Diotima, a prophetic woman and skilled in divine matters, predicted an imminent plague to the Athenians.</insert> <note>Diotima of Mantinea is the woman who taught Socrates the philosophy of Love in Plato's "Symposium."</note> Thus, having performed sacrifices ten years before the plague, she granted a delay of the disease. 

Likewise in the *Phaedrus*: 

> If we recall the **Sibyl** <note>A generic term for ancient prophetesses believed to be inspired by a deity.</note> and others whoever used prophecy, how many things they predicted that benefited the future, we would extend our speech far too long and bring forth a matter manifest to everyone. 

And a little later, he says: 

> The ancients testify that prophecy, proceeding from a certain <term>divine madness</term> <note>original: "divino quodam furore." For Ficino, this 'madness' or 'frenzy' is a state of being possessed by God, raising the soul above human reason.</note>, is far more excellent than human conjecture and prudence. 

And yet, against the most severe diseases and labors hanging over mortals sometimes by divine indignation because of ancient sins, a **divine madness** arriving to certain nations from elsewhere and predicting future things wonderfully found the remedies which were needed, fleeing to divine vows and worship. From this source, having obtained expiations and propitiations, it restored the possessor to safety, having obtained an absolution of present evils for both the present time and the future for the one who was rightly "maddened" and occupied [by the divine]. 

Furthermore, in the first book of the *Laws*, Plato says this: 

> **Epimenides of Crete** <note>A semi-mythical 6th-century BCE seer and philosopher.</note>, a divine man, warned by a divine oracle ten years before the Persian War, arrived at Athens and performed certain sacrifices commanded by the divine oracle; and to the Athenians who were fearing the Persian fleet, he predicted that the Persians would not come for ten years, and after they had come, they would depart without having accomplished their task. 

Plato certainly judges such a man to be the wisest of all, even though he is often commonly held to be the most foolish. Therefore, in the *Phaedrus*, he writes something wonderful in this manner: 

> He who rightly uses divine meditations and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, alone truly turns out perfect; but being separated from human studies and clinging to the divine, he is rebuked by the multitude as if he were out of his mind; but he, being full of God, is hidden from the multitude. 

After this, Plato, [discussing] the Prophet and the priest occupied with divine things...

<summary>Ficino argues that God allows evil and suffering to lead humans back to the divine and to demonstrate His power through healing. He uses Platonic examples like Diotima and Epimenides to show how "divine madness" and prophecy serve as a bridge between human distress and divine intervention.</summary>

...having placed it far above human wisdom by a very great interval, he describes a mind burning with a truly divine love, experiencing an amatory ecstasy, as well as a madness and alienation of this kind, which he prefers not only to human **prudence** <note>original: "prudentiæ," or practical wisdom.</note>, but even to all other divine gifts. In this, he clearly confirms that Apostolic saying: *The greatest of these is charity.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:13. Ficino frequently aligns Platonic "divine madness" with Christian "charity" or love.</note> That Prophets are sent by God, and the reason why they are sent, is a point where **Avicenna** <note>An influential Persian philosopher (Ibn Sina) whose work on the soul and prophecy was often synthesized with Plato by Renaissance thinkers.</note> also agrees with Plato through many arguments in his *Book of Divine Things*. 

But, setting aside longer digressions for now, let us return briefly to the matter at hand. It is certainly worthy of no small notice that Plato says in his earlier works that God, being indignant because of ancient sins, had in a way destined calamities for mankind. From this is asserted that oracle: *adversity comes because of sins.* Also that Mosaic teaching: *that all adversities have befallen us from the sin of our first parents.* <note>Referring to the Fall of Adam and Eve in Genesis.</note> Where Plato further adds that God, moved by a certain mercy, frequently inspires Prophets to announce future scourges to us, so that being warned by this, we may flee to vows and sacred expiations; when these are duly performed, we frequently escape unharmed. In this, he truly seems to confirm all the mysteries of our Church. 

Furthermore, lest examples of such a great matter be sought from too far away: was it not because of many sins that total destruction loomed over this city this autumn, a destruction absolutely unavoidable by any human virtue? Did not the divine mercy, most indulgent toward the **Florentines** <note>The people of Florence.</note>, foretell this very thing to us four full years before this autumn? This was done through a man outstanding in holiness and wisdom, **Jerome of the Order of Preachers** <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar who became the de facto spiritual leader of Florence. Ficino here credits Savonarola’s prophecies for saving the city from the French King Charles VIII.</note>, chosen by God for this purpose. Have we not, through the fulfillment of the divine presages and warnings given through him, wonderfully avoided the destruction even now hanging over our heads—a destruction absolutely unavoidable by our own power, but escaped beyond our hope and expectation? *This was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes.* <note>A quote from Psalm 118:23.</note> 

It remains, my dearest Giovanni, that from now on, obeying the saving counsels of such a great man, not only you and I, but all Florentines, may become grateful to God, who is most merciful to us, and cry out with a public voice: *Confirm, O God, this work which you have performed in us.* <note>A quote from Psalm 68:28.</note>

### *Congratulations for long-awaited letters.*
->Marsilio Ficino to his most beloved Germain de Ganay, sends greetings.<-

**T**he same injustice of these stormy times has often intercepted both your letters to me and mine to you. Yesterday at last, devotion conquered the hard journey and granted me your long-expected letter. Arise now, my present letter; now use better fates for our honor. But what shall I write first? Certainly that which first occurred to me as most pleasing: namely, that I have been commended through your letter to your brother **Jean** <note>Jean de Ganay, a high-ranking French legal official.</note>, the royal **official** <note>original: "Achati regio," likely implying a loyal counselor or "Achates" to the King.</note> currently in Paris. That was and will be of great value to us. For almost all of Italy, certainly all of Tuscany, and especially Florence, is agitated daily by both external and internal tumults. I indeed met our Jean here with your exalted King in recent days, a man most worthy of frequent greeting. I rejoiced at the sight of him, not only because of his own brilliance, but also greatly because in your excellent brother I seemed to see my dearest friend, comforting me meanwhile in these present hardships. Therefore, even if our profession is the work of a tranquil mind, I nevertheless persist among these noises in my **Platonic commentaries** <note>Ficino was working on his massive translation and explanation of Plato's works.</note> as diligently as I can, intending to finish them soon (if God breathes upon the work).

### *The pious opinion of Plato, concerning the friends and enemies of God.*
->Marsilio Ficino to his unique friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, sends greetings.<-

**I** conferred yesterday with you and with your son-in-law **Gherardo Gianfigliazzi** <note>original: "Gerardo Ianfilatio."</note> regarding what Plato thinks in the *Philebus* about the friends or enemies of God. These are the words of Plato: *Is not the just, pious, and upright man a friend to God? And the unjust and wicked man an enemy? Certainly. Each one is led by a very great hope. For there are certain internal discourses in each of us, which...*

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s philosophical commentary on the relationship between divine friendship and the human psyche, specifically focusing on how the virtuous possess "true" hopes compared to the "false" pleasures of the wicked. It also contains the concluding letters of Book XII of his "Familiar Letters," addressed to French dignitaries following his retreat from Florence during the political upheavals of 1494.</meta>

<page-num>964</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...and what we are accustomed to call opinions and hopes are, furthermore, like **painted fantasies** <note>original: "Phantasmata picta." Ficino is using a Platonic metaphor where the soul "paints" images of its expectations.</note>. For anyone is permitted to imagine that they possess a massive pile of gold, abounding in various delights, and are drenched in every sweetness. Must we not say that opinions and imaginations of this kind frequently turn out to be true for good men, because they are **friends of God**? But for the wicked, are they not frequently false? It must certainly be said. Indeed, certain pleasures are present to depraved men, often fabricated, and ultimately false; therefore, the wicked frequently exult in false pleasures. Good men, however, are always nourished by true joys. Thus far Plato. Our exposition follows. A good man is judged by Plato to be one who is indeed temperate within himself, pious toward God, and just toward men. Because of this likeness, such a soul is a friend to God above all others, while the evil man, because of unlikeness, is an enemy. Therefore, since God both moves us from within and provides for us everywhere, it is no wonder that the opinions, imaginations, and hopes of good men frequently turn out to be true, while those of the wicked are false. Both groups devise, desire, and hope for certain joys; for good men, as they are divine and truth-telling, these often happen truly. For the wicked, however, they are false; for the wicked are, as it were, liars to themselves. Just as they are frequently deceived in opinion, so they more often fabricate false delights. Finally, if hopes ought not to succeed for the depraved, as they are in discord with **divine truth** <note>original: "divina veritate"</note>, yet they often seem to have success in external matters; it follows at least that they do not succeed inwardly. Therefore, they are always troubled and languishing within, and their pleasures are like the false pleasures of the sick, the dreaming, or the insane. December 20, 1494.

### For the book *On the Sun*.
### Marsilio Ficino to Jean de Ganay, most worthy President in Paris, sends greetings.

**S**ince, on account of the crowd of guests in my home and public tumults, I was unable to practice philosophy there in tranquility, yet I did not wish to interrupt my perpetual philosophical duty, I have withdrawn from the city into **rural solitude** <note>Ficino likely retreated to his villa at Careggi or another country estate to escape the "public tumults"—the invasion of the French army and the expulsion of the Medici from Florence in late 1494.</note>. But before I departed, I often sought your splendor, which I have long desired. To you, whom I have not yet greeted in person, I send this greeting from afar with a certain **Phoebian gift** <note>original: "munere quodam Phœbeo." A reference to his work *De Sole* (On the Sun), as Phoebus is a name for the Sun god Apollo.</note>. For if **Phoebus** <term>Phoebus: a classical name for the sun, representing divine light and intellectual clarity</term> himself does not happen to touch something with his globe, he nevertheless touches everything with his rays; likewise, your own splendor has touched me with its rays even until now. Through that very heat of Phoebian light, I beseech you, my most splendid Jean, to love Marsilio, who loves you ardently. Farewell.

### For the book *On the Sun*.
### Marsilio Ficino to Paul of Verona, a man of distinguished learning, sends greetings.

**I** was indeed able to see you in Florence, and that happened to be quite pleasing to me. It would also have been most pleasing to visit the President in Paris, a man most worthy of being seen. Although, if you are both bound by such **charity** (as I believe) that one exists within the other, when I first looked upon Paul, I saw Jean within Paul. Thus truly, while Phoebus looks upon the outside with his splendor, he meanwhile (so to speak) looks within with his heat. Finally, through this Phoebian gift, which I also send to you, I vehemently beseech you to frequently commend me to the "Apolline" Jean. Farewell.

<page-num>965</page-num>
->BOOK OF THE SUN.<-

In this little work on the Sun and light, there are certain things which are also found in other works of Marsilio; but since the author himself wrote this compendium wishing, no doubt, to gratify and advise those who were not able to have his large volumes, we have wished to change nothing.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## On the book of the Sun to the magnanimous
### Piero de’ Medici,
### PREFACE.

**I** am daily pursuing the new interpretation of Plato, <note>Marsilio Ficino spent much of his life translating and commentating on Plato’s works under the patronage of the Medici family.</note> which has long been undertaken under your auspices, Magnanimous Piero; <note>Piero de' Medici (1472–1503), known as "Piero the Unfortunate," the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note> and (as is well known to you) I explain it with frequent distinctions of the sections and with longer arguments, insofar as the subject itself requires. Thus, when I recently came to that Platonic mystery where he most skillfully compares the Sun to God himself, it pleased me to explain so great a matter somewhat more extensively, especially because our Dionysius the Areopagite, <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic whom Ficino believed was a student of St. Paul and a "Christian Platonist."</note> the first of the Platonists, whose interpretation I have in hand, gladly embraces a similar comparison of the Sun to God. Therefore, while I worked by this Sun as if by a lamp for many nights now, I thought to select this most choice material from the great work and to commend it in its own compendium. And I thought to send this mystery concerning the Sun, like a gift from Phoebus <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, the god of the Sun and the arts.</note>, especially to you, a student of Phoebus the leader of the Muses, and a patron of the Muses, to whom also this entire new interpretation of Plato is dedicated. This is so that in the meantime, by this light, you might foresee—as if by a certain Moon—what the whole Platonic work will be like, just as the Sun relates to the Moon; and if ever you have loved my Plato, or rather your Plato for a long time now, you may hereafter, kindled by this light, love him more ardently and embrace the beloved with your whole mind.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Words to the reader, that this book is
### allegorical and anagogical rather than dog-
### matic, Chapter I.

**I**t is a Pythagorean precept, magnanimous Piero, and indeed a divine one, that one must not speak of divine matters and mysteries without light. In these words (as I judge), that wise man signifies not only that nothing should be attempted in divine matters unless the light of God itself has opened it to minds inspired from that source, but he also seems to warn that we should not proceed to the hidden light of divine things—either to perceive it or to declare it—without the comparison of this manifest light. From this light, therefore, we shall approach that one to the best of our ability, not so much by reasons at present as by certain comparisons drawn from light. But in the meantime, you, most careful reader—and I hope most indulgent toward us—remembering that these things are permitted under the Sun in an Apollonian and, as it were, poetic manner, do not hereafter demand from us more severe and (as the Greeks say) <note>original: "Gręci aiunt." Ficino is referring to the Greek term *dogmatika*.</note> dogmatic things. Indeed, I have promised only an allegorical and <term>anagogical</term> <note>anagogical: A method of spiritual interpretation that "leads upward," seeking to explain how earthly things point toward the divine or the afterlife.</note> exercise of wits, with Phoebus—whose gifts these are—acting as guarantor. The Muses never dispute with Apollo, but they sing. Even Mercury himself, the first inventor of disputations, although he treats grave matters with Saturn or Jupiter, nevertheless plays with Apollo. Those gods indeed joke not only aptly, but divinely. I hope that we, at least, may play not inaptly. But now, let us go forth into the light to perform these preludes of ours, of whatever kind they may be, with the Good itself—that is, the highest God—happily inspiring us.

<page-num>966</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO<-

## How the light of the Sun is similar to the Good itself, namely to God. Chapter II.

**N**othing represents the nature of the Good <note>The "Good" refers to the Platonic concept of the ultimate source of all being and value, often identified by Ficino with God.</note> more than light. First, indeed, light in the realm of the senses appears the most pure and most eminent. Second, it is spread most easily of all things, most widely, and in an instant. Third, it meets all things without harm and penetrates them; it is most gentle and most alluring. Fourth, it carries with it a life-giving heat, fostering, generating, and moving all things. Fifth, while it is present and within all things, it is defiled by none and mixed with none. Similarly, the Good itself towers over the entire order of things, spreads most widely, and soothes and attracts all things. It compels nothing; it has love, like heat, as its companion everywhere, by which it entices individual things here and there, and they willingly adopt the Good. Being most present in the innermost parts of things everywhere, it has no commerce <note>In the sense of "mixture" or "pollution" by material things.</note> with them. Finally, just as the Good itself is beyond estimation and ineffable, so is light nearly the same. For no philosopher has yet defined this, so that nothing is clearer than light in some respects, yet nothing again seems more obscure—just as the Good is both the most known of all things and equally the most unknown. 

For this reason, Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino's views on theurgy and the divinity of the cosmos.</note> the Platonist finally took refuge in this: he called light a certain act and a visible image of the divine intelligence. Just as a ray flashing from the sight is an image of the sight itself. Perhaps, truly, light is the celestial soul's own sight, or the very act of vision extended to the exterior, acting from a distance while meanwhile not leaving the heaven, but always continuous there, not mixed with exterior things—acting by seeing and touching at the same time. At least we are accustomed to call light a certain trace of the world’s life, as if it were offering itself to our eyes in a certain proportion; or like a vital spirit <term>spiritum uitalem</term> <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, "spirit" is the subtle medium that links the immaterial soul to the material body.</note> between the soul and the body of the world. 

But of this we have said enough in our *Theology*. <note>A reference to Ficino's major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note> Therefore, when you strive to affirm many angelic minds above the heaven as if they were lights, and their order both among themselves and toward the one God, the Father of Lights, why will you need long, winding paths of investigation? Look up at the heaven, I pray, citizen of the heavenly fatherland; the heaven was made by God in a most orderly way and most openly to declare this very thing clearly. Therefore, as you look upward, the celestial things immediately declare the glory of God through the rays of the stars themselves—as if they were the gazes and nods of His eyes—and the firmament announces the works of His hands. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 19:1.</note> But the Sun, most of all, can signify God Himself to you. "The Sun will give you signs; who would dare to call the Sun a liar?" <note>original: "Sol tibi signa dabit, Solem quis dicere falsum audeat?" — A quote from Virgil’s *Georgics* (1.463-4), traditionally referring to political omens but here applied to divine truth.</note> Thus, finally, the invisible things of God—that is, the angelic powers—are perceived most especially through the stars; but through the Sun, the eternal power and divinity of God are also seen.

## The Sun as the illuminator, Lord, and governor of the heavenly bodies. Chapter III.

**T**he Sun, as the manifest Lord of heaven, rules and governs all heavenly things without exception. I shall for the present pass over its immense size, by which it is thought to contain the earth one hundred and sixty-three times. <note>A standard astronomical measurement of the period, derived from Alfraganus.</note> In the first place, it implants light into all the stars—whether they have a small native light of their own (as some suspect) or none at all (as most think). Then, it is said and appears to be living, especially because of the twelve signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note>, as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> say, because the Sun gives life to the sign it is in at that time. 

Indeed, the Sun fills two signs on either side with such virtue that both spaces are called by the Arabs the "chariots of the Sun," that is, the "royal throne." While the planets are in these, though they meanwhile avoid being scorched <note>original: "incendium" — a technical term for a planet being too close to the Sun (combust).</note>, they are powerful with miraculous virtue—especially if the planets placed in this interval happen to be "superior" planets rising before the Sun, or "inferior" planets rising after the Sun. <note>In traditional astronomy, the superior planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; the inferior are Venus and Mercury.</note> 

Again, that sign in which the Sun reigns, namely Aries <note>The Sun is "exalted" in the sign of Aries.</note>, becomes the head of the signs and signifies the head in every living thing. Also, that sign which is the domicile of the Sun, namely Leo, is both the heart of the signs and holds the heart in any living thing. Truly, when the Sun reaches Leo, it extinguishes epidemics like "Pythonic venom" <note>A reference to the myth of Apollo (the Sun god) slaying the serpent Python; Ficino uses it to describe the Sun's power to clear the air of pestilence.</note> in many regions. Furthermore, the annual fortune of the whole world always depends on the entry of the Sun into Aries. From this comes the proper nature of Spring. From the entry of the Sun into Cancer, the quality of Summer is judged. From its entrance into Libra, the nature of Autumn. From its approach into Capricorn, the quality of Winter is found. This is clearly discovered by looking at the present figure of the heavens. Deservedly, since time depends on motion, the Sun creates the seasons through the four movable signs...

<summary>Ficino explains the metaphysical parallels between the Sun's light and God's goodness, and then details the Sun's astrological sovereignty over the stars, the zodiac, and the four seasons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the Sun’s physical and metaphysical properties in "De Sole." Having established the Sun as a symbol for the Divine, Ficino now moves into the technical astrological and astronomical ways the Sun governs the other planets and human destiny.</meta>

<page-num>967</page-num>
->BOOK ON THE SUN<-

...distinguishes the four seasons of the year. Likewise, from the return of the Sun to the same degree and minute of each person's birth, their own fortune is revolved in pairs throughout the year. To this is added that the motion of the Sun, as the first and chief of the planets (as Aristotle <note>referring to Aristotle's "On the Heavens" or "Metaphysics," where the Sun is central to the generation of life</note> says), is the most simple; it never leaves the middle of the Zodiac like the others, nor does it ever move backward.

## The Conditions of the Planets in relation to the Sun. Chapter IV.

**L**ikewise, certain defined spaces are seen everywhere in the heavens governed by the Sun itself, which, as soon as the planets have crossed them, they change their motion and condition. For Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, when they arrive at a trine <note>A "trine" is an astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, or one-third of the 360-degree zodiac.</note> aspect with the Sun (one third of the sky), immediately change their motion, moving either forward or backward. If they are oriental <note>Rising before the Sun in the morning.</note> to the Sun, they move backward; if they are occidental <note>Setting after the Sun in the evening.</note>, they move forward. Venus and Mercury wander through shorter, yet certain, spaces to and from the Sun. Indeed, Venus is forbidden to move further than 49 degrees away, and Mercury 28 degrees. The Moon changes her shape and nature in every aspect <note>The angular relationship between two celestial bodies.</note> with the Sun. And like a second Sun, acting out four ages, she represents the four seasons of the year. And whenever she is joined with the Sun, the figure of the heavens at that very degree of conjunction declares the nature of the coming month. Furthermore, all the planets, as soon as they touch the heart of the Sun <note>original: "cor Solis." In astrology, this is called "Cazimi," when a planet is within 17 minutes of the Sun, considered a position of great strength.</note>, dominate the others at that time, however brief it may be. But otherwise, when approaching the Sun, they are meanwhile vacant from their usual duty <note>This refers to "combustion," where a planet's influence is thought to be overwhelmed by the Sun's light.</note>. Indeed, when Saturn meets with the Sun, he is judged to lay aside his old rigidity, and Mars likewise his usual ferocity. The superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note> ascend as the Sun approaches them, but as it departs, they conversely descend. When joined to the Sun, they are at the highest point of their epicycle <note>In Ptolemaic astronomy, an "epicycle" is a small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves around a larger circle called a deferent.</note>. When opposite, they are at the lowest. In a square aspect <note>90 degrees apart.</note>, they are in the middle of their height. The Moon is high in both positions on the deferent <note>original: "perferente," likely a variant of "deferente."</note>; in the square aspect, she descends. Venus and Mercury, if they are joined to the Sun while moving forward, are high; if while moving backward, they are at their lowest. Nor is it permitted for the planets to complete the circuit of their epicycle before they have revisited the Sun, as if their Lord, in conjunction. In these things we have mentioned, the superior planets certainly seem to revere the royal gaze of the Sun when they change their step at the trine aspect. And when joined with the Sun, they are at their highest and most direct because they are meanwhile in harmony with the king. On the other hand, when they are in discord—that is, in opposition—they move backward and are at their lowest. When Venus and Mercury reach the Sun, if they are then walking straight—that is, obedient to their Lord—they emerge sublime. But if they are oblique, like rebels, they are meanwhile cast down. Indeed, if the Moon is high even when opposite the Sun, it should cause us no wonder. For what is the light of the Moon but that very same light of the Sun reflected here and there by the lunar mirror? And at the full moon, it is reflected back into the Sun from across the sky. The Moon seems to descend in the square aspect, however, because she then looks sternly <note>original: "torua," implying a harsh or grim gaze, typical of the "square" aspect which was traditionally considered challenging.</note> at her Lord. Again, just as the Sun does not step backward, so the Moon does not move backward, the speed of her epicycle preventing a retreat. Finally, by solar power, when the Moon seeks the north in the path of the Sun where the Dragon’s Head <note>term: <term>Dragon's Head</term> (Caput Draconis), the North Node of the Moon where its orbit crosses the ecliptic. It was associated with increase and gain.</note> is situated, she provides an increase to the signs there. But where she seeks the south, she provides a decrease where the Tail <note>term: <term>Dragon's Tail</term> (Cauda Draconis), the South Node, associated with decrease or loss.</note> is cast. All planets, having become oriental or occidental to the Sun, change their condition and their name. All indeed revere the path of the Sun, which they call the ecliptic. The inferior planets <note>Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> do so more and more. Finally, the females—namely the Moon and Venus—do so most of all. Therefore, they diverge most into the side <note>Meaning they have the greatest "latitude" or deviation from the central path of the Sun.</note>. Finally, all those placed either in this path or departing from it, while proceeding meanwhile to the north or south, are thought to change their condition everywhere. The Moon, the mistress of generation, has no manifest light except from the Sun. And from a perfect aspect with the Sun, she receives the powers of all celestial things, as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a major Neoplatonist philosopher whom Ficino translated and studied extensively.</note> says, as if all powers were in the Sun, and she sends down similar powers to our world.

## The power of the Sun in generations and times, in the nativity and in all things. Chapter V.

**F**inally, in the birth of every human being, the place of the Moon itself declares the Lord of the birth and the moment of conception. And the conjunction or opposition of the Moon with the Sun occurring before the birth of the person reveals the truth of the birth and its fortune. And in the present figure <note>The astrological chart or "horoscope."</note>, that portion of the sky in which the Part of Fortune <note>term: <term>Part of Fortune</term> (Pars Fortunae), a mathematical point in a horoscope calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant, representing prosperity.</note> falls, demonstrates for the birth...

He describes the Sun as the source of all planetary power, specifically highlighting how the Moon reflects solar light and how solar-lunar cycles determine human destiny.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s astrological and philosophical treatise "On the Sun." Having previously discussed the Sun’s physical movements and its relationship to the planets, he now moves into its role in determining the "tenor of life," its influence on the human spirit, and its exalted status in ancient theology and scripture.</meta>

<page-num>968</page-num>
->MARSILIO FICINO<-

...is said by the ancients, and it portends, or leads (as the Egyptians prefer) the entire tenor of life. The **Part of Fortune** <term>Pars Fortunae; a mathematical point in an astrology chart used to represent prosperity and health</term> designates the space first observed between the Sun and the Moon, projected forward from the degree of the Ascendant. Furthermore, astronomers find and measure the movements of the planets through the already discovered movement of the Sun. And the Sun, by its own motion, distinguishes nights and days, hours, months, and years. Likewise, by its light and heat, it generates, nourishes, moves, and regenerates all things; it cheers and fosters them, and makes manifest at its first arrival those things which had been hidden. By its approach and retreat, it creates the four parts of the year, and those regions too far removed from the Sun are equally removed from life. **Spring** is indeed the best of the seasons, since it begins with Aries, the kingdom of the Sun. **Autumn** is truly the worst, because Libra takes its beginning from the fall <note>In astrology, a "fall" is a sign where a planet's influence is weakened; the Sun "falls" in Libra as the days grow shorter.</note> of the Sun. Finally, a birth during the day is commonly thought to be better than one at night; the former is judged mostly by the Sun, while the latter is judged by the Moon as if by a mirror of the Sun. They divide the celestial figure <note>the horoscope or birth chart</note> at birth into twelve parts. Since they assign the ninth part to the Sun and the third to the Moon, they certainly name the former "God" and the latter "Goddess," and they believe these signify all the best things: wisdom, faith, religion, and eternal glory. For the Sun signifies all these things, as well as all truth, prophecy, and kingship. Added to this is the fact that as the Sun ascends to the midheaven, it wonderfully fosters the **vital and animal spirit** <note>spiritus; in Ficino's medical philosophy, this is a subtle vapor that connects the soul to the physical body</note> within us. But as it descends, both spirits are weakened. For this reason, David—the trumpet of the omnipotent God—rising at dawn to the lyre and songs, and meanwhile crying out: *It is vain for us to rise before the light* <note>original: "Vanum est nobis ante lucem surgere"; a reference to Psalm 127:2</note>, declares that the Sun coming toward us brings all good things with it, and wonderfully recalls our excited and illuminated spirits to sublime things. I pass over how the Sun, as they say, is thought to bring certain prophecies like a seer to those sleeping soberly upon its approach. The Moon also—the "lesser Sun" as Aristotle calls it—similarly recreates the natural spirit and moisture by ascending, and deserts them by descending. And the more it abounds in the light of the Sun, the more it is healthful to all. I pass over for now how the Moon must be observed in relation to the aspect of the Sun, making sure its light does not fail in this sign or that, as it signifies this or that limb. And thus, through the Moon, the virtue of all celestial things is to be transferred from the Sun to foster the limbs through medicines properly composed at that time. For we have already said enough about these things in the book *On Life* <note>Ficino's famous medical-astrological work, "De Vita Libri Tres" (Three Books on Life)</note>.

### *Praise of the Sun by the Ancients, and how the powers of the celestial bodies are all in the Sun and from the Sun. Chapter VI.*

**F**or these reasons, Orpheus called Apollo the life-giving eye of heaven. In summary, these things I say are gathered from the *Orphic Hymns*. The Sun is the eternal eye seeing all things. The supereminent celestial light, tempering the heavenly and pure things. Leading, or rather drawing, the harmonic course of the world. Master of the world, immortal Jupiter, the encircling eye of the world, possessing the seal, shaping all worldly things. The Moon is pregnant with stars, the Moon is the queen of stars. These are the words of Orpheus. Among the Egyptians, this was read inscribed in gold in the temples of Minerva <note>Minerva is the Roman name for the Greek Athena or Egyptian Neith</note>: *I am what is, what will be, and what has been. My veil no one has revealed. The fruit I have borne is the born Sun.* Where it appears, the Sun is the offspring, flower, and fruit of Minerva—that is, of divine intelligence. The ancient theologians, with Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino</note> as witness, used to say that Justice, the queen of all, proceeds through all things from the middle throne of the Sun, directing all things. It is as if the Sun itself is the moderator of all. Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist</note> recounts the opinion of the Egyptians thus: whatever good we have, we have from the Sun—namely, either from it alone, or if from others, it is either derived from the Sun or through the Sun via others. Likewise, the Sun is the Master of all elemental virtues. The Moon, by the virtue of the Sun, is the mistress of generation. Therefore, Abumashar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note> says that life is infused into all things through the Sun and the Moon. Moses thinks the Sun is the Master of the heavens by day, and the Moon by night, as if it were a nocturnal Sun. All have placed the Sun in the middle of the world as Master, though for different reasons. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers/astrologers</note> placed it in the middle of the planets, but the Egyptians placed it between two groups of five in the world: namely, five planets above it, and the Moon and four elements below it. But the closer...

of the earth, which they believe was placed in the firmament by providence so that by its burning spirit and fire, the moisture of the <term>Moon</term>, the air, and the water, and the thick matter of earthly things might be fostered. For another reason also, the very prosperity of the planets has declared this middle position. Indeed, their arrangement requires a relationship to the <term>Sun</term> of such a kind that <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, and <term>Mars</term> rise before the <term>Sun</term>. <term>Venus</term>, however, and <term>Mercury</term>, as well as the <term>Moon</term>, rise after the <term>Sun</term>, as if they were performing their journey with a king in the middle. If they move otherwise, they turn out to be weaker. Among those, however, those are held to be more excellent whom the <term>Sun</term> as Lord has commanded to precede him. But let us return to the ancients. The ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "Physici ueteres"</note> named the <term>Sun</term> the heart of heaven. <term>Heraclitus</term> called it the fountain of celestial light. Many <term>Platonists</term> located the <term>World Soul</term> in the <term>Sun</term>; filling the entire sphere of the <term>Sun</term>, it pours out rays—just like spirits—through that fiery globe as if through a heart. Thence it distributes life, sense, and motion to the universe through all things. For these reasons, perhaps, most astrologers think that just as God alone grants us an intellectual soul, so He sends it only under the influence of the <term>Sun</term>—that is, specifically in the fourth month after conception. <note>Ficino refers to a traditional belief that the soul is "infused" into the fetus at a specific stage of development, governed here by solar influence.</note> But let them see to that. <term>Mercury</term> certainly, signifying the movement of our mind, departs the least of all from the <term>Sun</term> in its motion. <term>Saturn</term>, finally, signifying the state of the withdrawn mind, least of all deserts the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky; Saturn's orbit is very closely aligned with this plane.</note>. Furthermore, <term>Jupiter</term> and <term>Mars</term>—since the former through its sign <term>Sagittarius</term>, and the latter through <term>Aries</term>, harmonize with the <term>Apollonian</term> <note>referring to Apollo, the god of the Sun</note> <term>Leo</term>—have obtained so great a gift that <term>Jupiter</term> indeed signifies religious justice, civil laws, and prosperity, while <term>Mars</term> signifies magnanimity, fortitude, and victory. The <term>Moon</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> are called the companions of the <term>Sun</term>; the <term>Moon</term> indeed because of its frequent conjunction <note>original: "coitum"</note> or aspect with the <term>Sun</term>. <term>Venus</term> and <term>Mercury</term>, however, beyond their proximity, are called so because of their equal progress with the <term>Sun</term>. From this, therefore, they received the empire of all generation. Since the more moist <term>Moon</term>, having obtained vital heat in its conjunction and sight of the <term>Sun</term>, immediately supplies warm and vital moisture for things to be generated. <term>Mercury</term>, however, mixes these two and all parts in the production of things by a certain numerical proportion. <term>Venus</term>, moreover, applies fitting forms, grace, and joy to such mixtures. Truly, just as the <term>Sun</term> distributes the whole light collected in itself through various stars differing from one another in appearance, so also it distributes all-formed virtues with all-formed light. From which it can be clearly conjectured that at least as many virtues exist in the <term>Sun</term> as there are stars existing in the heavens.

### Chapter VII: The arrangements of the signs and planets around the Sun and Moon.

**T**herefore, that the <term>Sun</term> is king, and the <term>Moon</term> (who is both the sister and the spouse of the <term>Sun</term>) is queen of the heavens, the very arrangement of the signs in the <term>Zodiac</term> clearly declares. For <term>Leo</term>, the seat of the <term>Sun</term>, and <term>Cancer</term>, the seat of the <term>Moon</term>, touch each other. Likewise, <term>Aries</term> is the kingdom of the <term>Sun</term>, and <term>Taurus</term> the kingdom of the <term>Moon</term>. The other planets, however, each have their own seats around the king and queen on all sides, which they place around them as intermediaries. <term>Mercury</term> on this side indeed has <term>Virgo</term> near <term>Leo</term>, and on that side has <term>Gemini</term> near <term>Cancer</term>. <term>Venus</term>, however, has <term>Libra</term> on this side and <term>Taurus</term> on that side. <term>Mars</term> also has <term>Scorpio</term> on this side and <term>Aries</term> on the other. <term>Jupiter</term> has <term>Sagittarius</term> on this side and <term>Pisces</term> on the other. <term>Saturn</term> has <term>Capricorn</term> on this side and <term>Aquarius</term> on the other. But formerly, when I was thus arranging the seats of the planets in relation to the <term>Sun</term> and the <term>Moon</term>, my close friend **Bindanius Recasolanus**, a man of profound judgment, objected in this way: "Do you not see, **Marsilio**, that those same seats, although in a reversed order, are arranged on both sides by those same degrees in relation to the houses of <term>Saturn</term>?" "I see," I said, "that this is especially fitting for the <term>Sun</term> itself, yet in the meantime, it also happens to the very high <term>Saturn</term>. What if, indeed, <term>Saturn</term> is worthy of this honor because it seems to deviate least of all from the royal way of the <term>Sun</term>?" But let us return to the task. These five planets, therefore, each have two seats. One indeed following the <term>Sun</term> as if from behind, the other in the sight of the <term>Moon</term>; those are called western from the <term>Sun</term>, these eastern from the <term>Moon</term>. Nevertheless, the <term>Sun</term> and the <term>Moon</term> claim the whole <term>Zodiac</term> for themselves. For the province of the <term>Sun</term> occupies <term>Leo</term>, <term>Virgo</term>, <term>Libra</term>, <term>Scorpio</term>, <term>Sagittarius</term>, and <term>Capricorn</term>. The province of the <term>Moon</term> occupies <term>Aquarius</term>, <term>Pisces</term>, <term>Aries</term>, <term>Taurus</term>, <term>Gemini</term>, and <term>Cancer</term>. Perhaps, indeed, they called <term>Cancer</term> the gate of men, because the <term>Sun</term> being about to descend there now seems almost to be so. <term>Capricorn</term>, however, they called the gate of gods, since the <term>Sun</term> is immediately seen to ascend there. <note>In Neoplatonic thought, souls were believed to descend into human bodies through the sign of Cancer and ascend back to the divine realm through Capricorn.</note> But we have also declared these things otherwise elsewhere. Certainly two...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s treatise "On the Sun" (De Sole). While the previous page established the Sun as the "heart" of the world and the source of life-giving spirit, Ficino now transitions into the astrological relationships between the Sun, the Moon, and the other planets, using these cosmic harmonies as an allegory for the soul's relationship with God.</meta>

<page-num>970</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

These signs—Aries and Libra—have claimed dignity for themselves so that they are called the "hinges" <term>cardines</term> <note>In ancient astrology, the "cardinal" points are the equinoxes and solstices where the seasons turn.</note> of heaven. This is because there the Sun determines the four changes of the seasons; and because the Sun, as it passes through Aries and Libra, holds a middle course in its ascent or descent and balances the day with the night. Therefore, the circle drawn from Aries to Libra is called the "Circle of Minerva"—that is, the circle of wisdom and justice—among the Egyptians. Indeed, the order of the celestial bodies is so wonderful that it declares the world was established not by chance, but by providence. Furthermore, the way all things look toward the one Sun as the moderator of everyone shows that both the angelic minds and all celestial beings obey the one supreme God above the heavens, and that our souls ought to obey Him even more.

-> *Planets in harmony with the Sun and Moon are fortunate; those in discord are not. Also, how they salute the Sun and Moon. Chapter VIII.* <-

**P**tolemy considers the Sun and Moon to be the authors of life: the Moon provides what pertains to growth and vegetation, while the Sun provides what pertains to the senses. Furthermore, Jupiter and Venus exist as life-giving <term>salutary</term> influences because they harmonize with the Sun and Moon through a certain musical <term>harmonic</term> proportion. Jupiter harmonizes mostly with the Sun and somewhat with the Moon; Venus, in turn, does the reverse. However, Saturn and Mars are adverse because they are dissonant from the Sun and Moon; Saturn is more discordant from the Sun, while Mars is more at odds with the Moon. But Jupiter is nurturing above all others, for if the lights of the Sun and the Moon were perfectly blended, Jupiter would be formed from both.

Nor should we overlook that when the planets revisit the "face" of the Sun or Moon in a kind of "salutation," they suddenly acquire a new power which the Arabs called <term>almugea</term> <note>original: "almugeam." This is a technical term in medieval astrology referring to a planet's strength gained by being at a specific distance from the Sun or Moon that mirrors the distance between their respective zodiacal houses.</note>. This happens when planets following the Sun are as far from it as their own house is distant from the Sun's house, or when planets preceding the Moon are at the same interval from the Moon as their residence is from the Moon’s residence. 

Thus, Saturn will salute the Sun whenever it is occidental—that is, rising after the Sun—in the sixth sign from the Sun's sign. Jupiter, however, will revisit the Sun when it is in the fifth sign, Mars in the fourth, Venus in the third, and Mercury in the second. Similarly, they will salute the Moon when they are oriental to the Moon—that is, rising before it—looking upon her at these same intervals. From this, the harmony of Jupiter and Venus with the Sun and Moon is again apparent, as is the discord of Saturn and Mars from both. Indeed, in relation to Leo (the Sun's seat), Jupiter placed its own seat, Sagittarius, in a <term>trine</term> <note>original: "trigono." An aspect of 120 degrees, considered the most harmonious.</note> aspect, which is surely favorable. Venus placed Libra in a <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "exagono." An aspect of 60 degrees, also considered favorable.</note> aspect to Leo, which is also propitious. But Mars placed Scorpio in the fourth space, which is dissonant [a square]. Saturn is in the sixth, which is not harmonious, and in the seventh, which is directly opposite. For Saturn opposes Leo with Aquarius, and likewise opposes Cancer with Capricorn. Similarly, in relation to Cancer [the Moon's seat], Venus arranges Taurus in a sextile; Jupiter arranges Pisces in a trine; Mars arranges Aries in a <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrato." An aspect of 90 degrees, traditionally associated with tension or conflict.</note>. Saturn, as we have said, is in both the sixth and seventh. 

Therefore, Jupiter and Venus are called "fortunate," as they are in harmony with the King and Queen of the heavens. Saturn and Mars are "unfortunate" because they are discordant with them; but Saturn is more unhappy because it seems to be most at odds with the Sun, even more than Mars is with the Moon. From this we are warned that those souls who harmonize with the divine will shall be happy, while those in discord will be wretched.

-> *The Sun is the statue of God. A comparison of the Sun to God. Chapter IX.* <-

**O**ur divine Plato, having most diligently contemplated these things, called the Sun the visible "son of the Good itself." He also believed the Sun to be the visible statue of God in this worldly temple, placed by God Himself to be admired by all observers above all other things. The ancients, as Plotinus says, and Plato too, venerated the Sun as a god. In the Sun, the ancient theologians of the nations located all the pagan deities, as Iamblichus, Julian, and Macrobius testify. Finally, whoever does not see that the Sun is the image and vicar of God in the world has surely never considered the night, nor looked up at the rising Sun, nor thought about how much it exceeds the senses—how suddenly living things return to life, which, far from the Sun, were thought to be dead! Nor [can they ignore] the gifts of the Sun...

Ficino transitions from astronomical observations to high Platonic theology, drawing parallels between the Sun's light and the Divine Intellect.</meta>

...observed, by which he alone performs what all the other stars together cannot achieve. Therefore, conclude alongside the Platonists and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who often used light metaphors for God.</note> that the Sun, or Phœbus <note>Phœbus is another name for Apollo, the god of light and the sun.</note>, the leader of the Muses—that is, the leader of intelligence—is the visible image of God. Also, that Phœbe, namely the Moon, is the image of Phœbus in much the same way he is the image of God. And as Hipparchus <note>A famous Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE).</note> says, she is the mirror of the Sun; that is, she reflects the light falling upon her from the Sun down toward us—though it is not expedient to dispute this at present.

Yet, it is not fitting to overlook that Platonic comparison, which I have described more extensively elsewhere. Just as the Sun creates both eyes and colors, and provides the eyes with the power to see and colors the power to be seen, and joins both into one through the mediation of light, so God is understood to relate to all intellects and all intelligible things. For He Himself procreates both the intelligible forms of things <term>species</term> and all intellects, and provides to both their own natural and effective power. Moreover, He constantly surrounds them with a common light, through which He excites the powers of both the intelligible things and the intellects into mutual action, and couples them together in that act. This light, in things to be understood, Plato calls "truth," and in minds he calls it "knowledge." He further considers that the Good itself—namely God—surpasses all these things at least as much as the Sun surpasses light, eyes, and colors.

But when Plato says that the Sun surpasses all visible things, he undoubtedly sensed an incorporeal Sun above the corporeal Sun—that is, the Divine Intellect. Since one may ascend from the image to the archetype, partly by removing what is inferior and partly by adding what is superior, you may do the same regarding the Sun if you wish. Following Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Islamic philosopher who argued that the heavens were not composed of the four earthly elements.</note>, who stripped the Sun of dense matter, you should likewise leave it its certain quantity, but meanwhile leave it its power along with its light. In this way, there remains the light itself, filled with a miraculous power, defined by neither a certain quantity nor any particular shape, and thus touching the immense space of the imagination with its own presence. In this way, it now exceeds the understanding just as it now surpasses the sharpest eyesight in its own right. By this reasoning, you will seem to have found God—who "set His tabernacle in the sun" <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4.</note>—and the Sun itself, according to your capacity.

Finally, just as nothing is further from the divine light than matter which is utterly without form, so nothing is more different from the light of the Sun than the earth. Therefore, bodies in which the earthy condition prevails, being most unsuitable for light, receive no light within themselves. This is not because the light is powerless to penetrate; for while it does not illuminate the inside of wool or a leaf, it simultaneously penetrates a mass of crystal, which otherwise would be much more difficult to pierce. In the same way, the divine light "shines even in the darkness" of the soul, "but the darkness does not comprehend it" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:5.</note>; yet this too has a similarity to God. For God first implants the knowledge of divine things into angelic and blessed minds, and then love. But for our souls here, He kindles in those who believe a love that purifies and converts them before they can grasp the understanding of divine things. In the same way, the Sun instantly illuminates transparent and pure natures everywhere, as if they were already celestial; but it first warms, kindles, and refines opaque materials unsuitable for light, and only then illuminates them. And once they have become light and permeable, it sometimes raises both their heat and light to sublime heights. Hence Apollo, with the arrows of his rays, pierces, purges, dissolves, and lifts up the massive Python <note>The Python was a monstrous serpent of the earth slain by Apollo; here it represents the "heavy" or "damp" qualities of matter being overcome by the sun.</note>.

Nor is it right to overlook that, just as we hope that Christ will eventually come into His kingdom and, by the overflowing splendor of His body, will utterly raise human bodies from the earth, so too after the deathly winter we yearly expect the Sun reigning in Aries <note>The astrological sign marking the beginning of Spring.</note> to immediately recall the seeds of things in the earth—which are like dead animals—back to life and beauty as half-living beings. Hence Mercury, as the companion <term>Achates</term> <note>Achates was the loyal companion of Aeneas; here Mercury is the Sun's loyal attendant.</note> of the Sun, is said to wake the sleepers with his staff <term>caduceus</term>. And Plato describes a certain similar resurrection in his book *The Statesman* <note>Ficino refers to the myth of the "reversed cosmos" in Plato's *Politicus*.</note>.

## *The Sun was created first, and in the middle of heaven.* Chapter X.

**I**t is asked among these things: what did God create first of all? Moses answers: Light. For it is fitting that from that divine light, which is more than intelligible, there should immediately emanate the light that is most similar to God. Intelligible light exists in the incorporeal world above us—that is, the purest intellect. Sensible light, however, exists in the corporeal world—that is, the solar light itself. But these perhaps, in their first degree as if on the first day, simply have the property of shining within and illuminating without. Secondarily...

He further compares the Sun's power to rejuvenate the earth in spring to the Christian resurrection and the purification of the soul.</summary>
