<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 97, where Ficino compares the Sun’s role in the physical universe to God’s role in the intellectual realm. Here, he interprets the Genesis creation account through a Platonic lens, arguing that the Sun’s physical form and its "royal" light were distinct stages of creation.</meta>

<page-num>972</page-num>
<header>MARSILII FICINI</header>

...indeed, so that it might both possess heating power itself and nourish everything else. Third, that by its own efficacy and the command of God, it might propagate itself into the physical mass. Fourth, in the fourth step of nature and order—as if on the fourth day—that it might obtain its mass in a sphere, just as the light of the divine intelligence, from which it flowed, is reflected back into itself. Therefore, Moses says on the first day that light itself was created simply, but on the fourth day, he asserts that light was created again, endowed with this solar, that is, circular shape <note>Ficino is reconciling the account in Genesis, where light is created on the first day but the Sun on the fourth.</note>. Plato also repeats the constitution of the Sun twice in the *Timaeus* <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>. First, among the number of the planets as a companion. Second, as being divinely gifted above the others with a wonderful light and royal authority. 

Most astronomers teach that at the beginning of the world, the Sun first held the habitable horizon in Aries, its own kingdom, and held the middle of the sky like a citadel and head, as if it were the king of the heavens. Moses also, when he says that "one day" was made—not indeed "morning and evening," but rather "evening and morning"—signifies that after midday when the Sun was lit, the day having been born then declined toward evening, to be completed the following morning. He certainly confirmed the royal authority of the Sun when he assigned the first day in the world to be the Lord’s day, that is, the solar day <note>original: *dominico... id est, solarem*. Ficino links the Christian "Lord's Day" (Sunday) with the pagan "Sun's Day."</note>. For if God finished the world in six days and rested on the seventh, then indeed he seems to have inaugurated the world's beginning from the day of the Sun itself—that is, from solar power. 

But he judged Saturn, the furthest from the Sun, to be adverse to generations and actions when he commanded that on Saturn's day <note>Saturday, the Sabbath.</note> one must refrain from action. Did not also that author of life, Christ—whom the Sun in the middle of heaven, like a prophet with a darkened face, had mourned as he expired—rise again from the dead on the day and hour of the Sun, thus to return to us an <term>intelligible light</term> <note>Light that can be perceived by the mind/intellect rather than the eyes, representing divine truth.</note> just as the Sun returns a visible one?

### *The two lights of the Sun. The gift of Apollo. The levels of light. The Sun reflects all divine things. Chapter XI.*

**I**F we consider the Sun in that first property of its nature, which it obtained at the first moment of its creation, as if counted in the company of the planets, we will realize that its natural and primary light was not as great at first as it soon became. For it does not surpass the other stars in size as much as it does in light. For it surpasses the size of Jupiter by less than double, but its light perhaps a hundredfold. The quantities of these are certainly measured by comparison to the Earth. We said at the beginning how many times the Sun contains the Earth. Jupiter is indeed thought to equal the Earth ninety-five times. 

Therefore, this immense light shone from another source entirely, added from above to the natural light of the Sun. Truly all celestial bodies brought their own light with them at birth, but it was either tiny or hidden from us, whether it lies hidden because of a certain rarity and brightness or some other cause. It seems the Sun brought with it from the beginning a similar light, slightly larger in proportion to its size. But besides that proper and native light—so to speak, an obscure one—immediately this other light, most manifest to the eyes, was divinely applied, like a more expressive image of divine intelligence and most bountiful goodness. 

God, as our theologians teach, gave a twin light to minds. The first is naturally kindled in them. The second, however, is now added as if for merit and moreover freely, making the blessed ones happy with wonderful abundance. Therefore, since stars are images of minds, it is consistent that they similarly received two lights. Just as God wonderfully added this great light in the Sun to the first light of the Sun, so the Sun, immediately as God’s deputy in this duty, adds this light added to itself to the native lights of the stars. Nay, just as we are accustomed to say that the light appearing in the Moon is not the Moon’s own, but the light of the Sun sent down to us through the Moon, so by the most secret reasoning of the Platonists, we shall say that such splendor manifest in the Sun proceeds not from itself, but from God through it to all things, as if it were not the light of that sphere, but of God Himself, now thus manifest to the eyes. 

God, indeed, while he filled the solar sphere—a tiny particle of heaven—with such splendor that brilliance overflowed from one into all things, undoubtedly declared both that the little body of the Sun received such an incomparable gift not from itself but from above, and that from the one God—the Sun of the Sun—absolutely all good things are propagated through all. Just as this sensible light in the Sun illuminates all sensible things and the senses, and nourishes...

He uses this to explain the biblical creation of light and the Sun, as well as the astrological significance of Sunday and Saturday.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic treatise on the Sun. In the previous section, he reconciled the Biblical creation account (Genesis) with Platonic philosophy, arguing that the Sun acts as a "king" or "citadel" of the heavens, established by God to govern the physical world through light.</meta>

<page-num>571</page-num>
<header>THE BOOK ON THE SUN</header>

...it shapes and forms, and turns toward higher things; likewise, a certain intelligible light in the soul of the Sun itself illuminates, ignites, and recalls the innermost eyes of souls. For this reason, I believe the Sun was called **Apollo** by the ancient theologians <note>Ficino refers to "ancient theologians" like Orpheus, Hermes Trismegistus, and Plato, who he believed shared a unified ancient wisdom (*prisca theologia*).</note> and the author of all harmony and the leader of the Muses, since it releases souls from a certain confused crowd through the hidden, rather than manifest, influences of its rays, moderates them harmoniously, and finally leads them to understanding. 

Nor indeed should it be thought that this most ample and effective light—granted as the best and perfect gift among all worldly things—takes its primary origin from the small body of the Sun. Rather, it comes from the **Good** itself as the "Father of Lights," <note>original: *patre luminum*</note> in whom whatever light exists is certainly more than "intelligible," surpassing all intelligence entirely. But from there, descending soon into the divine or angelic intellect, it now becomes **intelligible** <note>In Platonic terms, "intelligible" refers to things that can be understood by the mind but not seen by the eyes.</note>. Next, coming into the mind of the **World Soul**, it becomes **intellectual**, and furthermore it is made **imaginable**. Immediately passing into the heavens, it becomes **sensual** <note>Capable of being perceived by the senses.</note> and **sensible** <note>The object of the senses.</note> at the same time. Finally, having been sent down to the lower regions, it is now as if divided; in some places it becomes "sensual"—that is, in the eyes of living creatures—and in other places "sensible"—that is, in objects. In a few cases, however, it preserves both, as in those creatures that see at night. 

But let us return to the first principles. The Platonists posit three principles: **The Good itself**, the **Divine Intellect**, and the **World Soul**. A single light represents all these things more clearly than anything else. Indeed, it represents the Good itself, because while it marvelously precedes all things, it meanwhile diffuses itself through all things and recalls them to sublime heights, all while its excellence and purity are marvelously preserved. It represents the Divine Intellect because it declares, distinguishes, and adorns all things. It also represents the World Soul because, with its nourishing heat, it generates, fosters, enlivens, and moves all things. 

Again, just as light descends into the heavens from the three principles above the heavens, it reflects those parents everywhere beneath the heavens. Thus, in the heavens, light represents the Good itself through the **Sun**; it represents the Divine Intellect—that is, the fullness of Ideas—through the **firmament** full of stars; and finally, it represents the World Soul (as a mobile thing) through the **Moon**, which is changeable in its light. Similarly, beneath the heavens, it represents the first through **fire**, the second through **air**, and the third through **water**. Finally, just as the higher stars are immutably illuminated by the Sun, while the Moon receives light from it changeably, so too are the angels illuminated immovably by God, while souls are illuminated movably.

->*The Likeness of the Sun to the Divine Trinity, and the nine orders of angels. Also regarding the nine divinities in the Sun, and the nine Muses around the Sun.*<-

### Chapter XII.

**N**othing is found in the world more similar to the divine Trinity than the Sun. For in the single substance of the Sun, three things are distinct from one another and yet united. First is its **natural fecundity** <note>The inherent power to produce or create.</note>, which is entirely hidden from our senses. Second is its **manifest light**, flowing from that same fecundity and always equal to it. Third is the **heating power** from both, which is entirely equal to the other two. Therefore, fecundity represents the **Father**; the light, like intelligence, represents the **Son** conceived in the manner of intelligence; and the heat represents the **Loving Spirit** <note>The Holy Spirit.</note>. 

Concerning the divine Trinity, our theologians conceive of three **Hierarchies** of angels, each containing three orders. The first is consecrated to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Spirit. We find a similar grouping of three and nine regarding the Solar Trinity. Indeed, from the fecund nature of the Sun itself, three "natural fecundities" proceed through all things: the first occurs in the nature of the heavens, the second in the simple nature of the elements, and the third in the nature of mixed bodies. 

Again, from the vital heat of the Sun, life is propagated everywhere beyond these natures, and it is threefold: first, the **vegetative** life in plants; second, the **immobile sensual** life in "zoophytes" <note>Organisms like sponges or corals that appear to be both plant and animal.</note>; and third, the **sensual and moving** life in the higher animals. 

Finally, three species of brightness are derived from the light of the Sun, whether through the heavens or beneath them. For the light is either entirely **white**, or entirely **red**, or a **mixture**. Since light exists as both the closest image of knowledge and the principle of it (especially sensory knowledge), three types of senses rightfully seem to correspond to the three species of light. To the **Redness** belong the purely corporeal senses—namely, **touch** and **taste**. To the **Whiteness** belong the most incorporeal <note>Meaning "not tied to gross matter."</note> senses—namely, **imagination** and **sight**. But to the **mixed light** belong the senses that are middle points between the incorporeal and corporeal—namely, **hearing** and **smell**. 

Thus far, the light of the Sun is not only the image of these things, but also their cause. However, it is only an image of the **pure Intelligence**; for just as pure Intelligence acts in a moment, penetrates depths, and clarifies things while remaining unmixed with any and sublime in its...

<meta>Catchword: bilem (This catchword from the previous page likely completes the word "existens," meaning "existing.")</meta>

...existing, so light spreads through all things in a single moment and makes each thing visible; it is at once a whole, individual thing everywhere, yet mixed with nothing. Indeed, if the Sun departs, light does not remain in the air for even a moment, for it everywhere accompanies its own **Phoebus** <note>A common name for Apollo as the sun god, meaning "bright" or "radiant."</note> as he goes. 

But since, somehow, here under Apollo we are acting as if we were poets—even if not good ones—let us converse together for a little while. First, the ancients placed deities in the Sun; these were (to speak in the Platonic manner) the "higher gods," and then the nine **Muses**. For whether we contemplate its substance or its powers: in its substance, we name its essence, life, and intelligence, calling the essence "Heaven," the life "**Rhea**," <note>In Greek mythology, Rhea is the mother of the gods, representing the flow of life.</note> and the intelligence "**Saturn**," according to their custom. 

If we contemplate the powers of the Sun after its substance, we shall call its fertility **Jupiter and Juno**; its light, **Apollo and Minerva**; and finally its heat, **Venus and Bacchus**. Now, the ancients always depicted Phoebus and Bacchus—who rule most prominently in the Sun—as young men. They did this because if anyone knew how to receive the light and heat of the Sun with that purity and property with which they exist there, and could adapt them to their own use and measure, they would bring back perpetual youth from it, or at least fulfill one hundred and twenty "solar years." <note>120 years was considered the natural limit of human life in both Biblical (Genesis 6:3) and classical traditions.</note>

But after these nine deities deep within the Sun, let us proceed to the nine Muses around the Sun. What, therefore, are the nine Muses around Phoebus, if not the nine types of Apollonian spirits distributed through the nine spheres of the world? For the ancients recognized only eight heavens. But beneath the celestial fire, they added the **air** as a ninth heaven, being celestial in its quality and motion. In each sphere, they arranged divine spirits hidden from our eyes, dedicated step-by-step to individual stars; **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who detailed the hierarchy of spiritual beings.</note> calls these "angels," and **Iamblichus** <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist who emphasized the use of ritual to connect with the divine.</note> further calls them "archangels" and "principalities." But those among them who are primarily "solar" everywhere, the ancients called **Muses**, presiding over all the sciences, but especially over poetry, music, medicine, purifications, oracles, and prophecies. 

Now let us return to the Sun. We foolishly admire every tiny thing, provided it is rare; but we have long since ceased to admire the most common and greatest things, being both blind and ungrateful. No one wonders at fire, which burns like the heaven and the Sun, purest without mixture, perpetually moving, shining far and wide, growing from the smallest to the largest instantly as it converts all things into itself. No one admires the Sun as much as is right—the Sun which incomparably surpasses all things, the parent and moderator of all, the Sun that cheers the sorrowful, gives life to what is not yet living, and raises up the already dead. 

Truly, if the house of the omnipotent **Olympus** <note>A poetic reference to God’s dwelling or the highest heaven.</note> were opened but once a year, and such great splendor were suddenly looked upon, everyone would admire the Sun alone beyond measure. All would either humbly adore the Sun as the supreme God, or at least would have no doubt it was sent by the divine. They would give immense thanks daily to God, the author of the gift, however hidden He might be. Therefore, Iamblichus and **Julian the Platonist** <note>Referring to Emperor Julian, who wrote a famous hymn to the Sun.</note> command us to imagine a night without any light from the Moon or stars—wherein the gift of the Sun is also made manifest—so that we may more certainly know what we would be without the Sun, and how much we owe to this Sun and the one above.

<margin>405</margin>
### *The Sun is not to be worshiped as the author of all things. Chapter XIII.*

**Socrates**, while in military camps, often stood astonished in the same tracks, beneath the open sky, looking at the rising Sun. His limbs were unmoved and his eyes unblinking like a statue, until he greeted the Sun rising again the next day. Led by these and similar signs, the Platonists might say that Socrates—perhaps led by a certain <term>Phoeban daemon</term> <note>original: *Phoebeo quodam dæmone*. In this context, a "daemon" is not an evil spirit, but a protective guiding spirit or "genius" linked to the god Apollo.</note> from his very childhood—was accustomed to venerating Phoebus himself above all else, and for that same reason he was judged the wisest of all Greeks by the oracle of Apollo. 

For my part, I will for the present pass over what ought most to be affirmed regarding Socrates' daemon, or genius, or angel. I would certainly dare to affirm this: in that ecstasy of mind, Socrates did not admire *this* Sun, but another. For since novelty alone usually brings admiration, why would the admiring Socrates be so stunned by this Sun which he sees every day, and whose motions and powers he had long ago comprehended through both mathematical and physical reasoning? This Sun which, according to Plato, he called not the "first God," but the "Son of God." Not the *first* son of God, I say, but the *second*, and one that is already visible. For the first Son of God is not this Sun manifest to the eyes, but another far superior **Intellect**, namely the first one, which can be contemplated by the mind alone.

He also argues that while the physical Sun is a magnificent "second son" of God, philosophers like Socrates actually look past it to worship the "intelligible" Sun or the divine Intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s "Book on the Sun." It picks up from the previous discussion of how light and solar power can be used to restore the human spirit, moving now to a theological distinction between the physical Sun and God as the "Father of Lights."</meta>

<page-num>975</page-num>
<header>BOOK ON THE SUN.</header>

...[intelligi]ble through the intellect. <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "intelligibilem," continuing from the previous page's discussion of things perceived by the mind versus the senses.</note> Socrates, therefore, being occasionally prompted by the celestial Sun, and having conjectured from it a Sun above the heavens, contemplated the majesty of that higher Sun more attentively and was astonished as he admired the incomprehensible goodness of its Father. James the Apostle called him the "Father of Lights"—of lights, I say, that are more than celestial. <note>original: "patrem luminum"; a reference to the Epistle of James 1:17.</note> With Him, there is no change, nor any shadow of turning. For James thinks that even those super-celestial created things are naturally subject to change, and he does not doubt that many celestial things are also shadowed in some way, and sub-celestial things are shadowed every day. For this reason, James judges that "every best gift"—namely, that which is naturally implanted in the mind—and "every perfect gift"—namely, that which is added to us after our natural endowments—descends not from this Sun and the worldly stars, but from higher up, from the Father of Lights himself. 

For relying on the powers of the intellect as if on certain steps received not from the heavens, but from above, we ascend above the heavens; there we know, love, and worship many things more excellent than the heavens, and we venerate the maker of the heaven itself above all things. Nor could we understand or love anything incorporeal or better than the heaven if we received our intelligence only from the heavens. Now, lest anyone, admiring the Sun, Moon, and stars too much, should both worship them and venerate them as the authors and fathers of intellectual gifts, James wisely warned that this physical Sun is not the first principle <term>principle (principium) — in philosophy, the ultimate source or fundamental cause from which all other things arise.</term> of the universe. 

For the present, I shall set aside the arguments by which we affirm in our Theology that the principle of the universe is neither a body, nor a soul, nor an intellect, but something far more exalted, from which the celestial Sun is indeed very distant—so distant that the Sun should be judged a certain shadow of that principle rather than its true image. However, I will briefly touch upon the arguments that James alludes to here. Since stability—as the source, ruler, and goal of motion—is more perfect than any motion, certainly God himself, the ruler of all, cannot be subject to movement. The Sun, however, is constantly moving. Furthermore, the power of the first principle, being infinite, reaches all things strongly and cannot be restrained anywhere. But the power of the Sun, acting through rays, is hindered here and there when its rays are blocked; it suffers a failing when the Moon stands in its way, is often hemmed in by clouds, repelled by the density of the earth, and weakened by the distance of space. 

Moreover, the Sun itself is but a tiny particle of the world, confined to a narrow seat, drawn along by a sphere, and in turn pulled back. <note>Ficino refers to the Ptolemaic system where the Sun is carried by a celestial sphere but also has its own motion.</note> Against the impetus of its own sphere, it is revolved by a sphere that is always higher, and it is hindered by contrary signs and stars, and is sometimes weakened by the "aspect" (so to speak) of evil things. <note>In Renaissance astrology, "evil things" refers to malefic planets like Saturn or Mars which, when positioned at certain angles (aspects) to the Sun, were thought to weaken its influence.</note> Finally, the principle of the universe works all things, everywhere and always, and in all things. But the Sun itself neither creates the globes of the world, nor can it by its own power produce things that are cold, or moist, or dense, and the like. Nor do any similar powers, if there are any in the heaven, take their origin from the Sun. 

Otherwise, although the Sun is very far distant from the Author of the world, nevertheless all celestial things seem to have been divinely coordinated toward the unique Sun as their ruler and measure in the heaven. From this we are utterly warned that all things which are in the heaven, under the heaven, and above the heaven are similarly referred to the one principle of all things. And therefore, considering this at last, let us venerate that Principle with at least the same devotion with which celestial things venerate the
->Sun.<-

<page-num>976</page-num>

# OF MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine, on the Book of Light

->To the magnanimous Piero de' Medici,<-
->P R E F A C E.<-

<note>Historiated woodcut initial C depicting a scholar at a desk, likely Marsilio Ficino.</note>
**W**HEN I had destined for you, most illustrious Piero, my little work on the Sun, I remembered shortly thereafter that I had long ago composed a small book on Light. Therefore, I thought it entirely fitting that this light should soon follow its Sun, as if following a leader. On earth, indeed, the first glow of the dawning gold precedes the Sun about to rise immediately. But in the heavens, conversely, the Sun himself, the father, precedes the splendor emanating from him. Indeed, having long followed the earthly order, I have—I know not how—contemplated light first, before I did the Sun. But now, conversely, imitating the heavenly order, I have placed the Sun before Light, as the father before the son, as was fitting. Nor was it my intention in this book or in the preceding one to curiously pursue the more minute questions of mathematicians regarding the Sun or light, which are often not so much useful as they are certainly difficult. Rather, [my intention was] to attain, through their examples and certain comparisons—acting as if they were steps—the rules for contemplating the character of the soul and the divine mysteries, according to my strength. Indeed, there is no more certain sign or argument for clearly perceiving these things than light. For that heavenly father has illuminated the earth for us with Phoebean <note>original: "Phœbea"; relating to Phoebus Apollo, the god of light and the sun.</note> lamps, certainly not so that we might hunt flies <note>Ficino uses this metaphor to describe pursuing trivial or petty matters.</note>—if I may put it that way—under such great light, but so that we might look up at ourselves, our homeland, and our heavenly father, seeing divine things through light of this kind, as if through a mirror in an enigma, <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly [in an enigma]; but then face to face."</note> though at some point we shall see them through a more exalted light face to face.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine: a discourse through all the senses 
### on what light is in the body of the world, in the soul, 
### in the angel, and in God. Chapter 1.

<note>Large historiated woodcut initial O depicting figures pointing toward a source of light.</note>
**I** HATE darkness most of all things; by its fault, whatever displeases me does so either because it is with darkness, or because things slipping away from darkness slide back and are depressed down toward it. I love light above all things, for whose sake I love other things too—either because they are with it, or because, flowing from it, they flow back and are led back to it. Therefore, tell me, my senses—you who report almost innumerable other things—tell me, I beseech you: what is light? Hearing responds: "I am of the air; let it be enough if I report airy sounds to you." Smell also responds: "Indeed, I am not so bright; I am of vapor; learn about vapors from me." "Why do you seek what belongs to another from me?" says Taste. "Being born in liquid, I indicate liquids to you." "Do not," says Touch, "extort from me what I cannot do; I am corporeal, I report corporeal things; seek light higher up."

->Description of visible light. Chapter 2.<-

**H**aving thus been warned [to move] from the lowest point to which I had fallen, I shall now ascend to the highest parts of my body, so that I may receive light, which is smoother and higher than all else. Come then, my shining eyes, I beseech you by that light by which you, above all others—indeed, by which you alone—are so greatly delighted: indicate to your queen, Reason, what light is. Sight suddenly responds: "I am a splendid spirit, and I am a spiritual splendor." Wherefore, since by me...

--- Page 986 ---
<meta>This page continues from the preface to the "Book on Light," where Ficino transitioned from discussing the Sun to its primary manifestation: light. Here, he begins the philosophical investigation of light's nature, its relationship to color, and its role as a bridge between the physical and the divine.</meta>

<page-num>977</page-num>
<header>THE BOOK ON LIGHT</header>

Since you rightfully ask for the duties belonging to me, I most willingly bestow as much as I have. Light is a certain spiritual, sudden, and most wide-reaching emanation from bodies, occurring without any loss to the bodies themselves; specifically, it is a brightness proceeding from <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphanis"; transparent or translucent materials that allow light to pass through.</note> things. From their opposites, however, comes color; and from all of them come quantity, figure, and motion. Gather every kind of color into one: what will this whole be? Nothing other than a certain "all-colored" light, or light made opaque within the more solid and darker matter of the earth. Separate the earth that is mixed into it. What will remain but a certain quality—indeed, a clarity and the <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; in Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, this refers to the state of being "in action" or the full realization of a potential.</note> of the transparent, just as color is the act of the opaque? Color is indeed opaque light. Light, however, is clear color; or rather, it is a certain flower and vigor of the transparent body and of colors—in act it is "one-colored," but in power <note>original: "uirtute"; referring to its latent potential or essence.</note> it is all-colored. Perhaps, indeed, when light departs, colors do not exist. For they may be light itself, now varied, appearing in different places, and differently affected and reflected. Perhaps even in the power of light, those colors are always present, to be unfolded differently in different places.

### *Nothing is clearer than light and God, yet nothing is more obscure. Chapter III.*

<margin>*</margin> This is a sketch, oh my eyes, rather than a painting. I have never heard anything defined more obscurely. Oh, truly marvelous thing! In what way can it be that nothing is more obscure than light? For nothing is clearer, since through it all things become clear and are made manifest. I shall therefore ascend from here to the sublime watchtower of the mind, so that I may at least see this from there, since I am unable to see anything else anywhere else. O Mind, you who rightly measure all things, tell me: could it be that God himself is light, than whom also nothing is clearer, and nothing more obscure? Nothing is clearer than that God exists, and that He is supremely powerful, wise, and good. For every single thing made by Him proclaims this to our ears. Thus, no one is more deaf than he who does not hear such a great sound and noise of all things. Conversely, nothing is more obscure than *what* God is; so much so that nothing is more dark than the man who imagines this to be very clear to himself.

### *Intelligible light is the cause of intelligible things, visible light of visible things. Chapter IV.*

The mind responds that God is the "Father of lights," <note>A reference to the Epistle of James 1:17: "Every good gift... comes down from the Father of lights."</note> in whom there is no change by which He might be extinguished or diminished. Nor is there any shadow of turning, through which He might either undergo night in His turn or suffer an eclipse. It responds again that God is light, in which there are no shadows. That is, the Form in which nothing is unformed, and the Beauty in which nothing is deformed. God, certainly, as the mind (which is His ray) shows, is an unsearchable and infinite light, the very truth of every truth, and the cause of all things. This visible and finite light, the cause of visible things, is His splendor—or rather, His shadow. Truly, because it is the nature of light and truth to truly manifest other things to others, all things are truly clear and conspicuous through God by His own power. It is just as if visible light, since it is the source of eyes and of visible things, were to look upon itself as being all-colored, and were to see in itself all colors and all sensible things.

### *Light: visible, rational, intelligible, and divine. Chapter V.*

But the mind warns that one must not leap so suddenly toward such sublime speculation, but must ascend step by step, lest we be forced to grow dizzy and be blinded by too much splendor. Reason, do not trust in the senses; your touch does not report enough to you, and the others do not report at all. Sight, because it is a "sensual light," receives and gives only a sensible splendor. And conversely, because it receives and gives a sensible splendor, you recognize this to be a certain sensual light. Beyond that point, however, one may not proceed. But learn this from me: first, that I, the Intelligence, am a certain intellectual light, since my object is <term>intelligible light</term> <note>Light that is perceived by the mind or intellect rather than the physical eyes; the light of pure ideas or truth.</note>, which I seek to be sought in any thing, and having found it, I find it again. For the light of any thing and its truth are the same. Truth is the internal light; light is truth pouring itself out toward the external. Learn then that you, namely Reason, are a certain rational light and a shining reason. For you seek after the "reason of light" <note>Ficino plays on the word *ratio*, which means both "reason" and "the underlying principle/account" of something.</note> as your origin with such great greed through reasoning. But do you wish to attain the reason of light more conveniently? Seek it in the "reason" of any light. There is the reason of light, where the reason of all things exists: in the highest truth, which is itself both the highest certainty and clarity; there you will find the truth of light, and the clarity—

<meta>catchword: —ty (claritatem)</meta>

<summary>Ficino defines light as a spiritual emanation and the "act" of transparent bodies, proposing a hierarchy of light that moves from the physical (sensual) to the rational, the intellectual, and finally to God, the "Father of lights." He explores the paradox that both God and light are simultaneously the most obvious things in existence and the most difficult to define in their essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s metaphysical exploration of light. Having previously defined light as a "spiritual emanation," he now maps its presence across the hierarchy of being—from God down to inanimate matter—and argues that the visible light we see is merely a shadow of a higher, incorporeal reality.</meta>

# MARSILIUS FICINUS

<page-num>973</page-num>

Indeed, the clarity and truth you seek are the same thing as this light. What is light in God? An immeasurable exuberance of His goodness and truth. What is it in the angels? A certainty of intelligence flowing from God, and a profuse joy of the will. What is it in the heavenly bodies? An abundance of life from the angels, an unfolding of <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtutis"; in this context, it refers to the inherent power or efficacy of a celestial body to influence the world below.</note> from the heavens, and the laughter of the sky. What is it in fire? A certain vital vigor implanted by the celestial bodies, and an effective propagation. Then, in those things that lack sense, it is a grace poured down from heaven. In sentient beings, it is the exhilaration of the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; for Ficino, this is a subtle vapor in the body that links the soul to the physical organs.</note> itself and the vigor of the senses. In all things, in summary, it is the outpouring of an innermost fertility. Everywhere, it is the image of divine truth and goodness.

->By what reasons we may ascend from visible light to the invisible. Chapter VI.<-

**B**ut lest we seem perhaps to imagine things at our own whim when we so often affirm a certain substance of light that is entirely incorporeal and divine, it is worth considering that this light manifest to our eyes cannot be the primary light. This is partly because it holds some proportion with all—or at least some—corporeal eyes, and partly because it is mobile, exists within something else, and depends upon something else. We must, therefore, ascend to some higher light, free from such conditions, already existing through itself and in itself, and entirely incorporeal. For even this manifest light is almost incorporeal, being the cause of similarly incorporeal images, and is not bound by any dimensions, divisions, or mixtures. From this, it is clear that it cannot have its primary origin from a corporeal mass, or form, or virtue; it therefore has it from a light higher than bodies and, so to speak, immeasurably more ample and clearer. Indeed, just as heavenly matter spreads light descending there from the divine, so the dark mass beneath the heavens used to obscure the light received from above. Therefore, it is worthwhile to separate this light under the moon from the darkness, and that celestial light from matter, and from there to climb to the super-celestial light; and from there again from the <term>rational</term> light to the <term>intellectual</term>, from this to the <term>intelligible</term>, and from this—according to our strength—to the divine. Thus, with "unveiled face," led evidently by the spirit of the Lord, we may be "transformed from glory into glory" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18.</note> into that same image.

->For the joy of the divinities, their celestial eyes laugh with splendor and exult with motion. Chapter VII.<-

**W**e see that after perfection, life, sense, certainty, grace, and joy are given to all things by the celestial rays—which descend to us from super-celestial things through the heavens as if through certain glasses—it is necessary that the light in the spirits above the heaven is their own perfection, the fertility of their life, the keenness of their sense, the clearest certainty of the truest intelligence, the abundance of grace, and the fullness of joy. The splendor of the heaven is an image of all these things; indeed, it is like a shadow compared to their clarity, because the body of the heaven can no more exactly imitate the clarity of the spirit than the earth can imitate the brilliance of the heaven. At the wonderful joy of the divinities, the heaven—acting as their body, or rather as their eye (for Orpheus calls the Sun an eye)—laughs with splendor and exults with motion. Just so, the earth, being furthest from them, mourns in darkness and grows numb in its position and idleness. Nor should we think that the heaven is moved by any force or defect, for its motion is perpetual by nature and it does not leave its natural place; its substance is also most absolute, from which nothing of itself departs. Rather, it moves out of a certain excess of joy, because of which, in its exultation, it knows not how to remain still. At the song of the joyful <term>numina</term> <note>original: "numinum"; refers to divine powers or deities inhabiting the spheres.</note>, as the Pythagoreans believe, the spheres lead their dances. From this, they produce a wonderful harmony through various and most orderly motions; at the laughter of the stars, which is especially indicated by their rays, all things that are under the heaven and upon the earth laugh; at darkness, as if at sadness, all things mourn. For we are accustomed to congratulate those who laugh and to be saddened with those who weep.

->The laughter of heaven, proceeding from the joy of the divinities—that is, light—nourishes and delights all things. Chapter VIII.<-

**T**hat light is the laughter of heaven proceeding from the joy of celestial spirits is indicated by human beings. Whenever they rejoice in spirit and laugh in their countenance, they certainly shine within and are expanded in spirit; they also seem to shine in their countenance, especially in the eyes, which are most "celestial" and which, in laughter, produce a circular motion like that of the heavens. In those who mourn, however, everything is darkened, constricted, and numb. Indeed, the rays from the laughing stars—directed most kindly and joyfully into the seeds of things as if from the eyes of divine minds—foster and generate all things, not otherwise than the gaze of the ostrich <note>Ficino refers to the classical and medieval belief that the ostrich hatches its eggs simply by looking at them intensely.</note>...

<summary>Ficino describes light as a universal hierarchy of joy and truth, moving from God down to the physical world, where the "laughter" of the stars (light) acts as a creative, life-giving force.</summary>

<sig>Qqq 2</sig>

...into the egg. For by their <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtute"; refers to the inherent power or life-force of the celestial bodies.</note> natural heat is inserted into all things, from which life arises, is nourished, and increases. From this it happens that all things seek pleasure, because they are generated not only by earthly pleasure, but also by celestial joy. Who would deny that the deities move and generate all things with a certain joyful affection? Since we see that from the nature of animals and from art, all things are procreated and perfected by pleasure.

->Light is incorporeal; it is form, or rather the act of a celestial nature. It can exist even without a subject body; it is<-
->everywhere, even under the earth, together with the <term>diaphanous</term>. <note>original: "diaphano"; the transparent medium, such as air or water, that allows light to pass through.</note> Chapter IX.<-

**B**ut it is helpful sometimes to wander more widely about these same matters along with our Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher whose works Ficino translated and commented upon.</note>. At the moment light penetrates a soft transparent medium, it strikes through even the hardest. Likewise, in the same moment it traverses a short space, it also traverses the longest. It is therefore incorporeal, for neither hardness nor space offers resistance. Nevertheless, because it is celestial, a nature that is earthy and foul—even if it be less hard—does not receive the bright purity of light because of its obstruction. Hence Plotinus forbids attributing corporeal passions to light—that is, to approach, to recede, to flow away, to flow out, to be contracted, or to be dilated. Instead, he thinks it should be said that where a transparent thing is exposed in the presence of a lucid body, light immediately exists there and acts there. If not, it does not exist there and does not act. Nor, however, does it simply cease to be, as long as the lucid body remains. Just as a visual ray does not cease, as long as sight remains. Indeed, light is the first form of the first body <note>The "first body" usually refers to the highest heaven or the empyrean.</note>. Thus it is so perfect that it does not exist by way of some idle quality distinct from action, but rather by way of a more vigorous act—so effective, evidently, that it extends itself through all things in a moment, not disconnected from its own source.

Furthermore, in whatever body beneath the heavens a certain fiery vigor similar to celestial fire prevails, light or a certain brightness flashes forth from there like a familiar color. Therefore, the nature of the heavens and of light, in order to foster all things, is not forced to begin anew through all things—if the paradox be true—that this light was once and for all infused into all. Hence that <term>Er</term> <note>original: "Hærus"; referring to the Myth of Er from the end of Plato's Republic.</note>, who rose from the dead in Plato's writing, had meanwhile looked upon the light, clearly with a celestial vision even then, but one hidden from mortal eyes. This light, indeed, being extended through all things entirely, would rule the universe. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who emphasized theurgy and the divine presence in the physical world.</note>, following the theology of the Phoenicians, asserts that the vehicle of this light—that is, the transparent medium—is infused into all things, even opaque ones; clearly a certain color, which is a portion of light, is present in all these. Light, however, cannot exist apart from the transparent in opaque things, although perhaps it can exist in itself within a luminous source.

If we rightly prophesy the secret meaning of the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>Plato's dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world.</note>, we recognize that the fire itself and the celestial spirit—the closest vehicle to the world-soul—thrive everywhere together with it. For this soul, by its vital motion, produces heat and motion everywhere; by its intelligence, it produces light, and simultaneously the transparent vehicle of light everywhere. Yet it is not proper to say that the earth shines. Since neither is the transparent mixed with it, nor is light communicated to it, even though it is infused. If anyone, relying on the rule of the astrologers, considers how much force the innumerable rays of the immense celestial machine have everywhere to penetrate the earth (the very center-point of the world), he will at least recognize from this that celestial light and the transparent medium necessary for light are also diffused everywhere through it. Although these cannot be open to most eyes in the earth, they are open, perhaps, to certain animals living there. For the Platonists say that just as cold is to heat, and blackness to whiteness, so darkness relates to light; such that darkness is not a pure deprivation of light, but the smallest or most opaque light. Blackness is a less opaque light. The transparent is like a certain beginning of a slightly clearer light. Color is a certain termination of light. This indeed happens everywhere in some way together with a certain color. For the light of both the soul and the heavens is so powerful that no place is open to pure darkness. Since many effects testify that heat (which is weaker than light in its extent) is everywhere beneath the earth. Perhaps led by this, the Pythagoreans built a certain "Tower of Jove" in the center of the world. They certainly (as we have said elsewhere) lit the <term>Vestal fire</term> <note>The sacred eternal flame of Rome, here used metaphorically for the central heat of the earth.</note> there. Because of this, they also dared to call the earth a "certain star." Along with these, the ancient theologians and Plato—as the effects themselves confirm—derived certain fiery rivers through the passages of the earth and found fiery <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones"; in this context, these are intermediary spirits or elemental beings, not necessarily malevolent.</note> there.

<summary>Ficino argues that light is an incorporeal, celestial act that penetrates all matter instantaneously, asserting that even the dark interior of the earth contains a degree of light and the world-soul's vitality. He integrates Plotinian physics with Pythagorean and Platonic myths to suggest that pure darkness does not exist, as light is the universal governing force.</summary>

Having argued that light is an incorporeal substance present throughout the universe, he now distinguishes light from heat and explores its status as a pure "act" of a source rather than a physical property of the medium it inhabits.</meta>

<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

## Light is one thing, heat is another; and light precedes heat. Chapter X.

It is clear that brightness is one thing and heat is another. For many things shine or glisten which are not hot, and many are even cold. Likewise, many things are hot which are dark. The heat of a fire often penetrates where its splendor does not pass, and splendor is propagated much further and more swiftly than heat. Anyone who considers it will find that heat comes from light; even in the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritibus"; in Neoplatonic psychology, these are the subtle vapors that connect the soul to the body and facilitate thought.</note> of the mind, the clarity of understanding precedes the affection of the will by a certain origin, and in the machine of the world, the rays of the Sun are the origin of the heat that follows them. In higher things, indeed, union reigns; but in the things that follow, there is diversity. Thus, in this fire near us, although heat is in the same body in which light is, it is nonetheless not *in* the light, just as the rest of the elements is not found in motion. But in celestial things, heat is in the light as if it were light itself, and in the motion of the heavens is the very rest of the heavens, to speak <term>physically</term>. <note>original: "Physicè"; referring to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world.</note> Finally, above the heavens in the Intelligence itself, the will is as if it were the same as the understanding, and in the will, joy is as if it were the same as the will.

## Light does not become a quality of the illuminated thing, but is the act of the illuminator. Nor are lights confused. Light is the bond of the universe. Chapter XI.

Since light is the cause of heat, and yet is of the same kind, it is rightly established as being in a certain higher category; it so excels the heat here among us that while light depends only on the luminous body, heat depends on the <term>subject</term> <note>original: "subiecto patiente"; the material or object that receives an action or quality.</note> that receives it. Light, therefore, exists as the proper and natural <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; a philosophical term for the active expression or operation of a thing's essence, as opposed to a passive quality.</note> of the illuminator alone. It does not become a <term>quality</term> <note>original: "qualitas"; a property that belongs to a material object, like being "green" or "hot."</note> of the illuminated body, nor is it so much *in* the illuminated thing as it is *present* to it. Therefore, it neither changes the nature of the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: "diaphani"; the transparent medium, such as air.</note> medium, nor is it changed by a change of place, nor does it have a fixed space through this. For it always occurs that it will propagate itself further, and in the same moment it performs multiple reflections: from mirrors to mirrors, from water to a mirror, and from there back to a wall, and so on. Nor does it ever desert the source from which it is reflected through these reflections. And in any point of the air, it forms multiple spiritual images of things, through which the eye can perceive the whole thing in any given point.

By all these things it is confirmed that light is not something corporeal, nor a quality of a body. But to return for a moment to the comparison of light with heat: light does not illuminate gradually, nor does it remain here even for a moment when the illuminator departs from above, as we have often said. Heat, however, since it is a quality of the heated air, arrives and departs gradually, and remains in the subject when the light departs. Light can therefore pass through from substance to substance as the same thing, provided it is not an <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidens"; a non-essential property that can change without destroying the substance.</note>, or quality, or a certain passion of some subject, but a separable act of the agent. Rightly, between a substance (which subsists in itself) and a quality (which depends on both the agent and the receiver), there exists the luminous act, suspended only from the agent. 

When light heats the air, the heating depends on both the light and the air, and it holds a middle place between the light and the generated heat. Therefore, since this heat remains when the light is withdrawn, light—if the air were removed—could still exist in the power of the Sun, because it is his own property. For a property is inseparable. Thus, between the light that is deeply internal to the shining body and the heat now made internal to the air, light is the medium—partly internal to the shining thing, and partly proceeding outside, like the radial act of a sight directed into a mirror, or a visual ray flashing from the eye. 

From this it is clear that light is proper to the celestial nature, nor is it communicated to any bodies except those that are celestial—that is, the transparent and the fiery, as we have said—and in these, it preserves its celestial property. By its gift, light is neither mixed with the illuminated transparent medium, nor are lights confused with other lights. For that kind of confusion does not belong to celestial acts and virtues (that is, to rays), but to elemental qualities, none of which are necessary for the presence of light. For it is enough for light if it does not strike earthly opacity, which is unfit for perceiving celestial things, as if light were everywhere its own master, never losing its celestial sublimity. 

That lights are not confused with other lights is apparent from this: if you walk toward three lamps, you will cast three shadows on the opposite side, namely because of the three lights not being mixed together. Likewise, if you place a huge board in front of these three, in the middle of which there is a single small hole, three lights from the three lamps will immediately shine out on the opposite side. This is because they are clearly not confused. Finally, if you were to lift one lamp, that light of its own which is seen to accompany it, in the common splendor...

<summary>Ficino distinguishes light from heat, defining light as an incorporeal "act" of a source that remains distinct and does not become a physical property of the air it passes through. He uses the behavior of shadows and reflections to prove that light maintains its celestial purity and individual identity even when multiple sources overlap.</summary>

Having established that light precedes heat, he now discusses how light rays concentrate power and how light serves as a physical and spiritual bridge between the heavens and the earth, concluding with a "negative theology" of light.</meta>

...diminished in the meantime. I pass over for now that Dionysian <note>original: "Dionysiacum"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who used light as a primary metaphor for God.</note> thought, that three rays in one splendor represent the divine Trinity to us. Astronomers and Magi <note>original: "Magi"; here meaning wise men or "natural magicians" who study the hidden properties of the stars and nature.</note> confirm that there are marvelous but hidden powers in rays. But a thing most worthy of wonder, known to many, is when many rays from a concave brass <note>A parabolic or "burning" mirror used to focus sunlight.</note> are reflected toward a center from every sight-line through equal angles; they burn even a distant body, or one that is quite hard. From this it is established, moreover, that rays are naturally hot, since by their gathering alone they soon become most fervent. Such, without doubt, is the power of light, that it easily, suddenly, and greatly unites celestial things with terrestrial ones, which are otherwise distant beyond proportion. Not only does it transfer all the virtues of the stars to what follows them, but it casts the Sun itself and the stars down to the lower realms. Just as our spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the subtle, airy substance that Ficino believed connected the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> carries the powers of the soul and the soul itself to the humors and limbs, and just as in us the spirit is the knot of the soul and body, so light is the bond of the universe. For the Sun and any star do not hurl their light as if through a very thin line, but pour it out from their entire circumference. But this light immediately gathers itself from everywhere into a cone, lest perhaps by flowing outside its source it should vanish. For in this way, because of the union, it will act more strongly, and the whole will be easier to find everywhere. And while the entire base is narrowed into a cone, the whole star and all its virtue will be present through the angle, and it will act powerfully everywhere; its entire magnitude can be seen in that angle. Thus also, since in the stars the center and the circumference are their light, insofar as it flows from the whole circumference, it imitates the circumference; but insofar as it is gathered into a narrow space, it imitates both the center and (to speak in a Platonic way) the World Soul <note>original: "mundianimam"; the Neoplatonic concept of an animating spirit that gives life and order to the physical cosmos.</note> itself. It imitates the Soul's intelligence by its clarity, its life by its heat, and finally its motion by its own motion. But enough of all these things is found in the commentaries on Plotinus and the *Timaeus* <note>Two of Ficino's primary sources: the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus and Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>.

### *Light imitates God; the degrees of lights, colors, and sciences. The numbers seven and nine. Chapter XII.*

**I**n a certain way, light also imitates God. For no eye, however sharp, perceives light itself in its pure and solitary state, inasmuch as it is incorporeal and <margin>10</margin> surpasses every proportion of the eyes, just like the divine. Indeed, the eyes see light only in an illuminated or luminous body, and in one that is somewhat dense—that is, one that tempers the light for the eyes. Perhaps, indeed, they perceive the illuminated thing rather than the light. The weakest eyes cannot even endure this. Stronger eyes look upon this, but not around the Sun. The most vigorous eyes look around the Sun, but by no means into the Sun. Similarly, you will recognize that various intellects stand in relation to God. Recognize, I pray, that the Sun can do all things simultaneously with a single nod, even to the most distant things, namely by light and heat. And God similarly does all things most easily, by intelligence and will simultaneously. Think again, that God creates three kinds of things: Angels, which are entirely incorporeal; likewise forms, which are entirely corporeal; and in the middle, souls, which are indeed incorporeal in substance, but in their affection and motion are as if corporeal. Similarly, look at the Sun: by heat it always generates corporeal things, and by light it generates spiritual images of bodies reflecting through the air. In the middle are the colors. There are especially seven effects, both of the Sun regarding bodies, and of the divine light regarding minds and souls. For it penetrates, illuminates, kindles, awakens, amplifies, elevates, and forms. Remember, finally, that neither the Sun nor anything else can be seen without the light of the Sun, since every light depends on the Sun. Similarly, all intellects stand in relation to the divine light, the first truth, and the fullness of all true things. But Theology treats these things most extensively. To these things add: no one defines absolutely what light is, but we always argue what it is *not*. It is not color, not transparency, not an image of the heavens (which would be merely an image). For it does not belong to an image to act upon substances beyond images and imaginary knowledge. Therefore, we know light only by negations <note>The "Via Negativa" or "Negative Theology"—defining a higher reality by stating what it is not, because it transcends human language.</note> and certain comparisons, just like God. It is helpful, however, to pursue such comparisons for a little while. But you, meanwhile, kindly grant pardon to my words about light. Divine light is distributed through nine orders of angels. The Platonists also accepted this number in regards to minds. Blessed souls also receive similar degrees. Similarly, the light of the Sun is distributed especially through nine degrees. The first degree of light is in the Sun; the second is the white light in the firmament...

<summary>Ficino explains how light acts as the "bond of the universe" by concentrating stellar power into geometric cones and argues that light, like God, can only be understood through negations because its pure form transcends human sight.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s classification of the degrees of light, moving from the celestial and elemental realms into a comparison between the degrees of light and the structure of human knowledge (the Nine Muses). It then transitions into Chapter 13, which argues for the spiritual nature of light and its resemblance to the human soul.</meta>

...truth also hidden from us; the third is of conspicuous light in the stars, but for you these are threefold: white, raw, and mixed. Thus, there are five degrees so far. Fire is referred to as red. The sixth degree is in the simple transparent <term>diaphanis</term><note>Transparent or translucent materials that allow light to pass through.</note> things beneath the Moon; the seventh is in the composite transparent things beneath the Moon, such as glass and crystals, which do not preserve light at all; the eighth is in composite transparent things that *do* preserve light, such as many eyes, glow-worms, and carbuncles <note>original: "carbunculi"; ancient and medieval terms for red gemstones, like garnets or rubies, which were legendary for supposedly "shining" in the dark.</note>. In these, there is a certain fatty tenacity combined with transparency that acts as a preserver of light. The ninth degree ends in colors and the images of colors. Furthermore, if colors are, as it were, certain kinds of lights, they also possess just as many degrees. The extremes are indeed white and black; between these, equally distant, is green, about which enough was said in the second book of *On Life* <note>Ficino's famous work *De vita libri tres*, where he discusses the medical and magical properties of colors and herbs.</note>. Between white and green is saffron, which is more similar to white; clear red is near green, while sapphire-blue is in the middle. There are likewise three degrees between green and black, mixed from the preceding ones in a threefold proportion. Since, indeed, the sciences can be compared to the lights and luminous colors, there are rightly nine of them, like the nine Muses under Apollo. Science deals either with things entirely separate from matter, or entirely corporeal, or those in the middle; the first is Divine <note>Theology or Metaphysics.</note>, the second is Natural <note>Physics.</note>, and the third is Mathematical. Each of these is cut into three. For the Divine either contemplates God, or entirely divine substances like angels, or intellectual souls—which are divine by nature but in a certain way incline toward bodies, though they remain separable. This is the extent of Divine science. Natural science also considers three things: elemental bodies, celestial bodies, or the souls joined to them. Mathematics is also threefold: for it treats either quantity alone—whether numerical or continuous, such as Arithmetic and Geometry—or quantity of this kind joined with the principle of motion, as in Astronomy <note>original: "Astrologus"; in Ficino's time, "astrologer" and "astronomer" were often used interchangeably for the study of the stars.</note>, or even joined with the principle of sense, whether of sight or hearing, such as Optics <note>original: "perspectiua".</note> or Music. Therefore, there are nine common lights of the sciences. But we seem to have wandered too far.

### *Light is a kind of spiritual thing. And spirits are a kind of light. The likeness of light to the soul and angels. Chapter XIII.*

**T**hat light is a certain spiritual thing, rather than corporeal, is established from this (as we have said elsewhere): that it is propagated everywhere without time <note>Ficino believed light traveled instantaneously.</note>, it fills transparent bodies without clashing, and it surrounds itself with filthy things without being defiled. Furthermore, it bestows itself more easily upon bodies that depart further from heavy, corporeal mass. Whence the most pure bodies of the heavens and fire (which is celestial, as the Platonists believe) shine within themselves, while air and water shine because of them. Meanwhile, even terrestrial things do not shine clearly of themselves, but from those others. On the surface of the earth, light—infused into various mixtures of the four elements, especially the terrestrial ones—takes on the forms of different colors, which are like the little bodies whose "souls" are the sparks of light infused into them. If you were to segregate and preserve these sparks from those mixtures, you would perhaps see what rational souls are like when separated from bodies. For they are certain lights, formerly more confused while in bodies, but now restored to their own nature, and therefore most bright. For in this way, the body, being most different from the soul, draws a kind of eclipse over it, just as the Moon does when joined to the Sun; or rather, just as a terrestrial mixture renders the light from heaven opaque and makes color out of light, so the body around the soul turns intelligence into sense. Just as a ray mixes heat into the air but keeps its light unmixed, so the soul communicates life to the body, but intelligence not at all; like light, it collects itself into a narrow space without being compressed, and again unfolds into a wide space without being distracted. It does not grow when the body increases, nor decrease when it is diminished. Light, depending on a wide source, collects itself through a shape and leaps forward in the opposite direction with transverse rays, soon recovering its original figure and gradually its width, finally to return to the same state. Similarly, the soul, brought down from the wide Divinity into the narrow body and its affections among us, can depart from here unharmed, destined to eventually recover its original form and amplitude. The rays also declare what the descent and ascent of angels is like: leaping forward and leaping back in a moment, and in leaping forward, never abandoning the Sun.

### Light in God, in the angel, in reason, in the spirit, in the body.
#### Chapter XIV.

**B**ut to return to the point from which we digressed: although the heavens shine and rejoice in themselves, it is not *from* themselves, but from the clarity and joy of the things above them, just as the eye shines from the clarity of the spirit <term>spiritus</term><note>In Renaissance medicine and philosophy, "spirit" was a subtle bodily fluid that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> and the gladness of the soul. The spirit, moreover, rejoices most of all in its own clarity and that of the Sun; the soul rejoices in the clarity of the spirit and the mind. It seems, then, that this light is the mind reflecting through a transparent body, like glass, and thus it is made visible. But the mind itself is a light that is entirely invisible within itself because of its extreme abundance and fineness. For even if light is everywhere during the day, it appears nowhere unless there is something dense and resisting. Remove the density, and even if it is not seen, it is still there. Add the density again, and immediately it appears once more. From this it is clearly established that light itself, in its own nature, is something intellectual. It soon becomes sensible when something dense is placed under it, but remains hidden when that density is removed. How we might imagine visible light to have emerged from the invisible—just as a glowing circle is formed from a spark in motion—we discuss in the sixth book of our *Theology* <note>Referring to his major work, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>. Accordingly, light in the mind is truth rejoicing and a true joy; light from the mind in bodies is a certain declaration of the truth of sensible things, the flower of beauty, and the delight of the senses. But consider this more correctly: light, as if it were the property of a circular body perpetually returning to the same point—or rather, like an intelligence reflecting itself in a circle—seems to touch everything and return to its origin. As it is reflected upward into itself, it leads us back, by both contemplation and love of itself, to our fatherland <note>original: "patriam"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the divine realm from which the soul originated and to which it seeks to return.</note>. But in the meantime, it also compels me, as I speak, to return repeatedly to the same point in the manner of a circle. You, however—who are yourself a friend of light—please indulge this long-winded friend of light. With your kind permission, then, I shall repeat: Light in the divine mind surpasses understanding. From there, the same light is infused into the angelic mind, where it is rendered according to understanding, but stays above the limits of reason. This divine and angelic light then emerges in the minds of men according to reason, but it surpasses the imagination <term>phantasiam</term><note>The "phantasia" or imagination was considered the faculty that processed sensory images before they reached the rational mind.</note>. In the spirit, it exists according to imagination and is above sense; in the body, however, it becomes familiar to sense (though not to matter), especially in the eyes, which are like the celestial stars of the soul. For even that flower of beauty appearing in bodies was placed by Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, a major influence on Ficino.</note> within a certain non-corporeal splendor. Certainly, the first beauty itself is nothing other than the "splendor of the glory of the Father of Lights" and the "figure of His substance" <note>Ficino here weaves together Neoplatonic thought with the New Testament (James 1:17 and Hebrews 1:3).</note>. From this, a triple beauty shines forth: the first through the angelic intellects, the second through intellectual souls, and the third through bodies that are beautiful everywhere. It is like one light passing through three paths that vary in color, and thus it reflects a varied splendor from the first. Therefore, the very grace of beauty—which turns those who look and meditate upon it so wonderfully toward itself, even in bodies—is nothing other than splendor shining down through these stages. It acts most powerfully through the rays of the eyes, seizing those who look and, with a certain hidden heat, transforming lovers wonderfully into itself. But enough of this has been said in the book *On Love* <note>Ficino's *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note>. Let us return to the established order. In all minds, light is exuberant life, clear and certain truth, and full joy; from there, in bodies, it is the unfolding and outpouring of divine life, the declaration of the truth of things and their Author, the grace of form, and the incentive for pleasure. Empedocles and Zeno <note>Ancient Greek philosophers; Zeno was the founder of Stoicism.</note> maintain that just as a flame is related to a coal, so in a way light is related to a flame; they say flame is like dense light, while light is the rarest flame and the life of all things. Plotinus and Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a late Neoplatonist who wrote extensively on the metaphysics of light.</note> think that light is a certain vision and gaze of the gods, sent forth from afar through the rays of celestial eyes. They say it is a certain divine spirit that sees all things and, as far as it is able, is seen by all. They add that a spirit of this kind is never extinguished but follows the stars, just as the visual ray of animals that see at night sometimes flashes outward and sometimes does not, yet is not meanwhile entirely extinguished, continuously accompanying the life of its eye. For if the entire nature of heaven is eternal, and in this nature nothing is more familiar, beautiful, effective, or divine than light, then surely light is also eternal. Perhaps one might also conjecture that the fire beneath the Moon, along with its light, is eternal as well. For it is a certain portion of celestial fire, enclosed in denser bodies by a certain celestial force. This, the E- <margin>Egyptians</margin>

...the Egyptians recognized a celestial spirit infused into the elements. The Pythagoreans discovered this to be the Vesta-like fire <note>original: "Vestalem ignem"; referring to Vesta, the Roman goddess of the hearth, symbolizing the central fire of the cosmos.</note>, or a fire burning in the center of the world. The Stoics conceived of this as an intellectual fire running through all things. Plato also held this view, as we have proved in the *Timaeus*, and so did Plotinus. The ancient theologians, as Virgil <note>original: "Marone"; Ficino refers to Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> testifies, called this the divine ether inhaled by living creatures, which passes through all lands, the reaches of the sea, and the deep heavens. "Fiery is their vigor and celestial their origin." <note>original: "Igneus est ollis vigor & coelestis origo"; a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, line 730, describing the spark of life.</note> Perhaps, therefore, when fire seems to be extinguished, it is resolved into a hidden fire, and the light of this fire into that hidden light.

---

### *Even if souls are called lights, they cannot be resolved into one common light.*
### *Chapter XV.*

**W**hat I was just imagining—even if it is perhaps not true—can be imagined more freely. But regarding the soul, it truly cannot be imagined. For those things which have a common matter between them can be confused with one another. Likewise, things that are parts of others can be restored to them. Again, those which are certain subservient acts of a superior substance can be, as it were, resolved into it; and those which are accidents <term>accidents</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature (like the color of a shirt).</note> can more easily vanish. But rational souls are incorporeal substances, rulers of bodies and resisting them; they act through themselves, turn back by themselves, and subsist in themselves. They are sometimes even rebellious toward what is superior and differ greatly among themselves. Reason distinguishes accidents from substances and separates incorporeal things from corporeal ones. Therefore, they can neither be confused, nor restored, nor resolved. Concerning these matters, I have written most extensively in the *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, the *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note> and in the second book of my *Letters*. And if souls are imagined as lights, they are not indeed like rays, but like lamps <note>original: "luces"; implying individual sources of light rather than mere reflections.</note>; and these are substantial, far more excellent than sensible light, more like stars than dependent lights, endowed with a certain native light almost like the stars, and moreover about to receive another light from God, just as stars receive it from the Sun. Just as visible light is not perceived except by some visual light <note>The "visual spirit" believed to reside in the eye.</note>, nor is intelligible light perceived except by some intellectual light, so too a distinct and eternal substantial light is not perceived except by a distinct and eternal substantial light. This is especially true if that light is to be perceived under the very principle of eternity. Therefore, through this principle, looking out as if through a mirror, the specific immortality of our mind will immediately shine forth.

---

### *Light is like a visible divinity, reflecting God and leading us step by step to divine habits.*
### *Chapter XVI.*

**F**inally, light is like a certain divinity in this worldly temple, reflecting the likeness of God. So much so that our Plato, in his book on the *Republic*, called it the son of the Good itself. For it is, like God, to be venerated before all things in its appearance. It is also a certain sudden and very wide expansion, without detriment to itself, most willingly and most happily bestowing itself upon all things on account of its exuberant goodness and bounty. It is the cause, the preservation, and the awakening of all things that are born. Accordingly, it lifts up all other things toward the life, truth, and joy from which it descends. Without its presence, all things seem to die; but by its presence, they seem to come to life again. Meanwhile, since it is not only from the Sun but is also preserved by it and does not depart from it, it warns us that we are not only made by God but are also preserved by Him, and that we must not depart from Him in the least. Indeed, when it seems to be farther from the Sun, it is then that it reflects more intensely toward the Sun. And if perhaps I seem too inquisitive to someone, I will nevertheless say what has now come to mind concerning justice, carried away by the love of light and justice. For what limit is there to love? Indeed, it seems to me that light often exhorts us to justice and deters us from injustice, where it clearly declares how powerful justice itself is and how weak injustice is. For a ray that falls straight, as if just, making equal angles on both sides, acts powerfully and penetrates. And where it passes from the air into water, it is not refracted <note>original: "frangitur"; literally "broken."</note> obliquely. And when it touches a solid, it reflects back into itself like a strong thing. On the contrary, a ray that falls obliquely, as if unjust, making unequal angles on both sides, accomplishes hardly anything as if weak, is suddenly refracted obliquely, and never returns to itself but settles in the opposite direction. How much constancy, equality, and purity are everywhere pleasing to light as something divine is shown by its behavior in mirrored bodies. In these and from these, it is multiplied in a wonderful way on account of these three qualities.

<summary>Ficino explores light as a bridge between the physical and divine, arguing that souls are individual substantial lights that cannot be dissolved into a common source. He concludes by using the physics of light rays (refraction and reflection) as a moral allegory for justice and injustice.</summary>
