# BOOK OF LIGHT.

Perhaps some poet might say that just as Apollo <note>original: "Phœbus"; the Greek and Roman god of the sun, who famously pursued the nymph Daphne.</note> loved Daphne, so light loves virginity. For the very flower of brightness <note>original: "candoris"; referring to a white, pure brilliance.</note> flourishes alongside the flower of virginity and is lost at the same time. This is especially true in the circles of the eyes, through which character is testified. From this, Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher known for his sharp observation of the natural world.</note> wisely detected that a girl, whom he had recently judged a virgin, had soon after been defiled. But let us now return to our purpose. Light not only instructs us in our conduct, but—what is best of all—it is commemorated through divine worship by the human race, so that neither the impious dare to deny there is a God (since nothing is clearer to the senses than His image), nor can the wicked trust that they can hide from His eye or escape His hand, for clarity itself is His image.

And more swiftly than can be said, light spreads through all things in an instant, and there is no one who can hide from its heat. <note>original: "nec est qui se abscondat à calore eius"; a quotation from Psalm 19:6, describing the sun's reach.</note> Light is one in all things and around all things. Light in all things made by God is a certain splendor of divine brightness, and (if I may put it this way) it is God as if limiting Himself and accommodating Himself to the capacity of His works. But God Himself is an immense light consisting in Himself, and through Himself in all things and outside all things throughout the infinite. He is that fountain of life in whose light (as David says) we see light. <note>original: "in cuius lumine... uidemus lumen"; from Psalm 36:9.</note> He is also the eye by which all eyes see, and as Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet of Greek myth.</note> says, the eye that looks into all things in each individual, and in truth beholds all things in itself, while it perceives itself to be all things.

Moreover, He established that all things should be seen in one light, not only bodily things but also incorporeal ones. You see light in the matter of the world, full of all the forms of all things and constantly turning. Subtract the matter, leave the rest, and you have the soul: an incorporeal light separable from bodies, taking all forms, yet changeable. Remove change from this again, and you have reached the angelic intellect: a separate light, all-forming, and now also unchangeable. Take away from this that diversity by which any form is different from the light, and where some forms are different from others and infused from elsewhere. This light shines infinitely because it shines by its own nature, and it is simply absolute. In this way, finally, God will shine upon the eyes of the mind through this light with a certain higher light, most full of life and sense—since His image, that is, the light of the Sun, bestows life and sense upon all. And the more excellent that light is than ours, the greater the joy it will bring to the mind than this light brings to the eyes.

->*On the state of the blessed under divine light, and the miserable. Chapter XVII.*<-

**T**he Sun in the heavenly Jerusalem, as the Prophet says, is God Himself. He undoubtedly promises the light of universal truth and full joy in light to His worshippers on earth who are to return to their heavenly homeland. He promises this light especially to the wise who instruct others in justice. "The learned shall shine," says Daniel, "like the splendor of the firmament; and those who have instructed many in justice, like the stars for all eternity." <note>original: "Fulgebunt... docti sicut splendor firmamenti"; quoting Daniel 12:3.</note> He does not say they shall shine like the Sun, for there the Sun is God Himself. 

Indeed, the splendor of the firmament is that brightness of the heavens which is always hidden from our eyes because of its refined nature. For since all fire shines, the entire substance of the heavens shines much more, even where there are no stars; but like a fire shining far off in the thinnest matter, it is scarcely visible to anyone. Those wise men who among us were content with contemplation alone will shine with that kind of splendor. But those who, having contemplated divine things, then turned themselves to action to instruct others in justice and wisdom, will shine with a more abundant and manifest light, like the stars. For since the wise have loved and worshipped nothing other than light—for they seek only this in seeking any truth—they deservedly receive the rewards of light. And those who illuminate others forever are not unjustly themselves illuminated by divine power for all eternity. 

Just as the reward of the pious is a certain wonderful participation in light, so the punishment of the impious is the very deprivation of light. Indeed, the divine Sun itself, which wonderfully nourishes the healthy and vigorous eyes of the pious, strikes the weak eyes of the impious and torments their conscience with a burning heat. In the same way, the light of the Sun delights in the open, but when forced into a narrow space, it burns completely. But we gladly return to the blessed. To us, the light of the air is indeed pleasing to all, because it is most closely related to the vital and animal spirit, and it delights us with the variety of countless things. More pleasant is the light in the spirits of the body, which are of the blood;

A most pleasing light, innermost to the minds of the blessed, fills the mind to such an extent that it immediately overflows from there into the body: into the body, I say, both the celestial body (to speak in the Platonic manner <note>original: "Platonicè loquar"; Ficino refers to the "astral body" or "chariot of the soul," a Neoplatonic concept of a subtle body that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical world</note>) belonging to each individual soul, and also the human body, which has at last been made as if celestial. In that state, every person is like a great eye, entirely transparent from every side and shining. For this reason, as each person directs the rays of both their mind and their visible body toward one another, they understand each other completely with a very easy nod. Each will shine within the others by the mutual casting of rays. God, however, like the Sun among the stars, will shine as abundantly as He does happily in all things.

# MARSILIO FICINO
## Of Florence, while still a youth; his Book
### on Pleasure, to Antonio Canisiano, a
### Florentine citizen. <note>Antonio Canisiano was a contemporary of Ficino and a fellow member of the Florentine intellectual circle.</note>

## PREFACE.

### *Three types of disputation.*

I remember when I was together with you at your estate in Campoliano, and we were led along by the exceptional beauty of that region as well as the sweetness of the various fruits in which that villa especially abounds, that we happened upon a discussion regarding pleasure. You requested this of me yourself, asking that I should commit it to writing as soon as leisure was granted. Therefore, I have composed this little work on pleasure for you as soon as I returned to Figline <note>original: "Figinum"; Ficino’s birthplace in the Arno Valley</note>, with the greatest pleasure itself. Truly, so that we may begin from this point especially, there are three types of disputation among philosophers. The first is that by which we defend and approve a certain specific side of a question through argument, as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle, known for their systematic and often dogmatic approach to logic and science</term> and the Stoics <term>Stoics: Philosophers who taught that virtue is the only good and advocated for the control of emotions</term> have done. The second is that where, after a question has been proposed, we report various opinions and reasons regarding the matter sought, so that—having proposed many views and compared them in turn—we may choose which of them appears more probable and likely. This was the method used by the Academics <term>Academics: Followers of the Platonic Academy who, in its middle period, emphasized the difficulty of reaching absolute certainty</term> and almost all the Socratics. The third type is most characteristic of the Sceptics, who, because they think all things are indifferent, hold nothing certain or probable to follow; for they confuse and mix together those things which are separated and distinct by the order of nature, and they are rejected by all the more excellent philosophers. I have, therefore, decided to propose for myself at this time the method of the Academics and Socratics from among all these. For indeed Plato—whom we follow and venerate as the God of Philosophers—forbids those who are still in their tender years from offering their own opinion on a matter, lest (as often happens with the young) what we approved most in our early years must later be revoked in mature age and by weightier judgment, and be turned into a contrary opinion. I thought it better, therefore, to run through the opinions of the other philosophers on pleasure in a brief discourse than to express my own, lest I should boldly assert something against what we are taught by our Plato, and so that I might satisfy your will, which I know to be most ardent in the studies of philosophy.

-> But so much for these matters; let us now <-
-> arrive at the opinions of the philosophers. <-

# MARSILIO FICINO
## The Florentine, On the Parts of the Soul,
### Chapter One.

->Also on Gladness, Joy, and Pleasure, according to Plato.<-

Plato, therefore—to begin with the prince of philosophers—having divided the soul into two parts, namely the mind and the senses, attributed gladness <note>original: *laetitia*; often used for a more expansive or visible cheerfulness</note> and joy to the mind, and pleasure to the senses. However, he considers that the first two differ from one another in that all joy is worthy of praise, whereas gladness is partly to be praised and partly to be censured. For gladness is a certain elevation of the mind in the possession of some good, which can nonetheless exceed the bounds of modesty or preserve them; joy, however, is that very pleasantness which is received from contemplation or some other practice of the virtues. 

Therefore, in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul, beauty, and eros</note>, when speaking of that first and true life which the soul enjoys in its celestial seats, he says that it is nourished and rejoices in the contemplation of truth. For this reason, he frequently calls joy the "nourishment of the mind," for he wishes truth itself to be like a field, and the contemplation of that truth to be the harvest. The nourishment then taken from these two is joy, by which the mind fully enjoys the contemplation of truth. 

On this account, in the same *Phaedrus*, when he discusses those shadows into which the soul has been cast and submerged from the highest and true light, he says: "there is much effort to see where the plain of truth lies; for the fitting food for the soul comes from there, and the nature of the wings, by which the soul is raised, is nourished by this." Plato uses the term "wings" <term>wings of the soul <gloss>the intellectual and moral virtues that allow the soul to "fly" back to the divine</gloss></term> for those things by which the mind flies back to the higher realms, from which it had descended due to the contemplation of earthly things. Since one can achieve this through two virtues—namely, the contemplative and the moral—Plato understands these virtues, as I interpret him, to be the very wings of the soul, which it recovers through the contemplation of truth and divine things, just as it had lost them through the desire for these earthly things. 

When, through the exercise of both natural and moral philosophy, the soul has recovered its wings and flown back to the heavens, Plato believes two rewards are returned to the returning soul: one is the contemplation of divinity, and the other is a certain perfect and absolute joy, which the soul enjoys in that very knowledge of God. Plato calls the former "Ambrosia" <note>The food of the gods in Greek mythology, granting immortality</note> and the latter "Nectar" <note>The drink of the gods</note> in the *Phaedrus*, using these words: "the soul which has truly looked upon these things and been nourished by them, entering again within the heavens, returns home." When the charioteer has returned, standing the horses at the manger, he sets before them Ambrosia, and after it, Nectar to drink. 

Following the custom of Pythagoras, he calls Reason the "charioteer," and the other parts and natures of the soul the "horses," because reason leads, while the others are led and governed entirely. I believe the same is signified by several of the most excellent poets when they mention ambrosia, nectar, or the charioteer in relation to the soul. These things, then, come from the divine opinion of our Plato concerning the nature of joy itself. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of mystical and philosophical writings called the *Hermetica*</note> seems to have understood the same when he said these things concerning the Most High God:
> You grant us reason, sense, and intelligence. Reason, so that we may track you through our perceptions; sense, so that we may come to know you; and knowledge, so that in knowing you, we may rejoice because you have shown yourself to us in your entirety.

But enough concerning joy for now.

->What pleasure is, and that it is not a good in itself, by many reasons, according to Plato. Chapter II.<-

Plato maintains that pleasure <note>original: *voluptas*; here referring specifically to sensory gratification</note> is a certain sweet motion in the senses that proceeds from the filling of a deficiency. For he argues that deficiency and the filling of it are in a way at war with each other; from the former, desire and pain arise in our senses, and from the latter, pleasure. He does not think this pleasure of which we now speak should be numbered among the "goods." Although he demonstrated this with many very true reasons, this one is the first and most powerful of all: just as the presence of heat makes those things to which heat arrives hot, so too by that which is "Good" being present, all things lacking goodness are made good. 

Yet, no one is made better by the possession of pleasure, since even beasts possess pleasure—greater even than that of humans—who are nonetheless not better than humans, nor even good at all. Furthermore, women and children, and finally the foolish and the cowardly, all seek pleasure and embrace it with all their might, much more so even than men who are good and outstanding in character. <note>original: *ingenio*</note>

<meta>Catchword: character:</meta>

<summary>Ficino distinguishes between intellectual joy (gaudium), which nourishes the soul in the contemplation of truth, and sensory pleasure (voluptas), which he argues is not an inherent good as it is shared by animals and the base-minded.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: his own (suum)</meta>

with their nature. But it would be absurd if a thing were the "Good" if it belonged more to the wicked and the lazy than to upright and excellent men. Nor can contraries be mixed with one another as that man <note>referring to a hypothetical opponent or a hedonist like Aristippus</note> thinks; yet pleasure is undoubtedly found even where there are evils, since it is not lacking in the wicked and the unjust. Therefore, in no way is it the "Good": for it joins with that which is evil. The Good, however, can in no way unite with the evil, because they are repugnant to one another. 

Add to this what is said by Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning rhetoric and ethics</note>: that good and evil are never found simultaneously in the same man. Nevertheless, the same man is often affected by pain and pleasure at the very same time. Indeed, he says every deficiency <note>original: *indigentiam*; also meaning "want" or "lack"</note> is painful, and every sensory replenishment of it is pleasant. He calls thirst a deficiency of nature, and drinking a replenishment. Therefore, that [thirst] is troublesome, while this [drinking], on the contrary, is delightful; furthermore, it happens that one drinks and thirsts at the same time, from which he wishes to conclude that one can have pain and pleasure simultaneously. 

Indeed, desire, anxiety, suspicion, envy, and pity—all of which contain pain within themselves—are companions of pleasure. Whence, fearing desire, he says that it proceeds from the senses permitted to both pain and pleasure at once, whereby it happens that pleasure is coupled and confused with pain. And since the Good is not mixed with evil, he denies that pain can be evil and pleasure can be the Good. 

Furthermore, since every good ought to be stable and permanent, who would say that pleasure, which has no stability, is the Good? And yet, it cannot be denied. For if anyone considers its definition, pleasure is unstable and uncertain, for it was called a "motion" <note>original: *motio*; a technical term in Platonic physics for change or process as opposed to a fixed state</note> in its definition (as we recalled above). Nothing is more contrary to stability than motion; nor is there anyone who has ever tasted any pleasure of the body who does not know how fragile it is, how brief, with what speed it glides and flows away, and how quickly it is turned into its opposite. 

Moreover, that which is good can never be contrary to the Good. Since pleasure hinders many and great goods, who would doubt that it is contrary to the Good? For pleasures hinder <term>prudence</term> <note>original: *prudentia*; practical wisdom or the ability to judge what is right</note>, they pour darkness into the mind, they deprave judgment, and with their flatteries and enticements—like certain little harlots—they allure and ensnare the minds of men, prostrating the entire nature of man in the mud and filth of vices and crimes. For the divine Plato, in his letter to Dionysius, says: "pleasure brings detriment to men, giving birth to ignorance, restlessness, folly, and petulance." 

Furthermore, there is no good that is not worthy of either praise or veneration. But no one of sound mind praises pleasure, nor is anyone judged worthy of honor and glory because he enjoys the greatest pleasures. Rather, he who is of such a character that he may despise and neglect them with a high and invincible soul is honored. Added to these things is the fact that nothing can rightly be called "ours" unless it is either within our very nature or has proceeded from ourselves. And we are nothing else besides mind and reason. 

The body, however, is a prison and a tomb <note>original: *carcer, & sepulchrum*; a reference to the Platonic/Orphic wordplay on *soma* (body) and *sema* (tomb)</note> for us. The senses, indeed, are like certain attendants or ambushers, who seem to care for and strive for this most of all: to plunge and bind us more deeply in the darkness of this prison, so that the souls may neither fly back to their own place and heavenly homeland, nor look back at the breezes, being shut in by darkness and a blind prison. By this, it is brought about that only those things seem to be ours and to exist in us which have proceeded from the soul and reason. Other things, however, arise from fortune or from our enemy, the prison; they are not so much ours as they are the body’s and fortune’s. And Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar and writer</note> says rightly: "let no one call his own that which is outside himself." 

Therefore, since pleasure is innate and implanted in the body and the senses, he who numbers it among our goods will without doubt seem to be insane. Add to these things, if you please, what Socrates says in Plato’s *Gorgias*: that all goods of the soul proceed from art, righteousness, order, and choice. In this, the entire discipline of the moral philosophers also agrees: that the whole power of virtue and of the goods of the soul consists in choice <note>original: *electio*; the deliberate decision of the will</note>. But who would say that pleasure proceeds from choice? Must not counsel and deliberation have first held a place in those things that fall under choice? For nothing is chosen unless it has been previously consulted and judged. But no one deliberates in order to have pleasure in himself, for that is innate in us. Wherefore Socrates thinks there are two ideas <note>original: *ideae*; here meaning guiding principles or drives</note> in each one of us which we follow wherever they lead: one is an affectation for the best opinion, the other is a desire for pleasures; the former he calls "acquired," but the latter "innate." Therefore, pleasure follows neither art, nor reason, nor any order at all, but rather the nature of the senses...

<summary>Ficino presents a Platonic argument against identifying physical pleasure with the "Highest Good," noting its instability, its presence in the wicked, and its tendency to cloud the rational mind. He concludes by contrasting the innate, animalistic drive for pleasure with the acquired, deliberate pursuit of virtue through reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical critique of physical pleasure, contrasting its volatile and destructive nature with the stability of true "goods." It builds on the previous page's discussion of how pleasure is intertwined with pain.</meta>

<page-num>313</page-num>

-># BOOK ON PLEASURE.<-

...its own sudden and rash impulse, rather than by any certain judgment or counsel, it is stirred up in us, flatters the senses, charms the body with a certain destructive sweetness, and tickles and weakens the spirit; it displaces the mind and reason from their proper state. Moreover, such is the nature of all good things that while they are in the future, they raise a person's hope, but when they are present, they make the mind of the possessor tranquil and quiet, rendering them content with what is at hand. They fill the possessor so completely that he lacks nothing further, seeks nothing, and desires nothing, as if he possessed that one thing which is by its nature sufficient and perfect. Even if one who enjoys the possession of some good should desire something more, he nevertheless seems to be entirely free from anxiety and distress. Future pleasures, however, affect the senses with an intolerable heat of desire; they kindle worry, burden the mind with anxiety, and (to put it briefly) drive one into a certain madness and rage. When a person finally embraces those present pleasures for which he had burned with desire, they immediately bring fear and suspicion along with them. They blind us while we enjoy them and reduce us to the ferocity of wild beasts. Not yet even fully drained—indeed, to speak more truly, not yet even tasted with the tips of the lips—they affect the mind with an incredible repentance, shame, weariness, resentment, and utter listlessness. Thus, that saying of Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>A Platonic dialogue focusing on the soul and its immortality</note> is most true: that pain and pleasure are both connected to the same head, and nature has joined their tips into one. For that reason, it happens that whichever of them is present, the other follows afterward. From this, the fires of lust rise again, and the more greedily pleasures are drained, the more numerous and fertile the seeds and sprouts of lust spring back. Hence (as I believe), the poets in the underworld depict Tityos <note>A giant in Greek mythology punished in Tartarus</note>, whose body is stretched across nine whole acres:

> A huge vulture with a hooked beak 
> plucking at his immortal liver and his entrails 
> fertile with punishments, searches for his feast, 
> and dwells deep in his chest; nor is any rest 
> given to the fibers as they grow back. 
<note>original: "Porrigitur, rostroq; immanis uultur adunco / Immortale iecur tondens fœcundaq; pœnis / Viscera rimatur epulis, habitatq; sub alto / Pectore, nec fibris requies datur illa renatis." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI.</note>

For this reason, the divine Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician</note> and Plato wished for a mind of this sort to be like a leaky vessel, because of the insatiable and infinite whirlpool of craving, which is satisfied by no pleasures. Epicharmus the Pythagorean and Socrates compared the lustful mind not only to a broken vessel but even to the Euripus <term>Euripus</term> <note>A narrow sea channel famous for its violent, reversing currents</note>, because just as the water in the Euripus flows in and out, and is tossed up and down, so too in a mind of this kind, now desire or pleasure persists, now it ceases and flows away, and again it is reborn and flows back. At one moment the lustful mind rejoices and hopes, and is as if lifted upward; at another it grieves, despairs, fears, is anxious, and falls downward. Now it wants this, then it does not want it; indeed, at the very same time, reason wants one thing while the senses affect another. Thus it happens that such a mind is not only pulled now to this and now to that, but even at one and the same time, it is distracted by contrary emotions and differing opinions. Therefore, Socrates used to say he would prefer that his lyre be out of tune, or the choir he led, and that many other men should contradict him, rather than that he, being one, should be at odds and dissonant with himself. Whence Pythagoras reasonably calls virtue a certain "harmony." Next follow the remaining three arguments of Plato against pleasure. For he considers the nature of good and evil to be opposites: we attain the former with difficulty, but into the latter we slide easily, as if down a slippery path. Therefore, it would happen that evils would so increase that the entire nature of good would necessarily be destroyed and uprooted, unless nature had applied a most suitable remedy to this deadly plague. For it is so ordained that individual "goods," because of their great natural kinship, seek one another out. They tend toward a single point and can in no way be distinguished from one another, but unite in a kind of fusion; whoever possesses one of these cannot lack any good thing. The virtues follow one another with such a connection that he who has attained one already enjoys the possession of all virtues. For this reason, God seems to have placed the union and coupling of good things as an offset to the labor and difficulties of attaining them. But evils, on the other hand, disagree and conflict among themselves, nor can they in any way unite or be confused with one another. Correctlty does Aristotle say that evil destroys itself, because if it were entirely whole, it would be intolerable. Nor do prodigality and greed, or boldness and cowardice, ever meet in the same...

It concludes by asserting that while virtues are harmoniously united, vices are inherently conflicting and self-destructive.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument that sensory pleasure is not the "highest good," contrasting it with the unity of virtues and its role as a mere biological tool rather than a final goal.</meta>

<page-num>990</page-num>
->## OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

<margin>S.</margin>
Finally, in no other way are the extremes of vices connected to one another, since they are entirely opposite. For this reason, it seems that nature has applied the best remedy against the tendency to sin: although someone may be prone to falling, they cannot fall toward every precipice at once. However, one who ascends to the top with the greatest difficulty must necessarily reach the peak in its entirety and integrity. Since the condition of evils and goods is of this kind, it is concluded by necessary reason that those things which do not follow one another cannot be "goods." Pleasures, however, far from coming together, actually seem to conflict with one another and quite often bring about an obstacle. For while one bodily sense is moved by the greatest sweetness <note>original: "suauitate"</note>, the remaining senses hardly perceive the delight of those things then offered to them. It also happens that one person perceives more and greater pleasures than another, and not all living creatures are delighted equally. But virtues—and absolutely all things that are truly good—are, for the reason we reported a little earlier, so joined to one another that they are all present at once in the same person; nor can more of these be present in one person than in another. If, therefore, it is clear that the nature of goods and the nature of pleasures are different from each other, surely no one would call bodily pleasure a "good," unless he were an excessive friend to it.

Next, another argument of Plato proves that the property of "the good" is to tend toward the common utility and safety of the human race. He says that pleasure, however, produces its own <term>lust and love</term> <note>original: "libidinem, amoremq;"</note>, and whoever is subject to this always focuses only on their own private desire. Such a person has no care for anyone else, provided he may more vigilantly obey his own "whirlpool" of greed. Everything he does is referred back to that sweetness and delight perceived by the senses.

The final reasoning of the Platonists is that which says "the good" and "the end" <note>the Greek concept of *Telos*, or the ultimate purpose of a thing</note> are entirely the same thing; and they define the "end" as that toward which appetite is directed as its ultimate point. Therefore, since the natural appetite in man desires pleasure only for the sake of something else, how could anyone of sound mind think that this is the "end" or the "good" at all? In fact, they believe that this kind of sweet perception was given to living things by nature for this reason: so that they might acquire and prepare what is necessary for living. For that which lives requires two things above all: that it rejects and repels what can harm it, and that it takes and adopts what can benefit it. Since it is laborious and difficult to drive the former away and pursue the latter, nature—lest living things be too slow to provide what they need because of that very difficulty—intertwined a certain pleasure in every such action. Thus it happens that, charmed and utterly captured by this sweetness as if by a **lure** <note>original: "esca," literally "bait" or "food used as a lure"</note>, they do not flee from any dangers or labor, nor do they perceive the difficulty of preparing their food, but are more ready to provide the necessities of life. They demonstrate that nature gave us pleasure for the sake of these things by this sign: that all living creatures are moved by this sweetness (which we have already mentioned so often) whenever they expel something from the body which is superfluous, or when they take in what is necessary. The more they do this, the more delight they perceive. Yet, when they have entirely filled the lack in their nature, they feel no further pleasure; we see them moved only as long as they are filling that lack. It is as if nature directed the pleasure of the senses toward the goal of attaining the necessities of life and fulfilling a physical need. Pleasure was therefore handed down for the sake of both preserving life and propagating the species; it is not to be sought for its own sake, nor is it the "end," and therefore it should not even be called "the good," as we have demonstrated many times.

**Archytas the Pythagorean** <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician, contemporary of Plato</note> also used this argument against bodily pleasure: he said that causes and the things that follow from those causes are always related. Therefore, he thinks there is no doubt that something from which many evils follow cannot be a good. It is clear that for the sake of pleasure, all pestilential disturbances of the soul are born: adulteries, debaucheries, murders, thefts, dissensions, and finally all crimes. From these it is brought about (as he thinks) that pleasure seems not only "not a good," but a certain "greatest and detestable evil." By the same reasoning, **Antisthenes the Socratic** <note>A pupil of Socrates and a precursor to the Cynic school of philosophy</note> proves that bodily pleasure is the extreme and highest of evils, because that which is the cause and origin of all evils can deservedly be judged the worst of the rest. Since all sins proceed from ignorance, and nothing can corrupt judgment and sound counsel as much as pleasure, it is necessary (as he concludes) that both ignorance and all evils arise from this...

<summary>Ficino argues that pleasure is a biological tool used by nature to ensure survival and reproduction, rather than a moral good. He cites ancient philosophers like Plato, Archytas, and Antisthenes to claim that pleasure is the root of vice and the corruption of reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument against bodily pleasure, moving from the interconnectedness of virtues to the specific teachings of ancient authorities like Hermes Trismegistus, Socrates, and Hippocrates, before transitioning to the critiques raised by the Peripatetics (Aristotelians).</meta>

...all things proceed. Wherefore he used to say: "May I be seized by madness rather than by pleasure." <note>This is a famous quote attributed to Antisthenes, a student of Socrates, emphasizing that the loss of reason in madness is preferable to the loss of self-control in pleasure.</note> Furthermore, **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>The legendary "Thrice-Great Hermes," an Egyptian sage believed in the Renaissance to be a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom.</note>, the wisest of all Egyptians, attempts to uproot this wicked blight from the souls of men for two primary reasons. For he judges that a "good" is something that either contains the very thing in its own nature or leads to a better result. We see that the virtues placed in action are of the first kind; for it is their specific property to return the soul to a state of tranquility, free from the tumult of all disturbances. Indeed, the removal of disturbances and a certain serenity of mind is the natural property of each soul. It is established that those virtues engaged in contemplation are of the second kind. Indeed, since they raise and refine the soul through the study and understanding of divine things—somewhat beyond human nature—it seems to approach as closely as possible the life of God, which consists solely in contemplation.

It is clear, however, that the condition of pleasure is contrary to both. For it agitates the soul with countless burning passions, like so many Furies <note>In Greek mythology, the Furies (Erinyes) were deities of vengeance who drove people to madness.</note>, so that it remains far from that tranquility which nature so greatly requires. And since the human race holds a middle position between God and the beasts, and for that reason seems to share in the nature of both, Trismegistus believes we can migrate or be transformed into either. Truly, he who primarily uses his mind lives the most blessed life of the immortal gods; he who uses his body and senses lives the life of beasts. Therefore, since the use of pleasure exists in the body and the senses, he who is most devoted to it not only fails to ascend to those things which are better and more divine, but does not even retain the status and dignity of his own nature. He slides, as it were, from soul to body, from mind to senses, and from man to beast.

Socrates speaks divinely in Plato’s *Phaedo*: pleasure, he says, holding as it were a <term>nail</term> <note>In the "Phaedo," Plato describes pleasure and pain as nails that fasten the soul to the body, making the soul believe that bodily experiences are the only reality.</note>, fixes and joins the soul to the body. It causes the soul, infected by the appearance of the body, to think those things are true which the body suggests. For when the soul is moved by the same things and feels the same things as the body, it is forced (I believe) to adopt the same habits and the same "nourishment."

From these points, another argument is woven by Trismegistus. In every category of things, he maintains there is one thing that is greatest and supreme, by participation in which all other things are placed in that same category. For example, all things that are hot become hot by the nature of fire, in which the highest heat resides. In the same way, whatever things are "good" ought to be called good because they follow and imitate the supreme and primary Good. Who can doubt that the supreme Good is God? Anyone who doubts this understands nothing at all. Therefore, whatever things are called good are worthy of that name because they imitate God in some way; hence all virtues, because they are most closely related to God, are not undeservedly judged to be perfect and best. For (as we said above) the work of the first kind of virtue is to bring tranquility. The work of the other is to lead to the knowledge of truth. Truly, tranquility and the knowledge of truth (as Plato also argues) are the most characteristic properties of divinity.

Therefore, no one can doubt that both kinds of virtue make men related to the immortal God. But what relationship can pleasure have with divinity? God exists free and released from all bodily composition, but pleasure moves the body and flatters the senses. It causes us to be submerged in the <note>original: "luto," meaning mud or filth</note> mud of the body and the senses, so that we seem to degenerate not only from the excellence of the immortal gods but even from the nature of men. Having stripped off all human reason, we put on the most filthy dregs of pigs. Therefore, Plato said not without cause that pleasure is separated from the nature of the Gods. But what can be said more truly or more aptly against this plague than what they say was spoken by **Hippocrates**, a truly divine man? For when he spoke of the pleasure of Venus <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note>, he said it was a part of that most foul disease which our people call the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbus comitialis," the historical term for epilepsy.</note>.

->Objections of the Peripatetics against the Platonic definition of pleasure. Chapter III.<-

**T**his, then, is the divine opinion of Plato concerning pleasure, in which Mercurius Trismegistus, and all the Pythagoreans, and the more excellent Socratics agree without any doubt. But the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking (peripatētikos) while teaching.</note>—men who are certainly sharp, but in this matter perhaps more eager for contention than for the truth—strive to pervert and deprave this most excellent and divine opinion of Plato with certain subtleties of their own. There are three points in which they attempt to criticize the Platonists. First, because Plato [defined] pleasure as a motion <meta>The text cuts off here, matching the catchword "in defi" (meaning "in definitione" or "in defining") which leads to the next page.</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino cites Hermes Trismegistus and Socrates to argue that pleasure degrades humans to the level of beasts and separates the soul from God, unlike virtue which leads to divine tranquility. He concludes by introducing the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) counter-arguments against Plato's definition of pleasure.</summary>

<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Plato, Socrates, Hippocrates, Peripatetics, virtue, tranquility, contemplation, epilepsy, Great Chain of Being</keywords>

--- Page 1001 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general critiques of pleasure to specific technical objections raised by the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) school against Plato's definitions, followed by Ficino's systematic defense of the Platonic position.</meta>

<page-num>992</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

In defining pleasure, they <note>The Peripatetics, or followers of Aristotle.</note> say that every motion is local—that is, it occurs through space—and is either slow or fast. Pleasure, however, they claim can be called neither fast nor slow. Instead, it must be called either brief or long-lasting. Furthermore, they argue that no motion can exist as a complete whole all at once; rather, one part of a motion must always succeed another, so that as one part ceases, another is born. Two parts of a motion cannot wait for one another in the same moment. Pleasure, by contrast, becomes a whole all at once, and all its parts (so to speak) remain together. For when the mind knows it enjoys the possession of some good, they believe it perceives pleasure immediately. Thus, it follows that the pleasure of the mind follows cognition and perception; and just as perception of an object that appears good is completed entirely in an instant, so pleasure—which follows such an apprehension—is also perfected in an instant. Things that happen in this way are whole and equal at once, consisting of an indivisible and simple nature. From this, they wish to conclude that pleasure is born in the senses at a simple, singular point in time, and is whole and perfect from its very first beginning, requiring no further part to make it more complete. For this reason, they argue it cannot be a "motion." 

Next, they reprove Plato because he called pleasure "the replenishment of a lack" <note>original: "repletionem indigentiæ." This refers to the idea that pleasure is the process of returning to a natural state of balance, like eating when hungry.</note>. They think this is false because pleasure resides in the soul, whereas replenishment occurs in the body. Nor do they agree that every pleasure is of such a kind that it corresponds to the filling of a need. Indeed, the pleasures perceived by the eyes, ears, and nose—arising from shapes, sounds, and smells—fill no prior lack. Furthermore, they argue there is a certain ineffable pleasure in contemplation that fills no great void; this pleasure is proper to the mind. The mind, however, neither requires a physical support nor can it be "filled" in any literal sense. For "filling" and its opposite, "exhausting," are properties of bodies, which can be full or empty. But for the soul, since it is simple and incorporeal, these things can in no way occur. 

Thirdly, they argue against the fact that Plato said no pleasures are truly good, and that most are bad. But they themselves judge many pleasures to be excellent and most worthy of praise, such as those arising from honorable actions. They believe such actions are the most delightful of all, and that the pleasure within them is the best and purest.

### Responses to the Objections. Chapter IV.

These are the arguments of the Peripatetics, which I would despair of answering if the very man they fight against did not defend himself "by his own Mars" <note>original: "suo Marte," a Latin idiom meaning by one's own strength or independent efforts.</note>. The first argument, then, by which they conclude that pleasure cannot be a motion, may perhaps be true in a sense, yet it carries no weight against the Platonists. For Plato himself taught that there are two kinds of motion: one of bodies and another of souls. The motion of bodies is that which follows the nature of the body, which cannot be gathered into an indivisible and simple state. Instead, one part must necessarily lie outside the other; otherwise, it would lack division. But that which remains undivided has already stripped off the nature of a body. Therefore, since every body is extended and divisible, it is necessary that whenever it acts or is acted upon, or is moved from one place to another, the nearer and more forward parts must act, suffer, or turn before the rest. Thus, every motion of bodies requires a span of time and is stretched out by a certain succession from what is first to what is later. 

The soul, however, is indivisible and simple, having no internal separation or distance between parts. Therefore, the motion of the soul is indivisible and simple, and is completed as a whole in a single point of time. Hence **Thales of Miletus** <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, often cited as the first philosopher.</note> said that nothing is swifter than the mind. Since, therefore, pleasure in Plato's view was defined as a motion not of the body but of the soul, nothing prevents it from being a "motion" while also being whole all at once—especially since in Platonic books, "motion" signifies not only flow and succession (as the Peripatetics would have it), but also every operation and act. 

Next, regarding their claim that Plato called pleasure the replenishment of a lack and called lack "pain," this might perhaps seem less than true. For he himself in the *Gorgias* <note>original: "Georgia." Ficino refers to Plato's dialogue on rhetoric and ethics.</note> maintains that pleasure consists in the process of replenishment. But no one, except those most unlike Plato, would say that pleasure consists in pleasure, or that anything else produced by nature consists within itself. Furthermore, in the same book, he says that replenishment is "pleasurable" and lack is for the most part "painful." But who would speak so foolishly as to call pleasure itself "pleasurable," or pain "painful"

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of Plato’s definition of pleasure against the criticisms of Aristotle and the Peripatetic school. Ficino is specifically addressing the argument that pleasure cannot be a "replenishment of a lack" (repletio indigentiæ).</meta>

<page-num>993</page-num>
<header>BOOK ON PLEASURE</header>
<sig>Rrr</sig>

...called painful? Who, likewise, would call beauty "beautiful," or justice "just"? In the same way, Plato would not have called pleasure "pleasurable," nor pain "painful." Therefore, he did not intend for pain to be the state of lack itself, nor for pleasure to be the state of replenishment itself. Furthermore, he says that pleasure is *produced* by replenishment, and pain *by* lack. Yet he himself believes that nothing can be produced by itself. By what logic, then, could pleasure be replenishment if it is produced *by* replenishment? Or how could pain be lack if it is born *from* lack? Indeed, this same man in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato’s late dialogues concerning the nature of the physical world and the soul.</note> placed pleasure in the senses and called it a "motion" and an "affection"; and such a great man would never say that an affection or a motion of the senses is the same thing as a replenishment. 

If anyone reads in the *Gorgias* <note>Plato’s dialogue on rhetoric and ethics, where the character Callicles argues for the pursuit of unrestrained desire.</note> that pleasure is the replenishment of the body, let him consider that passage more carefully; he will eventually find that this is not Plato’s own opinion, but the opinion of Callicles—the most pleasure-seeking of men—against whom Socrates disputes most fiercely. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> grant us these points, yet some still deny that all pleasure is produced by the replenishment of a lack. They argue that the pleasure brought to us by contemplation, which resides in the mind, does not arise from the replenishment of any lack. 

Even though I could show more clearly than daylight that the mental delight taken from contemplation also takes its origin from a certain replenishment, let us grant them this point so that we do not appear overly litigious. Let it be as they wish; what then? Did not Plato (as we said above) locate "pleasure" in the senses and "**joy**" in the mind? If the Peripatetics also place it in the mind, what is that to us? For Plato does not hold that view. Therefore, what is perceived in contemplating we call "joy," not "pleasure." Even if it is not born from replenishment, it is nothing against Plato, who says not that joy (which is in the mind) but pleasure (which resides in the senses) is created from replenishment.

But Aristotle presses more sharply in the tenth book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book X, which deals extensively with pleasure and the contemplative life.</note>, proving that even sensory pleasure does not always proceed from the replenishment of a lack. He admits this is true for touch and taste, but argues it does not happen in those pleasures we take from smells, sights, and sounds. For he argues that a person who delights in sounds or sights is not "replenished" by those things in any way, nor did they previously "lack" them. However, even if these arguments seem plausible, they are not of such a kind that they can detract from Plato in any way.

For those words of Plato, in which he says pleasure is born from the replenishment of a lack, can be interpreted (it seems) in two ways. These two things—**lack** and **appetite**—are so interconnected that one cannot be separated from the other. For we desire (*appetimus*) those things we lack, and we do not desire anything unless we lacked it before the longing arose. No one is in lack without desiring, and no one desires without lacking. Thus, both seem so joined together that one always accompanies the other. For this reason, it is the custom among the most excellent philosophers to frequently use the name of "lack" to signify "appetite," and in the same way, they wish for "appetite" to be understood by the term "lack." 

Hence Cicero rightly said that "he who does not desire does not lack." <note>A reference to Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*.</note> Socrates also denied that he lacked our riches and luxuries (which others strive for most ardently) because he did not desire them at all. Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher often associated with the pursuit of pleasure, though he advocated for simple living.</note> said that the person who lacks is not the one who has little, but the one who desires more. Thus, if one wishes to drive away lack, one should not add to one's money, but rather take away from one's desire. 

In the same way, when Plato says "the replenishment of a lack," he wanted the "replenishment of appetite" to be understood. Desire is replenished when it attains what it was seeking. The replenishment of appetite is nothing other than the attainment of that which had entered into desire. Therefore, from what we have said, we interpret Plato thus: the replenishment of a lack is the *cause* of pleasure. That is, when the appetite (which lacks, and which we call "lack") has obtained what it longed for and enjoys its presence, and is as it were "replenished," that motion is immediately born in the senses which we call sweetness, delight, and pleasure. 

Hence the Delian inscription <note>An ancient Greek epigram famously cited by Aristotle, often translated as: "Justice is the loveliest; health is the best; but the sweetest thing is to obtain what one loves."</note> says that the most pleasant thing is "to obtain the thing loved." This interpretation holds true for all the senses and even for the mind (if one wishes). For all the senses, having attained the object they previously desired, are soothed by a certain ineffable pleasure. 

This is the first way of responding, by which the Platonists can escape the traps of the Peripatetics. If this interpretation seems perhaps too forced to anyone, come, let us try another, so that our side does not appear to have succumbed to their arrows. Let us explore, then: what is lack but that which we need to attain? And what do we lack, or what things do we need? Only those things which can either protect our health while it is present, restore it if it is lost, or bring us some other utility. Now, we are humans. But "man" is—as the Peripatetics and Stoics believe—that which consists of a rational soul and a body. The Pythagoreans and Platonists...

<summary>Ficino defends Plato’s definition of pleasure as the "replenishment of a lack" by arguing that "lack" is synonymous with "appetite." He distinguishes between sensory pleasure and mental joy, and refutes Aristotle's claim that certain sensory pleasures do not require a prior state of need.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the nature of the human being and the physiological basis of pleasure, transitioning from metaphysical definitions to the mechanics of the five senses as described in Platonic tradition.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

Above all others, those who remain distinct <note>The Platonists.</note> think that man is a certain divine mind bound by earthly chains. Thus, while among other philosophers the soul has the nature and name of a certain part of man, among the Platonists our soul is the whole man. For this reason, when Socrates was asked by Crito how he wished to be buried, he said: "However you like, if only you can catch me and I do not escape you." <note>A famous scene from Plato’s *Phaedo* where Socrates argues that his true self is his soul, not his corpse.</note> Likewise, when disputing with Alcibiades in Plato, he proves by many arguments that man is nothing other than the soul; that the body is not the man, but belongs to the man; and that external things belong not to the man, but to fortune. Yet he does not call our soul "man" at all times and in all places. Rather, as long as it leads its life in the celestial seats, it is called a God, and also a <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Greek sense, a *daemon* is a tutelary spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> by the Platonists. But when it is enclosed in earthly dwellings, it receives the name "humanity" from the very nature of the <term>ground</term> <note>Ficino here plays on the Latin etymology of *homo* (man) and *humanitas* (humanity) being derived from *humus* (earth/ground).</note> in which it is immersed. Thus, the most noble Platonist Origen <note>Referring here to Origen the Platonist, a contemporary of Plotinus, rather than the Christian Church Father.</note> asserts that a man can be turned into a daemon or a God, and sometimes even migrate into beasts. Likewise Seneca, a great student of Plato, called our soul "a God guesting in a human body." But all these men, and even Plato himself, imitated Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Pythagoras. For Pythagoras asserts in these verses that our soul is transferred from man into God:

> ->Having laid aside the body, when you go free to the aether,<-
> ->You shall escape the state of man, becoming a God of the nourishing aether.<-
<note>original: "Corpore depoſito cum liber ad æthera perges, / Euades hominem factus Deus ætheris almi." These are the *Golden Verses* attributed to Pythagoras.</note>

Since, therefore (to return to the point), man is in the opinion of the Aristotelians that which consists of a rational soul and a body, but as Plato wishes, he is a certain divine soul that makes use of the service of an earthly body, it follows that we must surely undertake the care of two things: the soul and the body. The care of the soul indeed (as he commands) should be for its own sake alone, but all care for the body ought to be referred to the soul, just as a servant is referred to a master. 

Of those things we need, there are therefore two kinds. For we need those things which will benefit the soul, and those which will benefit the body. Those things benefit the body which either restore or preserve life, health, strength, beauty, or its own proper nature. But to the soul belong all those things which contribute something to the best character and to the knowledge of things. Add to these, above all, those things which seem similar and kin to either one, for they benefit both soul and body. For by the similar (as it is said) similar things are preserved, and each individual thing seeks its own well-being. These, then, are the things which men need. For this reason, when these things are present, or at least those things which have a certain appearance and likeness of them, we are affected by pleasure. Indeed, those things which seem good to us, if they are present, bring pleasure. Thus it happens that opinion precedes pleasure; for as the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized logic, physics, and ethics, often contrasting with Platonism on the nature of emotions.</note> like it, nothing can be pleasant to anyone unless each person considers it kin to himself and good. 

Since, however, the pleasure of the body is perceived by the senses, and there are five kinds of these, there will likewise be five kinds of pleasures: one is perceived by touching, another by tasting; smells provide another; and the ears and eyes suggest the rest. And these senses are related to one another in such a way that they maintain a certain order, equally of place and of nature. For the eyes are the purest and, as Timaeus the Platonist <note>The speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus* who explains the creation of the universe.</note> disputes and proves, they are kin to the nature of fire and light. The ears hold the second rank of purity and are compared to the air. The nostrils then possess the third degree of thinness and, being composed of a certain thicker nature, they touch the middle ground between air and water. Next, however, the organ of tasting is thicker and most similar to the nature of water. Finally, in the [lowest] degree of thinness are distributed those parts with which we touch; for these approach more closely to the nature of the body and are assigned to the thickness of the earth. You see these five senses arranged step by step in such a way that those placed in the more eminent part of the body also obtain a superior rank of purity, and some exist as kin to different things than others. 

Because we have disputed this more widely in those commentaries which we published on Plato’s *Timaeus*, let it suffice to have touched upon it briefly in this place. Therefore, when certain solid and thicker bodies are moved toward the sense of touch, endowed with the same nature of moisture and heat by which the sense itself is affected, then by the presence of these bodies—because they are kin to it, because they have the same nature, and because they protect its own specific composition and quality—the sense in a way exults and gestures, and is entirely bathed in sweetness. Taste, however, is refreshed (as is evident) by more liquid bodies; for it is delighted by those flavors which have the nature of something boiled and ripened by moisture. Indeed, since it itself (as the Platonists think) is composed in the same proportion, it happens that when something similar and, as it were, its own "familiar" approaches, it rests most sweetly with it. Furthermore, the power of smelling is most refreshed by those odors which are mixed between the nature of water and air, which is perceived in fruits and flowers; for it too was allotted the same nature from its origin. In addition, the ears are delighted by sounds of this kind, which are fashioned from the purest air...

<summary>Ficino defines man as essentially a divine soul using a body and explains that pleasure arises when the senses encounter substances that are "kin" to their own elemental composition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the nature of the soul and its relationship to the senses, specifically focusing on how the soul is replenished through sensory experiences and the philosophical debate between Plato and Aristotle regarding the definition of pleasure.</meta>

# BOOK ON PLEASURE.

<meta>catchword: indeed</meta>

and are composed of the same substance as the harmonies themselves; thus we see that because of a diversity of nature, some people are delighted by softer harmonies, others by more intense ones, some by deeper tones, and others by clearer ones. To the eyes, however, since they are most familiar with light, those things seem most pleasing whose nature is tempered by a light very similar to their own. Truly, all such things result from a most beautiful tempering of colors, all of which proceed from light. And we do not require these things, which we draw in through the senses, merely to sustain and restore our physical life, but also to achieve an understanding of the mind. From this it follows that the senses require certain excellent things offered from the outside for two reasons: first, because these things are kindred and similar to themselves (for it is necessary that individual things be preserved and perfected by things similar to them), and second, because they can provide instruction for the knowledge of things and arts—the pursuit of which is our greatest goal. Therefore, whenever those things of which we have spoken are offered to the senses and admitted deep within for enjoyment, they satisfy that deficiency of the senses which previously gave birth to desire. And that **pleasure** <term>voluptas</term> which we seek happens because of this replenishment of deficiency. This, therefore, is the second interpretation of the Platonic definition, which I believe no one—provided they are of sound mind—will find fault with; therefore, enough on these matters, let us proceed to the rest.

There are three questions proposed by the followers of Aristotle against Plato: first, that he falsely called pleasure a "motion"; second, that not all pleasure can be a replenishment, nor can it arise from replenishment. To all these, I believe enough has already been answered—not indeed by my own meager wit, for I do not claim so much for myself, but by those arguments which were most extensively disputed by Plato himself. The final objection of Aristotle, however, was that many pleasures (contrary to what Plato supposedly denied) were good and honorable, such as those which proceed from the action and use of the virtues and from contemplation. Truly, I would say that the answer to this objection was proposed above by our leader and teacher <note>Ficino refers to Plato as his "prince and preceptor."</note>. For those things which consist in the mind and follow the virtues, our Plato (as we recorded above) named not with the word **pleasure** but with the name **joy** <term>gaudium</term>. Therefore, we will grant to Aristotle that because it is mixed with virtue, it is good; yet we will not grant that *pleasure* is good, but rather *joy*. For each man uses his own vocabulary according to his judgment; and while Aristotle differs from Plato in name, he agrees in reality. The Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Cynics, however, agree with our views both in reality and in name.

### Various opinions on what pleasure is; the first opinion of Aristotle. Chap. V.

**A**ristotle, however—to come to his opinion—uses the name of pleasure more broadly, and by it he wishes to signify not only that sweetness which inheres in the senses, but also that which consists in the mind. Yet he seems to hint at what pleasure itself is rather than to express it clearly. Nevertheless, what he disputes concerning this in the seventh and tenth books of the *Ethics*, we can interpret in the following way. There are (to use Aristotle’s words) three powers of the soul: one is common to us and the plants, which they call the vegetative power, whose duties are three—to nourish its own body, to grow it, and finally to beget another similar to itself outside itself. Then he calls the second nature of the soul the sensitive power, which exists in us in common with all other animals. Of the senses, however, some are internal and others external; the external ones, which pertain more to the present purpose, are five, very well known by the common division. The third power of the soul belongs to humans alone out of every kind of mortal living being, and he calls this the **intellect** or **mind**. To these he adds the power of movement, but let us set that aside as it has no bearing on the present purpose.

Regarding the first nature of the soul, which belongs to plants, the ancient philosophers held diverse views. Indeed, Plato thinks that the souls of trees and herbs have a certain silent appetite, which he calls the "striving of nature." Empedocles wanted not only a natural inclination but even sensation to be present in plants. Anaxagoras and Democritus, however, judge that plants are affected by pleasure and pain, and that they possess not only the power of sensation but also of thinking and understanding. But Aristotle judges them to be endowed with neither reason nor sensation at all, nor to be participants in any pleasure; hence it follows that the power of nourishing and growing contributes nothing to Aristotle’s opinion on pleasure.

The remaining powers of the soul, therefore, to which he attributes pleasure, are two: one of which (to use his words) he names the **intellect**, and the other the **sense**; and to these he assigns their own actions, which he calls "cognitions." The operation of the intellect, or (to speak in Latin) of the **mind** and **reason**, he wishes to be called "intelligence," "thought," or "contemplation." Of the sight, indeed, "vision"; of hearing, "audition"; of smell, "smelling"; of taste, "tasting"; and finally of touch, "touching." Thus sight is the power and nature of the soul itself by which one can see, while vision is the action itself—that is, the act of seeing. The same applies to the other senses. Vision (to follow one as an example for all) has two primary principles from which it arises as if from certain causes: namely, the sight itself in which it resides, and furthermore the external object which is perceived, by which the sight is stimulated so that it may see.

It details how sensory actions (like vision) arise from the interaction between internal faculties and external objects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's exploration of the definition of pleasure, moving from Platonic views to a detailed analysis of Aristotle’s perspective and how it differs from other philosophical schools.</meta>

-># MARSILIO FICINO<-

Aristotle calls a certain power and potency of the soul. That which is perceived by sight is an object, but **vision** is said to be "perfect" when the power of the soul is in its best state and the object to be seen is, by its own nature, excellent and, moreover, compatible with the nature of the soul. If either of these is lacking, the vision will be imperfect; but when both concur, it is perfect. Furthermore, whatever vision is perfect is also delightful; the more perfect it is, the more delightful; and the most perfect vision is the most delightful. Therefore, to repeat myself: because vision is perfect, it is delightful, and thus the perfection of vision is seen as a certain delight. For this reason—and vice versa—delight is the perfection of vision. Since delight and pleasure <term>voluptas; in this context, Ficino uses the terms interchangeably</term>, as far as our purpose is concerned, mean the same thing, he intends to show that pleasure is the perfection of vision. 

What has been said about sight we wish to be understood also concerning the other senses and the mind itself, for in all of them there is a proper activity <term>operatio; the functional exercise of a faculty</term>: in hearing, the act of hearing; in smelling, the act of smelling; and similarly for the rest. Therefore, according to Aristotle’s general definition, pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection of the soul's activity, and likewise a perfection of cognition. Since pleasure is inherent in all the senses, the pleasure of sight will be the perfection of vision, that of hearing the perfection of listening, that of taste the perfection of tasting, and so on for the others, so that the pleasure of each is the perfection of its own proper activity.

In Aristotle's view, however, there are two kinds of perfection: one is **primary**, the other is **annexed**. The primary perfection is that which exists as a part of the nature to which it is called a perfection—just as the soul of a human is the perfection of the human, being a certain part of the human substance. We call that an "annexed" perfection which, while not being a part of the substance, nevertheless follows the substance itself and is joined to its nature like a companion to the thing it perfects. An example of this is beauty in the flower of youth <note>original: "in iuuētutis flore pulchritudo"; this is a famous analogy from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, Book X, where he describes pleasure as being like the "bloom of youth."</note>. For beauty is neither youth itself nor some part of youth, but it follows youth, adorns it, and makes it perfect. 

Since pleasure is the perfection of that activity which consists in the senses or the mind, what kind of perfection will it be? A primary one? Aristotle would certainly deny this. For the pleasure produced by sight is neither vision itself nor a part of vision. Therefore, pleasure in sight will be a certain annexed and joined perfection to the vision. For even if it is implicit in the vision itself, it is nevertheless no part of the vision, nor is it the vision as a whole. Otherwise, vision without pleasure—which I have often noted occurs—could in no way happen. Rather, it arises from the vision itself, follows it like a companion, mingles with it, clings to it, adorns it, and makes it perfect; for everyone performs more diligently and perfectly that which delights them—a fact so well known that it seems to require no proof. 

For this reason, pleasure is defined with good reason as a certain annexed perfection of that activity to which it belongs—such as contemplation, vision, hearing, and all others. If the action is honorable, Aristotle calls the pleasure itself honorable; if it is base, the pleasure is base; if it is intermediate, the pleasure is intermediate. In this matter, Aristotle differs from most of the ancient philosophers. Some thought that pleasure was a natural quality impressed upon the senses by a thing that suits us, such as the sweet taste of honey absorbed by the tongue. Others defined pleasure as the **perception** of a suitable thing—for instance, when the sweetness of a liquid is presented to the taste, they did not call the sweetness itself, nor the liquid, nor the sense of taste "pleasure," but rather the tasting itself, that is, the perception of sweetness. Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (980–1037 AD) whose medical and philosophical works were central to Renaissance learning.</note> seems to approve of their opinion. 

Some, however, did not even want the perception of the sweet liquid itself to be pleasure, but rather that judgment of the soul which follows the first apprehension of the senses (which many call the **imagination** <term>phantasia; the faculty that processes sensory data before the intellect judges it</term>). For first, the sense knows that the taste is sweet; afterward, it judges that it is good and to be accepted. Many think that this judgment is what is meant by the name of pleasure. 

Nor were there lacking those who called neither the sweet quality impressed on the senses, nor the perception of that quality, nor the judgment "pleasure," but rather a certain commotion of the body and sense which follows the perception and judgment—such as liquefaction, pouring out, elation, exultation, wantonness, and similar things. Yet others judged that pleasure was the sweet and pleasing agitation and titillation of the limbs themselves that occurs before judgment.

### Opinions of the Peripatetics concerning pleasure. Chapter VI.

**A**ristotle, however, seems to call none of these things pleasure. Instead, he sees it as a certain perfection of the apprehension itself; just as there is a prior perception of sweetness, something else is born from this, existing as its companion and annexed perfection, and that is pleasure. But what exactly this kind of perfection is, which he names pleasure, he never (it seems) sufficiently explained. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum where they studied.</note> who followed Aristotle, while wishing to explain and bring to light what had been obscurely stated by their leader, were divided into various opinions. For...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the nature of pleasure (voluptas), specifically moving from the general definition of pleasure as the "perfection of an activity" to the specific debates among later followers of Aristotle (the Peripatetics) regarding whether pleasure resides in the senses or the appetite.</meta>

<page-num>997</page-num>
->#### BOOK ON PLEASURE<-
<sig>Rrr 3</sig>

# BOOK ON PLEASURE.

Some have placed pleasure in the senses, while others have placed it in that appetite which follows the senses. Among those who place it in the senses, they interpret Aristotle in various ways. Indeed, some think there are two perceptions in the senses: the first seems to proceed and flow into the soul from those things offered from the outside; the second, however, being more perfected by the soul, is extended toward those things which are outside. For first, for example, the soul perceives sweetness—this first perception seems to arise from the sweetness of the object itself. Then, it considers that it has attained that sweetness, perceives it, holds it, and enjoys it. This second perception of the soul—whether one calls it thought, meditation, or notice—is what they believe Aristotle called "pleasure," so that pleasure is that very consideration by which one thinks of oneself as enjoying the presence of good things.

Others do not think it is the sense itself, but rather when the soul notices it has attained sweetness, it is offered up, raised as it were, and conceives a certain cheerfulness <term>hilaritas; a state of joyful elevation</term> and carries it within itself; they judge this to be what Aristotle called pleasure. Thus, pleasure is the elevation or cheerfulness of the soul having attained the good it had desired.

But those who have placed pleasure in that part of the soul by which we desire <term>appetitus; the faculty of wanting or seeking</term> think there are two properties of the appetite. One is that we are moved and inclined toward those goods which are far from us and which we have not yet attained. The other consists in that which we have already acquired and reached. They call the first "desire" <term>cupiditas</term> and the second "rest" <term>quies</term>. They maintain that the former is full of annoyance, solicitation, care, and anxiety, while the latter is infused with a certain ineffable sweetness; they say this is what the Prince of the Peripatetics <note>A common title for Aristotle</note> called pleasure, so that pleasure is said to be nothing other than a certain limit or rest of the appetite in a good that has already been attained. Whence Lucretius says: "the rest of men and the pleasure of the gods." <note>original: "requies hominum divumque voluptas"</note>

However, not everyone explains what this "rest" is in the same way. For some define rest as the cessation itself, like an end to desiring. For when the appetite has attained the good it wanted, it stops desiring. Therefore, it is free from solicitation and anxiety; this vacancy is rest itself, and the same is called pleasure by Aristotle. Therefore, pleasure is, as these people define it, the acquisition of a desired good and a vacancy from all the anxiety and solicitation of desiring.

Yet some Peripatetics have added something else to this "vacancy." Indeed, to be free from all annoyance is not yet to possess the full and perfect nature of pleasure. It becomes whole and absolute if, in that very state, every desire comes to rest in such a way that it not only desires nothing further, but clings to this good which it enjoys with all its nerves and strength, agrees within itself that it is enough, and is thoroughly diffused into it. Therefore, as these men believe, pleasure is the assent and the diffusion of the appetite into the good it possesses. This is why, in the midst of pleasures, the whole body seems to melt and flow away, since every force and motion of the soul and body is inclined toward that which is presented from the outside and is utterly carried away. Such a diffusion, however, must be not only in the members and parts of the body, but also in the natural appetite of the soul; for the body cannot be diffused into anything else except by the power of the appetite in the pulse of the soul. For this reason, it is necessary that the appetite and the soul itself be diffused, and most greedily fixed and clinging to that which seems to agree with its own nature.

Therefore, every such effort of the soul and appetite—of coupling, clinging, and fixing itself to the good already possessed—contains pleasure. Nothing else, as it pleases these men, seems to be pleasure except to assent, to cling, and to be fixed to a present good, and to flow into it and be thoroughly diffused—provided you understand that these things happen in the soul, and in that part of the soul which is called the power of desiring. For a motion of this kind is also found in the heat of the blood, the spirits, and the whole body, which is nonetheless neither pleasure nor any part of pleasure; rather, from that diffusion and assent which is in the soul (which they call pleasure), that liquefaction and effusion of the body proceeds like certain traces of intimate pleasure. For as these things are in the body, so pleasure exists in the soul.

### *The agreement of the Platonists with the Aristotelians, and what Plato says about the senses and the affects. Chapter VII.*

**T**his, then, is the opinion of the Peripatetics regarding the definition of pleasure, which I myself judge does not differ in the least part from the opinion of our Plato, except that Aristotle speaks more broadly using the same name of "pleasure" for both that delight which is in the mind and that which is in the senses. Plato, however, calls "pleasure" <term>voluptas</term> that which happens to the senses, but that which is in the mind he calls "joy" <term>gaudium</term>. Furthermore, occasionally even Plato himself confuses the names of pleasure and joy, using either word to signify either thing. Therefore, in name they differ either not at all, or scarcely and minimally; but that they agree in reality, many of Plato's books can be witnesses, as well as many Platonists who are by no means philosophers to be looked down upon. For Apuleius, Calcidius, Contius, and Ptolemy, noble Platonists...

<summary>This page explores various Peripatetic interpretations of Aristotle’s definition of pleasure, debating whether it is a conscious reflection on a good, a state of "rest" after desire, or an active "diffusion" and "melting" of the soul into a possessed good. Ficino concludes by arguing that Aristotle and Plato essentially agree on the nature of pleasure, differing primarily in their terminology (voluptas vs. gaudium).</summary>
