...whom I will briefly recall. They interpret Plato's opinion, set down in the most obscure words in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe and the nature of the physical world</note>, by saying that sensation is understood by Plato to be the first perception of the soul which is born from the body's own suffering <term>passio; here meaning the state of being acted upon by an external force</term>. For indeed, they say that the "species" <term>species; the formal images or likenesses of things</term> of all things that are to be known flow toward us, are drawn in through the openings of the senses, and are imprinted and sealed upon the spirit that resides in the ventricles of the brain. These species of things, formed within the spirit—which is itself a most thin and translucent body—strike the soul and cause it to gaze upon and perceive those very external objects of which these are the images. We see that this perception of the soul is born from the stroke and impulse of the body's own suffering; since the spirit is clearly moved by external bodies, it strikes the soul in a similar way and shapes it with an image. Therefore, since a perception of this kind is born from the impulse of the spirit, it follows that it proceeds from the suffering of the body—that is, from its being struck and moved. In this, the good Platonist Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, whom Ficino identifies as a Platonist</note> followed Plato in that book titled *On the Quantity of the Soul*. He says, "Sensation is a suffering of the body that is not hidden from the soul," <note>original: "Sensus est passio corporis per seipsam non latens animam"</note> meaning that through that very image of the body drawn in by the senses, the suffering of the same body is perceived by a certain primary and proper image.

From this it follows that we feel through a twin suffering of the body. For by the impulse of the brain and the spirit, we apprehend the sufferings caused by external bodies. But the Platonists divide that suffering which the body itself receives from the outside into two parts: one which soothes and caresses the body, not so much striking the limbs and organs as stroking and tickling them; the other which agitates more sharply and harshly. They assert that when the soul consents to that first motion of the body, whose property is to soothe, **pleasure** is created; but when it shrinks and fails from the other motion, which we call harsh, **pain** is created. The soul "consents" to the motion of the body when it willingly adheres to it, is fastened to it, joined with it, suffused by it, and rests most sweetly within it. For this reason, Aurelius Augustine defines pleasure as the union of the appetite itself with that which it has loved. Do not the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> also define pleasure above in the same way, as the soul resting, being suffused, and being inwardly joined? What then remains to prevent the Platonists and Peripatetics from saying one and the same thing about pleasure, and both speaking and feeling alike? In what else do they differ, except that the former say the soul "consents," while the latter say it "rests" and "stops"? Indeed, they differ in nothing at all, for the soul never rests unless it consents, nor does it consent unless it also rests.

### How the Peripatetics divide pleasure, and concerning the powers of the soul. Chapter VIII.

**I** believe it has now been sufficiently declared what the Platonists and Peripatetics handed down concerning the definition of pleasure, and how the arguments of both agree on the same point. Now let us follow what the Peripatetics felt regarding the division of pleasure. The Peripatetics think that the whole nature of man consists of soul and body, and that the soul—as it pertains to the question at hand—is distributed into two parts: the mind and the sense. Furthermore, they believe the mind has a twin power and nature. One of these is occupied with the investigation of truth, the other with deliberation and action; the former they call the "contemplative intellect" (to use their words), and the latter the "active intellect." They say the property of the contemplative is to search out the causes, qualities, and progressions of those things contained in the order of nature, and to be content with the contemplation of truth alone. But they want the work of the active intellect to be the discerning, through deliberation, of what things should be increased or avoided.

Of the senses, they call some "internal" and others "external." The internal senses (as Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note>, the most acute of the Peripatetic interpreters, maintains) are divided into four types. The first of these collects and perceives all the images drawn in through the five external senses, and for this reason they call it the **common sense**. Then another power was named by them "imagination," whose duty is—though it perceives nothing itself—to retain the images received from the prior senses, and to bring them to a third nature of sensing which they call **phantasy**, or the power of estimating and thinking. They believe the work of this power is to judge and perceive, once those images are received, what or of what sort the thing is whose images they are. Once it has discerned, joined, or conceived of them by judging, it commends them to be kept by the final part of the brain and sense, which they call **memory**.

Those external senses, which are more significant to our inquiry, they divide into five species known to everyone. They think these are related to one another such that those which occupy a more eminent place in the body are purer and simpler, while the rest are coarser. Therefore, sight seems purer than hearing, hearing than smell, the power of smelling than taste, and finally taste than touch. For light and colors belong to sight; sounds to the ears; smells to the nostrils; flavors to taste; but solidity, softness, heat, and cold belong to the power of touch. Therefore, just as light and color are purer than sound, sound than smells, and these than flavor—or flavors are purer than those things subjected to touch—so is sight to hearing, and hearing to the sense of the nostrils.

<summary>Ficino harmonizes Plato and Aristotle's views on pleasure, defining it as the soul's restful union with a soothing bodily state, and outlines the Peripatetic hierarchy of the soul's powers, from the contemplative intellect down to the five external senses.</summary>

These senses <note>Referring to sight and hearing mentioned on the previous page</note> excel over taste, and taste finally over touch, in purity and dignity. To these five powers of sensing, five corresponding organs and subjects—and, as it were, certain foundations—are attributed in the body (as they call them). Nor do these seem to be anything other than certain **affections** <term>affectio; a state, condition, or "disposition" of the body</term> of the body, which some call **dispositions**, others **qualities**, and some **complexions** <term>complexio; the specific mixture of the four elements/humors in a body part</term>, which are born differently in various parts of the body through the varied mixing of the elements, and are the foundations of the various senses. For there is one affection of the body by which the power of **seeing** is sustained and flourishes; and another, truly, by which **hearing** [is sustained], and the same is to be judged regarding all the others. Besides these five affections or subjects, five corresponding **instruments**—more solid than the members of the body—were discovered and established as certain receptacles in which both the senses and the affections themselves might reside. For the **eyes**, like little vessels, receive the affection and the power of seeing, and the other members of the body, as is evident, are assigned to the other qualities and senses in a certain fixed order. Furthermore, certain **movements** are innate to these members and instruments, which seem to demonstrate the innermost affection of each. Thus, in the very disturbances of the mind, we see them now turn red, now turn pale, and at one time indeed contract and stiffen, but at another time flow abroad and, as it were, melt away. To all these things which we have now enumerated in a long sequence, Aristotle thinks **pleasure** pertains in such a way that in that mind which he calls **contemplative**, a certain perfect and absolute pleasure resides.

Then, in the other parts of man, it gradually degenerates. For (as he thinks) for seven reasons, that first pleasure seems to be more perfect than the other pleasure which he places in the **active mind**. For every pleasure that is taken from the investigation and contemplation of truth is honorable and most worthy of praise. But when the other mind deliberates on things to be done or avoided, and rejoices in the choice of such things, not every such pleasure is usually praised. That which comes from those counsels and actions which oppose the best laws is deservedly blamed—as if, for example, the mind should rejoice in a plan undertaken against the safety of the fatherland or parents. When it is delighted by honorable actions, the pleasure is honorable; but when by neutral ones, that pleasure too is neutral. Thus it happens that in the first mind, only one kind of joy exists, and that is worthy of praise. But in the other [the active mind], as we have said, three kinds are found: the honorable, the shameful, and the neutral. 

That reasoning also, which he uses in the tenth book *On Ethics* <note>original: "de morib."; referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book X</note>, is of no small value to the matter we are discussing. For he says that we are able to **contemplate** longer than we can do anything else; and since the inquiry into truth is firmer and more stable than any duty of acting, it is necessary that the pleasure which proceeds from it also exists as more stable and more perfect. Add to this that the life of the wise man needs fewer things for contemplation than the civil life does; wherefore his pleasure, since it too is content with few and very small things, will without doubt be more self-sufficient and be judged more perfect. 

Furthermore, that part of the mind to which we attribute the contemplation of nature is—as no one would deny—more perfect than the other, and for that reason, it brings a pleasure more excellent than all the others. And since the movement and agitation of the **active mind** is directed toward something else—either to be chosen or rejected—while the contemplation of the **primary mind** is content with itself and desires nothing else at all besides itself, it is established by necessary reason that the pleasure proper to contemplation is desired for its own sake alone. The other [active pleasure], however, seeks something else besides itself as an end, and therefore that first one is to be judged much more excellent. 

Added to this is that the first and more perfect part of anything carries, as it were, the role and name of the whole. From this it follows that, although each man is constituted of many parts, that part which is deputed to contemplation—because it excels the others in dignity—embraces almost the entire nature of man, and man (as Aristotle says) exists chiefly as that part. For which reason, its action especially suits us and contains an ineffable pleasure; for those things which are more related by nature usually bring greater pleasure. 

Finally, Aristotle's argumentation proves that the proper operation of the **immortal Gods** consists in contemplation alone. Therefore, nothing in us except the primary mind and contemplation (as we have said), and the pleasure which arises from it, seems to be related to God. Because this kind of pleasure alone is fitting for the immortal Gods, it is most divine, and will deservedly be judged more excellent than all other pleasures. Aristotle used these arguments to prefer the pleasure of contemplating over that which is perceived by acting; but let us now come to those pleasures which, as it were, tickle the senses, and flow into and glide over them with a certain sweetness. We find these divided by Aristotle into two species, of which some are indeed **natural**, others appear to be **against nature**; and he calls those "natural" which, when nature is right...

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

# MARSILIO FICINO

...they are desired by all, or by the majority. He <note>Referring to Aristotle, whom Ficino is paraphrasing</note> likewise divides these into two groups: some are equally common to all living creatures, while others are, in a sense, proper and innate to specific individuals according to their diverse natures. For the fact that all creatures seek food, drink, and the use of **Venus** <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> is a characteristic of common and natural desire and pleasure. But the fact that individuals are variously delighted by specific and certain things according to their different natures—and that some things happen to be more pleasing to some than to others—belongs to natural, yet "specific" pleasure. For since that which agrees with one’s nature seems pleasant to each, and since the dispositions and natures of various living things are diverse, it is necessary that those things which agree with different animals should also differ. And therefore, a certain and, as it were, "proper" desire and pleasure belongs to individual living things (as **Heraclitus** says). For that which is suited to his own nature delights each man; "his own pleasure draws each." <note>original: "trahit sua quenque voluptas." A famous quote from Virgil's Eclogues, here used to support the Heraclitean idea of individual nature.</note>

And these are what he calls "natural." Conversely, he maintains that those pleasures which almost the entire human race finds abhorrent are "against nature," and he divides them into three kinds. Some arise from a certain shameful and corrupt nature, others from the worst habits, and some from diseases and unfortunate accidents. **Aristotle** writes that it happened through a perversity of nature that a certain woman would rip open the wombs of pregnant women to eagerly devour the fetuses, or what they say of certain savage nations around the **Black Sea** <note>original: "Pontum"</note>: that some delight in raw meat, others in human flesh, and some are said to trade their own children to be eaten at feasts. The **Troglodytes** <term>Troglodytae; "cave-dwellers," often described by ancient geographers as having strange diets</term>, truly, feed on the flesh of serpents. 

It also happens to many through long-standing habit that they take delight in plucking out hair or biting their nails. Often this also happens because of diseases of the mind or body, like that man who sacrificed and ate his mother, or the one who cooked the flesh of his father and daughter so that he might eat both, or the one who ardently lusted after the liver of his fellow servant and, having killed him, devoured it with the highest pleasure. We ourselves have also seen those afflicted with certain bodily diseases—some grinding little stones with their teeth most greedily, others gypsum, some earth, certain others charcoal, and others lime—as often happens to pregnant women <note>This condition is known today as pica</note>. These three types of pleasures "against nature" he considers to belong not to a human, but to a wild and monstrous character; whence he calls such pleasures "monstrous" in the seventh book of his work *On Morals* <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*</note>.

From these things which we have listed so far, there appear to be three kinds of pleasures according to Aristotle: the first consists in **contemplation**, the second in **deliberation** and **action**, and both indeed reside in the mind, but (as we have said) in a different manner. The third we have placed in the senses, and we have divided it into two species: namely, "natural" and "against nature." Of the natural ones, we call one "common" and the other "proper." Furthermore, among the monstrous ones, one happens from a corrupt and shameful nature, another from a vicious habit, and the third from diseases. 

Therefore, he calls the first pleasure—which is born from contemplation—"divine," because it is most like God, and because it happens to us not as we are men, but as we are gods. But that which is proper to the **active mind** he calls "honest" <term>honesta; meaning morally beautiful, noble, or honorable</term>, yet not divine. For **honesty** is not divinity itself, but a certain perfect likeness and image of divinity; thus the second mind and its pleasure degenerate from the first, since divinity is attributed to the first, but the likeness of divinity to the second. 

As for those pleasures which soothe the body, they can no longer be participants in divinity, nor any more in honesty, since honesty exists as the grace, beauty, and ornament of the mind alone. Yet this ornament and the agreement of all parts is called "honesty" in the habit of the mind, "moderation" in the affections, "modesty" in actions, "order" in works, and "beauty" in the body by most **Platonists**. Nevertheless, even those pleasures which move the senses have a certain tiny image of honesty. For those which obey the laws of the mind and reason, and for that reason become "moderate," seem to imitate the nature of the honest and the graceful because of this very moderation; and although they are not entirely worthy of the name "honest," they are called "good" by the **Aristotelians**. Those which are more unbridled and participate less in reason, he judges to be neither divine, nor honest, nor finally good, but rather worthy of reproach and evil. And when they have not exceeded the limit so much that they seem to shrink entirely from human morals and character, he calls them "vicious" yet "human" pleasures. These he divides into two parts: some only corrupt the **appetite** <term>appetitio; the faculty of desiring</term>, so that he who is affected by them desires and acts indeed contrary to reason, yet he does not do so by deliberate choice, nor does he think he ought to act this way when he is outside of the disturbance; but then, as a certain heat of lust grows, he is inclined and drawn against that which his right mind had chosen. He thinks the pleasures of an **incontinent** <note>Someone who knows what is right but lacks the self-control to do it</note> mind are of this sort. But others deprave not only the appetite, but also the judgment of the mind, so that he both desires contrary to what is fitting, and the mind judges that very thing as something to be done and as a good...

Ficino moves from the Aristotelian classification of "human" versus "beastly" pleasures into a deeper Neoplatonic explanation of why sight and hearing are spiritually superior to touch, taste, and smell.</meta>

<note>original catchword: "filiæ" (daughters)</note>

choosing with purpose and according to one's strength to indulge in the pleasure of the body; he proves that these are the pleasures of an intemperate man which blind the mind. All those pleasures which we have thus far placed within the senses seem to be human. But truly, when pleasures that are foreign to human custom and character dominate a man—whether because he was born with a most wicked nature, or was poorly raised, or is driven outside himself by disease—Aristotle calls these "slavish" and "monstrous," since they are characteristic of beasts rather than the human character. But all these pleasures which the senses offer to us are arranged by the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about while teaching.</note> into five grades, according to the number of the senses themselves. They believe these pleasures hold the same order as the senses: thus, the pleasure of seeing, and that which the ears provide, is purer and more worthy, while the others are similarly superior to one another in that same order of purity and dignity.

## The pleasure of hearing and sight are more excellent than the other pleasures of the senses. Likewise regarding all the senses and their organs. Chapter IX.

**E**xcellent indeed is the reasoning discovered by the leaders of the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Ficino was the primary figure in the revival of Plato's philosophy in the Renaissance.</note>, by which they prefer the pleasures of the eyes and ears to all others offered by the body. For indeed, those figures perceived by the eyes are created by a certain optimal and most fitting joining of parts. This cannot happen without proportion, nor is there any proportion without order. Order, however, is most uniquely characteristic of reason. Thus it happens that in many sounds and figures containing that order of composition, a certain "trace of reason" seems to be present. The Platonists call this image of reason "harmony" when found in the rhythms of songs and voices, and "beauty" <note>original: "pulchritudo"</note> when found in the agreement of parts and limbs. Consequently, these things do not merely charm the ears and eyes, but they also move the mind and reason through these very traces of reason contained within them. Since they have the greatest natural kinship with the mind, they occupy it deeply, seize it, and fill the soul with an ineffable pleasure. From these two images and pleasures arise the two types of <term>divine frenzy</term> <note>Ficino refers to his own theory that beauty and harmony can trigger a state of inspired "madness" or poetic/religious ecstasy.</note>, as we have discussed more extensively in our booklet on divine frenzy. But truly, smells, tastes, heat, cold, and other such things belonging to smell, taste, and touch, seem to possess neither harmony, nor proportion, nor order—and much less any resemblance to reason. Therefore, they soothe only the nature of the body and the senses; they do not harmonize with the mind at all, or only barely. For this reason, the pleasures arising from them possess neither reason nor dignity, nor do they provide any "food" (so to speak) for the mind. Added to this is what the Peripatetics argued a little earlier: that the power of sensation is shared by more living creatures the "thicker" <note>meaning more material or less refined</note> it is. Thus, the power of seeing or hearing is not granted by nature to all things. The power of smelling is granted to more, of tasting perhaps to all, and finally, no one would doubt that the power of touching is present in all animals. In this same way, their pleasures will be ranked: some are judged more common and cheaper than others. Truly, it is established that of all of them, those located in taste and touch are the most common and most useful; therefore, Aristotle calls them "beastly," "slavish," and "absurd." Plato calls them the most "incontinent" and "frenzied." <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>An ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, however, (as we said above) judged one of them <note>specifically sexual pleasure</note> to be similar to the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "comitiali morbo" (epilepsy).</note>. Nor is it of little weight that almost all who philosophize about morals wish those who exceed the limit in these two pleasures to be called "incontinent" or "intemperate." Yet regarding the remaining pleasures, because they are much more refined, they have assigned neither "incontinence" nor "intemperance" to them. Thus far, we have recounted the three things to which pleasure is attributed: namely, the contemplative mind, the active mind, and the senses. But truly, after the powers of sensing, the affections themselves and the limbs of the body—which are subject to the senses—are arranged. Although these parts do not perceive delight or distress through themselves, they are nevertheless subjected to those very bodily motions and agitations by which either sweetness or pain is brought to the senses. From this it happens that the limbs themselves seem to hold certain traces of intimate pleasure. Most of the ancient philosophers called this very agitation of the internal organs and parts of the body, which occurs during joy and pain, "pleasure" and "pain." Others, however, believed that pleasure is the restoration of nature made manifest to the senses, while pain is the weakening and dissolution of that which is proper to nature. Moreover, besides these internal motions, certain external gestures follow which provide signs of hidden affections; there have even been some who called those very signs by the names of pleasure and pain. But the brevity of this little work seems to demand that we bring an end to the Aristotelian discussion, and that shall now be done.

<summary>Ficino ranks the senses, arguing that sight and hearing are superior because they reflect rational "harmony" and "beauty," whereas touch and taste are shared with beasts and lack intellectual value.</summary>

<page-num>1002</page-num>
<header>OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>
<note>original catchword: quædam (some)</note>

...if we first offer this reminder: that whenever in this discussion pleasure is placed by us within the mind, it should be understood to be placed in that part of the mind which desires and wills something. For one part of the mind thinks and considers, another remembers, and a third wills; though the mind can be divided in other ways, these categories will suffice for the present. Nor is the pleasure of the mind anything other than that perfect and grateful assent, by which the will finds total rest in that which the mind considers, as if in something familiar and its own.

### Opinions of the Stoics and others regarding pleasure and all the affections. Chapter X.

**H**aving said this, it should be enough to satisfy the opinion of Aristotle. Let us now come to the Stoics. The Stoics, whose leader was Zeno, define joy <note>original: "gaudium"</note> no differently than Plato does; however, they frequently confuse the terms for "pleasure" <note>original: "uoluptas"</note> and "gladness" <note>original: "lætitia"</note> with one another, and in their disputes they often use both names to designate the same thing. For when we are moved in such a way that we are in possession of some good, they believe this happens in two ways. For when the soul is moved by reason, calmly and constantly, they wish for this to be called "joy"; but when it exults effusively and in vain, they call it "wanton gladness" and "pleasure." They define this as an irrational elevation of the soul arising from the belief that one is enjoying some great good. 

Cicero, however, in his second book *On Ends* <note>Cicero’s *De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum*, a major Roman work on ethics.</note>, wishes for us to use these names in Latin such that "joy" and "gladness" reside only in the mind, while "pleasure"—though it is primarily attributed to the senses—can also be transferred to the mind. He holds that gladness is an elevation of the mind believing it enjoys a great good, while joy is a *rational* elevation of the mind; pleasure is that sweetness perceived by the senses, which can also be transferred to the mind, though in the mind it is always to be censured. He says this when he disputes concerning philosophy and expresses the differences between these things. Yet in other places, he often uses the word "pleasure" in place of "joy" or "gladness."

Aristotle, however, seems to disagree greatly with Cicero and the Stoics, since he does not wish for either joy or any pleasure to be called "gladness." For when he enumerated the affections <note>original: "affectus" - the emotions or passions</note> in the book titled the second on morals <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book II.</note>, he included gladness among them. He then added that those are affections which are followed by pleasure or pain; from this it follows that, for Aristotle, pleasure cannot be an affection, otherwise what he said just before would necessarily be false. For since pleasure cannot follow itself, anyone who calls pleasure an affection would seem to deny Aristotle’s premise that pleasure follows all affections. 

Furthermore, since in that same second book he called the affections "motions of the soul," yet in the tenth book of that same work he demonstrates that pleasure is in no way to be called a motion, who would not understand that Aristotle utterly denied that pleasure is an affection? Since, therefore, according to this opinion, pleasure is neither a motion nor an affection, yet he wished for gladness to be an affection, it is concluded by necessary reason that pleasure and gladness differ greatly from one another. 

Indeed, among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note>, gladness is not of such a nature that it is absent while the soul enjoys a present good; for no one among the Peripatetics doubts that it is a motion of the soul. For since the affections are defined by them as certain "passions of the appetite," and since passion in their opinion consists of a flow and a motion, the affections must be motions. Therefore, gladness being an affection, it will necessarily seem to be a motion. 

But the soul, having now attained what it desired, is no longer moved, but rather all the agitation of seeking ceases, and it rests most sweetly in the good it has acquired. Because of this, while it enjoys the object, one must remove from the appetite all affections that revolve around the process of acquiring that good. Therefore, we shall also remove gladness from the soul when it enjoys some good. 

Someone might perhaps ask: what then is gladness, if it is neither pleasure nor joy, nor consists in the appetite while it enjoys a present good? Even if this has not been sufficiently explained by the followers of Aristotle, I believe I can interpret Aristotle in this manner without any absurdity: When something that appears good is presented to us, the mind first judges that it should be seized; then the appetite is inclined toward that which was judged, which we call "desire" or "lust." Then the mind inquires within itself whether it can easily attain what it desires, which we call "care" and "solicitude." If it finds it cannot easily attain it, then this very opinion is called "diffidence," which is followed by "despair"—that is, when it no longer expects it will easily enjoy what it desires. From this arises "sadness" <note>original: "tristitia"</note>, which is the depression and dejection of a despairing and diffident soul (though those who care for Latin speech place this term no less on the face than in the soul). 

But if one believes he will easily attain what he desires, this very faith is called "confidence." Then "hope" follows confidence—that is, a firm and easy expectation of a future good. From this is born gladness, a certain lifting up... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>Ficino distinguishes between the Stoic view of pleasure (which conflates joy and gladness) and the Aristotelian view, which defines pleasure as a state of rest rather than an active emotional motion (affection).</summary>

<meta>Catchword: lum</meta>

...a certain elevation of the soul that hopes, without any doubt, that it will possess what it has sought. For certain confidence, the firmest hope, and the intense consideration of the very thing we hope for represents the object of our desire to the mind in such a way that it is not far from appearing entirely present. From this, it follows that something very similar to pleasure is born from this hope and thought. I believe Aristotle called this same gladness <note>original: "lætitia"</note> a certain image and appearance of future pleasure, which Lucretius the Epicurean called the "drop of Venus" <note>original: "guttam Veneris"</note>, because it is a small and light perception of the beloved thing, whereas pleasure is the perfect and absolute enjoyment of the desired thing (to speak in the Platonic manner). Wherefore, the same Lucretius, in the fourth book of his *On the Nature of Things*, when speaking of this first "drop of Venus," says:

> For mute Cupid foretells pleasure. 
> From this comes Venus to us, and from this the name of love. 
> From this, that drop of Venus’s sweetness first trickled 
> into the heart, and was followed by burning care.

That is to say, when Cupid herself—whom we name Venereal love—is "mute" (meaning still hidden and considering within herself, so to speak, by an internal movement), she perceives and, as it were, foretastes future pleasure because of that hope and confidence. In that moment, the first "drop of Venus" arises, which we call gladness. Therefore, among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who walked while teaching.</note>, let gladness be a certain sweet forefeeling of future pleasure born from hope itself; just as pleasure is found in the appetite while it enjoys, so gladness is found in the appetite while it hopes. And this is the controversy regarding these terms—gladness, joy, and pleasure—between Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, and Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero.</note>. But let them use their own names as they please; let us return to the Stoics. 

A disturbance <note>original: "perturbatio"; also translated as "passion" or "emotion" in a Stoic context.</note> is (as the Stoics like to say) a commotion of the soul turned away from right reason and contrary to nature, and they believe it is born from opinion. For as soon as the appearance of something is presented, the mind forms an opinion that it is either an evil and a plague, or a good. From this opinion, four disturbances of the soul proceed. For the things presented to us, whether they be bad or good, appear to be either future or present. 

But if the mind considers certain future evils, it immediately tries to turn away from them. If this turning away is done with reason, it is called "caution," and it is neither a disturbance nor foreign to the mind of a wise man. But that which is done without reason, and with a lowly and broken examination, is called "fear." Fear is a turning away from reason, or the anxious expectation of a future evil. When, however, that which seems evil is already imminent and affects the mind as a present thing, that disturbance arises which they call either "distress" <note>original: "ægritudinem"</note> or "pain." Distress is a contraction of the mind in opposition to reason, but in the wise man, there is no such affection toward a present evil. 

On the other hand, when the appearance of something that seems to be a future good is offered, the opinion itself impels one to attain it (to speak in the Stoic way). When this is done with constancy and prudence, we call such an appetite "will" <note>original: "uoluntatem"</note>; they believe this exists only in the wise man and should in no way be called a disturbance. They define it thus: will is that which desires something with reason. But that which is incited more violently, in opposition to reason, is "lust" or "unbridled desire" <note>original: "libido, uel cupiditas effrænata"</note>, which is found in all fools. 

Furthermore, when we are moved so as to enjoy some good, it happens in two ways: for the soul is moved either seriously or tranquilly, and they call this "joy" <note>original: "gaudium"</note>. But when the soul exults lightly, they call it "wanton gladness" <note>original: "lætitiam gestientem"</note> and "pleasure," which they define as an irrational and wanton elevation of the mind, thinking that it enjoys a great good. On this point, they agree with those Peripatetics whose opinion we cited in the second place when speaking of Aristotle; for both agree that pleasure is the very elevation of the mind that believes it has attained some maximum good. 

The Stoics divide pleasure into several parts: for they held there are five in the senses, and four in the mind while it assents to the senses. Those things which move the senses do not have distinct or proper names among the Stoics, except for that which is perceived by hearing; this they call "delectation" <note>original: "delectationem"</note>, and they define it thus: delectation is the pleasure soothing the mind through the sweetness of hearing. The others charm the remaining senses. Truly, besides those by which the body is affected, four others have been devised which are also found in the mind after it has been corrupted by appetite. These are "oblectation," "effusion," "boasting," and "malevolence." 

"Oblectation" is a softening inclination of the mind toward pleasure. I do not think this is anything other than the very softness of the mind and the assent by which the mind most willingly joins itself to the sweetness offered by the senses, agreeing with it, obeying it, and following it. "Effusion," however, they define as the loosening and dissolution of the soul's virtue. Nor indeed...

<header>MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...the mind itself is inclined and drawn by a certain softness so that it obeys the pleasures of the senses, which we have said happens through delight. But what is even greater is that all the power of our mind, and all its interior, melts and flows away with the sweetness of a present good; it lifts itself up to enjoy it and diffuses itself completely. This, therefore, the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that emotions like pleasure should be governed by reason.</note> name (I believe) **effusion** <note>original: "effusionem"</note>. Next follows **boasting**, a leaping pleasure, and those who carry themselves too insolently. This also is a disease of the mind, when it exults in the possession of that which appears good and glories in it vainly. **Malevolence**, however, is pleasure derived from the misfortune of another without any benefit to oneself. For when someone is affected by pleasure at another's misfortune for the sake of their own utility, it seems to be benevolence toward themselves rather than any malevolence toward others. Therefore, the phrase "without benefit to oneself" was rightly added in defining it.

### Cyrenaics on pleasure, that it is the goal. Chapter XI.

Let these things said about the opinion of the Stoics suffice. Let us now hear the Cyrenaic philosophers <note>A Greek school of philosophy founded by Aristippus; they believed pleasure was the supreme good, particularly physical, immediate pleasure.</note>, who descended from Aristippus, the disciple of Socrates. The Cyrenaics established two disturbances: pain and pleasure; calling the latter a **smooth motion** and the former a **rough motion**. They claim that one pleasure does not differ from another, nor does one soothe more than another; they say all living creatures seek pleasure and shun pain. By "pleasure," they mean that of the body, which they say is the goal <note>original: "finem"</note>. This is not the pleasure that exists in a stable state or consists in the absence of pain—acting as a rest from disturbance—which Epicurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who defined pleasure as the absence of pain (aponia) and trouble in the soul (ataraxia).</note> accepted and established as the goal. They believe the proof that pleasure is held as our goal is that nature has reconciled us to it from childhood, even without the judgment of reason; when the mind's judgment is neither depraved by habit nor shaped by opinion, it follows that by the instinct of nature alone, we seem to consider pleasure the highest good. 

And when we enjoy it, we seek nothing else besides it, as if it stands as the ultimate, extreme, and highest of all things to be sought, and the goal. Nor is there anything we naturally flee from as much as pain. Therefore, we seek pleasure most of all. Furthermore, they believe pleasure is good even if it proceeds from the most disgraceful things; for even if the act is foul, pleasure itself is to be chosen for its own sake and considered a good. Further, that casting off of pain which Epicurus defends does not seem to them to be pleasure, nor is the absence of pleasure pain; for they believe both states are rooted in fear. They do not hold that pleasures belong only to the body, but also to the soul—namely those perceived from the memory of past things, the hope of future goods, or the study of the sciences. Yet, they claim the pleasures of the body are far more excellent than those of the soul, and bodily pains worse than those of the soul. They believe the virtues, and indeed anything else besides pleasure, are good and desirable only for the sake of pleasure. Likewise, whatever evils appear are seen as evil and to be avoided only because of pain. 

Truly, pleasure alone is good and desirable for its own sake, while pain is evil and to be rejected for its own sake. They also believe that pleasure and pain reach the soul from its assent to and compassion with the body. For the body is agitated by various and diverse motions; if these are smooth and soothing, the soul assents to them, and that is pleasure. But if the body is struck by some harsher passion, the soul contracts, suffers with it, and feels pain. Therefore, in this definition of pain and pleasure, they agree with many of the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>. They disagree, however, in certain other matters, as can be clear from what we have reported, and furthermore because they thought nothing was inherently pleasant or unpleasant, but rather that some people rejoice while others are distressed by any given thing, whether due to its novelty, variety, or satiety.

### The opinion of Eudoxus, that pleasure is the highest good. Chapter XII.

The opinion of Eudoxus <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus, a Greek astronomer and mathematician who was a student of Archytas and Plato.</note>, the student of Archytas, is nearly the same. By these reasons which I shall set forth, he proves pleasure to be the highest good: he says that what is desirable seems to be good. That which is more desired is better. Finally, that which is desired most of all, no one would doubt to be the greatest and highest good. He considers it evident from two points that pleasure is sought above all else. For there is nothing among all things that living beings desire more vehemently and ardently than pleasure. Nor is there any good besides it that is sought by all. For not only humans, but also all other animals, and furthermore infants as soon as they are born, and then youths and the elderly, all affect it. But nothing else among the other goods can be found that is sought by all of them. Likewise, no one—not even the unlearned—would deny that what is most in accordance with nature is the highest good; and that pleasure fits nature most of all is evident from these—

<meta>catchword: (as he wishes</meta>

...[it follows] <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's argument regarding why pleasure is considered the primary good.</note> that living creatures are brought into being, and it is so necessary for procreation itself that many of the ancient philosophers even argued that plants join together through a mixture of both sexes and give birth through pleasure, sending forth their shoots. Furthermore, living things crave pleasure immediately upon being brought into the light, even before they desire anything else or are able to choose what they seek through any rational counsel. Moreover, we are nourished, educated, and increased by the charms of pleasure from our very nurse's milk throughout our entire lives; we are instructed by its delights, and we spend our lives in its lap. This pleasure is innate to all our senses, and like a **bait** <note>original: "esca"</note>, all the necessary duties of life are fulfilled through it. For we do not expel what is poisonous, nor do we pursue what is useful, without pleasure; for which reason it seems most of all to agree with nature and to be (as Aristotle says) most familiar to our race. 

Furthermore, a good is to be considered more divine the more widely it extends. Since pleasure is common to all living things and is mixed with all goods, who could doubt that it is most widely open and diffused everywhere? Indeed, there is no virtue that is present in all other virtues, or that belongs by nature to all animals, but pleasure is mixed with all virtues, and no virtue at all can be found without pleasure. Yet pleasure itself is found in many things without virtue, nor can there be any possession of a good without pleasure. From these points it is concluded that pleasure is inherent in all goods, and for that reason, it is the most ample and the best. 

Besides, there is nothing except pleasure that we do not look for for the sake of something else. On the contrary—and this seems even greater—we desire all other things for the sake of pleasure itself. For we do not strive for what is good for any other reason than that, having finally acquired it, we may enjoy it if it is at all possible. Therefore, all goods are sought for the sake of **enjoyment** <note>original: "fruitionis"</note> (if I may put it that way). Since pleasure is nothing other than a certain most sweet enjoyment of a good already acquired, who would deny that other goods are desired for its sake? There is no one who seeks any good except to attain it according to his strength, and he does not want to attain it except to possess it and rest most sweetly in it. That sweet rest, or that sweetness of rest, by which we enjoy the good we have already obtained, has been named "pleasure" by almost all who practice philosophy. For its sake, as we have proved, all goods are desired. Nor can pleasure ever happen to anyone unless he has first attained the good he desired. Thus, pleasure follows the acquisition of goods; and since that which necessarily follows another thing is also its **end** <note>In philosophy, the "end" or "telos" refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of an action.</note>, it is necessary that pleasure exists as that very end for the sake of which we seek all goods. 

There are, therefore, two principal points in the dispute of Aristippus <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cyrenaic school, which taught that immediate physical pleasure is the highest good.</note> and Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician who argued that pleasure is the supreme good because all creatures seek it.</note>: namely, that the pleasure of the body is more powerful than that of the mind, and that all happiness consists in that very **smooth motion** of the body.

### Aristotle's reasons against Aristippus and Eudoxus regarding pleasure, proving that the pleasure of the mind is superior to the pleasure of the body. Chapter XIII.

**B**UT Aristotle weaves together most true and approved reasons against both opinions. First, he demonstrates by many arguments that the pleasure of the mind is more powerful than that of the body. For of all bodily pleasures, the most intense are those perceived by touching and tasting. Yet the nature of these is such that they can move the body either not at all, or certainly hardly at all, without **indigence** <note>A state of lack or physical need, such as hunger or thirst.</note>. Hence Socrates used to say that hunger was the seasoning for food, and thirst for drink. 

But all indigence, since it is an enemy to nature, brings pain. And since pleasures of this kind cannot occur without indigence, it is necessary that they are always participants in pain; for that reason, they are considered neither complete nor pure, especially since they produce repentance, satiety, and diseases. The pleasure of the mind, however, has no inward lack mixed with it; for that reason, it does not share in pain, nor does it affect the mind with any satiety or distress. 

What of the fact that the more greedily the delights of the senses are drained, the more quickly they fall back into their opposite? But the joy of the mind, the more it is sought, the greater and more perfect it becomes. Furthermore, there are two causes or principles of pleasure: namely, the power of the soul itself which receives such a motion, and that which is presented to us from the outside. They call the former the **subject** of pleasure and the latter the **object**. The subject of bodily sweetness is the sense, while the object is the quality and nature of the body which the species drawn in by the senses offer. But the subject of that joy which the mind enjoys is indeed the intellect, and the object is an incorporeal, simple, absolute, and eternal thing: namely, **Truth**. Therefore, because the principles of this mental pleasure are more divine than those of the former, this one is more perfect than that. 

And (as Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age; his work heavily influenced Medieval and Renaissance European thought.</note> argues), the senses touch the surfaces or certain external properties of things, and are joined not to the things themselves, but rather to their images. The mind, however, inspects the intimate and absolute nature of that which is the object, and is so joined with that which it considers that one thing is made out of the two...

# MARSILII FICINI

(as Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> wishes) it happens, or (as Aurelius Augustine says) they cohere in an indissoluble connection. From this comprehension and union, a much greater <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "voluptas"; here referring to a state of supreme satisfaction or delight</note> belongs to the mind than to the senses, which are unable to achieve such a state. Add to this that the nature of the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "mens"; the rational and intellectual part of the soul</note> is always one and the same; therefore, it is always similar to itself and its own. From this it follows that the same thing is always delightful to it, and the same pleasure is always present. 

But the nature of the <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus"</note> either never remains in the same state (as Heraclitus and Plato hold) or is quickly transferred into many different affections (as Aristotle thinks). One quality follows another, which is why the same thing does not suit the body at all times. What now seems to agree with its nature immediately, or certainly a little later, disagrees and is at odds. For this reason, the same thing is not always pleasurable to it. By this, it is clearly understood that the pleasure of the mind is certain and stable, while the pleasure of the body is brief, fleeting, and fragile.

Likewise, the <term>senses</term> are moved only by the sweetness of present things, and they receive no pleasure from anything except physical objects. The mind, however, is equally delighted by the memory of the past, the hope of the future, and the contemplation of the present. It can rejoice not only in those things which lack a body, but even in the knowledge of bodies themselves. And since the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "animus"; the broader animating spirit of the human being</note> is the most excellent part of man, no one can doubt that what is agreeable to the mind should be judged as more kindred and similar to man than what suits the senses. Whatever is most kindred to someone is undoubtedly the most pleasant; from this, it is understood that the joy of the soul is greater and more excellent than the sweetness of the body.

Added to this is the fact that the soul is indivisible and simple, and the knowledge of truth is likewise indivisible. Therefore, the pleasure of the mind, since it flows from these two as if from certain causes, will be seen to be simple, unable to become smaller or larger than itself, especially since its principles do not undergo such variety. The senses, however, are disseminated and distributed through the limbs, and for that reason, they are composed of manifold variety. The objects of the senses seem to be nothing other than certain forms and qualities of bodies, which arise from a certain harmony of their parts, such as shapes, colors, sounds, smells, and other things of this sort. 

When that very proportion of bodies, by which the senses are moved, is consonant and similar to the proportion of the senses, the senses adopt it as something proper, familiar, and good, and they are affected by pleasure. But since such a <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "harmonia"; here meaning the mathematical or structural balance of physical qualities</note> of bodies can approach the likeness of the senses' harmony more or less, it follows that the sense may receive a greater pleasure at one time and a smaller one at another from the proportion of the same body. This can be seen in songs and sounds; for at the same moment of time (so to speak), the very same delight perceived from the same song is made more intense or more relaxed by voices uttered now more sweetly, now more discordantly. Since, therefore, the pleasure of the soul remains simple and immutable, while the delight of the body is mixed and becomes greater or smaller, no one of sound mind will deny that the former is more excellent and more perfect than the latter.

Finally, Aristotle’s argument for this same point is clear: he says those things which are sought for their own sake are seen to be better than those sought for the sake of another. That the joy of the mind is loved for its own sake is declared most of all by the fact that the mind and its motion greatly surpass all other things within us in dignity. From this, it follows that nothing exists within us to which we might refer the mind as if to some end; and by the same reasoning, we do not desire the pleasure inherent in the mind for the sake of anything else.

We desire the pleasure of the body, however, chiefly for the sake of three things: one of these is the mind, another is natural indigence <note>The state of being in need or lacking something necessary for survival, such as hunger or thirst.</note>, and the last is internal and perpetual pain. For since nature has referred the lesser things to those which are more powerful—so that there might be a certain inexplicable order of things and a perfect connection of parts among themselves—it is necessary that the senses of the body and their motions be referred to the mind as if to a mistress and queen. 

Next (as we also said above), nature implanted such a vehement pleasure in the senses for this reason: so that we might be made more inclined by these allurements to acquire those things necessary for life. This is most evident from the fact that as long as we admit into the body that which nature lacks, we are moved by this kind of sweetness; but after every natural lack has been filled, we not only taste no more pleasure, but what is more, we are affected by either regret or satiety. I believe nature established it for this reason: so that just as we are enticed toward our needs by pleasure, we are deterred by regret and satiety, so that we do not harm nature by admitting more than is necessary.

For the sake of soothing hidden <term>pain</term> <note>original: "dolor"; used here to mean physical distress or the lack of equilibrium in the body</note> (as Aristotle disputes in the seventh book of the *Ethics* <note>original: "de moribus"; referring to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>), we seek the pleasant motion of the body as a kind of medicine. For not only manifest pains but also certain hidden and middle pains occur. Indeed, violent motions brought in from the outside cause manifest pain...

It explores the idea that bodily pleasure is a restorative "medicine" for an inherent, hidden pain caused by the body's natural processes, before transitioning into Aristotle's arguments against identifying bodily pleasure as the "Highest Good."</meta>

->**1007**<-

Moreover, the natural movements that occur within us are quiet and intermediate. Some believe that the <term>spirits of nature</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> and the movements of the senses and the mind are perpetually present within us. For the soul both contains and nourishes the body; it generates and transfers <term>humor</term> <note>Vital bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> and spirit from limb to limb in an alternating and perpetual motion. It then employs the instruments of the body for sensing, and the senses themselves for contemplation. 

It seems reasonable that these movements—so great, so varied, and so constant—would weary nature and affect it with a certain hidden pain (if I may call it that). We notice this pain less because we have endured it perpetually from our very birth until our final day. Therefore, long habit makes it familiar to our senses in a way, and dissolves the mind’s focus on it. However, nature—the very artisan and teacher of things—has ordained that because this long habit has dulled our awareness, the animal should not perish through such negligence. Instead, it is stirred by a certain necessary and blind instinct, by which all things are almost compelled to desire bodily pleasure as a <term>medicine</term> opposed to this internal pain. 

For this reason, even those to whom no obvious lack has occurred still pursue pleasure because of this innate and blind indigence. This confirms that famous saying of **Plato**, which we discussed earlier: that all pleasure proceeds from the fulfillment of a lack. For even those who appear to have no open lack cannot be said to be free of this internal and hidden one as long as they live. 

This inherent indigence of which we speak happens most especially to the young and to those of a <term>Melancholic</term> <note>Referring to the "melancholic" temperament, associated with an excess of black bile, often thought to lead to intense or brooding personalities.</note> disposition. To the young, certainly, because by the necessity of growing and perfecting the body, they are stirred by many violent movements; thus, they require a greater medicine and for this reason seek the greatest pleasures of all. But to those in whom <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis", translated from the Greek "μελαγχολίαν" (melancholia).</note> dominates, the body (as the saying goes) is continually consumed and gnawed away by the intense dryness of that humor. On that account, they also greatly indulge in pleasures. This is why the young and the Melancholic are usually the most incontinent and intemperate of all. 

Hunger, thirst, and any other bodily desire can be called an "intermediate" pain; for this is neither a completely hidden pain, nor does it torture the body with an open or more violent movement. Thus it is not undeservedly called intermediate, and as everyone can see, we seek pleasures for the sake of driving it away.

### Aristotelian Arguments against the same, that bodily pleasure is not the highest good. Chapter XIV.

**L**ong have we declared in order the opinion of **Aristotle**, who judges that the pleasure of the mind excels the sweetness of the body. Now remains another dispute of Aristotle against **Eudoxus** <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician who argued that pleasure is the supreme good.</note> and the **Cyrenaics** <note>A school of philosophy that taught that the pleasure of the moment is the only certain good.</note>, by which he demonstrates that bodily pleasure is in no way the <term>Highest Good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum"; the ultimate end or goal of human life.</note>. By the authority of all philosophers, the Highest Good must be such that nothing better exists beyond it, and it is in no way referred to something else. 

However, bodily pleasure is significantly inferior to the joy of the mind (as we showed a little earlier), and it is desired for the sake of other things (of which we have spoken). Furthermore, that which is the Highest Good in itself must always seem good and desirable to everyone, and must be approved in all its parts. Yet, not every bodily delight is sought by all people at all times. For what provides pleasure to one often brings annoyance to another; things that are pleasing to boys seem bothersome to men; and what we crave when we are sober, we find nauseating to even look at once we are full. 

To this is added the fact that the nature of the Highest Good is such that whatever we do, we choose it as if compelled by necessity for its own sake. Yet there are many very laborious tasks and many duties full of danger which we do not hesitate to undertake—not for any bodily pleasure they might bring (for we know for certain they will bring none), but for the sake of honor, or virtue, or the joy of the mind. Indeed, many very brave and wise men have gone to certain death for the sake of virtue, for their country, or for their parents. If anyone were to say that they did this because they were ensnared by bodily sweetness or inflamed by lust—or if one prefers the opinion and impulse of the common rabble and beasts to the judgment of these men—that person must surely be judged the most foolish of all. 

Moreover, anyone, even the most abject person, can enjoy bodily pleasures no less than the best man. But no one would say that happiness belongs to the abject. Nor is it reasonable to assert that the lowliest and half-dead wretches are as blessed as great and wise men. Likewise, the Highest Good of any nature ought to be proper to it; but since bodily pleasure is common even to the lowliest living beasts, it should in no way be judged the Highest Good of man. Would you truly call that the Highest Good which does not even seem to be a good? How shameful, how wicked, and how pestilential this empty elation of the senses is, I believe has been sufficiently proven by our **Plato** above. But why Eudoxus and Aristippus <note>Founder of the Cyrenaic school.</note> [judged it so] especially...

The text draws heavily on the authority of Aristotle, Plato, and Cicero to explain why humans are often led astray by sensory desires despite their natural inclination toward truth.</meta>

...they relied most heavily on the argument that bodily pleasure is sought by everyone. To the <term>Aristotelians</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Aristotle.</note>, this seems to carry little weight for what they intend to prove. For Aristotle thinks that the various conditions of different bodies—and because these conditions are related to their specific natures and thus produce pleasure through that very kinship—differ greatly among themselves. From this, it is understood that quite varied and different pleasures belong to different living creatures. If you were to run through all the pleasures of the body, you would eventually find none that is supremely desired by everyone. However, it is established that the mind is either one in all people or, at the very least, entirely similar. Therefore, that which is proper to the mind appears to be the proper and natural concern of everyone who uses a mind.

The proper work of the mind is the investigation and knowledge of truth. It is clear, then, that this is agreeable to all humans and, for that reason, is to be desired. On this account, all humans (as Aristotle says) naturally desire knowledge, because appetite usually generates distress if the object is absent, but pleasure if it is present. Therefore, there is one thing naturally akin to all humans, one thing to be sought by all, and finally, one thing most delightful of all: and all of this consists in the contemplation of truth. This is (as Plato says) the <term>nourishment</term> <note>original: "pabulum"</note> of the mind, and it fills the soul with a certain ineffable pleasure. Thus, while some bodily pleasures are sought by some and different ones by others, the joy of the mind is one and the same, loved by all.

### Why humans are prone to bodily pleasure. Chapter XV.

**B UT** perhaps someone might ask why nearly countless humans are more prone to bodily pleasure. Aristotle considers the cause of this to be that the sweetness of the senses is a certain shadow and image of that joy upon which the mind feeds. Therefore, from our earliest years, since we use only our senses—which can attain neither the nature of truth nor its joy—we follow that which charms the senses, being deceived by this resemblance, and we embrace it greedily in place of that pleasure toward which nature's primary intention is directed. 

When, however, we have reached adulthood, and with the eyes of the soul awakened, as it were, we begin to suspect the truth and taste its joy, even then very many people continue the course of their past life right through to old age. For a long time, they have been accustomed to believing the senses and obeying their movements, and that very habit has now driven its roots deeper and more profoundly, so that it is impossible, or certainly most difficult, to tear out roots so solid and deep. 

From this, it is clear that there are two chief obstacles—namely ignorance and shameful habit—which force us to wander in the "forests of misery" outside the path of blessedness. <term>Cicero</term> describes this most elegantly in the third book of his *Tusculan Disputations* with these words:

> Nature, he says, has given us tiny sparks <note>original: "igniculos"</note> which we quickly extinguish with evil customs and depraved opinions, so that the light of nature appears nowhere. For there are seeds of virtues innate in our talents, which, if they were allowed to mature, nature itself would lead us to a blessed life. But now, as soon as we are brought into the light and received, we are continually engaged in every depravity and the greatest perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error with our nurse's milk. When we are returned to our parents—that is, handed over to teachers—we are then so imbued with various errors that nature itself yields to vanity and confirmed opinion.

These are the words of Cicero. But to return to the proposal: pleasure is varied and uncertain according to the diversity of men, but the unique joy of the mind is naturally sought by everyone. And since these two things—namely the contemplation of truth and its pleasure—reside in the mind, and the nature of the "Highest Good" seems to consist of these, the ancient philosophers doubted which of them was more essential and excellent for <term>Beatitude</term> <note>The state of perfect happiness or the "Highest Good".</note>. 

For <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic.</note>, and <term>Theodorus</term> the disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician, <term>Democritus</term>, <term>Plato</term>, <term>Eurilochus</term>, <term>Philatimon</term>, <term>Phliasius</term>, <term>Nausiphanes</term>, <term>Theius</term>, <term>Epicurus</term>, <term>Origen</term>, <term>Avicenna</term>, and <term>Al-Ghazali</term> seem to judge that joy, which is the companion of contemplation, is the principal part of the nature of blessedness. 

On the other hand, <term>Thales</term>, <term>Bias</term>, <term>Anaxagoras</term>, <term>Socrates</term>, <term>Euclid of Megara</term>, <term>Aristotle</term>, <term>Herillus</term>, <term>Chalcedonius</term>, and <term>Averroes</term> prefer contemplation itself. Indeed, this debate and controversy has flourished right up to our own age, and it is even argued among Christian theologians. But regarding this, I will speak elsewhere. For now, it will suffice to have reminded you how Aristotle differs from Eudoxus and Aristippus in two chief ways (as we explained above).

### What the Sceptics felt about pleasure, and what Dionysius and Theodorus felt. Chapter XVI.

**P YRRHO** of Elis, and all the philosophers who descended from him called <term>Sceptics</term>, agreed with <term>Aristippus</term> the leader of the <term>Cyrenaics</term> <note>A school of philosophy that believed pleasure was the ultimate good.</note> on this one point: that nothing can be pleasant or harsh by nature, but that pleasure and pain arise either from human opinion, or habit, or a certain condition of our bodies. For what appears pleasant now will tomorrow, on the contrary, be troublesome; and what is harsh to one person, is otherwise <margin>otherwise</margin> to another...

<summary>This page argues that mental joy—the contemplation of truth—is the only universal pleasure, whereas bodily pleasures are varied and deceptive. It also outlines the historical debate over whether the Highest Good consists in the act of contemplation itself or the joy that accompanies it.</summary>

is most sweet to one differently affected. Since he denies that such a variety exists in its own nature, he thinks instead that things appear varied because of the diversity of the men who are warned by their senses. Dionysius of Heraclea <note>A philosopher known as "the Renegade" because he abandoned Stoicism for the Cyrenaic school after suffering an eye disease.</note>, however, defended not only this one point but all the institutions of the <term>Cyrenaics</term> <note>A school of philosophy that believed pleasure was the supreme good, specifically physical pleasure.</note>. He says that the goal of goods is pleasure; for when he had run into a pain of the eyes, he refused to call pain "indifferent" <note>original: "indifferentē". In Stoic philosophy, "indifferents" (adiaphora) are things that do not contribute to or detract from a happy life, such as health or pain.</note> after he had been sharply tortured by it. Although he had listened to Zeno the Stoic, he afterwards brought himself over to the Cyrenaics. Yet Theodorus <note>Theodorus the Atheist, a later philosopher of the Cyrenaic school.</note>, the disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician, differs greatly from both this man and the Cyrenaics. For he uses the name of "pleasure" only to signify that sweetness which touches the senses; he thinks such pleasure is not only not the supreme good, but not even a good at all. Indeed, he thinks the supreme good is the joy of the mind, and its distress is the supreme evil; he believes the one consists in <term>prudence</term> <note>Practical wisdom.</note> and the other in imprudence. Among the goods by which we obtain happiness, he places prudence and justice, but the contrary habits among the evils; pleasure and pain, however, he considers <term>indifferent</term>, just as the Stoics do.

### What the Epicureans think about the origins of things, about pleasure and the emotions, and about character. Chapter XVII.

**B**ut the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus, who taught that pleasure—defined as the absence of pain—is the greatest good and that the world is composed of atoms.</note> establish the name of pleasure as a kind of genus, of which there are two species. Furthermore, they judge that one pleasure consists in motion, and the other in a state of rest. They divide that which is placed in motion into two parts: one indeed is in the mind, the other in the senses. They most often call the former "joy" <note>original: "gaudiū"</note> and the latter "delight" <note>original: "lætitiā"</note>. They define joy as a sweet commotion of the mind, enjoying that which it had sought; but delight as a pleasant motion by which the senses open up and overflow. They teach how this very pleasantness, which is placed in motion, arises in the following way.

They say that the origins of all things that exist are certain very small and entirely indivisible bodies, which for this reason—because they are "uncuttable"—they call <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "ἀτόμους"</note>. They say these differ among themselves in size and shape, so that some seeds are larger, others smaller; some are round and smooth, others are curved, hooked, and rough. All of these fly through the immense void in perpetual motions, touching one another and, clinging together by accidental collisions, they constitute whatever exists in the nature of things. They think that by the grouping of these, three main kinds of things are made. Some things are produced from these atoms which are round, small, and smooth; others from larger and rougher ones. Some, however, hold a middle ground between these two, being neither smooth nor entirely rough. 

They also maintain that our body and soul are composed of these same seeds; however, there is this difference: the body is composed of larger and thicker ones, while the soul is fashioned from small, smooth, and round ones. Furthermore, they say that there is void mixed into all bodies and natures, which they call "passages" and "pores," through which it happens that bodies are able to receive and, as it were, drink one another in. Therefore, when those first types of seeds are presented to us—because (as we said) they are very small—they penetrate the body and soul from every side without any offense. Because they are round and smooth, and therefore related to the nature of the soul, they continually soothe it and flatter the senses. They think that mild fruits, the liquids of honey and milk, songs, the sweetest scents, and other things of this kind are of this genus. 

For this reason, when the seeds from which the soul is woven are touched by these smooth and flattering little bodies, they indeed yield to this sweet commotion. They spread themselves out with a certain great greediness into those little bodies that have been drawn into the senses and passages; they adhere pleasantly, are firmly joined, and are most sweetly embraced. This very yielding, spreading, joining, and embracing they judge to be "pleasure placed in motion." On the other hand, it happens that when that third genus of bodies, which is constructed from rough and heavy seeds, is moved toward the senses—for those elements of which they consist are large—they are pushed with difficulty into the openings of the body and soul. By a certain force, they strike, break through, and pull apart the little bodies of the soul. Those which are rough and hooked "bite" the soul sharply in a way and prick the body. They judge such things to be wormwood, gall, harsh colors, sounds, and smells—in short, everything else that touches the senses with a certain roughness and bitterness. Indeed, by the seeds of these things, the origins of the soul are stirred up and pulled apart; they shudder, flee, and quickly contract themselves. Such dispersion and contraction they define as "pain according to motion."

The noble Epicurean Lucretius expresses this in his second book *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "de rerum natura"</note> with these verses:

> So that you may easily recognize that those things
> are made of smooth and round elements
> which are able to touch the senses pleasantly.
> But on the contrary, those which appear hooked and rough,
> are held bound among themselves by more hooked parts,
> and because of this, they are accustomed to tear the paths
> of our senses and break into the body by their entrance.
