### These things also appear in the same book <note>original: "eodem in libro", referring to Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things), Book II.</note>.

> Furthermore, since pain occurs when material
> Particles <note>original: "Corpora", referring to atoms.</note> by some force through the living viscera and limbs,
> Are shaken in their seats deep within.
> And when they return to their place, a charming pleasure is born.

But truly those things, which are mixtures of certain middle elements, are divided into several kinds. For some indeed closely approach smooth and charming bodies; others rather approach those that are rough to the senses; while some are distant from both by almost an equal difference. The first kind, by a certain quiet motion, entice the soul to pleasure; the second seem to incite it gradually and secretly toward sadness and pain. Those, however, which are said to be in the "difference" <note>An intermediate state between smooth and rough.</note>, produce an ambiguous and doubtful motion. For this reason, the mind grows sluggish and numb by their impulse, and is not excited to action unless some new motion is added. 

Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that between those things which are entirely smooth and round, and those besides which are completely hooked and rough, a certain middle genus of bodies is interposed. This consists of those atoms which are neither entirely round nor bent and hooked, but stand out with certain small and soft angles. Some would have it that certain wines and apples, which are moderately tempered with a rustic, sharp, and (as they say) acute flavor, are of this kind. These neither soothe the mind nor dissipate it, and they do not force it to languish; rather, they prick it lightly and moderately, and, as it were, <term>titillate</term> <note>From the Latin "titillatio," a term used by Epicureans to describe a light, pleasant stimulation of the senses.</note> it and produce pleasure. This whole concept is understood from these verses of Lucretius:

> There are also things which are rightly thought to be neither 
> Smooth, nor entirely hooked with curved points,
> But rather with angles projecting slightly, and which
> Can titillate the senses rather than hurt them.
> Of this kind are wine-lees and the flavors of wine.

Thus it happens that there are three species of pleasures in the senses following motion: one indeed is a certain effect toward softness, which they call intellection <note>original: "intellectionē". This may be a scribal or OCR error for "inflexionem" (bending/refraction), as "intellection" (understanding) fits poorly with a physical description of atoms; however, I have translated it as written while noting the context.</note>; another is a smooth and sweet commotion; and the last is a certain small pricking and (as they say) a sort of itch and titillation. 

Epicurus also uses another division of pleasures: for he calls some **natural and necessary**, such as those which settle pain and the vehement longing of nature through food, drink, and everything else to which a powerful natural motion impels us. Others he calls **natural, but not necessary**, which are of the sort that only vary delight but do not remove pain nor increase pleasure—since the need of nature is already fulfilled and the pain following that need is removed. Epicurus thinks that the highest pleasure of the body is limited by this; so that afterward pleasure can be varied and distinguished, but it cannot be increased or enlarged. Therefore, in this second genus, the Epicureans place those pleasures perceived through various seasonings and the exquisite delights of banquets. 

Then he adds a **third genus** of those pleasures which are neither natural nor necessary, such as those derived from the spectacle of external things that contribute nothing to life or skill, and absolutely all those which are taken from an immense heap of riches and wealth. 

The logic of all these pleasures is this: the lust for those which are necessary is satisfied without much labor or expense; nor do the desires for natural pleasures require much, because nature herself keeps the riches she is contented with both easy to obtain and limited. However, for empty desires, which affect pleasures that are neither natural nor necessary, no limit (as he thinks) and no end can be found. Whence Epicurus says:

> If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if according to opinion, you will never be rich.

Indeed, nature herself enriches the wise man, for her riches are easy to find; nor truly are the pleasures perceived from the most meager and contemptible food less than those from the most exquisite things for banqueting. For nature is contented with few and minimal things. 

Nor does Epicurus follow that pleasure alone which moves nature with some sweetness, of which we have already said enough; but he considers that the greatest pleasure which is perceived when all pain is removed, which he says is placed in a "state." <note>This refers to "katastematic" pleasure, the pleasure of being in a state of equilibrium without disturbance.</note> And when the <term>Cyrenaics</term> <note>Followers of Aristippus who believed only the "smooth motion" of active pleasure was good.</note> denied that this was pleasure, Epicurus conversely taught that this must be called pleasure, since when we are deprived of pain, we rejoice in that very liberation and vacancy from all trouble. Now, everything in which we rejoice is pleasure, just as everything by which we are offended is pain; the privation of all pain is rightly named pleasure. For just as when hunger and thirst are driven away by food and drink, the very removal of the trouble brings the attainment of pleasure, so in every thing, the removal of pain effects a succession of pleasure. Therefore, it did not please Epicurus that there was something middle between pain and pleasure. For that very thing which...

<summary>Ficino explains the Epicurean physical theory of pleasure using Lucretius’s atoms, categorizing sensations based on atomic shape. He further details Epicurus's ethical division of desires into natural/necessary, natural/unnecessary, and vain, concluding that the highest pleasure is the absence of pain.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Epicurean ethics, transitioning from the physical nature of atoms to the psychological and ethical definitions of pleasure and tranquility.</meta>

What seems to some to be a middle state—when we are free from all pain—is not only pleasure, but indeed the highest pleasure. For whoever perceives how they are affected must necessarily be either in a state of pain or in a state of pleasure. Furthermore, they divide this "pleasure in a stable state" into two parts. One they place in the soul, and the other in the body; they call the latter "freedom from pain" <note>original: "indolentiam"</note> and the former "tranquility" <note>original: "tranquillitatem"</note>. Now, freedom from pain in the body (as they see it) is the removal of all suffering. Tranquility, however, is a certain peaceful and constant freedom of the soul from every disturbance. Sometimes they encompass both types of pleasure under a single term, calling it "absolute and complete tranquility." Thus, there is a double tranquility: one of the soul alone, and another of the whole human being, which is entirely perfect and absolute.

## Moderation in pleasures, and that happiness consists not in stimulated pleasure, but in tranquility according to Epicurus and Democritus. Chapter XVIII.

**O**MNEM <note>The text begins with a decorative initial O. The word is "Omnem," meaning "All."</note> Furthermore, all pleasure is by its own nature good and to be sought after, yet it must sometimes be avoided for the sake of something else. For example, pleasures arising from immoderate and shameful actions ought to be avoided for this reason: they are very brief and fragile, and they bring with them regret, care, anxiety, and pain. Likewise, all pains should be avoided for their own sake, yet they must sometimes be endured for the sake of something else; those pains which, although light and very brief, will provide us with the greatest pleasures and advantages. 

And even if all pleasures are good, a happy life is not found in all of them. For that "active" pleasure <note>original: "quae motu fit," referring to kinetic pleasure, which involves a process of stimulation</note> is not sufficient in itself for a happy life, nor is it entirely necessary for living happily for its own sake. Rather, they think that the "absolute tranquility" which contains the peaceful rest of the soul and the body's freedom from pain is the highest good of all <note>original: "summum omnino bonum"</note>. For in these two things, the entire nature of man—namely of the body and the soul alike—is perfected. This is the state to which all activities are referred; indeed, we undergo all labors so that we may eventually be in leisure and rest. 

Those pleasures which we categorized as "active" <note>original: "in motione"</note> are pursued so that they may drive away pain and satisfy the needs of nature. By driving away pain and satisfying need, we become released and free from all the pain that arises from natural want. This is that "freedom from pain" which they wish to be understood as a stable state, and which they judge to hold one part of happiness; the other part is governed by tranquility of the soul, for the sake of which all virtues are sought. Indeed, the virtues desire nothing else except to free the soul from every disturbance; and that very thing is tranquility itself. For this reason, they maintain that all virtues were sought for the sake of tranquility, and much more so all other human actions. 

Furthermore, while the other goods of man belong either specifically to the soul or to the body alone, that absolute and perfect tranquility alone among all things encompasses the universal nature of man. Therefore, it ought to be rightly judged as the most excellent of all goods. To this also belongs what has been confirmed by the authority of all philosophers: that the "highest" <note>The *summum bonum* or ultimate end.</note> is seen to be that to which nothing else can be added. 

But what can you add to tranquility? Indeed, you would only do so if something were missing from it. But if any good were lacking, the person who lacks it would necessarily desire it; and he who desires cannot be tranquil in any way. Where there is tranquility, therefore, there is no desire; where there is no desire, there is no need; where there is no need, there is finally a perfect state, an abundance of things to be sought, and an absolute embrace of all goods. Therefore, where there is tranquility, all goods are present; where all goods are present, there is tranquility. By this, it is understood that nothing is lacking to it, nothing can be added, and it encompasses the nature and reason of all goods within itself. 

Thus, it is the perfect and ultimate good toward which every natural desire is referred. Since there are many goods, happiness is either one of these, or all of them gathered together, or rather something that is made from the accumulated possession of all other goods. A single good separated from the rest cannot be seen as the highest good, since many other things could be added to it. Nor can all things merely collected together be the end. For happiness is a certain ultimate and final end of human life; but the final end ought to be one and simple. Therefore, the highest good will be that which results from the accumulation of all others. That can be nothing other than tranquility. 

For the nature of goods is twofold: they fill the soul and they free it from all distress. Such a filling and liberation is undoubtedly tranquility itself. Since this follows the possession of other goods, it follows that it is the end and extreme of them all, and for that reason is rightly seen as the highest. For the soul never rests unless it has obtained all goods; and rest and tranquility are one and the same. It succeeds the possession of other goods; therefore all goods seem to be sought for its sake, as if this were the ultimate and best end to be sought by everyone.

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s treatise "On Pleasure," summarizing the Epicurean definition of the "blessed life" through quotes from Epicurus and Lucretius, emphasizing that true happiness is found in mental tranquility and physical freedom from pain, even in the face of suffering.</meta>

<page-num>1012</page-num>
<header>MARSILIO FICINO’S BOOK ON PLEASURE.</header>

Therefore, Epicurus believes that the blessed life consists in the tranquility of the soul; indeed, he considers that life most blessed which contains both tranquility of the soul and <term>freedom from pain</term> <note>original: "indolentia," a technical term in Epicureanism meaning the total absence of physical suffering</note> of the body. But so that I do not seem to be asserting these reports about Epicurus on my own authority, he himself testifies in his own words in his *Letter to Menoeceus*, saying: "When we say that pleasure is the goal, we do not mean the pleasures of the profligate, nor those consisting in the sense of taste, as some who are ignorant and disagree with our opinion believe; rather, we mean being free from pain in the body and being tranquil and free from disturbance in the soul. For it is not drinking bouts and continuous partying, nor the company of boys and women, nor the consumption of fish and other things which a costly table offers, that produce a sweet life; but rather sober reasoning, which searches out the causes of why things should be chosen or avoided, and which drives out those opinions through which the greatest tumult occupies the soul." Likewise, in the same letter: "The absence of pain and disturbance," he says, "are <term>stable pleasures</term> <note>original: "constantes voluptates." These are pleasures of rest, as opposed to pleasures of movement</note>, whereas joy and gladness are called actions according to movement; the highest pleasure is the privation of pain. Indeed, the pleasures of the soul are greater than those of the body, for the flesh is bathed only in present sweetness, but the soul rejoices together in the thought of things past, present, and future." Likewise, in the same letter: "It is not possible to live pleasantly unless one lives prudently, honorably, and justly; nor can one live prudently, honorably, and justly without living pleasantly." From these points, Epicurus shows that the highest good consists neither in pleasures according to movement, nor in those taken from turbulent actions, but rather that these two—namely, freedom from physical pain and tranquility of the soul—make life most blessed. Lucretius the Epicurean also testifies to the same in his second book *On the Nature of Things*, where, while he censures the empty desires of men and their luxurious delights, he says:

> O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts!
> In what shadows of life and in how great perils
> Is this span of time spent, however much it is! Do you not see
> That nature barks for nothing else for itself, except that
> Pain be absent and separated from the body, and that the mind enjoy
> A pleasant sense, with care and fear removed?

Here, therefore, censuring the luxury of men, he calls them blind and wretched because they burden themselves with every trouble and do not see what nature desires as the supreme goal and good. He himself explains what that is, saying that nature hungers for this: that pain be absent from the body (which signifies that freedom from pain of which we spoke), and that care and fear be removed. By these words, he certainly wants tranquility of the soul to be understood, and that one may enjoy the benefit of these two through a pleasant sense and the mind—as if he were saying that the highest pleasantness of body and soul consists in these things. Therefore, that the most blessed life consists in these two—freedom from pain and tranquility of soul—these testimonies of Epicurus and Lucretius ought to be sufficient. Furthermore, that even a man in whom there is tranquility of mind remains blessed even though the members of his body are tortured, Epicurus is a witness in his *Letter to Metrodorus*, saying that he who has once become a wise man cannot pass into the opposite condition, nor err by yielding to disturbances; and even if he is tortured or racked with pain, the wise man will nonetheless be happy. Also, in that letter which he wrote to Hermarchus while dying, he said: "While we were spending a happy day and our final one, we were writing these things; yet such great diseases of the bladder and intestines were present that nothing could be added to their bitterness. Nevertheless, all these things were compensated by the joy of soul which I took from the memory of our reasonings and discoveries." In these words, he says he is spending a blessed day, yet is tortured by the greatest pains. The same is said to have been the opinion of Leucippus, Democritus, and Theodorus: that happiness is in the tranquility of the mind, and if freedom from physical pain is added to this, then absolute and perfect happiness consists in this disposition of soul and body.

I have written down for you these things disputed by various philosophers concerning Pleasure; however, as to which of these opinions you should follow, I want you to be persuaded by the authority and reasons of those who dispute here, rather than by my own judgment. For me, it will have been enough to have related the opinions of almost all the philosophers for the sake of exercising the memory.

->**THE END.**<-
